Book 3, chapter 33: The shafan
------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/shafan.html

II, 409 col. 1001 CAP. XXXIII.

II, 409 col. 1001 Chapter 33.


Probatur, שפן saphan non esse Cuniculum, ut volunt, sed majoris Muris genus in Palaestina, Aegypto et Libya, qui Herodoto et aliis Δίπους, Senioribus Χοιρογρύλλιος, Hieronymo Ἀρκτομῦς, et Arabibus dicitur اليربوع aljarbuo, de quo multa, nondum vulgata, ex Arabum scriptis produntur.

It is proved that שפן saphan is not the rabbit, as they hold, but a kind of larger mouse in Eretz Yisrael, Egypt and Libya, which is called Δίπους [Dipous] by Herodotus and others, Χοιρογρύλλιος [Choirogryllios] by the Elders [=the translators of the Septuagint], Ἀρκτομῦς [Arktomys] by Jerome, and اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo by the Arabs; many things about it, not yet published, are brought forward from the writings of the Arabs.


Levit, XI, 5. et Deut. XIV, 7. in iis animalibus, quae ruminant quidem, sed col. 1002 non habent bifidam ungulam, ac proinde sunt immunda, cum camelo et lepore recensetur השפן, ὁ σαφάν. Plurale שפנים sephanim habetur Psal. CIV. 18. Petra refugium לשפנים, τοῖς σεφανίμ. Et Prov. XXX, 26. שפנים sephanim populus invalidus, ponunt in petra domum suam. Cuniculos explicant plerique recentiorum. Cui interpretationi in speciem multa favent. 1. Quod bis in lege השפן cum הארנבת, id est, cum lepore jungitur, tanquam animal congener. 2. Quod Psalmi locus, quem modo citavimus, in Graeca editione sic redditur, Πέτρα καταφυγὴ τοῖς λαγωοῖς, Petra refugium leporibus. Quaedam exemplaria habent τοῖς χοιρογρυλλίοις, id est, ut volunt, herinaceis. Sed priorem lectionem sequuntur vetustissimi scriptores. Hieronymus Epistola 135. ad Suniam et Fretelam: Omnes χοιρογρυλλίους voce simili transtulerunt: soli LXX. lepores interpretati sunt. Ita etiam legerunt Theodoretus Commentario in hunc Psalmum, Basilius in Esaiam capite secundo, et Apollinaris in Paraphrasi,

In Lev 11:5 and Deut 14:7, among those animals which do chew the cud but col. 1002 do not have a cloven hoof, and are therefore unclean, השפן, ὁ σαφάν [ho saphan], is listed together with the camel and the hare. The plural שפנים sephanim occurs in Ps 104:18: The rock is a refuge לשפנים, τοῖς σεφανίμ [tois sephanim]. And in Prov 30:26: שפנים sephanim, a feeble folk, make their house in the rock. Most of the more recent interpreters explain them as rabbits. Many things seem on the face of it to favour this interpretation. 1. That twice in the Law השפן is joined with הארנבת, that is, with the hare, as a kindred animal. 2. That the passage of the Psalm which we have just cited is rendered thus in the Greek edition: Πέτρα καταφυγὴ τοῖς λαγωοῖς [Petra kataphygē tois lagōois], The rock is a refuge for the hares. Some copies have τοῖς χοιρογρυλλίοις [tois choirogrylliois], that is, as they hold, for the hedgehogs. But the most ancient writers follow the former reading. Jerome, Epistle 135, to Sunia and Fretela: All translated it with a similar word, χοιρογρυλλίους [choirogryllious]; only the LXX rendered it hares. So too read Theodoret in his Commentary on this Psalm, Basil on Isaiah, chapter 2, and Apollinaris in his Paraphrase:


Πέτροις ἠλιβάτοις περιθάρσεες εἰσὶ λαγωοὶ,

Πέτροις ἠλιβάτοις περιθάρσεες εἰσὶ λαγωοὶ [Petrois ēlibatois peritharsees eisi lagōoi],


Saxis praeruptis fidentes sunt lepores: et Arabica versio, quae ex Graeca est expressa, Petrae refugium الارانب leporum. Alii utrumque jungunt: ut in hunc locum Augustinus, Petra refugium hericiis et leporibus. Arnobius, Ibi est petra, praestans refugium sive erinaceorum filiis, etc. sive leporibus. Beda in Proverbia capite trigesimo, Notandumque, quod in Psalmo, ubi nos canimus: „Petra refugium herinaciis, in quibusdam codicibus leporibus, in quibusdam choerogrylliis invenitur “. 3. Hebraea Prov. XXX, 26. שפנים עם לא עצום, Vulgatus interpres sic transtulit, Lepusculus plebs invalida, sequutus, nisi fallor, II, 410 Graecum aliquem interpretem, qui שפנים, λαγίδεις lepusculos explicaverat, id est, cuniculos. Sic enim in Strabone libro tertio λαγίδεις, lepusculi sumuntur pro cuniculis. Graeci aliud cuniculi nomen non habent. Nam in Aeliano κόνι-λος, in Polybio et Galeno κούνικλος Hispanorum, in Strabone et Erotiano λεβη-ρὶς Massiliensium propria erant vocabula, in Graecia non usurpata. 4. Nominum liber vetus, quem Philoni adscribunt, in Ieremia sic habet, SAPHAN, choerogryllius, lepus, vel hericius. Et in Ezechiele, SAPHAN, hericius, vel lepus. 5. In Arabico Giggeji Lexico pag. 854. tom. 2. سفن saphan redditur cuniculus. Quod tamen unde habeat, haud quaquam scio. Nam alibi nusquam reperi. 6. Hebraeum nomen שפן saphan videtur alludere ad Hebraea verba ספן et צפן, quorum illud tegere, hoc abscondere significat. Et quadrare videtur in cuniculum, qui scrobum latebras quaerit, ut in iis delitescat, et obtegatur quasi. Martialis,

The hares trust in the sheer rocks; and the Arabic version, which was made from the Greek: The rock is the refuge الارانب [al-arānib] of the hares. Others join both: thus Augustine on this passage: The rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs and the hares. Arnobius: There is the rock, affording a refuge either to the young of the hedgehogs, etc., or to the hares. Bede on Proverbs, chapter 30: And it is to be noted that in the Psalm, where we sing „The rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs, in some manuscripts for the hares is found, in some for the choerogryllii“. 3. The Hebrew of Prov 30:26, שפנים עם לא עצום, the Vulgate translator rendered thus: The little hare, a feeble folk, following, if I am not mistaken, II, 410 some Greek translator who had explained שפנים as λαγίδεις [lagideis], little hares, that is, rabbits. For thus in Strabo, book 3, λαγίδεις [lagideis], little hares, are taken for rabbits. The Greeks have no other name for the rabbit. For κόνιλος [konilos] in Aelian, κούνικλος [kouniklos] in Polybius and Galen, words of the Spaniards, and λεβηρὶς [lebēris] in Strabo and Erotian, a word of the Massilians, were local terms not used in Greece. 4. The old Book of Names, which they ascribe to Philo, has this under Jeremiah: SAPHAN, choerogryllius, hare, or hedgehog. And under Ezekiel: SAPHAN, hedgehog, or hare. 5. In Giggeius' [=Antonio Giggei, Thesaurus linguae Arabicae (Milan 1632)] Arabic Lexicon, p. 854, vol. 2, سفن [safan] saphan is rendered cuniculus [rabbit]. Where he got this from, however, I do not know at all, for I have found it nowhere else. 6. The Hebrew name שפן saphan seems to allude to the Hebrew verbs ספן and צפן, of which the former means to cover, the latter to hide. And it seems to fit the rabbit, which seeks the hiding places of burrows, so as to lurk in them and be, as it were, covered over. Martial:


Gaudet in effossis habitare cuniculus antris.

The rabbit delights to dwell in dug-out caves.


7. Certum est, Hebraeos cuniculum abhinc aliquot saeculis sic appellasse. Ita Baal Aruch ante annos fere quingentos in voce תלא אילן thela Aelan, aut ilan, de viverris: ושמענו שמצויין הן במקומות שצדין בהן שפנים Audivimus, eas reperiri in certis locis, in quibus iis venantur cuniculos. Et apud R. Isaacum, Selomonis filium, uno circiter saeculo posteriorem, in libro, cui titulus Masal Kadmoni, in quo habentur fabulae, Aesopicis similes, stricta oratione scriptae, fabula quinquagesima colloquuntur השפן והזרזיר, id est, cuniculus et sturnus; ut palam faciunt picturae appositae. Et in Porta coeli, cujus auctor R. Gersom, Tract. 4. cap. 1. fol. 19. d. וקצתם יולידו ולדות רבות כחתול ושפן וארנבת ועכבר Et eorum (animalium) nonnulla multos foetus generant; ut felis, et cuniculus, et col. 1003 lepus, et mus. Et fol. 20. d. ויש מב״ח אשר ביציהם תלוים בכיס ויש מהם שהם דבוקים בבטן כשפן וארנבת וחחול Quorundam animalium testiculi in scroto pendent, at aliorum ventri adhaerent; ut cuniculi, leporis et felis. David de Pomis in Lexico, שפן ב״ח או חיה הנקרא קוני״לו בלעז Saphan, animal, aut fera, quae lingua vernacula (id est, Italica) vocatur Coniglio. Et alibi טפז שפן, cuniculus, coniglio, animaletto. Et rursus, חגס שפן, cuniculus, coniglio. Nec Hebraeorum ullus occurrit, qui aliter interpretetur. 8. Denique, si שפן saphan est cuniculus, jam liquido patebit, unde Σπανία Spania, vel Hispania nomen traxerit. Et Σπανία Hebraice erit שפניה cuniculosa. Quo nomine a Phoenicibus dicta fuerit, quia hoc animali maxime scatet. Quod alibi multis probamus. Unde est, quod in Hadriani nummo pro Hispania habetur mulier sedens cum oleae ramo in manu, et cuniculo ad pedes. Ex his igitur videtur confici, שפן esse cuniculum.

7. It is certain that the Hebrews have called the rabbit by this name for some centuries now. Thus Baal Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome] [=Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome, the ʿArukh], almost five hundred years ago, under the word תלא אילן thela Aelan, or ilan, says of ferrets: ושמענו שמצויין הן במקומות שצדין בהן שפנים We have heard that they are found in certain places where rabbits are hunted with them. And in R. Isaac, son of Solomon [=Isaac ibn Sahula, Meshal ha-qadmoni], about one century later, in the book entitled Masal Kadmoni, which contains fables similar to Aesop's, written in bound language, the speakers in the fiftieth fable are השפן והזרזיר, that is, the rabbit and the starling, as the accompanying pictures make plain. And in the Porta coeli, whose author is R. Gersom [=Gershon ben Solomon of Arles, Shaʿar ha-shamayim (Porta coeli)], tract. 4, ch. 1, fol. 19d: וקצתם יולידו ולדות רבות כחתול ושפן וארנבת ועכבר And some of them (the animals) produce many young; such as the cat, and the rabbit, and col. 1003 the hare, and the mouse. And fol. 20d: ויש מב״ח אשר ביציהם תלוים בכיס ויש מהם שהם דבוקים בבטן כשפן וארנבת וחחול In some animals the testicles hang in a scrotum, but in others they adhere to the belly, as in the rabbit, the hare and the cat. David de Pomis [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587), a Hebrew-Latin-Italian dictionary], in his Lexicon: שפן ב״ח או חיה הנקרא קוני״לו בלעז Saphan, an animal, or wild beast, which in the vernacular (that is, Italian) is called Coniglio. And elsewhere: טפז שפן, rabbit, coniglio, animaletto. And again: חגס שפן, rabbit, coniglio. Nor is there any of the Hebrews who interprets it otherwise. 8. Finally, if שפן saphan is the rabbit, it will at once be perfectly clear whence Σπανία [Spania] Spania, or Hispania, took its name. And Σπανία [Spania] will be in Hebrew שפניה, abounding in rabbits. It would have been so called by the Phoenicians because it teems above all with this animal. This we prove at length elsewhere. Hence it is that on a coin of Hadrian, representing Hispania, there is a seated woman with an olive branch in her hand and a rabbit at her feet. From all this, then, it seems to follow that שפן is the rabbit.


Tamen in hanc interpretationem tria possunt objici. 1. Non ruminare cuniculos, ut expresse asseritur in Porta coeli fol. 20. b. אין השפן והארנבת מעלה II, 411 גרה, Cuniculus et lepus non ruminant. 2. In petris non habitare, sed in terreno solo, quod facile perfodiatur. 3. Id animal olim fuisse Hispaniae peculiare, quae a Iudaea distat immensum quantum. Varro de re Rustica libri tertii capite duodecimo, Tertii generis est, quod in Hispania nascitur, simile nostro lepori ex quadam parte, sed humile, quem cuniculum appellant. Plinius libri octavi capite quinquagesimo quinto, Leporum generis sunt et quos Hispania cuniculos appellat. Aelianus libri decimi tertii De animalibus capite decimo quinto, Κόνιλος ὄνομα αὐτῷ, Conilus nomen ipsi (malim κένικλος, ut in Galeno). Et paullo post, Φυλάττω τὴν ἐπωνυμίαν τὴν ἐξ ἀρχῆς, ἥνπερ οὖν Ἰβηρίαν Ἑσπέριοι ἔθεντο οἱ πάρος, παρ᾽ οἷς καὶ γίνεταί τε, καὶ ἔστι πάμπολις. Servo Ibericum nomen vetus, quod ab initio imposuerant prisci Hispani, apud quos et nascitur, et maxime abundat. Galenus libro tertio De alimentis, Οὐκοῦν ἔτι δεήσομαι λόγων μακρῶν εἰς τὸ τὰ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον ἔθνος ἐπιχώρια τῶν ζώων ἅπαντα διέρχεσθαι· καθά-περ ἐν Ἰβηρίᾳ τὸ τοῖς λαγωοῖς ὅμοιον ζωΰφιον, ὃ καλοῦσι κένικλον. Non opus erit pluribus animalia omnia exsequi, quae apud singulas gentes propria sunt et indigena: quale est in Hispania leporibus simile animalculum, quod cuniculum appellant. Ex his igitur cum cuniculum constet Hispanicum fuisse animal, quid opus fuit illius esum Iudaeis prohibere, quibus erat prorsus ignotus? (1)

Yet three objections can be raised against this interpretation. 1. That rabbits do not ruminate, as is expressly asserted in the Porta coeli, fol. 20b: אין השפן והארנבת מעלה II, 411 גרה, The rabbit and the hare do not chew the cud. 2. That they do not live in rocks, but in earthy soil that is easily dug through. 3. That this animal was formerly peculiar to Spain, which is an immense distance from Judaea. Varro, On Agriculture, book 3, chapter 12: There is a third kind, which is born in Spain, in some respects similar to our hare, but low, which they call the rabbit. Pliny, book 8, chapter 55: Of the hare kind also are those which Spain calls rabbits. Aelian, On Animals, book 13, chapter 15: Κόνιλος ὄνομα αὐτῷ [Konilos onoma autō], Its name is conilus (I would prefer κένικλος [keniklos], as in Galen). And a little later: Φυλάττω τὴν ἐπωνυμίαν τὴν ἐξ ἀρχῆς, ἥνπερ οὖν Ἰβηρίαν Ἑσπέριοι ἔθεντο οἱ πάρος, παρ᾽ οἷς καὶ γίνεταί τε, καὶ ἔστι πάμπολις [Phylattō tēn epōnymian tēn ex archēs, hēnper oun Ibērian Hesperioi ethento hoi paros, par' hois kai ginetai te, kai esti pampolis]. I keep the old Iberian name, which the ancient Spaniards had given it from the beginning, among whom it is both born and most abounds. Galen, book 3 On Foods: Οὐκοῦν ἔτι δεήσομαι λόγων μακρῶν εἰς τὸ τὰ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον ἔθνος ἐπιχώρια τῶν ζώων ἅπαντα διέρχεσθαι· καθάπερ ἐν Ἰβηρίᾳ τὸ τοῖς λαγωοῖς ὅμοιον ζωΰφιον, ὃ καλοῦσι κένικλον [Oukoun eti deēsomai logōn makrōn eis to ta kath' hekaston ethnos epichōria tōn zōōn hapanta dierchesthai; kathaper en Ibēria to tois lagōois homoion zōyphion, ho kalousi keniklon]. There will be no need of more words to go through all the animals that are peculiar and native to the individual nations: such as in Spain the little animal similar to hares, which they call the rabbit. Since, then, it is established from these passages that the rabbit was a Spanish animal, what need was there to forbid the eating of it to the Jews, to whom it was entirely unknown? R1


Gesnerus, qui cum plerisque recentiorum interpretum contendit, שפן esse cuniculum, ad primam objectionem respondet, se mandentes cuniculos deprehendisse post cibum, eis ante horae dimidium exhibitum. Et frustra opponatur, quod citavimus ex Porta coeli. Locum enim scribae corruperunt, negatione in textum insulta perperam, et contra mentem auctoris, quem credibile non est tam fuisse ineptum, ut השפן והארנבת ruminare negaverit. Sic enim expresse negaret, quod expresse asserit Moses Levit. XI, 6. et Deut. XIV, 7. et Scriptori θεοπνεύστῳ mendacii dicam impingeret. Tollenda igitur negatio אין. Quod insuper arguit tota series orationis, quae, si negationem auferas, talis erit: Sunt animalia, quae ruminant, et alia, quae non ruminant. Ratio est, quia, quae ruminant, non habent dentes superiores, nisi molitores. Ideo non possunt concidere cibum una vice. Et stomachus non potest eum accipere perfectum, donec altera vice sit commolitus. Proinde duplex est ipsis ingluvies: superior, in quam descendit cibus prima vice; et inferior, qua recipitur, postquam altera vice est II, 412 commolitus. אך השפן והארנבת מעלה גרה ויש להם שינים למעלה אבל שיניהם הם חדות מאד ולא יוכלו לטחון האוכל היטב והגמל יש לו שינים col. 1004 למעלה אבל הם קטנות וחלושות Tamen cuniculus et lepus ruminant, licet habeant dentes superiores. Sed dentes eorum sunt valde acuti, nec possunt perfecte commolere cibum. Camelus quoque habet dentes superiores, sed parvos et infirmos.

Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium], who maintains with most of the more recent interpreters that שפן is the rabbit, answers the first objection by saying that he caught rabbits chewing after their meal, half an hour after the food had been given them. And it would be vain to object with what we cited from the Porta coeli. For the scribes corrupted the passage by wrongly inserting a negation into the text, against the intention of the author. It is not credible that he was so foolish as to deny that השפן והארנבת ruminate. For he would then be expressly denying what Moses expressly asserts in Lev 11:6 and Deut. XIV, 7., and he would be charging the divinely inspired (θεοπνεύστῳ [theopneustō]) writer with falsehood. The negation אין must therefore be removed. This is further shown by the whole sequence of the passage, which, if you take away the negation, will run as follows: There are animals which ruminate, and others which do not ruminate. The reason is that those which ruminate have no upper teeth except molars. Therefore they cannot cut up their food at one time. And the stomach cannot receive it complete until it has been ground a second time. Hence they have a double crop: an upper one, into which the food descends the first time, and a lower one, by which it is received after it has been II, 412 ground the second time. אך השפן והארנבת מעלה גרה ויש להם שינים למעלה אבל שיניהם הם חדות מאד ולא יוכלו לטחון האוכל היטב והגמל יש לו שינים col. 1004 למעלה אבל הם קטנות וחלושות Nevertheless the rabbit and the hare ruminate, although they have upper teeth. But their teeth are very sharp and cannot grind the food perfectly. The camel also has upper teeth, but small and weak.


Ad secundam objectionem respondet utcunque Gesnerus, sed cunctanter admodum. Dubitet, inquit, aliquis, an sephanim sint cuniculi, cum non in saxis, aut saxosis locis versari soleant, quod sciam, quod fodere illic impediantur, sed terreno potius solo, etc. Sed quoniam inter saxa quaedam in collibus specus, vel meatus oblongi reperiuntur, et cuniculorum receptaculis apti, quaerendum est, an in iis quoque cuniculi in aliis regionibus versari soleant. Nec multo certius consultus a Gesnero hac de re Hispanus quidam, Cuniculi apud nos copiosissimi sunt in montanis locis atque in praeruptis montibus. Neque dubium mihi est, eos habere subterraneos meatus in locis asperioribus et petricosis, quanquam id nunquam accurate observavi. Item, Fui ego in venatione cuniculorum in loco montoso et saxis oppleto; inter quae videbam cavernulas perfossas: utrum autem in locis interioribus fuerint saxa, an terra mollior, non possum asseverare. Neque ad rem magis facit, quod scribit Papirius Massonus in Descriptione Franciae per flumina, lepusculos, id est, cuniculos paene innumeros nutriri in insule Caloneso ad litus Armoricanum, quamvis tota sit rupes, nec nisi superficiem habeat, terra adopertam. Hoc, inquam, ad rem non facit; quia in terrena illa superficie possunt haerere cuniculi, nec rupem, ei subjectam, excavare necesse habent. Sed consulendus Petrus Quinqueranus in Provinciae descriptione, ex qua haec citat Camerarius Historiae tom. 2. lib. 5. cap. 20.

To the second objection Gesner gives some sort of answer, but very hesitantly. Someone may doubt, he says, whether the sephanim are rabbits, since, as far as I know, these do not usually live among rocks or in rocky places, because they are prevented from digging there, but rather in earthy ground, etc. But since among rocks on hills certain caves or long passages are found which are suitable as dens for rabbits, it should be asked whether in other regions rabbits also usually live in these. Nor is a certain Spaniard, whom Gesner consulted on this matter, much more certain: Among us rabbits are very plentiful in mountainous places and on steep mountains. And I have no doubt that they have underground passages in rougher and stony places, although I have never observed it closely. Again: I once took part in a rabbit hunt in a mountainous place full of rocks, among which I saw little burrows dug out; but whether in the inner parts there was rock or softer earth, I cannot affirm. Nor is it more to the point that Papire Masson writes in his Descriptio Franciae per flumina that little hares, that is, rabbits, almost without number are bred on the island of Calonesus off the Armorican coast, although it is entirely rock and has only its surface covered with earth. This, I say, is not to the point, because the rabbits can stay in that earthy surface and have no need to hollow out the rock beneath it. But one should consult Pierre Quiqueran de Beaujeu [=De laudibus Provinciae] in his description of Provence, from which Camerarius quotes these things in his Historiae vol. 2, book 5, ch. 20.


Superest tertia objectio, in qua refellenda plus est operae, cum veteres tam diserte asserant, cuniculum fuisse animal, olim Hispaniae peculiare. Unde est, quod illud e Graecis soli noverant Massilienses, qui fere sunt in Hispaniae confinio. Itaque haec ratio facit, ut subdubitem, an vere שפן sit cuniculus, et putem quaerendum amplius, nec standum magistris Hebraeorum, sed consulendos potius vetustiores interpretes: quamvis sibi non satis constent, ac proinde verum ex iis eruere sit difficillimum. Chaldaeos, et Syrum, et Samaritanum praetereo, quia pro Hebraea שפן voces adhibent prorsus ignotas. Neque enim quisquam est, qui sciat, quid sit in Onkelo טפזא taphza, pro quo in Ionathane legitur טווזא tauza; et in Samaritano ࠈࠐࠎࠄ taphsa, nisi quod videtur ἁλτικὸν esse animal, quia טפז tephaz Chaldaeis et Syris est salire, aut subsultare. Neque notius Syrum ܚܓܣܐ chagasa, cujus Plurale חגסי chagase etiam Chaldaeus usurpat pro שפנים sephanim, Prov. XXX, 26. Sed Aethiopicum ለጊሔ፡ legiche, II, 413 Psal. CIII. (Hebraeis CIV,) 19. reddendum puto leporibus, quia respondet Graeco τοῖς λαγωοῖς. Quod idem sequuti Arabes ita habent الارنب lepores. At iidem aliter habent in Proverbiis, nempe القنافد hericios. Et in Lege rursus aliter: ibi enim, pro השפן, unus habet الوبر alwebro, et alius الفنك alpheneco.

There remains the third objection, which takes more effort to refute, since the ancients state so plainly that the rabbit was an animal formerly peculiar to Spain. This is why, of the Greeks, only the Massilians, who live almost on the border of Spain, knew it. This argument therefore makes me somewhat doubtful whether שפן is really the rabbit. I think the question should be examined further, and that we should not rely on the masters of the Hebrews but rather consult the older interpreters, although they are not consistent with one another, so that it is very difficult to extract the truth from them. I pass over the Chaldee versions, the Syriac and the Samaritan, because for the Hebrew שפן they use words that are entirely unknown. For no one knows what טפזא taphza is in Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos], for which Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] reads טווזא tauza, and the Samaritan ࠈࠐࠎࠄ [טפסה] taphsa, except that it seems to be a leaping (ἁλτικὸν [haltikon]) animal, because טפז tephaz in Chaldee and Syriac means to leap or to jump up. Nor is the Syriac ܚܓܣܐ [חגסא] chagasa better known, whose plural חגסי chagase the Chaldee also uses for שפנים sephanim, Prov 30:26. But the Ethiopic ለጊሔ፡ [lagiḥē] legiche, II, 413 Psal. CIII. (in the Hebrew CIV,) 19., I think should be rendered hares, because it corresponds to the Greek τοῖς λαγωοῖς [tois lagōois]. The Arabs, following the same, have الارنب [al-arnab] hares. But the same translators have something else in Proverbs, namely القنافد [al-qanāfid] hedgehogs. And in the Law something else again: there, for השפן, one has الوبر [al-wabr] alwebro, and another الفنك [al-fanak] alpheneco.


Quorum animalium prius ita describit Giauhari, الوبر دويبة اصغر من السنور كحلا اللون لا ذنب لها تدجن في البيوت Alwebro est animalculum, fele minus, fusci coloris, sine cauda, residens in domibus. Sed, ut observat Damir, قوله لا ذنب لها اي لا ذنب لها col. 1005 طويل والا فالوبر له ذنب قصير جدا Cum negat habere caudam, significat, caudam illi non esse longam; quia alwebro caudam quidem habet, sed valde brevem. Idem asserit, a nonnullis vocari غنم بني اسرايل ovem filiorum Israelis; لان ذنبها مع صغره يشبه الية الخروف quia cauda ejus brevitate sua refert caudam agninam (2). Sed in Giauhari زلم zulem appellatur, qua de causa, non satis scio. In libro, cui titulus كفاية المتحفظة legitur, الوبر alwebro esse دويبة قريبة من السنور ولها بول يتخثر فيتداوي به الناس animalculum instar felis, cujus urina spissatur, et usurpatur inter morborum remedia. Mawardi et Rujiani animal esse dicunt في عظم الجرذ الا انه انبل منه والعرب تاكله magnitudine majoris muris, sed praestantius, quo vescuntur Arabes. Ab aliis describitur دويبة سودا في قدر الارنب واكبر من ابن عرس animalculum nigrum, accedens ad staturam leporis, et mustela majus. Idem, ut nonnulli addunt, كالارنب يعتلف النبات والبقول leporis instar herbis vescitur, atque oleribus. Marmotam intelligo, vel murem montanum, quem Gesnerus ita describit: Fele corpulentior est, sed brevior cruribus, etc. Colore ut plurimum rufo, qui in aliis clarior, in aliis obscurior et fuscus est. Et Scaliger in Cardanum. Exercitatione ducentesima tertia, Melis sunt magnitudine et pilo, cauda item nulla pene. Addit, se unam aluisse in Taurinis mansuetam. Et Gesnerus, Historiam ejus describam, partim ut ipse II, 414 observavi, cum domi alerem hoc animal. Et Stumpfius, Ex feris nostri orbis vix ullam reperias, quae adeo mansueta et familiaris homini reddatur. Nempe unam habuerat domi per biennium. Murem alpinum vocat Plinius libri octavi capite trigesimo septimo; quia frequens est in Alpibus. Sed, ne quis hos mures putet Alpibus esse peculiares, idem in Aegypto pares describit (3). Nec solis Arabibus שפן saphan Mosis est الوبر alvvebro, seu mus montanus. Quippe etiam e nostris Iunius, qui Arabes haudquaquam consuluerat, Hebraeum שפן constanter II, 415 ita reddit. Et anonymus alius, de quo Gesnerus in capite De mure Al-pino : Saphan, Hebraicam vocem, etc. eruditus quidam apud nos murem Alpinum interpretatur. Obiter nota, montani, vel Alpini muris nomen Italicum marmota in Bereschith Rabba duobus locis reperiri leviter immutatum. Primus est sectione decima septima, ubi in verba Gen. II, 21. Immisit Dominus Deus תרדמה thardema (id est, soporem) in Adamum. רב אמר שלש תרדמת הן תרדמת שינה תרדמת נבואה ותרדמת מרמיטה תרדמת שינה ויפול יהוה תרדמה על האדם col. 1006 וישן תרדמת נבואה ויהי השמש לבא ותרדמה נפלה על אברם תרדמת מרמיטה אין רואה ואין יודע ואין מקיץ כי כלם ישנים כי תרדמת י״ נפלה עליהם Rab dixit, tres sunt soporum species : sopor somni, sopor prophetiae, et sopor מרמיטה marmita. Sopor somni Gen. II, 21. „Immisit Dominus Deus soporem super Ada-„mum, et dormiit. Sopor prophetiae Gen. XV, 12. Et cum occumberet sol, so-„por in Abramum incidit. Sopor מרמיטה marmitae 1 Sam. XXVI, 12. Non erat „qui videret, nec qui intelligeret, nec qui expergisceretur, sed omnes dormiebant; „quia sopor Domini super eos inciderat“. Alter locus est sectione quadragesima tertia, ubi in Gen. XV, 12. haec eadem repetuntur. Et utroque loco vox מרמיטה marmita interpretes non parum torquet. R. Selomo reddit בהלה, id est, terrorem et conturbationem. Ita etiam Scholiastes in haec loca, et Clarissimus Buxtorfius. Baal Aruch, marmor; quasi somnus marmoris dicatur, quo marmoris, aut, in genere, lapidis instar obstupescimus: prout dicitur de Aegyptiis Exod. XV, 16. ידמו כאבן, sileant sicut lapis. Postellus sopor carri, seu vehementiae somni profundioris. Legendum cari, id est, κάρου. Boderianus, Pomarius, Aquinas, pro מרמיטה marmita, emendant דורמיטה dormita, ut sit, dormitatio. Tamen מרמיטה marmita constanter legunt nostra exemplaria, et Baal Aruch sine Jod מרמטה. Sed vera lectio est מרמוטה marmota: quomodo in ipsis Alpibus appellatur hoc animal, quo ne glis quidem est somniculosior. Scaliger De subtilitate Exercitatione 203. Cum glirium specie (marmotae) in somno conveniunt. Hybernos enim totos menses transigunt sopore. Gesnerus, Hi mures multum dormiunt, et in cavernis suis delitescunt, quas miro artificio fodiunt, etc. Agricola, Somno plurimum indulget, etc. In montibus quidem foenum, quod in saxis mollissimum crescit, collectum, in cavernam deferunt, ut hyeme mollius dormiant. Stumpfius, in Helvetiae Chronicis: Cibi gratia hyeme tantum dormientes effodiuntur. Item, Terraque effossa dormientes auferunt. Et paullo post, loco effosso dormientes deprehenduntur, etc. portanturque dormientes quo libuerit. Neque enim facile expergiscuntur, nisi calor solis, ignis, aut hypocausti eos resolverit. Et rursus, Occiduntur etiamnum dormientes, cultro in jugulum adacto, unde parum prioribus pedibus moveri incipiunt. Sed exspirant prius quam prorsus expergiscantur. Et multo ante Plinius, qui hujus muris meminit solus veterum libri octavi capite trigesimo septimo: Conduntur hyeme II, 416 et Pontici mures etc. Conduntur et Alpini. Nempe in cavis suis altum dormituri. Itaque somnus Saulis et militum circumstantium, qui tam altum dormiebant, ut Davidem et Abisaeum, usque ad regium tentorium procedentes, et Saulis lanceam auferentes, non senserint, recte ab Hebraeo scriptore vocatur תרדמת מרמוטה, somnus marmotae.

Of these animals, Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ] describes the former as follows: الوبر دويبة اصغر من السنور كحلا اللون لا ذنب لها تدجن في البيوت [al-wabr duwayba aṣghar min al-sinnawr kaḥlā al-lawn lā dhanab lahā tadjun fī al-buyūt], Alwebro is a small animal, smaller than a cat, of dusky colour, without a tail, living in houses. But, as Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] observes, قوله لا ذنب لها اي لا ذنب لها col. 1005 طويل والا فالوبر له ذنب قصير جدا [qawluhu lā dhanab lahā ay lā dhanab lahā ṭawīl wa-illā fa-l-wabr lahu dhanab qaṣīr jiddan] When he denies that it has a tail, he means that its tail is not long; for alwebro does indeed have a tail, but a very short one. He also states that some call it غنم بني اسرايل [ghanam banī Isrāyil] the sheep of the children of Israel; لان ذنبها مع صغره يشبه الية الخروف [li-anna dhanabahā maʿa ṣigharihi yushbih alyat al-kharūf] because its tail, by its shortness, resembles a lamb's tail R2. But in Giauhari it is called زلم [zulam] zulem, for what reason I do not sufficiently know. In the book entitled كفاية المتحفظة [Kifāyat al-mutaḥaffiẓa] we read that الوبر [al-wabr] alwebro is دويبة قريبة من السنور ولها بول يتخثر فيتداوي به الناس [duwayba qarība min al-sinnawr wa-lahā bawl yatakhaththar fa-yatadāwī bihi al-nās] a small animal like a cat, whose urine thickens and is used among the remedies for diseases. Mawardi and Rujiani say that it is an animal في عظم الجرذ الا انه انبل منه والعرب تاكله [fī ʿiẓam al-juradh illā annahu anbal minhu wa-l-ʿArab taʾkuluhu] of the size of a larger mouse, but finer, which the Arabs eat. By others it is described as دويبة سودا في قدر الارنب واكبر من ابن عرس [duwayba sūdā fī qadr al-arnab wa-akbar min ibn ʿirs] a small black animal, approaching the size of a hare, and larger than a weasel. The same animal, as some add, كالارنب يعتلف النبات والبقول [ka-l-arnab yaʿtalif al-nabāt wa-l-buqūl] feeds, like the hare, on herbs and vegetables. I take it to be the marmot, or mountain mouse, which Gesner describes thus: It is more corpulent than a cat, but shorter in the legs, etc. Its colour is for the most part reddish, brighter in some, darker and dusky in others. And Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)] against Cardano, Exercise 203: They are of the size and fur of badgers, and likewise have almost no tail. He adds that he kept a tame one among the Taurini. And Gesner: I shall describe its natural history, partly as I myself II, 414 observed it when I kept this animal at home. And Stumpf [=Johannes Stumpf, Swiss chronicle]: Of the wild animals of our part of the world you will scarcely find any that becomes so tame and familiar to man. He had, namely, kept one at home for two years. Pliny, book 8, chapter 37, calls it the Alpine mouse, because it is common in the Alps. But lest anyone think that these mice are peculiar to the Alps, he describes similar ones in Egypt R3. Nor is it only for the Arabs that the שפן saphan of Moses is الوبر [al-wabr] alvvebro, or the mountain mouse. For among our own scholars too Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], who had by no means consulted the Arabs, consistently renders the Hebrew שפן II, 415 in this way. So too another anonymous writer, of whom Gesner says in the chapter On the Alpine mouse: Saphan, a Hebrew word, etc., a certain learned man among us interprets as the Alpine mouse. Note in passing that the Italian name of the mountain or Alpine mouse, marmota, is found, slightly altered, in two places in Bereschith Rabba. The first is section 17, on the words of Gen 2:21. The Lord God caused תרדמה thardema (that is, a deep sleep) to fall upon Adam. רב אמר שלש תרדמת הן תרדמת שינה תרדמת נבואה ותרדמת מרמיטה תרדמת שינה ויפול יהוה תרדמה על האדם col. 1006 וישן תרדמת נבואה ויהי השמש לבא ותרדמה נפלה על אברם תרדמת מרמיטה אין רואה ואין יודע ואין מקיץ כי כלם ישנים כי תרדמת י״ נפלה עליהם Rab said: there are three kinds of deep sleep: the deep sleep of slumber, the deep sleep of prophecy, and the deep sleep of מרמיטה marmita. The deep sleep of slumber, Gen 2:21: “The Lord God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept. The deep sleep of prophecy, Gen 15:12: And when the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell upon Abram. The deep sleep of מרמיטה marmita, 1 Sam 26:12: There was no one who saw, nor who understood, nor who awoke, but they were all asleep; because a deep sleep from the Lord had fallen upon them.” The other place is section 43, where these same words are repeated on Gen 15:12. In both places the word מרמיטה marmita has tormented the interpreters not a little. R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] renders it בהלה, that is, terror and confusion. So too the Scholiast on these passages, and the most distinguished Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum]. Baal Aruch renders it marble; as if it were called the sleep of marble, in which we become stupefied like marble or, in general, like stone: as is said of the Egyptians in Exod 15:16. ידמו כאבן, let them be still as a stone. Postel [=Guillaume Postel]: the deep sleep of carrus, or of the vehemence of a more profound sleep. One should read cari, that is, κάρου [karou]. Boderianus [=Guy Le Fèvre de la Boderie], Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)] and Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)] emend מרמיטה marmita to דורמיטה dormita, so that it would mean dormitatio [dozing]. Yet our copies consistently read מרמיטה marmita, and Baal Aruch, without Yod, מרמטה. But the true reading is מרמוטה marmota: as this animal is called in the Alps themselves, an animal than which not even the dormouse is sleepier. Scaliger, On Subtlety, Exercise 203: They (the marmots) agree with the dormouse kind in sleep. For they pass whole winter months in torpor. Gesner: These mice sleep a great deal, and lie hidden in their burrows, which they dig with wonderful skill, etc. Agricola [=Georgius Agricola]: It indulges very much in sleep, etc. In the mountains they gather the hay that grows softest among the rocks and carry it into the burrow, so that they may sleep more softly in winter. Stumpf, in the Chronicles of Switzerland: For the sake of food they are dug out only in winter, while asleep. Likewise: And having dug up the earth, they carry them off asleep. And a little later: when the place is dug up, they are found asleep, etc., and they are carried asleep wherever one pleases. For they do not easily wake up unless the heat of the sun, of a fire or of a stove has loosened them. And again: They are even killed while still asleep, by driving a knife into the throat, whereupon they begin to move their forefeet a little. But they expire before they are fully awake. And long before, Pliny, the only one of the ancients who mentions this mouse, book 8, chapter 37: In winter II, 416 the Pontic mice also hide away, etc. The Alpine ones also hide away. That is, to sleep deeply in their burrows. Therefore the sleep of Saul and of the soldiers around him, who slept so deeply that they did not notice David and Abishai advancing right up to the royal tent and carrying off Saul's spear, is rightly called by the Hebrew writer תרדמת מרמוטה, the sleep of the marmot.


Iam dicendum, quid sit الفنك alphenec, qua voce alios Arabes Hebraeum שפן saphan reddidisse diximus. Gabriel Sionita Geographiae Nubiensis Clim. 1. part. 1. mustelam albam interpretatur. Golius, mustelam foenariam, vulgo fovinam (quia putavit vir doctissimus, فنك phenec ad foenum alludere, et fovinam a foeno dici, cum a Gallico fagi vocabulo nomen habeat). Giggeio فنك phenec est brutum quoddam utilissimum, ex cujus pelle vestes pelliceae accipiuntur. Sed praestat audire ipsos Arabes. Abenbitar, الفنك حر طيب الرايحة اطيب من جميع انواع الفرأء يجلب كثيرا col. 1007 من الصقالبة ويشبه ان يكون في لحمه حلاوة وهو ابرد من السمور واحر من السنجاب واكثر الناس علي اختلاف اسنانهم يحتملون لبس الفنك Phenec animal est, cujus pellis est calida, boni odoris, in omnibus pelliciorum speciebus odoratissima. Affertur magna copia ex Secalia. Videtur esse carne dulci. Frigidior est pellis pelle τοῦ simor, sed calidior pelle τοῦ sungiab. Ea maxime pelle, vergente aetate, vestiri mos est. Razi, الفنك والقماقم والحواصل معتدلة في الحرارة وهو مع ذلك خفيفة Pelles alphenec, et alkamakim, et alhawasil, sunt caloris temperati, et praeterea leves. Damir, الفنك دويبة يوخذ منها الفرو قال ابن البيطار انه اطيب من جميع الفراء يجلب كثيرا من بلاد الصقلاب Alphenec, animalculum, ex quo sumitur pellicium. Dixit Abenbitar, fragrantissimum esse omnium pelliciorum, et plurimum afferri ex regione Sclava: quomodo legendum supra, non صقالية Secalia (regio Sclava, id est, Sclavorum, fuit olim in Scythia Europaea versus Oceanum occidentalem, teste Simocatta libri sexti capite secundo). Ibnomar Ben Abdalbar in libro, cui titulus غهيد id est, Explanatio, الفنك والسنجاب والسمور كل ذلك سبع كالثعلب وابن عرس Phenec, et sungiab, et simur ferae sunt omnes instar vulpis et mustelae. Haec illi: ex quibus colligi videatur, has pelles esse in martis speciebus. Tamen الفنك alphenec po[?]

Now we must say what الفنك [al-fanak] alphenec is, the word by which, as we said, other Arabs rendered the Hebrew שפן saphan. Gabriel Sionita [=translator of al-Idrīsī's geography into Latin (Geographia Nubiensis, Paris 1619)], in the Geography of Nubia, Clim. [=climate (section) of al-Idrīsī's geography, in the Latin Geographia Nubiensis] 1, section 1, interprets it as white weasel. Golius [=Jacobus Golius, Lexicon Arabico-Latinum (1653)] renders it mustela foenaria, vulgo fovina [hay-weasel, commonly called fovina], because that most learned man thought that فنك [fanak] phenec alludes to foenum [hay], and that fovina is named from foenum, whereas it takes its name from the French word for the beech. For Giggeius فنك [fanak] phenec is a certain very useful beast, from whose skin fur garments are made. But it is better to hear the Arabs themselves. Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār]: الفنك حر طيب الرايحة اطيب من جميع انواع الفرأء يجلب كثيرا [al-fanak ḥarr ṭayyib al-rāyiḥa aṭyab min jamīʿ anwāʿ al-farāʾ yujlab kathīran] col. 1007 من الصقالبة ويشبه ان يكون في لحمه حلاوة وهو ابرد من السمور واحر من السنجاب واكثر الناس علي اختلاف اسنانهم يحتملون لبس الفنك [min al-ṣaqāliba wa-yushbih an yakūn fī laḥmihi ḥalāwa wa-huwa abrad min al-sammūr wa-aḥarr min al-sinjāb wa-akthar al-nās ʿalī ikhtilāf asnānihim yaḥtamilūn lubs al-fanak]: Phenec is an animal whose skin is warm and of good odour, the most fragrant of all kinds of furs. It is brought in great quantity from Secalia. It seems to have sweet flesh. Its skin is cooler than the skin of τοῦ [tou] simor, but warmer than the skin of τοῦ [tou] sungiab. It is the custom above all for those advancing in age to be clothed in this skin. Razi: الفنك والقماقم والحواصل معتدلة في الحرارة وهو مع ذلك خفيفة [al-fanak wa-l-qamāqim wa-l-ḥawāṣil muʿtadila fī al-ḥarāra wa-huwa maʿa dhālika khafīfa]: The skins alphenec, and alkamakim, and alhawasil are of moderate warmth, and moreover light. Damir: الفنك دويبة يوخذ منها الفرو قال ابن البيطار انه اطيب من جميع الفراء يجلب كثيرا من بلاد الصقلاب [al-fanak duwayba yūkhadh minhā al-farw qāla Ibn al-Bayṭār innahu aṭyab min jamīʿ al-firāʾ yujlab kathīran min bilād al-ṣaqlāb]: Alphenec, a small animal from which fur is taken. Abenbitar said that it is the most fragrant of all furs, and that it is brought in great quantity from the Sclavic region. This is how it should be read above, not صقالية [ṣaqāliya] Secalia (the Sclavic region, that is, the region of the Sclavs, was once in European Scythia, toward the Western Ocean, as Simocatta attests, book 6, ch. 2). Ibnomar Ben Abdalbar [=Abū ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, author of al-Tamhīd], in the book entitled غهيد [ghhyd], that is, Explanation: الفنك والسنجاب والسمور كل ذلك سبع كالثعلب وابن عرس [al-fanak wa-l-sinjāb wa-l-sammūr kull dhālika sabʿ ka-l-thaʿlab wa-ibn ʿirs]: Phenec, and sungiab, and simur are all wild beasts like the fox and the weasel. So they say; from which one might gather that these skins belong to the species of marten. Yet, rather[?], الفنك [al-fanak] alphenec


II, 417 est mus Ponticus, id est, muris, aut sciuri species, quem Venetum Hermolaus, et Finnicum Agricola nominat, a Venetis et Finnis, populis ad Vistulam in Borussia, a quibus defertur ad nos in pelliciorum usum. De his populis ita Ptolemaeus in descriptione Sarmatiae, Παρὰ μὲν τὸν Οὐιστούλαν ποταμὸν ὑπὸ τοὺς Οὐενέδας Γύθωνες, εἶτα Φίννοι· Ad Vistulam quidem fluvium sub Venetis sunt Gythones, deinde Finni. Ab his, inquam, Finnis dici videtur mus Finnicus, et Arabice فنك phenec, qui a statura et colore Gallis dicitur petigris (4). Sed et سنجاب sungiab Golio est sciurus, animal cinerei coloris, ejusque pellis, qua suffulciuntur vestes, seu potius minium (voluit, credo, herminium). Damir animal esse dicit, ad formam talpae, mure majus, degens in summis arboribus, pellis coeruleae, mollissimae, pulcherrimae, qua delicati vestiuntur. Apparet, sciuri speciem describi. Est et simur genus muris, Graecis non prorsus ignoti. Hesychius, Σίμωρ παρὰ Πάρθοις καλεῖταί τι μυὸς ἀγρίου εἶδος, οὗ ταῖς δοραῖς col. 1008 χρῶνται πρὸς χιτῶνας· Simor apud Parthos vocatur quaedam agrestis muri species, cujus pelles cedunt in usum vestium. Aliis simur est martes. Damir ait, esse animal, feli simile, aut النمس furoni, ex quorundam sententia, cujus pellis mollitie, levitate, calore et pulchritudine ita excellit, ut ea reges et magnates induantur. De utraque pelle multo plura possem addere, petita ex Arabum li-bris: sed singula haec accuratius explicare non est nostri otii, neque multum facit ad rem praesentem.

II, 417 is the Pontic mouse, that is, a species of mouse or squirrel, which Hermolaus calls Venetian and Agricola Finnish, after the Veneti and the Finni, peoples on the Vistula in Prussia, from whom it is brought to us for use as fur. Of these peoples Ptolemy writes thus in his description of Sarmatia: Παρὰ μὲν τὸν Οὐιστούλαν ποταμὸν ὑπὸ τοὺς Οὐενέδας Γύθωνες, εἶτα Φίννοι [Para men ton Ouistoulan potamon hypo tous Ouenedas Gythōnes, eita Phinnoi]· Along the Vistula river, below the Veneti, are the Gythones, then the Finni. From these Finni, I say, the Finnish mouse seems to be named, in Arabic فنك [fanak] phenec, which the French, from its size and colour, call petigris R4. But سنجاب [sinjāb] sungiab too is for Golius the squirrel, an animal of ash-grey colour, and its skin, with which garments are lined, or rather minium (he meant, I believe, herminium [ermine]). Damir says it is an animal in the shape of a mole, larger than a mouse, living at the tops of trees, with a bluish, very soft and very beautiful skin, in which people of refinement are clothed. It is evident that a species of squirrel is being described. Simur, too, is a kind of mouse, not entirely unknown to the Greeks. Hesychius: Σίμωρ παρὰ Πάρθοις καλεῖταί τι μυὸς ἀγρίου εἶδος, οὗ ταῖς δοραῖς [Simōr para Parthois kaleitai ti myos agriou eidos, hou tais dorais] col. 1008 χρῶνται πρὸς χιτῶνας [chrōntai pros chitōnas]· Simor is the name among the Parthians of a certain species of wild mouse whose skins are used for garments. For others simur is the marten. Damir says it is an animal similar to a cat, or, in the opinion of some, النمس [al-nims] to a ferret, whose skin so excels in softness, lightness, warmth and beauty that kings and magnates are clothed in it. About both skins I could add much more, drawn from the books of the Arabs; but to explain these particulars more precisely is not a matter for our leisure, nor does it contribute much to the present subject.


Graecis par est inconstantia in explicatione vocis שפן saphan.

Among the Greeks there is equal inconsistency in explaining the word שפן saphan.


1. Sunt, qui λαγωοὺς reddunt; ut Vulgatus, lepusculos: quod jam supra expendimus.

1. There are some who render it λαγωοὺς [lagōous]; so the Vulgate translator, little hares: this we have already examined above.


2. Fuere, qui hyaenam mallent; ut Clemens Alexandrinus libri secundi Paedagogi capite decimo, ubi Mosem inducit dicentem, Οὐκ ἔδεσαι τὸν λαγὼν, οὐδὲ τὴν ὕαιναν, Non comedes leporem, neque hyaenam, id est הארנבת והשפן. Cui simile est, quod legitur in Epistola Barnabae: Ἀλλὰ καὶ δασύποδα οὐ φά-γῃ, Sed nec leporem manducabis. Et paullo post Ἀλλὰ οὐδὲ τὴν ὕαιναν φάγῃ, pro quo habet versio vetus, Sed nec belluam manducabis. Malim beluum, aut belbum. Ita enim Iulius Capitolinus in Gordiano tertio: Fuerunt sub Gordiano Romae elephanti XXXII, alces X, tigres X, leones mansueti LX, leopardi mansueti II, 418 XXX, belbi, id est, hyaenae X. Tamen in Glossario Philoxenus, Ὕαινα· ζῶον, bellua.

2. There were some who preferred the hyena; so Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus book 2, ch. 10, where he presents Moses as saying, Οὐκ ἔδεσαι τὸν λαγὼν, οὐδὲ τὴν ὕαιναν [Ouk edesai ton lagōn, oude tēn hyainan], You shall not eat the hare, nor the hyena, that is הארנבת והשפן. Similar to this is what is read in the Epistle of Barnabas: Ἀλλὰ καὶ δασύποδα οὐ φάγῃ [Alla kai dasypoda ou phagē], But neither shall you eat the hare. And a little later, Ἀλλὰ οὐδὲ τὴν ὕαιναν φάγῃ [Alla oude tēn hyainan phagē], for which the old version has, But neither shall you eat the beast [belluam]. I would prefer beluum or belbum. For so Julius Capitolinus in Gordian III: Under Gordian there were at Rome 32 elephants, 10 elks, 10 tigers, 60 tame lions, 30 tame leopards II, 418, 10 belbi, that is, hyenas. Yet in the Glossary Philoxenus has: Ὕαινα· ζῶον [Hyaina; zōon], bellua [beast].


3. Plerisque Graecis שפן saphan est χοιρογρύλλιος· quae versio est receptissima, adeoque vetustissima. Ita enim reddunt Seniores, Levit. XI, 5. Deut. XIV, 7. et Prov. XXX, 26. Sed et Psalm. CIII, (Hebraeis CIV,) 18. pro τοῖς λαγωοῖς, alii omnes, id est, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, etc. voce simili χοιρογρυλλίους transtulerunt, ut testatur Hieronymus in Epistola ad Suniam. Unde in nonnulla etiam irrepsit Seniorum exemplaria. Atque, idem sequutus, Aethiops Pentateuchi interpres, Romae manu - scriptus, pro השפן, habet ኮሮገሬሊወን፡ choerogryllion. Verum ignotum pene dixerim sic explicari per ignotius. Neque enim constat satis, quid sit χοιρογρύλλιος, cum de eo nil quidquam habeant ii veterum, qui de animalibus scripserunt, Aristoteles puta, Plinius, Aelianus, Oppianus, Phile, etc. Tamen Aristophanis Scholiastes in Pace vocem Graecam esse agnoscit: sed de illa hoc solum habet, Ἔστι δὲ ζῶον, ὃ καλεῖται ὑπό τινων χοιρογρύλλιος· Animal est, quod a nonnullis vocatur choerogryllius. Alii veterum Lexicographi hericium, aut hystricem interpretantur. Hesychius, Χοιρογρύλλιον· ὁ ἐχῖνος. Philoxeni Glossae, Χοιρογρύλλιος, ἤγουν ἐχῖνος χερσαῖος, Erinacius. Suidas, Χοιρογρύλλιος· ὕστριξ, ἀκανθόχοιρος, τουτέστιν ἐχῖνος χερσαῖος. Sed et Vulgatus interpres Psal. CIII, (Hebraeis CIV,) 18. Petra refugium herinaciis, id est, τοῖς χοιρογρυλλίοις· quomodo etiam Hieronymus in Psalmorum versione, quae extat inter ipsius Opera, a Vulgata in multis plane diversa. Et Eucherius in libro De nominibus Hebraeorum capite duodecimo, Erinacii chirogrylli nuncupantur, etc. Et Vincentius in Doctrinali, libri decimi sexti capite octuagesimo sexto: Erinacius, qui et cirogryllus, est animal, porcelli formam habens, sed spinosum, etc. Et Graecus Scholiastes in proverbia perabsurde, οἱ χοιρογρύλλιοι· εἶδος ἰχθύος, ἤτοι οἱ λαγωοὶ, ἢ οἱ καλού-μενοι οἶστροι. Choerogryllii piscis species, aut lepores, aut qui vocantur asili.

3. For most Greeks שפן saphan is χοιρογρύλλιος [choirogryllios]. This rendering is the most widely accepted, and accordingly also the most ancient. For so the Elders render it in Levit. XI, 5., Deut. XIV, 7. and Prov 30:26. Moreover, in Psalm. CIII, (Hebraeis CIV,) 18., in place of τοῖς λαγωοῖς [tois lagōois], all the others, that is, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, etc., translated with the similar word χοιρογρυλλίους [choirogryllious], as Jerome testifies in his Epistle to Sunia. From there it also crept into some copies of the Elders. And following the same, the Ethiopic translator of the Pentateuch, in a manuscript at Rome, has for השפן ኮሮገሬሊወን፡ [korogarēliwan] choerogryllion. But this, I would almost say, is to explain the unknown by the more unknown. For it is not sufficiently established what the χοιρογρύλλιος [choirogryllios] is, since those of the ancients who wrote about animals, Aristotle, for instance, Pliny, Aelian, Oppian, Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)], etc., say nothing whatever about it. Yet the Scholiast on Aristophanes, on the Peace, acknowledges that the word is Greek; but about it he has only this: Ἔστι δὲ ζῶον, ὃ καλεῖται ὑπό τινων χοιρογρύλλιος [Esti de zōon, ho kaleitai hypo tinōn choirogryllios]; It is an animal which is called choerogryllius by some. Other ancient Lexicographers interpret it as the hedgehog or the porcupine. Hesychius: Χοιρογρύλλιον· ὁ ἐχῖνος [Choirogryllion; ho echinos]. The Glosses of Philoxenus: Χοιρογρύλλιος, ἤγουν ἐχῖνος χερσαῖος [Choirogryllios, ēgoun echinos chersaios], Erinacius [hedgehog]. Suidas: Χοιρογρύλλιος· ὕστριξ, ἀκανθόχοιρος, τουτέστιν ἐχῖνος χερσαῖος [Choirogryllios; hystrix, akanthochoiros, toutestin echinos chersaios]. Moreover, the Vulgate translator at Psal. CIII, (Hebraeis CIV,) 18. has The rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs, that is, τοῖς χοιρογρυλλίοις [tois choirogrylliois]; and so too Jerome in his version of the Psalms, which is extant among his Works and in many places differs entirely from the Vulgate. And Eucherius, in the book On the Hebrew Names, chapter 12: Hedgehogs are called chirogrylli, etc. And Vincent, in the Doctrinale, book 16, chapter 86: The hedgehog, which is also called cirogryllus, is an animal having the form of a piglet, but spiny, etc. And the Greek Scholiast on Proverbs, most absurdly: οἱ χοιρογρύλλιοι· εἶδος ἰχθύος, ἤτοι οἱ λαγωοὶ, ἢ οἱ καλούμενοι οἶστροι [hoi choirogryllioi; eidos ichthyos, ētoi hoi lagōoi, ē hoi kaloumenoi oistroi]. Choerogryllii: a species of fish, or hares, or what are called gadflies.


Atque haec fere sunt veterum interpretamenta vocis שפן saphan, in quibus quid eligas nondum apparet; quia horum nullum est, quod non habeat sua incommoda. الوبر alvvebro, id est, mus montanus, in eo differt a שפן saphan, quod non ruminat, neque degit in petris, neque in Iudaea nascitur, neque in locis vicinis (5). Et frustra opponi Plinium dicetur infra. Plus in iis est rationis, qui saphan volunt esse الغنك alphenec, sciuri speciem, quem veteres murem Ponticum appellabant. Ruminant enim mures Pontici. Aristoteles Historiae col. 1009 II, 419 animalium fere in fine libri noni, Μηρυκάζουσι δὲ καὶ τῶν ἀμφοδόντων ἔνια, οἷον οἱ μῦες οἱ Ποντικοί. Sunt etiam ex utrimque dentatis, quae ruminant, ut mures Pontici. Plinius libri decimi capite septuagesimo tertio, Pontici quoque mures simili modo remandunt. Et quamvis in frigidis locis fere nascantur, tamen in calidis non desunt. Getulici quippe sciuri meminere scriptores. Et de eo multa habet Iohannes Cajus Anglus in Epistola ad Gesnerum. Ut de Arabe Geographo a) taceam, qui in censu animalium, quae in intima Africa nutriunt Nigrorum sylvae, etiam habet افناك Finnicos mures, sive Ponticos. In petris tamen non degunt, sed in arborum fastigio nidificant et foetus fovent. Itaque الفنك alphenec, seu mus Finnicus, non potest esse שפן saphan. Idem de hyaena judicium, quae non ruminat, neque in petris degit, sed in sepulchris potius. Unde est, quod antrum hyaenae Arabice رجمة rugma dicitur, id est, sepulchrum. Praeterea שפנים sephanim Solomon dicit esse populum invalidum Prov. XXX, 26. quod de hyaenis nemo dixerit. Sed neque est hericius in censu ruminantium, neque in petris habitat, sed in cavis arborum, aut in dumetis, aut sepibus. Unde est, quod hericium Angli vocant Hedge-hog, quasi dicas porcum sepium. Nec temere praetereundum, quod dicturus sum. Marmotta et hyaena solitaria sunt animalia: hericius quoque, qui Graece χὴρ ἀπὸ τῆς χη-ρώσεως, ἤτοι ἐρημώσεως, a solitudine dicitur. At שפן saphan gregarium est animal. Quo pertinet, quod Solomon שפנים sephanim populum appellat ubi supra, שפנים עם לא עצום, Sephanim populus invalidus: ut paullo ante de formicis, הנמלים עם לא עז, Formicae populus non fortis. Et Ioel. I, 6. de locustis, גוי עלה על ארצי עצום, Contra terram meam ascendit gens valida. Quale est, quod Lucianus in Icaro-Menippo dixit μυρμήκων ἀγορὰν formicarum concionem. Et Philippus Anthologiae libri primi capite vigesimo tertio, Βωλοτόμοι μύρμηκες, ὁ γῆς στρατός· Glebas excavantes formicae, terrae exercitus. Et Philostratus πιθήκων δῆμος· ut Solinus, plebes simiarum; et Smyrnaeus, μελισσάων κλυτὰ φῦλα, nobiles apum gentes: et multo ante Poeta summus Iliad. β′.

These, then, are roughly the interpretations of the word שפן saphan given by the ancients. Which of them one should choose is not yet clear, for there is none of them that does not have its own difficulties. الوبر [al-wabr] alvvebro, that is, the mountain mouse, differs from the שפן saphan in that it does not ruminate, does not live among rocks, and is not native to Judaea or to the neighbouring regions R5. That Pliny is objected against this to no purpose will be shown below. There is more reason on the side of those who hold that the saphan is الغنك [al-ghnk] alphenec, a species of squirrel, which the ancients called the Pontic mouse. For Pontic mice do ruminate. Aristotle, near the end of book 9 of the History col. 1009 II, 419 of Animals: Μηρυκάζουσι δὲ καὶ τῶν ἀμφοδόντων ἔνια, οἷον οἱ μῦες οἱ Ποντικοί [Mērykazousi de kai tōn amphodontōn enia, hoion hoi myes hoi Pontikoi]. There are also some among the animals with teeth in both jaws that ruminate, such as the Pontic mice. Pliny, book 10, chapter 73: Pontic mice also chew the cud in a similar way. And although they are mostly born in cold places, they are not lacking in hot ones either. Writers, indeed, mention a Gaetulian squirrel, and John Caius the Englishman has a good deal about it in his Letter to Gesner. I pass over the Arabian Geographer a), who, in his list of the animals nourished by the forests of the Negroes in the interior of Africa, also includes افناك [afnāk], Finnic or Pontic mice. They do not, however, live among rocks; rather, they build their nests and rear their young at the tops of trees. Therefore الفنك [al-fanak] alphenec, or the Finnic mouse, cannot be the שפן saphan. The same judgement applies to the hyaena, which does not ruminate and does not live among rocks, but rather in tombs. Hence the den of a hyaena is called in Arabic رجمة [rujma] rugma, that is, a tomb. Moreover, Solomon says that the שפנים sephanim are a feeble folk, Prov 30:26, which no one would say of hyaenas. Nor is the hedgehog among the ruminants, nor does it live among rocks, but in hollow trees, or in thickets or hedges. Hence the English call the hedgehog Hedge-hog, as if one were to say pig of the hedges. Nor should what I am about to say be lightly passed over. The marmot and the hyaena are solitary animals; so too is the hedgehog, which in Greek is called χὴρ [chēr] ἀπὸ τῆς χηρώσεως, ἤτοι ἐρημώσεως [apo tēs chērōseōs, ētoi erēmōseōs], from solitude. But the שפן saphan is a gregarious animal. To this belongs the fact that Solomon, in the place cited above, calls the שפנים sephanim a people: שפנים עם לא עצום, The Sephanim are a feeble people; just as a little earlier he says of the ants, הנמלים עם לא עז, The ants are a people not strong. And Joel. I, 6. of the locusts: גוי עלה על ארצי עצום, A strong nation has come up against my land. Of the same kind is what Lucian said in the Icaromenippus, μυρμήκων ἀγορὰν [myrmēkōn agoran], an assembly of ants. And Philip in the Anthology, book 1, chapter 23: Βωλοτόμοι μύρμηκες, ὁ γῆς στρατός [Bōlotomoi myrmēkes, ho gēs stratos]; Clod-hollowing ants, the army of the earth. And Philostratus says πιθήκων δῆμος [pithēkōn dēmos], as Solinus says the commons of the apes; and Smyrnaeus says μελισσάων κλυτὰ φῦλα [melissaōn klyta phyla], the noble nations of bees; and long before them the supreme Poet, Iliad 2:


Ἠΰτε ἔθνεα εἶσι μελισσάων ἀδινάων,

Ἠΰτε ἔθνεα εἶσι μελισσάων ἀδινάων, [Ēyte ethnea eisi melissaōn adinaōn,]


ut apum frequentium gentes eunt, id est, examina. De qua phrasi plura alibi. Itaque quidquid sit שפן saphan, solitarium animal non est. Et vel saphan non est χοιρογρύλλιος, quomodo reddiderunt vetustissimi interpretes, vel χοιρο-γρύλλιος non est ἐχῖνος herinacius, ut volunt. Et vero idem Hieronymus, qui Psalmo centesimo quarto, aliorum interpretum torrente abreptus, herinacium reddit, in Epistola ad Suniam χοιρογρύλλιον diversum esse ab herinacio animal, diserte docet, nempe ἀρκτομῦν. Verba sunt: Sciendum est, animal esse non II, 420 majus hericio, habens similitudinem muris et ursi. Unde et in Palaestina ἀρκτο-μῦς dicitur. Et magna est in istis regionibus hujus generis abundantia, semperque in cavernis petrarum, et terrae foveis habitare consueverunt. Et in Lexico Coptico ΠΙΧΙΡΟΓΡΙΛΛΙΟΝ, id est, ὁ χοιρογρύλλιος, Arabice redditur اليربوع aljarbuo. Itaque cardo quaestionis in hoc versatur, ut sciamus, quid sit Graecum ἀρκτομῦς, et Arabicum اليربوع. Neque lectori debet esse grave, si id perpendam accuratius, cum non possimus aliter scire rem, ignoratam hactenus, nempe quod animal Seniores χοιρογρύλλιον, et Hebraei שפן saphan appellaverint.

as the nations of thronging bees go forth, that is, swarms. Of this phrase more elsewhere. Therefore, whatever the שפן saphan may be, it is not a solitary animal. And either the saphan is not the χοιρογρύλλιος [choirogryllios], as the most ancient translators rendered it, or the χοιρογρύλλιος [choirogryllios] is not the ἐχῖνος [echinos], the hedgehog, as they hold. And indeed the same Jerome who, in Psalm 104, carried away by the torrent of the other translators, renders it hedgehog, expressly teaches in his Letter to Sunia that the χοιρογρύλλιον [choirogryllion] is an animal different from the hedgehog, namely the ἀρκτομῦν [arktomyn]. His words are: It should be known that it is an animal not II, 420 larger than a hedgehog, resembling a mouse and a bear. Hence in Palestine it is called ἀρκτομῦς [arktomys] [bear-mouse]. And there is a great abundance of this kind in those regions, and they are always accustomed to live in the caverns of rocks and in holes in the ground. And in the Coptic Lexicon ΠΙΧΙΡΟΓΡΙΛΛΙΟΝ, that is, ὁ χοιρογρύλλιος [ho choirogryllios], is rendered in Arabic اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo. The crux of the question therefore turns on this: that we should know what the Greek ἀρκτομῦς [arktomys] and the Arabic اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] are. Nor should the reader find it tedious if I examine this more carefully, since we cannot otherwise come to know something hitherto unknown, namely what animal the Elders called χοιρογρύλλιον [choirogryllion] and the Hebrews שפן saphan.


Ut ab origine rem ordiar, vetustissimi scriptores meminere murium in Aegypto et in Africa, qui posteriores pedes prioribus habent longiores, adeoque iis bipedes gradiuntur (6). Herodotus, ubi de Lybia, libri quarti capite cen- col. 1010 tesimo nonagesimo secundo: Μυῶν δὲ γενεὰ τριξὰ αὐτόθι ἐστί. οἱ μὲν δίποδες καλέονται, etc. Murium autem ibi est triplex genus. Alii quidem bipedes vocantur, etc. Aristoteles Historiae libro sexto in fine, Οἱ δ' ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ μῦες σκληρὰν ἔχουσι τὴν τρίχα, σχεδὸν ὥσπερ οἱ χερσαῖοι ἐχῖνοι. Εἰσὶ δὲ καὶ ἕτεροι, οἱ βα-δίζουσιν ἐπὶ τοῖς δυσὶ ποσί. τὰ γὰρ πρόσθια μικρὰ ἔχουσι, τὰ δ' ὀπίσθια με-γάλα (7). γίνονται δὲ πλήθει πολλοί. Mures autem, qui in Aegypto sunt, duros habent pilos, fere ut echini terrestres. Sunt autem et alii, qui bipedes incedunt. Habent enim priora crura brevia, posteriora longa. Sunt autem multi numero. Theophrastus apud Aelianum Historiae libri decimi quinti capite vigesimo sexto, Ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ δὲ ἀκούω δίποδας εἶναι μῦς, καὶ μεγίστους μεγέθει φύε-σθαι· τοῖς γε μὴν ἐμπροσθίοις ποσὶν, ὡς χερσὶ, χρῆσθαι. εἶναι γὰρ αὐτοὺς τοὺς ὄπισθε βραχυτέρους. εἶδον τούτους. Λιβυκοί εἰσι. βαδίζουσι δὲ ὀρθοὶ ἐπὶ τοῖν ποδοῖν, ὅταν δὲ διώκωνται, πηδῶσι. Audio, in Aegypto mures esse bipedes, et statura maximos, et prioribus pedibus, tanquam manibus, uti. Eos enim breviores esse posterioribus. Illos vidi. Libyci sunt. Recti duobus pedibus nitentes gradiuntur. Si quis autem insequatur, saliunt. Et ex eodem Photius, Ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ II, 421 δίποδάς φασι μῦας γίνεσθαι, καὶ μεγάλους. ἔχουσι δὲ οὗτοι καὶ τοὺς ἐμ-προσθίους πόδας, ἀλλ᾽ οὐ βαδίζουσιν ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῖς. χρῶνται δὲ αὐτοῖς, οἷα χερσίν. ὅταν δὲ φεύγωσιν, πηδῶσι. Bipedes in Aegypto mures, et magnos, nasci perhibent. Habent autem etiam anteriores pedes. At iis non incedunt, sed ut manibus utuntur. Et saltu fugiunt. Plinius libri octavi capite trigesimo septimo, postquam egit de muribus Alpinis, sunt his pares et in Aegypto (nempe in eo, quod sequitur, cum sint caetera valde dispares) similiterque residunt in clunes, et binis pedibus gradiuntur, prioribusque ut manibus utuntur. Et libri decimi capite sexagesimo quinto, Aegyptiis muribus durus pilus sicut herinaceis; iidem bi-pedes ambulant ceu Alpini.

To begin the matter from its origin: the most ancient writers mention mice in Egypt and in Africa which have hind feet longer than their fore feet, and therefore walk on them as bipeds R6. Herodotus, where he deals with Libya, book 4, chapter 192 col. 1010: Μυῶν δὲ γενεὰ τριξὰ αὐτόθι ἐστί. οἱ μὲν δίποδες καλέονται [Myōn de genea trixa autothi esti. hoi men dipodes kaleontai], etc. And there are three kinds of mice there. Some are called bipeds, etc. Aristotle, History, book 6, at the end: Οἱ δ' ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ μῦες σκληρὰν ἔχουσι τὴν τρίχα, σχεδὸν ὥσπερ οἱ χερσαῖοι ἐχῖνοι. Εἰσὶ δὲ καὶ ἕτεροι, οἱ βαδίζουσιν ἐπὶ τοῖς δυσὶ ποσί. τὰ γὰρ πρόσθια μικρὰ ἔχουσι, τὰ δ' ὀπίσθια μεγάλα R7. γίνονται δὲ πλήθει πολλοί. [Hoi d' en Aigyptō myes sklēran echousi tēn tricha, schedon hōsper hoi chersaioi echinoi. Eisi de kai heteroi, hoi badizousin epi tois dysi posi. ta gar prosthia mikra echousi, ta d' opisthia megala. ginontai de plēthei polloi.] The mice that are in Egypt have hard hair, almost like land hedgehogs. There are also others which walk on two feet. For they have short fore legs and long hind legs. And they are many in number. Theophrastus in Aelian, History, book 15, chapter 26: Ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ δὲ ἀκούω δίποδας εἶναι μῦς, καὶ μεγίστους μεγέθει φύεσθαι· τοῖς γε μὴν ἐμπροσθίοις ποσὶν, ὡς χερσὶ, χρῆσθαι. εἶναι γὰρ αὐτοὺς τοὺς ὄπισθε βραχυτέρους. εἶδον τούτους. Λιβυκοί εἰσι. βαδίζουσι δὲ ὀρθοὶ ἐπὶ τοῖν ποδοῖν, ὅταν δὲ διώκωνται, πηδῶσι. [En Aigyptō de akouō dipodas einai mys, kai megistous megethei phyesthai; tois ge mēn emprosthiois posin, hōs chersi, chrēsthai. einai gar autous tous opisthe brachyterous. eidon toutous. Libykoi eisi. badizousi de orthoi epi toin podoin, hotan de diōkōntai, pēdōsi.] I hear that in Egypt there are biped mice, very large in size, and that they use their fore feet as hands. For these are shorter than the hind ones. I have seen them. They are Libyan. They walk upright, supporting themselves on their two feet. But if anyone pursues them, they leap. And from the same source Photius: Ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ II, 421 δίποδάς φασι μῦας γίνεσθαι, καὶ μεγάλους. ἔχουσι δὲ οὗτοι καὶ τοὺς ἐμπροσθίους πόδας, ἀλλ᾽ οὐ βαδίζουσιν ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῖς. χρῶνται δὲ αὐτοῖς, οἷα χερσίν. ὅταν δὲ φεύγωσιν, πηδῶσι. [En Aigyptō dipodas phasi myas ginesthai, kai megalous. echousi de houtoi kai tous emprosthious podas, all' ou badizousin ep' autois. chrōntai de autois, hoia chersin. hotan de pheugōsin, pēdōsi.] They report that in Egypt biped mice are born, and large ones. They also have fore feet, but they do not walk on them; rather they use them as hands. And they flee by leaping. Pliny, book 8, chapter 37, after treating of the Alpine mice: there are also animals equal to these in Egypt (namely in what follows, since in other respects they are very unlike) and they likewise sit back on their haunches, walk on two feet, and use their fore feet as hands. And book 10, chapter 65: Egyptian mice have hard hair, like hedgehogs; they also walk on two feet, like the Alpine ones.


Hoc muris genus, etiam in Palaestina frequens, Hellenistae ideo vocarunt ἀρκτομῦν, id est, ursinum murem, quod incederet bipes, et prioribus pedibus tanquam manibus uteretur. Id enim est ursorum proprium. Oppianus libro tertio Cynegeticῶν in ursi descriptione,

This kind of mouse, which is also common in Eretz Yisrael, the Hellenists therefore called ἀρκτομῦν [arktomyn], that is, bear-mouse, because it walked on two feet and used its fore feet as hands. For this is characteristic of bears. Oppian, book 3 of the Cynegetica, in his description of the bear:


Χεῖρες χερσὶ βροτῶν ἴκελαι, πόδες ἠδὲ πόδεσσι,

Χεῖρες χερσὶ βροτῶν ἴκελαι, πόδες ἠδὲ πόδεσσι, [Cheires chersi brotōn ikelai, podes ēde podessi,]


Manus hominum manibus, pedesque pedibus similes. Solinus in capite De Numidia, et in ea ursis: Vis maxima in brachiis, et lumbis: unde interdum posticis pedibus insistunt.

Hands like the hands of men, and feet like their feet. Solinus, in the chapter On Numidia, and there on the bears: Their greatest strength is in the arms and loins; hence they sometimes stand on their hind feet.


Hoc idem animal Arabice vocatur اليربوع aljarbuo, et falluntur Lexicographi, qui talpam interpretantur. Res ex descriptione patebit. Damir in capite De اليربوع aljarbuo, هو حيوان طويل الرجلين وقصير اليدين جدا Est animal, cujus pedes posteriores longi sunt, et priores breves admodum. Et paullo post, فهي قصيرة اليدين لانها اذا خافت شي لاذت بالصعود فلا يلحقها شي Et pedes anteriores ideo breves habet, ut, cum aliquid timet, ad superiora confugiat, neque ul-lum animal id assequatur. Et infra, قال الجاحظ والقزويني وهو من نوع الفار Dixerunt Algiahid et Alkazuinius, esse inter species muris. col. 1011 Itaque vere est ἀρκτομῦς, id est, mus, cum urso hoc commune habens, quod pedibus posterioribus ingreditur, quos longiores habet. Gesnerus, in capite De mure Alpino, Graecum scriptorem anonymum citat, nondum editum, qui in libello De animalibus haec habet de arctomye: Arctomys unus custodit, caeteris pascentibus; et singuli partem pabuli ad eum deferunt: at, si negligentior fuerit in custodia, et homo aliquis supervenerit, cujus adventum ille voce non prodiderit, a caeteris occiditur. En his simillima de Aljarbuo in Damire, ut scias, idem esse animal! هو من الحيوان الذي له رييس مطاع يناقده II, 422 اليه واذا كان فيها يكون بيتها في مكان مشرف او علي صخرة ينظر الي الطريق من كل ناحية فان راي ما يخافه صر باسنانه وصوت فاذا سمعته انصرفت الي حجرتها فان قصر الرييس حتي ادركهم احد وصاد منهم شيا اجتمعوا علي الرييس وقتلوا وولوا غيره Est ille mus e numero animalium, quae ducem habent, quem colant, cuique obsequantur. Qui cum est inter eos, quorum domus est in sublimi loco, aut super petram, inde in viam ab omni parte prospicit. Et, si videat aliquid, unde sit metus, dentibus stridet et clamat: quo audito, illi secedunt ad latibula sua. At, si se contineat, donec eos assequatur aliquis, aut e numero suo aliquem intercipiat, conjuratione contra ducem inita, eum interficiunt, aliumque illi substituunt. De eodem animali si plura desideras, audi reliqua Damiris: ويسمى الدرص وذو الرمح ورمحه ذنبه وله ذنب كذنب الجرد يرفعه صعدا في طرفه شبه النوارة ولونه كلون الغزال Vocatur etiam dirs et dur-romchi (id est, hastatus); nempe pro hasta caudam ha-bet, similem caudae muris, quam sursum tollit: et in extremo est floris species (8). Color est ut color gazellae, seu capreae (9). Sequitur, وهذا الحيوان يسكن بطن الارض ليقوم رطوبتها له مقام الما Habitat hoc animal in ventre terrae, ut humiditas ejus praestet ipsi locum aquae. Et paullo infra, واليربوع يتخذ حجره في نشر من الارض ثم يحفر بيته في مهب والرياح الاربع ويتخذ col. 1012 فيه كوي وتسمي النافقا والقاصعا والراهطا فاذا طلب من احدي هذه الكوي نافق اي خرج من النافقا وان طلب من النافقا خرج من القاصعا وان طلب من القاصعا خرج من الراهطا |Aljarbuo parat latibulum suum dispergendo terram, et domum sibi fodit ad flatus quatuor ventorum, eamque fenestris II, 423 instruit, quarum una vocatur naphika, alia kasia, et rahita. A quibus, si impetatur, exit per naphikam. Et, si a naphika impetatur, exit per kasiam; aut per rahitam, si a kasia. Quomodo de mure nostro Plautus in Truculento Actu quarto,

In Arabic this same animal is called اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo, and the lexicographers who render it as talpa [mole] are mistaken. The matter will become clear from the description. Damir, in the chapter On اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo, says: هو حيوان طويل الرجلين وقصير اليدين جدا [huwa ḥayawān ṭawīl al-rijlayn wa-qaṣīr al-yadayn jiddan] It is an animal whose hind feet are long and whose fore feet are very short. And a little later: فهي قصيرة اليدين لانها اذا خافت شي لاذت بالصعود فلا يلحقها شي [fa-hiya qaṣīrat al-yadayn li-annahā idhā khāfat shay lādhat bi-l-ṣuʿūd fa-lā yalḥaquhā shay] And it has short fore feet so that, when it fears something, it may flee upward, and no animal can overtake it. And further on: قال الجاحظ والقزويني وهو من نوع الفار [qāla al-Jāḥiẓ wa-l-Qazwīnī wa-huwa min nawʿ al-fār] Algiahid and Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt] have said that it is among the species of mouse. col. 1011 It is therefore truly an ἀρκτομῦς [arktomys], that is, a mouse that has this in common with the bear, that it walks on its hind feet, which are the longer. Gesner, in the chapter On the Alpine mouse, cites an anonymous Greek writer, not yet published, who in a little book On animals has the following about the arctomys: One arctomys keeps watch while the others feed, and each of them brings it a share of the fodder. But if it has been too careless in its watch, and some man has come upon them whose approach it did not betray with its voice, it is killed by the others. See how very similar to this is what Damir says of the aljarbuo, so that you may know that it is the same animal! هو من الحيوان الذي له رييس مطاع يناقده [huwa min al-ḥayawān alladhī lahu raʾīs muṭāʿ yunāqiduhu] II, 422 اليه واذا كان فيها يكون بيتها في مكان مشرف او علي صخرة ينظر الي الطريق من كل ناحية فان راي ما يخافه صر باسنانه وصوت فاذا سمعته انصرفت الي حجرتها فان قصر الرييس حتي ادركهم احد وصاد منهم شيا اجتمعوا علي الرييس وقتلوا وولوا غيره [ilayhi wa-idhā kāna fīhā yakūn baytuhā fī makān mushrif aw ʿalā ṣakhra yanẓuru ilā al-ṭarīq min kull nāḥiya fa-in raʾā mā yakhāfuhu ṣarra bi-asnānihi wa-ṣawwata fa-idhā samiʿathu inṣarafat ilā ḥujratihā fa-in qaṣṣara al-raʾīs ḥattā adrakahum aḥad wa-ṣāda minhum shayʾan ijtamaʿū ʿalā al-raʾīs wa-qatalū wa-wallaw ghayrahu] That mouse is one of the animals that have a leader whom they honour and obey. When it is among those whose dwelling is in a high place or on a rock, it looks out from there over the path in every direction. And if it sees anything to be feared, it gnashes its teeth and cries out; on hearing this, they withdraw to their hiding-places. But if it holds back until someone overtakes them, or catches one of their number, they conspire against the leader, kill it, and put another in its place. If you want more about the same animal, hear the rest of Damir: ويسمى الدرص وذو الرمح ورمحه ذنبه وله ذنب كذنب الجرد يرفعه صعدا في طرفه شبه النوارة ولونه كلون الغزال [wa-yusammā al-dirṣ wa-dhū al-rumḥ wa-rumḥuhu dhanabuhu wa-lahu dhanab ka-dhanab al-jurd yarfaʿuhu ṣuʿudan fī ṭarafihi shibh al-nawwāra wa-lawnuhu ka-lawn al-ghazāl] It is also called dirs and dur-romchi (that is, the spear-bearer); for in place of a spear it has a tail, like the tail of a mouse, which it raises upward; and at its tip there is something like a flower R8. Its colour is like the colour of the gazelle, or roe-deer R9. There follows: وهذا الحيوان يسكن بطن الارض ليقوم رطوبتها له مقام الما [wa-hādhā al-ḥayawān yaskun baṭn al-arḍ li-yaqūm ruṭūbatuhā lahu maqām al-mā] This animal lives in the belly of the earth, so that its moisture may serve it in place of water. And a little further on: واليربوع يتخذ حجره في نشر من الارض ثم يحفر بيته في مهب والرياح الاربع ويتخذ [wa-l-yarbūʿ yattakhidhu juḥrahu fī nashr min al-arḍ thumma yaḥfiru baytahu fī mahabb wa-l-riyāḥ al-arbaʿ wa-yattakhidhu] col. 1012 فيه كوي وتسمي النافقا والقاصعا والراهطا فاذا طلب من احدي هذه الكوي نافق اي خرج من النافقا وان طلب من النافقا خرج من القاصعا وان طلب من القاصعا خرج من الراهطا [fīhi kuwā wa-tusammā al-nāfiqā wa-l-qāṣiʿā wa-l-rāhiṭā fa-idhā ṭuliba min iḥdā hādhihi al-kuwā nāfaqa ay kharaja min al-nāfiqā wa-in ṭuliba min al-nāfiqā kharaja min al-qāṣiʿā wa-in ṭuliba min al-qāṣiʿā kharaja min al-rāhiṭā] The aljarbuo prepares its hiding-place by scattering the earth, and digs itself a dwelling open to the blowing of the four winds, and furnishes it with windows II, 423 one of which is called naphika, another kasia, and rahita. If it is attacked from these, it goes out through the naphika. And if it is attacked from the naphika, it goes out through the kasia; or through the rahita, if from the kasia. Just as Plautus says of our mouse in the Truculentus, act 4:


Cogitato, mus pusillus quam sit sapiens bestia,
Aetatem qui uni cubili nunquam committit suam:
Quia si unum ostium obsideatur, aliud perfugium gerit b).

Consider what a wise beast the tiny mouse is, which never entrusts its life to a single lair: for if one entrance is besieged, it has another refuge b).


Sed et aliud comminisci dicitur aljarbuo. Fenestras, aut foramina sua verius, quandoque terra obducit in summa superficie, ne extrinsecus appareant (10). Id Arabice دم damma dicitur. Alcamus, دم اليربوع حجره غطاه وسواه Damma aljarbuo latibulum suum, id est, texit istud et complanavit. Unde et latibulo دممة dumama nomen. Idem Alcamus, الدممة حجرة اليربوع وتراب يجمعه اليربوع ويخرجه من الحجر فيسوي به بابه Dumama, latibulum aljarbui, et terra, quam colligit et e latibulo suo effodit, ut ea complanet ejus aditum. Proinde ut نافقا naphika dicitur ejus latibuli foramen, terra obtectum, inde sumta metaphora نافق naphaka, verbum tertiae Conjugationis, est in religione dissimulare, et aliud ore profiteri, aliud habere in animo reconditum. Et منافق munaphik est hypocrita. Damir, ظاهر بيته تراب وباطنه حفر وكذلك المنافق ظاهره ايمان وباطنه كفر Pars exterior domus ejus terra est, sed interior est concava. Hypocrita itidem fidem habet extrinsecus, sed intrinsecus infidelitatem. Algiahid, et alii, واسم المنافق لم يكن في الجاهلية لكن لمن اسر الكفر واظهر الايمان Nomen munaphik non erit in Ethnicismo, sed de eo (dicitur), qui celat infidelitatem, et ostentat fidem. Albazi, تعالي اشتق له هذا الاسم من هذا الاصل وهو من نافقا اليربوع لانه لما ابطن الكفر col. 1013 واظهر الايمان Excelsus Deus hypocritae nomen derivavit ex ista radice, nempe ex naphika, seu foramine muris, aljarbuo dicti; quia intus est infidelitas, et extra fides. Haec et alia plura Arabes in Azoaram Alcorani LXXIII. cui titulus المنافقون hypocritae. In Alcamus nidus hujus animalis vocatur لغز II, 424 logoz, quasi labyrinthum dicas, quia in hujusmodi nidis viae sinuosae sunt et intricatae admodum. Ac proinde الغاز algaz Arabice dicuntur طرق تلطوي وتشكل علي مسالكها viae, quae in tractu suo contortae sunt et implicatae. Ad haec muris genus referenda sunt, quae dicit Synesius de Iohanne quodam duce sub finem Epistolae centesimae quartae, Δίκην ἀρουραίου μυὸς ἐνεδεδύκει τῇ πέτρᾳ, Agrestis muris instar sese in petram abdiderat, id est, in Bombaeam, castrum in cavo rupis munitissimum. Neque enim alii agrestes mures in petra nidificant, sed solus aljarbuo (11). Quod probant haec Ibnolgiauzi, اليربوع لا يتخذ بيته الا في موضع صلب مرتفع ليسلم من سيل او حافر ثم لا يجعلة الا عند اكمة او شجرة او صخرة ليلا يضل اذا عاد اليه Aljarbuo domum suam non parat nisi in loco duro (id est, petricoso) et sublimi, ut ab aquarum influxu et ab (equorum) ungula tuta sit. Nec eam statuit, nisi in tumulis, aut arboribus, aut petris, ne, cum ad illam redit, aberret. Quod hujus animalculi catulis maxime accidit. Unde proverbium in Damire, اضل من ولد اليربوع Catulo aljarbui magis errat, de eo, qui vagatur, nec pedem figit uspiam. Ibidem, وفي طباعه انه اذا مشي في ارض سهلة او لينة مشي علي موخر كفه حتي لا يعرف اثر وطيه كما يفعل الارنب Etiam e natura ejus est, ut, cum in terra molli et in tenera graditur, summis pedibus insistat, ne in locis, quae calcavit, ejus vestigia agnoscantur: quod lepori quoque in more est. Item, وهو II, 425 يجتر ويبعر وله كرش واسنان واضراس من الفك الاعلي والاسفلي Ruminat etiam, et stercus egerit, et ingluviem habet (more ruminantium); quamvis dentes et maxillares illi sint, tam in superiore, quam in inferiore maxilla. Eidem muri hoc singulare, quod salit. Quod efferunt Arabes verbo بحظل bachdala maxime proprio. Alcamus, بحظل قفز قفزان اليربوع Bachdala, saliit saltu aljarbui. Ita etiam Giauhari. Quod ipsum Theophrastus de muribus illis, qui bipedes incedunt, supra observavit, Ὅταν δὲ διώκωνται, πηδῶσι· Si quis insequatur, saliunt. In ejusdem latibulis nidificat anguinum genus, quos Arabes appellant جنادع gianadio, vel جنادب gianadibo. Alcamus الجنادع الاجناش اوجنادب تكون في حجرة اليرابيع Algianadio, serpentum (genus) aut gia- col. 1014 nadibo: hi sunt in nido aljarabii, quod Plurale est vocis اليربوع aljarbuo. Si cum mure vulgari coëat aljarbuo, mus hybrida inde natus vocatur فرنب pharnab, aut phirnib. Alcamus, الفرنب الفارة او ولدها من اليربوع Alpharnab, (aut alphirnib) mus, aut foetus ejus ex aljarbuo. Est et hoc illi peculiare, quod ab Arabibus comeditur aljarbuo, cum de caetero muris esus sit eis interdictus. Damir in capite الفار alphar, id est, De mure, يحرم اكل جميع انواع الفار الا اليربوع Prohibitus est esus omnium muris specierum, praeterquam aljarbui. Est tamen inter Arabes aliquis ea de re dissensus. Nam ex sententia Abuchaniphae, لا يوكل لانه من الحشرات Non comeditur (aljarbuo); quia est ex subterraneis animalibus. Et Algazali, in libro, cui titulus الوسيط Mediator, negat, quidquam esse comedendum من الحشرات الا الضب ex subterraneis animalibus praeter crocodilum terrestrem. Tamen ab aliis insuper excipiuntur اليربوع وابن عرس وام حبين والقنفد والدلدل aljarbuo, et mustela, et chamaeleon, et hericius, et hystrix. Hinc de aljarbuo Damir, يحل اكله لان العرب تستطيبه وتحله Conceditur illius esus; quia permittunt Arabes, et eo delectantur. Ita nimirum definiunt magni Arabum Canonistae, Ata, et Achmed Ben-Hantal, et Ibnolmandsar, et Abutsaur, etc. Proinde non solum aljarbuo, sed et latibulum ejus emitur, id est, jus illud rimandi et perscrutandi, ut in eo capiatur hoc animal. Quod tamen, quia plerumque parum succedit, in proverbium cessit apud Arabes: ut cum dicunt, كالمشتري القاصعا باليربوع Ut qui pro II, 426 aljarbuo emit foramen ejus. Quod proverbium يضرب الذي يدع العين ويتبع الاثر ferit eum, qui, fonte relicto, solum sequitur vestigium. Graece dixeris, Σκιὰν ἀντὶ τοῦ σώματος, Umbram pro corpore. Atque hic quoque Arabes delicati sunt, et caeteris hujus generis muribus Suphariensem praeferunt, quem sic describit Alcamus: يربوع شفاري ضخم الاذنين وطويلهما العاري البراثين ولا يلحق سريعا والطويل والغوايم الرخو اللحم الدسم Suphariensis jarbuo crassis et longis est auribus, nudus unguibus, ita, ut non facile apprehendat, pedibus longis, teneraque et pingui carne.
