In Abenbitare, يربوع الاسراييلي لحم اليربوع يقد وغذا كثير ويلين البطن Iarbuo Israëliticus vocatur caro aljarbui, quae exsiccatur. Est autem multi nutrimenti, et mollit ventrem. Exsiccare Arabice est قد kadda, quod proprie signi- col. 1015 ficat carnem, in longitudinem scissam, vento exponere, quomodo apud nos fumo, ut humor absumatur. Unde قداد kedad dicitur tam hericius, quam aljarbuo; quia utrumque animal sic exsiccatur. Alkamus, القداد القنفد واليربوع Alkedado, hericius et Aljarbuo. In Arabicis Sacri textus versionibus vox aljarbuo occurrit semel omnino, nempe Es. LXVI, 17. ubi sic habet Arabs interpres, الذين ياكلون لحم الخنازير والرذالات واليربوع Qui comedunt carnem porcinam, et abominationes, et Aljarbua, id est, speciem pro genere. Nam Hebraea habent והעכבר, et murem. Sed Arabi causa non defuit, cur redderet اليربوع aljarbua. Iam enim docuimus, in toto murium genere hunc solum apud Arabes edulem esse. Praeterea, quamvis עכבר achbar Hebraeis murem in genere significet, tamen Arabice haec ipsa vox عكبر achbar in Plurali عكابر achabiro, significat marem اليربوع aljarbui. Alcamus, العكابر ذكور من اليرابيع Alachabiro, mares Aljarabii: quod jam diximus Plurale esse vocis اليربوع aljarbuo. Itaque cum اليربوع sit speciei nomen العكبر alachbar marem significat, ut العطيوطة alatiuta foeminam. Alcamus, العطيوطة اليربوع الانثي Alatiuta, Aljarbuo foemina. Teixeira Lusitanus appellat ratones del mato, id est, mures dumeti, et his verbis describit Indici itinerarii capite quarto, Son estos ratones del grandor de los grandes nuestros communes, tienen el pelo pardo tirante à blanco. Tienen de raton las orejas, manos, y la cola: cuya punta, y los ojos, y cabeça, son de conejo; y las piernas como de gazela. Corren mucho saltando, hazen cueua como conejo. Y ay dellos grande quantidad II, 427 por aquel de sierto. Los Arabes los comen, y dizen, que son muy buenos. Id est, Sunt isti mures vulgarium maximis mole pares, coloris leucophaei. Muris habent auriculas, pedes anteriores, et caudam: cujus acumen, oculi et caput sunt cuniculi; et pernae (id est, crura posteriora) capreae. Saltando plerumque currunt, et cuniculos agunt quomodo cuniculi. Horum in illo deserto (in Arabiae parte, Babyloniae vicina) maxima est copia. Arabes in cibis usurpant, et optimi saporis esse asserunt. Quibus verbis omnino describitur aljarbuo, quod nemo non fatebitur. De eodem sic Olearius libri sexti Itinerarii Persici pagina sexagesima quarta, Vidimus prope Terkin (in Circassia) muris agrestis genus, Arabice IERBUA dicti. Huic sciuri magnitudo est, neque forma dissimilis; pilus tamen fuscior; et caput muris; aures longae; crura anterius brevia, posterius longiora. Proinde non nisi in ascensu currunt; in planis fere reptitant, aut saltu supra terram ad quinque, vel sex pedes efferuntur. Cauda longa, dorso incumbens, in caule glabra, in vertice hirta et albicans. Multos videre eodem impetu sursum prosilientes jucundum erat spectaculum. Babyloniam et Arabiam his scatere ajunt, et incolis esse pro cibo. Sunt, qui ex agris in domos se conferunt, et pecuniam suffurantur.

The aljarbuo is also said to devise another stratagem. Its windows, or rather its holes, it sometimes covers over with earth at the very surface, so that they may not be visible from outside R10. In Arabic this is called دم [damma] damma. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: دم اليربوع حجره غطاه وسواه [damma al-yarbūʿ juḥrahu ghaṭṭāhu wa-sawwāhu] Damma aljarbuo its hiding place, that is, it covered it and levelled it. Hence the hiding place also has the name دممة [dumama] dumama. The same Alcamus: الدممة حجرة اليربوع وتراب يجمعه اليربوع ويخرجه من الحجر فيسوي به بابه [al-dumama juḥrat al-yarbūʿ wa-turāb yajmaʿuhu al-yarbūʿ wa-yukhrijuhu min al-juḥr fa-yusawwī bihi bābahu] Dumama is the hiding place of the aljarbuo, and the earth which it gathers and digs out of its hiding place in order to level its entrance with it. Accordingly, since the hole of its hiding place, covered with earth, is called نافقا [nāfiqā] naphika, by a metaphor taken from this نافق [nāfaqa] naphaka, a verb of the third conjugation, means to dissemble in religion, and to profess one thing with the mouth while keeping another hidden in the mind. And منافق [munāfiq] munaphik is a hypocrite. Damir: ظاهر بيته تراب وباطنه حفر وكذلك المنافق ظاهره ايمان وباطنه كفر [ẓāhir baytihi turāb wa-bāṭinuhu ḥafr wa-ka-dhālika al-munāfiq ẓāhiruhu īmān wa-bāṭinuhu kufr] The outer part of its house is earth, but the inner part is hollow. Likewise the hypocrite has faith on the outside, but unbelief on the inside. Algiahid and others: واسم المنافق لم يكن في الجاهلية لكن لمن اسر الكفر واظهر الايمان [wa-ism al-munāfiq lam yakun fī al-jāhiliyya lākin li-man asarra al-kufr wa-aẓhara al-īmān] The name munaphik will not be found in heathendom, but (it is said) of him who conceals unbelief and displays faith. Albazi: تعالي اشتق له هذا الاسم من هذا الاصل وهو من نافقا اليربوع لانه لما ابطن الكفر [taʿālā ishtaqqa lahu hādhā al-ism min hādhā al-aṣl wa-huwa min nāfiqā al-yarbūʿ li-annahu lammā abṭana al-kufr] col. 1013 واظهر الايمان [wa-aẓhara al-īmān] God Most High derived the name of the hypocrite from this root, namely from naphika, or the hole of the mouse called aljarbuo; because within there is unbelief, and without, faith. These and many other things the Arabs say on Azoara 73 of the Qur'an, which is entitled المنافقون [al-munāfiqūn] The Hypocrites. In Alcamus the nest of this animal is called لغز [lughz] II, 424 logoz, as if you were to say labyrinth, because in nests of this kind the passages are winding and very intricate. And accordingly in Arabic الغاز [alghāz] algaz is the term for طرق تلطوي وتشكل علي مسالكها [ṭuruq talṭawī wa-tushkilu ʿalā masālikihā] paths that are twisted and entangled in their course. To this kind of mouse must be referred what Synesius says of a certain commander John near the end of Epistle 104: Δίκην ἀρουραίου μυὸς ἐνεδεδύκει τῇ πέτρᾳ [dikēn arouraiou myos enededykei tē petra], Like a field mouse he had hidden himself in the rock, that is, in Bombaea, a very strongly fortified stronghold in the hollow of a cliff. For no other field mice nest in rock except the aljarbuo alone R11. This is proved by these words of Ibnolgiauzi: اليربوع لا يتخذ بيته الا في موضع صلب مرتفع ليسلم من سيل او حافر ثم لا يجعلة الا عند اكمة او شجرة او صخرة ليلا يضل اذا عاد اليه [al-yarbūʿ lā yattakhidhu baytahu illā fī mawḍiʿ ṣulb murtafiʿ li-yaslama min sayl aw ḥāfir thumma lā yajʿaluhu illā ʿinda akama aw shajara aw ṣakhra li-allā yaḍilla idhā ʿāda ilayhi] The aljarbuo makes its home only in a hard (that is, rocky) and elevated place, so that it may be safe from the inflow of water and from the hoof (of horses). Nor does it set it anywhere but by mounds, or trees, or rocks, lest it go astray when it returns to it. This happens above all to the young of this little animal. Hence the proverb in Damir: اضل من ولد اليربوع [aḍallu min walad al-yarbūʿ] More astray than the young of the aljarbuo, said of one who wanders about and never sets his foot firmly anywhere. In the same place: وفي طباعه انه اذا مشي في ارض سهلة او لينة مشي علي موخر كفه حتي لا يعرف اثر وطيه كما يفعل الارنب [wa-fī ṭibāʿihi annahu idhā mashā fī arḍ sahla aw layyina mashā ʿalā muʾakhkhar kaffihi ḥattā lā yuʿrafa athar waṭʾihi kamā yafʿalu al-arnab] It is also in its nature that, when it walks on soft and yielding ground, it stands on the tips of its feet, so that its tracks may not be recognized in the places it has trodden: which is also the habit of the hare. Likewise: وهو [wa-huwa] II, 425 يجتر ويبعر وله كرش واسنان واضراس من الفك الاعلي والاسفلي [yajtarru wa-yabʿaru wa-lahu karish wa-asnān wa-aḍrās min al-fakk al-aʿlā wa-al-asfalī] It also ruminates, and voids dung, and has a crop (in the manner of ruminants); although it has teeth and molars both in the upper and in the lower jaw. Peculiar to this same mouse is that it leaps. The Arabs express this by the verb بحظل [baḥẓala] bachdala, which is entirely proper to it. Alcamus: بحظل قفز قفزان اليربوع [baḥẓala qafaza qafazān al-yarbūʿ] Bachdala: he leapt with the leap of the aljarbuo. So also Giauhari. This very thing Theophrastus observed above of those mice that walk on two feet: Ὅταν δὲ διώκωνται, πηδῶσι [hotan de diōkōntai, pēdōsi]· If anyone pursues them, they leap. In its burrows a kind of snake nests, which the Arabs call جنادع [janādiʿ] gianadio, or جنادب [janādib] gianadibo. Alcamus: الجنادع الاجناش اوجنادب تكون في حجرة اليرابيع [al-janādiʿ al-ajnāsh aw janādib takūnu fī juḥrat al-yarābīʿ] Algianadio, (a kind of) serpents, or gianadibo: these are in the nest of the aljarabii col. 1014, which is the plural of the word اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo. If the aljarbuo mates with the common mouse, the hybrid mouse born of it is called فرنب [farnab] pharnab, or phirnib. Alcamus: الفرنب الفارة او ولدها من اليربوع [al-farnab al-fāra aw waladuhā min al-yarbūʿ] Alpharnab (or alphirnib) is the mouse, or its offspring by the aljarbuo. This too is peculiar to it, that the aljarbuo is eaten by the Arabs, whereas otherwise the eating of mice is forbidden to them. Damir, in the chapter الفار [al-fār] alphar, that is, On the mouse: يحرم اكل جميع انواع الفار الا اليربوع [yaḥrumu akl jamīʿ anwāʿ al-fār illā al-yarbūʿ] The eating of all species of mouse is forbidden, except the aljarbuo. There is, however, some disagreement among the Arabs on this matter. For according to the opinion of Abuchanipha: لا يوكل لانه من الحشرات [lā yuʾkalu li-annahu min al-ḥasharāt] It (the aljarbuo) is not eaten, because it is one of the subterranean animals. And Algazali, in the book entitled الوسيط [al-Wasīṭ] The Mediator, denies that anything should be eaten من الحشرات الا الضب [min al-ḥasharāt illā al-ḍabb] of the subterranean animals except the land crocodile. Yet others further except اليربوع وابن عرس وام حبين والقنفد والدلدل [al-yarbūʿ wa-ibn ʿirs wa-umm ḥubayn wa-al-qunfud wa-al-duldul] the aljarbuo, and the weasel, and the chameleon, and the hedgehog, and the porcupine. Hence Damir on the aljarbuo: يحل اكله لان العرب تستطيبه وتحله [yaḥillu akluhu li-anna al-ʿArab tastaṭībuhu wa-tuḥilluhu] Its eating is permitted, because the Arabs allow it and delight in it. So indeed the great canonists of the Arabs decide: Ata, and Achmed Ben-Hantal, and Ibnolmandsar, and Abutsaur, etc. Accordingly not only the aljarbuo but also its burrow is bought, that is, the right of searching and probing it so that this animal may be caught in it. Since this, however, usually meets with little success, it has passed into a proverb among the Arabs: as when they say كالمشتري القاصعا باليربوع [ka-al-mushtarī al-qāṣiʿā bi-al-yarbūʿ] Like one who buys, in place of II, 426 the aljarbuo, its hole. This proverb يضرب الذي يدع العين ويتبع الاثر [yuḍrabu alladhī yadaʿu al-ʿayn wa-yatbaʿu al-athar] is aimed at him who leaves the spring and follows only the track. In Greek you would say Σκιὰν ἀντὶ τοῦ σώματος [skian anti tou sōmatos], The shadow instead of the body. Here too the Arabs are fastidious, and prefer the Supharian to the other mice of this kind, which Alcamus describes thus: يربوع شفاري ضخم الاذنين وطويلهما العاري البراثين ولا يلحق سريعا والطويل والغوايم الرخو اللحم الدسم [yarbūʿ shafārī ḍakhm al-udhunayn wa-ṭawīluhumā al-ʿārī al-barāthīn wa-lā yulḥaqu sarīʿan wa-al-ṭawīl wa-al-ghawāyim al-rikhw al-laḥm al-dasim] The Supharian jarbuo has thick and long ears, is bare of claws, so that it does not easily grip, has long feet, and tender and fat flesh. In Abenbitar: يربوع الاسراييلي لحم اليربوع يقد وغذا كثير ويلين البطن [yarbūʿ al-isrāyīlī laḥm al-yarbūʿ yuqaddu wa-ghadhā kathīr wa-yulayyinu al-baṭn] The Israelite jarbuo is the name for the flesh of the aljarbuo that is dried. It is very nourishing and loosens the bowels. To dry in Arabic is قد [qadda] kadda, which properly col. 1015 means to expose to the wind meat cut lengthwise, as we do with smoke, so that the moisture may be drawn off. Hence قداد [qaddād] kedad is the name both of the hedgehog and of the aljarbuo, because both animals are dried in this way. Alkamus: القداد القنفد واليربوع [al-qaddād al-qunfud wa-al-yarbūʿ] Alkedado: the hedgehog and the aljarbuo. In the Arabic versions of the Sacred Text the word aljarbuo occurs only once in all, namely at Es. LXVI, 17, where the Arabic translator has: الذين ياكلون لحم الخنازير والرذالات واليربوع [alladhīna yaʾkulūna laḥm al-khanāzīr wa-al-radhālāt wa-al-yarbūʿ] Who eat the flesh of swine, and abominations, and the aljarbua, that is, the species for the genus. For the Hebrew has והעכבר, and the mouse. But the Arab did not lack a reason for rendering it اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbua. For we have already shown that among the Arabs, in the whole genus of mice, this one alone is edible. Moreover, although עכבר achbar means mouse in general for the Hebrews, yet in Arabic this very word عكبر [ʿakbar] achbar, in the plural عكابر [ʿakābir] achabiro, means the male of اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] the aljarbuo. Alcamus: العكابر ذكور من اليرابيع [al-ʿakābir dhukūr min al-yarābīʿ] Alachabiro: the males of the aljarabii, which, as we have already said, is the plural of the word اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo. Thus, since اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] is the name of the species, العكبر [al-ʿakbar] alachbar denotes the male, as العطيوطة [al-ʿaṭyūṭa] alatiuta denotes the female. Alcamus: العطيوطة اليربوع الانثي [al-ʿaṭyūṭa al-yarbūʿ al-unthā] Alatiuta: the female aljarbuo. The Portuguese Teixeira [=Pedro Teixeira, Relaciones (1610)] calls them ratones del mato, that is, mice of the thicket, and describes them in these words in chapter 4 of his Indian Itinerary: Son estos ratones del grandor de los grandes nuestros communes, tienen el pelo pardo tirante à blanco. Tienen de raton las orejas, manos, y la cola: cuya punta, y los ojos, y cabeça, son de conejo; y las piernas como de gazela. Corren mucho saltando, hazen cueua como conejo. Y ay dellos grande quantidad II, 427 por aquel de sierto. Los Arabes los comen, y dizen, que son muy buenos. That is: These mice are equal in size to the largest of the common ones, and of a whitish-grey colour. They have the ears, forefeet and tail of a mouse; the tip of the tail, the eyes and the head are those of a rabbit; and the haunches (that is, the hind legs) those of a roe deer. They mostly run by leaping, and dig burrows as rabbits do. In that desert (in the part of Arabia bordering on Babylonia) there is a very great abundance of them. The Arabs use them as food, and assert that they are of excellent flavour. In these words the aljarbuo is described in every respect, as no one will deny. Of the same animal Olearius [=Adam Olearius, travels in Persia] writes thus in book 6 of his Persian Itinerary, page 64: Near Terkin (in Circassia) we saw a kind of field mouse, called in Arabic IERBUA. It has the size of a squirrel, and a form not unlike it; but its fur is darker; and it has the head of a mouse; long ears; the front legs short, the hind legs longer. Hence they run only when going uphill; on level ground they mostly creep, or are carried by a leap above the ground for five or six feet. The tail is long, lying along the back, bare on the stem, hairy and whitish at the tip. It was a pleasant sight to see many of them springing upward at the same moment. They say that Babylonia and Arabia teem with them, and that they serve the inhabitants as food. There are some that come from the fields into houses and steal money.


His ita explicatis, tria sunt, quae lectori non oscitanti clara et manifesta fient. I. Murem illum, qui Arabice vocatur aljarbuo, eundem esse cum Herodoti, Aristotelis, Theophrasti, Plinii, Aeliani et Photii mure, qui pedum posteriorum longitudine et saltu insignis est. Nam in aljarbuo suo utrumque ob- col. 1016 servant Arabes. Bipedes quidem incedere non addunt; quia res est infrequentior. Fallitur enim Photius, qui pedibus anterioribus eos unquam niti negat. Quod apud Aelianum non refert Theophrastus, nec quisquam alius veterum. II. Hunc ipsum murem patet eundem esse cum Hieronymi arctomye. Naturam enim habet cum mure et urso communem, habitatque in cavernis petrarum, et terrae foveis, et in singulis saxis et collibus custodem habet in excubiis, cujus negligentia morte mulctatur. III. Denique اليربوع aljarbuo idem est animal cum Hebraeorum שפן saphan. Concurrunt enim omnes notae, nulla excepta. Quod probare est obvium. Primo enim neutrum est bisulcum. 2. Utrumque ruminat. 3. Utrumque edule est, quamvis immundum. 4. Utrumque gregarium. 5. Utrumque infirmum. 6. Utrumque domum habet in petra. 7. Aristoteles, Theophrastus, Plinius et alii scribunt, Aegyptium esse animal; et Hieronymus, magnam esse in Palaestina hujus generis abundantiam. Arabiam quoque eo scatere, Arabum scripta abunde docent, et Teixeira testis αὐτόπτης (12).

With these matters thus explained, there are three things that will become clear and evident to an attentive reader. I. The mouse called aljarbuo in Arabic is the same as the mouse of Herodotus, Aristotle, Theophrastus, Pliny, Aelian and Photius, which is remarkable for the length of its hind feet and for its leaping. For the Arabs observe col. 1016 both features in their aljarbuo. They do not, indeed, add that it walks on two feet, because this is a less frequent occurrence. Photius is mistaken when he denies that these mice ever rest on their forefeet. Theophrastus, as reported in Aelian, does not say this, nor does any other of the ancients. II. It is evident that this very mouse is the same as Jerome's arctomys. For it shares a nature with the mouse and the bear; it lives in caves in the rocks and in holes in the earth; and on each rock and hill it has a sentinel on watch, whose negligence is punished with death. III. Finally, اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo is the same animal as the Hebrews' שפן saphan. For all the marks agree, without exception. This is easy to prove. First, neither has a cloven hoof. 2. Both chew the cud. 3. Both are edible, though unclean. 4. Both are gregarious. 5. Both are feeble. 6. Both have their home in the rock. 7. Aristotle, Theophrastus, Pliny and others write that it is an Egyptian animal; and Jerome, that there is a great abundance of this kind in Eretz Yisrael. That Arabia too teems with it, the writings of the Arabs amply show, and Teixeira, an eyewitness, αὐτόπτης [autoptēs], attests it R12.


II, 428 Superest, ut varia hujus animalis nomina explicare conemur. Hebraice שפן saphan per Sin dici videtur pro ספן saphan, per Samech, tanquam a tegendo; quia latibuli sui foramina terra obtegit, ut abunde docuimus. Vel pro צפן tsaphan, per Tsade, tanquam a delitescendo; quia ibi sub terra latet, et ex hominum conspectu se subtrahit (13). Idem Arabice اليربوع aljarbuo, quasi quaternarius appellatur; quia domum sibi fodit في مهب الرياح الاربع ad flatus quatuor ventorum, ut didicimus ex Arabibus. Et Chaldaice טפזא taphza, a saltu. Murem enim esse ἁλτικὸν, e veteribus nos docent Theophrastus, Aelianus, Photius, e recentioribus Alcamus, Teixeira, Olearius. Syrum ܚܓܣ chagas factum suspicor ex Graeco χοιρογρύλλιος, per compendium ita scripto χγς. Vel ܚܓܣ chagas est claudum animal. Syris enim claudus tam ܚܓܝܣܐ chagisa dicitur, quam ܚܓܝܪܐ chagira. Claudicare porro videtur hoc animalculum propter pedum inaequalitatem. Dictus ille ipse mus χοιρογρύλλιος a porci sagina, aut specie. Nam compositae vocis etiam ultima pars porcum significat. Hesychius, Γρύλλιος· χοῖρος. Item, Γρυλλίων· ὁ χοῖ-ρος. Tale, quod ὕραξ, sus Aeolibus, a Nicandro pro mure usurpatur; quia mures παρεοίκασι χοίροις τῶ ῥάμφει, rostro porcos referunt, ut ibi habet Seholiastes. Et a Graeco ὕραξ deductum sorex. Cur Seniorum χοιρογρύλλιος Hieronymi aetate vocatus fuerit ἀρκτομῦς, abunde jam explicatum. Nec sine causa pro herinaceo est sumtus, si vere scribit Plinius, hoc muris genus herinacii pilum habere: Aegyptiis, inquit, muribus durus pilus sicut herinaceis; iidem bi-pedes ambulant ceu Alpini. Sed is videtur duas murium species sumsisse promiscue. Nam alii distinguunt inter mures δίποδας, et ἐχῖνας, vel ἐχινώδεις. Herodotus, Οἱ μὲν δίποδες καλέονται, οἱ δὲ ζεγέριες, οἱ δὲ ἐχῖνες· Alii quidem bipedes appellantur, alii zegeries, et alii echines, nempe ab asperitate pilorum echini instar. Aristoteles, Οἱ δὲ ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ μῦες σκληρὰν ἔχουσι τὴν τρίχα, ὥσπερ οἱ χερσαῖοι ἐχῖνοι. εἰσὶ δὲ καὶ ἕτεροι, οἳ βαδίζουσιν ἐπὶ τοῖς δυσὶ ποσί. Aegyptii mures duros habent pilos, ut herinacei terrestres. Sed et ibidem alii bi-pedes gradiuntur. Sed quo errore Plinius, eodem Scripturae interpretes murium II, 429 haec duo genera confudisse putaverim, et mures ἐχῖνας, vel ἐχινώδεις, herinaceos appellasse.

II, 428 It remains for us to try to explain the various names of this animal. In Hebrew it seems to be called שפן saphan, with Sin, for ספן saphan, with Samech, as if from covering, because it covers the openings of its hiding place with earth, as we have amply shown. Or for צפן tsaphan, with Tsade, as if from lying hidden, because it lies hidden there under the earth and withdraws itself from the sight of men R13. In Arabic the same animal is called اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo, as if "the fourfold one", because it digs its home في مهب الرياح الاربع [fī mahabb al-riyāḥ al-arbaʿ] toward the blowing of the four winds, as we have learned from the Arabs. And in Chaldee it is called טפזא taphza, from leaping. For that the mouse is ἁλτικὸν [haltikon], a leaper, we are taught among the ancients by Theophrastus, Aelian and Photius, and among the more recent writers by Alcamus, Teixeira and Olearius. The Syriac ܚܓܣ [חגס] chagas, I suspect, was formed from the Greek χοιρογρύλλιος [choirogryllios], written in abbreviated form thus: χγς [chgs]. Or ܚܓܣ [חגס] chagas means a lame animal. For among the Syrians a lame person is called both ܚܓܝܣܐ [חגיסא] chagisa and ܚܓܝܪܐ [חגירא] chagira. And this little animal seems to limp because of the inequality of its feet. That same mouse was called χοιρογρύλλιος [choirogryllios] from the fatness of a pig, or from its appearance. For the last part of the compound word also means pig. Hesychius: Γρύλλιος· χοῖρος [Gryllios; choiros]. Likewise: Γρυλλίων· ὁ χοῖρος [Grylliōn; ho choiros]. Similarly ὕραξ [hyrax], which is sus [pig] among the Aeolians, is used by Nicander for mouse, because mice παρεοίκασι χοίροις τῶ ῥάμφει [pareoikasi choirois tō rhamphei], resemble pigs in their snout, as the scholiast says there. And from the Greek ὕραξ [hyrax] comes sorex [shrew]. Why the χοιρογρύλλιος [choirogryllios] of the Elders was called ἀρκτομῦς [arktomys] in Jerome's time has already been amply explained. Nor was it without reason taken for the hedgehog, if Pliny writes truly that this kind of mouse has the bristles of a hedgehog: The Egyptian mice, he says, have hard hair like hedgehogs; they also walk on two feet, like the Alpine ones. But he seems to have taken two species of mice indiscriminately. For others distinguish between mice that are δίποδας [dipodas], two-footed, and those that are ἐχῖνας [echinas] or ἐχινώδεις [echinōdeis]. Herodotus: Οἱ μὲν δίποδες καλέονται, οἱ δὲ ζεγέριες, οἱ δὲ ἐχῖνες [Hoi men dipodes kaleontai, hoi de zegeries, hoi de echines]· Some are called two-footed, others zegeries, and others echines, namely from the roughness of their hair, like that of a hedgehog. Aristotle: Οἱ δὲ ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ μῦες σκληρὰν ἔχουσι τὴν τρίχα, ὥσπερ οἱ χερσαῖοι ἐχῖνοι. εἰσὶ δὲ καὶ ἕτεροι, οἳ βαδίζουσιν ἐπὶ τοῖς δυσὶ ποσί. [Hoi de en Aigyptō myes sklēran echousi tēn tricha, hōsper hoi chersaioi echinoi. eisi de kai heteroi, hoi badizousin epi tois dysi posi.] The Egyptian mice have hard hair, like land hedgehogs. But there are also others there that walk on two feet. I would suppose, however, that the interpreters of Scripture fell into the same error as Pliny and confused II, 429 these two kinds of mice, and called the mice that are ἐχῖνας [echinas] or ἐχινώδεις [echinōdeis] hedgehogs.


Notandum quoque, Iudaeorum שפנים sephanim, id est, χοιρογρυλλίους, vel ἀρκτομῦας, si mavis, quaedam habere communia cum Hispaniae cuniculis; oculos scilicet, et caput, et imam caudam, ut a Teixeira observatur: et quod col. 1017 posteriores pedes prioribus sunt longiores, quodque subsultim gradiuntur, et pariter ruminant, quamvis utrimque dentati, et subterranea sibi latibula defodiunt, in quibus interdiu latent. Itaque ut Hebraei hodie, ita Poeni videntur olim Hebraeum nomen שפן saphan cuniculis indidisse, atque inde esse, quod Hispania שפניה, Σπάνια, id est, cuniculosa dicta est, ut in Catullo Celtiberia, quod jam supra c) monuimus. Aliorum tamen esto judicium.

It should also be noted that the שפנים sephanim of the Jews, that is, χοιρογρυλλίους [choirogryllious], or ἀρκτομῦας [arktomyas] if you prefer, have certain features in common with the rabbits of Spain: namely the eyes, the head and the tip of the tail, as Teixeira observes. Moreover, col. 1017 their hind feet are longer than their fore feet, they move by leaping, and they likewise ruminate, although they have teeth in both jaws, and they dig themselves underground hiding places in which they lie hidden by day. Therefore, as the Jews do today, so the Carthaginians seem once to have given the Hebrew name שפן saphan to rabbits; and hence it is that Spain was called שפניה, Σπάνια [Spania], that is, cuniculosa [full of rabbits], as Celtiberia is in Catullus, which we have already pointed out above c). Let others, however, be the judges of this.

(3) Rosenmüller, II, 414 In hoc erravit haud dubie Stumpfius. Marmottam enim animal esse, Sabaudicis, Helveticis, Pyrenaicis alpibus prorsus peculiare, sciunt omnes. Vid. Bruce p. 151. 4. Utrumque gregarium, Bruce p. 146. conf. Prov. XXX, 26. 5. Utrumque infirmum, Prov. l. c. 6. Utrumque domum habet in petra, Shaw. p. 301. Bruce p. 146. cf. Ps. CIV, 18. 7. Utrumque in Syria et Palaestina frequens, testibus iisdem illis peregrinatoribus. Quae singula tamen deprehendemus etiam in Mure iaculo, Arabum يربوع, de quo multa Bochartus in iis, quae sequuntur.

R3 Rosenmüller, II, 414 In this Stumpf undoubtedly erred. For everyone knows that the marmot is an animal peculiar to the Savoyard, Swiss and Pyrenean Alps. Nor has any of those who have visited the regions of the East found that animal there. But the animals that Stumpf thinks are like Alpine mice in Egypt seem to be the Syrian hyraces or sorices, the ἔχινοι χερσαῖοι [echinoi chersaioi] of Aelian (book 3, ch. 10, where their foresight and skill in storing away food are recounted; cf. Bochart below, p. 1008. 3, and p. 1016), in which we find everything that the Arabs relate of the وبر [wabr]. The animal has the size of a marmot, but a more elongated body; the back is marked with bristles projecting from the ridge (from which the Greeks undoubtedly gave it the name ἐχῖνος [echinos]); it is dark above and whitish below; the snout is oblong; the claws very short; there is no tail; its gait is creeping, its diet vegetable; it lives in the hollows of rocks. See Schreber, Mammalia 4, pl. 211. B. Shaw [=Thomas Shaw, Travels (1738)] described this animal under the name of lamb of Israel (see Bochart above) (Travels p. 301, German trans., where, however, Daman Israel is wrongly written for Ganam Israel غنم اسرايل [ghanam isrāyl], an error that has crept into many other books); he found the animal frequent on Mount Lebanon and in other places of Syria. It was also known to Prosper Alpinus, who mentioned a certain low animal, not unlike a rabbit, which they call the lamb of Israel, in Hist. Nat. Aegypti vol. 1, ch. 20, p. 80, and book 4, ch. 9. Shaw, loc. cit., was the first to contend that the Hebrew name of this Syrian hyrax was שפן. He has recently found an ally in Bruce, Travels vol. 5, p. 149, Leipzig trans., who carefully describes this animal, which he saw frequently not only in Syria but also in Ethiopia, under the name Aschkoko, by which it is known among the Amharas, from the bristles projecting from the ridge of its back like thorns (for the Amharic Aschok means thorn: see Ludolf [=Hiob Ludolf, Historia Aethiopica (1681) and its Commentarius (1691)], Lexic. Amhar. [=Hiob Ludolf, Lexicon Amharico-Latinum (1698)] p. 58). He also gave an illustration of it, plate 29. And it must be admitted that everything we read in the Hebrew text about the שפן is found in the Syrian hyrax, the وبر [wabr]. First, neither is cloven-footed. 2. Both chew the cud; Bruce, l. p. 148, attests that he observed this in the Aschkoko, that is, a hyrax, which he kept at home; cf. Lev 11:5 and Deut 14:7 3. Both are edible, though unclean: the flesh of the Syrian hyrax is eaten by those Arabs who live on Lebanon and in Arabia Petraea (see the words of Mavardius quoted by Bochart above), although the other Muslims and the Abyssinian Christians abstain from it as from an unclean food. See Bruce p. 151. 4. Both are gregarious, Bruce p. 146; cf. Prov 30:26 5. Both are feeble, Prov. loc. cit. 6. Both have their home in the rock, Shaw p. 301, Bruce p. 146; cf. Ps 104:18 7. Both are frequent in Syria and Eretz Yisrael, on the testimony of those same travellers. Yet we shall find every one of these points in the jerboa (mus iaculus) as well, the يربوع [yarbūʿ] of the Arabs, about which Bochart says much in what follows.

Book 3, chapter 34: The common mouse

II, 429 col. 1017 CAP. XXXIV.

II, 429 col. 1017 Chapter 34.


De vulgari Mure.

On the Common Mouse.


Hebraei murem עכבר achbar appellant, voce fortasse Chaldaea magis, quaeque proprie murem agrestem sonat. Videtur enim עכבר achbar dici pro עכלבר achalbar, eliso L: ut in vocibus Babel pro Balbel, et Samuel pro שאול-מאל Saul-meel, quasi petitum a Deo dicas. Nempe Chaldaeis עכל achal est consumere; et בר bar est ager: itaque עכלבר achalbar, et per contractionem עכבר achbar est agri consumtor, seu vastator (1). Nomen agresti muri valde congruum, qui agrorum est certa pestis. Aristoteles Hist. lib. 6. cap. 37. Ἀπορεῖται δὲ καὶ ἡ τῶν ἐπιπολαζόντων μυῶν γένεσις ἐν ταῖς χώραις, καὶ ἡ φορά. πολλα-χοῦ γὰρ εἴωθε γίνεσθαι πλῆθος ἀμύθητον τῶν ἀρουραίων, ὥστε ὀλίγον λείπε-θαι τοῦ σίτου παντός. γίνεται δὲ οὕτω ταχεῖα ἡ φορὰ, ὥστε ἔνιοι τῶν μὴ μεγά-λας γεωργίας ἐργαζομένων, τῇ προτέρᾳ ἰδόντες ὅτι θερίζειν ὥρα, τῇ ὑστεραίᾳ ἕωθεν ἄγοντες τοὺς θεριστὰς, καταβεβρωμένα ἅπαντα καταλαμβάνουσιν. In quaestionem etiam vocatur murium in agris emergentium generatio et proventus. II, 430 Saepe enim exoritur agrestium murium tanta vis, ut relinquatur parum frumenti. Et illorum proventus tam est subitus, ut nonnulli eorum, qui non multum agrum araverunt, cum pridie metere statuerint, postridie mane messores adducentes, se- getes omnes absumtas deprehendant. Hinc Plinius de prodigiosa murium foecunditate loquutus lib. 10. cap. 65. Itaque, inquit, desinit mirum esse, unde vis tanta messes populetur murium agrestium. Et apud Horum lib. I. cap. 47. Aegyptii, ἀφανισμὸν δηλοῦντες, μῦν ζωγραφοῦσιν, ἐπειδὴ πάντα ἐσθίων μιαίνει καὶ ἀχρη-στοῖ, destructionem significantes, murem pingunt, quia omnia consumens inquinat et deperdit.

The Hebrews call the mouse עכבר achbar, a word that is perhaps rather Chaldee, and which properly means field mouse. For עכבר achbar seems to be said for עכלבר achalbar, with the L elided, as in the words Babel for Balbel, and Samuel for שאול-מאל Saul-meel, as if you were to say asked of God. For in Chaldee עכל achal is to consume; and בר bar is field: therefore עכלבר achalbar, and by contraction עכבר achbar, is consumer or devastator of the field R1. The name fits the field mouse very well, which is a sure plague of the fields. Aristotle, Hist. book 6, ch. 37: Ἀπορεῖται δὲ καὶ ἡ τῶν ἐπιπολαζόντων μυῶν γένεσις ἐν ταῖς χώραις, καὶ ἡ φορά. πολλαχοῦ γὰρ εἴωθε γίνεσθαι πλῆθος ἀμύθητον τῶν ἀρουραίων, ὥστε ὀλίγον λείπεθαι τοῦ σίτου παντός. γίνεται δὲ οὕτω ταχεῖα ἡ φορὰ, ὥστε ἔνιοι τῶν μὴ μεγάλας γεωργίας ἐργαζομένων, τῇ προτέρᾳ ἰδόντες ὅτι θερίζειν ὥρα, τῇ ὑστεραίᾳ ἕωθεν ἄγοντες τοὺς θεριστὰς, καταβεβρωμένα ἅπαντα καταλαμβάνουσιν. [Aporeitai de kai hē tōn epipolazontōn myōn genesis en tais chōrais, kai hē phora. pollachou gar eiōthe ginesthai plēthos amythēton tōn arouraiōn, hōste oligon leipethai tou sitou pantos. ginetai de houtō tacheia hē phora, hōste enioi tōn mē megalas geōrgias ergazomenōn, tē protera idontes hoti therizein hōra, tē hysteraia heōthen agontes tous theristas, katabebrōmena hapanta katalambanousin.] The generation and increase of the mice that appear in the fields is also called into question. II, 430 For often so great a multitude of field mice arises that little grain is left. And their increase is so sudden that some of those who have not ploughed much land, having decided the day before to reap, on bringing the reapers early the next morning find all the crops consumed. Hence Pliny, having spoken of the prodigious fertility of mice, book 10, ch. 65, says: And so it ceases to be a wonder whence so great a multitude of field mice ravages the harvests. And in Horus, book 1, ch. 47: the Egyptians, ἀφανισμὸν δηλοῦντες, μῦν ζωγραφοῦσιν, ἐπειδὴ πάντα ἐσθίων μιαίνει καὶ ἀχρηστοῖ [aphanismon dēlountes, myn zōgraphousin, epeidē panta esthiōn miainei kai achrēstoi], signifying destruction, paint a mouse, because in consuming everything it defiles and ruins it.


Exempla sunt passim obvia. Sic 1 Sam. V, 6. in Graeca versione scribitur de iis Philistaeis, qui captivam arcam tenebant: Μέσον τῆς χώρας αὐτῆς ἀνε-φύησαν μύες. Et in Vulgata, Et ebullierunt villae et agri in medio regionis illius, et nati sunt mures. Et cap. VI, 1. rursus in Graeca, Καὶ ἐξέζεσεν ἡ γῆ αὐτῶν col. 1018 μύας. Et terra eorum mures ebulliit. Quae quidem sunt Glossemata: cum neque Hebraea origo, neque reliquae versiones, Chaldaea, inquam, Syra et Ara- bica, tale quidquam agnoscant. Tamen res in se vera est. Nam ejusdem sexti capitis versu quinto etiam Hebraea habent, Facietis, etc. צלמי עכבריכם המשחיתים את הארץ, imagines murium vestrorum, qui vastant terram مثال الجرذان التي تسلطت علي الارض لتفسدها Imagines murium (2), qui terrae incumbunt, ut eam vastent, ut habet Arabs interpres. Proinde merito Iosephus Antiquitatum lib. 6. capite 1. Τὰ δὲ ἐπὶ τῆς χώρας μυῶν πλῆθος, ἀνελθὸν ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς, κατέβλαψε, μήτε φυτῶν, μήτε καρπῶν ἀποσχόμενον· Quae autem in regione erant murium copia, e terra emergens, de- vastabat, neque stirpibus, neque fructibus parcens. Et Philastrius in Musoritis, Cum fuisset capta arca Testamenti ab Allophylis, atque ex ira Dei produxisset ter- ra sorices, ut eorum fruges deperirent. Et Maginus in Palaestina sua, Nonnul- lis in locis Palaestinae agri sunt pene deserti ob murium et soricum abundantiam, quos nisi quaedam aves devorarent, nullam sementem facere possent incolae (3).

Examples are met with everywhere. Thus at 1 Sam 5:6 in the Greek version it is written of those Philistines who held the captured ark: Μέσον τῆς χώρας αὐτῆς ἀνεφύησαν μύες [Meson tēs chōras autēs anephyēsan myes]. And in the Vulgate: And the villages and fields in the midst of that region boiled up, and mice were born. And again at ch. VI, 1. in the Greek: Καὶ ἐξέζεσεν ἡ γῆ αὐτῶν col. 1018 μύας [Kai exezesen hē gē autōn myas]. And their land boiled up with mice. These are indeed glosses, since neither the Hebrew original nor the other versions, the Chaldee, I mean, the Syriac and the Arabic, recognize anything of the kind. Yet the thing is true in itself. For in verse five of the same sixth chapter the Hebrew too has: You shall make, etc. צלמי עכבריכם המשחיתים את הארץ, images of your mice that ravage the land; مثال الجرذان التي تسلطت علي الارض لتفسدها [mithāl al-jirdhān allatī tasallaṭat ʿalī al-arḍ li-tufsidahā], images of the mice R2 that fall upon the land to ravage it, as the Arabic translator has it. Accordingly Josephus, Antiquities book 6, chapter 1, rightly says: Τὰ δὲ ἐπὶ τῆς χώρας μυῶν πλῆθος, ἀνελθὸν ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς, κατέβλαψε, μήτε φυτῶν, μήτε καρπῶν ἀποσχόμενον· [Ta de epi tēs chōras myōn plēthos, anelthon apo tēs gēs, keteblapse, mēte phytōn, mēte karpōn aposchomenon] And a multitude of mice, emerging from the earth, laid waste what was in the region, sparing neither plants nor fruits. And Philastrius, on the Musorites: When the ark of the Covenant had been captured by the Allophyli, and the earth, through the wrath of God, had produced shrews, so that their crops perished. And Maginus in his Palestine: In some places of Palestine the fields are almost deserted because of the abundance of mice and shrews, so that, if certain birds did not devour them, the inhabitants could make no sowing R3.


II, 431 Quod malum ne quis putet esse Palaestinae peculiare, Strabo lib. 3. etiam in Hispania nonnunquam increbuisse memorat μυῶν πλῆθος, ἀφ᾽ οὗ καὶ λοιμι-καὶ νόσοι πολλάκις ἠκολούθησαν, murium copiam, quam saepe pestifera lues subsequuta sit. Et in Cantabria Romani, pretio dato, μυοθηροῦντες πρὸς μέτρον ἀποδειχθὲν διεσώζοντο μόλις, mures ad certam mensuram venantes vix servabantur. Nec desunt, qui de Italia idem referant. Diodorus lib. 3. Περὶ τὴν Ἰτα-λίαν μυῶν πλῆθος ἀρουραίων. ἐγγενηθὲν τοῖς πεδίοις, ἐξέβαλέ τινας τῆς πα-τρίου χώρας· Circa Italiam murium agrestium vis, ex agris emersa, quosdam e patrio solo pepulit. Quod ipsum in Aeliano est Historiae lib. 17. cap. 41. Et uterque sequitur Agatharchidem lib. 5. cap. 28. Porro Cosanos intelligi verissimile est; quia de Cosa canit Rutilius Rufus,

II, 431 Lest anyone think this evil peculiar to Eretz Yisrael, Strabo, book 3, records that in Spain too there has sometimes arisen μυῶν πλῆθος, ἀφ᾽ οὗ καὶ λοιμικαὶ νόσοι πολλάκις ἠκολούθησαν [myōn plēthos, aph᾽ hou kai loimikai nosoi pollakis ēkolouthēsan], a multitude of mice, which has often been followed by a pestilential plague. And in Cantabria the Romans, a reward being offered, μυοθηροῦντες πρὸς μέτρον ἀποδειχθὲν διεσώζοντο μόλις [myothērountes pros metron apodeichthen diesōzonto molis], hunting mice to a fixed measure, were scarcely saved. Nor are there lacking those who report the same of Italy. Diodorus, book 3: Περὶ τὴν Ἰταλίαν μυῶν πλῆθος ἀρουραίων. ἐγγενηθὲν τοῖς πεδίοις, ἐξέβαλέ τινας τῆς πατρίου χώρας· [Peri tēn Italian myōn plēthos arouraiōn. engenēthen tois pediois, exebale tinas tēs patriou chōras] Around Italy a multitude of field mice, having emerged from the fields, drove some people from their native soil. This very thing is in Aelian, History book 17, ch. 41. And both follow Agatharchides, book 5, ch. 28. Further, it is most likely that the people of Cosa are meant, because Rutilius Rufus sings of Cosa:


Dicuntur cives, quondam migrare coacti,
Muribus infestos deseruisse lares.

The citizens, it is said, once forced to emigrate, abandoned their homes, infested by mice.


Thraciae quoque Abderitis, qui, propter ranarum muriumque multitudinem relicto patriae solo, sedes quaerebant, Cassander agros in ultimis Macedoniae finibus assignavit, ut testatur Trogus, lib. 15. Chalcidenses itidem narrat Heraclides in Politiis Cleonas incoluisse, ἐν τῷ Ἄθῳ ἐξαναστάντας ἐξ Ἐλυμνίου ὑπὸ μυῶν, οἳ τὰ τ᾽ ἄλλα κατήθιον αὐτῶν, καὶ τὸν σίδηρον, Elymnio in Atho monte pulsos a muribus, qui cum alia devorabant, tum ipsum ferrum. Quod de Gyaro alii referunt. Plinius libri octavi capite vigesimo nono, M. Varro auctor est, etc. ex Gyaro, Cycladum insula, incolas a muribus fugatos. Et capite quinquagesimo septimo, Theophrastus auctor est, in Cyaro insula, cum incolas fugassent, ferrum quoque rosisse eos. Hinc Antigonus Mirabilium capite vigesimo primo, Τῆς δὲ Καρυστίας καὶ τῆς Ἀνδρίας χώρας ἐστὶν πλησίον νῆσος ἡ καλουμέ-νη Γύαρος· ἐνταῦθα οἱ μύες διατρώγουσι τὸν σίδηρον. Prope Carystiam et An-driam insula est nomine Gyarus, in qua mures ferrum exedunt. Et de eadem insula Stephanus Byzantius, Ἀντίγονος δ᾽ ὁ Καρύστιός φησι, ὅτι ἐν ταύτῃ οἱ μύες διατρώγουσι σίδηρον· Antigonus Carystius autem inquit, quod in hac insula mures II, 432 ferrum comedunt (4). Nec multo aliter Suidas. Mendose igitur Aristoteles in Mirabilibus [c. 24.], Ἐν Κύπρῳ τῇ νήσῳ λέγεται τοὺς μέτας τὸν σίδηρον ἐσθίειν· In Cypro insula metas ajunt ferrum devorare. Mendose etiam in Aeliano Historiae libri quinti capite decimo quarto, Ἐν τῇ Πάρῳ τῇ νήσῳ Ἀριστοτέλης λέγει μῦς εἶναι, καὶ μέν τοι καὶ γῆν σιτεῖσθαι τὴν σιδηρῶτιν· In Paro insula dicit Aristoteles mures esse, qui ferrariam terram exedant. Utrobique enim pro Κύπρῳ, vel Πάρῳ legendum Γυάρῳ· et in priore loco μύας pro μέτας, in posteriore τὴν σιδηρῖτιν. Quid quod Troadis incolae, quos Graeci decennali bello vix subegerunt, huic malo cedere coacti, patriam deseruerunt? Plinius libri decimi col. 1019 capite sexagesimo quinto, Plurimi mures ita ad Troadem proveniunt, et jam inde fugaverunt accolas. Et in Chrysa, Mysiae urbe, Crini sacerdoti infensus Apollo ἔπεμψεν αὐτοῦ τοῖς ἄγροις μύας, οἵτινες τοὺς καρποὺς ἐλυμαίνοντο, agris ipsius mures immisit, qui fructus deperdebant. Ita Homeri vetus Scholiastes ad vocem Σμινθεῦ libro primo Iliados. Quale est, quod tradit Aelianus Historiae libri duodecimi capite quinto, Τῶν Αἰολέων καὶ τῶν Τρώων τὰ λήϊα πολλὰς μυῶν μυριάδας ἐπελθούσας ἄωρα ὑποκείρειν, καὶ ἀτελῆ τὰ θέρη τοῖς σπείρα-σιν ὑποφαίνειν· Permultas olim murium myriades Aeolorum et Trojanorum segetes invasisse, atque immaturas succidisse, iisque, qui sementem fecissent, messem infructuosam reddidisse (5).

Likewise, to the Abderites of Thrace, who had left their native soil because of the multitude of frogs and mice and were seeking a place to settle, Cassander assigned lands in the farthest borders of Macedonia, as Trogus attests, book 15. Heraclides in the Politiae likewise relates that the Chalcidians settled in Cleonae, ἐν τῷ Ἄθῳ ἐξαναστάντας ἐξ Ἐλυμνίου ὑπὸ μυῶν, οἳ τὰ τ᾽ ἄλλα κατήθιον αὐτῶν, καὶ τὸν σίδηρον [en tō Athō exanastantas ex Elymniou hypo myōn, hoi ta t' alla katēthion autōn, kai ton sidēron], having been driven out of Elymnium on Mount Athos by mice, which devoured not only other things but even iron itself. Others report the same of Gyarus. Pliny, book 8, chapter 29: M. Varro is the authority, etc., that the inhabitants of Gyarus, an island of the Cyclades, were put to flight by mice. And in chapter 57: Theophrastus is the authority that on the island of Cyarus, after they had driven out the inhabitants, they gnawed even iron. Hence Antigonus, Mirabilia, chapter 21: Τῆς δὲ Καρυστίας καὶ τῆς Ἀνδρίας χώρας ἐστὶν πλησίον νῆσος ἡ καλουμένη Γύαρος· ἐνταῦθα οἱ μύες διατρώγουσι τὸν σίδηρον [Tēs de Karystias kai tēs Andrias chōras estin plēsion nēsos hē kaloumenē Gyaros; entautha hoi myes diatrōgousi ton sidēron]. Near Carystia and Andria there is an island named Gyarus, in which mice eat iron. And of the same island Stephanus of Byzantium: Ἀντίγονος δ᾽ ὁ Καρύστιός φησι, ὅτι ἐν ταύτῃ οἱ μύες διατρώγουσι σίδηρον [Antigonos d' ho Karystios phēsi, hoti en tautē hoi myes diatrōgousi sidēron]; and Antigonus of Carystus says that on this island mice II, 432 eat iron R4. Suidas says much the same. Thus the text of Aristotle in the Mirabilia [ch. 24] is corrupt: Ἐν Κύπρῳ τῇ νήσῳ λέγεται τοὺς μέτας τὸν σίδηρον ἐσθίειν [En Kyprō tē nēsō legetai tous metas ton sidēron esthiein]; On the island of Cyprus they say that the metae devour iron. Corrupt also is Aelian, History, book 5, chapter 14: Ἐν τῇ Πάρῳ τῇ νήσῳ Ἀριστοτέλης λέγει μῦς εἶναι, καὶ μέν τοι καὶ γῆν σιτεῖσθαι τὴν σιδηρῶτιν [En tē Parō tē nēsō Aristotelēs legei mys einai, kai men toi kai gēn siteisthai tēn sidērōtin]; Aristotle says that on the island of Paros there are mice which eat iron-bearing earth. For in both places, instead of Κύπρῳ [Kyprō] or Πάρῳ [Parō], one should read Γυάρῳ [Gyarō]; and in the former passage μύας [myas] instead of μέτας [metas], in the latter τὴν σιδηρῖτιν [tēn sidēritin]. What of the fact that the inhabitants of the Troad, whom the Greeks barely subdued in a ten-year war, were forced to yield to this plague and abandoned their homeland? Pliny, book 10, col. 1019 chapter 65: Very many mice thus spring up in the Troad, and they have already driven out the inhabitants from there. And at Chryse, a city of Mysia, Apollo, angered at the priest Crinis, ἔπεμψεν αὐτοῦ τοῖς ἄγροις μύας, οἵτινες τοὺς καρποὺς ἐλυμαίνοντο [epempsen autou tois agrois myas, hoitines tous karpous elymainonto], sent mice into his fields, which destroyed the crops. So the old Scholiast on Homer, on the word Σμινθεῦ [Smintheu] in book 1 of the Iliad. Of the same kind is what Aelian relates, History, book 12, chapter 5: Τῶν Αἰολέων καὶ τῶν Τρώων τὰ λήϊα πολλὰς μυῶν μυριάδας ἐπελθούσας ἄωρα ὑποκείρειν, καὶ ἀτελῆ τὰ θέρη τοῖς σπείρασιν ὑποφαίνειν [Tōn Aioleōn kai tōn Trōōn ta lēia pollas myōn myriadas epelthousas aōra hypokeirein, kai atelē ta therē tois speirasin hypophainein]; that once very many myriads of mice invaded the crops of the Aeolians and Trojans, cut them down unripe, and made the harvest fruitless for those who had sown R5.


Ex his abunde patet, muribus, iisque agrestibus, vix indi potuisse nomen aptius, quam ab agrorum vastatione. Itaque id proprie עכבר achbar, quod confirmat usus Arabum, quibus عكبر achbar non est mus quivis, sed muris agrestis species, nempe aljarbuo mas, ut supra a) docuimus. Proinde Esa. LXVI, 17. pro Hebraeo העכבר haachbar Arabs habet اليربوع aljarbuo, quasi haec duo fere sint synonyma. Atque hoc ipsum, quod Esaias ibi Iudaeis exprobrat, nonnullos eorum porcinam edere, et העכבר haachbar, suadet, עכבר esse murem agrestem, eumque اليربوع aljarbuo, quem solum comedi tradunt Arabes. Nam μύωξος, id est, glis, quem Hieronymus hic intelligit, non II, 433 censetur ab Arabibus in genere murium (6). Fateor quidem, in Historia Hebraica Templi secundi pag. 241. cum Hierosolymitani, a Romanis obsessi, comedisse leguntur נבלות הכלבים ועכברים, cadavera canum, et mures, domesticos necessario intelligi; quia in urbe, tam arcte obsessa, agrestes non erant obvii. Et in extrema fame in cibum admittere necesse erat, quidquid offerebatur. At Esaias agit de cibis, quos Iudaei sui temporis, in Dei legem rebelles, ultro sibi deligebant, neque ulla necessitate coacti. Murem porro domesticum nemo est qui in cibum expetat, cum aliae escae suppetant. Itaque in Esaia mures illi, qui in cibum erant, agrestes fuere, non domestici. Eodem facit, quod in Samuelis loco, quem citavimus, עכברים achbarim Philistaeorum agros devastant. Illud enim est murium agrestium proprium. Certum tamen est, posteriores Hebraeos עכבר achbar accipere pro mure quovis. Et potuit ipse Moses sic usurpare, latius accepta voce. Quod ut doceret Ionathan, Hebraeum העכבר haachbar sic παραφράζει Lev. XI, 29. ועכברא אוכמא וסמוקא וחיורא, id est, Achbar niger, rufus et albus: qui tres sunt murium colores. In his albus est rarissimus, non tamen ignotus Graecis. Aelianus Historiae lib. 12. cap. 5. ubi de templo Sminthii Apollinis in Troadis urbe Hamaxito: Ὑπὸ δὲ τῷ βωμῷ φω-λεύουσι λευκοὶ μῦες, Sub altari nidificant albi mures. Hi putantur omnium salacissimi: unde in proverbium abiit, Μῦς λευκὸς, ἐπὶ τῶν ἀκρατῶν περὶ τὰ Ἀφροδίσια· Mus albus, de iis, qui ad res venereas sunt maxime incontinentes. Vide Suidam, et quid ex Philemone habeat Aelianus Historiae libri duodecimi capite decimo.

From this it is abundantly clear that hardly any name could have been given more aptly to mice, and specifically field mice, than one taken from the laying waste of fields. Therefore עכבר achbar properly denotes this. This is confirmed by the usage of the Arabs, for whom عكبر [ʿkbr] achbar is not just any mouse, but a species of field mouse, namely the male aljarbuo, as we showed above a). Accordingly, at Esa. LXVI, 17, for the Hebrew העכבר haachbar the Arabic has اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo, as though these two were nearly synonyms. And the very thing with which Isaiah there reproaches the Jews, that some of them ate swine's flesh and העכבר haachbar, suggests that עכבר is a field mouse, and indeed the اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo, which alone, the Arabs report, is eaten. For the μύωξος [myōxos], that is, the glis [dormouse], which Jerome understands here, is not II, 433 reckoned by the Arabs among the mice R6. I admit, indeed, that in the Hebrew History of the Second Temple, p. 241, where the inhabitants of Jerusalem, besieged by the Romans, are said to have eaten נבלות הכלבים ועכברים, the carcasses of dogs, and mice, domestic mice must necessarily be understood, since in a city so closely besieged field mice were not at hand. And in extreme famine they had to accept as food whatever presented itself. But Isaiah is speaking of foods which the Jews of his time, in rebellion against God's law, chose for themselves of their own accord, under no compulsion of necessity. Moreover, no one seeks out the house mouse as food when other fare is available. Therefore in Isaiah the mice that were eaten were field mice, not house mice. The same point is supported by the fact that in the passage of Samuel we cited, the עכברים achbarim lay waste the fields of the Philistines. For that is characteristic of field mice. It is certain, however, that the later Hebrews take עכבר achbar for any mouse whatever. And Moses himself may have used it so, taking the word in a broader sense. To show this, Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] paraphrases the Hebrew העכבר haachbar at Lev 11:29 thus: ועכברא אוכמא וסמוקא וחיורא, that is, the black, red and white achbar: these are the three colours of mice. Of these the white is very rare, yet not unknown to the Greeks. Aelian, History book 12, ch. 5, on the temple of Apollo Smintheus in Hamaxitus, a city of the Troad: Ὑπὸ δὲ τῷ βωμῷ φωλεύουσι λευκοὶ μῦες [Hypo de tō bōmō phōleuousi leukoi myes], Under the altar white mice make their nests. These are thought the most lustful of all; hence the proverb, Μῦς λευκὸς, ἐπὶ τῶν ἀκρατῶν περὶ τὰ Ἀφροδίσια [Mys leukos, epi tōn akratōn peri ta Aphrodisia]· A white mouse, of those who are utterly incontinent in sexual matters. See Suidas, and what Aelian reports from Philemon, History, book 12, chapter 10.


Murem cur Lex pronunciet immundum esse animal, praeter causas, quae cuivis se offerunt, hae quoque afferuntur, quod inutile et noxium est, et typus eorum, qui dicunt,

As to why the Law declares the mouse an unclean animal, besides the reasons that occur to anyone, these too are offered: that it is useless and harmful, and a type of those who say,


Nos numerus sumus, et fruges consumere nati.

We are mere numbers, born to consume the fruits of the earth.


In Cyrillo contra Iulianum libro nono γαλῆ καὶ μῦς γράφουσί πως ἐφ᾽ ἑαυ- col. 1020 τοῖς τὰ δειλὰ, καὶ ἄνανδρα, καὶ ψοφώδη τῶν κλεπτῶν γένη, mustela et mus II, 434 furum referant timida, et imbellia genera, atque obstrepera. In quibus cum illud obstreperum sit plane extra rem, pro ψοφώδη legendum contendo ψοφοδεῆ, id est, ad omnem strepitum metuentia. Quo verbo utuntur Lucianus in Scytha, et Plutarchus in lib. De sanitate tuenda: sed et idem in lib. Utra anim. de chamaeleonte dicit, Ὑπὸ δέους ἄλλως τρέπεται, φύσει ψοφοδεὴς ὢν, καὶ δειλός· Prae timore in aliud mutatur, cum natura meticulosus sit et timidus. Hinc in Hesychio ψοφοδεὴς est δειλὸς, κενοφόβος, ὁ καὶ τοὺς ψόφους καὶ τὰ ἐλάχιστα φοβούμε-νος. Quod muri quam conveniat, Poeta eximius sic docet in Apologo de mure rustico et urbano Satyra 6. lib. 2.

In Cyril, Against Julian, book 9: γαλῆ καὶ μῦς γράφουσί πως ἐφ᾽ ἑαυτοῖς τὰ δειλὰ, καὶ ἄνανδρα, καὶ ψοφώδη τῶν κλεπτῶν γένη [galē kai mys graphousi pōs eph᾽ heautois ta deila, kai ananda, kai psophōdē tōn kleptōn genē], col. 1020 the weasel and the mouse II, 434 represent the timid, unwarlike and noisy kinds of thieves. Since noisy is here entirely beside the point, I maintain that for ψοφώδη [psophōdē] we should read ψοφοδεῆ [psophodeē], that is, afraid of every noise. This word is used by Lucian in the Scythian, and by Plutarch in the book On Preserving Health; and the same author in the book Utra anim. says of the chameleon: Ὑπὸ δέους ἄλλως τρέπεται, φύσει ψοφοδεὴς ὢν, καὶ δειλός [Hypo deous allōs trepetai, physei psophodeēs ōn, kai deilos]· From fear it changes into another colour, being by nature fearful and timid. Hence in Hesychius ψοφοδεὴς [psophodeēs] is δειλὸς, κενοφόβος, ὁ καὶ τοὺς ψόφους καὶ τὰ ἐλάχιστα φοβούμενος [deilos, kenophobos, ho kai tous psophous kai ta elachista phoboumenos]. How well this suits the mouse the excellent Poet shows in his fable of the country mouse and the town mouse, Satire 6, book 2:


Valvarum strepitus lectis excussit utrumque:
Currere per totum pavidi conclave, magisque
Exanimes trepidare, simul domus alta molossis
Personuit canibus. — — — —

The clatter of the doors shook both from their couches: in panic they ran through the whole room, and trembled the more, half dead, as soon as the lofty house rang with Molossian hounds. — — — —


Aliud Hebraei afferunt, nempe murinae carnis esum oblivionem inducere. Quod doctissimus Buxtorfius probat ex Avoda Zera cap. 3. (ubi tamen non reperio) et ex Beth Iacob fol. 181. ubi ad quaestionem, Cur canis dominum suum agnoscat, felis autem non agnoscat? respondetur, feles ideo esse obliviosos, quia comedunt mures, quorum caro, imo quorum arrosa, si comedantur, turbant cerebrum et memoriam. Unde elicitur haec conclusio, האוכל ממה שהעכבר אוכל משכח תלמודו האוכל עכבר עצמו לא כ״ש Comedens de eo, quod comedit mus, obliviscitur doctrinae suae: comedens ergo murem ipsum quanto magis?

The Hebrews offer another reason, namely that eating mouse flesh induces forgetfulness. The most learned Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum] proves this from Avoda Zera ch. 3 (where, however, I do not find it) and from Beth Iacob fol. 181, where to the question why a dog recognizes its master but a cat does not, the answer is given that cats are forgetful because they eat mice, whose flesh, and indeed whatever they have gnawed, if eaten, disturbs the brain and the memory. Hence this conclusion is drawn: האוכל ממה שהעכבר אוכל משכח תלמודו האוכל עכבר עצמו לא כ״ש He who eats of what a mouse has eaten forgets his learning: how much more, then, he who eats the mouse itself?


Sennacheribi cladem, quam angelo tribuunt Sacri Scriptores b), et Iosephus c) ex Beroso pesti, immissae divinitus, mirum, cur ad agrestes mures referant Aegyptii in Herodoto d), quos narrant τοῖσι ἐναντίοισι αὐτοῖσι ἐπιχυθέντας νυκτὸς, κατὰ μὲν φαγέειν τοὺς φαρετρεῶνας αὐτέων, κατὰ δὲ τὰ τόξα, πρὸς δὲ τῶν ἀσπίδων τὰ ὄχανα· ὥς τε τῇ ὑστεραίῃ φευγόντων σφέων, γυμνῶν ὅπλων, πεσέειν πολλούς· hostibus ipsis noctu circumfusos, illorum tum pharetras, tum arcus, tum scutorum ansas exedisse, ita, ut postridie, armis exuti, multis amissis, fugam fecerint. An huc facit, quod λοιμὸς lues, et λαμὰς mus in Hesychio, sunt voces ita vicinae, ut una potuerit pro altera usurpari, atque sic muribus tribui clades, a lue accepta? Utut sit, Cretensibus illis, qui Troadis urbem Hamaxitum condiderunt, tale quidpiam accidisse memoratur. Cum enim consultus II, 435 Apollo de loco condendae urbis, illam ibi condendam esse respondisset, ἔνθα ἂν αὐτοῖς οἱ γηγενεῖς πολεμήσωσι, ubi terrigenae iis bellum inferrent, intellexerunt, Haxamitum designari; quia, castris ibi positis, μυῶν ἄφατόν τι πλῆθος ἐφερπύσαν τά τε ὄχανα αὐτοῖς τῶν ἀσπίδων διέτραγε, καὶ τὰς τῶν τόξων νευρὰς διέφαγεν, murium immensa vis erumpens clypeorum rosit ansas, et arcuum nervos exedit. Ita Aelianus Historiae libri duodecimi capite quinto. Nec multo aliter Homeri vetus Scholiastes ad librum primum Iliados, Νυκτὸς ἐπιγενομένης, μῦες ἔκοψαν αὐτῶν τοὺς τελαμῶνας τῶν ὅπλων, Cum nox venisset, mures armorum lora ipsis absciderunt. Proinde apud Aristotelem, Rhetorices libri secundi capite vigesimo quarto, mures ideo laudat Polycrates, ὅτι ἐβοήθησαν διατραγόντες τὰς νευρὰς, quia (popularibus suis) opem tulerunt, cum hostilium arcuum nervos corroserunt. Et, apud Clementem in Protreptico, Polemo refert populos, Troadi vicinos, τοὺς ἐπιχωρίους μῦς, οὓς σμίνθους καλοῦ-σι θρησβεύειν, ὅτι τὰς νευρὰς τῶν πολεμίων διέτρωγον τῶν τόξων· colere mures illius loci, quos sminthos vocant, quoniam hostilium arcuum nervos arroserant. Quae cum iis simillima sint, quae de Assyriis referunt Aegyptii, illos Creticam hanc, aut Troicam, si mavis, historiam interpolasse putaverim.

The defeat of Sennacherib, which the sacred writers ascribe to an angel b), and Josephus c), following Berosus, to a plague sent by God, the Egyptians in Herodotus d) strangely refer to field mice. They relate that these, τοῖσι ἐναντίοισι αὐτοῖσι ἐπιχυθέντας νυκτὸς, κατὰ μὲν φαγέειν τοὺς φαρετρεῶνας αὐτέων, κατὰ δὲ τὰ τόξα, πρὸς δὲ τῶν ἀσπίδων τὰ ὄχανα· ὥς τε τῇ ὑστεραίῃ φευγόντων σφέων, γυμνῶν ὅπλων, πεσέειν πολλούς· [toisi enantioisi autoisi epichythentas nyktos, kata men phagein tous pharetreōnas auteōn, kata de ta toxa, pros de tōn aspidōn ta ochana; hōs te tē hysteraiē pheugontōn spheōn, gymnōn hoplōn, peseein pollous] poured over the enemy themselves by night, gnawed through their quivers, their bows, and the handles of their shields, so that the next day, stripped of their arms and with many lost, they took to flight. Is it relevant here that λοιμὸς [loimos] plague and λαμὰς [lamas] mouse in Hesychius are words so close that one could have been used for the other, and thus a defeat brought about by plague was ascribed to mice? However that may be, something of the kind is recorded to have happened to those Cretans who founded Hamaxitus, a city of the Troad. For when Apollo II, 435, consulted about where to found their city, had answered that it must be founded ἔνθα ἂν αὐτοῖς οἱ γηγενεῖς πολεμήσωσι [entha an autois hoi gēgeneis polemēsōsi], where the earth-born should make war on them, they understood that Hamaxitus was meant; because, when they had pitched camp there, μυῶν ἄφατόν τι πλῆθος ἐφερπύσαν τά τε ὄχανα αὐτοῖς τῶν ἀσπίδων διέτραγε, καὶ τὰς τῶν τόξων νευρὰς διέφαγεν [myōn aphaton ti plēthos epherpysan ta te ochana autois tōn aspidōn dietrage, kai tas tōn toxōn neuras diephagen], an immense host of mice, bursting forth, gnawed the handles of their shields and ate through the strings of their bows. So Aelian, History, book 12, chapter 5. Not very differently the old Scholiast of Homer on book 1 of the Iliad: Νυκτὸς ἐπιγενομένης, μῦες ἔκοψαν αὐτῶν τοὺς τελαμῶνας τῶν ὅπλων [Nyktos epigenomenēs, myes ekopsan autōn tous telamōnas tōn hoplōn], When night had come, mice cut through the straps of their arms. Accordingly, in Aristotle, Rhetoric, book 2, chapter 24, Polycrates praises mice ὅτι ἐβοήθησαν διατραγόντες τὰς νευρὰς [hoti eboēthēsan diatragontes tas neuras], because they brought help (to his countrymen) when they gnawed through the strings of the enemy's bows. And in Clement's Protrepticus, Polemo reports that the peoples neighbouring the Troad τοὺς ἐπιχωρίους μῦς, οὓς σμίνθους καλοῦσι θρησβεύειν, ὅτι τὰς νευρὰς τῶν πολεμίων διέτρωγον τῶν τόξων· [tous epichōrious mys, hous sminthous kalousi thrēsbeuein, hoti tas neuras tōn polemiōn dietrōgon tōn toxōn] worship the mice of that place, which they call sminthoi, because they had gnawed the strings of the enemy's bows. Since these accounts are very similar to what the Egyptians relate of the Assyrians, I would think that they worked this Cretan, or if you prefer Trojan, story into their own.

Quod quam sit frigidum, quisque sponte sentiet. Nec magis placet, quod protulit MICHAELIS Supplemm. ad Lexx. P. V. p. 1908., Hebraeum עכבר referens ad Arabum عُكَبٌ agilis, alacer.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 429 Simonis, in his Lexicon and in the Arcanum Formarum p. 660, thinks the word עכבר is compounded from the verb עכר, which he supposes has the same meaning as the Arabic عرك [ʿarak] he rubbed, and from the word בר, so that it denotes the animal rubbing grain. How frigid this is, anyone will feel at once. Nor do I like any better what Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer] put forward in Supplemm. ad Lexx. [=J. D. Michaelis, Supplementa ad lexica Hebraica] vol. 5, p. 1908, referring the Hebrew עכבר to the Arabic عُكَبٌ [ʿukabun] nimble, brisk.

Under the name جِرْذ [jirdh], Dschird, Shaw [=Thomas Shaw, Travels (1738)] described this animal in Travels p. 156 of the German trans., from which it is clear that it is the mus Glis with a hairy tail, the body dark ash-grey above, whitish below, or the sciurus canus subtus albidus of Linnaeus, p. 155, ed. 13, the μυωξον [myōxon] of Oppian, Cyneg. 2, 574.


(3) Rosenmüller, II, 430 Praetermisit Bochartus Syrum interpretem, qui posuit ܥܘܟܒܪܐ, quod vocabulum tam murem significat, quam mor- bum serpentem, et intorquentem se instar serpentis, Barbahlule, Lexicographo, teste. Huc pertinet, quod et Henslerus, regis II, 431 gis Daniae archiater, vocabulo עכברים 1 Sam. VI, 5. non mures intelligi censet, sed carbunculos, bubones forsan Venereos; quam conjecturam ex literis Hensleri, ad se datis, refert MICHAELIS in Supplemm. P. V. p. 1909. nec sine approbatione: „Est, inquit, in tota narratione, quod ejusmodi bubones, aut mariscas intelligere suadet. In malis, quae Philisthaeos vexarant, nulla 1 Sam. V. murium mentio, quod ita molestum fuit interpretibus, ut LXX. et Vulgatus 1 Sam. V, 6. mures adderent; placuit Hubigantio, sed codex nullus confirmavit. Omni dubio liberamur, si mures Capitis VI. sunt idem fere, quod עפלים, carbunculi, aut tumoris, ulcerisve genus“. — Sed mox addit: „obstare tamen videtur, ac pro muribus, agrum vastantibus, facere versus capitis VI. quintus: עכבריכם המשחיתים את הארץ“.

R3 Rosenmüller, II, 430 Bochart passed over the Syriac translator, who put ܥܘܟܒܪܐ [עוכברא], a word that signifies both a mouse and a creeping disease, one that twists itself like a serpent, on the testimony of the lexicographer Bar Bahlul. To this belongs the view of Hensler too, chief physician to the king II, 431 of Denmark, that by the word עכברים in 1 Sam 6:5 not mice are meant but carbuncles, perhaps venereal buboes. Michaelis reports this conjecture, from a letter Hensler sent him, in the Supplemm. vol. 5, p. 1909, and not without approval: “There is,” he says, “something in the whole narrative that urges us to understand buboes or piles of this kind. Among the evils that had afflicted the Philistines, 1 Sam. V makes no mention of mice, which so troubled the translators that the LXX and the Vulgate translator added mice at 1 Sam 5:6; Houbigant approved this, but no manuscript has confirmed it. We are freed from all doubt if the mice of Chapter VI are much the same as עפלים, carbuncles, or a kind of tumour or ulcer.” But he soon adds: “Yet verse five of chapter VI seems to stand in the way and to favour mice that lay waste the field: עכבריכם המשחיתים את הארץ.”

This argument would hardly satisfy others. I would think the Hebrew names שפן and עכבר differ thus: the former signifies the Syrian sorex, Arab. وَبْر [wabr] (cf. note 3 to the preceding Chapter), the other, עכבר, the mus jaculus, on the authority of the Arabic dialect, in which عَكْبَر [ʿakbar] and يربوع [yarbūʿ] are nearly synonyms; see Bochart above and p. 1015.

Book 3, chapter 35: The choled

II, 435 CAP. XXXV. col. 1021

II, 435 CHAPTER 35. col. 1021


Probatur, חולד choled non esse Mustelam, ut volunt; sed Talpam. Alia Talpae nomina.

It is proved that חולד choled is not the weasel, as they hold, but the mole. Other names of the mole.


Levit. XI, 29. Hebraeum חלד choled Graeci γαλῆν, et Hieronymus mustelam col. 1022 reddit, et Ionathan כרכושתא carcoustha; et Syrus ܟܟܘܫܬܐ cacaustho, quod id ipsum est (1). In Hesychio quidem κέρκος est ἀρουραῖος μῦς, mus agrestis. II, 436 Et suspicabar olim, ex κέρκος deductum fuisse כרכושתא carcoustha, eadem significatione. Sed כרכושתא carcoustha esse animal, feli quadamtenus simile, probat proverbium Talmudicum in Sanhedrin cap. II. fol. 85. I. כרכושתא ושונרא עבדו הלולא מחרבא דבישא גדא Carcoustha et felis cum faciunt nuptias, extollit se is, qui fuerat infortunatus. Et mustelam esse, ex eo constat, quod Psal. CXIII, 9. Hebraea verba עקרת הבית, sterilem domus, Elia teste, sic redduntur in nonnullis exemplaribus Chaldaeae Paraphrasis, דיתבא מוריקא לאינשי ביתה היך כרכושתא דיתבא מדורא בעקרי ביתא Eam, quae assidet livida viris domus suae, ut carcoustha, quae statuit mansionem in fundamentis domus. Quasi עקרת eo loco sterilem non significet, sed eam, quae prae moerore habitat בעקרי in fundamentis, id est, in infima parte) aedium, quomodo carcoustha solet. Quae ad mustelae κατοικιδίου descriptionem pertinere, patebit ex sequentibus. Itaque, cum חולד choled in Mose sit mustela, ex tot veterum sententia, videbuntur id merito sequi Hebraei omnes, Baal Aruch, R. Selomo, Kimchius, Pomarius, Aquinas: et recentiores Scripturae interpretes, Pagninus, Arias, Castalio, Iunius, Tremellius, etc. vernaculi etiam, quotquot videre licuit, Galli puta, Itali, Angli, Belgae, Germani. Ut Lexicographos taceam, quorum nullus est, quod quidem sciam, qui חולד choled aliter quam mustelam, aut martem reddat, quae est mustelae species. Et Hebraeum Aristeae paraphrastem, qui Graeca haec verba, Κακοποιητικὸς γὰρ ὁ τρόπος ἐστὶ, καὶ γαλῆς, καὶ μυῶν, Hebraice sic reddit:

Lev 11:29. The Hebrew חלד choled the Greeks render γαλῆν [galēn], and Jerome mustela [weasel] col. 1022; Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] renders it כרכושתא carcoustha, and the Syriac ܟܟܘܫܬܐ [ככושתא] cacaustho, which is the very same thing R1. In Hesychius, indeed, κέρκος [kerkos] is ἀρουραῖος μῦς [arouraios mys], field mouse. II, 436 And I once suspected that כרכושתא carcoustha was derived from κέρκος [kerkos], with the same meaning. But that כרכושתא carcoustha is an animal somewhat like the cat is proved by the Talmudic proverb in Sanhedrin ch. 2, fol. 85. 1: כרכושתא ושונרא עבדו הלולא מחרבא דבישא גדא, "When the carcoustha and the cat make a wedding, he who had been unfortunate lifts himself up." And that it is the weasel is clear from the fact that in Ps 113:9 the Hebrew words עקרת הבית, the barren woman of the house, are rendered thus, on the testimony of Elias [=Elijah Levita (1469–1549), author of the Aramaic lexicon Meturgeman and of Tishbi], in some copies of the Chaldee Paraphrase: דיתבא מוריקא לאינשי ביתה היך כרכושתא דיתבא מדורא בעקרי ביתא, "She who sits pale before the men of her house, like the carcoustha, which sets its dwelling in the foundations of the house." As if עקרת in that place did not mean barren, but she who out of grief dwells בעקרי in the foundations, that is, in the lowest part of the house, as the carcoustha is wont to do. That this fits the description of the κατοικιδίου [katoikidiou] [domestic] weasel will be evident from what follows. Therefore, since חולד choled in Moses is the weasel, according to the opinion of so many ancients, all the Hebrews will seem to follow this with good reason: Baal Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome] [=Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome, the ʿArukh], R. Solomon, Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)], Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)]; and the more recent interpreters of Scripture, Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae], Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], Castellio, Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], Tremellius [=Immanuel Tremellius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], etc.; also the vernacular ones, as many as I have been able to see, namely the French, Italian, English, Dutch, German. Not to mention the lexicographers, of whom there is none, as far as I know, who renders חולד choled otherwise than as weasel, or martes [marten], which is a species of weasel. And the Hebrew paraphrast of Aristeas, who renders these Greek words, Κακοποιητικὸς γὰρ ὁ τρόπος ἐστὶ, καὶ γαλῆς, καὶ μυῶν [Kakopoiētikos gar ho tropos esti, kai galēs, kai myōn], into Hebrew thus:


II, 437 כי הנה החולד והעכבר הם בטבעם דורכים אל ההשחתה ומועדים תמיד להרע, Ecce enim choled et achbar, (id est, mustela et mus) natura sua ad deperditionem tendunt, et ad malum sunt semper proclives.

II, 437 כי הנה החולד והעכבר הם בטבעם דורכים אל ההשחתה ומועדים תמיד להרע, "For behold, the choled and the achbar (that is, the weasel and the mouse) by their nature tend toward destruction, and are always inclined to evil."


Tamen habeo causas dubitandi, an haec sit vera versio. Quarum prima est, quod palam inde formatum Syrum ܚܘܠܕܐ chuldo significat talpam, non mustelam. Ita statuunt Iohannes Baptista Ferrarius, et Thomas a Novaria in Le-xicis, aut Nomenclatoribus Syriacis, Romae editis, annis 1622. et 1636. (2). Et confirmat Maronitarum doctissimus Gabriel Sionita, qui verba Syri interpretis Proverb. XXIV, 31. ܘܚܦܝܘ ܐܦܘܗܝ ܚܘܠܕܐ Latine ita reddidit: Et cooperuerunt superficiem ejus talpae. Neque vero locus patitur, ut mustelae intelligantur. Agitur enim de agro pigri hominis, qui ita negligitur, ut illum urticae obtegant. Urticae, id est, חרלים, ita habetur in Hebraeo. Sed Syrus legit חלדים, litera Res sede sua mota, et in Daleth mutata; quia sunt literae similes: ac proinde reddidit ܚܘܠܕܐ (3). Qua voce non mustelas, sed talpas significari, res ipsa docet. Neque enim mustelis scatet ager neglectus, sed talpis scatere potest, ut docet Poeta summus lib. 1. Georgicorum,

Yet I have reasons to doubt whether this is the true rendering. The first of them is that the Syriac ܚܘܠܕܐ [חולדא] chuldo, plainly formed from it, means the mole, not the weasel. So Giovanni Battista Ferrari and Thomas a Novaria determine in their Lexicons, or Syriac Nomenclators, published at Rome in the years 1622 and 1636 R2. And this is confirmed by the most learned of the Maronites, Gabriel Sionita [=translator of al-Idrīsī's geography into Latin (Geographia Nubiensis, Paris 1619)], who rendered the words of the Syriac translator in Proverb. XXIV, 31., ܘܚܦܝܘ ܐܦܘܗܝ ܚܘܠܕܐ [וחפיו אפוהי חולדא], into Latin thus: And moles covered its surface. Nor indeed does the passage allow weasels to be understood. For it concerns the field of a lazy man, which is so neglected that nettles cover it. Nettles, that is, חרלים, is what stands in the Hebrew. But the Syriac read חלדים, the letter Resh being moved from its place and changed into Daleth, because the letters are similar; and accordingly he rendered ܚܘܠܕܐ [חולדא] R3. That this word signifies not weasels but moles the matter itself shows. For a neglected field does not swarm with weasels, but it can swarm with moles, as the greatest Poet teaches in book 1 of the Georgics:


— — — — saepe exiguus mus
Sub terris posuitque domos, atque horrea fecit:
Aut oculis capti fodere cubilia talpae.

— — — — often the tiny mouse has set up its home beneath the ground and built its granaries; or blinded moles have dug their chambers.


Quae maxima est agri pernicies. Unde Simocatta in Epistolis, Τί δῆτα περὶ τῶν ἀσπαλάκων λέξαιμι, φοβερὸν γὰρ τῷ γεωργῷ τὸ κακὸν, καὶ δυσανταγώνι-στον τὸ πολέμιον. De talpis igitur quid dixerim? Aratori enim terribile hoc ma- col. 1023 lum est, et hostis non facile expugnabilis. Proinde hoc animal finxit Stesimbrotus ὑπὸ τῆς Γῆς τυφλωθῆναι, διὰ τὸ φθείρειν τοὺς καρποὺς, a Tellure fuisse excaecatum, eo quod fruges corrumperet. Ita Suidas et Apostolius in Τυφλότερος ἀσπάλακος.

This is the greatest bane of a field. Hence Simocatta in his Epistles: Τί δῆτα περὶ τῶν ἀσπαλάκων λέξαιμι, φοβερὸν γὰρ τῷ γεωργῷ τὸ κακὸν, καὶ δυσανταγώνιστον τὸ πολέμιον [Ti dēta peri tōn aspalakōn lexaimi, phoberon gar tō geōrgō to kakon, kai dysantagōniston to polemion]. What then shall I say about moles? For to the ploughman this col. 1023 evil is terrible, and the enemy not easily overcome. Accordingly Stesimbrotus fabled that this animal ὑπὸ τῆς Γῆς τυφλωθῆναι, διὰ τὸ φθείρειν τοὺς καρποὺς [hypo tēs Gēs typhlōthēnai, dia to phtheirein tous karpous], had been blinded by Earth, because it ruined the crops. So Suidas and Apostolius under Τυφλότερος ἀσπάλακος [Typhloteros aspalakos].


Praeterea non Syris solum, sed et Arabibus خلد chuld, vel chold, est talpa. Quod, ut caetera taceam, aperte docent ejus descriptiones. Alcamus II, 438 الخلد الغارة العميا Alchold, mus caecus. Liber, cui titulus est الفلاحة الفارسية Agricultura Persica apud Abenbitarem, الخلد دابة عميا تحت الارض تاكل عروق الشجر ويحب رايحة البصل والكراث وتخرج من حجرتها في طلب الرايحتها Alchold, animal coecum, sub terra arborum radices comedens, quodque cepae et porri odore a) ita delectatur, ut eo allectum exeat e latibulo suo (4). Et Giahid, الخلد دويبة عميا صما لا تعرف ما بين يديها الا بالشم تخرج من حجرها وهي تعلم انها لا سمع لها ولا بصر فتنفتح فاها وتقف عند حجرها فياتي الذباب فيسقط علي شدقيها ويمر بين لحييها فيستد خله جوفها بنفسها وهي تعرض لذلك في الساعات التي يكون فيها الذباب اكثر Alchold est animalculum caecum, et surdum, quodque non novit objecta, nisi per odoratum. Cum e latibulo suo exit, auditu et visu se carere non ignarus, aperto ore stat prope latibulum, et venientes muscae in buccam ejus incidunt, et ambulant inter maxillas, et per ejus halitum in ventrem attrahuntur. Ac proinde os dilatat iis horis, quibus muscae sunt frequentiores. Haec ille, quibus الخلد alchold, id est, talpam, non solum visu, sed et auditu privat. At aliter statuit Damir, cujus verba sunt: كل حيوان له عينان الا الخلد وانما خلق كذلك لانه ترابي جعل الله له الارض كالما للسمك وغذاوه في بطنها وليس له في ظاهرها قوة ولا نشاط ولما لم يكن له بصر عوضه الله حدة حاسة الشمع فيدرك الوطي col. 1024 الخفي من مسافة بعيدة فانا احس بذلك جعل يحفر الارض Omne animal habet oculos praeter alchold, qui creatus est sine oculis; quia in terra degit, quam assignavit ipsi Deus, ut aquam piscibus: ita, ut in ventre terrae sit alimentum ejus, et extra eam robore et alacritate careat. II, 439 Sed visus defectum compensavit Deus acumine sensus aurium, quibus etiam e longinquo spatio suspenso gradu incedentes percipit, et, quamprimum percepit, in terram reconditur. Quibus haec Plinii consona: Liquidius audiunt talpae obrutae terra, tam denso atque surdo Naturae elemento. Sed ex nonnullorum sententia duplex est talpae genus, nempe خلد chold, et زباب zebab: quarum illa visu, haec auditu caret. Damir in capite الفار, id est, De mure, ومنها اليرابوع والزباب والخلد فالزباب صم والخلد اعمي Etiam in speciebus murium sunt aljarbuo (seu choerogryllius), et zebab, et chold; quorum zebab est surdus, et chold caecus. Multo plura possem addere: sed ex his patet plus satis, tam Arabibus, quam Syris, chold, vel chuld esse talpam.

Moreover, not only for the Syrians but also for the Arabs خلد [khuld] chuld, or chold, is the mole. This is plainly shown, to say nothing of the rest, by the descriptions of it. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] II, 438: الخلد الغارة العميا [al-khuld al-ghāra al-ʿamyā] Alchold, the blind mouse. The book entitled الفلاحة الفارسية [al-Filāḥa al-Fārisiyya] Persian Agriculture, cited by Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār]: الخلد دابة عميا تحت الارض تاكل عروق الشجر ويحب رايحة البصل والكراث وتخرج من حجرتها في طلب الرايحتها [al-khuld dābba ʿamyā taḥt al-arḍ taʾkul ʿurūq al-shajar wa-yuḥibb rāyiḥat al-baṣal wa-l-kurrāth wa-takhruj min ḥujratihā fī ṭalab al-rāyiḥatihā] Alchold, a blind animal that eats the roots of trees under the ground, and that takes such delight in the smell of onion and leek a) that, lured by it, it comes out of its hiding-place R4. And Giahid: الخلد دويبة عميا صما لا تعرف ما بين يديها الا بالشم تخرج من حجرها وهي تعلم انها لا سمع لها ولا بصر فتنفتح فاها وتقف عند حجرها فياتي الذباب فيسقط علي شدقيها ويمر بين لحييها فيستد خله جوفها بنفسها وهي تعرض لذلك في الساعات التي يكون فيها الذباب اكثر [al-khuld duwaybba ʿamyā ṣammāʾ lā taʿrif mā bayn yadayhā illā bi-l-shamm takhruj min ḥujrihā wa-hiya taʿlam annahā lā samʿ lahā wa-lā baṣar fa-tanfatiḥ fāhā wa-taqif ʿind ḥujrihā fa-yaʾtī al-dhubāb fa-yasquṭ ʿalā shidqayhā wa-yamurr bayn laḥyayhā fa-yastad khalahu jawfahā bi-nafsihā wa-hiya taʿriḍ li-dhālika fī al-sāʿāt allatī yakūn fīhā al-dhubāb akthar] Alchold is a small animal, blind and deaf, which does not recognize what is in front of it except by smell. When it comes out of its hiding-place, well aware that it lacks hearing and sight, it stands with open mouth near its hiding-place; and flies that come fall into its mouth and walk between its jaws, and are drawn by its breath into its belly. And so it opens its mouth wide at those hours when flies are most numerous. So he, who deprives الخلد [al-khuld] alchold, that is, the mole, not only of sight but also of hearing. But Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] judges otherwise; his words are: كل حيوان له عينان الا الخلد وانما خلق كذلك لانه ترابي جعل الله له الارض كالما للسمك وغذاوه في بطنها وليس له في ظاهرها قوة ولا نشاط ولما لم يكن له بصر عوضه الله حدة حاسة الشمع فيدرك الوطي [kull ḥayawān lahu ʿaynān illā al-khuld wa-innamā khuliqa ka-dhālika li-annahu turābī jaʿala Allāh lahu al-arḍ ka-l-māʾ li-l-samak wa-ghidhāʾuhu fī baṭnihā wa-laysa lahu fī ẓāhirihā quwwa wa-lā nashāṭ wa-lammā lam yakun lahu baṣar ʿawwaḍahu Allāh ḥiddat ḥāssat al-shamʿ fa-yudrik al-waṭʾ] col. 1024 الخفي من مسافة بعيدة فانا احس بذلك جعل يحفر الارض [al-khafī min masāfa baʿīda fa-anā aḥass bi-dhālika jaʿala yaḥfur al-arḍ] Every animal has eyes except alchold, which was created without eyes, because it lives in the earth, which God assigned to it as water to the fishes, so that its food is in the belly of the earth, and outside it it lacks strength and vigour. II, 439 But God compensated for the lack of sight by the keenness of the sense of hearing, by which it perceives even from a great distance those who walk with stealthy step; and as soon as it perceives them, it hides itself in the earth. With this agrees the statement of Pliny: Moles, though buried in the earth, so dense and deaf an element of Nature, hear more clearly. But in the opinion of some there are two kinds of mole, namely خلد [khuld] chold and زباب [zabāb] zebab, of which the former lacks sight, the latter hearing. Damir, in the chapter الفار [al-fār], that is, On the mouse: ومنها اليرابوع والزباب والخلد فالزباب صم والخلد اعمي [wa-minhā al-yarābūʿ wa-l-zabāb wa-l-khuld fa-l-zabāb ṣumm wa-l-khuld aʿmā] Among the species of mice there are also aljarbuo (or choerogryllius), zebab, and chold; of which zebab is deaf and chold blind. I could add much more, but from this it is more than sufficiently clear that for the Arabs as well as the Syrians, chold or chuld is the mole.


Tertio, in Talmude Babylonico tractatu Moëd Katon cap. 1. fol. 6. b. in Misnae verbis, צדין את האישות ואת העכברים, Venantur licite talpas et mures, in his (inquam) verbis האישות, id est, talpa, vel talpae (quod omnes agnoscunt, et nos infra pluribus docebimus) in Talmude Hierosolymitano redditur, חולדה chulda. Quod quidem in eo non legi; quia liber non est ad manum: sed ita asserit Glossa ad locum Moëd Katon, quem nuper citavimus, אישות מפירש בירושלמי חולדה Vox אישות in Hierosolymitana Talmude redditur חולדה chulda. Ibi igitur חולדה chulda est talpa, non mustela.

Third, in the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Moëd Katon, ch. 1, fol. 6b, in the words of the Mishnah צדין את האישות ואת העכברים, One may lawfully hunt moles and mice, in these words (I say) האישות, that is, the mole or moles (as all acknowledge, and as we shall show at greater length below), is rendered in the Jerusalem Talmud as חולדה chulda. I have not, indeed, read this in it myself, since the book is not at hand; but so the Gloss asserts on the passage of Moëd Katon just cited: אישות מפירש בירושלמי חולדה The word אישות is rendered in the Jerusalem Talmud as חולדה chulda. There, therefore, חולדה chulda is the mole, not the weasel.


Quarto, Levit. XI, 29. חולד choled ordinem ducit in iis animalibus, quae continentur nomine שרץ. Horum porro duo propria sunt. Unum, quod, propter exiguitatem pedum, repere videntur potius, quam ambulare. Alterum, quod in immensum sobolescunt. Id enim propriè significat verbum שרץ, ac proinde piscibus tribuitur Gen. I, 20. et ranis Exod. VIII, 3. et Psal. CV, 30. et καθ' ὑπερβολὴν Israelitis in Aegypto Exod. I, 7. quia in illa servitute Dei be-nedictio eorum numerum auxit, pene dixero, supra omnem fidem.
