Has autem notas nemo nescit, mustelis minus convenire, quam talpis, quarum crura sunt brevissima, et (alicubi auctore Plinio) tam numerosa est multitudo, ut tota arva subruant.

Fourth, in Lev 11:29. חולד choled heads the list of those animals which are comprised under the name שרץ. Two things, moreover, are characteristic of these. One, that because of the shortness of their feet they seem to creep rather than walk. The other, that they multiply beyond measure. For this is what the verb שרץ properly signifies, and accordingly it is applied to fishes in Gen 1:20, to frogs in Exod 8:3 and Ps 105:30, and, καθ' ὑπερβολὴν [kath' hyperbolēn], to the Israelites in Egypt, Exod 1:7, because in that servitude God's blessing increased their number, I might almost say, beyond all belief. Everyone knows that these marks suit weasels less than moles, whose legs are very short and whose multitude (on the authority of Pliny somewhere) is so great that they undermine whole fields.


Quinto, si חולד choled est talpa, recte iunguntur in Mose חולד choled, et עכבר achbar, id est, talpa et mus: cum talpa sit muri congener, adeoque muris species, si Arabibus credimus: et Hesychio, cui Λὼτ est ἀσπάλαξ, talpa, seu μῦς τυφλὸς ὁ τὴν γῆν τρυπῶν, mus caecus, terram penetrans: et Scholiasti Aristophanis in Acharnan. ubi σκάλοπας definit μύας τινὰς, οὓς φαμεν σπά-λακας, mures quosdam, quos vocamus talpas: et Oecumenio in 2 Petri I, 9. ubi μυωπάζειν vult idem esse, quod τυφλώττειν, caecutire, ἀπὸ τῶν ὑπὸ τὴν γῆν μυῶν τυφλῶν εἰς ἅπαν διατελούντων, a muribus, qui sub terra omnino caeci degunt, II, 440 id est, a talpis. Proinde juxta Scaligerum b) talpa est in genere murium. Aliis talpa solum est animal, muri simile. Suidas, Ἔστι δὲ ὁ ἀσπάλαξ ζῶον μυῒ ἐμφερὲς, ὑπὸ γῆν διάγον, τῷ ὀφθαλμῷ ἐστερημένον· Talpa est animal, muri simile, sub terra degens, oculis privatum. Proinde junguntur in Talmu- col. 1025 dis loco, quem citavimus, צדין אישות ועכברים, Venantur talpas et mures. At mustela plane diversum est animal, mure majus et validius, eique tam infensum, quam felis. Hinc Theophrastus in libello De animalibus, quae cum copi[?] visuntur, quo loco de muribus agit: Φθείρουσι δ' αὐτοὺς καὶ αἱ ἄγριαι γαλαῖ· Occidunt illos mustelae agrestes. Et Batrachomyomachiae auctor, quisquis est, vs. 9[?].

Fifth, if חולד choled is the mole, then חולד choled and עכבר achbar, that is, the mole and the mouse, are rightly joined in Moses, since the mole is akin to the mouse, and indeed a species of mouse, if we believe the Arabs; and Hesychius, for whom Λὼτ [Lōt] is ἀσπάλαξ [aspalax], the mole, or μῦς τυφλὸς ὁ τὴν γῆν τρυπῶν [mys typhlos ho tēn gēn trypōn], a blind mouse that bores through the earth; and the Scholiast on Aristophanes in the Acharnians, where he defines σκάλοπας [skalopas] as μύας τινὰς, οὓς φαμεν σπάλακας [myas tinas, hous phamen spalakas], certain mice, which we call moles; and Oecumenius on 2 Petri I, 9., where he holds that μυωπάζειν [myōpazein] is the same as τυφλώττειν [typhlōttein], to be blind, ἀπὸ τῶν ὑπὸ τὴν γῆν μυῶν τυφλῶν εἰς ἅπαν διατελούντων [apo tōn hypo tēn gēn myōn typhlōn eis hapan diatelountōn], from the mice which live under the earth entirely blind, II, 440 that is, from moles. Accordingly, according to Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)] b), the mole belongs to the genus of mice. For others the mole is merely an animal similar to the mouse. Suidas: Ἔστι δὲ ὁ ἀσπάλαξ ζῶον μυῒ ἐμφερὲς, ὑπὸ γῆν διάγον, τῷ ὀφθαλμῷ ἐστερημένον [Esti de ho aspalax zōon myi empheres, hypo gēn diagon, tō ophthalmō esterēmenon]; The mole is an animal similar to the mouse, living under the earth, deprived of eyes. Accordingly they are joined in the passage of the Talmud col. 1025 that we cited, צדין אישות ועכברים, They hunt moles and mice. But the weasel is a quite different animal, larger and stronger than the mouse, and as hostile to it as the cat. Hence Theophrastus, in the little book On the animals that appear in multitudes [?], in the passage where he treats of mice: Φθείρουσι δ' αὐτοὺς καὶ αἱ ἄγριαι γαλαῖ [Phtheirousi d' autous kai hai agriai galai]; Wild weasels kill them. And the author of the Batrachomyomachia, whoever he is, line 9[?]:


Μῦς ποτε διψαλέος, γαλέης κίνδυνον ἀλύξας,

Μῦς ποτε διψαλέος, γαλέης κίνδυνον ἀλύξας, [Mys pote dipsaleos, galeēs kindynon alyxas,]


Mus aliquando sitibundus, mustelae periculo evitato. Et apud Athenaeum poeta Carcinus Fabulam scripsit, titulo Μῦες, in qua mustela nocturnos mures strangulat. Plautus quoque in Sticho Actu tertio,

A mouse once, thirsty, having escaped the danger of a weasel. And in Athenaeus the poet Carcinus wrote a play entitled Μῦες [Myes], in which a weasel strangles mice by night. Plautus too, in the Stichus, Act 3:


Mustela murem mihi abstulit praeter pedes.
Eum strenue obsonavit. — — —

A weasel snatched a mouse away from right before my feet.
It did its shopping briskly. — — —


Plinius itidem libri octavi capite vigesimo septimo, Mustela ruta (vires refovet) in venatu murium, cum iis dimicatione conserta. Isidorus Originum libri duodecimi capite tertio, Serpentes etiam muresque mustela persequitur. Abdollat[?]f Bagdadensis (5), ربما عادي الفار وقتله لكن الخوف الفار من السنور اشد خوفه منه Mures nonnunquam inse- quitur (mustela), et interimit. Mus tamen a fele gravius sibi timet, quam mustela.

Likewise Pliny, book 8, chapter 27: The weasel (restores its strength) with rue when hunting mice, once it has joined battle with them. Isidore, Etymologies, book 12, chapter 3: The weasel also pursues serpents and mice. Abdollatif of Baghdad R5: ربما عادي الفار وقتله لكن الخوف الفار من السنور اشد خوفه منه [rubbamā ʿādā al-fār wa-qatalahu lākin al-khawf al-fār min al-sinnawr ashadd khawfihi minhu] It (the weasel) sometimes pursues mice and kills them. Yet the mouse fears the cat more gravely than the weasel.


Sexto, verbum חלד chalad (unde deductum חולד choled) penetrare et suffo- dere est. De terra proprie dicitur, quod haec exempla doceant. Talmud Hie- rosolymitanum in Kelaim capite ultimo, ut Cl. Buxtorfius citat, מחליד הקב״ה לפניהם את הארץ Deus Sanctus Benedictus terram coram iis suffodiens. Et Talmud Babylonicum in Bava Bathra fol. 19. b. de vitibus, מפני שמחלידין את הקרקע ומעלין עפר תיחוח Quia solum suffodiunt, et terram emolliunt. Et Syrus interpres de herinaceo Es. XXXIV, 15. ܘܢܚܠܕ ܘܢܥܘܠ ܒܛܠܠܗ Et effodiet, et penetrabit in umbram illius. Unde ad alia transfertur per metaphoram. II, 441 Ita חלד de metallis, est rubeginem contrahere; et חלודה, rubigo, in Ionathane חלדות Num. XXXI, 22. quia metalla penetrat, et usque ad intima exedit. Gangraena item in Syra paraphrasi ܡܣܟܝܢܘܬܐ dicitur 2 Tim. II, 17. quia morbus est ὑπόνομος, et in carnem altius penetrans. Rursus in victimae mactatione חלדה vocabatur cultri in victimam profunda immersio, quae mactationem reddebat illegitimam, ut habetur in tractatu Talmudico Cholin cap. 2. fol. 20. b. et in Maimonis tractatu De mactatione cap. 3. §. 9 et 10. Eodem pertinet, quod 2 Tim. III, 6. pro Pauli verbis, οἱ ἐνδύνοντες εἰς τὰς οἰκίας, id est, qui penetrant in domos, Syrus habet ܕܡܣܟܝܢ ܒܒܝܬ ܒܬܐ. De iis enim ibi agitur, qui, quasi aedium profundum petentes, occultissima quaeque rimantur et perscrutantur. Proinde Arabs, Parisiis editus, non absimili metaphora reddidit, الذين يغوصون في المنازل qui in domos sese immergunt. Nec sua specie caret doctissimi Fulleri conjectura Miscellaneorum libri tertii capite decimo quarto, Chalybes prope Trapezuntem et Pharnaciam, Chaldaeos a Phoenicibus ideo fuisse dictos, non quod commune quidquam haberent cum Chaldaeis Babyloniis: sed quasi חלדיא, seu καταδύτας, quia terrae viscera perscrutabantur, ut metalla inde eruerent. Cui rei primi omnium operam impendisse, putantur. Callimachus in Elegia De coma Berenices,

Sixth, the verb חלד chalad (from which חולד choled is derived) means to penetrate and to dig under. It is properly said of the earth, as these examples show. The Jerusalem Talmud, in Kilayim, last chapter, as the distinguished Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum] cites it: מחליד הקב״ה לפניהם את הארץ God, the Holy One, Blessed be He, digging under the earth before them. And the Babylonian Talmud, in Bava Batra fol. 19b, of vines: מפני שמחלידין את הקרקע ומעלין עפר תיחוח Because they dig under the ground and loosen the soil. And the Syriac translator of the hedgehog in Es. XXXIV, 15.: ܘܢܚܠܕ ܘܢܥܘܠ ܒܛܠܠܗ [ונחלד ונעול בטללה] And it will dig out, and penetrate into its shade. From this it is transferred metaphorically to other things. II, 441 Thus חלד, of metals, is to contract rust; and חלודה, rust, in Jonathan חלדות, Num 31:22, because it penetrates metals and eats into them to their innermost parts. Likewise gangrene is called ܡܣܟܝܢܘܬܐ [מסכינותא] in the Syriac paraphrase, 2 Tim. II, 17., because it is a disease that is ὑπόνομος [hyponomos], penetrating deeper into the flesh. Again, in slaughtering a victim, חלדה was the name for the deep plunging of the knife into the victim, which rendered the slaughter illegitimate, as is found in the Talmudic tractate Chullin, ch. 2, fol. 20b, and in Maimonides [=Moses Maimonides (Rambam), Mishneh Torah]' treatise On Slaughtering, ch. 3, §§ 9 and 10. To the same belongs the fact that in 2 Tim. III, 6., for Paul's words οἱ ἐνδύνοντες εἰς τὰς οἰκίας [hoi endynontes eis tas oikias], that is, who penetrate into houses, the Syriac has ܕܡܣܟܝܢ ܒܒܝܬ ܒܬܐ [דמסכין בבית בתא]. For it speaks there of those who, as if making for the depths of houses, search and scrutinize everything most hidden. Accordingly the Arabic version published at Paris rendered it with a not dissimilar metaphor: الذين يغوصون في المنازل [alladhīna yaghūṣūna fī al-manāzil] who plunge themselves into houses. Nor does the conjecture of the most learned Fuller [=Nicholas Fuller, Miscellanea theologica / sacra (1612–22)], Miscellanies, book 3, chapter 14, lack plausibility: that the Chalybes near Trapezus and Pharnacia were called Chaldaeans by the Phoenicians not because they had anything in common with the Babylonian Chaldaeans, but as חלדיא, or καταδύτας [katadytas], because they searched the bowels of the earth to dig metals out of it. They are thought to have been the first of all to devote effort to this. Callimachus, in the elegy On the Lock of Berenice:


— — Χαλύβων ὡς ἀπόλοιτο γένος, col. 1026
Γειόθεν ἀντέλλον τι κακὸν φυτὸν οἵ μιν ἔφηναν.

— — Χαλύβων ὡς ἀπόλοιτο γένος, [Chalybōn hōs apoloito genos,] col. 1026 Γειόθεν ἀντέλλον τι κακὸν φυτὸν οἵ μιν ἔφηναν. [Geiothen antellon ti kakon phyton hoi min ephēnan.]


Quod Catullus ita reddidit:

Which Catullus rendered thus:


— — Chalybon omne genus pereat, Et qui principio sub terra quaerere venas Institit, etc.

— — May the whole race of the Chalybes perish, And he who first began to seek veins beneath the earth, etc.


Valerius quoque libro quinto Argonauticῶν de iisdem eleganter,

Valerius too, in book 5 of the Argonautica, says elegantly of the same people:


Pervigil auditur Chalybum labor: arma fatigant
Ruricolae, Gradive, tui: sonat illa creatrix
Prima manus belli terras crudelis in omnes.
Nam prius ignoti quam dura cubilia ferri
Eruerent, ensesque darent, odia aegra sine armis
Errabant, iraeque inopes, et segnis Erinnys.

The sleepless toil of the Chalybes is heard; the country-dwellers wear out arms for you, Gradivus; there sounds that hand, the first creator of war, cruel against all lands. For before they dug out the hard beds of unknown iron and supplied swords, sick hatreds wandered without arms, and wraths lacked means, and Erinys was sluggish.


Et Arrianus in Alexandro, Χάλυβες πρῶτοι ἀνθρώπων αἰτίαν ἔχουσι χαλκεύ-σασθαι σίδηρον· Chalybibus crimini datur, quod primi ferrum cuderint. Et Ammianus libro vigesimo secundo, Chalybes, per quos erutum et domitum est primitus ferrum. Tamen idem inventum alii Cyclopibus tribuunt. Plinius libri septimi capite quinquagesimo sexto, Aerariam fabricam alii Chalybas, alii Cyclopas II, 442 monstrasse putant. Utut sit, a metallorum frequenti effossione terra Chalybum dici potuit Chaldia, et incolae Chaldi, Chaldii et Chaldaei. Nam tot modis scripsisse veteres, testatur Eustathius in Notis ad Dionysium Periegeten pagina 101. b. Et haec nomina omnino alludunt ad verbum חלד chalad; quod, cum de terra dicitur, fodere significat, ut pluribus supra c) probatum. Iam quis non videt, eodem commode revocari nomen חולד choled, pro talpa, quae ad id videtur nata et instituta, ut indesinenti labore terram subruat et suffodiat. Ideo talpam nemo definit, qui non hoc ponat in parte definitionis. Sic apud Hesychium in vocibus Λὼτ et Σκάλοψ legitur, esse μῦς τυφλὸς ὁ τὴν γῆν τρυ-πῶν, mus caecus, qui terram perforat; et ζῶον γεώρυχον τυφλὸν, caecum animal, terram fodiens. Epiphanius in Adamitis statim initio, Ἀσπάλακα κα-λοῦσί τι ζῶον ἐν τῇ γῇ κάτω ἐμφωλεῦον, τετράπουν, ὅπερ ὀρύττει τὴν γῆν, etc. Talpam vocant animal quoddam quadrupes, latebras habens in terrae penetralibus, quam effodit, etc. In Hieronymo in Esaiam capite secundo, Est animal absque oculis, quod semper terram fodit, et humum egerit. In R. Selomone ibidem, חפרפרות מיני שרצים שחופרין הארץ שקורין טלפא בלעז, Chaphorpheroth sunt reptilium species, quae terram fodiunt, et vulgari lingua vocantur talpae. Et in Moed Katon fol. 6. b. בריה שאין לה עיניים חופרת בקרקע Creatura est, oculis carens, et terram fodiens. Proinde naturae consulti notant, eo pertinere, quod rostro est acutissimo. Et priorum crurum pars anterior hoc habet peculiare, quod ossibus constat geminis et brevissimis, quaeque in os humeri statim inseruntur, ut sic fortius fodiant. Qua ipsa de causa priores etiam pedes et digiti non deorsum, sed ad latera spectant; et volam habent bene latam, et ungues robustissimos, et ad corporis modulum longe majores, quam in reliquis animalibus. Unde est, quod tam facile tamque expedite terram fodiunt, ut fidem id prope superet: quod rerum nostrarum damno quotidie experimur. Itaque etiam alterum talparum nomen חפרפרות, Es. II, 20. est a fossione sumtum. Nam, ut חלד chalad, ita etiam חפר chaphar, fodere significat: quod nemo nescit. Unde geminatum חפרפרות significationem intendit, ut eo nomine designetur animal, quod in terrae fossione totum est. Sed et eodem revocandum Graecum σπάλαξ, vel ἀσπάλαξ, cujus vera origo doctos latuit hactenus. Nam, qui παρὰ τὸ σπᾶν, id est, a trahendo deducunt, nugas agunt. Quin σπάλαξ, per metathesin factum ex σκάλοψ, quod vetus fuit talpae vocabulum apud Athenienses, ut ex Nicocle scimus: Σκάλοψ, ὁ σπάλαξ λέγεται παρὰ col. 1027 Ἀττικοῖς, ὡς λέγει Νικοκλῆς. Ita Etymologus. Et confirmat Aristoteles in Acharnan. Ubi pro talpis habet σκάλοπας. Ad quem locum Scholiastes, Σκά-λοπας] μύας τινὰς, οὓς φαμεν σπάλακας. Dicitur autem σκάλοψ, non II, 443 quasi κεκαλυμμένους ἔχων τοὺς ὦπας, ut nugatur Etymologus: sed ἀπὸ τοῦ σκάλ-λειν, ἢ σκαλεύειν, a fodiendo; et voce composita σκαλόπεζα, quasi fossorios habens pedes, ut apud Poetam ἀργυρόπεζα Θέτις, argenteis pedibus Thetis. Hesychius, Σκάλοψ· σκαλόπεζα, ἀσπάλαξ. Ita legendum, non σκαλόπετα, quomodo habent nostrae editiones. Rursus, παρὰ τοῦ σκάλοπος, a talpa fit σκαλοπιὰ pro talparum latibulo, vel terrae cumulo, a talpis excitato. Et sic omnino sumendum in his Theophrasti Historiae libri septimi capite undecimo, de phasgani (seu gladioli) radicibus, Πολλὰς δὲ εὑρίσκουσι παρὰ ταῖς σκαλοπιαῖς· χαίρει γὰρ, καὶ συλλέγεται τὸ ζῶον. Multas reperiunt prope scalopias, seu talparum foramina; illas enim appetit et colligit hoc animal. Pessime igitur interpretes, Permultas juxta eam scolopendras reperiunt. Neque verum, quod alii volunt, τὴν σκαλοπιὰν idem esse, quod τὴν σκάλοπα. Ac si quis τὴν μυρμη-κιὰν, formicarum latibulum idem esse vellet, quod τὴν μύρμηκα, formicam. Quod prope omiseram, etiam in quadam Galliae parte talpa vocatur foyon, ut fovir Gallis est fodere, quod observat Capellus ὁ μακαρίτης Sacrae Criticae pagina 382. Et Germanica talpae plura nomina d), eodem pertinentia, refert Gesnerus in Talpa, pagina 932. Itaque id commune est Hebraeis, Graecis, Germanis et nonnullis Gallorum, ut a fodiendo talpam nominent.

And Arrian in the Alexander: Χάλυβες πρῶτοι ἀνθρώπων αἰτίαν ἔχουσι χαλκεύσασθαι σίδηρον [Chalybes prōtoi anthrōpōn aitian echousi chalkeusasthai sidēron]; the Chalybes are charged with having been the first to forge iron. And Ammianus, book 22: the Chalybes, by whom iron was first dug out and worked. Yet others attribute the same invention to the Cyclopes. Pliny, book 7, chapter 56: Some think that the Chalybes, others that the Cyclopes II, 442 first showed the craft of working bronze. However that may be, from the frequent digging of metals the land of the Chalybes could be called Chaldia, and its inhabitants Chaldi, Chaldii and Chaldaei. For that the ancients wrote it in all these ways is attested by Eustathius in his Notes on Dionysius Periegetes, page 101 b. And these names clearly allude to the verb חלד chalad, which, when said of the earth, means to dig, as was proved at length above c). Now who does not see that the name חולד choled can fittingly be referred to the same root, for the mole, which seems born and designed for this very purpose: to undermine and dig beneath the earth with unceasing labour? That is why no one defines the mole without making this part of the definition. Thus in Hesychius, under the words Λὼτ [Lōt] and Σκάλοψ [Skalops], we read that it is μῦς τυφλὸς ὁ τὴν γῆν τρυπῶν [mys typhlos ho tēn gēn trypōn], a blind mouse that bores through the earth; and ζῶον γεώρυχον τυφλὸν [zōon geōrychon typhlon], a blind animal that digs the earth. Epiphanius, on the Adamites, right at the beginning: Ἀσπάλακα καλοῦσί τι ζῶον ἐν τῇ γῇ κάτω ἐμφωλεῦον, τετράπουν, ὅπερ ὀρύττει τὴν γῆν [Aspalaka kalousi ti zōon en tē gē katō emphōleuon, tetrapoun, hoper oryttei tēn gēn], etc. They call mole a certain four-footed animal that has its lairs in the depths of the earth, which it digs out, etc. In Jerome on Isaiah, chapter 2: It is an animal without eyes, which is always digging the earth and throwing up the soil. In R. Solomon on the same passage: חפרפרות מיני שרצים שחופרין הארץ שקורין טלפא בלעז, Chaphorpheroth are kinds of creeping things that dig the earth, and in the vernacular are called talpae [moles]. And in Moed Katan fol. 6b: בריה שאין לה עיניים חופרת בקרקע It is a creature that lacks eyes and digs in the earth. Accordingly, naturalists note that its very sharp snout serves this purpose. And the forward part of its forelegs has this peculiarity, that it consists of paired and very short bones, which are inserted directly into the humerus, so that they may dig more powerfully. For the same reason the forefeet and toes point not downward but sideways; and they have a quite broad palm and very strong claws, far larger in proportion to the size of the body than in other animals. Hence they dig the earth so easily and so swiftly as almost to pass belief, as we experience daily to the damage of our property. Therefore the other name for moles, חפרפרות, Isa 2:20, is also taken from digging. For, like חלד chalad, חפר chaphar also means to dig, as everyone knows. Hence the reduplicated חפרפרות intensifies the meaning, so that the name designates an animal wholly given over to digging the earth. But the Greek σπάλαξ [spalax] or ἀσπάλαξ [aspalax] must also be referred to the same idea; its true origin has so far escaped the learned. For those who derive it παρὰ τὸ σπᾶν [para to span], that is, from drawing, talk nonsense. Rather, σπάλαξ [spalax] was formed by metathesis from σκάλοψ [skalops], which was the old word for the mole among the Athenians, as we know from Nicocles: Σκάλοψ, ὁ σπάλαξ λέγεται παρὰ col. 1027 Ἀττικοῖς, ὡς λέγει Νικοκλῆς [Skalops, ho spalax legetai para Attikois, hōs legei Nikoklēs]. So the Etymologicum. And Aristotle confirms it in the Acharnians, where he has σκάλοπας [skalopas] for moles. On this passage the Scholiast: Σκάλοπας] μύας τινὰς, οὓς φαμεν σπάλακας [Skalopas] myas tinas, hous phamen spalakas]. It is called σκάλοψ [skalops], however, not II, 443 as if κεκαλυμμένους ἔχων τοὺς ὦπας [kekalymmenous echōn tous ōpas], as the Etymologicum idly claims, but ἀπὸ τοῦ σκάλλειν, ἢ σκαλεύειν [apo tou skallein, ē skaleuein], from digging; and by the compound word σκαλόπεζα [skalopeza], as if having digging feet, as in the Poet ἀργυρόπεζα Θέτις [argyropeza Thetis], silver-footed Thetis. Hesychius: Σκάλοψ· σκαλόπεζα, ἀσπάλαξ [Skalops; skalopeza, aspalax]. So it should be read, not σκαλόπετα [skalopeta], as our editions have it. Again, from σκάλοψ [skalops], mole, comes σκαλοπιὰ [skalopia] for a mole's lair, or a heap of earth thrown up by moles. And it must certainly be taken so in these words of Theophrastus, History, book 7, chapter 11, on the roots of the phasganon (or gladiolus): Πολλὰς δὲ εὑρίσκουσι παρὰ ταῖς σκαλοπιαῖς· χαίρει γὰρ, καὶ συλλέγεται τὸ ζῶον [Pollas de heuriskousi para tais skalopiais; chairei gar, kai syllegetai to zōon]. They find many near the scalopiae, or mole-holes; for this animal seeks them and gathers them. Very badly, then, do the translators render it: They find a great many scolopendras near it. Nor is it true, as others hold, that τὴν σκαλοπιὰν [tēn skalopian] is the same as τὴν σκάλοπα [tēn skalopa]. As if someone held that τὴν μυρμηκιὰν [tēn myrmēkian], the ants' nest, were the same as τὴν μύρμηκα [tēn myrmēka], the ant. What I had nearly omitted: in a certain part of France too the mole is called foyon, as fovir is French for to dig, as the late Cappel (ὁ μακαρίτης [ho makaritēs]) observes in the Critica Sacra, page 382. And Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium], under Talpa, page 932, records several German names for the mole d) that belong to the same idea. Thus it is common to the Hebrews, the Greeks, the Germans and some of the French to name the mole from digging.


Cum ex iis, quae dicta sunt, liquido constare putem, חולד choled Mosi fuisse talpam, aeque ac Syrum ܚܘܠܕܐ chulda, et Arabicum خلد chuld, vel chold: non tamen dissimulandum, apud Talmudicos doctores חולדה chulda plerumque esse mustelam. Quod haec loca palam faciunt. In tractatu Cholin ubi supra, חלדה הר בחלדה הדרה בעיקרי בתים דמכסי הכא Cultri immersio in mactatione Chalada dicitur, phrasi mutuata ex chulda, quae degit in fundamentis aedium, ut ibi lateat. Non quadrat in talpam, quae non nisi in agro degit, sed in mustelam κατοικίδιον. Cui passim opponitur חולדת סנאים, aut חולדת הסניים, mustela ruborum, id est, sylvestris: ut in Kilaim cap. 8. fol. 32. a. b. הקופד וחולדת הסניים, hericius et mustela ruborum. Ubi Glossa Maimonidis, וחולדת הסניים חיה דומה לחולדה ממיני השועלים, id est, Mustela ruborum fera est similis vulgari mustelae inter vulpium species. Et in Bava kama cap. 4. fol. 80. 1. מגדלין כלבין כופרין וחתולין וקופין וחולדות סנאים מפני שעושין לנקראת הבית, Nutrire lices canes villaticos, et feles, et simias, et mustelas ruborum (quae vocantur חולדות), quia factae sunt ad perfodiendas aedes. Et paullo post, אמר ר׳ יהודה שרצא חרצא ואיכא דאמר חרזא דקטני שקי דרעיא ביני וורדיני, Dixit R. Iuda, Est reptile (CHARTSA) exscindens. Et sunt, qui dicunt (CHAR-ZA) perforans, quod gracilia habet crura, et pascit inter dumeta. Sic apud Plinium II, 444 libri vigesimi noni capite quarto, Mustelarum duo genera: alterum sylvestre. Distant magnitudine. Graeci vocant ictidas, etc. Haec autem, quae in domibus nostris oberrat, etc. Id ipsum, quod diximus, חולדה chulda, Talmudicis fere mustelam esse, non talpam, sequitur ex eo, quod hoc animal pueros strangulare volunt, quod de talpa nemo dixerit. In quam rem affertur locus ex tractatu Thaanith cap. 1. fol. 8. 1. בא וראה כמה גדולים בעלי אמנה מניין מחולדה ובור ומה המאמין בחולדה ובור כך המאמין בהקב״ה על אחת כמה וכמה, Veni, et vide, quomodo in magnis fidei testibus censeantur chulda et puteus. Et quis chul- col. 1028 dae et puteo fidit, qui Deo Sancto Benedicto non fidat multo magis? Ad quem locum hanc fabellam refert Glossator Talmudicus: מחולדה ובור שהמיתו שני בני אדם מצוי הוא באגדה מעשה בבחור אחד שנתן אמונתו לריבה אחת שישאנה אמרה מי העיד והיה שם בור א׳ וחולדה אמר הבחור בור וחולדה עדים בדבר לימים עבר על אמונתו ונשא אחרת והוליד שני בנים אחד נפל לבור ומת ואחד נשכתו חולדה ומת אמרה לו אשתו מה מעשה הוא זה שבנינו מתים במיתה משונה ואמר לה כך וכך היה מעשה, Chulda et puteus, a quibus duo homines letho dati. Historia habetur in Aggada de juvene quodam, qui, cum puellae cui- dam fidem suam obstringeret, fore, ut eam duceret in uxorem, Quis erit testis, inquit illa? Ibi autem erant puteus et chulda (mustela). Et dixit juvenis, Puteus et chulda rei gestae testes erunt. Sed post aliquot dies is idem, violata fide, aliam duxit, ex qua cum peperisset duos filios: horum unus in puteum delapsus exspira- vit; alter quoque a chulda, seu mustela, morsus obiit. Tum ab uxore interro- gatus, quamobrem ambo filii violenta morte obiissent, narravit illi, quomodo res se haberet. Ejusdem historiae multo plures circumstantias refert Baal Aruch, et in his marem fuisse puerum, et jam trimestrem a chulda fuisse strangulatum. Verba sunt: וילדה בן זכר כשהגיע לג׳ חרשים חנקתו חולדה Et illa peperit fili- um marem, quem chulda strangulavit, cum tertium mensem jam attigisset. Ita de الزبزب zebzeb, mustelae majoris, seu viverrae specie, Bagdadi capta anno Hegirae 304. suprae) narraverunt Arabes انه ياكل اطفالهم eam infantes suos vorasse, et virorum manus, et mulierum mammas momordisse. His addenda, quae Talmudici afferunt in Collatione vocum חולדה chulda, vel חולד choled, et חלד cheled: quarum haec orbem significat Ps. XLIX, 2. ubi homines vocantur יושבי חלד, incolae cheled, id est, terreni orbis. Et doctores inter se disputant, quorsum terra dicatur חלד cheled, et quaerunt, quid commune habeat cum חולד choled, animali. Et in Talmude Babylonico tractatu Cholin cap. 9. fol. 127. a. quidam respondet, כל שיש ביבשה יש בים חוץ מן החולדה, Quidquid animalium est in terra, esse etiam in mari, sola chulda excepta. Quod ne putetur II, 445 dici gratis, en bellam historiam, quam ex Rabbinorum scriptis profert doctissimus Buxtorfius in Lexico Talmudico ad vocem חלד! Comitia fuerunt principum mundi de administratione recta. Princeps maris conquestus est, se non habere subditos sufficientes. Permissum ipsi proinde fuit, ut ex terra peteret plures, modo de alimento provideret. Conjecit omnia animalia terrestria in mare, cum mandato, ut illic quoque suam speciem propagarent. Factum est: unde dicitur, omnia animalia terrestria esse quoque in mari, nisi quod quaedam in monstrosam formam conversa sunt. Ad mustelam cum pervenisset, ea, in littore stans, dixit principi maris: Quorsum me denuo in mare projicies? Nunquid vides, me in mari jam esse? Id autem dixit, effigiem suam in mari ostendens. Princeps contentus mustelam dimisit. Hinc dicunt Talmudici, omnia terrestria in mari esse praeter mustelam, quae astutia sua evasit. Et terra dicitur חלד cheled, quod propria remanserit mustelae, quae vocatur חולדה chulda, vel חולד choled. In Talmude Hierosolymitano, initio capitis De octo reptilibus, tractatur eadem quaestio, et a nonnullis respondetur id ipsum, quod jam diximus, terram et terrenos homines cum chulda comparari; לפי שכל מה שיש ביבשה יש בים והרבה מינין יש col. 1029 בים מה שאין כן ביבשה ואין חולדה בים eo quod, cum omnia, quae sunt in terra, sint etiam in mari, et multae sint in mari species, quae non sunt in terra, tamen chulda non est in mari. Altera responsio haec est: חולדה זו גוררת ומנחת ואינה וודעת למי מנחת כך כל באי העולם גוררין ומניחין ואינן יודעין למי מניחין כמו שנאמר יצבור ולא ידע מי אספם, Chulda multa attrahit et relinquit; ignara, cui relinquat. Ita quoque mundani omnes multa attrahunt, et relinquunt; nescientes, cui ea sint relicturi. Quomodo dicitur Psal. CXXXIX, 2. „Congregabit, et nesciet, quis ea sit collecturus“. Ita haec citat Aruch, quae, utut nugacissima, tamen ad scopum nostrum faciunt. Docent enim, voce chulda a plerisque Talmudicis non significari talpam. Neque enim talpa, quae caeca est, imaginem suam in mari vidisse diceretur, et aliis ostendisse. Neque in latibulis suis quidquam reponere legitur et recondere. Sed mustelae hoc ingenium est, de qua scribit ubi supra Abdollatiph Bagdadensis, في طبعه انه يسرق ما وجد من فضة او ذهب كما يفعل الغار E natura ejus est, ut suffuretur, quidquid argenti (aut auri) reperit, quomodo mures solent. Itaque de mustela ibidem haec historia narratur: رجل صاد فرخا منها وحبسه في قفص بحيث تراه امه فلما اراته ذهبت ثم جات وفي فمها دينار فالقته بين يديه كانها تفدي ولدها فلم يتركه لها فذهبت وعادت بدينار اخر حتي بلغت من العدد خمسا فلما II, 446 ان لا يطلق لها ذهبت وعادت بخرقة كانها تشير الي فراغ حاصلها فلم يكترث بها فلما رات ذلك عادت الي دينار فاخذته منه فخشي الرجل من ذلك فاطلق لها ولدها Quidam mustelae catulum cepit, et cavea inclusit, ita, ut videret mater. Quae, cum illum vidisset, abiit, et rediit cum denario in ore, quem coram eo projecit, tanquam catulum redemptura. Sed, cum is non dimisisset, profecta rursus alios attulit denarios, donec ad quinarium numerum pervenisset. Et, cum vidit, catulum suum nondum dimitti, pannum etiam attulit (in quo erant nummi), ut doceret, se totum peculium exhausisse. Cumque se non respici animadvertit, ad nummos rediit, ut illos reciperet. Sed vir ille, metu perculsus, restituit ei catulum. Patet igitur, a Talmudicis voce חולדה chulda plerumque significari mustelam. Sed illorum auctoritas hac in parte nos parum movet, cum ipsi sibi non constent, et apud Arabes et Syros chuld, col. 1030 vel chulda sit talpa; et tam origo vocis, quam Mosaici textus circumstantiae palam doceant, vocem ita esse sumendam.

From what has been said I think it is clear that the חולד choled of Moses was the mole, just like the Syriac ܚܘܠܕܐ [חולדא] chulda and the Arabic خلد [khuld] chuld or chold. Yet it must not be concealed that among the Talmudic doctors חולדה chulda is for the most part the weasel. The following passages make this plain. In the tractate Cholin, cited above: חלדה הר בחלדה הדרה בעיקרי בתים דמכסי הכא, "The thrusting in of the knife in slaughtering is called Chalada, an expression borrowed from chulda, which lives in the foundations of houses so as to lie hidden there." This does not fit the mole, which lives only in the field, but it fits the house-dwelling weasel, κατοικίδιον [katoikidion]. To this is regularly opposed חולדת סנאים or חולדת הסניים, the weasel of the brambles, that is, the wild weasel: as in Kilaim ch. 8, fol. 32a b., הקופד וחולדת הסניים, "the hedgehog and the weasel of the brambles." There the Gloss of Maimonides says: וחולדת הסניים חיה דומה לחולדה ממיני השועלים, that is, "The weasel of the brambles is a wild animal similar to the common weasel, among the species of foxes." And in Bava kama ch. 4, fol. 80. 1: מגדלין כלבין כופרין וחתולין וקופין וחולדות סנאים מפני שעושין לנקראת הבית, "One may raise village dogs, and cats, and monkeys, and weasels of the brambles (which are called חולדות), because they are made for digging through houses." And shortly after: אמר ר׳ יהודה שרצא חרצא ואיכא דאמר חרזא דקטני שקי דרעיא ביני וורדיני, "R. Iuda said: It is a creeping thing (CHARTSA) that cuts. And there are those who say (CHARZA) that bores, because it has slender legs and feeds among thickets." So too Pliny, II, 444 book 29, chapter 4: "There are two kinds of weasels: one is wild. They differ in size. The Greeks call them ictidas, etc. But this one, which roams about in our houses," etc. That the Talmudists generally take חולדה chulda to be the weasel, not the mole, as we have said, also follows from their claim that this animal strangles children, which no one would say of the mole. To this end a passage is cited from the tractate Thaanith ch. 1, fol. 8. 1: בא וראה כמה גדולים בעלי אמנה מניין מחולדה ובור ומה המאמין בחולדה ובור כך המאמין בהקב״ה על אחת כמה וכמה, "Come and see how the chulda and the pit are reckoned among the great witnesses of faith. And who trusts the chulda col. 1028 and the pit, and would not trust much more the Holy One, Blessed be He?" On this passage the Talmudic Glossator relates this tale: מחולדה ובור שהמיתו שני בני אדם מצוי הוא באגדה מעשה בבחור אחד שנתן אמונתו לריבה אחת שישאנה אמרה מי העיד והיה שם בור א׳ וחולדה אמר הבחור בור וחולדה עדים בדבר לימים עבר על אמונתו ונשא אחרת והוליד שני בנים אחד נפל לבור ומת ואחד נשכתו חולדה ומת אמרה לו אשתו מה מעשה הוא זה שבנינו מתים במיתה משונה ואמר לה כך וכך היה מעשה, "The chulda and the pit, by which two people were put to death. The story is found in the Aggada about a certain young man who pledged his faith to a girl that he would marry her. 'Who will be witness?' she said. Now there were there a pit and a chulda (weasel). And the young man said: 'The pit and the chulda will be witnesses of the matter.' But some days later he broke his pledge and married another, who bore him two sons. One of these fell into the pit and died; the other also died, bitten by a chulda, or weasel. Then, when his wife asked him why both sons had died a violent death, he told her how the matter stood." Baal Aruch relates many more details of the same story, among them that the child was a boy, already three months old, strangled by the chulda. The words are: וילדה בן זכר כשהגיע לג׳ חרשים חנקתו חולדה, "And she bore a male son, whom the chulda strangled when he had already reached the third month." Likewise, of the الزبزب [al-zabzab] zebzeb, a kind of larger weasel or ferret, caught at Baghdad in the year 304 of the Hegira, the Arabs related abovee) انه ياكل اطفالهم [annahu yaʾkul aṭfālahum], that it devoured their infants, and bit men's hands and women's breasts. To this must be added what the Talmudists adduce in comparing the words חולדה chulda or חולד choled and חלד cheled. The latter means the world in Ps. XLIX, 2., where men are called יושבי חלד, inhabitants of cheled, that is, of the earthly world. And the doctors dispute among themselves why the earth is called חלד cheled, and ask what it has in common with חולד choled, the animal. In the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Cholin ch. 9, fol. 127a, someone answers: כל שיש ביבשה יש בים חוץ מן החולדה, "Whatever animal is on land is also in the sea, except only the chulda." Lest this be thought said without grounds, II, 445 here is a pretty story which the most learned Buxtorf brings from the writings of the Rabbis in his Lexicon Talmudicum under the word חלד: "The princes of the world held an assembly on right government. The prince of the sea complained that he did not have enough subjects. He was therefore permitted to seek more from the land, provided he made provision for their food. He cast all the land animals into the sea, with the command that they should propagate their kind there too. So it was done; hence it is said that all land animals are also in the sea, except that some have been changed into monstrous form. When he came to the weasel, she, standing on the shore, said to the prince of the sea: 'Why will you throw me into the sea again? Do you not see that I am already in the sea?' She said this showing her image in the sea. The prince was satisfied and let the weasel go. Hence the Talmudists say that all land creatures are in the sea except the weasel, which escaped by her cunning. And the earth is called חלד cheled because it remained the property of the weasel, which is called חולדה chulda or חולד choled." In the Jerusalem Talmud, at the beginning of the chapter On the eight creeping things, the same question is treated, and some answer the very thing we have just said, that the earth and earthly men are compared with the chulda: לפי שכל מה שיש ביבשה יש בים והרבה מינין יש col. 1029 בים מה שאין כן ביבשה ואין חולדה בים, "because, although everything that is on land is also in the sea, and there are many species in the sea that are not on land, yet the chulda is not in the sea." The other answer is this: חולדה זו גוררת ומנחת ואינה וודעת למי מנחת כך כל באי העולם גוררין ומניחין ואינן יודעין למי מניחין כמו שנאמר יצבור ולא ידע מי אספם, "The chulda drags in many things and leaves them behind, not knowing for whom she leaves them. So also all worldly people drag in many things and leave them behind, not knowing for whom they will leave them. As it is said Ps 139:2: 'He will heap up, and will not know who will gather them'." So the Aruch cites these things, which, however utterly trifling, nevertheless serve our purpose. For they show that by the word chulda most Talmudists do not mean the mole. For the mole, which is blind, would not be said to have seen its image in the sea and shown it to others. Nor is it read to store up and hide anything in its burrows. But this is the disposition of the weasel, of which Abdollatiph of Baghdad writes, in the place cited above: في طبعه انه يسرق ما وجد من فضة او ذهب كما يفعل الغار [fī ṭabʿihi annahu yasriq mā wajada min fiḍḍa aw dhahab kamā yafʿal al-ghār], "It is in its nature to steal whatever silver (or gold) it finds, as mice do." And so in the same place this story is told of the weasel: رجل صاد فرخا منها وحبسه في قفص بحيث تراه امه فلما اراته ذهبت ثم جات وفي فمها دينار فالقته بين يديه كانها تفدي ولدها فلم يتركه لها فذهبت وعادت بدينار اخر حتي بلغت من العدد خمسا فلما II, 446 ان لا يطلق لها ذهبت وعادت بخرقة كانها تشير الي فراغ حاصلها فلم يكترث بها فلما رات ذلك عادت الي دينار فاخذته منه فخشي الرجل من ذلك فاطلق لها ولدها [rajul ṣāda farkhan minhā wa-ḥabasahu fī qafaṣ bi-ḥaythu tarāhu ummuhu fa-lammā arāthu dhahabat thumma jāʾat wa-fī famihā dīnār fa-alqathu bayna yadayhi kaʾannahā tafdī waladahā fa-lam yatrukhu lahā fa-dhahabat wa-ʿādat bi-dīnār ākhar ḥattā balaghat min al-ʿadad khamsan fa-lammā an lā yuṭliq lahā dhahabat wa-ʿādat bi-khirqa kaʾannahā tushīr ilā farāgh ḥāṣilihā fa-lam yaktarith bihā fa-lammā raʾat dhālika ʿādat ilā dīnār fa-akhadhathu minhu fa-khashiya al-rajul min dhālika fa-aṭlaqa lahā waladahā] "A certain man caught a weasel's young and shut it in a cage, so that the mother could see it. When she had seen it, she went away and came back with a denarius in her mouth, which she threw down before him, as though to ransom her young. But when he did not release it, she went off again and brought more denarii, until she reached the number five. And when she saw that her young was still not released, she also brought a cloth (in which the coins had been), to show that she had exhausted her whole store. And when she noticed that no heed was paid to her, she went back to the coins to take them back. But the man, struck with fear, returned her young to her." It is clear, then, that by the word חולדה chulda the Talmudists mostly mean the weasel. But their authority in this matter moves us little, since they are not consistent with themselves, and among the Arabs and Syrians chuld col. 1030 or chulda is the mole; and both the origin of the word and the circumstances of the Mosaic text plainly show that the word is to be taken in this way.


Obiter nota, non solum Hebraeos, sed et nostrorum doctissimos in eo laborare, ut concilient voces חולד choled, et חלד cheled: quarum illa mustelam, ut volunt; haec terram, aut aevum sonat, et doceant, qui factum sit, ut tam diversae vocis notiones ab una origine deductae sint. Et sunt, qui voce חלד cheled nonnisi breve tempus intelligant, ut inde mustela dicatur חולד choled, tanquam animal βραχύβιον. Ita Mercerus. Aliis חלד verbum est sensim abire et irrepere: ac proinde, ut quidem volunt, non solum mustela חולד choled dicitur a furtivo progressu; sed tempus quoque חלד cheled, quia tacite decurrit, neque sentitur ejus motus.

Note in passing that not only the Hebrews but also the most learned of our own scholars labour to reconcile the words חולד choled and חלד cheled, of which the former means, as they would have it, weasel, the latter earth or age, and to show how it came about that the senses of such different words were derived from one origin. There are some who understand by the word חלד cheled nothing but a short time, so that the weasel would hence be called חולד choled as a βραχύβιον [brachybion] animal. So Mercerus [=Jean Mercier (d. 1570), commentaries on Job and Proverbs]. For others חלד is a verb meaning to pass away gradually and to creep in; and accordingly, as they would have it, not only is the weasel called חולד choled from its stealthy movement, but time too is called חלד cheled, because it runs by silently and its motion is not perceived.


Tempora labuntur, tacitisque senescimus annis.

The times glide by, and we grow old with the silent years.


Quae Schindleri sententia est. At Fullero ut חלד chalad, verbum est καταδῦ-ναι, id est, in profunda loca penetrare: ita mustela חולד choled vocatur, tanquam ζῶον καταδυτικὸν, et tam terra ipsa, quam tempus, quo in terra vivimus, חלד cheled, quasi κατάδυσις, ut ab Aquila redditur, id est, latibulum, aut demersio: quia densae caliginis hic plena sunt omnia, neque conferenda cum luce rerum supercoelestium. Quae quidem speciose dicuntur, sed minus solide, ut quidem puto. Certum enim est, verbum חלד chalad duo habere significata diversissima: quorum unum apud Syros; alterum apud Arabes invaluit. Syris nimirum ܚܠܕ chalad proprie est profunda loca fodere et penetrare, ut abunde supra probatum est. At Arabibus خلد chalada plane aliud sonat, nempe manere, durare, perennare, aeternum esse. Atque, ut ex priore significatu factum חולד II, 447 choled, pro talpa: ita ex posteriore חלד cheled, quod primo durationem sonat: ut Ps. XXXIX, 6. וחלדי, Et duratio mea tanquam nihil est coram te; et Ps. LXXXIX, 48. זכור אני מה חלד, Memento, qualis ego sim durationis, id est, quam brevis aevi. Deinde חלד cheled etiam mundum sonat: ut Ps. XLIX, 2. Audite, omnes incolae חלד, mundi: quia mundus, et res, quae in eo sunt, certa duratione constant. Sic עולם olam, huic synonymum, primo saeculum et aeternitatem, deinde etiam mundum significat; quod omnes sciunt.

This is the opinion of Schindler. But for Fuller, just as חלד chalad is a verb meaning καταδῦναι [katadynai], that is, to penetrate into deep places, so the weasel is called חולד choled as a ζῶον καταδυτικὸν [zōon katadytikon], and both the earth itself and the time during which we live on earth are called חלד cheled, as it were κατάδυσις [katadysis], as Aquila renders it, that is, a hiding-place or a submersion: because here all things are full of thick darkness and are not to be compared with the light of supercelestial things. These things are indeed attractively said, but with too little solidity, as I at least think. For it is certain that the verb חלד chalad has two very different meanings, of which one prevailed among the Syrians, the other among the Arabs. For the Syrians, namely, ܚܠܕ [חלד] chalad properly means to dig deep places and to penetrate, as was amply proved above. But for the Arabs خلد [khalada] chalada means something quite different, namely to remain, to endure, to last for ever, to be eternal. And just as from the former meaning came חולד II, 447 choled for the mole, so from the latter came חלד cheled, which first means duration, as in Ps 39:6. וחלדי, And my duration is as nothing before thee; and Ps 89:48. זכור אני מה חלד, Remember of what duration I am, that is, of how brief a span. Then חלד cheled also means the world, as in Ps 49:2 Hear, all ye inhabitants of חלד, the world: because the world and the things in it consist of a fixed duration. So also עולם olam, its synonym, first means age and eternity, and then also the world, as everyone knows.


Pro vero talpae nomine, nempe חולד choled, Levit. XI, 29. aliud substituunt interpretes: nimirum תנשמת thinsemeth, sequente versu, quod talpam reddunt Onkelos, Graeci, Hieronymus, Iarchius, Kimchius, Pomarius, Pagninus, Arias, Itali, Angli, Genevenses, et novae versiones fere quotquot sunt. Sed, quamvis eos

In place of the true name of the mole, namely חולד choled, Lev 11:29, the interpreters substitute another: namely תנשמת thinsemeth in the following verse, which is rendered mole by Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos], the Greeks, Jerome, Jarchi [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac), called Jarchi by the Christian Hebraists], Kimchi, Pomarius, Pagninus, Arias, the Italians, the English, the Genevans, and nearly all the new versions there are. But although


Defendat numerus, junctaeque umbone phalanges,

Their number defends them, and phalanxes joined boss to boss,


in hac tamen versione nihil certi video. Quin, si vere חולד choled est talpa, quod putamus jam esse firmum, aliud est תנשמת thinsemeth. Nam in censu reptilium, quae ut immunda rejiciuntur, haec duo separatim nominat Moses, tanquam diversa animalia. Et, cum octo sint in universum, primum in illo censu est חולד choled, et תנשמת thinsemeth ultimum. Ita, ut non potuerint magis ab invicem removeri. Sed libro sequenti docebimus, quid sit תנשמת thinsemeth.

I nevertheless see nothing certain in this rendering. Indeed, if חולד choled truly is the mole, which we consider now established, then תנשמת thinsemeth is something else. For in the list of creeping things rejected as unclean, Moses names these two separately, as different animals. And since there are eight in all, the first in that list is חולד choled and the last is תנשמת thinsemeth, so that they could not have been placed further apart from each other. But in the following book we shall show what תנשמת thinsemeth is.


Volunt etiam, אשת eseth esse talpam in his Davidis Ps. LVIII, 9. כפל אשת בל חזו שמש, quae sic reddunt multi Hebraeorum: Ut abortivus et talpa non viderunt solem. In his R. Selomo, et R. Obadias Gaon in Psalmos, et Pomarius in Lexico, et Elias in Methurgeman, a majoribus suis scilicet sic edocti. Nam in ipsa Misna Talmudis, qua Iudaei secundum Biblia, neque sanctius, neque antiquius quidquam habent, talpa vocatur אישות esuth; voce ab אשת eseth deducta. Sic in tractatu Kelim cap. 11. fol. 34. a. מצודת האשות טהורה Rete talpae mundum est. Et in Moëd Katon ubi supra, צדין את האשות ואת העכברים משדה האילן ומשדה הלבן כדרכו במועד ובשביעית Venari licet talpam, et mures, tam in agro consito, quam in agro arabili, minore festo, et anno septimo. col. 1031 Et ibi Gemara מאי אישות אמר רב יהודה בריה שאין לה עיניים Quid est esuth? Dixit Rabbi Iuda, Animal est carens oculis. Et paullo post, מאי קרא כמו שבלול תמס יהלך כפל אשת בל חזו שמש, Cur ita vocatur? (quia dicitur Ps. LVIII, 9.) ut limax liquescens abit, ut abortivus et eseth (seu talpa) non viderunt solem. Et ibidem in Glossa אשות esuth definitur בריה שאין לה עיניים וחופרת בקרקע animal lumine cassum, et terram fodiens. Proinde Chaldaeus interpres Psalmi locum sic παραφράζει· היך נפול ואישותא די סמין ולא חמין שמשא Ut abortivus foetus, et esutha (talpa), qui caeci sunt, nec vident solem. II, 448 Certum tamen est, hanc versionem nihil habere sani. Nam Hebraea verba נפל אשת, quae reddunt abortivum et talpam, nil quidquam sonant, quam ἔκτρωμα γυναικὸς, abortum mulieris; ut e veteribus optime illa exposuerunt Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion et Hieronymus. נפל nephel, pro abortivo, a cadendo nomen habet, ut Arabicum سقط sikt, vel sukt. Neque solum hic extat, sed et Iob. III, 16. et Eccles. VI, 3. Et אשת eseth, pro muliere in statu constructo frequentius, sed et in Absoluto occurrit. Sic Deut. XXI, 11. Et si videris in captivitate אשת יפת תאר eseth (id est, mulierem), forma venustam. Et 1 Sam. XXVIII, 7. Quaerite mihi אשת בעלת אוב eseth (seu mulierem), Pythonissam. Et Ierem. XIII, 21. Dolores corripient te כמו אשת לדה, ut eseth (seu mulierem) corripit partus. Ita hic נפל אשת, abortivus foetus eseth (seu mulieris). Itaque in his verbis nihil est difficile, nihil ambiguum, et quod in diversa trahi possit. Et sensus quoque est apertissimus. Qui vitae luce brevi carituri sunt, conferuntur cum abortivo mulieris foetu, cui vitae usura fuit tam brevis, et in tam obscuro loco, ut solem nunquam viderit. Ut nihil opus fuerit hic talpam sibi fingere; maxime, cum Scripturae solenne sit de abortivis foetibus id ipsum asserere, quod hic Psaltes, nempe illos non vidisse lucem. Ita Iob. III, 16. Sicut abortivus latens, non amplius essem; ut infantes, qui non viderunt lumen: quod additur ἐπεξηγητικῶς. Et Eccles. VI, 3. 4. 5. Beatior illo est abortivus, quamvis in cassum venerit, et in tenebras iverit, et tenebris opertum fuerit nomen ejus, neque solem viderit, neque cognoverit, etc. Proinde videtur esse ἀντίθετον in Pauli verbis 1 Cor. XV, 8. Ὡσπερεὶ τῷ ἐκτρώματι ὤφθη κἀμοί· quasi dicat, „A me etiam visus est Christus, quamvis in rebus, quae ad salutem pertinent, „olim tam coeco, quam caecus est abortivus ad lumen solis. Dato tamen, non concesso, אשת eseth, in loco Psalmi talpam significare, ne sic quidem haberent, quod volunt. Nam verba נפל אשת, abortivum talpae significarent, non abortivum et talpam, quomodo illi reddunt, Conjunctionem ET supplentes, quae in textu non comparet. Quod tamen ne videantur facere sine exemplo, R. Selomo hic citat similem locum ex Ierem. XI, 19. ubi Hebraea verba ככבש אלוף reddi vult ut agnus et bos, pariter addita Conjunctione. Sed nos suo loco f) docuimus, nihil ibi esse supplendum, et Hebraice כבש אלוף esse agnum mansuetum, et الوف aluph apud Arabes hodieque sic sumi.

They also hold that אשת eseth is the mole in these words of David, Ps 58:9, כפל אשת בל חזו שמש, which many of the Hebrews render thus: Like the abortive and the mole, they have not seen the sun. Among them are R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)], R. Obadias Gaon on the Psalms, Pomarius in his Lexicon, and Elias in the Methurgeman, having no doubt been so taught by their forebears. For in the very Mishnah of the Talmud, than which the Jews have nothing, after the Bible, either more sacred or more ancient, the mole is called אישות esuth, a word derived from אשת eseth. So in the tractate Kelim, ch. 11, fol. 34a: מצודת האשות טהורה The net for the mole is clean. And in Moëd Katon, cited above: צדין את האשות ואת העכברים משדה האילן ומשדה הלבן כדרכו במועד ובשביעית It is permitted to hunt the mole and mice, both in a planted field and in an arable field, during the minor festival and in the seventh year. col. 1031 And there the Gemara: מאי אישות אמר רב יהודה בריה שאין לה עיניים What is esuth? Rabbi Judah said: It is an animal lacking eyes. And a little later: מאי קרא כמו שבלול תמס יהלך כפל אשת בל חזו שמש, Why is it so called? (because it is said in Ps 58:9) as a snail that melts away, as the abortive and the eseth (or mole) have not seen the sun. And in the same place, in the Gloss, אשות esuth is defined as בריה שאין לה עיניים וחופרת בקרקע, an animal deprived of sight, and digging in the earth. Accordingly the Chaldee translator paraphrases [παραφράζει, paraphrazei] the passage of the Psalm thus: היך נפול ואישותא די סמין ולא חמין שמשא Like an abortive fetus, and the esutha (mole), which are blind and do not see the sun. II, 448 It is certain, however, that this version has nothing sound in it. For the Hebrew words נפל אשת, which they render the abortive and the mole, mean nothing other than ἔκτρωμα γυναικὸς [ektrōma gynaikos], the miscarriage of a woman, as among the ancients Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion and Jerome explained them very well. נפל nephel, for an abortive, takes its name from falling, like the Arabic سقط [saqṭ] sikt, or sukt. Nor does it occur only here, but also in Job 3:16 and Eccl 6:3. And אשת eseth, for woman, occurs more often in the construct state, but also in the absolute. So Deut 21:11. And if you see among the captives אשת יפת תאר an eseth (that is, a woman) beautiful in form. And 1 Sam 28:7. Seek me אשת בעלת אוב an eseth (or woman), a Pythoness. And Jer 13:21. Pains will seize you כמו אשת לדה, as labour seizes an eseth (or woman). So here נפל אשת is the abortive fetus of an eseth (or woman). Thus in these words there is nothing difficult, nothing ambiguous, nothing that could be drawn in different directions. And the sense too is perfectly plain. Those who are soon to lose the light of life are compared with the abortive fetus of a woman, whose enjoyment of life was so brief, and in so dark a place, that it never saw the sun. So there was no need to imagine a mole here, especially since it is customary in Scripture to assert of abortive fetuses the very thing the Psalmist asserts here, namely that they have not seen the light. So Job 3:16. Like a hidden abortive, I would no longer be; like infants who have not seen the light, which is added by way of explanation [ἐπεξηγητικῶς, epexēgētikōs]. And Eccl 6:3–4. 5. The abortive is happier than he, though it came in vain, and went into darkness, and its name was covered with darkness, and it neither saw the sun nor knew, etc. Accordingly there seems to be an antithesis [ἀντίθετον, antitheton] in the words of Paul, 1 Cor 15:8 Ὡσπερεὶ τῷ ἐκτρώματι ὤφθη κἀμοί· [Hōsperei tō ektrōmati ōphthē kamoi], as if he were saying: “Christ was seen even by me, though in matters pertaining to salvation I was once as blind as an abortive is to the light of the sun.” Yet granted, though not conceded, that אשת eseth in the passage of the Psalm means the mole, even so they would not have what they want. For the words נפל אשת would mean the abortive of a mole, not the abortive and the mole, as they render it, supplying the conjunction AND, which does not appear in the text. Yet lest they seem to do this without precedent, R. Selomo here cites a similar passage from Jer 11:19, where he would have the Hebrew words ככבש אלוף rendered like a lamb and an ox, likewise adding the conjunction. But we have shown in its place f) that nothing is to be supplied there, and that in Hebrew כבש אלוף is a tame lamb, and that الوف [alūf] aluph is still taken in this sense among the Arabs today.


Plus in iis est rationis, qui חפרפרות chapharpheroth talpas esse volunt in his Es. II, 20. In illa die projiciet homo idola sua argentea, et idola sua aurea, quae ad adorandum sibi fecerat, לחפרפרות ולעטלפים, ad chaphorpheroth (seu talpas) et vespertiliones. Sed ad hanc vocem multa notanda: quorum primum II, 449 hoc esto, quod, quamvis vox una sit, tamen divisim scribitur לחפר פרות, quasi duae essent voces, quomodo nonnullae aliae. Sic 2 Par. XXXIV, 6. in pleris- col. 1032 que editionibus scribitur בחר בתיהם pro בחרבותיהם, malleis eorum. Ierem. XLVI, 20. יפה פיה pro יפהפיה, formosissima. Thren. IV, 3. כי ענים pro כיענים, ut struthiones, Ezech. XXVII, 6. בת אשורים pro בתאשורים, buxis. Idem in hac voce accidit, ut in duas divelleretur. Unde est, quod quidam explicant tanquam divisas voces. Puta ad fossorem fructuum; quasi sit avis genus, sic appellata, quod arborum fructus perforet atque pertundat. Vel ad fodiendum scrobes, quasi פירות sit pro חפירות, quomodo scrobes Hebraei vocant. Sed certum est, veteres interpretes, nempe Septuaginta, Seniores, Aquilam, Symmachum, Theodotionem, Hieronymum, Chaldaeum, Syrum, Arabem, una voce legisse לחפרפרות; quia una voce illam expresserunt. Iarchius quoque et Aben Ezra vocem unicam esse sentiunt. At unica illa vox varie explicatur. Seniores τὰ μάταια, vana reddunt; Aquila ὄρυγας, fossuras; Symmachus ἄκαρ-πα, infructuosa; Theodotion ipsum verbum Hebraicum posuit ἀφαρφερώθ Chaldaeus טעותא, idola; Syrus ܣܪܝܩܘܬܐ, vanitates; Aben Ezra putat esse שם עוף יעוף בלילה כעטלף ומביא עצמו ביום במקום סתר nomen avis, quae noctu volat vespertilionis instar, et interdiu se subducit in occultum locum. Quae singula expendere nostri otii non est (6). Et monuisse sufficiet, his omnibus merito suo praeferri e nostris Hieronymum, et ex Hebraeis R. Selomonem, qui talpas hic intelligunt. Nam a verbo חפר chaphar, quod fodere est, commodissime nominantur animalia maxime ὀρυκτικὰ, quaeque in fodiendo totam aetatem degunt. Et, quod jam supra g) obiter attigimus, ideo in חפרפרות chaphorpheroth, Radicales geminantur, ut significatio sit intensior. Tale אדמדם adamdem, pro summe rubro; ירקרק jerakrak, pro summe flavo; שחרחר secharchor, pro valde fusco; עקלקל akalkal, pro summe tortuoso; הפכפך haphachphach, pro summe versatili; פתלתל pethalthol, pro summe contorto; יפהפיה jephephija, pro summe pulchra. Praeterea haec eadem versio jungit talpas vespertilionibus, quae sunt animalia, in multis similia, quamvis unum sub terra repat, alterum in aërem volatu se attollat. Primo enim, utrumque vile est et immundum animalculum. Secundo, utrumque ad murinum genus aliquo modo refertur. Quod de talpa h) jam probatum est. Et de vespertilione neminem latet. Hinc apud Nonnium Varro, in Agathone, Factus sum vespertilio, neque in muribus plane, neque in volucribus sum. In Aesopo pro ave captus a mustela vespertilio, II, 450 ut evaderet, ἔλεγεν, ὀυκ ὄρνις, ἀλλὰ μῦς εἶναι, se non avem esse, sed murem. Scaliger mediam habere naturam contendit inter soricem et hirundinem. Proinde apud Eustathium τρισμὸς muri et vespertilioni communis est. Et vespertilionem Victorinus in libro De orthographia nominat soricem avem; Kimchius העטלף בעל כנפים, murem alatum; Lombardi ratto penago, id est, murem pennatum; Hispani morcego, id est, murem caecum; Galli chauve-souris, id est, calvum soricem. Tertio, talpa caeca est, et parum videt vespertilio. Unde Arabice خغاش chuphas. Nam خغش chaphas apud illos oculi parvitatem et debilitatem sonat: et اخغش achphaso est μύωψ. Proinde, ut talpae sub terra, ita vespertiliones interdiu in antris et locis obscuris degunt.

There is more reason in those who hold that חפרפרות chapharpheroth are moles in this passage, Isa 2:20. In that day a man shall cast away his idols of silver and his idols of gold, which he had made for himself to worship, לחפרפרות ולעטלפים, to the chaphorpheroth (or moles) and the bats. But much must be noted about this word. Let the first point II, 449 be this: although it is a single word, it is nevertheless written separately, לחפר פרות, as if there were two words, as happens with some others. Thus at 2 Chr 34:6 in most col. 1032 editions בחר בתיהם is written for בחרבותיהם, with their hammers. Jer 46:20. יפה פיה for יפהפיה, most beautiful. Lam 4:3. כי ענים for כיענים, like ostriches; Ezek 27:6. בת אשורים for בתאשורים, of boxwood. The same happened with this word, so that it was split in two. Hence some explain it as though the words were separate: for instance, to the digger of fruits, as if it were a kind of bird so called because it pierces and bores through the fruits of trees; or to the digging of pits, as if פירות stood for חפירות, which is what the Hebrews call pits. But it is certain that the ancient interpreters, namely the Septuagint, the Elders, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, Jerome, the Chaldee, the Syriac and the Arabic, read לחפרפרות as one word, since they rendered it by one word. Iarchius and Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] also hold that it is a single word. But this single word is explained in various ways. The Elders render τὰ μάταια [ta mataia], vain things; Aquila ὄρυγας [orygas], diggings; Symmachus ἄκαρπα [akarpa], fruitless things; Theodotion put the Hebrew word itself, ἀφαρφερώθ [apharpherōth]; the Chaldee טעותא, idols; the Syriac ܣܪܝܩܘܬܐ [סריקותא], vanities; Aben Ezra thinks it is שם עוף יעוף בלילה כעטלף ומביא עצמו ביום במקום סתר, the name of a bird which flies by night like a bat and by day withdraws into a hidden place. To weigh each of these is not for our present leisure R6. It will suffice to point out that, deservedly, all of these are surpassed by Jerome among our writers, and among the Hebrews by R. Selomo, who understand moles here. For from the verb חפר chaphar, which means to dig, animals that are supremely ὀρυκτικὰ [oryktika], and that spend their whole life digging, are most fittingly named. And, as we already touched on in passing above g), in חפרפרות chaphorpheroth the radicals are doubled so that the meaning may be intensified. So too אדמדם adamdem for intensely red; ירקרק jerakrak for intensely yellow; שחרחר secharchor for very dark; עקלקל akalkal for exceedingly winding; הפכפך haphachphach for exceedingly changeable; פתלתל pethalthol for exceedingly twisted; יפהפיה jephephija for exceedingly beautiful. Moreover, this same rendering joins moles with bats, which are animals alike in many respects, although the one creeps beneath the earth and the other rises into the air in flight. First, both are lowly and unclean little animals. Second, both are in some way referred to the mouse kind. This has already been proved of the mole h), and in the case of the bat it is known to everyone. Hence in Nonius, Varro says in the Agathon: I have become a bat; I am neither wholly among the mice nor among the birds. In Aesop a bat, caught by a weasel as a bird, II, 450 in order to escape ἔλεγεν, ὀυκ ὄρνις, ἀλλὰ μῦς εἶναι [elegen, ouk ornis, alla mys einai], said that it was not a bird but a mouse. Scaliger maintains that it has a nature midway between the shrew and the swallow. Accordingly in Eustathius τρισμὸς [trismos] is common to the mouse and the bat. And Victorinus in his book De orthographia calls the bat sorex avis [bird-shrew]; Kimchi calls it העטלף בעל כנפים, a winged mouse; the Lombards ratto penago, that is, feathered mouse; the Spaniards morcego, that is, blind mouse; the French chauve-souris, that is, bald shrew. Third, the mole is blind, and the bat sees little. Hence in Arabic it is خغاش [khughāsh] chuphas. For خغش [khaghash] chaphas among them denotes smallness and weakness of the eyes, and اخغش [akhghash] achphaso is μύωψ [myōps]. Accordingly, as moles live beneath the earth, so bats spend the day in caves and dark places.


— — — lucemque perosi
Nocte volant, seroque tenent a vespere nomen i).

— — — and, hating the light,
they fly by night, and take their name from the late evening i).


Quod maxime ad rem facit. Idola enim dicuntur ad talpas et vespertiliones projici, cum e sublimi loco, in quo eminebant, tanquam in tenebras detruduntur, ut ne amplius superstitiosis hominibus suo fulgore illudant. Et videtur col. 1033 fuisse apud Hebraeos proverbialis locutio, qua ad talpas et vespertiliones projici dicebatur, quod erat plane despectum atque in summo contemtu. Proinde recte Kimchius haec dici vult דרך בזיון, id est, per modum contemtus. Quamvis etiam ad literam id impleverit Iacobus Patriarcha, cum idola suae familiae infodit sub terebintho, Gen. XXXV, 4. Aliter Hieronymus, In die illa projiciet homo idola, etc. quae fecerat sibi, ut adoraret, talpas et vespertiliones. Quomodo etiam ex Hebraeis Rabbi Selomo. Quod ideo minus placet, licet Hebraea id ferre possint; quia, talpas et vespertiliones a veteribus pro diis fuisse cultos, nusquam legi.

This is very much to the point. For idols are said to be cast to the moles and the bats when they are thrust down, as it were into darkness, from the lofty place in which they stood out, so that they may no longer deceive superstitious people with their splendour. And among the Hebrews there seems col. 1033 to have been a proverbial expression by which something utterly despised and held in the greatest contempt was said to be cast to the moles and the bats. Accordingly Kimchi rightly holds that this is said דרך בזיון, that is, by way of contempt. Although the Patriarch Jacob also fulfilled it literally when he buried the idols of his household under the terebinth, Gen. XXXV, 4. Jerome renders it otherwise: In that day a man shall cast away the idols, etc. which he had made for himself to worship, moles and bats. So also, among the Hebrews, Rabbi Solomon. This pleases me less, although the Hebrew could bear it, because I have nowhere read that moles and bats were worshipped as gods by the ancients.


Quis nescit, Volusi Bithynice, qualia demens
Aegyptus portenta colat? — — —

Who does not know, Bithynian Volusius, what monsters mad Egypt worships? — — —


Tamen ne in Aegypto quidem eo usque descendit idololatrarum vesanus furor. Quamvis huic sit proximum, quod μυγάλην, id est, murem araneum, colebant Athribitae, ut testatur Strabo lib. 7. Ut Musoritas taceam, Christianos haereticos, a quibus cultos fuisse sorices legitur in Philastrio (7).

Yet not even in Egypt did the insane frenzy of the idolaters descend so far. Though the nearest thing to it is that the Athribites worshipped the μυγάλην [mygalēn], that is, the shrew-mouse, as Strabo testifies in book 7. Not to mention the Musorites, heretical Christians, by whom shrews are read in Philastrius to have been worshipped R7.


II, 451 Inter Opera Hieronymi extat Liber nominum, a Philone inchoatus, ab Origene auctus, et ab Hieronymo perfectus, in quo explicantur nomina propria, quotquot extant in Prophetarum libris. In his פרפר Farfar, fluvii Damasceni nomen, 2 Reg. V, 12. talpam explicari videas; cujus explicationis auctor, quisquis est, putavit, פרפר decurtatum fuisse ex praecedenti חפרפר. Quomodo fossa in Talmude פירה per aphaeresin dicitur pro חפירא.

II, 451 Among the works of Jerome there is extant a Book of Names, begun by Philo, enlarged by Origen, and completed by Jerome, in which are explained all the proper names that occur in the books of the Prophets. Among these you may see פרפר Farfar, the name of a river of Damascus, 2 Reg. V, 12., explained as mole; the author of this explanation, whoever he is, thought that פרפר had been shortened from the preceding חפרפר. In the same way in the Talmud a ditch is called פירה by aphaeresis for חפירא.


Talpa immerito in lege immundis animalibus accensetur, cum neque bisulca sit, neque ruminet. Praeterea caecitate sua typus est eorum, quorum mentes excaecavit Deus hujus saeculi, ne iis oboriatur splendor Evangelii, 2 Cor. IV, 4. Et dum in terra fodienda jugiter occupatur, refert eos homines, qui nihil nisi terrestria curant, Philipp. III, 19. et quorsum sapientia terrena est, animalis, diabolica, Iacobi III, 15. At mustelam, quam interpretes per vocem חולד choled designari voluerunt hactenus, significare τὰ δειλὰ, καὶ ἄνανδρα, καὶ ψοφοδεῆ τῶν κλεπτῶν γένη supra nos docuit Cyrillus, ut a nobis emendatus est. Quale illud in Aristea, Κακοποιητικὸς ὁ τρόπος ἐστὶ καὶ γαλῆς, καὶ μυῶν· Malefici sunt mores tam mustelae, quam murium. Et paullo post, Τότε τῆς γαλῆς γέ-νος ἰδιάζον ἐστί. χωρὶς γὰρ τοῦ προειρημένου, ἔχει λυμαντικὸν κατάστημα· διὰ γὰρ τῶν ὤτων συλλαμβάνει, τεκνοποιεῖ δὲ τῷ στόματι. Quod ita in Hebraeo: הנה עוד בסגולת טבעו התועבה הזאת שהנקבה תהר מאזנה ותלד מפיה, Ecce insuper inter propria naturae ejus est haec abominatio, quod foemina aure concipit, et ore parit. Et Algiahid, haec invertens, Aristotelem docuisse fingit, in libris De natura et proprietatibus animalium, ان الانثي من بنات عرس تلقح من افواهها وتلد من اذانها foeminas in mustelis ore concipere, et aure parere. Tamen in scriptis Aristotelis nihil occurrit simile. Quin eos, qui mustelam ore parere nugantur, non refellit modo, sed et fabulae originem aperit libri tertii De generatione animalium capite sexto; ubi, postquam mustelae vulvam eodem modo se habere dixit, quo reliquorum quadrupedum, neque foetum inde posse ad os devenire, addit, natam esse hanc opinionem διὰ τὸ τίκτειν πάμπαν τὴν γαλῆν σμικρὰ, τῷ δὲ στόματι πολλάκις μεταφέρειν τοὺς νεοττοὺς, ex eo, quod mustela catulos parit parvos admodum, II, 452 eosque ore saepe transfert. At aliud mihi se offert, quod videtur vero similius. Puto, ad mustelam translatum, quod in mustelo pisce veteres observaverunt. Quippe etiam ὁ γαλεὸς, seu mustelus piscis creditur ore parere. Aelianus Hi- storiae libri secundi capite quinquagesimo quinto, Ὁ γαλεὸς ὠδίνει διὰ τοῦ στό- col. 1034 ματος ἐν τῇ θαλάττῃ, Mustelus in mari per os parit. Et libri noni capite sexagesimo quinto, Οἱ μυούμενοι τοῖν Θεοῖν οὐκ ἂν πάσαιντο γαλεοῦ φασιν· οὐ γὰρ εἶναι αὐτὸν καθαρὸν ὄψον ἐπεὶ τῷ στόματι τίκτει. Dearum (nempe Cereris et Proserpinae) sacerdotes ajunt, mustelum piscem nunquam edere: neque enim mun- dum esse cibum, quoniam ore parit. Et ideo creditur ore parere, quia parvulos suos quandoque in os recipit, unde exeuntes qui vident, hunc partum esse sibi fingunt. Quod ipse Philosophus obiter tangit, cum de mustelis, seu galeis piscibus dicit Historiae libri sexti capite decimo, Ἐξαφιᾶσι καὶ δέχονται εἰς ἑαυ-τοὺς τοὺς νεοττούς· Foetus suos emissos intra se ipsos recipiunt. Sed alii multo disertius. Antigonus Historia vigesima quinta, Τῶν δὲ γαλεῶν τὰ ἔμβρυα, ἐξί-όντα ἐκ τῆς κοιλίας, νέμεται· καὶ πάλιν ἐκδύεται (lege εἰσδύεται) κατὰ τὸ στό-μα. Galeorum foetus, ex utero exeuntes, pascunt; rursusque per os intrant. Athenaeus libri septimi capite duodecimo, Τίκτει δὲ ὁ γαλεὸς τὰ πλεῖστα τρία, καὶ εἰσδέχεται τὰ γεννηθέντα εἰς τὸ στόμα,. καὶ πάλιν ἀφίησι· Plerumque pa- rit mustelus tres catulos, eosque ore recipit, et rursus emittit. Plutarchus catulos in ipso matris utero ex ovo formari dicit, deinde per os emitti tanquam secunda generatione. Verba sunt in libro Utra anim. Τίκτουσι μὲν γὰρ ὠὸν, εἶτα ζῶον, οὐκ ἐκτὸς, ἀλλὰ ἐντὸς ἐν ἑαυτοῖς. καὶ τρέφουσιν οὕτως, καὶ φέρουσιν, ὥσπερ ἐκ δευτέρας γενέσεως. Et in Περὶ Φιλοστοργίας dicit emissos rursus ad-mittere, et dormientes suis visceribus involvere: Οἱ γαλεοὶ ζωογονοῦσι μὲν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς, ἐκβαίνειν δὲ παρέχουσιν ἐκτὸς, καὶ νέμεσθαι τοῖς σκύμνοις, εἶτα πά-λιν ἀναλαμβάνουσι, καὶ περιπτύσσουσιν ἐγκοιμώμενοι τοῖς σπλάγχνοις. Aelia- nus etiam libri secundi capite quinquagesimo quinto, Πάλιν τε εἰσδέχεται τὰ βρέφη, κἀνεμεῖ ταῖς αὐταῖς ὁδοῖς ζῶντα, καὶ ἀπαθῆ· Foetus (ore) denuo re- cipit, eademque via revomit vivos et incolumes. Nempe in subito metu illis ita consulit. Idem Aelianus libri noni capite sexagesimo quinto, Οὐ τίκτειν δὲ αὐ-τὸν ἔνιοι λέγουσιν· ἀλλὰ, δείσαντά τι τῶν ἐπιβουλευόντων, τὰ σκυλάκια κα-ταπίνειν, καὶ ἀποκρύπτειν. εἶτα τοῦ φοβήσαντος παραδραμόντος, ζῶντα αὖθις ἀνεμεῖν. Eum non ore parere, quidam dicunt; sed, insidiarum timore per- culsum, catulos suos devorare et abscondere: deinde, metu ablato, vivos rursus evomere. Idem de glauco pisce multi referunt, ut idem Aelianus libri primi capite decimo sexto, Oppianus Halieuticῶν libri primi versu 749. Phile capite sexagesimo nono: Tzetzes etiam Chiliados quartae Historia centesima vigesima sexta, glaucum, canem et galeum scribit in metu catulos abscondere, glaucum et canem in ore, et galeum in ventre, καὶ πάλιν ταῦτα γεννᾷν, τοῦ φόβου II, 453 παρελθόντος, et eos rursus parere, cum praeteriit timor. Itaque ex hac nube testium apparet, non τὴν γαλῆν, id est, mustelam quadrupedem, sed τὸν γα-λεὸν, id est, mustelum piscem, catulos ex ore emittere; quod aut verum esse partum, aut partus instar se habere creditum. Merito igitur Isidorus Originum libri duodecimi capite tertio, eos refellit, qui dicunt, mustelam aure concipere, et ore effundere partum (ita legendum, non, ut vulgo, ore concipere, et aure, etc. quamvis hoc sequantur Arabes). Et ore quidem parere mustelam multi dixerunt, ut ex Philosopho scimus. Sed aure concipere nescio an quisquam dixerit ante Aristeam, qui fabulam videtur ideo sic adornasse, ut mustela delatorum et calumniatorum esset typus. Illi enim, inquit, alios malis involvunt, ὅσα διὰ ἀκοῆς λαβόντες, ταῦτα τῷ λόγῳ σωματοποιήσαντες, ea, quae auribus acceperant, verbis quasi corporantes, id est, exaggerantes, et in majus augentes: quae nova et prorsus inusitata est acceptio verbi σωματοποιεῖν. Falsus quoque Barnabas, ut in mustelam horribile fellatorum crimen impingat, illam ore parere non dicit, sed κύειν, concipere. Ἀλλὰ, inquit, καὶ τὴν γαλῆν ἐμίσησε καλῶς. οὐ μὴ γάρ φησιν, ὁμοιωθήσῃ τοῖς τοιούτοις, οἵους ἀκούομεν ἀνομίαν ποιοῦντας τῷ στόματι, διὰ ἀκαθαρσίαν, etc. Τὸ γὰρ ζῶον τοῦτο τῷ στόματι κύει. Itaque in eo loco non putamus quidquam mutandum: neque hac in parte accedimus col. 1035 viri optimi, doctissimi, et nobis amicissimi sententiae, qui in Notis ad hanc Epistolam, mirum, quam eruditis! censet, hunc locum esse corruptum, et ex Aristea restituendum. Aegyptii quoque voluere lasciviae tribadum in mustelis esse exemplum, ut docet Horus Hieroglyphicῶν libri secundi capite trigesimo quarto: sed alii honestiores apud Plutarchum in Iside statuunt τὴν γαλῆν κατὰ τὸ οὖς ὀχευομένην, τῷ δὲ στόματι τίκτουσαν, εἴκασμα τῆς τοῦ λόγου γενέσεως εἶναι, mustelam, cum aure ineatur, et ore pariat, sermonis generationem referre. Ita nonnunquam

The mole is deservedly counted among the unclean animals in the Law, since it neither divides the hoof nor chews the cud. Moreover, by its blindness it is a type of those whose minds the god of this world has blinded, lest the splendour of the Gospel should dawn upon them, 2 Cor 4:4. And while it is continually busy digging in the earth, it represents those men who care for nothing but earthly things, Philipp. III, 19. and whose wisdom is earthly, sensual, devilish, Iacobi III, 15. But the weasel (mustela), which the interpreters have hitherto wanted to be designated by the word חולד choled, signifies, as Cyril taught us above (as emended by us), τὰ δειλὰ, καὶ ἄνανδρα, καὶ ψοφοδεῆ τῶν κλεπτῶν γένη [ta deila, kai ananda, kai psophodeē tōn kleptōn genē]. Of the same sort is that in Aristeas: Κακοποιητικὸς ὁ τρόπος ἐστὶ καὶ γαλῆς, καὶ μυῶν [Kakopoiētikos ho tropos esti kai galēs, kai myōn]; Mischievous are the habits both of the weasel and of mice. And a little later: Τότε τῆς γαλῆς γένος ἰδιάζον ἐστί. χωρὶς γὰρ τοῦ προειρημένου, ἔχει λυμαντικὸν κατάστημα· διὰ γὰρ τῶν ὤτων συλλαμβάνει, τεκνοποιεῖ δὲ τῷ στόματι [Tote tēs galēs genos idiazon esti. chōris gar tou proeirēmenou, echei lymantikon katastēma; dia gar tōn ōtōn syllambanei, teknopoiei de tō stomati]. Which in the Hebrew runs thus: הנה עוד בסגולת טבעו התועבה הזאת שהנקבה תהר מאזנה ותלד מפיה, Behold, moreover, among the peculiarities of its nature is this abomination, that the female conceives through the ear and gives birth through the mouth. And Algiahid, inverting this, pretends that Aristotle taught, in the books On the Nature and Properties of Animals, ان الانثي من بنات عرس تلقح من افواهها وتلد من اذانها [inna al-unthī min banāt ʿirs tulqaḥ min afwāhihā wa-talid min ādhānihā] that the females among weasels conceive through the mouth and give birth through the ear. Yet nothing similar occurs in the writings of Aristotle. Indeed, those who idly claim that the weasel gives birth through the mouth he not only refutes but also reveals the origin of the tale, in book 3 On the Generation of Animals, chapter 6. There, after saying that the womb of the weasel is arranged in the same way as that of other quadrupeds, and that the foetus cannot pass from it to the mouth, he adds that this opinion arose διὰ τὸ τίκτειν πάμπαν τὴν γαλῆν σμικρὰ, τῷ δὲ στόματι πολλάκις μεταφέρειν τοὺς νεοττοὺς [dia to tiktein pampan tēn galēn smikra, tō de stomati pollakis metapherein tous neottous], from the fact that the weasel bears very small young, II, 452 and often carries them about in its mouth. But another explanation presents itself to me, which seems closer to the truth. I think that what the ancients observed in the fish called mustelus [dogfish] was transferred to the weasel. For ὁ γαλεὸς [ho galeos], or the fish mustelus, is also believed to give birth through the mouth. Aelian, History, book 2, chapter 55: Ὁ γαλεὸς ὠδίνει διὰ τοῦ στόματος ἐν τῇ θαλάττῃ [Ho galeos ōdinei dia tou stomatos en tē thalattē], The mustelus gives birth in the sea through the mouth. col. 1034 And in book 9, chapter 65: Οἱ μυούμενοι τοῖν Θεοῖν οὐκ ἂν πάσαιντο γαλεοῦ φασιν· οὐ γὰρ εἶναι αὐτὸν καθαρὸν ὄψον ἐπεὶ τῷ στόματι τίκτει [Hoi myoumenoi toin Theoin ouk an pasainto galeou phasin; ou gar einai auton katharon opson epei tō stomati tiktei]. They say that the priests of the Goddesses (namely Ceres and Proserpina) never eat the mustelus fish, for it is not clean food, since it gives birth through the mouth. And it is believed to give birth through the mouth because it sometimes takes its little ones into its mouth, and those who see them coming out imagine this to be a birth. The Philosopher himself touches on this in passing when he says of the mustelus or galeus fishes, in History, book 6, chapter 10: Ἐξαφιᾶσι καὶ δέχονται εἰς ἑαυτοὺς τοὺς νεοττούς [Exaphiasi kai dechontai eis heautous tous neottous]; They take their young back into themselves after letting them out. But others say it much more explicitly. Antigonus, History 25: Τῶν δὲ γαλεῶν τὰ ἔμβρυα, ἐξιόντα ἐκ τῆς κοιλίας, νέμεται· καὶ πάλιν ἐκδύεται (read εἰσδύεται [eisdyetai]) κατὰ τὸ στόμα [Tōn de galeōn ta embrya, exionta ek tēs koilias, nemetai; kai palin ekdyetai … kata to stoma]. The foetuses of the galei, coming out of the womb, feed, and enter again through the mouth. Athenaeus, book 7, chapter 12: Τίκτει δὲ ὁ γαλεὸς τὰ πλεῖστα τρία, καὶ εἰσδέχεται τὰ γεννηθέντα εἰς τὸ στόμα,. καὶ πάλιν ἀφίησι [Tiktei de ho galeos ta pleista tria, kai eisdechetai ta gennēthenta eis to stoma, kai palin aphiēsi]; The mustelus usually bears three young, and takes them into its mouth, and lets them out again. Plutarch says that the young are formed from an egg within the mother's womb itself, and then let out through the mouth as if by a second generation. The words are in the book Utra anim.: Τίκτουσι μὲν γὰρ ὠὸν, εἶτα ζῶον, οὐκ ἐκτὸς, ἀλλὰ ἐντὸς ἐν ἑαυτοῖς. καὶ τρέφουσιν οὕτως, καὶ φέρουσιν, ὥσπερ ἐκ δευτέρας γενέσεως [Tiktousi men gar ōon, eita zōon, ouk ektos, alla entos en heautois. kai trephousin houtōs, kai pherousin, hōsper ek deuteras geneseōs]. And in Περὶ Φιλοστοργίας [Peri Philostorgias] he says that they take back those they have let out, and wrap them, as they sleep, in their own entrails: Οἱ γαλεοὶ ζωογονοῦσι μὲν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς, ἐκβαίνειν δὲ παρέχουσιν ἐκτὸς, καὶ νέμεσθαι τοῖς σκύμνοις, εἶτα πάλιν ἀναλαμβάνουσι, καὶ περιπτύσσουσιν ἐγκοιμώμενοι τοῖς σπλάγχνοις [Hoi galeoi zōogonousi men en heautois, ekbainein de parechousin ektos, kai nemesthai tois skymnois, eita palin analambanousi, kai periptyssousin enkoimōmenoi tois splanchnois]. Aelian too, book 2, chapter 55: Πάλιν τε εἰσδέχεται τὰ βρέφη, κἀνεμεῖ ταῖς αὐταῖς ὁδοῖς ζῶντα, καὶ ἀπαθῆ [Palin te eisdechetai ta brephē, kanemei tais autais hodois zōnta, kai apathē]; It takes its young back (through the mouth) and by the same way vomits them up again alive and unharmed. That is, it protects them in this way in sudden fear. The same Aelian, book 9, chapter 65: Οὐ τίκτειν δὲ αὐτὸν ἔνιοι λέγουσιν· ἀλλὰ, δείσαντά τι τῶν ἐπιβουλευόντων, τὰ σκυλάκια καταπίνειν, καὶ ἀποκρύπτειν. εἶτα τοῦ φοβήσαντος παραδραμόντος, ζῶντα αὖθις ἀνεμεῖν [Ou tiktein de auton enioi legousin; alla, deisanta ti tōn epibouleuontōn, ta skylakia katapinein, kai apokryptein. eita tou phobēsantos paradramontos, zōnta authis anemein]. Some say that it does not give birth through the mouth, but that, struck with fear of some attacker, it swallows its young and hides them; then, when the fear is removed, it vomits them up again alive. Many report the same of the glaucus fish, as the same Aelian, book 1, chapter 16; Oppian, Halieutica, book 1, line 749; Phile, chapter 69. Tzetzes too, Chiliad 4, History 126, writes that the glaucus, the dogfish and the galeus hide their young in fear, the glaucus and the dogfish in the mouth, the galeus in the belly, καὶ πάλιν ταῦτα γεννᾷν, τοῦ φόβου [kai palin tauta gennan, tou phobou] II, 453 παρελθόντος [parelthontos], and bring them forth again when the fear has passed. Thus from this cloud of witnesses it appears that it is not τὴν γαλῆν [tēn galēn], that is, the four-footed weasel, but τὸν γαλεὸν [ton galeon], that is, the mustelus fish, that emits its young from the mouth; and that this was believed either to be a true birth or to be like a birth. Rightly, therefore, Isidore, Etymologies, book 12, chapter 3, refutes those who say that the weasel conceives through the ear and pours forth its offspring through the mouth (so it must be read, not, as commonly, conceives through the mouth and through the ear, etc., although the Arabs follow the latter). And many indeed said that the weasel gives birth through the mouth, as we know from the Philosopher. But whether anyone said that it conceives through the ear before Aristeas, I do not know; he seems to have embellished the tale in this way so that the weasel might be a type of informers and slanderers.
