For these, he says, entangle others in evils, ὅσα διὰ ἀκοῆς λαβόντες, ταῦτα τῷ λόγῳ σωματοποιήσαντες [hosa dia akoēs labontes, tauta tō logō sōmatopoiēsantes], as it were embodying in words what they had received through their ears, that is, exaggerating and magnifying them: which is a new and wholly unusual sense of the verb σωματοποιεῖν [sōmatopoiein]. Barnabas too is mistaken when, in order to fasten on the weasel the horrible crime of fellators, he says not that it gives birth through the mouth but κύειν [kyein], conceives. Ἀλλὰ, he says, καὶ τὴν γαλῆν ἐμίσησε καλῶς. οὐ μὴ γάρ φησιν, ὁμοιωθήσῃ τοῖς τοιούτοις, οἵους ἀκούομεν ἀνομίαν ποιοῦντας τῷ στόματι, διὰ ἀκαθαρσίαν, etc. Τὸ γὰρ ζῶον τοῦτο τῷ στόματι κύει [Alla … kai tēn galēn emisēse kalōs. ou mē gar phēsin, homoiōthēsē tois toioutois, hoious akouomen anomian poiountas tō stomati, dia akatharsian … To gar zōon touto tō stomati kyei]. Therefore we do not think anything should be changed in that passage; nor in this respect do we agree col. 1035 with the opinion of a most excellent and most learned man, and a very dear friend of ours, who in his Notes on this Epistle (how learned they are!) holds that this passage is corrupt and must be restored from Aristeas. The Egyptians also wanted the weasels to be an example of the lewdness of tribades, as Horapollo teaches, Hieroglyphica, book 2, chapter 34; but others, more decent, in Plutarch's Isis, hold that τὴν γαλῆν κατὰ τὸ οὖς ὀχευομένην, τῷ δὲ στόματι τίκτουσαν, εἴκασμα τῆς τοῦ λόγου γενέσεως εἶναι [tēn galēn kata to ous ocheuomenēn, tō de stomati tiktousan, eikasma tēs tou logou geneseōs einai], the weasel, since it is covered through the ear and gives birth through the mouth, represents the generation of speech. Maxima de nihilo nascitur historia.

A very great history is born from nothing.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 435 That the Syriac word means cat, and not weasel, was recently argued by Geo. Guil. Kirsch in the Preface to the Chronicle of Gregory Barhebraeus translated into Latin, p. VIII. He was moved by two passages of Barhebraeus in which he judges that no meaning other than cat fits the word ܟܟܘܣܬܐ [ככוסתא]. One of these passages is on p. 216, line 16 of the Syriac text, where Barhebraeus speaks of a great famine that arose in the region of Khorasan: So great was the famine that a litra of bread was sold for one gold denarius, and people ate dogs and ܟܟܘܫܬܐ [ככושתא]. On these words Kirsch remarks: "Since the meaning weasel hardly fits, it is not difficult to guess what ܟܟܘܫܬܐ [ככושתא] was. Yet this passage, which would not settle the matter, II, 436 should be compared with another, much clearer one, which leaves no room for doubt. On p. 268, line 4, he describes a famine that afflicted above all the city of Damascus, of whose inhabitants, who numbered 300,000 before the famine, he reports that only 3,000 survived it. He then continues: Because of this failure of the grain supply the mice, troublesome to people, increased beyond measure, because the ܟܪܟܘܫܬܐ [כרכושתא] were lacking, having long since been eaten by the people. Since ܥܘܟܒܪ̈ܐ [עוכברא] are by general agreement mice, it is evident without my pointing it out that ܟܪܟܘܫܬܐ [כרכושתא] means cat, the animal more hostile to mice than any other. Although I do not deny that weasels also hunt mice, everyone will think of the cat as soon as the question arises which kind of animal, when lacking, lets mice multiply." So Kirsch. Against this, however, Lorsbach rightly objected, in the book entitled Archiv für die morgenländische Litteratur, vol. 1, p. 204, first, the corresponding Chaldee word כרכושתא, which Bochart has amply proved on this very page to mean weasel, not cat. The name was aptly given to the weasel from its agile and swift movement, for כרכש, كركس [karkas], means he moved, drove to and fro. As to the point on which Kirsch's view chiefly rests, that mice multiplied when the animals called ܟܪܟܘܫܬܐ [כרכושתא] were lacking, Lorsbach answers well that weasels hunt mice no less than cats do, indeed better, because the slenderness of their bodies lets them get into mouse-holes more easily.

III. p. 82. 83 vocem Hebraeam interpretatus exploratorem vaccarum, avem quandam noctivagam significari contendit, quam vaccarum mammas exsugere fabulantur: Linnaeo audit Caprimulgus (Euro(Europaeus), II, 451 Germanis Nachtrabe. Quod doctum magis, quam vero simile, aut loco Iesaiano aptum videtur. Melius placet, quod attulit PAULUS in Clavi Philolog. in Iesaiam. Divisim is scribendum censet לחפר פרות, quod vertit foraminibus murium agrestium (חפר excavatum quid, foramen, Arab. حُفْرٌ, et פר mus agrestis, sive montanus, iuxta Arabum فَأْر). Favet huic interpretationi, quod לחפר פרות in paucis tantummodo codicibus conjunctim una voce scriptum reperitur.

R7 Rosenmüller, II, 450 Koppe held (in his notes on Lowth's Commentary on Isaiah) that the word חפרפר means two-legged jumping mice, without adequate reason; for this he was also criticized by Michaelis in the Supplemm. vol. 3, p. 876, who himself attempted other explanations, though no more certain ones. Oedmann, in the Vermischte Sammlungen, fascicle 3, p. 82. 83, interpreting the Hebrew word as spy of the cows, argues that it means a certain night-roving bird which, according to the fable, sucks the udders of cows: in Linnaeus it is called Caprimulgus (Europaeus), II, 451 in German Nachtrabe. This seems more learned than probable or suited to the passage of Isaiah. More satisfying is what Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)] offered in the Clavis Philolog. in Iesaiam. He thinks it should be written as two words, לחפר פרות, which he renders into the holes of field mice (חפר, something dug out, a hole, Arab. حُفْرٌ [ḥufr], and פר, a field mouse or mountain mouse, after the Arabic فَأْر [faʾr]). In favour of this interpretation is the fact that לחפר פרות is found written together as one word in only a few manuscripts.


Book 3, chapter 36: The kippod
------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/kippod.html

II, 454 col. 1035 CAP. XXXVI.

II, 454 col. 1035 Chapter 36.


Probatur, קפוד kippod esse Hericium et Hystricem.

It is proved that קפוד kippod is the hedgehog and the porcupine.


Tria elementa certant de animali קפוד kippod: quod alii terrae adscribunt, alii aquae, alii aëri cum volucribus. In primo ordine pono Graecos et Hieronymum; quibus קפוד kippod est ἐχῖνος hericius, nempe terrestris, qui aestate in sepibus, hyeme in truncis arborum, aut in terrae scrobibus degit. Alii aquaticum animal esse inferunt ex his Esa. XIV, 23. de Babylone, Ponam eam in possessionem hereditariam τοῦ kippod et stagna aquarum. Sed horum agmen aut bi-partitum est, aut tripartitum etiam. Pars testudinem esse vult, pars castorem, pars lutram. Nituntur omnes etymologia vocis. Nempe Esa. XXXVIII, 12. קפד est praecidere, ubi textor stamen praecidit, tela tota jam praetexta. H[?]s autem animalibus praecidendi mira vis. De castore res notissima. Animal est horrendi morsus (inquit Plinius libri octavi capite trigesimo), arbores juxta flumina, ut ferro caedit. Sed et lutram Varro libro quarto De lingua Latina di[?]i vult ἀπὸ τοῦ λύειν, quod succidere dicitur arborum radices in ripa, atque eas dissolvere. Eandem in testudine vim eo mirere magis, quod, cum illi dentes non sint, rostri tamen acie comminuit omnia. Rostri scilicet margines acuti sunt, superna parte inferiorem claudente pyxidum modo. Ita Plinius lib. 11. cap. 37. et lib. 9. cap. 10. Cui simile, quod de marina testudine legitur in Porta coeli fo[?]. col. 1036 34. a. ויש לה כח גדול בפיה ובשיניה ואם תקח אבן בפיה תשבור אותה בחוק גדול לחלקים קטנים, Ipsi est robur ingens in ore et dentibus. Et, si o[?] lapidem accipit, viribus magnis conterit eum in minutissimas partes. Huc accedi[?], quod Arabice, si utrique Kimchio fides, testudinis nomen est קנפאר, quod a[?]b Hebraeo קפוד non multum differt. Sed ab iis objicitur, qui in tertia sentent[?]a sunt, nempe קפוד kippod esse avis speciem: alibi ab Esaia et Sophonia kipp[?]d nominari cum avibus. Esaiae locus sic habet capitis trigesimi quarti capite und[?]-cimo, Possidebunt eum pelecanus et kippod. Nec multo aliter Sophonias capit[?]s secundi versu decimo quarto, Etiam pelecanus, etiam kippod in superliminarib[?]s ejus pernoctabunt. Rursus ab his dubitatur, quod avis genus sit kippod: ali[?]is noctuam explicantibus; aliis vulturem; aliis merulam; aliis butaurum, sive ard[?]-am stellarem; aliis cypselum, qui et apus; aliis plancum, aut aquilam anatariam[?]; et quid non? Et plerasque illas interpretationes ita inter se confert doctissim[?]s Fullerus Miscellaneorum libri primi capite decimo octavo, ut nullam rejiciat pra[?]-ter illam, quae sola vera est. Antiquissimam illam dico, qua קפוד kippod h[?]-ricius exponitur: cui firmandae multa faciunt.

Three elements contend over the animal קפוד kippod: some assign it to the earth, others to the water, others to the air along with the birds. In the first rank I place the Greeks and Jerome, for whom קפוד kippod is ἐχῖνος [echinos], the hedgehog, namely the land hedgehog, which lives in hedges in summer and in winter in tree trunks or in holes in the ground. Others infer that it is an aquatic animal from Isa 14:23, on Babylon: I will make it a hereditary possession of the kippod and pools of water. But the ranks of these are divided in two, or even in three. Some hold it to be the tortoise, some the beaver, some the otter. All rely on the etymology of the word. For in Isa 38:12. קפד means to cut off, where the weaver cuts off the warp when the whole web has been woven. And these animals have a remarkable power of cutting. With the beaver the matter is very well known. It is an animal with a fearsome bite (says Pliny, book 8, chapter 30); it cuts down trees by rivers as if with iron. But Varro too, in book 4 On the Latin Language, would have the otter [lutra] named from λύειν [lyein], because it is said to undercut the roots of trees on the bank and to loosen them. The same power in the tortoise is all the more remarkable because, though it has no teeth, it nevertheless crushes everything with the edge of its beak. That is, the edges of the beak are sharp, the upper part closing over the lower in the manner of a box. So Pliny, book 11, ch. 37, and book 9, ch. 10. Similar to this is what is read of the sea turtle in Porta coeli, fol. col. 1036 34a: ויש לה כח גדול בפיה ובשיניה ואם תקח אבן בפיה תשבור אותה בחוק גדול לחלקים קטנים, It has enormous strength in its mouth and teeth. And if it takes a stone into its mouth, it crushes it with great force into the tiniest pieces. Add to this that in Arabic, if both Kimchis are to be believed, the name of the tortoise is קנפאר, which does not differ much from the Hebrew קפוד. But those who hold the third opinion, namely that קפוד kippod is a species of bird, object that elsewhere kippod is named by Isaiah and Zephaniah together with birds. The passage of Isaiah, chapter 34, verse 11, reads thus: The pelican and the kippod shall possess it. And Zephaniah, chapter 2, verse 14, not very differently: Both the pelican and the kippod shall lodge on its lintels. Again, these are in doubt as to what kind of bird kippod is: some explain it as the owl; others as the vulture; others as the blackbird; others as the bittern, or starry heron; others as the cypselus, which is also the apus; others as the plancus, or duck-eagle[?]; and what not? And the most learned Fuller [=Nicholas Fuller, Miscellanea theologica / sacra (1612–22)], in his Miscellanea, book 1, chapter 18, compares most of those interpretations with one another in such a way that he rejects none except the one which alone is true. I mean that most ancient one, by which קפוד kippod is explained as the hedgehog; and many things serve to confirm it.


Primo, Graecorum auctoritas et Hieronymi, qui constanter ita exponu[?]t. Ab iis autem recedere tutum non puto, nisi graves causae subsint, quales h[?]c II, 455 nullas video. 2. Graecis Hebraeos addo, apud quorum doctissimos pridem invaluit haec sententia, קפוד esse hericium. Hispanica voce R. Nathan explicat ריצ"ו rizo, vel erizo; Italica Poniarius ריצ"יו riccio, Gallica Rabbi Selomo הריצ"ון herisson, Germanica Elias איג"יל Igel. Et in Talmude קפוד kippod, vel קופד kuphad, quod idem est in Chaldaica inflexione, saepe ponitur inter terrestres be-stias quadrupedes. Ut in Berachoth capite nono folio quinquagesimo septimo b. כל מיני חיות יפות לחלום חוץ מן הפיל והקוף והקפוד, Omnes ferarum species bonae sunt ad somnium (id est, boni ominis in somnis visae) praeter elephantem, simiam et kippod, id est, hericium. Nugatur enim R. Selomo, qui exponit cercopithecum. Et in tractatu Kelaim cap. octavo folio trigesimo secundo a. והקופד וחולדת הסניים, Et kuphad (hericius) et mustela ruborum. Et in Bava Kama capite septimo, אין מגדלין חתולים וקופדים, Non alunt feles, et kuphadim (hericios). Et in Sabbatho capite quinto folio quinquagesimo septimo b. ואין העגל יוצא בגימון ולא פרא בעור הקופד, Vitulus (die Sabbathi) non exit cum gemon, nec vacca cum pelle kuphad. גימון gemon Hebraeis puto esse κημὸν, camum, et vocem inde deduci; quamvis hoc vocabulo non designent camum quemvis, sed quo vitulus prohibetur, ne lactet. Aruch definit לוח בפיו שלא יוכל לשתות החלב, Tabulam, quae ori ejus inditur, ne possit lac exsugere. Graece πύσσαχον dixeris. Hesychius, Πύσσαχος· ξύλον καμπύλον τοῖς μόσχοις περὶ τοὺς μυκτῆρας τιθέμενον, ὃ κωλύει θηλάζειν· Lignum curvum vitulis circa nares appositum, quo prohibentur, ne lacteant. Et pellis kuphad (id est, hericii) vaccae mammis alligabatur eodem fine, id est, ne vel vitulus, vel aliud animal ipsam exsugeret. Rabbi Selomo in hunc locum, קופד שרץ הוא שנימיו חדים כמחט וקורין לו הריצון וקושרין עורו בדדי הפרה שלא יניקוה שרצים, Kuphad reptile est (ita Hebraei vocant minima quadrupedum), cujus pili in acus col. 1037 modum acuti sunt, vulgo vocatur herisson. Hujus pellis vaccae mammis alligatur, ne reptilia eas exsugant. Neque enim a solo vitulo lacti cavendum, sed et a serpentibus, e quorum numero boae aluntur primo bubuli lactis succo, unde nomen traxere. Ita Plinius libri octavi capite decimo quarto. Et, qui hunc sequitur, Solinus: Captat (boa) greges bubulos, et quae plurimo lacte rigua bos est, ejus se uberibus innectit, suctuque continuo saginata, etc. 4. Arabice denique قنفذ kunphud, Plurali قنافذ kanaphido, est hericius. Barbari interpretes scribunt caused, ceufud, ceufund, etc. Res notior est, quam ut probatione egeat. Tantum lectorem monebo, nomine قنفذ kunphud, praeter herinaceum, etiam hystricem contineri. Id clarum est ex Avicenna, qui inter species kunphud unum dicit esse montanum, spinas habentem missiles, cujus proprium nomen est دلدل duldul, id est, hystrix. Hinc in Damire hericii foemina vocatur أم دلدل mater τοῦ duldul, id est, hystricis. Et duldul, seu hystrix, ibidem definitur II, 456 عظيم القنافد, hericius major. Et juxta Algiahid, الفرق بين الدلدل والقنافد كالفرق بين البقر والجوامس والبخاتي من الابل العراب Duldul, et kanaphido (id est, hystrix, et hericii proprie dicti) non aliter differunt, quam a bubalis boves, et cameli Ba-ctriani ab Arabicis. Elmacinus denique Saracenicae Historiae libri primi capite quinto videtur per القنفد alkunphud hystricem potius quam hericium significasse, cum de Aisiae camelo scribit, صار كالقنفد من السهام Factus est ut alkunphud prae telis, id est, prae telorum copia, quibus transfixus est. Sed hac in parte habuerunt Arabes, quos sequerentur, Plinium et Oppianum: quorum ille libri octavi capite trigesimo quinto hystrices expresse ponit in herinaceorum genere; hic libri secundi Cynegeticῶν versu 603. echinorum terrestrium duo genera faciens, alios parvos et imbelles, alios μεγέθει πολὺ μείζονας, longe majores, et circumquaque horrentes — ἀρειοτέρῃσιν ἀκωκαῖς, majoribus cuspidibus, per majores illos echinos videtur hystrices intelligere. Sed et Suidae ἡ ὕστριξ hystrix est ὁ ἀκανθόχοιρος, ὁ χερσαῖος ἐχῖνος, porcus spinosus, hericius terrestris.

First, the authority of the Greeks and of Jerome, who consistently explain it so. I do not think it safe to depart from them unless there are weighty reasons, and here II, 455 I see none. 2. To the Greeks I add the Hebrews, among whose most learned men this opinion has long prevailed, that קפוד is the hedgehog. R. Nathan explains it with the Spanish word ריצ"ו rizo, or erizo; Poniarius with the Italian ריצ"יו riccio; Rabbi Selomo with the French הריצ"ון herisson; Elias [=Elijah Levita (1469–1549), author of the Aramaic lexicon Meturgeman and of Tishbi] with the German איג"יל Igel. And in the Talmud קפוד kippod, or קופד kuphad, which is the same in the Chaldee inflection, is often placed among land quadrupeds. Thus in Berachoth, chapter 9, folio 57b: כל מיני חיות יפות לחלום חוץ מן הפיל והקוף והקפוד, All species of wild beasts are good for a dream (that is, of good omen when seen in sleep), except the elephant, the ape and the kippod, that is, the hedgehog. For R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] talks nonsense when he explains it as the long-tailed monkey. And in the tractate Kelaim, ch. 8, folio 32a: והקופד וחולדת הסניים, And the kuphad (hedgehog) and the bramble weasel. And in Bava Kama, chapter 7: אין מגדלין חתולים וקופדים, They do not raise cats and kuphadim (hedgehogs). And in Sabbath, chapter 5, folio 57b: ואין העגל יוצא בגימון ולא פרא בעור הקופד, A calf may not go out (on the Sabbath) with a gemon, nor a cow with the skin of a kuphad. I think the Hebrew גימון gemon is κημὸν [kēmon], a muzzle, and that the word is derived from it; although by this term they do not mean any muzzle whatever, but the one by which a calf is prevented from sucking. The Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome] defines it: לוח בפיו שלא יוכל לשתות החלב, A board that is put in its mouth so that it cannot suck the milk. In Greek you would call it πύσσαχον [pyssachon]. Hesychius: Πύσσαχος· ξύλον καμπύλον τοῖς μόσχοις περὶ τοὺς μυκτῆρας τιθέμενον, ὃ κωλύει θηλάζειν· [Pyssachos; xylon kampylon tois moschois peri tous myktēras tithemenon, ho kōlyei thēlazein] A curved piece of wood placed around the nostrils of calves, by which they are prevented from sucking. And the skin of a kuphad (that is, of a hedgehog) was tied to the cow's udder for the same purpose, that is, so that neither the calf nor any other animal might suck it. Rabbi Selomo on this passage: קופד שרץ הוא שנימיו חדים כמחט וקורין לו הריצון וקושרין עורו בדדי הפרה שלא יניקוה שרצים, Kuphad is a creeping thing (so the Hebrews call the smallest quadrupeds) whose hairs are sharp like col. 1037 needles; it is commonly called herisson. Its skin is tied to the cow's udder so that creeping things may not suck it. For the milk had to be guarded not from the calf alone, but also from serpents, among which boas are fed at first on the juice of cow's milk, whence they took their name. So Pliny, book 8, chapter 14. And Solinus, who follows him: It (the boa) lies in wait for herds of cattle, and fastens itself to the udder of whichever cow is most abundant in milk, and fattened by continual sucking, etc. 4. Finally, in Arabic قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud, plural قنافذ [qanāfidh] kanaphido, is the hedgehog. Barbarous translators write caused, ceufud, ceufund, etc. The matter is too well known to need proof. I will only advise the reader that the name قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud includes, besides the hedgehog, also the porcupine. This is clear from Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)], who says that among the species of kunphud one is the mountain kind, having spines that can be shot, whose proper name is دلدل [duldul] duldul, that is, the porcupine. Hence in Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] the female hedgehog is called أم دلدل [umm duldul] mother τοῦ [tou] duldul, that is, of the porcupine. And duldul, or porcupine, is defined in the same place II, 456 as عظيم القنافد [ʿaẓīm al-qanāfid], the larger hedgehog. And according to Algiahid: الفرق بين الدلدل والقنافد كالفرق بين البقر والجوامس والبخاتي من الابل العراب [al-farq bayna al-duldul wa-al-qanāfid ka-al-farq bayna al-baqar wa-al-jawāmis wa-al-bakhātī min al-ibil al-ʿirāb] Duldul and kanaphido (that is, the porcupine and hedgehogs properly so called) differ no otherwise than oxen from buffaloes, and Bactrian camels from Arabian ones. Finally Elmacinus, in the Saracen History, book 1, chapter 5, seems to have meant by القنفد [al-qunfud] alkunphud the porcupine rather than the hedgehog, when he writes of Aisha's camel: صار كالقنفد من السهام [ṣāra ka-al-qunfud min al-sihām] It became like an alkunphud from the darts, that is, from the multitude of darts with which it was pierced. But in this the Arabs had Pliny and Oppian to follow: the former, in book 8, chapter 35, expressly places porcupines in the hedgehog kind; the latter, in book 2 of the Cynegetica, line 603, making two kinds of land hedgehogs, some small and unwarlike, others μεγέθει πολὺ μείζονας [megethei poly meizonas], far larger, and bristling all round — ἀρειοτέρῃσιν ἀκωκαῖς [areioterēsin akōkais], with stronger points, seems to understand porcupines by those larger hedgehogs. And for Suidas too ἡ ὕστριξ [hē hystrix], the porcupine, is ὁ ἀκανθόχοιρος, ὁ χερσαῖος ἐχῖνος [ho akanthochoiros, ho chersaios echinos], the spiny pig, the land hedgehog.


Iam, ne quis objiciat ex utroque Kimchio Arabum قنفذ kunphud esse testudinem, ajo, illos hac in parte graviter hallucinari. Cum Arabice testudo non dicatur kunphud, sed سلخفاة sulachpha, vel سلخفية sulachphia, quasi cortice, vel putamine latentem dicas: nempe خفا chapha est occultare; et سلخ silch, vel sulch, φολὶς cortex, proprie serpentis, sed et testudinis: ut γῆρας, quam vocem plerique usurpant pro leberide, seu spolio serpentis, sed et nonnulli pro χελωνίω, ut Aelianus Historiae lib. II. cap. 37. et Suidas in Φολίδωτον. At قنفذ kunphud esse hericium, nemo ibit inficias, qui Damirem legerit: ubi قنفذ kunphud cognominatur ابو الشوك abussuchi, id est, pater spinarum: et انقد ankado, id est, decorticator: et ابو سفين abusaphin, id est, pater, qui abradit, vel expolit; quia hujus col. 1038 cute vestes expoliuntur: et العساعس alasaiso, quia noctu vagatur. Id enim proprie est عس assa, ut et سري sara; unde proverbium apud illos in usu, اسري من قنفذ Magis noctivagus quam kunphud. Ibidem multa reperias, quae ad ejus descriptionem pertinent, in quibus haec eximia: القنفذ ان جاع صعد الكرم منكسا فيقطع العناقيد ويرمي بها ثم ينزل فياكل منها ما اطاق واذا كان له فراخ تمرغ في العناقيد لتشتبك في شوكه ويذهب به الي فراخه وهو لا يظهر الا ليلا وهو مولع باكل الافاع II, 457 ولا يتالم لها وانا لذعته الحية اكل الصعتر البري فيبري وله خمسة اسنان في فيه والبرية منها تسفد قايمة وظهر الذكر لاصق بظهر الانثي Alkunphud, cum esurit, ascendit in vitem inversus, et decerpit racemos, quos abjicit. Postea inde descendens ex iis comedit, quantum potest. Si catulos habeat, volutatur in racemis, ut spinis suis implicentur, et cum iis contendit ad catulos suos. Non apparet nisi nocte. Viperarum esum mire appetit, nec ab illis laeditur. A serpente demorsus, origani sylvestris esu sanatur. Quinque dentes habet in ore. Terrestris kunphud coit erectus, ita, ut maris dorsum haereat dorso foeminae. Haec ad hericium pertinere, nemo non videt, quamvis in iis nonnulla sint, quae in Graecis frustra quaeras. Iam, si medicos consulamus, Avicennam puta, Abenbitarem atque illum ipsum Damirem, de quo supra, eos non solum reperiemus easdem virtutes tribuere τῷ kunphud, quas τῷ ἐχίνῳ Graeci scriptores: sed et Dioscoridis et Galeni loca de echino terrestri et marino reddentes, illum القنفذ البري alkunphud albarri, seu terrestrem, hunc القنفذ البحري alkunphud al- bahari, seu marinum, constanter nominare. Ut taceam Prophetarum interpretes, qui Arabicam versionem ex Graeca expresserunt, ubique Graecum ἐχίνους reddidisse القنافذ alkanaphido, quod est Plurale τοῦ kunphud. Exempla vide Esa. XIV, 23. et XXXIV, 11. et Sophon. II, 14. Proinde ex Hebraeis id ul-tro agnoscit R. Nathan, Arabice Kimchio longe doctior, قنفذ kunphud esse hericium. Porro Hebraeorum קפוד kippod, Chaldaeorum קופד kuphad, et Ara- bum قنفذ kunphud idem esse animal, statim agnoscet, quisquis harum linguarum aliquem habebit gustum. Longa vocalis in קופד kuphad supplet defectum puncti Daghes, quod habetur in קפוד kippod. Atque illud ipsum Daghes supplet litera Nun, quae se prodit in Arabico قنفذ kunphud, ut etiam in col. 1039 Aethiopico ቀንፈዝ፡ konphoz ejusdem notionis. Sic חטה chitta, id est, triti- cum, est pro חנטה chinta, ut scribunt Arabes. Lignum, ex quo facta fuit arca testimonii, שטה sitta dicitur, pro שנטה sinta; ut Arabice سنط sent. Ara- nea עכביש accabis, pro ancabis; ut Arabice عنكبوث ancabuths. Et עז ez, id est, capra, Plurali עזים izzim, Arabice est عنز enz. Quod hic in eos observandum, qui vocem קפוד kippod revocant ad Radicem קפד kaphad, ut significet animal, quod peculiari aliqua vi incidendi polleat. Atqui vera Radix non est קפד kaphad, sed inusitata קנפד kanphad: nisi quis putet, compositam esse vocem, Gutturalibus (ut fit) elisis, ex קנה kana, quod est spiculum, et אפד aphad, quod est amicire: quia hoc animal spinis et aculeis tanquam spiculis amictus et circumvallatus est. Aut, si malis, in قنفذ kunphud Nun esse epentheticum, etiam radix קפד kaphad quaedam habet significata, quae huc referre II, 458 possis. Ut cum קפדן kaphdan usurpatur de homine aspero et iracundo. Quo sensu in Sanhedrin capite undecimo propheta Elias dicitur fuisse קפדן. Et in tractatu De Sabbatho cap. 2. fol. 30. b. לעולם יהא אדם ענותן כהלל ואל יהא קפדן כשמאי, Semper sit homo mansuetus sicut Hillel, neque sit kaphdan (seu iracundus) ut Sammai. Quia, ut ait Pomarius, homo asper et iracundus est כמו הקפוד עם קוצים, ut hericius cum spinis. Ita Graeca haec adagia, Ἐχῖνου τρα-χύτερος, et Ἅπας ἐχῖνος τραχὺς, hominem morosum significant et intractabilem. Eodem pertinet, quod קפד kaphad, vel הקפיד hikphid attentum et sollicitum esse significat: et הקפדה hakkephada attentionem et sollicitudinem; quia, ut est in Pomario, cum hericius קורץ כל גופו, spinis obtegit totum corpus suum, facie inter pedes delitescente, et aculeos erigit, quibus ut clypeo se muniat, et eos laedat, qui violentas manus in eum injicere volunt, פעולת הזאת היא השגחה והרגשה נמרצת, haec actio est providentiae et attentionis acerrimae. Praeterea ܩܦܕ Syris est horrere, vel horripilari; ut cum pili prae metu eriguntur, quomodo in hericiis. Sic Psami Syri centesimi decimi noni versu 120. ܩܦܕ ܒܣܪܝ ܡܢ ܕܚܠܬܟ, Horruit caro mea prae timore tui, id est, horruerunt pili carnis meae, ut habetur Iob. IV, 15. Gallice herisser dixeris eadem metaphora. Nam herisser, id est, ὀρθοτριχεῖν, horripilari, et herisson sunt Conjugata.

Now, lest anyone object, on the authority of both Kimchis, that the Arabs' قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud is the tortoise, I say that they are gravely mistaken on this point. For in Arabic the tortoise is not called kunphud but سلخفاة [sulaḥfāh] sulachpha, or سلخفية [sulaḥfiya] sulachphia, as if you were to say hiding in a shell or husk: for خفا [khafā] chapha means to hide, and سلخ [salkh] silch, or sulch, is φολὶς [pholis], a covering, properly of a serpent, but also of a tortoise; just as γῆρας [gēras], a word most use for the leberis, or slough of a serpent, but some also for χελωνίω [chelōniō], as Aelian, History book 2, ch. 37, and Suidas under Φολίδωτον [Pholidōton]. But that قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud is the hedgehog no one will deny who has read Damiri, where قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud is surnamed ابو الشوك [abū al-shawk] abussuchi, that is, father of thorns; and انقد [anqad] ankado, that is, the stripper of bark; and ابو سفين [abū safīn] abusaphin, that is, the father who scrapes or polishes, because garments are polished with its col. 1038 skin; and العساعس [al-ʿasāʿis] alasaiso, because it roams at night. For that is properly عس [ʿassa] assa, as also سري [sarā] sara; hence the proverb in use among them, اسري من قنفذ [asrā min qunfudh], More night-roaming than the kunphud. In the same place you may find many things pertaining to its description, among which these are remarkable: القنفذ ان جاع صعد الكرم منكسا فيقطع العناقيد ويرمي بها ثم ينزل فياكل منها ما اطاق واذا كان له فراخ تمرغ في العناقيد لتشتبك في شوكه ويذهب به الي فراخه وهو لا يظهر الا ليلا وهو مولع باكل الافاع II, 457 ولا يتالم لها وانا لذعته الحية اكل الصعتر البري فيبري وله خمسة اسنان في فيه والبرية منها تسفد قايمة وظهر الذكر لاصق بظهر الانثي [al-qunfudh in jāʿa ṣaʿida al-karm munakkasan fa-yaqṭaʿu al-ʿanāqīd wa-yarmī bihā thumma yanzilu fa-yaʾkulu minhā mā aṭāqa wa-idhā kāna lahu firākh tamarragha fī al-ʿanāqīd li-tashtabika fī shawkihi wa-yadhhabu bihi ilā firākhihi wa-huwa lā yaẓharu illā laylan wa-huwa mūlaʿ bi-akl al-afāʿ wa-lā yataʾallamu lahā wa-anā ladhaʿathu al-ḥayya akala al-ṣaʿtar al-barrī fa-yabraʾ wa-lahu khamsat asnān fī fīhi wa-al-barriyya minhā tusfadu qāʾima wa-ẓahr al-dhakar lāṣiq bi-ẓahr al-unthā] Alkunphud, when it is hungry, climbs a vine upside down and plucks off the clusters, which it throws down. Then, coming down from there, it eats of them as much as it can. If it has young, it rolls about in the clusters so that they become entangled in its spines, and with them it hurries to its young. It does not appear except at night. It has a wonderful appetite for eating vipers, and is not harmed by them. When bitten by a serpent, it is healed by eating wild marjoram. It has five teeth in its mouth. The land kunphud copulates upright, so that the back of the male clings to the back of the female. Everyone sees that these things pertain to the hedgehog, although among them there are some that you would seek in vain in the Greeks. Now, if we consult the physicians, say Avicenna, Ibn al-Baitar and that same Damiri mentioned above, we shall find not only that they attribute to the kunphud the same virtues that the Greek writers attribute to the ἐχίνῳ [echinō], but also that, in rendering the passages of Dioscorides and Galen on the land and sea hedgehog, they consistently call the former القنفذ البري [al-qunfudh al-barrī] alkunphud albarri, or land hedgehog, the latter القنفذ البحري [al-qunfudh al-baḥrī] alkunphud albahari, or sea hedgehog. Not to mention that the translators of the Prophets, who made the Arabic version from the Greek, everywhere rendered the Greek ἐχίνους [echinous] by القنافذ [al-qanāfidh] alkanaphido, which is the plural of kunphud. For examples see Isa 14:23 and XXXIV, 11. and Zeph 2:14. Accordingly, among the Hebrews, R. Nathan, far more learned in Arabic than Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], readily acknowledges that قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud is the hedgehog. Further, that the Hebrews' קפוד kippod, the Chaldeans' קופד kuphad, and the Arabs' قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud are the same animal, anyone who has some taste of these languages will at once recognize. The long vowel in קופד kuphad makes up for the lack of the Daghesh point found in קפוד kippod. And that very Daghesh is replaced by the letter Nun, which shows itself in the Arabic قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud, as also in col. 1039 the Ethiopic ቀንፈዝ፡ [qanəfaz] konphoz of the same meaning. Thus חטה chitta, that is, wheat, stands for חנטה chinta, as the Arabs write it. The wood of which the ark of the testimony was made is called שטה sitta, for שנטה sinta; as in Arabic سنط [sanṭ] sent. The spider is עכביש accabis, for ancabis; as in Arabic عنكبوث [ʿankabūth] ancabuths. And עז ez, that is, goat, plural עזים izzim, is in Arabic عنز [ʿanz] enz. This is to be noted here against those who trace the word קפוד kippod to the root קפד kaphad, so that it would signify an animal endowed with some peculiar power of cutting. But the true root is not קפד kaphad, but the unused קנפד kanphad; unless someone thinks that the word is a compound, with the gutturals elided (as happens), of קנה kana, which is a dart, and אפד aphad, which is to clothe, because this animal is clothed and fenced about with spines and prickles as with darts. Or, if you prefer that the Nun in قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud is epenthetic, even the root קפד kaphad has certain meanings which II, 458 you could refer here. As when קפדן kaphdan is used of a harsh and irascible man. In this sense, in Sanhedrin, chapter 11, the prophet Elijah is said to have been קפדן. And in the tractate On the Sabbath, ch. 2, fol. 30b: לעולם יהא אדם ענותן כהלל ואל יהא קפדן כשמאי, Let a man always be gentle like Hillel, and not kaphdan (or irascible) like Shammai. Because, as the Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)] says, a harsh and irascible man is כמו הקפוד עם קוצים, like a hedgehog with spines. So these Greek proverbs, Ἐχῖνου τραχύτερος [Echinou trachyteros] and Ἅπας ἐχῖνος τραχὺς [Hapas echinos trachys], signify a morose and intractable man. To the same point belongs the fact that קפד kaphad, or הקפיד hikphid, means to be attentive and anxious, and הקפדה hakkephada means attention and anxiety; because, as is in the Pomarius, when the hedgehog קורץ כל גופו, covers its whole body with spines, its face hiding between its feet, and raises its prickles, with which it defends itself as with a shield and wounds those who wish to lay violent hands on it, פעולת הזאת היא השגחה והרגשה נמרצת, this action is one of providence and the keenest attention. Moreover, ܩܦܕ [קפד] for the Syrians is to shudder, or to bristle, as when the hairs stand on end from fear, as in hedgehogs. So in the Syriac Psalm 119, verse 120: ܩܦܕ ܒܣܪܝ ܡܢ ܕܚܠܬܟ [קפד בסרי מן דחלתך], My flesh shuddered for fear of you, that is, the hairs of my flesh stood on end, as is found in Iob. IV, 15. In French you would say herisser by the same metaphor. For herisser, that is, ὀρθοτριχεῖν [orthotrichein], to bristle, and herisson are cognates.


Iam, ut ad objectiones respondeam, negat Fullerus, in herinacei natura quidquam esse, quod conveniat τῷ kippod. Quod non possum mirari satis, cum ab Esaia et Sophonia semper describatur kippod ut animal solivagum et φιλέρη-μον, habitans in Babylonis, Bostrae et Ninives desolatis urbibus. Qualem esse herinaceum, nemo est qui nesciat, ζῶον χῆρον, ἤτοι ἔρημον, quodque adeo ab omni aliorum animalium societate prohibent aculei, quos impune nemo attigerit. Unde factum, ut Graece χὴρ diceretur. Hesychius, χήρ· ἐχῖνος. nempe ἀπὸ τῆς χηρώσεως, ἤτοι ἐρημώσεως. Unde etiam Latinum nomen; non ab haerendo, aut horrendo, ut volunt. Nam, ut hir, pro vola manus apud Probum et Charisium, factum ex Graeco χεὶρ, ita her pro hericio omnino est ex Graeco χήρ. Quem scilicet posterior aetas, crescente voce, appellavit hericem, hericium, herinacium, eum veteres herem vocabant. Nemesianus in Cynegetico:

Now, to reply to the objections: Fuller denies that there is anything in the nature of the hedgehog that suits the kippod. This I cannot sufficiently wonder at, since Isaiah and Zephaniah always describe the kippod as a solitary animal and φιλέρημον [phileremon], dwelling in the desolate cities of Babylon, Bozrah and Nineveh. That the hedgehog is such, there is no one who does not know: ζῶον χῆρον, ἤτοι ἔρημον [zōon chēron, ētoi erēmon], an animal which its spines, which no one touches with impunity, keep from all society with other animals. Hence it came about that in Greek it was called χὴρ [chēr]. Hesychius: χήρ· ἐχῖνος [chēr: echinos], namely from χηρώσις [chērōsis], that is, ἐρημώσις [erēmōsis]. Hence also the Latin name; not ab haerendo [from clinging] or horrendo [from bristling], as some would have it. For just as hir for vola manus [the palm of the hand] in Probus and Charisius was made from the Greek χεὶρ [cheir], so her for hericius [hedgehog] comes entirely from the Greek χήρ [chēr]. The animal which a later age, as the word grew longer, called herix, hericius, herinacius, the ancients called her. Nemesianus in the Cynegetica:


Implicitumque sinu spinosi corporis herem.

And the hedgehog wrapped up in the fold of its spiny body.


Et multo ante Plautus in Captivis Actu primo ex emendatione Cl. Salmasii:

And long before, Plautus in the Captivi, Act 1, as emended by the distinguished Salmasius [=Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), Plinianae exercitationes]:


I, modo venare leporem, nunc herem tenes.

Go now, hunt a hare: now you hold a hedgehog.


Aut, si nomine kippod apud Prophetas hystricem intelligamus (quem [?] col. 1040 eodem cum herinaceo genere contineri, probavimus ex veteribus), res videbi[?]

Or, if by the name kippod in the Prophets we understand the porcupine (which [?] col. 1040 we have proved from the ancients to be included in the same genus as the hedgehog), the matter will seem[?]


II, 459 eo magis ad horrorem comparata, si Prophetae minentur, fore, ut populosae urbes, quales in Chaldaeis Babylon, in Assyriis Ninive, et Bostra in Idumaeis, hystricibus in haereditatem cedant. Hystrix enim hericio et major, et ferocior est, et propter missiles spinas, quas in canes et venatores certo destinatoque ictu vibrat, longe terribilior (1). Proinde eximius Poeta, postquam hystricem pilis, in sagittarum modum acutis, horrentem graphice descripsit, his verbis docet, quantum hystrix echino, id est, herinaceo praestet:

II, 459 all the more fitted to inspire horror, if the Prophets threaten that populous cities, such as Babylon among the Chaldeans, Nineveh among the Assyrians, and Bozrah among the Idumaeans, will pass as an inheritance to porcupines. For the porcupine is both larger and fiercer than the hedgehog, and, because of the missile spines which it hurls at dogs and hunters with a sure and well-aimed stroke, far more terrible R1. Accordingly the excellent Poet, after vividly describing the porcupine bristling with hairs sharp like arrows, teaches in these words how far the porcupine surpasses the echinus, that is, the hedgehog:


Sed non haec acies ritu sylvestris echini
Fixa manet. Crebris propugnat jactibus ultro,
Et longe sua membra regit, tortumque per auras
Evolat excusso nativum missile tergo.

But this array does not stay fixed, in the manner of the woodland hedgehog.
It fights on the offensive with frequent volleys,
and guards its limbs from afar, and, whirled through the air,
its native missile flies out from its shaken back.


Et cum Ion in Phoenice a) rideat herinacii οἰζυρὰς τέχνας, miseras artes, qui, ab aliis feris impetitus,

And whereas Ion in the Phoenix a) mocks the οἰζυρὰς τέχνας [oizyras technas], the wretched arts, of the hedgehog, which, when attacked by other beasts,


Στρόβιλον ἀμφ' ἄκανθαν εἰλίξας δέμας, Κεῖται δακεῖν τε καὶ θιγεῖν ἀμήχανος· Denso sub orbe sentium corpus degens, Mordere et ultro tangere ignarus jacet:

Στρόβιλον ἀμφ' ἄκανθαν εἰλίξας δέμας, Κεῖται δακεῖν τε καὶ θιγεῖν ἀμήχανος· [Strobilon amph' akanthan eilixas demas, keitai dakein te kai thigein amēchanos] Keeping its body under a dense ball of thorns, it lies there, unable to bite or to touch in return:


hystricis in pugna virtus et solertia perillustrem Poetam in admirationem ita rapuit, ut hos versus ab illo expresserit:

the porcupine's courage and skill in fighting so carried the most illustrious Poet away in admiration that it drew these verses from him:


Interdum fugiens Parthorum more sequentem Vulnerat: interdum, positis velut ordine castris, Terrificum densa mucronem verberat unda, Et consanguineis hastilibus asperat armos. Militat omne ferae corpus, vibrataque rauco Terga fragore sonant; stimulis accensa tubarum Agmina collatis credas concurrere signis. Tantus in angusto strepitus furit. Additur armis Calliditas, parcusque sui timor, iraque nunquam Prodiga telorum, caute contenta minari, Nec nisi servandae jactus impendere vitae. Error abest, certum solertia destinat ictum, Nil spatio fallente modum, servatque tenorem Muta cutis, doctique regit conamina visus.

Sometimes, fleeing in the manner of the Parthians, it wounds its pursuer: sometimes, as if pitching camp in order, it lashes out its terrifying point in a dense wave, and roughens its shoulders with kindred shafts. The whole body of the beast does battle, and its back, shaken, resounds with a harsh crash; you would think columns roused by the goad of trumpets were clashing with standards joined. So great a din rages in so small a space. To its arms is added cunning, and a fear sparing of itself, and an anger never prodigal of its darts, cautiously content to threaten, and spending its shots only to save its life. Error is absent; skill directs a sure stroke, the distance never deceiving its measure; and the mute skin keeps its course and guides the efforts of a practised eye.


Et paullo post,

And a little later,


Ecce, brevis propriis munitur bestia telis, Externam nec quaerit opem, fert omnia secum, II, 460 Se pharetra, sese jaculo, sese utitur arcu. Unum animal cunctas bellorum possidet artes.

Behold, a small beast is armed with its own weapons, and seeks no outside help; it carries everything with it; II, 460 it is its own quiver, its own javelin, its own bow. One animal possesses all the arts of war.


Denique jaculandi artem ab hac fera nos didicisse concludit. Et de eadem Ha-drianus, imperator,

Finally he concludes that we learned the art of shooting from this beast. And of the same the emperor Hadrian:


Spinis missilibus canes virosque
Arcebat procul et fugabat omnes.

With missile spines it kept dogs and men
far off, and put them all to flight.


Et Phile cap. 59. De animalibus,

And Phile, ch. 59, On Animals:


Ὕστριξ δὲ τὰς ἄνωθεν ἐκπέμπει τρίχας, Ἃς ἡ φύσις γ᾽ ἔθηξε καὶ πρὸ τῆς μάχης. Φρίξασα γὰρ τὰ νῶτα βάλλει τοὺς πέλους Οἷον ἀπὸ νευρᾶς εὐτυχῶν b) τις τοξότης. Ut tela villos asper hystrix conjicit, Natura quas ad praelium exacuit sagax. Cum nempe dorsum contrahit, nervo velut Intenso, in hostes tela torquet eminus.

Ὕστριξ δὲ τὰς ἄνωθεν ἐκπέμπει τρίχας, Ἃς ἡ φύσις γ᾽ ἔθηξε καὶ πρὸ τῆς μάχης. Φρίξασα γὰρ τὰ νῶτα βάλλει τοὺς πέλους Οἷον ἀπὸ νευρᾶς εὐτυχῶν b) τις τοξότης. [Hystrix de tas anōthen ekpempei trichas, has hē physis g' ethēxe kai pro tēs machēs. Phrixasa gar ta nōta ballei tous pelous hoion apo neuras eutychōn tis toxotēs.] As the rough porcupine hurls its hairs like darts, which shrewd nature has sharpened for battle, for when it draws in its back, as with a bowstring drawn taut, it hurls darts at its enemies from afar.


Et Oppianus lib. 3. Cynegeticῶν, vs. 398.

And Oppian, book 3 of the Cynegetica, v. 398:


— — — Θοὰς δ᾽ ἔφριξεν ἐθείρας
Καί τ᾽ ὀπίσω νώτοισιν ἀκαχμένον ὠκυπέτῃσιν
Ἰθὺς ἀκοντίζει μαλερὸν βέλος. — —

— — — Θοὰς δ᾽ ἔφριξεν ἐθείρας
Καί τ᾽ ὀπίσω νώτοισιν ἀκαχμένον ὠκυπέτῃσιν
Ἰθὺς ἀκοντίζει μαλερὸν βέλος. — — [Thoas d' ephrixen etheiras kai t' opisō nōtoisin akachmenon ōkypetēisin ithys akontizei maleron belos.]


Acutos erigit aculeos, atque retro dorso volucri affixum perniciosum telum recta ejaculantur. Et paullo post,

It raises its sharp spines, and shoots straight backwards the deadly dart fixed on its swift-flying back. And a little later,


Δηθάκις ἔκτεινεν κύνα κάρχαρον,

Δηθάκις ἔκτεινεν κύνα κάρχαρον, [Dēthakis ekteinen kyna karcharon,]


Dentibus asperum canem saepenumero interfecit. Proinde venatores, cum canes non audeant in hystricem immittere, illum quodam dolo capiunt, quem in sequentibus se scripturum professus idem Oppianus, morte praeventus promissis non stetit. Nec est, quod quis putet, haec poetica fide dici, cum idem tradant, quotquot scripserunt de natura animalium. Ita Philosophus Historiae libri noni col. 1041 capite trigesimo nono animalia quaedam memorat τὰ βάλλοντα ταῖς θριξὶν, οἷον αἱ ὕστριχες, quae villos jaculantur, ut hystrices. Et Plinius libri octavi capite trigesimo quinto, Hystrici longiores aculei, et, cum intendit cutem, missiles. Ora urgentium figit canum, et paullo longius jaculatur. Solinus quoque, Spinis tergum hispida (hystrix), quas plerumque laxatas jaculatione emittit voluntaria, ut assiduis aculeorum nimbis canes vulneret ingruentes. Et Aelianus libri primi capite trigesimo primo, Τὰς ἄνωθεν τρίχας οἱονεὶ βέλη ἐκπέμπει, καὶ εὐστόχως βάλ-λει πολλάκις, τὰ νῶτα φρίξασα, καὶ ἐκεῖναί γε πηδῶσιν. ὥσπερ οὖν ἔκ τινος ἀφειμέναι νευρᾶς· Superiores pilos ut sagittas emittit, et tanquam ad scopum saepe recta destinat, dorsum horrendo contrahens. Illi autem insiliunt tanquam ex nervo emissi. Aristophanis Scholiastes in Pace, et ex illo Suidas, Ἔστι δὲ ὕστριξ II, 461 θηρίον τρίχας ἔχον ὑὸς, ἂν ἐν τῷ διώκεσθαι ἐπακοντίζει κατὰ τῶν διωκόντων· Hystrix fera horret suillis setis (unde illi nomen), quas, cum quis illam persequitur, ejaculatur in insequentes. Porta coeli pag. 19. d. גם יש מין מחוירי הבר שיש להם שערות גסים כמו חצים וזה לסבת גסות העור, Species est porcorum sylvestrium, quibus sagittarum instar densi sunt pili, nempe propter pellis densitatem et duritiem. Avicenna libri secundi Canonis capite قنفذ Kunphud, والجبلي هو الدلدل ذو الشوك السهمي Et montanus (kunphud) est duldul (hystrix), qui spinas habet sagittales, id est missiles. Damir in capite دلدل Duldul, واذا راي ما يكرهه انقبض فيخرج منه شوك كالمسال يخرج من اصابه والشوك الذي علي ظهره بحو الذراع Et cum videt aliquid infensum, sese contrahit. Et exeunt ex eo spinae ut acus, quibus vulnerantur imminentes. Spinae autem, quae sunt super dorsum ejus, sunt fere cubitales. Paulus Venetus libri primi capite trigesimo tertio, ubi de Scassem, Tartariae civitate: Sunt in regione illa multi sues spinosi (hystrices), qui, cum capiuntur, spinis suis saepe homines et canes laedunt. Nam canes, a venatoribus in porcos provocati, adeo irritant et commovent feras illas, ut simul concurrentes (contrahentes) terga sua, quibus spinae innituntur, vehementer commoveant, atque stimulos ipsos vehementia quadam excutiant, et in viciniores homines et canes vibrent. Gesnerus, Certo destinatoque ictu ferit, quem voluerit, vulnere interdum incurabili propemodum, utpote angusto et profundo, periculoso nimirum, si nervus pungatur. Ut Oppianus non immerito canat,

it has often killed a dog rough with teeth. Accordingly hunters, since they do not dare to set dogs on the porcupine, take it by a certain stratagem, which the same Oppian professed he would describe in what follows, but, prevented by death, he did not keep his promise. Nor is there reason for anyone to think that these things are said on poetic authority, since all who have written on the nature of animals report the same. Thus the Philosopher, History, book 9, col. 1041 chapter 39, mentions certain animals τὰ βάλλοντα ταῖς θριξὶν, οἷον αἱ ὕστριχες [ta ballonta tais thrixin, hoion hai hystriches], which shoot their hairs, like porcupines. And Pliny, book 8, chapter 35: The porcupine has longer quills, and, when it stretches its skin, they can be shot. It pierces the mouths of dogs pressing on it, and shoots a little farther off. Solinus also: Bristling on its back with spines (the porcupine), which, often loosened, it discharges by voluntary shooting, so as to wound attacking dogs with continual showers of quills. And Aelian, book 1, chapter 31: Τὰς ἄνωθεν τρίχας οἱονεὶ βέλη ἐκπέμπει, καὶ εὐστόχως βάλλει πολλάκις, τὰ νῶτα φρίξασα, καὶ ἐκεῖναί γε πηδῶσιν. ὥσπερ οὖν ἔκ τινος ἀφειμέναι νευρᾶς· [Tas anōthen trichas hoionei belē ekpempei, kai eustochōs ballei pollakis, ta nōta phrixasa, kai ekeinai ge pēdōsin. hōsper oun ek tinos apheimenai neuras] It sends forth its upper hairs like arrows, and often aims them straight as at a target, contracting its back as it bristles. And they leap out as if shot from a bowstring. The Scholiast on Aristophanes on the Peace, and from him Suidas: Ἔστι δὲ ὕστριξ II, 461 θηρίον τρίχας ἔχον ὑὸς, ἂν ἐν τῷ διώκεσθαι ἐπακοντίζει κατὰ τῶν διωκόντων· [Esti de hystrix thērion trichas echon hyos, an en tō diōkesthai epakontizei kata tōn diōkontōn] The porcupine is a wild beast bristling with swine's bristles (whence its name), which, when someone pursues it, it shoots out at its pursuers. Porta coeli p. 19 d: גם יש מין מחוירי הבר שיש להם שערות גסים כמו חצים וזה לסבת גסות העור, There is a species of wild swine whose hairs are thick like arrows, namely because of the thickness and hardness of the skin. Avicenna, book 2 of the Canon, in the chapter قنفذ [qunfudh] Kunphud, والجبلي هو الدلدل ذو الشوك السهمي [wa-l-jabalī huwa al-duldul dhū al-shawk al-sahmī] And the mountain one (kunphud) is the duldul (porcupine), which has arrow-like spines, that is, missiles. Damir in the chapter دلدل [duldul] Duldul: واذا راي ما يكرهه انقبض فيخرج منه شوك كالمسال يخرج من اصابه والشوك الذي علي ظهره بحو الذراع [wa-idhā rāy mā yakrahuhu inqabaḍa fa-yakhruju minhu shawk ka-l-masāl yakhruju min aṣābahu wa-l-shawk alladhī ʿalī ẓahrihi bḥw al-dhirāʿ] And when it sees anything hostile, it contracts itself. And spines like needles come out of it, by which those pressing on it are wounded. And the spines that are on its back are about a cubit long. Marco Polo, book 1, chapter 33, on Scassem, a city of Tartary: In that region there are many spiny swine (porcupines), which, when they are caught, often injure men and dogs with their spines. For the dogs, set on the swine by the hunters, so provoke and stir up those beasts that, running together (contracting) their backs, on which the spines rest, they shake them violently, and with a certain violence discharge the very quills and hurl them at the nearer men and dogs. Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium]: It strikes whomever it wishes with a sure and aimed blow, with a wound sometimes almost incurable, being narrow and deep, dangerous indeed if a nerve is pierced. So that Oppian not without reason sings,


Ὑστρίγγων οὔπω τι πέλει κατὰ δάσκιον ὕλην
Ῥίγιον εἰσιδέειν, ὅτ' ἀργαλεώτερον ἄλλο,

Ὑστρίγγων οὔπω τι πέλει κατὰ δάσκιον ὕλην Ῥίγιον εἰσιδέειν, ὅτ' ἀργαλεώτερον ἄλλο, [Hystringōn oupō ti pelei kata daskion hylēn Rhigion eisideein, hot' argaleōteron allo]


Quae ita contraxit Stephanus in Notis ad Callimachum,

Which Stephanus condensed thus in his Notes on Callimachus:


Hystrice nil silvis visu magis horret opacis.

Nothing in the shady woods is more dreadful to behold than the porcupine.


De hoc Prophetas egisse eo sit verissimilius, quod ab Arabibus disco rem, ignotam hactenus, hystricem animal esse in Syria frequens. Damir in capite دلدل Duldul, seu De Hystrice, هو كثير ببلاد الشام والعراق وبلاد المغارب Abundat in regione Syriae et Irak (Mesopotamiae et Babyloniae), et col. 1042 in regione Megareb, id est, Africa occidentali. Quod ipsum de hericio sic docet: وهو صنفان قنفد يكون بارض مصر قدر الفار وقنفد يكون بارض الشام وعراق في قدر الكلب القلطي والفرق بينهما كالفرق بين الفار والجرذ Hericius duarum est specierum. Unus enim est in terra Aegypti, soricis magnitudine; et alter in terris Syriae et Irak (Mesopotamiae et Babyloniae), Melitensis canis magnitudine, ita, ut tam differant, quam differunt sorex et mus. II, 462 Qui aquaticum animal קפוד kippod esse colligunt ex his Esaiae de Babylone, Ponam eam in possessionem τοῦ kippod, et stagna aquarum, ne sic quidem quidquam afferunt, quod sententiae nostrae officiat. Cum in aquatilibus etiam sit echini species, qui Avicennae, Damiri, Abenbitari قنفد بحري, aliis ἐχῖνος θαλάσσιος, echinus marinus dicitur, aut vero ποτάμιος, fluviatilis. Ha-beri enim et fluviatiles echinos, Paulus Aegineta prodidit. Quibus scatere potuit Euphrates ad Babylonem. Ad eas saltem insulas, quae Euphratis ori objectae sunt, insignis magnitudinis echinos reperiri, ex Nearcho discimus. Strabo, Λέ-γει δὲ (ὁ Νέαρχος) ἐν ταῖς πρὸ τοῦ Εὐφράτου νήσοις φύεσθαι παγούρων καὶ ἐχί-νων μεγέθη· Sed nos Esaiae locum multo aliter interpretamur, nempe hoc modo: Ponam eam in possessionem τοῦ kippod (id est, terrestris echini), etiam stagna aquarum. Id est, Non modo desolabitur urbs, sed et vicina stagna sic exarescent, ut tam apta futura sit in iis, quam in urbe echino terrestri sedes, qui locis aridis maxime delectatur. Sic Sophon. II, 13. poni dicitur Ninive לשממה וציה, in desolationem et siccitatem, atque ita demum fieri, ut kippod in ea diversetur. Et Esa. XXXIV, 11. antequam Idumaea tradatur in possessionem τοῦ kippod, mutantur in picem torrentes, et pulvis in sulphurem.

That the Prophets spoke of this animal may be the more probable because I learn from the Arabs something hitherto unknown, that the porcupine is an animal common in Syria. Damir, in the chapter دلدل [duldul] Duldul, or On the Porcupine: هو كثير ببلاد الشام والعراق وبلاد المغارب [huwa kathīr bi-bilād al-Shām wa-l-ʿIrāq wa-bilād al-Maghārib] It abounds in the region of Syria and Iraq (Mesopotamia and Babylonia), and col. 1042 in the region of Megareb, that is, western Africa. He teaches the same about the hedgehog, thus: وهو صنفان قنفد يكون بارض مصر قدر الفار وقنفد يكون بارض الشام وعراق في قدر الكلب القلطي والفرق بينهما كالفرق بين الفار والجرذ [wa-huwa ṣinfān qunfud yakūn bi-arḍ Miṣr qadr al-fār wa-qunfud yakūn bi-arḍ al-Shām wa-ʿIrāq fī qadr al-kalb al-qalṭī wa-l-farq baynahumā ka-l-farq bayn al-fār wa-l-jurdh] The hedgehog is of two species. One is in the land of Egypt, of the size of a shrew; the other in the lands of Syria and Iraq (Mesopotamia and Babylonia), of the size of a Maltese dog, so that they differ as much as the shrew and the mouse differ. II, 462 Those who infer that the kippod kippod קפוד is an aquatic animal from these words of Isaiah about Babylon, I will make it a possession of the kippod, and pools of water, do not even so adduce anything that stands in the way of our view. For among aquatic creatures too there is a species of hedgehog, which by Avicenna, Damir and Ibn al-Baitar is called قنفد بحري [qunfud baḥrī], by others ἐχῖνος θαλάσσιος [echinos thalassios], sea hedgehog, or else ποτάμιος [potamios], river hedgehog. For Paul of Aegina reported that there are also river hedgehogs. The Euphrates near Babylon could have teemed with them. At least we learn from Nearchus that hedgehogs of remarkable size are found near the islands lying off the mouth of the Euphrates. Strabo: Λέγει δὲ (ὁ Νέαρχος) ἐν ταῖς πρὸ τοῦ Εὐφράτου νήσοις φύεσθαι παγούρων καὶ ἐχίνων μεγέθη· [Legei de (ho Nearchos) en tais pro tou Euphratou nēsois phyesthai pagourōn kai echinōn megethē]. But we interpret the passage of Isaiah very differently, namely in this way: I will make it a possession of the kippod (that is, of the land hedgehog), even the pools of water. That is, not only will the city be laid waste, but the neighbouring pools too will dry up, so that they will be as fit a dwelling as the city for the land hedgehog, which delights above all in dry places. Thus in Zeph 2:13 Nineveh is said to be made לשממה וציה, a desolation and dryness, and only then does it come about that the kippod lodges in it. And in Isa 34:11, before Idumaea is handed over as a possession of the kippod, the streams are turned into pitch and the dust into brimstone.


Ut קפוד kippod probetur esse avis, parum in eo momenti est, quod Es. XXXIV, 11. cum avibus nominatur. Statim enim versu decimo tertio junguntur simul dracones et struthionss, quamvis animalia toto genere diversa. Et Sophonias greges, bestias, pelecanum et kippod simul in unum fascem congerit. Quod ipsum magis afficit lectorem, cum in descriptione vastitatis ea, quae ad horrorem pertinent, ita confusaneo ordine proponuntur. Cum inter multas aves leporum meminit Sophocles in hoc versu in Amyco Satyrico,

To prove that the kippod kippod קפוד is a bird, it carries little weight that in Es. XXXIV, 11. it is named together with birds. For right in verse thirteen dragons and ostriches are joined together, although they are animals of entirely different kinds. And Zephaniah gathers flocks, beasts, the pelican and the kippod together into one bundle. This affects the reader all the more, since in a description of devastation the things that inspire horror are set forth in such a jumbled order. When Sophocles, in this line of the satyr play Amycus, mentions hares among many birds,


Γέρανοι, κορῶναι, γλαῦκες ἴκτινοι, λαγοὶ,

Γέρανοι, κορῶναι, γλαῦκες ἴκτινοι, λαγοὶ, [Geranoi, korōnai, glaukes iktinoi, lagoi,]


Grues, cornices, noctuae, milvi, lepores: quis inde concluserit, leporem esse avis genus? Scio, non neminem pro λαγοὶ reposuisse λάροι, quod avis aquaticae genus est. Sed frustra. Athenaeus enim libri noni capite decimo quarto hunc versum citat, ut probet, λαγοὶ tam Atticum esse, quam λαγώ. Itaque retinendum λαγοί. Contra, in Luciani Syria Dea, inter multas quadrupedes aquilas sic nominari videas: Ἐν δὲ τῇ αὐλῇ ἄφετοι νέμονται βόες μεγάλοι, καὶ ἵπποι, καὶ αἐτοὶ, καὶ ἄρκτοι, καὶ λέοντες· In atrio autem liberi pascuntur boves magni, et equi, et aquilae, et ursi, et leones. Unde inepte colligatur, ibi aquilas non esse aves, sed genus quadrupedis.

Cranes, crows, owls, kites, hares: who would conclude from this that the hare is a kind of bird? I know that someone has substituted λάροι [laroi], a kind of water bird, for λαγοὶ [lagoi]. But in vain. For Athenaeus, book 9, chapter 14, cites this line to prove that λαγοὶ [lagoi] is as much Attic as λαγώ [lagō]. So λαγοί [lagoi] must be retained. Conversely, in Lucian's Syrian Goddess you may see eagles named among many quadrupeds thus: Ἐν δὲ τῇ αὐλῇ ἄφετοι νέμονται βόες μεγάλοι, καὶ ἵπποι, καὶ αἐτοὶ, καὶ ἄρκτοι, καὶ λέοντες· [En de tē aulē aphetoi nemontai boes megaloi, kai hippoi, kai aetoi, kai arktoi, kai leontes] In the court, moreover, there graze freely great oxen, and horses, and eagles, and bears, and lions. From which it would be absurd to infer that the eagles there are not birds but a kind of quadruped.

Book 4, chapter 1: The tsab

https://openseforim.org/bochart/tsab.html

II, 463 DE SCRIPTURAE ANIMALIBUS LIBER QUARTUS DE QUADRUPEDIBUS OVIPARIS. col. 1043

II, 463 ON THE ANIMALS OF SCRIPTURE BOOK FOUR ON THE OVIPAROUS QUADRUPEDS. col. 1043


CAP. I.

CHAPTER I.


Probatur, צב tsab Levit. XI, 29. esse Crocodilum terrestrem, de quo ex Arabum monumentis multa afferuntur, nondum vulgata.

It is proved that צב tsab in Lev 11:29 is the land crocodile, concerning which much is brought forward from the records of the Arabs that has not yet been published.


Post quadrupedes viviparas sequentur oviparae, quae et in natura paucae sunt, et in Scriptura pauciores. Harum sex species a Mose recensentur Levit. XI, 29. 30. nempe צב tsab, אנקה anaka, כח coach, לטאה letaa, חמט chomet, תנשמת thinsemeth. Septima videbitur addi posse, שממית semamith, ex Prov. XXX, 28. Sed, semamith ab anaka solo nomine differre, suo loco docebimus. Et octava, לויתן leviathan, qui palam est crocodilus, Iob. XL et XLI. Sed crocodilum maluimus in aquaticis describere; quia ἀμφίβιον est animal. Testudo col. 1044 denique hic locum habebit, si Seniores sequimur Os. XII, 12. Oviparae quadrupedes, quas ex Mose recensuimus, ad lacertorum species aliquo modo pertinent, et ita sunt inter se similes, ut eas certis notis ab invicem distinguere non sit cujusvis. Nobis certe fuit valde operosum; quia hic ab Hebraeis prorsus destituimur. Neque ex aliis Scripturae interpretibus multo plus fuit subsidii, qui in tenebris plerique palpant, cum ad has minutias deveniunt: sed longe plus affulsit lucis ex monumentis Arabum, in quorum solo hae pestes nascuntur et edu- col. 1045 cantur. Quod sequentia palam facient. In his singula verba explicare conabimur, illo ipso ordine, quo a Mose proponuntur.

After the viviparous quadrupeds follow the oviparous, which are few in nature and fewer still in Scripture. Moses lists six species of them in Lev 11:29–30., namely צב tsab, אנקה anaka, כח coach, לטאה letaa, חמט chomet, תנשמת thinsemeth. It will seem that a seventh can be added, שממית semamith, from Prov 30:28. But we shall show in its place that semamith differs from anaka in name only. And an eighth, לויתן leviathan, which is plainly the crocodile, Iob. XL et XLI. But we have preferred to describe the crocodile among the aquatic animals, because it is an ἀμφίβιον [amphibion] animal. Finally, the tortoise col. 1044 will have a place here, if we follow the Elders at Hos 12:12. The oviparous quadrupeds that we have listed from Moses belong in some way to the species of lizards, and are so similar to one another that it is not for just anyone to distinguish them from each other by definite marks. For us it was certainly very laborious, because here the Hebrews leave us entirely destitute. Nor was there much more help from the other interpreters of Scripture, most of whom grope in the dark when they come to these minutiae. But far more light has shone from the records of the Arabs, in whose soil these pests are born and reared. col. 1045 What follows will make this plain. In it we shall try to explain the individual words in the very order in which Moses sets them out.


II, 464 Levit. XI, 29. Hebraeum צב tsab Hieronymo est crocodilus, Graecis ὁ κρο-κόδειλος ὁ χερσαῖος. At recentiorum alii bufonem, aut rubetam; alii testudinem reddunt: Castalio autem testaceorum genera. Horum, nisi fallor, agmen ducit R. Selomo, Iudaeus Gallus, qui scripsit ante annos fere DL. Is enim primus, quod quidem sciam, צב tsab animal esse scripsit ranae simile, nomine פויוט. Sed legendum פרוט frot, Germanicum bufonis nomen in Gallia tum in usu. Huc refero, quod צב tsab Kimchius Hispanice reddit גריישנט graissant. Tum scilicet Hispanis graissant erat rubeta, ut Gallis graisset et croisset, et Germanis Grasfrosch, ad verbum rana graminis. Hos sequuti Pomarius, Aquinas, Munsterus, Pagninus, Arias, Robertus Olivetanus, צב tsab bufonem, aut rubetam, aut ranam interpretantur, aut שרץ שדומה לצפרדע, reptile, ranae simile. Putarunt nempe, hoc animal a tumore sic appellari; quia צבה tumere est. Quomodo a bufone factum est nomen vernaculum bouffi, quod tumidum sonat. Accedit, quod Illyrice zaba est rana, tanquam a צב tsab deducta voce. At Elias, Iudaeorum in Germania facile doctissimus, צב tsab sua lingua שלטפרוט schildfrot, id est, testudinem exponit; quia putamina testudinum tectum referre videntur cameratorum curruum, qui Hebraice dicuntur צבים tsabbim. In tantula ratione tantum fuit virium, ut in assensum traxerit Iunium, Tremellium, Schindlerum, Anglos, Italos et Genevenses interpretes. Buxtorfius, in Lexico, quorum se partibus addicat, haud satis sciens, צב tsab et bufonem reddit, et testudinem.

II, 464 Lev 11:29. For Jerome the Hebrew צב tsab is the crocodile; for the Greeks ὁ κροκόδειλος ὁ χερσαῖος [ho krokodeilos ho chersaios]. But among more recent interpreters some render it toad or bramble-toad [rubeta], others tortoise; Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)], however, "kinds of shellfish." The first group, if I am not mistaken, is led by R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)], a French Jew, who wrote about 550 years ago. For he was the first, so far as I know, to write that צב tsab is an animal similar to a frog, called פויוט. But one should read פרוט frot, the German name for the toad, then in use in France. To this I refer the fact that Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] renders צב tsab in Spanish as גריישנט graissant. At that time, namely, graissant was for the Spaniards the bramble-toad, as graisset and croisset for the French, and Grasfrosch for the Germans, literally "grass frog." Following these, Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)], Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)], Munster, Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae], Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], and Robert Olivetan interpret צב tsab as toad, or bramble-toad, or frog, or שרץ שדומה לצפרדע, "a creeping thing similar to a frog." They thought, namely, that this animal was so called from swelling, because צבה means to swell; just as from bufo [toad] the vernacular word bouffi was formed, which means swollen. Add that in Illyrian zaba is frog, as if the word were derived from צב tsab. But Elias [=Elijah Levita (1469–1549), author of the Aramaic lexicon Meturgeman and of Tishbi], easily the most learned of the Jews in Germany, explains צב tsab in his language as שלטפרוט schildfrot, that is, tortoise, because the shells of tortoises seem to resemble the roofs of covered wagons, which in Hebrew are called צבים tsabbim. So slight a reason had such force that it drew to assent Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], Tremellius [=Immanuel Tremellius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], Schindler, and the English, Italian and Genevan translators. Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum], in his Lexicon, not quite knowing which side to join, renders צב tsab both as toad and as tortoise.


In hac tantorum virorum haesitatione, addo etiam hallucinatione, quod illorum pace dixerim, erudito lectori spero me facturum rem pergratam, si veram et genuinam vocis significationem, non jam ex conjectura, sed certis et solidis rationibus adstruam. Id vero, vel me tacente, nullo negotio praestabit, quisquis ea perpendet, quae de hoc animali scribunt Arabes. Quibus non potest non esse notissimum, quia in Arabia frequentius est, quam ullibi terrarum. At illis quam notum est animal, tam nobis est ignotum. Proinde necesse habeo, haec accuratius persequi.

Amid this hesitation of such great men, I will add also this hallucination, if I may say so with their leave, I hope I shall do the learned reader a most welcome service if I establish the true and genuine meaning of the word, not now from conjecture, but by certain and solid reasons. Indeed, even if I said nothing, anyone who weighs what the Arabs write about this animal will accomplish this without any trouble. To them it cannot but be very well known, because it is more common in Arabia than anywhere else on earth. But as well known as the animal is to them, so unknown is it to us. Therefore I find it necessary to pursue these matters more carefully.


Ut a nomine ordiamur, sciendum, ut Hebraice צב, ita Arabice ضب iisdem scribi literis. Sed, ut Dialecti variant, Tsade Arabicum initio vocis effertur ut d, vel dh, propter punctum adscriptum. Itaque haec vocula sonat ضب dhab apud Arabes. Plurale est ضباب dhibab, vel أضب adhab, et Foemininum ضبة dhabba. Unde ضبب dhabab, et مضب mudhab, et مضبب mudhbib, locus dicitur, his animalibus refertus; et مضبب mudhabbib eorum venator. Porro ضب dhab a Damire definitur حيوان بري معروف من الحشرات يشبه الورل animal agreste notum e reptilibus, simile τῷ guaril, seu stellioni majori: ut Avicenna illud a guaril differre scribit, وان كان II, 465 يشبهه وكان قريب الاحوال والقوي منه Quamvis illi sit similis, et tam constitutione, quam virtute proximus. Haec ille libro secundo Canonis in capite ضب dhab, seu tsab, si mavis. Et in capite حردون char- col. 1046 daun, quod a Latino interprete prorsus omissum est. هو الضب وطبعه قريب من طبع الورل وهو اشبه الوزغ بما يتعزي به Chardaun idem est, quod dhab: cujus natura accedit ad guaril, et attributa ea- dem, quae guezgae. Et in capite ورل guaril, هو غير الضب والضب لا يكون او قل ما يكون الا في البادية وراسه وبدنه وذنبه خالف من الورل وربما قريب في طبايعه Guaril alius est a dhab. Nam dhab non est, aut raro est alibi, quam in deserto. Et ca- pite, trunco et cauda differt a guaril, quamvis natura sit vicinus. Et Abdollatif Bagdadensis, الورل والضب والحربا وشحمة الارض والوزغ كلها متناسبة في الخلق Guaril, et dhab, et hirba, et adeps terrae, et guezga, sunt omnes ejusdem naturae participes. Hae nempe sunt totidem lacertorum species, de quibus infra dicemus. Itaque ضب dhab, vel צב tsab, quod idem est, neque bufo est, neque rubeta, neque testudo, neque testaceum animal, sed in lacertorum genere. Nunc, ut cognoscatur plenius, dicemus, quid Arabum Critici, Philosophi, Theologi, Magi, Medici de illo scripserint, quorum pleraque nondum in vulgus prodierunt.

To begin with the name: it should be known that, like the Hebrew צב, the Arabic ضب [ḍabb] is written with the same letters. But, as the dialects vary, the Arabic Tsade at the beginning of a word is pronounced as d or dh, because of the dot added to it. Thus this little word is pronounced ضب [ḍabb] dhab among the Arabs. The plural is ضباب [ḍibāb] dhibab, or أضب [aḍubb] adhab, and the feminine ضبة [ḍabba] dhabba. Hence ضبب [ḍabab] dhabab, and مضب [maḍabb] mudhab, and مضبب [muḍbib] mudhbib denote a place full of these animals; and مضبب [muḍabbib] mudhabbib their hunter. Further, ضب [ḍabb] dhab is defined by Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] as حيوان بري معروف من الحشرات يشبه الورل [ḥayawān barrī maʿrūf min al-ḥasharāt yushbih al-waral] a well-known wild animal among the reptiles, similar to the guaril, or greater stellio: just as Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] writes that it differs from the guaril, وان كان [wa-in kāna] II, 465 يشبهه وكان قريب الاحوال والقوي منه [yushbihuhu wa-kāna qarīb al-aḥwāl wa-al-quwā minhu] although it is similar to it, and very close to it both in constitution and in powers. So he writes in the second book of the Canon, in the chapter ضب [ḍabb] dhab, or tsab, if you prefer. And in the chapter حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun, col. 1046 which was entirely omitted by the Latin translator: هو الضب وطبعه قريب من طبع الورل وهو اشبه الوزغ بما يتعزي به [huwa al-ḍabb wa-ṭabʿuhu qarīb min ṭabʿ al-waral wa-huwa ashbah al-wazagh bi-mā yataʿazzī bihi] Chardaun is the same as dhab: its nature comes close to the guaril, and its attributes are the same as those of the guezga. And in the chapter ورل [waral] guaril, هو غير الضب والضب لا يكون او قل ما يكون الا في البادية وراسه وبدنه وذنبه خالف من الورل وربما قريب في طبايعه [huwa ghayr al-ḍabb wa-al-ḍabb lā yakūn aw qalla mā yakūn illā fī al-bādiya wa-raʾsuhu wa-badanuhu wa-dhanabuhu khālif min al-waral wa-rubbamā qarīb fī ṭabāyiʿihi] The guaril is different from the dhab. For the dhab is not found, or only rarely, anywhere but in the desert. And it differs from the guaril in head, trunk and tail, although it is close to it in nature. And Abdollatif of Baghdad: الورل والضب والحربا وشحمة الارض والوزغ كلها متناسبة في الخلق [al-waral wa-al-ḍabb wa-al-ḥirbā wa-shaḥmat al-arḍ wa-al-wazagh kulluhā mutanāsiba fī al-khalq] The guaril, and the dhab, and the hirba, and the fat of the earth, and the guezga all share the same nature. These, namely, are so many species of lizards, of which we shall speak below. Therefore ضب [ḍabb] dhab, or צב tsab, which is the same, is neither a toad, nor a bramble-toad, nor a tortoise, nor a shelled animal, but belongs to the lizard kind. Now, so that it may be known more fully, we shall say what the Critics, Philosophers, Theologians, Magicians and Physicians of the Arabs have written about it, most of which has not yet been published.


Et Critici quidem docent, animal esse πολυώνυμον· Nam praeter ضب dhab, seu צב tsab, commune nomen, insuper vocatur حردون chardaun (Chaldaei חרדונא chara[?]· Syri ܚܕܪܘܢܐ chadrona, et Samaritani [?] adrona scribunt, ut infra docebitur). Vocatur item برق bork, et علين alin, et هيقل haikal. Et, si pinguis est, سبحل [?] aut سحبل sichbal: si annosus, قرسم kirsem; si pravae indolis, ضغطار dhiphtar: ut foemina vulgo ضبة dhabba; sed, cum pinguis est, حيكانا chaicana; cum foeta, مكون machun, et ممكن mamchin. A verbo مكن machi- na, huic et locustae proprio, cum ova ponunt, ovum مكين machin, et شلقة silka. Foetus in genere, حضرم chidhrim; primus, مطبح mutbich; cum ab ovo nuper prodiit, حسل chisel; jam maturior, غيداق chaidak. Adeps, quem habet circa ventrem et caudae radicem, كشية chusia. Et حلم halama proprie est, adipem illum eximere, ut عكد acha- da, pinguem esse, de solo ضب dhab usurpatur. Veretrum Duali numero نزكان nazachani; quia bifidum. Unde etiam ipse سديم sadim, id est, II, 466 illa parte bene instructus. Latibulum ejus عكدة ochda, et عرن arin, et col. 1047 لغز logoz, sed vulgatius جحر giochar, unde جحر الضب dhab in la- tibulum suum ingressus est. Et اجحر فلان aliquis eum in latibulum suum impulit. At ادلق adlaka aquam in illud effudit, ut dhab exiret. Et دلق الضب dalaka dhab, id est, ex latibulo exiit propter aquam affusam. Et اهوي يده الي الضب immisit manum, ut caperet τὸν dhab. Et حرش charasa, venatus est, proprie de hoc animali. Haec in Giauhari, Alcamus et aliis ex Criticorum libris hinc inde collecta et excerpta.

The Critics, then, teach that it is an animal πολυώνυμον [polyōnymon], with many names. For besides ضب [ḍabb] dhab, or צב tsab, the common name, it is also called حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun (the Chaldeans write חרדונא chara[?], the Syrians ܚܕܪܘܢܐ [חדרונא] chadrona, and the Samaritans [?] adrona, as will be shown below). It is likewise called برق [barq] bork, and علين [ʿlyn] alin, and هيقل [hayqal] haikal. And, if it is fat, سبحل [?] or سحبل [siḥbal] sichbal: if old, قرسم [qirsim] kirsem; if of bad disposition, ضغطار [ḍighṭār] dhiphtar: just as the female is commonly ضبة [ḍabba] dhabba; but, when fat, حيكانا [ḥaykānā] chaicana; when with young, مكون [makūn] machun, and ممكن [mumkin] mamchin. From the verb مكن [makina] machina, proper to this animal and to the locust when they lay eggs, the egg is مكين [makīn] machin, and شلقة [shalqa] silka. The young in general, حضرم [ḥiḍrim] chidhrim; the first, مطبح [muṭbiḥ] mutbich; when just hatched from the egg, حسل [ḥisl] chisel; when already more grown, غيداق [ghaydāq] chaidak. The fat which it has around the belly and the root of the tail, كشية [kushya] chusia. And حلم [ḥalama] halama properly means to take out that fat, just as عكد [ʿakida] achada, to be fat, is used of the dhab ضب [ḍabb] alone. The male member, in the dual, نزكان [nazkān] nazachani; because it is forked. Hence the animal itself is also called سديم [sadīm] sadim, that is, II, 466 well furnished in that part. Its hiding-place is عكدة [ʿukda] ochda, and عرن [ʿirn] arin, and col. 1047 لغز [lughz] logoz, but more commonly جحر [juḥr] giochar, whence جحر الضب [jaḥara al-ḍabb] the dhab has entered its hiding-place. And اجحر فلان [ajḥara fulān] someone drove it into its hiding-place. But ادلق [adlaqa] adlaka he poured water into it, so that the dhab would come out. And دلق الضب [dalaqa al-ḍabb] dalaka dhab, that is, it came out of its hiding-place because of the water poured in. And اهوي يده الي الضب [ahwā yadahu ilā al-ḍabb] he put in his hand to catch the dhab. And حرش [ḥarasha] charasa, he hunted, used properly of this animal. These things have been gathered and excerpted here and there from Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ], Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] and other books of the Critics.


At Philosophi de natura τοῦ ضب dhab non pauca afferunt insignia. Quod veretrum diximus illi esse bifidum, Damir his verbis docet: للضب نكران وللانثي فرجان كما للورل وللحردون Dhab mas duo ha- bet veretra, et foemina eius duas vulvas, ut guaril et chardaun. Et Alcamus, للنزك نكر الضب والورل ولهم نزكان Nazach, veretrum τοῦ dhab et τοῦ guaril, qui geminum habent (Quae verba Lexicographi, cum non intelligerent, alio detorserunt). Proinde veretrum τοῦ ضب dhab sacerdos Abuchanipha scribit esse كلسان الحية اصل واحد له فرعان vt linguam serpentis, quae, ex una radice nata, tamen bifida est. Caudam habet mire nodosam, unde proverbium in Damire, اعقد من ذنب الضب Nodosior cauda τοῦ dhab. In ea enim esse ajunt حد وعشرون عقدة no- dos XXI. cum scorpionis cauda, quae et ipsa valde nodosa est, nodos [?] ticulos, ad summum septem habeat. Additur, idem animal [?] habere continuos, qui proinde nunquam decidant. [?] يقال ان اسنانه قطعة واحدة : [?] dentes ipsius in unum cohaerere. Alcamus, لا اتيك سن الحسل اي ابدا لان سنه لا تسقط Non ad te veniet dens τοῦ chisel (seu catuli τοῦ dhab): id est, nunquam ad te veniet; quia dentes ejus non cadunt. Ecce aliud de eodem simile proverbium in Damire! لا افعله حتي يرد الضب لان الضب لا يرد Hoc non faciam, donec dhab ad aquas descenderit (id est, nunquam faciam), quia dhab ad aquas nunquam descendit. Nempe non bibit prorsus, itaque raro mingit. Idem, الضب لا يشرب الما Dhab ab aquarum potu prorsus abstinet. Et paullo post, يقال انه يبول في كل اربعين يوما مرة Dicitur singulis quadraginta diebus mejere tantum semel, aut قطرة unam gut- col. 1048 tulam, ut habet aliud exemplar. De oculis ibidem, الضب يخرج من II, 467 حجره كليل البصر فيجلوه بالتحدق في الشمس Dhab e latibulo suo exit hebetiore visu: sed, pupilla ad solem abstersa, clarius videt. Epiphanius in Sampsaeis σαῦραν ἡλιακὴν, lacertam Solarem visum eodem modo recuperare asserit, cum caligare incipit: Ἐκείνη, inquit, ἀμβλυωπήσασα χρόνῳ ἀναβλέπει, διὰ ἡλιακῆς στροφάλιγγος ἐν φωλεῷ πρὸς ἀνατολὴν προσέχοντι ἑαυτὴν προσθλίψασα, καὶ νηστεύσασα πρὸς ἀνατολὴν κατανοοῦσα· Cum illa obtusum habet visum, eum aliquando post recuperat per conversionem ad solem, in lustro ad ortum obverso se ipsam comprimens, et jejuna ad Orientem respiciens. Rursus Damir de τῷ dhab ويتغذي بالنسيم ويعيش بالبره الهوا وذلك عند الهرم وفنا الرطوبات ونقص الحرارت Et alitur halitu, vesciturque aëre frigido, idque usque ad aetatem decrepitam, et donec absumatur humor (radicalis), et deficiat calor. Et infra, وهو طويل العمر ومن هذه الجهة يناسب الحيات والافاعي Longaevum est animal; quod cum serpentibus et viperis commune habet. Et Ibno-chalvia, يعيش سبع ماية فصاعدا Vivit annos septingentos, et amplius. Quod ab illis confictum puto, qui de magnis majora loquuntur. Sed et falsum omnino est, et ex chamaeleontis historia perperam huc translatum, quod ali halitu suo et frigido aëre vesci traditur. Est enim animal pene παμφάγον, quodque radicibus potissimum fructibusque vescitur. Hinc Alcamus, postquam خبلة chobla vocari scripsit vitis radices, et fructus spinosarum arborum, addit ضب خابل ياكلها dhab chabil est dhab, qui illis vescitur. Et foemina, a scorpione puncta, اكلت من حشيشة تسمي اذان الفار يزول عنها الم اللسع edit herbam, quam vocant auriculam muris, et remittitur puncturae dolor. Ita est in Alkazuinio. Sed et, auctore ipso Damire (ut pluribus infra dicetur), dhab ad vomitum redit ut canis, et proprios catulos vorat. Illum igitur solo aëre vesci, merum commentum est. Hoc commune habet cum jarboa, seu choerogryllio, quod in petrosis et arduis locis latibulum sibi deligit. Alkazuinius, من كيسه انه لا يتخذ البيت الا في موضع صلب ليلا ينهدر عليه في حوافر الدواب ولما علم انه نساء لا يتخذ البيت الي عند الاكمته او صخرة عظيمة او شجرة ليستدل بها علي بيته اذا عاب ويتباعد عن col. 1049 بيته E solertia ejus est, quod domum sibi non sumit, nisi in loco duro, ne jumentorum ungulis obtrita in se corruat. Sed et quia se novit esse valde obliviosum, eam in sublimi colle, aut in celsa rupe deligit, aut ad arborem, quam pro II, 468 indice habeat, cum ab illa abest, aut procul excedit. Damir etiam لا يتخذ حجره الا في كدية حجر خوفا من السيل والحافر ولذلك براثنه ناقصة كليلة لحفره بها في الاماكن الصلبة Neque latibulum alibi habet, quam in petris durissimis; quia ab inundationibus et fossoribus sibi timet. Ac proinde ungues illi detriti et obtusi sunt, ut qui lapidosa loca iis fodiat. Item, وفي طبعه النسيان وعدم الهداية وبه يضرب المثل في الحيرة ولذلك يحفر جحره عند الاكمة او صخرة ليلا يضل عنه اذا خرج لطلب والطعم Naturalis ipsis est oblivio, et ἀβλε-ψία. Itaque stupor ejus in proverbium cessit. Proinde lustrum suum in colle fodit, aut in rupe, ne ab eo aberret, cum exit, ut victum sibi quaerat. Proverbium, de quo Damir, ab eodem sic citatur in titulo De Proverbiis, اضل من الضب Qui a via magis aberrat, quam dhab. Quia ضب dhab pravum est animal, unde vocatur ضغطار dhiphtar, ut jam observatum, ecce aliud proverbium in usu apud Arabes, quod me docuit Alcamus, اطعم اخاك كشية الضب حشة على المواسات Cibavit fratrem tuum pinguedine τοῦ dhab, id est, ad malum patrandum eum incitavit! Partum quod attinet: اذا ارادت الضبة ان تخرج بيضها حفرت في الارض حفرة ورمت فيها البيض وطمته بالتراب وتعاهده كل يوم حتي يخرج وذلك في اربعين يوما Cum dhabba (id est, foemina τοῦ dhab) ova sua positura est, scrobem in terra defodit, in quam ova conjecta pulvere obtegit, et quotidie visitat, donec excludantur, id est, usque ad diem quadragesimum.
