Sic Damir, Alkazuinium ex parte sequutus, cujus verba sunt, فاذا اراد ان يبيض حفر مثل ادحي النعام ويرمي فيها ثمانين بيضة ويدفنها col. 1050 في التراب وبيضها مثل بيض الحمام ويدعها اربعين يوما ثم ياتي وحسول قد خرجت منها فيتعدون فياكل منها ما قدرت Cum in eo est, ut ovisivet, fodit tanquam struthionis nidum, in quem ova octoginta, columbarum ovis similia, conjicit et in pulvere sepelit. Ad quae, per dies quadraginta relicta, cum revertitur, catuli, inde exeuntes, cursitant. Ex quibus ille comedit quantumcunque potest. Nempe, ut ait Damir, يوصف العقوق لانه ياكل حسوله describitur crudelitate insignis; quia proprios catulos vorat. Unde Poeta, II, 469 اكلت بنيك كاكل الضب حتي تركت بنيك ليس لهم غذي

But the philosophers report a good many notable things about the nature of the ضب [ḍabb] dhab. That its penis is forked, as we said, Damir teaches in these words: للضب نكران وللانثي فرجان كما للورل وللحردون [li-l-ḍabb nakrān wa-li-l-unthā farjān kamā li-l-waral wa-li-l-ḥardūn] The male dhab has two penises, and its female two vulvas, like the guaril and the chardaun. And Alcamus: للنزك نكر الضب والورل ولهم نزكان [li-l-nazk nakr al-ḍabb wa-l-waral wa-lahum nazkān] Nazach is the penis of the dhab and of the guaril, which have a double one (the lexicographers, not understanding these words, twisted them to another sense). Accordingly the priest Abuchanipha writes that the penis of the ضب [ḍabb] dhab is كلسان الحية اصل واحد له فرعان [ka-lisān al-ḥayya aṣl wāḥid lahu farʿān] like the tongue of a serpent, which, though born from one root, is nevertheless forked. It has a remarkably knotty tail, whence the proverb in Damir, اعقد من ذنب الضب [aʿqad min dhanab al-ḍabb] Knottier than the tail of the dhab. For they say there are حد وعشرون عقدة [ḥd wa-ʿishrūn ʿuqda] 21 knots in it, whereas the scorpion's tail, which is itself very knotty, has at most seven knots [?] joints. It is added that the same animal [?] has continuous [teeth], which therefore never fall out. [?] يقال ان اسنانه قطعة واحدة [yuqāl anna asnānahu qiṭʿa wāḥida]: [?] its teeth cohere into one. Alcamus: لا اتيك سن الحسل اي ابدا لان سنه لا تسقط [lā ātīka sinn al-ḥisl ay abadan li-anna sinnahu lā tasquṭ] The tooth of the chisel (that is, of the young of the dhab) will not come to you: that is, it will never come to you, because its teeth do not fall out. Here is another similar proverb about the same animal in Damir! لا افعله حتي يرد الضب لان الضب لا يرد [lā afʿaluhu ḥattā yarida al-ḍabb li-anna al-ḍabb lā yarid] I will not do this until the dhab goes down to the water (that is, I will never do it), because the dhab never goes down to the water. For it does not drink at all, and so it rarely urinates. The same: الضب لا يشرب الما [al-ḍabb lā yashrab al-mā] The dhab abstains entirely from drinking water. And a little later: يقال انه يبول في كل اربعين يوما مرة [yuqāl annahu yabūl fī kull arbaʿīn yawman marra] It is said to urinate only once every forty days, or قطرة [qaṭra] one little col. 1048 drop, as another copy has it. On its eyes, in the same place: الضب يخرج من II, 467 حجره كليل البصر فيجلوه بالتحدق في الشمس [al-ḍabb yakhruj min juḥrihi kalīl al-baṣar fa-yajlūhu bi-l-taḥadduq fī al-shams] The dhab comes out of its hiding place with rather dim sight; but when its pupil has been cleansed against the sun, it sees more clearly. Epiphanius, in the Sampsaeans, asserts that the σαῦραν ἡλιακὴν [sauran hēliakēn], the solar lizard, recovers its sight in the same way when it begins to grow dim: Ἐκείνη, he says, ἀμβλυωπήσασα χρόνῳ ἀναβλέπει, διὰ ἡλιακῆς στροφάλιγγος ἐν φωλεῷ πρὸς ἀνατολὴν προσέχοντι ἑαυτὴν προσθλίψασα, καὶ νηστεύσασα πρὸς ἀνατολὴν κατανοοῦσα· [Ekeinē amblyōpēsasa chronō anablepei, dia hēliakēs strophalingos en phōleō pros anatolēn prosechonti heautēn prosthlipsasa, kai nēsteusasa pros anatolēn katanoousa] When it has dulled sight, it recovers it some time later by turning toward the sun, pressing itself into a den facing the east, and, fasting, looking toward the East. Again Damir on the dhab: ويتغذي بالنسيم ويعيش بالبره الهوا وذلك عند الهرم وفنا الرطوبات ونقص الحرارت [wa-yataghadhdhā bi-l-nasīm wa-yaʿīsh bi-l-barh al-hawā wa-dhālika ʿind al-haram wa-fanā al-ruṭūbāt wa-naqṣ al-ḥarārāt] And it is nourished by breath and lives on cold air, and this until decrepit old age, and until the (radical) moisture is consumed and the heat fails. And below: وهو طويل العمر ومن هذه الجهة يناسب الحيات والافاعي [wa-huwa ṭawīl al-ʿumr wa-min hādhihi al-jiha yunāsib al-ḥayyāt wa-l-afāʿī] It is a long-lived animal, which it has in common with serpents and vipers. And Ibno-chalvia: يعيش سبع ماية فصاعدا [yaʿīsh sabʿ māya fa-ṣāʿidan] It lives seven hundred years and more. This I think was invented by those who say greater things about great matters. But it is also altogether false, and wrongly transferred here from the account of the chameleon, that it is said to be fed by its own breath and to live on cold air. For it is an almost παμφάγον [pamphagon] animal, feeding chiefly on roots and fruits. Hence Alcamus, after writing that خبلة [khabla] chobla is the name for the roots of the vine and the fruits of thorny trees, adds: ضب خابل ياكلها [ḍabb khābil yaʾkuluhā] dhab chabil is a dhab that feeds on them. And the female, when stung by a scorpion, اكلت من حشيشة تسمي اذان الفار يزول عنها الم اللسع [akalat min ḥashīsha tusammā ādhān al-fār yazūl ʿanhā alam al-lasʿ] eats a herb called mouse-ear, and the pain of the sting abates. So it is in Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt]. Moreover, on the authority of Damir himself (as will be said more fully below), the dhab returns to its vomit like a dog, and devours its own young. That it lives on air alone is therefore a mere fiction. It has this in common with the jarboa, or choerogryllius, that it chooses its hiding place in rocky and steep places. Alkazuinius: من كيسه انه لا يتخذ البيت الا في موضع صلب ليلا ينهدر عليه في حوافر الدواب ولما علم انه نساء لا يتخذ البيت الي عند الاكمته او صخرة عظيمة او شجرة ليستدل بها علي بيته اذا عاب ويتباعد عن col. 1049 بيته [min kaysihi annahu lā yattakhidh al-bayt illā fī mawḍiʿ ṣulb laylā yanhadir ʿalayhi fī ḥawāfir al-dawābb wa-lammā ʿalima annahu nassāʾ lā yattakhidh al-bayt ilā ʿind al-akamatih aw ṣakhra ʿaẓīma aw shajara li-yastadill bihā ʿalā baytihi idhā ʿāb wa-yatabāʿad ʿan baytihi] It is part of its shrewdness that it does not take a home except in hard ground, lest, trampled by the hooves of beasts of burden, it collapse upon it. And since it knows itself to be very forgetful, it chooses it on a high hill or a lofty rock, or by a tree, which it may have as II, 468 a marker when it is away from it or goes far off. Damir also: لا يتخذ حجره الا في كدية حجر خوفا من السيل والحافر ولذلك براثنه ناقصة كليلة لحفره بها في الاماكن الصلبة [lā yattakhidh juḥrahu illā fī kudyat ḥajar khawfan min al-sayl wa-l-ḥāfir wa-li-dhālika barāthinuhu nāqiṣa kalīla li-ḥafrihi bihā fī al-amākin al-ṣulba] Nor does it have a hiding place anywhere but in the hardest rocks, because it fears floods and diggers. And accordingly its claws are worn and blunt, since it digs stony places with them. Likewise: وفي طبعه النسيان وعدم الهداية وبه يضرب المثل في الحيرة ولذلك يحفر جحره عند الاكمة او صخرة ليلا يضل عنه اذا خرج لطلب والطعم [wa-fī ṭabʿihi al-nisyān wa-ʿadam al-hidāya wa-bihi yuḍrab al-mathal fī al-ḥayra wa-li-dhālika yaḥfir juḥrahu ʿind al-akama aw ṣakhra laylā yaḍill ʿanhu idhā kharaja li-ṭalab wa-l-ṭuʿm] Forgetfulness and ἀβλεψία [ablepsia] are natural to them. So its bewilderment has become proverbial. Accordingly it digs its den on a hill or in a rock, so as not to stray from it when it goes out to seek its food. The proverb Damir mentions is cited by him thus under the heading On Proverbs: اضل من الضب [aḍall min al-ḍabb] More apt to stray from the way than the dhab. Because the ضب [ḍabb] dhab is a wicked animal, whence it is called ضغطار [ḍghṭār] dhiphtar, as already observed, here is another proverb in use among the Arabs, which Alcamus taught me: اطعم اخاك كشية الضب حشة على المواسات [aṭʿim akhāka kushyat al-ḍabb ḥashsha ʿalā al-muwāsāt] He fed your brother the fat of the dhab, that is, he incited him to commit evil! As for breeding: اذا ارادت الضبة ان تخرج بيضها حفرت في الارض حفرة ورمت فيها البيض وطمته بالتراب وتعاهده كل يوم حتي يخرج وذلك في اربعين يوما [idhā arādat al-ḍabba an tukhrija bayḍahā ḥafarat fī al-arḍ ḥufra wa-ramat fīhā al-bayḍ wa-ṭammathu bi-l-turāb wa-taʿāhadathu kull yawm ḥattā yakhruj wa-dhālika fī arbaʿīn yawman] When the dhabba (that is, the female of the dhab) is about to lay her eggs, she digs a pit in the ground, into which she throws the eggs and covers them with dust, and visits them daily until they hatch, that is, until the fortieth day. So Damir, following Alkazuinius in part, whose words are: فاذا اراد ان يبيض حفر مثل ادحي النعام ويرمي فيها ثمانين بيضة ويدفنها col. 1050 في التراب وبيضها مثل بيض الحمام ويدعها اربعين يوما ثم ياتي وحسول قد خرجت منها فيتعدون فياكل منها ما قدرت [fa-idhā arāda an yabīḍa ḥafara mithl udḥī al-naʿām wa-yarmī fīhā thamānīn bayḍa wa-yadfinuhā fī al-turāb wa-bayḍuhā mithl bayḍ al-ḥamām wa-yadaʿuhā arbaʿīn yawman thumma yaʾtī wa-ḥusūl qad kharajat minhā fa-yataʿaddawn fa-yaʾkul minhā mā qadarat] When it is about to lay, it digs something like an ostrich's nest, into which it throws eighty eggs, like pigeons' eggs, and buries them in the dust. When it returns to them after leaving them forty days, the young, coming out of them, run about. Of these it eats as many as it can. Indeed, as Damir says, يوصف العقوق لانه ياكل حسوله [yūṣaf al-ʿuqūq li-annahu yaʾkul ḥusūlahu] it is described as notable for cruelty, because it devours its own young. Hence the poet: II, 469 اكلت بنيك كاكل الضب حتي تركت بنيك ليس لهم غذي [akalta banīka ka-akl al-ḍabb ḥattā tarakta banīka laysa lahum ghidhā]


Liberos tuos comedisti, quomodo dhab foetus suos; ita ut prae alimenti inopia de- fecerint. Eidem tribuunt Arᵃbes, quod cani Petrus a)). Rursus Damir, من طبعه انه يرجع في قيه كالكلب وياكل رجيعه Etiam e natura ejus est, quod, canis instar, ad vomitum suum redit, et id, ad quod re- diit, rursus vorat. Et hoc quoque, quod في الشتا لا يخرج من حجره tota hyeme ex antro suo non excedit. Vivit tamen et pinguescit, et sic illi providet Deus, ut prae fame non deficiat. Unde Poeta Chatimolasem,

You have eaten your children, as the dhab eats its young, so that they have perished for lack of food. The Arabs attribute the same thing to it that Peter attributes to the dog a)). Again Damir: من طبعه انه يرجع في قيه كالكلب وياكل رجيعه [min ṭabʿihi annahu yarjiʿu fī qayʾihi ka-l-kalb wa-yaʾkulu rajīʿahu] It is also in its nature that, like a dog, it returns to its vomit, and devours again that to which it has returned. And this too: في الشتا لا يخرج من حجره [fī al-shitā lā yakhruju min juḥrihi] through the whole winter it does not come out of its burrow. Yet it lives and grows fat, and God so provides for it that it does not perish from hunger. Hence the poet Chatimolasem:


وكيف اخاف الفقر والله رازقن ورازق هذا الخلق في العسر واليسر تكفل بالارزاقي للخلق كلهم وللضب في البيداء وللحوت في البحر

وكيف اخاف الفقر والله رازقن [wa-kayfa akhāfu al-faqra wa-llāhu rāziqun] ورازق هذا الخلق في العسر واليسر [wa-rāziqu hādhā al-khalqi fī al-ʿusri wa-l-yusri] تكفل بالارزاقي للخلق كلهم [takaffala bi-l-arzāqi li-l-khalqi kullihim] وللضب في البيداء وللحوت في البحر [wa-li-l-ḍabbi fī al-baydāʾi wa-li-l-ḥūti fī al-baḥri]


Cur timerem paupertatem, cum Deus provideat mihi? Providet is creaturis in angustia et egestate. Victum largitur creaturis omnibus, etiam τῷ dhab in deser- to et piscibus in mari. Etiam observarunt Arabes, quibus animalibus dhab συμ-παθεῖ et ἀντιπαθεῖ. Damir, بينه وبين العقارب مودة فلذلك يويها في حجره لتلسع المتحرش به اذا ادخل يده لاخذه Inter eum et scorpiones mutuus amor intercedit. Proinde illos in latibulo suo recipit, ut venatorem pungant, cum manum suam immittit, ut eam capiat. Idem in capite فالية الافاعي quasi Viperarum scrutatorem dixeris, sic appellari asserit ضرب من الخنافس رقط تالف العقارب في col. 1051 حجرة الضب لانها اذا اخرجت يعلم ان الضب خارج لا محالة واذا زويت في الحجر علم ان وراها العقارب والحيات Speciem scarabaeorum varii coloris, quae cum scorpionibus junctim habitat in latibulis τοῦ dhab. Nempe hoc animalculum, cum exit e latibulo, signi- ficat etiam τὸν dhab sine dolo exiisse. At illud repetens significat, post eum la- tere serpentes et scorpiones. Sed τῷ dhab maxime infensus est الورل alvvarlo, seu stellio major, quem guaril vocant barbari scriptores. Abdollatif Bagdaden- sis, ubi de guaril: بينه وبين الضب عداوة فيغلب الورل II, 470 الضب ويقتله لكنه لا ياكله كما يفعل بالحية وهو لا يتخذ بيتا لنفشه ولا يحفر حجر بل يخرج الضب من حجره صارعا يستولي عليه, Inter τὸν guaril et τὸν dhab gravis est inimicitia. Sed guaril illum vincit et interimit. Non edit tamen, quomodo serpentes solet: sed, cum domum sibi non exstruat, nec latibulum fodiat, e lustro suo τὸν dhab luctando ejicit et illi praevalet. Habet et alterum hostem, serpentem nigrum, qui Arabice vocatur اسود سالخ asvvad-salich. Alcamus, الحراش الاسود السالخ لانه يحرش الضباب Sensus est, hunc serpentem alio nomine charras, id est, venatorem vocari; quia τὸν dhab venatur. Nam حرش charrasa verbum est venari, non in genere, sed peculiariter venari τὸν dhab, ut jam ante b) monuimus. His tertius hostis addatur ظربان dhorban, id est putorius, ut vocant, animal foetidissimum ex mustelarum genere, a quo non debellatur viribus, sed posticae partis flatibus ad illius antrum obversae. الظربان يقصد حجر الضب وفيه حسوله وبيضه فياتي اضيق موضع فيه فيسده بذنبه فيحول دبره ويفسوا ثلاث فسوات حتي يغشي علي الضب فياكله ويقيم في حجره حتي ياتي علي اخر حسولة Dhorban (seu putorius) ad antrum τοῦ dhab accedit, cum ibi habet catulos et ova sua, et ejus angustissimum locum occupat, quem cauda sua obstruit, tergoque ad id obuerso, tres ventris flatus emittit, donec dhab in animi deliquium incidat. Quo vorato in antro manet, donec ad ultimum usque catulorum col. 1052 ejus pervenerit. Haec Philosophi de lacerti specie, in qua versamur.

Why should I fear poverty, when God provides for me? He provides for His creatures in hardship and want. He bestows sustenance on all creatures, even on the dhab in the desert and on the fish in the sea. The Arabs have also observed with which animals the dhab has sympathy and antipathy. Damir: بينه وبين العقارب مودة فلذلك يويها في حجره لتلسع المتحرش به اذا ادخل يده لاخذه [baynahu wa-bayna al-ʿaqārib mawadda fa-li-dhālika yuwīhā fī juḥrihi li-talsaʿa al-mutaḥarrish bihi idhā adkhala yadahu li-akhdhihi] There is mutual love between it and scorpions. It therefore receives them into its hiding place, so that they may sting the hunter when he puts his hand in to catch it. The same author, in the chapter on فالية الافاعي [fāliyat al-afāʿī], as if you were to say searcher of vipers, asserts that this name is given to ضرب من الخنافس رقط تالف العقارب في col. 1051 حجرة الضب لانها اذا اخرجت يعلم ان الضب خارج لا محالة واذا زويت في الحجر علم ان وراها العقارب والحيات [ḍarb min al-khanāfis ruqṭ taʾlafu al-ʿaqārib fī ḥujrat al-ḍabb li-annahā idhā kharajat yuʿlamu anna al-ḍabba khārij lā maḥāla wa-idhā zuwiyat fī al-juḥr ʿulima anna warāhā al-ʿaqārib wa-l-ḥayyāt] a species of beetle of varied colour, which lives together with scorpions in the hiding places of the dhab. That is, when this little creature comes out of the hiding place, it signifies that the dhab has certainly gone out too. But when it goes back in, it signifies that serpents and scorpions lurk behind it. But the dhab is most hostile to الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, or the greater stellio, which barbarous writers call guaril. Abdollatif of Baghdad, on the guaril: بينه وبين الضب عداوة فيغلب الورل II, 470 الضب ويقتله لكنه لا ياكله كما يفعل بالحية وهو لا يتخذ بيتا لنفشه ولا يحفر حجر بل يخرج الضب من حجره صارعا يستولي عليه [baynahu wa-bayna al-ḍabb ʿadāwa fa-yaghlibu al-waral al-ḍabba wa-yaqtuluhu lākinnahu lā yaʾkuluhu kamā yafʿalu bi-l-ḥayya wa-huwa lā yattakhidhu baytan li-nafshihi wa-lā yaḥfiru juḥr bal yukhriju al-ḍabba min juḥrihi ṣāriʿan yastawlī ʿalayhi], Between the guaril and the dhab there is grave enmity. The guaril overcomes it and kills it. Yet it does not eat it, as it usually does serpents; but, since it builds no home for itself nor digs a hiding place, it drives the dhab out of its lair by fighting and prevails over it. It also has a second enemy, a black serpent, which in Arabic is called اسود سالخ [aswad sālikh] asvvad-salich. Alcamus: الحراش الاسود السالخ لانه يحرش الضباب [al-ḥarrāsh al-aswad al-sālikh li-annahu yaḥrushu al-ḍibāb]. The sense is that this serpent is called by another name charras, that is, hunter, because it hunts the dhab. For حرش [ḥarasha] charrasa is a verb meaning to hunt, not in general, but specifically to hunt the dhab, as we noted earlier b). To these let a third enemy be added, ظربان [ẓarbān] dhorban, that is, the putorius [polecat], as they call it, a most fetid animal of the weasel kind, by which it is vanquished not by strength but by blasts from its hind parts turned toward its burrow. الظربان يقصد حجر الضب وفيه حسوله وبيضه فياتي اضيق موضع فيه فيسده بذنبه فيحول دبره ويفسوا ثلاث فسوات حتي يغشي علي الضب فياكله ويقيم في حجره حتي ياتي علي اخر حسولة [al-ẓarbān yaqṣidu juḥr al-ḍabb wa-fīhi ḥusūluhu wa-bayḍuhu fa-yaʾtī aḍyaqa mawḍiʿ fīhi fa-yasudduhu bi-dhanabihi fa-yuḥawwilu duburahu wa-yafsū thalāth faswāt ḥattā yughshā ʿalā al-ḍabb fa-yaʾkuluhu wa-yuqīmu fī juḥrihi ḥattā yaʾtī ʿalā ākhir ḥusūlih] The dhorban (or putorius) approaches the burrow of the dhab when it has its young and its eggs there, and occupies its narrowest spot, which it blocks with its tail; and, turning its rear toward it, it emits three blasts of wind, until the dhab falls into a swoon. Having devoured it, it stays in the burrow until it has finished off its young, down to the last one col. 1052. So much from the philosophers about the species of lizard with which we are dealing.


Theologis quoque hoc idem animal magnam suggessit disputandi materiam. Quaeritur enim, quorsum concedatur ejus esus, cum sit e numero الحشرات reptilium, quorum esus est prohibitus. Et nonnulli regerunt, hoc solum excipi. Ita enim habet الوسيط id est, liber, cui titulus Mediator, in quo hae quaestiones plene deciduntur, لا يوكل من الحشرات الا الضب Nullum reptile comedatur praeter τὸν dhab. Ab aliis τῷ dhab junguntur اليربوع والقنفد jarbuo et kunphud, id est, choerogryllus et hericius, quae et ipsa reptilia sunt, et tamen ad esum conceduntur. Alii rem in medio relinquunt, postquam in utramque partem multa disputaverunt, quamvis in II, 471 Arabia hunc cibum agnoscant esse in frequenti usu. Iidem pseudo-Theologi de hoc animali magnas congerunt ineptias, quarum unam hic referre sit satis, imo plus satis. Quidam juraverat in Mahomethem, se haud unquam crediturum, nisi prior crederet هذا الضب iste dhab, qui in ore speluncae suae forte fortuna apparuit. Tum is, e spelunca exiens, ad Prophetam accessit, et dixit ipsi بلسان طلق فصيح عربي مبين يفهمه القوم جميعا لبيك وسعديك يا رسول رب العالمين lingua diserta et perspicua, et sermone Arabico manifesto, quemque omnes intellexerunt: Tibi addictus sum, et beatus sis, O Apostole Domini saeculorum. Et cum propheta dixisset, من تعبد Quem colis? Respondit dhab, Eum colo, cujus thronus est in coelis, et in terra dominatio ejus, et in mari semita ejus, et in inferis indignatio et supplicium ejus. Tum illi dixit Propheta, Quis sum ego? Et dhab regessit, Tu es Apostolus Domini saeculorum, et sigillum Prophetarum. Bene sit illi, qui in te credet et tibi obsequetur. Et male pereat, quisquis a te recedet, aut te falsitatis arguet.

This same animal has also given the theologians ample matter for dispute. For it is asked why it is permitted to eat it, since it is one of الحشرات [al-ḥasharāt], the reptiles, which are forbidden as food. Some reply that this one alone is excepted. For so says الوسيط [al-Wasīṭ], that is, the book entitled The Mediator, in which these questions are fully settled: لا يوكل من الحشرات الا الضب [lā yūkal min al-ḥasharāt illā al-ḍabb] No reptile may be eaten except τὸν [ton] dhab. Others join to the dhab اليربوع والقنفد [al-yarbūʿ wa-l-qunfud] jarbuo and kunphud, that is, the choerogryllus and the hedgehog, which are themselves reptiles too and yet are permitted as food. Others leave the matter undecided, after arguing at length on both sides, although they admit that in II, 471 Arabia this food is in frequent use. These same pseudo-theologians heap up great absurdities about this animal, of which it will be enough, indeed more than enough, to relate one here. A certain man had sworn concerning Muhammad that he would never believe unless هذا الضب [hādhā al-ḍabb] this dhab, which by chance had appeared at the mouth of its burrow, believed first. Then the dhab came out of the burrow, approached the Prophet, and said to him بلسان طلق فصيح عربي مبين يفهمه القوم جميعا لبيك وسعديك يا رسول رب العالمين [bi-lisān ṭalq faṣīḥ ʿarabī mubīn yafhamuhu al-qawm jamīʿan labbayka wa-saʿdayka yā rasūl rabb al-ʿālamīn] in eloquent and clear speech, in plain Arabic language, which all understood: I am devoted to you, and may you be blessed, O Apostle of the Lord of the worlds. And when the Prophet had said من تعبد [man taʿbud] Whom do you worship?, the dhab answered: I worship Him whose throne is in heaven, and His dominion on earth, and His path in the sea, and His wrath and punishment in the underworld. Then the Prophet said to it: Who am I? And the dhab replied: You are the Apostle of the Lord of the worlds, and the seal of the Prophets. Well be it for him who believes in you and obeys you; and may whoever turns away from you or accuses you of falsehood perish miserably.


Magi quoque suas partes hic habent. Ad eos enim refero superstitiosa illa, quae in Damire et Alkazuinio lego. Si e medio pedum hominis ضب dhab exeat, non poterit is, cui id accidit, cum ulla muliere coire. Testiculos ejus si quis deferat, illum servi sui maxime amabunt. Equum, qui talum τοῦ dhab fronti alligatum habuerit, non praeveniet ullus alius in cursus certamine. Quisquis ensi قرابا vaginam. aut thecam potius ex illius pelle fecerit, strenuus erit. Alii solum نصاب السيف capulum ensis hac pelle involvi malunt, quasi id multum referat. In vanissimis scriptoribus plura reperias hujus farinae, quae referre pudet ac piget.

The magicians also play their part here. For to them I attribute those superstitions which I read in Damir and Alkazuini. If a ضب [ḍabb] dhab comes out from between a man's feet, the man to whom this happens will be unable to have intercourse with any woman. If anyone carries its testicles, his slaves will love him greatly. A horse that has the ankle-bone of the dhab tied to its forehead will not be outrun by any other in a race. Whoever makes for his sword a قرابا [qirāban] scabbard, or rather a sheath, from its skin will be valiant. Others prefer that only the نصاب السيف [niṣāb al-sayf] hilt of the sword be wrapped in this skin, as though that mattered much. In the most frivolous writers you may find more of this sort, which one is ashamed and loath to relate.


Medici pauciora habent, sed certiora. Avicenna in capite ضب dhab, يطلي بعره علي الكلف والنمش فينفع ۞ زبله نافع لبياض العين ونزول الما ۞ Confert stercus ejus lentigini, illitum, et col. 1053 maculis faciei. Albugini item, et oculorum suffosionibus. Et in capite حردون Chardaun, postquam monuit, chardaun idem esse, quod dhab, زبله للبياض والحكة ويحد البصر Stercus ejus (confert) albugini, et oculorum pruritui, et acuit visum. Et in capite دم Dam, seu De sanguine animalium, دم الورل والحردون يقوي البصر Sanguis guaril et chardaun roborat visum. Et in capite زبل Zebel, seu De stercore, Stercus locustarum tollit e facie maculas et vitiligines; ut et stercus turdorum, qui oryza aluntur. II, 472 وكذلك زبل الحردون والورل ويحسن اللون Quod idem praestat stercus chardaun et guaril, et bonum colorem facit. Et infra, بعر الضب يجلو الكلف مجرب Fimus dhab abstergit maculas a facie: quod expertum est. Item, زبل الورل والضب والتمساح لبياض العين Stercus guaril et dhab, et crocodili ad oculorum albuginem supple adhibeatur. Et in capite بعر الحيوان id est, De fimo animalium, بعر الضب ينفع من البرص والكلف بجلايه Fimus dhab abstersoria vi sua elephantiasi medetur, et maculis in facie. Et paullo post, بعر الضب يجلو بياض العين Fimus τοῦ dhab abstergit oculorum albu- gines. Ita etiam Damir, بعرة ينفع من البرص والكلف طلا ومن البياض ونزول الما في العين اكتحالا Fimus ejus illitus leprae medetur et faciei maculis. Et collyria ex eo amovent albugines et hu- morum fluxum in oculos. Quae sumta sunt ex Alkazuinio, ubi habentur paene totidem verbis. Etiam in Abenbitare similia legas, et in aliis anonymis, qui penes me sunt (1).

The physicians have less, but more reliable. Avicenna, in the chapter ضب [ḍabb] dhab: يطلي بعره علي الكلف والنمش فينفع ۞ زبله نافع لبياض العين ونزول الما ۞ [yuṭlī baʿruhu ʿalā al-kalaf wa-l-namash fa-yanfaʿ ۞ zibluhu nāfiʿ li-bayāḍ al-ʿayn wa-nuzūl al-mā ۞] Its dung, smeared on, helps freckles and col. 1053 spots of the face; likewise white specks of the eye and cataracts. And in the chapter حردون [ḥardūn] Chardaun, after noting that the chardaun is the same as the dhab: زبله للبياض والحكة ويحد البصر [zibluhu li-l-bayāḍ wa-l-ḥikka wa-yuḥidd al-baṣar] Its dung (helps) white specks and itching of the eyes, and sharpens the sight. And in the chapter دم [dam] Dam, or On the blood of animals: دم الورل والحردون يقوي البصر [dam al-waral wa-l-ḥardūn yuqawwī al-baṣar] The blood of the guaril and the chardaun strengthens the sight. And in the chapter زبل [zibl] Zebel, or On dung: The dung of locusts removes spots and vitiligo from the face; as does the dung of thrushes fed on rice. II, 472 وكذلك زبل الحردون والورل ويحسن اللون [wa-ka-dhālika zibl al-ḥardūn wa-l-waral wa-yuḥassin al-lawn] The dung of the chardaun and the guaril does the same, and makes a good complexion. And below: بعر الضب يجلو الكلف مجرب [baʿr al-ḍabb yajlū al-kalaf mujarrab] The dung of the dhab cleanses spots from the face: this has been tested. Likewise: زبل الورل والضب والتمساح لبياض العين [zibl al-waral wa-l-ḍabb wa-l-timsāḥ li-bayāḍ al-ʿayn] The dung of the guaril, the dhab and the crocodile for white specks of the eyes; supply is to be applied. And in the chapter بعر الحيوان [baʿr al-ḥayawān], that is, On the dung of animals: بعر الضب ينفع من البرص والكلف بجلايه [baʿr al-ḍabb yanfaʿ min al-baraṣ wa-l-kalaf bi-jalāyih] The dung of the dhab by its cleansing power heals elephantiasis and spots on the face. And shortly after: بعر الضب يجلو بياض العين [baʿr al-ḍabb yajlū bayāḍ al-ʿayn] The dung of the dhab cleanses white specks of the eyes. So too Damir: بعرة ينفع من البرص والكلف طلا ومن البياض ونزول الما في العين اكتحالا [baʿra yanfaʿ min al-baraṣ wa-l-kalaf ṭilā wa-min al-bayāḍ wa-nuzūl al-mā fī al-ʿayn iktiḥālan] Its dung, smeared on, heals leprosy and spots of the face; and eye-salves made from it remove white specks and the flux of humours into the eyes. This is taken from Alkazuini, where it is found in almost the same words. You may also read similar things in Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār], and in other anonymous writers that I have R1.


II, 473 Iam id animal, quod nobis descripserunt Arabes sub nominibus ضب dhab et حردون chardaun, id ipsum esse, quod צב tsab Mosis, tam multa docent, ut de II, 474 eo dubitare sit nefas. Primo enim id adstruit similitudo nominis Hebraici cum Arabico. Utut enim sono differant Hebraicum צב tsab et Arabicum ضب dhab; tamen utrobique litera initialis est Tsade, quae Arabibus aliter sonat propter punctum adscriptum. Qua mutatione nihil frequentius. Sic צאן tson Hebraeis ovis, Arabibus est ضان dhan. Hyaena illis צבוע tsebua: his ضبع dhebu. Rana illis צפרדע tsephardea: his ضفدع dhephda. Costa illis צלע tsela: his ضلع dhila. Diadema, aut plexus crinium, illis צפירה tsephira: his ضفيرة col. 1054 dhephira. Stercus illis צפיע tsephia: his ضفع dhepha. Angustia illis צוק tsuk: his ضيق dhik. Ridere illis צחק tsachak: his ضحق dhachika. 2. Secundo, צב tsab id esse, quod diximus, planum facit series homogeneorum animalium in eodem contextu orationis. Nam sequente versu lacertae mentio fit, et stellionis, et chamaeleontis, et salamandrae, etc. ut suo loco docebitur. Et par fuit ratio, cur ea lacertae species ut immunda rejiceretur. Neque illa omitti debuit, cum in Arabia nascatur, quae Iudaeae est contermina, et sit edulis apud Arabes. 3. Huc accedit veterum auctoritas, quorum assero nullum esse, qui aliter sumserit. Certe quatuor Arabes, quos consulere licuit, editi duo, et manu-scripti II, 475 duo, cum in aliis inter se multum differant, tamen hic constanter ha-bent الضب aldhab, et Onkelos צבא tsaba, quae est ipsa vox Hebraea, sola terminatione ad Chaldaismum inflexa. In Ionathane pro צב tsab legas חרדונא chardona; in Syro ܚܕܪܘܢܐ chadrona; et in Samaritano [?] adrona: quae tria eodem recidunt. Significatur scilicet Arabum حردون chardaun, quod idem esse cum ضب dhab supra c) asseruit Avicenna. Alii similem esse volunt, alii ejus marem. Damir, الحردون دويبة شبيه بالضب وقيل هو ذكر الضب لان له ذكرين مثله Alchardaun (vel al-chirdaun potius, jubet enim ita scribere) animalculum, simile τῷ dhab: quin mas ejus esse dicitur, quia ad instar illius duo habet veretra. Alcamus, الحردون لذكر الضب ودويبة احري Alchardaun de mare τοῦ dhab (dicitur). Est et aliud (huic simile) animalculum (2).

II, 473 Now, that the animal which the Arabs have described to us under the names ضب [ḍabb] dhab and حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun is the very same as the צב tsab of Moses is shown by so many considerations that to doubt it II, 474 would be wrong. First, it is supported by the similarity of the Hebrew name to the Arabic. For although the Hebrew צב tsab and the Arabic ضب [ḍabb] dhab differ in sound, in both the initial letter is Tsade, which among the Arabs sounds differently because of the dot added to it. Nothing is more frequent than this change. Thus sheep, צאן tson to the Hebrews, is ضان [ḍān] dhan to the Arabs. Hyena is צבוע tsebua to the former, ضبع [ḍabuʿ] dhebu to the latter. Frog is צפרדע tsephardea to the former, ضفدع [ḍifdaʿ] dhephda to the latter. Rib is צלע tsela to the former, ضلع [ḍilʿ] dhila to the latter. Diadem, or braid of hair, is צפירה tsephira to the former, ضفيرة [ḍafīra] col. 1054 dhephira to the latter. Dung is צפיע tsephia to the former, ضفع [ḍfʿ] dhepha to the latter. Distress is צוק tsuk to the former, ضيق [ḍīq] dhik to the latter. To laugh is צחק tsachak to the former, ضحق [ḍḥq] dhachika to the latter. 2. Secondly, that צב tsab is what we have said is made plain by the series of related animals in the same context. For in the following verse mention is made of the lizard, the stellio, the chameleon, the salamander, etc., as will be shown in its place. And there was equal reason why this species of lizard should be rejected as unclean. Nor ought it to have been omitted, since it is native to Arabia, which borders on Judaea, and is eaten among the Arabs. 3. To this is added the authority of the ancients, none of whom, I assert, took it otherwise. Certainly the four Arabic versions I was able to consult, two printed and two in manuscript, II, 475 though they differ greatly among themselves elsewhere, here consistently have الضب [al-ḍabb] aldhab; and Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] has צבא tsaba, which is the Hebrew word itself, with only its ending adapted to Chaldee usage. In Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan], for צב tsab you read חרדונא chardona; in the Syriac ܚܕܪܘܢܐ [חדרונא] chadrona; and in the Samaritan [?] adrona: all three come to the same thing. What is meant, namely, is the حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun of the Arabs, which Avicenna asserted above c) to be the same as the ضب [ḍabb] dhab. Some hold it to be similar to it, others its male. Damir: الحردون دويبة شبيه بالضب وقيل هو ذكر الضب لان له ذكرين مثله [al-ḥardūn duwaybba shabīh bi-l-ḍabb wa-qīla huwa dhakar al-ḍabb li-anna lahu dhakarayn mithlahu] Alchardaun (or rather alchirdaun, for he directs it to be written so) is a small animal, similar to τῷ [tō] dhab: indeed it is said to be its male, because like it it has two penises. Alcamus: الحردون لذكر الضب ودويبة احري [al-ḥardūn li-dhakar al-ḍabb wa-duwaybba aḥrī] Alchardaun is said of the male τοῦ [tou] dhab. There is also another (similar) small animal R2.


Arabibus et Chaldaeis addo veteres Hebraeos, qui צב tsab, vel חרדון chardon, aperte ponunt inter lacertorum species. Quod planum facient duo loca, quae proferam, a multis jam observata, nec tamen explicata hactenus. Prior est in tractatu Talmudico Cholin cap. 9. fol. 127. a. ubi sub nomine צב tsab, in Le-ge prohibiti, Hebraei volunt similes species contineri; quia additum est juxta speciem suam. Sic enim habent verba Legis: Immunda vobis erunt inter reptilia, quae repunt super terram, talpa et mus, והצב למינהו, et tsab, juxta speciem II, 476 suam. Nempe inquiunt: להביא העריד ובן־נפילים וסלמנדרא, ut includantur arod et ben-nephilim, et salamandra, tanquam vicinae species τῷ dhab. Et recentiores quidem ignorant, quid hic sint ערוד arod et בן־נפילים ben-nephilim. Sed salamandram saltem notum est in lacertorum esse genere. Itaque צב tsab necesse est ut referatur ad idem genus. Res erit manifestior, si doceamus, quid hic sint ערוד arod et בן־נפילים ben-nephilim: et prius quidem alibi onagrum, posterius filium gigantum significat. Quae videntur esse extra rem. Itaque hic haerent interpretes, neque Talmudis Glossatores, aut Lexicographi quidquam afferunt, quod veri speciem habeat. Sed prior vox est corrupta, et pro ערוד arod, vel iruad scribendum עסוד isvvad. Id lacerti genus est album, in arenis degens, cum quo puellarum digitos conferunt poetae Arabes. Nonnulli عذفوط odphut, et عضرفوط adhraphut vocant. Alcamus, العذفوط دويبة col. 1055 بيضا ناعمة يشبة بها اصابع الجواري Alodphut, animalculum album, amoenum, quocum puellarum digiti conferuntur. Et alibi, العضرفوط العذفوط او ذكر العظا Aladhraphut, idem, quod alodphut, aut lacertae mas. Et rursus, العسود للعضرفوط من العظاء Aliswad, de adraphut lacerti genere dicitur. Item, العسودة دويبة بضا يشبه بها بنان العذاري وتكني بنة النقا Aliswada, animalculum album, cui comparantur extremae pulpae digitorum in virginibus, cognominatur Binth-onnakai, id est, arenae filia. Itaque cum inter lacertorum species ערוד censetur a Talmudicis, levi mutatione, pro ערוד legendum עסוד, ut significetur illa lacerta, quam descripsimus. Parum usitatum עסוד, nec fortasse aliunde notum, imperiti scriptores in ערוד mutaverunt, quod plane aliud, nempe onagrum sonat. Superest, ut dicamus, quod animal sit בן־נפילים ben-nephilim, istis homogeneum. Vir in his literis eximius, quique hodie parem non habet, recte colligit, hoc animal esse aquaticum; quia legitur Semoth rabba Sect. 15. וזיע את הימים והראהו את בן־הנפילים שנאמר קול יי על המים Movit (Deus) maria, et ostendit ei (Mosi) Ben-nephilim, prout dicitur Ps. XXIX, 3. „ Vox Domini super aquas. Sed idem errat gravissime, cum ex vocum affinitate et animalium (ut asserit) similitudine colligit, בן־נפילים ben-nephilim esse nauplium, sive nautilum. Nam utut nephilim ad nauplium aliquo modo alludere concedamus, tamen in rebus ipsis nulla est similitudo. Nauplius enim, sive nautilus, cum τῷ tsab nihil habet commune, sive hac voce, quod ille vult, bufo, aut testudo significetur, aut aliqua lacerti species, quod apud me est firmissimum. Lacerti enim, bufones et testudines a nauplio, vel nautilo pisce, toto genere differunt. Nec verissimile est, Hebraeos suum נפילים nephilim, a nauplii nomine deduxisse, quod parum est in usu, II, 477 nec usquam occurrit, quod meminerim, quam in uno loco Plinii. Sed neque ex נפילים nephilim factum nauplius. Patet enim, hoc nomen sumtum esse ex argumento, et nautilum dici nauplium, quia navigat tanquam in nave, ex nomine ναῦς, et verbo πλεῖν. Quid igitur est בן־נפילים ben-nephilim? Is omnino videtur esse scincus Aegyptius, de quo Avicenna libri secundi capite اسقنقور Iscancur, quomodo Arabes scincum vocant: هو ورل الماي يصاد من نيل مصر ويقولون انه من نسل التمساح اذا وضعه خارج الما ونشا خارجا Is est guaril aquaticus, qui in Aegypto capitur in Nili ripa: eum ex crocodili semine nasci ajunt, cum extra aquam illud effundit; et extra aquam crescere (3). Et rursus in capite سقنقور Scancur, ورل نيلي يصاد بمصر ويزعمون انه من نتاج التمساح في البر Est guaril Niloticus, quem in Aegypto capiunt, et col. 1056 ex crocodili semine ajunt in terra nasci. Et Alkazuinius, postquam citavit Avicennam, وقال غيره انه من نسل التمساح اذا وضعه خارج الما فما قصد الما صار تمساحا وما قصد البر صار سقنقورا Alii, inquit, dixerunt, illum esse ex crocodili semine, cum extra aquas illud ejecit, et, quidquid ad aquas pervenit, fieri crocodilum; et scincum, quod in terra manet. Et Damir, الاسقنقور نوعان هندي ومصري فالمصري منه ما يتولد ببحر القلزم وهو يغتذي بالسمك في الما وفي البر بالقطا يسرطه كالحيات Scincus duarum est specierum; Indus et Aegyptius. In Aegyptiis autem est, qui nascitur in mari Kelzem (seu Rubro), et piscibus in aqua alitur, et in terra palumbis, quos ut serpentes deglutit. Quod quia ridiculum est, pro بالقطا id est, palumbis, legendum بالعظا lacertis. Et infra, disquirens, quid inter se differant guaril et scincus, praecipuum discrimen in eo ponit, أن ورل لا ياوي الا البراري الاسقنقور لا ياوي الا بالقرب من الما او فيه quod guaril nonnisi in terra degit; scincus autem nonnisi prope II, 478 aquas, aut etiam in ipsis aquis. Et infra, لا نعرف اليوم في عصرنا الاسقنقور في ديار المصرية الا ببلاد الفيوم ومنها يجلب الي القاهرة لمن اعتني بطلبه ولا يصاد الا في ايام الشتا لانه اذا اشتد حليه البرد خرج الي البر فيصاد Hodie aetate nostra scincum in Aegyptiaca ditione alibi non novimus, quam in provincia Phium, unde Cairam defertur ad eum, cui curae est ejus disquisitio. Nec nisi hyeme capitur. Frigoris enim vi coactus in terram exit, atque inibi capitur. Et paullo post, يحل اكل الاسقنقور الهندي لانه سمك ويحتمل ان ياتي فيه وجه الحرمة لان له شبهين في البر احدهما احرام وهو الورل واخر حلال وهو الضب واما الاسقنقور المصري فهو حرام col. 1057 لانه متولد من التمساح فهو حرام كاصله Licitum est edere scincum Indicum; quia piscis est (4): quamvis illi attribuatur species rei prohibitae; quia in terra similes illi sunt guaril et dhab; quorum unus prohibitus est, alter concessus. At scincus Aegyptius prohibetur; quia ex crocodilo nascitur: itaque est vetitus ut radix ejus. E multis, quae de scinco habent Arabes (5), pauca haec excerpsimus, quia faciunt ad nostrum institutum. Ex his enim tria colliguntur. Primo, scincum sub eodem genere contineri cum τῷ dhab et τῷ guaril, cum sit illis specie similis. Secundo, esse amphibium, et plerumque in Nili aquis, adeoque etiam in mari versari. Ita, ut recte dici queat Deus movisse את הימים, maria, ut Mosi scincum ostenderet. Quamvis in ea voce sit mendum, et pro הימים, id est maria, sit legendum המים, aquas, una literula minus: quod docent sequentia, Prout dicitur, „Vox Domini super aquas“. Tertio, cum credatur scincus (quam vere, non jam quaerimus) nasci ex crocodili semine, ut Arabes constanter scribunt, apparet, quorsum ab Hebraeis appellatus sit בן-נפילים, id est, filius gigantum. Nam gigantum nomine Orientales non solum homines significant, sed et bruta quaevis majoris molis. Sic scriptor Arabs apud Damirem, في جرادة خلق عشرة من جبابرة من الحيوان In locusta natura est decem gigantum ex animalibus; ita habetur ad verbum: id est, decem majorum animalium. Nempe, ut sequitur, locusta II, 479 habet equi faciem, oculos elephanti, collum tauri, cornua cervi, etc. Eodem exemplo scincus ab Hebraeis dicitur gigantum filius, id est, crocodilorum, quibus collatus nihil quidquam est, quam perpusillum animal. His ita explicatis, veritas magis ac magis elucescet, si legatur locus integer, cujus non nisi partem citavimus. Is vero ita habet: Deus commovit aquas, ut ei (Mosi) ostenderet filium gigantum: Prout dicitur Psalm. XXIX, 3. „Vox Domini super aquas“. Commovit terram, ut ostenderet ei τὸν צב tsab: prout habetur Psalm. XXIX, 8. „Vox Domini parere facit desertum“. Ignem commovit, ut ostenderet ei salamandram: sicut dicitur Psal. XXIX, 7. „Vox Domini exscindit flammas ignis“. Ex tribus elementis ita petuntur tria diversae speciei, sed ejusdem generis animalia. Gigantum, seu crocodilorum filius, scincus, ex aquis, in quibus plerumque degit. צב tsab ex terra, cui tanquam glebae sic affixus est, ut ad aquas nunquam descendat, quod supra d) probavimus. Salamandra denique ex igne, in quo nasci, et ex quo vesci a multis putatur perperam.

To the Arabs and Chaldeans I add the ancient Hebrews, who openly place צב tsab, or חרדון chardon, among the species of lizards. This will be made plain by two passages which I shall cite; many have already noticed them, but they have not yet been explained. The first is in the Talmudic tractate Cholin, ch. 9, fol. 127a, where the Hebrews hold that similar species are included under the name צב tsab, forbidden in the Law, because the words after its kind are added. For the words of the Law run thus: These shall be unclean to you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth: the mole and the mouse, והצב למינהו, and the tsab after its II, 476 kind. They say: להביא העריד ובן־נפילים וסלמנדרא, to include the arod and the ben-nephilim and the salamander, as species close to the dhab. Now the more recent writers do not know what ערוד arod and בן־נפילים ben-nephilim are here. But it is at least known that the salamander belongs to the lizard kind. Therefore צב tsab must necessarily be assigned to the same kind. The matter will be clearer if we show what ערוד arod and בן־נפילים ben-nephilim are here. Elsewhere the former means wild ass, the latter son of giants. These seem beside the point. Here, therefore, the interpreters are at a loss, and neither the Glossators of the Talmud nor the Lexicographers offer anything with the appearance of truth. But the first word is corrupt, and instead of ערוד arod, or iruad, one should write עסוד isvvad. This is a white kind of lizard, living in the sands, to which the Arab poets compare the fingers of girls. Some call it عذفوط [ʿadhfūṭ] odphut, and عضرفوط [ʿaḍrafūṭ] adhraphut. Alcamus: العذفوط دويبة col. 1055 بيضا ناعمة يشبة بها اصابع الجواري [al-ʿadhfūṭ duwaybba bayḍā nāʿima yushbih bihā aṣābiʿ al-jawārī] Alodphut, a small animal, white and pleasing, to which the fingers of girls are compared. And elsewhere: العضرفوط العذفوط او ذكر العظا [al-ʿaḍrafūṭ al-ʿadhfūṭ aw dhakar al-ʿaẓā] Aladhraphut, the same as alodphut, or the male lizard. And again: العسود للعضرفوط من العظاء [al-ʿaswad li-l-ʿaḍrafūṭ min al-ʿaẓāʾ] Aliswad is said of the adraphut, a kind of lizard. Likewise: العسودة دويبة بضا يشبه بها بنان العذاري وتكني بنة النقا [al-ʿaswada duwaybba baḍā yushbah bihā banān al-ʿadhārī wa-tukannā binat al-naqā] Aliswada, a small white animal, to which the fingertips of virgins are compared; it is surnamed Binth-onnakai, that is, daughter of the sand. Therefore, since ערוד is reckoned by the Talmudists among the species of lizards, by a slight change we should read עסוד instead of ערוד, so that the lizard we have described is meant. Unskilled scribes changed עסוד, a little-used word and perhaps not known from elsewhere, into ערוד, which means something quite different, namely wild ass. It remains for us to say what animal the בן־נפילים ben-nephilim is, of the same kind as these. A man outstanding in these studies, who today has no equal, rightly infers that this animal is aquatic, because we read in Semoth rabba, sect. 15: וזיע את הימים והראהו את בן־הנפילים שנאמר קול יי על המים He (God) moved the seas and showed him (Moses) the Ben-nephilim, as it is said Ps 29:3: „The voice of the Lord is upon the waters.“ But the same man errs very gravely when, from the affinity of the words and the similarity of the animals (as he asserts), he infers that בן־נפילים ben-nephilim is the nauplius, or nautilus. For even if we grant that nephilim alludes in some way to nauplius, in the things themselves there is no similarity. For the nauplius, or nautilus, has nothing in common with the tsab, whether this word signifies, as he holds, a toad or a tortoise, or some species of lizard, which with me is most firmly established. For lizards, toads and tortoises differ in their whole kind from the nauplius or nautilus fish. Nor is it at all likely that the Hebrews derived their נפילים nephilim from the name nauplius, which is little used, II, 477 and occurs nowhere, so far as I remember, except in one passage of Pliny. Nor, conversely, was nauplius made from נפילים nephilim. For it is evident that this name was taken from the thing itself, and that the nautilus is called nauplius because it sails as in a ship, from the noun ναῦς [naus] and the verb πλεῖν [plein]. What, then, is the בן־נפילים ben-nephilim? It seems altogether to be the Egyptian skink, of which Avicenna says in book 2, in the chapter اسقنقور [isqanqūr] Iscancur, as the Arabs call the skink: هو ورل الماي يصاد من نيل مصر ويقولون انه من نسل التمساح اذا وضعه خارج الما ونشا خارجا [huwa waral al-māy yuṣād min Nīl Miṣr wa-yaqūlūn innahu min nasl al-timsāḥ idhā waḍaʿahu khārij al-mā wa-nashaʾa khārijan] It is the aquatic guaril, which is caught in Egypt on the bank of the Nile. They say that it is born from the seed of the crocodile when it sheds it outside the water, and that it grows up outside the water R3. And again in the chapter سقنقور [saqanqūr] Scancur: ورل نيلي يصاد بمصر ويزعمون انه من نتاج التمساح في البر [waral nīlī yuṣād bi-Miṣr wa-yazʿumūn annahu min nitāj al-timsāḥ fī al-barr] It is the Nile guaril, which they catch in Egypt, and col. 1056 they say it is born on land from the seed of the crocodile. And Alkazuinius, after citing Avicenna: وقال غيره انه من نسل التمساح اذا وضعه خارج الما فما قصد الما صار تمساحا وما قصد البر صار سقنقورا [wa-qāla ghayruhu innahu min nasl al-timsāḥ idhā waḍaʿahu khārij al-mā fa-mā qaṣada al-mā ṣāra timsāḥan wa-mā qaṣada al-barr ṣāra saqanqūran] Others, he says, have said that it comes from the seed of the crocodile when it has cast it out of the waters; and that whatever reaches the waters becomes a crocodile, and whatever stays on land a skink. And Damir: الاسقنقور نوعان هندي ومصري فالمصري منه ما يتولد ببحر القلزم وهو يغتذي بالسمك في الما وفي البر بالقطا يسرطه كالحيات [al-isqanqūr nawʿān hindī wa-miṣrī fa-l-miṣrī minhu mā yatawallad bi-baḥr al-Qulzum wa-huwa yaghtadhī bi-l-samak fī al-mā wa-fī al-barr bi-l-qaṭā yasruṭuhu ka-l-ḥayyāt] The skink is of two species, the Indian and the Egyptian. Among the Egyptian ones is one that is born in the sea of Kelzem (that is, the Red Sea), and feeds on fish in the water, and on land on doves, which it swallows like snakes. Since this is absurd, instead of بالقطا [bi-l-qaṭā], that is, on doves, one should read بالعظا [bi-l-ʿaẓā] on lizards. And further on, inquiring how the guaril and the skink differ from each other, he places the chief difference in this: أن ورل لا ياوي الا البراري الاسقنقور لا ياوي الا بالقرب من الما او فيه [anna waral lā yaʾwī illā al-barārī al-isqanqūr lā yaʾwī illā bi-l-qurb min al-mā aw fīhi] that the guaril lives only on land, but the skink only near II, 478 the waters, or even in the waters themselves. And further on: لا نعرف اليوم في عصرنا الاسقنقور في ديار المصرية الا ببلاد الفيوم ومنها يجلب الي القاهرة لمن اعتني بطلبه ولا يصاد الا في ايام الشتا لانه اذا اشتد حليه البرد خرج الي البر فيصاد [lā naʿrif al-yawm fī ʿaṣrinā al-isqanqūr fī diyār al-miṣriyya illā bi-bilād al-Fayyūm wa-minhā yujlab ilā al-Qāhira li-man iʿtanā bi-ṭalabihi wa-lā yuṣād illā fī ayyām al-shitā li-annahu idhā ishtadda ḥlyh al-bard kharaja ilā al-barr fa-yuṣād] Today, in our age, we know of the skink in the Egyptian territory nowhere but in the province of Phium, from which it is brought to Cairo for whoever takes the trouble to seek it. It is caught only in winter; for, driven by the force of the cold, it comes out onto land, and is caught there. And shortly after: يحل اكل الاسقنقور الهندي لانه سمك ويحتمل ان ياتي فيه وجه الحرمة لان له شبهين في البر احدهما احرام وهو الورل واخر حلال وهو الضب واما الاسقنقور المصري فهو حرام col. 1057 لانه متولد من التمساح فهو حرام كاصله [yaḥill akl al-isqanqūr al-hindī li-annahu samak wa-yuḥtamal an yaʾtī fīhi wajh al-ḥurma li-anna lahu shibhayn fī al-barr aḥaduhumā aḥrām wa-huwa al-waral wa-ākhar ḥalāl wa-huwa al-ḍabb wa-ammā al-isqanqūr al-miṣrī fa-huwa ḥarām li-annahu mutawallid min al-timsāḥ fa-huwa ḥarām ka-aṣlihi] It is lawful to eat the Indian skink, because it is a fish R4, although an aspect of something forbidden may be attributed to it, because on land the guaril and the dhab resemble it, of which one is forbidden and the other permitted. But the Egyptian skink is forbidden, because it is born from the crocodile; it is therefore forbidden like its root. Of the many things the Arabs R5 say about the skink, we have excerpted these few, because they serve our purpose. For three things are inferred from them. First, that the skink is contained under the same kind as the dhab and the guaril, since it is similar to them in appearance. Second, that it is amphibious, and lives mostly in the waters of the Nile, and so also in the sea, so that God can rightly be said to have moved את הימים, the seas, in order to show the skink to Moses. Though there is an error in that word, and instead of הימים, that is, seas, one should read המים, waters, with one small letter fewer, as what follows shows: As it is said, „The voice of the Lord is upon the waters“. Third, since the skink is believed (how truly, we do not now ask) to be born from the seed of the crocodile, as the Arabs consistently write, it is clear why it was called by the Hebrews בן-נפילים, that is, son of giants. For by the name of giants the Orientals denote not only men but also any beasts of greater bulk. Thus an Arab writer in Damir: في جرادة خلق عشرة من جبابرة من الحيوان [fī jarāda khalq ʿashara min jabābira min al-ḥayawān] In the locust is the nature of ten giants among animals; so it reads word for word, that is, of ten larger animals. For, as follows, the locust II, 479 has the face of a horse, the eyes of an elephant, the neck of a bull, the horns of a stag, etc. On the same pattern the skink is called by the Hebrews son of giants, that is, of crocodiles, compared with which it is nothing but a very tiny animal. These things being thus explained, the truth will shine out more and more if the whole passage is read, of which we have cited only a part. It runs thus: God stirred the waters, to show him (Moses) the son of giants, as it is said Ps 29:3: „The voice of the Lord is upon the waters“. He stirred the earth, to show him the צב tsab, as it is written Ps 29:8: „The voice of the Lord makes the desert bring forth“. He stirred fire, to show him the salamander, as it is said Ps 29:7: „The voice of the Lord cuts out flames of fire“. Thus from three elements are drawn three animals of different species but of the same kind: the son of giants, or of crocodiles, the skink, from the waters, in which it mostly lives; the צב tsab from the earth, to which it is so attached, as if to the soil, that it never goes down to the waters, as we proved above d); and finally the salamander from fire, in which many wrongly suppose it is born and on which it feeds.


Alter locus est ex Berescith Rabba Sectione octuagesima tertia, qui nou magis intelligitur, quam prior: הביא חכינא וזיוג לה חרדון ויצאת מהם חברבר, Adduxit chacina, et copulavit eam τῷ chardon, et ex iis natus est chabarber. Agitur de Ana, qui legitur הימים jemim, in deserto invenisse, id est, Hemaeis occurrisse, ut alibi e) docuimus. Sed Hebraei mulos intelligunt, quorum Ana fuerit primus inventor, asina equo, aut onagro admota. Quae diversarum specierum copulatio cum ex Lege Mosis sit illicita, Deus, ut ajunt, in hujus criminis ultionem, voluit et ipse miscere diversae speciei animalia, unde id nasceretur, quod homini esset noxium. Itaque τὸν חרדון chardon cum חכינה chacina copulavit; unde nata est tertia species, utraque pejor, nempe חברבר cha- col. 1058 barber, cujus morsus est tam noxius, ut מעולם לא נשך אדם חברבר וחיה, nunquam convalescat homo, quem momorderit chabarber. Hinc Talmud Hierusalem in Berachoth fol. 12. b. מימיו לא יאמר לך אדם שעקצו חברבר וחיה שנשכו כלב שיטה וחיה שבעטתו פרדה וחיה Nemo unquam tibi dicet, se punctum a chabarber convaluisse, aut a cane rabioso morsum convaluisse, aut a mula calcibus petitum convaluisse. Et fol. 9. a. narratur historiola de R. Chanina, Dusae filio, qui, dum orabat, morsus a chabarber, ab oratione non destitit. Non tamen ipse obiit, sed obiit chabarber, qui illum momorderat. Ac proinde dictum est, אי לו לאדם שנשכו חברבר ואי לו לחברבר שנשך את רבי חנינה Vae illi homini, quem momorderit chabarber! Sed vae illi chabarber, qui momorderit Rabbi Chaninam! Iam si consulas Lexicographos, ut discas, quid sit חרדון chardon; quid חכינא chacina; quid חברבר chabarber: ii te docebunt, chardon esse bufonem, II, 480 vel testudinem, et chacina, serpentis genus; et ex eorum concubitu natum esse chabarber, id est, bestiam, utriusque naturae participem. Quae cum sint absurdissima, quidni hic cum Poeta dicamus,

The other passage is from Bereshit Rabbah, section 83, and it is no better understood than the former: הביא חכינא וזיוג לה חרדון ויצאת מהם חברבר, He brought a chacina and coupled it with the chardon, and from them was born the chabarber. The subject is Anah, who is read to have found הימים jemim in the desert, that is, to have come upon the Emim, as we have shown elsewhere e). But the Hebrews understand mules, of which Anah was supposedly the first inventor, by bringing a she-ass to a horse or a wild ass. Since such a coupling of different species is forbidden by the Law of Moses, God, they say, in punishment for this crime, chose himself also to mix animals of different species, so that something harmful to man would be born from them. So he coupled the חרדון chardon with the חכינה chacina; from these was born a third species, worse than either, namely the חברבר chabarber col. 1058, whose bite is so harmful that מעולם לא נשך אדם חברבר וחיה, a man whom the chabarber has bitten never recovers. Hence the Jerusalem Talmud, in Berakhot, fol. 12b: מימיו לא יאמר לך אדם שעקצו חברבר וחיה שנשכו כלב שיטה וחיה שבעטתו פרדה וחיה No one will ever tell you that he recovered after being stung by a chabarber, or recovered after being bitten by a rabid dog, or recovered after being kicked by a she-mule. And on fol. 9a a little story is told of R. Chanina, son of Dosa, who, while he was praying, was bitten by a chabarber and did not stop praying. Yet he himself did not die; rather the chabarber that had bitten him died. And so it was said: אי לו לאדם שנשכו חברבר ואי לו לחברבר שנשך את רבי חנינה Woe to the man whom the chabarber has bitten! But woe to the chabarber that has bitten Rabbi Chanina! Now if you consult the lexicographers to learn what the חרדון chardon is, what the חכינא chacina is, and what the חברבר chabarber is, they will teach you that the chardon is a toad II, 480 or a tortoise, and the chacina a kind of serpent, and that from their union the chabarber was born, that is, a beast sharing the nature of both. Since this is utterly absurd, why should we not say here with the Poet,


Iungentur jam gryphes equis? — — —

Shall griffins now be mated with horses? — — —


Bufoni enim, aut testudini nihil est commune cum serpentibus: nec copulari possunt tam diversa animalia: nec, si miscerentur, posset ex iis tertium aliquid nasci. Proinde nemo indicavit hactenus, quae sit tertia illa species, ex angue et bufone (aut testudine) nata. Itaque, utut inepti sint Hebraeorum magistri, absit tamen, ut illos putem eo stultitiae devenisse, ut haec monstra sibi fingerent. Omnino igitur his tribus vocibus, חרדון chardon, חכינא chacina, et חברבר chabarber, tria designantur animalia, quae, licet specie diversa, genere tamen conveniunt. Nec usque adeo difficile est indicare, quaenam illa sint. Iam enim didicimus, חרדון chardon idem esse, quod צב tsab, vel ضب dhab, lacerti genus, de quo tam multa nos docuerunt Arabes. Et pro חכינא chacina est certo certius legendum חבינא chabina, Beth et Caph permutatis, quae literae sunt simillimae, et per librariorum incuriam non raro permutantur. Proinde hanc vocem in Ialkut per Beth, חבנא chabna, vel chabina legi, observat Buxtorfius, quae scriptura est verissima. Nam Arabice حبن chabna est hydropisi laborare. Nulla vox est frequentior in medicorum libris. Atque hinc ام حبين ummo chubaini, quasi mater hydropisis: et حبينة chubaina, vel chabina, quasi hydropica, dicitur foemina chamaeleontis, aut lacertae quaedam species, huic simillima; quia ventrem habet turgidum, ac si hydropisi laboraret (6). Utrumque nomen est in Alcamus. Et prius in Damire sic explicatur, واغا سميت بذلك من الحبن لكبر بطنها وهي علي خلقة الحربا غير صدر Utique sic vocatur ab hydropisi, propter ventris magnitudinem, et est naturae chamaeleontis, solo pectore excepto. Et Ibnossachith, هي اعرض العظاة وراسها عرض Haec est vulgari lacerta latior, et latum habet caput. Et Ibnokatiba, ام حبين تستقبل للشمس col. 1059 وتدور معها كيف دارت وهذه صفة الحربا Ummo chubain ad solem se obvertit, et cum illo convertitur, quod est chamaeleontis attributum. Et auctor المرصع id est, Gemmati operis, اختلف في ام حبين فقيل هي ضرب من العظا وقيل هي اعرض منها وقيل هي انثي الحرابي يتحاماها الاعراب فلا II, 481 ياكلونها لنتنها De ea dissentiunt. Alii enim dicunt, vulgaris lacerti genus esse, alii latiorem esse, alii chamaeleontis esse foeminam. Propter foetorem Arabes ab ea abhorrent, neque in cibos recipiunt. Haec igitur est chabina, ex cujus coitu cum chardon fingitur oriri chabarber, id est, salamandra, ni fallor. Cujus venenum quam sit potens, in calidioribus scilicet locis, doceant haec Plinii libri vigesimi noni capite quarto: Intra omnia venenata salamandrae scelus maximum est. Caetera enim singulos feriunt, nec plures pariter interimunt. Salamandra populos necare improvidos potest. Nam, si arbori irrepsit, omnia poma inficit veneno, et eos, qui ederint, necat, frigida vi nihil ab aconito distans. Quinimo si contacto ab ea ligno, vel pede crusta panis incoquatur, idem veneficium est, vel si in puteum cadat. Quippe, cum saliva ejus quacunque parte corporis vel in pede imo respersa, omnis in toto corpore defluat pilus. Et libri decimi capite sexagesimo septimo, Ejusdem sanie, quae lactea ore vomitur, quacunque parte corporis humani contacta, toti defluunt pili: idque, quod contactum est, colorem in vitiliginem mutat. Et haec Aeliani de sue, quae salamandram ederit, libri noni capite vigesimo octavo: Τοὺς γε μὲν αὐτῆς γευσαμένους ἀποκτείνει. Illos, qui carnibus ejus vescuntur, interimit. Et haec Theophrasti: Aquas, quibus admixta fuerit, exitiales reddit; item fructus, praesertim mortua. Et haec Gesneri pagina octogesima nona, Galli quidam olim mihi narrarunt, vulgo apud eos ferri, si Blanda (sic Salamandram Narbonenses vocant) in acervo tritici reperiatur, totum infici, adeo, vt vel gallinae vescentes inde pereant. Et infra, Hanc lacertam in quibusdam Galliae locis arressadam vocant, cujus morsum adeo exitialem esse putant, ut nulla vitae spes relinquatur (quod ipsum ab Hebraeis dicitur de chabarber). Itaque vulgo haec metra celebrant:

For the toad, or the tortoise, has nothing in common with serpents. Such different animals cannot copulate, nor, if they did mate, could some third thing be born from them. Accordingly no one has so far shown what that third species, born of a snake and a toad (or a tortoise), might be. Therefore, however inept the masters of the Hebrews may be, far be it from me to think that they reached such a degree of folly as to invent these monsters. These three words, then, חרדון chardon, חכינא chacina, and חברבר chabarber, certainly designate three animals which, though different in species, nevertheless agree in genus. Nor is it so very difficult to show what they are. For we have already learned that חרדון chardon is the same as צב tsab, or ضب [ḍabb] dhab, a kind of lizard about which the Arabs have taught us so much. And for חכינא chacina we must most certainly read חבינא chabina, with Beth and Caph interchanged; these letters are very similar and are not rarely confused through the carelessness of copyists. Accordingly Buxtorf observes that in the Ialkut this word is read with Beth, חבנא chabna, or chabina, and this spelling is entirely correct. For in Arabic حبن [ḥabana] chabna means to suffer from dropsy. No word is more frequent in the books of the physicians. And hence ام حبين [umm ḥubayn] ummo chubaini, as it were mother of dropsy, and حبينة [ḥubayna] chubaina, or chabina, as it were the dropsical one, is the name of the female chameleon, or of a certain species of lizard very like it, because it has a swollen belly, as if it suffered from dropsy R6. Both names are in Alcamus. And the former is explained thus in Damir: واغا سميت بذلك من الحبن لكبر بطنها وهي علي خلقة الحربا غير صدر [wāghā summiyat bi-dhālika min al-ḥabn li-kibar baṭnihā wa-hiya ʿalī khilqat al-ḥirbā ghayr ṣadr] It is so called from dropsy, because of the size of its belly, and it is of the nature of the chameleon, the chest alone excepted. And Ibnossachith: هي اعرض العظاة وراسها عرض [hiya aʿraḍ al-ʿaẓāh wa-raʾsuhā ʿarḍ] This is broader than the common lizard, and has a broad head. And Ibnokatiba: ام حبين تستقبل للشمس col. 1059 وتدور معها كيف دارت وهذه صفة الحربا [umm ḥubayn tastaqbil lil-shams wa-tadūr maʿahā kayfa dārat wa-hādhihi ṣifat al-ḥirbā] Ummo chubain turns itself toward the sun and turns round with it, which is the property of the chameleon. And the author of المرصع [al-Muraṣṣaʿ], that is, the Inlaid Work: اختلف في ام حبين فقيل هي ضرب من العظا وقيل هي اعرض منها وقيل هي انثي الحرابي يتحاماها الاعراب فلا II, 481 ياكلونها لنتنها [ukhtulifa fī umm ḥubayn fa-qīla hiya ḍarb min al-ʿaẓā wa-qīla hiya aʿraḍ minhā wa-qīla hiya unthā al-ḥarābī yataḥāmāhā al-aʿrāb fa-lā yaʾkulūnahā li-natnihā] There is disagreement about it. Some say it is a kind of common lizard, others that it is broader, others that it is the female of the chameleon. Because of its stench the Arabs shun it and do not take it as food. This, then, is the chabina, from whose coupling with the chardon the chabarber is imagined to arise, that is, the salamander, if I am not mistaken. How potent its venom is, namely in warmer places, these words of Pliny, book 29, chapter 4, may show: Among all venomous creatures the salamander's wickedness is the greatest. For the others strike individuals and do not kill many at once. The salamander can kill whole peoples unawares. For if it has crept onto a tree, it infects all the fruit with poison and kills those who eat it, with a cold force no different from aconite. Indeed, if a crust of bread is baked on wood it has touched, or with its foot, the same poisoning results, or if it falls into a well. For when its saliva is sprinkled on any part of the body, even the sole of the foot, all the hair on the whole body falls out. And book 10, chapter 67: By its fluid, which it vomits milky from its mouth, whatever part of the human body is touched, all the hair falls out; and the part touched changes its colour into a leprous blotch. And these words of Aelian, book 9, chapter 28, about a pig that has eaten a salamander: Τοὺς γε μὲν αὐτῆς γευσαμένους ἀποκτείνει [Tous ge men autēs geusamenous apokteinei]. It kills those who eat its flesh. And these of Theophrastus: It makes waters with which it has been mixed deadly; likewise fruits, especially when it is dead. And these of Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium], page 89: Certain Frenchmen once told me that it is commonly said among them that if a Blanda (so the people of Narbonne call the salamander) is found in a heap of wheat, the whole is infected, so much so that even hens feeding on it die. And further on: In certain places of France they call this lizard arressada; they think its bite so deadly that no hope of life remains (which is the very thing the Hebrews say of the chabarber). So they commonly repeat these verses:


Si mordu tá une arressade,
Pren ton linceul, et ta flessade.

Si mordu tá une arressade, Pren ton linceul, et ta flessade.


Si te salamandra momorderit, accipe linteum tuum, et tuum lodicem: id est, in lecto decumbito, tanquam moriturus. Et Rhoeti a salamandra morsum ajunt tot medicis opus habere, quot distinguitur maculis. Atque hoc quoque notandum venit, maculosum esse animal, ac proinde varium a Dioscoride, et a Plinio stellatum dici. Quod cum stellione illi commune est. Inde igitur ab Hebraeis חברבר chabarber est appellata. Nam Ierem. XIII, 23. חברברות chabarburoth sunt pardorum maculae. Ita Maal germanice dici conjectat Gesnerus a maculis et punctis, quibus toto corpore pingitur atque distinguitur. Maal enim (inquit) maculam, et maalen pingere, nostri dicunt.

If a salamander bites you, take your linen and your blanket: that is, lie down in bed as one about to die. And the Rhaetians say that one bitten by a salamander needs as many physicians as the spots with which it is marked. This too should be noted: the animal is spotted, and is therefore called varius [variegated] by Dioscorides and stellatus [starred] by Pliny. This it has in common with the stellio. Hence, then, it was called חברבר chabarber by the Hebrews. For in Jer 13:23. חברברות chabarburoth are the spots of leopards. So Gesner conjectures that it is called Maal in German from the spots and dots with which its whole body is painted and marked. For (he says) our people say Maal for a spot, and maalen for to paint.


Sequitur, ut dicamus, quorsum in Graeca versione pro צב tsab legatur ὁ κροκόδειλος ὁ χερσαῖος· et in Vulgata crocodilus, absque epitheto. Hujus interpretationis ratio non potest plene percipi, nisi rem altius repetamus in rudiorum col. 1060 II, 482 gratiam, qui crocodili nomine nihil aliud intelligunt, quam Aegyptiam belluam magnae molis. At Ionibus, qui primi mortalium hanc vocem usurparunt, crocodilus erat lacertae genus in sepibus et maceriis commorari solitae. Ridiculum igitur Grammaticorum commentum est, quo crocodilum dici somniant aut a colore croceo, aut quia crocum timet, aut τὰς κρόκας, id est, littora: cum non alia fuerit causa nominis, quam formae similitudo cum Ionicis crocodilis, id est, lacertis sepium. Herodotus libro secundo: Κροκοδείλους δὲ Ἴωνες ὠνόμασαν, εἰκάζοντες αὐτῶν τὰ εἴδεα τοῖσι παρὰ σφίσι γινομένοισι κροκοδεί-λοισι, τοῖσιν ἐν τῇσιν αἱμασίῃσι. De talibus crccodilis accipiendum, quod Plinius f) excerpsit ex Democrito, crocodilo magnitudine similem esse chamaeleontem. Idem enim alibi chamaeleonti tribuit lacertae magnitudinem. Neque aliud cogitabat vetus Grammaticus, quisquis est, ex quo haec verba descripserunt Etymologus et Phavorinus: Ὁ δὲ κροκόδειλος ζωΰφιόν ἐστι μικρόν (nisi cum Eustathio, pro κροκόδειλος, legamus κροκύδειλος). Et potest id esse sumtum ex historia de fonte Zareta, vel Azaritia, prope Chalcedonem, in quo parvos crocodilos, id est, aquaticas lacertas veteres descripserunt. Antigonus Mirabilium capite centesimo sexagesimo secundo, Εὔδοξον δ’ ἱστορεῖν τὴν μὲν ἐν Καρχηδόνι (lege Χαλκηδόνι) κρήνην κροκοδείλους ἐν αὐτῇ μικροὺς (ἔχουσαν) ὁμοίους τοῖς ἐν Αἰ-γύπτῳ. Strabo libro duodecimo, ubi de Chalcedone: Ἔχει δ’ ἡ χώρα μὲν μι-κρὰν ὑπὲρ τῆς θαλάττης κρήνην Ἀζαριτίαν, τρέφουσαν κροκοδείλους μικρούς. Stephanus, Ζάρητα· κρήνη ὑπὲρ τῆς Καλχηδονίας θαλάσσης, μικροὺς τρέφου-σα κροκοδείλους, οἱ καλοῦνται Ζαρήτιοι. In risu Saturnalicio g) Statius hos crocodilos vocat Byzantiacos lacertos, cum scribit de libro, ad se misso:

It remains for us to say why in the Greek version ὁ κροκόδειλος ὁ χερσαῖος [ho krokodeilos ho chersaios] is read for צב tsab, and in the Vulgate crocodilus [crocodile], without an epithet. The reason for this rendering cannot be fully grasped unless we go further back, for the sake of the less learned, col. 1060 II, 482 who understand by the name crocodile nothing other than the Egyptian beast of great bulk. But for the Ionians, the first of mortals to use this word, the crocodile was a kind of lizard that usually lives in hedges and dry-stone walls. Ridiculous, therefore, is the invention of the grammarians, who dream that the crocodile is so called either from its saffron colour, or because it fears saffron, or from τὰς κρόκας [tas krokas], that is, the shores. For there was no other reason for the name than its likeness in form to the Ionian crocodiles, that is, the lizards of the hedges. Herodotus, book 2: Κροκοδείλους δὲ Ἴωνες ὠνόμασαν, εἰκάζοντες αὐτῶν τὰ εἴδεα τοῖσι παρὰ σφίσι γινομένοισι κροκοδείλοισι, τοῖσιν ἐν τῇσιν αἱμασίῃσι [Krokodeilous de Iōnes ōnomasan, eikazontes autōn ta eidea toisi para sphisi ginomenoisi krokodeiloisi, toisin en tēisin haimasiēisi]. To such crocodiles must be referred what Pliny f) excerpted from Democritus, that the chameleon is similar in size to the crocodile. For elsewhere he ascribes to the chameleon the size of a lizard. Nor did the old grammarian, whoever he is, from whom the Etymologicum and Phavorinus copied these words, have anything else in mind: Ὁ δὲ κροκόδειλος ζωΰφιόν ἐστι μικρόν [Ho de krokodeilos zōyphion esti mikron] (unless, with Eustathius, we read κροκύδειλος [krokydeilos] for κροκόδειλος [krokodeilos]). And this may have been taken from the account of the spring Zareta, or Azaritia, near Chalcedon, in which the ancients described small crocodiles, that is, water lizards. Antigonus, Mirabilia, chapter 162: Εὔδοξον δ’ ἱστορεῖν τὴν μὲν ἐν Καρχηδόνι [Eudoxon d’ historein tēn men en Karchēdoni] (read Χαλκηδόνι [Chalkēdoni]) κρήνην κροκοδείλους ἐν αὐτῇ μικροὺς (ἔχουσαν) ὁμοίους τοῖς ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ [krēnēn krokodeilous en autēi mikrous (echousan) homoious tois en Aigyptōi]. Strabo, book 12, on Chalcedon: Ἔχει δ’ ἡ χώρα μὲν μικρὰν ὑπὲρ τῆς θαλάττης κρήνην Ἀζαριτίαν, τρέφουσαν κροκοδείλους μικρούς [Echei d’ hē chōra men mikran hyper tēs thalattēs krēnēn Azaritian, trephousan krokodeilous mikrous]. Stephanus: Ζάρητα· κρήνη ὑπὲρ τῆς Καλχηδονίας θαλάσσης, μικροὺς τρέφουσα κροκοδείλους, οἱ καλοῦνται Ζαρήτιοι [Zarēta; krēnē hyper tēs Kalchēdonias thalassēs, mikrous trephousa krokodeilous, hoi kalountai Zarētioi]. In his Saturnalian jest g) Statius calls these crocodiles Byzantine lizards, when he writes of a book sent to him:


Tu rosum tineis, situque putrem,
Quales aut Libycis madent olivis,
Aut thus Niliacum piperve servant,
Aut Byzantiacos colunt lacertos.

You [sent] one gnawed by moths and rotten with mould,
such as those that are soaked with Libyan olives,
or keep Nilotic incense or pepper,
or house Byzantine lizards.


Eum habuit usum crocodili vox apud Graecos vetustissimos. Sed iidem ad Niloticas belluas translatum nomen paullatim lacertis ademerunt. Nisi quod peregrinas quasdam in eo genere species, quae visae sunt usu, aut figura, aut magnitudine prae caeteris insignes, aut ad majoris crocodili formam propius accedere, sic vocare non destiterunt. Terrestris tamen epitheto fere addito ad fluviatilis differentiam. Sic Aristoteles Histeriae libri secundi capite decimo septimo, ubi de ventre animalium, eandem ventris rationem esse dicit τοῖς κροκοδεί-λοις ἀμφοῖν, utrisque crocodilis, id est, tam terrestribus, quam aquaticis. Et libri quinti capite trigesimo tertio, Τίκτουσι δὲ καὶ σαῦροι, καὶ κροκόδειλοι οἱ II, 483 χερσαῖοι, καὶ οἱ ποταμιοὶ, εἰς τὴν γῆν. Apollonius Mirabilium capite trigesimo nono ex Aristotelis Eclogis τῶν ἀνατομῶν· Ὄφις ὤφθη ἐν Πάφῳ πόδας ἔχων δύο, ὁμοίους χερσαίῳ κροκοδείλῳ. Aelianus Historiae libri primi capite quinquagesimo octavo, Καὶ αἱ σαῦραι δὲ ἐπιβουλεύουσι ταῖς μελίτταις, καὶ οἱ κροκόδειλοι οἱ χερσαῖοι. Et libri decimi sexti capite sexto de Indico phattage, Ἐν Ἰνδοῖς γίνεται ζῶον κροκοδείλῳ χερσαίῳ παραπλήσιον ἰδεῖν, etc. Nicandri Scholiastes de salamandra, Ἔοικε δὲ τῷ χερσαίῳ κροκοδείλῳ. Hieronymus in Iovinianum libri secundi capite sexto, Quanquam Syri et crocodilis terrenis, Afri etiam viridibus lacertis vesci solebant. Proinde Hesychius, ut crocodili nomen doceat ad utrumque esse homonymum: Κροκόδειλος, inquit, τὸ ζῶον· καὶ τὸ ἐν τῷ Νείλῳ, καὶ τὸ χερσαῖον. Interim non constat satis, quae demum sint illae lacertorum species, quibus attribuitur crocodili terrestris nomen. In Corinthiacis sic agit Pausanias, quasi nulli sint alii hujus nominis lacerti, quam magni illi bicubitales in Mauritania Libyae. Haec enim illius verba sunt: Λιβύη μέν γε μόνη κροκοδείλους τρέφει χερσαίους διπήχεων οὐκ ἐλάσσονας. Iidem in Herodoto dicuntur esse κροκόδειλοι, ὅσον τε τριπήχεες χερσαῖοι, τῇσι σαυρῇσι ἐμ-φερέστατοι, crocodili circiter tricubitales, terrestres, lacertis similes. Strabo vo- col. 1061 cat σαύρας, διπήχεις. Et Aristoteles his pares in Arabia describit, si vera sunt haec Aeliani libri decimi sexti capite quadragesimo primo: Σαύρους δὲ Ἀριστοτέ-λης ἐν τῇ τῶν Ἀράβων γῇ τίκτεσθαί φησι, καὶ δύο πήχεις ἔχειν αὐτούς. Sed in loco Aristotelis, ex quo haec hausit Aelianus, solum dicuntur πηχυαῖοι cubitales, nusquam διπήχεις bicubitales. Verba sunt Historiae libri octavi capite vigesimo octavo, Ἐν δὲ τῇ Ἀραβίᾳ σαῦροι μείζους πηχυαίων. Unde Plinius li-bri octavi capite trigesimo nono: Lacerti Arabiae cubitales. In Dioscoride scincus et crocodilus terrestris aliter non differunt, quam species et genus. Is enim definit scincum κροκόδειλον χερσαῖον ἰδιογενῆ, crocodilum terrestrem sui generis. At eos castigat Plinius, qui sic sentiunt, et certos characteres scinco assignat, quibus a crocodilo terrestri dignoscatur, sed quam vere, non satis scio: Ex eadem, inquit, similitudine est scincus, quem quidam terrestrem crocodilum esse dixerunt, candidiore tantum et tenuiore cute. Praecipua tamen differentia dignoscitur a crocodilo, squamarum seta ad caput versa. Recentiorum alii scincum et crocodilum terrestrem promiscue usurpant, ac si sint idem animal. Ita Gesnerus, Rondeletius et Marcellus Vergilius in Dioscoridem. Alii pro terrestri crocodilo belluam ingentem sibi fingunt, fluviatili pene parem. Vide Bellonium, et Cardanum libro nono De subtilitate.

This was the use of the word crocodile among the most ancient Greeks. But the same Greeks, having transferred the name to the beasts of the Nile, gradually took it away from lizards. Except that they did not cease to call by this name certain foreign species of that kind which seemed remarkable above the rest in use, shape or size, or to come closer to the form of the larger crocodile. Yet the epithet land was generally added, to distinguish them from the river crocodile. Thus Aristotle, History, book 2, chapter 17, on the belly of animals, says that the belly is of the same structure τοῖς κροκοδείλοις ἀμφοῖν [tois krokodeilois amphoin], in both crocodiles, that is, the land as well as the aquatic. And in book 5, chapter 33: Τίκτουσι δὲ καὶ σαῦροι, καὶ κροκόδειλοι οἱ II, 483 χερσαῖοι, καὶ οἱ ποταμιοὶ, εἰς τὴν γῆν [Tiktousi de kai sauroi, kai krokodeiloi hoi chersaioi, kai hoi potamioi, eis tēn gēn]. Apollonius, Marvels, chapter 39, from Aristotle's Extracts τῶν ἀνατομῶν [tōn anatomōn]: Ὄφις ὤφθη ἐν Πάφῳ πόδας ἔχων δύο, ὁμοίους χερσαίῳ κροκοδείλῳ [Ophis ōphthē en Paphō podas echōn dyo, homoious chersaiō krokodeilō]. Aelian, History, book 1, chapter 58: Καὶ αἱ σαῦραι δὲ ἐπιβουλεύουσι ταῖς μελίτταις, καὶ οἱ κροκόδειλοι οἱ χερσαῖοι [Kai hai saurai de epibouleuousi tais melittais, kai hoi krokodeiloi hoi chersaioi]. And in book 16, chapter 6, on the Indian phattages: Ἐν Ἰνδοῖς γίνεται ζῶον κροκοδείλῳ χερσαίῳ παραπλήσιον ἰδεῖν [En Indois ginetai zōon krokodeilō chersaiō paraplēsion idein], etc. The Scholiast on Nicander, on the salamander: Ἔοικε δὲ τῷ χερσαίῳ κροκοδείλῳ [Eoike de tō chersaiō krokodeilō]. Jerome, Against Jovinian, book 2, chapter 6: Although the Syrians used to eat land crocodiles too, and the Africans even green lizards. Accordingly Hesychius, to show that the name crocodile is a homonym applying to both, says: Κροκόδειλος, τὸ ζῶον· καὶ τὸ ἐν τῷ Νείλῳ, καὶ τὸ χερσαῖον [Krokodeilos, to zōon; kai to en tō Neilō, kai to chersaion]. Meanwhile it is not sufficiently established which species of lizards, exactly, are given the name land crocodile. In his Corinthiaca Pausanias writes as though there were no other lizards of this name than those large ones two cubits long in Mauretania in Libya. For these are his words: Λιβύη μέν γε μόνη κροκοδείλους τρέφει χερσαίους διπήχεων οὐκ ἐλάσσονας [Libyē men ge monē krokodeilous trephei chersaious dipēcheōn ouk elassonas]. In Herodotus the same are said to be κροκόδειλοι, ὅσον τε τριπήχεες χερσαῖοι, τῇσι σαυρῇσι ἐμφερέστατοι [krokodeiloi, hoson te tripēchees chersaioi, tēsi saurēsi empherestatoi], crocodiles about three cubits long, living on land, very like lizards. Strabo calls col. 1061 them σαύρας, διπήχεις [sauras, dipēcheis]. And Aristotle describes similar ones in Arabia, if these words of Aelian, book 16, chapter 41, are true: Σαύρους δὲ Ἀριστοτέλης ἐν τῇ τῶν Ἀράβων γῇ τίκτεσθαί φησι, καὶ δύο πήχεις ἔχειν αὐτούς [Saurous de Aristotelēs en tē tōn Arabōn gē tiktesthai phēsi, kai dyo pēcheis echein autous]. But in the passage of Aristotle from which Aelian drew this, they are said only to be πηχυαῖοι [pēchyaioi], a cubit long, nowhere διπήχεις [dipēcheis], two cubits long. The words are in the History, book 8, chapter 28: Ἐν δὲ τῇ Ἀραβίᾳ σαῦροι μείζους πηχυαίων [En de tē Arabia sauroi meizous pēchyaiōn]. Hence Pliny, book 8, chapter 39: The lizards of Arabia are a cubit long. In Dioscorides the skink and the land crocodile differ only as species and genus. For he defines the skink as κροκόδειλον χερσαῖον ἰδιογενῆ [krokodeilon chersaion idiogenē], a land crocodile of its own kind. But Pliny rebukes those who hold this view and assigns to the skink definite marks by which it may be distinguished from the land crocodile, though how truly, I do not quite know: Of the same likeness, he says, is the skink, which some have said is a land crocodile, only with a whiter and thinner skin. Its chief difference from the crocodile, however, is recognized in that the set of its scales is turned toward the head. Some of the moderns use skink and land crocodile indiscriminately, as if they were the same animal. So Gesner, Rondeletius and Marcellus Vergilius on Dioscorides. Others imagine the land crocodile to be a huge beast, almost equal to the river crocodile. See Bellonius, and Cardano, book 9, On Subtlety.


Sed credat hic quisque, quod volet. Mihi tamen persuasissimum est, terrestrem crocodilum apud plerosque veteres neque fuisse scincum, neque vastam belluam, sed illud ipsum animal, quod ab Hebraeis צב tsab, a Chaldaeis et Syris ܚܪܕܘܢܐ chardona, ab Arabibus ضب dhab et حردون chardaun appellari II, 484 diximus: quod a scinco quid differat, illi ipsi nos abunde docent. Rem ita se habere, statim animadvertet, quisquis utriusque naturam et vires inter se contulerit. 1. Sanguis τοῦ dhab roborat visum. Sic in Plinio, libri vigesimi octavi capite octavo, crocodili terrestris sanguis claritatem visus inunctus donat, et cicatrices oculorum emendat. Unde Galenus Simplicium libri decimi capite sexto, Εἰ δὲ τὸ τοῦ χερσαίου κροκοδείλου (αἷμα) ποιητικὸν ὀξυδερκίας ἐστὶν, οὐ δε πειράζειν ἔμελλον, ἔχων ὀξυδερκῆ φάρμακα δόκιμα· An crocodili terrestris sanguis visum acuat, experiri non debui, cum alia ad id haberem probata pharmaca. 2. Sed plus virtutis ضب dhab habet in stercore, quo ex oculis tolluntur albugines et suffusiones. Ecce id ipsum in Plinio de crocodilea, sive terrestris crocodili stercore! In terra tantum odoratissimisque floribus vivit. Ob id intestina ejus diligenter exquiruntur, jucundo nidore farta. Crocodileam vocant oculorum vitiis utilissimam, cum porri succo inunctis, et contra suffusiones, vel caligines. Etiam Trallianus libri secundi capite quinto crocodili terrestris fimum misceri vult in collyrio ad cicatrices oculorum, et λευκώματα exterenda. 3. Stercus ضب dhab faciei nitorem conciliat, maculas tollens, et verrucas, et furfures, et lentigines. Eadem crocodileae vis: Plinius.
