Illita quoque ex oleo Cyprino, molestias in facie crescentes tollit. Ex aqua vero morbos omnes, quorum natura serpit in facie, nitoremque reddit. Lentigines tollit, ac varos, omnesque maculas. Dioscorides libro secundo capite De fimo animalium, Ἡ δὲ τοῦ χερσαίου κροκοδείλου ἄφοδος ἁρμώζει ἐπὶ τῶν γυναικῶν πρὸς εὔχροιαν, καὶ στίλβωσιν τῶν προσώπων. Galenus libri decimi Simplicium capite vigesimo nono, Τὴν δὲ τῶν χερσαίων κρο-κοδείλων τούτων, τῶν μικρῶν τε, καὶ χαμαιρεπῶν, κόπρον ἔντιμον αἱ τρυφῶ-σαι πεποιήκασι, γυναῖκες· αἷς οὐκ ἀρκεῖ τοῖς ἄλλοις φαρμάκοις, τοσούτοις οὖσι, λαμπρόν τε καὶ τετανὸν ἐργάζεσθαι τὸ περὶ τὸ πρόσωπον δέρμα. προστιθέα-σι δὲ αὐταῖς καὶ τῶν κροκοδείλων κόπρον. Quo nomine mulieres sui temporis Clemens Alexandrinus libro tertio Paedagogi dignas esse pronuntiat, quae non col. 1062 semel, sed ter pereant. Τρὶς γὰρ, inquit, οὐχ ἅπαξ ἀπολωλέναι δίκαιαι κροκοδείλων ἀποπάτοις χρώμεναι. Nota inprimis verba Dioscoridis, quae nuper citavimus, in Arabica versione apud Abenbitarem ita reddi: خرو الحردون يصلح للغمرة ولتحسين اللون وصقال الوجه والبشرة Stercus alchardaun conducit ad linimentum, quo nitor mulieribus conciliatur, et color fit pulchrior, et facies ac caro nitidior. Ita pro crocodilo terrestri ibi est chardaun. Et chardaun idem esse, quod ضب dhab, vel צב tsab, abunde probatum est supra h)). 4. Stercus τοῦ dhab praescribunt Arabes contra alphos, vitiligines et elephantiasim. Sic, Aegineta auctore, ἡ τῶν χερσαίων II, 485 κροκοδείλων κόπρος, ἀλφοὺς ἀποῤῥύπτει· Et <ⁱ>Aetius multis describit i), quomodo contra elephantiasim Indi utantur crocodilo terrestri. Et Galenus ubi supra, Ἡ δέ γε τῶν κροκοδείλων κόπρος ὥσπερ τῶν προσώπων τὴν ἔφηλιν ἀφαιρεῖν πέφυκεν, οὕτω καὶ ἑλεῖν ἀλφοὺς, καὶ λειχῆνας. 5. Serapio capite quadringentesimo quadragesimo sexto eadem habet ad verbum de stercore stellionis, quae de crocodili terrestris stercore Dioscorides et Galenus. Sed ibi stellio Arabice est ضب dhab, vel حردون chardaun. Sic Galeni et Dioscoridis veteres interpretes stellionis nomine passim utuntur pro crocodilo terrestri. Quo eodem errore حردون chardaun, in Locmani Fabulis, stellionem interpretatur Erpenius ὁ μακαρίτης. 6. In Avicenna ضب dhab rarum animal, prope Arabiae peculiare. Ita terrestris crocodilus, cujus stercus in Galeno ἔντιμον· in Aetio, inventu difficile; in Plinio, diligenter exquiritur. At scincos Dioscorides in Mauritania, Aegypto, India et Arabia reperiri auctor est. Solinus ait, circa Nilum esse frequentissimos. 7. Denique nulla causa est, cur scincus dicatur crocodilus terrestris, cum sit animal aeque ἀμφίβιον, ac major crocodilus, ac in aquis plerumque degat. Nec eaedem tribuantur vires scinco et crocodilo terrestri: de quo nemo scripsit, quod sciam, id, quod omnes de scinco tradunt, ejus usu nervorum stuporem excitari, et veneni vires exstingui. Ut vel hinc appareat, diversa esse animalia.

But here let everyone believe what he will. I, however, am fully persuaded that the land crocodile among most of the ancients was neither the skink nor a huge beast, but that very animal which, as we have said, is called צב tsab by the Hebrews, ܚܪܕܘܢܐ [חרדונא] chardona by the Chaldeans and Syrians, and ضب [ḍabb] dhab and حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun by the Arabs II, 484. How it differs from the skink, these same writers teach us abundantly. That the matter is so will at once be noticed by anyone who compares the nature and powers of the two. 1. The blood of the dhab strengthens the sight. So in Pliny, book 28, chapter 8: the blood of the land crocodile, applied as an ointment, gives clearness of sight and remedies scars of the eyes. Hence Galen, On Simples, book 10, chapter 6: Εἰ δὲ τὸ τοῦ χερσαίου κροκοδείλου (αἷμα) ποιητικὸν ὀξυδερκίας ἐστὶν, οὐ δε πειράζειν ἔμελλον, ἔχων ὀξυδερκῆ φάρμακα δόκιμα· [Ei de to tou chersaiou krokodeilou (haima) poiētikon oxyderkias estin, ou de peirazein emellon, echōn oxyderkē pharmaka dokima] Whether the blood of the land crocodile sharpens the sight I had no need to test, since I had other proven drugs for that purpose. 2. But the ضب [ḍabb] dhab has more potency in its dung, by which white spots and cataracts are removed from the eyes. See this very thing in Pliny concerning crocodilea, that is, the dung of the land crocodile! It lives only on land and among the most fragrant flowers. For this reason its intestines are diligently sought out, stuffed with a pleasant scent. They call it crocodilea; it is most useful for defects of the eyes, applied with leek juice, and against cataracts or dimness. Alexander of Tralles too, book 2, chapter 5, wants the dung of the land crocodile mixed into an eye-salve for scars of the eyes and for wiping away λευκώματα [leukōmata]. 3. The dung of the ضب [ḍabb] dhab gives brightness to the face, removing spots, warts, scurf and freckles. The same is the power of crocodilea; Pliny: Smeared on with Cyprus oil, it also removes blemishes growing on the face; with water, all diseases whose nature is to spread over the face, and it restores brightness. It removes freckles and pimples and all spots. Dioscorides, book 2, in the chapter On the dung of animals: Ἡ δὲ τοῦ χερσαίου κροκοδείλου ἄφοδος ἁρμώζει ἐπὶ τῶν γυναικῶν πρὸς εὔχροιαν, καὶ στίλβωσιν τῶν προσώπων. [Hē de tou chersaiou krokodeilou aphodos harmōzei epi tōn gynaikōn pros euchroian, kai stilbōsin tōn prosōpōn.] Galen, On Simples, book 10, chapter 29: Τὴν δὲ τῶν χερσαίων κροκοδείλων τούτων, τῶν μικρῶν τε, καὶ χαμαιρεπῶν, κόπρον ἔντιμον αἱ τρυφῶσαι πεποιήκασι, γυναῖκες· αἷς οὐκ ἀρκεῖ τοῖς ἄλλοις φαρμάκοις, τοσούτοις οὖσι, λαμπρόν τε καὶ τετανὸν ἐργάζεσθαι τὸ περὶ τὸ πρόσωπον δέρμα. προστιθέασι δὲ αὐταῖς καὶ τῶν κροκοδείλων κόπρον. [Tēn de tōn chersaiōn krokodeilōn toutōn, tōn mikrōn te, kai chamairepōn, kopron entimon hai tryphōsai pepoiēkasi, gynaikes· hais ouk arkei tois allois pharmakois, tosoutois ousi, lampron te kai tetanon ergazesthai to peri to prosōpon derma. prostitheasi de autais kai tōn krokodeilōn kopron.] On this account Clement of Alexandria, in book 3 of the Paedagogus, declares the women of his time deserving to perish not col. 1062 once but three times. Τρὶς γὰρ, he says, οὐχ ἅπαξ ἀπολωλέναι δίκαιαι κροκοδείλων ἀποπάτοις χρώμεναι. [Tris gar … ouch hapax apolōlenai dikaiai krokodeilōn apopatois chrōmenai.] Note especially that the words of Dioscorides just cited are rendered thus in the Arabic version in Ibn al-Baitar: خرو الحردون يصلح للغمرة ولتحسين اللون وصقال الوجه والبشرة [khurū al-ḥardūn yaṣluḥu li-l-ghumra wa-li-taḥsīn al-lawn wa-ṣiqāl al-wajh wa-l-bashara] The dung of alchardaun is useful for a liniment by which brightness is given to women, and the colour becomes more beautiful, and the face and skin more shining. Thus in place of the land crocodile there stands chardaun. And that chardaun is the same as ضب [ḍabb] dhab, or צב tsab, has been abundantly proved above h)). 4. The Arabs prescribe the dung of the dhab against alphoi, vitiligo and elephantiasis. So, on the authority of Paul of Aegina, ἡ τῶν χερσαίων II, 485 κροκοδείλων κόπρος, ἀλφοὺς ἀποῤῥύπτει· [hē tōn chersaiōn krokodeilōn kopros, alphous aporrhyptei] And Aetius describes at length i) how the Indians use the land crocodile against elephantiasis. And Galen, in the place cited: Ἡ δέ γε τῶν κροκοδείλων κόπρος ὥσπερ τῶν προσώπων τὴν ἔφηλιν ἀφαιρεῖν πέφυκεν, οὕτω καὶ ἑλεῖν ἀλφοὺς, καὶ λειχῆνας. [Hē de ge tōn krokodeilōn kopros hōsper tōn prosōpōn tēn ephēlin aphairein pephyken, houtō kai helein alphous, kai leichēnas.] 5. Serapion [=Serapion, Liber de simplicibus medicinis (the Arabic-Latin pharmacopoeia)], chapter 446, says word for word about the dung of the stellio the same things that Dioscorides and Galen say about the dung of the land crocodile. But there stellio in Arabic is ضب [ḍabb] dhab, or حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun. So too the old translators of Galen and Dioscorides everywhere use the name stellio for the land crocodile. By the same error the late Erpenius renders حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun in Luqman's Fables as stellio. 6. In Avicenna the ضب [ḍabb] dhab is a rare animal, almost peculiar to Arabia. So is the land crocodile, whose dung in Galen is ἔντιμον [entimon]; in Aetius, hard to find; in Pliny, diligently sought out. But Dioscorides states that skinks are found in Mauretania, Egypt, India and Arabia; Solinus says they are very numerous around the Nile. 7. Finally, there is no reason why the skink should be called the land crocodile, since it is an animal just as ἀμφίβιον [amphibion] as the larger crocodile, and lives mostly in the water. Nor are the same powers attributed to the skink and the land crocodile: of the latter no one, as far as I know, has written what all report of the skink, that its use rouses torpor of the nerves and extinguishes the force of poison. So that from this too it appears that they are different animals.

Meanwhile this abbreviated expression has given many people occasion for error, who thought that the crocodile, the great beast, was meant. Among them is the poet Ovid, when he says in book 3 of the Art,


Pallida purpureis tingit sua corpora virgis;

id est, ad majorem crocodilum Aegyptium, e cujus stercore fieri credidit crocodileam, qua faciei nitor redditur. Avicenna pariter errat, cum scribit, stercus تمساح thimsach, id est, crocodili majoris, auferre albuginem. Id enim est minoris proprium. Et Radulphus, qui crocodili nomine in Levitico vult latrones publicos significari. Et Cornelius a Lapide, qui crocodilum in Lege ideo immundum esse statuit, quia amphibius est, durus et rapax. Haec enim dici apparet II, 486 de majori crocodilo, cum de minore Moses egerit. Nec minus falli puto Palaestinae recentiores geographos, Breidenbachium et Zieglerum, cum prope col. 1063 Caesaream et Ptolemaidem paludes nobis describunt, majorum crocodilorum multitudine scatentes: quia Crocodilorum oppidi circa haec loca Plinius et Strabo meminerunt. Certe, si Phoenicum littora, aut lacus infestassent belluae tam immanes, non tam altum de iis esset silentium in veterum monumentis. Et ex hodiernis saltem peregrinationibus Hierosolymam res esset compertissima. Itaque illud oppidum Syros appellasse puto non a majore crocodilo ܟܦܪ ܬܡܣܚ Caphar-timsach, sed a minore ܟܦܪ ܨܒܐ Caphar-tsaba. Cujus nominis aliud oppidum fuit in illo ipso littore, non procul a Caesarea. Testem habeo Iosephum, qui vetus nomen Antipatridis modo scribit Καφαρσαβᾶ k), modo Καφαρζαβά l)· quia Hebraeum Tsade Graeci aut per σ, aut per ζ efferunt. Atque hoc ipsum argumento est, crocodilum terrestrem etiam in Phoenice reperiri.

that is, to the larger Egyptian crocodile, from whose dung he believed crocodilea was made, by which the face is given its sheen. Avicenna likewise errs when he writes that the dung of the تمساح [timsāḥ] thimsach, that is, of the larger crocodile, removes albugo. For this is proper to the smaller one. So too Radulphus, who holds that by the name crocodile in Leviticus public robbers are signified. And Cornelius a Lapide, who decides that the crocodile is unclean in the Law because it is amphibious, hard and rapacious. For it is evident that these things are said II, 486 of the larger crocodile, whereas Moses dealt with the smaller. Nor, I think, are the more recent geographers of Eretz Yisrael, Breidenbach and Ziegler, less mistaken when they describe to us marshes near col. 1063 Caesarea and Ptolemais teeming with a multitude of larger crocodiles, because Pliny and Strabo mention a Town of the Crocodiles around these places. Certainly, if such monstrous beasts had infested the shores or lakes of the Phoenicians, there would not be so deep a silence about them in the records of the ancients. And at least from present-day pilgrimages to Jerusalem the matter would be thoroughly known. I therefore think that the Syrians named that town not after the larger crocodile, ܟܦܪ ܬܡܣܚ [כפר תמסח] Caphar-timsach, but after the smaller, ܟܦܪ ܨܒܐ [כפר צבא] Caphar-tsaba. Another town of this name lay on that very coast, not far from Caesarea. My witness is Josephus, who writes the old name of Antipatris sometimes Καφαρσαβᾶ [Kapharsaba] k), sometimes Καφαρζαβά [Kapharzaba] l), because the Greeks render the Hebrew Tsade either by σ or by ζ. And this very fact is evidence that the land crocodile is also found in Phoenicia.


Crocodili terrestris aliquot hic addam nomina, quae vulgo sunt minus nota. Unum ex Hesychio, Κίκερος· ὁ χερσαῖος κροκόδειλος. Sed quod scinco potius convenire putaverim. Videtur enim κίκερος decurtatum esse nomen ex Aegyptio et Arabico سقنقور skankur, vel skinkur apud Avicennam et alios. Alludit tamen κίκερος ad Copticum nomen ΧΑΡΟΥΚῚ, quo in Lexico vocatur الضب seu crocodilus terrestris. Quid si κίκερος dictus sit a parvitate, quia altero est longe minor? Nam in Hesychio κύκερος redditur τὸ ἐλάχιστον. Et Hebraeum רקיק rekik, est ejusdem notionis, si Pomario et Boderiano credimus, qui קטן parvum exponunt, tanquam ex Aruch, ubi tamen non reperio. Proinde רקיק rekic videtur perperam scribi pro דקיק dekik; Res pro Daleth. Ejusdem animalculi barbara habentur duo nomina in Arabe Pandectario: Dhab (inquit) est quoddam animal ut lacerta magna, ventricosum: et Latine vocatur ballecola. Est species stellionis Arabiti. Hispanice dicitur botrax. Ballecola quid sit, nescio. Puto corruptam esse vocem, cum alibi scribatur balleccara. Sed botrax in Isidoro est inter lacerti species. Genera, inquit, lacertorum plura, ut botrax, salamandra, saura, stellio. Botrax dicta, quod ranae habeat speciem. Forte est rana scincoides. Hinc lapis borax (lege botrax) crapaudine in Pandectario.

I shall add here some names of the land crocodile that are less commonly known. One is from Hesychius: Κίκερος· ὁ χερσαῖος κροκόδειλος [Kikeros; ho chersaios krokodeilos]. But I would think this fits the skink rather. For κίκερος [kikeros] seems to be a name shortened from the Egyptian and Arabic سقنقور [saqanqūr] skankur, or skinkur, in Avicenna and others. Yet κίκερος [kikeros] also echoes the Coptic name ΧΑΡΟΥΚῚ, by which الضب [al-ḍabb], or the land crocodile, is called in the Lexicon. What if it was called κίκερος [kikeros] from its smallness, because it is far smaller than the other? For in Hesychius κύκερος [kykeros] is rendered τὸ ἐλάχιστον [to elachiston]. And the Hebrew רקיק rekik has the same meaning, if we believe Pomis and Boderianus [=Guy Le Fèvre de la Boderie], who explain it as קטן, small, as if from the Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome], where, however, I do not find it. Accordingly רקיק rekic seems to be wrongly written for דקיק dekik, Res for Daleth. Two barbarous names of the same little animal are found in the Arabic Pandectarius: Dhab (he says) is a certain animal like a large lizard, big-bellied; and in Latin it is called ballecola. It is a species of Arabian stellio. In Spanish it is called botrax. What ballecola is, I do not know. I think the word is corrupt, since elsewhere it is written balleccara. But botrax appears in Isidore among the species of lizard. There are several kinds of lizards, he says, such as the botrax, the salamander, the saura, the stellio. The botrax is so called because it has the appearance of a frog. Perhaps it is a skink-like frog. Hence the borax stone (read botrax), crapaudine, in the Pandectarius.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 472 We hope we shall do our readers a welcome service if, to what Bochart has so far adduced from the Arabs on the lizard ضب [ḍabb], we add what experts in these matters among our own writers report about it. Among these let the first be LEO AFRICANUS, who in Descript. Africae book 9, ch. 52, p. [?], Zurich ed. 1559, has this: The Dub (otherwise Dab) is an animal living in the deserts; in form it resembles the stellio, though it is somewhat thicker; in length it fills a forearm, in breadth four fingers. It does not drink water, and if anyone pours water on them, it dies on the spot. It hatches eggs in the manner of the tortoise, and it lacks venom. They are caught by the Arabs in the deserts; indeed I myself cut the throat of one I had caught, yet it gives out little blood. It is eaten roasted, with the skin removed, and has the flavour and taste of a small frog. In speed it resembles the lizard, and if during the hunt it is driven into an underground hole, with its tail remaining outside, it cannot be pulled out by any force; but when the opening has been widened with mattocks, it is taken by the hunters. When, three days after being killed, it is put on the fire, it moves no differently than if it had been freshly killed. But far more accurately HASSELQUIST described this animal in his Itiner. p. 353, German trans., under the name Lacerta Aegyptia cauda verticillata squamis denticulatis, pedibus pentadactylis [Egyptian lizard with whorled tail, denticulate scales, five-toed feet]. — Head roughly triangular, elongated, continuous with the neck and a little higher than it. — Snout blunt, very short, scarcely distinguishable from the head, flattened above, uneven, ending behind at the sides in two prominences, one on each side. — Eyes behind the snout, at the sides of the head, nearer the upper part of the head than the throat. Pupil black. Iris dark. Two small pits, one on each side, oblong, immediately above the eyes, behind the prominences of the snout. The area of the eyes deeper [relative to the prominences of the head and snout], oblong, sprinkled with very small tubercles. The space between the eyes oblong, slightly raised, slightly narrowed. Lips mobile, covering the jaws; the upper one ends on each side at the edges in scaly tubercles, which surround its margin and imitate small teeth. Each jaw is composed of bones. These tubercles number 12 on each side, of which the 4 rear ones are pointed, the rest convex and very blunt. The tip of this lip smooth. Jaws equal. — Nostrils in front of the eyes, at the sides of the head, near the snout, round. — Eyes at the sides of the head, in the middle. Orbit protruding at its upper margin, keeled. Crown depressed, scaly, slightly concave, raised beside the eyes. — Neck folded and wrinkled, as are the sides of the head behind the eyes. Throat with a pouch; the pouch longitudinal, compressed, keeled. Ear area hollowed out. Body depressed, ovate; sides of the abdomen protruding. Back furrowed, scaly, the scales ending in a point. Three lines of spiny tubercles on each side of the abdomen, each tubercle composed of about 7 raised, prickly scales. — Tail cylindrical, longer than the body, covered with spiny-angular scales in whorls. — Loins and legs scaly-spiny. Toes 5 on each foot, the middle ones longer. Claws curved. — Colour dusky with black and whitish spots, but it sometimes also takes on bright greenish spots and admits them on the sides of the abdomen and head, by which it comes somewhat close to the nature of the chameleon, which is thus not the only one to enjoy this faculty of changing colours. — Length of body under a span; of tail 1 span. — Habitat: ruins of Natolia, Syria and Eretz Yisrael.

Book 4, chapter 2: The anaka
----------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/anaqah.html

II, 487 col. 1063 CAP. II.

II, 487 col. 1063 CHAPTER II.


Probatur, אנקה anaka Levit. XI, 30. esse Stellionis genus, ab acerbo stridore sic appellati.

It is proved that אנקה anaka of Lev 11:30 is a kind of stellio, so called from its harsh shrill cry.


Iam sequentur Levit. XI, 30. reptilium quinque species, quorum nomina ex- col. 1064 plicare non est facile, cum alibi nusquam reperiantur. Nempe אנקה anaka, כח coach, לטאה letaa, חמט chomet, תנשמת thinsemeth. Horum אנקה anaka Graecis et Hieronymo est μυγάλη mygale, seu mus araneus. Μυγάλην dici volunt, quia ἐκ μύος καὶ γαλῆς, ex mure et mustela nascitur. Nicandri Scholia- stes, Ἀμύντας δή φησι τὴν μυγάλην ἐκ μύος καὶ γαλῆς γίνεσθαι. Quod est absurdissimum, cum et mustela sit mure multo major, et illi tam infensa, quam felis, ut supra a) observavimus. Itaque ut mustela cum mure coëat, atque inde nascatur mus araneus, plane vero est absimile. Melius igitur Aetius Tetrabibli libri quarti Sermone primo, capite decimo quarto: Mus araneus colore quidem mustelae similis est, magnitudine autem muri, unde et mygales obtinuit nomen. Quamvis mus araneus muris habeat speciem potius, quam magnitudinem. Omnino enim est mure minor. Romanis mus araneus a veneno dici videtur, quod illi commune est cum aranea. Et Hebraice אנקה anaka dici credita est ratione vocis, quam habet acutissimam. Ita, ut pro gemitu et ejulatu possit haberi. Alioqui enim אנקה anaka Hebraeis gemitum, aut clamorem sonat. Si idem sensit Onkelos, in ejus Paraphrasi, pro ילא jala (qua voce ibi redditur אנקה anaka) rescribendum est פלא pala, vel phala. Arabes enim murem araneum sic appellant. Avicenna libro quarto Fen. 6. Tract. 3. capite ultimo in titulo, فصل في عضة موغالي وهو الغلا Caput de morsu mygales, quae (Arabibus) est alphala. In Latina versione legitur alcale, quod esset الغلا. Alterutrum semidoctos mutasse putaverim in ילא jala. Cujus nominis occurrunt in libris Talmudicis animalia duo diversissima, nempe sanguisuga et hericius. Sed quorum neutrum hic habet locum. Neutrum enim Hebraice אנקה anaka; sed hericius קפוד kippod; et hirudo עלוקה aluka dicitur, vel עלקה alka potius. Praeterea hic agitur de iis reptilibus, quae super terram repunt, e quo numero non est hirudo. Haec de prima et antiquissima interpretatione vocis אנקה anaka.

Next, in Lev 11:30, follow five species of creeping things whose names are not easy to ex- col. 1064 plain, since they are found nowhere else. They are אנקה anaka, כח coach, לטאה letaa, חמט chomet, תנשמת thinsemeth. Of these, אנקה anaka is for the Greeks and for Jerome μυγάλη [mygalē] mygale, that is, the mus araneus [shrew]. They hold that it is called Μυγάλην [Mygalēn] because it is born ἐκ μύος καὶ γαλῆς [ek myos kai galēs], from a mouse and a weasel. The scholiast on Nicander says: Ἀμύντας δή φησι τὴν μυγάλην ἐκ μύος καὶ γαλῆς γίνεσθαι [Amyntas dē phēsi tēn mygalēn ek myos kai galēs ginesthai]. This is utterly absurd, since the weasel is much larger than the mouse and as hostile to it as the cat, as we observed above a). That a weasel should mate with a mouse and a shrew be born of it is therefore wholly improbable. Aetius puts it better in the Tetrabiblos, book 4, sermon 1, chapter 14: The shrew is like the weasel in colour, but like the mouse in size; hence it also obtained the name mygale. Yet the shrew has the appearance of a mouse rather than its size, for it is altogether smaller than a mouse. The Romans seem to call it mus araneus [spider mouse] from its venom, which it shares with the spider. And in Hebrew it has been thought to be called אנקה anaka by reason of its voice, which is extremely shrill, so that it can be taken for a groan and a wail; for otherwise אנקה anaka means groaning or outcry to the Hebrews. If Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] understood the same, then in his Paraphrase, instead of ילא jala (the word by which אנקה anaka is rendered there), one must read פלא pala, or phala. For the Arabs call the shrew so. Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)], book 4, Fen 6, tract. 3, last chapter, in the title: فصل في عضة موغالي وهو الغلا [faṣl fī ʿaḍḍat mūghālī wa-huwa al-ghalā] Chapter on the bite of the mygale, which (for the Arabs) is alphala. In the Latin version one reads alcale, which would be الغلا [al-ghalā]. I should think that half-learned men changed one or the other into ילא jala. Under this name two very different animals occur in the Talmudic books, namely the leech and the hedgehog. But neither of them has a place here. For neither is called אנקה anaka in Hebrew; rather the hedgehog is called קפוד kippod, and the leech עלוקה aluka, or rather עלקה alka. Moreover, the subject here is those creeping things that creep upon the earth, and the leech is not of that number. So much for the first and most ancient interpretation of the word אנקה anaka.


Secunda Ionathanis est, et Ierosolymitani Interpretis: quorum unus hic habet מינקת חויא, et alter פלית חויא, vel פיילת חויא. Ita legendum, non חיוא, in Lexico Baal-Aruch. Lexicographi neutrum intelligunt. Est enim II, 488 alienum, quod פליית pro locusta hic sumunt, ut פליא ביארי, capite nono tractatus Talmudici De Sabbatho. Aliud enim פליא ביארי, aliud פליית חויא. Nempe id ipsum, quod Arabibus فالية الافاعي phaliath alaphai, id est, scrutatrix serpentum, aut viperarum, (quomodo appellari supra b)) nos docuerunt pictum genus scarabaeorum, quod cum scorpionibus et serpentibus degere solet in latibulo crocodili terrestris) id ipsum, inquam, est Chaldaeum פליית חויא. Illis enim חויא est serpens, et פליית paljath, seu phaljath, palam deductum est ex Arabico فالية phaliath, quod scrutatricem reddimus; quia فلي phala est scrutari. Sic فلي الراس caput scrutatus est, pediculos in eo col. 1065 quaesiturus, فلي الشعر carmen scrutatus est, id est, exploravit et examinavit, ut in Poetae mentem penetraret. Et merito serpentes scrutari dicitur hoc scarabaeorum genus, quod in eodem latibulo cum iis jugiter degit, adeoque serpentes, vel venientes, vel discedsntes, perpetuo comitatur: ita, ut eos, vel adventu suo, vel recessu suo abesse significet. Unde proverbium, apud Arabes receptum, اتكلم فالية الافاعي An alloquutus es phaliath alaphai, scrutatricem serpentum? Quod usurpatur لاول شر ينتظر بعده شر منه de priore malo, post quod aliud expectatur, ex eo oboriturum: sed, quia فلي phala verbum non solum scrutari significat, sed et nutrire et educare; Ionathan, pro פליית חויא, habet מינקת חויא, i. e. nutricem serpentis. Porro, cur voce אנקה anaka hoc scarabaei genus designari voluerint Chaldaei duo interpretes, causa mihi nulla apparet praeter ipsum vocum ordinem. Nempe, ut vox צב tsab crocodilum terrestrem significat, quod multis c) probavimus, ita sequens אנקה anaka פליית חויא, id est, serpentis scrutatricem significare visa est, quae crocodili terrestris perpetua est assecla, et in eodem cum illo latibulo degere solet. Sed haec qualiscunque ratio non est apud me magni momenti, ut neque ipsa versio, quae videtur ea niti. Quod paene omiseram, haec animalcula nonnullis Arabum non sunt scarabaei, sed بنات وردان benath vvardan, quomodo Dioscoridis σίλφας, seu blattas appellat Abenbitar.

The second is that of Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] and of the Jerusalem Targum: the one of them has here מינקת חויא, and the other פלית חויא, or פיילת חויא. So it should be read, not חיוא, in the Lexicon of Baal-Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome]. The lexicographers understand neither. For it is II, 488 beside the point that they take פליית here for a locust, as in פליא ביארי in chapter 9 of the Talmudic tractate On the Sabbath. For פליא ביארי is one thing, פליית חויא another. Namely, the very thing that the Arabs call فالية الافاعي [fāliyat al-afāʿī] phaliath alaphai, that is, the searcher of serpents, or of vipers (they taught us above b) that this name is given to a painted kind of beetle which usually lives with scorpions and serpents in the lair of the land crocodile), that very thing, I say, is the Chaldee פליית חויא. For to them חויא is serpent, and פליית paljath, or phaljath, is plainly derived from the Arabic فالية [fāliya] phaliath, which we render searcher, because فلي [falā] phala means to search. Thus فلي الراس [falā al-raʾs] he searched the head, to look for lice in it; col. 1065 فلي الشعر [falā al-shiʿr] he searched the poem, that is, he explored and examined it in order to penetrate the poet's mind. And this kind of beetle is rightly said to search the serpents, since it lives continually with them in the same lair, and so constantly accompanies the serpents, whether coming or going, in such a way that by its arrival or its departure it signals whether they are near or away. Hence the proverb current among the Arabs: اتكلم فالية الافاعي [a-takallama fāliyat al-afāʿī] Have you spoken to the phaliath alaphai, the searcher of serpents? It is used لاول شر ينتظر بعده شر منه [li-awwal sharr yuntaẓar baʿdahu sharr minhu] of a first evil after which another is expected to arise from it. But since the verb فلي [falā] phala means not only to search but also to nourish and to rear, Jonathan has, instead of פליית חויא, מינקת חויא, i.e. the nurse of the serpent. Further, why the two Chaldee translators wished this kind of beetle to be designated by the word אנקה anaka, I see no reason except the very order of the words. Namely, as the word צב tsab signifies the land crocodile, as we have proved at length c), so the following אנקה anaka seemed to signify פליית חויא, that is, the searcher of the serpent, which is the constant companion of the land crocodile and usually lives in the same lair with it. But this reason, such as it is, carries little weight with me, as does the version itself, which seems to rest on it. Something I had almost omitted: for some of the Arabs these little creatures are not beetles but بنات وردان [banāt wardān] benath vvardan, which is what Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār] calls the σίλφας [silphas] of Dioscorides, or blattae [cockroaches].


Tertio loco eos numero, quibus אנקה anaka est lacertae genus, qui nec pauci sunt, nec contemnendi. In Syro enim sic habetur, ܐܡܩܬܐ amaktha, vel amkatha, quod lacertam exposuit Maronitarum doctissimus Gabriel Sionita ὁ μακαρίτης. In Samaritano [?] semamitha, id est, stellio, ut suo loco palam fiet. In Arabe Erpeniano الورل alvvarlo, id est, lacertae species, quae barbaris est guaril. In Arabe, Parisiis edito, الورك alvvarco, quod idem II, 489 est. Nam nescio, quo fato factum est, ut in Avicenna et aliis multo saepius scribatur الورك alvvarco, quamvis vera scriptura sit الورل alvvarlo: quod docent omnes Arabum Lexicographi, et barbarum nomen guaril inde deductum. Ut taceam criticam observationem, quae sic habet apud Damirem capite ورل Guaril, لا تلتقي الراء مع اللام الا في اربع مواضع الورل وهو الحيوان المذكور وارل اسم جبل والغرلة وهو القلفة وحرل وهو ضرب من الحجارة. Re non occurrit cum Lam (id est, R cum L) nisi quatuor locis. 1. In alvvarlo animalis nomine, de quo supra. 2. In Aral, montis nomine, de quo supra. 3. In alghorla, quod praeputium sonat (ut Hebraeum ערלה). 4. In charal, quod lapidis est genus. Hi sunt igitur quatuor veteres, Syrus, Samaritanus et Arabes duo, quibus anaka est lacertae species. Quibus cur calculum addam, causas habeo non leves. 1. Quod praecesserat צב tsab, id est, crocodilus terrestris: et statim adduntur col. 1066 aliae quatuor lacertorum species, ut constabit ex sequentibus. Proinde videtur anaka esse in eodem genere. Nam mygale, vel aliud quodvis animal, inter tot lacertorum species, minus opportuno loco esset insertum. 2. Ex Hebraeo אנקה anaka plane ortum est Syrum ܐܡܩܬܐ amaktha, vel amkatha. Nam haec duo vocabula (praeter terminationem, quae in illo Hebraea, in hoc Syra est) nulla ex parte differunt: nisi quod Hebraicum NUN Syri mutarunt in MEM, qua mutatione in illis linguis nihil est frequentius. Sic Chaldaeis, aut Syris fortis dicitur ܚܣܝܢ chasin, et ܚܣܝܡ chasim: Ratio ܛܥܢܐ taana, et ܛܥܡܐ taama: Nympha ܢܝܢܦܐ ninphe, et ܢܝܡܦܐ nimphe: Fustis ܩܘܪܢܣܐ kurnesa, et ܩܘܪܡܙܐ kurmeza: Terebinthus, vel arbor, quae fert pistacium, ܒܘܛܡܐ butem, ut Hebraice בוטן boten. Et Arabice pollex ابهام ibham dicitur pro Hebraeo בהן bohen: ut pinguescere, دسم dasama, pro Hebraeo דשן dasen: et canere رنم ranima pro Hebraeo רנן ranan. Aethiopice ዘመወ፡ zamavva, scortatus est, pro Hebraeo זנה zana: እድሜ፡ edem, tempus pro Chaldaeo עדן iddan: አደመ፡ adam, jucundus, suavis, ex Hebraeo עדן adan, deliciari. Tale Aegyptium ΜΕΤΩΠΟΝ, unguenti genus ex Hebraeo נטף nataph, aut Chaldaeo נטופא netopha: ΜΕΙΣΙ serpens ex Hebraeo נחש naas. Ut Aegyptia urbs Memphis a Prophetis modo נוף Noph, modo מוף Moph appellatur. Pari exemplo hic Syrum ܐܡܩܬܐ amaktha deducitur ex Hebraeo אנקה anaka, N et M permutatis. Itaque, quidquid sit Syrum amaktha, id ipsum esse Hebraeum anaka, vero valde consentaneum est. Certum autem est, ܐܡܩܬܐ lacertae genus esse, adeoque stellionem, Prov. XXX, 28. ubi habetur in Syra II, 490 Paraphrasi pro Hebraeo שממית semamith. Ut in Chaldaea per literarum μετά-θεσιν אקמתא akmetha, quod idem est. Itaque ut ܐܡܩܬܐ amaktha, vel amkatha, Syrum; et אקמתא akmetha Chaldaeum est stellio: ita etiam Hebraeum אנקה anaka. Unde est, quod etiam a Samaritano אנקה anaka redditur * [?] semamitha, id est, stellio: et ab utroque Arabe الورل alvvarlo, vel الورك alvvarco, lacertae genus, ad stellionem accedentis, quamque adeo pro stellione multi habent, quia est formae similis. Proinde sic de illo Alkazuinius, هو العظيم من شكل الوزغ وسوام ابرص Hic est magnus, ejusdem formae cum guezga et savvamabras, id est, cum stellionibus minoribus et majoribus. Quae ex Avicenna sumta sunt. Et Al-camus, الورل دابة كالضب والعظيم من اشكال الوزغ Alvvarlo (vulgo guaril), animal ut dhab (seu crocodilus terrestris). Et magnus est in iis, qui formam habent guezgae, seu stellionis. 3. Hebraeis אנקה anaka gemitum et acutum clamorem sonat, qualis fit in magno luctu. Unde stellionem dici posse si quis neget, quasi sit mutum animal, eum refellent haec Plinii de Graeciae stellione libri 29. capite 4. Hunc Graeci coloten vocant, et ascalaboten, et galeoten. In Italia non nascitur. Est enim hic plenus lentigine, stridoris acerbi, et * vescitur. Quae omnia á nostris stellionibus aliena sunt. Nota, stridoris acerbi. Graece dixeris τρισμοῦ τραχέος, unde merito אנקה anaka dictus. At-que ut apud Hebraeos ex Foeminino Singulari saepe fit Plurale Masculinum, ut col. 1067 יעלים ex יעלה, et יענים ex יענה: ita ex אנקה anaka Plurale potuit esse אנקים. Et in secundo Thargum Esther capitis primi versu secundo, cum inter diversa animalia, quae singula coram Solomone propriam vocem edunt, describuntur אנקין בכיין anakin flentes, aut ejulantes, fortasse id accipiendum est, non (ut vulgo sumitur) de aquilarum clangore, sed de stellionum clamore, et acerbo stridore, quem ad ejulatum accedere testatur ipsa vox אנקה anaka. Atque ob id ipsum Arabes, cum hoc saltem scirent, anakam esse lacerti genus, reddiderunt الورل alvvarlo, qui et ipse vocem habet, quamvis fortasse minus sonoram. Hinc Alcamus, ضغث الورل صوت Dhagathsa alvvarlo, id est, clamavit. Quod e nostris, qui Arabica Lexica ediderunt, non intellexerunt satis. Alius enim reddidit, Femur fragorem reddidit: alius, Sonuit coxa. Quia legerunt الورك alvvarco, quod ירך, i. e. coxam sonat. Sed meminisse debuerant, illud ipsum الورك passim occurrere pro الورل, ut jam supra d) notavimus. Ne dicam in exemplari τοῦ Alcamus, quo sum usus, optime scribi الورل alvvarlo. Itaque, quod nostros homines latuerat hactenus, hoc pro II, 491 comperto maneat, in lacertarum genere quasdam esse vocales, atque in his stellionem esse, qui acutissime stridet. Sed de stellione plura dicemus in explicatione vocis שממית semamith.

In third place I count those for whom אנקה anaka is a kind of lizard; they are neither few nor to be despised. For in the Syriac we read ܐܡܩܬܐ [אמקתא] amaktha, or amkatha, which the most learned of the Maronites, the late Gabriel Sionita [=translator of al-Idrīsī's geography into Latin (Geographia Nubiensis, Paris 1619)] (ὁ μακαρίτης [ho makaritēs]), rendered lacerta [lizard]. In the Samaritan it is [?] semamitha, that is, stellio, as will become clear in its proper place. In Erpenianus [=the Arabic version edited by Thomas Erpenius (Pentateuch 1622; New Testament 1616)] it is الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, that is, a species of lizard which the barbarous writers call guaril. In the Arabic edition published at Paris it is الورك [al-warak] alvvarco, which is the same thing II, 489. For by what chance I do not know, in Avicenna and others الورك [al-warak] alvvarco is written far more often, although the true spelling is الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo. This is taught by all the Arabic lexicographers, and the barbarous name guaril is derived from it. Not to mention the critical observation which is found in Damiri, in the chapter ورل [waral] Guaril: لا تلتقي الراء مع اللام الا في اربع مواضع الورل وهو الحيوان المذكور وارل اسم جبل والغرلة وهو القلفة وحرل وهو ضرب من الحجارة [lā taltaqī al-rāʾ maʿa al-lām illā fī arbaʿ mawāḍiʿ al-waral wa-huwa al-ḥayawān al-madhkūr wa-aral ism jabal wa-al-ghurla wa-hiya al-qulfa wa-ḥaral wa-huwa ḍarb min al-ḥijāra]. Re does not meet with Lam (that is, R with L) except in four places. 1. In alvvarlo, the name of the animal discussed above. 2. In Aral, the name of a mountain discussed above. 3. In alghorla, which means foreskin (like the Hebrew ערלה). 4. In charal, which is a kind of stone. These, then, are the four ancient versions, the Syriac, the Samaritan and the two Arabic, for which anaka is a species of lizard. I have weighty reasons for casting my vote with them. 1. צב tsab, that is, the land crocodile, had preceded, and four other species of lizards are added immediately afterwards col. 1066, as will be evident from what follows. Accordingly anaka seems to belong to the same genus. For the mygale, or any other animal, would be inserted rather inappropriately among so many species of lizards. 2. The Syriac ܐܡܩܬܐ [אמקתא] amaktha, or amkatha, plainly arose from the Hebrew אנקה anaka. For these two words (apart from the ending, which is Hebrew in the one and Syriac in the other) differ in no respect, except that the Syrians changed the Hebrew NUN into MEM, a change than which nothing is more frequent in those languages. Thus among the Chaldeans or Syrians strong is ܚܣܝܢ [חסין] chasin and ܚܣܝܡ [חסים] chasim; reason, ܛܥܢܐ [טענא] taana and ܛܥܡܐ [טעמא] taama; nymph, ܢܝܢܦܐ [נינפא] ninphe and ܢܝܡܦܐ [נימפא] nimphe; cudgel, ܩܘܪܢܣܐ [קורנסא] kurnesa and ܩܘܪܡܙܐ [קורמזא] kurmeza; the terebinth, or the tree that bears the pistachio, ܒܘܛܡܐ [בוטמא] butem, as in Hebrew בוטן boten. And in Arabic thumb is ابهام [ibhām] ibham for the Hebrew בהן bohen; likewise to grow fat, دسم [dasama] dasama, for the Hebrew דשן dasen; and to sing, رنم [ranima] ranima, for the Hebrew רנן ranan. In Ethiopic ዘመወ፡ [zamawa] zamavva, he committed fornication, for the Hebrew זנה zana; እድሜ፡ [ʾədəmē] edem, time, for the Chaldee עדן iddan; አደመ፡ [ʾadama] adam, pleasant, sweet, from the Hebrew עדן adan, to take delight. Of the same kind is the Egyptian ΜΕΤΩΠΟΝ [metōpon], a kind of ointment, from the Hebrew נטף nataph or the Chaldee נטופא netopha; and ΜΕΙΣΙ [meisi], serpent, from the Hebrew נחש naas. So too the Egyptian city of Memphis is called by the Prophets now נוף Noph, now מוף Moph. By a like example the Syriac ܐܡܩܬܐ [אמקתא] amaktha is here derived from the Hebrew אנקה anaka, with N and M interchanged. Therefore, whatever the Syriac amaktha may be, it is highly probable that the Hebrew anaka is the very same. Now it is certain that ܐܡܩܬܐ [אמקתא] is a kind of lizard, and indeed the stellio, Prov. XXX, 28, where it stands in the Syriac II, 490 Paraphrase for the Hebrew שממית semamith; just as in the Chaldee, by metathesis (μετάθεσιν [metathesin]) of the letters, אקמתא akmetha, which is the same. Therefore, as the Syriac ܐܡܩܬܐ [אמקתא] amaktha, or amkatha, and the Chaldee אקמתא akmetha is the stellio, so also is the Hebrew אנקה anaka. Hence it is that the Samaritan too renders אנקה anaka by * [?] semamitha, that is, stellio; and both Arabic versions by الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, or الورك [al-warak] alvvarco, a kind of lizard close to the stellio, which many therefore take for the stellio, because it is similar in form. Accordingly Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt] says of it: هو العظيم من شكل الوزغ وسوام ابرص [huwa al-ʿaẓīm min shakl al-wazagh wa-sawām abraṣ] It is a large one, of the same form as the guezga and savvamabras, that is, as the smaller and larger stellios. This is taken from Avicenna. And Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: الورل دابة كالضب والعظيم من اشكال الوزغ [al-waral dābba ka-al-ḍabb wa-al-ʿaẓīm min ashkāl al-wazagh] Alvvarlo (commonly guaril), an animal like the dhab (or land crocodile). And it is the large one among those which have the form of the guezga, or stellio. 3. In Hebrew אנקה anaka means a groan and a shrill cry, such as is uttered in great mourning. If anyone should deny that the stellio can be so called, as though it were a mute animal, he will be refuted by these words of Pliny on the stellio of Greece, book 29, chapter 4: The Greeks call it colotes, and ascalabotes, and galeotes. It does not occur in Italy. For it is covered with spots, has a harsh shriek, and feeds on *. All of which is foreign to our stellios. Note: a harsh shriek. In Greek you would say τρισμοῦ τραχέος [trismou tracheos], whence it is rightly called אנקה anaka. And as among the Hebrews a masculine plural is often formed from a feminine singular, as col. 1067 יעלים from יעלה, and יענים from יענה, so from אנקה anaka the plural could be אנקים. And in the second Targum of Esther, chapter 1, verse 2, where among the various animals which each utter their own cry before Solomon are described אנקין בכיין anakin weeping, or wailing, this should perhaps be understood not (as it is commonly taken) of the screaming of eagles, but of the cry and harsh shriek of stellios, which the very word אנקה anaka attests approaches wailing. And for this very reason the Arabs, since they knew at least this much, that the anaka is a kind of lizard, rendered it الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, which itself also has a voice, though perhaps less resonant. Hence Alcamus: ضغث الورل صوت [ḍaghatha al-waral ṣawt] Dhagathsa alvvarlo, that is, it cried out. This those of our scholars who have published Arabic lexicons did not sufficiently understand. For one rendered it The thigh made a cracking noise; another, The hip sounded. For they read الورك [al-warak] alvvarco, which means ירך, i.e. hip. But they ought to have remembered that this very الورك [al-warak] occurs everywhere for الورل [al-waral], as we noted above d). Not to mention that in the copy of Alcamus which I used, الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo is quite correctly written. Therefore, what has hitherto escaped our scholars, let this stand as II, 491 established: that among the lizards some are vocal, and among them is the stellio, which shrieks very shrilly. But we shall say more about the stellio in the explanation of the word שממית semamith.


Tribus interpretationibus hujus vocis, quas adduximus, jungi queant tres aliae, in quibus ne gutta quidem apparet bonae mentis. Prima est paraphrastarum Arabum, quos legi manuscriptos, ubi אנקה anaka est عنكبوت an-cabuths, id est, aranea. Quae aranea fortasse nata est ex Graecorum et Hieronymi mygale, seu mure araneo: quasi mus araneus idem sit cum aranea, quae summa fuerit imperitia: aut ex Syrorum ܐܡܟܬܐ amkatha; quia Chaldaeum אקמתא akmetha, huic synonymum, plerique Hebraeorum pro aranea sumunt. At aranea Hebraeis non est אנקה anaka, sed עכביש accabis. Neque Prophetam verissimile est hic araneae meminisse inter lacertarum species.

To the three interpretations of this word that we have adduced, three others may be added, in which not even a drop of good sense appears. The first is that of the Arabic paraphrasts, whom I have read in manuscript, where אנקה anaka is عنكبوت [ʿankabūt] ancabuths, that is, aranea [spider]. This aranea perhaps arose from the mygale of the Greeks and of Jerome, or mus araneus [shrew-mouse]: as though the shrew-mouse were the same as the spider, which would be the height of ignorance; or from the Syriac ܐܡܟܬܐ [אמכתא] amkatha, since most of the Hebrews take the Chaldee אקמתא akmetha, which is synonymous with it, for the spider. But for the Hebrews the spider is not אנקה anaka but עכביש accabis. Nor is it at all likely that the Prophet mentions the spider here among the species of lizards.


Secunda interpretatio est R. Mardochaei in Hebraicis Concordantiis, ubi hoc animal definit שרץ העוף reptile volans, cum Moses illud diserte ponat inter reptilia, quae repunt super terram, Levit. XI, 29. 30.

The second interpretation is that of R. Mardochai in the Hebrew Concordance, where he defines this animal as שרץ העוף, a flying creeping thing, although Moses expressly places it among the creeping things that creep upon the earth, Lev 11:29–30.


Tertia est R. Selomonis, qui Gallica voce reddidit בברא bieure, id est, fibrum, seu castorem, ut est in Pomario: animal ita amphibium, ut sit potius aquaticum. Piscis enim habet caudam, et pedes, ad natandum potius, quam ad incessum comparatos, degitque in fluminum ripis, unde alimentum petat. Dioscorides, Ζῶόν ἐστιν ἀμφίβιον, τὸ πλεῖστον ἐν ὕδασι σὺν ἰχθύσι, καὶ καρκί-νοις τρεφόμενον· Animal est amphibium, plerumque in aquis cum piscibus et cancris vescens. Alkazuinius, القندر بري بحري يكون في الانهار العظيمة من بلاد ايسو يتخذ في البر بيتا الي جانب النهر Alkundur (id est, castor) amphibium animal. Reperitur in magnis amnibus regionis Aisu, et domum sibi deligit ad amnis ripam. Proinde fibrum dici volunt Varro et Festus ab extremis fluminum oris. Nam fibrum dicebant veteres pro extremo. Unde fibrae jecoris, et vestium fimbriae appellatae. Tale igitur animal quis credat, Mosem recensuisse inter re- col. 1068 ptilia terrae? Maxime, cum proportio sit valde dispar. Reptilia enim hic vocat Moses talpas, et mures, et lacertarum genera. Praeterea ratio nulla est, cur a clamore et ejulatu castor dicatur אנקה anaka, cum vox castoris nihil quidquam habeat insigne, quod quidem sciam. Sed hujus sententiae primus auctor, quisquis fuit, promiscue sumsisse videtur castores et castorides: quae marina esse animalia dictitant, tam horrendi ejulatus, ut brevi moriatur, qui audierit. Aelianus Historiae libri noni capite quinquagesimo, Αἱ καστορίδες ζῶόν εἰσι θα-λάττιον, καὶ ἐπὶ ταῖς ἀκταῖς, καὶ ταῖς πέτραις ταῖς προβεβλημέναις, ἀπόΦημόν II, 492 τινα κωκυτὸν μεθιᾶσι, καὶ ὠρύονται βαρύτατα. Τούτου τοίνυν τοῦ ἤχου ὅστις ἂν ὑπακούσῃ, ἄφυκτα οἵ ἐστι, καὶ οὐ μετὰ μικρὸν ἀποθνήσκει· Castorides, marinum animal, ad littora et saxa eminentia infaustum edunt ululatum, et gravissime rugiunt. Ita, ut earum clamorem qui audierit, non effugiat, quin paullo post excedat e vita. Oppianus libro primo Halieuticῶν, vs. 398. seqq.

The third is that of R. Solomon, who rendered it with the French word בברא bieure, that is, fiber or castor [beaver], as it is in the Pomarium: an animal so amphibious that it is rather aquatic. For it has the tail of a fish, and feet fitted for swimming rather than for walking, and it lives on the banks of rivers, from which it seeks its food. Dioscorides: Ζῶόν ἐστιν ἀμφίβιον, τὸ πλεῖστον ἐν ὕδασι σὺν ἰχθύσι, καὶ καρκίνοις τρεφόμενον [Zōon estin amphibion, to pleiston en hydasi syn ichthysi, kai karkinois trephomenon]; It is an amphibious animal, mostly feeding in the waters on fish and crabs. Alkazuini: القندر بري بحري يكون في الانهار العظيمة من بلاد ايسو يتخذ في البر بيتا الي جانب النهر [al-qundur barrī baḥrī yakūn fī al-anhār al-ʿaẓīma min bilād Īsū yattakhidh fī al-barr baytan ilā jānib al-nahr] Alkundur (that is, the beaver) is an amphibious animal. It is found in the great rivers of the region of Aisu, and chooses a home for itself on the river bank. Accordingly Varro and Festus hold that it is called fiber from the outermost edges of rivers. For the ancients said fibrum for extremum [outermost]. Hence the fibrae [lobes] of the liver and the fimbriae [fringes] of garments were so named. Who then would believe that Moses listed such an animal among the creeping things of the col. 1068 earth? Especially since the proportion is very unequal. For here Moses calls moles, mice and kinds of lizards creeping things. Moreover, there is no reason why the beaver should be called אנקה anaka from crying and wailing, since the voice of the beaver has nothing remarkable about it, so far as I know. But the first author of this opinion, whoever he was, seems to have confused castores and castorides: these are said to be marine animals of so horrible a wailing that whoever hears it soon dies. Aelian, History, book 9, chapter 50: Αἱ καστορίδες ζῶόν εἰσι θαλάττιον, καὶ ἐπὶ ταῖς ἀκταῖς, καὶ ταῖς πέτραις ταῖς προβεβλημέναις, ἀπόΦημόν II, 492 τινα κωκυτὸν μεθιᾶσι, καὶ ὠρύονται βαρύτατα. Τούτου τοίνυν τοῦ ἤχου ὅστις ἂν ὑπακούσῃ, ἄφυκτα οἵ ἐστι, καὶ οὐ μετὰ μικρὸν ἀποθνήσκει [Hai kastorides zōon eisi thalattion, kai epi tais aktais, kai tais petrais tais probeblēmenais, apophēmon tina kōkyton methiasi, kai ōryontai barytata. Toutou toinyn tou ēchou hostis an hypakousē, aphykta hoi esti, kai ou meta mikron apothnēskei]; The castorides, a marine animal, utter an ill-omened wail on the shores and the jutting rocks, and roar most heavily. So that whoever hears their cry cannot escape departing from life shortly afterwards. Oppian, Halieutica, book 1, v. 398 ff.


Καστορίδες τ᾽ ὀλοαὶ δυσπενθέες, αἵ τ᾽ ἀλεγεινὴν
Ὅσσαν ἐπὶ κροκαλοίσιον ἀπαίσιον ὠρύονται
Ἀνδράσιν· ὃς δέ κε γῆρυν ἐν οὔασιν ἀλγινόεσσαν
Δέξηται, στυγερῆς τ᾽ ἐνοπῆς κωκυτὸν ἀκούσῃ,
Οὐ τηλοῦ θανάτοιο τάχ᾽ ἔσσεται· ἀλλὰ οἱ ἄτην
Καὶ μόρον αἰνοτάτη κείνη μαντεύεται αὐδή.

Καστορίδες τ᾽ ὀλοαὶ δυσπενθέες, αἵ τ᾽ ἀλεγεινὴν Ὅσσαν ἐπὶ κροκαλοίσιον ἀπαίσιον ὠρύονται Ἀνδράσιν· ὃς δέ κε γῆρυν ἐν οὔασιν ἀλγινόεσσαν Δέξηται, στυγερῆς τ᾽ ἐνοπῆς κωκυτὸν ἀκούσῃ, Οὐ τηλοῦ θανάτοιο τάχ᾽ ἔσσεται· ἀλλὰ οἱ ἄτην Καὶ μόρον αἰνοτάτη κείνη μαντεύεται αὐδή. [Kastorides t᾽ oloai dyspenthees, hai t᾽ alegeinēn Ossan epi krokaloision apaision ōryontai Andrasin; hos de ke gēryn en ousin alginoessan Dexētai, stygerēs t᾽ enopēs kōkyton akousē, Ou tēlou thanatoio tach᾽ essetai; alla hoi atēn Kai moron ainotatē keinē manteuetai audē.]


Castoridesque perniciosae et gravis luctus, quaeque in littoribus tristem vocem et hominibus infaustam emittunt. Qui vero moestum clamorem auribus perceperit, et quaerulae vocis ejulatum audierit, non procul erit a morte: sed ipsi cladem et mortem praesagit gravissima illa vox. Tzetzes Chiliadis sextae Historia quadragesima septima,

And the deadly castorides of grievous mourning, which on the shores utter a sad voice, ill-omened for men. Whoever receives the doleful cry in his ears and hears the wailing of the plaintive voice will not be far from death: that most grievous voice foretells ruin and death for him. Tzetzes, Chiliad 6, History 47:


Ἡ καστορὶς δ᾽ ὠρύεται, ὃς δ᾽ ἂν ἀκούσῃ ταύτης
Χρόνῳ βραχεῖ παρέρχεται τοῦ ταλαιπώρου βίου·

Ἡ καστορὶς δ᾽ ὠρύεται, ὃς δ᾽ ἂν ἀκούσῃ ταύτης Χρόνῳ βραχεῖ παρέρχεται τοῦ ταλαιπώρου βίου· [Hē kastoris d᾽ ōryetai, hos d᾽ an akousē tautēs Chronō brachei parerchetai tou talaipōrou biou;]


Rugit autem castoris, et quisquis illam audierit, ex misera hac vita brevi excedet. Haec de castoridum ejulatu et rugitu reperio. Sed falluntur, qui castoridem pro fibro, aut castore habent, in quibus doctissimus Rittershusius in Notis ad Oppianum. Aliud enim castor, aliud castoris. Ille quadrupes amphibium, haec piscis est. Tzetzes ubi supra,

And the castoris roars, and whoever hears it will shortly depart from this wretched life. This is what I find about the wailing and roaring of the castorides. But those are mistaken who take the castoris for the fiber or castor [beaver], among them the most learned Rittershusius in his Notes on Oppian. For the castor is one thing, the castoris another. The former is an amphibious quadruped, the latter is a fish. Tzetzes, in the place cited above:


Πάντες δ᾽ ἰχθύες ἄφωνοι, πλὴν σκάρου, καὶ καστορίδος·

Πάντες δ᾽ ἰχθύες ἄφωνοι, πλὴν σκάρου, καὶ καστορίδος· [Pantes d᾽ ichthyes aphōnoi, plēn skarou, kai kastoridos;]


Omnes autem pisces muti sunt, exceptis scaro et castoride. Ille in ripis fluminum, haec circa maris littora describitur et censetur ab Oppiano inter ea cete, quae nonnunquam e mari in siccum exeunt: cum contra castor ex terra in amnes feratur. Denique castor est verum animal: castoris fabulosum, ut quidem puto, cum animal in mari nullum noverim, in quod quadret haec descriptio.

But all fishes are mute, except the scarus and the castoris. The former is described on the banks of rivers, the latter around the shores of the sea, and it is counted by Oppian among those sea monsters that sometimes come out of the sea onto dry land; whereas the beaver, on the contrary, goes from land into rivers. Finally, the beaver is a real animal; the castoris is fabulous, as I at least think, since I know of no animal in the sea to which this description fits.


E recentioribus אנקה anaka, Pagnino, Graecos et Hieronymum sequuto, est mygale: et Deodatio mus araneus: Munstero et Genevensibus ericius, tanquam ex Onkelo, cujus Paraphrasis hic corrupta est: Iunio et Buxtorfio attelabus, tanquam ex Hierosolymitano interprete, quem non satis intellexerant: Castalioni fiber ex Rabbi Selomone: Ariae viverra, tanquam ex eodem. Sed ב״ברא Selomonis non debuit legi viverra, quia viverra vox Romana est, sed ב״ברא mere Gallica. II, 493 Gallus enim fuit Rabbi Selomo, nec nisi Gallicis vocibus Hebraeas interpretatur. Tamen ex eodem fonte Angli quoque a ferret, id est, furonem, hic habent, animal, viverrae simile. Sed nihil mirum in devia abiisse tot interpretes, qui neque Syram viderant, neque Samaritanam paraphrasim, neque duas illas Arabicas, ex quibus veram vocis אנקה anaka notionem exsculpsimus.

Among the more recent writers, אנקה anaka is, for Pagnino, who followed the Greeks and Jerome, the mygale; for Deodati the mus araneus [shrew-mouse]; for Münster and the Genevans the ericius [hedgehog], as if on the authority of Onkelos, whose Paraphrase is corrupt here; for Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] and Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum] the attelabus, as if on the authority of the Jerusalem translator, whom they had not sufficiently understood; for Castellio the fiber [beaver], on the authority of Rabbi Solomon; for Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot] the viverra [ferret], as if from the same source. But Solomon's ב״ברא should not have been read as viverra, since viverra is a Roman word, whereas ב״ברא is purely French. II, 493 For Rabbi Solomon was a Frenchman, and he interprets Hebrew words only by French ones. Yet from the same source the English too have here a ferret, that is, furo, an animal similar to the viverra. But it is no wonder that so many translators went astray, since they had seen neither the Syriac nor the Samaritan paraphrase, nor those two Arabic ones, from which we have extracted the true meaning of the word אנקה anaka.

Book 4, chapter 3: The coach
----------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/koach.html

II, 493 CAP. III. col. 1069

II, 493 Chapter III. col. 1069


Probatur, כח coach esse ورل guaril, lacertorum in Arabia maximum et validissimum.

It is proved that כח coach is the ورل [waral] guaril, the largest and strongest of the lizards in Arabia.


Sequitur כח coach, quem in lacertorum genere ponunt veteres fere quotquot sunt. Graeci et Hieronymus chamaeleontem reddunt. Uterque Arabs editus حردون chardaun, id est, crocodilum terrestrem, vel ejus speciem. Ita etiam R. Ionas et David Kimchi. Lacertam R. Selomo. Hebraeam vocem retinent Chaldaei et Samaritanus, sola terminatione mutata. Sed magno errore Syrus ܚܘܠܕܐ chulda: et Arabes manuscripti الخلد alchuld, id est, talpam, hic habent. E recentioribus Pagninus, Munsterus, Castalio, Angli, Itali reddunt chamaeleontem: Arias et Iunius lacertam: Petrus Robertus testudinem: Pomarius limacem: Iudaei quidam (apud Gesnerum) sciurum: Genevenses crocodilum. Nos iis accedimus, qui lacertae genus intelligunt; quia de lacertis hic agitur, et sic sumunt plerique veteres, iique antiquissimi. Quo semel concesso, facile erit statuere, Hebraeo nomine כח coach significari الورل id est, Arabum guaril, quomodo barbari scriptores vocant. Patet id ex ipso nomine, quod a robore sumtum est. Alibi enim Scripturae locis plus centum כח coach pro robore sumitur. Et Arabice كوح iisdem literis significat, in pugna superiorem esse. Itaque in lacertorum genere vero consentaneum est, כח coach illum appellari, qui robore maxime valet, et in pugna reliquis praecellit. Is autem haud dubie est الورل alvvarlo, seu guaril, cujus robur maxime eminet in pugna contra serpentes et crocodilum terrestrem. Quod ne quisquam in dubium vocet, en ea de re disertissima scriptorum Arabum testimonia! Alkazuinius, هو عدو للضب وللحية يدخل بيتها وياكلها وليس شي من الحيوان اقوي علي قتل الحيات منه ولا يحتفر لنفسه بل يغتصب كل شي II, 494 بيته لان اي بيت دخله هرب ساكنه وبغتصب بيت الحية كما يغتصب الحية بيت ساير الاجناس Infensus est crocodilo terrestri, et serpenti, cujus latibulum ingre- col. 1070 ditur, ut eum voret. Neque ullum est animal eo fortius ad serpentes occidendos. Neque latibulum sibi ipsi fodit: sed aliorum omnium latibula invadit. Nam quod- cunque latibula adeat, ejus incola fugam capessit. Quin serpentis lustrum invadit, quomodo aliorum generum (malim الاحناش ساير aliorum reptilium) lustra invadit serpens. Algiahid de eodem, وهو يقوي علي الحيات وياكلها اكلا ذريعا ويخرجها من حجرها ويسكن فيه فهو اظلم من ظالم Is serpentibus praevalet, et eos avide com- edit, et e latibulis suis expellit, ut ea occupet, et violento violentior est. Abdol- latif, ex quo Damir: وبينه وبين الضب عداوة فيغلب الورل الضب ويقتله لكنه لا ياكله كما يفعل بالحيه وهو لا يتخذ بيتا لنفسه ولا يحفر حجرا بل يخرج الضب من حجره صارعا ويستولي عليه وانه كان اكثر براثن منه واقوي لكن الظلم يمنعه ولهذا يضرب به المثل في الظلم ويكفي في ظلمه انه يغصب الحية حجرها ويبلعها وربما قتل فوجد في بطنه الحية العظيمة وهو لا يتبلعها حتي يشدخ راسها Inter eum et τὸν dhab (seu crocodilum terrestrem) gravis est inimicitia. Sed guaril est superior, et eum occidit. Nec tamen eum comedit, quo- modo serpentes solent. Neque domum sibi deligit, aut latibulum fodit. Sed croco- dilum terrestrem ex proprio domicilio colluctando extrudit, et ei praevalet. Quam- vis crocodilus unguium viribus praepolleat; tamen hic violentia potior est. Unde est, quod in proverbium cessit ejus violentia. Quae in illo tanta est, ut sufficiat ad serpentem e lustro suo extrudendum ac devorandum. Ac proinde in occisi ventre magnum serpentem nonnunquam reperire est, quem non vorat, nisi prius fracto capite. Proverbia de eo multa sunt apud Arabes, in quibus haec notanda sunt: اجبر من الورل Ferocior (aut superbior) τῷ guaril. Et اظلم من الورل Iniquior (aut violentior) τῷ guaril: ad quod supra allusit Abdollatif. Et اسرع من تلظم الورل Citius quam guaril cibum in ore versat. Quo pertinet, quod scribit Algiahid, eum serpentem avide comedere, vel II, 495 اكلا نريعا id est ad verbum, veloci et praecipiti comestione (1). Ex col. 1071 Ex hac descriptione apparet, nomen כח coach, a robore sumtum, huic lacertae apprime convenire (2).

Next comes כח coach, which almost all the ancients, as many as there are, place in the lizard family. The Greeks and Jerome render it chameleon. Both printed Arabic versions have حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun, that is, the land crocodile, or a species of it. So also R. Jonah [=Jonah ibn Janāḥ, Sefer ha-Shorashim] and David Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim]. R. Solomon has lizard. The Chaldee versions and the Samaritan keep the Hebrew word, with only the ending changed. But the Syriac, by a great error, has ܚܘܠܕܐ [חולדא] chulda here, and the manuscript Arabic versions الخلد [al-khuld] alchuld, that is, mole. Among the more recent translators, Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae], Münster, Castellio, the English and the Italians render it chameleon; Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot] and Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] lizard; Petrus Robertus tortoise; Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)] slug; certain Jews (in Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium]) squirrel; the Genevans crocodile. We side with those who understand a kind of lizard, because lizards are the subject here, and this is how most of the ancients take it, and the most ancient of them. Once this is granted, it will be easy to establish that the Hebrew name כח coach signifies الورل [al-waral], that is, the guaril of the Arabs, as the barbarous writers call it. This is clear from the name itself, which is taken from strength. For in more than a hundred other passages of Scripture כח coach is used for strength. And in Arabic كوح [kawḥ], with the same letters, means to be superior in a fight. It is therefore entirely fitting that, within the lizard family, the one called כח coach should be the one that is most powerful in strength and surpasses the rest in fighting. And that is undoubtedly الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, or guaril, whose strength stands out above all in fighting against serpents and the land crocodile. Lest anyone call this into doubt, here are the most explicit testimonies of the Arabic writers on the matter! Alkazuini: هو عدو للضب وللحية يدخل بيتها وياكلها وليس شي من الحيوان اقوي علي قتل الحيات منه ولا يحتفر لنفسه بل يغتصب كل شي II, 494 بيته لان اي بيت دخله هرب ساكنه وبغتصب بيت الحية كما يغتصب الحية بيت ساير الاجناس [huwa ʿaduww li-l-ḍabb wa-li-l-ḥayya yadkhulu baytahā wa-yaʾkuluhā wa-laysa shayʾ min al-ḥayawān aqwā ʿalā qatl al-ḥayyāt minhu wa-lā yaḥtafiru li-nafsihi bal yaghtaṣibu kull shayʾ baytahu li-anna ayy bayt dakhalahu haraba sākinuhu wa-byaghtaṣibu bayt al-ḥayya kamā yaghtaṣibu al-ḥayya bayt sāyir al-ajnās] It is hostile to the land crocodile and to the serpent, whose hiding place it enters in order to devour it. And no animal is stronger than it at killing serpents. col. 1070 Nor does it dig a hiding place for itself, but it invades the hiding places of all others. For whatever hiding place it approaches, its occupant takes flight. Indeed, it invades the serpent's den, just as the serpent invades the dens of other kinds (I would prefer الاحناش ساير [sāyir al-aḥnāsh], of other reptiles). Algiahid on the same animal: وهو يقوي علي الحيات وياكلها اكلا ذريعا ويخرجها من حجرها ويسكن فيه فهو اظلم من ظالم [wa-huwa yaqwā ʿalā al-ḥayyāt wa-yaʾkuluhā aklan dharīʿan wa-yukhrijuhā min juḥrihā wa-yaskunu fīhi fa-huwa aẓlam min ẓālim] It prevails over serpents and eats them greedily, and drives them out of their hiding places in order to occupy them, and it is more violent than the violent. Abdollatif, followed by Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: وبينه وبين الضب عداوة فيغلب الورل الضب ويقتله لكنه لا ياكله كما يفعل بالحيه وهو لا يتخذ بيتا لنفسه ولا يحفر حجرا بل يخرج الضب من حجره صارعا ويستولي عليه وانه كان اكثر براثن منه واقوي لكن الظلم يمنعه ولهذا يضرب به المثل في الظلم ويكفي في ظلمه انه يغصب الحية حجرها ويبلعها وربما قتل فوجد في بطنه الحية العظيمة وهو لا يتبلعها حتي يشدخ راسها [wa-baynahu wa-bayna al-ḍabb ʿadāwa fa-yaghlibu al-waral al-ḍabb wa-yaqtuluhu lākinnahu lā yaʾkuluhu kamā yafʿalu bi-l-ḥayya wa-huwa lā yattakhidhu baytan li-nafsihi wa-lā yaḥfiru juḥran bal yukhriju al-ḍabb min juḥrihi ṣāriʿan wa-yastawlī ʿalayhi wa-innahu kāna akthar barāthin minhu wa-aqwā lākin al-ẓulm yamnaʿuhu wa-li-hādhā yuḍrabu bihi al-mathal fī al-ẓulm wa-yakfī fī ẓulmihi annahu yaghṣibu al-ḥayya juḥrahā wa-yablaʿuhā wa-rubbamā qutila fa-wujida fī baṭnihi al-ḥayya al-ʿaẓīma wa-huwa lā yatabalaʿuhā ḥattā yashdakha raʾsahā] Between it and the τὸν [ton] dhab (or land crocodile) there is fierce enmity. But the guaril is superior and kills it. Yet it does not eat it, as it does with serpents. Nor does it choose a dwelling for itself or dig a hiding place. Rather, it thrusts the land crocodile out of its own home by wrestling, and prevails over it. Although the crocodile excels in the strength of its claws, this one is superior in violence. Hence its violence has become proverbial. It is so great in it that it suffices to thrust a serpent out of its den and devour it. Accordingly, a large serpent is sometimes found in the belly of one that has been killed; it does not swallow it without first crushing its head. There are many proverbs about it among the Arabs, of which these are worth noting: اجبر من الورل [ajbar min al-waral] Fiercer (or prouder) than the τῷ [tō] guaril. And اظلم من الورل [aẓlam min al-waral] More unjust (or more violent) than the τῷ [tō] guaril, to which Abdollatif alluded above. And اسرع من تلظم الورل [asraʿ min talaẓẓum al-waral] Quicker than the guaril turns food over in its mouth. To this belongs what Algiahid writes, that it eats the serpent greedily, or II, 495 اكلا نريعا [aklan narīʿan], that is, literally, with a swift and headlong eating R1. col. 1071 From this description it appears that the name כח coach, taken from strength, suits this lizard exceedingly well R2.


Si quis de lacerti genere, in his terris ignoto, plura scire aveat, illum describit Ibno-saida, دابة علي خلق الضب الا انه اعظم منه animal naturae τοῦ dhab, nisi quod est majus. Et Abdollatif, فاما الورل وهو الحردون Guaril utique idem est, quod chardaun. Sed contra Algiahid apud Damirem tradit, ان الحردون غير الورل ووصفه دابة تكون غالبا بارض مصر موشاة بالوان كثير ولها كف ككف الانسان مقسومة اصابعها الي الانامل Chardaun a guaril esse diversum, quem describit animal in Aegypto frequens, multis distinctum coloribus, manus habens, quales hominis, et digitos in articulos divisos. Et Alkazuinius, هو العظيم من شكل الوزغ وسام ابرص الطويل الذنب الصغير الراس وهو سريع السير خفيف الحركة Maximus est lacertorum, qui formam habent guezgae et sam-mabras (sunt stellionum species, quarum illa minor, haec major), longae caudae, parvi capitis, celeris incessus, et motus expediti. Avicenna quoque, postquam illum cum stellionibus contulit, caudamque et caput eodem modo descripsit, quo Alkazuinius, وهو غير الضب والضب لا يكون او قل ما يكون الا في البادية وراسه وبدنه وذنبه خالف الورل وربما قاربة في طبايعه Et alius est a dhab (seu terrestri crocodilo).

If anyone wishes to know more about this kind of lizard, unknown in these lands, Ibno-saida describes it: دابة علي خلق الضب الا انه اعظم منه [dābba ʿalā khalq al-ḍabb illā annahu aʿẓam minhu] an animal of the nature of the dhab, except that it is larger. And Abdollatif: فاما الورل وهو الحردون [fa-ammā al-waral wa-huwa al-ḥardūn] Guaril is indeed the same as chardaun. But on the contrary Algiahid, in Damir, reports ان الحردون غير الورل ووصفه دابة تكون غالبا بارض مصر موشاة بالوان كثير ولها كف ككف الانسان مقسومة اصابعها الي الانامل [anna al-ḥardūn ghayr al-waral wa-waṣafahu dābba takūn ghāliban bi-arḍ Miṣr muwashshāh bi-alwān kathīr wa-lahā kaff ka-kaff al-insān maqsūma aṣābiʿuhā ilā al-anāmil] that chardaun is different from guaril; he describes it as an animal common in Egypt, marked with many colours, having hands like those of a man, and fingers divided into joints. And Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt]: هو العظيم من شكل الوزغ وسام ابرص الطويل الذنب الصغير الراس وهو سريع السير خفيف الحركة [huwa al-ʿaẓīm min shakl al-wazagh wa-sāmm abraṣ al-ṭawīl al-dhanab al-ṣaghīr al-raʾs wa-huwa sarīʿ al-sayr khafīf al-ḥaraka] It is the largest of the lizards that have the form of the guezga and the sam-mabras (these are species of stellio, the former smaller, the latter larger), with a long tail, a small head, a swift gait and nimble movement. Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] too, after comparing it with the stellios and describing its tail and head in the same way as Alkazuinius, says: وهو غير الضب والضب لا يكون او قل ما يكون الا في البادية وراسه وبدنه وذنبه خالف الورل وربما قاربة في طبايعه [wa-huwa ghayr al-ḍabb wa-al-ḍabb lā yakūn aw qall mā yakūn illā fī al-bādiya wa-raʾsuhu wa-badanuhu wa-dhanabuhu khālaf al-waral wa-rubbamā qārabahu fī ṭabāʾiʿihi] And it is different from the dhab (or land crocodile).


II, 496 Nam dhab nunquam est, aut valde raro est alibi, quam in deserto. Et capite, et corpore, et cauda differt a guaril. Naturae tamen illi vicinae est. Unde Al-camus, الورل دابة كالضب والعظيم من اشكال الوزغ طويل الذنب صغير الراس Guaril animal, ut dhab magnum, in iis, quae guezgae forma sunt, longae caudae, parvi capitis. Sunt, qui ex crocodili semine nasci putant, quomodo scincum: sed eos refellit Damir, cum quia cute et pelle multum differunt, tum quia statura est valde dispar: والورل لا يزيد قدره علي ذراعين او ذراع ونصف والتمساح عشرة col. 1072 اذرع واكثر Guaril enim non crescit supra duos cubitos, aut unum et semi, cum crocodilus crescat supra decem cubitos et amplius. Idem animal describitur ut valde libidinosum. Abdollatif, فليس في الحيوان اكثر سفاد منه Nullum est animal, quod coëat frequentius. Et, si creditur Alcamus, شحمه يعظم الذكر دلكا. Quod qui potest intelligat. Idem de carnis esu, لحمه حار جدا يسمن بقوة Caro ejus calidissima est, et maxime pinguefacit. Et Alkazuinius, لحمه وشحمه سمن طبقات الناس Ejus caro et adeps mulieres inprimis pinguefacit. Ita etiam Avicenna et Damir. Addunt, in eadem carne vim esse, qua e corpore avellit السلي والشوك surculos et spinas. Pilos, brachio mulieris alligatos, conceptum impedire. Excitari membra torpentia, si combustae pellis cinere, cum olei faecibus misto, illinantur. Stercus albugines, lentigines et verrucas amovere. Sanguinem denique visum roborare et acuere. Quod idem scribunt de crocodilo terrestri.

II, 496 For the dhab is never, or very rarely, found anywhere but in the desert. And in head, body and tail it differs from the guaril. Yet it is close to it in nature. Hence Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: الورل دابة كالضب والعظيم من اشكال الوزغ طويل الذنب صغير الراس [al-waral dābba ka-al-ḍabb wa-al-ʿaẓīm min ashkāl al-wazagh ṭawīl al-dhanab ṣaghīr al-raʾs] Guaril is an animal like the dhab, large among those which have the form of the guezga, with a long tail and a small head. Some think it is born from the seed of the crocodile, like the skink; but Damir refutes them, both because they differ much in skin and hide, and because their size is very unequal: والورل لا يزيد قدره علي ذراعين او ذراع ونصف والتمساح عشرة col. 1072 اذرع واكثر [wa-al-waral lā yazīd qadruhu ʿalā dhirāʿayn aw dhirāʿ wa-niṣf wa-al-timsāḥ ʿashara adhruʿ wa-akthar] For the guaril does not grow beyond two cubits, or one and a half, whereas the crocodile grows beyond ten cubits and more. The same animal is described as very lustful. Abdollatif: فليس في الحيوان اكثر سفاد منه [fa-laysa fī al-ḥayawān akthar sifādan minhu] There is no animal that copulates more often. And, if Alcamus is to be believed, شحمه يعظم الذكر دلكا [shaḥmuhu yuʿaẓẓim al-dhakar dalkan]. Let him understand this who can. He says the same about eating its flesh: لحمه حار جدا يسمن بقوة [laḥmuhu ḥārr jiddan yusamminu bi-quwwa] Its flesh is very hot and fattens greatly. And Alkazuinius: لحمه وشحمه سمن طبقات الناس [laḥmuhu wa-shaḥmuhu samman ṭabaqāt al-nās] Its flesh and fat fatten women above all. So also Avicenna and Damir. They add that the same flesh has a power by which it draws out of the body السلي والشوك [al-salā wa-al-shawk] splinters and thorns; that its hairs, tied to a woman's arm, prevent conception; that numb limbs are revived if smeared with the ash of its burnt skin mixed with the dregs of oil; that its dung removes white spots of the eye, freckles and warts; and finally that its blood strengthens and sharpens the sight. They write the same of the land crocodile.


Quaeri potest, an hic lacertus sit idem cum lacerto viridi: quod videbuntur multa suadere. 1. Quod lacertus viridis eorum est maximus, qui apud nos sunt. Erasmus in Dialogo De Amicitia: Italia magnas habet lacertas, et virides. Gesnerus: Majores fere duplo sunt communibus lacertis. 2. Lacerti virides sunt ὀφιομάχοι. Erasmus ibidem, Hoc animal natura et homini amicum est, et serpentibus inimicum. Et paullo post, Quodam die vidi praegrandem et mire viridem, in ostio cavi decertantem cum serpente. Primum mirabamur, quid esset rei. Nam serpens nobis non erat conspicuus. Italus admonebat, in antro esse hostem. Paullo post venit ad nos lacerta, velut ostendens sua vulnera, ac remedium flagitans, etc. Serpens alterum latus paene totum eroserat, et ex viridi rubrum fecerat. Itaque ad has lacertas id referendum, quod in Plinio legitur, lacertas cum serpentibus pugnare. Unde illi nomen ὀφιονίκος a recentioribus inditum.

It may be asked whether this lizard is the same as the green lizard, which many things will seem to suggest. 1. The green lizard is the largest of those found among us. Erasmus [=Desiderius Erasmus, Adagia] in the Dialogue On Friendship: Italy has large lizards, and green ones. Gesner: They are almost twice as large as common lizards. 2. Green lizards are ὀφιομάχοι [ophiomachoi]. Erasmus in the same place: This animal is by nature both friendly to man and hostile to serpents. And a little later: One day I saw a very large and wonderfully green one fighting with a serpent at the mouth of a hole. At first we wondered what was going on, for the serpent was not visible to us. An Italian told us that the enemy was in the cave. A little later the lizard came to us, as if showing its wounds and begging for a remedy, etc. The serpent had gnawed away almost the whole of one side and had turned it from green to red. So what we read in Pliny, that lizards fight with serpents, should be referred to these lizards. Hence the more recent writers gave it the name ὀφιονίκος [ophionikos].


II, 497 Pandectarius: OFIONICOS Graece, id est, lacerta. 3. Ut esu τοῦ guaril Arabes pinguescere se scribunt: ita phtisicis lacertam viridem esse utilissimam, et incredibiliter prodesse tradunt Plinius et Marcellus. 4. Utriusque stercora, faciei il-lita, maculas delere leguntur. Tamen guaril a lacerto viridi distinguit color. Varium enim describit Algiahid. Praeterea videtur guaril, qualis ab Arabibus describitur, lacertam viridem viribus et animi ferocia longe antecellere. Puto igitur, τὸν guaril lacerti genus esse, Arabiae peculiare, et lacertum viridem ita illi similem, ut sit

II, 497 The Pandectarius: OFIONICOS in Greek, that is, lizard. 3. Just as the Arabs write that they grow fat by eating the guaril, so Pliny and Marcellus report that the green lizard is most useful for consumptives and benefits them incredibly. 4. The dung of both, smeared on the face, is said to remove blemishes. Yet colour distinguishes the guaril from the green lizard, for Algiahid describes it as variegated. Moreover the guaril, as the Arabs describe it, seems far to surpass the green lizard in strength and fierceness of spirit. I therefore think that the guaril is a kind of lizard peculiar to Arabia, and that the green lizard is so similar to it that it is


Proximus huic, longo sed proximus intervallo.

Next to it, but next by a long interval.


(1) Rosenmüller, II, 495 In Leonis Africani Descript. Africae Lib. IX. cap. 53. haec lacerta Guaral sonat. Animal, inquit, praedicto [Dub, ضبّ] simile, vero paullo grandius, in capite pariter et cauda venenum gerit, quibus partibus excisis, Arabes eo vesci solent, alioquin deforme et tetri coloris. Sed ورل non est permutandum cum وَرَنٌ, quod in Giggejo vertitur species reptilis, Forskalio autem teste nomen est lacertae niloticae, vid. Descriptiones Animalium, quae in itinere Orientali observavit Petrus Forskal, p. 13.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 495 In Leo Africanus, Descript. Africae book 9, ch. 53, this lizard is called Guaral. An animal, he says, similar to the aforementioned [Dub, ضبّ [ḍabb]] but somewhat larger; it likewise carries venom in its head and tail, and when these parts have been cut off the Arabs are accustomed to eat it; otherwise it is ugly and of a foul colour. But ورل [waral] must not be confused with وَرَنٌ [waranun], which in Giggeius [=Antonio Giggei, Thesaurus linguae Arabicae (Milan 1632)] is rendered a species of reptile, but which, on Forskål's testimony, is the name of the Nile lizard; see Descriptiones Animalium, quae in itinere Orientali observavit Petrus Forskal, p. 13.


(2) Rosenmüller, II, 495 Sed recte monet MICHAELIS in Supplemm. P. IV. p. 1221. plura se offerre etyma, a Bocharto non expensa, ad quae il-lius lacertae nomen possit referri. Prorsus incertam esse hanc rationem, meris etymologiis expiscari eorum nominum, quae animalia indicant, significationes, jam saepius monuimus. Videtur nomen כח unum esse ex iis, de quorum significatione definienda plane est desperandum, cum destituamur tam reliquarum dialectorum, quam eorum locorum adminiculis, ex quibus hujus animalis natura et indoles ita cognoscatur, ut de eo certi quidquam possit statui.

R2 Rosenmüller, II, 495 But Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer] rightly points out in the Supplemm. vol. 4, p. 1221, that several further etymologies present themselves, not considered by Bochart, to which the name of that lizard could be referred. We have already noted quite often that this method, fishing out the meanings of the names that denote animals by etymologies alone, is wholly uncertain. The name כח seems to be one of those whose meaning we must utterly despair of determining, since we lack the aid both of the other dialects and of passages from which the nature and character of this animal might be known well enough for anything certain to be established about it.


Book 4, chapter 4: The leta
