https://openseforim.org/bochart/letaah.html

II, 497 CAP. IV. col. 1073

II, 497 Chapter IV. col. 1073


Probatur, voce לטאה letaa Lacertam significari, stellioni similem, maxime venenatam et terrae adhaerentem, quae Arabice وحرة vvachara dicitur.

It is proved that the word לטאה letaa signifies a lizard, similar to the stellio, extremely venomous and clinging to the ground, which in Arabic is called وحرة [waḥra] vvachara.


Hebraeum לטאה letaa conantur quidam recentiorum ex Graeca lingua interpretari, qua λὼτ est talpa. Hesychius Λώτ· ἀσπάλαξ, μῦς τυφλὸς ὁ τὴν γῆν τρυπῶν. Et λάταξ animal amphibium, castori et lutrae congener, de quo Philosophus Historiae libri octavi capite quinto. Itaque ex illorum mente לטאה letaa, aut talpa esset, aut latax. Alii murem araneum malunt, in quem Λητὼ, id est, Latona, mutata fuisse fingatur, propter allusionem vocum Λητὼ et letaa, quae sit μυγάλη. Atque illud quidem verum est, fingi Latonam, Typhonis metu, in murem araneum fuisse mutatam. Antonius Liberalis, Metam. 28. Ἀπόλλων μὲν ἐγένετο ἱέραξ, Ἑρμῆς δὲ ἴβις· Ἄρης δὲ λεπιδωτὸς ἰχθύς· Ἄρ-τεμις δὲ αἴλουρος (non σίλουρος, ut perperam habent nostrae editiones). Τρά-γῳ δὲ εἰκάζεται Διόνυσος· ἔλλῳ δ᾽ Ἡρακλῆς· βοῒ δ᾽ Ἥφαιστος· μυγάλῃ δὲ Λητώ. Sed non inde sequitur, voce letaa murem araneum significari: ut neque talpam, aut latacem; quia alludunt λὼτ et λάταξ. De talpa enim versu praecedente jam actum. Et latax in terrae reptilibus computari non potest (ut neque castor, de quo supra) a), quia in aquis potius vivit, et pilos habet, ex parte similes vituli marini pilis. Praestat igitur sequi veteres, qui hoc quoque animal numerant in lacertorum speciebus. Ita Graecis est καλαβώτης, vel ἀσκα-λαβώτης, et Hieronymo stellio: et Ionathani שממיתא semamitha; quod id II, 498 ipsum est: et Syro ܨܪܘܪܝܬܐ tseruritha, id est, salamandra, ut volunt: et Arabibus العظاة aladha, vel العظاية aladhaja, lacertus. Ita etiam Selomoni, et Kimchio, et Pomario. Quomodo etiam sumsisse Talmudicos constat ex tractatu Oholoth (cap. 1. fol. 45. b.), ubi pecudes quaedam et aves, post caput amputatum palpitare leguntur, כגון הזנב של הלטאה שהיא מפרכסת, quomodo cauda τῆς letaae, quae (abscissa) adhuc se motitat. Quo haec alludunt in Porta coeli, ויש מב״ח אם יכרתו מזנבותיהם יתנועעו זמן רב אחר כן כזנב הלטאה וזנבות השרצים, Sunt quaedam animalia, quorum caudae, si abscindantur, moventur aliquamdiu, ut cauda letaae et aliorum reptilium. Quale est, quod lacertae, virgae ictu bifariam divisi, singulas partes vivere, et duobus pedibus repere, et nonnunquam iterum coalescere asserunt Aelianus Historiae libri secundi capite vigesimo tertio, et Phile capite quinquagesimo tertio. Non tamen temere crediderim, quod habetur in Porta coeli de caudis, ita abscissis, כי הן יגדלו אחרי כריתותם, eas post abscissionem crescere, cum non nisi tantillum temporis divisas vivere pro comperto habeatur.

Some of the more recent writers try to interpret the Hebrew לטאה letaa from the Greek language, in which λὼτ [lōt] is the mole. Hesychius: Λώτ· ἀσπάλαξ, μῦς τυφλὸς ὁ τὴν γῆν τρυπῶν [Lōt· aspalax, mys typhlos ho tēn gēn trypōn]. And λάταξ [latax] is an amphibious animal, akin to the beaver and the otter, of which the Philosopher speaks in History, book 8, chapter 5. Thus in their view לטאה letaa would be either the mole or the latax. Others prefer the shrew-mouse, into which Λητὼ [Lētō], that is, Latona, is fabled to have been changed, on account of the allusion between the words Λητὼ [Lētō] and letaa, which would be the μυγάλη [mygalē]. And it is indeed true that Latona is fabled to have been changed into a shrew-mouse for fear of Typhon. Antoninus Liberalis, Metam. 28: Ἀπόλλων μὲν ἐγένετο ἱέραξ, Ἑρμῆς δὲ ἴβις· Ἄρης δὲ λεπιδωτὸς ἰχθύς· Ἄρτεμις δὲ αἴλουρος [Apollōn men egeneto hierax, Hermēs de ibis; Arēs de lepidōtos ichthys; Artemis de ailouros] (not σίλουρος [silouros], as our editions wrongly have it). Τράγῳ δὲ εἰκάζεται Διόνυσος· ἔλλῳ δ᾽ Ἡρακλῆς· βοῒ δ᾽ Ἥφαιστος· μυγάλῃ δὲ Λητώ [Tragō de eikazetai Dionysos; ellō d᾽ Hēraklēs; boi d᾽ Hēphaistos; mygalē de Lētō]. But it does not follow from this that the word letaa signifies the shrew-mouse, any more than the mole or the latax because λὼτ [lōt] and λάταξ [latax] sound alike. For the mole has already been dealt with in the preceding verse. And the latax cannot be counted among the reptiles of the earth (any more than the beaver, discussed above) a), since it lives rather in the water and has hair partly like that of the seal. It is better, therefore, to follow the ancients, who also number this animal among the species of lizards. Thus for the Greeks it is καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs] or ἀσκαλαβώτης [askalabōtēs], and for Jerome the stellio; for Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] שממיתא semamitha, which is the II, 498 very same thing; for the Syrian ܨܪܘܪܝܬܐ [צרוריתא] tseruritha, that is, the salamander, as they claim; and for the Arabs العظاة [al-ʿaẓāh] aladha or العظاية [al-ʿaẓāya] aladhaja, the lizard. So also Solomon [Rashi], Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] and the Pomarium. That the Talmudists also took it so is clear from the tractate Oholoth (ch. 1, fol. 45b), where certain beasts and birds are said to quiver after the head has been cut off, כגון הזנב של הלטאה שהיא מפרכסת, like the tail of the letaa, which (when cut off) still keeps moving. To this the words in the Porta coeli allude: ויש מב״ח אם יכרתו מזנבותיהם יתנועעו זמן רב אחר כן כזנב הלטאה וזנבות השרצים, There are certain animals whose tails, if cut off, move for some time, like the tail of the letaa and of other reptiles. Of the same kind is what Aelian, History, book 2, chapter 23, and Phile, chapter 53, assert: that when a lizard is cut in two by the blow of a rod, each part lives and crawls on two feet, and sometimes they grow together again. I would not, however, lightly believe what is said in the Porta coeli about tails so cut off, כי הן יגדלו אחרי כריתותם, that they grow after being cut off, since it is held as established that once divided they live only a very short time.


Constat igitur hactenus, letaam esse in lacertorum genere, cum magno consensu veteres ita statuant. Sed speciem definire non est cujusvis. Syrus salamandram exponit. Recentiorum alii stellionem, alii lacertam malunt. Quo- col. 1074 rum prius sequuntur Pagninus, Arias, Iunius, Castalio: posterius Munsterus, Schindlerus, Genevenses, Angli, Itali. Ego lacertae speciem intelligo, quae Arabice وحرة wachra, vel wachara dicitur. De ea scilicet Arabes tria potissimum observant: 1. Stellioni similem esse. 2. Terrae maxime adhaerere. 3. Veneno ejus cibos infici, quoscumque calcat. Quae tria rem conficiunt, ut postmodum docebimus. Sed Arabes prius audiendi. Giauhari, الوحرة دويبة حمرا تلتصق بالارض كالعظا Alvvachra, animalculum rubrum, terrae adhaerens, ut lacerta. Damir, هي دويبة شبيهة بسام ابرص تلتصق بالارض او ضرب من العظا لا تطا طعاما ولا سرابا الا سميته Est animalculum, simile τῷ sammabras (seu stellioni majori) terrae adhaerens, aut lacertae species, quemcunque cibum aut potum calcet, veneno suo inficiens. Ibidem alii, وقيل هي علي شكل سام ابرص Dicitur esse formae sammabras. Et Alcamus, الوحرة وزغة كسام ابرص او ضرب من العظا لا تطا شي لا سميته Alvvachara est guezga, sicut sammabras, aut lacertae species, quae nihil calcat, quod non inficiat. Inde وحر vvachara verbum est veneno inficere. Proinde dicunt, وحر الصدر عشه ووسواسه II, 499 Pectus infecit dolus ejus, et suggestio ejus. Item, الغل اللازق به كما تلزق الوحرة بالارض Dolus ipsi adhaeret, ut alvvachara adhaeret terrae.

So far, then, it is established that the letaa belongs to the lizard kind, since the ancients so determine with great agreement. But to define the species is not for just anyone. The Syrian explains it as the salamander. Of the more recent writers some prefer the stellio, others the lizard. The col. 1074 former is followed by Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae], Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)]; the latter by Munster, Schindler, the Genevans, the English, the Italians. I understand a species of lizard which in Arabic is called وحرة [waḥra] wachra or wachara. Concerning it the Arabs note chiefly three things: 1. That it is similar to the stellio. 2. That it clings very closely to the ground. 3. That whatever food it treads on is infected with its venom. These three settle the matter, as we shall show later. But first the Arabs must be heard. Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ]: الوحرة دويبة حمرا تلتصق بالارض كالعظا [al-waḥra duwaybba ḥamrā taltaṣiqu bi-l-arḍ ka-l-ʿaẓā] Alvvachra, a small red animal, clinging to the ground, like a lizard. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: هي دويبة شبيهة بسام ابرص تلتصق بالارض او ضرب من العظا لا تطا طعاما ولا سرابا الا سميته [hiya duwaybba shabīha bi-sām abraṣ taltaṣiqu bi-l-arḍ aw ḍarb min al-ʿaẓā lā taṭaʾ ṭaʿāman wa-lā sarāban illā sammathu] It is a small animal, similar to the sammabras (or greater stellio), clinging to the ground, or a species of lizard, infecting with its venom whatever food or drink it treads on. In the same place others say: وقيل هي علي شكل سام ابرص [wa-qīla hiya ʿalī shakl sām abraṣ] It is said to be of the form of the sammabras. And Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: الوحرة وزغة كسام ابرص او ضرب من العظا لا تطا شي لا سميته [al-waḥra wazagha ka-sām abraṣ aw ḍarb min al-ʿaẓā lā taṭaʾ shay lā sammathu] Alvvachara is a guezga, like the sammabras, or a species of lizard, which treads on nothing that it does not infect. Hence وحر [waḥira] vvachara is a verb meaning to infect with venom. Accordingly they say: وحر الصدر عشه ووسواسه [waḥira al-ṣadr ʿishshuhu wa-waswāsuhu] II, 499 His deceit and his insinuation infected the breast. Likewise: الغل اللازق به كما تلزق الوحرة بالارض [al-ghill al-lāziq bihi kamā talzaqu al-waḥra bi-l-arḍ] Deceit clings to him, as the alvvachara clings to the ground.


Iam hoc, quidquid est, letaae convenire, nullo negotio probavero. 1. Id enim lacertae genus stellioni esse simile, aut etiam ejus speciem, suadet, quod interpretum antiquissimi, Graeci, Chaldaei et Romani stellionem explicant. 2. Terrae adhaerere, colligitur ex ipso nomine. Nam Arabice verbum لطا lataa, vel لطئ latia, proprie adhaerere sonat, non ubivis, sed terrae. Nusquam aliter sumitur. Hinc Damir in capite قبرة Kobbara, seu De Alauda, E natura ejus est, ut strepitus eam non terreat: et quandoque lapide molari conteratur, ولطي بالارض حتي يتجاوزها الحجر et terrae adhaereat, donec eam lapis pertransierit. Et in capite عنكبوت seu De Aranea, فانا اراد صيد الذباب لطي بالارض Et, cum vult venari muscas, terrae adhaeret. Itaque לטאה letaa, inde deducta, proprie id animal significat, quod terrae adhaeret. Quod in vvacharae definitione observant Giauhari et Damir. 3. Letaam denique venenatum esse animal, et a quo maxime cavendum, docet majusculum Lamed initio nominis. Neque enim scribitur לטאה, sed לטאה. Unde Buxtorfius in Commentario Masorethico cap. 14. La- col. 1075 med majusculum Masora parva notat in voce והלטאה, Levit. XI, 30. quam alii lacertam, alii stellionem reddunt. Litera autem majuscula denotat, inter reliqua reptilia vel maxime ab hoc reptili esse cavendum.

Now I shall prove without any difficulty that this, whatever it is, fits the letaa. 1. That this kind of lizard is similar to the stellio, or even a species of it, is suggested by the fact that the most ancient of the interpreters, the Greek, the Chaldee and the Roman, render it stellio. 2. That it clings to the ground is gathered from the name itself. For in Arabic the verb لطا [laṭā] lataa, or لطئ [laṭiʾa] latia, properly means to cling, not to anything at all, but to the ground. It is never taken otherwise. Hence Damir, in the chapter قبرة [qubbara] Kobbara, or On the Lark: It is its nature that noise does not frighten it; and sometimes it is crushed by a millstone, ولطي بالارض حتي يتجاوزها الحجر [wa-laṭiya bi-l-arḍ ḥattā yatajāwazahā al-ḥajar] and it clings to the ground until the stone has passed over it. And in the chapter عنكبوت [ʿankabūt], or On the Spider, فانا اراد صيد الذباب لطي بالارض [fa-nā arāda ṣayd al-dhubāb laṭiya bi-l-arḍ] And when it wants to hunt flies, it clings to the ground. Thus לטאה letaa, derived from it, properly signifies the animal that clings to the ground. This is what Giauhari and Damir note in the definition of the vvachara. 3. Finally, that the letaa is a venomous animal, and one to be guarded against above all, is taught by the enlarged Lamed at the beginning of the name. For it is not written לטאה, but לטאה. Hence Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum] in the Commentarius Masorethicus, ch. 14: The small Masora notes an enlarged La- col. 1075 med in the word והלטאה, Lev 11:30, which some render lizard, others stellio. The enlarged letter indicates that among the other reptiles this reptile is to be guarded against most of all.


De caetero hoc animal quomodo Graece vocetur, nemo facile dixerit, nisi quis putet, esse salamandrae speciem. Nempe cum stellione salamandram veterum nonnulli conferunt, tanquam illi similem, aut etiam ejus speciem. Aëtius Tetrab. 4. Serm. 1. cap. 52. Salamandra animal est simile stellioni. Nicandri Scholiastes in Alexipharmaca, Ἡ σαλαμάνδρα, εἶδος ἀσκαλαβώτου. 2. Eadem inficere legitur, quidquid calcat. Plinius ubi supra: Si arbori irrepsit, omnia poma inficit veneno. Item, Si contacto ab ea ligno, vel pede, crusta panis incoquatur, idem veneficium est. Quo pertinet, quod Narbonenses apud Gesnerum dictitant: Si Blanda (id est, salamandra) in acervo tritici reperiatur, totum infici, adeo, ut vel gallinae vescentes inde pereant. Proinde الوحرة alvvachara, cui Arabes haec eadem tribuunt, videri queat, idem esse cum salamandra, nisi quod non convenit color. Is enim in wachara ruber est, in salamandra varius. Itaque wachara aliud est Arabicae lacertae genus, nobis ignotae, similis tamen, in II, 500 multis, stellioni et salamandrae. Unde est, quod לטאה letaa, quam putamus esse Arabum vvacharam, a Syro ܣܡܢܕܪܐ salamandra, et a veterum plerisque aliis stellio redditur (1).

As for the rest, what this animal is called in Greek no one could easily say, unless one thinks it to be a species of salamander. For some of the ancients compare the salamander with the stellio, as similar to it, or even a species of it. Aëtius, Tetrab. 4, Serm. 1, ch. 52: The salamander is an animal similar to the stellio. The Scholiast of Nicander on the Alexipharmaca: Ἡ σαλαμάνδρα, εἶδος ἀσκαλαβώτου [Hē salamandra, eidos askalabōtou]. 2. The same animal is said to infect whatever it treads on. Pliny, in the place cited above: If it has crept onto a tree, it infects all the fruit with poison. Likewise: If a crust of bread is baked over wood or a foot touched by it, the poisoning is the same. To this belongs what the people of Narbonne keep saying, according to Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium]: If a Blanda (that is, a salamander) is found in a heap of wheat, the whole is infected, so much that even hens feeding on it die. Accordingly الوحرة [al-waḥara] alvvachara, to which the Arabs attribute these same things, might seem to be the same as the salamander, except that the colour does not agree. For in the wachara it is red, in the salamander variegated. Therefore the wachara is another kind of Arabian lizard, unknown to us, yet similar in II, 500 many respects to the stellio and the salamander. Hence it is that לטאה letaa, which we take to be the vvachara of the Arabs, is rendered ܣܡܢܕܪܐ [סמנדרא] salamandra by the Syriac, and stellio by most of the other ancients R1.


a) Bochart, II, 497 cap. 2. pag. 1007.

a) Bochart, II, 497 ch. 2, p. 1007.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 500 What we noted on the preceding chapter, note 2, applies here too in every respect. Nor have I been able to find anything about the lizard which the Arabs call وحرة [waḥra] in the accounts of those who have visited those regions.


Book 4, chapter 5: The chomet
-----------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/chomet.html

II, 500 col. 1075 CAP. V.

II, 500 col. 1075 Chapter 5.


Probatur, חומט chomet esse lacertam, in arena degentem, quae Arabibus حلكا chulaca dicitur.

It is proved that חומט chomet is a lizard living in the sand, which the Arabs call حلكا [ḥlkā] chulaca.


Hbraeis recentioribus, Selomoni, Kimchio, Pomario et Aquinati חומט chomet est limax. Neque aliud volunt Hispani illi, qui in Kimchio vernacule כרבר reddunt. Legendum enim כר״כול caracol, quomodo limacem illi appellant. Id sequuntur Arias, Munsterus, Petrus Robertus, Genevenses et Angli, qui hic quoque limacem habent. Tamen aliter veteres. Graecis enim et Hieronymo חומט chomet est σαῦρα, lacerta. Et Arabibus editis حربا chirba, chamaeleon: manu-scriptis سام ابرص sammabras, stellio. Neque aliud hic Syrus ܚܘܠܡܛܐ chaulmata juxta Gabrielem Sionitam, cui malo credere, quam Baptistae Ferrario, qui reddit: avem, dorsum habentem, nigris et purpureis pennis distinctum; plane ἀπροσδιονύσως. Neque enim de avibus hic agitur, sed de terrae reptilibus. Itaque, ut superiora, ita etiam חומט chomet videtur esse in lacertorum specie. Neque latet origo vocis. Talmudicis enim חומטון chometon est arena. Hinc in tractatu De Sabbatho cap. 5. fol. 54. a. (ubi Talmudici disputant, quorsum 1 Reg. IX, 13. Hiramus, rex Tyriorum, ארץ כבול, terram chabul appellaverit tractum illum, quo donaverat eum Solomon) dicit R. Nach- col. 1076 man, Isaaci filius, ארץ חומטין היתה אמאי קרו לה כבול דמשתרגה בה כרעא עד כבלא Terra erat chometon, unde est, quod vocarunt eam terram chabul quia in ea crus usque ad talum immergebatur. Et Kimchius, hunc locum citans in Lexico Radice כבל, sed verbis paullum immutatis, חומטון chometon explicat חול chol, id est, arenam. Ita, ut illi terra chometon sit terra arenae, vel arenosa. Baal Aruch itidem totum locum ita exponit: פי׳ שרגליו של אדם משתקעות בה מחמת החול כאילו הן כבולין לכן אינה עושה פירות Significat pedes hominis in ea (terra) fuisse immersos propter arenae (copiam) ac si fuissent II, 501 compediti, ac proinde illam fuisse infrugiferam. In Glossa Talmudis terra chome- ton est terra מלחה ומתבקעת salsuginosa et diffissa. Et ejusdem tractatus cap. 2. fol. 31. a. חומטון Glossatori est ארץ מלחה ומשמרת את הפירות מהתליע, ter- ra salsuginosa, quae fructus a vermiculatione servat. Sed prior interpretatio est verior, et utrique loco apprime convenit. Nam et incedentium pedibus arena molesta est, et in calidis locis vim habet ἀρτυτικὴν, qua res a corruptione diu servat. Itaque in Africae arenis cadavera condiri multi asserunt et pro mumia distrahi. Quin vox חומטון chometon, quamvis non extet in libris Propheticis, videtur esse valde antiqua (1). Et Graecos puto, aspiratione demta, inde deduxisse ἄμαθον, et, cum προθέσει, ψάμαθον. Quorum utrumque in vetustissimis scriptoribus, Homero puta et aliis, in arenae notione reperitur. Ita tamen, ut ἄμαθον Grammatici velint arenam esse μεσόγειον, mediterraneam, et ψάμαθον παραθαλασσίαν, seu littoralem. Sic fere distinguunt Hesychius, Suidas, alii.

For the more recent Hebrews, Solomon, Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)] and Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)], חומט chomet is the limax [slug]. Nor do those Spaniards mean anything else who in Kimchi render it in the vernacular as כרבר. For one should read כר״כול caracol, which is what they call the slug. This is followed by Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], Münster, Pierre Robert, the Genevans and the English, who here too have limax [slug]. The ancients, however, thought otherwise. For to the Greeks and to Jerome חומט chomet is σαῦρα [saura], a lizard. And in the printed Arabic versions it is حربا [ḥirbā] chirba, the chameleon; in the manuscript ones سام ابرص [sām abraṣ] sammabras, the stellio. Nor does the Syriac ܚܘܠܡܛܐ [חולמטא] chaulmata mean anything else here, according to Gabriel Sionita [=translator of al-Idrīsī's geography into Latin (Geographia Nubiensis, Paris 1619)], whom I prefer to believe rather than Battista Ferrari, who renders it: a bird having a back marked with black and purple feathers; plainly ἀπροσδιονύσως [aprosdionysōs]. For the subject here is not birds but creeping things of the earth. Therefore, like the preceding ones, חומט chomet also seems to belong to the lizard kind. Nor is the origin of the word obscure. For to the Talmudists חומטון chometon is sand. Hence in the tractate On the Sabbath, ch. 5, fol. 54a (where the Talmudists discuss why in 1 Reg. IX, 13 Hiram, king of the Tyrians, called ארץ כבול, the land of Chabul, the district which Solomon had given him), R. Nachman, son of Isaac, says: col. 1076 ארץ חומטין היתה אמאי קרו לה כבול דמשתרגה בה כרעא עד כבלא It was a land of chometon; hence they called it the land of chabul, because in it the leg sank down to the ankle. And Kimchi, citing this passage in his Lexicon under the root כבל, though with slightly altered words, explains חומטון chometon as חול chol, that is, sand. So for them land of chometon is land of sand, or sandy land. Baal Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome] [=Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome, the ʿArukh] likewise explains the whole passage thus: פי׳ שרגליו של אדם משתקעות בה מחמת החול כאילו הן כבולין לכן אינה עושה פירות It means that a man's feet sank into it (the land) because of the (abundance of) sand, as if they had been II, 501 fettered, and that it was therefore unfruitful. In the Gloss on the Talmud, the land of chometon is land מלחה ומתבקעת, salty and cracked. And in ch. 2 of the same tractate, fol. 31a, חומטון for the Glossator is ארץ מלחה ומשמרת את הפירות מהתליע, salty soil, which preserves fruits from worms. But the former interpretation is the truer, and suits both passages exceedingly well. For sand is both troublesome to the feet of those walking, and in hot places has a ἀρτυτικὴν [artytikēn] power, by which it preserves things from corruption for a long time. Thus many assert that in the sands of Africa corpses are embalmed and sold as mummy. Indeed the word חומטון chometon, although it does not occur in the Prophetic books, seems to be very ancient R1. And I think the Greeks, dropping the aspiration, derived from it ἄμαθον [amathon], and, with a prefix, ψάμαθον [psamathon]. Both are found in the most ancient writers, Homer for instance and others, in the sense of sand. Yet the Grammarians hold that ἄμαθον [amathon] is μεσόγειον [mesogeion], inland sand, and ψάμαθον [psamathon] παραθαλασσίαν [parathalassian], or shore sand. So, roughly, Hesychius, the Suda and others distinguish them.


Itaque, ut חימטון chometon est arena: sic חומט chomet est lacerti species, quae in arenis degit. Et videtur intelligi Arabum حلكا chulaca, vel لحكا lucha, et luchaca; de qua Alcamus, الحلكا دويبة تغوص في الرمل او ضرب من العظا كالحلكا Alchulaca, animalculum, quod in arena mergitur: aut lacertae species, quae etiam chulaca vocatur. Idem, اللحكا دويبة زرقا تشبه العظا Luchaca, animalculum coeru- leum, lacertae simile. Damir, لحلكا دويبة شبيهة بالعغناة تغوص في الرمل Alchulaca, animalculum, lacertae simile, quod in arenis immergitur. Alazhari, اللحكا دويبة كانها سمكة تكون في الرمل فاذا احست الانسان دارت في الرمل وغاصت فيه Luchaca, animalculum, in arena degens, ut piscis (in aqua); quod, cum sentit hominem, in arena volvitur, atque in ea immergitur. Et Ibnosacith, اللحكا دوبة شبيهة بالعظاية وقوايم خفيفة Luchaca, animalculum, lacertae simile, pedibus levissimis. Asseidalanius et Arruvianus, دويبة مثل الاصبع تجري في الرمل ثم تغوص col. 1077 فيه وهذا يقوي قول الجوهري انه مقلوبة من الحلكا II, 502 Animalculum est digitale, quod per arenas currit, et in iis demergitur. Id confirmat dictum Giauhari, Nomen luchaca inversum esse ex chulaca. Rursus Damir, العرب تسيها بنات النقا لانها تسكن نقيات Arabes etiam appellant filias tumuli arenae; quia in arenae tumulis degit.

Therefore, just as חימטון chometon is sand, so חומט chomet is a species of lizard that lives in the sands. And it seems that the Arabs' حلكا [ḥlkā] chulaca, or لحكا [lḥkā] lucha, and luchaca, is meant; of which Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] says: الحلكا دويبة تغوص في الرمل او ضرب من العظا كالحلكا [al-ḥlkā duwaybba taghūṣu fī al-raml aw ḍarb min al-ʿaẓā ka-al-ḥlkā] Alchulaca, a little animal that plunges into the sand; or a species of lizard, which is also called chulaca. The same: اللحكا دويبة زرقا تشبه العظا [al-lḥkā duwaybba zarqā tushbihu al-ʿaẓā] Luchaca, a little blue animal, like a lizard. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: لحلكا دويبة شبيهة بالعغناة تغوص في الرمل [lḥlkā duwaybba shabīha bi-al-ʿghnāt taghūṣu fī al-raml] Alchulaca, a little animal like a lizard, which plunges into the sands. Alazhari: اللحكا دويبة كانها سمكة تكون في الرمل فاذا احست الانسان دارت في الرمل وغاصت فيه [al-lḥkā duwaybba ka-annahā samaka takūnu fī al-raml fa-idhā aḥassat al-insān dārat fī al-raml wa-ghāṣat fīhi] Luchaca, a little animal living in the sand like a fish (in water); which, when it senses a man, rolls about in the sand and plunges into it. And Ibnosacith: اللحكا دوبة شبيهة بالعظاية وقوايم خفيفة [al-lḥkā dwba shabīha bi-al-ʿaẓāya wa-qawāyim khafīfa] Luchaca, a little animal like a lizard, with very light feet. Asseidalanius and Arruvianus: دويبة مثل الاصبع تجري في الرمل ثم تغوص [duwaybba mithl al-iṣbaʿ tajrī fī al-raml thumma taghūṣu] col. 1077 فيه وهذا يقوي قول الجوهري انه مقلوبة من الحلكا [fīhi wa-hādhā yuqawwī qawl al-Jawharī annahu maqlūba min al-ḥlkā] II, 502 It is a little animal the size of a finger, which runs through the sands and plunges into them. This confirms the statement of Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ] that the name luchaca is inverted from chulaca. Again Damir: العرب تسيها بنات النقا لانها تسكن نقيات [al-ʿarab tsyhā banāt al-naqā li-annahā taskunu nqyāt] The Arabs also call them daughters of the sand-hill, because it lives in sand-hills.


Sed et lacerti communis una species est ἀμμώδης. Damir capite العظاة Aladha, seu De Lacerta, وهي انواع كثيرة منها الابيض والاحمر والاصغر وكلها منقطه بالسواد والوان بحسب مساكنها فان منها ما يسكن الرمال ومنها ما يسكن قريبا من الما والعشب Earum multae sunt species: quaedam albae, quaedam rubrae, quaedam flavae; quae omnes sunt nigro distinctae. Et colores illis sunt pro ratione loci, quem occupant. Aliae enim in arenis degunt: aliae prope aquas et in herbosis locis. Et Alazhari, هي دويبة ملسا تعدوا وتترد كثيرا تشبه سام ابرص الا انها احسن منه وتسي العظاه وشحمة الارض وشحمة الرمل Est animal molle, multum cursitans, et ultro citroque commeans, simile τῷ sammabras, seu stellioni, nisi quod eo est pulchrius. Vocatur aladha, et Adeps terrae, et adeps arenae. Vides, lector, tam hanc lacertam, quam alteram, minus vulgarem, de qua supra, ab arena nomen ha-bere, aeque ac Hebraeum חומט chomet. Itaque חומט chomet vel alterutrum, vel utrumque significat (2).

But there is also one species of the common lizard that is ἀμμώδης [ammōdēs]. Damir, in the chapter العظاة [al-ʿaẓāh] Aladha, or On the Lizard: وهي انواع كثيرة منها الابيض والاحمر والاصغر وكلها منقطه بالسواد والوان بحسب مساكنها فان منها ما يسكن الرمال ومنها ما يسكن قريبا من الما والعشب [wa-hiya anwāʿ kathīra minhā al-abyaḍ wa-al-aḥmar wa-al-aṣghar wa-kulluhā munaqqaṭa bi-al-sawād wa-alwān bi-ḥasab masākinihā fa-inna minhā mā yaskun al-rimāl wa-minhā mā yaskun qarīban min al-mā wa-al-ʿushb] There are many species of them: some white, some red, some yellow; all of them are spotted with black. And their colours correspond to the place they occupy. For some live in the sands, others near waters and in grassy places. And Alazhari: هي دويبة ملسا تعدوا وتترد كثيرا تشبه سام ابرص الا انها احسن منه وتسي العظاه وشحمة الارض وشحمة الرمل [hiya duwaybba malsā taʿdū wa-tataraddad kathīran tushbih sāmm abraṣ illā annahā aḥsan minhu wa-tusī al-ʿaẓāh wa-shaḥmat al-arḍ wa-shaḥmat al-raml] It is a soft animal, running about a great deal and going back and forth, similar to the sammabras, or stellio, except that it is prettier than it. It is called aladha, and Fat of the earth, and fat of the sand. You see, reader, that both this lizard and the other, less common one discussed above take their name from sand, just as the Hebrew חומט chomet does. Therefore חומט chomet signifies either one of the two, or both R2.


Obiter nota, عظاية vel عضاية in Avicenna pro salamandra poni, et in Abenbitare modo pro salamandra, modo pro sepe, vel lacerta Chalcidica, non sine gravi errore. Utraque enim est venenata. At العظاة veneno caret, ut Arabes diserte docent. Damir, ومن خرافات العرب قالوا ان السوم لما فرق علي الحيوان احتبست العظاة II, 503 عند التفرقة حتي نفد السم واخذ كل حيوان قسطه منه علي قدر السبق اليه فلم يكن لها فيه نصيب وفي طبعها انها عتشي مشيا سريعا ثم تقف ويقال col. 1078 ان ذلك يعرض لها من التذكرة والاسف علي ما فاتها من السم Est ex Arabum Apologis, quod dicunt, quod, cum divisa sunt venena inter animalia, continuit se aladha, dum divisio fiebat, donec venena defecerunt, cum unumquodque animal portionem suam sumsisset, prout ordine primum fuerat. Neque illi fuit sua portio. Proinde, cum illi naturale sit, ut citato gressu incedat, et mox subsistat, ajunt id illi accidere, quia meminit, et moesta est, eo quod defuit ipsi venenum. Ibidem Damir, وتمسي بارض مصر السحلية In terra Aegypti vocatur SUCHLIA, quam Azhari asserit stellioni similem esse, الا انها لا تودي وهي احسن منه nisi quod non est noxia, et est eo pulchrior. Eos igitur falli necesse est, qui hoc animalculum cum salamandra confundunt, aut cum lacerta Chalcidica, quae sunt maxime noxiae.

Note in passing that عظاية [ʿaẓāya] or عضاية [ʿaḍāya] is used in Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] for the salamander, and in Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār] sometimes for the salamander, sometimes for the seps or Chalcidian lizard, not without serious error. For both of these are venomous. But العظاة [al-ʿaẓāh] lacks venom, as the Arabs explicitly teach. Damir: ومن خرافات العرب قالوا ان السوم لما فرق علي الحيوان احتبست العظاة II, 503 عند التفرقة حتي نفد السم واخذ كل حيوان قسطه منه علي قدر السبق اليه فلم يكن لها فيه نصيب وفي طبعها انها عتشي مشيا سريعا ثم تقف ويقال col. 1078 ان ذلك يعرض لها من التذكرة والاسف علي ما فاتها من السم [wa-min khurāfāt al-ʿArab qālū anna al-sūm lammā furriqa ʿalā al-ḥayawān iḥtabasat al-ʿaẓāh ʿinda al-tafriqa ḥattā nafida al-summ wa-akhadha kull ḥayawān qisṭahu minhu ʿalā qadr al-sabq ilayhi fa-lam yakun lahā fīhi naṣīb wa-fī ṭabʿihā annahā ʿatmshī mashyan sarīʿan thumma taqif wa-yuqāl anna dhālika yaʿriḍ lahā min al-tadhkira wa-al-asaf ʿalā mā fātahā min al-summ] It is one of the fables of the Arabs that they say that, when venoms were distributed among the animals, the aladha held back while the distribution was taking place, until the venoms ran out, each animal having taken its portion according to the order in which it had come first. And it got no portion. Accordingly, since it is natural to it to move at a rapid pace and then suddenly stop, they say this happens to it because it remembers and grieves that venom was denied it. In the same place Damir: وتمسي بارض مصر السحلية [wa-tumsī bi-arḍ Miṣr al-suḥliyya] In the land of Egypt it is called SUCHLIA, which Azhari asserts is similar to the stellio, الا انها لا تودي وهي احسن منه [illā annahā lā tūdī wa-hiya aḥsan minhu] except that it is not harmful, and is prettier than it. Those, therefore, must be mistaken who confuse this little animal with the salamander or with the Chalcidian lizard, which are extremely harmful.


(1) Rosenmüller, II, 501 Hoc dictum in Buxtorfium, quippe qui Talmudicorum חוממון a Graeco vocabulo factum autumat (in Lexico Chald. p. 782). Certe arenae significatio in reliquarum dialectorum cognatarum nulla est usitata.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 501 This is said against Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum], who holds that the Talmudists' חוממון was formed from a Greek word (in the Lexicon Chald. p. 782). Certainly the meaning sand is in no common use in any of the other cognate dialects.


(2) Rosenmüller, II, 502 Sed omnis haec disputatio ea nititur opinione, חומט esse arenam; quo quidem fundamento nil esse potest infirmius, vid. supra not. 1. Apud Chaldaeos verbum חמט denotat, incurvavit, flexit, inflexit se. Unde fortassis Arabibus eruca خُمَّاطٌ est appellata (vid. Golii Lexic. p. 652.), nisi ea potius dicta sit ab eo, quod plantas derodit; est enim خَمَطَ decorticavit arborem. Sed ab inflectendo potuit quoque limax nomen nancisci, qui nonnullis ex eruditis Levit. XI, 30. placuit (vid. Bochart sub hujus Capit. initio). Doceris itaque novo exemplo, quam vana res sit, solis etymologiis elicere significationes eorum nominum, quae animalia designant.

R2 Rosenmüller, II, 502 But this whole discussion rests on the opinion that חומט means sand; and no foundation could be weaker than that, see above note 1. Among the Chaldeans the verb חמט denotes he bent, curved, bent himself. Hence perhaps the caterpillar is called خُمَّاطٌ [khummāṭ] by the Arabs (see Golius [=Jacobus Golius, Lexicon Arabico-Latinum (1653)], Lexic. p. 652), unless it was rather named from the fact that it gnaws plants; for خَمَطَ [khamaṭa] means he stripped the bark from a tree. But from bending the snail could also have got its name, which some of the learned favoured at Lev 11:30 (see Bochart at the beginning of this Chapter). You are thus taught by a new example how vain a thing it is to derive the meanings of names that designate animals from etymologies alone.


Book 4, chapter 6: The tinshemeth
---------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/tinshemet.html

II, 503 col. 1078 CAP. VI.

II, 503 col. 1078 CHAPTER VI.


Probatur, תנשמת thinsemeth Levit. XI, 30. esse Chamaeleontem.

It is proved that תנשמת thinsemeth in Levit. XI, 30. is the chameleon.


In loco, in quo versamur, sola superest תנשמת thinsemeth, id est, talpa, si Graecos sequimur et Hieronymum, et e Chaldaeis Onkelosum, et Hebraeos recentis aevi, Selomonem, Kimchium, Pomarium, Aquinatem; et novos Bibliorum interpretes, Pagninum, Munsterum, Ariam, Genevenses, Anglos, Italos, etc. Quorum omnium auctoritas cum apud me multum valeat, tamen quo minus in assensum trahat, duo potissimum obstant, quae jam alibi observavi. Unum, quod praecedenti versu de talpa jam actum est. Id enim esse חולד choled, iis rationibus probavimus a), quas nemo facile refellet. Aliud igitur est in hoc versu תנשמת thinsemeth: nisi Mosem velimus in eadem contextus serie idem animal bis vetasse, et eum fingamus sic loquutum: Inter reptilia, quae repunt super terram, haec erunt vobis immunda, talpa, et mus, et crocodilus terrestris, col. 1079 etc. et talpa. Praeterea nomen תנשמת thinsemeth, quod ab halitu et aspiratione ductum est, quomodo in talpam quadret, nullus video, cui tam tenuis est aspiratio, II, 504 ut totos dies sub terra degat, quomodo pisces sub aqua. Unde est, quod talpae et muris subterranei cuniculi hac nota distinguuntur: quod terra obrutos mus statim aperit, ne suffocetur, ac talpa saepe nonnisi secunda, aut tertia die reserat. Proinde תנשמת non esse talpam, viderunt multi veterum, apud quos extant hujus vocis tres aliae versiones diversissimae.

In the passage we are dealing with, only תנשמת thinsemeth remains, that is, the mole, if we follow the Greeks and Jerome, and among the Chaldees Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos], and the Hebrews of recent times, Solomon, Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)], Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)]; and the modern translators of the Bible, Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae], Münster, Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], the Genevans, the English, the Italians, etc. Although the authority of all these carries great weight with me, two things above all keep it from drawing my assent, which I have already noted elsewhere. The first is that the mole was already dealt with in the preceding verse. For we have proved, with arguments that no one will easily refute a), that it is חולד choled. Therefore תנשמת thinsemeth in this verse is something else, unless we wish Moses to have forbidden the same animal twice in one and the same sequence of text, and imagine him to have spoken thus: Among the creeping things that creep upon the earth, these shall be unclean to you: the mole, and the mouse, and the land crocodile, col. 1079 etc. and the mole. Moreover, I do not see at all how the name תנשמת thinsemeth, which is derived from breath and breathing, can fit the mole, whose breathing is so slight II, 504 that it spends whole days under the earth, as fish do under water. Hence the burrows of the mole and of the underground mouse are distinguished by this mark: when they are buried with earth, the mouse opens them at once so as not to suffocate, whereas the mole often unseals them only on the second or third day. Accordingly many of the ancients saw that תנשמת is not the mole; among them three other, very different, renderings of this word are found.


Primo enim Samaritano interpreti תנשמת est [?], id est, mustela, quae Chaldaeis est כרכושתא, et Syris ܟܒܟܘܫܬܐ, prima Radicali geminata, cum Samaritani secundam geminent.

First, to the Samaritan translator תנשמת is [?], that is, the weasel, which in Chaldee is כרכושתא, and in Syriac ܟܒܟܘܫܬܐ [כבכושתא], with the first radical doubled, whereas the Samaritans double the second.


Secundo, pro eadem voce תנשמת Syrus habet ܝܘܕܥܝܕܐ jodaida, multipedam: et Arabes manu-scripti, البدال وهو أم اربعة اربعين Albedal, quae mater est quadraginta quatuor, supple pedum; seu cui sunt pedes XLIV, id est, julum, aut scolopendram. Sed pro بدال bedal, voce nihili, legendum ندال nedal. Chaldaeis enim et Talmudicis נדל nedal, vel nedel est scolopendra. Sic infra versu quadragesimo secundo, ubi e reptilibus terrae prohibetur כל מרבה רגלים, quodcumque reptile multos habet pedes, Gr. ὃ πολυπληθεῖ πο-σὶν, Ionathan habet נדל דמסגי ריגלין, nedal, qui est multipes, id est, scolopendram. Et Talmudici in Cholin cap. 3. fol. 67. b. מרבה רגלים זה נדל, qui multos habet pedes, id est, nedal. Et ibi Glossa, נדל מאה רגלים קורין לו Nedal centi-pedam vulgo vocant. Numero scilicet certo pro incerto. Sed Arabes, qui solent praecise loqui, matrem pedum XLIV. appellant. Sic Avicenna lib. 4. Fen. 6. Tract. 6. ubi de animalculis, quorum morsus est venenosus, capite decimo nono animal الاربعة والاربعين id est, quadraginta quatuor pedum, ita describit, هو الحيوان المعروف بدخال الاذن وربما كان في طول شبر وله في كل جانب اثنان وعشرون قايمة وقد يمشي قدما وقد ينكص بحاله Illud est animal notum; quia in aurem ingreditur. Plerumque est palmi longitudine. Ab unoquoque latere pedes habet viginti duos, et modo incedit antrorsum, modo in posteriora fertur. Scolopendram in aurem ingredi, alibi nusquam legi. Sed eam ἐπὶ τὴν οὐρὰν, caudam versus ferri, dicit Philosophus, Historiae libri quarti capite septimo. Unde a Nicandro Theriacῶν versu 812. vocatur ἀμφικαρὴς σκολόπενδρα. Ad quae verba Scholiastes, Ἀμφικαρὴς δὲ, ἤγουν δικέφαλος. Ψευδῶς δέ φησιν, οὐ γάρ ἐστιν. Ἀλλ᾽, ὡς Ἀριστοτέλης φησὶν, εἰς τοὐπίσω πολλάκις ἕρπει, καὶ παρ-έχει δόξαν τοῦ δικέφαλος εἶναι. Pedum numerum quod attinet, illum alii aliter definiunt, ut ubique locorum eundem esse necesse non est. Utut sit, scolopendram hoc nomine intelligi, nos docet Abenbitar ad caput Dioscoridis Περὶ σκολοπένδρας θαλασσίας, cujus nomen, postquam Arabicis literis ita expressit, II, 505 سقولوفندريا تالاسيا هو حيوان بحري وسمي باسم الحيوان الذي يقال له اربعة واربعون Hoc est marinum animal, col. 1080 quod XLIV pedum vocant.

Second, for the same word תנשמת the Syriac has ܝܘܕܥܝܕܐ [יודעידא] jodaida, the many-footed one; and the Arabic manuscripts have البدال وهو أم اربعة اربعين [al-badāl wa-huwa umm arbaʿa arbaʿīn] Albedal, which is the mother of forty-four, supply feet; that is, which has 44 feet, i.e. the iulus or scolopendra. But for بدال [badāl] bedal, a meaningless word, one should read ندال [nadāl] nedal. For in Chaldee and among the Talmudists נדל nedal or nedel is the scolopendra. Thus below in verse 42, where among the creeping things of the earth כל מרבה רגלים is forbidden, whatever creeping thing has many feet, Gr. ὃ πολυπληθεῖ ποσὶν [ho polyplēthei posin], Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] has נדל דמסגי ריגלין, nedal, which is many-footed, that is, the scolopendra. And the Talmudists in Chullin ch. 3, fol. 67b: מרבה רגלים זה נדל, that which has many feet, that is, nedal. And there the Gloss: נדל מאה רגלים קורין לו, Nedal is commonly called the hundred-footed, a definite number, of course, for an indefinite one. But the Arabs, who usually speak precisely, call it the mother of 44 feet. Thus Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)], book 4, Fen 6, tract. 6, where he treats of small animals whose bite is venomous, in chapter 19 describes the animal الاربعة والاربعين [al-arbaʿa wa-l-arbaʿīn], that is, of forty-four feet, as follows: هو الحيوان المعروف بدخال الاذن وربما كان في طول شبر وله في كل جانب اثنان وعشرون قايمة وقد يمشي قدما وقد ينكص بحاله [huwa al-ḥayawān al-maʿrūf bi-dakhkhāl al-udhn wa-rubbamā kāna fī ṭūl shibr wa-lahu fī kull jānib ithnān wa-ʿishrūn qāyima wa-qad yamshī quduman wa-qad yankuṣu bi-ḥālihi] It is a well-known animal, because it enters the ear. Usually it is a span in length. On each side it has twenty-two feet, and it sometimes walks forward, sometimes moves backward. That the scolopendra enters the ear I have read nowhere else. But that it moves ἐπὶ τὴν οὐρὰν [epi tēn ouran], toward the tail, is said by the Philosopher, History, book 4, chapter 7. Hence Nicander, Theriaca verse 812, calls it ἀμφικαρὴς σκολόπενδρα [amphikarēs skolopendra]. On which words the Scholiast: Ἀμφικαρὴς δὲ, ἤγουν δικέφαλος. Ψευδῶς δέ φησιν, οὐ γάρ ἐστιν. Ἀλλ᾽, ὡς Ἀριστοτέλης φησὶν, εἰς τοὐπίσω πολλάκις ἕρπει, καὶ παρέχει δόξαν τοῦ δικέφαλος εἶναι [Amphikarēs de, ēgoun dikephalos. Pseudōs de phēsin, ou gar estin. All', hōs Aristotelēs phēsin, eis toupisō pollakis herpei, kai parechei doxan tou dikephalos einai]. As for the number of feet, different authors define it differently, so that it need not be the same in every place. However that may be, that the scolopendra is meant by this name is taught us by Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār] on the chapter of Dioscorides Περὶ σκολοπένδρας θαλασσίας [Peri skolopendras thalassias], whose name, after he has rendered it in Arabic letters thus, II, 505 سقولوفندريا تالاسيا هو حيوان بحري وسمي باسم الحيوان الذي يقال له اربعة واربعون [sqūlūfandriyā tālāsiyā huwa ḥayawān baḥrī wa-summiya bi-ism al-ḥayawān alladhī yuqāl lahu arbaʿa wa-arbaʿūn] This is a sea animal, col. 1080 which they call the 44-footed.


Tertio, Ionathani תנשמת thinsemeth est סלמנדרא salamandra. Et Arabi Erpeniano صنبرص senabras, corrupte pro سامابرص sammabras, quomodo habet Parisiensis editio. Hos ad verum proxime accessisse puto, atque ut quinque illis, quae praecesserunt, ita hoc quoque nomine aliquam lacerti speciem contineri, nempe chamaeleontem, qui a spiratione ita vocetur. Hebraeis enim נשם spirare est, et נשמה non solum spiritus, sed et halitus, vel spiratio, ut et נשימה. Unde est, quod ad haec verba Psal. CL, 6. כל נשמה תהלל יה, Omnis spiritus laudet Deum; sic habet auctor Berescith Rabba cap. 14. על כל נשימה ונשימה שאדם נישם צריך לקלס לבוראו מה טעם כל נשמה תהלל יה כל הנשימה תהלל יה Ad omnem halitum, quem homo spirat, necesse est ut laudet creatorem suum. Qua ratione? (Quia dicitur) „Omnis spiritus laudet Dominum“, id est, Omnis halitus laudet Dominum. A spirando autem, vel ab aspirando recte dici chamaeleontem, fateatur necesse est, quisquis naturam ejus habet perspectam: cum, os diducens hiatu perpetuo, atque spiritu aërem ducens, a multis putetur eo solo vesci. Plinius libri octavi capite trigesimo tertio, Ipse celsus, hianti semper ore, solus animalium nec cibo, nec potu alitur, nec alio quam aëris alimento. Solinus, Hiatus ejus aeternus, ac sine ullius usus ministerio; quippe cum neque cibum capiat, neque potu alatur, aut alimento alio, quam haustu aëris vivat. Ovidius Metamorphoseωs libro decimo quinto,

Third, for Jonathan תנשמת thinsemeth is סלמנדרא salamandra. And for Erpenius' Arabic translator it is صنبرص [ṣnbrṣ] senabras, a corruption of سامابرص [sāmābrṣ] sammabras, as the Paris edition has it. I think these have come closest to the truth, and that, as with the five preceding names, this name too denotes some species of lizard, namely the chameleon, which is so called from breathing. For in Hebrew נשם is to breathe, and נשמה means not only spirit but also breath or breathing, as does נשימה. Hence, on these words of Ps 150:6. כל נשמה תהלל יה, Let every spirit praise God, the author of Bereshit Rabba, ch. 14, says: על כל נשימה ונשימה שאדם נישם צריך לקלס לבוראו מה טעם כל נשמה תהלל יה כל הנשימה תהלל יה For every breath that a man breathes he must praise his Creator. For what reason? (Because it is said) „Let every spirit praise the Lord“, that is, Let every breath praise the Lord. Anyone who has a clear understanding of its nature must admit that the chameleon is rightly named from breathing, or from breathing in: for since it keeps its mouth open in a perpetual gape and draws in air with its breath, many believe that it feeds on air alone. Pliny, book 8, chapter 33: It holds itself erect, with its mouth always open, and alone of animals is nourished neither by food nor by drink, nor by any nourishment other than air. Solinus: Its gaping is perpetual and serves no use; for it takes no food, is not nourished by drink, and lives on no other nourishment than the air it draws in. Ovid, Metamorphoses, book 15:


Id quoque, quod ventis animal nutritur, et aura.

That too, the animal that is fed on winds and air.


Nempe pulmo est illi maximus. Plinius libri undecimi capite trigesimo septimo, Chamaeleoni pulmo portione maximus, et nihil aliud intus. Plutarchus in libro Utra anim. Συνέπεται δὲ καὶ πνεύματος πλῆθος, ὡς Θεόφραστος. Ὀλί-γον γὰρ ἀποδεῖ πᾶν τὸ σῶμα τοῦ ζώου πλῆρες εἶναι πνεύμονος, ᾧ τεκμαίρεται τὸ πνευματικὸν αὐτοῦ· Accedit etiam spiritus in ipso copia, ut tradit Theophrastus. Parum enim abest, quin totum corpus pulmone sit plenum, unde conjicit, quam sit flatilis. Bellonius, Cum pulmonibus magnis per ventris latera exporrectis praeditus sit, ventum intro magno impetu attrahit atque intumescit (1). Tertullianus II, 506 in libro De pallio, Oscitans vescitur, follicans ruminat, de vento cibus, etc. Sed et, quod mirere magis, etiam post dissectionem diu spirare creditur. Philosophus in eximia illa chamaeleonis descriptione Historiae libri secundi capite undecimo, Ἐνεργεῖ δὲ καὶ τῷ πνεύματι, ἀνατετμημένος ὅλος ἐπὶ πολὺν χρόνον, βραχείας ἰσχυρῶς ἔτι κινήσεως ἐν αὐτῷ περὶ τὴν καρδίαν οὔσης· Etiam, cum totus dissectus est, flatu pollet per longum tempus, quamdiu scilicet motus, quantumvis exiguus, circa cor manet. Is porro halitus Arabice نسيم nasim vocatur ab ea ipsa radice, a qua illi nomen תנשמת thinsemeth. Damir, يغتذي بالنسيم ويعيش بالبرد الهوا Alitur τῷ nasim (id est, halitu) et frigido aëre vescitur. Quod tamen per summum errorem is transfert ad crocodilum terrestrem, ut supra b) notavimus, cum sit proprium chamaeleonis. Quamvis neque chamaeleon solo aëre vesci satis vere scribatur. Quippe linguam habet praelongam in imo glutinosam, cujus jaculatu muscas et culices captat e ramo arboris, cui insidet. Damir, لسانه طويل جدا مقدار col. 1081 ذراع وذلك دليل علي انه يكون مطوي في حلقه وهو يبلع ما بعد عنه من الذباب Lingua ejus valde longa est, nempe ad mensuram cubiti. Proinde eam habet in faucibus complicatam, quam emittit, ut muscas, a se dissitas, (captet et) comedat. Algazel in Mirabilibus, والحربا خلق الله لسانها بخلاف المعتاد لتلحق به ما بعد عنها بثلاث اشبار ونحوه وتصتاد به علي هذه المسافة Chamaeleoni creavit Deus linguam, a solito prorsus diversam, ut ea attingeret, quae a se dissita sunt tribus circiter palmis, et venaretur, quae sunt intra hoc spatium. Arabibus suffragatur apud Scaligerum Iohannes Landius, qui in ultima Syria cum esset, ait, se vidisse unum e quinque, quos emerat, chamaeleonibus, linguae repentino momentaneoque jaculatu muscam, quae in ejus esset pectore, le-gisse. Et Bellonius, qui in Aegypto et in Arabia vivos viderat: Linguam habet teretem, sesquipalmum longam, quam a longe in insecta, quibus maxime vescitur, vibrat: et mucore, quem in extremo spongiosum habet, muscas, scarabaeos, locustas, formicas ad se adducit (2). Inde illi nomen حربا chirba, quasi jaculatritricem dicas. Nam حربة charba est jaculi, aut brevioris lanceae genus. Proinde herba lonchitis, cujus semen est lanceae cuspidi simile, Arabice حربة II, 507 charba dicitur (3). At Graece χαμαιλέων unde vocetur, minus patet, cum animali pigerrimo et timidissimo vix quidquam videatur esse cum leone commune. Tertullianus ubi supra, Chamaeleontem qui audieris, haud ante gnarus, jam timebis aliquid amplius cum leone. At, cum offenderis apud vineam ferme sub pampino totum, ridebis illico audaciam nominis. Tamen etiam poëtis Arabibus باقرة bakira dicitur, id est, leaena. Iisdem enim باقر bakir est leo. Et chamaeleoni simile animalculum vocatur ليث عفرين leo Iphrin a loco, ubi nascitur. Alcamus, ليث عفرين دابة كالحربا يتعرض للراكب ويضربه بذنبه Leo Iphrin, animal, ut chamaeleon, quod equitem invadit, et cauda sua percutit. Itaque leo merito dicitur, cum in chamaeleontis corpore leonis habeat animum. Proinde, si constaret, hoc animal notum fuisse Graecis, dicerem, huic primo inditum chamaeleontis nomen, postmodum ad alterum simile fuisse translatum. Sed, cum hujus animalculi meminerit nemo veterum, mihi fit verissimilius, chamaeleontem ut Arabes جمل gemel vocant, vel جمل يهود gemel jehoud, id est, camelum Iudaicum, ut afferunt Damir et Abenbitar: ita Poenos in Africa גמל gamal appellasse, vel גמליון gamalion, unde facta sit vox χαμαιλέων, Graeco more inflexa, ut videretur II, 508 esse Graeca. Neque obscurum est, cur camelum Arabes appellaverint. Quippe ut vituli caput et pisciculi corpus, et stellionis pedes, ita سنام col. 1082 البعير cameli gibbum illi tribuunt apud Damirem; quia cameli instar dorsum habet tuberosum. Sunt et, qui مجوسي vocant, id est, Magum, vel Magusaeum; quia solem videtur adorare, cum ad illum perpetuo obvertatur. Dicitur in horas mutari, prout lux solis est vegetior, aut calor ejus intensior; et mane esse cineritius, deinde flavus, postremo viridis, cum sol maxime calet (4). Sed et in metu, aut si aliquid illi objiciatur, alios colores induit. Unde proverbium de eo, qui in eodem statu non permanet. تلون الحرباء Mutavit colorem chamaeleon. Ut olim Alcibiades dictus est χαμαιλέοντος εὐμε-ταβολώτερος, chamaeleonte mutabilior. Esum ejus interdicunt Arabes, quia venenatus est, et species وزغ guezgae, seu stellionis. Apud Avicennam et Abenbitarem, sanguis ejus depilat palpebras. Apud Damirem fel removet caliginem, et adeps ad ulcera et cicatrices adhibetur. Apud Alkazuinium remedia ex chamaeleone praescribuntur in epilepsiam, grandinem, locustas et incantationem. Sed his immorari diutius, nostri non est otii.

Its lung, namely, is very large. Pliny, book 11, chapter 37: The chameleon has a lung very large in proportion, and nothing else inside. Plutarch, in the book Utra anim.: Συνέπεται δὲ καὶ πνεύματος πλῆθος, ὡς Θεόφραστος. Ὀλίγον γὰρ ἀποδεῖ πᾶν τὸ σῶμα τοῦ ζώου πλῆρες εἶναι πνεύμονος, ᾧ τεκμαίρεται τὸ πνευματικὸν αὐτοῦ [synepetai de kai pneumatos plēthos, hōs Theophrastos. Oligon gar apodei pan to sōma tou zōou plēres einai pneumonos, hō tekmairetai to pneumatikon autou]; There is also an abundance of breath in it, as Theophrastus reports. For the whole body is very nearly full of lung, from which he infers how full of air it is. Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)]: Since it is furnished with large lungs extending along the sides of the belly, it draws air inward with great force and swells up R1. Tertullian II, 506 in the book De pallio: It feeds by gaping, ruminates by puffing like bellows; its food comes from the wind, etc. But, what is more surprising, it is also believed to go on breathing for a long time after being dissected. The Philosopher, in that excellent description of the chameleon in book 2, chapter 11 of the History: Ἐνεργεῖ δὲ καὶ τῷ πνεύματι, ἀνατετμημένος ὅλος ἐπὶ πολὺν χρόνον, βραχείας ἰσχυρῶς ἔτι κινήσεως ἐν αὐτῷ περὶ τὴν καρδίαν οὔσης [energei de kai tō pneumati, anatetmēmenos holos epi polyn chronon, bracheias ischyrōs eti kinēseōs en autō peri tēn kardian ousēs]; Even when it has been dissected entirely, it retains the power of breath for a long time, that is, as long as some motion, however slight, remains around the heart. This breath is called in Arabic نسيم [nasīm] nasim, from the very root from which its name תנשמת thinsemeth comes. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: يغتذي بالنسيم ويعيش بالبرد الهوا [yaghtadhī bi-l-nasīm wa-yaʿīsh bi-l-bard al-hawā] It is nourished by τῷ [tō] nasim (that is, by breath) and feeds on cold air. Yet by a very great error he transfers this to the land crocodile, as we noted above b), although it is proper to the chameleon. And yet it is not quite truly written that the chameleon lives on air alone. For it has a very long tongue, sticky at the tip, by darting which it catches flies and gnats from the branch of the tree on which it sits. Damir: لسانه طويل جدا مقدار col. 1081 ذراع وذلك دليل علي انه يكون مطوي في حلقه وهو يبلع ما بعد عنه من الذباب [lisānuhu ṭawīl jiddan miqdār dhirāʿ wa-dhālika dalīl ʿalā annahu yakūn maṭwī fī ḥalqihi wa-huwa yablaʿ mā baʿuda ʿanhu min al-dhubāb] Its tongue is very long, namely a cubit in measure. Accordingly it keeps it folded in its throat, and shoots it out in order to (catch and) eat flies that are at a distance from it. Algazel in the Mirabilia: والحربا خلق الله لسانها بخلاف المعتاد لتلحق به ما بعد عنها بثلاث اشبار ونحوه وتصتاد به علي هذه المسافة [wa-l-ḥirbā khalaqa Allāh lisānahā bi-khilāf al-muʿtād li-talḥaqa bihi mā baʿuda ʿanhā bi-thalāth ashbār wa-naḥwihi wa-taṣtād bihi ʿalā hādhihi al-masāfa] God created for the chameleon a tongue quite different from the usual, so that with it it might reach things about three spans away from it, and hunt what lies within this distance. Johannes Landius, cited by Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)], supports the Arabs: he says that when he was in farthest Syria he saw one of the five chameleons he had bought pick off, by a sudden, instantaneous dart of its tongue, a fly that was on its breast. And Belon, who had seen them alive in Egypt and Arabia: It has a round tongue, a palm and a half long, which it darts from afar at the insects on which it chiefly feeds; and with the spongy slime it has at the tip it draws flies, beetles, locusts and ants to itself R2. Hence its name حربا [ḥirbā] chirba, as if one were to say the darter. For حربة [ḥarba] charba is a kind of javelin or short lance. Accordingly the herb lonchitis, whose seed resembles the point of a lance, is called in Arabic حربة [ḥarba] II, 507 charba R3. But why it is called χαμαιλέων [chamaileōn] in Greek is less clear, since this most sluggish and timid animal seems to have scarcely anything in common with the lion. Tertullian, in the place cited above: When you hear of a chameleon, not knowing it before, you will at once fear something more than a lion. But when you come upon it in a vineyard, almost entirely under a vine leaf, you will immediately laugh at the boldness of the name. Yet by the Arab poets too it is called باقرة [bāqira] bakira, that is, lioness. For with them باقر [bāqir] bakir is lion. And an animalcule similar to the chameleon is called ليث عفرين [layth ʿIfrīn] lion of Iphrin, from the place where it is born. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: ليث عفرين دابة كالحربا يتعرض للراكب ويضربه بذنبه [layth ʿIfrīn dābba ka-l-ḥirbā yataʿarraḍ li-l-rākib wa-yaḍribuhu bi-dhanabihi] The lion of Iphrin, an animal like the chameleon, which attacks a rider and strikes him with its tail. So it is rightly called a lion, since in a chameleon's body it has a lion's spirit. Accordingly, if it were established that this animal was known to the Greeks, I would say that the name chameleon was first given to it and afterwards transferred to the other, similar animal. But since none of the ancients mentions this animalcule, it seems to me more probable that, just as the Arabs call the chameleon جمل [jamal] gemel, or جمل يهود [jamal yahūd] gemel jehoud, that is, the Jewish camel, as Damir and Abenbitar report, so the Phoenicians in Africa called it גמל gamal, or גמליון gamalion, from which the word χαμαιλέων [chamaileōn] was formed, inflected in the Greek manner so that it would seem II, 508 to be Greek. Nor is it obscure why the Arabs called it a camel. For, just as they attribute to it the head of a calf, the body of a little fish and the feet of a gecko, so too, in Damir, سنام col. 1082 البعير [sanām al-baʿīr] the hump of a camel, because like a camel it has a humped back. There are also those who call it مجوسي [majūsī], that is, a Magian or Magusaean, because it seems to worship the sun, since it is constantly turned towards it. It is said to change hour by hour, according as the sunlight is stronger or its heat more intense: in the morning it is ash-grey, then yellow, and finally green when the sun is hottest R4. But in fear too, or if something is put in its way, it takes on other colours. Hence the proverb about one who does not remain in the same state: تلون الحرباء [talawwana al-ḥirbāʾ] The chameleon has changed colour. So Alcibiades was once called χαμαιλέοντος εὐμεταβολώτερος [chamaileontos eumetabolōteros], more changeable than a chameleon. The Arabs forbid eating it, because it is venomous and a species of وزغ [wazagh] guezga, or gecko. In Avicenna and Abenbitar, its blood removes the hair of the eyelids. In Damir, its gall removes dimness of sight, and its fat is applied to ulcers and scars. In Alkazuini, remedies from the chameleon are prescribed against epilepsy, hail, locusts and enchantment. But to dwell on these any longer is not a matter for our leisure.


Tantum observabo, Hebraeos usque adeo ignorasse, quod animal sit chamaeleon, ut avem esse voluerint. Testem habeo Kimchium, qui, in Lexico disquirens, quid sit לילית lilith, Es. XXXIV, 14. scribit, quosdam asserere, שהוא עוף גדל מן הרוח כמו סלמנדרא מן האש שקורין לו קמליאן Lilith avem esse, quae aëre vescitur (ut igne salamandra), quam chamaeleonem vocant. Quale est, quod in Tanchuma sectione וישב fol. 18. a. salamandra describitur araneae similis. Verba sic habent, Vitrarii, qui vitrum conficiunt, cum fornacem accende- runt septem diebus et 7 noctibus continuis, ex vi ignis היוצא משם בריה הדומה לעכבית והבריה קורין אותה סלמנדרא egreditur animal, simile araneae, quod animal vocatur salamandra. Sunt, qui pro לעכבית, araneae, legi volunt לעכבר, muri; quod nihilo est sanius, cum salamandra non sit muri similior, quam araneae. Hebraeis igitur animalium natura cum sit tam parum perspecta, illis temere credendum non est in harum vocum explicatione.

I shall only observe that the Hebrews were so ignorant of what kind of animal the chameleon is that they took it to be a bird. My witness is Kimchi, who, inquiring in his Lexicon what לילית lilith is, Isa 34:14, writes that some assert שהוא עוף גדל מן הרוח כמו סלמנדרא מן האש שקורין לו קמליאן that Lilith is a bird which feeds on air (as the salamander on fire), which they call the chameleon. Of the same kind is the description of the salamander in the Tanchuma, section וישב, fol. 18a, as similar to a spider. The words run thus: When glassmakers, who make glass, have kept the furnace burning for seven days and 7 nights without interruption, from the force of the fire היוצא משם בריה הדומה לעכבית והבריה קורין אותה סלמנדרא there comes forth an animal similar to a spider, which animal is called the salamander. Some would read לעכבר, to a mouse, instead of לעכבית, to a spider; but this is no sounder, since the salamander is no more like a mouse than like a spider. Since, then, the nature of animals was so little understood by the Hebrews, they are not to be trusted rashly in explaining these words.


II, 509 In Graeca versione de Ninive dicitur Soph. II, 4. χαμαιλέοντες, καὶ ἐχῖ-νοι ἐν τοῖς φατνώμασιν αὐτῆς κοιταθήσονται· Chamaeleontes et hericii in laquearibus ejus cubabunt. At in Hebraeo textu pro chamaeleonte est קאת, quod illi ipsi pelicanum reddunt Levit. XI, 18. et Ps. CI, (Hebr. CII,) 7. Quorsum igitur hic vox eadem pro chamaeleonte sumitur? Si cum Complutensibus λέοντες pro χαμαιλέοντες scribamus, malo non medebimur; quia Hebraeum קאת non magis leonem, quam chamaeleontem sonat. Graecos pro קאת legisse suspicor לטאה, lacertae genus, quod illis in Levitico καλαβώτης, stellio, hic χαμαιλέων fuerit, ut hae species non raro confunduntur: aut καλαβώτης, vel quod idem est, γαλεώτης, mutatum in χαμαιλέοντες (5), Huc facit, quod chamaeleon ἐν τοῖς φατνώμασιν, in laquearibus recubare nusquam legitur. Sed proprium id του καλαβώτου, vel γαλεώτου, stellionis. Hinc Dioscorides libri sexti capite primo sub dio parari jubet esculenta; aut, si parentur ἐν ὑποστέγῳ, in loco operto, ἐπιμελῶς καταμανθάνειν τὰς ὀροφὰς, πολλάκις γὰρ ἐκ τῶν ὑπερκειμέ-νων πίπτει ζωΰφια φθοροποιὰ, ὥσπερ φαλάγγια, καὶ ἄλλα τινὰ ἑρπετὰ, καὶ ὁ καλούμενος ἀσκαλαβώτης, tecti convexa, aut laquearia (si mavis) studiose considerare: saepe enim superne decidunt lethifera animalcula, ut araneae, et alia quaedam reptilia, et qui vocatur stellio. Et in Nubibus Aristophanis Actu primo de Socrate dicitur,

II, 509 In the Greek version it is said of Nineveh, Soph. II, 4.: χαμαιλέοντες, καὶ ἐχῖνοι ἐν τοῖς φατνώμασιν αὐτῆς κοιταθήσονται [chamaileontes, kai echinoi en tois phatnōmasin autēs koitathēsontai]; Chameleons and hedgehogs shall lie in its coffered ceilings. But in the Hebrew text, in place of the chameleon, there is קאת, which the same translators render pelican in Lev 11:18 and Ps. CI, (Hebr. CII,) 7. Why, then, is the same word taken here for the chameleon? If, with the Complutensian editors, we write λέοντες [leontes] for χαμαιλέοντες [chamaileontes], we shall not cure the fault, because the Hebrew קאת no more means lion than chameleon. I suspect that the Greeks read לטאה in place of קאת, a kind of lizard, which for them in Leviticus is καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs], stellio [gecko], and here would have been χαμαιλέων [chamaileōn], since these species are not infrequently confused; or else that καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs], or, what is the same, γαλεώτης [galeōtēs], was changed into χαμαιλέοντες [chamaileontes] R5. In support of this is the fact that the chameleon is nowhere said to lie ἐν τοῖς φατνώμασιν [en tois phatnōmasin], in coffered ceilings. But this is characteristic of the καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs], or γαλεώτης [galeōtēs], the stellio. Hence Dioscorides, book 6, chapter 1, directs that food be prepared in the open air; or, if it is prepared ἐν ὑποστέγῳ [en hypostegō], in a covered place, ἐπιμελῶς καταμανθάνειν τὰς ὀροφὰς, πολλάκις γὰρ ἐκ τῶν ὑπερκειμένων πίπτει ζωΰφια φθοροποιὰ, ὥσπερ φαλάγγια, καὶ ἄλλα τινὰ ἑρπετὰ, καὶ ὁ καλούμενος ἀσκαλαβώτης [epimelōs katamanthanein tas orophas, pollakis gar ek tōn hyperkeimenōn piptei zōyphia phthoropoia, hōsper phalangia, kai alla tina herpeta, kai ho kaloumenos askalabōtēs], to examine carefully the vault of the roof, or the coffered ceiling (if you prefer): for deadly little creatures often fall from above, such as spiders and certain other reptiles, and the one called the stellio. And in the Clouds of Aristophanes, Act 1, it is said of Socrates:


Ζητοῦντες αὐτοῦ τῆς σελήνης τὰς ὁδοὺς, col. 1083
Καὶ τὰς περιφορὰς, εἶτ᾽ ἄνω κεχηνότος,
Ἀπὸ τῆς ὀροφῆς νύκτωρ γαλεώτης κατέχεσεν·

Ζητοῦντες αὐτοῦ τῆς σελήνης τὰς ὁδοὺς, col. 1083 Καὶ τὰς περιφορὰς, εἶτ᾽ ἄνω κεχηνότος, Ἀπὸ τῆς ὀροφῆς νύκτωρ γαλεώτης κατέχεσεν· [Zētountes autou tēs selēnēs tas hodous, kai tas periphoras, eit᾽ anō kechēnotos, apo tēs orophēs nyktōr galeōtēs katechesen]


Eum, lunae vias et circuitus quaerentem, et sursum hiantem, e tecti laqueari noctu concacavit stellio. Sunt, quibus τὰ φατνώματα sunt praesepia. In quo errore perridiculo fuisse video Graeci textus interpretes. Quos tamen si sequaris, nihil egeris. Quia tam in praesepibus, quam in tectorum laquearibus versari solet stellio. Aristoteles Historiae libri noni capite primo, Κωλωτῇ δ᾽ ὄνος πολέμιος. Κοιμᾶται γὰρ ἐν τῇ φάτνῃ αὐτῆς, καὶ κωλύει ἐθίειν, εἰς τοὺς μυκτῆρας ἐνδυό-μενος· Stellioni asinus hostis est. In ejus enim praesepi dormit stellio, et in nares penetrans prohibet, ne comedat. Cum chamaeleon in desertis locis degat. Sed capite sequenti de stellione plura dicentur.

As he was investigating the paths and revolutions of the moon, and gaping upward, a stellio from the ceiling of the roof dropped its excrement on him at night. Some take τὰ φατνώματα [ta phatnōmata] to be mangers. I see that the translators of the Greek text were in this very ridiculous error. Yet even if you follow them, you will gain nothing, because the stellio is accustomed to frequent mangers as much as the coffered ceilings of roofs. Aristotle, History, book 9, chapter 1: Κωλωτῇ δ᾽ ὄνος πολέμιος. Κοιμᾶται γὰρ ἐν τῇ φάτνῃ αὐτῆς, καὶ κωλύει ἐθίειν, εἰς τοὺς μυκτῆρας ἐνδυόμενος· [Kōlōtē d᾽ onos polemios. Koimatai gar en tē phatnē autēs, kai kōlyei ethiein, eis tous myktēras endyomenos] The ass is an enemy to the stellio. For the stellio sleeps in its manger and, entering its nostrils, prevents it from eating. Whereas the chameleon lives in desert places. But more will be said about the stellio in the following chapter.

(3) Rosenmüller, II, 507 Errasse Bochartum in hae nominis حربا explicatione, convincere voluit I. E. FABER in Dissertatione de Animalibus, quorum mentio fit Zeph. II, 14. (adnexa est a C. F. CRAMERO libro, cui inscriptum: Scythische Denkmäler in Palaestina). Is, postquam recensuisset Bocharti de voce حربا sententiam, ita pergit (p. 305. libri laudati): „Sed oppido fallitur Bochartus. Dictus potius [chamaeleon] a חרב, cujus propria vis et potestas apud Hebraeos, Chaldaeos et Syros est in exsiccando, ut יבש, quapropter de aquis exsiccandis Ies. XIX, 5. LI, 10. dictum, et cum יבש, exsiccari conjunctum legitur. Nam sole gaudet chamaeleon, ejusque quasi calore exsiccatur“. Haec Faber, qui tam longe abest, ut correxerit Bochartum, ut ipse potius aperte falsa protulerit. Nomini حِرْباء enim, in sola usitato dialecto Arabica, notionem exsiccandi subjicit, a verbo Arabico حَرِبَ prorsus alienam. Deinde, quam parum commode chamaeleon, propterea quod loca aprica amat, nuncupatus putetur ab exsiccando, quisque sentiet ipse. Nec magis placet, quod idem Faber Hebraicum חרב Zephan. II, 14. chamaeleontis nomen esse statuit. Non reputavit ille linguae Hebraicae usum, qui vocem istam constanter adhibet mox ad vastitatem, mox ad siccitatem declarandam. Vastitatis vero notionem cur respuamus in Zephaniae loco, nulla apparet necessitas. Nos quemadmodum illum interpretandum censeamus, exposuimus supra ad Lib. III. cap. VIII. not. 7. pag. 115.

R3 Rosenmüller, II, 507 J. E. FABER sought to prove that Bochart erred in this explanation of the name حربا [ḥrbā] in his Dissertation de Animalibus, quorum mentio fit Zeph 2:14 (appended by C. F. CRAMER to the book entitled Scythische Denkmäler in Palaestina). After reviewing Bochart's opinion on the word حربا [ḥrbā], he continues thus (p. 305 of the book cited): "But Bochart is quite mistaken. For the name of the spear is rather far from the root, and was derived from it by another route. Rather, [the chameleon] is named from חרב, whose proper force and meaning among the Hebrews, Chaldeans and Syrians lies in drying up, like יבש; for this reason it is said of the drying up of waters, Isa 19:5. LI, 10., and is found joined with יבש, to be dried up. For the chameleon delights in the sun and is, as it were, dried up by its heat." So Faber [=J. E. Faber, notes to the German edition of Harmer's Observations (Beobachtungen über den Orient, 1772–79)], who is so far from having corrected Bochart that he has rather himself put forward plain falsehoods. For to the name حِرْباء [ḥirbāʾ], used only in the Arabic dialect, he attributes the notion of drying up, which is entirely foreign to the Arabic verb حَرِبَ [ḥariba]. Next, anyone will feel for himself how unsuitably the chameleon would be thought to be named from drying up because it loves sunny places. Nor is it any more satisfactory that the same Faber holds the Hebrew חרב in Zeph 2:14 to be the name of the chameleon. He did not consider the usage of the Hebrew language, which consistently employs this word now to denote desolation, now dryness. And there appears no need to reject the notion of desolation in the passage of Zephaniah. How we think that passage should be interpreted we have set out above at book 3, ch. 8, note 7, p. 115.
