R5 Rosenmüller, II, 509 In the Alexandrian version of the passage of Zephaniah, χαμαιλεοντες [chamaileontes] corresponds to the Hebrew קאת, while κορακα [koraka] corresponds to חרב. But Faber, to add strength and weight to his opinion that חרב means the chameleon, would have the order of those two words disturbed in the manuscripts of the Alexandrian version, so that in place of χαμαιλεοντες [chamaileontes] κορακες [korakes] should be restored, and in place of κορακες [korakes] χαμαιλεοντες [chamaileontes]. Since this has been devised in favour of a rather flimsy opinion and rests on no authority, we think it needs no refutation.


Book 4, chapter 7: The semamith
-------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/semamit.html

II, 510 col. 1083 CAP. VII.

II, 510 col. 1083 Chapter 7.


Probatur, שממית semamith Prov. XXX, 28. non esse Simiam, neque Araneam, sed Stellionem.

It is proved that שממית semamith in Prov 30:28 is neither the ape nor the spider, but the stellio.


E quatuor animalibus, quorum solertiam depraedicat Solomon XXX, 28. ul-timum est שממית semamith, quod manibus apprehendere scribit, et esse in Regum palatiis. De hoc animali magna lis inter doctores Hebraeos. Quibusdam explicantibus תולעת של מטר pluvialem vermem, aliis שרץ של כנפים, re- ptile alatum, aut שרץ מה מהעופים, reptile aliquod ex eorum numero, quae vo- lant. R. Ionas semamith Arabica voce خطاف chottaph, id est, hirundinem, exponit, quasi sit idem, quod סנונית senunith, quomodo hirundinem Chaldaei vocant, et Talmudici doctores. Quod est prorsus absurdum, cum hirundo non col. 1084 habeat manus, quibus contrectet et apprehendat, neque sit ex terrestribus animalculis, de quibus hic agit Solomon. Quatuor sunt, inquit, pusilla terrae. Itaque haec explicatio nihil habet sanum. Aben Ezra, Emmanuel et Kabuenaki, ut haec vitarent incommoda, שממית semamith maluerunt esse simiam, animal solertissimum, et in regum deliciis, et manibus instructum hominis instar. Sed meo judicio majus, quam ut censeri possit בקטני ארץ in pusillis animalculis, qualia sunt formica, choerogryllius et locusta. His enim exemplis Solomon antea usus est. Allusionem vocis semamith ad simiam quidam incassum urgent. Neque enim aliunde simiae nomen, quam a simis naribus. Ideo iidem enares a) olim dicti. Et Πιθηκοῦσσαι Graecorum Latinis Enariae insulae, ut in Solinum observat Cl. Salmasius. Multo aliter sentiunt R. Levi, Kimchius et Elias, nempe שממית semamith esse araneam, tam in regum turribus, quam in pauperum tabernis diversari solitam, atque inibi telam texere tanto pedum artificio, ut manuum vicem supplere queant. Ita etiam Arabs interpres manu-scriptus, qui hic habet العنكبوت araneam. Cui interpretationi summo consensu subscribunt Santes, Arias, Mercerus, Munsterus, Castalio, Iunius, Tremellius, Angli, Itali, Genevenses, et si qui alii sunt recentiores interpretes. At observare debuerant viri, Hebraicae linguae longe peritissimi, nullibi, nec in Scriptura, nec in veterum Hebraeorum scriptis araneam dici שממית semamith; sed ubique עכביש accabis, unde Chaldaicum עכובית accobith; et Arabicum عنكبوت ancabuths hodieque in usu. Praeterea fateor, pedes aranearum quandoque vocari digitos. Ut in Ranis Aristophanis Actu quinto, II, 511 Εἰλίσσετε δακτύλοις φάλαγγες ἰσότονα πηνίσματα,

Of the four animals whose cleverness Solomon extols in XXX, 28., the last is שממית semamith, which he writes takes hold with its hands, and is in kings' palaces. Over this animal there is a great dispute among the Hebrew doctors. Some explain it as תולעת של מטר, a rain-worm; others as שרץ של כנפים, a winged creeping thing, or שרץ מה מהעופים, some creeping thing of the number of those that fly. R. Jonah [=Jonah ibn Janāḥ, Sefer ha-Shorashim] explains semamith by the Arabic word خطاف [khaṭṭāf] chottaph, that is, the swallow, as though it were the same as סנונית senunith, as the Chaldeans and the Talmudic doctors call the swallow. This is utterly absurd, since the swallow does not col. 1084 have hands with which to handle and grasp, nor is it one of the small land creatures with which Solomon deals here: There are four, he says, little things of the earth. So this explanation has nothing sound in it. Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra], Emmanuel and Kabuenaki, to avoid these difficulties, preferred that שממית semamith be the ape, a most clever animal, a delight of kings, and furnished with hands like a man. But in my judgement it is too large to be counted בקטני ארץ among the little creatures, such as are the ant, the choerogryllius and the locust; for these are the examples Solomon used before. Some press in vain the resemblance of the word semamith to simia [ape]. For the name simia comes from nowhere else than from the simae [snub] noses. That is why the same animals were once called enares [noseless] a), and the Πιθηκοῦσσαι [Pithēkoussai] of the Greeks are the Enariae islands of the Latins, as the distinguished Salmasius [=Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), Plinianae exercitationes] observes on Solinus. Quite otherwise think R. Levi, Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] and Elias [=Elijah Levita (1469–1549), author of the Aramaic lexicon Meturgeman and of Tishbi]: namely, that שממית semamith is the spider, which is accustomed to dwell in the towers of kings as much as in the huts of the poor, and there to weave its web with such skill of its feet that they can take the place of hands. So too the manuscript Arabic translator, who has here العنكبوت [al-ʿankabūt], the spider. To this interpretation Santes, Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], Mercerus [=Jean Mercier (d. 1570), commentaries on Job and Proverbs], Munster, Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)], Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], Tremellius [=Immanuel Tremellius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], the English, Italian and Genevan versions, and any other more recent translators subscribe with complete agreement. But these men, by far the most skilled in the Hebrew language, ought to have observed that nowhere, neither in Scripture nor in the writings of the ancient Hebrews, is the spider called שממית semamith, but everywhere עכביש accabis, whence the Chaldee עכובית accobith and the Arabic عنكبوت [ʿankabūt] ancabuths, still in use today. Moreover, I admit that the feet of spiders are sometimes called fingers, as in the Frogs of Aristophanes, Act 5, II, 511 Εἰλίσσετε δακτύλοις φάλαγγες ἰσότονα πηνίσματα [Eilissete daktylois phalanges isotona pēnismata],


Digitis torquete, o araneae, licia, quibus textorium jugum intenditur. Et Ovi- dii Metamorphoseως libri sexti Fabula secunda,

Twist with your fingers, o spiders, the threads by which the weaver's beam is stretched. And in Ovid's Metamorphoses, book 6, fable 2,


In latere exiles digiti pro cruribus haerent.

Thin fingers cling to her sides in place of legs.


Et in Pisidae Hexaëmero versu 1152.

And in Pisides' Hexaemeron, line 1152:


Τίς τοὺς ἀράχνας λεπτοδακτύλους πλάσας,
Νήθειν διδάσκει, καὶ πρὸς ἔργα τοὺς μίτους
Ἐκ τῶν παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς ἐντέρων ἀναπτύειν;

Τίς τοὺς ἀράχνας λεπτοδακτύλους πλάσας, Νήθειν διδάσκει, καὶ πρὸς ἔργα τοὺς μίτους Ἐκ τῶν παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς ἐντέρων ἀναπτύειν; [Tis tous arachnas leptodaktylous plasas, Nēthein didaskei, kai pros erga tous mitous Ek tōn par' autois enterōn anaptyein?]


Quis araneas tenuibus digitis factas nere docet, et ad opera filos ex propriis visce- ribus exspuere? Sed qui manus illis tribuat, neminem reperire est. Quamvis enim araneae pedes digitos utcumque imitentur, tamen in iis nihil est, quod ad manus formam accedat. Quin apud Symposium Aenigmate decimo septimo aranea diserte negat, ullas sibi esse manus,

Who teaches the spiders, made with slender fingers, to spin, and to spit out threads for their works from their own entrails? But one cannot find anyone who attributes hands to them. For although the spider's feet imitate fingers after a fashion, there is nothing in them that approaches the form of hands. Indeed, in Symphosius, Riddle 17, the spider expressly denies that it has any hands:


Nulla mihi manus est, pedibus tamen omnia fiunt.

I have no hand, yet everything is done by my feet.


Dato tamen, non concesso, araneae pedes pro manibus posse haberi, quia manuum vice funguntur: tamen, eam manibus apprehendere, non dixisset Divinus Scriptor, sed nere, vel texere, vel stamina ducere: quia, quod pedibus contrectat et apprehendit, leve est, et illi commune cum multis animalibus; quod texit, peculiare et θαυματῶδες. Sed neque eam dixisset esse in regum palatiis; quia ad regalis aulae cultum non satis conveniunt aranearum sordes. Et diversantur potius in pauperis Euclionis aedibus, in quibus

But granting, without conceding, that the spider's feet can be taken for hands because they perform the office of hands, the Divine Writer would still not have said that it takes hold with its hands, but that it spins, or weaves, or draws out threads: for that it handles and grasps with its feet is a slight matter, and shared with many animals; that it weaves is peculiar and θαυματῶδες [thaumatōdes]. Nor would he have said that it is in kings' palaces, since the filth of spiders does not well suit the elegance of a royal court. They rather dwell in the house of poor Euclio, in which


— — — nihil est quaesti furibus,
Ita inaniis sunt oppletae, atque araneis.

— — — there is nothing for thieves to gain, so filled is it with emptiness and spiders.


Ut in Aulularia scribit Plautus. In omnium ore versatur Apologus de podagra et aranea, inter quas convenisse ajunt, ut illa in opulentiorum palatiis, haec in pauperum tuguriis diversaretur. Proinde cum aliquis araneas in aedibus, aut in arca, aut in vasis, aut in loculis habere dicitur, idem est, ac si dicatur, in te- nui re vivere. Hinc apud Festum Afranius,

As Plautus writes in the Aulularia. Everyone knows the fable of the gout and the spider, who, they say, agreed that the former should dwell in the palaces of the rich and the latter in the hovels of the poor. Accordingly, when someone is said to have spiders in his house, or in his chest, or in his vessels, or in his purse, it is the same as saying that he lives in slender circumstances. Hence Afranius in Festus:


Tamne arcula tua plena est aranearum?

Is your little chest so full of spiders?


Et Catullus, ut se excuset apud Fabullum, quod vocatum ad coenam minus laute excipiat:

And Catullus, excusing himself to Fabullus for entertaining him, invited to dinner, less sumptuously:


— — — —, tui Catulli
Plenus sacculus est aranearum. col. 1085

— — — —, your Catullus's purse is full of cobwebs. col. 1085


Hinc Hesiodus Operum versu 473.

Hence Hesiod, Works, line 473.


Ἐκ δ᾽ ἀγγέων ἐλάσειας ἀράχνια, II, 512 E vasis autem ejicies araneas, id est, inanitatem et inopiam. Proinde sic explicat Scholiastes, Εἰ καλῶς ἀροτριάσεις, καὶ σπείρεις, ἁδροὺς ἕξεις στάχους (lege στά-χυας). Ἐκ δὲ τῶν σιτοφόρων σου κιβωτίων τῶν μέχρι τότε κενῶν ἑστηκότων, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἀραχνιέντων, ἐξελάσειας τὰ ἀράχνια, καὶ ἐμπλήσεις δηλονότι ταῦτα τοῦ σίτου· Si bene araveris et seminaveris, densas habebis spicas: et ex frumentariis vasis tuis, quae eo usque vacua fuerant, ac proinde araneis plena, araneas ejicies, ut scilicet illa frumento impleas. Ideo Solomonem araneis domum assignasse in regum palatiis, parum est verissimile.

Ἐκ δ᾽ ἀγγέων ἐλάσειας ἀράχνια [Ek d᾽ angeōn elaseias arachnia], II, 512 But you will drive the spiders out of the vessels, that is, emptiness and want. Accordingly the Scholiast explains it thus: Εἰ καλῶς ἀροτριάσεις, καὶ σπείρεις, ἁδροὺς ἕξεις στάχους (lege στάχυας). Ἐκ δὲ τῶν σιτοφόρων σου κιβωτίων τῶν μέχρι τότε κενῶν ἑστηκότων, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἀραχνιέντων, ἐξελάσειας τὰ ἀράχνια, καὶ ἐμπλήσεις δηλονότι ταῦτα τοῦ σίτου [Ei kalōs arotriaseis, kai speireis, hadrous hexeis stachous (lege stachyas). Ek de tōn sitophorōn sou kibōtiōn tōn mechri tote kenōn hestēkotōn, kai dia touto arachnientōn, exelaseias ta arachnia, kai emplēseis dēlonoti tauta tou sitou]; If you plough and sow well, you will have thick ears of grain; and from your grain vessels, which until then had been empty and therefore full of spiders, you will drive out the spiders, namely so that you may fill them with grain. Therefore it is hardly likely that Solomon assigned spiders a home in the palaces of kings.


Quid igitur erit שממית semamith? Plane aliud animal, nempe stellio: quod tam multa probant, ut in alia interpretatione quaerenda docti frustra se fatigent, cum haec vera et certa sit, et loco maxime congrua. Hujus auctores habeo primum LXX Interpretes, quibus שממית semamith est καλαβώτης, stellio. Fallitur enim Mercerus post Complutenses, qui καλαβώτην ibi piscis genus esse affirmant. In piscium quidem genere est καλαβώτης, sed et in lacertorum. Utrumque est in Hesychio: Καλαβώτης· ἰχθῦς ποῖος, καὶ σαῦρος. Nimirum καλαβώτης idem, qui ἀσκαλαβώτης. Hinc Levit. XI, 30. Complutensis et Parisiensis editio, pro Hebraeo הלטאה, καλαβώτην habent, ubi reliquae ἀσκα-λαβώτην. Neque vero quisquam credat, Graecos ita insanivisse, ut ἐν ἐλαχί-στοις ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς piscem computaverint. 2. Graecis addo Hieronymum, apud quem שממית semamith hic est stellio. 3. Syrum quoque interpretem, cui ܐܡܩܬܐ amaktha, vel amkatha, id ipsum est, ut supra b) abunde probavimus in capite de אנקה anaka. 4. Ut et Chaldaeum אקמתא akmetha, mutato literarum ordine, ut in forma ex μόρφη.

What, then, will שממית semamith be? Plainly another animal, namely the stellio. This is proved by so many arguments that learned men weary themselves in vain seeking another interpretation, since this one is true and certain, and fits the passage best. As its authorities I have, first, the LXX translators, for whom שממית semamith is καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs], the stellio. For Mercerus, following the Complutensians, is mistaken in asserting that καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs] there is a kind of fish. Καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs] is indeed among the fishes, but also among the lizards. Both are in Hesychius: Καλαβώτης· ἰχθῦς ποῖος, καὶ σαῦρος [Kalabōtēs; ichthys poios, kai sauros]. Clearly καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs] is the same as ἀσκαλαβώτης [askalabōtēs]. Hence at Lev 11:30 the Complutensian and Parisian editions have καλαβώτην [kalabōtēn] for the Hebrew הלטאה, where the others have ἀσκαλαβώτην [askalabōtēn]. Nor should anyone believe that the Greeks were so mad as to count a fish among ἐν ἐλαχίστοις ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς [en elachistois epi tēs gēs]. 2. To the Greeks I add Jerome, in whom שממית semamith here is the stellio. 3. Also the Syriac translator, for whom ܐܡܩܬܐ [אמקתא] amaktha, or amkatha, is the very same thing, as we proved abundantly above b) in the chapter on אנקה anaka. 4. As also the Chaldee אקמתא akmetha, with the order of the letters changed, as in forma [form] from μόρφη [morphē].


Praeterea illa ipsa vox שממית semamith, pro lacertae genere, adeoque pro stellione, nobis etiam aliunde nota est. Quippe Lev. XI, 30. legitur [?] vel [?] semamitha, in Samaritano interprete, et in Chaldaeis duobus, Ionathane, et altero, cui ab urbe nomen. In illo, pro אנקה anaka: in his pro לטאה letaa, ubi in Graeca versione καλαβώτης, et stellio in Romana. Hebraeos denique veteres sic usurpavisse, palam est ex eo, quod legitur in Talmudico tractatu De Sabbatho cap. 8. pag. 77. b. אימת שממית על העקרב, Terror semamith super scorpionem. Quibus verbis innuunt, hoc animal scorpioni esse terrori. Unde apparet, semamith non esse araneam. Eam enim cum scorpione inimicitias exercere, aut illi terrori esse, nemo scripsit. At de scorpione sic Plinius libri vigesimi noni capite quarto, Scorpionibus contrarius maxime stellio traditur, ut visu quoque pavorem iis afferat, et torporem frigidi sudoris. Et Aelianus II, 513 Historiae libri sexti capite vigesimo secundo, Ἔχθιστα δὲ τῷ μὲν λέοντι πῦρ, καὶ ἀλεκτρυών· ὕαινα δὲ τῇ παρδάλει· σκορπίος δὲ ἀσκαλαβώτῃ, νάρ-κη γοῦν τὸν σκορπίον καταλαμβάνει προαχθέντος οἱ τοῦ ζώου τοῦ προειρημένου· Inimicissima sunt leoni quidem ignis, et gallus; et hyaena pantherae; et stellioni scorpius, quo admoto, torpore afficitur. Et Galenus libri primi De theriaca ad Pisonem capite nono, Ὁ οὖν ἀσκαλαβώτης, ὁραθεὶς ὑπὸ τῶν σκορπίων, πή-γνυσιν αὐτοὺς, καὶ οὕτως ἀναιρεῖ· Stellio, visus a scorpionibus, obstupefacit eos, atque ita interimit. Et Isidorus libri duodecimi capite quarto, Scorpionibus stellio adeo contrarius traditur, ut, viso eo, pavorem iis afferat et terrorem. Et Phile capite vigesimo nono ex Aeliano, perperam lecto et intellecto:

Moreover, that very word שממית semamith, for a kind of lizard, and indeed for the stellio, is known to us from elsewhere as well. For at Lev 11:30 one reads [?] or [?] semamitha in the Samaritan translator and in the two Chaldee ones, Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] and the other, named after the city: in the former for אנקה anaka, in the latter for לטאה letaa, where the Greek version has καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs] and the Roman stellio. Finally, that the ancient Hebrews used it in this way is evident from what is read in the Talmudic tractate On the Sabbath, ch. 8, p. 77b: אימת שממית על העקרב, The terror of the semamith is upon the scorpion. By these words they indicate that this animal is a terror to the scorpion. Hence it appears that the semamith is not the spider. For no one has written that it carries on enmity with the scorpion or is a terror to it. But concerning the scorpion Pliny, book 29, chapter 4, says thus: The stellio is reported to be especially hostile to scorpions, so that even by its sight it brings them fear and a torpor of cold sweat. And Aelian, History II, 513 book 6, chapter 22: Ἔχθιστα δὲ τῷ μὲν λέοντι πῦρ, καὶ ἀλεκτρυών· ὕαινα δὲ τῇ παρδάλει· σκορπίος δὲ ἀσκαλαβώτῃ, νάρκη γοῦν τὸν σκορπίον καταλαμβάνει προαχθέντος οἱ τοῦ ζώου τοῦ προειρημένου [Echthista de tō men leonti pyr, kai alektryōn; hyaina de tē pardalei; skorpios de askalabōtē, narkē goun ton skorpion katalambanei proachthentos hoi tou zōou tou proeirēmenou]; Most hostile to the lion are fire and the cock; the hyena to the panther; and the scorpion to the stellio, at whose approach it is seized with torpor. And Galen, On Theriac, to Piso, book 1, chapter 9: Ὁ οὖν ἀσκαλαβώτης, ὁραθεὶς ὑπὸ τῶν σκορπίων, πήγνυσιν αὐτοὺς, καὶ οὕτως ἀναιρεῖ [Ho oun askalabōtēs, horatheis hypo tōn skorpiōn, pēgnysin autous, kai houtōs anairei]; The stellio, when seen by scorpions, stupefies them and so kills them. And Isidore, book 12, chapter 4: The stellio is reported to be so hostile to scorpions that, when it is seen, it brings them fear and terror. And Phile, chapter 29, from Aelian, wrongly read and understood:


— — — ἡ δ᾽ ὕαινα πάρδαλιν,
Καὶ ἀσκαλαβώτην ὁ φθορεὺς κλὼψ σκορπίος,
Νάρκη δὲ τοῦτον· — — — — —

— — — ἡ δ᾽ ὕαινα πάρδαλιν, Καὶ ἀσκαλαβώτην ὁ φθορεὺς κλὼψ σκορπίος, Νάρκη δὲ τοῦτον· — — — — — [hē d᾽ hyaina pardalin, Kai askalabōtēn ho phthoreus klōps skorpios, Narkē de touton]


Et hyaena pantheram (supple δυσμενῆ κρινεῖ, infensam putat, quod e superiori- col. 1086 bus repetendum) et stellionem perditor fur scorpius, torpedo autem illum. Cum in Aeliani verbis, νάρκη γοῦν τὸν σκορπίον καταλαμβάνει, vox νάρκη non sit torpedo piscis, sed torpor, qui scorpionem invadit, stellione viso. Si cum nonnullis corrigas ναρκοῖ δὲ τοῦτον, eum autem (stellionem) obstupefacit (scorpius), Phile rem falsissimam dixerit, nempe stellionem a scorpione obstupefieri, cum contra scorpionem obstupefaciat stellio. Quin Democritus, Plinius, Galenus, Aëtius, Diophanes, alii stellionem dissectum, et in oleo mersum, et putrefactum praescribunt, ut remedium efficax contra scorpionum ictus. Neque in eo leve momentum est, quod hodieque vulgari Graecorum lingua stellio appellatur σαμιαμίνθη, palam detorto nomine ex Hebraeo שממית semamith. Glossae, Ἀσκαλαβώτης· τὸ σαμιαμίνθη. A Gesnero scribitur θαμιάμιθος, et ψαμα-μύθη· a Bellonio SAMIAMITOS, qui pro Chalcidica lacerta perperam sumit. Vide Salmasium in Solinum pag. 1161.

And the hyena the panther (supply δυσμενῆ κρινεῖ [dysmenē krinei], considers hostile, which is to be repeated from the preceding col. 1086) and the thieving destroyer scorpion the stellio, but numbness seizes it. For in Aelian's words, νάρκη γοῦν τὸν σκορπίον καταλαμβάνει [narkē goun ton skorpion katalambanei], the word νάρκη [narkē] is not the torpedo [electric ray] fish, but the torpor [numbness] which seizes the scorpion when it sees the stellio. If, with some, you correct it to ναρκοῖ δὲ τοῦτον [narkoi de touton], but it (the scorpion) numbs it (the stellio), Phile would have said something utterly false, namely that the stellio is numbed by the scorpion, whereas on the contrary the stellio numbs the scorpion. Indeed Democritus, Pliny, Galen, Aëtius, Diophanes and others prescribe a stellio cut open, steeped in oil and left to putrefy, as an effective remedy against the stings of scorpions. Nor is it of slight weight that even today in the vulgar tongue of the Greeks the stellio is called σαμιαμίνθη [samiaminthē], a name plainly distorted from the Hebrew שממית semamith. The Glossae: Ἀσκαλαβώτης· τὸ σαμιαμίνθη [Askalabōtēs; to samiaminthē]. By Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium] it is written θαμιάμιθος [thamiamithos] and ψαμαμύθη [psamamythē]; by Bellonius SAMIAMITOS, who wrongly takes it for the Chalcidian lizard. See Salmasius on Solinus, p. 1161.


Sunt, qui שׁממית schemamith per Schin scribunt, ac si fiat a שמם schamam, id est, obstupefacere. Quod ipsum recte convenit naturae stellionis, qui scorpionem solo visu obstupefacit, ut docuimus. Sed in Kimchio et Bibliorum purissimis exemplaribus שׂממית semamith scribitur per Sin Semol; ut סממית per Samech in Talmudicis, et in paraphrasi Samaritana. Ita, ut deducatur a סמם, non a שמם, id est, a veneno, non a stupore. Ut igitur vera ratio nominis intelligatur, sciendum est, duas tradi stellionum species; unam innocui morsus, alteram venenati. Quamvis, quibus nascantur locis, non conveniat inter scriptores. Venenatos Philosophus c) Italiae et Siciliae adscribit, innoxios Graeciae. II, 514 Contra Theophrastus apud Plinium libri octavi capite trigesimo primo auctor est, stelliones, mortiferi in Graecia morsus, innoxios esse in Sicilia. Etiam in Thracia stellio perniciosi morsus est, ut habetur in Nicandro. Et Compluti Bustamantinus stelliones tam perniciosos esse asserit, ut, casu cibis permisti, integros populos vastaverint. Hinc in stellionis morsum tot remedia praescribunt Aëtius, Paulus et Avicenna. Et Columella libri decimi capite septimo alvearium foramina vult esse angustissima, ne venenatus stellio per laxiora spatia januae favos populetur. Venenati epithetum addidit διακριτικῶς, quia alius est innoxius. Venenato stellionis nomen magis convenit, si vere asserit Verrius apud Varronem et Festum, stellionem ideo dici, quod virus stillet. Eidem nomen סממית semamith impositum; quia סם sam Hebraeis et Syris est φάρμακον, seu venenum; et Arabice سم samma verbum veneno inficere. Ergo proprie סממית semamith est σαῦρα φαρμακὶς, vel φαρμακῖτις. Quod ipsum nomen a Graecis usurpari video sensu parum diverso. Nicander in Alexipharmacis versu 537.

There are some who write שׁממית schemamith with Shin, as if it came from שמם schamam, that is, to stupefy. This itself fits well the nature of the stellio, which stupefies the scorpion by its mere sight, as we have shown. But in Kimchi and in the purest copies of the Bible it is written שׂממית semamith with Sin Semol, just as סממית with Samech in the Talmudic writings and in the Samaritan paraphrase. Thus it is to be derived from סמם, not from שמם, that is, from poison, not from stupor. So, to understand the true reason for the name, one must know that two species of stellio are reported: one with a harmless bite, the other with a venomous one. The writers, however, do not agree in which places they are born. The Philosopher c) assigns the venomous ones to Italy and Sicily, the harmless ones to Greece. II, 514 On the other hand Theophrastus, in Pliny, book 8, chapter 31, states that stellios, deadly in their bite in Greece, are harmless in Sicily. In Thrace too the stellio has a pernicious bite, as is found in Nicander. And Bustamantinus of Complutum asserts that stellios are so pernicious that, mixed by chance with food, they have laid waste entire populations. Hence Aëtius, Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)] and Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] prescribe so many remedies against the bite of the stellio. And Columella, book 10, chapter 7, wants the openings of beehives to be very narrow, lest the venomous stellio ravage the combs through the wider spaces of the entrance. He added the epithet venomous διακριτικῶς [diakritikōs], because another kind is harmless. The name stellio suits the venomous one better, if Verrius, in Varro and Festus, truly asserts that the stellio is so called because it drips venom. To the same was given the name סממית semamith, because סם sam among the Hebrews and Syrians is φάρμακον [pharmakon], or poison; and in Arabic سم [samm] samma is the verb to infect with poison. Therefore סממית semamith is properly σαῦρα φαρμακὶς [saura pharmakis], or φαρμακῖτις [pharmakitis]. I see that this very name is used by the Greeks in a sense little different. Nicander in the Alexipharmaca, line 537:


Φαρμακίδος σαύρης πολυμήδεος, ἣν σαλαμάνδρην
Κλείουσιν. — — — — — — —

Φαρμακίδος σαύρης πολυμήδεος, ἣν σαλαμάνδρην Κλείουσιν. — — — — — — — [Pharmakidos saurēs polymēdeos, hēn salamandrēn Kleiousin.]


Vides, ibi σαῦραν φαρμακίδα salamandram esse, lacertae genus, stellioni tam simile, ut pro stellionis specie a nonnullis habeatur. Proinde ibi Scholiastes, Ἡ σαλαμάνδρα· εἶδος ἀσκαλαβώτου. Tamen in Aëtii Tetrab. 4. Serm. 4. cap. 52. salamandra, stellio et lacerta venenata Graecis σαῦρα φαρμακῖτις, diversa sunt animalcula, sed inter se simillima. Salamandra, inquit, animal est, stellioni simile, asperius, et scabrum magis lacerta venenata. Forte stellionis nomine solum innoxium, et nomine lacertae pharmacitidis, seu venenatae, a salamandra diversae, stellionem, morsu noxium, intelligit. Sic lacerta pharmacitis erit eadem, quae סממית semamith.

You see that there the σαῦρα φαρμακίς [saura pharmakis] is the salamander, a kind of lizard so similar to the stellio that some take it for a species of stellio. Accordingly the Scholiast there: Ἡ σαλαμάνδρα· εἶδος ἀσκαλαβώτου [Hē salamandra; eidos askalabōtou]. Yet in Aëtius, Tetrab. 4, Serm. 4, ch. 52, the salamander, the stellio and the venomous lizard, in Greek σαῦρα φαρμακῖτις [saura pharmakitis], are different little animals, but very similar to one another. The salamander, he says, is an animal similar to the stellio, rougher, and more scaly than the venomous lizard. Perhaps by the name stellio he means only the harmless one, and by the name pharmacitis lizard, or venomous lizard, distinct from the salamander, the stellio with a harmful bite. Thus the pharmacitis lizard will be the same as the סממית semamith.


Eodem facit, quod Arabes duas memorant stellionis venenati species, quae differunt sola magnitudine. Major vocatur سام ابرص sammabras, et minor col. 1087 وزغة vvezga. Et nominis sammabras, compositi ex سام et ابرص pars prior ex semamith decurtata est, et venenatum sonat; posterior leprosum, vel le-prae maculis infectum. Ergo, ad verbum, sammabras est semamith leprosa, vel lacertae species, veneno et leprae maculis insignis. Nempe in stellione haec duo notanda sunt: primo, quod venenatus est, de quo jam actum; secundo, quod leprosus est, id est, maculis distinctus tanquam leprae. Quorum utrumque continet Arabicum SAMMABRAS, Hebraicum SEMAMITH solum prius. Damir, وانما سمي هذا النوع سام ابرص لانه سم اي جعل الله فيه السم وجعله ابرص Utique haec lacerti species nomen habet sammabras, II, 515 quia venenatus est, id est, venenum in eo posuit Deus, et (insuper) fecit cum leprosum (1). Stellionis maculas Romani honestiori nomine stellas vocarunt, unde stellionem ipsum animal. Ovidius Metamorphoseωs libri quinti Fabula 7.

The same point is supported by the fact that the Arabs record two species of venomous stellio, which differ only in size. The larger is called سام ابرص [sām abraṣ] sammabras, and the smaller col. 1087 وزغة [wazagha] vvezga. In the name sammabras, compounded of سام [sām] and ابرص [abraṣ], the first part is shortened from semamith and means venomous; the second means leprous, or marked with spots of leprosy. So, literally, sammabras is leprous semamith, or a species of lizard notable for venom and for spots of leprosy. For two things are to be noted in the stellio: first, that it is venomous, which has already been treated; second, that it is leprous, that is, marked with spots as if of leprosy. The Arabic SAMMABRAS contains both of these, the Hebrew SEMAMITH only the first. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: وانما سمي هذا النوع سام ابرص لانه سم اي جعل الله فيه السم وجعله ابرص [wa-innamā summiya hādhā al-nawʿ sām abraṣ li-annahu summa ay jaʿala Allāh fīhi al-summ wa-jaʿalahu abraṣ] This species of lizard indeed has the name sammabras, II, 515 because it is venomous, that is, God put venom in it, and (moreover) made it leprous R1. The Romans called the stellio's spots by a more honourable name, stellae [stars], whence the animal itself is called stellio. Ovid, Metamorphoses, book 5, fable 7:


— — — — aptumque colori
Nomen habet variis stellatus corpora guttis.

— — — — and it has a name suited to its colour,
its body starred with varied drops.


Salonius in Proverbia: Quod genus animalis est stellio? Genus lacertae valde pi- grum et colore varium. ' Unde nomen accepit stellio, quia quasi stellis, id est, gut- tis, distinctus et variatus est. In quibus Poetam ita sequitur, ut stellas pro stil- lis, seu guttis accepisse videatur. Ut contrario errore מרים Marjam, Syrum Mariae nomen, maris stellam multi exponunt pro maris stilla. Sed et lentigines vocat Plinius, cum de Graeco stellione scribit libri vigesimi noni capite quarto; Est hic plenus lentigine. Hinc eunuchus lentiginosus a Menandro γαλεώτης, id est, stellio nuncupatus, propter faciei maculas. Quod Terentius in Eunucho d) perperam reddidit, colore mustelino, quasi γαλεώτης ἀπὸ τῆς γαλῆς, id est, a mustela dictus fuisset, ut Donatus ibi observat.

Salonius on Proverbs: What kind of animal is the stellio? A kind of lizard, very sluggish and of varied colour. ' Hence it got the name stellio, because it is marked and variegated as if with stellae, that is, drops. Here he follows the Poet in such a way that he seems to have taken stellae [stars] for stillae [drops], or guttae [drops]. By the opposite error many explain מרים Marjam, the Syrian name of Mary, as maris stella [star of the sea] instead of maris stilla [drop of the sea]. Pliny also calls them lentigines [freckles], when he writes of the Greek stellio in book 29, chapter 4: This one is full of freckles. Hence a freckled eunuch is called by Menander γαλεώτης [galeōtēs], that is, stellio, because of the spots on his face. Terence in the Eunuch d) wrongly rendered this colore mustelino [of weasel colour], as if γαλεώτης [galeōtēs] were named ἀπὸ τῆς γαλῆς [apo tēs galēs], that is, from the weasel, as Donatus observes there.


II, 516 In Alkazuinio sammabras definitur الوزغ الصغير الراس الطويل الذنب alvvezgo (seu stellio) parvi capitis et longae caudae. In Damire et Al-camus, animal من كبار الوزغ e magnis guezgis, seu stellionibus, Fabulantur Arabes, lepram illi fuisse immissam in poenam admissi criminis, quia scilicet flatu suo accendit ignem, in quem conjectus est Abraham. Lepram generari addunt esu salis, in quo volutatus est, aut mucilaginem emisit. Proinde hoc animal Arabibus est maxime odiosum (2). Et dicit Iahius, Iameri filius, chariorem sibi esse eum, qui occidit centum stelliones, quam qui redemit ماية رقبة centum colla, id est, centum servos. In quam rem multa citantur a Mahomete dicta. Nec minus odiosus fuit veteribus Graecis stellio. Antonius Liberalis ubi supra de stellione, Ὑπὸ Θεῶν καὶ ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπων μεμίσηται· ὁ δ' ἀποκτείνας κεχαρισμένος γίνεται Δημῆτρι. Diis et hominibus est odiosus: et Cereri rem gratam praestat, qui eum interficit. Tamen ad multa est utilis, quae non sunt hujus loci. Sed non possum non observare, quod in capite De sammabras habet Alkazuinius, لحمه يوضع علي لسع العقرب ينفع نفعا بينا Caro ejus, cum ponitur super puncturam scorpio- col. 1088 nis, habet usum manifestum. Ita etiam Damir. Ut constet, idem esse animal cum stellione, de quo supra: quamvis Avicenna quandoque usurpet pro vulgari lacerto.

II, 516 In Alkazuini, sammabras is defined as الوزغ الصغير الراس الطويل الذنب [al-wazagh al-ṣaghīr al-raʾs al-ṭawīl al-dhanab] alvvezgo (or stellio) with a small head and a long tail. In Damir and Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī], an animal من كبار الوزغ [min kibār al-wazagh] of the large guezgi, or stellios. The Arabs tell the fable that leprosy was inflicted on it as punishment for a crime it committed, namely because with its breath it kindled the fire into which Abraham was thrown. They add that leprosy is produced by eating salt in which it has rolled, or on which it has discharged slime. Hence this animal is most hateful to the Arabs R2. And Iahius, son of Iamer, says that he holds dearer one who has killed a hundred stellios than one who has redeemed ماية رقبة [māya raqaba] a hundred necks, that is, a hundred slaves. Many sayings of Muhammad are cited on this matter. Nor was the stellio less hateful to the ancient Greeks. Antoninus Liberalis, in the passage cited above on the stellio: Ὑπὸ Θεῶν καὶ ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπων μεμίσηται· ὁ δ' ἀποκτείνας κεχαρισμένος γίνεται Δημῆτρι [Hypo Theōn kai hypo anthrōpōn memisētai; ho d' apokteinas kecharismenos ginetai Dēmētri]. It is hateful to gods and men; and he who kills it does a thing pleasing to Ceres. Yet it is useful for many things, which do not belong here. But I cannot fail to note what Alkazuini has in the chapter On sammabras: لحمه يوضع علي لسع العقرب ينفع نفعا بينا [laḥmuhu yūḍaʿ ʿalī lasʿ al-ʿaqrab yanfaʿ nafʿan bayyinan] Its flesh, when placed on a scorpion's col. 1088 sting, is of evident benefit. So also Damir. It is thus established that it is the same animal as the stellio discussed above, although Avicenna sometimes uses the word for the common lizard.


Iam, si ea excutiantur, quae de semamith habet Solomon, omnia reperientur quadrare in stellionem. Quatuor sunt, inquit, pusilla terrae (Graeci ἐλά-χιστα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς) sapientia tamen, tanquam sapientiam edocta. In his merito censetur stellio, pusillum animal, et valde solers (3). De brevitate staturae sic Ovidius:

Now, if what Solomon says of the semamith is examined, everything will be found to fit the stellio. There are four things, he says, little upon the earth (the Greeks ἐλάχιστα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς [elachista epi tēs gēs]), yet wise, as if taught wisdom. Among these the stellio is rightly counted, a small animal and very clever R3. On its small stature Ovid writes thus:


Inque brevem formam, ne sit vis magna nocendi,
Contrahitur, parvaque minor mensura lacerta est.

And it is contracted into a small form, lest it have great power to harm, and its size is less than a small lizard.


Claudianus, vel quisquis est in Cereris aerumnis:

Claudian, or whoever is the author of the Sorrows of Ceres:


Apparent maculae, forma est brevis, illita cauda
Surgit, et exiguae similat vaga membra lacertae.

Spots appear, its form is small, a tail smeared on rises, and it imitates the wandering limbs of a tiny lizard.


Porphyrius apud Eusebium libro quinto Praeparationis, II, 517 Ζώοισιν λεπτοίσι κατοικιδίοις σκαλαβώταις, Parvis animalculis, domesticis stellionibus.

Porphyry in Eusebius, book 5 of the Praeparatio, II, 517 Ζώοισιν λεπτοίσι κατοικιδίοις σκαλαβώταις [Zōoisin leptoisi katoikidiois skalabōtais], To small little animals, domestic stellios.


Solertiae stellionis multa sunt argumenta. Hesychius in Κωλώτης, stellionem ait, εὐστόχως ἅλλεσθαι περὶ τὰς μυίας, industrie salire circa muscas; nempe, ut eas captet. Phavorinus inepte, περὶ τοὺς μῦς, circa mures: quibus cum stellione nihil est negotii. Sed de muscis etiam Augustinus libri decimi Confessionum capite trigesimo quinto: Quid, cum me domi sedentem stellio, muscas captans, vel aranea, retibus suis irruentes implicans, saepe intentum facit? Aliud affert Theophrastus in libro De anim. invid. sed minus certum: Ὅτι ὁ γαλεώτης, φθονῶν τῆς ὠφελείας τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, καταπίνει τὸ δέρμα, ὅταν ἐκδύηται· ἔστι γὰρ βοήθημα ἐπιλήπτῳ· Stellionem, hominum utilitati invidentem, proprium vorare corium, quamprimum eo exuitur. Iuvat enim illud comitiali morbo laborantes. Idem habent Antigonus Mirabilium capite vigesimo quarto, et Apulejus Apologia pro se prima. Et inde concludit Plinius libri trigesimi capite decimo, nullum animal fraudulentius invidere homini. Indidem stellionum et stellionatus nomen in maledictum translatum. Sunt et qui Galeotas, in Sicilia portentorum interpretes solertissimos, ab hujus animalis industria nomen traxisse putent. Quo haec Stephani referunt: Γαλεῶται μάντεων εἶδος Σικελῶν· Γα-λεὸς δὲ, ὁ ἀσκαλαβώτης (ubi pro γαλεὸς legendum γαλεώτης). Sed quia Hebraice גלה gala est revelare, quod vatum maxime proprium, Galeotarum nomen Hebraicum esse suspicor, ut et alia magno numero, quae, cum Phoenicum coloniis, in Siciliam translata fuisse, alibi probavimus.

There are many proofs of the stellio's skill. Hesychius, under Κωλώτης [Kōlōtēs], says that the stellio εὐστόχως ἅλλεσθαι περὶ τὰς μυίας [eustochōs hallesthai peri tas myias], leaps skilfully about flies; that is, in order to catch them. Phavorinus ineptly has περὶ τοὺς μῦς [peri tous mys], about mice: with which the stellio has nothing to do. But Augustine also speaks of flies in book 10 of the Confessions, chapter 35: What of it, when, as I sit at home, a stellio catching flies, or a spider entangling them as they rush into its webs, often holds my attention? Theophrastus, in the book De anim. invid., adduces another proof, but a less certain one: Ὅτι ὁ γαλεώτης, φθονῶν τῆς ὠφελείας τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, καταπίνει τὸ δέρμα, ὅταν ἐκδύηται· ἔστι γὰρ βοήθημα ἐπιλήπτῳ· [Hoti ho galeōtēs, phthonōn tēs ōpheleias tois anthrōpois, katapinei to derma, hotan ekdyētai; esti gar boēthēma epilēptō;] The stellio, begrudging men the benefit, devours its own skin as soon as it has shed it. For it helps those suffering from epilepsy. Antigonus has the same in the Mirabilia, chapter 24, and Apuleius in his first Apology for himself. And from this Pliny, book 30, chapter 10, concludes that no animal more deceitfully begrudges man. From the same source the names stelliones [swindlers] and stellionatus [fraud] were transferred into terms of abuse. There are also those who think that the Galeotae, the most skilful interpreters of portents in Sicily, took their name from the cleverness of this animal. To this Stephanus refers these words: Γαλεῶται μάντεων εἶδος Σικελῶν· Γαλεὸς δὲ, ὁ ἀσκαλαβώτης [Galeōtai manteōn eidos Sikelōn; Galeos de, ho askalabōtēs] (where for γαλεὸς [galeos] one should read γαλεώτης [galeōtēs]). But since in Hebrew גלה gala means to reveal, which is most characteristic of seers, I suspect that the name of the Galeotae is Hebrew, like a great many others which, as I have proved elsewhere, were carried over into Sicily with the colonies of the Phoenicians.


At ipse Solomon stellionis industriam abunde probat his verbis: Manibus apprehendit, et est in palatiis regum. Cur illi manus tribuat, nemini est obscurum. Ut lacertus a lacertis, id est, brachiis, nominatur: ita stellio Graece κωλώτης a τοῖς κώλοις. Κῶλα sunt manus et pedes. Manus appello pedes anteriores cum Avicenna e), qui غظاية adhajam, id est, salamandram (ex Avicennae mente) non aliter in melle servari scribit, quam si evisceretur et resecentur يداها ورجلاها illius manus et pedes: pro eo, quod Dioscorides, φυ-λάσσεται ἐν μέλιτι ἐξεντεριθεῖσα, τῶν ποδῶν ἀφαιρεθέντων. Si salamandra habet manus, quidni etiam stellio, animal, salamandrae simillimum? Ita Damir capite حردون Chardaun, seu De terrestri crocodilo, له كف ككف الانسان مقسومة الاصابع الا انامل Illi manus est instar manus hominis, cum digitis, in articulos divisis. Sed et lacerti cujusvis pedes, praesertim II, 518 anteriores, recte manus appellaveris, cum sint instar manuum. Gesnerus, ex propria inspectione: Lacertus a similitudine lacertorum hominis, quod pedes col. 1089 eorum similiter in digitos, tanquam e volis, aut palmis, findantur. Idem, Digiti perexiles ante et retro quini cum unguiculis. In posterioribus longissimus, qui indicis situm obtinet; pollex inferiore loco, ut in manibus hominis: anteriores vero pollicem cum caeteris eodem situ habent. Vides, anteriores pedes, seu lacertos verius, ad humani brachii et manus formam esse, pares numero digitos, et in eodem situ. Talibus lacertis manuum appellatio quanto convenit magis, quam phalangis aranearum?

But Solomon himself amply proves the stellio's skill with these words: It takes hold with its hands, and is in kings' palaces. Why he attributes hands to it is obscure to no one. Just as lacertus [lizard] is named from lacerti, that is, arms, so the stellio is called in Greek κωλώτης [kōlōtēs] from τοῖς κώλοις [tois kōlois]. Κῶλα [Kōla] are hands and feet. I call the forefeet hands together with Avicenna e), who writes that غظاية [ghaẓāya] adhajam, that is, the salamander (in Avicenna's view), is preserved in honey only if it is gutted and يداها ورجلاها [yadāhā wa-rijlāhā] its hands and feet are cut off: where Dioscorides has φυλάσσεται ἐν μέλιτι ἐξεντεριθεῖσα, τῶν ποδῶν ἀφαιρεθέντων [phylassetai en meliti exenteritheisa, tōn podōn aphairethentōn]. If the salamander has hands, why not also the stellio, an animal very like the salamander? Thus Damir, in the chapter حردون [ḥardūn] Chardaun, or On the land crocodile: له كف ككف الانسان مقسومة الاصابع الا انامل [lahu kaff ka-kaff al-insān maqsūmat al-aṣābiʿ illā anāmil] It has a hand like the hand of a man, with fingers divided into joints. Indeed, you may rightly call the feet of any lizard, especially II, 518 the forefeet, hands, since they are like hands. Gesner, from his own observation: The lacertus is named from its likeness to the lacerti [arms] of a man, because their feet col. 1089 are likewise split into fingers, as if from hollow hands or palms. The same: Very slender fingers, five in front and five behind, with little claws. On the hind feet the longest is the one that occupies the place of the index finger; the thumb is in a lower position, as in the hands of man: but the front feet have the thumb in the same position as the other fingers. You see that the forefeet, or more truly the arms, are in the shape of a human arm and hand, with the same number of fingers, and in the same position. How much better does the name hands suit such arms than the legs of spiders?


Iam, quod stellio manibus dicitur apprehendere, vel ad incessum refero, vel ad venatum. Cum enim supinus incedit e laqueari pendulus, eum vel in rimulis necesse est unguiculos defigere, vel amplecti manibus, quidquid eminet, aut scabrum est. Supinum autem incedere, disertis verbis asserit Philosophus Historiae libri noni capite nono, ubi de pico sic agit: Πορεύεται ὕπτιος καθάπερ οἱ ἀσκαλαβῶται· Ingreditur supinus ut stelliones. Et in Mirabilibus, Τὸν δρυο-κολάπτην τὸ ὄρνεον ἐπὶ τῶν δένδρων βαδίζειν φασὶν ὥσπερ τοὺς ἀσκαλαβώτας, καὶ ὕπτιον, καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν γαστέρα· Picum in arboribus incedere ajunt, ut stelliones, tam supinum, quam pronum. Mirum cur ἀσκαλαβώτας feles reddat Plinius, et ὕπτιον in subrectum pro supino, cum dicit libri decimi capite decimo octavo, arborum cavatores (id est, δρυοκολάπτας picos) scandere in subrectum felium modo. Maxime, cum idem libri vigesimi noni capite quarto agnoscat, stellionem Graece vocari coloten, ascalaboten et galeoten: ne quis Graeca stellionis vocabula Plinium ignorasse putet. Tale est, quod legitur in Plutarchi libro De facie in orbe Lunae, esse valde paradoxum, quod Geographi docent, ἀντίποδας οἰκεῖν, ὥσπερ θρίπας, ἢ γαλεώτας, τραπέντα ἄνω τὰ κάτω, τῇ γῇ προϊσχομένους, terram inhabitare antipodes, qui, instar teredinum, aut stellionum, imis corporum partibus sursum obversis, terrae adhaereant, Ubi itidem primi interpretes pro stellionibus feles scripserant.

Now, the statement that the stellio takes hold with its hands I refer either to its walking or to its hunting. For when it walks upside down, hanging from a ceiling, it must either fix its little claws in small cracks or clasp with its hands whatever projects or is rough. That it walks upside down is asserted in express words by the Philosopher in the History, book 9, chapter 9, where he speaks of the woodpecker thus: Πορεύεται ὕπτιος καθάπερ οἱ ἀσκαλαβῶται [poreuetai hyptios kathaper hoi askalabōtai]; It walks upside down like stellios. And in the Marvels: Τὸν δρυοκολάπτην τὸ ὄρνεον ἐπὶ τῶν δένδρων βαδίζειν φασὶν ὥσπερ τοὺς ἀσκαλαβώτας, καὶ ὕπτιον, καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν γαστέρα [ton dryokolaptēn to orneon epi tōn dendrōn badizein phasin hōsper tous askalabōtas, kai hyption, kai epi tēn gastera]; They say that the woodpecker walks on trees like stellios, upside down as well as face down. It is strange why Pliny renders ἀσκαλαβώτας [askalabōtas] as feles [cats], and ὕπτιον [hyption] as in subrectum [upright] instead of supinum [upside down], when he says in book 10, chapter 18, that the hollowers of trees (that is, δρυοκολάπτας [dryokolaptas], woodpeckers) climb upright in the manner of cats. All the more so since the same author, in book 29, chapter 4, acknowledges that the stellio is called in Greek colotes, ascalabotes and galeotes, so that no one should think Pliny was ignorant of the Greek names of the stellio. Similar is what we read in Plutarch's book On the Face in the Orb of the Moon: that what the geographers teach is highly paradoxical, ἀντίποδας οἰκεῖν, ὥσπερ θρίπας, ἢ γαλεώτας, τραπέντα ἄνω τὰ κάτω, τῇ γῇ προϊσχομένους [antipodas oikein, hōsper thripas, ē galeōtas, trapenta anō ta katō, tē gē proischomenous], that antipodes inhabit the earth, who, like woodworms or stellios, with the lower parts of their bodies turned upward, cling to the earth. Here likewise the first translators had written feles [cats] instead of stelliones.


Manibus etiam ad venationem stellionem uti diximus, cum muscas captat, aut araneas. Bustamantinus: Arripit manibus secura pollicentibus. Pedes imo fallaces, qui motui inservire tenebantur, vice manuum succedunt, rapinam exercent, et manus sunt illi pedes, quibus innititur in motu, et pedes manus, quibus arripit praedam. Merito igitur Solomon, Manibus apprehendit stellio, seu gradiatur supinus, aut in praedam se conjiciat. Utrumque mirabile et notatu dignissimum in tenui animalculo. Graeci hic habent, Καλαβώτης χερσὶν ἐρειδό-μενος· et Hieronymus, Stellio manibus nititur; Arabs etiam يتنسد بيديه nititur manibus suis: tanquam ad incessum haec referentes. Sed nemo facile dixerit, quid in Chaldaeo sit אקמתא דמסככה בידיה. Neque enim II, 519 capio, quid sibi velit Latina versio, Aranea manibus tegumenta facit. Nec multo melius Gabriel, qui Syrae paraphrasis eadem verba sic reddidit: Stellio, quae serpit manibus suis. Et legerim potius sepit; quia סכך sepire est. Sed quorsum stellio sepire dicatur, aut tegumenta facere, nullus capio. Hic quoque haesit Drusius Observationum libri decimi capite sexto, et locus illi est de mendo suspectus. Et, pro מסככה, sepit, aut tegit, modo legi vult מסבכה, per Beth, implicans, aut perplexum opus faciens; quod dicatur de araneae tela: modo מסמכה, nitens; quod de stellione dicatur: ut sic Chaldaeo conveniat cum Graecis et Romano interprete. Sed Chaldaeum interpretem praestat cum Hebraeo textu conciliare, in quo תפש est apprehendere. Proinde Theodotion reddiderat ἐλλαμβανόμενος. Malim igitur pro מסככה mesacceca legere מפככה mephacceca, Pe pro Samech, quae literae figura non sunt prorsus absimiles. Nempe פכך Chaldaeis idem, quod Hebraeis תפש, capere, apprehendere. Sic Prov. V, 22. in editione Veneta, Funibus peccatorum suorum אתפכך, captus, aut apprehensus est.

We have also said that the stellio uses its hands for hunting, when it catches flies or spiders. Bustamantinus: It seizes with hands that promise security. Indeed the deceitful feet, which were bound to serve for motion, take the place of hands and carry out the plunder; and to it the feet on which it rests in moving are hands, and the hands with which it seizes its prey are feet. Rightly therefore Solomon says, The stellio takes hold with its hands, whether it walks upside down or throws itself upon its prey. Both are marvellous and most worthy of note in a tiny creature. The Greeks have here Καλαβώτης χερσὶν ἐρειδόμενος [Kalabōtēs chersin ereidomenos], and Jerome The stellio leans on its hands; the Arabic too has يتنسد بيديه [yatanassadu bi-yadayhi] it leans on its hands: as if referring this to walking. But no one could easily say what אקמתא דמסככה בידיה in the Chaldee means. For I do not II, 519 understand what the Latin version means, The spider makes coverings with its hands. Nor much better is Gabriel, who rendered the same words of the Syriac paraphrase thus: The stellio, which creeps with its hands. I would rather read sepit [fences]; for סכך is to fence. But why the stellio should be said to fence, or to make coverings, I do not understand at all. Here too Drusius was at a loss in the Observations, book 10, chapter 6, and he suspects the passage of corruption. And instead of מסככה, fences or covers, he would sometimes read מסבכה, with Beth, entangling or making an intricate work, which would be said of the spider's web; sometimes מסמכה, leaning, which would be said of the stellio; so that the Chaldee would thus agree with the Greek and the Roman translators. But it is better to reconcile the Chaldee translator with the Hebrew text, in which תפש is to take hold. Accordingly Theodotion had rendered ἐλλαμβανόμενος [ellambanomenos]. I would therefore prefer to read, instead of מסככה mesacceca, מפככה mephacceca, Pe for Samech, letters not entirely dissimilar in shape. For פכך in Chaldee is the same as תפש in Hebrew, to take, to take hold. Thus Prov 5:22 in the Venice edition: With the cords of his sins אתפכך, he is taken, or held fast.


Semamith in palatiis regum versari addit Solomon: quod unum habuit col. 1090 Mercerus, quod objiceret. Semamith, inquit, noster interpres stellionem exponit, quod quadrare non videtur, quia in aulis regum non versatur. At in domibus versari stellionem, credo, non ignoravit vir doctissimus, cum in uno ore clament fere, quotquot sunt, qui de stellione scripserunt. Proinde apud Eusebium Porphyrius vocat κατοικιδίους σκαλαβώτας, domesticos stelliones. Suidas, Etymologus, Phavorinus et Graecorum alii definiunt, ζωΰφιον ἐοικὸς σαύρᾳ ἐν τοῖς τοίχοις τῶν οἰκημάτων ἀνέρπον, lacertae simile animalculum, per domorum parietes serpens. Ita etiam Elluchasem, Bagdadensis medicus, in libro De animalibus: Stellio est lacerta, inhabitans domos. Hinc τοιχοβάτην appellat Kiranides. Et in Hispania Catalauni dragon de las casas, id est, draconem domorum. In veteribus praesertim aedificiis habitare, tradunt Niphus in Aristotelem, et Ponzettus in libro De venenis. Sed et in novis conspici, Marcellinus apud Hermolaum asserit. Iuxta Philosophum f) degit in praesepibus: juxta Antonium Liberalem g), παρ᾽ ὀχετὸν, prope cloacas: juxta Plinium h), in locis hostiorum fenestrarumque, aut cavernis sepulcrisve: juxta Arnobium i), sub simulacrorum cavis nidamenta ponit. Eidem assignat Matthiolus k) cava murorum prope terram. Sed laquearia veteres, et convexa tectorum, ubi supinus ambulet. Proinde, praeter Aristophanem et Dioscoridem, quos supra l) jam citavi, etiam in Avicenna m) legas, quandoque stellionem superne in potum cadere, et in venenum II, 520 illud vertere, si in eo moriatur (4). Haec, nisi fallor, abunde probant, agreste animal non esse stellionem, sed domesticum. Porro nullus video, quo privilegio regales domus ab hac peste sint immunes. Imo, quo major in illis est lapidum strues et congeries, eo sunt profundiores in parietibus fissurae et rimulae. Unde non absurde colligas, talia animalcula, quae in murorum foraminibus fere versantur, in regum aulis et palatiis etiam tutius degere, quam in privata domo.

Solomon adds that the semamith is in kings' palaces. This was the one objection that Mercerus had to raise col. 1090. "Our translator," he says, "renders semamith as stellio, which does not seem to fit, because it does not live in the courts of kings." But that the stellio lives in houses was not, I believe, unknown to this most learned man, since nearly all who have written about the stellio proclaim it with one voice. Thus in Eusebius, Porphyry speaks of κατοικιδίους σκαλαβώτας [katoikidious skalabōtas], domestic stellios. Suidas, the Etymologicum, Phavorinus and others among the Greeks define it as ζωΰφιον ἐοικὸς σαύρᾳ ἐν τοῖς τοίχοις τῶν οἰκημάτων ἀνέρπον [zōyphion eoikos saura en tois toichois tōn oikēmatōn anerpon], a little animal like a lizard, creeping along the walls of houses. So also Elluchasem, a physician of Baghdad, in his book On Animals: The stellio is a lizard that inhabits houses. Hence Kiranides calls it τοιχοβάτην [toichobatēn]. And in Spain the Catalans call it dragon de las casas, that is, dragon of the houses. That it lives especially in old buildings is reported by Niphus on Aristotle and by Ponzettus in his book On Poisons. But that it is also seen in new ones is asserted by Marcellinus in Hermolaus. According to the Philosopher f) it lives in mangers; according to Antoninus Liberalis g), παρ᾽ ὀχετὸν [par᾽ ocheton], near drains; according to Pliny h), about doors and windows, or in caves or tombs; according to Arnobius i), it builds its nests under the hollows of statues. Matthiolus k) assigns to it the hollows of walls near the ground. But the ancients assign it ceiling panels and the vaults of roofs, where it may walk upside down. Accordingly, besides Aristophanes and Dioscorides, whom I have already cited above l), you may also read in Avicenna m) that the stellio sometimes falls from above into a drink and turns it II, 520 into poison if it dies in it R4. These things, if I am not mistaken, amply prove that the stellio is not a wild animal but a domestic one. Further, I see no privilege by which royal houses should be immune from this pest. Indeed, the greater the pile and mass of stones in them, the deeper are the fissures and cracks in the walls. From this you may not unreasonably conclude that such little animals, which live mostly in holes in walls, dwell even more safely in the courts and palaces of kings than in a private house.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 515 This lizard was carefully described by HASSELQUIST, Travels p. 356-358, under this name: Lacerta (Gecko) cauda tereti mediocri, pedibus cristatis, subtus longitudinaliter lamellosis [lizard (gecko) with a moderate, rounded tail, crested feet, lamellate lengthwise underneath]. "The body," he says, "the head and the feet are hairless and smooth. Very small, raised, shining points are scattered over the whole back. Very small pores run along the abdomen. Rather large, soft scales cover the very small space between the loins underneath. The back, head and tail are whitish above, with grey transverse spots scattered irregularly; the throat, abdomen and tail are whitish underneath." From these words it is clear enough that the name leprous was not undeservedly given to this lizard. Now hear the same Hasselquist [=Fredrik Hasselquist, Iter Palaestinum (1757)] on the animal's poison, from which it is called سام [sām]. "Most remarkable is this animal's poison, which it exhales from the lobes of its toes. The little animal seeks out places and any things soaked or tinged with sea salt; when it finds such a thing, it runs over it several times, and as it runs it leaves behind it a highly noxious poison. In Cairo, in July 1750, I saw two women and a girl close to death who had eaten fresh salted cheese, bought in the market, on which this little animal had deposited its poison. How acrid the exhalations of its toes are I once saw in Cairo, when the little animal ran over the hand of a certain monk who wanted to catch it: at once, over the whole area the animal had touched, very small pustules arose, with redness, heat and slight pain, exactly as in those who have touched a nettle." FORSKAL also mentions this lizard, in Descriptt. Animall. p. 13: "Lacerta Gecko. By the Egyptians it is called ابو برص [abū baraṣ], i.e. father of leprosy, or leprous; by the people of Aleppo Burs." Schultens [=Albert Schultens, Liber Jobi (1737)], in Comment. ad Proverb. Chapter XXX. vs. 28. p. 486 b, interprets سام ابرص [sām abraṣ] as leprous breather, from سُمَام [sumām], which he says means pestilent blast.

Nomen animalis ortum putant alii a similitudine coloris leprae“.

Book 4, chapter 8: Altars like tortoises

https://openseforim.org/bochart/chelonai.html

II, 520 col. 1090 CAP. VIII.

II, 520 col. 1090 Chapter VIII.


Cur Idolorum arae dicantur esse ὡς χελῶναι, ut testudines, in Graeca versione Os. XII, 12. Et de chelonide Holofernis, Iudith. XIV, 13.

Why the altars of the idols are said to be ὡς χελῶναι [hōs chelōnai], like tortoises, in the Greek version of Hos 12:12. And on the chelonis of Holofernes, Jdt 14:13.


Nulla vox est Hebraeis notior, quam גל gal, pro acervo lapidum. Inde nomen habuit Galaad, mons celeberrimus in terra Chanaan, Gen. XXXI, 48. Et Gallim, oppidum prope Accaronem, de quo 1 Sam. XXV, 44. Es. X, 30. col. 1091 Eusebius et Hieronymus in locis. Achane lapidibus obruto, quia de anathemate acceperat, in rei memoriam super eum congestus est lapidum magnus גל gal, (seu acervus) Ios. VII, 26. Ita etiam super rebellis Absalomi cadaver, 2 Sam. XVIII, 17. Domus quoque, et urbes, quae diruuntur, redigi leguntur לגל, in gal (id est, acervum), Es. XXV, 2. aut לגלים, in gallim (id est, acervos), Iob. XV, 28. et Ierem. IX, 11. et LI, 37. Et fieri גלים נצים gallim nitsim (id est, vasti acervi), 2 Reg. XIX, 25. Itaque nihil obscurum est in his Os. XII, 11. (al. 12.): Arae eorum כגלים, ut gallim (seu lapidum acervi) super porcas agri. Agit Propheta de aris, quas Galgalis idololatrae Diis suis non solum in urbe exstruxerant, sed et in vicinis agris: et confert cum acervis lapidum, ab iis congeri solitis, qui lapidosos agros expurgant. Graeci tamen interpretes, quibus גל gal alibi est βουνὸς, tumulus, χῶμα agger, σωρὸς acervus, συναγωγὴ λίθων collectio lapidum, in hoc Oseae loco Plurale גלים gallim plane aliter, nempe χε-λώνας testudines reddunt. Τὰ θυσιαστήρια αὐτῶν (inquiunt), ὡς χελῶναι ἐπὶ χέρσον ἀγροῦ, Altaria eorum ut testudines super desertum agri. Et ad illa verba II, 521 Theodoretus testudinem observat, in aquis natantem, piscatorum manus facilius evadere, cum eadem in terra gradiens sit πρόχειρος, καὶ εὐάλωτως· quomodo futurum erat, ut Galgalitarum arae facile caperentur, et ab hostibus subverterentur. Maluit Hieronymus, quae de altaribus dicuntur, transferre ad haereticos, qui, testudinum instar, sunt tardi gressibus, et in uno moventur loco, etc. Quibus fortasse prudentior videbitur Cyrillus, cui χελῶναι hoc loco non sunt animalia, sed αἱ τῶν χωμάτων ἐγέρσεις, aggerum exstructiones: ut Drusio etiam testudines significant γεωλόφους terrae tumulos. Et his libenter accederem, si quod daretur exemplum similis locutionis. Sed, cum nullum proferatur, duo habeo, quae conjiciam. Unum, pro ὡς χελῶναι, legendum esse ὡς κολῶναι, quae vox pro tumulis saepe usurpatur. Ut Iliad. β΄. versu 811.

No word is better known to the Hebrews than גל gal, for a heap of stones. From it Galaad, a very famous mountain in the land of Canaan, took its name, Gen 31:48. So too Gallim, a town near Accaron, on which see 1 Sam 25:44. Isa 10:30 col. 1091 and Eusebius and Jerome in the Places. When Achan had been stoned because he had taken from the devoted things, a great גל gal of stones (that is, a heap) was piled over him as a memorial of the deed, Josh 7:26. Likewise over the corpse of the rebel Absalom, 2 Sam 18:17. Houses, too, and cities that are demolished are said to be reduced לגל, to a gal (that is, a heap), Isa 25:2 or לגלים, to gallim (that is, heaps), Job 15:28 and Jer 9:11 and LI, 37. And to become גלים נצים gallim nitsim (that is, desolate heaps), 2 Reg. XIX, 25. There is therefore nothing obscure in these words of Hos 12:11 (var. 12.): Their altars are כגלים, like gallim (or heaps of stones) on the furrows of the field. The Prophet is speaking of the altars which the idolaters of Gilgal had built to their gods not only in the city but also in the neighbouring fields; and he compares them with the heaps of stones customarily piled up by those who clear stony fields. The Greek translators, however, for whom גל gal is elsewhere βουνὸς [bounos], a mound, χῶμα [chōma] an embankment, σωρὸς [sōros] a heap, συναγωγὴ λίθων [synagōgē lithōn] a collection of stones, render the plural גלים gallim in this passage of Hosea quite differently, namely as χελώνας [chelōnas], tortoises. Τὰ θυσιαστήρια αὐτῶν [Ta thysiastēria autōn] (they say), ὡς χελῶναι ἐπὶ χέρσον ἀγροῦ [hōs chelōnai epi cherson agrou], Their altars are like tortoises on the waste of the field. And on these words II, 521 Theodoret observes that the tortoise, when swimming in the water, escapes the hands of fishermen more easily, whereas when walking on land it is πρόχειρος, καὶ εὐάλωτως [procheiros, kai eualōtōs], ready to hand and easily caught; so it would come about that the altars of the Gilgalites would easily be taken and overthrown by their enemies. Jerome preferred to apply what is said of the altars to the heretics, who, like tortoises, are slow of step and move about in one place, etc. Wiser than these, perhaps, will seem Cyril, for whom χελῶναι [chelōnai] in this passage are not animals but αἱ τῶν χωμάτων ἐγέρσεις [hai tōn chōmatōn egerseis], the raising of embankments; just as for Drusius too tortoises signify γεωλόφους [geōlophous], mounds of earth. And I would gladly agree with them if any example of a similar expression were given. But since none is adduced, I have two conjectures. The first is that instead of ὡς χελῶναι [hōs chelōnai] we should read ὡς κολῶναι [hōs kolōnai], a word often used for mounds. As in the Iliad, β΄ [book 2], line 811.


Ἔστι δέ τις προπάροιθε πόλεως αἰπεῖα κολώνη,

Ἔστι δέ τις προπάροιθε πόλεως αἰπεῖα κολώνη, [Esti de tis propároithe poleōs aipeia kolōnē,]


Est autem prope urbem celsus quidam tumulus. Et Apollonii Argonauticῶn lib. 1. versu 1114.

Now there is near the city a certain lofty mound. And in Apollonius' Argonautica, book 1, line 1114.


Φαίνετο δ᾽ ἠερόεν στόμα Βοσπόρου, ἠδὲ κολῶναι
Μύσιαι. — — — — — —

Φαίνετο δ᾽ ἠερόεν στόμα Βοσπόρου, ἠδὲ κολῶναι Μύσιαι. — — — — — — [Phaineto d' ēeroen stoma Bosporou, ēde kolōnai Mysiai.]


Apparebat autem nebulosum os Bosphori et juga Mysiae. Utuntur et prosaici scriptores: ut Polemo apud Athenaeum libro decimo tertio, et alius apud Suidam: et Pausanias in Laconicis, ubi de Colona, Spartae loco. Hesychio κολώ-νη est τόπος ὑψηλὸς, καὶ ἐπανάστημα γῆς βουνοειδὲς, locus celsus, et terrae eminentia in tumuli modum. Et Homeri Scholiastae, τόπος εἰς ὕψος ἀνήκων, καὶ γεώλεφος ἐξοχὴ, locus in altum elatus, et clivosa prominentia. Altera conjectura est גלים gallim, hic χελώνας, seu testudines, ex usu Syrae linguae, reddi, qua ܓܠܐ gala est testudo. Itaque Syrus hic habet ܐܝܟ ܓܠܐ, id est, quasi testudines, juxta Gabrielem Sionitam. Et in Syro Lexico Iohannis Baptistae Ferrarii pagina 107. ܓܠܐ gala testudo redditur. Tamen in Thesauro Thomae a Novaria pagina 241. Syrae voces ܫܠܘܦܝܬܐ seluphita, et ܥܓܠܐ gala, sic distinguuntur, ut illa testudinem in genere significet, haec nonnisi masculum testudinis. Quod puto esse verius; quia eundem Arabes non nisi allusione ad hoc verbum غيلم gailam vocant. Ita testantur Giauhari, Alcamus, Damir, alii. Et nomen a libidine factum. Quippe غلم galam libidinem sonat, et غلم galima Verbum libidine ardere. Unde marem testudinis merito غيلم col. 1092 gailam appellari, doceant haec Aeliani Historiae libri decimi quinti capite decimo nono, Χερσαία χελώνη ζῶον λαγνίστατον· ἀλλὰ ὅγε ἄῤῥην. ὁμιλεῖ δὲ ἡ θή-λεια ἄκουσα. Terrestris testudo animal est salacissimum; illius mas scilicet: foemina enim nonnisi invita coit. Et a coitu scribit Damostratus illam ideo abhorrere; quia, cum a mare resupinata propter nimium testae pondus non possit se II, 522 erigere, post coitum aquilae in praedam patet et aliis animantibus. Sed puto verius, quod alii scribunt, eam in ipso coitu gravi dolore affici; quia durum et aculeatum est maris veretrum. Taceo Damostrati fabulam, a Damire non praetermissam, de herba quadam ignota, quam mas in ore habens repugnantem ad se allicit. Interim licet non solis Graecis, sed Syro quoque et Arabi גלים gallim in Osea sint testudines, causam tamen non video, cur a recepta illius loci versione discedamus. Idolorum aras, in agris passim obvias, cum propter vilitatem, tum propter frequentiam, cum iis lapidum acervis, quos diximus, recte conferri, nemo non videt. Ut taceam, eminus intuentibus non absimilem esse speciem. Sed coactum et longe petitum est, quidquid affertur, ut inter easdem aras et testudines adstruatur similitudo. Possunt etiam Oseae verba sumi tanquam prophetice dicta, quasi vaticinetur, Galgalitarum aras brevi futuras כגלים, ut lapidum acervos, qui sunt in agris, id est, brevi diruendas. Neque negligenda est allusio vocis Galgal ad גלים gallim. Ita, ut Galgal et illius arae futurae dicantur ut gallim, seu lapidum acervi. Quomodo Sophon. II, 4. Aza (seu Gaza) erit עזובה (azuba) derelicta. Et Accaron תעקר (theaker) eradicabitur. Ut in Pseudo-Sibyllinis,

And the misty mouth of the Bosphorus and the ridges of Mysia appeared. Prose writers also use it: for example Polemo in Athenaeus, book 13, and another in the Suda; and Pausanias in the Laconica, where he speaks of Colona, a place in Sparta. In Hesychius κολώνη [kolōnē] is τόπος ὑψηλὸς, καὶ ἐπανάστημα γῆς βουνοειδὲς [topos hypsēlos, kai epanastēma gēs bounoeides], a lofty place, and an elevation of the ground in the manner of a mound. And in the scholiasts on Homer, τόπος εἰς ὕψος ἀνήκων, καὶ γεώλεφος ἐξοχὴ [topos eis hypsos anēkōn, kai geōlephos exochē], a place rising to a height, and a hilly prominence. The other conjecture is that גלים gallim is rendered here as χελώνας [chelōnas], or tortoises, following the usage of the Syriac language, in which ܓܠܐ [גלא] gala is tortoise. Accordingly the Syriac here has ܐܝܟ ܓܠܐ [איך גלא], that is, like tortoises, according to Gabriel Sionita [=translator of al-Idrīsī's geography into Latin (Geographia Nubiensis, Paris 1619)]. And in the Syriac Lexicon of Giovanni Battista Ferrari, page 107, ܓܠܐ [גלא] gala is rendered tortoise. Yet in the Thesaurus of Thomas of Novara, page 241, the Syriac words ܫܠܘܦܝܬܐ [שלופיתא] seluphita and ܥܓܠܐ [עגלא] gala are distinguished in such a way that the former signifies the tortoise in general, the latter only the male tortoise. This I think is more correct, since the Arabs call the same animal غيلم [ghaylam] gailam, surely in allusion to this word. So testify Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ], Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī], Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] and others. And the name is formed from lust. For غلم [ghalam] galam means lust, and the verb غلم [ghalima] galima means to burn with lust. That the male tortoise is rightly called غيلم [ghaylam] col. 1092 gailam may be shown by these words of Aelian, Historia, book 15, chapter 19: Χερσαία χελώνη ζῶον λαγνίστατον· ἀλλὰ ὅγε ἄῤῥην. ὁμιλεῖ δὲ ἡ θήλεια ἄκουσα [Chersaia chelōnē zōon lagnistaton; alla hoge arrhēn. homilei de hē thēleia akousa]. The land tortoise is a most lustful animal; that is, its male: for the female mates only unwillingly. And Damostratus writes that she shrinks from mating for this reason: because, when she has been turned on her back by the male, she cannot right herself on account of the excessive weight of her shell, II, 522 and after mating lies open as prey to the eagle and to other animals. But I think what others write is more correct, that in the very act of mating she suffers severe pain, because the male's member is hard and spiny. I pass over the fable of Damostratus, not omitted by Damir, about a certain unknown herb which the male holds in his mouth and so draws the resisting female to himself. Meanwhile, although not only for the Greeks but also for the Syriac and the Arabic translators גלים gallim in Hosea are tortoises, I nevertheless see no reason why we should depart from the received rendering of that passage. Everyone sees that the altars of the idols, met everywhere in the fields, are rightly compared with those heaps of stones we have mentioned, both on account of their cheapness and on account of their frequency. Not to mention that to those viewing them from afar their appearance is not dissimilar. But whatever is adduced to establish a likeness between these altars and tortoises is forced and far-fetched. Hosea's words can also be taken as spoken prophetically, as if he foretold that the altars of the people of Gilgal would shortly be כגלים, like heaps of stones that are in the fields, that is, would shortly be demolished. Nor should the allusion of the word Galgal to גלים gallim be neglected, so that Galgal and its altars are said to be destined to become like gallim, or heaps of stones. Just as in Zeph 2:4: Aza (or Gaza) shall be עזובה (azuba) forsaken. And Accaron תעקר (theaker) shall be uprooted. As in the Pseudo-Sibyllines,


Καὶ Ῥώμη ῥύμη ἔσεται, καὶ Δῆλος ἄδηλος·

Καὶ Ῥώμη ῥύμη ἔσεται, καὶ Δῆλος ἄδηλος· [Kai Rhōmē rhymē esetai, kai Dēlos adēlos;]


et in historia Susannae σχίσαι et πρίσαι alludunt ad arborum nomina σχί-νον et πρίνον.

and in the history of Susanna σχίσαι [schisai] and πρίσαι [prisai] allude to the names of the trees σχίνον [schinon] and πρίνον [prinon].


Cum truncum Holofernis projectum reperisse legitur Bagoas ἐπὶ τῆς χε-τλωνίδος, Iudith. XIV, 13. alii recte observant, pro χετλωνίδος, voce nihili, legendum χελωνίδος, quomodo legerunt Hesychius et Suidas: et χελωνίδα dici ἀπὸ τῆς χελώνης, a testudine. Sed quid tandem sit χελωνὶς, non satis constat. Vulgatus interpres cortinam reddit. Plerique recentiorum stratum, aut lectum; quos facile est refellere. Iudith enim Holoferni caput amputaverat, καὶ ἐπεκύ-λισε τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς στρωμνῆς, et corpus ejus a strato evolverat, cap. XIII, v. 10. Χελωνὶς igitur, in qua hoc corpus ἐῤῥιμμένον projectum reperit Bagoas, a strato et lecto quid diversum est. Hesychius, in χελωνίδος, exponit οὐδὸς τῆς θύρας τῆς σκηνῆς, limen januae tabernaculi. Ita etiam Suidas ex eo corrigendus, cum scribit ὅδου pro οὐδοῦ. Quod parum est verissimile; cum quia nomen non quadrat, tum quia Holofernis corpus e strato devolutum est in chelonidem. Chelonis igitur non fuit prope limen januae: sed in intimo tabernaculo, in quo etiam ipse Imperatoris lectus. Ne lectorem pluribus detineam, mihi χελωνὶς est קבה kubba. Vox semel in scriptura legitur, nec satis intelligitur: nempe Num. XXV, 8. ubi, Zimri et Kozbi scortantibus, ingressus est Phinees אל הקבה, in kubba, et utrumque transfodit. Quod varii varie explicant. Sed Arabibus قبة kubba, vel kobba, et cum Articulo القبة alkobba, conclave est camerati operis, quo lectus circumdatur. Hispanis alcoba II, 523 dicitur, et alcova, quae vox apud nos quoque est vicinae significationis. Radix قب kabba in secunda Conjugatione concamerare significat, aut cameratum opus struere. Itaque ut musicum instrumentum χέλυς, seu testudo, Arabice vocatur العود alaud, unde Hispanis laud, vel laut, et nobis lut: ita القبة alkobba, col. 1093 seu conclave, quod descripsimus, Arabice alio nomine dicitur ام العود ommolaudi, id est, mater testudinis; quia est camerati et testudinei operis. Apud Arabes in tali القبة alkobba est sponsae thalamus. Et illam eo deducere بنا bana, et زف zappha dicitur. Holofernis igitur thalamus, cum Iuditha, ut putabat, concubituri, in hujusmodi alcobba fuit, quae cur Graece χελωνὶς appelletur, jam cuivis patet. Fortasse etiam χελωνὶς a materia dicta. Olim enim in magnatum lectis et spondis multus fuit testudinis usus. Qui luxus in Oriente primum usurpatus tandem ad Romanos devenit. Tempus, a Plinio notatum libri noni capite undecimo, Testudinum, inquit, putamina secare in laminas, lectosque, et repositoria his vestire, Carbilius Pollio instituit. Et libri decimi sexti col. 1094 capite quadragesimo tertio: Testudo in hoc secta. Nuperque portentosis ingeniis principatu Neronis inventum, ut pigmentis perderet se, plurisque veniret imitata lignum. Sic lectis pretia quaeruntur. Hinc Martialis libri duodecimi Epigrammate 67.

When we read that Bagoas found the trunk of Holofernes thrown down ἐπὶ τῆς χετλωνίδος [epi tēs chetlōnidos], Jdt 14:13, others rightly observe that in place of χετλωνίδος [chetlōnidos], a meaningless word, we should read χελωνίδος [chelōnidos], as Hesychius and Suidas read it, and that χελωνίς [chelōnis] is so called ἀπὸ τῆς χελώνης [apo tēs chelōnēs], from the tortoise. But what exactly a χελωνὶς [chelōnis] is, is not sufficiently clear. The Vulgate translator renders it cortina [curtain]. Most of the more recent interpreters render it stratum [couch] or lectus [bed]; they are easily refuted. For Judith had cut off Holofernes' head, καὶ ἐπεκύλισε τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς στρωμνῆς [kai epekylise to sōma autou apo tēs strōmnēs], and had rolled his body off the couch, ch. 13, v. 10. Therefore the χελωνὶς [chelōnis], in which Bagoas found this body ἐῤῥιμμένον [erhrimmenon], thrown down, is something different from the couch and the bed. Hesychius, under χελωνίδος [chelōnidos], explains it as οὐδὸς τῆς θύρας τῆς σκηνῆς [oudos tēs thyras tēs skēnēs], the threshold of the door of the tent. So Suidas too must be corrected from him, since he writes ὅδου [hodou] for οὐδοῦ [oudou]. This is hardly likely, both because the name does not fit, and because Holofernes' body was rolled from the couch into the chelonis. The chelonis, then, was not near the threshold of the door, but in the innermost part of the tent, where the commander's bed itself also stood. Not to detain the reader any longer: to me the χελωνὶς [chelōnis] is קבה kubba. The word occurs once in Scripture and is not well understood, namely Num 25:8, where, while Zimri and Kozbi were fornicating, Phinehas went אל הקבה, into the kubba, and pierced them both through. Different people explain this differently. But among the Arabs قبة [qubba] kubba, or kobba, and with the article القبة [al-qubba] alkobba, is a chamber of vaulted work, by which a bed is enclosed. The Spaniards call it alcoba II, 523 and alcova, a word which among us too has a similar meaning. The root قب [qabba] kabba in the second conjugation means to vault, or to build vaulted work. So, just as the musical instrument χέλυς [chelys], or testudo [tortoise], is called in Arabic العود [al-ʿūd] alaud, whence the Spanish laud or laut, and our lut, so القبة [al-qubba] alkobba, col. 1093 or the chamber we have described, is called in Arabic by another name ام العود [umm al-ʿūd] ommolaudi, that is, mother of the tortoise, because it is of vaulted, tortoise-shaped work. Among the Arabs the bridal chamber is in such an القبة [al-qubba] alkobba. And leading the bride there is called بنا [banā] bana and زف [zaff] zappha. So Holofernes' bedchamber, when he was about to lie with Judith, as he thought, was in an alcobba of this kind; and why it is called χελωνὶς [chelōnis] in Greek is now clear to anyone. Perhaps the χελωνὶς [chelōnis] was also named from its material. For in former times tortoise shell was much used in the beds and bedsteads of the great. This luxury, first adopted in the East, finally reached the Romans. The date is noted by Pliny, book 9, chapter 11: To cut tortoise shells into plates, he says, and to veneer beds and sideboards with them, was introduced by Carbilius Pollio. And book 16, col. 1094 chapter 43: Tortoise shell is cut for this purpose. And recently, in the principate of Nero, it was devised by monstrous ingenuity that it should destroy itself with paints and sell for more by imitating wood. Thus high prices are sought for beds. Hence Martial, book 12, Epigram 67:


Gemmantes prima fulgent testudine lecti.

Beds jewelled with the finest tortoise shell gleam.


Et Iuvenalis Satyra undecima,

And Juvenal, Satire 11:


Qualis in Oceani fluctu testudo nataret,
Clarum Trojugenis factura et nobile fulcrum.

What kind of tortoise swam in the waves of Ocean, to make a splendid and noble headrest for the Trojan-born.


Ubi Scholiastes, Ut lectum testudineum haberet. Lectos namque antiqui testudine Oceani ornabant. Apulejus quoque non procul a fine libri decimi, Lectus Indica testudine perlucidus, plumea congerie tumidus, etc. Sed haec plus satis de re non magni momenti. Itaque hic definimus, jam ad aves transituri.

Where the Scholiast says: That he might have a tortoise-shell bed. For the ancients adorned beds with the tortoise shell of Ocean. Apuleius too, not far from the end of book 10: A bed shining with Indian tortoise shell, swelling with a heap of feathers, etc. But this is more than enough on a matter of no great importance. So here we end, and now pass on to the birds.


Part 2, Book 1, chapter 1: The Hebrew name of the dove
