https://openseforim.org/bochart/jonah.html

II, 524 DE SCRIPTURAE ANIMALIBUS PARS SECUNDA LIBER PRIMUS DE DE MUNDIS AVIBUS. col. 1

II, 524 ON THE ANIMALS OF SCRIPTURE PART TWO BOOK ONE ON ON THE CLEAN BIRDS. col. 1


CAP. I.

CHAPTER I.


De Hebraeo Columbae nomine.

On the Hebrew name of the dove.


Mundas aves Sacri Scriptores paucis attingunt, una columba excepta, de qua plura habent, quam de reliquis omnibus simul sumtis. Itaque de illa necesse est agere accuratius. Columbam Hebraice יונה jona dici volunt a verbo ינה jana, quod opprimere significat, quasi omnium praedae pateat. Quam in rem poetae proferuntur,

The sacred writers touch on the clean birds only briefly, with the single exception of the dove, about which they say more than about all the others taken together. It is therefore necessary to treat it more carefully. It is held that the dove is called in Hebrew יונה jona from the verb ינה jana, which means to oppress, as if it lay open to the plundering of all. On this point the poets are cited:


Dat veniam corvis, vexat censura columbas.

Censure pardons the ravens and harasses the doves.


Quod videtur longe petitum. Itaque conabor aliquid afferre verosimilius. Ie- rem. XLVI, 16. et L, 16. Hebraea verba מפני חרב היונה Graeci reddunt ἀπὸ προσώπου μαχαίρας Ἑλληνικῆς, a facie gladii Graeci; Hieronymus, a facie gla- dii columbae; Syrus, a facie gladii ܡܣܝܒܐ cruciantis; R. Selomo et Kimchius, האונסת, opprimentis: sed Chaldaeus Paraphrastes, מן קדם חרב סנאה דהיא כחמר מרויא, a facie gladii hostilis, qui est ut vinum inebrians; quasi היונה fiat a יין, id est, a vino, Iod et Vau permutatis. Indidem igitur יונה jona pro co- lumba deduci queat. Quod si sequamur, יונה jona proprie erit οἰνὰς, columbae ferae genus, a vino sic appellatum. 1. Quia, Eustathio auctore, est οἰνωπὸς τὸ χρῶμα, id est, quia vinum, vel uvas maturas colore refert. 2. Quia vindemiae tempore fere apparet. Aristoteles Hist. lib. 8. cap. 3. Οἰνὰς δὲ τοῦ col. 2 φθινοπώρου καὶ φαίνεται μάλιστα, καὶ ἁλίσκεται· Oenas (vel, ut Gaza reddit, vinago) Autumno maxime apparet et capitur. Athenaeus lib. 9. cap. 11. Ἡ δὲ φὰψ, καὶ ἡ περιστερὰ ἀεὶ φαίνονται· ἡ δὲ οἰνὰς φθινοπώρῳ μόνῳ· Palumbus minor et columba semper apparent; sed vinago solum autumno. Sed huic etymo II, 525 repugnat Hebraeorum usus, apud quos יונה jona, vel יון jon non est οἰνὰς, sed columba in genere, et proprie domestica. Itaque columba οἰνὰς a Syris dicta est ܟܪܡܝܘܢ charmion, vel ܟܪܡܝܘܢܐ charmiona, voce composita ex duabus, ܟܪܡ et ܝܘܢ, vel ܝܘܢܐ, quarum illa vitem, haec columbam sonat. Quod ipsissimum fuit nomen unius illustrium illarum Cleopatrae ancillarum. Graece id Χάρμιον scribitur, vel Χαρμιόνη, vel Χαρμιουνώ. Plutarchus in Antonio, Εἴρας ἡ Κλεοπάτρας κουρεύτρια, καὶ Χάρμιον, ὑφ᾽ ὧν τὰ μέγιστα διοικεῖται τῆς ἡγεμονίας· Iras Cleopatrae tonstrix, et Charmion, a quibus maxima imperii negotia administrabantur. Et infra, ubi de morte Cleopatrae, Τῶν δὲ γυναι-κῶν ἡ μὲν Εἴρας λεγομένη πρὸς τοῖς ποσὶν ἀπέθνησκεν· ἡ δὲ Χάρμιον, ἤδη σφαλλομένη, καὶ καρηβαροῦσα, κατεκόσμει τὸ διάδημα περὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐ-τῆς. Mulierum ejus quae vocabatur Iras, ad pedes ejus expiraverat: Charmion autem, jam lapsabunda, et capite gravata, caput illius diademate exornabat. Galenus De theriaca ad Pisonem libri primi capite octavo, Καὶ τοῖς ὀνόμασι λεγό-μεναι Νάειρα, καὶ Καρμιόνη· ἡ μὲν ἀναπλέκουσα τὰς τρίχας εὐπρεπῶς, ἡ δὲ col. 3 ἀποτέμνουσα τὰς ὑπεροχὰς τῶν ὀνύχων εὐφυῶς. Et (Cleopatrae ancillae) Naira et Carmione dictae; quarum illa comam decenter implicabat, haec extremos ungues dextre praecidebat. Tzetzes Chil. 6. Hist. 44.

This seems far-fetched. I shall therefore try to offer something more probable. In Jer 46:16 and L, 16. the Hebrew words מפני חרב היונה are rendered by the Greeks ἀπὸ προσώπου μαχαίρας Ἑλληνικῆς [apo prosōpou machairas Hellēnikēs], from the face of the Greek sword; by Jerome, from the face of the sword of the dove; by the Syriac, from the face of the sword ܡܣܝܒܐ [מסיבא] of the tormentor; by R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] and Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], האונסת, of the oppressor. But the Chaldee Paraphrast has מן קדם חרב סנאה דהיא כחמר מרויא, from the face of the hostile sword, which is like intoxicating wine, as if היונה were formed from יין, that is, from wine, with Yod and Vav interchanged. From the same source, then, יונה jona for the dove could be derived. If we follow this, יונה jona will properly be the οἰνὰς [oinas], a kind of wild dove so named from wine. 1. Because, on the authority of Eustathius, it is οἰνωπὸς τὸ χρῶμα [oinōpos to chrōma], that is, because it resembles wine, or ripe grapes, in colour. 2. Because it usually appears at the time of the vintage. Aristotle, Hist. book 8, ch. 3: Οἰνὰς δὲ τοῦ col. 2 φθινοπώρου καὶ φαίνεται μάλιστα, καὶ ἁλίσκεται· [Oinas de tou phthinopōrou kai phainetai malista, kai halisketai] The oenas (or, as Gaza renders it, vinago) appears and is caught chiefly in autumn. Athenaeus book 9, ch. 11: Ἡ δὲ φὰψ, καὶ ἡ περιστερὰ ἀεὶ φαίνονται· ἡ δὲ οἰνὰς φθινοπώρῳ μόνῳ· [Hē de phaps, kai hē peristera aei phainontai; hē de oinas phthinopōrō monō] The smaller wood pigeon and the dove are always to be seen; but the vinago only in autumn. But this etymology II, 525 is contradicted by the usage of the Hebrews, among whom יונה jona, or יון jon, is not the οἰνὰς [oinas] but the dove in general, and properly the domestic one. Accordingly the οἰνὰς [oinas] dove was called by the Syrians ܟܪܡܝܘܢ [כרמיון] charmion, or ܟܪܡܝܘܢܐ [כרמיונא] charmiona, a word compounded of two, ܟܪܡ [כרם] and ܝܘܢ [יון], or ܝܘܢܐ [יונא], of which the former means vine and the latter dove. This was the very name of one of those famous handmaids of Cleopatra. In Greek it is written Χάρμιον [Charmion], or Χαρμιόνη [Charmionē], or Χαρμιουνώ [Charmiounō]. Plutarch in the Antony: Εἴρας ἡ Κλεοπάτρας κουρεύτρια, καὶ Χάρμιον, ὑφ᾽ ὧν τὰ μέγιστα διοικεῖται τῆς ἡγεμονίας· [Eiras hē Kleopatras koureutria, kai Charmion, hyph᾽ hōn ta megista dioikeitai tēs hēgemonias] Iras, Cleopatra's hairdresser, and Charmion, by whom the most important affairs of the realm were managed. And further on, regarding the death of Cleopatra: Τῶν δὲ γυναικῶν ἡ μὲν Εἴρας λεγομένη πρὸς τοῖς ποσὶν ἀπέθνησκεν· ἡ δὲ Χάρμιον, ἤδη σφαλλομένη, καὶ καρηβαροῦσα, κατεκόσμει τὸ διάδημα περὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτῆς. [Tōn de gynaikōn hē men Eiras legomenē pros tois posin apethnēsken; hē de Charmion, ēdē sphallomenē, kai karēbarousa, katekosmei to diadēma peri tēn kephalēn autēs] Of her women, the one called Iras had died at her feet; Charmion, however, already tottering and heavy-headed, was adorning her head with the diadem. Galen, On theriac to Piso, book 1, chapter 8: Καὶ τοῖς ὀνόμασι λεγόμεναι Νάειρα, καὶ Καρμιόνη· ἡ μὲν ἀναπλέκουσα τὰς τρίχας εὐπρεπῶς, ἡ δὲ col. 3 ἀποτέμνουσα τὰς ὑπεροχὰς τῶν ὀνύχων εὐφυῶς. [Kai tois onomasi legomenai Naeira, kai Karmionē; hē men anaplekousa tas trichas euprepōs, hē de apotemnousa tas hyperochas tōn onychōn euphyōs] And (Cleopatra's handmaids) called Naira and Carmione, of whom the former braided her hair becomingly, the latter skilfully trimmed the tips of her nails. Tzetzes, Chil. 6, Hist. 44:


Τῇ Κλεοπάτρᾳ τῇ σοφῇ, τῇ καὶ ὡραιοτάτῃ, Καὶ τοῖς λοιποῖς δὲ σύμπασι a) πολλῶν ὑπερφερούσῃ, Πρὸς ἐπιμέλειαν τριχῶν, καὶ τῶν ὀνύχων, ἦσαν Χαρμιουνὼ, καὶ Τάειρα τί δε δηλοῦσι τάδε; Σύρον τὸν Τζέτζην βλέπε νῦν, Ἰσμαηλίτην ἅμα, Καὶ ταῦτα διαρθροῦντα σοι ταῖς γλώσσαις ταῖς ἐκείνων. Κατὰ Ἑβραίων γλῶσσάν τε, καὶ τὴν τῶν Σύρων ἅμα, Χαρμὶ δηλοῖ τὴν ἀμπελον, Οὐνὼ περιστεράν δε, Τὴν, ἣν b) φησιν οἱ Ἕλληνες περιστερὰν οἰνάδα, Κατὰ Ἰσμαηλίτας δὲ, τοὺς Ἄγαρ γόνους λέγω, Περιστερὰν τὴν Γάειραν σημαίνουσάν μοι νόει.

Τῇ Κλεοπάτρᾳ τῇ σοφῇ, τῇ καὶ ὡραιοτάτῃ, Καὶ τοῖς λοιποῖς δὲ σύμπασι a) πολλῶν ὑπερφερούσῃ, Πρὸς ἐπιμέλειαν τριχῶν, καὶ τῶν ὀνύχων, ἦσαν Χαρμιουνὼ, καὶ Τάειρα τί δε δηλοῦσι τάδε; Σύρον τὸν Τζέτζην βλέπε νῦν, Ἰσμαηλίτην ἅμα, Καὶ ταῦτα διαρθροῦντα σοι ταῖς γλώσσαις ταῖς ἐκείνων. Κατὰ Ἑβραίων γλῶσσάν τε, καὶ τὴν τῶν Σύρων ἅμα, Χαρμὶ δηλοῖ τὴν ἀμπελον, Οὐνὼ περιστεράν δε, Τὴν, ἣν b) φησιν οἱ Ἕλληνες περιστερὰν οἰνάδα, Κατὰ Ἰσμαηλίτας δὲ, τοὺς Ἄγαρ γόνους λέγω, Περιστερὰν τὴν Γάειραν σημαίνουσάν μοι νόει. [Tē Kleopatra tē sophē, tē kai hōraiotatē, / Kai tois loipois de sympasi a) pollōn hyperpherousē, / Pros epimeleian trichōn, kai tōn onychōn, ēsan / Charmiounō, kai Taeira ti de dēlousi tade? / Syron ton Tzetzēn blepe nyn, Ismaēlitēn hama, / Kai tauta diarthrounta soi tais glōssais tais ekeinōn. / Kata Hebraiōn glōssan te, kai tēn tōn Syrōn hama, / Charmi dēloi tēn ampelon, Ounō peristeran de, / Tēn, hēn b) phēsin hoi Hellēnes peristeran oinada, / Kata Ismaēlitas de, tous Agar gonous legō, / Peristeran tēn Gaeiran sēmainousan moi noei.]


Cleopatrae sapienti, et formosissimae, et supra reliquas omnes mulieres longe praestanti, ad curam capillorum et unguium, erant Charmiuno et Taïra. Haec autem nomina quid designant? Syrum vide nunc Tzetzem et Ismaëlitem simul, et haec illorum linguis tibi explicantem. Tam Hebraeorum, quam Syrorum lingua Charmi vitem significat, et Uno columbam, quam Graeci columbam oenadem vocant. At juxta Ismaëlitas, ex Agare oriundos, dico, Taïram mihi columbam significare II, 526 intellige. Ex his collige, in Plutarcho pro Εἴρας, et in Galeno pro Νά-ειρα, rescribendum esse Τάειρας, vel Τάειρα, ut in Tzetze, qui recte quidem scribit hanc vocem, sed male interpretatur. Quippe Arabicum طاير taïr, vel طايرة taira, columbam non significat, sed avem in genere. Unde Chaldaeis טייר tajer est augurari. Neque dividi debuit Charmiuno in Charmi et Uno; sed in כרם charm, et יונא juno. Interim non dubitandum, quin Charmiuno, vel Charmiona vere sit οἰνάς. Itaque יונה jona per se non est οἰνὰς, sed columba quaevis. Quo posito nulla apparet ratio, cur a vino dicta sit יונה jona. Proinde aliud quaerendum. Neque fortasse absurdum erit, ut patriae columbae יונים jonim, quasi Graecae, putentur fuisse appellatae. Graeci enim olim Ἴω-νες Iones dicebantur, ut alibi probavimus: et Hebraice יונים jonim, iisdem literis, quamvis javanim hodie efferant, quia Masorethis ita placuit. Columbas inde appellari, duo potissimum suadent. Unum, quod apud Plinium, libri decimi capite vigesimo nono, Theophrastus tradit, invectitias esse in Asia columbas. Alterum, quod in Graecia columbas fuisse ab omni aevo historia fabularis abunde docet. Sic 1. Dodonaeam columbam ajunt c) ἱζομένην ἐπὶ φηγὸν, αὐδάξασθαι φωνῇ ἀνθρωπίνῃ, ὡς χρεὼν εἴη, μαντήϊον αὐτόθι Διὸς γένεσθαι, fago insidentem, humana voce dixisse, in fatis esse, ut eo loci Iovis oraculum conderetur, quod fuit Graeciae totius longe antiquissimum. 2. Ut a Noacho, sic a Deucalione ferunt d) περιστερὰν, ἐκ τῆς λάρνακος ἀφιεμένην, δήλωμα γενέσθαι, χειμῶνος μὲν εἴσω πάλιν ἐνδυομένην, εὐδίας δὲ, ἀποπτᾶσαν, columbam, ex arca emissam, tempestatis signum fuisse, cum eodem rediit, et serenitatis, cum avolavit. 3. Columbae Iovem, in Creta vagientem, ambrosia dicuntur aluisse, ex Oceano allata Moero Byzantia, Athenaei libro undecimo,

Cleopatra, wise, most beautiful, and far surpassing all other women, had for the care of her hair and nails Charmiuno and Taïra. But what do these names signify? See now Tzetzes, at once a Syrian and an Ishmaelite, explaining them to you in their languages. In the language of the Hebrews as well as of the Syrians, Charmi signifies the vine, and Uno the dove, which the Greeks call the oenas dove. But among the Ishmaelites, I mean those descended from Hagar, understand that Taïra signifies II, 526 the dove to me. From this gather that in Plutarch for Εἴρας [Eiras], and in Galen for Νάειρα [Naeira], one must write Τάειρας [Taeiras] or Τάειρα [Taeira], as in Tzetzes, who indeed writes this word correctly but interprets it wrongly. For the Arabic طاير [ṭāyir] taïr, or طايرة [ṭāyira] taira, does not signify a dove, but a bird in general. Hence for the Chaldeans טייר tajer means to take auguries. Nor should Charmiuno have been divided into Charmi and Uno, but into כרם charm and יונא juno. Meanwhile there is no doubt that Charmiuno, or Charmiona, is truly οἰνάς [oinas]. So יונה jona by itself is not οἰνὰς [oinas], but any dove. This being granted, no reason appears why יונה jona should be named from wine. Therefore something else must be sought. Nor perhaps will it be absurd to think that doves were called by their native name יונים jonim, as if Greek ones. For the Greeks were formerly called Ἴωνες [Iōnes] Iones, as we have proved elsewhere; and in Hebrew יונים jonim, with the same letters, although today they pronounce javanim, because that pleased the Masoretes. Two things chiefly suggest that doves were named from this. One, that in Pliny, book 10, chapter 29, Theophrastus reports that doves were imported into Asia. The other, that mythical history amply shows that there were doves in Greece from all time. Thus 1. they say that the Dodonaean dove c) ἱζομένην ἐπὶ φηγὸν, αὐδάξασθαι φωνῇ ἀνθρωπίνῃ, ὡς χρεὼν εἴη, μαντήϊον αὐτόθι Διὸς γένεσθαι [hizomenēn epi phēgon, audaxasthai phōnē anthrōpinē, hōs chreōn eiē, mantēion autothi Dios genesthai], sitting on a beech tree, said with a human voice that it was fated that an oracle of Jupiter should be founded in that place, which was by far the most ancient of all Greece. 2. As from Noah, so from Deucalion they relate d) περιστερὰν, ἐκ τῆς λάρνακος ἀφιεμένην, δήλωμα γενέσθαι, χειμῶνος μὲν εἴσω πάλιν ἐνδυομένην, εὐδίας δὲ, ἀποπτᾶσαν [peristeran, ek tēs larnakos aphiemenēn, dēlōma genesthai, cheimōnos men eisō palin endyomenēn, eudias de, apoptasan], that a dove, sent out from the ark, was a sign of storm when it returned there, and of fair weather when it flew away. 3. Doves are said to have fed Jupiter, crying as an infant in Crete, with ambrosia brought from Ocean, according to Moero of Byzantium in Athenaeus, book 11,


Ζεὺς δ᾽ ἀρ᾽ ἐνὶ Κρήτῃ τρέφετο μέγας, οὐδ᾽ ἄρα τίς νιν
Ἠήδει μακάρων. ὁ δ᾽ ἀέξετο πᾶσι μέλεσσι
Τὸν μὲν ἄρα τρήρωνες ὑπὸ ζαθέῳ τρέφον ἄντρῳ,
Ἀμβροσίην φορέουσαι ἀπ᾽ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων.

Ζεὺς δ᾽ ἀρ᾽ ἐνὶ Κρήτῃ τρέφετο μέγας, οὐδ᾽ ἄρα τίς νιν Ἠήδει μακάρων. ὁ δ᾽ ἀέξετο πᾶσι μέλεσσι Τὸν μὲν ἄρα τρήρωνες ὑπὸ ζαθέῳ τρέφον ἄντρῳ, Ἀμβροσίην φορέουσαι ἀπ᾽ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων. [Zeus d᾽ ar᾽ eni Krētē trepheto megas, oud᾽ ara tis nin ēēdei makarōn. ho d᾽ aexeto pasi melessi; ton men ara trērōnes hypo zatheō trephon antrō, ambrosiēn phoreousai ap᾽ Ōkeanoio rhoaōn.]


In Creta nutriebatur magnus Iupiter, neque eum Beatorum quisquam noverat. Is autem omnibus membris crescebat. Ipsum porro alebant in antro divino columbae, ambrosiam ex Oceani fluentis afferentes. Quod sumtum ex Odyss. μ´. ubi columbae

In Crete great Jupiter was nourished, and none of the Blessed knew him. And he grew in all his limbs. Doves, moreover, fed him in the divine cave, bringing ambrosia from the streams of Ocean. This is taken from Odyssey μ´ [12], where doves


— — ἀμβροσίην Διῒ πατρὶ φέρουσιν, — — ambrosiam Iovi patri ferunt. II, 527 Unde est, quod in Plutarchi Symposio Cleodemus Chersiae poetae dicit, Εἰ τὴν col. 4 ἀμβροσίαν τῷ Διῒ πελειάδες τινὲς κομίζουσιν, ὡς ὑμεῖς λέγετε, Si ambrosiam Iovi columbae quaedam afferunt, ut vos, poetae, dicitis. 4. In Aegio, Achaiae urbe, Iupiter, in columbam mutatus, Pthiam virginem iniisse fertur. Athenaeus, libro nono, Αὐτοκράτης ἐν τοῖς Ἀχαικοῖς καὶ τὸν Διὰ ἱστορεῖ μεταβα-λεῖν τὴν μορφὴν εἰς περιστερὰν, ἐρασθέντα παρθένου Φθίας ὄνομα ἐν Αἰγείῳ. Autocrates in Achaicis narrat etiam, ipsum Iovem, virginem, Pthiam nomine, in Aegio adamantem, formam in columbam mutasse. Ita etiam Aelianus Variorum libri primi capite decimo quinto. 5. Argonautae, inter coëuntes Symplegades trajecturi, a Phineo vate moniti sunt, columbam emittere, quae si salva per il-las transiisset, ipsi quoque sequerentur: quod et fecerunt. Hujus columbae meminerunt Apollonius libro secundo Argonauticων, Asclepiades libro secundo Τραγῳδουμένων, Apollodorus libro primo Bibliothecae, Hyginus Fabula decima nona, et alii non pauci. 6. Ctesylla, Alcidamantis Cei filia, in partu mortua, cum efferretur, ἐκ τῆς στρομνῆς πελειὰς ἐξέπτη, καὶ τὸ σῶμα τῆς Κτησύλλης ἀφανὲς ἐγένετο, columba e sandapila evolavit, et Ctesyllae corpus evanuit. Ita Nicander libro tertio Ἑτεροιουμένων. Hinc Ovidius de Medea, in aëre vecta, Metamorphoseως libri septimi Fabula duodecima,

— — ἀμβροσίην Διῒ πατρὶ φέρουσιν [ambrosiēn Dii patri pherousin], — — bring ambrosia to father Jupiter. II, 527 Hence it is that in Plutarch's Symposium Cleodemus says to the poet Chersias: Εἰ τὴν col. 4 ἀμβροσίαν τῷ Διῒ πελειάδες τινὲς κομίζουσιν, ὡς ὑμεῖς λέγετε [Ei tēn ambrosian tō Dii peleiades tines komizousin, hōs hymeis legete], If certain doves bring ambrosia to Jupiter, as you poets say. 4. At Aegium, a city of Achaea, Jupiter, changed into a dove, is said to have lain with the maiden Phthia. Athenaeus, book 9: Αὐτοκράτης ἐν τοῖς Ἀχαικοῖς καὶ τὸν Διὰ ἱστορεῖ μεταβαλεῖν τὴν μορφὴν εἰς περιστερὰν, ἐρασθέντα παρθένου Φθίας ὄνομα ἐν Αἰγείῳ [Autokratēs en tois Achaikois kai ton Dia historei metabalein tēn morphēn eis peristeran, erasthenta parthenou Phthias onoma en Aigeiō]. Autocrates in his Achaica relates that Jupiter himself, loving a maiden named Phthia in Aegium, changed his form into a dove. So too Aelian, Varia book 1, chapter 15. 5. The Argonauts, about to pass between the clashing Symplegades, were advised by the seer Phineus to send out a dove, and if it passed through them safely, they too should follow; and this they did. This dove is mentioned by Apollonius, book 2 of the Argonautica, Asclepiades, book 2 of the Τραγῳδούμενα [Tragōdoumena], Apollodorus, book 1 of the Bibliotheca, Hyginus, Fable 19, and not a few others. 6. When Ctesylla, daughter of Alcidamas of Ceos, who died in childbirth, was being carried out for burial, ἐκ τῆς στρομνῆς πελειὰς ἐξέπτη, καὶ τὸ σῶμα τῆς Κτησύλλης ἀφανὲς ἐγένετο [ek tēs stromnēs peleias exeptē, kai to sōma tēs Ktēsyllēs aphanes egeneto], a dove flew out of the bier, and the body of Ctesylla vanished. So Nicander, book 3 of the Ἑτεροιούμενα [Heteroioumena]. Hence Ovid, of Medea borne through the air, Metamorphoses book 7, Fable 12,


Transit et antiquae Cartheïa moenia Ceae,
Qua pater Alcidamas placidam de corpore natae
Miraturus erat nasci potuisse columbam.

He passes also the walls of ancient Carthaea on Ceos,
where the father Alcidamas was to marvel that a gentle dove
could be born from the body of his daughter.


7. Apud eundem (Metam. lib. 13. Fab. 4.) Oenotropae, Anii filiae, ut pater Anius Anchisae narrat,

7. In the same author (Metam. book 13, Fable 4), the Oenotropae, daughters of Anius, as their father Anius tells Anchises,


— — — pennas sumsere, tuaeque
Conjugis in volucres niveas abiere columbas.

— — — took on wings, and
were turned into the snow-white birds of your consort, doves.


Id est, in Veneris aves, quae Anchisae conjux fuerat. Quae, utut fabulosa, tamen ad scopum nostrum faciunt. Inde enim hoc saltem colligas, ex eorum sententia, qui has fabulas confinxerunt, columbas in Graacia semper fuisse. 8. Quid quod Boeoticam Thisben, et Lacedaemoniam Messenem a copia columbarum Homerus vocat πολυτρήρωνας Iliad. 2.? Et juxta Smyrnam septem insulas Peristerides, id est, Columbarias, recenset Plinius libri quinti capite trigesimo primo. Columbas igitur, post diluvium, primo in Graeciam et vicina loca contendisse, verissimile est, atque inde paullatim in reliquum orbem esse dispersas.

That is, into the birds of Venus, who had been the consort of Anchises. These stories, however fabulous, nevertheless serve our purpose. For from them you may at least gather that, in the opinion of those who invented these fables, there had always been doves in Greece. 8. What of the fact that Homer calls Boeotian Thisbe and Laconian Messene πολυτρήρωνας [polytērōnas], from their abundance of doves, Iliad 2? And Pliny, book 5, chapter 31, lists near Smyrna seven islands called Peristerides, that is, Columbariae [Dove Islands]. It is therefore very likely that after the Flood doves first made their way into Greece and the neighbouring places, and from there were gradually dispersed over the rest of the world.


Dices, haec afferri frustra, cum antiquissimis illis a diluvio temporibus Syriam etiam fuisse πολυτρήρονα tam ex sacris probetur, quam ex profanis historiis. Nam in sacris Abraham, quo apud Graecos nihil antiquius, jubetur offerre Deo turturem et columbam, Gen. XV, 9. Et passim in Lege Mosis praescribuntur II, 528 sacrificia ex turturibus et pullis columbarum. Exempla vide Levit. I, 14. et V, 7. 11. et XII, 6. et XIV, 22. et XXV, 14. 29. et Num. VI, 10. In profanis etiam Abrahamo aequalis, ut creditur, Semiramis, in locis desertis et petrosis, circa Ascalonem exposita fuisse narratur, ἐν οἷς πολλοῦ πλήθους περιστε-ρῶν ἐννοσσεύειν εἰωθότος, παραδόξως τροφῆς καὶ σωτηρίας τυχεῖν τὸ βρέφος, in quibus cum columbarum magna copia nidificare consuevisset, infans miro modo nutrita et servata sit. Quin Semiramidis nomen indidem deducitur, quasi sit κα-τὰ τὴν τῶν Σύρων διάλεκτον παρωνομασμένον ἀπὸ τῶν περιστερῶν, Syrorum lingua sumtum a columbis. Ita ex Ctesia Diodorus libro secundo. Et R. Azarias, in Meor Enajim capite vigesimo primo, deducit a voce זמיר zemir, quae cantum avium, et speciatim turturis, designat Cant. II, 12. verba sic habent: נקראת סמיראמיס אשר לפי דבריו בלשון הארמי יורה על צפצוף העוף ולדעתי הוא מלשון עת הזמיר הגיע בחלוף הזין בסמך וכן בארמי פק דנטין זמרא דמנא זמרא דפומא ולזה אות דגלה היה יונה Vocatur Semiramis, quod, juxta ipsius verba, (id est, Diodori, quem citaverat) lingua Syra cantum avium significat. Quod videtur sumtum ex voce זמיר zemir, cum dicitur Cant. II, 12. col. 5 „Tempus zemir, id est, cantus, advenit, et vox turturis audita est in terra nostra.“ Nam etiam Syriace in Talmudico tractatu Gittin capite primo זמרא דמנא zemara demana est cantus organicus, et זמרא דפומא zemara dephuma cantus oralis. Atque ideo pro vexilli signo columbam habuit Semiramis. Quin contendit in sequentibus, non solam Semiramidem, sed et omnes Assyriae reges columbam habuisse pro vexillorum symbolo. Atque inde esse, quod pro Assyriorum ira et gladio, Ieremias dixerat חרון היונה, iram columbae, Ierem. XXV, 38. et חרב היונה, gladium columbae, Ierem. XLVI, 16, et L, 16. Quod ex Hieronymi versione confirmat, et Thomae Aquinatis Commentariis in Ieremiam. Eodem etiam id refert, quod Ierusalem Sophon. III, 1. vocatur היונה, columba, quasi Propheta eam arguat, שהיא במעשיו דומה לבבל אשר אות דגלה יונה, quod in operibus suis sit Babyloni similis, quae pro militari signo in vexillo columbam habuit. Et hunc sequutus R. David Ganz, libro secundo Chronologiae ad annum 1958. Signum vexilli Semiramidis fuit figura columbae. Quod vexilli signum imitati sunt omnes Assyriae reges. Unde Ieremias capitis XXV, versu 28. „Propter iram columbae“; et capitis XLVI, versu 6. „Coram gladio columbae“. His addunt veteres, Semiramidem in columbam fuisse mutatam. Diodorus ubi supra, Ἔνιοι δὲ μυθολογοῦντές φασιν αὐτὴν γενέσθαι περιστερὰν, καὶ πολλῶν ὀρνέ-ων εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν καταπετασθέντων, μετ᾽ ἐκείνων ἐκπετασθῆναι· Alii autem eam fabulantur factam esse columbam, et cum plures aves in domum advolassent, cum iis avolasse. Ovidius, Metam. lib. 4. Fab. 2. ubi de matre Derceto,

You will say that these things are adduced in vain, since in those most ancient times after the Flood Syria too was πολυτρήρονα [polytērona], as is proved both from sacred and from profane histories. For in the sacred histories Abraham, than whom the Greeks have nothing more ancient, is commanded to offer to God a turtledove and a dove, Gen 15:9. And throughout the Law of Moses sacrifices of turtledoves and young doves are prescribed II, 528. For examples see Lev 1:14 and V, 7. 11. and XII, 6. and XIV, 22. and XXV, 14. 29. and Num 6:10. In the profane histories too, Semiramis, believed to be a contemporary of Abraham, is said to have been exposed in desert and rocky places near Ascalon, ἐν οἷς πολλοῦ πλήθους περιστερῶν ἐννοσσεύειν εἰωθότος, παραδόξως τροφῆς καὶ σωτηρίας τυχεῖν τὸ βρέφος [en hois pollou plēthous peristerōn ennosseuein eiōthotos, paradoxōs trophēs kai sōtērias tychein to brephos], where, since a great multitude of doves was accustomed to nest, the infant was wondrously fed and preserved. Indeed, the name of Semiramis is derived from the same source, as being κατὰ τὴν τῶν Σύρων διάλεκτον παρωνομασμένον ἀπὸ τῶν περιστερῶν [kata tēn tōn Syrōn dialekton parōnomasmenon apo tōn peristerōn], taken from doves in the language of the Syrians. So Diodorus, from Ctesias, in book 2. And R. Azarias [=Azariah de' Rossi, Meʾor ʿEnayim], in Meor Enajim, chapter 21, derives it from the word זמיר zemir, which denotes the song of birds, and specifically of the turtledove, Song 2:12. His words are as follows: נקראת סמיראמיס אשר לפי דבריו בלשון הארמי יורה על צפצוף העוף ולדעתי הוא מלשון עת הזמיר הגיע בחלוף הזין בסמך וכן בארמי פק דנטין זמרא דמנא זמרא דפומא ולזה אות דגלה היה יונה She is called Semiramis, which, according to his words, (that is, those of Diodorus, whom he had cited) signifies in the Syrian language the song of birds. This seems to be taken from the word זמיר zemir, as it is said in Song 2:12 col. 5 "The time of zemir, that is, of song, has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land." For also in Syriac, in the Talmudic tractate Gittin, chapter 1, זמרא דמנא zemara demana is instrumental music, and זמרא דפומא zemara dephuma vocal music. And therefore Semiramis had a dove as the emblem of her banner. Indeed, he contends in what follows that not only Semiramis but all the kings of Assyria had a dove as the symbol of their banners. And that this is why, for the wrath and sword of the Assyrians, Jeremiah had said חרון היונה, the wrath of the dove, Jer 25:38 and חרב היונה, the sword of the dove, Jer 46:16, and L, 16. This he confirms from the version of Jerome and from the Commentaries of Thomas Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)] on Jeremiah. To the same he also refers the fact that Jerusalem in Zeph 3:1 is called היונה, the dove, as if the Prophet were reproaching her שהיא במעשיו דומה לבבל אשר אות דגלה יונה, that in her deeds she is like Babylon, which had a dove on its banner as its military emblem. And following him, R. David Ganz, in book 2 of his Chronology, at the year 1958: The emblem of the banner of Semiramis was the figure of a dove. This banner emblem all the kings of Assyria imitated. Hence Jeremiah, chapter XXV, verse 28: "Because of the wrath of the dove"; and chapter XLVI, verse 6: "Before the sword of the dove". To this the ancients add that Semiramis was changed into a dove. Diodorus, in the place cited above: Ἔνιοι δὲ μυθολογοῦντές φασιν αὐτὴν γενέσθαι περιστερὰν, καὶ πολλῶν ὀρνέων εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν καταπετασθέντων, μετ᾽ ἐκείνων ἐκπετασθῆναι· [Enioi de mythologountes phasin autēn genesthai peristeran, kai pollōn orneōn eis tēn oikian katapetasthentōn, met᾽ ekeinōn ekpetasthēnai] But others tell the fable that she became a dove, and that when many birds had flown into the house, she flew away with them. Ovid, Metam. book 4, Fable 2, where, concerning her mother Derceto,


An magis, ut sumtis illius filia pennis, Extremos aleis in turribus egerit annos? II, 529 Lucianus in Syria Dea, Τὸ Σεμιράμιος τέλος εἰς περιστερὰν ἀπίκετο, Semiramis in columbam versa tandem est. Athenagoras, in Legatione de eadem, Τὸ γὰρ ἀδύνατον, εἰς περιστερὰν μετέβαλεν ἡ γυνή· ὁ μύθος παρὰ Κτησίᾳ. Nam, quod impossibile est, in columbam scilicet mulier mutata est. Fabula extat apud Ctesiam. Unde est, quod apud Syros et Assyrios columbae fuerunt in multo cultu: ut in Diodoro docet Ctesias, postquam Semiramidem a columbis enutritam, et nomen sumsisse narravit: Ἃς ἀπ᾽ ἐκείνων τῶν χρόνων, οἱ κατὰ Συρίαν ἅπαντες διετέλεσαν, ὡς Θεὰς τιμῶντες· Quas ab illis temporibus Syri omnes ut Deas colere non destiterunt. Et post historiam ejusdem in columbam metamorphosis idem addit, Διὸ καὶ τοὺς Ἀσσυρίους τὴν περιστερὰν τιμᾷν ὡς Θεὸν, ἀπαθανατίζοντες τὴν Σεμίραμιν· Proinde etiam Assyrios columbam ut Deam venerari, ut Semiramim a morte vindicent. Xenophon quoque Cyri minoris li-bro primo, ubi de Chali, Syriae amnis, piscibus: Οὓς οἱ Σύροι Θεοὺς ἐνόμιζον, καὶ ἀδικεῖν οὐκ εἴων, οὐδὲ τὰς περιστεράς. Quos Syri Deos putabant, eosque violare, ut et columbas, vetabant. Philo apud Eusebium circa finem libri octavi Praeparationis Evangelicae, Ἀμήχανόν τι πελειάδων πλῆθος ἐπὶ τῶν τριόδων, καὶ κατ᾽ οἰκίαν ἑκάστην, ἐθεασάμην. πυνθανομένῳ δέ μοι τὴν αἰτίαν ἔφασαν, οὐ θεμιτὸν εἶναι συλλαμβάνειν. ἀπειρῆσθαι γὰρ ἐκ παλαίου τοῖς οἰκήτορσι τὴν χρῆσιν. Immensam columbarum multitudinem in triviis, et per singulas aedes (Ascalone) vidi. Et mihi causam sciscitanti responderunt, capere nefas esse. Incolis enim jam olim illarum usum fuisse interdictum. Tibullus Elegia octava,

Or rather, that, having taken wings from that daughter of hers, she spent her last years in lofty towers? II, 529 Lucian in De Syria Dea: Τὸ Σεμιράμιος τέλος εἰς περιστερὰν ἀπίκετο [To Semiramios telos eis peristeran apiketo], Semiramis was at last turned into a dove. Athenagoras, in the Legatio, on the same woman: Τὸ γὰρ ἀδύνατον, εἰς περιστερὰν μετέβαλεν ἡ γυνή· ὁ μύθος παρὰ Κτησίᾳ [To gar adynaton, eis peristeran metebalen hē gynē; ho mythos para Ktēsia]. For, what is impossible, the woman was changed into a dove. The tale is found in Ctesias. This is why among the Syrians and Assyrians doves were held in great veneration, as Ctesias teaches in Diodorus, after relating that Semiramis was nourished by doves and also took her name from them: Ἃς ἀπ᾽ ἐκείνων τῶν χρόνων, οἱ κατὰ Συρίαν ἅπαντες διετέλεσαν, ὡς Θεὰς τιμῶντες [Has ap᾽ ekeinōn tōn chronōn, hoi kata Syrian hapantes dietelesan, hōs Theas timōntes]; These, from those times on, all the Syrians have never ceased to worship as goddesses. And after the story of her metamorphosis into a dove the same author adds: Διὸ καὶ τοὺς Ἀσσυρίους τὴν περιστερὰν τιμᾷν ὡς Θεὸν, ἀπαθανατίζοντες τὴν Σεμίραμιν [Dio kai tous Assyrious tēn peristeran timan hōs Theon, apathanatizontes tēn Semiramin]; Hence the Assyrians also venerate the dove as a goddess, in order to rescue Semiramis from death. Xenophon too, in book 1 of the Cyrus the Younger, speaking of the fish of the Chalus, a river of Syria: Οὓς οἱ Σύροι Θεοὺς ἐνόμιζον, καὶ ἀδικεῖν οὐκ εἴων, οὐδὲ τὰς περιστεράς [Hous hoi Syroi Theous enomizon, kai adikein ouk eiōn, oude tas peristeras]. These the Syrians regarded as gods, and forbade anyone to harm them, as also the doves. Philo in Eusebius, near the end of book 8 of the Praeparatio Evangelica: Ἀμήχανόν τι πελειάδων πλῆθος ἐπὶ τῶν τριόδων, καὶ κατ᾽ οἰκίαν ἑκάστην, ἐθεασάμην. πυνθανομένῳ δέ μοι τὴν αἰτίαν ἔφασαν, οὐ θεμιτὸν εἶναι συλλαμβάνειν. ἀπειρῆσθαι γὰρ ἐκ παλαίου τοῖς οἰκήτορσι τὴν χρῆσιν [Amēchanon ti peleiadōn plēthos epi tōn triodōn, kai kat᾽ oikian hekastēn, etheasamēn. pynthanomenō de moi tēn aitian ephasan, ou themiton einai syllambanein. apeirēsthai gar ek palaiou tois oikētorsi tēn chrēsin]. I saw an immense multitude of doves at the crossroads and in every house (at Ascalon). And when I asked the reason, they answered that it was unlawful to catch them, for their use had long ago been forbidden to the inhabitants. Tibullus, Elegy 8:


Alba Palaestino culta columba viro.

The white dove, sacred to the man of Palestine.


Al. Syro, aut suo. Hyginus Fab. 197. Syri pisces et columbas ex Deorum numero habent; non edunt. Lucianus, ubi supra, de Hierapolitanis: Ὀρνίθων τε αὐτέοισι περιστερὴ δοκέει χρῆμα ἱρώτατον, καὶ οὐδὲ ψαύειν αὐτέων δικαιεῦσι· Columba ipsis videtur avium sanctissima, ac ne eam quidem tangere aequum putant. Item, Ὄρνιθας τοὺς μὲν ἄλλους σιτέονται· περιστερὴν δὲ μούνην οὐ σιτέονται, ἀλ- col. 6 λὰ σφίσι ἥδε ἱερή. Avibus quidem aliis vescuntur, sed a sola columba abstinent, quae illis sacra est. Phornutus libro De Diis in capite de Rhea, Ἔοικε δὲ ἡ αὐτὴ ἡ παρὰ Σύροις Ἄρταγα εἶναι, ἣν διὰ τὸ περιστερὰς καὶ ἰχθύος ἀπέχεσθαι τι-μῶσι· Videtur haec eadem esse, quae apud Syros Artaga (aliis Atergatis et Derceto) quam abstinendo a pisce et columba colunt. Clemens Alexandrinus in Protreptico, Οὐδέ γε τῶν τὴν Φοινίκην Σύρων κατοικούντων (ἐκλήσομαι) ὧν οἱ μὲν τὰς περιστερὰς, οἱ δὲ τοὺς ἰχθῦς οὕτω σέβουσι περιττῶς, ὡς Ἠλεῖοι τὸν Δία· Neque eorum, qui in Phoenice degunt, Syrorum obliviscar, quorum alii columbas, alii pisces tam impense colunt, quam Elei Iovem. Meor enajim, ונמצאו קצת אמות שבכה אהבו את זכר סמיראמיס ואות דגלה שאסרו על עצמן לאכול את בני היונה Et gentes quaedam repertae sunt, quae Semiramidis memoriam et II, 530 signum vexilli ejus ita coluerunt, ut columbarum esum sibi interdixerint. Neque Samaritani fuerunt ab hac superstitione immunes, si quidem Iudaeis credimus. Talmud, tractatu Cholin cap. 1. fol. 6. a. de Cuthaeis, seu Samaritanis, אמר רב נחמן בר יצחק דמות יונה מצאו להן בראש הר גריזים שהיו עובדין אותה Dixit Rab Nachman, Isaaci filins, columbae imaginem iis invenerunt, quam colebant in monte Garizim. Glossa Talmudici tractatus Avodazera fol. 26. b. אל ימול כותי שמל לשם דמות שנמצאו בראש הר גריזים ועובדין לה עבודה כדאמר בהכל שיחטין ומלו את בניהם לשם יונה זו, Non circumcidet Cuthaeus, qui circumcidit in nomine imaginis, quam invenerunt in vertice montis Garizim, et il-lam colunt, ut traditur in capite (Cholin supra citato, cujus initium est) Omnes mactant: et circumcidunt filios suos in nomine columbae hujus. Meor enajim, קרוב בעיני להאמין שהכותיים אשר הושיב מלך אשור ובבל בשומרון לאות ולעד הכנעם באהבה אל מלכם ההוא אשר אות דגלה יונה חבבו אותה והקימוהו ליראתם בראש הר גריזים אשר עם שכם ראש ממלכת שומרון בימים ההם, Mihi persuasissimum est, Cuthaeos, quos Assyriae et Babyloniae rex in Samariam deportaverat, in amoris cultusque signum, et testimonium erga regem suum, qui columbam habebat pro vexilli symbolo, columbam amasse, et statuam, quam colevent ei erexisse in vertice montis Garizim prope urbem Sichem, quae tum erat metropolis regni Samaritici. Tsemach David in Templi secundi Chronologia ad an-num 881. Diebus R. Meir invenerunt Cuthaeorum imaginem columbae in monte Garizim, ut habetur capite primo Cholin. Et decrevit is, ut omnino judicarentur tanquam gentiles terrae. (1).

Al. Syro, or suo. Hyginus, Fab. 197: the Syrians regard fish and doves as among the gods; they do not eat them. Lucian, in the place cited above, on the Hierapolitans: Ὀρνίθων τε αὐτέοισι περιστερὴ δοκέει χρῆμα ἱρώτατον, καὶ οὐδὲ ψαύειν αὐτέων δικαιεῦσι· [Ornithōn te auteoisi peristerē dokeei chrēma hirōtaton, kai oude psauein auteōn dikaieusi] Among birds the dove seems to them the most sacred, and they do not think it right even to touch it. Likewise: Ὄρνιθας τοὺς μὲν ἄλλους σιτέονται· περιστερὴν δὲ μούνην οὐ σιτέονται, ἀλλὰ σφίσι ἥδε ἱερή. [Ornithas tous men allous siteontai; peristerēn de mounēn ou siteontai, alla sphisi hēde hierē] col. 6 They eat other birds, but abstain from the dove alone, which is sacred to them. Phornutus [=L. Annaeus Cornutus, De natura deorum], in the book On the Gods, in the chapter on Rhea: Ἔοικε δὲ ἡ αὐτὴ ἡ παρὰ Σύροις Ἄρταγα εἶναι, ἣν διὰ τὸ περιστερὰς καὶ ἰχθύος ἀπέχεσθαι τιμῶσι· [Eoike de hē autē hē para Syrois Artaga einai, hēn dia to peristeras kai ichthyos apechesthai timōsi] She seems to be the same as the one whom the Syrians call Artaga (others Atergatis and Derceto) and whom they worship by abstaining from fish and the dove. Clement of Alexandria in the Protrepticus: Οὐδέ γε τῶν τὴν Φοινίκην Σύρων κατοικούντων (ἐκλήσομαι) ὧν οἱ μὲν τὰς περιστερὰς, οἱ δὲ τοὺς ἰχθῦς οὕτω σέβουσι περιττῶς, ὡς Ἠλεῖοι τὸν Δία· [Oude ge tōn tēn Phoinikēn Syrōn katoikountōn (eklēsomai) hōn hoi men tas peristeras, hoi de tous ichthys houtō sebousi perittōs, hōs Ēleioi ton Dia] Nor shall I forget the Syrians who live in Phoenicia, some of whom worship doves, others fish, as fervently as the Eleans worship Jupiter. Meor enajim: ונמצאו קצת אמות שבכה אהבו את זכר סמיראמיס ואות דגלה שאסרו על עצמן לאכול את בני היונה And certain nations were found who so revered the memory of Semiramis and the II, 530 emblem of her banner that they forbade themselves to eat doves. Nor were the Samaritans free from this superstition, if indeed we believe the Jews. The Talmud, tractate Cholin, ch. 1, fol. 6a, on the Cuthaeans or Samaritans: אמר רב נחמן בר יצחק דמות יונה מצאו להן בראש הר גריזים שהיו עובדין אותה Said Rab Nachman, son of Isaac: they found among them the image of a dove, which they worshipped on Mount Gerizim. The gloss on the Talmudic tractate Avodazera, fol. 26b: אל ימול כותי שמל לשם דמות שנמצאו בראש הר גריזים ועובדין לה עבודה כדאמר בהכל שיחטין ומלו את בניהם לשם יונה זו, A Cuthaean shall not circumcise, for he circumcises in the name of the image which they found on the summit of Mount Gerizim, and they worship it, as is related in the chapter (of Cholin, cited above, which begins) "All slaughter": and they circumcise their sons in the name of this dove. Meor enajim: קרוב בעיני להאמין שהכותיים אשר הושיב מלך אשור ובבל בשומרון לאות ולעד הכנעם באהבה אל מלכם ההוא אשר אות דגלה יונה חבבו אותה והקימוהו ליראתם בראש הר גריזים אשר עם שכם ראש ממלכת שומרון בימים ההם, I am fully persuaded that the Cuthaeans, whom the king of Assyria and Babylonia had deported to Samaria, as a sign and testimony of their love and devotion toward their king, who had the dove as the emblem of his banner, loved the dove, and erected a statue, which they worshipped, on the summit of Mount Gerizim, near the city of Shechem, which was then the capital of the Samaritan kingdom. Tsemach David, in the Chronology of the Second Temple, at the year 881: In the days of R. Meir they found the Cuthaeans' image of a dove on Mount Gerizim, as is stated in the first chapter of Cholin. And he decreed that they should be treated in every respect as gentiles of the land. R1.


Ex his videatur posse confici, tam in Syria, quam in Graecia columbas ab omni aevo nidificasse. Tamen est, quod regeratur, nempe Mosis quidem aetate etiam a plebejis in Israele oblatos fuisse בני יונה, pullos columbarum, ut Lex diserte praecipit: sed, an Abraham idem obtulerit, in quaestionem posse vocari. Neque enim legitur obtulisse תור ובן יונה turturem et pullum columbae, ut jubetur II, 531 in Lege Mosis, sed תור וגוזל turturum et gozal, quae vox non solum significat pullum columbae, proprie dictae, sed et pullum turturis, et palumbi, et liviae, et vinaginis, et avis alia, si qua est, quae ad columbinum genus referatur. Damir in capite De القطا alkata, quomodo vocant Arabes quoddam palumbi genus, يقال القطا والحمام وانواعها امهات الجوازل والجوازل فراخها الواحد جوزل Alkata et columba, et col. 7 aves homogeneae dicuntur matres algavvazil. Et Algavvazil sunt pulli earum a singulari gauzal. Porro جوزل gauzal Arabibus id ipsum est, quod Hebraeis גוזל gozal. Proinde, quia τοῦ gozal sunt variae species, cum pipio praecise significatur, quandoque additur διακριτικῶς, gozal, columbae pullus. Ita in Chal- daeo Cantici paraphraste capitis primi versu decimo quinto, Oculi tui sunt כגוזלין בני יונתא, ut gozalin pulli columbae. Et Vajikra Rabba capite vigesimo secundo de Tito, imperatore, קראו לרופאים ומצאו בו כמו גוזל בן יונה והיה בו משקל שתי לטראות, Vocaverunt medicos, qui (cerebro ejus discisso), in illo in- venerunt tanquam gozal columbae filium, ponderis duarum librarum. A pipitu dicitur gozal, vel gauzal, ut latine pipio. Nam الجزل algezel est pipitus. In Alcamus redditur صوت الحمام vox columbae; nempe pipientis adhuc, et nondum adultae. Itaque falluntur, qui גוזל gozal referunt ad verbum גזל gazal, id est, rapere; quia rapinae est obnoxius. Syri per metathesim ܙܘܓܠ zogal dicunt pro ܓܘܙܠ gozal. Sed Poeni olim gozol. Unde peristereon Punice חציר־גוזול azirgozol, id est, herba pipionis, in Herbario Apuleii capite sexagesimo quinto.

From this it might seem possible to conclude that doves have nested in Syria as well as in Greece from all time. Yet there is an objection to be raised: in the age of Moses, it is true, בני יונה, young of doves, were offered even by common people in Israel, as the Law expressly prescribes; but whether Abraham offered the same can be called into question. For we do not read that he offered תור ובן יונה, a turtledove and a young dove, as is commanded II, 531 in the Law of Moses, but תור וגוזל, a turtledove and a gozal. This word signifies not only the young of the dove properly so called, but also the young of the turtledove, of the wood pigeon, of the livia, of the vinago, and of any other bird that may be assigned to the dove kind. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], in the chapter On القطا [al-qaṭā] alkata, as the Arabs call a certain kind of wood pigeon, writes: يقال القطا والحمام وانواعها امهات الجوازل والجوازل فراخها الواحد جوزل [yuqāl al-qaṭā wa-l-ḥamām wa-anwāʿuhā ummahāt al-jawāzil wa-l-jawāzil firākhuhā al-wāḥid jawzal] "Alkata and the dove, and col. 7 birds of the same kind are called the mothers of the algavvazil. And the algavvazil are their young, from the singular gauzal." Now جوزل [jawzal] gauzal is for the Arabs exactly what גוזל gozal is for the Hebrews. Accordingly, since there are various species of gozal, when a pipio [squab] is meant precisely, there is sometimes added, by way of distinction, "gozal, young of the dove." Thus in the Chaldee paraphrast of the Song of Songs, chapter 1, verse 15: "Your eyes are כגוזלין בני יונתא, like gozalin, young of the dove." And Vajikra Rabba [=Leviticus Rabbah], chapter 22, on the emperor Titus: קראו לרופאים ומצאו בו כמו גוזל בן יונה והיה בו משקל שתי לטראות, "They called the physicians, who (when his skull had been cut open) found in it something like a gozal, a young of the dove, weighing two pounds." It is called gozal, or gauzal, from its peeping, just as in Latin pipio. For الجزل [al-jazl] algezel is pipitus [peeping]. In the Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] it is rendered صوت الحمام [ṣawt al-ḥamām] the voice of the dove, namely of one still peeping and not yet grown. Therefore those are mistaken who derive גוזל gozal from the verb גזל gazal, that is, to seize, because it is exposed to plunder. The Syrians, by metathesis, say ܙܘܓܠ [זוגל] zogal instead of ܓܘܙܠ [גוזל] gozal. But the Phoenicians of old said gozol. Hence peristereon is in Punic חציר־גוזול azirgozol, that is, herb of the squab, in the Herbarium of Apuleius, chapter 65.


Iam de columbis Semiramidis posset id ipsum regeri. Quippe, licet etiam יונים jonim, id est, columbas domesticas, et quae proprie sic dicuntur, coluerint Syri posteriores in gratiam Semiramidis; sylvestres tamen columbas illi adfuisse, vel ex Ctesia videtur posse colligi. Cum loca, in quibus degebant illae columbae, deserta et petrosa vocet, ἐρήμους, καὶ πετρώδεις τόπους. Proinde nomen Semiramidis, inde sumptum, ab Hesychio explicatur περιστερὰ ὄρειος, columba montana. Quam vocem esse Arabicam, non Syram, ut putatur, alibi docuimus, et scriptam fuisse Serimam, quod διὰ τὴν εὐφωνίαν Graeci mutarunt in Σεμίραμιν. Nempe Arabibus حمام himam est columba, et سراة sera mons, شعرا sera sylva, صحرا sahra desertum: ex quarum vocum una aliqua eum حمام himam juncta factum nomen Serimam pro montis, aut sylvae, aut deserti columba. Qualis est compositio in verbis כרמיון charmion, vel כרמיונא charmiona, de quibus dictum, et חריונים chirjonim, vel דביונים dibjonim, de II, 532 quibus dicturi sumus. Sed haec praecipuum, quod ex historia Semiramidis columbas jam olim fuisse in Syria nullo modo probari potest; quia illius tempus est plane incertum. Nam, si Ctesiae stamus, Scriptori valde fabuloso, Nini uxor fuit Semiramis, cujus regnum incidet in Abrahami tempora. Sed Semiramin alii Belochi filiam faciunt, qui annis plus quingentis Nino posterior fuit. Hinc Eusebius ad numerum 582. qui decimus est a morte Iosuae: Assyriorum octavus decimus Belochus annis XXV. cujus filia Atossa, quae et Semiramis, regnavit cum patre annis XII. Et Photius auctore 186. de Canone Hist. 9. Ὅσα οἱ ἄλλοι περὶ Ἀττόσης Ἀσσυρίου ἀναγράφουσι, ταῦθ᾽ οὗτος εἰς Σεμίραμιν ἀνα-φέρει· Quaecunque alii de Atossa Assyria scribunt, is refert ad Semiramin. Sed, quod mirere magis, si Herodoto credimus libro primo, Semiramis nonnisi πέν-τε γενεαῖς, quinque generationibus, id est, annis ad summum ducentis, Nitocri vetustior fuit, illius Laboniti matre, quem devicit Cyrus. Cum inter Cyrum et Belochum anni plus mille, inter eundem et Ninum anni intercedant mille quingenti, vel sexcenti. Neque vero referri possunt gesta Semiramidis ad Abrahami aetatem, qua regem שנער, seu Babyloniae, regulum fuisse colligere est ex Gen. XIV. Et aeque incertum, quod quidam asserunt, Babyloniae reges columbam col. 8 habuisse pro signo militari: cum vetus auctor nullus citetur, qui hoc referat (2). Et Cyrum verissimile est, postquam Babylonios imperio suo subjecit, eadem usurpasse signa militaria, quae habuerant Medi et Assyrii, antecessores. Eum autem pro signo aquilam habuisse, constat ex his Xenophontis libro septimo Cyropaediae, Ἦν δ᾽ αὐτῷ τὸ σημεῖον ἀετὸς χρυσοῦς ἐπὶ δόρατος μακροῦ ἀνατεταμέ-νος. Erat autem ipsi pro signo aquila aurea, in longa hasta extensa. Quod exinde Persarum reges omnes imitati sunt. Idem Xenophon, Καὶ νῦν δὲ ἔτι τοῦτο τὸ σημεῖον τῷ Περσῶν βασιλεῖ διαμένει· Hoc etiam signum hodieque restat Persarum regi. Curtius libro tertio, ubi de exercitu Darii: Inter haec aquilam auream, pennas extendenti similem, sacraverant. Philostratus in Heroicis capite de Themistocle, Μῆδοι ταῦτα, καὶ Βαβυλὼν μέση, καὶ τὸ σημεῖον τὸ βασίλειον ὁ χρυσοῦς ἐπὶ τῆς πέλτης ἀετός· Medi haec, et Babylon media, et signum militare aurea super hastam aquila. Itaque in Ieremia [XXV, 38. XLVI,16. L,16.] חרב היונה non est gladius columbae, ut quidem puto, sed gladius opprimens, vel devastans, qualis Babyloniorum fuit sub rege Nebucadnetsare (3). Proinde II, 533 de eodem dicit propheta Ierem. XLVI, 14. אכלה חרב סביביך, Te consumsit gladius circumquaque. Sed et Samaritanos columbas coluisse, prorsus est fabulosum. Quae idola coluerint, cum primum ex Assyria in Samariam translati sunt, refertur 2 Reg. XVII, 30. 31. Viri Babylonii fecerunt Succoth-Benoth, Chuthaei fecerunt Nergal, etc. At ibi de columba, aut ejus imagine, ab iis culta, ne γρῦ quidem Sacra Historia. Neque id iis uspiam a Iosepho objectum, qui multis locis acriter in eos invehitur. Videsis Antiquitatum Iudaicarum li-brum nonum, et undecimum in fine; et libri duodecimi caput primum et septimum; et libri decimi tertii caput sextum; et libri decimi octavi caput tertium et quintum; et libri vigesimi caput quintum. Neque ulla ratione potuisset consistere columbae, aut ejus imaginis cultus cum Lege Mosis, quam admittebant. Nam, ut taceam, simulachra omnia toties et tam diserte a Mose prohiberi, quo tandem praetextu ab iis coli potuisset id ipsum animal, quod in sacrificiis ad Deum mactare jubebantur? Tamen haud dubie verum est, quod Xenophon, Ctesias, Lucianus atque alii testes αὐτόπται asserunt, Syros et Assyrios aut columbas ut Deas coluisse, aut saltem ab iis abstinuisse tanquam a re sacra. Sed quo praecise tempore in Syriam, aut Assyriam invecta fuerit haec superstitio, nemo facile dixerit.

Now, the same objection could be raised regarding the doves of Semiramis. For although the later Syrians also worshipped יונים jonim, that is, domestic doves, those properly so called, out of regard for Semiramis, it nevertheless seems possible to infer, even from Ctesias, that wild doves were attendant on her. For he calls the places in which those doves lived desert and rocky, ἐρήμους, καὶ πετρώδεις τόπους [erēmous, kai petrōdeis topous]. Accordingly the name of Semiramis, taken from this, is explained by Hesychius as περιστερὰ ὄρειος [peristera oreios], mountain dove. We have shown elsewhere that this word is Arabic, not Syrian as is supposed, and that it was written Serimam, which the Greeks changed διὰ τὴν εὐφωνίαν [dia tēn euphōnian] into Σεμίραμιν [Semiramin]. For among the Arabs حمام [ḥmām] himam is dove, and سراة [srāh] sera mountain, شعرا [shʿrā] sera forest, صحرا [ṣḥrā] sahra desert; from some one of these words joined with حمام [ḥmām] himam the name Serimam was formed, for dove of the mountain, or of the forest, or of the desert. Such is the composition in the words כרמיון charmion or כרמיונא charmiona, of which we have spoken, and חריונים chirjonim or דביונים dibjonim, of II, 532 which we shall speak. But the chief point is this: from the history of Semiramis it can in no way be proved that doves were already worshipped in Syria in ancient times, because her date is quite uncertain. For if we follow Ctesias, a highly fabulous writer, Semiramis was the wife of Ninus, whose reign would fall in the times of Abraham. But others make Semiramis the daughter of Belochus, who was more than five hundred years later than Ninus. Hence Eusebius at the number 582, which is the tenth year from the death of Joshua: Eighteenth king of the Assyrians, Belochus, for 25 years; whose daughter Atossa, who is also Semiramis, reigned with her father for 12 years. And Photius, on author 186, concerning the Canon, Hist. 9: Ὅσα οἱ ἄλλοι περὶ Ἀττόσης Ἀσσυρίου ἀναγράφουσι, ταῦθ᾽ οὗτος εἰς Σεμίραμιν ἀναφέρει· [Hosa hoi alloi peri Attosēs Assyriou anagraphousi, tauth᾽ houtos eis Semiramin anapherei] Whatever others write about Atossa the Assyrian, he refers to Semiramis. But, what is more surprising, if we believe Herodotus in his first book, Semiramis was older only by πέντε γενεαῖς [pente geneais], five generations, that is, at most two hundred years, than Nitocris, the mother of that Labonitus whom Cyrus defeated. Yet between Cyrus and Belochus more than a thousand years intervene, and between him and Ninus fifteen or sixteen hundred. Nor can the deeds of Semiramis be referred to the age of Abraham, when, as may be gathered from Gen. XIV, the king of שנער, or Babylonia, was a petty prince. And equally uncertain is what some assert, that the kings of Babylonia had the dove col. 8 as a military standard, since no ancient author is cited who reports this R2. And it is most probable that Cyrus, after subjecting the Babylonians to his rule, adopted the same military standards that his predecessors, the Medes and Assyrians, had had. But that he had an eagle as his standard is clear from these words of Xenophon in the seventh book of the Cyropaedia: Ἦν δ᾽ αὐτῷ τὸ σημεῖον ἀετὸς χρυσοῦς ἐπὶ δόρατος μακροῦ ἀνατεταμένος [Ēn d᾽ autō to sēmeion aetos chrysous epi doratos makrou anatetamenos]. His standard was a golden eagle, stretched out upon a long spear. This all the kings of the Persians thereafter imitated. The same Xenophon: Καὶ νῦν δὲ ἔτι τοῦτο τὸ σημεῖον τῷ Περσῶν βασιλεῖ διαμένει· [Kai nyn de eti touto to sēmeion tō Persōn basilei diamenei] This standard still remains even today for the king of the Persians. Curtius, book 3, on the army of Darius: Among these they had consecrated a golden eagle, resembling one spreading its wings. Philostratus in the Heroica, in the chapter on Themistocles: Μῆδοι ταῦτα, καὶ Βαβυλὼν μέση, καὶ τὸ σημεῖον τὸ βασίλειον ὁ χρυσοῦς ἐπὶ τῆς πέλτης ἀετός· [Mēdoi tauta, kai Babylōn mesē, kai to sēmeion to basileion ho chrysous epi tēs peltēs aetos] These things are the Medes, and Babylon in the middle, and the military standard, a golden eagle upon a spear. Therefore in Jeremiah [XXV, 38. XLVI,16. L,16.] חרב היונה is not, as I at least think, the sword of the dove, but the oppressing or devastating sword, such as that of the Babylonians was under King Nebuchadnezzar R3. Accordingly II, 533 the prophet says of the same, Jer 46:14: אכלה חרב סביביך, The sword has devoured round about you. But that the Samaritans also worshipped doves is entirely fabulous. What idols they worshipped when they were first transplanted from Assyria into Samaria is related in 2 Reg. XVII, 30. 31.: The men of Babylon made Succoth-Benoth, the Cuthites made Nergal, etc. But there the Sacred History says not a γρῦ [gry] about a dove, or its image, worshipped by them. Nor was this anywhere charged against them by Josephus, who in many places inveighs sharply against them. See the ninth book of the Jewish Antiquities, and the end of the eleventh; and chapters 1 and 7 of book 12; and chapter 6 of book 13; and chapters 3 and 5 of book 18; and chapter 5 of book 20. Nor could the worship of the dove, or of its image, in any way have been consistent with the Law of Moses, which they accepted. For, to say nothing of the fact that all images are forbidden so often and so expressly by Moses, on what pretext could they possibly have worshipped the very animal which they were commanded to slaughter to God in sacrifice? Nevertheless it is undoubtedly true, as Xenophon, Ctesias, Lucian and other eyewitnesses, αὐτόπται [autoptai], assert, that the Syrians and Assyrians either worshipped doves as goddesses, or at least abstained from them as from something sacred. But at what precise time this superstition was introduced into Syria or Assyria, no one could easily say.

(1) Rosenmüller, II, 530 Columbam nomine יונה ideo esse nuncupatam, quod e Graecia invecta esset in Asiam, parum videtur verosimile. Quod enim magno eruditionis apparatu evincit Bochartus, ab omni retro tempore columbas memorari in Graecia, nihil facit ad rem. Hincne enim consequitur, columbas in nulla alia regione fuisse indigenas, aut e Graecia eas invectas in Asiam? Quare miror, illam sententiam placuisse Michaeli, ita, ut novis etiam argumentis eam exornaret, in Supplemm. ad Lexx. P. IV, p. 1094. sequ. Ego columbae a mansuetudine nomen inditum putem, quae notio inest verbis Arabicis أَانَ et هَانَ, unde أون est lenitas, comitas, هون mansuetudo, le-nitas, ut igitur quodammodo respondeat Chaldaico הון, quies, commoditas. Alia opinionum commenta de nominis illius ratione dabit SIMONIS in Arcano Formarr. p. 42.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 530 That the dove was given the name יונה because it had been brought from Greece into Asia seems hardly probable. For what Bochart proves with a great display of learning, that doves are mentioned in Greece from all time past, is irrelevant to the matter. Does it follow from this that doves were native to no other region, or that they were brought from Greece into Asia? I am therefore surprised that this opinion pleased Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], so much that he even adorned it with new arguments, in the Supplemm. ad Lexx. [=J. D. Michaelis, Supplementa ad lexica Hebraica] vol. 4, p. 1094 ff. I would think that the dove was given its name from its gentleness, a notion present in the Arabic verbs أَانَ [ʾāna] and هَانَ [hāna], whence أون [ʾawn] is mildness, affability, and هون [hawn] gentleness, mildness, so that it corresponds in a way to the Chaldee הון, rest, ease. Other conjectures on the reason for that name will be given by Simonis in the Arcanum Formarum, p. 42.


(2) Rosenmüller, II, 532 Hujus opinionis vanitatem pluribus demonstravit I. D. MICHAELIS in Supplemm. P. IV. p. 1096. sequ., et in Observationibus Criticis et Philologg. in Ieremiae Vaticinia, ad Cap. XXV, 38., cum quo conferendus SCHLEUSNERUS, Vir S. R., ad Michaëlis Observatt. in Ierem. XLVI, 16. p. 309.

R2 Rosenmüller, II, 532 The emptiness of this opinion has been shown at length by J. D. Michaelis in the Supplemm. vol. 4, p. 1096 ff., and in the Observationes Criticae et Philologicae in Ieremiae Vaticinia, on Chapter XXV, 38., with which compare Schleusner, a most reverend man, on Michaelis' Observationes in Ierem. XLVI, 16, p. 309.


(3) Rosenmüller, II, 532 Hanc interpretationem vindicarunt duumviri, in nota praecedente laudati, locis ibidem commemoratis.

R3 Rosenmüller, II, 532 This interpretation has been defended by the two men praised in the preceding note, in the places mentioned there.


Part 2, Book 1, chapter 2: The dove's feathers, neck, eyes, moaning and flight

II, 533 CAP. II.

II, 533 Chapter 2.


De Columbae pennis, collo, oculis, gemitu et volatu.

On the dove's feathers, neck, eyes, moaning and flight.


Columbae descriptionem a plumis et pennis ordiri lubet, quarum pulchritudi- col. 9 nem sacer vates ita commendat Psal. LXVIII, 14. Alae columbae argento obductae, et pennae ejus pallore auri. Alae et pennae per συνεκδοχὴν hic pro toto corpore. Argento obductae, id est, argenti instar summe albae, et cum splendore quodam candidae. Quippe argentum Graece ἀργύριον dicitur παρὰ τὸ ἀργὸν, τὸ λευκόν· et argentea vocantur, quae maxime candent. Unde poetae ἀργυρόπεζα Θέτις, id est, λευκόπους. Ita est in Hesychio, qui idem ἀργυρο-δίνην κρήνην explicat λευκὰ ῥεύματα ἔχουσαν, et Aeneidos libro octavo,

I am pleased to begin the description of the dove with its plumage and feathers, whose beauty col. 9 the sacred poet commends thus, Ps 68:14: The wings of the dove covered with silver, and its feathers with the paleness of gold. Wings and feathers stand here by συνεκδοχὴν [synekdochēn] for the whole body. Covered with silver, that is, supremely white like silver, and bright with a certain splendour. For silver is called in Greek ἀργύριον [argyrion], from τὸ ἀργὸν, τὸ λευκόν [to argon, to leukon, "the bright, the white"]; and things that are most brilliantly white are called silver. Hence in the poets ἀργυρόπεζα Θέτις [argyropeza Thetis], that is, λευκόπους [leukopous]. So it is in Hesychius, who likewise explains ἀργυροδίνην κρήνην [argyrodinēn krēnēn] as λευκὰ ῥεύματα ἔχουσαν [leuka rheumata echousan]; and in the eighth book of the Aeneid,


— — — — argenteus anser,

— — — — the silver goose,


teste Servio est epithetum coloris. Corvus quoque tum ales erat argentea, cum columbas aequabat albedine. Ovidius Metam. lib. 2. Fab. 7.

is, on the testimony of Servius, an epithet of colour. The raven too was once a silver bird, when it equalled doves in whiteness. Ovid, Metam. book 2, Fable 7:


Nam fuit haec quondam niveis argentea pennis Ales, ut aequaret totas sine labe columbas. II, 534 In columbis enim quaedam sunt maxime albae (1). Varro De re rustica lib. 3. cap. 7. Alterum genus illud columbarum est clementius, quod cibo domestico contentum intra limina januae solet pasci. Hoc genus maxime est colore albo. Aliquando scilicet, et alicubi, non semper, nec ubivis locorum. Nam in Graecia albae columbae sero visae sunt, nempe cum Xerxis copiae ad montem Atho sunt profligatae. Quod in Persicis diserte tradit Charon Lampsacenus, qui tum vivebat, et scripsit ante Herodotum. Athenaeus libro nono, Χάρων δ᾽ ὁ Λαμψακη-νὸς, ἐν τοῖς Περσικοῖς περὶ Μαρδονίου ἱστορῶν, καὶ τοῦ διαφθαρέντος στρατοῦ Περ-σικοῦ περὶ τὸν Ἄθω, γράφει ταῦτα· „Καὶ λευκαὶ περιστεραὶ τότε πρῶτον εἰς „Ἕλληνας ἐφάνησαν, πρότερον οὐ γιγνόμεναι“. Charon Lampsacenus in Persicis de Mardonio agens, et de Persico exercitu, ad montem Atho profligato, haec scribit: „Et candidae columbae apud Graecos tum primum visae sunt, cùm antea „nullae fuissent“, nempe in Graecia, non usquam, ut perperam ibi habet interpres. Aelianus in Variis lib. 1. cap. 15. Χάρων δὲ ὁ Λαμψακηνὸς περὶ τὸν Ἄθω φανῆναι περιστερὰς λευκὰς λέγει, ὅτε ἐνταῦθα ἀπώλοντο αἱ τῶν Περσῶν τριέρεις παρακάμπτουσαι τὸν Ἄθω· Charon vero Lampsacenus asserit, circa Athon visas esse columbas albas, cum ibi perierunt Persarum triremes, Athon praeterlegentes. Sequitur in Psalmo, ואברותיה בירקרק חרוץ, Et pennae ejus pallore auri, supple obductae, quod repetendum ex priore hemistichio. Pallore auri, id est, auro palloris, seu pallido. Tale Habac. II, 6. עב טיט, densitas luti, pro luto densitatis, seu denso. התואר במקום המתואר, praedicatum pro subjecto, ut hic habet Kimchius. Aurum vocatur חרוץ charuts, id est, e terra effossum, hic, et Zach. IX, 3. et passim in Solomonis Proverbiis (2). Und fit Graecum χρυσός. Et pallor auri est ירקרק, geminatis literis, ut significatio sit intensior. Itaque ab hoc ipso verbo fit Aethiopum ወርቅ፡ vvark pro auro. Pallorem auri Graeci interpretes recte vocant χλωρότητα χρυσίου. Is enim verus est auri color. Hinc Diogenes rogatus, Διὰ τί τὸ χρυσίον χλωρόν ἐστιν; Cur II, 535 aurum palleat? respondit, Ὅτι πολλοὺς ἔχει τοὺς ἐπιβουλεύοντας, Quia multos habet insidiatores. Ita est in Laertio, et Catullus in nuptiis Pelei et Thetidos,

For this was once a silver bird with snowy feathers, so that it equalled doves wholly without blemish. II, 534 For among doves some are extremely white R1. Varro, On Agriculture book 3, ch. 7: The other kind of doves is the tamer, which, content with household food, is usually fed within the threshold of the door. This kind is mostly white in colour. That is, at some times and in some places, not always nor everywhere. For in Greece white doves were seen late, namely when the forces of Xerxes were routed at Mount Athos. This is expressly reported in the Persica by Charon of Lampsacus, who lived at that time and wrote before Herodotus. Athenaeus, book 9: Χάρων δ᾽ ὁ Λαμψακηνὸς, ἐν τοῖς Περσικοῖς περὶ Μαρδονίου ἱστορῶν, καὶ τοῦ διαφθαρέντος στρατοῦ Περσικοῦ περὶ τὸν Ἄθω, γράφει ταῦτα· „Καὶ λευκαὶ περιστεραὶ τότε πρῶτον εἰς „Ἕλληνας ἐφάνησαν, πρότερον οὐ γιγνόμεναι“ [Charōn d᾽ ho Lampsakēnos, en tois Persikois peri Mardoniou historōn, kai tou diaphtharentos stratou Persikou peri ton Athō, graphei tauta: "Kai leukai peristerai tote prōton eis Hellēnas ephanēsan, proteron ou gignomenai"]. Charon of Lampsacus, in the Persica, treating of Mardonius and of the Persian army routed at Mount Athos, writes this: "And white doves were then first seen among the Greeks, there having been none before", namely in Greece, not anywhere, as the translator there wrongly has it. Aelian in the Varia book 1, ch. 15: Χάρων δὲ ὁ Λαμψακηνὸς περὶ τὸν Ἄθω φανῆναι περιστερὰς λευκὰς λέγει, ὅτε ἐνταῦθα ἀπώλοντο αἱ τῶν Περσῶν τριέρεις παρακάμπτουσαι τὸν Ἄθω [Charōn de ho Lampsakēnos peri ton Athō phanēnai peristeras leukas legei, hote entautha apōlonto hai tōn Persōn triereis parakamptousai ton Athō]; But Charon of Lampsacus asserts that white doves were seen around Athos when the triremes of the Persians perished there while sailing past Athos. There follows in the Psalm ואברותיה בירקרק חרוץ, And its feathers with the paleness of gold; supply covered, which must be repeated from the preceding hemistich. Paleness of gold, that is, gold of paleness, or pale gold. Similar is Hab 2:6. עב טיט, thickness of mud, for mud of thickness, or thick mud. התואר במקום המתואר, the predicate for the subject, as Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] has it here. Gold is called חרוץ charuts, that is, dug out of the earth, here and in Zech 9:3 and frequently in Solomon's Proverbs R2. From this comes the Greek χρυσός [chrysos]. And the paleness of gold is ירקרק, with doubled letters, so that the meaning is intensified. Accordingly from this very word comes the Ethiopic ወርቅ፡ [warəq] vvark for gold. The Greek translators rightly call the paleness of gold χλωρότητα χρυσίου [chlōrotēta chrysiou]. For this is the true colour of gold. Hence Diogenes, asked Διὰ τί τὸ χρυσίον χλωρόν ἐστιν; [Dia ti to chrysion chlōron estin?] Why II, 535 is gold pale?, answered Ὅτι πολλοὺς ἔχει τοὺς ἐπιβουλεύοντας [Hoti pollous echei tous epibouleuontas], Because it has many plotting against it. So it is in Laertius; and Catullus in the wedding of Peleus and Thetis,


O quam saepe magis lurore expalluit auri!

O how often she grew paler than the sallow hue of gold!


Et rursus ad Iuventium, col. 10

And again, to Juventius, col. 10


Hospes inaurata pallidior statua.

A guest paler than a gilded statue.


Et Statius ad Maximum Iunium libro quarto Sylvarum,

And Statius to Maximus Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] in the fourth book of the Silvae,


Quando te dulci Latio remittent
Dalmatae montes, ubi Dite viso
Pallidus fossor redit, erutoque
Concolor auro.

When will the Dalmatian mountains send you back to sweet Latium, where, having seen Dis, the pale miner returns, of the same colour as the gold he has dug up?


Et Lucianus in Gallo ad divitem avarum, Οἴμωζε, καὶ ἀγρυπνεῖ, καὶ ὅμοιος γίγνου τὸ χρῶμα τῷ χρυσῷ, προσετηκὼς αὐτῷ· Plora ac vigila, auroque inta- bescens, illi fias colore similis. Iam, si quaeras, quorsum hic auri color columbis tribuatur, respondet Kimchius, שיש בכנפי היונה נוצה שהמצהבת כזהב, In columbarum alis plumam esse auri instar flavam: nempe in juniorum alis, postquam e nido excesserunt. Quod ipsum de turturibus Talmudici observant, atque hinc disci quando ad sacrificia aptae, vel ineptae sint. Cum enim e columbis nonnisi pullos, et e turturibus nonnisi adultas offerri Lex jubeat, illos ad sacrificia ineptos, has vero aptas tum demum esse volunt, cum plumae in auri colorem flavescere incipiunt. Verba sunt in tractatu Cholin capitis primi folio vigesimo secundo b. מאימתי התורים כשרים משיצהיבו מאימתי בני יונה פסולים משיצהיבו Quando turtures (ad oblationem) rectae sunt? ex quo auri instar fla- vescere inceperunt. Quando pulli columbarum (ad oblationem) profani sunt? ex quo auri instar flavescere inceperunt. Et ad vocem משיצהיבו Glossa habet שיהא כנפי גופן גדולים ואדומים ומזהיבים כזהב, quia pennae corporis magnae et ru- brae fiunt, et flavae ut aurum. Et aliquando ante, תחילה הציהב כשמתחילין לצהב כנפים שמסביבות צוארן Initium flavedinis est, cum auri instar flavescere incipiunt pennae, quas habent circa collum. Ita etiam Maimonides in Issure Miz- beach cap. 3. §. 2. והתורים כשרים משיזהבו Turtures ad oblationem aptae sunt, ex quo aureum colorem habent. Ubi Glossa eadem, quae in Talmude supra. Sed et colla columbarum, soli opposita, aureo colore splendent. Philosophus in libro De coloribus, Οἱ τῶν περιστερῶν τράχηλοι, καὶ τῶν ὑδάτων οἱ στα-λαγμοὶ φαίνονται χρυσοειδεῖς, τοῦ φωτὸς ἀνακλωμένου. Columbarum colla et aquarum stillae videntur esse aurei coloris, tum cum lux repercutitur. Alii solum variis coloribus fulgere scribunt. Lucretius lib. 2. versu 800.

And Lucian in the Cock, to a greedy rich man: Οἴμωζε, καὶ ἀγρυπνεῖ, καὶ ὅμοιος γίγνου τὸ χρῶμα τῷ χρυσῷ, προσετηκὼς αὐτῷ [oimōze, kai agrypnei, kai homoios gignou to chrōma tō chrysō, prosetēkōs autō]; Lament and keep watch, and, wasting away over your gold, become like it in colour. Now, if you ask why this golden colour is attributed to doves, Kimchi answers: שיש בכנפי היונה נוצה שהמצהבת כזהב, In the wings of doves there is plumage yellow like gold: namely in the wings of the younger birds, after they have left the nest. The Talmudists observe the same of turtledoves, and say that from this one learns when they are fit or unfit for sacrifice. For since the Law commands that of doves only the young, and of turtledoves only the adults, be offered, they hold that the former become unfit for sacrifice, and the latter fit, precisely when the feathers begin to turn yellow like gold. The words are in the tractate Cholin, chapter 1, folio 22b: מאימתי התורים כשרים משיצהיבו מאימתי בני יונה פסולים משיצהיבו When are turtledoves (for offering) fit? From the time they begin to turn yellow like gold. When are young doves (for offering) unfit? From the time they begin to turn yellow like gold. And on the word משיצהיבו the Gloss has: שיהא כנפי גופן גדולים ואדומים ומזהיבים כזהב, because the feathers of the body become large and red, and yellow like gold. And somewhat earlier: תחילה הציהב כשמתחילין לצהב כנפים שמסביבות צוארן The beginning of the yellowing is when the feathers they have around the neck begin to turn yellow like gold. So also Maimonides [=Moses Maimonides (Rambam), Mishneh Torah] in Issure Mizbeach ch. 3, §2: והתורים כשרים משיזהבו Turtledoves are fit for offering from the time they have a golden colour. Where the Gloss is the same as in the Talmud above. But the necks of doves too, when facing the sun, shine with a golden colour. The Philosopher, in the book On Colours: Οἱ τῶν περιστερῶν τράχηλοι, καὶ τῶν ὑδάτων οἱ σταλαγμοὶ φαίνονται χρυσοειδεῖς, τοῦ φωτὸς ἀνακλωμένου [Hoi tōn peristerōn trachēloi, kai tōn hydatōn hoi stalagmoi phainontai chrysoeideis, tou phōtos anaklōmenou]. The necks of doves and drops of water appear to be of a golden colour when the light is reflected. Others write only that they gleam with various colours. Lucretius, book 2, line 800:


Pluma columbarum quo pacto in sole videtur, Quae sita cervices circum collumque coronat. II, 536 Namque alias fit uti claro fit rubra pyropo, Interdum quodam sensu fit uti videatur Inter coeruleum virides miscere smaragdos.

As the plumage of doves appears in the sun, which, set about the nape, crowns the neck: II, 536 for at times it comes to be red with bright fire-bronze, at times, by a certain way of seeing, it seems to mingle green emeralds with sky-blue.


Philo in libro De Temulentia, Τὸν αὐχένα τῆς περιστερᾶς ἐν ἡλιακαῖς αὐγαῖς οὐ κατενόησας μυρίας χρωμάτων ἀλλάττοντα ἰδέας; ἢ οὐχὶ φοινικοῦν, καὶ κυα-νοῦν, πυροπόν τε, καὶ ἀνθρακοειδὲς, ἔτι τε ὠχρὸν, καὶ ἐρυθρὸν, καὶ ἄλλα παντόδαπα ἴσχει χρώματα, ὧν οὐδὲ τὰς κλήσεις ῥάδιον ἀπομνημονεῦσαι. Vidistine unquam columbae cervicem ad solis radios in sexcentos colores variatam? Nonne puniceum, et coeruleum, et pyropi, et carbunculi, et pallidum, et rubrum, et alios habet colores omnigenos, quorum ne nuda quidem nomina referre facile sit? Quae pene ad verbum exscripsit Eustathius in Hexaëmeron pagina 29. Nero apud Senecam Naturalium Quaestionum lib. 1. cap. 5.

Philo, in the book On Drunkenness: Τὸν αὐχένα τῆς περιστερᾶς ἐν ἡλιακαῖς αὐγαῖς οὐ κατενόησας μυρίας χρωμάτων ἀλλάττοντα ἰδέας; ἢ οὐχὶ φοινικοῦν, καὶ κυανοῦν, πυροπόν τε, καὶ ἀνθρακοειδὲς, ἔτι τε ὠχρὸν, καὶ ἐρυθρὸν, καὶ ἄλλα παντόδαπα ἴσχει χρώματα, ὧν οὐδὲ τὰς κλήσεις ῥάδιον ἀπομνημονεῦσαι [Ton auchena tēs peristeras en hēliakais augais ou katenoēsas myrias chrōmatōn allattonta ideas? ē ouchi phoinikoun, kai kyanoun, pyropon te, kai anthrakoeides, eti te ōchron, kai erythron, kai alla pantodapa ischei chrōmata, hōn oude tas klēseis rhadion apomnēmoneusai]. Have you never seen a dove's neck in the sun's rays varied into countless colours? Does it not have crimson, and sky-blue, and the colours of fire-bronze and of carbuncle, and pale, and red, and colours of every other kind, whose mere names it would not be easy to recount? This Eustathius copied almost word for word in the Hexaemeron, page 29. Nero, in Seneca, Natural Questions book 1, ch. 5:


Colla Cytheriacae splendent agitata columbae.

The necks of Cytherea's dove shine as it moves.


Plinius, libri decimi capite vigesimo sexto, Columbis inest quidam et gloriae intellectus. Nosse credas suos colores et varietatem dispositam. Et libri trigesimi septimi capite quinto, Carchedonii, etc. Colore incerti, et virentium in caudis pavonum, columbarumque collo plumis similes. Ausonius de anatibus Epistola tertia,

Pliny, book 10, chapter 26: Doves have a certain sense even of glory. You would think they know their own colours and the ordered variety of them. And book 37, chapter 5: The Carchedonian, etc. uncertain in colour, and like the feathers of the green in peacocks' tails and on the necks of doves. Ausonius, on ducks, Epistle 3:


Iricolor vario pinxit quas pluma colore,
Collum columbis aemulas.

Whom iridescent plumage has painted with varied colour,
rivals of doves in their necks.


Sed hi colores solum sunt apparentes. Itaque apud Martianum libro secundo col. 11 Arcesilas, collum columbarum intuens, hac permotus varietatis incertitudine, amplius adstruere ἀκαταληψίαν coepit. Et Carneades, ut probaret, incertos esse sensus nostros, columbarum colla proferebat, ad singulas conversiones colorem mutantia. Ita testatur Hieronymus ad Pammachium contra errores Iohannis Hierosolymitani. At Oppianus lib. 1. Cynegeticῶν pullos etiam in ovo variis coloribus, iisque veris, posse distingui docuit. Nempe si coituris foeminis objiciantur

But these colours are only apparent. Thus in Martianus, book 2, col. 11 Arcesilas, gazing at the neck of doves and moved by this uncertainty of variation, began to build up further his doctrine of ἀκαταληψία [akatalēpsia]. And Carneades, to prove that our senses are uncertain, brought forward the necks of doves, which change colour at every turn. So Jerome attests in his letter to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem. But Oppian, in book 1 of the Cynegetica, taught that the young even in the egg can be marked with various colours, and real ones at that: namely if, when the females are about to mate, there are set before them
