— — — — — δαίδαλα πολλὰ Εἵματα πορφύρεα· ταὶ δὲ κλιδὸν ὄσσε βαλοῦσαι, Θυμὸν ἰαινόμεναι τίκτουσ᾽ ἁλιπόρφυρα τέκνα, [— — — — — daidala polla heimata porphyrea; tai de klidon osse balousai, thymon iainomenai tiktous' haliporphyra tekna,]


daedala multa vestimenta purpurea: illae vero limis oculis conjectis, animoque oblectatae, pariunt purpureos pullos. Quod adduco libentius, quia simili arte Iacobus oves sibi comparavit versicolores.

many richly wrought purple garments: and they, casting sidelong glances at them and delighted in mind, bring forth purple young. I cite this the more gladly because by a similar art Jacob obtained parti-coloured sheep for himself.


Oculi columbarum sponsae tribuuntur Cant. I, 15. et IV, 1. Et sponso quoque Cant. V, 12. id est, puri, venusti, simplices, casti denique. Quod potissimum Hebraei hic intelligunt; quia columba solum conjugem respicit, neque II, 537 oculos in ullum alium conjicit. Rabbi Selomo, משמכרת את בן זוגה אונה מניחתו שיזדווג לאחר, Postquam compari suo desponsata est, alteri sociari non gaudet. Et Aben Ezra, מנהג בני יונה שלא להתחבר אלא עם זוגה שלה, Columbae non solent ulli alteri, quam compari suo consociari. Quod idem de palumbe postquam docuit Aelianus Hist. lib. 3. cap. 44. Ἐὰν δὲ, inquit, ἐποφθαλ-μιάσωσιν ἑτέροις, περιέρχονται αὐτοὺς οἱ λοιποὶ, καὶ τὸν μὲν ἄῤῥενα οἱ ὁμογε-νεῖς διασπῶσιν, αἱ θήλειαι δὲ τὸν θῆλυν· Si autem libidinosos oculos in alios conjiciant, eos reliqui circumsedentes, marem quidem mares discerpunt, foeminam vero foeminae. Ubi nota, verbum ἐποφθαλμιᾶν de libidinoso aspectu usurpari, quia oculi sunt in amore duces. Et ἐκ τοῦ ὁρᾷν γίνεται ἐρᾷν. Unde Iohannes a), Ἡ ἐπιθυμία τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν· et Petrus b), ὀφθαλμοὺς ἔχοντες μεστοὺς μοιχαλίδος. Quod malo suo expertus David c) a Deo obnixe petiit, ut oculos suos averteret, ne viderent vanitatem. Et Iob d) cum iis foedus pepigit, ut ne virginem aspicerent. Anxie quaerunt interpretes, quo haec pertineant Cant. V, 12. Oculi ejus (sponsi) tanquam (oculi) columbarum ad decursus aquarum lotarum in lacte, manentium ad plenitudinem. Ego Sacrum Scriptorem hoc solum respexisse puto, quod columbae ad aquas oculos habent excitatiores, quia ad eas libentius degunt. Proinde Varro (De re rustica libri tertii capite septimo) in descriptione τῆς περιστεροφείου, Aquam puram, inquit, esse oportet, quae influat; unde et bibere, et ubi lavari possint: permundae enim sunt hae volucres. Neque solum ad aquas describuntur, sed et ad plenitudinem, supple aquarum, (quomodo Scriptura passim agit e) de maris plenitudine) id est, ad loca, ubi aquae scatent, et ad riparum altitudinem prope accedunt, ita, ut sint potu faciles. Eaedem lacte lotae dicuntur, id est, candidissimae: ac si alba fierent, quae lacte lavantur; ut nigra, quae atramento. Tale illud Iob. IX, 30. Si lavero me aquis nivalibus, et mundavero smegmate manus meas. Remotum est, nec alibi reperitur, quod quidem sciam, quod Gregorius in Cantica capite quinto columbas ideo putat juxta fluenta residere, ut volantium avium umbram in aqua videant, super quam se projicientes, ungues rapacium sic effugiant. Sed videtur id ex parte sumtum ex historia cujusdam avis, quae Arabice vocatur خاطف ظله chatipho-dhillihi, quasi dicas raptorem umbrae suae; quia اذا راي ظله في الما اقبل اليه ليخطفه cum umbram suam in aqua videt, accedit ad eam, ut rapiat eam. Ita Alcamus. In Damire aliter vocatur col. 12 قرلا koralla voce Persica, et رفراف riphraph a motitatione alarum, et II, 538 ملاعب ظله mulaibo dhillihi, ludens cum umbra sua, et asseritur esse في جنس العصافير in genere passerum, seu avicularum. Itaque non est graculus, in qua sententia quandoque fui, quia de iis dicit Tzetzes Chiliade 4. Hist. 119.

The eyes of doves are attributed to the bride in Song 1:15 and IV, 1., and to the bridegroom as well in Song 5:12; that is, eyes that are pure, lovely, simple, and finally chaste. This last is what the Hebrews chiefly understand here, because the dove looks only to its mate and does not II, 537 cast its eyes on any other. Rabbi Selomo: משמכרת את בן זוגה אונה מניחתו שיזדווג לאחר, After she has been betrothed to her mate, she does not delight in being joined to another. And Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra]: מנהג בני יונה שלא להתחבר אלא עם זוגה שלה, Doves are not accustomed to associate with any other than their own mate. Aelian teaches the same of the wood pigeon in Hist. book 3, ch. 44, and then says: Ἐὰν δὲ ἐποφθαλμιάσωσιν ἑτέροις, περιέρχονται αὐτοὺς οἱ λοιποὶ, καὶ τὸν μὲν ἄῤῥενα οἱ ὁμογενεῖς διασπῶσιν, αἱ θήλειαι δὲ τὸν θῆλυν [Ean de epophthalmiasōsin heterois, perierchontai autous hoi loipoi, kai ton men arrena hoi homogeneis diaspōsin, hai thēleiai de ton thēlyn]; But if they cast lustful eyes on others, the rest surround them, and the males tear the male to pieces, the females the female. Note here that the verb ἐποφθαλμιᾶν [epophthalmian] is used of a lustful look, because the eyes are the leaders in love, and ἐκ τοῦ ὁρᾷν γίνεται ἐρᾷν [ek tou horan ginetai eran]. Hence John a) speaks of Ἡ ἐπιθυμία τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν [Hē epithymia tōn ophthalmōn], and Peter b) of ὀφθαλμοὺς ἔχοντες μεστοὺς μοιχαλίδος [ophthalmous echontes mestous moichalidos]. David c), having learned this to his own cost, earnestly asked God to turn his eyes away so that they should not behold vanity. And Job d) made a covenant with them that they should not look upon a virgin. The interpreters inquire anxiously what these words refer to in Song 5:12: His eyes (the bridegroom's) are like (the eyes) of doves by the streams of waters, washed in milk, dwelling by the fullness. I think the sacred writer had only this in view: that doves have livelier eyes by the waters, because they prefer to live near them. Accordingly Varro (De re rustica, book 3, chapter 7), in his description of the dovecote, τῆς περιστεροφείου [tēs peristeropheiou], says: There should be pure water flowing in, from which they can both drink and bathe; for these birds are very clean. And they are described not only as by the waters but also as by the fullness (supply "of the waters", as Scripture repeatedly speaks e) of the fullness of the sea), that is, by places where waters gush forth and come up close to the top of the banks, so that they are easy to drink from. The same doves are said to be washed in milk, that is, very white, as if things washed in milk became white, as things washed in ink become black. Compare Job. IX, 30.: If I wash myself with snow water, and cleanse my hands with soap. Far-fetched, and found nowhere else so far as I know, is the view of Gregory on the Canticle, chapter 5, that doves sit beside streams so that they may see in the water the shadow of birds flying overhead, and by throwing themselves upon it may thus escape the talons of birds of prey. But this seems to have been taken in part from the story of a certain bird which in Arabic is called خاطف ظله [khāṭif ẓillihi] chatipho-dhillihi, as if to say snatcher of its own shadow, because اذا راي ظله في الما اقبل اليه ليخطفه [idhā rāy ẓillahu fī al-mā aqbala ilayhi li-yakhṭafahu], when it sees its shadow in the water, it approaches it in order to snatch it. So Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]. In Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] it is called otherwise: col. 12 قرلا [qirlā] koralla, a Persian word; رفراف [rafrāf] riphraph, from the fluttering of its wings; and II, 538 ملاعب ظله [mulāʿib ẓillihi] mulaibo dhillihi, playing with its shadow. It is asserted to be في جنس العصافير [fī jins al-ʿaṣāfīr] of the kind of sparrows, or small birds. It is therefore not the jackdaw, which I once thought it was, because Tzetzes says of jackdaws in Chiliad 4, Hist. 119:


— εἴπερ χέεις ἔλαιον ἔν τινι λεκανίσκῃ,
Πρὸς τὴν σκιὰν τὴν ἑαυτῶν τοὺς κολοιοὺς κρατήσῃς.
Ναρκίσσους ἄλλους Λάκωνας ὄντας τῶν φιλοσκίων.

— εἴπερ χέεις ἔλαιον ἔν τινι λεκανίσκῃ, Πρὸς τὴν σκιὰν τὴν ἑαυτῶν τοὺς κολοιοὺς κρατήσῃς. Ναρκίσσους ἄλλους Λάκωνας ὄντας τῶν φιλοσκίων. [— eiper cheeis elaion en tini lekaniskē, Pros tēn skian tēn heautōn tous koloious kratēsēs. Narkissous allous Lakōnas ontas tōn philoskiōn.]


Si in parva pelve oleum fundas, ad umbram suam graculos detinebis, ac si essent Narcissi Lacones, ex iis, qui propriam umbram amant. Obiter nota, Narcissum non fuisse Laconem, sed Boeotum, ut testantur Ovidius Metam. lib. 3. Fab. 5. Conon Hist. 24. Strabo lib. 9. Hyginus Fab. 271. Pausanias in Boeoticis, Claudianus lib. 2. de raptu, atque alii sine numero. Tamen Laconem facit Tzetzes hic, et Chil. 1. Hist. 9. quasi fuerit Hyacinthi popularis, quem illi confert Hist. 11. Quod μνημονικὸν σφάλμα in eo ferendum non est, qui in eo ipso loco ita se jactat,

If you pour oil into a small basin, you will hold the jackdaws fast at their own shadow, as if they were Laconian Narcissi, of those who love their own shadow. Note in passing that Narcissus was not a Laconian but a Boeotian, as Ovid, Metam. book 3, Fab. 5, Conon, Hist. 24, Strabo, book 9, Hyginus, Fab. 271, Pausanias in the Boeotica, Claudian, book 2 de raptu, and countless others attest. Yet Tzetzes makes him a Laconian both here and in Chil. 1, Hist. 9, as if he were a countryman of Hyacinthus, with whom he compares him in Hist. 11. This μνημονικὸν σφάλμα [mnēmonikon sphalma] is not to be tolerated in a man who, in that very passage, boasts thus:


Οὐδὲ γὰρ μνημονέστερον τοῦ Τζέτζου Θεὸς ἄλλον
Ἄνδρα τῶν πρίν τε, καὶ τῶν νῦν ἐξέφηνεν ἐν βίῳ.

Οὐδὲ γὰρ μνημονέστερον τοῦ Τζέτζου Θεὸς ἄλλον Ἄνδρα τῶν πρίν τε, καὶ τῶν νῦν ἐξέφηνεν ἐν βίῳ. [Oude gar mnēmonesteron tou Tzetzou Theos allon Andra tōn prin te, kai tōn nyn exephēnen en biō.]


Neque enim magis Tzetze memorem Deus ullum alium in vitam produxit, eorum, qui fuerunt, aut nunc sunt. Et paullo ante dixerat, se scire omnes libros. Sed, ut eo redeamus, unde digressi sumus, Hebraei, quae nos ad columbas, ut ad columbarum oculos referant, sacra verba sic reddunt, Oculi ejus ut columbarum (oculi) ad decursus aquarum, lacte loti, insiti in plenitudine, id est, locum suum implentes ut gemma palam. Quod Hebraice dicitur מלואת אבן, plenitudo, vel impletio lapidis, Exod. XXVIII, 17. Ita Aben Ezra et R. Selomo, qui oculos designari vult לא בולטות יותר מדאי ולא שיקעות אלא יושבות מלאת גומא שלהם, non plus aequo prominentes, aut depressos, sed ita sitos, ut fossam suam impleant. Atque id sequuntur novi interpretes. Sed in hac interpretatione nonnulla desidero: primo, quod sic color lacteus oculis tribui videtur, quorum praecipua pars, id est, pupilla, nigra est, aut coerulea, etc. Secundo, quod, quamvis lapides pala inclusi, Hebraice dicantur אבני מלואים, lapides impletionum, id est, qui palam implent, et insitio lapidis in palam מלואת אבן, impletio lapidis, tamen lapis, in palam insitus, nusquam dicitur יושב על מלאת, manens ad plenitudinem. Neque vero id dici potest. Quis enim pecuniam ad sacci, aut vinum ad dolii plenitudinem manere vel stare dixerit, cum saccus pecunia, aut vinum dolio plenum est (3).

For God has not brought into life any other man more mindful than Tzetzes, of those who have been or who now are. And shortly before he had said that he knew all books. But, to return to the point from which we digressed, the Hebrews render the sacred words, which we refer to doves as to the eyes of doves, thus: His eyes are like doves' (eyes) by the courses of waters, washed with milk, set in fullness, that is, filling their place like a gem its setting. This is what in Hebrew is called מלואת אבן, fullness or filling of stone, Exod 28:17. So Aben Ezra and R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)], who holds that the eyes are described as לא בולטות יותר מדאי ולא שיקעות אלא יושבות מלאת גומא שלהם, neither more prominent than is fitting, nor sunken, but so placed that they fill their socket. And the recent interpreters follow this. But in this interpretation I find some things lacking. First, that in this way a milky colour seems to be attributed to the eyes, whose principal part, that is, the pupil, is black, or blue, etc. Second, that although stones enclosed in a setting are called in Hebrew אבני מלואים, stones of fillings, that is, which fill the setting, and the setting of a stone in a bezel is called מלואת אבן, filling of stone, yet a stone set in a bezel is nowhere said to be יושב על מלאת, remaining at fullness. Nor indeed can this be said. For who would say that money remains or stands at the fullness of a bag, or wine at the fullness of a cask, when the bag is full of money, or the cask full of wine R3?


II, 539 In columbae voce aliquid querulum et gemebundum est. Proinde gemere dicuntur. Auctor Philomelae,

II, 539 In the voice of the dove there is something plaintive and moaning. Hence doves are said to moan. The author of the Philomela:


Et castus turtur, atque columba gemunt.

And the chaste turtledove and the dove moan.


Virgilius Ecloga prima, Nec tamen interea raucae tua cura palumbes, Nec gemere aëria cessabit turtur ab ulmo.

Virgil, Eclogue 1: Yet meanwhile neither will the hoarse wood-pigeons, your care, nor the turtledove cease to moan from the airy elm.


Martialis lib. 3. Epigr. 57.

Martial, book 3, Epigr. 57:


Gemit hinc palumbus, inde cereus turtur.

Here moans the wood-pigeon, there the wax-coloured turtledove.


Gregorius in Iobum lib. 32. cap. 4. Scimus quia columbarum pulli, vel turtures pro cantu gemitum habent. Et in Cant. cap. 1. Columba in amore suo pro cantu gemit. Graecis quoque id ipsum στένειν. Theocritus Idyll. 7. versu 141.

Gregory on Job, book 32, ch. 4: We know that the young of doves, or turtledoves, have moaning instead of song. And on the Song, ch. 1: The dove in its love moans instead of singing. For the Greeks too this same thing is στένειν [stenein]. Theocritus, Idyll 7, verse 141:


Ἄειδον κόρυδοι, καὶ ἀκανθίδες, ἔστενε τρυγὼν,

Ἄειδον κόρυδοι, καὶ ἀκανθίδες, ἔστενε τρυγὼν, [Aeidon korydoi, kai akanthides, estene trygōn,]


Cantabant alaudae et cardueles, gemebat turtur. Hinc Chrysostomus Homilia De turture, Ἡ τρυγὼν ἡ φιλέρημος, ὅτε ἐν ὕλαις συγκοιταζομένη καλεῖ τὸν ὁμόζυγον, γοεραῖς κολακείαις τὰς κοιλάδας δονήσασα· Solitarius turtur, cum in sylvis decumbens conjugem vocat, lugubribus adulationibus valles commovens. col. 13 Alii turtures τρύζειν dicunt, et columbas γογγύζειν. Pollux lib. 5. capite 13. §. 2. cui titulus Ὄρνεων φωναὶ, Avium voces, Εἴποις ἂν τρυγόνας τρύζειν, πε-ριστερὰς γογγύζειν. Γογγύζειν est murmurare. Hinc murmura reperias pro columbarum gemitu: ut cum Gallienus, imperator, apud Trebellium in Epithalamio carmine de sponsis dicit,

The larks and goldfinches were singing, the turtledove was moaning. Hence Chrysostom, in the Homily On the Turtledove: Ἡ τρυγὼν ἡ φιλέρημος, ὅτε ἐν ὕλαις συγκοιταζομένη καλεῖ τὸν ὁμόζυγον, γοεραῖς κολακείαις τὰς κοιλάδας δονήσασα· [Hē trygōn hē philerēmos, hote en hylais synkoitazomenē kalei ton homozygon, goerais kolakeiais tas koilada donēsasa;] The solitary turtledove, when lying in the woods it calls its mate, stirring the valleys with mournful blandishments. col. 13 Others say that turtledoves τρύζειν [tryzein] and doves γογγύζειν [gongyzein]. Pollux, book 5, chapter 13, §. 2, which is entitled Ὄρνεων φωναὶ [Orneōn phōnai], Voices of Birds: Εἴποις ἂν τρυγόνας τρύζειν, περιστερὰς γογγύζειν [Eipois an trygonas tryzein, peristeras gongyzein]. Γογγύζειν [Gongyzein] means to murmur. Hence you may find murmura [murmurs] for the moaning of doves: as when the emperor Gallienus, in Trebellius, says of the bride and groom in an epithalamium,


— — — non murmura vestra columbae,
Brachia non hederae, non vincant oscula conchae.

— — — let not doves surpass your murmurs,
nor ivy your arms, nor shells your kisses.


At Hebraicum est הגה, quod gemendi verbo recte redditur, cum ad luctum ubique referatur. Ita in Ezechiae, regis, cantico de morbo suo Es. XXXVIII,14. II, 540 אהגה כיונה, gemebam ut columba. Et Es. LIX, 11. ubi agitur de Iudaeorum rebus afflictis, Uncamus ut ursi nos omnes, וכיונים הגה נהגה, et ut columbae gemendo gemimus, id est, gravi et continuo gemitu (4). Sed et המה, quod proprie fremere est, ad columbarum gemitum pertinet, cum dicitur Ezech. VII, 16. כיוני הגאות כלם הומות איש בעונו, ut columbae vallium omnes illi fremebant, (id est, gemebant) quisque propter peccatum suum. Septuaginta pro כיוני הגיאות, ut columbae vallium, legerunt כיונה הגות. Unde nata illa versio, ὡς περιστεραὶ μελετητικαὶ, ut columbae gemebundae. Nam de columbis μελετᾷν illis gemere est. Proinde in hunc locum Theodoretus, Ὀδυρόμενοι γὰρ καὶ θρηνοῦντες πε-ριστεραῖς μελετώσαις ἀπεικαθήσονται· στένουσι γὰρ ἔοικε τῶν περιστερῶν ἡ φωνή. Quae omnino sic reddenda: Conquerentes enim et lugentes columbis gementibus conferentur (non columbis sublimibus, ut hic habet interpres). Gementibus quippe similis est vox columbarum. Sumitur quoque pro luctuoso gemitu vox columbae Nahum II, 7. ubi regina Ninives, cum in captivitatem abducitur, comitantur ancillae gementes, tanquam voce columbarum, et pectora sua tundentes. Hebraea habent מנהגות כקול יונים, deducentes tanquam voce columbarum. Deducentes, ut volunt, hic idem, quod comitantes, et supplendum gementes. Nam deducere positum pro deducere et gemere. Unum pro duobus. Quale Prov. XXV, 22. Capies carbones ignis supra caput ejus, pro capies et pones Et Psal. LXVIII, 19. Accepisti dona hominibus, pro, accepisti et dedisti, vel accepisti quae dares. Proinde reddit Paulus, dedit dona hominibus, Ephes. IV, 8. Quid si pro מנהגות, deducentes, legatur מהגות, gementes, una literula minus? Sic planior esset sensus: tamen non ausim quidquam mutare, quia vetustissimos interpretes constat legisse מנהגות (5).

But the Hebrew has הגה, which is rightly rendered by the verb to moan, since it everywhere refers to mourning. So in the song of King Hezekiah about his illness, Isa 38:14 II, 540 אהגה כיונה, I moaned like a dove. And Isa 59:11, where the afflicted condition of the Jews is treated: We all growl like bears, וכיונים הגה נהגה, and like doves we moan with moaning, that is, with heavy and continuous moaning R4. But המה too, which properly means to roar, applies to the moaning of doves, when it is said in Ezek 7:16. כיוני הגאות כלם הומות איש בעונו, like doves of the valleys they all roared (that is, moaned), each for his own sin. For כיוני הגיאות, like doves of the valleys, the Septuagint read כיונה הגות. Hence arose that rendering ὡς περιστεραὶ μελετητικαὶ [hōs peristerai meletētikai], like moaning doves. For with them μελετᾷν [meletan], said of doves, means to moan. Accordingly Theodoret on this passage: Ὀδυρόμενοι γὰρ καὶ θρηνοῦντες περιστεραῖς μελετώσαις ἀπεικαθήσονται· στένουσι γὰρ ἔοικε τῶν περιστερῶν ἡ φωνή [Odyromenoi gar kai thrēnountes peristerais meletōsais apeikasthēsontai; stenousi gar eoike tōn peristerōn hē phōnē]. This must certainly be rendered thus: For those who lament and mourn will be compared to moaning doves (not to doves on high, as the translator has it here). For the voice of doves is like that of people moaning. The voice of the dove is also taken for mournful moaning in Nahum II, 7., where the queen of Nineveh, as she is led into captivity, is accompanied by maidservants moaning, as with the voice of doves, and beating their breasts. The Hebrew has מנהגות כקול יונים, leading away as with the voice of doves. Leading away here, as they hold, is the same as accompanying, and moaning must be supplied. For to lead away is put for to lead away and to moan: one for two. So in Prov 25:22, You will take coals of fire upon his head, for you will take and put; and Ps 68:19, You received gifts for men, for you received and gave, or you received things to give. Accordingly Paul renders it he gave gifts to men, Ephes. IV, 8. What if for מנהגות, leading away, one were to read מהגות, moaning, with one small letter less? The sense would thus be plainer; yet I would not dare to change anything, since it is established that the most ancient translators read מנהגות R5.


Columbae volatum Scriptura laudat non semel. Sic Esa. LX, 8. Qui sunt isti, qui ut nubes convolant, et ut columbae ad fenestras suas? Magistri haec referunt II, 541 ad Israelitas, ex captivitate Babylonica cum summa alacritate redituros. Hinc Chaldaeus paraphrastes, Qui sunt isti, qui palam veniunt ut nubes veloces sine mora? Transmigratio Israël, quae congregatur, et redit ad terram suam, כיונין דתיבין לגו שובכיהן, ut columbae, quae redeunt ad columbaria sua. In quae verba Kimchius, יותר יעופו מהרה בשובם אל קניהם ממה שיעופו בצאתם מהם מפני שהם ממהרות לשוב אל גוזליהם שהניחו להאכילם מאשר בפיהם Citius volant, eum redeunt ad nidos suos, quam cum ex iis exeunt, quia ad pullos, quos reliquerunt, redire properant, ut cibum, quem in ore habent, iis offerant. Similis est locus Os. XI, 11. Trepidabunt ut avicula ex Aegypto, et ut columba e terra Assriae. Trepidabunt יחרדו, id est, trepide accurrent. Sic 1 Sam. XVI, 4. cum Samuel venit Bethlehem, ויחרדו, Et trepidarunt (id est, trepide accurrerunt) seniores urbis in occursum ejus. Et in hoc ipso propheta Ose. III, 5. Trepidabunt ad Dominum et bonitatem ejus, id est, Trepide accurrent. Aben Ezra, col. 14 ישובו במהרה במרוצא פתע פתאום, Redibunt festinanter, cursim, cito, velociter. Tamen in sacro textu non est חרדו, sed synonymum פחדו. Nempe trepitandi verba quandoque ad festinationem pertinent. Virgilius libro nono Aeneidos,

Scripture praises the flight of the dove more than once. Thus Isa 60:8: Who are these that fly together like clouds, and like doves to their windows? The Rabbis refer this II, 541 to the Israelites, who were to return from the Babylonian captivity with the greatest eagerness. Hence the Chaldee paraphrast: Who are these who come openly like swift clouds without delay? The exiles of Israel, who are gathered and return to their land, כיונין דתיבין לגו שובכיהן, like doves that return to their dovecotes. On these words Kimchi: יותר יעופו מהרה בשובם אל קניהם ממה שיעופו בצאתם מהם מפני שהם ממהרות לשוב אל גוזליהם שהניחו להאכילם מאשר בפיהם, They fly faster when they return to their nests than when they go out from them, because they hasten to return to the young they have left, to offer them the food which they have in their mouth. A similar passage is Hos 11:11: They will tremble like a little bird out of Egypt, and like a dove from the land of Assyria. They will tremble, יחרדו, that is, they will hurry up in agitation. So 1 Sam. XVI, 4., when Samuel came to Bethlehem, ויחרדו, And the elders of the city trembled (that is, hurried in agitation) to meet him. And in this same prophet, Ose. III, 5.: They will tremble to the Lord and to his goodness, that is, they will hurry up in agitation. Aben Ezra: col. 14 ישובו במהרה במרוצא פתע פתאום, They will return hastily, at a run, quickly, swiftly. Yet in the sacred text there is not חרדו but its synonym פחדו. Indeed, verbs of trembling sometimes relate to haste. Virgil, in the ninth book of the Aeneid:


Ne trepidate meas, Teucri, defendere naves.

Do not tremble, Teucrians, to defend my ships.


id est, ne festinetis. Ita Servius et Nonius Marcellus. Et Livius lib. 23. Moxque, dum in sua quisque ministeria discursu trepidat ad prima signa. Trepidat, id est, festinat. Ita omnino in Osea, Trepidabunt ut columba (id est, summa festinatione fugient) ex Assyria (6). Quia columbae volatus est pernicissimus. Unde est, quod Psal. LV, 7. alas columbae optat David, ut celeri fuga se subducat ex imminenti periculo. Quis (inquit) mihi dabit alam velut columbae, qua in tutum evolem? Ecce! quam longissime evagarer, commoraturus in deserto. Et maturarem effugium, ocyus vento rapidissimo et turbine. Quomodo Chorus apud Sophoclem in Oedipo Coloneo,

that is, do not hurry. So Servius and Nonius Marcellus. And Livy, book 23: And soon, while each hurries [trepidat] running about to his own duties at the first signals. Trepidat, that is, festinat [hurries]. So certainly in Hosea: They will tremble like a dove (that is, they will flee with the utmost haste) from Assyria R6. For the flight of the dove is extremely swift. Hence it is that in Psal. LV, 7. David wishes for the wings of a dove, to withdraw by swift flight from imminent danger. Who (he says) will give me a wing like a dove's, with which I might fly away to safety? Behold, I would wander as far away as possible, to stay in the wilderness. And I would hasten my escape, swifter than the most rapid wind and whirlwind. Just as the Chorus in Sophocles' Oedipus at Colonus:


Εἴτ᾽, ἀελλαία ταχύῤ- Utinam, ut turbinea celeri ῥωστος πελειὰς, Impetu columba, Αἰθερίας νεφέλας Aethereas nubes Κύρσαί με, etc. Permearem, etc.

Εἴτ᾽, ἀελλαία ταχύῤ- [Eit', aellaia tachyr-] Would that, like a dove of swift ῥωστος πελειὰς, [rhōstos peleias,] whirlwind onrush, Αἰθερίας νεφέλας [Aitherias nephelas] I might pass through Κύρσαί με, [Kyrsai me,] etc. the ethereal clouds, etc.


Gregorius Nazianzenus Oratione decima septima dicit, columbae alas a Davide exoptari, ὡς κουφοτέρας, καὶ ταχυτέρας, ut leviores et perniciores. Et Iansenius in Paraphrasi, O utinam mihi dentur alae tales, quales habet columba, velocissimi inter aves volatus; ut quomodo pernicissimo suo volatu, eoque solo, sese ab II, 542 hoste accipitre liberat, etc. Plinius quoque libri decimi capite trigesimo sexto columbas dicit soluto volatu esse accipitre in multum velociores. Et Phaedrus libri primi Fab. 31.

Gregory of Nazianzus, in Oration 17, says that David longed for the wings of a dove ὡς κουφοτέρας, καὶ ταχυτέρας [hōs kouphoteras, kai tachyteras], as being lighter and swifter. And Jansenius [=Cornelius Jansen of Ghent (d. 1576), commentary on Wisdom] in his Paraphrase: O that wings were given me such as the dove has, which of all birds is the swiftest in flight; so that, as by its most rapid flight, and by that alone, it frees itself from II, 542 its enemy the hawk, etc. Pliny too, book 10, chapter 36, says that doves in free flight are much swifter than the hawk. And Phaedrus, book 1, Fable 31:


Columbae saepe cum fugissent milvium,
Et celeritate pennae vitassent necem.

The doves, when they had often fled the kite,
And by the swiftness of their wings escaped death.


Et Euripides de Bacchis, ad Penthei caedem properantibus,

And Euripides, of the Bacchae hastening to the slaughter of Pentheus:


Ἤιξαν πελέιας ὠκύτητ᾽ οὐκ ἥσσονες,

Ἤιξαν πελέιας ὠκύτητ᾽ οὐκ ἥσσονες, [Ēixan peleias ōkytēt᾽ ouk hēssones,]


Irruerunt columbae celeritate non inferiores. Proinde Virgilius Aeneidos libro quinto Mnesthei navem, quae

They rushed on, not inferior to doves in swiftness. Accordingly Virgil, Aeneid book 5, compares the ship of Mnestheus, which


Agmine remorum celeri, ventisque vocatis
Prona petit maria, et pelago decurrit aperto,

With the swift stroke of oars, and the winds called up,
Makes for the sloping seas, and runs down the open main,


eum columba volante confert tum cum

to a dove in flight, at the moment when


Fertur in arva volans, atque aëre lapsa quieto
Radit iter liquidum, celeres neque commovet alas.

It is borne flying into the fields, and gliding through the still air
Skims its liquid path, and does not move its swift wings.


Et, ut credatur Argo navis fuisse expeditissima, illam poetae ὅσον πελειάδος, columbae instar, citam describunt. Et columbam ab Argonautis inter Symplegades missam fuisse fingunt, quae cum evasisset, inde conjecerunt etiam Argo evasuram, ut ab Eustathio docetur in Odyss. μ´. Quibus consonant Arabes et Hebraei. Sic Damir, postquam docuit الشهرمان والشاهين saharman et sahin, accipitrum species, columbae esse infensissimos, وهو اطير منهما ومن ساير الطير كلها Et haec, inquit, eos volatu superat, atque aves omnes, quotquot sunt. Et ad locum Psalmi, quem citavimus, R. Simon, R. Iodan, R. Ionas, et R. Kimchius ad quaestionem, cur David alas columbae aliarum avium alis praeferat, sic respondent כל העופות בשעה שיגעים הם נסים על גבי הסלע או על גבי האילן ונתפסין אבל יונה בשעה שיגעה היא קובצת אחת מאגפיה ופורחת באחת והיא נצולת ואינה נתפסת, Reliquae omnes aves, cum volando fessae sunt, super petram, aut super arborem fugiunt, et capiuntur: sed columba, cum est fessa, alarum unam comprimit, et altera volat, sicque evadit, nec capitur. Et Aben Ezra, והזכיר יונה col. 15 שהיא עם בני אדם ועמה ישגרו המלכים ספריהם, Meminit columbae, quia illa degit cum hominibus, et literas per eam mittunt reges. Nempe saeculo post Christum duodecimo, quo scripsit Aben Ezra, fuit id in multo usu. Paulus Aemylius, de gestis Francorum libro quarto, ubi de Hasarchi, Syriae oppidi praefecto: Ejus oratores (ad Balduinum missi, ut auxilium implorarent) epistolam caudae columbae, quam, cum in legationem proficiscerentur, domo secum attulerant, alligaverunt, illamque ex composito remisere. Ita Praefectus certior factus egregie II, 543 se tutatus est. Et ubi de Hierosolymis, per Christianos obsessis: Casus tulit, ut columba, super castra Latinorum volitans, accipitre opprimente se demittens, a nostris exciperetur. Sub alis ejus inventa est epistola Arabicis, et verbis et literis, exarata. Et libro quinto, Cum assidetur (Tyri) moenibus, sunt auctores, columbam advolasse. Eam cum nostri, usu docti, tabellariam esse cognoscerent, clamorem tantum a terrestribus navalibusque Latinorum copiis sublatum, ut ales, tanquam turbine moti coeli acta, in terram delaberetur. Demptam epistolam, barbarorum literis ad Tyrios exaratam, brevi auxilia occursura, bono animo essent, paucos dies obsidionem tolerarent. Nostros contra alteram epistolam curasse scribendam manu linguaque eorum barbarorum, quos in manu habebant etc. Volucremque cum subdititiis fallacibusque literis remissam, sibi ex usu praesenti obsessi consulerent, etc. spem propinquam auxilii nullam ostendi posse, etc. Dolo cessere Tyrii. Marmolius Africae suae libri secundi capite trigesimo primo id refert ad annum 1123. De iisdem vide Iacobum Vitriacum, Histor. Orient. lib. 1. Arnoldum Lubecensem in Historia Slavorum, Vincentium in Doctrinali lib. 16. cap. 154. et Wildebrandum ab Oldenborg in Itinerario Hierosolymitano, ubi Tripolitanis id perperam adscribit, quod alii Tyriis tribuunt. Sed et historiae vetustiores ejusdem artis specimina nobis exhibent. Nam, ut fabulosa taceam; ut quod Samaritani scribunt adulterini Iosuae libri capite vigesimo, illum victis quinque regibus, per epistolam, avicularum alis alligatam, Eleazarum hujus victoriae certiorem reddidisse; et capite trigesimo quarto eundem, columbae ministerio, literas ad Nebichum misisse; et quod apud Aelianum Historiae libri sexti capite septimo, Mares, Aegypti rex, cornicis opera legitur usus in literis quocunque vellet perferendis: haec, inquam, ut praeteream, quia palam fabulosa sunt, quidni credamus, quod habetur in Aeliani Variis lib. noni capite secundo, Taurosthenem Ὀλυμπιονίκην victoriam suam eodem die patri ex Olympia Aeginam significasse per columbam internunciam. Ajunt nimirum, περιστερὰν τὸν Ταυροσθένην ἐπάγεσθαι ἀπολιποῦσαν τοὺς ἑαυτῆς νεοσσοὺς ὑγροὺς ἔτι, καὶ ἀπτῆνας, νικήσαντα, καὶ ἀφεῖναι τὴν πελειάδα, προσάψαντα πορφύραν αὐτῇ· τὴν δὲ ἐπειγομένην πρὸς τοὺς νεοττοὺς, ἀπαυθημερῆσαι ἐκ Πίσσης εἰς Αἴγιναν· Taurosthenem columbam, a suis pullis teneris adhuc et implumibus abstractam, secum deportasse. Cumque vicisset, purpura alligata eandem remisisse, atque illam, summa cum festinatione ad pullos properantem, eodem die Pisa Aeginam advolasse. Quale quid in obsidione Mutinensi evenisse, Plinius et Frontinus referunt, quamvis inter illos parum conveniat. Hic enim libro tertio Stratagematum Hirtium scribit literas, collo columbae seta religatas, ad Decium Brutum, Mutinae obsessum, ab Antonio misisse: ille libri decimi capite trigesimo septimo internuncias in rebus magnis fuisse columbas, epistolas annexas earum pedibus obsidione Mutinensi in castra Consulum D. Bruto mittente. Sed in eadem obsidione II, 544 potuit idem Brutus literas columbarum ministerio et accepisse, et remisisse. Ad hanc columbarum industriam poetas alludere saepe videas. In quibus Anacreon Oda nona columbae suae haec affingit:

And, so that the Argo may be believed to have been a very swift ship, the poets describe it as quick ὅσον πελειάδος [hoson peleiados], like a dove. And they invent the story that a dove was sent by the Argonauts between the Symplegades, and that when it had got through, they concluded from this that the Argo too would get through, as Eustathius teaches on Odyssey μ´. The Arabs and Hebrews agree with this. Thus Damir, after teaching that الشهرمان والشاهين [al-shahramān wa-l-shāhīn], the saharman and the sahin, species of hawk, are most hostile to the dove, says: وهو اطير منهما ومن ساير الطير كلها [wa-huwa aṭyar minhumā wa-min sāyir al-ṭayr kullihā] And it surpasses them in flight, and all birds whatsoever. And on the passage of the Psalm that we have cited, R. Simon, R. Iodan, R. Jonah [=Jonah ibn Janāḥ, Sefer ha-Shorashim], and R. Kimchi, to the question why David prefers the wings of the dove to the wings of other birds, answer thus: כל העופות בשעה שיגעים הם נסים על גבי הסלע או על גבי האילן ונתפסין אבל יונה בשעה שיגעה היא קובצת אחת מאגפיה ופורחת באחת והיא נצולת ואינה נתפסת, All other birds, when they are tired from flying, flee onto a rock or onto a tree, and are caught; but the dove, when it is tired, folds one of its wings and flies with the other, and so escapes and is not caught. And Aben Ezra: והזכיר יונה col. 15 שהיא עם בני אדם ועמה ישגרו המלכים ספריהם, He mentions the dove because it lives with men, and kings send letters by it. Indeed, in the twelfth century after Christ, when Aben Ezra wrote, this was much practised. Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)] Aemilius, On the Deeds of the Franks, book 4, where he speaks of the governor of Hasarchum, a town of Syria: His envoys (sent to Baldwin to beg for help) tied a letter to the tail of a dove which they had brought with them from home when they set out on their embassy, and sent it back as agreed. Thus informed, the governor defended himself excellently II, 543. And where he speaks of Jerusalem besieged by the Christians: It happened that a dove flying over the camp of the Latins, descending as a hawk pressed upon it, was caught by our men. Under its wings was found a letter written in Arabic, both in words and in letters. And in book 5: While they were encamped before the walls (of Tyre), some authors say that a dove flew up. When our men, taught by experience, recognized it as a letter-carrier, so great a shout was raised by the land and naval forces of the Latins that the bird, as if driven by a whirlwind of the disturbed air, fell to the ground. The letter taken from it, written in barbarian characters to the Tyrians, said that help would soon come, that they should be of good courage and endure the siege a few days. Our men, on the other hand, had another letter written in the hand and language of those barbarians whom they held in their power etc. and sent the bird back with the forged and deceitful letter, telling the besieged to take counsel for themselves according to their present need, etc. that no hope of help near at hand could be held out, etc. The Tyrians yielded to the trick. Marmol, in his Africa, book 2, chapter 31, refers this to the year 1123. On the same matter see Jacques de Vitry, Histor. Orient. book 1; Arnold of Lübeck in the History of the Slavs; Vincent in the Doctrinale book 16, ch. 154; and Wildebrand of Oldenburg in the Itinerarium Hierosolymitanum, where he wrongly ascribes to the people of Tripoli what others attribute to the Tyrians. But older histories too offer us examples of the same art. For, to pass over fables, such as what the Samaritans write in chapter 20 of their spurious book of Joshua, that after defeating the five kings he informed Eleazar of this victory by a letter tied to the wings of birds, and in chapter 34 that he sent a letter to Nebichus by the service of a dove; and what we read in Aelian, History, book 6, chapter 7, that Mares, king of Egypt, used a crow to carry letters wherever he wished: to pass over these, I say, since they are plainly fabulous, why should we not believe what is found in Aelian's Varia, book 9, chapter 2, that Taurosthenes, the Ὀλυμπιονίκην [Olympionikēn], announced his victory to his father in Aegina from Olympia on the same day by a dove as messenger? They say, namely, περιστερὰν τὸν Ταυροσθένην ἐπάγεσθαι ἀπολιποῦσαν τοὺς ἑαυτῆς νεοσσοὺς ὑγροὺς ἔτι, καὶ ἀπτῆνας, νικήσαντα, καὶ ἀφεῖναι τὴν πελειάδα, προσάψαντα πορφύραν αὐτῇ· τὴν δὲ ἐπειγομένην πρὸς τοὺς νεοττοὺς, ἀπαυθημερῆσαι ἐκ Πίσσης εἰς Αἴγιναν· [peristeran ton Taurosthenēn epagesthai apolipousan tous heautēs neossous hygrous eti, kai aptēnas, nikēsanta, kai apheinai tēn peleiada, prosapsanta porphyran autē; tēn de epeigomenēn pros tous neottous, apauthēmerēsai ek Pissēs eis Aiginan] that Taurosthenes took with him a dove taken away from its chicks, still tender and unfledged; and when he had won, he sent it back with a piece of purple tied to it, and it, hastening with all speed to its chicks, flew on the same day from Pisa to Aegina. Pliny and Frontinus report that something similar happened at the siege of Mutina, although they hardly agree with each other. For the latter, in book 3 of the Stratagems, writes that Hirtius sent letters, tied with a bristle to a dove's neck, to Decimus Brutus, besieged in Mutina by Antony; the former, in book 10, chapter 37, says that doves were messengers in great affairs, with letters attached to their feet, at the siege of Mutina, when D. Brutus sent them to the consuls' camp. But in the same siege II, 544 the same Brutus could have both received and sent back letters by the service of doves. You may often see the poets allude to this skill of doves. Among them Anacreon, in Ode 9, attributes the following to his dove:


Ἐγὼ δ᾽ Ἀνακρέοντι Egoque Anacreonti Διακονῶ τοσαῦτα, In talibus ministro, Καὶ νῦν οἵας ἐκείνου Ejusque nunc videte col. 16 Ἐπιστολὰς κομίζω. Quales fero tabellas.

Ἐγὼ δ᾽ Ἀνακρέοντι [Egō d᾽ Anakreonti] And I, for Anacreon, Διακονῶ τοσαῦτα, [Diakonō tosauta,] serve in such matters, Καὶ νῦν οἵας ἐκείνου [Kai nyn hoias ekeinou] And now see col. 16 Ἐπιστολὰς κομίζω. [Epistolas komizō.] what letters of his I carry.


Pherecrates in Pictoribus apud Athenaeum libro nono,

Pherecrates in the Painters, in Athenaeus, book 9:


Ἀπόπεμψον ἀγγέλλοντα, τὸν περιστερὸν,

Ἀπόπεμψον ἀγγέλλοντα, τὸν περιστερὸν, [Apopempson angellonta, ton peristeron,]


Remitte columbam nunciam. Martialis de columba in Aretullae sinum delapsa, libri octavi Epigram. 32.

Send back the dove as messenger. Martial, on a dove that flew down into the lap of Aretulla, book 8, Epigram 32:


Haec a Sardois tibi forsitan exulis oris,
Fratre reversuro nuncia venit avis.

Perhaps this bird has come to you from the Sardinian shores of the exile,
a messenger that your brother will return.


His non possum non addere pauca haec ex suavissima Heinsii τοῦ μακαρίτου Elegia de columbis Leidensibus, libri tertii Elegia decima,

To these I cannot help adding these few lines from the most charming Elegy of the late Heinsius on the doves of Leiden, book 3, Elegy 10:


Hic volucrem sacram trepida demittit ab urbe,
Quae referat ductus illius; illa volat.
Moxque domum gaudens dulcesque revisere nidos,
Per medium rursus aera lapsa fuit.
Scriptaque Boisoti mandataque gestat in alis,
Iamque ministerii dulce peregit opus.

Here he sends the sacred bird down from the anxious city,
to carry back his directions; she flies.
And soon, rejoicing to see her home and sweet nest again,
she glided back through the midst of the air.
She carries in her wings the letters and orders of Boisot, and has now completed the sweet work of her service.


Hanc scilicet artem, intermortuam patrum nostrorum memoria, Belgae excitarunt. Et Turcae quoque, quorum imperatorem scribit Linschottus in Armuziae descriptione capite sexto per columbas brevi addiscere, quid fiat in remotissimis imperii sui partibus. Proinde in libro De Animalibus, quem ex Arabico Abulsaphe in Hebraeum sermonem transtulit Calonymus anno Christi 1316. de columba dicitur, היונה המסולסל הוא זה המגביה לעוף נושה כתבים ואגרות מארץ אל ארץ לחבונתו, Columba, in sublime se attollens, id est, quae volatu suo exaltatur, cum per intelligentiam suam fert literas e loco in locum. Nempe, ut ait Alkazuinius, اذا ارسل من موضع بعيد يصعد نحو الهوا وتكون صعوده مدورا فلا يزال يصعد وينظر حتي يري شيا من علامات بلده فعند ذلك يهبط اليها بادني زمان Cum mittitur e loco valde dissito, ascendit in summum aërem. Et ascensus ejus fit in orbem. Neque ascendere et circumspicere desinit, donec regionis suae signum aliquod animadvertat. Tum vero ad illud descendit II, 545 brevi tempore. Et Damir, في طبعه انه يطلب وكره ولو ارسل من الف فرسخ ويحمل الاخبار وياتي بها من المسافة البعيدة في المده القريبة وفيه ما يقطع ثلاثة الاف فرسخ في يوم واحد Et natura ejus est, ut nidum suum repetat, etiamsi mittatur e mille parasangis, et nuncia e locis remotissimis brevissimo tempore ferat: ita, ut unica die quaedam confecisse dicatur tria parasangarum millia. Quod superat omnem fidem, et ab iis confictum puto, qui de magnis majora loquuntur. Epistolium, quod columbae alligatur, Arabice speciali nomine بطاقة bittaka vocatur, id est, πιττάκιον, pittacium. Et زجل zagiala est, columbam in hunc finem emittere. Et columba sic emissa زجال zigial dicitur. Ita est in Alcamus (7).

This art, which had nearly died out in our fathers' time, the Dutch revived. So too did the Turks: Linschoten, in his description of Ormuz, chapter 6, writes that their emperor learns within a short time by means of doves what is happening in the most remote parts of his empire. Accordingly, in the book On Animals, which Calonymus translated from the Arabic of Abulsaphe into Hebrew in the year of Christ 1316, it is said of the dove: היונה המסולסל הוא זה המגביה לעוף נושה כתבים ואגרות מארץ אל ארץ לחבונתו, The dove, raising itself on high, that is, which is exalted in its flight, when by its intelligence it carries letters from place to place. For, as Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt] says, اذا ارسل من موضع بعيد يصعد نحو الهوا وتكون صعوده مدورا فلا يزال يصعد وينظر حتي يري شيا من علامات بلده فعند ذلك يهبط اليها بادني زمان [idhā ursila min mawḍiʿ baʿīd yaṣʿad naḥwa al-hawā wa-takūn ṣuʿūduhu mudawwaran fa-lā yazāl yaṣʿad wa-yanẓur ḥattī yarī shayan min ʿalāmāt baladihi fa-ʿinda dhālika yahbiṭ ilayhā bi-adnā zamān] When it is sent from a very distant place, it climbs into the highest air, and its ascent is made in a circle. Nor does it stop climbing and looking about until it notices some sign of its own region. Then it descends to it II, 545 in a short time. And Damir: في طبعه انه يطلب وكره ولو ارسل من الف فرسخ ويحمل الاخبار وياتي بها من المسافة البعيدة في المده القريبة وفيه ما يقطع ثلاثة الاف فرسخ في يوم واحد [fī ṭabʿihi annahu yaṭlub wakrahu wa-law ursila min alf farsakh wa-yaḥmil al-akhbār wa-yātī bihā min al-masāfa al-baʿīda fī al-mudda al-qarība wa-fīhi mā yaqṭaʿ thalāthat ālāf farsakh fī yawm wāḥid] And its nature is to seek its nest again, even if it is sent from a thousand parasangs, and to carry messages from the most remote places in the shortest time, so that some are said to have covered three thousand parasangs in a single day. This exceeds all belief, and I think it was invented by those who tell of great things as still greater. The little letter that is tied to the dove is called in Arabic by a special name, بطاقة [biṭāqa] bittaka, that is, πιττάκιον [pittakion], pittacium [slip]. And زجل [zajala] zagiala means to send out a dove for this purpose; and a dove so sent is called زجال [zijāl] zigial. So it is in Alcamus R7.

Cana sunt collum, caput, pectus et humeri. Dorsum canum cum maculis fuscis. Rectrices et remiges apice candidae. Oculi et pedes rubescunt“.

The same author has this on the dove of Palestine, p. 553: “The size of a wood pigeon. The neck, head, breast and shoulders are grey. The back grey with dark spots. The tail feathers and flight feathers white at the tip. The eyes and feet are reddish.”


(2) Rosenmüller, II, 534 Sed nimis late patere hoc etymon, quum omnia omnino metalla e terra effodiantur, recte monuit Michaelis in Supplemm. ad Lexx. P. III, p. 950. not., qui tamen omisit, quae de hac voce disputavit A. SCHULTENSIUS in Commentar. ad Prov. XXI, 5. p. 252. Videtur aurum inde חרוץ appellatum esse, quod in nonnullis Arabiae felicis locis, ubi fundum, auri divitem, largius perfundit pluvia, illud enudatur, adeoque quasi jam effissum invenitur, non arte, sed sua sponte. Vide locum ex Taurizio, Grammatico, prolatum a Schultensio, loco laudato.

R2 Rosenmüller, II, 534 But Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], in Supplemm. ad Lexx. [=J. D. Michaelis, Supplementa ad lexica Hebraica] vol. III, p. 950, note, rightly pointed out that this etymology is far too broad, since absolutely all metals are dug out of the earth. He nevertheless omitted what A. Schultens [=Albert Schultens, Liber Jobi (1737)] discussed concerning this word in Commentar. ad Prov. [=Albert Schultens, Commentarius in Proverbia Salomonis (1748)] XXI, 5, p. 252. Gold seems to have been called חרוץ because in some places of Arabia Felix, where rain pours heavily over ground rich in gold, the gold is laid bare and so is found as if already dug out, not by art but of its own accord. Ad imaginis ornatum pertinet, quod eae columbae ad aquas sedere finguntur; nec in hoc nova similitudo captanda. Aliorum interpretum hariolationes referre taedet.

R3 Rosenmüller, II, 538 The ancient interpreters also understood the word מלאת, with unanimous agreement, of the fullness of waters, as Bochart explained above. See HUFNAGEL's II, 539 Observationes in Canticum Canticorum (under the title Auch etwas übers hohe Lied) in the Repertorium für bibl. und morgenl. Litterat. edited by Eichhorn, vol. XI, p. 131. Moreover, what Bochart remarks here about the interpretation of the word מלאת devised by some of the Hebrews applies also to Velthusen [=J. C. Velthusen, in Symbolae litterariae Kilonienses], who in his commentary on this passage (Der Schwesternhandel, eine morgenländische Idyllenkette, mit historischkritischen Untersuchungen pp. 425–428) brings forward much from his manifold store of learning to explain the simile used by the Hebrew poet, but little, I suspect, that bears on the matter. By doves washed in milk our poet undoubtedly meant to express the pure and, as it were, radiant whiteness of the eyes around the pupils. That these doves are pictured as sitting by the waters belongs to the ornament of the image; no further simile should be sought in this. It is tedious to report the guesses of other interpreters.


(4) Rosenmüller, II, 540 Verbi הגה primigeniam vim, quae est in fervore aestuante, ceterarumque inde deductam significationum seriem, cum deinceps transferatur ad incitatiores quosque et vehementiores animi motus, sive ii intus in animo aestuent (unde etiam de meditatione usurpatur, quae Orientali quaedam animi est agitatio et commotio) sive exaestuent et erumpant in murmura, gemitus, ululatus, clamores (hinc de leonis etiam rugitu), et carmina, tam lugubria, quam satyrica, ope Arabici هجى detexit atque exposuit ALB. SCHULTENSIUS in Commentario in Prov. p. 320. seqq coll. p. 71., porro in Commentar. in Iob. pag. 1040. et in Animadverss. Philologg. in Thren. Ierem. Cap. III. vs. 62. p. 509.

R4 Rosenmüller, II, 540 The original sense of the verb הגה, which lies in seething heat, and the series of meanings derived from it, since it is then transferred to all the more agitated and vehement emotions, whether these seethe inwardly in the mind (hence it is also used of meditation, which for an Oriental is a kind of agitation and commotion of the mind) or boil over and burst out into murmurs, moaning, howls, cries (hence also of the roaring of a lion), and into songs, both mournful and satirical: all this ALB. Schultens uncovered and expounded with the help of the Arabic هجى [hajā] in his Commentarius in Prov. p. 320 ff., compare p. 71; further in his Commentar. in Iob. p. 1040, and in the Animadverss. Philologg. in Thren. Ierem. Chapter III, v. 62, p. 509.


(5) Rosenmüller, II, 540 Sed plana sunt omnia, nec verbi alicujus supplemento, nec receptae lectionis mutatione est opus, si verbum נהג ex Arabum نهج suspirare, gemere, suspiria ducere, explicatur, ut primus docuit ALB. SCHULTENS in Animadverss. Philoll. ad Nah. II, 7. p. 342. cui addendus I. D. MICHAELIS in Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. P. V. pag. 1603.

R5 Rosenmüller, II, 540 But everything is plain, and there is no need either to supply some verb or to alter the received reading, if the verb נהג is explained from the Arabic نهج [nahaja] to sigh, to moan, to draw sighs, as ALB. Schultens first showed in Animadverss. Philoll. ad Nah. II, 7, p. 342; to whom add I. D. Michaelis in Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. vol. V, p. 1603.

R6 Rosenmüller, II, 541 Compare ALB. Schultens, Animadverss. Philologg. on Esaj. XIX. 17., p. 265 of the Opera minora, Leiden 1769. ED. Pococke [=Edward Pococke, Commentary on Hosea (1685)] shows a similar use of the Arabic verb فزع [fazaʿa] in his Commentar. on Hos. III, 5.

Part 2, Book 1, chapter 3: The dwellings of doves

II, 545 CAP. III. col. 17

II, 545 Chapter III. col. 17


De Columbarum sedibus.

On the dwelling places of doves.


Columbae in columbariis habent ארבות arubboth, id est, fenestras, seu foramina, in quibus latere et nidificare solent. Es. LX, 8. Qui sunt isti, qui ut nubes volant, et ut columbae אל ארבותיהם, ad fenestras suas? Id est, לגו שובכיהון, ad columbaria sua, ut in Chaldaeo habetur. Sed in metu latent ubivis in fossis, in petris, in montibus, etc. Hinc Ierem. XLVIII, 28. Moabitae, qui prae metu hostium relictis urbibus suis, in rupium antris delitescunt, dicuntur esse כיונה תקנן בעברי פי פחת, ut columba, quae (in simili metu praeter naturam) nidificat in lateribus oris fossae: ubi Chaldaeus, כיונא דשבקא פום שובכה ונחתא ושריא בארעית גובא, ut columba, quae foramine columbarii relicto, descendit, ut habitet in ima fossa (1). Et Cant. II, 14. per columbam, quae II, 546 latet בחגוי הסלע בסתר המדרגה, in fissuris petrae, in latibulo praecipitii, Hebraei Israelitas intelligunt, quos in exitu ex Aegypto ab una parte persequebatur Pharao, ab altera concludebat desertum, anguibus plenum. Unde Chaldaeus interpres, הות מתילא כנישתא דישראל ליונתא דסגירא בחגוי טנרא והיוא מעיק לה מגיו וגצא מעיק לה מברא, Similis erat ecclesia Israelitica columbae, quae inclusa est in fissuris petrae. Et serpens illam intrinsecus obsidet, et accipiter extrinsecus. Quod R. Selomo pluribus persequitur. Sic apud Smyrnaeum lib. 12.

In dovecotes, doves have ארבות arubboth, that is, windows or openings, in which they usually hide and nest. Isa 60:8. Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves אל ארבותיהם, to their windows? That is, לגו שובכיהון, to their dovecotes, as the Chaldee has it. But when afraid they hide anywhere: in pits, in rocks, in mountains, etc. Hence in Jer 48:28 the Moabites, who for fear of the enemy abandon their cities and hide in caves in the cliffs, are said to be כיונה תקנן בעברי פי פחת, like the dove that (in a similar fear, contrary to its nature) nests in the sides of the mouth of a pit. There the Chaldee has כיונא דשבקא פום שובכה ונחתא ושריא בארעית גובא, like a dove that leaves the opening of the dovecote and goes down to dwell at the bottom of a pit R1. And in Song 2:14 by the dove that II, 546 hides בחגוי הסלע בסתר המדרגה, in the clefts of the rock, in the hiding place of the cliff, the Hebrews understand the Israelites, whom at the exodus from Egypt Pharaoh pursued on one side, while on the other the desert, full of snakes, hemmed them in. Hence the Chaldee translator: הות מתילא כנישתא דישראל ליונתא דסגירא בחגוי טנרא והיוא מעיק לה מגיו וגצא מעיק לה מברא, The Israelite congregation was like a dove shut up in the clefts of the rock. And the serpent besieges it from within, and the hawk from without. R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] develops this at greater length. So too in Quintus of Smyrna, book 12:


Ἴρηξ σεῦε πέλειαν· ἐπειγομένη δ᾽ ἄρα κείνη
Κηραμον ἐς πέτρης κατεδύσατο· — —

Ἴρηξ σεῦε πέλειαν· ἐπειγομένη δ᾽ ἄρα κείνη Κηραμον ἐς πέτρης κατεδύσατο· — — [Irēx seue peleian; epeigomenē d' ara keinē Kēramon es petrēs katedysato]


Accipiter columbam persequebatur: illa autem, cum urgeretur, in scopuli cavernam se subduxit. Quod ex his Homeri sumptum Iliad. φ᾽. versu 495.

A hawk was pursuing a dove; and she, hard pressed, slipped into a hollow of the rock. This is taken from these lines of Homer, Iliad φ᾽ [phi], line 495:


— — — φύγεν, ὥς τε πέλεια,
Ἥ ῥάθ᾽ ὑφ᾽ ἴρηκος κοίλην εἰσέπτατο πέτρην·

— — — φύγεν, ὥς τε πέλεια, Ἥ ῥάθ᾽ ὑφ᾽ ἴρηκος κοίλην εἰσέπτατο πέτρην· [phygen, hōs te peleia, Hē rhath' hyph' irēkos koilēn eiseptato petrēn]


Fugit ut columba, quae ab accipitre volavit in cavam petram, in antrum. Quamvis etiam extra metum columbas in antris nidificare suadent haec Poetae:

She fled like a dove that, before a hawk, has flown into a hollow rock, into a cave. Yet these lines of the Poet suggest that doves nest in caves even apart from fear:


Qualis spelunca subito commota columba,
Cui domus, et dulces latebroso in pumice nidi.

As a dove suddenly startled from a cave, whose home and sweet nests are in the hollow rock.


Et quod in Diodoro Semiramis exposita fuisse legitur εἰς τινας ἐρήμους, καὶ πε-τρώδεις τόπους, ἐν οἷς πολλοῦ πλήθους περιστερῶν ἐννοσσεύειν εἰωθότος, in quibusdam desertis et petrosis locis, in quibus cum magna columbarum copia nidificare soleret, etc. Si quidem ibi agatur de columbis proprie dictis. Etiam Ezech. VII, 16. qui ex magna clade evaserunt, oberrare leguntur in montibus כיוני הגיאות, ut columbae convallium. Quae nempe metu aucupis, aut accipitris, naturali sede deserta, coguntur alio secedere, ut vitae suae consulant. Columbis convallium montanae opponuntur, quomodo ferae domesticis. Sic Hesychio Semiramis est περιστερὰ ὄρειος, quod jam ante est expositum. Et in Alcamus العزف Alozpho est الحمام الطورانية columba montana.

So too we read in Diodorus that Semiramis was exposed εἰς τινας ἐρήμους, καὶ πετρώδεις τόπους, ἐν οἷς πολλοῦ πλήθους περιστερῶν ἐννοσσεύειν εἰωθότος [eis tinas erēmous, kai petrōdeis topous, en hois pollou plēthous peristerōn ennosseuein eiōthotos], in certain desert and rocky places, in which, since a great number of doves used to nest there, etc., if indeed doves in the proper sense are meant there. Also in Ezek 7:16 those who escaped a great slaughter are said to wander on the mountains כיוני הגיאות, like doves of the valleys. These, that is, for fear of the fowler or the hawk, abandon their natural home and are forced to withdraw elsewhere to save their lives. Mountain doves are contrasted with doves of the valleys, as wild animals are with domestic ones. Thus in Hesychius, Semiramis is περιστερὰ ὄρειος [peristera oreios], as has already been explained. And in the Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] العزف [al-ʿazf] Alozpho is الحمام الطورانية [al-ḥamām al-ṭūrāniyya], mountain dove.


Fallor, aut etiam columbae arborum, vel lucorum memorantur in titulo col. 18 Psal. LVI. in cujus versione puto interpretes hactenus frustra desudasse. Nam, ut veteres praeteream, qui in diversissima abeunt, quis Selomonem, aut Kimchium ferat, Hebraea verba על יונת אלם רחוקים, reddentes, de columba silentii remotorum, II, 547 ut ad Davidem referant? Nempe, ut ait Selomo, David tum erat inter Philistaeos, procul a terra Israelis. Et Kimchius columbam vocari addit, quia Os. VII, 11. columba vocatur fatua, et David se fatuum esse simulabat. Et columbam silentii, id est mutam; quia non loquebatur more suo, sed tanquam insanus. Nec multo magis probo virum magnum (2) e nostris, qui, sequutus auctores τοῦ Midras, eadem verba ita exponit: De anima vim patiente a manipulo longinquorum. Quae interpretatio, ut et prior, de qua diximus, Hebraeo textui vim facit tam manifestam, ut cuivis Hebraice vel mediocriter docto pateat, cur a me rejiciatur. His igitur relictis, dicam, quod res est. Aben Ezra recte vidit, verba יונת אלם רחוקים initium esse cantici, ad cujus modulos David hunc Psalmum composuit: sed ea reliquit ἀνερμήνευτα. Nos vero hic quaerimus, quid illa verba significent. Et certum est ex iis, prout leguntur a Masorethis, nullum posse commodum sensum erui. Itaque periti videant, annon iisdem literis manentibus, sed uno puncto mutato, sit consultius אלם elim, pro אלם elem, id est, Hirec pro Segol. Quo dato, sacrae cantionis, cujus modulos in hoc Psalmo sequitur David, initium hoc fuerit, Columba nemorum remotorum. Hoc fefellit interpretes, adeoque ipsos Masorethas, quod in אלם deest Iod, nota Pluralis numeri. Sed, ut recte observat Cl. Buxtorfius, Thesauri Grammatici libri primi capite nono, Iod saepe excidit ex Plurali, ut in תנינם, dracones, Deut. XXXII, 33. תמימם, integri, Levit. IX, 2. Addo solum exemplum similis Ellipseως in hac voce, quamvis in alia notione, באלם, in Diis fortibus, pro באלים, Exod. XV, 11. Porro יונת אלים, columba arborum, seu nemorum, est columba sylvestris, id est, palumbus, qui in sylvis degit, et in arboribus nidificat. Theocritus Idyll. 5.

Unless I am mistaken, doves of the trees, or of the groves, are also mentioned in the title col. 18 of Psal. LVI., in the rendering of which I think interpreters have so far laboured in vain. For, to pass over the ancients, who go off in the most diverse directions, who could tolerate Selomo or Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], who render the Hebrew words על יונת אלם רחוקים as concerning the dove of silence of those far off, II, 547 so as to refer them to David? For, as Selomo says, David was then among the Philistines, far from the land of Israel. And Kimchi adds that he is called a dove because in Hos 7:11 the dove is called silly, and David was feigning to be a fool; and a dove of silence, that is, mute, because he did not speak in his usual manner but like a madman. Nor do I much more approve of a great man R2 from among our own, who, following the authors of the Midrash, explains the same words thus: Concerning the soul suffering violence from a band of those far off. This interpretation, like the former one we have discussed, does such manifest violence to the Hebrew text that anyone even moderately learned in Hebrew will see why I reject it. Leaving these aside, then, I shall say what the matter is. Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] rightly saw that the words יונת אלם רחוקים are the opening of a song to whose melody David composed this Psalm; but he left them ἀνερμήνευτα [anermēneuta]. Here, however, we are asking what those words mean. And it is certain that no suitable sense can be drawn from them as they are read by the Masoretes. Let the experts therefore consider whether, keeping the same letters but changing one vowel point, it would not be wiser to read אלם elim instead of אלם elem, that is, Hirec for Segol. Granted this, the opening of the sacred song whose melody David follows in this Psalm would be: The dove of the distant groves. What misled the interpreters, and even the Masoretes themselves, is that אלם lacks the Iod, the mark of the plural. But, as the distinguished Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum] rightly observes in Thesaurus Grammaticus, book 1, ch. 9, Iod often drops out of the plural, as in תנינם, dragons, Deut 32:33, תמימם, unblemished, Lev 9:2. I add only an example of a similar ellipsis in this very word, though in another sense: באלם, among the mighty gods, for באלים, Exod 15:11. Further, יונת אלים, the dove of the trees, or of the groves, is the wild dove, that is, the wood pigeon (palumbus), which lives in woods and nests in trees. Theocritus, Idyll 5:


Κἠγὼ μὲν δώσω τᾷ παρθένῳ αὐτίκα φάσσαν,
Ἐκ τᾶς ἀρκεύθω καθελών· τηνεὶ γὰρ ἐφίσδει·

Κἠγὼ μὲν δώσω τᾷ παρθένῳ αὐτίκα φάσσαν, Ἐκ τᾶς ἀρκεύθω καθελών· τηνεὶ γὰρ ἐφίσδει· [Kēgō men dōsō tai parthenōi autika phassan, Ek tas arkeuthō kathelōn; tēnei gar ephisdei]


Et ego quidem mox puellae palumbum dabo, ex Iunipero abreptum: ibi enim sedet. Nemesianus Ecloga secunda,

And I will soon give the girl a wood pigeon, taken from the juniper: for there it sits. Nemesianus, Eclogue 2:


Praeterea tenerum leporem, geminasque palumbes,
Nuper quae potui, sylvarum praemia, misi.

Besides, I have sent a tender hare and a pair of wood pigeons, the spoils of the woods, which I lately could.


Auctor Philomelae,

The author of the Philomela:


Plausitat arborea clamans de fronde palumbes.

The wood pigeon claps its wings, calling from the leafy tree.


Proinde ramier Galli vocant a ramis arborum, quibus insidet. Idem de liviis quoque scribitur, quae Graecis πελειάδες. Ita Herodotus in Euterpe πελειά-δα liviam describit ἰζομένην ἐπὶ φηγὸν, fago insidentem. Et de turture Origenes II, 548 in Cantica Homil. 2. Semper in montium jugis et in arborum verticibus commoratur. Theodoretus quoque in Cant. 2. turturem dicit ἐν δένδροις ἀμφιλα-φέσι τὰς καλιὰς πηγνύναι, in umbrosis arboribus nidos construere. Et Chrysostomus in Homilia De turture, Ἐπὶ τῶν στερεμνίων πρέμνων τὴν καλίαν αὐτῶν πήξασαι, καὶ ἀφόβως ἐπωάζουσαι, τοὺς νεοττοὺς ἑαυτῶν ἐκεῖθεν πετάζουσι· Firmis arborum stipitibus nidum suum defigentes et secure incubantes, pullos suos ibi extendunt. Quod columbis, proprie dictis, est infrequens, non tamen sine exemplo. Hinc Anacreon Oda nona περιστερὰν dicit πέτασθαι ὄρη τε, καὶ κατ᾽ ἄγρους, καὶ δένδρεσιν καθίζειν, per montes et agros volare, et arboribus insidere. Et Horatius libri primi Oda secunda,

Accordingly the French call it ramier, from the branches (rami) of the trees on which it perches. The same is written also of the rock doves (liviae), which the Greeks call πελειάδες [peleiades]. Thus Herodotus in Euterpe describes a πελειάδα [peleiada], a rock dove, ἰζομένην ἐπὶ φηγὸν [izomenēn epi phēgon], perching on a beech. And of the turtledove Origen II, 548 on the Song of Songs, Homily 2: It always lingers on the ridges of mountains and on the tops of trees. Theodoret also, on Cant. 2, says that the turtledove ἐν δένδροις ἀμφιλαφέσι τὰς καλιὰς πηγνύναι [en dendrois amphilaphesi tas kalias pēgnynai], builds its nests in shady trees. And Chrysostom in the homily On the Turtledove: Ἐπὶ τῶν στερεμνίων πρέμνων τὴν καλίαν αὐτῶν πήξασαι, καὶ ἀφόβως ἐπωάζουσαι, τοὺς νεοττοὺς ἑαυτῶν ἐκεῖθεν πετάζουσι· [Epi tōn steremniōn premnōn tēn kalian autōn pēxasai, kai aphobōs epōazousai, tous neottous heautōn ekeithen petazousi] Fixing their nest on firm tree trunks and brooding securely, they spread out their young there. This is infrequent in doves properly so called, yet not without example. Hence Anacreon, Ode 9, says that a περιστερὰν [peristeran] πέτασθαι ὄρη τε, καὶ κατ᾽ ἄγρους, καὶ δένδρεσιν καθίζειν [petasthai orē te, kai kat' agrous, kai dendresin kathizein], flies over mountains and fields and perches on trees. And Horace, book 1, Ode 2:


Piscium et summa genus haesit ulmo,
Nota quae sedes fuerat columbis.

And the race of fishes clung to the top of the elm, which had been the familiar seat of doves.


Et Virgilius libro sexto de columbis, Aeneae a Venere immissis,

And Virgil in book 6, of the doves sent to Aeneas by Venus:


Sedibus optatis gemina super arbore sidunt. col. 19

They settle in the longed-for seat upon the twofold tree. col. 19


Et Suetonius in Octavio capite nonagesimo quarto, ubi de palma prope Mundam, quam ut omen victoriae D. Iulius conservari jusserat. Ex ea continuo enata soboles, adeo in paucis diebus adolevit, ut non aequipararet modo matricem, verum etiam obtegeret, frequentareturque columbarum nidis: quamvis id avium genus duram et prosperam frondem maxime vitet. Ex his planum est, quid sit in Psalmi titulo Columba arborum, aut nemorum remotorum, nempe ab urbibus et locis cultis (3).

And Suetonius in the Octavius, ch. 94, on the palm near Munda which the deified Julius had ordered to be preserved as an omen of victory: From it a shoot at once sprang up and in a few days grew so much that it not only equalled the parent tree but even overshadowed it, and was frequented by the nests of doves, although that kind of bird especially avoids hard and rough foliage. From these it is plain what the dove of the trees, or of the distant groves, in the title of the Psalm is: namely, distant from cities and cultivated places R3.


(1) Rosenmüller, II, 545 Quod columba in lateribus oris foraminis nidificare hic dicitur, id GUSSETIUS in Lexico p. 573. eo refert, quod columbae non directe e regione orificii ponere solent nidum, sed ad alterum latus orificii hinc et illinc; unde qui peristereones struunt, cellularum fenestras non in earum medio, sed in latere faciei extremo aperiunt. Sed mihi praeplacet Grotii sententia, vocabula עברי פי - פחת intelligentis de lateribus II, 546 scissae rupis. Veterum interpretum hariolationes, quae nihil iuvant sententiae intelligentiam, enumeravit I. D. MICHAE-LIS in Observatt. Critt. et Philologg. ad Ierem. p. 256.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 545 That the dove is here said to nest in the sides of the mouth of the hole, Gussetius, in his Lexicon p. 573, refers to the fact that doves are not accustomed to place their nest directly opposite the opening, but to one side or the other of the opening; hence those who build dovecotes open the windows of the cells not in their middle but at the outer edge of the face. But I much prefer the opinion of Grotius, who understands the words עברי פי - פחת of the sides II, 546 of a split rock. The guesses of the ancient interpreters, which contribute nothing to understanding the meaning, have been listed by J. D. Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer] in Observatt. Critt. et Philologg. ad Ierem. p. 256.


(2) Rosenmüller, II, 547 Franciscum Iunium.

R2 Rosenmüller, II, 547 Franciscus Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible].


(3) Rosenmüller, II, 548 Ex animo ego Bocharto assentior in eo, quod verba יונה אלם רחוקים initium esse dicit carminis, ad cujus modulos Davides hunc Psalmum composuit (repetenda sunt, quae de simili Syrorum usu in carminibus inscribendis monuimus supra ad P. I. L. III. cap. XVII. not. 8.); sed in verbis ipsis explicandis frustra hodie laboretur. Quis enim ex his verbis: Sey Lob und Ehr, quae multis cantilenis inscripta inveniuntur, sanum sensum elicuerit, nisi cui notus sit primus versus cantici ejus, cuius moduli praescribuntur? Sine damno igitur ignorabimus sensum trium illorum vocabulorum Hebraicorum. Conjecturae tamen, a Bocharto allatae, nemo facile sagacitatis laudem denegaverit, maxime si cum ea contuleris, quae alii interpretes de verbis vexatissimis nugati sunt, quae, si lubet, in unum congesta legi possunt in PFEIFFERI Dubiis Vexatt. p. 605., porro in SIMONIS Lex. Hebr. sub vocc. אלם et עלם, atque in I. B. KOEHLERI Animadverss. Critt. in Psal. LVI. 1. in Repertorio für bibl. und morgenl. Litterat., Eichhornii cura instructo, P. VIII. p. 252. seqq.

R3 Rosenmüller, II, 548 I wholeheartedly agree with Bochart in saying that the words יונה אלם רחוקים are the beginning of a song to whose tune David composed this Psalm (what we noted above, at vol. 1, book 3, ch. 17, note 8, about a similar custom of the Syrians in titling songs should be recalled here); but in explaining the words themselves one would labour in vain today. For who could draw a sound meaning from the words Sey Lob und Ehr, which are found written above many hymns, unless he knew the first line of the song whose tune is prescribed? We may therefore remain ignorant of the sense of those three Hebrew words without loss. Yet no one would readily deny the conjecture put forward by Bochart the praise of acuteness, especially if one compares it with the trifles other interpreters have produced about these much-vexed words, which, if one wishes, can be read gathered together in Pfeiffer's Dubia Vexata p. 605, further in Simonis' Lex. Hebr. under the words אלם and עלם, and in J. B. Koehler's Animadverss. Critt. on Ps 56:1 in the Repertorium für bibl. und morgenl. Litterat., edited by Eichhorn, vol. 8, p. 252 ff.
