II, 549 CAP. IV.

II, 549 Chapter IV.


De Columbae simplicitate, mansuetudine, castitate et timiditate.

On the dove's simplicity, gentleness, chastity and timidity.


Iam de columbarum acturi moribus, incipiemus a celebri Christi dicto Matth. X, 16. Γίνεσθε φρόνιμοι ὡς οἱ ὄφεις, καὶ ἀκέραιοι ὡς αἱ περιστεραί· Estote prudentes ut serpentes, et simplices ut columbae. A Tzetze Chiliade 9. Hist. 263. φρόνιμοι et ἀκέραιοι pro eodem sumuntur. Postquam enim prudentes eos dici asseruit, cum ut serpentes caput servant, id est, fidem in Deum, addit continuo post:

Now, as we are about to treat of the habits of doves, we shall begin with the famous saying of Christ, Matt 10:16 Γίνεσθε φρόνιμοι ὡς οἱ ὄφεις, καὶ ἀκέραιοι ὡς αἱ περιστεραί [Ginesthe phronimoi hōs hoi opheis, kai akeraioi hōs hai peristerai]· Be ye prudent as serpents, and simple as doves. By Tzetzes, Chiliad 9, Hist. 263, φρόνιμοι [phronimoi] and ἀκέραιοι [akeraioi] are taken as meaning the same thing. For after he has asserted that they are called prudent when, like serpents, they guard their head, that is, their faith in God, he immediately adds:


Ἀκέραιοι δὲ γίνεσθε, ὡς αἱ περιστεραί μοι·
Καὶ τοῦτο πάλιν τὸ αὐτὸ δηλοῖ τε, καὶ σημαίνει.
Ἀκέραιοι γὰρ λέγονται περιστεραὶ τοιώς δε,
Φρόνιμοι, ὥσπερ λέγεται περιστερὰ τοῦ Νῶε.

Ἀκέραιοι δὲ γίνεσθε, ὡς αἱ περιστεραί μοι· Καὶ τοῦτο πάλιν τὸ αὐτὸ δηλοῖ τε, καὶ σημαίνει. Ἀκέραιοι γὰρ λέγονται περιστεραὶ τοιώς δε, Φρόνιμοι, ὥσπερ λέγεται περιστερὰ τοῦ Νῶε. [Akeraioi de ginesthe, hōs hai peristerai moi; Kai touto palin to auto dēloi te, kai sēmainei. Akeraioi gar legontai peristerai toiōs de, Phronimoi, hōsper legetai peristera tou Nōe.]


Simplices autem mihi sitis sicut columbae. Et hoc rursus idem indicat et significat. Simplices enim dicuntur columbae, tali modo prudentes, ut dicitur columba Noe. Quae nempe ad arcam rediit, id est, ad ecclesiam, a qua non secedendum. Quo nihil absurdius fingi potuit. Nam, ut serpens et columba, ita φρόνιμος et ἀκέραιος nullo modo sunt synonyma. Neque Christus ut synonyma, sed ut opposita junxit, egregia antithesi, quali utitur Martialis, cum dicit libri decimi Epigr. 47.

But be ye simple for me as doves. And this again indicates and signifies the same thing. For doves are called simple, prudent in such a way as Noah's dove is spoken of. That is, the dove which returned to the ark, that is, to the church, from which one must not depart. Nothing more absurd could have been devised. For, like the serpent and the dove, so φρόνιμος [phronimos] and ἀκέραιος [akeraios] are in no way synonyms. Nor did Christ join them as synonyms, but as opposites, in a striking antithesis, such as Martial uses when he says, in book 10, Epigr. 47:


Prudens simplicitas, pares amici.

Prudent simplicity, friends who are equals.


Nempe, ut prudentia sine simplicitate in versutiam degenerat, ita simplicitas sine prudentia nihil quidquam est, quam fatuitas et stultitia. Prudentes Hebraice sunt ערומים, et simplices פתיים, vel פתאים. Quae duo Solomon saepe opponit. Sic Prov. I, 4. לתת לפתאים ערמה, ad dandum simplicibus prudentiam. Prov. VIII, 5. Intelligite simplices prudentiam. Prov. XIV, 15. פתי, simplex cre- dit omni verbo, וערום, et prudens advertit ad gressum suum. Prov. XIX, 25. ופתי יערים, Et simplex prudens fiet. Prov. XXII, 3. ערום, Prudens, cum videt malum, abscondit se, ופתיים, At simplices, transeunt et mulctantur. Atque, col. 20 ut serpens dicitur ערום, φρόνιμος, Gen. III, 1. ita columba dicitur פתה, sim- plex Os. VII, 11. Et factus est Ephraim כיונה פתה אין לב, ut columba simplex, carens corde, id est, vecors. Ad quae duo loca haud dubie respexit Christus. Si objicias, utrumque in vitio poni, et serpentem ערום dici, non quia prudens, sed quia callidus est, et versipellis: Et columbam פתה, non quia simplex, sed quia fatua est, et אין לב, vecors, ut statim sequitur. Respondeo, primo tam II, 550 ערום, quam פתי, vel פתה voces esse medias, quaeque pro subjecti ratione etiam in laudem cedant. Ita ערום non solum callidum et versutum, sed et prudentem, et ערמה prudentiam sonat, quod abunde docent loca Solomonis supra al-lata. Vicissim פתי non solum ἄφρονα fatuum, sed et ἀκέραιον simplicem significat, ut Ps. CXVI, 6. שמר פתאים יהוה. simplices servat Dominus. Eas igitur voces potuit Christus etiam in laudem usurpare. Secundo, nec serpentis prudentia, nec columbae simplicitas, laudantur a Christo solae et ab invicem divulsae, sed tum demum laudantur, cum simul conjunctae sunt, ita, ut una suppleat, quod deest in altera, aut corrigat, quod excedit. Quomodo e duobus pharmacis, quae separatim noxia sunt, tertium componitur, quod utile est et salutare, quia se mutuo temperant. Unde est, quod haec duo veteres tam saepe jungunt. Gregorius Nazianzenus de patre Oratione 19. Τὸ γὰρ τοῦ ὄφεως φρόνιμον περὶ τὸ κακὸν τῷ τῆς περιστερᾶς ἀκεραίῳ περὶ τὸ καλὸν ἀναμίξας, οὐδὲ τὸ φρόνιμον εἴασε κακοῦργον γενέσθαι. οὔτε τὸ ἁπλοῦν ἀνόητον, ἀλλ᾽ ἓν ἀρε-τῆς εἶδος, ὡς μάλιστα ἐνῆν, ἐξ ἀμφοτέρων ἀπηκριβώσατο. Cum serpentis ad malum prudentiam cum columbae ad bonum simplicitate conjunxisset, ita se comparavit, ut nec prudentiam in versutam improbitatem, nec simplicitatem in stoliditatem degenerare sineret: verum ex ambabus, quoad ejus fieri poterat, unam virtutis speciem efficeret, numeris omnibus perfectam et absolutam. Hieronymus ad Paulinum de institutione monachi, Habeto simplicitatem columbae, ne cuiquam machineris dolos, et serpentis astutiam, ne aliorum supplanteris insidiis. Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 3. epist. 175. Ἡ φρόνησις τῇ ἁπλότητι κιρνωμένη θεῖόν τι χρῆμα· φημὶ δὲ ἐντελεστάτην ἀρετὴν ἀποτελεῖ· εἰ δὲ θατέρα θατέρας χωρισθείη, ἡ μὲν εἰς πονηρίαν ἐμπίπτει, ἡ δὲ εἰς μωρίαν τελευτᾷ· Prudentia, simplicitate temperata, divinam quandam rem, hoc est, numeris omnibus absolutam virtutem parit. At si altera ab altera sejungatur, illa in perversitatem incidit, haec vero in stultitiam desinit. Faustus, De libero arbitrio lib. 2. capite ultimo, Faciamus hominem simplicem, faciamus astutum: simplicem, ne malum callidus inferat, astutum, ne incautus incurrat. Gregorius in Iobum lib. 1. cap. 2. Utraque necessario in admonitione conjunxit, ut et simplicitatem columbae astutia serpentis instrueret, et rursum serpentis astutiam columbae simplicitas temperaret. Sidonius lib. 7. Epist. 13. de Lupo, Tricassiensi episcopo, Simplicitatem columbae in ecclesia servat, in foro serpentis astutiam. Bonis prudens, malis cautus, neutris callidus judicatur. S. Bernardus Epist. 327. ad Papam Innocentium: in ecclesia ergo simplicitas, in foro astutia servanda est; hic, ne decipiaris, illic, ne decipias. Videsis plura de hoc argumento Caesarii Dial. 4. Quaest. 190. Porro simplices hic ἁπλοὶ non dicuntur, sed ἀκέραιοι. Res tamen eodem redit. Nam ex κεράω, misceo, factum ἀκέραιος proprie id significat, quod externum et peregrinum nihil habet admixtum. Sunt, quibus ἀκέραιος idem est, quod ἀκερᾶς, vel ἀκέρατος, II, 551 qui cornua non habet, adeoque est ἀβλαβὴς, et innoxius, metaphora ab iis animalibus sumta, quae cornu feriunt. Quomodo sumsisse videntur Arabs et Aethiops, quorum illi ἀκέραιοι sunt ودعا, huic የዋሃን፡ id est, mites, et mansueti. Sed prius etymon videtur magis analogicum. Nec satis convenit, ut excornis dicatur pro innoxio, cum aquilis, et leonibus, et pluribus aliis feris, col. 21 quae cornua non habent, multae sint nocendi artes, quibus in aliorum animalium perniciem abutuntur. Praeterea prudentibus simplices opponuntur, mites et mansueti non item. Itaque, si mites reddas, peribit gratia oppositionis, quae hic est manifesta inter serpentis prudentiam et columbae simplicitatem. Cujusmodi est illa Pauli Rom. XVI, 19. Vos quidem volo σοφοὺς sapientes esse in bono, ἀκεραίους δὲ, simplices vero in malo. Innocentes verterat Cl. Beza in primis editionibus. Sed in posterioribus idem in simplices recte mutavit, ut constaret oppositio (1). Eodem facit, quod in vetustissimo illo Beza exemplari pro ἀκέραιοι legebatur ἁπλούστατοι simplicissimi. Nec leve est, quod, ut ex Mose sumtum est, quod serpens vocatur prudens, ita ex Osea, quod columba vocatur simplex. At ubi mitis vocetur, Prophetarum locus nullus occurrit. Itaque Christiani Arabes videntur minus intellexisse, quid hoc loco sint ἀκέραιοι, quam Mahumetani doctores, qui بلها bulhan, id est, simplices reddunt. Ita in libro sacerdotis Achmed, cui titulus الزهد id est, abstinentia, dicit Iazid, Malzarae filius, Iesum discipulis suis praecepisse ان يكون بلها في الله مشل الحمام ut essent bulhan (id est, simplices) in Deo sicut columbae. Ita بلها bulhan reddimus cum Arabum peritissimis a Singulari ابله ablaho, cui كيس chaison opponitur, id est, versutus et callidus. Et sic sumendum docent, quae ibidem sequuntur: ليس شي ابله من الحمام وذلك انك تاخذ فرخيه من تحته فتذبحهما ثم يعود الي مكانه فيفرخ فيه Nihil est columba simplicius. Etsi enim pullos illi subtractos mactaveris, tamen ad locum suum subinde redit, et in eo pullos excludit. Quod ipsum scribunt Patres in Oseae locum, quem citavimus. Theodoretus, Ἐκείνη τῶν ἰδίων νεοττῶν ἀφαιρουμένη οὐκ ἀφίπταται, ἀλλὰ τοῖς αὐ-τοῖς προστρέχει χωρίοις. Et ex illo Theophylactus, Illa pullis sublatis non avolat, verum in iisdem locis remanet. Paullo aliter Hieronymus: Aves caeterae pullos suos etiam cum periculo vitae suae protegere festinant, et cum ad nidum II, 552 suum accipitrem, colubrum, corvum, sive cornicem accedere viderint, huc illucque volitant, et immittunt se morsu, et unguibus lacerant, et dolorem parentis querula voce testantur. Sola columba ablatos pullos non dolet, non requirit. Sed quam vere, non satis scio, cum columbae, aut palumbis genus الورشان alvvarsen describatur ab Arabibus بالحنو علي اولاده حتي انه ربما قتل نفسه اذا راها في يد القانص tanto affectu fervens erga pullos suos, ut quandoque se ipsum interimat, cum illos videt in manu aucupis. Ita ha-betur in Damire. Et in genere scriptores columbam commendant ab amore in prolem. Plinius lib. 10. cap. 34. de columba mare et foemina: Amor utrique sobolis aequalis: saepe ex hac causa castigatio, pigrius intrante foemina ad pullos. De quibus plura Aristoteles Hist. lib. 9. cap. 7. Aelianus Hist. lib. 3. cap. 45. Al-ter Aelianus Var. lib. 1. cap. 15. Athenaeus lib. 9. cap. 11. Porphyrius Περὶ ἀποχῆς, etc. lib. 3. quae non vacat hic describere. Alii columbae simplicitatem in eo patere asserunt, quod retia non evitat, neque laqueos, sibi paratos, col. 22 cum se demittit ad cibum. Et huic columbae stupori Oseam Israelitarum socordiam conferre volunt, qui pericula non praecavebant, et se ipsos in hostium potestatem conjiciebant. Utut se res habeat, hanc columbae simplicitatem agnoverunt etiam οἱ ἔξωθεν. Sic ad illud Iuvenalis,

For just as prudence without simplicity degenerates into cunning, so simplicity without prudence is nothing but foolishness and stupidity. The prudent in Hebrew are ערומים, and the simple פתיים, or פתאים. Solomon often sets these two against each other. Thus Prov 1:4. לתת לפתאים ערמה, to give prudence to the simple. Prov 8:5 O ye simple, understand prudence. Prov 14:15. פתי, the simple believes every word, וערום, but the prudent considers his step. Prov 19:25. ופתי יערים, And the simple will become prudent. Prov 22:3. ערום, The prudent, when he sees evil, hides himself, ופתיים, but the simple pass on and are punished. And, col. 20 just as the serpent is called ערום, φρόνιμος [phronimos], Gen 3:1, so the dove is called פתה, simple, Hos 7:11 And Ephraim has become כיונה פתה אין לב, like a simple dove, lacking heart, that is, senseless. To these two passages Christ no doubt alluded. You may object that both are put as vices: that the serpent is called ערום not because it is prudent but because it is crafty and wily, and the dove פתה not because it is simple but because it is foolish, and אין לב, senseless, as immediately follows. I reply, first, that both II, 550 ערום and פתי or פתה are neutral words, which according to their subject may also turn to praise. Thus ערום means not only crafty and cunning but also prudent, and ערמה prudence, as the passages of Solomon cited above amply show. Conversely פתי signifies not only ἄφρονα [aphrona], foolish, but also ἀκέραιον [akeraion], simple, as in Ps 116:6. שמר פתאים יהוה, the Lord preserves the simple. Christ could therefore use these words in praise as well. Second, neither the serpent's prudence nor the dove's simplicity is praised by Christ on its own and torn from the other; they are praised only when joined together, so that the one supplies what is lacking in the other, or corrects what is excessive. In the same way, from two drugs that are harmful separately a third is compounded that is useful and wholesome, because they temper each other. Hence the ancients so often join these two. Gregory of Nazianzus, on his father, Oration 19: Τὸ γὰρ τοῦ ὄφεως φρόνιμον περὶ τὸ κακὸν τῷ τῆς περιστερᾶς ἀκεραίῳ περὶ τὸ καλὸν ἀναμίξας, οὐδὲ τὸ φρόνιμον εἴασε κακοῦργον γενέσθαι. οὔτε τὸ ἁπλοῦν ἀνόητον, ἀλλ᾽ ἓν ἀρετῆς εἶδος, ὡς μάλιστα ἐνῆν, ἐξ ἀμφοτέρων ἀπηκριβώσατο. [To gar tou opheōs phronimon peri to kakon tō tēs peristeras akeraiō peri to kalon anamixas, oude to phronimon eiase kakourgon genesthai. oute to haploun anoēton, all᾽ hen aretēs eidos, hōs malista enēn, ex amphoterōn apēkribōsato.] Having joined the serpent's prudence regarding evil with the dove's simplicity regarding good, he so conducted himself that he let neither prudence degenerate into cunning wickedness nor simplicity into stupidity, but from both, as far as was possible, he produced a single form of virtue, perfect and complete in every respect. Jerome, to Paulinus on the training of a monk: Have the simplicity of the dove, so as not to contrive snares against anyone, and the cunning of the serpent, so as not to be tripped up by the plots of others. Isidore of Pelusium, book 3, epist. 175: Ἡ φρόνησις τῇ ἁπλότητι κιρνωμένη θεῖόν τι χρῆμα· φημὶ δὲ ἐντελεστάτην ἀρετὴν ἀποτελεῖ· εἰ δὲ θατέρα θατέρας χωρισθείη, ἡ μὲν εἰς πονηρίαν ἐμπίπτει, ἡ δὲ εἰς μωρίαν τελευτᾷ· [Hē phronēsis tē haplotēti kirnōmenē theion ti chrēma; phēmi de entelestatēn aretēn apotelei; ei de thatera thateras chōristheiē, hē men eis ponērian empiptei, hē de eis mōrian teleuta;] Prudence tempered with simplicity produces something divine, that is, a virtue complete in every respect. But if the one is separated from the other, the former falls into perversity, while the latter ends in folly. Faustus, On Free Will, book 2, last chapter: Let us make man simple, let us make him astute: simple, so that being crafty he may not inflict evil; astute, so that being incautious he may not fall into it. Gregory on Job, book 1, ch. 2: He necessarily joined both in the admonition, so that the cunning of the serpent might equip the simplicity of the dove, and in turn the simplicity of the dove might temper the cunning of the serpent. Sidonius, book 7, Epist. 13, on Lupus, bishop of Troyes: In the church he keeps the simplicity of the dove, in the forum the cunning of the serpent. To the good he is judged prudent, to the wicked wary, to neither crafty. St Bernard [=Bernard of Clairvaux], Epist. 327, to Pope Innocent: in the church, then, simplicity must be kept, in the forum cunning; here, lest you be deceived, there, lest you deceive. See more on this subject in Caesarius, Dial. 4, Quaest. 190. Further, the simple are here called not ἁπλοί [haploi] but ἀκέραιοι [akeraioi]. Yet it comes to the same thing. For ἀκέραιος [akeraios], formed from κεράω [keraō], misceo [I mix], properly signifies that which has nothing external and foreign mixed into it. Some take ἀκέραιος [akeraios] to be the same as ἀκερᾶς [akeras] or ἀκέρατος [akeratos], II, 551 that which has no horns, and hence is ἀβλαβής [ablabēs] and harmless, a metaphor taken from animals that strike with the horn. So the Arabic and Ethiopic translators seem to have taken it: in the former ἀκέραιοι [akeraioi] are ودعا [wudaʿā], in the latter የዋሃን፡ [yawāhān], that is, mild and gentle. But the first etymology seems more regular. Nor is it quite fitting that hornless should be said for harmless, since eagles, lions and many other wild beasts col. 21 that have no horns possess many ways of doing harm, which they employ to destroy other animals. Moreover, the simple are opposed to the prudent, but the mild and gentle are not. So if you render mild, the grace of the opposition will be lost, which is evident here between the serpent's prudence and the dove's simplicity. Of the same kind is that of Paul, Rom 16:19: I would have you σοφούς [sophous] wise in what is good, ἀκεραίους δέ [akeraious de], but simple in what is evil. The illustrious Beza had rendered innocent in his first editions, but in later ones he rightly changed it to simple, so that the opposition might stand R1. To the same effect is the fact that in that very ancient manuscript of Beza ἁπλούστατοι [haploustatoi], most simple, was read for ἀκέραιοι [akeraioi]. Nor is it a slight point that, just as the serpent's being called prudent is taken from Moses, so the dove's being called simple is taken from Hosea. But no passage of the Prophets occurs where it is called mild. Thus the Christian Arabs seem to have understood less well what ἀκέραιοι [akeraioi] means here than the Muslim doctors, who render بلها [bulhan] bulhan, that is, simple. So in the book of the priest Achmed entitled الزهد [al-zuhd], that is, abstinence, Iazid, son of Malzara, says that Jesus commanded his disciples ان يكون بلها في الله مشل الحمام [an yakūna bulhan fī Allāh mashl al-ḥamām] that they should be bulhan (that is, simple) in God like doves. Thus we render بلها [bulhan] bulhan, with the most learned of the Arabs, from the singular ابله [ablah] ablaho, to which كيس [kayyis] chaison is opposed, that is, cunning and crafty. And that it is to be so taken is shown by what follows in the same place: ليس شي ابله من الحمام وذلك انك تاخذ فرخيه من تحته فتذبحهما ثم يعود الي مكانه فيفرخ فيه [laysa shay ablah min al-ḥamām wa-dhālika annaka taʾkhudh farkhayhi min taḥtihi fa-tadhbaḥuhumā thumma yaʿūd ilā makānihi fa-yufarrikh fīhi] Nothing is simpler than the dove. For even if you kill the young taken from under it, it nevertheless soon returns to its place and hatches young in it. The very same thing the Fathers write on the passage of Hosea we have cited. Theodoret: Ἐκείνη τῶν ἰδίων νεοττῶν ἀφαιρουμένη οὐκ ἀφίπταται, ἀλλὰ τοῖς αὐτοῖς προστρέχει χωρίοις. [Ekeinē tōn idiōn neottōn aphairoumenē ouk aphiptatai, alla tois autois prostrechei chōriois.] And following him Theophylact: When its young are taken away it does not fly off, but remains in the same places. Somewhat differently Jerome: Other birds hasten to protect their young even at the risk of their own life, and when they see a hawk, a snake, a raven or a crow approach their nest, II, 552 they flutter this way and that, throw themselves at it, tear it with beak and claws, and bear witness to a parent's grief with plaintive cry. The dove alone does not grieve for its young when they are taken away, nor seek them. But how truly, I do not quite know, since a kind of dove or wood-pigeon, الورشان [al-warashān] alvvarsen, is described by the Arabs بالحنو علي اولاده حتي انه ربما قتل نفسه اذا راها في يد القانص [bi-l-ḥunuww ʿalā awlādihi ḥattā annahu rubbamā qatala nafsahu idhā rāhā fī yad al-qāniṣ] as burning with such affection for its young that it sometimes kills itself when it sees them in the fowler's hand. So it is found in Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]. And in general writers commend the dove for its love of its offspring. Pliny, book 10, ch. 34, on the male and female dove: Both have equal love for their offspring; often for this reason there is chastisement, when the female is slow in going in to the young. On which more in Aristotle, Hist. book 9, ch. 7; Aelian, Hist. book 3, ch. 45; again Aelian, Var. book 1, ch. 15; Athenaeus, book 9, ch. 11; Porphyry, Περὶ ἀποχῆς [Peri apochēs], etc., book 3; which there is no room to copy out here. Others assert that the dove's simplicity is evident in the fact that it does not avoid nets, nor the snares laid for it, col. 22 when it comes down to feed. And with this stupidity of the dove they would have Hosea compare the sloth of the Israelites, who took no precaution against dangers and threw themselves into the power of their enemies. However that may be, this simplicity of the dove was recognized also by οἱ ἔξωθεν [hoi exōthen]. Thus on that line of Juvenal,


— — — vexat censura columbas,

— — — censure harasses the doves,


dicit vetus Scholiastes, Columbas retulit ad simplicitatem. Et in Suida ἡμένη πε-λειὰς, columba sedens proverbio dicitur ἐπὶ τῶν ἁπλουστάτων, de simplicissimis. Nempe διὰ τὸ εὔηθες τοῦ ζώου, propter ejus stoliditatem, ut habet Eustathius in Iliad. ψ΄. Non tamen de omni columba usurpatur hoc proverbium: sed de iis, quae allectatrici assident, atque, ut ait Suidas, κατὰ ἀντιπαρεξέτασιν τῆς πα-λευτρίας, per oppositionem ad columbam allectatricem, id est, qua abutuntur aucupes ad caeteras alliciendas. Aristophanes in Avibus,

the old Scholiast says: He referred "doves" to simplicity. And in the Suda ἡμένη πελειὰς [hēmenē peleias], a sitting dove, is used as a proverb ἐπὶ τῶν ἁπλουστάτων [epi tōn haploustatōn], of the most simple-minded. This is, of course, διὰ τὸ εὔηθες τοῦ ζώου [dia to euēthes tou zōou], because of the creature's stupidity, as Eustathius has it on Iliad ψ΄ [psi]. The proverb, however, is not used of every dove, but of those that sit beside the decoy dove. As the Suda says, it is κατὰ ἀντιπαρεξέτασιν τῆς παλευτρίας [kata antiparexetasin tēs paleutrias], by contrast with the decoy dove, that is, the dove that fowlers misuse to lure the others. Aristophanes in the Birds:


Τὰς περιστερὰς θ᾽ ὁμοίως ξυλλαβὼν εἵρξας ἔχει
Κἀπαναγκάζει παλεύειν δεδεμένας ἐν δικτύῳ·

Τὰς περιστερὰς θ᾽ ὁμοίως ξυλλαβὼν εἵρξας ἔχει Κἀπαναγκάζει παλεύειν δεδεμένας ἐν δικτύῳ· [Tas peristeras th' homoiōs xyllabōn heirxas echei / Kapanankazei paleuein dedemenas en diktyō]


Columbasque similiter correptas coercens detinet, et ligatas in reti cogit alias alli- cere. Et ibi Scholiastes: Εἰώθασιν ἐκτυφλοῦντές τινα τῶν ὀρνέων ἱστάναι ἐν δι-κτύῳ, ὅπως τῇ φωνῇ προσκαλεῖτο τὰ ὁμοιογενῆ· Solent excaecatam avem in la- queo detinere, ut voce congeneres advocet. Et columbas in hunc usum fuisse ad-hibitas, praeter Aristophanem Philosophus quoque asserit Hist. lib. 9. cap. 7. Αἱ περιστεραὶ, inquit, ζῶσι καὶ ὀκτὼ ἔτη, αἱ τετυφλωμέναι ὑπὸ τῶν παλευτρίας τρεφόντων αὐτάς· Octo annos vivunt columbae, quae excaecatae aluntur, ut sint allectatrices. Iam, si consulas recentiores, quae dicta sunt de columbarum simplicitate et facili captura, non parum confirmabit, quod sibi contigisse narrat II, 553 Aloisius Cadamustus Navigat. cap. 40. cum in Canarias insulas primum appulit. Columbi capiebantur, ait, pro libito manu hominis. Non enim pavebant ad viri conspectum. Et capite sexto de Madera insula, Memini ab indigenis accepisse, ibi, cum primo culta est insula, copiam maximam columborum fuisse: quibus capiendis non alia arte usi sunt aucupes, quam alligato perticae uncino, ut ex arboribus, quibus illic insident, traherentur ad se, non paventibus avibus, sed mirantibus, veluti ad rem, non visam hactenus.

And likewise he seizes the doves, keeps them confined, and forces them, bound in a net, to lure others. And there the Scholiast says: Εἰώθασιν ἐκτυφλοῦντές τινα τῶν ὀρνέων ἱστάναι ἐν δικτύῳ, ὅπως τῇ φωνῇ προσκαλεῖτο τὰ ὁμοιογενῆ· [Eiōthasin ektyphlountes tina tōn orneōn histanai en diktyō, hopōs tē phōnē proskaleito ta homoiogenē] They are accustomed to keep a blinded bird in a snare, so that by its voice it may call others of its kind. That doves were used for this purpose is asserted not only by Aristophanes but also by the Philosopher, Hist. book 9, ch. 7: Αἱ περισταὶ, he says, ζῶσι καὶ ὀκτὼ ἔτη, αἱ τετυφλωμέναι ὑπὸ τῶν παλευτρίας τρεφόντων αὐτάς· [Hai peristerai … zōsi kai oktō etē, hai tetyphlōmenai hypo tōn paleutrias trephontōn autas] Doves that are blinded and kept as decoys live as long as eight years. Now, if you consult more recent writers, what has been said about the simplicity of doves and the ease of catching them will be considerably confirmed by what II, 553 Cadamosto [=Alvise Cadamosto, Navigazioni (1455-56)] relates happened to him, Navigat. ch. 40, when he first landed on the Canary Islands. The doves, he says, were caught at will by a man's hand. For they were not frightened at the sight of a man. And in chapter 6, on the island of Madeira: I remember hearing from the inhabitants that when the island was first settled there was a very great abundance of doves there. To catch them the fowlers used no other device than a hook tied to a pole, so that they might be drawn to them from the trees on which they perch there; the birds were not frightened but full of wonder, as at something never seen before.


Interim, qui ἀκεραίους in Christi dicto mites et mansuetos esse volunt, praeterquam quod Grammaticorum non paucos sequuti sunt, quibus ἀκέραιον, de animali dictum, excorne significat, et benignum et innoxium, columbae naturam respexerunt, quae re vera est mitissimum et mansuetissimum animal. Proinde placidam vocat Ovidius Metam. lib. 7. Fab. 12. Et Cyrillus columbam dicit πρὸς ἄκρον ἥκειν πρᾳότητος, supremum mansuetudinis fastigium attingere, libro decimo quinto De adoratione. Quin eam felle prorsus carere multi putant. Inde ἄχολον vocat Clemens Paedag. lib. 1. cap. 5. Et Isidorus Orig. lib. 12. aves mansuetas ac sine felle. Quale est, quod Tertullianus, De Baptismo cap. 8. scribit, etiam corporaliter ipso felle carere columbam. Et Sedulius lib. 2. Carm. ubi de Baptismo Christi,

Meanwhile, those who take ἀκεραίους [akeraious] in Christ's saying to mean mild and gentle have followed a good many Grammarians, for whom ἀκέραιον [akeraion], said of an animal, means hornless, as well as kindly and harmless. Beyond this, they have had regard to the nature of the dove, which is in truth a most mild and gentle animal. Accordingly Ovid calls it placid, Metam. book 7, Fable 12. And Cyril says that the dove πρὸς ἄκρον ἥκειν πρᾳότητος [pros akron hēkein praotētos], reaches the highest summit of gentleness, in book 15 On Adoration. Indeed, many think it entirely lacks gall. Hence Clement calls it ἄχολον [acholon], Paedag. book 1, ch. 5; and Isidore, Orig. book 12, calls doves gentle birds without gall. Of the same kind is what Tertullian writes, On Baptism ch. 8, that the dove, even bodily, lacks gall itself. And Sedulius, book 2 of the Carmen, on the Baptism of Christ:


Mansuetumque decet, multumque incedere mitem,
Per volucrem, quae felle caret. — —

And it befits the Gentle One, the greatly Mild, to come forth through the bird that lacks gall. — —


Et Horus Hieroglyph. lib. 1. cap. 54. Ἱστορεῖται δὲ ὅτι οὐ χολὴν ἔχει τοῦτο τὸ ζῶον, Traditur et hoc animal felle carere. Quod tamen ipse refellit lib. 2. cap. 45. Columbam dicens ἐν ὀπισθίοις τὴν χολὴν ἔχειν, in tergo fel habere. Et Galenus in libro De atra bile ridiculos eos esse ait, qui columbam felle carere putant, quoniam τὴν ἐπὶ τῷ ἤπατι κύστιν, vesicam fellis prope jecur non habeat. Neque id fugit Philosophum, cujus verba sunt Hist. lib. 2. cap. 15. Ἔνιοι πρὸς τῇ κοιλίᾳ ἔχουσιν, οἱ δὲ πρὸς τοῖς ἐντέροις τὴν χολὴν, οἷον περιστερά. Unde Plinius lib. 11. cap. 37. Quibusdam intestino tantum fel jungitur, ut columbis.

And Horapollo, Hieroglyph. book 1, ch. 54: Ἱστορεῖται δὲ ὅτι οὐ χολὴν ἔχει τοῦτο τὸ ζῶον [Historeitai de hoti ou cholēn echei touto to zōon], It is also reported that this animal lacks gall. Yet he himself refutes this in book 2, ch. 45, saying that the dove ἐν ὀπισθίοις τὴν χολὴν ἔχειν [en opisthiois tēn cholēn echein], has its gall at the back. And Galen, in the book On Black Bile, says those people are ridiculous who think the dove lacks gall because it does not have τὴν ἐπὶ τῷ ἤπατι κύστιν [tēn epi tō hēpati kystin], the gall bladder next to the liver. Nor did this escape the Philosopher, whose words are, Hist. book 2, ch. 15: Ἔνιοι πρὸς τῇ κοιλίᾳ ἔχουσιν, οἱ δὲ πρὸς τοῖς ἐντέροις τὴν χολὴν, οἷον περιστερά [Enioi pros tē koilia echousin, hoi de pros tois enterois tēn cholēn, hoion peristera]. Hence Pliny, book 11, ch. 37: In some the gall is attached only to the intestine, as in doves.


Aliud in columbis nobis hic notandum venit, nempe conjugalis castitas, quam veteres mire depraedicant. Aristoteles Hist. lib. 9. cap. 7. Οὔτε γὰρ συν- col. 23 δυάζεσθαι θέλουσι πλείοσιν, οὔτε προσλείπουσι τὴν κοινωνίαν, πλὴν ἐὰν χῆρος, ἢ χήρα γένηται· Neque enim pluribus copulari volunt, neque mutuum consortium unquam deserunt, nisi per viduitatem. Plinius lib. 10. cap. 34. Pudicitia illis prima, et neutri nota adulteria. Conjugii fidem non violant, communemque servant domum. Nisi coelebs, aut vidua, nidum non relinquit. Propertius libro 2. Eleg. 12.

Another point to be noted here in doves is their conjugal chastity, which the ancients praise remarkably. Aristotle, Hist. book 9, ch. 7: Οὔτε γὰρ συν- col. 23 δυάζεσθαι θέλουσι πλείοσιν, οὔτε προσλείπουσι τὴν κοινωνίαν, πλὴν ἐὰν χῆρος, ἢ χήρα γένηται· [Oute gar syndyazesthai thelousi pleiosin, oute proleipousi tēn koinōnian, plēn ean chēros ē chēra genētai] For they will not pair with more than one, nor do they ever abandon their partnership, except through widowhood. Pliny, book 10, ch. 34: Chastity is foremost with them, and adultery is known to neither. They do not violate conjugal fidelity, and they keep a common home. Unless unmated or widowed, a dove does not leave its nest. Propertius, book 2, Eleg. 12:


II, 554 Exemplo junctae sic sint in amore columbae,
Masculus et totum foemina conjugium.

II, 554 So let doves joined in love be my example, male and female, a whole marriage.


De turture quoque et palumbe Philosophus idem scribit: Ἔχει δὲ τὸν ἄῤῥενα ἡ τρυγὼν τὸν αὐτὸν καὶ φάττα, καὶ ἄλλον οὐ προσίενται, Turtur quoque, et palumbus marem unum habent., neque alterum admittunt. Quin palumbos adulteria morte punire, tradunt Porphyrius, De abstin. anim. lib. 3. et Phile, De anim. cap. 19. Uterque ex Aeliano Hist. lib. 3. cap. 44. ubi turtures addit eandem legem sancte servare: sed columbas albas ex adulteriis solos mares perimere, foeminarum misertas. Clemens quoque Stromatων libro secundo animalia quaedam esse tradit, ἃ τὴν ἐπιμιξίαν οὐ ποιεῖται πρὸς πολλὰ καὶ ἀναίδην, ἀλλὰ πρὸς ἓν, καὶ ὁμόφυλον· οἷαι αἱ πελειάδες, καὶ αἱ φάσσαι, καὶ τὸ τρυγόνων γένος, καὶ ὅσα τούτοις παραπλήσια, quae cum multis et imprudenter non congrediuntur, sed cum uno, eoque ejusdem generis, ut sunt columbae, et palumbes, et turturum genus, et quae sunt his similia. Quid quod columbam nigram post conjugis obitum viduam ajunt permanere, atque ideo apud Aegyptios symbolum fuisse mulieris, quae a secundis nuptiis abhorret. Horus lib. 2. cap. 30. Γυναῖ-κα χήραν ἐπιμείνασαν ἄχρι θανάτου θέλοντες σημῆναι, περιστερὰν μέλαιναν ζωγραφοῦσιν· αὕτη γὰρ οὐ συμμίγνυται ἑτέρῳ ἀνδρὶ ἕως οὗ χηρεύει Mulierem, quae ad mortem usque vidua manet, significare cum volunt, nigram pingunt columbam: haec enim, quamdiu vidua est, alteri mari non jungitur. Proinde Tertullianus monogamiam suam columbae exemplo stabilire conatur: Avis, inquit, non tantum innocuae, sed et pudicae, quam unam unus masculus novit. At id ipsum in turtures magno consensu transtulerunt Patres posteriores, qua de causa nullus scio. Origenes in Cant. Homil. 2. Turturum ferunt hujusmodi naturam esse, ut neque masculum praeter unam foeminam adeat aliam, nec foemina plus quam unum patiatur marem. Ita, ut, si accidat, altero intercepto superesse alterum, pariter cum conjuge extinctus sit ei concubitus amor. Basilius in Hexaëmeron Homil. 8. Τὴν τρυγόνα φασὶ διαζευχθεῖσάν ποτε τοῦ ὁμόζυγος, μηκέτι τὴν πρὸς ἕτερον καταδέχεσθαι κοινωνίαν, ἀλλὰ μένειν ἀσυνδύαστον, μνήμῃ τοῦ ποτε συζευχθέντος τὴν πρὸς ἕτερον κοινωνίαν ἀπαρνημένην· Turturem ajunt sejugatam a conjuge, nunquam societatem inire cum alio, sed sine conjuge manere coelibem, recordatione amissi consortis conjugium alterius abnuentem. Gregor. Nazianz. in Praeceptis ad virgines Carm. 3.

Of the turtledove and the wood pigeon the same Philosopher writes: Ἔχει δὲ τὸν ἄῤῥενα ἡ τρυγὼν τὸν αὐτὸν καὶ φάττα, καὶ ἄλλον οὐ προσίενται [Echei de ton arrhena hē trygōn ton auton kai phatta, kai allon ou prosientai], The turtledove too, and the wood pigeon, have one male, and do not admit another. Indeed, Porphyry, On Abstinence from Animal Food book 3, and Phile, On Animals ch. 19, report that wood pigeons punish adultery with death. Both take this from Aelian, Hist. book 3, ch. 44, where he adds that turtledoves keep the same law scrupulously, but that white doves kill only the males caught in adultery, taking pity on the females. Clement, too, in the second book of the Stromata, reports that there are certain animals ἃ τὴν ἐπιμιξίαν οὐ ποιεῖται πρὸς πολλὰ καὶ ἀναίδην, ἀλλὰ πρὸς ἓν, καὶ ὁμόφυλον· οἷαι αἱ πελειάδες, καὶ αἱ φάσσαι, καὶ τὸ τρυγόνων γένος, καὶ ὅσα τούτοις παραπλήσια [ha tēn epimixian ou poieitai pros polla kai anaidēn, alla pros hen, kai homophylon; hoiai hai peleiades, kai hai phassai, kai to trygonōn genos, kai hosa toutois paraplēsia], which do not mate with many and shamelessly, but with one, and that of the same kind, as are doves, and wood pigeons, and the turtledove kind, and those that are like them. What is more, they say that the black dove remains a widow after the death of its mate, and that for this reason among the Egyptians it was the symbol of a woman who shrinks from a second marriage. Horus book 2, ch. 30: Γυναῖκα χήραν ἐπιμείνασαν ἄχρι θανάτου θέλοντες σημῆναι, περιστερὰν μέλαιναν ζωγραφοῦσιν· αὕτη γὰρ οὐ συμμίγνυται ἑτέρῳ ἀνδρὶ ἕως οὗ χηρεύει [Gynaika chēran epimeinasan achri thanatou thelontes sēmēnai, peristeran melainan zōgraphousin; hautē gar ou symmignytai heterō andri heōs hou chēreuei] When they wish to signify a woman who remains a widow until death, they paint a black dove: for this bird, as long as it is widowed, does not join with another male. Accordingly Tertullian tries to establish his monogamy by the example of the dove: A bird, he says, not only harmless but also chaste, which one male alone knows. But the later Fathers, with great unanimity, transferred this very thing to turtledoves, for what reason I do not know. Origen on the Song of Songs, Homily 2: They say that the nature of turtledoves is such that the male does not approach any female besides one, nor does the female accept more than one male; so that, if it happens that one is taken away and the other survives, the love of mating is extinguished together with the mate. Basil in the Hexaemeron, Homily 8: Τὴν τρυγόνα φασὶ διαζευχθεῖσάν ποτε τοῦ ὁμόζυγος, μηκέτι τὴν πρὸς ἕτερον καταδέχεσθαι κοινωνίαν, ἀλλὰ μένειν ἀσυνδύαστον, μνήμῃ τοῦ ποτε συζευχθέντος τὴν πρὸς ἕτερον κοινωνίαν ἀπαρνημένην· [Tēn trygona phasi diazeuchtheisan pote tou homozygos, mēketi tēn pros heteron katadechesthai koinōnian, alla menein asyndyaston, mnēmē tou pote syzeuchthentos tēn pros heteron koinōnian aparnēmenēn] They say that the turtledove, once separated from its mate, never enters into union with another, but remains single without a mate, refusing marriage with another in remembrance of the partner it has lost. Gregory of Nazianzus in the Precepts to Virgins, Poem 3:


Πυνθάνομ᾽ ὡς πτερόεσσα τρυγὼν τρυγόνος φιλίοιο
Χηρωθεῖσ᾽ ὁμόλεκτρον ἑὸν ποθέουσα σαόφρων,
Οὐ δέχεται πόσιν ἄλλον ἑῆς καθύπερθε καλιῆς·

Πυνθάνομ᾽ ὡς πτερόεσσα τρυγὼν τρυγόνος φιλίοιο Χηρωθεῖσ᾽ ὁμόλεκτρον ἑὸν ποθέουσα σαόφρων, Οὐ δέχεται πόσιν ἄλλον ἑῆς καθύπερθε καλιῆς· [Pynthanom᾽ hōs pteroessa trygōn trygonos philioio Chērōtheis᾽ homolektron heon potheousa saophrōn, Ou dechetai posin allon heēs kathyperthe kaliēs]


Alatam turturis foeminam audio, amico turture viduatam, conjugis suae desiderio temperantem, in nido suo nullum alium conjugem admittere. Chrysostomus Homilia II, 555 De turture, edit. Anglic. tom. 7. pag. 264. Φασί τινες τὴν τρυγόνα φίλ-ανδρον εἶναι, καὶ φίλαγνον· ὥς τε κἂν συμβῇ τὸν ταύτης ἄῤῥενα ὑπὸ ἀετοῦ ἀναλωθῆναι, ἢ ὑπὸ ἰξευτοῦ θηρευθῆναι, ταύτην ἑτέρῳ ἀνδρὶ μὴ ἐπιμίγνυσθαι, ἀλλ᾽ αὐτὸν ποθεῖν, αὐτὸν ἀναμένειν, καὶ τῇ τούτου μνήμῃ συναποθνήσκειν. Foeminam turturis quidam ajunt conjugis amore teneri, et castitatis ita esse studiosam, ut, si marem suum ab aquila, aut ab aucupe capi contingat, alteri non misceatur, sed hunc unum desideret et exspectet, ejusque adeo recordatione commoriatur. Ita etiam Gregorius Nyssenus Homil. 3. in Cant. Epiphanius in Physiologo cap. 10. Philo Carpathius in Cant. 1. Ambrosius in Hexaëm. lib. 5. cap. 19. et in Psalm. CXVIII. Hieronymus contra Iovinianum lib. 1. cap. 17. Iustus Orgelita- col. 24 nus, Theodoretus, Aponius et Gregorius Magnus in Cant. I, 10. Eustathius in Hexaëm. Hildephonsus Toletanus Serm. in Purificat. S. Mariae, si vere est illius; Theophylactus in Lucam cap. 2. Pisidas de mundi opificio versu 998. Goffridus Abbas Vindocinus Serm. 7. Michael Glycas part. 1. Annal. Bernardus in Cant. Serm. 40. et 59. et Serm. in Nativitate S. Mariae de Aquaeductu, Baal Hatturim in Levit. XII, 6. R. Selomo in Psalm. LXXIV, 19. Damir capite De شفنين siphnin, seu turture. Hi, inquam, omnes turturi tribuunt, quod de sola columba scripserant vetustiores, eam uni conjugi sic esse addictam, ut, eo mortuo, alterum non admittat. Unde factum, ut qui in Solomonis Canticum commentati sunt, non satis intellexerint, quorsum sponsam toties columbae suae nomine Solomon indigitet. Sic Cant. II, 14. Columba mea in foraminibus petrae, etc. Et Cant. V, 2. Aperi mihi, soror mea, amica mea, columba mea. Et Cant. VI, 8. Unica est columba mea, perfecta mea, etc. Ita nimirum significari voluit, hanc a se unice diligi, seque illi vicissim unice charum esse. Quomodo in columbis mirus est amor inter conjuges, et conjugii lex firmissima. Quod si in typo, id est, in Solomone, minus verum fuit, qui tot habuit conjugum ἑκατοντάδας, tamen verissimum est ἐν τῷ τυπωθέντι, id est, in Christo, quem ut pro sponso solum agnoscimus, ita ille unam habet ecclesiam, quam sibi in aeternum desponsavit in justitia, judicio, benignitate et misericordia, Os. II, 19. Hinc Apostolus 2 Cor. XI, 2. Despondi vos uni viro, ut tanquam virginem castam Christo exhibeam.

I hear that the female of the turtledove, once widowed of her mate, restrains herself out of longing for her spouse and admits no other mate into her nest. Chrysostom, Homily II, 555 On the Turtledove, English edition, vol. 7, p. 264: Φασί τινες τὴν τρυγόνα φίλανδρον εἶναι, καὶ φίλαγνον· ὥς τε κἂν συμβῇ τὸν ταύτης ἄῤῥενα ὑπὸ ἀετοῦ ἀναλωθῆναι, ἢ ὑπὸ ἰξευτοῦ θηρευθῆναι, ταύτην ἑτέρῳ ἀνδρὶ μὴ ἐπιμίγνυσθαι, ἀλλ᾽ αὐτὸν ποθεῖν, αὐτὸν ἀναμένειν, καὶ τῇ τούτου μνήμῃ συναποθνήσκειν. [Phasi tines tēn trygona philandron einai, kai philagnon; hōs te kan symbē ton tautēs arrena hypo aetou analōthēnai, ē hypo ixeutou thēreuthēnai, tautēn heterō andri mē epimignysthai, all᾽ auton pothein, auton anamenein, kai tē toutou mnēmē synapothnēskein.] Some say that the female turtledove is held by love for her mate and is so devoted to chastity that, if her male happens to be taken by an eagle or by a fowler, she does not mate with another, but longs for and awaits him alone, and even dies together with the memory of him. So also Gregory of Nyssa, Homily 3 on the Song; Epiphanius in the Physiologus, ch. 10; Philo of Carpasia on Cant. 1.; Ambrose in the Hexaemeron, book 5, ch. 19, and on Psalm. CXVIII.; Jerome, Against Jovinian, book 1, ch. 17; Justus of Urgel, col. 24 Theodoret, Aponius and Gregory the Great on Song 1:10; Eustathius on the Hexaemeron; Ildefonsus of Toledo, Sermon on the Purification of St Mary, if it is really his; Theophylact on Luke, ch. 2; Pisides, On the Creation of the World, line 998; Geoffrey, Abbot of Vendôme, Sermon 7; Michael Glycas, Annals, section 1; Bernard on the Song, Sermons 40 and 59, and the Sermon on the Nativity of St Mary, On the Aqueduct; the Baal Hatturim [=Jacob ben Asher (d. 1343), commentary on the Torah] on Lev 12:6; R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] on Ps 74:19; Damir in the chapter On شفنين [shifnīn] siphnin, that is, the turtledove. All these, I say, attribute to the turtledove what the older writers had written of the dove alone: that she is so devoted to one mate that, when he dies, she does not admit another. As a result, those who have commented on the Song of Solomon have not sufficiently understood why Solomon so often designates the bride by the name of his dove. Thus Song 2:14: My dove, in the clefts of the rock, etc. And Song 5:2: Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove. And Song 6:8: My dove, my perfect one, is but one, etc. By this, clearly, he wished to signify that she was loved by him alone, and that he in turn was uniquely dear to her, just as among doves there is a remarkable love between mates and a very firm law of marriage. If this was less true in the type, that is, in Solomon, who had wives by the ἑκατοντάδας [hekatontadas], it is nevertheless most true ἐν τῷ τυπωθέντι [en tō typōthenti], that is, in Christ: just as we acknowledge him alone as bridegroom, so he has one church, which he has betrothed to himself for ever in righteousness, judgment, lovingkindness and mercy, Hos 2:19. Hence the Apostle, 2 Cor 11:2: I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.


Quamvis המה strepere et tumultuari proprie sonat, tamen Hebraea מעי המו Cant. V, 4. Graeci reddunt ἡ κοιλία μου ἐθροήθη· et Hieronymus, Venter meus intremuit. Sic Ezech. VII, 16. ubi idem habet, Erunt in montibus quasi columbae omnes trepidi: et Iunius, Erunt in ipsis montibus velut columbae vallium, trepidantes omnes: verba, omnes trepidi, vel trepidantes omnes, respondent Hebraeis כלם המות. At Os. XI, 11. pro ויחרדו in Iunio legas, trepidi accurrent, etc. ut columba e terra Assyriae. In aliis trepidabunt, aut pavebunt, aut contremiscent sicut columba, etc. Quae coluinbae ingenium prorsus exprimunt. Columba II, 556 enim est animal pavidissimum. Hinc Varro de columbis Rust. lib. 3. cap. 7. Propter timorem naturalem summa loca in tectis captant. Et paullo post, Nihil enim timidius columba. Et apud Ovidium Metam. lib. 5. Fab. 10. Arethusa Nympha de se et insequente Alpheo,

Although המה properly means to make a noise and to be in tumult, nevertheless the Hebrew מעי המו in Song 5:4 the Greeks render ἡ κοιλία μου ἐθροήθη [hē koilia mou ethroēthē], and Jerome, My belly trembled. So too in Ezek 7:16, where the same Jerome has, They shall be on the mountains like doves, all trembling, and Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], They shall be on the mountains themselves like doves of the valleys, all trembling: the words all trembling correspond to the Hebrew כלם המות. And in Hos 11:11, for ויחרדו you may read in Junius, they shall come running in trepidation, etc., like a dove from the land of Assyria. In others: they shall tremble, or they shall fear, or they tremble like a dove, etc. These expressions exactly capture the dove's nature. For the dove II, 556 is a most fearful animal. Hence Varro on doves, On Agriculture, book 3, ch. 7: Because of their natural fear they seek the highest places on roofs. And a little later: For nothing is more timid than a dove. And in Ovid, Metam. book 5, Fable 10, the nymph Arethusa says of herself and of Alpheus pursuing her:


Sic ego currebam, sic me ferus ille premebat,
Ut fugere accipitrem penna trepidante columba,
Et solet accipiter trepidas urgere columbas.

So I ran, so that wild one pressed upon me,
As the dove flees the hawk on trembling wing,
And as the hawk is wont to harry trembling doves.


Et Trist. lib. 1. Eleg. 1.

And Tristia, book 1, Elegy 1:


Terretur minimo pennae stridore columba, col. 24
Unguibus accipiter saucia facta tuis.

The dove, once wounded by your talons, hawk, col. 24
is terrified by the slightest whirring of a wing.


Et Valerius Flaccus libro octavo Argonauticων de Medea,

And Valerius Flaccus, in the eighth book of the Argonautica, of Medea:


Ecce! autem pavidae virgo de more columbae, Cum semper ingenti circumdata praepetis umbra, In quemcunque tremens hominem cadit. Haud secus illa, Icta timore gravi, mediam se misit, etc.

But lo! the maiden, after the manner of a frightened dove, When, encompassed by the huge shadow of a bird of prey, She falls trembling upon whatever man she meets. Just so she, Struck with heavy fear, threw herself into the midst, etc.


Ut Chorus in Ajace Sophoclis versu 139.

As the Chorus in Sophocles' Ajax, line 139:


— — — πεφόβημαι
Πτηνῆς ὡς ὄμμα πελειάς.

— — — πεφόβημαι
Πτηνῆς ὡς ὄμμα πελειάς. [pephobēmai / Ptēnēs hōs omma peleias.]


Timeo ut volucris oculus columbae. Et alius poeta apud Suidam in Πελειάδες

I fear, like the eye of the winged dove. And another poet in the Suda, under Πελειάδες [Peleiades]:


Δειλαί τοι δείλοισιν ἐφεδρεύουσι πέλειαι,

Δειλαί τοι δείλοισιν ἐφεδρεύουσι πέλειαι, [Deilai toi deiloisin ephedreuousi peleiai,]


Timidae timidis insident columbae. Quo pertinet, quod columba τρήρων toties ab Homero dicitur, ἐπεὶ διὰ τὴν ἀθένειαν εὐλαβὴς ἡ ὄρνις αὕτη, τρεῖν δ' ἐστὶ τὸ εὐλαβεῖσθαι, quia propter imbecillitatem avis est meticulosa, nam τρεῖν est me- col. 25 tuere. Ita Athenaeus libro nono. Neque aliter vetus Homeri Scholiastes, Eu- stathius in Odyss. μ'. Hesychius, Suidas, Etymologus, etc. Et Homerum sic imitatur Apollonius, Argonauticων libro 3. versu 541.

Timid doves sit upon timid [eggs]. To this belongs the fact that the dove is so often called τρήρων [trērōn] by Homer, ἐπεὶ διὰ τὴν ἀθένειαν εὐλαβὴς ἡ ὄρνις αὕτη, τρεῖν δ' ἐστὶ τὸ εὐλαβεῖσθαι [epei dia tēn atheneian eulabēs hē ornis hautē, trein d' esti to eulabeisthai], because on account of its weakness this bird is fearful, for τρεῖν [trein] means to col. 25 fear. So Athenaeus in book 9. Nor otherwise the old Scholiast on Homer, Eustathius on Odyssey μ' [mu], Hesychius, Suidas, the Etymologicum, etc. And Apollonius imitates Homer thus, in book 3 of the Argonautica, verse 541:


Τρήρων μὲν φεύγουσα βίην κίρκοιο πελειὰς,
Ὑψόθεν Αἰσονίδεω πεφοβημένη ἔμπεσε κόλποις·

Τρήρων μὲν φεύγουσα βίην κίρκοιο πελειὰς, Ὑψόθεν Αἰσονίδεω πεφοβημένη ἔμπεσε κόλποις· [Trērōn men pheugousa biēn kirkoio peleias, Hypsothen Aisonideō pephobēmenē empese kolpois]


Pavida quidem fugiens vim accipitris columba, ex alto terrefacta in Aesoni-dae sinum incidit.

A timid dove, fleeing the violence of a hawk, fell terrified from on high into the bosom of Aeson's son.


(1) Rosenmüller, II, 551 Rectius fortasse vocabulum ἀκέραιος cum Eustathio ad Iliad. II, 855. refertur ad κεραΐζειν, laedere, nocere, ut significet eum, qui neminem laedit, unde transfertur in omnem a dolo ac fraude alienum. Aliorum sententias qui nosse cupit, adeat SUI-CERI Thesaur. Ecclesiast. T. I. p. 155.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 551 Perhaps the word ἀκέραιος [akeraios] is more correctly referred, with Eustathius on Iliad 2, 855, to κεραΐζειν [keraizein], to harm, to injure, so that it denotes one who harms no one; from which it is transferred to anyone free from guile and deceit. Whoever wishes to know the opinions of others should consult SUICER, Thesaur. Ecclesiast. vol. 1, p. 155.


Part 2, Book 1, chapter 5: The sacrifices of doves and turtledoves
------------------------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/columba-sacrificia.html

II, 557 CAP. V.

II, 557 Chapter V.


De Columbarum et Turturum sacrificiis.

On the sacrifices of doves and turtledoves.


Iudaei columbas non solum ad esum, sed etiam ad sacrificia exquirebant, quae multorum erant generum. Sic Levit. I, 14. agitur de spontaneo holocausto e turturibus, aut pullis columbarum. Levit. V, 7. qui blasphemantem alium non correxerat, aut ipse temere juraverat, aut immundae rei contactu se polluerat, jubetur offerre par turturum, aut columbarum, unam pro peccato, alteram pro holocausto. Levit. XII, 6. a puerpera, post expletos dies purificationis, Deus agnum anniculum in holocaustum exigit, et pullum columbae, vel turturem, pro peccato; aut, si agnum offerre non possit, duos turtures, aut duos pullos columbarum. Easdem quoque oblationes praescribi videas ei, qui a lepra sanatus est, Levit. XIV, 22. Illi item, qui gonorrhoea laboravit, cum mundatus est a profluvio suo, Levit. XV, 13. 14. Et ἐν τῷ τῆς αἱμοῤῥοούσης κα-θαρισμῷ, Levit. XV, 28. 29. Et in purgatione Naziraei, qui mortui contactu se contaminavit, Num. VI, 10.

The Jews sought doves not only for eating but also for sacrifices, which were of many kinds. Thus Lev 1:14 deals with a voluntary burnt offering of turtledoves or young doves. In Levit. V, 7. one who had not rebuked another who blasphemed, or had himself sworn rashly, or had defiled himself by touching an unclean thing, is commanded to offer a pair of turtledoves or doves, one for a sin offering, the other for a burnt offering. In Lev 12:6. God requires of a woman after childbirth, once the days of her purification are completed, a yearling lamb for a burnt offering and a young dove or a turtledove for a sin offering; or, if she cannot offer a lamb, two turtledoves or two young doves. You may see the same offerings prescribed also for one who has been healed of leprosy, Levit. XIV, 22; likewise for one who has suffered from a discharge, when he has been cleansed of his flux, Levit. XV, 13. 14; and ἐν τῷ τῆς αἱμοῤῥοούσης καθαρισμῷ [en tō tēs haimorrhoousēs katharismō], Levit. XV, 28. 29; and in the purification of the Nazirite who has defiled himself by contact with a dead body, Num. VI, 10.


In quibus sacrificiis nota primo, Deum columbas et turtures caeteris avibus praetulisse, propter puritatem, castitatem, simplicitatem, mansuetudinem et reliquas virtutum umbras, quae in his observatae sunt. 2. Turtures adultos, sed columbarum nonnisi pullos in altari fuisse oblatos, quia turtures in matura, columbae in tenera aetate maxime praestant. 3. Pleraque haec sacrificia nonnisi tenuiorum fuisse, ut expresse observatur Levit. V, 7. et XII, 6. Itaque vel hinc collige, quam pauper fuerit sancta virgo, Christi mater, quae post purificationem non obtulit agnum, sed turtures, aut pullos columbarum, Luc. II, 24. 4. Iam ante Legem hujusmodi sacrificia fuisse in usu, constat ex Abrahami exemplo, qui cum juvenca, capra et ariete, trimis, turturem et גוזל gozal, id est, columbini generis pullum, Deo offerre jussus est. Nempe, ut hoc sacrificium omnia victimarum genera complecteretur, quae postmodum in Lege constituta sunt. Quod puto simplicissimum, quamvis varia mysteria hic multi quaerunt. Et per quinque haec animalia alii Christi dotes: alii eos significari velint, quibus Deus terram Chanaan destinaverat, et virtutes, in iis requisitas: alii denique posterorum Abrahami quis futurus esset status. Per bovem enim, hircum et agnum, quae terrestria sunt animalia, et sub hominum jugo vivere col. 26 solita, designari tempus illud, quo abjecti et humiles et sub Aegyptiorum servitute victuri essent; per turturem, quae solitaria est, Iudaeorum in deserto moram: et per columbam, quae gregalis est, et in cultis locis degit, eorum ha-bitationem in Chanaanitide. 5. Columbarum sacrificia prava quadam κακοζηλίᾳ gentes etiam usurpasse. Propertius libro quarto Elegia ad Lenam, II, 558 Sed cape torquatae, Venus o regina, columbae, Ob meritum ante tuos guttura secta focos.

In these sacrifices note, first, that God preferred doves and turtledoves to other birds because of the purity, chastity, simplicity, gentleness and the other shadows of virtues that have been observed in them. 2. That adult turtledoves, but only young doves, were offered on the altar, because turtledoves are best at a mature age, doves at a tender age. 3. That most of these sacrifices were only those of the poorer people, as is expressly noted in Levit. V, 7. and XII, 6. So gather even from this how poor the holy Virgin, the mother of Christ, was, who after her purification offered not a lamb but turtledoves or young doves, Luc. II, 24. 4. That sacrifices of this kind were already in use before the Law is clear from the example of Abraham, who was commanded to offer to God, together with a three-year-old heifer, she-goat and ram, a turtledove and a גוזל gozal, that is, a young bird of the dove kind: namely, so that this sacrifice might embrace all the kinds of victims that were afterwards established in the Law. This I think the simplest explanation, although many seek various mysteries here. Some would have these five animals signify the gifts of Christ; others, those for whom God had destined the land of Canaan, and the virtues required in them; others, finally, what the condition of Abraham's descendants would be. For by the ox, the goat and the lamb, which are land animals and accustomed to live under the yoke of men, col. 26 they say is signified the time when they would live abased and humble and in servitude to the Egyptians; by the turtledove, which is solitary, the sojourn of the Jews in the desert; and by the dove, which is gregarious and lives in cultivated places, their dwelling in Canaan. 5. That the gentiles too, through a certain perverse κακοζηλίᾳ [kakozēlia], adopted sacrifices of doves. Propertius, book 4, in the Elegy to the Procuress: II, 558 “But take, o queen Venus, the throat of a ringed dove, cut before your hearths for its desert.”


Ovidius lib. 1. Fastorum,

Ovid, book 1 of the Fasti:


Ergo saepe suo conjux abducta marito
Uritur in calidis alba columba focis.

“Therefore often the white dove, a wife taken from her husband,
is burned on the hot hearths.”


Columbarum tamen esum Veneris mystis fuisse interdictum, colligi videtur ex his Martialis libro 13. Epigr. 66.

Yet the eating of doves seems to have been forbidden to the initiates of Venus, as may be gathered from these lines of Martial, book 13, Epigr. 66:


Ne violes teneras praeduro dente columbas,
Tradita si Cnidiae sunt tibi sacra Deae.

“Do not violate tender doves with too hard a tooth,
if the rites of the Cnidian Goddess have been handed down to you.”


Quo ritu turtures et columbas Iudaei mactaverint, breviter docet Moses Le-vit. I, 15. 16. 17. et V, 8. et pluribus Talmudici in Zebachim cap. 6. fol. 64. Et Maimonides in libro De sacrificiis offerendis cap. 6. §. 20. 21. 22. 23. et cap. 7. §. 6. 7. 8. unde multa possent elici non usquequaque trita, si id ageretur in praesens. Sed hic notasse sufficiet, Hebraeos alias quidem victimas ferro mactasse, at aves ungue solo, quo, capite versus reflexo, guttur illis discerpebatur. Id Hebrais est מלק, quod Graeci ἀποκνίζειν, id est, ungue lacerare, vel abscindere, Levit. I, 15. et V, 8. quibus solum locis occurrit. Ierosolymitanus עום, et Ionathan חום, quod idem est, ח et ע permutatis. Arabice idem حذم vel خذم quod secare reddunt, et discerpere. Sic خذمت الصقر unguibus discerpsit accipiter, in Alcamus. Avem discerpendi ritum Kimchius in Lexico in voce מלק, ita describit: ואר״זל כיצד מולקין חטאת העוף נותן שתי גפיה בין שתי אצבעותיו ושתי רגליה בין שתי אצבעותיו והיה מותח צוארה על שתי אצבעותיו והיה מולק בצפורן ממול עורף עד שמגיע לסימנים וקוצץ אותן או רובן ואינו מבדיל שנאמר ולא יבדיל אבל בעולה העוף שאמר ומלק את ראשו ולא אמר ולא יבדיל הוא מולק ומבדיל הראש בעצמו הגוף בעצמו Dixerunt magistri nostri beatae memoriae: Quomodo lacerabatur sacrificium pro peccato ex ave? Ponebat (sacerdos) alas ejus inter duos digitos, et pedes inter duos digitos, et extendebat collum super duos digitos suos, et secabat ungue versus cervicem, donec attingeret signa (in jugulo), quae amputabat, aut majorem partem, ita tamen, ut non divideret, quia dicitur Levit. V, 8. „Et non dividet“. Sed in holocausto ex ave, quia dicitur, „Secabit caput ejus“, neque additur, „Et non dividet“, Levit. I, 15. ita secabat, ut caput a trunco corporis separeretur. Haec ille ex Talmudis loco, quem citavimus. Videndus etiam Maimonides, qui hoc esse asserit מעבודות קשות שבמקדש, unum ex operosissimis Sanctuarii cultibus, in libro De offerendis sacrificiis cap. 7. §. 8. (1).

The rite by which the Jews slaughtered turtledoves and doves is taught briefly by Moses in Levit. I, 15. 16. 17. and V, 8., and at greater length by the Talmudists in Zebachim ch. 6, fol. 64, and by Maimonides [=Moses Maimonides (Rambam), Mishneh Torah] in the book On the offering of sacrifices ch. 6, §§ 20, 21, 22, 23, and ch. 7, §§ 6, 7, 8. Much could be drawn from these that is not altogether commonplace, if that were our present business. But here it will suffice to have noted that the Hebrews slaughtered other victims with a blade, but birds with the fingernail alone, by which, with the head bent back, their throat was torn open. In Hebrew this is מלק, which the Greeks render ἀποκνίζειν [apoknizein], that is, to tear with the nail, or to cut off, Lev 1:15 and V, 8., the only places where it occurs. The Jerusalem Targum has עום, and Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] חום, which is the same, ח and ע being interchanged. In Arabic the same is حذم [ḥadhama] or خذم [khadhama], which they render to cut and to tear apart. Thus خذمت الصقر [khadhamat al-ṣaqr], the hawk tore with its talons, in Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]. Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], in his Lexicon under the word מלק, describes the rite of tearing the bird thus: ואר״זל כיצד מולקין חטאת העוף נותן שתי גפיה בין שתי אצבעותיו ושתי רגליה בין שתי אצבעותיו והיה מותח צוארה על שתי אצבעותיו והיה מולק בצפורן ממול עורף עד שמגיע לסימנים וקוצץ אותן או רובן ואינו מבדיל שנאמר ולא יבדיל אבל בעולה העוף שאמר ומלק את ראשו ולא אמר ולא יבדיל הוא מולק ומבדיל הראש בעצמו הגוף בעצמו Our masters of blessed memory said: How was the sin offering of a bird torn? He (the priest) placed its wings between two fingers and its feet between two fingers, and stretched its neck over his two fingers, and cut with his nail opposite the nape until he reached the signs (in the throat), which he severed, or the greater part of them, yet so that he did not divide it, because it is said Lev 5:8 „And he shall not divide it“. But in the burnt offering of a bird, because it is said, „He shall wring off its head“, and it is not added, „And he shall not divide it“, Lev 1:15, he cut so that the head was separated from the trunk of the body. So he, from the passage of the Talmud we have cited. See also Maimonides, who asserts that this was מעבודות קשות שבמקדש, one of the most laborious services of the Sanctuary, in the book On the offering of sacrifices ch. 7, § 8 R1.


II, 559 Ne victimae deessent, in prima templi parte, quae פרבר parbar vocabatur 1 Paral. XXVI, 18. vendebantur boves, et oves, et columbae, Ioh. II, 14. Itaque in Maimonidis tractatu De vasis Sanctuarii cap. 7. §. 9. (inter templi praefectos, quos Hebraei vocabant ממוני המקדש, et Graeci στρατηγοὺς τοῦ ἱεροῦ, Luc. XXII, 52.) recensetur הממונה שעל הקינים, praefectus super nidos, id est, super aves. Atque is ita describitur: הדא שפוסקין עמו שימכור הקנים לקורבנות כך וכך בסלע וכל מי שהוא חייב תורים או שני בני יונה יביא דמיהם למקדשי col. 27 וזה הממונה נותן הקנים לבעלי הקורבנות ועושה חשבון עם הגוברים ונותנין לו משלושים יום לשלושים יום, Is est, cum quo paciscuntur, ut ad oblationes aves comparet, has vel illas pro siclo. Et quisquis tenebatur vel turtures offerre, vel pullos columbarum, pretium ad sanctuarium afferebat. Et iste praefectus dabat aves iis, quorum erat offerre, et cum quaestoribus eas aestimabat; et, postquam de pretio convenerat, eas intra triduum dabant. Et paullo post, וכן קן שנמצא פסול או שנפסל קודם שיקרוב נותן אחר תחתיו, Et, si quae avis profana erat, aut profana fiebat (per pollutionem ceremonialem) antequam offerretur, aliam pro ea dabat. Quae ad quaestum a lucripetis et avaris sacerdotibus fuisse excogitata, his verbis docet Hieronymus in Matthaei cap. 21. Iuxta mandata Legis an-gustissimo in toto orbe templo Domini, et de cunctis pene regionibus Iudaeorum illuc populo confluente, innumerabiles immolabantur hostiae, maxime festis diebus, taurorum, arietum, hircorum, pauperibus, ne absque sacrificio essent, pullos columbarum et turtures offerentibus, accidebat plerumque, ut, qui de longe venerant, non haberent victimas. Excogitaverunt igitur sacerdotes, quomodo praedam de populo facerent; et omnia animalia, quibus opus erat ad sacrificia, vendebant, ut et venderent non habentibus, et ipsi rursum empta susciperent. Proinde Christus in hos lucriones jure merito irritatus, evertit eorum cathedras, qui columbas vendebant, Matth. XXI, 12. et Marc. XI, 15. Et columbarum venditoribus dixit, Auferte ista hinc. Ne facite domum patris mei domum emporii, Ioh. II, 16.

II, 559 So that victims should not be lacking, in the first part of the temple, which was called פרבר parbar, 1 Chr 26:18, oxen, sheep and doves were sold, John 2:14. Accordingly in Maimonides' treatise On the vessels of the Sanctuary ch. 7, § 9 (among the officers of the temple, whom the Hebrews called ממוני המקדש and the Greeks στρατηγοὺς τοῦ ἱεροῦ [stratēgous tou hierou], Luke 22:52) there is listed הממונה שעל הקינים, the officer over the nests, that is, over the birds. And he is described thus: הדא שפוסקין עמו שימכור הקנים לקורבנות כך וכך בסלע וכל מי שהוא חייב תורים או שני בני יונה יביא דמיהם למקדשי col. 27 וזה הממונה נותן הקנים לבעלי הקורבנות ועושה חשבון עם הגוברים ונותנין לו משלושים יום לשלושים יום, He is the one with whom they contract that he provide birds for the offerings, so many or so many for a shekel. And whoever was obliged to offer either turtledoves or young doves brought the price to the sanctuary. And this officer gave the birds to those whose duty it was to offer, and valued them with the treasurers; and, once he had agreed on the price, they paid him within three days. And a little later: וכן קן שנמצא פסול או שנפסל קודם שיקרוב נותן אחר תחתיו, And if any bird was found unfit, or became unfit (through ceremonial defilement) before it was offered, he gave another in its place. That these arrangements were devised for gain by greedy and avaricious priests, Jerome teaches in these words on Matthew ch. 21: According to the commandments of the Law, in the temple of the Lord, the most confined in the whole world, with the people flocking there from almost all the regions of the Jews, innumerable victims were sacrificed, especially on feast days: bulls, rams and he-goats, while the poor, so as not to be without a sacrifice, offered young doves and turtledoves. It often happened that those who had come from afar had no victims. The priests therefore devised a way to make a prey of the people: they sold all the animals needed for the sacrifices, so that they might both sell to those who had none and themselves receive back again what had been bought. Hence Christ, rightly and justly angered against these profiteers, overturned the seats of those who sold doves, Matth. XXI, 12. and Marc. XI, 15. And to those who sold doves he said, Take these things hence. Do not make my father's house a house of trade, John 2:16.


(1) Rosenmüller, II, 558 Multa de hoc ritu ex magistrorum Hebraeorum scriptis congessit THEODOR. DASSOVIUS in Dissertat., cui titulum fecit: Avis, ungue secta, inque sacrificium oblata, ad illustranda commata Levit. I, 14. seqq. et V, 7. seqq. Vitemb. 1697.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 558 Much on this rite has been collected from the writings of the Hebrew masters by THEODOR. DASSOVIUS in a dissertation to which he gave the title Avis, ungue secta, inque sacrificium oblata, ad illustranda commata Lev 1:14 ff. et V, 7. ff. Wittenberg 1697.


Part 2, Book 1, chapter 6: Noah's dove, and the dove at the baptism of Christ
------------------------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/columba-noachi.html

II, 560 CAP. VI.

II, 560 CHAPTER 6.


De Columba Noachi, et de Columbae specie, quae in Baptismo Christi apparuit.

On Noah's Dove, and on the Form of a Dove which appeared at the Baptism of Christ.


Noachus, in arca inclusus, cum ex corvo non didicisset, quod scire avebat, quousque decrevissent aquae diluvii, columbam quoque emisit, avem docilem et homini amicam, quaeque diu et procul volat, Ps. V, 7. et libenter humi pascitur, quia est ἐκ τῶν σπερμολόγων, hocque habet a natura sua insi- col. 28 tum, ut ad nidum suum redeat undequaque, etiam e locis remotissimis. His igitur de causis columba a Noacho emissa est; sed rediit non multo post, quia quietis locum non reperit: quamvis enim montium cacumina jamdudum apparuissent, tamen in terra adhuc λιμναζομένῃ, ut ait Iosephus, id est, vel adhuc stagnante, vel lacunosa saltem et uliginosa, nihil tum erat firmum. At eadem, septiduo post rursus emissa, rediit sub vesperam, ramum olivae in ore gestans. Sunt ex Hebraeis, qui ramum illum velint in monte Oliveti prope Ierusalem fuisse decerptum, aut alibi in Iudaea, quae a diluvii aquis immunis fuerit. Be-resith Rabba cap. 33. מהיכן הביאה אותו רבי אבא בר כהנא אמר משבשושין שבארץ ישראל הביאה אותו רבי לוי אמר מהר המשחה הביאה אותו דלא טפת ארעה דישראל במבולא והוא שהקבה אומר ליחזקיאל ארץ לא מטוהרה היא ולא גושמה ביום זעם, Unde attulit (columba ramum) illum? Rabbi Abba, filius Cahana (sacerdotis) dixit: Ex arbustis terrae Israelis illum attulit. R. Levi dixit, Ex monte Oliveto attulit illum, quia terra Israelis diluvio non est submersa. Prout Deus Sanctus Benedictus Ezechieli dixit capitis vigesimi secundi versu vigesimo quarto: Terra illa non mundata est, neque pluviis aspersa die indignationis. Quae sunt absurdissima, cum aquis diluvii operti fuisse legantur etiam altissimi montes, qui sub universo coelo sunt, Gen. VII, 19. Praeterea quorsum terram Chanaan, nondum sacram, Deus ab inundatione praestitisset immunem? Quorsum Noachum jussisset arcam tanto molimine fabricare? Quidni potius eo secedere jussus est cum bestiis, feris et avibus? Et, si terrae Chanaan pepercerunt aquae diluvii, quid factum est de illius terrae incolis? An hi quoque communem cladem evaserunt, et horum posteri scilicet alium parentem agnoscunt praeter Noachum, e quo totum genus humanum deduxit Moses? Et e tanta clade superstites quomodo pelli permisit Deus a maledicto Chanaane, qui non diu post diluvii tempus illorum sedem invaserit? Denique cum aquae vicinos montes tot cubitis exsuperabant, quid obstabat, quo minus terram Chanaan obruerent? Dicent Dei virtute id factum, et fateor potuisse fieri. Sed, si miracula credimus cum scripta sunt, non tamen cuivis licet ea de suo sibi fingere, quod hi homines palam faciunt. Nam Ezechielem frustra citant, qui de diluvio II, 561 ne γρῦ quidem habet. Tantum, dum Israelitis varia crimina objicit, et varias poenas commemorat, illis inflictas, vel infligendas, inter caetera terram illorum pluviis aut aspersam fuisse, aut aspersum iri negat in die indignationis. Nempe juxta Legis minas Deuter. XI, 17. Ne in vos ira excandescens Dominus claudat coelos, ut non sit pluvia, et terra non edat proventum suum. Et prophetae Amosi IV, 7. ubi Deus ita loquitur: Ego quoque prohibui a vobis imbrem, etc. Et plui super unam civitatem, et super alteram non plui: pars una compluta est, et pars, super quam non pluit, exaruit. Quod illustri exemplo patuit, cum ad Eliae verbum coelum clausum est, neque in Iudaeam descendit ros et pluvia per triennium et amplius, 1 Reg. XVII. et XVIII. At frustra disputamus, cum ipsa Mosis verba abunde doceant, olivae ramum ex iis locis fuisse decerptum, quae diluvium inundaverat. Ita enim habet Moses de Noa Genes. VIII, 8. Emisit columbam a se, ut videret, an esset levata aquis terrae superficies. Et versu 11. Et venit ad eum columba vespertino tempore. Ecce autem folium olivae decerptum in ore ejus. Et sic cognovit Noe, levatam esse aquis terrae superficiem. Id falso diceretur, si folium illud fuisset allatum ex ea terra, quam diluvium non attigisset. Nam inde potuisset afferri, etiam tum, cum aquae alibi erant maxime elatae. Unde etiam id sequitur, folium hoc non fuisse decerptum in Paradiso terrestri, ut alii Iudaeorum asserunt. Beresith Rabba ubi supra, רב ביבי אמר col. 29 נפתחו לה שערי גן עדן והביאה אותו משם, R. Bibi dixit, Portae horti Edenis illi apertae sunt, unde hoc folium attulit. Quae eadem sententia cuidam Barachiae tribuitur in Vajekra Rabba in fine cap. 31. Nempe, si Hebraeis credimus, hortus Eden evectus est supra montium summos vertices, ita, ut aquae diluvii eo usque non pertigerint. Quo eodem inclinant multi veterum. In his Lactantius, vel Venantius potius, qui de Paradiso terrestri sic habet in carmine De Phoenice,

Noah, shut up in the ark, since he had not learned from the raven what he longed to know, namely how far the waters of the flood had decreased, also sent out the dove, a docile bird and friendly to man, which flies long and far, Ps. V, 7. and gladly feeds on the ground, because it is one of the ἐκ τῶν σπερμολόγων [ek tōn spermologōn], and has this implanted in it by its nature, that it returns to its nest from anywhere, even from the most remote places. col. 28 For these reasons, then, the dove was sent out by Noah; but it returned not long after, because it found no place of rest: for although the tops of the mountains had long since appeared, yet on an earth still λιμναζομένῃ [limnazomenē], as Josephus says, that is, either still standing under water, or at least full of pools and marshy, nothing was then firm. But the same dove, sent out again seven days later, returned toward evening, carrying an olive branch in its mouth. There are some among the Hebrews who will have it that this branch was plucked on the Mount of Olives near Jerusalem, or elsewhere in Judaea, which was untouched by the waters of the flood. Bereshit Rabbah ch. 33: מהיכן הביאה אותו רבי אבא בר כהנא אמר משבשושין שבארץ ישראל הביאה אותו רבי לוי אמר מהר המשחה הביאה אותו דלא טפת ארעה דישראל במבולא והוא שהקבה אומר ליחזקיאל ארץ לא מטוהרה היא ולא גושמה ביום זעם, Whence did it (the dove) bring it (the branch)? Rabbi Abba, son of Cahana (the priest), said: It brought it from the shrubs of the land of Israel. R. Levi said: It brought it from the Mount of Olives, because the land of Israel was not submerged by the flood. As God, the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Ezekiel in chapter 22, verse 24: That land is not cleansed, nor rained upon in the day of indignation. These things are utterly absurd, since we read that even the highest mountains under the whole heaven were covered by the waters of the flood, Gen 7:19. Moreover, to what end would God have kept the land of Canaan, not yet holy, free from the inundation? To what end would he have ordered Noah to build the ark with such great labour? Why was he not rather ordered to withdraw there with the beasts, wild animals and birds? And if the waters of the flood spared the land of Canaan, what became of the inhabitants of that land? Did they too escape the common destruction, and do their descendants, forsooth, acknowledge another ancestor besides Noah, from whom Moses derived the whole human race? And how did God allow the survivors of so great a destruction to be driven out by the accursed Canaan, who not long after the time of the flood seized their dwelling place? Finally, since the waters rose so many cubits above the neighbouring mountains, what prevented them from overwhelming the land of Canaan? They will say this was done by the power of God, and I grant that it could have been done. But although we believe miracles when they are written, still no one is permitted to invent them for himself on his own authority, which these men openly do. For they cite Ezekiel in vain, who has not one γρῦ [gry] about the flood. II, 561 He only, while reproaching the Israelites with various crimes and recounting the various punishments inflicted, or to be inflicted, on them, denies among other things that their land was, or would be, rained upon in the day of indignation. That is, in keeping with the threats of the Law, Deuter. XI, 17. Lest the Lord, his wrath kindled against you, shut up the heavens, so that there be no rain, and the land yield not its produce. And of the prophet Amos 4:7, where God speaks thus: I also withheld the rain from you, etc. And I caused it to rain upon one city, and upon another I caused it not to rain: one part was rained upon, and the part on which it did not rain withered. This was shown by a famous example when, at Elijah's word, the heaven was shut, and neither dew nor rain came down upon Judaea for three years and more, 1 Reg. XVII. and XVIII. But we argue in vain, since the very words of Moses amply show that the olive branch was plucked from those places that the flood had inundated. For thus Moses says of Noah, Genes. VIII, 8. He sent forth the dove from him, to see whether the surface of the earth was relieved of the waters. And in verse 11: And the dove came to him in the evening; and behold, a plucked olive leaf in her mouth. And so Noah knew that the surface of the earth was relieved of the waters. This would be falsely said if that leaf had been brought from a land that the flood had not touched. For it could have been brought from there even at the time when the waters elsewhere were at their very highest. From this it also follows that this leaf was not plucked in the earthly Paradise, as others of the Jews assert. Bereshit Rabbah, in the place cited above: רב ביבי אמר col. 29 נפתחו לה שערי גן עדן והביאה אותו משם, R. Bibi said: The gates of the garden of Eden were opened to it, and from there it brought this leaf. The same opinion is attributed to a certain Berechiah in Vayikra Rabbah at the end of ch. 31. That is, if we believe the Hebrews, the garden of Eden was raised above the highest summits of the mountains, so that the waters of the flood did not reach that far. Many of the ancients incline to the same view. Among them is Lactantius, or rather Venantius, who speaks thus of the earthly Paradise in the poem On the Phoenix,


Et cum diluvium mersisset fluctibus orbem,
Deucalionaeas exsuperavit aquas.

And when the deluge had drowned the world in its waves, it rose above the Deucalionian waters.


Ita etiam statuunt plerique Scholasticorum in libro 2. Sententiarum Dist. 17. Tostatus quoque et Cajetanus in Genesim, et Bellarminus libri De gratia primi hominis cap. 14. et Malvenda cap. 84. De Paradiso. Sed huic sententiae multa opponimus in peculiari opere De Paradiso terrestri. Hoc igitur olivae folium unde dicetur allatum? Ex Assyria, ut videtur, quae 2 Reg. XVII, 32. legitur esse ארץ זית יצהר, vel, ut Chaldaeus habet, ארע דזיתהא עבדין משחא, terra, cujus oleae faciunt oleum, id est, terra, oleis foecunda, iisque fertilissimis. Noae scilicet arca substiterat in montibus Ararat, seu Gordyaeorum, quibus Assyria versus Austrum vicina est. In quam coeli partem columbam, ex arca exeuntem, devolasse putaverim, invitante austri calore, et vento etiam eo impellente. Vero II, 562 enim consentaneum est, ventum illum, quem excitaverat Deus, ut aquas exsiccaret, Gen. VIII, 1. ex aquilone flavisse in austrum. Ut apud Ovidium in Deucalionis diluvio pacatus Iupiter,

This is also the view of most of the Scholastics on book 2 of the Sentences, Dist. 17; of Tostatus and Cajetan on Genesis; of Bellarmine in the book De gratia primi hominis, ch. 14; and of Malvenda, De Paradiso, ch. 84. But we raise many objections to this view in a separate work, De Paradiso terrestri. From where, then, shall we say this olive leaf was brought? From Assyria, it seems, which in 2 Reg. XVII, 32. is said to be ארץ זית יצהר, or, as the Chaldee has it, ארע דזיתהא עבדין משחא, a land whose olive trees make oil, that is, a land abounding in olive trees, and very fruitful ones. For Noah's ark had come to rest on the mountains of Ararat, or of the Gordyaeans, to which Assyria lies adjacent toward the south. I would suppose that the dove, on leaving the ark, flew off toward that quarter of the sky, drawn by the warmth of the south and also driven by the wind. For II, 562 it is probable that the wind which God had raised to dry up the waters, Gen. VIII, 1., blew from the north toward the south. So in Ovid, in the flood of Deucalion, Jupiter, appeased,


Nubila disjecit, nimbisque Aquilone remotis,
Et coelo terras ostendit, et aethera terris.

Scattered the clouds, and, the rain-clouds removed by the North Wind, Showed the lands to the sky, and the heavens to the lands.


Haec igitur columba, versus austrum in Assyriam volans, potuit olivae folium ex monte aliquo decerpere, cujus partem aquae decedentes aperuerint.

This dove, then, flying south into Assyria, could have plucked an olive leaf from some mountain, part of which the receding waters had laid bare.


Si quaeratur, quomodo sub aquis ramus olivae virentibus foliis tamdiu duraverit, duo habebo, quae respondeam. Primo, quamvis in Hieronymi versione columba Noae legatur in ore suo portasse ramum virentibus foliis, tamen in Hebraeo solum legi, eam in ore habuisse עלה זית טרף, folium oleae decerptum. Secundo, a veteribus tradi, sub aquis vivere et virere non solum oleae, sed et aliarum arborum quasdam species. Theophrastus Hist. Plant. libri quarti capite octavo, Ἐν δὲ τῇ θαλάττῃ ἐρυθρᾷ δενδρά τινα φύεται· καὶ καλοῦσιν αὐτὰ δάφνην, καὶ ἐλαίαν. Ἔστι δὲ ἡ μὲν δάφνη ὅμοια τῇ ἀρίᾳ, ἡ δὲ ἐλαία τῷ φύλ-λῳ· καρπὸν δὲ ἔχει ἡ ἐλαία παραπλήσιον δὲ ταῖς ἐλαίαις. Quae ita contrahit Plinius lib. decimi tertii cap. vigesimo quinto, In mari vero rubro (mirum est) sylvas vivere, laurum maxime, et olivam, ferentem baccas. Et Theophrastus rursus, Ἐν δὲ ταῖς νήσοις ταῖς ὑπὸ τῆς πλυμμυρίδος καταλαμβανομέναις, δένδρα μεγάλα πεφυκέναι ἡλίκα πλάτανοι· συμβαίνειν δὲ ὅθ᾽ ἡ πλημμυρὶς ἐπέλθοι, τὰ μὲν ἄλλα κατακρύπτεσθαι ὅλα, τῶν δὲ μεγίστων ὑπερέχειν τοὺς κλάδους, etc. ἔχειν δὲ τὰ δένδρα φύλλον μὲν ὅμοιον τῇ δάφνῃ, ἄνθος δὲ τοῖς οἴσοις (cum Plinio lege τοῖς ἴοις) καὶ τῷ χρώματι, καὶ τῇ ὀσμῇ, καρπὸν δ᾽ ἡλίκον ἐλαίᾳ, καὶ τοῦτον εὐώδη σφόδρα, καὶ τὰ μὲν φύλλα οὐκ ἀποβάλλειν, τὸ δὲ ἄνθος, καὶ τὸν καρπὸν ἅμα τῷ φθινοπώρῳ γίνεσθαι· τοῦ δὲ ἔαρος ἀποῤῥεῖν. Quae Plinius ita reddidit, ordine non nihil mutato, Eodem tractu insularum sylvas operit aestus, quanquam altiores platanis populisque altissimis. Folia iis lauri, flos violae odore et colore, baccae, ut oleis, et ipsae odoris jucundi, autumno nascentes, foliis nunquam deciduis. Harum minores totas integit mare; maximarum cacumina extant. Addit Theophrastus, Ἀλλὰ δὲ ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ θαλάττῃ πεφυκέναι, ἀεί-φυλλα μὲν, τὸν δὲ καρπὸν ὅμοιον ἔχειν τοῖς θέρμοις. Unde Plinius, Alias quoque arbores in alto, etc. eodem in mari visas, semper folia retinentes, fructu earum lupino simili. Plutarchus etiam in libro De facie in orbe Lunae, Τῆς δὲ Γεδρωσίας καὶ Τρωγλοδύτιδος ἡ καθήκει πρὸς τὸν ὠκεανὸν, ἀφόρου διὰ ξηρότη-τα, καὶ ἀδένδρου παντάπασιν οὔσης, ἐν τῇ παρακειμένῃ καὶ παρακεχυμένῃ col. 30 θαλάττῃ θαυμαστὰ μεγέθη φυτῶν τρέφεται, καὶ κατὰ βυθοῦ τέθηλεν· ὧν τὰ μὲν ἐλαίας, τὰ δὲ δάφνας, τὰ Ἴσιδος τρίχας καλοῦσιν. Gedrosiae autem et Troglodyticae regionis ea pars, quae ad oceanum pertingit, cum sit omnino II, 563 sterilis ob siccitatem, et arboribus careat: in mari vicino, quo alluitur, inusitatae magnitudinis plantae nascuntur, et ex profundo pullulant, quarum alias oleas, alias lauros, alias crines Isidis nominant. Quod puto Plutarchum habere ex Aga- tharchide, ubi quaedam leguntur libri quinti capite quinquagesimo tertio, de olivis in mari, et crinibus Isidis, sed a Photio interpolata. Arbor in mari platani instar, de qua Theophrastus et Plinius, Arabice vocatur قرم Karam. Alcamus, القرم نبت كالدلب غلظا وبياضا ينبت في البحر جوف Crescit alkaram instar platani, ampla arbor et alba.
