If it is asked how an olive branch with green leaves could have lasted so long under the waters, I shall have two things to answer. First, although in Jerome's version Noah's dove is read to have carried in her mouth a branch with green leaves, yet in the Hebrew we read only that she had in her mouth עלה זית טרף, an olive leaf plucked off. Second, the ancients report that certain species not only of the olive but of other trees too live and stay green under water. Theophrastus, Hist. Plant. book 4, chapter 8: Ἐν δὲ τῇ θαλάττῃ ἐρυθρᾷ δενδρά τινα φύεται· καὶ καλοῦσιν αὐτὰ δάφνην, καὶ ἐλαίαν. Ἔστι δὲ ἡ μὲν δάφνη ὅμοια τῇ ἀρίᾳ, ἡ δὲ ἐλαία τῷ φύλλῳ· καρπὸν δὲ ἔχει ἡ ἐλαία παραπλήσιον δὲ ταῖς ἐλαίαις [En de tē thalattē erythra dendra tina phyetai; kai kalousin auta daphnēn, kai elaian. Esti de hē men daphnē homoia tē aria, hē de elaia tō phyllō; karpon de echei hē elaia paraplēsion de tais elaiais]. Pliny condenses this in book 13, ch. 25: But in the Red Sea (it is a marvel) woods live, chiefly the laurel and the olive, bearing berries. And Theophrastus again: Ἐν δὲ ταῖς νήσοις ταῖς ὑπὸ τῆς πλυμμυρίδος καταλαμβανομέναις, δένδρα μεγάλα πεφυκέναι ἡλίκα πλάτανοι· συμβαίνειν δὲ ὅθ᾽ ἡ πλημμυρὶς ἐπέλθοι, τὰ μὲν ἄλλα κατακρύπτεσθαι ὅλα, τῶν δὲ μεγίστων ὑπερέχειν τοὺς κλάδους [En de tais nēsois tais hypo tēs plymmyridos katalambanomenais, dendra megala pephykenai hēlika platanoi; symbainein de hoth᾽ hē plēmmyris epelthoi, ta men alla katakryptesthai hola, tōn de megistōn hyperechein tous kladous], etc. ἔχειν δὲ τὰ δένδρα φύλλον μὲν ὅμοιον τῇ δάφνῃ, ἄνθος δὲ τοῖς οἴσοις [echein de ta dendra phyllon men homoion tē daphnē, anthos de tois oisois] (read with Pliny τοῖς ἴοις [tois iois]) καὶ τῷ χρώματι, καὶ τῇ ὀσμῇ, καρπὸν δ᾽ ἡλίκον ἐλαίᾳ, καὶ τοῦτον εὐώδη σφόδρα, καὶ τὰ μὲν φύλλα οὐκ ἀποβάλλειν, τὸ δὲ ἄνθος, καὶ τὸν καρπὸν ἅμα τῷ φθινοπώρῳ γίνεσθαι· τοῦ δὲ ἔαρος ἀποῤῥεῖν [kai tō chrōmati, kai tē osmē, karpon d᾽ hēlikon elaia, kai touton euōdē sphodra, kai ta men phylla ouk apoballein, to de anthos, kai ton karpon hama tō phthinopōrō ginesthai; tou de earos aporrhein]. Pliny rendered this as follows, with the order somewhat changed: In the same region the tide covers woods of islands, although they are taller than plane trees and the tallest poplars. Their leaves are those of the laurel, the flower is that of the violet in scent and colour, the berries are like olives, and they too have a pleasant scent; they grow in autumn, and the leaves never fall. The sea covers the smaller of these entirely; the tops of the largest stand out. Theophrastus adds: Ἀλλὰ δὲ ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ θαλάττῃ πεφυκέναι, ἀείφυλλα μὲν, τὸν δὲ καρπὸν ὅμοιον ἔχειν τοῖς θέρμοις [Alla de en autē tē thalattē pephykenai, aeiphylla men, ton de karpon homoion echein tois thermois]. Hence Pliny: Other trees too have been seen in the deep, etc. in the same sea, always retaining their leaves, their fruit like the lupine. Plutarch too, in the book On the Face in the Orb of the Moon: Τῆς δὲ Γεδρωσίας καὶ Τρωγλοδύτιδος ἡ καθήκει πρὸς τὸν ὠκεανὸν, ἀφόρου διὰ ξηρότητα, καὶ ἀδένδρου παντάπασιν οὔσης, ἐν τῇ παρακειμένῃ καὶ παρακεχυμένῃ col. 30 θαλάττῃ θαυμαστὰ μεγέθη φυτῶν τρέφεται, καὶ κατὰ βυθοῦ τέθηλεν· ὧν τὰ μὲν ἐλαίας, τὰ δὲ δάφνας, τὰ Ἴσιδος τρίχας καλοῦσιν [Tēs de Gedrōsias kai Trōglodytidos hē kathēkei pros ton ōkeanon, aphorou dia xērotēta, kai adendrou pantapasin ousēs, en tē parakeimenē kai parakechymenē thalattē thaumasta megethē phytōn trephetai, kai kata bythou tethēlen; hōn ta men elaias, ta de daphnas, ta Isidos trichas kalousin]. But that part of the Gedrosian and Troglodytic region which reaches to the ocean, although it is wholly II, 563 barren through dryness and lacks trees, yet in the neighbouring sea that washes it plants of unusual size grow and sprout from the depths; some of them they call olives, others laurels, others hairs of Isis. I think Plutarch has this from Agatharchides, in whom some things are read, book 5, chapter 53, about olives in the sea and the hairs of Isis, but interpolated by Photius. The tree in the sea like a plane tree, of which Theophrastus and Pliny speak, is called in Arabic قرم [qurm] Karam. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: القرم نبت كالدلب غلظا وبياضا ينبت في البحر جوف [al-qurm nabt ka-l-dulb ghilaẓan wa-bayāḍan yanbut fī al-baḥr jawf] The alkaram grows like a plane tree, a large and white tree. It comes up in the middle of the sea R1. Since it is clear from these passages that true trees live in the sea itself, and among them a tree most like the olive, which therefore not only Pliny but also the inhabitants of those places simply call an olive: why should not an olive, whose leaves never fall (whence the Poet,


— — ramum semper frondentis olivae)

— — a branch of the ever-leafy olive)


folia sua, aut saltem eorum unum aliquod sub aquis per aliquot menses retinuerit, quod fuerit a columba decerptum? Maxime, cum oleae folia aquis et imbribus diu obsistere ex eo colligatur, quod his Ichthyophagi tuguria sua obtegunt. Strabo libro decimo sexto vocat μάνδρας στεγαστὰς ἀπὸ φυλλάδος ἐλαίνης, ca- sas olei folio tectas. Et Agatharchides lib. 5. cap. 17. Οἱ δὲ τὰς τῶν ἐλαιῶν κο-ρυφὰς ἀλλήλαις συνάπτοντες εἶτα χρῶνται σκηνώμασι· Alii olearum vertices, inter se connexos, pro tabernaculis usurpant. Et Diodorus lib. 3. p. 109. Ἐλαίαι φύονται πάνυ πολλαὶ περὶ τοὺς τόπους τούτους, τὰ μὲν πρὸς τὴν ῥίζαν ἔχουσαι προσκλυζόμενα τῇ θαλάττη, πυκναὶ δὲ τοῖς φυλλώμασι, etc. ταύτας ἀλλήλαις συμπλέκοντες, καὶ συνεχῆ σκιὰν ποιοῦντες, ἰδιαζούσαις σκηναῖς ἐμβιοῦσιν. Pro ἐλαίαι, id est, oleae, nostrae editiones perperam habent ἐλάται, abietes, cujus folia angustiora sunt, quam ut continuam umbram possint facere. Diodorus igitur ex Agatharchide et Strabone corrigendus est.

All the more so, since it may be gathered that olive leaves long withstand water and rain from the fact that the Ichthyophagi cover their huts with them. Strabo, book 16, speaks of μάνδρας στεγαστὰς ἀπὸ φυλλάδος ἐλαίνης [mandras stegastas apo phyllados elainēs], huts roofed with olive leaf. And Agatharchides, book 5, ch. 17: Οἱ δὲ τὰς τῶν ἐλαιῶν κορυφὰς ἀλλήλαις συνάπτοντες εἶτα χρῶνται σκηνώμασι [Hoi de tas tōn elaiōn koryphas allēlais synaptontes eita chrōntai skēnōmasi]; Others use the tops of olives, joined to one another, as tents. And Diodorus, book 3, p. 109: Ἐλαίαι φύονται πάνυ πολλαὶ περὶ τοὺς τόπους τούτους, τὰ μὲν πρὸς τὴν ῥίζαν ἔχουσαι προσκλυζόμενα τῇ θαλάττη, πυκναὶ δὲ τοῖς φυλλώμασι [Elaiai phyontai pany pollai peri tous topous toutous, ta men pros tēn rhizan echousai prosklyzomena tē thalattē, pyknai de tois phyllōmasi], etc. ταύτας ἀλλήλαις συμπλέκοντες, καὶ συνεχῆ σκιὰν ποιοῦντες, ἰδιαζούσαις σκηναῖς ἐμβιοῦσιν [tautas allēlais symplekontes, kai synechē skian poiountes, idiazousais skēnais embiousin]. Very many olives grow around those places, with their roots immersed in the sea and with very dense foliage. Weaving these together and making a continuous shade, they live in them privately as in tents. For ἐλαίαι [elaiai], that is, olives, our editions wrongly have ἐλάται [elatai], firs, whose leaves are too narrow to make a continuous shade. Diodorus must therefore be corrected from Agatharchides and Strabo.


II, 564 Iam nihil necesse est dicere, quam Noacho volupe fuerit columbam videre redeuntem cum oleae folio in ore. Unde duo collegit, 1. Quod Propheta observat, terram aquis esse levatam, id est, non solum montes altissimos, quorum vertices jam multo ante apparuerant Gen. VIII, 5. sed et loca plana, aut saltem colles, quibus oleae maxime gaudent. Columella libri sexti capite sexto, Sed neque depressa loca, neque ardua, magisque modicos clivos amat (olea) quales in Italia Sabinorum, vel tota provincia Baetica videmus. Palladius libri tertii capite decimo octavo, Locis aestuosis Septentrionali colle, frigidis meridiano gaudet. Mediis clivis delectatur. Neque imum locum, neque arduum patitur, magis modicos clivos, sicut est regio Sabina, vel Baetica (lege magis amat modicos clivos). Florentinus libro nono Geoponicων, capite Περὶ ἀέρος ἐπιτηδείου ἐλαίας καὶ γῆς σχημάτιον, De aëre oleae opportuno et terrae figuris; Συναίρεται δὲ τῇ τοῦ ἀέρος ἐπιτηδειότητι καὶ τὰ τῆς γῆς σχήματα προσκλινῆ καὶ ὑψηλά. Αἱ γὰρ ἐν τοῖς τοιούτοις τόποις, διὰ τὸ ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνέμων καταψύχεσθαι· τὸ ὑπερ-βάλλον τοῦ ἡλίου πυρῶδες, κάλλιστον ἔλαιον ποιοῦσι. Ad aëris oportunitatem conferunt etiam figurae terrarum declives et celsae. Nam quae sunt in tali situ, quia nimius solis fervor a ventis refrigeratur, pulcherrimum oleum faciunt. Perdicca in Ierosolymorum thematibus pag. 71.

II, 564 There is now no need to say how pleased Noah was to see the dove returning with an olive leaf in its mouth. From this he inferred two things. 1. What the Prophet observes: that the land had been relieved of the waters, that is, not only the highest mountains, whose summits had appeared long before (Gen 8:5), but also the level places, or at least the hills, in which olives most delight. Columella, book 6, chapter 6: But it (the olive) loves neither low-lying places nor steep ones, but rather moderate slopes, such as we see in Italy among the Sabines, or in the whole province of Baetica. Palladius, book 3, chapter 18: In hot places it delights in a northern hill, in cold places in a southern one. It takes pleasure in middling slopes. It tolerates neither the lowest place nor a steep one, rather moderate slopes, such as the Sabine region or Baetica (read it rather loves moderate slopes). Florentinus, book 9 of the Geoponica, in the chapter Περὶ ἀέρος ἐπιτηδείου ἐλαίας καὶ γῆς σχημάτιον [Peri aeros epitēdeiou elaias kai gēs schēmation], On the air suitable for the olive and on the shapes of the ground: Συναίρεται δὲ τῇ τοῦ ἀέρος ἐπιτηδειότητι καὶ τὰ τῆς γῆς σχήματα προσκλινῆ καὶ ὑψηλά. Αἱ γὰρ ἐν τοῖς τοιούτοις τόποις, διὰ τὸ ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνέμων καταψύχεσθαι· τὸ ὑπερβάλλον τοῦ ἡλίου πυρῶδες, κάλλιστον ἔλαιον ποιοῦσι. [Synairetai de tē tou aeros epitēdeiotēti kai ta tēs gēs schēmata prosklinē kai hypsēla. Hai gar en tois toioutois topois, dia to hypo tōn anemōn katapsychesthai; to hyperballon tou hēliou pyrōdes, kalliston elaion poiousi.] Sloping and elevated shapes of ground also contribute to the suitability of the air. For those that are in such a situation, because the excessive heat of the sun is cooled by the winds, produce the finest oil. Perdicca, in the Themes of Jerusalem, p. 71:


Ὄρος μικρὸν ἀνεστηκώς ἐστι τοῦ Ἐλαιῶνος, col. 31

Ὄρος μικρὸν ἀνεστηκώς ἐστι τοῦ Ἐλαιῶνος, [Oros mikron anestēkōs esti tou Elaiōnos,] col. 31


Pusillus Oliveti mons erectus est. Et paullo post,

The small mount of Olivet rises up. And a little later,


Πρὸς δέ γε τὸ μεσαίτατον μέρος τοῦ ὄρους τούτου
Ὁ Ἐλαιῶν κατάκαρπος ὑπὲρ τὴν φύσιν ὄντως.

Πρὸς δέ γε τὸ μεσαίτατον μέρος τοῦ ὄρους τούτου Ὁ Ἐλαιῶν κατάκαρπος ὑπὲρ τὴν φύσιν ὄντως. [Pros de ge to mesaitaton meros tou orous toutou Ho Elaiōn katakarpos hyper tēn physin ontōs.]


Ad mediam partem montis illius Olivetum est foecundum omnino supra naturam. Pusillus mons, id est, collis, in cujus medio olivae proveniunt. Quod ipsum dixerat Palladius, illas mediis clivis delectari. Secundo, hinc didicit Noachus, terram diluvii aquis non ita fuisse vastatam, ut non adhuc superessent aliquot frugiferae arbores, unde homines et bruta post diluvium vescerentur. Potuit enim ex oliva de reliquis ferri judicium. Quin, quod columba non confestim, ut ante, sed nonnisi sub vesperam redierat, suadebat, eam loca reperisse ubi quiesceret. Neque enim erat credibile, illam tota die volasse. Vespere tamen ad arcam revolavit, vel quia quies in arborum ramis non visa est satis commoda, vel inopia ciborum, vel desiderio conjugis et pullorum, si quos habuit, vel denique Deo sic providente, ut anxium Noachi animum suo reditu recrearet, et eum excitaret in spem proximae liberationis. Sed post septiduum tertio emissa, non reversa est amplius in arcam, quia tum aquis magis ac magis secedentibus, neque victus illi defuit, neque nidus, in quo lateret. Unde aquas destitisse animadversum.

Toward the middle part of that mount the olive grove is fruitful wholly beyond nature. A small mount, that is, a hill, in the middle of which olives grow. This is just what Palladius had said, that they take pleasure in middling slopes. Second, Noah learned from this that the earth had not been so devastated by the waters of the flood that some fruit-bearing trees did not still survive, on which men and beasts might feed after the flood. For from the olive a judgement could be made about the rest. Indeed, the fact that the dove had returned not at once, as before, but only toward evening, suggested that it had found places where it could rest. For it was not credible that it had flown the whole day. Yet in the evening it flew back to the ark, either because resting on the branches of trees did not seem comfortable enough, or for lack of food, or from longing for its mate and its young, if it had any, or finally because God so provided, that by its return it might refresh Noah's anxious mind and rouse him to hope of an imminent deliverance. But when it was sent out a third time after seven days, it did not return to the ark any more, because then, as the waters receded more and more, it lacked neither food nor a nest in which to hide. From this it was perceived that the waters had ceased.


II, 565 En hujus historiae vestigia in Abydeni Chaldaicis apud Eusebium lib. 9. Praepar. et Cyrillum libro primo contra Iulianum! Τρίτη δὲ ἡμέρᾳ ἔπειτα ὑὼν ἐκό-πασε, μεθίει τῶν ὀρνίθων πείρην ποιούμενος, εἴπου γῆν ἴδοι, τοῦ ὕδατος ἐκδῦσαν. αἱ δὲ ἐκδεχομένου σφέας πελάγεος ἀχανέος, ἀπορέουσαι ὅπη καθορμίσονται, παρὰ τὸν Ξίσουθρον ὀπίσω κομίζονται, καὶ ἐπ᾽ αὐτῇσιν ἕτεραι, ὡς δὲ τῇσι τρί-τησιν εὐτύχεεν· ἀφίκατο γὰρ δὴ πηλοῦ κατάπλεοι τοὺς ταρσοὺς, θεοί μιν ἐξ ἀνθρώπων ἀφανίζουσιν, Tertio autem die postquam pluere desiit, aliquas aves dimisit (Xisuthrus, sic ille Noam vocat) periculum facturus, sicubi terram videret ex aqua emergentem. Quae quidem excipiente semper eas immenso pelago, incertae, quo appellerent, retro ad eum rediere; et post istas aliae. Ut vero tertiis emissis successit illi, redierant enim pedibus lutosis, Dii illum ex hominum medio sustulerunt. Aves dicit Plurali numero, quia Noe corvum et columbam emisit. Et rediisse lutosas, quomodo etiam de columba Eutychius pag. 40. رجعت رجلتها مبلولة بالماء Rediit pedibus suis aqua madentibus. Et ante eum Iosephus, ὑπανελθούσης δὲ πεπηλομένης, cum autem lutosa rediisset. Quia Hebraice habetur ותבא אליו היונה, et rediit ad eum columba. Et ad columbae nomen יונה alludit יון, quod lutum sonat. Denique quod de avibus dictum, aut saltem de columba, illam avolasse, nec rediisse, inepte ad Xisuthrum, seu Noam transtulit Abydenus, quasi tum fuerit e medio sublatus. Plutarchus in libro Utra animalia, etc. Οἱ μὲν οὖν μυθολόγοι τῷ Δευκαλίωνί φασι περιστερὰν ἐκ τῆς λάρνακος ἀφιεμένην δήλωμα γενέσθαι, χειμῶνος μὲν εἴσω πάλιν ἐνδυομένην, εὐδίας δὲ ἀποπτᾶσαν. Columbam, ex arca emissam, tempestatem Deucalioni significasse, mythologi dicunt, cum intus remeabat, et serenitatem, cum avolavit. II, 565 See the traces of this story in the Chaldaica of Abydenus, cited by Eusebius, book 9 of the Praeparatio, and by Cyril in the first book against Julian: Τρίτη δὲ ἡμέρᾳ ἔπειτα ὑὼν ἐκόπασε, μεθίει τῶν ὀρνίθων πείρην ποιούμενος, εἴπου γῆν ἴδοι, τοῦ ὕδατος ἐκδῦσαν. αἱ δὲ ἐκδεχομένου σφέας πελάγεος ἀχανέος, ἀπορέουσαι ὅπη καθορμίσονται, παρὰ τὸν Ξίσουθρον ὀπίσω κομίζονται, καὶ ἐπ᾽ αὐτῇσιν ἕτεραι, ὡς δὲ τῇσι τρίτησιν εὐτύχεεν· ἀφίκατο γὰρ δὴ πηλοῦ κατάπλεοι τοὺς ταρσοὺς, θεοί μιν ἐξ ἀνθρώπων ἀφανίζουσιν [Tritē de hēmera epeita hyōn ekopase, methiei tōn ornithōn peirēn poioumenos, eipou gēn idoi, tou hydatos ekdysan. hai de ekdechomenou spheas pelageos achaneos, aporeousai hopē kathormisontai, para ton Xisouthron opisō komizontai, kai ep᾽ autēsin heterai, hōs de tēsi tritēsin eutycheen; aphikato gar dē pēlou katapleoi tous tarsous, theoi min ex anthrōpōn aphanizousin], On the third day after it had stopped raining, he (Xisuthrus, as he calls Noah) sent out some birds to make a trial, whether he might see land emerging from the water. But since the boundless sea everywhere received them, and they were uncertain where to land, they came back to him; and after these, others. When he succeeded with the third ones sent out, for they had returned with muddy feet, the gods removed him from among men. He says birds in the plural, because Noah sent out a raven and a dove. And that they returned muddy, just as Eutychius also says of the dove, p. 40: رجعت رجلتها مبلولة بالماء [rajaʿat rijlatuhā mablūla bi-l-māʾ] It returned with its feet wet with water. And before him Josephus: ὑπανελθούσης δὲ πεπηλομένης [hypanelthousēs de pepēlomenēs], but when it had returned muddy. For in Hebrew we have ותבא אליו היונה, and the dove came back to him. And יון, which means mud, alludes to the name of the dove, יונה. Finally, what was said of the birds, or at least of the dove, that it flew away and did not return, Abydenus ineptly transferred to Xisuthrus, or Noah, as if he had then been removed from the midst. But the Greeks report this very thing in such a way that you would hardly find anything lacking in them, except that they substitute their own Deucalion for Noah. Plutarch, in the book Whether Land or Sea Animals, etc.: Οἱ μὲν οὖν μυθολόγοι τῷ Δευκαλίωνί φασι περιστερὰν ἐκ τῆς λάρνακος ἀφιεμένην δήλωμα γενέσθαι, χειμῶνος μὲν εἴσω πάλιν ἐνδυομένην, εὐδίας δὲ ἀποπτᾶσαν [Hoi men oun mythologoi tō Deukalioni phasi peristeran ek tēs larnakos aphiemenēn dēlōma genesthai, cheimōnos men eisō palin endyomenēn, eudias de apoptasan]. The mythographers say that a dove, sent out of the ark, signalled a storm to Deucalion when it came back inside, and fair weather when it flew away. The Arab dream-interpreters attribute to the ورشان [warashān] vvarsen, that is, the wood pigeon, what Moses attributes to the dove. For thus they say of the wood pigeon in Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], in the chapter الورشان [al-warashān] Alvvarsen: وهو في المنام رجل غريب يدل علي اخبار ورسل لانه اخبر توحا عليه col. 32 السلام تنقص الما لما كان في السفينة [wa-huwa fī l-manām rajul gharīb yadullu ʿalā akhbār wa-rusul li-annahu akhbara Tūḥan ʿalayhi al-salām tanaqquṣ al-mā lammā kāna fī l-safīna] Seen in sleep by a stranger, it signifies messengers and couriers, because it announced to Noah, peace be upon him, when he was in the ark, the decrease of the waters. The Arabs, namely, prefer the wood pigeon to the dove because God is believed to have appeared to Muhammad in the form of a wood pigeon and to have inspired many things. Ludovico di Varthema, Navigation, book 1, ch. 18: While we were on our way (towards Mecca) countless wood pigeons darkened the sky. They say that birds of this kind descend from that bird which spoke into the ear of Muhammad under the guise of the Holy Spirit. See the rest there.


II, 566 Haec ad literam de historia columbae, quam ex arca emisit Noe. Mystieum sensum quod attinet, multis olivae folium, aut termes fuisse videtur pacis symbolum et foederis, quod Deus cum Noacho paullo post erat initurus. Tertullianus, De Baptismo lib. 8. Post baptismum (ut ita dixerim) mundi pacem coelestis irae praeco columba terris annuntiavit, dimissa ex arca, et cum olea reversa, quod signum etiam apud nationes paci praetenditur. Hieronymus Epist. 83. ad Oceanum cap. 3. Ramo refectionis ac luminis pacem mundo adnuntiat. Et in Dialogo adversus Luciferum, Pacem terrae columba nuntiat. Chrysostomus in Matth. Homil. 12. Κλάδον φέρον ἐλαίας, τὴν κοινὴν τῆς οἰκουμένης γαλήνην εὐηγγελίσατο· Ramum oleae ferens, communem orbis serenitatem evangelizavit. Amoenus in Enchiridio Veteris et Novi Testamenti,

II, 566 So much for the literal sense of the story of the dove which Noah sent out of the ark. As for the mystical sense, many hold that the olive leaf, or twig, was a symbol of the peace and covenant which God was shortly to make with Noah. Tertullian, On Baptism, book 8: After the baptism (so to speak) of the world, the dove, herald of heaven's wrath appeased, announced peace to the earth, sent out of the ark and returning with the olive, a sign which is held out for peace among the nations too. Jerome, Epist. 83 to Oceanus, ch. 3: With a branch of refreshment and light it announces peace to the world. And in the Dialogue against Lucifer: The dove announces peace to the earth. Chrysostom on Matthew, Homily 12: Κλάδον φέρον ἐλαίας, τὴν κοινὴν τῆς οἰκουμένης γαλήνην εὐηγγελίσατο [Kladon pheron elaias, tēn koinēn tēs oikoumenēs galēnēn euēngelisato]; Bearing an olive branch, it proclaimed the common calm of the world. Amoenus in the Enchiridion of the Old and New Testament:


Nuntia diluvii jam decrescentis ad arcam
Ore columba refert ramum viridantis olivae:
Corvus enim, ingluvie per foeda cadavera captus,
Haeserat; illa datae revehit nova gaudia pacis.

Messenger of the flood now abating, the dove brings back to the ark in its beak a branch of the green olive: for the raven, caught by gluttony among foul carcasses, had stayed; she brings back the new joys of peace granted.

Polybius, book 3, on Hannibal crossing the Alps: Οἱ περὶ τὴν δίοδον οἰκοῦντες, συμφρονήσαντες ἐπὶ δόλῳ συνήντων αὐτῷ, θάλλους ἔχοντες, καὶ στεφάνους· II, 567 τοῦτο γὰρ σχεδὸν πᾶσι τοῖς Βαρβάροις ἐπὶ σύνθημα φιλίας, καθάπερ τὸ κηρύκειον τοῖς Ἕλλησιν. [Hoi peri tēn diodon oikountes, symphronēsantes epi dolō synēntōn autō, thallous echontes, kai stephanous; touto gar schedon pasi tois Barbarois epi synthēma philias, kathaper to kērykeion tois Hellēsin.] The inhabitants along the route, having secretly conspired, come to meet him with branches of green olive and with garlands. For almost everywhere among the barbarians this is a sign of peace and friendship, as the caduceus is among the Greeks. Hence Ovid, Fasti book 1:


Frondibus Actiacis comptos redimita capillos
Pax ades, et toto mitis in orbe veni.

With your tresses bound with Actian leaves,
come, Peace, and gently visit all the world.


Frondibus Actiacis, id est, oleae, ex cujus foliis Paci corona texitur. Quomodo Minervam volunt pacem cum Neptuno iniisse, ex hac arbore coronatam, ut habet Tertullianus De corona militis capite 13. Ita omnes interpretantur. Sed, cur Actiacae dicantur oleae frondes, nondum constat, nec mihi satisfacit, quod interpretes afferunt. Itaque legere malim frondibus Actaeis, id est, Atticis: col. 33 quia olea creditur in Attica esse nata, quae Graece Ἀκτὴ dicitur, unde gentile Ἀκταῖος. Stephanus, Ἀκτὴ, οὕτως ἡ Ἀττικὴ ἐκαλεῖτο. Et paullo post, Τὸ ἐθνικὸν Ἀκταῖος καὶ Ἀκταῖα. Proinde ut mel Actaeum est mel Atticum apud Columellam in horto,

With Actian leaves, that is, of the olive, from whose leaves a crown is woven for Peace. In the same way they hold that Minerva made peace with Neptune crowned with this tree, as Tertullian has it in De corona militis, chapter 13. So all interpret it. But why the olive's leaves are called Actian is not yet clear, and what the commentators offer does not satisfy me. I would therefore rather read frondibus Actaeis, that is, Attic leaves: col. 33 because the olive is believed to have originated in Attica, which in Greek is called Ἀκτὴ [Aktē], whence the gentile adjective Ἀκταῖος [Aktaios]. Stephanus: Ἀκτὴ, οὕτως ἡ Ἀττικὴ ἐκαλεῖτο [Aktē, houtōs hē Attikē ekaleito]. And a little later: Τὸ ἐθνικὸν Ἀκταῖος καὶ Ἀκταῖα [To ethnikon Aktaios kai Aktaia]. Accordingly, just as Actaean honey is Attic honey in Columella on the garden,


Nariciae picis: aut Actaei mellis Hymetti:

Of Narycian pitch, or the honey of Actaean Hymettus:


ita oliva Actaea est oliva Attica. Nonnus Dionysiac. lib. 27. versu 287.

so an Actaean olive is an Attic olive. Nonnus, Dionysiaca book 27, line 287:


Ἀκταίης τε γέραιρε φερέπτολιν ὄζον ἐλαίης,

Ἀκταίης τε γέραιρε φερέπτολιν ὄζον ἐλαίης, [Aktaiēs te geraire pheréptolin ozon elaiēs,]


Et urbem venerare ferentem Actaeae ramum olivae. Ausonius in Mosella de siluro,

And honour the city-bearing branch of the Actaean olive. Ausonius, in the Mosella, on the sheatfish:


Quem velut Actaeo perductum tergora olivo,
Amnicolam delphina reor. — —

Whom, as if his back were smeared with Actaean olive oil,
I take for a river-dwelling dolphin. — —


Obiter nota, in Luciani Tragopodagra aliud esse φύλλα ἀκτέας, cum dicit,

Note in passing that in Lucian's Tragopodagra φύλλα ἀκτέας [phylla akteas] is something else, when he says:


Τίνες γὰρ οἵδε βάκτρα νωμᾶντες χεροῖν,
Κάρηνα φύλλοις ἀκτέας καταστεφεῖς;

Τίνες γὰρ οἵδε βάκτρα νωμᾶντες χεροῖν, Κάρηνα φύλλοις ἀκτέας καταστεφεῖς; [Tines gar hoide baktra nōmantes cheroin, Karēna phyllois akteas katastepheis?]


Quae interpres male reddidit,

which the translator rendered badly:


Quaenam ista turba est, qui manu fustes tenent,
Cincti coronis frondis Actaeae caput?

What crowd is this, who hold staves in their hands,
their heads bound with garlands of Actaean leaf?


Cum ibi ἀκτέα sit ἀκτὴ, id est, sambucus: cujus foliis podagrosi finguntur caput cingere, quia sambuci folia ποδαγρικοῖς βοηθεῖ μετὰ στέατος ταυρείου, ἢ τραγείου. Ita Dioscorides: nec multo aliter Plinius. Et Samonicus in capite De podagra depellenda,

For there ἀκτέα [aktea] is ἀκτὴ [aktē], that is, sambucus [elder]: the gouty are depicted as binding their heads with its leaves, because elder leaves ποδαγρικοῖς βοηθεῖ μετὰ στέατος ταυρείου, ἢ τραγείου [podagrikois boēthei meta steatos taureiou, ē trageiou]. So Dioscorides; and Pliny not very differently. And Samonicus, in the chapter On driving away gout:


Parua sambucus item hircino collita sevo. II, 568 Iam de oliva hoc solum addo, etiam in America jam olim hunc morem invaluisse, ut rami olivae haberentur pro signo pacis. Columbus Navigat. cap. 103. ubi de Americana quadam insula, non procul ab Hispaniola: Primo adventu occurrerunt adolescentulae triginta, quae, etc. ramos olivarum manibus gestabant, et ubi appropinquabant praefecto, in signum foederis pacisque illi ramos porrigebant (2).

Likewise dwarf elder smeared with goat's tallow. II, 568 Of the olive I add only this: that even in America the custom had long prevailed that olive branches were held to be a sign of peace. Columbus, Navigat. ch. 103, on a certain American island not far from Hispaniola: On our first arrival thirty young girls came to meet us, who, etc. carried olive branches in their hands, and when they approached the commander, they held out the branches to him as a sign of alliance and peace R2.


In Christi baptismo, sunt e Patribus, qui veram columbam descendisse vo- col. 35 lunt. Ita Tertullianus in libro De carne Christi capite tertio de Spiritu, in Christum descendente, scribit: Tam vere erat columba, quam et spiritus: nec interfecerat a) substantiam propriam, assumpta substantia extranea. Et Augustinus, De Agone Christiano cap. 22. Christi corpus cum hac columba conferens, Neque hoc ita dicimus, ut Dominum Iesum dicamus solum verum corpus habuisse, Spiritum autem Sanctum fallaciter apparuisse oculis hominum: sed ambo illa corpora vera corpora credimus. Sicut enim non oportebat, ut homines falleret filius Dei, sic non decebat, ut homines falleret Spiritus Sanctus. Sed omnipotenti Deo, qui universam creaturam de nihilo fabricavit, non erat difficile, verum corpus columbae sine aliarum columbarum ministerio figurare, sicut ei non fuit difficile, verum corpus in utero Mariae sine virili semine fabricare. Tamen quatuor Evangelistae b) columbam in Christum descendisse non dicunt, sed ὡσεὶ περιστερὰν, tanquam columbam. Et disertius Lucas, descendisse Spiritum Sanctum σωματικῷ εἴδει ὡσεὶ περιστερὰν, corporali specie tanquam columbam. Ubi Syrus, ܒܕܡܘܬܐ ܓܘܫܡܐ ܕܝܘܢܐ, juxta similitudinem corporis columbae. Et Arabs, شبه جسد حمامة similitudine corporis columbae. Et Aethiops, በሥጋ፡ ከመ፡ ርእየተ፡ ርግብ፡ In corpore tanquam specie columbae. Unde concludi queat, juxta mentem Aethiopis, corpus fuisse, quod apparuit, sed non corpus verae columbae. S. Augustinum sequitur Thomas in summa parte 3. quaest. 39. art. 7. Quin omnes fere Scholares theologos idem sentire, scribit Sixtus Senensis Biblioth. lib. 6. annot. 13. Tamen aliter sentiunt plerique recentiorum, nempe non in vera columba, sed in columbae specie Spiritum descendisse. Et de Tertulliano parum solliciti, Augustini auctoritatem bifariam eludunt. Alii enim, ut Pamelius, negant, librum De Agone Christiano vere esse Augustini. Alii, ut Maldonatus, pro genuino agnoscunt, sed ab Augustino contendunt solum asseri, verum apparuisse corpus, non tamen veram columbam. Sed neutri satisfaciunt.

At the baptism of Christ there are some of the Fathers who hold that a real dove descended. col. 35 Thus Tertullian, in the book On the Flesh of Christ, chapter 3, writes of the Spirit descending upon Christ: It was as truly a dove as it was also spirit; nor had it destroyed a) its own substance by assuming a foreign substance. And Augustine, On the Christian Combat, ch. 22, comparing the body of Christ with this dove, says: Nor do we say this in such a way as to say that the Lord Jesus alone had a true body, while the Holy Spirit appeared deceptively to the eyes of men; rather, we believe both those bodies to be true bodies. For just as it was not fitting that the Son of God should deceive men, so it was not becoming that the Holy Spirit should deceive men. But for almighty God, who made the whole creation out of nothing, it was not difficult to form a true body of a dove without the agency of other doves, just as it was not difficult for him to make a true body in the womb of Mary without male seed. Yet the four Evangelists b) do not say that a dove descended upon Christ, but ὡσεὶ περιστερὰν [hōsei peristeran], as a dove. And Luke more explicitly says that the Holy Spirit descended σωματικῷ εἴδει ὡσεὶ περιστερὰν [sōmatikō eidei hōsei peristeran], in bodily form as a dove. There the Syriac has ܒܕܡܘܬܐ ܓܘܫܡܐ ܕܝܘܢܐ [בדמותא גושמא דיונא], after the likeness of the body of a dove. And the Arabic, شبه جسد حمامة [shibh jasad ḥamāma] in the likeness of the body of a dove. And the Ethiopic, በሥጋ፡ ከመ፡ ርእየተ፡ ርግብ፡ [baśəgā kama rəʾəyata rəgəb] In a body as in the appearance of a dove. From this one may conclude that, in the Ethiopic translator's mind, what appeared was a body, but not the body of a real dove. St Augustine is followed by Thomas in the Summa, part 3, question 39, article 7. Indeed Sixtus of Siena, Biblioth. book 6, annotation 13, writes that almost all the Scholastic theologians hold the same view. Most of the more recent writers, however, think otherwise, namely that the Spirit descended not in a real dove but in the appearance of a dove. Caring little about Tertullian, they evade Augustine's authority in two ways. Some, like Pamelius, deny that the book On the Christian Combat is really Augustine's. Others, like Maldonatus, accept it as genuine, but contend that Augustine asserts only that a true body appeared, not however a real dove. But neither party is convincing.


II, 569 Non primi, cum librum De Agone Augustini esse constet, tam ex stylo, quam ex Possidii Indiculo et ipso Augustino, qui librum illum pro suo agnoscit lib. 2. Retract. cap. 3. Non secundi, quia Augustinus columbam illam non solum verum corpus vocat, sed et verum corpus columbae. Non erat, inquit, Deo difficile verum corpus columbae sine aliarum columbarum ministerio figurare. Quod, juxta ipsius sententiam, ideo necesse fuit, ne homines falleret Spiritus S. si colum- col. 36 ba illa non fuisset id, quod videbatur esse. Vult igitur, hanc columbam tam vere fuisse columbam, quam Christus vere fuit homo. Proinde utrumque dixerim, id est, tam Augustinum, quam Tertullianum, disputantes in eos, qui Christi corpus tam imaginarium fuisse volebant, quam fuit illa columba, peccasse, quod saepe accidit, τῇ τῆς ἀνθόλκης ἀμετρίᾳ. Nam, cum suffecisset asserere veritatem Christi corporis, etiam hoc φάσμα ὄρνιθος, ut recte vocat Origenes, voluerunt pro vera columba haberi. Sed hic quatuor notanda sunt. Primo, extra disputationis aestum eosdem aliter id definire. Nam in Tertulliano libro De Baptismo cap. 8. legitur Spiritus Sanctus columbae figura delapsus in Dominum. Et Augustini Epistola 102. ad Euodium, haec columba dicitur sola specie corporali oculis reddita, non natura viventis animalis expressa. Et De Trinit. lib. 2. cap. 5. In ipsum Dominum (Spiritus Sanctus) corporali specie, velut columba, descendit. Secundo, alios Patres hanc columbam habuisse pro imaginaria. Iustinus in Dialogo cum Tryphone Iudaeo, Τοῦ ἐπελθόντος ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς πνεύ-ματος. Irenaeus lib. 3. cap. 19. Dixerunt, Spiritum Dei sicut columbam descendisse in eum. Origenes in Lucam Serm. 27. Descendit Spiritus Sanctus super Salvatorem in specie columbae. Epiphanius adversus Sabellianos Haeresi 62. Ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς σχηματίζεται. Et interpres, Ad columbae effigiem se conformavit. Hilarius in Matth. Can. 2. Spiritus Sanctus emittitur, et specie columbae visibilis agnoscitur. Nonnus in Paraphrasi S. Iohannis vocat Ἀντίτυπον μίμημα πελειάδος. Iuvencus Evang. Hist. lib. 1.

II, 569 Not the first, since it is established that the book On the Combat is Augustine's, both from its style and from Possidius' Indiculus and from Augustine himself, who acknowledges that book as his own in book 2 of the Retractations, ch. 3. Not the second, because Augustine calls that dove not only a true body but also a true body of a dove. It was not difficult for God, he says, to form a true body of a dove without the agency of other doves. In his opinion this was necessary so that the Holy Spirit should not deceive men, if that dove col. 36 had not been what it seemed to be. He holds, therefore, that this dove was as truly a dove as Christ was truly a man. Accordingly I would say of both, that is, of Augustine as well as of Tertullian, that in arguing against those who held that Christ's body was as imaginary as that dove was, they erred, as often happens, τῇ τῆς ἀνθόλκης ἀμετρίᾳ [tē tēs anthol kēs ametria]. For although it would have sufficed to assert the reality of Christ's body, they wanted even this φάσμα ὄρνιθος [phasma ornithos], as Origen rightly calls it, to be taken for a real dove. But four things are to be noted here. First, outside the heat of controversy the same writers define it otherwise. For in Tertullian, book On Baptism, ch. 8, we read that the Holy Spirit descended upon the Lord in the figure of a dove. And in Augustine's Letter 102 to Evodius this dove is said to have been presented to the eyes in bodily appearance only, not expressed in the nature of a living animal. And in On the Trinity, book 2, ch. 5: Upon the Lord himself (the Holy Spirit) descended in bodily form, like a dove. Second, other Fathers regarded this dove as imaginary. Justin, in the Dialogue with Trypho the Jew: Τοῦ ἐπελθόντος ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς πνεύματος [tou epelthontos en eidei peristeras pneumatos]. Irenaeus, book 3, ch. 19: They said that the Spirit of God descended upon him like a dove. Origen on Luke, Homily 27: The Holy Spirit descended upon the Saviour in the appearance of a dove. Epiphanius against the Sabellians, Heresy 62: Ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς σχηματίζεται [en eidei peristeras schēmatizetai]. And the translator: He conformed himself to the likeness of a dove. Hilary on Matthew, Canon 2: The Holy Spirit is sent forth, and is recognized as visible in the appearance of a dove. Nonnus in the Paraphrase of St John calls it Ἀντίτυπον μίμημα πελειάδος [antitypon mimēma peleiados]. Juvencus, Evang. Hist. book 1:


Corporeamque gerens speciem, descendit ab alto
Spiritus aëriam simulans ex nube columbam.

And bearing bodily form, the Spirit descended from on high, imitating from the cloud an airy dove.


Sedulius Carm. lib. 2.

Sedulius, Carm. book 2:


Confestim patuere poli, Sanctusque columbae
Spiritus in specie Christum vestivit honore.

At once the heavens opened, and the Holy Spirit in the appearance of a dove clothed Christ with honour.


Chrysostomus in Matth. Homil. 12. Ἦλθε τὸ πνεῦμα ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς. Isidorus Pelusiota Epist. 106. Ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς τὸ θεῖον ἐπεφάνη πνεῦμα. Cyrillus in Iohannem, Περιστερᾶς ἐν σχήματι. Et ἐν τῷ τῆς περιστερᾶς σχηματισμῷ. Auctor libri De Mirabilibus Scripturae sub Augustini nomine lib. 3. cap. 5. Quamvis vero corporali specie Spiritus Sanctus super Dominum descendere dicitur, non tamen de avibus sumsisse columbam, sed ex aëre, minime dubitatur. Auctor libri II, 570 De Sacramentis sub Ambrosii nomine lib. 1. cap. 5. Et, ecce! quasi columba Spiritus descendit: non columba descendit, sed quasi columba. Et paullo post, Non in veritate columbae, sed in specie columbae descendit de coelo. Procopius Gazaeus in Gen. XVIII. Spiritus Sanctus in nostrum conspectum venit in specie columbae; nec tamen erat columba, quia non eam, quam columba, habebat proprietatem. Tertio, notandum, Tertullianum gravissime errare. Nam ea dicit de Spiritu Sancto, quae vera esse non possunt, nisi fingatur Spiritus Sanctus columbam unione hypostatica sibi assumsisse. Spiritus, inquit, tam vere erat columba, quam et Spiritus, nec interfecerat substantiam propriam assumta extranea. Unde alius error natus est, nempe Spiritum Sanctum tam esse infra Christum, quam columba est infra hominem. Ut Martialis, columbam Stellae cum Catulli passere conferens, Stellam contendit Catullo tanto meliorem esse poetam,

Chrysostom on Matth., Homil. 12: Ἦλθε τὸ πνεῦμα ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς [Ēlthe to pneuma en eidei peristeras]. Isidore of Pelusium, Epist. 106: Ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς τὸ θεῖον ἐπεφάνη πνεῦμα [En eidei peristeras to theion epephanē pneuma]. Cyril on John: Περιστερᾶς ἐν σχήματι [Peristeras en schēmati]. And: ἐν τῷ τῆς περιστερᾶς σχηματισμῷ [en tō tēs peristeras schēmatismō]. The author of the book On the Wonders of Scripture, under Augustine's name, book 3, ch. 5: “But although the Holy Spirit is said to have descended upon the Lord in bodily form, there is not the least doubt that he did not take the dove from among the birds, but from the air.” The author of the book II, 570 On the Sacraments, under Ambrose's name, book 1, ch. 5: “And behold! the Spirit descended as a dove: not a dove descended, but as it were a dove.” And a little later: “He descended from heaven not in the reality of a dove, but in the appearance of a dove.” Procopius of Gaza on Gen. XVIII: “The Holy Spirit came into our sight in the appearance of a dove; yet it was not a dove, because it did not have the nature that a dove has.” Third, it must be noted that Tertullian errs very gravely. For he says things of the Holy Spirit that cannot be true unless one imagines that the Holy Spirit took a dove to himself in hypostatic union. “The Spirit,” he says, “was as truly a dove as he was Spirit, and he had not destroyed his own substance by assuming a foreign one.” From this another error arose, namely that the Holy Spirit is as far below Christ as a dove is below a man. So Martial, comparing Stella's dove with Catullus's sparrow, maintains that Stella is a better poet than Catullus by as much


Quanto passere major est columba.

As a dove is greater than a sparrow.


Sed hunc errorem ita refellit Chrysostomus in Matthaeum Homilia 12. Ὁ μὲν ἐν τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ φύσει, τὸ δὲ ἐν ὄψει περιστερᾶς ἐφάνη· Christus quidem in natura nostra: sed Spiritus in columbae specie apparuit. Item, Ὁ μὲν υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ φύσιν ἀνθρώπου ἀνέλαβε· τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα οὐ φύσιν ἀνέλαβε περιστερᾶς. Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ὁ Εὐαγγελιστὴς οὐκ εἶπεν, ὅτι ἐν φύσει περιστερᾶς, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς· οὐκοῦν οὐδὲ μετὰ ταῦτα ὤφθη ἐν τούτῳ τῷ σχήματι, ἀλλὰ τότε μόνον. Hominis quidem naturam suscepit Dei filius; sed columbae naturam non suscepit Spiritus. Proinde non dixit Evangelista, eum in natura columbae, sed in specie columbae col. 37 (descendisse). Neque postmodum in ea specie apparuit, sed tunc solum. At Augustinus, ab hoc errore prorsus alienus, tantum credidit, veram columbam, a Deo in hunc usum creatam, symbolum fuisse praesentiae Sancti Spiritus, qui error est multo levior. Quamvis enim haec sententia cum Evangelistarum verbis non possit conciliari, tamen in eo a priore differt, quod nihil habet indignum majestate Sancti Spiritus. Nam, salva dignitate sua, tam potuit per veram columbam, quam per columbae imaginem significari. Quarto, notandum, Augustini argumentum, quo probare nititur, veram fuisse hanc columbam, parum habere virium. Ambo, inquit, illa corpora, nempe Christi et Sancti Spiritus, vera corpora credimus. Sicut enim non oportebat, ut homines falleret Filius Dei, sic non decebat, ut homines falleret Spiritus Sanctus. Fateor: sed hanc columbae speciem nego quemquam vidisse praeter Christum ipsum, Matth. III, 16. et Marc. I, 10. et Iohannem Ioh. I, 32. In mediis quidem turbis Christus baptizatus est Luc. III, 21. Sed his columbam apparuisse, nemo scripsit. Et praeter Christum a nullo fuisse visam, praeterquam a Iohanne, aperte docent haec Ioh. I, 32. Ei testimonium exhibuit Iohannes, dicens, Vidi Spiritum, de coelo descendentem quasi columbam, qui etiam mansit super eum. Quid enim opus fuisset tanti II, 571 viri testimonio ad id probandum, quod alii quoque vidissent, adeoque omnes turbae, quae tum Christum et Iohannem circumstabant? Haec porro columbae species Christo non imposuit, qui erat erroris expers: nec Iohanni, qui, a Deo praemonitus, fore, ut Spiritus suus visibili specie descenderet, et maneret super filium suum, cum hanc columbae speciem super Christum descendere et desidere vidit, pro comperto habuit, haec in visione fieri, prout praedixerat Deus. Proinde non dicit, se vidisse columbam, sed tanquam columbam. Dato tamen, non concesso, hoc columbae φάσμα ab omnibus esse conspectum, et a plerisque creditum, veram fuisse columbam, ne sic quidem eos fefellisset Spiritus Sanctus. Neque enim is vere fallit, qui ob oculos imaginem ponit, non fallendi animo, sed docendi. Talis autem fuit haec visio, qua ob oculos columbae species proposita est, non ut crederetur, vera esse columba, sed ut per eam Sancti Spiritus praesentia significaretur, et quae sint ejus virtutes. Hoc si putetur esse falsitas, abolebitur omnium visionum usus, in quibus aliud oculis, aliud animo exhibetur. Neque solum in columbae, sed et in linguarum ignearum visione fefellerit Spiritus Sanctus. Hae quippe linguae verae linguae non erant, nec verus ignis. Proinde, ut hic descendisse legitur ὡσεὶ περιστερὰ, ita ibi visae linguae dicuntur ὡσεὶ πυρὸς, Act. II, 3. Et paullo ante auditus esse sonus, non venti, sed tanquam venti, ὥσπερ φερομένης πνοῆς βιαίας, ut sciamus, haec omnia in visione obtigisse.

But Chrysostom refutes this error as follows in Homily 12 on Matthew: Ὁ μὲν ἐν τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ φύσει, τὸ δὲ ἐν ὄψει περιστερᾶς ἐφάνη· [Ho men en tē hēmetera physei, to de en opsei peristeras ephanē] Christ appeared in our nature, but the Spirit in the form of a dove. Again: Ὁ μὲν υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ φύσιν ἀνθρώπου ἀνέλαβε· τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα οὐ φύσιν ἀνέλαβε περιστερᾶς. Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ὁ Εὐαγγελιστὴς οὐκ εἶπεν, ὅτι ἐν φύσει περιστερᾶς, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς· οὐκοῦν οὐδὲ μετὰ ταῦτα ὤφθη ἐν τούτῳ τῷ σχήματι, ἀλλὰ τότε μόνον. [Ho men huios tou Theou physin anthrōpou anelabe; to de pneuma ou physin anelabe peristeras. Dia touto kai ho Euangelistēs ouk eipen, hoti en physei peristeras, all' en eidei peristeras; oukoun oude meta tauta ōphthē en toutō tō schēmati, alla tote monon.] The Son of God took on the nature of a man, but the Spirit did not take on the nature of a dove. Therefore the Evangelist did not say that he (descended) in the nature of a dove, but in the form of a dove. col. 37 Nor did he appear in that form afterwards, but only then. Augustine, however, who was wholly free of this error, believed only that a real dove, created by God for this purpose, was the symbol of the presence of the Holy Spirit. This is a much lighter error. For although this opinion cannot be reconciled with the words of the Evangelists, it differs from the former in that it contains nothing unworthy of the majesty of the Holy Spirit; for, without detriment to his dignity, he could be signified as well by a real dove as by the image of a dove. Fourth, it should be noted that Augustine's argument, by which he tries to prove that this was a real dove, has little force. We believe, he says, that both those bodies, namely those of Christ and of the Holy Spirit, were real bodies. For just as it was not fitting that the Son of God should deceive men, so it was not proper that the Holy Spirit should deceive men. I grant this. But I deny that anyone saw this form of a dove except Christ himself, Matt 3:16 and Mark 1:10, and John, John 1:32 Christ was indeed baptized in the midst of the crowds, Luke 3:21, but no one has written that the dove appeared to them. And that it was seen by no one apart from Christ except John is plainly taught by John 1:32: John bore witness to him, saying, I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and he remained upon him. For what need would there have been of the testimony of so great a II, 571 man to prove what others too had seen, indeed all the crowds that then stood around Christ and John? Moreover, this form of a dove did not deceive Christ, who was free from error; nor John, who had been forewarned by God that his Spirit would descend in visible form and remain upon his Son, and so, when he saw this form of a dove descend and settle upon Christ, he knew for certain that this was taking place in a vision, as God had foretold. Accordingly he does not say that he saw a dove, but as it were a dove. Yet even supposing, without conceding it, that this φάσμα [phasma] of a dove was seen by all and was believed by most to have been a real dove, not even so would the Holy Spirit have deceived them. For he does not truly deceive who places an image before the eyes with the intention not of deceiving but of teaching. Such was this vision, in which the form of a dove was set before the eyes, not so that it should be believed to be a real dove, but so that through it the presence of the Holy Spirit, and what his powers are, might be signified. If this is held to be falsehood, the use of all visions will be abolished, in which one thing is shown to the eyes and another to the mind. And the Holy Spirit would then have deceived not only in the vision of the dove but also in that of the fiery tongues. For those tongues were not real tongues, nor was it real fire. Accordingly, just as here he is said to have descended ὡσεὶ περιστερὰ [hōsei peristera], so there the tongues are said to have been seen ὡσεὶ πυρὸς [hōsei pyros], Acts 2:3. And a little before, a sound is said to have been heard, not of wind, but as of wind, ὥσπερ φερομένης πνοῆς βιαίας [hōsper pheromenēs pnoēs biaias], so that we may know that all these things happened in a vision.


Non possum non addere, Hebraeos quoque Cant. II, 12. turturis nomine, quae avis est columbini generis, Spiritum Sanctum intelligere. Unde est, quod verba Sacri textus, Vox turturis audita est in terra nostra, Chaldaeus sic παρα-φράζει· וקול רוחא דקודשא דפורקנא דאמרית לאברהם אביכון כבר שמעתון Et vocem Spiritus Sancti, id est, liberationem, quam Abrahamo, patri vestro, praedixi, Gen. XV, 14. 16. jam audivistis. Sed et haec ipsa verba Origenes refert ad Spiritum Sanctum, quem per turturem significari vult, cum occultiora revelat, et per columbam, cum ea docet, quae ad vulgi captum sunt magis accommodata. Spiritus Sanctus, inquit, quando de magnis et occultioribus sacramentis, et quae multi capere non possunt, loquitur, in turturis appellatione signatur, id est, eius avis, quae semper in montium jugis et in arborum verticibus commoratur. In vallibus autem, et his, quae ad homines usque perveniunt, columba assumitur. Haec ille in Cantici verba: Vox turturis, etc. col. 38

I cannot refrain from adding that the Hebrews too, in Song 2:12, understand the Holy Spirit by the name of the turtledove, a bird of the dove kind. Hence the words of the sacred text, The voice of the turtledove is heard in our land, are paraphrased by the Chaldee thus: וקול רוחא דקודשא דפורקנא דאמרית לאברהם אביכון כבר שמעתון And the voice of the Holy Spirit, that is, the deliverance which I foretold to Abraham, your father, Gen 15:14 16., you have already heard. Origen too refers these very words to the Holy Spirit, who, he holds, is signified by the turtledove when he reveals more hidden things, and by the dove when he teaches things better suited to the understanding of the common people. The Holy Spirit, he says, when he speaks of great and more hidden mysteries, which many cannot grasp, is designated by the name of the turtledove, that is, of that bird which always dwells on mountain ridges and in the tops of trees. But in the valleys, and in those things which reach down to men, the dove is taken. So he writes on the words of the Canticle: The voice of the turtledove, etc. col. 38
