Part 2, Book 1, chapter 7: Chiryonim, dove's dung or chickpeas
------------------------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/chiryonim.html

II, 572 CAP. VII.

II, 572 Chapter VII.


Probatur, חריונים, vel דביונים, 2 Reg. VI, 25. esse ciceris genus, non stercus columbarum, ut hactenus creditum.

It is proved that חריונים, or דביונים, 2 Reg. VI, 25, is a kind of chickpea, not dove's dung, as has hitherto been believed.


Narratur 2 Reg. VI, 25. Samariae famis tempore רובע הקב חריונים, quartam partem cabi stercoris columbarum venditam fuisse quinque argenteis. Nummos argenteos intellige semunciales, quorum singuli fere valent triginta sex as-ses Turonicos, ut summa fuerit praeter propter novem librarum nostrae monetae. Porro cabum Hebraei omnes summo consensu tradunt capacem fuisse duntaxat ovorum viginti quatuor. Ergo cabi quarta pars fuerit logus, id est, mensura sex ovorum. Haec probare non aggrediar, ne videar actum agere. Tantum conabor satisfacere quaestioni difficillimae, quamque nemo solvit hactenus, cur mensura tantula rei tam vilis, nempe columbini stercoris, tanti aestimata fuerit, et in quem usum comparata.

It is related in 2 Reg. VI, 25 that in the time of the famine at Samaria רובע הקב חריונים, the fourth part of a cab of dove's dung, was sold for five pieces of silver. Understand by these silver coins half-ounce pieces, each worth about thirty-six Tours sous, so that the total came to roughly nine livres of our money. Further, all the Hebrews with complete agreement report that the cab held only twenty-four eggs. So the fourth part of a cab would be a log, that is, a measure of six eggs. I shall not undertake to prove these things, lest I seem to do what has already been done. I shall only try to answer a most difficult question, which no one has solved so far: why so tiny a measure of so worthless a thing, namely dove's dung, was valued so highly, and for what use it was bought.


I. Sunt, qui dicunt, Samaritanos, urgente fame, hoc stercus in cibum adhibuisse. In his Eutychius, Alexandrinus patriarcha, in Annalibus, ubi de fame Samariae pag. 213. واكلوا زبل الحمام Et comederunt stercus columbarum. Quomodo Rabsakes, Ierosolymam obsessurus, minabatur se facturum, ut incolae comederent stercus suum, et lotium suum biberent, 2 Reg. XVIII, 27. et Es. XXXVI, 12. Verum haec verba Rabsakis aliud non sunt, quam jactabundi Thrasonis inanis insultatio, qua futurum significabat, ut Hierosolymitani summa rerum omnium inopia premerentur. Et merito Hebraei di-col. 39 ctum interpretantur על דרך גוזמא, per viam hyperboles; cum res sine exemplo sit, ut quisquam, porcorum instar, vel aliena deglutierit stercora, nedum sua. A tam immani cibo natura plane abhorret. Aut si, ingruente fame, quemquam eo adigeret ferro trabali vincta necessitas, tamen id faceret frustra: quia in excrementis nihil superest, quod concoquatur. Quod de columbino stercore, quam de humano multo verius, quia multo calidius est. Hoc cum res ipsa nos docet, tum medicorum libri atque eorum omnium, qui de stercoratione scripserunt. Varro, De re rust. lib. 1. cap. 38. Stercus (stercorandis agris) optimum scribit esse Cassius volucrium, etc. De hisce praestare columbinum, quia calidissimum. Columella lib. 2. cap. 15. Tria igitur stercoris genera sunt praecipua, quod ex avibus, quod ex hominibus, quod ex pecudibus consit. Avium primum habetur, quod ex columbariis egeritur. Plinius lib. 17. cap. 9. Marcus Varro principatum dat turdorum fimo ex aviariis. Proximum Columella columbariis, II, 573 mox gallinariis facit. Aliqui columbaria praeferunt. Palladius lib. 2. cap. 33. Columbinum (stercus) fervidissimum, caeterarumque avium satis utile est. Quintilius lib. 2. Geopon. Ἔστι δὲ κόπρος μὲν καλὴ ἡ τῶν πτηνῶν ἁπάντων, πλὴν τῶν χηνῶν, καὶ τῶν ἐνύδρων ὀρνέων, διὰ τὴν ὑγρότητα, etc. Πολὺ δὲ καλλίων ἡ τῶν περιστερῶν, πολὺ τὸ θερμὸν ἔχουσα· Avium omnium stercus bonum est, praeterquam anserum et aquaticarum volucrium, propter humiditatem, etc. sed longe praestat columbinum, quia fervidissimum. Avicenna lib. 2. Canonis, capite زبل seu De stercore, زبل الحمام اسخان الازبال المستعمل Stercus columbarum calidissimum est omnium eorum, quorum aliquis usus. Causa patet ex Aristotele, qui columbam primam recenset inter ea, quae θερμὴν κοι-λίαν, ventriculum ferventiorem habent, De part. anim. lib. 2. cap. 7. Itaque e recentioribus columbam nonnulli scribunt, struthionis instar, lapillos devorare et concoquere. Et columbae nomen Arabicum حمام himam est a calore factum. Quae, ut puto, abunde docent, in columbino stercore nihil superesse, quod ab homine possit digeri (1).

I. There are those who say that the Samaritans, pressed by hunger, used this dung as food. Among them is Eutychius, patriarch of Alexandria, in his Annals, where he speaks of the famine of Samaria, p. 213: واكلوا زبل الحمام [wa-akalū zibl al-ḥamām] And they ate dove's dung. In the same way Rabshakeh, about to besiege Jerusalem, threatened that he would make the inhabitants eat their own dung and drink their own urine, 2 Reg. XVIII, 27, and Es. XXXVI, 12. But these words of Rabshakeh are nothing but the empty taunt of a boastful Thraso, by which he meant that the people of Jerusalem would be oppressed by the utmost want of all things. And the Hebrews rightly interpret the col. 39 saying על דרך גוזמא, by way of hyperbole; for it is a thing without precedent that anyone should, like swine, have swallowed the dung of others, let alone his own. Nature utterly recoils from so monstrous a food. Or if, when famine struck, necessity bound with iron spikes drove someone to it, he would still do it in vain, because nothing remains in excrement that can be digested. This is far more true of dove's dung than of human dung, because it is much hotter. This is taught both by experience itself and by the books of the physicians and of all who have written on manuring. Varro, De re rust. book 1, ch. 38: Cassius writes that the best dung (for manuring fields) is that of birds, etc. Of these, that of doves is the best, because it is the hottest. Columella book 2, ch. 15: There are, then, three chief kinds of dung: that from birds, that from men, and that from cattle. Of birds' dung the first is held to be that which is cleared out of dovecotes. Pliny book 17, ch. 9: Marcus Varro gives first place to the dung of thrushes from aviaries. Columella puts that from dovecotes next, II, 573 then that from henhouses. Some prefer that from dovecotes. Palladius book 2, ch. 33: That of doves (dung) is the most fiery, and that of other birds is quite useful. Quintilius book 2 of the Geopon.: Ἔστι δὲ κόπρος μὲν καλὴ ἡ τῶν πτηνῶν ἁπάντων, πλὴν τῶν χηνῶν, καὶ τῶν ἐνύδρων ὀρνέων, διὰ τὴν ὑγρότητα [esti de kopros men kalē hē tōn ptēnōn hapantōn, plēn tōn chēnōn, kai tōn enydrōn orneōn, dia tēn hygrotēta], etc. Πολὺ δὲ καλλίων ἡ τῶν περιστερῶν, πολὺ τὸ θερμὸν ἔχουσα [poly de kalliōn hē tōn peristerōn, poly to thermon echousa]· The dung of all birds is good, except that of geese and water-birds, because of its moisture, etc. but that of doves is far superior, because it is the most fiery. Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] book 2 of the Canon, in the chapter زبل [zibl], or On dung: زبل الحمام اسخان الازبال المستعمل [zibl al-ḥamām askhan al-azbāl al-mustaʿmal] Dove's dung is the hottest of all those that have any use. The cause is clear from Aristotle, who lists the dove first among those that have θερμὴν κοιλίαν [thermēn koilian], a hotter stomach, De part. anim. book 2, ch. 7. Accordingly some of the moderns write that the dove, like the ostrich, swallows and digests small stones. And the Arabic name of the dove, حمام [ḥamām] himam, is formed from heat. These things, I think, show abundantly that nothing remains in dove's dung that a human being could digest R1.


II, 574 II. Itaque hinc dejecti R. Ionas et R. David aliud comminiscuntur, nimirum Israelitas stercore pro ligno usos, cum tempore obsidionis Samariae non li-ceret ire lignatum: quod est paullo minus absurdum, cum stercus columbinum possit ligni vices praestare. Nam pro comperto tradit Galenus, stercus columbinum tam facile incendi, ut alicubi in Mysia fimo columbario, a solis radiis sponte accenso, vicina domus conflagraverit. Nempe prope domum illam κόπρος ἀπέκειτο περιστερῶν, ἤδη σεσηπυῖα, καὶ τεθερμαμένη, καὶ ἀτμὸν ἀναπέμπου-σα, καὶ ἁπτομένοις ἱκανῶς θερμή. ταύτης δὲ πλησίον ἦν, ὡς καὶ ψαύειν ἤδη θυρὶς ἔχουσα ξύλα νεωστὶ καταληλιμμένα ῥητίνῃ πολλῇ, θέρους οὖν μέσου λαῦρος ἥλιος προσβαλὼν ἐξῆψε τὴν ῥητίνην τε, καὶ τὰ ξύλα, jacebat fimus columbarius jam putridus et fervidus, et fumum emittens, et tactu abunde calidus, et illi domui tam vicinus, ut fenestram tangeret, cujus ligna nuper multa resina inuncta fuerant: media igitur aestate sol plurimus, desuper feriens, ligna et resinam incendit. Ita Galenus libro tertio De temperam. Quale est, quod apud eundem le-gas libro primo De different. febr. et libro De morborum causis, agrestium columbarum stercus ignem concipere tardius, sed retinere diutius. Ne quis hanc materiam putet igni fovendo esse prorsus ineptam. Verum enimvero quis credat, in urbe Samaria, quam, cum esset regum sedes, a rusticanis moribus plurimum abhorruisse par est, tantum fuisse columbini stercoris, ut inde strueretur ignis? Aut ullum fuisse, qui non mallet igne carere ad tempus, quam materiae col. 40 in flammis foetidissimae tantillum tam grandi pretio comparare? Quid quod haec non cohaerent? Samariae fames erat magna, quia nihil erat, unde aleretur ignis, praeter columbinum stercus, magno emptum.

II, 574 II. Driven from this position, R. Jonah [=Jonah ibn Janāḥ, Sefer ha-Shorashim] and R. David devise something else, namely that the Israelites used the dung in place of wood, since during the siege of Samaria they could not go out to gather firewood. This is a little less absurd, since dove's dung can serve in place of wood. For Galen reports as an established fact that dove's dung catches fire so easily that somewhere in Mysia a neighbouring house burned down because dove's dung had ignited spontaneously from the sun's rays. Near that house, namely, κόπρος ἀπέκειτο περιστερῶν, ἤδη σεσηπυῖα, καὶ τεθερμαμένη, καὶ ἀτμὸν ἀναπέμπουσα, καὶ ἁπτομένοις ἱκανῶς θερμή. ταύτης δὲ πλησίον ἦν, ὡς καὶ ψαύειν ἤδη θυρὶς ἔχουσα ξύλα νεωστὶ καταληλιμμένα ῥητίνῃ πολλῇ, θέρους οὖν μέσου λαῦρος ἥλιος προσβαλὼν ἐξῆψε τὴν ῥητίνην τε, καὶ τὰ ξύλα [kopros apekeito peristerōn, ēdē sesēpuia, kai tethermamenē, kai atmon anapempousa, kai haptomenois hikanōs thermē. tautēs de plēsion ēn, hōs kai psauein ēdē thyris echousa xyla neōsti katalēlimmena rhētinē pollē, therous oun mesou lauros hēlios prosbalōn exēpse tēn rhētinēn te, kai ta xyla], there lay dove's dung, already putrid and hot, giving off steam, and quite hot to the touch, and so close to that house, that it touched a window, whose wood had recently been smeared with much resin: so in midsummer the blazing sun, striking from above, set the wood and the resin alight. So Galen, book 3 De temperam. Similar is what one reads in the same author, book 1 De different. febr. and in the book De morborum causis: that the dung of wild doves catches fire more slowly but holds it longer. So no one should think this material wholly unfit for feeding a fire. But truly, who would believe that in the city of Samaria, which, being the royal seat, we may fairly suppose was very far removed from rustic ways, there was so much dove's dung that fires could be built from it? Or that there was anyone who would not rather go without fire for a time than buy so tiny a quantity of a substance most foul-smelling in the flames at so great a price? col. 40 Moreover, these things do not hang together: that there was a great famine in Samaria because there was nothing to feed a fire with except dove's dung, bought at a high price.


III. Tertia sententia est eorum, qui volunt, Israelitas ideo comparasse hoc stercus, ut agri, in urbe inclusi, melius stercorarentur, atque sic futurae fami in annum prospiceretur: quasi verissimile sit, in urbe populosissima tantum agri fuisse, aut eos, quibus deerat, unde viverent in dies, habuisse, unde sererent; aut Samariae cives de futuro tam fuisse sollicitos, cum nihil esset in praesens; aut in seligendo stercore tam delicatos, ut, cum aliud stercus, paullo minus utile, magna copia suppeteret, columbinum tanti emerint.

III. The third opinion is that of those who hold that the Israelites bought this dung in order to manure better the fields enclosed within the city, and so provide against famine in the coming year. As if it were very likely that in a most populous city there was so much farmland; or that those who lacked the means to live from day to day had the means to sow; or that the citizens of Samaria were so anxious about the future when they had nothing for the present; or so fastidious in choosing dung that, when other dung, only a little less useful, was available in great abundance, they bought dove's dung at so high a price.


IV. Quarta sententia, aeque absurda, Iosephi est, columbarum stercus illis fuisse ἀντὶ ἁλῶν, pro sale. Quamvis enim agnoscam, in eo non deesse salem, tamen si excrementitio sale iis utendum erat, nemo est, qui nesciat, in urina II, 575 multo plus esse salis, et facilius elici, et minori cum fastidio. Ut nihil opus fuerit tanti emere, quod unusquisque domi habebat. Praeterea, quorsum ille sal in tanta fame? Si libeat rhetoricari, scio, multa posse congeri in laudem salis, et secundum panem vix quidquam esse ad vitam utilius: quo sine, cum ci-borum magna pars fatua sit atque insipida, nunquid comeditur insipidum absque sale? Iob. VI, 6. Itaque, ut sub Lege absque sale nullum sacrificium, Levit. II, 13. et Marc. IX, 49. Adeoque etiam inter ethnicos, auctore Plinio, nulla sacra conficiebantur sine mola salsa. Ita vix ulla mensa est paullo lautior, quae sale vacet. Sed et sal pauperum videatur fuisse cibus. Solebant enim tenuiores πρὸς ἅλα δειπνεῖν, καὶ κύμινον, sale et cumino coenare, ut ex Plutarcho colligere est. Proinde Cratero, se invitanti, respondit Diogenes apud Laërtium li-bro sexto, Ἀλλὰ βούλομαι ἐν Ἀθήναις ἅλα λείχειν, ἢ παρὰ Κρατερῷ τῆς πο-λυτελοῦς τραπέζης ἀπολαύειν· At malo Athenis salem lingere, quam apud Craterum opipara mensa frui. Et Persius Satyra quinta,

IV. The fourth opinion, equally absurd, is that of Josephus: that dove's dung served them ἀντὶ ἁλῶν [anti halōn], in place of salt. For although I grant that it does not lack salt, yet if they had to use salt from excrement, everyone knows that there is II, 575 much more salt in urine, and that it is extracted more easily and with less disgust. So there would have been no need to buy at so high a price what everyone had at home. Besides, what would be the point of that salt in so great a famine? If one cared to play the rhetorician, I know that much could be gathered in praise of salt, and that after bread hardly anything is more useful for life: without it a great part of foods is flat and tasteless, can that which is unsavoury be eaten without salt? Job 6:6. Thus, under the Law no sacrifice was without salt, Lev 2:13 and Mark 9:49. And even among the heathen, on the authority of Pliny, no rites were performed without salted meal. So too there is hardly any table of some refinement that lacks salt. But salt also seems to have been the food of the poor. For people of slender means used πρὸς ἅλα δειπνεῖν, καὶ κύμινον [pros hala deipnein, kai kyminon], to dine on salt and cumin, as can be gathered from Plutarch. Hence Diogenes, in Laertius book 6, answered Craterus when he invited him: Ἀλλὰ βούλομαι ἐν Ἀθήναις ἅλα λείχειν, ἢ παρὰ Κρατερῷ τῆς πολυτελοῦς τραπέζης ἀπολαύειν [Alla boulomai en Athēnais hala leichein, ē para Kraterō tēs polytelous trapezēs apolauein]· But I would rather lick salt at Athens than enjoy a sumptuous table at the house of Craterus. And Persius, Satire 5,


Varo regustatum digito terebrare salinum
Contentus perages, si vivere cum Iove tendis.

You will live content to bore with your finger into a salt-cellar tasted again and again, if you strive to live with Jove.


id est, summe pauper eris, si pius. Et Horatii libri primi Satyra tertia, Tigellius, de quo Seneca Epistola centesima vigesima sexta, ut videatur homo frugi, divitum, inquit, lautitias nihil moror,

that is, you will be extremely poor if you are pious. And in Horace, book 1, Satire 3, Tigellius, of whom Seneca speaks in Epistle 126, in order to seem a frugal man, says: I care nothing for the luxuries of the rich,


— — — modo sit mihi mensa tripes, et
Concha salis puri. — — — —

— — — let me only have a three-legged table, and a shell of pure salt. — — — —


Varro etiam (sale) pulmentarii vice usos veteres auctor est: esitasse enim salem cum pane et caseo, ut proverbio apparet. Ita Plinius lib. 31. cap. 7. ubi idem paullo ante, Honoribus etiam militiaeque interponitur: Salariis inde dictis, magna apud antiquos auctoritate. Item, Ancus Martius, rex, salis modia sex millia in congiario dedit populo. Sed et Assyriae reges salem dabant pro stipendio. Proinde Esdr. IV, 14. ad Artaxerxem regem haec scribunt Samariae praefecti: Propterea quod די־מלח היכלא מלחנא, sale palatii salimur. Ita ad verbum, id est, ut recte Iunius, salarium de regis palatio percipimus. Sed salem nemo laudat uberius Plutarcho Sympos. lib. 5. Probl. 10. ubi ad quaestionem, cur Homerus a) salem divinum appellet, inter caetera salem asserit τῶν ἄλλων ὄψων ὄψον εἶναι, καὶ ἥδυσμα, aliorum esse obsoniorum obsonium et condimentum. Item, Θρίγκω ⁠-μα τῆς τροφῆς γινόμενον εἰς τὸ σῶμα, καὶ παρέχον ἐναρμοσίαν αὐτῇ προς τὴν ὄρεξιν, quod in corpore fit cibi tutela, eum palato nostro congruum et convenientem reddens. Unde est, quod Sirach. XXXIX, 31. quaedam laudantur tanquam II, 576 ἀρχὴ πάσης χρείας εἰς ζωὴν ἀνθρώπου, principium (id est, praecipua) omnium eorum, quae ad vitam necessaria sunt. Et in his sal ante omnem cibum. Sed de sale quidquid dicatur, tamen hoc certum, salem nihil quidquam esse, quam col. 41 condimentum, nec magno pretio comparari solere condimenta in magna fame, et cum alimenta desunt; cum optimum condimentum sit ipsa fames: neque id quaeratur, quod gulam irritet, sed quod satiet.

Varro also reports that the ancients used (salt) as a relish: for they ate salt with bread and cheese, as the proverb shows. So Pliny, book 31, ch. 7, where shortly before the same author says: It is also involved in honours and in military service: hence salaries are so called, with great authority among the ancients. Likewise, Ancus Martius, the king, gave the people six thousand modii of salt as a largess. The kings of Assyria also gave salt as pay. Accordingly, in Ezra 4:14 the governors of Samaria write this to King Artaxerxes: Because די־מלח היכלא מלחנא, we are salted with the salt of the palace. That is the literal rendering; that is, as Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] rightly puts it, we receive a salary from the king's palace. But no one praises salt more fully than Plutarch, Sympos. book 5, Probl. 10, where, on the question why Homer a) calls salt divine, he asserts among other things that salt is τῶν ἄλλων ὄψων ὄψον εἶναι, καὶ ἥδυσμα [tōn allōn opsōn opson einai, kai hēdysma], the relish and seasoning of all other relishes. Likewise, Θρίγκωμα τῆς τροφῆς γινόμενον εἰς τὸ σῶμα, καὶ παρέχον ἐναρμοσίαν αὐτῇ προς τὴν ὄρεξιν [thrinkōma tēs trophēs ginomenon eis to sōma, kai parechon enarmosian autē pros tēn orexin], that which becomes a safeguard of food in the body, making it agreeable and suited to our palate. Hence in Sir 39:31 certain things are praised as II, 576 ἀρχὴ πάσης χρείας εἰς ζωὴν ἀνθρώπου [archē pasēs chreias eis zōēn anthrōpou], the beginning (that is, the chief) of all things necessary for life. And among these salt comes before all food. But whatever may be said of salt, this much is certain: salt is nothing but col. 41 a seasoning, and seasonings are not usually bought at a great price in a severe famine, when food is lacking. For hunger itself is the best seasoning, and one does not then seek what stimulates the palate, but what satisfies.


V. Quinta sententia Talmudicorum est, quae ut intelligatur, lector praemonendus est, axioma hoc esse Talmudicum codicis Megilla c. 3. כל המקראות הכתובין בתורה לגנאי קורין אותן לשבח, Omnes voces, quae in Lege obscoenae scriptae sunt, honeste legi. Quapropter, ubicunque in Scriptura occurrunt vocabula, in communi usu minus honesta, Hebraeorum magistri, honestati consulentes, ea voluerunt aliter legi, quam scripta sunt. Adeoque pro verbo, quod in textu habetur, honestius aliud in margine substituunt, quod pro eo in synagogis legere moris hodieque est. Hinc est, quod pro שגלb), coire, legunt שכב, concumbere: pro עפוליםc), ani morbis, טחורים, mariscas: pro טחוראותd), latrinis, proprie locis stercoris, מוצאות, secessus: pro חורים et שיניםe), stercoribus et urinis, צואה et מימי רגלים, excrementum et aquas pedum. Non aliter hoc loco pro חריונים, stercore columbarum, legi volunt דביונים, fluxum columbarum, voce composita ex דב fluxu, et יונים columbis. Sed Talmudici דביונים aliter interpretantur, quasi sit compositum ex Chaldaico pronomine ד, quod respondet Hebraeo אשר, qui, quae, quod, et Praepositione ב, in, et nomine יונים, columbae. Illis itaque דביונים significat quod in columbis, supple, est, vel erat. Samariae nempe volunt columbas ad hoc fuisse institutas, ut pabulatum irent in agros, si ita loqui liceat. Unde, cum fartae et distentae rediissent, dominos excussa ingluvie grana elicuisse et magno vendidisse. Ita, ut ex horum mente verba Sacri textus sic sonent: Fames tanta erat Samariae, ut quarta pars cabi granorum, quae erant in columbis, et ex earum ingluvie eliciebantur, veniret quinque siclis. Unde Comestor in Historia Scholastica lib. 4. Regum cap. 10. Tradunt quidam, nomine stercoris dici vesiculam columbae, in qua reperiebantur grana deforis allata. Quo commento non puto quidquam fingi potuisse absurdius. Non, quod negem, columbas amore sobolis sic institui posse, ut ex urbe obsessa emissae domum redeant. Talibus enim internuntiis veteres et recentiores saepe esse usos, probavimus in capite proxime antecedenti. Sed quis Samariae credat columbas tam dociles magno fuisse numero? Aut eas in agro, ab hostibus longe lateque vastato, fruges habuisse passim obvias? Aut, ingluvie II, 577 plena reduces, quidquid in agro absorpserant, tam facile expectorasse? Atque his demum artibus vel unum frumenti cabum toto obsidionis tempore potuisse congeri? Aut, si Deus hunc populum tam miraculosa ratione aliquamdiu sustentasset, Scripturam rem inauditam tam leviter fuisse praeterituram? Sed frustra disputamus, cum vox חריונים , quae in textu est, nulla ratione huc trahi possit. Imo vix, ac ne vix quidem, vox marginalis דביונים , verti queat, id, quod est in columbis. Nisi Hebraeo Nomine Chaldaicum Pronomen praefixum fuisse velimus, atque ita conflatam fuisse vocem hybridam et semibarbaram.

V. The fifth opinion is that of the Talmudists. To understand it, the reader must first be told that there is this Talmudic axiom in the tractate Megilla, ch. 3: כל המקראות הכתובין בתורה לגנאי קורין אותן לשבח, All words written indecently in the Law are read decently. Therefore, wherever words occur in Scripture that are less decent in common usage, the teachers of the Hebrews, out of regard for decency, wanted them read otherwise than they are written. So in place of the word found in the text they substitute in the margin another, more decent one, which it is still the custom today to read in its place in the synagogues. Hence for שגלb), to have intercourse, they read שכב, to lie with; for עפוליםc), diseases of the anus, טחורים, haemorrhoids; for טחוראותd), latrines, properly places of dung, מוצאות, privies; for חורים and שיניםe), dung and urine, צואה and מימי רגלים, excrement and water of the feet. In the same way, in this passage, for חריונים, dove's dung, they want דביונים to be read, the flux of doves, a word compounded of דב, flux, and יונים, doves. But the Talmudists interpret דביונים differently, as if it were compounded of the Chaldee pronoun ד, which corresponds to the Hebrew אשר, who, which, that, the preposition ב, in, and the noun יונים, doves. For them, then, דביונים means that which (supply: is or was) in the doves. For they hold that at Samaria doves had been trained to go out foraging in the fields, so to speak; and that when they returned stuffed and swollen, their owners shook out their crops, extracted the grain and sold it at a high price. So, in their view, the words of the sacred text run thus: The famine in Samaria was so great that a quarter of a kab of the grains that were in the doves, and were extracted from their crops, sold for five shekels. Hence Comestor in the Historia Scholastica, book 4 of Kings, ch. 10: Some relate that by the word dung is meant the little bladder of the dove, in which were found grains brought from outside. I do not think anything more absurd than this fiction could have been devised. Not that I deny that doves, through love of their young, can be so trained that, released from a besieged city, they return home; for we have shown in the immediately preceding chapter that ancient and more recent people often used such messengers. But who would believe that at Samaria there were so many such docile doves? Or that in fields laid waste far and wide by the enemy they found crops everywhere at hand? Or that, returning with full crops, II, 577 they so easily disgorged whatever they had swallowed in the field? And that by such arts even one kab of grain could have been gathered in the whole time of the siege? Or, if God had sustained this people for some time in so miraculous a way, that Scripture would have passed over so unheard-of a thing so lightly? But we argue in vain, since the word חריונים, which is in the text, can in no way be drawn to this sense. Indeed, hardly, or not even hardly, can the marginal word דביונים be rendered that which is in the doves, unless we suppose that a Chaldee pronoun was prefixed to a Hebrew noun, and so a hybrid, half-barbarous word was formed.


VI. Iunius, has Symplegadas nova interpretatione vitare posse se putans, hunc locum ita reddidit: Extitit fames magna Samariae, etc. Adeo, ut esset quarta pars, venter ipse, qui est in cavo columbarum, quinum siclorum argenti. Sed prima lectione statim apparet, virum, impense doctum, non fuisse ita redditurum, prope dixerim nullo sensu, nisi in magnis angustiis versari se sensisset. Quid enim sit quarta pars, venter ipse columbarum? Et quid attinebat definire, ventrem esse in cavo? Quamvis cavum potius in ventre sit, quam in cavo venter. col. 42 Rursus quomodo illi viro, qui fuit perspicacissimus, venire potuit in mentem, seorsim venisse columbarum ventrem? Sed neque ex Hebraeis verbis רובע הקב חריונים , ullis fidiculis elici queant, quae in illius versione habentur, quarta pars, venter ipse, qui est in cavo columbarum. Nam si רבע , quarta pars, et הקב , venter, ut quidem reddit Cl. Iunius, essent apposita, utrumque nomen praefixum haberet He hajedia, seu Articulum: ut Graece diceretur τὸ τέταρτον, ἡ κοιλία. Addo, hac versione confundi perperam קב kab, cum קבה keba. Quorum קבה keba ventrem, seu ingluviem sonat: sed קב kab plane aliud est, nempe κάβος cabus, mensurae genus. Ita ex Hebraeis explicant Aruch, Kimchius, Pomarius, Elias et Aquinas in Lexicis suis, Mardochaeus in Concordantiis, Al-phes in tractatu De Paschate cap. 5. fol. 176. Et Glossa Talmudis passim. Unde compositum תרקב tharkab aliis duos cabos sonat, quasi contractum ex תרי קבין there kabin, duo cabi; aliis verius tres cabos, quasi sit תרי וקב , duo et cabus, unus insuper. Ita R. Selomo in variis locis Talmudis. Et κάβος quoque mensura est Hesychio, Philoxeno, Suidae, Etymologo, Phavorino, et aliis. Denique חריונים nemo veterum aliter reddit, quam stercus columbarum. Consulantur Iosephus, Graeci, Chaldaei, Syri, Arabes, Romani interpretes. Et, ex Hebraeis, Iarchius, Kimchius et R. Levi in hunc locum. Inter eos reperietur mirus esse consensus, quod in obscuri loci interpretatione raro contingit. Quin e recentioribus nemo dissentit praeter Iunium et Fullerum, de quo jam pauca.

VI. Junius, thinking he could avoid these Symplegades by a new interpretation, rendered this passage as follows: There arose a great famine in Samaria, etc. so that the fourth part, the belly itself, which is in the hollow of doves, was of five shekels of silver. But at first reading it is immediately apparent that this exceedingly learned man would not have rendered it thus, almost, I would say, without any sense, had he not felt himself to be in great straits. For what would the fourth part, the belly itself of doves be? And what point was there in specifying that the belly is in the hollow? Although the hollow is rather in the belly than the belly in the hollow. col. 42 Again, how could it have entered the mind of that man, who was most perspicacious, that the belly of doves was sold separately? Nor can what is found in his version, the fourth part, the belly itself, which is in the hollow of doves, be extracted by any torture from the Hebrew words רובע הקב חריונים. For if רבע, the fourth part, and הקב, the belly, as the distinguished Junius renders it, were in apposition, each noun would have the He hajedia, or article, prefixed, as one would say in Greek τὸ τέταρτον, ἡ κοιλία [to tetarton, hē koilia]. I add that in this version קב kab is wrongly confused with קבה keba. Of these, קבה keba means belly or crop; but קב kab is something quite different, namely κάβος [kabos], cabus, a kind of measure. So it is explained among the Hebrews by the Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome], Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)], Elias [=Elijah Levita (1469–1549), author of the Aramaic lexicon Meturgeman and of Tishbi] and Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)] in their Lexicons, by Mardochaeus in his Concordance, by Alphes in the tractate On Passover, ch. 5, fol. 176, and by the Gloss on the Talmud passim. Hence the compound תרקב tharkab means to some two cabs, as if contracted from תרי קבין there kabin, two cabs; to others, more correctly, three cabs, as if it were תרי וקב, two and a cab, one more. So R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] in various places of the Talmud. And κάβος [kabos] is also a measure in Hesychius, Philoxenus, the Suda, the Etymologicum, Phavorinus and others. Finally, none of the ancients renders חריונים otherwise than as dove's dung. Let Josephus and the Greek, Chaldee, Syriac, Arabic and Latin translators be consulted, and, among the Hebrews, Iarchius, Kimchi and R. Levi on this passage. Among them a remarkable agreement will be found, which rarely happens in the interpretation of an obscure passage. Indeed, of the more recent writers no one dissents except Junius and Fuller [=Nicholas Fuller, Miscellanea theologica / sacra (1612–22)], about whom now a few words.


VII. Is in Sacris Miscellaneis lib. 6. cap. 11.) tam per דביונים , quam per חריונים (quorum illud in margine scribitur, hoc in textu) columbarum ingluviem, II, 578 alvum et interanea intelligit. Quasi vocentur דביונים, id est, fluxus columbarum, eo quod, qui columbas dissecant et exenterant, ea defluere, seu delabi in terram sinant. Et חריונים, id est, κοιλία, seu alvus columbarum. Nam חריונים esse columbarum alvum et interanea, conatur ita probare: „Hebraeum חור primo „album sonat: 2. foramen, a candore lucis, quae per illud solet conspici: 3. „τρώγλην cavernam, quae foraminis est species: 4. alvum, Graece κοιλίαν, „quae insignis est humani corporis caverna; unde alvus, quasi alveus, κοιλία „ἀπὸ τοῦ κοίλου denominatur: 5. stercora alvo inclusa, metonymia contenti „pro continente. Quarum hujus verbi notionum cum liceat elicere commo-„dissimam, quidni columbarum alvum et interanea hic putemus intelligenda, quae „cum abjici soleant, tamen gravissimae famis tempore non solum servata sint, „sed et grandi pretio distracta et divendita“. Haec Fulleri sententia est, in qua (quod accuratissimi scriptoris pace dixero) non pauca reperisse mihi videor, quae veri ne speciem quidem habent. Ita, quod columbarum interanea vult Hebraice dici דביונים, ne per somnium quidem ulli unquam venit in mentem. Quin stercora omnes exponunt, a fluxu sic appellata, ut Graece ῥεῦμα γαστρὸς et δι-άῤῥοια, et Latine alvi profluvium de hujusmodi fluxu dicitur. Et Celso febres fluentes, Graece ῥοώδεις πυρετοὶ, eae sunt, quae alvum laxant. Rursus in eo, quod asserit idem Fullerus, vocem חור 1. album, 2. foramen, 3. cavernam, 4. alvum, ingluviem, interanea, 5. stercus significare, pleraque sunt commentitia. חור pro albo non tam Hebraeum est, quam Chaldaeum et Arabicum. At pro foramine, aut caverna Hebraeum est, et a diversa Radice. Illud enim est a חור chavar, albescere: hoc a geminato חרר charar, perforare. Proinde in Talmude legas tractatus Succa fol. 20. b. חור שחררוהו מים, foramen, quod aquae perforarunt. Et iisdem Talmudicis חריר est foramen acus, ut ܚܪܘܪܐ Syris Matth. XIX, 24. Porro illud חור alvum quoque, aut ingluviem, aut interanea col. 43 sonare, merum commentum est, cujus auctor non profertur, neque vero potest proferri, cum nemo unquam ita usurpaverit. Denique חר, vel חרי potius, aut חרא pro stercore vox est diversa prorsus, cujus Radix neque est חור, neque est חרר, sed חרה, vel חרא. Itaque Talmudici חרי, vel חריא constanter scribunt. Et Arabice خري charia, cum hamza in fine, est stercus egerere, خرء stercus, مخرأة latrina. Quin et Hebraei, cum plene scribunt, Aleph inserunt, ut Esa. XXXVI, 12. לאכול את חראיהם, ad comedenda stercora sua. Et 2 Reg. X, 27. Destruxerunt domum Baalis, et posuerunt למחראות, in latrinas. Neque Aleph ibi est adventitium, ut putant, sed Radicale, et supplendum, ubi deest, ut ex Arabismo patet. His observatis, Cl. Fullerum apparet vocis etymon, et veram scripturam ignorasse, et promiscue sumsisse tres voces diversae originis, quod illum in devia traxit. Cum enim, quidquid affert, solis nitatur II, 579 vocum etymis, si haec etyma falsa sunt, falsum etiam esse necesse est, quidquid his superstruitur. Et vero futilissimum est, quod auctori sacro affingit, cabum alvorum et extorum columbinorum Samariae venisse quinque siclis. Neque enim fando unquam auditum est, columbarum ingluviem et exta separatim fuisse distracta. Fateor, de gallinis id legi, et Arabice تبودك thabudach eum dici, qui vendit interanea gallinae, puta cor, ingluviem, etc. Alcamus interpretatur من يبيع ما في بطون الدجاج من القلب والقانصة Sed de columbinis nihil tale occurrit uspiam, quod quidem sciam. Neque etiam id convenit, ut columbarum intestina per cabos fuerint dimensa. Cabus enim non est extorum mensura, sed granorum, ut satum, epha et corus. Nempe sex cabi satum constituunt, tria sata epham, decem ephae corum, mensuram in aridis maximam. Proinde in Talmude et in Aruch, passim legas קב חטין, cabum tritici. Et ab Elia definitur מדת היובש, mensura aridorum; a Pomario מדת של חטים, mensura frumentaria, ab Aquinate מדת למדות דבר היבש, mensura ad dimentiendam rem aridam. Sic in Polluce, Κάβασον δὲ ἐκάλουν τὸν περὶ τὴν τροφὴν ἄπληστον, etc. Κάβος γὰρ σίτου μέτρον. Cabasum autem vocabant cibo insatiabilem, etc. Cabus enim frumenti mensura est. Et in Hesychio, Κάβαισος· ἄπληστος· κάβος γὰρ μέτρον σιτικόν· Cabasus, insatiabilis; cabus enim est mensura frumentaria. Inde corrige Suidam, qui pro κάβαισος habet κάβαιστος. Et Etymologicon, quod pro μέτρον σιτικὸν habet μετασιτικὸν, vocem nihili. Sed in Hesychio mendosa sunt, quae sequuntur paullo infra, Κά-βος· μέτρον σιτικὸν, καὶ οἰνικὸν, Cabus, mensura frumenti et vini. Cabum enim vini, vel liquidorum esse mensuram, alibi nusquam legas. Itaque sic emendo, Κάβος· μέτρον σιτικὸν, καὶ κάδος οἰνικόν· Cabus frumenti mensura, et cadus vini. Confert inter se duas voces, ut sono, ita et significatione vicinas. Nam utraque mensuram sonat, sed haec vini, illa frumenti. Quippe ut cabum frumenti, ita cadum vini mensuram esse, nemo est, qui nesciat. Sic Herodotus libri tertii capite vigesimo dicit Φοινικηΐου οἴνου κάδον, cadum vini palmei. Et Athenaei libro undecimo Anacreon,

VII. He (in the Sacred Miscellanies, book 6, ch. 11) understands both by דביונים and by חריונים (the former is written in the margin, the latter in the text) the crop of doves, II, 578 their belly and entrails. It is as if they were called דביונים, that is, the flux of doves, because those who cut up and gut doves let these flow down, or slip, to the ground; and חריונים, that is, κοιλία [koilia], or the belly of doves. For he tries to prove that חריונים are the belly and entrails of doves as follows: "The Hebrew חור first "means white; 2. a hole, from the brightness of the light that is usually seen through it; 3. "τρώγλην [trōglēn], a cavity, which is a kind of hole; 4. the belly, in Greek κοιλίαν [koilian], "which is the chief cavity of the human body; whence alvus [belly] is named as if alveus [hollow], and κοιλία [koilia] "from κοῖλον [koilon]; 5. the excrement enclosed in the belly, by a metonymy of the content "for the container. Since we may choose the most "suitable of these meanings of the word, why should we not take it here to mean the belly and entrails of doves, which, "though usually thrown away, in a time of most severe famine were not only kept, "but were even sold off and disposed of at a high price." This is the opinion of Fuller, in which (if I may say so with the leave of a most careful writer) I seem to have found a good many things that have not even the appearance of truth. Thus, that the entrails of doves should be called דביונים in Hebrew never occurred to anyone even in a dream. Rather, all explain it as dung, so called from flowing, just as in Greek ῥεῦμα γαστρὸς [rheuma gastros] and διάῤῥοια [diarrhoia], and in Latin alvi profluvium [flux of the belly], are said of such a flux. And in Celsus febres fluentes [flowing fevers], in Greek ῥοώδεις πυρετοὶ [rhoōdeis pyretoi], are those that loosen the bowels. Again, in what the same Fuller asserts, that the word חור means 1. white, 2. a hole, 3. a cavity, 4. the belly, crop, entrails, 5. dung, most of it is invented. חור for white is not so much Hebrew as Chaldee and Arabic. But for a hole or a cavity it is Hebrew, and from a different root. For the former is from חור chavar, to grow white; the latter from the geminate חרר charar, to perforate. Accordingly in the Talmud, tractate Succa, fol. 20b, you may read חור שחררוהו מים, a hole which the waters have bored. And for the same Talmudists חריר is the eye of a needle, as ܚܪܘܪܐ [חרורא] is for the Syrians in Matt 19:24. Further, that this חור also means belly, or crop, or entrails col. 43 is a pure invention, for which no authority is cited, nor indeed can be, since no one has ever used it so. Finally, חר, or rather חרי or חרא, for dung is an entirely different word, whose root is neither חור nor חרר, but חרה or חרא. Hence the Talmudists consistently write חרי or חריא. And in Arabic خري [khriy] charia, with hamza at the end, is to void excrement, خرء [khurʾ] is dung, مخرأة [makhraʾa] a latrine. Indeed the Hebrews too, when they write plene, insert an Aleph, as in Isa 36:12. לאכול את חראיהם, to eat their own dung. And 2 Reg. X, 27. They destroyed the house of Baal and made it למחראות, into latrines. Nor is the Aleph there adventitious, as they think, but radical, and to be supplied where it is missing, as is clear from Arabic usage. With these observations made, it is evident that the distinguished Fuller did not know the etymology of the word or its true spelling, and indiscriminately took three words of different origin, which led him astray. For since everything he adduces rests solely II, 579 on the etymologies of words, if these etymologies are false, whatever is built upon them must also be false. And indeed it is most frivolous, what he attributes to the sacred author, that a cab of the bellies and entrails of doves sold at Samaria for five shekels. For it has never been heard tell that the crop and entrails of doves were sold separately. I admit that I have read this of hens, and that in Arabic تبودك [tbwdk] thabudach is said of one who sells the entrails of a hen, namely the heart, crop, etc. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] explains it as من يبيع ما في بطون الدجاج من القلب والقانصة [man yabīʿu mā fī buṭūn al-dajāj min al-qalb wa-l-qāniṣa]. But of those of doves nothing of the kind occurs anywhere, so far as I know. Nor is it fitting that the intestines of doves should have been measured by cabs. For the cab is a measure not of entrails but of grain, like the seah, the ephah and the cor. Namely, six cabs make a seah, three seahs an ephah, ten ephahs a cor, the largest dry measure. Accordingly in the Talmud and in the Aruch you may read everywhere קב חטין, a cab of wheat. And it is defined by Elias as מדת היובש, a measure of dry things; by Pomarius as מדת של חטים, a measure of grain; by Aquinas as מדת למדות דבר היבש, a measure for measuring a dry thing. So in Pollux: Κάβασον δὲ ἐκάλουν τὸν περὶ τὴν τροφὴν ἄπληστον, etc. Κάβος γὰρ σίτου μέτρον. [Kabason de ekaloun ton peri tēn trophēn aplēston, etc. Kabos gar sitou metron.] And they called a man insatiable for food a cabasus, etc. For the cab is a measure of grain. And in Hesychius: Κάβαισος· ἄπληστος· κάβος γὰρ μέτρον σιτικόν· [Kabaisos; aplēstos; kabos gar metron sitikon;] Cabasus, insatiable; for the cab is a measure of grain. From this correct Suidas, who has κάβαιστος [kabaistos] for κάβαισος [kabaisos]; and the Etymologicon, which has μετασιτικὸν [metasitikon], a word of no meaning, for μέτρον σιτικὸν [metron sitikon]. But in Hesychius what follows a little below is corrupt: Κάβος· μέτρον σιτικὸν, καὶ οἰνικὸν [Kabos; metron sitikon, kai oinikon], Cab, a measure of grain and of wine. For that the cab is a measure of wine, or of liquids, you will read nowhere else. So I emend thus: Κάβος· μέτρον σιτικὸν, καὶ κάδος οἰνικόν· [Kabos; metron sitikon, kai kados oinikon;] The cab is a measure of grain, and the cadus of wine. He compares two words close to each other in sound as well as in meaning. For both mean a measure, but the latter of wine, the former of grain. Indeed, that the cab is a measure of grain, as the cadus is of wine, there is no one who does not know. Thus Herodotus, book 3, chapter 20, says Φοινικηΐου οἴνου κάδον [Phoinikēiou oinou kadon], a cadus of palm wine. And in book 11 of Athenaeus, Anacreon:


Οἴνου δ᾽ ἐξέπιον κάδον,

Οἴνου δ᾽ ἐξέπιον κάδον, [Oinou d' exepion kadon,]


Vini cadum exhausi. Et ibidem Hedylus in Epigrammate,

I drained a cadus of wine. And in the same place Hedylus in an Epigram,


Ἀλλὰ κάδοις Χίου με κατάβρεχε,

Ἀλλὰ κάδοις Χίου με κατάβρεχε, [Alla kadois Chiou me katabreche,]


Ubi interpres ridicule, At cadis vinum effundens irriga, pro At Chii vini cadis col. 44 me irriga: ut Tibulli lib. 2. Elegia 1.

Here the translator ridiculously has But water by pouring wine from casks, instead of But drench me with casks of Chian wine col. 44: as in Tibullus, book 2, Elegy 1:


— — — Chio solvite vinc'la cado.

— — — loosen the bonds of the Chian cask.


Et Horatii lib. 3. Oda 19.

And Horace, book 3, Ode 19:


II, 580 Quo Chium pretio cadum.
Mercemur? — — —

Et ut cabus, ita cadus Hebraeae est originis. Nempe ut קב kab est cabus, ita כד cad, cadus. Quamvis Hebraeum כד pateat latius. Nam a Mose, Solomone et Elia sumitur pro hydria. Vide Gen. XXIV, 14. Eccles. XII, 8. et 1 Reg. XVIII, 34.

And like cabus, so cadus is of Hebrew origin. Just as קב kab is cabus, so כד cad is cadus, although the Hebrew כד has a wider range. For Moses, Solomon and Elijah use it for a water jar. See Gen. XXIV, 14. Eccles. XII, 8. and 1 Reg. XVIII, 34.


Aliorum sententiis ita expensis, jam superest, ut nostram quoque proferamus. Quae ut stabiliatur, primo hoc ponendum ut certissimum, per columbinum stercus cibi genus significari. Alioqui nulla esset in hac oratione series, Fames erat magna Samariae: nam caput asini venibat octoginta argenteis, et quar- ta pars cabi stercoris columbini quinque argenteis. Porro, cum probatum sit, columbarum stercus, ut vulgo accipiuntur hae voces, nullo modo esse in cibis, iis aliud significari necesse est. Qua de re cum Arabes consuluissem, reperi, duo quaedam esse hoc epitheto apud illos insigniri solita. Quorum unum illud est, quod alio nomine vocatur كوز كندم kuz kendem, vel جوز جندم giauz gendem, id est, nucem a loco sic dicto. Nux enim Persice كوز kuz, et Arabice جوز giauz dicitur. Et Kendem, vel Gendem eadem vox. Nam Caph Persicum ibi sonat G propter tria puncta superposita. Porro de hac nuce sic Avicenna lib. 2. Can. كوز كندم الماهية هو خفيف كالاشنة طيني وبالرقة يسمونه حرا الحمام وببغداد يسمي جوز جندم الاختيار اجوده المربري والذفني ضغيف Kuzkendem, quid est? Res est levis, ut muscus arboreus, lutea. Quam in urbe Racca (ad Euphratem infra Samosatam in Mesopotamia) vocant ster- cus columbarum. Et Bagdadi giauz Gendem. Electio. Optima est Barbarica, sed Daphnensis est debilis. Reliqua ibi vide. Idem alibi, جوز جندم الطبع قال بولس له قوة مبردة مطفية مجففة قليلا Giauz, seu nux Gendem. Natura ejus. Dixit Paulus, virtutem ha- bere refrigerandi, extinguendi et exsiccandi parumper. Sed ibi omissa est definitio, quae in Latina versione sic habet: Nux Kendem quid est? Est terra granosa sicut cicer, alba, declinans, ad citrinitatem, quae exportatur de Barca et de Co- rascena, ex qua cum melle fit vinum. Quae definitio si vera est, nihil nos juvat. Est enim terrae species, quarum nulla est esculenta.

Having thus weighed the opinions of others, it now remains for us to put forward our own as well. To establish it, we must first lay down as most certain that by dove's dung some kind of food is meant. Otherwise there would be no coherence in this sentence: There was a great famine in Samaria: for an ass's head was sold for eighty pieces of silver, and the fourth part of a cab of dove's dung for five pieces of silver. Further, since it has been proved that dove's dung, as these words are commonly understood, is in no way a food, something else must necessarily be meant by them. When I consulted the Arabs on this matter, I found that two things are customarily marked with this epithet among them. One of them is what is called by another name كوز كندم [kūz kandum] kuz kendem, or جوز جندم [jawz jandum] giauz gendem, that is, a nut named after a place. For a nut is called كوز [kūz] kuz in Persian and جوز [jawz] giauz in Arabic. And Kendem or Gendem is the same word, for the Persian Caph there sounds as G because of the three dots placed over it. Of this nut Avicenna, book 2 of the Canon, says: كوز كندم الماهية هو خفيف كالاشنة طيني وبالرقة يسمونه حرا الحمام وببغداد يسمي جوز جندم الاختيار اجوده المربري والذفني ضغيف [kūz kandum al-māhiyya huwa khafīf ka-l-ushna ṭīnī wa-bi-l-Raqqa yusammūnahu ḥurā al-ḥamām wa-bi-Baghdād yusammā jawz jandum al-ikhtiyār ajwaduhu al-mrbrī wa-l-dhfnī ḍghīf] Kuzkendem, what is it? It is a light thing, like tree moss, clay-like. In the city of Raqqa (on the Euphrates below Samosata in Mesopotamia) they call it dove's dung. And in Baghdad giauz Gendem. Selection: the best is the Barbaric, but the Daphnensian is weak. See the rest there. The same author elsewhere: جوز جندم الطبع قال بولس له قوة مبردة مطفية مجففة قليلا [jawz jandum al-ṭabʿ qāla Būlus lahu quwwa mubarrida muṭfiya mujaffifa qalīlan] Giauz, or the nut Gendem. Its nature. Paul said that it has the power of cooling, quenching and drying somewhat. But the definition is omitted there; in the Latin version it reads thus: What is the nut Kendem? It is a granular earth like a chickpea, white, inclining to yellow, which is exported from Barca and from Corascena, from which wine is made with honey. If this definition is true, it does not help us at all. For it is a kind of earth, and no kind of earth is edible.


Sed et aliud est genus columbini stercoris apud Arabes, ab hoc plane diversum. Nempe id ipsum, quod vulgo vocatur usnen. Id enim alio nomine appellari constat stercus passerum, aut columbarum.
