But there is also another kind of dove's dung among the Arabs, entirely different from this one: namely the very thing commonly called usnen. For it is established that this is called by another name sparrows' dung, or doves' dung. Avicenna, book 2: اشنان [ushnān] II, 581 الماهية هي انواع الطغها الابيض ويسمي خرو العصافير [al-māhiyya hiya anwāʿ al-ṭghhā al-abyaḍ wa-yusammā khurūʾ al-ʿaṣāfīr] What is usnen? It has several species, of which the finest is white, and it is called sparrows' dung. Sylvaticus: Sparrows' dung, usnen. Giggeius [=Antonio Giggei, Thesaurus linguae Arabicae (Milan 1632)]: col. 45 الاشنان [al-ushnān] Alusnen, a cleansing powder, which is called dove's dung. The same elsewhere: الحرض [al-ḥuruḍ] Alhord, usnen, or dove's dung. Likewise: خرو العصافير [khurūʾ al-ʿaṣāfīr] dove's dung, a certain cleansing powder. Likewise: الوشنان [al-wushnān] dove's dung, a kind of medicinal powder. But even so the matter is not settled, since it is not well enough known what usnen properly is. Most hold that it is the same as القلي [al-qilī] alkali, from which a very well-known salt is named. The Pandectarius: The salt alkali is made in this way: Take of the herb otherwise called usnen, etc. The same: Antifilos (read anthyllion) or antili (read anthyllis) in Greek, in Arabic usnen, in Latin salsola, is a herb from which alkali is made. And elsewhere: Usnen, etc. is a herb whose leaves are like those of stonecrop or of the lentil, having a salty taste, from which salt is made. Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)] against Cardano, Exercitation 104, Section 18: The Arabs call Chali (better kali) the plant which we call Soda. It is a shrub in the province of Narbonne. By grinding and pressing it they produce what they call salicornum, others soda, others alumen catini, from the shape of the basin into which the juice drips, etc. In Serapion [=Serapion, Liber de simplicibus medicinis (the Arabic-Latin pharmacopoeia)] it is called usnen. Giggeius: القلي [al-qilī] alkali, etc. or usnen. Golius [=Jacobus Golius, Lexicon Arabico-Latinum (1653)]: اشنان [ushnān] Usnen, the herb alkali, and the ashes made from it, the best and in great quantity in الحوران [al-Ḥawrān] Auranitis, a region of Syria. Likewise: بلس [bils] bils, the same as اشنان [ushnān] usnen. Ashes of alkali. And that Alcanzius, or Alchindus, a most celebrated Arab physician and almost a contemporary of Avicenna, held this opinion, you may gather from the fact that in the chapter On usnen he describes, almost word for word, everything that Avicenna had said about kali, as though usnen and kali did not differ at all. This is partly true, partly false. قلي [qilī] kali, for the Arabs as for the Hebrews, means roasted or fried. So usnen, roasted so that from its ash a kind of lye or soap is made, is rightly called kali. And by this name it is also known to the Hebrews, who write קליא kalia, in the Talmudic tractate Erubim, ch. 3, fol. 28b. In Pomarius קליא is defined as עשב שנשרף ומשימין אפרו בבורית, A kind of herb whose ash, when it is burnt, is put into soap. And in the Aruch: עשב שורפין ונותנין אותו בבורית ורוחצין ידיהם, A herb which they burn and put into soap, in order to wash their hands with it. The Arabs say the very same of their اشنان [ushnān] usnen, or قلي [qilī] R2. Thus the verb تاشن [taʾashshana], formed from the noun اشنان [ushnān] usnen, is rendered by the distinguished Golius: He cleansed his hands with ashes of alkali, or with their lye. II, 582 And Alcamus: غسل يده فيه [ghasala yadahu fīhi] He washed his hand in it, because it is useful للجرب والحكك [li-l-jarab wa-l-ḥakak] for scabies and itching, as is stated in the same place. But as for the view of Sylvaticus, Scaliger, Salmasius [=Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), Plinianae exercitationes] on Solinus, and other more recent writers, that this usuen or kali is our soda, or solida R3, from which they make glass R4, I would not grant it, except for some single species. For the most learned of the Arabs teach that usnen, or kali, is a species in the genus of the chickpea R5, which has nothing in common with our soda or solida. Abuchanipha: اجناس الاشنان كثيرة وكلها من الحمص والاشنان الحرض الذي يغسل به الثياب [ajnās al-ushnān kathīra wa-kulluhā min al-ḥimmaṣ wa-l-ushnān al-ḥuruḍ alladhī yughsalu bihi al-thiyāb] The kinds of usnen are many, col. 46 all of which are from the chickpeas (if the word may be pardoned), and usnen is alhord, with which garments are washed. II, 583 In agreement with this is Serapion, chapter 257: Usnen is a very hot herb, whose species are from amoch (read from amos, من حمص [min ḥimmaṣ] from chickpeas) and usnen is haron (read hord حرض [ḥuruḍ]) and it is that with which cloths are washed. Again elsewhere Abuchanipha: القلي يتخذ من الجمص واجوده ما يتخذ من الحرض وهو قلي الصباغين وساير ذلك الزجاجين [al-qilī yuttakhadhu min al-jmṣ wa-ajwaduhu mā yuttakhadhu min al-ḥuruḍ wa-huwa qilī al-ṣabbāghīn wa-sāʾir dhālika al-zajjājīn] Alkali is taken from the chickpea; but the best is that taken from alhord, which is the kali of the dyers, as the rest is that of the glassmakers. Albacra: الاشنان نبات لا ورق له وله اعضان دقاق شبه العقر وهي رخصة كثيرة الما وتعظم حتي يكون له خشب غليظ يتوقد به وناره حر جدا ورايحته ودخانه كريهة وطعمة الي الملوحة وهو من الحمص [al-ushnān nabāt lā waraq lahu wa-lahu aʿḍān diqāq shibh al-ʿqr wa-hiya rakhṣa kathīrat al-māʾ wa-taʿẓumu ḥattā yakūna lahu khashab ghalīẓ yutawaqqadu bihi wa-nāruhu ḥarr jiddan wa-rāʾiḥatuhu wa-dukhānuhu karīha wa-ṭaʿmuhu ilā al-mulūḥa wa-huwa min al-ḥimmaṣ] Usnen is a plant without leaves, having slender branches like a root, tender, full of moisture, which grow until there is dense wood in them, with which fire is kindled, which is very hot. Its smell and smoke are abominable, its taste salty. And it is in the genus of chickpeas. Alcamus: القلي شي يتخذ من حريق الحمص [al-qilī shayʾ yuttakhadhu min ḥarīq al-ḥimmaṣ] Alkali, a thing obtained from the burning of chickpeas. Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār], from Abuchanipha, in the chapter قاقلي [qāqulī] kakeli,: هو من الحمص والناس ياكولونه مع اللبن وهو مثل الاشنان الا ان القلام اعظم منه وورقه شبيه بورق الحرف [huwa min al-ḥimmaṣ wa-l-nās yaʾkulūnahu maʿa al-laban wa-huwa mithl al-ushnān illā anna al-qlām aʿẓam minhu wa-waraquhu shabīh bi-waraq al-ḥurf] It is a species of chickpea, which is eaten with milk, and it is like usnen, except that it has a larger stalk, and a leaf like the leaf of cress. Giggeius: الغولان [al-ghawlān] Algaulano, a kind of chickpea similar to alusnen R6. What of the fact that in 2 Sam 17:28 the Hebrew קלי kali is rendered by Jerome fried chickpea? This will seem novel to those who know that the Hebrew kali does not mean chickpea but roasted grain, Lev 23:14. Ruth 2:14 1 Sam 17:17 and XXV, 18. etc. Yet Jerome's version is doubtless correct. For there the Ammonites and Gileadites are said to have brought to David, a fugitive in the desert, wheat, and barley, and flour, וקלי, and kali, and beans, and lentils, וקלי, and kali. So in the same verse the noun kali is repeated twice. The first, joined to wheat, barley and flour, means roasted grain. But the second, which follows beans and lentils, denotes some roasted or fried legume, namely fried chickpea. For the chickpea was customarily fried or roasted. Thus in Aristophanes' play Peace, a countryman is described


᾿Ανθρακίζων τὲρεβίνθου col. 47 II, 584 cicer super carbones torrens. Et in Ἐκκλησιαζουσῶν pagina secunda Scholiastes, Ὑποπίνοντες ἔκοπτον φρυκτοὺς ἐρεβίνθους, Largius poti frictum cicer tundebant. Sed et fricti ciceris non semel meminere Romani scriptores. Plautus in Bacchidibus Actus quarti Scena quinta,

᾿Ανθρακίζων τὲρεβίνθου [anthrakizōn tērebinthou] col. 47 II, 584 roasting chickpeas over the coals. And on the second page of the Ecclesiazusae the Scholiast has: Ὑποπίνοντες ἔκοπτον φρυκτοὺς ἐρεβίνθους [hypopinontes ekopton phryktous erebinthous], when they had drunk rather freely, they pounded roasted chickpeas. The Roman writers, too, mention roasted chickpeas more than once. Plautus in the Bacchides, Act 4, Scene 5:


Tam frictum ego illum reddam, quam frictum est cicer.

I will make him as roasted as a roasted chickpea.


Horatius in Arte,

Horace in the Art of Poetry:


Nec si quid fricti ciceris probat, aut nucis emptor.

Nor if the buyer of roasted chickpeas or of nuts approves of something.


Cassianus Collat. 8. cap. 1. Superintulit canistrum, habens cicer frictum, quod illi trogalia vocant. Τρωγάλια, id est, bellaria. Et frictum cicer Arabes hodieque قلي kali vocant, ut jam modo docuimus (7). Proinde Hebraei omnes in Samuelis loco, quem diximus, duo genera τοῦ kali agnoscunt: quorum ut prius ex frugibus, ita posterius מקטניות, ex leguminibus, vel ממיני קטניות, ex leguminum speciebus. Ita Kimchius, et R. Levi, et R. Esaias in eum locum. Et R. Selomo kali posterius ita describit: וקלי ממינים של קטניות מיבישין אותו בתנור כשהן לחין והם מתוקין לעולם וטוחנין אותן ועושין מהם מאכל שקורין שתית, Kali sunt leguminum species, quae adhuc recentia in furno exsiccantur, et semper manent dulcia, et commoluntur, et fit ex iis cibus, quem vocant sethith. Quod sumptum est ex Talmudico tractatu De idololatria cap. 2. fol. 38. a. ubi Barzillai Galaadites Davidi misisse legitur תרי מיני שתיתאה, duas species sethithae, id est, duas species kali: et ibi Glossa, שתיתא תבשיל העשוי מקמח של קליות שייבשין בתנור ויש שעושין אותו מקמח עדשין ולפי שהן מתוקין יותר מדאי נותנים שם חומץ, Sethita est pulmentum, factum ex farina τοῦ kali, in furno exsiccata. Sunt etiam, qui faciunt ex farina lentium, quibus, quia sunt praedulces (id est, fatuae) acetum infunditur. Et verum est, quod שתיתא sethitha fieri dicitur ex lentibus. Nam in tractatu Gittin capitis septimi folio septuagesimo a. in ipso Talmudis textu memoratur שתיתא דטלפחי, sethitha ex lentibus. Sed quod de aceto additur, puto esse σφάλμα Glossatoris, qui alicubi le-gerat, hoc pulmentum fieri ex lente, וחמצא, et cicere. Et pro cicere acetum intellexit, quia Chaldaice חמצא chimtza, cicer, et חמצא chumtsa, acetum, iisdem scribuntur literis. Utut sit usnen, seu kali, cicer esse, vel ciceris speciem, abunde probavimus. Et cur vocetur קלי kali, docuimus, nempe quia torretur, aut frigitur. At اشنان usnen, vel وشنان vvsnen potius, ut multi scribunt, II, 585 fit a verbo وشن, quod de terra, camelo, etc. tumere significat, et eminere. Unde cicer merito usnen appellatum, propter inaequales angulos, quibus tumet atque eminet. Neque enim pisi instar rotundum est, sed angulosum et turbinatum (8). At quorsum stercus passerum aut columbarum appelletur, plane me latet. Tantum scio, sic appellari. Neque dubium, quin nux Kendem, vel Gendem, ob id ipsum vocetur stercus columbarum, quod granis, seu calculis suis ciceris formam imitetur. Est enim terra granosa, sicut cicer, ut habet Avicennae vetus interpres, ubi supra.

Cassian, Collat. 8, ch. 1: He brought in a basket containing roasted chickpeas, which they call trogalia. Τρωγάλια [trōgalia], that is, sweetmeats. And the Arabs still today call roasted chickpeas قلي [qly] kali, as we have just shown R7. Accordingly all the Hebrews, on the passage of Samuel we mentioned, recognize two kinds of kali: the first from grain, the second מקטניות, from legumes, or ממיני קטניות, from kinds of legumes. So Kimchi, R. Levi and R. Esaias on that passage. And R. Selomo describes the second kali thus: וקלי ממינים של קטניות מיבישין אותו בתנור כשהן לחין והם מתוקין לעולם וטוחנין אותן ועושין מהם מאכל שקורין שתית, Kali are kinds of legumes which are dried in the oven while still fresh; they always remain sweet, they are ground, and from them is made a food which they call sethith. This is taken from the Talmudic tractate On Idolatry, ch. 2, fol. 38a, where we read that Barzillai the Gileadite sent David תרי מיני שתיתאה, two kinds of sethitha, that is, two kinds of kali. And there the Gloss says: שתיתא תבשיל העשוי מקמח של קליות שייבשין בתנור ויש שעושין אותו מקמח עדשין ולפי שהן מתוקין יותר מדאי נותנים שם חומץ, Sethita is a pottage made from the flour of kali dried in the oven. There are also some who make it from lentil flour, into which, because they are very sweet (that is, insipid), vinegar is poured. And it is true that שתיתא sethitha is said to be made from lentils. For in the tractate Gittin, ch. 7, fol. 70a, in the very text of the Talmud, שתיתא דטלפחי is mentioned, sethitha from lentils. But what is added about vinegar I think is a σφάλμα [sphalma] of the Glossator, who had read somewhere that this pottage is made from lentils וחמצא, and chickpeas, and understood vinegar instead of chickpeas, because in Chaldee חמצא chimtza, chickpea, and חמצא chumtsa, vinegar, are written with the same letters. However that may be, we have amply proved that usnen, or kali, is the chickpea or a kind of chickpea. And we have shown why it is called קלי kali: namely because it is roasted or fried. But اشنان [ushnān] usnen, or rather وشنان [wshnān] vvsnen, as many write it, II, 585 comes from the verb وشن [wshn], which, of earth, a camel, etc., means to swell and to stand out. Hence the chickpea is rightly called usnen, because of the uneven angles with which it swells and stands out. For it is not round like a pea, but angular and top-shaped R8. But why it should be called sparrows' dung or dove's dung is entirely hidden from me. I only know that it is so called. And there is no doubt that the nut Kendem or Gendem is called dove's dung for this very reason, that with its grains or little stones it imitates the form of the chickpea. For it is a granular earth, like chickpeas, as the old translator of Avicenna has it, in the place cited above.


Cum igitur in Sacro textu legimus, in fame Samaritica quartam partem cabi columbini stercoris venisse quinque argenteis, quidni cicer, vel ciceris speciem intelligamus? Certe sic omnia belle quadrabunt. 1. Primo enim in Iudaea cicer fuisse notissimum, praeter aliquot loca Talmudis, docet Sacra Historia loco supra citato ex 2 Sam. XVII, 28. ubi Galaaditae et Ammonitae Davidi inter caetera קלי kali, id est, frictum cicer afferunt. Proinde חמצה, id est, Emesa, col. 48 urbs illustris in confinio Iudaeae, quaeque habuit reges suos, a cicere videtur dicta. Bellonius Singularium libri secundi capite quinquagesimo tertio observat, in Aegypti urbe Cairo multas esse officinas, in quibus nihil venditur praeter frictum cicer, quod magna copia comparatur a peregrinis, qui quotannis inde Meccham proficiscuntur. Et capite nonagesimo nono, idem de Damasco refert. Damasci, inquit, plures sunt officinae, in quibus frigendo ciceri omnes vacant. Erevithia vocant (ἐρεβίνθια) Graeco nomine. Illa autem in aereis sartaginibus fricta et exsiccata, iis percommoda sunt, qui longum iter suscipiunt. 2. Praeterea cabus tam leguminum, quam frugum est mensura. Nempe legumina aeque ac fruges grana sua habent, quae designant Arabes communi nomine حبوب. 3. Per stercus columbarum vile aliquod cibi genus significari, patet in his verbis Sacri textus, Caput asini venibat octoginta siclis, et quarta pars cabi stercoris columbarum quinque siclis. Ibi enim cum asini capite confertur stercus columbarum: et illud quidem octoginta siclis, hujus cabi quarta pars quinque siclis venalis erat. Cabo igitur integro, quae cibi diurni mensura est, pretium erant viginti sicli, et cabis quatuor octoginta sicli. Quo pretio tunc venibat caput asini. Itaque quidquid ibi intelligas per columbinum stercus, vilissimum fuisse cibum plane necesse est, cum ejus cabi quatuor, id est, quantum homini sobrio ad quatriduanum victum sufficiat, non pluris aestimati fuerint, quam unius asini caput. Porro inter cibos, usu receptos, vix quidquam est cicere vilius. Proinde nonnisi II, 586 frugalium aut tenuiorum cibus est cicer. Ita in Aristophanis Pace, ut jam supra notatum, rusticus quidam optat esse cum sodalibus,

So when we read in the Sacred text that in the famine of Samaria a quarter of a cab of dove's dung sold for five pieces of silver, why should we not understand the chickpea, or a kind of chickpea? Certainly everything will then fit nicely. 1. First, that the chickpea was very well known in Judaea is shown, besides several places of the Talmud, by the Sacred History in the passage cited above from 2 Sam 17:28, where the Gileadites and Ammonites bring David, among other things, קלי kali, that is, roasted chickpea. Accordingly חמצה, that is, Emesa, col. 48 a famous city on the border of Judaea, which had its own kings, seems to have been named from the chickpea. Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)], in book 2, chapter 53 of his Singularia, observes that in the Egyptian city of Cairo there are many shops in which nothing is sold but roasted chickpea, which is bought in great quantity by the pilgrims who set out from there every year for Mecca. And in chapter 99 he reports the same of Damascus: In Damascus, he says, there are many shops in which all are occupied with roasting chickpeas. They call them Erevithia (ἐρεβίνθια [erebinthia]) by a Greek name. Roasted and dried in bronze pans, they are very convenient for those who undertake a long journey. 2. Further, the cab is a measure of legumes as well as of grain. For legumes, just like grain, have their seeds, which the Arabs designate by the common name حبوب [ḥubūb]. 3. That some cheap kind of food is signified by dove's dung is clear from these words of the Sacred text: An ass's head was sold for eighty shekels, and a quarter of a cab of dove's dung for five shekels. For there dove's dung is compared with the ass's head: the latter was for sale at eighty shekels, a quarter of a cab of the former at five shekels. So a whole cab, which is the measure of a day's food, cost twenty shekels, and four cabs eighty shekels, the price at which an ass's head was then sold. Therefore, whatever you understand there by dove's dung, it must plainly have been a very cheap food, since four cabs of it, that is, as much as suffices a sober man for four days' sustenance, were valued no higher than one ass's head. Now among foods in common use hardly anything is cheaper than the chickpea. Accordingly the chickpea is the food only of II, 586 the frugal or the poorer sort. Thus in Aristophanes' Peace, as noted above, a certain countryman wishes to be with his companions,


Ἀνθρακίζων τοὐρεβίνθου,
Τήν τε φηγὸν ἐμπυρεύων·

Ἀνθρακίζων τοὐρεβίνθου, Τήν τε φηγὸν ἐμπυρεύων· [Anthrakizōn tourebinthou, Tēn te phēgon empyreuōn]


Cicer super carbones torrens, et faginam glandem ad ignem assans. In Alexi Comico apud Athenaeum libro secundo vetula quaedam, inopiam suam deflens, inter plebejos cibos, quibus miseram vitam aegre sustinet, ἐρέβινθον et λάθυρον recenset, id est, cicer et cicerculam. Horatius libri primi Satyra sexta, ut se parvo contentum esse doceat, et victum tenuem sibi sufficere,

Toasting the chickpea over the coals, and roasting the beech-nut at the fire. In Alexis the Comic poet, in Athenaeus book 2, an old woman lamenting her poverty lists, among the common foods by which she barely sustains her wretched life, ἐρέβινθον [erebinthon] and λάθυρον [lathyron], that is, chickpea and chickling. Horace, book 1, Satire 6, to show that he is content with little and that a meagre diet suffices him:


— — — inde domum me
Ad porri et ciceris refero lachanique catinum.

— — — thence I take myself home
to a dish of leeks and chickpeas and fritters.


Et in De Arte iis, qui ex fricto cicere et nucibus victitant, divites sic opponit,

And in the De Arte he thus contrasts the rich with those who live on roasted chickpeas and nuts:


Offenduntur enim, quibus est equus, et pater, et res,
Nec si quid fricti ciceris probat, aut nucis emptor,
Aequis accipiunt animis, donantve corona.

For those who have a horse, a father and property take offence,
nor, if the buyer of roasted chickpeas and nuts approves something,
do they receive it with fair minds or bestow a crown.


Unde illud Martialis lib. 5. Epigramm. 79.

Hence that line of Martial, book 5, Epigram 79:


Et fervens cicer, et tepens lupinus,
Parva est coenula, quis potest negare?

Both hot chickpea and warm lupin,
it is a small little dinner, who can deny it?


Et lib. 1. Epigramm. 104. ubi de avaro Scaevola, qui genium suum defraudabat:

And book 1, Epigram 104, on the miser Scaevola, who cheated his own appetite:


Et Vejentani bibitur fax crassa rubelli:
Asse cicer tepidum constat, et asse Venus.

And the thick dregs of reddish Veientan are drunk:
warm chickpea costs an as, and an as buys Venus.


Et ejusdem libri Epigramm. 42.

And Epigram 42 of the same book:


— — — — — — otiosae
Vendit qui madidum cicer coronae. — —

— — — — — — he who sells soaked chickpea
to the idle crowd. — —


Id est, qui plebeculae feriatae, Circoque, et scenae vacanti vilissimos cibos venditat, in quibus maceratum cicer. Eodem facit, quod Romae in spectaculis qui honores ambibant, plebeculae gratiam captaturi, inter missilia, cum fabis et lupinis cicer spargebant. Quo alludunt haec Horatii lib. 2. Satyra 3.

That is, he who peddles the cheapest foods, among them soaked chickpea, to the common people on holiday, at leisure for the Circus and the stage. To the same effect is the fact that at Rome, at the shows, those canvassing for office, to win the favour of the populace, scattered chickpeas along with beans and lupins among the gifts thrown to the crowd. To this allude these words of Horace, book 2, Satire 3:


In cicere, atque faba, bona tu perdasque lupinis,
Latus ut in Circo spatiere, atque aeneus ut stes.

May you squander your goods on chickpeas, beans and lupins,
so that you may strut broad in the Circus and stand in bronze.


Et haec Persii Satyra 5.

And these words of Persius, Satire 5.


— — — — cicer ingere large Rixanti populo, nostra ut Floralia possint Aprici meminisse senes. — — — II, 587 Sic in Aegypti eremo Scetica, ubi monachi miram frugalitatem profitebantur, col. 49 frictum cicer illis pro cibo fuit. Cassianus, ubi supra, de Sereno Abbate: Superintulit canistrum, habens cicer frictum, quod illi trogalia vocant, ex quibus quina tantum sumpsimus grana. Hinc Tertullianus cicerculam pro re minimi pretii usurpat, cum in Marcionem sic scribit libri primi capite undecimo, Unam saltem cicerculam Deus Marcionis protulisse debuerat, ut novus aliquis Triptolemus praedicaretur. Sed et apud Graecos ἐρεβίνθινος, id est, cicernus, pro vili sumitur. Hesychius, Ἐρεβίνθινος Διόνυσος· οὐδενὸς ἄξιος, παρά τινα παροιμίαν ἐρεβίνθινος ζωμός· Cicernus Bacchus (cicernum vinum) id est, nullius pretii; Proverbio quodam ita vocatur jus cicernum. Suidas item, Ἐρεβίνθινος Διόνυσος· ἐπὶ τῶν μηδενὸς ἀξίων. Cicernus Bacchus, de rebus nullius pretii. Plutarchus in Rom. Quaest. capite 95. Τὸν λάθυρον, καὶ τὸν ἐρέβινθον, cicerculam et cicer observat nonnullis fuisse cibos vetitos et exosos, sed joculari de causa: nempe ὡς παρωνύμους τοῦ Ἐρέβους, καὶ τῆς Λήθης, tanquam ad Erebum et Lethen (Inferorum amnem) alludentes. Nam, ut ad Erebum ἐρέβινθος, ita λάθυρος ad Lethen. Addit, leguminum plurimum fuisse usum πρὸς τὰ περίδειπνα, καὶ τὰς προκλήσεις τῶν νεκρῶν, in inferalibus coenis et ad mortuorum evocationes. Sed ad fabam potius aut lentem id pertinet. De faba enim Plinius lib. 18. cap. 12. Pythagorica sententia (fabacia) damnata, ut alii tradidere, quoniam mortuorum animae sint in ea. Qua de causa parentando utique assumitur. Varro et ob haec Flaminem ea non vesci tradit, quoniam et in flore ejus literae lugubres reperiuntur. Et Festus, Fabam nec tangere, nec nominare, Diali Flamini licet, quod ea putatur ad mortuos pertinere. Nam et Lemuralibus jacitur larvis, et parentalibus adhibetur sacrificiis, et in flore ejus luctus literae apparere videntur. Quale est, quod lentem veteres censent inter τὰ πένθιμα lugubria, καὶ προτίθεν-ται τοῖς νέκυσιν, et mortuis opponunt, ut notant Plutarchus in Crasso, et Appianus in Parthicis. A qua superstitione Iudaeos non fuisse prorsus immunes, testantur haec Hieronymi ad Paulam de Blaesillae obitu, Flentesque hodie Iudaei, et nudatis pedibus in pulvere volutati sacco incubant: ac, ne quid desit superstitioni, ex ritu vanissimo Pharisaeorum, primum cibum lentis accipiunt, videlicet ostendentes, quali edulio primogenita perdiderint. At de cicere solum in Plinio reperi, religionem illud pervigiliis adhibere. Si tamen cum faba et lente cicer etiam, et cicercula ad ferales pertinuit coenas, ut videtur Plutarchus subinnuere, cum, quae afferuntur, parum sint ad rem, veteres crediderim nihil aliud spectasse, quam quod lugubre tempus decent tenues et frugales cibi, ut sunt legumina omnia, quae corpus quidem implent, sed parum alunt. Proinde princeps Eunuchorum Nabuchodonozoris timuit, ne, si Daniel et socii leguminibus vescerentur, vultus eorum tristiores et macilentiores viderentur, quam reliquorum adolescentum, quos habebat rex in comitatu suo. Vide Dan. I, 8. etc. Notandum II, 588 ibi versu 12 et 16. legumina non dici קטניות, ut alibi ab Hebraeis, sed זרעים, vel זרענים. Quae vox generalior est. Nam זרעים, vel זרענים sunt quaevis semina. Proinde Graeca versio, quae Theodotionis est, habet σπέρματα. Et Maimonides sic definit, quid sint זרעונים, semina, in tractatu De heterogeneis libri 1. cap. 8. הזרעונים נחלקין לשלושה חלקים האחד מהם הוא הנקרא תבואה והיא חמשה מינין החטים והכוסמין והשעורין ושבולת שועל והשיפון והשני מהן הוא הנקרא קטנית והן כל זרעים הנאכל לאדם חוץ מן התבואה כגון הפול והאפונים והדוחן והאורז והשומשמין והפרגין והספיר וכיוצא בהן והשלישי מהן הוא הנקרא זרעוני גנה והן שאר זרעונין שאינן ראויין למאכל אדם והפרי col. 50 של אותר הזרע מאכל אדם כגון זרע הבצלין והשומין וזרע החציר והקצח וזרע לפת וכיוצא בהן, Semina dividuntur in tres species. Prima est eorum, quae vocantur proventus (fruges σιτώδη). Eorum sunt quinque species, triticum, spelta, ordeum, spica vulpis (avena, cujus spica caudae vulpis similis est) secale. Secunda eorum, quae legumina vocant, id est, omnia semina, quae ab homine comeduntur, ut fabae, pisa, panicum, oryza, sesamum, papaver, cicercula et similia. Tertia eorum, quae vocantur hortensia semina, quae quidem ipsa non sunt apta ad esum; sed quod ab iis provenit, ab homine comeditur, ut caepe, allia, porri, nigella, rapa et similia. Tamen in Daniele זרעי ὄσπρια legumina explicant Iosephus et Graecus Scholiastes, Tertullianus, Hieronymus, R. Selomo, Saadias Gaon, Aben Ezra, Ioseph, Iachiae filius, etc. Et tam potuere Hebraice זרעים, id est, semina nominari, quam Graece ὄσπρια. Dicuntur enim ὄσπρια, pro σπόρια, ἀπὸ τῆς σπορᾶς, a satu. Itaque Graecum hoc nomen prorsus respondet Hebraico. Sed et Graece vocantur χεδροπὰ quasi χειρόδροπα, ut Latine legumina, quia manu leguntur. Quo respiciens Nicander Theriacῶν versu 752. ait.

— — — — pour out chickpeas generously to the brawling people, so that the old men may remember our sunny Floralia. — — — II, 587 Thus in the Scetic desert of Egypt, where the monks professed a remarkable frugality, col. 49 roasted chickpeas served them as food. Cassian, in the place cited above, on Abbot Serenus: He brought in a basket containing roasted chickpeas, which they call trogalia, of which we took only five grains each. Hence Tertullian uses cicercula [chickling] for a thing of very little value, when he writes thus against Marcion, book 1, chapter 11: The God of Marcion ought to have produced at least one chickling, so that he might be proclaimed a new Triptolemus. Among the Greeks too, ἐρεβίνθινος [erebinthinos], that is, cicernus [of chickpea], is taken for worthless. Hesychius: Ἐρεβίνθινος Διόνυσος· οὐδενὸς ἄξιος, παρά τινα παροιμίαν ἐρεβίνθινος ζωμός [Erebinthinos Dionysos; oudenos axios, para tina paroimian erebinthinos zōmos]; Chickpea Bacchus (chickpea wine), that is, of no value; in a certain proverb chickpea broth is so called. Likewise Suidas: Ἐρεβίνθινος Διόνυσος· ἐπὶ τῶν μηδενὸς ἀξίων [Erebinthinos Dionysos; epi tōn mēdenos axiōn]. Chickpea Bacchus, of things of no value. Plutarch, in the Rom. Quaest., chapter 95, observes that τὸν λάθυρον, καὶ τὸν ἐρέβινθον [ton lathyron, kai ton erebinthon], the chickling and the chickpea, were forbidden and detested foods for some, but for a jocular reason: namely ὡς παρωνύμους τοῦ Ἐρέβους, καὶ τῆς Λήθης [hōs parōnymous tou Erebous, kai tēs Lēthēs], as alluding to Erebus and Lethe (the river of the underworld). For as ἐρέβινθος [erebinthos] alludes to Erebus, so λάθυρος [lathyros] to Lethe. He adds that pulses were very much used πρὸς τὰ περίδειπνα, καὶ τὰς προκλήσεις τῶν νεκρῶν [pros ta perideipna, kai tas prosklēseis tōn nekrōn], at funeral meals and for the summoning of the dead. But this pertains rather to the bean or the lentil. For on the bean Pliny, book 18, ch. 12: The Pythagorean opinion (on the bean) condemned it, as others have reported, because the souls of the dead are in it. For this reason it is certainly used in rites for deceased parents. Varro also reports that for these reasons the Flamen does not eat it, since mournful letters are also found on its flower. And Festus: It is not permitted to the Flamen Dialis either to touch or to name the bean, because it is thought to pertain to the dead. For it is thrown to the ghosts at the Lemuria, and used in sacrifices to deceased parents, and the letters of mourning seem to appear on its flower. Similar is the fact that the ancients counted the lentil among τὰ πένθιμα [ta penthima], mournful things, καὶ προτίθενται τοῖς νέκυσιν [kai protithentai tois nekysin], and set it before the dead, as Plutarch notes in the Crassus and Appian in the Parthica. That the Jews were not entirely free of this superstition is attested by these words of Jerome to Paula on the death of Blaesilla: And to this day the Jews, weeping, with bare feet, rolled in the dust, lie on sackcloth; and, so that nothing may be lacking to superstition, by a most empty rite of the Pharisees they take lentils as their first food, showing, no doubt, for what kind of dish they lost the birthright. But concerning the chickpea I have found only in Pliny that religion uses it at night vigils. If, however, along with the bean and the lentil, the chickpea and the chickling also belonged to funeral meals, as Plutarch seems to hint, then, since the reasons adduced have little to do with the matter, I would believe the ancients had nothing else in view than that a time of mourning befits thin and frugal foods, such as all pulses are, which fill the body but nourish it little. Accordingly the chief of Nebuchadnezzar's eunuchs feared that if Daniel and his companions ate pulses, their faces would look sadder and leaner than those of the other youths whom the king kept in his retinue. See Dan 1:8 etc. It should be noted II, 588 that there, in verses 12 and 16, pulses are not called קטניות, as elsewhere by the Hebrews, but זרעים, or זרענים. This word is more general. For זרעים or זרענים are any seeds whatever. Accordingly the Greek version, which is that of Theodotion, has σπέρματα [spermata]. And Maimonides [=Moses Maimonides (Rambam), Mishneh Torah] defines what זרעונים, seeds, are in the treatise On Mixed Kinds, book 1, ch. 8: הזרעונים נחלקין לשלושה חלקים האחד מהם הוא הנקרא תבואה והיא חמשה מינין החטים והכוסמין והשעורין ושבולת שועל והשיפון והשני מהן הוא הנקרא קטנית והן כל זרעים הנאכל לאדם חוץ מן התבואה כגון הפול והאפונים והדוחן והאורז והשומשמין והפרגין והספיר וכיוצא בהן והשלישי מהן הוא הנקרא זרעוני גנה והן שאר זרעונין שאינן ראויין למאכל אדם והפרי col. 50 של אותר הזרע מאכל אדם כגון זרע הבצלין והשומין וזרע החציר והקצח וזרע לפת וכיוצא בהן, Seeds are divided into three kinds. The first is of those called produce (grain crops, σιτώδη [sitōdē]). Of these there are five kinds: wheat, spelt, barley, fox's ear (oats, whose ear resembles a fox's tail), rye. The second is of those they call pulses, that is, all seeds eaten by man, such as beans, peas, millet, rice, sesame, poppy, chickling and the like. The third is of those called garden seeds, which are themselves not fit for eating, but what grows from them is eaten by man, such as onions, garlic, leeks, nigella, turnips and the like. Yet in Daniel זרעי is explained as ὄσπρια [ospria], pulses, by Josephus and the Greek Scholiast, Tertullian, Jerome, R. Selomo, Saadias Gaon, Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra], Joseph son of Jachia, etc. And they could just as well be called זרעים, that is, seeds, in Hebrew as ὄσπρια [ospria] in Greek. For they are called ὄσπρια [ospria] for σπόρια [sporia], ἀπὸ τῆς σπορᾶς [apo tēs sporas], from sowing. So this Greek name corresponds exactly to the Hebrew. But in Greek they are also called χεδροπὰ [chedropa], as if χειρόδροπα [cheirodropa], just as in Latin legumina [pulses], because they are gathered (leguntur) by hand. Referring to this, Nicander, Theriaca, verse 752, says.


Χειροδροπὰ δ' ἵνα φῶτες ἄνευ δρεπάνοιο λέγονται
Ὄσπρια, χεδροπά τ' ἄλλα, μεσοχλόου ἐντὸς ἀρούρης·

Χειροδροπὰ δ' ἵνα φῶτες ἄνευ δρεπάνοιο λέγονται Ὄσπρια, χεδροπά τ' ἄλλα, μεσοχλόου ἐντὸς ἀρούρης· [Cheirodropa d' hina phōtes aneu drepanoio legontai / Ospria, chedropa t' alla, mesochlou entos arourēs]


Ubi manulegi homines sine falce legumina, atque alia ejus generis, legunt in semivirente terra. His observatis statim patebit, quorsum velit Iosephus, columbinum stercus Samaritanis fuisse loco salis. Theophrastus (De causis plantarum li-bri quarti capite nono) exquirens, quibus de causis cicer aliis leguminibus citius maturescat, inter caetera hanc affert, Ἡ ἅλμη πρὸς τὴν τελείωσιν συμβάλλε-ται, Salsedo ciceris ad promptam illam maturitatem confert. Et libri quinti capite undecimo, Ὁ ἐρέβινθος ἀπόλλυται σφακελίας, ὅταν ἀνθοῦσιν ὕδωρ ἐπιγι-νόμενον ἐπικλύσῃ τὴν ἄλμην· τὸ γὰρ ἔφαλμα οἷον σφακελίζειν ἐστί. Cicer sphacelisco perit, cum in flore salsuginem imber eluit: salsuginis enim jactura ei veluti sphacelismus est. Cato quoque de cicere, Rusticorum capite tr[?]igesimo septimo: Si cariosam in terram jacies cicer, quod vellitur, salsum est et malum. Et Columella libri secundi capite decimo quarto, Tremellius obesse maxime ait II, 589 solo virus ciceris et lini: alterum, quia sit salsae; alterum, quia sit fervidae naturae. Et Plinius libri decimi octavi capite duodecimo, Ciceris natura est gigni cùm salsedine, ideo solum urit. Et libro decimo septimo, Commune omnium satorum vitium urica, etiam ciceris, cum salsilaginem ejus obluendo imber dulcius id facit. Id Galenus libro sexto De simplic. amaritudinem vocat, cum de ciceribus dicit: Μετέχουσι δέ τι καὶ τῆς πικρότητος· Etiam amaritudinis aliquid ha-bent. Et de cicere sylvestri, Δριμύτερός τ᾽ ἐστι, καὶ πικρότερος, Acrius est et amarius. Sed amarum pro salso posuit, ut cum Poeta dicit de mari,

Where men gather by hand, without a sickle, pulses and other things of that kind, in the half-green field. Once these points are noted, it will at once be clear what Josephus means when he says that dove's dung served the Samaritans in place of salt. Theophrastus (De causis plantarum, book 4, chapter 9), inquiring into the reasons why the chickpea ripens sooner than other pulses, gives this one among others: Ἡ ἅλμη πρὸς τὴν τελείωσιν συμβάλλεται [Hē halmē pros tēn teleiōsin symballetai], The saltiness of the chickpea contributes to that quick ripening. And in book 5, chapter 11: Ὁ ἐρέβινθος ἀπόλλυται σφακελίας, ὅταν ἀνθοῦσιν ὕδωρ ἐπιγινόμενον ἐπικλύσῃ τὴν ἄλμην· τὸ γὰρ ἔφαλμα οἷον σφακελίζειν ἐστί [Ho erebinthos apollytai sphakelias, hotan anthousin hydōr epiginomenon epiklysē tēn halmēn; to gar ephalma hoion sphakelizein esti]. The chickpea perishes of blight when rain washes off its saltiness while it is in flower: for the loss of its saltiness is to it a kind of blight. Cato too says of the chickpea, in De re rustica, chapter 37: If you sow chickpea in crumbly soil, since it is pulled up, it is salty and harmful. And Columella, book 2, chapter 14, says that Tremellius [=Immanuel Tremellius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] states that the soil is harmed most II, 589 by the poison of chickpea and flax: the one because it is of a salty nature, the other because it is of a hot nature. And Pliny, book 18, chapter 12: It is the nature of the chickpea to grow with saltiness; therefore it burns the soil. And in book 17: A defect common to all crops is blight, the chickpea's too, when the rain, washing off its saltiness, makes it sweeter. Galen, in book 6 of De simplic., calls this bitterness, when he says of chickpeas: Μετέχουσι δέ τι καὶ τῆς πικρότητος [Metechousi de ti kai tēs pikrotētos]; They also have something of bitterness. And of the wild chickpea: Δριμύτερός τ᾽ ἐστι, καὶ πικρότερος [Drimyteros t' esti, kai pikroteros], It is sharper and more bitter. But he put bitter for salty, as when the Poet says of the sea,


Doris amara suam non intermisceat undam.

let bitter Doris not mingle her wave.


Proinde ex ciceris quodam genere, ut notavimus, Arabes celeberrimum illud sal eliciunt, quod inde vocatur sal alkali, id est, sal adusti ciceris. Ad locum igitur, in quo versamur, cum monuissent Hebraei vetustiores, stercus columbarum id esse, unde elicitur sal: id mala manu acceptum a Iosepho, qui scripsit, columbarum stercus Samariae fuisse ἀντὶ ἁλῶν, pro sale. Ex quo Theodoretus in 4. Reg. Quaest. 21. Ἡ τῆς πολιορκίας ἀνάγκη, καὶ τοῦ λίμου τὸ μέγεθος ἠνάγκασεν αὐτοὺς ἀντὶ ἁλῶν κεχρῆσθαι τῷ κόπρῳ. Necessitas obsidionis et famis magnitudo cogebat eos stercore uti pro sale (9).

Accordingly, as we have noted, the Arabs extract from a certain kind of chickpea that very famous salt which is therefore called sal alkali, that is, salt of burnt chickpea. So, on the passage with which we are dealing, when the older Hebrews had remarked that it was dove's dung, from which salt is extracted, this was misunderstood by Josephus, who wrote that at Samaria dove's dung was used ἀντὶ ἁλῶν [anti halōn], in place of salt. Hence Theodoret on 4 Kings, Question 21: Ἡ τῆς πολιορκίας ἀνάγκη, καὶ τοῦ λίμου τὸ μέγεθος ἠνάγκασεν αὐτοὺς ἀντὶ ἁλῶν κεχρῆσθαι τῷ κόπρῳ [Hē tēs poliorkias anankē, kai tou limou to megethos ēnankasen autous anti halōn kechrēsthai tō koprō]. The necessity of the siege and the severity of the famine compelled them to use dung in place of salt R9.

Celsius [=Olof Celsius, Hierobotanicon (1745-47)] in Hierobot. vol. 2, p. 82, rightly points out that there is no lack of examples of others who, in the want of a long siege, turned to food things that human nature otherwise abhors. "Wretched mortals," he says, "shudder at perishing of hunger so long as anything remains, however foul and abominable, by which they may put off the fatal moment. Hence histories everywhere record that many have yielded to necessity and in sieges have used even the excrement of animals as food and drink." Eusebius, Hist. Eccles. book 3, ch. 6, writes of the final siege of the Jews: "Necessity set everything before their teeth in place of food, and they brought themselves to eat things that would not have been fit even for the most unclean brute beasts. — For some, even the stalks of old hay served as food. Some gathered refuse." In Josephus, Jewish War book 6, last chapter, near the end, we read: προσελθῶν τινὰς εἰς τοσοῦτον ἀνάγκης, ὥστε τὰς ἀμάρας ἐρευνῶντας καὶ παλαιὸν ὄνθον βοῶν, προσφέρεσθαι τὰ ἐκ τούτων σκύβαλα, καὶ τὸ μηδὲ ὄψει φορητὸν πάλαι τότε γενέσθαι τροφήν [proselthōn tinas eis tosouton anankēs, hōste tas amaras ereunōntas kai palaion onthon boōn, prospheresthai ta ek toutōn skybala, kai to mēde opsei phorēton palai tote genesthai trophēn]. In the great famine that raged in Egypt in the year 1200 AD II, 574 1200, اكلوا الميتات والجيف والكلاب والبعر والاروات [akalū al-maytāt wa-al-jiyaf wa-al-kilāb wa-al-baʿr wa-al-arwāt] they fed on the dead, on stinking carcasses, on camel dung and on dung. The annals of the Orientals are full of examples of this kind.

(5) Rosenmüller, II, 582 Quod ipsum aperte est falsum nititurque miro Nostri errore, quo in iis locis, quae statim ex scriptoribus Arabicis adducet, pro حمض i. e. herbae salsugino- sae, legit حمص cicer. Quae observatio debetur OL. CELSIO, qui Hierobot. P. II. pag. 234. de Hebraeorum קלי agens, haec habet: „Bochartus doctissime, ceu solet, laborat, ut ex Kali 2 Sam. XVII, 28. efficiat cicer. Verum sive minus correctis Arabum codicibus, sive aliunde deceptus, حمص cicer, pro حمض apud Arabes, quos laudat, continuo legit, et res confundit diversas. Quod ex Abul Fadli meo planum facio. Is sub tit. اشنان haec dicit: اشنان معروف ويسمي الحرض وهو من الحمض وهو كل نابت فيه ملوحة Usnen notum est, et dicitur Alhord, estque ex الحمض quo nomine herbae appellantur omnes, in quibus est salsedo. Ipsum verbum est apud Golium Lex. Arab. pag. 653. حمض de- pastus fuit camelus amaram et salsam plantam, quae حمض dicitur. Et in IV. Coniug. plantis salsis amarisque abun- davit terra“. Haec Celsius, quae confirmantur re ipsa. Nam cum ii, quos Bochartus in medium profert, scriptores omnes unanimi consensu plantis Usnen et Alkali salsuginosum saporem tribuant, per se patet, esse illas non inter ciceres, حمص, verum inter herbas salsuginosas, حمض, referendas. Neque movet me hoc, quod non in uno tantummodo loco ex unico scriptore, sed in omnibus omnino, quae ex variis auctoribus Noster adfert, constanter حمص hic legitur pro حمض. Nam cum Bochartus in uno horum scriptorum librarii negligentia pro حمض scriptum حمص haud dubie inveniret, cicerem, opinionis suae anteceptae in gratiam, eupide arripuit eumque intrudit ceteris quoque locis, quae ex aliis scriptoribus adducit, dum in iis حمص tacite posuit pro حمض. Certe non satis fideliter hic egisse Bochartum, argumento est, quod not. sequ. observabitur. Itaque in iis, quae sequuntur, semper pro حمص, cicer, reponendum est: حمض plantae salsu- ginosae, excepto ultimo Abenbitari loco de قاقلي,

R5 Rosenmüller, II, 582 This itself is plainly false, and rests on a strange error of our author, by which, in the passages which he will presently adduce from Arabic writers, he reads حمص [ḥimmaṣ] chickpea instead of حمض [ḥamḍ], i.e. saline herbs. This observation is owed to Ol. Celsius, who in Hierobot. vol. II, p. 234, treating the קלי of the Hebrews, says the following: "Bochart labours most learnedly, as is his habit, to make Kali in 2 Sam 17:28 into chickpea. But, deceived either by less correct manuscripts of the Arabs or by something else, he consistently reads حمص [ḥimmaṣ] chickpea instead of حمض [ḥamḍ] in the Arabs whom he cites, and confuses different things. This I make clear from my Abu'l-Fadl. Under the heading اشنان [ushnān] he says this: اشنان معروف ويسمي الحرض وهو من الحمض وهو كل نابت فيه ملوحة [ushnān maʿrūf wa-yusmī al-ḥurḍ wa-huwa min al-ḥamḍ wa-huwa kull nābit fīhi mulūḥa] Usnen is well known, and is called Alhord, and it belongs to الحمض [al-ḥamḍ], the name by which all herbs are called in which there is saltiness. The verb itself is in Golius, Lex. Arab. p. 653: حمض [ḥamaḍa] the camel grazed on the bitter and salty plant which is called حمض [ḥamḍ]. And in the 4th conjugation: the land abounded in salty and bitter plants." Thus Celsius, and his words are confirmed by the matter itself. For since all the writers whom Bochart brings forward unanimously attribute a saline taste to the plants Usnen and Alkali, it is self-evident that these are to be classed not among chickpeas, حمص [ḥimmaṣ], but among saline herbs, حمض [ḥamḍ]. Nor am I moved by the fact that حمص [ḥimmaṣ] is read here instead of حمض [ḥamḍ] not in just one passage of a single writer, but consistently in absolutely all the passages that our author adduces from various authors. For when Bochart found, no doubt through a copyist's carelessness, حمص [ḥimmaṣ] written instead of حمض [ḥamḍ] in one of these writers, he eagerly seized upon the chickpea in favour of his preconceived opinion, and inserted it into the other passages too which he cites from other writers, silently putting حمص [ḥimmaṣ] in them instead of حمض [ḥamḍ]. That Bochart did not act faithfully enough here is certainly shown by what will be observed in the following note. Therefore in what follows, حمص [ḥimmaṣ], chickpea, must always be replaced by حمض [ḥamḍ], saline plants, except for the last passage of Ibn al-Baytar on قاقلي [qāqulī],


(6) Rosenmüller, II, 583 Imo ibi legitur: plantae salsuginosae species, τῷ اشنان similis.

R6 Rosenmüller, II, 583 Rather, what is read there is: a species of saline plant, similar to اشنان [ushnān].


(7) Rosenmüller, II, 584 Id quod vere ita se haberet, si قلي esset e حمص, id est, ciceribus. Nunc, quum e salsuginosarum herbarum (حمض) numero sit, nil commune ha-bere potest cum Hebraeorum קלי, quod recte exponi frumentum tostum, ostendit CELSIUS Hierobot. P. II. p. 231. seqq.

R7 Rosenmüller, II, 584 This would truly be so, if قلي [qilī] belonged to the حمض [ḥimmaṣ]—that is, the chickpeas. (8) Rosenmüller, II, 585 Quae argumentatio, cum hac nitatur opinione, Usnen et Kali esse ciceris (حمص) speciem; ea sublata (iis, quae not. 5. observavimus) plane concidit.

(9) Rosenmüller, II, 589 Vix opus videtur, ut lectorem moneamus, haec omnia in vanum esse disputata, quum ea res, quam Arabes stercus columbarum vocant, non ex ciceris genere sit (quo, tanquam fundamento, omnis nititur Bocharti argumentatio), verum salsuginosae plantae species, ut abunde probavimus not. 5. Minoris momenti sunt, quae in Bocharti sententiam dixit OTHO VERBRUG-GE in Observatt. Philologg. de nominum Hebraeorum plurali numero Groen. 1730. in duoden. pag. 7. 8. Ipse חרייונים exiguos panes significari existimat a Singulari חרייון, quod diminutivum esse vult τοῦ חרי, panis species apud Chaldaeos atque Talmudicos. Quae opinio vix cuiquam probetur, quum panibus nullo modo conveniat, quod de חרייונים dicitur in sacro textu, ea per cabos esse mensurata. Multo ineptius est, quod HILLERUS in medium protulit in Hierophyt. P. II. C. XXII. Sect. III. p. 129. חריינים esse foramina columbina, hoc est, columbarum exta, quae perforata e corpore cibum et incrementa educunt. Quibus omnibus expensis praestat eam vocis vexatissimae interpretationem retinere, quam hujus capitis initio primo loco recensuit Bochartus, verum ibidem repudiavit; sed immerito, ut ostendimus nota prima.

R9 Rosenmüller, II, 589 It hardly seems necessary to warn the reader that all this has been argued in vain, since the thing which the Arabs call dove's dung is not of the chickpea kind (on which, as on a foundation, Bochart's whole argument rests), but a species of saline plant, as we have amply proved in note 5. Of lesser weight is what Otho Verbrugge said in support of Bochart's opinion in Observatt. Philologg. de nominum Hebraeorum plurali numero, Groningen 1730, in duodecimo, p. 7–8. He himself thinks that חרייונים means small loaves, from a singular חרייון, which he takes to be a diminutive of חרי, a kind of bread among the Chaldeans and Talmudists. This opinion will hardly win anyone's approval, since what is said of the חרייונים in the sacred text, that they were measured by kabs, in no way suits loaves. Much more absurd is what Hiller put forward in Hierophyt. vol. II, ch. 22, sect. 3, p. 129: that חריינים are dove's holes, that is, the entrails of doves, which, being perforated, draw nourishment and growth out of the body. All these things weighed, it is best to retain that interpretation of this much-vexed word which Bochart listed in first place at the beginning of this chapter, but rejected there; yet undeservedly, as we have shown in note 1.


Part 2, Book 1, chapter 8: The deror

II, 590 CAP. VIII. col. 51

II, 590 Chapter VIII. col. 51


Avem דרור deror non esse Hirundinem, ut volunt, sed Columbae ferae speciem, puta Turturem, aut Palumbum.

That the bird דרור deror is not the swallow, as is held, but a kind of wild dove, namely the turtledove or the wood pigeon.


Ex avium genere una est, quam Hebraei דרור deror, id est, libertatem, aut libe- ram appellant; מפני שדרה בבית כבשדה, quia tam libere versatur in domo, quam in agro. Ita statuit R. Ismael in tractatu Talmudico Betsa cap. 3. pag. 24. a. Hinc Hebraei recentiores, quique illos sequuti sunt nuperi Lexicographi et Bi- bliorum interpretes, summo consensu statuunt, דרור deror esse hirundinem: quia duae leguntur esse species hirundinum,

Among the birds there is one which the Hebrews call דרור deror, that is, freedom or free; מפני שדרה בבית כבשדה, because it dwells as freely in the house as in the field. So R. Ishmael determined in the Talmudic tractate Betsa, ch. 3, p. 24a. Hence the later Hebrews, and the recent lexicographers and interpreters of the Bible who have followed them, hold with the greatest unanimity that דרור deror is the swallow, because there are said to be two species of swallows,


quarum petit altera sylvas,
Altera tecta subit. — — — — a)

of which one seeks the woods, the other enters under roofs. — — — — a)


Sed haec ratio non sufficit, cum et aliae sint aves partim domesticae, partim agrestes. In his principem locum columbae tenent, quarum unum genus κατοικί-διον, domesticum, alterum νομαδικὸν, vagum, et in agris pascens, ut in Galeno habetur libro decimo De Simplic. Quomodo etiam distinguit Varro Rustic. lib. 3. cap. 7. Ita tamen, ut utrumque genus in tectis habitare dicat; sed agreste in summa parte turrium, unde in agros evolet ac remeet: cum clementius alterum, cibo domestico contentum, intra limina januae soleat pasci. Ego nomine דרור deror et agreste hoc columbae genus, et quascumque columbarum species in feris Graeci recensent, significari puto: sed maxime φάτταν, palumbum, et τρυ-γόνα, turturem. Huc me movet primo veterum interpretum auctoritas, qui דרור, vel turturem, vel palumbum explicant. Sic Ps. LXXXIV, 4. דרור tur- tur exponitur in Graeca versione, et Vulgata, Chaldaea, Syra, et utraque Arabe, et in Apollinaris paraphrasi. Sed Aethiops habet መዐንቅ፡ id est, tor- quatum: quo epitheto palumbum insigniri nemo nescit, propter torquem, quem habet circa collum. Martialis in Xeniis,

But this reason is not sufficient, since there are also other birds that are partly domestic, partly wild. Among these the first place belongs to the doves, of which one kind is κατοικίδιον [katoikidion], domestic, the other νομαδικὸν [nomadikon], roaming, and feeding in the fields, as is found in Galen, book 10 On Simples. Varro also makes this distinction in On Agriculture, book 3, ch. 7, yet in such a way that he says both kinds dwell under roofs: but the wild kind in the highest part of towers, from which it flies out into the fields and returns, whereas the other, tamer kind, content with domestic food, usually feeds within the threshold of the door. For my part, I think that by the name דרור deror are meant both this wild kind of dove and whatever species of doves the Greeks list among the wild ones, but above all φάτταν [phattan], the wood pigeon, and τρυγόνα [trygona], the turtledove. I am moved to this, first, by the authority of the ancient interpreters, who explain דרור as either the turtledove or the wood pigeon. Thus in Ps. LXXXIV, 4 דרור is rendered turtledove in the Greek version, and in the Vulgate, the Chaldee, the Syriac, and both Arabic versions, and in the paraphrase of Apollinaris. But the Ethiopic has መዐንቅ፡ [maʿanəq], that is, the collared one: everyone knows that the wood pigeon is distinguished by this epithet, on account of the collar it has around its neck. Martial in the Xenia:


Inguina torquati tardant hebetantque palumbi.

The collared wood pigeons slow and dull the loins.


Abdorrachman, Abubecri filius, in carmine De repudio Aticae, uxoris olim charissimae,

Abdorrachman, son of Abubecr, in his poem On the Divorce of Atica, once his dearest wife,


ما ناح قمري الحمام المطوق col. 52 II, 591 Quam luget palumbus columba torquata. Alkazuinius, ان بيض القماري يجعل تحت الفواخت وبيض الفواخت يجعل تحت القماري كلاهما ينغقان قماري كافورية مطوقة Sive palumbi ova sub phabe ponantur, aut ova phabis sub palumbo, inde nihil edetur praeter palumbos camphoratos, torquatos. Altera ducitur ex Arabica lingua, qua الحر alhorro est pullus columbae, aut turturis, et ساق حر sako horrin palumbus. Alcamus, الحر فرخ الحمامة Alhorro pullus columbae, Giggejus addit, vel turturis. ساق حر ذكر القماري Sako horrin, mas palumborum. Et alibi, الورشان طاير وهو ساق حر لحمه اخف من الحمام Alvvarsen avis, nempe sako horrin, cujus caro levior est, quam columbae. Ajunt Arabes, a voce sic appellari. Ibnosaida, سمي القماري ساق حر لصوته فانه يقول ساق حر ساق حر Vocatur palumbus sako horrin propter vocem suam, quia dicit Sako horrin, Sako horrin. Sic alia palumbi species قطا kata, vel katta, etiam a voce dici putatur. Damir, سميت بحكاية صوته Nomen habet a similitudine vocis. Nempe, cum ad pullos venit, inquiunt, aquam in ingluvie afferens, صاحت قطا قطا clamat Katta, Katta. Sed merum hoc commentum est. Nam قطا katta, deflexum ex palumbi Graeco nomine φάττα. Graecum φ et π Arabes in Kaph saepe mutant, quia ف Phe et ق Kaph apud illos sunt ejusdem figurae, nec nisi puncto differunt, quod Phe simplex, Kaph duplex habet. Proinde in Avicenna قوقي kauke sunt phocae. In Arabico Dioscoride قوطوما φύτευμα, قوقي keuke, πεύκη· قرقسيون karkesion, καρπήσιον· قوقس البحر kukos albahri, φύκος θαλάσσιον· Neque scribarum id esse mendum, sed auctorum, inde apparet, quod hae voces digestae sunt per ordinem Alphabeticum, et referuntur ad literam Kaph. Ita igitur قطا Kata, vel katta, est φάττα, seu palumbus: neque a voce dicitur, ut sibi fingunt Arabes. Idem judicium de ساق حر sako horrin. Nam ساق sako per se est columbae mas. Et ساق حر sako horrin, mas columbae libertatis, seu liberae, id est, palumbi, vel etiam turturis, ut quidam volunt. Nam ut Hebraeum דרור deror, ita Arabicum حر horro, liberum sonat. Et Radix حر harra, Syris et Chaldaeis חרר harar, liberum esse, et libertate donare. Itaque quoties דרור in Sacro textu pro libertate sumitur, toties col. 53 II, 592 pro eo Chaldaei interpretes habent חירות, et Arabes حرية. Neque vero est obscurum, cur apud Orientales columbae ferae et agrestes a libertate nomen habeant. Cum etiam Basilius Epistola 175. ad Iulittam talium columbarum turmam appellet αὐτόνομον ἀγέλην, liberum gregem, et suis legibus utentem. Graece enim αὐτόνομος idem, quod ἐλεύθερος. Hinc eosdem populos Thucydides libro secundo promiscue vocat αὐτονόμους et ἐλευθέρους. Et apud Plutarchum in Dialogo De Daemonio Socratis, Epaminondas profitetur se civem ἐλευ-θέρας καὶ αὐτονόμου πόλεως. Et Demosthenes in prima Philippica de populis, qui Philippi partium erant, αὐτονομούμενα καὶ ἐλεύθερα (ἔθνη) ὑπῆρχε. Itaque Isocrates servituti opponit αὐτονομίαν, Graecos habuisse dicens sub Evagora ἀντὶ δουλείας αὐτονομίαν. Quocirca Hebraeum דרור deror ex Basilio recte verteris αὐτόνομον περιστεράν.

ما ناح قمري الحمام المطوق [mā nāḥa qumrī al-ḥamām al-muṭawwaq] col. 52 II, 591 How the wood pigeon, the ring-necked dove, laments. Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt]: ان بيض القماري يجعل تحت الفواخت وبيض الفواخت يجعل تحت القماري كلاهما ينغقان قماري كافورية مطوقة [inna bayḍ al-qamārī yujʿal taḥt al-fawākhit wa-bayḍ al-fawākhit yujʿal taḥt al-qamārī kilāhumā yanghaqān qamārī kāfūriyya muṭawwaqa] Whether the eggs of the wood pigeon are placed under the phabe, or the eggs of the phabe under the wood pigeon, nothing will be hatched from them but camphor-coloured, ring-necked wood pigeons. The other derivation is taken from the Arabic language, in which الحر [al-ḥurr] alhorro is the young of a dove or of a turtledove, and ساق حر [sāq ḥurr] sako horrin is the wood pigeon. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: الحر فرخ الحمامة [al-ḥurr farkh al-ḥamāma] Alhorro, the young of a dove; Giggeius [=Antonio Giggei, Thesaurus linguae Arabicae (Milan 1632)] adds, or of a turtledove. ساق حر ذكر القماري [sāq ḥurr dhakar al-qamārī] Sako horrin, the male of the wood pigeons. And elsewhere: الورشان طاير وهو ساق حر لحمه اخف من الحمام [al-warashān ṭāyir wa-huwa sāq ḥurr laḥmuhu akhaff min al-ḥamām] Alvvarsen, a bird, namely sako horrin, whose flesh is lighter than that of the dove. The Arabs say it is so called from its call. Ibn Sida: سمي القماري ساق حر لصوته فانه يقول ساق حر ساق حر [summiya al-qamārī sāq ḥurr li-ṣawtihi fa-innahu yaqūl sāq ḥurr sāq ḥurr] The wood pigeon is called sako horrin on account of its call, because it says Sako horrin, Sako horrin. In the same way another species of wood pigeon, قطا [qaṭā] kata or katta, is also thought to be named from its call. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: سميت بحكاية صوته [summiyat bi-ḥikāyat ṣawtihi] It has its name from the likeness of its call. For, they say, when it comes to its young, bringing water in its crop, صاحت قطا قطا [ṣāḥat qaṭā qaṭā] it cries Katta, Katta. But this is pure invention. For قطا [qaṭā] katta is bent from the Greek name of the wood pigeon, φάττα [phatta]. The Arabs often change Greek φ and π into Kaph, because among them ف Phe and ق Kaph have the same shape and differ only in the dots, Phe having a single one and Kaph a double. Accordingly in Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] قوقي [qūqī] kauke are seals. In the Arabic Dioscorides قوطوما [qūṭūmā] is φύτευμα [phyteuma], قوقي [qūqī] keuke is πεύκη [peukē], قرقسيون [qarqasiyūn] karkesion is καρπήσιον [karpēsion], قوقس البحر [qūqas al-baḥr] kukos albahri is φύκος θαλάσσιον [phykos thalassion]. That this is not a slip of the copyists but of the authors is clear from the fact that these words are arranged in alphabetical order and are listed under the letter Kaph. Thus, then, قطا [qaṭā] Kata or katta is φάττα [phatta], that is, the wood pigeon, and it is not named from its call, as the Arabs imagine. The same judgement applies to ساق حر [sāq ḥurr] sako horrin. For ساق [sāq] sako by itself is the male of the dove. And ساق حر [sāq ḥurr] sako horrin is the male of the dove of liberty, or of the free dove, that is, of the wood pigeon, or also of the turtledove, as some hold. For like the Hebrew דרור deror, so the Arabic حر [ḥurr] horro means free. And the root حر [ḥarra], in Syriac and Chaldee חרר harar, means to be free and to grant freedom. Therefore, whenever דרור is taken in the sacred text for liberty, the Chaldee col. 53 II, 592 translators have חירות in its place, and the Arabic ones حرية [ḥurriyya]. Nor indeed is it obscure why among the Orientals wild and field doves are named from liberty. For Basil too, in Epistle 175 to Julitta, calls a flock of such doves αὐτόνομον ἀγέλην [autonomon agelēn], a free flock, living by its own laws. For in Greek αὐτόνομος [autonomos] is the same as ἐλεύθερος [eleutheros]. Hence Thucydides in book 2 calls the same peoples indiscriminately αὐτονόμους [autonomous] and ἐλευθέρους [eleutherous]. And in Plutarch, in the dialogue On the Daemon of Socrates, Epaminondas declares himself a citizen ἐλευθέρας καὶ αὐτονόμου πόλεως [eleutheras kai autonomou poleōs]. And Demosthenes, in the First Philippic, says of the peoples who were of Philip's party: αὐτονομούμενα καὶ ἐλεύθερα (ἔθνη) ὑπῆρχε [autonomoumena kai eleuthera (ethnē) hypērche]. Accordingly Isocrates opposes αὐτονομίαν [autonomian] to servitude, saying that under Evagoras the Greeks had ἀντὶ δουλείας αὐτονομίαν [anti douleias autonomian]. Therefore, following Basil, you would rightly render the Hebrew דרור deror as αὐτόνομον περιστεράν [autonomon peristeran].


In Scripturae duobus locis, quibus pro ave occurrit דרור deror, nihil est, quod vel minimum huic interpretationi repugnet. Prov. XXVI, 2. דרור commendari videtur a pernicitate volatus, qua vel cum quavis alite decertare posse columbam, suo loco docuimus (1). Et Psal. LXXXIV, 4. ingemiscit Psaltes, sortem suam conferens cum vilissimis avibus, passere puta, et דרור deror, id est, agresti columba, quibus ad altare Dei non modo liber accessus, sed et ibi nidificare, et pullos excludere concessum: dum ipse vagus erat, et extorris, et ab aede sacra remotus. In altaris nomine figuram esse oportet. Neque enim in tanta hominum et sacrificiorum frequentia tuta fuisset avibus in ipso altari commoratio. Itaque altare pro tabernaculo ponitur, vel pro templo. Pro tabernaculo, si David loquitur in hoc Psalmo; pro templo, si quis alius post Davidem (2). Dubitant enim Hebraei, ut ex Kimchio discere est. Utut sit, tam II, 593 tabernaculum, quam templum b) nitebatur magnis trabibus cedrinis, et ἀρκευ-θίναις, in quo cedri genere palumbum libenter nidificare, docent haec Theocriti Idyll. 5.

In the two passages of Scripture in which דרור deror occurs for a bird, there is nothing that conflicts in the least with this interpretation. In Prov 26:2 the דרור seems to be commended for the swiftness of its flight, in which, as we have shown in its place R1, the dove can compete with any bird whatever. And in Ps 84:4 the Psalmist groans, comparing his lot with the meanest birds, namely the sparrow and the דרור deror, that is, the field dove, to which not only free access to the altar of God was granted, but also to nest and hatch their young there, while he himself was a wanderer, an exile, and far from the sacred house. In the name of the altar there must be a figure of speech. For amid so great a throng of men and sacrifices, staying on the altar itself would not have been safe for birds. Therefore altar is put for the tabernacle, or for the temple: for the tabernacle if David speaks in this Psalm; for the temple if someone else after David R2. For the Hebrews are in doubt, as one may learn from Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim]. However that may be, both the tabernacle II, 593 and the temple b) rested on great beams of cedar and of ἀρκευθίναις [arkeuthinais], in which kind of cedar the wood pigeon likes to nest, as these lines of Theocritus, Idyll 5, teach.


Κἠγὼ μὲν δώσω τᾷ παρθένῳ αὐτίκα φάσσαν, Ἐκ τᾶς ἀρκεύθῳ καθελὼν, τηνεὶ γὰρ ἐφείσδει. At mea, tu felix, donabere virgo palumbo, Cui suus arceuthi celsa latet in trabe nidus.

Κἠγὼ μὲν δώσω τᾷ παρθένῳ αὐτίκα φάσσαν, Ἐκ τᾶς ἀρκεύθῳ καθελὼν, τηνεὶ γὰρ ἐφείσδει. [Kēgō men dōsō tai parthenōi autika phassan, Ek tas arkeuthō kathelōn, tēnei gar epheisdei.] But you, my maiden, happy one, shall be given a wood pigeon, whose nest lies hidden in the lofty timber of a juniper.


Sed et liviam columbam in templis nidificare, asserunt Albertus et Turnerus. Et ex Herodoto c) notum, quid Aristodico acciderit, cum ἐξαῖρε τοὺς στρουθοὺς, καὶ ἄλλα ὅσα ἦν νενοσσευμένα ὀρνίθων γένεα ἐν τῷ νηῷ, passeres exemit, aliaque avium genera, quae in templo nidulabantur (3). Hebraei quidem ullas aves templo Hierosolymitano insedisse negant, quia aves id abigebat, quod כולה עורב II, 594 vocabant in summo tecti fastigio positum. Kimchius in Psal. LXXXIV. בגג הבית עשו דבר שם כדי שלא ינוח שם עוף והיו קורין אותו כולה עורב, Aliquid fecerunt in templi tecto, ne aves ibi quiescerent, quod vocabatur chole oreb, id est, arcens corvos. Hujus in Talmude frequens mentio. Sic in tractatu Middoth cap. 4. fol. 71. a. in Glossa, וכולה עורב מאבד העורבים לפי שהיה מקיף ההיכל למעלה מן המעקה מארבע רוחותיו בחשק של ברזל גובה אמה חד כמו הסיף כדי שלו ישב עליו שום עוף על ההיכל מפני שנחתכים רגליו באותו הסיף, Et chole oreb perdebat corvos, quia templum cingebat super loricam a quatuor ventis ferreo cingulo cubitum alto, gladii instar acuto, ne ulla avis templo insideret, quia per gladium illum pedes ejus exscindebantur. Et in tractatu De Sabbato cap. 9. fol. 90. a. ad vocem לכליא עורב (ita enim ibi habetur) Glossator scribit, טבלאת של אמה היו עושין והן חדין כסכין סביבותיה ומסמרין חדין בכלן ומחפין בהן גגו של היכל למנוע את העורבי׳ מלישב, Tabulas cubitales faciebant in circuitu in modum cultri acutas, et acutis clavis omnes instructas, quibus templi tectum tegebant ad corvos arcendos, ne illi insiderent. Et in tracta- col. 54 tu Menachoth cap. 13. fol. 107. a. כולה העורב Glossa definit, מסמרות חדין תחובין בראש גג ההיכל לכלות העורבי׳ שלא ישבו עליו, clavos acutos summo templi tecto defixos, ad prohibendos corvos, ne super illud sedeant. Et alia Glossa ibidem, כמין טבלה חדה וקיפה על צידה וחדודה לחתוך כמו סכין, Speciem tabulae acutae in latus erectae, et cultri instar aciem habentis ad incidendum. Et Aruch, עשה צורה להבריח בה העופות מגג ההיכל כדרך שעושין עכשיו שומרי זרעים, Faciebant μορμολύκειον, quo aves e templi tecto fugarent, ut nunc faciunt, qui sata servant. Et rursus, במקדש ראשון ששכינה שרוייה בו לא היו צורכין כלה עורב שלא היו עופות פורחין עליו אבל במקדש שני שלו היתה קדושתו כקדושת ראשון הוצרכו לכלה עורב, Quia in primo Sanctuario habitabat divina majestas, non opus erat προβασκανίῳ. Aves enim in illud non volabant. Sed illo opus fuit in secundo, quia secundi sanctitas non fuit qualis primi. Tamen etiam in templo Solomonis tale aliquid describitur ab Eupolemo, cum eum fecisse dicit d) δακτυλίους δύο χαλκοῦς ἀλυσιδωτοὺς, καὶ στῆσαι αὐτοὺς (lege δικτύας δύο χαλκᾶς ἀλυσιδωτὰς, καὶ στῆσαι αὐτὰς) ἐπὶ μηχανημάτων ὑπερ-εχόντων τῷ ὕψει τὸν ναὸν πήχεις κ΄, καὶ σκιάζειν ἐπάνω παντὸς τοῦ ἱεροῦ, καὶ προσκρεμάσαι ἑκάστῃ δικτύϊ κώδωνας χαλκοῦς ταλαντιαίους τετρακοσίους, καὶ ποιῆσαι ὅλας τὰς δικτύας πρὸς τὸ ψοφεῖν τοὺς κώδωνας, καὶ ἀποσοβεῖν τὰ ὄρνεα, ὅπως μὴ καθίζῃ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἱεροῦ, μηδὲ νοσσεύῃ ἐπὶ τοῖς φατνώμασι τῶν πυλῶν, καὶ στοῶν, καὶ μολύνῃ τοῖς ἀποπατήμασι τὸ ἱερὸν, retia duo aerea an-nulis conserta, et machinis imposuisse, quae viginti cubitis supra templum eminebant, et totum illud obumbrabant, et ex singulis retibus appendisse tintinnabula II, 595 quadringenta magni ponderis, et tota illa retia sic adaptasse, ut sonarent tintinna- bula, et aves sonitu suo abigerent, ne templo insiderent, et in portarum, aut por- ticuum laquearibus nidificarent, et stercoribus templum polluerent. Sed libro primo Regum, ubi Solomonis templum accurate describitur, nihil tale reperias: ut neque in Iosepho, quamvis idem scribat de templo, ab Herode exstructo, De bello Iudaico lib. 6. cap. 6. Κατὰ κορυφὴν δὲ χρυσέους ὀβελοὺς ἀνεῖχε τεθηγμένους, ὡς μή τινι προσκαθεζομένῳ μολύνοιτο τῶν ὀρνέων, In summo autem aureis verubus horrebat acutissimis, ne ab insidentibus avibus pollueretur. Quae descriptioni τοῦ כלה עורב, a Talmudicis traditae, sunt consona satis. Pone tamen, etiam Solomo- nis templum in tecti vertice hujusmodi verubus inhorruisse: hoc quidem aves a summo, non tamen a toto tecto, aut ab aliis templi partibus arcuisset. Si ἐπὶ τὸ πτερύγιον τοῦ ἱεροῦ, super pinnaculum templi stare potuisset Christus illaesus Matth. IV, 5. quanto magis aviculae (4)?

But Albertus and Turner [=William Turner, Avium praecipuarum historia (1544)] also assert that the livia dove nests in temples. And it is known from Herodotus c) what happened to Aristodicus when ἐξαῖρε τοὺς στρουθοὺς, καὶ ἄλλα ὅσα ἦν νενοσσευμένα ὀρνίθων γένεα ἐν τῷ νηῷ [exaire tous strouthous, kai alla hosa ēn nenosseumena ornithōn genea en tō nēō], he took out the sparrows and the other kinds of birds that were nesting in the temple R3. The Hebrews, it is true, deny that any birds settled on the temple at Jerusalem, because they were driven off by what they called כולה עורב II, 594, placed on the very top of the roof. Kimchi on Psal. LXXXIV.: בגג הבית עשו דבר שם כדי שלא ינוח שם עוף והיו קורין אותו כולה עורב, They made something on the roof of the temple so that birds should not rest there, and it was called chole oreb, that is, keeping off ravens. This is frequently mentioned in the Talmud. Thus in the tractate Middoth, ch. 4, fol. 71a, in the Gloss: וכולה עורב מאבד העורבים לפי שהיה מקיף ההיכל למעלה מן המעקה מארבע רוחותיו בחשק של ברזל גובה אמה חד כמו הסיף כדי שלו ישב עליו שום עוף על ההיכל מפני שנחתכים רגליו באותו הסיף, And the chole oreb destroyed ravens, because it surrounded the temple above the parapet on all four sides with an iron band a cubit high, sharp like a sword, so that no bird should settle on the temple, since its feet would be cut off by that sword. And in the tractate On the Sabbath, ch. 9, fol. 90a, on the word לכליא עורב (for so it reads there), the Glossator writes: טבלאת של אמה היו עושין והן חדין כסכין סביבותיה ומסמרין חדין בכלן ומחפין בהן גגו של היכל למנוע את העורבי׳ מלישב, They made plates a cubit in size, sharp all round like a knife and all furnished with sharp nails, with which they covered the roof of the temple to keep off the ravens, so that they would not settle on it. And in the tractate col. 54 Menachoth, ch. 13, fol. 107a, the Gloss defines כולה העורב as מסמרות חדין תחובין בראש גג ההיכל לכלות העורבי׳ שלא ישבו עליו, sharp nails fixed in the top of the temple roof to prevent the ravens from sitting on it. And another Gloss in the same place: כמין טבלה חדה וקיפה על צידה וחדודה לחתוך כמו סכין, A kind of sharp plate set up on its edge, with an edge like a knife for cutting. And the Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome]: עשה צורה להבריח בה העופות מגג ההיכל כדרך שעושין עכשיו שומרי זרעים, They made a μορμολύκειον [mormolykeion], with which to chase birds from the temple roof, as those who guard crops do now. And again: במקדש ראשון ששכינה שרוייה בו לא היו צורכין כלה עורב שלא היו עופות פורחין עליו אבל במקדש שני שלו היתה קדושתו כקדושת ראשון הוצרכו לכלה עורב, Because the divine majesty dwelt in the first Sanctuary, there was no need for a προβασκανίῳ [probaskaniō]. For birds did not fly over it. But it was needed in the second, because the holiness of the second was not like that of the first. Yet something of the kind is described even in Solomon's temple by Eupolemus, when he says d) that he made δακτυλίους δύο χαλκοῦς ἀλυσιδωτοὺς, καὶ στῆσαι αὐτοὺς [daktylious dyo chalkous halysidōtous, kai stēsai autous] (read δικτύας δύο χαλκᾶς ἀλυσιδωτὰς, καὶ στῆσαι αὐτὰς [diktyas dyo chalkas halysidōtas, kai stēsai autas]) ἐπὶ μηχανημάτων ὑπερεχόντων τῷ ὕψει τὸν ναὸν πήχεις κ΄, καὶ σκιάζειν ἐπάνω παντὸς τοῦ ἱεροῦ, καὶ προσκρεμάσαι ἑκάστῃ δικτύϊ κώδωνας χαλκοῦς ταλαντιαίους τετρακοσίους, καὶ ποιῆσαι ὅλας τὰς δικτύας πρὸς τὸ ψοφεῖν τοὺς κώδωνας, καὶ ἀποσοβεῖν τὰ ὄρνεα, ὅπως μὴ καθίζῃ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἱεροῦ, μηδὲ νοσσεύῃ ἐπὶ τοῖς φατνώμασι τῶν πυλῶν, καὶ στοῶν, καὶ μολύνῃ τοῖς ἀποπατήμασι τὸ ἱερὸν [epi mēchanēmatōn hyperechontōn tō hypsei ton naon pēcheis k', kai skiazein epanō pantos tou hierou, kai proskremasai hekastē diktyi kōdōnas chalkous talantiaious tetrakosious, kai poiēsai holas tas diktyas pros to psophein tous kōdōnas, kai aposobein ta ornea, hopōs mē kathizē epi tou hierou, mēde nosseuē epi tois phatnōmasi tōn pylōn, kai stoōn, kai molynē tois apopatēmasi to hieron], two bronze nets linked with rings, and that he set them on machines which rose twenty cubits above the temple and overshadowed the whole of it, and hung from each net II, 595 four hundred bells of great weight, and fitted all those nets so that the bells would ring and drive off the birds with their sound, so that they would not settle on the temple, nor nest in the coffered ceilings of the gates or porticoes, nor pollute the temple with their droppings. But in the first book of Kings, where Solomon's temple is accurately described, you will find nothing of the sort; nor in Josephus, although he writes the same of the temple built by Herod, On the Jewish War book 6, ch. 6: Κατὰ κορυφὴν δὲ χρυσέους ὀβελοὺς ἀνεῖχε τεθηγμένους, ὡς μή τινι προσκαθεζομένῳ μολύνοιτο τῶν ὀρνέων [Kata koryphēn de chryseous obelous aneiche tethēgmenous, hōs mē tini proskathezomenō molynoito tōn orneōn], On the top it bristled with very sharp golden spits, so that it should not be polluted by birds settling on it. This agrees well enough with the description of the כלה עורב handed down by the Talmudists. Yet suppose that Solomon's temple too bristled with such spits on the ridge of the roof: this would have kept the birds off the top, but not off the whole roof or the other parts of the temple. If Christ could stand unharmed ἐπὶ τὸ πτερύγιον τοῦ ἱεροῦ [epi to pterygion tou hierou], on the pinnacle of the temple, Matt 4:5, how much more little birds R4?

SCHULTENSIUS in Commentar. ad h. l. pag. 345. seqq. simili Arabum usu, qui temerariam levitatem denotare solent hoc adagio: طارت عصافيره, volant passeres ejus, cum quo convenit alterum: طارت خطاطيفه volant hirundines ejus, de blaterone futili ac temerario usurpari solitum.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 592 In that passage rash words and curses are compared with the wandering and circling sparrow and with the דרור. A. Schultens [=Albert Schultens, Liber Jobi (1737)], in his Commentary on this passage, p. 345 ff., shows that the latter may not unreasonably be understood of the swallow, from a similar usage of the Arabs, who are accustomed to denote rash levity by this proverb: طارت عصافيره [ṭārat ʿaṣāfīruhu], his sparrows fly. With this agrees another: طارت خطاطيفه [ṭārat khaṭāṭīfuhu] his swallows fly, customarily used of an empty and rash babbler.

SCHNUR-RERUS quidem in Animadverss. ad h. l. (in Dissertatt. junctim editt. p. 162.) hanc interpretationem repudiat eam ob causam, quod ab Hebraeis nomen מזבח eodem sensu fuisse usurpatum, exemplis haud sit demonstrabile. Mihi tamen ejusmodi synecdoche ita prona videtur cujusque gentis poetae, ut eam in Hebraeo nostro et sine exemplorum autoritate agnoverim.

R2 Rosenmüller, II, 592 Merrick, in his notes on the passage, shows from Eustathius and Hesychius that it is not unusual among the Greeks either to put the word βωμου [bōmou], altar, sometimes for temple. Schnurrer [=C. F. Schnurrer, Dissertationes philologico-criticae (1790)], it is true, in his Animadversions on this passage (in the Dissertations Published Together, p. 162), rejects this interpretation on the ground that it cannot be demonstrated by examples that the Hebrews used the word מזבח in the same sense. To me, however, a synecdoche of this kind seems so natural to the poets of every nation that I would recognize it in our Hebrew poet even without the authority of examples.
