(3) Rosenmüller, II, 593 Digna est, quae apponatur ANT. DRIESSENII observatio ad h. l. in Ejus Specimine Observationum, quibus quaedam Veteris Testamenti loca explicantur, vindicantur, emendantur, Praef. Nicol. Guil. Schroedero, Groening. 1774. (inserta est haec dissertat. Συλλογη Dissertt. Philologico-Exegeticar. a diversis auctoribus editarum, sub praesidio A. Schultens, I. I. Schultens et N. G. Schroeder defensarr. Leid. et Leovard. 1775. P. II. p. 1094. sequ.). „Hunc locum respicere ad morem, inter veteres populos receptum, quo animalia, in sacra quadam aede commorantia, praesertim volucria, in ejus muris aut altarium lateribus nidulantia, habebantur tanquam Numinis in tutelam admissa, quae violare, aut ex sua sede exturbare nefas esset, jam ab aliis est observatum. Non tamen inutile, aut injucundum erit, similem prorsus locum contulisse ex Monumentis vetustioribus Arabiae [ab A. Schultensio editt. Lugd. 1740.] Carm. I., ubi, quemadmodum Psaltes sacri loci praestantiam numinisque benignitatem eo nomine celebrat, quod etiam animalia ibi tutam sedem inveniant, ita excellentiam aedis Meccanae simili ratione extollit Amru Ben Elharith, ونبكي لبيت ليس يوذي حمامة يظل دها امنا وفيه العصافر وفيه وحوش لا تراب انيسة انا خرجت منه فليست تغادم Et flemus ob aedem, cujus non laeditur columba, Quae umbra ejus gaudet secura, ibidemque passeres, Ibidem quoque ferae, quae non conterreantur, cicures, Si vel exierint inde; quaeque noxam non inferant. Ratio autem, cur hoc carmen cum Hymno sacro conferre operae pretium duxerim, haec est, quod utrobique eadem occurrant animalia, scil. passeres et columbae. Arabicum hocce fragmentum ad aetatem Salomonis refert Cl. Schultensius. Caeterum particula את in verbis את מזבחותיך sine dubio valet apud, juxta, ut saepius alibi.“ Haec Driessenius; quae, etsi apposite observata, nihil tamen faciunt ad definiendam vocabuli דרור significationem. Hirundines enim aeque ac palumbes in templo nidulari poterant.

R3 Rosenmüller, II, 593 The observation of ANT. DRIESSEN on this passage deserves to be added, from his Specimen of Observations in which Certain Passages of the Old Testament are Explained, Defended and Emended, with a preface by Nicol. Guil. Schroeder, Groningen 1774 (this dissertation is included in the Συλλογη [Syllogē] of Philological-Exegetical Dissertations Published by Various Authors and Defended under the Presidency of A. Schultens, I. I. Schultens and N. G. Schroeder, Leiden and Leeuwarden 1775, vol. 2, p. 1094 ff.): „It has already been observed by others that this passage refers to a custom accepted among ancient peoples, whereby animals dwelling in a sacred building, especially birds nesting in its walls or on the sides of the altars, were regarded as admitted into the protection of the Deity, so that it was sacrilege to harm them or drive them from their abode. Yet it will not be useless or unpleasant to compare an altogether similar passage from the Older Monuments of Arabia [edited by A. Schultens, Leiden 1740], Poem 1, where, just as the Psalmist celebrates the excellence of the holy place and the kindness of the Deity on the ground that even animals find a safe abode there, so Amru Ben Elharith extols the excellence of the Meccan sanctuary in a similar way: ونبكي لبيت ليس يوذي حمامة [wa-nabkī li-baytin laysa yūdhī ḥamāmatun] يظل دها امنا وفيه العصافر [yaẓallu dahā āminan wa-fīhi al-ʿaṣāfir] وفيه وحوش لا تراب انيسة [wa-fīhi wuḥūshun lā turābu anīsatun] انا خرجت منه فليست تغادم [anā kharajat minhu fa-laysat tughādim] And we weep for the sanctuary, whose dove is not harmed, which rejoices secure in its shade, and the sparrows there too; there also wild beasts that are not frightened, tame, even if they go out from it; and they inflict no harm. The reason why I thought it worthwhile to compare this poem with the sacred hymn is that the same animals occur in both, namely sparrows and doves. The celebrated Schultens dates this Arabic fragment to the age of Solomon. Moreover, the particle את in the words את מזבחותיך undoubtedly means at, beside, as often elsewhere.“ Thus Driessen. These remarks, though aptly made, contribute nothing to determining the meaning of the word דרור; for swallows could nest in the temple just as well as wood pigeons.


d) Bochart, II, 594 Vide Eusebium lib. 19.

d) Bochart, II, 594 See Eusebius, book 19.


(4) Rosenmüller, II, 595 In tota hac disputatione feliciorem ego Bochartum versatum esse putem in aliorum commentis refellendis, quam in sua sententia stabilienda. Nam quum hujus capitis initio iis, qui hirundinem interpretantur, quasi a libertate ea dicta esset, recte opponeret, non sufficere hanc rationem, quum et aliae aves sint partim domesticae, partim agrestes, mox tamen ipse eadem ratione utitur, ut ostendat, דרור esse columbae ferae speciem. Etenim tota Nostri argumentatio huc redit: Hebraeorum דרור ut Arabum حرّ liberum sonat: atqui Arabibus حرّ epitheton est columbae ferae; ergo Hebraeorum דרור, eandem li-bertatis notionem gerens, idem illud animal indicat. Quod quam leve sit, sponte quisque intelligit, cum Arabibus حرّ non sit nomen columbae, sed epitheton ferae columbae, additum nomini ساق, columbam marem significanti. Quod autem at-tinet duo loca, quibus vocabulum דרור occurrit, priori illi (Proverb. XXVI, 2.) hirundinem satis aptam, alteri vero hirundinem aeque atque columbam convenire vidimus (not. 1. et 3.). — Memorat FORS-KALIUS in Descript. Animalium in Itinere Orientali observatorum p. 10. inter migratorias Alexandriae aves quandam nomine Dururi, quae venit, cum Dactyli maturuerunt, fine Octobris, ex Aegypto superiore, hisque consumtis post tres menses abit. Alexandria cum non multum australior sit Hierosolymis, MICHAELIS (in Supplemm. P. II. p. 477.) suspicatur, posse hanc avem Hebraeorum דרור esse: nec tamen certi quidquam definit, cum dubium sit, quibusnam literis Arabice nomen scribatur, دُرُوري an ضُرُوري? Attamen sub finem addit: „Estne ea passeris species, lusciniae colore, cantu dulcissimo, quam circa Capsam in locis palmiferis vidit Shawius, p. 185. Itiner. vers. germ. 164.? Vide et Buffons Naturgeschichte der Voegel T. X. p. 161. vers germ. Sic Dattelnsperling vocare potuissem.“ Quae, etsi dubitanter a Michaele proposita, pro certo tamen ha-buit Zieglerus, in vers. Proverbiorum. — Tandem avem omnino ullam voce דרור indicari, prorsus negat PAULUS in Clavi Psalmorr. p. 209. quod opponatur ea τῷ צפור, id vero est, toti avium generi. Unde ipse vocabulum Hebraeum interpretatur formicam exiguam, coll. Arab. ذرّ, vid. CASTELCASTELLI II, 596 Lexic. Hexapl. pag. 77c. Sed צפור et aves quasvis significat, et speciatim passerem. Formica vero parum apta fuerit loco Proverb. XXVI, 2. (דרור לעוף). Neque formicae tribui potest nidus, קן, quod fit Psal. LXXXIV, 4. — Ego דרור turturis nomen ὀνοματοποιητικον crediderim, quum in eo consentiant interpretes veteres omnes.

R4 Rosenmüller, II, 595 In this whole discussion I would think Bochart more successful in refuting the fancies of others than in establishing his own opinion. For at the beginning of this chapter he rightly objected to those who render it swallow, as if it were named from freedom, that this reason is not sufficient, since there are also other birds, some domestic, some wild; yet soon he himself uses the same reason to show that דרור is a species of wild dove. Indeed, our author's whole argument comes to this: the Hebrew דרור, like the Arabic حرّ [ḥurr], means free; but among the Arabs حرّ [ḥurr] is an epithet of the wild dove; therefore the Hebrew דרור, carrying the same notion of freedom, denotes that same animal. How weak this is, anyone understands at once, since among the Arabs حرّ [ḥurr] is not the name of the dove but an epithet of the wild dove, added to the noun ساق [sāq], which signifies the male dove. As for the two passages in which the word דרור occurs, we have seen (note 1 and 3) that the swallow fits the former (Proverb. XXVI, 2.) well enough, while for the other the swallow suits as well as the dove. — Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)], in Descript. Animalium in Itinere Orientali observatorum p. 10, mentions among the migratory birds of Alexandria one named Dururi, which comes when the dates have ripened, at the end of October, from Upper Egypt, and, when these have been consumed, leaves after three months. Since Alexandria is not much further south than Jerusalem, Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer] (in Supplemm. vol. 2, p. 477) suspects that this bird may be the Hebrew דרור; yet he determines nothing certain, since it is doubtful in which letters the name is written in Arabic, دُرُوري [durūrī] or ضُرُوري [ḍurūrī]. Nevertheless, toward the end he adds: “Is it the species of sparrow, of the colour of a nightingale, with a very sweet song, which Shaw [=Thomas Shaw, Travels (1738)] saw around Capsa in palm-bearing places, p. 185, Travels, German trans. 164? See also Buffons Naturgeschichte der Voegel vol. 10, p. 161, German trans. Thus I could have called it Dattelnsperling.” Although Michaelis proposed this with hesitation, Ziegler nevertheless took it as certain, in his translation of Proverbs. — Finally, Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)], in Clavis Psalmorr. p. 209, flatly denies that any bird at all is denoted by the word דרור, because it is contrasted with τῷ [tō] צפור, that is, with the whole class of birds. Hence he himself renders the Hebrew word tiny ant, comparing the Arabic ذرّ [dharr]; see Castell [=Edmund Castell, Lexicon heptaglotton (London 1669)] II, 596 Lexic. Hexapl. p. 77c. But צפור signifies both any birds whatever and specifically the sparrow. An ant, moreover, would hardly fit the passage Proverb. XXVI, 2. (דרור לעוף). Nor can a nest, קן, be attributed to an ant, as is done in Ps 84:4 — I would believe that דרור is an onomatopoeic (ὀνοματοποιητικον [onomatopoiētikon]) name of the turtledove, since all the ancient translators agree on this.

II, 596 col. 54 CAP. IX.

II, 596 col. 54 Chapter IX.


De Turture.

On the Turtledove.


Turtur Hebraice תור thor dicitur, et Graece τρυγών. Quae nomina, utut col. 55 similia, non tamen sunt ab invicem deducta, sed ὀνοματοποιητικά. Facta nimirum ad imitationem cantus turturis, qui Graece dicitur τρυσμὸς, a verbo τρύζειν, id est, turturis more gemere, Pollux lib. 5. cap. 14. sectione De avium vocibus, Εἴποις δ' ἂν τρυγόνας τρύζειν, περιστερὰς γογγύζειν. Sed et τρύζειν Suidae et Etymologo est ψιθυρίζειν, γογγύζειν, ἀσήμως λαλεῖν παρὰ καὶ ἡ τρυγὼν, ἐπεὶ καὶ ἀσήμως φθέγγεται καὶ γογγυστικῶς, susurrare, murmurare, obscure loqui, ut et turtur, quia obscure canit et cum murmure. Unde Clemens libro quinto Stromatων, Γογγύζουσα ἡ τρυγὼν, μέμψεως καταλαλιὰν ἀχάρι-στον ἐμφαίνουσα, εἰκότως ἐξοικίζεται. Turtur murmurans, quaerelae ingratam ostendens maledicentiam, merito domo expellitur. Aliis τρύζειν est πολυφωνεῖν, καὶ πολυλογεῖν, multa garrire. Quia τὴν τρυγόνα ἡ παροιμία ἐπὶ σκώμματι τῶν πολυλογούντων παραλαμβάνει, λαλιστέρους τῶν τρυγόνων τοιούτους καλοῦσα, turturem adhibet proverbium, in eorum suggillationem, qui multa garriunt, eos turturibus loquaciores appellans. Haec Eustathius, in illud Homeri Iliad. l. versu 31.

The turtledove is called תור thor in Hebrew and τρυγών [trygōn] in Greek. These names, however col. 55 similar, are not derived from one another but are onomatopoeic (ὀνοματοποιητικά [onomatopoiētika]). They were formed, that is, in imitation of the song of the turtledove, which in Greek is called τρυσμὸς [trysmos], from the verb τρύζειν [tryzein], that is, to moan in the manner of a turtledove. So Pollux, book 5, ch. 14, in the section On the calls of birds: Εἴποις δ' ἂν τρυγόνας τρύζειν, περιστερὰς γογγύζειν [Eipois d' an trygonas tryzein, peristeras gongyzein]. But for Suidas and the Etymologicum, too, τρύζειν [tryzein] is ψιθυρίζειν, γογγύζειν, ἀσήμως λαλεῖν παρὰ καὶ ἡ τρυγὼν, ἐπεὶ καὶ ἀσήμως φθέγγεται καὶ γογγυστικῶς [psithyrizein, gongyzein, asēmōs lalein para kai hē trygōn, epei kai asēmōs phthengetai kai gongystikōs], to whisper, to murmur, to speak indistinctly, like the turtledove too, because it sings indistinctly and with a murmur. Hence Clement, in the fifth book of the Stromata: Γογγύζουσα ἡ τρυγὼν, μέμψεως καταλαλιὰν ἀχάριστον ἐμφαίνουσα, εἰκότως ἐξοικίζεται [Gongyzousa hē trygōn, mempseōs katalalian acharistōn emphainousa, eikotōs exoikizetai]. The murmuring turtledove, displaying the ungrateful slander of complaint, is rightly driven from the house. For others τρύζειν [tryzein] is πολυφωνεῖν, καὶ πολυλογεῖν [polyphōnein, kai polylogein], to chatter a great deal. Because τὴν τρυγόνα ἡ παροιμία ἐπὶ σκώμματι τῶν πολυλογούντων παραλαμβάνει, λαλιστέρους τῶν τρυγόνων τοιούτους καλοῦσα [tēn trygona hē paroimia epi skōmmati tōn polylogountōn paralambanei, lalisterous tōn trygonōn toioutous kalousa], the proverb uses the turtledove to mock those who chatter a great deal, calling them more talkative than turtledoves. So Eustathius, on that line of Homer, Iliad 1, verse 31:


Ὡς μή μοι τρύζητε παρήμενοι ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος,

Ὡς μή μοι τρύζητε παρήμενοι ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος, [Hōs mē moi tryzēte parēmenoi allothen allos,]


Ut ne mihi garriatis assidentes aliunde alius. Proverbii meminere, praeter Paroemiographos, Alexis in Thrasone apud Athenaeum libro quarto, Menander in Plocio, Demetrius in Sicilia apud Aelianum De animalibus libri duodecimi capite duodecimo, et Clemens libro primo Stromatων. Quo pertinet, quod de garrulis mulierculis habetur in Theocriti Syracusiis,

So that you may not chatter at me, sitting by, one from here, another from there. Besides the paroemiographers, the proverb is mentioned by Alexis in the Thraso in Athenaeus, book 4; by Menander in the Plocium; by Demetrius in the Sicilia in Aelian, On Animals, book 12, chapter 12; and by Clement in the first book of the Stromata. To this belongs what is said of chattering women in Theocritus' Syracusan Women:


Τρυγόνες ἐκκναισεῦντι πλατυάσδοισαι ἅπαντα,

Τρυγόνες ἐκκναισεῦντι πλατυάσδοισαι ἅπαντα, [Trygones ekknaiseunti platyasdoisai hapanta,]


Ut turtures obtundunt ad omnia os diducentes. Nec placet, quod vir magnus pro ἐκκναισεῦντι legi vult ἐκ Ναύσοιο, id est, ex insula Sicilia. Ναῦσος, ait, sicut Νᾶσος, Dorum et Siculorum est, qui ita vocabant suam Siciliam. Poeta igitur urbanissime τοὺς Δωριζούσας, et ore lato omnia pronuntiantes, τρυγόνας ἐκ II, 597 Ναύσοιο vocat. Haec, inquam, conjectura non placet: quia nihil opus est quidquam mutare, cum ex recepta lectione sensus emergat commodissimus. Ἐκκναίειν est aures obtundere, ut ἀποκναίειν. Pollux, Ἀποκναίων ἀηδίᾳ, κό-πτων τὰ ὦτα, Insuavitate, seu ineptiis suis, ἀποκναίων, id est, aures obtundens. Quod scripsit Demosthenes contra Midiam pag. 362. Ἀποκναίει γὰρ ἀη-δίᾳ, δήπου καὶ ἀναιθησίᾳ καθ᾽ ἑκάστην τὴν ἐκκλησίαν ταῦτα λέγων· Obtundit enim ineptiis et stoliditate sua, in singulis concionibus eadem subinde inculcans. Ita igitur de loquaculis dictum, Τρυγόνες ἐκκναισεῦντι, Dorice pro ἐκκναίσουσι, Turtures (seu turturum instar) loquacitate sua aures obtundunt. Est in Proverbiis apud Suidam Τρυγόνα ψάλλειν Turturem canere, ἐπὶ τῶν φαύλως πρατ-των, de iis, qui rem aliquam perperam agunt, quia turturis vox est prorsus incondita. Atque eo fortasse pertinet, quod ab Hebraeis צלצל, et a Chaldaeis צרצילתא nominatur, et Arabice etiam صلصل, tanquam a cymbalo facto nomine, quia vocem habet tinnulam et obstreperam. Quin, si Gesnero credimus, ob id ipsum cum turture confertur cicadae species cercope in his Athenaei lib. 4. cap. 4. Ἔστι δ᾽ ἡ κερκώπη ζῶον ὅμοιον τέττιγι, καὶ τρυγονίῳ· Cercope autem est animal, cicadae et turturi simile. Ad quae verba sic ille habet, Non alia re cercope turturi similis est, quam obstrepera garrulitate. Sed conjectat Dale- col. 56 champius, gryllum ita vocari a soni tri proprietate. Et magnus Casaubonus secure praeteriit hunc locum. Quem tamen esse mendosum, tam certum est, quam quod est certissimum. Et τρυγονίῳ perperam legi pro τεττιγονίῳ, quae una est cicadae species. Aristoteles Hist. lib. 5. cap. 30. Καλοῦσι δέ τινες τοὺς μὲν μεγά-λους (τῶν τεττίγων) καὶ ᾄδοντας ἄχετας· τοὺς δὲ μικροὺς τεττιγόνια. Unde Plinius lib. 11. cap. 26. Quae canunt vocantur achetae, et quae minores ex iis, tettigonia. Itaque nihil habet hic locus, quod ad turturum garrulitatem possit referri. Quae, utut saepe molesta, habet tamen aliquid gratum, nempe ver et aestatem venisse significat, quia hyeme turtures non apparent. Unde dicitur Cant. II, 11. 12. Iam enim hyems transiit, pluvia praeteriit et recessit. Flores in terra conspiciuntur. Tempus cantus advenit, et vox turturis audita est in terra nostra. Et Ierem. VIII, 7. Turtur et hirundo, et grus observarunt tempus ad-ventus sui. Turtur enim est avis migratoria (1). Aristoteles Hist. lib. 8. cap. 3.

Like turtledoves they deafen us, broadening their mouths on every word. Nor do I approve the proposal of a great man to read ἐκ Ναύσοιο [ek Nausoio], that is, from the island of Sicily, instead of ἐκκναισεῦντι [ekknaiseunti]. Ναῦσος [Nausos], he says, like Νᾶσος [Nasos], is a word of the Dorians and the Sicilians, who so called their Sicily. The poet therefore very wittily calls the Dorian-speaking women (τοὺς Δωριζούσας [tous Dōrizousas]), who pronounce everything with a broad mouth, τρυγόνας ἐκ II, 597 Ναύσοιο [trygonas ek Nausoio]. This conjecture, I say, I do not approve, because there is no need to change anything, since the received reading yields a most fitting sense. Ἐκκναίειν [Ekknaiein] means to deafen the ears, like ἀποκναίειν [apoknaiein]. Pollux: Ἀποκναίων ἀηδίᾳ, κόπτων τὰ ὦτα [Apoknaiōn aēdia, koptōn ta ōta], ἀποκναίων [apoknaiōn] by his unpleasantness, or by his inanities, that is, deafening the ears. As Demosthenes wrote against Midias, p. 362: Ἀποκναίει γὰρ ἀηδίᾳ, δήπου καὶ ἀναιθησίᾳ καθ᾽ ἑκάστην τὴν ἐκκλησίαν ταῦτα λέγων· [Apoknaiei gar aēdia, dēpou kai anaithēsia kath' hekastēn tēn ekklēsian tauta legōn;] For he deafens us with his inanities and stupidity, hammering the same things in at every assembly. Thus, then, it is said of chatterboxes, Τρυγόνες ἐκκναισεῦντι [Trygones ekknaiseunti], Doric for ἐκκναίσουσι [ekknaisousi], Turtledoves (or like turtledoves) deafen the ears with their talkativeness. Among the Proverbs in Suidas there is Τρυγόνα ψάλλειν [Trygona psallein], To sing the turtledove, ἐπὶ τῶν φαύλως πραττων [epi tōn phaulōs prattōn], said of those who do something badly, because the voice of the turtledove is utterly unmusical. And perhaps this is why it is called צלצל by the Hebrews, צרצילתא by the Chaldeans, and in Arabic also صلصل [ṣalṣal], as if the name were formed from a cymbal, because it has a ringing and noisy voice. Indeed, if we believe Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium], for this very reason a species of cicada, the cercope, is compared with the turtledove in these words of Athenaeus, book 4, ch. 4: Ἔστι δ᾽ ἡ κερκώπη ζῶον ὅμοιον τέττιγι, καὶ τρυγονίῳ· [Esti d' hē kerkōpē zōon homoion tettigi, kai trygoniō;] The cercope is an animal like a cicada and a turtledove. On these words he says: The cercope resembles the turtledove in nothing else than its noisy chatter. But Dale- col. 56 champius conjectures that a cricket is so called from the peculiarity of the sound tri. And the great Casaubon passed over this passage unconcerned. Yet that it is corrupt is as certain as whatever is most certain, and τρυγονίῳ [trygoniō] is wrongly read for τεττιγονίῳ [tettigoniō], which is a species of cicada. Aristotle, Hist. book 5, ch. 30: Καλοῦσι δέ τινες τοὺς μὲν μεγάλους (τῶν τεττίγων) καὶ ᾄδοντας ἄχετας· τοὺς δὲ μικροὺς τεττιγόνια [Kalousi de tines tous men megalous (tōn tettigōn) kai adontas achetas; tous de mikrous tettigonia]. Hence Pliny, book 11, ch. 26: Those that sing are called achetae, and the smaller of them tettigonia. So this passage contains nothing that can be referred to the chattering of turtledoves. That chattering, though often annoying, nevertheless has something pleasing: it signals that spring and summer have come, since turtledoves do not appear in winter. Hence it is said in Cant. II, 11. 12.: For now the winter is past, the rain is over and gone. Flowers are seen on the earth. The time of song has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land. And Ierem. VIII, 7.: The turtledove and the swallow and the crane have observed the time of their coming. For the turtledove is a migratory bird R1. Aristotle, Hist. book 8, ch. 3.


II, 598 φάττα μὲν οὖν, καὶ περιστερὰ ἀεὶ φαίνονται· τρυγὼν δὲ τοῦ θέρους· τοῦ γὰρ χειμῶνος ἀφανίζεται· Palumbus et columba semper apparent: sed turtur aestate tantum. Nam hyeme non conspicitur. Et libri octavi capite duodecimo, de palumbo id ipsum negans, quod hic affirmaverat, solas columbas jugiter manere scribit. Verba sunt: Ἀπαίρουσι δὲ καὶ αἱ φάτται, καὶ αἱ πελειάδες, καὶ οὐ χει-μάζουσι, καὶ αἱ χελιδόνες, καὶ αἱ τρυγόνες, αἱ δὲ περιστεραὶ καταμένουσιν· Discedunt autem et palumbi, et liviae, et hirundines, et turtures, neque (hic) hyemant, sed columbae manent. Et capite decimo sexto docet, hoc turturis maxime esse proprium, ut hyeme lateat. Φωλεῖ γὰρ, inquit, καὶ πελαργὸς, καὶ κόττυφος, καὶ τρυγὼν, καὶ κόρυδος. καὶ ἥ γε τρυγὼν ὁμολογουμένως μάλιστα πάντων. οὐδεὶς γὰρ, ὡς εἰπεῖν, λέγεται τρυγόνα ἰδεῖν οὐδαμοῦ χειμῶνος· Nam et ciconia latet, et merula, et turtur, et alauda. Sed de turture maxime omnium constat: nemo enim, prope dixerim, turturem per hyemem uspiam vidisse memoratur. Varro etiam Rustic. lib. 3. cap. 5. Turdi quotannis in Italiam trans mare advolant circiter aequinoctium autumnale, et eodem revolant ad aequinoctium vernum. Et alio tempore turtures ac coturnices immani numero. Et Cicero, De Finib. libro secundo, Turtures cursu et peregrinatione laetantur. Et Gregorius Nyssenus in Cant. Homil. 5. Ἐν γὰρ τῇ χειμῶνι φεύγει ἡ ἀηδὼν, ναρκᾷ ἡ χε-λιδὼν, ἀποξενοῦται τῆς καλίας ἡ τρυγών· Hyeme enim fugit luscinia, torpet hirundo, a nido peregrinatur turtur. Sunt tamen, qui turturem putant non tam abire, quam occultari. Plinius libri decimi capite vigesimo quarto, Verius turtur occultatur, pennasque amittit. Alii vere perperam legunt. Neque enim turtur vere occultatur, sed hyeme. Quin ipse Aristoteles ubi supra capite duodecimo turtures nonnullos remanere ἐν εὐηλίοις χωρίοις non diffitetur.

II, 598 φάττα μὲν οὖν, καὶ περιστερὰ ἀεὶ φαίνονται· τρυγὼν δὲ τοῦ θέρους· τοῦ γὰρ χειμῶνος ἀφανίζεται· [phatta men oun, kai peristera aei phainontai; trygōn de tou therous; tou gar cheimōnos aphanizetai] The wood-pigeon and the dove are always to be seen, but the turtledove only in summer. For in winter it is not seen. And in book 8, chapter 12, denying of the wood-pigeon the very thing he had affirmed here, he writes that only doves remain all year. His words are: Ἀπαίρουσι δὲ καὶ αἱ φάτται, καὶ αἱ πελειάδες, καὶ οὐ χειμάζουσι, καὶ αἱ χελιδόνες, καὶ αἱ τρυγόνες, αἱ δὲ περιστεραὶ καταμένουσιν· [Apairousi de kai hai phattai, kai hai peleiades, kai ou cheimazousi, kai hai chelidones, kai hai trygones, hai de peristerai katamenousin] But the wood-pigeons, the rock-doves, the swallows and the turtledoves depart, and do not winter (here), but the doves remain. And in chapter 16 he teaches that it is above all characteristic of the turtledove to hide in winter. Φωλεῖ γὰρ [Phōlei gar], he says, καὶ πελαργὸς, καὶ κόττυφος, καὶ τρυγὼν, καὶ κόρυδος. καὶ ἥ γε τρυγὼν ὁμολογουμένως μάλιστα πάντων. οὐδεὶς γὰρ, ὡς εἰπεῖν, λέγεται τρυγόνα ἰδεῖν οὐδαμοῦ χειμῶνος· [kai pelargos, kai kottyphos, kai trygōn, kai korydos. kai hē ge trygōn homologoumenōs malista pantōn. oudeis gar, hōs eipein, legetai trygona idein oudamou cheimōnos] For the stork also hides, and the blackbird, and the turtledove, and the lark. But of the turtledove this is agreed most of all: for no one, I might almost say, is reported to have seen a turtledove anywhere in winter. Varro too, Rustic. book 3, ch. 5: Thrushes fly every year across the sea into Italy around the autumn equinox, and fly back to the same place at the spring equinox. And at another season turtledoves and quails in enormous numbers. And Cicero, De Finib. book 2: Turtledoves delight in running and in travel. And Gregory of Nyssa on the Song, Homily 5: Ἐν γὰρ τῇ χειμῶνι φεύγει ἡ ἀηδὼν, ναρκᾷ ἡ χελιδὼν, ἀποξενοῦται τῆς καλίας ἡ τρυγών· [En gar tē cheimōni pheugei hē aēdōn, narka hē chelidōn, apoxenoutai tēs kalias hē trygōn] For in winter the nightingale flees, the swallow grows torpid, the turtledove goes abroad from its nest. There are some, however, who think that the turtledove does not so much go away as hide. Pliny, book 10, chapter 24: More truly, the turtledove hides and loses its feathers. Others wrongly read vere [in spring]. For the turtledove does not hide in spring, but in winter. Indeed Aristotle himself, in chapter 12 cited above, does not deny that some turtledoves remain ἐν εὐηλίοις χωρίοις [en euēliois chōriois].


Cant. I, 10. sponsae dicitur in Graeca versione, Τί ὡραιώθησαν σιαγόνες σου ὡς τρυγόνος; et in Vulgata, Quam speciosae factae sunt genae tuae tanquam turturis? Ad quem locum multa habent de castitate turturis, et sede pudoris in genis Graeci doctores, Origenes, Gregorius Nyssenus, Philo Carpathius, Theodoretus et Romani, Iustus Orgelitanus, Gregorius Magnus, Beda, Aponius, Bernardus, atque alii magni nominis viri. Sed omnia praeter rem, quod illorum pace dixerim. Neque enim ibi agitur de turture, quae cum σιαγόνες, id est, genas, aut malas non habeat, quis credat, sponsae genas cum turturis genis conferri? Ἡ δὲ ὄρνις (inquit Philosophus De partib. animal. libro 2. cap. 16.)

In Song 1:10 it is said to the bride in the Greek version, Τί ὡραιώθησαν σιαγόνες σου ὡς τρυγόνος; [Ti hōraiōthēsan siagones sou hōs trygonos?] and in the Vulgate, How beautiful are your cheeks become, like the turtledove's! On this passage the Greek doctors, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Philo of Carpasia, Theodoret, and the Latin ones, Justus of Urgel, Gregory the Great, Bede, Aponius, Bernard [=Bernard of Clairvaux], and other men of great name, have much to say about the chastity of the turtledove and about the seat of modesty in the cheeks. But all of it is beside the point, if I may say so with their leave. For the passage is not about the turtledove there: since it has no σιαγόνες [siagones], that is, cheeks or jaws, who would believe that the bride's cheeks are compared with the cheeks of a turtledove? Ἡ δὲ ὄρνις [Hē de ornis] (says the Philosopher, De partib. animal. book 2, ch. 16)


II, 599 ἀντὶ σιαγόνων ἔχει τὸ καλούμενον ῥύγχος, pro malis id habet, quod rostrum vocant. Frustra Ovidium objeceris reliquas aves invitare ad genas lacerandas in morte psittaci sui Amorum libri secundi Elegia sexta,

II, 599 ἀντὶ σιαγόνων ἔχει τὸ καλούμενον ῥύγχος [anti siagonōn echei to kaloumenon rhynchos], in place of jaws it has what they call a beak. In vain would you object that Ovid, at the death of his parrot, invites the other birds to tear their cheeks, in Amores book 2, Elegy 6:


Ite, piae volucres, et plangite pectora pennis,
Et rigido teneras ungue notate genas.

Go, pious birds, and beat your breasts with your wings, and mark your tender cheeks with rigid claw.


Haec enim ille ποιητικῶς, et πρωσοποποιητικῶς ad aves accommodans, quae col. 57 hominum in luctu propria sunt. Proinde idem Tristium lib. 3. Elegia 3.

For he is applying to birds ποιητικῶς [poiētikōs], and πρωσοποποιητικῶς [prōsopopoiētikōs], things that are proper to human beings in mourning. col. 57 Accordingly the same poet, Tristia book 3, Elegy 3:


Parce tamen lacerare genas, nec scinde capillos.

Yet forbear to tear your cheeks, and do not rend your hair.


Et Tibullus lib. 1. Elegia 1.

And Tibullus book 1, Elegy 1:


Tu manes ne laede meos, sed parce solutis
Crinibus, et teneris, Delia, parce genis,

Do not wound my shade, but spare your loosened hair, and spare, Delia, your tender cheeks,


Et Artemidorus Onirocriticῶν lib. 1. cap. 30. Παρειὰς ἴσχνας ἔχειν, ἢ ἑλκομέ-νας, λύπας, ἢ πένθος σημαίνει. ἴσχνας μὲν λύπας, ἑλκομένας δὲ πένθος. καὶ γὰρ ἐν τοῖς πένθεσι λωβῶνται τὰς παρειὰς οἱ ἄνθρωποι· Genas (in somnis) habere graciles, aut exulceratas, tristitiam et luctum significat. Graciles quidem tristitiam, exulceratas autem luctum. Nam in luctu homines genas dilacerant. Fateor, in Horo legi, turturem habere dentes Hieroglyph. lib. 2. cap. 50. Lactantem, ait, mulierem, et quae bene nutriat, ut significent (Aegyptii) τρυ-γόνα ζωγραφοῦσιν· αὕτη γὰρ μόνη τῶν ἄλλων πτηνῶν ὀδόντας, καὶ μασθοὺς ἔχει, turturem pingunt: sola enim haec inter volucres dentes et mammas habet. Quae si vera sunt, malas etiam habet et genas. Sed a doctis jam observatum, haec ad vespertilionem pertinere, cui soli conveniunt. Itaque τρυγόνα in τρι-γόνα nonnulli mutant: quo nomine vespertilionem ibi appellari conjectant, quia illius est proprium τρίζειν. Alii melius in νυκτερίδα, quae cur permutata fuerint, caussa est obvia. Proxime antecesserat, Imbecillum hominem, et magna molientem significare volentes, νυκτερίδα ζωγραφοῦσιν, vespertilionem pingunt, qui sine pennis volat. Et proxime sequitur, Hominem, qui saltatione et tibia delinitur, designaturi, τρυγόνα ζωγραφοῦσιν, turturem pingunt, quae tibia et saltatione capitur. Turturem reddidi cum Mercero, Caussino et aliis. Quamvis, quod eos fugisse miror, τρυγὼν ibi non sit turtur, sed pastinaca, quam infra cap. 105. τρυγόνα simpliciter appellat hic idem scriptor, et alii θαλαττίαν τρυ-γόνα marinum turturem διακριτικῶς. Neque enim turtur avis, sed ἡ θαλατ-τία τρυγὼν, turtur marinus, id est, pastinaca, tibia et saltatione delinitus in nassam inducitur, ut pluribus narrat Aelianus De animal. lib. 17. cap. 18. Quamvis etiam Philo ad turturem avem id referat. Iam, ut eo redeat, unde digressa est oratio, Sacri Cantici verba Hebraice sic habent: נאוו לחייך בתורים צוארך בחרוזים, Ornatae sunt genae tuae (gemmarum) ordinibus, collum tuum torquibus. II, 600 Pro quibus Graeci, Τί ὡραιώθησαν σιαγόνες σου ὡς τρυγόνος, τραχηλός σου ὡς ὅρμισκοι; et Hieronymus, Quam speciosae factae sunt genae tuae tanquam turturis, collum tuum sicut monile. Quia ב et כ permutatis, pro בתורים, legerunt כתורים, et כחרוזים pro בחרוזים, et תורי ab iisdem sumptum pro turturibus, cum ibi ordines significet, puta gemmarum, aut clavorum aureorum. Quomodo esse reddendum multa docent: 1. Quod תורים et חרוזים hic fere sunt synonyma. Porro, quamvis vox חרוזים alibi in Scriptura non extet, tamen ex Arabica lingua est notissima, qua خرز Verbum est subula consuere, et الخرز monile ex gemmis consertis, item spina dorsi, cujus spondilia tanquam consuta et conserta sunt. Itaque חרוזים Graece ὁρμισκοὺς, et Hieronymus monilia explicant, recte omnino. 2. Statim sequitur, תורי זהב נעשה לך, ubi palam est, תורי non esse turtures, sed aurei ornamenti genus, nempe torques, aut quid simile. Proinde ibi Hieronymus, Muraenulas aureas faciemus tibi. Et Syrus ܕܕܗܒܐ ܥܢܩܐ, torquem aureum. Et quinta editio στρεπτὸν χρυσίου, ita le-gendum, non στρεπτοῦ. Nam στρεπτὸς, vel στρεπτὸν, pro torque ab Herodoto, Xenophonte, Plutarcho, et aliis passim usurpatur. In Symmacho, pro περίβλε-πτα χρυσίου, legerim περίπλεκτα. Nempe στρέφειν, unde στρεπτὸν, et πλέ-κειν, unde πλεκτὸν, sunt fere synonyma. Proinde in Hesychio πλόκιον est εἶ-δος περιδεραίου, monilis species. Atque eadem ratio Syri ܥܢܩܐ pro torque. Nam ܥܢܩ verbum plicare et torquere est. At Seniores quorsum reddunt ὁμοιώματα? An pro תורי legerunt ציורי, id est, imagines? vel תורי זהב dici putarunt turturum similitudines, ex auro factas: quae fuit Aben Ezrae sententia? 3. Quin תור per Thau hic idem est, quod טור per Teth, qua voce pro gemmarum ordine passim utitur Moses: ut Exod. XXVIII, 17. ארבעה טורים אבן, quatuor ordines gemmarum. Item, אדם פטדת וברקת הטור האחד, Sardius, topazius et smaragdus, ordo primus. 5. Neque obscurum est, quomodo gemmarum ordinibus ornentur genae. Nempe si ex auribus pendeant, aut si inspergantur mitrarum redimiculis, id est, latis fasciis, quae per malas productae mento subligabantur. Nam in Syria mitra muliebre fuit capitis integumentum. Virgilius in Catalectis, col. 58

And Artemidorus, Onirocritica book 1, ch. 30: Παρειὰς ἴσχνας ἔχειν, ἢ ἑλκομένας, λύπας, ἢ πένθος σημαίνει. ἴσχνας μὲν λύπας, ἑλκομένας δὲ πένθος. καὶ γὰρ ἐν τοῖς πένθεσι λωβῶνται τὰς παρειὰς οἱ ἄνθρωποι· [Pareias ischnas echein, ē helkomenas, lypas, ē penthos sēmainei. ischnas men lypas, helkomenas de penthos. kai gar en tois penthesi lōbōntai tas pareias hoi anthrōpoi] To have thin or ulcerated cheeks (in dreams) signifies sorrow and mourning: thin cheeks sorrow, ulcerated ones mourning. For in mourning people tear their cheeks. I admit that I have read in Horus, Hieroglyph. book 2, ch. 50, that the turtledove has teeth. To signify a nursing woman, and one who nourishes well, he says, (the Egyptians) τρυγόνα ζωγραφοῦσιν· αὕτη γὰρ μόνη τῶν ἄλλων πτηνῶν ὀδόντας, καὶ μασθοὺς ἔχει [trygona zōgraphousin; hautē gar monē tōn allōn ptēnōn odontas, kai masthous echei], paint a turtledove: for she alone among birds has teeth and breasts. If this were true, she would also have jaws and cheeks. But learned men have already observed that this belongs to the bat, to which alone it applies. So some change τρυγόνα [trygona] into τριγόνα [trigona], conjecturing that the bat is called by that name there, because τρίζειν [trizein, to squeak] is proper to it. Others more correctly change it into νυκτερίδα [nykterida]; and the reason why the words were interchanged is obvious. Immediately before it had said: Wishing to signify a weak man who attempts great things, νυκτερίδα ζωγραφοῦσιν [nykterida zōgraphousin], they paint a bat, which flies without feathers. And immediately after follows: To designate a man who is charmed by dancing and the pipe, τρυγόνα ζωγραφοῦσιν [trygona zōgraphousin], they paint a turtledove, which is caught by the pipe and dancing. I have rendered turtledove with Mercerus [=Jean Mercier (d. 1570), commentaries on Job and Proverbs], Caussinus and others. Yet — and I am surprised this escaped them — τρυγὼν [trygōn] there is not the turtledove but the stingray, which this same writer below, in ch. 105, calls simply τρυγόνα [trygona], and others, to distinguish it, θαλαττίαν τρυγόνα [thalattian trygona], the sea turtledove. For it is not the bird, the turtledove, but ἡ θαλαττία τρυγὼν [hē thalattia trygōn], the sea turtledove, that is, the stingray, that, charmed by the pipe and dancing, is lured into the fish-trap, as Aelian relates at length, On Animals book 17, ch. 18; although Philo too refers this to the turtledove, the bird. Now, to return to where the discussion digressed: the words of the Sacred Song in Hebrew read thus: נאוו לחייך בתורים צוארך בחרוזים, Your cheeks are adorned with rows (of gems), your neck with chains. II, 600 For this the Greeks have Τί ὡραιώθησαν σιαγόνες σου ὡς τρυγόνος, τραχηλός σου ὡς ὅρμισκοι; [Ti hōraiōthēsan siagones sou hōs trygonos, trachēlos sou hōs hormiskoi?] and Jerome: How beautiful have your cheeks become, like the turtledove's; your neck like a necklace. For, interchanging ב and כ, they read כתורים for בתורים, and כחרוזים for בחרוזים, and they took תורי for turtledoves, whereas there it means rows, namely of gems, or of golden studs. That it must be rendered so is shown by many things: 1. תורים and חרוזים are here nearly synonymous. Moreover, although the word חרוזים does not occur elsewhere in Scripture, it is very well known from the Arabic language, in which the verb خرز [kharaza] means to sew with an awl, and الخرز [al-kharaz] a necklace of gems strung together, and also the spine, whose vertebrae are as it were sewn and strung together. Accordingly the Greek renders חרוזים as ὁρμισκοὺς [hormiskous], and Jerome as necklaces, entirely correctly. 2. Immediately there follows תורי זהב נעשה לך, where it is plain that תורי are not turtledoves but a kind of golden ornament, namely chains or something similar. Hence there Jerome has: We will make you golden chains. And the Syriac ܕܕܗܒܐ ܥܢܩܐ [דדהבא ענקא], a golden chain. And the fifth edition στρεπτὸν χρυσίου [strepton chrysiou]; so it should be read, not στρεπτοῦ [streptou]. For στρεπτὸς [streptos] or στρεπτὸν [strepton] is used everywhere for a torque by Herodotus, Xenophon, Plutarch and others. In Symmachus, for περίβλεπτα χρυσίου [periblepta chrysiou] I would read περίπλεκτα [periplekta]. For στρέφειν [strephein], whence στρεπτὸν [strepton], and πλέκειν [plekein], whence πλεκτὸν [plekton], are nearly synonymous. Hence in Hesychius πλόκιον [plokion] is εἶδος περιδεραίου [eidos perideraiou], a kind of necklace. And the same reasoning holds for the Syriac ܥܢܩܐ [ענקא] for torque, for the verb ܥܢܩ [ענק] means to fold and to twist. But why do the Elders render ὁμοιώματα [homoiōmata]? Did they read ציורי, that is, images, for תורי? Or did they think that תורי זהב meant likenesses of turtledoves made of gold, which was the opinion of Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra]? 3. Indeed, תור with Thau here is the same as טור with Teth, a word Moses uses repeatedly for a row of gems, as in Exod. XXVIII, 17: ארבעה טורים אבן, four rows of stones. Likewise, אדם פטדת וברקת הטור האחד, sardius, topaz and emerald, the first row. 5. Nor is it obscure how cheeks are adorned with rows of gems: namely if these hang from the ears, or if they are scattered over the ribbons of the mitres, that is, the broad bands that were drawn down along the cheeks and tied under the chin. For in Syria the mitre was a woman's head-covering. Virgil in the Catalecta: col. 58


Copa Syrisca caput Graia redimita mitella.

The Syrian tavern-hostess, her head bound with a Greek little mitre.


Iuvenalis Satyra 3.

Juvenal, Satire 3:


Ite, quibus grata est picta lupa barbara mitra.

Go, you who fancy a barbarian harlot with a painted mitre.


Barbara, id est, Syra; nam praecesserat,

Barbarian, that is, Syrian; for there had preceded:


Iam pridem Syrus in Tiberim defluxit Orontes Et linguam, et mores, et cum tibicine chordas II, 601 Obliquas, nec non gentilia tympana secum Vexit, et ad Circum jussas prostare puellas.

Long since has the Syrian Orontes flowed down into the Tiber, and brought with it its language and its manners, the slanting strings along with the piper, II, 601 and its native timbrels too, and the girls bidden to sell themselves at the Circus.


De turturum sacrificiis supra diximus. Actum etiam de castitate: et ex Aristotele, Aeliano et Clemente probatum, turtures nonnisi unum conjugem ad-mittere. Unde natum, quod magno consensu scripsere posteriores, mortuo conjuge turturem viduam permanere. Quo pertinere volunt haec verba Psaltis Psal. LXXIV, 19. Ne tradas catervae (hostium) animam turturis tuae, id est, inquiunt, Ecclesiae Israelis, quae, etiam a te deserta, alii Deo non adhaeret. Rabbi Selomo, התור הזה משמת הזכר בן זוגה אינה מזדווגת לאחר אף ישראל לא התחליפוך באל אחר אף על פי שרחקתה מהם והיו כאלמנה, Turtur foe- mina, ex quo obiit mas conjux ejus, alteri non copulatur. Ita nec Israelitae te cum alio Deo commutarunt, etiamsi ab iis recesseris, sed viduae instar manserunt. Sed nihil opus est eo usque descendere. Neque enim id satis certum est, turturem in viduitate alteri non copulari. Quamvis scriptores, qui id asserunt,

We have spoken above about the sacrifices of turtledoves. Their chastity has also been treated, and it was proved from Aristotle, Aelian and Clement that turtledoves admit only one mate. From this arose what later writers have stated with great unanimity: that when its mate has died, the turtledove remains a widow. To this they would refer these words of the Psalmist, Ps 74:19. Deliver not the soul of thy turtledove unto the multitude (of the enemies), that is, they say, the Church of Israel, which, even when forsaken by you, does not cleave to another God. R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)]: התור הזה משמת הזכר בן זוגה אינה מזדווגת לאחר אף ישראל לא התחליפוך באל אחר אף על פי שרחקתה מהם והיו כאלמנה, The female turtledove, once her male mate has died, does not pair with another. So too the Israelites have not exchanged you for another God, even though you have withdrawn from them, but have remained like a widow. But there is no need to go so far. For it is not sufficiently certain that the turtledove in widowhood does not pair with another, even though the writers who assert it


Defendat numerus, junctaeque umbone phalanges.

may be defended by their number and by phalanxes joined shield to shield.


At constat, saltem turturem, vivo conjuge, cum altero non commisceri. Ad quod exemplum ecclesia si se conformaverit, alios deos nunquam colet; quia Deus, quem colit, semper vivus est. Potuere etiam Israelitae cum turture conferri; לפי שהם חלושי הכח ונטרפים ואינם טורפים וכן ישראל, quia turtures viribus infirmae sunt, et diripiuntur, nec diripiunt, et sic Israelitae. Quae Kim- chii conjectura est. Nam et columbae genus est turtur, et in columbino genere omnium minima. Philosophus Hist. lib. 5. cap. 13. Ἐλάχιστον δὲ τῶν τοιούτων ἡ τρυγών· Minimum ex iis turtur est. Eodem quoque referri queant quaecunque de columbae simplicitate dicta sunt, cum turtur sit columbae genus. Mirabere, cur veterum interpretum, quotquot extant, nullus turturis meminerit in versione hujus loci. Nam, pro anima turturis tuae, Graeci habent ψυχὴν ἐξομολογουμένην σοι, animam, confitentem tibi. Quod idem sequuntur Syrus et Aethiops. Nempe תודך legerunt pro תורך, Daleth pro Res, quae litera sunt simillimae. Arabes editi habent نفسا عارفة بك animam, quae te no- vit. Et unus e manuscriptis, qui penes me sunt, انفس يايسيك animas, qui te sciunt, id est, qui te noverunt. Quasi legerint נפש תדעך, ani- col. 59 mam, quae novit te. At Hieronymus, Animam eruditam in Lege tua. Et Chal- daica versio Iosephi Coeci, נפשת מאלפי אוריתך, animas docentium Legem tuam. Quasi תורך alluderet ad vocem תורה, quae Legem sonat. Sed haec remota et aliena sunt. Et, si Graecos excipias, his omnibus vetustior Ionathan recte viderat, תור hic esse turturem. Atque is quidem non extat. Sed illum ita vertisse, II, 602 docent haec Selomonis: יונתן תירגם לשון תורים ובני יונה, Ionathan reddidit, ut in legis locis, quibus agitur de turturibus et filiis columbarum. Quod Hebraei merito sequuntur, et recentiores interpretes, quotquot habentur.

But it is certain at least that the turtledove does not mate with another while its mate is alive. If the Church conforms itself to this example, it will never worship other gods, because the God whom it worships is ever living. The Israelites could also be compared with the turtledove לפי שהם חלושי הכח ונטרפים ואינם טורפים וכן ישראל, because turtledoves are weak in strength, and are torn as prey but do not prey, and so are the Israelites. This is Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim]'s conjecture. For the turtledove is a kind of dove, and the smallest of all in the dove kind. The Philosopher, Hist. book 5, ch. 13: Ἐλάχιστον δὲ τῶν τοιούτων ἡ τρυγών [Elachiston de tōn toioutōn hē trygōn]· The smallest of these is the turtledove. To the same purpose could also be referred whatever has been said of the simplicity of the dove, since the turtledove is a kind of dove. You will wonder why none of the ancient translators, as many as are extant, mentioned the turtledove in rendering this passage. For in place of the soul of thy turtledove the Greeks have ψυχὴν ἐξομολογουμένην σοι [psychēn exomologoumenēn soi], a soul confessing to thee. The Syriac and the Ethiopic follow the same. They evidently read תודך for תורך, Daleth for Resh, which are very similar letters. The printed Arabic versions have نفسا عارفة بك [nafsan ʿārifatan bika] a soul that knows thee. And one of the manuscripts in my possession has انفس يايسيك [anfus yāysīk] souls who know thee, that is, who have known thee. As if they had read נפש תדעך, a soul col. 59 that knows thee. But Jerome has A soul instructed in thy Law. And the Chaldee version of Joseph the Blind has נפשת מאלפי אוריתך, the souls of those teaching thy Law, as though תורך alluded to the word תורה, which means Law. But these renderings are far-fetched and beside the point. And, apart from the Greeks, Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan], older than all of these, had rightly seen that תור here is the turtledove. His version, indeed, is not extant. But that he rendered it so is shown by these words of Selomo: II, 602 יונתן תירגם לשון תורים ובני יונה, Jonathan rendered it as in the passages of the Law dealing with turtledoves and young doves. The Hebrews rightly follow this, as do the more recent translators, as many as there are.

But he wrongly wrote the name of the animal as كمري [kmry] for قمري [qumrī]; see Golius [=Jacobus Golius, Lexicon Arabico-Latinum (1653)], Lexic. Arab. p. 1964, whose feminine is قُمْرِيَّة [qumriyya]; the male is also called ساق حرّ [sāq ḥurr], on which see Bochart, preceding Chapter, p. 52, marginal note. By a strange error Hufnagel [=W. F. Hufnagel, in Paulus's [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)] Repertorium für biblische und morgenländische Litteratur], V. S. V., in the Annotatt. in Cantic. in the Repertorium für biblische und morgenl. Litterat. vol. 10, p. 243 II, 598 243, note b), confuses the turtur [turtledove] with the turdus [thrush], Arab. سمرمر [smrmr], which Forsskål, p. 6 of the book cited, says arrives at Aleppo in the months of July and August. But there is no one who does not know that the turdus [thrush] is of an entirely different kind from the turtur [turtledove].


Part 2, Book 1, chapter 10: The swallow
---------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/sis.html

II, 602 col. 59 CAP. X.

II, 602 col. 59 CHAPTER X.


De Hirundine.

On the Swallow.


Cum תור thor, id est turture, junguntur סיס sis et עגור agor, ut aves pariter migratoriae, in his Ierem. VIII, 7. Et thor, et sis, et agor custodierunt tempus adventus sui. Et de turture cum sit actum, sequitur, ut agamus de sis et agor. Quae voces rursus occurrunt in Ezechiae, regis, cantico Es. XXXVIII, 14. Ut sis (inquit) et agor pipiebam, gemebam ut columba. Sed harum alibi nulla mentio. Et cum utroque loco סוס in textu scribatur per Vau, tamen in Ieremia Hebraei סיס sis, per Iod legunt. Quam lectionem maxime probo, cum ut col. 60 סיס sis, a voce סוס sus, differat, qua significatur equus, tum quia סיס sis videtur magis exprimere naturam rei, quae hoc nomine significatur (1). Quod ipsum, quia in quaestione est, jam disquirendum. Pagninus, Munsterus, Buxtorfius, Schindlerus, Iunius, et Tremellius, Angli, Itali, etc. et plerique alii novi interpretes סיס sis gruem constanter exponunt. Ita nimirum statuunt Hebraeorum doctissimi, Iarchius, Kimchius et Pomarius, Ionathanem sequuti in Chaldaica Paraphrasi, quae pro סיס sis habet כורכיא kurkeja. Porro כורכיא kurkeja gruem esse, tam ex Talmude constat, quam ex Arabum scriptoribus, qui scribunt كركي kurki. Pro כורכיא kurkeja quandoque reperias כרוכיא krukeja, ut in tractatu Kiddusim cap. 2. fol. 44. a. Cui voci simillima est vox כרוכא kruka, quae pro חגב chagab, seu cicada, apud Ionathanem occurrit Levit. XI, 22. Extabat etiam olim in Paraphrasi Ierusalem, ex qua citatur ab Elia in Methurgeman. Unde natus jocularis error in Symmacho, qui, promiscue sumens voces כרוכא kruka et כרוכיא krukeja, ex grue in Ieremia cicadam fecit. Hinc Hieronymus in Ieremiam: Symmachus cicadam transtulit, quae Hebraice dicitur סיס sis. Et ibidem Theodoretus, Τρυγὼν, καὶ τέττιξ, καὶ χελιδὼν, ἀγροῦ στρουθία, ἐφύλαξαν καιροὺς εἰσόδων αὐτῶν· Turtur, et cicada, et hirundo, II, 603 agri aviculae, observarunt tempus adventus sui. Quae ipsa verba postquam citavit Chrysostomus in Homilia De turture, tanquam ex Ieremia, addit pro commentario, Τρυγόνα λέγων τὴν πάνσεμνον ἐκκλησίαν, χελιδόνα τὸν φιλέρημον Ἰωάννην, τέττιγα τὸν εὔλαλον Παῦλον. Turturem vocans venerabilem ecclesiam, hirundinem deserti incolam, Ioannem, cicadam eloquentem Paulum. Qui er-ror ex alio errore ortus. Tam enim falluntur, qui סיס sis gruem, quam qui cicadam reddunt: cum סיס sis neque grus, neque cicada sit, sed hirundo. Id probat primo consensus vetustiorum interpretum, qui apud me multum potest, cum ei non repugnat necessaria ratio, qualis hoc loco nulla se offert. Vetustiores hic appello, 1. Graecos Seniores, a quibus סיס sis χελιδὼν utroque loco exponitur; 2. Theodotionem; 3. Hieronymum, qui id ipsum sequuntur; 4. Il-lum ipsum Symmachum, cui סיס sis in Ieremia est cicada. Ab eodem enim Ezechiae verba כסוס עגור redduntur ὡς χελιδὼν ἐγκλεισθεῖσα, ut hirundo inclusa. 5. His adde Arabem, cui סיס sis est سنونوه sununua, id est, hirundo. In Abi Ubid, Cent. 1. Prov. 32. سنونية senunia scribitur, et hirundinem recte explicaverat Erpenius ὁ μακαρίτης, sed solum ex conjectura. Avis, inquit, nomen esse, satis liquet: at cujusmodi nescio. Verti hirundinem, quod sic fere verti soleat סנוניתא senunitha Chaldaicum. Alioqui hirundo خطاف chottaph vocatur, etc. His viri, in Arabicis literis longe doctissimi, et de me olim optime meriti, dubiis ut occurratur, libet vocem explicare accuratius. خطاف chottaph est hirundo in genere, a volatus rapiditate sic dicta, ut Chaldaice חטפיתא chatphitha. Sed hujus plures sunt species, quas in Damire sic definiunt Arabes: الخطاطيف انواع منها نوع يالف السواحل عند البحر يحفر بيتها هناك ويعشش هناك وهو صغير الجثة دون عصغور الجنة ولونه رمادي col. 61 والناس يسمونه سنونوا بضم السين المهملة ونونين ومنها نوع لخضرته علي ظهرة بعض حمرة اصغر من الدرة تسميه اهل مصر الخضري لخضرته يغتات الغراش والذباب ونحو ذلك ومنها طويل الاجنحة رقيقها يالف الجبال وياكل النمل وهذا النوع يقال له السايم مغرب سامه ومنهم من يسمي هذا النوع السنونوا الوحدة سنونوة وهو كثير في المسجد الحرام بمكة يعشش في سقف المسجد في مقام ابراهيم وباب بني شيبة وبعض الناس II, 604 يزعم انه الطير الابابيل الذي عذب الله به اصحاب الغيل Hirundinum variae sunt species: quarum una degit in maris littoribus, et ibi effossa domo sua nidulatur. Haec corpore minor est ave Paradisi, et cinerei coloris. Vocatur sununu per Sin Semol dammatum et duo Nun. Est et species viridis cum aliqua rubedine super dorsum, minor psittaco, quam Aegyptii ratione coloris vocant chadra, id est, viridem. Vescitur papilionibus, muscis atque aliis similibus animalculis. Est et alia species longis alis, et tenuibus, incola montium, formicas edens. Has semaim appellant a Singulari semama. Sed et nonnulli sununu vocant. Singulare unitatis est sununua. Hujus speciei multae sunt in templo Charam Mecchanae urbis, quae in templi tecto nidificant, in Abrahami statione, in porta filiorum Seibae. Quidam asserunt, aves esse ababil dictas, per quas Deus castigavit socios elephantis: jactis scilicet in eorum capita حجارة من سجيل lapidibus ex siggil. Ita illi vocant lapides, in inferorum igne excoctos et induratos, cum eorum, in quos cadebant, nominibus inscriptis. Il-lorum dux Abraheth, rex Abasenorum in Arabia Felici intima, eo ipso anno, quo natus est Mahometh, magno elephante vectus cum multis copiis venerat, ut Mecchanum templum exscinderet. Quod pseudo-propheta obiter tangit Azoara cxv, cui titulus الغيل Elephas. Sed haec sunt alterius loci. Hic notasse sufficiat, constare ex iis, quae allata sunt, سنونوة sununua proprie dici ripariam hirundinem (2), de qua Plinius lib. 10. cap. 33. Tertium est earum genus, quae ripas excavant, atque ita internidificant. Et lib. 30. cap. 4. Multo tamen efficacissimi ripariarum (hirundinum) pulli. Ita vocant in riparum cavis nidificantes. Riparia Graece dicitur δρεπανὶς a falcatis pedibus. Ita vocat Philosophus Hist. col. 62 lib. 1. cap. 1. Sed et eodem nomine سنونوة sununua illas hirundines significari addunt, quae in montibus et templis nidificant. Hae sunt rusticae, seu agrestes Plinii hirundines, de quibus Gesnerus pag. 565. (3). Interim certum est, hoc nomen quandoque patere latius, et pro quavis hirundine sumi. Ut, cum lapis اليرقان icterias, id est, quo sanantur icterici, alio nomine vocatur حجر السنونوة lapis sununuae, id est, hirundinis; quia in ejus nido reperitur. Nam hirundinis pullos croco tingunt Arabes; et pater, eos ictero laborare suspicatus, lapidem illum ex India in nidum affert et pullis supponit. Parvum describit Damir, lineis rubris striatum, quae ad nigredinem vergunt. Ita etiam qui scripsit De Naturae mirabilibus, ubi صنونو sununu per Sad perperam legi notat Damir. Et Baruch. VI, 21. Graeca haec verba, Ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν II, 605 αὐτῶν ἐφίπτανται χελιδόνες, Arabs ita reddidit: السنونو تلمسهم علي راسهم Assununu (seu hirundines) tangunt eos super capita sua. Tangunt, id est, ἐφάπτονται, quomodo legit pro ἐφίπτανται involant.

With תור thor, that is, the turtledove, are joined סיס sis and עגור agor, as birds that are likewise migratory, in these words of Jer 8:7. Both thor and sis and agor have kept the time of their coming. And since the turtledove has been dealt with, it follows that we treat of sis and agor. These words occur again in the song of King Hezekiah, Isa 38:14. Like sis (he says) and agor I chirped, I moaned like a dove. But elsewhere there is no mention of them. And although in both places סוס is written in the text with Vau, yet in Jeremiah the Hebrews read סיס sis, with Iod. This reading I strongly approve, both so that סיס sis may differ from the word סוס sus, which means horse, and because סיס sis seems better to express the nature of the thing signified by this name R1. This very point, since it is in question, must now be examined. Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae], Munster, Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum], Schindler, Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] and Tremellius [=Immanuel Tremellius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], the English, the Italians, etc., and most other modern interpreters consistently render סיס sis as crane. So, of course, the most learned of the Hebrews hold, Jarchi [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac), called Jarchi by the Christian Hebraists], Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] and Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)], following Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] in the Chaldee Paraphrase, which has כורכיא kurkeja for סיס sis. Further, that כורכיא kurkeja is the crane is clear both from the Talmud and from the Arab writers, who write كركي [kurkī] kurki. For כורכיא kurkeja you sometimes find כרוכיא krukeja, as in the tractate Kiddusim, ch. 2, fol. 44a. Very similar to this word is the word כרוכא kruka, which occurs in Jonathan at Lev 11:22 for חגב chagab, or cicada. It once also stood in the Jerusalem Paraphrase, from which it is cited by Elias [=Elijah Levita (1469–1549), author of the Aramaic lexicon Meturgeman and of Tishbi] in the Methurgeman. Hence arose an amusing error in Symmachus, who, taking the words כרוכא kruka and כרוכיא krukeja indiscriminately, made a cicada out of the crane in Jeremiah. Hence Jerome on Jeremiah: Symmachus translated it 'cicada', which in Hebrew is called סיס sis. And in the same place Theodoret: Τρυγὼν, καὶ τέττιξ, καὶ χελιδὼν, ἀγροῦ στρουθία, ἐφύλαξαν καιροὺς εἰσόδων αὐτῶν· [Trygōn, kai tettix, kai chelidōn, agrou strouthia, ephylaxan kairous eisodōn autōn] The turtledove, and the cicada, and the swallow, II, 603 little birds of the field, have observed the time of their coming. After Chrysostom quoted these very words in the Homily On the Turtledove, as if from Jeremiah, he adds by way of commentary: Τρυγόνα λέγων τὴν πάνσεμνον ἐκκλησίαν, χελιδόνα τὸν φιλέρημον Ἰωάννην, τέττιγα τὸν εὔλαλον Παῦλον [Trygona legōn tēn pansemnon ekklēsian, chelidona ton philerēmon Iōannēn, tettiga ton eulalon Paulon]. Calling the venerable church the turtledove, the dweller in the desert, John, the swallow, and the eloquent Paul the cicada. This error arose from another error. For those who render סיס sis as crane are as mistaken as those who render it cicada: since סיס sis is neither the crane nor the cicada, but the swallow. This is proved first by the agreement of the older interpreters, which carries great weight with me when no compelling reason opposes it, and here none presents itself. As older interpreters I here name: 1. the Greek Elders, by whom סיס sis is rendered χελιδὼν [chelidōn] in both places; 2. Theodotion; 3. Jerome, who follow the same; 4. that very Symmachus for whom סיס sis in Jeremiah is the cicada. For by him Hezekiah's words כסוס עגור are rendered ὡς χελιδὼν ἐγκλεισθεῖσα [hōs chelidōn enkleistheisa], like a swallow shut in. 5. Add to these the Arabic translator, for whom סיס sis is سنونوه [sunūnūh] sununua, that is, swallow. In Abi Ubid, Century 1, Proverb 32, it is written سنونية [sunūniya] senunia, and the late Erpenius ὁ μακαρίτης [ho makaritēs] had rightly explained it as swallow, but only by conjecture. That it is the name of a bird, he says, is clear enough; but of what kind I do not know. I translated it swallow, because the Chaldee סנוניתא senunitha is usually so translated. Otherwise the swallow is called خطاف [khuṭṭāf] chottaph, etc. To meet these doubts of a man by far the most learned in Arabic letters, and once most deserving of my gratitude, I wish to explain the word more precisely. خطاف [khuṭṭāf] chottaph is the swallow in general, so called from the swiftness of its flight, like the Chaldee חטפיתא chatphitha. But of this there are several species, which the Arabs in Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] define thus: الخطاطيف انواع منها نوع يالف السواحل عند البحر يحفر بيتها هناك ويعشش هناك وهو صغير الجثة دون عصغور الجنة ولونه رمادي [al-khaṭāṭīf anwāʿ minhā nawʿ yaʾlaf al-sawāḥil ʿinda al-baḥr yaḥfir baytahā hunāka wa-yuʿashshish hunāka wa-huwa ṣaghīr al-jutha dūna ʿaṣghūr al-janna wa-lawnuhu ramādī] col. 61 والناس يسمونه سنونوا بضم السين المهملة ونونين ومنها نوع لخضرته علي ظهرة بعض حمرة اصغر من الدرة تسميه اهل مصر الخضري لخضرته يغتات الغراش والذباب ونحو ذلك ومنها طويل الاجنحة رقيقها يالف الجبال وياكل النمل وهذا النوع يقال له السايم مغرب سامه ومنهم من يسمي هذا النوع السنونوا الوحدة سنونوة وهو كثير في المسجد الحرام بمكة يعشش في سقف المسجد في مقام ابراهيم وباب بني شيبة وبعض الناس [wa-al-nās yusammūnahu sunūnū bi-ḍamm al-sīn al-muhmala wa-nūnayn wa-minhā nawʿ li-khuḍratihi ʿalā ẓahrih baʿḍ ḥumra aṣghar min al-durra tusammīhi ahl Miṣr al-khuḍarī li-khuḍratihi yaghtāt al-gharāsh wa-al-dhubāb wa-naḥw dhālika wa-minhā ṭawīl al-ajniḥa raqīquhā yaʾlaf al-jibāl wa-yaʾkul al-naml wa-hādhā al-nawʿ yuqāl lahu al-sāyim mughrib sāmih wa-minhum man yusammī hādhā al-nawʿ al-sunūnū al-waḥda sunūnūa wa-huwa kathīr fī al-masjid al-ḥarām bi-Makka yuʿashshish fī saqf al-masjid fī maqām Ibrāhīm wa-bāb banī Shayba wa-baʿḍ al-nās] II, 604 يزعم انه الطير الابابيل الذي عذب الله به اصحاب الغيل [yazʿum annahu al-ṭayr al-abābīl alladhī ʿadhdhaba Allāh bihi aṣḥāb al-ghīl] There are various species of swallows. One of them lives on the shores of the sea, and there digs out its home and nests. It is smaller in body than the bird of Paradise, and ash-grey in colour. It is called sununu, with Sin Semol given damma and two Nun. There is also a green species with some redness on the back, smaller than a parrot, which the Egyptians on account of its colour call chadra, that is, green. It feeds on butterflies, flies and other similar small creatures. There is also another species, with long and slender wings, a dweller in the mountains, which eats ants. These they call semaim, from the singular semama. But some also call them sununu. The singular of unity is sununua. Of this species there are many in the Charam temple of the city of Mecca, which nest in the roof of the temple, at the station of Abraham and at the gate of the sons of Seiba. Some assert that these are the birds called ababil, by which God punished the companions of the elephant: namely by throwing on their heads حجارة من سجيل [ḥijāra min sijjīl] stones of siggil. So they call stones baked and hardened in the fire of hell, inscribed with the names of those on whom they fell. Their leader Abraheth, king of the Abyssinians in the interior of Arabia Felix, in the very year in which Muhammad was born, had come riding a great elephant with large forces in order to destroy the temple of Mecca. The pseudo-prophet touches on this in passing in Azoara 115, entitled الغيل [al-ghīl] The Elephant. But these matters belong elsewhere. Here it suffices to have noted that it is clear from what has been adduced that سنونوة [sunūnūa] sununua properly denotes the sand martin [hirundo riparia] R2, of which Pliny, book 10, ch. 33: The third kind of them is those which hollow out banks and so nest within. And book 30, ch. 4: Yet by far the most efficacious are the young of the bank (swallows). So they call those that nest in hollows of riverbanks. The riparia [bank swallow] is called in Greek δρεπανὶς [drepanis], from its sickle-shaped feet. So the Philosopher calls it, Hist. col. 62 book 1, ch. 1. But they add that by the same name سنونوة [sunūnūa] sununua are also signified those swallows which nest in mountains and temples. These are the rustic or field swallows of Pliny, on which see Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium], p. 565 R3. Meanwhile it is certain that this name sometimes extends more widely and is used for any swallow. Thus the stone اليرقان [al-yaraqān] icterias, that is, by which jaundice sufferers are healed, is by another name called حجر السنونوة [ḥajar al-sunūnūa] the stone of the sununua, that is, of the swallow, because it is found in its nest. For the Arabs dye the swallow's young with saffron; and the father, suspecting that they suffer from jaundice, brings that stone from India into the nest and places it under the young. Damir describes it as small, streaked with red lines that verge on black. So too the author On the Wonders of Nature, where, as Damir notes, صنونو [ṣunūnū] sununu is wrongly read with Sad. And at Bar 6:21 the Arabic translator rendered these Greek words, Ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν II, 605 αὐτῶν ἐφίπτανται χελιδόνες [Epi tēn kephalēn autōn ephiptantai chelidones], thus: السنونو تلمسهم علي راسهم [al-sunūnū talmisuhum ʿalā raʾsihim] Assununu (or swallows) touch them upon their heads. Touch, that is, ἐφάπτονται [ephaptontai], as he read instead of ἐφίπτανται [ephiptantai], fly upon.


Probatum est hactenus, plerisque veterum סיס sis esse hirundinem. Quibus Ionathan frustra opponitur, quasi כורכיא, id est, gruem, reddiderit. Ille enim duas voces סיס sis, et עגור agor, recte explicavit per כורכיא kurkeja, et סנוניתא sununitha, id est, gruem et hirundinem. Nam, ut סיס sis est hirundo, sic עגור agor est grus, ut sequenti capite docebitur. Sed invertit ordinem, et hirundinem, quae in Hebraeo textu prior est, posteriore loco posuit. Quod interpretibus saepe accidit. Et, ne longius exempla petantur, in loco Baruch, quem nuper citavimus, pro Graecis verbis νυκτερίδες, χελιδόνες, vespertiliones et hirundines, Arabs habet, inverso ordine, السنونو والوطاويط hirundines et vespertiliones. Proinde Chaldaeum etiam, quem Syrus sequutus est, iis veterum addimus, quibus סיס sis est hirundo. Ita, ut priscorum interpretum jam nullus sit, qui non assentiatur versioni, quam asserimus.

It has been proved so far that for most of the ancients סיס sis is the swallow. Against them Jonathan is cited in vain, as though he had rendered it כורכיא, that is, crane. For he correctly explained the two words סיס sis and עגור agor by כורכיא kurkeja and סנוניתא sununitha, that is, crane and swallow. For as סיס sis is the swallow, so עגור agor is the crane, as will be shown in the following chapter. But he inverted the order, and put the swallow, which comes first in the Hebrew text, in the second place. This often happens with translators. And, not to seek examples further afield, in the passage of Baruch which we cited a little earlier, for the Greek words νυκτερίδες, χελιδόνες [nykterides, chelidones], bats and swallows, the Arabic has, in inverted order, السنونو والوطاويط [al-sunūnū wa-l-waṭāwīṭ] swallows and bats. Accordingly we add the Chaldee also, whom the Syriac followed, to those of the ancients for whom סיס sis is the swallow. Thus there is now none of the early translators who does not agree with the rendering we maintain.


Ad hanc veterum auctoritatem accedit manifesta ratio. Vox סיס sis est ὀνοματοποιητικὴ, qua Hebraeus fuit animus hirundinis ψιθυρισμὸν utcunque imitari. Ut Italis circa Venetiam, quibus zisilla est hirundo, et zisillare hirundinis more τιτυβίζειν, vel ψιθυρίζειν. Zinzilulare dixit auctor Philomelae,

To this authority of the ancients is added a clear reason. The word סיס sis is ὀνοματοποιητικὴ [onomatopoiētikē], by which the Hebrew intended to imitate, after a fashion, the swallow's ψιθυρισμὸν [psithyrismon]. So with the Italians around Venice, for whom zisilla is the swallow, and zisillare means to τιτυβίζειν [titybizein] or ψιθυρίζειν [psithyrizein] in the manner of a swallow. The author of the Philomela said zinzilulare:


Regulus, atque merops, et rubro pectore Progne,
Consimili modulo zinzilulare sciunt.

The wren and the bee-eater, and Procne with red breast,
Know how to zinzilulare with a like measure.


Quasi Prognes, id est, hirundinis vox sit zizi, unde zizilulare dici debuit, ut Italice zisillare. Sed euphoniae causa additum est N epentheticum, quod in Romanis vocibus frequens. Tale lingo ex λείχω, linquo, ex Aeolico λείκω, pro λείπω, tango, ex θίγω, pango, ex πάγω pro πήγω, densus, ex δασὺς, pinguis, ex παχὺς, etc. (4).

As though the voice of Procne, that is, of the swallow, were zizi, from which zizilulare ought to have been said, as in Italian zisillare. But for the sake of euphony an epenthetic N was added, which is frequent in Roman words. Such are lingo from λείχω [leichō], linquo from the Aeolic λείκω [leikō] for λείπω [leipō], tango from θίγω [thigō], pango from πάγω [pagō] for πήγω [pēgō], densus from δασὺς [dasys], pinguis from παχὺς [pachys], etc. R4.


Nec leve in eo momentum est, quod Isidem in hirundinem mutatam fuisse fabulantur Aegyptii. Plutarchus in Iside, Αὐτὴν δὲ γενομένην χελιδόνα (φασὶ)

Nor is it of slight weight that the Egyptians relate in their fables that Isis was changed into a swallow. Plutarch in the Isis: Αὐτὴν δὲ γενομένην χελιδόνα (φασὶ) [Autēn de genomenēn chelidona (phasi)]


II, 606 τῇ κίονι περιπέτεσθαι, καὶ θρηνεῖν· Eam autem hirundinem factam (ajunt) circa columnam volasse et luxisse. Nam Isis palam ad sis alludit. Et fabulosae Deorum metamorphoses vocum allusionibus saepe nituntur. Sic Anubis fingebatur cum canino capite, quia Hebraice נובח nobeah latrantem sonat. Et rex Apis in bove cultus est, propter allusionem ad אביר abir: Hebraei enim bovem ita nominant. Unde LXX. Ier. XLVI, 15. Διὰ τί ἔφυγεν ὁ Ἄπις, pro Hebraeis col. 63 מדוע נסחף אבירך, quomodo legerunt pro אביריך. Et in historia Gigantomachiae, Dii, gigantum metu in Aegyptum arrepta fuga, in varias formas se mutaverunt. Ovidius lib. 5. Metamorphoseωs,

II, 606 τῇ κίονι περιπέτεσθαι, καὶ θρηνεῖν· [tē kioni peripetesthai, kai thrēnein] And she, having become a swallow (they say), flew around the pillar and lamented. For Isis plainly alludes to sis. And the fabulous metamorphoses of the gods often rest on allusions of words. Thus Anubis was represented with a dog's head, because in Hebrew נובח nobeah means barking. And king Apis was worshipped in a bull, because of the allusion to אביר abir: for the Hebrews so name the bull. Hence the LXX at Ier. XLVI, 15: Διὰ τί ἔφυγεν ὁ Ἄπις [Dia ti ephygen ho Apis], for the Hebrew col. 63 מדוע נסחף אבירך, as they read in place of אביריך. And in the story of the Gigantomachy the gods, having taken flight into Egypt for fear of the giants, changed themselves into various forms. Ovid, book 5 of the Metamorphoses:


Duxque gregis, dixit, sis Iuppiter, unde recurvis Nunc quoque formatus Libys est cum cornibus Hammon: Delius in corvo, proles Semeleïa capro, Fele soror Phoebi, nivea Saturnia vacca, Pisce Venus latuit, Cyllenius ibidis alis.

Jupiter, she said, became leader of the flock, whence even now Libyan Hammon is fashioned with curved horns: The Delian hid in a raven, the offspring of Semele in a goat, The sister of Phoebus in a cat, the daughter of Saturn in a snow-white cow, Venus in a fish, the Cyllenian in the wings of an ibis.


Antonius Liberalis Fab. 28. ex Nicandro, Ἀπόλλων μὲν ἐγένετο ἱέραξ, Ἑρμῆς δὲ ἴβις, Ἄρης δὲ λεπιδωτὸς ἰχθὺς, Ἄρτεμις δὲ αἴλουρος (sic legendum pro σί-λουρος, ut ex Ovidio patet) τράγῳ δὲ εἰκάζεται Διόνυσος, ἔλλῳ δὲ Ἡρακλῆς, βοὶ δ᾽ Ἥφαιστος, μυγάλῃ δὲ Λητώ· Apollo in accipitrem mutatus est, Mercurius in ibin, Mars in lepidotum piscem, Diana in felem, Bacchus in caprum, Hercules in hinnulum, Vulcanus in bovem, Latona in murem araneum. Quae omnia hic explicare non aggredimur, sed pauca,. quibus confingendis occasio ex paranomasiis sumpta est. Iupiter, summus Deus, in arietem mutatus est, quia אל el Deus fortis, et איל ajil aries sunt paronyma, et utriusque Plurale est אלים elim; Bacchus, Aegyptiis Osiris, in hircum, quia ad Osirim alludit שעיר seir, Hebraice hircus. Diana in felem, quia Aegyptiace ΒΟΥΒΑΣΤΟΣ erat felis, et Bubastis Diana. Unum est in Stephano voce Βούβαστος, Οἱ δὲ Αἰγύπτιοι βού-βαστον τὴν αἴλουρόν φασι· Aegyptii autem felem bubaston vocant: alterum Herodoti lib. 2. cap. 156. Αἰγυπτιστὶ δὲ Ἀπόλλων Ὧρος, Δημήτηρ δὲ Ἶσις, Ἄρτεμις δὲ Βούβαστις· Aegyptiace quidem Apollo est Horus, Ceres Isis, Diana Bubastis. Unde est, quod in Apuleji Herbario cap. 10. Artemisiam Aegyptii Βουβαστέως καρδίαν, cor Bubastis vocant, id est, herbam, Dianae charam, quod et Graecum nomen prae se fert. Iuno sumpsit bovis figuram. Nam עשתרות, unde Iuno dicta est Astarte, non solum ovium greges, sed et armenta boum significare, suo loco observavimus, atque inde esse, quod apud Sanchoniathonem Astarte ἐπέθηκε τῇ ἰδίᾳ κεφαλῇ βασιλείας παράσημον κεφαλὴν ταύρου, capiti pro regni insignibus caput tauri imposuit. Quod pisce Venus latuit, ad Atergatin referunt, quasi sit Dagon, cui דג dag, id est, piscis nomen fecerit: quod tamen minus probo ob rationes, alibi allatas.

Antoninus Liberalis, Fab. 28, from Nicander: Ἀπόλλων μὲν ἐγένετο ἱέραξ, Ἑρμῆς δὲ ἴβις, Ἄρης δὲ λεπιδωτὸς ἰχθὺς, Ἄρτεμις δὲ αἴλουρος [Apollōn men egeneto hierax, Hermēs de ibis, Arēs de lepidōtos ichthys, Artemis de ailouros] (so it must be read instead of σίλουρος [silouros], as is clear from Ovid) τράγῳ δὲ εἰκάζεται Διόνυσος, ἔλλῳ δὲ Ἡρακλῆς, βοὶ δ᾽ Ἥφαιστος, μυγάλῃ δὲ Λητώ [tragō de eikazetai Dionysos, ellō de Hēraklēs, boi d' Hēphaistos, mygalē de Lētō]: Apollo was changed into a hawk, Mercury into an ibis, Mars into a scaly fish, Diana into a cat, Bacchus into a goat, Hercules into a fawn, Vulcan into an ox, Latona into a shrew-mouse. We do not undertake to explain all of these here, but only a few, for whose invention the occasion was taken from paronomasias. Jupiter, the supreme God, was changed into a ram, because אל el, God the strong, and איל ajil, ram, are paronyms, and the plural of both is אלים elim. Bacchus, the Osiris of the Egyptians, into a he-goat, because שעיר seir, in Hebrew he-goat, alludes to Osiris. Diana into a cat, because in Egyptian ΒΟΥΒΑΣΤΟΣ was the cat, and Bubastis was Diana. The one is in Stephanus, under the word Βούβαστος [Boubastos]: Οἱ δὲ Αἰγύπτιοι βούβαστον τὴν αἴλουρόν φασι [Hoi de Aigyptioi boubaston tēn ailouron phasi]: but the Egyptians call the cat bubastos; the other in Herodotus, book 2, ch. 156: Αἰγυπτιστὶ δὲ Ἀπόλλων Ὧρος, Δημήτηρ δὲ Ἶσις, Ἄρτεμις δὲ Βούβαστις [Aigyptisti de Apollōn Hōros, Dēmētēr de Isis, Artemis de Boubastis]: in Egyptian Apollo is Horus, Ceres Isis, Diana Bubastis. Hence it is that in the Herbarium of Apuleius, ch. 10, the Egyptians call Artemisia Βουβαστέως καρδίαν [Boubasteōs kardian], the heart of Bubastis, that is, the herb dear to Diana, as its Greek name also displays. Juno took the shape of a cow. For we have observed in its place that עשתרות, from which Juno was called Astarte, signifies not only flocks of sheep but also herds of cattle, and that this is why in Sanchuniathon Astarte ἐπέθηκε τῇ ἰδίᾳ κεφαλῇ βασιλείας παράσημον κεφαλὴν ταύρου [epethēke tē idia kephalē basileias parasēmon kephalēn taurou], placed a bull's head on her own head as the insignia of royalty. That Venus hid in a fish they refer to Atargatis, as if she were Dagon, to whom דג dag, that is, fish, gave the name; but I approve this less, for reasons given elsewhere.


II, 607 Ezechias in morbo dicit se ut hirundinem pipivisse [Ies. XXXVIII, 14.], quia vox hirundinis videtur aliquid habere querulum et luctuosum. Hoc uno ore clamant omnes poetae. Hesiodus in Operibus versu 366.

II, 607 Hezekiah in his illness says that he chirped like a swallow [Isa 38:14], because the swallow's voice seems to have something plaintive and mournful about it. All the poets proclaim this with one voice. Hesiod, in the Works, verse 366:


Τὸν δὲ μετ' ὀρθρογόη Πανδιονὶς ὦρτο χελιδὼν,

Τὸν δὲ μετ' ὀρθρογόη Πανδιονὶς ὦρτο χελιδὼν, [Ton de met' orthrogoē Pandionis ōrto chelidōn,]


Post hunc mane lugens Pandionis filia prodiit hirundo. Unde Suidas, Ὀρθρογόη· χελιδών. Alii malunt ὀρθογόη. Hesychius, Ὀρθογόη· ἡ χελιδών. Itaque hinc corrigenda in Cyrilli Lexico apud me MSS. Ὀρθογόν· χελιδών. In Etymologico ὀρθογόη redditur ἡ μεγάλως θρηνοῦσα, quae multum luget. Ita etiam in Phavorino, qui addit, de hirundine dici. Aristophanes in Ranis,

After him, lamenting at dawn, came forth the swallow, daughter of Pandion. Hence Suidas: Ὀρθρογόη· χελιδών [Orthrogoē: chelidōn]. Others prefer ὀρθογόη [orthogoē]. Hesychius: Ὀρθογόη· ἡ χελιδών [Orthogoē: hē chelidōn]. Accordingly, from this, Ὀρθογόν· χελιδών [Orthogon: chelidōn] must be corrected in the manuscript Lexicon of Cyril in my possession. In the Etymologicum ὀρθογόη [orthogoē] is rendered ἡ μεγάλως θρηνοῦσα [hē megalōs thrēnousa], she who laments greatly. So too in Phavorinus, who adds that it is said of the swallow. Aristophanes in the Frogs:


Δὴ χείλεσιν ἀμφιλάλοις
Δεινὸν ἐπιβρέμεται
Θρηΐκια χελιδὼν,
Ἐπὶ βάρβαρον ἑζομένη πέταλον,
Κελαδεῖ δ' ἐπίκλαυτον ἀηδόνιον νόμον,

Δὴ χείλεσιν ἀμφιλάλοις Δεινὸν ἐπιβρέμεται Θρηΐκια χελιδὼν, Ἐπὶ βάρβαρον ἑζομένη πέταλον, Κελαδεῖ δ' ἐπίκλαυτον ἀηδόνιον νόμον, [Dē cheilesin amphilalois Deinon epibremetai Thrēikia chelidōn, Epi barbaron hezomenē petalon, Keladei d' epiklauton aēdonion nomon,]


Iam labris loquacibus
Grave resonat
Thracia hirundo,
Supra barbarum sedens folium,
Canit autem luctuosam stridulam cantilenam.

Now with chattering lips
the Thracian swallow
resounds heavily, sitting upon a barbarian leaf, and sings a mournful, shrill song.

Ἀλλ' Ἴτυλον κλαίοιτε κατ' οὔρεα, καὶ γοάοιτε,
