Sed his opponitur, quod Plato, eos refellens, qui cygnos dicunt, θρηνοῦντας τὸν θάνατον ὑπὸ λύπης ἐξάδειν, mortem deflentes, prae moerore canere: Οὐδὲν, inquit, ὄρνεον ᾄδει ὅταν πεινῇ, ἢ ῥιγοῖ, ἤ τινα ἄλλην λύπην λυπεῖται· οὐδὲ αὐτὴ ἥ τε ἀηδὼν, καὶ χελιδὼν, καὶ ὁ ἔποψ, ὃν δή φασι διὰ λύπην θρηνοῦντα ᾄδειν (lege οὓς δὴ φ. δ. λ. θρηνοῦντας ᾄδειν) Nulla avis canit cum esurit, aut alget, aut alia de causa tristis est, ne luscinia quidem, et hirundo, et upupa, quas ajunt prae moerore lugubriter canere. Proinde Proclus ferre non potest, ut hirundo ab Hesiodo vocetur ὀρθογόη, et legi vult ὀρθοβόη, mane clamans, ne a Platone videatur Poeta dissentire. At aliter respondet Tzetzes: Ὑμεῖς δ' ἴσμεν καὶ δίχα μάρτυρος Πλάτωνος, ὅτι οὐδὲν ὄρνεον λυπούμενον ᾄδει· ἀλλὰ δεινῶς, καὶ ῥητο-ρικῶς ὁ ποιητὴς τὴν λαλιὰν τῆς χελιδόνος θρῆνον εἶναι λέγει κατὰ τὸν μῦθον τῆς τοῦ Πανδίονος ἐκείνης θυγατρός. Nos vero etiam sine Platone teste scimus, nullam avem in moerore canere. Sed perite et rhetorice Poeta cantum hirundinis lamentationem vocat, juxta fabulam de Pandionis filia. Haec ille, quasi nonnisi col. 65 propter fabulam lugere dicatur hirundo. Quin cum Pausania in Atticis, σφίσι τὴν ἐς ἀηδόνα, καὶ χελιδόνα, μεταβολὴν ἐπεφήμισαν, ὅτι οἶμαι, καὶ αὗται αἱ ὄρνιθες ἐλεεινὸν, καὶ θρήνῳ ὅμοιον ᾄδουσιν, vulgatam fabulam de Pandionis filiabus, earum unam in lusciniam, alteram in hirundinem esse mutatam, ex eo ex- istimo. quod avis utraque miserabiles et luctuosos cantus edit. Itaque in Hesiodo nihil mutandum. Et hirundo ridicule diceretur ὀρθοβόη, vel ὀρθροβόη, cum non sit avis clamosa, sed minuriens, et ψιθυρίζουσα. Proinde dixit Sidonius, Prognen inter asseres minurientem, libri secundi Epistola secunda. Ut in Antho- logia Poeta incertus,

Against these, however, it is objected that Plato, refuting those who say that swans θρηνοῦντας τὸν θάνατον ὑπὸ λύπης ἐξάδειν [thrēnountas ton thanaton hypo lypēs exadein], sing for grief as they bewail their death, says: Οὐδὲν ὄρνεον ᾄδει ὅταν πεινῇ, ἢ ῥιγοῖ, ἤ τινα ἄλλην λύπην λυπεῖται· οὐδὲ αὐτὴ ἥ τε ἀηδὼν, καὶ χελιδὼν, καὶ ὁ ἔποψ, ὃν δή φασι διὰ λύπην θρηνοῦντα ᾄδειν [Ouden orneon adei hotan peinē, ē rhigoi, ē tina allēn lypēn lypeitai; oude autē hē te aēdōn, kai chelidōn, kai ho epops, hon dē phasi dia lypēn thrēnounta adein] (read οὓς δὴ φ. δ. λ. θρηνοῦντας ᾄδειν [hous dē ph. d. l. thrēnountas adein]), No bird sings when it is hungry, or cold, or sad for any other reason; not even the nightingale, the swallow and the hoopoe, which they say sing mournfully for grief. Accordingly Proclus cannot bear that the swallow should be called ὀρθογόη [orthogoē] by Hesiod, and wants to read ὀρθοβόη [orthoboē], crying in the morning, so that the Poet may not seem to disagree with Plato. But Tzetzes answers otherwise: Ὑμεῖς δ' ἴσμεν καὶ δίχα μάρτυρος Πλάτωνος, ὅτι οὐδὲν ὄρνεον λυπούμενον ᾄδει· ἀλλὰ δεινῶς, καὶ ῥητορικῶς ὁ ποιητὴς τὴν λαλιὰν τῆς χελιδόνος θρῆνον εἶναι λέγει κατὰ τὸν μῦθον τῆς τοῦ Πανδίονος ἐκείνης θυγατρός [Hymeis d' ismen kai dicha martyros Platōnos, hoti ouden orneon lypoumenon adei; alla deinōs, kai rhētorikōs ho poiētēs tēn lalian tēs chelidonos thrēnon einai legei kata ton mython tēs tou Pandionos ekeinēs thygatros]. We know even without Plato as witness that no bird sings in grief. But the Poet skilfully and rhetorically calls the swallow's song a lament, in keeping with the fable of Pandion's daughter. So he, as though the swallow were said to mourn only because of the fable. Indeed, as Pausanias says in the Attica, σφίσι τὴν ἐς ἀηδόνα, καὶ χελιδόνα, μεταβολὴν ἐπεφήμισαν, ὅτι οἶμαι, καὶ αὗται αἱ ὄρνιθες ἐλεεινὸν, καὶ θρήνῳ ὅμοιον ᾄδουσιν [sphisi tēn es aēdona, kai chelidona, metabolēn epephēmisan, hoti oimai, kai hautai hai ornithes eleeinon, kai thrēnō homoion adousin], I think the common fable about Pandion's daughters, that one of them was changed into a nightingale and the other into a swallow, arose from the fact that each bird utters pitiful and mournful songs. col. 65 Therefore nothing is to be changed in Hesiod. And the swallow would absurdly be called ὀρθοβόη [orthoboē] or ὀρθροβόη [orthroboē], since it is not a clamorous bird but one that twitters softly and ψιθυρίζουσα [psithyrizousa]. Hence Sidonius, book 2, letter 2, spoke of Procne twittering among the rafters. Likewise an unknown Poet in the Anthology,


Τραυλὰ μινυρομένη Πανδιονὶ κάμμορε φωνᾷ,

Τραυλὰ μινυρομένη Πανδιονὶ κάμμορε φωνᾷ, [Traula minyromenē Pandioni kammore phōna,]


O misera Pandionis filia, voce blaesa cantica minuriens. Cui simile, quod Pol- lux, in capite De avium vocibus, χελιδόνας ψιθυρίζειν, hirundines susurrare dicit. Et ille ψιθυρισμὸς, vel minuritio illa, si mavis, videtur aliquid habere commune cum querelis et susurris, qui in moerore nobis excidunt, aut alia quavis de causa. Proinde ψιθύρους, id est, susurrones, seu delatores, qui clam in aurem insusurrant, per hirundinem Pythagoram significasse volunt nonnulli veterum apud Plutarchum in Symposiacis. Verum tamen est, quod ait Plato, hirundines II, 610 prae moerore non sic canere. Avis enim cantus, quamlibet sit in speciem lugubris, non est moeroris effectus, sed naturae.

O wretched daughter of Pandion, twittering songs with lisping voice. Similar is what Pollux says in the chapter On the voices of birds, χελιδόνας ψιθυρίζειν [chelidonas psithyrizein], that swallows whisper. And that ψιθυρισμὸς [psithyrismos], or that twittering if you prefer, seems to have something in common with the complaints and murmurs that escape us in grief or for any other cause. Hence some of the ancients in Plutarch's Table Talk hold that by the swallow Pythagoras meant ψιθύρους [psithyrous], that is, whisperers or informers who secretly whisper into the ear. Still, what Plato says is true: swallows II, 610 do not sing thus for grief. For a bird's song, however mournful it may seem, is the effect not of grief but of nature.


Iam pauca de migratione hirundinum in Ierem. VIII, 7. Et migratorias quidem esse aves, lippis notum et tonsoribus. Idque observatum ab omni aevo. Homerus in Εἰρεσιώνῃ apud Herodotum in ejus vita,

Now a few words on the migration of swallows in Ierem. VIII, 7. That they are migratory birds is known to the bleary-eyed and the barbers, and it has been observed in every age. Homer in the Εἰρεσιώνη [Eiresiōnē], quoted by Herodotus in his life,


Νεῦμαι σοι, νεῦμαι ἐνιαύσιος, ὥστε χελιδὼν,

Νεῦμαι σοι, νεῦμαι ἐνιαύσιος, ὥστε χελιδὼν, [Neumai soi, neumai eniausios, hōste chelidōn,]


Apud te redeo quotannis, ut hirundo. Anacreon Oda trigesima tertia,

I return to you every year, like the swallow. Anacreon, Ode 33,


Σὺ μὲν, φίλη χελιδὼν Tu quidem, amica hirundo, Ἐτησίη μολοῦσα, Annuatim veniens, Θέρει πλέκεις καλίην, Aestate nidum texis, Χειμῶσι δ' εἶς ἄφαντος. Et hyeme non appares.

Σὺ μὲν, φίλη χελιδὼν [Sy men, philē chelidōn] You, dear swallow, Ἐτησίη μολοῦσα [Etēsiē molousa], coming every year, Θέρει πλέκεις καλίην [Therei plekeis kaliēn], weave your nest in summer, Χειμῶσι δ' εἶς ἄφαντος [Cheimōsi d' eis aphantos]. And in winter you do not appear.


Aristoteles Hist. lib. 8. cap. 12. Ἀπαίρουσι δὲ, etc. καὶ οὐ χειμάζουσι, καὶ αἱ χε-λιδόνες, καὶ αἱ τρυγόνες· Abeunt autem, et apud nos non hyemant tam hirundines, quam turtures. Auctor ad Herennium, Hirundines aestivo tempore praesto sunt, hieme pulsae recedunt. Plinius libri decimi capite vigesimo quarto, Abeunt et hirundines hybernis mensibus. Damir, وهو من الطيور القواطع Est ex avibus migratoriis. Columella in prosa De cultu hortorum libri duodecimi capite tertio, Mox ubi bruma confecta est, intermissis quadraginta diebus, circa hirundinis adventum, cum jam Favonius exoritur. Et libri decimi capite decimo quarto, Dum Arcturi ortus, et hirundinis adventus commodiores polliceantur tempestates. Apud Plinium libri secundi capite quadragesimo septimo, Favonium quidam ad VII. Calendas Martias Chelidoniam vocant ab hirundinis visu. Favonium, id est, Zephyrum. Hinc Horatius libri primi Epistola septima ad Maecenatem,

Aristotle, Hist. book 8, ch. 12: Ἀπαίρουσι δὲ, etc. καὶ οὐ χειμάζουσι, καὶ αἱ χελιδόνες, καὶ αἱ τρυγόνες [Apairousi de, etc. kai ou cheimazousi, kai hai chelidones, kai hai trygones]; Both swallows and turtledoves depart, and do not winter among us. The author To Herennius: Swallows are at hand in summertime; driven off by winter, they withdraw. Pliny, book 10, chapter 24: Swallows too depart in the winter months. Damir: وهو من الطيور القواطع [wa-huwa min al-ṭuyūr al-qawāṭiʿ] It is one of the migratory birds. Columella, in his prose On the Cultivation of Gardens, book 12, chapter 3: Soon, when the winter solstice is over, after an interval of forty days, around the arrival of the swallow, when Favonius is already rising. And book 10, chapter 14: While the rising of Arcturus and the arrival of the swallow promise more favourable weather. In Pliny, book 2, chapter 47: Some call Favonius, on the 7th day before the Calends of March, Chelidonias, from the sighting of the swallow. Favonius, that is, Zephyr. Hence Horace, book 1, Epistle 7, to Maecenas:


Cum Zephyris si concedes, et hirundine prima.

If you will allow me, with the Zephyrs and the first swallow.


Et Oppianus de hirundine lib. 3. Halieuticῶν versu 244.

And Oppian on the swallow, book 3 of the Halieutica, line 244:


— — εἰαρινὴ Ζεφύρου πρωτάγγελος ὄρνις,

— — εἰαρινὴ Ζεφύρου πρωτάγγελος ὄρνις, [eiarinē Zephyrou prōtangelos ornis,]


Avis verna Zephyri prima nuntia. Et Nonnus libro secundo Dionysiacῶν,

The spring bird, first messenger of Zephyr. And Nonnus, book 2 of the Dionysiaca:


— — εἰαρινοῖο φίλη Ζεφύροιο χελιδὼν,

— — εἰαρινοῖο φίλη Ζεφύροιο χελιδὼν, [eiarinoio philē Zephyroio chelidōn,]


Verni amica Zephyri hirundo. Et libro quadragesimo septimo,

The swallow, friend of the spring Zephyr. And in book 47:


Καὶ Ζεφύρου καλὸς ὄρνις ὑπωροφίην χέε μολπὴν,

Καὶ Ζεφύρου καλὸς ὄρνις ὑπωροφίην χέε μολπὴν, [Kai Zephyrou kalos ornis hypōrophiēn chee molpēn,]


Et Zephyri pulchra avis sub tecto fudit cantilenam. Tanquam alludentes ad Graecum proverbium, Νέα χελιδὼν, Nova hirundo, quod lapsu memoriae citat Suidas ex Aristophanis Avibus, cum alibi non legatur, quam in Equitibus Actu primo his verbis, II, 611 Σκέψασθε παῖδες, οὐχ' ὁρᾶθ'; ὥρα, νέα χελιδὼν, col. 66

And the beautiful bird of Zephyr poured out its song beneath the roof. As if alluding to the Greek proverb Νέα χελιδὼν [Nea chelidōn], A new swallow, which Suidas, by a lapse of memory, cites from the Birds of Aristophanes, although it is read nowhere but in the Knights, Act 1, in these words: II, 611 Σκέψασθε παῖδες, οὐχ' ὁρᾶθ'; ὥρα, νέα χελιδὼν, [Skepsasthe paides, ouch' horath'; hōra, nea chelidōn,] col. 66


Aspicite pueri, non videtis? ver est, nova hirundo. Ad quae Scholiastes, Ἔστιν ἔαρος ἀρχή· δοκεῖ γάρ πως ἅμα τῷ ἔαρι φαίνεσθαι χελιδών. Veris initium est, videtur enim simul cum vere hirundo apparere. Itaque in Avibus (quod Suidam potuit fallere) hirundo apparens docet,

Look, boys, don't you see? It is spring, a new swallow. On which the Scholiast: Ἔστιν ἔαρος ἀρχή· δοκεῖ γάρ πως ἅμα τῷ ἔαρι φαίνεσθαι χελιδών. [Estin earos archē; dokei gar pōs hama tō eari phainesthai chelidōn.] It is the beginning of spring, for the swallow seems to appear together with the spring. So in the Birds (which may have misled Suidas) the appearing swallow teaches


Ὅτε χρὴ χλαῖναν πωλεῖν ἤδη, καὶ ληϊδάριόν τι πρίασθαι,

Ὅτε χρὴ χλαῖναν πωλεῖν ἤδη, καὶ ληϊδάριόν τι πρίασθαι, [Hote chrē chlainan pōlein ēdē, kai lēidarion ti priasthai,]


Quando laena sit vendenda, ut ematur aestiva vestis. Et in Pace canit Chorus,

When the cloak is to be sold, so that a summer garment may be bought. And in the Peace the Chorus sings:


— — ὅταν ἠρινᾷ μὲν — — cum verna quidem Φωνῇ χελιδὼν Voce hirundo Ἑζομένη κελαδῇ. Sedens resonat.

— — ὅταν ἠρινᾷ μὲν [hotan ērina men] — — when indeed with spring Φωνῇ χελιδὼν [Phōnē chelidōn] voice the swallow Ἑζομένη κελαδῇ. [Hezomenē keladē.] sitting resounds.


Quibus similia haec Stesichori, ut monet Scholiastes, Ὅταν ἦρος ὥρᾳ κελαδῇ χε-λιδών· Cum veris tempore resonabit hirundo. Neque abludunt haec Simonidis in Athenaeo, Ἄγγελε κλυτὰ ἔαρος ἁδυόδμου κυανέα χελιδὼν, Inclyta suaveolentis veris nuntia, o cyanea hirundo*). Et apud Theognin libro tertio de Rodiorum sacrificiis ita incipit cantilena, quam ostiatim canebant οἱ χελιδονίζοντες, id est, agyrtae, qui hirundinem venisse nuntiabant (Hesychio χελιδονισταὶ) Ἦλθ', ἦλθε χελιδὼν καλὰς ὥρας ἄγουσα, καὶ καλοὺς ἐνιαυτοὺς, ἐπὶ γαστέρα λευκὰ κἀπὶ νῶτα μέλαινα· Venit, venit hirundo albo ventre et nigro dorso, pulchra tempora adducens et pulchros annos. Caetera ibi vide. Proinde, ut Theon ad Aratum scribit, piscem borealem veteres cum hirundinis capite pingebant, et ἰχθὺν χελιδόνιαν vocabant, quia veris praeludium ortu suo significabat. Eodem pertinent haec Aeliani Hist. lib. 1. cap. 52. Χελιδὼν δ' ἄρα τῆς ὥρας τῆς ἀρίστης ὑποσημαίνει τὴν ἐπιδημίαν· Hirundo pulcherrimae anni tempestatis adventum significat. Et Ovidii pene in fine libri secundi Fastorum,

Similar to which are these words of Stesichorus, as the Scholiast notes: Ὅταν ἦρος ὥρᾳ κελαδῇ χελιδών· [Hotan ēros hōra keladē chelidōn;] When the swallow shall resound in springtime. Nor are these words of Simonides in Athenaeus far off: Ἄγγελε κλυτὰ ἔαρος ἁδυόδμου κυανέα χελιδὼν [Angele klyta earos hadyodmou kyanea chelidōn], O famed messenger of sweet-scented spring, dark-blue swallow*). And in Theognis, book 3, on the sacrifices of the Rhodians, the song which οἱ χελιδονίζοντες [hoi chelidonizontes] sang from door to door, that is, the beggar-minstrels who announced that the swallow had come (in Hesychius χελιδονισταὶ [chelidonistai]), begins thus: Ἦλθ', ἦλθε χελιδὼν καλὰς ὥρας ἄγουσα, καὶ καλοὺς ἐνιαυτοὺς, ἐπὶ γαστέρα λευκὰ κἀπὶ νῶτα μέλαινα· [Ēlth', ēlthe chelidōn kalas hōras agousa, kai kalous eniautous, epi gastera leuka kapi nōta melaina;] The swallow has come, has come, with white belly and black back, bringing fair seasons and fair years. See the rest there. Accordingly, as Theon writes on Aratus, the ancients painted the northern Fish with a swallow's head and called it ἰχθὺν χελιδόνιαν [ichthyn chelidonian], because by its rising it signified the prelude of spring. To the same point belong these words of Aelian, Hist. book 1, ch. 52: Χελιδὼν δ' ἄρα τῆς ὥρας τῆς ἀρίστης ὑποσημαίνει τὴν ἐπιδημίαν· [Chelidōn d' ara tēs hōras tēs aristēs hyposēmainei tēn epidēmian;] The swallow signals the arrival of the most beautiful season of the year. And Ovid, almost at the end of book 2 of the Fasti:


Fallimur, an veris praenuntia venit hirundo?

Am I deceived, or has the swallow, harbinger of spring, come?


Et Columellae in Horto,

And Columella in the Garden:


Veris et adventum nidis cantarit hirundo.

And the swallow will have sung of spring's arrival from her nest.


Et Calphurnii Ecloga quinta,

And Calpurnius, Eclogue 5:


— — vere novo, cum jam tinnire volucres
Incipiant, nidosque reversa lutabit hirundo.

— — in early spring, when the birds are already beginning to twitter, and the returning swallow plasters her nests with mud.


Et incerti poetae inter Epigrammata veterum libro quarto,

And an unknown poet among the Epigrams of the ancients, book 4:


Tempus vernum hoedus petulans, et garrula hirundo, Indicat, et sinus lactis, et herba virens. II, 612 Et quinto Avieni,

The frisky kid and the chattering swallow announce springtime, and the bowl of milk, and the green grass. II, 612 And in book 5, Avienus:


Nam, cum vere novo tellus se dura relaxat,
Culminibusque cavis blandum strepit ales hirundo.

For when in early spring the hard earth loosens itself,
and the swallow, winged one, chirps sweetly in the hollow rooftops.


Sed, si una duntaxat aut altera hirundo appareat, ex Aristotele notum est Grae- corum proverbium Moralium libri primi capite sexto, Μία χελιδὼν ἔαρ οὐ ποιεῖ, Una hirundo non facit ver. Hirundinis apud nos mora solet esse sex mensium Plinius libri decimi capite vigesimo quinto, Temporum magna differentia avi- bus. Perennes, ut columbae; semestres, ut hirundines; trimestres, ut turdi et turtures. Nempe hirundines initio veris veniunt, et abeunt in fine aestatis. Plinius de Arcturo libri decimi octavi capite trigesimo primo, Signum orientis ejus sideris servetur hirundinum abitu. Arcturus autem oritur Septembri mense. Galenus, Ἔστι μὲν ὡραιότατον τῆς ἐλάτης τὸ σπέρμα περὶ τὴν ἐπιτολὴν τοῦ Ἀρκτούρου, ὅστις καιρὸς ἐν Ῥώμῃ ὁ καλούμενος μὲν Σεπτέμβριός ἐστι. Et circa autumni aequinoctium. Theophrastus de ceronia Historiae plantarum libri quarti capite secundo, Ἀνθεῖ περὶ Ἀρκτοῦρον, καὶ ἰσημερίαν· vel (ut Plinius expressius libri secundi capite quadragesimo septimo) Arcturus oritur undecim diebus ante aequinoctium. Itaque quando migrent hirundines, satis compertum est, sed quo migrent, non itidem. Isidorus in genere, maria transvolat (hirundo) ibique commoratur. Anacreon ubi supra,

But if only one or two swallows appear, the proverb of the Greeks is known from Aristotle, Ethics book 1, chapter 6: Μία χελιδὼν ἔαρ οὐ ποιεῖ [mia chelidōn ear ou poiei], One swallow does not make a spring. Among us the swallow's stay is usually six months. Pliny, book 10, chapter 25: Birds differ greatly in their seasons. Some are perennial, like doves; some stay six months, like swallows; some three months, like thrushes and turtledoves. That is, swallows come at the beginning of spring and depart at the end of summer. Pliny on Arcturus, book 18, chapter 31: Let the sign of the rising of that star be observed in the departure of the swallows. Arcturus, moreover, rises in the month of September. Galen: Ἔστι μὲν ὡραιότατον τῆς ἐλάτης τὸ σπέρμα περὶ τὴν ἐπιτολὴν τοῦ Ἀρκτούρου, ὅστις καιρὸς ἐν Ῥώμῃ ὁ καλούμενος μὲν Σεπτέμβριός ἐστι [esti men hōraiotaton tēs elatēs to sperma peri tēn epitolēn tou Arktourou, hostis kairos en Rhōmē ho kaloumenos men Septembrios esti]. It is also around the autumn equinox. Theophrastus on the carob, History of Plants book 4, chapter 2: Ἀνθεῖ περὶ Ἀρκτοῦρον, καὶ ἰσημερίαν [anthei peri Arktouron, kai isēmerian]; or (as Pliny says more explicitly, book 2, chapter 47) Arcturus rises eleven days before the equinox. So when swallows migrate is well enough established, but where they migrate is not likewise. Isidore says in general: (the swallow) flies across the seas and stays there. Anacreon, in the place cited above:


Χειμῶνι δ' εἷς ἄφαντος, Ἦ Νεῖλον, ἢ 'πὶ Μέμφιν. Hyeme autem non conspiceris, col. 67 Sive Nilum aut Memphim petas.

Χειμῶνι δ' εἷς ἄφαντος, Ἢ Νεῖλον, ἢ 'πὶ Μέμφιν. [cheimōni d' heis aphantos, ē Neilon, ē 'pi Memphin.] But in winter you are not seen, col. 67 Whether you make for the Nile or Memphis.


Herodotus libri secundi capite vigesimo secundo, de Aethiopia sub Aegypto, Ἰκτῖνοι δὲ, καὶ χελιδόνες δι' ἔτεος ἐόντες οὐκ ἀπολείπουσι· Milvi et hirundines toto anni tempore ibi sunt, nec per hyemem discedunt. Utut sit, discedens agmen deserere apud eas grave crimen est, si vera sunt haec Martialis libri quinti Epi- grammate 68.

Herodotus, book 2, chapter 22, on Ethiopia below Egypt: Ἰκτῖνοι δὲ, καὶ χελιδόνες δι' ἔτεος ἐόντες οὐκ ἀπολείπουσι [iktinoi de, kai chelidones di' eteos eontes ouk apoleipousi]; Kites and swallows are there the whole year round, and do not depart in winter. However that may be, among them it is a grave crime to desert the departing flock, if these lines of Martial, book 5, Epigram 68, are true:


Hibernos peterent solito cum more recessus
Atthides in nidis una remansit avis:
Deprendere nefas ad tempora verna reversae,
Et profugam volucres diripuere suae.

When the Attic birds sought their winter retreats in their accustomed manner, one bird stayed behind in the nests: the crime was detected when they returned in springtime, and her own kind tore the deserter to pieces.


Sed et a frigore manentibus non leve imminet periculum. Plinius in loco jam citato de Arcturo, sidere, Signum orientis ejus sideris servetur hirundinum abitu; namque deprehensae intereunt. Tamen in apricis locis quasdam manere, certum est, quae non moriuntur omnes, sed nudantur et deplumantur. Quocirca Phi- losophus Historiae animalium libri octavi capite decimo sexto, postquam milvos II, 613 et hirundines hyeme in tepidiora loca conferre se docuit, cum non sunt remota nimis, Οἱ δὲ ποῤῥοτέρω ὄντες τῶν τοιούτων, inquit, οὐκ ἐκτοπίζουσι, ἀλλὰ κρύπτουσιν ἑαυτούς· ἤδη γὰρ ὠμμέναι εἰσὶ πολλαὶ χελιδόνες ἐν ἀγγείοις (lege ἐν ἄγκεσι, vel ἐν ἀγκείαις) ἐψιλωμέναι πάμπαν· Quae autem aves ab hujusmodi locis sunt remotiores, inde non migrant, sed se abscondunt: jam enim in convallibus visae sunt multae hirundines, plane deplumes. Et hunc sequutus Plinius libri decimi capite vigesimo quarto, In vicina abeunt (hirundines) apricos sequutae montium recessus, inventaeque jam sunt ibi nudae atque deplumes. Cujusmodi hirundini Eutropii, eunuchi jam effoeti depile caput, et tinea exesum, Claudianus his verbis confert libro primo in Eutropium,

But those that remain also face no slight danger from the cold. Pliny, in the passage already cited on the star Arcturus: Let the sign of the rising of that star be observed in the departure of the swallows; for those caught behind perish. Yet it is certain that some remain in sunny places; not all of these die, but they are stripped bare and lose their feathers. Accordingly the Philosopher, History of Animals book 8, chapter 16, after teaching that kites and II, 613 swallows betake themselves in winter to warmer places when these are not too far away, says: Οἱ δὲ ποῤῥοτέρω ὄντες τῶν τοιούτων οὐκ ἐκτοπίζουσι, ἀλλὰ κρύπτουσιν ἑαυτούς· ἤδη γὰρ ὠμμέναι εἰσὶ πολλαὶ χελιδόνες ἐν ἀγγείοις [hoi de porrhoterō ontes tōn toioutōn ouk ektopizousi, alla kryptousin heautous; ēdē gar ōmmenai eisi pollai chelidones en angeiois] (read ἐν ἄγκεσι [en ankesi], or ἐν ἀγκείαις [en ankeiais]) ἐψιλωμέναι πάμπαν [epsilōmenai pampan]; But the birds that are farther from such places do not migrate from there, but hide themselves: for many swallows have already been seen in valleys, completely featherless. And following him Pliny, book 10, chapter 24: (swallows) go off into neighbouring places, seeking the sunny recesses of the mountains, and have already been found there naked and featherless. To such a swallow Claudian compares the hairless, moth-eaten head of Eutropius, an already worn-out eunuch, in these words, book 1 Against Eutropius:


Vel qualis gelidis pluma labente pruinis
Arboris immoritur trunco brumalis hirundo.

Or like the winter swallow that, its feathers falling in the icy frosts, dies upon the trunk of a tree.


Sed cum Propheta dicit, hirundines nosse tempus adventus, aut recessus sui, non necesse est id de omnibus intelligere, nulla excepta. Et sufficit, ut in plerisque id impleatur, ut hoc exemplo moneamur, quam recte dixerit Hesiodus,

But when the Prophet says that swallows know the time of their coming or their departure, it need not be understood of all of them without exception. It suffices that it holds for most, so that by this example we may be reminded how rightly Hesiod said:


— — καιρὸς δ᾽ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἄριστος,

— — καιρὸς δ᾽ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἄριστος [kairos d' epi pasin aristos],


et unus e septem Sapientibus, quos Graecia celebravit, Καιρὸν γνῶθι, Nosce tempus. Quae ipsissima Sacri vatis verba sunt.

and one of the Seven Sages whom Greece celebrated: Καιρὸν γνῶθι [kairon gnōthi], Know the time. These are the very words of the sacred prophet.


Unum addo, in Graeco Tobiae exemplari legi capitis secundi versu undecimo, τὰ στρουθία, aviculas in ejus oculos stercus egessisse, quod pertinere ad hirundines, recte vidit Hieronymus, qui sic reddit: Contigit, ut ex nido hirundinum dormienti illi calida stercora inciderent super oculos ejus. Quia id hirundini peculiare est, quod pullorum stercora aut ipsa mater ex nido ejicit, cum parvuli sunt, aut eos docet ex nido egerere, cum sint grandiusculi. Aristoteles Historiae animalium libri noni capite septimo, Καὶ κόπρον τὸ πρῶτον αὐταὶ ἐκ-βάλλουσιν· ὅταν δὲ αὐξηθῶσι μεταστρέφοντας ἔξω διδάσκουσι τοὺς νεοττοὺς προΐ-εσθαι. Quae a Plinio sic reddita libri decimi capite trigesimo tertio, Notabili munditia egerunt excrementa pullorum: adultioresque circumagi docent, et foras saturitatem emittere. Neque dissimilia haec Arabum in Damire, ولا يلقي في عشه زبلا بل يلقيه الي خارج فانا اكبر فراخه علمها ذلك Neque in nidum, sed foras stercus excernit, quod ipsum pullos edocet, cum adoleverunt. Gorgiae legitur quid simile accidisse. In eum enim hirundo stercus egessit. Plutarchus Symposiacων libri octavi capite septi- col. 68 mo, Γοργίας δὲ ὁ Σοφιστὴς, χελιδόνος ἀφείσης ἐπ᾽ αὐτὸν ἀπόπατον, ἀναβλέ-ψας πρὸς αὐτὴν, Οὐ καλὰ ταῦτα (εἶπεν) ὦ Φιλομῆλα· Gorgias Sophista, cum hirundo stercus in eum emisisset, oculis ad illam conversis, haec, inquit, decora II, 614 non sunt, o Philomela. Quod laudat Philosophus tanquam apposite dictum Rhetoricorum libri tertii capite tertio. Quia ὄρνιθι μὲν, εἰ ἐποίησεν, οὐκ αἰσχρὸν, παρθένῳ δὲ αἰσχρόν· εὖ οὖν ἐλοιδόρησεν, εἰπὼν ὃ ἦν ἀλλ᾽ οὐχ᾽ ὅ ἐστιν, avi quidem, si fecerat, id turpe non est, sed puellae turpe est. Recte igitur eam convitiatus est, id dicens, quod fuerat, non autem, quod tum erat. Nec est, quod quis miretur, hirundini indi Philomelae nomen, cum vulgo sit persuasissimum, Philomelam esse lusciniam. Res enim est in ambiguo. Et multi veterum Prognen in lusciniam, ac Philomelam in hirundinem mutatam fuisse diserte tradunt. Quod nullo negotio probaverim, si haec res ageretur. Sed alio jam properamus.

I add one point: in the Greek copy of Tobit, chapter 2, verse 11, we read that τὰ στρουθία [ta strouthia], little birds, dropped dung into his eyes. Jerome rightly saw that this refers to swallows, and renders it thus: It happened that, as he slept, warm dung fell from a nest of swallows onto his eyes. For this is peculiar to the swallow: the mother herself either throws the droppings of the chicks out of the nest while they are small, or teaches them to void outside the nest when they are somewhat bigger. Aristotle, History of Animals, book 9, chapter 7: Καὶ κόπρον τὸ πρῶτον αὐταὶ ἐκβάλλουσιν· ὅταν δὲ αὐξηθῶσι μεταστρέφοντας ἔξω διδάσκουσι τοὺς νεοττοὺς προΐεσθαι [Kai kopron to prōton autai ekballousin; hotan de auxēthōsi metastrephontas exō didaskousi tous neottous proiesthai]. This is rendered by Pliny, book 10, chapter 33, as follows: With remarkable cleanliness they carry out the excrement of the chicks; and when these are older they teach them to turn round and discharge their fullness outside. Nor is this statement of the Arabs in Damir unlike it: ولا يلقي في عشه زبلا بل يلقيه الي خارج فانا اكبر فراخه علمها ذلك [wa-lā yulqī fī ʿushshihi ziblan bal yulqīhi ilā khārij fa-anā akbar firākhihi ʿallamahā dhālik] It does not void its dung into the nest but outside, and it teaches this very thing to its chicks when they have grown up. Something similar is recorded to have happened to Gorgias, for a swallow dropped dung on him. Plutarch, Table Talk, book 8, chapter 7: col. 68 Γοργίας δὲ ὁ Σοφιστὴς, χελιδόνος ἀφείσης ἐπ᾽ αὐτὸν ἀπόπατον, ἀναβλέψας πρὸς αὐτὴν, Οὐ καλὰ ταῦτα (εἶπεν) ὦ Φιλομῆλα [Gorgias de ho Sophistēs, chelidonos apheisēs ep᾽ auton apopaton, anablepsas pros autēn, Ou kala tauta (eipen) ō Philomēla]· Gorgias the Sophist, when a swallow had let fall its dung on him, turned his eyes towards it and said, "This is not becoming II, 614, Philomela." The Philosopher praises this as an apt saying in the Rhetoric, book 3, chapter 3, because ὄρνιθι μὲν, εἰ ἐποίησεν, οὐκ αἰσχρὸν, παρθένῳ δὲ αἰσχρόν· εὖ οὖν ἐλοιδόρησεν, εἰπὼν ὃ ἦν ἀλλ᾽ οὐχ᾽ ὅ ἐστιν [ornithi men, ei epoiēsen, ouk aischron, parthenō de aischron; eu oun eloidorēsen, eipōn ho ēn all᾽ ouch ho estin], for a bird, if it had done it, it is not shameful, but for a maiden it is shameful. So he rebuked her well, saying what she had been, not what she then was. Nor should anyone be surprised that the swallow is given the name Philomela, although it is very commonly believed that Philomela is the nightingale. For the matter is uncertain, and many of the ancients state explicitly that Procne was changed into a nightingale and Philomela into a swallow. I could prove this without any trouble, if that were the subject at hand. But we now hasten to other matters.


(1) Rosenmüller, II, 602 Quam scriptionis diversitatem VELT-HUSEN (Beytrag zur Aufklär. des Dankliedes Hiskiae, in den Beyträgen zur Be-förderung theologischer Kenntnisse a I. A. CRAMERO editt. P. I. p. 60. 61. not.) inde ortam putat, quod, quum veteres Hebraei carerent signo aliquo certo, quo sonum il-lum, ex u et i mixtum (ü), exprimerent, qui in Ssüs, סוס, auditur, nunc littera י nunc ו essent usi.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 602 Velthusen [=J. C. Velthusen, in Symbolae litterariae Kilonienses] (Beytrag zur Aufklär. des Dankliedes Hiskiae, in den Beyträgen zur Beförderung theologischer Kenntnisse, edited by J. A. Cramer, vol. 1, p. 60. 61. note) thinks that this difference in spelling arose because the ancient Hebrews lacked any fixed sign by which to express the sound mixed from u and i (ü), which is heard in Ssüs, סוס, and so used now the letter י, now ו.

Quasi vero non plura essent vocabula, uni tantummodo, aut alteri dialecto priva. Cf. Velthusen ad Cantic. Hisk. in Symbolis Kiloniens. P. II. pag. 325. not. 51. Deinde quo jure Ierem. R4 Rosenmüller, II, 605 But because the swallow is called by the name סוס neither in the Arabic dialect nor in the Syriac, Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)], in his Clavis in Iesaj., p. 216, denies that this word was used by the Hebrews to signify the swallow, and holds that it was used only of the horse. As if there were not many words peculiar to only one dialect or another! Cf. Velthusen on the Song of Hezekiah in the Symbolae Kilonienses, vol. 2, p. 325, note 51. Moreover, by what right the horse should be counted among the migratory birds in Jer 8:7, I can scarcely understand.

II, 614 col. 68 CAP. XI.

II, 614 col. 68 Chapter 11.


De Grue.

On the Crane.


In anatomia gruis aliquid peculiare observasse se scribit Bellonius libri quarti capite primo De Avibus, quod nimirum canna pulmonis aliter se habet, quam in aliis. Sterno enim, inquit, adhaerens carnem utrimque penetrat. Ac proinde mirum non est, quod vox ejus tam longe auditur. Neque enim ulla est avis tam vocalis atque grus. Hinc Ezechias in eucharistico carmine, postquam a morbo col. 69 convaluit Es. XXXVIII, 14. כסיס עגור כן אצפצף, ut sis et agor pipiebam, id est, ut hirundo et grus; quarum avium una querulam, altera contentissimam habet vocem. Inter sis et agor deest Copulativa Vau; ut Hab. III, 11. שמש ירח עמד זבלה, sol, luna (id est, sol et luna) steterunt in loco suo. Et 1 Par. II, 1. Ruben, Simeon, Levi, pro Ruben, et Simeon, et Levi. Itaque mens Ezechiae haec est, se, gravi morbo afflictum, non modo instar hirundinis leni murmure gemuisse, sed et gruis instar contenta voce ejulasse. Sic Talmudici in tractatu Kiddusim cap. 2. fol. 44. a. וצווח ר״ל ככורכיא, Et clamabat ut grus dominus Lakis. Et Smyrnaeus libro tertio de Nereidum planctu in morte Achillis,

In the anatomy of the crane, Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)] writes in book 4, chapter 1 of De Avibus that he observed something peculiar: namely, that the windpipe is arranged otherwise than in other birds. For, adhering to the breastbone, he says, it penetrates the flesh on both sides. And so it is no wonder that its voice is heard so far away. For no bird is as vocal as the crane. Hence Hezekiah, in his song of thanksgiving after he recovered from his illness col. 69, Es. XXXVIII, 14: כסיס עגור כן אצפצף, like sis and agor I chirped, that is, like the swallow and the crane; of these birds the one has a plaintive voice, the other a very strained one. Between sis and agor the copulative Vau is missing, as in Hab 3:11. שמש ירח עמד זבלה, sun, moon (that is, sun and moon) stood still in their place. And 1 Chr 2:1. Reuben, Simeon, Levi, for Reuben, and Simeon, and Levi. Thus Hezekiah's meaning is this: afflicted by grave illness, he not only moaned with a gentle murmur like a swallow, but also wailed with a strained voice like a crane. So the Talmudists in the tractate Kiddushin, ch. 2, fol. 44a: וצווח ר״ל ככורכיא, And Resh Lakish cried out like a crane. And Quintus of Smyrna, in book 3, on the lament of the Nereids at the death of Achilles,


— — — — ταί δ᾽ ἐφέροντο
Κλαγγηδὸν κραιπνῇσιν ἐειδόμεναι γεράνοισιν,
Ὀσσόμεναι a) μέγα χεῖμα, — —

— — — — ταί δ᾽ ἐφέροντο [tai d’ epheronto] Κλαγγηδὸν κραιπνῇσιν ἐειδόμεναι γεράνοισιν [klangēdon kraipnēsin eeidomenai geranoisin], Ὀσσόμεναι a) μέγα χεῖμα [Ossomenai mega cheima], — —


Illae vero ferebantur cum clangore, citis gruibus similes, quae magnam tempestatem praesentiscunt. Et libro decimo tertio, ubi de Trojae excidio,

But they were borne along with clangor, like swift cranes that sense a great storm in advance. And in book 13, on the destruction of Troy,


— — στοναχὴ δὲ δαϊκταμένων αἰζηῶν Ἔπλετο λευγαλέη, περὶ δ᾽ ἴαχε πάντα μέλαθρα II, 615 Ἄσπετον· οἰμωγὴ δὲ πέλεν στονόεσσα γυναίκων Εἰδομένων γεράνοισιν, ὅτ᾽ αἰετὸν ἀθρήσωσιν. Ὑψόθεν αἴσσοντα δι᾽ αἰθέρος, οὐδ᾽ ἄρα τῇσι Θαρσαλέον στέρνοισι πέλει μένος, ἀλλὰ ἑ μοῦνον Μακρὸν ἀνατρύζουσι, φοβούμεναι ἱερὸν ὄρνιν.

— — στοναχὴ δὲ δαϊκταμένων αἰζηῶν [stonachē de daiktamenōn aizēōn] Ἔπλετο λευγαλέη, περὶ δ᾽ ἴαχε πάντα μέλαθρα [Epleto leugaleē, peri d’ iache panta melathra] II, 615 Ἄσπετον· οἰμωγὴ δὲ πέλεν στονόεσσα γυναίκων [Aspeton; oimōgē de pelen stonoessa gynaikōn] Εἰδομένων γεράνοισιν, ὅτ᾽ αἰετὸν ἀθρήσωσιν [Eidomenōn geranoisin, hot’ aieton athrēsōsin]. Ὑψόθεν αἴσσοντα δι᾽ αἰθέρος, οὐδ᾽ ἄρα τῇσι [Hypsothen aissonta di’ aitheros, oud’ ara tēsi] Θαρσαλέον στέρνοισι πέλει μένος, ἀλλὰ ἑ μοῦνον [Tharsaleon sternoisi pelei menos, alla he mounon] Μακρὸν ἀνατρύζουσι, φοβούμεναι ἱερὸν ὄρνιν [Makron anatryzousi, phoboumenai hieron ornin].


Et juvenum caesorum gemitus erat miserabilis, omnesque domus horrendum resonabant. Et tristissimus erat mulierum ejulatus, gruibus similium, cum aquilam vident, ex alto per aetherem irruentem. Nec fortis illis in pectore vis residet, sed tantummodo multum strident, sacram Iovis alitem formidantes. Homerus quoque militum barritum cum gruum clangore conferens initio libri tertii Iliados,

And the groaning of the slain young men was pitiful, and all the houses resounded dreadfully. And most mournful was the wailing of the women, like cranes when they see an eagle swooping from on high through the air. Nor does any brave strength remain in their breasts; they only shriek long, dreading the sacred bird of Jove. Homer too, comparing the battle cry of soldiers with the clangor of cranes at the beginning of book 3 of the Iliad,


Τρῶες μὲν κλαγγῇ τ᾽ ἐνοπῇ τ᾽ ἴσαν ὄρνιθες ὥς,
Ἠΰτε περ κλαγγὴ γεράνων πέλει οὐρανόθι πρό.

Τρῶες μὲν κλαγγῇ τ᾽ ἐνοπῇ τ᾽ ἴσαν ὄρνιθες ὥς [Trōes men klangē t’ enopē t’ isan ornithes hōs], Ἠΰτε περ κλαγγὴ γεράνων πέλει οὐρανόθι πρό [Ēute per klangē geranōn pelei ouranothi pro].


Trojani quidem cum clangore et clamore ibant ut aves, qualis est gruum clangor ad coelum usque. Quod Maro imitatus Aeneidos libro decimo,

The Trojans went with clangor and clamor like birds, like the clangor of cranes up to the sky. Which Virgil imitated in book 10 of the Aeneid,


— — clamorem ad sidera tollunt
Dardanidae e muris, quales sub nubibus atris
Strymoniae dant signa grues, atque aethera tranant
Cum sonitu, fugiuntque Notos clamore secundo.

— — the Dardanians raise a shout to the stars from the walls, as beneath black clouds Strymonian cranes give their signals and swim through the air with noise, and flee the South Winds with favoring clamor.


Et Martialis, ut anum Philenidem non loquacem solum, sed et vocalem ac Stentoream fuisse significet, libri noni Epigrammate 30.

And Martial, to indicate that the old woman Philaenis was not only talkative but also loud-voiced and Stentorian, in book 9, Epigram 30:


Heu, quae lingua silet! Non illam mille catastae
Vincebant, nec quae turba Serapin amat.
Nec matutini cirrata caterva magistri,
Nec quae Strymonio de grege ripa sonat.

Alas, what a tongue is silent! A thousand slave-auction platforms could not outdo it, nor the throng that loves Serapis, nor the curly-haired troop of the morning schoolmaster, nor the bank that resounds with the Strymonian flock.


Sed et ad gruum clamorem pertinent, quae sequuntur. Homerus iterum ubi supra,

The following also pertain to the cry of cranes. Homer again, in the place cited above,


Κλαγγῇ ταί γε πέτονται ἐπ᾽ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων,

Κλαγγῇ ταί γε πέτονται ἐπ᾽ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων [Klangē tai ge petontai ep’ Ōkeanoio rhoaōn],


Cum clangore hae volant ad Oceani fluenta. Hesiodus in Operibus,

With clangor they fly toward the streams of Ocean. Hesiod in the Works,


Φράζεσθαι δ᾽ εὖτ᾽ ἂν φωνὴν γεράνου ἐπακούσης,
Ὑψόθεν ἐκ νεφέων ἐνιαύσια κεκλαγυίης,

Φράζεσθαι δ᾽ εὖτ᾽ ἂν φωνὴν γεράνου ἐπακούσης [Phrazesthai d’ eut’ an phōnēn geranou epakousēs], Ὑψόθεν ἐκ νεφέων ἐνιαύσια κεκλαγυίης [Hypsothen ek nepheōn eniausia keklagyiēs],


Attende, cum vocem gruis audieris sursum ex nubibus quotannis clangentis. Lucretius libri quarti versu 18.

Take heed when you hear the voice of the crane clangoring yearly from the clouds on high. Lucretius, book 4, verse 18:


Parvus ut est cygni melior canor, ille gruum quam Clamor in aethereis dispersis nubibus austri.

As the small song of the swan is better than the clamor of cranes scattered among the ethereal clouds of the South Wind.


II, 616 Claudianus de bello Gildonico,

II, 616 Claudian on the Gildonic War,


Ingenti clamore grues aestiva relinquunt
Thracia, cum tepido permutant Strymona Nilo.

With great clamor the cranes leave their summer Thrace, when they exchange the Strymon for the warm Nile.


Proinde Eustathius gruem dicit avem esse φωνητικὴν, vocalem. Et notandum, plerasque linguas ipso avis nomine vocem illius utcumque imitari. Ita Hebraeum עגור agor, Chaldaeum כורכיא kurkeja, Arabica كركي kurki (1), et غرنوق gurnuk (2), Graecum γέρανος, Cambro-Britannicum garan, German. cran, Romanum grus sunt totidem voces ὀνοματοποιητικαί. Hinc Isidorus, col. 70 Grues nomen de propria voce sumpserunt. Tali enim voce susurrant. Et gruere est gruum more clangere. Festus, Gruere dicuntur grues, ut sues grunnire. Poëmatium De cantu Philomelae,

Accordingly Eustathius says the crane is a φωνητικὴν [phōnētikēn], vocal, bird. And it should be noted that most languages, in the very name of the bird, imitate its voice in some way. Thus the Hebrew עגור agor, the Chaldee כורכיא kurkeja, the Arabic كركي [kurkī] kurki R1 and غرنوق [gharnūq] gurnuk R2, the Greek γέρανος [geranos], the Cambro-British garan, the German cran, the Roman grus are so many onomatopoeic (ὀνοματοποιητικαί [onomatopoiētikai]) words. Hence Isidore, col. 70 Cranes took their name from their own voice. For they whisper with such a sound. And gruere is to clangor in the manner of cranes. Festus: Cranes are said gruere, as swine grunnire. The little poem On the Song of Philomela:


Grus gruit, inque glomis cygni prope flumina drensant.

The crane cries gru, and the swans in flocks drensant near the rivers.


Glossarium vetus: Gruunt, γερανίζουσι. Interim, ne quis putet, grues semper sonora voce clangere, Damir haec habet de grue, quae excubias agit, dum reliquae dormiunt: والذي يحرس يهتف خافي كانه ينذر بانه جارس Et quae in custodia est nonnisi submissa voce murmurat, ac si sciret, se esse in custodia. Quod ipsum ad Ezechiae locum non absurde referatur, quasi hoc gruis lene murmur cum hirundinis minuritione junxerit.

An old Glossary: Gruunt, γερανίζουσι [geranizousi]. Meanwhile, lest anyone think that cranes always clangor with a resounding voice, Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] says this of the crane that keeps watch while the rest sleep: والذي يحرس يهتف خافي كانه ينذر بانه جارس [wa-lladhī yaḥrus yahtif khāfī ka-annahu yundhir bi-annahu jāris] And the one on guard murmurs only in a low voice, as if it knew that it was on guard. This very thing might not absurdly be referred to the passage of Hezekiah, as though he joined this gentle murmur of the crane with the twittering of the swallow.


II, 617 Nunc de migratione gruum agemus in illud Ierem. VIII, 7. Turtur, et hirundo, et grus custodierunt tempus adventus sui. In genere gruem non solum alio migrare constat, sed et fuga frigoris in remotissima loca proficisci. Symeon Sethi, Τὸ δὲ τοιοῦτον πτηνὸν διέρχεται τὴν οἰκουμένην ἅπασαν, μὴ μένον ἐν ἑνὶ κλίματι· Haec avis omnem terrarum orbem peragrat, in una regione haud quaquam manens. Aristoteles Historiae animalium libri octavi capite duodecimo, Ἐκτοπίζουσιν εἰς τὰ ἔσχατα ἐκ τῶν ἐσχάτων· Ex ultimis in ultima (grues) migrant. Id est, ut ipse interpretatur, ἐκ τῶν Σκυθικῶν εἰς τὰ ἕλη τὰ ἄνω τῆς Αἰγύπτου, ὅθεν ὁ Νεῖλος ῥεῖ, ex Scythicis oris ad paludes, quae sunt supra Aegyptum, unde fluit Nilus. Herodotum sequutus, qui, de Nili fontibus et vicino Oceano agens libri secundi capite vigesimo secundo, Γέρανοι δὲ, inquit, φεύγου-σαι τὸν χειμῶνα, τὸν ἐν τῇ Σκυθικῇ χώρῃ γενόμενον, φοιτῶσι εἰς χειμαδίην ἐς τοὺς τόπους τούτους· Grues, Scythicae plagae hyemem fugientes, ad illa loca hyematum se conferunt. Aelianus etiam Historiae animalium libri tertii capite decimo tertio, Εἰς Αἴγυπτόν τε, καὶ Λιβύην ἀπαίρουσι, καὶ Αἰθιόπιαν, ὥσπερ γὰρ οὖν γῆς περίοδον εἰδυῖαι, καὶ φύσεις ἀέρων, καὶ ὡρῶν διαφορὰς στέλλονται αἱ πᾶσαι· Quasi terrae ambitum, et coeli naturam, et temporum varietatem nossent, in Aegyptum, Lybiam et Aethiopiam abeunt, et proficiscuntur omnes. Et Homerus multo ante,

II, 617 Now we shall treat the migration of cranes, with reference to Jer 8:7. The turtledove, and the swallow, and the crane have kept the time of their coming. In general it is agreed that the crane not only migrates elsewhere, but also travels to the most remote places to escape the cold. Symeon Seth [=Symeon Seth (11th c.), Syntagma de alimentorum facultatibus]: Τὸ δὲ τοιοῦτον πτηνὸν διέρχεται τὴν οἰκουμένην ἅπασαν, μὴ μένον ἐν ἑνὶ κλίματι [To de toiouton ptēnon dierchetai tēn oikoumenēn hapasan, mē menon en heni klimati]; This bird traverses the whole world, by no means staying in one region. Aristotle, History of Animals, book 8, chapter 12: Ἐκτοπίζουσιν εἰς τὰ ἔσχατα ἐκ τῶν ἐσχάτων [Ektopizousin eis ta eschata ek tōn eschatōn]; They (the cranes) migrate from the farthest regions to the farthest. That is, as he himself explains, ἐκ τῶν Σκυθικῶν εἰς τὰ ἕλη τὰ ἄνω τῆς Αἰγύπτου, ὅθεν ὁ Νεῖλος ῥεῖ [ek tōn Skythikōn eis ta helē ta anō tēs Aigyptou, hothen ho Neilos rhei], from the Scythian shores to the marshes that lie above Egypt, whence the Nile flows. He followed Herodotus, who, treating the sources of the Nile and the neighbouring Ocean in book 2, chapter 22, says: Γέρανοι δὲ φεύγουσαι τὸν χειμῶνα, τὸν ἐν τῇ Σκυθικῇ χώρῃ γενόμενον, φοιτῶσι εἰς χειμαδίην ἐς τοὺς τόπους τούτους [Geranoi de pheugousai ton cheimōna, ton en tē Skythikē chōrē genomenon, phoitōsi eis cheimadiēn es tous topous toutous]; Cranes, fleeing the winter of the Scythian region, betake themselves to those places to spend the winter. Aelian too, History of Animals, book 3, chapter 13: Εἰς Αἴγυπτόν τε, καὶ Λιβύην ἀπαίρουσι, καὶ Αἰθιόπιαν, ὥσπερ γὰρ οὖν γῆς περίοδον εἰδυῖαι, καὶ φύσεις ἀέρων, καὶ ὡρῶν διαφορὰς στέλλονται αἱ πᾶσαι [Eis Aigypton te, kai Libyēn apairousi, kai Aithiopian, hōsper gar oun gēs periodon eiduiai, kai physeis aerōn, kai hōrōn diaphoras stellontai hai pasai]; As though they knew the circuit of the earth, the nature of the sky and the variation of the seasons, they depart for Egypt, Libya and Ethiopia, and all set out. And Homer long before:


— — — ταί γε πέτονται ἐπ᾽ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων,

— — — ταί γε πέτονται ἐπ᾽ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων [tai ge petontai ep᾽ Ōkeanoio rhoaōn],


Ad Oceani fluenta hae volant, nempe australis, ubi Pygmaei; quod docent sequentia. Unde Pompejo Lucullus apud Plutarchum, Εἶτά σοι δοκῶ ἐλάττονα τῶν γεράνων νοῦν ἔχειν, καὶ τῶν πελαργῶν, ὥς τε ταῖς ὥραις μὴ συμμετα-βάλλειν τὰς διαίτας· An tibi videor gruibus et ciconiis minus sapere, ita, ut cum anni tempestatibus stationes non mutem?

These fly to the streams of Ocean, namely the southern Ocean, where the Pygmies are, as what follows shows. Hence Lucullus to Pompey in Plutarch: Εἶτά σοι δοκῶ ἐλάττονα τῶν γεράνων νοῦν ἔχειν, καὶ τῶν πελαργῶν, ὥς τε ταῖς ὥραις μὴ συμμεταβάλλειν τὰς διαίτας [Eita soi dokō elattona tōn geranōn noun echein, kai tōn pelargōn, hōs te tais hōrais mē symmetaballein tas diaitas]; Do I seem to you to have less sense than cranes and storks, so as not to change my abode with the seasons of the year?


Plerasque in Thracia nasci, veteres crediderunt. Aelianus ubi supra, Αἱ γέρανοι γίνονται μὲν ἐν Θράκῃ· Grues quidem in Thracia nascuntur. Et paullo post, Οὐκοῦν φιλοῦσι τὴν χώραν, ἐν ᾗ γεγόνασι· Regionem igitur amant, in qua nati sunt. Inde Thraciae aves dicuntur, et Strymoniae, et Bistoniae, a Strymone, fluvio, et Bistone, lacu Thraciae, unde creduntur proficisci. Virgilius libro decimo Aeneidos,

The ancients believed that most of them are born in Thrace. Aelian, in the place cited above: Αἱ γέρανοι γίνονται μὲν ἐν Θράκῃ [Hai geranoi ginontai men en Thrakē]; Cranes are born in Thrace. And shortly after: Οὐκοῦν φιλοῦσι τὴν χώραν, ἐν ᾗ γεγόνασι [Oukoun philousi tēn chōran, en hē gegonasi]; They therefore love the region in which they were born. Hence they are called birds of Thrace, and Strymonian and Bistonian, from the Strymon, a river, and the Biston, a lake of Thrace, from which they are believed to set out. Virgil, Aeneid, book 10:


— — — quales sub nubibus altis
Strymoniae dant signa grues. — —

— — — as beneath the high clouds Strymonian cranes give their signals. — —


Lucanus libri tertii versu 199.

Lucan, book 3, line 199:


Deseritur Strymon tepido committere Nilo Bistonias consuetus aves. — — — II, 618 Et libri quinti versu 711.

The Strymon is deserted, which is wont to commit the Bistonian birds to the warm Nile. — — — II, 618 And book 5, line 711:

Seneca, Oedipus, Act 3:

Not so many birds, fleeing the threats of the icy Strymon, exchange their winters, and, cleaving the sky, offset the Arctic snows with the warm Nile.

Antipater Sidonius capite decimo sexto libri tertii Anthologiae,

Antipater of Sidon, Anthology, book 3, chapter 16:


— — — — καὶ ἁρπάκτειραν ἐρύκων
Σπέρματος ὑψιπετῆ Βιστονίαν γέρανον· — —

— — — — καὶ ἁρπάκτειραν ἐρύκων Σπέρματος ὑψιπετῆ Βιστονίαν γέρανον [kai harpakteiran erykōn Spermatos hypsipetē Bistonian geranon]· — —


Et seminis direptricem arcens altivolam Bistoniam gruem. E Thracia discessurae dicuntur ad Hebrum amnem convenire. Aelianus libri secundi capite primo, Ὅταν τὰ ἤθη τὰ τῶν Θρακῶν καὶ τοὺς κρυμοὺς ἀπολείπωσι τοὺς Θρακίους αἱ γέ-ρανοι, ἀθροίζονται μὲν ἐς τὸν Ἕβρον· Cum Thracum sedes et frigora grues relinquunt, congregantur ad Hebrum. Tzetzes Chiliad. 4. Hist. 120.

And warding off the high-flying Bistonian crane, plunderer of seed. When about to leave Thrace, they are said to gather at the river Hebrus. Aelian, book 2, chapter 1: Ὅταν τὰ ἤθη τὰ τῶν Θρακῶν καὶ τοὺς κρυμοὺς ἀπολείπωσι τοὺς Θρακίους αἱ γέρανοι, ἀθροίζονται μὲν ἐς τὸν Ἕβρον [Hotan ta ēthē ta tōn Thrakōn kai tous krymous apoleipōsi tous Thrakious hai geranoi, athroizontai men es ton Hebron]; When the cranes leave the abodes and the cold of the Thracians, they gather at the Hebrus. Tzetzes, Chiliad 4, Hist. 120:


Ὅταν γοῦν πρὸς τὸν Αἴγυπτον μέλλουσιν ἀποτρέχειν,
Ὡς πρὸς τὸν Ἕβρον ποταμὸν τὸν Θρακικὸν ἐλθοῦσαι·

Ὅταν γοῦν πρὸς τὸν Αἴγυπτον μέλλουσιν ἀποτρέχειν, Ὡς πρὸς τὸν Ἕβρον ποταμὸν τὸν Θρακικὸν ἐλθοῦσαι [Hotan goun pros ton Aigypton mellousin apotrechein, Hōs pros ton Hebron potamon ton Thrakikon elthousai]·


Cum in Aegyptum evolaturae sunt, ubi ad Hebrum Thraciae fluvium venerint.

When they are about to fly off to Egypt, having come to the Hebrus, a river of Thrace.


Sed Scythicis gruibus alio est iter, nempe per Pontum, quem transvolant. Unde Virgilius libro sexto Aeneidos,

But the Scythian cranes take another route, namely across the Pontus, which they fly over. Hence Virgil, Aeneid, book 6:


— — — ad terram gurgite ab alto
Cum multae glomerantur aves, ubi frigidus annus
Trans Pontum fugat, et terris immittit apricis.

— — — as when many birds flock to land from the deep sea, when the cold season drives them across the Pontus and sends them to sunny lands.


Atque illas certum est, inquit Plinius, Pontum transvolaturas, primum omnium angustias petere inter duo promontoria Criu-metopon et Carambin. Quae nonnisi CLXXM passuum intervallo distant, ut idem asserit libri quarti capite duodecimo. II, 619 Alii quidem aliter statuunt, nempe tridui navigatione, vel, quod fere idem est, bis mille quingentis stadiis ab invicem distare duo haec promontoria. Dionysius Periegetes versu 155.

And it is certain, says Pliny, that when they are about to fly across the Pontus, they first of all make for the narrows between the two promontories Criu-metopon and Carambis. These are only 170,000 paces apart, as he likewise asserts in book 4, chapter 12. II, 619 Others indeed judge differently, namely that these two promontories are three days' sailing apart, or, what is nearly the same, 2,500 stadia. Dionysius Periegetes, line 155:


Αἵτ' ἄμφω ξυνίασιν ἐναντίαι, οὐ μὲν ἐοῦσαι
Ἐγγύθεν, ἀλλ᾽ ὅσον ὁλκὰς ἐπὶ τρίτον ἦμαρ ἀνύσσῃ.

Αἵτ' ἄμφω ξυνίασιν ἐναντίαι, οὐ μὲν ἐοῦσαι Ἐγγύθεν, ἀλλ᾽ ὅσον ὁλκὰς ἐπὶ τρίτον ἦμαρ ἀνύσσῃ [Hait' amphō xyniasin enantiai, ou men eousai Engythen, all᾽ hoson holkas epi triton ēmar anyssē].


Quae Priscianus itá reddidit:

These Priscian rendered thus:


Ergo conveniunt adversi gurgite tanto
Distantes, quantum ternis transire diebus
Evaleat navis. — — —

So they come together facing each other, across so great a gulf
Separated, as far as a ship could cross in three days. — — —


Et Ammianus libro vigesimo secundo, Haud procul inde attollitur Carambis etc. Cujus e regione Criu-metopon, Tauricae promontorium, duobus millibus et quingentis stadiis disparatum. Strabo etiam libro secundo, Τὸ μὲν οὖν τῆς Εὐρώπης ἀκρωτήριον καλεῖται Κριοῦ μέτωπον, τὸ δὲ τῆς Ἀσίας Κάραμβις, διέχοντα ἀλλήλων περὶ δισχιλίους σαδίους, καὶ πεντακοσίους· Europae quidem promontorium vocatur Criu-metopon (frons arietis), Asiae autem Carambis, ab invicem distantia stadiis circiter MMD. Quae tamen sunt falsissima, et palam refelluntur ipsius Strabonis verbis libro tertio, Διέσηκε δὲ ἡ Κάραμβις τῆς μὲν τῶν Χερσο-νησιτῶν πόλεως σταδίους δισχιλίους, καὶ πεντακοσίους, τοῦ δὲ Κριοῦ μετώπου πολὺ ἐλάττους τὸν ἀριθμόν· Carambis quidem distat ab urbe Chersonesitarum stadiis bis mille quingentis, sed Criu-metopon longe minus. Recte omnino: nam aliud Chersonesus urbs, aliud Chersonesus regio, in qua urbs illa sita. Et urbs quidem, quae est in boreali Chersonesi parte, a Carambi vere distat MMD stadiis. Sed in opposita parte Chersonesi Criu-metopon est Carambi multo propius. Tamen haec promiscue sumpta sunt: et quod de urbe Chersoneso nonnulli scripserant, illam a Carambi distare stadiis MMD, ita sumptum est, quasi de tota Chersoneso dictum, atque illius parte maxime australi, nempe Criu-metopo. Sed hujus commenti vanitas ex eo maxime apparet, quod ibidem a Strabone additur, Συ-χνοὶ γοῦν τῶν διαπλευσάντων τὸν πορθμὸν, ἅμα φασὶν ἀμφοτέρας ἰδεῖν τὰς ἄκρας ἑκατέρωθεν· Multi eorum, qui hoc fretum enavigarunt, se simul vidisse ajunt utrumque promontorium, in medio scilicet spatio constituti; quod non fie- col. 72 ret, si fretum pateret MMD stadiis. Imbecillior enim est humani oculi acies, quam ut ad MCCL stadia possit penetrare, quae faciunt horarias leucas plus LII.

And Ammianus, book 22: Not far from there rises Carambis etc. Opposite which lies Criu-metopon, a promontory of the Taurica, separated from it by two thousand five hundred stadia. Strabo too, in book 2: Τὸ μὲν οὖν τῆς Εὐρώπης ἀκρωτήριον καλεῖται Κριοῦ μέτωπον, τὸ δὲ τῆς Ἀσίας Κάραμβις, διέχοντα ἀλλήλων περὶ δισχιλίους σαδίους, καὶ πεντακοσίους [To men oun tēs Eurōpēs akrōtērion kaleitai Kriou metōpon, to de tēs Asias Karambis, diechonta allēlōn peri dischilious sadious, kai pentakosious]· The promontory of Europe is called Criu-metopon (ram's forehead), and that of Asia Carambis, distant from each other about 2,500 stadia. These statements, however, are utterly false, and are openly refuted by Strabo's own words in book 3: Διέσηκε δὲ ἡ Κάραμβις τῆς μὲν τῶν Χερσονησιτῶν πόλεως σταδίους δισχιλίους, καὶ πεντακοσίους, τοῦ δὲ Κριοῦ μετώπου πολὺ ἐλάττους τὸν ἀριθμόν [Diesēke de hē Karambis tēs men tōn Chersonēsitōn poleōs stadious dischilious, kai pentakosious, tou de Kriou metōpou poly elattous ton arithmon]· Carambis is distant from the city of the Chersonesites by two thousand five hundred stadia, but from Criu-metopon by far less. Quite rightly: for Chersonesus the city is one thing, and Chersonesus the region, in which that city lies, another. The city, which is in the northern part of the Chersonese, is indeed 2,500 stadia distant from Carambis. But on the opposite side of the Chersonese, Criu-metopon is much nearer to Carambis. Yet these have been confused: what some had written about the city of Chersonesus, that it is 2,500 stadia from Carambis, was taken as if said of the whole Chersonese, and of its most southern part, namely Criu-metopon. The emptiness of this invention is especially apparent from what Strabo adds in the same place: Συχνοὶ γοῦν τῶν διαπλευσάντων τὸν πορθμὸν, ἅμα φασὶν ἀμφοτέρας ἰδεῖν τὰς ἄκρας ἑκατέρωθεν [Sychnoi goun tōn diapleusantōn ton porthmon, hama phasin amphoteras idein tas akras hekaterōthen]· Many of those who have sailed through this strait say that they saw both promontories at once, that is, when placed in the middle of the passage; which would not col. 72 happen if the strait were 2,500 stadia wide. For the sight of the human eye is too weak to reach 1,250 stadia, which make more than 52 hourly leagues.


Utut sit, tam in hujus freti trajectu, quam in reliquo itinere, miram emicare gruum industriam tradunt veteres. Plinius Pontum transvolaturas saburra stabiliri asserit, et, cum medium transierint, abjici lapillos e pedibus, cum attigerint continentem, et e gutture arenam. Id est, tum demum non jam lapillos, sed arenam etiam evomi. Quod Solinus disertius, Ne pergentibus ad destinata II, 620 vis flatuum renitatur, arenas devorant, sublatisque lapillulis ad moderatam gravitatem saburrantur. Et paullo post, Cum contra medium (Pontum) adventasse se sciunt, scrupulorum sarcina pedes liberant. Ita nautae prodiderunt, compluti saepe ex illo casu imbre saxatili. Arenas non prius revomunt, quam securi sedis suae fuerint. Cassiodorus quoque horum lapillorum ita meminit Variorum libri quarti Epistola quadragesima septima, Grues, pelagus transiturae, parvos lapillos uncis pedibus amplectuntur, ut nec earum levitas nimio vento rapiatur, nec nativa celeritas iniquis ponderibus ingravetur. Scholiastes Aristophanis in Avibus, et ex eo Suidas diversa plane de causa lapillos istos a gruibus gestari et projici putant: nempe, ut ex cadentis sono sentiant πότερον ἐπὶ γῆς, ἢ ἐπὶ θαλάσσης φέρωνται· καὶ εἰ μὲν ἐπὶ θαλάσσης ἥκοι ὁ λίθος ἀνύουσι τὴν ὁδόν· εἰ δὲ ἐπὶ γῆς, ἀναπαύονται, an supra terram, aut supra mare ferantur; si autem lapis in mare deciderit, ire pergunt; at si in terram, quiescunt. At Maximus Tyrius Oratione quadragesima grues hunc lapidem asserit in ore pro saburra gestare. Οὐ πρότε-ρον, inquit, ἀνίπταται, πρὶν ξυλλάβῃ λίθον τῷ στόματι, ἕρμα μὲν εἶναι αὐ-τῇ πρὸς τὴν πτῆσιν, φυλακὴν δὲ πρὸς σωτηρίαν· Non ante volat, quam lapidem rostro susceperit, ut firmamentum ad volatum ipsi sit, et ad salutem custodia. Neque aliter Nonnus Dionisiacων libri quadragesimi versu 521.

However that may be, the ancients relate that both in crossing this strait and on the rest of their journey the remarkable ingenuity of cranes shines forth. Pliny asserts that when about to fly across the Pontus they are steadied with ballast, and that when they have passed the middle, the pebbles are dropped from their feet, and when they have reached the mainland, the sand from their throat. That is, only then do they disgorge not pebbles but sand too. Solinus puts this more explicitly: Lest the force of the winds should resist them as they proceed to their destination, they swallow sand, and taking up little pebbles they II, 620 ballast themselves to a moderate weight. And shortly after: When they know that they have come to the middle (of the Pontus), they free their feet of the load of stones. So sailors have reported, who have often been rained on by a shower of stones from this cause. The sand they do not disgorge until they are secure of their abode. Cassiodorus also mentions these pebbles, in Variae book 4, Letter 47: Cranes, when about to cross the sea, clasp small pebbles in their hooked feet, so that their lightness may not be carried off by too strong a wind, nor their native speed be weighed down by unequal burdens. The scholiast on Aristophanes' Birds, and Suidas following him, think that these pebbles are carried and thrown down by cranes for an entirely different reason: namely, so that from the sound of the falling stone they may perceive πότερον ἐπὶ γῆς, ἢ ἐπὶ θαλάσσης φέρωνται· καὶ εἰ μὲν ἐπὶ θαλάσσης ἥκοι ὁ λίθος ἀνύουσι τὴν ὁδόν· εἰ δὲ ἐπὶ γῆς, ἀναπαύονται [poteron epi gēs, ē epi thalassēs pherōntai; kai ei men epi thalassēs hēkoi ho lithos anyousi tēn hodon; ei de epi gēs, anapauontai], whether they are borne over land or over sea; if the stone falls into the sea, they continue on; but if onto land, they rest. But Maximus of Tyre, Oration 40, asserts that cranes carry this stone in their mouth as ballast. Οὐ πρότερον, he says, ἀνίπταται, πρὶν ξυλλάβῃ λίθον τῷ στόματι, ἕρμα μὲν εἶναι αὐτῇ πρὸς τὴν πτῆσιν, φυλακὴν δὲ πρὸς σωτηρίαν [Ou proteron … anuptatai, prin xyllabē lithon tō stomati, herma men einai autē pros tēn ptēsin, phylakēn de pros sōtērian]· It does not fly before it has taken up a stone in its beak, to be a support for its flight and a safeguard for its safety. Nor otherwise Nonnus, Dionysiaca book 40, line 521:


Αἱ στομάτων ἔκτοσθεν ἀοσσητῆρα κελεύθου
Λᾶαν ἐλαφρίζουσι καταχθέα, μήποτε κείνων
Ἱπταμένων πτερὰ κοῦφα παρακλάγξειεν ἀήτης.

Αἱ στομάτων ἔκτοσθεν ἀοσσητῆρα κελεύθου Λᾶαν ἐλαφρίζουσι καταχθέα, μήποτε κείνων Ἱπταμένων πτερὰ κοῦφα παρακλάγξειεν ἀήτης. [Hai stomatōn ektosthen aossētēra keleuthou / Laan elaphrizousi katachthea, mēpote keinōn / Hiptamenōn ptera koupha paraklangxeien aētēs.]


Quae in ore auxiliatorem viae gravem lapidem ferunt, ne quando ipsarum volantium alas leves aberrare faciat ventus. Et Phile capite decimo,

Which carry in their mouth a heavy stone as a helper on their way, lest the wind should ever make the light wings of them as they fly go astray. And Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)], chapter 10:


Τίς ἕρμα ποιεῖ τῇσι γεράνοις τὰς λίθους,
Ἃς ἐγκαθειργνύουσι τοῖς παρισθμίοις,
Πρὸς τὰς ὑπὲρ γῆς ἐμβολὰς τῶν πνευμάτων;

Τίς ἕρμα ποιεῖ τῇσι γεράνοις τὰς λίθους, Ἃς ἐγκαθειργνύουσι τοῖς παρισθμίοις, Πρὸς τὰς ὑπὲρ γῆς ἐμβολὰς τῶν πνευμάτων; [Tis herma poiei tēsi geranois tas lithous, / Has enkatheirgnyousi tois paristhmiois, / Pros tas hyper gēs embolas tōn pneumatōn?]


Quis fecit, ut gruibus pro saburra essent lapides, quos faucibus includunt ad ventorum impetus, qui sunt super terram? Male legunt ἀμβολάς. Id enim ex his Aeliani sumptum, Λίθον δὲ ἑκάστη καταπιοῦσα, ὡς ἔχειν καὶ δεῖ-πνον, καὶ πρὸς τὰς ἐμβολὰς τῶν ἀνέμων ἕρμα, πειρῶνται τοῦ μετοικισμοῦ· Unaquaeque, lapide vorato, quem et coenae et saburrae loco habeat, adversus ventorum impetus, migrationem aggreditur. Alii hunc lapidem auri indicem esse dictitant. Idem Aelianus libri tertii, capite decimo tertio, Γέρανος δὲ λίθον ὅν-περ οὖν καταπίνει πετομένη ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἔχειν ἕρμα, χρυσοῦ βάσανός ἐστιν· Lapis, quem volatura grus pro saburra devorat, est auri index. Itaque Phile vocat

Who has made the cranes carry stones as ballast, which they hold in their throats against the onslaughts of the winds that are upon the earth? They wrongly read ἀμβολάς [ambolas]. For this is taken from these words of Aelian: Λίθον δὲ ἑκάστη καταπιοῦσα, ὡς ἔχειν καὶ δεῖπνον, καὶ πρὸς τὰς ἐμβολὰς τῶν ἀνέμων ἕρμα, πειρῶνται τοῦ μετοικισμοῦ· [Lithon de hekastē katapiousa, hōs echein kai deipnon, kai pros tas embolas tōn anemōn herma, peirōntai tou metoikismou] Each one, having swallowed a stone to serve both as a meal and as ballast against the onslaughts of the winds, sets out on its migration. Others keep saying that this stone is a touchstone for gold. The same Aelian, book 3, chapter 13: Γέρανος δὲ λίθον ὅνπερ οὖν καταπίνει πετομένη ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἔχειν ἕρμα, χρυσοῦ βάσανός ἐστιν· [Geranos de lithon honper oun katapinei petomenē hyper tou echein herma, chrysou basanos estin] The stone which the crane swallows as ballast when about to fly is a touchstone for gold. Accordingly Philes calls them


Λίθους κριτικὰς τοῦ χρυσοῦ τοῖς ἐμπόροις, II, 621 lapides mercatoribus auri indices. Sed hoc commentum ita refellit Aristoteles, Historiae animalium libri octavi capite duodecimo, Τὸ δὲ περὶ τοῦ λίθου ψεῦδός ἐστι· λέγεται γὰρ ὡς ἔχουσιν ἕρμα λίθον, ὃς γίνεται χρήσιμος πρὸς τὰς τοῦ χρυσοῦ βασάνους, ὅταν ἐκπέσῃ. Quod de lapide narrant, falsum est; lapidem nempe eas pro saburra habere, qui, cum deciderit, utilis sit ad auri probationem. Sed, si hoc sit commentitium, erunt fortasse veriora, quae jam sequentur.

Λίθους κριτικὰς τοῦ χρυσοῦ τοῖς ἐμπόροις [Lithous kritikas tou chrysou tois emporois], II, 621 stones that test gold for merchants. But Aristotle refutes this fiction as follows, History of Animals, book 8, chapter 12: Τὸ δὲ περὶ τοῦ λίθου ψεῦδός ἐστι· λέγεται γὰρ ὡς ἔχουσιν ἕρμα λίθον, ὃς γίνεται χρήσιμος πρὸς τὰς τοῦ χρυσοῦ βασάνους, ὅταν ἐκπέσῃ. [To de peri tou lithou pseudos esti; legetai gar hōs echousin herma lithon, hos ginetai chrēsimos pros tas tou chrysou basanous, hotan ekpesē.] What they tell about the stone is false: namely, that they carry a stone as ballast which, when it has fallen out, is useful for testing gold. But if this is a fiction, perhaps what follows now will be truer.


Mirus est inter illas concentus, consensusque, mira animorum concordia. Plinius, Quando proficiscuntur, consentiunt. Solinus, Concors cura omnium pro fatigatis, adeo, ut, si quae defecerunt, congruant universae, lassatasque sustol- col. 73 lant, usque dum vires otio recuperentur. Ubi nota congruendi verbum, a gruibus sumptum: de gruibus proprie usurpari, unde ad alia transfertur. Festus, Congruere dictum est a gruibus, quae non se segregant, sive cum volant, sive cum pascunt. Ita ingruere est gruum instar magno agmine irruere. Unde ad milites, ad imbrem, ad grandinem, et ad alia translatum. Et in Solino leguntur fluctus ingrui.

There is among them a wonderful harmony and agreement, a wonderful concord of minds. Pliny: When they set out, they agree together. Solinus: All share a common care for the weary, so that, if any have failed, they all gather together and lift up the exhausted ones, col. 73 until their strength is recovered by rest. Note here the verb congruere [to come together], taken from cranes: it is properly used of cranes, and from them transferred to other things. Festus: Congruere is said from cranes, which do not separate from one another, whether they are flying or feeding. So also ingruere means to rush upon in a great host like cranes. From this it was transferred to soldiers, to rain, to hail and to other things. And in Solinus we read fluctus ingrui [waves rushing in].


Nec immerito Oppianus,

Not without reason does Oppian speak of

altivolantem gruum chorum: et Antipater Sidonius,

the high-flying chorus of cranes; and Antipater of Sidon

altivolantem Bistoniam gruem dixit. Et Virgilius,

spoke of the high-flying Bistonian crane. And Virgil:

The airy cranes have fled, — — —


id est, interprete Servio, in altum volantes. Et Ausonius in Monosyllabis,

that is, as Servius explains, flying on high. And Ausonius in the Monosyllables:
