When Ibycus perished, the high-flying crane was the informer.


Et grus de seipsa in Avieno, Fabula 15.

And the crane says of itself in Avienus, Fable 15:


— — — Sublimis in aera penna
Proxima sideribus numinibusque feror.

— — — Lofty on my wing into the air
I am borne, next to the stars and the gods.


In altum enim volant grues, ad omnes aeris mutationes intentae, ne a tempestate obruantur. Aristoteles, Historiae animalium lib. 9. cap. 10. Εἰς ὕψος πέ-τονται πρὸς τὸ καθορᾶν τὰ πόῤῥω, καὶ ἐὰν ἴδωσι νέφη, καὶ χειμέρια (Antigo- nus καὶ συστροφὴν) καταπτᾶσαι ἡσυχάζουσιν· In altum volant, ut procul prospi- ciant: et si nubes et tempestatem (aut turbinem) videant, infra devolantes quietae manent. Itaque est inter prognostica futurae tempestatis, cum nauta e medio mari videt γεράνους ὑποστρεφούσας, καὶ τὴν ἔμπαλιν πετομένας, grues rever- tentes, et retro volantes. Ita Aelianus Historiae libri 3. capite 14. Quibus similia videas apud Aratum, Virgilium, Plinium, Theonem et Avienum. Sed et II, 622 grues contendunt in altissima, ut de excelsiori specula metentur, quas petant terras. Ita Solinus et Isidorus. Videntur etiam ad summa niti, quia ibi tranquillior est aër, quod his verbis testatur Horus lib. 2. cap. 93. Ὑψηλῶς πάνυ ἵπτάται (γέ-ρανος) ἵνα θεάσηται τὰ νέφη, μὴ ἄρα χειμάζῃ, ἵνα ἐν ἡσυχίᾳ διαμένῃ· Grus alte admodum volat, ut nubes conspiciat, neque tempestate agitetur, sed quieta maneat. Quartam denique hanc causam affert Alkazuinius, فاذا طارت ترفعت في الهوا جدا كي لا يعرض لها شي من السباع الطير Et cum volat in sublime, multum evehitur, ne rapacium avium ulla ei occurrat.

For cranes fly on high, attentive to every change of the air, so as not to be overwhelmed by a storm. Aristotle, History of Animals, book 9, ch. 10: Εἰς ὕψος πέτονται πρὸς τὸ καθορᾶν τὰ πόῤῥω, καὶ ἐὰν ἴδωσι νέφη, καὶ χειμέρια [Eis hypsos petontai pros to kathoran ta porrhō, kai ean idōsi nephē, kai cheimeria] (Antigonus has καὶ συστροφὴν [kai systrophēn]) καταπτᾶσαι ἡσυχάζουσιν· [kataptasai hēsychazousin] They fly on high in order to see far ahead; and if they see clouds and stormy weather (or a whirlwind), they fly down and stay quiet. Accordingly it is among the signs of a coming storm when a sailor in mid-sea sees γεράνους ὑποστρεφούσας, καὶ τὴν ἔμπαλιν πετομένας [geranous hypostrephousas, kai tēn empalin petomenas], cranes turning back and flying in the opposite direction. So Aelian, History, book 3, chapter 14. You may see similar statements in Aratus, Virgil, Pliny, Theon and Avienus. But II, 622 cranes also strive toward the greatest heights, so that from a loftier watchtower they may survey the lands they are heading for. So Solinus and Isidore. They also seem to strive for the heights because the air is calmer there, as Horus attests in these words, book 2, ch. 93: Ὑψηλῶς πάνυ ἵπτάται (γέρανος) ἵνα θεάσηται τὰ νέφη, μὴ ἄρα χειμάζῃ, ἵνα ἐν ἡσυχίᾳ διαμένῃ· [Hypsēlōs pany hiptatai (geranos) hina theasētai ta nephē, mē ara cheimazē, hina en hēsychia diamenē] The crane flies very high in order to observe the clouds, so that it may not be tossed by a storm but remain at rest. Finally, Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt] gives this fourth reason: فاذا طارت ترفعت في الهوا جدا كي لا يعرض لها شي من السباع الطير [fa-idhā ṭārat taraffaʿat fī al-hawā jiddan kay lā yaʿriḍ lahā shay min al-sibāʿ al-ṭayr] And when it flies aloft, it rises very high, so that none of the birds of prey may meet it.


Agmen in ipso volatu formam habet trianguli, qui basi a ventis impulsus summa parte aërem secat. Cicero lib. 2. De natura Deorum, Illud vero ab Aristotele animadversum, grues, cum loca calidiora petentes maria transmittunt, tri- anguli formam efficere. Ejus autem summo angulo aër ab iis adversus pellitur. Deinde sensim ab utroque latere, tanquam remis, ita pennis cursus avium levatur. Basis autem trianguli, quam grues efficiunt, ea tanquam a puppi ventis adjuvatur. Plutarchus in libro Utra animalia, etc. Εἰς τρίγωνον συνάγουσαι σχίζουσι τῇ κορυφῇ τὸ πνεῦμα περιῤῥέον, ὥστε μὴ διασπᾶσθαι τὴν τάξιν· In triangulum collectae illius vertice ventum circumfusum incidunt, ne distrahatur earum acies. Aelianus lib. 13. cap. 13. Τρίγωνον ὀξύγονον τὸ σχῆμα τῆς πτήσεως ἀποφαίνουσι, ἵνα ἐμπίπτουσαι τῷ ἀέρι διακόπτωσιν αὐτόν· In triangulum oxygonum volatum suum configurant, ut in aërem incidentes eum facilius secent. Phile etiam eas volare asserit,

In flight itself the flock has the form of a triangle, which, driven at its base by the winds, cuts the air with its apex. Cicero, book 2 On the Nature of the Gods: "This too was observed by Aristotle: that cranes, when they cross the seas seeking warmer regions, form the shape of a triangle. With its apex the air in front of them is pushed aside. Then gradually, on either side, the course of the birds is borne up by their wings as by oars. And the base of the triangle which the cranes form is helped by the winds, as if from the stern." Plutarch, in the book Whether Land or Sea Animals, etc.: Εἰς τρίγωνον συνάγουσαι σχίζουσι τῇ κορυφῇ τὸ πνεῦμα περιῤῥέον, ὥστε μὴ διασπᾶσθαι τὴν τάξιν· [Eis trigōnon synagousai schizousi tē koryphē to pneuma perirrheon, hōste mē diaspasthai tēn taxin] "Gathered into a triangle, they cut with its apex the wind flowing around them, so that their line is not broken up." Aelian, book 13, ch. 13: Τρίγωνον ὀξύγονον τὸ σχῆμα τῆς πτήσεως ἀποφαίνουσι, ἵνα ἐμπίπτουσαι τῷ ἀέρι διακόπτωσιν αὐτόν· [Trigōnon oxygonon to schēma tēs ptēseōs apophainousi, hina empiptousai tō aeri diakoptōsin auton] "They shape their flight into an acute-angled triangle, so that, striking into the air, they may cut it more easily." Philes also asserts that they fly


Εἰς ὀρμαθὸν τρίστοιχον ὀξυγωνίου,

Εἰς ὀρμαθὸν τρίστοιχον ὀξυγωνίου, [Eis hormathon tristoichon oxygōniou]


in ordinem triquetrum acutis angulis. Et Tzetzes,

"in a three-sided formation with acute angles." And Tzetzes:


Τρίγωνον ὀξυγώνιον ποιοῦνται τούτων πτῆσιν, a) col. 74
Ὡς τὸν ἀέρα τέμνωσιν οὕτως εὐμαρεστέρως,

Τρίγωνον ὀξυγώνιον ποιοῦνται τούτων πτῆσιν, [Trigōnon oxygōnion poiountai toutōn ptēsin] a) col. 74 Ὡς τὸν ἀέρα τέμνωσιν οὕτως εὐμαρεστέρως, [Hōs ton aera temnōsin houtōs eumaresterōs]


Triangulum oxygonium faciunt earum volatus, ut aerem sic facilius dividant. Quin triangulum hac figura quasdam litteras imitari putantur, puta A. V. Δ. Λ. Υ. Unde Hieronymus Epist. 4. ad Rusticum, Grues unum sequuntur ordine literato. Ita etiam Isidorus. Unde lux his Lucani de gruibus lib. 5. versu 712.

"They make their flight an acute-angled triangle, so that they may thus divide the air more easily." Indeed, by this triangular figure they are thought to imitate certain letters, namely A, V, Δ, Λ, Υ. Hence Jerome, Epist. 4 to Rusticus: "Cranes follow one leader in a lettered order." So too Isidore. This sheds light on these lines of Lucan on cranes, book 5, line 712:


— — — primoque volatu Effingunt varias casu monstrante figuras: Mox, ubi percussit tensas Notus altior alas, II, 623 Confusos temere immistae glomerantur in orbes, Et turbata perit dispersis littera pennis.

— — — and in their first flight they form various figures, as chance directs; soon, when Notus strikes their outstretched wings from higher up, II, 623 they are heedlessly mingled and massed into confused circles, and the letter, thrown into disorder, perishes as their feathers scatter.


Et Martialis in Xeniis,

And Martial in the Xenia:


Turbabis versus, nec litera tota volabit,
Unam perdideris si Palamedis avem.

You will throw the lines into disorder, and the letter will not fly whole,
if you lose a single bird of Palamedes.


Et de nomine Earini libri noni Epigrammate decimo quarto,

And on the name of Earinus, book 9, Epigram 14:


Quod penna scribente grues ad sidera tollunt.

Which cranes, with writing wing, raise to the stars.


Et Symposius, Aenigmate trigesimo sexto, ubi grus dicit,

And Symphosius, Riddle 36, where the crane says:


Litera sum coeli penna perscripta volantis.

I am a letter of the sky, written out by a flying wing.


Malim perscripta volante. Et Claudianus de bello Gildonico, ubi de gruibus,

I would prefer perscripta volante [written out by (me) flying]. And Claudian, in The Gildonic War, where he speaks of cranes:


Ordinibus variis per nubila texitur ingens
Littera, pennarumque notis inscribitur aër.

In varied ranks a huge letter is woven across the clouds,
and the air is inscribed with the marks of their wings.


Et Cassiodorus Variorum lib. 8. Epistola 12. Nam et hodie grues, qui classem consociant, alphabeti formas, natura imbuente, describunt. Et in Philostrati Heroicis Ulysses, grues videns solito more volantes, in Palamedem respiciens, Αἱ γέρανοι, ἔφη, μαρτύρονται τοὺς Ἀχαιοὺς, ὅτι αὗται γράμματα εὗρον, οὐχὶ σύ· Grues, inquit, Graecis testantur se, non te literas invenisse. Legerim τοῖς Ἀχαιοῖς, non τοὺς Ἀχαιούς· Et Nazianzenus Oratione 34. Τίνος Παλαμήδους τακτικὰ, κινήματά τε, καὶ σχήματα γεράνων, ὡς πᾶσι, καὶ ταῦτα παι-δεύματα, κινουμένων ἐν τάξει, καὶ μετὰ ποικίλης τῆς πτήσεως; Cujus Palamedis sunt ordinati gruum motus, et figurae, et praecepta, quibus, ut ajunt, in acie vario volatu se movent? Eaedem aquila visa b) κολπωσάμεναι, μηνοειδὲς τὸ μέ-σον ἀποφήνασαι, ἀπειλοῦσιν ὡς ἀντιταξόμεναι, sinu ita aperto, ut crescentis lunae speciem imitentur, minantur tanquam obstiturae; et retrocedit aquila, volatumque inhibet.

And Cassiodorus, Variae book 8, Epistle 12: "For even today cranes, which form a fleet together, trace the shapes of the alphabet, nature instructing them." And in Philostratus' Heroicus, Ulysses, seeing cranes flying in their usual manner, looked at Palamedes and said: Αἱ γέρανοι, ἔφη, μαρτύρονται τοὺς Ἀχαιοὺς, ὅτι αὗται γράμματα εὗρον, οὐχὶ σύ· [Hai geranoi, ephē, martyrontai tous Achaious, hoti hautai grammata heuron, ouchi sy] "The cranes," he said, "testify to the Greeks that they, not you, invented letters." I would read τοῖς Ἀχαιοῖς [tois Achaiois], not τοὺς Ἀχαιούς [tous Achaious]. And Nazianzen, Oration 34: Τίνος Παλαμήδους τακτικὰ, κινήματά τε, καὶ σχήματα γεράνων, ὡς πᾶσι, καὶ ταῦτα παιδεύματα, κινουμένων ἐν τάξει, καὶ μετὰ ποικίλης τῆς πτήσεως; [Tinos Palamēdous taktika, kinēmata te, kai schēmata geranōn, hōs pasi, kai tauta paideumata, kinoumenōn en taxei, kai meta poikilēs tēs ptēseōs] "Of what Palamedes are the ordered movements, figures and precepts of the cranes, by which, as they say, they move in battle line with varied flight?" The same birds, when an eagle is sighted, b) κολπωσάμεναι, μηνοειδὲς τὸ μέσον ἀποφήνασαι, ἀπειλοῦσιν ὡς ἀντιταξόμεναι, [kolpōsamenai, mēnoeides to meson apophēnasai, apeilousin hōs antitaxomenai] "opening a hollow so that they imitate the appearance of the crescent moon, threaten as if about to resist"; and the eagle retreats and checks its flight.


Habent duces in primo agmine, et οὐραγοὺς in extremo, quos describit Philosophus ἐπισυρίττοντας ἐν τοῖς ἐσχάτοις, ὥστε ἀκούεσθαι τὴν φωνὴν, inter postremos insibilantes, ita, ut vox audiri possit. Unde Plinius: Ducem, quem sequantur, eligunt. Iam extremo agmine, per vices qui acclament, dispositos ha-bent, et qui gregem voce contineant. Et Solinus, Fidens meatu praeit catervas, volatus desidiam castigat voce, quae cogit agmen. Ea ubi obraucata est, succedit alia. Aelianus seniores, ac viarum peritas, et esse ἡγεμόνας τῆς πτήσεως, volatus duces, et οὐραγεῖν asserit, id est, extremum agmen regere, dum in medio II, 624 sunt natu minores. Inprimis mirabile illud est, quomodo se inter volandum mutuo juvent. Cicero, In tergo praevolantium colla et capita reponunt. Quod quia ipse dux facere non potest, quia non habet, ubi nitatur, revolat, ut ipse quoque quiescat. In ejus locum succedit ex iis, quae acquieverant, proxima, eaque vicissitudo in omni cursu servatur. Basilius in Hexaëmeron Homilia octava, Ἄλ-λό τε γὰρ ἄλλη τὴν ὁδηγίαν ἐκδέχεται, καὶ τακτόν τινα χρόνον προκαθηγη-σαμένη τῆς πτήσεως, εἰς τὸ κατόπιν περιελθοῦσα, τῇ μεθ᾽ ἑαυτὴν τὴν ἡγεμο-νίαν τῆς ὁδοῦ παραδίδωσι. Unde Ambrosius in Hexaëmeron libri quinti capite decimo quinto, Praecedit una caeteris, praestituto sibi tempore, et quasi ante signa praecurrit: deinde convertitur, et sequenti sortem ducendi agminis cedit. Cassiodorus libri noni Epistola secunda, His etiam volatus vicaria aequalitate disponitur, ultima fit prima, et quae primatum tenuit, esse posterior non recusat. Damir Arabs, يقدمها واحد منها كالرايس لها وهي col. 75 تتبعه ويكون ذلك حينا ثم يخلفه اخر منها مقدما حتي يصير الذي كان مقدما موخرا Praecedit una ex illis, tanquam ducis vices praestans, et aliae sequuntur, idque ad tempus. Deinde succedit alia ex illo numero, donec, quae prima fuerat, fiat ultima.

They have leaders at the head of the column and οὐραγοὺς [ouragous] at the rear, whom the Philosopher describes as ἐπισυρίττοντας ἐν τοῖς ἐσχάτοις, ὥστε ἀκούεσθαι τὴν φωνὴν [episyrittontas en tois eschatois, hōste akouesthai tēn phōnēn], whistling among the hindmost, so that their voice can be heard. Hence Pliny: They choose a leader to follow. At the rear of the column they have birds posted to call out in turn and to keep the flock together with their voice. And Solinus: Confident of its course, it goes before the flocks and rebukes sluggishness in flight with its voice, which keeps the column together. When that voice has grown hoarse, another takes its place. Aelian asserts that the older birds, experienced in the routes, are ἡγεμόνας τῆς πτήσεως [hēgemonas tēs ptēseōs], leaders of the flight, and that they οὐραγεῖν [ouragein], that is, command the rear of the column, while the younger ones are in the middle. II, 624 Especially remarkable is the way they help one another in flight. Cicero: They rest their necks and heads on the backs of those flying in front. Because the leader himself cannot do this, since he has nothing to lean on, he flies back so that he too may rest. His place is taken by the nearest of those that have been resting, and this alternation is kept up throughout the whole journey. Basil, Hexaëmeron, Homily 8: Ἄλλό τε γὰρ ἄλλη τὴν ὁδηγίαν ἐκδέχεται, καὶ τακτόν τινα χρόνον προκαθηγησαμένη τῆς πτήσεως, εἰς τὸ κατόπιν περιελθοῦσα, τῇ μεθ᾽ ἑαυτὴν τὴν ἡγεμονίαν τῆς ὁδοῦ παραδίδωσι [Allo te gar allē tēn hodēgian ekdechetai, kai takton tina chronon prokathēgēsamenē tēs ptēseōs, eis to katopin perielthousa, tē meth᾽ heautēn tēn hēgemonian tēs hodou paradidōsi]. Hence Ambrose, Hexaëmeron, book 5, chapter 15: One goes before the rest for a set time and, as it were, runs ahead of the standards; then it turns back and yields the office of leading the column to the one following. Cassiodorus, book 9, Letter 2: Their flight, too, is arranged by an equal alternation: the last becomes first, and the one that held first place does not refuse to be behind. Damir the Arab: يقدمها واحد منها كالرايس لها وهي [yuqaddimuhā wāḥid minhā ka-l-rāyis lahā wa-hiya] col. 75 تتبعه ويكون ذلك حينا ثم يخلفه اخر منها مقدما حتي يصير الذي كان مقدما موخرا [tatbaʿuhu wa-yakūnu dhālika ḥīnan thumma yakhlufuhu ākhar minhā muqaddaman ḥattā yaṣīra alladhī kāna muqaddaman muʾakhkharan] One of them goes ahead, acting as leader, and the others follow, and this for a time. Then another from their number takes its place, until the one that had been first becomes last.


Eadem in vigiliis servatur vicissitudo, cum enim, volatu fessae, in terram descendunt, ut quiescant et somnos captent, reliquis dormientibus, una, aut altera, aut e toto numero paucae per vices toti gregi invigilant. Aristoteles lib. 9. cap. 10. Ὅταν δὲ καθίζωνται, αἱ μὲν ἄλλαι, ὑπὸ τῇ πτέρυγι τὴν κεφαλὴν ἔχουσαι, καθεύδουσιν ἐπὶ ἑνὸς ποδὸς ἐναλλάξ, ὁ δὲ ἡγεμὼν γυμνὴν ἔχων τὴν κεφαλὴν προορᾷ, καὶ ὅταν αἴσθηταί τι, σημαίνει βοῶν, Cum consistunt, caeterae dormiunt capite subter alam condito, alternis pedibus insistentes. Dux autem (id est, vigil) detecto capite prospicit, et quod senserat, voce significat. Antigonus idem sequitur Mirabilium cap. 46. et Alkazuinius cum Auctario, واذا ارادت النوم ادخل كل واحد راسه تحت جناحها لعلمها ان الجناح احمل للصدمة من الراس لما فيه من العين التي هي اشرف الاعضا والدماغ الذي هو ملاك البدن ونام كل واحد منها قايما علي احدي رجليه حتي لا يكون نومها ثقيل واما قايدها وحارسها فلا ينام ولا يدخل راسه في جناحه ولا يزال ينظر من جميع الجوانب فان احس باحد صاح باعلا صوته فاخبر اصحابه بالعدو Cum dormire volunt, caput II, 625 ponunt sub alis; quia sciunt, alas collisionem melius ferre, quam caput, in quo est oculus partium nobilissima, et cerebrum, a quo pendet reliquum corpus. Dormi- unt autem stantes in uno pede, ne gravis sit somnus. Sed, qui dux et custos est, a somno abstinet, nec subter alis caput condit. Quin ab omni parte continuo pro- spicit. Et, si quem sentit, edita voce clamat, ut sociis suis hostem adesse signifi- cet. Alii duo quaedam addunt, unum, grues per vices vigilare. Horus lib. 2. cap. 90. Αὗται γὰρ ἑαυτὰς φυλάττουσι γρηγοροῦσαι κατ᾽ ὄρδινον ἐν πάσῃ τῇ νυκτί. Eae se ipsas custodiunt, ordine tota nocte vigilantes. Solinus, Excubias nocte dividunt, ut exsomnis sit decima quaeque. Isidorus, Nocte excubias divi- dunt, et ordinem vigiliarum per vices faciunt. Cassiodorus, Vigilant vicissim, communi se cautela custodiunt. Basilius, Τοῦ καιροῦ τῆς φυλακῆς πληρομένου, ἡ μὲν βοήσασα πρὸς ὕπνον ἐτράπετο. ἡ δὲ τὴν διαδοχὴν ὑποδεξαμένη, ἧς ἔτυ- col. 76 χεν ἀσφαλείας, ἀντέδωκεν ἐν τῷ μέρει. Quod Ambrosius ita diducit: Ubi vi- giliarum fuerit tempus impletum, perfuncto munere in somnum se praemisso clan- gore componit, ut excitet dormientem, cui vicem muneris traditura est. At illa volens suscipit sortem, nec, usu nostro, invita et pigrior somno renuntiat. Sed impigre suis excutitur stratis, vicem exequitur, et quam accepit gratiam pari cura atque officio repraesentat. Et Damir, في طبعه الخوف والتحارس بالنوبة فاذا قضي نوبتة قام الذي كان نايما يحرس مكانه حتي تقضي كله ما يلزمها من الحراسة E natura ejus est, ut timeat et custodias agat per vices. Et, cum absolvit vices suas, surgit una ex iis, quae dormiebant, ut excubias agat ejus loco, donec omnes egerint excubias, quibus tenentur. Alterum, lapidem vigiles pede ferre, qui casu suo dormientes aut dormiturientes excitet. Plinius, Excubias habent nocturnis temporibus, lapillum pede sustinentes, qui laxatus somno et deci- dens indiligentiam coarguat. Solinus, Vigiles ponduscula digitis amplectuntur, quae, si forte exciderint, somnum coarguant. Plutarchus, Αἱ προφυλακὴν ἔχου-σαι νυκτὸς, ἐπὶ θατέρου σκέλους ὀχοῦνται τὸ σῶμα, τῷ δ᾽ ἑτέρῳ ποδὶ λίθον πε-ριλαβοῦσαι κρατοῦσι· συνέχει γὰρ ὁ τῆς ἀφῆς τόνος ἐν τῷ μὴ καθεύδειν πολὺν χρόνον. Ὅταν δὲ ἀνῶσιν, ἐκπεσὼν ὁ λίθος ταχὺ διήγειρε τὴν προεμένην. Quae noctu excubias agunt crurum alterutro corpus sustinent, et altero pede lapil- lum prehensum tenent. Et apprehensionis contentio somnum aliquamdiu cohibet. Sed, quamprimum remisere, decidens calculus negligentem statim excitat. Aelianus [III, 13.], Ἑστᾶσι μὲν ἀσκωλιάζουσαι, τῷ γε μὲν μετεώρῳ ποδὶ λίθον κατέχουσι τοῖς ὄνυξι μάλα ἐγκρατῶς τε καὶ εὐλαβῶς· ἵνα ἐάν ποτε λάθωσιν ἑαυτὰς εἰς ὕπνον ὑπολισθαίνουσαι, πεσὼν καὶ ὑποκτυπήσας ὁ λίθος, ἀποδαρθάνειν κατα-ναγκάσῃ. Unico quidem pede innituntur, et in altero, qui sublimis est, lapillum II, 626 unguibus firmissime et summa cautione tenent; ut, si quando somnus obrepserit, lapillus cadens strepitu suo eas excitet. Quae eadem Phile et Tzetzes. Itaque, cum grues Aelianus lapillos vorare dicit, ὡς ἔχειν καὶ δεῖπνον, καὶ πρὸς τὰς ἐμβολὰς τῶν ἀνέμων ἕρμα, ut et pro coena habeant, et pro saburra adversus ventorum impetus, videndum, annon pro δεῖπνον legi debeat δι᾽ ὕπνον, propter somnum. Lapillos enim gruibus esse pro coena, valde absurdum est. Sed voluit forte Aelianus, lapides a gruibus vorari, non solum ut Pontum transvolaturis pro saburra sit, sed et ut, mari trajecto, evomiti ad somnum, qua ratione diximus, arcendum inserviant.

The same alternation is observed in keeping watch. For when, tired from flying, they come down to the ground to rest and sleep, while the rest sleep, one or two, or a few out of the whole number, keep watch in turn over the entire flock. Aristotle, book 9, ch. 10: Ὅταν δὲ καθίζωνται, αἱ μὲν ἄλλαι, ὑπὸ τῇ πτέρυγι τὴν κεφαλὴν ἔχουσαι, καθεύδουσιν ἐπὶ ἑνὸς ποδὸς ἐναλλάξ, ὁ δὲ ἡγεμὼν γυμνὴν ἔχων τὴν κεφαλὴν προορᾷ, καὶ ὅταν αἴσθηταί τι, σημαίνει βοῶν [Hotan de kathizōntai, hai men allai, hypo tē pterygi tēn kephalēn echousai, katheudousin epi henos podos enallax, ho de hēgemōn gymnēn echōn tēn kephalēn proora, kai hotan aisthētai ti, sēmainei boōn], When they settle, the others sleep with the head hidden under the wing, standing on one foot and then the other. But the leader (that is, the watchman) looks out with his head uncovered, and signals by his voice what he has perceived. Antigonus follows the same in the Mirabilia, ch. 46, and so does Alkazuinius with the Auctarium: واذا ارادت النوم ادخل كل واحد راسه تحت جناحها لعلمها ان الجناح احمل للصدمة من الراس لما فيه من العين التي هي اشرف الاعضا والدماغ الذي هو ملاك البدن ونام كل واحد منها قايما علي احدي رجليه حتي لا يكون نومها ثقيل واما قايدها وحارسها فلا ينام ولا يدخل راسه في جناحه ولا يزال ينظر من جميع الجوانب فان احس باحد صاح باعلا صوته فاخبر اصحابه بالعدو [wa-idhā arādat al-nawm adkhala kull wāḥid raʾsahu taḥt janāḥihā li-ʿilmihā anna al-janāḥ aḥmal li-l-ṣadma min al-raʾs li-mā fīhi min al-ʿayn allatī hiya ashraf al-aʿḍā wa-l-dimāgh alladhī huwa milāk al-badan wa-nāma kull wāḥid minhā qāyiman ʿalā iḥdā rijlayhi ḥattā lā yakūn nawmuhā thaqīl wa-ammā qāyiduhā wa-ḥārisuhā fa-lā yanām wa-lā yudkhil raʾsahu fī janāḥihi wa-lā yazāl yanẓur min jamīʿ al-jawānib fa-in aḥassa bi-aḥad ṣāḥa bi-aʿlā ṣawtihi fa-akhbara aṣḥābahu bi-l-ʿaduww] When they wish to sleep, they put their heads II, 625 under their wings, because they know that the wings bear a blow better than the head, in which is the eye, the noblest of the parts, and the brain, on which the rest of the body depends. They sleep, moreover, standing on one foot, so that their sleep may not be heavy. But the one who is leader and guard abstains from sleep and does not hide his head under his wings. Rather, he continually looks out on every side. And if he perceives anyone, he cries out with a loud voice to signal to his companions that an enemy is near. Others add two further points. The first is that cranes keep watch in turn. Horus, book 2, ch. 90: Αὗται γὰρ ἑαυτὰς φυλάττουσι γρηγοροῦσαι κατ᾽ ὄρδινον ἐν πάσῃ τῇ νυκτί [Hautai gar heautas phylattousi grēgorousai kat᾽ ordinon en pasē tē nykti]. They guard themselves, keeping watch in order through the whole night. Solinus: They divide the night watches, so that every tenth one is sleepless. Isidore: At night they divide the watches, and keep the order of the vigils by turns. Cassiodorus: They watch in turn, and guard themselves by common caution. Basil: Τοῦ καιροῦ τῆς φυλακῆς πληρομένου, ἡ μὲν βοήσασα πρὸς ὕπνον ἐτράπετο. ἡ δὲ τὴν διαδοχὴν ὑποδεξαμένη, ἧς ἔτυχεν ἀσφαλείας, col. 76 ἀντέδωκεν ἐν τῷ μέρει [Tou kairou tēs phylakēs plēromenou, hē men boēsasa pros hypnon etrapeto. hē de tēn diadochēn hypodexamenē, hēs etychen asphaleias, antedōken en tō merei]. Ambrose expands this as follows: When the time of the watch has been completed, having discharged its duty it settles down to sleep after first giving a cry, so as to wake the sleeper to whom it is to hand over its turn of duty. And that one willingly takes up its lot, and does not, as is our habit, renounce sleep unwillingly and sluggishly. Rather, it briskly shakes itself from its bed, performs its turn, and repays the favour it received with equal care and service. And Damir: في طبعه الخوف والتحارس بالنوبة فاذا قضي نوبتة قام الذي كان نايما يحرس مكانه حتي تقضي كله ما يلزمها من الحراسة [fī ṭabʿihi al-khawf wa-l-taḥārus bi-l-nawba fa-idhā qaḍā nawbatahu qāma alladhī kāna nāyiman yaḥrus makānahu ḥattā taqḍī kulluhu mā yalzamuhā min al-ḥirāsa] It is in its nature to be fearful and to keep guard by turns. And when one has completed its turn, one of those that were sleeping rises to keep watch in its place, until all have kept the watches incumbent on them. The second is that the watchmen carry a stone in the foot, which by its fall wakes them when asleep or about to fall asleep. Pliny: They keep watches at night, holding a pebble in the foot, which, loosened by sleep and falling, betrays their negligence. Solinus: The watchmen grasp small weights in their toes, which, if they should happen to fall, betray sleep. Plutarch: Αἱ προφυλακὴν ἔχουσαι νυκτὸς, ἐπὶ θατέρου σκέλους ὀχοῦνται τὸ σῶμα, τῷ δ᾽ ἑτέρῳ ποδὶ λίθον περιλαβοῦσαι κρατοῦσι· συνέχει γὰρ ὁ τῆς ἀφῆς τόνος ἐν τῷ μὴ καθεύδειν πολὺν χρόνον. Ὅταν δὲ ἀνῶσιν, ἐκπεσὼν ὁ λίθος ταχὺ διήγειρε τὴν προεμένην [Hai prophylakēn echousai nyktos, epi thaterou skelous ochountai to sōma, tō d᾽ heterō podi lithon perilabousai kratousi; synechei gar ho tēs haphēs tonos en tō mē katheudein polyn chronon. Hotan de anōsin, ekpesōn ho lithos tachy diēgeire tēn proemenēn]. Those that keep watch at night support the body on one of their legs, and hold a pebble grasped in the other foot. The effort of gripping holds off sleep for some time. But as soon as they relax, the falling stone at once wakes the negligent one. Aelian [III, 13.]: Ἑστᾶσι μὲν ἀσκωλιάζουσαι, τῷ γε μὲν μετεώρῳ ποδὶ λίθον κατέχουσι τοῖς ὄνυξι μάλα ἐγκρατῶς τε καὶ εὐλαβῶς· ἵνα ἐάν ποτε λάθωσιν ἑαυτὰς εἰς ὕπνον ὑπολισθαίνουσαι, πεσὼν καὶ ὑποκτυπήσας ὁ λίθος, ἀποδαρθάνειν καταναγκάσῃ [Hestasi men askōliazousai, tō ge men meteōrō podi lithon katechousi tois onyxi mala enkratōs te kai eulabōs; hina ean pote lathōsin heautas eis hypnon hypolisthainousai, pesōn kai hypoktypēsas ho lithos, apodarthanein katanankasē]. They rest on one foot only, and in the other, which is raised, they hold a pebble II, 626 with their claws very firmly and with the greatest care, so that, if sleep should ever steal upon them, the falling pebble may wake them with its noise. Philes and Tzetzes say the same. Accordingly, when Aelian says that cranes swallow pebbles ὡς ἔχειν καὶ δεῖπνον, καὶ πρὸς τὰς ἐμβολὰς τῶν ἀνέμων ἕρμα [hōs echein kai deipnon, kai pros tas embolas tōn anemōn herma], so as to have them both for a meal and as ballast against the onslaught of the winds, one should consider whether instead of δεῖπνον [deipnon] we ought to read δι᾽ ὕπνον [di᾽ hypnon], on account of sleep. For that pebbles should serve cranes as a meal is quite absurd. But perhaps Aelian meant that stones are swallowed by cranes not only to serve as ballast when they are about to fly across the Pontus, but also so that, once the sea has been crossed, they may be vomited up and serve to ward off sleep in the manner we have described.


Gruum cum Pygmaeis pugnas ad australem Oceanum et Nili fontes, de quibus post Homerum multi multa nugantur, libenter praeterimus. Quamvis in ea fabula hoc saltem verum esse asserat Philosophus, pusillos homines in iis locis degere, Hist. lib. 8. cap. 12. Μεταβάλλουσιν, inquit, αἱ γέρανοι ἐκ τῶν Σκυ-θικῶν εἰς τὰ ἕλη τὰ ἄνω τῆς Αἰγύπτου, ὅθεν ὁ Νεῖλος ῥεῖ. Ἔστι δὲ ὁ τόπος οὗτος, περὶ ὃν οἱ Πυγμαῖοι κατοικοῦσιν. Οὐ γάρ ἐστι τοῦτο μῦθος, ἀλλ᾽ ἔστι κα-τὰ τὴν ἀλήθειαν γένος μικρὸν μὲν, ὥσπερ λέγεται, καὶ αὐτοὶ, καὶ οἱ ἵπποι. Τρωγλοδύται δ᾽ εἰσὶ τὸν βίον. Ex Scythicis oris grues migrant ad paludes, quae supra Aegyptum sunt, unde profluit Nilus. Circa quem locum Pygmaei habitant. Neque enim id est fabula. Sed re vera, ut ajunt, genus ibi parvum est tam homi- num, quam equorum. Vitam autem Troglodyticam, hoc est, in cavernis sub terra degunt. Veros Nili fontes veteribus fuisse prorsus ignotos, nemo est, qui nesciat. Itaque hic Nili nomine intelligitur Astaboras, quem Nili ramum esse col. 77 veteres crediderunt, ut alibi probavimus. Oritur autem Astaboras ex locis, Ava- litui sinui proximis, et Mosylo emporio. Unde est, quod Aethicus Nili fontes ibi describit. Fluviumque Nilum, inquit, qui de littore incipientis maris Rubri, videtur emergere in loco, qui dicitur Mossylon emporium. Et re vera Nonnosus, circa haec loca navigans, ut ex Homeritis iret ad Auxumitas, Ἐνέτυχέ τισι μορ-φὴν μὲν καὶ ἰδέαν ἔχουσιν ἀνθρωπίνην, βραχυτάτοις δὲ τὸ μέγεθος, καὶ μέ-λασι τὴν χρόαν· ὑπὸ δὲ τριχῶν δεδασυμμένοις διὰ παντὸς τοῦ σώματος· εἵπον-το δὲ τοῖς ἀνδράσι καὶ γυναῖκες παραπλήσιαι, καὶ παιδάρια ἔτι βραχύτερα. Incidit in quosdam forma quidem et figura humana, sed statura brevissimos, et co- lore nigros, et toto corpore pilosos. Sequebantur autem viros prope aequales foe- minae, et pueri adhuc breviores. Ita Photius in Excerptis ex Nonnosi historia, qui sub Iustiniano vixit. Sed et in Hesychio Νῶβαι sunt Πυγμαῖοι. Nobae, id est, Nubae, qui in illis locis degunt. Et Strabo de Aethiopibus sub Aegypto lib. 17. τά τε βοσκήματα αὐτοῖς ἐστι μικρὰ πρόβατα, καὶ αἶγες, καὶ βόες, καὶ κύνες μικροί· τραχεῖς δὲ καὶ μάχιμοι οἰκοῦντες μικροὶ ὄντες. Τάχα δὲ τοὺς Πυγμαίους ἀπὸ τῆς τούτων μικροφυΐας ἐπενόησαν καὶ ἀνέπλασαν· ἑωρακὼς II, 627 μὲν γὰρ οὐδεὶς ἐξηγεῖται τῶν πίστεως ἀξίων ἀνδρῶν. Pecora ipsis sunt parvae oves, et caprae, boves etiam, et canes parvi. Sed et ipsi incolae pusilli sunt, asperi ta- men et pugnaces. Et fortasse ob naturalem horum parvitatem (veteres ibi locorum) Pygmaeos confinxerunt. Eos enim fide dignus nemo est qui viderit. Nempe quales esse finguntur, trium palmorum altitudine, quales ne Homerus quidem dixerat. Sed hoc commentum auctores habet fabulosissimos scriptores, Megasthenem et Daimachum, de quibus Strabo lib. 2. Ἐνεκαίνισαν δὲ καὶ τὴν Ὁμηρικὴν τῶν Πυγμαίων γερανομαχίαν τρισπιθάμους εἴποντες· Homericam Pygmaeorum in grues pugnam interpolarunt, trium palmorum eos esse dicentes. Sed et Arabes idem referunt ex cujusdam Graeculi fide, qui Iacobo, Isaaci filio, Siragensi, fertur ita narrasse. ركبت في بحر الزنج والقتني الريح الي بعض الجزاير فوصلت منها الي مدينة اهلها ناس قاماتهم قدم نراع واكثرهم عور فاجتمع علي منهم جمع وانتهوا بي الي ملكهم فامر بحبسي فحبست في شبه قفص ثم رايتهم في بعض الايام يستعدون القتال وقالوا لنا عدو ياتينا في هذا الاوان فلم يلبث الي ان طلعت عليهم عصابة من الغرانيق وكان عورهم من نقرها اعينهم فاخذت عصي وشددت عليها وهربت واكرموني لذلك Navigabam aliquando in mari Zingitano, et impulit me ventus in quan- dam insulam. In cujus oppidum cum devenissem, reperi incolas cubitalis esse sta- turae, et plerosque coclites. Quorum multitudo, in me congregata, me deduxit ad col. 78 regem suum. Iussit is, ut captivus detinerer. Et in quandam caveae speciem con- jectus sum. Eos autem aliquando ad bellum instrui cum viderem, dixerunt, hostem imminere, et fore, ut propediem ingrueret. Nec multo post gruum exercitus in eos insurrexit. Atque ideo erant coclites, quod illorum oculos hae confodissent. At ego, virga sumpta, in eas impetum feci, et illae avolarunt atque aufugerunt. Ob quod facinus in honore fui apud illos.

The battles of the cranes with the Pygmies near the southern Ocean and the sources of the Nile, about which many writers since Homer have spun many tales, we gladly pass over. Yet the Philosopher asserts that in that fable at least this much is true, that very small men live in those places, Hist. book 8, ch. 12: Μεταβάλλουσιν, he says, αἱ γέρανοι ἐκ τῶν Σκυθικῶν εἰς τὰ ἕλη τὰ ἄνω τῆς Αἰγύπτου, ὅθεν ὁ Νεῖλος ῥεῖ. Ἔστι δὲ ὁ τόπος οὗτος, περὶ ὃν οἱ Πυγμαῖοι κατοικοῦσιν. Οὐ γάρ ἐστι τοῦτο μῦθος, ἀλλ᾽ ἔστι κατὰ τὴν ἀλήθειαν γένος μικρὸν μὲν, ὥσπερ λέγεται, καὶ αὐτοὶ, καὶ οἱ ἵπποι. Τρωγλοδύται δ᾽ εἰσὶ τὸν βίον. [Metaballousin hai geranoi ek tōn Skythikōn eis ta helē ta anō tēs Aigyptou, hothen ho Neilos rhei. Esti de ho topos houtos, peri hon hoi Pygmaioi katoikousin. Ou gar esti touto mythos, all᾽ esti kata tēn alētheian genos mikron men, hōsper legetai, kai autoi, kai hoi hippoi. Trōglodytai d᾽ eisi ton bion.] From the Scythian regions the cranes migrate to the marshes that lie above Egypt, whence the Nile flows. Around this place the Pygmies live. For this is no fable; in truth, as they say, there is a small race there, both of men and of horses. They lead a Troglodyte life, that is, they live in caves under the earth. Everyone knows that the true sources of the Nile were entirely unknown to the ancients. Here, therefore, by the name Nile is meant the Astaboras, which col. 77 the ancients believed to be a branch of the Nile, as we have shown elsewhere. The Astaboras rises in places nearest to the Avalites gulf and the trading-post of Mosylon. That is why Aethicus places the sources of the Nile there: And the river Nile, he says, which seems to emerge from the shore of the beginning of the Red Sea, in the place called the Mossylon trading-post. And indeed Nonnosus, sailing about these places on his way from the Homerites to the Axumites, Ἐνέτυχέ τισι μορφὴν μὲν καὶ ἰδέαν ἔχουσιν ἀνθρωπίνην, βραχυτάτοις δὲ τὸ μέγεθος, καὶ μέλασι τὴν χρόαν· ὑπὸ δὲ τριχῶν δεδασυμμένοις διὰ παντὸς τοῦ σώματος· εἵποντο δὲ τοῖς ἀνδράσι καὶ γυναῖκες παραπλήσιαι, καὶ παιδάρια ἔτι βραχύτερα. [Enetyche tisi morphēn men kai idean echousin anthrōpinēn, brachytatois de to megethos, kai melasi tēn chroan; hypo de trichōn dedasymmenois dia pantos tou sōmatos; heiponto de tois andrasi kai gynaikes paraplēsiai, kai paidaria eti brachytera.] came upon certain people, human indeed in form and shape, but very short in stature, black in colour, and hairy over the whole body. The men were followed by women of nearly the same size, and by children still shorter. So Photius in the Excerpts from the history of Nonnosus, who lived under Justinian. Moreover, in Hesychius Νῶβαι [Nōbai] are Πυγμαῖοι [Pygmaioi]: the Nobae, that is, the Nubae, who live in those places. And Strabo, book 17, on the Ethiopians below Egypt: τά τε βοσκήματα αὐτοῖς ἐστι μικρὰ πρόβατα, καὶ αἶγες, καὶ βόες, καὶ κύνες μικροί· τραχεῖς δὲ καὶ μάχιμοι οἰκοῦντες μικροὶ ὄντες. Τάχα δὲ τοὺς Πυγμαίους ἀπὸ τῆς τούτων μικροφυΐας ἐπενόησαν καὶ ἀνέπλασαν· ἑωρακὼς II, 627 μὲν γὰρ οὐδεὶς ἐξηγεῖται τῶν πίστεως ἀξίων ἀνδρῶν. [ta te boskēmata autois esti mikra probata, kai aiges, kai boes, kai kynes mikroi; tracheis de kai machimoi oikountes mikroi ontes. Tacha de tous Pygmaious apo tēs toutōn mikrophyias epenoēsan kai aneplasan; heōrakōs men gar oudeis exēgeitai tōn pisteōs axiōn andrōn.] Their livestock are small sheep and goats, oxen too, and small dogs. The inhabitants themselves are also tiny, yet rough and warlike. And perhaps on account of their natural smallness (the ancients of those parts) invented the Pygmies. For no one worthy of credit has seen them. That is, Pygmies such as they are imagined to be, three spans tall, such as not even Homer had described. But this invention has as its authors the most fabulous of writers, Megasthenes and Daimachus, of whom Strabo says in book 2: Ἐνεκαίνισαν δὲ καὶ τὴν Ὁμηρικὴν τῶν Πυγμαίων γερανομαχίαν τρισπιθάμους εἴποντες· [Enekainisan de kai tēn Homērikēn tōn Pygmaiōn geranomachian trispithamous eipontes;] They embellished the Homeric battle of the Pygmies with the cranes, saying that they were three spans tall. The Arabs too report the same on the word of a certain little Greek, who is said to have told it thus to Jacob, son of Isaac, of Siraf: ركبت في بحر الزنج والقتني الريح الي بعض الجزاير فوصلت منها الي مدينة اهلها ناس قاماتهم قدم نراع واكثرهم عور فاجتمع علي منهم جمع وانتهوا بي الي ملكهم فامر بحبسي فحبست في شبه قفص ثم رايتهم في بعض الايام يستعدون القتال وقالوا لنا عدو ياتينا في هذا الاوان فلم يلبث الي ان طلعت عليهم عصابة من الغرانيق وكان عورهم من نقرها اعينهم فاخذت عصي وشددت عليها وهربت واكرموني لذلك [rakibtu fī baḥr al-Zanj wa-alqatnī al-rīḥ ilā baʿḍ al-jazāyir fa-waṣaltu minhā ilā madīna ahluhā nās qāmātuhum qadm nrāʿ wa-aktharuhum ʿūr fa-ijtamaʿa ʿalayya minhum jamʿ wa-intahaw bī ilā malikihim fa-amara bi-ḥabsī fa-ḥubistu fī shibh qafaṣ thumma raʾaytuhum fī baʿḍ al-ayyām yastaʿiddūn al-qitāl wa-qālū lanā ʿaduww yaʾtīnā fī hādhā al-awān fa-lam yalbath ilā an ṭalaʿat ʿalayhim ʿiṣāba min al-gharānīq wa-kāna ʿawaruhum min naqrihā aʿyunahum fa-akhadhtu ʿaṣā wa-shadadtu ʿalayhā wa-harabat wa-akramūnī li-dhālik] I was once sailing on the Zanj sea, and the wind drove me to a certain island. When I reached its town, I found the inhabitants to be a cubit tall, and most of them one-eyed. A crowd of them gathered around me and led me to col. 78 their king. He ordered that I be held captive, and I was thrown into a kind of cage. When one day I saw them preparing for war, they said that an enemy was threatening and would soon fall upon them. Not long after, an army of cranes rose up against them. And they were one-eyed because the cranes had pecked out their eyes. But I took a stick and charged at them, and they flew off and fled. For this deed I was held in honour among them.


Philosophus (Hist. lib. 8. cap. 12.) grues e Thracia migrare scribit τοῦ Μαι-μακτηριῶνος, Maemacterione mense: et Aelianus lib. 3. cap. 13. Φθινοπώρου ἤδη μεσοῦντος, medio autumno. Unde maxime confirmatur, quod contra Gazam contendit Scaliger, et contra Petavium Samuel Petit in Eclogis chronologicis lib. 4. in mensibus Atticis Maemacterionem non esse primum, sed secundum Au- tumnalium. Reditus tempus Aelianus ita definit, Ὅταν ὑπεύδια ἄρξηται, καὶ εἰρηναῖα τοῦ ἀέρος ὑποστρέφουσιν ὀπίσω· Cum incipit aëris serenitas et tranquillitas II, 628 postliminio revertitur. Et Maximus Tyrius, Αἱ γέρανοι ἐξ Αἰγύπτου ὥρα-θέρους ἀφισάμεναι, οὐκ ἀνεχόμεναι τὸ θάλπος, τείνασαι πτέρυγας ὥσπερ ἱςία, φέρονται διὰ τοῦ ἀέρος εὐθὺ τῶν Σκυθῶν γῆς· Grues per aestatem ex Aegypto abscedentes, quia calorem pati non possunt, alis velorum instar expansis per aërem ad Scythicam plagam recta feruntur. Proinde aestatis advenas vocat Plinius. Quod ita excipio, ut aestatis nomine etiam ver intelligam. In haec Theocriti Idyll. 10.

The Philosopher (Hist. book 8, ch. 12) writes that cranes migrate from Thrace τοῦ Μαιμακτηριῶνος [tou Maimaktēriōnos], in the month Maemacterion; and Aelian, book 3, ch. 13, Φθινοπώρου ἤδη μεσοῦντος [Phthinopōrou ēdē mesountos], in mid-autumn. This strongly confirms what Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)] maintained against Gaza, and Samuel Petit against Petavius in his Eclogae chronologicae, book 4: that among the Attic months Maemacterion is not the first but the second of the autumn months. Aelian defines the time of their return thus: Ὅταν ὑπεύδια ἄρξηται, καὶ εἰρηναῖα τοῦ ἀέρος ὑποστρέφουσιν ὀπίσω [Hotan hypeudia arxētai, kai eirēnaia tou aeros hypostrephousin opisō]; when the fair weather begins and the calm of the air II, 628 returns, they come back. And Maximus of Tyre: Αἱ γέρανοι ἐξ Αἰγύπτου ὥραθέρους ἀφισάμεναι, οὐκ ἀνεχόμεναι τὸ θάλπος, τείνασαι πτέρυγας ὥσπερ ἱςία, φέρονται διὰ τοῦ ἀέρος εὐθὺ τῶν Σκυθῶν γῆς [Hai geranoi ex Aigyptou hōratherous aphisamenai, ouk anechomenai to thalpos, teinasai pterygas hōsper histia, pherontai dia tou aeros euthy tōn Skythōn gēs]; The cranes, departing from Egypt in summer because they cannot endure the heat, spread their wings like sails and are carried straight through the air to the Scythian region. Accordingly Pliny calls them summer visitors. I take this in such a way that under the name of summer I also understand spring. On these lines of Theocritus, Idyll 10,


Ἁ αἶξ τὸν κύτισον, ὁ λύκος τὰν αἶγα διώκει,
Ἁ γέρανος τ᾽ ὤροτρον, — — —

Ἁ αἶξ τὸν κύτισον, ὁ λύκος τὰν αἶγα διώκει, Ἁ γέρανος τ᾽ ὤροτρον, — — — [Ha aix ton kytison, ho lykos tan aiga diōkei, Ha geranos t᾽ ōrotron]


Capra cytisum, lupus capram sequitur, grus aratrum, sic habet Scholiastes: Ἀρ-χομένου γὰρ σπόρου αἱ γέρανοι φαίνονται, Sementis enim initio grues apparent. Quod non capio, quia sementis tempore non veniunt grues, sed migrant. Gruum enim migratio in autumnum incidit, qui est sationis solemne tempus. Virgi- lius lib. 1. Georgicorum,

The goat follows the clover, the wolf the goat, the crane the plough, the Scholiast says: Ἀρχομένου γὰρ σπόρου αἱ γέρανοι φαίνονται [Archomenou gar sporou hai geranoi phainontai], For cranes appear at the beginning of sowing. This I do not understand, since cranes do not arrive at sowing time but depart. For the migration of cranes falls in autumn, which is the customary time of sowing. Virgil, Georgics book 1:


Libra die somnique pares ubi fecerit horas,
Et medium luci atque umbris jam dividit orbem,
Exercete viri tauros, serite ordea campis.

When Libra has made the hours of day and sleep equal, and now divides the globe in the middle between light and shade, work your bulls, men, sow barley in the fields.


Ad quae verba Servius, Dicit frumenta serenda esse autumnali tempore. Itaque nugatur Graeculus, a quo haec Scholia scripta sunt. Huic proinde Aristopha- nes est διαῤῥήδην oppositus. Is enim in Avibus nos jubet

On these words Servius says: He says that grain is to be sown in the autumn season. So the Greekling who wrote these Scholia is talking nonsense. Aristophanes is therefore διαῤῥήδην [diarrhēdēn] opposed to him. For in the Birds he bids us


Σπείρειν μὲν ὅταν γέρανος κρώζουσ᾽ ἐς τὴν Λιβύην μεταχωρῇ,

Σπείρειν μὲν ὅταν γέρανος κρώζουσ᾽ ἐς τὴν Λιβύην μεταχωρῇ, [Speirein men hotan geranos krōzous᾽ es tēn Libyēn metachōrē]


Seminare cum grus clamans in Libyam migrat. Quod Scholiastes observat sumptum esse ex Hesiodi Operibus versu 446.

Sow when the crane migrates, crying, to Libya. The Scholiast notes that this is taken from Hesiod's Works, line 446:


Φράζεσθαι δ᾽ εὖ τ᾽ ἂν φωνὴν γεράνου ἐπακούσης,
Ὑψόθεν ἐκ νεφέων ἐνιαύσια κεκληγυίης,
Ἡτ᾽ ἀρότοιό τε σῆμα φέρει, καὶ χείματος ὥρην
Δεικνύει ὀμβρηροῦ· — — —

Φράζεσθαι δ᾽ εὖ τ᾽ ἂν φωνὴν γεράνου ἐπακούσης, Ὑψόθεν ἐκ νεφέων ἐνιαύσια κεκληγυίης, Ἡτ᾽ ἀρότοιό τε σῆμα φέρει, καὶ χείματος ὥρην Δεικνύει ὀμβρηροῦ· — — — [Phrazesthai d᾽ eu t᾽ an phōnēn geranou epakousēs, Hypsothen ek nepheōn eniausia keklēgyiēs, Hēt᾽ arotoio te sēma pherei, kai cheimatos hōrēn Deiknyei ombrērou]


Adverte, cum migrantis gruis vocem audiveris, ex alto in nubibus quotannis clan- gentis, quae arationis signum edit, et hyemis umbriferae tempus indicat.

Take heed when you hear the voice of the migrating crane, crying every year from on high in the clouds, which gives the signal for ploughing and shows the season of rainy winter.


Ex iis, quae de gruum migratione dicta sunt, constat, eas a Propheta in prudentiae naturalis exemplum non immerito proponi. Hirundo, inquit, et grus custodierunt tempus adventus sui: at populus meus non novit jus Domini. Proinde Philosophus (Histor. lib. 9. cap. 10.) migrationis gruum historiam ita orditur, Φρόνιμα δὲ πολλὰ καὶ περὶ τὰς γεράνους δοκεῖ συμβαίνειν· A gruibus quoque videntur multa prudenter fieri. Et τὸ κυβερνητικὸν, gubernandi, artem ab iis homines didicisse, contendit Aelianus Historiae lib. 3. capite 14. Et Mercurium II, 629 Cassiodorus, Palamedem Philostratus grues pro magistris habuisse volunt. Proinde apud Aegyptios grus vigilans, ut Horus auctor est, cautum hominem, et grus volans ἄνθρωπον εἰδότα τὰ μετέωρα, hominem sublimium rerum peri- col. 79 tum significabat. Et apud Arabes vulgato proverbio dicitur احرس من الكركي Grue cautior is, qui valde cautus est.

From what has been said about the migration of cranes it is clear that the Prophet not without reason sets them forth as an example of natural prudence. The swallow, he says, and the crane have kept the time of their coming; but my people has not known the judgment of the Lord. Accordingly the Philosopher (Hist. book 9, ch. 10) begins his account of the migration of cranes thus: Φρόνιμα δὲ πολλὰ καὶ περὶ τὰς γεράνους δοκεῖ συμβαίνειν [Phronima de polla kai peri tas geranous dokei symbainein]; Many things also seem to be done prudently by cranes. And Aelian, History book 3, chapter 14, maintains that men learned τὸ κυβερνητικὸν [to kybernētikon], the art of steering, from them. And Cassiodorus holds that Mercury, II, 629 Philostratus that Palamedes, had cranes as teachers. Accordingly among the Egyptians, as Horus reports, a watchful crane signified a cautious man, and a flying crane ἄνθρωπον εἰδότα τὰ μετέωρα [anthrōpon eidota ta meteōra], a man skilled in lofty matters. col. 79 And among the Arabs one who is very cautious is called, in a common proverb, احرس من الكركي [aḥras min al-kurkī], more cautious than a crane.


Nec est, quod quisquam gruem miretur esse in avibus mundis potius quam ciconiam, volucrem illi simillimam, cum serpentibus vescatur ciconia, grus frugibus et seminibus. Vetus auctor apud Suidam, Γέρανοι γεωργοῦ κατενέμον-το χώραν ἐσπαρμένην νεωστὶ πυρίνῳ σίτῳ, Grues agricolae agrum tritico nuper satum depascebantur. Aelianus lib. 2. cap. 1. Σπείραντας δὲ τοὺς Αἰγυπτίους κα-ταλαμβάνουσι, καὶ τράπεζαν, ὡς ἂν εἴποις, ἄφθονον τὴν ἐν ταῖς ἀρούραις εὑρόντες, εἶτα ἄκλητοι ξενίων μεταλαγχάνουσιν· Aegyptios sementem facientes offendunt, et in arvis, ut ita dicam, mensam, cibis affluentem, invenientes, hospitalitatis jure non vocatae fruuntur. Proinde Mela Pygmaeos scribit pro satis frugibus contra grues dimicasse: et Antipater Sidonius, ubi supra, in Aucupis Epitaphio:

Nor should anyone wonder that the crane is among the clean birds rather than the stork, a bird very like it, since the stork feeds on serpents, the crane on crops and seeds. An old author in Suidas: Γέρανοι γεωργοῦ κατενέμοντο χώραν ἐσπαρμένην νεωστὶ πυρίνῳ σίτῳ [Geranoi geōrgou katenemonto chōran esparmenēn neōsti pyrinō sitō], Cranes were grazing on a farmer's field newly sown with wheat. Aelian, book 2, ch. 1: Σπείραντας δὲ τοὺς Αἰγυπτίους καταλαμβάνουσι, καὶ τράπεζαν, ὡς ἂν εἴποις, ἄφθονον τὴν ἐν ταῖς ἀρούραις εὑρόντες, εἶτα ἄκλητοι ξενίων μεταλαγχάνουσιν [Speirantas de tous Aigyptious katalambanousi, kai trapezan, hōs an eipois, aphthonon tēn en tais arourais heurontes, eita aklētoi xeniōn metalanchanousin]; They come upon the Egyptians as they are sowing, and finding in the fields a table, so to speak, abounding in food, they enjoy, uninvited, the rights of hospitality. Hence Mela writes that the Pygmies fought against the cranes for their sown crops; and Antipater of Sidon, as cited above, in the Epitaph of a Fowler:


Ὁ πρὶν ἐγὼ καὶ ψῆρα καὶ ἁρπάκτειραν ἐρύκων
Σπέρματος ὑψιπετῆ Βιστόνιαν γέρανον.

Ὁ πρὶν ἐγὼ καὶ ψῆρα καὶ ἁρπάκτειραν ἐρύκων Σπέρματος ὑψιπετῆ Βιστόνιαν γέρανον. [Ho prin egō kai psēra kai harpakteiran erykōn Spermatos hypsipetē Bistonian geranon]


Ego qui prius a semine (id est a granis) prohibens sturnum et altivolam Bistoniam gruem. Mundae igitur grues fuerint ex Aristeae definitione, qui pro mundis habet τῶν πτηνῶν τὰ πυροῖς καὶ ὀσπρίοις χρώμενα πρὸς τὴν τροφὴν, eas aves, quae tritico et leguminibus nutriuntur. Quid quod apud Graecos veteres grues non solum in cibis, sed et in deliciis fuere, maxime circa Thessaliam, ubi in villis opulentiores suas habuere γερανοβοτίας, vel γερανοβοσίας, id est, gruum pascua, quorum meminit Pollux post Platonem in Politico. Et Balearibus insulis in honore mensarum erat vipio, quomodo vocabant minorem gruem. Ita Plinius lib. 10. cap. 49. Miratur idem, cur sub Augusto scripserit Cornelius Nepos, ciconias magis placere quam grues, cum haec nunc ales, inquit, inter primas expetatur: illam nemo velit attigisse. Hinc Horatius in Nasidieni coena, cui Mecoenas interfuit lib. 2. Satyra 8.

I, who formerly kept the starling and the high-flying Bistonian crane away from the seed (that is, from the grains). Cranes, then, will have been clean by the definition of Aristeas, who counts as clean τῶν πτηνῶν τὰ πυροῖς καὶ ὀσπρίοις χρώμενα πρὸς τὴν τροφὴν [tōn ptēnōn ta pyrois kai ospriois chrōmena pros tēn trophēn], those birds which are nourished on wheat and pulse. What is more, among the ancient Greeks cranes were not only eaten but even counted among the delicacies, especially around Thessaly, where the wealthier had on their estates their own γερανοβοτίας [geranobotias] or γερανοβοσίας [geranobosias], that is, crane pastures, which Pollux mentions, following Plato in the Statesman. And in the Balearic islands the vipio, as they called the smaller crane, was held in honour at table. So Pliny, book 10, ch. 49. The same author wonders why Cornelius Nepos, writing under Augustus, said that storks were preferred to cranes, since this bird is now, he says, sought after among the very first, while no one would want to touch the other. Hence Horace, in the dinner of Nasidienus, at which Maecenas was present, book 2, Satire 8:


— — — — deinde sequuti
Mazonomo pueri magno discerpta ferentes
Membra gruis sparsi sale multo, non sine farre.

— — — — then followed
slaves carrying on a great platter the carved limbs of a crane, sprinkled with much salt, not without meal.


Et Ovidius, agens de veterum frugalitate, Fastorum lib. 6.

And Ovid, treating of the frugality of the ancients, Fasti book 6:


Nec Latium norat quam praebet Ionia dives, Nec quae Pygmaëo sanguine gaudet avem. II, 630 Id est, attagen et grus nondum erant in Romanorum deliciis. Et Statius etiam in Hercule Vindic. sui temporis catillones, quibus palatum erat aequo doctius, ita perstringit:

Nor did Latium know the bird that rich Ionia supplies, nor the one that delights in Pygmy blood. II, 630 That is, the francolin and the crane were not yet among the delicacies of the Romans. And Statius too, in Hercules Vindex, censures thus the gluttons of his own time, whose palate was more learned than was fitting:


Ah miseri! quos nosse juvat quid Phasidis ales
Distet ab hiberna Rhodopes grue. — —

Ah, wretches! who delight to know how the bird of the Phasis differs from the wintering crane of Rhodope. — —


Haec de voce עגור agor hactenus, in qua haesisse video priscos interpretes. In Esaia pro verbis כסוס עגור, ut hirundo et agor, id est, grus, Graeci Seniores solum habent ὡς χελιδὼν, et Arabs, مثل سنونوة ut hirundo, sequenti voce prorsus omissa: et Hieronymus, Sicut pullus hirundinis: Aquila, ὡς ἵππος ἀγώρ· et Theodotion, ὡς χελιδὼν ἀγὼρ, quia vocem ignotam describere sat habuerunt. At Syrus, ܐܝܟ ܣܢܘܢܝܬܐ ܕܡܨܦܪܐ, sicut hirundo quae garrit: et Chaldaeus כסוסיא דאחיד, sicut hirundo, quae capta est: cui gemina Symmachi versio, ὡς χελιδὼν ἐγκλειθεῖσα, ut hirundo inclusa; quasi legerint סגור sagur, pro עגור agor. Sed legendum esse עגור agor, docent Aquila, Symmachus, Hebraei omnes, et hujus loci collatio cum Ierem. VIII, 7. Ubi rursus eaedem voces סיס sis et עגור agor junctae sunt, et quidem ita junctae, ut appareat, עגור agor esse avis nomen, ut תור thor et סיס sis, quae praecedunt. Hieronymus ciconiam reddit, et Graeci ἀγροῦ στρουθία. Sed ἀγροῦ factum ex ἀγὼρ, et στρου-ϑία est Glossema, quod ex margine in textum irrepsit. Chaldaeus et Syrus optime ܟܘܪܟܝܐ kurkeja, id est, gruem exponunt, quamvis ordine non suo, ut col. 80 supra notavimus (3).

So much, then, for the word עגור agor, over which I see that the ancient translators stumbled. In Isaiah, for the words כסוס עגור, like a swallow and agor, that is, a crane, the Greek Elders have only ὡς χελιδὼν [hōs chelidōn], and the Arabic translator مثل سنونوة [mithl sunūnwa] like a swallow, the following word being omitted altogether; and Jerome, Like a young swallow; Aquila, ὡς ἵππος ἀγώρ [hōs hippos agōr]; and Theodotion, ὡς χελιδὼν ἀγὼρ [hōs chelidōn agōr], because they were content to transcribe an unknown word. But the Syriac has ܐܝܟ ܣܢܘܢܝܬܐ ܕܡܨܦܪܐ [איך סנוניתא דמצפרא], like a swallow that chatters; and the Chaldee כסוסיא דאחיד, like a swallow that has been caught; with which Symmachus's version agrees, ὡς χελιδὼν ἐγκλειθεῖσα [hōs chelidōn enkleitheisa], like a swallow shut in; as if they had read סגור sagur instead of עגור agor. But that עגור agor is to be read is shown by Aquila, Symmachus, all the Hebrews, and the comparison of this passage with Ierem. VIII, 7. There again the same words סיס sis and עגור agor are joined, and indeed so joined that it is clear that עגור agor is the name of a bird, like תור thor and סיס sis, which precede it. Jerome renders it stork, and the Greeks ἀγροῦ στρουθία [agrou strouthia]. But ἀγροῦ [agrou] arose from ἀγὼρ [agōr], and στρουθία [strouthia] is a gloss that crept from the margin into the text. The Chaldee and the Syriac very well explain it as ܟܘܪܟܝܐ [כורכיא] kurkeja, that is, crane, although not in its proper order, as col. 80 we noted above R3.


Quamvis עגור agor pro grue hodie non usurpetur apud Arabes, tamen potuit olim usurpari, atque inde fieri, quod verbo عجر agara significant aliquem ad lares suos postliminio reverti, vel aufugere, quod gruum est maxime proprium. Illas enim amore patriae in Scythiam et Thraciam, unde ortae sunt, quotannis redire constat, adeoque τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἕκαστον καλιὰν ἀναγνωρίζειν, ὡς τὴν οἰκίαν ἀνθρώπους, unamquamque nidum suum recognoscere, ut homines domum: quod pluribus docet Aelianus lib. 3. cap. 13. et 23. Atque indidem fortasse factum, quod a Syris et Persis Ἄγγαροι aggari, vel angari dicebantur cursores regii. Angari enim cum gruibus certare credebantur celeritate cursus. Φασί τινες (inquit Xenophon libro octavo Cyropaediae) θᾶττον τῶν γεράνων ταύτην τὴν πορείαν ἀνύττειν· Quidam hoc iter gruum volatu celerius confici referunt. II, 631 De angarorum cursu ibi agi, patebit legenti locum. At Cypriis agor erat avis, a grue diversissima, nempe aquila, si his Hesychii credimus, Ἀγώρ· ἀετὸς, Κύπριοι. Sed fortasse scriptum fuerat Ἀγώρ· γερανός· Et vocis γερα-νὸς priore parte omissa propter praecedentis τὸ ὁμοιόπτωτον, ex ἀνὸς factum ἀετός (4).

Although עגור agor is not used today for the crane among the Arabs, it may nevertheless once have been so used, and may derive from the fact that by the verb عجر [ʿajara] agara they mean that someone returns home by right of return, or flees away, which is most characteristic of cranes. For it is well known that out of love of their homeland they return every year to Scythia and Thrace, where they were born, and indeed τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἕκαστον καλιὰν ἀναγνωρίζειν, ὡς τὴν οἰκίαν ἀνθρώπους [tēn heautōn hekaston kalian anagnōrizein, hōs tēn oikian anthrōpous], that each recognizes its own nest, as men do their house: which Aelian sets out at length in book 3, ch. 13 and 23. And perhaps from the same source it came about that the royal couriers were called by the Syrians and Persians Ἄγγαροι [Angaroi], aggari or angari. For the angari were believed to rival cranes in speed of running. Φασί τινες θᾶττον τῶν γεράνων ταύτην τὴν πορείαν ἀνύττειν [Phasi tines thatton tōn geranōn tautēn tēn poreian anyttein] (says Xenophon in book 8 of the Cyropaedia): Some report that this journey is accomplished faster than the flight of cranes. II, 631 That the running of the angari is treated there will be clear to anyone who reads the passage. Among the Cypriots, however, agor was a bird very different from the crane, namely the eagle, if we believe these words of Hesychius: Ἀγώρ· ἀετὸς, Κύπριοι [Agōr: aetos, Kyprioi]. But perhaps it had been written Ἀγώρ· γερανός [Agōr: geranos]; and, the first part of the word γερανὸς [geranos] having been omitted because of its similar ending to the preceding word, ἀετός [aetos] was made out of ἀνὸς [anos] R4.


a) Bochart, II, 614 Lege Ὀσσομέναις.

a) Bochart, II, 614 Read Ὀσσομέναις [Ossomenais].


(1) Rosenmüller, II, 616 Inter Alexandriae aves migratorias FORSKALIUS in Descript. Animall. p. 9. recenset quoque Kurki: „vocatur et Vaes araki [إوز أرقي anas vigilans, quod quidem gruis nomen esse possit, quum gruis vigilantia satis sit celebrata, vid. Bochart. infra]. Constantinopoli advenit Octobri, post tres menses redit, vel ad Indiam, ut perhibetur, transit“. Sed p. 3. idem Forskalius Vaes araki anatis anseris nomen refert. Vnde VELTHUSEN (in Animadverss. ad Cantic. Hisk. Symbolis Kiloniensibus insertis P. II. pag. 323. sequ.) recte concludit, fuisse pluribus avibus unum nomen commune. Certe tamen Kurki, كركي, et gruem vocari ab Arabibus, vel patet ex proverbio, quod deinceps Bochartus afferet de homine cauto, احرس من الكركي vigilantior grue.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 616 Among the migratory birds of Alexandria, Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)] in Descript. Animall. p. 9 also lists the Kurki: "it is also called Vaes araki [إوز أرقي [iwazz arqī] anas vigilans [wakeful duck], which might indeed be a name of the crane, since the crane's vigilance is well known; see Bochart below]. (2) Rosenmüller, II, 616 Idem nomen inter aves Arabiae obscuras habet Forskal pag. VIII. „Ghornak alba; oestris pascitur, in tergo boum nidificantibus“. Patet, hanc avem non esse gruem. R2 Rosenmüller, II, 616 Forsskål has the same name among the obscure birds of Arabia, p. VIII: "Ghornak, white; it feeds on gadflies that nest on the backs of oxen." Clearly this bird is not the crane. However, since in the fable of the Pygmies, which Bochart will give us from a certain Arab below, p. 77, cranes are plainly to be understood by غرانيق [gharānīq], I would think that this same name was used of different animals in different regions. In Mauretania a certain species of vulture is called by that name; see Hoest, Descript. regni Fessani et Maroccani p. 298, German trans. Cf. Velthusen loc. cit. p. 321.

(4) Rosenmüller, II, 631 Sed tota hac doctissima disputatione vix credam certi quidquam effectum esse a Bocharto. Perpendamus argumentorum ejus momenta. Atque illa quidem diserte exposita frustra quaeras in toto hoc capite. עגור esse gruem, initio statim sumit, quibus vero rationibus ductus, plane silet. Tamen quantum colligere est ex totius disputationis serie, ita ratiocinatus videtur: „E duobus Iesaiae et Ieremiae locis patet, עגור esse avem advenam et voce utentem contenta: atque hoc utrumque deprehendimus in grue, ergo עגור est grus“. Quo nil esset certius, si duo illa gruibus essent priva; nunc, quum multae essent volucres advenae voce contenta utentes, vides, quam parum tutum hoc argumentum sit, nisi accedant graviora. Sed iis plane destitutus est Bochartus, ita, ut ne veterum quidem ul-lus sit, cujus auctoritate niti tuto possit. Syrus enim et Chaldaeus, ubi in textu Hebraeo est סוס, ponunt gruem, loco עגור vero hirundinem; nisi transpositas in utroque interprete voces dixeris, id quod Bochartus sine omni idonea ratione tantummodo opinionis suae anteceptae in gratiam sumit. Aeque infirmum est alterum pro grue argumentum, ex eo petitum, quod Arabum عجر rediit significat, nam inde omnes omnino aves migratoriae poterant appellari. Sed quod praecipue me inhibet, עגור pro gruis nomine habere, est hoc, quod in Iesaia avibus סוס et עגור pipitus (צפצף) tribuitur. — Multum allaborat VELTHUSEN (in Symbolis Kiloniens. P. II. p. 273—390.), ut demonstret, Hebraeum עגור idem esse vocabulum cum نغر Arabico lusciniae nomine, permutatis inter se ن et ע (quorum sonus cognatus in pronunciando olim accesserit ad ng, Gallorum n in mon, ton), atque ג et غ, quorum commutatorum exempla adfert SCHULTEN-SIUS in Clavi Dialector. p. 199. Porro de luscinia cogitasse cum Alexandrinos, dum στρουθια, passeres, posuerunt in Ieremia, ex quorum genere illa sit avis; tum Chaldaeum Syrumque, qui in Ieremia suo כורכיא (a verbo כָּרַךְ operire) indicarent avem, luctu inter densas frondes sese occultantem, i. e. lusciniam, eoque vocabulo simul exprimere voluerint eandem illam verbi עגר occultandi notionem, quae peti possit ex Arabum عجر, in Conjug. V. operuit se. Quae omnia quam sint artificiosa, atque e longo petita, facile quisque animadvertet ipse. — EVERARD. SCHEIDIUS in Dissertat. ad Cantic. Hiskiae p. 86. seqq. in Iesaia nostrum עגור participium ratus passivum verbi עגר, quod Geuhario et Firuzabadio testibus, torquendi flectendique notionem habet, epitheton hirundinis putat, quae metu exterrita huc illuc gyrat, et sese identidem in via inflectit. — Pro participio vocabulum habuit quoque PAU-LUS in Clavi Iesai., sed quum ibi סוס equi nomen censeat (conf. not. 4. ad Cap. praeced.), עגור interpretatur perturbatum, an-xium, in auxilium vocato Syriaco ܥܓܘܪܐ, etiam ab Arabum عجر, inflectere in via, gyrare, ut poeta sese febris aestu jactatum comparet cum equo defatigato, at-que ex imo pectore anhelante, stridula acrique voce emissa, quae exprimatur verbo II, 632 צפצף.— Mihi et in Iesaia עגור avis videtur nomen esse, ob eam maxime caussam, quod Ierem. VIII, 7. eaedem voces סיס et עגור junctae sunt, et quidem ita junctae, ut appareat, עגור esse avis nomen, ut תור et סיס, quae praecedunt. Quaenam autem volucrium indicetur species, silentibus reliquis dialectis, mirumque in modum dissentientibus veteribus, hodie nemo dixerit.

R4 Rosenmüller, II, 631 But I can scarcely believe that Bochart has established anything certain by this whole very learned discussion. Let us weigh the force of his arguments. One will look in vain in this entire chapter for any explicit statement of them. At the very outset he assumes that עגור is the crane, but he is completely silent about the reasons that led him to it. Yet, so far as one can gather from the course of the whole discussion, he seems to have reasoned thus: "From the two passages of Isaiah and Jeremiah it is clear that עגור is a migratory bird and one using a strained voice; and we find both of these in the crane; therefore עגור is the crane." Nothing would be more certain than this, if those two features were peculiar to cranes. As it is, since there are many migratory birds that use a strained voice, you see how unsafe this argument is unless weightier ones are added. But Bochart is wholly without these, so that there is not even one of the ancients on whose authority he can safely rely. For the Syriac and the Chaldee put crane where the Hebrew text has סוס, but swallow in place of עגור; unless you say that the words have been transposed in both translators, which Bochart assumes without any adequate reason, merely in favour of his preconceived opinion. Equally weak is the other argument for the crane, drawn from the fact that the Arabic عجر [ʿjr] means he returned; for on that basis all migratory birds whatsoever could have been so named. But what chiefly restrains me from taking עגור as the name of the crane is this: that in Isaiah chirping (צפצף) is attributed to the birds סוס and עגור. — VELTHUSEN (in Symbolae Kilonienses vol. 2, p. 273—390) labours hard to show that the Hebrew עגור is the same word as نغر [nughar], the Arabic name of the nightingale, with an interchange of ن and ע (whose related sound in pronunciation once approached ng, like the French n in mon, ton), and of ג and غ, examples of whose interchange Schultens [=Albert Schultens, Liber Jobi (1737)] gives in the Clavis Dialectorum p. 199. He further argues that the nightingale was in the minds both of the Alexandrians, when they put στρουθια [strouthia], sparrows, in Jeremiah, that bird being of their kind; and of the Chaldee and the Syriac, who in their Jeremiah by כורכיא (from the verb כָּרַךְ to cover) would indicate a bird that hides itself amid thick foliage in mourning, i.e. the nightingale, and by that word sought at the same time to express the same notion of hiding in the verb עגר that can be derived from the Arabic عجر [ʿjr], in Conjugation 5 he covered himself. How contrived and far-fetched all this is, anyone will easily notice for himself. — EVERARD SCHEIDIUS, in his Dissertatio ad Canticum Hiskiae p. 86 ff., taking our עגור in Isaiah as a passive participle of the verb עגר, which, on the testimony of Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ] and Firuzabadi, has the notion of twisting and bending, considers it an epithet of the swallow, which, struck with fear, wheels this way and that and repeatedly turns aside in its course. — Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)] too, in the Clavis to Isaiah, took the word for a participle; but since he there regards סוס as the name of the horse (cf. note 4 to the preceding Chapter), he interprets עגור as disturbed, anxious, calling to his aid the Syriac ܥܓܘܪܐ [עגורא] and also the Arabic عجر [ʿjr], to turn aside in the way, to wheel, so that the poet, tossed by the heat of fever, compares himself with an exhausted horse, panting from the depths of its chest and uttering a shrill and sharp sound, which is expressed by the verb II, 632 צפצף. — To me עגור seems to be the name of a bird in Isaiah too, chiefly for this reason: that in Jer 8:7 the same words סיס and עגור are joined, and joined in such a way that it is evident that עגור is the name of a bird, like תור and סיס, which precede. But which species of bird is meant, since the other dialects are silent and the ancients disagree remarkably, no one today can say.


Part 2, Book 1, chapter 12: The kore
