II, 645 col. 89 CAP. XIII.

II, 645 col. 89 Chapter 13.


Quid sit πέρδιξ θηρευτὴς ἐν καρτάλλῳ, perdix venator in cavea, Sirach. XI, 31. al. 37.

What is πέρδιξ θηρευτὴς ἐν καρτάλλῳ [perdix thēreutēs en kartallō], the hunter partridge in a cage, Sir 11:31 var. 37.


Postquam de spurio perdice actum, de genuino pauca dicemus ad celebrem Sirachidis locum Eccles. XI, 31. al. 37. Πέρδιξ θηρευτὴς ἐν καρτάλλῳ, οὕτως καρδία ὑπερηφάνου, καὶ ὡς ὁ κατάσκοπος ἐπιβλέπει πτῶσιν· Ut perdix venator in cavea, ita cor superbi, qui ut speculator observat casum. Sensus est, hominem superbum, altero in ruinam impulso, sic in illum insultare, quomodo perdix venator in cavea in sui generis aves, quas in laqueum induxit. Ibi enim πέρδιξ θηρευτὴς est perdix cicur, qui feros perdices suis artibus in caveam aut laqueos allicit. Aristoteles Historiae lib. 9. cap. 8. Καὶ τῶν περδίκων δ᾽ οἱ τι-θασσοὶ τοὺς ἀγρίους πέρδικας ὀχεύουσι, καὶ ἐπικορίζουσι (lege ἐπικοῤῥίζουσι) καὶ ὑβρίζουσιν. Ἐπὶ δὲ τὸν θηρευτὴν πέρδικα ὠθεῖται τῶν ἀγρίων ὁ ἡγεμὼν, ἀν-τιάσας ὡς μαχούμενος, τούτου δ᾽ ἁλόντος ἐν ταῖς πηκταῖς, πάλιν προσέρχεται ἄλλος, ἀντιάσας τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον. Cicures quoque perdices feros subagitant, et verberant, et contumelia afficiunt. Et in venatorem perdicem impetum facit agrestium dux, contra congrediens ut pugnaturus. Eo vero capto in viminea cavea, denuo contra procedit alter eodem modo. Vides utrobique τὸν θηρευτὴν πέρ- col. 90 δικα, perdicem venatorem, et caveam vimineam. Id enim proprie κάρταλλος in Syrachide, ut in Philosopho αἱ πήκται. Hesychius Κάρταλον (lege Κάρταλλον)· τὸ πλεκτὸν ἀγγεῖον (malim πηκτὸν, ut in Aristotele) ἐν τοῖς ὀψαρτυτικοῖς κλωβός. Recte omnino. Cavea enim hujusmodi vocatur etiam κλωβὸς, ut Hebraice כלוב club, et Syriace ܩܠܘܒܝܐ klubja. Sic Ierem. V, 27. ככלוב מלא עוף, ut cluub (cavea) scatens avibus. Ubi Syrus, ܐܝܟ ܩܠܘܒܝܐ, ut klubja (quamvis Graeci, ὡς παγὶς ἐφεσταμένη, et Arabs مثل فخ منصوب II, 646 ܡܨܝܕܬܐ ut laqueus tensus, et Hieronymus, sicut decipula). Agitur enim de cavea, in quam alliciuntur aves, quod patet ex tota serie. Ita enim habet versus proxime praecedens: Quia inventi sunt in populo meo insidiantes quasi aucupes, laqueos ponentes ad capiendos homines. Et hic ipse, Sicut club, scatens avibus, ita domus eorum plenae sunt fraude: id est, rebus, per fraudem partis et comparatis. Itaque quod fugit Lexicographos, ut in Hebraeo Ieremiae textu כלוב club, ita etiam in Graecis scriptoribus κλουβὸς, aut κλωβὸς, vel pro dolosa hac cavea, vel pro cavea quavis etiam alibi occurrit. Oppianus in Ixeuticis [III, 14.] de aegitho, Capitur κλωβῷ, cavea, cui alius, pridem captus, ad alliciendum voce includitur. Poeta vetus apud Suidam, in Ἀμφιῤῥῶγας· Κλωβοὺς τ᾽ ἀμφιῤῥῶγας, caveas undique diruptas. Philostorgius lib. 10. cap. 11. (in manuscripto meo, quod edito exemplari saepe est emendatius) de Aegyptio pumilione, Ὁ δὲ Αἰγύπτιος οὕτω κατεβραχύνετο, ὥστε μηδ᾽ ἀχαρίστως τοὺς ἐν τοῖς κλουβοῖς πέρδικας ἐκμιμεῖσθαι, καὶ συναθύρειν αὐτῷ πρὸς ἔριν ἐκείνους· Aegyptius vero ita contrahebatur, ut perdices in clubis (seu caveis) inclusos non injucunde imitaretur, qui et ipsi cum eo per lusum contendebant. Et eundem Nicephorus lib. 12. cap. 37. fuisse dicit παραπλήσιον πέρδικι, καὶ μὴ ἀχάριστον ἐν κλωβῷ τὴν ἐκείνου προσομιλίαν. Et Cedrenus editionis Parisiensis pag. 592. B. Ζῶον ἦν τι πτῆνον ἐν κλωβῷ κατὰ τὰ βασίλεια αἰωρούμενον. Avis quaedam in regia erat in clobo (id est, cavea) appensa. Glossae Philoxeni, Κλωβὸς, cavea. Itaque frustra vir doctissimus in Philostorgio pro κλουβοῖς rescribi vult κλοιοῖς, vel κλυβοῖς. Et Nicephori interpres voces ἐν κλωβῷ perridicule reddidit, In globo scilicet hominum. Caveam capiendis avibus Talmudici in tractatu Kilaim פלצור paltsur vocant, et Romani transennam. Plautus in Bacchidibus Actus quarti Scena Nimio,

Having dealt with the spurious partridge, we shall say a little about the genuine one, with reference to the well-known passage of Sirach, Sir 11:31 var. 37: Πέρδιξ θηρευτὴς ἐν καρτάλλῳ, οὕτως καρδία ὑπερηφάνου, καὶ ὡς ὁ κατάσκοπος ἐπιβλέπει πτῶσιν [Perdix thēreutēs en kartallō, houtōs kardia hyperēphanou, kai hōs ho kataskopos epiblepei ptōsin]; Like a hunter partridge in a cage, so is the heart of the proud man, who like a spy watches for a fall. The sense is that a proud man, when another has been driven to ruin, exults over him in the same way as the hunter partridge in a cage exults over the birds of its own kind that it has led into the snare. For there πέρδιξ θηρευτὴς [perdix thēreutēs] is a tame partridge, which by its arts lures wild partridges into the cage or the snares. Aristotle, History book 9, ch. 8: Καὶ τῶν περδίκων δ᾽ οἱ τιθασσοὶ τοὺς ἀγρίους πέρδικας ὀχεύουσι, καὶ ἐπικορίζουσι [kai tōn perdikōn d᾽ hoi tithassoi tous agrious perdikas ocheuousi, kai epikorizousi] (read ἐπικοῤῥίζουσι [epikorrizousi]) καὶ ὑβρίζουσιν. Ἐπὶ δὲ τὸν θηρευτὴν πέρδικα ὠθεῖται τῶν ἀγρίων ὁ ἡγεμὼν, ἀντιάσας ὡς μαχούμενος, τούτου δ᾽ ἁλόντος ἐν ταῖς πηκταῖς, πάλιν προσέρχεται ἄλλος, ἀντιάσας τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον [kai hybrizousin. Epi de ton thēreutēn perdika ōtheitai tōn agriōn ho hēgemōn, antiasas hōs machoumenos, toutou d᾽ halontos en tais pēktais, palin proserchetai allos, antiasas ton auton tropon]. Tame partridges also tread the wild partridges, and beat them, and treat them with insult. And the leader of the wild ones rushes at the hunter partridge, advancing against it as if to fight. When he has been caught in the wicker cage, another in turn comes forward against it in the same way. You see in both places τὸν θηρευτὴν πέρ- col. 90 δικα [ton thēreutēn perdika], the hunter partridge, and the wicker cage. For that is properly κάρταλλος [kartallos] in Sirach, as αἱ πήκται [hai pēktai] is in the Philosopher. Hesychius: Κάρταλον [Kartalon] (read Κάρταλλον [Kartallon]): τὸ πλεκτὸν ἀγγεῖον [to plekton angeion] (I would prefer πηκτὸν [pēkton], as in Aristotle) ἐν τοῖς ὀψαρτυτικοῖς κλωβός [en tois opsartytikois klōbos]. Quite correctly. For a cage of this kind is also called κλωβὸς [klōbos], as in Hebrew כלוב club, and in Syriac ܩܠܘܒܝܐ [קלוביא] klubja. Thus Ierem. V, 27: ככלוב מלא עוף, like a cluub (cage) teeming with birds. Here the Syriac has ܐܝܟ ܩܠܘܒܝܐ [איך קלוביא], like a klubja (although the Greeks have ὡς παγὶς ἐφεσταμένη [hōs pagis ephestamenē], and the Arabic مثل فخ منصوب [mithl fakhkh manṣūb] II, 646 ܡܨܝܕܬܐ [מצידתא] like a set snare, and Jerome like a trap). For the subject is a cage into which birds are lured, as is clear from the whole context. For the verse immediately preceding reads: For among my people are found those who lie in wait like fowlers, setting snares to catch men. And this verse itself: Like a club teeming with birds, so their houses are full of deceit, that is, of things gained and acquired by deceit. Thus, a point that has escaped the lexicographers: just as כלוב club occurs in the Hebrew text of Jeremiah, so also in Greek writers κλουβὸς [kloubos] or κλωβὸς [klōbos] occurs elsewhere too, either for this deceitful cage or for any cage at all. Oppian in the Ixeutica [III, 14.], on the aegithus: It is caught κλωβῷ [klōbō], in a cage, in which another bird, caught earlier, is shut up to lure it by its voice. An old poet in Suidas, under Ἀμφιῤῥῶγας [Amphirrhōgas]: Κλωβοὺς τ᾽ ἀμφιῤῥῶγας [Klōbous t᾽ amphirrhōgas], cages broken on all sides. Philostorgius book 10, ch. 11 (in my manuscript, which is often more correct than the printed copy), on the Egyptian dwarf: Ὁ δὲ Αἰγύπτιος οὕτω κατεβραχύνετο, ὥστε μηδ᾽ ἀχαρίστως τοὺς ἐν τοῖς κλουβοῖς πέρδικας ἐκμιμεῖσθαι, καὶ συναθύρειν αὐτῷ πρὸς ἔριν ἐκείνους [Ho de Aigyptios houtō katebrachyneto, hōste mēd᾽ acharistōs tous en tois kloubois perdikas ekmimeisthai, kai synathyrein autō pros erin ekeinous]; The Egyptian was so stunted that he imitated, not unpleasingly, the partridges shut up in clubs (or cages), which themselves contended with him in play. And Nicephorus, book 12, ch. 37, says that the same man was παραπλήσιον πέρδικι, καὶ μὴ ἀχάριστον ἐν κλωβῷ τὴν ἐκείνου προσομιλίαν [paraplēsion perdiki, kai mē acharislon en klōbō tēn ekeinou prosomilian]. And Cedrenus, Paris edition, p. 592 B: Ζῶον ἦν τι πτῆνον ἐν κλωβῷ κατὰ τὰ βασίλεια αἰωρούμενον [Zōon ēn ti ptēnon en klōbō kata ta basileia aiōroumenon]. There was a certain bird in the palace, hung up in a clobus (that is, a cage). The Glosses of Philoxenus: Κλωβὸς [Klōbos], cavea [cage]. Therefore a very learned man wishes in vain to change κλουβοῖς [klouhois] in Philostorgius to κλοιοῖς [kloiois] or κλυβοῖς [klybois]. And the translator of Nicephorus rendered the words ἐν κλωβῷ [en klōbō] quite absurdly: In a globe, namely of men. The Talmudists, in the tractate Kilaim, call a cage for catching birds פלצור paltsur, and the Romans transenna. Plautus in the Bacchides, act 4, the scene Nimio:


Nunc ab transenna hic turdus lumbricum petit.
Pendebit hodie pulchre, ita intendi tenus.

Now this thrush is going for the worm from the trap. He will hang there nicely today, so well have I set the snare.


Et in Persa Act. 4. Scena Cui homini,

And in the Persa, act 4, the scene Cui homini:


Hunc ego hominem hodie in transennam doctis ducam dolis.

Today I shall lead this man into the trap with clever tricks.


Et in Rudente Act. 4. Scena Quam mox,

And in the Rudens, act 4, the scene Quam mox:


O Gripe, Gripe, in aetate hominum plurimae
Fiant transennae, ubi capiuntur dolis (1).

O Gripus, Gripus, in men's lifetime there come to be very many traps, in which they are caught by tricks R1.


II, 647 Porro de perdice venatore etiam alii meminerunt. Nisi quod pro venatore Athenaeus lib. 9. θηρεύοντα πέρδικα, venantem perdicem vocat. Plinius a), aucupis indicem, aut illicem potius, ut Turnebus b) et Scaliger c) legendum monent. Aelianus d) eodem sensu τὸν παλεύοντα πέρδικα. Eustathius Antiochenus τὸν πέρδικα συμπράττοντα τοῖς θηρευταῖς πρὸς τὴν ἄγραν. Theodoretus in Catena in Ieremiam πέρδικα θηρατικὸν, tales addens e Babylone haberi. Nempe id aucupii genus in Oriente jam olim fuit in usu. Proinde in Xenophonte lib. 1. Cyropaediae Cambyses Cyrum filium sic alloquitur: Ὄρνιθες δὲ ἐπεπαί-δευτό σοι, ὥς τέ σοι μὲν τὰ συμφέροντα ὑπερητεῖν, τὰς δὲ ὁμοφύλους ὄρνιθας ἐξαπατᾷν, Aves a te ita edoctae fuerant, ut et tibi utilia subministrarent, et aves ejusdem generis deciperent. Qui plura de hoc argumento volet, eos consulat, quos citavimus. Et Albertum Magnum ubi de cubeth e), id est, perdice foemina, col. 91 Arabice القبج quam cavea inclusam ait mares ad se allicere. Quamvis Damir id ipsum mari his verbis tribuit, في طبع الذكر ان يخدع امثاله بقرقرته ولهذا اتخذه الصيادون في اشراكهم ليكثر القرقرة فيجتمع الحجل فيقعن معه De maris natura hoc est, ut aves sibi similes cantu suo alliciat: proinde venatores illum secum assumunt, ut frequenti cantu suo perdices foeminas congreget, quae ad eum volent. Sed ad id utrumque sexum et vario successu adhiberi, pluribus docent Philosophus, Aelianus et Athenaeus ubi supra. Arabica versio in Sirachide, pro القبج في القفص perdix in cavea, nullo sensu habet الصنج في الرقص sistrum, vel cymbalum in tripudio. Quod factum esse per scribarum imperitiam, docet literarum similitudo. Pagnino, Castalioni, Ariae, Camerario, Iansenio, aliis πέρδιξ θηρευτὴς est capta perdix, quod esset πέρδιξ θη-ρευθεὶς. Pari errore in Syro habetur ܐܝܟ ܩܩܒܢܐ ܕܨܝܕܐ ut perdix venatione capta; et in Vulgata, sicut perdix inducitur in caveam.

II, 647 Moreover, others also mention the hunter partridge. Except that instead of "hunter" Athenaeus, book 9, calls it θηρεύοντα πέρδικα [thēreuonta perdika], a hunting partridge. Pliny a) calls it the fowler's informer, or rather his decoy [illicem], as Turnebus b) and Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)] c) advise reading. Aelian d), in the same sense, says τὸν παλεύοντα πέρδικα [ton paleuonta perdika]. Eustathius of Antioch says τὸν πέρδικα συμπράττοντα τοῖς θηρευταῖς πρὸς τὴν ἄγραν [ton perdika sympratonta tois thēreutais pros tēn agran]. Theodoret, in the Catena on Jeremiah, says πέρδικα θηρατικὸν [perdika thēratikon], adding that such birds are obtained from Babylon. Indeed, this kind of fowling was already in use in the East long ago. Accordingly, in Xenophon, book 1 of the Cyropaedia, Cambyses addresses his son Cyrus thus: Ὄρνιθες δὲ ἐπεπαίδευτό σοι, ὥς τέ σοι μὲν τὰ συμφέροντα ὑπερητεῖν, τὰς δὲ ὁμοφύλους ὄρνιθας ἐξαπατᾷν [Ornithes de epepaideuto soi, hōs te soi men ta sympheronta hypērētein, tas de homophylous ornithas exapatan], "You had trained birds so that they would both serve you in what was useful and deceive birds of the same kind." Whoever wants more on this subject should consult those we have cited. Also Albertus Magnus, where he treats of the cubeth e), that is, the female partridge, col. 91 in Arabic القبج [al-qabj], which he says, when shut in a cage, lures the males to itself. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], however, attributes this very thing to the male in these words: في طبع الذكر ان يخدع امثاله بقرقرته ولهذا اتخذه الصيادون في اشراكهم ليكثر القرقرة فيجتمع الحجل فيقعن معه [fī ṭabʿ al-dhakar an yakhdaʿa amthālahu bi-qarqaratihi wa-li-hādhā ittakhadhahu al-ṣayyādūn fī ashrākihim li-yukthira al-qarqara fa-yajtamiʿa al-ḥajal fa-yaqaʿna maʿahu] "It is the nature of the male to lure birds like itself by its call; therefore hunters take it with them, so that by its frequent calling it may gather the female partridges, which fly to it." But that both sexes are used for this, with varying success, is shown at length by the Philosopher, Aelian and Athenaeus in the places cited above. The Arabic version of Sirach, instead of القبج في القفص [al-qabj fī al-qafaṣ] a partridge in a cage, has, without any sense, الصنج في الرقص [al-ṣanj fī al-raqṣ] a sistrum, or a cymbal in the dance. That this arose through the ignorance of scribes is shown by the similarity of the letters. For Pagnino, Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)], Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], Camerarius, Jansenius [=Cornelius Jansen of Ghent (d. 1576), commentary on Wisdom] and others, πέρδιξ θηρευτὴς [perdix thēreutēs] is a captured partridge, as though it were πέρδιξ θηρευθεὶς [perdix thēreutheis]. By the same error the Syriac has ܐܝܟ ܩܩܒܢܐ ܕܨܝܕܐ [איך קקבנא דצידא] like a partridge taken in hunting; and the Vulgate, "as a partridge is led into the cage."


(1) Rosenmüller, II, 646 Transennam non esse caveam vimineam, ut Bochartus vult, sed rete, duobus orbibus ligneis inclusum, et per terram tensum, Ioh. Gottl. Schneiderus contendit ad Oppiani Ixeutic. III, 13. p. 435.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 646 That a transenna is not a wicker cage, as Bochart holds, but a net enclosed by two wooden hoops and stretched along the ground, is argued by Joh. Gottl. Schneider on Oppian, Ixeutic. 3, 13, p. 435.

Part 2, Book 1, chapter 14: The names of the quail
--------------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/selav.html

II, 648 col. 91 CAP. XIV.

II, 648 col. 91 Chapter XIV.


Varia Coturnicum nomina, שלו, سلوي, سماني, ፈርፈርት et variae species juxta Hebraeos, 1. שיכלי, Συκαλὶς, 2. קכלי, Κίχλη. 3. פסיוני, Phasianus. 4. שליו.

The various names of the quail, שלו, سلوي [salwā], سماني [sumānā], ፈርፈርት [farəfarət] and the various kinds according to the Hebrews: 1. שיכלי, Συκαλὶς [Sykalis], 2. קכלי, Κίχλη [Kichlē]. 3. פסיוני, the pheasant. 4. שליו.


De coturnicibus, quas Israelitis, in deserto fame enectis, liberaliter indulsit Deus, ita Moses Exod. XVI, 13. Et vespere contigit, ut adscendentes coturnices castra tegerent. Et Num. XI, 31. Tum ventus profectus a Domino abripuit coturnices a mari, et in castra dispersit, quasi itinere unius diei hinc, et quasi iti- col. 92 nere unius diei illinc circa castra, idque ad duos cubitos in superficie terrae. 32. Surgensque populus toto die illo, et tota nocte illa, et toto die postero collegerunt coturnices. Qui minimum, decem coros collegit, et eas circa castra late expandebant. 33. Sed cum caro adhuc esset inter dentes nondum conscissa, ira Domini in populum accensa est; et populum percussit Dominus plaga valde magna. 34. Quamobrem vocaverunt nomen loci illius kibroth thaava, (id est, sepulchra concupiscentiae) quia ibi sepeliverant populum eorum, qui concupiverant. David etiam Psal. LXXVIII, 26. Impulit Eurum in coelos, et virtute sua austrum induxit. 27. Et carnem depluit super eos tanquam pulverem, et volucres alatas tanquam arenam maris. 28. Quas in media eorum castra conjecit, circa illorum tabernacula. 29. Et ad satietatem usque comederunt, ab illo, quae concupiverant, adepti. 30. Nondum cupiditatem suam deposuerant, et adhuc in ore cibum habebant. 31. Cum eos invadens ira Dei pinguissimos eorum interfecit, et Israelis lectissimos prostravit. Et Psal. CV, 40. Peientibus coturnices invexit, et pane coelorum satiavit eos.

Of the quails which God generously granted to the Israelites when they were perishing of hunger in the desert, Moses writes thus, Exod 16:13: And it came to pass in the evening that quails came up and covered the camp. And Num 11:31: Then a wind going forth from the Lord swept quails from the sea and scattered them over the camp, about a day's journey on this side and about a day's journey on that side, round about the camp, and that to two cubits above the face of the earth. 32. And the people rose up all that day, and all that night, and all the next day, and gathered the quails. He who gathered least gathered ten cors, and they spread them out widely round about the camp. 33. But while the flesh was still between their teeth, not yet chewed, the wrath of the Lord was kindled against the people, and the Lord smote the people with a very great plague. 34. Therefore they called the name of that place kibroth thaava (that is, graves of craving), because there they had buried the people of those who had craved. David also, Ps 78:26: He drove the east wind into the heavens, and by his power he brought in the south wind. 27. And he rained flesh upon them as dust, and winged fowl as the sand of the sea. 28. These he cast into the midst of their camp, round about their tents. 29. And they ate until they were filled, having received from him what they had craved. 30. They had not yet put away their craving, and the food was still in their mouth, 31. when the wrath of God came upon them and slew the fattest of them, and laid low the choicest of Israel. And Ps 105:40: When they asked, he brought quails, and satisfied them with the bread of heaven.


Hebraeum coturnicis nomen est שלו selau; Chaldaicum quoque סליו selau; Syriacum ܣܠܘܝ salvai, et Arabicum سلوي iisdem literis, quamvis efferant selvva. Unde Alcoranus Azoara 17. cui titulus اعراف seu Limbi انزلنا عليهم المن والسلوي Super eos manna demisimus, et coturnices. Nonnulli mel explicant, quia vox Arabica سلوي selvva tam mel significat, quam coturnices. Quomodo si sumeretur, من manna, et سلوي selvva essent synonyma. Manna enim est mel aerium. Unde est, quod a medicorum filiis vocatur ἀερόμελι, et ab Amynta libro 1. τῶν τῆς Ἀσίας σταθμῶν apud Athenaeum lib. 11. Sed melius Alkazuinius et Ibnobitar, qui asserunt انه السماني eam esse coturnicem. Et Alachphas, هو طاير الذي انزله الله تعالي علي بني اسرايل علي القول المشهور وغلط II, 649 الهزلي فظنه الغسل Avis est, quam demisit Deus Excelsus super filios Israelis, juxta receptam sententiam. Erravit igitur Alhazelius, qui putavit, esse mel. Sunt ex Arabibus, qui scribant, سلوي vocari coturnicem لانه يسلي الانسان عن ساير الادام Quia facit, ut homo reliquos cibos oblivioni tradat. Sed est Hebraeum שלו selau, quod referendum puto ad verbum שלה sala, quamvis hoc Masorethae per Sin dextrum, illud per sinistrum scripserint διακριτικῶς. Proprie שלה est pacate vivere, deinde etiam abundare. Unde est, quod a Graecis saepe redditur εὐθηνεῖν, et שליה εὐθηνία. Coturnices igitur a copia dici verissimile est, cum in calidis regionibus vix ulla sit fertilior avis, ut patebit ex sequentibus (1). Aliud coturnicum nomen سماني II, 650 sumana apud Arabes duci constat a pinguedine; quia pinguissima est avis. Hinc Rabbi Selomo in Exod. XVI. השלו מין עוף ושמן מאד, Coturnix, avis species, quae est obesissima. Et Kimchius in Lexico הוא שמן מאד, est pinguis valde. In Aethiopum Psalterio Psal. CIV, 38. ፈርፈርት፡ phorphorath est coturnix, nomi- col. 93 ne generis, ut videtur, ad speciem translato (2). Talmudicis enim פרפרות parperoth, vel pharpheroth, ἀρχαϊκῶς sunt cupediae quaevis ex rebus minutis et delicatis, cujusmodi afferri solebant, vel statim initio, vel in fine convivii. Unde in tractatu Berachoth cap. 6. fol. 42. a. ברך על הפרפרות שלפני המזון פטר את הפרפרות שלאחר המזון, Qui benedictionem dicit super pharpheroth (id est, cupedias), quae afferuntur ante cibum, liberas facit (a benedictione) pharpheroth, quae post cibum afferuntur. Quia utrisque sufficit una benedictio. Et ibi Glossa, ומביאין לפני הם פרפרות להמשיך אכילה כגון פרגיות ודגים ואח״כ מביאין השלחן Et iis offerebant pharpheroth (seu cupedias) ad irritandam orexin, ut aviculas et pisces: deinde mensam afferebant, id est, consuetos cibos.

The Hebrew name of the quail is שלו selau; the Chaldee is likewise סליו selau; the Syriac ܣܠܘܝ [סלוי] salvai; and the Arabic سلوي [salwā] in the same letters, although they pronounce it selvva. Hence the Qur'an, Azoara 17, entitled اعراف [Aʿrāf] or The Limbo: انزلنا عليهم المن والسلوي [anzalnā ʿalayhim al-manna wa-l-salwā] We sent down upon them manna and quails. Some explain it as honey, because the Arabic word سلوي [salwā] selvva signifies honey as well as quails. Taken in that way, من [mann] manna and سلوي [salwā] selvva would be synonyms. For manna is aerial honey. That is why it is called ἀερόμελι [aeromeli] by the sons of the physicians, and by Amyntas in book 1 of τῶν τῆς Ἀσίας σταθμῶν [tōn tēs Asias stathmōn], cited by Athenaeus, book 11. But Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt] and Ibnobitar do better, who assert انه السماني [annahu al-sumānā] that it is the quail. And Alachphas: هو طاير الذي انزله الله تعالي علي بني اسرايل علي القول المشهور وغلط [huwa ṭāʾir alladhī anzalahu Allāh taʿālā ʿalā banī Isrāʾīl ʿalā al-qawl al-mashhūr wa-ghalaṭa] II, 649 الهزلي فظنه الغسل [al-Hudhalī fa-ẓannahu al-ghasl] It is the bird which God Most High sent down upon the children of Israel, according to the received opinion. So Alhazelius erred, who thought it was honey. There are some among the Arabs who write that the quail is called سلوي [salwā] لانه يسلي الانسان عن ساير الادام [li-annahu yuslī al-insān ʿan sāʾir al-idām] because it makes a man forget other foods. But the Hebrew is שלו selau, which I think should be referred to the verb שלה sala, although the Masoretes wrote the latter with right-hand Sin and the former with left-hand, διακριτικῶς [diakritikōs]. Properly שלה means to live in peace, and then also to abound. Hence it is often rendered by the Greeks εὐθηνεῖν [euthēnein], and שליה εὐθηνία [euthēnia]. It is therefore most likely that quails are named from abundance, since in warm regions scarcely any bird is more prolific, as will appear from what follows R1. Another name of the quail among the Arabs, سماني [sumānā] II, 650 sumana, is agreed to be derived from fatness, because it is a very fat bird. Hence R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] on Exod. XVI.: השלו מין עוף ושמן מאד, The quail, a species of bird which is very fat. And Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] in his Lexicon: הוא שמן מאד, it is very fat. In the Ethiopic Psalter, Ps 104:38, ፈርፈርት፡ [farəfarət] phorphorath is the quail, the name of the genus having been transferred, as it seems, to the species R2. col. 93 For among the Talmudists פרפרות parperoth or pharpheroth, ἀρχαϊκῶς [archaikōs], are any delicacies made of small and dainty things, such as used to be served either right at the beginning or at the end of a banquet. Hence in the tractate Berachoth, ch. 6, fol. 42a: ברך על הפרפרות שלפני המזון פטר את הפרפרות שלאחר המזון, He who says the blessing over the pharpheroth (that is, delicacies) that are served before the meal exempts (from the blessing) the pharpheroth that are served after the meal. For one blessing suffices for both. And there the Gloss: ומביאין לפני הם פרפרות להמשיך אכילה כגון פרגיות ודגים ואח״כ מביאין השלחן And they served them pharpheroth (or delicacies) to whet the appetite, such as small birds and fish; then they brought the table, that is, the usual foods.


A Graecis interpretibus שלו selau non redditur ὄρτυξ coturnix; sed ὀρτυ-γομήτρα ortygometra. Ita Exod. XVI, 13. Ἀνέβη ὀρτυγομήτρα. Et Num. XI, 31. Ἐξεπέρασεν ὀρτυγομήτραν. Et versu sequente, Καὶ συνέλεγον τὴν ὀρ-τυγομήτραν. Et Psal. CIV, 40. Ἤιτησαν, καὶ ἦλθεν ὀρτυγομήτρα. Et Apollinaris in Paraphrasi,

By the Greek translators שלו selau is rendered not ὄρτυξ [ortyx] coturnix [quail], but ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra] ortygometra. Thus Exod 16:13 Ἀνέβη ὀρτυγομήτρα [Anebē ortygomētra]. And Num 11:31 Ἐξεπέρασεν ὀρτυγομήτραν [Exeperasen ortygomētran]. And in the following verse, Καὶ συνέλεγον τὴν ὀρτυγομήτραν [Kai synelegon tēn ortygomētran]. And Ps 104:40 Ἤιτησαν, καὶ ἦλθεν ὀρτυγομήτρα [Ētēsan, kai ēlthen ortygomētra]. And Apollinaris in his Paraphrase,


Ἦλθε μάλ᾽ αἰτίζουσιν ἀπείριτος ὀρτυγομήτρα.

Ἦλθε μάλ᾽ αἰτίζουσιν ἀπείριτος ὀρτυγομήτρα. [Ēlthe mal' aitizousin apeiritos ortygomētra.]


II, 651 Et Sap. XVI, 2. Τροφὴν ἡτοίμασας ὀρτυγομήτραν. Et Sap. XIX, 12. Ἀνέβη αὐτοῖς ἐκ θαλάσσης ὀρτυγομήτρα. Et Philo lib. 1. De vita Moysis, Ὀρτυγο-μητρῶν νέφος συνεχὲς ἐκ θαλάττης ἐπιφερόμενον πᾶν τὸ στρατόπεδον ἐπεσκία-ζε. Nec desunt, quibus ortygometra videatur esse avis, a coturnice diversa. Augustinus in Exodum Quaest. 62. Illis ortygometra data est, id est, aves, quas coturnices multi Latini interpretati sunt, cum sit aliud genus avium ortygometra, quamvis coturnicibus non usquequaque dissimile. Et multo ante Philosophus Hist. lib. 8. cap. 12. Ὅταν δ' ἐντεῦθεν ἀπάρωσιν (οἱ ὄρτυγες) ἥ τε γλωττὶς συν-απαίρει, καὶ ἡ ὀρτυγομήτρα, καὶ ὁ ὠτὸς, καὶ ὁ κύγχραμος· Cum hinc disce- dunt (coturnices), simul discedit lingulaca, et ortygometra, et otus, et cynchra- mus. Quibus verbis, ut lingulacam, et otum, et cynchramum, ita etiam ortygometram a coturnice distingui, palam est. Proinde ibidem infra sequitur, Ἡ δὲ ὀρτυγομήτρα παραπλήσιος τὴν μορφὴν τοῖς λιμναίοις ἐστὶ· Ortygometra for- ma lacustribus est similis. Et apud Athenaeum lib. 9. ab Alexandro Myndio describitur eadem avis τὸ μέγεθος ἡ λίκη τρυγὼν, σκέλη δὲ μακρὰ, δυσθαλπὴς καὶ δειλὴ, magnitudine turturis, longis cruribus, alsiosa et timida. Δυσθαλὴς, id est, male virescens, nullo sensu scribitur, sed rescripsi δυσθαλπής. Ex horum igitur sententia planum est, ortygometran a coturnice specie differre (3). Hesychio tamen ὀρτυγομήτρα nihil quidquam est, quam ὄρτυξ ὑπερμεγέθης, co- turnix praemagna, tanquam aliorum mater, aut matrix. Qualis in cicadis τετ-τιγομήτρα, et in echinis ἐχινομήτρα, et in vermibus ἰουλομήτρα Hesychio pro ἰουλυμήτρα· et in loti speciebus Plinii λωτομήτρα· et in urbibus ac pagis, μη-τρόπολις et μητροκωμία. Nam gravi errore Iansenius in librum Sapientiae cap. 16. ortygometran dici vult tanquam μέτρον τῆς ὄρτυγος, quasi aliarum co- turnicum mensura sit et moderatrix. Neque enim per ε scribitur ὀρτυγόμετρα, sed per η ὀρτυγομήτρα, ut plane sit, quod diximus, coturnicum mater, aut ma- trix. Et vel hinc colligas, ortygometran a vulgari coturnice sola magnitudine differre. Itaque ὀρτυγομήτραν et coturnicem multi promiscue sumunt. In his Iosephus, qui pro ortygometris habet simpliciter ὀρτύγων πλῆθος, coturnicum copiam, lib. 3. cap. 1. Et rursus cap. 12. Πίμπλαται τὸ στρατόπεδον ὀρτύγων ἅπαν, Coturnicibus replentur tota castra. Hieronymus quoque, qui pro voce ortygometrae, quam retinuit in Psalmis et in libro Sapientiae, in Lege habet coturnices. Et auctor Mirabilium, inter opera Augustini, lib. 1. cap. 27. haec II, 652 palam habet pro synonymis, cum de hoc miraculo scribit, Ventus, a Domino egrediens, arreptas trans mare coturnices ad castrorum loca detulit. Et paullo col. 94 post, Circa castrorum loca ortygometran inseruit. Neque alia mens Aristopha- nis in Avibus, ubi vota fieri vult

II, 651 And Sap. XVI, 2. Τροφὴν ἡτοίμασας ὀρτυγομήτραν [Trophēn hētoimasas ortygomētran]. And Sap. XIX, 12. Ἀνέβη αὐτοῖς ἐκ θαλάσσης ὀρτυγομήτρα [Anebē autois ek thalassēs ortygomētra]. And Philo, book 1 On the Life of Moses, Ὀρτυγομητρῶν νέφος συνεχὲς ἐκ θαλάττης ἐπιφερόμενον πᾶν τὸ στρατόπεδον ἐπεσκίαζε [Ortygomētrōn nephos syneches ek thalattēs epipheromenon pan to stratopedon epeskiaze]. Nor are there lacking those to whom the ortygometra seems to be a bird different from the quail. Augustine on Exodus, Question 62: To them the ortygometra was given, that is, birds which many Latin translators have rendered quails, although the ortygometra is another kind of bird, though not altogether unlike quails. And long before, the Philosopher, Hist. book 8, ch. 12: Ὅταν δ' ἐντεῦθεν ἀπάρωσιν (οἱ ὄρτυγες) ἥ τε γλωττὶς συναπαίρει, καὶ ἡ ὀρτυγομήτρα, καὶ ὁ ὠτὸς, καὶ ὁ κύγχραμος [Hotan d' enteuthen aparōsin (hoi ortyges) hē te glōttis synapairei, kai hē ortygomētra, kai ho ōtos, kai ho kynchramos]· When they (the quails) depart from here, the lingulaca departs together with them, and the ortygometra, and the otus, and the cynchramus. From these words it is evident that the ortygometra, like the lingulaca, the otus and the cynchramus, is distinguished from the quail. Accordingly, further on in the same place there follows: Ἡ δὲ ὀρτυγομήτρα παραπλήσιος τὴν μορφὴν τοῖς λιμναίοις ἐστὶ [Hē de ortygomētra paraplēsios tēn morphēn tois limnaiois esti]· The ortygometra is similar in form to the marsh birds. And in Athenaeus, book 9, the same bird is described by Alexander of Myndus as τὸ μέγεθος ἡ λίκη τρυγὼν, σκέλη δὲ μακρὰ, δυσθαλπὴς καὶ δειλὴ [to megethos hē likē trygōn, skelē de makra, dysthalpēs kai deilē], of the size of a turtle-dove, with long legs, sensitive to cold and timid. Δυσθαλὴς [Dysthalēs], that is, ill-flourishing, is written there without any sense; but I have emended it to δυσθαλπής [dysthalpēs]. In the opinion of these authors, then, it is plain that the ortygometra differs in species from the quail R3. For Hesychius, however, ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra] is nothing other than ὄρτυξ ὑπερμεγέθης [ortyx hypermegethēs], a very large quail, as if the mother or matrix of the others. So among cicadas there is the τεττιγομήτρα [tettigomētra], among sea-urchins the ἐχινομήτρα [echinomētra], among worms the ἰουλομήτρα [ioulomētra] (in Hesychius written ἰουλυμήτρα [ioulymētra]), among the species of lotus Pliny's λωτομήτρα [lōtomētra], and among cities and villages μητρόπολις [mētropolis] and μητροκωμία [mētrokōmia]. For Jansenius [=Cornelius Jansen of Ghent (d. 1576), commentary on Wisdom], on the book of Wisdom, ch. 16, gravely errs in holding that the ortygometra is so called as if μέτρον τῆς ὄρτυγος [metron tēs ortygos], as though it were the measure and regulator of the other quails. For the word is not written with ε, ὀρτυγόμετρα [ortygometra], but with η, ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra], so that it plainly means what we said: mother or matrix of quails. And even from this you may infer that the ortygometra differs from the common quail only in size. Therefore many use ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra] and coturnix [quail] indiscriminately. Among them is Josephus, who instead of ortygometras has simply ὀρτύγων πλῆθος [ortygōn plēthos], an abundance of quails, book 3, ch. 1. And again in ch. 12: Πίμπλαται τὸ στρατόπεδον ὀρτύγων ἅπαν [Pimplatai to stratopedon ortygōn hapan], The whole camp is filled with quails. Jerome too, who for the word ortygometra, which he retained in the Psalms and in the book of Wisdom, has coturnices [quails] in the Law. And the author of the Mirabilia, among the works of Augustine, book 1, ch. 27, II, 652 plainly treats these as synonyms when he writes of this miracle: A wind, going forth from the Lord, seized quails across the sea and carried them to the places of the camp. And a little col. 94 later: Around the places of the camp it set down the ortygometra. Nor was the intention of Aristophanes any different in the Birds, where he would have vows made


Λητοῖ ὀρτυγομήτρᾳ,

Λητοῖ ὀρτυγομήτρᾳ, [Lētoi ortygomētra,]


Latonae ortygometrae, id est, coturnici. Latona enim paritura fingitur, in coturnicem mutata, Delum venisse, quae inde Ortygia dicta fuerit, quasi coturnicis insula. Iupiter quoque eam iniisse fingitur ὄρτυγι εἰκασθείς. Ita habet Pin- dari Scholiastes in Pythiorum argumento. Plinium etiam et Solinum ortygometran in coturnicum genere censuisse, probat Vir magnus in Plinianis Exercita- tionibus pag. 182. Nec dubito, quin id ipsum senserint Graeci interpretes, et auctor libri Sapientiae, et Philo, et Apollinaris, quibus שלו selau est ὀρτυγομή-τρα. Qua tamen voce libentius usi sunt, quam simplici ὄρτυγος, ne crederetur Deus gregarias coturnices Israelitis immisisse, sed earum nobilissimas.

to Latona the ortygometra, that is, the quail. For Latona, when about to give birth, is fabled to have come to Delos changed into a quail, and the island was therefore called Ortygia, as if the quail's island. Jupiter too is fabled to have lain with her ὄρτυγι εἰκασθείς [ortygi eikastheis]. So the Scholiast on Pindar has it, in the argument of the Pythians. That Pliny and Solinus also counted the ortygometra among the kind of quails is proved by a great man in the Plinianae Exercitationes, p. 182. Nor do I doubt that the same was the view of the Greek translators, of the author of the book of Wisdom, of Philo and of Apollinaris, for whom שלו selau is ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra]. They preferred this word, however, to the simple ὄρτυξ [ortyx], lest it be thought that God had sent the Israelites common quails, rather than the noblest of them.


Quod ferendum, nec conferendum cum magistrorum ineptiis in Talmudico tractatu Ioma cap. 8. fol. 75. b. ubi, ex definitione Rabbi Chaninae Barabbae, ד׳ מיני סליו הן ואלו הן שיכלי וקיכלי ופסיוני ושליו מעליא דכולהו שיכלי גריעי דכולהו שליו, Quatuor sunt coturnicum species, nempe sicli (id est, συκα-λὶς, ficedula), et kichli (id est κίχλη, turdus), et phisioni (φασιανὸς, phasianus), et selau (coturnix proprie dicta), quarum praestantissima est sicli (ficedula), et vilissima omnium selau (coturnix proprie dicta). Inde est, quod שלו, vel שלוים nonnulli interpretes פסיונין, id est, phasianos reddunt. Ita Ionathan Exod. XVI, 13. וסליקו פסיינין וחפו ית משריתא, Et ascenderunt phasiani, et coope- ruerunt castra. Et R. Ioseph Caecus Psal. CV, 40. שאלו בסרא ואיתי פסיונין, Carnem petierunt, et adduxit phasianos: nempe hominibus, qui ventri et gulae nati sunt, non sufficit, quod patribus coturnices liberali manu indulsit Deus; his itaque placuit, eas aves adjungere, quae palato maxime arrident, ficedulas, turdos et phasianos. In illis ducit ordinem

This is tolerable, and not to be compared with the absurdities of the masters in the Talmudic tractate Ioma, ch. 8, fol. 75b, where, by the definition of Rabbi Chanina Barabba, ד׳ מיני סליו הן ואלו הן שיכלי וקיכלי ופסיוני ושליו מעליא דכולהו שיכלי גריעי דכולהו שליו, There are four kinds of quails, namely sicli (that is, συκαλὶς [sykalis], ficedula [fig-pecker]), and kichli (that is, κίχλη [kichlē], turdus [thrush]), and phisioni (φασιανὸς [phasianos], phasianus [pheasant]), and selau (the quail properly so called); of which the most excellent is sicli (the fig-pecker), and the meanest of all selau (the quail properly so called). Hence it is that some interpreters render שלו or שלוים as פסיונין, that is, pheasants. So Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] on Exod. XVI, 13: וסליקו פסיינין וחפו ית משריתא, And pheasants came up and covered the camp. And R. Joseph the Blind on Ps 105:40: שאלו בסרא ואיתי פסיונין, They asked for meat, and he brought pheasants: evidently, for men born for the belly and the gullet it is not enough that God granted quails to the fathers with a liberal hand; so they chose to add those birds that most delight the palate: fig-peckers, thrushes and pheasants. Among these the fig-pecker leads the line,


Cerea quae patulo lucet ficedula lumbo

The waxen fig-pecker that gleams with its broad loin


apud Martialem lib. 5. Unde Iuvenalis Satyra 14.

in Martial, book 5. Hence Juvenal, Satire 14:


— — — qui radere tubera terrae,
Boletum condire, et eodem jure natantes
Mergere ficedulas didicit nebulone parente.

— — — who, from a spendthrift father, learned to scrape truffles, to season a mushroom, and to drown fig-peckers swimming in the same sauce.


Ficedulae peculiare hoc fuit, quod lurconibus tota placuit, non, ut reliqua avitia, solis clunibus. Gellius lib. 15. cap. 8. ex Phavorino: Praefecti popinae, atque luxuriae, etc. negant, ullam avem, praeter ficedulam, totam comesse oportere. II, 653 Caeterarum avium atque altilium, nisi tantum apponatur, ut a cluniculis inferiori parte saturi fiant, convivium putant inopia sordere; superiorem partem avium atque altilium, qui edunt, eos palatum non habere. Hinc Martialis lib. 3. Epigrammate 59.

It was peculiar to the fig-pecker that gluttons liked the whole of it, not, as with other birds, the rump alone. Gellius, book 15, ch. 8, from Favorinus: The masters of the cookshop and of luxury, etc., deny that any bird except the fig-pecker ought to be eaten whole. II, 653 Of other birds and fattened fowls, unless so much is served that the guests are filled from the rump and the lower part, they think the banquet mean through scarcity; and that those who eat the upper part of birds and fowls have no palate. Hence Martial, book 3, Epigram 59:


Aureus immodicis turtur te clunibus implet.

A golden turtle-dove fills you with its huge rump.


Et Epigrammate 81.

And Epigram 81:


Et concubino turturum nates donat.

And gives the turtle-doves' rumps to his concubine.


Ficedulam sequitur קיכלי κίχλη, turdus, quae aves saepe junguntur, tanquam deliciis aut pares, aut suppares. Cornelius Celsus lib. 2. cap. 18. Ex avibus, quae volatu fidunt, firmioris sunt nutrimenti, quae grandiores, quam quae minutae, ut ficedulae et turdus. Suetonius in Tiberio cap. 42. Asellio Sabino HS ducenta donavit pro dialogo, in quo boleti, et ficedulae, et ostreae, et turdi certamen induxerat. Plautus in Captivis ad utramque avem alludens,

After the fig-pecker follows קיכלי, κίχλη [kichlē], the thrush; these birds are often joined as equal, or nearly equal, delicacies. Cornelius Celsus, book 2, ch. 18: Of the birds that rely on flight, the larger give firmer nourishment than the small, such as fig-peckers and the thrush. Suetonius, Tiberius, ch. 42: He gave Asellius Sabinus two hundred thousand sesterces for a dialogue in which he had staged a contest of the mushroom, the fig-pecker, the oyster and the thrush. Plautus in the Captivi, alluding to both birds:


Opus Turdetanis, opus Ficedulensibus,

There is need of the Turdetani, need of the Ficedulenses,


Sed contra quam Hebraei sentiunt pingui turdo datur principatus ab iis, qui palati deliciis omnia metiuntur. Aristophanis Scholiastes in Pace, Αἱ κίχλαι εἶδος στρουθῶν, δοκοῦσι δὲ πρὸς τρυφὴν ἐκ τῶν ἄλλων πτηνῶν περισπούδαστοι εἶναι μᾶλ-λον· Turdi genus avicularum, quae prae caeteris ad delicias maxime exquiruntur. Horatius lib. 1. Epist. 15.

But, contrary to the opinion of the Hebrews, those who measure everything by the delights of the palate give first place to the fat thrush. The Scholiast of Aristophanes on the Peace: Αἱ κίχλαι εἶδος στρουθῶν, δοκοῦσι δὲ πρὸς τρυφὴν ἐκ τῶν ἄλλων πτηνῶν περισπούδαστοι εἶναι μᾶλλον· [Hai kichlai eidos strouthōn, dokousi de pros tryphēn ek tōn allōn ptēnōn perispoudastoi einai mallon] Thrushes are a kind of small bird which are sought out above others for delicacies. Horace, book 1, Epist. 15:


Ajebat, si qui comedunt bona, cum sit obeso col. 95
Nil melius turdo. — — — —

He used to say that those who devour their goods are right, since nothing is better than a fat col. 95 thrush. — — — —


Martialis Xenio 92.

Martial, Xenium 92:


Inter aves turdus, si quis me judice certet,
Inter quadrupedes gloria prima lepus.

Among birds the thrush, if anyone contends with me as judge, among quadrupeds the hare holds the first glory.


Et alibi,

And elsewhere:


Texta rosis fortasse tibi, vel divite nardo,
At mihi de turdis facta corona placet.

Perhaps you like a crown woven of roses or rich nard, but I like a crown made of thrushes.


Et rursus,

And again:


Illic coronam pinguibus gravem turdis.

There a crown heavy with fat thrushes.


Persius Satyra 6.

Persius, Satire 6:


Nec tenuem solers turdorum nosse salivam.

Nor skilled to know the delicate savour of thrushes.


Id est, non liguritor, et λίχνος, qui probe calleat, quo sapore sint turdi. Itaque olim Athenis, cum disciplina erat adstrictior, junioribus a) ὀψοφαγεῖν, II, 654 οὐδὲ κιχλίζειν ἐξῆν, pisces edere, neque turdos licebat, id est, delicate vesci. Et Pompejus aeger a Lucullo turdum peti noluit, quamvis jubente medico, hoc celebri dicto usus, Οὐκοῦν, εἰ μὴ Λούκουλλος ἐτρύφα, Πομπήϊος οὐκ ἂν ἔζησεν; An igitur absque Luculli luxu Pompejus non viveret? Quod Plutarcho ita placuit, ut id referret quater minimum, nempe in Lucullo, et in Pompejo, et in Apophthegmatis, et in libro An seni gerenda sit respublica?

That is, not a gourmand, a λίχνος [lichnos], who knows well what flavour thrushes have. So formerly at Athens, when discipline was stricter, the young a) were not permitted ὀψοφαγεῖν [opsophagein], II, 654 οὐδὲ κιχλίζειν [oude kichlizein], to eat fish, nor thrushes, that is, to dine delicately. And Pompey, when ill, refused to have a thrush sought from Lucullus, although the physician ordered it, using this famous saying: Οὐκοῦν, εἰ μὴ Λούκουλλος ἐτρύφα, Πομπήϊος οὐκ ἂν ἔζησεν; [Oukoun, ei mē Loukoullos etrypha, Pompēios ouk an ezēsen?] Would Pompey then not live without the luxury of Lucullus? This so pleased Plutarch that he related it at least four times: in the Lucullus, in the Pompey, in the Apophthegmata, and in the book Whether an old man should engage in public affairs.


Superest phasianus, qui olim videtur fuisse deliciarum ultimus finis. Proinde Athenaei lib. 14. Ptolemaeus Physcon, quamvis in Aegypto phasianos magno numero aleret, οὐδὲ φασιανικοῦ ὄρνιθός ποτε γεύσασθαι ὡμολόγησεν, ἀλλ᾽ ὥσπερ τι κειμήλιον ἀνακείμενον εἶχε τοὺς δὲ τοὺς ὄρνιθας, se phasianum nunquam gustasse professus est, sed has aves habuit ut repositum thesaurum. Sic apud Capitolinum Pertinax fasianum (nam per f ibi scribitur) nunquam privato convivio comedit, aut alicui misit. Apud Lampridium Alexander Severus nonnisi Calendis Ianuariis, et Hilariis matris Deum, et ludis Apollinaribus, et Iovis epulo, et Saturnalibus, et hujusmodi festis diebus fasianum mensis adhibebat. Apud Vopiscum Tacitus imperator Fasianam avem nonnisi suo et suorum natali, et diebus festivissimis posuit. Et, Ammiano teste lib. 2. Iulianus in convivio Caesaris phasianum exigi vetuit, et inferri. Nempe avi, per se eximiae, raritas pretium addebat. Petronius in Satyrico,

There remains the pheasant, which in former times seems to have been the very summit of delicacies. Thus, according to Athenaeus, book 14, Ptolemy Physcon, although he kept pheasants in great numbers in Egypt, οὐδὲ φασιανικοῦ ὄρνιθός ποτε γεύσασθαι ὡμολόγησεν, ἀλλ᾽ ὥσπερ τι κειμήλιον ἀνακείμενον εἶχε τοὺς δὲ τοὺς ὄρνιθας [oude phasianikou ornithos pote geusasthai hōmologēsen, all᾽ hōsper ti keimēlion anakeimenon eiche tous de tous ornithas], declared that he had never tasted a pheasant, but kept these birds as a stored-up treasure. So in Capitolinus Pertinax never ate a pheasant (fasianus, for there it is written with f) at a private banquet, nor sent one to anyone. In Lampridius, Alexander Severus served pheasant at his table only on the Kalends of January, at the Hilaria of the Mother of the Gods, at the Apollinarian games, at the feast of Jupiter, at the Saturnalia, and on festival days of that kind. In Vopiscus, the emperor Tacitus served the pheasant bird only on his own birthday and those of his family, and on the most festive days. And, as Ammianus attests in book 2, Julian forbade a pheasant to be demanded or brought in at the banquet of the Caesar. Evidently rarity added value to a bird that was excellent in itself. Petronius in the Satyricon:


Ales Phasiacis petita Colchis,
Atque Afrae volucres placent palato,
Quod non sunt faciles. — — —

The bird sought from Phasian Colchis,
And African fowl please the palate,
Because they are not easy to get. — — —


Ales Phasiacis petita Colchis, id est, phasianus, ex Phaside petitus, Colchidis amne. Inde enim afferebatur, quod ipsum nomen indicat. Agatharchides de Phaside apud Athenaeum libro nono, Πλῆθος δὲ ὀρνίθων τῶν καλουμένων φα-σιανῶν φοιτᾷ τροφῆς χάριν πρὸς τὰς ἐμβολὰς τῶν στομάτων· Avium, quas phasianos vocant, magna copia cibi causa ad fluminis ostia se confert. Petronius idem alibi,

The bird sought from Phasian Colchis, that is, the pheasant, fetched from the Phasis, a river of Colchis. For it was brought from there, as the name itself shows. Agatharchides on the Phasis, in Athenaeus, book 9: Πλῆθος δὲ ὀρνίθων τῶν καλουμένων φασιανῶν φοιτᾷ τροφῆς χάριν πρὸς τὰς ἐμβολὰς τῶν στομάτων [Plēthos de ornithōn tōn kaloumenōn phasianōn phoita trophēs charin pros tas embolas tōn stomatōn]; A great multitude of the birds they call pheasants resorts to the mouths of the river for the sake of food. Petronius likewise elsewhere:


— — — — Iam Phasidis unda
Orbata est avibus. — — — —

— — — — Now the Phasis' wave
Is bereft of its birds. — — — —


Martialis in Xeniis,

Martial in the Xenia:


Argiva primum sum transportata carina:
Ante mihi notum nil nisi Phasis erat.

I was first carried over in the Argive keel:
Before that nothing was known to me but the Phasis.


Statius in Psittaco Melioris lib. 2. Sylvarum,

Statius in The Parrot of Melior, book 2 of the Silvae:


Quem non gemmata volucris Iunonia cauda Vinceret aspectu, gelidi non Phasidis ales. II, 655 Clemens in Paedagogo lib. 2. cap. 1. Ὄρνεις ἐπὶ τούτοις συνωνοῦνται ἀπὸ Φάσιδος· Praeterea volucres ex Phaside coëmunt. Apollonius apud Philostratum lib. 8. cap. 3. Οὐ κρίνω τοὺς τρυφῶντας ὑπὲρ τοῦ φοινικέου ὄρνιθος, οὐδ' ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἐκ Φάσιδος, ἢ Παιόνων· In judicium eos non voco, qui deliciis dediti sunt, propter avem puniceam (phoenicopterum) nec propter avem ex Phaside, aut Paeonibus, id est, phasianum, aut gruem. Iornandes, De rebus Geticis cap. 21. Ad Phasim fluvium, a quo Phasides aves exortae, in toto mundo epulis potentum exuberant. Eustathius in Dionysium, Οἱ φασιανοὶ δὲ τὸ ὄρνεον ἐκεῖθεν παρονομα-σθῆναι δοκοῦσιν ὡς αὐτόθι πλεονάσαντες· Phasiani, avis species, videntur inde col. 96 nomen habuisse, ut qui ibi abundaverint. Quae, utut protrita, Talmudicos tamen latuerunt, et Chaldaeos paraphrastas. Neque enim pro phasianis habuissent aves, quas auster advexerat in castra Israelitarum, si scivissent, phasianos ex septentrione afferri. Phasianos quidem, fateor, non peti ex sola Colchide. Nam ad Ptolemaeum, Aegypti regem, ἐκ Μηδείας μετεπέμποντο, ex Media accersebantur, ut testatur Athenaeus ubi supra. Et in provincia Ergimul Paulus Venetus lib. 1. cap. 62. maximos describit fasianos, caudas habentes longitudinis decem palmorum, aut octo. Sed ut Colchis et Media, ita etiam Ergimul ad septentriones est obversa. Est enim Tartariae pars. Videtur esse Arabum جرمق giormok, quia nomen accedit, et utrobique est muscus. Vide Geographum Nubiensem part. 9. Clim. 3. Phasianus alio nomine τατύρας tatyras appellatur. Ita testantur Hesychius et Athenaeus libro nono post Pamphilum Alexandrinum in Glossis, et Epaenetum in Opsartytico. Quod ideo duxi notandum, quia huc alludit Persicum phasiani nomen تذرو tazeru, et Arabicum تدرج tadrug.

Whom neither the Junonian bird with jewelled tail Could surpass in beauty, nor the bird of the icy Phasis. II, 655 Clement in the Paedagogus, book 2, ch. 1: Ὄρνεις ἐπὶ τούτοις συνωνοῦνται ἀπὸ Φάσιδος [Orneis epi toutois synōnountai apo Phasidos]; Besides, they buy up birds from the Phasis. Apollonius in Philostratus, book 8, ch. 3: Οὐ κρίνω τοὺς τρυφῶντας ὑπὲρ τοῦ φοινικέου ὄρνιθος, οὐδ' ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἐκ Φάσιδος, ἢ Παιόνων [Ou krinō tous tryphōntas hyper tou phoinikeou ornithos, oud' hyper tou ek Phasidos, ē Paionōn]; I do not bring to judgement those given to luxury on account of the crimson bird (the flamingo), nor on account of the bird from the Phasis or from the Paeonians, that is, the pheasant or the crane. Jordanes, On the Affairs of the Goths, ch. 21: To the river Phasis, from which the Phasian birds have come forth that abound throughout the whole world at the banquets of the powerful. Eustathius on Dionysius: Οἱ φασιανοὶ δὲ τὸ ὄρνεον ἐκεῖθεν παρονομασθῆναι δοκοῦσιν ὡς αὐτόθι πλεονάσαντες [Hoi phasianoi de to orneon ekeithen paronomasthēnai dokousin hōs autothi pleonasantes]; The pheasants, a species of bird, seem to have had their col. 96 name from there, as having abounded in that place. These things, however commonplace, nevertheless escaped the Talmudists and the Chaldee paraphrasts. For they would not have taken for pheasants the birds that the south wind had brought into the camp of the Israelites, had they known that pheasants are brought from the north. I admit, indeed, that pheasants are not sought from Colchis alone. For to Ptolemy, king of Egypt, ἐκ Μηδείας μετεπέμποντο [ek Mēdeias metepempontō], they were fetched from Media, as Athenaeus testifies in the place cited above. And in the province of Ergimul, Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)] Venetus [=Marco Polo], book 1, ch. 62, describes very large pheasants, having tails ten or eight palms long. But like Colchis and Media, Ergimul too faces the north, for it is part of Tartary. It seems to be the جرمق [jrmq] giormok of the Arabs, because the name is close and in both places there is musk. See the Nubian Geographer, section 9, Clim. [=climate (section) of al-Idrīsī's geography, in the Latin Geographia Nubiensis] 3. The pheasant is called by another name τατύρας [tatyras] tatyras. So testify Hesychius, and Athenaeus in book 9, following Pamphilus of Alexandria in his Glossary and Epaenetus in his Opsartyticus. I have thought this worth noting because the Persian name of the pheasant, تذرو [tadhrū] tazeru, and the Arabic تدرج [tadruj] tadrug, allude to it.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 649 Since the other name of quails, سماني [sumānā], has plainly been given them from their fatness, as Bochart presently notes, ALB. Schultens [=Albert Schultens, Liber Jobi (1737)], in Originib. Hebr. book 1, ch. 3, §39, p. 231, believes that these birds were also called שלו, سلوي [salwā], from that same quality; there he shows that the root سلي [s-l-y], שלה, also contains the notion of rich and fat. — HIOB Ludolf [=Hiob Ludolf, Historia Aethiopica (1681) and its Commentarius (1691)] (in Commentar. ad Histor. Aethiop. on book 1, ch. 13, no. 96, p. 172, and in Adpend. ad Histor. Aethiop.), having come upon a passage of Porphyry, περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψυχῶν [peri apochēs empsychōn] book 1, §2, where he says that an army in Africa suffering from famine was saved by the arrival of locusts, contends that the שלוים are locusts. For it is well known that locusts are a very common food in almost the whole of the East. The Jews living in Arabia today also think that the שלוים are locusts, and Niebuhr [=Carsten Niebuhr, Beschreibung von Arabien (1772)] himself agrees with them, Beschreib. von Arab. p. 172. But the strongest objection is that in the Arabic, Syriac and Chaldee dialects this word without any doubt means quails. Nor is שלו found among the names of locusts in Lev 11:22. Hasselquist [=Fredrik Hasselquist, Iter Palaestinum (1757)] p. 255; Niebuhr Beschreib. von Arab. p. 176; Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)] Descriptt. Animal. p. 16), was formerly the conjecture of OL. RUDBECK (Ichthyol. Bibl. Specim. I.), which I. D. Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer] elaborated further in his Commentat. super lege Mosaica Deut 22:6–7. §9, and in the Addition to §9, in Syntagm. Commentatt. vol. 2, p. 104 and 115; afterwards, however, he himself rejected it, and rightly so, since in the Red Sea there is no such abundance of flying fish that many thousands of people could be fed with them daily. Nor can these fish rise more than three or four feet above the sea. In addition, flying fish are not an ordinary food; rather, dried, they serve as a medicine for strengthening the stomach. Cf. Niebuhr p. 177. For other points see Faber and Oedmann, loc. cit. — The Seleucid birds [Turdus Seleucis Forsskål vol. 6 a, p. 5, no. 16, Arabic سمرمر [samarmar], Turdus roseus Linnaeus 2, p. 819, no. 15, 13th ed.; Oedmann 2, ch. 6, p. 103], whose coming (as Pliny reports, Hist. Nat. 10, ch. 26, sect. 39) the inhabitants of Mount Casius obtain by prayer from Jupiter when locusts are ravaging their crops; it has not been discovered where they come from or where they go, and they are never seen except when their protection is needed, were suspected by II, 650 HERMANN VON DER HARDT to be the same as the שלוים; RATHLEF also fought for this opinion in his Append. Acridotheol., but with futile arguments, which I. D. Michaelis long ago refuted in the commentary cited, p. 104 ff. — There is a bird, common in Syria, Arabia and Egypt, of the size of a partridge or turtle-dove, of the grouse family, with hard and dry flesh, which the Arabs, from the call it utters, call قَطًّا [qaṭṭan] Katta (as Hasselquist and Russell [=Alexander Russell, The Natural History of Aleppo (1756)] write it) (see Golius's [=Jacobus Golius, Lexicon Arabico-Latinum (1653)] Lexic. p. 1934, where a description of this bird is also found); in Linnaeus it is Tetrao supra varius; rectricibus duabus intermediis duplo longioribus subulatis, see Syst. Nat. vol. 1, part 2, p. 754, no. 11, under the heading Alchata, where the synonyms and those who have treated of it are also listed. That this bird is the שלו of the Hebrews is so certain to Hasselquist that in his Travels p. 333, after describing it fairly accurately under the name Tetrao Israelitarum, he uses these words: this, if any, is the bird taken as food by the Israelites in the desert, since it is common in the places through which they wandered. But this very point holds also of the quail, and what is read of the שלוים in Moses does not fit any other bird, as we shall see in the following Chapter. — I. E. Faber, ad Harmar. 2, p. 442, thinks the Arabs' Katta is the same as the quail, though these birds are carefully distinguished by all who have written on the natural history of birds.


(2) Rosenmüller, II, 650 Cum Aethiopico vocabulo videtur convenire Arabum فُرْفُر et فُرْفُور quod GOLIUS in Lexico p. 1773. Firuzabadio auctore dicit avis alicujus nomen esse.

R2 Rosenmüller, II, 650 The Arabs' فُرْفُر [furfur] and فُرْفُور [furfūr] seem to agree with the Ethiopic word; Golius, in his Lexicon p. 1773, on the authority of Firuzabadi, says it is the name of some bird.


(3) Rosenmüller, II, 651 Aristotelis et Athenaei ὀρτυγομήτρα est Rallus alis rufo-ferrugineis Linn., sive Crex (Syst. T. I. P. II. p. 711.), Gallice, Roi de cailles, German. Wiesenschnar- re, s. Wachtelkönig. Ea avis Alexandriae hodie سلوى vocatur, teste Niebuhrio, p. 176. Descr. Arab. Sed Graecos interpp. sub ὀρτυγομήτραις potius praegrandes cotur- nices intellexisse censeo, quod Bocharto probabile est, cujus quae sequuntur legas.

R3 Rosenmüller, II, 651 The ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra] of Aristotle and Athenaeus is the Rallus alis rufo-ferrugineis of Linnaeus, or Crex (Syst. vol. 1, part 2, p. 711), in French Roi de cailles, in German Wiesenschnarre or Wachtelkönig. At Alexandria this bird is today called سلوى [salwā], according to Niebuhr, p. 176, Descr. Arab. But I think that the Greek translators understood by ὀρτυγομήτραις [ortygomētrais] rather very large quails, which Bochart considers probable; read what follows from him.

Part 2, Book 1, chapter 15: Five questions about the quails of Moses
------------------------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/selav-quaestiones.html

II, 656 col. 96 CAP. XV.

II, 656 col. 96 CHAPTER XV.


Solvuntur quinque quaestiones de Mosis Coturnicibus. I. Quoties coturnices Israelitis Deus dederit? II. An salubris sit cibus? III. Hae coturnices unde venerint? IV. Quanta copia venerint? V. Qualis fuerit poena coturnices comedentium?

Five questions about the quails of Moses are resolved. I. How many times did God give quails to the Israelites? II. Are they wholesome food? III. From where did these quails come? IV. In what quantity did they come? V. What was the punishment of those who ate the quails?


De Mosis coturnicibus quinque potissimum quaeruntur. 1. Quoties Israelitis col. 97 eas immiserit Deus? 2. An salubris fuerit cibus? 3. Unde venerint? 4. Quanta copia? 5. Cur illarum esu Israelitae Deum in se concitaverint?

Concerning the quails of Moses five questions above all are asked. 1. How many times did God send them to the Israelites? col. 97 2. Were they wholesome food? 3. From where did they come? 4. In what quantity? 5. Why did the Israelites provoke God against themselves by eating them?


I. Et ad primam quaestionem, re non satis explorata, multi respondent, semel tantum fuisse immissas. Tamen repetitum fuisse hoc miraculum, multa non suadent solum, sed et plane persuadent. Nam Exod. XVI, 13. una cum Manna dantur coturnices in deserto Sin paullo post exitum ex Aegypto die decima quinta secundi mensis, antequam venissent in montem Sinai, ut apparet ex initio capitis. Sed Num. XI, 6. cum populus obmurmurasset, eo quod praeter Manna nihil viderent, ibidem versu trigesimo primo Deus illis coturnices largitur in Kibroth-thaava, quo demum venerunt post excessum e deserto Sinai, Num. XXXIII, 16. Idque tertia die, Num. X, 33. E Sinai autem discesserant anno secundo, die vigesima secundi mensis, Num. X, 11. Ut uno anno serius priore contigisse necesse sit hoc miraculum. Praeterea priores coturnices solum in diem, posteriores in totum mensem a Deo indultae fuerunt. Proinde illae solum castra tegebant; hae etiam extra castra erant, hinc et inde dispersae ad iter unius diei. Et harum, non illarum, esu Deus graviter irritatus populum magna plaga percussit. Itaque utramque historiam refert Iosephus diversis locis; illam capite primo, hanc capite decimo tertio libri tertii Antiquitatum. Quomodo etiam Hieronymus Epist. CXXVII. ad Fabiolam, mansionibus X et XIII. Quod objiciunt, nihil esse causae, cur Deus his potius, quam illis fuerit infensus, refelluntur in fine capitis. Iam, si quaeras, quomodo Moses Num. XI, 21. dubitaverit, an possent reperiri carnes, quae sufficerent tot millibus, si jam aliud simile miraculum viderat, Exod. XVI, 13. Respondeo, prius miraculum posteriori non fuisse omni ex parte simile. Nam in priori, quod jam observavimus, hunc populum Deus carnibus nonnisi in unum diem paverat. At hic id ipsum se facturum pollicetur in mensem integrum, quod Mosi visum est multo majus. Itaque hoc ipsum Deo objicit. Sexcenties mille peditum, inquit, populus iste est, in cujus medio ego sum: et tu dicis, te carnem eis daturum per mensem integrum. II, 657 Praeterea quis nescit, Mosem, cum in Raphidim aquas e rupe percussa elicuisset, Exod. XVII, 1. etc. dubitasse tamen, cum jussus est idem miraculum repetere in deserto Sin et Kades, Num. X, 1. etc. Ne quis miretur, quod hoc ipsum illi acciderit, cum Deus carnes populo promisit, quas alibi jam ante dederat.

I. To the first question many, without having examined the matter sufficiently, answer that they were sent only once. Yet many things not only suggest but plainly prove that this miracle was repeated. For in Exod 16:13 quails are given together with the manna in the desert of Sin, shortly after the exodus from Egypt, on the fifteenth day of the second month, before they had come to Mount Sinai, as is clear from the beginning of the chapter. But in Num 11:6, when the people had murmured because they saw nothing but manna, God, in verse 31 of the same chapter, grants them quails at Kibroth-thaava, where they finally arrived after leaving the desert of Sinai, Num 33:16, and that on the third day, Num 10:33. They had departed from Sinai, moreover, in the second year, on the twentieth day of the second month, Num 10:11. So this miracle must have happened a year later than the former. Furthermore, the first quails were granted by God for only one day, the later ones for a whole month. Accordingly the former covered only the camp; the latter were also outside the camp, scattered on this side and that for a day's journey. And it was at the eating of these, not of the former, that God, gravely angered, struck the people with a great plague. Therefore Josephus relates the two stories in different places: the former in chapter 1, the latter in chapter 13 of book 3 of the Antiquities. So also Jerome, Epistle 127 to Fabiola, at stations 10 and 13. Their objection, that there is no reason why God should have been angry at these rather than at the former, is refuted at the end of the chapter. Now, if you ask how Moses in Num 11:21 could doubt whether flesh could be found sufficient for so many thousands, if he had already seen a similar miracle, Exod 16:13, I answer that the earlier miracle was not in every respect like the later. For in the earlier one, as we have already observed, God had fed this people with flesh for only one day. But here he promises to do the same for a whole month, which seemed to Moses far greater. Therefore he raises this very point against God: The people, he says, among whom I am, are six hundred thousand footmen; and you say that you will give them flesh for a whole month. II, 657 Besides, who does not know that Moses, although at Raphidim he had drawn water from the struck rock, Exod 17:1 etc., nevertheless doubted when he was ordered to repeat the same miracle in the desert of Sin and at Kades, Num 10:1 etc.? So let no one be surprised that the same happened to him when God promised the people flesh which he had already given before elsewhere.


II. Ad secundam quaestionem, coturnices elleboro, aut, quod idem est, veratro vesci observant. Aristoteles libri primi capite quinto De plantis, Ὁ ἐλ-λέβορος ἀνθρώποις μὲν δηλητήριον, τροφὴ δὲ τοῖς ὄρτυξι· Hominibus quidem elleborus venenum est, sed coturnicibus alimentum. Galenus ad Pisonem, Ὁ ἐλ-λέβορος τῶν ὀρτυγίων ἐστὶ τροφή· Elleborus coturnicum est cibus. Et libri secundi De aliment. cap. 6. Καὶ μὲν τὸν ἐλλέβορον οἱ ὄρτυγες, καὶ οἱ ψᾶρες τὸ κώ-νειον ἐσθίοντες οὐδὲν βλάπτονται· Coturnices ellebori, ut sturni cicutae esu nihil quidquam laeduntur. Et libri tertii De temperam. cap. 4. Τοῖς μὲν ὄρτυξιν ἐλλέ-βορος τροφὴ, τοῖς δὲ ἀνθρώποις φάρμακον· Coturnicibus quidem elleborus cibus est, hominibus autem venenum. Ita etiam Alexander Aphrodisaeus libro primo Problematum in Praefatione, Basilius, Ambrosius et Eustathius in Hexaëmeron. Eodem haec Lucretii pertinent libri quarti versu 641.

II. On the second question, writers observe that quails feed on hellebore, or, what is the same, veratrum. Aristotle, On Plants, book 1, chapter 5: Ὁ ἐλλέβορος ἀνθρώποις μὲν δηλητήριον, τροφὴ δὲ τοῖς ὄρτυξι· [Ho elleboros anthrōpois men dēlētērion, trophē de tois ortyxi]; Hellebore is poison to men, but food to quails. Galen, to Piso: Ὁ ἐλλέβορος τῶν ὀρτυγίων ἐστὶ τροφή· [Ho elleboros tōn ortygiōn esti trophē]; Hellebore is the food of quails. And On Foods, book 2, ch. 6: Καὶ μὲν τὸν ἐλλέβορον οἱ ὄρτυγες, καὶ οἱ ψᾶρες τὸ κώνειον ἐσθίοντες οὐδὲν βλάπτονται· [Kai men ton elleboron hoi ortyges, kai hoi psares to kōneion esthiontes ouden blaptontai]; Quails are not harmed at all by eating hellebore, nor starlings by eating hemlock. And On Temperaments, book 3, ch. 4: Τοῖς μὲν ὄρτυξιν ἐλλέβορος τροφὴ, τοῖς δὲ ἀνθρώποις φάρμακον· [Tois men ortyxin elleboros trophē, tois de anthrōpois pharmakon]; To quails hellebore is food, but to men poison. So also Alexander of Aphrodisias in the Preface to book 1 of the Problems, and Basil, Ambrose and Eustathius on the Hexaemeron. To the same point belong these lines of Lucretius, book 4, verse 641:


Praeterea nobis veratrum est acre venenum,
At capreis adipes et coturnicibus auget.

Moreover, veratrum is a sharp poison to us, but it fattens goats and quails.


Sed aliter Sextus Empiricus libro primo, Τὸ γοῦν κώνειον πιαίνει τοὺς ὄρτυγας. Cicuta coturnices pinguefacit. Quod alii de sturno referunt. Et Arabes rursus aliter. Alkazuinius in Coturnice, يغتدي بالبيش والبيش col. 98 هو سم قاتل Alitur napello, quod est venenum lethiferum. Avicenna capite بيش seu De napello, والسماني يغتدي به ولا يموت منه Eo aluntur coturnices, neque ideo moriuntur. Quod ipsum est in Alcamus. Napellus autem neque est elleborus, neque cicuta, sed aconitum λυκο-κτόνον· utut sit, apud omnes in confesso est, coturnices vesci venenis. Atque eas ob id ipsum ut insalubres non pauci vetant. Plinius lib. 10. cap. 23. Coturnicibus veneni semen gratissimus cibus: quam ob causam eos damnavere mensis. Et ex eo Solinus, Cibos gratissimos habent semina venenorum: quam ob causam eos damnavere prudentium mensae. Didymus in Geoponicis lib. 14. Οἱ ὄρτυγες, ἐλ-λέβορον ἐπινεμόμενοι, τοὺς ἐσθίοντας εἰς κίνδυνον ἐμβάλλουσι, κατατεινομένους, καὶ ἰλιγγιῶντας· Coturnices, quae elleboro pascuntur, eos, a quibus comestae fuerint, in tantum discrimen agunt, ut distendantur convellanturque, ceu correpti vertigine (1). Quod tamen refert Avicenna non tam ad esum ellebori, quam II, 658 ad pravam qualitatem, illis insitam. Verba sunt libro secundo Canonis, capite سماني seu De coturnice, اكل لحمه يخاف منه التمدد والتشنج لا لانه ياكل الخربق فقط بل لان في جوهره هذه القوة واظن ان اغتداه بالخربق هو والمشاكلة المزاج Ex esu carnis ejus timetur tetanus et spasmus, non solum quia comedit elleborum, sed et quia ejus substantiae inest haec virtus: quin eam puto elleboro ideo ali, quia temperamento ejus congruit hoc alimentum. Ex Plinio et Solino additur, comitialem propter morbum despui suetum, quem solae animalium timeant praeter hominem. Rasis tamen multo aliter in libro ad Al-mansorem capite De carnibus volatilium, qui decimus est tractatus tertii: Starnae (perdicis) caro omni carne avium levior invenitur, atqui his, qui subtili volunt custodiri regimine, convenientior. Post istam autem coturnicis caro secunda in bonitate existit. Et paullo post, Caro itidem pullorum post ipsam ponitur. Coturnicis tamen caro melioris est generativa sanguinis, et spermatis augmentativa. Et Ibnozohar in libro De alimentis capite De coturnicibus, وامزاجها فكانها وسط بين مزاج الدجاج والحجل وهي الي مزاج الدجاج اميل وهي الطف جوهرا واميل الي حر قليلا وهي جيدة الكيموص طيبة الطعم نافعه للاصحا والناقهين ولحومها تفتت الحصا وتدر البول Medium fere temperamentum habet inter gallinam et perdicem, ita tamen, ut ad gallinae temperamentum magis accedat. Sed substantia subtilior est, et ad calidum paullo magis inclinat. Est et boni chymi et egregii saporis, sanis et valentibus utilis. Et carnes ejus calculum frangunt atque urinam provocant. Et superiore saeculo Nicolaus Massa in Epistolis Medicinalibus apud Gesnerum: Coturnices, col. 99 id est, qualeae, ejusdem temperamenti sunt, cujus perdices, sed siccioris. Probe nutriunt. Et Aloysius Mundella, Aristoteles de coturnicibus et perdicibus in eodem capite tradit, quasi utraeque natura non multum inter se differant. Quamobrem cum ejusdem generis esse videantur, manifestum relinquitur, coturnicem, non ita, ut vulgo fertur, pravi succi esse, neque a mensis ablegandam, nisi pauperum fortasse, ut qui minoris impensae cibis vesci consueverint. Neque etiam quod morbo comitiali corripiatur, quodque veneno pascatur, ab hujus esu abstinendum esse censuerim. Nonnulla enim novimus animalia, quae, licet venenis quandoque nutriantur, bonum tamen et innocuum succum generant. Exempli gratia Sturni cicuta, ut idemmet Galenus autor est, aluntur, quibus quis non impune vescitur? II, 659 triantur, boni tamen succi sunt, quemadmodum sturni, qui cicuta vescuntur. Quod si elleboro vescitur coturnix, quod nobis nondum constat, eo cibo juvari eam probabilius est, quam laedi. Quare coturnicis nutrimentum, quod non ingrati etiam saporis sit, laudandum potius quam damnandum censeo. Nam et Averroes mirifice coturnicum carnem laudat, tanquam bonum generantem succum. Et licet veneno interdum vescantur, et interdum comitiali morbo vexentur, non tamen semper, nec omnes existimo, sed illas fortasse, quae in aviariis captae reservantur. Nam et hac ratione galli gallinacei, quod nonnulli eorum quandoque comitiali morbo corripiantur, improbandi essent. Id quoque non praetermiserim, Dominum Deum nostrum Israelis populum, quem ardentissime diligebat, dum per deserta illa transiret loca, ad satietatem usque coturnicibus non pasturum fuisse, nisi probati illae fuissent alimenti et salutaris. Haec, et plura Mundella, quae lector ibi videat. Quod si altius ascendere libet, constabit, fabularum architectos coturnicem magni fecisse, ex eo quod Herculem fingunt, a Typhone interemptum, nidore coturnicis, illi ab Iolao admotae, in vitam fuisse revocatum, atque inde esse, quod Phoenices illi coturnices immolabant. Athenaeus libro nono, Εὔδο-ξος δὲ ὁ Κνίδιος ἐν πρώτῳ γῆς περιόδου τοὺς Φοίνικας λέγει θύειν τῷ Ἡρακλεῖ ὄρ-τυγας, διὰ τὸ τὸν Ἡρακλέα, τὸν Ἀστερίας καὶ Διὸς, πορευόμενον εἰς Λιβύην, ἀναιρεθῆναι μὲν ὑπὸ Τυφῶνος. Ἰολάου δ᾽ αὐτῷ προσενέγκαντος ὄρτυγα, καὶ προσαγάγοντος, ὀσφρανθέντα ἀναβιῶναι. Quod dedit locum proverbio, apud Graecos recepto,

But Sextus Empiricus, book 1, says otherwise: Τὸ γοῦν κώνειον πιαίνει τοὺς ὄρτυγας [to goun kōneion piainei tous ortygas]. Hemlock fattens quails. Others report this of the starling. And the Arabs, again, say otherwise. Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt], under The Quail: يغتدي بالبيش والبيش [yaghtadī bi-l-bīsh wa-l-bīsh] col. 98 هو سم قاتل [huwa samm qātil] It feeds on napellus, which is a deadly poison. Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)], in the chapter بيش [bīsh], that is On napellus: والسماني يغتدي به ولا يموت منه [wa-l-summānā yaghtadī bihi wa-lā yamūtu minhu] Quails feed on it, and yet do not die from it. The same is in Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]. Napellus, however, is neither hellebore nor hemlock, but aconite, λυκοκτόνον [lykoktonon]. However that may be, all agree that quails feed on poisons. And for that very reason not a few forbid them as unwholesome. Pliny, book 10, ch. 23: To quails the seed of poison is the most welcome food; for which reason they have banished them from the table. And following him Solinus: Their most welcome food is the seeds of poisonous plants; for which reason the tables of the prudent have banished them. Didymus in the Geoponica, book 14: Οἱ ὄρτυγες, ἐλλέβορον ἐπινεμόμενοι, τοὺς ἐσθίοντας εἰς κίνδυνον ἐμβάλλουσι, κατατεινομένους, καὶ ἰλιγγιῶντας· [Hoi ortyges, elleboron epinemomenoi, tous esthiontas eis kindynon emballousi, katateinomenous, kai ilingiōntas] Quails that feed on hellebore bring those who eat them into such danger that they are distended and convulsed, as if seized by vertigo R1. Avicenna, however, attributes this not so much to their eating hellebore as II, 658 to a bad quality inherent in them. His words are in book 2 of the Canon, in the chapter سماني [summānī], that is On the quail: اكل لحمه يخاف منه التمدد والتشنج لا لانه ياكل الخربق فقط بل لان في جوهره هذه القوة واظن ان اغتداه بالخربق هو والمشاكلة المزاج [akl laḥmihi yukhāfu minhu al-tamaddud wa-l-tashannuj lā li-annahu yaʾkulu al-kharbaq faqaṭ bal li-anna fī jawharihi hādhihi al-quwwa wa-aẓunnu anna ightidāʾahu bi-l-kharbaq huwa wa-l-mushākala al-mizāj] From eating its flesh tetanus and spasm are to be feared, not only because it eats hellebore, but also because this property is inherent in its substance; indeed I think it feeds on hellebore precisely because this food suits its temperament. From Pliny and Solinus it is added that it is customary to spit at it on account of the falling sickness, which alone of animals, apart from man, they fear. Rasis, however, says something very different in his book to Almansor, in the chapter On the flesh of birds, which is the tenth of the third treatise: The flesh of the starna (the partridge) is found to be lighter than the flesh of any other bird, and so more suitable for those who wish to be kept on a delicate regimen. After it the flesh of the quail stands second in goodness. And a little later: The flesh of chickens likewise is placed after it. The flesh of the quail, however, is more productive of good blood, and increases semen. And Ibnozohar, in the book On Foods, chapter On quails: وامزاجها فكانها وسط بين مزاج الدجاج والحجل وهي الي مزاج الدجاج اميل وهي الطف جوهرا واميل الي حر قليلا وهي جيدة الكيموص طيبة الطعم نافعه للاصحا والناقهين ولحومها تفتت الحصا وتدر البول [wa-amzājuhā fa-ka-annahā wasaṭ bayna mizāj al-dajāj wa-l-ḥajal wa-hiya ilā mizāj al-dajāj amyal wa-hiya alṭaf jawharan wa-amyal ilā ḥarr qalīlan wa-hiya jayyidat al-kaymūs ṭayyibat al-ṭaʿm nāfiʿa li-l-aṣiḥḥāʾ wa-l-nāqihīn wa-luḥūmuhā tufattitu al-ḥaṣā wa-tudirru al-bawl] It has a temperament roughly midway between the hen and the partridge, yet so that it comes closer to the temperament of the hen. But its substance is finer, and inclines a little more to the hot. It also yields good chyme and has an excellent flavour, and is beneficial to the healthy and strong. And its flesh breaks up the stone and promotes urine. And in the last century Nicolaus Massa [=Niccolò Massa, physician of Venice (d. 1569), Epistolae medicinales], in his Medical Letters, cited by Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium]: Quails, col. 99 that is, qualeae, are of the same temperament as partridges, but drier. They nourish well. And Aloysius Mundella [=Luigi Mondella, physician of Brescia (16th c.), Epistolae medicinales]: Aristotle treats of quails and partridges in the same chapter, as if the two did not differ much in nature. Therefore, since they seem to be of the same kind, it remains clear that the quail is not, as is commonly said, of bad juice, nor to be banished from the table, except perhaps that of the poor, who are accustomed to eat cheaper foods. Nor would I judge that one should abstain from eating it because it is seized by the falling sickness, or because it feeds on poison. For we know some animals which, although they are sometimes nourished by poisons, nevertheless produce good and harmless juice. For example, starlings feed on hemlock, as the same Galen attests; who does not eat them without harm? II, 659 nourished, are nevertheless of good juice, like starlings, which feed on hemlock. And if the quail does feed on hellebore, which is not yet established for us, it is more probable that it is helped by that food than harmed. Therefore I judge that the nourishment of the quail, which is also of no unpleasant flavour, is to be praised rather than condemned. For Averroes too praises the flesh of quails wonderfully, as producing good juice. And although they sometimes feed on poison, and are sometimes afflicted with the falling sickness, I think this is not always so, nor true of all, but perhaps of those that are caught and kept in aviaries. For on this reasoning cocks too would have to be rejected, because some of them are sometimes seized by the falling sickness. Nor would I pass over this: that the Lord our God would not have fed the people of Israel, whom he loved most ardently, with quails to the point of satiety while they passed through those desert places, had they not been an approved and wholesome food. So Mundella, and more, which the reader may see there. And if one wishes to go further back, it will appear that the makers of myths thought highly of the quail, since they relate that Hercules, slain by Typhon, was recalled to life by the smell of a quail brought to him by Iolaus, and that this is why the Phoenicians sacrificed quails to him. Athenaeus, book 9: Εὔδοξος δὲ ὁ Κνίδιος ἐν πρώτῳ γῆς περιόδου τοὺς Φοίνικας λέγει θύειν τῷ Ἡρακλεῖ ὄρτυγας, διὰ τὸ τὸν Ἡρακλέα, τὸν Ἀστερίας καὶ Διὸς, πορευόμενον εἰς Λιβύην, ἀναιρεθῆναι μὲν ὑπὸ Τυφῶνος. Ἰολάου δ᾽ αὐτῷ προσενέγκαντος ὄρτυγα, καὶ προσαγάγοντος, ὀσφρανθέντα ἀναβιῶναι. [Eudoxos de ho Knidios en prōtō gēs periodou tous Phoinikas legei thyein tō Hēraklei ortygas, dia to ton Hērakléa, ton Asterias kai Dios, poreuomenon eis Libyēn, anairethēnai men hypo Typhōnos. Iolaou d᾽ autō prosenenkantos ortyga, kai prosagagontos, osphranthenta anabiōnai.] This gave rise to a proverb current among the Greeks,


Ὄρτυξ ἔσωσεν Ἡρακλῆν τὸν καρτερὸν, Fortem coturnix liberavit Herculem.

Ὄρτυξ ἔσωσεν Ἡρακλῆν τὸν καρτερὸν [Ortyx esōsen Hēraklēn ton karteron], The quail rescued mighty Hercules.


In qua fabula si quid verum est, Herculem putaverim, comitiali morbo correptum, (quem Herculeum vocari a)) ajunt, quia Hercules huic fuit obnoxius) tanquam mortuum jacuisse, et admotae coturnicis odore recreatum et refocillatum convaluisse. Saltem inter remedia, ad morbum comitialem maxime efficacia, praescribitur coturnicum cerebrum, quod in myrteo unguento tritum, et stanneo vase repositum, si aegri faciei illinatur, is statim sanus exsurget. Galenus, libri tertii Paratu facilium capite 155. Ad morbum comitialem remedium valde efficax. Coturnicum cerebrum ex unguento myrteo tritum stanneo vase reponito: et cum quempiam, morbo comitiali prolapsum, videris, eo faciem illinito. Admiraberis enim hujusce naturalis remedii efficaciam. Nam statim aegrotus exsurget. Et Assariph in Abenbitare de coturnice, اذا لعقت مرارته نفعت من الصرع Fel ejus si lingatur, confert ad epilepsiam. Itaque ad epilepsiam II, 660 coturnix se habet ut alce, quae huic morbo creditur maxime esse obnoxia: tamen ejus ungulis curari epilepticos, apud medicos constans fama est. Non solum igitur coturnix morbi, quo laborat, contagione homines non inficit, sed et adversus illum potens est amuletum (2). Dato tamen, non concesso, frequentem coturnicis esum corpori minus esse salubrem, non sequeretur, Deum Israelitis in deserto male consuluisse, dum eos pavit coturnicibus. 1. Quia non fuit cibus ordinarius. 2. Quia, qui coturnices per miraculum populo suo indulgebat, potuit etiam, quidquid in iis noxium erat, eximere, et hoc ipso bonitatem et col. 100 potentiam suam testari, quod eos sanos servabat et incolumes, quocunque uterentur cibo.

If there is any truth in this fable, I would suppose that Hercules, seized by the falling sickness (which, they say, is called Herculean a) because Hercules was subject to it), lay as if dead, and, revived and refreshed by the smell of a quail brought to him, recovered. At any rate, among the remedies most effective against the falling sickness, the brain of quails is prescribed: ground in myrtle ointment and stored in a tin vessel, if it is smeared on the patient's face, he will at once rise up healthy. Galen, On Easily Prepared Remedies, book 3, chapter 155: A very effective remedy for the falling sickness. Store the brain of quails, ground in myrtle ointment, in a tin vessel; and when you see someone who has collapsed from the falling sickness, smear his face with it. You will marvel at the efficacy of this natural remedy, for the patient will rise up at once. And Assariph [=al-Sharif (probably al-Idrisi), a source that Ibn al-Baytar quotes], in Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār], on the quail: اذا لعقت مرارته نفعت من الصرع [idhā luʿiqat marāratuhu nafaʿat min al-ṣarʿ] If its gall is licked, it is beneficial for epilepsy. Thus, with regard to epilepsy, II, 660 the quail is like the elk, which is believed to be especially subject to this disease; yet there is a constant tradition among physicians that epileptics are cured by its hooves. So the quail not only does not infect people with the contagion of the disease it suffers from, but is even a powerful amulet against it R2.
