Yet even granting, though not conceding, that frequent eating of quail is less wholesome for the body, it would not follow that God provided badly for the Israelites in the desert when He fed them with quails. 1. Because it was not their ordinary food. 2. Because He who granted quails to His people by a miracle could also remove whatever was harmful in them, and col. 100 by this very fact bear witness to His goodness and power, that He kept them healthy and unharmed whatever food they used.


III. Ad tertiam quaestionem, unde venerint hae coturnices, respondet Moses Num. XI, 31. ventum, a Domino profectum, eas advexisse מן הים, e mari. Et auctor libri Sapientiae capitis decimi noni versu duodecimo, In solatium ex mari ascendit ipsis ortygometra. Quod nonnulli sic acceperunt, quasi in ipso mari ortae fuissent. In qua sententia video esse quosdam Arabum. Idem Assariph, qui supra, سماني هو طاير يخرج من البحر Coturnix avis est, quae exit ex mari. Damir, وهو من الطيور القواطع لا يدري من اين يابي حتي ان بعض الناس يقول انه يخرج من البحر المالح فانه يري طاير عليه واحد جناحية فيه منغمس والاخر منشور كالقلع والاهل مصر به عنايه ويتغالون في ثمنه Est ex avibus migratoriis: atque ita ignotum est, unde veniat, ut quidam eam asserant exire ex mari salso, et in illo videri volantem, alarum una immersa, et altera in veli modum expansa. De quo Aegyptii valde sunt solliciti, ac proinde eam avem pro pretiosa habent. Nec Aben Ezra videtur aliud voluisse, cum ad verba Mosis Exod. XVI, 13. Et ascendit coturnix, et cooperuit castra, hanc notulam apposuit, אולי עלתה מפאת ים, Fortasse ascenderat ex plaga maris. Sed et e Graecis Phanodemus idem sensisse putatur, cum in Atthide scripsit, Delum a veteribus Ortygiam fuisse appellatam, id est, coturnicum insulam, παρὰ τὰς ἀγέλας τῶν ζώων τούτων, φερομένας ἐκ τοῦ πελά-γους, ἱζάνειν εἰς τὴν νῆσον διὰ τὸ εὔορμον εἶναι, eo quod horum animantium multi II, 661 greges, ex mari delati, in ea insula sedeant, quia commoda est statio. Et nugatur Kiranides libro primo, e thynnis, in Lybiae littus ejectis, cum putrescunt, enasci vermes, qui primo muscarum, deinde locustarum, et tandem coturnicum speciem et magnitudinem habeant. Verum, quidquid illi senserint, certum est, coturnices in nudo solo nasci et pasci. Eas itaque Sacer Scriptor e mari venisse scribit, quo sensu dixit Plinius libro 10. cap. 29. In agrum Volaterranum palumbium vim e mari quotannis advolare. Non, quod in eo creentur, sed quod, eo trajecto, circa Volaterras se conferant. Ita igitur ventus coturnices e mari detulisse legitur, quia, Arabico mari traducto, illas ex Aegypto vexerat in castra Israelitarum. Quo haec Iosephi pertinent Antiqu. lib. 3. cap. 1. Καὶ μετ᾽ ὀλίγον ὀρτύγων πλῆθος· τρέφει δὲ τοῦτο τὸ ὄρνεον, ὡς οὐδὲν ἕτερον, ὁ Ἀράβιος κόλ-πος, ἐπίπταται τὴν μεταξὺ θάλασσαν ὑπερελθόν. Et paullo post advolavit magna vis coturnicum, intermedium mare transgressa, hoc enim avium genus prae caeteris alit Arabicus sinus. Nec procul inde Rhinocolura, ubi magnam vim coturnicum, e mari advolantem, capi, his verbis tradit Diodorus libri primi pagina 38. Καλάμην γὰρ κείροντες ἐκ τῆς ὁμόρου χώρας, καὶ ταύτην σχίζοντες λίνα παραμήκη κατασκεύαζον. ταῦτα δὲ παρὰ τὸν αἰγιαλὸν ἐπὶ πολλοὺς σταδίους ἱστάντες τὰς θήρας τῶν ὀρτύγων ἐποιοῦντο (φέρονται γὰρ οὗτοι κατ᾽ ἀγέλας μείζους ἐκ τοῦ πελάγους) οὓς θηρεύοντες ἤθροιζον πλῆθος ἱκανὸν εἰς διατροφὴν col. 101 ἑαυτοῖς· Calamis, ex vicina regione detonsis et fissis, longa retia parabant, quibus prope littus in multa stadia constitutis, coturnices, quae per magnos greges ex mari eo se conferunt, capientes, earum colligebant, quantum ad victum sufficeret. Ubi notandum, quod coturnices dicit φέρεσθαι ἐκ τοῦ πελάγους, quomodo Moses supra.

III. To the third question, from where these quails came, Moses answers in Num 11:31 that a wind, proceeding from the Lord, brought them מן הים, from the sea. And the author of the book of Wisdom, chapter 19, verse 12: For their comfort the ortygometra came up to them from the sea. Some have taken this as though they had been born in the sea itself. I see that some of the Arabs hold this opinion. The same Assariph as above: سماني هو طاير يخرج من البحر [samānī huwa ṭāyir yakhruj min al-baḥr] The quail is a bird that comes out of the sea. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: وهو من الطيور القواطع لا يدري من اين يابي حتي ان بعض الناس يقول انه يخرج من البحر المالح فانه يري طاير عليه واحد جناحية فيه منغمس والاخر منشور كالقلع والاهل مصر به عنايه ويتغالون في ثمنه [wa-huwa min al-ṭuyūr al-qawāṭiʿ lā yudrā min ayna yābī ḥattā anna baʿḍ al-nās yaqūl annahu yakhruj min al-baḥr al-māliḥ fa-innahu yurā ṭāyir ʿalayhi wāḥid janāḥiyya fīhi munghamis wa-al-ākhar manshūr ka-al-qilʿ wa-al-ahl miṣr bihi ʿināya wa-yataghālūn fī thamanihi] It is one of the migratory birds, and it is so unknown where it comes from that some assert that it comes out of the salt sea and is seen flying over it, with one of its wings immersed and the other spread out like a sail. The Egyptians are very keen on it, and therefore hold this bird to be precious. Nor does Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] seem to have meant anything else when, on the words of Moses in Exod 16:13, And the quail came up and covered the camp, he added this little note: אולי עלתה מפאת ים, Perhaps it had come up from the region of the sea. And among the Greeks, Phanodemus is thought to have held the same view, when he wrote in his Atthis that Delos was called Ortygia by the ancients, that is, the island of quails, παρὰ τὰς ἀγέλας τῶν ζώων τούτων, φερομένας ἐκ τοῦ πελάγους, ἱζάνειν εἰς τὴν νῆσον διὰ τὸ εὔορμον εἶναι [para tas agelas tōn zōōn toutōn, pheromenas ek tou pelagous, hizanein eis tēn nēson dia to euormon einai], because many flocks of these creatures, II, 661 borne from the sea, settle on that island, since it is a convenient resting place. And Kiranides, in book 1, talks nonsense: that from tunnies cast up on the shore of Libya, as they rot, worms are born which have first the form and size of flies, then of locusts, and finally of quails. But whatever they thought, it is certain that quails are born and feed on bare ground. The Sacred Writer therefore writes that they came from the sea in the sense in which Pliny, book 10, ch. 29, said: A great number of wood pigeons flies every year from the sea into the territory of Volaterrae. Not that they are produced in it, but that, having crossed it, they betake themselves to the area around Volaterrae. So, then, the wind is said to have brought the quails from the sea because, having crossed the Arabian sea, it had carried them from Egypt into the camp of the Israelites. To this belong these words of Josephus, Antiqu. book 3, ch. 1: Καὶ μετ᾽ ὀλίγον ὀρτύγων πλῆθος· τρέφει δὲ τοῦτο τὸ ὄρνεον, ὡς οὐδὲν ἕτερον, ὁ Ἀράβιος κόλπος, ἐπίπταται τὴν μεταξὺ θάλασσαν ὑπερελθόν [Kai met' oligon ortygōn plēthos; trephei de touto to orneon, hōs ouden heteron, ho Arabios kolpos, epiptatai tēn metaxy thalassan hyperelthon]. And shortly afterwards a great number of quails flew in, having crossed the intervening sea; for the Arabian gulf nourishes this kind of bird more than any other. Not far from there is Rhinocolura, where, as Diodorus reports in book 1, page 38, a great number of quails flying in from the sea is caught, in these words: Καλάμην γὰρ κείροντες ἐκ τῆς ὁμόρου χώρας, καὶ ταύτην σχίζοντες λίνα παραμήκη κατασκεύαζον. ταῦτα δὲ παρὰ τὸν αἰγιαλὸν ἐπὶ πολλοὺς σταδίους ἱστάντες τὰς θήρας τῶν ὀρτύγων ἐποιοῦντο (φέρονται γὰρ οὗτοι κατ᾽ ἀγέλας μείζους ἐκ τοῦ πελάγους) οὓς θηρεύοντες ἤθροιζον πλῆθος ἱκανὸν εἰς διατροφὴν col. 101 ἑαυτοῖς· [Kalamēn gar keirontes ek tēs homorou chōras, kai tautēn schizontes lina paramēkē kateskeuazon. tauta de para ton aigialon epi pollous stadious histantes tas thēras tōn ortygōn epoiounto (pherontai gar houtoi kat' agelas meizous ek tou pelagous) hous thēreuontes ēthroizon plēthos hikanon eis diatrophēn heautois] Cutting reeds from the neighbouring region and splitting them, they made long nets; setting these up near the shore over many stadia, they caught the quails, which betake themselves there in great flocks from the sea, and gathered as many of them as sufficed for their sustenance. Here it should be noted that he says the quails φέρεσθαι ἐκ τοῦ πελάγους [pheresthai ek tou pelagous], just as Moses above.


Atque haec quidem satis obvia sunt: sed nemo facile dixerit, quomodo concilientur cum his Davidis de eodem miraculo Psal. LXXVIII, 26. 27.(3) Eurum in coelo excitavit, et austrum vi sua impulit, et depluit super eos carnem tanquam pulverem, et volucres alatas sicut arenam maris. Quid enim opus fuit Eurum excitari, ut ex Aegypto in Arabiam per sinum Arabicum deveherentur coturnices, cum ad Favonium potius id pertineat et ventos occidentales? Aegypti enim et Africae respectu, non flat Eurus in Arabiam, sed flat ex Arabia, juxta illud Poetae,

These things, indeed, are obvious enough. But no one could easily say how they are to be reconciled with these words of David on the same miracle, Ps 78:26–27.R3 He stirred up the east wind in the heaven, and by his power drove on the south wind, and rained flesh upon them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea. For what need was there for the east wind to be stirred up so that quails might be carried from Egypt into Arabia across the Arabian gulf, when this would rather be the task of Favonius and the western winds? For with respect to Egypt and Africa, the east wind does not blow into Arabia but blows out of Arabia, according to the line of the Poet:


Eurus ad Auroram Nabataeaque regna recessit.

The east wind withdrew to the Dawn and the Nabataean realms.


Ad Nabataea regna, id est, in Arabiam, ubi Nabataei Arabes, oriundi ex Nabajot, Ismaelis primogenito, Gen. XXV, 13. In quibus locis tum erant Israelitae. II, 662 Itaque Exod. X, 19. locustas ex Aegypto in mare rubrum non impellit Eurus, sed ventus alius, huic contrarius, nempe occidentalis. Ita enim habet Moses, Immisit Dominus ventum occidentalem valde vehementem, qui, exportans locustas illas, dejecit in mare rubrum. Debuit igitur hic idem ventus coturnices ex Aegypto per mare rubrum in Arabiam deferre, non Eurus, ut in Psalmo habetur. Huic objectioni videtur facile posse occurri ex Hieronymi versione, quae sic habet, Abstulit Eurum de coelo, et induxit in fortitudine sua Africum. Quasi uno sublato, alter fuerit inductus. Quae eadem est Graecorum versio et Vulgati interpretis, nisi quod pro Euro Νότον austrum habent. Ita enim Graeci: Ἀπῆρεν Νότον ἐξ οὐρανοῦ, καὶ ἐπήγαγεν ἐν τῇ δυναστείᾳ αὐτοῦ Λίβα. Et Vulgatus, Transtulit austrum de coelo, et induxit in virtute sua Africum. Itaque ex eorum mente Hebraea vox יסע reddi debet ἀπῆρεν, transtulit, vel abstulit. Quae versio si recipiatur, jam nulla erit objectio. Nec ea videbitur facile posse rejici, cum, quia magnos habet auctores, tum, quia verbum הסיע, unde יסע, in amovendi et auferendi notione passim occurrit. Est enim Hiphil verbi נסע, quod proficisci significat, sive e loco, sive ad locum. Itaque in Hiphil הסיע est facere, ut quis aut e loco, aut ad locum proficiscatur. Et, de vento dictum, tam potest significare ventum auferri, quam immitti. Sonticae tamen causae sunt, ut quidem puto, cur hoc loco יסע in auferendi significatione non possit sumi. Primo enim illud יסע Psaltes ex Mose mutuatur, cujus verba sunt Num. XI, 31. Et ventus a Domino נסע profectus est, et e mari transvexit coturnices. Itaque, ut in Mose נסע ventum recedere non significat, sed progredi, ut coturnices advehat: ita in Psalte יסע, quod est Hiphil ejusdem verbi, ventum amotum fuisse non significat, sed immissum, ut coturnices adduceret. Secundo, ἀπῆρεν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ, abstulit e coelo, Hebraice esset יסע מן השמים. Sed textus habet בשמים, quod significat in coelo, vel in coelum, non e coelo. Proinde ibi יסע non est auferre, sed inferre et immittere. Nam, ut res e loco aufertur, ita in locum infertur. Tertio, quorsum diceretur, ut in Hieronymo, Abstulit Eurum, et induxit Africum, et in Graeca versione, Ἀπῆρεν Νότον, καὶ ἐπήγαγεν Λίβα, Abstulit notum; et induxit Africum: cum hi venti non sint contrarii, et simul stare et flare possint? Unde Poeta summus,

To the Nabataean realms, that is, into Arabia, where the Nabataean Arabs live, descended from Nebaioth, the firstborn of Ishmael, Gen 25:13. The Israelites were in those places at that time. II, 662 Thus in Exod 10:19 it is not the east wind that drives the locusts from Egypt into the Red Sea, but another wind, contrary to it, namely the west wind. For Moses says: The Lord sent a very strong west wind, which carried off those locusts and cast them into the Red Sea. This same wind, then, ought to have carried the quails from Egypt across the Red Sea into Arabia, not the east wind, as the Psalm has it. This objection seems easy to meet from Jerome's version, which reads: He took away the east wind from heaven, and brought in by his strength the south-west wind (Africus). As if, when the one was removed, the other was brought in. The version of the Greeks and of the Vulgate translator is the same, except that instead of the east wind they have Νότον [Noton], the south wind. For the Greeks read: Ἀπῆρεν Νότον ἐξ οὐρανοῦ, καὶ ἐπήγαγεν ἐν τῇ δυναστείᾳ αὐτοῦ Λίβα [Apēren Noton ex ouranou, kai epēgagen en tē dynasteia autou Liba]. And the Vulgate translator: He removed the south wind from heaven, and brought in by his power the south-west wind. Thus in their view the Hebrew word יסע should be rendered ἀπῆρεν [apēren], he removed or he took away. If this version is accepted, there will be no objection left. Nor will it seem easy to reject, both because it has weighty authorities and because the verb הסיע, from which יסע comes, frequently occurs in the sense of removing and taking away. For it is the Hiphil of the verb נסע, which means to set out, whether from a place or to a place. So in the Hiphil הסיע is to cause someone to set out either from a place or to a place. And said of a wind, it can mean that the wind is taken away as well as that it is sent in. Yet there are, as I at least think, compelling reasons why יסע cannot be taken in this passage in the sense of taking away. First, the Psalmist borrows this יסע from Moses, whose words are, Num 11:31. And a wind from the Lord נסע went forth, and brought quails across from the sea. Thus, just as in Moses נסע does not mean that the wind withdrew but that it advanced to bring the quails, so in the Psalmist יסע, which is the Hiphil of the same verb, does not mean that the wind was removed but that it was sent in to bring the quails. Second, ἀπῆρεν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ [apēren ex ouranou], he took away from heaven, would in Hebrew be יסע מן השמים. But the text has בשמים, which means in heaven or into heaven, not from heaven. Accordingly יסע there is not to take away but to bring in and to send in. For as a thing is taken away from a place, so it is brought into a place. Third, to what purpose would it be said, as in Jerome, He took away the east wind and brought in the south-west wind, and in the Greek version, Ἀπῆρεν Νότον, καὶ ἐπήγαγεν Λίβα [Apēren Noton, kai epēgagen Liba], He took away the south wind, and brought in the south-west wind, since these winds are not contrary and can stand and blow at the same time? Hence the greatest Poet:


Una Eurusque Notusque ruunt, creberque procellis
Africus. — — — — — —

Together rush Eurus and Notus, and, thick with storms, Africus. — — — — — —


Et multo ante Homerus Iliad. π΄. versu 765.

And long before, Homer, Iliad 16, line 765:


Ὡς δ᾽ Εὖρός τε Νότος τ᾽ ἐριδαίνετον ἀλλήλοιϊν·

Ὡς δ᾽ Εὖρός τε Νότος τ᾽ ἐριδαίνετον ἀλλήλοιϊν· [Hōs d' Euros te Notos t' eridaineton allēloiin]


Quarto in hoc toto Psalmo, ut saepe alibi in Hebraeorum Poeticis libris, duo hemistichia fere sunt parallela, et sese mutuo explicant. Unde sequitur, יסע col. 102 II, 663 hic fere idem esse, quod וינהג, et induxit, in posteriore hemistichio, in quo le-gitur Deus vi sua austrum induxisse. Quinto, si auctoritate certatur, Graecis et Hieronymo Chaldaeum et Syrum opponimus, et utrumque Arabem (4) et Hebraeos, quotquot sunt, et recentiores interpretes, quotquod videre licuit. Neque enim occurrit ullus, cui יסע hic sit auferre. Quin omnes intelligunt, Eurum a Deo excitatum fuisse et immissum. Pagninus, Excitavit Eurum in coelo, Arias, Profecisci fecit Eurum in coelis. Felix Pratensis, Movit Eurum in coelis. Castellio, Acto per coelum Euro. Quibus adde omnes vernaculas. Hoc igitur maneat, Deum, juxta Davidis mentem, hunc ventum movisse, non amovisse; intulisse, non abstulisse. Sed, ut res intelligatur, notandum est, Israelitas fuisse tum in deserto Pharan, et jam triduano itinere progressos ultra montem Sinai, Num. X, 12. 33. et extremum sinum Arabicum habuisse ad meridiem, ac proinde merito תימן Theman, id est, australem, a Davide vocari ventum, qui coturnices a mari rubro ad illorum castra advexit. At cur idem vocatur קדים kadim, id est, orientalis? Respondent Aben Ezra et Kimchius, utroque nomine appellari; quia fuit מזרחי דרומי, id est, partim orientalis, partim australis, quem uno verbo dixeris Euro-Notum (5). Quod est oppido falsum. Neque enim orientalis ullo modo fuit ille ventus, ut norunt locorum periti. Tamen dicitur קדים Kadim, qua de causa jam dicturus sum. Quamvis venti cardinales quatuor constituantur, qui rursus subdividuntur in multo plures, nihilominus docti b) observant, in antiquis philosophorum ac medicorum libris, et praecipue apud Aristotelem et Theophrastum, ad designandas tempestatum et aëris constitutiones, quas venti faciunt, τὰ βόρεια solum et τὰ νότια nominari, nusquam τὰ ἑσπέρια, aut τὰ ἑῷα. Unde Aristoteles lib. 2. Meteorol. cap. 6. postquam octo principales ventos cum suis lateronibus nominavit, Ὅλως δὲ, inquit, τὰ μὲν βόρεια τούτων καλεῖται, τὰ δὲ νότια. Universaliter quidem horum alii boreales, alii vocantur australes. Nempe venti occidentales, tanquam frigidiores, boreae apponuntur; et austro orientales, quia sunt calidiores. Quod his verbis idem addit, Προστίθηται δὲ τὰ μὲν ζεφυρικὰ τῷ βορέᾳ, ψυχρότερα γὰρ, διὰ τὸ ἀπὸ δυσμῶν πνεῖν· τῷ δὲ νότῳ ἀπηλιωτικὰ, θερμότερα γὰρ, τῷ (lege διὰ τὸ) ἀπὸ ἀνατολῆς πνεῖν. Vento autem occidentali orientalis ideo calidior est, ὅτι πλείω χρόνον ὑπὸ τὸν ἥλιόν ἐστι, quia diutius est sub sole. Unde est, quod II, 664 Graece vocatur ἀπηλιώτης, et Latine Subsolanus. Proinde in Politicis lib. 4. cap. 3. idem Aristoteles omnes reipubl. formas vel ad democratiam, vel oligarchiam contendit esse referendas; καθάπερ ἐπὶ τῶν πνευμάτων λέγεται τὰ μὲν βόρεια, τὰ δὲ νότια, τάδ' ἄλλα τούτων παρεκβάσεις, Quomodo in ventis alii boreales, alii dicuntur australes, et reliqui sunt horum excessus. Unde est, ait, quod τὸν μὲν ζέφυρον τοῦ βορέου, τοῦ δὲ νότου τὸν εὖρον, Zephyrum Boreae, austri vero Eurum esse dicunt. Quo pertinent Lucillii versus libro de Coty, Thracum rege, quos corruptissimos in Nonio, voce Demagis, Salmasius sic restituit:

Fourth, in this whole Psalm, as often elsewhere in the poetic books of the Hebrews, the two hemistichs are generally parallel and explain each other. From this it follows that יסע col. 102 II, 663 here is roughly the same as וינהג, and he brought in, in the second hemistich, in which we read that God by his power brought in the south wind. Fifth, if the matter is decided by authority, against the Greeks and Jerome we set the Chaldee and the Syriac, and both Arabic versions R4, and the Hebrews, as many as there are, and the more recent interpreters, as many as I have been able to see. For not one of them occurs for whom יסע here means to take away. Rather, all understand that the east wind was stirred up and sent in by God. Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae]: He stirred up the east wind in the heaven; Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot]: He made the east wind set out in the heavens; Felix Pratensis [=Felix of Prato, Latin Psalter from the Hebrew (1515)]: He moved the east wind in the heavens; Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)]: The east wind having been driven through the heaven. Add to these all the vernacular versions. Let this therefore stand: that God, according to David's meaning, moved this wind, not removed it; brought it in, not took it away. But for the matter to be understood, it must be noted that the Israelites were then in the desert of Paran, having already advanced a three days' journey beyond Mount Sinai, Num 10:12 33., and had the farthest gulf of the Arabian sea to the south; and therefore the wind that carried the quails from the Red Sea to their camp is rightly called by David תימן Theman, that is, southern. But why is the same wind called קדים kadim, that is, eastern? Aben Ezra and Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] answer that it is called by both names because it was מזרחי דרומי, that is, partly eastern, partly southern, which you might call in one word Euro-Notus R5. This is utterly false. For that wind was in no way eastern, as those acquainted with the region know. Yet it is called קדים Kadim, and I shall now say why. Although four cardinal winds are established, which are in turn subdivided into many more, nevertheless the learned b) observe that in the ancient books of the philosophers and physicians, and especially in Aristotle and Theophrastus, to designate the conditions of weather and air produced by the winds, only τὰ βόρεια [ta boreia] and τὰ νότια [ta notia] are named, never τὰ ἑσπέρια [ta hesperia] or τὰ ἑῷα [ta heōa]. Hence Aristotle, Meteorol. book 2, ch. 6, after naming eight principal winds with their side-winds, says: Ὅλως δὲ τὰ μὲν βόρεια τούτων καλεῖται, τὰ δὲ νότια [Holōs de ta men boreia toutōn kaleitai, ta de notia]. In general, of these some are called northern, others southern. That is, the western winds, as colder, are assigned to the north wind, and the eastern ones to the south wind, because they are warmer. He adds this in these words: Προστίθηται δὲ τὰ μὲν ζεφυρικὰ τῷ βορέᾳ, ψυχρότερα γὰρ, διὰ τὸ ἀπὸ δυσμῶν πνεῖν· τῷ δὲ νότῳ ἀπηλιωτικὰ, θερμότερα γὰρ, τῷ (read διὰ τὸ) ἀπὸ ἀνατολῆς πνεῖν [Prostithētai de ta men zephyrika tō borea, psychrotera gar, dia to apo dysmōn pnein; tō de notō apēliōtika, thermotera gar, tō (dia to) apo anatolēs pnein]. The eastern wind is warmer than the western for this reason, ὅτι πλείω χρόνον ὑπὸ τὸν ἥλιόν ἐστι [hoti pleiō chronon hypo ton hēlion esti], because it is longer under the sun. That is why II, 664 in Greek it is called ἀπηλιώτης [apēliōtēs], and in Latin Subsolanus. Accordingly, in the Politics, book 4, ch. 3, the same Aristotle contends that all forms of commonwealth are to be referred either to democracy or to oligarchy, καθάπερ ἐπὶ τῶν πνευμάτων λέγεται τὰ μὲν βόρεια, τὰ δὲ νότια, τάδ' ἄλλα τούτων παρεκβάσεις [kathaper epi tōn pneumatōn legetai ta men boreia, ta de notia, tad' alla toutōn parekbaseis], just as among the winds some are called northern, others southern, and the rest are deviations from these. Hence it is, he says, that they say τὸν μὲν ζέφυρον τοῦ βορέου, τοῦ δὲ νότου τὸν εὖρον [ton men zephyron tou boreou, tou de notou ton euron], that the zephyr belongs to the north wind, and the east wind to the south wind. To this belong the verses of Lucilius in the book on Cotys, king of the Thracians, which, badly corrupted in Nonius under the word Demagis, Salmasius [=Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), Plinianae exercitationes] restores thus:


Rex Cotys ille duos ventos, austrum atque aquilonem, Novisse ajebat solos se demagis, istos Ex nimbo Austellos nec nosse, nec esse putare.

King Cotys used to say that he knew only two winds, the south wind and the north wind, and moreover, that those little south winds from the storm-cloud he neither knew nor thought existed.


Ex his cum Eurum pateat ad australem ventum referri, potuere apud Davidem קדים Kadim, et תימן Theman, id est, Eurus et auster, haberi pro synonymis, ita, ut hoc loco Kadim non sit aliud, quam sequens Theman. Neque vero hic solum, sed et passim alibi, vento Kadim Sacri Scriptores ea tribuunt, quae potius venti australis videntur esse propria. Is enim fruges exurit, Gen. XLI, 6. Vites quoque et fructus arborum, Ezech. XVII, 10. et XIX, 12. Maris et fontium aquas exsiccat, Exod. XIV, 21. et Os. XIII, 15. Vi sua naves conterit, col. 103 Psal. XLVIII, 8. et Ezech. XXVII, 26. Omnia denique subvertit et dispergit, Iob. XXVII, 21. et Ierem. XVIII, 17. Proinde vocatur ventus durus, Es. XXVII, 8. et חרשית, strepitu suo homines surdos faciens, Ion. IV, 8. Neque a Graecis Εὖρος uspiam, sed Νότος vocatur, aut Καύσων, id est, auster, et ventus urens. Et Dei verba Deut. XXXII, 22. Ignis succensus est in furore meo, et ardebit usque ad imos inferos, consumetque terram et proventum ejus, Ionathan et Onkelos ad hunc eundem ventum referunt hac sua periphrasi, קדום תקיף כאשא, Ventus orientalis validus ut ignis a me in furore exiit, etc. A Theodoreto denique Eurus et Notus conferuntur ut venti similes, et prope iidem, cum scribit Quaestione octava in Genesin, Εὔρου ἢ Νότου πνέοντος, τὸ πεπηγὸς ὕδωρ διαλύεσθαι, Euro, aut noto flante, aquam congelatam dissolvi. Quamvis igitur רוח הקדים, proprie et praecise loquendo, ventum orientalem sonet (quod et vocis origo docet, et locus Ezech. XLII, 16. etc. ubi a vento Kadim Borealis, Australis et Occidentalis distinguuntur) tamen quia venti Kadim et Theman, id est, Eurus et Auster, quaedam habent inter se communia, Hebraeos puto has voces promiscue usurpasse. Atque inde esse, quod קדים Kadim passim a Graecis Νότος redditur: ut Exod. X, 13. et XIV, 21. Num. XXXIV, 15. Iob. XXXVIII, 24. Ezech. XXVII, 26. atque in illo ipso Psalmi loco, in quo versamur, ubi Kadim et Theman explicant Νότον καὶ Λίβα. Quocirca utraque voce II, 665 idem ventus videtur significari, Auster nimirum, aut Africus (6), qui ex intima Aegypto coturnices Israelitis advexerit (7).

Since it is clear from this that the east wind is related to the south wind, in David קדים Kadim and תימן Theman, that is, the east wind and the south wind, could be taken as synonyms, so that in this passage Kadim is nothing other than the following Theman. And not only here but frequently elsewhere the sacred writers attribute to the wind Kadim things that seem rather to be proper to the south wind. For it scorches the crops, Gen 41:6. It also scorches vines and the fruits of trees, Ezek 17:10 and XIX, 12. It dries up the waters of the sea and of springs, Exod 14:21 and Hos 13:15. By its force it shatters ships, col. 103 Ps 48:8 and Ezek 27:26. Finally, it overturns and scatters everything, Job 27:21 and Jer 18:17. Accordingly it is called a harsh wind, Isa 27:8 and חרשית, making people deaf with its roar, Jonah 4:8. Nor is it anywhere called Εὖρος [Euros] by the Greeks, but Νότος [Notos] or Καύσων [Kausōn], that is, the south wind and the burning wind. And God's words in Deut 32:22. A fire is kindled in my anger, and it shall burn to the lowest hell, and shall consume the earth and its produce, Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] and Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] refer to this same wind by this paraphrase of theirs, קדום תקיף כאשא, An east wind, strong as fire, has gone out from me in anger, etc. Finally, Theodoret compares the east wind and the south wind as similar winds, almost the same, when he writes in Question 8 on Genesis, Εὔρου ἢ Νότου πνέοντος, τὸ πεπηγὸς ὕδωρ διαλύεσθαι [Eurou ē Notou pneontos, to pepēgos hydōr dialyesthai], When the east wind or the south wind blows, frozen water is dissolved. Therefore, although רוח הקדים, properly and strictly speaking, means the east wind (as both the origin of the word shows and the passage Ezek 42:16 etc., where the north, south and west winds are distinguished from the wind Kadim), nevertheless, because the winds Kadim and Theman, that is, the east wind and the south wind, have certain things in common, I think the Hebrews used these words interchangeably. And hence it is that קדים Kadim is frequently rendered Νότος [Notos] by the Greeks: as in Exod 10:13 and XIV, 21. Num 34:15. Job 38:24. Ezek 27:26 and in that very passage of the Psalm with which we are dealing, where they render Kadim and Theman as Νότον καὶ Λίβα [Noton kai Liba]. Therefore the same wind seems to be meant by both words II, 665, namely the south wind or the south-west wind R6, which brought the quails to the Israelites from the interior of Egypt R7.


At unum potest objici, nempe austro flante non volare coturnices, Aristoteles Hist. lib. 8. cap. 12. Οἱ δὲ ὄρτυγες, ὅταν πέσωσιν, ἐὰν μὲν εὐδία ᾖ βόρειον ᾖ, συνδυάζονταί τε, καὶ ἠρεμοῦσιν. ἐὰν δὲ νότος, χαλεπῶς ἔχουσι, διὰ τὸ μὴ εἶναι πτητικοί· ὑγρὸς γὰρ καὶ βαρὺς ὁ ἄνεμος· διὸ καὶ οἱ θηρεύοντες ἐπι-χειροῦσι τοῖς νοτίοις· Coturnices, cum cadunt (imo ὅταν πέτονται, cum volant), si sudum coelum, et ventus ab aquilone est, sociantur, et quiete degunt. At, si auster est, graviter se habent, quia non facile volant; humidus enim et gravis est ventus. Quamobrem qui aucupantur, austrinis ventis eas aggrediuntur. Et Plinius libro decimo capite vigesimo tertio, Austro non volant, humido scilicet et gravi vento. Aura tamen vehi volunt, propter pondus corporum viresque parvas, etc. Aquilone ergo maxime volant. Et Solinus, Austro nunquam exeunt: nam metuunt vim flatus tumidioris. Plurimum se aquilonibus credunt, ut corpora pinguiuscula, atque eo tarda, facilius provehat siccior et vehementior spiritus. Eodem facit, quod venti, Ornithiae dicti, quasi aves adducant, ab aquilone, aut saltem ab occasu flare scribuntur. Aristoteles libro De mundo, Οἱ δὲ ὀρνιθίαι κα-λούμενοι, ἐαρινοί τινες ὄντες ἄνεμοι, βόρειοί εἰσι τῷ γένει. Quae Budaeus ita reddidit, Ornithiae, quasi Aviarii, venti quidam dicti sunt ex Aquilonio genere, verno tempore invalescentes. Sed Apulejus multo aliter, Ornithiae verni (alii venti) aquilonum genus ex aëre prolati minori nisu, nec jugi perseverantia spiritus perferentes. Quae scilicet non tam ex hoc loco petita sunt, quam ex Meteorologicorum libri secundi capite quinto, ubi Ornithiae dicuntur esse Ἐτησίαι ἀσθενεῖς· ἐλάττους δὲ, καὶ ὀψιαίτεροι τῶν Ἐτησίων πνέοντες, Etesiae debiles, sed quae veris Etesiis minores et tardiores sunt. Quibus verbis Ornithiae Etesiis adscribuntur. Etesiae autem vel ab occiduo axe flant, vel a septentrionali plaga. Diodorus libro primo, Τοὺς Ἐτησίας ἰδεῖν ἐστιν οὐδέν τι μᾶλλον ἀπὸ τῆς ἄρκτου II, 666 πνέοντας, ἤπερ τῆς ἑσπέρας· οὐ βορέαι γὰρ, οὐδ᾽ ἀπαρκτίαι μόνοι, ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ πνέοντες ἀπὸ τῆς θηρινῆς δύσεως ἀργέσαι κοινωνοῦσι τῆς τῶν Ἐτησίων προση-γορίας. Itaque Ornithiae indidem oriuntur. Et eos Plinius libri secundi capite quadragesimo septimo modo ad Favonium refert, modo ad Etesias. Favonium, inquit, quidam ad VII. Calend. Martii Chelidoniam vocant ab hirundinis visu. col. 104 Nonnulli vero Ornithiam, LXXI die post brumam, ab adventu avium, flantem per dies novem. Et infra ubi de Etesiis, Spirant autem et a bruma qui vocantur Ornithiae, sed leniores, et paucis diebus. In Aristophanis Acharnensibus aliter sumitur χειμὼν ὀρνιθίας, nempe pro hyeme frigidissimo, in quo τὰ ὄρνεα δια-φθείρεται, aves prae frigore pereunt, vt volunt Scholiastes et Suidas voce Ὀρνι-θίας. Itaque iisdem ventus ὀρνιθίας est ὁ ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν τὰ ὄρνεα στρωννὺς ὑπὸ τῆς ψυχρᾶς πνοῆς, qui frigido suo flatu aves humi sternit. Sed Philosophis Ornithias ventus nihil quidquam est, quam quod diximus, nempe ventus, ex aquilone aut occasu aves adducens. Itaque videri possit praeter naturam id contigisse, ut auster coturnices ad Israelitas adveheret. Atque ex eo ipso contendunt, majus fuisse miraculum. Sed nihil opus eo recurrere. Utut enim Plinius et Solinus eas austro volare simpliciter negent, tamen ex Philosopho hoc solum elicias, tum volare difficilius, et facilius capi (8). Quod ipsum hic momentum habet:

But one objection can be raised: namely, that quails do not fly when the south wind blows. Aristotle, Hist. book 8, ch. 12: Οἱ δὲ ὄρτυγες, ὅταν πέσωσιν, ἐὰν μὲν εὐδία ᾖ βόρειον ᾖ, συνδυάζονταί τε, καὶ ἠρεμοῦσιν. ἐὰν δὲ νότος, χαλεπῶς ἔχουσι, διὰ τὸ μὴ εἶναι πτητικοί· ὑγρὸς γὰρ καὶ βαρὺς ὁ ἄνεμος· διὸ καὶ οἱ θηρεύοντες ἐπιχειροῦσι τοῖς νοτίοις· [Hoi de ortyges, hotan pesōsin, ean men eudia ē boreion ē, syndyazontai te, kai ēremousin. ean de notos, chalepōs echousi, dia to mē einai ptētikoi; hygros gar kai barys ho anemos; dio kai hoi thēreuontes epicheirousi tois notiois] "When quails fall (rather, ὅταν πέτονται [hotan petontai], when they fly), if the sky is clear and the wind is from the north, they pair and stay quiet. But if the south wind blows, they fare badly, because they do not fly easily; for that wind is moist and heavy. That is why fowlers go after them when the winds are southerly." And Pliny, book 10, chapter 23: "They do not fly with the south wind, that is, a moist and heavy wind. Yet they want to be carried by a breeze, because of the weight of their bodies and their small strength," etc. "Thus they fly most with the north wind." And Solinus: "They never set out with the south wind, for they fear the force of its swollen blast. They entrust themselves mostly to the north winds, so that a drier and stronger breath may more easily carry forward their rather fat and therefore sluggish bodies." To the same effect is the fact that the winds called Ornithiae, as if they brought birds, are described as blowing from the north, or at least from the west. Aristotle, in the book De mundo: Οἱ δὲ ὀρνιθίαι καλούμενοι, ἐαρινοί τινες ὄντες ἄνεμοι, βόρειοί εἰσι τῷ γένει [Hoi de ornithiai kaloumenoi, earinoi tines ontes anemoi, boreioi eisi tō genei]. Budaeus rendered this: "Certain winds of the northern kind, gaining strength in springtime, are called Ornithiae, as it were 'bird-winds'." But Apuleius quite differently: "The spring Ornithiae (others read winds) are a kind of north wind, issuing from the air with lesser force and not maintaining their blowing with continuous persistence." These words, indeed, are taken not so much from this passage as from the Meteorologica, book 2, chapter 5, where the Ornithiae are said to be Ἐτησίαι ἀσθενεῖς· ἐλάττους δὲ, καὶ ὀψιαίτεροι τῶν Ἐτησίων πνέοντες [Etēsiai astheneis; elattous de, kai opsiaiteroi tōn Etēsiōn pneontes], "weak Etesians, but smaller and later than the true Etesians." In these words the Ornithiae are assigned to the Etesians. The Etesians, however, blow either from the western quarter or from the northern region. Diodorus, book 1: Τοὺς Ἐτησίας ἰδεῖν ἐστιν οὐδέν τι μᾶλλον ἀπὸ τῆς ἄρκτου II, 666 πνέοντας, ἤπερ τῆς ἑσπέρας· οὐ βορέαι γὰρ, οὐδ᾽ ἀπαρκτίαι μόνοι, ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ πνέοντες ἀπὸ τῆς θηρινῆς δύσεως ἀργέσαι κοινωνοῦσι τῆς τῶν Ἐτησίων προσηγορίας [Tous Etēsias idein estin ouden ti mallon apo tēs arktou pneontas, ēper tēs hesperas; ou boreai gar, oud' aparktiai monoi, alla kai hoi pneontes apo tēs thērinēs dyseōs argesai koinōnousi tēs tōn Etēsiōn prosēgorias]. So the Ornithiae arise from the same quarter. And Pliny, book 2, chapter 47, relates them now to the Favonius, now to the Etesians. "Some," he says, "call the Favonius around the 7th day before the Kalends of March Chelidonias, from the sighting of the swallow. col. 104 Some, however, call it Ornithias, blowing on the 71st day after the winter solstice, from the arrival of the birds, for nine days." And further on, concerning the Etesians: "There also blow after the winter solstice those called Ornithiae, but gentler, and for a few days." In Aristophanes' Acharnians χειμὼν ὀρνιθίας [cheimōn ornithias] is taken otherwise, namely for a most bitterly cold winter, in which τὰ ὄρνεα διαφθείρεται [ta ornea diaphtheiretai], birds perish from the cold, as the Scholiast and Suidas under the word Ὀρνιθίας [Ornithias] hold. Accordingly, for them the ὀρνιθίας [ornithias] wind is ὁ ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν τὰ ὄρνεα στρωννὺς ὑπὸ τῆς ψυχρᾶς πνοῆς [ho epi tēn gēn ta ornea strōnnys hypo tēs psychras pnoēs], "the one that lays birds low on the ground with its cold blast." But for the philosophers the Ornithias wind is nothing other than what we have said, namely a wind bringing birds from the north or the west. It might therefore seem that it happened contrary to nature that the south wind carried the quails to the Israelites. And from this very point some argue that the miracle was greater. But there is no need to resort to this. For although Pliny and Solinus flatly deny that they fly with the south wind, from the Philosopher you can draw only this: that they then fly with more difficulty and are more easily caught R8. And this very point carries weight here:


II, 667 quia ab austro non solum advectas, sed et in terram dejectas fuisse scribunt Moses Num. XI, 31. et David Psal. LXXVIII, 28. Et vero falsissimum est, illas austro volare nunquam. Sunt enim aves migratoriae, quas ut aquilones autumno a nobis avehunt, ita austri vere ad nos revehunt. Aristoteles ubi supra, Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ οἱ ὄρτυγες (ἀπαίρουσι)· ἐὰν μή τινες ὑπολειφθῶσι ἐν εὐηλίοις χωρίοις· Similiter et coturnices (abeunt); nisi paucae locis apricis remanserint. Varro Rustic. lib. 3. cap. 5. Turdi quotannis in Italiam trans mare advolant circiter aequinoctium autumnale, et eodem revolant ad aequinoctium vernum. Et alio tempore turtures ac coturnices immani numero. Plinius, Coturnices ante etiam semper adveniunt quam grues. Solinus, Adveniendi habent tempora aestate depulsa: imo hyeme, ut multis docet magnus auctor in Solinum. Aloysius Mundella in Epistolis, Ad maritimam regionem circa Pisaurum ingens coturnicum copia adventare consuevit, et mille insidiis capi: sed potissimum sub extremum verni temporis illarum adventu observato. Bellonius Observat. lib. 2. cap. 17. ubi de itinere e Rhodo in Alexandriam, Plurimae coturnices, a septentrione meridiem versus volantes, in navi nostra captae sunt. Unde certo persuasus sum, coturnices aves esse migratorias. Nam prius cum verno tempore e Zacyntho in Euboeam navigarem, alias observaveram contraria profectione a meridie in septentrionem volantes. Gesnerus, Coturnices ad nos, ut audio, medio fere Aprili veniunt, et abeunt cum prima pruina ingruit. Ex quibus non solum constat, coturnices solum mutare, sed et medio vere ab austro in septentrionem migrare. Quod ideo hic observo, quia illo ipso tempore coturnices advexit auster in Israelitarum castra, nempe die XXIV secundi mensis. Nam vicesima discesserant e deserto Sinai; et post triduanum iter, cum carnem petiissent non sine multo murmure, promisit Deus, crastina die se daturum in mensem integrum, et misit coturnices. Vide Num. X, 11. 12. 33. et XI, 18.

II, 667 because Moses (Num 11:31) and David (Ps 78:28) write that they were not only carried by the south wind but also thrown down onto the ground. And indeed it is utterly false that they never fly with the south wind. For they are migratory birds: just as the north winds carry them away from us in autumn, so the south winds bring them back to us in spring. Aristotle, in the place cited above: Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ οἱ ὄρτυγες (ἀπαίρουσι)· ἐὰν μή τινες ὑπολειφθῶσι ἐν εὐηλίοις χωρίοις· [Homoiōs de kai hoi ortyges (apairousi)· ean mē tines hypoleiphthōsi en euēliois chōriois·] Likewise the quails also (depart), unless a few have remained in sunny places. Varro, Rustic. book 3, ch. 5: Thrushes fly every year across the sea into Italy around the autumn equinox, and fly back to the same place at the spring equinox. And at another time turtledoves and quails, in enormous numbers. Pliny: Quails also always arrive before the cranes. Solinus: They have their times of arrival when summer has been driven off; or rather winter, as the great commentator on Solinus shows at length. Aloysius Mundella in his Letters: To the coastal region around Pesaro a huge number of quails usually arrives, and they are caught with a thousand snares; but their arrival has been observed chiefly toward the end of spring. Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)], Observat. book 2, ch. 17, on the voyage from Rhodes to Alexandria: Very many quails, flying from the north toward the south, were caught on our ship. From this I am firmly convinced that quails are migratory birds. For earlier, when I was sailing in spring from Zacynthus to Euboea, I had observed others flying in the opposite direction, from the south to the north. Gesner: Quails come to us, as I hear, at about the middle of April, and leave when the first frost sets in. From these it is clear not only that quails change their country, but also that in mid-spring they migrate from the south to the north. I note this here because at precisely that time the south wind brought quails into the camp of the Israelites, namely on the 24th day of the second month. For on the twentieth they had departed from the wilderness of Sinai; and after a three days' journey, when they had demanded meat with much murmuring, God promised that on the next day he would give it for a whole month, and he sent quails. See Num 10:11–12. 33. and XI, 18.


IV. Copiam quod attinet, Psaltes coturnices Deum pluisse dicit ut pulverem atque ut arenam maris, Psal. LXXVIII, 27. id est, magna copia et ubertate demisisse. Sic apud Athenaeum libro octavo Phaenias narrat, ἐν Χεῤῥονήσῳ ἐπὶ τρισὶν ἡμέραις ὗσαι τὸν Θεὸν ἰχθύας, in Chersoneso Deum per tres dies pisces pluisse. Et Phylarchus ibidem, ἑωρακέναι τινὰς πολλαχοῦ τὸν Θεὸν ὕσαντα ἰχθῦσιν, πολλάκις δὲ καὶ πυροῖς, quosdam observasse, Deum multis in locis pluisse piscibus, saepe etiam tritico. Et Heraclides Lembus, Περὶ τὴν Παιονίαν II, 668 καὶ Δαρδανίαν βατράχους, φησὶν, ὕσεν ὁ Θεὸς καὶ τοσοῦτον αὐτῶν ἐγένετο τὸ πλῆθος, ὡς τὰς οἰκίας καὶ τὰς ὁδοὺς πλήρεις εἶναι· Circa Paeoniam et Dardaniam, inquit, tantam ranarum vim pluit Deus, ut domos et vias implerent. Caetera ibi vide, et nota in Exodi VIII, 3. Pari ratione coturnices Deus pluit tanta col. 105 copia, ut essent instar pulveris,

IV. As to the quantity, the Psalmist says that God rained quails like dust and like the sand of the sea, Ps 78:27, that is, sent them down in great quantity and abundance. Thus in Athenaeus, book 8, Phaenias relates ἐν Χεῤῥονήσῳ ἐπὶ τρισὶν ἡμέραις ὗσαι τὸν Θεὸν ἰχθύας [en Cherrhonēsō epi trisin hēmerais hysai ton Theon ichthyas], that in the Chersonese God rained fish for three days. And Phylarchus in the same place: ἑωρακέναι τινὰς πολλαχοῦ τὸν Θεὸν ὕσαντα ἰχθῦσιν, πολλάκις δὲ καὶ πυροῖς [heōrakenai tinas pollachou ton Theon hysanta ichthysin, pollakis de kai pyrois], that some have observed God raining fish in many places, and often wheat too. And Heraclides Lembus: Περὶ τὴν Παιονίαν II, 668 καὶ Δαρδανίαν βατράχους, φησὶν, ὕσεν ὁ Θεὸς καὶ τοσοῦτον αὐτῶν ἐγένετο τὸ πλῆθος, ὡς τὰς οἰκίας καὶ τὰς ὁδοὺς πλήρεις εἶναι· [Peri tēn Paionian kai Dardanian batrachous, phēsin, hysen ho Theos kai tosouton autōn egeneto to plēthos, hōs tas oikias kai tas hodous plēreis einai·] Around Paeonia and Dardania, he says, God rained such a mass of frogs that they filled the houses and the roads. See the rest there, and the note on Exodi VIII, 3. In the same way God rained quails in such col. 105 quantity that they were like dust,


— — — numeroque carentis arenae.

— — — and of the sand that has no number.


Et immani numero fuisse, probat Moses duobus argumentis: uno, quod non per castra solum, sed et undequaque dispersae erant, ad iter unius diei, et ad al-titudinem duorum cubitorum supra terram extabant. Alterum, quod in iis aucupandis et colligendis toto biduo sic laborarunt tot hominum myriades, ut, qui minimum collegerat illarum, congesserit decem coros [Numer. XI, 31. 32.]. Haec igitur coturnicum nubes circumquaque patuit minimum quadraginta millia, (nam diurnum iter minimum est viginti millium) et duobus cubitis supra terram eminebat. Quod trifariam potest intelligi. 1. Ut sonet, coturnices in toto illo spatio ita fuisse coacervatas, ut ubique ad duos cubitos eminuerint. 2. Ut coturnicum bicubitales acervos significet hinc ita fuisse dispersos, ut vacua subinde spatia remanserint, per quae populus iter faceret, cibos, a Deo oblatos, collecturus. 3. Ut in ipso volatu significentur ita se demisisse, ut a terra non abfuerint plusquam duobus cubitis, quasi captantium manibus ultro se offerrent. Quod sequutus Hieronymus sacra verba ita reddidit: Volabantque in aëre duobus cubitis altitudine super terram. Et Ionathan, וכרום תרתין אמין הוה פרח על אנפי ארעא והוו מהלכין בהון עד פרתהון מטול דלא ילעון בזמן מכנשהון יתהון, Et ad duorum cubitorum altitudinem volabant super faciem terrae, et ibant inter illos (Israelitas) usque ad umbilicum, ne laborarent in iis colligendis. Et R. Selomo in Notis, פורחות בגובה עד שהן כנגד לבו של אדם כדי שלא יהא טורח באסיפתן לא להגביה ולא לשחות, Volabant ad humani pectoris altitudinem, ne quisquam in earum collectione se attollendo aut deprimendo fatigaret. Neque dubito, quin Philo id ipsum in animo habuerit, cum describit ὀρτυγομη-τρῶν νέφος τὰς πτήσεις προσγειοτάτας ποιούμενον εἰς τὸ εὔθηρον, coturnicum nubem terrae proxime volantem, ut facile esset aucupium. Quod coturnicis naturae non male convenit, quae cum ad nos venit, inquit Plinius, terrestris potius quam sublimis est. Itaque ab hac interpretatione non sum alienus, quamvis secundam praeferam; quia David diserte dicit, coturnices cecidisse in medio castrorum, et Moses, fusas fuisse super terram. Quibus verbis describi videntur humi plane jacentes, potius quam in infimo aëre volitantes. Eodem pertinet pluendi vox. Neque enim pluere dicuntur, nisi quae in terram usque prolabuntur. Praeterea volantes vix potuissent in biduo tam multae capi, ut quisque habuisset II, 669 decem coros (9). Corus enim Hebraeorum maxima fuit mensura, continens decem batos, ut batus tria sata, satum sex cabos, cabus quatuor logos, logus sex ova. Hebraice חומר chomer dicitur, quod ad חמור chamor, id est, asinum, revocant nonnulli Hebraeorum, quasi fuerit onus asini. Sed alii verius corum contendunt duplo fuisse graviorem, adeoque camelum oneravisse. Itaque verissimile est, in spatio, quod definit Moses, id est, per iter diurnum circa castra, non ubique, sed passim coturnicum acervos jacuisse (10), alicubi super terram ad duos cubitos eminentes. Quas longo volatu fessas vel divina vis, vel angeli a Deo missi, vel venti vehementiores hinc inde disjecerant, ut huic populo pro cibo essent.

That they were immense in number, Moses proves by two arguments. The first is that they were scattered not only through the camp but on every side, for a day's journey, and stood two cubits high above the ground. The second is that so many myriads of men laboured for two whole days in catching and gathering them that he who had gathered the least of them heaped up ten cors [Numer. XI, 31. 32.]. This cloud of quails, then, extended on every side at least forty miles (for a day's journey is at least twenty miles), and rose two cubits above the ground. This can be understood in three ways. 1. That it means the quails were so heaped up over that whole space that everywhere they rose to two cubits. 2. That it signifies heaps of quails two cubits high, scattered here and there in such a way that empty spaces were left between them, through which the people might make their way to gather the food offered by God. 3. That it signifies that in their very flight they came down so low that they were no more than two cubits from the ground, as though offering themselves of their own accord to the hands of those catching them. Following this, Jerome rendered the sacred words thus: And they flew in the air at a height of two cubits above the ground. And Jonathan: וכרום תרתין אמין הוה פרח על אנפי ארעא והוו מהלכין בהון עד פרתהון מטול דלא ילעון בזמן מכנשהון יתהון, And they flew at a height of two cubits over the face of the ground, and (the Israelites) walked among them up to the navel, so that they might not toil in gathering them. And R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] in his Notes: פורחות בגובה עד שהן כנגד לבו של אדם כדי שלא יהא טורח באסיפתן לא להגביה ולא לשחות, They flew at the height of a man's breast, so that no one in gathering them should tire himself by stretching up or bending down. Nor do I doubt that Philo had this very thing in mind when he describes ὀρτυγομητρῶν νέφος τὰς πτήσεις προσγειοτάτας ποιούμενον εἰς τὸ εὔθηρον [ortygomētrōn nephos tas ptēseis prosgeiotatas poioumenon eis to euthēron], a cloud of quails flying very close to the ground, so that catching them was easy. This fits the nature of the quail not badly, which, when it comes to us, says Pliny, is a ground bird rather than a high-flying one. I am therefore not averse to this interpretation, although I prefer the second, because David says expressly that the quails fell in the midst of the camp, and Moses that they were spread out upon the ground. These words seem to describe birds lying flat on the ground rather than fluttering in the lowest air. The word raining points the same way, for only things that fall all the way to the ground are said to rain. Moreover, had they been flying, hardly so many could have been caught in two days that each man had II, 669 ten cors R9. For the cor was the largest measure of the Hebrews, containing ten baths, as the bath contained three seahs, the seah six kabs, the kab four logs, the log six eggs. In Hebrew it is called חומר chomer, which some of the Hebrews derive from חמור chamor, that is, ass, as though it had been an ass's load. But others more correctly contend that the cor was twice as heavy, and so would have loaded a camel. It is therefore most probable that in the space Moses defines, that is, a day's journey around the camp, heaps of quails lay not everywhere but here and there R10, in places rising two cubits above the ground. These, wearied by their long flight, either divine power, or angels sent by God, or rather violent winds had scattered hither and thither, to serve this people as food.


Fateor interim, me ultima illa ratione, a decem coris sumpta, quos ex illo populo quisque collegisse creditur, non magnopere niti. Neque enim opus fuit, ut singuli coturnicum decem coros colligerent. Deus huic populo carnes in mensem promiserat, cui promisso fecisset satis, si unicuique pro decem coris solum dedisset cori trientem. Quod probare est in proclivi. Singulis Israelitis in diurnum cibum assignatur gomor Mannae Exod. XVI, 16. id est, ephae decima pars ibidem versu 36. [al. 35.]. Et Epha est decima pars cori Ezech. XLV, col. 106 11. Itaque in coro sunt centum mensurae gomor. Et, si gomor in diem sufficit, corus sufficit in centum dies, id est, in tres menses et amplius. Proinde, si singuli Israelitae coturnicum colligerunt decem coros, collegerunt plus trigesies quam Deus promiserat. Sed cum dicit Moses, etiam illum, qui minimum collegerat, decem coros collegisse, fortasse nonnisi ad familiarum capita hoc referendum est: neque in illo censu numerantur uxores, liberi, servi. Vel, quod puto verius, ibi loci עשרה חמרים non sunt decem cori, sed decem acervi. Nam et חמר chomer acervum sonat. Ita Habac. III, 15. חמר מים רבים, est acervus aquarum multarum. Et eodem sensu de ranis dicitur Exod. VIII, 10. ויצברו אותם חמרים חמרים, Et congregaverunt eos in acervos, acervos, id est, in multos acervos. Et Iudic. XV, 17. [al. 16.] חמרתים in Duali sunt duo acervi. Sed et hoc ipso loco עשרה חמרים; Onkelos reddit עשרא דגורים, et Arabs Parisiis editus عشرة انابير, et Erpenianus عشرة اجداس decem acervos. Quomodo si sumpseris, Moses non praecise definiverit, quam coturnicum mensuram II, 670 unusquisque collegerit. Sed solum decem acervos collectos fuisse dixerit ab eo, qui minimum. Decem acervos, id est, plurimos, phrasi Hebraeis familiari, qua decem pro multis passim usurpant. Sic Gen. XXXI, 7. Mutavit mercedem meam decies. Num. XIV, 22. Tentarunt me jam decies. Nehem. IV, 6. Iam decies nobis dixerunt. Iob. XIX, 3. Iam decies ignominia me affecistis, id est, multoties. Levit. XXVI, 26. Decem mulieres panem vestrum coquent, id est, multae. 1 Sam. I, 8. Annon melior sum tibi, quam decem filii? Eccles. VII, 19. Sapientia robur confert sapienti, plus quam decem principes, qui sunt in eadem civitate. Zachar. VIII, 23. Decem homines apprehendent alam hominis Iudaei, id est, plurimi. Ita igitur decem coturnicum acervos pro pluribus dixerit Moses (11). Et sic vertendum potius quam decem choros, praeter ea, quae jam diximus, etiam haec ratio suadet, quod כור, corus, seu חומר chomer, granorum est mensura, non carnium (12). Haec observatio non est nihili. Quia, si singuli Israelitae decem coturnicum coros collegisse dicantur, illarum numerus erit immanis, et superabit omnem fidem. Cornelius a Lapide, qui supputare conatus est in Commentariis in hunc locum, ita subducit calculos, ut probet, Israelitas collegisse circiter duodecim millia millionum coturnicum. At nos, pro decem coris, singulos statuimus ne tertiam quidem cori partem collegisse, aut absumpsisse. Non, ut minuamus Dei virtutem, sed ne fidei vim faciamus, ab illa plura extorquentes, quam Deus nobis in verbo suo revelavit (13).

Meanwhile I confess that I do not rely much on that last argument, taken from the ten cors which each of that people is believed to have gathered. For there was no need for each person to gather ten cors of quails. God had promised this people meat for a month, and he would have fulfilled this promise if, instead of ten cors, he had given each person only a third of a cor. This is easy to prove. To each of the Israelites an omer of manna is assigned as daily food, Exod 16:16, that is, the tenth part of an ephah, in the same place, verse 36 [var. 35]. And an ephah is the tenth part of a cor, Ezech. XLV, col. 106 11. Therefore a cor contains a hundred omer measures. And if an omer suffices for a day, a cor suffices for a hundred days, that is, for three months and more. Accordingly, if each of the Israelites gathered ten cors of quails, they gathered more than thirty times what God had promised. But when Moses says that even he who had gathered least gathered ten cors, perhaps this is to be referred only to the heads of families; and wives, children and slaves are not counted in that census. Or, what I think truer, in that place עשרה חמרים are not ten cors but ten heaps. For חמר chomer also means heap. Thus in Hab 3:15. חמר מים רבים is a heap of many waters. And in the same sense it is said of the frogs in Exod 8:10. ויצברו אותם חמרים חמרים, And they gathered them into heaps, heaps, that is, into many heaps. And in Judg 15:17 [var. 16.] חמרתים in the dual is two heaps. But also in this very passage עשרה חמרים, Onkelos renders עשרא דגורים, and the Arabic edited at Paris عشرة انابير [ʿashrat anābīr], and Erpenianus [=the Arabic version edited by Thomas Erpenius (Pentateuch 1622; New Testament 1616)] عشرة اجداس [ʿashrat ajdās], ten heaps. If you take it this way, Moses will not have defined precisely what measure of quails II, 670 each person gathered, but will only have said that ten heaps were gathered by him who gathered least. Ten heaps, that is, very many, by a phrase familiar to the Hebrews, who everywhere use ten for many. Thus Gen. XXXI, 7: He has changed my wages ten times. Num 14:22: They have tempted me now ten times. Neh 4:6: They have told us now ten times. Job 19:3: These ten times you have reproached me, that is, many times. Lev 26:26: Ten women shall bake your bread, that is, many. 1 Sam 1:8: Am I not better to you than ten sons? Eccl 7:19: Wisdom gives strength to the wise more than ten rulers who are in the same city. Zech 8:23: Ten men shall take hold of the skirt of a Jew, that is, very many. So, then, Moses will have said ten heaps of quails for many R11. And that it should be translated thus rather than ten cors is suggested, besides what we have already said, also by this reason: that כור, cor, or חומר chomer, is a measure of grain, not of meat R12. This observation is not worthless. For if each of the Israelites is said to have gathered ten cors of quails, their number will be enormous and will exceed all belief. Cornelius a Lapide, who tried to compute it in his Commentaries on this passage, reckons the figures so as to prove that the Israelites gathered about twelve thousand million quails. But we, instead of ten cors, maintain that each did not gather or consume even a third part of a cor. We do this not to diminish God's power, but so as not to do violence to faith by extorting from it more than God has revealed to us in his word R13.


II, 671 At, inquies, hoc saltem constat a Mose asseri, Deum per mensem pavisse coturnicibus omnes Israelitas, in quibus fuere peditum sexaginta myriades. Fateor et hanc avem in nostris regionibus minus esse frequentem, quam ut tale quid possit fieri absque nova creatione. Sed in calidis regionibus longe aliter haec res se habet. In iis enim coturnicum ubertas longe major est. Sic in Graecia coturnice nihil fuisse vulgatius, colligere est ex his Aristophonis Comici de pavonibus apud Athenaeum lib. 14.

II, 671 But, you will say, this at least is certain: Moses asserts that God fed all the Israelites with quails for a month, among whom there were six hundred thousand footmen. I admit too that this bird is less frequent in our regions than that such a thing could happen without a new creation. But in hot regions the matter is quite otherwise, for there the abundance of quails is far greater. Thus that in Greece nothing was more common than the quail may be gathered from these lines of the comic poet Aristophon on peacocks in Athenaeus, book 14.


Τὸν ταὼν μὲν ὡς ἅπαξ τις ζεῦγος ἤγαγεν μόνον,
Σπάνιον ὂν τὸ χρῆμα· πλείους δ’ εἰσὶ νῦν τῶν ὀρτύγων·

Τὸν ταὼν μὲν ὡς ἅπαξ τις ζεῦγος ἤγαγεν μόνον, [Ton taōn men hōs hapax tis zeugos ēgagen monon,] Σπάνιον ὂν τὸ χρῆμα· πλείους δ’ εἰσὶ νῦν τῶν ὀρτύγων· [Spanion on to chrēma; pleious d’ eisi nyn tōn ortygōn;]


Pavonum olim solum par unum quispiam adduxerat, rem illo aevo raram: nunc vero plures sunt quam coturnices. Et Romae etiam eas viluisse, docent haec Iuvenalis in haeredipetas, Satyra 12.

Of peacocks someone had once brought only a single pair, a rare thing in that age; but now there are more of them than quails. And that at Rome too they were cheap is shown by these lines of Juvenal against legacy-hunters, Satire 12.


Tres habet haeredes; libet exspectare quis aegram
Et claudentem oculos gallinam impendat amico
Tam sterili: verum haec nimia est impensa, coturnix
Nulla unquam pro patre cadet. — —

He has three heirs; I should like to see who would spend a sick hen, closing its eyes, on so barren a friend: but this is too great an expense; no quail will ever fall for a father. — —


Negat, pro salute amici, qui jam pater est, et haeredes habet, a quoquam offer- col. 107 ri gallinam, quamvis aegram et moribundam: sed ne coturnicem quidem, quae vilissima est avis, atque impensae multo minoris. Neque id mirum; si vera sunt, quae ex Flavio Blondo narrat Gesnerus, in Antiatum littore, cum primo vere hirundines et coturnices, transmisso mari infero, in Italiam redeunt, intra passuum quinque millia nonnunquam in dies capi centies mille hujus generis aviculas, et hoc aucupium fere per mensem continuari. Neque dissimilia tradunt veteres (14). Ita Varro, postquam turdos ex Italia trans mare avolare, II, 672 et eodem revolare scripsit circa aequinoctia, Et alio tempore, inquit, turtures, ac coturnices immani numero. Unde est, quod volando fessae quandoque in naves incidunt tanta copia, ut illas pondere suo demergant. Plinius, Ad-volant et hae (coturnices) simili modo, non sine periculo navigantium, cum appropinquavere terris. Quippe velis insidunt, et hoc semper noctu, merguntque navigia. Solinus, Ubi terram persentiscunt, coëunt catervatim. Deinde globatae vehementius properant: quae festinatio plerumque exitium portat navigantibus. Accidit enim in noctibus, ut vela insidant, et praeponderatis finibus alveos vertant, alias vergant, aut mergant, ut in Plinio. Eodem facit, quod a coturnicum copia Ortygia nomen olim commune fuit pluribus locis. Sic Delus Ortygia dicta est, et insula Syracusarum, et urbs Ephesus, et lucus illi proximus, et alius prope Miletum. Quid quod eapse de causa universae Libyae veteres Ortygiae nomen indiderunt? Testis Stephanus in Λιβύῃ.

He says that no one offers a hen for the health of a friend who is already a father and has heirs, however sick and dying he may be col. 107; not even a quail, which is the cheapest of birds and costs much less. Nor is this surprising, if what Gesner relates from Flavius Blondus is true: on the shore of Antium, when in early spring the swallows and quails cross the Tyrrhenian Sea and return to Italy, within five thousand paces sometimes a hundred thousand little birds of this kind are caught daily, and this fowling continues for about a month. The ancients report similar things R14. Thus Varro, after writing that thrushes fly away from Italy across the sea, II, 672 and fly back again about the equinoxes, says: And at another time turtledoves and quails, in enormous numbers. Hence, exhausted by flying, they sometimes fall upon ships in such numbers that they sink them by their weight. Pliny: These (quails) also fly in in a similar way, not without danger to sailors, when they have come near land. For they settle on the sails, and always at night, and sink the vessels. Solinus: When they perceive land, they gather in flocks. Then, massed together, they hasten more vehemently; and this haste generally brings destruction to sailors. For it happens at night that they settle on the sails and, weighing down the edges, overturn the hulls, elsewhere tilt, or sink, as in Pliny. To the same effect is the fact that from the abundance of quails the name Ortygia was once common to several places. Thus Delos was called Ortygia, and the island of Syracuse, and the city of Ephesus, and the grove nearest to it, and another near Miletus. What of the fact that for this very reason the ancients gave the name Ortygia to the whole of Libya? The witness is Stephanus under Λιβύῃ [Libyē].


Sed nullibi coturnicum copia major, quam in Aegypto et vicinis locis; sive aëris tepor eas alliciat, seu soli ubertas et foecunditas. Hinc Iosephus, Τρέφει δὲ τοῦτο τὸ ὄρνεον, ὡς οὐδὲν ἕτερον, ὁ Ἀράβιος κόλπος· Hanc avem prae caeteris alit Arabicus sinus. Diodorum quoque jam audivimus de immensa coturnicum copia circa Rhinocoluram. Et multa veteres de chenniis, coturnicis specie, Aegypto peculiari, qua certa anni tempestate Aegyptii sic abundabant, ut, cum omnes absumere non possent, eas in posterum sale condire cogerentur. Quod maxime notandum in regione tam populosa, ut Theocritus c) in ea censeat oppidorum plus triginta millia: et Iosephus d) hominum septingentas et quinquaginta myriades, absque incolis Alexandriae. Quae de chenniis diximus, probant haec loca: Athenaeus lib. 9. cap. 11. in fine tractatus De coturnicibus, Τῶν δὲ καλουμένων χεννίων, μικρὸν δ᾽ ἐστὶν ὀρτύγιον, μνημονεύει Κλεομένης ἐν τῇ πρὸς Ἀλέξανδρον ἐπιστολῇ γράφων οὕτως· Φαληρίδας ταριχηρὰς μυρίας, τυλάδας πεντακισχι-λίας, χέννια ταριχηρὰ μύρια. Chenniorum, quae vocant, sunt autem parvae coturnices, meminit Cleomenes in epistola ad Alexandrum, sic scribens: Phalarides salsas decies mille, tyladum quinque millia, chennia salsa decies mille. Phalaris mergi, et tylas turdi genus est, et chennium coturnicis; ut auctor est ipse Athenaeus. Ibidem Hipparchus in Iliade Aegyptia,

But nowhere is the abundance of quails greater than in Egypt and the neighbouring places, whether the warmth of the air attracts them or the richness and fertility of the soil. Hence Josephus: Τρέφει δὲ τοῦτο τὸ ὄρνεον, ὡς οὐδὲν ἕτερον, ὁ Ἀράβιος κόλπος· [Trephei de touto to orneon, hōs ouden heteron, ho Arabios kolpos] The Arabian Gulf nourishes this bird above all others. We have also already heard Diodorus on the immense abundance of quails around Rhinocolura. And the ancients say much about the chennia, a kind of quail peculiar to Egypt, with which at a certain season of the year the Egyptians so abounded that, since they could not consume them all, they were forced to preserve them in salt for later. This is especially noteworthy in a region so populous that Theocritus c) reckons more than thirty thousand towns in it, and Josephus d) seven hundred and fifty myriads of people, apart from the inhabitants of Alexandria. What we have said about the chennia is proved by these passages: Athenaeus book 9, ch. 11, at the end of the treatise On quails: Τῶν δὲ καλουμένων χεννίων, μικρὸν δ᾽ ἐστὶν ὀρτύγιον, μνημονεύει Κλεομένης ἐν τῇ πρὸς Ἀλέξανδρον ἐπιστολῇ γράφων οὕτως· Φαληρίδας ταριχηρὰς μυρίας, τυλάδας πεντακισχιλίας, χέννια ταριχηρὰ μύρια. [Tōn de kaloumenōn chenniōn, mikron d᾽ estin ortygion, mnēmoneuei Kleomenēs en tē pros Alexandron epistolē graphōn houtōs· Phalēridas tarichēras myrias, tyladas pentakischilias, chennia tarichēra myria.] Cleomenes mentions the so-called chennia, which are small quails, in his letter to Alexander, writing thus: ten thousand salted phalarides, five thousand tylades, ten thousand salted chennia. The phalaris is a kind of diver, the tylas a kind of thrush, and the chennium a kind of quail, as Athenaeus himself states. In the same place Hipparchus in the Egyptian Iliad:


Οὔ μοι Αἰγυπτίων βίος ἤρεσεν, οἷον ἔχουσιν
Χέννια τίλλοντες· — — — —

Οὔ μοι Αἰγυπτίων βίος ἤρεσεν, οἷον ἔχουσιν Χέννια τίλλοντες· — — — — [Ou moi Aigyptiōn bios ēresen, hoion echousin Chennia tillontes]


Mihi non placet vita, quam Aegyptii degunt, chennia vellentes. Poeta vetus in sordidum convivatorem, qui hospitibus vilia et salsa omnia apponebat, Anthologiae lib. 2. cap. 47.

I do not like the life which the Egyptians lead, plucking chennia. An old poet, against a stingy host who served his guests everything cheap and salted, Anthology book 2, ch. 47:


II, 673 Ἡμεῖς δ᾽ ἐσθίομεν κεκλημένοι ἅλμυρα πάντα,
Χέννια, καὶ τυροὺς, χηνὸς ἁλιστὰ λίπη.

II, 673 Ἡμεῖς δ᾽ ἐσθίομεν κεκλημένοι ἅλμυρα πάντα, Χέννια, καὶ τυροὺς, χηνὸς ἁλιστὰ λίπη. [Hēmeis d᾽ esthiomen keklēmenoi halmyra panta, Chennia, kai tyrous, chēnos halista lipē.]


Nos vero invitati comedimus salsa omnia, chennia, et caseos, et anseris salsas adipes. Hesychius, Χέννιον· ὀρνιθάριόν τι κατ᾽ Αἴγυπτον ταριχευόμενον· Chennium avitium quoddam in Aegypto, sale conditum. Chenniorum igitur et coturnicum in Aegypto et tota Africa cum tanta copia fuerit, unde ventorum alis vectae sunt in castra Israelitarum? Non opus hic, quod quidam faciunt, nova miracula sibi fingere, et creavisse Deum, aut multiplicavisse coturnices, quomo- col. 108 do Christus panes inter manus Apostolorum. Nostrum est, Sacro textui mordicus adhaerere, in quo coturnices, virtute Dei creatas, aut multiplicatas fuisse non legimus, sed a ventis fuisse advectas ex transmarinis regionibus. Non me latet, has appellari novam creaturam avium in Vulgata versione Sap. XIX, 10. Atque inde a multis colligi, Deum illas de novo creasse. Sed, ut de auctore libri taceam, cui fidem nostram non adstrinximus, Graecum exemplar non ha-bet κτίσιν, creaturam, sed γένεσιν νέαν ὀρνέων, generationem novam avium; Syrus itidem, ܡܘܠܕܐ ܚܕܬܐ ܕܦܪܚܬܐ, et Arabs, توالد طيور جديدة Et nova vocatur non in se, sed Israelitis, qui nihil tale experti erant. Quale est, quod idem auctor huic ipsi cibo tribuit ξένην γεῦσιν, novum saporem, Sap. XVI, 2. id est, illo vescentibus insuetum et inexpertum. Hic igitur nullam agnoscimus coturnicum creationem. Sed miraculosum id fuit, quod tanta copia advectae sunt, atque eo praecise tempore, quod Deus definiverat, et omnes prolapsae sunt circa castra Israelitarum, ut ipsis essent pro cibo divinitus oblato.

But we, having been invited, ate all the salted things, chennia, and cheeses, and salted goose fat. Hesychius: Χέννιον· ὀρνιθάριόν τι κατ᾽ Αἴγυπτον ταριχευόμενον [Chennion· ornitharion ti kat᾽ Aigypton taricheuomenon]; Chennium, a certain small bird in Egypt, preserved in salt. Since, then, there was so great an abundance of chennia and quails in Egypt and in all Africa, from where were they carried on the wings of the winds into the camp of the Israelites? There is no need here, as some do, to invent new miracles for ourselves, and to say that God created or multiplied the quails, as Christ multiplied the loaves in the hands of the Apostles. col. 108 It is our part to hold fast to the sacred text, in which we do not read that the quails were created or multiplied by the power of God, but that they were brought by the winds from regions beyond the sea. I am not unaware that in the Vulgate version, Wis 19:10, they are called a new creature of birds, and that many infer from this that God created them anew. But, to say nothing of the author of the book, to whom we have not bound our faith, the Greek copy does not have κτίσιν [ktisin], creature, but γένεσιν νέαν ὀρνέων [genesin nean orneōn], a new generation of birds; the Syriac likewise has ܡܘܠܕܐ ܚܕܬܐ ܕܦܪܚܬܐ [מולדא חדתא דפרחתא], and the Arabic توالد طيور جديدة [tawālud ṭuyūr jadīda]. And it is called new not in itself, but to the Israelites, who had experienced nothing of the kind. Similar is the fact that the same author attributes to this very food ξένην γεῦσιν [xenēn geusin], a new taste, Wis 16:2, that is, one unaccustomed and unknown to those who ate it. Here, therefore, we recognize no creation of quails. But this was miraculous: that they were brought in such great abundance, and at precisely the time that God had appointed, and that they all fell down around the camp of the Israelites, so as to serve them as food divinely provided.


V. Superest quinta quaestio de Iudaeorum poena, quam inflixit Deus coturnices comedentibus. Et peccatum quidem id fuit, quod, pertaesi suae conditionis, ita in Deum obmurmuraverant: Quis dabit nobis carnem comedendam! Recordamur piscium, quos in Aegypto gratis edebamus, cucumerumque, et peponum, et porrorum, et ceparum, et alliorum: at nunc anima nostra arida est, nec quidquam praeter Manna oculis nostris obversatur, Num. XI, 4. 5. 6. Unde Psaltes Ps. LXXVIII, 19. Obloquentes contra Deum dixerunt, An posset Deus instruere mensam in hoc deserto? En! ita percussit rupem, ut fluxerint aquae, et torrentes exundaverint. An etiam cibum posset dare? An parabit carnem populo suo? In quibus verbis 1. mire ingratos se produnt, dum praesenti praeferunt praeteritam conditionem, id est, servitutem Aegyptiacam, e qua Deus eos asseruerat forti manu et extenso brachio, libertati, qua fruebantur. Haec audiens quis non putasset, eos in Aegypto laute vixisse et in ampla fortuna? In qua tamen misere vixerant, sub Pharaonis jugo pressi et prope oppressi: sed ingratis id solenne est, ut, licet ad majora evecti, tamen praeterita extollant, et fastidiant II, 674 praesentia, ne in melius mutati status gratias ulli se debere agnoscant. 2. Miram aperiunt ἀῤῥωστίαν τῆς διανοίας in eo, quod pisciculos, cucumeres, pepones, porros, caepe, et allia, carnalia denique praeferunt spiritualibus bonis et gloriosae Dei praesentiae, quam testatam fecerat tot signis et miraculis. 3. Non contenti Manna, unde victus necessarius abunde illis suppetebat, carnem insuper petierant, et Deum circumscripserant, ut habetur Psal. LXXVIII, 41. hoc est, potentiam ejus arbitratu suo definiverant, non solum liberari petentes, sed et hoc vel illo modo. 4. Post expertam toties Dei virtutem, tamen haec sunt verba diffidentiae, An posset Deus mensam in hoc deserto instruere? An posset etiam cibum dare? Deus igitur, ad iram merito provocatus, spondet, se daturum carnes, non solum in unum aut alterum diem, sed et in mensem integrum, quasque, non tantum ad satietatem, sed et ad nauseam et fastidium usque comesas, tandem respuant ac rejiciant. Quae verba sunt animi concitati, quique nonnisi in ira sua populi preces exaudierat. Mense igitur jam expleto, cum cibum, quo se ingurgitaverant, adhuc in ore haberent, Deus, in eos excandescens, populum percussit plaga magna. Hanc Aben Ezra pestem esse vult. Sunt, qui רזון, id est, maciem, seu phthisim, significari colligunt ex Psal. CVI, 15. Alii aliter exponunt. Sed iis accedo, quibus haec plaga est ignis, a quo absumpti sint ex hoc populo nonnulli. Ita enim habet David Psal. LXXVIII, col. 109 21. Ideo audiens Dominus excanduit (audiens scilicet quae allata sunt ex praecedente versu, An posset Deus mensam, etc.) et ignis accensus est in Iacob. Ignem intellige, de quo Num. XI, 1. Et, cum populus quiritaretur, malum fuit in auribus Domini. Audiens igitur Dominus excanduit, et exardescens ignis Domini consumpsit extrema castrorum, etc. usque ad versum quartum, ubi breviter narrari videntur per πρόληψιν, quae postea uberius reliquo capite explicantur. Et eidem loco duplex nomen inditum: unum Tabera ab incendio, Num. XI, 3. alterum Kibrot-taava, quia ibi sepulti sunt, qui carnes concupiverant, Num. XI, 34. (15). Est et aliud exemplum in hoc eodem populo similis pervicaciae.

V. There remains the fifth question, concerning the punishment that God inflicted on the Jews who ate the quails. The sin was this: weary of their condition, they had murmured against God as follows: Who will give us meat to eat! We remember the fish that we ate in Egypt for nothing, and the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlic: but now our soul is dried up, and nothing is before our eyes except the Manna, Num 11:4–5. 6. Hence the Psalmist, Ps 78:19: Speaking against God they said, Can God furnish a table in this wilderness? Behold! he struck the rock so that waters flowed and streams overflowed. Can he also give food? Will he provide meat for his people? In these words, 1. they show themselves remarkably ungrateful, since they prefer their former condition, that is, the Egyptian servitude, from which God had rescued them with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, to the liberty they now enjoyed. Who, hearing this, would not have thought that they had lived sumptuously in Egypt and in great prosperity? Yet there they had lived wretchedly, pressed and nearly crushed under Pharaoh's yoke. But it is customary for the ungrateful, even when raised to greater things, to extol the past and disdain II, 674 the present, lest they acknowledge that they owe thanks to anyone for the improvement of their state. 2. They reveal a remarkable ἀῤῥωστίαν τῆς διανοίας [arrhōstian tēs dianoias] in that they prefer little fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic, in short carnal things, to spiritual goods and to the glorious presence of God, which he had attested by so many signs and miracles. 3. Not content with the Manna, from which the necessary sustenance was abundantly supplied to them, they had demanded meat besides, and had limited God, as it says in Ps 78:41, that is, they had defined his power by their own judgement, asking not only to be delivered, but to be delivered in this or that way. 4. After having experienced God's power so many times, these are nevertheless words of distrust: Can God furnish a table in this wilderness? Can he also give food? God therefore, justly provoked to anger, promises that he will give meat, not only for one or two days but for a whole month, so that, having eaten it not only to satiety but even to nausea and loathing, they would at last spit it out and reject it. These are the words of one whose mind is stirred, and who had heard the people's prayers only in his anger. So when the month was over, while they still had in their mouths the food with which they had gorged themselves, God, blazing against them, struck the people with a great plague. Aben Ezra takes this to be pestilence. There are some who infer from Ps 106:15 that רזון, that is, leanness or consumption, is meant. Others explain it otherwise. But I side with those for whom this plague is fire, by which some of this people were consumed. For so David has it, Psal. LXXVIII, col. 109 21: Therefore the Lord heard and was enraged (hearing, that is, what is reported in the preceding verse, Can God furnish a table, etc.) and a fire was kindled in Jacob. Understand the fire spoken of in Num 11:1: And when the people complained, it was evil in the ears of the Lord. So the Lord heard and was enraged, and the fire of the Lord, blazing up, consumed the outermost parts of the camp, etc., up to the fourth verse, where the things that are afterwards explained more fully in the rest of the chapter seem to be narrated briefly by πρόληψιν [prolēpsin]. And the same place was given a double name: one, Tabera, from the burning, Num 11:3; the other, Kibrot-taava, because those who had craved meat were buried there, Num 11:34 R15. There is also another example of similar obstinacy in this same people.


II, 675 Nam Exod. XVI, 2. murmurasse legitur congregatio, et dixisse Mosi et Aaroni: Utinam mortui essemus per manum Domini in terra Aegypti, cum assidentes ollis carnium panem comedebamus usque ad satietatem! At in hanc solitudinem nos adduxistis, ut universus hic coetus fame conficiatur. Sed in pari, ut videtur, causa, dispar fuit judicium. His enim murmuratoribus Deus illa ipsa vespera coturnices, et postridie Mannam indulsit, nullas ab iis poenas reposcens, Exod. XVI, 12. 13. Nempe Deus eadem peccata potest vel in justitia punire, vel in misericordia condonare et remittere. Quamvis cur in posterioribus graviter puniverit, quod prioribus benigne remiserat, multae possint afferri causae. Primo enim in peccata, quae semel remisit Deus, si quis rursus incidat, gravius peccat; quia praeter Dei justitiam spernit insuper misericordiam, et ideo malus est, quia Deus fuit bonus. Praeterea priores ideo murmuraverant, quia fame premebantur et omnium rerum inopia. At his Manna erat pro cibo, qua satietati, quod carnes tam avide expetebant, et petebant tam importune, vox non fuit a necessitate extorta, sed ab improba libidine. Denique priores adhuc rudes, et nondum data Lege, statim ab excessu Aegypti, posteriores jam edocti murmurant, et post legem acceptam, unde peccatum sit gravius. Ut non mirum sit, quod Deus, qui prioribus pepercerat, in hos tam rigide animadvertit.

II, 675 For in Exod 16:2 we read that the congregation murmured and said to Moses and Aaron: Would that we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the pots of meat and ate bread to the full! But you have brought us into this wilderness, so that this whole assembly may be destroyed by hunger. But in what seems a like case, the judgement was unlike. For to these murmurers God granted quails that very evening and Manna the next day, exacting no punishment from them, Exod 16:12–13. Indeed, God can either punish the same sins in justice or pardon and remit them in mercy. Yet many reasons can be given why he punished the latter severely for what he had kindly remitted to the former. First, if anyone falls again into sins which God has once remitted, he sins more gravely, because besides God's justice he also spurns his mercy, and so he is evil because God was good. Moreover, the former had murmured because they were pressed by hunger and the want of everything. But the latter had Manna for food, which satisfied them, so that their so greedily desiring meat and demanding it so importunately was a cry wrung not by necessity but by wicked lust. Finally, the former were still untaught, and the Law had not yet been given, immediately after the departure from Egypt; the latter murmur when already instructed, and after receiving the Law, so that the sin is graver. So it is not surprising that God, who had spared the former, dealt so severely with these.


Si Iudaeis credimus, Dii Sepharvaeorum, Adramelech et Anamelech, de quibus 2 Reg. XVII, 31. sub pavonum et phasianorum, aut coturnicum specie culti sunt. Kimchius in eum locum, ובירושלמי אדרמלך וענמלך זה טווס ופסיוני וטווס הוא הנקרא בלשון לע״ז פאון וידוע הוא ופסיוני הוא שלו והרגים שאלו ויבא שלו שאלו בסרא ואייתי פסיונין, In Talmude Hierosolymitano (tractatu De Idololatria) Adramelech et Anamelech, id est, ταὼς, et phasianus. Et ταὼς idem est, quod pavo, idoli nomen, quod notum. Et phasianus, id est, coturnix. Nam Ps. CV, 40. pro verbis, „Petierunt, et adduxit coturnices, „Thargum habet, Petierunt carnes, et adduxit phasianos“. Sed in Talmude Babylonico tractatu Sanhedrin cap. 7. fol. 63. b.
