De Pavonibus.

On Peacocks.


De pavone est insignis locus 1 Reg. X, 22. et 2 Par. IX, 21. Semel singulis tri- col. 136 enniis ibat (Solomonis) classis in Tharsis, et afferebat aurum et argentum, dentes elephantinos, simias et pavones. Hebraeum pavonum nomen תכיים thou- cijim, vel תוכיים thuccijim, Graeci interpretes reliquerunt ἀνεϱμήνευτον, quia non intellexerunt. Sed pavones explicant Chaldaeus, Syrus, Arabs et Latinus interpres, et ex Hebraeis quotquot sunt alicujus nominis, R. Selomo, R. Levi, Kimchius, Pomarius, Aquinas. Obscuri enim et ignoti sunt, qui apud Kim- chium in Lexico גאטו מימון gato maimon, id est, cercopithecum reddunt. Ita etiam qui psittacum, quod in margine notat Iunius (1). Itaque cur hos sequi maluerit Deodatius ὁ μακαρίτης, nullus capio. A recepta versione recedere parum tutum est, nisi graves causae subsint, quales hic nullas video. De vocis origine ita Mercerus in Thesauro: Vox videtur peregrina. Etymon enim est igno- tum. Forsan a percutiendo per onomatopaeam. Galli nimirum vocibus toc, toc, ὀνοματοποιητικῶς sonum exprimunt pulsantis fores. Unde toquer est percutere, ut Italice toccare. Sed, ut haec fere arbitraria sunt, Hebraeis תוך תוך thoc thoc dicitur de sono bullientis ollae. Sic in Berachoth cap. 6. fol. 39. a. דיתיב אבי תפי ועביד תוך תוך, Quod positum est in loco positionis (ollarum ad ignem), et facit thoc thoc. Sed quoquomodo intelligas, nihil hoc ad pavonem. Neque ulla potest fingi ratio, cur a percutiendo dicatur. Aliud igitur sentio, nempe pavones inversa voce dictos תוכיים thuccijim, pro כותיים cuthijim, quasi Cuthae- os dixeris, seu Persicos. Nam Cuth (al. Chuth) est in Perside. Iosephus Anti- quitatum libro nono fere in fine, Οἱ δὲ μετοικισθέντες εἰς Σαμάρειαν Χουθαῖοι (ταύτῃ γὰρ ἐχρῶντο μέχρι δεῦρο τῇ προσηγορίᾳ, διὰ τὸ ἐκ τῆς Χουθᾶς καλου-μένης χώρας μεταχθῆναι, αὕτη δ᾽ ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ Περσίδι, καὶ ποταμὸς τοῦ τ᾽ ἔχων ὄνομα). Chuthaei in Samariam deportati (Sic enim tum appellabantur, quia ex Chutha regione translati fuerant, quae regio est in Perside, ubi et amnis ejusdem II, 710 nominis). Neque novum est, ut aves a locis denominentur. Sic a Phaside dicitur phasianus: Afrae aves et Numidicae, a Numidia et Africa: a Seleucia Seleucides: Garamantides a Garamantibus. Et, ne petantur exempla longius, ille ipse pavo, de quo agimus, passim a veteribus Medica, aut Persica vocatur avis. Aristophanes in Avibus,

There is a notable passage on the peacock in 1 Reg. X, 22. and 2 Chr 9:21: Once every three col. 136 years the fleet (of Solomon) went to Tarshish, and brought gold and silver, elephants' teeth, apes and peacocks. The Hebrew name of the peacocks, תכיים thoucijim, or תוכיים thuccijim, the Greek translators left ἀνεϱμήνευτον [anermēneuton] [untranslated], because they did not understand it. But the Chaldee, the Syriac, the Arabic and the Latin translators explain it as peacocks, and so do all the Hebrews of any repute: R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)], R. Levi, Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)], Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)]. For those who, in Kimchi's Lexicon, render it גאטו מימון gato maimon, that is, long-tailed monkey, are obscure and unknown. So too are those who render it parrot, as Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] notes in the margin R1. Therefore I cannot at all understand why the late Diodati preferred to follow them. It is hardly safe to depart from the received version unless there are weighty reasons, and I see none here. On the origin of the word, Mercerus [=Jean Mercier (d. 1570), commentaries on Job and Proverbs] says in his Thesaurus: The word seems foreign, for its etymology is unknown. Perhaps it is from striking, by onomatopoeia. The French, to be sure, express onomatopoeically the sound of someone knocking at a door with the words toc, toc; hence toquer means to strike, as does toccare in Italian. But since such things are largely arbitrary: among the Hebrews תוך תוך thoc thoc is said of the sound of a boiling pot. Thus in Berachoth ch. 6, fol. 39a: דיתיב אבי תפי ועביד תוך תוך, That which is placed in the place of setting (of pots on the fire), and makes thoc thoc. But however you understand it, this has nothing to do with the peacock. Nor can any reason be devised why it should be named from striking. I therefore hold a different view: namely, that peacocks are called תוכיים thuccijim by an inversion of the word, for כותיים cuthijim, as if you were to say Cuthaeans, or Persians. For Cuth (var. Chuth) is in Persia. Josephus, Antiquities, book 9, near the end: Οἱ δὲ μετοικισθέντες εἰς Σαμάρειαν Χουθαῖοι (ταύτῃ γὰρ ἐχρῶντο μέχρι δεῦρο τῇ προσηγορίᾳ, διὰ τὸ ἐκ τῆς Χουθᾶς καλουμένης χώρας μεταχθῆναι, αὕτη δ᾽ ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ Περσίδι, καὶ ποταμὸς τοῦ τ᾽ ἔχων ὄνομα) [Hoi de metoikisthentes eis Samareian Chouthaioi (tautē gar echrōnto mechri deuro tē prosēgoria, dia to ek tēs Chouthas kaloumenēs chōras metachthēnai, hautē d᾽ estin en tē Persidi, kai potamos tou t᾽ echōn onoma)]. The Cuthaeans deported into Samaria (for so they were then called, because they had been transferred from the region of Chutha, which is in Persia, where there is also a river of the same II, 710 name). Nor is it anything new for birds to be named after places. Thus the pheasant is named from the Phasis; African and Numidian birds from Numidia and Africa; Seleucides from Seleucia; Garamantides from the Garamantes. And, not to seek examples further afield, the very peacock we are discussing is often called the Median or Persian bird by the ancients. Aristophanes in the Birds:


Ὁ μὲν ὄρτυγα δοὺς, ὁ δὲ πορφυρίων᾽, ὁ δὲ χῆν᾽, ὁ δὲ Περσικὸν ὄρνιν᾽

Ὁ μὲν ὄρτυγα δοὺς, ὁ δὲ πορφυρίων᾽, ὁ δὲ χῆν᾽, ὁ δὲ Περσικὸν ὄρνιν᾽ [Ho men ortyga dous, ho de porphyriōn᾽, ho de chēn᾽, ho de Persikon ornin᾽]


Hic quidem coturnicem dans, ille porphyrionem, alius anserem, alius Persicam avem. Et ibi Scholiastes, Τὰ πολυτελῆ πάντα, οἷς μόνος βασιλεὺς ἐχρῆτο, ἐκαλεῖτο Περσικά· καὶ νῦν οὐκ ἰδίως τις ὄρνις Περσικός. τινὲς δὲ τὸν ἀλεκτρυό-να, οἱ δὲ τὸν ταῶ. Pretiosa omnia, quibus rex solus utebatur, vocabantur Persica. Quidam tamen gallum intelligunt, et alii pavonem. Et in Acharnan. de le-gatis Persicis,

One giving a quail, another a porphyrion, another a goose, another a Persian bird. And there the Scholiast: Τὰ πολυτελῆ πάντα, οἷς μόνος βασιλεὺς ἐχρῆτο, ἐκαλεῖτο Περσικά· καὶ νῦν οὐκ ἰδίως τις ὄρνις Περσικός. τινὲς δὲ τὸν ἀλεκτρυόνα, οἱ δὲ τὸν ταῶ [Ta polytelē panta, hois monos basileus echrēto, ekaleito Persika; kai nyn ouk idiōs tis ornis Persikos. tines de ton alektryona, hoi de ton taō]. All costly things, which the king alone used, were called Persian. Some, however, understand the cock, and others the peacock. And in the Acharnians, of the Persian envoys:


Ἥκοντες ἀπὸ Περσίδος ταὼν ἔχοντες ἐληλύθασιν,

Ἥκοντες ἀπὸ Περσίδος ταὼν ἔχοντες ἐληλύθασιν, [Hēkontes apo Persidos taōn echontes elēlythasin,]


cum ex Perside profecti essent, pavonem habentes venerant. Suidas, Μηδικὸς ὄρ-νις· ὁ ταώς· Medica avis, pavo. Item, Ταὼς εὐπήληξ· ὁ Μηδικὸς καὶ χρυ-σόπτερος, καὶ ἀλαζονικὸς ὄρνις. Pavo bene galeatus, Medica avis, aureis aleis instructa et superba. Hinc Clemens Paedag. lib. 2. cap. 1. Ὄρνεις ἐπὶ τούτοις συν- col. 137 ωνοῦνται τοὺς ἀπὸ Φάσιδος, ἀτταγὰς Αἰγυπτίας, Μῆδον ταῶνα· Aves praeterea coëmunt ex Phaside, attagenes Aegyptios, Medum pavonem. Et lib. 3. cap. 4. Ὄρνεις Ἰνδικοὺς, καὶ ταῶνας Μηδικοὺς ἐκτρέφουσι· Aves Indicas et pavones Medicos nutriunt. Et Diodorus lib. 2. Ἡ μὲν γὰρ Βαβυλωνία ταώνων ἐκτρέφει πλῆθος παντοίαις χρόαις ἐπηνθισμένων. Babylonia enim plurimos nutrit pavones, omnigenis coloribus distinctos. Quamvis enim in India fuerint pavonum veri natales, ut alibi probamus: Medici tamen et Persici ideo vocabantur, quod ex India primo in Persidem et Mediam transvecti, atque inde in Iudaeam, Aegyptum, Graeciam, Latium aliasque orbis regiones paullatim dispersi sunt. Quin illi ipsi pavones, quos Solomonis classis in Iudaeam advexit, potuerunt e Perside peti. Neque enim in triennali illa navigatione, qua Taprobanam se conferebant (ut suo loco docemus), eos semper rectam viam institisse verisimile est. Sed per varia viarum diverticula quaesiisse, quidquid in rem suam erat: etiam in Persico sinu, ubi celeberrimae Phoenicum insulae fuere, Tyrus, vel Tylus, et Aradus, a Perside parum dissitae. Potuit quoque nomen תוכיים thuccijim imponi pavonibus post Solomonis tempora; postquam terrestri itinere coeperunt e Perside et Babylone in Iudaeam advehi.

when they had set out from Persia, they had come bringing a peacock. Suidas: Μηδικὸς ὄρνις· ὁ ταώς [Mēdikos ornis; ho taōs]· The Median bird, the peacock. Likewise: Ταὼς εὐπήληξ· ὁ Μηδικὸς καὶ χρυσόπτερος, καὶ ἀλαζονικὸς ὄρνις [Taōs eupēlēx; ho Mēdikos kai chrysopteros, kai alazonikos ornis]. The well-helmeted peacock, the Median bird, furnished with golden wings, and proud. Hence Clement, Paedag. book 2, ch. 1: Ὄρνεις ἐπὶ τούτοις συνωνοῦνται τοὺς ἀπὸ Φάσιδος, ἀτταγὰς Αἰγυπτίας, Μῆδον ταῶνα [Orneis epi toutois synōnountai tous apo Phasidos, attagas Aigyptias, Mēdon taōna] col. 137· Besides, they buy up birds from the Phasis, Egyptian francolins, the Median peacock. And book 3, ch. 4: Ὄρνεις Ἰνδικοὺς, καὶ ταῶνας Μηδικοὺς ἐκτρέφουσι [Orneis Indikous, kai taōnas Mēdikous ektrephousi]· They rear Indian birds and Median peacocks. And Diodorus, book 2: Ἡ μὲν γὰρ Βαβυλωνία ταώνων ἐκτρέφει πλῆθος παντοίαις χρόαις ἐπηνθισμένων [Hē men gar Babylōnia taōnōn ektrephei plēthos pantoiais chroais epēnthismenōn]. For Babylonia rears a great many peacocks, variegated with colours of every kind. For although the true homeland of peacocks was India, as we prove elsewhere, they were nevertheless called Median and Persian because they were first carried from India into Persia and Media, and from there gradually dispersed into Judaea, Egypt, Greece, Latium and other regions of the world. Indeed, the very peacocks which Solomon's fleet brought into Judaea may have been obtained from Persia. For it is not likely that on that three-year voyage, by which they made their way to Taprobane (as we show in its place), they always kept a straight course. Rather, by various detours they sought out whatever served their purpose: also in the Persian Gulf, where lay the most celebrated islands of the Phoenicians, Tyrus or Tylus, and Aradus, not far distant from Persia. The name תוכיים thuccijim could also have been given to peacocks after Solomon's time, once they began to be brought overland from Persia and Babylon into Judaea.


Iam, quod inversis literis תוכיים dicti sunt pro כותיים, res non est sine exemplo, sive librariorum incuria id acciderit, sive, quod credo verius, certo II, 711 consilio sit factum, ut a gentis nomine avis nomen distingueretur. Sic eadem ligna dici videas אלמוגים almugin, 1 Reg. X, 11. et אלגומים algumim, 2 Paral. II, 7. Eandem urbem, in qua Iosue sepultus est, vocari תמנת־סרח Thimnath-Serach, Ios. XXIV, 30. et תמנת־חרס Thimnath-Cheres, Iudic. II, 9. Eundem Danis filium חושים Chusim, appellari Gen. XLVI, 23. et שוחם Sucham, Num. XXVI, 42. Virum eundem רחום Rechum, Nehem. XII, 3. et חרם Charim, ibidem versu 15. Alium שמלי Samlai, Esd. II, 46. et שלמי Salmai, Nehem. VII, 48. Ita ovis modo כבס chebes vocatur, modo כשב cheseb. Et Aethiopes Hebraea verba quandoque prorsus invertunt. Sic רחם, misereri, illis est ምሕረ፡ קלס, illudere, illis ሰለቀ፡ זנק, salire, illis ቀነጸ፡ Itaque eodem exemplo pro כותיים pavones dici potuere תוכיים. Tamen haec pono, non statuo: et liberum unicuique suum permitto judicium.

Now, that they were called תוכיים with the letters inverted, instead of כותיים, is not without precedent, whether this happened through the carelessness of copyists or, as I believe more likely, was done by deliberate II, 711 design, so that the name of the bird might be distinguished from the name of the people. Thus you may see the same wood called אלמוגים almugin, 1 Reg. X, 11. and אלגומים algumim, 2 Chr 2:7. The same city in which Joshua was buried is called תמנת־סרח Thimnath-Serach, Josh 24:30 and תמנת־חרס Thimnath-Cheres, Judg 2:9. The same son of Dan is called חושים Chusim, Gen 46:23 and שוחם Sucham, Num 26:42. The same man is רחום Rechum, Neh 12:3 and חרם Charim, in the same place, verse 15. Another is שמלי Samlai, Esd. II, 46. and שלמי Salmai, Neh 7:48. So the sheep is called now כבס chebes, now כשב cheseb. And the Ethiopians sometimes invert Hebrew words entirely. Thus רחם, to have pity, is for them ምሕረ፡ [məḥəra]; קלס, to mock, for them ሰለቀ፡ [salaqa]; זנק, to leap, for them ቀነጸ፡ [qanaṣa]. Therefore, on the same pattern, peacocks could have been called תוכיים instead of כותיים. However, I propose this, I do not decide it, and I leave everyone free to judge for himself.


Si pavo esset ignotus, quaereremus, quid Solomonem moverit, ut cum auri et argenti gazis aves non magni usus e tam longinquo accerseret. Aut quorsum id observare sacri scriptores operae pretium esse duxerint? Sed haec dubia solvit aspectus avis eximiae, quae ad id videtur facta, ut intuentium oculos jucundo pascat spectaculo. Proinde Varro naturam asserit huic e volucribus formae dedisse palmam. Et post Graecos, qui certatim in ejus descriptionem operam suam contulerunt, illam ita pingit Tertullianus, De Pallio cap. 3. Quanquam et pavo pluma vestis, et quidem de cataclitis: ita omni conchylio pressior, qua colla florent: et omni patagio inauratior, qua terga fulgent: et omni syrmate solutior, qua caudae jacent. Multicolor, et discolor, et versicolor. Nunquam ipsa, semper alia: etsi semper ipsa, quando alia. Toties denique mutanda, quoties movenda. Sudarunt quoque Arabes in eadem palaestra, in quibus Alkazuinius, تري في وسط كل ريش دايرة من الذهب مخلطة بالزرقة والصفرة والخضرة وغيرها من الاوان التي col. 138 تلايم بعضها بعضا لينشا من تركيبها Videbis in medio omnium plumarum ejus circulum aureum, mixtum coeruleo, flavo, et viridi, et aliis coloribus, quae inter se conveniunt, ut ex eorum coalitione summa pulchritudo exsurgat. Addit, aurum, quibusvis coloribus impositum, nihil esse ad hunc splendorem, quamvis e terra vix eruatur, nec nisi multo labore expurge-tur; cum avis tam speciosa ex ovo sponte emergat, et absque hominum opera. Multo plura habet Damir, quae praeterire malui, ne in argumento omnium tritissimo lectori sim taediosus. Itaque sufficiet, in praesens paucos versus ad-dere ex Arabico poeta anonymo, II, 712 سبحان من خلق الطاوس * طير علي اشكاله رييس * كانه من نقشه عروس * في الريش منه ركبت فلوس * تشرق في داراته شموس * في راس منه شجرة مغروس * كانه ببنفسج يميس *

If the peacock were unknown, we would ask what moved Solomon to fetch from so far away, along with treasures of gold and silver, birds of no great use. Or why the sacred writers thought it worth recording? But these doubts are resolved by the appearance of this exceptional bird, which seems made for the very purpose of feasting the eyes of beholders with a delightful spectacle. Accordingly Varro asserts that nature gave it the prize for beauty among birds. And after the Greeks, who vied with one another in describing it, Tertullian paints it thus, De Pallio ch. 3: And yet the peacock too has a garment of feathers, and indeed one of the finest: deeper than any purple where the neck blooms, more gilded than any border where the back gleams, more flowing than any trailing robe where the tail lies. Many-coloured, and diverse-coloured, and changing-coloured. Never itself, always other; and yet always itself when other. In short, changed as often as it is moved. The Arabs too have toiled in the same arena, among them Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt]: تري في وسط كل ريش دايرة من الذهب مخلطة بالزرقة والصفرة والخضرة وغيرها من الاوان التي [tarī fī wasaṭ kull rīsh dāyira min al-dhahab mukhallaṭa bi-l-zurqa wa-l-ṣufra wa-l-khuḍra wa-ghayrihā min al-awān allatī] col. 138 تلايم بعضها بعضا لينشا من تركيبها [talāyam baʿḍuhā baʿḍan li-yansha min tarkībihā] You will see in the middle of all its feathers a golden circle, mixed with blue, yellow and green, and other colours which harmonize with one another, so that from their combination the highest beauty arises. He adds that gold, laid over any colours whatever, is nothing compared with this splendour, although it is scarcely dug out of the earth and only refined with much labour; whereas so beautiful a bird emerges from the egg of its own accord, without human effort. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] has much more, which I have preferred to pass over, lest I weary the reader on a subject most hackneyed of all. So for the present it will suffice to add a few verses from an anonymous Arabic poet: II, 712 سبحان من خلق الطاوس [subḥān man khalaqa al-ṭāwūs] * طير علي اشكاله رييس [ṭayr ʿalā ashkālihi rayīs] * كانه من نقشه عروس [ka-annahu min naqshihi ʿarūs] * في الريش منه ركبت فلوس [fī al-rīsh minhu rukkibat fulūs] * تشرق في داراته شموس [tushriqu fī dārātihi shumūs] * في راس منه شجرة مغروس [fī raʾs minhu shajara maghrūs] * كانه ببنفسج يميس [ka-annahu bi-banafsaj yamīs] *


Gloria sit illi, qui pavonem creavit, avem, specie eximiam, quae varietate colorum sponsam refert. Pennis ipsius squamae insitae sunt. In aedibus ejus plures oriuntur soles. Super verticem arbuscula a) est consita. Tanquam in janthina veste cum pompa incedit. Arabice tanquam in viola. Sed ibi viola sumitur pro veste violacei, seu purpurei coloris, qui inter reliquos in collo et cauda pavonis maxime eminet. Hinc supra Tertullianus, Omni conchylio pressior, qua colla florent. Et Achilles Tatius lib. 1. Ὁ δὲ τοῦ ταῶ λειμὼν εὐανθέστερος· πεφύτευται γὰρ αὐτῷ καὶ χρυσὸς ἐν τοῖς πτεροῖς, κύκλῳ δὲ τὸ ἁλουργὲς τὸν χρυσὸν περιθέει τὸν ἴσον κύκλον. Pavonis pratum (prato quovis) est floridius: in ejus quippe pennis etiam aurum insitum est: et aurum ambit purpura pari circulo. Quo refertur, quod pavo a Publio Syro describitur

Glory be to him who created the peacock, a bird of exceptional beauty, which in the variety of its colours resembles a bride. Scales are set into its feathers. In its dwelling many suns rise. On its crown a little tree a) is planted. It struts in pomp as though in a violet garment. In Arabic, as though in a violet. But there violet is taken for a garment of violet, or purple colour, which stands out most among the other colours in the neck and tail of the peacock. Hence Tertullian above: Deeper than any purple dye, where the neck blooms. And Achilles Tatius, book 1: Ὁ δὲ τοῦ ταῶ λειμὼν εὐανθέστερος· πεφύτευται γὰρ αὐτῷ καὶ χρυσὸς ἐν τοῖς πτεροῖς, κύκλῳ δὲ τὸ ἁλουργὲς τὸν χρυσὸν περιθέει τὸν ἴσον κύκλον [Ho de tou taō leimōn euanthesteros; pephyteutai gar autō kai chrysos en tois pterois, kyklō de to halourges ton chryson peritheei ton ison kyklon]. The meadow of the peacock (than any meadow) is more flowery: for in its feathers gold also is set, and purple surrounds the gold in an equal circle. To this belongs the description of the peacock by Publilius Syrus:


Plumato amictus aureo Babylonico.

Clad in a feathered golden Babylonian mantle.


Ac si Babylonico sit idem quod purpureo. Quia in Periplo Arrianus purpurae meminit ex Apologo, Babylonis urbe, ad Euphratis ostium. Et τὸν Βαβυλώνιον κόκκον laudat Philostratus Epistola 28. ad mulierem. Proinde אדרת שנער , pallium Sinar, seu Babylonicum, Ios. VII, 21. Rabbi Chaninae est pallium מן פרפרא בבלאה , ex purpura Babylonica; et Hieronymo coccineum. Sed per plumatum Babylonicum nos varium intelligimus. Quia, ut ex Plinio et aliis alibi probavimus, colores diversos picturae intexere Babylon maxime celebravit et nomen imposuit. Eo nos ducunt haec Aeliani de pavone lib. 5. cap. 21. Δεικνὺς φιλοπόνως τὸ τῆς πτερώσεως πολύμορφον ὑπὲρ τὴν τῶν Μήδων ἐσθῆτα, καὶ τὰ τῶν Περ-σῶν ποικίλματα· Ambitiose ostentans pennarum speciem multiformem, supra Medorum vestem, et Persarum varios colores. Proinde Antiphon in oratione De pavonibus contra Erasistratum, quam citant Athenaeus lib. 9. et Aelianus ubi supra, pavones vero nomine, id est, ταῶνας nusquam appellat, sed solum ὄρνεις ποικίλους, aves varias; quasi hoc ipso ab aliis maxime distinguantur.

As though Babylonian were the same as purple, since Arrian in the Periplus mentions purple from Apologus, a city of Babylonia, at the mouth of the Euphrates. And Philostratus, Epistle 28, to a woman, praises τὸν Βαβυλώνιον κόκκον [ton Babylōnion kokkon]. Accordingly, אדרת שנער, the mantle of Shinar, or Babylonian mantle, Josh 7:21, is for Rabbi Chanina a mantle מן פרפרא בבלאה, of Babylonian purple; and for Jerome scarlet. But by feathered Babylonian we understand variegated. For, as we have proved elsewhere from Pliny and others, to weave different colours into a picture Babylon most made famous and gave it its name. We are led to this by these words of Aelian on the peacock, book 5, ch. 21: Δεικνὺς φιλοπόνως τὸ τῆς πτερώσεως πολύμορφον ὑπὲρ τὴν τῶν Μήδων ἐσθῆτα, καὶ τὰ τῶν Περσῶν ποικίλματα [Deiknys philoponōs to tēs pterōseōs polymorphon hyper tēn tōn Mēdōn esthēta, kai ta tōn Persōn poikilmata]; Ostentatiously displaying the multiform appearance of its plumage, surpassing the garment of the Medes and the varied colours of the Persians. Accordingly Antiphon, in his speech On the Peacocks against Erasistratus, cited by Athenaeus, book 9, and by Aelian in the place above, nowhere calls peacocks by their proper name, that is, ταῶνας [taōnas], but only ὄρνεις ποικίλους [orneis poikilous], variegated birds; as if by this very feature they were most distinguished from others.


II, 713 Ex hac eadem oratione collata cum vita Periclis apud Plutarchum colligitur, col. 139 circa Periclis aetatem pavones ali coepisse Athenis in Demi cujusdam aedibus, Pyrilambis filii, qui magnum ex eo quaestum fecit. Eos enim certo pretio videndos exhibebat singulis noviluniis. Et ad hoc spectaculum ex Lacedaemone et Thessalia, id est, ex utrisque Graeciae extremis, curiosi confluebant. Idem pavonini generis marem et foeminam vendidit mille drachmis. Quin in Graecia pavones nondum vulgares erant aevo Alexandri, qui, teste Aeliano, ἐν Ἰνδοῖς ἰδὼν τοὺς δὲ τοὺς ὄρνιθας ἐξεπλάγη, καὶ τοῦ κάλλους θαυμάσας, ἠπείλησε τῷ καταθύσαντι ταὼν ἀπειλὰς βαρυτάτας, illas aves in Indis videns obstupuit, et speciem admiratus, in eos, qui has occiderent, gravem poenam constituit. Ita Romae Hortensius, ut idem refert, καταθύσας ἐπὶ δείπνῳ ταὼν πρῶτος, ἐκρί-θη, cum in coena pavonem primus mactasset, in jus vocatus est: aut, ut alii le-gunt, κατεκρίθη, damnatus est, seu mulctatus. Tamen, praevalente luxu, Hortensium sequuti multi extulerunt pavonum pretia; ita, ut in Varrone Merula ova eorum asserat suo tempore denariis venisse quinis, ipsos facile quinquagenis. Et ex pavonum gregibus M. Aufidium Lurconem supra sexagena millia nummûm annui reditus confecisse. Quamvis enim pavonis caro gallinae carne non plus sapiat, tamen multo pluris fiebat pavo propter caudam et pennas: quasi ad palatum hoc pertineret, aut cum carne pennas edissent. Quam helluonum stultitiam Horatius his verbis salse deridet lib. 2. Satyra 2.

II, 713 From this same speech, compared with the life of Pericles in Plutarch, it is gathered col. 139 that around the time of Pericles peacocks began to be kept at Athens in the house of a certain Demus, son of Pyrilampes, who made great profit from it. For he exhibited them to be viewed for a fixed fee at every new moon. And to this spectacle the curious flocked from Lacedaemon and Thessaly, that is, from both extremities of Greece. He also sold a male and female of the peacock kind for a thousand drachmas. Indeed, in Greece peacocks were not yet common in the age of Alexander, who, on the testimony of Aelian, ἐν Ἰνδοῖς ἰδὼν τοὺς δὲ τοὺς ὄρνιθας ἐξεπλάγη, καὶ τοῦ κάλλους θαυμάσας, ἠπείλησε τῷ καταθύσαντι ταὼν ἀπειλὰς βαρυτάτας [en Indois idōn tous de tous ornithas exeplagē, kai tou kallous thaumasas, ēpeilēse tō katathysanti taōn apeilas barytatas], seeing those birds among the Indians was astonished, and, admiring their beauty, fixed a heavy penalty for those who should kill them. Likewise at Rome Hortensius, as the same author reports, καταθύσας ἐπὶ δείπνῳ ταὼν πρῶτος, ἐκρίθη [katathysas epi deipnō taōn prōtos, ekrithē], having been the first to slaughter a peacock for a dinner, was summoned to court: or, as others read, κατεκρίθη [katekrithē], was condemned, or fined. Yet, as luxury prevailed, many following Hortensius raised the prices of peacocks; so much so that in Varro Merula asserts that in his time their eggs sold for five denarii each, the birds themselves easily for fifty. And that M. Aufidius Lurco made an annual income of over sixty thousand sesterces from flocks of peacocks. For although the flesh of the peacock tastes no better than the flesh of a hen, the peacock was valued much more highly because of its tail and feathers: as if this concerned the palate, or as if they ate the feathers with the flesh. This folly of gluttons Horace wittily mocks in these words, book 2, Satire 2:


Vix tamen eripiam, posito pavone, velis quin
Hoc potius quam gallina tergere palatum,
Corruptas vanis rerum: quia veneat auro
Rara avis, et picta pandat spectacula cauda.
Tanquam ad rem attineat quidquam. Num vesceris ista
Quam laudas pluma? Cocto num adest honor idem?
Carne tamen quamvis distat nihil, hac magis illa
Imparibus formis deceptum te patet. — —

Yet I shall hardly keep you, when a peacock is served, from wishing to wipe your palate with it rather than with a hen, corrupted as you are by empty things: because the rare bird is sold for gold and spreads a spectacle with its painted tail. As if that mattered at all. Do you eat that plumage you praise? Once it is cooked, does the same glory remain? Yet though in flesh there is no difference, it is plain that you are deceived by the unequal appearance into preferring this to that. — —


Neque enim sapore, sed pretio aestimabantur hae dapes: neque alia de causa exquirebantur, quam quia carius venibant, ut ex India allati psittaci. Claudianus in Eutropium lib. 2.

For these dishes were valued not for their flavour but for their price; nor were they sought for any other reason than that they sold more dearly, like parrots brought from India. Claudian, Against Eutropius, book 2:


Qui ventrem invitant pretio, traduntque palato
Sidereas Iunonis aves, et si qua loquendi
Gnara coloratis viridis defertur ab Indis.

Who whet the belly with price, and hand over to the palate the starry birds of Juno, and any green bird skilled in speech brought from the coloured Indians.


Quid quod in Symeone Sethi pavonis caro ἰνώδης, καὶ περιττωματικὴ, καὶ δύσ-πεπτος, καὶ κακόχυμος, fibrosa, excrementitia, concoctu difficilis, et mali succi? Quomodo in Galeno σκληροτέρα, καὶ δυσπεπτοτέρα, καὶ ἰνωδεστέρα.

What of the fact that in Symeon Seth [=Symeon Seth (11th c.), Syntagma de alimentorum facultatibus] the flesh of the peacock is ἰνώδης, καὶ περιττωματικὴ, καὶ δύσπεπτος, καὶ κακόχυμος [inōdēs, kai perittōmatikē, kai dyspeptos, kai kakochymos], fibrous, productive of excrements, hard to digest, and of bad juice? Just as in Galen it is σκληροτέρα, καὶ δυσπεπτοτέρα, καὶ ἰνωδεστέρα [sklērotera, kai dyspeptotera, kai inōdestera].


II, 714 Et in Damire, لحمه عسر الهضم ردي المزاج وهي يولد كيموسا غليظا Caro ejus difficilis est concoctionis, mali temperamenti, et crassum chymum generat. In Avicenna, لحوم الطواويس صلبة Carnes pavonum durae sunt. In Mesue, ردي المزاج mali succi, unde Iuvenalis Satyra prima,

II, 714 And in Damir: لحمه عسر الهضم ردي المزاج وهي يولد كيموسا غليظا [laḥmuhu ʿasir al-haḍm radī al-mizāj wa-hiya yuwallid kaymūsan ghalīẓan], Its flesh is difficult to digest, of a bad temperament, and it produces a thick chyme. In Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)]: لحوم الطواويس صلبة [luḥūm al-ṭawāwīs ṣulba], The flesh of peacocks is hard. In Mesue: ردي المزاج [radī al-mizāj], of bad juice; whence Juvenal in his first Satire:


— — crudum pavonem in balnea portas:
Hinc subitae mortes, atque intestata senectus.

— — you carry the undigested peacock into the baths: hence sudden deaths, and an old age without a will.


Itaque, praeter eximiam illam speciem, causa nulla fuit, cur pavo apud veteres tanti fieret. Quin pavonem, quamlibet formosam, tamen avem esse mali ominis, sibi fingunt Arabes: quia, ut fabulantur, كان سببا لدخول ابليس الجنة وخروج ادم منها Causa fuit, cur in Paradisum ingrederetur diabolus, et ex eo egrederetur Adam. Sed qua ratione, nondum reperi. Ejusdem farinae est, quod refert incertus auctor روضة العلما Vi- col. 140 ridarii doctorum, vitem quatuor animalium sanguine a diabolo fuisse adspersam: nempe pavonis, cum primum consita est: simiae, cum incepit folia edere: leonis, cum protrusit uvas: porci denique, jam maturescente fructu. Atque inde esse, quod qui vinum bibit 1. ut pavo fit venustior: 2. in simiae modum ludit, saltat, gesticulatur: 3. leonis instar furit: 4. ut porcus

Therefore, apart from that exceptional beauty, there was no reason why the peacock was so highly valued among the ancients. Indeed, the Arabs imagine that the peacock, however beautiful, is nonetheless a bird of ill omen, because, as they tell the tale, كان سببا لدخول ابليس الجنة وخروج ادم منها [kāna sababan li-dukhūl Iblīs al-janna wa-khurūj Ādam minhā], it was the reason why the devil entered Paradise, and why Adam went out of it. But for what reason, I have not yet found. Of the same sort is what the anonymous author of the روضة العلما [Rawḍat al-ʿulamā], Garden col. 140 of the Learned, reports: that the vine was sprinkled by the devil with the blood of four animals, namely of the peacock when it was first planted, of the ape when it began to put out leaves, of the lion when it pushed out its grapes, and finally of the pig when the fruit was already ripening. And that this is why whoever drinks wine 1. becomes more handsome, like the peacock; 2. plays, dances and gesticulates in the manner of an ape; 3. rages like a lion; 4. like a pig


— — jacet somno vinoque sepultus.

— — lies buried in sleep and wine.


Dei verba Iob. XXXIX, 13. כנף רננים נעלסה, post Kimchium et Pomarium, plerique recentiorum explicant, Ala pavonum exultat. Quasi de pavonibus agatur, qui pennarum pulchritudine superbiunt; cum eo loco רננים sint struthiones, non pavones: quod in tractatu De struthione multis probamus: nec ulla ratione niti, qui pavones interpretantur, quamvis hodie hujus vocis expositio nulla sit receptior.

God's words in Job 39:13, כנף רננים נעלסה, are explained by most of the more recent writers, following Kimchi and Pomarius, as The wing of the peacocks exults, as though it dealt with peacocks, which take pride in the beauty of their feathers. Yet in that passage רננים are ostriches, not peacocks, as we prove at length in the treatise On the Ostrich; and those who interpret them as peacocks rest on no reasoning, although today no explanation of this word is more widely accepted.


Nihilo magis placet, quod Ezech. XXVII, 15. Hebraea voce הבנים hobnim pavones significari voluit Chaldaeus interpres. Quamvis id sequatur R. Selomo. Et reliqui Hebraeorum ambigant. Et e nostris Santes Pagninus totum hunc locum sic reddiderit: Filii Dedan negotiatores tui. Insulae multae negotiatio manus tuae. Cornua eburnea et pavones reddiderunt in munus tuum. Graeci (quos sequitur Arabs) et Syrus hoc idem verbum videntur prave legisse. Illi enim reddunt τοῖς εἰσαγομένοις, illis, qui introducuntur, id est, הובאים. Hic לבונתא, thus, quod Hebraice esset לבנה. Itaque soli veterum Symmachus et Hieronymus viderunt, הובנים hobnim esse hebenum. Quam interpretationem multa II, 715 confirmant. Primo enim hobnim et hebenus sunt voces non absimiles. In principe syllaba Vocales O et E permutatae sunt, quod frequens esse omnes sciunt. Priscianus lib. 1. O transit in E, ut tutor tutela, bonus bene, γόνυ genu, ποῦς pes. Antiqui compes pro compos. In quo Aeoles sequimur. Illi enim ἐδόντα pro ὀδόντα dicunt. Quintilianus lib. 1. cap. 7. Quid dicam vortices et vorsus, caeteraque ad eundem modum, quae primo Scipio Africanus in E literam secundam vertisse dicitur. Hinc iidem Ὀσσηνοὶ et Ἐσσηνοί. Et a Ptolemaeo dicitur Ὁρ-κύνιος δρυμὸς, qui aliis Ἑρκύνιος, id est, Hercynia sylva. Secundo, קרנות שן והבננים, cornua eboris et ebenus, in Propheta recte junguntur, tanquam merces, aliquo modo homogeneae, quamvis unum ex animali, alterum ex arbore petatur. Quippe, ut notat Fullerus in Miscellaneis lib. 6. cap. 14. utrique est extremus color eodem excellentiae gradu. Ebori videlicet pulcherrimi candoris, hebeno speciosissimi nigroris. Utrumque politissimum, nitidissimum, et incomparabili laevore conspicuum. Unde est, quod in eosdem usus fere adhibentur; et ex utroque arcus fiunt, pectines, tabulae lusoriae, cultrorum manubria, etc. Tertio, verba Ezechielis sic reddi queant, cornua (elephantini) dentis et ebeni secundo casu, ita, ut vox קרנות, cornua, ad utrumque pertineat. Nam, ut ebur cornu vocatur propter similitudinem, quam habet cum vero cornu, hebenus quoque potuit eadem καταχρήσει cornu vocari, cum a Dioscoride describatur ἐμφερὴς κέρατι εἰργασμένῳ τῇ λειότητι, levore cornu levigato simile. Et ab Isidoro lignum nigrum, leve et corneum. Et ab Avicenna يشبه في ملاسته قرنا محكوكا وقيل مخروطا levore suo referens cornu laevigatum, aut, ut alii dicunt, dedolatum. Hebenus igitur dici potuit cornu καταχρηστικῶς. Non tamen dentem dixerim cum Hieronymo, qui hic habet, dentes eburneos et ebeninos. Quarto, in iisdem locis nascuntur ebur col. 141 et ebenus. Nam, ut elephantes in Indicos et Aethiopicos distinguunt Polybius, Plinius, Philostratus, et apud Pindari Scholiastem Amyntianus in libro De elephantis: sic ebenum in India et Aethiopia nasci tradunt Dioscorides, Plinius, Isidorus. Atque, ut Indicae ebeni speciatim meminerunt Theophrastus, Arrianus et Ennodius; ita Aethiopicae Herodotus, Diodorus, Mela, Avicenna et Nubiensis Geographus. Quibus ne opponas haec summi vatis Georgicorum lib. 2.

No more acceptable is the view of the Chaldee translator, who held that in Ezek 27:15 the Hebrew word הבנים hobnim means peacocks, although R. Selomo follows it, and the other Hebrews are in doubt, and among our own scholars Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae] rendered the whole passage thus: The sons of Dedan were thy merchants. Many isles were the merchandise of thy hand. They brought horns of ivory and peacocks as thy present. The Greeks (whom the Arab follows) and the Syrian seem to have misread this same word. For the former render τοῖς εἰσαγομένοις [tois eisagomenois], to those who are brought in, that is, הובאים; the latter לבונתא, frankincense, which in Hebrew would be לבנה. Thus of the ancients only Symmachus and Jerome saw that הובנים hobnim is ebony. Many things confirm this interpretation. II, 715 First, hobnim and hebenus are not dissimilar words. In the first syllable the vowels O and E have been interchanged, which everyone knows to be frequent. Priscian, book 1: O passes into E, as tutor tutela, bonus bene, γόνυ [gony] genu, ποῦς [pous] pes. The ancients said compes for compos. In this we follow the Aeolians, for they say ἐδόντα [edonta] for ὀδόντα [odonta]. Quintilian, book 1, ch. 7: What shall I say of vortices and vorsus, and the rest of the same kind, which Scipio Africanus is said to have been the first to turn into the second letter, E. Hence the same people are called Ὀσσηνοὶ [Ossēnoi] and Ἐσσηνοί [Essēnoi]. And Ptolemy speaks of the Ὁρκύνιος δρυμὸς [Horkynios drymos], which others call Ἑρκύνιος [Herkynios], that is, the Hercynian forest. Second, קרנות שן והבננים, horns of ivory and ebony, are rightly joined in the Prophet as wares in some way homogeneous, although the one is obtained from an animal, the other from a tree. For, as Fuller [=Nicholas Fuller, Miscellanea theologica / sacra (1612–22)] notes in his Miscellanea, book 6, ch. 14, each has an extreme colour in the same degree of excellence: ivory, namely, of the most beautiful whiteness, ebony of the most splendid blackness. Both are highly polished, very lustrous, and remarkable for an incomparable smoothness. Hence they are applied to almost the same uses; and from both are made bows, combs, gaming boards, knife handles, etc. Third, the words of Ezekiel could be rendered thus: horns of (elephant) tooth and of ebony, in the genitive, so that the word קרנות, horns, belongs to both. For as ivory is called horn because of its resemblance to true horn, ebony too could be called horn by the same καταχρήσει [katachrēsei], since Dioscorides describes it as ἐμφερὴς κέρατι εἰργασμένῳ τῇ λειότητι [empherēs kerati eirgasmenō tē leiotēti], like polished horn in smoothness; and Isidore as a black wood, smooth and horn-like; and Avicenna as يشبه في ملاسته قرنا محكوكا وقيل مخروطا [yushbihu fī malāsatihi qarnan maḥkūkan wa-qīla makhrūṭan] resembling in its smoothness polished horn, or, as others say, horn worked smooth. Ebony therefore could be called horn καταχρηστικῶς [katachrēstikōs]. I would not, however, call it a tooth with Jerome, who has here teeth of ivory and of ebony. Fourth, ivory and ebony originate in the same places. col. 141 For just as Polybius, Pliny, Philostratus, and, in the Scholiast on Pindar, Amyntianus in his book On Elephants distinguish elephants into Indian and Ethiopian, so Dioscorides, Pliny and Isidore report that ebony grows in India and Ethiopia. And as Theophrastus, Arrian and Ennodius mention Indian ebony specifically, so Herodotus, Diodorus, Mela, Avicenna and the Nubian Geographer mention Ethiopian. Lest you object to them these words of the supreme poet in Georgics book 2,


— — — sola India nigrum
Fert ebenum: — — —

— — — India alone bears black ebony: — — —


sciendum, Indiae nomine etiam Aethiopiam intelligi. Hinc ad illum locum Servius, Indiam omnem plagam Aethiopiae accipimus. Quod verissimum esse docent haec ejusdem poetae de Nili Origine lib. 4. Georgicorum,

one must know that by the name India Ethiopia is also understood. Hence Servius on that passage: By India we understand the whole region of Ethiopia. That this is very true is shown by these words of the same poet on the Source of the Nile in Georgics book 4,


Usque coloratis amnis devexus ab Indis, II, 716 Id est, ex intima Aethiopia. Sunt, qui Indicae et Aethiopicae Aegyptiam ebenum addunt, tanquam auctore Lucano, cujus verba sunt lib. 10.

The river flowing down all the way from the dark-coloured Indians, II, 716 that is, from innermost Ethiopia. There are some who add Egyptian ebony to the Indian and Ethiopian, as on the authority of Lucan, whose words in book 10 are:


— — — ebenus Mareotica vastos
Non operit postes. — — —

— — — Mareotic ebony
does not cover the vast doorposts. — — —


Maereotica, id est, ex Mareotide, Aegypti parte, ut volunt, prope Alexandriam. Quibus consona haec Servii, Atqui et in Aegypto nascitur ebenus. Sed utrobique mendum est. Nam in Lucano legendum Meroitica, quod egregie probat Cl. Salmasius in Solinum; qui infra habetur in eodem Lucani libro,

Maereotic, that is, from Mareotis, a part of Egypt near Alexandria, as they would have it. Consonant with them are these words of Servius: And yet ebony also grows in Egypt. But in both places there is an error. For in Lucan one must read Meroitica, as the distinguished Salmasius [=Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), Plinianae exercitationes] excellently proves in his work on Solinus; Meroë, which appears below in the same book of Lucan,


— — nigris Meroe foecunda colonis,
Laeta comis ebeni. — — —

— — Meroë, fertile with black settlers, rich in the foliage of ebony. — — —


Proinde Diodorus lib. 1. ubi de insula Meroe, Πρὸς δὲ τούτοις (λέγουσιν) ἔχειν πλῆθος ἐβένου, Eam insuper ajunt copiam habere ebeni. Et Plinius allatam fuisse Neroni memorat raram arborem ebenum, Meroen usque a Syene fine imperii (petitam) per nongenta nonaginta sex millia passuum. Sed et in his Servii, At-qui et in Aegypto nascitur, mendum est manifestum. Omnino enim scripserat, Atqui et in Aethiopia nascitur, quod sequentia docent, Sed Indiam omnem plagam Aethiopiae accipimus. Quae erunt ἀνακόλουθα, si legamus, in Aegypto. Haec enim habet Servius ad Virgilii locum, de quo supra,

Accordingly Diodorus, book 1, where he speaks of the island of Meroe: Πρὸς δὲ τούτοις (λέγουσιν) ἔχειν πλῆθος ἐβένου [Pros de toutois (legousin) echein plēthos ebenou], Moreover they say that it has an abundance of ebony. And Pliny records that the rare tree ebony was brought to Nero (fetched) from as far as Meroe, a distance of 996 miles from Syene, the boundary of the empire. But in these words of Servius too, And yet it grows also in Egypt, there is an obvious error. For he had certainly written, And yet it grows also in Ethiopia, as what follows shows: But by India we understand the whole region of Ethiopia. This would be ἀνακόλουθα [anakoloutha] if we read in Egypt. For Servius says this on the passage of Virgil discussed above,


— — — sola India nigrum
Fert ebenum. — — —

— — — India alone bears
black ebony. — — —


Quem verum esse contendit, etsi ebenus etiam in Aethiopia nascatur; quia Indiae nomen Aethiopiam complectitur. At, si ebenum in Aegypto nasci dixeris, nulla erit haec excusatio. Aliud enim Aegyptus, aliud Aethiopia. Nec quisquam est, qui Indiae nomine Aegyptum intelligat. Quinto, ebenus et ebur una cum auro perpetuum fuit Aethiopum tributum. Hinc apud Diodorum lib. 1. pag. 35. cum Aegyptiorum rex antiquissimus Sesoosis (al. Sesostres) Aethiopes debellasset, ἠνάγκασε τὸ ἔθνος φόρους τελεῖν, ἔβενον, καὶ χρυσὸν, καὶ τῶν ἐλεφάντων τοὺς ὀδόντας, genti pro tributo imposuit ebenum, et aurum, et elephantorum dentes. Quae eadem ab iisdem Aethiopibus exegisse Persae leguntur. Herodotus Musa 3. cap. 97. Ἀγινέουσι δὲ καὶ τὸ μέχρι ἐμεῦ δύο χοίνικας ἀπύρου χρυσίου, καὶ διηκοσίας φαλάγγας ἐβένου, καὶ ἐλέφαντος ὀδόντας μεγάλους εἴκοσι· Ad meam usque aetatem (Aethiopes Persis pro triennali tributo) vehunt duos choenices auri apyri (id est, ignem nondum experti), et ducentas ebeni phalangas, et magnos elephantis dentes viginti. Nempe horum trium ferax est regio, ut idem scribit cap. 114. Αὕτη δὲ χρυσόν τε φέρει πολλὸν, καὶ ἐλέφαντας ἀμφιλαφέας, καὶ δένδρεα πάντα ἄγρια, καὶ ἔβενον· Haec auri multum fert, et elephantes amplissimos, et sylvestres arbores omne genus, et ebenum. Plinius quoque libri II, 717 12. cap. 4. ubi de ebeno asserit, tributi vice regibus Persidis e materie ejus centenas palangas tertio quoque anno pensitasse Aethiopes cum auro et ebore. Et in Ptolemaei Philadelphi pompa apud Callixenum Rhodium Aethiopes haec eadem col. 142 gestasse referuntur. Ἐχόμενοι τούτων ἦσαν (inquit) Αἰθίοπες δωροφόροι, ὧν οἱ μὲν ἔφερον ὀδόντας ἑξακοσίους, ἕτεροι δὲ ἐβένου κορμοὺς δισχιλίους, ἄλλοι χρυ-σοῦ καὶ ἀργυρίου κρατῆρας ἑξήκοντα, καὶ ψήγματα χρυσίου. His juncti erant Aethiopes, dona ferentes, quorum alii quidem sexcentos (elephantorum) dentes ferebant, alii ebeni stipitum duo millia, alii sexaginta auri et argenti crateres, et auri ramenta. Proinde in festo Adonidis, Alexandriae sub eodem rege cum magna pompa celebrato, Syracusanae mulieres, viso ebeno, et auro, et ebore multo, in haec verba prorumpunt, Idyll. 15. versu 123.

which he maintains is true, even though ebony also grows in Ethiopia, because the name of India includes Ethiopia. But if you say that ebony grows in Egypt, this excuse will not hold. For Egypt is one thing, Ethiopia another; nor is there anyone who understands Egypt by the name of India. Fifth, ebony and ivory, together with gold, were the constant tribute of the Ethiopians. Hence in Diodorus, book 1, p. 35, when Sesoosis (var. Sesostres), the most ancient king of the Egyptians, had subdued the Ethiopians, ἠνάγκασε τὸ ἔθνος φόρους τελεῖν, ἔβενον, καὶ χρυσὸν, καὶ τῶν ἐλεφάντων τοὺς ὀδόντας [ēnankase to ethnos phorous telein, ebenon, kai chryson, kai tōn elephantōn tous odontas], he imposed on the nation as tribute ebony, and gold, and elephants' teeth. The Persians are read to have exacted the same things from the same Ethiopians. Herodotus, Muse 3, ch. 97: Ἀγινέουσι δὲ καὶ τὸ μέχρι ἐμεῦ δύο χοίνικας ἀπύρου χρυσίου, καὶ διηκοσίας φαλάγγας ἐβένου, καὶ ἐλέφαντος ὀδόντας μεγάλους εἴκοσι· [Agineousi de kai to mechri emeu dyo choinikas apyrou chrysiou, kai diēkosias phalangas ebenou, kai elephantos odontas megalous eikosi] Down to my own time (the Ethiopians, as a triennial tribute to the Persians) bring two choenixes of apyrous gold (that is, not yet tried by fire), and two hundred logs of ebony, and twenty large elephant tusks. For the region is rich in these three things, as the same author writes in ch. 114: Αὕτη δὲ χρυσόν τε φέρει πολλὸν, καὶ ἐλέφαντας ἀμφιλαφέας, καὶ δένδρεα πάντα ἄγρια, καὶ ἔβενον· [Hautē de chryson te pherei pollon, kai elephantas amphilapheas, kai dendrea panta agria, kai ebenon] This land produces much gold, and very large elephants, and wild trees of every kind, and ebony. Pliny too, book II, 717 12, ch. 4, where he states of ebony that by way of tribute the Ethiopians paid to the kings of Persia every third year a hundred logs of its wood, together with gold and ivory. And in the procession of Ptolemy Philadelphus, according to Callixenus of Rhodes, Ethiopians are reported to have carried these same things. col. 142 Ἐχόμενοι τούτων ἦσαν (he says) Αἰθίοπες δωροφόροι, ὧν οἱ μὲν ἔφερον ὀδόντας ἑξακοσίους, ἕτεροι δὲ ἐβένου κορμοὺς δισχιλίους, ἄλλοι χρυσοῦ καὶ ἀργυρίου κρατῆρας ἑξήκοντα, καὶ ψήγματα χρυσίου [Echomenoi toutōn ēsan … Aithiopes dōrophoroi, hōn hoi men epheron odontas hexakosious, heteroi de ebenou kormous dischilious, alloi chrysou kai argyriou kratēras hexēkonta, kai psēgmata chrysiou]. Next to these came Ethiopians bearing gifts, some of whom carried six hundred (elephants') tusks, others two thousand logs of ebony, others sixty bowls of gold and silver, and gold dust. Accordingly, at the festival of Adonis celebrated with great pomp at Alexandria under the same king, the Syracusan women, on seeing the ebony and the gold and the abundant ivory, burst out in these words, Idyll 15, line 123:


Ὦ ἔβενος, ὢ χρυσὸς, ὢ ἐκ λευκῶ ἐλέφαντος
Αἰετώ!

Ὦ ἔβενος, ὢ χρυσὸς, ὢ ἐκ λευκῶ ἐλέφαντος Αἰετώ! [Ō ebenos, ō chrysos, ō ek leukō elephantos Aietō!]


O ebenum, o aurum, o ex albo ebore aquilae! Quin et Romae, ut docet Plinius, in tributorum auctoritate tertia res fuit ebenus. Sexto, quamvis Hebraei Chaldaeo paraphrasti multum deferant, cui הבנים hobnim sunt pavones: tamen agnoscunt, nonnullos ebenum interpretari, et inter utramque sententiam ambigui sunt. Hinc Kimchius in Commentariis, הובנים פירשו בו העץ הנקרא בערבי אבנוס Hob nim lignum interpretantur, quod Arabice vocatur ebenus. Melius quam in Lexico יבנים jabnim, aut jebenim. Et Abarbanel, פירשו בו שהוא העץ הנקרא בערבי אוינוס שמביאין גם כן מארצות המזרח, Lignum explicant, quod Arabice dicitur evenus, quod etiam (ut ebur) ex orientalibus terris afferunt. Mardochaeus et Aquinas, עצם חיה מה או מין עץ, Os animalis alicujus, aut ligni species. Quod os animalis esse dictitant, tertia est sententia, quam in Lexico Kimchius ita explicat, הבנים הם חיות שעושין מלאכה מהעצם שלהן או מהקרנות כמו שעושין מעצם הפיל שהוא השן, Hobnim sunt animalia, ex quorum ossibus, aut cornibus, quaedam opera fiunt, quomodo ex osse elephantis, quod est ebur. Sed tertiam hanc sententiam idem reducit ad primam; quae hobnim pavones explicat, addens, fieri posse, שיעשו מלאכה מעצם שלהם, ut ex eorum ossibus opus aliquod fiat. Ut ex ebore scilicet, quocum hic jungitur הבנים hobnim. Quod monstrum est opinionis. Quis enim unquam fando audiit, pavonum ossa scalpi, aut sculpi, aut ad ullum opus eboris instar adhiberi? Itaque hoc ipsum, quod qui הבנים hobnim volunt esse pavones, ad tam absurda commenta delabuntur, docet, quanto sanius sentiant, qui ebenum hic intelligunt, in quo versione nihil est, quod non quadret ad amussim.

O ebony, O gold, O eagles of white ivory! Moreover, at Rome, as Pliny teaches, ebony held the third place in the esteem of tributes. Sixthly, although the Hebrews defer greatly to the Chaldee paraphrast, for whom הבנים hobnim are peacocks, they nevertheless acknowledge that some interpret it as ebony, and they waver between the two opinions. Hence Kimchi in his Commentaries: הובנים פירשו בו העץ הנקרא בערבי אבנוס, They interpret hobnim as the wood which is called ebony in Arabic. This is better than in his Lexicon, where it is יבנים jabnim, or jebenim. And Abarbanel [=Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), commentary on the Bible]: פירשו בו שהוא העץ הנקרא בערבי אוינוס שמביאין גם כן מארצות המזרח, They explain it as the wood which in Arabic is called evenus, which they also (like ivory) bring from the eastern lands. Mardochaeus and Aquinas: עצם חיה מה או מין עץ, The bone of some animal, or a kind of wood. Their repeated claim that it is the bone of an animal is a third opinion, which Kimchi explains in his Lexicon thus: הבנים הם חיות שעושין מלאכה מהעצם שלהן או מהקרנות כמו שעושין מעצם הפיל שהוא השן, Hobnim are animals from whose bones or horns certain works are made, as they are made from the bone of the elephant, which is ivory. But he reduces this third opinion to the first, which explains hobnim as peacocks, adding that it may be שיעשו מלאכה מעצם שלהם, that some work is made from their bones, namely as from ivory, with which הבנים hobnim is joined here. This is a monstrous opinion. For who has ever heard tell of peacock bones being carved or engraved, or used for any work in the manner of ivory? Thus the very fact that those who would have הבנים hobnim be peacocks slide into such absurd fictions shows how much more soundly those judge who understand ebony here; in that rendering there is nothing that does not fit exactly.


Tamen unum potest objici, nempe Plurale esse Hebraeum הבנים hobnim, cum ebeni vox sit solum Singularis. Varie quidem illa flectitur et scribitur. Dicitur enim haec ebenus, vel evenus, vel hebenus, et hoc ebenum, vel evenum, II, 718 vel hebenum. Et Graece ἡ ἔβενος, vel ἔβελος, ut in Suida; vel ἐβένη, ut in Theophrasto. Sed in Plurali ἐβένους Graece solus dixit Symmachus: et Latine ebenos, vel ebena soli, quod meminerim, Arias, et Mercerus in hujus loci interpretatione. Respondet Iunius, Plurali numero ab Hebraeis appellari; quia duo sunt genera ebeni. Nempe ita docet Theophrastus Hist. lib. 4. cap. 5. ubi de Indiae arboribus, Ἴδιον δὲ καὶ ἡ ἐβένη τῆς χώρας ταύτης. Ταύτης δὲ δύο γένη τὸ μὲν εὔξυλον, καὶ καλόν· τὸ δὲ φαῦλον. σπάνιον δὲ τὸ καλὸν, θάτε-ρον δὲ πολύ. Τὴν δὲ χρόαν οὐ θησαυριζομένη λαμβάνει τὴν εὔχρουν, ἀλλ᾽ εὐ-θὺς τῇ φύσει ἐστὶ δὲ τὸ δένδρον θαμνῶδες, ὥσπερ ὁ κύτισος. Est et ebenus hujus regionis propria. Illius autem duo sunt genera: unum ligni praestantis, et bonum; alterum malum. Rarum vero est illud, quod bonum, at alterum frequens. Nec bonum colorem accipit ebenus recondita, sed statim a natura habet. Fruticis porro instar est, ut cytisus. Hanc veram esse mentem Theophrasti, multis probat in Solinianis Salmasius, non qualem Plinius libri duodecimi capite quarto illi affingit his verbis: Duo genera ejus. Rarum id, quod melius arboreum, trunco col. 143 enodi, materie nigri splendoris, ac vel sine arte protinus jucundi. Alterum fruticosum cytisi modo, et tota India dispersum. Bona ebenus non dicitur εὔξυλος, quia est arborea, id est, magna ut arbor, sed a ligni praestantia. Neque malae proprium, sed utrique commune, quod sit θαμνώδης. Et ibi θαμνῶδες non sonat fruticosum, id est, multis virgultis densum, sed fruticis modo se habens, quomodo arbusta omnia. Dioscorides etiam duo ebeni genera facit, sed quae pro ratione loci ita distinguit: Ἔβενος κρατίστη ἡ Αἰθιοπικὴ, καὶ μέλαινα, καὶ μὴ ἔχουσα κτηδόνας· Ebenus optima est Aethiopica et nigra, venas, in pectinis modum discurrentes, non habens. Arabs interpres طبقات vocat. Et paullo post, Ἔστι δέ τις καὶ Ἰνδικὴ, ἔχουσα διαφύσεις λευκὰς, καὶ κιῤῥὰς, καὶ σπί-λους ὁμοίως πυκνούς· πλὴν βελτίων ἡ πρώτη. Est et alia Indica, candidis et rutilis intercurrentibus lineis, crebris etiam maculis. Sed prior est melior. Ita etiam Isidorus, Ebenus in India et Aethiopia nascitur, quae caesa durescit in lapidem, cujus lignum nigrum est, et cortex levis ut lauri. Sed Indicum maculosum est, in parvis distinctionibus albis et fulvis. Aethiopicum vero, quod praestantius accipitur, in nullo est maculatum, sed nigrum, leve et corneum. Et Serapio, Ejus duae sunt species, scilicet Absi et Inda. Et Absi est lignum nigrum, non ha-bens lineationes, etc. In Indo vero sunt lineationes albae, et coloris subrufi, etc. Quae ex Dioscoride sumpta sunt. Absi est حبشي Habasi, id est, Aethiopicum. His omnibus id commune est, quod ebeni nonnisi duas species agnoscunt. Quo non pertinet Hebraeum הבנים hobnim, quia Plurale, non Duale nomen est. Nam Duale esset hobnajim. Itaque aliud quaerendum. Et Fullerus quidem hoc Plurale refert ad ebeni palangas, quae ex India et Æthiopia magno II, 719 numero afferebantur. Φάλαγγας vocant Herodotus et Arrianus in Periplo. Plinius palangas, aut phalangas, variante scriptura, id est, fustes teretes, ut qui navibus supponuntur, aut quibus idem onus plures bajulant. Pollux lib. 7. cap. 33. §. 9. Τὰ δὲ τῶν νεῶν ξύλα, οἷς ὑποβληθεῖσιν ἐφέλκονται αἱ νῆες, φάλαγγες, καὶ φαλάγγια. Hesychius, Φαλάγγια· στρόγγυλα ξύλα, καὶ σύμμετρα. Nonnius, Palangae dicuntur fustes teretes, qui navibus subjiciuntur, cum attrahuntur ad pelagus, vel cum ad littora subducuntur. Glossae, Phalangarii, Οἱ τοῖς δοκοῖς ἀποκρεμῶντες βάρη, καὶ πλείονες ἅμα βαστάζοντες. Rursus Nonius, Palangarios dicimus, qui aliquid oneris fustibus transvehunt. Origo vocis videtur esse Hebraica. Nam Hebraice פלך pelec, vel ἀρχαϊκῶς phelec est baculus, 2 Sam. III, 29. Et Arabice فلك phalaca, rotundum esse. Itaque hinc φάλαγγες, phalanges, vel palanges dici potuere baculi teretes ebenini, quos Tyrii mercatores פלכין pelakin, aut phelakin appellabant. Callixenus lib. 5. Athenaei nominat ἐβένου κορμοὺς, ebeni stipites. Apulejus Apologia prima hebeni baculos, quamvis ibi loculos legere quidam malint. Hos igitur, sive baculos, sive κορμοὺς, aut has ebeni palangas Plurali voce הבנים hobnim significari putat Fullerus. Sed viri docti videntur hic frustra se fatigare, cum hujusmodi pretiosa ligna Hebraei vix aliter quam Plurali voce nominent. Sic arbor, ex qua arca fabricata est, Singulari numero semel שטה sitta dicitur Es. XLI, 19. Sed Plurali שטים sittim in Exodo plus vigesies. Et arbor alia, ex qua tigna et fulcra facta sunt in templo Solomonis, citharaeque et nablia cantorum, nonnisi Plurali voce dicitur אלגומים algumim, vel אלמוגים almugim, 1 Reg. X, 11. 12. et 2 Par. IX, 10. 11. Et in Chaldaeis paraphrasibus Ionathanis et Ierusalem, Gen. L, 1. Iosephus patrem suum decumbere fecit בערס דסנדפין, in sponda ex sindaphin, id est, ut volunt, in lecto, facto ex praestantissimi ligni genere, Plurali voce sic col. 144 dicti. Et ego suspicabar olim, a duobus Aegypti pagis سندف Sendapha nomine sic appellari. Tamen in tractatu De Elephanto supra alia habetur hujus vocis verior expositio.

Yet one objection can be raised, namely that the Hebrew הבנים hobnim is a plural, whereas the word for ebony is only singular. It is indeed inflected and spelled in various ways. For one says haec ebenus, or evenus, or hebenus, and hoc ebenum, or evenum, II, 718 or hebenum. And in Greek ἡ ἔβενος [hē ebenos], or ἔβελος [ebelos], as in the Suda; or ἐβένη [ebenē], as in Theophrastus. But in the plural, ἐβένους [ebenous] in Greek was said only by Symmachus; and in Latin ebenos or ebena only, as far as I remember, by Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot] and Mercerus in their rendering of this passage. Junius answers that it is named in the plural by the Hebrews because there are two kinds of ebony. That is indeed what Theophrastus teaches, Hist. book 4, ch. 5, where he treats the trees of India: Ἴδιον δὲ καὶ ἡ ἐβένη τῆς χώρας ταύτης. Ταύτης δὲ δύο γένη τὸ μὲν εὔξυλον, καὶ καλόν· τὸ δὲ φαῦλον. σπάνιον δὲ τὸ καλὸν, θάτερον δὲ πολύ. Τὴν δὲ χρόαν οὐ θησαυριζομένη λαμβάνει τὴν εὔχρουν, ἀλλ᾽ εὐθὺς τῇ φύσει ἐστὶ δὲ τὸ δένδρον θαμνῶδες, ὥσπερ ὁ κύτισος [Idion de kai hē ebenē tēs chōras tautēs. Tautēs de dyo genē to men euxylon, kai kalon; to de phaulon. spanion de to kalon, thateron de poly. Tēn de chroan ou thēsaurizomenē lambanei tēn euchroun, all᾽ euthys tē physei estin de to dendron thamnōdes, hōsper ho kytisos]. Ebony too is peculiar to this region. Of it there are two kinds: one of excellent wood, and good; the other bad. The good one is rare, but the other common. Nor does ebony acquire its fine colour by being stored away, but has it at once from nature. Moreover it is like a shrub, as the cytisus is. That this is the true meaning of Theophrastus Salmasius proves at length in his Exercitations on Solinus, and not the one that Pliny, book 12, chapter 4, ascribes to him in these words: There are two kinds of it. The rarer is the better one, tree-like, with a trunk col. 143 free of knots, its wood of a black lustre, and pleasing at once even without craftsmanship. The other is shrubby, like the cytisus, and spread over all India. Good ebony is not called εὔξυλος [euxylos] because it is tree-like, that is, large like a tree, but from the excellence of its wood. Nor is being θαμνώδης [thamnōdēs] peculiar to the bad kind; it is common to both. And there θαμνῶδες [thamnōdes] does not mean fruticosum [shrubby], that is, dense with many twigs, but behaving like a shrub, as all bushes do. Dioscorides also makes two kinds of ebony, but distinguishes them by place: Ἔβενος κρατίστη ἡ Αἰθιοπικὴ, καὶ μέλαινα, καὶ μὴ ἔχουσα κτηδόνας [Ebenos kratistē hē Aithiopikē, kai melaina, kai mē echousa ktēdonas]; The best ebony is the Ethiopian, black, and without veins running through it like the teeth of a comb. The Arabic translator calls them طبقات [ṭabaqāt]. And a little later: Ἔστι δέ τις καὶ Ἰνδικὴ, ἔχουσα διαφύσεις λευκὰς, καὶ κιῤῥὰς, καὶ σπίλους ὁμοίως πυκνούς· πλὴν βελτίων ἡ πρώτη [Esti de tis kai Indikē, echousa diaphyseis leukas, kai kirrhas, kai spilous homoiōs pyknous; plēn beltiōn hē prōtē]. There is also another, Indian, with white and reddish lines running through it, and frequent spots as well. But the former is better. So also Isidore: Ebony grows in India and Ethiopia; when cut it hardens into stone; its wood is black, and its bark smooth like that of the laurel. But the Indian is spotted, with small white and tawny markings. The Ethiopian, however, which is held to be superior, is spotted nowhere, but black, smooth and horn-like. And Serapion [=Serapion, Liber de simplicibus medicinis (the Arabic-Latin pharmacopoeia)]: It has two species, namely Absi and Inda. And Absi is a black wood, without lines, etc. In the Indian, however, there are white lines, and of a reddish colour, etc. This is taken from Dioscorides. Absi is حبشي [ḥabashī] Habasi, that is, Ethiopian. Common to all of these is that they recognize only two species of ebony. To which the Hebrew הבנים hobnim does not correspond, because it is a plural, not a dual noun. For the dual would be hobnajim. So something else must be sought. Fuller indeed refers this plural to the palangae of ebony, which were brought from India and Ethiopia in great II, 719 numbers. Herodotus and Arrian in the Periplus call them φάλαγγας [phalangas]; Pliny palangae or phalangae, the spelling varying; that is, round poles, such as are placed under ships, or on which several men carry the same load. Pollux, book 7, ch. 33, §. 9: Τὰ δὲ τῶν νεῶν ξύλα, οἷς ὑποβληθεῖσιν ἐφέλκονται αἱ νῆες, φάλαγγες, καὶ φαλάγγια [Ta de tōn neōn xyla, hois hypoblētheisin ephelkontai hai nēes, phalanges, kai phalangia]. Hesychius: Φαλάγγια· στρόγγυλα ξύλα, καὶ σύμμετρα [Phalangia; strongyla xyla, kai symmetra]. Nonius: Palangae is the name for round poles which are put under ships when they are drawn down to the sea, or when they are hauled up onto the shore. The Glosses: Phalangarii, Οἱ τοῖς δοκοῖς ἀποκρεμῶντες βάρη, καὶ πλείονες ἅμα βαστάζοντες [Hoi tois dokois apokremōntes barē, kai pleiones hama bastazontes]. Again Nonius: We call palangarii those who carry some load on poles. The origin of the word seems to be Hebrew. For in Hebrew פלך pelec, or in archaic form phelec, is baculus [staff], 2 Sam 3:29. And in Arabic فلك [falaka] phalaca means to be round. Hence the round ebony staves which the Tyrian merchants called פלכין pelakin or phelakin could have been called φάλαγγες [phalanges], phalanges, or palanges. Callixenus, in book 5 of Athenaeus, names ἐβένου κορμοὺς [ebenou kormous], logs of ebony. Apuleius, in the first Apology, staves of ebony, though some prefer to read loculos [little boxes] there. These, then, whether staves or κορμοὺς [kormous], or these palangae of ebony, Fuller thinks are signified by the plural הבנים hobnim. But learned men seem to weary themselves here in vain, since the Hebrews scarcely name precious woods of this kind otherwise than with a plural word. Thus the tree from which the ark was made is called once in the singular שטה sitta, Isa 41:19. But in the plural שטים sittim more than twenty times in Exodus. And another tree, from which the beams and supports in the temple of Solomon were made, and the harps and lutes of the singers, is called only by a plural word, אלגומים algumim or אלמוגים almugim, 1 Reg. X, 11. 12. and 2 Chr 9:10–11. And in the Chaldee paraphrases of Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] and Jerusalem, Gen 50:1: Joseph laid his father בערס דסנדפין, on a couch of sindaphin, that is, as they hold, on a bed made of the most excellent kind of wood, so called with a plural word. col. 144 And I once suspected that it was so named after two villages of Egypt called سندف [Sndf] Sendapha. Yet in the treatise On the Elephant above, a truer explanation of this word is given.


Obiter notandum, in Arabum libris memorari quaedam ligna ebeno tam similia, ut illa pro ebeno nonnulli sumant. In his lignum شيز Siz, vel شيزي Siza, a loco sic appellatum: et lignum ساسم sasem, vel سمسم semsem, et in Plurali سماسم semasim eodem nomine dictum, quo sesamum, quamvis a sesamo diversissimum. Quo haec pertinent in Alcamus, الشيز والشيزي خشب اسود للقصاع وهو الابنوس والساسم او خشب الجوز وناحية بارض بادر بيجان Siz, vel Siza, nigrum lignum ad patinas conficiendas. Aut est ebenus, aut sasim, aut li-gnum nucis, et regio quaedam in terra Adarbigian (id est, Atropatia Strabonis et II, 720 Ptolemaei Atropatena), ex qua nempe hoc lignum affertur, et nomen sumit. Idem alibi, الساسم شجر اسود او الابنوس او الشيز او شجر يعمل منه القسي Sasim; arbor nigra, aut ebenus, aut siz, aut arbor, ex qua fiunt arcus. Damir in capite De سمسمة simsima, quod formicae rubrae genus est, ut Chaldaeis שומשמנא, dicit hoc idem lignum سمسم semsem vocari, et Plurali سماسم semasim, quod probat ex his pseudo-prophetae verbis de الجهنميين, id est, de iis, qui in gehenna torquentur, تخرجون من النار بعد ان يكونوا فيها فيخرجون كانها عيدان السماسم Exibunt ex igne post aliquam in eo moram; exibunt, inquam, tanquam ligna semasim, id est, pariter nigri propter adustionem ex igne. In quae verba commentatores multa afferunt absurdissima. Sed peritiores agnoscunt, ligna semasim esse ebenina ligna, aut ebeno atrore similia, ita, ut exusta videantur. Unde lux his Dioscoridis in capite De ebeno, Ἔνιοι δὲ τὰ σησάμινα, ἢ ἀκάνθινα ξύλα ἐμφερῆ ὄντα, ἀντὶ ἐβένου πωλοῦσι· Quae Marcellus Virgilius ita reddidit: Vendunt pro ebeno qui- dam spinae Indicae, aut mori, fallente similitudine, materiam. Putat nempe, pro σησάμινα legendum συκάμινα, quia sesamum nihil habet commune cum ebeno. Sed neque sycaminus, seu sycomorus, nisi quod utrumque lignum est. Cave igitur, ne quidquam mutes. Aliud enim hic sesamina, quam vulgo. Nempe ligna illius arboris, quae Arabice sasim et semsem appellatur, et in Plurali sema- sim. Itaque Dioscoridis Arabs interpres hic recte habet ومن الناس من ياخذ اعضان خشب بعض اصناف الشوك والخشب الذي يقال له سيساما فيبيعه بدل الابنوس لانه col. 145 شبيه به Sunt, qui sumunt lignum cujusdam spinae speciei, et lignum, quod sesamum vocant, et pro ebeno vendunt, quia illi simile est. Quid quod praeter Dioscoridem etiam Arrianus in Periplo meminit φαλάγγων σησαμίνων, καὶ ἐβενίνων, palangarum sesaminarum et ebeninarum, quae ex Indiae urbe Baryga- sis in Persidem afferuntur. Itaque haec lectio certa est et indubitata.

It should be noted in passing that the books of the Arabs mention certain woods so similar to ebony that some take them for ebony. Among these is the wood شيز [shīz] Siz, or شيزي [shīzī] Siza, so called from a place; and the wood ساسم [sāsam] sasem, or سمسم [simsim] semsem, in the plural سماسم [samāsim] semasim, called by the same name as sesame, although it is entirely different from sesame. To this belong these words in Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: الشيز والشيزي خشب اسود للقصاع وهو الابنوس والساسم او خشب الجوز وناحية بارض بادر بيجان [al-shīz wa-l-shīzī khashab aswad li-l-qiṣāʿ wa-huwa al-abanūs wa-l-sāsam aw khashab al-jawz wa-nāḥiya bi-arḍ bādr bījān] Siz, or Siza, a black wood for making dishes. It is either ebony, or sasim, or the wood of the walnut; and also a certain region in the land of Adarbigian (that is, the Atropatia of Strabo and II, 720 the Atropatena of Ptolemy), from which, namely, this wood is brought and takes its name. The same author elsewhere: الساسم شجر اسود او الابنوس او الشيز او شجر يعمل منه القسي [al-sāsam shajar aswad aw al-abanūs aw al-shīz aw shajar yuʿmal minhu al-qisī] Sasim: a black tree, or ebony, or siz, or a tree from which bows are made. Damir, in the chapter On سمسمة [simsima] simsima, which is a kind of red ant, like שומשמנא among the Chaldeans, says that this same wood is called سمسم [simsim] semsem, in the plural سماسم [samāsim] semasim. He proves this from these words of the pseudo-prophet about الجهنميين [al-jahannamiyyīn], that is, about those who are tormented in Gehenna: تخرجون من النار بعد ان يكونوا فيها فيخرجون كانها عيدان السماسم [takhrujūn min al-nār baʿd an yakūnū fīhā fa-yakhrujūn ka-annahā ʿīdān al-samāsim] They will come out of the fire after some stay in it; they will come out, I say, like the woods semasim, that is, equally black from being scorched by the fire. On these words the commentators offer many quite absurd things. But the more learned recognize that the semasim woods are ebony woods, or woods resembling ebony in blackness, so that they seem burnt. This throws light on these words of Dioscorides in the chapter On ebony: Ἔνιοι δὲ τὰ σησάμινα, ἢ ἀκάνθινα ξύλα ἐμφερῆ ὄντα, ἀντὶ ἐβένου πωλοῦσι· [Enioi de ta sēsamina, ē akanthina xyla empherē onta, anti ebenou pōlousi]. Marcellus Virgilius rendered this as follows: Some sell in place of ebony the timber of the Indian thorn, or of the mulberry, the resemblance deceiving. He thinks, namely, that σησάμινα [sēsamina] should be read συκάμινα [sykamina], because sesame has nothing in common with ebony. But neither has the sycamine or sycomore, except that both are wood. Beware, therefore, of changing anything. For sesamina here means something other than in common usage: namely, the wood of that tree which is called sasim and semsem in Arabic, and in the plural semasim. Accordingly the Arabic translator of Dioscorides rightly has here: ومن الناس من ياخذ اعضان خشب بعض اصناف الشوك والخشب الذي يقال له سيساما فيبيعه بدل الابنوس لانه col. 145 شبيه به [wa-min al-nās man yaʾkhudh aʿḍān khashab baʿḍ aṣnāf al-shawk wa-l-khashab alladhī yuqāl lahu sīsāmā fa-yabīʿuhu badal al-abanūs li-annahu shabīh bihi] There are some who take the wood of a certain kind of thorn, and the wood which they call sesamum, and sell it in place of ebony, because it resembles it. What is more, besides Dioscorides, Arrian too in the Periplus mentions φαλάγγων σησαμίνων, καὶ ἐβενίνων [phalangōn sēsaminōn, kai ebeninōn], beams of sesamine and of ebony, which are brought from the Indian city of Barygaza to Persia. This reading is therefore certain and beyond doubt.


(1) Rosenmüller, II, 709 Scribit PLINIUS Hist. Nat. L. X. c. 42. §. 58. Psittacum in India vocari Sit- tacen. Quod nomen ADR. RELANDUS in Dissertatt. Miscellann. P. I. p. 184. factum existimat ex Tedac, et hoc a תך: „sive, inquit, a תך geminata prima, vel addita, similis soni litera, fecerint alii تدك, sive ex Tedac, rejecta ob soni similitudinem alterutra priorum literarum, natum sit תך“. Quod quam lubricum sit atque incertum, quisque intelliget ipse. Praetermitto aliorum de hoc vocabulo somnia, quae qui scire cupit, adeat SIMONIS Lexic. sub voce. Equidem acquiescendum putem in iis, quae Bochartus acute non minus quam docte hic disputavit.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 709 Pliny writes, Hist. Nat. book 10, ch. 42, §. 58, that the psittacus [parrot] is called Sittace in India. Reland [=Adriaan Reland, Dissertationes miscellaneae (1706–08)], in Dissertatt. Miscellann. vol. 1, p. 184, thinks this name was formed from Tedac, and this from תך: "whether," he says, "from תך others made تدك [tdk] by doubling the first letter or adding a letter of similar sound, or whether תך arose from Tedac by dropping one of the first two letters because of the similarity of sound." How slippery and uncertain this is, everyone will see for himself. I pass over the dreams of others about this word; whoever wishes to know them may consult Simonis, Lexic. under the word. For my part, I would think one should rest content with what Bochart has argued here no less acutely than learnedly.

Part 2, Book 1, chapter 21: The word tsippor
