https://openseforim.org/bochart/tsippor.html

II, 721 col. 145 CAP. XXI.

II, 721 col. 145 Chapter 21.


De voce צפור tsippor, quae et quasvis aves sonat, et speciatim passerem. Hujus species juxta Arabes, et de passere domestico et ejus pipitu.

On the word צפור tsippor, which denotes both birds of any kind and specifically the sparrow. Its kinds according to the Arabs; and on the house sparrow and its chirping.


Inter senilis aetatis incommoda, quae graphice depingit Solomon, hoc quoque recensetur Eccles. XII, 6. quod excitatur, et surgit לקול הצפור, ad vocem τοῦ tsippor, seu avis, id est, galli, ut multi putant. Quos doctissimus Mercerus ita refellit: Qui gallum intelligunt, ad cujus vocem excitetur, vim vocis Hebraicae צפור (tsippor) non intelligunt, quae aviculam significat, etc. nec de majoribus avibus dicitur. Et idem in Thesauro, צפור (tsippor) significat minutiores aves, etc. עוף (oph) autem generaliter est avis, aut volucris. Et Schindlerus, צפור (tsippor) avicula circumvolitans, aut quae in aëre gyratur. Comprehendit aves minores, et harum frequentiorem hominibus passerem, avem communissimam. Ita etiam plerique alii recentiores lexicographi. Et in Philonis libro, Quis rerum divinarum sit haeres, Sepphora est ὀρνίθιον avicula. Tamen apud Hebraeos עוף oph et צפור tsippor, sunt aeque generalia, et omnes omnino volucres complectitur utrumque nomen. Hinc Kimchius et Pomarius in Lexicis suis ad vocem צפור tsippor, שם כלל לכל עוף, omni avi commune nomen est. Et Aquinas, שם כולל לכל מיני עוף שיעופף, Nomen hoc complectitur omnem avis speciem, quae volat. Quod verissimum esse, apparebit conferenti loca Scripturae. Nam Deut. IV, 17. cum Deus coli prohibet תבנית כל צפור כנף אשר תעוף בשמים, similitudinem omnis tsippor alatae, quae per coelum volat, quis solum prohiberi dixerit avicularum cultum, non etiam majorum avium? et Deut. XIV, 11. cum idem Deus concedit esum כל צפור טהורה, omnis tsippor mundae, an solum aviculas concessisse dicetur, non gallinas, et meleagrides, et phasianos? Aut quis unquam ad aviculas restrinxit legem, quae habetur Deut. XXII, 6. Si obviam tibi fiat קן צפור, nidus tsippor in ulla arbore, aut humi, nidus pullorum, aut ovorum, ubi mater incubet pullis, aut ovis, ne accipito matrem cum pullis? Rursus quis negaverit, omnes aves significari, cum Deus homini subjecisse legitur bestias agri, צפור שמים, tsippor coelorum, et pisces maris, Psal. VIII, 9.? Aut cum col. 146 ad celebrandum Deum invitantur ferae, et jumenta omnia, reptilia, וצפור כנף, et tsippor alata, Psal. CXLVIII, 10.? Aut cum in mysticae arboris ramis ha-bitare leguntur כל צפור כל כנף, omnis tsippor, omne alatum, Ezech. XVII, 23.? Et Plurali numero צפרי שמיא, tsippare coelorum, Dan. IV, 9. 18.? Denique rapaces aves, quae fere sunt multo maximae, hoc nomine designari patet, cum Ezech. XXXIX, 4. 17. copias Gog et Magog Deus tradit vorandas לעיט צפור, II, 722 rapaci tsippor alatae. Et Daniel IV, 20. ubi Babylonii regis ungues crevisse dicuntur כצפרין, ut tsipparin, ut rapacium avium ungues, quae ab unguium curvatura et amplitudine Graece dicuntur γαμψώνυχες. Itaque palam est, extendi nomen צפור tsippor etiam ad maximas aves. Rabbi Moses, filius Guersom, aves ita dici contendit; שבעלות השחר מתחילות לרנן ולצפצוף quia ad ortum aurorae canere et minurire incipiunt. Ego non quidem a cantu, qui non est communis omnibus, sed a צפר, id est, mane, dici autumo; quia solenne est avibus, summo mane surgere, sive canorae sint, aut non canorae: cum ferae tum altum dormiant, quia noctem ducunt insomnem, Psal. CIV, 20.

Among the infirmities of old age which Solomon vividly depicts, this too is listed, Eccl 12:6: that one is roused and rises לקול הצפור, at the voice of the tsippor, or bird, that is, of the cock, as many think. The most learned Mercerus [=Jean Mercier (d. 1570), commentaries on Job and Proverbs] refutes them thus: Those who understand the cock, at whose voice one is roused, do not understand the force of the Hebrew word צפור (tsippor), which means a little bird, etc., and is not said of larger birds. And the same author in his Thesaurus: צפור (tsippor) means smaller birds, etc.; עוף (oph), however, is a bird or winged creature in general. And Schindler: צפור (tsippor) is a little bird flying about, or one that circles in the air. It comprises the smaller birds, and among them the sparrow, the one most frequently found among men, a very common bird. So too most other recent lexicographers. And in Philo's book Who is the Heir of Divine Things, Sepphora is ὀρνίθιον [ornithion], a little bird. Yet among the Hebrews עוף oph and צפור tsippor are equally general, and both names embrace absolutely all winged creatures. Hence Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] and Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)] in their Lexicons, under the word צפור tsippor: שם כלל לכל עוף, it is a name common to every bird. And Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)]: שם כולל לכל מיני עוף שיעופף, This name comprises every species of bird that flies. That this is entirely true will be clear to anyone who compares the passages of Scripture. For in Deut 4:17, when God forbids the worship of תבנית כל צפור כנף אשר תעוף בשמים, the likeness of any winged tsippor that flies through the heavens, who would say that only the worship of little birds is forbidden, and not that of larger birds as well? And in Deut 14:11, when the same God permits the eating of כל צפור טהורה, every clean tsippor, will he be said to have permitted only little birds, and not hens, guinea fowl and pheasants? Or who ever restricted to little birds the law found in Deut 22:6: If there come before you קן צפור, a nest of a tsippor, in any tree or on the ground, a nest of young or of eggs, where the mother is sitting on the young or on the eggs, do not take the mother with the young? Again, who would deny that all birds are meant when we read that God subjected to man the beasts of the field, צפור שמים, the tsippor of the heavens, and the fish of the sea, Ps 8:9? Or when col. 146 wild beasts, and all cattle, creeping things, וצפור כנף, and the winged tsippor are invited to praise God, Ps 148:10? Or when we read that in the branches of the mystical tree dwell כל צפור כל כנף, every tsippor, everything winged, Ezek 17:23? And in the plural, צפרי שמיא, the tsippare of the heavens, Dan 4:9 18.? Finally, it is clear that birds of prey, which are generally by far the largest, are designated by this name, when in Ezek 39:4 17. God hands over the hosts of Gog and Magog to be devoured לעיט צפור, II, 722 by the ravenous winged tsippor. And in Daniel IV, 20, where the nails of the Babylonian king are said to have grown כצפרין, like tsipparin, that is, like the talons of birds of prey, which from the curvature and size of their talons are called in Greek γαμψώνυχες [gampsōnyches]. It is therefore evident that the name צפור tsippor extends even to the largest birds. Rabbi Moses, son of Gershom, maintains that birds are so called שבעלות השחר מתחילות לרנן ולצפצוף, because at the rising of the dawn they begin to sing and to warble. I, for my part, hold that they are named not from singing, which is not common to all, but from צפר, that is, morning; because it is customary for birds to rise very early in the morning, whether they are songbirds or not, while wild beasts are then sound asleep, because they spend the night awake, Psal. CIV, 20.


Sed, utut omnibus avibus commune sit nomen צפור tsippor, tamen Hebraei asserunt, quandoque hoc eodem nomine passerem speciatim significari. Kimchius in Psal. LXXXIV, 4. וצפור הוא עוף קטן וקורין לו בלעז פשרא Et tsippor (ibi loci) parva est avis, quam vulgari lingua (id est, Hispanica) vocant paxaro (id est, passerem). Hinc Pomarius, קמחי אומר שלפעמים יוקח בעד עוף קטן שקורין לו בלעז פאסרו, Dixit Kimchius, aliquando sumi pro avicula, quam vernaculo (seu Italico) sermone vocant passaro. Aquinas, הוא שם מין עוף מה, Nomen est certae avis speciei. Et paullo post, והוא עוף קטן וידוע, Est avicula nota, nempe passer. Proinde ut Hieronymus passerem reddit Lev. XIV, 4. ita etiam vetus interpres Psal. X, 1. et LXXXIII, 4. et CI, 8. et CIII, 16. et CXXIII, 7. Graecos sequutus, qui στρουθίον exponunt in iisdem Psalmorum locis, et Eccles. XII, 6. et Thren. III, 52. Et vicissim Graecum στρουθία, id est, passeres, Matth. X, 29. et Luc. XII, 6. Syrus ܨܦܪܝܢ tsipparin interpretatur: pro quo Arabs عصافير atsaphiro. Illis enim عصفور otsphur est passer, voce facta ex צפור tsippor, gutturali praefixa. Quod cum ignoraret Chamza, Grammaticus Arabs non incelebris, putavit عصفور voce composita passerem dici; quia عصي وفر percutit et fugit. Nec Hebraeis peculiare est, quod ea voce passerem vocant, qua etiam majores aves. Graecum enim passeris nomen στρουθὸς de gallina quoque usurpatur. Nicander in Alexipharmacis versu 60.

But although the name צפור tsippor is common to all birds, the Hebrews nevertheless assert that this same name sometimes signifies the sparrow specifically. Kimchi on Psal. LXXXIV, 4: וצפור הוא עוף קטן וקורין לו בלעז פשרא And tsippor (in that place) is a small bird, which in the vernacular (that is, Spanish) they call paxaro (that is, sparrow). Hence Pomarius: קמחי אומר שלפעמים יוקח בעד עוף קטן שקורין לו בלעז פאסרו, Kimchi said that it is sometimes taken for a little bird, which in the vernacular (or Italian) tongue they call passaro. Aquinas: הוא שם מין עוף מה, It is the name of a certain species of bird. And a little later: והוא עוף קטן וידוע, It is a well-known little bird, namely the sparrow. Accordingly, just as Jerome renders it sparrow in Lev. XIV, 4, so too does the old translator in Psal. X, 1, and LXXXIII, 4, and CI, 8, and CIII, 16, and CXXIII, 7, following the Greeks, who render it στρουθίον [strouthion] in those same passages of the Psalms, and in Eccles. XII, 6, and Thren. III, 52. And conversely, the Greek στρουθία [strouthia], that is, sparrows, in Matth. X, 29, and Luc. XII, 6, the Syriac translator renders ܨܦܪܝܢ [צפרין] tsipparin, for which the Arabic has عصافير [ʿaṣāfīr] atsaphiro. For to them عصفور [ʿuṣfūr] otsphur is the sparrow, a word formed from צפור tsippor with a guttural prefixed. Not knowing this, Chamza, a not undistinguished Arab grammarian, thought that the sparrow is called عصفور by a compound word, because عصي وفر [ʿaṣá wa-farra] it strikes and flees. Nor is it peculiar to the Hebrews that they call the sparrow by the same word as they also call larger birds. For the Greek name of the sparrow, στρουθὸς [strouthos], is also used of the hen. Nicander in the Alexipharmaca, line 60:


Ἠέ τι μηελόεντα χαλικρότερον ποτὸν ἴσχοις
Ὄρνιθος στρουθοῖο κατοικάδος, — — —

Ἠέ τι μηελόεντα χαλικρότερον ποτὸν ἴσχοις Ὄρνιθος στρουθοῖο κατοικάδος, — — — [Ēe ti mēeloenta chalikroteron poton ischois / Ornithos strouthoio katoikados]


Sive aliquod medullosum meracum potabile pharmacum habeas ex ave passere domestica, id est, ex gallina. Et rursus versu 535.

Or may you have some marrowy, undiluted drinkable remedy from the domestic sparrow-bird, that is, from the hen. And again, line 535:


Ἠὲ πάτον στρουθοῖο κατοικάδος, — —

Ἠὲ πάτον στρουθοῖο κατοικάδος, — — [Ēe paton strouthoio katoikados]


Aut stercus passeris domestici, id est, gallinae. Unde factum, ut στρουθὸς diceretur gallina illa Libyca, avium longe maxima, uno verbo struthio. Quod imitati II, 723 Romani scriptores struthionem appellant marinum passerem. Plautus in Persa Actu secundo,

Or the dung of the domestic sparrow, that is, of the hen. Hence it came about that the great Libyan hen, by far the largest of birds, was called στρουθὸς [strouthos], in a word the ostrich. Imitating this, the II, 723 Roman writers call the ostrich the sea sparrow. Plautus in the Persa, Act 2:


Vola curriculo. P. Istuc marinus passer per circum solet.

Fly at a run. P. That is what the sea sparrow usually does around the circus.


Ausonius Epistola undecima,

Ausonius, Epistle 11:


Ovum tu coque passeris marini. col. 147

Cook you the egg of the sea sparrow. col. 147


Festus, Passer marinus, quem vocat vulgus struthiocamelum. Passeris Romana vox putatur ad Hebraeam צפור tsippor alludere, et ab illa esse orta. Sed vir magnus in Solinum observat, passerem etiam passam dici, ut Gallice paisse passerem foeminam. Hinc Glossae, Passa, εἶδος ὀρνέου. Et passa factum ex Aeolico πίζα, pro σπίζα. Nempe σπίζα est fringillus, avis, passeri similis. Hesychius, Σπίζα· ὀρνιθάριον στρουθῷ παρεμφερές. Et quandoque latius sumitur pro avicula in genere. Ut in Timone apud Laërtium de Arcesilao,

Festus: The sea sparrow, which the common people call the struthiocamelus. The Roman word passer is thought to allude to the Hebrew צפור tsippor and to have arisen from it. But a great man, commenting on Solinus, observes that the sparrow was also called passa, as the female sparrow is called paisse in French. Hence the Glosses: Passa, εἶδος ὀρνέου [eidos orneou]. And passa was formed from the Aeolic πίζα [piza], for σπίζα [spiza]. For σπίζα [spiza] is the finch, a bird similar to the sparrow. Hesychius: Σπίζα· ὀρνιθάριον στρουθῷ παρεμφερές [Spiza: ornitharion strouthō paremferes]. And sometimes it is taken more broadly for a little bird in general, as in Timon, quoted by Laertius, on Arcesilaus:


Οἱ δέ μιν ἠΰ τε γλαῦκα περὶ σπίζαι τερατοῦντο,

Οἱ δέ μιν ἠΰ τε γλαῦκα περὶ σπίζαι τερατοῦντο, [Hoi de min ēy te glauka peri spizai teratounto]


Illum autem mirabuntur ut aviculae, quae noctuam circumstant, proinde Hesychius, Σπίζια· ὄρνεα ἅπαντα. Recte, si modo ὄρνεα illi sunt ὀρνίθια, vel ὀρνιθάρια· aviculae, non aves. Sic Arabicum عصفور, quamvis proprie passerem sonat, tamen avicularum multas species complectitur. Damir, وهى انواع منها ما هو مطرب بصوته ومنها ما يعجب بصورته وحسنه والعصفور الصوار هو الذي يجيب اذا ادعي من الصرورة وعصفور الجنة وهو الخطاف والعصفور البيوت فان في طباعه اختلافا Passerum sunt variae species: alii enim placent vocis modulatione; alii specie et forma sunt mirabiles. Et passer suar dictus is est, qui vocatus stridendo respondet. Et passer paradisi est hirundo. Et passer domesticus is, qui natura sua est pugnax, etc. Et infra, ومن انواعه عصفور الشوك واكثر ماواه السياج وزعم ارسطو ان بينه وبين الحمار عداوة E speciebus ejus est passer spinarum, qui in vepretis plerumque degit. Refert Aristoteles, inter eum et asinum mutuum esse odium; palam est, acanthidem intelligi, quam alii carduelem, alii spinum, alii ligurinum explicant. De ea enim Philosophus Hist. libri octavi capite tertio, Τὰ δὲ τοιάδε ἀκανθοφάγα, ἀκανθὶς, θραυπίς· ἔτι ἡ καλουμένη χρυσομήτρις. Ταῦτα γὰρ πάντα ἐπὶ τῶν ἀκανθῶν νέμεται. Quae Gaza sic reddidit: Spinam appetunt illa, spinus, sive ligurinus, carduelis, item quae aurivittis appellatur. Haec enim omnia victitant in spinis. Et libri noni capite primo, Ὄνος δὲ, καὶ ἀκανθίδες πολέμιοι· αἱ μὲν γὰρ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀκανθῶν βοητεύουσιν (legendum II, 724 βιοτεύουσιν), ὁ δὲ ἁπαλὰς οὔσας ἐσθίει τὰς ἀκάνθας· Inimici sunt asinus et acanthides: illis enim victus ex spinis, quas adhuc teneras pascit asinus. Et hanc avem merito Arabes referunt ad passerum genus. Acanthis enim eadem, quae acánthyllis, de qua Hesychius, Ἀκανθυλλίς· στρουθοῦ γένος, Acanthyllis, passeris genus. Gallice dicitur serin. An a Sirenum cantu, ut vult Bellonius Ornithologiae libri septimi capite decimo quarto. Sequitur in Damire, ومن انواعه القبرة والحسون والبلبل والصعوة والحمرة والعندليب والمكاكي والصافر والتنوط والوصع والابوبراقش col. 148 والقبعة Etiam e speciebus ejus sunt kubbara (corydalus), et hassun (alibi non reperio, videtur a pulchritudine dicta) (1), et bulbul (philomela), et savva (avicula rubro vertice), et hamra (alaudae species rubra), et andalib (avis species, philomelae similis,), et mechachi (Plurale a Singulari مكا maccha, avis, a sibilo dicta,), et saphir (quae et ipsa tota nocte sibilat capite inclinato, et pedibus ad arborem applicatis), et thenavvut (avicula, huic non absimilis, a nido appellata, quem ex arbore suspendit,), et vvasa (regulus), et abubarakis (avicula canora, longo collo et pedibus, pennis rubris, flavis, virilibus et coeruleis, quae colores subinde mutant), et kubaa (avicula varia, collum in metu contrahens, unde illi nomen). Hae sunt aves, quas ad passerum genus referunt Arabes. Quomodo etiam apud Hebraeos, auctore Kimchio in Lexico, הוא רב המין לפיכך כלל כל עוף בזה השם, Passer multas habet species: unde est, quod hoc nomen ad omnes aves refertur.

But they will marvel at him like little birds that surround an owl. Accordingly Hesychius: Σπίζια· ὄρνεα ἅπαντα [Spizia; ornea hapanta]. Rightly, provided that his ὄρνεα [ornea] are ὀρνίθια [ornithia] or ὀρνιθάρια [ornitharia], that is, little birds, not birds. Thus the Arabic عصفور [ʿuṣfūr], although properly it means sparrow, nevertheless embraces many species of little birds. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: وهى انواع منها ما هو مطرب بصوته ومنها ما يعجب بصورته وحسنه والعصفور الصوار هو الذي يجيب اذا ادعي من الصرورة وعصفور الجنة وهو الخطاف والعصفور البيوت فان في طباعه اختلافا [wa-hiya anwāʿ minhā mā huwa muṭrib bi-ṣawtihi wa-minhā mā yuʿjib bi-ṣūratihi wa-ḥusnihi wa-l-ʿuṣfūr al-ṣawwār huwa alladhī yujību idhā duʿiya min al-ṣarūra wa-ʿuṣfūr al-janna wa-huwa al-khuṭṭāf wa-l-ʿuṣfūr al-buyūt fa-inna fī ṭibāʿihi ikhtilāfan] There are various species of sparrows: some please by the modulation of their voice; others are admirable for their appearance and form. And the sparrow called suar is the one that, when called, answers by chirping. And the sparrow of paradise is the swallow. And the house sparrow is the one that is quarrelsome by nature, etc. And further on: ومن انواعه عصفور الشوك واكثر ماواه السياج وزعم ارسطو ان بينه وبين الحمار عداوة [wa-min anwāʿihi ʿuṣfūr al-shawk wa-akthar maʾwāhu al-siyāj wa-zaʿama Arisṭū anna baynahu wa-bayna al-ḥimār ʿadāwa] Among its species is the sparrow of thorns, which mostly lives in thickets. Aristotle reports that there is mutual hatred between it and the ass. It is plain that the acanthis is meant, which some explain as the goldfinch, others as the siskin, others as the ligurinus. For of it the Philosopher writes in Hist. book 8, chapter 3: Τὰ δὲ τοιάδε ἀκανθοφάγα, ἀκανθὶς, θραυπίς· ἔτι ἡ καλουμένη χρυσομήτρις. Ταῦτα γὰρ πάντα ἐπὶ τῶν ἀκανθῶν νέμεται [Ta de toiade akanthophaga, akanthis, thraupis; eti hē kaloumenē chrysomētris. Tauta gar panta epi tōn akanthōn nemetai]. Gaza rendered this as follows: These seek thorns: the siskin or ligurinus, the goldfinch, and also the one called aurivittis. For all these live on thorns. And in book 9, chapter 1: Ὄνος δὲ, καὶ ἀκανθίδες πολέμιοι· αἱ μὲν γὰρ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀκανθῶν βοητεύουσιν [Onos de, kai akanthides polemioi; hai men gar apo tōn akanthōn boēteuousin] (read II, 724 βιοτεύουσιν [bioteuousin]), ὁ δὲ ἁπαλὰς οὔσας ἐσθίει τὰς ἀκάνθας [ho de hapalas ousas esthiei tas akanthas]: The ass and the acanthides are enemies: for they get their living from thorns, which the ass eats while they are still tender. And the Arabs rightly assign this bird to the sparrow kind. For the acanthis is the same as the acanthyllis, of which Hesychius says: Ἀκανθυλλίς· στρουθοῦ γένος [Akanthyllis; strouthou genos], Acanthyllis, a kind of sparrow. In French it is called serin; whether from the song of the Sirens, as Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)] holds in the Ornithology, book 7, chapter 14. There follows in Damir: ومن انواعه القبرة والحسون والبلبل والصعوة والحمرة والعندليب والمكاكي والصافر والتنوط والوصع والابوبراقش col. 148 والقبعة [wa-min anwāʿihi al-qubbara wa-l-ḥassūn wa-l-bulbul wa-l-ṣaʿwa wa-l-ḥumra wa-l-ʿandalīb wa-l-makākī wa-l-ṣāfir wa-l-tanawwuṭ wa-l-waṣaʿ wa-l-abū barāqish wa-l-qubaʿa] Also among its species are the kubbara (the crested lark), and the hassun (I do not find it elsewhere; it seems to be named from its beauty) R1, and the bulbul (the nightingale), and the savva (a little bird with a red crown), and the hamra (a red species of lark), and the andalib (a species of bird similar to the nightingale), and the mechachi (plural of the singular مكا [mukkā] maccha, a bird named from its whistling), and the saphir (which also whistles all night long with its head bent down and its feet fastened to the tree), and the thenavvut (a little bird not unlike this one, named from the nest that it hangs from a tree), and the vvasa (the wren), and the abubarakis (a songbird with long neck and legs, and red, yellow, green and blue feathers, which repeatedly change their colours), and the kubaa (a variegated little bird that draws in its neck when afraid, whence its name). These are the birds that the Arabs assign to the sparrow kind. So too among the Hebrews, according to Kimchi in his Lexicon: הוא רב המין לפיכך כלל כל עוף בזה השם, The sparrow has many species: hence this name is applied to all birds.


Passerem البيوتي domesticum ita describit:- في طباعه اختلاف وذلك فيه من الطباعه ما يشبه السباع وهو اكله اللحم ولا يزق فراخه ومن البهايم انه ليس بذي مخلب ولا منسر وياكل الحب والبقول وهو اذا سقط علي العود قدم اصابعه الثلاث واخر الدايرة وساير الطير تقدم اصبعين وتوخر اصبعين وتميز الذكر منها بلحيه سودا كما الرجل والتيس والديك وليس في الارض طاير ولا سبع ولا بهيمة احني من العصفور علي II, 725 ولده ولا اشد له عشقا a) وذلك مشاهد عند اخذ فراخه ووكره في الغمران تحت السقوف خوف من الجوارح واذا حلت مدينة من اهلها ذهبت العصافير منها فاذا عاد واعادت العصافير والعصفور لا يعرف المشي وانما يثب وثبا وهو كثير السفاد فربما سفد في الساعة الواحدة ماية مرة ولذلك قصر عمره فانه لا يعيش في الغالب اكثر من سنة والفرخه تدرب علي col. 149 الطيران حتي انه يدعي فيجيب قال الجاحظ انه رجع من فرسخ Pugnacis est naturae. Nempe ferinum aliquid illi a natura insitum est. Proinde carne vescitur, et pullos suos non cibat rostro in illorum ora inserto. Sed cum avibus non rapacibus hoc illi commune est, quod non habet ungues, quibus laniet, neque rostrum aduncum, et grana ac olera comedit. Cum in arborem incidit, e quatuor digitis tres in anteriora porrigit, et unum retro. At in reliquis avibus bini digiti sunt anterius, et totidem posterius. Mas a foemina distinguitur nigra barba, quam habet ad instar viri, hirci, aut galli. Nusquam est avis, aut fera, aut jumentum in prolem propensius, quodque amet vehementius. Unde est, quod pullos et nidum suum in locis cultis collocat, et sub aedium tectis metu rapacium. Cum desolatur urbs, ex ea excedunt passeres, et simul cum incolis redeunt. Passer ambulare nescit, nec nisi saltuatim fertur. Avis est tam multi coitus, ut quandoque in hora centies coëat, ac proinde brevis est aevi, et plerumque ultra annum non vivit. Dociles habet pullos supra vulgus avium, ita, ut vocati respondeant. Passerem a parasanga redire, testatur Algiahid. His plura liceat addere Alkazuinio, sed quae toti passerum generi conveniunt, non soli domestico.

He describes the البيوتي [al-buyūtī] domestic sparrow as follows: في طباعه اختلاف وذلك فيه من الطباعه ما يشبه السباع وهو اكله اللحم ولا يزق فراخه ومن البهايم انه ليس بذي مخلب ولا منسر وياكل الحب والبقول وهو اذا سقط علي العود قدم اصابعه الثلاث واخر الدايرة وساير الطير تقدم اصبعين وتوخر اصبعين وتميز الذكر منها بلحيه سودا كما الرجل والتيس والديك وليس في الارض طاير ولا سبع ولا بهيمة احني من العصفور علي II, 725 ولده ولا اشد له عشقا a) وذلك مشاهد عند اخذ فراخه ووكره في الغمران تحت السقوف خوف من الجوارح واذا حلت مدينة من اهلها ذهبت العصافير منها فاذا عاد واعادت العصافير والعصفور لا يعرف المشي وانما يثب وثبا وهو كثير السفاد فربما سفد في الساعة الواحدة ماية مرة ولذلك قصر عمره فانه لا يعيش في الغالب اكثر من سنة والفرخه تدرب علي col. 149 الطيران حتي انه يدعي فيجيب قال الجاحظ انه رجع من فرسخ It is of a pugnacious nature. For something wild has been implanted in it by nature. Accordingly it feeds on flesh, and does not feed its young by inserting its beak into their mouths. But it has this in common with non-raptorial birds, that it has no talons with which to tear, nor a hooked beak, and it eats grain and vegetables. When it alights on a tree, of its four toes it stretches three forward and one backward, whereas in other birds two toes are in front and as many behind. The male is distinguished from the female by a black beard, which it has like a man, a he-goat, or a cock. Nowhere is there a bird, wild beast, or beast of burden more devoted to its offspring or loving it more ardently. Hence it places its young and its nest in inhabited places and under the roofs of houses, for fear of birds of prey. When a city is deserted, the sparrows leave it, and return together with the inhabitants. The sparrow does not know how to walk, and moves only by hopping. It is a bird of such frequent coition that it sometimes mates a hundred times in an hour, and consequently it is short-lived, and generally does not live beyond a year. Its young are more teachable than the common run of birds, so that when called they answer. Algiahid testifies that a sparrow returns from a parasang away. One could add more from Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt], but these things apply to the whole sparrow genus, not to the domestic sparrow alone.


Hebraice צפצף tsiphseph est murmurare et mussitare, Es. VIII, 19. et XXIX, 4. Quod sumtum ex garritu avium. R. Selomo in Es. XXIX. ציפצוף הוא לשון קול לחש כקול עופות דקין, Tsiphtsuph significat vocem mussitationis, instar vocis avicularum. Constat id ex Es. XXXVIII, 14. ubi ad hirundinem refertur. Tamen magis proprie צפצוף est pipitus passerum. Pomarius, צפצף עשה קול צפורים, Tsiphseph, pipivit more passerum. Quod verum esse constat ex Arabibus, quibus صفصف tsophtsoph est عصفور passer, et صفصفة tsaphtsapha صوته vox ejus. Ita habetur in Alcamus. Inde est, quod Es. II, 726 X, 14. Hebraea verba, ופצה פה ומצפצף, Et os aperiens, et pipiens, Graece ita redduntur: Καὶ ἀνοίγων στόμα, καὶ στρουθίζων. Ad quae Theodoretus, Ἀπὸ τῆς κρατούσης συνηθείας παρὰ ἀνθρώποις εἴρηται τῇ γραφῇ. εἰώθαμεν γὰρ λέγειν περὶ τῶν λίαν ἀγωνιώντων, Οὐκ ἐτόλμησε γρύξαι· οἱ δὲ λοιποί φασιν, Οὐκ ἐτόλμησε τρύσαι. τὸ οὖν Ἀνοίγων στόμα, καὶ στρουθίζων, ἀντὶ τοῦ Οὐ μόνον οὐδεὶς ἀντιπαρατάξασθαί μοι τολμήσει, ἀλλ᾽ οὐδὲ γρύζειν στρουθοῖς παραπλησί-ως ἐπιχειρήσει. Ex humana consuetudine a Scriptura usurpatum est. Solemus enim dicere de iis, qui in magnis sunt angustiis, Non ausus est mutire. Alii autem dicunt, Non ausus est stridere. Os igitur aperiens et pipiens (nemo erit), idem est, ac si diceret, Non solum nemo audebit mihi obsistere, sed ne passerum quidem more pipire conabitur. Indidem sumptum illud Suidae, Στρουθίζων· τρίζων. Nam τρίζειν, stridere, etiam est passerum, ut patet ex Iliad. β΄. versu 314. ubi draco passerculos octo cum matre

In Hebrew צפצף tsiphseph means to murmur and to mutter, Isa 8:19 and XXIX, 4. This is taken from the twittering of birds. R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] on Es. XXIX.: ציפצוף הוא לשון קול לחש כקול עופות דקין, tsiphtsuph signifies a muttering voice, like the voice of little birds. This is evident from Isa 38:14, where it is applied to the swallow. Yet more properly צפצוף is the chirping of sparrows. Pomarius: צפצף עשה קול צפורים, tsiphseph, he chirped in the manner of sparrows. That this is true is clear from the Arabs, for whom صفصف [ṣafṣaf] tsophtsoph is عصفور [ʿuṣfūr] sparrow, and صفصفة [ṣafṣafa] tsaphtsapha is صوته [ṣawtuhu] its voice. So it is given in the Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]. Hence in Es. II, 726 X, 14. the Hebrew words ופצה פה ומצפצף, And opening the mouth, and chirping, are rendered in Greek thus: Καὶ ἀνοίγων στόμα, καὶ στρουθίζων [Kai anoigōn stoma, kai strouthizōn]. On which Theodoret says: Ἀπὸ τῆς κρατούσης συνηθείας παρὰ ἀνθρώποις εἴρηται τῇ γραφῇ. εἰώθαμεν γὰρ λέγειν περὶ τῶν λίαν ἀγωνιώντων, Οὐκ ἐτόλμησε γρύξαι· οἱ δὲ λοιποί φασιν, Οὐκ ἐτόλμησε τρύσαι. τὸ οὖν Ἀνοίγων στόμα, καὶ στρουθίζων, ἀντὶ τοῦ Οὐ μόνον οὐδεὶς ἀντιπαρατάξασθαί μοι τολμήσει, ἀλλ᾽ οὐδὲ γρύζειν στρουθοῖς παραπλησίως ἐπιχειρήσει [Apo tēs kratousēs synētheias para anthrōpois eirētai tē graphē. eiōthamen gar legein peri tōn lian agōniōntōn, Ouk etolmēse gryxai; hoi de loipoi phasin, Ouk etolmēse trysai. to oun Anoigōn stoma, kai strouthizōn, anti tou Ou monon oudeis antiparataxasthai moi tolmēsei, all' oude gryzein strouthois paraplēsiōs epicheirēsei]. Scripture has taken this from human usage. For we are accustomed to say of those who are in great distress, He did not dare to mutter. Others, however, say, He did not dare to squeak. Thus "opening the mouth and chirping" (there will be no one) is the same as if he said, Not only will no one dare to oppose me, but no one will even attempt to chirp in the manner of sparrows. From the same source is taken that gloss of Suidas: Στρουθίζων· τρίζων [Strouthizōn; trizōn]. For τρίζειν [trizein], to squeak, is also said of sparrows, as is clear from Iliad 2, line 314, where the serpent devoured eight little sparrows together with their mother


— — ἐλεεινὰ κατήσθιε τετριγῶτας,

voravit miserabiliter stridentes: non τιτίζοντας, ut legi voluit Zenodotus. Nec est, quod quis miretur, homines ab Esaia describi avium instar pipientes. Est enim metaphorae continuatio. Ibi nempe Propheta loquitur verbis Assyriae regis, Thrasonice se efferentis, et populos, a se devictos, conferentis cum nido avium, quas metus aucupis ita percellit, ut ne pipire quidem audeant. Itaque totus versus sic habet: Et manus mea tanquam (avium) nidum populorum opulentiam assequuta est. Et quasi reciperem ova derelicta, totam terram ego recepi: neque est, qui agitet alam, aut aperiat os, aut pipiat. Verba Καὶ ἀνοίγων στό- col. 150 μα, καὶ στρουθίζων, desunt in plerisque editionibus, nec a Basilio lecta sunt, nec a Cyrillo. Ita tamen exhibent editio Complutensis et Parisiensis nupera. Eadem quoque legerunt Theodoretus et Arabs, qui versionem suam ex Graeca expressit. Et in Procopio habentur in margine cum asterisco. Seniorum scilicet versio saepe liberior est, qui, modo sensum utcunque exprimant, saepe de verbis sunt parum solliciti. Hebraea igitur, Neque est, qui agitet alam, aut aperiat os, aut pipiat, sic illi reddiderant, Καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ὃς διαφεύξεταί με, ἢ ἀντείπῃ μοί· Neque est, qui me effugiat, aut mihi contradicat. Sed reliqua supplevit aliquis ex alio interprete. An is Aquila, qui linguae Hebraicae fuit peritissimus, et verbum verbo reddere solitus?

devoured, miserably shrieking: not τιτίζοντας [titizontas], as Zenodotus wanted it read. Nor should anyone be surprised that Isaiah describes men chirping like birds. For it is a continuation of the metaphor. There the Prophet speaks in the words of the king of Assyria, who boasts like a Thraso and compares the peoples he has conquered with a nest of birds which fear of the fowler so dismays that they do not even dare to chirp. So the whole verse reads thus: And my hand has reached the wealth of the peoples as (birds') nest. And as one gathers abandoned eggs, I have gathered the whole earth; and there is none who moves a wing, or opens the mouth, or chirps. The words Καὶ ἀνοίγων στόμα, καὶ στρουθίζων [Kai anoigōn stoma, kai strouthizōn] col. 150 are missing in most editions, and were read neither by Basil nor by Cyril. Yet the Complutensian edition and the recent Paris edition present them so. Theodoret also read them, and so did the Arabic translator, who made his version from the Greek. And in Procopius they are found in the margin with an asterisk. The version of the Elders [=the translators of the Septuagint], namely, is often rather free: provided they express the sense in some way, they are often little concerned about the words. Thus the Hebrew, And there is none who moves a wing, or opens the mouth, or chirps, they had rendered thus: Καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ὃς διαφεύξεταί με, ἢ ἀντείπῃ μοί [Kai ouk estin hos diapheuxetai me, ē anteipē moi]: And there is none who escapes me, or contradicts me. But someone supplied the rest from another translator. Was it Aquila, who was most skilled in the Hebrew language and accustomed to render word for word?

The Arabic مصع [maṣʿ] matsaon for the male sparrow echoes the Dutch name of the sparrow, mosche, and the Norman moisson. Alcamus: المصع العصفور الذكرة [al-maṣʿ al-ʿuṣfūr al-dhakara].

II, 727 col. 150 CAP. XXII.

II, 727 col. 150 CHAPTER XXII.


Prophetarum loca novem, quae ad Passeres referunt nonnulli interpretes, plerumque parum certa. I. Levit. XIV. passim. II. Iob. XL, 24. III. Psal. X, 1. IV. Psal. LXXXIV, 4. V. Psal. CII, 8. VI. Psal. CIV, 16. VII. Psal. CXXIV, 7. VIII. Eccles. XII, 4. IX. Thren. III, 52.

Nine passages of the Prophets which some interpreters refer to sparrows, for the most part rather uncertain. I. Levit. XIV. passim. II. Job 40:24. III. Ps 10:1. IV. Ps 84:4. V. Ps 102:8. VI. Ps 104:16. VII. Ps 124:7. VIII. Eccl 12:4. IX. Lam 3:52.


Inter interpretes non convenit satis, quibus Scripturae locis צפור tsippor sumatur pro passere. Nam ex novem locis, quae proferuntur, pleraque sunt valde dubia.

Interpreters do not sufficiently agree in which passages of Scripture צפור tsippor is taken for the sparrow. For of the nine passages that are adduced, most are very doubtful.


I. Primus est Levit. XIV. initio capitis, et in fine, ubi agitur de duabus צפורים tsipporim, quarum una caesa, altera emissa purgabatur leprosus, et domus etiam lepra infecta. Ibi tsipporim esse passeres, plerique volunt, quomodo reddunt Hieronymus, Pagninus, Arias, Genevenses, alii. Sed aves in genere significari, constabit haec attente legenti versu quarto, Et accipiat qui mundandus est שתי צפורים חיות טהרות, duas tsipporim vivas mundas. Quae in passerem non quadrant, sive mundus fuisse statuatur, aut immundus. Mundus enim dici non potuit, si ex Lege fuit immundus. Contra, si fuit mundus, Lex incassum jusserit capi passeres mundos, cum immundi nulli fuerint. Mundas columbas, col. 151 aut turtures offerri nusquam jubetur; quia omnes erant mundae. Apparet igitur, צפורים tsipporim ibi esse aves in genere, quarum cum aliae mundae, aliae immundae fuerint, mundas accipi Deus jubet, puta columbas, aut turtures, quae vocantur הצפור Gen. XV, 10. aut alias quasvis, modo mundae sint et ad esum concessae juxta legem Deut. XIV, 11. כל צפור טהרה תאכלו, Omnem tsippor mundam comedetis. Itaque gallinas etiam a nonnullis hic intelligi, supra docuimus, atque eo referri posse Graecum ὀρνίθια. Nec Hebraei speciem designant, modo sint צפרים דרור טהורות, aves liberae et mundae. De hujus purificationis ritu multa habet insignia Maimonides in tractatu De lepra capite undecimo, quae non sunt hujus loci.

I. The first is Levit. XIV., at the beginning of the chapter and at the end, where it treats of two צפורים tsipporim, by which, one being killed and the other released, the leper was purified, and also a house infected with leprosy. Most hold that the tsipporim there are sparrows, as Jerome, Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae], Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], the Genevans and others render it. But that birds in general are meant will be clear to anyone who reads attentively verse four: And let him that is to be cleansed take שתי צפורים חיות טהרות, two living clean tsipporim. This does not fit the sparrow, whether it is held to have been clean or unclean. For it could not be called clean if by the Law it was unclean. Conversely, if it was clean, the Law would have commanded in vain that clean sparrows be taken, since there were no unclean ones. Nowhere is it commanded that clean doves col. 151 or turtledoves be offered, because all were clean. It appears, therefore, that צפורים tsipporim there are birds in general; and since some of these were clean and others unclean, God commands that clean ones be taken, for instance doves or turtledoves, which are called הצפור in Gen 15:10, or any others, provided they are clean and permitted as food according to the law of Deut 14:11. כל צפור טהרה תאכלו, Every clean tsippor you shall eat. Thus, as we showed above, some understand hens here too, and the Greek ὀρνίθια [ornithia] can be referred to this. Nor do the Hebrews specify a species, provided they are צפרים דרור טהורות, free and clean birds. On the rite of this purification Maimonides [=Moses Maimonides (Rambam), Mishneh Torah] has much that is notable in the treatise On Leprosy, chapter 11, which does not belong here.


II. Secundus locus est in descriptione τοῦ Leviathan Iob. XL, 24. (al. 29.), et Hebraice sic habet: An eo ludes כצפור, ut tsippor? Et ligabis eum puellis tuis? Et in Graeca versione, Παίξῃ δὲ ἐν αὐτῷ ὥσπερ ὀρνέῳ; ἢ δήσεις αὐτὸν ὥσπερ col. 152 στρουθίον παιδίῳ; An ludes eo tanquam ave? et ligabis eum ut passerem puero? Et in Arabica, هل تضحك عليه مثل العصفور An ludes eo tanquam passere, etc. Quod ad diabolum referunt, qui mysteria consectantur, II, 728 quasi per baptismum et conversionem nobis vinctus tradatur, ut puero passerculus. Origenes de fideli homine, Ὅ γε δράκων αὐτῷ ὥσπερ στρουθίον πα-ραδέδοται παιδίῳ· Draco illi ut passer puero traditus est. Et paullo post, Τῇ χάριτι τοῦ Κυρίου, ὡς στρουθίον ὑποχείριον, ὁ Σατανᾶς δεδεμένος γεγένηται τοῖς νηπίοις, καὶ θηλάζουσιν, ὧν ἐκ στόματος κατηρτίσατο αἶνον ὁ Θεός· Domini gratia, ut passer mansuetus, Satan vinctus est pueris et lactentibus, ex quorum ore Deus perfecit laudem suam. Chrysostomus, Δήσας τὸν ἐχθρὸν ὁ Κύριος ἡμῶν δέδωκε καταπαίζειν αὐτοῦ, ὡς στρουθίου, τοῖς στραφεῖσι, καὶ γενομένοις ὡς τὰ παιδία. Conversis, et iis, qui ut infantes facti sunt, Dominus noster vinctum adversarium tanquam passerem illudendum tradidit. Quo alludens auctor vitae Pachomii capite quadragesimo nono diabolis haec tribuit, Ex quo mirabilis incarnatio Christi facta est in terris, nos sine viribus prorsus existere coepimus; Ita, ut ab his, qui credunt in nomine ejus, illudamur ut passeres. Quibus missis solum quaerimus, an Hebraea bene reddantur: An eo ludes tanquam passere? et ligabis eum pullis tuis? Et commodam hic esse mentionem passeris, suadebit Catullianum illud notissimum,

II. The second passage is in the description of the Leviathan, Job 40:24 (var. 29.), and in Hebrew it reads thus: Will you play with him כצפור, as with a tsippor? And will you bind him for your girls? And in the Greek version: Παίξῃ δὲ ἐν αὐτῷ ὥσπερ ὀρνέῳ; ἢ δήσεις αὐτὸν ὥσπερ col. 152 στρουθίον παιδίῳ; [Paixē de en autō hōsper orneō; ē dēseis auton hōsper strouthion paidiō?] Will you play with him as with a bird? and will you bind him like a sparrow for a child? And in the Arabic: هل تضحك عليه مثل العصفور [hal taḍḥaku ʿalayhi mithla al-ʿuṣfūr] Will you play with him as with a sparrow, etc. Those who pursue mysteries refer this to the devil, as though through baptism and conversion he were handed over to us bound, II, 728 like a little sparrow to a child. Origen, of the faithful man: Ὅ γε δράκων αὐτῷ ὥσπερ στρουθίον παραδέδοται παιδίῳ· [Ho ge drakōn autō hōsper strouthion paradedotai paidiō] The dragon has been handed over to him as a sparrow to a child. And shortly after: Τῇ χάριτι τοῦ Κυρίου, ὡς στρουθίον ὑποχείριον, ὁ Σατανᾶς δεδεμένος γεγένηται τοῖς νηπίοις, καὶ θηλάζουσιν, ὧν ἐκ στόματος κατηρτίσατο αἶνον ὁ Θεός· [Tē chariti tou Kyriou, hōs strouthion hypocheirion, ho Satanas dedemenos gegenētai tois nēpiois, kai thēlazousin, hōn ek stomatos katērtisato ainon ho Theos] By the grace of the Lord, like a tame sparrow, Satan has been bound for children and sucklings, out of whose mouth God has perfected his praise. Chrysostom: Δήσας τὸν ἐχθρὸν ὁ Κύριος ἡμῶν δέδωκε καταπαίζειν αὐτοῦ, ὡς στρουθίου, τοῖς στραφεῖσι, καὶ γενομένοις ὡς τὰ παιδία. [Dēsas ton echthron ho Kyrios hēmōn dedōke katapaizein autou, hōs strouthiou, tois strapheisi, kai genomenois hōs ta paidia.] To those who have been converted and have become as infants, our Lord has handed over the adversary, bound, to be mocked like a sparrow. Alluding to this, the author of the life of Pachomius, chapter 49, attributes these words to the devils: Since the wonderful incarnation of Christ took place on earth, we have begun to exist wholly without strength; so that we are mocked like sparrows by those who believe in his name. Leaving these aside, we ask only whether the Hebrew is well rendered: Will you play with him as with a sparrow? and will you bind him for your young ones? That a mention of the sparrow is fitting here is suggested by that very well-known line of Catullus,


Passer deliciae meae puellae
Quicum ludere, quem in sinu tenere,
Quoi primum digitum dare adpetenti
Et acris solet incitare morsus.

Sparrow, darling of my girl, with whom she is wont to play, whom to hold in her lap, to whom, as it seeks it, to give her fingertip and to provoke its sharp bites.


Unde Arnobius libro septimo, ut parvuli pusiones (ut animis parcant, abstineantque ploratibus) passerculos, populos, panes accipiunt, quibus avocare se possint. Et Arabs poeta, quem citat Ibno Rasik in libro, cui titulus غرايب garaibo, id est, Peregrinitates:

Hence Arnobius, book 7: as little boys (to spare their feelings and keep from crying) are given little sparrows, poplar toys, loaves, with which they can divert themselves. And an Arab poet, whom Ibno Rasik cites in the book entitled غرايب [gharāyib] garaibo, that is, Curiosities:


كعصفورة في كف طفل يسوخها * حياض الردي والطفل يلهو ويلعب *

كعصفورة في كف طفل يسوخها * حياض الردي والطفل يلهو ويلعب * [ka-ʿuṣfūratin fī kaffi ṭiflin yasūkhuhā * ḥiyāḍa al-radī wa-l-ṭiflu yalhū wa-yalʿabu *]


Ut passer foemina in manu pueri, quam is in malis luteribus demergens jocatur et ludit. Tamen in Iobo nihil necesse est praecise passerem intelligere, cam aliae aves non desint, quibus pueri et puellae aeque oblectentur. Plautus in Captivis Actu quinto,

Like a hen sparrow in a boy's hand, which he plunges into the evil troughs while he jests and plays. Yet in Job there is no need to understand the sparrow precisely, since there is no lack of other birds with which boys and girls are equally amused. Plautus in the Captivi, Act 5:


— — quasi patriciis pueris aut monedulae,
Aut anates, aut coturnices dantur, qui cum lusitent.

— — as jackdaws, or ducks, or quails are given to patrician boys to play with.


Plinius ad Clementem de Reguli filio libri quarti Epistola secunda, Habebat puer mannulos multos, et vinctos, et solutos, habebat canes majores minoresque, habebat luscinias, psittacos, merulas. Iulius Capitolinus in Clodio Albino, Septem aquilae parvae de nido allatae sunt, et quasi ad jocum circa cunas pueri constitutae. Pausanias in Corinthiacis, Κόκκυγα δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ σκήπτρῳ καθῆσθαί φασι, λέγοντες II, 729 τὸν Δία, ὅτε ἤρα παρθένου τῆς Ἥρας ἐς τοῦτον τὸν ὄρνιθα ἀλλαγῆναι· τὴν δὲ ἅτε παίγνιον θηρᾶσαι· Cucullum vero avem idcirco sceptro Iovis ajunt impositum, quod virginis Iunonis amore captus Iupiter in eam se avem verterit, quam puella tanquam ludicrum captarit. Unde Iupiter Coccygius, de quo idem infra meminit. Itaque Iobi locum, quem diximus, Hieronymus ita explicat: Nunquid illudes ei quasi avi? aut ligabis eum ancillis tuis? nulla passeris mentione facta. Atqui idem sequuntur plerique recentiorum.

Pliny, writing to Clemens about the son of Regulus in Letter 2 of book 4: "The boy had many ponies, both harnessed and unharnessed; he had dogs large and small; he had nightingales, parrots, blackbirds." Julius Capitolinus in Clodius Albinus: "Seven small eagles were brought from the nest and placed, as if in play, around the boy's cradle." Pausanias in the Corinthiaca: Κόκκυγα δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ σκήπτρῳ καθῆσθαί φασι, λέγοντες II, 729 τὸν Δία, ὅτε ἤρα παρθένου τῆς Ἥρας ἐς τοῦτον τὸν ὄρνιθα ἀλλαγῆναι· τὴν δὲ ἅτε παίγνιον θηρᾶσαι· [Kokkyga de epi tō skēptrō kathēsthai phasi, legontes ton Dia, hote ēra parthenou tēs Hēras es touton ton ornitha allagēnai; tēn de hate paignion thērasai] "They say the cuckoo sits on the sceptre of Jove because Jupiter, seized with love for the maiden Juno, turned himself into that bird, which the girl caught as a plaything." Hence Jupiter Coccygius, whom the same author mentions further on. Accordingly Jerome explains the passage of Job we mentioned thus: "Will you play with him as with a bird? Or will you bind him for your maidservants?", making no mention of a sparrow. And most of the more recent interpreters follow the same.


III. Tertius locus est Psal. X, 1. (Hebraeis XI, 1.), ubi Graeca versio, Μεταναστεύου ἐπὶ τὰ ὄρη ὡς στρουθίον· Et Vulgata, Transmigra in montem sicut passer. Arabs quoque مثل العصفور, ut passer. Et Apollinaris in col. 153 Metaphrasi,

III. The third passage is Ps 10:1 (in the Hebrew XI, 1.), where the Greek version has Μεταναστεύου ἐπὶ τὰ ὄρη ὡς στρουθίον· [Metanasteuou epi ta orē hōs strouthion], and the Vulgate, "Flee to the mountain like a sparrow." The Arabic also has مثل العصفور [mithl al-ʿuṣfūr], like a sparrow. And Apollinaris in col. 153 his Metaphrase:


Στρουθὸν ὀρεσσιβότοισιν ὅπως θρώσκοντα νομῆσι,

Στρουθὸν ὀρεσσιβότοισιν ὅπως θρώσκοντα νομῆσι, [Strouthon oressibotoisin hopōs thrōskonta nomēsi]


Ut passerem montanis salientem pascuis. Et Theodoretus in Commentario, Τί δή ποτέ φησι παραινεῖτέ μοι φυγεῖν, καὶ τὰ ὄρη περινοστεῖν στρουθίου δίκην ἐπτοη-μένου; Quorsum, inquit, me hortamini, ut fugiam, et montes pererrem more passeris exterriti? Sed Hieronymus melius, ut quidem puto, Transvola in montem, ut avis, ut et plerique recentiores. Quia passer avis montana non est. Et David, de quo hic agitur, Saulem dicit se persequi, ac si quis persequeretur, non passerem, sed avem Kore in montibus, 1 Sam. XXVI, 20. id est, rusticulam, ut docuimus. Frustra objeceris, avem esse juxta Larium in Italia lacum, quam passerem montanum vocant. Neque enim illa avis vere est passer, sed e merularum genere, ut pluribus probat Gesnerus pag. 608. Nec magis ad rem est hic Galeni locus De ingenio sanitatis cap. 2. Ex avibus laudantur perdices cum montanis omnibus passeribus. Neque enim ibi intelliguntur passeres, proprie dicti, qui calidissimi sunt, et libidinem incitant, sed ex avibus minutis in genere eae, quae montanae sunt. Minutas enim aves quandoque στρουθία vocari, in confesso est. Moschopulus, Περὶ σχεδῶν pag. 178. Τρώγλη· ἡ τρύπα, ἀφ᾽ οὗ τρωγλίτης, ὃς καὶ στρουθὸς λέγεται· στρουθία δὲ οὐδετέρως πάντα τὰ μικρὰ τῶν ὀρνίθων. Ita etiam Phavorinus in Στρουθία.

"Like a sparrow leaping in mountain pastures." And Theodoret in his Commentary: Τί δή ποτέ φησι παραινεῖτέ μοι φυγεῖν, καὶ τὰ ὄρη περινοστεῖν στρουθίου δίκην ἐπτοημένου; [Ti dē pote phēsi paraineite moi phygein, kai ta orē perinostein strouthiou dikēn eptoēmenou?] "Why," he says, "do you urge me to flee and wander over the mountains like a frightened sparrow?" But Jerome does better, as I at least think, with "Fly over to the mountain like a bird", as do most of the more recent interpreters. For the sparrow is not a mountain bird. And David, who is the subject here, says that Saul is pursuing him as one would hunt, not a sparrow, but the bird Kore in the mountains, 1 Sam 26:20, that is, the woodcock, as we have shown. It would be vain to object that near Lake Larius in Italy there is a bird which they call the mountain sparrow. For that bird is not truly a sparrow, but of the blackbird kind, as Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium] proves at length, p. 608. Nor is this passage of Galen, De ingenio sanitatis ch. 2, more to the point: "Among birds, partridges are praised, together with all mountain sparrows." For there not sparrows properly so called are meant, which are very hot and incite lust, but those small birds in general that live in the mountains. For it is agreed that small birds are sometimes called στρουθία [strouthia]. Moschopulus, Περὶ σχεδῶν [Peri schedōn] p. 178: Τρώγλη· ἡ τρύπα, ἀφ᾽ οὗ τρωγλίτης, ὃς καὶ στρουθὸς λέγεται· στρουθία δὲ οὐδετέρως πάντα τὰ μικρὰ τῶν ὀρνίθων. [Trōglē; hē trypa, aph᾽ hou trōglitēs, hos kai strouthos legetai; strouthia de oudeterōs panta ta mikra tōn ornithōn.] So also Phavorinus under Στρουθία [Strouthia].


IV. Quartus locus est Ps. LXXXIV, 4. גם צפור מצאה בית, pro quo Graeci, Καὶ γὰρ στρουθίον εὗρεν ἑαυτῷ οἰκίαν. Et Arabs eodem sensu, لان العصفور وجد له مسكنا Et Vulgatus, Etenim passer invenit sibi domum. Et Hieronymus, Siquidem passer invenit domum. Et Kimchius in Lexico probat hoc loco, צפור tsippor non esse nomen generale ad omnes aves, sed certae speciei peculiare, quia in hemistichio sequente דרור deror est hirundo, ut is quidem asserit. Itaque, inquit, אחר שאחרון פרט הראשון גם כן פרט, II, 730 quandoquidem posterius (id est, דרור deror) peculiaris avis nomen est, ita etiam prius (nempe צפור tsippor). Proinde in Commentariis idem statuit, צפור ibi esse aviculam, quam Hispani vocant פשׂרא paxaro, id est, passerem. Ita igitur reddendus est hic versus ex mente Kimchii: Etiam passer invenit domum, et hi- rundo nidum sibi, ubi poneret pullos suos, nempe altaria tua, o Deus exercituum. Cui sententiae nos accedimus, nisi quod דרור deror pro hirundine palumbum interpretati sumus. Et altarium nomine per senecdochen partis pro toto taberna- culum intelleximus, ad cujus trabes nidulati sint tam passeres, quam palumbi, ut jam alibi dictum.

IV. The fourth passage is Ps. LXXXIV, 4. גם צפור מצאה בית, for which the Greeks have Καὶ γὰρ στρουθίον εὗρεν ἑαυτῷ οἰκίαν [Kai gar strouthion heuren heautō oikian]. And the Arabic in the same sense: لان العصفور وجد له مسكنا [li-anna al-ʿuṣfūr wajada lahu maskanan]. And the Vulgate translator: "For the sparrow has found itself a home." And Jerome: "Since the sparrow has found a home." And Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] in his Lexicon proves from this passage that צפור tsippor is not a general name for all birds but proper to a certain species, because in the following hemistich דרור deror is the swallow, as he at least asserts. "Therefore," he says, אחר שאחרון פרט הראשון גם כן פרט, II, 730 "since the latter (that is, דרור deror) is the name of a particular bird, so also is the former (namely צפור tsippor)." Accordingly in his Commentaries he likewise holds that צפור there is the little bird which the Spaniards call פשׂרא paxaro, that is, the sparrow. So this verse is to be rendered according to Kimchi's mind: "Even the sparrow has found a home, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, namely your altars, O God of hosts." We agree with this view, except that we have interpreted דרור deror as the wood pigeon instead of the swallow. And by the name altars, by synecdoche of part for whole, we have understood the tabernacle, on whose beams both sparrows and wood pigeons nested, as has already been said elsewhere.


V. Quintus locus Psal. CII, 8. Vigilavi, et fui כצפור בודד על גג, ubi Graeci, ὡσεὶ στρουθίον μονάζων ἐπὶ δώματι· et Vulgatus, Sicut passer solitarius in tecto: et Arabum unus, Fui in solitudine mea كالعصفور ut passer super tectum: et alter, Factus sum ut passer, qui manet super tectum solus. Et Apol- linaris,

V. The fifth passage is Ps 102:8 "I have kept watch, and I have become כצפור בודד על גג", where the Greeks have ὡσεὶ στρουθίον μονάζων ἐπὶ δώματι· [hōsei strouthion monazōn epi dōmati], and the Vulgate translator, "like a solitary sparrow on the roof"; and one of the Arabic versions, "I was in my solitude كالعصفور [ka-l-ʿuṣfūr] like a sparrow upon the roof"; and the other, "I have become like a sparrow that stays alone upon the roof." And Apollinaris:


Ἢ στρουθόν τιν᾽ ἄϋπνον ἐόντ᾽ ἐν δώματι μοῦνον,

Ἢ στρουθόν τιν᾽ ἄϋπνον ἐόντ᾽ ἐν δώματι μοῦνον, [Ē strouthon tin᾽ aypnon eont᾽ en dōmati mounon]


Aut passerem aliquem, qui insomnis est in tecto solus. Nempe Damir supra passerem nidificare dixit تحت السقوف خوف من الجوارح sub tecto, rapacium avium metu. Et Suidas in Νυκτικόραξ passerem describit tanquam δειλὸν ὄρνεον, timidam avem; quaeque ὑπὸ ἀγωνίας ἐλαύνει τὸν ὕπνον, prae sollicitudine somnum repellat. Quae videbuntur ad hunc locum maxime pertinere, quo David, ut quidam volunt, se vigilasse dicit instar passeris, qui super tectum solus est. Eodem facere putatur, quod pro passere solitario in Augusti- no legitur passer singularis. Id enim Graece esset στρουθὸς μόνιος, vel στρουθίον col. 154 μόνιον. Et ex μόνιος facta videbitur vox vernacula moineau pro passere. Denique circa Tridentum avis est, quam vulgus vocat passerem solitarium, quae solivaga est, et in tectis versari solita. Itaque, ut multi veterum, ita recentiorum interpretum fere quotquot sunt, Latini, Galli, Itali, Germani, Belgae, Angli passerem hic intelligunt. Tamen aliter Hieronymus, Fui sicut avis solitaria su- per tectum. Nec Hebraeorum quisquam est, qui moneat, hic agi de passere, quomodo in superiore loco. Et vero nihil esse puto a Prophetae mente remotius. Omnino enim haec pertinent ad avis nocturnae descriptionem. Quod in mentem interpretum nondum venisse miror, cum id aperte clament omnes loci circumstantiae. Nam in hoc Psalmo quisquis loquitur, cum gravi moerore confectus hominum consortium fugeret, gemitusque perpetuos ex imo pectore funderet, cum feralibus avibus se confert, quae et solitariae sunt, et in voce lugubre aliquid habent et ominosum. Propter vocem gemitus mei, inquit, ossa mea carni adhaeserunt. Similis factus sum pelicano deserti. Fui instar noctuae (vel II, 731 bubonis) solitudinum. Haec ille in duobus versibus, qui proxime antecedunt. Deinde in instituta comparatione pergens, Vigilavi, inquit, et fui ut avis solitaria super tectum. Vigilavi, id est, noctem egi insomnem. Proinde ibi habet Chaldaeus, שקדת כל ליליא, Vigilavi tota nocte. Nempe, ut nocturnae aves lucifugae, quae quia lucem oderunt, postquam interdiu latuere, e latebris noctu prodeunt, ut in praedam invigilent. Philosophus Hist. lib. 9. cap. 34. Γλαῦ-κες δὲ, καὶ νυκτικόρακες, καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ, ὅσα τῆς ἡμέρας ἀδυνατεῖ βλέπειν, τῆς νυκτὸς μὲν θηρεύοντα τὴν τροφὴν αὐτοῖς πορίζεται· Noctuae et nycticoraces, et reliquae aves, quae interdiu cernere nequeunt, noctu venando cibum sibi comparant. Unde corrigendus Athenaeus, qui haec verba sic contrahit lib. 8. cap. 12. Γλαῦκες δὲ, καὶ κόρακες ἡμέρας ἀδυνατοῦσι βλέπειν, διὸ νύκτωρ τὴν τροφὴν ἑαυτοῖς θηρεύουσιν· et pro κόρακες rescribendum νυκτικόρακες. Proinde nocturnis avibus vigilias fere perpetuas tribuunt omnes scriptores. Et in Aristophanis Lysistrata mulier quaedam ita loquitur:

Or some sparrow, which is sleepless, alone on the roof. For Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] said above that the sparrow nests تحت السقوف خوف من الجوارح [taḥta al-suqūf khawf min al-jawāriḥ] under the roof, for fear of birds of prey. And Suidas, under Νυκτικόραξ [Nyktikorax], describes the sparrow as δειλὸν ὄρνεον [deilon orneon], a timid bird, and one that ὑπὸ ἀγωνίας ἐλαύνει τὸν ὕπνον [hypo agōnias elaunei ton hypnon], drives away sleep out of anxiety. These things will seem to bear most closely on this passage, in which David, as some would have it, says that he kept watch like a sparrow that is alone on the roof. The same point is thought to be supported by the fact that, instead of passer solitarius [solitary sparrow], Augustine reads passer singularis [single sparrow]. In Greek this would be στρουθὸς μόνιος [strouthos monios], or στρουθίον col. 154 μόνιον [strouthion monion]. And the vernacular word moineau for the sparrow will seem to have been formed from μόνιος [monios]. Finally, around Trent there is a bird which the common people call the passer solitarius [solitary sparrow], which wanders alone and usually stays on roofs. Accordingly, like many of the ancients, nearly all the more recent interpreters, Latin, French, Italian, German, Dutch and English, understand the sparrow here. Jerome, however, renders it otherwise: I was like a solitary bird upon the roof. Nor is there any of the Hebrews who points out that the sparrow is meant here, as in the preceding passage. And indeed I think nothing is further from the Prophet's mind. For these words belong entirely to the description of a nocturnal bird. I am surprised that this has not yet occurred to the interpreters, since all the circumstances of the passage openly proclaim it. For whoever speaks in this Psalm, since, worn out by heavy grief, he was fleeing the company of men and pouring out continual groans from the depths of his breast, compares himself with funereal birds, which are both solitary and have something mournful and ominous in their voice. By reason of the voice of my groaning, he says, my bones cleave to my flesh. I am become like a pelican of the wilderness. I was like an owl (or II, 731 a horned owl) of the desert places. So he speaks in the two verses immediately preceding. Then, continuing the comparison he has begun, he says: I kept watch, and was like a solitary bird upon the roof. I kept watch, that is, I spent a sleepless night. Accordingly the Chaldee has there שקדת כל ליליא, I kept watch all night. That is, like the light-shunning nocturnal birds, which, because they hate the light, after hiding by day come out of their hiding places at night to watch for prey. The Philosopher, Hist. book 9, ch. 34: Γλαῦκες δὲ, καὶ νυκτικόρακες, καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ, ὅσα τῆς ἡμέρας ἀδυνατεῖ βλέπειν, τῆς νυκτὸς μὲν θηρεύοντα τὴν τροφὴν αὐτοῖς πορίζεται· [Glaukes de, kai nyktikorakes, kai ta loipa, hosa tēs hēmeras adynatei blepein, tēs nyktos men thēreuonta tēn trophēn autois porizetai] Owls and nycticoraces, and the other birds that cannot see by day, obtain their food by hunting at night. Hence Athenaeus must be corrected, who condenses these words thus, book 8, ch. 12: Γλαῦκες δὲ, καὶ κόρακες ἡμέρας ἀδυνατοῦσι βλέπειν, διὸ νύκτωρ τὴν τροφὴν ἑαυτοῖς θηρεύουσιν· [Glaukes de, kai korakes hēmeras adynatousi blepein, dio nyktōr tēn trophēn heautois thēreuousin]; and instead of κόρακες [korakes] one must write νυκτικόρακες [nyktikorakes]. Accordingly all writers attribute almost continual wakefulness to nocturnal birds. And in Aristophanes' Lysistrata a certain woman speaks thus:


Ἐγὼ δ᾽ ὑπὸ τῶν γλαυκῶν γε τάλαιν᾽ ἀπόλλυμαι,
Ταῖς ἀγρυπνίαισι κακκαβιζουσῶν ἀεί.

Ἐγὼ δ᾽ ὑπὸ τῶν γλαυκῶν γε τάλαιν᾽ ἀπόλλυμαι, Ταῖς ἀγρυπνίαισι κακκαβιζουσῶν ἀεί. [Egō d' hypo tōn glaukōn ge talain' apollymai, Tais agrypniaisi kakkabizousōn aei.]


Ego autem propter noctuas misera perii, quae in vigiliis semper caccabant. Et Aelianus Hist. lib. 1. cap. 29. de noctua, Νύκτωρ μὲν ἀγρυπνεῖ· Noctu quidem vigilat. Et de eadem Varro De ling. Lat. lib. 4. Noctu canit ac vigilat. Hoc igitur Psaltes respiciens, Vigilavi, inquit, et fui ut avis solitaria super tectum. Atque id quidem ad passerem referunt, quasi prae metu vigilet, quod ex Theodoreto habet Suidas. Sed nihil tale apud eos legas, qui de avium natura scripserunt. Et qui passeres domi alunt, sciunt, illos noctu dormire, ut omnes aves praeter nocturnas. Alioqui cum die vigilent, perpetuo essent insomnes. Praeterea צפור בודד, avis solitaria, merito dicitur bubo, vel noctua; quia in desertis locis degit, ut versu praecedente dictum. Hinc Damir, وكنية الانثي ام الخراب Et cognominatur (noctua) foemina mater solitudinis. Et infra, البوم اصناف وكلها تهب الخلوة بانفسها والتفرد Noctuarum plures sunt species, quae omnes secessum et solitudinem amant. Itaque ut onager בודד boded, id est, solitarius, dicitur Os. VIII, 9. quia est eremicola, pari ratione bubo, vel noctua צפור בודד, avis boded, id est solitaria, hic appellatur merito, cum in iis locis nidificet, quae ab hominum frequentia sunt remotissima. Quocirca Plinius lib. vigesimi noni cap. quarto, magos irridens, qui ex bubonis ovo ad capillos remedia praescribunt: Quis, quaeso (inquit) ovum bubonis unquam videre potuit, cum ipsam avem vidisse pro- col. 155 digium sit? Et Alcamus de الصدي id est, Bubone, طاير يصر بالليل يقفر قفرانا Avis est, quae noctu stridet, et in desertis II, 732 locis degit. Quin eo pertinet, quod Arabice صدي tsada dicitur, ut Chaldaice צדיא tsadja. Nam צדו tsadu, vel צדות tsaduth, Chaldaeis est vastitas, desolatio; et Verbum צדה tseda est vastari, desolari. Qua notione in Niphal a Sophonia usurpatur cap. 3. vers. 6. Itaque ex ipso bubonis nomine, quod illi indiderunt Chaldaei, Syri et Arabes, eum colligas avem esse solitariam, et in desolatis locis degentem. Sed et ideo bubo vocatur avis solitaria, quia gregale non est animal, sed solivagum. Unde Poetae lib. 4. Aeneidos,

But I, wretched woman, have perished because of the owls, which were always hooting in the night watches. And Aelian, Hist. book 1, ch. 29, on the owl: Νύκτωρ μὲν ἀγρυπνεῖ· [Nyktōr men agrypnei] By night it keeps awake. And of the same bird Varro, De ling. Lat. book 4: By night it sings and keeps awake. With this in view, then, the Psalmist says: I have watched, and was like a solitary bird upon the roof. Some, however, refer this to the sparrow, as though it kept awake for fear, which Suidas has from Theodoret. But you will read nothing of the kind in those who have written on the nature of birds. And those who keep sparrows at home know that they sleep at night, like all birds except the nocturnal ones. Otherwise, since they are awake by day, they would never sleep at all. Moreover, צפור בודד, a solitary bird, is rightly said of the eagle-owl or the owl, because it lives in desert places, as was said in the preceding verse. Hence Damir: وكنية الانثي ام الخراب [wa-kunyat al-unthī umm al-kharāb] And the female (owl) is surnamed mother of desolation. And further on: البوم اصناف وكلها تهب الخلوة بانفسها والتفرد [al-būm aṣnāf wa-kulluhā thb al-khalwa bi-anfusihā wa-l-tafarrud] There are several species of owls, all of which love seclusion and solitude. Therefore, just as the wild ass is called בודד boded, that is, solitary, in Hos 8:9, because it dwells in the wilderness, by the same reasoning the eagle-owl or owl is here rightly called צפור בודד, bird boded, that is, solitary, since it nests in places very far removed from human traffic. Accordingly Pliny, book 29, ch. 4, mocking the magi who prescribe remedies for the hair from the egg of the eagle-owl, says: Who, I ask, could ever have seen an eagle-owl's egg, when to have seen the bird itself is a por- col. 155 tent? And Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] on الصدي [al-ṣadā], that is, the eagle-owl: طاير يصر بالليل يقفر قفرانا [ṭāyir yaṣirr bi-l-layl yaqfur qafrānan] It is a bird that shrieks at night and lives in desert II, 732 places. Indeed, to this point belongs the fact that in Arabic it is called صدي tsada, as in Chaldee צדיא tsadja. For צדו tsadu or צדות tsaduth means to the Chaldeans waste, desolation; and the verb צדה tseda means to be laid waste, to be made desolate. In this sense it is used in the Niphal by Zephaniah, ch. 3, v. 6. Thus from the very name which the Chaldeans, Syrians and Arabs gave the eagle-owl, you may infer that it is a solitary bird, living in desolate places. But the eagle-owl is also called a solitary bird because it is not a gregarious animal but one that wanders alone. Hence the Poet, in book 4 of the Aeneid:


Solaque culminibus ferali carmine bubo
Visa queri, et longas in fletum ducere voces.

And the eagle-owl alone on the rooftops with funereal song was seen to lament, and to draw out its long notes into weeping.


At passer quorsum dicatur solitarius, cum et gregaria sit avis, et sub aedium tectis nidificet? Fateor quidem, in passerum genere quosdam esse sylvestres. Unde est, quod Athenaei lib. 9. Alexander Myndius docet, δύο γένη εἶναι τῶν στρου-θῶν, τὸ μὲν ἥμερον, τὸ δὲ ἄγριον, passerum duo esse genera, unum domesticum, alterum sylvestre. Sed sylvestres passeres ad aedium tecta se non conferunt, quomodo avis, de qua Psaltes, quam super tectum describit. Itaque, si de passere agitur, non potest intelligi passer sylvestris, sed solum domesticus. Respondent, domesticum passerem ideo dici solitarium, quia compare viduatus est. Quod ferri posset, si passer, aeque ac turtur, aut columba, conjuge amissa, maneret viduus. Sed aliis moribus vivitur inter passeres, animal salacissimum et tam multae Veneris, ut non quidem centies, quomodo referunt Arabes, sed septies saltem in hora foeminam ineat. Unde est, quod illum currui Veneris poetae jungunt. Proinde nulli legi addictus in promiscuam Venerem ruit, neque habet certam conjugem. Itaque ut maritus non fuit, ita neque fit coelebs. Hinc est, quod de passere solitario nihil habent Philosophorum libri. Et toto coelo errant, qui Gallicum passeris nomen deducunt ex Graeco μόνιος. Apri enim est epithetum μόνιος, non passeris. Nobisque adeo moineau plane aliud, nempe μοναχίσκος, monachulus. Quo nomine mas appellatur; quia monachorum more videtur esse cucullatus. Aliud item Tridentinis passer solitarius. Is enim non est e passerum, sed e merularum genere, qui a Philosopho describitur βαιὸς, fuscus, et ἐπὶ τῶν πετρῶν, καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν κεράμων τὰς δια-τριβὰς ποιῶν, in saxis et tegulis degens. Itaque hoc nihil ad rhombum. Iam si rogaveris, quorsum nocturnam avem, puta bubonem, aut noctuam, Psaltes supra tectum describat, responsio erit obvia. Quamvis enim bubones et noctuae in desertis locis nidificent; noctu tamen ad urbes et ad loca culta nonnunquam se conferre, et ex aedium tectis et culminibus ferale suum carmen occentare, in more habent. Quod nemo est qui non aliquando audiverit. Itaque nihil tam frequens apud poetas. Ovidius Metam. lib. 6. Fab. 7.

But why should the sparrow be called solitary, since it is a gregarious bird and nests under the roofs of houses? I admit that within the sparrow kind some are wild. Hence Alexander of Myndus teaches, in Athenaeus book 9, δύο γένη εἶναι τῶν στρουθῶν, τὸ μὲν ἥμερον, τὸ δὲ ἄγριον [dyo genē einai tōn strouthōn, to men hēmeron, to de agrion], that there are two kinds of sparrows, one domestic, the other wild. But wild sparrows do not betake themselves to the roofs of houses, as does the bird of which the Psalmist speaks, whom he describes upon the roof. Therefore, if a sparrow is meant, it cannot be the wild sparrow but only the domestic one. They answer that the domestic sparrow is called solitary because it has been bereaved of its mate. This might be tolerable if the sparrow, like the turtledove or the dove, remained widowed after losing its spouse. But sparrows live by other customs: it is a most lustful animal, so given to Venus that it covers the female, if not a hundred times, as the Arabs report, at least seven times in an hour. Hence the poets yoke it to the chariot of Venus. Bound by no law, then, it rushes into promiscuous love and has no fixed spouse. So, as it was never a husband, neither does it become a widower. That is why the books of the Philosophers say nothing of a solitary sparrow. And those err by the whole breadth of heaven who derive the French name of the sparrow from the Greek μόνιος [monios]. For μόνιος [monios] is an epithet of the boar, not of the sparrow. And to us moineau is something quite different, namely μοναχίσκος [monachiskos], monachulus [little monk]. By this name the male is called, because, like monks, it seems to be hooded. Something else again is the passer solitarius [solitary sparrow] of the people of Trent. For it belongs not to the sparrows but to the blackbird kind, which the Philosopher describes as βαιὸς [baios], dusky, and ἐπὶ τῶν πετρῶν, καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν κεράμων τὰς διατριβὰς ποιῶν [epi tōn petrōn, kai epi tōn keramōn tas diatribas poiōn], living on rocks and roof-tiles. So this is nothing to the point. Now if you ask why the Psalmist describes a nocturnal bird, say the eagle-owl or the owl, upon the roof, the answer is ready. For although eagle-owls and owls nest in desert places, yet at night they are accustomed sometimes to come to towns and cultivated places and to sound their funereal song from the roofs and gables of houses. There is no one who has not heard this at some time. So nothing is more frequent in the poets. Ovid, Metam. book 6, Fable 7:


II, 733 — — — — tectoque profanus
Incubuit bubo, thalamique in culmine sedit.

II, 733 — — — — and on the roof the unholy eagle-owl brooded, and sat on the gable of the bridal chamber.


Et in Ibin versu 223.

And in the Ibis, verse 223:


Sedit in adverso nocturnus culmine bubo.

The nocturnal eagle-owl sat on the opposite gable.


Tibullus lib. 1. Elegia 6.

Tibullus, book 1, Elegy 6:


— — — e tectis strix violenta canat.

— — — let the violent screech-owl sing from the roofs.


Propertius lib. 4. in Epistola Arethusae ad Lycotam,

Propertius, book 4, in the Letter of Arethusa to Lycotas:


Sive in finitimo gemuit stans noctua tigno.

Or whether the owl moaned, perched on the neighbouring beam.


Et Poeta summus lib. 1. Georgicorum,

And the greatest Poet, book 1 of the Georgics:


— — — — de culmine summo
Nequicquam seros exercet noctua cantus.

— — — — from the highest rooftop
the owl plies her late songs in vain.


Et in loco, nuper citato,

And in the passage cited a little earlier:


Solaque culminibus ferali carmine bubo.

And alone on the rooftops the eagle-owl with funereal song.


Sed et apud Historicos hujusmodi exempla passim occurrunt. Lampridius ubi de col. 156 morte Commodi imperatoris, Bubo etiam supra cubiculum ejus deprehensus est tam Romae, quam Lavinii. Supra cubiculum, id est, supra tectum cubiculi. Dio etiam in Commodo, Ὁ βύας ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῦ ἔβυξεν, Bubo super illud (id est, super Capitolii tectum) bubulavit. Ita enim legunt nonnulli pro ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ, ab eo. Et in ejusdem Augusto bellum Actiacum significavit bubo, in templum Concordiae volans, καὶ ἐπὶ τοὺς ἄλλους ἐπικαθήμενος, et aliis (id est, aliorum tectis) insidens. Ammianus denique lib. 30. ubi de Valentiniani obitu, Apud Sabariam eodem adhuc constituto, bubo culminibus regii lavacri insidens occentansque funebria, etc. Concludimus igitur, Psaltis avem solitariam, quaeque noctu vigilat et tectis insidet, non esse passerem, ut volunt, sed bubonem, aut noctuam. Passer quidem sub tecto nidificat, sed non על גג super tectum, quod ait Psaltes.

But examples of this kind also occur everywhere in the Historians. Lampridius, on the col. 156 death of the emperor Commodus: An eagle-owl was also caught above his bedchamber, both at Rome and at Lavinium. Above the bedchamber, that is, above the roof of the bedchamber. Dio also, in his Commodus: Ὁ βύας ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῦ ἔβυξεν [Ho byas ep᾽ autou ebyxen], the eagle-owl hooted upon it (that is, upon the roof of the Capitol). For so some read instead of ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ [ap᾽ autou], from it. And in his Augustus an eagle-owl portended the war of Actium, flying into the temple of Concord, καὶ ἐπὶ τοὺς ἄλλους ἐπικαθήμενος [kai epi tous allous epikathēmenos], and perching on the others (that is, on the roofs of other buildings). Finally Ammianus, book 30, on the death of Valentinian: While he was still staying at Sabaria, an eagle-owl perched on the rooftops of the royal bath and hooted funereal notes, etc. We conclude, therefore, that the Psalmist's solitary bird, which keeps watch at night and perches on roofs, is not the sparrow, as they would have it, but the eagle-owl or the owl. The sparrow does indeed nest under the roof, but not על גג, upon the roof, as the Psalmist says.


VI. Sextus locus est Psal. CIV, 16. Saturabuntur arbores Dei, cedri Libani, quas plantavit, ubi צפורים tsipporim nidificant. Arbores Dei, id est, arbores celsissimae. Tale Cedri Dei, Psal. LXXX, 11. Montes Dei, Psal. XXXVI, 7. Flamma Dei, Cantic. VIII, 6. id est, flamma vehementissima. Luctationes Dei, Gen. XXX, 5. id est, luctationes gravissimae. Itaque arbores Dei et cedri Libani proponuntur ut synonyma; quia cedri sunt inter arbores procerissimas. Et saturari dicuntur arbores Dei et cedri Libani, imbre scilicet, de quo versu 13. Et Deus has plantare, ut arbores aloës Num. XXIV, 6. quia sponte proveniunt, et solo Dei nutu, absque hominum labore et cura. Additur, in his nidificare צפורים tsipporim, id est, passeres, ut multi putant. Ita enim LXX. Ἐκεῖ II, 734 στρουθία ἐννοσσεύσουσι. Et Symmachus, Ὅπου στρουθία ἐννοσσεύσει. Et Vulgatus, Illic passeres nidificabunt. Et Apollinaris,

VI. The sixth passage is Ps 104:16: The trees of God shall be satisfied, the cedars of Lebanon, which he planted, where צפורים tsipporim make their nests. Trees of God, that is, very lofty trees. So also cedars of God, Ps 80:11; mountains of God, Ps 36:7; flame of God, Song 8:6, that is, a most vehement flame; wrestlings of God, Gen 30:5, that is, most severe wrestlings. Thus trees of God and cedars of Lebanon are put forward as synonyms, since cedars are among the tallest of trees. And the trees of God and cedars of Lebanon are said to be satisfied, namely with rain, of which verse 13 speaks. And God is said to have planted them, like the aloe trees in Num 24:6, because they grow of their own accord, by God's will alone, without human labour and care. It is added that צפורים tsipporim nest in them, that is, sparrows, as many think. For so the LXX: Ἐκεῖ II, 734 στρουθία ἐννοσσεύσουσι [Ekei strouthia ennosseusousi]. And Symmachus: Ὅπου στρουθία ἐννοσσεύσει [Hopou strouthia ennosseusei]. And the Vulgate translator: There the sparrows shall make their nests. And Apollinaris:


Κεῖσε νεηγενέων πέλεται στρουθῶν ἀλεωρὴ,

Κεῖσε νεηγενέων πέλεται στρουθῶν ἀλεωρὴ [Keise neēgeneōn peletai strouthōn aleōrē],


Illic nuper-natorum passerum est perfugium. Et Arabs uterque, هناك عششت العصافير Illic nidificant passeres. Sed Aquila, ut videtur, melius, Ἐκεῖ ὄρνεα νοσσεύσουσιν. Et Hieronymus, Ibi aves nidificabunt. Sammusenim, Libani vertex, ubi cedri, passeribus est inaccessus, quos aves montanas non esse, jam docuimus.

There is the refuge of newly hatched sparrows. And both Arabic versions: هناك عششت العصافير [hunāka ʿashshashat al-ʿaṣāfīr] There the sparrows nest. But Aquila, it seems, does better: Ἐκεῖ ὄρνεα νοσσεύσουσιν [Ekei ornea nosseusousin]. And Jerome: There the birds shall make their nests. For the summit of Lebanon, where the cedars are, is inaccessible to sparrows, which, as we have already shown, are not mountain birds.


VII. Septimus locus Psal. CXXIV, 7. Anima nostra כצפור, ut tsippor erepta est ex venatorum laqueo: Graeci, ὡς στρυθίον· Vulgata, sicut passer: Arabs itidem مثل العصفور ut passer: Apollinaris, στρουθοῦ πανομοίϊος, passeri plane similis: sed Hieronymus, quasi avis. Quod probo magis, quia passeres et similes aviculae visco potius, quam laqueo capiuntur. Quod docet Baal Aruch ad vocem שפשף, qua significatur pertica, visco illita, ad aviculas capiendas.

VII. The seventh passage is Psal. CXXIV, 7: Our soul has escaped כצפור, like a tsippor, from the snare of the fowlers. The Greeks: ὡς στρυθίον [hōs strythion]; the Vulgate: like a sparrow; the Arabic likewise: مثل العصفور [mithl al-ʿuṣfūr] like the sparrow; Apollinaris: στρουθοῦ πανομοίϊος [strouthou panomoiios], entirely like a sparrow; but Jerome: as a bird. This I approve more, because sparrows and similar little birds are caught with birdlime rather than with a snare. This is taught by Baal Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome] [=Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome, the ʿArukh] on the word שפשף, which signifies a pole smeared with birdlime for catching little birds.


VIII. Octavus Eccles. XII, 4. al. 6. ubi de sene Graeci dicunt, Καὶ ἀνα-στήσεται εἰς φωνὴν τοῦ στρουθίου, Et surget ad vocem passeris. Sed Hieronymus, Et consurget ad vocem volucris. Et Chaldaeus, Et excitaberis a somno tuo על עסק קול דעופא, propter vocem avis, id est, ad avis cantum, quam gallum esse nonnulli volunt, et gallicinium significari. Ut gallus, homines matutino cantu excitans, simpliciter ales vocatur in his Poetae Amorum lib. 1. Eleg. 6.

VIII. The eighth is Eccles. XII, 4 (var. 6), where the Greeks say of the old man: Καὶ ἀναστήσεται εἰς φωνὴν τοῦ στρουθίου [Kai anastēsetai eis phōnēn tou strouthiou], And he shall rise up at the voice of the sparrow. But Jerome: And he shall rise up at the voice of the bird. And the Chaldee: And you shall be roused from your sleep על עסק קול דעופא, because of the voice of the bird, that is, at the song of a bird, which some take to be the cock, and cockcrow to be meant. Just as the cock, which wakes people with its morning song, is simply called ales [the bird] in these lines of the Poet of the Amores, book 1, Eleg. 6:


Iamque pruinosus molitur Lucifer axes,
Inque suum miseros excitat ales opus.

And now Lucifer drives forth his frosty axles,
and the bird rouses wretched men to their work.


Alii malunt, passeris aut aviculae cantum intelligi, quo, quamlibet tenui, senex e somno excitetur, dum juvenes tam alte dormiunt, ut ne tonitruum quidem fragorem audiant. Nec facile est statuere, utra versio sit sanior. Eos enim abunde confutavimus, qui gallum negant, aut ullam majorum avium voce צפור significari. Potest etiam id accipi de matutino garritu avium, qui Arabice voce col. 157 maxime propria dicitur زقزقة zakzaka. Alcamus, الزقزقة صوت طير عند الصبح garritus avium circa auroram.

Others prefer to understand the song of the sparrow or of a little bird, by which, however faint, the old man is woken from sleep, while the young sleep so deeply that they do not hear even the crash of thunder. Nor is it easy to decide which version is sounder. For we have amply refuted those who deny that the cock, or any of the larger birds, is signified by the word צפור. It can also be taken of the morning chatter of birds, which in Arabic is called by a most proper word, col. 157 زقزقة [zaqzaqa] zakzaka. Alcamus: الزقزقة صوت طير عند الصبح [al-zaqzaqa ṣawt ṭayr ʿinda al-ṣubḥ] the chatter of birds about dawn.


IX. Nonus locus sic habet Thren. III, 32. Me venantur כצפור, ut tsippor inimici mei merito: ubi Graeci, ὡς στρουθίον· sed Hieronymus, quasi avem. Quod acceperim potius de majoribus avibus, quibus aucupandis opera libentius insumitur, et majore cum fructu.

IX. The ninth passage reads thus, Thren. III, 32: My enemies hunt me כצפור, like a tsippor, deservedly [sic]. Here the Greeks: ὡς στρουθίον [hōs strouthion]; but Jerome: like a bird. This I would rather take of the larger birds, on the catching of which effort is more willingly spent, and with greater profit.


II, 735 In Tobia Latinum exemplar a Graeco in hac voce dissidet Tob. II, 9. (al. 11.). Nam in Graeco dicit Tobias, Καὶ οὐκ ᾔδειν ὅτι στρουθία ἐν τῷ τοίχῳ ἐστί· καὶ, τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν μου ἀνεωγότων, ἀφώδευσαν τὰ στρουθία θερμὸν εἰς τοὺς ὀφθαλ-μούς μου· Et passeres in pariete esse nesciebam: et, oculis meis apertis, passeres calidum stercus in oculos meos egesserunt. At Latinum quadam die contigisse narrat, ut, cum juxta parietem Tobias obdormisset, ex nido hirundinum dormienti illi calida stercora inciderent. Quae aliter conciliari posse non video, quam si dicas, Graece στρουθία ibi non esse passeres, sed aviculas, prout supra asserebant Moschopulus et Phavorinus, aviculae omne genus Graece dici στρουθία. Aut passerum nomine hirundines significari Arabum more, qui hirundinem vocant عصفور الجنة passerem Paradisi. Quale est, quod Prov. XXVI, 2. Hebraeum דרור deror alii hirundinem reddunt: sed Graeci interpretes στρουθοὺς passeres.

II, 735 In Tobit the Latin copy disagrees with the Greek on this word, Tob 2:9 (var. 11.). For in the Greek Tobit says, Καὶ οὐκ ᾔδειν ὅτι στρουθία ἐν τῷ τοίχῳ ἐστί· καὶ, τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν μου ἀνεωγότων, ἀφώδευσαν τὰ στρουθία θερμὸν εἰς τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς μου [Kai ouk ēdein hoti strouthia en tō toichō esti; kai, tōn ophthalmōn mou aneōgotōn, aphōdeusan ta strouthia thermon eis tous ophthalmous mou]; And I did not know that there were sparrows in the wall; and, my eyes being open, the sparrows voided warm dung into my eyes. But the Latin relates that it happened one day that, when Tobit had fallen asleep beside a wall, warm dung fell upon him as he slept from a swallows' nest. I do not see how these can be reconciled otherwise than by saying that στρουθία [strouthia] in the Greek there are not sparrows but little birds, just as Moschopulus and Phavorinus asserted above that every kind of little bird is called στρουθία [strouthia] in Greek. Or else that by the name of sparrows swallows are meant, after the manner of the Arabs, who call the swallow عصفور الجنة [ʿuṣfūr al-janna] the sparrow of Paradise. Similar is the case of Prov 26:2, where some render the Hebrew דרור deror as swallow, but the Greek interpreters as στρουθοὺς [strouthous], sparrows.
