De providentia Dei circa Passeres et aviculas, in Matth. X, 29. et Luc. XII, 6.

On the providence of God concerning sparrows and little birds, in Matt 10:29 and Luke 12:6.


Christus Matth. X, 29. dicit, duos passeres assario vendi, nec tamen eorum ul-lum in terram cadere sine Deo. Et Luc. XII, 6. quinque passeres duobus assariis venire, nec tamen eorum ullum in oblivione esse apud Deum. Itaque singuli passeres semisse vendebantur, aut paullo minus. Falluntur enim, qui as-sarium semissem esse volunt. Quin assarium est idem, quod as. Glossae Latino-Graecae, Asse, Ἀσσάριον, lege Ἀσσαρίου. Et alibi, Sesquas, Ἓι ἥμισυ ἀσσάριον. Lege, Ἓν ἥμισυ καὶ ἀσσάριον. Glossae Graeco-latinae Phloxeni, Ἀσσάριον, Hic as. Ἀσσαρίου ἥμισυ, Sesquas, lege Ἓν ἀσσάριον καὶ ἥμισυ. As, ex Budaei supputatione, quaternos denariolos nostros valuit et pauxillo plus. Syrus interpres habet ܐܣܪ assar, qua voce pro assario Hebraei etiam saepe utuntur. A Davide Cohen de Lara, in libro De convenientia Rabbinismi col. 158 cum Graeco, אסר assar Hispanice definitur moneda de tres maravedis, quod ad Budaei λογισμὸν proxime accedit. In Maimonidis tractatu De siclis cap. 1. 3. הסלע ארבעה דינרין והדינר שש מעין ומעה היא היקראת בימי משה רבינו גרה ומאה היא שני פונדיונין ופונדיון שני אסרין ופרוטה אחת משמונה באסר נמצא משקל המעה והיא הגרה שש עשרה שעורות ומשקל האסר ארבע שעורות ומשקל פרוטה חצי שעורה, Siclus valet quatuor denarios. Denarius sex obolos. Obolus autem gera vocabatur diebus Mosis, magistri nostri. Obolus valet duo II, 736 pondia: et pondium duo assaria. Et peruta est assarii octava pars. Oboli pondus, qui gera dicitur, est sedecim granorum hordei. Pondus assarii quatuor granorum, peruta dimidii grani. Similem locum citat Drusius ex libro Mandatorum. Pro assario فلس follem, et pro duobus assariis فلسين duos folles habet Arabs interpres, et Hieronymus dipondium. Sed Matth. V, 26. in eodem Arabe follis est pro quadrante. Et Marc. XIV, 42. فلسين duo folles sunt pro duobus minutis, seu duabus פרוטות perutoth: quae simul junctae unum quadrantem efficiunt. Apparet igitur, hunc interpretem, de vero nummorum pretio parum sollicitum, sat habuisse, si pro vili nummo vilem alium poneret, quamvis diversi pretii. Et vero assario, vel asse, vendi nihil aliud est, quam vili pretio distrahi. Nam vilia esse oportet, quaecunque asse veneunt, vel aestimantur. Hinc Catullus Lesbiae suae,

Christ, in Matt 10:29, says that two sparrows are sold for an assarion, and yet not one of them falls to the ground without God. And in Luke 12:6 he says that five sparrows are sold for two assaria, and yet not one of them is forgotten before God. Thus individual sparrows were sold for half an as, or a little less. For those are mistaken who hold that the assarion is half an as. Rather, the assarion is the same as the as. The Latin-Greek Glosses: Asse, Ἀσσάριον [assarion]; read Ἀσσαρίου [assariou]. And elsewhere: Sesquas, Ἓι ἥμισυ ἀσσάριον [hei hēmisy assarion]. Read Ἓν ἥμισυ καὶ ἀσσάριον [hen hēmisy kai assarion]. The Greek-Latin Glosses of Philoxenus: Ἀσσάριον [assarion], Hic as.; Ἀσσαρίου ἥμισυ [assariou hēmisy], Sesquas; read Ἓν ἀσσάριον καὶ ἥμισυ [hen assarion kai hēmisy]. The as, by Budé's reckoning, was worth four of our little deniers and a trifle more. The Syriac translator has ܐܣܪ [אסר] assar, a word which the Hebrews also often use for the assarion. David Cohen de Lara, in his book De convenientia Rabbinismi col. 158 cum Graeco, defines אסר assar in Spanish as moneda de tres maravedis, which comes very close to Budé's λογισμὸν [logismon]. In Maimonides' [=Moses Maimonides (Rambam), Mishneh Torah] treatise On Shekels, ch. 1. 3.: הסלע ארבעה דינרין והדינר שש מעין ומעה היא היקראת בימי משה רבינו גרה ומאה היא שני פונדיונין ופונדיון שני אסרין ופרוטה אחת משמונה באסר נמצא משקל המעה והיא הגרה שש עשרה שעורות ומשקל האסר ארבע שעורות ומשקל פרוטה חצי שעורה, The shekel is worth four denarii. The denarius six obols. The obol was called a gerah in the days of Moses our master. The obol is worth two II, 736 pondia, and the pondion two assaria. And the perutah is the eighth part of an assarion. The weight of the obol, which is called a gerah, is sixteen barley grains. The weight of the assarion four grains, of the perutah half a grain. Drusius cites a similar passage from the Book of Commandments. For assarion the Arabic translator has فلس [fals] follis, and for two assaria فلسين [falsayn] two folles; and Jerome has dipondium. But in Matt 5:26 the same Arabic version has follis for quadrans. And in Mark 14:42 فلسين [falsayn] two folles stands for two mites, that is, two פרוטות perutoth, which together make one quadrans. It is evident, therefore, that this translator, caring little about the true value of the coins, was content to put one cheap coin for another cheap coin, though of different value. And indeed, to be sold for an assarion or an as means nothing other than to be sold off at a low price. For whatever is sold or valued at an as must be cheap. Hence Catullus to his Lesbia:


Rumoresque senum severiorum,
Omnes unius aestimemus assis.

And the gossip of stern old men, let us value it all at a single as.


Et in Vivennios,

And against the Vibennii:


Fili, non potes asse venditare.

Son, you cannot sell it for an as.


Et in quendam,

And against a certain man:


Non assis facis? O lutum, lupanar!

You think it not worth an as? O filth, O brothel!


Et Cicero pro Quintio, Assem sese negat daturum, nisi prius de rebus rationibusque socitatis omnibus decidisset. Et pro Roscio Comoedo, Dic LLS. CCCIↃↃↃ dedisse, qui assem nullum dedit. Et Iuvenalis Satyra 10.

And Cicero, for Quinctius: He says he will not pay an as unless he has first settled all the affairs and accounts of the partnership. And for Roscius the Comedian: Say he gave LLS. CCCIↃↃↃ, he who gave not a single as. And Juvenal, Satire 10:


Quisquis adhuc uno partam colit asse Minervam.

Whoever still worships Minerva, acquired for a single as.


Et Misna in fine tractatus Cholin, ubi de praecepto, quo jubentur Israelitae matrem dmittere, cum ova et pullos in nido capiunt, ut illis bene sit, et prorogenturdies, Deut. XXII, 6. 7. אם מצוה קלה שהיא באסר אמרה תורה למען ייטב לך והארכת ימים קל וחומר על מצות חמורות שבתורה, Si in praecepto leviore, de re, quae vix assarii est, Lex ait, „Ut bene sit tibi, et proroget dies „tuos:“ quanto magis (idem sperandum) de gravioribus praeceptis, qui sunt in Lege? Pro assario obolum dixissent Graeci vetustiores. Sic in Avibus Aristophanis graviter queruntur aves de quodam Philocrate, qui,

And the Mishnah at the end of the tractate Chullin, concerning the precept by which the Israelites are commanded to let the mother go when they take eggs and young from a nest, that it may be well with them and their days be prolonged, Deut 22:6–7.: אם מצוה קלה שהיא באסר אמרה תורה למען ייטב לך והארכת ימים קל וחומר על מצות חמורות שבתורה, If concerning a lighter precept, about a thing that is scarcely worth an assarion, the Law says, “That it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days,” how much more (is the same to be hoped) for the weightier precepts that are in the Law? For assarion the older Greeks would have said obol. Thus in the Birds of Aristophanes the birds complain bitterly of a certain Philocrates, who,


— συνείρων τοὺς σπίνους, πωλεῖ καθ᾽ ἑπτὰ ὀβολοῦ,

— συνείρων τοὺς σπίνους, πωλεῖ καθ᾽ ἑπτὰ ὀβολοῦ, [syneirōn tous spinous, pōlei kath᾽ hepta obolou,]


Fringillos connectens, septem vendit uno obolo. Obolo, id est, duobus assariis, sive assibus. Quod docent haec Polybii Historiarum lib. 2. Ὡς μὲν οὖν ἐπιτοπο-λὺ παρίενται τοὺς καταλύτας οἱ πανδοχεῖς ἡμιασσαρίου, τοῦτο δ᾽ ἐστὶ τέταρ-τον μέρος ὀβολοῦ. Hospites suos plerumque caupones accipiunt semisse, seu dimidio assario, quod est oboli quarta pars. Cum igitur quinque passeres duobus II, 737 assariis venire dicit Christus, idem est, ac si dixisset, obolo vendi. Unde colligis, Athenis aevo Aristophanis aliquanto viliorem fuisse annonam, quam in Iudaea Christi aetate. Nam quo pretio Athenienses septem fringillos, nonnisi quinque passeres Iudaei comparabant. Latinus porro Aristophanis interpres pro fringillis habet passeres; quia passer et fringillus sunt aves simillimae. Hinc Glos- col. 159 sae Philoxeni, Σπίνος· ὁ στρουθὸς, Frincillus, fringillus. Quasi σπίνος idem esset, quod στρουθὸς, seu passer. Fringillus, Gallis pinson, olim forte pintion, ut Hesychio σπίνθιον. Tale chanson ex cantione, maison ex mansione, raison ex ratione, etc. Sed, sive quinque, vel septem hujusmodi aviculae obolo distrahantur, et matrem solam, aut matrem cum pullis, Misnae auctor assem aestimaverit, vilissima oportet esse animalia, cum tam levi pretio prostent. Tamen hic Christus nos docet, etiam haec animalcula Deo ita esse curae, ut eorum nullum absque eo in terram cadat, id est, eo non permittente pereat. Quibus haec Lucae consona: Ἓν ἐξ αὐτῶν οὐκ ἔστιν ἐπιλελησμένον ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ· Unus ex illis non est in oblivione coram Deo. Phrasi sumpta ex Psal. IX, 19. ubi de paupere dicitur, Οὐκ εἰς τέλος ἐπιλησθήσεται, Non in aeternum oblivioni erit. Hebraice לא לנצח ישכח. Unde regius Psaltes tam de pusillis, quam de magnis animalibus Psal. CIV, 27. Omnia ista a te exspectant, ut des illis escam in tempore suo. Tamen, ut de Iudaeis taceam in praesens, quorum plerique in diversa sunt sententia, Hieronymus in Habacucum cap. 1. haec habet: Absurdum est, ad hoc Dei deducere majestatem, ut sciat, per momenta singula quot nascantur culices, quotve moriantur: quae cimicum, et pulicum, et muscarum sit in terra multitudo: quanti pisces in aqua natent: et qui de minoribus majorum praedae cedere debeant. Ne simus tam fatui adulatores Dei, ut, dum potentiam ejus ad ima detrahimus, in nos ipsos injuriosi simus; eandem rationabilium quam irrationabilium providentiam esse dicentes. Quae duriora videri poterunt, nisi benigna interpretatione molliantur; ita, ut intelligamus, haec comparate dici (quod sub finem innuit), ne putetur Deus brutorum eandem habere rationem, quam hominum, quos creavit ad suam imaginem: cum bruta servet praecipue propter homines, in quorum usum creata sunt. Diversos igitur agnoscimus divinae providentiae gradus, neque Deum curare boves eodem modo, quo homines, quod docet Paulus 1 Cor. IX, 9. Tamen tam boves, quam homines, et vilis- col. 160 simas etiam creaturas Deo subesse, certum est. Neque is regere et conservare dedignatur, quae creare dignatus est. Et cavendum, ne fingamus limites illius providentiae, quam, ut nec maxima onerant, sic nec minima effugiunt, aut ab ea negliguntur. Quis credat, Deum ignorasse numerum coturnicum, quibus Israelitas in deserto pavit, aut piscium, qui natabant in lacu Genesareth, cum Christi jussu Petrus jecit retia? Aut nescivisse, quot ranis aut pediculis usurus esset in Aegyptios; aut locustas illas, quae vocantur Dei copiae Ioel. II, 11. ipsi II, 738 non fuisse curae, et summum illum ducem fugisse, quot milites in exercitu suo conscripserit? Denique quid Christi verbis disertius, nullum ex passeribus in terram cadere sine Deo, aut in oblivione esse coram illo? In quem locum haec observanda, quae ex Talmude Hierosolymitano profert doctissimus Buxtorfius Lexici Talmudici pag. 553. Rabbi Simeon Ben Iochai latebat in quadam spelunca. Die quodam sedens ad ostium speluncae, et videns aucupem, aves capientem et rete extendentem, audivit filiam vocis (oraculum), quae cum dicebat דימוס dimos (id est, liberatio), tum evadebat avis. Quando vero filia vocis dicebat ספיקולא, spicula (id est, sententia mortis), tum avis capiebatur. Proinde dixit oraculum, צפור מבלברי שמיא לא יבדא כל שכן בר נשא, Avicula sine coelo (id est, sine Dei voluntate et providentia) non perit: quanto minus homo! Pro לא יבדא lege לא יאבד. His etiam ethnici non dissimilia scribunt. Sic Plutarchus alicubi ex Homero probat, veteres in ea fuisse sententia, Dei numine curari οὐ μόνον βόας, ἀλλὰ καὶ πάντα τὰ ἄλλα ζῶα, non solum boves, sed et omnia alia animalia. Et Aelianus Hist. lib. 11. cap. 31. Ἴδιον δὲ ἄρα τῶν ζώων καὶ ἐκεῖνο ἀγαθὸν, πρόνοιαν αὐτῶν καὶ οἱ Θεοὶ ποιοῦνται, καὶ οὔτε αὐτῶν καταφρονοῦσιν, οὐδὲ μὴν ὀλιγώρως ἔχουσιν· Etiam brutis competit hoc bonum, quod iis Dii provident, neque illa despiciunt, aut susque deque habent.

Tying finches together, he sells seven for one obol. For an obol, that is, for two assaria, or asses. This is shown by these words of Polybius, Histories book 2: Ὡς μὲν οὖν ἐπιτοπολὺ παρίενται τοὺς καταλύτας οἱ πανδοχεῖς ἡμιασσαρίου, τοῦτο δ᾽ ἐστὶ τέταρτον μέρος ὀβολοῦ [Hōs men oun epitopoly parieнтai tous katalytas hoi pandocheis hēmiassariou, touto d᾽ esti tetarton meros obolou]. Innkeepers generally receive their guests for half an as, or half an assarion, which is a quarter of an obol. So when Christ says that five sparrows are sold for two II, 737 assaria, it is the same as if he had said they are sold for an obol. From this you may infer that at Athens in the time of Aristophanes provisions were somewhat cheaper than in Judaea in the time of Christ. For at the price for which the Athenians bought seven finches, the Jews bought only five sparrows. Further, the Latin translator of Aristophanes has passeres [sparrows] for fringilli [finches], because the sparrow and the finch are very similar birds. Hence the Glosses col. 159 of Philoxenus: Σπίνος· ὁ στρουθὸς [Spinos; ho strouthos], Frincillus, fringillus, as if σπίνος [spinos] were the same as στρουθὸς [strouthos], or passer [sparrow]. Fringillus is in French pinson, formerly perhaps pintion, like σπίνθιον [spinthion] in Hesychius. So too chanson from cantione, maison from mansione, raison from ratione, etc. But whether five or seven such little birds are sold for an obol, and whether the author of the Mishnah valued the mother alone, or the mother with her young, at an as, they must be very cheap animals, since they are on sale for so slight a price. Yet here Christ teaches us that even these little creatures are such a concern to God that none of them falls to the ground without him, that is, perishes without his permission. With this agrees Luke: Ἓν ἐξ αὐτῶν οὐκ ἔστιν ἐπιλελησμένον ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ [Hen ex autōn ouk estin epilelēsmenon enōpion tou Theou]; Not one of them is forgotten before God. The phrase is taken from Ps 9:19, where it is said of the poor man: Οὐκ εἰς τέλος ἐπιλησθήσεται [Ouk eis telos epilēsthēsetai], He shall not be forgotten for ever; in Hebrew לא לנצח ישכח. Hence the royal Psalmist, of small and great animals alike, Ps 104:27: These all wait upon you, that you may give them their food in due season. Yet, to say nothing for the present of the Jews, most of whom hold a different opinion, Jerome on Habakkuk ch. 1 says this: It is absurd to lower the majesty of God to this, that he should know at every moment how many gnats are born and how many die; how great is the multitude of bugs, fleas and flies on the earth; how many fish swim in the water; and which of the smaller must fall prey to the larger. Let us not be such foolish flatterers of God that, while we drag his power down to the lowest things, we do injury to ourselves, saying that the providence over rational and irrational creatures is the same. These words might seem rather harsh unless softened by a kindly interpretation, so that we understand them to be said comparatively (as he hints toward the end): lest God be thought to have the same regard for brutes as for men, whom he created in his own image, since he preserves the brutes chiefly for the sake of men, for whose use they were created. We therefore recognize different degrees of divine providence, and that God does not care for oxen in the same way as for men, as Paul teaches, 1 Cor 9:9. Yet it is certain that oxen as well as men, and even the meanest col. 160 creatures, are subject to God. Nor does he disdain to govern and preserve what he deigned to create. And we must beware of inventing limits to that providence, which, as the greatest things do not burden it, so the smallest do not escape it or go neglected by it. Who would believe that God did not know the number of the quails with which he fed the Israelites in the desert, or of the fish that swam in the lake of Gennesaret when Peter cast his nets at Christ's command? Or that he did not know how many frogs or lice he would use against the Egyptians; or that those locusts which are called God's army, Joel 2:11, were of no II, 738 concern to him, and that this supreme commander did not know how many soldiers he had enlisted in his army? Finally, what could be plainer than Christ's words, that none of the sparrows falls to the ground without God, or is forgotten before him? On this passage note what the most learned Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum] cites from the Jerusalem Talmud in his Lexicon Talmudicum, p. 553: Rabbi Simeon ben Yochai was hiding in a cave. One day, sitting at the mouth of the cave and seeing a fowler catching birds and spreading his net, he heard a daughter of the voice (an oracle); when it said דימוס dimos (that is, release), the bird escaped. But when the daughter of the voice said ספיקולא, spicula (that is, sentence of death), the bird was caught. Then the oracle said, צפור מבלברי שמיא לא יבדא כל שכן בר נשא, A little bird does not perish without heaven (that is, without God's will and providence): how much less a man! For לא יבדא read לא יאבד. The pagans too write things not unlike these. Thus Plutarch somewhere proves from Homer that the ancients held the opinion that by the divine power are cared for οὐ μόνον βόας, ἀλλὰ καὶ πάντα τὰ ἄλλα ζῶα [ou monon boas, alla kai panta ta alla zōa], not only oxen, but all other animals too. And Aelian, Hist. book 11, ch. 31: Ἴδιον δὲ ἄρα τῶν ζώων καὶ ἐκεῖνο ἀγαθὸν, πρόνοιαν αὐτῶν καὶ οἱ Θεοὶ ποιοῦνται, καὶ οὔτε αὐτῶν καταφρονοῦσιν, οὐδὲ μὴν ὀλιγώρως ἔχουσιν [Idion de ara tōn zōōn kai ekeino agathon, pronoian autōn kai hoi Theoi poiountai, kai oute autōn kataphronousin, oude mēn oligōrōs echousin]; The brutes too have this good, that the gods provide for them, and neither despise them nor treat them with indifference.

II, 739 DE SCRIPTURAE ANIMALIBUS col. 161 PARS SECUNDA LIBER SECUNDUS DE DE IMMUNDIS AVIBUS.

II, 739 ON THE ANIMALS OF SCRIPTURE col. 161 PART TWO BOOK TWO ON ON THE UNCLEAN BIRDS.


CAP. I.

CHAPTER I.


Aquila, rex avium; ejus nomen, rostrum, ungues, pluma, calvitium, renovatio, color.

The eagle, king of the birds; its name, beak, talons, plumage, baldness, renewal, colour.


Immundas aves in hoc libro eodem ordine proponemus, quo Moses Levit. XI, 13. et Deut. XIV, 2. Prima omnium est aquila. Quo pertinet, quod hic habet Baal Hatturim, פתח בנשר שהוא מלך בעופות, Incepit ab aquila, quia est rex avium. In earum scilicet avium censu, quarum esum Iudaeis interdixit Deus, vult aquilam merito ducere ordinem, cum in reliquas aves regnum ei dederit consensus gentium, propter eximias dotes, quibus supra illas eminet. De Graecis res manifesta est. Aquilam enim vocat Pindarus Olymp. 13.

In this book we shall set out the unclean birds in the same order as Moses in Lev 11:13 and Deut 14:2. First of all is the eagle. To this pertains what Baal Hatturim [=Jacob ben Asher (d. 1343), commentary on the Torah] has here: פתח בנשר שהוא מלך בעופות, He began with the eagle, because it is king of the birds. That is, in the list of those birds whose eating God forbade the Jews, he holds that the eagle rightly leads the line, since the consensus of nations has given it kingship over the other birds because of the outstanding gifts by which it surpasses them. As to the Greeks the matter is plain. For Pindar, Olymp. 13, calls the eagle


— — οἰωνῶν βασιλῆα,

— — οἰωνῶν βασιλῆα [oiōnōn basilēa],


avium regem. Et Pyth. 1.

king of the birds. And Pyth. 1:


Διὸς αἰετὸν, ἀρχὸν οἰωνῶν,

Διὸς αἰετὸν, ἀρχὸν οἰωνῶν [Dios aieton, archon oiōnōn],


Iovis aquilam, ducem avium. Et Istm. 6.

the eagle of Jupiter, leader of the birds. And Isthm. 6:


— — — ἀρχὸν οἰωνῶν μέγαν αἰετὸν,

— — — ἀρχὸν οἰωνῶν μέγαν αἰετὸν [archon oiōnōn megan aieton],


principem avium, magnam aquilam. Et oraculum de Atheniensibus in Equitibus col. 162 Aristophanis Actu tertio,

the prince of the birds, the great eagle. And the oracle about the Athenians in the Knights col. 162 of Aristophanes, Act 3:


Αἰετὸς ὡς γίνει, καὶ πάσης γῆς βασιλεύσεις,

Αἰετὸς ὡς γίνει, καὶ πάσης γῆς βασιλεύσεις [Aietos hōs ginei, kai pasēs gēs basileuseis],


Esto ut aquila, et toti orbi dominabere. Nicander etiam, ubi de aquilae et draconis pugna, Theriacων versu 448.

Be like an eagle, and you will rule the whole world. Nicander too, where he speaks of the fight of the eagle and the serpent, Theriaca, line 448:

Αἰετὸς, — — — — — —

II, 740 Τῷ μέν τ᾽ ἔκπαγλον κοτέων βασιλήϊος ὄρνις Αἰετὸς, — — — — — — [Tō men t᾽ ekpaglon koteōn basilēios ornis Aietos]


In hunc autem immanem in modum exaestuans regia avis aquila. Et Boëus libro primo Ornithogoniae, de Periphante, a Iove in aquilam mutato, Ποιεῖ γὰρ αὐτὸν ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ὄρνισι βασιλέα. Facit enim eum regem inter omnes aves. Et Dionysius in Bassaricis apud Stephanum in Κάσπειρος,

But against him the royal bird, the eagle, raging in monstrous fashion. And Boeus, in book 1 of the Ornithogonia, on Periphas, changed by Jupiter into an eagle: Ποιεῖ γὰρ αὐτὸν ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ὄρνισι βασιλέα [Poiei gar auton en pasi tois ornisi basilea]. For he makes him king among all the birds. And Dionysius in the Bassarica, cited by Stephanus under Κάσπειρος [Kaspeiros]:


Αἰετὸς εἰν ὄρνισι μεταπρέπει ἀγρομένοισιν,

Αἰετὸς εἰν ὄρνισι μεταπρέπει ἀγρομένοισιν [Aietos ein ornisi metaprepei agromenoisin],


Aquila inter agrestes aves excellit. Et Quintus Smyrnaeus libri tertii versu 353.

The eagle excels among the wild birds. And Quintus Smyrnaeus, book 3, line 353:


Αἰετὸς οἰωνῶν προφερέστατος,

Αἰετὸς οἰωνῶν προφερέστατος [Aietos oiōnōn propherestatos],


Aquila avium praestantissima. Et Oppianus Halieuticων libri secundi versu 539.

The eagle, most excellent of birds. And Oppian, Halieutica, book 2, line 539:


Ὅσσον γὰρ κέφοισι μετ᾽ οἰωνοῖσιν ἄνακτες
Αἰετοί. — — — — — —

Ὅσσον γὰρ κέφοισι μετ᾽ οἰωνοῖσιν ἄνακτες Αἰετοί. — — — — — — [Hosson gar kephoisi met᾽ oiōnoisin anaktes Aietoi]


Quantum leves inter aves (excellunt) reges aquilae. Et Aelianus Hist. lib. 9. cap. col. 163 2. Τὸν ἀετὸν, τὸν τῶν ὀρνίθων βασιλέα, οὐ μόνον παρόντα, καὶ ζῶντα δέδοι-κε τὰ ὄρνεα· Avium regem aquilam, non solum viventem et praesentem timent aves. Phile denique πτηνοκράτορα nominat, id est, avium principem. Et Tzetzes Chiliad. 5. Hist. 9. tam aquilas, quam leones cadavera negat attingere, ut qui reges sint, ille avium, hic ferarum. Et e Romanis scriptoribus Horatius libri quarti Oda quarta,

As much as among the light birds the eagles, their kings (excel). And Aelian, Hist. book 9, ch. col. 163 2: Τὸν ἀετὸν, τὸν τῶν ὀρνίθων βασιλέα, οὐ μόνον παρόντα, καὶ ζῶντα δέδοικε τὰ ὄρνεα [Ton aeton, ton tōn ornithōn basilea, ou monon paronta, kai zōnta dedoike ta ornea]; The birds fear the eagle, king of the birds, not only when it is alive and present. Finally Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)] calls it πτηνοκράτορα [ptēnokratora], that is, prince of the birds. And Tzetzes, Chiliad. 5, Hist. 9, denies that either eagles or lions touch carrion, since they are kings, the former of birds, the latter of wild beasts. And among the Roman writers, Horace, book 4, Ode 4:


Qualem ministrum fulminis alitem, Cui rex Deorum regnum in aves vagas Permisit, etc.

Like the winged minister of the thunderbolt, to whom the king of the gods granted kingship over the wandering birds, etc.


Martialis libri quinti Epigrammate quinquagesimo sexto,

Martial, book 5, Epigram 56:


Dic mihi quem portes, volucrum regina.

Tell me whom you carry, queen of the birds.


Apulejus asini libro sexto, Primi Iovis regalis avis illa. Clandianus Praefatione in tertium consulatum Honorii,

Apuleius, The Ass, book 6: that royal bird of supreme Jupiter. Claudian, Preface to the Third Consulship of Honorius:


— — volucrumque potens, et fulminis haeres.

— — both mighty over the birds and heir of the thunderbolt.


Aegyptios quoque idem sensisse, docent haec Diodori libro primo: Τὸν δ᾽ ἀε-τὸν Θηβαῖοι τιμῶσι, διὰ τὸ βασιλικὸν εἶναι δοκεῖν τοῦτο ζῶον, καὶ τοῦ Διὸς ἄξιον· Aquilam Thebani colunt, quia regium esse putant hoc animal, et Iove dignum. Unde etiam apud Arabes manaverat aquilae cultus. Talmudici in libro De Idololatria cap. 1. fol. 11. b. בתי ע״ז קבועין אלו הן בית בל בבבל בית נבו בכורסי תרעתא שבמפג צריפא שבאשקלון נשרא שבערביא, Templa idololatrica II, 741 fixa haec sunt, templum Beli Babylone, templum Nebo Borsippae, Atergatis Hierapoli, Uraniae Veneris Ascalone, et Aquilae in Arabia. Fixa templa vocantur, quorum idola coluntur omnibus anni diebus, ut explicatur in Glossa. Quomodo Bel Babylone cultus est, et Nebo Borsippae (nam pro בכורסי lege בבורסיף). Et Hierapoli Derceto, vel Atergatis, quam Hierapoli fuisse cultam, multis docet Lucianus in libro De Syria Dea. Derceto, vel Atergatis, Hebraice est תרעתא Tirgata. Et Hierapolis ממבג Mambeg, ut Arabice منبج Manbeg. In Plinio quoque olim Bambyca et Mambeg, quod mutatum in Magog. Itaque in Talmude pro שבמפג legendum שבממבג. Uraniam porro Venerem Ascalone fuisse in summo cultu, ex Herodoto scimus. Proinde haec videtur esse צריפא שבאשקלון, Tseripha, quae Ascalone est. Quamvis, cur vocetur צריפא Tseripha, non satis constet. Nisi a conflando dictam putes. Hebraeis enim צרף tsaraph est conflare. Unde Talmudicis בית נצרפי, domus conflatilium, id est, idolorum templum. Aut a libidine, cui praeest. Nam Arabice صرف tsarapha est ardere libidine, et صارفة tsaripha dicitur canis foemina, cum catulit et ardet libidine in marem. Superest de Arabum aquila dicamus. Fuit id idolum Dulkelaitarum in Homeritis, populo Arabiae felicis notissimo. Alcamus, النسر الصنم كان لذي الكلا بارض حمير Aquila fuit idolum Dulkelae in terra Humeir, id est, Homeritarum. Nempe etiam apud Arabes invaluerat haec opinio, aquilam esse avium principem. Itaque Muaphius in li-bro, qui inscribitur نفحات الازهار Odores florum, hoc tribuit impuro Mahometi: هبط علي جبرييل فقال يا محمد ان لكل شي سيد فسيد البشر ادم وسيد ولد ادم انت وسيد الروم صحيب وسيد فارس سليمان وسيد col. 164 الحبش بلال وسيد الشجر السدر وسيد الطير النسر Descendit ad me Gabriel, et dixit, O Mahomed, unicuique rei suus est dominus. Dominus hominum fuit Adamus. Tu vero dominus es filiorum Adami. Et Graecorum dominus est Sahib, et Persarum Soliman, et Abissinorum Bilal. Et arborum connarus, loti species, et avium aquila, etc. Iam si libet audire Hebraeos, Iosephus De bello Iudaico libri tertii capite quinto, Romanos in prima legionis cohorte aquilam pro signo ideo habuisse scribit, quia ἀετὸς est βασιλεύς τε οἰωνῶν ἁπάντων, καὶ ἀλκιμώτατος, omnium avium rex, et validissimus. Et Kimchius in Ezech. XVII, 3. הנשר הוא משל לנבוכדנצר מלך בבל כי הנשר מלך העופות וכן נבוכדנצר היה מלך על כל מלכי הארץ, Aquila ibi est typus Nebucadnetsaris, regis Babyloniae, quia, ut aquila rex est avium, ita II, 742 Nebucadnetsar rex fuit omnium terrae regum. Hinc in Masal Kadmoni Fabula tricesima octava hanc habet inscriptionem:

That the Egyptians too held the same view is shown by these words of Diodorus in book 1: Τὸν δ᾽ ἀετὸν Θηβαῖοι τιμῶσι, διὰ τὸ βασιλικὸν εἶναι δοκεῖν τοῦτο ζῶον, καὶ τοῦ Διὸς ἄξιον [Ton d᾽ aeton Thēbaioi timōsi, dia to basilikon einai dokein touto zōon, kai tou Dios axion]· The Thebans worship the eagle, because they think this animal is royal and worthy of Jupiter. From there the cult of the eagle had also spread to the Arabs. The Talmudists, in the treatise On Idolatry, ch. 1, fol. 11b: בתי ע״ז קבועין אלו הן בית בל בבבל בית נבו בכורסי תרעתא שבמפג צריפא שבאשקלון נשרא שבערביא, These are the fixed idolatrous II, 741 temples: the temple of Bel at Babylon, the temple of Nebo at Borsippa, Atergatis at Hierapolis, Venus Urania at Ascalon, and the Eagle in Arabia. Those temples are called fixed whose idols are worshipped on every day of the year, as the Gloss explains. Thus Bel was worshipped at Babylon and Nebo at Borsippa (for instead of בכורסי read בבורסיף). And at Hierapolis Derceto, or Atergatis, whose worship at Hierapolis Lucian describes at length in his book On the Syrian Goddess. Derceto, or Atergatis, is in Hebrew תרעתא Tirgata. And Hierapolis is ממבג Mambeg, as in Arabic منبج [Manbij] Manbeg. In Pliny too the text once read Bambyca and Mambeg, which was altered into Magog. Accordingly in the Talmud one should read שבממבג instead of שבמפג. Further, we know from Herodotus that Venus Urania was held in the highest worship at Ascalon. Hence she seems to be the צריפא שבאשקלון, Tseripha, which is at Ascalon. Why she is called צריפא Tseripha, however, is not quite clear. Unless you think she was named from casting [metal]; for among the Hebrews צרף tsaraph means to cast. Hence the Talmudists' בית נצרפי, house of molten images, that is, a temple of idols. Or from lust, over which she presides. For in Arabic صرف [ṣarafa] tsarapha means to burn with lust, and صارفة [ṣārifa] tsaripha is said of a female dog when she is in heat and burns with lust for the male. It remains for us to speak of the eagle of the Arabs. It was the idol of the Dulkelaites among the Homerites, a very well-known people of Arabia Felix. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: النسر الصنم كان لذي الكلا بارض حمير [al-nasr al-ṣanam kāna li-Dhī al-Kalāʿ bi-arḍ Ḥimyar] The Eagle was the idol of Dulkela in the land of Humeir, that is, of the Homerites. Evidently among the Arabs too this opinion had prevailed, that the eagle is the chief of the birds. So Muaphius, in the book entitled نفحات الازهار [Nafaḥāt al-azhār] Fragrances of Flowers, attributes this to the impure Muhammad: هبط علي جبرييل فقال يا محمد ان لكل شي سيد فسيد البشر ادم وسيد ولد ادم انت وسيد الروم صحيب وسيد فارس سليمان وسيد col. 164 الحبش بلال وسيد الشجر السدر وسيد الطير النسر [habaṭa ʿalayya Jabrīl fa-qāla yā Muḥammad inna li-kull shayʾ sayyid fa-sayyid al-bashar Ādam wa-sayyid walad Ādam anta wa-sayyid al-Rūm Ṣuhayb wa-sayyid Fāris Salmān wa-sayyid al-Ḥabash Bilāl wa-sayyid al-shajar al-sidr wa-sayyid al-ṭayr al-nasr] Gabriel came down to me and said: O Muhammad, every thing has its lord. The lord of men was Adam; but you are the lord of the sons of Adam. And the lord of the Greeks is Sahib, and of the Persians Soliman, and of the Abyssinians Bilal. And of trees the connarus, a species of lotus, and of birds the eagle, etc. Now, if one wishes to hear the Hebrews: Josephus, On the Jewish War, book 3, chapter 5, writes that the Romans had the eagle as the standard in the first cohort of the legion because the ἀετὸς [aetos] is βασιλεύς τε οἰωνῶν ἁπάντων, καὶ ἀλκιμώτατος [basileus te oiōnōn hapantōn, kai alkimōtatos], king of all birds, and the strongest. And Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] on Ezek 17:3: הנשר הוא משל לנבוכדנצר מלך בבל כי הנשר מלך העופות וכן נבוכדנצר היה מלך על כל מלכי הארץ, The eagle there is a figure of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, because, as the eagle is king of the birds, so II, 742 Nebuchadnezzar was king over all the kings of the earth. Hence in the Masal Kadmoni the thirty-eighth Fable bears this title:


צורת הנשר על מושבו : וסנהדרי׳ העוף יושבים סביבו :

צורת הנשר על מושבו : וסנהדרי׳ העוף יושבים סביבו :


Figura aquilae super folium suum, et synhedrium avium, circa illam sedentium. Nempe in avium concilio pingitur aquila, corona insignis, et in solio sublimis, et illi adstant aves reliquae. Et de aquila Baal Hatturim hujus capitis statim initio, הוא מלך העופות, Ea in aves regnum obtinet. Patres denique id ipsum sic definiunt. Ita Ambrosius Hexaëm. lib. 5. cap. 18. aquilam appellat regalem avem, et ei tribuit regale fastigium. Hieronymus in Mich. 1. Aquila, quae regi- na est avium. Et in Dan. VII. Ut leo inter bestias, ita aquila inter aves regnum tenet. Epiphanius in Physiologo capite sexto, Ἔστι γὰρ ὁ ἀετὸς βασιλεὺς τῶν ὀρνέων· Aquila enim est avium rex, aut regina, si mavis. Theodoretus Praefatione in Canticum, de loco Ezech. XVII, 3. Ἀετὸν μὲν τὸν βασιλέα (ἐνόησεν), ἐπειδὰν καὶ τὸ ζῶον βασιλικόν· Aquilae nomine regem intellexit, quia regium est animal. Theodorus Heracleensis in Psal. CII. Ἐπειδὴ ὁ ἀετὸς δοκεῖ βασι-λεύειν τῶν πετεινῶν ἁπάντων· Quia aquila imperare videtur omnibus volucribus Et paullo post, Διὰ γὰρ τοῦ ὄρνιθος τοῦ ἀετοῦ τὴν βασιλείαν αἰνίττεται, Nam per aquilam regnum significat. Quid quod vulgo persuasum fuit, aquilae cum trochilo ideo esse certamen, quia καλεῖται πρέσβυς, καὶ βασιλεὺς, vocatur senator et rex, quasi hoc illi nomen invideat? Ita testatur Philosophus Hist. lib. 9. cap. 11. Unde Plinius lib. 10. cap. 74. Dissident aquilae et trochilus, si credimus, quoniam rex appellatur avium.

The figure of the eagle upon its throne, and the council of birds sitting around it. That is, in the council of the birds the eagle is depicted, distinguished by a crown and raised high on a throne, and the other birds stand by it. And of the eagle Baal Hatturim says, right at the beginning of this chapter, הוא מלך העופות, It holds kingship over the birds. Finally, the Fathers define the very same thing. Thus Ambrose, Hexaëm. book 5, ch. 18, calls the eagle a royal bird and attributes to it royal eminence. Jerome on Mich. 1: The eagle, which is queen of the birds. And on Dan. VII.: As the lion holds kingship among the beasts, so the eagle among the birds. Epiphanius in the Physiologus, chapter 6: Ἔστι γὰρ ὁ ἀετὸς βασιλεὺς τῶν ὀρνέων· [Esti gar ho aetos basileus tōn orneōn] For the eagle is king of the birds, or queen, if you prefer. Theodoret, in the Preface to the Song, on the passage Ezek 17:3: Ἀετὸν μὲν τὸν βασιλέα (ἐνόησεν), ἐπειδὰν καὶ τὸ ζῶον βασιλικόν· [Aeton men ton basilea (enoēsen), epeidan kai to zōon basilikon] By the name of eagle he meant the king, because it is a royal animal. Theodore of Heraclea on Psal. CII.: Ἐπειδὴ ὁ ἀετὸς δοκεῖ βασιλεύειν τῶν πετεινῶν ἁπάντων· [Epeidē ho aetos dokei basileuein tōn peteinōn hapantōn] Because the eagle seems to rule over all the birds. And a little later: Διὰ γὰρ τοῦ ὄρνιθος τοῦ ἀετοῦ τὴν βασιλείαν αἰνίττεται, [Dia gar tou ornithos tou aetou tēn basileian ainittetai] For by the eagle he signifies the kingdom. What of the fact that it was commonly believed that the eagle is at war with the wren because the latter καλεῖται πρέσβυς, καὶ βασιλεὺς [kaleitai presbys, kai basileus], is called senator and king, as though it begrudged it this name? So the Philosopher attests, Hist. book 9, ch. 11. Hence Pliny, book 10, ch. 74: The eagle and the wren are at odds, if we believe it, because the latter is called king of the birds.


Aquila Hebraice נשר neser unde dicatur, magistros latuit hactenus. Absurdum enim est commentum Rabbi Bechai in Gen. II. deduci a Chaldaeo נשר nesar, quod decidere est; quia, cum volatu se sustulit ad elementum ignis, ut quidem volunt, inde praeceps in mare decidit. Nec iis assentior, qui a defluvio pennarum dictam asserunt, quia נשר Rabbinis est defluere. Aut a visu; quia נשר neser videtur alludere ad verbum שור sur, quod videre est. Sed Arabes maxime probo, quibus نسر nasara est rostro vellicare: et منسر minsar, ro- strum, idque proprie rapacis avis. Inde igitur aquilam نسر nesr appellari volunt; لانه ينسر الشي ويقتلعه quia rem rostro carpit et vellicat. Ita Giauhari, et Damir, et Alcamus. Rostro quidem vellicant etiam aliae rapaces aves; tamen rapacium principi, aquilae, id speciali jure tribuitur, col. 165 quia rostro est magis adunco, et eo carpit fortius. Ita in praedam involare commune est omnibus, quod Hebraeis est העיט. Unde עיט ajit est in genere II, 743 avis rapax. Tamen ἀετὸν vel αἰετὸν, inde deflexum, proprium esse aquilae nomen, voluit usus apud Graecos (1).

Whence the eagle, in Hebrew נשר neser, gets its name has so far escaped the masters. For absurd is the fancy of Rabbi Bechai on Gen. II. that it derives from the Chaldee נשר nesar, which means to fall down, because, after it has risen in flight to the element of fire, as they indeed would have it, it then falls headlong into the sea. Nor do I agree with those who assert that it is named from the shedding of its feathers, because נשר among the Rabbis means to fall off; or from sight, because נשר neser seems to allude to the verb שור sur, which means to see. Rather, I most approve of the Arabs, for whom نسر [nasara] nasara means to pluck with the beak, and منسر [minsar] minsar means beak, and properly that of a bird of prey. From this, then, they hold that the eagle is called نسر [nasr] nesr, لانه ينسر الشي ويقتلعه [li-annahu yansiru al-shay wa-yaqtaliʿuhu] because it tears and plucks a thing with its beak. So Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ], Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] and Alcamus. Other birds of prey also pluck with the beak; yet this is ascribed by special right to the prince of the birds of prey, the eagle, col. 165 because its beak is more hooked and it tears more forcefully with it. Likewise, swooping upon prey is common to all, which in Hebrew is העיט. Hence עיט ajit is in general II, 743 a bird of prey. Yet usage among the Greeks made ἀετόν [aeton] or αἰετόν [aieton], derived from it, the proper name of the eagle R1.


Aquila, ut rostro, ita etiam unguibus est insignis, quos non habet rectos, ut homo, sed leonis instar incurvos et aduncos. Animalium enim, quae ungues habent, τὰ μέν εἰσιν εὐθυόνυχα, ὥσπερ ἄνθρωπος· τὰ δὲ γαμψώνυχα, ὥσπερ καὶ τῶν πεζῶν λέων, καὶ τῶν πτηνῶν αἰετὸς, aliae sunt rectis unguibus, ut homo; alia aduncis, ut leo inter pedestria, et aquila in volucribus. Ita Philosophus Hist. lib. 3. cap. 9. Nempe ungues in avibus rostri formam imitantur. Suidas, Γαμψώνυχα ὅσα τῶν ζώων τὴν ἐπιρυγχίδα γεγάμψωκεν ὑπὸ τὴν γέ-νυν, οἷα ἐστὶν ἀετός· Aduncis sunt unguibus quotquot animalium sub malis rostrum habent incurvum, in quo genere est aquila. Grammatici dubitant, ad utrum pertineat, quod aquila, quam Penelope vidit insomnis, vocatur

The eagle is remarkable not only for its beak but also for its talons, which it has not straight, like a man, but curved and hooked like a lion's. For of the animals that have claws, τὰ μέν εἰσιν εὐθυόνυχα, ὥσπερ ἄνθρωπος· τὰ δὲ γαμψώνυχα, ὥσπερ καὶ τῶν πεζῶν λέων, καὶ τῶν πτηνῶν αἰετὸς [ta men eisin euthyonycha, hōsper anthrōpos; ta de gampsōnycha, hōsper kai tōn pezōn leōn, kai tōn ptēnōn aietos], some have straight claws, like man; others hooked, like the lion among land animals and the eagle among birds. So the Philosopher, Hist. book 3, ch. 9. In birds, that is, the talons imitate the shape of the beak. Suidas: Γαμψώνυχα ὅσα τῶν ζώων τὴν ἐπιρυγχίδα γεγάμψωκεν ὑπὸ τὴν γένυν, οἷα ἐστὶν ἀετός· [Gampsōnycha hosa tōn zōōn tēn epirynchida gegampsōken hypo tēn genyn, hoia estin aetos] Those animals have hooked claws which have a beak curved beneath the jaws, to which kind the eagle belongs. The Grammarians are uncertain to which of the two it refers that the eagle which the sleepless Penelope saw is called


— — — μέγας αἰετὸς ἀγκυλοχείλης·

— — — μέγας αἰετὸς ἀγκυλοχείλης· [megas aietos ankylocheilēs]


Aliis enim ἀγκυλοχείλης est ὁ ἔχων ἀγκύλα χείλη, ἤτοι τὸ ῥάμφος, qui labia, II, 744 aut rostrum incurvum habet: aliis ἐπικαμπεῖς τὰς χηλὰς ἔχων, qui ungues habet inflexos. Quo sensu in Aristophanis Equitibus Cleo appellatur

For to some ἀγκυλοχείλης [ankylocheilēs] is ὁ ἔχων ἀγκύλα χείλη, ἤτοι τὸ ῥάμφος [ho echōn ankyla cheilē, ētoi to rhamphos], one that has curved lips, II, 744 that is, a curved beak; to others ἐπικαμπεῖς τὰς χηλὰς ἔχων [epikampeis tas chēlas echōn], one that has bent talons. In this sense, in Aristophanes' Knights, Cleon is called


— — βυρσαίετος ἀγκυλοχείλης,

— — βυρσαίετος ἀγκυλοχείλης, [byrsaietos ankylocheilēs]


quia instar aquilae aduncos seu rapaces habebat ungues, ut interpretatur non solum Scholiastes, sed et ipse Aristophanes. Et in Plauti Pseudolo coquus dicit,

because like an eagle he had hooked or rapacious claws, as not only the Scholiast but also Aristophanes himself explains. And in Plautus' Pseudolus the cook says,


An invenire postulas quemquam coquum,
Nisi milvinis, aut aquilinis ungulis?

Do you expect to find any cook
who has not a kite's or an eagle's talons?


Sed et Ezech. XVII, 3. 7. unguium ratione aquilam dici מלא הנוצה et רב הנוצה, credidere multi veterum. Id enim a Graecis redditur ὁ ἀετὸς πλήρης ὀνύχων, aquila plena unguibus, et πολὺς ὄνυξι, multa unguibus, seu quae multos habet ungues. Quod ipsum sequitur Arabs. Nec multo aliter Syrus versu tertio, ܡܠܝܢ ܛܦܪ̈ܘܗܝ, pleni ungues ejus, et versu septimo, ܣܓܝܐܢ ܛܦܪܘܗܝ multi ungues ejus. Illis nempe נוצה est unguis. Sed Chaldaeus, Hieronymus et Hebraei omnes rectius pennam aut plumam explicant. Adeoque ipsi Graeci Levit. I, 16. pro בנצתא habent σὺν τοῖς πτεροῖς, et Theodotion σὺν τοῖς πτίλοις. Nempe נצה est volare, unde נצו volarunt, vel avolarunt, Thren. IV, 15. et נוצה penna, vel pluma, quae aves ad volatum attollit. Quod huic loco convenit magis. Nam quid sit aquila, plena unguibus, aut multis unguibus, nullus capio, cum aquilis omnibus sit idem unguium numerus. Sed aquila recte dicitur plena esse plumis, aut multas habere plumas, ut glabrae opponatur (2), de qua Mich. I, 16. Dilata calvitium tuum ut aquila. Nempe in ingressu veris rapaces aves plumarum defluvio sunt obnoxiae. Quod nos muer dicimus, id est, mutare pennas. Ita enim loquuntur, qui de hoc argumento scribunt. Et id ipsum est μουτεύειν apud Graecos recentioris aevi. Demetrius Ὀρνεοσοφίου libro secundo capite quinquagesimo tertio, Ἐὰν δὲ βραδύνῃ εἰς τὸ μουτεῦσαι. Quamvis propriae voces non desint, ut μαδίζεσθαι, πτεροῤῥυῆσαι, et ἀποβάλλειν τὰ πτερὰ, quibus utitur idem scriptor. Arabice كرز curiza dixeris. Alcamus, كرز البازي سقط ريشه curiza albazi, seu accipiter, decidit plu- ma ejus. Unde كرز corraz, accipiter, vel quaecunque avis rapax, cui pen- nae defluunt. Itaque in Michaea calvitium aquilae est illud tempus, quo pleraeque ejus pennae exciderunt. Quamvis enim calvitium proprie homini tribuatur, col. 166 II, 745 tamen etiam aves calvae dicuntur. Plinius libri undecimi capite trigesimo septimo: Quaedam animalium naturaliter calvent, sicut struthiocameli et corvi aquatici, quibus apud Graecos nomen est inde, id est, οἱ φαλακροκόρακες. Itaque tam Graeci, quam Hebraei calvitium avibus tribuunt. Ita, ut hoc solo differant, quod cum avium calvitium juxta Graecos pertineat ad solum caput, id Hebraei extendunt ad totum corpus: et avis calva illis dicitur, quae glabra et deplumis est (3).

But many of the ancients also believed that in Ezek 17:3 7. the eagle is called מלא הנוצה and רב הנוצה on account of its talons. For this is rendered by the Greeks ὁ ἀετὸς πλήρης ὀνύχων [ho aetos plērēs onychōn], the eagle full of talons, and πολὺς ὄνυξι [polys onyxi], great in talons, or having many talons. The Arabic follows the same. Nor does the Syriac differ much in verse 3, ܡܠܝܢ ܛܦܪ̈ܘܗܝ [מלין טפרוהי], its talons are full, and in verse 7, ܣܓܝܐܢ ܛܦܪܘܗܝ [סגיאן טפרוהי] its talons are many. For them, that is, נוצה is talon. But the Chaldee, Jerome and all the Hebrews more correctly explain it as feather or plumage. Indeed the Greeks themselves in Lev 1:16 have σὺν τοῖς πτεροῖς [syn tois pterois] for בנצתא, and Theodotion σὺν τοῖς πτίλοις [syn tois ptilois]. For נצה means to fly, whence נצו they flew, or flew away, Lam 4:15, and נוצה feather or plumage, which lifts birds up to flight. This suits this passage better. For I, at least, cannot understand what an eagle full of talons, or with many talons, would be, since all eagles have the same number of talons. But an eagle is rightly said to be full of feathers, or to have many feathers, in contrast to the bald one R2, of which Mic 1:16 speaks: Enlarge thy baldness as the eagle. For at the onset of spring birds of prey are subject to the shedding of their feathers. This we call muer, that is, to change feathers. For so those speak who write on this subject. And this is precisely μουτεύειν [mouteuein] among the Greeks of a later age. Demetrius, Orneosophion, book 2, chapter 53: Ἐὰν δὲ βραδύνῃ εἰς τὸ μουτεῦσαι [Ean de bradynē eis to mouteusai]. Though proper words are not lacking, such as μαδίζεσθαι [madizesthai], πτεροῤῥυῆσαι [pterorrhyēsai], and ἀποβάλλειν τὰ πτερὰ [apoballein ta ptera], which the same writer uses. In Arabic you would say كرز [kariza] curiza. Alcamus: كرز البازي سقط ريشه [kariza al-bāzī saqaṭa rīshuhu] curiza albazi, that is, of the hawk, its plumage fell out. Whence كرز [kurraz] corraz, a hawk, or any bird of prey whose feathers are falling out. Thus in Micah the baldness of the eagle is the time when most of its feathers have dropped out. For although baldness is properly attributed to man, col. 166 II, 745 birds too are called bald. Pliny, book 11, chapter 37: Some animals are naturally bald, such as ostriches and water ravens, which among the Greeks take their name from this, that is, οἱ φαλακροκόρακες [hoi phalakrokorakes]. Thus both the Greeks and the Hebrews attribute baldness to birds, differing only in this, that whereas among the Greeks the baldness of birds concerns the head alone, the Hebrews extend it to the whole body; and they call a bird bald which is smooth and stripped of feathers R3.


At cum in locum pennarum, quae decidêre, aliae subinde succreverunt, tum demum aquila (Hebraice נשר) dicitur מלא הנוצה, plena plumis, et רב נוצה, plumis scatens. Et pennas in aquilis renasci, insinuat Scriptura non uno in loco. Sic in celebri loco Davidis Psal. CIII, 5. תתחדש כנשר נעוריכי, Renovabis ut aquila juventutem tuam. Ita malo cum Chaldaeo reddere quam cum aliis, Renovabitur ut aquilae juventus tua. Quia verbum תתחדש tertiae personae, cum sit Singulare et Foemininum, neque genere, neque numero convenit cum נעוריכי, quod Plurale et Masculinum est. Utut sit, in aquila juventus non aliter renovatur, quam cum vteribus pennis novae succedunt. Quomodo serpens senectam exuere dicitur, cum veterem pellem deponit. Unde est, quod serpentis exuvias Graeci γήρας, Romani senium et senectutem appellant. Itaque verba Psaltis eodem pertinent, quo haec Esaiae capitis quadragesimi versu 31. Sperantibus in Dominum instaurabuntur vires. Ascendent (succrescent) pennae sicut aquilarum. Ubi Septuaginta eleganter Πτεροφυήσουσιν ὡς ἀετοί. Sed mira metamorphosi aquilas Syrus in columbas transmutavit hac sua versione, ܢܦܩܘܢ ܓܦܐ ܐܝܟ ܕܝܘܢܐ, Alas emittent, similes columbinis. Nec minore errore ex aquilis facti leones in his Theodotionis de rege Nebucadnetsare Dan. IV, 30. al. 33. Αἱ τρίχες αὐτοῦ ὡς λεόντων ἐμεγαλύνθησαν. Pili ipsius ut leonum creverunt. Nam in fonte est כנשרין, ut aquilarum. Sed scribarum est error, non interpretis. Haud dubie enim interpres ἀετῶν scripserat, quod in λεόντων ideo mutarunt scribae imperiti, quia αἱ τρίχες, id est pili, non videbantur aquilis posse convenire. Itaque aquilis substituerunt pilosi animalis nomen. futili tamen scrupulo. Quippe in Prophetae verbis suppleri potuit vox analoga, Pili ipsius creverunt, ut aquilarum, supple plumae, quae id sunt in avibus, quod in hominibus II, 746 pili. Praeterea quandoque etiam avibus pili et capilli tribuuntur. Qua κα-ταχρήσει Oppianus libro tertio Cynegeticῶν dicit de gallina, quae accipitrem videt, pullis suis inhiantem,

But when others have gradually grown in place of the feathers that fell out, then at last the eagle (in Hebrew נשר) is called מלא הנוצה, full of plumage, and רב נוצה, teeming with plumage. And Scripture indicates in more than one place that feathers grow again in eagles. So in the famous passage of David, Psal. CIII, 5. תתחדש כנשר נעוריכי, You will renew your youth like the eagle. I prefer to render it so with the Chaldee rather than with others, Your youth will be renewed like the eagle's, because the verb תתחדש, of the third person, since it is singular and feminine, agrees neither in gender nor in number with נעוריכי, which is plural and masculine. However that may be, youth is renewed in the eagle in no other way than when new feathers succeed the old, just as a serpent is said to shed its old age when it lays aside its old skin. Hence the Greeks call the slough of a serpent γήρας [gēras], the Romans senium [old age] and senectus [old age]. Thus the words of the Psalmist have the same sense as these of Isaiah, chapter 40, verse 31: Those who hope in the Lord shall renew their strength. They shall mount up (grow) feathers like eagles. Where the Seventy elegantly have Πτεροφυήσουσιν ὡς ἀετοί [Pterophyēsousin hōs aetoi]. But by a strange metamorphosis the Syriac has transformed the eagles into doves in this version of his, ܢܦܩܘܢ ܓܦܐ ܐܝܟ ܕܝܘܢܐ [נפקון גפא איך דיונא], They will put forth wings like those of doves. And by no smaller error eagles have been made lions in these words of Theodotion about king Nebuchadnezzar, Dan 4:30 var. 33. Αἱ τρίχες αὐτοῦ ὡς λεόντων ἐμεγαλύνθησαν [Hai triches autou hōs leontōn emegalynthēsan]. His hairs grew like those of lions. For in the original it is כנשרין, like those of eagles. But this is an error of the scribes, not of the translator. For no doubt the translator had written ἀετῶν [aetōn], which ignorant scribes changed to λεόντων [leontōn] because αἱ τρίχες [hai triches], that is hairs, did not seem able to fit eagles. So they substituted for eagles the name of a hairy animal, but from a pointless scruple. For in the Prophet's words an analogous word could be supplied: His hairs grew like those of eagles, supply feathers, which are in birds what II, 746 hairs are in men. Moreover, hairs and locks are sometimes attributed even to birds. By this catachresis Oppian, in book 3 of the Cynegetica, says of the hen that sees a hawk gaping after her chicks,


— — — ἑαῖς ἔφριξεν ἐθείραις,

— — — ἑαῖς ἔφριξεν ἐθείραις [heais ephrixen etheirais],


suis inhorruit pilis. Et Matron in Parodiis apud Athenaeum libro decimo quarto gallinas describit, in convivio oblatas,

bristled with its hair. And Matron, in the Parodies quoted by Athenaeus in book 14, describes hens served at a banquet,


Ἄτριχας, οἰετέας, λαγάνοις κατὰ νῶτον ἐΐσας,

Ἄτριχας, οἰετέας, λαγάνοις κατὰ νῶτον ἐΐσας, [Atrichas, oieteas, laganois kata nōton eïsas,]


Depiles, aetate pares, dorso laganis similes. Depiles, id est, deplumes. Neque opus ὄτριχας cum Casaubono restituere, quia sic legitur in Homeri versu, ad quem alludit, Iliad. β΄. versu 765. Nam in hoc ipso sita est παρῳδία, quod vox similis non eadem reponitur. Quod palam faciunt multa exempla. Itaque, ut gallinarum plumae pili vocantur, ita etiam aquilarum. Unde Tertullianus in libro De Poenitentia pene extremo, ubi de rege Nabuchodonozore: Capilli incuria horrorem aquilinum praeferente. Pro quo Pamelius rescripsit leoninum, quasi aquilam pilis horrere dici non possit. Quod refellunt quae jam docuimus, etiam avium plumas pilorum nomine censeri. Et vero cum aquilas calvescere dicat Michaeas (cap. 1. vers. 16.) quidni pilos eis tribuere potuerit Propheta Daniel? Eadem certe utrobique est κατάχρησις. Proprie enim calvitium est capillorum col. 167 defluvium. Interim recens non est loci Danielis corruptio, cum praeter Arabem interpretem illam sequantur Theodoretus in Danielem, et auctor Quaestionum, quae Iustino tribuuntur, Quaestione 44. et qui Prophetarum vitas scripserunt sub Epiphanii et Dorothei nominibus, qui, quamvis spurii scriptores et ψευδώνυμοι, sunt tamen satis vetusti. Iam, si conferas tria haec loca, primum Psaltis, renovabis ut aquila juventutem tuam; secundum Esaiae, Sperantibus in Dominum instaurabuntur vires, succrescent pennae sicut aquilis; tertium Danielis, Pili ipsius ut aquilarum creverunt (4): videbis, in omnibus agi de aquilarum plumis, quae post ψίλωσιν redintegrantur. Unde fit, ut aquila vegetior, adeoque etiam junior esse videatur. Neque his absurde jungatur Iobi locus de accipitre capitis trigesimi noni versu 26. Nunquid ex intelligentia tua יאבר נץ, plumescet accipiter, alis ad austrum expansis? Nempe, ut in illa ψιλώσει solis blando calore refocilletur, et novae plumae in deperditarum locum facilius renascantur.

Hairless, equal in age, like flat cakes on the back. Hairless, that is, featherless. Nor is there any need to restore ὄτριχας [otrichas] with Casaubon, because that is the reading in the verse of Homer to which he alludes, Iliad 2, line 765. For the parody [παρῳδία, parōdia] consists precisely in this, that a similar word, not the same one, is substituted. Many examples make this plain. So, just as the feathers of hens are called hairs, so too are those of eagles. Hence Tertullian, near the end of his book On Penitence, speaking of King Nebuchadnezzar: his hair, through neglect, displaying an eagle-like shagginess. For this Pamelius substituted leoninum [lion-like], as if an eagle could not be said to bristle with hair. This is refuted by what we have already shown, that the feathers of birds too are reckoned under the name of hairs. And indeed, since Micah (ch. 1, v. 16) says that eagles grow bald, why could not the Prophet Daniel have attributed hairs to them? Certainly the same catachresis [κατάχρησις, katachrēsis] occurs in both places. For baldness is properly the falling out of the hair of the head. col. 167 Meanwhile the corruption of the passage of Daniel is not recent, since besides the Arabic translator it is followed by Theodoret on Daniel, by the author of the Questions attributed to Justin, Question 44, and by those who wrote the Lives of the Prophets under the names of Epiphanius and Dorotheus, who, though spurious and pseudonymous [ψευδώνυμοι, pseudōnymoi] writers, are nevertheless fairly ancient. Now, if you compare these three passages, first that of the Psalmist, you will renew your youth like the eagle; second that of Isaiah, For those who hope in the Lord their strength will be restored, their wings will grow again like eagles'; third that of Daniel, His hairs grew like those of eagles R4: you will see that all of them concern the feathers of eagles, which are restored after moulting [ψίλωσιν, psilōsin]. Hence the eagle comes to seem more vigorous, and so even younger. Nor would it be absurd to join to these the passage of Job about the hawk, chapter 39, verse 26: Is it by your understanding that יאבר נץ, the hawk grows its feathers, spreading its wings toward the south? That is, so that during that moulting [ψιλώσει, psilōsei] it may be revived by the gentle warmth of the sun, and new feathers may more easily grow back in place of those it has lost.


II, 747 Ad haec cum non satis attenderent multi veteres, de aquilarum ἀνακαι-νώσει et ἀνανεώσει multa commenti sunt, quae piget hic referre (5). Notum est Saadiae commentum apud Kimchium in Psal. CIII. et Es. XL. הנשר יעוף על כל העופות ויעלה מאד על פני רקיע השמים ויקרוב לחום האש היסודי ויפול עצמו בים מרוב חום ויתחדש ויעלה אבר וישוב לימי עלומיו כן כל עשר עד מאה וכשיגיע למאה יעלה כמנהגו ויפול בים וימות שם, Aquila volat sublimius quam ulla avium, et firmamentum versus multum effertur, donec ad ignem elementarem accesserit. Tum vero calore aestuans in mare se dat praecipitem, et renovatur, et plumae ejus renascuntur, et redit ad dies juventutis suae: atque id fit singulis decenniis usque ad annum centesimum, quem ubi attigit, illa de more sursum effertur, et in mare praeceps decidit, et ibi moritur. Quale est, quod legitur in Porta coeli fol. 22. col. 2. ויש אומרים כי הנשר טבעו לעלות קרוב לגבול האש ומתלהב בסוף עשר שנים לעשר שנים ומרוב חמומו מפיל עצמו בים לקרר חומו ושם ימרט נוצתו ויתחדש נוצה אחרת ויתחדש כחו עד ק׳ שנה שיעלה שם ויפול בים ויטבע, Sunt, qui aquilae naturale esse dicunt, ut prope terminum ignis ascendat, et incendatur singulis decenniis, et calore aestuans in mare se dejiciat, ut aestum illum refrigeret, et ibi defluere pennas ejus, et alias succrescere, et vires ejus confirmari usque ad annum centesimum, quo eodem subvecta cadit praeceps, et in mare demergitur. Alii non in mare, sed in fontem immergi dicunt, in quo abluta juvenescat. Damir, ubi de العقاب alokab, id est, περὶ τοῦ μελαναιέτου, quod est aquilae genus, in Arabia felici maxime frequens, متي ثقلت عن النهوض او عميت حملتها الفراخ ونقلتها من مكان الي مكان تلتمس لها عينا صافيتا بارض الهند علي راس جبل فيتغمسها فيها ثم تضعها في شعاع الشمس فيذهب ريشها وينبت لها ريش جديد ويذهب ظلمة بصرها ثم تعوص في تلك العين col. 168 فاذا هي قد عادت شابة Et cum volatu tarda fit et excaecatur, ferunt eam pulli, et e loco in locum transferunt, et in India fontem purum ei quaerunt in vertice montis, in quem demersam radiis solis opponunt. Tum defluunt ejus pennae, et novae illi succrescunt, et oculorum caligo dissipatur: atque eidem II, 748 fonti rursus immergitur, cum rediit canities ejus. Auctor Epistolae ad Praesidium, quae Hieronymo tribuitur: Aquila cum senuerit, gravantur ipsius pennae et oculi, quaeritque fontem, et erigit pennas, et colligit in se calorem, et sic oculi ejus sanantur, et in fontem se ter mergit, et ita ad juventutem redit. Eustathius in Hexaëmeron pag. 27. Φασὶ γηράσαντα τὸν ἀετὸν ἀμαυροῦσθαι τὰς ὄψεις, καὶ βαρεῖσθαι αὐτοῦ τὰς πτέρυγας, καὶ εἰς πηγὴν ἀφικνεῖσθαι, καὶ εἰς τὸν αἰθέρα ἀνιπτάμενον, ὑπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου τὰς πτέρυγας καταφλέγεσθαι, καὶ ἀναβλέπειν· εἶθ᾽ εὐθὺς ἐπὶ τὴν πηγὴν καταβάντα τρίτον βαπτίζεσθαι, καὶ ἀνανεοῦσθαι. Διὸ καὶ τὸν Ψαλμὸν φάσκειν φησὶν, Ἀνακαινισθήσεται ὡς ἀετοῦ ἡ νεότης σου. Ferunt, aquilam, senio confectam, oculorum acie obtundi, alasque ejus ingravescere, et ad fontem contendere, et dum in aëre volatu effertur, alas à sole exuri, et visum recuperare: deinde cum descendit in fontem, in eo ter immergi et renovari. Ac proinde Psalmum dixisse, „Renovabitur sicut aquilae juventus tua“. Anonymus in Psalmos, Ὁ ἀετὸς κατὰ φ´ ἔτη ἀνακαινίζεται. καιόμε-νος ὑπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου, καὶ καταδυόμενος εἰς πηγὴν ὕδατος, πάλιν νέος εὑρίσκεται. Aquila quingentesimo quoque anno renovatur. Adusta a sole, et mersa in fontem aquae, juvenis iterum reperitur. Sunt, qui pro φ´, hoc est, quingentesimo, ϱ´, hoc est, centesimum rescribunt, ut huic scriptori cum Epiphanio conveniat, cujus verba sunt: Ἀετὸς δὲ καλεῖται διὰ τὴν πολυετίαν αὐτοῦ. οὗτος μὲν ζῇ ἔτη ἑκατὸν, καὶ γηράσαντος γρυποῦται ὁ προμυκτὴρ, καὶ ἀμβλυώττουσιν οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ αὐτοῦ, τοῦ μὴ ὁρᾷν, καὶ οὐκ ἰσχύει φαγεῖν. ἀνέρχεται δὲ εἰς ὕψος λίαν, καὶ ῥίπτει ἑαυτὸν ἐπὶ ἀκροτόμου πέτρας, προσκρούσας αὐτῇ τὸ ῥάμφος, καὶ λούεται ἐπὶ τὴν ψυγρὰν λίμνην, καὶ κάθηται κατὰ τὸ ἡλιακὸν θερμὸν, πίπτουσι δὲ λεπίδες ἀπὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν, καὶ πάλιν εἰς νέους τελεῖν ἄρχεται. Aquila vocatur ἀετὸς propter longaevitatem. Vivit enim annos centum. Cum vero senescit, rostrum ei incurvatur, caligantque oculi, ita, ut nec videre, nec comedere possit. Igitur in altum se attollit, et in praeruptam se projicit rupem, ad quam rostrum allidit, et frigido lacu se abluit, et ad calorem solis residet, caduntque ex oculis squamae, atque iterum juvenescit. Augustinus quoque in Psalmum 102. aquilae senescentis rostrum superius ita crescere scribit, ut claudatur edendi aditus. Quod ipsum Aristoteles a), Plinius b) et Horus Apollo c) diserte docent. Sed cum rostro sic accrescente fame interire iidem addant, illam asserit Augustinus, rostro ad petram attrito, vires collapsas esu reparare. Quod tamen ne quis putet ab eo pro certo tradi, en tibi viri Sancti verba in Psalmum LXVI. Renovabitur juventus nostra sicut aquila, tantummodò nos vetustatem nostram ad petram conteramus. Sive illa vera sunt, etc. quae dicuntur de aquila, II, 749 sive sit fama potius hominum, quam veritas: veritas est tamen in Scripturis, et non sine causa hoc dixerunt Scripturae. Nos quidquid illud significat faciamus, et quam sit verum, non laboremus. Quin cum vel falsa, vel incerta sint, quae de aquilae ἀνανεώσει tradunt scriptores, quos citavimus, id solum amplectamur, quod pro vero et certo omnes agnoscunt, nempe aquilam stato tempore, veteribus plumis abjectis, alias subinde resumere, atque hoc modo renovari. Unde verus Hieronymus in Esaiam capite 40. Crebro diximus, aquilarum senectutem revirescere mutatione pennarum. Et Euthymius in Psalmum CII. Depones debi- lem senectam, quam morbi et peccata contraxerant, ὡς ἐκεῖνος τὸ γῆρας τῶν ἑαυ- col. 169 τοῦ πτερῶν, sicut illa senectam pennarum. Renovaberis per poenitentiam, ὡς ἐκεῖνος διὰ τῆς παλιφυΐας πτερῶν, sicut illa per pennarum repullulationem.

II, 747 Because many ancient writers did not pay sufficient attention to these points, they invented a great deal about the ἀνακαίνωσις [anakainōsis] and ἀνανέωσις [ananeōsis] of eagles, which it is tedious to report here R5. Well known is the fiction of Saadia, cited by Kimchi on Psal. CIII. and Es. XL.: הנשר יעוף על כל העופות ויעלה מאד על פני רקיע השמים ויקרוב לחום האש היסודי ויפול עצמו בים מרוב חום ויתחדש ויעלה אבר וישוב לימי עלומיו כן כל עשר עד מאה וכשיגיע למאה יעלה כמנהגו ויפול בים וימות שם, The eagle flies higher than any of the birds and is carried far up towards the firmament, until it comes near the elemental fire. Then, burning with the heat, it throws itself headlong into the sea, and is renewed; its feathers grow again, and it returns to the days of its youth. And this happens every ten years up to the hundredth year; when it has reached that, it is carried upward as usual, falls headlong into the sea, and dies there. Similar is what we read in Porta coeli fol. 22, col. 2: ויש אומרים כי הנשר טבעו לעלות קרוב לגבול האש ומתלהב בסוף עשר שנים לעשר שנים ומרוב חמומו מפיל עצמו בים לקרר חומו ושם ימרט נוצתו ויתחדש נוצה אחרת ויתחדש כחו עד ק׳ שנה שיעלה שם ויפול בים ויטבע, There are some who say that it is natural to the eagle to ascend close to the boundary of fire and to be set ablaze every ten years, and, burning with the heat, to cast itself into the sea to cool that heat; and that there its feathers fall out and others grow in their place, and its strength is restored, up to the hundredth year, when, carried up to the same place, it falls headlong and is drowned in the sea. Others say it is plunged not into the sea but into a spring, and, washed in it, grows young again. Damir, on العقاب [al-ʿuqāb] alokab, that is, περὶ τοῦ μελαναιέτου [peri tou melanaietou] [on the black eagle], which is a kind of eagle especially common in Arabia Felix: متي ثقلت عن النهوض او عميت حملتها الفراخ ونقلتها من مكان الي مكان تلتمس لها عينا صافيتا بارض الهند علي راس جبل فيتغمسها فيها ثم تضعها في شعاع الشمس فيذهب ريشها وينبت لها ريش جديد ويذهب ظلمة بصرها ثم تعوص في تلك العين [matā thaqulat ʿan al-nuhūḍ aw ʿamiyat ḥamalathā al-firākh wa-naqalathā min makān ilā makān taltamisu lahā ʿaynan ṣāfiyatan bi-arḍ al-Hind ʿalā raʾs jabal fa-yataghammasuhā fīhā thumma taḍaʿuhā fī shuʿāʿ al-shams fa-yadhhabu rīshuhā wa-yanbutu lahā rīsh jadīd wa-yadhhabu ẓulmat baṣarihā thumma taʿūṣu fī tilka al-ʿayn] col. 168 فاذا هي قد عادت شابة [fa-idhā hiya qad ʿādat shābba] And when it becomes slow in flight and goes blind, its chicks carry it and move it from place to place, and in India they seek for it a pure spring on the summit of a mountain; they plunge it into this and set it facing the rays of the sun. Then its feathers fall out and new ones grow for it, and the dimness of its eyes is dispelled; and it is plunged II, 748 again into the same spring, when its grey age has returned. The author of the Letter to Praesidius, which is attributed to Jerome: When the eagle has grown old, its feathers and eyes become heavy; it seeks a spring, raises its feathers, and gathers heat into itself, and so its eyes are healed; and it plunges itself three times into the spring, and thus returns to youth. Eustathius, on the Hexaëmeron, p. 27: Φασὶ γηράσαντα τὸν ἀετὸν ἀμαυροῦσθαι τὰς ὄψεις, καὶ βαρεῖσθαι αὐτοῦ τὰς πτέρυγας, καὶ εἰς πηγὴν ἀφικνεῖσθαι, καὶ εἰς τὸν αἰθέρα ἀνιπτάμενον, ὑπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου τὰς πτέρυγας καταφλέγεσθαι, καὶ ἀναβλέπειν· εἶθ᾽ εὐθὺς ἐπὶ τὴν πηγὴν καταβάντα τρίτον βαπτίζεσθαι, καὶ ἀνανεοῦσθαι. Διὸ καὶ τὸν Ψαλμὸν φάσκειν φησὶν, Ἀνακαινισθήσεται ὡς ἀετοῦ ἡ νεότης σου. [Phasi gērasanta ton aeton amaurousthai tas opseis, kai bareisthai autou tas pterygas, kai eis pēgēn aphikneisthai, kai eis ton aithera aniptamenon, hypo tou hēliou tas pterygas kataphlegesthai, kai anablepein; eith᾽ euthys epi tēn pēgēn katabanta triton baptizesthai, kai ananeousthai. Dio kai ton Psalmon phaskein phēsin, Anakainisthēsetai hōs aetou hē neotēs sou.] They say that the eagle, worn out by old age, has the sharpness of its eyes dulled and its wings grow heavy, and it makes for a spring; and while it is carried up in flight into the air, its wings are scorched by the sun and it recovers its sight; then, when it comes down into the spring, it is plunged into it three times and renewed. And therefore the Psalm said, „Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's“. An Anonymous writer on the Psalms: Ὁ ἀετὸς κατὰ φ´ ἔτη ἀνακαινίζεται. καιόμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου, καὶ καταδυόμενος εἰς πηγὴν ὕδατος, πάλιν νέος εὑρίσκεται. [Ho aetos kata ph´ etē anakainizetai. kaiomenos hypo tou hēliou, kai katadyomenos eis pēgēn hydatos, palin neos heurisketai.] The eagle is renewed every five hundredth year. Scorched by the sun and plunged into a spring of water, it is found young again. Some write ϱ´ [r´], that is, hundredth, instead of φ´ [ph´], that is, five hundredth, so that this writer may agree with Epiphanius, whose words are: Ἀετὸς δὲ καλεῖται διὰ τὴν πολυετίαν αὐτοῦ. οὗτος μὲν ζῇ ἔτη ἑκατὸν, καὶ γηράσαντος γρυποῦται ὁ προμυκτὴρ, καὶ ἀμβλυώττουσιν οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ αὐτοῦ, τοῦ μὴ ὁρᾷν, καὶ οὐκ ἰσχύει φαγεῖν. ἀνέρχεται δὲ εἰς ὕψος λίαν, καὶ ῥίπτει ἑαυτὸν ἐπὶ ἀκροτόμου πέτρας, προσκρούσας αὐτῇ τὸ ῥάμφος, καὶ λούεται ἐπὶ τὴν ψυγρὰν λίμνην, καὶ κάθηται κατὰ τὸ ἡλιακὸν θερμὸν, πίπτουσι δὲ λεπίδες ἀπὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν, καὶ πάλιν εἰς νέους τελεῖν ἄρχεται. [Aetos de kaleitai dia tēn polyetian autou. houtos men zē etē hekaton, kai gērasantos gryproutai ho promyktēr, kai amblyōttousin hoi ophthalmoi autou, tou mē horan, kai ouk ischyei phagein. anerchetai de eis hypsos lian, kai rhiptei heauton epi akrotomou petras, proskrousas autē to rhamphos, kai louetai epi tēn psygran limnēn, kai kathētai kata to hēliakon thermon, piptousi de lepides apo tōn ophthalmōn, kai palin eis neous telein archetai.] The eagle is called ἀετὸς [aetos] on account of its long life. For it lives a hundred years. But when it grows old, its beak becomes hooked and its eyes grow dim, so that it can neither see nor eat. So it rises on high and hurls itself against a sheer rock, against which it strikes its beak; and it washes itself in a cold lake and sits in the heat of the sun; and scales fall from its eyes, and it grows young again. Augustine too, on Psalm 102, writes that the upper beak of an ageing eagle grows so much that the passage for eating is closed. This very thing Aristotle a), Pliny b) and Horapollo c) expressly teach. But whereas they add that with its beak growing in this way it dies of hunger, Augustine asserts that, having worn down its beak against a rock, it restores its failing strength by eating. Yet lest anyone think this is handed down by him as certain, here are the holy man's words on Psalm LXVI.: Our youth shall be renewed like the eagle, provided only that we wear down our old age against the rock. Whether those things are true, etc., which are said about the eagle, II, 749 or whether it is rather a report of men than the truth, yet the truth is in the Scriptures, and not without reason have the Scriptures said this. Let us do whatever it signifies, and not trouble ourselves how true it is. Indeed, since the things that the writers we have cited relate about the ἀνανέωσις [ananeōsis] of the eagle are either false or uncertain, let us embrace only what all acknowledge as true and certain: namely, that the eagle at a fixed time casts off its old feathers and then takes on others, and is renewed in this way. Hence the genuine Jerome, on Isaiah chapter 40: We have often said that the old age of eagles grows young again by the changing of their feathers. And Euthymius on Psalm CII.: You will lay aside the feeble old age which diseases and sins had brought on, ὡς ἐκεῖνος τὸ γῆρας τῶν ἑαυτοῦ πτερῶν [hōs ekeinos to gēras tōn heautou pterōn], col. 169 as it does the old age of its feathers. You will be renewed through repentance, ὡς ἐκεῖνος διὰ τῆς παλιφυΐας πτερῶν [hōs ekeinos dia tēs paliphyias pterōn], as it is through the regrowth of its feathers.


In aquilarum generibus multis a colore nomen est. Ita πύγαργος d) dicitur ab albicante cauda, a fusco colore μορφνὸς, a nigro μελαναίετος, ab alarum notis περκνόπτερος, et χρυσαίετος, quae et ἀστερίας, ab aureo fulgore, et maculis aspersis stellarum instar. Ad quam refero haec Ezech. XVII, 3. Aqui- la grandis, magnis alis, longis pennis, plena pluma, in qua רקמה rekama, id est, Phrygium opus. Nam aquilam illam ἀστερίαν, sive stellarem, aquilarum esse maximam, haec Aeliani nos docent Hist. lib. 2. cap. 39. Ἀκούω δέ τι καὶ γένος ἀετῶν, καὶ ὄνομα αὐτῶν χρυσαίετον ἔθεντο· ἄλλοι δὲ ἀστερίαν τὸν αὐτὸν κα-λοῦσιν· ὁρᾶται δὲ οὐ πολλάκις, etc. μέγιστος δὲ ἀετῶν εἶναι πεπίστευται. Audio, etiam aliquod aquilarum genus esse, quam alii Chrysaeton, alii Asteriam, aut stellarem appellant. Non saepe apparet, etc. Maxima autem aquilarum esse cre- ditur (6). Sed aquilae genus sanguinea cauda nullum novi, qualem his verbis describit Syrus interpres Apoc. VIII, 13. Et vidi, et audivi aquilam unam, volan- tem in medio, ܕܢܫܪܐ ܕܕܡܐ ܐܝܬ ܠܗ, cui sanguinea erat cauda. Itaque hic haereret calculus, nisi paterent fontes erroris. Graece est μεσουρανή-ματι, hoc est, in medio coelo. Id interpres accepit, quasi legisset ἐν μέσῳ οὐρὰν αἵματι, supple βεβαμμένην ἔχοντος, aquilam in medio caudam sanguine, supple tinctam habentem, quo nihil fingi potuit ineptius. Vide in hunc locum Notas Edvvardi Pocockii, viri, in his literis longe doctissimi.

Among the kinds of eagles, many take their name from their colour. Thus the πύγαργος [pygargos] d) is so called from its whitish tail, the μορφνὸς [morphnos] from its dusky colour, the μελαναίετος [melanaietos] from its black colour, the περκνόπτερος [perknopteros] from the markings of its wings, and the χρυσαίετος [chrysaietos], also called ἀστερίας [asterias], from its golden gleam and from the spots sprinkled over it like stars. To this last I refer these words of Ezek 17:3: A great eagle, with great wings, long pinions, full of plumage, in which was רקמה rekama, that is, Phrygian work. For that this eagle, the ἀστερίας [asterias] or starry eagle, is the largest of the eagles, we learn from these words of Aelian, Hist. book 2, ch. 39: Ἀκούω δέ τι καὶ γένος ἀετῶν, καὶ ὄνομα αὐτῶν χρυσαίετον ἔθεντο· ἄλλοι δὲ ἀστερίαν τὸν αὐτὸν καλοῦσιν· ὁρᾶται δὲ οὐ πολλάκις, etc. μέγιστος δὲ ἀετῶν εἶναι πεπίστευται. [Akouō de ti kai genos aetōn, kai onoma autōn chrysaieton ethento; alloi de asterian ton auton kalousin; horatai de ou pollakis, etc. megistos de aetōn einai pepisteutai.] I hear that there is also a certain kind of eagle which some call Chrysaetos, others Asterias or the starry eagle. It is not often seen, etc. It is believed to be the largest of the eagles R6. But I know of no kind of eagle with a blood-red tail, such as the Syriac translator describes in these words at Rev 8:13: And I saw, and heard one eagle flying in the midst, ܕܢܫܪܐ ܕܕܡܐ ܐܝܬ ܠܗ [דנשרא דדמא אית לה], which had a blood-red tail. So the matter would be stuck here, were the sources of the error not plain. The Greek has μεσουρανήματι [mesouranēmati], that is, in mid-heaven. The translator took this as if he had read ἐν μέσῳ οὐρὰν αἵματι [en mesō ouran haimati], supplying βεβαμμένην ἔχοντος [bebammenēn echontos]: an eagle in the midst, having its tail (supply dyed) with blood, than which nothing more absurd could be devised. On this passage see the Notes of Edward Pococke [=Edward Pococke, Commentary on Hosea (1685)], a man by far the most learned in these studies.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 743 That نِسْر [nisr] is today the Arabic name of eagles is also confirmed by Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)] in Descriptt. Animall. p. 12. But just as the Arabs often take eagles, نِسْر [nisr], and vultures, رخم [rakham], indiscriminately, and attribute to the eagle many things that are proper to the vulture, as Bochart will show at length below in Chapter XXVII, so it is likely that the Hebrews too sometimes confused birds of both kinds and took one for the other. Medieval writers also confuse vultures with eagles, as Jo. Gottl. Schneider observes on Frederick II, De arte venandi cum avibus, p. 52. "Of eagles," says Leo Africanus, Descript. Afr. book 9, ch. 56, "there are various species, differing in their properties, size and colour: the larger are called Nesir in the Arabic idiom." And in ch. 57: Nesir "is the largest of the birds of Africa; in body it exceeds the crane, yet it is shorter in beak, neck and legs." These marks are rather uncertain and fit more than one bird of the eagle kind. This one thing seems certain: the word نسر [nsr] comprehends birds similar to one another but different in species. Alb. Schultens [=Albert Schultens, Liber Jobi (1737)] rightly says in his Commentary on Job XXXIX, p. 1136: "See Pliny, book 10, ch. 3, where six kinds of eagles are indicated. The name common to all is נשר, نسر [nsr]. The species noted in Scripture are פרס, the ossifrage, and עזניה, the Melanaetos or Valeria." Therefore I cannot agree with Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde] [Vermischte Sammlungen, fasc. 1, ch. 5; fasc. 3, p. 164; and fasc. 5, p. 73], who assigns the name נשר to the bearded vulture alone, although I do not think it should be excluded altogether. But most of what is recorded of the נשר in the sacred books fits the whole kind of eagles and vultures. — Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], in Supplemm. p. 1695, which should be read, inclines more to the eagle; with him may be compared what a certain learned man notes in the Sylloge of observations on Bruce's [=James Bruce, Travels to discover the source of the Nile (1790)] travels, edited by Hassencamp, p. 161.

(6) Rosenmüller, II, 749 Hanc ipsam aquilam, a se diligenter observatam, accuratissime descripsit ULYSS. ALDROVANDUS Ornithol. P. I. L. II. p. 112. Ubi inter alia Alarum, inquit, et caudae color fuscus, eoque magis, quo pennae majores. Caeterarum totius corporis mi- nutiorum plumarum ex fusco ferrugine- us seu castaneus erat, maculis sparsim intercurrentibus albis, paucis dorso, pluribus ventre, radicibus ubique albis. Re- ctrices alarum pennae utrinque senae erant, dodrantes binos, et palmum lon- gae, calamis firmissimis et duris. Vides, optimo jure Ezechielis verba a Bocharto referri ad ἀστερίαν, quae et χρυσάετος, aquilarum maximam. Sed vulturem suum bar- batum et hic videt Oedmann. I. p. 74.

R6 Rosenmüller, II, 749 This very eagle, which he had carefully observed, was described most accurately by Aldrovandi [=Ulisse Aldrovandi, Ornithologia (1599–1603)], Ornithol. vol. 1, book 2, p. 112. There, among other things, he says: "The colour of the wings and tail was dusky, the more so the larger the feathers. That of the other, smaller feathers of the whole body was a rusty or chestnut brown," with white spots scattered here and there, few on the back, more on the belly, the roots everywhere white. "The flight feathers of the wings were six on each side, two spans and a palm long, with very firm and hard quills." You see that Bochart, with every right, refers Ezekiel's words to the ἀστερίας [asterias], which is also the χρυσάετος [chrysaetos], the largest of the eagles. But here too Oedmann, vol. 1, p. 74, sees his bearded vulture.


Part 2, Book 2, chapter 2: The eagle's wings, flight, nest, sight and food
