Part 2, Book 2, chapter 5: Peres is the ossifrage
-------------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/peres.html

II, 770 col. 185 CAP. V.

II, 770 col. 185 Chapter 5.


Probatur, פרס peres esse Ossifragam.

It is proved that פרס peres is the ossifrage.


In censu immundarum avium פרס peres est ordine secunda. Graeci τὸν γρύπα explicant. Unde gryphum Hieronymus, Pagninus et Arias. Et ex Hebraeis Pomarius, qui Perusiam, Tuscorum oppidum, ex eo vult sumsisse nomen, ac proinde פרס peres, seu gryphem habere in insignibus. Gryphem tamen nunquam ὑποχείριον ἀνθρώπων γεγονέναι, vere observat Origenes lib. 4. in Celsum. Et de gryphibus quidquid afferunt nugacissimi scriptores, Ctesias et Aristeas Proconnesius, jure merito rejiciunt ut fabulosum Plinius, Arrianus et Pausanias, ut alibi docemus. Itaque non potest stare haec versio, nisi gryphis nomine aliud intelligatur, quam vulgo, γρυπαίετος nimirum, id est, aquila rostro insigniter adunco. Id enim proprie γρυπότης. Nempe in rostro eadem esse solet, quae in unguibus aduncitas. Porro nomine פרס peres avem significari maxime ungulatam, ex eo puto conjecisse vetustos illos interpretes, quod Hebraeum פרסה parsa, pro ungula iisdem fere literis scribitur. Sed conjectura haec minus placet; quia פרסה parsa nonnisi quadrupedum est ungula: ut avium צפרן tsipporen, Chaldaeis טפר tephar, Dan. IV, 30.

In the list of unclean birds פרס peres is second in order. The Greeks render it τὸν γρύπα [ton grypa]. Hence Jerome, Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae] and Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot] have "griffin". So too, among the Hebrews, Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)], who holds that Perusia, a town of the Etruscans, took its name from it, and therefore has the פרס peres, or griffin, in its arms. Yet Origen, book 4 Against Celsus, rightly observes that the griffin has never ὑποχείριον ἀνθρώπων γεγονέναι [hypocheirion anthrōpōn gegonenai]. And whatever those most frivolous writers Ctesias and Aristeas of Proconnesus relate about griffins, Pliny, Arrian and Pausanias quite rightly reject as fabulous, as we show elsewhere. This rendering, therefore, cannot stand, unless by the name gryps [griffin] something other than the common meaning is understood, namely γρυπαίετος [grypaietos], that is, an eagle with a remarkably hooked beak. For that is properly γρυπότης [grypotēs]. The beak, of course, usually has the same hookedness as the talons. Further, I think those ancient interpreters conjectured that the name פרס peres signifies a bird with especially large talons because the Hebrew פרסה parsa, "hoof", is written with almost the same letters. But this conjecture pleases me less, because פרסה parsa is only the hoof of quadrupeds, while that of birds is צפרן tsipporen, in Chaldee טפר tephar, Dan 4:30.


Samaritano פרס peres est ࠁࠆࠀࠄ bezaa, accipiter: Munstero quoque et Schindlero. Sed Ionathani עוזא uza, de qua sequenti capite. Arabibus عقاب okab, μελαναίετος. Iudaeis in Germania בלאבֿוז blafus, quasi cyanopodem dicas. Ita vocant falconis genus a coeruleis pedibus, de quo Albertus, Nonum genus falconum, et jam declinans ab excellentia nobilium falconum, est id, col. 186 II, 771 cujus pedes hyacinthini, sive azurini sunt, etc. Ab Italis apud Gesnerum zafiro dicitur a sapphirino colore pedum. Id sequutus Deodatius in Italica versione falconem reddidit, et in Gallica girofalcum. Cujus versionis prima origo jam dicetur. A prasino deducta vox Gallica vetus pers primo viridem, deinde etiam coeruleum colorem significavit. Quod cum animadvertissent Iudaei, qui in Gallia olim frequentes habitabant, inde collegerunt insulsi homines, avem פרס peres saltem ex parte coerulei esse coloris, quasi nostrum pers pro coeruleo ab Hebraeo esset factum. Quod quidem est perabsurdum. Sed illis hominibus insanire solenne est. Nec minus ridiculo errore eam ipsam vocem פרס peres fecisse Perusiae nomen (Tuscorum oppido veteri, cujus praeter Ptolemaeum, Silius, Appianus, Eutropius, Stephanus atque alii meminerunt), nuper asserebat David de Pomis.

For the Samaritan, פרס peres is ࠁࠆࠀࠄ [בזאה] bezaa, the hawk; so too for Münster and Schindler. But for Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] it is עוזא uza, of which in the next chapter. For the Arabs it is عقاب [ʿuqāb] okab, the melanaeetus. For the Jews in Germany it is בלאבֿוז blafus, as if you were to say "blue-foot". So they call a kind of falcon from its blue feet, of which Albertus says: The ninth kind of falcons, already falling short of the excellence of the noble falcons, is the one col. 186 II, 771 whose feet are hyacinthine or azure, etc. By the Italians, according to Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium], it is called zafiro from the sapphire colour of its feet. Following this, Diodati rendered it "falcon" in his Italian version, and "gerfalcon" in the French. The first origin of this rendering will now be explained. The old French word pers, derived from prasinus [leek-green], first meant a green, then also a blue colour. When the Jews, who once lived in large numbers in France, noticed this, those witless men inferred that the bird פרס peres is at least partly blue in colour, as if our pers for blue were formed from the Hebrew. This is utterly absurd. But raving is customary with those men. And by no less ridiculous an error David de Pomis [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587), a Hebrew-Latin-Italian dictionary] recently asserted that this very word פרס peres produced the name of Perusia (an old town of the Etruscans, mentioned besides Ptolemy by Silius, Appian, Eutropius, Stephanus and others).


Ex eodem grege non nemo apud Munsterum פרס peres avem esse statuit, quae in sola Perside reperiatur; quasi פרס peres alludat ad Hebraeum Persidis vocabulum פרס paras. Sed et haec conjectura duabus de causis inanis est. 1. Quia Persidis nomen Mose recentius est annis circiter nongentis: Cyri nempe tempore natum, qui primus populares suos equitare docuit. Unde פרסין, vel פרשין, Persae vel equites dici coeperunt, qui olim Cuthaei, vel Cissii, Susiani et Elamitae, ut probavimus in nostro Phaleg. 2. Quia Moses non prohibuisset Iudaeis avem, Persidi peculiarem, quae a Iudaea immensum distat. Interim agnoscendum est, quandam avem a Perside nomen habuisse, quam Aristophanes in Avibus vocat Περσικὸν ὄρνιν. Sed scribit Scholiastes, quosdam τὸν ἀλεκτρυόνα, alios τὸν ταῶ pavonem intelligere; quarum avium utraque munda, cum peres sit immunda.

From the same flock, someone cited by Münster decided that the פרס peres is a bird found only in Persia, as if פרס peres alluded to the Hebrew word for Persia, פרס paras. But this conjecture too is empty, for two reasons. 1. Because the name of Persia is about nine hundred years more recent than Moses: it arose in the time of Cyrus, who first taught his countrymen to ride. Hence those who were formerly Cuthaeans, or Cissians, Susians and Elamites began to be called פרסין or פרשין, Persians or horsemen, as we proved in our Phaleg. 2. Because Moses would not have forbidden the Jews a bird peculiar to Persia, which is immensely distant from Judaea. Meanwhile it must be acknowledged that a certain bird had its name from Persia, which Aristophanes in the Birds calls Περσικὸν ὄρνιν [Persikon ornin]. But the Scholiast writes that some understand τὸν ἀλεκτρυόνα [ton alektryona], others τὸν ταῶ [ton taō], the peacock; both of these birds are clean, whereas the peres is unclean.


Iam scire est operae pretium, cur פרס, peres, Iunius ossifragam, Castalio anatariam interpretetur, quae sunt aquilarum species. Verbum פרס paras, unde פרס peres, primo dividere et distribuere, deinde etiam frangere significat; quia res frangendo dividuntur. Quod respexit Castalio, quia de anataria aquila scribit Plinius lib. 10. cap. 3. Ingenium est ei testudines raptas frangere e sublimi jaciendo, quae sors interemit poetam Aeschylum. Sed Iunius, quasi פרס peres a distribuendo dicatur, hanc suae versionis rationem affert in Notis: Ossifraga nomen habet a distribuendo, quod huic animanti sic tribuit Plinius: Ejectos ab aquilis cognatum genus ossifragae excipiunt, et educunt cum suis. In quibus tamen Plinii verbis de distributione ne γρῦ quidem, nisi καθ᾽ ἀκολούθησιν· quia cum ossifraga foetus alienos cum suis alit, necesse est, ut alimenta inter utrosque partiatur. Nec ossifragae nomen est a distribuendo, sed ab ossium fractione, quod omnes sciunt.

Now it is worth knowing why Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] renders פרס, peres, "ossifrage", and Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)] anataria [duck-eagle], which are species of eagles. The verb פרס paras, from which פרס peres comes, first means to divide and to distribute, then also to break, because things are divided by breaking. Castalio had this in view, because Pliny, book 10, ch. 3, writes of the duck-eagle: It has the habit of breaking tortoises it has seized by dropping them from on high, a fate which killed the poet Aeschylus. But Junius, as if פרס peres were named from distributing, gives this reason for his rendering in his Notes: The ossifrage has its name from distributing, because Pliny attributes this to the creature: The related kind, the ossifrages, take in the young cast out by the eagles and rear them with their own. Yet in these words of Pliny there is not even a γρῦ [gry] about distribution, except καθ᾽ ἀκολούθησιν [kath᾽ akolouthēsin]; for since the ossifrage feeds strange young with its own, it must divide the food between both. Nor is the name of the ossifrage from distributing, but from the breaking of bones, as everyone knows.


II, 772 Aliorum sententiis sic explicatis, nostram quoque hic afferemus, et idoneis argumentis statuminare conabimur. Ac primo quidem iis accedo, qui פרס peres aquilae speciem esse volunt. In quibus Graeci, Hieronymus, Chaldaei, Arabes et plerique recentiorum. Huc facit, quod apud Macedones, qui ex Orientis spoliis non solum opes, sed et linguam suam auxerunt, aquila dicebatur παραὸς, allusione manifesta ad Hebraeum פרס peres. Hesychius, Παραός· ἀετὸς ὑπὸ Μακεδόνων· Paraos aquila Macedonibus. Praeterea, ut ex omnium consensu נשר genuinam aquilam sonat, ita vocibus, in Mose proxime sequentibus, nempe פרס et עזניה, alias aquilarum species, Iudaeis notas, designari, valde verisimile est. Neque tutum est se opponere tam multis interpretibus, qui sic statuunt. Hoc igitur firmum maneat, פרס esse in aquilarum speciebus. Sed de specie jam inquirendum, quae aliunde exsculpi non potest, quam ex vocis origine, cum de ea praeter nudum nomen nihil quidquam habeamus. Et recte col. 187 notat Aben Ezra, sumendam esse originem ex his Es. LVIII, 7. פרוס לרעב לחמך Frange esurienti panem tuum. Qua nota significatum voluit aquilae genus esse a frangendo sic appellatae. Sed, ut res sit manifestior, expende, Le-ctor, haec Mich. III, 3. quae in hoc argumento nondum fuisse citata, mirum est: ואת עצמותיהם פצחו ופרשו כאשר בסיר וכבשר בתוך קלחת, Et ossa eorum ruperunt, et fregerunt tanquam in olla, et sicut carnem in medio lebetis. Ex quibus constat, Verbum פרס (vel פרש per Sin Semol, quod idem est) etiam de fractione ossium usurpari. Inde igitur nemo est, qui non colligat, פרס peres esse ossifragam, hoc est, illam aquilae speciem, quae a frangendis ossibus Romana lingua ossifraga, vel ossifragus appellatur: et Arabica vel simpliciter كاسر id est, fractor, vel كاسر اعظام fractor ossium (1). Itaque Iunius ossifragam recte reddidit, quamvis illum latuerit hujus versionis vera ratio. Et fortasse eodem pertinet, quod pro פרס Onkelos et Hierosolymitanus ha-bent ער, vel עריא. Quippe voces ער et עריא, inversis radicalibus, deduci potuere ex verbis רעע, vel רעה, quae frangere et conterere significant. De ossifraga sic Lucretius lib. 5. versu 1077.

II, 772 Having thus set out the opinions of others, we shall here also present our own and try to support it with suitable arguments. First, I side with those who hold that פרס peres is a species of eagle. Among them are the Greeks, Jerome, the Chaldeans, the Arabs and most of the more recent writers. In favour of this is the fact that among the Macedonians, who enriched from the spoils of the East not only their wealth but also their language, the eagle was called παραὸς [paraos], in manifest allusion to the Hebrew פרס peres. Hesychius: Παραός· ἀετὸς ὑπὸ Μακεδόνων· [Paraos; aetos hypo Makedonōn;] Paraos, the eagle among the Macedonians. Moreover, just as by universal agreement נשר denotes the true eagle, so it is very probable that the words immediately following in Moses, namely פרס and עזניה, designate other species of eagles known to the Jews. Nor is it safe to oppose so many interpreters who hold this view. Let it stand firm, then, that פרס is among the species of eagles. But now we must inquire into the species, which can be extracted from nothing else than the origin of the word, since apart from the bare name we have nothing whatever about it. And Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] rightly col. 187 notes that the origin is to be taken from these words of Es. LVIII, 7: פרוס לרעב לחמך Break your bread for the hungry. By this note he meant to indicate that it is a kind of eagle so called from breaking. But to make the matter clearer, consider, reader, these words of Mic 3:3, which it is surprising have not yet been cited in this discussion: ואת עצמותיהם פצחו ופרשו כאשר בסיר וכבשר בתוך קלחת, And they broke their bones and shattered them as in a pot, and as flesh in the midst of a cauldron. From this it is evident that the verb פרס (or פרש with Sin Semol, which is the same) is also used of the breaking of bones. From this, then, there is no one who would not conclude that פרס peres is the ossifrage, that is, that species of eagle which from breaking bones is called in the Roman tongue ossifraga or ossifragus [bone-breaker], and in Arabic either simply كاسر [kāsir], that is, breaker, or كاسر اعظام [kāsir aʿẓām] breaker of bones R1. Thus Junius rightly rendered it ossifrage, although the true reason for this rendering escaped him. And perhaps it bears on the same point that for פרס Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] and the Jerusalem Targum have ער or עריא. For the words ער and עריא, with the radicals inverted, could have been derived from the verbs רעע or רעה, which mean to break and to crush. Of the ossifrage Lucretius writes thus, book 5, line 1077:


Postremo genus alituum, variaeque volucres,
Accipitres, atque ossifragae. — — —

Lastly the race of winged things, and the various birds, hawks and ossifrages — — —


Et Plinius passim, ut lib. 10. cap. 3. ubi de haliaeetis, Id quidem, quod ex iis natum est, in ossifragis genus habet. Et paullo post, Quidam adjiciunt genus aquilae, quam barbatam vocant; Thusci vero ossifragam. Et rursus ubi de pullis, II, 773 quos ejiciunt aquilae taedio nutriendi: Ejectos ab his cognatum genus ossifragae excipiunt et educant cum suis. Et cap. 7. Immussulum aliqui vulturis pullum arbi- trantur esse, et sanqualem ossifragae. Item, Massurius sanqualem ossifragam esse dicit. Et lib. 30. cap. 7. Unum est ossifrago intestinum mirabili natura, omnia devorata conficienti. Et paullo ante, Ossifragi venter arefactus; et potus, iis, qui cibos non conficiunt, utilissimus. Et capite statim sequenti eundem sumi jubet ad calculos pellendos. Isidorus quoque lib. 12. cap. 7. Ossifrangus (lege Ossi- fragus) vulgo appellatur avis, quae ossa ab alto demittit et frangit, unde et a frangendo ossa nomen accepit. Vide etiam Festum in vocibus immussulus et san- qualis. Ossifragus in uno Glossario Graece dicitur ὀστοκόπος, ὀστοκλάστης, ὀστο-κατεάκτης· in altero, sed perperam, ὀστοκόραξ, Dioscoridi φίνις. Φίνις, inquit, τὸ ὄρνεον, ὃ Ῥωμαϊστὶ καλοῦσιν ὀσσίφραγον. Et vetustioribus φήνη, voce ex Homero et Aristotele notissima, quamque Arabes quoque usurpant. Damir ex Ibnosaida, الفينة طاير يشبه العقاب فاذا خاف البرد انحدر الي اليمن Phena, avis, aquilae similis, quae, cum timet frigus, proficiscitur in Ieman, id est, in Arabiam felicem. Sed vulgo vocatur, ut diximus, nempe كاسر fractor, et كاسر اعظام fractor ossium. Item, مكلفة mechalapha, a colore nigro cum rufedine, vel flavedine admixta. Damir, الكاسر العقاب Alchasir (seu fractor) aqui- lae genus. Idem alibi, كاسر العظام المكلفة Fractor ossium, id est, mechalepha. Et in capite De mechalepha, الفرخ الذي ترمي col. 188 به العقاب من الثلثة يحضنه طاير يقال له المكلفه ويقال له كاسر العظام وتربيه Pullum, quem ejecit aquila e tribus, fovet et nutrit avis, quae mechalepha dicitur, et fra- ctor ossium. Et capite العقاب seu De aquila, والعرب يسمي العقاب الكاسر Etiam Arabes aquilam (id est, aquilae speciem) fra- ctorem vocant. Et infra, والفرخ الذي تلقيه يعطف عليه طاير يسمي كاسر العظام ويسمي المكلفه ايضا فيربيه Et pulli, ab aquila projecti, miseretur avis, quae ossifra- ga et mechalepha nominatur, ita, ut eum nutriat. Ab ossifraga deduci palam est Gallicum orfraye; quamvis apud nos aliud sonet, nempe haliaeetum, sive aqui- lam marinam. Quod pridem observavit Bellonius lib. 2. cap. 7. De avibus.

And Pliny uses it throughout, as in book 10, ch. 3, where he speaks of the haliaeetus: That which is born from them has its kind among the ossifrages. And a little later: Some add a kind of eagle which they call the bearded eagle; the Tuscans, however, call it the ossifrage. And again, where he speaks of the chicks II, 773 that eagles throw out because they are weary of feeding them: When they have been thrown out by these, the related kind of the ossifrage takes them up and rears them with its own. And in ch. 7: Some think that the immussulus is the chick of the vulture, and the sanqualis that of the ossifrage. Likewise Massurius says that the sanqualis is the ossifrage. And in book 30, ch. 7: The ossifrage has a single intestine of wonderful nature, which digests everything it has swallowed. And a little before: The stomach of the ossifrage, dried and taken in drink, is very useful to those who do not digest their food. And in the chapter immediately following he prescribes that the same be taken to expel stones. Isidore too, book 12, ch. 7: The bird that drops bones from on high and breaks them is commonly called ossifrangus (read ossifragus), and hence it received its name from breaking bones. See also Festus under the words immussulus and sanqualis. Ossifragus is rendered in Greek in one Glossary as ὀστοκόπος [ostokopos], ὀστοκλάστης [ostoklastēs], ὀστοκατεάκτης [ostokateaktēs]; in another, but wrongly, as ὀστοκόραξ [ostokorax]; in Dioscorides as φίνις [phinis]. Φίνις [Phinis], he says, τὸ ὄρνεον, ὃ Ῥωμαϊστὶ καλοῦσιν ὀσσίφραγον [to orneon, ho Rhōmaisti kalousin ossiphragon]. And among older writers it is φήνη [phēnē], a word very well known from Homer and Aristotle, and one which the Arabs also use. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], from Ibnosaida [=Ibn Sīda (d. 1066), lexicographer, as cited by al-Damīrī]: الفينة طاير يشبه العقاب فاذا خاف البرد انحدر الي اليمن [al-fīna ṭāyir yushbih al-ʿuqāb fa-idhā khāfa al-bard inḥadara ilā al-Yaman] Phena, a bird resembling the eagle, which, when it fears the cold, goes off to Ieman, that is, to Arabia Felix. But it is commonly called, as we have said, كاسر [kāsir] breaker, and كاسر اعظام [kāsir aʿẓām] breaker of bones. Also مكلفة [mukallafa] mechalapha, from its black colour mixed with reddish or yellowish. Damir: الكاسر العقاب [al-kāsir al-ʿuqāb] Alchasir (or breaker) is a kind of eagle. The same elsewhere: كاسر العظام المكلفة [kāsir al-ʿiẓām al-mukallafa] The breaker of bones, that is, the mechalepha. And in the chapter On the mechalepha: الفرخ الذي ترمي col. 188 به العقاب من الثلثة يحضنه طاير يقال له المكلفه ويقال له كاسر العظام وتربيه [al-farkh alladhī tarmī bihi al-ʿuqāb min al-thalatha yaḥḍunuhu ṭāyir yuqāl lahu al-mukallafa wa-yuqāl lahu kāsir al-ʿiẓām wa-turabbīhi] The chick which the eagle has thrown out of the three is warmed and fed by a bird which is called mechalepha and breaker of bones. And in the chapter العقاب [al-ʿuqāb], or On the eagle: والعرب يسمي العقاب الكاسر [wa-al-ʿarab yusammī al-ʿuqāb al-kāsir] The Arabs also call the eagle (that is, a species of eagle) the breaker. And below: والفرخ الذي تلقيه يعطف عليه طاير يسمي كاسر العظام ويسمي المكلفه ايضا فيربيه [wa-al-farkh alladhī tulqīhi yaʿṭifu ʿalayhi ṭāyir yusammā kāsir al-ʿiẓām wa-yusammā al-mukallafa ayḍan fa-yurabbīhi] And on the chick thrown out by the eagle a bird takes pity, which is named ossifrage and mechalepha, so that it rears it. It is evident that the French orfraye is derived from ossifraga, although among us it denotes something else, namely the haliaeetus or sea eagle. This was observed long ago by Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)], On Birds, book 2, ch. 7.

Part 2, Book 2, chapter 6: Oznija is the black eagle

II, 774 col. 188 CAP. VI.

II, 774 col. 188 Chapter VI.


Probatur, עזניה oznija non esse Haliaeetum, ut plerique volunt, sed Melanaeetum, seu Valeriam aquilam.

It is proved that עזניה oznija is not the haliaeetus, as most hold, but the melanaeetus, or Valerian eagle.


In immundis avibus tertia est עזניא oznija. Ἁλιαίετον Graeci reddunt, unde Hieronymus, Munsterus, Castalio, Pagninus, Arias, Iunius, Deodatius, haliaeetum, vel aquilam marinam: et Angli ospray, quod idem est: Genevenses falconem, quorsum, non satis scio, nisi quod aquilam marinam pro falcone nonnulli habent, quos tamen refellit Gesnerus. In voce עזניה oznija Hebraei monent, Nun esse נוסף, seu epentheticum: et עזניה oznija dici pro עזיה ozja. Proinde Onkelos hic habet עזיה ozja. Et hanc aquilae speciem ab עוז oz, seu robore sic appellari, in confesso est. Unde valde verissimili ratione colligo, potius esse μελαναίετον, id est, nigram aquilam; quae, utut aquilarum minima, tamen est robustissima. Proinde Valeriam Romani vocant, ut quae viribus maxime valeat. Plinius ubi supra, Melanaeetos a Graecis dicta, eademque Valeria, minima magnitudine, viribus praecipua, colore nigricans, etc. Et ante Plinium Philosophus lib. 9. cap. 32. Ἕτερος δὲ μέλας τὴν χρόαν, καὶ μέγεθος ἐλάχιστος, καὶ κράτιστος τούτων. οὗτος οἰκεῖ ὄρη, καὶ ὕλας· καλεῖται δὲ μελαναίετος, καὶ λαγωφόνος. Alia autem est aquila, colore nigra, magni- col. 189 tudine minima, sed viribus praestantissima. Ea montes et sylvas colit: vocaturque melanaeetus (id est, nigra aquila) et leporicida. Et ante Philosophum Poeta summus de Achille Iliad. φ΄. versu 252.

Third among the unclean birds is עזניא oznija. The Greeks render it Ἁλιαίετον [Haliaieton], whence Jerome, Munster, Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)], Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae], Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] and Diodati have haliaeetus or sea eagle; the English have ospray, which is the same; the Genevans have falcon, for what reason I do not well know, unless because some take the sea eagle for a falcon, whom, however, Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium] refutes. In the word עזניה oznija the Hebrews note that the Nun is נוסף, that is, epenthetic, and that עזניה oznija is said for עזיה ozja. Accordingly Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] here has עזיה ozja. And it is agreed that this species of eagle is so named from עוז oz, that is, strength. Hence I infer on very probable grounds that it is rather the μελαναίετον [melanaieton], that is, the black eagle, which, though the smallest of eagles, is nevertheless the strongest. For this reason the Romans call it Valeria, as being most powerful (valeat) in strength. Pliny, in the place cited above: "Called melanaeetos by the Greeks, and also Valeria, smallest in size, outstanding in strength, blackish in colour", etc. And before Pliny, the Philosopher, book 9, ch. 32: Ἕτερος δὲ μέλας τὴν χρόαν, καὶ μέγεθος ἐλάχιστος, καὶ κράτιστος τούτων. οὗτος οἰκεῖ ὄρη, καὶ ὕλας· καλεῖται δὲ μελαναίετος, καὶ λαγωφόνος. [Heteros de melas tēn chroan, kai megethos elachistos, kai kratistos toutōn. houtos oikei orē, kai hylas; kaleitai de melanaietos, kai lagōphonos.] "But there is another eagle, black in colour, smallest in col. 189 size, but most excellent in strength. It inhabits mountains and forests, and is called melanaeetus" (that is, black eagle) "and hare-killer." And before the Philosopher, the greatest Poet, of Achilles, Iliad 21, line 252:


Αἰετοῦ οἴματ᾽ ἔχων μέλανος, τοῦ θηρητῆρος·
Ὅς θ᾽ ἅμα κάρτιστός τε, καὶ ὤκιστος πετεηνῶν·

Αἰετοῦ οἴματ᾽ ἔχων μέλανος, τοῦ θηρητῆρος· Ὅς θ᾽ ἅμα κάρτιστός τε, καὶ ὤκιστος πετεηνῶν· [Aietou oimat' echōn melanos, tou thērētēros; Hos th' hama kartistos te, kai ōkistos peteēnōn;]


Aquilae impetum habens nigrae, venatricis, quae alitum simul est fortissima et celerrima. Ad quem locum Eustathius, Αἰετοῦ μέλανος τῆς θηρητῆρος, ὃν καὶ μελαναίετόν τινες συνθέτως φασὶ, τὸν καὶ φασσοφόνον (forte legendum λα-γωφόνον) μικρὸν μέν φασιν ὄντα, τῶν ἄλλων δὲ ἰσχυρότερον· Aquilae nigrae venatricis, quam composita voce quidam melanaeetum et palumbariam, parvam quidem, ut ajunt, sed aliis robustiorem. Homeri vetus Scholiastes scribit, Aristotelem pro μέλανος τοῦ, conjunctis vocibus legisse μελανόστου, ut significetur, aquilam habere nigra ossa, et alios μελανόσσου, quasi sit nigris oculis. Sed in Aristotelis libris, qui extant, nihil occurrit simile. Et frustra sollicitatur Poetae le-ctio, quae commoda est et erudita, eum conciliat in descriptione nigrae aquilae cum Aristotele et Plinio. Horum igitur consensu cum nigra aquila sit omnium validissima, quidni a robore עזניה osnija ab Hebraeis dicta fuerit. ut a Romanis valeria? Praeterea inter aquilarum species hanc a Mose fuisse omissam, verissimile II, 775 non est, cum post majorem illam et genuinam aquilam, quae proprie נשר vocatur, haec sit aquilarum omnium ἀξιομνημονεύτατος. Nam praeter eximium robur plurimas habet dotes, quae illam maxime commendant. Has ita describit Philosophus ubi supra, Ἐκτρέφει δὲ μόνος οὗτος τὰ τέκνα, καὶ ἐξ-άγει· ἔστι δὲ ὠκυβόλος, καὶ εὐθήμων, καὶ ἄφθονος, καὶ ἄφοβος, καὶ μάχι-μος, καὶ εὔφημος· οὐ γὰρ μινυρίζει, οὐδὲ λέληκεν. Una haec foetus suos alit at-que educit. Est et pernix, elegans, sine invidia, sine metu, strenua, boni ominis; neque clangit, neque murmurat. Proinde illam cum chrysaëto ita confert amplissimus Thuanus lib. I. De re accipitraria,

"Having the onset of the black eagle, the hunter, which is at once the strongest and swiftest of birds." On this passage Eustathius: Αἰετοῦ μέλανος τῆς θηρητῆρος, ὃν καὶ μελαναίετόν τινες συνθέτως φασὶ, τὸν καὶ φασσοφόνον [Aietou melanos tēs thērētēros, hon kai melanaieton tines synthetōs phasi, ton kai phassophonon] (perhaps one should read λαγωφόνον [lagōphonon]) μικρὸν μέν φασιν ὄντα, τῶν ἄλλων δὲ ἰσχυρότερον· [mikron men phasin onta, tōn allōn de ischyroteron;] "Of the black hunting eagle, which some call by a compound word melanaeetus, and dove-killer; small indeed, as they say, but stronger than the others." The old Scholiast of Homer writes that Aristotle, instead of μέλανος τοῦ [melanos tou], read with the words joined μελανόστου [melanostou], meaning that the eagle has black bones, and others μελανόσσου [melanossou], as if with black eyes. But in the extant books of Aristotle nothing similar occurs. And the Poet's reading is tampered with in vain, for it is apt and learned, and brings him into agreement with Aristotle and Pliny in describing the black eagle. Since, then, by their consensus the black eagle is the strongest of all, why should it not have been called עזניה osnija by the Hebrews from its strength, as valeria by the Romans? Moreover, it is not at all likely II, 775 that this species was omitted by Moses among the eagles, since after that greater and genuine eagle, properly called נשר, this is the most noteworthy (ἀξιομνημονεύτατος [axiomnēmoneutatos]) of all eagles. For besides its exceptional strength it has very many qualities that especially commend it. The Philosopher describes them thus in the place cited: Ἐκτρέφει δὲ μόνος οὗτος τὰ τέκνα, καὶ ἐξάγει· ἔστι δὲ ὠκυβόλος, καὶ εὐθήμων, καὶ ἄφθονος, καὶ ἄφοβος, καὶ μάχιμος, καὶ εὔφημος· οὐ γὰρ μινυρίζει, οὐδὲ λέληκεν. [Ektrephei de monos houtos ta tekna, kai exagei; esti de ōkybolos, kai euthēmōn, kai aphthonos, kai aphobos, kai machimos, kai euphēmos; ou gar minyrizei, oude lelēken.] "This one alone rears and brings out its young. It is also swift, elegant, without envy, without fear, vigorous, of good omen; it neither screams nor murmurs." Accordingly the most distinguished Thuanus, book 1 De re accipitraria, compares it with the chrysaetus thus:


Optima et ipsa aequans animis ingentibus illam, Corporis inferior quamvis sit mole, nec ungue, Aut rostro tantum valeat, digitisve: sed ortus Non mentita suos, animive oblita virilis, Accipitres collata nothos facit. Hanc quoque nostri Valeriam dicunt, Graeci μελαναίετον, atrum Quod referat rostro, pennis atque ungue colorem (1).

"Excellent, she too equals that one in mighty spirit, though she is inferior in bulk of body, and not so strong in talon, beak or toes; but, not belying her birth nor forgetful of a manly spirit, she makes hawks look bastard by comparison. Her too our people call Valeria, the Greeks μελαναίετον [melanaieton], because in beak, feathers and talon she shows a dark colour" R1.


Notandum, tam עזניה oznija, quam פרס peres, a nonnullis pro gryphe haberi. Ac proinde utrumque עוז uz, vel עוזא uza reddi, quae vox paraphrastis et Talmudicis gryphem sonat. Ita in Ionathanis paraphrasi עוזא uza habetur pro פרס peres. At in Samaritana ࠏࠅࠆࠀ uza est pro ࠏࠆࠍࠉࠄ oznija. Et in Talmudico tractatu Kelim cap. 17. §. 14. ubi agitur de vasis, quae fiunt מכנף העוז, ex ala τοῦ uz, id est, gryphis, Glossator haec habet: עוף הוא ששמו עזניה ורגילים היו לעשות כלים מכנף אותו העוז, Avis est, quae (in textu sacro) vocatur oznija, ex cujus alis solebant fieri vasa. Ubi fortasse pro מכנף miccanaph (ex ala) legendum מכף miccaph (ex planta). Et paullo post, כף העוז מכל הכפים, Planta (avis) uz omni alia praestat, pro כנף העוז מכל הכנפים, Ala avis uz omni ala praestat. Planta, id est, pes et unguis. Id enim כף caph in avibus. Sic Gen. VIII, 9. Columba non invenit requiem לכף רגלה: et Arabs Erpenianus لكف رجلها Plantae pedis sui, id est, τοῖς ποσὶν αὐτῆς, pedibus suis, ut ibi Graeci habent. Porro ex gryphis pedibus, vel unguibus vasa fieri dictitant, non item ex ejus alis. Damir capite De col. 190 عنقا anka, seu Gryphe, فيصنع من مخاليبها اقداح II, 776 عظام للشرب Et ex unguibus ejus fiunt vasa potoria magna. Gesnerus de gryphe, Iohannes de Montevilla scribit, ungues ejus tanquam cornua bovis esse, e quibus magni pretii pocula fiunt. Et paullo post, Memini ego me videre apud aurifabrum in civitate nostra cornu nigrum laeve, et in summo aduncum, fere ut in rupicapris, triplo forte crassius, cujus labris argentum inducturus erat auri- faber, ut pro poculo mensis adhiberetur. Id forte bovis alicujus peregrini, ut quem Indicum vocant, aut bubali cornu erat. Ille vero pro gryphis ungue accepe- rat. Aliud afferam, unde constet, עזניה oznija gryphem esse ex Hebraeorum sententia. In libro בעל החיים, seu De naturis animalium, quem ex Arabico Abulsaphae in Hebraeum transtulit Calonymus, עזניה oznija, in aves rapaces late imperans, eas undequaque convocat, et in illarum concilio ita loquitur: הנה אני עם גודל גופי ואומץ כוחי ומהירות עופפותי עזבתי בתיהם וברחתי מהם אל האיים הרחוקים ואל ההרים הרמים והנשואים, Ego quidem, utut corpore vasta, et viribus praestans, et alis pernix, domos eorum (hominum) reliqui, et ab iis in remotas insulas fugi; et in arduos celsosque montes. Nec multo aliter Maimonides de peres et oznija, in tractatu De cibis vetitis cap. 1. §. 17. פרס ועזניה אינן מצויין בישוב אלא במדברות איי הים הרחוקות עד מאד שהן סוף הישוב, Perez et oznija in habitato orbe (ἐν τῇ οἰκουμένῃ) non reperiuntur, sed in maris insulis remotissimis in extrema parte orbis. Haec ad Arabum ancam, seu gryphem pertinere, palam est, quem fabulantur olim inter homines in Arabia vixisse, ferasque et aves habuisse pro pabulo: sed, cum aliquando pueros et sponsam etiam rapuisset, Handalae Prophetae precibus relegatum fuisse in insulam, ab hominum commercio remotissimam, unde egredi, ut ad loca cultiora se conferat, sit illi nefas. Proinde pro Hebraeo עזניה oznija in Arabicis paraphrasibus, tam Saadiae, quam aliorum, legere est العنقا alanka. Atque ideo Saadiae succenset Aben Ezra, quod Deum prohibuisse velit הדבר שלא היה, rem, quae non extat. Quod ipsi fatentur Arabes. In his Alcamus, a quo العنقا alanka definitur eleganti paronomasia طاير معروف الاسم ومجهول الجسم avis noti alismi, id est, nominis, sed ignoti algismi, id est, corporis. Et poeta, qui dicit, الجود والغول والعنقا ثلاثة اسما اشيا لم توجد ولم تكن Probitas, et algol (seu empusa) et alanca (seu gryphus) tria sunt nomina rerum, quae non reperiuntur, nec usquam extant. Sed alibi Saadiam atque alios paraphrastas, qui hac voce utuntur, excusari posse doceo. Quia, utut anca plerunque sit avis fictitiae nomen, ut nobis gryphes, tamen etiam pro vera ave quandoque occurrit. Sed, quidquid illi in mente ha-buerint, hoc certum est, עזניה oznija in Mose significare veram avem, et valde verissimile, aquilam esse nigram, quam Graeci composita voce μελαναίετον appellant.

It should be noted that both עזניה oznija and פרס peres are taken by some for the griffin, and that accordingly both are rendered עוז uz or עוזא uza, a word that among the paraphrasts and the Talmudists means griffin. Thus in Jonathan's [=Targum Jonathan] paraphrase עוזא uza stands for פרס peres, while in the Samaritan ࠏࠅࠆࠀ [עוזא] uza stands for ࠏࠆࠍࠉࠄ [עזניה] oznija. And in the Talmudic tractate Kelim, ch. 17, § 14, where vessels made מכנף העוז, from the wing of the uz, that is, of the griffin, are discussed, the Glossator has this: עוף הוא ששמו עזניה ורגילים היו לעשות כלים מכנף אותו העוז, It is a bird which (in the sacred text) is called oznija, from whose wings vessels used to be made. Here perhaps instead of מכנף miccanaph (from the wing) we should read מכף miccaph (from the sole). And shortly after, כף העוז מכל הכפים, The sole (of the bird) uz surpasses every other, instead of כנף העוז מכל הכנפים, The wing of the bird uz surpasses every wing. Sole, that is, foot and talon; for that is what כף caph means in birds. So Gen 8:9. The dove found no rest לכף רגלה: and Erpenianus [=the Arabic version edited by Thomas Erpenius (Pentateuch 1622; New Testament 1616)] has لكف رجلها [li-kaff rijlihā] for the sole of her foot, that is, τοῖς ποσὶν αὐτῆς [tois posin autēs], for her feet, as the Greeks have there. Moreover, they commonly say that vessels are made from the griffin's feet or talons, not from its wings. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], in the chapter On col. 190 عنقا [ʿanqā] anka, or the Griffin: فيصنع من مخاليبها اقداح II, 776 عظام للشرب [fa-yuṣnaʿ min makhālībihā aqdāḥ ʿiẓām li-l-shurb] And from its talons large drinking vessels are made. Gesner, on the griffin: John Mandeville writes that its talons are like the horns of an ox, from which cups of great value are made. And shortly after: I remember seeing at a goldsmith's in our city a smooth black horn, hooked at the top, almost as in chamois, perhaps three times as thick, whose rim the goldsmith was about to mount in silver, so that it might be used as a cup at table. It was perhaps the horn of some foreign ox, such as the one they call Indian, or of a buffalo. But he had received it as a griffin's talon. I shall adduce another testimony showing that עזניה oznija is the griffin in the opinion of the Hebrews. In the book בעל החיים, or On the Natures of Animals, which Calonymus translated from the Arabic of Abulsapha into Hebrew, the עזניה oznija, ruling far and wide over the birds of prey, summons them from every side and speaks thus in their council: הנה אני עם גודל גופי ואומץ כוחי ומהירות עופפותי עזבתי בתיהם וברחתי מהם אל האיים הרחוקים ואל ההרים הרמים והנשואים, I indeed, though vast in body, outstanding in strength and swift of wing, have left their (men's) dwellings and fled from them to remote islands and to steep and lofty mountains. Not very differently Maimonides [=Moses Maimonides (Rambam), Mishneh Torah] on the peres and the oznija, in the tractate On Forbidden Foods, ch. 1, § 17: פרס ועזניה אינן מצויין בישוב אלא במדברות איי הים הרחוקות עד מאד שהן סוף הישוב, The Perez and the oznija are not found in the inhabited world (ἐν τῇ οἰκουμένῃ [en tē oikoumenē]), but in the most remote islands of the sea at the farthest edge of the world. It is obvious that this refers to the anca of the Arabs, or griffin, which they fable once lived among men in Arabia and fed on beasts and birds; but when it had once carried off children and even a bride, it was banished at the prayers of the Prophet Handala to an island most remote from human intercourse, from which it is forbidden to come out to betake itself to more cultivated places. Accordingly, for the Hebrew עזניה oznija one reads in the Arabic paraphrases, of Saadia as of others, العنقا [al-ʿanqā] alanka. And for this reason Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] is angry with Saadia for holding that God forbade הדבר שלא היה, a thing that does not exist. The Arabs themselves admit this. Among them is Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī], by whom العنقا [al-ʿanqā] alanka is defined with an elegant paronomasia as طاير معروف الاسم ومجهول الجسم [ṭāʾir maʿrūf al-ism wa-majhūl al-jism], a bird of known alism, that is, name, but unknown algism, that is, body. And the poet who says الجود والغول والعنقا ثلاثة اسما اشيا لم توجد ولم تكن [al-jūd wa-l-ghūl wa-l-ʿanqā thalātha asmā ashyā lam tūjad wa-lam takun] Liberality, and algol (or empusa) and alanca (or griffin) are three names of things that are not found and exist nowhere. But elsewhere I show that Saadia and the other paraphrasts who use this word can be excused, because, although anca is mostly the name of a fictitious bird, as griffins are for us, yet it sometimes also occurs for a real bird. But whatever they had in mind, this is certain: עזניה oznija in Moses signifies a real bird, and very probably it is the black eagle, which the Greeks call by the compound word μελαναίετον [melanaieton].

Part 2, Book 2, chapter 7: Daa or raa, the kite
-----------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/daah.html

II, 777 CAP. VII. col. 191

II, 777 CHAPTER 7. col. 191


Milvum potius a volatu dici דאה daa, ut in Levitico; quam a visu ראה raa, ut in Deuteronomio.

That the kite is named from flying, דאה daa, as in Leviticus, rather than from sight, ראה raa, as in Deuteronomy.


Sequitur דאה daa, vel ראה raa. Neque enim certum est, utro modo sit scribendum. Quia eadem avis in Levitico דאה vocatur, et in Deuteronomio ראה raa: quorum unum a volatu, alterum a visu sumptum. Nam דאה daa verbum volare est, et ראה raa, videre. Nempe literas Daleth et Res, quia sunt valde affines, librarii saepe confundunt. Sic iidem sunt דודנים Dodanim, Gen. X, 4. et רודנים Rodanim, 1 Par. I, 7. ריפת Riphath, Gen. X, 3. et דיפת Diphath, 1 Par. I, 6. הדר Hadar, Gen. XXXVI, 39. et הדד Hadad, 1 Par. I, 46. הדד־עזר Hadad-ezer, 2 Sam. VIII, 3. et הדר־עזר Hadar-ezer, 1 Par. XVIII, 3. ההרודי Harodites, 2 Sam. XXIII, 25. et ההרורי Harorites, 1 Paral. XI, 27. חמדן Hamdan, Gen. XXXVI, 26. et חמרן Hamran, 1 Par. I, 39. (al. 41.). דעואל Daguel, Num. I, 14. et VII, 42. et רעואל Raguel, Num. II, 14. Et de Deo dicitur 2 Sam. XXII, 11. וירא vajera, et apparuit, pro וידא vajeda, et volavit, Psal. XVIII, 11. Qua omnino ratione eadem avis alibi דאה daa vocatur; alibi ראה raa. Sed illa avis, si vere milvus est, prout statuunt plerique veterum et recentiorum interpretum, in his Hieronymus, Arabes, Munsterus, Castalio, Iunius, Deodatius, Buxtorfius, Schindlerus, etc. malim דאה daa scribi, quam ראה raa; a volatu ducto nomine potius, quam a visu. Quia cum in milvi visu peculiare nihil observent rerum naturae scriptores: in volatu primo hoc habet eximium, quod alis prope immotis in aëre omnium avium diutissime libratur. Munsterus, רחף, Motus est, ut milvus scilicet in aëre movetur, alis non motis, etc. Budaeus, Horam integram, aut plus eo, milvos observavimus, non jactatis alis, captare praedam, etc. Hoc Itali aucupes tendere vocant, Galli planare. Elata namque paullisper ala, motum aëris in reliquum etiam corpus excipiunt, at-que ita sustinentur. Praeterea vix ulla est avis, quae milvo volet altius. Martialis lib. 9. Epigrammate 55.

Next comes דאה daa, or ראה raa. For it is not certain which way it should be written, since the same bird is called דאה in Leviticus and ראה raa in Deuteronomy; of these, one is taken from flying, the other from sight. For דאה daa is the verb to fly, and ראה raa to see. The letters Daleth and Resh, being very similar, are often confused by scribes. Thus דודנים Dodanim, Gen 10:4 and רודנים Rodanim, 1 Chr 1:7 are the same; so are ריפת Riphath, Gen 10:3 and דיפת Diphath, 1 Chr 1:6; הדר Hadar, Gen 36:39 and הדד Hadad, 1 Chr 1:46; הדד־עזר Hadad-ezer, 2 Sam 8:3 and הדר־עזר Hadar-ezer, 1 Chr 18:3; ההרודי Harodites, 2 Sam 23:25 and ההרורי Harorites, 1 Chr 11:27; חמדן Hamdan, Gen 36:26 and חמרן Hamran, 1 Chr 1:39 (var. 41.); דעואל Daguel, Num 1:14 and VII, 42. and רעואל Raguel, Num 2:14. And of God it is said in 2 Sam 22:11. וירא vajera, and he appeared, instead of וידא vajeda, and he flew, Ps 18:11. In exactly the same way the same bird is called דאה daa in one place and ראה raa in another. But if that bird is truly the kite, as most of the ancient and more recent interpreters hold, among them Jerome, the Arabs, Munster, Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)], Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], Diodati, Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum], Schindler, etc., I would rather have it written דאה daa than ראה raa, with the name derived from flying rather than from sight. For while writers on natural history observe nothing peculiar in the kite's sight, in its flight it has this first distinctive feature: with its wings almost motionless it hovers in the air longer than any other bird. Munster: רחף, It moved, namely as the kite moves in the air without moving its wings, etc. Budaeus: We have watched kites for a whole hour or more catching prey without beating their wings, etc. This the Italian fowlers call tendere, the French planare. For by raising the wing a little they take the movement of the air into the rest of the body as well, and are thus held up. Moreover, there is scarcely any bird that flies higher than the kite. Martial, book 9, Epigram 55:


Hinc prope summa rapax milvus in astra volat.

Hence the rapacious kite flies almost to the highest stars.


Bellonius, De Avibus lib. 2. cap. 26. Cum accipiter in milvum immittitur, utrique in summum aërem ita evehuntur, ut hominum visus fugiant. Budaeus in Philologia, Nec ardeae, nec milvi, intra nubes conditi, evadere humanas manus possunt. Volando denique milvus non facile delassatur. Unde Persius de Vectidio Satyra 4.

Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)], De Avibus book 2, ch. 26: When a hawk is let loose at a kite, both are carried up into the highest air, so that they escape human sight. Budaeus in his Philologia: Neither herons nor kites, though hidden within the clouds, can escape human hands. Finally, the kite does not easily tire in flying. Hence Persius on Vectidius, Satire 4:


— arat Curibus quantum non milvus oberret.

— he ploughs at Cures more than a kite could fly over.


Ubi Cornutus, Quod dici solet secundum proverbium, „Quantum milvi non volant“, quia milvi multum volant. Et Iuvenalis Satyra 9.

Where Cornutus comments: As is commonly said in the proverb, "As far as kites do not fly", because kites fly a great deal. And Juvenal, Satire 9:


II, 778 — — cui tot montes, tot praedia servas
Appula, tot milvos intra tua pascua lassos.

II, 778 — — for whom are you keeping so many mountains, so many Apulian estates, so many kites wearied within your pastures?


Et ibi vetus Scholiastes, Vult ostendere magnitudinem possessionum Poeta, quam latae sint agris, ut nec milvi transvolare eas possint. Id igitur naturae milvi con- col. 192 venit magis, ut a volatus praestantia dictus fuerit דאה daa potius quam a visu ראה raa. Si objicias haec Apuleji lib. 6. Metamorphoseωs, Nec tamen astutulae anus milvinos oculos effugere potui: quibus milvo tribui videtur insignis perspicacitas. Respondebo, 1. rapacibus omnibus idem tribui, 2. singularem esse hunc Apuleji locum. Quod his verbis agnoscit illustris commentator Philippus Beroaldus, Milvinos oculos scriptor nullus, quod quidem sciam, celebrat, velut acumine oculorum praepollentes. Addo, in Samaritano exemplari, tam in Deu- teronomio, quam in Levitico legi ࠃࠀࠄ per Daleth, nusquam ࠓࠀࠄ per Res. Et ex Hebraeo דאה daa factum videri Arabicum حدا hida, Gutturali praeposita; ut in Hebraeo Tigris nomine חדקל Hiddekel, facto ex Chaldaeo דגלה Digla. Saltem id certum, apud Arabes milvum حداة hida vocari (1). Quod ex Abenbitare clarum, capite قاطاننقي Catananke, in quo Graeca haec Dioscoridis de exsiccato catanankes herbae semine, Ἰκτίνου ὄνυξιν ὁμοιοῦται νεκροῦ, Milvi mortui unguibus assimilatur, in Arabica paraphrasi sic redduntur: وكان شكلها شبيها شكل مخالب الحداة الميتة Et forma ejus similis est formae unguium hidae mortuae. Hidae, id est, milvi. Ut de Damire taceam, qui in capite De حداة hida illi tribuit, quidquid de milvo habet Philosophus Hist. lib. 6. cap. 6. Et de Andrea Bellunensi, cujus verba sunt: Alhada est avis, quae dicitur milvus. Recte, nisi quod alhida scribendum, non alhada. Nam الحداة alhada per Fata est bipennis, ut notant Damir et Alca- mus: sed alhida per Kesra est avis nomen. Sunt, qui tam דאה daa, quam ראה raa, multo aliter interpretentur: sed illorum versiones ideo praetermitto, quia non videntur ullo modo verisimiles (2).

And there the old Scholiast says: The poet wishes to show the size of the estates, how widely they extend in fields, so that not even kites can fly across them. This, then, suits the nature of the kite col. 192 better: that it was called דאה daa from the excellence of its flight rather than ראה raa from its sight. You may object these words of Apuleius, Metamorphoses book 6: Yet I could not escape the kite's eyes of the crafty little old woman, in which remarkable keenness of sight seems to be attributed to the kite. I shall reply, 1. that the same is attributed to all birds of prey; 2. that this passage of Apuleius is unique. This the illustrious commentator Philippus Beroaldus acknowledges in these words: No writer, so far as I know, celebrates the eyes of the kite as excelling in keenness of sight. I add that in the Samaritan copy, both in Deuteronomy and in Leviticus, ࠃࠀࠄ [דאה] is read with Daleth, nowhere ࠓࠀࠄ [ראה] with Resh. And from the Hebrew דאה daa the Arabic حدا [ḥdā] hida seems to have been formed, with a guttural prefixed, as in the Hebrew name of the Tigris, חדקל Hiddekel, formed from the Chaldee דגלה Digla. At least this is certain: among the Arabs the kite is called حداة [ḥidāh] hida R1. This is clear from Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār], in the chapter قاطاننقي [qāṭānanqī] Catananke, in which these Greek words of Dioscorides on the dried seed of the herb catananke, Ἰκτίνου ὄνυξιν ὁμοιοῦται νεκροῦ [Iktinou onyxin homoioutai nekrou], It resembles the claws of a dead kite, are rendered thus in the Arabic paraphrase: وكان شكلها شبيها شكل مخالب الحداة الميتة [wa-kāna shakluhā shabīhan shakla makhālib al-ḥidāh al-mayyita] And its shape is similar to the shape of the claws of a dead hida. Hida, that is, kite. To say nothing of Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], who in the chapter On حداة [ḥidāh] hida attributes to it whatever the Philosopher has about the kite, Hist. book 6, ch. 6. Nor of Andrea Bellunensis, whose words are: Alhada is a bird which is called the kite. Correct, except that alhida should be written, not alhada. For الحداة [al-ḥadāh] alhada with Fatha is a double axe, as Damir and Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] note; but alhida with Kasra is the name of the bird. There are some who interpret both דאה daa and ראה raa quite differently; but I pass over their versions because they do not seem in any way probable R2.

Part 2, Book 2, chapter 8: Aja is the merlin

II, 779 col. 192 CAP. VIII.

II, 779 col. 192 CHAPTER VIII.


Probatur, איה aja esse Accipitris speciem, quam veteres aesalonem, Germani Smirle appellant, nos esmerillon.

It is proved that איה aja is a species of hawk, which the ancients call the aesalon, the Germans Smirle, and we esmerillon [merlin].


Post tractatum De Aquila tres avium appellationes explicare conati sumus, nempe פרס peres, עזניה oznija, et דאה daa, vel ראה raa: quae extra immundarum catalogum nusquam reperiuntur. Itaque cum in harum interpretatione tam veteres, quam novi interpretes maxime dissentiant, aliunde exsculpi non potuit vera significatio, quam ex sola vocum origine. Nunc quatuor subsequentur, איה aja nimirum, et דיה daja, et עורב oreb, et בת־יענה bath-jaana: quae cum alibi reperiantur, in harum explicatione plus affulgebit lucis. Tamen de prima valde ambigitur. Graeci modo vulturem, modo milvum explicant. col. 193 Prius sequuntur Hieronymus, Munsterus, Pagninus, Castalio, Anglica et Itali- ca versio: posterius Arabs in Iobo, Schindlerus et Genevenses. Ionathan reddit דייתא אוכמתא, vulturem nigrum. Ierosolymitanus, אבו ibbu, quod puto idem esse. Onkelos, טרפיתא, rapacem avem, nomine generico, quia ignoravit speciem. Arabes in Mose الصدا bubonem. Kimchius, יגא״וא, picam. Iunius et Buxtorfius, picam, aut cornicem. Arias, variam avem. Pomarius, vultu- rem, aut accipitrem. Aben Ezra, avem insularem, tanquam ab אי, id est, ab insula facto nomine. Alii Hebraeorum, ut R. Levi, Mardochaeus, Aquinas, caeteris prudentiores, solum dicunt esse שם עוף, nomen avis.

After the treatise On the Eagle we tried to explain three names of birds, namely פרס peres, עזניה oznija, and דאה daa, or ראה raa, which are found nowhere outside the catalogue of unclean birds. Since in interpreting these the ancient and modern interpreters disagree greatly, their true meaning could be extracted from no other source than the origin of the words alone. Now four follow, namely איה aja, דיה daja, עורב oreb, and בת־יענה bath-jaana; since these are found elsewhere, more light will shine on their explanation. Yet there is much doubt about the first. The Greeks explain it sometimes as vulture, sometimes as kite. col. 193 The former is followed by Jerome, Munster, Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae], Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)], and the English and Italian versions; the latter by the Arabic translator in Job, Schindler, and the Genevans. Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] renders it דייתא אוכמתא, black vulture; the Jerusalem Targum, אבו ibbu, which I think is the same. Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] has טרפיתא, bird of prey, a generic name, because he did not know the species. The Arabs in Moses have الصدا [al-ṣadā] owl. Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] has יגא״וא, magpie. Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] and Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum], magpie or crow. Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], variegated bird. Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)], vulture or hawk. Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra], island bird, as if the name were formed from אי, that is, from island. Other Hebrews, such as R. Levi, Mordecai, and Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)], more prudent than the rest, say only that it is שם עוף, the name of a bird.


Nobis Hebraeorum האיה haaja avis eadem, quae Arabum اليويو aljuju. Avis est a clamore sic dicta. Nam ut aquilarum clangere est, milvorum jugere vel lipire, accipitrum pipare, et crocitare corvorum: ita hujus avis proprium est يايا jaja, secundum Arabes, et clamor ipse dicitur اليايا aljajao. Inde igitur ipsa avis Hebraice dicta videtur איה aja, ut Arabice يويو juju, et in plurali يايي jaji. Neque novum id videri debet, ut avis nomen a voce sumatur, si vere Varro libro quarto De lingua Latina, Pleraeque (aves) a suis vocibus, ut hae, upupa, cuculus, corvus, hirundo, ulula, bubo: item hae: pavo, anser, gallina, columba. Est porro اليويو aljuju in accipitrum speciebus, quorum ut Aristoteles decem, Plinius sedecim censet genera: ita Arabes multa numerant. Atque in his est صقر sacer, vernaculo sermone sacre, qui rursus in tres species subdividitur, nempe in sacrum proprie dictum II, 780 (1), كونج chauneg, et يويو juju, de quo sic Damir: الصنف الثالث من الصغور اليويو وتسميه اهل مصر والشام الجلم لخغة جناحه وسرعته ولان الجلم هو الذي منجز به وهو المقص وهو طاير صغير قصير الذنب ومزاجه بالنسبة الي الباشق بارد رطب لانه اصبر منه نغسا واثغل حركة ويشرب الما شربا ضروريا كما يشربه الباسق الا انه ابخر ومزاجه بالنسبة الي الصغر حار يابس واذلك هو اشجع منه ويغال ان اول من ضراه واصطاد به بهرام جور وذلك انه شاهد يويو يطارد قبرة ويراوغها ويترفع وينخغض معها وما تركها الي ان صادها فاعجبه ذلك وامر به فادب وصاد به col. 194 Tertia SACRORUM species est aljuju, quem Aegyptii et Syri vocant algelem, propter alarum levitatem et celeritatem. Nempe algelem secula, seu falce instructum sonat (quasi aërem alis tanquam falce dividat). Est autem avis parva, brevis caudae: cujus temperamentum si conferas cum albasik (alio genere accipitris), est frigidum et humidum; quia spiritum diutius continet, et motu gravior est, et bibit aquam, cum necesse est, quomodo bibit albasik; eo tamen est foetidior. At, si conferas cum sacro (proprie dicto), temperamenti calidi et sicci videbitur, ac proinde illo est audacior. Quidam porro, nomine Behram Giur, primus eum ad venationem adhibuisse dicitur. Cum scilicet eo praesente avis juju alaudam insequutus fuisset, et ei colluctatus, cum illa sese efferens, et demittens, neque relinquens donec cepisset: id ille admiratus, avem erudiri jussit, et postmodum ad venationem ea usus est. Haec in Damire, unde constat, eam avem describi, quae Germanice Smirle, Italice smerlo et smeriglio, Gallice dicitur esmerillon. Quippe etiam is censetur inter accipitrum et falconum species. Sed quantitate minimus est (inquit Albertus libri vigesimi tertii capite decimo quarto), nulli tamen animo et audacia cedit pro corporis et virium suarum portione, etc. Itaque Guilielmus Falconarius refert, se harum avium opera aliquando gruem cepisse. Alioqui enim alaudas et similes aves tantum II, 781 vincere potest, etc. Alas habet longissimas respectu sui corporis, caudam mensuratam (id est, mediocrem), crura et pedes planos, etc. Sunt celerrimi, et insidiosi, et in capiendo ascendunt, ac descendunt feriendo, etc. Et Crescentiensis, Ismerli sunt quasi falconelli, id est, falcones parvi, quos et corporis specie et colore pennarum referunt, etc. Capiunt praecipue alaudas, quas tanto desiderio et impetu persequuntur, ut vel ad clibanum usque ardentem quandoque, vel in puteum, vel hominum vestes offendant. Alius apud Gesnerum, Smerillo formam habet falconis, minor sperverio, volacior quam ulla avis alia. Aves capit easdem, quas sperverius, praecipue vero parvas, ut passerem, alaudam et similes (2). Vides, le-ctor, ut Arabum aljuju, ita nostrum smirlum, vel smerillonem esse in accipitrum specie, eumque statura parvum, et cauda brevi, et volatu celerem, et audacia insignem, et alaudarum venationi maxime addictum: ut minime sit dubitandum, quin diversis nominibus eadem avis designetur. Sed et aliud est notandum inprimis, quia maxime ad rem nostram facit. Si quis vivaces oculos habet et maxime perspicaces, eum vulgato adagio Galli smerillonis oculos habere dicunt; quia tales habet haec avis. Et Arabum quoque poetae oculos sui juju multum commendant. In his anonymus apud Damirem,

In our view the Hebrew האיה haaja is the same bird as the Arabic اليويو [al-yūyū] aljuju. The bird is so called from its cry. For just as eagles are said to clangere, kites jugere or lipire, hawks pipare, and ravens crocitare, so the proper sound of this bird, according to the Arabs, is يايا [yāyā] jaja, and the cry itself is called اليايا [al-yāyā] aljajao. From this, then, the bird itself seems to have been called in Hebrew איה aja, as in Arabic يويو [yūyū] juju, and in the plural يايي [yāyī] jaji. Nor should it seem strange that a bird's name is taken from its voice, if Varro is right in book 4 of On the Latin Language: Most (birds) are named from their own calls, such as these: upupa, cuculus, corvus, hirundo, ulula, bubo; likewise these: pavo, anser, gallina, columba. Further, اليويو [al-yūyū] aljuju is among the species of hawks; and as Aristotle reckons ten kinds of them and Pliny sixteen, so the Arabs too count many. Among these is the صقر [ṣaqr] sacer, in the vernacular sacre, which is again subdivided into three species, namely the saker properly so called II, 780 R1, the كونج [kawnaj] chauneg, and the يويو [yūyū] juju, of which Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] says: الصنف الثالث من الصغور اليويو وتسميه اهل مصر والشام الجلم لخغة جناحه وسرعته ولان الجلم هو الذي منجز به وهو المقص وهو طاير صغير قصير الذنب ومزاجه بالنسبة الي الباشق بارد رطب لانه اصبر منه نغسا واثغل حركة ويشرب الما شربا ضروريا كما يشربه الباسق الا انه ابخر ومزاجه بالنسبة الي الصغر حار يابس واذلك هو اشجع منه ويغال ان اول من ضراه واصطاد به بهرام جور وذلك انه شاهد يويو يطارد قبرة ويراوغها ويترفع وينخغض معها وما تركها الي ان صادها فاعجبه ذلك وامر به فادب وصاد به [al-ṣinf al-thālith min al-ṣughūr al-yūyū wa-tusammīhi ahl Miṣr wa-l-Shām al-jalam li-khiffat janāḥihi wa-surʿatihi wa-li-anna al-jalam huwa alladhī munjaz bihi wa-huwa al-miqaṣṣ wa-huwa ṭāyir ṣaghīr qaṣīr al-dhanab wa-mizājuhu bi-l-nisba ilā al-bāshiq bārid raṭb li-annahu aṣbar minhu nafasan wa-athqal ḥarakatan wa-yashrab al-mā shurban ḍarūriyyan kamā yashrabuhu al-bāsiq illā annahu abkhar wa-mizājuhu bi-l-nisba ilā al-ṣaqr ḥārr yābis wa-li-dhālika huwa ashjaʿ minhu wa-yuqāl anna awwal man ḍarrāhu wa-iṣṭāda bihi Bahrām Jūr wa-dhālika annahu shāhada yūyū yuṭārid qubbara wa-yurāwighuhā wa-yatarafaʿ wa-yankhafiḍ maʿahā wa-mā tarakahā ilā an ṣādahā fa-aʿjabahu dhālika wa-amara bihi fa-uddiba wa-ṣāda bihi] col. 194 The third species of SAKERS is aljuju, which the Egyptians and Syrians call algelem, because of the lightness and swiftness of its wings. For algelem means a sickle, or one furnished with a sickle (as though it cut the air with its wings as with a sickle). It is a small bird with a short tail. If you compare its temperament with that of albasik (another kind of hawk), it is cold and moist, because it holds its breath longer and is heavier in movement, and it drinks water when it must, as albasik drinks; yet it is more foul-smelling than it. But if you compare it with the saker (properly so called), it will appear to be of a hot and dry temperament, and is accordingly bolder than it. Moreover, a certain man named Behram Giur is said to have been the first to use it for hunting. For when, in his presence, a juju bird had pursued a lark and grappled with it, rising and descending with it, and not leaving it until it had caught it, he marvelled at this, ordered the bird to be trained, and afterwards used it for hunting. So far Damir. From this it is clear that the bird described is the one called in German Smirle, in Italian smerlo and smeriglio, in French esmerillon [merlin]. For it too is reckoned among the species of hawks and falcons. But in size it is the smallest (says Albertus, book 23, chapter 14), yet it yields to none in spirit and daring, in proportion to its body and strength, etc. Thus William the Falconer reports that he once caught a crane by means of these birds. Otherwise it can overcome only larks and similar birds II, 781 etc. Its wings are very long in relation to its body, its tail moderate (that is, of middling size), its legs and feet flat, etc. They are very swift and crafty, and in taking their prey they ascend, and descend as they strike, etc. And Crescentiensis: The Ismerli are like falconelli, that is, little falcons, which they resemble both in shape of body and in colour of plumage, etc. They take chiefly larks, which they pursue with such eagerness and impetus that they sometimes dash even against a burning oven, or into a well, or against men's clothing. Another writer in Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium]: The Smerillo has the form of a falcon, is smaller than the sparrowhawk, and flies faster than any other bird. It takes the same birds as the sparrowhawk, but especially small ones, such as the sparrow, the lark and the like R2. You see, reader, that like the Arabs' aljuju, our smirlus or smerillon belongs to the hawk species, is small in stature, short-tailed, swift in flight, remarkable for daring, and especially given to hunting larks; so that there can be no doubt at all that the same bird is designated by different names. But another point must above all be noted, because it bears most on our subject. If someone has lively and very keen eyes, the French say by a common proverb that he has the eyes of a smerillon, because this bird has such eyes. And the Arab poets too greatly praise the eyes of their juju. Among them an anonymous poet in Damir:


يويو مهذب رشيق ۞ كان عينيه لذي التحقيق ۞ فصان مخروطان من عقيق ۞

يويو مهذب رشيق ۞ كان عينيه لذي التحقيق ۞ فصان مخروطان من عقيق ۞ [yūyū muhadhdhab rashīq ۞ ka-anna ʿaynayhi li-dhī al-taḥqīq ۞ faṣṣān makhrūṭān min ʿaqīq ۞]


Iuju (volatu) celer et pernix, cujus oculi sunt vere suaves, et pupillae tanquam torno expolitae plus quam sapphirus. Et Abu Navvas in opere De aucupiis, cui titulus طريدة Tarida, de eadem ave inter caetera haec habet:

The Iuju is swift and nimble (in flight), whose eyes are truly lovely, and its pupils, as if polished on the lathe, more than sapphire. And Abu Nuwas, in his work On Fowling, entitled طريدة [Ṭarīda] Tarida, says of the same bird, among other things:


ازرق لا تكذب عيناه ۞ فلا يري القانص ما يراه ۞

ازرق لا تكذب عيناه ۞ فلا يري القانص ما يراه ۞ [azraq lā takdhib ʿaynāhu ۞ fa-lā yarā al-qāniṣ mā yarāhu ۞]


Quae Latinis verbis pene ad verbum sic expressimus, col. 195

These we have rendered in Latin words almost word for word thus: col. 195


Caesius, atque oculis nunquam fallentibus usus,
Et quod venator non videt, ille videt.

Grey-eyed, and with eyes that never deceive,
What the hunter does not see, that bird sees.


Haec porro ad rem nostram ideo maxime pertinere diximus; quia de ejusdem avis oculo haec leguntur, Iob. XXVIII, 7. Semitam non novit עיט, avis, neque eam vidit עין איה, oculus τοῦ aja. Agit de fodinis, unde hominum industria metalla eruuntur. Quae cum in intimis terrae visceribus lateant, harum semitam, II, 782 inquit sacer scriptor, non novit עיט ajit, id est, avis non quaevis, sed avis rapax, quod genus multo est perspicacius. Haec in priore hemistichio, et in al-tero, huic parallelo, Neque eam vidit oculus τοῦ aja, vel juju, si mavis, id est, smerillonis, licet illa avis sit oculatissima, et tam cernat acutum, quam ut aquila, aut serpens Epidaurius. Smerillonem esse veterum αἰσαλῶνα, aesalonem, multa probant. 1. Quod Aristoteles (Hist. lib. 9. cap. 36.) et Plinius (lib. 10. cap. 8.) aesalonem recensent inter accipitrum species. 2. Quod ab Aeliano (lib. 2. cap. 51.) vocatur ὄρνις ἰσχυρός (3). 3. Et a Plinio (lib. 10. cap. 74.) parva avis. 4. Quod idem Plinius (lib. 10. cap. 8.) aesalonem scribit omni tempore apparere, cum caeteri hyeme abeant. Id enim smerilloni prorsus convenit, ut a Turnero notatum. Verba sunt: Inter minores accipitres sola merlina, ut Angli vocant, sive smerla, ut Germani, semper apparet. Tamen id falsum esse, contendit nobilissimus Dominus de Grentemesnil. Sunt, qui pro aesalone aesaronem scribant. Hesychius, Αἰσάρων· εἶδος ἱέρακος. Utrumque fortasse ab αἶσα, quia est avis αἴσιος, auspicata, et boni ominis, ut accipitrum omne genus. Quod nullo negotio probaverim, si tanti esset.

We have said that these words bear especially on our subject, because the following is read of the eye of this same bird, Iob. XXVIII, 7: The bird עיט knew not the path, nor has עין איה, the eye of the aja, seen it. He is speaking of mines, from which metals are dug out by human industry. Since these lie hidden in the innermost bowels of the earth, their path, II, 782 says the sacred writer, the עיט ajit knew not, that is, not just any bird, but the bird of prey, a kind that is far more keen-sighted. This is in the first hemistich; and in the other, parallel to it: Nor has the eye of the aja, or juju if you prefer, seen it, that is, of the smerillon [merlin], although that bird is most sharp-eyed and sees as keenly as the eagle or the Epidaurian serpent. Many things prove that the smerillon is the αἰσαλών [aisalōn], the aesalon, of the ancients. 1. Aristotle (Hist. book 9, ch. 36) and Pliny (book 10, ch. 8) list the aesalon among the species of hawks. 2. By Aelian (book 2, ch. 51) it is called ὄρνις ἰσχυρός [ornis ischyros] R3. 3. And by Pliny (book 10, ch. 74) a small bird. 4. The same Pliny (book 10, ch. 8) writes that the aesalon appears at every season, whereas the others depart in winter. This fits the smerillon exactly, as Turner [=William Turner, Avium praecipuarum historia (1544)] has noted. His words are: Among the smaller hawks only the merlin, as the English call it, or smerla, as the Germans do, is always seen. Yet the most noble Lord de Grentemesnil contends that this is false. Some write aesaron instead of aesalon. Hesychius: Αἰσάρων· εἶδος ἱέρακος [Aisarōn; eidos hierakos]. Both perhaps come from αἶσα [aisa], because it is a bird αἴσιος [aisios], auspicious and of good omen, like every kind of hawk. This I could prove without any trouble, if it were worth the effort.

Part 2, Book 2, chapter 9: Daja is the black vulture
