II, 782 col. 195 CAP. IX.

II, 782 col. 195 CHAPTER IX.


Probatur, דיה daja esse Vulturem nigrum.

It is proved that דיה daja is the black vulture.


Post איה aja sequitur דיה daja, Deut. XIV, 13. Quod omissum in Levitico, vel ab ipso Propheta, qua de causa nescimus, vel a scribis post Prophetam propter τὸ ὁμοιόπτωτον duarum vocum האיה haaja et הדיה hadaja, quod ultimum puto esse vero propius. Quid sit דיה daja, non satis notum est. Hieronymus, et Arabes (1), et multi recentiorum milvum interpretantur, quasi sit II, 783 idem, quod דאה daa, Levit. XI, 14. (2). Quod vix videtur posse ferri: quia, ut probavimus, דאה daa et ראה raa idem sunt. Porro, ראה raa et דיה daja non possunt idem esse, cum in eodem versu Iudaeis prohibeantur tanquam diversa animalia. Ita enim habet sacer textus: Haec sunt, ex quibus non comedetis, aquila, etc. והראה ואת האיה והדיה, et raa, et aja, et daja. Ubi cum ראה raa sit idem, quod in Levitico דאה daa, milvus scilicet, omnino דיה daja aliud est: nempe vultur, ut quidem puto. Quomodo reddunt R. Selomo, Castalio, col. 196 Schindlerus, Anglica et Italica versio. Fullerus quoque Miscellaneorum lib. 6. cap. 4. Cui versioni firmandae multum faciunt haec Es. XXXIV, 15. de Idumaeae desolatione, Ibi דיות dajoth inter se convenerunt. Nam דיות dajoth, Plurale τοῦ דיה daja, non possunt esse milvi, qui non sunt gregales aves, neque unquam inter se conveniunt, aut congregantur (3). Sed possunt esse vultures, de quibus Gesnerus pag. 785. Vultures soli uncunguium gregatim degunt, ita, ut aliquando quinquaginta in uno grege appareant, ut in Aegypto se observasse scribit II, 784 Bellonius. Hinc Philosophus Hist. libro sexto capite quinto, Πολλοὶ ἐξαί-φνης φαίνονται ἀκολουθοῦντες τοῖς στρατεύμασι· Multi derepente apparent, qui sequuntur exercitus. Et libri noni capite undecimo idem scribit, φαίνεσθαι τα-χὺ πολλοὺς, subito apparere multos. Basilius quoque in Hexaëmeron Homilia octava, Ἴδοις ἂν μυρίας ἀγέλας γυπῶν τοῖς στρατοπέδοις παρεπομένας· Vulturum videas innumeros greges exercitus sequentes. Et Ambrosius, hunc imitatus, in Hexaëmeron libri quinti capite vigesimo tertio, Cum bellum lacrymabile inter se adversae acies instaurant, multo praedictae volucres sequuntur agmine. Petrus Bembus Historiae Venetae libro quinto, Constat illis diebus, quibus bellum contra Bajazetem parabatur in Apulia, corvos vulturesque tanta ex aëre vi, tantisque agminibus inter se conflixisse, ut carri duodecim eorum cadaveribus explerentur. Non possum hic omittere duodecim vultures, a Romulo visos, tum, cum Romam urbem condidit: unde collegit Vectius, Romano imperio post exacta totidem saecula finem fore. Quod post Varronem scripsit Censorinus capite decimo quarto, anno ab urbe condita circiter millesimo. Quot, inquit, saecula urbi Romae debeantur, dicere meum non est. Sed, quid apud Varronem legerim, non tacebo, qui libro Antiquitatum duodevigesimo ait fuisse Vectium Romae in augurio non ignobilem ingenio, cuivis doctori in disceptando parem. Eum se audivisse dicentem, Si ita essent, ut tradebant Historici de Romuli urbis condendae auguriis, ac duodecim vulturibus, quoniam CXX annos incolumis praeteriisset, populum Romanum ad mille et ducentos perventurum. Neque defuit eventus vaticinio. Nam paullo post exacta duodecim illa saecula, reipublicae viribus ex Occidente in Orientem translatis, Romana dignitas consumpta est, et occidentale imperium defecit in Augustulo. Is enim purpuram deposuit Herulorum metu, qui Adovacre duce in Italiam irruperant, ut scribit Paulus Diaconus libro decimo sexto. Ita Caesari, cum in campum Martium exercitum deduceret, sex vultures apparuerunt. Conscendenti deinde rostra creato consuli iterum sex vultures conspecti, veluti Romuli auspiciis novam urbem condituro, signum dederunt. Ita tradit Iulius Obsequens. Et apud Suetonium Octavio Augusto, primo consulatu augurium capienti, duodecim se vultures, ut Romulo, ostenderunt. Quod paullo aliter refert Dio, Πρώτῃ τῶν ἀρχαιρεσιῶν ἐς τὸ πεδίον τὸ Ἄρειον εἰσελθὼν, γύπας ἓξ· καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα δημηγορῶν τι πρὸς τοὺς στρατειώ-τας, ἄλλους δώδεκα εἶδε. Comitiorum prima die, in campum Martium ingressus, sex vultures: nec paullo post, cum militibus orationem haberet, duodecim alios vidit. Ex quibus hoc saltem colligere est, vultures saepe congregari, quod de avibus aliis rapacibus non scribitur. Frustra objeceris, quod legitur Matth. XXIV, 28. et Luc. XVII, 37. etiam aquilas ad cadaver congregari. Neque enim ibi agitur de genuinis aquilis, sed de percnopteris, seu gypaeetis, quae sunt aquilae degeneres, et vulturina specie, atque ex aquilae cum vulture concubitu, II, 785 ut videtur, ortae; quod supraa) docuimus. Utut sit, quisquis in Esaiae verbis, quibus דיות dajoth convenire, aut congregari scribit, milvos intelligi volet, is necesse habebit docere, vel experientia teste, vel ex idoneis scriptoribus, milvos quandoque congregari. Quod a milvorum genio tam abhorret, quam vulturum naturae convenit. Omnino igitur דיות dajoth sunt vultures, non mil- col. 197 vi. Non tamen putaverim, omne vulturum genus hoc nomine contineri, sed solum nigros. 1. Quia Deut. XIV, 13. 17. a Mose distinguuntur tanquam diversa animalia דיה daja et רחם racham; quorum hoc significare vulturis genus, magna ex parte album, infra dicetur. 2. Quia דיה daja et דיו dejo, atramen- tum, sunt Conjugata. Ne dicam, a Syris et Persis daemonem dici ܕܝܘܐ dajava, vel deva, ab atri coloris specie, qua potissimum hominibus se conspiciendum exhibet, ut graviorem intuentibus terrorem incutiat. Unde est, quod quaedam sabinae species Persice ديودار diudar dicitur, id est, daemonis ar- bor. Itaque etiam a colore דיה daja vocatur id vulturis genus, quod nigrum est. Et recte Elias, דיה Daja dicitur avis, quae nigra est כדיו, ut atramentum. Nec immerito Kimchius דיה et דיו revocat ad eandem Radicem. Porro de nigro vulture multa legere est apud veteres. Ita Plinius libri decimi capite sexto dicit, vulturum praevalere nigros. Et apud poëtas inter inferorum poenas una est e gravissimis, ab atro vulture rodi. Hinc Iuvenalis Satyra decima tertia,

After איה aja comes דיה daja, Deut 14:13. It is omitted in Leviticus, either by the Prophet himself, for a reason we do not know, or by scribes after the Prophet because of the τὸ ὁμοιόπτωτον [to homoioptōton] of the two words האיה haaja and הדיה hadaja; I think the latter is nearer the truth. What דיה daja is, is not sufficiently known. Jerome, the Arabs R1, and many of the more recent writers interpret it as the kite, as though it were II, 783 the same as דאה daa, Lev 11:14 R2. This seems scarcely tenable, because, as we have proved, דאה daa and ראה raa are the same. Moreover, ראה raa and דיה daja cannot be the same, since in the same verse they are forbidden to the Jews as different animals. For the sacred text reads: These are the ones of which you shall not eat: the eagle, etc. והראה ואת האיה והדיה, and the raa, and the aja, and the daja. Here, since ראה raa is the same as דאה daa in Leviticus, namely the kite, דיה daja is certainly something else: namely the vulture, as I at least think. So render R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)], Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)], col. 196 Schindler, and the English and Italian versions; also Fuller [=Nicholas Fuller, Miscellanea theologica / sacra (1612–22)], Miscellanea book 6, ch. 4. This rendering is strongly confirmed by Es. XXXIV, 15., on the desolation of Idumaea: There the דיות dajoth have gathered together. For דיות dajoth, the plural of דיה daja, cannot be kites, which are not gregarious birds and never gather or flock together R3. But they can be vultures, of which Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium] says, p. 785: Vultures alone among the birds with hooked talons live in flocks, so that sometimes fifty appear in a single flock, as Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)] writes that he observed II, 784 in Egypt. Hence the Philosopher, Hist. book 6, chapter 5: Πολλοὶ ἐξαίφνης φαίνονται ἀκολουθοῦντες τοῖς στρατεύμασι [polloi exaiphnēs phainontai akolouthountes tois strateumasi]; Many suddenly appear, following armies. And in book 9, chapter 11, he writes likewise, φαίνεσθαι ταχὺ πολλοὺς [phainesthai tachy pollous], that many suddenly appear. Basil too, in the Hexaemeron, Homily 8: Ἴδοις ἂν μυρίας ἀγέλας γυπῶν τοῖς στρατοπέδοις παρεπομένας [Idois an myrias agelas gypōn tois stratopedois parepomenas]; You may see countless flocks of vultures following armies. And Ambrose, imitating him, in the Hexaemeron, book 5, chapter 23: When opposing lines renew a lamentable war among themselves, the aforesaid birds follow in a great column. Pietro Bembo [=Pietro Bembo, Historia Veneta (1551)], History of Venice, book 5: It is established that in those days when war against Bajazet was being prepared in Apulia, ravens and vultures fought one another in the air with such force and in such hosts that twelve carts were filled with their carcasses. I cannot here omit the twelve vultures seen by Romulus when he founded the city of Rome, from which Vettius inferred that the Roman empire would end after as many centuries had passed. Censorinus, following Varro, wrote of this in chapter 14, about the thousandth year from the founding of the city. How many centuries, he says, are owed to the city of Rome it is not for me to say. But I will not keep silent about what I have read in Varro, who in book 18 of the Antiquities says that there was at Rome one Vettius, not undistinguished in augury for his talent, equal to any learned man in debate; and that he had heard him say that if things were as the historians reported about the auguries of Romulus at the founding of the city and the twelve vultures, then, since the Roman people had passed 120 years unharmed, it would reach a thousand two hundred. Nor did the prophecy lack fulfilment. For shortly after those twelve centuries had passed, when the strength of the state had been transferred from the West to the East, the Roman dignity was exhausted and the Western empire came to an end in Augustulus. For he laid down the purple out of fear of the Heruli, who under their leader Odoacer had burst into Italy, as Paul the Deacon writes in book 16. Likewise, when Caesar was leading his army down into the Campus Martius, six vultures appeared to him. Then, when he mounted the rostra after being made consul, six vultures were again seen and gave a sign, as though he were to found a new city under the auspices of Romulus. So Julius Obsequens reports. And in Suetonius, twelve vultures showed themselves to Octavius Augustus, as to Romulus, when he was taking the auspices in his first consulship. Dio reports this somewhat differently: Πρώτῃ τῶν ἀρχαιρεσιῶν ἐς τὸ πεδίον τὸ Ἄρειον εἰσελθὼν, γύπας ἓξ· καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα δημηγορῶν τι πρὸς τοὺς στρατειώτας, ἄλλους δώδεκα εἶδε [Prōtē tōn archairesiōn es to pedion to Areion eiselthōn, gypas hex; kai meta tauta dēmēgorōn ti pros tous strateiōtas, allous dōdeka eide]. On the first day of the elections, having entered the Campus Martius, he saw six vultures; and shortly afterwards, while addressing the soldiers, twelve others. From these it can at least be inferred that vultures often flock together, which is not written of other birds of prey. In vain would you object what we read in Matt 24:28 and Luke 17:37, that eagles too gather at a carcass. For there it is not a question of true eagles but of percnopteri, or gypaeeti, which are degenerate eagles of vulturine appearance, born, II, 785 as it seems, from the mating of an eagle with a vulture, as we showed abovea). However that may be, whoever would have kites understood in the words of Isaiah where he writes that the דיות dajoth gather or flock together, will have to show, either from experience or from reliable writers, that kites sometimes flock together. This is as foreign to the disposition of kites as it is suited to the nature of vultures. Therefore the דיות dajoth are certainly vultures, not kites. col. 197 Yet I would not think that every kind of vulture is contained under this name, but only the black ones. 1. Because in Deut 14:13 17. Moses distinguishes דיה daja and רחם racham as different animals; and that the latter signifies a kind of vulture largely white will be shown below. 2. Because דיה daja and דיו dejo, ink, are cognates. Not to mention that the Syrians and Persians call a demon ܕܝܘܐ [דיוא] dajava, or deva, from the appearance of a black colour, in which it chiefly shows itself to men, to strike greater terror into those who see it. Hence a certain species of savin is called in Persian ديودار [dīvdār] diudar, that is, demon's tree. So also that kind of vulture which is black is called דיה daja from its colour. And Elias [=Elijah Levita (1469–1549), author of the Aramaic lexicon Meturgeman and of Tishbi] rightly says: The bird that is black כדיו, like ink, is called דיה Daja. Nor without reason does Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] refer דיה and דיו to the same root. Moreover, much can be read about the black vulture in the ancients. Thus Pliny, book 10, chapter 6, says that among vultures the black ones prevail. And among the poets, one of the gravest punishments of the underworld is to be gnawed by a black vulture. Hence Juvenal, Satire 13,


— — — nec saxum, aut vulturis atri
Poena. — — — — — —

— — — nor the rock, or the punishment
of the black vulture. — — — — — —


Et Seneca in Thyeste de Tityo,

And Seneca in the Thyestes, of Tityus:


Visceribus atras pascit effossis aves.

With his dug-out entrails he feeds the black birds.


Atras aves, id est, vultures nigros. Medici quoque in pharmacis suis li-bentius utuntur atro vulture. Sic Samonicus capit decimo quarto ad oculorum dolorem mitigandum adhiberi vult

Black birds, that is, black vultures. Physicians, too, prefer to use the black vulture in their remedies. Thus Samonicus, in chapter 14, would have applied, to soothe pain of the eyes,


— — — — vulturis atri
Fella, chelidoniae fuerint quis gramina mista.

— — — — the gall of the black vulture,
with which blades of celandine have been mixed.


Et capite trigesimo quarto πρὸς εὐτοκίαν

And in chapter 34, πρὸς εὐτοκίαν [pros eutokian] [for an easy delivery]:


— — stercus supponunt vulturis atri, Sentiat ut minime partus quam proximus urget. II, 786 Et capite quinquagesimo octavo ad comitialem morbum,

— — they place beneath the dung of the black vulture, so that she may scarcely feel the birth that presses close. II, 786 And in chapter 58, for the falling sickness:


Prodest cum veteri Baccho fel vulturis atri.

The gall of the black vulture is of help with old Bacchus.


Quamvis alii ampli legant: et excipiat Plinius remedia contra serpentes, in quibus nigros vultures minus valere scribit libri vigesimi noni capite quarto. Ex volucribus (inquit) in auxilio contra serpentes primum vultur est. Annotatum quoque, minus virium esse nigris. Nigros illos vultures αἰγυπιοὺς proprie dici, ac utriusque sexus, contra quam alios vultures, et inter aquilinum et vulturinum genus, Aelianus his verbis tradit libri secundi capite quadragesimo sexto: Τοὺς δὲ αἰγυπιοὺς (λέγουσιν) ἐν μεθορίῳ γυπῶν ὄντας καὶ αἰετῶν, εἶναι καὶ ἄῤῥενας, καὶ τὴν χρόαν πεφυκέναι μέλανας. Et Phile aegypios pro Aegyptiis dici insinuat, cum capite secundo scribit, εἶναι δὲ καὶ τοὺς μέλανας ὡς Αἰγυπτίους, eos etiam esse nigros, ut Aegyptios(4). Sed aliud αἰγυπιὸς, aliud Αἰγύπτιος. Illud ἀπὸ τῆς γυπός· hoc vero factum ex Cophti.

Others, however, read ampli [large]; and Pliny makes an exception for remedies against serpents, in which, he writes in book 29, chapter 4, black vultures are less effective. Among birds (he says) the vulture is foremost as a help against serpents. It has also been noted that the black ones have less power. That those black vultures are properly called αἰγυπιοὺς [aigypious], that they are of both sexes, unlike other vultures, and that they stand between the eagle kind and the vulture kind, Aelian reports in book 2, chapter 46, in these words: Τοὺς δὲ αἰγυπιοὺς (λέγουσιν) ἐν μεθορίῳ γυπῶν ὄντας καὶ αἰετῶν, εἶναι καὶ ἄῤῥενας, καὶ τὴν χρόαν πεφυκέναι μέλανας [tous de aigypious (legousin) en methoriō gypōn ontas kai aietōn, einai kai arrhenas, kai tēn chroan pephykenai melanas]. And Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)] hints that aegypii are so called for Aegyptii [Egyptians], when he writes in chapter 2: εἶναι δὲ καὶ τοὺς μέλανας ὡς Αἰγυπτίους [einai de kai tous melanas hōs Aigyptious], that they too are black, like EgyptiansR4. But αἰγυπιὸς [aigypios] is one thing, Αἰγύπτιος [Aigyptios] another. The former comes from γυπός [gypos]; the latter is formed from Cophti.

(3) Rosenmüller, II, 783 Sed contrarium asserit Oedmann pag. 81. Bellonium producens testem, quippe qui magnas milvorum catervas a se visas esse scribat, et quidem ita densas, ut volantium turba solis radios obscurasset. Sed, quod pace viri doctissimi dictum sit, videtur is Bellonii verbis sinistre usus esse. En ipsa Bellonii verba (de avibus Lib. II. cap. 28.): Cum aliquando in littore Ponti Euxini ea parte, qua Thracia est, versaremur, ultimo fere Aprili, in colle quodam eminentissimo, columnae illi, quae ad ostium Bosphori est, proximo, ubi rete tenderet auceps capiendis Nisis, qui a dextra maris plaga ad-volabant, observavimus Milvos, gregatim eo adventantes recto tractu, frequenti adeo numero ac denso agmine, ut miraculi loco nobis ea res esset. — Aestate vero adventante, ut nimium illarum regionum aestum effugiant, in Europam revertuntur. T. I. Lib. V. Cap. XV. pag. 401. Bellonius etiam l. c. in Aegypto milvos prae mansuetudine ad fenestras usque domuum advolare, scribit.

R3 Rosenmüller, II, 783 But Oedmann, p. 81, asserts the contrary, producing Belon as witness, who writes that he saw great flocks of kites, and so dense that the crowd of birds in flight darkened the rays of the sun. But, with all respect to that most learned man, he seems to have made poor use of Belon's words. For in the passage Oedmann cites, Belon is speaking of kites changing their abode as winter approaches, and then, like absolutely all migratory birds, flying in great swarms. Here are Belon's own words (de avibus book 2, ch. 28): Once, when we were on the shore of the Euxine Sea, in the part where Thrace lies, at about the end of April, on a very lofty hill next to the column that stands at the mouth of the Bosporus, where a fowler was spreading a net to catch sparrowhawks flying in from the right-hand stretch of the sea, we observed kites arriving there in flocks on a straight course, in such numbers and so dense a column that it seemed a marvel to us. — But when summer comes on, they return to Europe to escape the excessive heat of those regions. But there is yet another thing that prevents us from taking דיות as kites. It is clear from Isa 34:15 that the דיות inhabit desolate places and wildernesses, whereas kites shun the wilderness and seek out cities and places frequented by men, as Aldrovandi [=Ulisse Aldrovandi, Ornithologia (1599–1603)] reports from his own observation and the testimony of many others, Ornithol. vol. 1, book 5, ch. 15, p. 401. Belon too, loc. cit., writes that in Egypt kites are so tame that they fly right up to the windows of houses.


a) Bochart, II, 785 Cap. 2. pag. 175.

a) Bochart, II, 785 Chapter 2, p. 175.


(4) Rosenmüller, II, 786 Αἰγυπιον Schneiderus ad Aelian. II, 46. eundem suspicatur, quem Bellonius (de avibus Lib. II. cap. 23.) in Aegypto frequentem vidit, et vulturem nigrum appellavit, de quo tamen nondum satis constet, an idem sit cum percnoptero Linnaei. R4 Rosenmüller, II, 786 Schneider, on Aelian 2, 46, suspects that the Αἰγυπιον [Aigypion] is the same bird that Belon (de avibus book 2, ch. 23) saw frequently in Egypt and called the black vulture, although it is not yet sufficiently established whether it is the same as Linnaeus' percnopterus. The same Schneider, on the Reliqua of Frederick II, p. 14, observes that the vultur ater [dark vulture] of the ancients is the Emperor's Galeranus niger (p. 28), the Avoltoio nero of Cetti [=Francesco Cetti, Storia naturale di Sardegna (1774–77)] in the Histor. Nat. Sardin. vol. 2, p. 9 ff., German trans. In the newest edition of the Linnaean System, vol. 1, part 1, p. 248, no. 9, this species of vulture appears under the heading Vultur niger, with dusky primaries and tail feathers, the feathers of the feet black. Yet Gmelin [=J. F. Gmelin, 13th edition of Linnaeus, Systema naturae (1788–93)] too doubts whether it is a mere variety of the percnopterus (which is the Hebrew and Arabic רחם). — But by what argument Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)], in the Clavis in Iesaj. p. 234, was moved to take the דיות as white vultures, I for my part cannot grasp.


Part 2, Book 2, chapter 10: The raven

https://openseforim.org/bochart/corvus.html

II, 787 col. 197 CAP. X.

II, 787 col. 197 Chapter X.


Corvi nomina, vox, color, sedes, victus, species, etc.

The names of the raven, its voice, colour, abode, food, kinds, etc.


Corvus, de quo jam agendum, duo habet, quae in sensus maxime se inge- col. 198 runt, crocitationem et nigredinem. Crocitatio, Graece κρωγμὸς, est vox rauca et aspera, ex imis ducta faucibus, quam corvi, quasi certatim, magna contentione ingeminant; inprimis, cum pluvias et tempestates praesagiunt. Hinc Nicander Theriacῶν versu 406.

The raven, which we must now treat, has two features that most force themselves upon the senses: col. 198 its croaking and its blackness. Croaking, in Greek κρωγμὸς [krōgmos], is a hoarse and harsh sound drawn from the depths of the throat, which ravens repeat over and over with great effort, as if in competition; above all when they foretell rains and storms. Hence Nicander, Theriaca, line 406:


Αἰγυπιοὶ, γῦπές τε, κόραξ τ᾽ ὀμβρήρεα κρώζων,

Αἰγυπιοὶ, γῦπές τε, κόραξ τ᾽ ὀμβρήρεα κρώζων, [Aigypioi, gypes te, korax t᾽ ombrērea krōzōn,]


Aegypii, et vultures, et corvus pluvia crocitans, id est, pluvium tempus futurum crocitatione praenuntians. Lucretius libri quinti versu 1082.

Aegypii, and vultures, and the raven croaking of rain, that is, announcing rainy weather to come by its croaking. Lucretius, book 5, line 1082:


Et partim mutant cum tempestatibus una
Raucisonos cantus cornicum, et saec'la vetusta,
Corvorumque greges, ubi aquas dicuntur et imbres
Poscere, et interdum ventos aurasque vocare.

And in part they change together with the weather
The hoarse-sounding songs of the crows, and the long-lived generations,
And the flocks of ravens, when they are said to call for
Waters and rains, and at times to summon winds and breezes.


Nigredo quoque corvi propria, eaque intensissima, et per totum corpus diffusa. Non tamen usquequaque verum est, quod a Porphyrio scribitur capite quinto Isagoges: Τὸ δὲ μέλαν εἶναι ἀχωρίστως τῷ κόρακι καὶ τῷ Αἰθίοπι συμ-βέβηκε· Nigredo corvo et Aethiopi sic inest, ut separari non possit. Quippe etiam albi corvi visi sunt. Aristoteles, De generatione animalium libri quinti capite sexto, Ὦπται καὶ πέρδιξ λευκὴ, καὶ κόραξ· Perdix visa est alba, et corvus. Heraclides in Republica Cyren. Ἀρκεσιλάου δὲ βασιλεύοντος λευκὸς κόραξ ἐφά-νη· Regnante Arcesilao, corvus albus apparuit. Quales hodieque in Suecia et Norvegia reperiuntur, ubi frigus est intensius. Tamen in confesso est, corvum alvum raro inveniri. Hinc Iuvenalis Satyra septima,

Blackness, too, is proper to the raven, and that most intense, and spread over its whole body. Yet what Porphyry writes in chapter 5 of the Isagoge is not true without exception: Τὸ δὲ μέλαν εἶναι ἀχωρίστως τῷ κόρακι καὶ τῷ Αἰθίοπι συμβέβηκε· [To de melan einai achōristōs tō koraki kai tō Aithiopi symbebēke;] Blackness is so present in the raven and the Ethiopian that it cannot be separated. For white ravens too have been seen. Aristotle, On the Generation of Animals, book 5, chapter 6: Ὦπται καὶ πέρδιξ λευκὴ, καὶ κόραξ· [Ōptai kai perdix leukē, kai korax;] A white partridge has been seen, and a raven. Heraclides in the Constitution of Cyrene: Ἀρκεσιλάου δὲ βασιλεύοντος λευκὸς κόραξ ἐφάνη· [Arkesilaou de basileuontos leukos korax ephanē;] When Arcesilaus was king, a white raven appeared. Such are found even today in Sweden and Norway, where the cold is more intense. Yet it is admitted that a white raven is rarely found. Hence Juvenal, Satire 7:


Felix ille tamen, corvo quoque rarior albo.

Yet he is fortunate, rarer even than a white raven.


Et Ammianus Anthologiae libri secundi capite quadragesimo sexto, Epigrammate decimo septimo,

And Ammianus in the Anthology, book 2, chapter 46, Epigram 17:


Θᾶττον ἔην λευκοὺς κόρακας, πτηνάς τε χελώνας
Εὑρεῖν, ἢ δόκιμον ῥήτορα Καππαδόκην·

Θᾶττον ἔην λευκοὺς κόρακας, πτηνάς τε χελώνας Εὑρεῖν, ἢ δόκιμον ῥήτορα Καππαδόκην· [Thatton eēn leukous korakas, ptēnas te chelōnas heurein, ē dokimon rhētora Kappadokēn;]


Facilius est, albos corvos et testudines volantes reperire, quam probum rhetorem Cappadocem. Itaque, ut haec duo, crocitatio, inquam, et nigredo, sunt corvo maxime propria: ita pleraque corvi nomina ex alterutro sumpta sunt. Sic a crocitatione ܢܥܒܐ neab; et Arabice نعاب noab, a verbo نعب naa- ba scilicet, quod crocitare significat. Et in Aethiopico corvi nomine ቋዕ፡ II, 788 koe manifesta est imitatio corvinae vocis. Indidem natum Graecum κόραξ, ut κρώζειν· et Romana crocire, et crocitare. Nam frustra sunt, qui κόρακα dici volunt παρὰ τὸν κόρον, ὃ σημαίνει τὸ μέλαν· cum κόρος pro nigro apud veteres nusquam occurrat. At Hebraicum עורב oreb, Chaldaicum ערבא orba, Arabicum غراب gorab (unde Romani corvum dixere), palam ad colorem pertinent. Hebraice enim ערב ereb est vespera, et ערב arab, Verbum advesperascere, obtenebrescere. Unde Arabice غربيب garbib est niger (Ain initiali mutata in Gain propter punctum appositum); itaque hic idem accidit, quod Graecis vocibus δνοφερὸς, ὄρφνιος et ὄρφνινος, quae a tenebris ad nigredinem significandam trans- col. 199 feruntur. Et a tenebroso, vel, quod idem est, nigro colore corvum Hebraei עורב oreb, et Arabes غراب gorab dixerunt. Interim agnoscendum est, colorem κοράκινον, seu corvinum, aliquid habere luminis, cum color pullus sit ἄστιλπνος. Unde est, quod coracinum a pullo his verbis distinguit Vitruvius libri octavi capite tertio: Quamvis sint alba, procreant aliis locis leucophaea, aliis locis pulla, aliis coracino colore. Et κοράκινον χρῶμα docti definiunt colorem cum aliquo splendore nigerrimum; qualis est gagatis lapidis, et nostri serici villosi. Quem colorem lanis tribuit Strabo lib. duodecimo circa Laodiceam Phrygiae, illam regionem ferre dicens προβάτων ἀρετὰς, οὐκ εἰς μα-λακότητας μόνον τῶν ἐρίων, ᾗ καὶ τῶν Μιλησίων διαφέρει, ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰς τὴν κόραξιν χρόαν, praestantes oves, non solum mollitie lanarum, qua Milesias etiam superant, sed et colore, quali in corvis. Legendum enim τὴν ἐν κόραξιν χρόαν· sed post τὴν omissum illud ἐν, quia τὴν et ἐν sunt voces fere ὁμοιόπτωτοι. Placet etiam is color in capillis. Hinc Apuleji libro secundo laudatur capillus, corvina nigredine coerulus: coerulus, id est, niger, ut Graece κυάνεος. Itaque cum corvo confertur etiam, qui arte nigrum habet capillitium. Martialis libri tertii Epigrammate quadragesimo tertio,

It is easier to find white ravens and flying tortoises than a good orator from Cappadocia. Therefore, as these two things, croaking, I say, and blackness, are most proper to the raven, so most of the raven's names are taken from one or the other. Thus from croaking comes ܢܥܒܐ [נעבא] neab; and in Arabic نعاب [nuʿāb] noab, namely from the verb نعب [naʿaba] naaba, which means to croak. And in the Ethiopic name of the raven, ቋዕ፡ II, 788 koe, there is a manifest imitation of the raven's voice. From the same source arose the Greek κόραξ [korax], as well as κρώζειν [krōzein]; and the Roman crocire and crocitare. For those are mistaken who would have κόραξ [korax] so called παρὰ τὸν κόρον, ὃ σημαίνει τὸ μέλαν [para ton koron, ho sēmainei to melan], since κόρος [koros] in the sense of black occurs nowhere among the ancients. But the Hebrew עורב oreb, the Chaldee ערבא orba, and the Arabic غراب [ghurāb] gorab (whence the Romans said corvus) plainly relate to colour. For in Hebrew ערב ereb is evening, and ערב arab, the verb, is to grow towards evening, to grow dark. Hence in Arabic غربيب [ghirbīb] garbib is black (the initial Ain being changed into Gain by the added dot); so here the same thing happens as with the Greek words δνοφερὸς [dnopheros], ὄρφνιος [orphnios] and ὄρφνινος [orphninos], which are transferred from darkness to signify col. 199 blackness. And from the dark, or, what is the same, black colour, the Hebrews called the raven עורב oreb, and the Arabs غراب [ghurāb] gorab. Meanwhile it must be acknowledged that the κοράκινον [korakinon], or raven-coloured, has some lustre, whereas the dusky colour is ἄστιλπνος [astilpnos]. That is why Vitruvius, book 8, chapter 3, distinguishes raven-black from dusky in these words: Though they are white, in some places they produce grey-white, in other places dusky, in others raven-black. And learned men define κοράκινον χρῶμα [korakinon chrōma] as a deepest black with some sheen, such as that of jet and of our velvet. Strabo, book 12, attributes this colour to the wool around Laodicea in Phrygia, saying that region bears προβάτων ἀρετὰς, οὐκ εἰς μαλακότητας μόνον τῶν ἐρίων, ᾗ καὶ τῶν Μιλησίων διαφέρει, ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰς τὴν κόραξιν χρόαν [probatōn aretas, ouk eis malakotētas monon tōn eriōn, hē kai tōn Milēsiōn diapherei, alla kai eis tēn koraxin chroan], excellent sheep, not only in the softness of their wool, in which they surpass even the Milesian, but also in colour, such as is in ravens. For one must read τὴν ἐν κόραξιν χρόαν [tēn en koraxin chroan]; but after τὴν [tēn] that ἐν [en] was omitted, because τὴν [tēn] and ἐν [en] are nearly ὁμοιόπτωτοι [homoioptōtoi]. This colour is also pleasing in hair. Hence in Apuleius, book 2, hair is praised as dark-blue with raven blackness: coerulus, that is, black, as in Greek κυάνεος [kyaneos]. So even one who has hair made black by art is compared with the raven. Martial, book 3, Epigram 43:


Mentiris juvenem tinctis, Lentine, capillis,
Tam subito corvus, qui modo cygnus eras.

You feign youth with dyed hair, Lentinus, so suddenly a raven, you who were lately a swan.


Et de Theoro balbutiens dicit Alcibiades apud Aristophanem in Vespis,

And Alcibiades, lisping, says of Theorus in Aristophanes, in the Wasps:


Ὁλᾷς Θέωλον τὴν κεφαλὴν κόλακος ἔχει,

Ὁλᾷς Θέωλον τὴν κεφαλὴν κόλακος ἔχει, [Holas Theōlon tēn kephalēn kolakos echei,]


κόλακος, id est, adulatoris, caput illi tribuens pro κόρακος, id est, corvi, capite; quia R non poterat aliter efferre, quam per L. Sed sequitur,

κόλακος [kolakos], that is, of a flatterer, attributing to him the head of a flatterer instead of κόρακος [korakos], that is, of a raven; because he could not pronounce R otherwise than as L. But there follows,


Ὀρθῶς γε τοῦτ᾽ Ἀλκιβιάδης ἐθραύλισεν,

Ὀρθῶς γε τοῦτ᾽ Ἀλκιβιάδης ἐθραύλισεν [Orthōs ge tout᾽ Alkibiadēs ethraulisen],


Hoc recte balbutiit Alcibiades; quia re vera Theorus adulator erat insignis. Haec eo pertinent, ut doceamus, quorsum de sponso dicatur Cant. V, 2. קוצותיו תלתלים שחורות כעורב, Antiae ejus pendulae nigrae ut corvus. Ita enim interpretamur: II, 789 quia Arabice قُصَّة Kutssa est comae portio, quae fronti imminet, aut ex anteriore capitis parte propendet. Et תלתלים, pendulas cum Selomone explicamus, tanquam geminatum a verbo תלה, quod pendere est. Sic ex יפה geminato factum יפיפית pulcher es, Ps. XLV, 3. Illae igitur antiae, quae in frontem, aures et genas pendulae sunt, nigrae dicuntur esse ut corvus, id est, coracini coloris, qui splendore suo est conspicuus. Neque obscurum est, cur solum antiarum meminerit. Agitur de rege coronato: proinde dicitur Cant. III, 11. Videte, filiae Sion, regem Solomonem cum corona, qua mater illum coronavit, in die sponsaliorum ejus. Et in hoc ipso versu, Capite ejus auro optimo (supple coronato) antiae ejus pendulae, nigrae ut corvus. Quae capillitii pars fere sola apparet, cum caput est corona cinctum. Porro ad formae decus id pertinere, ut coracino colore crines fulgeant, omnes sciunt, ac proinde id a nonnullis summo studio affectari, atque ab ipso corvo remedia a curiosis expeti, quibus hoc consequantur. Hinc Plinius libri vigesimi noni capite sexto, Corvi ovum, in aereo vase permixtum, illitumque deraso capite, nigritiam capillis affert, etc. Et paullo post, Alii sanguine et cerebro ejus utuntur cum vino nigro. Alii excoquunt ipsum, et nocte concubia in plumbeum vas condunt. Et Aelianus libri primi capite quadragesimo octavo Hist. Προσακούω δὲ καὶ ὠὰ κόρακος με-λαίνειν τρίχας· Corvi ova audio nigros efficere pilos. Quae eadem praescribunt Sextus, et Marcellus, et Rasis, et Arabum non pauci alii. Meritò igitur Solomonis species ex eo in Cantico commendatur, quod comam nigram habuerit, adeoque corvi instar nigram, id est coracini coloris. Si Solomonem objicias in col. 200 hoc libro nobis proponi ut Christi typum, qui contra Dan. VII, 9. et Apoc. I, 14. senex et canis capillis describitur; respondeo, utrumque Christo convenire diverso respectu. Nempe, ut nigri capilli juvenilem vigorem arguunt, ita cani senilem gravitatem et sapientiam. Corvi nigredinem Arabes حلك chalac, aut حنك chanac vocant, voce maxime propria. Alcamus, حلك الغراب حنكه او سواده Chalac corvi, id est, chanac, aut nigredo ejus. Et alibi, حنك الغراب منقاره او سواده Chanac corvi, rostrum, aut nigredo ejus. Item, اسود حانك حالك Niger, chanic, chalic, id est, nigerrimus, ut corvus, cujus nigredo est intensissima.

This Alcibiades lisped rightly; because in truth Theorus was a notorious flatterer. All this serves to show why it is said of the bridegroom in Cant. V, 2: קוצותיו תלתלים שחורות כעורב, His locks are hanging, black as a raven. For so we interpret it: II, 789 because in Arabic قُصَّة [quṣṣa] Kutssa is the portion of the hair that overhangs the forehead, or hangs down from the front part of the head. And we explain תלתלים, with Solomon, as hanging, as if a reduplicated form of the verb תלה, which means to hang. Thus from יפה reduplicated comes יפיפית, thou art fair, Ps 45:3. Those locks, then, which hang down over the forehead, ears and cheeks, are said to be black as a raven, that is, of raven colour, which is conspicuous for its sheen. Nor is it obscure why he mentions only the locks. The subject is a crowned king: accordingly it is said in Song 3:11. Behold, daughters of Zion, King Solomon with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his espousals. And in this very verse: His head of finest gold (supply crowned), his locks hanging, black as a raven. This is almost the only part of the hair that is visible when the head is encircled with a crown. Moreover, everyone knows that it belongs to beauty of appearance that the hair should shine with a raven colour; hence some strive after it with the greatest zeal, and the curious seek remedies from the raven itself by which to obtain it. Hence Pliny, book 29, chapter 6: A raven's egg, mixed in a bronze vessel and smeared on the shaven head, gives blackness to the hair, etc. And a little later: Others use its blood and brain with dark wine. Others boil the bird itself down and at dead of night store it in a lead vessel. And Aelian, Hist. book 1, chapter 48: Προσακούω δὲ καὶ ὠὰ κόρακος μελαίνειν τρίχας [Prosakouō de kai ōa korakos melainein trichas]; I hear that raven's eggs make the hair black. The same things are prescribed by Sextus, Marcellus, Rhazes, and not a few other Arabs. Rightly, therefore, Solomon's appearance is praised in the Song for his having black hair, indeed black like a raven, that is, of raven colour. If you object that in col. 200 this book Solomon is set before us as a type of Christ, who on the contrary in Dan 7:9 and Rev 1:14 is described as old and with white hair, I reply that both befit Christ in different respects. For as black hair signifies youthful vigour, so white hair signifies the gravity and wisdom of age. The Arabs call the blackness of the raven حلك [ḥalak] chalac, or حنك [ḥanak] chanac, a most proper term. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: حلك الغراب حنكه او سواده [ḥalak al-ghurāb ḥanakuhu aw sawāduhu], Chalac of the raven, that is, chanac, or its blackness. And elsewhere: حنك الغراب منقاره او سواده [ḥanak al-ghurāb minqāruhu aw sawāduhu], Chanac of the raven: its beak, or its blackness. Likewise, اسود حانك حالك [aswad ḥānik ḥālik], Black, chanic, chalic, that is, very black, like the raven, whose blackness is most intense.


Corvum solitudinis amicum esse animal, in confesso est. Proinde Hesychius, Σκορακίζει· εἰς ἔρημον πέμπει, καὶ ἀρᾶται, ἀπὸ τοῦ εἰς κόρακας πέμ-πειν. Sensus est, ad corvos mittere, idem esse, quod alicui imprecari, ut in solitudinem amandetur et relegetur. Quale est, quod ad proverbium, Βάλλ᾽ ἐς κόρ κας, Scholiastes Aristophanis in Nubibus corvos asserit ἐν τοῖς ἐρημοτέροις τόποις ἐπιτηρεῖν τὰ σώματα, in solitariis locis observare cadavera. Huc quoque II, 790 pertinet, quod praedicitur Es. XXXIV, 10. fore, ut post vastatam Idumaeam in Bosrae metropolis ruderibus noctua et corvus habitent. Additur ex Sophon. II, 14. ubi de vastatione Ninives, Vox cantantis in fenestra, corvus in superliminari. Ita enim habet Hieronymus. Et Graecorum versio, Θηρία φωνήσει ἐν τοῖς διορύγμασιν αὐτῶν, καὶ κόρακες ἐν τοῖς πυλῶσιν αὐτῆς· Bestiae clamabunt in eorum (Ninivitarum) fossis, et corvi in portis ejus (Ninives). Et a Theodoreto ad hunc locum censentur inter vastitatis signa κοράκων νεοττίαι, corvorum nidi. Et a Cyrillo per corvos intelliguntur nycticoraces, qui in ipsis urbis portis non habitarent, nisi plurimum ibi quietis et otii esset, eorum naturae gratissimi: Οὐδ᾽ ἂν ἐμφιλοχωρήσειαν αὐτοῖς πυλῶσιν οἱ νυκτικόρακες, εἰ μὴ πλείστη τις ὅση καὶ ἁνδάνουσα λίαν τοῖς ὧδε φύσεως ἔχουσιν ὑπάρχῃ σχολή. Sed Hebraea vox חרב choreb, quam corvum explicant (1), siccitatem et vastitatem significat: aut, si chereb legas, gladium. Proinde Syrus interpres gladium reddit, quomodo etiam Aquila. Et Graecorum alii siccitatem, ut testatur Hieronymus, qui cur maluerit corvum reddere, nullus capio. In Hebraeo (inquit) ponitur חרב, quod secundum lectionis diversitatem vel siccitas, vel gladius, vel corvus accipitur. Quasi idem sint, חרב, per Cheth, et ערב, per Ajin. Quod Hieronymo nullus concesserit. Nam ערב, per Ajin et Cholem, corvum sonat: sed חרב, per Cheth et Cholem, siccitatem et vastitatem; aut gladium, si sit Segol. Hic igitur cum חרב per Cheth et Cholem scribant, Sophoniae verba sic reddenda sunt: Vox resonabit e fenestra: vastitas erit in limine, cum cedrus nudata fuerit, id est, cedrinum tabulatum. Vocem hic intelligo, qualem Es. XIII, 21.

That the raven is an animal fond of solitude is generally agreed. Accordingly Hesychius has: Σκορακίζει· εἰς ἔρημον πέμπει, καὶ ἀρᾶται, ἀπὸ τοῦ εἰς κόρακας πέμπειν [Skorakizei; eis erēmon pempei, kai aratai, apo tou eis korakas pempein]. The sense is that to send to the ravens is the same as to curse someone, wishing that he be banished and relegated to the wilderness. Of the same kind is the remark of the Scholiast on Aristophanes in the Clouds, on the proverb Βάλλ᾽ ἐς κόρ κας [Ball᾽ es kor kas], that ravens ἐν τοῖς ἐρημοτέροις τόποις ἐπιτηρεῖν τὰ σώματα [en tois erēmoterois topois epitērein ta sōmata], watch for corpses in solitary places. Here too II, 790 belongs the prediction in Es. XXXIV, 10, that after Idumaea has been laid waste, the owl and the raven will dwell in the ruins of its metropolis Bosra. To this is added Sophon. II, 14, on the devastation of Nineveh: The voice of one singing in the window, the raven on the lintel. For so Jerome has it. And the version of the Greeks: Θηρία φωνήσει ἐν τοῖς διορύγμασιν αὐτῶν, καὶ κόρακες ἐν τοῖς πυλῶσιν αὐτῆς [Thēria phōnēsei en tois diorygmasin autōn, kai korakes en tois pylōsin autēs]; Beasts will cry out in their (the Ninevites') ditches, and ravens in her gates (Nineveh's). And Theodoret, on this passage, counts among the signs of devastation κοράκων νεοττίαι [korakōn neottiai], nests of ravens. And Cyril understands by the ravens night-ravens, which would not dwell in the very gates of the city unless there were a great deal of quiet and leisure there, which is most agreeable to their nature: Οὐδ᾽ ἂν ἐμφιλοχωρήσειαν αὐτοῖς πυλῶσιν οἱ νυκτικόρακες, εἰ μὴ πλείστη τις ὅση καὶ ἁνδάνουσα λίαν τοῖς ὧδε φύσεως ἔχουσιν ὑπάρχῃ σχολή [Oud᾽ an emphilochōrēseian autois pylōsin hoi nyktikorakes, ei mē pleistē tis hosē kai handanousa lian tois hōde physeōs echousin hyparchē scholē]. But the Hebrew word חרב choreb, which they explain as raven R1, means dryness and devastation; or, if you read chereb, sword. Accordingly the Syriac translator renders it sword, as does Aquila too. And others among the Greeks render it dryness, as Jerome attests; why he preferred to render it raven, I cannot grasp at all. In the Hebrew (he says) is written חרב, which, according to the difference of reading, is taken as either dryness, or sword, or raven. As if חרב with Cheth and ערב with Ajin were the same. No one would grant Jerome that. For ערב, with Ajin and Cholem, means raven; but חרב, with Cheth and Cholem, means dryness and devastation, or sword if it has Segol. Since here, then, they write חרב with Cheth and Cholem, the words of Zephaniah are to be rendered thus: A voice will resound from the window; devastation will be on the threshold, when the cedar has been laid bare, that is, the cedar panelling. By voice here I understand one such as in Es. XIII, 21.


Hic quaeri potest, quorsum corvos Solomon appellet ערבי נחל, corvos vallis, aut, si mavis, corvos torrentis, Prov. XXX, 17. Nam נחל et vallem, et torrentem sonat (2). Ego crediderim corvos vallis cum Graecis, qui habent κόρακες ἐκ τῶν φαράγγων, id est, corvos ex vallibus, seu, qui nidificare amant in reductis vallibus, quas Hebraice recte dixeris נחלי הבתות, valles solitudinum II, 791 cum Propheta Es. VII, 19. Potest etiam intelligi vallis aliqua, corvis frequens, et ab iis denominata. De tali aliqua valle intelligi posset Esaias, nisi per Masorethas staret, cum de Moabitarum opibus dicit Es. XV, 7. על נחל הערבים ישאום, id est, ut vulgo reddunt, Ad vallem Arabum, aut Ad torrentem salicum deferent eas. Atque id quidem recte; quia Vocales, a Masorethis appositae, col. 201 non patiuntur, ut aliter interpretemur. Sed illae si abessent, aeque commode legeretur, Ad vallem corvorum deferent eas. Quo sensu Graece dicitur Βάλλ᾽ ἐς κόρακας, id est, εἰς ἀπώλειαν, καὶ εἰς φθοράν. Et in ipso Esaia II, 20. idola, ad talpas et vespertiliones projicere, est, ea perdere et exscindere. Iam conjecturis indulgere si libet, vallis corvorum illa ipsa fuit, quae vallis cadaverum appellatur Ierem. XXXI, 40. Et utroque nomine vocata est vallis eadem, eo quod damnatorum in illa conjecta cadavera corvi, undecunque confluentes, absumerent. Quo dato, cum dicit Solomon, fore, ut oculum, qui subsannat patrem, eruant corvi vallis, idem erit, ac si dixisset, eum tam tetri criminis, infami supplicio affectum, in vallum cadaverum conjiciendum, ut a corvis ibi absumatur. Id enim reis cedit in partem poenae, ut insepulta jaceant, aut pendeant eorum cadavera, vel a feris, vel ab avibus carnivoris dilanianda. Hinc in Aristophanis Θεσμοφορούσαις Mnesilochus hoc nomine supplicium deprecatur, ne a mulieribus rideretur vir senex τοῖς κόραξιν ἑστιῶν, corvis convivium exhibens. Et paullo post, Ἐκρέμασε κόραξι δεῖπνον, Suspendit, ut corvis esset pro coena. Horatius quoque Epistola 16. ad Quintium,

Here it may be asked why Solomon calls ravens ערבי נחל, ravens of the valley, or, if you prefer, ravens of the torrent, Prov 30:17. For נחל means both valley and torrent R2. I would take it as ravens of the valley, with the Greeks, who have κόρακες ἐκ τῶν φαράγγων [korakes ek tōn pharangōn], that is, ravens from the valleys, or those that like to nest in secluded valleys, which in Hebrew you might rightly call נחלי הבתות, valleys of the wastes II, 791, with the Prophet Isa 7:19. One may also understand some particular valley frequented by ravens and named after them. Isaiah could be understood of some such valley, were it not for the Masoretes, when he says of the riches of the Moabites, Es. XV, 7: על נחל הערבים ישאום, that is, as it is commonly rendered, They will carry them to the valley of the Arabs, or to the torrent of willows. And that indeed rightly, since the vowels supplied by the Masoretes col. 201 do not allow us to interpret otherwise. But if they were absent, one could just as well read, They will carry them to the valley of the ravens. In this sense it is said in Greek Βάλλ᾽ ἐς κόρακας [Ball᾽ es korakas], that is, εἰς ἀπώλειαν, καὶ εἰς φθοράν [eis apōleian, kai eis phthoran]. And in Isaiah himself, II, 20, to cast idols to the moles and the bats is to destroy and cut them off. Now, if one may indulge in conjecture, that valley of the ravens was the very one that is called the valley of corpses in Jer 31:40. And the same valley was called by both names because ravens, flocking together from every side, consumed the corpses of the condemned thrown into it. Granting this, when Solomon says that the ravens of the valley will pick out the eye that mocks its father, it will be as if he had said that one guilty of so foul a crime, having suffered an infamous punishment, is to be thrown into the valley of corpses, to be consumed there by ravens. For it counts as part of the penalty for the guilty that their corpses lie unburied or hang, to be torn apart by wild beasts or by carnivorous birds. Hence in Aristophanes' Θεσμοφορούσαις [Thesmophorousais] Mnesilochus begs to be spared punishment on this account, that he, an old man, should not be laughed at by the women τοῖς κόραξιν ἑστιῶν [tois koraxin hestiōn], providing a banquet for ravens. And shortly after, Ἐκρέμασε κόραξι δεῖπνον [Ekremase koraxi deipnon], He hung him up, to be a dinner for ravens. Horace too, Epistle 16 to Quintius,


— — — non pasces in cruce corvos:

— — — you will not feed the ravens on the cross:


ut in Philostrati Heroicis, et Tzetze Chil. 5. cap. 22. Centaurus Asbolus,

as in Philostratus' Heroica, and Tzetzes, Chil. 5, ch. 22, the Centaur Asbolus,


Ὑψικόμοιο κρεμαστὸς ἀπ᾽ εὐλιπέος κατὰ πεύκης
Σύγκειται, μέγα δεῖπνον ἀμετροβίοις κοράκεσσιν·

Ὑψικόμοιο κρεμαστὸς ἀπ᾽ εὐλιπέος κατὰ πεύκης Σύγκειται, μέγα δεῖπνον ἀμετροβίοις κοράκεσσιν· [Hypsikomoio kremastos ap' eulipeos kata peukēs synkeitai, mega deipnon ametrobiois korakessin]


Pendet in excelsae suffixus stipite pinus,
Suavia inexpletis ut det convivia corvis.

He hangs fixed to the trunk of a lofty pine, to give a sweet banquet to the insatiable ravens.


Et nominatim oculi meminit Solomon, Oculum, inquit, qui subsannat patrem, effodient corvi vallis; quia corvus oculum maxime appetit. Et, Isidoro teste, prior (lege primo) in cadaveribus oculum petit. Unde Epictetus, Οἱ μὲν κόρα-κες τῶν τετελευτηκότων τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς λυμαίνονται· Corvi mortuorum oculos vastant. (Vide reliqua in capite De aquila a)) Catullus quoque, Cominio mortem imprecatus, hoc addit:

And Solomon mentions the eye by name: The eye, he says, that mocks its father, the ravens of the valley shall dig out; for the raven goes for the eye above all. And, as Isidore attests, first (read primo) it goes for the eye in corpses. Hence Epictetus: Οἱ μὲν κόρακες τῶν τετελευτηκότων τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς λυμαίνονται· [Hoi men korakes tōn teteleutēkotōn tous ophthalmous lymainontai] Ravens ravage the eyes of the dead. (See the rest in the chapter On the eagle a).) Catullus too, calling down death on Cominius, adds this:


Effossos oculos voret atro gutture corvus, Intestina canes, caetera membra lupi. II, 792 Quid quod ne vivorum quidem oculis parcunt? Hinc Aristophanes in Avibus,

Let the raven devour his dug-out eyes with its black gullet, the dogs his entrails, the wolves his other limbs. II, 792 What of the fact that they do not spare even the eyes of the living? Hence Aristophanes in the Birds:


Ὁ κόραξ παρελθὼν τοῦπιορκοῦντος λάθρα
Προσπτάμενος ἐκκόψει τὸν ὀφθαλμὸν θένων·

Ὁ κόραξ παρελθὼν τοῦπιορκοῦντος λάθρα Προσπτάμενος ἐκκόψει τὸν ὀφθαλμὸν θένων· [Ho korax parelthōn toupiorkountos lathra prosptamenos ekkopsei ton ophthalmon thenōn]


Corvus adveniens, et clam advolans, pejerantis oculum percutiens effodiat. Item,

Let the raven, coming up and flying at him unseen, strike and dig out the eye of the perjurer. Likewise:


Οἱ δ' αὖ κόρακες τῶν ζευγαρίων, οἷσι τὴν γῆν καταροῦσι,
Καὶ τῶν προβάτων τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ἐκκοψάντων·

Οἱ δ' αὖ κόρακες τῶν ζευγαρίων, οἷσι τὴν γῆν καταροῦσι, Καὶ τῶν προβάτων τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ἐκκοψάντων· [Hoi d' au korakes tōn zeugariōn, hoisi tēn gēn katarousi, kai tōn probatōn tous ophthalmous ekkopsantōn]


Rursus corvi boum jugalium, quibus terram arant et ovium oculos ejiciant. Et Gregorius Nyssenus Homilia 13. corvum vocat σαρκοβόρον τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ἀφανιστικὸν, carnivorum oculorum corruptorem. Et Alkazuinius in capite غراب gorab, seu Ce Corvo, يجتمع علي كل الحيوانات الكبار البادية كالجمل والفرس وكذا الادمي ويقصد قلع عينها ولا يمتنع بالدفع والضرب لشدة جوعه Versatur super omnia magna animalia, quae sunt in agris, ut super camelos et equos, adeoque super homines, et eorum oculos conatur evellere: nec propellendo, aut verberando prohibetur propter vim famis. Quanquam id corvo non sit peculiare, si vere scribit Carduanus lib. 7. capite 35. De rerum varietate: Nullum ge- col. 202 nus avium magnarum, seu gallinae, seu pavones, aut corvi sint, vel grues, aut ciconiae, ita mansuescit, ut, si propius sint, non conentur tibi oculos eruere. De struthionibus idem audivi ab iis, qui illas circumducunt. Et hanc causam affert Plinius lib. 11. cap. 37. Adeoque oculis absoluta vis speculi, ut tam parva illa pupilla totam imaginem reddat hominis. Ea causa est, ut pleraeque alitum e manibus hominum oculos potissimum appetant, quod, effigiem suam in iis cernentes, velut ad cognata desideria sua tendunt. Interim veteri proverbio jactatur, Corvum corvi oculum non eruere. Gregor. Turonensis de Chilpericho, rege, (Historiae lib. 5. cap. 18.), Visoque me, rex ait, o episcope, justitiam cunctis largiri debes: et, ecce! ego justitiam a te non accipio. Sed, ut video, consentis iniquitati, et in te impletur proverbium illud, quod „Corvus oculum corvi non eruit“. Quo proverbio innuebat, Gregorium episcopum in alterum episcopum, laesae majestatis reum, noluisse quidquam pronuntiare.

Again, let the ravens pluck out the eyes of the yoked oxen with which they plough the land, and of the sheep. And Gregory of Nyssa, Homily 13, calls the raven σαρκοβόρον τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ἀφανιστικὸν [sarkoboron tōn ophthalmōn aphanistikon], a flesh-eater, a destroyer of eyes. And Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt], in the chapter غراب [ghurāb] gorab, or On the Raven: يجتمع علي كل الحيوانات الكبار البادية كالجمل والفرس وكذا الادمي ويقصد قلع عينها ولا يمتنع بالدفع والضرب لشدة جوعه [yajtamiʿ ʿalī kull al-ḥayawānāt al-kibār al-bādiya ka-l-jamal wa-l-faras wa-kadhā al-ādamī wa-yaqṣid qalʿ ʿaynihā wa-lā yamtaniʿ bi-l-dafʿ wa-l-ḍarb li-shiddat jūʿihi] It settles on all the large animals that are in the open country, such as camels and horses, and even on men, and tries to pluck out their eyes; nor is it kept off by driving away or beating, because of the violence of its hunger. Although this is not peculiar to the raven, if Cardanus writes truly in book 7, chapter 35 of De rerum varietate: No kind of large bird, whether hens, or peacocks, or ravens, or cranes, or col. 202 storks, becomes so tame that, if they are rather close, they do not try to tear out your eyes. I have heard the same about ostriches from those who lead them about. And Pliny gives this reason, book 11, ch. 37: And so perfect is the mirror-like power in the eyes that that tiny pupil gives back the whole image of a man. This is the reason why most birds, when in men's hands, go chiefly for the eyes: seeing their own likeness in them, they make for them as if toward the objects of their natural longing. Meanwhile an old proverb is bandied about, A raven does not pluck out a raven's eye. Gregory of Tours on King Chilperic (History, book 5, ch. 18): And on seeing me the king said, "O bishop, you ought to bestow justice on all; and, behold! I do not receive justice from you. But, as I see, you consent to iniquity, and in you is fulfilled that proverb, 'A raven does not pluck out a raven's eye.'" By this proverb he was hinting that Bishop Gregory had been unwilling to pronounce anything against another bishop accused of high treason.


Ex iis, quae dicta sunt, aperte constat, τὸ σκορακίζειν, seu ad corvos mittere, aut abjicere, non solum id esse, quod supra definiebat Hesychius, secessum, aut relegationem in solitudinem alicui imprecari, sed et ad necem eum devovere, et ultima quaeque illi exoptare. Tamen apud sacros scriptores σκορα-κίζειν et ἀποσκορακίζειν solum est relinquere, repellere, increpare. Et σκορα-κισμὸς, vel ἀποσκορακισμὸς, repulsio et increpatio. Sic Eccles. XLI, 19. (Αἰ-σχύνεθε) ἀπὸ σκορακισμοῦ λήψεως, καὶ δόσεως· Vos pudeat ob repulsionem dati II, 793 et accepti. Septuaginta Psal. XXVI, 9. Μὴ ἀποσκορακίσῃς με (3)· Ne me derelinquas: Hebr. אל תטשני. Esa. XVII, 13. Καὶ ἀποσκορακιεῖ αὐτόν· Hebr. וגער בו, Et increpavit eum. Es. LXVI, 15. Καὶ ἀποσκορακισμὸν ἐν φλογὶ πυ-ρός· Hebraice וגערתו בלהבי אש, Et increpationem ejus in flamma ignis. Sed ibi increpatio pro perditione sumitur; quomodo saepe apud Hebraeos. Tamen Cyrillus ἀποβολὴν abjectionem explicat; quia Deus dicet reprobis, Discedite a me, maledicti, in ignem aeternum.

From what has been said it is plainly evident that τὸ σκορακίζειν [to skorakizein], or to send or cast to the ravens, is not only what Hesychius defined above, to wish on someone withdrawal or banishment into the wilderness, but also to devote him to death and to wish him every extremity. Yet among the sacred writers σκορακίζειν [skorakizein] and ἀποσκορακίζειν [aposkorakizein] mean only to abandon, to repel, to rebuke. And σκορακισμὸς [skorakismos], or ἀποσκορακισμὸς [aposkorakismos], means repulse and rebuke. Thus Sir 41:19 (Αἰσχύνεθε [Aischynethe]) ἀπὸ σκορακισμοῦ λήψεως, καὶ δόσεως· [apo skorakismou lēpseōs, kai doseōs] Be ashamed on account of the rejection of what is given II, 793 and received. The Septuagint, Ps 26:9 Μὴ ἀποσκορακίσῃς με R3· [Mē aposkorakisēs me] Do not forsake me: Hebrew אל תטשני. Isa 17:13 Καὶ ἀποσκορακιεῖ αὐτόν· [Kai aposkorakiei auton] Hebrew וגער בו, And he rebuked him. Isa 66:15 Καὶ ἀποσκορακισμὸν ἐν φλογὶ πυρός· [Kai aposkorakismon en phlogi pyros] in Hebrew וגערתו בלהבי אש, And his rebuke in a flame of fire. But there rebuke is taken for destruction, as often among the Hebrews. Yet Cyril explains it as ἀποβολὴν [apobolēn], rejection, because God will say to the reprobate, Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire.


Corvum Iudaeis prohibet Moses למינו, secundum genus suum, aut secundum speciem suam: ut et alias quasdam aves in immundarum censu. Et, ut notat R. Selomo, cum ad nomen avis additur juxta genus suum, יש באותו המין שאין דומין זה לזה לא כמראיהם ולא בשמותיהם וכולן מין אחד, Species habet figura et nomine dissimiles, quae tamen ad unum genus revocantur. Sed haec infra docebimus parum esse solita. Tamen, si corvorum species quaeras, eo referri queant cornix, graculus, monedula, pica, sturnus etiam, si creditur Baal Hatturim, Cabalistica ratione fretus; ista nimirum, quod verba עורב למינו, corvus secundum genus suum, et vox זרזר, id est, sturnus, sunt ἰσόψηφα. Utraque enim valent 414. Corvi species in Damire Arabes ita describunt: والغربان اربعة اجناس اسود حالك وابلق ومطرف ببياض لطيف الجرم ياكل الحب واسود طاووسي براق الريش ورجلاه بلون المرجان يعرف بالزاغ, Corvorum sunt quatuor species. 1. Perfecte niger (is est corvus, proprie dictus.). 2. Varius, seu ex nigro et albo mixtus (cornicem intelligo, quam vernaculo sermone palliatam vocamus). 3. Qui extrema habet alba, corpore gracilis, granis vescens (id est, cornix σπερμολόγος). 4. Niger pavoninus, lucentibus plumis, pedibus corallinis, qui pica vocatur. Ara- col. 203 bes cornicem referre ad corvinum genus, ex eo maxime constat, quod herbam κορωνοπόδα constanter appellant رجل الغراب pedem corvi.

Moses forbids the raven to the Jews למינו, after its kind, or after its species, as he does certain other birds in the list of the unclean. And, as R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] notes, when after its kind is added to the name of a bird, יש באותו המין שאין דומין זה לזה לא כמראיהם ולא בשמותיהם וכולן מין אחד, it has species unlike in form and name, which are nevertheless referred to one kind. But we shall show below that this is hardly well founded. Still, if you ask for the species of ravens, there may be referred to it the crow, the graculus [jackdaw], the jackdaw, the magpie, and even the starling, if one believes Baal Hatturim [=Jacob ben Asher (d. 1343), commentary on the Torah], who relies on a Cabbalistic argument: namely, that the words עורב למינו, the raven after its kind, and the word זרזר, that is, starling, are ἰσόψηφα [isopsēpha]. For both amount to 414. The Arabs in Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] describe the species of the raven thus: والغربان اربعة اجناس اسود حالك وابلق ومطرف ببياض لطيف الجرم ياكل الحب واسود طاووسي براق الريش ورجلاه بلون المرجان يعرف بالزاغ [wa-l-ghirbān arbaʿat ajnās aswad ḥālik wa-ablaq wa-muṭarraf bi-bayāḍ laṭīf al-jirm yaʾkul al-ḥabb wa-aswad ṭāwūsī barrāq al-rīsh wa-rijlāhu bi-lawn al-marjān yuʿraf bi-l-zāgh], There are four species of ravens. 1. The perfectly black (this is the raven properly so called). 2. The pied, or mixed of black and white (I understand the crow which in our vernacular we call the palliata [hooded]). 3. The one that has white extremities, slender in body, feeding on grains (that is, the σπερμολόγος [spermologos] crow). 4. The peacock-like black one, with shining plumage and coral-coloured feet, which is called the magpie. That the Arabs col. 203 refer the crow to the raven kind is clearest from the fact that they consistently call the plant κορωνόπους [korōnopous] رجل الغراب [rijl al-ghurāb] raven's foot.


Unus principum Madian עורב Oreb, id est, corvus, dictus est. Et locus, in quo ab Ephraimitis caesus est Petra Oreb, Iudic. VII, 25. et Esa. X, 26. Sic Κόρακος πέτρη, Coracis, seu corvi petra, Ithacae locus fuit, in quo ὁ Κόραξ κυνηγῶν ἀπὸ τῆς πέτρας πεσῶν ἐτελεύτησε, venator quidam Corax (seu corvus nomine), ex petra delapsus, obiit. Ita Scholiastes vetus ad Homeri versum Odyss. ν'.

One of the princes of Midian was called עורב Oreb, that is, raven. And the place in which he was slain by the Ephraimites is the Rock of Oreb, Judg 7:25 and Isa 10:26. Likewise Κόρακος πέτρη [Korakos petrē], the rock of Corax, or of the raven, was a place on Ithaca, at which ὁ Κόραξ κυνηγῶν ἀπὸ τῆς πέτρας πεσῶν ἐτελεύτησε [ho Korax kynēgōn apo tēs petras pesōn eteleutēse], a certain hunter Corax (that is, named raven) died after falling from the rock. So the old Scholiast on the verse of Homer, Odyss. 13:


Παρ' Κόρακος πέτρῃ, ἐπί τε κρήνῃ Ἀρεθούσῃ.

Παρ' Κόρακος πέτρῃ, ἐπί τε κρήνῃ Ἀρεθούσῃ. [Par' Korakos petrē, epi te krēnē Arethousē.]


(1) Rosenmüller, II, 790 Quod ipsum negat I. E. FABER in Dissertat. de animalibus, quorum mentio fit Zephan. II, 14., ad calcem libri Crameriani, qui inscribitur: Scythische Denkmaehler in Palaestina, p. 304. κορακος nomen ab interpretibus pro קאת positum autumans, pro חרב vero χαμαιλεωντος: utrumque sine idonea ratione, nec alium in finem, nisi ut tueatur conjecturas suas leves de animalium istorum nominibus. Cf. supra p. 507. not. et 509. not.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 790 This very thing is denied by I. E. Faber [=J. E. Faber, notes to the German edition of Harmer's Observations (Beobachtungen über den Orient, 1772–79)] in his dissertation On the animals mentioned in Zeph 2:14, at the end of Cramer's book entitled Scythische Denkmaehler in Palaestina, p. 304. He maintains that the name κορακος [korakos] was put by the translators for קאת, and that of χαμαιλεωντος [chamaileōntos] for חרב: both without adequate reason, and for no other purpose than to defend his own flimsy conjectures about the names of those animals. Compare above p. 507, note, and 509, note.
