Part 2, Book 2, chapter 11: The providence of God for ravens
------------------------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/corvus-providentia.html

II, 794 col. 203 CAP. XI.

II, 794 col. 203 CHAPTER XI.


Dei providentia circa Corvos.

The providence of God concerning ravens.


Cum corvum appareat hactenus vile et abjectum esse animal, et hominibus odiosum, nonnulli mirantur, cur corvos Deo esse curae sacra scriptura toties et tam diserte testetur. Sic Iob. XXXIX, 3. (al. XXXVIII, 41.) Quis corvo praeparat escam suam, cum pulli eius ad Deum clamant, errantes inopia cibi? Et Psal. CXLVII, (al. CXLVI,) 9. Qui dat jumentis escam suam, et pullis corvorum, qui clamant. Et Luc. XII, 24. Considerate corvos, qui neque serunt, neque metunt, neque cellam, neque horreum habent, et tamen Deus alit illos. Nec patiuntur multi veteres haec ad literam intelligi. Deum invocare (inquit Hilarius in Psalmum CXLVI.) proprium hominis officium est. Corvorum vero pulli quomodo Deum invocant? Et cur pulli corvorum potius, quam corvi etc.? Aut quae esca praebetur? Nunquid ut foenum jumentis, et ut herbam hominibus, sic corruptorum cadaverum foetidas sordes Deus orantibus se corvorum pullis, et pecudum mortes ad cibum vitae praesentis impertiet? Haec ita intelligere, non dicam erroris, sed irreligiositatis extremae est. Et Augustinus, Hoc forte putabimus, quia corvi Deum invocant, ut det illis escam. Ne hoc cogitetis, irrationalem animam invocare Deum etc. In figura accipite dictum. Et auctor Commentariorum in Psalmos sub Hieronymi nomine, Responde, Iudaee, responde, qui Iudaicam literam tantum sequeris. Dicis istos corvos vere corvos esse? Si ergo de pullis corvorum scriptum est, „Et pullis corvorum invocantibus eum;“ Et scriptum est Ioel. II. a). Omnis, qui invocaverit nomen Domini, salvus erit: Ergo et pulli corvorum salvi erunt in resurrectione. Itaque ad allegorias, tanquam ad sacram anchoram, confugiunt sacri Doctores. Et per corvos intelligunt gentes; per pullos corvorum, Christianos, qui, utut orti ex gentibus, ta- col. 204 men verum Deum invocant. At, quod illorum pace dixero, Allegoriae literalem sensum non destruunt, sed praesupponunt. Illis igitur indulgere nolim, antequam de literali sensu constet. Quem in his locis si rejicimus, nihil erit in scriptura certum, et quod non facile possit alio detorqueri. Iobum enim quidni fateamur tam de veris corvis egisse capite XXXIX. quam de veris ibicibus, leonibus, onagris, equis, aquilis, struthionibus etc. in iis, quae hoc eodem capite vel sequuntur, vel antecedunt? In tot animalium descriptionibus cum vltro fateamur, reliquas ad literam sumi, cur haec sola nihil habebit, quod non sit allegoricum? Ita enim in his Davidis, Quae dat jumentis escam suam, et pullis II, 795 corvorum, qui clamant, cum versiculi pars prior vera jumenta, quidni posterior quoque veros cervos significabit? Et in Christi verbis, Considerate corvos, qui neque serunt, neque metunt etc. aves intelligi, non homines, aperte docet 1. hujus loci collatio cum parallelo Matth. VI, 26. Intuemini volucres coeli, quae non serunt, neque metunt, etc. 2. Quod negantur serere, et metere, et horrea habere, in quae proventus suos cogant. 3. Quod in fine versus Christus addit, Quanto vos praestatis volucribus? ut in Luca: aut, Nonne vos illis longe praestatis? ut in Matthaeo habetur. 4. Denique si corvi, aut aves allegoricae intelligantur, lilia quoque in sequentibus non erunt vera lilia, sed quidquid τοῖς ἀλ-ληγορηταῖς libuerit confingere. Hoc igitur certum maneat, in locis, quae citavimus, veros corvos significari. Nec est, quod quemquam moveat, quod ex Psalmo objicitur, τοῖς νεοσσοῖς τῶν κοράκων τοῖς ἐπικαλουμένοις αὐτὸν, pullis corvorum invocantibus eum, cum Hebraea solum habeant, Deum escam suam dare לבני עורב אשר יקראו, filiis corvi, qui clamant. Quod sequuntur Chaldaea, Syra, et Hieronymiana versio. Sed, post Graecos, Vulgatus interpres, Aethiops, et Arabes duo, Pronomen addiderunt; quasi Propheta expresse dixerit, corvorum pullos Deum invocare, aut clamare ad Deum. Tamen si, post verba Davidis, pullis corvorum, qui clamant, aliquis supplendum censeat ad Deum, non vehementer pugnabo, cum in Iobo diserte legantur pulli corvorum ad Deum clamare: sed quo sensu dicuntur leunculi rugire ad praedam, et ut quaerant a Deo escam suam, Psal. CIV, 21. Et omnium animalium oculi ad Deum spectare, qui dat illis escam tempore suo, Psal. CXLV, 15. Et bestiae agri ad eum glocitare, eo quod exaruerunt alvei aquarum, Ioel. I, 20. Recte igitur Theodoretus, Οὐ λογικὴ τῶν κοράκων ἡ φύσις, οὐδ᾽ ὅτι λογικῶς ἐπικαλεῖται τὸν ποιητήν· ἀλλ᾽ ἡ διὰ τὴν χρείαν κραυγὴ μιμεῖται τὴν αἴτησιν. Non est rationalis corvorum natura, neque rationis ductu opificem invocat: sed clamor, ob necessitatem emissus, petitionem imitatur. Quae Elias Cretensis fere totidem verbis exscripsit in Notis ad Gregorii Orationem LI. Et metaphora ubique elegans, cum de corvis agitur, ideo elegantior est, quod, cum aves pleraeque Deum celebrare cantu suo, et hymnos εὐχαριστικοὺς in illius laudes canere videantur, corvus vocem clamosam habet, et obstreperam, tanquam importuni flagitatoris. Et re vera crocitatu suo nonnunquam stipem rogare creditur. Proinde (ut narrat Aelianus Historiae lib. 2. cap. 48.) Κόρακες Αἰγύπτιοι, ὅσοι τῷ Νείλῳ προσδιαιτῶνται, τῶν πλεόντων ἐοίκασιν ἱκέται εἶναι, λαβεῖν τι αἰτοῦντες, corvi Aegyptii, Nilum accolentes, nauigantibus quasi supplices esse videntur, sibi quidpiam dari efflagitantes. Et in Hesychio, Κοράξαι, ἄγαν προσλιπαρῆσαι· πεποίηται παρὰ τοὺς κόρακας (malim παρὰ τοῦ κόρακος.). Quibus verbis vult τὸ κοράξαι idem esse, quod obnixe rogare, et vocem esse a corvis sumptam. Et rationem addit Suidas in Κοράττειν, addens, sumptam esse ἀπὸ τῶν περὶ τὰς θύρας κοράκων περιπετομένων, II, 796 καὶ μὴ ἀποχωρούντων, a corvis, qui (aliquid petentes) aedium fores circumvolitant, neque inde discedunt.

Since it appears from what has been said so far that the raven is a base and abject animal, and hateful to men, some wonder why sacred Scripture so often and so explicitly testifies that ravens are a care to God. Thus Job 39:3 (var. XXXVIII, 41.): Who prepares for the raven its food, when its young cry to God, wandering for lack of food? And Psal. CXLVII, (var. CXLVI,) 9. Who gives to the beasts their food, and to the young of the ravens that cry. And Luc. XII, 24: Consider the ravens, which neither sow nor reap, which have neither storeroom nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Nor do many of the ancients allow these passages to be understood literally. To call upon God (says Hilary on Psalm 146) is the proper office of man. But how do the young of ravens call upon God? And why the young of ravens rather than the ravens etc.? Or what food is supplied? Will God, as he gives hay to the beasts and grass to men, so bestow the stinking filth of rotting carcasses and the deaths of cattle as food for the present life on the young ravens that pray to him? To understand these things so is, I will not say an error, but the height of irreligion. And Augustine: Shall we perhaps think this, that ravens call upon God to give them food? Do not imagine this, that an irrational soul calls upon God etc. Take what is said as a figure. And the author of the Commentaries on the Psalms under the name of Jerome: Answer, Jew, answer, you who follow only the Jewish letter. Do you say these ravens are truly ravens? If then it is written of the young of ravens, „And to the young of ravens calling upon him;“ and it is written Ioel. II. a), Whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved: then the young of ravens too will be saved in the resurrection. And so the sacred Doctors take refuge in allegories as in a sacred anchor. By ravens they understand the gentiles; by the young of ravens, Christians, who, though sprung from the gentiles, col. 204 nevertheless call upon the true God. But, if I may say so with their leave, allegories do not destroy the literal sense but presuppose it. I would therefore not indulge in them before the literal sense is established. If we reject it in these passages, nothing in Scripture will be certain, nothing that cannot easily be twisted elsewhere. For why should we not admit that Job in chapter 39 treated of real ravens just as of real ibexes, lions, wild asses, horses, eagles, ostriches etc. in what follows or precedes in this same chapter? Since in so many descriptions of animals we freely admit that the rest are taken literally, why should this one alone contain nothing that is not allegorical? So too in these words of David, Who gives to the beasts their food, and to the young II, 795 of the ravens that cry: since the first part of the verse signifies real beasts, why should the latter not also signify real ravens? And in Christ's words, Consider the ravens, which neither sow nor reap etc., that birds are meant, not men, is plainly shown 1. by comparing this passage with the parallel Matt 6:26. Behold the birds of the air, which do not sow, nor reap, etc. 2. Because they are denied to sow, reap and have barns into which to gather their produce. 3. Because at the end of the verse Christ adds, How much more are you worth than the birds? as in Luke; or, Are you not of much more value than they? as in Matthew. 4. Finally, if ravens or birds are understood allegorically, the lilies in what follows will not be real lilies either, but whatever it pleases τοῖς ἀλληγορηταῖς [tois allēgorētais] to invent. Let this therefore stand certain, that in the passages we have cited real ravens are meant. Nor should anyone be moved by the objection from the Psalm, τοῖς νεοσσοῖς τῶν κοράκων τοῖς ἐπικαλουμένοις αὐτὸν [tois neossois tōn korakōn tois epikaloumenois auton], to the young of ravens calling upon him, since the Hebrew has only that God gives his food לבני עורב אשר יקראו, to the sons of the raven, which cry. This is followed by the Chaldee, the Syriac, and Jerome's version. But, after the Greeks, the Vulgate translator, the Ethiopic, and the two Arabic versions added the pronoun, as if the Prophet had expressly said that the young of ravens call upon God, or cry to God. Yet if anyone thinks that after David's words, to the young of ravens that cry, one should supply to God, I will not strongly contest it, since in Job the young of ravens are explicitly said to cry to God: but in the sense in which young lions are said to roar after their prey, and to seek their food from God, Ps 104:21; and the eyes of all animals to look to God, who gives them their food in its season, Ps 145:15; and the beasts of the field to cry out to him, because the watercourses are dried up, Joel 1:20. Rightly therefore Theodoret: Οὐ λογικὴ τῶν κοράκων ἡ φύσις, οὐδ᾽ ὅτι λογικῶς ἐπικαλεῖται τὸν ποιητήν· ἀλλ᾽ ἡ διὰ τὴν χρείαν κραυγὴ μιμεῖται τὴν αἴτησιν [Ou logikē tōn korakōn hē physis, oud᾽ hoti logikōs epikaleitai ton poiētēn; all᾽ hē dia tēn chreian kraugē mimeitai tēn aitēsin]. The nature of ravens is not rational, nor does it call upon its maker by the guidance of reason: but the cry uttered from need imitates a petition. Elias of Crete copied this almost word for word in his Notes on Gregory's Oration 51. And the metaphor, elegant everywhere, is the more elegant where ravens are concerned, because, while most birds seem to celebrate God with their song and to sing hymns εὐχαριστικοὺς [eucharistikous] in his praise, the raven has a clamorous and noisy voice, like an importunate beggar. And in fact it is believed sometimes to ask for alms with its croaking. Hence (as Aelian relates, History book 2, ch. 48) Κόρακες Αἰγύπτιοι, ὅσοι τῷ Νείλῳ προσδιαιτῶνται, τῶν πλεόντων ἐοίκασιν ἱκέται εἶναι, λαβεῖν τι αἰτοῦντες [Korakes Aigyptioi, hosoi tō Neilō prosdiaitōntai, tōn pleontōn eoikasin hiketai einai, labein ti aitountes], the Egyptian ravens that live along the Nile seem to be suppliants, as it were, of those sailing by, begging that something be given them. And in Hesychius: Κοράξαι, ἄγαν προσλιπαρῆσαι· πεποίηται παρὰ τοὺς κόρακας [Koraxai, agan prosliparēsai; pepoiētai para tous korakas] (I would prefer παρὰ τοῦ κόρακος [para tou korakos]). By these words he means that τὸ κοράξαι [to koraxai] is the same as to ask insistently, and that the word is taken from ravens. And Suidas under Κοράττειν [Korattein] adds the reason, saying it was taken ἀπὸ τῶν περὶ τὰς θύρας κοράκων περιπετομένων, II, 796 καὶ μὴ ἀποχωρούντων [apo tōn peri tas thyras korakōn peripetomenōn, kai mē apochōrountōn], from ravens which (seeking something) fly around the doors of houses and do not depart from there.


At, inquiunt, cur a Iobo et Davide non ipsis corvis, sed corvorum pullis col. 205 tribuitur haec escae flagitatio? Cui quaestioni ut satisfiat, Hebraei et Arabes multa comminiscuntur, ut patebit ex sequentibus. Rabbi Eliezer in Capitulis fere in fine cap. 21. Cum corvi genuerunt pullos suos, videntes, eos esse albos, aufugiunt ab illis, existimantes, illos esse pullos serpentis: tum Deus Sanctus Benedictus illis largitur alimentum absque penuria. Rabbi Selomo in Iobum, יתעו מבלי אכל שאביהם שונאם והקב״ה מזמן להם יתושים הנבראים מצואתן ונכנסין לתוך פיהם, Vagantur absque cibo; quia patri suo sunt exosi: sed Deus Sanctus Benedictus culices ipsis praeparat, ex proprio ipsorum stercore procreatos, qui in os eorum ingrediantur, Aben Ezra in Psalmum CXLVII. חכמי הגויים אומרים כי אבותם יעזבום בהולדם, Philosophi gentilium asserunt, eos a parentibus deseri, quam primum nati sunt. Et Kimchius, לפי שהם לבנים בהולדם ואמותיהם מניחים אותם ולא יביאו להם טרפם כי יחשבו כי אינם בניהם לפי שהם לבנים והם צווחים כאלו יקראו לאל בעד טרפם והקב״ה מזמין להם יתושין ואוכלים אותם, quia nascuntur albi, matres eos deserunt, neque iis cibum afferunt: neque enim pro suis agnoscunt, cum albi sint. Proinde clamant, quasi a Deo cibum suum peterent. Et Deus ipsis culices praeparat, quibus vescantur. Haec Hebraei: jam audi Arabes. In his Haririus poeta sic canit in مقامة Mekama, seu stantia 13.

But, they ask, why do Job and David attribute this demand for food not to the ravens themselves, but to the chicks of the ravens? col. 205 To answer this question the Hebrews and Arabs devise many things, as will be clear from what follows. Rabbi Eliezer in the Capitula, near the end of ch. 21: When the ravens have hatched their chicks and see that they are white, they flee from them, thinking that they are the young of a serpent; then God, the Holy One, Blessed be He, grants them food without want. R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] on Job: יתעו מבלי אכל שאביהם שונאם והקב״ה מזמן להם יתושים הנבראים מצואתן ונכנסין לתוך פיהם, They wander without food, because they are hateful to their father; but God, the Holy One, Blessed be He, prepares for them gnats, generated from their own dung, which enter into their mouth. Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] on Psalm CXLVII.: חכמי הגויים אומרים כי אבותם יעזבום בהולדם, The philosophers of the gentiles assert that they are deserted by their parents as soon as they are born. And Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim]: לפי שהם לבנים בהולדם ואמותיהם מניחים אותם ולא יביאו להם טרפם כי יחשבו כי אינם בניהם לפי שהם לבנים והם צווחים כאלו יקראו לאל בעד טרפם והקב״ה מזמין להם יתושין ואוכלים אותם, because they are born white, their mothers desert them and do not bring them food; for they do not recognize them as their own, since they are white. Therefore they cry out, as if they were asking God for their food. And God prepares gnats for them to feed on. So much for the Hebrews; now hear the Arabs. Among them the poet Hariri sings thus in مقامة [maqāma] Mekama, or stantia, 13.


يا رازق النعاب في عشه وجابر العظم الكسير المهيض

يا رازق النعاب في عشه [yā rāziq al-naʿʿāb fī ʿushshihi] وجابر العظم الكسير المهيض [wa-jābir al-ʿaẓm al-kasīr al-mahīḍ]


O qui corvum alis in nido suo, et onagri os fractum et contritum reparas. Cujus distichi primam partem Davidi tribuit Scholiastes, et sic exponit: الغراب اذا فقس عن فراخه خرجت بيضا فاذا راها ابواها كذلك نفرا عنها فتفتح افواها فيرسل الله تبارك وتعالي لها ذبابا فيدخل في افواها فيركون لها غذا حتي تسود فاذا اسودت عاد ابواها اليها فغذياها ويرفع الله الذباب عنها Corvus cum pullos excludit, albi prodeunt. Quales cum vident parentes, fugam capessunt. Illi autem ora aperiunt. Et Deus Benedictus et excelsus, muscas iis mittit, quae, in ora ingredientes, sunt ipsis pro cibo, donec nigrescant. Et tum demum parentes redeuntes eos alunt. Deus autem ab illis muscas amovet. Quae eadem docet Alkazuinius verbis parum diversis. Et Damir aliquanto uberius, اذا خرجت الفراخ II, 797 الغراخ من البيض طردتها لانها تخرج قبيحة المنظر حدا انا تكون صغار الاجرام عظيم الروس والمناقر جرد اللون الاجساد متفواتا الاعضا فالابوان col. 206 ينظران الفرخ كذلك فيتركانه فيجعل الله تعالي قوته في الذباب والبعوض الكاين في عشه الي ان يقوي وينبت ريشه فيعود اليه ابواه فيرزقانه Cum pulli ex ovo exeunt, pellunt eos (parentes); quia exeunt admodum foedi visu. Quippe sunt parvo corpore, magno capite, et rostro, glabra specie, corporis membris divulsis et male cohaerentibus. Parentes igitur pullum deserunt, cum eum talem vident. Sed summus Deus dat ei pro cibo muscas et culices: qui cibus in nido est, donec viribus confirmetur (pullus), et plumae crescant, et ad eum redeant parentes, a quibus alatur. Quod ipsum, ut confirmet alius Arabs, Chalpholachmar nomine, pullorum corvi foetiditatem ita describit: رايت فرخ الغراب فلم ار صورة اقبح منه ولا اسمج الا اقذر ولا اشر رايت راسا كبيرا ومنقارا طويلا وذلك مع صغر البدن وصغر الجناح وهو امرط نتن الريح Vidi pullum corvi, quo nihil unquam foedius, deformius, impurius et nequius a me conspectum est. Vidi magnum caput, et longum rostrum, cum parvo corpore et parvis alis. Etiam glaber is erat et foetentis halitus, etc. Plura ex Arabum scriptis describere non vacat, et haec abunde sufficiunt. Itaque hoc solum addam, etiam e veteribus ecclesiae doctoribus fuisse, qui hanc fabulam non multo aliter adornaverint. Chrysostomus in Sermone De Elia, Κεχηνότες εἰς ἀέρα τῶν κοράκων οἱ νεοσσοὶ, καὶ παρὰ τῶν γονέων μὴ τρεφόμενοι, ἔχουσιν αὐτοὶ ζῶα μικρά τινα τὴν θείαν ἐπιπέμπουσαν πρόνοιαν διακονούμενα· καὶ οὕτως ἐκ τοῦ ἀέρος ἐκεῖνα δεχόμενοι πρὸς αὔξησιν τρέφονται· Ad aërem hiantes corvorum pulli, cum a parentibus non alantur, habent animalcula quaedam, quae Dei providentiae, a quo mittuntur, inserviunt; et iis, ex aëre acceptis, nutriuntur, donec adolescant. Olympiodorus in Iobum, Λέγεται ὁ κόραξ μὴ ἐκτρέφειν τὰ ἔκγονα ὑπὸ λαι-μαργίας, ἀλλ᾽ ἀτημελήτους ἐᾶν τοὺς νεοσσούς· τοὺς δὲ, ὑπὸ τῆς ἐνδείας πιεζο-μένους, φυσικῇ τινι κεχρῆσθαι πρὸς Θεὸν τῇ βοῇ, καὶ ὑπὸ μικρῶν τινων ζωϋ-φίων, γινομένων ἐν ταῖς νεοσσιαῖς, ἐκτρέφεσθαι. Dicitur corvus prae ingluvie foetum suum non alere, sed pullos neglectos deserere: illos vero, urgente fame, clamore quodam naturali ad Deum uti, et parvis quibusdam bestiolis, quae in nidis nascuntur, nutriri. Gregorius in Iobum lib. 30. Editis pullis (corvus), ut fertur, escam praebere dissimulat, priusquam plumescendo nigrescant, eosque inedia II, 798 affici patitur, quoad usque in illis per pennarum nigredinem sua similitudo videatur. Qui huc illucque vagantur in nido, et ciborum expetunt aperto ore subsidium. At, cum nigrescere coeperint, tanto illis praebenda alimenta ardentius requirit, quanto illos alere diutius distulit. Isidorus, Originum lib. 12. cap. 7. Fertur haec col. 207 avis, quod editis pullis escam plene non praebeat, priusquam in iis pennarum nigredinem, similitudinem proprii coloris, agnoscat. Postquam vero tetros (malim atros) plumis aspexerit, in toto agnitos abundantius pascit. Cassiodorus in Psalmos, et qui sub Hieronymi nomine circumfertur, pullos, ajunt, ita neglectos, rore coelesti pasci, qui cicadarum victus est, non corvorum. Muscas vero et culices quis in corvi nido credat nasci tanta copia, ut pluribus pullis, iisque avidissimis, alendis sufficiat? Et statim natos culices in pullorum os devorandos ultro se ingerere? Aut parentes pullos suos ideo odisse, quod nascantur ex parte implumes, cum reliquis avibus id ipsum accidat? Aut ad eos, semel desertos, iterum se conferre, quam primum plumis vestiti sunt, vel cum eae sunt nigriores; ac si ab aliquo moneantur, jam pullos suos melius se habere, nec causam esse amplius, cur ab iis abhorreant? Uno verbo, hoc certum est et jam in ore vulgi, avi nulli nidum suum sordere; et nullum esse animal, cui sibi similium forma non placeat. Hinc Epicharmus apud Laertium in Platone,

O you who nourish the raven in its nest, and repair the broken and crushed jaw of the wild ass. The first part of this distich the Scholiast attributes to David, and explains it thus: الغراب اذا فقس عن فراخه خرجت بيضا فاذا راها ابواها كذلك نفرا عنها فتفتح افواها فيرسل الله تبارك وتعالي لها ذبابا فيدخل في افواها فيركون لها غذا حتي تسود فاذا اسودت عاد ابواها اليها فغذياها ويرفع الله الذباب عنها [al-ghurāb idhā faqasa ʿan firākhihi kharajat bīḍan fa-idhā raʾāhā abawāhā ka-dhālika nafarā ʿanhā fa-taftaḥ afwāhā fa-yursil Allāh tabāraka wa-taʿālī lahā dhubāban fa-yadkhul fī afwāhā fa-yarkūn lahā ghidhā ḥattī taswadd fa-idhā iswaddat ʿāda abawāhā ilayhā fa-ghadhdhayāhā wa-yarfaʿ Allāh al-dhubāb ʿanhā] When the raven hatches its chicks, they come out white. When the parents see them so, they take to flight. But the chicks open their mouths, and God, blessed and exalted, sends them flies, which, entering their mouths, serve them as food until they turn black. Only then do the parents return and feed them, and God removes the flies from them. Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt] teaches the same in words little different. And Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] somewhat more fully: اذا خرجت الفراخ II, 797 الغراخ من البيض طردتها لانها تخرج قبيحة المنظر حدا انا تكون صغار الاجرام عظيم الروس والمناقر جرد اللون الاجساد متفواتا الاعضا فالابوان [idhā kharajat al-firākh al-ghirākh min al-bayḍ ṭaradathā li-annahā takhruj qabīḥat al-manẓar ḥadā anā takūn ṣighār al-ajrām ʿaẓīm al-rūs wa-al-manāqir jurd al-lawn al-ajsād mutafawwatā al-aʿḍā fa-al-abawān] col. 206 ينظران الفرخ كذلك فيتركانه فيجعل الله تعالي قوته في الذباب والبعوض الكاين في عشه الي ان يقوي وينبت ريشه فيعود اليه ابواه فيرزقانه [yanẓurān al-farkh ka-dhālika fa-yatrukānih fa-yajʿal Allāh taʿālī qūtah fī al-dhubāb wa-al-baʿūḍ al-kāyin fī ʿushshih ilī an yaqwā wa-yanbut rīshuh fa-yaʿūd ilayh abawāh fa-yarzuqānih] When the chicks come out of the egg, they (the parents) drive them away, because they come out exceedingly ugly to look at. For they have a small body, a large head and beak, a bare appearance, and the limbs of the body disjointed and badly knit together. So the parents, seeing the chick in such a state, desert it. But God most high gives it flies and gnats for food; this food is in the nest until (the chick) gains strength and its feathers grow, and the parents return to it and it is fed by them. To confirm this, another Arab, named Chalpholachmar, describes the foulness of the raven's chicks thus: رايت فرخ الغراب فلم ار صورة اقبح منه ولا اسمج الا اقذر ولا اشر رايت راسا كبيرا ومنقارا طويلا وذلك مع صغر البدن وصغر الجناح وهو امرط نتن الريح [raʾaytu farkh al-ghurāb fa-lam ara ṣūra aqbaḥ minhu wa-lā asmaj al-ā aqdhar wa-lā asharr raʾaytu raʾsan kabīran wa-minqāran ṭawīlan wa-dhālika maʿa ṣighar al-badan wa-ṣighar al-janāḥ wa-huwa amraṭ natin al-rīḥ] I saw a raven's chick, and I have never beheld anything fouler, more misshapen, more unclean or more vile. I saw a large head and a long beak, with a small body and small wings. It was also bare and of fetid breath, etc. There is no time to copy out more from the writings of the Arabs, and these suffice abundantly. So I shall add only this: among the ancient doctors of the church too there were some who embellished this fable in much the same way. Chrysostom, in the Sermon On Elias: Κεχηνότες εἰς ἀέρα τῶν κοράκων οἱ νεοσσοὶ, καὶ παρὰ τῶν γονέων μὴ τρεφόμενοι, ἔχουσιν αὐτοὶ ζῶα μικρά τινα τὴν θείαν ἐπιπέμπουσαν πρόνοιαν διακονούμενα· καὶ οὕτως ἐκ τοῦ ἀέρος ἐκεῖνα δεχόμενοι πρὸς αὔξησιν τρέφονται· [Kechēnotes eis aera tōn korakōn hoi neossoi, kai para tōn goneōn mē trephomenoi, echousin autoi zōa mikra tina tēn theian epipempousan pronoian diakonoumena; kai houtōs ek tou aeros ekeina dechomenoi pros auxēsin trephontai] The ravens' chicks, gaping into the air, since they are not fed by their parents, have certain tiny creatures which serve the providence of God, by whom they are sent; and receiving these from the air, they are nourished until they grow up. Olympiodorus on Job: Λέγεται ὁ κόραξ μὴ ἐκτρέφειν τὰ ἔκγονα ὑπὸ λαιμαργίας, ἀλλ᾽ ἀτημελήτους ἐᾶν τοὺς νεοσσούς· τοὺς δὲ, ὑπὸ τῆς ἐνδείας πιεζομένους, φυσικῇ τινι κεχρῆσθαι πρὸς Θεὸν τῇ βοῇ, καὶ ὑπὸ μικρῶν τινων ζωϋφίων, γινομένων ἐν ταῖς νεοσσιαῖς, ἐκτρέφεσθαι. [Legetai ho korax mē ektrephein ta ekgona hypo laimargias, all᾽ atēmelētous ean tous neossous; tous de, hypo tēs endeias piezomenous, physikē tini kechrēsthai pros Theon tē boē, kai hypo mikrōn tinōn zōyphiōn, ginomenōn en tais neossiais, ektrephesthai] The raven is said, out of gluttony, not to rear its offspring, but to abandon its chicks uncared for; and they, pressed by hunger, use a kind of natural cry to God, and are nourished by certain small creatures which are born in the nests. Gregory on Job, book 30: When its chicks are hatched (the raven), as is reported, neglects to provide them food before they turn black by growing feathers, and lets them suffer hunger II, 798 until its own likeness is seen in them through the blackness of their feathers. They wander here and there in the nest and seek the help of food with open mouth. But when they have begun to turn black, it seeks the food to be given them all the more eagerly, the longer it has put off feeding them. Isidore, Etymologies book 12, ch. 7: This bird is said col. 207 not to give its hatched chicks full food until it recognizes in them the blackness of the feathers, the likeness of its own colour. But after it has seen them foul (I would prefer black) with feathers, having recognized them wholly, it feeds them more abundantly. Cassiodorus on the Psalms, and the author who circulates under the name of Jerome, say that the chicks, thus neglected, are fed by heavenly dew, which is the food of cicadas, not of ravens. But who would believe that flies and gnats are born in a raven's nest in such abundance as to suffice to feed several chicks, and very greedy ones at that? And that the gnats, as soon as they are born, of their own accord thrust themselves into the chicks' mouths to be devoured? Or that the parents hate their chicks because they are born partly featherless, when the very same thing happens to other birds? Or that, having once deserted them, they return to them as soon as they are clothed with feathers, or when these are blacker, as if someone had told them that their chicks are now in better shape and there is no longer reason to shrink from them? In a word, this is certain and already a common saying: to no bird is its own nest foul; and there is no animal that is not pleased by the form of its like. Hence Epicharmus in Laertius, in the Life of Plato:


— — — Καὶ γὰρ ὁ κύων κυνὶ
Κάλλιστον εἶναι φαίνεται, καὶ βοῦς βοΐ,
῎Ονος δ᾽ ὄνῳ κάλλιστον, ὗς δ᾽ ὑΐ·

— — — Καὶ γὰρ ὁ κύων κυνὶ Κάλλιστον εἶναι φαίνεται, καὶ βοῦς βοΐ, ῎Ονος δ᾽ ὄνῳ κάλλιστον, ὗς δ᾽ ὑΐ· [Kai gar ho kyōn kyni kalliston einai phainetai, kai bous boi, onos d᾽ onō kalliston, hys d᾽ hyi]


Etenim canis cani videtur esse quid pulcherrimum, et bos bovi, asinus asino, sus sui. Et Cicero lib. 1. De natura Deorum, An putas, ullam esse terra marique belluam, quae non sui generis bellua maxime delectetur? Quod ni ita esset, cur non gestiret taurus equae contrectatione, equus vaccae? An tu aquilam, aut leonem, aut delphinum ullam anteferre censes figuram suae? Itaque nugantur Hebraei, et Arabes, cum corvum a pullis suis, modo natis, ideo abhorrere dictitant, quia sunt mire deformes. Nam si nobis sordent τὰ κορακίδια, non sequitur, eadem sordere etiam parentibus, qui aliis oculis illa intuentur. Et vero cum ideo solum fictae fuerint istae fabulae, ut scripturam explicarent, tamen scripturae verbis nullo modo sunt consonae. Neque enim Iob dicit, corvorum pullos in nido clamare ad Deum, sed tum, cum inopia cibi errant, et divagantur. Agitur ergo de pullis, qui jam e nido excesserunt. Nam pullos in ipso nido huc illucque divagari, quod ait Gregorius, animo concipi non potest. Hanc pullorum evagationem nidi angustiae non ferunt. Neque vero corvus foetus suos negligit, dum in nido sunt, sed jam enutritos, et ad volatum habiles, nido pellit, ut in posterum sibi prospiciant. Philosophus Hist. lib. 9. cap. 31. Οἱ δὲ κόρακες τοὺς ἑαυτῶν νεοττοὺς, ὅταν οἷοί τ᾽ ὦσιν ἤδη πέτεσθαι, τὸ μὲν πρῶτον ἐκβάλλουσιν, II, 799 ὕστερον δὲ καὶ ἐκ τοῦ τόπου ἐκδιώκουσι· Corvi autem pullos suos, cum jam potestas volandi est, primum nido ejiciunt, deinde regione tota expellunt. Plinius lib. 10. cap. 12. de cornice, Sola haec etiam volantes pullos aliquamdiu pascit. Caeterae omnes ex eodem genere pellunt nidis pullos, ac volare cogunt, sicut et corvi, qui robustos quosque foetus suos pellunt longius. Aeliani lib. 2. cap. 49. De animali- bus, Τούς γε μὴν νεοττοὺς τοὺς ἐκτραφέντας διώκουσι, καὶ τῆς ἑαυτῶν ἕκαστος καλιᾶς φυγάδας ἀποφαίνουσιν ὑπὲρ ὅτου τροφὰς μαστεύουσι. Pullos quidem suos enutritos persequuntur; et eos unusquisque ex nido suo fugat: quamobrem pulli deinceps victum quaerunt. Pullis igitur sic ejectis tum demum id evenit, col. 208 quod tradit sacer scriptor, ut, cibi penuria vagantes, quasi ad Deum clament. Cum enim nondum sint plenis viribus, nec in perfecto vigore aetatis, neque dum ad victum proprio labore atque industria sibi comparandum assueverint, consilii prorsus inopes magna voce crocitant, et aërem querulis clamoribus implent, tanquam de parentum ἀστοργίᾳ ad Deum expostulantes. Et in his angustiis illis succurrit Deus, non per miraculum muscas et culices procreans, quae in illorum ora ultro se ingerant, sed eis suggerens, quid facto sit opus, et quomodo urgenti fami sit consulendum, ne inedia pereant. Itaque corvorum pullis hic idem accidit, quod leonum catulis, qui, a matre deserti, egent, atque esu- riunt, Psal. XXXIV, 11. et rugiunt ad praedam, tanquam a Deo quaerentes escam suam, Psal. CIV, 21. Et eos explet Deus, Iob. XXXIX, 1. (al. XXXVIII, 39.) Quamvis non multum sit laborandum, cur pullis corvorum id tribuatur potius, quam ipsis corvis. Cum etiam de corvis Christus dixerit, Luc. XII, 24. Consi- derate corvos, qui neque serunt etc. et tamen Deus alit illos. Nec causa fuit, cur pro corvis Arabs redderet فراخا الغربان pullos corvorum. Neque enim interpreti licet quidquam mutare in verbis sacri textus, nisi necessitas eo adigat, qualis hic nulla apparet; cum de corvis nihil dicat Christus, quod universae speciei non conveniat. Considerate, inquit, corvos, qui neque serunt, neque me- tunt, neque cellam, neque horreum habent, et tamen Deus alit illos. Quae de patribus tam vera sunt, quam de pullis; neutri enim serunt, aut metunt; neutri cellas, aut horrea habent. Denique Deus utrisque ex aequo prospicit. Quin ad quascunque aves haec eadem refert Christus Matth. VI, 26. Considerate, ait, aves coeli, quae neque serunt, neque metunt etc. Sed, quod ibi asserit de avibus in genere, Matth. X, 29. restringit ad passeres, qui, quamvis vilissimi sint, et bini assario veneant, tamen eos non judicat Deus sua cura indignos. Et Luc. XII, 24. etiam ad corvos idem extendit, quos, utut deformes aves, et inconditae vocis, et infausti ominis, tamen alere non dedignatur. Itaque nihil hic corvis, aut corvorum pullis peculiare tribuitur. Sed illorum, aeque ac passerum, inter reliquas aves fit diserta mentio, ut pateat, Dei providentiam non solum avibus in genere prospicere; sed et vsque ad earum vilissimas et despicatissimas II, 800 se extendere: ut homines, iique fideles, inde certius concludant, se Deo curae esse, qui, quod infimi ordinis animalculis tam benigne indulget, iis non denegabit, a quibus colitur, et invocatur. His ita explicatis, non dissimulabo, apud Servium in Notis ad lib. 1. Georgicorum haec legi: Plinius in Naturali Historia dicit, corvos obliviosos esse, et plerumque minime ad nidos suos reverti; sed quadam ratione naturae congerunt ad suos nidos quae vermes possint creare, ex quibus relicti eorum pulli aluntur interdum. Unde ex Plinii auctoritate firmari posse videbitur fabula, quam confutavimus. Sed non est, quod quemquam haec commoveant. Fallit enim Servius, aut fallitur: cum neque in Plinio, neque in ullo philosophorum, qui aetatem Servii praecesserunt, legatur tale quidquam. Itaque hoc merum somnium est ex eburnea porta: qualia multa illi excidere viri docti jam observarunt.

For to a dog a dog seems the most beautiful thing, and an ox to an ox, an ass to an ass, a pig to a pig. And Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods book 1: Do you think there is any beast on land or sea that does not take the greatest delight in a beast of its own kind? If it were not so, why would a bull not long to touch a mare, or a stallion a cow? Or do you suppose that an eagle, or a lion, or a dolphin prefers any shape to its own? So the Hebrews and the Arabs talk nonsense when they keep saying that the raven shrinks from its newly hatched chicks because they are wonderfully ugly. For if τὰ κορακίδια [ta korakidia] look vile to us, it does not follow that they look vile also to their parents, who view them with other eyes. And indeed, although these fables were invented solely to explain Scripture, they in no way agree with the words of Scripture. For Job does not say that the chicks of the ravens cry to God in the nest, but when they wander and stray about for lack of food. The subject, therefore, is chicks that have already left the nest. For that chicks should wander here and there within the nest itself, as Gregory says, cannot be conceived; the narrowness of a nest does not allow such wandering of the chicks. Nor in fact does the raven neglect its young while they are in the nest; rather, once they are fully reared and able to fly, it drives them from the nest, so that thereafter they may provide for themselves. The Philosopher, Hist. book 9, ch. 31: Οἱ δὲ κόρακες τοὺς ἑαυτῶν νεοττοὺς, ὅταν οἷοί τ᾽ ὦσιν ἤδη πέτεσθαι, τὸ μὲν πρῶτον ἐκβάλλουσιν, II, 799 ὕστερον δὲ καὶ ἐκ τοῦ τόπου ἐκδιώκουσι· [Hoi de korakes tous heautōn neottous, hotan hoioi t᾽ ōsin ēdē petesthai, to men prōton ekballousin, hysteron de kai ek tou topou ekdiōkousi] But ravens, when their chicks are now able to fly, first cast them out of the nest, then drive them out of the whole district. Pliny, book 10, ch. 12, on the crow: This bird alone even feeds its chicks for some time after they can fly. All the others of the same kind drive their chicks from the nests and force them to fly, as do the ravens too, which drive each of their young, once strong, farther away. Aelian, On Animals book 2, ch. 49: Τούς γε μὴν νεοττοὺς τοὺς ἐκτραφέντας διώκουσι, καὶ τῆς ἑαυτῶν ἕκαστος καλιᾶς φυγάδας ἀποφαίνουσιν ὑπὲρ ὅτου τροφὰς μαστεύουσι. [Tous ge mēn neottous tous ektraphentas diōkousi, kai tēs heautōn hekastos kalias phygadas apophainousin hyper hotou trophas masteuousi.] Their chicks, indeed, once reared, they chase away; and each drives them from its nest, for which reason the chicks thereafter seek their own food. It is only when the chicks have been cast out in this way, then, that there happens col. 208 what the sacred writer relates: that, wandering for lack of food, they as it were cry to God. For since they are not yet at full strength, nor in the perfect vigour of their age, and have not yet grown used to procuring food for themselves by their own effort and industry, they are utterly at a loss, croak loudly, and fill the air with plaintive cries, as though complaining to God of their parents' ἀστοργία [astorgia]. And in these straits God comes to their aid, not by miraculously producing flies and gnats that thrust themselves of their own accord into their mouths, but by suggesting to them what must be done and how to provide against pressing hunger, so that they do not perish of starvation. Thus the same thing happens here to the chicks of ravens as to the whelps of lions, which, deserted by their mother, lack and suffer hunger, Ps 34:11, and roar after their prey, as though seeking their food from God, Ps 104:21. And God satisfies them, Job 39:1 (var. XXXVIII, 39). Yet one need not trouble much over why this is attributed to the chicks of ravens rather than to the ravens themselves, since Christ said it of ravens too, Luke 12:24: Consider the ravens, which neither sow etc. and yet God feeds them. Nor was there any reason for the Arabic translator to render ravens as فراخا الغربان [firākhā al-ghirbān] chicks of ravens. For a translator may not change anything in the words of the sacred text unless necessity compels him, and here no such necessity appears, since Christ says nothing of ravens that does not suit the whole species. Consider, he says, the ravens, which neither sow nor reap, which have neither storeroom nor barn, and yet God feeds them. This is as true of the parents as of the chicks: neither sows or reaps; neither has storerooms or barns. Finally, God provides for both alike. Indeed, Christ applies these same words to all birds, Matt 6:26: Consider, he says, the birds of the air, which neither sow nor reap etc. But what he asserts there of birds in general he narrows, Matt 10:29, to sparrows, which, though very cheap and sold two for a farthing, God nevertheless does not judge unworthy of his care. And in Luke 12:24 he extends the same to ravens too, which, ugly birds though they are, harsh of voice and of ill omen, he nevertheless does not disdain to feed. So nothing peculiar is attributed here to ravens or to the chicks of ravens. Rather, they, like the sparrows, are expressly mentioned among the other birds, to make clear that God's providence not only cares for birds in general, but extends even to the cheapest and most despised of them, II, 800 so that men, and faithful men above all, may conclude the more surely that they are in God's care: what he so kindly grants to little creatures of the lowest order, he will not deny to those by whom he is worshipped and invoked. Having explained these things thus, I will not conceal that in Servius, in his Notes on book 1 of the Georgics, one reads this: Pliny in his Natural History says that ravens are forgetful and for the most part do not return to their nests at all; but by a certain provision of nature they gather at their nests things that can produce worms, by which their abandoned chicks are sometimes fed. Hence it may seem that the fable we have refuted can be confirmed by the authority of Pliny. But there is no reason for this to trouble anyone. For Servius either deceives or is deceived, since nothing of the kind is read either in Pliny or in any of the philosophers who preceded the age of Servius. So this is a mere dream from the ivory gate, of the sort that learned men have already observed slipped from him in large numbers.

II, 800 Chapter XII. col. 209


De Corvo, quem ex arca emisit Noë.

On the Raven that Noah Sent Out of the Ark.


De corvo in sacro textu duae habentur historiae: una de corvo, a Noa ex arca emisso; altera de corvis, qui Eliam in deserto paverunt. Prior sic habet juxta Hebraeos Gen. VIII, 7. Et emisit corvum, et is exivit exeundo, et redeundo, donec aquae exaruissent a superficie terrae. Causam emissionis corvi Graeca editio sic effert in quibusdam exemplaribus, Καὶ ἀπέστειλε τὸν κόρακα ἰδεῖν, εἰ κεκόπακε τὸ ὕδωρ· Et corvum emisit, ut videret, an cessavissent aquae. Quod ex versu sequenti sumptum, ubi de columba habetur, Emisit quoque columbam a se, ut videret, an extenuatae fuissent aquae a superficie terrae. Et vero Noam eodem animo corvum, quo columbam emisisse constat. Sed, ut repetitionis taedium vitaret Moses, id solum de columba dixit, cujus historiam ideo expressit disertius; quia est majoris momenti. Die igitur prima decimi mensis, cum aquae diluvii non parum decrevissent, apparere jam inceperant celsissimorum montium summi vertices, Gen. VIII, 5. Et post quadraginta dies elapsos, id est, undecimi mensis die undecima, Noë, aperta arcae fenestra, corvum emisit; cum terram aquis obruissent quadragesimales pluviae, Gen. VII, 12. Noë speraverat fore, ut pari numero dierum aquae exsiccarentur. Quod cum non successisset, corvum emisit, quem sciebat odore cadaverum allici posse, ut longius evolaret, si jam animalibus patuisset terra. At corvus, arcam circumvolitans, ab ea non abscessit longius. Exivit (inquit Moses) exeundo, et redeundo. Emissus enim, non nisi foedas paludes cernens, statim receptum quaesiit vel in arcam, aut super arcam. A qua subinde rursus avolans redibat identidem: neque II, 801 aliud quidquam praestitit, donec aquae exaruissent. Hebraei nugantur in Agudda, corvum ideo non desiisse arcam circumvolitare, nec ivisse quo missus fuerat: שהיה חושדו על בת זוגו, quia de conjuge (seu foemina) sua sollicitus erat; ne scilicet, se absente, ab alio iniretur. Quod cum de alio corvo non possit intelligi, cum Noë solum duos servasset, nolo attexere, quae monstra sibi fingant impuri homines, et mortalium insulsissimi. In Beresith Rabba sect. 33. Noë et corvus colloquuntur invicem: et, hoc quaerente, cur ex omnibus pecudibus, col. 210 feris, et avibus solus mitteretur, respondet Noë, mundum corvis posse facile carere, cum neque לאכילה, ad esum, neque לקרבן, ad sacrificia sint utiles. Sed intercedit Deus, monens, futuris saeculis magnum fore corvorum usum, nempe Eliae tempore, qui pane et carne, a corvis allata, aliquamdiu pastus fuit. Atque ob id ipsum scilicet noluit Deus, ut corvus ab arca longius secederet. Et illi dixit, אתה מזומן לשליחות אחרת בימי אליהו, Tu Eliae diebus aliam (majoris momenti) legationem obire debes: ac proinde in illa tempora servandus es. Quod ipsa Mosis verba volunt obscure subinnuere, cum dicit עד יבשת, donec exaruissent. Quia vox יבשת easdem habet literas, quas vox תשבי Thisbi. Itaque עד יבשת, id est, עד תשבי, Ad usque Thisbitem, supple Eliam, quod observat Baal Hatturim; et literas יבשת המים, Exaruerunt aquae, per Gematriam idem valere, quod נחל כרית, torrentem Cerith, vbi Eliam corvi paverunt: quod tamen verum non est.

Concerning the raven, the sacred text contains two narratives: one about the raven sent out of the ark by Noah; the other about the ravens that fed Elias in the desert. According to the Hebrews, the former reads as follows, Gen 8:7: And he sent out the raven, and it went out, going forth and returning, until the waters had dried up from the face of the earth. In some copies the Greek edition states the reason for sending out the raven thus: Καὶ ἀπέστειλε τὸν κόρακα ἰδεῖν, εἰ κεκόπακε τὸ ὕδωρ [Kai apesteile ton koraka idein, ei kekopake to hydōr]; And he sent out the raven, to see whether the waters had ceased. This is taken from the following verse, which concerns the dove: He also sent out the dove from him, to see whether the waters had abated from the face of the earth. And indeed it is evident that Noah sent out the raven with the same intention as the dove. But Moses, to avoid the tedium of repetition, stated this only of the dove, whose story he therefore set out more explicitly, because it is of greater importance. So on the first day of the tenth month, when the waters of the flood had decreased considerably, the topmost peaks of the highest mountains had already begun to appear, Gen 8:5. And after forty days had passed, that is, on the eleventh day of the eleventh month, Noah opened the window of the ark and sent out the raven. Since forty days of rain had overwhelmed the earth with waters, Gen 7:12, Noah had hoped that the waters would dry up in the same number of days. When this did not happen, he sent out the raven, which he knew could be lured by the smell of carcasses to fly farther off, if the earth were already open to animals. But the raven, flying round the ark, did not go far from it. It went out (says Moses) going forth and returning. For once sent out, seeing nothing but foul swamps, it at once sought refuge either in the ark or on top of the ark. Flying off from it again and again, it kept returning; and it did nothing II, 801 else until the waters had dried up. The Hebrews talk nonsense in the Agudda, saying that the raven did not stop circling the ark, nor go where it had been sent, שהיה חושדו על בת זוגו, because he was anxious about his mate (or female); that is, lest in his absence she be covered by another. Since this cannot be understood of another raven, as Noah had kept only two, I will not add the monstrosities that these impure men, the most senseless of mortals, invent for themselves. In Bereshit Rabbah, section 33, Noah and the raven converse with each other. When the raven asks why, out of all the cattle, col. 210 wild beasts and birds, he alone was sent, Noah replies that the world could easily do without ravens, since they are useful neither לאכילה, for eating, nor לקרבן, for sacrifices. But God intervenes, warning that in future ages ravens would be of great use, namely in the time of Elias, who was fed for some time on bread and meat brought by ravens. And for that very reason, of course, God did not want the raven to go far from the ark. And He said to it, אתה מזומן לשליחות אחרת בימי אליהו, In the days of Elias you must undertake another mission (of greater importance); and therefore you must be preserved for those times. This, they say, the very words of Moses obscurely hint at when he says עד יבשת, until they had dried up, because the word יבשת has the same letters as the word תשבי Tishbi. Thus עד יבשת means עד תשבי, Until the Tishbite, supply Elias, as Baal Hatturim [=Jacob ben Asher (d. 1343), commentary on the Torah] observes; and he adds that the letters of יבשת המים, The waters dried up, by Gematria are equivalent to נחל כרית, the brook Cherith, where the ravens fed Elias: which, however, is not true.


Haec de corvo Noae juxta Hebraeos: sed multo aliter Graeci; quorum versio in speciem id ipsum negat, quod diserte asserit Moses, nempe rediisse corvum. Habet enim, Ἐξελθὼν οὐκ ἀνέστρεψεν, Egressus (ex arca corvus) non reversus est, pro Hebraeis ויצא יצוא ושוב, Et egressus est egrediendo, et redeundo. Syrus itidem, ܘܢܦܩ ܡܦܩ ܘܠܐ ܗܦܟ, Et egressus est egrediendo, et non rediit. Et Hieronymus, Qui egrediebatur, et non revertebatur. Et Arabes manuscripti duo, quos in Suecia vidi, لم يعون non rediit, aut فلم يعد et non rediit. Sed ille ex Graeca, hic ex Syra versione palam expressi. Quod ipsum sequuntur prisci doctores, Hilarius, Arnobius et Pseudo-Hieronymus in Psalmum centesimum quadragesimum sextum, verus Hieronymus in Dialogo contra Luciferianos capite octavo, Ambrosius libri De Noë et arca capite decimo septimo, Sulpitius Severus Historiae libro primo, Augustinus in Genesim libro primo, Quaestione decima tertia, et passim, Chrysostomus in Genesim li-bro secundo. Eutychius quoque Alexandrinus pag. 40. فذهب الغراب ولم يرجع Et abiit corvus, nec reversus est. Omnes denique veteres, in quos incidere licuit, praeter unum Procopium, qui negationem non admittit. Unde nata duplex quaestio: prior, unde ortum sumpserit haec lectionum diversitas; II, 802 altera, utra lectio vera sit, atque alteri praeferenda. Atque ad illam multi respondent, Hebraeos et Graecos posse optime conciliari; utrumque enim vere dici, et corvum esse reversum, et corvum non esse reversum. Cum ad arcam reversus sit, vel super arcam, sed non reversus sit in arcam. Quae responsio est inanis. Cum neutra lectio corvum dicat in arcam, aut super arcam rediisse, vel non rediisse: sed harum una simpliciter corvum rediisse habet, altera non rediisse; quae omnino sunt contraria. Mosis verba Gen. XXII, 1. Deus tentavit Abrahamum, si quis ita reddiderit, Deus non tentavit Abrahamum, nonne esset falsus interpres; etiamsi verum sit aliquo modo, Deum non tentasse Abrahamum, nempe quomodo dixit Iacobus a), Deum neminem tentare? Praeterea, licet in Hebraeo textu non diserte dicatur corvus rediisse in arcam, tamen palam subintelligitur. Ita enim habent verba: Egressus est egrediendo, et redeundo, donec, etc. Id est, saepe egressus est, et saepe rediit. Ex arca porro ut saepe egrederetur, necesse illi fuit in eandem saepe regredi. Neque enim e domo quisquam egreditur, qui in eam non sit ingressus. Aliis Hebraeum שוב col. 211 non solum redire, sed et recedere est: ut hujus ipsius capitis versu tertio, וישבו המים מעל הארץ הלוך ושוב, Et redierunt aquae a facie terrae, eundo et redeundo, id est, recesserunt recedendo. Et pari ratione, inquiunt, corvus ex arca egressus est exeundo, ושוב, et redeundo, id est, recedendo. Ex arca porro recedere idem est, ut asserunt, quod ad eam non reverti. Sed neque haec responsio satis est idonea. Nam, quidquid dicant, שוב proprie redire est. Etiam cum dicuntur aquae a facie terrae rediisse, ideo rediisse dicuntur, quia prius eam demerserant, et a facie terrae se conferebant in naturalem suum locum, id est, in mare, etc. Praeterea שוב in recedendi notione non sumitur, nisi addita particula מן, id est, ab, vel ex, quae hic nusquam comparet. Denique haec non cohaerent, Corvus exiit exeundo et recedendo, donec exaruissent aquae. Exiit enim corvus mensis undecimi die undecima, Gen. VIII, 5. 6. Et aquae demum exaruerunt anni sequentis initio, Gen. VIII, 13. id est, diebus quinquaginta post corvi exitum. Quo toto tempore corvum semper ex arca recessisse, nemo dixerit. Dato tamen, non concesso, Hebraea verba sic posse reddi: Corvus exiit exeundo et recedendo, ab iis valde diversa esset Graeca versio, Corvus egressus non rediit. Abire enim et recedere alicunde per quinquaginta dierum iter, non idem est, quod inde abire, nec redire ante diem quinquagesimum. Alii Iudaeos volunt negationem ex Hebraeo textu exemisse, quos refellit Samaritani codicis cum Hebraico consensus. Praeterea Chaldaei duo, Ionathan et Onkelos, hic habent, ונפק מפק ותאיב. Et Samaritanus interpres, ࠅࠍࠐࠒ ࠌࠐࠅࠒ ࠅࠕࠁ Et egressus est egrediendo et revertendo. Et Arabs Parisiis editus, II, 803 فجعل يخرج ويرجع Et exibat, et redibat. Et Erpenianus, وخرج خارجا وراجعا Et exiit exiens, et rediens. Iosephus quoque Antiqu. lib. 1. cap. 4. πρὸς Νῶχον ἐπανῆλθε, Ad Noam rediit. Sed et in Beresith Rabba, et in Agudda, qui Hebraeorum libri sunt vetustissimi, legitur iste locus plane ut in nostris codicibus. Hieronymum denique sic legisse, mihi persuasissimum est, et in Quaestionibus Hebraicis haberi perperam: „Et de corvo aliter (in Hebraeo textu) dicitur, Et emisit corvum, et egressus est exiens, et non revertens“. Le-gendum enim, Exiens et revertens. Nam, si legas, et non revertens, quorsum asserit, in Hebraeo textu aliter, quam in Graeco dici? Quae Chisamensis episcopi observatio est verissima. Neque vero causam habuere Iudaei, cur illum locum corrumperent, cum eorum nihil intersit, utrum corvus rediisse, vel non rediisse credatur. Sunt denique, qui Graecis codicibus, vel certo consilio, vel per scribarum incuriam putant insertam fuisse negationem: quorum neutrum est verissimile. Non prius; quia ut reliquis Hebraeorum causa non fuit, cur negationem ex Hebraeo textu eximerent, ita nec Graecis interpretibus causa fuit, cur illam suae versioni adderent: neque posterius; quia ex Graecis verbis (Ἐξελ-θὼν οὐκ ἀνέστρεψεν, ἕως τοῦ ξηρανθῆναι τὸ ὕδωρ, Egressus non rediit, donec aquae exaruissent) negationem si demas, dissolvetur orationis tota compages. Et haec erunt sine ullo sensu, Egressus rediit, donec aquae exaruissent. Cum igitur haec versio iis verbis concepta sit, ex quibus negatio nullo modo potest abesse, eam patet ab ipsis auctoribus esse adscriptam, non scribarum errore insultam, atque in textum insertam.

So much on Noah's raven according to the Hebrews. The Greeks, however, put it very differently: their version appears to deny the very thing that Moses expressly asserts, namely that the raven came back. For it has Ἐξελθὼν οὐκ ἀνέστρεψεν [Exelthōn ouk anestrepsen], Having gone out (from the ark, the raven) did not return, for the Hebrew ויצא יצוא ושוב, And it went out, going out and returning. The Syriac likewise has ܘܢܦܩ ܡܦܩ ܘܠܐ ܗܦܟ [ונפק מפק ולא הפך], And it went out, going out, and did not return. And Jerome: Which went out and did not return. And two Arabic manuscripts which I saw in Sweden have لم يعون [lam yaʿūn] it did not return, or فلم يعد [fa-lam yaʿud] and it did not return. But the former is plainly rendered from the Greek version, the latter from the Syriac. The early doctors follow the same reading: Hilary, Arnobius and Pseudo-Jerome on Psalm 146; the genuine Jerome in the Dialogue against the Luciferians, chapter 8; Ambrose, On Noah and the Ark, chapter 17; Sulpicius Severus, History, book 1; Augustine on Genesis, book 1, Question 13, and elsewhere; Chrysostom on Genesis, book 2. Also Eutychius of Alexandria, p. 40: فذهب الغراب ولم يرجع [fa-dhahaba al-ghurāb wa-lam yarjiʿ] And the raven went away, and did not return. In short, all the ancients whom I have been able to come across, except Procopius alone, who does not admit the negation. Hence a twofold question arises: first, where this difference of readings originated; II, 802 second, which reading is true and to be preferred to the other. To the first many reply that the Hebrews and the Greeks can very well be reconciled, since both statements are truly made: that the raven returned and that the raven did not return. For it returned to the ark, or onto the ark, but did not return into the ark. This answer is empty. For neither reading says that the raven returned or did not return into the ark or onto the ark; rather, one of them says simply that the raven returned, the other that it did not return, which are flatly contrary. If someone rendered the words of Moses, Gen 22:1. God tested Abraham, as God did not test Abraham, would he not be a false translator, even though it is in some sense true that God did not test Abraham, namely in the sense in which James said a) that God tempts no one? Moreover, although the Hebrew text does not expressly say that the raven returned into the ark, it is nevertheless plainly implied. For the words run thus: It went out, going out and returning, until, etc. That is, it often went out and often returned. And in order to go out of the ark often, it had necessarily to go back into it often. For no one goes out of a house who has not gone into it. According to others the Hebrew שוב col. 211 means not only to return but also to recede, as in verse 3 of this very chapter: וישבו המים מעל הארץ הלוך ושוב, And the waters returned from the face of the earth, going and returning, that is, they receded steadily. And in the same way, they say, the raven went out, going out from the ark, ושוב, and returning, that is, receding. And to recede from the ark, they assert, is the same as not returning to it. But neither is this answer adequate. For whatever they say, שוב properly means to return. Even when the waters are said to have returned from the face of the earth, they are said to have returned because they had previously submerged it and were withdrawing from the face of the earth to their natural place, that is, into the sea, etc. Moreover, שוב is not taken in the sense of receding unless the particle מן, that is, from or out of, is added, which nowhere appears here. Finally, these words do not hang together: The raven went out, going out and receding, until the waters had dried up. For the raven went out on the eleventh day of the eleventh month, Gen 8:5–6., and the waters dried up only at the beginning of the following year, Gen 8:13, that is, fifty days after the raven went out. No one would say that the raven kept receding from the ark during that whole time. But granting, without conceding, that the Hebrew words could be rendered thus, The raven went out, going out and receding, the Greek version, The raven having gone out did not return, would still differ greatly from them. For to go away and recede from somewhere over a fifty days' journey is not the same as to go away from there and not return before the fiftieth day. Others hold that the Jews removed the negation from the Hebrew text; they are refuted by the agreement of the Samaritan codex with the Hebrew. Moreover the two Chaldees, Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] and Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos], have here ונפק מפק ותאיב. And the Samaritan translator has ࠅࠍࠐࠒ [ונפק] ࠌࠐࠅࠒ [מפוק] ࠅࠕࠁ [ותב] And it went out, going out and returning. And the Arabic edited at Paris, II, 803 فجعل يخرج ويرجع [fa-jaʿala yakhruju wa-yarjiʿu] And it kept going out and coming back. And Erpenianus [=the Arabic version edited by Thomas Erpenius (Pentateuch 1622; New Testament 1616)], وخرج خارجا وراجعا [wa-kharaja khārijan wa-rājiʿan] And it went out, going out and returning. Josephus also, Antiqu. book 1, ch. 4: πρὸς Νῶχον ἐπανῆλθε [pros Nōchon epanēlthe], It returned to Noah. Moreover, in Bereshit Rabbah and in the Agudda, which are very ancient books of the Hebrews, this passage reads exactly as in our codices. Finally, I am entirely convinced that Jerome read it thus, and that the Hebrew Questions read wrongly: „And of the raven it is said otherwise (in the Hebrew text): And he sent out the raven, and it went out, going out and not returning“. For one should read going out and returning. For if you read and not returning, why does he assert that the Hebrew text says something different from the Greek? This observation of the bishop of Chisamus is entirely true. Nor indeed did the Jews have any reason to corrupt that passage, since it makes no difference to them whether the raven is believed to have returned or not. Finally, there are those who think the negation was inserted into the Greek codices, either deliberately or through the carelessness of scribes; neither of these is at all likely. Not the former, because just as the Hebrews had no reason to remove the negation from the Hebrew text, so the Greek translators had no reason to add it to their version. Nor the latter, because if you take the negation out of the Greek words (Ἐξελθὼν οὐκ ἀνέστρεψεν, ἕως τοῦ ξηρανθῆναι τὸ ὕδωρ [Exelthōn ouk anestrepsen, heōs tou xēranthēnai to hydōr], Having gone out it did not return until the waters had dried up), the whole structure of the sentence falls apart, and it will make no sense at all: Having gone out it returned until the waters had dried up. Since, therefore, this version is framed in words from which the negation can in no way be absent, it is clear that it was written by the translators themselves, not slipped in and inserted into the text by scribal error.


Nempe, si recte conjicimus, Hebraea verba, יצוא ושוב, Egrediendo et redeundo, Graeci interpretes sic legerunt, ולוא ישוב, Et non reversus est. Ad col. 212 verbum, Et non revertetur. Sed Futurum pro Praeterito tam frequenter occurrit, ut in uno Psalmo centesimo septimo huius καταχρήσεως viginti minimum exempla reperire sit. Neque scriptura multum differunt יצוא ושוב, et ולוא ישוב. Nam Vau et Iod in veteribus manuscriptis literae sunt tam similes, ut saepissime permutentur. Et Lamed a Tsade fere solo cornu differt: quod Tsade dextrum habet, et demissius; Lamed sinistrum, et elatius. Sciunt quid velim, qui Rabbinorum lectioni assueverunt. Hinc igitur, nisi fallor, diversae lectionis et versionis horum verborum vera est origo. Neque facile dixerim, utra sit praeferenda. Et quamvis Hebraicam lectionem venerari soleam, ut ab ea nunquam discedam nisi valde invitus: tamen Graecam fateor hoc loco esse perspicuam magis, Egressus est corvus, neque rediit donec etc. id est, nunquam ad arcam rediit. At, inquiunt, si non rediit; quid de illo factum est? Respondet Augustinus in Iohannem Tractatu sexto, Mortuus est in his aquis. Et II, 804 In Faustum libri duodecimi capite vigesimo, Emissus corvus non est reversus, aut aquis utique interceptus, aut aliquo supernatante cadavere illectus. Et Cyrillus in Glaphyris libro secundo, Ἐνεπνίγη δὲ, οἶμαι, τοῖς ὕδασιν, ἔρεισμά τε, καὶ στάσιν οὐχ εὑρηκώς· Submersus est, ut arbitror, aquis, cum, ubi subsisteret, non invenisset. Quod potest sine periculo concedi. Et frustra objicitur, ex uno corvo superstite non potuisse post diluvium corvorum speciem reparari. Poterat enim ille corvus foeminam inivisse, antequam emitteretur. Et vero sunt ex Hebraeis, qui ob id ipsum volunt a Noa fuisse emissum, quod arcam intempestiva libidine polluisset, atque incestasset. Potuit etiam superesse corvus, etsi in arcam non redierit, sive cadaveri aquis innatanti insederit, aut montium verticibus, qui aquis nudari jam inceperant diebus quadraginta, antequam fuisset emissus, Gen. VIII, 5. 6. 7. Cur igitur columba, septiduo post emissa, non reperiens, ubi pedem figeret, in arcam redire coacta est, quia aquae adhuc universae terrae incumbebant, Gen. VIII, 8? Respondeo: Primo, gratis id dici, columbam septiduo post corvum fuisse emissam. Illam quidem emisit Noë ὀπίσω αὐτοῦ post eum, id est, post corvum, si Graecos et Hieronymum sequimur: sed ne id quidem habet Moses, cuius verba sunt, Et emisit columbam מאתו a se: quomodo recte reddunt Ionathan, et Onkelos, et Syrus, et Samaritanus, et uterque Arabs. Itaque potuerunt corvus et columba simul emitti. Pone tamen, columbam post corvum fuisse emissam; quid opus est hanc emissionem in septiduum differre, cum, corvo non reverso, Noë potuerit illam emittere die proxime sequente? Secundo, columba rediit, quia in humidis et uliginosis locis pedem non figit libenter. At corvum, utpote temperamenti siccissimi, aquis maxime gaudere notum. Unde est, quod corvi, futuram pluviam praesentientes, multa edunt laetitiae signa, tam voce, quam motu alarum: quae videre est in Arato versu 963. etc. Quia φιληδοῦσι τοῖς ὑγροῖς, humidis oblectantur, ut ibi habet Theon.

That is, if we conjecture rightly, the Greek translators read the Hebrew words יצוא ושוב, going out and returning, as ולוא ישוב, and it did not return. Literally col. 212 and it will not return. But the future for the past occurs so frequently that in Psalm 107 alone one can find at least twenty examples of this κατάχρησις [katachrēsis]. Nor do יצוא ושוב and ולוא ישוב differ much in writing. For in old manuscripts the letters Vau and Iod are so similar that they are very often interchanged. And Lamed differs from Tsade almost only by its horn: Tsade has it on the right and lower, Lamed on the left and higher. Those who are accustomed to reading the Rabbis know what I mean. Here, then, if I am not mistaken, is the true origin of the different reading and rendering of these words. Nor would I readily say which is to be preferred. And although I am accustomed to revere the Hebrew reading, so that I never depart from it except very reluctantly, I nevertheless admit that in this passage the Greek is clearer: The raven went out, and did not return until etc., that is, it never returned to the ark. But, they say, if it did not return, what became of it? Augustine answers in his sixth Tractate on John: It died in these waters. And II, 804 in Against Faustus, book 12, chapter 20: The raven, when sent out, did not return, being either overtaken by the waters or lured by some floating corpse. And Cyril in the Glaphyra, book 2: Ἐνεπνίγη δὲ, οἶμαι, τοῖς ὕδασιν, ἔρεισμά τε, καὶ στάσιν οὐχ εὑρηκώς· [Enepnigē de, oimai, tois hydasin, ereisma te, kai stasin ouch heurēkōs] It was drowned, I think, in the waters, since it had not found where to stand. This can be granted without risk. And it is objected in vain that the species of ravens could not have been restored after the flood from a single surviving raven. For that raven could have mated with the female before it was sent out. Indeed, there are some among the Hebrews who hold that it was sent out by Noah for precisely this reason, that it had polluted and defiled the ark with untimely lust. The raven could also have survived even though it did not return to the ark, whether by perching on a corpse floating on the waters, or on the mountain tops, which had already begun to be laid bare of the waters forty days before it was sent out, Gen 8:5–6. 7. Why then was the dove, sent out seven days later, forced to return to the ark, not finding where to set its foot, because the waters still lay over the whole earth, Gen 8:8? I answer: First, it is asserted without grounds that the dove was sent out seven days after the raven. Noah did indeed send it out ὀπίσω αὐτοῦ [opisō autou] after it, that is, after the raven, if we follow the Greeks and Jerome; but Moses does not even say this. His words are: And he sent out the dove מאתו from himself, as Jonathan, Onkelos, the Syriac, the Samaritan and both Arabic versions rightly render it. So the raven and the dove could have been sent out at the same time. But suppose the dove was sent out after the raven: what need was there to delay this sending for seven days, when, the raven not having returned, Noah could have sent it out on the very next day? Second, the dove returned because it does not willingly set its foot in wet and marshy places. But the raven, being of a very dry temperament, is known to delight greatly in water. Hence ravens, sensing coming rain, give many signs of joy, both by their voice and by the movement of their wings, as can be seen in Aratus, line 963 etc. Because φιληδοῦσι τοῖς ὑγροῖς [philēdousi tois hygrois], they delight in moist things, as Theon puts it there.


Sed et Graecorum lectioni favere videtur Ethnica fabula de corvo, qui, ab Apolline aquatum missus, non rediit, nisi post ficus maturas. Ovidius libro secundo Fastorum,

The pagan fable of the raven also seems to favour the Greek reading: sent by Apollo to fetch water, it did not return until the figs were ripe. Ovid, Fasti, book 2:


Immemor imperii sedisse sub arbore fertur,
Dum fierent tarda dulcia poma mora.

Forgetful of its orders, it is said to have sat beneath a tree,
Until the fruit grew sweet with slow delay.


Hyginus Astronomicῶn libro secundo in Hydra; Corvus, Apollinis tutela usus, eo sacrificante missus a fonte aquam puram petitum, vidit arbores complures ficorum immaturas: eas expectans, dum maturescerent, in arbore quadam earum consedit. Et Germanicus in Aratum capite De Hydra, Corvus ideo inter astra col. 213 collocatus dicitur, eo quod fuerit in tutela Apollinis, a quo missus ad fontem, etc. cum vidisset arbores, grossos ficus habentes, volans consedit in eis, donec maturae II, 805 fierent, et aquam deferre distulit. A quo parum diversus Arati Scholiastes nondum editus, quem habeo manuscriptum; Τιμὴν γὰρ ἔχει ὁ κόραξ παρὰ τῷ Ἀπόλλωνι· ἑκάστῳ γὰρ τῶν Θεῶν ὄρνεόν ἐστι ἀνακείμενον. Θυσίας δὲ γενομέ-νης τοῖς Θεοῖς, σπονδὴν πεμφθεὶς ἐνέγκαι ἀπὸ κρήνης τινος, ἰδὼν παρὰ τὴν κρήνην συκὴν ὀλύνθους ἔχουσαν, ἔμεινεν, ὡςb) πεπανθῶσιν. Sed paulo aliter Aelianus Hist. lib. 1. cap. 47. Ὁ Ἀπολλὼν αὐτὸν θεράποντα ὄντα ὑδρευσάμενον ἀποπέμπει· ὁ δὲ ἐντυγχάνει λήϊῳ βαθεῖ μὲν, ἔτι δὲ χλωρῷ, καὶ μένει ἕως ἂν αὖον γένηται, τῶν πυρῶν περαχναῦσαιc) βουλόμενος, καὶ τοῦ προστάγματος ὠλιγώρησεν. Cum ad aquationem eum famulum suum misisset Apollo, ille in magnam segetem, adhuc viridem, cum incidisset, expectavit dum maturuisset, granis frumenti frui volens, et mandatum neglexit. Et aliter rursus apud Gesnerum Oppiani Scholiastes in librum primum Ἰξευτικῶν, Cum Coronis in Tricca Aesculapium pareret, Corax (servus) aquari jussus, re neglecta ἐλαγνεύετο lasciviebat: quamobrem iratus Apollo convertit eum in avem atram, etc. Sed haec ita diversa sunt, ut appareat, ex eodem fonte esse orta. Ut et vetus Proverbium de cessatore apud Hesychium, et Suidam, Κόραξ ὑδρεύει, Corvus aquatur. Et plerique, ut corvi moram longissimam fuisse significent, illum expectasse fingunt, donec ficus maturuisset; quia ficus serotina est, nec nisi cum uvis maturescit, ut constat ex Cant. II, 13. et Num. XIII, 24. Unde Epictetus apud Arrianum libri primi capite decimo quinto, Ἄν μοι λέγῃς, ὅτι θέλω σῦκον, ἀποκρινοῦμαί σοι, ὅτι χρόνου δεῖ· ἄφες ἀνθήσῃ πρῶτον, εἶτα προβαλεῖ τὸν καρπὸν, εἶτα πε-πανθῇ. εἶτα συκῆς μὲν καρπὸς ἄφνω, καὶ μίᾳ ὥρᾳ οὐ τελειοῦται. Si mihi dicas, te velle ficum, respondebo tibi, tempore opus esse. Permitte, ut primum floreat, deinde fructum emittat, deinde maturescat. Neque enim fici fructus cito et una hora ad maturitatem perducitur. Proinde ficus apta visa est ad designandam corvi moram, et cunctationem ad aquas. Quod ipsum natum videtur ex historia de corvo Noae, qui, ad aquas emissus, non rediit, donec, etc. Atque eodem fortasse pertinet, quod tradunt veteres apud Servium, corvos obliviosos esse, et plerumque minime ad nidos suos reverti. Neque enim id corvo tribuunt philosophorum libri. Sed fama de corvo Noae, qui reditus fuit immemor, causa potuit esse, cur vulgus corvino generi affingeret, quod huic fuit peculiare. Hae conjecturae si verae sunt, ut saltem habent aliquam veri speciem, vetustissima est illa lectio, qua corvus, ex arca emissus, ad Noam rediisse negatur.

Hyginus, in the second book of the Astronomica, under Hydra: The raven, which was under the protection of Apollo, was sent by him, while he was sacrificing, to fetch pure water from a spring. It saw a number of fig trees with unripe fruit; waiting for them to ripen, it settled on one of those trees. And Germanicus on Aratus, in the chapter On the Hydra: The raven is said to have been placed among the stars col. 213 because it was under the protection of Apollo, by whom it was sent to a spring, etc. When it had seen trees bearing unripe figs, it flew and settled on them until they II, 805 became ripe, and put off bringing the water. Little different from him is the still unpublished Scholiast on Aratus, whom I have in manuscript: Τιμὴν γὰρ ἔχει ὁ κόραξ παρὰ τῷ Ἀπόλλωνι· ἑκάστῳ γὰρ τῶν Θεῶν ὄρνεόν ἐστι ἀνακείμενον. Θυσίας δὲ γενομένης τοῖς Θεοῖς, σπονδὴν πεμφθεὶς ἐνέγκαι ἀπὸ κρήνης τινος, ἰδὼν παρὰ τὴν κρήνην συκὴν ὀλύνθους ἔχουσαν, ἔμεινεν, ὡςb) πεπανθῶσιν [Timēn gar echei ho korax para tō Apollōni; hekastō gar tōn Theōn orneon esti anakeimenon. Thysias de genomenēs tois Theois, spondēn pemphtheis enenkai apo krēnēs tinos, idōn para tēn krēnēn sykēn olynthous echousan, emeinen, hōs pepanthōsin]. But Aelian puts it somewhat differently, Hist. book 1, ch. 47: Ὁ Ἀπολλὼν αὐτὸν θεράποντα ὄντα ὑδρευσάμενον ἀποπέμπει· ὁ δὲ ἐντυγχάνει λήϊῳ βαθεῖ μὲν, ἔτι δὲ χλωρῷ, καὶ μένει ἕως ἂν αὖον γένηται, τῶν πυρῶν περαχναῦσαιc) βουλόμενος, καὶ τοῦ προστάγματος ὠλιγώρησεν [Ho Apollōn auton theraponta onta hydreusamenon apopempei; ho de entynchanei lēïō bathei men, eti de chlōrō, kai menei heōs an auon genētai, tōn pyrōn perachnausai boulomenos, kai tou prostagmatos ōligōrēsen]. When Apollo had sent it, his servant, to fetch water, it came upon a large field of grain, still green, and waited until it had ripened, wishing to enjoy the grains of wheat, and it neglected its errand. And differently again the Scholiast on Oppian, cited by Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium], on the first book of the Ἰξευτικά [Ixeutika]: When Coronis was giving birth to Asclepius in Tricca, Corax (a servant), ordered to fetch water, neglected the task and ἐλαγνεύετο [elagneueto] was wanton; for this reason the angry Apollo turned him into a black bird, etc. But these accounts differ in such a way that it is evident they arose from the same source. So too the old proverb about an idler in Hesychius and the Suda: Κόραξ ὑδρεύει [Korax hydreuei], The raven is fetching water. And most writers, to indicate that the raven's delay was very long, imagine that it waited until the fig had ripened; for the fig is late and ripens only with the grapes, as is clear from Song 2:13 and Num 13:24. Hence Epictetus in Arrian, book 1, chapter 15: Ἄν μοι λέγῃς, ὅτι θέλω σῦκον, ἀποκρινοῦμαί σοι, ὅτι χρόνου δεῖ· ἄφες ἀνθήσῃ πρῶτον, εἶτα προβαλεῖ τὸν καρπὸν, εἶτα πεπανθῇ. εἶτα συκῆς μὲν καρπὸς ἄφνω, καὶ μίᾳ ὥρᾳ οὐ τελειοῦται [An moi legēs, hoti thelō sykon, apokrinoumai soi, hoti chronou dei; aphes anthēsē prōton, eita probalei ton karpon, eita pepanthē. eita sykēs men karpos aphnō, kai mia hōra ou teleioutai]. If you tell me that you want a fig, I shall answer you that it takes time. Let it first blossom, then put forth its fruit, then ripen. For the fruit of the fig tree is not brought to ripeness quickly and in a single hour. Accordingly the fig seemed suitable for denoting the raven's delay and its dawdling at the water. This very idea seems to have sprung from the story of Noah's raven, which, sent out to the waters, did not return until, etc. And perhaps to the same thing belongs what the ancients report in Servius, that ravens are forgetful, and for the most part do not return to their nests at all. For the books of the philosophers do not attribute this to the raven. But the report of Noah's raven, which forgot to return, may have been the reason why the common people ascribed to the whole raven kind what was peculiar to this one. If these conjectures are true, as at least they have some appearance of truth, then that reading by which the raven sent out of the ark is denied to have returned to Noah is very ancient.


Quid quod ex verbis Hebraeis, prout hodie leguntur, non facile est se expedire, Exiit exeundo, et redeundo, donec aquae exaruissent? Illud enim, Exiit exeundo, est Ἑβραϊκώτατον. Sed quod sequitur, Exiit redeundo, poterit II, 806 videri durius, et esse oppositum in apposito. Et dubito, an alibi dicatur animal exire redeundo. Nec patet, quorsum Noë corvum, in arcam semel regressum, passus sit ex ea toties egredi, et per quinquaginta dies divagari nullo successu: maxime, postquam ex columba didicit, quod scire avebat. Has quippe volitationes clausa fenestra potuisset prohibere. Nam, quod ajunt, corvum ad arcam, non in arcam rediisse, jam supra confutavimus. Itaque non displicet Graeca lectio, quae non laborat his incommodis. Tamen haec pono, non statuo, et peritiorum judicio non illibenter submitto (0).

What of the fact that it is not easy to make sense of the Hebrew words as they are read today: It went out going out, and returning, until the waters had dried up? For It went out going out is thoroughly Hebraic. But what follows, It went out returning, may II, 806 seem rather harsh, and a contradiction in terms. And I doubt whether an animal is anywhere else said to go out returning. Nor is it clear why Noah should have allowed the raven, once it had come back into the ark, to go out of it so many times and wander about for fifty days to no purpose, especially after he had learned from the dove what he was eager to know. For he could have prevented these flights by shutting the window. As for the claim that the raven returned to the ark, not into the ark, we have already refuted it above. Therefore the Greek reading, which does not suffer from these difficulties, does not displease me. Yet I put this forward, I do not decide it, and I not unwillingly submit it to the judgement of those more expert R0.
