CXXXIII, 2. על הזקן זקן אהרן, super barbam, barbam Aaronis. Et Ezech. XLVII, 3. במים מי אפסים, in aquis, aquis talorum. Ita in loco, in quo versamur, legeretur, si plena esset oratio, אברה אברת חסידה, penna, penna, inquam, ciconiae: vel potest suppleri, si mavis, כף דמיון, Caph similitudinis; ita ut אברה חסידה, sit pro אברה כחסידה, penna sicut ciconiae. Cujusmodi locutiones passim occurrunt. Ut Gen. XLIX, 9. Catulus leonis, Iuda. Et Deut. XXXIII, 22. Dan catulus leonis, id est, ut catulus leonis. Gen. XLIX, 14. Issachar, asinus robustus, id est, ut asinus Deut. XXVIII, 23. Coeli tui aes, terra ferrum, id est, ut aes, ut ferrum. 2 Sam. I, 21. Clypeus Saul non unctus, id est, quasi non unctus. Iob VII, 9. Defecit nubes, et abiit, sic qui descendit in sepulchrum, etc. Defecit II, 852 כלה, pro ככלה, sicut defecit. Iob. XI, 12. Onager homo nascitur, id est, sicut onager. Psal. XI, 1. Quomodo dicitis animae meae, ut transmigret a monte vestro צפור, avis, id est, כצפור, sicut avis. Psal. XIV, 4. Comedentes populum meum, comedunt panem, id est, ut comedunt panem. Psal. CXIX, 119. Scorias removisti omnes impios terrae, id est, ut scorias. Proverb. XVII, 22. Cor laetum ייטב גהה, benefacit medicina, id est, כגהה ut medicina. Cant. I, 15. Oculi tui columbarum, id est, ut columbarum. Can. VII, 5. Oculi tui piscinae in Hesbon, pro ut piscinae. Thren. IV, 7. Polities eorum sapphiri, id est, ut sapphiri. Mich. III, 12. Sion ager arabitur, pro ut ager.

With these preliminaries, we shall now try to interpret the whole verse. In Hebrew it reads thus: כנף רננים נעלסה אם אברה חסידה ונוצה, which we render word for word as follows: The wing of the ostriches exults, truly the wing of the stork, and the plumage: that is, which is truly a wing and plumage such as in the stork. The particle אם im is mostly the same as IF, or is a mark of interrogation, like WHETHER, ἄρα [ara], πότερον [poteron]; but also, as Kimchi points out, ויש שהוא כמו האמת. It also occurs for TRULY, and is a particle of affirmation, as if formed from אמן, amen, with the Nun dropped, as in אמת for אמנת R2. Examples of this meaning are found at Gen 47:18. Num 16:30. Job 22:20. Ps 59:16 and LXIII, 7. Prov 3:34 and XXIII, 18. Isa 4:4 and XXIX, 16. etc. The wing of the stork, אברה חסידה, for אברת חסידה: the absolute state for the construct, which is not without examples. Thus Deut 16:21. אשרה כל עץ, a grove of any tree, for אשרת. Ruth 2:17. איפה שערים, an ephah of barley, for איפת. 2 Reg. VII, 1. סאה סולת, a seah of fine flour, for סאת. Ps 45:5. וענוה צדק, and of the meekness of righteousness, for וענות. Isa 24:22. אספה אסיר, with the gathering of a prisoner, for אספת. Isa 42:25. חמה אפו, the heat of his anger, for חמת. These Kimchi in his Commentaries repeatedly explains by ellipsis, as if one said אשרה אשרת כל עץ, a grove, a grove, I say, of any tree: col. 248 as when we read at Exod 38:21. אלה פקודי המשכן משכן העדה, These are the things numbered of the tabernacle, of the tabernacle of the testimony. And Num 32:1. המקום מקום מקנה, the place, a place of cattle. And Ps 133:2. על הזקן זקן אהרן, upon the beard, the beard of Aaron. And Ezek 47:3. במים מי אפסים, in the waters, waters of the ankles. So in the passage we are dealing with, if the expression were complete, it would read אברה אברת חסידה, a wing, a wing, I say, of the stork: or, if you prefer, one may supply כף דמיון, the Caph of similitude, so that אברה חסידה stands for אברה כחסידה, a wing like that of the stork. Expressions of this kind occur everywhere. As Gen 49:9. Judah, a lion's whelp. And Deut 33:22. Dan, a lion's whelp, that is, like a lion's whelp. Gen 49:14. Issachar, a strong ass, that is, like an ass. Deut 28:23 Your heavens bronze, the earth iron, that is, like bronze, like iron. 2 Sam 1:21. The shield of Saul not anointed, that is, as if not anointed. Job 7:9 The cloud has vanished and gone, so he who goes down to the grave, etc. Has vanished II, 852 כלה, for ככלה, as it vanished. Job 11:12 Man is born a wild ass, that is, like a wild ass. Ps 11:1 How do you say to my soul, that it should flee from your mountain צפור, a bird, that is, כצפור, like a bird. Ps 14:4 Eating my people, they eat bread, that is, as they eat bread. Ps 119:119 You have removed all the wicked of the earth as dross, that is, like dross. Proverb. XVII, 22. A merry heart ייטב גהה, does good, a medicine, that is, כגהה, like a medicine. Song 1:15 Your eyes doves', that is, like doves'. Can. VII, 5. Your eyes the pools in Heshbon, for like the pools. Lam 4:7 Their polish sapphires, that is, like sapphires. Mic 3:12. Zion shall be ploughed a field, for like a field.


Haec de verbis: sensum quod attinet, jam prius hemistichium abunde explicavimus, et docuimus, quo sensu struthionum ala dicatur exultare, aut laeta esse: sed de posteriore hemistichio, vere ala ciconiae, et pluma; vel vere ala tanquam ciconiae, et pluma, duo quaeri possunt. 1. Quo pertineat illa asseveratio, VE-RE ala, et pluma. 2. Cur ala et pluma ciconiae dicatur, aut tanquam ciconiae. Ad primum respondeo, struthionem avem esse non avem, quae in multis accedit ad naturam quadrupedis. Quod pridem observavit Philosophus libro quarto De partibus fere in fine. Verba sunt, Quaedam habet avis, quaedam quadrupedis propria. Non esse quadrupedem, suadet, quod pennas habet, et non esse avem, quod non volat in sublime, nec pennas ad volatum commodas, sed pilosas habet. Insuper tanquam quadrupes superiora habet cilia, et capite glaber est, et parte colli superiore; adeoque cilia habet pilosiora. Sed, ut avis, inferiora habet plumis operta. Et bipes etiam est, ut avis; sed bisulcus ut quadrupes. Neque enim ha-bet digitos, sed bifidam ungulam: cuius causa est magnitudo, quam non habet avis, sed quadrupedis. Hinc Diodorus de Arabia libro secundo, Φέρει δὲ καὶ ζῶα διφυῆ, καὶ μεμιγμένα ταῖς ἰδέαις, ὧν αἱ μὲν ὀνομαζόμεναι στρουθοκάμηλοι περιειλήφασι τοῖς τύποις μίγματα χηνῶν, καὶ καμήλων· Fert etiam animalia naturae duplicis, et biformia, in quibus qui struthio-cameli vocantur, speciem, ex anseribus et camelis mixtam, habent. Pro χηνῶν lege πτηνῶν· quia, cum id probavit per partes, struthionem concludit χερσαῖον ἅμα φαίνεσθαι, καὶ πτη-νὸν, terrestrem simul, et volucrem videri. Hinc Herodotus στρουθὸς καταγαίους appellat, id est, passeres terrestres. Et Plinius scribit esse pene bestiarum generis. Et Tertullianus, Bestia quaedam magis quam avis. Et Alkazuinius, حيوان مركب من خلقة الطير والجمل Animal est compositum ex natura avis et cameli. Hinc Arabum proverbium est in Damire, de eo, col. 249 qui sibi non constat, nec bonum dignoscit a malo, النعامة لا طير ولا جمل Struthio neque avis, neque camelus est. Proinde Gabriae Fabula vigesima II, 853 octava, cum ferae et volucres inter se disceptarent, utrosque decipiebat Λί-βυσσα στρουθὸς, Libycus struthio, cum videretur

So much for the words. As for the sense, we have already explained the first hemistich fully and shown in what sense the wing of ostriches is said to exult, or to be glad. But concerning the second hemistich, truly the wing of the stork, and plumage, or truly a wing as of a stork, and plumage, two questions can be asked. 1. What is the point of that affirmation, TRULY a wing, and plumage? 2. Why is it called the wing and plumage of a stork, or as of a stork? To the first I answer that the ostrich is a bird that is not a bird, which in many respects approaches the nature of a quadruped. This was long ago observed by the Philosopher in book 4 of On the Parts, near the end. His words are: It has some features proper to a bird and some proper to a quadruped. That it is not a quadruped is suggested by its having feathers; that it is not a bird, by its not flying aloft and having feathers not suited to flight but hair-like. Moreover, like a quadruped it has upper eyelashes, and it is bare on the head and on the upper part of the neck, so that its eyelashes are rather hairy. But, like a bird, its lower parts are covered with plumage. And it is two-footed like a bird, but cloven-hoofed like a quadruped. For it does not have toes but a divided hoof; the cause of this is its size, which is not that of a bird but of a quadruped. Hence Diodorus, on Arabia, in book 2: Φέρει δὲ καὶ ζῶα διφυῆ, καὶ μεμιγμένα ταῖς ἰδέαις, ὧν αἱ μὲν ὀνομαζόμεναι στρουθοκάμηλοι περιειλήφασι τοῖς τύποις μίγματα χηνῶν, καὶ καμήλων· [Pherei de kai zōa diphyē, kai memigmena tais ideais, hōn hai men onomazomenai strouthokamēloi perieilēphasi tois typois migmata chēnōn, kai kamēlōn] It also produces animals of a double nature and of two forms, among which those called ostriches have an appearance mixed of geese and camels. For χηνῶν [chēnōn] read πτηνῶν [ptēnōn], because, having proved this part by part, he concludes that the ostrich χερσαῖον ἅμα φαίνεσθαι, καὶ πτηνὸν [chersaion hama phainesthai, kai ptēnon], seems at once a land animal and a winged one. Hence Herodotus calls them στρουθὸς καταγαίους [strouthous katagaious], that is, ground sparrows. And Pliny writes that they are almost of the genus of beasts. And Tertullian: A beast of some kind rather than a bird. And Alkazuinius: حيوان مركب من خلقة الطير والجمل [ḥayawān murakkab min khilqat al-ṭayr wa-l-jamal] It is an animal composed of the nature of a bird and of a camel. Hence there is a proverb of the Arabs in Damir, about one col. 249 who is inconsistent and does not distinguish good from bad: النعامة لا طير ولا جمل [al-naʿāma lā ṭayr wa-lā jamal] The ostrich is neither bird nor camel. Accordingly, in Fable 28 of Gabrias II, 853, when the wild beasts and the birds were disputing with each other, Λίβυσσα στρουθὸς [Libyssa strouthos], the Libyan ostrich, deceived both sides, since it seemed


Εἶναι μὲν ὄρνις, ἐκ μέρους δὲ θηρίον,
Πτηνοῖς κάραν δεικνύσα, τοῖς θερσὶ πόδας,

Εἶναι μὲν ὄρνις, ἐκ μέρους δὲ θηρίον, Πτηνοῖς κάραν δεικνύσα, τοῖς θερσὶ πόδας, [Einai men ornis, ek merous de thērion, Ptēnois karan deiknysa, tois thersi podas,]


Avis quidem esse, ex parte autem fera, volucribus caput, pedes feris ostendens. Cum igitur hoc animal quadrupedis tam multa habeat, hic a sacro scriptore describitur cum feris quadrupedibus. Et quia res παράδοξος videri queat, tale animal pennas et plumas habere, ut veras aves: ideo proponitur cum hac asseveratione, Vere penna, etc. et pluma, supple illis est. Neque obscurum est, cur non solum pennas habere dicatur, sed et ciconiae pennas. Struthio colore pennarum plane ciconiam refert. Marmolius ubi supra, En las alas y en la cola tiene grandes plumas negras y blancas, come las de la cigueña. In alis et in cauda magnas ha-bet pennas, nigras et albas, ut ciconiae pennas. Hinc Scaliger i), Cardanum arguens, quod struthioni tribuat pennas coeruleas, candidas, nigras, rubras, virides, quibus ornantur militum galeae, Risum, inquit, movent colores, quos ab infectorum officinis in apothecas naturae transtulisti. Quis enim te non rideat, illa venditantem, hosce colores, quos in galeis infigunt, nativos esse struthio-camelis? Omnes enim fusco et albo picti sunt, ut mihi dixerunt multi mercatores Africani. Quod ut melius intelligerem, ciconiae colori comparabant. Versus iste, sic expositus, sequentibus lucem inferet (3).

To be a bird indeed, but in part a wild beast, showing its head to the birds and its feet to the beasts. Since, then, this animal has so much of the quadruped, it is described here by the sacred writer together with the wild quadrupeds. And because it might seem a παράδοξος [paradoxos] thing that such an animal should have feathers and plumage like true birds, it is therefore set forth with this affirmation: Truly a wing, etc., and plumage; supply they have. Nor is it obscure why it is said to have not only feathers but the feathers of a stork. In the colour of its feathers the ostrich plainly resembles the stork. Marmol, in the place cited above: En las alas y en la cola tiene grandes plumas negras y blancas, come las de la cigueña. In its wings and tail it has large feathers, black and white, like the feathers of the stork. Hence Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)] i), criticizing Cardano for attributing to the ostrich blue, white, black, red and green feathers, with which soldiers' helmets are adorned, says: The colours provoke laughter which you have transferred from the dyers' workshops into the storehouses of nature. For who would not laugh at you, peddling the claim that these colours which they fix on helmets are native to ostriches? For all are marked with dusky and white, as many African merchants told me. That I might understand it better, they compared it to the colour of the stork. This verse, thus explained, will shed light on those that follow R3.

(1) Rosenmüller, II, 850 Quod ipsum tamen verisimile est REISKIO in Conjecturis in Iobum et Proverbia Salomonis Lips. 1779. p. 162., qui non persuadere sibi potest, רננים esse struthionis nomen. Verba ejus sunt: „Sed illo quidem expresso nomine valde opus non est. Nam Arabum ille mos est, de re quadam longe lateque disserere, et eam tamen non nominare. Interrogati, quare sic faciant, respondent, لعلم السمع بها propter scire audientem id, propterea quod audiens et proinde quoque legens ex epithetorum et praedicatorum et descriptionis qualitate totoque filo sermonis assequi facillime queat, qua de re sermo sit. [Cf. eundem Reiskium in Nott. ad Taraphae Moallacah pag. 86.]. Ipse Iobus noster hoc schema supra adhibuit cap. XXVI, 2-5. ubi Deum describit absque ut illum nominet. Conf. XL, 10.“ Haec Reiskius, cui assentiuntur Doederlein in Scholiis ad Li-bros Poeticos V. T. ad loc. et Dathius; qui haec verba ita vertunt: Est, quae alis stridulis exultat, etc. Quod an praeferendum sit interpretationi, quam statim Bochartus subjiciet, quisque judicet ipse. Omitto audaces Reiskii et Michaelis conjecturas, quibus textum receptum sine necessitate turbant. Quas qui scire cupit, ipsos is adeat.

R1 Rosenmüller, II, 850 This very thing, however, seems probable to REISKE in his Conjecturis in Iobum et Proverbia Salomonis, Leipzig 1779, p. 162, who cannot persuade himself that רננים is a name of the ostrich. His words are: "But there is no great need for that name to be expressed. For it is the custom of the Arabs to discourse at length on some thing and yet not to name it. Asked why they do so, they answer, لعلم السمع بها [li-ʿilm al-samʿ bihā], because the hearer knows it, since the hearer, and hence also the reader, can very easily grasp from the character of the epithets, the predicates and the description, and from the whole thread of the discourse, what the subject is. [Cf. the same Reiske in the notes on Tarafa's Moallaka, p. 86.] Our Job himself used this figure above, ch. XXVI, 2-5, where he describes God without naming him. Compare XL, 10." So Reiske, with whom Doederlein in his Scholia ad Libros Poeticos V. T. on the passage, and Dathe agree; they translate these words thus: There is one that exults with whirring wings, etc. Whether this is to be preferred to the interpretation that Bochart will give presently, let each judge for himself. I pass over the bold conjectures of Reiske and Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], by which they needlessly disturb the received text. Whoever wishes to know them should consult the authors themselves.

SCHULTENSIUS ad Iob. XLII, 8. pag. 1214. contulit. Cf. STORRII Observatt. ad Analog. et Synt. Hebr. p. 348. not. *).

SCHULTENS compared on Job 42:8, p. 1214. Cf. STORR, Observatt. ad Analog. et Synt. Hebr. p. 348, note *).

Part 2, Book 2, chapter 17: The rest of Job on the ostrich
----------------------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/struthio-iob-reliqua.html

II, 854 col. 249 CAP. XVII.

II, 854 col. 249 Chapter 17.


Explicantur Iobi reliqua de Struthione capitis trigesimi noni versibus decimo septimo, decimo octavo, decimo nono, vigesimo et vigesimo primo.

The rest of what Job says about the ostrich in chapter 39, verses 17, 18, 19, 20 and 21, is explained.


Postquam in Iobo de struthione id explicavimus, quod erat longe difficillimum, col. 250 in caeteris minus laboris, plus erit utilitatis. Et post ἀκανθολογίαν, seu spinilegium, sequetur ἀνθολογία, aut verius spicilegium. Sacra autem verba sic habent: Sed relinquit in terra ova sua, et super pulverem calefiunt. Et obliviscitur, fore, ut illa pes comprimat, et agri fera conterat. Duriter tractat pullos suos, ac si non essent sui. Frustra laboravit, absque timore est. Quia privavit eam Deus sapientia, nec prudentiam ei impertitus est. Quo tempore in altum se attollit, ridet equum et sessorem ejus. Quae singula jam exponemus.

Now that we have explained in Job what was by far the most difficult point about the ostrich, col. 250 in the rest there will be less labour and more profit. After the ἀκανθολογίαν [akanthologian], or gathering of thorns, will follow the ἀνθολογία [anthologia], or more truly the gleaning of ears. The sacred words run thus: But she leaves her eggs on the ground, and they are warmed upon the dust. And she forgets that the foot may crush them, and the beast of the field trample them. She deals harshly with her chicks, as if they were not hers. She has laboured in vain, she is without fear. For God has deprived her of wisdom, and has not imparted understanding to her. When she raises herself on high, she laughs at the horse and its rider. We shall now expound these one by one.


Sed relinquit in terra ova sua] Hebraice, כי תעזוב לארץ ביציה. Connexio hujus versus cum praecedente talis est: „Struthio alis suis exultat, quas alacres „et pulchras habet; sed eadem est ἄστοργος, et ova sua negligit. Aliquas habet „in corpore dotes, sed duram mentem atque immisericordem.“ Itaque כי hoc loco idem, quod sed: ut Gen. XLV, 8. Non vos me huc misistis, כי האלהים, sed Deus. Relinquit, תעזוב, est Numeri enallage. Nam plurale praecesserat, Ala struthionum exultat. Sed haec enallage nihil est frequentius in Iobi libro. Sic in hoc ipso loco, Relinquit in terra ova sua, etc. Et obliviscitur, fore, ut pes conculcet illud. Et paullo infra de equo, Nunquid dedisti equo fortitudinem, etc. Fodiunt vallem, et gestit fortitudine. Idem verbum תעזוב, relinquit, licet genere Foemininum, tamen refertur ad Nomen רננים renanim, masculinae terminationis. Sed et יענים, struthiones, יעלים, ibices, רמכים, equae, רחלים, oves, et hoc ipso loco ביצים, ova, utut masculina terminatione, tamen genere sunt foemina (1). Quod porro haec avis ova sua in terra dicitur relinquere, plane docet, esse struthionem. Nam in toto genere avium alia nulla se offert, quae hujus criminis vere insimuletur. Indi quidem apud Aelianum (Hist. lib. 14. cap. 13.) ideo cygnos oderunt, quod illos fama fert ἐπιβουλεύειν ἐκγόνοις, καὶ διαφθείρειν τὰ ὠὰ, foetui suo insidiari, et propria ova perdere. Sed famae non semper credendum, quae

But she leaves her eggs on the ground] In Hebrew, כי תעזוב לארץ ביציה. The connection of this verse with the preceding one is as follows: "The ostrich exults in her wings, which she has swift and beautiful; but she is also ἄστοργος [astorgos], and neglects her eggs. She has some endowments of body, but a hard and pitiless mind." Thus כי in this place means the same as but, as in Gen 45:8. It was not you who sent me here, כי האלהים, but God. She leaves, תעזוב, is an enallage of number. For the plural had preceded: The wing of the ostriches exults. But nothing is more frequent than this enallage in the book of Job. So in this very passage: She leaves her eggs on the ground, etc. And she forgets that the foot may tread on it. And a little below, of the horse: Have you given the horse strength, etc. They paw in the valley, and he rejoices in strength. The same verb תעזוב, she leaves, though feminine in gender, nevertheless refers to the noun רננים renanim, of masculine ending. But יענים, ostriches, יעלים, ibexes, רמכים, mares, רחלים, ewes, and in this very place ביצים, eggs, although of masculine ending, are nevertheless feminine in gender R1. Further, the fact that this bird is said to leave her eggs on the ground plainly shows that it is the ostrich. For in the whole class of birds no other presents itself which is truly charged with this crime. The Indians, it is true, according to Aelian (Hist. book 14, ch. 13), hate swans because report has it that they ἐπιβουλεύειν ἐκγόνοις, καὶ διαφθείρειν τὰ ὠὰ [epibouleuein ekgonois, kai diaphtheirein ta ōa], lay snares for their offspring and destroy their own eggs. But report is not always to be believed, which


Tam ficti est, pravique tenax, quam conscia veri. II, 855 Neque necesse habemus, ad extremos Indos currere, ut discamus cygni naturam, qui cum in Batavia et Britannia sit frequens, negant tamen Batavi et Britanni omnes, se tale quidquam in cygno observasse. Ejusdem est commatis, quod apud Athenaeum libro decimo quarto scribit Clytus, Aristotelis discipulus, de ave meleagride: Ἔστι δὲ ἄστοργον πρὸς τὰ ἔκγονα τὸ ὄρνεον, καὶ ὀλιγωρεῖ τῶν νεω-τέρων, ὥστε ἀνάγκη τοῖς ἱερεῦσιν ἐπιμελεῖσθαι αὐτῶν· Animal hoc exiguo est erga prolem affectu, pullosque adeo negligit, ut sacerdotibus eos curare sit necesse. A Clyto enim nomine meleagridis sive gallina describitur, quam Indicam, aut quam Barbaricam nos appellamus, et veteres Numidicam: utraque erga pullos suos naturali φιλοστοργίᾳ vulgari gallinae vix cedit. Neque verius quidam Ara- bes idem crimen impingunt in الحباري alhubara, id est, otidem. Alkazuinius, قالوا ما في الطيور اشد منه بلها يترك بيضها col. 251 وتحضن بيض غيرها وفي المثل كل شي يحب ولده حتي الحباري Ajunt, nullam avem illa stultiorem esse, cum, propriis ovis relictis, aliena foveat. Unde proverbium, Omne animal foetum suum amat praeter otidem. Sed Damir, qui de otide plura scripsit, quam quisquam alius, quem noverim, foeminam saltem his verbis liberat a tam foedo crimine: قال عثمان رضي الله عنه كل شي يحب ولده حتي الحباري خصها بالذكر لانها يضرب بها المثل في الحمق وهي علي حمقها تحب ولدها فتطعمها وتعلمها الطيران كغيرها من الحيوان Dixit Ottomannus, cui Deus sit propitius, omne animal prolem suam amare prae- ter otidem. Sed id proprie ad marem pertinet. Quamvis enim foeminae stultitiam imputet commune proverbium, tamen stultitia sua pullos amat, et cibat, et volare docet, aeque ac reliqua animalia. Sed et aliquem Hieronymo imposuisse necesse est, cum de columba scripsit in Os. VII. Aves caeterae pullos suos etiam cum periculo vitae suae protegere festinant, etc. Sola columba ablàtos pullos non dolet, non requirit. Certe nemo est, qui nesciat, tam erga pullos, quam erga conjuges affectus columbarum esse tenerrimos. Ovis ἐκ διαδοχῆς, id est, per vi- ces, incubant mas et foemina: et pullos natos pari ratione συνθερμαίνουσι, con- junctim fovent. Foeminamque, si post dolores partus pigrius redeat, mas ad nidum revocat levi castigatione. Iisdem pullos ψωμίζειν mutua cura est, praemansum cibum in eorum ora ingerendo: et a nido abductae a quantocunque spatio eum repetunt amore prolis. Unde factum, ut columbis internuntiis quidam usi sint, illas cum alligata schedula in oppidum remittentes, in quo ovis aut pullis incubuerant. Hinc Oppianus libri tertii [Cyneget.] versu 115.

She clings to the false and the wrong as firmly as she proclaims the true. II, 855 Nor do we need to run to the farthest Indians to learn the nature of the swan; although it is common in Holland and Britain, all the Dutch and British nevertheless deny that they have observed any such thing in the swan. Of the same stamp is what Clytus, the disciple of Aristotle, writes in Athenaeus, book 14, about the bird meleagris: Ἔστι δὲ ἄστοργον πρὸς τὰ ἔκγονα τὸ ὄρνεον, καὶ ὀλιγωρεῖ τῶν νεωτέρων, ὥστε ἀνάγκη τοῖς ἱερεῦσιν ἐπιμελεῖσθαι αὐτῶν [Esti de astorgon pros ta ekgona to orneon, kai oligōrei tōn neōterōn, hōste anankē tois hiereusin epimeleisthai autōn]; This animal has little affection for its offspring, and neglects its chicks so much that the priests must take care of them. For by the name meleagris Clytus describes the hen which we call the Indian or the Barbary hen, and the ancients the Numidian: both scarcely yield to the common hen in natural φιλοστοργίᾳ [philostorgia] toward their chicks. Nor do certain Arabs more truly lay the same charge against الحباري [al-ḥubārā] alhubara, that is, the bustard. Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt]: قالوا ما في الطيور اشد منه بلها يترك بيضها [qālū mā fī al-ṭuyūr ashadd minhu balahan yatruku bayḍahā] col. 251 وتحضن بيض غيرها وفي المثل كل شي يحب ولده حتي الحباري [wa-taḥḍunu bayḍ ghayrihā wa-fī al-mathal kull shay yuḥibbu waladahu ḥattā al-ḥubārā] They say that no bird is more foolish than it, since it abandons its own eggs and sits on those of others. Hence the proverb: Every animal loves its young except the bustard. But Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], who has written more about the bustard than anyone else I know of, at least clears the female of so shameful a charge in these words: قال عثمان رضي الله عنه كل شي يحب ولده حتي الحباري خصها بالذكر لانها يضرب بها المثل في الحمق وهي علي حمقها تحب ولدها فتطعمها وتعلمها الطيران كغيرها من الحيوان [qāla ʿUthmān raḍiya Allāh ʿanhu kull shay yuḥibbu waladahu ḥattā al-ḥubārā khaṣṣahā bi-al-dhikr li-annahā yuḍrabu bihā al-mathal fī al-ḥumq wa-hiya ʿalā ḥumqihā tuḥibbu waladahā fa-tuṭʿimuhā wa-tuʿallimuhā al-ṭayarān ka-ghayrihā min al-ḥayawān] Othman, to whom may God be gracious, said that every animal loves its offspring except the bustard. But this properly applies to the male. For although the common proverb imputes folly to the female, yet for all her folly she loves her chicks, feeds them and teaches them to fly, just like the other animals. Someone must also have deceived Jerome when he wrote of the dove on Os. VII.: The other birds hasten to protect their chicks even at the peril of their own life, etc. The dove alone does not grieve for its chicks when they are taken away, and does not seek them. Surely there is no one who does not know that the affection of doves, both toward their chicks and toward their mates, is most tender. Male and female sit on the eggs ἐκ διαδοχῆς [ek diadochēs], that is, by turns; and in like manner they συνθερμαίνουσι [synthermainousi], warm together, the hatched chicks. And if the female returns too sluggishly after the pains of laying, the male calls her back to the nest with a light chastisement. They share the care of ψωμίζειν [psōmizein] the chicks, putting predigested food into their mouths; and when taken away from the nest, however great the distance, they return to it out of love for their offspring. Hence it has come about that some have used doves as messengers, sending them back with a note attached to the town where they had sat on eggs or chicks. Hence Oppian, book 3 [Cyneget.], verse 115.


II, 856 Πῶς δ᾽ ἄρ ἐν οἰωνοῖσι ποθὴν ἀλίαστον ἔχουσιν
Ὧν τεκέων φῆναί τε, βαρύφθογγοί τε πέλειαι.

II, 856 Πῶς δ᾽ ἄρ ἐν οἰωνοῖσι ποθὴν ἀλίαστον ἔχουσιν Ὧν τεκέων φῆναί τε, βαρύφθογγοί τε πέλειαι. [Pōs d' ar en oiōnoisi pothēn aliaston echousin / Hōn tekeōn phēnai te, barypthongoi te peleiai.]


Quomodo etiam inter aves amorem perpetuum suorum pullorum habent ossifragae, et gravi gemitu columbae. Corvis quoque pullos esse odio, licet permulti asserant, res tamen est commentitia, quod abunde supra probatum a): et aquilam b) ovum aut pullum unum non alia de causa e nido suo ejicere, quam quia omnibus alendis et fovendis impar est. Sed struthionem ova sua non raro in terra relinquere et negligere, quamvis non tradant Graeci et Romani scriptores, quibus hujus animalis natura non fuit satis cognita, mihi tamen ex Arabum monumentis est compertissimum. Damir, وهي تخرج لطلب الطعم فمتي وجدت بيض نعامة اخري تحضنه وتنسي بيضها ولعلها ان تصاد فلا ترجع اليه ولهذا توصف بالحمق ويضرب بها المثل في ذلك Cum e col. 252 nido prodit, ut cibum quaerat, si reperiat ovum struthionis alterius, illi incubat, et proprii obliviscitur, et a venatoribus inde pulsa nunquam redit. Unde est, quod stulta describitur, et illam ferit proverbium ea de re (2). Nempe احمق نعامة Struthione stultior, quod in sectione De Proverbiis idem exponit. Et singula haec designant Arabes propriis nominibus. بيضة in genere est ovum, ut Hebraice ביצה, iisdem literis. Unde hic Plurale cum Affixo ביציה, ova sua. Cur ovum sic dicatur, Hebraeos latet, sed Arabes deducunt ab albedine. Illis enim باض Verbum album esse sonat. At struthionis ovum speciali nomine تومة thauma dicitur, quod Graece est miraculum. Et تريكة tharicha, cum ex eo pullus exiit. Et نتل nethel, cum a mare relictum est, vel بيضة البلد ovum regionis. Alcamus, تومة بيضة النعام Thauma, ovum struthionis. التريكة البيضة بعد II, 857 ان يخرج منه الفرخ ويخص بالنعام Tharicha, ovum, postquam ex eo exiit pullus: sed proprie dicitur de struthione. النتل بيضة النعام يملا ماء فيدفن في المفازة Nethel, ovum struthio- nis aqua plenum, quod in deserto sepultum est, nempe in mediis arenis. Et alibi, هو اذل من بيضة البلد اي من بيضة النعام التي تركها Ille est vilior ovo regionis, id est, ovo struthionis, quae il- lud reliquit. Struthionis nidus, in quo solent ova hujusmodi reperiri, vocatur ادحي udcha, ادحوة udchua, et ادحية udchia, propter arenam, circumquaque oppansam. Nam دحا est oppandere. Idem Alcamus, الادحي والادحوة والادحية مبيض النعام في الرمل Udcha, et udchua, et udchia, struthionis nidus in arenis. De quo sic Phile in Iambis:

Just as among birds too the ossifrages have a constant love for their chicks, and the doves with their heavy moaning. That ravens, too, hate their chicks, though very many assert it, is nevertheless a fiction, as was amply proved above a); and the eagle b) casts one egg or chick out of its nest for no other reason than that it is unequal to feeding and warming them all. But that the ostrich not infrequently leaves its eggs on the ground and neglects them, although the Greek and Roman writers, to whom the nature of this animal was not sufficiently known, do not report it, is nevertheless quite certain to me from the records of the Arabs. Damir: وهي تخرج لطلب الطعم فمتي وجدت بيض نعامة اخري تحضنه وتنسي بيضها ولعلها ان تصاد فلا ترجع اليه ولهذا توصف بالحمق ويضرب بها المثل في ذلك [wa-hiya takhruju li-ṭalab al-ṭuʿm fa-matī wajadat bayḍ naʿāma ukhrī taḥḍunuhu wa-tansī bayḍahā wa-laʿallahā an tuṣād fa-lā tarjiʿ ilayhi wa-li-hādhā tūṣaf bi-l-ḥumq wa-yuḍrab bihā al-mathal fī dhālika] When it goes out of col. 252 the nest to seek food, if it finds the egg of another ostrich, it sits on it and forgets its own; and, driven away from there by hunters, it never returns. Hence it is described as foolish, and the proverb strikes it on this account R2. Namely احمق نعامة [aḥmaq naʿāma] More foolish than an ostrich, which the same author explains in the section On Proverbs. And the Arabs designate each of these things by proper names. بيضة [bayḍa] in general is egg, as in Hebrew ביצה, with the same letters. Hence here the plural with the suffix, ביציה, its eggs. Why an egg is so called is hidden from the Hebrews, but the Arabs derive it from whiteness. For with them the verb باض [bāḍa] means to be white. But the ostrich's egg is called by a special name تومة [tūma] thauma, which in Greek means marvel. And تريكة [tarīka] tharicha, when the chick has come out of it. And نتل [natl] nethel, when it has been left by the male, or بيضة البلد [bayḍat al-balad] egg of the region. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: تومة بيضة النعام [tūma bayḍat al-naʿām] Thauma, the ostrich's egg. التريكة البيضة بعد II, 857 ان يخرج منه الفرخ ويخص بالنعام [al-tarīka al-bayḍa baʿda an yakhruja minhu al-farkh wa-yakhuṣṣu bi-l-naʿām] Tharicha, an egg after the chick has come out of it; but it is said properly of the ostrich. النتل بيضة النعام يملا ماء فيدفن في المفازة [al-natl bayḍat al-naʿām yumlaʾ māʾan fa-yudfan fī al-mafāza] Nethel, an ostrich egg full of water, which is buried in the desert, that is, in the midst of the sands. And elsewhere: هو اذل من بيضة البلد اي من بيضة النعام التي تركها [huwa adhallu min bayḍat al-balad ay min bayḍat al-naʿām allatī tarakathā] He is more worthless than the egg of the region, that is, than the ostrich's egg, which it has abandoned. The ostrich's nest, in which such eggs are usually found, is called ادحي [udḥī] udcha, ادحوة [udḥuwwa] udchua, and ادحية [udḥiyya] udchia, on account of the sand spread out all around. For دحا [daḥā] is to spread out. The same Alcamus: الادحي والادحوة والادحية مبيض النعام في الرمل [al-udḥī wa-l-udḥuwwa wa-l-udḥiyya mabīḍ al-naʿām fī al-raml] Udcha, and udchua, and udchia, the ostrich's nest in the sands. Of which Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)] says thus in his Iambics:


Καὶ τὴν καλιὰν τοῖς ποσὶν διαγλύφειν
Εἰς ἀνέχουσαν ψάμμον ἐν τῷ δαπέδῳ,

Καὶ τὴν καλιὰν τοῖς ποσὶν διαγλύφειν Εἰς ἀνέχουσαν ψάμμον ἐν τῷ δαπέδῳ, [Kai tēn kalian tois posin diaglyphein Eis anechousan psammon en tō dapedō,]


Et nidum (ajunt) pedibus excavare super eminentem arenam in solo. Sed multo uberius Aelianus, ex quo mutata est, libri decimi quarti capite septimo, Καλιὰν ἐργάζεται ταπεινὴν ἐν τῷ δαπέδῳ, τὴν ψάμμον διαγλύψασα τοῖς ποσὶ, καὶ τὸ μὲν μεσαίτατον αὐτῆς κοῖλόν ἐστι· τὰ χείλη δὲ τὰ κύκλῳ ὑψηλὰ ἐργάζε-ται, ἀποτειχίζουσα τρόπον τινά· ἵνα τὸ ἐκ Διὸς ὕδωρ ἀποστέξῃ, καὶ μὴ εἰσρέῃ τῇ καλιᾷ, καὶ ἐπικλύζῃ τῆς στρουθοῦ τοὺς νεοττοὺς, ὄντας ἁπαλούς. Humilem in solo nidum construit, arenam pedibus excavans. Medium ejus cavum est: la- bra autem ambientia in altum extollit, et tanquam muro circummunit; ut labra illa pluviam arceant, ne in nidum influat, et struthionis pullos adhuc teneros alluat. Ut jam non sit obscurum, cur Arabice vocetur ادحي ab arena, circumquaque oppansa. Obiter nota, in Aeliani textu legi perperam ἀποστάξῃ, et veram le-ctionem esse ἀποστέξῃ, quae in marginem rejecta est. Sed et tam Aelianus, quam Phile corrigendi sunt in vocibus διαγλύψασα et διαγλύφειν. Legendum enim διαγλάψασα, et διαγλάφειν. Vox sumpta est ex Homeri versu 437. col. 253 Odyss. δ. de Idothea, Protei filia:

And (they say) that it hollows out its nest with its feet upon raised sand on the ground. But much more fully Aelian, from whom this was adapted, book 14, chapter 7: Καλιὰν ἐργάζεται ταπεινὴν ἐν τῷ δαπέδῳ, τὴν ψάμμον διαγλύψασα τοῖς ποσὶ, καὶ τὸ μὲν μεσαίτατον αὐτῆς κοῖλόν ἐστι· τὰ χείλη δὲ τὰ κύκλῳ ὑψηλὰ ἐργάζεται, ἀποτειχίζουσα τρόπον τινά· ἵνα τὸ ἐκ Διὸς ὕδωρ ἀποστέξῃ, καὶ μὴ εἰσρέῃ τῇ καλιᾷ, καὶ ἐπικλύζῃ τῆς στρουθοῦ τοὺς νεοττοὺς, ὄντας ἁπαλούς. [Kalian ergazetai tapeinēn en tō dapedō, tēn psammon diaglypsasa tois posi, kai to men mesaitaton autēs koilon estin; ta cheilē de ta kyklō hypsēla ergazetai, apoteichizousa tropon tina; hina to ek Dios hydōr apostexē, kai mē eisreē tē kalia, kai epiklyzē tēs strouthou tous neottous, ontas hapalous.] It builds a low nest on the ground, hollowing out the sand with its feet. Its middle is hollow, but it raises the surrounding rims high and, as it were, walls it round, so that those rims may keep out the rain, lest it flow into the nest and wash over the ostrich's still tender chicks. So it is now not obscure why in Arabic it is called ادحي [udḥī] from the sand spread out all around. Note in passing that in Aelian's text ἀποστάξῃ [apostaxē] is wrongly read, and that the true reading is ἀποστέξῃ [apostexē], which has been relegated to the margin. But both Aelian and Philes must also be corrected in the words διαγλύψασα [diaglypsasa] and διαγλύφειν [diaglyphein]. For one should read διαγλάψασα [diaglapsasa] and διαγλάφειν [diaglaphein]. The word is taken from Homer, line 437 col. 253 of Odyssey δ [delta], about Idothea, daughter of Proteus:


Εὐνὰς δ᾽ ἐν ψαμάθοισι διαγλάψασ᾽ ἁλίῃσιν,

Εὐνὰς δ᾽ ἐν ψαμάθοισι διαγλάψασ᾽ ἁλίῃσιν, [Eunas d' en psamathoisi diaglaps' haliēsin,]


Cum cubilia in marinis arenis excavasset. Ubi Scholiastae, Διαγλάψασα· δια-κοιλάνασα, excavans. At διαγλύφειν est insculpere, persculpere.

When she had hollowed out beds in the sands of the sea. Where the Scholiasts have: Διαγλάψασα· διακοιλάνασα [Diaglapsasa; diakoilanasa], hollowing out. But διαγλύφειν [diaglyphein] is to engrave, to carve through.


Et super pulverem calefiunt] Hebraice תחמם, calefit supple unumquodque ovorum. Enallage Numeri, de qua modo. Alii calefacit, quod cum praecedentibus II, 858 non cohaeret; Relinquit ova sua, et calefacit. Neque enim struthio calefacit ea ipsa ova, quae reliquit. Quod incommodum ut vitaret sanctus Hieronymus, personam ita mutavit; Quando derelinquit in terra ova sua, tu forsitan in pulvere calefacies ea? Quia verbum תחמם, tam potest esse secundae Personae Masculinae, quam tertiae Foemininae. Sed de suo addidit, tu forsitan; et omisit Conjunctionem ET, quae hanc Personae mutationem non patitur. Neque enim recte dicitur, Cum in terra relinquit ova sua, et in pulvere calefacies, pro tune in pulvere illa calefacies? Itaque malui reddere, et super pulverem calefit; quamvis תחמם sit in Piel, quae Conjugatio saepissime Activam significationem habet, sed et quandoque Neutram. Ova porro, a matre deserta, calefieri dicuntur, non eo calore, qui vivificat, sed qui corrumpit. Nam quod ea volunt interpretes solo calore solis, aut solo fotu pulveris excludi, sine matris opera, merum somnium est: quod ex Isidoro, Alberto, Cardano, Vallesio, etc. hauriunt Commentatores. At Arabes deserta haec ova docent corrumpi, et putrescere; ut infra observabitur. Tamen, si Damiri credimus, ومن اعاجيب النعامة انها تضع بيضها طولا بحيث لو مد عليه خيط لم يجد لشي منه خروجا عن الاخر ثم تعطي كل بيضة نصيبها من الحضن ان كان كل بدنها لا يشتمل علي عدد بيضها Inter ea, quae in struthione mirabilia sunt, etiam illud habetur, quod ova sua in longitudinem ita disponit, ut, si super illa filum extendatur, ne unum quidem reperiatur alterum excedere. Quo facto, ova singula ex illius incubatu suam partem accipiunt, quamvis universa complecti non possit corpus ejus. Quod fit, ut illi volunt, per contactum virtutis, quomodo in annulorum ferreorum serie, si unus magneti affricetur, reliqui primum illum sequuntur.

And on the dust they are warmed] In Hebrew תחמם, is warmed; supply each one of the eggs. This is an enallage of number, of which we spoke just now. Others render warms, which does not fit with what precedes II, 858: She leaves her eggs, and warms them. For the ostrich does not warm the very eggs it has left. To avoid this difficulty Saint Jerome changed the person thus: When she abandons her eggs on the ground, will you perhaps warm them in the dust? For the verb תחמם can be second person masculine as well as third person feminine. But he added you perhaps of his own, and omitted the conjunction AND, which does not allow this change of person. For it is not correct to say, When she leaves her eggs on the ground, and you will warm them in the dust, for will you warm them in the dust? I have therefore preferred to render and on the dust it is warmed, although תחמם is in Piel, a conjugation which very often has an active meaning, but sometimes also an intransitive one. Further, the eggs, deserted by the mother, are said to be warmed, not with the heat that gives life, but with the heat that corrupts. For the interpreters' view that they are hatched by the heat of the sun alone, or by the warmth of the dust alone, without the mother's help, is a mere dream, which the commentators draw from Isidore, Albertus, Cardano, Vallés, etc. But the Arabs teach that these deserted eggs are corrupted and rot, as will be noted below. Yet, if we believe Damiri, ومن اعاجيب النعامة انها تضع بيضها طولا بحيث لو مد عليه خيط لم يجد لشي منه خروجا عن الاخر ثم تعطي كل بيضة نصيبها من الحضن ان كان كل بدنها لا يشتمل علي عدد بيضها [wa-min aʿājīb al-naʿāma annahā taḍaʿu bayḍahā ṭūlan bi-ḥaythu law mudda ʿalayhi khayṭ lam yajid li-shay minhu khurūjan ʿan al-ākhar thumma tuʿṭī kull bayḍa naṣībahā min al-ḥaḍn in kāna kull badanihā lā yashtamil ʿalī ʿadad bayḍihā] Among the marvels of the ostrich is also this, that it arranges its eggs lengthwise in such a way that, if a thread were stretched over them, not a single one would be found to project beyond another. When this is done, each egg receives its share of her incubation, although her body cannot cover them all. This happens, as they would have it, through the transmission of a power, as in a chain of iron rings, if one is rubbed on a magnet, the rest follow the first.


Et oblivi scitur fore, ut pes comprimat ea] Graeci σκορπιεῖ, et Chaldaeus תבדרנה, dispergat ea; sed Hebraeum תזורה est a Verbo זור, comprimere, non a זרה, spargere. Syrus nullo sensu, ܘܛܥܝܐ ܕܪܓܠܐ ܕܦܪܚܬܐ ܐܝܬ ܠܗ̇, Et obliviscitur, se pedem avis habere: quasi pro רגל תזורה legerit רגל צפור לה: quod plane alienum, adeoque falsum est. Struthio enim pedem non habet digitatum, ut aves; sed bisulcum, ut quadrupedes. Philosophus libri quarti capite decimo quarto De partibus, Δίπους μέν ἐστιν, ὡς ὄρνις· διχηλὸς δὲ ὡς τετράπους· οὐ γὰρ δακτύλους ἔχει, ἀλλὰ χηλάς. Bipes etiam est, ut avis; sed bisulcus, ut quadrupes: neque enim habet digitos, sed bifidam ungulam. Itaque pedem avis vere non habet. Sed Hebraea sunt manifesta, col. 254 Obliviscitur, fore, ut pes ea comprimat: id est, ita stolida est, ut non cogitet, II, 859 fieri posse, ut ova sua, quae humi reliquit, ferarum, aut hominum pedibus premantur. Quasi illi perinde sit, utrum atterantur, nec ne. Ac si Ulysses aratrum non avertisset, cum illi aranti filius in sulco, quem ducebat, objectus est.

And she forgets that a foot may crush them] The Greeks have σκορπιεῖ [skorpiei], and the Chaldee תבדרנה, may scatter them; but the Hebrew תזורה is from the verb זור, to crush, not from זרה, to scatter. The Syriac, with no sense at all, has ܘܛܥܝܐ ܕܪܓܠܐ ܕܦܪܚܬܐ ܐܝܬ ܠܗ̇ [וטעיא דרגלא דפרחתא אית לה], And she forgets that she has the foot of a bird: as if for רגל תזורה he had read רגל צפור לה; which is quite beside the point, and indeed false. For the ostrich does not have a toed foot like birds, but a cloven one like quadrupeds. The Philosopher, On the Parts of Animals, book 4, chapter 14: Δίπους μέν ἐστιν, ὡς ὄρνις· διχηλὸς δὲ ὡς τετράπους· οὐ γὰρ δακτύλους ἔχει, ἀλλὰ χηλάς [Dipous men estin, hōs ornis; dichēlos de hōs tetrapous; ou gar daktylous echei, alla chēlas]. It is two-footed, like a bird, but cloven-hoofed, like a quadruped; for it does not have toes, but a cloven hoof. So it truly does not have the foot of a bird. But the Hebrew is plain col. 254: She forgets that a foot may crush them; that is, she is so stupid that she does not consider II, 859 that it may happen that her eggs, which she has left on the ground, are trodden by the feet of wild beasts or of men. As if it made no difference to her whether they are crushed or not. As if Ulysses had not turned aside his plough when, as he was ploughing, his son was laid in the furrow he was drawing.


Duriter tractat pullos suos, ac si non essent sui] Chaldaeus multo aliter, שיחנא על בניא דלא דילה, Fovet filios, qui non sunt sui: id est, ova aliena, unde pulli emergant. Syrus, ܐܣܓܝܬ, multiplicat filios non suos. Quod idem sequitur Arabs, et struthionis mores optime refert, de qua Damir: متي وجدت بيضة نعامة اخري تحضنها وتنسي بيضها Si in alius struthionis ova incidat, illa fovet, et suorum est immemor. Tamen Hebraea hanc versionem non ferunt. Pagninus, Oblivisci facit illam pullorum suorum, in quo non erunt. Quae non capio. Iunius, Deus torrefaciens excludit pullos suos aliena opera: id est, Solis aestu fovet ova, quae struthio-camelus in arena posuerat, donec excludantur pulli; ut idem habet in Notis. Cum enim a viris doctis de struthione videret id affirmari, eo textum Hebraeum inflectere conatus est. Sed simplicissima est versio, quam adduximus, adeoque antiquissima: Duriter tractat pullos suos. Hebraice הקשיח בניה. Verbum הקשיח hic solum extat, et in his Esa. LXIII, 17. Cur nos aberrare sineres a viis tuis, O Domine, et תקשיח לבנו מיראתך, indurares cor nostrum a timore tuo? Ubi Septuaginta, Ἐσκλήρυνας τὰς καρδίας ἡμῶν; et Hieronymus, Indurasti cor nostrum? Neque aliter Syrus et Arabs. Nempe קשח, cum Cheth, idem est, quod הקשה, cum He, nisi quod in illo videtur aspiratio fortior significationem intendere. Itaque etiam Arabice قسي durum esse, sed قسح praedurum et rigidum esse sonat. Unde قساح hyaena; quia collum habet rigidum, nec ullo modo flexibile. Et رمح قاسح est hasta dura et rigida; ut hasta Lausi, de qua Poeta Aeneidos libro decimo,

She deals harshly with her young, as if they were not hers] The Chaldee renders it very differently: שיחנא על בניא דלא דילה, She broods over young that are not hers, that is, over the eggs of others, from which chicks may emerge. The Syriac has ܐܣܓܝܬ [אסגית], she multiplies young not her own. The Arabic follows the same sense, and it describes the habits of the ostrich very well; of it Damir says: متي وجدت بيضة نعامة اخري تحضنها وتنسي بيضها [matā wajadat bayḍat naʿāma ukhrā taḥḍinuhā wa-tansā bayḍahā] If she comes upon the eggs of another ostrich, she broods them and forgets her own. Yet the Hebrew does not bear this rendering. Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae] has: He makes her forget her young, in which they will not be. This I do not understand. Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] has: God, parching, hatches her young by another's work; that is, by the heat of the sun He warms the eggs which the ostrich had laid in the sand, until the chicks are hatched, as he also says in his Notes. For since he saw this asserted about the ostrich by learned men, he tried to bend the Hebrew text in that direction. But the simplest rendering is the one we have given, and it is therefore also the most ancient: She deals harshly with her young. In Hebrew, הקשיח בניה. The verb הקשיח occurs only here and in these words of Isa 63:17. Why hast thou let us stray from thy ways, O Lord, and תקשיח לבנו מיראתך, hardened our heart from thy fear? There the Septuagint has Ἐσκλήρυνας τὰς καρδίας ἡμῶν [Esklērynas tas kardias hēmōn]; and Jerome, Thou hast hardened our heart? Nor do the Syriac and the Arabic differ. For קשח, with Cheth, is the same as הקשה, with He, except that in the former the stronger aspiration seems to intensify the meaning. So also in Arabic قسي [qasā] means to be hard, but قسح [qasaḥa] to be very hard and to be rigid. Hence قساح [qassāḥ] hyena, because it has a rigid neck, not flexible in any way. And رمح قاسح [rumḥ qāsiḥ] is a hard and rigid spear, like the spear of Lausus, of which the Poet speaks in book 10 of the Aeneid:


Advenit, et rigida Dryopem ferit eminus hasta.

He comes up, and strikes Dryops from afar with his rigid spear.


Inde igitur ad animum قسح, vel קשח, significat animo duro esse et inflexo: et הקשיח vel obdurari, vel duriter agere cum aliquo (3). Proinde hic Hieronymus, Duravit ad filios suos. Et Augustinus, Obduravit contra filios suos. Et Graeci, Ἀπεσκλήρυνε τὰ τέκνα αὐτῆς, id est, τὴν περὶ τὰ τέκνα φυσικὴν στορ-γήν· Obduravit naturalem affectum erga pullos suos: ut Olympiodorus recte exponit. Quo pertinent haec Ierem. Thren. IV, 3. Filia populi mei crudelis est, II, 860 ut struthiones in deserto. Et quod struthio-camelus Hebraice dicitur תחמס, et Arabice ظليم, id est, impius, iniquus, ut jam supra c) docuimus. Verbum הקשיח Masculinum hic pro Foeminino usurpari, mirabitur, qui nesciet, quam in Hebraismo sit frequens haec Generis enallage, maxime circa animalia. Ut Esa. XIV, 11. תחתיך יצע רמה ומכסיך תולעה, Sub te sternitur lumbricus, et obtegit te vermis. Ubi nomina Foeminina, sed verba Masculina sunt. Contra, Exod. VIII, 2. [al. 6.] ותעל הצפרדע, Et ascendit rana; et versu decimo quarto [al. sexto], ותהי הכנים, Et fuit pediculus: Masculinis nominibus foeminina verba junguntur. Quem esse Scripturae morem, dicit Kimchius in Esaiam, col. 255 cum non loquitur de hoc, vel illo animali, sed על דרך כלל universaliter de tota specie, quomodo hic de struthione. Pullos suos, Hebraice בניה, filios suos, id est, ova, ex quibus pulli emersissent, si fovisset. Itaque filii vocantur δυνω-τικῶς. Quale illud Martialis libri noni Epigrammate 42.

Hence, then, applied to the mind, قسح [qasaḥa] or קשח means to be hard and unbending in mind; and הקשיח means either to be hardened or to deal harshly with someone R3. Accordingly Jerome here has: She was hard toward her young. And Augustine: She hardened herself against her young. And the Greeks: Ἀπεσκλήρυνε τὰ τέκνα αὐτῆς [Apesklēryne ta tekna autēs], that is, τὴν περὶ τὰ τέκνα φυσικὴν στοργήν [tēn peri ta tekna physikēn storgēn]: She hardened her natural affection toward her young, as Olympiodorus rightly explains. To this belong these words of Jeremiah, Lam 4:3: The daughter of my people is cruel, II, 860 like the ostriches in the desert. So too the fact that the ostrich is called תחמס in Hebrew and ظليم [ẓalīm] in Arabic, that is, impious, unjust, as we have already shown above c). That the masculine verb הקשיח is used here for the feminine will surprise only someone who does not know how frequent this change of gender is in Hebrew idiom, especially with animals. Thus Isa 14:11. תחתיך יצע רמה ומכסיך תולעה, Beneath thee the worm is spread, and the maggot covers thee. There the nouns are feminine, but the verbs masculine. Conversely, in Exod 8:2 [var. 6.] ותעל הצפרדע, And the frog came up; and in verse 14 [var. 16], ותהי הכנים, And there was the louse: feminine verbs are joined to masculine nouns. Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], on Isaiah, says this is the custom of Scripture col. 255 when it speaks not of this or that animal, but על דרך כלל, universally, of the whole species, as here of the ostrich. Her young, in Hebrew בניה, her sons, that is, the eggs from which chicks would have emerged had she brooded them. They are therefore called sons δυνωτικῶς [dynōtikōs]. Compare that line of Martial, book 9, Epigram 42:


Istud, quod digitis, Pontice, perdis, homo est.

What you waste with your fingers, Ponticus, is a man.


Ac si sui non essent] Hebraice ללא לה. Plenum esset כאשר לא יהיו לה. Ut Iob. X, 19. כאשר לא הייתי, Ac si non fuissem (4). Sed in hoc libro stylus quandoque est valde concisus; quia soluta non est oratio, sed stricta. Et huic oppositioni suus est lepos, Filios suos, tanquam non suos. Quale illud Pauli 1 Cor. VII, 30. Οἱ κλαίοντες ὡς μὴ κλαίοντες, καὶ οἱ χαίροντες ὡς μὴ χαίρον-τες, etc. Lacrymantes tanquam non lacrymantes, et gaudentes tanquam non gaudentes, etc. Et Hebr. XI, 27. Τὸν γὰρ ἀόρατον ὡς ὁρῶν· Tanquam videns invisibilem.

As if they were not hers] In Hebrew, ללא לה. In full it would be כאשר לא יהיו לה, as in Job 10:19. כאשר לא הייתי, As if I had not been R4. But in this book the style is sometimes very concise, because it is not prose but verse. And this antithesis has its own charm: her young, as though not hers. Compare that of Paul, 1 Cor 7:30: Οἱ κλαίοντες ὡς μὴ κλαίοντες, καὶ οἱ χαίροντες ὡς μὴ χαίροντες [Hoi klaiontes hōs mē klaiontes, kai hoi chairontes hōs mē chairontes], etc. Those who weep as though not weeping, and those who rejoice as though not rejoicing, etc. And Heb 11:27 Τὸν γὰρ ἀόρατον ὡς ὁρῶν [Ton gar aoraton hōs horōn]: As seeing him who is invisible.


Frustra laborat, absque metu est] Frustra laborasse dicuntur matres, quae filios pariunt non victuros. Ut Esa. LXV, 23. Non frustra laborabunt, nec generabunt ad conturbationem. Ut in Aeschyli Agamemnone propter ablatos pullos dolent vultures δεμνιοτήρη πόνον ὀρταλίχων ὀλέσαντες, amisso labore, quem in pullorum nido servando insumpserant. Hoc eodem sensu struthionem frustra laborare Iob scribit, cum ova, a se non sine labore edita, negligit: quia scilicet absque metu est. Non absque omni metu. Nam struthio est animal timidissimum. Proinde apud Arabes unum e variis struthionum nominibus est اجفيل igphil; quasi timidum dixeris. Alcamus, الاجفيل الجبن والظليم ينفر من كل شي Igphil, id est, timidus: item struthio-camelus, qui quacunque de causa fugit. Est et Arabicum proverbium, اجبن II, 861 نعامة من اجبن struthione timidior: خافت انها لانها وذلك ابدا اليه ترجع لا موضع من idque quia, cum prae metu alicunde fu- git, eo nunquam revertitur. Ita Damir in sectione De Proverbiis. Sed hic struthio dicitur esse metus expers; quia provido illo timore caret, quo parentes impelluntur ad prospiciendum suis. Qui timor ex amore oritur. Ovidius in Epistola Penelopes,

She labors in vain, without fear] Mothers are said to have labored in vain when they bear children who will not live. So Isa 65:23. They shall not labor in vain, nor bring forth for trouble. So in the Agamemnon of Aeschylus the vultures grieve over their stolen young, δεμνιοτήρη πόνον ὀρταλίχων ὀλέσαντες [demniotērē ponon ortalichōn olesantes], having lost the labor they had spent in guarding the nest of their chicks. In this same sense Job writes that the ostrich labors in vain when it neglects the eggs it has laid, not without labor: namely, because it is without fear. Not without all fear, for the ostrich is a most timid animal. Accordingly, among the Arabs one of the various names of the ostrich is اجفيل [ijfīl] igphil, as if you were to say timid. Alcamus: الاجفيل الجبن والظليم ينفر من كل شي [al-ijfīl al-jabān wa-al-ẓalīm yanfiru min kull shī], Igphil, that is, timid; also the male ostrich, which flees for any cause whatever. There is also an Arabic proverb, اجبن II, 861 نعامة من اجبن [ajban naʿāma min ajban], more timid than an ostrich: خافت انها لانها وذلك ابدا اليه ترجع لا موضع من [khāfat annahā li-annahā wa-dhālika abadan ilayhi tarjiʿ lā mawḍiʿ min], and this because, when it flees from some place out of fear, it never returns there. So Damir in the section On Proverbs. But here the ostrich is said to be devoid of fear, because it lacks that provident fear by which parents are driven to look out for their young. This fear springs from love. Ovid in the Epistle of Penelope:


Res est solliciti plena timoris amor.

Love is a thing full of anxious fear.


Et parentes hic timor semper tenet anxios, ac sollicitos. Unde pater ille apud Comicum,

And this fear always keeps parents anxious and troubled. Hence that father in the Comic poet:


Ego, quia non rediit filius, quae cogito, et
Quibus nunc sollicitor rebus, ne aut ille alserit,
Aut uspiam ceciderit, aut perfregerit aliquid.

I, because my son has not come back, what things I think of, and
by what things I am now troubled: lest he has caught cold,
or fallen somewhere, or broken something.


Sed struthio, quia non amat, ita nec suis timet. Quamprimum e nido excessit, ovorum suorum oblita, alienis eodem affectu, quo propriis, incubat. At, inquies, in Aeliano (Hist. lib. 14. cap. 7.) describitur struthio tanquam ἐρῶσα τῶν νεοττῶν ἰσχυρῶς, καὶ διψῶσα αὐτῶν τῆς συνουσίας, pullos suos impense amans, et eorum consortii sitiens, id est, summe avida. Ita ut, ex venatione rediens, quamvis nidum reperiat ferreis mucronibus a venatore obseptum, tamen νικω-μένη ὑπὸ τοῦ ἱμέρου, καὶ οἰστρουμένη, eorum desiderio victa, et tanquam oestro per- cita, passis alis, cum cursu, et stridore in medium ferrum ruat, atque ita proprio impetu transfixa misere pereat. Respondeo, e tot scriptoribus, qui de struthione egerunt, unum Aelianum hoc referre: et in hac relatione tam potuisse decipi, quam in iis, quae praecedunt, struthionem ova parere ὑπὲρ τὰ ὀγδοή- col. 256 κοντα, supra octoginta: cum Alkazuinius solum viginti, Leo Africanus, et Marmolius solum decem, aut duodecim censeant. Aut, si vera sit historia, non esse amoris, sed stuporis effectum, quod tam coeco impetu struthio in ferrum ruit: De quo stupore in Iobo sequitur,

But the ostrich, because it does not love, likewise does not fear for its young. As soon as it has left the nest, it forgets its own eggs and sits on those of others with the same affection as on its own. But, you will say, in Aelian (Hist. book 14, ch. 7) the ostrich is described as ἐρῶσα τῶν νεοττῶν ἰσχυρῶς, καὶ διψῶσα αὐτῶν τῆς συνουσίας [erōsa tōn neottōn ischyrōs, kai dipsōsa autōn tēs synousias], loving its chicks intensely, and thirsting for their company, that is, supremely eager for it. So much so that, returning from foraging, although it finds the nest fenced about by the hunter with iron points, nevertheless νικωμένη ὑπὸ τοῦ ἱμέρου, καὶ οἰστρουμένη [nikōmenē hypo tou himerou, kai oistroumenē], overcome by longing for them, and roused as if by a gadfly, it rushes with spread wings, running and screeching, into the midst of the iron, and so, pierced by its own onrush, perishes miserably. I reply that, of all the writers who have treated the ostrich, Aelian alone reports this; and that he could have been deceived in this report just as in what precedes it, that the ostrich lays ὑπὲρ τὰ ὀγδοή- col. 256 κοντα [hyper ta ogdoēkonta], more than eighty eggs, whereas Alkazuinius reckons only twenty, and Leo Africanus and Marmolius only ten or twelve. Or, if the story is true, that it is the effect not of love but of stupidity that the ostrich rushes onto the iron with so blind an impulse. Of this stupidity there follows in Job:


Quia privavit eum Deus sapientia, nec prudentiam ei impertitus est] Utut enim sapientia, et prudentia, si proprie loqui velimus, non sint nisi hominum, qui ratione sunt praediti: tamen etiam brutis in Scriptura tribuuntur. Ita serpens legitur esse omnium animalium φρονιμώτατος, Gen. III, 1. Et Christus ipse nos jubet ejus prudentiam imitari, Matth. X, 16. Esaias quoque nobis proponit bovis et asini exemplum, qui agnoscunt possessorem suum, et praesepe domini sui, Esa. I, 3. Ieremias ciconiam, quae novit tempora sua; et turturem, gruem, atque hirundinem, quae observant tempus adventus sui, Ierem. VIII, 7. Et Solomon formicam, ut, perspectis viis ejus, sapiamus, Prov. II, 862 VI, 6. Quin, quamvis idem hominum fuerit longe sapientissimus, tamen quatuor bestiolas laudat tamquam חכמים מחכמים, eximie sapientes: nempe praeter formicas, choerogryllios, locustas, et stelliones, Prov. XXX, 24. Sed eximie sapere dicuntur bruta quaedam: 1. Quia sapiunt, quantum necesse est, ad sui conservationem. 2. Quia in reliquis brutis hac sua sapientia eminent. Quae tamen infra humanam multis subsidit gradibus, cum rationis lumine destituatur, et ad unum sit determinata. Sed hanc qualemcunque sapientiam struthioni hic denegasse dicitur Deus. Qui non humanae solum, sed et brutorum solertiae unus auctor est. Quo referunt quod habetur Iob. XXXVIII, 36. juxta Chaldaeum, et Vulgatum, Quis dedit gallo intelligentiam? id est, nemo alius praeter Deum. Hebraea porro sic habent de struthione כי השה אלוה חכמה, ad verbum quia eam oblivisci fecit Deus sapientiae. Nam a נשה, oblivisci Hiphil est השה. Sed Graeci, Κατεσιώπησεν αὐτῇ ὁ Θεὸς σοφίαν, Tacere fecit ei Deus sapientiam. Et Syrus ܐܣܓܝ, et Arabs أكثر multiplicavit, sensu non diverso solum, sed et prorsus contrario. Graeci nempe pro השה, per He, le-gerunt חשה, per Cheth, siluit, vel silere fecit. Et Syrus, ex quo Arabs, Gimel inserto, השגה, multiplicavit. Sed recte Chaldaeus, אנשיה, oblivisci fecit eam sapientiae. Dicitur autem Deus rerum, quae praeteritae sunt, oblivionem inducere, cum magna fit mutatio. Puta, si adversa laetis, aut adversis laeta succedant. Sic Iosephus, in Aegypto ad honorum fastigium evectus, primogenitum suum ab oblivione Manassem appellavit. Fecit enim Deus, inquit, ut prisci laboris mei obliviscerer, Gen. XLI, 51. Contra, in captivitate Babylonica lamentatur Ieremias, eo quod in Sione Deus oblivisci fecerit solennia festa, et sabbatha, Thren. II, 6. Non eo sensu sumendum, quod hic habetur Deum fecisse, ut struthio sapientiae oblivisceretur. Quasi meminisset prius, et aliqua in ejus natura mutatio intervenisset. Hic enim oblivisci nihil aliud est, quam non meminisse. Non privativa est haec oblivio, sed negativa. Quomodo ante lucem creatam tenebras vocat Moses, non privationem lucis, sed meram negationem, Gen. I, 3. Ac proinde in sequente hemistichio additur ἐξηγητικῶς, ולא חלק לה בבינה, Et non impertivit ei intelligentiam, seu prudentiam. Itaque oblivisci fecit, id est, non impertivit. חלק, vulgo dividere, hic impertiri significat, ut Graece νέμειν. Recte igitur Symmachus, Οὐκ ἔνειμεν αὐτῇ σύνε-σιν, pro eo, quod Seniores, Οὐκ ἐπεμέρισεν αὐτῇ ἐν τῇ συνέσει, Non distribuit ei, vel Non dedit ei partem in intelligentia. Ut Simoni Mago dicitur Actor. VIII, 21. Οὐκ ἔστι σοι μερὶς, οὐδὲ κλῆρος ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τούτῳ· Non est tibi pars, col. 257 neque sors in hac re; Act. VIII, 21.

Because God has deprived her of wisdom, nor has he imparted understanding to her] For although wisdom and understanding, if we wish to speak properly, belong only to human beings, who are endowed with reason, they are nevertheless also attributed to brute animals in Scripture. Thus the serpent is said to be the φρονιμώτατος [phronimōtatos] of all animals, Gen 3:1. And Christ himself bids us imitate its prudence, Matt 10:16 Isaiah too sets before us the example of the ox and the ass, which know their owner and their master's crib, Isa 1:3 Jeremiah sets before us the stork, which knows her appointed times, and the turtledove, the crane and the swallow, which observe the time of their coming, Jer 8:7. And Solomon sets before us the ant, so that, having considered her ways, we may be wise, Prov. II, 862 VI, 6. Indeed, although he was by far the wisest of men, he nevertheless praises four small creatures as חכמים מחכמים, exceedingly wise: namely, besides the ants, the choerogryllii, the locusts and the stellions, Prov 30:24. But certain brute animals are said to be exceedingly wise: 1. Because they are as wise as is necessary for their own preservation. 2. Because they excel among the other brutes in this wisdom of theirs. Yet this wisdom falls short of human wisdom by many degrees, since it lacks the light of reason and is determined to a single end. But here God is said to have denied even this wisdom, such as it is, to the ostrich. He alone is the author not only of human ingenuity but also of that of the brutes. To this they refer what is found in Job 38:36 according to the Chaldee and the Vulgate: Who gave the cock understanding? that is, no one other than God. Further, the Hebrew says of the ostrich כי השה אלוה חכמה, literally because God made her forget wisdom. For from נשה, to forget, the Hiphil is השה. But the Greeks have Κατεσιώπησεν αὐτῇ ὁ Θεὸς σοφίαν [Katesiōpēsen autē ho Theos sophian], God made wisdom silent for her. And the Syriac has ܐܣܓܝ [אסגי], and the Arabic أكثر [akthara], he multiplied, in a sense not only different but entirely contrary. The Greeks, that is, read instead of השה, with He, חשה, with Cheth, he was silent or he made silent. And the Syriac, followed by the Arabic, inserting a Gimel, read השגה, he multiplied. But the Chaldee rightly has אנשיה, he made her forget wisdom. Now God is said to bring about forgetfulness of things past when a great change takes place: for instance, if prosperity follows adversity, or adversity prosperity. Thus Joseph, raised to the height of honours in Egypt, named his firstborn Manasseh, from forgetting. For God, he says, has made me forget my former toil, Gen 41:51. Conversely, in the Babylonian captivity Jeremiah laments that God has caused the solemn feasts and sabbaths to be forgotten in Zion, Lam 2:6. What is said here, that God made the ostrich forget wisdom, is not to be taken in that sense, as though she had previously remembered it and some change had occurred in her nature. For here to forget is nothing other than not to remember. This forgetfulness is not privative but negative, just as Moses calls the state before the creation of light darkness, not as a privation of light but as a mere negation, Gen 1:3. Accordingly, in the following hemistich there is added ἐξηγητικῶς [exēgētikōs], ולא חלק לה בבינה, And he did not impart to her understanding, or prudence. Thus made her forget means did not impart. חלק, commonly to divide, here means to impart, like the Greek νέμειν [nemein]. Symmachus therefore rightly has Οὐκ ἔνειμεν αὐτῇ σύνεσιν [Ouk eneimen autē synesin], where the Elders have Οὐκ ἐπεμέρισεν αὐτῇ ἐν τῇ συνέσει [Ouk epemerisen autē en tē synesei], He did not distribute to her, or He did not give her a share in understanding. As it is said to Simon Magus in Actor. VIII, 21. Οὐκ ἔστι σοι μερὶς, οὐδὲ κλῆρος ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τούτῳ· [Ouk esti soi meris, oude klēros en tō logō toutō] You have neither part col. 257 nor lot in this matter; Acts 8:21.


Sunt, qui nec per imprudentiam, nec per incuriam, aut ἀστοργίαν, sed certo consilio partem ovorum a struthione negligi volunt, atque id ab illa fieri II, 863 cum delectu, et solum τὰ ὑπηνέμια rejici, aut quae ad pullos alendos servari necesse est. Aelianus Historiae libri quarti capite trigesimo septimo, Ἡ στρουθὸς ἡ μεγάλη ὠὰ μὲν ἀποτίκτει πολλὰ, οὐ πάντα δὲ ἀποκύει, ἀλλ᾽ ἀποκρίνει τὰ ἄγονα, τοῖς δὲ ἐγκάρποις ἐπῳάζει, καὶ ἐκ μὲν τούτων τοὺς νεοττοὺς ἐξέλεψεν, ἐκεῖνα δὲ τὰ ἐκφαυλισθέντα τούτοις τροφὴν παρατίθησιν. Struthio etsi multa ova parit, non tamen omnia ad pullationem adhibet, sed sterilia secernit, nec nisi foecundis incubat. Ex quibus cum pullos exclusit, ova, male affecta, pro alimento eis apponit. Et Phile ubi supra,

There are some who hold that part of the eggs is neglected by the ostrich neither through imprudence nor through carelessness or ἀστοργίαν [astorgian], but by deliberate design, and that she does this II, 863 with discrimination, rejecting only τὰ ὑπηνέμια [ta hypēnemia], or those which must be kept for feeding the chicks. Aelian, History, book 4, chapter 37: Ἡ στρουθὸς ἡ μεγάλη ὠὰ μὲν ἀποτίκτει πολλὰ, οὐ πάντα δὲ ἀποκύει, ἀλλ᾽ ἀποκρίνει τὰ ἄγονα, τοῖς δὲ ἐγκάρποις ἐπῳάζει, καὶ ἐκ μὲν τούτων τοὺς νεοττοὺς ἐξέλεψεν, ἐκεῖνα δὲ τὰ ἐκφαυλισθέντα τούτοις τροφὴν παρατίθησιν. [Hē strouthos hē megalē ōa men apotiktei polla, ou panta de apokyei, alla apokrinei ta agona, tois de enkarpois epōazei, kai ek men toutōn tous neottous exelepsen, ekeina de ta ekphaulisthenta toutois trophēn paratithēsin.] Although the ostrich lays many eggs, she does not use all of them for hatching, but sets apart the sterile ones and broods only on the fertile ones. When she has hatched the chicks from these, she sets the spoiled eggs before them as food. And Philes, in the place cited above:


Ὠῶν δὲ συχνῶν εὑρεθεῖσαν ἐργάτιν
Τὰ μὴ καθαρά γε τῆς γονῆς ἀποκρίνειν·
Ὅσους γὰρ ἐξέλεψεν ἡ ζέσις τόκους,
Ἐν τοῖς ἀποῤῥεύσασι κυλίνδροις τρέφειν.

Ὠῶν δὲ συχνῶν εὑρεθεῖσαν ἐργάτιν Τὰ μὴ καθαρά γε τῆς γονῆς ἀποκρίνειν· Ὅσους γὰρ ἐξέλεψεν ἡ ζέσις τόκους, Ἐν τοῖς ἀποῤῥεύσασι κυλίνδροις τρέφειν. [Ōōn de sychnōn heuretheisan ergatin / Ta mē kathara ge tēs gonēs apokrinein· / Hosous gar exelepsen hē zesis tokous, / En tois aporrheusasi kylindrois trephein.]


Et cum reperiatur multorum ovorum operatrix, a generatione secernere (dicitur) quae impura sunt: et quotquot pullos calor exclusit in defluentibus cylindris enutrire. Ita vocat valde improprie ova subventanea, quorum humor, et testa defluens, pullos nutrit. Damir, يقال انها تقسم بيضها ثلاثا فمنه ما تحضنه ومنه ما تجعل صغارة غذ ومنه ما تفتحه وتجعله في الهوا حتي يتعفن ويتولد دودا فتتغذي به فراخها اذا خرجت من البيض Dicitur ova sua in tres partes dividere: ita, ut ex iis quaedam sint, quibus incubet; quaedam etiam, ex quorum vitello alatur; quaedam denique, quae aperta exponit aëri, donec putrescant, et ex iis producantur vermes, unde pulli sui alantur, cum ex ovo exclusi sunt. Alkazuinius, واذا باضت يبيض عشرين بيضة او اكثر فيجعلها ثلاثة اقسام تدفن ثلثها في التراب وتترك ثلثها في الشمس وتخضن ثلثها فاذا اخرجت فراخها كسرت ما كان في الشمس وغذتها بما فيها من الرطوبة التي ذوبتها الشمس ورقتها فاذا اشتدت فراخها وقويت اخرجت المدفون وفتحت لها ثقبا فتجمع عليها الذباب والبق والنمل وغيرها من فرعت فغذت تقوي ان الي فراخها فتاكلها الهوام col. 258 Ova cum parit, parit autem viginti, aut amplius, ea in tres partes dividit, quarum unam terrae infodit, unam soli exponit, uni incubat. Et, pullis exclusis, frangit eam partem, quae ad solem erat, et pullos alit eo humore, quem continent, II, 864 postquam a sole liquefactus et emollitus est. Et cum pulli invalescunt et ro- borantur, ova infossa effodit et perforat; ut ad ea congregentur muscae, cimices, formicae et similia animalcula, quibus pulli vescantur, donec, firmiores facti, cur- rant, et per se pascantur. Sed haec fabulis propiora sunt, cum non prudentiam solum, sed et providentiam tribuant animali: quod stupidissimum esse, constabit ex iis, quae dicturus sum.

And since it is found to be the producer of many eggs, it (is said) to separate from the brood those that are impure, and to nourish with the flowing cylinders as many chicks as the heat has hatched. So he calls, very improperly, the wind-eggs, whose fluid, and the shell flowing away, nourish the chicks. Damir: يقال انها تقسم بيضها ثلاثا فمنه ما تحضنه ومنه ما تجعل صغارة غذ ومنه ما تفتحه وتجعله في الهوا حتي يتعفن ويتولد دودا فتتغذي به فراخها اذا خرجت من البيض [yuqāl annahā taqsim bayḍahā thalāthan fa-minhu mā taḥḍunuhu wa-minhu mā tajʿal ṣighāra ghadh wa-minhu mā taftaḥuhu wa-tajʿaluhu fī al-hawā ḥattī yataʿaffan wa-yatawallad dūdan fa-tataghadhdhī bihi firākhuhā idhā kharajat min al-bayḍ] It is said to divide its eggs into three parts, so that some of them are those on which it sits; some also, from whose yolk it is fed; and some, finally, which it opens and exposes to the air until they rot and worms are produced from them, by which its chicks are fed when they have been hatched from the egg. Alkazuinius: واذا باضت يبيض عشرين بيضة او اكثر فيجعلها ثلاثة اقسام تدفن ثلثها في التراب وتترك ثلثها في الشمس وتخضن ثلثها فاذا اخرجت فراخها كسرت ما كان في الشمس وغذتها بما فيها من الرطوبة التي ذوبتها الشمس ورقتها فاذا اشتدت فراخها وقويت اخرجت المدفون وفتحت لها ثقبا فتجمع عليها الذباب والبق والنمل وغيرها من فرعت فغذت تقوي ان الي فراخها فتاكلها الهوام [wa-idhā bāḍat yabīḍ ʿishrīn bayḍa aw akthar fa-yajʿaluhā thalāthat aqsām tadfin thuluthahā fī al-turāb wa-tatruk thuluthahā fī al-shams wa-takhḍin thuluthahā fa-idhā akhrajat firākhahā kasarat mā kāna fī al-shams wa-ghadhdhathā bi-mā fīhā min al-ruṭūba allatī dhawwabathā al-shams wa-raqqathā fa-idhā ishtaddat firākhuhā wa-qawiyat akhrajat al-madfūn wa-fataḥat lahā thuqban fa-tajammaʿ ʿalayhā al-dhubāb wa-al-baqq wa-al-naml wa-ghayruhā min frʿt fghdht tqwy an ilā firākhihā fa-taʾkuluhā al-hawāmm] col. 258 When it lays eggs — and it lays twenty or more — it divides them into three parts: one of these it buries in the earth, one it exposes to the sun, and on one it sits. And when the chicks have hatched, it breaks the part that was in the sun and feeds the chicks with the fluid they contain, II, 864 after it has been liquefied and softened by the sun. And when the chicks grow strong and sturdy, it digs up the buried eggs and pierces them, so that flies, bugs, ants and similar little creatures gather to them, on which the chicks feed until, having become stronger, they run and feed themselves. But these things are closer to fables, since they attribute to the animal not only prudence but also foresight; yet that it is most stupid will be evident from what I am about to say.


1. Caetera animantia cibos, naturae suae congruos, deligunt: hoc, quodcunque se offert, ferrum, ossa, vitrum, lapides, terrae glebas, carbones, candentes prunas, gemmas, ex adstantium auribus pendentes, sine ullo delectu vorat; quae quidem non deglutire solum, sed et concoquere dicitur. Plinius li-bri decimi capite primo; Concoquendi sine delectu devorata mira natura. Aelia- nus libri decimi quarti capite septimo in occisae ventre lapides reperiri ait, ὥσπερ οὖν καταπιοῦσα ἡ στρουθὸς ἐν τῷ ἐχίνῳ φυλάττει, καὶ πέττει τῷ χρόνῳ, quos voratos, et in omaso asservatos tandem concoquit. Porta coeli fol. 22. d. כתב אבן רשד כי בהלעיטה את הזהב הוא נתך בגופה מחמם יותר מן האש בסגולה שלהם, Scripsit Averroës, eam voratum aurum in corpore suo li- quefacere, ac si sit igne calidius, per proprietatem illi insitam. Alkazuinius, ياكل الحصاة فتذوب في قانصته حتي يصير كالما بالخاصية خلقها الله فيه Lapides vorat, et in sto- macho suo liquefacit, donec ut aqua fiant, per facultatem, a Deo illi inditam. Et paullo post, وايضا يبلع الجمر ولا يضرها Etiam carbones vorat, qui illi non nocent. Item, وتحمي صنجة ماية دينار من الحديد حتي تحمر وترمي الي النعامة فتبلعها وتسترها Et ad ruborem usque calefit ferreum cymbalum centum denariorum ponderis, et struthioni projicitur, quae illud vorat et recondit. Ita etiam Damir, وتتبلع العظم الصلب والحجر والمدر والحديد وتذيبه d) كالماء Et vorat ossa dura, et lapides, et glebas, et ferrum quae instar aquae liquefacit. Item, واذا رات في اذن صغير لولوة خطفتها Et cum videt in aure parvam margaritam, rapit eam. Et rursus, وتتبلع الجمر فيكون جوفها هو العامل في اطفايه II, 865 ولا يكون الجمر عاملا في احراقة وفي ذلك اعجوبتان احدا col. 259 هما التغذي بما لا يتغذي به والثانية الاستمرا والهضم Prunas quoque deglutit, et in earum extinctionem efficax est corpus ejus. At prunae non sunt efficaces in ejus adustionem. In quo duplex est miraculum: unum in eo, quod iis alitur, quae non alunt; alterum, eorum digestio et concoctio. Haec illi, sed, ut solent, hyperbolice in majus aucta. Aelianus in ejus ventre reperiri ait lapides, quos voratos concoxit, quae mira est ἐναντιολογία. Alexander Aphrodi- saeus in Praefatione ad Aristotelis Problemata, ferrum a struthione concoqui diserte negat. Et Albertus eam asserit, quos lapides avide devoravit, postea respuere, id est, ore ejectare. Et Ulysses Aldrovandus ferri frustula deglutire, quae incocta rursus excernit. Et Gesnerus, postquam, quidquid tetigerit, lintea, ferrum, lapides vorare dixit. Verum, ait, haec incocta et integra in ejus ven- triculo manent. Et, si nimia fuerint, tandem animal ad mortem, vel ad tabem deducunt, ut in dissectis apparuit.

1. Other animals choose foods suited to their nature; this one devours without any discrimination whatever presents itself: iron, bones, glass, stones, clods of earth, coals, glowing embers, gems hanging from the ears of bystanders; and it is said not only to swallow these but also to digest them. Pliny, book 10, chapter 1: Of a wondrous nature in digesting what it has devoured without discrimination. Aelian, book 14, chapter 7, says that stones are found in the belly of a slain one, ὥσπερ οὖν καταπιοῦσα ἡ στρουθὸς ἐν τῷ ἐχίνῳ φυλάττει, καὶ πέττει τῷ χρόνῳ [hōsper oun katapiousa hē strouthos en tō echinō phylattei, kai pettei tō chronō], which, having swallowed them and kept them in its omasum, it at length digests. Porta coeli fol. 22. d.: כתב אבן רשד כי בהלעיטה את הזהב הוא נתך בגופה מחמם יותר מן האש בסגולה שלהם, Averroës wrote that it melts swallowed gold in its body, as if it were hotter than fire, through a property implanted in it. Alkazuinius: ياكل الحصاة فتذوب في قانصته حتي يصير كالما بالخاصية خلقها الله فيه [yaʾkul al-ḥaṣāh fa-tadhūb fī qāniṣatihi ḥattī yaṣīr ka-l-mā bi-l-khāṣṣiyya khalaqahā allāh fīhi] It devours stones and melts them in its stomach until they become like water, through a faculty placed in it by God. And a little later: وايضا يبلع الجمر ولا يضرها [wa-ayḍan yablaʿ al-jamr wa-lā yaḍurruhā] It also devours coals, which do it no harm. Likewise: وتحمي صنجة ماية دينار من الحديد حتي تحمر وترمي الي النعامة فتبلعها وتسترها [wa-tuḥmā ṣanjat māyat dīnār min al-ḥadīd ḥattā taḥmarr wa-turmā ilā al-naʿāma fa-tablaʿuhā wa-tasturuhā] And an iron weight of a hundred denarii is heated until red-hot and thrown to the ostrich, which devours it and stores it away. So also Damir: وتتبلع العظم الصلب والحجر والمدر والحديد وتذيبه d) كالماء [wa-tatabalaʿ al-ʿaẓm al-ṣulb wa-al-ḥajar wa-al-madar wa-al-ḥadīd wa-tudhībuhu d) ka-l-māʾ] And it devours hard bones, and stones, and clods, and iron, which it liquefies like water. Likewise: واذا رات في اذن صغير لولوة خطفتها [wa-idhā raʾat fī udhn ṣaghīr luʾluʾa khaṭifathā] And when it sees a small pearl in an ear, it snatches it. And again: وتتبلع الجمر فيكون جوفها هو العامل في اطفايه II, 865 ولا يكون الجمر عاملا في احراقة وفي ذلك اعجوبتان احدا col. 259 هما التغذي بما لا يتغذي به والثانية الاستمرا والهضم [wa-tatabalaʿ al-jamr fa-yakūn jawfuhā huwa al-ʿāmil fī iṭfāyih II, 865 wa-lā yakūn al-jamr ʿāmilan fī iḥrāqih wa-fī dhālika uʿjūbatān aḥad col. 259 humā al-taghadhdhī bi-mā lā yutaghadhdhā bihi wa-al-thāniya al-istimrā wa-al-haḍm] It also swallows embers, and its body is effective in extinguishing them, but the embers are not effective in burning it. In this there is a double marvel: one, that it is nourished by things that do not nourish; the other, their digestion and concoction. So they say, but, as usual, hyperbolically exaggerated. Aelian says stones are found in its belly which it has swallowed and digested, which is a remarkable ἐναντιολογία [enantiologia]. Alexander of Aphrodisias, in the Preface to Aristotle's Problems, expressly denies that iron is digested by the ostrich. And Albertus asserts that the stones it has greedily devoured it afterwards spits out, that is, ejects through the mouth. And Ulysses Aldrovandi [=Ulisse Aldrovandi, Ornithologia (1599–1603)] says it swallows bits of iron which it excretes again undigested. And Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium], after saying that it devours whatever it touches, linen, iron, stones, says: But these remain undigested and whole in its stomach. And if they are too many, they finally bring the animal to death or to wasting, as has appeared in dissected ones.


2. Alterum stuporis argumentum illud est, quod struthio, capite inter frutices abdito, putat se totum latere. Plinius, Non minus (mira) stoliditas in tanta corporis altitudine, cum colla frutice occultaverint, latere se existimantium. Oppianus, postquam id ipsum de bubalide narravit, Halieuticῶn libri quarti versu 630.

2. The second proof of its stupidity is that the ostrich, having hidden its head among bushes, thinks that it is entirely concealed. Pliny: No less (remarkable) is the stupidity, in so great a height of body, of those who, when they have hidden their necks in a bush, think that they are concealed. Oppian, after telling this very thing of the bubalis, Halieutica book 4, line 630:


Τοῖα δὲ καὶ Λιβύης πτερόεν βοτὸν ἀγκυλόδειρον
Νήπια τεχνάζει· — —

Τοῖα δὲ καὶ Λιβύης πτερόεν βοτὸν ἀγκυλόδειρον Νήπια τεχνάζει· — — [Toia de kai Libyēs pteroen boton ankyloderon / Nēpia technazei]


Talis etiam et Libyae alatum incurvi-cervicum pecus puerilia exercet. Tertullianus De velandis virginibus capite decimo septimo, Hanc ajunt, cum delitescen- dum habet, caput solum plane totum in condensum abscondere, reliquum se in aper- to relinquere. Claudianus in Eutropium libro secundo,

Such childish tricks does the winged, crook-necked beast of Libya also practise. Tertullian, On the Veiling of Virgins, chapter 17: They say that this bird, when it has to hide, buries only its head, plainly and wholly, in a thicket, and leaves the rest of itself in the open. Claudian, Against Eutropius, book 2:


— — stat lumine clauso
Ridendum revoluta caput, creditque latere
Quae non ipsa videt. —

— — it stands with eyes shut, its head ridiculously turned back, and believes that what it does not itself see is hidden. —


Damir, من حمق النعامة انها اذا ادركها القناص ادخلت راسها في كثيب رمل تقدر انها قد استخفت منه E struthionis ineptiis una haec est, quod, cum venator illam insequitur, ca- put suum in arenae cumulum immittit, eum se latere putans. Aut انها قد استحصنت منه ab eo se tutam esse, ut habet aliud exemplar. Tamen, ut varia sunt hominum judicia, hic quoque stultitiae suae patronum habet Dio- dorum his verbis: Ἐπειδὰν δὲ περικατάληπτον ᾖ, τὴν κεφαλὴν εἴς τινα θάμνον, ἢ τοιαύτην σκέπην ἀποκρύπτεται, οὐχ᾽, ὡς οἴονταί τινες. ἀφροσύνῃ, II, 866 καὶ νωθρότητι ψυχῆς, διὰ τὸ μὴ βλέπειν ἑτέρους, μηδ᾽ αὐτὸ βλέπεσθαι δια-λάμβανον ὑφ᾽ ἑτέρων· ἀλλὰ, διὰ τὸ τοῦ σώματος ἔχειν τοῦτο τὸ μέρος ἀσθενέ-στατον, σκέπην αὐτῷ πρὸς σωτηρίαν περιποιεῖν. Cum in proximo est, ut capiatur, caput in arbustum aliquod, aut aliud simile latibulum recondit, non quod prae stultitia, aut stupore mentis, ut quidam putant, ex eo quod non videt alios, se etiam ab aliis non videri concludat: sed, quia haec pars corporis in eo est infirmissima, hoc se latibulo tuetur ad salutem.
