Sed hoc effugium Tertullianus paucis ita refellit, Dum in capite secura est, nuda, qua major est, capitur tota cum capite. Vult frustra caput occultari, dum venatori patet reliquum corpus, quo capto, vel lethaliter icto, caput non potest evadere.

Damir: من حمق النعامة انها اذا ادركها القناص ادخلت راسها في كثيب رمل تقدر انها قد استخفت منه [min ḥumq al-naʿāma annahā idhā adrakahā al-qannāṣ adkhalat raʾsahā fī kathīb raml taqdiru annahā qad istakhfat minhu] Among the follies of the ostrich is this: when the hunter pursues it, it thrusts its head into a heap of sand, thinking that it is hidden from him. Or انها قد استحصنت منه [annahā qad istaḥṣanat minhu] that it is safe from him, as another copy has it. Yet, since men's judgements vary, here too the bird has a defender of its folly in Diodorus, in these words: Ἐπειδὰν δὲ περικατάληπτον ᾖ, τὴν κεφαλὴν εἴς τινα θάμνον, ἢ τοιαύτην σκέπην ἀποκρύπτεται, οὐχ᾽, ὡς οἴονταί τινες. ἀφροσύνῃ, II, 866 καὶ νωθρότητι ψυχῆς, διὰ τὸ μὴ βλέπειν ἑτέρους, μηδ᾽ αὐτὸ βλέπεσθαι διαλάμβανον ὑφ᾽ ἑτέρων· ἀλλὰ, διὰ τὸ τοῦ σώματος ἔχειν τοῦτο τὸ μέρος ἀσθενέστατον, σκέπην αὐτῷ πρὸς σωτηρίαν περιποιεῖν. [Epeidan de perikatalēpton ē, tēn kephalēn eis tina thamnon, ē toiautēn skepēn apokryptetai, ouch, hōs oiontai tines, aphrosynē kai nōthrotēti psychēs, dia to mē blepein heterous, mēd' auto blepesthai dialambanon hyph' heterōn; alla, dia to tou sōmatos echein touto to meros asthenestaton, skepēn autō pros sōtērian peripoiein.] When it is on the point of being caught, it hides its head in some shrub or other such hiding place. It does not do so because, out of stupidity or dullness of mind, as some think, it concludes from the fact that it does not see others that it is not itself seen by others, but because this part of its body is the weakest, it protects itself with this cover for its safety. But Tertullian refutes this excuse in a few words: While it is secure in its head, it is caught, naked where it is larger, whole along with its head. He means that the head is hidden in vain while the rest of the body lies open to the hunter; once that is caught, or mortally struck, the head cannot escape.


3. Sed et stupidissimum patet esse hoc animal, si verum est, quod ait Stra- col. 260 bo libro decimo sexto, de ratione illud venandi, apud Struthophagos recepta: Θηρεύουσι δὲ αὐτοὺς οἱ μὲν τόξοις, οἱ δὲ ταῖς δοραῖς τῶν στρουθῶν σκεπασθέντες· τὴν μὲν δεξιὰν καλύπτουσι τῷ τραχηλιμαίῳ μέρει, καὶ κινοῦσιν οὕτως ὥσπερ τὰ ζῶα κινεῖται τοῖς τραχήλοις· τῇ δὲ ἀριστερᾷ σπέρμα προχέουσιν ἀπὸ πήρας παρηρτημένης, καὶ τούτῳ δελεάσαντες τὰ ζῶα εἰς φάραγγας συνωθοῦσιν. Alii quidem struthiones arcu venantur, alii autem eorum tecti pellibus: nam dextram manum colli pelle induunt, atque eam sic movent, ut animalia collum; sinistra vero semen spargunt, ab appensa pera eductum, quo avem allicientes in convalles detrudunt. Quamvis enim a struthionis specie humana differat immensum quantum, tamen hac arte stultae aves propter mentis hebetudinem patiebantur sibi imponi. Neque hic fuit opus Zeuxidis penicillo, qui uvas, tanto successu pictas, in scenam detulit, ut ad eas aves advolarent; nec caelo Myronis, cujus bucula tauros in amorem incendebat: cum isto allectae fuerint, quamlibet crasso, atque informi, suae figurae rudimento.

3. And this animal is also plainly most stupid, if what Strabo col. 260 says in book 16 is true, about the method of hunting it practised among the Struthophagi: Θηρεύουσι δὲ αὐτοὺς οἱ μὲν τόξοις, οἱ δὲ ταῖς δοραῖς τῶν στρουθῶν σκεπασθέντες· τὴν μὲν δεξιὰν καλύπτουσι τῷ τραχηλιμαίῳ μέρει, καὶ κινοῦσιν οὕτως ὥσπερ τὰ ζῶα κινεῖται τοῖς τραχήλοις· τῇ δὲ ἀριστερᾷ σπέρμα προχέουσιν ἀπὸ πήρας παρηρτημένης, καὶ τούτῳ δελεάσαντες τὰ ζῶα εἰς φάραγγας συνωθοῦσιν. [Thēreuousi de autous hoi men toxois, hoi de tais dorais tōn strouthōn skepasthentes; tēn men dexian kalyptousi tō trachēlimaiō merei, kai kinousin houtōs hōsper ta zōa kineitai tois trachēlois; tē de aristera sperma procheousin apo pēras parērtēmenēs, kai toutō deleasantes ta zōa eis pharangas synōthousin.] Some hunt the ostriches with bows, others covered with their skins: for they clothe the right hand in the skin of the neck and move it as the animals move their necks, while with the left they scatter seed taken from a bag hanging at their side; luring the birds with this, they drive them into ravines. For although the human form differs immeasurably from the shape of the ostrich, yet these foolish birds, through dullness of mind, let themselves be deceived by this trick. Nor was there any need here for the brush of Zeuxis, who brought onto the stage grapes painted with such success that birds flew to them; nor for the chisel of Myron, whose heifer kindled bulls to love: since they were lured by this rough sketch of their own figure, however crude and shapeless.


4. Quartum stuporis in struthione indicium est illud ipsum, quod a Iobo urgetur, quod ova sua derelinquit, et illorum est immemor. Notum Esaiae ἐπιφώνημα tanquam de re impossibili, Esa. XLIX, 15. An oblivisci potest mulier foetus sui, ut non misereatur filii uteri sui? Et reliquis animantibus eundem illum affectum erga prolem a natura esse inditum, ut conserventur species, cetisque adeo tribui, quae omnium animalium longe immanissima sunt, Thren. IV, 3. Sed struthio hic excipitur, quae ova sua in terra deserit, etc. Unde Damir supra, Cum e nido exit, ut cibum quaerat, si reperiat ova struthionis alterius, تحضنه وتنسى بيضها illis incubat, et suorum obliviscitur. Et Leo Africanus libro nono, Ova, numero decem aut duodecim, in arena emittit, etc. Ac brevissimimae cum sit memoriae, loci confestim obliviscitur. Quare foemina, in haec ova incidens, sive propria, sive aliena, excubat et calefacit. Quae eadem in Marmolio. II, 867 5. Denique apud Arabes, quibus haec avis est notissima, احمق من النعامة Struthione stultiorem dici notavimus pro stultissimo. Quod corporis ipse habitus abunde docet. Nam caput habet valde exile, et cerebrum fere nullum. Unde Arabice صعون sivvan dicitur, id est, الدقيق العنق والصغير الراس او العام colli tenuis, et parvi capitis, aut verticis. Vocatur etiam انقخ ankach, id est, قليل الدماغ exigui cerebri. Ita Al-camus. Quocirca sexcentorum struthionum capita Heliogabalus una coena exhibuit ad edenda cerebella. Tam multa enim esse oportuit, ut convivis abunde esset; quia singuli struthiones cerebri vix quidquam habent. Struthionis porro caput, longo exili collo vectum, firmum esse non potest. Unde est, quod نغض nigd appellant ipsum animal; quia نغض nagada est nutare caput. Rursus Al-camus, نغض اسم الظليم معرفة للجوال منه Nigd, nomen struthionis, ab agitatione illi inditum. Et ad eandem vocem Damir, الظليم سمي بذلك لانه يحرك راسه Ita vocatur struthio, quia movet caput suum. In qua capitis agitatione facultas imaginativa firma esse vix potest, et in gradu suo consistere. Et cum auris etiam in brutis suo modo sit disciplinae sensus, in struthione stuporem auget surditas, quae illi naturalis est. Chaluia in libro ليس Laisa, seu Non est (quem diximus esse De reb. quae alicui, aut alicubi desunt) ليس في الدنيا حيوان لا يسمع الا النعام Nullum est in mundo animal (perfectum), quod non audiat, praeter struthionem. col. 261 Leo Africanus libro nono, Struthio est animal simplex et surdum. Marmolius, El abestruez es simple, y sordò, que no oye cosa ninguna. Quae omnia lucem addunt his Iobi, Deus destituit eam sapientia, etc. Superest, ut explicentur ultima verba sacri scriproris, qui struthionis descriptionem ita claudit:

4. The fourth sign of stupidity in the ostrich is the very thing that Job presses: that it abandons its eggs and is unmindful of them. Isaiah's ἐπιφώνημα [epiphōnēma] is well known, as if about something impossible, Isa 49:15. Can a woman forget her offspring, so as not to have compassion on the son of her womb? And the same affection toward offspring has been implanted by nature in the other animals, so that the species may be preserved; it is attributed even to the cetaceans, which are by far the most savage of all animals, Lam 4:3. But the ostrich is here excepted, which leaves its eggs on the ground, etc. Hence Damir above: When it leaves the nest to seek food, if it finds the eggs of another ostrich, تحضنه وتنسى بيضها [taḥḍunuhu wa-tansā bayḍahā] it broods on them and forgets its own. And Leo Africanus, book 9: It lays its eggs, ten or twelve in number, in the sand, etc. And since it has a very short memory, it immediately forgets the place. Therefore the female, coming upon these eggs, whether her own or another's, sits on them and warms them. The same is found in Marmol. II, 867 5. Finally, among the Arabs, to whom this bird is very well known, we have noted that احمق من النعامة [aḥmaq min al-naʿāma] more foolish than an ostrich is said for "most foolish." The very build of its body amply shows this. For it has a very small head and almost no brain. Hence in Arabic it is called صعون [ṣaʿwan] sivvan, that is, الدقيق العنق والصغير الراس او العام [al-daqīq al-ʿunuq wa-al-ṣaghīr al-rās aw al-ʿām] thin of neck and small of head, or of crown. It is also called انقخ [anqakh] ankach, that is, قليل الدماغ [qalīl al-dimāgh] of little brain. So Alcamus. For this reason Heliogabalus served the heads of six hundred ostriches at a single dinner, so that their little brains might be eaten. So many were needed for there to be plenty for the guests, since individual ostriches have hardly any brain. Further, the head of the ostrich, carried on a long thin neck, cannot be steady. That is why they call the animal itself نغض [nighḍ] nigd, because نغض [naghaḍa] nagada means to nod the head. Again Alcamus: نغض اسم الظليم معرفة للجوال منه [nighḍ ism al-ẓalīm maʿrifa lil-jawwāl minhu] Nigd, a name of the ostrich, given to it from its agitation. And on the same word Damir: الظليم سمي بذلك لانه يحرك راسه [al-ẓalīm summiya bi-dhālika li-annahu yuḥarriku rasahu] The ostrich is so called because it moves its head. With such agitation of the head the imaginative faculty can hardly be steady and keep to its own level. And since the ear, even in brute animals, is in its own way the sense of learning, in the ostrich stupidity is increased by deafness, which is natural to it. Khalawayh, in the book ليس [laysa] Laisa, or There is not (which we said is On things that are lacking to someone, or somewhere): ليس في الدنيا حيوان لا يسمع الا النعام [laysa fī al-dunyā ḥayawān lā yasmaʿu illā al-naʿām] There is no animal in the world (no perfect animal) that does not hear, except the ostrich. col. 261 Leo Africanus, book 9: The ostrich is a simple and deaf animal. Marmol: El abestruez es simple, y sordò, que no oye cosa ninguna. All this sheds light on these words of Job: God has deprived her of wisdom, etc. It remains to explain the last words of the sacred writer, who closes the description of the ostrich thus:


Quo tempore in altum se attollit, ridet equum, et sessorem ejus] Sensus est, Deum hanc avem ita privasse sapientia, ut tamen ejus saluti, et conservationi prospexerit: cum homini etiam equiti illam assequi non sit facile. Quo tempore כעת, vel κατὰ καιρὸν, cum tempus fuerit; ut Graeci, Hieronymus, Pagninus, Genevenses, etc. quomodo sumi videtur Num. XXIII, 23. Alioqui כעת, saepius jungitur cum sequentibus, ut כעת מחר, tempore crastino, 1 Sam. IX, 16. et passim, כעת מנחת ערב, tempore oblationis vespertinae, Dan. IX, 21. כעת הראשון יקל, Quo tempore primus levis fuit, Esa. VIII, 23. Quomodo hic malo cum Chaldaeo sumere, Quo tempore in altum se attollit, ridet, etc. Quia sic melius cohaerent duo hemistichia. In altum se attollit] Hebraice במרום תמריא. Quia vox תמריא hic solum occurrit, illam varie exponunt prisci interpretes. II, 868 Syrus ܬܬܬܪܝܡ ܐܝܟ ܕܩܠܐ, Arabs itidem ترتفع مثل النخلة Erigitur, ut palma. Quasi תמריא thamri, ad תמר thamar, id est, ad palmam alludat. Quod absurdum est, cum in תמריא Thau sit servile. Chaldaeus vero טיסא, volat. Et vetus Scholiastes ad hunc locum, Ἐν τῇ πτήσει τὸ θαῤῥεῖν ἔχουσα ἵπταται. Volatu fidens volat. Hieronymus melius, alas erigit. Septuaginta optime ὑψώσει, attolletur. Neque enim volat struthio, cum sit volatus expers, sed in altum alas erigit, vel ipsa potius in altum attollitur, id est, cum venatores ad nidum accedunt, e cubili suo exsurgens, staturae proceritate, et colli extensione supra fidem eminet, quod voce תמריא commode significatur. Est enim Futurum Hiphil. Et Kal est מרא mara; quod, literis trajectis, factum videtur ex ראם raam, id est, altum esse. Nam רום rum, et ראם raam, idem sonare, alibi e) probavimus (5). Itaque his verbis, in altum erigitur, commendatur in struthione staturae proceritas, de qua multa scriptores. Aristoteles De partibus animalium in fine libri quarti, Τὸ μέγεθος οὐκ ὄρνιθος ἔχει, ἀλλὰ τε-τράποδος· Magnitudinem avis non habet, sed quadrupedis. Diodorus lib. 2. Τὸ μέγεθος ἔχουσι νεογονεῖ καμήλῳ παραπλήσιον· Recens nati cameli magnitudinem prope habet. Oppianus libro tertio Venaticorum,

At the time when it lifts itself on high, it laughs at the horse and its rider] The sense is that God so deprived this bird of wisdom that he nevertheless provided for its safety and preservation, since it is not easy for a man, even a horseman, to overtake it. At the time when: כעת, or κατὰ καιρὸν [kata kairon], when the time has come; so the Greeks, Jerome, Pagninus, the Genevans, etc., which is how it seems to be taken in Num 23:23. Otherwise כעת is more often joined with what follows, as כעת מחר, at the time of tomorrow, 1 Sam 9:16, and passim; כעת מנחת ערב, at the time of the evening offering, Dan 9:21; כעת הראשון יקל, At the time when the first was light, Isa 8:23. So here I prefer, with the Chaldee, to take it as At the time when it lifts itself on high, it laughs, etc., because the two hemistichs cohere better this way. It lifts itself on high] In Hebrew במרום תמריא. Because the word תמריא occurs only here, the ancient interpreters explain it variously. II, 868 The Syriac has ܬܬܬܪܝܡ ܐܝܟ ܕܩܠܐ [תתתרים איך דקלא], and the Arabic likewise ترتفع مثل النخلة [tartafiʿ mithl al-nakhla], It is raised up like a palm, as if תמריא thamri alluded to תמר thamar, that is, to the palm. This is absurd, since in תמריא the Thau is servile. The Chaldee, however, has טיסא, it flies. And the old Scholiast on this passage: Ἐν τῇ πτήσει τὸ θαῤῥεῖν ἔχουσα ἵπταται [En tē ptēsei to tharrhein echousa hiptatai], Trusting in its flight it flies. Jerome better: it raises its wings. The Seventy best of all: ὑψώσει [hypsōsei], it will be lifted up. For the ostrich does not fly, since it is incapable of flight; rather it raises its wings on high, or rather it is itself lifted on high. That is, when hunters approach the nest, it rises from its resting place and towers up beyond belief through the tallness of its stature and the stretching out of its neck, which is aptly signified by the word תמריא. For it is the future of Hiphil, and the Kal is מרא mara; which, with the letters transposed, seems to have been formed from ראם raam, that is, to be high. For we have proved elsewhere e) that רום rum and ראם raam mean the same R5. So by these words, it is raised on high, the tallness of the ostrich's stature is commended, about which writers say much. Aristotle, On the Parts of Animals, at the end of the fourth book: Τὸ μέγεθος οὐκ ὄρνιθος ἔχει, ἀλλὰ τετράποδος [To megethos ouk ornithos echei, alla tetrapodos]· It has the size not of a bird but of a quadruped. Diodorus, book 2: Τὸ μέγεθος ἔχουσι νεογονεῖ καμήλῳ παραπλήσιον [To megethos echousi neogonei kamēlō paraplēsion]· It has nearly the size of a newborn camel. Oppian, in the third book of the Cynegetica:


Τῆς ἤτοι μέγεθος μὲν ὑπέρβιον, ὅσσον ὕπερθεν
Νώτοις εὐρυτάτοισι φέρειν νεοθήλεα κοῦρον·

Τῆς ἤτοι μέγεθος μὲν ὑπέρβιον, ὅσσον ὕπερθεν Νώτοις εὐρυτάτοισι φέρειν νεοθήλεα κοῦρον· [Tēs ētoi megethos men hyperbion, hosson hyperthen / Nōtois eurytatoisi pherein neothēlea kouron·]


Cujus immensa est magnitudo, ita, ut lato dorso puerum, nuper natum ferat. Plinius, Altitudinem equitis insidentis equo excedunt. Albertus, Struthio alta est a pedibus ad dorsum circiter quinque, vel sex pedes: collum habet longissimum, etc. Itaque Arabes هيق heic, et هيقم heicam vocant a colli longitudine, et اسقف ascaph ab eminentia. Quomodo etiam Christianorum episcopos, sed ex Graeco deflexa voce. Et de herba استرال isterala est in altum crescere ut struthionis pullus, qui Arabice رال raal dicitur. II, 869 Struthio igitur, ita in altum se erigens, ridet equum, et sessorem ejus. col. 262 Ridet, id est, spernit; ut habet Graecus Scholiastes, Καταφρονοῦσα ἵππου σὺν τῷ ἀναβάτῃ διὰ τὴν ἰσχὺν, ὥς φασι, καὶ τὸ μέγεθος. Equum cum ascensore despiciens, propter vires, ut ajunt, et magnitudinem. Recte, nisi quod equum, et equitem, struthio spernere dicendus erat, non virium, sed celeritatis fiducia. Unde Plinius, Altitudinem equi insidentis equo excedunt, celeritate vincunt. Et Xenophon, libro primo Anabaseως, Cyri equites dicit onagros et capreas in Arabia cepisse, sed struthiones nullo modo potuisse assequi. Στρουθὸν δὲ οὐδεὶς ἔλαβεν· οἱ δὲ διώξαντες τῶν ἱππέων ταχὺ ἐπαύοντο· πολὺ γὰρ ἀπέσπα απο-φεύγουσα. Struthionem nemo cepit; et, qui insequebantur, cito cessabant: nam fuga longius se proripiebat. Quod in exercitu, multis equitum millibus, instructo notabile est. Ajunt quidem, in Africa, in equorum illo genere, quos Arabicos appellant, nonnullos reperiri, qui struthionem cursu assequantur, sed paucos admodum, eosque immensi pretii. Marmolius libri primi capite vigesimo tertio, Cavallos Barbaros son llamados en toda Europa los, que vienen de Berberia: mas ay una especie de cavallos en Africa, y en Egypto, y en las Arabias, y en toda Asia, que llaman cavallos Arabes, que son de casta de cavallos salvages, que se crian por los desiertos de Arabia, etc. Son est rañamente ligeros, y la mayor experiencia, que se haze de su ligereza es quando alcançan una fiera llamada Lamte, o a un abestruz. Porque este tal cavallos es apreciado en mil ducados de oro, o en cien camellos. Mas ay pocos dellos en Berberia. Id est, In tota Europa Barbari vocantur equi, e Barbaria advecti: sed in Africa, Aegypto, Arabia, et tota Asia una est equorum species, quos Arabicos appellant, ex eorum prosapia, qui in Arabiae desertis procreantur, etc. Ii sunt mire veloces: neque majus ullum est eorum celeritatis experimentum, quam cum feram, Lamten nomine, aut struthiocamelum assequuntur. Ideo talis equus mille ducatis aureis, aut centum camelis aestimatur. Sed in Barbaria tales pauci sunt. Et certe haec est Arabum communis sententia, nullum esse animal, quod struthionem cursu superet. In quam rem diserta sunt haec Alkazuinii, لا يصبقها شي من الحيوانات Nullum animalium illam antevertit. Quod qua ratione fiat, supra f) docuimus; et alas pro velo habentem in aëre natare quasi. Unde Oppianus libri terti Cynegeticῶn versu 500.

Whose size is immense, so that on its broad back it could carry a newborn boy. Pliny: They exceed the height of a horseman sitting on a horse. Albertus: The ostrich is about five or six feet tall from the feet to the back; it has a very long neck, etc. Therefore the Arabs call it هيق [hayq] heic and هيقم [hayqam] heicam from the length of its neck, and اسقف [usquf] ascaph from its height. This is also what they call the bishops of the Christians, but there the word is derived from the Greek. And of a plant, استرال [istarāl] isterala means to grow tall like the chick of an ostrich, which in Arabic is called رال [rāl] raal. II, 869 The ostrich, then, raising itself so high, laughs at the horse and its rider. col. 262 Laughs, that is, scorns, as the Greek Scholiast has it: Καταφρονοῦσα ἵππου σὺν τῷ ἀναβάτῃ διὰ τὴν ἰσχὺν, ὥς φασι, καὶ τὸ μέγεθος [kataphronousa hippou syn tō anabatē dia tēn ischyn, hōs phasi, kai to megethos]. Despising the horse with its rider, on account of its strength, as they say, and its size. Rightly, except that the ostrich should have been said to scorn horse and horseman not in reliance on its strength but on its speed. Hence Pliny: They exceed the height of a horseman sitting on a horse, and surpass him in speed. And Xenophon, in book 1 of the Anabasis, says that the horsemen of Cyrus caught wild asses and roe deer in Arabia, but could in no way overtake the ostriches: Στρουθὸν δὲ οὐδεὶς ἔλαβεν· οἱ δὲ διώξαντες τῶν ἱππέων ταχὺ ἐπαύοντο· πολὺ γὰρ ἀπέσπα αποφεύγουσα [strouthon de oudeis elaben; hoi de diōxantes tōn hippeōn tachy epauonto; poly gar apespa apopheugousa]. No one caught an ostrich; and those who pursued it soon gave up, for in its flight it drew far ahead. This is remarkable in an army equipped with many thousands of horsemen. It is said, indeed, that in Africa, among the breed of horses called Arabian, some are found that can overtake an ostrich in running, but very few, and these of immense price. Marmol, book 1, chapter 23: Cavallos Barbaros son llamados en toda Europa los, que vienen de Berberia: mas ay una especie de cavallos en Africa, y en Egypto, y en las Arabias, y en toda Asia, que llaman cavallos Arabes, que son de casta de cavallos salvages, que se crian por los desiertos de Arabia, etc. Son est rañamente ligeros, y la mayor experiencia, que se haze de su ligereza es quando alcançan una fiera llamada Lamte, o a un abestruz. Porque este tal cavallos es apreciado en mil ducados de oro, o en cien camellos. Mas ay pocos dellos en Berberia. That is: Throughout Europe the horses brought from Barbary are called Barbary horses; but in Africa, Egypt, Arabia and all Asia there is a breed of horses which they call Arabian, descended from those bred in the deserts of Arabia, etc. They are wonderfully swift, and there is no greater proof of their speed than when they overtake the wild beast called the Lamte, or an ostrich. Therefore such a horse is valued at a thousand gold ducats, or a hundred camels. But in Barbary there are few such. And certainly this is the common opinion of the Arabs, that there is no animal which surpasses the ostrich in running. On this point these words of Alkazuinius are explicit: لا يصبقها شي من الحيوانات [lā yaṣbiquhā shay min al-ḥayawānāt] None of the animals outruns it. How this comes about we have shown above f): that, using its wings as a sail, it swims, as it were, in the air. Hence Oppian, Cynegetica book 3, verse 500:


Ἠέρος ὑψιπόροισιν ἐπιπλώουσι κελεύθοις,

Ἠέρος ὑψιπόροισιν ἐπιπλώουσι κελεύθοις, [Ēeros hypsiporoisin epiplōousi keleuthois,]


Aëris sublimibus natant viis. Et mox, II, 870 Αὐτοῖσιν φορέουσιν ἴσον τάχος οἰωνοῖσιν,

They swim along the lofty paths of the air. And shortly after, II, 870 Αὐτοῖσιν φορέουσιν ἴσον τάχος οἰωνοῖσιν, [Autoisin phoreousin ison tachos oiōnoisin,]


Ipsis avibus aequali sunt celeritate. Itaque Arabes multa cuderunt vocabula, quibus id designarent. Sic de struthione زازا zaza est capite, alis, et cauda elatis fluere potius quam incedere: رفرف raphrapha alas motitando currere, ut Tal- mudicum רפרף riphreph: كحص chahatsa, ire tam propere, ut visum prope fugiat. Atque ob id ipsum struthio عصوف id est, turbo vocatur, et aliis nominibus, minimum decem, a cursus rapiditate ductis (6). Quin ipsa sese ad cursum incitat spiculis quibusdam osseis, qui sub alis latent, et pro calcaribus illi sunt. De quibus multo plura facile esset adducere: sed haec docere sigillatim non est praesentis locis; et Sacri Scriptoris mentem explicasse nobis sufficit.

They are of equal speed with the birds themselves. Accordingly the Arabs coined many words to express this. Thus of the ostrich, زازا [zāzā] zaza means to flow rather than walk, with head, wings and tail raised; رفرف [rafrafa] raphrapha, to run while flapping the wings, like the Talmudic רפרף riphreph; كحص [kaḥaṣa] chahatsa, to go so swiftly as almost to escape the sight. And for this very reason the ostrich is called عصوف [ʿaṣūf], that is, whirlwind, and by other names, at least ten, derived from the rapidity of its running R6. Indeed it spurs itself on to run with certain bony spikes which lie hidden under its wings and serve it as spurs. On these it would be easy to adduce much more; but to set this out point by point is not the business of the present place, and it is enough for us to have explained the meaning of the Sacred Writer.

(5) Rosenmüller, II, 868 Sed rectius ALB. SCHULTENS pag. 1126. reddit: ad cursum sese incitat. Etenim verbum مري significat ad vehementiorem cursum scutica incussa adegit equum. Geuhari: مريت الفرس اذا استخرجت ما عنده من الجري بسوط او غيره Dicitur מריח אלפרש strinxi equum, quum elicio, admota scutica, aut alia re (calcaribus), quicquid cursu pollet. Quod quidem verbum perquam apte adhibitum est a poeta Hebraeo. Habet enim struthio, Shawio teste (pag. 387. vers. germ.), sub alis unguiculum aliquem, quo ipse se acrius currens vulnerat, adeoque sanguinem elicit. Quod ipsum et Bochartus observat infra ad finem capitis nostri.

R5 Rosenmüller, II, 868 But ALB. SCHULTENS, p. 1126, renders it more correctly: it urges itself on to running. For the verb مري [marā] means he drove a horse to a faster run by striking it with the whip. Giauhari: مريت الفرس اذا استخرجت ما عنده من الجري بسوط او غيره [maraytu al-faras idhā istakhrajtu mā ʿindahu min al-jary bi-sawṭ aw ghayrihi] One says מריח אלפרש I urged the horse, when I draw out, by applying the whip, or something else (spurs), whatever it has in running. This verb is indeed most aptly used by the Hebrew poet. For the ostrich, as Shaw [=Thomas Shaw, Travels (1738)] testifies (p. 387, German trans.), has under its wings a small claw with which it wounds itself as it runs harder, and so draws blood. Bochart too notes this very thing below, at the end of our chapter.

Part 2, Book 2, chapter 18: Sachaph is the gull, or the cepphus
------------------------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/sachaph.html

III, 1 CAP. XVIII. col. 263

III, 1 Chapter XVIII. col. 263


Probatur, שחף sachaph esse Larum, aut Cepphum, unde κεπφωθεὶς Prov. VII, 22.

It is proved that שחף sachaph is the gull or the cepphus, whence κεπφωθεὶς [kepphōtheis] Prov. VII, 22.


Ut struthio vasta est avis, ita nos diu detinuit. Iam in iis, quae sequentur, rem peragemus paucioribus. Et primo se offert שחף sachaph, a Syro prorsus omissus; a Chaldaeis שחפא sachpha redditus; ab Arabibus سَاف saph; a Samaritano ࠔࠅࠐࠀ sopha: vocibus aeque ignotis. Itaque hinc nullum subsidium. Graeci, Hieronymus, Munsterus, Castalio explicant larum: Iunius aesalonem, tanquam ex R. Iuda: Deodatius la folica, id est, fulicam, in Italica versione; sed idem in Gallica, la movette, id est, larum: Genevenses et Angli, cuculum; Arias phthiticam avem, tanquam a phthisi sumto nomine. Nempe Hebraeorum plerique observant, hujus avis nomen שחף sachaph alludere ad שחפת sachepheth, morbi speciem, Levit. XXVI, 16. et Deut. XXVIII, 22. Sive ipsa avis huic morbo sit obnoxia, aut sua carne vescentibus illum ingeneret. Sed neque id satis notum, quod morbi genus sit שחפת sachepheth. Rabbi Selomo definit חולי שמשחפת את הבשר אנפו״ליש בלע״ז דומה לנפוח שהוקלה כפיחהו ומראית פניו זעיפה, morbum, qui carnem inflat. Gallice ampullas dixeris, quo qui laborat, similis est viro, qui buccam inflat leviter, et speciem habeat irati. Et David de Pomis, הוא חולי אשר יוליד אבעבועות כמו תפוחים לפי רש״י, Morbus est, pustulas gignens ut poma, ut ait Rabbi Selomo Iarchi. Quamvis de pomis R. Selomo nihil habeat. Sed pro דומה לנפוח, Pomarius videtur in Selomone legisse דומה לתפוח, pomo similis: quam lectionem sequentia palam refellunt. Utut sit, Rabbi Ionas hunc eundem morbum multo aliter definit, ut docent haec Kimchii in Lexico: פירשו רבי יונה בל׳שון ערבי סחא״ף והוא החולי שהגוף מתנונה בו, R. Ionas explicat morbum Arabice dictum sochaph; quo sit, ut corpus fit מתנונה mathnuna, id est, מתחלשת ומתכחשת ומתדלדלת, debilitatum, et emaciatum, et attenuatum. Ita enim in Aruch redditur vox מתנונה mathnuna, sumta ex Talmudico tractatu Sota cap. 4. fol. 26 a.

As the ostrich is a huge bird, so it has detained us long. Now in what follows we shall settle matters more briefly. And first presents itself שחף sachaph, entirely omitted by the Syrian; rendered by the Chaldeans שחפא sachpha; by the Arabs سَاف [sāf] saph; by the Samaritan ࠔࠅࠐࠀ [שופא] sopha: words equally unknown. So no help comes from here. The Greeks, Jerome, Munster and Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)] explain it as the gull; Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] as the aesalon [merlin], as if on the authority of R. Judah; Diodati as la folica, that is, the fulica [coot], in the Italian version, but the same man in the French as la movette, that is, the gull; the Genevans and the English as the cuckoo; Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot] as the phthisic bird, as if the name were taken from phthisis. For most of the Hebrews observe that this bird's name שחף sachaph alludes to שחפת sachepheth, a kind of disease, Lev 26:16 and Deut. XXVIII, 22, whether because the bird itself is subject to this disease, or because it produces it in those who eat its flesh. But it is not well enough known either what kind of disease שחפת sachepheth is. R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] defines it: חולי שמשחפת את הבשר אנפו״ליש בלע״ז דומה לנפוח שהוקלה כפיחהו ומראית פניו זעיפה, a disease that inflates the flesh; in French you would call them blisters; one who suffers from it is like a man who puffs his cheek slightly, and has the look of an angry man. And David de Pomis [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587), a Hebrew-Latin-Italian dictionary]: הוא חולי אשר יוליד אבעבועות כמו תפוחים לפי רש״י, It is a disease producing pustules like apples, as R. Selomo Jarchi [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac), called Jarchi by the Christian Hebraists] says. Yet R. Selomo says nothing about apples. But instead of דומה לנפוח, Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)] seems to have read in R. Selomo דומה לתפוח, like an apple: a reading which what follows plainly refutes. However that may be, R. Jonah [=Jonah ibn Janāḥ, Sefer ha-Shorashim] defines this same disease very differently, as these words of Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] in his Lexicon show: פירשו רבי יונה בל׳שון ערבי סחא״ף והוא החולי שהגוף מתנונה בו, R. Jonah explains it as the disease called in Arabic sochaph, through which the body becomes מתנונה mathnuna, that is, מתחלשת ומתכחשת ומתדלדלת, weakened, and emaciated, and wasted. For so the word מתנונה mathnuna is rendered in the Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome], taken from the Talmudic tractate Sota, ch. 4, fol. 26a


III, 2 Hinc idem Pomarius, qui supra אבל לפי קמחי הוא חולי שיוליד דקות הגוף ואבודו, Sed juxta Kimchium morbus est attenuationem corporis gignens, et perditionem ejus. Et Aquinas, חולי מה שגורם כיחוש ודלות לגוף עד שמאבדו והוא מן קדחא, Morbus est, qui causatur maciem, et corporis attenuationem, donec illud plane consumat, idque fit ex febri. Quibus verbis phthisim, seu tabem describi nemo non videt. Et vero سحاف sochaph Arabum in Giauhari col. 264 est idem, quod سل sil. Qua voce phthisim significari docet praeter alios Avicenna in tractatu De Phthisi lib. 3. Fen. 10. tract. 4. cap. 18. Porro Hebraeum שחפת sachepheth, et Arabicum سحاف sochaph easdem habent Radicales, nisi quod Arabes de more Scin Hebraeum in Sin mutant. Omnino igitur utraque voce idem morbus significatur. Proinde in Mose, pro שחפת, habent Arabes السل phthisim, vel حمي السل, febrim phthisicam. Graecos quoque suspicor ἀτροφίαν reddidisse, quae est inter phthisis species. Quamvis ἀπορίαν exhibeant nostra exemplaria jam inde a multis saeculis. Ita enim legit Hieronymus, ac proinde שחפת egestatem interpretatur. Utut sit, שחפת non esse ἀπορίαν, egestatem, ex eo patet, quod in utroque loco Legis censetur inter morborum species. Itaque שחפת est morbus, isque adeo, quem diximus; nempe phthisis, seu tabes. Id confirmatur ex Talmudicis, apud quos שחוף tabidum sonat, ut probat Cl. Buxtorfius ex Sota fol. 26. b. Sed et Hebraeorum aliis שחף, in Kal est tabere, in Niphal, tabidum fieri; in Piel, tabefacere: ut ab eodem affirmatur. Verisimile est igitur, שחף sachaph avem esse, a tabe dictam. Et Hieronymum, post Graecos, larum recte reddidisse (id est movette Gall.) de qua ave Bellonius libri tertii capite decimo tertio, Nulla est avis molis ratione tam levis. Cum enim sit gallina crassior, non habet tantum carnis, quantum coturnix. Id in ceppho maxime deprehenditur, lari specie levissima, quaeque plumae plurimum, sed carnis habet minimum. Aristophanis Scholiastes in Pace, Εὔηθες ζῶον ὁ κέπφος, etc. Ἐκ δὲ τῆς θαλάττης ζῆν αὐτὸν λέγουσιν, ἐσθίοντα τὸν ἀφρόν· εἶναι δὲ αὐτὸν πολὺν μὲν ἐν τοῖς πτεροῖς, ὀλίγον δὲ ἐν τοῖς κρέασι. Cepphus est animal stolidum, etc. Eum autem ajunt ex mari vivere, spumam edentem, et plumarum quidem multum habere, sed parum carnium. Hinc Hesychius, Κέπφος· εἶδος ὀρνέου κουφοτάτου, περὶ τὴν θάλασσαν διατρίβον-τος, ὃ εὐχερῶς ὑπὸ ἀνέμου μετάγεται. Cepphus, species avis levissimae, circa mare versari solitae, quae a vento facile abducitur. Et Suidas, Κέπφος· εἶδος ὀρνέου ὁ λεγόμενος λάρος· ἔστι δὲ κοῦφον, καὶ ἐπιπλέον τοῖς κύμασιν· Cepphus, avis species, quae et larus vocatur: est autem levis, et fluctibus supernatat. Quod alio nomine larum vocari dicit, habet ex Scholiaste Aristophanis in Plutum, cujus de ceppho verba sunt: Καλεῖται δὲ κοινῶς λάρος. Vulgo autem vocatur larus. Itaque junguntur ut synonyma in Proverbio Κέπφος λάρος apud Erasmum et alios. Et in Hesychio Κὴξ Apioni est ὁ λάρος, at alii κέπφον reddunt, III, 3 alii etiam ἐφυϊάν· lege αἰθυϊὰν, id est, mergum. Tamen larum et cepphum differre colligas ex his Aristotelis Historiae libri octavi capite tertio, Περὶ δὲ τὴν θάλατταν καὶ ἀλκύων, καὶ κήρυλος, etc. Ἔτι δὲ ὁ λάρος ὁ λευ-κὸς, καὶ κέπφος, καὶ χαράδριος· At circa mare sunt et alcyon, et cerylus, etc. Larus albus etiam, et cepphus, et charadrius. Cepphus igitur et larus non plane idem sunt, sed aves valde similes. Unde Nicandri Scholiastes in Alexipharmaca, Ὁ δὲ κέπφος θαλάσσιόν ἐστι ὄρνεον παραπλήσιον λάρῳ. Gesnerus putat, esse aves congeneres, aut cepphum lari speciem. Quoquo modo res se ha-beat, nomen שחף tam laro, quam ceppho apprime convenit, cum avis utraque describatur fere carnis expers, ac si sit tabe consumta (1).

III, 2 Hence the same Pomarius, who above wrote אבל לפי קמחי הוא חולי שיוליד דקות הגוף ואבודו, But according to Kimchi it is a disease producing wasting of the body and its destruction. And Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)]: חולי מה שגורם כיחוש ודלות לגוף עד שמאבדו והוא מן קדחא, It is a disease which causes leanness and wasting of the body, until it consumes it entirely; and this comes from fever. Everyone can see that these words describe phthisis, or consumption. And indeed the Arabic سحاف [suḥāf] sochaph in Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ] col. 264 is the same as سل [sill] sil. That this word signifies phthisis is taught, among others, by Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] in the treatise On Phthisis, book 3, Fen 10, tract. 4, ch. 18. Moreover, the Hebrew שחפת sachepheth and the Arabic سحاف [suḥāf] sochaph have the same radicals, except that the Arabs, as is their custom, change the Hebrew Shin into Sin. So the two words certainly signify the same disease. Accordingly, in Moses, for שחפת the Arabs have السل [al-sill] phthisis, or حمي السل [ḥummā al-sill], phthisical fever. I also suspect that the Greeks rendered it ἀτροφίαν [atrophian], which is among the species of phthisis, although our copies have shown ἀπορίαν [aporian] for many centuries now. For so Jerome read, and accordingly he interprets שחפת as poverty. However that may be, that שחפת is not ἀπορίαν [aporian], poverty, is clear from the fact that in both passages of the Law it is counted among the kinds of diseases. Therefore שחפת is a disease, and indeed the one we have named: namely phthisis, or consumption. This is confirmed from the Talmudists, among whom שחוף means consumptive, as the distinguished Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum] proves from Sota fol. 26b Moreover, among other Hebrew writers שחף in Kal is to waste away, in Niphal to become consumptive, in Piel to cause to waste away, as the same author affirms. It is therefore probable that שחף sachaph is a bird named from wasting, and that Jerome, following the Greeks, rightly rendered it larus [gull] (that is, French movette). Of this bird Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)], book 3, chapter 13, says: No bird is so light in proportion to its bulk. For though it is bigger than a hen, it has not as much flesh as a quail. This is found above all in the cepphus, a very light species of gull, which has a great deal of plumage but very little flesh. The Scholiast on Aristophanes, on the Peace: Εὔηθες ζῶον ὁ κέπφος, etc. Ἐκ δὲ τῆς θαλάττης ζῆν αὐτὸν λέγουσιν, ἐσθίοντα τὸν ἀφρόν· εἶναι δὲ αὐτὸν πολὺν μὲν ἐν τοῖς πτεροῖς, ὀλίγον δὲ ἐν τοῖς κρέασι [Euēthes zōon ho kepphos, etc. Ek de tēs thalattēs zēn auton legousin, esthionta ton aphron; einai de auton polyn men en tois pterois, oligon de en tois kreasi]. The cepphus is a stupid animal, etc. They say that it lives from the sea, eating the foam, and that it has much plumage but little flesh. Hence Hesychius: Κέπφος· εἶδος ὀρνέου κουφοτάτου, περὶ τὴν θάλασσαν διατρίβοντος, ὃ εὐχερῶς ὑπὸ ἀνέμου μετάγεται [Kepphos; eidos orneou kouphotatou, peri tēn thalassan diatribontos, ho eucherōs hypo anemou metagetai]. Cepphus: a species of very light bird, accustomed to spend its time about the sea, which is easily carried off by the wind. And Suidas: Κέπφος· εἶδος ὀρνέου ὁ λεγόμενος λάρος· ἔστι δὲ κοῦφον, καὶ ἐπιπλέον τοῖς κύμασιν [Kepphos; eidos orneou ho legomenos laros; esti de kouphon, kai epipleon tois kymasin]; Cepphus: a species of bird, which is also called larus; it is light, and floats on the waves. His statement that it is called by another name larus comes from the Scholiast on Aristophanes, on the Plutus, whose words on the cepphus are: Καλεῖται δὲ κοινῶς λάρος [Kaleitai de koinōs laros]. It is commonly called larus. Accordingly they are joined as synonyms in the proverb Κέπφος λάρος [Kepphos laros] in Erasmus [=Desiderius Erasmus, Adagia] and others. And in Hesychius, Κὴξ [Kēx] for Apion is ὁ λάρος [ho laros], but others render it κέπφον [kephon], III, 3 and others again ἐφυϊάν [ephyian]; read αἰθυϊὰν [aithyian], that is, diver. Yet you may gather that the gull and the cepphus differ from these words of Aristotle, History, book 8, chapter 3: Περὶ δὲ τὴν θάλατταν καὶ ἀλκύων, καὶ κήρυλος, etc. Ἔτι δὲ ὁ λάρος ὁ λευκὸς, καὶ κέπφος, καὶ χαράδριος [Peri de tēn thalattan kai alkyōn, kai kērylos, etc. Eti de ho laros ho leukos, kai kepphos, kai charadrios]; But about the sea there are also the alcyon and the cerylus, etc. Also the white gull, and the cepphus, and the charadrius. The cepphus and the gull, then, are not entirely the same, but very similar birds. Hence the Scholiast on Nicander, on the Alexipharmaca: Ὁ δὲ κέπφος θαλάσσιόν ἐστι ὄρνεον παραπλήσιον λάρῳ [Ho de kepphos thalassion esti orneon paraplēsion larō]. Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium] thinks they are birds of the same genus, or that the cepphus is a species of gull. However the matter stands, the name שחף suits both the gull and the cepphus exceedingly well, since both birds are described as almost devoid of flesh, as if consumed by wasting R1.


A ceppho factum verbum κεπφοῦσθαι non solum efferri significat, et le-viter circumagi cepphi instar ad omnem ventum, sed et facile decipi et inescari. Sic Prov. VII, 22. de incauto juvene, quem lenociniis suis demulsit adultera: Ὁ δὲ ἐπηκολούθησεν αὐτῇ κεπφωθείς· Eam autem ille sequitur, cepphi instar, facile actus, aut facile deceptus. Hesychius, Κεπφωθείς· ἐπαρθεὶς, ἀπατη- col. 265 θείς· Elatus, deceptus. Et rursus post Κέφαλον· Κεπφωθεὶς, καταγελα-σθείς· εἴρηται δὲ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀλόγου δίκην ἀνοήτως συνεπαγομένων· Derisus: Dicitur autem de iis, qui, bruti instar, stulte ducuntur. Suidas, Κεπφωθείς· ἐπαρ-θεὶς, ἐρεθισθεὶς, ὀξέως ἐλαυνόμενος· Elatus, concitatus, celeriter actus. Quae sunt ejusdem loci varia interpretamenta. Sed ἀπατηθεὶς maxime placet. 1. Quia quo loco diximus κεπφωθεὶς est pro Hebraeo פתאים, pro quo Graeci legerunt פתאים, id est, simplices, εὐαπάτητοι. Fit enim a verbo פתה, quod plerumque reddunt ἀπατᾷν. 2. Quia cepphus est avis deceptu facilis, quamque, spuma oblata, pueri nullo negotio ad se alliciunt, atque injecta manu capiunt. Unde est, quod κέπφος a Graecis pro stulto passim usurpatur. Ita proverbium, Κέπφος λάρος, vecordem ferit, qui cujusvis rei cupiditate deceptus capitur. Et apud Aristophanem in Pace,

The verb κεπφοῦσθαι [kepphousthai], formed from cepphus, means not only to be carried away and to be lightly driven about by every wind like a cepphus, but also to be easily deceived and lured with bait. So in Prov. VII, 22, of the heedless young man whom the adulteress has charmed with her enticements: Ὁ δὲ ἐπηκολούθησεν αὐτῇ κεπφωθείς [Ho de epēkolouthēsen autē kepphōtheis]; But he follows her, like a cepphus, easily driven, or easily deceived. Hesychius: Κεπφωθείς· ἐπαρθεὶς, ἀπατηθείς [Kepphōtheis; epartheis, apatētheis]; col. 265 Carried away, deceived. And again, after Κέφαλον [Kephalon]: Κεπφωθεὶς, καταγελασθείς· εἴρηται δὲ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀλόγου δίκην ἀνοήτως συνεπαγομένων [Kepphōtheis, katagelastheis; eirētai de epi tōn alogou dikēn anoētōs synepagomenōn]; Mocked: it is said of those who, like a brute beast, are foolishly led along. Suidas: Κεπφωθείς· ἐπαρθεὶς, ἐρεθισθεὶς, ὀξέως ἐλαυνόμενος [Kepphōtheis; epartheis, erethistheis, oxeōs elaunomenos]; Carried away, stirred up, swiftly driven. These are various interpretations of the same passage. But ἀπατηθεὶς [apatētheis] pleases me most. 1. Because in the passage we have cited κεπφωθεὶς [kepphōtheis] stands for the Hebrew פתאים, for which the Greeks read פתאים, that is, simple ones, εὐαπάτητοι [euapatētoi]. For it comes from the verb פתה, which they usually render ἀπατᾷν [apatan]. 2. Because the cepphus is a bird easily deceived, which boys, by offering it foam, draw to themselves without any trouble and catch by laying hands on it. Hence κέπφος [kepphos] is commonly used by the Greeks for a fool. Thus the proverb Κέπφος λάρος [Kepphos laros] strikes at the senseless man who is deceived by desire for anything and is caught. And in Aristophanes, in the Peace,


Καὶ κέπφοι τρήρωνες ἀλωπεκίδεσσι πέπεισθε, III, 4 Et cepphi, et columbae (id est, stulti et simplices) vulpeculis fiditis. Et rursus in Pluto, Ὦ κέπφε, O cepphe, id est, O faute. Proinde ad priorem locum Scholiastes, Εὔηθες ζῶον ὁ κέπφος, Fatuum est animal cepphus. Et ad posteriorem, Ὄρνεον γὰρ ἄφρον, ὅπερ φιλεῖ ἀφρὸν θαλάττιον ἐσθίειν. Τοῦτο βουλό-μενοι οἱ τῶν ἁλιέων παῖδες χειρώσασθαι, ῥίπτουσι τὸ πρῶτον πόῤῥωθεν ἀφρὸν, εἶτα ἐγγύτατα, εἶτα φέρουσιν τοῦτο ἐν ταῖς χερσὶν, καὶ οὕτω κατὰ μικρὸν ἀπατῶντες, εὐχερῶς ἀγρεύουσι τοῦτο ἐμπεσὸν εἰς τὰς χεῖρας αὐτῶν· εἴλη-πται οὖν εἰς παροιμίαν ἐπὶ τῶν ἀλογίστων ἀνδρῶν, καὶ ἀνοήτων. Stulta enim est avis, quae marinae spumae esu delectatur. Cum igitur hanc capere volunt piscatorum filii, primo spumam eminus jaciunt, deinde propius propiusque, postea manibus ferunt, atque ita paullatim inescantes, in manus suas incidentem facile capiunt. Cessit itaque in proverbium in vecordes homines, atque dementes. Quod ipsum de hac ave tradiderant antiquiores. Sic Philosophus Historiae animalium libri noni capite trigesimo quinto, Οἱ δὲ κέπφοι ἁλίσκονται τῷ ἀφρῷ, κόπτου-σι γὰρ αὐτόν· διὸ προσραίνοντες θηρεύουσιν. Cepphi autem spuma capiuntur; eam enim appetunt: proinde spuma injecta eos venantur. Et Nicander Alexipharmacωn versu 165.

Καὶ κέπφοι τρήρωνες ἀλωπεκίδεσσι πέπεισθε [Kai kepphoi trērōnes alōpekidessi pepeisthe], III, 4 And you cepphi and doves (that is, fools and simpletons) trust little foxes. And again in the Plutus, Ὦ κέπφε [Ō kepphe], O cepphus, that is, O fool. Accordingly, on the former passage the Scholiast says: Εὔηθες ζῶον ὁ κέπφος [Euēthes zōon ho kepphos], The cepphus is a foolish animal. And on the latter: Ὄρνεον γὰρ ἄφρον, ὅπερ φιλεῖ ἀφρὸν θαλάττιον ἐσθίειν. Τοῦτο βουλόμενοι οἱ τῶν ἁλιέων παῖδες χειρώσασθαι, ῥίπτουσι τὸ πρῶτον πόῤῥωθεν ἀφρὸν, εἶτα ἐγγύτατα, εἶτα φέρουσιν τοῦτο ἐν ταῖς χερσὶν, καὶ οὕτω κατὰ μικρὸν ἀπατῶντες, εὐχερῶς ἀγρεύουσι τοῦτο ἐμπεσὸν εἰς τὰς χεῖρας αὐτῶν· εἴληπται οὖν εἰς παροιμίαν ἐπὶ τῶν ἀλογίστων ἀνδρῶν, καὶ ἀνοήτων [Orneon gar aphron, hoper philei aphron thalattion esthiein. Touto boulomenoi hoi tōn halieōn paides cheirōsasthai, rhiptousi to prōton porrhōthen aphron, eita engytata, eita pherousin touto en tais chersin, kai houtō kata mikron apatōntes, eucherōs agreuousi touto empeson eis tas cheiras autōn; eilēptai oun eis paroimian epi tōn alogistōn andrōn, kai anoētōn]. For it is a foolish bird, which delights in eating sea foam. So when the fishermen's sons wish to catch it, they first throw foam from a distance, then nearer and nearer, afterwards they carry it in their hands, and so, luring it little by little, they easily catch it as it falls into their hands. Hence it has become a proverb for senseless and witless men. The older writers had reported this very thing about this bird. So the Philosopher, History of Animals, book 9, chapter 35: Οἱ δὲ κέπφοι ἁλίσκονται τῷ ἀφρῷ, κόπτουσι γὰρ αὐτόν· διὸ προσραίνοντες θηρεύουσιν [Hoi de kepphoi haliskontai tō aphrō, koptousi gar auton; dio prosrainontes thēreuousin]. The cepphi are caught with foam, for they go after it; therefore they hunt them by throwing foam at them. And Nicander, Alexipharmaca, verse 165:


Ἀφρὸν ἐπεγκεράσοιο θοοῦ δορπήϊα κέπφου.
Τῷ γὰρ δὴ ζωήν τε σαοῖ, καὶ πότμον ἐπισπεῖ.
Εὖτε δόλοις νήχοντα κακοφθόρα τέκν᾽ ἁλιήων
Οἰωνὸν χραίνωσιν. ὁ δ᾽ ἐς χέρας ἔμπεσε παίδων,
Θηρεύων ἀφροῖο νέην κλύδα λευκαίνουσαν.

Ἀφρὸν ἐπεγκεράσοιο θοοῦ δορπήϊα κέπφου. Τῷ γὰρ δὴ ζωήν τε σαοῖ, καὶ πότμον ἐπισπεῖ. Εὖτε δόλοις νήχοντα κακοφθόρα τέκν᾽ ἁλιήων Οἰωνὸν χραίνωσιν. ὁ δ᾽ ἐς χέρας ἔμπεσε παίδων, Θηρεύων ἀφροῖο νέην κλύδα λευκαίνουσαν. [Aphron epenkerasoio thoou dorpēia kepphou. Tō gar dē zōēn te saoi, kai potmon epispei. Eute dolois nēchonta kakophthora tekn᾽ haliēōn Oiōnon chrainōsin. ho d᾽ es cheras empese paidōn, Thēreuōn aphroio neēn klyda leukainousan.]


Spumam admisce citi cepphi pabulum. Illo enim et vitam servat, et fatum accersit: cum natantem avem ea dolose inquinant perniciosi piscatorum filii. Is autem in puerorum manus incidit, persequens spumae recentem adspersionem albicantem. Plura vide apud Nicandri Scholiastem, Hesychium, Suidam, Etymologum (2) et alios, quos exscribere jam non vacat. Neque vero est opus, cum, quae jam dicta sunt, nude repetant. Tantum monebo, in his Hesychii et Suidae Κεπφωθεὶς· ἐπαρθεὶς, pro ἐπαρθεὶς legendum esse ἐπαχθεὶς; Ipso enim Hesychio auctore Κεπφωθεὶς dicitur ἐπὶ τῶν ἀλόγου δίκην ἀνοήτως συνεπαγομένων de iis, qui bruti ad instar stulte ducuntur.

Mix in foam, the food of the swift cepphus. For by it the bird both preserves its life and brings on its doom, when the destructive sons of fishermen craftily spatter the swimming bird with it. And it falls into the boys' hands, chasing the fresh white spray of foam. See more in the Scholiast on Nicander, Hesychius, Suidas, the Etymologicum R2 and others, whom I have no time to copy out now. Nor is there need, since they merely repeat what has already been said. I will only note that in these words of Hesychius and Suidas, Κεπφωθεὶς· ἐπαρθεὶς [Kepphōtheis; epartheis], one should read ἐπαχθεὶς [epachtheis] instead of ἐπαρθεὶς [epartheis]. For on Hesychius's own authority Κεπφωθεὶς [Kepphōtheis] is said ἐπὶ τῶν ἀλόγου δίκην ἀνοήτως συνεπαγομένων [epi tōn alogou dikēn anoētōs synepagomenōn], of those who are foolishly led along like a brute beast.


(1) Rosenmüller, III, 3 Cepphum esse avem e genere Linnaeano Procellariarum (der Sturmvoegel), docuit I. G. SCHNEIDER in Promtuario Lipsiensi Historiae naturalis (Leipziger Magazin zur Naturgeschichte und Oeconomie) anni 1786. pag. 501 seqq. Hebraeorum vero שחף eandem esse avem, ego neque affirmem, neque negem, quum praeter nomen in codice Hebraeo de eo animali nil occurrat, Bocharti autem conjectura nullo alio fundamento nitatur, nisi etymologia vocis שחף: quo quidem ratiocinandi modo, ubi de animalium nominibus quaestio agitur, nil esse incertius, jam saepius vidimus.

R1 Rosenmüller, III, 3 That the cepphus is a bird of the Linnaean genus Procellaria (der Sturmvoegel [the storm-birds]) was shown by J. G. SCHNEIDER in the Leipzig Repository of Natural History (Leipziger Magazin zur Naturgeschichte und Oeconomie) for the year 1786, p. 501 ff. But whether the שחף of the Hebrews is the same bird I would neither affirm nor deny, since apart from the name nothing about this animal occurs in the Hebrew text, and Bochart's conjecture rests on no other foundation than the etymology of the word שחף. We have already seen quite often that, where the question concerns the names of animals, nothing is more uncertain than this way of reasoning.


(2) Rosenmüller, III, 4 Et apud OPPIANUM in Ἰξευτικ. Lib. II. c. 10. p. 189. ed. Schneider.

R2 Rosenmüller, III, 4 And in OPPIAN, Ἰξευτικ. [Ixeutik.] book 2, ch. 10, p. 189, ed. Schneider.


Part 2, Book 2, chapter 19: The hawk
