III, 40 col. 292 CAP. XXIV.

III, 40 col. 292 CHAPTER XXIV.


Probatur, קאת kaath esse Pelicanum, et Ardeam, praecipue stellarem, id est, Butaurum.

It is proved that קאת kaath is the pelican and the heron, especially the starred heron, that is, the bittern.


Graecis hic, et Psalmi centesimi primi (Hebraeis centesimi secundi) versu septimo קאת kaath est pelicanus. Hieronymo etiam in loco Psalmi, quamvis alibi reddat onocrotalum. Onkelos et Samaritanus vocem Hebraeam retinent. Et pro illa Ionathan et Syrus habent ܩܩܐ kaka; Arabs Erpenianus القوق alkuk, et alter القيق alkik. Neque aliter Talmudici scriptores. Ita Talmud Babylonicum tractatu Cholin cap. 3. fol. 63. a. אמר רב יהודה קאת זו הקוק, Dixit R. Iuda, Kaath est kuk. Ita etiam R. Ismael in Talmude Hierosolymitano. Et pro קוק kuk nonnulli קיק kik scribunt. Proinde in tractatu De Sabbatho cap. 2. fol. 21. a. Rabbi Samuel rogatus, unde sumatur שמן קיק, oleum kik, ita respondet: שאלתי נהו לכל נחותי ימא ואמרו לי עוף אחד יש בכרכי הים וקיק שמו, Illud ipsum quaesivi ab iis omnibus, qui in mare descendunt, qui dixerunt, avem kik nomine reperiri in maritimis oppidis. Et Kimchius in Lexico loca Talmudis sic citat, quasi ubique kik legerit. Verba sunt, ובתלמוד אמר רב יהודה קאת זה הקיק ובתלמוד ירושלמי תני רבי ישמעאל קאת זה הקיק, Et in Talmude dixit Rabbi Iuda, kaath esse kik. Etiam in Hierosolymitano Talmude tradidit Rabbi Ismael, kaath esse kik. Arabes quoque paraphrastas notavimus utroque modo scribere. Tamen apud illos قوق kuk, et قيق kik, multum differunt. Nam قوق kuk est طاير ماي طويل العنق avis aquatica longo collo. Ita definiunt Alcamus et Damir, ex libro, cui titulus العباب Alobab, id est, Universitas. Sed القيق alkik est cornix. Damir ita describit, القيق طاير علي قدر اليمامة واهل الشام يسمونه ابو زريق وهو الوف للناس فيه قبول للتعليم وسرعة ادراك لما يعلم ويحاكي كلما يسمع وقد تقدم الكلام col. 293 عليه في باب الزاي المعجمة Alkik est avis, accedens ad turturis magnitudinem, quae ab incolis Syriae vocatur abu-zarik (id est, pater caesius). Habitat cum hominibus. In ea est doctrinae capacitas et facilitas apprehensionis eorum, quae docentur. Et recitat, quidquid audit. Sed de ea jam actum in capite de Ze. Nempe ad vocem زاغ Zag, quod est cornicis vulgare nomen, quamvis alii picam exponant (1) Cum igitur III, 41 avis קיק kik nomine ab ave קוק kuk ita differat, non debuerunt confundi (2).

For the Greeks, here and in the seventh verse of Psalm 101 (102 for the Hebrews), קאת kaath is the pelican. So too for Jerome in the passage of the Psalm, although elsewhere he renders it onocrotalus. Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] and the Samaritan retain the Hebrew word. In its place Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] and the Syriac have ܩܩܐ [קקא] kaka; Erpenianus [=the Arabic version edited by Thomas Erpenius (Pentateuch 1622; New Testament 1616)] has القوق [al-qūq] alkuk, and the other القيق [al-qīq] alkik. Nor do the Talmudic writers say otherwise. Thus the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Cholin, ch. 3, fol. 63a: אמר רב יהודה קאת זו הקוק, R. Judah said: Kaath is kuk. So also R. Ishmael in the Jerusalem Talmud. And for קוק kuk some write קיק kik. Accordingly, in the tractate On the Sabbath, ch. 2, fol. 21a, Rabbi Samuel, asked where שמן קיק, oil of kik, comes from, answers thus: שאלתי נהו לכל נחותי ימא ואמרו לי עוף אחד יש בכרכי הים וקיק שמו, I asked this very thing of all those who go down to the sea, and they told me that a bird named kik is found in the coastal towns. And Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] in his Lexicon cites the passages of the Talmud as if he had read kik everywhere. His words are: ובתלמוד אמר רב יהודה קאת זה הקיק ובתלמוד ירושלמי תני רבי ישמעאל קאת זה הקיק, And in the Talmud Rabbi Judah said that kaath is kik. Also in the Jerusalem Talmud Rabbi Ishmael taught that kaath is kik. We have noted that the Arabic paraphrasts also write it both ways. Yet among them قوق [qūq] kuk and قيق [qīq] kik differ greatly. For قوق [qūq] kuk is طاير ماي طويل العنق [ṭāyir māʾī ṭawīl al-ʿunuq], a water bird with a long neck. So Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] and Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] define it, from the book entitled العباب [al-ʿUbāb] Alobab, that is, The Universe. But القيق [al-qīq] alkik is the crow. Damir describes it thus: القيق طاير علي قدر اليمامة واهل الشام يسمونه ابو زريق وهو الوف للناس فيه قبول للتعليم وسرعة ادراك لما يعلم ويحاكي كلما يسمع وقد تقدم الكلام col. 293 عليه في باب الزاي المعجمة [al-qīq ṭāyir ʿalī qadr al-yamāma wa-ahl al-Shām yusammūnahu abū zurayq wa-huwa alūf li-l-nās fīhi qabūl li-l-taʿlīm wa-surʿat idrāk li-mā yuʿallam wa-yuḥākī kullamā yasmaʿ wa-qad taqaddama al-kalām ʿalayhi fī bāb al-zāy al-muʿjama] Alkik is a bird approaching the size of a turtledove, which is called by the inhabitants of Syria abu-zarik (that is, the grey-blue father). It lives with people. It has a capacity for learning and ease in grasping what it is taught. And it repeats whatever it hears. But it has already been dealt with in the chapter on Ze. That is, under the word زاغ [zāgh] Zag, which is the common name of the crow, although others explain it as the magpie R1 Since, then, the bird III, 41 named קיק kik differs so from the bird קוק kuk, they ought not to have been confused R2.


Sed et graviter falluntur ii Talmudicorum, qui שמן קיק, oleum kik volunt ab ave sumi, cum sit κίκινον ἔλαιον, id est, oleum, ex ejus plantae granis expressum, quam Aegyptii KIKI` vocabant. Hujus meminerunt multi veteres. Sic Herodotus libri primi capite nonagesimo secundo, palustres Aegyptios uti dicit unguento ἀπὸ τῶν σιλλικυπρίων τοῦ καρποῦ, τὸ καλεῦσι μὲν Αἰγύπτιοι KIKI`, ex fructu syllicypriorum, quod Aegyptii KIKI appellant. Et Strabo libro decimo septimo in Aegypti descriptione, Καὶ τὸ KIKKI` (lege KIKI`) καρπός τις σπειρόμενος ἐν ἀρούραις, ἐξ οὗ ἔλαιον ἀποθλίβεται. Et KIKI fructus quidam est, ex quo, in arvis sato, oleum exprimitur. Et Dioscorides libro quarto: KIKI`, ἢ κρότων, etc. ἐξ οὗ ἀποθλίβεται τὸ λεγόμενον κίκινον ἔλαιον. Et Plinius libri decimi quinti capite septimo, Fit oleum et e CICI arbore, in Aegypto copiosa. Hinc Hesychius, Κίκη· φυτόν· sed rescribendum Κικί. Atque id ipsum est Ionae קיקיון kikajon; et Arabum الخروع elcheroa. Quod jam ante annos fere mille trecentos ab Hieronymo est observatum. Pro cucurbita, sive hedera (inquit in Ionam) in Hebraeo legimus קיקיון: quae etiam lingua Syra et Punica elkeroa dicitur. Itaque in Lexico Coptico a) KOYKI` kuki vox III, 42 Aegyptia pro qua scripserim KIKI`) Arabice redditur حب الخروع granum elcheroa, vel alcheroa. Et in Abenbitare capite خروع cheroa, Dioscoridis verba de κικὶ, ἐξ οὗ ἀποθλίβεται τὸ λεγόμενον κίκινον ἔλαιον, Arabice ita redduntur, ومنها يتعصر الدهن المسمي قيقي وهو دهن الخروع Et inde exprimitur oleum, quod vocant oleum KIKI, quod est oleum ALCHEROA. Quin etiam e Talmudicis sunt, quibus kik, unde oleum, est idem, quod kikajon. Talmud ubi supra, ריש לקיש אמר קיקיון דיונה אמר רבה בר בר חנה לדידי חזי לי קיקיון דיונה ולצלוליבה דמי, Dominus Lakis dixit, Est kikajon Ionae. Dixit Rabba Bar, Annae filius, Me quod atti- net, videtur mihi esse Ionae kikajon, quae planta est selulibae similis. Imo eadem, si selulibae vere sit Arabum الخروع alcheroa, ut habetur in Responsionibus Geonim, id est, illustrium doctorum, ubi seluliba definitur, אילן סרק יש במקומינו ועושה גרעינים ועושין מהן שמן ומין סממנין וכל מי שיש בו צנה הרבה שותה ממנו ושמו בלשון ערבי אלכרו״ע ושמנו קורין דהן כרוע, Arbor sterilis in terris nostris proveniens, grana proferens, ex quibus fit oleum, et ru- bri coloris species. Et quisquis gravi frigore corripitur, ex hoc oleo bibit. Arabice autem vocatur alcheroa, et oleum ejus oleum cheroa. Ita citat Baal Aruch. Sed in Kimchii Commentariis, ubi profertur hic idem locus, nusquam compa- col. 294 rent verba ומין סממנין, et rubri coloris species. Itaque vel alicunde addita, vel corrupta fuisse suspicor, et pro iis legendum ומין שמשומין, et sesamorum species: ut seliluba, vel alcheroa, significetur esse inter sesami species, in qua sententia fuere nonnulli veterum. Plinius libri decimi quinti capite septimo, ubi de oleo factitio; Proximum fit e CICI arbore in Aegypto copiosa: alii crotonem, alii tri- xim (vel sili potius, ut legi vult Salmasius in Solinum), alii sesamum sylvestre appellant. Auctarium ad Dioscoridem, Κικὶ, ἢ κρότων, οἱ δὲ σήσαμον ἄγριον. Arabs Pandectarius, CICI Dioscoridis, aut sesamus agrestis, etc. kerva Arabice Notandum etiam, in Herodoto vocari τὰ σιλλικύπρια, in Auctario Dioscoridis σεσελὶ κύπριον, et in Plinio sili, quae voces videntur alludere ad barbarum se- luliba (3). Sed haec obiter; jam ad rem.

But those Talmudists are also gravely mistaken who will have שמן קיק, oleum kik [kik oil], taken from a bird, since it is κίκινον ἔλαιον [kikinon elaion], that is, oil pressed from the seeds of the plant which the Egyptians called KIKI` [kiki]. Many ancient writers mention it. Thus Herodotus, book 1, chapter 92, says that the marsh-dwelling Egyptians use an ointment ἀπὸ τῶν σιλλικυπρίων τοῦ καρποῦ, τὸ καλεῦσι μὲν Αἰγύπτιοι KIKI` [apo tōn sillikypriōn tou karpou, to kaleusi men Aigyptioi kiki], from the fruit of the syllicyprium, which the Egyptians call KIKI. And Strabo, book 17, in his description of Egypt: Καὶ τὸ KIKKI` (read KIKI`) καρπός τις σπειρόμενος ἐν ἀρούραις, ἐξ οὗ ἔλαιον ἀποθλίβεται [Kai to kikki … karpos tis speiromenos en arourais, ex hou elaion apothlibetai]. And KIKI is a certain fruit, sown in the fields, from which oil is pressed. And Dioscorides, book 4: KIKI`, ἢ κρότων [kiki, ē krotōn], etc. ἐξ οὗ ἀποθλίβεται τὸ λεγόμενον κίκινον ἔλαιον [ex hou apothlibetai to legomenon kikinon elaion]. And Pliny, book 15, chapter 7: Oil is also made from the CICI tree, abundant in Egypt. Hence Hesychius: Κίκη· φυτόν [Kikē· phyton]; but it should be corrected to Κικί [Kiki]. And this is the very kikajon קיקיון of Jonah, and the elcheroa الخروع [al-kharwaʿ] of the Arabs. This was already observed by Jerome nearly thirteen hundred years ago. For the gourd, or ivy (he says on Jonah) we read in the Hebrew קיקיון, which in the Syriac and Punic language is also called elkeroa. Accordingly, in the Coptic Lexicon a) the Egyptian word KOYKI` [kouki] kuki III, 42 (for which I would write KIKI` [kiki]) is rendered in Arabic حب الخروع [ḥabb al-kharwaʿ], the seed of elcheroa or alcheroa. And in Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār], in the chapter خروع [kharwaʿ] cheroa, the words of Dioscorides on κικὶ [kiki], ἐξ οὗ ἀποθλίβεται τὸ λεγόμενον κίκινον ἔλαιον [ex hou apothlibetai to legomenon kikinon elaion], are rendered in Arabic thus: ومنها يتعصر الدهن المسمي قيقي وهو دهن الخروع [wa-minhā yutaʿaṣṣar al-duhn al-musammī qīqī wa-huwa duhn al-kharwaʿ], And from it is pressed the oil which they call the oil KIKI, which is the oil ALCHEROA. Indeed there are even some among the Talmudists for whom kik, from which the oil comes, is the same as kikajon. The Talmud, in the place cited above: ריש לקיש אמר קיקיון דיונה אמר רבה בר בר חנה לדידי חזי לי קיקיון דיונה ולצלוליבה דמי, Resh Lakish said: It is the kikajon of Jonah. Rabba Bar son of Hana said: As for me, I have seen the kikajon of Jonah, and it is a plant resembling the selulibah. Indeed it is the same, if selulibah is truly the alcheroa الخروع [al-kharwaʿ] of the Arabs, as is found in the Responsa of the Geonim, that is, of the illustrious doctors, where seluliba is defined: אילן סרק יש במקומינו ועושה גרעינים ועושין מהן שמן ומין סממנין וכל מי שיש בו צנה הרבה שותה ממנו ושמו בלשון ערבי אלכרו״ע ושמנו קורין דהן כרוע, A barren tree growing in our lands, bearing seeds from which oil is made, and a kind of red colouring. And whoever is seized by a severe chill drinks of this oil. In Arabic it is called alcheroa, and its oil the oil cheroa. So Baal Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome] [=Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome, the ʿArukh] cites it. But in Kimchi's Commentaries, where this same passage is quoted, the words ומין סממנין, and a kind of red colouring, appear nowhere. col. 294 I therefore suspect that they were either added from elsewhere or corrupted, and that in their place we should read ומין שמשומין, and a kind of sesame, so that seliluba, or alcheroa, is said to be among the kinds of sesame, an opinion held by some of the ancients. Pliny, book 15, chapter 7, on manufactured oil: Next is that made from the CICI tree, abundant in Egypt; some call it croton, others trixis (or rather sili, as Salmasius [=Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), Plinianae exercitationes] on Solinus would have it read), others wild sesame. The Supplement to Dioscorides: Κικὶ, ἢ κρότων, οἱ δὲ σήσαμον ἄγριον [Kiki, ē krotōn, hoi de sēsamon agrion]. The Arabic Pandectarius: CICI of Dioscorides, or wild sesame, etc., kerva in Arabic. It should also be noted that in Herodotus it is called τὰ σιλλικύπρια [ta sillikypria], in the Supplement to Dioscorides σεσελὶ κύπριον [seseli kyprion], and in Pliny sili, words which seem to allude to the barbarian seluliba R3. But this in passing; now to the matter at hand.


III, 43 Hebraeum קאת kaath tam Arabes, quam Talmudici nos docuere idem esse, quod קוק huk et kuk avem esse aquaticam, et longo collo. Sed, cum hoc non sufficiat, quia multae sunt aves aquaticae, et longo collo, Graeci et Hieronymus pelicanum nobis designant: quam versionem ut verissimam amplector libens. Nam eo nos deducit origo vocis, quae palam orta est a Verbo קאה kaah, id est, vomere. Hinc Baal Hatturim, הקאת דרכו להקיא מאכלו, Kaath solet evomere cibum suum. Et, ne putetur, obstare Thau finale, id Rabbi Ionas docet esse Nominis formativum, et veram Radicem esse קאה kaah. Et Kimchius poetam citat, qui in Plurali dicit קאות kaoth. Itaque ut a פרה fit פרת, pro Euphrate, et שחת, fossa, a שחה, ita קאת, pelicanus, a קאה (4). Et cur a vomitu dicatur, iis non est obscurum, qui pelicanum sciunt conchas jam absorptas revomere, postquam calore ventris apertae sunt, ut ex iis esculenta legat. Quod veteres scriptores tanto consensu asserunt, ut res non possit in dubium revocari. Aristoteles Historiae libri noni capite decimo, Οἱ δὲ πελεκᾶνες, οἱ ἐν τοῖς ποτα-μοῖς γινόμενοι, καταπίνουσι τὰς μεγάλας κόγχας καὶ λείας· ὅταν δὲ ἐν τῷ πρὸ τῆς κοιλίας τόπῳ πέψωσιν, ἐξεμοῦσιν, ἵνα χασκουσῶν τὰ κρέα ἐξαφοῦντες ἐσθίωσι. Pelicani fluviatiles magnas levesque conchas deglutiunt, et in stomacho coctas evomunt, ut ex hiantibus carnes ablatas comedant. Et in libro Mirabilium [c. 13.], Φασὶ τοὺς πελεκᾶνας τὰς ἐν τοῖς ποταμοῖς γενομένας κόγχας ὀρύτ-τοντας κατεσθίειν· ἔπειτα, ὅταν πλῆθος εἰσφορήσωσιν αὐτῶν, ἐξεμεῖν, εἶθ᾽ οὕτως τὰ μὲν κρέα ἐσθίειν τῶν κογχῶν, τῶν δὲ ὀστράκων μὴ ἅπτεσθαι. Pelica- nos conchas, ex amnibus effossas, vorare ajunt, horumque copiam ingestam mox evo- mere, ut sic, ad esum lectis carnibus, a testis abstineant. Antigonus Carystius Histo- ria quadragesima septima, Τοὺς δὲ πελεκᾶνας τὰς θηλείας κόγχας καταπίνειν ἱστορεῖ· ἔπειτα ὀλίγας κατασχόντας ἐν τῷ ἄνω τῆς κοιλίας ἐξεμεῖν κεχηνυίας· εἶτα οὕτω τὰ κρέα ἐξαφοῦντας ἐσθίειν. Quae triplici mendo laborant: nam, pro τὰς θηλείας κόγχας, foeminas conchas, lege τὰς λείας κόγχας, leves conchas, ut in Aristotele; et pro ἱστορεῖ narrat, ἱστορεῖται narratur; et pro ὀλίγας κατα-σχόντας, cum parvas retinuerunt, ὀλίγον κατασχόντας, cum parum retinuerunt. Ac proinde sic vertendum, Pelicanos autem leves conchas deglutire narratur; deinde, III, 44 cum in summo ventriculo parum retinuerunt, dehiscentes evomere, atque ita carnes exemptas comedere. Plinius libri decimi capite quadragesimo, Eadem, cum devora- tis se implevit conchis, calore ventris coctas evomit, atque ita ex iis esculenta legit, testas excernens. Aelianus Historiae animalium libri tertii capite vigesimo, Οἱ πελεκᾶνες, ἐν τοῖς ποταμοῖς κόγχας περιχαίνοντες· εἶτα καταπίνουσιν· ἔν-δον δὲ καὶ ἐν μυχῷ τῆς γαστρὸς ὑποθάλψαντες ἀνεμοῦσιν, καὶ τὰ μὲν ὀστράκια ἐκ τῆς ἀλέας διέστη ὡσπεροῦν τῶν ἑφθῶν. οἱ δὲ ἐξορύττουσι τὰ κρέα, καὶ ἔχουσι δεῖπνον. Plateae fluviatilibus conchis inhiant, atque eas absorbent; et in imo sto- macho calefactas revomunt. Et ex testis alvi calore diductis, ut quae coctae sunt, carnes in cibum eruunt. Quae fere eadem in Apostolio Centuriae 15. Proverbio 93. Eustathius in Hexaëmeron, postquam conchas, ab iis deglutitas, calore faucium laxari dixit, ἐξεμέσαντες οὖν αὐτὰς, inquit, εὐμαρῶς τὸ ἐδώδιμον αὐτῶν col. 295 κατεσθίουσιν, iis evomitis, quod est esculentum facile comedunt. Phile De ani- malibus capite octavo,

III, 43 Both the Arabs and the Talmudists have taught us that the Hebrew קאת kaath is the same as קוק huk and kuk, a water bird with a long neck. But since this is not enough, because there are many water birds with long necks, the Greeks and Jerome point us to the pelican; and I gladly embrace this rendering as the truest. For the origin of the word leads us to it, which plainly derives from the verb קאה kaah, that is, to vomit. Hence Baal Hatturim [=Jacob ben Asher (d. 1343), commentary on the Torah]: הקאת דרכו להקיא מאכלו, "the kaath is accustomed to vomit up its food." And lest the final Tav be thought an obstacle, Rabbi Jonah teaches that it is a formative of the noun, and that the true root is קאה kaah. And Kimchi cites a poet who says קאות kaoth in the plural. So, just as from פרה comes פרת for the Euphrates, and שחת, pit, from שחה, so קאת, pelican, comes from קאה R4. And why it is named from vomiting is not obscure to those who know that the pelican brings back up shells it has already swallowed, after they have been opened by the heat of its belly, so as to pick out the edible parts from them. The ancient writers assert this with such agreement that the matter cannot be called into doubt. Aristotle, History, book 9, chapter 10: Οἱ δὲ πελεκᾶνες, οἱ ἐν τοῖς ποταμοῖς γινόμενοι, καταπίνουσι τὰς μεγάλας κόγχας καὶ λείας· ὅταν δὲ ἐν τῷ πρὸ τῆς κοιλίας τόπῳ πέψωσιν, ἐξεμοῦσιν, ἵνα χασκουσῶν τὰ κρέα ἐξαφοῦντες ἐσθίωσι. [Hoi de pelekanes, hoi en tois potamois ginomenoi, katapinousi tas megalas konchas kai leias; hotan de en tō pro tēs koilias topō pepsōsin, exemousin, hina chaskousōn ta krea exaphountes esthiōsi.] "River pelicans swallow large smooth shells, and when these have been cooked in the stomach they vomit them up, so as to take the flesh out of them as they gape and eat it." And in the book of Marvels [ch. 13]: Φασὶ τοὺς πελεκᾶνας τὰς ἐν τοῖς ποταμοῖς γενομένας κόγχας ὀρύττοντας κατεσθίειν· ἔπειτα, ὅταν πλῆθος εἰσφορήσωσιν αὐτῶν, ἐξεμεῖν, εἶθ᾽ οὕτως τὰ μὲν κρέα ἐσθίειν τῶν κογχῶν, τῶν δὲ ὀστράκων μὴ ἅπτεσθαι. [Phasi tous pelekanas tas en tois potamois genomenas konchas oryttontas katesthiein; epeita, hotan plēthos eisphorēsōsin autōn, exemein, eith' houtōs ta men krea esthiein tōn konchōn, tōn de ostrakōn mē haptesthai.] "They say that pelicans devour shells dug out of the rivers, and, having taken in a quantity of them, soon vomit them up, so that they pick out the flesh to eat and leave the shells alone." Antigonus of Carystus, Story 47: Τοὺς δὲ πελεκᾶνας τὰς θηλείας κόγχας καταπίνειν ἱστορεῖ· ἔπειτα ὀλίγας κατασχόντας ἐν τῷ ἄνω τῆς κοιλίας ἐξεμεῖν κεχηνυίας· εἶτα οὕτω τὰ κρέα ἐξαφοῦντας ἐσθίειν. [Tous de pelekanas tas thēleias konchas katapinein historei; epeita oligas kataschontas en tō anō tēs koilias exemein kechēnuias; eita houtō ta krea exaphountas esthiein.] This suffers from three errors: for τὰς θηλείας κόγχας [tas thēleias konchas], female shells, read τὰς λείας κόγχας [tas leias konchas], smooth shells, as in Aristotle; for ἱστορεῖ [historei], he relates, read ἱστορεῖται [historeitai], it is related; and for ὀλίγας κατασχόντας [oligas kataschontas], having retained small ones, read ὀλίγον κατασχόντας [oligon kataschontas], having retained them a little while. It should therefore be translated thus: "It is related that pelicans swallow smooth shells; then, III, 44 after retaining them a little while in the top of the stomach, they vomit them up gaping, and so take out the flesh and eat it." Pliny, book 10, chapter 40: "The same bird, when it has filled itself with swallowed shells, vomits them up cooked by the heat of its belly, and so picks out the edible parts from them, rejecting the shells." Aelian, History of Animals, book 3, chapter 20: Οἱ πελεκᾶνες, ἐν τοῖς ποταμοῖς κόγχας περιχαίνοντες· εἶτα καταπίνουσιν· ἔνδον δὲ καὶ ἐν μυχῷ τῆς γαστρὸς ὑποθάλψαντες ἀνεμοῦσιν, καὶ τὰ μὲν ὀστράκια ἐκ τῆς ἀλέας διέστη ὡσπεροῦν τῶν ἑφθῶν. οἱ δὲ ἐξορύττουσι τὰ κρέα, καὶ ἔχουσι δεῖπνον. [Hoi pelekanes, en tois potamois konchas perichainontes; eita katapinousin; endon de kai en mychō tēs gastros hypothalpsantes anemousin, kai ta men ostrakia ek tēs aleas diestē hōsperoun tōn hephthōn. hoi de exoryttousi ta krea, kai echousi deipnon.] "Spoonbills gape after river shells and swallow them; and having warmed them in the depth of the stomach they vomit them up. And from the shells, forced apart by the heat of the belly, as if they had been cooked, they dig out the flesh for food." Almost the same is found in Apostolius, Century 15, Proverb 93. Eustathius on the Hexaemeron, after saying that the shells they swallow are loosened by the heat of the throat, says: ἐξεμέσαντες οὖν αὐτὰς εὐμαρῶς τὸ ἐδώδιμον αὐτῶν [exemesantes oun autas eumarōs to edōdimon autōn] col. 295 κατεσθίουσιν [katesthiousin], "having vomited them up, they easily eat what is edible." Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)], On Animals, chapter 8:


Κόγχην δὲ πελεκὰν ἐμβαλὼν τοῖς ἐγκάτοις,
Κἀνάπαλιν αὐτὴν ἐξενεγκὼν ὀστράκοις
Τὸ σαρκίον βέβρωκε ληφθὲν εὐστόχως.

Κόγχην δὲ πελεκὰν ἐμβαλὼν τοῖς ἐγκάτοις, Κἀνάπαλιν αὐτὴν ἐξενεγκὼν ὀστράκοις Τὸ σαρκίον βέβρωκε ληφθὲν εὐστόχως. [Konchēn de pelekan embalōn tois enkatois, Kanapalin autēn exenenkōn ostrakois To sarkion bebrōke lēphthen eustochōs.]


Pelicanus, concham, in viscera immissam, rursus revocans, carne testis exempta perite vescitur. Pisidas quoque De mundi opificio testas ab iis demitti dicit in ignem viscerum, cum aliter recludi non possint,

"The pelican, having sent a shell down into its innards and brought it back up again, skilfully feeds on the flesh taken out of the shell." Pisides too, On the Creation of the World, says that they send the shells down into the fire of their innards, since they cannot be opened otherwise:


Λύσιν δὲ πάσχει τῶν πτυχῶν ἡ στεῤῥότης,
Τῇ θερμότητι τῶν ἔσω χαυνουμένη.
Θᾶττον δὲ τὰς πρὶν ἐξεμοῦντες συνδέσεις,
Γυμνῇ διαρπάζουσι τὰς σάρκας μάχῃ,
Τὴν ὀστρακώδη μὴ φορούσας ἀσπίδα.

Λύσιν δὲ πάσχει τῶν πτυχῶν ἡ στεῤῥότης, Τῇ θερμότητι τῶν ἔσω χαυνουμένη. Θᾶττον δὲ τὰς πρὶν ἐξεμοῦντες συνδέσεις, Γυμνῇ διαρπάζουσι τὰς σάρκας μάχῃ, Τὴν ὀστρακώδη μὴ φορούσας ἀσπίδα. [Lysin de paschei tōn ptychōn hē sterrotēs, Tē thermotēti tōn esō chaunoumenē. Thatton de tas prin exemountes syndeseis, Gymnē diarpazousi tas sarkas machē, Tēn ostrakōdē mē phorousas aspida.]


Tum vero solutionem patitur valvarum firmitas, interiore calore laxata. Et mox vomentes quae prius colligata erant, nuda pugna carnes diripiunt, testaceo clypeo non amplius instructas. Fatendum interim, Plutarchum in libro Utra anim. hoc idem ardeis tribuere, cum dicit, artem aperiendi ostrea deberi τοῖς ἐρωδίων σοφίσμασιν· ὅταν γὰρ τὴν κόγχην καταπίῃ μεμυκυῖαν, ἐνοχλούμενος ἐγκαρ-τερεῖ, μέχρις ἂν αἴσθηται μαλασσομένην, καὶ χαλῶσαν ὑπὸ τῆς θερμότητος· τότε δὲ ἐκβαλὼν κεχηνυῖαν, καὶ ἀπεσπασμένην, ἐξεῖλε τὸ ἐδώδιμον, ardea- rum industriae: cum enim clausam testam ardea deglutiit, quamvis eam moleste fe- rat, tamen patitur, donec a calore emollitam et laxatam sentiat; tum vero hian- tem et avulsam ejiciens, ex ea esculentum eximit. Et Aelianus libri tertii capite vigesimo quarto, postquam narravit, ciconias proprios cibos evomitos pullis offerre, si nihil aliud suppetat, quo illos alant, addit, καὶ τοὺς ἐρωδίους ποιεῖν III, 45 ταὐτὸ, καὶ τοὺς πελεκᾶνας μέντοι, ardeas quoque et pelicanos idem facere. Sed quod de pelicanis diximus constanti fama atque omnium sermone est celebratum: cum valde obscurum sit, quod de ardeis et ciconeis scribunt Plutarchus et Aelianus, neque alios habeat auctores, quod meminerim. Quin ardearum nomine pelicanos a Plutarcho intelligi putaverim: quos ardeis multi accensent; quia pelicanus ab ardea solo pene rostro differt, quod in extremo latius habet, et in cochlearis formam (5). Gesnerus, Videtur sane mihi pelecanus noster ardearum generi adnumerandus, a quo non tam alio insigni, quam rostri latitudine, differt. Item, Albertus etiam avem, quam cochleariam vocamus (id est, pelicanum) ardeam albam esse putavit. Turnerus; Albardeolam (id est, albam ardeam) si non vidissem in Italia, Anglorum shovelardam (id est, pelicanum) albardeolam esse judicassem. Bellonio quoque, libri quarti De Avibus capite quinto, Aristotelis λευκερώδιος (id est, ardea alba) avis est, quam a rostri forma vocant, pale poche ou cullier, id est, veterum pelicanum. Plutarchus igitur pari ratione promiscue sumere potuit ardeas et pelicanos. Vel, si verum est, ardeam quoque, pelicani instar, testas evomere (6), ut vult Plutarchus, quidni Hebraeum nomen קאת kaath, a vomitu factum, ardeae cum pelicano potuerit esse commune, cum sint aves congeneres, atque in tam multis similes.

Then the firmness of the valves gives way, loosened by the inner heat. And soon, vomiting up what had previously been bound shut, they tear apart the flesh, no longer protected by its shelly shield, in an unequal fight. It must be admitted, however, that Plutarch, in the book Utra anim., attributes this same thing to herons, when he says that the art of opening oysters is owed τοῖς ἐρωδίων σοφίσμασιν· ὅταν γὰρ τὴν κόγχην καταπίῃ μεμυκυῖαν, ἐνοχλούμενος ἐγκαρτερεῖ, μέχρις ἂν αἴσθηται μαλασσομένην, καὶ χαλῶσαν ὑπὸ τῆς θερμότητος· τότε δὲ ἐκβαλὼν κεχηνυῖαν, καὶ ἀπεσπασμένην, ἐξεῖλε τὸ ἐδώδιμον [tois erōdiōn sophismasin; hotan gar tēn konchēn katapiē memykuian, enochloumenos enkarterei, mechris an aisthētai malassomenēn, kai chalōsan hypo tēs thermotētos; tote de ekbalōn kechēnuian, kai apespasmenēn, exeile to edōdimon], to the ingenuity of herons: for when the heron has swallowed a closed shell, although it finds it troublesome, it nevertheless endures it until it feels it softened and loosened by the heat; then, casting it out gaping and torn open, it takes the edible part out of it. And Aelian, book 3, chapter 24, after relating that storks offer their own food, vomited up, to their young if nothing else is available with which to feed them, adds καὶ τοὺς ἐρωδίους ποιεῖν III, 45 ταὐτὸ, καὶ τοὺς πελεκᾶνας μέντοι [kai tous erōdious poiein tauto, kai tous pelekanas mentoi], that herons too, and pelicans, do the same. But what we have said about pelicans is celebrated by constant report and by everyone's talk, whereas what Plutarch and Aelian write about herons and storks is very obscure, and has no other authorities, as far as I remember. Indeed, I would think that by the name herons Plutarch means pelicans, which many count among the herons, because the pelican differs from the heron almost only in its bill, which it has broader at the tip and in the shape of a spoon R5. Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium]: It certainly seems to me that our pelican should be counted in the heron kind, from which it differs not so much by any other mark as by the breadth of its bill. Likewise: Albertus also thought that the bird which we call the spoonbill (that is, the pelican) was the white heron. Turner [=William Turner, Avium praecipuarum historia (1544)]: If I had not seen the albardeola (that is, the white heron) in Italy, I would have judged the English shovelard (that is, the pelican) to be the albardeola. For Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)] too, book 4 De Avibus, chapter 5, Aristotle's λευκερώδιος [leukerōdios] (that is, white heron) is the bird which from the shape of its bill they call pale poche ou cullier, that is, the pelican of the ancients. Plutarch, therefore, could on the same grounds take herons and pelicans indiscriminately. Or, if it is true that the heron too, like the pelican, vomits up shells R6, as Plutarch holds, why could the Hebrew name קאת kaath, formed from vomiting, not have been common to the heron and the pelican, since they are kindred birds and alike in so many respects?


Quo dato, planiora erunt haec verba Psaltis, Psalm. CII, 7. Propter vocem gemitus mei ossa mea carni adhaeserunt, similis factus sum τῷ kaath deserti: fui instar τοῦ chos solitudinum. In quibus ratione planctuum et gemituum duabus avibus se confert, nempe τῷ kaath, et τῷ chos. Unde has aves colligere est habere aliquid querulum et gemebundum. Atque e multis rationibus, quae nobis pene persuadent, chos esse onocrotalum, haec una fuit, quod onocrotalus avis est horrendae vocis, quaeque hominis graviter dolentis ululatus egregie referat. III, 46 Proinde, ut sibi constet Psaltes, etiam de ave kaath idem esse docendum. Quod difficulter fiet, si kaath praeter pelicanum nihil significet, cum de pelecani voce nihil quidquam reperiatur. At, si nomen kaath sit ardeae cum pe- col. 296 licano commune, quod puto esse vero consentaneum, facile erit se expedire. Ardeae enim est clara vox (7). Homerus clangorem vocat: et Iliad. κ'. de ardea dicit, quam Pallas pro fausto omine Diomedi et Ulyssi misit, noctu ad hostium castra euntibus,

Granting this, these words of the Psalmist, Ps 102:7, will be plainer: Because of the voice of my groaning my bones have cleaved to my flesh; I have become like the kaath of the wilderness; I have been like the chos of the desolate places. In these he compares himself, on account of his laments and groans, to two birds, namely the kaath and the chos. From this one may infer that these birds have something plaintive and groaning about them. And among the many reasons which almost persuade us that the chos is the onocrotalus, this was one: that the onocrotalus is a bird of dreadful voice, which admirably imitates the wailing of a man in grievous pain. III, 46 Accordingly, so that the Psalmist be consistent, the same must be shown of the bird kaath too. This will be difficult if kaath means nothing but the pelican, since nothing whatever is found about the voice of the pelican. But if the name kaath is common to the heron and the pelican, col. 296 which I think agrees with the truth, it will be easy to find a way out. For the heron has a loud voice R7. Homer calls it a clangor, and in Iliad 10 he says of the heron which Pallas sent as a favourable omen to Diomedes and Ulysses as they went by night to the enemy camp:


— — — τοὶ δ' οὐ ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσι
Νύκτα δι' ὀρφναίην, ἀλλὰ κλάγξαντος ἄκουσαν·

— — — τοὶ δ' οὐ ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσι Νύκτα δι' ὀρφναίην, ἀλλὰ κλάγξαντος ἄκουσαν· [— — — toi d' ou idon ophthalmoisi / Nykta di' orphnaiēn, alla klanxantos akousan;]


Hi vero oculis non viderunt noctem per obscuram, sed clangentem audiverunt. Et Philosophus de ardea pella, Historiae libri noni capite primo, Τούτων (ἐρωδίων) ὁ πέλλος χαλεπῶς εὐνάζει τε, καὶ ὀχεύει. κράζει τε γὰρ, καὶ αἷμα, ὥς φα-σιν, ἀφίησιν ἐκ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ὀχεύων, καὶ τίκτει φαυλῶς, ὡς καὶ ὀδυνηρῶς. Quae sic Plinius libri primi capite sexagesimo, Hi in coitu anguntur. Mares quidem cum vociferatu sanguinem ex oculis profundunt: nec minus aegre pariunt gravidae. Sed, quod maxime notandum, ardea asterias, sive stellaris, quae butaurus vulgo dicitur, avis est mugitus tam horribilis, ut hac in parte onocrotalo vix cedat. Quod mirum tacuisse veteres: nisi ad illam referantur haec Plinii libri decimi capite quadragesimo secundo: Est, quae boum mugitus imitatur in agro Arelatensi, taurus appellata. Et auctoris Philomelae,

They did not see it with their eyes through the dark night, but heard it clanging. And the Philosopher, on the ash-coloured heron, History book 9, chapter 1: Τούτων (ἐρωδίων) ὁ πέλλος χαλεπῶς εὐνάζει τε, καὶ ὀχεύει. κράζει τε γὰρ, καὶ αἷμα, ὥς φασιν, ἀφίησιν ἐκ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ὀχεύων, καὶ τίκτει φαυλῶς, ὡς καὶ ὀδυνηρῶς. [Toutōn (erōdiōn) ho pellos chalepōs eunazei te, kai ocheuei. krazei te gar, kai haima, hōs phasin, aphiēsin ek tōn ophthalmōn ocheuōn, kai tiktei phaulōs, hōs kai odynērōs.] Which Pliny, book 1, chapter 60, renders thus: These suffer anguish in coupling. The males indeed shed blood from their eyes with loud cries; nor do the females give birth with less difficulty. But, what is most to be noted, the starry heron, or stellaris, which is commonly called the butaurus [bittern], is a bird whose bellowing is so dreadful that in this respect it scarcely yields to the onocrotalus. It is strange that the ancients were silent about this, unless these words of Pliny, book 10, chapter 42, refer to it: There is one that imitates the lowing of oxen in the territory of Arles, called the bull. And those of the author of the Philomela:


Inque paludiferis butio bubit aquis.

And in the marshy waters the butio booms.


Utut sit, hujus avis boatu nihil notius: tamen in rudiorum gratiam, ecce de eo loca recentiorum! Vincentius in Doctrinali libri 16. cap. 151. Butorius est avis sic dicta a sono vocis, etc. Pro cantu vocem horrificam edit. Nec hoc posse dicitur, nisi caput suum aquis immergat, ut intra se densitas elementi conceptam vocem, instar cujusdam tonitru, sonoram reddat. Albertus, Horribilem sonum tanquam cornu edit, rostrum coeno paludis immittens, ut vox in ipso rumpatur ad modum tonitrui. Tamen ad ripas lacuum et paludum desidet, ubi rostrum in aquas inserens tantos edit bombos, ut ad milliare Italicum facile possit audiri. Bellonius De Avibus libri quarti capite quarto, Cum in stagni aut paludis ripam incidit, rostro in aquam immisso tantum sonum edit, ut nullus bos possit tam contenta voce mugire. Et vicina loca ita personant, ut ad dimidiam leucam audiatur. III, 47 Gesnerus, Rostrum aquae immittere dicitur, et in aquae fundo maxime strepitum ciere, voce contenta instar tauri, quae ad dimidium fere milliare Germanicum (id est, horae unius itinere) exaudiatur. Vir doctus in Epistola ad Gesnerum butorium describens sub onocrotali nomine, Vocem cum emittere vult, rostrum, quod oblongum habet, vel aquis immergit, vel in ripam infigit. Idque facit post solis occasum, et boatum saepe totam noctem continuat. Inde Italis dicitur trombono a voce tubae: et tarabusa, vel terrabusa, quia, terram rostro perforans, sonum edit horribilem. Germanica ejus nomina, indidem sumta, vide apud Gesnerum (8). Itaque Beza, קאת kaath non male pro butauro accipiens, Psaltis verba sic reddidit:

However that may be, nothing is better known than the booming of this bird; yet for the benefit of the less learned, here are passages about it from more recent writers! Vincent, in the Doctrinale, book 16, ch. 151: The butorius is a bird so called from the sound of its voice, etc. Instead of a song it utters a terrifying cry. And it is said to be unable to do this unless it plunges its head into the water, so that the density of the element makes the voice it has formed within resound like a kind of thunder. Albertus: It utters a horrible sound like a horn, thrusting its bill into the mud of the marsh, so that its voice bursts forth in it like thunder. Yet it sits on the banks of lakes and marshes, where, putting its bill into the water, it produces such booms that it can easily be heard a mile away, an Italian mile. Belon, On Birds, book 4, chapter 4: When it comes upon the bank of a pool or marsh, it puts its bill into the water and produces so great a sound that no ox could bellow with so strained a voice. And the neighbouring places resound so that it is heard half a league away. III, 47 Gesner: It is said to put its bill into the water and to raise a very great noise at the bottom of the water, with a strained voice like a bull's, which can be heard almost half a German mile away (that is, an hour's journey). A learned man, in a letter to Gesner describing the butorius under the name onocrotalus, writes: When it wishes to give voice, it either plunges its bill, which is long, into the water or sticks it into the bank. It does this after sunset, and often continues its booming the whole night. Hence the Italians call it trombono, from the sound of a trumpet, and tarabusa or terrabusa, because it pierces the earth with its bill and utters a horrible sound. For its German names, taken from the same source, see Gesner R8. Thus Beza, not wrongly taking קאת kaath for the bittern, rendered the words of the Psalmist thus:


Ie suis au butor semblable
Du desert inhabitable.

Ie suis au butor semblable
Du desert inhabitable.


Quod ideo magis miror; quia neminem habuit, quem sequeretur: nam Graeci, Hieronymus et Pagninus pelicanum reddiderant, Munsterus upupam, Arias cuculum, Castalio onocrotalum, et in Lege ibin, Genevenses cormorant, id est, phalacrocoracem.

This surprises me all the more because he had no one to follow. For the Greeks, Jerome and Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae] had rendered it pelican, Munster hoopoe, Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot] cuckoo, Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)] onocrotalus, and in the Law ibis, and the Genevans cormorant, that is, phalacrocorax.


At, inquies, nomine קאת kaath sive ardeam, aut pelicanum intelligas, quorsum in desertis ponitur, cum dicitur in Psalmo, Similis factus sum כקאת מדבר, τῷ kaath deserti; et Es. XXXIV, 11. Et possidebunt illam kaath et ericius, et Soph. II, 14. Etiam kaath, etiam hericius in tabulatis ejus: in quibus locis agitur de desolatione Idumaeae et Assyriae? An aquaticis avibus, quales sunt pelicanus et ardea, recte assignatur sedes in locis desertis et inaquosis? Quisquis in Psalmos edidit Commentaria sub Hieronymi nomine, respondet, duo genera esse horum volatilium. Quorum unum in col. 297 aquis est, et esca ejus pisces sunt: et unum in solitudine, et esca ejus venenata animalia, hoc est, serpentes, et crocodili, et lacertae. Sed nihil opus est huc confugere, cum non omne desertum sit inaquosum. In Marmaricae intimis, quae regio maxime deserta est, ponuntur a Ptolemaeo Cleartis palus, Lacci palus, Lycomedis palus. In Arabiae desertis Israelitae inciderunt in aquas Mara et fontes Elim, Exod. XV, 23. 27. Falluntur ergo, si qui putant, aquaticis avibus nusquam esse in desertis commodam habitationem (9).

But, you will say, whether by the name קאת kaath you understand the heron or the pelican, why is it placed in deserts, when it is said in the Psalm, I am become like כקאת מדבר, the kaath of the desert; and in Isa 34:11. And the kaath and the hedgehog shall possess it; and in Soph. II, 14. Both the kaath and the hedgehog in its upper storeys, passages that deal with the desolation of Idumaea and Assyria? Is it right to assign to water birds, such as the pelican and the heron, a dwelling in desert and waterless places? Whoever published the Commentaries on the Psalms under the name of Jerome answers that there are two kinds of these birds, of which one lives in col. 297 the waters, and its food is fish; and the other in the wilderness, and its food is venomous animals, that is, serpents, crocodiles and lizards. But there is no need to take refuge in this, since not every desert is waterless. In the interior of Marmarica, a region that is extremely desert, Ptolemy places the marsh of Cleartes, the marsh of Laccus and the marsh of Lycomedes. In the deserts of Arabia the Israelites came upon the waters of Marah and the springs of Elim, Exod 15:23 27. Those, therefore, are mistaken who think that water birds nowhere find a suitable habitation in deserts R9.

Moreover, Moses in Lev 11:18 has already included the crow under the genus of ravens, ערב, so that there was no need to name this bird separately, as Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde] aptly points out, fasc. 3, Chapter 6, p. 58.

Christoph. Doederlein, in his Scholia on Ps 102:7, explains קאת as the viverra Zibetha or wild cat, comparing the Arabic قط البر [qiṭṭ al-barr], i.e. wild cat, in Forsskål, Descript. Animall. p. 1, no. 7, letter b. III, 48 col. 297 CAP. XXV.

III, 48 col. 297 CHAPTER XXV.


Variae interpretationes vocis רחם racham; ubi multa de avibus שרקרק serakrak, Cygno, Pelicano et Merope.

Various interpretations of the word רחם racham; with much on the birds שרקרק serakrak, the Swan, the Pelican and the Bee-eater.


Etiam anxie disputatur de ave רחם racham, vel רחמה rachama, ut scribitur Deut. XIV, 17.

There is also anxious dispute about the bird רחם racham, or רחמה rachama, as it is written in Deut. XIV, 17.


I. Ionathan et Syrus explicant ܣܪܩܪܩܐ serakreka; et Onkelos ירקרקא jerakreka. Quod idem esse puto, quamvis illud a sibilo dicatur, hoc a viridi colore. Sed et Talmudici שרקרק serakrak reddunt. Locus est in tractatu Cholin fol. 63. a. רחם זו שרקרק אמר רבי יוחנן למה נקרא שמו רחם כיון שבא רחם באו רחמים לעולם, „Racham avis eadem, quae serakrak. Dixit Rabbi „Iohannes, Cur vocatur racham? (Id est, cur illi nomen a misericordia inditum, „quae Hebraeis est רחם)? Cum venit racham, veniunt misericordiae in mun-„dum.“ Et ibi Glossa, רחמים מטר, Misericordiae, id est, pluvia, quam Deus III, 49 pro benignitate sua nobis indulget, juxta illud Lucae Act. XIV, 16. Non se reliquit sine testimonio ἀγαθοποιῶν benefaciens, coelitus dans nobis pluvias. Ibidem docent, שרקרק serakrak, a clamore suo dici. Sequitur enim, אמר רב בבי בר אביי והוא דיתיב אמידי ועביד שרקרק, Dixit Rabbi Bibi, filius Abii, Avis est, quae ubicunque sedeat, facit serakrak, id est, sibilo suo videtur id efferre. Ad-dunt, דאי יתיב בארעא ושריק אתי משיחא שנאמר אשרקה להם ואקבצם, Cum in terra sedebit sibilans, veniet Messias, prout dicitur Zachar. X, 8. „Sibi- col. 298 labo ad eos, et congregabo eos. “ Creditur nempe avis esse fausti ominis: atque ut habet Glossator, cum non stat, sed sedet et sibilat, סימן בשורה הוא, signum est boni nuncii. Inprimis si in terra sedeat, שאין דרכו, quod praeter morem facit. Illa igitur sic sedente et sibilante, aut Deo ipso per illam avem, si recutitis doctoribus credimus, venturus est Iudaicus Messias et Iudaei, toto terrarum orbe dispersi, congregabuntur juxta vaticinium, quod modo citavimus, Sibilabo ad eos, et congregabo eos. Itaque eorum multum interest, ut sciant, quaenam sit avis, quod tamen prorsus ignorant. Nam Iudaei Germaniae, Munstero et Fagio testibus, picam interpretantur. Quod sequitur in Latina versione Munsterus, et Deodatius in Italica. Et videri potest verisimile, cum apud Gesnerum dicat Gratarolus, picam a veteribus dictam fuisse pluviae avem; quia amplius solito stridens certo imbrem indicat. Et recens picae nomen καρακάξα, quo utuntur hodie Graeci, accedit ad serakraka. Tamen a pica differre docent Arabum descriptiones, qui eandem avem vocant شرقراق sirikrak, et per methathesim شقراق sikirrak, et شرشاق sirisak: et in Alcamus definiunt طاير مرقط بخضرة وحمرة وبياض ويكون بارض الاحرام Avem viridi, rubro et albo distinctam, quae est in terra Alachram, id est, circa Meccham et Medinam (1). Et in Alkazuinio, طاير يقال له بالفارسية III, 50 كاسينة اخضر اللون احمر المنقار وقد يكون اصفر عدو النحل ياكل منها ويقتل ما لا ياكل Avem, quae Persice CASINA dicitur, plumarum colore viridi, rostro rubro, quandoque etiam flavo; apibus inimicam, quas deglutit, quin et eas perimentem, quas non comedit. Et in Damire, طاير صغير يسمي الاخيل والعرب تتشام به وهو اخضر مليح بقدر الحمامة خضرته حسنة مشبعة وفي اجنحته سواد وله مشتا ومصيف يكثر في البلاد الروم والشام وخراسان ونواجد وفي طبعه شرة وشراسة وسرقة فراخ غيره وهو لا يزال الا متباعدا من الناس ويالف الروابي وروس الجبال لكنه يحضن بيضه في العمران العوالي الذي لا تناله الايدي وعشه شديد النتن Avem parvam alio nomine achial dictam (id est, maculosam, quam- col. 299 vis aliis achial sit avis صرد surad, quae vulgo lanius minor). Arabes inauspicatam putant. Est viridis, elegans, magnitudinis columbae. Viride ejus pulchrum et saturum. Aliis nigra est. Tam hyberna, quam aestiva est. Abundat in terris Graecorum, Syriae, Chorasan et Negid (in Arabia Felice). Pravae naturae est et malae indolis. Suffuratur pullos non suos. Est ab omni hominum consortio remotissima. In collibus habitat, et in vertice montium. Et ova sua fovet in locis celsissimis, ad quae manus non attingunt. Nidum habet summe foetidum. De eadem ave dicit Algiahid, انه نوع من الغربان وفي طبعه السرقة والعفة من السفاد وهو كثير الاستغاثة اذا طار بقربه طاير ضربه وصاحْ كانه المضروب, Esse corvi speciem, et furacis esse naturae, et a coitu multum abstinere, querulamque et clamosam esse, ita, ut, si alia avis prope advolet, ea verberata clamet, quasi vapulasset ipsa. Esum alii Arabum concedunt, alii vetant لاستخباثه propter foeditatem ejus. Tamen his verbis commendat Avicenna Canonis libro secundo, capite De carnibus, لحم الشقراق كاسر III, 51 الرياح وابعد اللحمان من تعفن اقله شحما وايبسه جوهرا Caro sikirrak pellit flatus, et, cum parum sit pinguis substantiaeque siccissimae, a corruptione maxime distat. In Paroemiographis hoc proverbium de illa ave occurrit: اشام من الاخيل وهو الشقراق Inauspicatius ave achial, id est, ave sikirrak. Proinde Damir supra dixerat, eam avem ab Arabibus pro inauspicata haberi. Talmudici tamen contra statuunt, avem esse fausti ominis: sed quis miretur in iis, quae ex opinione pendent, varia esse hominum judicia. صاحب الحيل, id est, auctor artium, felli ejus vim tribuit, quam hic intactam praeterire non possum. اذا كان الذهب ناقص العيار يذاب ويفرغ عليه من مرارته فانه يتحجر ويبردان عياره كما لو افرغ عليه مرارة الثعلب فانه ينقص عياره Si in auro pondus deficit, liquefit, et fel istius avis ipsi affunditur: et, cum aurum coaluit, gravius fit pondere. Ut contra fit levius, si vulpis fel affundatur. Minus mirum quod sequitur, اذا اتخذ من مرارته خضاب سود الشعر tincturam ex eo felle sumptam denigrare capillos. In Tartariae campestribus circa Caucasum et Caucasias portas, quas hodie Derbend, id est, angustias et Temir capi, id est, ferream portam, vocant, harum avium est copia, de quibus notatu dignum est, quod refert Haitho Armenus in libro De Tartaris capite quadragesimo septimo. In quadam planitie, quae vocatur Mon- col. 300 ga (lege Mongal) stant hyeme quaedam aves magnitudinis phasianorum, quae pulcherrimas habent plumas, et vocantur seicerach (شقراق) unde, quando aliquae gentes ingrediuntur illam planitiem, statim fugiunt illae aves, et transeunt per illas custodias, et fossata (ubi Derbend et Porta ferrea, de quibus paullo ante egerat), et qui sunt deputati ad custodiam illius loci per illas aves, manifeste cognoscunt inimicorum adventum, et ad defensionem continuo sunt parati. Ex his omnibus multa colligo: Primo has aves non esse picas, ut Hebraei sentiunt, et fortasse etiam ex Arabibus Algiahid; cum mole corporis, pennarum et rostri colore, victu, foetore, nido, quem sibi struunt in remotissimis montibus, prorsus a pica differant. Secundo, non esse picos virides, ut statuit vir doctissimus et mihi amicissimus, cum huic avi cum pico vix quidquam commune sit praeter colorem, qui in utroque est viridis, sed in pico dilutior. Tertio, quamvis non possum definire, quae avis sit شرقراق sirikrak; quia in Europaeis avibus nulla est huic similis; constat tamen, illi cum Hebraeo רחם racham nihil esse commune; et graviter falli Talmudicos, Chaldaeos, Syros et Hebraeos recentiores, qui racham et serakraka eandem avem esse definiunt. Sed jam alii sunt audiendi.

I. Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] and the Syriac explain it as ܣܪܩܪܩܐ [סרקרקא] serakreka; and Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] as ירקרקא jerakreka. I think these are the same, although the former is named from hissing, the latter from green colour. The Talmudists too render it שרקרק serakrak. The passage is in the tractate Cholin fol. 63a רחם זו שרקרק אמר רבי יוחנן למה נקרא שמו רחם כיון שבא רחם באו רחמים לעולם, "Racham is the same bird as serakrak. Rabbi Johanan said: Why is it called racham? (That is, why was it given a name from mercy, which in Hebrew is רחם?) When the racham comes, mercies come into the world." And there the Gloss says: רחמים מטר, Mercies, that is, rain, which God III, 49 in his kindness grants us, according to the words of Luke in Acts 14:16: He did not leave himself without witness, ἀγαθοποιῶν [agathopoiōn] doing good, giving us rains from heaven. In the same place they teach that שרקרק serakrak is named from its cry. For there follows: אמר רב בבי בר אביי והוא דיתיב אמידי ועביד שרקרק, Rabbi Bibi, son of Abii, said: It is a bird which, wherever it sits, makes serakrak, that is, it seems to utter this with its hissing. They add: דאי יתיב בארעא ושריק אתי משיחא שנאמר אשרקה להם ואקבצם, When it sits on the ground hissing, the Messiah will come, as it is said Zech 10:8: "I will hiss col. 298 for them, and gather them." The bird, namely, is believed to be of good omen; and, as the Glossator has it, when it does not stand but sits and hisses, סימן בשורה הוא, it is a sign of good tidings. Especially if it sits on the ground, שאין דרכו, which it does contrary to its habit. When it sits and hisses thus, therefore, or when God himself hisses through that bird, if we believe the circumcised doctors, the Jewish Messiah will come, and the Jews, scattered over the whole world, will be gathered according to the prophecy just cited, I will hiss for them, and gather them. So it matters greatly to them to know what bird this is; yet they are wholly ignorant of it. For the Jews of Germany, as Münster and Fagius testify, interpret it as the magpie. Münster follows this in his Latin version, and Diodati in his Italian. And it may seem probable, since in Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium] Gratarolus says that the magpie was called by the ancients the bird of rain, because when it chatters more than usual it surely signals a shower. And the recent name of the magpie, καρακάξα [karakaxa], which the Greeks use today, comes close to serakraka. Yet the descriptions of the Arabs show that it differs from the magpie. They call the same bird شرقراق [shirqirrāq] sirikrak, and by metathesis شقراق [shiqirrāq] sikirrak, and شرشاق [shirshāq] sirisak; and in the Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] they define it: طاير مرقط بخضرة وحمرة وبياض ويكون بارض الاحرام [ṭāyir muraqqaṭ bi-khuḍra wa-ḥumra wa-bayāḍ wa-yakūn bi-arḍ al-aḥrām] A bird spotted with green, red and white, which is found in the land of Alachram, that is, around Mecca and Medina R1. And in Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt]: طاير يقال له بالفارسية III, 50 كاسينة اخضر اللون احمر المنقار وقد يكون اصفر عدو النحل ياكل منها ويقتل ما لا ياكل [ṭāyir yuqāl lahu bi-l-fārisiyya kāsīna akhḍar al-lawn aḥmar al-minqār wa-qad yakūn aṣfar ʿaduww al-naḥl yaʾkul minhā wa-yaqtul mā lā yaʾkul] A bird which in Persian is called CASINA, green in the colour of its feathers, with a red beak, sometimes also yellow; hostile to bees, which it swallows, and indeed it also kills those which it does not eat. And in Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: طاير صغير يسمي الاخيل والعرب تتشام به وهو اخضر مليح بقدر الحمامة خضرته حسنة مشبعة وفي اجنحته سواد وله مشتا ومصيف يكثر في البلاد الروم والشام وخراسان ونواجد وفي طبعه شرة وشراسة وسرقة فراخ غيره وهو لا يزال الا متباعدا من الناس ويالف الروابي وروس الجبال لكنه يحضن بيضه في العمران العوالي الذي لا تناله الايدي وعشه شديد النتن [ṭāyir ṣaghīr yusammī al-akhyal wa-l-ʿarab tatashāʾam bihi wa-huwa akhḍar malīḥ bi-qadr al-ḥamāma khuḍratuhu ḥasana mushbaʿa wa-fī ajniḥatihi sawād wa-lahu mashtā wa-maṣīf yakthur fī al-bilād al-rūm wa-l-shām wa-khurāsān wa-nawājid wa-fī ṭabʿihi shirra wa-sharāsa wa-sariqat firākh ghayrihi wa-huwa lā yazāl illā mutabāʿidan min al-nās wa-yaʾlaf al-rawābī wa-rūs al-jibāl lākinnahu yaḥḍun bayḍahu fī al-ʿumrān al-ʿawālī alladhī lā tanāluhu al-aydī wa-ʿushshuhu shadīd al-natn] A small bird, by another name called achial (that is, spotted, col. 299 although for others achial is the bird صرد [ṣurad] surad, commonly the lesser shrike). The Arabs consider it ill-omened. It is green, elegant, of the size of a dove. Its green is beautiful and deep. Its wings have black. It has both winter and summer quarters. It abounds in the lands of the Greeks, Syria, Chorasan and Negid (in Arabia Felix). It is of a wicked nature and evil disposition. It steals chicks not its own. It keeps as far as possible from all company of men. It lives on hills and on the tops of mountains. And it broods its eggs in the highest places, which hands cannot reach. Its nest is extremely foul-smelling. Of the same bird Algiahid says: انه نوع من الغربان وفي طبعه السرقة والعفة من السفاد وهو كثير الاستغاثة اذا طار بقربه طاير ضربه وصاحْ كانه المضروب [annahu nawʿ min al-ghirbān wa-fī ṭabʿihi al-sariqa wa-l-ʿiffa min al-sifād wa-huwa kathīr al-istighātha idhā ṭār bi-qurbihi ṭāyir ḍarabahu wa-ṣāḥ kaʾannahu al-maḍrūb], that it is a species of raven, of thievish nature, much abstaining from coition, querulous and clamorous, so that, if another bird flies near, it strikes it and cries out as if it had itself been beaten. Some of the Arabs permit eating it, others forbid it لاستخباثه [li-stikhbāthihi] because of its foulness. Yet Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] commends it in these words in book 2 of the Canon, the chapter On meats: لحم الشقراق كاسر III, 51 الرياح وابعد اللحمان من تعفن اقله شحما وايبسه جوهرا [laḥm al-shiqirrāq kāsir al-riyāḥ wa-abʿad al-luḥmān min taʿaffun aqalluhu shaḥman wa-aybasuhu jawharan] The flesh of the sikirrak dispels flatulence, and, since it is little fatty and of very dry substance, it is the furthest from corruption. In the Paroemiographers this proverb about that bird occurs: اشام من الاخيل وهو الشقراق [ashʾam min al-akhyal wa-huwa al-shiqirrāq] More ill-omened than the bird achial, that is, the bird sikirrak. Accordingly Damir had said above that this bird is held ill-omened by the Arabs. The Talmudists, however, hold on the contrary that it is a bird of good omen; but who would wonder that in matters which depend on opinion men's judgements vary? صاحب الحيل [ṣāḥib al-ḥiyal], that is, the author of the arts, attributes a power to its gall which I cannot pass over here untouched: اذا كان الذهب ناقص العيار يذاب ويفرغ عليه من مرارته فانه يتحجر ويبردان عياره كما لو افرغ عليه مرارة الثعلب فانه ينقص عياره [idhā kān al-dhahab nāqiṣ al-ʿiyār yudhāb wa-yufragh ʿalayhi min marāratihi fa-innahu yataḥajjar wa-yabrudān ʿiyāruhu kamā law afragh ʿalayhi marārat al-thaʿlab fa-innahu yanquṣ ʿiyāruhu] If gold is deficient in weight, it is melted and the gall of this bird is poured on it; and when the gold has solidified, it becomes heavier in weight. Just as, on the contrary, it becomes lighter if the gall of a fox is poured on it. Less wonderful is what follows: اذا اتخذ من مرارته خضاب سود الشعر [idhā ittakhadh min marāratihi khiḍāb sawwad al-shaʿr] a dye made from that gall blackens the hair. In the plains of Tartary around the Caucasus and the Caucasian gates, which today they call Derbend, that is, the narrows, and Temir capi, that is, the iron gate, there is an abundance of these birds, about which what Hayton the Armenian relates in his book On the Tartars, chapter 47, is worth noting: In a certain plain, which is called Mon- col. 300 ga (read Mongal), there stay in winter certain birds of the size of pheasants, which have very beautiful feathers and are called seicerach (شقراق [shiqirrāq]); hence, when any peoples enter that plain, those birds immediately flee and pass through those guard-posts and ditches (where Derbend and the Iron Gate are, which he had treated a little before), and those who are appointed to guard that place clearly recognize by those birds the approach of enemies, and are at once prepared for defence. From all this I gather many things. First, that these birds are not magpies, as the Hebrews think, and perhaps also, among the Arabs, Algiahid; since they differ entirely from the magpie in bodily size, in the colour of feathers and beak, in diet, in stench, and in the nest they build in the most remote mountains. Second, that they are not green woodpeckers, as a most learned man and very dear friend of mine holds, since this bird has hardly anything in common with the woodpecker except colour, which in both is green, but paler in the woodpecker. Third, although I cannot determine what bird the شرقراق [shirqirrāq] sirikrak is, because among European birds none is like it, it is nevertheless certain that it has nothing in common with the Hebrew רחם racham; and that the Talmudists, the Chaldees, the Syrians and the more recent Hebrews, who determine that racham and serakraka are the same bird, are gravely mistaken. But now others must be heard.


III, 52 II. In Samaritana paraphrasi רחם racham est ࠍࠏࠌࠉࠕࠀ naamitha, struthio: quo nihil absurdius fingi potuit. Nam struthionem versu decimo sexto jam prohibuerat Moses, ut abunde a) probatum est. Itaque causa nulla est, cur versu decimo octavo eundem rursus prohibeat. Praeterea cum struthio sit avis immisericors et crudelis in suos, quorsum nomen habeat a misericordia factum, quae Hebraeis est רחם rechem.

III, 52 II. In the Samaritan paraphrase רחם racham is ࠍࠏࠌࠉࠕࠀ [נעמיתא] naamitha, ostrich; nothing more absurd could have been invented. For Moses had already forbidden the ostrich in verse 16, as has been amply a) proved. So there is no reason why he should forbid the same bird again in verse 18. Besides, since the ostrich is a bird without mercy and cruel to its own young, why should it have a name derived from mercy, which in Hebrew is רחם rechem?


III. Idem in Graecos potest objici, quibus רחם racham est κύκνος, cygnus. Utut enim cygnos Graeci poëtae summis laudibus evehant, tamen quam sint immites, docent haec Philosophi Historiae libri noni capite primo, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ κύκνοι ἀλληλοφάγοι μάλιστα τῶν ὀρνέων. Unde Plinius libri decimi capite vigesimo tertio, Iidem mutua carne vescuntur inter se. Is igitur in Aristotele legerat, cygnos ἀλληλοφαγεῖν, mutuo se vorare, nec simpliciter ἀλληλοκτονεῖν, se mutuo interimere, quomodo hunc locum citant Athenaeus libro nono, et Aelianus in Variis libri primi capite decimo quarto, ut diritatem facti emolliant. Unde est, quod in fabulis homines duri et immites in cygnos mutari narrantur. Antonius Liberalis de Cygno, Apollinis filio, qui a patre factus est cygnus: Οὗτος ἦν εὐσχήμων τὴν ὄψιν· τὸ δὲ ἦθος ἄχαρις καὶ ἄγροικός. Facie quidem erat formosus; sed moribus rudis et agrestis. Sunt et alii duo Cygni, quibus idem fatum affingunt b): Ὁ μὲν Ἄρεως υἱὸς, ὃς ἐν Θετταλίᾳ τοὺς παριόντας λοχῶν, καὶ ἀποκτείνων, καὶ βουλόμενος ταῖς κεφαλαῖς ναὸν ἀνεγεῖραι τῷ πατρὶ, ὃν Ἡρακλῆς ἀπέκτεινεν· ὁ δὲ Ποσειδῶνος, etc. ὃν Ἀχιλλεὺς ἀπέκτεινεν. Unus Martis filius, qui in Thessalia transeuntes insidiis appetens perimebat, ut ex eorum capitibus patri templum excitaret, quem interfecit Hercules: alius Neptuni filius, etc. quem occidit Achilles. Atque hic quoque narratur Philonomen uxorem propria manu necasse, et filium Tennem, arca inclusum, in mare conjecisse. Neque vero satis certum est, κύκνον hic haberi pro רחם racham: cum in Hieronymo, qui Graecos fere sequitur, alius sit ordo vocum; ita, ut cygnus τῷ תנשמת thinsemeth, et porphyrio τῷ racham respondeat. Quod videri queat minus alienum; quia רחם racham verbum est diligere: porphyrionem autem φιλοοίκειον εἶναί φασι, καὶ τὴν συντροφίαν τῶν συννόμων ἀγαπᾷν. Quod multis probat Aelianus Historiae libri quinti capite vigesimo octavo porphyrionis cujusdam exemplo, qui, convictore gallo privatus, inedia sibi mortem conscivit.

III. The same objection can be made against the Greeks, for whom רחם racham is κύκνος [kyknos], swan. For however highly the Greek poets extol swans, how savage they are is taught by these words of the Philosopher, History, book 9, chapter 1: Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ κύκνοι ἀλληλοφάγοι μάλιστα τῶν ὀρνέων [eisi de hoi kyknoi allēlophagoi malista tōn orneōn]. Hence Pliny, book 10, chapter 23: They also feed on one another's flesh. He had therefore read in Aristotle that swans ἀλληλοφαγεῖν [allēlophagein], devour one another, and not simply ἀλληλοκτονεῖν [allēloktonein], kill one another, as Athenaeus, book 9, and Aelian in the Varia, book 1, chapter 14, cite this passage, so as to soften the horror of the act. This is why in fables hard and savage men are said to be changed into swans. Antoninus Liberalis, on Cycnus, son of Apollo, who was made a swan by his father: Οὗτος ἦν εὐσχήμων τὴν ὄψιν· τὸ δὲ ἦθος ἄχαρις καὶ ἄγροικός [houtos ēn euschēmōn tēn opsin; to de ēthos acharis kai agroikos]. He was handsome in appearance, but rude and boorish in character. There are also two other Cycni to whom the same fate is ascribed b): Ὁ μὲν Ἄρεως υἱὸς, ὃς ἐν Θετταλίᾳ τοὺς παριόντας λοχῶν, καὶ ἀποκτείνων, καὶ βουλόμενος ταῖς κεφαλαῖς ναὸν ἀνεγεῖραι τῷ πατρὶ, ὃν Ἡρακλῆς ἀπέκτεινεν· ὁ δὲ Ποσειδῶνος, etc. ὃν Ἀχιλλεὺς ἀπέκτεινεν [ho men Areōs huios, hos en Thettalia tous pariontas lochōn, kai apokteinōn, kai boulomenos tais kephalais naon anegeirai tō patri, hon Hēraklēs apekteinen; ho de Poseidōnos, etc. hon Achilleus apekteinen]. One, the son of Mars, who in Thessaly ambushed and killed passers-by, in order to build a temple to his father from their heads, and whom Hercules slew; the other, the son of Neptune, etc., whom Achilles killed. This latter is also said to have killed his wife Philonome with his own hand and to have thrown his son Tennes, shut in a chest, into the sea. Yet it is not quite certain that κύκνος [kyknos] here stands for רחם racham, since in Jerome, who generally follows the Greeks, the order of the words is different, so that swan corresponds to תנשמת thinsemeth, and porphyrio to racham. This might seem less inappropriate, because רחם racham is the verb to love; and the porphyrio, they say, φιλοοίκειον εἶναί φασι, καὶ τὴν συντροφίαν τῶν συννόμων ἀγαπᾷν [philooikeion einai phasi, kai tēn syntrophian tōn synnomōn agapan]. Aelian, History, book 5, chapter 28, proves this at length by the example of a certain porphyrio which, deprived of the cock that was its companion, starved itself to death.


IV. Hebraei recentiores, nominis etymon respicientes, dicunt שהוא עוף col. 301 מרחם על בניו מאד, racham avem esse erga pullos suos valde misericordem. Sic III, 53 Aben Ezra, Kimchius, Pomarius, Aquinas et R. Iacob auctor Hatturim, sive Commentarii Cabalistici in Pentateuchum. Hinc apud Ariam in Levitico pro רחם racham est philostorgos. Sed hoc est etymologias interpretari, non verba, quod alicubi Aquilae objicit Hieronymus: cum in rerum natura nulla sit avis philostorgos nomine. Itaque idem, mutato consilio, pro philostorgo maluit in Deuteronomio pelicanum scribere, quem veterum ecclesiae doctorum multi narrant occidere natos suos, eosque per triduum lugere, deinde se ipsum rostro vulnerare, et aspersione sui sanguinis revocare ad vitam. Epiphanii Physiologus, capite octavo, Ἔστι γὰρ ἡ πελεκᾶν φιλότεκνον ὄρνεον παρὰ πάντα τὰ ὄρνεα, Prae omnibus volucribus pelecanus prolis est amans. Addit, parvulos a matre nimiis osculis sauciatos emori, sed post triduum marem accedere, qui, doloris impatiens, κολαφίζει τὴν ἰδίαν πλευρὰν, καὶ ὀπὰς αὐτῇ ἐμποίει, καὶ καταῤῥεῖ αἷμα, ἐπιστάζων ἐπὶ τὰς πληγὰς τῶν τεθνηκότων νεοσσῶν, καὶ οὕτως ζωοποιοῦνται, proprium latus percutit, et terebrat, emanatque sanguis, quem super mortuorum pullorum vulnera instillat, et illi sic vitae restituuntur. Ita etiam Eustathius in Hexaëmeron, nisi quod apud illum pater pullos occidit, et mater aperto latere eosdem exsuscitat. Neque Latini multo aliter. Augustinus in Psalmum centesimum primum, Dicuntur hae aves tanquam colaphis rostrorum occidere parvulos filios suos, eosdemque in nido occisos a se lugere per triduum. Postremo dicunt matrem se ipsam graviter vulnerare, et sanguinem suum super filios fundere, quo illi superfusi reviviscant. Et Gregorius, Ferunt philosophi, quod pelicanus filios suos, statim ut nati sunt, interficit, etc. Postea vero mater se ipsam vulnerat, eosque sanguine suo resuscitat. Et Isidorus Originum libri duodecimi capite septimo, Fertur, si verum est, eam occidere natos suos, eosque per triduum lugere, deinde se ipsam vulnerare, et aspersione sui sanguinis vivificare filios. Quibus similia narrant Pseudo-Hieronymus libro De cereo Paschali, Petrus Damianus libri secundi Epistola decima octava, Vincentius in Doctrinali libri decimi sexti capite centesimo sexagesimo sexto, Michael Glycas libro primo Annalium, atque alii sine numero. Unde est, quod pictores, quibus cum poëtis

IV. More recent Hebrews, looking to the etymology of the name, say שהוא עוף col. 301 מרחם על בניו מאד, that racham is a bird very compassionate toward its young. So III, 53 Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra], Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)], Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)] and R. Jacob, the author of the Turim, or Cabbalistic Commentary on the Pentateuch. Hence in Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], in Leviticus, for רחם racham there is philostorgos. But this is to translate etymologies, not words, as Jerome somewhere objects against Aquila, since in nature there is no bird by the name of philostorgos. Therefore the same man, changing his mind, preferred in Deuteronomy to write pelican instead of philostorgos. Many of the ancient doctors of the church relate that the pelican kills its young, mourns them for three days, then wounds itself with its beak and calls them back to life by sprinkling them with its own blood. The Physiologus of Epiphanius, chapter 8: Ἔστι γὰρ ἡ πελεκᾶν φιλότεκνον ὄρνεον παρὰ πάντα τὰ ὄρνεα [Esti gar hē pelekan philoteknon orneon para panta ta ornea], Above all birds the pelican loves its offspring. He adds that the little ones, wounded by the mother's excessive kisses, die, but after three days the male comes, who, unable to bear his grief, κολαφίζει τὴν ἰδίαν πλευρὰν, καὶ ὀπὰς αὐτῇ ἐμποίει, καὶ καταῤῥεῖ αἷμα, ἐπιστάζων ἐπὶ τὰς πληγὰς τῶν τεθνηκότων νεοσσῶν, καὶ οὕτως ζωοποιοῦνται [kolaphizei tēn idian pleuran, kai opas autē empoiei, kai katarrhei haima, epistazōn epi tas plēgas tōn tethnēkotōn neossōn, kai houtōs zōopoiountai], strikes his own side and pierces it, and blood flows out, which he drips upon the wounds of the dead chicks, and so they are restored to life. So also Eustathius on the Hexaemeron, except that in him the father kills the chicks and the mother revives them by opening her side. Nor do the Latins say much otherwise. Augustine on Psalm 101: These birds are said to kill their little offspring as if with blows of their beaks, and to mourn them, killed by themselves, in the nest for three days. Finally they say that the mother wounds herself severely and pours her blood over her offspring, and that, drenched with it, they come back to life. And Gregory: The philosophers say that the pelican kills its young as soon as they are born, etc. But afterwards the mother wounds herself and revives them with her blood. And Isidore, Etymologies, book 12, chapter 7: It is said, if it is true, that it kills its young, mourns them for three days, then wounds itself and brings its offspring to life by sprinkling them with its blood. Similar things are related by Pseudo-Jerome in the book On the Paschal Candle, Peter Damian, book 2, Letter 18, Vincent in the Doctrinale, book 16, chapter 166, Michael Glycas, book 1 of the Annals, and others without number. Hence it is that painters, to whom, as to poets,


Quidlibet audendi semper fuit aequa potestas,

There was always an equal licence to dare anything,


pelecanum nobis exhibent acuto rostro sauciantem pectus, aut latus, et pullos magno hiatu effluentem inde sanguinem excipientes. Sed imposuit viris sanctis, quisquis primus hanc fabellam mendacio suo adornavit: cum in philosophorum libris, qui de rerum natura scripserunt accuratius, tam insignis miraculi vestigia nulla sint. Ut taceam, resurrectionem esse supra naturae vires: et pelecanum non esse adunci rostri, sed latissimi, unde illi plateae Latinum nomen: neque רחם a misericordia, sed קאת a vomitu dici, ut pluribus probatum. Non tamen soli Ariae, sed Castalioni etiam, et Genevensibus racham est pelicanus. III, 54 V. At Iunio et Tremellio רחם racham est merops. Meropem nimirum volunt racham dici ab amore; quia genitores suos reconditos eum pascere Plinius auctor est libri decimi capite trigesimo tertio. Et Aelianus eapropter meropem haberi dicit c) δικαιότερον (lege δικαιότατον) καὶ εὐσεβέστατον ὀρνίθων ἁπάντων, avium omnium justissimum et piissimum. Isidorus etiam, Meropes eosdem, et gaulos, qui parentes suos recondere atque alere dicuntur. Quod ex Aristotele sumtum. Is enim Historiae libri noni capite decimo tertio, postquam col. 302 ciconiarum ἀντιπελαργίαν descripsit, de meropibus addit: Φασὶ δέ τινες καὶ τοὺς μέροπας ταυτὸ τοῦτο ποιεῖν, καὶ ἀντεκτρέφεσθαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἐκγόνων, οὐ μόνον γηράσκοντας, ἀλλὰ καὶ εὐθὺς, ὅταν οἷοί τ᾽ ὦσι· τὸν δὲ πατέρα, καὶ τὴν μητέρα μένειν ἔνδον. Sunt, qui meropes quoque idem facere asserant, et a pullis suis vicissim ali, non solum cum senes sunt, sed et quam primum pulli huic curae pares sunt: patrem vero et matrem intus manere. Nota obiter, ab Aristophanis Scholiaste in Aves, pro τοὺς μέροπας, scribi τοὺς ἀέροπας, et a Suida τοὺς ἀερόποδας in voce ἀντιπελαργεῖν· quamvis uterque profiteatur, se Aristotelem sequi. Sed et in Hesychio legas, Ἀέροπες· ἔθνος, etc. καὶ ὄρνεά τινα. Aëropes gens, et quaedam aves. Et cum de Eumelo dicit Boeus libro secundo Ornithog. Ἀπόλλων δὲ ὄρνιθα ἐποίησε τὸν παῖδα ἠέροπον, ὃς ἔτι νῦν τίκτει μὲν ὑπὸ γῆς, ἀεὶ δὲ μελετᾷ πέτεσθαι· Apollo autem puerum mutavit in avem aeropum, quae nunc etiam sub terra parit, et semper volatum molitur: aeropi nomine meropem intelligit, de quo Philosophus Historiae libri sexti capite primo, Ὃν δὲ οἱ Βοιώτιοι καλοῦσι μέροπα, εἰς τὰς ὀπὰς ἐν τῇ γῇ καταδυόμενος, νεοτ-τεύει μόνος· Is, quem Boeotii meropem vocant, solus subit terrae cavernas, ut ibi nidificet. Et libri noni capite tertio, Τίκτει ἐν τοῖς κρημνοῖς τοῖς μαλακοῖς εἰσδύεται δὲ εἴσω καὶ τέτταρας πήχεις· Parit in praecipitiis mollioribus, vel ad quatuor cubitos intro subiens. Et Plinius libri decimi capite trigesimo tertio, Cunabula in terra faciunt, corporis gravitate prohibitae sublime petere. Itaque meropes etiam ἀέροπες, ἀερόποδες, et ἠέροποι dictae. Tamen rectum est μέ-ροπες, quomodo dicuntur hae aves, quia habent μεμερισμένην τὴν ὄπα, ὅ ἐστι τὴν φωνήν. Unde Probus in Georgicorum librum quartum, MEROPES sic dicuntur Graece, quia earum vox multiplicem capit partitionem, a μερισμῷ ὀπὸς, id est, partitione vocis. Quem τῆς ὀπὸς μερισμὸν zinzilulandi vocabulo sic expressit auctor Philomelae,

show us the pelican wounding its breast or side with its sharp beak, and its young catching with wide-open mouths the blood that flows from it. But whoever first adorned this little fable with his lie imposed upon holy men, since in the books of the philosophers who wrote more carefully on the nature of things there is no trace of so remarkable a miracle. Not to mention that resurrection is beyond the powers of nature; that the pelican does not have a hooked beak but a very broad one, whence its Latin name platea; and that it is called not רחם from mercy but קאת from vomiting, as has been shown at length. Yet racham is the pelican not only for Arias, but also for Castellio and the Genevans. III, 54 V. For Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] and Tremellius [=Immanuel Tremellius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], however, רחם racham is the bee-eater. They hold, namely, that the bee-eater is called racham from love, because, as Pliny reports in book 10, chapter 33, it feeds its parents when they are hidden away. And Aelian says that for this reason the bee-eater is considered c) δικαιότερον [dikaioteron] (read δικαιότατον [dikaiotaton]) καὶ εὐσεβέστατον ὀρνίθων ἁπάντων [kai eusebestaton ornithōn hapantōn], the most just and most dutiful of all birds. Isidore too: Bee-eaters, the same as gauli, which are said to hide away and feed their parents. This is taken from Aristotle. For in History book 9, chapter 13, after col. 302 describing the ἀντιπελαργία [antipelargia] of storks, he adds about bee-eaters: Φασὶ δέ τινες καὶ τοὺς μέροπας ταυτὸ τοῦτο ποιεῖν, καὶ ἀντεκτρέφεσθαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἐκγόνων, οὐ μόνον γηράσκοντας, ἀλλὰ καὶ εὐθὺς, ὅταν οἷοί τ᾽ ὦσι· τὸν δὲ πατέρα, καὶ τὴν μητέρα μένειν ἔνδον [Phasi de tines kai tous meropas tauto touto poiein, kai antektrephesthai hypo tōn ekgonōn, ou monon gēraskontas, alla kai euthys, hotan hoioi t᾽ ōsi; ton de patera, kai tēn mētera menein endon]. There are some who assert that bee-eaters also do the same, and are fed in turn by their young, not only when they are old, but as soon as the young are equal to this task: the father and mother remain inside. Note in passing that the Scholiast on Aristophanes' Birds writes τοὺς ἀέροπας [tous aeropas] instead of τοὺς μέροπας [tous meropas], and Suidas, under the word ἀντιπελαργεῖν [antipelargein], τοὺς ἀερόποδας [tous aeropodas], although both profess to follow Aristotle. And in Hesychius too you may read: Ἀέροπες· ἔθνος, etc. καὶ ὄρνεά τινα [Aeropes; ethnos, etc. kai ornea tina]. Aëropes: a people, and certain birds. And when Boeus, in book 2 of the Ornithog., says of Eumelus: Ἀπόλλων δὲ ὄρνιθα ἐποίησε τὸν παῖδα ἠέροπον, ὃς ἔτι νῦν τίκτει μὲν ὑπὸ γῆς, ἀεὶ δὲ μελετᾷ πέτεσθαι [Apollōn de ornitha epoiēse ton paida ēeropon, hos eti nyn tiktei men hypo gēs, aei de meleta petesthai]; Apollo changed the boy into the bird aëropus, which even now gives birth under the earth and is always striving to fly: by the name aëropus he means the bee-eater, about which the Philosopher says in History book 6, chapter 1: Ὃν δὲ οἱ Βοιώτιοι καλοῦσι μέροπα, εἰς τὰς ὀπὰς ἐν τῇ γῇ καταδυόμενος, νεοττεύει μόνος [Hon de hoi Boiōtioi kalousi meropa, eis tas opas en tē gē katadyomenos, neotteuei monos]; The bird which the Boeotians call merops alone goes down into holes in the earth to nest there. And in book 9, chapter 3: Τίκτει ἐν τοῖς κρημνοῖς τοῖς μαλακοῖς εἰσδύεται δὲ εἴσω καὶ τέτταρας πήχεις [Tiktei en tois krēmnois tois malakois eisdyetai de eisō kai tettaras pēcheis]; It breeds in the softer cliffs, going in as far as four cubits. And Pliny, book 10, chapter 33: They make their nurseries in the earth, being prevented by the weight of their bodies from seeking a high place. Hence bee-eaters were also called ἀέροπες [aeropes], ἀερόποδες [aeropodes] and ἠέροποι [ēeropoi]. Yet μέροπες [meropes] is correct, as these birds are so called because they have μεμερισμένην τὴν ὄπα, ὅ ἐστι τὴν φωνήν [memerismenēn tēn opa, ho esti tēn phōnēn]. Hence Probus on book 4 of the Georgics: MEROPES are so called in Greek because their voice admits of manifold division, from μερισμῷ ὀπὸς [merismō opos], that is, division of the voice. This τῆς ὀπὸς μερισμὸν [tēs opos merismon] the author of the Philomela expressed by the word zinzilulare [to twitter], thus:


Regulus, atque merops, et rubro pectore Progne, Consimili modulo zinzilulare sciunt. III, 55 Utut sit, quidquid affertur de meropum amore et gratitudine erga parentes, non facit satis ad rem. Ita enim רחם racham non esset avis φιλότεκνος, ut Hebraei volunt, sed φιλοπάτωρ. Tamen Hebraeo verbo רחם racham potius significatur naturalis ille affectus et compassio parentum erga liberos. Et quandoque patri tribuitur: ut Psal. CIII, 13. כרחם אב על בנים, Ut pater est misericors erga filios. Et Esa. LXIII, 15. 16. Ubi commotio viscerum tuorum, ורחמיך, et miserationes tuae, quia tu pater noster es? Et Ierem. XXXI, 20. Annon filius mihi charus est Ephraim? Nonne est filius deliciarum? Idcirca commota sunt viscera mea propter eum, רחם ארחמנו, miserendo miserebor ejus. Sed et maternus affectus eodem verbo aptissime exprimitur: ut 1 Reg. III, 26. נכמרו רחמיו, Incaluerunt ejus (matris) affectus erga filium suum. Et Esa. XLIX, 15. Nunquid obliviscetur mulier foetus sui, מרחם, ut ne misereatur filii ventris sui. Et Thren. IV, 10. Manus mulierum (matrum) רחמניות, misericordes. Vult Propheta naturalem esse matrum erga liberos affectum. Nempe videtur ille affectus ortum ex vulva ducere, quae Hebraice est רחם rechem. Ex his abunde apparet, quae sit vera et nativa significatio verbi רחם, adeoque verum esse, quod Hebraei asserunt, nempe רחם racham, si ratio nominis habeatur, avem esse φιλό-τεκνον· quamvis avem illam definire non potuerint viri, tam imperiti rerum naturae, quam periti vocum interpretes.

The kinglet, and the bee-eater, and Progne with her red breast know how to zinzilulare [twitter] in a like measure. III, 55 However that may be, whatever is adduced about the love and gratitude of bee-eaters toward their parents does not meet the point. For in that case רחם racham would not be a φιλότεκνος [philoteknos] bird, as the Hebrews hold, but a φιλοπάτωρ [philopatōr] one. Yet the Hebrew verb רחם racham rather signifies that natural affection and compassion of parents toward their children. And sometimes it is attributed to a father: as in Ps 103:13. כרחם אב על בנים, As a father is merciful toward his children. And Isa 63:15–16. Where is the stirring of thy bowels, ורחמיך, and thy mercies, for thou art our father? And Jer 31:20. Is not Ephraim a dear son to me? Is he not a delightful child? Therefore my bowels are stirred for him, רחם ארחמנו, I will surely have mercy on him. But maternal affection too is most fittingly expressed by the same verb: as in 1 Reg. III, 26. נכמרו רחמיו, Her (the mother's) affections grew warm toward her son. And Isa 49:15. Can a woman forget her offspring, מרחם, so as not to have mercy on the son of her womb? And Lam 4:10. The hands of the merciful (רחמניות) women (mothers). The Prophet means that the affection of mothers toward their children is natural. Indeed, that affection seems to take its origin from the womb, which in Hebrew is רחם rechem. From these passages it is abundantly clear what the true and native meaning of the verb רחם is, and hence that what the Hebrews assert is true, namely that רחם racham, if the reason for the name is considered, is a φιλότεκνον [philoteknon] bird; although these men, as unskilled in natural history as they were skilled as interpreters of words, were unable to identify that bird.
