III, 56 CAP. XXVI. col. 303

III, 56 Chapter XXVI. col. 303


Ex Arabica lingua probatur, רחם racham esse Vulturis speciem.

It is proved from the Arabic language that רחם racham is a species of vulture.


Iam in ea, quam descripsimus, interpretum haesitatione Arabes consulere tutissimum esse quis neget, cum avis رخم racham, vel رخمة rachama, apud eos hodieque sit notissima, et describatur pluribus, quod sequentia palam facient? Damir, الرخمة طاير ابقع يشبه النسر في الخلقة Rachama, avis varii coloris, ad aquilae naturam accedens. Et paullo post, وفي طبع هذا الطاير انه لا يرضي من الجبال الا من بالوحش منها ولا من الاماكن الا بالاسحقها والابعدها من اماكن اعداية ولا من الهضاب الا بصخورها ويقال لها لانوق E natura hujus avis est, quod non amat montes, nisi maxime so- litarios; neque loca alia, nisi maxime dissita, et ab habitatis remotissima; et in lo- cis petrosis nonnisi rupes inaccessas. Alio nomine vocatur anuk. Et infra, وتبيض بيضة واحدة وربما اتامت وهي من ليام الطير وهن ثلاث الغراب والبوم والرخم والعرب تضرب المثل في الامتناع ببيضها فيقولون اعز من بيض الانوق وابعد من بيض الانوق فانه لا يكاد col. 304 يظفر به لان اوكارها في روس الجبال والاماكن الصعبة كما تقدم قال الشاعر ۞

Now, given the hesitation of the interpreters that we have described, who would deny that it is safest to consult the Arabs? For the bird رخم [rakham] racham, or رخمة [rakhama] rachama, is very well known among them even today, and it is described by many, as what follows will make plain. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: الرخمة طاير ابقع يشبه النسر في الخلقة [al-rakhama ṭāyir abqaʿ yushbih al-nasr fī al-khilqa] Rachama, a bird of variegated colour, approaching the nature of the eagle. And a little later: وفي طبع هذا الطاير انه لا يرضي من الجبال الا من بالوحش منها ولا من الاماكن الا بالاسحقها والابعدها من اماكن اعداية ولا من الهضاب الا بصخورها ويقال لها لانوق [wa-fī ṭabʿ hādhā al-ṭāyir annahu lā yarḍī min al-jibāl illā min bi-l-waḥsh minhā wa-lā min al-amākin illā bi-l-asḥaqihā wa-l-abʿadihā min amākin aʿdāyih wa-lā min al-hiḍāb illā bi-ṣukhūrihā wa-yuqāl lahā lānūq] It is the nature of this bird that it does not like mountains unless they are extremely solitary; nor other places, unless they are very far apart and most remote from inhabited places; and among rocky places only inaccessible crags. It is called by another name anuk. And below: وتبيض بيضة واحدة وربما اتامت وهي من ليام الطير وهن ثلاث الغراب والبوم والرخم والعرب تضرب المثل في الامتناع ببيضها فيقولون اعز من بيض الانوق وابعد من بيض الانوق فانه لا يكاد col. 304 يظفر به لان اوكارها في روس الجبال والاماكن الصعبة كما تقدم قال الشاعر ۞ [wa-tabīḍ bayḍa wāḥida wa-rubbamā atāmat wa-hiya min liyām al-ṭayr wa-hunna thalāth al-ghurāb wa-l-būm wa-l-rakham wa-l-ʿarab taḍrib al-mathal fī al-imtināʿ bi-bayḍihā fa-yaqūlūn aʿazz min bayḍ al-anūq wa-abʿad min bayḍ al-anūq fa-innahu lā yakād yuẓfar bihi li-anna awkārahā fī rūs al-jibāl wa-l-amākin al-ṣaʿba kamā taqaddam qāla al-shāʿir]


وكنت اذا استودعت سر ۞ اكتمت كبيض انوق لا ينال لها وكر ۞

وكنت اذا استودعت سر ۞ اكتمت كبيض انوق لا ينال لها وكر ۞ [wa-kuntu idhā istawdaʿtu sirr aktamtu ka-bayḍ anūq lā yunāl lahā wakr]


Et ovum parit unicum, sed et quandoque gemina edit. Est ex avibus liam (quasi ignobiles dixeris). Eae autem tres sunt, corvus, noctua et racham. Proverbium est apud Arabes, quo significatur, quam ova ejus sint inaccessa, „Rarius ovo anuk“, aut „Remotius ovo anuk“: quod vix quisquam assequitur, quia nidificat in vertice montium et in praeruptis locis, ut jam ante dictum est. Unde est, quod poëta dixit, „Et fui, cum seorsim in abditum locum evocatus sum, latens ut ovum „anuk, cujus nidus est inaccessus“. Alkazuinius, رخمه طاير النسر في خلقته يختار لبيضه اطراف الجبال III, 57 الشاهقة ليصعب الوصول الي بيضه يقال اعز من بيض الانوق فاذا جاء اوان بيضها ذهبت الي الهند واتت حجر يقال له ابوطاقيون وهو حجر مدور مثل خرزة اذا حركت تعقعق في جوفه حجر اخر ويترك ذلك الحجر تحتها فتبيض من غير وجع وتطير خلف العساكر لتاكل من جيف Rachama est avis aquila (id est, aquilini generis). E natura ejus est, ut eligat ovis suis summorum montium vertices, ut ad ea difficilior sit accessus. Unde est, quod dicitur, „Rarius ovo anuk (id est, rachamae)“. Quo tempore ova positura est, in Indiam se conferens inde affert lapidem, quem abutacium vocant (imo εὐτόκιον). Is lapis est margaritae instar rotundus. Cum movetur, sonat in ventre ejus lapis alius. Eo lapide sibi supposito, ova ponit sine dolore. Castra sequitur volatu suo, ut vescatur occisorum cadaveribus. Alcamus الانوق العقاب الرخمة وطاير اسود له كالعرف او اسود اصلع الراس اصفر المنقار وهو اعز من بيض الانوق لانها تحرزها فلا يكاد يظفر به لان اوكارها في التلل الصعبة قيل col. 305 فاخلاقها عشر خصال تحصن بيضها وتحمي فرجها وتالف ولدها ولا تمكن من نفسها غير زوجها وتقطع في اول القواطع وترجع في اول الرواجع وتطير في التحسير ولا تغتر بالشكير ولا ترب بالوكور ولا تسقط علي الجفر بالشكير Anuk, aquilae genus, quae et rachama dicitur. Avis nigra, quae habet tanquam jubam. Alii, avis nigra, calvi capitis, flavi rostri, de qua proverbium, „Rarius est ovo anuk“; quia ovo ita prospicit, ut vix possit invadi. Nidificat enim in montibus inaccessis. Huic propria decem tribuuntur. 1. Munit ova sua. 2. Pullos suos tuetur. 3. Proli suae semper adhaeret. 4. Nihil per se constituit absque compare suo. 5. Migrat cum primis migrantibus. 6. Redit cum primis redeuntibus. 7. Volat in pennarum defluvio. 8. Neque propter pennarum paucitatem periclitatur. 9. Neque manet in nido. 10. Neque cadit in coëundi impotentiam: quomodo reliquae aves, cum pennae defluxerunt. E quibus decem propriis prima quatuor etiam in Damire leguntur verbis fere totidem. Andreas Bellunensis, Alrachame est avis magna sicut milvus, plumis corporis albis, et pennis alarum nigris. Edit carnes putridas, et similia. In III, 58 Syria abundat (1). Ad Alcorani Suratam الاخراب Alachrab, quae in Latino interprete est Azoara quadragesima tertia, ubi de Mose agitur, versus finem, dicit Commentator, Abulabas Cordubensis, لم يعرف موضع قبره الا الرخم فلذلك جعله الله اصم ابكم Nemo novit locum sepulchri ejus praeter avem racham, ac proinde illam fecit Deus surdam et mutam. Id omni ex parte fabulosum est, ut pleraque hujusmodi nugatorum. Nam, ut caetera taceam, haec avis est maxime vocalis, ut aquilinum et vulturinum omne genus. Proinde, ut Arabes saepe avibus, veluti nos campanis, quidvis affingunt, Zamachsari scribit, rachamae clangorem haec fere verba sonare, سبحان ربي الاعلي Sobchan rabbi alali, id est, Laus Domino meo altissimo.

And it lays a single egg, but sometimes it also produces twins. It is one of the birds called liam (as if you were to say ignoble). These are three: the raven, the little owl and the racham. There is a proverb among the Arabs signifying how inaccessible its eggs are: “Rarer than the egg of the anuk”, or “More remote than the egg of the anuk”: for hardly anyone reaches it, because it nests on the summit of mountains and in precipitous places, as was said before. Hence the poet said: “And when I was called apart into a hidden place, I was concealed like the egg of the anuk, whose nest is inaccessible”. Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt]: رخمه طاير النسر في خلقته يختار لبيضه اطراف الجبال III, 57 الشاهقة ليصعب الوصول الي بيضه يقال اعز من بيض الانوق فاذا جاء اوان بيضها ذهبت الي الهند واتت حجر يقال له ابوطاقيون وهو حجر مدور مثل خرزة اذا حركت تعقعق في جوفه حجر اخر ويترك ذلك الحجر تحتها فتبيض من غير وجع وتطير خلف العساكر لتاكل من جيف [rakhama ṭāyir al-nasr fī khilqatih yakhtār li-bayḍih aṭrāf al-jibāl al-shāhiqa li-yaṣʿub al-wuṣūl ilā bayḍih yuqāl aʿazz min bayḍ al-anūq fa-idhā jāʾa awān bayḍihā dhahabat ilā al-hind wa-atat ḥajar yuqāl lahu abūṭāqiyūn wa-huwa ḥajar mudawwar mithl kharaza idhā ḥurrikat taʿaqʿaqa fī jawfih ḥajar ākhar wa-yutrak dhālika al-ḥajar taḥtahā fa-tabīḍ min ghayr wajaʿ wa-taṭīr khalf al-ʿasākir li-taʾkul min jiyaf] Rachama is an eagle bird (that is, of the aquiline kind). It is its nature to choose the summits of the highest mountains for its eggs, so that access to them may be more difficult. Hence the saying, “Rarer than the egg of the anuk” (that is, of the rachama). When it is about to lay its eggs, it goes to India and brings from there a stone which they call abutacium (rather, εὐτόκιον [eutokion]). This stone is round like a pearl. When it is moved, another stone sounds inside it. With this stone placed under itself, it lays its eggs without pain. It follows armies in its flight, to feed on the corpses of the slain. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: الانوق العقاب الرخمة وطاير اسود له كالعرف او اسود اصلع الراس اصفر المنقار وهو اعز من بيض الانوق لانها تحرزها فلا يكاد يظفر به لان اوكارها في التلل الصعبة قيل col. 305 فاخلاقها عشر خصال تحصن بيضها وتحمي فرجها وتالف ولدها ولا تمكن من نفسها غير زوجها وتقطع في اول القواطع وترجع في اول الرواجع وتطير في التحسير ولا تغتر بالشكير ولا ترب بالوكور ولا تسقط علي الجفر بالشكير [al-anūq al-ʿuqāb al-rakhama wa-ṭāyir aswad lahu ka-l-ʿurf aw aswad aṣlaʿ al-raʾs aṣfar al-minqār wa-huwa aʿazz min bayḍ al-anūq li-annahā taḥruzuhā fa-lā yakād yuẓfar bihi li-anna awkārahā fī al-tilal al-ṣaʿba qīla fa-akhlāquhā ʿashar khiṣāl tuḥaṣṣin bayḍahā wa-taḥmī farkhahā wa-taʾlaf waladahā wa-lā tumakkin min nafsihā ghayr zawjihā wa-taqṭaʿ fī awwal al-qawāṭiʿ wa-tarjiʿ fī awwal al-rawājiʿ wa-taṭīr fī al-taḥsīr wa-lā taghtarr bi-l-shakīr wa-lā tarubb bi-l-wukūr wa-lā tasquṭ ʿalā al-jafr bi-l-shakīr] Anuk, a kind of eagle, which is also called rachama. A black bird, which has something like a mane. Others say: a black bird with a bald head and a yellow beak, about which there is the proverb, “Rarer than the egg of the anuk”; because it guards its egg so well that it can hardly be attacked. For it nests in inaccessible mountains. Ten peculiarities are attributed to it. 1. It protects its eggs. 2. It guards its young. 3. It always stays close to its offspring. 4. It does nothing on its own without its mate. 5. It migrates with the first migrants. 6. It returns with the first to return. 7. It flies during the moulting of its feathers. 8. Nor is it endangered by the scantiness of its feathers. 9. Nor does it remain in the nest. 10. Nor does it fall into an inability to mate: as the other birds do when their feathers have fallen out. Of these ten peculiarities the first four are also found in Damir, in almost the same words. Andreas Bellunensis: Alrachame is a large bird like a kite, with white body plumage and black wing feathers. It eats putrid flesh and the like. In III, 58 Syria it is abundant R1. On the Sura of the Qur'an الاخراب [al-akhrāb] Alachrab, which in the Latin translator is Azoara 43, where Moses is treated, towards the end, the Commentator Abulabas Cordubensis says: لم يعرف موضع قبره الا الرخم فلذلك جعله الله اصم ابكم [lam yaʿrif mawḍiʿ qabrih illā al-rakham fa-li-dhālika jaʿalahu allāh aṣamm abkam] No one knew the place of his tomb except the bird racham, and therefore God made it deaf and dumb. This is entirely fabulous, like most things of such triflers. For, to say nothing of the rest, this bird is extremely vocal, like the whole aquiline and vulturine kind. Accordingly, as the Arabs often attribute any words they like to birds, as we do to bells, Zamachsari writes that the cry of the rachama sounds roughly like these words: سبحان ربي الاعلي [subḥān rabbī al-aʿlī] Sobchan rabbi alali, that is, Praise to my Lord most high.


Iam si liberet addere, quidquid habent Alkazuinius, Ibnolbatrik, Avicenna, Serapion, Sariph, Abenbitar, Alcamus et Arabum alii de hujus avis medicis virtutibus, res in immensum excresceret. Nobis igitur e multis sufficiet addere pauca quaedam, unde constet, quam avem Arabes sic indigetent. 1. Stercus rachamae embryonem excutit. Alkazuinius, ذرقها ان احتملته المراة القت جنينها, Stercus ejus si ferat mulier, embryonem ejicit. Avicenna, قيل ان زبله يسقط الجنين تبخيرا Stercus ejus embryonem suffitu ejicere dicitur. Ecce idem in Dioscoride de stercore vulturis in capite De stercore libro secundo, Γυπὸς ἄφοδος ὑποθυμιαθεῖ-σα ἔμβρυα ἐκτινάσσειν παραδέδοται, Vulturis stercus suffitu foetus pellere dicitur. Et in Samonico capite trigesimo quarto,

Now if I wished to add everything that Alkazuinius, Ibnolbatrik, Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)], Serapion [=Serapion, Liber de simplicibus medicinis (the Arabic-Latin pharmacopoeia)], Sariph, Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār], Alcamus and other Arabs say about the medicinal virtues of this bird, the matter would grow beyond measure. It will therefore suffice for us to add a few things out of many, from which it may be clear what bird the Arabs call by this name. 1. The dung of the rachama expels the embryo. Alkazuinius: ذرقها ان احتملته المراة القت جنينها [dharquhā in iḥtamalathu al-marʾa alqat janīnahā], If a woman applies its dung, she expels the embryo. Avicenna: قيل ان زبله يسقط الجنين تبخيرا [qīla inna zibluhu yusqiṭu al-janīn tabkhīran], Its dung is said to expel the embryo by fumigation. Behold, the same is found in Dioscorides concerning the dung of the vulture, in the chapter On dung in book 2: Γυπὸς ἄφοδος ὑποθυμιαθεῖσα ἔμβρυα ἐκτινάσσειν παραδέδοται [gypos aphodos hypothymiatheisa embrya ektinassein paradedotai], Vulture's dung, used as a fumigation, is said to drive out the foetus. And in Serenus Sammonicus [=Quintus Serenus Sammonicus, Liber medicinalis], chapter 34:


Quin etiam stercus supponunt vulturis atri, col. 306
Sentiat ut minime partus quam proximus urget.

Moreover, they place beneath the dung of the black vulture, col. 306 so that she may scarcely feel the birth that presses close.


2. Pluma quoque rachamae ad partum prodest. Sariph, وان اخذت ريشه من جناحها اليمن ووضعت بين رجلي المطلغة سهل اولادها Cum sumitur penna ex ala ejus dextera, et ad parturientis pedes ponitur, levat dolores partus. Ita etiam Alcamus in رخم racham. Quod idem de vulturis penna habet Plinius libri vigesimi noni capite quarto, Penna vulturina subjecta pedibus adjuvat parturientes. Et Sextus libri secundi capite secundo, Efficit, ut sine labore partum edant. III, 59 3. Fel rachamae medetur albugini. Alkazuinius, يكتحل بمرارتها وحدها لبياض العين Ex solo vulturis felle fit collyrium ad oculi albuginem. Avicenna, يكتحل بمرارتها لبياض العين بالما البارد Ex felle ejus cum aqua frigida fit collyrium ad oculorum albugines. Vulturino felli vis eadem. Plinius libri vigesimi noni capite sexto, postquam aquilae felle inungi dixit nubeculas, et caligationes, suffusionesque oculorum, Eadem vis et in vulturino felle, etc. Samonicus capite decimo quarto,

2. The feather of the rachama also assists childbirth. Sariph: وان اخذت ريشه من جناحها اليمن ووضعت بين رجلي المطلغة سهل اولادها [wa-in ukhidhat rīsha min janāḥihā al-yumn wa-wuḍiʿat bayna rijlay al-muṭlagha sahhala awlādahā], When a feather is taken from its right wing and placed at the feet of a woman in labour, it relieves the pains of childbirth. So also Alcamus under رخم [rakham] racham. Pliny says the same of the vulture's feather, book 29, chapter 4: A vulture's feather placed under the feet assists women in labour. And Sextus, book 2, chapter 2: It makes them give birth without labour. III, 59 3. The gall of the rachama cures albugo [white opacity of the eye]. Alkazuinius: يكتحل بمرارتها وحدها لبياض العين [yuktaḥalu bi-marāratihā waḥdahā li-bayāḍ al-ʿayn], From the vulture's gall alone an eye-salve is made for albugo of the eye. Avicenna: يكتحل بمرارتها لبياض العين بالما البارد [yuktaḥalu bi-marāratihā li-bayāḍ al-ʿayn bi-l-mā al-bārid], From its gall with cold water an eye-salve is made for albugo of the eyes. The vulture's gall has the same power. Pliny, book 29, chapter 6, after saying that eagle's gall is applied as an ointment for clouding, dimness and cataracts of the eyes: The same power is also in vulture's gall, etc. Serenus Sammonicus, chapter 14:


Si tenebras oculis obducit pigra senectus,
Expressae marathro guttae cum melle liquenti
Detergere malum potuerunt, vel vulturis atri
Fella, chelidoniae fuerint quis gramina mista.

If sluggish old age draws darkness over the eyes, drops pressed from fennel with flowing honey have been able to wipe away the ill, or the gall of the black vulture, if blades of celandine are mixed with it.


Marcellus, Fellēs gallinacei, vel vulturini, quod longe magis prodest, scrupulum, et mellis optimi unciam bene tritam conjunges, atque in pyxide cuprea habebis, et opportune ad inungendum uteris. Hoc nihil potentius caliginem relevat. Galenus Euporistων libri primi capite quadragesimo quarto, Omnem oculorum obscuritatem incipientemque suffusionem curat fel vulturis, cum marrubii succo et melle At-tico. Sextus, Vulturis fel, etc. omnem caliginem discutit.

Marcellus: Combine a scruple of the gall of a cock, or of a vulture, which is far more beneficial, with an ounce of the best honey, well ground, keep it in a copper box, and use it for anointing when needed. Nothing relieves dimness more powerfully than this. Galen, Euporista, book 1, chapter 44: Vulture's gall, with juice of horehound and Attic honey, cures every dimness of the eyes and incipient cataract. Sextus: Vulture's gall, etc. dispels all dimness.


4. Rachamae jecur a daemone obsessis utile. Alcamus, كبده يشوي ويسحق ويسقي المجنون ثلثة ايام كل يوم ثلاث مرات ويبريه Iecinore ejus tosto et contrito, per triduum potatur daemoniacus quotidie tribus vicibus, et convalescit. Ita etiam Damir. Nec multo aliter Abenbitar, كبدها شوي ويسحق ويداف بخل ويسقي من به جنون كل يوم ثلاث مرات ثلاثة ايام متواليه فيبريه Iecur ejus assatur, conteritur, et in aceto maceratur, et illi propinatur, quia a daemone obsessus est, per triduum quotidie tribus vicibus, per tres dies continuos, et sanat eum. Nempe de comitiali morbo, in quo videtur esse θεῖόν τι, aliquid simile tradiderant vetustiores. Plinius, Iecur vulturis, cum suo sanguine ter septenis diebus potum, adversus comitialem morbum praedicatur. Ita etiam Sextus et Aesculapius.

4. The liver of the rachama is useful for those possessed by a demon. Alcamus: كبده يشوي ويسحق ويسقي المجنون ثلثة ايام كل يوم ثلاث مرات ويبريه [kabiduhu yushwā wa-yusḥaqu wa-yusqā al-majnūn thalatha ayyām kull yawm thalāth marrāt wa-yubrīhi], Its liver, roasted and ground, is given to the demoniac to drink for three days, three times daily, and he recovers. So also Damir. And not much differently Abenbitar: كبدها شوي ويسحق ويداف بخل ويسقي من به جنون كل يوم ثلاث مرات ثلاثة ايام متواليه فيبريه [kabiduhā shuwiya wa-yusḥaqu wa-yudāfu bi-khall wa-yusqā man bihi junūn kull yawm thalāth marrāt thalātha ayyām mutawāliya fa-yubrīhi], Its liver is roasted, ground, and steeped in vinegar, and given to drink to one who is possessed by a demon, three times daily for three days, for three continuous days, and it heals him. Indeed, concerning epilepsy, in which there seems to be θεῖόν τι [theion ti], something divine, the older writers had handed down something similar. Pliny: Vulture's liver, drunk with its own blood for thrice seven days, is commended against epilepsy. So also Sextus and Aesculapius.


5. Ecce aliud de carne rachamae! Sariph, لحم الرخم اذا خلط بخردل وجفف وبخر به المعقود عن النسا سبع col. 307 مرات اطلقه ذلك Carne rachamae cum sinapi mixta et exsiccata, si suffiatur III, 60 ischiadicus septies, a morbo suo liberabitur. Alcamus, التبخير بتجفيف لحمه مخلوطا بخردل سبع مرات يحل المعقود عن النسا Suffimentum ex carne ejus sicca, cum sinapi mixta, septies repetitum, ischiadico morbo laborantem sanabit. Sed utroque loco, pro خردل chardal, id est, sinapi, legendum putamus حرمل charmal, id est, rutam: quia habetur in Samonico, capite quinquagesimo quinto,

5. Here is another remedy from the flesh of the rachama! Sariph: لحم الرخم اذا خلط بخردل وجفف وبخر به المعقود عن النسا سبع col. 307 مرات اطلقه ذلك [laḥm al-rakham idhā khuliṭa bi-khardal wa-juffifa wa-bukhkhira bihi al-maʿqūd ʿan al-nasā sabʿ marrāt aṭlaqahu dhālika], If the flesh of the rachama, mixed with mustard and dried, is used to fumigate a sufferer from sciatica III, 60 seven times, he will be freed from his illness. Alcamus: التبخير بتجفيف لحمه مخلوطا بخردل سبع مرات يحل المعقود عن النسا [al-tabkhīr bi-tajfīf laḥmihi makhlūṭan bi-khardal sabʿ marrāt yaḥullu al-maʿqūd ʿan al-nasā], A fumigation from its dried flesh, mixed with mustard, repeated seven times, will heal one suffering from sciatica. But in both places, instead of خردل [khardal] chardal, that is, mustard, we think one should read حرمل [ḥarmal] charmal, that is, rue: because in Serenus Sammonicus, chapter 55, we find:


Si vero occultus nervos dolor urit inertes, Vulturis excisos adipes, rutamque remitte, etc.

But if a hidden pain burns the sluggish sinews, apply the excised fat of a vulture, and rue, etc.


Sed et ad hemicranium et capitis dolores remedia praescribunt Avicenna ex rachama; Plinius, Galenus, Marcellus, Sextus, alii, ex vulture. Et ut stercus rachamae apud Abenbitarem, Damirem et Alcamus: ita vulturinus sanguis apud Plinium lepras sanat. Qui idem libri vigesimi noni capite quarto, Ex volucribus in auxilio contra serpentes primum vultur est. Quam vim uno ore rachamae tribuunt omnes Arabes. Pelli scilicet tradunt venenata omnia pennae suffitu et stercoris: felle illito sanari viperae et scorpionum morsum: et flavam pellem, qua continetur ingluvies, exsiccatam, contritam, et in potu sumtam, purgare ab omni veneno. De quibus praeter Avicennam consulendi Ibnolbatrik, Abenbitar, Damir, Alcamus, etc. Neque enim vacat eorum loca describere.

Moreover, for migraine and headaches remedies are prescribed by Avicenna from the rachama, and by Pliny, Galen, Marcellus, Sextus and others from the vulture. And just as the dung of the rachama in Abenbitar, Damir and Alcamus, so vulture's blood in Pliny cures leprosy. The same author, book 29, chapter 4: Among birds, the first aid against serpents is the vulture. All the Arabs with one voice attribute this power to the rachama. They report, namely, that all venomous creatures are driven off by fumigation with its feather and dung; that the bite of the viper and of scorpions is healed by smearing on its gall; and that the yellow skin which encloses the crop, dried, ground and taken in a drink, purges from every poison. On these matters, besides Avicenna, one should consult Ibnolbatrik, Abenbitar, Damir, Alcamus, etc. For there is no time to copy out their passages.


Iam, quod rachamam, vel anuk, quod idem est, in locis inaccessis nidificare perhibent, atque inde natum proverbium, apud illos receptissimum, Rarius ovo anuk, nemo vulturi negaverit maxime convenire; de quo Philosophus Historiae libri sexti capite quinto, Ὁ δὲ γὺψ νεοττεύει μὲν ἐπὶ πέτραις ἀπροσβάτοις· διὸ σπά-νιον ἰδεῖν νεοττείαν γυπὸς, καὶ νεοττούς. Καὶ διὰ τοῦτο Ἡρόδοτος (lege Ἡρόδωρος), ὁ Βρύσσωνος τοῦ Σοφιστοῦ πατὴρ, φησὶν εἶναι τοὺς γῦπας ἐφ᾽ ἑτέρας γῆς ἀδήλους (lege ἀδήλου) ἡμῖν τοῦτό γε λέγων τὸ σημεῖον, ὅτι οὐδεὶς ἑώρακε γυπὸς νεοτ-τείαν, καὶ ὅτι πολλοὶ ἐξαίφνης φαίνονται ἀκολουθοῦντες τοῖς στρατεύμασι. τὸ δέ ἐστι χαλεπὸν ἰδεῖν ὦπται δ᾽ ὅμως. Vultur autem nidificat in rupibus inaccessis: unde est, quod vulturis nidus et pulli raro videntur. Ac proinde Herodorus, Bryssonis, Sophistae, pater, vultures tradit in alia esse terra, nobis ignota: id ex hoc argumento constare addens, quod, cum vulturis nidum nemo viderit, multi derepente appareant exercitus sequentes. Sed, utut hunc videre difficile est, tamen quandoque visus est. Et rursus libri noni capite undecimo, Γυπὸς δὲ λέγεται ὑπό τινων ὡς οὐδεὶς ἑώρακεν οὔτε νεοττὸν, οὔτε νεοττίαν. Ἀλλὰ διὰ τοῦτο Ἡρό-δωρος ὁ τοῦ Βρύσωνος, τοῦ Σοφιστοῦ πατὴρ, ἀπό τινος αὐτὸν ἑτέρας εἶναι μετεώ-ρου γῆς ἔλεγεν, τεκμήριον τοῦτο λέγων, καὶ τὸ φαίνεσθαι ταχὺ πολλούς· ὅθεν δὲ μηδενὶ εἶναι δῆλον. τούτου δὲ αἴτιον, ὅτι τίκτει ἐν πέτραις ἀπροσβάτοις.

Further, they report that the rachama, or anuk, which is the same, builds its nest in inaccessible places, and that from this arose the proverb, very widely accepted among them, Rarer than the egg of the anuk. No one will deny that this fits the vulture above all. Of it the Philosopher says in the History, book 6, chapter 5: Ὁ δὲ γὺψ νεοττεύει μὲν ἐπὶ πέτραις ἀπροσβάτοις· διὸ σπάνιον ἰδεῖν νεοττείαν γυπὸς, καὶ νεοττούς. Καὶ διὰ τοῦτο Ἡρόδοτος [Ho de gyps neotteuei men epi petrais aprosbatois; dio spanion idein neotteian gypos, kai neottous. Kai dia touto Hērodotos] (read Ἡρόδωρος [Hērodōros]), ὁ Βρύσσωνος τοῦ Σοφιστοῦ πατὴρ, φησὶν εἶναι τοὺς γῦπας ἐφ᾽ ἑτέρας γῆς ἀδήλους [ho Bryssōnos tou Sophistou patēr, phēsin einai tous gypas eph᾽ heteras gēs adēlous] (read ἀδήλου [adēlou]) ἡμῖν τοῦτό γε λέγων τὸ σημεῖον, ὅτι οὐδεὶς ἑώρακε γυπὸς νεοττείαν, καὶ ὅτι πολλοὶ ἐξαίφνης φαίνονται ἀκολουθοῦντες τοῖς στρατεύμασι. τὸ δέ ἐστι χαλεπὸν ἰδεῖν ὦπται δ᾽ ὅμως [hēmin touto ge legōn to sēmeion, hoti oudeis heōrake gypos neotteian, kai hoti polloi exaiphnēs phainontai akolouthountes tois strateumasi. to de esti chalepon idein ōptai d᾽ homōs]. The vulture nests on inaccessible rocks; hence the vulture's nest and young are rarely seen. And therefore Herodorus, father of Bryson the Sophist, reports that vultures are from another land unknown to us, adding that this is established by the argument that, although no one has seen a vulture's nest, many suddenly appear following armies. But however difficult it is to see, it has nevertheless been seen at times. And again, book 9, chapter 11: Γυπὸς δὲ λέγεται ὑπό τινων ὡς οὐδεὶς ἑώρακεν οὔτε νεοττὸν, οὔτε νεοττίαν. Ἀλλὰ διὰ τοῦτο Ἡρόδωρος ὁ τοῦ Βρύσωνος, τοῦ Σοφιστοῦ πατὴρ, ἀπό τινος αὐτὸν ἑτέρας εἶναι μετεώρου γῆς ἔλεγεν, τεκμήριον τοῦτο λέγων, καὶ τὸ φαίνεσθαι ταχὺ πολλούς· ὅθεν δὲ μηδενὶ εἶναι δῆλον. τούτου δὲ αἴτιον, ὅτι τίκτει ἐν πέτραις ἀπροσβάτοις [Gypos de legetai hypo tinōn hōs oudeis heōraken oute neotton, oute neottian. Alla dia touto Hērodōros ho tou Brysōnos, tou Sophistou patēr, apo tinos auton heteras einai meteōrou gēs elegen, tekmērion touto legōn, kai to phainesthai tachy pollous; hothen de mēdeni einai dēlon. toutou de aition, hoti tiktei en petrais aprosbatois].


III, 61 Vulturis neque pullum, neque nidum quenquam vidisse, nonnulli asserunt. Quocirca Brysonis, Sophistae, pater, Herodorus, eos ex sublimiore aliqua terra venire, hoc argumento probabat, quod multi subito appareant, cum, unde venerint, nulli sit notum. Sed hujus rei causa est, quod in rupibus inaccessis vultur pariat. Quae etiam in Antigono Historia quadragesima octava reperire est. Plinius libri decimi capite sexto, Nidos (vulturum) nemo attigit. Ideo etiam fuere, qui putarent, illos ex adverso orbe advolare: falso. Nidificant enim in excelsissimis ru- col. 308 pibus. Foetus quidem saepe cernuntur. Quae non satis cohaerent. Nam, si vulturum nidum nemo attigit, illorum foetus saepe cerni verum esse non potest, cum foetus alibi non videantur, quam in nido, aut circa nidum. Sed prius ex Herodoro, alterum ex Aristotele sumptum, qui in contraria sunt sententia. Quamvis ne Aristoteles quidem vulturis pullos saepe cerni dixerit, sed nonnisi raro videri. Διὸ, inquit, σπάνιον ἰδεῖν νεοττείαν γυπὸς, καὶ νεοττοὺς· ut Plutarchus in Romulo, Νεοσσοῖς γυπὸς οὐ ῥᾳδίως ἴσμεν ἐντετυχηκότες, In vulturis pullos non facile incidimus: pro eo, quod idem dicit in Romanis Quaestionibus, Οὐδὲ γὰρ νεοττίᾳ γυπὸς ἐντυχεῖν ῥᾳδίως ἐστίν. Neque enim in vulturis nidum facile est incidere. Sed Aelianus multo absurdius Historiae libri secundi capite quadragesimo sexto, Λέγουσι δὲ νεοττιὰν μὴ ὑποπλέκειν γῦπα, Vulturem nidum contexere negant. Quid igitur? Γῦπας δὲ, inquit paullo post, ὠὰ μὴ τίκτειν πέπεισμαι (al. πέπυσμαι), νεοττοὺς δὲ ὠδίνειν, καὶ ὡς ἀπὸ γενεᾶς κα-τάπτεροί εἰσι, καὶ τοῦτο ἤκουσα· Vultures credo (aut audivi) ova non excludere, sed pullos parere, qui statim a partu sint volucres. Et Phile capite secundo,

III, 61 Some assert that no one has seen either the young or the nest of a vulture. Therefore Herodorus, father of Bryson the Sophist, proved that they come from some higher land by this argument, that many suddenly appear, while no one knows whence they have come. But the cause of this is that the vulture breeds on inaccessible rocks. This can also be found in Antigonus, History 48. Pliny, book 10, chapter 6: No one has reached their (the vultures') nests. Hence there were even those who thought that they fly here from the opposite side of the world: falsely. For they nest on the loftiest rocks. col. 308 Their young, indeed, are often seen. These statements do not hang together well. For if no one has reached the nest of vultures, it cannot be true that their young are often seen, since the young are not seen anywhere but in the nest or around it. But the first is taken from Herodorus, the second from Aristotle, who hold opposite views. Yet not even Aristotle said that the vulture's young are often seen, but only that they are rarely seen. Διὸ [Dio], he says, σπάνιον ἰδεῖν νεοττείαν γυπὸς, καὶ νεοττοὺς [spanion idein neotteian gypos, kai neottous]; as Plutarch in the Romulus: Νεοσσοῖς γυπὸς οὐ ῥᾳδίως ἴσμεν ἐντετυχηκότες [Neossois gypos ou rhadiōs ismen entetychēkotes], We do not easily come upon the young of a vulture; in place of which the same author says in the Roman Questions: Οὐδὲ γὰρ νεοττίᾳ γυπὸς ἐντυχεῖν ῥᾳδίως ἐστίν [Oude gar neottia gypos entychein rhadiōs estin]. For it is not easy to come upon a vulture's nest. But Aelian is far more absurd in the History, book 2, chapter 46: Λέγουσι δὲ νεοττιὰν μὴ ὑποπλέκειν γῦπα [Legousi de neottian mē hypoplekein gypa], They say that the vulture does not weave a nest. What then? Γῦπας δὲ [Gypas de], he says a little later, ὠὰ μὴ τίκτειν πέπεισμαι [ōa mē tiktein pepeismai] (var. πέπυσμαι [pepysmai]), νεοττοὺς δὲ ὠδίνειν, καὶ ὡς ἀπὸ γενεᾶς κατάπτεροί εἰσι, καὶ τοῦτο ἤκουσα [neottous de ōdinein, kai hōs apo geneas katapteroi eisi, kai touto ēkousa]; I believe (or I have heard) that vultures do not hatch eggs, but bear young which are winged immediately after birth. And Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)], chapter 2:


Στρουθοὺς πτερωτοὺς ἄρ᾽ ἀπὸ μήτρας ἐξάγει,
Οἱ ζῶσιν εὐθὺς ἐξ ὀνύχων ἁρπάγων,
Πνίγους καλιῶν εὑρεθέντες κρείττονες.

Στρουθοὺς πτερωτοὺς ἄρ᾽ ἀπὸ μήτρας ἐξάγει, Οἱ ζῶσιν εὐθὺς ἐξ ὀνύχων ἁρπάγων, Πνίγους καλιῶν εὑρεθέντες κρείττονες. [Strouthous pterōtous ar᾽ apo mētras exagei, Hoi zōsin euthys ex onychōn harpagōn, Pnigous kaliōn heurethentes kreittones.]


Pullos alatos e vulva educit, qui statim rapacibus unguibus sibi victum comparant, nidi suffocatione praestantiores reperti. Sed nemo non videt, unde nata sint haec opinionum monstra. Quia nidi vulturum raro cernuntur, alii nonnisi in altero orbe, alii nusquam extare crediderunt.

It brings forth winged young from the womb, who at once procure their food with rapacious talons, being found superior to the stifling of the nest. But everyone sees whence these monstrous opinions arose. Because vultures' nests are rarely seen, some believed that they exist only in another world, others that they exist nowhere.


Etiam id vulturi convenit, quod de rachama dicit Damir, illum aut unicum ovum, aut ad summum geminum edere. Aristoteles enim de vulture Historiae libri sexti capite quinto, Τίκτουσι δὲ δύο ὠὰ οἱ γῦπες, Duo ova pariunt vultures. Et libri noni capite undecimo, Τίκτει δ᾽ ἓν ὠὸν, ἢ δύο τὰ πλεῖστα· Unum ovum edit, aut ad summum duo. Plinius ubi supra, Foetus quidem saepe cernuntur, fere bini.

What Damir says of the rachama also fits the vulture, namely that it lays either a single egg or at most two. For Aristotle says of the vulture in History, book 6, chapter 5, Τίκτουσι δὲ δύο ὠὰ οἱ γῦπες [Tiktousi de dyo ōa hoi gypes], Vultures lay two eggs. And in book 9, chapter 11, Τίκτει δ᾽ ἓν ὠὸν, ἢ δύο τὰ πλεῖστα· [Tiktei d' hen ōon, ē dyo ta pleista] It lays one egg, or at most two. Pliny, in the place cited above: Their young are indeed often seen, usually in pairs.


Est et vulturis proprium, quod in Bellunensi rachama legitur edere carnes putridas: et in Alkazuinio, تطير خلف العساكر لتاكل من III, 62 جيف Post castra volat, ut cadaveribus vescatur. Inde in Homero passim eos, qui occisi sunt,

It is also characteristic of the vulture, as we read of the rachama in the Bellunensis, that it eats putrid flesh; and in Alkazuinius, تطير خلف العساكر لتاكل من [taṭīru khalfa al-ʿasākir li-taʾkula min] III, 62 جيف [jiyaf] It flies behind armies in order to feed on corpses. Hence in Homer, throughout, those who have been slain

the vultures devour. And the same men are said to be

Vulturibus multo chariores, quam uxoribus. Quin Herodoro Pontico teste apud Plutarchum Romanarum Quaestionum Quaestione nonagesima tertia, vultur οὐδε-νὸς ἅπτεται ζῶντος, χρῆται δὲ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἀποθανοῦσιν, nihil vivum attingit, sed mortuis solum vescitur. Hinc Lucretius libri quarti versu 680.

far dearer to the vultures than to their wives. Indeed, on the testimony of Herodorus of Pontus in Plutarch, Roman Questions, Question 93, the vulture οὐδενὸς ἅπτεται ζῶντος, χρῆται δὲ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἀποθανοῦσιν [oudenos haptetai zōntos, chrētai de tois allois apothanousin], touches nothing living, but feeds only on the dead. Hence Lucretius, book 4, line 680:


Mellis apes quamvis longe ducantur odore,
Vulturiique cadaveribus. — —

Though bees are drawn from far by the scent of honey,
And vultures by corpses. — —


Ovidius libri primi Tristium Elegia quinta,

Ovid, Tristia, book 1, Elegy 5:


Aut ut edax vultur corpus circumspicit, ecquod

That it can see lying beneath no earth.

Silius, book 13, line 396:

Plutarchus, de causis naturalibus Quaestione vigesima sexta, Τὰ κενέβρια τὸν γῦπα κινεῖ, καὶ προσάγεται πόῤῥωθεν· Morticinae carnes vulturem movent atque eminus trahunt. Et in libro De utilitate ex inimicis, Καθάπερ οἱ γῦπες ἐπὶ τὰς ὀσμὰς τῶν διεφθορότων σωμάτων φέρονται· Vt vultures ad cadaverum odorem feruntur. Aelianus Historiae libri secundi capite quadragesimo sexto, Γὺψ νεκρῷ πολέμιος, ἐσθίει γοῦν ἐμπεσὼν, ὡς ἐχθρόν· Vultur mortuo est infensus, et tanquam in hostem incidens vorat. Sed et brevi morituros praesentire creditur. Aelianus ibidem, Φυλάσσει τεθνηξόμενον. καὶ μέν τοι καὶ ταῖς ἐκ-δήμοις στρατιαῖς ἕπονται γῦπες, καὶ μάλα μαντικῶς, ὅτι γε εἰς πόλεμον χω-ροῦσιν εἰδότες, καὶ ὅτι μάχη πᾶσα ἐργάζεται νεκροὺς, καὶ τοῦτο ἐγνωκότες· Moriturum observat. Peregrinos etiam exercitus sequuntur vultures praesensione quadam, ut qui eos noverint ad bellum proficisci, atque hoc quoque sciant, omne praelium aliquam stragem edere. Phile De animalibus capite secundo, III, 63 Πλὴν μαντικὴν ἔχουσιν οἱ γῦπες φύσιν· Καὶ γὰρ συνεκδημοῦσι τοῖς μαχουμένοις, Τῶν σωμάτων ἐλπίδι πεσουμένων τότε.

Plutarch, On Natural Causes, Question 26: Τὰ κενέβρια τὸν γῦπα κινεῖ, καὶ προσάγεται πόῤῥωθεν· [Ta kenebria ton gypa kinei, kai prosagetai porrhōthen] Carrion flesh stirs the vulture and draws it from afar. And in the book On Profiting from One's Enemies: Καθάπερ οἱ γῦπες ἐπὶ τὰς ὀσμὰς τῶν διεφθορότων σωμάτων φέρονται· [Kathaper hoi gypes epi tas osmas tōn diephthorotōn sōmatōn pherontai] As vultures are borne towards the smell of corpses. Aelian, History, book 2, chapter 46: Γὺψ νεκρῷ πολέμιος, ἐσθίει γοῦν ἐμπεσὼν, ὡς ἐχθρόν· [Gyps nekrō polemios, esthiei goun empesōn, hōs echthron] The vulture is hostile to the dead, and falling upon it devours it as if it were an enemy. It is moreover believed to foresee those who will soon die. Aelian in the same place: Φυλάσσει τεθνηξόμενον. καὶ μέν τοι καὶ ταῖς ἐκδήμοις στρατιαῖς ἕπονται γῦπες, καὶ μάλα μαντικῶς, ὅτι γε εἰς πόλεμον χωροῦσιν εἰδότες, καὶ ὅτι μάχη πᾶσα ἐργάζεται νεκροὺς, καὶ τοῦτο ἐγνωκότες· [Phylassei tethnēxomenon. kai men toi kai tais ekdēmois stratiais hepontai gypes, kai mala mantikōs, hoti ge eis polemon chōrousin eidotes, kai hoti machē pasa ergazetai nekrous, kai touto egnōkotes] It watches one who is about to die. Vultures also follow armies marching abroad, by a kind of foreknowledge, since they know that they are setting out for war, and know this too, that every battle produces some slaughter. Philes, On Animals, chapter 2: III, 63 Πλὴν μαντικὴν ἔχουσιν οἱ γῦπες φύσιν· Καὶ γὰρ συνεκδημοῦσι τοῖς μαχουμένοις, Τῶν σωμάτων ἐλπίδι πεσουμένων τότε. [Plēn mantikēn echousin hoi gypes physin; kai gar synekdēmousi tois machoumenois, tōn sōmatōn elpidi pesoumenōn tote.]


Praeterea vultures naturam habent vaticinam: quippe cum iis peregrinantur, qui dimicaturi sunt, in spem cadaverum, quae tunc cadent. Apud Plinium tradit Umbricius, aruspicum peritissimus, triduo ante, aut biduo volare eos, ubi cadavera futura sint. Unde Plautus in Truculento Scena Piscis,

Moreover, vultures have a prophetic nature: for they travel abroad with those who are about to fight, in hope of the corpses that will then fall. In Pliny, Umbricius, the most skilled of the haruspices, reports that they fly three or two days beforehand to where there will be corpses. Hence Plautus in the Truculentus, in the scene Piscis:


— — vide, ut jam, quasi volturii, triduo
Prius praedivinant quo die esuri sient.

— — see how now, like vultures, they foretell three days
beforehand on what day they will eat.


Aegyptii non triduo, sed septiduo ante, vultures praelii locum designare asserunt, adeoque praevidere, ex qua parte major futura sit strages. Horus Hieroglyphicῶn libri primi capite undecimo, Πολέμου μέλλοντος τελειοῦσθαι, τὸν τόπον ὁρί-ζει, ἐν ᾧ μέλλει ὁ πόλεμος γίνεσθαι, πρὸ ἡμέρων ἑπτὰ ἐπ' αὐτὸν παραγινομένη· Cum belli conficiendi tempus instat, definit locum, in quo pugna committi debet, septem ante diebus ad eum accedens. Et rursus, Πλείονας σφαζομένους, καὶ ἡτ-τωμένους, βλέπει, ταμιευομένη τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἐκ τῶν πτωμάτων τροφήν· παρ' ὃ καὶ οἱ ἀρχαῖοι βασιλεῖς κατασκόπους ἔπεμπον σκεπτομένους κατὰ ποῖον τοῦ πολέμου οἱ γῦπες βλέπουσι μέρος, ἐντεῦθεν σημειούμενοι τοὺς ἡττωμένους. Ubi plures mactandi sint, et qui vincendi, praevidet, ut ex cadaveribus cibum sibi ipsi seponat. Proinde prisci reges exploratores mittebant, qui observarent, in utram aciei partem vultures respicerent, et inde colligerent, quinam esse vincendi. Quae, ut saltem ex parte vera, maxime mirantur ii Patres, qui in Hexaëmeron scripserunt. Basilius Homilia octava, Τίς τοῖς γυψὶ προαπαγγέλλων τῶν ἀνθρώ-πων τὸν θάνατον, ὅταν κατ' ἀλλήλων ἐπιστρατεύσωσιν; ἴδοις γὰρ ἂν μυρίας ἀγέλας γυπῶν τοῖς στρατοπέδοις παρεπομένας, ἐκ τῆς τῶν ὅπλων παρασκευῆς τεκμαιρομένων τὴν ἔκβασιν. Quae Ambrosius ita reddidit, Interrogabo te, tu autem responde mihi: Unde vultures mortem hominum signis quibusdam annuntiare consueverint? Quo indicio edocti atque instructi sint, ut, cum bellum lacrimabile inter se adversae acies instaurant, multo praedictae volucres sequantur agmine, et eo significent, quia multitudo hominum casura sit bello, futura praeda vulturibus? Et Eustathius, Ἡνίκα δέ φασιν ἄνδρες εἰς πόλεμον παρατάσσονται, ἐπ-ακολουθεῖ αὐτοῖς, καὶ οὐκ ἀφίσταται, σαρκοβόρος ὤν· Cum autem homines in aciem instruuntur, sequitur, neque abscedit, cum sit carnis avidus. Unde est, quod cum vulturibus conferuntur haeredipetae. Quo sensu dicit Seneca Epistola nonagesima quinta, Vultur est, cadaver exspectat. Et Martialis libri sexti Epigrammate sexagesimo secundo,

The Egyptians assert that vultures mark out the place of a battle not three days but seven days beforehand, and that they even foresee on which side the greater slaughter will be. Horus, Hieroglyphics book 1, chapter 11: Πολέμου μέλλοντος τελειοῦσθαι, τὸν τόπον ὁρίζει, ἐν ᾧ μέλλει ὁ πόλεμος γίνεσθαι, πρὸ ἡμέρων ἑπτὰ ἐπ' αὐτὸν παραγινομένη· [polemou mellontos teleiousthai, ton topon horizei, en hō mellei ho polemos ginesthai, pro hēmerōn hepta ep' auton paraginomenē] When the time for waging a war is at hand, it marks out the place in which the battle is to be joined, coming to it seven days beforehand. And again: Πλείονας σφαζομένους, καὶ ἡττωμένους, βλέπει, ταμιευομένη τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἐκ τῶν πτωμάτων τροφήν· παρ' ὃ καὶ οἱ ἀρχαῖοι βασιλεῖς κατασκόπους ἔπεμπον σκεπτομένους κατὰ ποῖον τοῦ πολέμου οἱ γῦπες βλέπουσι μέρος, ἐντεῦθεν σημειούμενοι τοὺς ἡττωμένους. [pleionas sphazomenous, kai hēttōmenous, blepei, tamieuomenē tēn heautou ek tōn ptōmatōn trophēn; par' ho kai hoi archaioi basileis kataskopous epempon skeptomenous kata poion tou polemou hoi gypes blepousi meros, enteuthen sēmeioumenoi tous hēttōmenous] It foresees where more are to be slain, and who are to be defeated, so as to set aside food for itself from the corpses. Accordingly the ancient kings used to send out scouts to observe towards which part of the battle line the vultures were looking, and to infer from this who were to be defeated. These things, as being at least partly true, are greatly marvelled at by those Fathers who wrote on the Hexaemeron. Basil, Homily 8: Τίς τοῖς γυψὶ προαπαγγέλλων τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὸν θάνατον, ὅταν κατ' ἀλλήλων ἐπιστρατεύσωσιν; ἴδοις γὰρ ἂν μυρίας ἀγέλας γυπῶν τοῖς στρατοπέδοις παρεπομένας, ἐκ τῆς τῶν ὅπλων παρασκευῆς τεκμαιρομένων τὴν ἔκβασιν. [tis tois gypsi proapangellōn tōn anthrōpōn ton thanaton, hotan kat' allēlōn epistrateusōsin? idois gar an myrias agelas gypōn tois stratopedois parepomenas, ek tēs tōn hoplōn paraskeuēs tekmairomenōn tēn ekbasin] Ambrose rendered this as follows: I will ask you, and you answer me: How is it that vultures are accustomed to announce the death of men by certain signs? By what indication have they been taught and instructed that, when opposing armies begin a lamentable war against each other, these birds follow in a great flock, having foretold it, and thereby signify that a multitude of men will fall in the war, to become prey for the vultures? And Eustathius: Ἡνίκα δέ φασιν ἄνδρες εἰς πόλεμον παρατάσσονται, ἐπακολουθεῖ αὐτοῖς, καὶ οὐκ ἀφίσταται, σαρκοβόρος ὤν· [hēnika de phasin andres eis polemon paratassontai, epakolouthei autois, kai ouk aphistatai, sarkoboros ōn] But when men are drawn up in battle array, it follows and does not depart, since it is greedy for flesh. Hence legacy hunters are compared to vultures. In this sense Seneca says in Epistle 95: He is a vulture, he is waiting for a corpse. And Martial, book 6, Epigram 62:


Cujus vulturis hoc erit cadaver? col. 310 III, 64 Unum addo, pro רחם racham, in Deuteronomio legi רחמה rachama, Foeminina terminatione. Neque enim iis assentior, qui volunt, He in רחמה esse paragogicum: cum etiam Arabice sciam Foemininum رخمة rachama longe saepius occurrere, quam Masculinum رخم racham. Atque, ut monet Damir, الها فيها للجنس in ea voce litera He pertinet ad genus, ne putetur esse He unitatis, ut passim apud Arabes. Sed, quod mirere magis, cum Graece dicatur ὁ γὺψ masculino genere, tamen in versione Graeca Hori Apollinis, scriptoris Aegyptii, semper legitur ἡ γύψ nempe ut respondeat Graeca vox Aegyptiae רחמה rachama, aut alteri huic analogae, quae foeminina erat. Quod ex errore vulgi videtur natum; quia plerisque Aegyptiis persuasum id fuit, vultures omnes esse foeminas, nec eas aliter concipere, quam Noto flanti, vel subsolano, obversas. Horus Hieroglyphicῶn libri primi capite undecimo, Ἄῤῥεν ἐν τούτῳ τῷ γένει τῶν ζώων οὐχ ὑπάρχει, In eo genere animalium mas nullus est. Et postquam alias aves ova solum ad esum, non etiam ad generationem apta, ex vento concipere narravit, Γυπῶν δὲ, ait, οὐχ' ὑπηνέμιον ποιουμένων τὴν ὀχεί-αν ἡ τῶν ὠῶν γένεσις ζωογονεῖται, Vultures autem, quamvis subventaneum faciant congressum (id est, quamvis non aliter concipiant, quam ex vento: nam pro οὐχ lego κἂν, vel εἰ καὶ, aut tale quid), tamen ex illorum ovis generatur animal. Plutarchus in Quaestionibus Romanis Quaestione nonagesima tertia, Εἰ δὲ (ὡς Αἰγύπτιοι μυθολογοῦσι) θῆλυ πᾶν τὸ γένος ἐστὶ καὶ κυΐσκονται δεχόμενοι καταπνέοντα τὸν Ἀπηλιώτην· Si verum est, quod narrant Aegyptii, totum vulturum genus esse foemininum, et concipere subsolani flatu excepto. Ammianus libro decimo septimo, de Aegyptiis; Per vulturem naturae vocabulum pandunt: quia mares nullos posse inter has alites inveniri rationes memorant Physicae. Fortasse pro naturae legendum matris, ut in Homero: Μητέρα δὲ γράφοντες γῦ-πα ζωγραφοῦσι, ἐπειδὴ ἄῤῥην ἐν τούτῳ τῷ γένει τῶν ζώων οὐχ' ὑπάρχει. Tzetzes etiam Chiliadis duodecimae Historia 439. id ipsum, postquam narravit multo uberius, profitetur se hausisse ἐξ Αἰγυπτίων, ex Aegyptiis. In Aegypto igitur haec fabula primum orta est: unde ad reliquas gentes paullatim dimanavit, praecipue post Christum natum, multis doctorum ecclesiae cupide illam amplectentibus, aut ea saltem utentibus, tanquam argumento ad hominem, quod vocant, in eos, qui Christum ex virgine nasci potuisse negabant. Proinde vultures foeminas sine coitu concipere et generare, scribunt e Patrum choro Tertullianus in Valentinianos capite decimo, Origenes contra Celsum libro primo, Ba-silius in Hexaëmeron libri quinti capite vigesimo, Eustathius in Hexaëmeron pagina vigesima septima, Procopius in Esaiam, Isidorus Originum libri duodecimi capite septimo. Quibus addi queant Theophylactus Simocatta Quaestione Physica octava, Phile et Pisidas in Iambis (quos alii tribuunt Cyrillo Alexandrino), Petrus Damianus libri secundi Epistola decima octava, Tzetzes ubi supra, Etymologicus, III, 65 Cyrillus, lexicographus, Scholiastae, quos citavimus, etc. Neque dubito, quin haec sententia, utut falsa et absurda, jam inde a Mosis tempore inter multos obtinuerit. Absit tamen, ut Mosem putemus, eo torrente abreptum, tale quidquam de vulture cogitasse vel per somnium. Hoc tantum volo, in Deu- col. 311 teronomio illum usum voce foeminina רחמה rachama, ut loqueretur cum vulgo. Sed, ne quisquam hoc traheret in erroris patrocinium, idem in Exodo רחם racham masculine dixit.

Whose vulture will this carcass be? col. 310 III, 64 I add one thing: instead of רחם racham, in Deuteronomy we read רחמה rachama, with a feminine ending. For I do not agree with those who hold that the He in רחמה is paragogic, since I know that in Arabic too the feminine رخمة [rakhama] rachama occurs far more often than the masculine رخم [rakham] racham. And, as Damir notes, الها فيها للجنس [al-hā fīhā li-l-jins] in that word the letter He pertains to the genus, lest it be thought to be the He of unity, as commonly among the Arabs. But, what is more surprising, although in Greek one says ὁ γὺψ [ho gyps] in the masculine gender, yet in the Greek version of Horapollo, an Egyptian writer, ἡ γύψ [hē gyps] is always read, evidently so that the Greek word should correspond to the Egyptian רחמה rachama, or to another word analogous to it, which was feminine. This seems to have arisen from a popular error, since most Egyptians were persuaded that all vultures are female, and that they conceive in no other way than by facing the south wind, or the east wind, when it blows. Horus, Hieroglyphica, book 1, chapter 11: Ἄῤῥεν ἐν τούτῳ τῷ γένει τῶν ζώων οὐχ ὑπάρχει [Arrhen en toutō tō genei tōn zōōn ouch hyparchei], In this kind of animal there is no male. And after relating that other birds conceive from the wind eggs fit only for eating, not also for generation, he says: Γυπῶν δὲ οὐχ' ὑπηνέμιον ποιουμένων τὴν ὀχείαν ἡ τῶν ὠῶν γένεσις ζωογονεῖται [Gypōn de ouch hypēnemion poioumenōn tēn ocheian hē tōn ōōn genesis zōogoneitai], But in vultures, although they make a wind-borne union (that is, although they conceive in no other way than from the wind: for instead of οὐχ [ouch] I read κἂν [kan], or εἰ καὶ [ei kai], or something of the kind), a living creature is nevertheless generated from their eggs. Plutarch in the Roman Questions, Question 93: Εἰ δὲ (ὡς Αἰγύπτιοι μυθολογοῦσι) θῆλυ πᾶν τὸ γένος ἐστὶ καὶ κυΐσκονται δεχόμενοι καταπνέοντα τὸν Ἀπηλιώτην· [Ei de (hōs Aigyptioi mythologousi) thēly pan to genos esti kai kyiskontai dechomenoi katapneonta ton Apēliōtēn] If it is true, as the Egyptians relate, that the whole race of vultures is female, and that they conceive by receiving the blast of the east wind. Ammianus, book 17, on the Egyptians: By the vulture they express the word for nature, because natural science records that no males can be found among these birds. Perhaps instead of naturae [nature] we should read matris [mother], as in Homer: Μητέρα δὲ γράφοντες γῦπα ζωγραφοῦσι, ἐπειδὴ ἄῤῥην ἐν τούτῳ τῷ γένει τῶν ζώων οὐχ' ὑπάρχει [Mētera de graphontes gypa zōgraphousi, epeidē arrhēn en toutō tō genei tōn zōōn ouch hyparchei]. Tzetzes too, Chiliad 12, History 439, after relating this very thing much more fully, declares that he drew it ἐξ Αἰγυπτίων [ex Aigyptiōn], from the Egyptians. This fable, then, first arose in Egypt; from there it gradually spread to the other nations, especially after the birth of Christ, since many doctors of the church eagerly embraced it, or at least used it as an argumentum ad hominem, as they call it, against those who denied that Christ could have been born of a virgin. Accordingly, that female vultures conceive and bear without intercourse is written, from the choir of the Fathers, by Tertullian against the Valentinians, chapter 10; Origen against Celsus, book 1; Basil on the Hexaemeron, book 5, chapter 20; Eustathius on the Hexaemeron, page 27; Procopius on Isaiah; Isidore, Etymologies, book 12, chapter 7. To these may be added Theophylact Simocatta, Physical Question 8; Philes, and Pisides in the Iambics (which others attribute to Cyril of Alexandria); Peter Damian, book 2, Letter 18; Tzetzes, as above; the Etymologicum, III, 65 Cyril the lexicographer, the Scholiasts whom we have cited, etc. Nor do I doubt that this opinion, however false and absurd, already prevailed among many from the time of Moses. Far be it from us, however, to think that Moses, swept away by that torrent, ever imagined any such thing about the vulture, even in a dream. I mean only this: that in Deu- col. 311 teronomy he used the feminine word רחמה rachama in order to speak with the common people. But, lest anyone should turn this into a defence of the error, in Exodus he said רחם racham in the masculine.


(1) Rosenmüller, III, 58 Descriptionem ejus avis, quae Arabibus Rachaeme audit, accuratissimam dedit HASSELQUIST in Itiner. p. 286 – 289. vers. germ. qui nomen ei indidit Vulturis percnopteri, capite nudo, gula plumulosa: quo nomine etiam comparet in System. Linn. T. I. P. I. p. 249.

R1 Rosenmüller, III, 58 A most accurate description of this bird, which the Arabs call Rachaeme, was given by Hasselquist [=Fredrik Hasselquist, Iter Palaestinum (1757)] in his Travels, p. 286–289 of the German trans.; he gave it the name Vultur percnopterus, capite nudo, gula plumulosa [with naked head, downy throat], and under this name it also appears in the System. Linn. vol. 1, part 1, p. 249.


Part 2, Book 2, chapter 27: Racham: answers to the objections
------------------------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/racham-objectiones.html

III, 65 col. 311 CAP. XXVII.

III, 65 col. 311 CHAPTER 27.


Ad ea respondetur, quae in Caput praecedens possunt objici.

A reply to the objections that can be made to the preceding chapter.


Cum probaverimus hactenus, רחם racham esse vulturem, nonnulla videntur posse objici, unde sequatur, avem esse, a vulture diversam. Primo enim Arabes, racham definientes, aquilam esse diserte dicunt. Alkazuinius, رخمة طاير النسر Rachama est avis aquila, seu aquilini generis. Alcamus, الانوق العقاب الرخمة Anuk, aquila, rachama. Proinde in Alka- col. 312 zuinio, rachama paritura lapidem afferre dicitur ex India, lapidem alium in ventre habentem, et dolores partus sublevantem, id est, lapidem ἀετίτην, seu aquilinum. Is enim ita describitur. Plinius libri decimi capite tertio, Est lapis iste praegnans, alio, cum quatias, intus in utero sonante. Dioscorides libro quinto, Ἀετίτης λίθος, ὁ ἐν τῷ κινεῖσθαι ἦχον ἀποτελῶν, ὡς ἑτέρου ἐγκύμων λίθου ὑπάρχων· Lapis aquilinus, qui commotus sonat, ceu lapide alio intra se concepto praegnans. Et paullo post, Ἐν δὲ τῷ καιρῷ τῆς ἀποτέξεως, περίαπτε τῷ μηρῷ, καὶ ἐκτὸς ὠδίνων τέξεται. Hora partus femori (parturientis) alliga, et pariet sine dolore. Chrysermus apud Stobaeum Sermone nonagesimo octavo, Ἐν Εὐφράτῃ, ποταμῷ τῆς Παρθίας, γεννᾶται λίθος ἀετίτης καλούμενος· ὃν αἱ μαῖαι ταῖς δυστοκούσαις ἐπὶ τὰς γαστέρας ἐπιτιθέασι, καὶ παραχρῆμα τί-κτουσιν ἄτερ ἀλγηδόνος. In Euphrate, Parthiae amne, lapis gignitur, aëtides dictus: quem obstetrices mulieribus in difficultate partus ventri imponunt, et statim sine dolore pariunt. Porro, cum ἀετίτην, seu aquilinum, ab aquila Graeci appellent, non a vulture γυπίτην, seu vulturinum, sequi videtur, lapidem illum ab aquila, non a vulture afferri. Quod et asserunt prisci scriptores. Plinius ubi supra, Tribus primis et quinto aquilarum generi inaedificatur nido lapis aëtites. Et libri 30. cap. 14. Lapis aëtites in aquilae repertus nido. Et libri trigesimi sexti capite vigesimo primo, Aëtites lapis ex argumento nominis magnam famam habet. III, 66 Reperitur in nidis aquilarum. Sextus, Aquilae lapis in ventre ejus aut nido invenitur. Isidorus Originum libri decimi sexti capite quinto, Aëtites (lege Aëtitae) lapides reperiuntur in nidis aquilarum. Horus de aquila, libri secundi capite quadragesimo sexto; Ἐκεῖνος ἀπὸ θαλάττης, ἢ ἀπὸ γῆς λίθον ἐπαίρει, καὶ τίθησιν εἰς τὴν ἰδίαν νεοττίαν· Haec e terra, vel mari sublatum lapidem in suum infert nidum. Philostratus libri secundi capite septimo, Τὰ δὲ τῶν ὀρνίθων τίς οὐκ οἶδεν, ὡς ἀετοὶ μὲν, καὶ πελαργοὶ, καλιὰς οὐκ ἂν πήξαιντο, μὴ πρό-τερον αὐταῖς ἐναρμόσαντες, ὁ μὲν τὸν ἀετίτην λίθον, ὁ δὲ τὸν λυχνίτην; Quid aves faciant, quis non novit, ut aquilae et ciconiae, quae nunquam nidos exstruunt, quin lapides illis imponant; illa quidem aëtitem, haec vero lychnitem lapidem? Aelianus quoque Historiae libri primi capite trigesimo quinto aquilas nidis imponere scribit τὸν λίθον, ὅσπερ οὖν ἐξ αὐτῶν ἀετίτης κέκληται, lapidem, qui ab ipsis aquilinus vocatur. Sed et ipsi Arabes hunc lapidem docent in aquilae nido reperiri. Damir in capite العقاب Alokab, quae est aquilae species, حجر العقاب حجر يشبه نوي التمر هندي اذا حرك سمع له صوي فاذا كسر لا يري فيه شي يوجد في عش العقاب والعقاب يجلبه من بلد الهند Lapis alokab (seu aquilae) lapis est similis nucleo tamarindi, quo commoto sonus auditur: tamen in eo fracto nihil videtur. Reperitur in nido alokab (aquilae). Et alokab (aquila) illum affert ex India. Et ipse Alkazuinius in capite De نسر seu aquila, اذا كان اوان بيضها فالنسر الذكر يمشي الي بلاد الهند وياتي بحجر يوجد في col. 313 بعض جبالها ويترك تحت الانثي لتخف عليه الالم Cum ova positura est aquila, mas, in Indiam se conferens, inde lapidem affert, qui in nonnullis terrae illius montibus reperitur, et foeminae supponit ad dolores ejus sublevandos. Itaque apud eundem Alkazuinium, cum avis rachama hunc ipsum lapidem dicatur ex India afferre, videtur omnino rachamam pro vera aquila sumsisse. Tertio, cum in censu avium prohibitarum דיה daja tam ex rationibus, quam ex veterum auctoritate, vulturem esse probaverimus, si רחם racham etiam est vultur, eadem avis in eadem serie orationis diversis nominibus bis a Mose interdicetur: quod non videtur posse ferri. Quarto, dici potest, in vulture nihil esse, quod respondeat nomini רחם, a misericordia ducto, et naturali στοργῇ erga pullos: cum vultur sit rapax avis et carnivora,

Since we have so far proved that רחם racham is the vulture, some objections seem possible from which it would follow that it is a bird different from the vulture. First, the Arabs, when they define the racham, say expressly that it is an eagle. Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt]: رخمة طاير النسر [rakhma ṭāyir al-nasr] "The rachama is the eagle bird", that is, of the eagle kind. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: الانوق العقاب الرخمة [al-anūq al-ʿuqāb al-rakhma] "Anuk, eagle, rachama." Accordingly, in Alkazuinius col. 312 the rachama, when about to give birth, is said to bring from India a stone that has another stone in its belly and relieves the pains of birth, that is, the ἀετίτης [aetitēs] stone, or eagle-stone. For it is described thus. Pliny, book 10, chapter 3: "This stone is pregnant, another stone sounding within, in its womb, when you shake it." Dioscorides, book 5: Ἀετίτης λίθος, ὁ ἐν τῷ κινεῖσθαι ἦχον ἀποτελῶν, ὡς ἑτέρου ἐγκύμων λίθου ὑπάρχων· [Aetitēs lithos, ho en tō kineisthai ēchon apotelōn, hōs heterou enkymōn lithou hyparchōn] "The eagle-stone, which makes a sound when moved, as though pregnant with another stone conceived within it." And a little later: Ἐν δὲ τῷ καιρῷ τῆς ἀποτέξεως, περίαπτε τῷ μηρῷ, καὶ ἐκτὸς ὠδίνων τέξεται. [En de tō kairō tēs apotexeōs, periapte tō mērō, kai ektos ōdinōn texetai] "At the hour of birth tie it to the thigh (of the woman in labour), and she will give birth without pain." Chrysermus in Stobaeus, Discourse 98: Ἐν Εὐφράτῃ, ποταμῷ τῆς Παρθίας, γεννᾶται λίθος ἀετίτης καλούμενος· ὃν αἱ μαῖαι ταῖς δυστοκούσαις ἐπὶ τὰς γαστέρας ἐπιτιθέασι, καὶ παραχρῆμα τίκτουσιν ἄτερ ἀλγηδόνος. [En Euphratē, potamō tēs Parthias, gennatai lithos aetitēs kaloumenos; hon hai maiai tais dystokousais epi tas gasteras epititheasi, kai parachrēma tiktousin ater algēdonos] "In the Euphrates, a river of Parthia, a stone is produced called aëtides, which midwives place on the bellies of women in difficult labour, and at once they give birth without pain." Further, since the Greeks call it ἀετίτης [aetitēs], or eagle-stone, from the eagle, and not γυπίτης [gypitēs], or vulture-stone, from the vulture, it seems to follow that this stone is brought by the eagle, not by the vulture. And this is what the ancient writers assert. Pliny, in the place cited: "In the nests of the first three kinds of eagles and of the fifth the aëtites stone is built in." And book 30, ch. 14: "The aëtites stone, found in the nest of the eagle." And book 36, chapter 21: "The aëtites stone has great fame from the meaning of its name. III, 66 It is found in the nests of eagles." Sextus: "The eagle's stone is found in its belly or nest." Isidore, Origines, book 16, chapter 5: "Aëtites (read Aëtitae) stones are found in the nests of eagles." Horus on the eagle, book 2, chapter 46: Ἐκεῖνος ἀπὸ θαλάττης, ἢ ἀπὸ γῆς λίθον ἐπαίρει, καὶ τίθησιν εἰς τὴν ἰδίαν νεοττίαν· [Ekeinos apo thalattēs, ē apo gēs lithon epairei, kai tithēsin eis tēn idian neottian] "It takes up a stone from the land or the sea and brings it into its own nest." Philostratus, book 2, chapter 7: Τὰ δὲ τῶν ὀρνίθων τίς οὐκ οἶδεν, ὡς ἀετοὶ μὲν, καὶ πελαργοὶ, καλιὰς οὐκ ἂν πήξαιντο, μὴ πρότερον αὐταῖς ἐναρμόσαντες, ὁ μὲν τὸν ἀετίτην λίθον, ὁ δὲ τὸν λυχνίτην; [Ta de tōn ornithōn tis ouk oiden, hōs aetoi men, kai pelargoi, kalias ouk an pēxainto, mē proteron autais enarmosantes, ho men ton aetitēn lithon, ho de ton lychnitēn] "Who does not know what birds do: that eagles and storks never build their nests without placing stones in them, the former the aëtites, the latter the lychnites stone?" Aelian too, History, book 1, chapter 35, writes that eagles place in their nests τὸν λίθον, ὅσπερ οὖν ἐξ αὐτῶν ἀετίτης κέκληται [ton lithon, hosper oun ex autōn aetitēs keklētai], "the stone which is called aquiline after them." But the Arabs themselves also teach that this stone is found in the eagle's nest. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], in the chapter on العقاب [al-ʿuqāb] Alokab, which is a species of eagle: حجر العقاب حجر يشبه نوي التمر هندي اذا حرك سمع له صوي فاذا كسر لا يري فيه شي يوجد في عش العقاب والعقاب يجلبه من بلد الهند [ḥajar al-ʿuqāb ḥajar yushbih nawā al-tamr hindī idhā ḥurrika sumiʿa lahu ṣawī fa-idhā kusira lā yurā fīhi shay yūjad fī ʿushsh al-ʿuqāb wa-l-ʿuqāb yajlibuhu min balad al-hind] "The stone of alokab (or of the eagle) is a stone like the kernel of the tamarind; when it is moved a sound is heard, yet when it is broken nothing is seen in it. It is found in the nest of alokab (the eagle). And alokab (the eagle) brings it from India." And Alkazuinius himself, in the chapter On نسر [nasr], or the eagle: اذا كان اوان بيضها فالنسر الذكر يمشي الي بلاد الهند وياتي بحجر يوجد في col. 313 بعض جبالها ويترك تحت الانثي لتخف عليه الالم [idhā kāna awān bayḍihā fa-l-nasr al-dhakar yamshī ilā bilād al-hind wa-yaʾtī bi-ḥajar yūjad fī baʿḍ jibālihā wa-yutrak taḥt al-unthā li-takhiff ʿalayhi al-alam] "When the eagle is about to lay its eggs, the male goes off to India and brings from there a stone that is found in some mountains of that land, and places it under the female to relieve her pains." Therefore, since in the same Alkazuinius the bird rachama is said to bring this very stone from India, he seems altogether to have taken the rachama for a true eagle. Third, since we have proved, both from reasons and from the authority of the ancients, that in the list of forbidden birds דיה daja is the vulture, if רחם racham is also the vulture, the same bird will be forbidden twice by Moses under different names in the same sequence of discourse, which does not seem tolerable. Fourth, it can be said that there is nothing in the vulture that answers to the name רחם, derived from mercy and natural στοργή [storgē] towards the young, since the vulture is a rapacious and carnivorous bird,


— — rostroque immanis adunco,

— — monstrous with its hooked beak,


ut est apud poetam, adeoque aliena maxime a tenerrimis illis affectibus, quibus mater in prolem exardescit: ut non immerito scribat Antonius Liberalis Fabula III, 67 vigesima prima, vulturem esse πάντων ὀρνίθων ἔχθιστον θεοῖς τε, καὶ ἀνθρώ-ποις· καὶ διὰ παντὸς ἵμερον αὐτῷ κρέως καὶ αἵματος ἐνέβαλον ἀνθρωπείου, omnium avium Diis hominibusque invisissimum; cui perpetuum humanae carnis et sanguis desiderium (dii) indiderunt. Quin apud Photium, Auctore ducentesimo vigesimo tertio, Theodorus, vel Diodorus potius, Tarsensis episcopus, vulturem pullos suos nutrire negat. Διὰ τί δέ τινα τῶν ζώων, inquit, οὐ τρέφει τὰ γεννήματα, ὥσπερ πτηνῶν γύπας, καὶ κόρακες; Cur quaedam animalia foetus suos non nutriunt, ut in avibus vultures et corvi? Et infra, Τίς δὲ κόρακας, καὶ γύπας ἐδίδαξεν ἵπτασθαι· οὓς οὐδὲ τρέφειν οἱ γεγεννηκότες πεφύκασι; Quis corvos, aut vultures volare docuit; quos ne quidem alere parentes solent? Sed hae objectiones nullo negotio diluentur.

as the poet has it, and so utterly foreign to those most tender affections with which a mother burns for her offspring. Hence Antoninus Liberalis, Fable III, 67 21, rightly writes that the vulture is πάντων ὀρνίθων ἔχθιστον θεοῖς τε, καὶ ἀνθρώποις· καὶ διὰ παντὸς ἵμερον αὐτῷ κρέως καὶ αἵματος ἐνέβαλον ἀνθρωπείου [pantōn ornithōn echthiston theois te, kai anthrōpois; kai dia pantos himeron autō kreōs kai haimatos enebalon anthrōpeiou], of all birds the most hateful to gods and men; in which (the gods) implanted a perpetual craving for human flesh and blood. Indeed, in Photius, Author 223, Theodore, or rather Diodorus, bishop of Tarsus, denies that the vulture feeds its young. Διὰ τί δέ τινα τῶν ζώων [Dia ti de tina tōn zōōn], he says, οὐ τρέφει τὰ γεννήματα, ὥσπερ πτηνῶν γύπας, καὶ κόρακες; [ou trephei ta gennēmata, hōsper ptēnōn gypas, kai korakes?] Why do some animals not feed their offspring, as among birds vultures and ravens? And below: Τίς δὲ κόρακας, καὶ γύπας ἐδίδαξεν ἵπτασθαι· οὓς οὐδὲ τρέφειν οἱ γεγεννηκότες πεφύκασι; [Tis de korakas, kai gypas edidaxen hiptasthai; hous oude trephein hoi gegennēkotes pephykasi?] Who taught ravens or vultures to fly, whom their parents are not even accustomed to feed? But these objections will be refuted with no trouble.


Arabibus, inquiunt, رخم racham est نسر neser, id est, aquila, non vultur. Respondemus, quosdam Arabes, non tamen omnes, sic definire. Damir enim diserte dicit الرخمه طاير ابقع يشبه النسر في الخلقة Rachama est avis varia, ad aquilae naturam accedens. Itaque ex Damiris sententia non est avis eadem cum aquila, sed duntaxat illi similis. Quod de vulture verissimum, de quo Phile:

Among the Arabs, they say, رخم [rakham] racham is نسر [nasr] neser, that is, the eagle, not the vulture. We answer that some Arabs, though not all, define it so. For Damir expressly says الرخمه طاير ابقع يشبه النسر في الخلقة [al-rakhma ṭāyir abqaʿ yushbih al-nasr fī al-khilqa]: The rachama is a variegated bird, approaching the nature of the eagle. Thus in Damir's opinion it is not the same bird as the eagle, but merely similar to it. This is most true of the vulture, of which Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)] says:


Οὗ τήν τε κεφαλήν γε, βασιλεῦ, καὶ τὸ στόμα,
Κἂν μακρόθεν βλέπῃ τις, αἰετὸν λέγει·

Οὗ τήν τε κεφαλήν γε, βασιλεῦ, καὶ τὸ στόμα, Κἂν μακρόθεν βλέπῃ τις, αἰετὸν λέγει· [Hou tēn te kephalēn ge, basileu, kai to stoma, Kan makrothen blepē tis, aieton legei;]


Cujus caput, o rex, et os si quis eminus videat, aquilam esse dicit. Maxime in aquilarum genere percnopteri vulturinam habent speciem. Unde vocantur γυπ-αίετοι, vultur-aquilae. Aristoteles Historiae libri noni capite trigesimo secundo, Ἔστι δ᾽ ἕτερον γένος (ἀετῶν) περκνόπτερος, etc. γυπὶ ὅμοιος· ὀρειπέλαρ-γος καλεῖται, καὶ γυπαίετος. Plinius libri decimi capite tertio, Quarti (aquilarum) generis est percnopterus, eadem oripelargus, vulturina specie. Alii aegypios vocant. Aelianus Historiae libri secundi capite quadragesimo sexto, Τοὺς δὲ αἰγυπιοὺς, ἐν μεθορίῳ γυπῶν ὄντας καὶ αἰετῶν· Aegypios, qui inter vultures et aquilas medii sunt. Sed et aquilas ex diverso coitu tandem in vultures degenerare, volunt magni scriptores. Plinius, Haliaeeti suum genus non habent, sed ex diverso aquilarum coitu nascuntur. Id quidem, quod ex iis natum est, in ossifragis genus habet, e quibus vultures progenerantur minores: et ex iis magni, qui omnino non generant. Quae sumta sunt ex his Aristotelis Mirabilium, Ἐκ τοῦ col. 314 ζεύγους δὲ τῶν ἀετῶν θάτερον τῶν ἀγόνων ἁλιαίετος γίνεται παραλλὰξ, ἕως ἂν σύζυγα γένηται, ἐκ δὲ τούτων οἱ περκνοὶ, καὶ γῦπες. οὗτοι δὲ οὐκέτι διορίζου-σι περὶ τοὺς γύπας, ἀλλὰ γεννῶσι τοὺς μεγάλους γύπας· οὗτοι δ᾽ εἰσὶν ἄγονοι· Sed locum Aristotelis ita reddidit Plinius, ut, quidquid erat difficile, (nempe verba θάτερον τῶν ἀγόνων, et παραλλὰξ ἕως ἂν σύζυγα γένηται) securo saltu III, 68 praeterierit. Ego priora, nimirum θάτερον τῶν ἀγόνων, corrupta esse puto, et pro iis legendum θάτερον τῶν ἀγενῶν· ut hic sit sensus loci totius, „Ex pa-„ribus aquilis unam ignobilem alternis nasci, haliaeetum scilicet. Et, cum σύ-„ζυγα nata sunt, id est, binae aquilae degeneres, seu bini haliaeeti; ex iis nasci „ossifragas, ex ossifragis percnos et vultures: quorum genus non mutatur am-„plius. Hi enim alios vultures generant, sed majores et steriles“. Cum ex iis, quae dicta sunt, sequatur, inter aquilas et vultures magnam esse cognationem, nemo mirabitur, has aves a scriptoribus saepe confundi, atque unam pro altera sumi. Quod ut exemplis probemus, Promethei jecur ab aquila fuisse exesum, tradunt Hesiodus Theogoniae versu 523. Aeschylus in Prometheo vincto versu 996. Apollonius Argonauticῶν libri secundi versu 1254. et libri tertii versu 851. Actius in Prometheo, Apollodorus libro primo et secundo, Diodorus libro quarto, Philostratus libro secundo, Plutarchus libro De fluminibus in Phasi, Lucianus in Prometheo et in Sacrificiis, Pherecydes libro secundo, Agroetas in Scythicis libro decimo tertio, Duris et Herodorus apud Apollonii Scholiastem, Servius in Virgilii Eclogam sextam, etc. Tamen Fulgentius libro secundo Mythologicῶn Prometheum nobis describit vulturi fero jecur perenne praebentem: et auctores citat Nicagoram in libro Distemithea (lego De Prometheo), et Aristoxenum in Epimetheiorum libro, et Petronium Arbitrum in his Hendecasyllabis,

Whose head and beak, O king, if anyone sees them from afar, he calls it an eagle. Especially among the kinds of eagle, the percnopteri have a vulture-like appearance. Hence they are called γυπαίετοι [gypaietoi], vulture-eagles. Aristotle, History, book 9, chapter 32: Ἔστι δ᾽ ἕτερον γένος (ἀετῶν) περκνόπτερος, etc. γυπὶ ὅμοιος· ὀρειπέλαργος καλεῖται, καὶ γυπαίετος [Esti d᾽ heteron genos (aetōn) perknopteros, etc. gypi homoios; oreipelargos kaleitai, kai gypaietos]. Pliny, book 10, chapter 3: Of the fourth (eagle) kind is the percnopterus, also called oripelargus, of vulture-like appearance. Others call them aegypii. Aelian, History, book 2, chapter 46: Τοὺς δὲ αἰγυπιοὺς, ἐν μεθορίῳ γυπῶν ὄντας καὶ αἰετῶν [Tous de aigypious, en methoriō gypōn ontas kai aietōn]: The aegypii, which are intermediate between vultures and eagles. Moreover, great writers hold that eagles, through mixed mating, at length degenerate into vultures. Pliny: Sea eagles have no kind of their own, but are born from the mixed mating of eagles. What is born of them in turn has its kind among the ossifrages, from which smaller vultures are produced; and from these the great ones, which do not breed at all. This is taken from these words of Aristotle's Marvels: Ἐκ τοῦ col. 314 ζεύγους δὲ τῶν ἀετῶν θάτερον τῶν ἀγόνων ἁλιαίετος γίνεται παραλλὰξ, ἕως ἂν σύζυγα γένηται, ἐκ δὲ τούτων οἱ περκνοὶ, καὶ γῦπες. οὗτοι δὲ οὐκέτι διορίζουσι περὶ τοὺς γύπας, ἀλλὰ γεννῶσι τοὺς μεγάλους γύπας· οὗτοι δ᾽ εἰσὶν ἄγονοι· [Ek tou zeugous de tōn aetōn thateron tōn agonōn haliaietos ginetai parallax, heōs an syzyga genētai, ek de toutōn hoi perknoi, kai gypes. houtoi de ouketi diorizousi peri tous gypas, alla gennōsi tous megalous gypas; houtoi d᾽ eisin agonoi;] But Pliny rendered this passage of Aristotle in such a way that whatever was difficult (namely the words θάτερον τῶν ἀγόνων [thateron tōn agonōn] and παραλλὰξ ἕως ἂν σύζυγα γένηται [parallax heōs an syzyga genētai]) he skipped over with a carefree leap. III, 68 I think the first words, namely θάτερον τῶν ἀγόνων [thateron tōn agonōn], are corrupt, and that θάτερον τῶν ἀγενῶν [thateron tōn agenōn] should be read instead, so that the sense of the whole passage is: "From a pair of eagles, one ignoble chick is born in alternation, namely the sea eagle. And when σύζυγα [syzyga] have been born, that is, two degenerate eagles, or two sea eagles, from them are born ossifrages; from the ossifrages, percni and vultures, whose kind changes no further. For these beget other vultures, but larger and sterile ones." Since it follows from what has been said that there is a close kinship between eagles and vultures, no one will be surprised that these birds are often confused by writers and one taken for the other. To prove this by examples: that the liver of Prometheus was devoured by an eagle is related by Hesiod, Theogony, verse 523; Aeschylus in Prometheus Bound, verse 996; Apollonius, Argonautica, book 2, verse 1254, and book 3, verse 851; Accius in Prometheus; Apollodorus, books 1 and 2; Diodorus, book 4; Philostratus, book 2; Plutarch in the book On Rivers, under Phasis; Lucian in Prometheus and in Sacrifices; Pherecydes, book 2; Agroetas in Scythica, book 13; Duris and Herodorus in the Scholiast on Apollonius; Servius on Virgil's sixth Eclogue, etc. Yet Fulgentius, in book 2 of the Mythologies, describes to us Prometheus offering his ever-renewed liver to a fierce vulture, and cites as authorities Nicagoras in the book Distemithea (I read On Prometheus), Aristoxenus in the book of Epimetheia, and Petronius Arbiter in these Hendecasyllables:


Cui vultur jecur ultimum a) pererrat, Et pectus trahit intimasque fibras, Non est, quem tepidi b) vocant poëtae; Sed cordis mala, livor atque luxus.

The vulture that roams through the depths of the liver a), and tears at the breast and the innermost fibres, is not the one the idle b) poets speak of, but the evils of the heart: envy and excess.


Ubi tamen, pro Non est, quem tepidi, aut lepidi, vocant poetae, quidam non male legunt, Non est, quem Tityum, etc. Quae lectio si admittatur, de Prometheo non egerit Petronius, sed de Tityo; de quo poeta summus libro sexto Aeneidos,

There, however, instead of There is none whom the warm or the charming poets call, some read, not badly, There is none whom Tityus, etc. If this reading is accepted, Petronius would be speaking not of Prometheus but of Tityus, of whom the greatest poet says in book 6 of the Aeneid:


— rostroque immanis vultur obunco
immortale jecur tundens. — —

— and a monstrous vulture with hooked beak, pecking at the immortal liver. — —


Et multo ante fabularum parens Odyss. λ'.

And long before, the father of fables, Odyss. λ' [l]:


Γῦπε δέ μιν ἑκάτερθε παρημένῳ ἧπαρ ἔκειρον,
Δέρτρον ἔσω δύνοντες,

Γῦπε δέ μιν ἑκάτερθε παρημένῳ ἧπαρ ἔκειρον, Δέρτρον ἔσω δύνοντες, [Gype de min hekaterthe parēmenō hēpar ekeiron, Dertron esō dynontes,]


Duo autem vultures utrimque incumbentes jecur fodiebant, cute intus penetrata. Fortasse igitur Petronii verborum prava lectio Fulgentium decepit. At illud Valerii Flacci de herba Promethea Argonauticῶn libri secundi versu 357.

And two vultures, perched on either side, were digging into his liver, having pierced the skin within. Perhaps, then, a corrupt reading of Petronius' words deceived Fulgentius. But consider the passage of Valerius Flaccus on the Promethean herb, Argonautica book 2, line 357:


III, 69 — Prometheae florem de sanguine fibrae
Caucaseum tonitru, nutrita gramina, promit,
Quae sacer ille, nives inter, tristesque pruinas,
Durat, editque cruor, cum gutture vultur adeso
Tollitur e scopulis, et rostro irrorat aperto.

III, 69 — it brings forth the Caucasian flower from the blood of the Promethean flesh, herbage nourished by the thunder,
which that sacred gore, amid the snows and the grim frosts,
hardens and puts forth, when the vulture, its gullet sated,
rises from the crags and sprinkles it from its open beak.


Illud, inquam, Valerii si conferas cum his Apollonii de hac eadem herba Argonauticῶn libri tertii versu 850.

If, I say, you compare this passage of Valerius with these lines of Apollonius on this same herb, Argonautica book 3, line 850:


Πρωτοφυὲς τό γ᾽ ἀνέσχε καταστάξαντος ἔραζε
Αἰετοῦ ὠμηστέω κνημοῖς ἐνὶ Καυκασίοισιν,
Αἱματόεντ᾽ ἰχῶρα Προμηθῆος μογεροῖο.

Πρωτοφυὲς τό γ᾽ ἀνέσχε καταστάξαντος ἔραζε Αἰετοῦ ὠμηστέω κνημοῖς ἐνὶ Καυκασίοισιν, Αἱματόεντ᾽ ἰχῶρα Προμηθῆος μογεροῖο. [Prōtophyes to g' anesche katastaxantos eraze Aietou ōmēsteō knēmois eni Kaukasioisin, Haimatoent' ichōra Promēthēos mogeroio.]


Palam videbis, Valerium ex aquila vulturem fecisse: quomodo e nostris Theophylactus, cum aquilas, de quibus Christus Matth. XXIV, 28. vult pro vulturibus haberi. Ἐπὶ νεκρὸν σῶμα, inquit, συνάγονται ὀξέως οἱ ἀετοὶ, οἱ γῦπες δηλαδή. Ad cadaver aquilae, id est, vultures, statim congregantur. Gesnerus col. 315 quoque, Albertum et alios quosdam recentiores vulturem cum aquila passim confundere, observat. Et se tuetur Albertus Aristotelis auctoritate, quem aquilam et vulturem ad idem genus referre scribit: quod Gesnerus merito negat. Tamen Alberto causa fuit, cur id crederet. Is enim neque Aristotelis Graecum textum legerat, neque Latinam versionem ex Graeco textu, sed ex Arabico expressam. Ita enim ferebant tempora, quibus vixit Albertus. Tum nemo erat inter Latinos, qui Graecos scriptores Graece legeret, aut Latine redderet: tantum Arabes consulebantur, qui, Graece quidquid extabat, in suam linguam transtulerant, et ex illorum versionibus Graeca Latine utcunque reddebant barbari interpretes. Arabes porro vocem نسر neser, quae proprie aquilam sonat, ad vulturem usque extendunt. Unde est, quod τῷ neser ea quandoque tribuunt, quae sunt vulturis propria. Sic ad vulturem pertinet, quod dicit Alkazuinius, النسر يتبع العساكر لطعمه في لحم القتال τὸν neser castra sequi, ut occisorum carnibus vescatur. Item, ياكل الجيف حتي لا يقدر علي الطيران Cadaveribus ita saturari, ut volare amplius non possit. Sed et vulturis potius, quam aquilae, sunt propria haec Damiris in cap. نسر Neser, وهو حاد البصر يري الجيفة من اربع ماية فرسخ وكذلك حاسة شمه الي النهايه لكنه اذا شم الطيب مات لوقت Est acutissimi visus, ita, ut cadaver videat a quadringentis parasangis. Et odoratus pariter in eo est intensissimus. Proinde, cum sentit unguentum, ipso momento moritur. Nam visu quidem III, 70 aquila maxime valet, ut suo loco c) probatum; sed odorandi vis in vulture major esse creditur. Unde Lucretius libro quarto,

you will plainly see that Valerius has made a vulture out of the eagle, just as among our own writers Theophylact does when he wants the eagles of which Christ speaks in Matth. XXIV, 28. to be taken as vultures. Ἐπὶ νεκρὸν σῶμα, he says, συνάγονται ὀξέως οἱ ἀετοὶ, οἱ γῦπες δηλαδή [Epi nekron sōma … synagontai oxeōs hoi aetoi, hoi gypes dēladē]. To a corpse the eagles, that is, the vultures, quickly gather. Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium] col. 315 also observes that Albertus and certain other more recent writers often confuse the vulture with the eagle. And Albertus defends himself with the authority of Aristotle, who, he writes, assigns the eagle and the vulture to the same genus; this Gesner rightly denies. Yet Albertus had a reason for believing it. For he had read neither the Greek text of Aristotle nor a Latin version made from the Greek text, but one made from the Arabic. Such were the times in which Albertus lived. Then there was no one among the Latins who read the Greek writers in Greek or rendered them into Latin: only the Arabs were consulted, who had translated into their own language whatever existed in Greek, and from their versions barbarous translators rendered the Greek works into Latin after a fashion. The Arabs, moreover, extend the word نسر [nasr] neser, which properly means eagle, even to the vulture. Hence they sometimes ascribe to the neser things that are proper to the vulture. Thus what Alkazuinius says belongs to the vulture: النسر يتبع العساكر لطعمه في لحم القتال [al-nasr yatbaʿu al-ʿasākir li-ṭuʿmihi fī laḥm al-qitāl] that the neser follows armies, in order to feed on the flesh of the slain. Likewise, ياكل الجيف حتي لا يقدر علي الطيران [yākulu al-jiyaf ḥattā lā yaqdiru ʿalā al-ṭayarān] that it gorges itself on carcasses so much that it can no longer fly. But these words of Damir too, in the chapter نسر [nasr] Neser, are proper to the vulture rather than to the eagle: وهو حاد البصر يري الجيفة من اربع ماية فرسخ وكذلك حاسة شمه الي النهايه لكنه اذا شم الطيب مات لوقت [wa-huwa ḥādd al-baṣar yarā al-jīfa min arbaʿ māya farsakh wa-kadhālika ḥāssat shammihi ilā al-nihāya lākinnahu idhā shamma al-ṭīb māta li-waqtihi] It has very keen sight, so that it sees a carcass from four hundred parasangs. Its sense of smell is likewise extremely intense. Accordingly, when it smells perfume, it dies on the instant. For in sight the III, 70 eagle is indeed strongest, as was proven in its place c); but the power of smell is believed to be greater in the vulture. Hence Lucretius, book 4:


Mellis apes quamvis longe ducantur odore,
Vulturiique cadaveribus. — —

Though bees are drawn from far by the scent of honey,
and vultures by carcasses. — —


Et Apuleius in Apologia prima, Sin vero e naribus nidorem domesticum praesensit, vincit idem sagacitate odorandi canes et vulturios. Cui enim cani, cui vulturio Alexandrini coeli quidquam ab usque Aeensium finibus oboleat? Et Sidonius libri septimi Epistola decima quarta, Proferunt odorandi subtilitatem, tanquam non praecedat vultur olfactu. Hinc versus in ore vulgi,

And Apuleius in the first Apology: But if he has caught with his nostrils the smell of home cooking, he surpasses dogs and vultures in keenness of scent. For to what dog, to what vulture would anything of the Alexandrian sky be perceptible as far away as the borders of the Aeenses? And Sidonius, book 7, letter 14: They display subtlety of smell, as if the vulture did not excel in scent. Hence the verse in common use:


Vultur odoratu, praecellit aranea tactu.

The vulture excels in smell, the spider in touch.


Isidorus tamen, Originum libri duodecimi capite septimo, vulturibus aquilas jungens, Vultures, inquit, sicut et aquilae, etiam ultra maria cadavera sentiunt. Sed illum, haec scribentem, visum potius, quam odoratum respexisse, palam faciunt sequentia: Altius quippe volantes, multa, quae montium obscuritate celantur, ex alto illi conspiciunt. Verum, ut caetera taceam, hoc saltem, quod addit Arabs, neser, seu aquilam unguenti odore offendi, nonnisi de vulture a veteribus scribi constat. Sic Aristoteles in Mirabilibus, Λέγεται καὶ τοὺς γῦπας ὑπὸ τῆς τῶν μύρων ὀσμῆς ἀποθνήσκειν· Ajunt etiam vultures ab unguentorum odore exanimari.
