d) Bochart, III, 132 P. 361.


(3) Rosenmüller, III, 132 Fabulas esse has de viperis narrationes, Continuator operum Buffonii DE LA CEPEDE T. II. Hist. Nat. des Serpens pag. 35. ostendit.

R3 Rosenmüller, III, 132 That these stories about vipers are fables is shown by Buffon's continuator, de La Cépède, vol. 2, Hist. Nat. des Serpens, p. 35.


(4) Rosenmüller, III, 132 Accuratius in verbi فعي originem variasque notiones inquisivit ALBERT. SCHULTENSIUS in Nott. ad Antholog. Hamasa, Grammaticae Erpenianae subjunct. pag. 420. 421. Ex Arabum Lexicographis ostendit, فعي significare proprie tumido ore flavit, unde usurpetur de parturiente femina, quae, represso diu spiritu, victa tandem dolore cum anhelitu vocem erumpit.

R4 Rosenmüller, III, 132 Albert Schultens inquired more precisely into the origin and various meanings of the verb فعي [faʿā] in his Notes on the Hamasa Anthology, appended to Erpenius's Grammar, pp. 420–421. From the Arab lexicographers he shows that فعي [faʿā] properly means he blew with puffed-out mouth, whence it is used of a woman in labour who, having long held her breath, at last, overcome by pain, bursts out with a gasping cry.


(5) Rosenmüller, III, 132 Non opus videtur hac artificiosa etymologia. Viperae a sibilando, et aperto, vel tumido potius ore flando nomen אפעה, افعي videtur inditum esse.

R5 Rosenmüller, III, 132 This artful etymology seems unnecessary. The viper seems to have been given the name אפעה, افعي [afʿī] from hissing and from blowing with open, or rather puffed-out, mouth.


Part 2, Book 3, chapter 2: The viper of Paul; the brood of vipers
------------------------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/vipera-pauli.html

III, 138 col. 367 CAP. II.

III, 138 col. 367 Chapter 2.


De Vipera Pauli, et cur Pharisaei dicantur progenies Viperarum.

On Paul's viper, and why the Pharisees are called a brood of vipers.


Quidam, naufragio facto, cum in Libyam salvus evasisset, mox in littore col. 368 dormiens, a vipera morsus interiisse narratur. De quo habetur non inelegans Statyllii Flacci Epigramma Anthologiae libri 3. cap. 22.

A certain man, after a shipwreck, is said to have escaped safely to Libya, and soon after, while sleeping on the shore, col. 368 to have died from the bite of a viper. On him there is a not inelegant epigram of Statyllius Flaccus in the Anthology, book 3, ch. 22.


Λαίλαπα καὶ μανίην ὀλοῆς προφυγόντα θαλάσσης
Ναυηγὸν, Λιβυκαῖς κείμενον ἐν ψαμάθοις,
Οὐκ ἑκὰς ἠϊόνων, πυμάτῳ βεβαρημένον ὕπνῳ,
Γυμνὸν, ἀπὸ στυγερῆς ὃς κάμε ναυφθορίης,
Ἔκτανε λυγρὸς ἔχις. τί μάτην πρὸς κύματ᾽ ἐμόχθει,
Τὴν ἐπὶ γῆς φεύγων μοῖραν ὀφειλομένην;

Λαίλαπα καὶ μανίην ὀλοῆς προφυγόντα θαλάσσης Ναυηγὸν, Λιβυκαῖς κείμενον ἐν ψαμάθοις, Οὐκ ἑκὰς ἠϊόνων, πυμάτῳ βεβαρημένον ὕπνῳ, Γυμνὸν, ἀπὸ στυγερῆς ὃς κάμε ναυφθορίης, Ἔκτανε λυγρὸς ἔχις. τί μάτην πρὸς κύματ᾽ ἐμόχθει, Τὴν ἐπὶ γῆς φεύγων μοῖραν ὀφειλομένην; [Lailapa kai maniēn oloēs prophygonta thalassēs / Nauēgon, Libykais keimenon en psamathois, / Ouk hekas ēïonōn, pymatō bebarēmenon hypnō, / Gymnon, apo stygerēs hos kame nauphthoriēs, / Ektane lygros echis. ti matēn pros kymat᾽ emochthei, / Tēn epi gēs pheugōn moiran opheilomenēn?]


Turbinem et insaniam perniciosi maris effugientem naufragum, Libycis in arenis jacentem, non procul a littore, ultimo gravatum somno, nudum, gravi naufragio adhuc laborantem, occidit funesta vipera. Quid cum fluctibus frustra laborabat, fatum, in terra debitum, frustra fugiens? Aliquid simile Paulo accidit. Illum enim, in insulam, Libyae vicinam, e naufragio vix elapsum, vipera statim aggressa est; sed eventu valde dispari. Neque enim Paulo, sed viperae fatalis fuit haec aggressio. Historiam ita incipit Lucas Actor. XXVIII, 3. Cum involvisset Paulus sarmentorum multitudinem, et in pyram imposuisset. Alii, cum congregasset, cum collegisset, cum converrisset. Et Syrus, ܫܩܠ, attulit, copiam sarmentorum. Quod sequitur Arabs Erpenianus. Et alter, usus longa paraphrasi, qua tamen Pauli mentem non assequitur, وبينما بولس يدور ويفتش ليجمع حطبا كثيرا Et, dum Paulus circuibat et disquirebat, ut lignum multum colligeret. Basilius in Hexaëmeron Homilia 9. uno verbo, φρυγανιζομένῳ τῷ Παύλῳ· quod Hebraice esset מקשש, ut Num. XV, 32. cujus Foemininum מקששת 1 Reg. XVII, 10. Sed, cum Lucas habeat συστρέψαντος τοῦ Παύλου φρυγάνων πλῆθος, non possumus aliud intelligere, quam Paulum sarmenta convolvisse (id enim proprie συστρέφειν), vel ut in fascem colligeret, vel, ut jam collecta ad pyram admoveret, cum fasci ferendo par non esset. Sic igitur convoluta sarmenta cum in ignem conjiceret, vipera, e calore prorepens, manui ejus se alligavit. Sarmenta proprie superflua luxuriantis vitis ligna sunt. Sed generalius est Graecum φρύγανα, quo hic utitur Lucas. Nam ἀπὸ τοῦ φρύγειν, ab urendo Graece dicuntur φρύγανα, virgulta quaevis arida, quae facile ignem concipiunt, uno verbo cremia. Porro, col. 369 III, 139 ex hujusmodi sarmentis et virgultis viperas, aliosque id genus serpentes, passim erumpere, satis notum est. Inde in Palladii Lausiacis capite vigesimo Macarius, puteum fodiens, πλησίον θρύων καὶ φρυγάνων ἐκεῖ κειμένων, ὑπὸ ἀσπί-δος ἐδήχθη, prope juncos et sarmenta seu virgulta ibi jacentia, ab aspide morsus est. Et Midam, vinitorem, ὑπὸ ἐχίδνης δηχθέντα, a vipera demorsum, jacuisse narrat Lucianus in Philopseude: Ἀναδοῦντι γὰρ αὐτῷ τὰ κλήματα, inquit, καὶ ταῖς χάραξι περιπλέκοντι, προσέρπυσαν τὸ θυρίον δακεῖν τὸν μέγαν δάκτυλον· Ei enim, dum ligaret palmites, et pedamentis circumligaret, inde adrepentem be-stiam maximum pedis digitum momordisse. Damir capite الاسود seu De Serpente nigro, وقال للذي قال انه يموت حل حطبك فحله فاذا فيه حيه اسود Et (Iesus) illi dixit, cui mortem interminatus fuerat, ut lignum suum (id est, fascem ligni) solveret; quo facto, in eo repertus est serpens niger. Thuanus De vita sua libro tertio, A templo proximo cum mane rediretur, et cuncti propere ad ignem, nondum bene accensum, accederent, ex fasciculo, sive ab imbre, sive a cella subterranea, unde allatus erat, madido, serpens prosiliit, qui expositus, et diu consideratus, amphisbaenae speciem praeferebat. Ita ex virgultis excessit Pauli vipera: nec attigit ea convolventem; quia tum torpebat frigore. Hyems enim erat. Hinc Prudentius ubi supra,

A shipwrecked man who had escaped the whirlwind and the madness of the deadly sea, lying on the Libyan sands not far from the shore, weighed down by his last sleep, naked, still suffering from his grievous shipwreck, a baleful viper killed. Why did he toil in vain against the waves, vainly fleeing the fate owed him on land? Something similar happened to Paul. For when he had barely escaped from shipwreck onto an island near Libya, a viper at once attacked him, but with a very different outcome: this attack proved fatal not to Paul but to the viper. Luke begins the story thus, Actor. XXVIII, 3: When Paul had gathered up a great quantity of brushwood and laid it on the fire. Others render: when he had assembled, when he had collected, when he had swept together. And the Syriac has ܫܩܠ [שקל], he brought, a quantity of brushwood. This is followed by Erpenianus [=the Arabic version edited by Thomas Erpenius (Pentateuch 1622; New Testament 1616)]. The other Arabic version uses a long paraphrase, which nevertheless does not capture Paul's meaning: وبينما بولس يدور ويفتش ليجمع حطبا كثيرا [wa-baynamā Būlus yadūru wa-yufattishu li-yajmaʿa ḥaṭaban kathīran] And while Paul was going about and searching in order to gather much wood. Basil, in Homily 9 on the Hexaemeron, says it in one word: φρυγανιζομένῳ τῷ Παύλῳ [phryganizomenō tō Paulō]; in Hebrew this would be מקשש, as in Num 15:32, whose feminine is מקששת in 1 Reg. XVII, 10. But since Luke has συστρέψαντος τοῦ Παύλου φρυγάνων πλῆθος [systrepsantos tou Paulou phryganōn plēthos], we can understand nothing else than that Paul rolled the brushwood together (for that is the proper sense of συστρέφειν [systrephein]), either to gather it into a bundle, or to move what was already gathered to the fire, since he was not equal to carrying the load. So when he was throwing the brushwood thus bundled into the fire, a viper, creeping out because of the heat, fastened itself on his hand. Sarmenta [brushwood] are properly the superfluous wood of a rank-growing vine. But the Greek φρύγανα [phrygana], which Luke uses here, is more general. For φρύγανα [phrygana] are so called in Greek ἀπὸ τοῦ φρύγειν [apo tou phrygein], from burning: any dry twigs that easily catch fire, in one word cremia [kindling]. Further, col. 369 III, 139 it is well enough known that vipers and other serpents of that kind everywhere burst out of brushwood and twigs of this sort. Hence in Palladius's Lausiac History, chapter 20, Macarius, while digging a well, πλησίον θρύων καὶ φρυγάνων ἐκεῖ κειμένων, ὑπὸ ἀσπίδος ἐδήχθη [plēsion thryōn kai phryganōn ekei keimenōn, hypo aspidos edēchthē], was bitten by an asp near rushes and brushwood or twigs lying there. And Lucian in the Philopseudes relates that Midas, a vinedresser, lay ὑπὸ ἐχίδνης δηχθέντα [hypo echidnēs dēchthenta], bitten by a viper: Ἀναδοῦντι γὰρ αὐτῷ τὰ κλήματα, he says, καὶ ταῖς χάραξι περιπλέκοντι, προσέρπυσαν τὸ θυρίον δακεῖν τὸν μέγαν δάκτυλον [Anadounti gar autō ta klēmata ... kai tais charaxi periplekonti, proserpysan to thyrion dakein ton megan daktylon]; For while he was tying up the vine shoots and binding them around the stakes, the creature crept up from there and bit the big toe of his foot. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], in the chapter الاسود [al-aswad], that is On the black serpent: وقال للذي قال انه يموت حل حطبك فحله فاذا فيه حيه اسود [wa-qāla li-lladhī qāla innahu yamūtu ḥull ḥaṭabaka fa-ḥallahu fa-idhā fīhi ḥayya aswad] And (Jesus) told the man whom he had threatened with death to untie his wood (that is, his bundle of wood); when this was done, a black serpent was found in it. Thuanus, On his own life, book 3: When we were returning in the morning from the nearby church, and all hurried to the fire, which was not yet well lit, a serpent leapt out of a bundle of wood that was wet, either from the rain or from the underground cellar from which it had been brought; when it was laid out and examined for a long time, it had the appearance of an amphisbaena. Thus Paul's viper came out of the twigs; nor did it touch him while he was bundling them, because it was then torpid with cold. For it was winter. Hence Prudentius, in the place cited above:


Paulus, dum fragiles cogere surculos,
Et densare foci congeriem studet,
Incautam cumulis inseruit manum,
Torpebat glacie pigra ubi vipera,
Sarmentis laqueos corporis implicans.

Paul, while he was eager to gather brittle shoots and heap up the pile for the hearth, thrust his unwary hand into the stacks, where a sluggish viper lay torpid with frost, twining the coils of its body in the brushwood.


Sed, cum sarmenta, in quibus latebat vipera, Paulus in pyram conjecisset, illa, sensu caloris vel modico recreata, vel nimio exasperata, Paulum aggressa est. Ut in Gabriae Fabulis,

But when Paul had thrown the brushwood in which the viper lay hidden onto the fire, it, either revived by a moderate sensation of heat or provoked by excessive heat, attacked Paul. As in the Fables of Gabrias:


Ἔθαλπέ τις γεωργὸς ἐν κόλποις ὄφιν,
Ὥρᾳ κρύους· ἐπεὶ δὲ θέρμης ᾔσθετο,
Ἔπληξε τὸν θάλψαντα, κἄκτεινεν τάχος.

Ἔθαλπέ τις γεωργὸς ἐν κόλποις ὄφιν, Ὥρᾳ κρύους· ἐπεὶ δὲ θέρμης ᾔσθετο, Ἔπληξε τὸν θάλψαντα, κἄκτεινεν τάχος. [Ethalpe tis geōrgos en kolpois ophin, / Hōra kryous; epei de thermēs ēstheto, / Eplēxe ton thalpsanta, kakteinen tachos.]


Et apud Phaedrum Fabula septuagesima quinta,

And in Phaedrus, Fable 75:


Gelu rigentem quidam colubram sustulit,
Sinuque fovit, contra se ipsum misericors:
Namque, ut refecta est, necuit hominem protinus.

A certain man picked up a snake stiff with frost and warmed it in his bosom, compassionate against himself: for as soon as it was revived, it straightway killed the man.


Porro Pauli manui haec vipera se illigavit, καθῆψε τῆς χειρὸς αὐτοῦ, nempe ut infenso dente morderet. Vulgatus, Erasmus, Castalio, Beza, reddunt invasit manum ejus; Aethiops, pependit e manu ejus; Syrus et uterque Arabs, momordit manum ejus. In qua ipsa sententia videntur fuisse nonnulli Patrum. III, 140 Ita enim Tertullianus in Scorpiaco, de Paulo: Morsum viperae sprevit. Et Ambrosius in Hexaëmeron libri sexti capite sexto, Paulum momordit vipera. Et Prudentius,

Further, this viper fastened itself to Paul's hand, καθῆψε τῆς χειρὸς αὐτοῦ [kathēpse tēs cheiros autou], namely in order to bite with hostile tooth. The Vulgate translator, Erasmus, Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)], Beza render it attacked his hand; the Ethiopic, it hung from his hand; the Syriac and both Arabic versions, it bit his hand. Some of the Fathers seem to have held this very opinion. III, 140 For thus Tertullian in the Scorpiace, of Paul: He scorned the bite of the viper. And Ambrose in the Hexaemeron, book 6, chapter 6: A viper bit Paul. And Prudentius,


Quae, postquam intepuit fomite fumeo,
Laxavitque ferox colla rigentia,
Iam flecti facilis rettulit ad manum,
Vibrato capite, spicula dentium,
Haerentem digiti vulnere mordicus
Pendentemque gerens Paulus inhorruit.

After it had warmed in the smoky kindling, and fiercely loosened its stiffened neck, now easy to bend, it carried to the hand, with darting head, the barbs of its teeth; and Paul shuddered, bearing it clinging and hanging by its bite from the wound in his finger.


Et Arator libro secundo Historiae Apostolicae,

And Arator, book 2 of the Apostolic History,


— — — — cui vipera fixit
Daemonis arma ferens, surgentibus obvia flammis,
Antiqua feritate manum, gelidique veneni
Vulnus in igne dedit. — — —

— — — — whose hand the viper, bearing the demon's weapons, meeting the rising flames, pierced with its ancient ferocity, and gave a wound of cold poison in the fire. — — —


Oecumenius quoque, Ἡ ἔχις, τῇ τοῦ Ἀποστόλου χειρὶ τοὺς ὀδόντας ἐμβαλοῦσα· Vipera, injectis manui Apostoli dentibus. Ego eundem Deum, qui, misso an-gelo suo, conclusit ora leonum, ne Prophetam morsu laederent, Dan. VI, 22. puto viperam cohibuisse, ne in Apostoli manum noxios dentes defigeret. Quod videntur palam docere haec verba Lucae, ἔπαθεν οὐδὲν κακὸν, nihil mali passus col. 370 est. Nam qui a vipera fuisset morsus, non diceretur fuisse immunis ab omni malo. Neque vero καθάπτειν mordere significat, quod quidem sciam, ut neque pendere, aut invadere, sed illigare, ut simplex ἅπτειν· Xenophon in Cynegetico, Ἐκ τῶν τριμμῶν εἰς τὰ συμφέροντα καθάπτων τοὺς περιδρόμους ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν· Ex tramitibus ad loca commoda humi plagas alligans. Anonymus in Venerem armatam Anthologiae libri quarti capite duodecimo,

Oecumenius likewise: Ἡ ἔχις, τῇ τοῦ Ἀποστόλου χειρὶ τοὺς ὀδόντας ἐμβαλοῦσα· [Hē echis, tē tou Apostolou cheiri tous odontas embalousa] The viper, having driven its teeth into the Apostle's hand. I, however, think that the same God who, sending his angel, shut the mouths of the lions lest they injure the Prophet with their bite, Dan 6:22, restrained the viper so that it did not fix its harmful teeth in the Apostle's hand. This these words of Luke seem plainly to teach: ἔπαθεν οὐδὲν κακὸν [epathen ouden kakon], he suffered no harm col. 370. For one who had been bitten by a viper would not be said to have been free of all harm. Nor indeed does καθάπτειν [kathaptein] mean to bite, so far as I know, nor to hang or to attack, but to fasten, like the simple ἅπτειν [haptein]. Xenophon in the Cynegeticus: Ἐκ τῶν τριμμῶν εἰς τὰ συμφέροντα καθάπτων τοὺς περιδρόμους ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν· [Ek tōn trimmōn eis ta sympheronta kathaptōn tous peridromous epi tēn gēn] Fastening the nets to the ground from the paths to suitable places. An anonymous poet on the armed Venus, Anthology, book 4, chapter 12,


Τίπτε μόθων ἄτλητος, Ἐνυαλίοιο λέλογχας,
Κύπρι; τίς ὁ ψεύσας συγνὰ καθᾶψε μάταν.

Τίπτε μόθων ἄτλητος, Ἐνυαλίοιο λέλογχας, Κύπρι; τίς ὁ ψεύσας συγνὰ καθᾶψε μάταν. [Tipte mothōn atlētos, Enyalioio lelonchas, Kypri; tis ho pseusas sygna kathapse matan.]


Cur, cum pugnas tolerare non possis, Martis arma sortita es, o Venus? Quis mendax molesta haec frustra adalligavit? Ita etiam περικαθάπτειν, circumalligare: ut libro quinto Dioscoridis capite De hydrargyro, Περικαθάπτουσιν ἄμβι-κα περιαλείψαντες πηλῷ, Calicem, luto illitum, circumalligant. Et Nomen καθαπτὸς ligatus. Sic in veteri proverbio apud Hesychium, Καθαπτὰ λύεις, vel, ut alii, κάθαμμα (male in Suida κάθαρμα) id est, Ligata, vel Nodos solvis, quaeque aliis sunt δύσλυτα, insolubilia. Itaque in Lucae verbis καθῆψε τῆς χειρὸς αὐτοῦ, Stephanus supplet ἑαυτὴν, et reddit, alligavit se ejus manui. Quomodo dixit Basilius, eandem historiam referens, Homilia nona in Hexaëmeron, Φρυγανιζομένῳ τῷ Παύλῳ ἐνάψας ὁ ἔχις, supple ἑαυτὸν, Sarmenta colligenti III, 141 Paulo cum vipera se illigasset. Tamen alii pependit reddunt; quia ἀφάπτειν et ἐξανάπτειν est appendere, aut suspendere: et statim sequitur, ὡς δὲ εἶδον οἱ βάρβαροι κρεμάμενον τὸ θηρίον ἐκ τῆς χειρὸς αὐτοῦ, cum barbari bestiam viderunt pendentem e manu ejus. Alii rursus momordit, quasi legerint καθήψατο. Nam καθάπτεσθαί τινος in Passiva voce est, aliquem mordere, non tamen dentibus, sed cavillis et dicteriis. Et vero Chrysostomus in hunc locum pro καθῆ-ψε legit καθήψατο. Quod tamen aliter sumit, nempe pro simplici ἥψατο, id est, invasit. Is enim ita habet in sequenti expositione, Εἶτα ἔχιδνα, ἐκ τῆς θέρμης ἐξελθοῦσα, τῆς χειρὸς αὐτοῦ ἅπτεται· καὶ ὅτι ἥψατο, δῆλον ποιεῖ τοῦ-το ἐκ τῆς ἐπαγωγῆς. Deinde vipera, e calore egressa, manum ipsius invadit: invasisse enim palam facit ex sequentibus. Ita omnino reddendum. Quippe ἅπτεσθαι ἀνθρώπου est hominem invadere, ut ex Platone, Thucydide et Plutarcho probat Stephanus. Unde factum, quod a multis καθῆψε τῆς χειρὸς redditur invasit manum; quasi καθῆψε, vel καθήψατο sit idem, quod ἥψατο. Sed nihil opus quidquam mutare, nec usitato verbo inusitatas notiones affingere, cum apprime id conveniat, ut dicatur vipera Pauli manui se alligasse. Nam id ligare dicitur serpens, quod spiris suis complectitur. Sic apud summum poetam angues duo Laocoontem

Why, since you cannot endure battles, have you been allotted the arms of Mars, O Venus? What liar has vainly fastened these burdensome things on you? Likewise περικαθάπτειν [perikathaptein], to fasten around: as in Dioscorides, book 5, the chapter On quicksilver: Περικαθάπτουσιν ἄμβικα περιαλείψαντες πηλῷ [Perikathaptousin ambika perialeipsantes pēlō], They fasten around a cup smeared with clay. And the noun καθαπτὸς [kathaptos], fastened. So in an old proverb in Hesychius: Καθαπτὰ λύεις [Kathapta lyeis], or, as others have it, κάθαμμα [kathamma] (wrongly κάθαρμα [katharma] in Suidas), that is, You untie things fastened, or knots, things which to others are δύσλυτα [dysluta], insoluble. Accordingly, in Luke's words καθῆψε τῆς χειρὸς αὐτοῦ [kathēpse tēs cheiros autou], Stephanus supplies ἑαυτὴν [heautēn] and renders it fastened itself to his hand. So Basil put it, relating the same story in the ninth Homily on the Hexaemeron: Φρυγανιζομένῳ τῷ Παύλῳ ἐνάψας ὁ ἔχις [Phryganizomenō tō Paulō enapsas ho echis], supply ἑαυτὸν [heauton], when the viper had fastened itself on Paul as he gathered brushwood III, 141. Yet others render it hung, because ἀφάπτειν [aphaptein] and ἐξανάπτειν [exanaptein] mean to hang on or to suspend: and there follows at once ὡς δὲ εἶδον οἱ βάρβαροι κρεμάμενον τὸ θηρίον ἐκ τῆς χειρὸς αὐτοῦ [hōs de eidon hoi barbaroi kremamenon to thērion ek tēs cheiros autou], when the barbarians saw the beast hanging from his hand. Others again render it bit, as if they had read καθήψατο [kathēpsato]. For καθάπτεσθαί τινος [kathaptesthai tinos] in the passive voice means to bite someone, yet not with teeth but with jibes and taunts. And indeed Chrysostom on this passage reads καθήψατο [kathēpsato] for καθῆψε [kathēpse]. But he takes it otherwise, namely for the simple ἥψατο [hēpsato], that is, it attacked. For he has this in the following exposition: Εἶτα ἔχιδνα, ἐκ τῆς θέρμης ἐξελθοῦσα, τῆς χειρὸς αὐτοῦ ἅπτεται· καὶ ὅτι ἥψατο, δῆλον ποιεῖ τοῦτο ἐκ τῆς ἐπαγωγῆς. [Eita echidna, ek tēs thermēs exelthousa, tēs cheiros autou haptetai; kai hoti hēpsato, dēlon poiei touto ek tēs epagōgēs.] Then the viper, coming out from the heat, attacks his hand: and that it attacked he makes plain from what follows. So it must certainly be rendered. For ἅπτεσθαι ἀνθρώπου [haptesthai anthrōpou] is to attack a man, as Stephanus proves from Plato, Thucydides and Plutarch. Hence many render καθῆψε τῆς χειρὸς [kathēpse tēs cheiros] it attacked the hand, as if καθῆψε [kathēpse] or καθήψατο [kathēpsato] were the same as ἥψατο [hēpsato]. But there is no need to change anything, nor to attach unusual meanings to a common word, since it fits perfectly to say that the viper fastened itself to Paul's hand. For a serpent is said to bind what it embraces with its coils. So in the greatest poet two snakes


Corripiunt, spirisque ligant ingentibus. — —

Seize Laocoön and bind him in huge coils. — —


Et in Plutarchi libro Utra anim. draco Aetolae puellae, quam amabat, subiratus, τῷ μὲν ἄλλῳ σπειρήματι τὰς χεῖρας αὐτῆς ἔδησε πρὸς τὸ σῶμα, τῷ δὲ ἀπολήγοντι τῆς οὐρᾶς ἐμαστίγου τὰς κνήμας, reliquo quidem volumine manus ejus corpori adalligavit, dum extrema cauda crura flagellabat. Sic Nicander in Theriacis versu 475. cavendum monet, ne cenchris

And in Plutarch's book Whether land or sea animals, a dragon, somewhat angry with the Aetolian girl whom it loved, τῷ μὲν ἄλλῳ σπειρήματι τὰς χεῖρας αὐτῆς ἔδησε πρὸς τὸ σῶμα, τῷ δὲ ἀπολήγοντι τῆς οὐρᾶς ἐμαστίγου τὰς κνήμας [tō men allō speirēmati tas cheiras autēs edēse pros to sōma, tō de apolēgonti tēs ouras emastigou tas knēmas], bound her hands to her body with the rest of its coil, while it lashed her legs with the tip of its tail. So Nicander in the Theriaca, line 475, warns one to beware lest the cenchris


— — — σε καταφλέξῃ, καὶ ἀνάγχῃ
Πάντοθι μαστίζων οὐρῇ δέμας, — —

— — — σε καταφλέξῃ, καὶ ἀνάγχῃ Πάντοθι μαστίζων οὐρῇ δέμας, — — [se kataphlexē, kai ananchē Pantothi mastizōn ourē demas]


te exurat et constringat corpus, undique cauda feriens. Et Leo Byzantius in Boeoticis apud Plutarchum libro De fluviis, de Cythaerone puero: Ὁ δὲ ὄφις, τοῖς κόλποις περισφίγξας, αὐτὸν ἀνεῖλεν· Serpens eum, nexibus suis constrictum, interemit. Et Cicero de Roscio libro primo De Divinatione; Noctu, lumine apposito exporrecta nutrix animadvertit puerum dormientem, circumplicatum serpentis amplexu. Et libro secundo, De ipso Roscio potest quidem esse falsum, ut circumligatus fuerit anguis. Quo facit, quod Aeliani Historiae libri sexti capite vigesimo primo, draco, qui in elephantem pugnat, τῷ τραχήλῳ περιερ-πόσας, θείνων τῷ οὐραίῳ μέρει, καὶ σφίγγων θατέρῳ, ἀπάγχει τὸ θηρίον ἀήθει βρόχῳ, καὶ καινῷ, cum in collum erepsit, a caudae parte verberans, et col. 371 altera constringens, novo et inusitato laqueo belluam strangulat. Et in caducei descriptione III, 142 apud Macrobium libri primi Saturnalium capite decimo nono: Hi dracones parte media voluminis sui, invicem nodo, quem vocant, Herculis obligantur.

it burns you and constricts the body, striking with its tail on every side. And Leo of Byzantium in the Boeotica, cited by Plutarch in the book On Rivers, says of the boy Cythaeron: Ὁ δὲ ὄφις, τοῖς κόλποις περισφίγξας, αὐτὸν ἀνεῖλεν· [Ho de ophis, tois kolpois perisphingxas, auton aneilen;] The serpent, having bound him tight in its coils, killed him. And Cicero, on Roscius, in the first book On Divination: At night, by the light of a lamp set beside him, the nurse, aroused, noticed the boy sleeping, encircled in the embrace of a serpent. And in the second book: About Roscius himself it may indeed be false that a snake was coiled around him. To this belongs the passage in Aelian's History, book 6, chapter 21, where the dragon that fights the elephant, τῷ τραχήλῳ περιερπόσας, θείνων τῷ οὐραίῳ μέρει, καὶ σφίγγων θατέρῳ, ἀπάγχει τὸ θηρίον ἀήθει βρόχῳ, καὶ καινῷ [tō trachēlō perierposas, theinōn tō ouraiō merei, kai sphingōn naterō, apanchei to thērion aēthei brochō, kai kainō], having crept around its neck, beating it with the tail end, and col. 371 constricting it with the other, strangles the beast with a new and unaccustomed noose. And in the description of the caduceus in Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 1, chapter 19: III, 142 These dragons are bound together at the middle of their coils by the knot they call the knot of Hercules.


Sequitur barbarorum judicium de isto casu, Ut vero barbari viderunt pendentem bestiam e manu ejus, alii aliis dicebant, „Omnino homicida est homo iste, „quem, e mari servatum, justitia non sinit vivere“. Barbari, id est, Melitenses. Tum enim erat Paulus in insula Melite, et Melitenses ideo pro barbaris habebantur, quia plerique insulae illius incolae neque Graeci, neque Romani erant; sed Φοινίκων, ἢ Καρχηδονίων ἄποικοι, Phoenicum, aut Carthaginiensium coloni; ut ex Scylace, Diodoro et Stephano alibi probavimus. Proinde primo bello Punico Romanus consul Atilius, in navali expeditione contra Carthaginienses, Liparam Melitamque, insulas Siciliae nobiles, pervagatus evertit, ut docet Orosius libri quarti capite octavo. Et Punico bello secundo, T. Sempronius a Lilybaeo in insulam Melitam, quae a Carthaginiensibus tenebatur, trajecit. Advenienti Amilcar, Gisgonis filius, praefectus praesidii, cum paullo minus duobus millibus militum, oppidumque in insula traditur. Ita Livius Decadis tertiae libro primo. Atque ipsum Melites nomen Punicum esse docuimus. Fuere igitur Melitenses pars Barbarorum, ut reliqui in Africa Poeni, a quibus tandem ipsa regio Barbaria denominata est. Hi porro, cum viderunt κρεμάμενον τὸ θηρίον, pendentem bestiam, seu viperam, e manu Pauli, etc. Nam θηρίον non solum bestiam in genere, sed et serpentem significat, seu venenatam bestiam. Ut Sirach. XII, 17. Τίς ἐλεήσει ἐπαοιδὸν ὀφιόδηκτον, καὶ πάντας τοὺς προσάγοντας θηρίοις; Quis miserebitur incantatoris, a serpente demorsi, aut ullius eorum, qui accedunt ad be-stias? supple venenatas, id est, viperas, seu serpentes. Dioscorides lib. 1. cap. De vitice; Τὰ φύλλα ὑποθυμιώμενά τε καὶ ὑποστρωννύμενα θηρία διώκει· quae sic reddit Plinius libri vigesimi quarti capite nono, Suffitu quoque (folia) aut substratu fugant venenata. Hinc passim in medicorum libris θηριόδηγμα et θηριόδη-κτος de eo, qui a serpente morsus est, et θηριακὰ φάρμακα, quae venenatis prosunt. Quale est, quod Iosepho Antiquitatum libri secundi capite quinto, Aethiopia terra est θηριοτρόφος, quia multos alit serpentes. Et Galeno θηριοτρό-φοι Μαρσοὶ, quia vescuntur serpentibus. Et Dionysio Halicarnasseo Σῖγμα litera θηριώδης, quia serpentum sibilum imitatur. Sic eadem vox חיה Hebraeis est fera quaevis, et Arabibus serpens. Et apud Chaldaeos parum differunt voces חיוא et חויא: quarum illa bestiam in genere, haec serpentem sonat. Ita igitur Lucae τὸ θηρίον est serpens, adeoque vipera, quam cum barbari pendere vidissent e manu Pauli, cui scilicet se alligaverat, eum homicidam esse collegerunt, id est, aut caedis, aut alius gravis criminis, reum. Species pro genere. Qua figura Furiarum una vocatur Τισιφόνη, ἀπὸ τοῦ τίειν τοὺς φόνους· neque enim caedis solius, sed et reliquorum criminum credebatur esse vindex. Haec autem III, 143 ratio fuit barbaris, cur tam barbarum judicium de viro sancto tulerint, quod il-lum videbant, ex uno malo vix elapsum, mox in aliud incidere: quasi ἡ Δίκη illum vivere non permitteret. Ἡ δίκη, id est, Iustitia, dea. Ita enim vocabant veteres. Hesiodus in Operibus versu 254.

There follows the judgment of the barbarians on this incident: And when the barbarians saw the beast hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though saved from the sea, justice does not allow to live.” The barbarians, that is, the Melitans. For Paul was then on the island of Melite, and the Melitans were counted as barbarians because most of the inhabitants of that island were neither Greeks nor Romans, but Φοινίκων, ἢ Καρχηδονίων ἄποικοι [Phoinikōn, ē Karchēdoniōn apoikoi], colonists of the Phoenicians or of the Carthaginians, as we have proved elsewhere from Scylax, Diodorus and Stephanus. Accordingly, in the First Punic War the Roman consul Atilius, in a naval expedition against the Carthaginians, ranged over and laid waste Lipara and Melita, famous islands of Sicily, as Orosius relates in book 4, chapter 8. And in the Second Punic War, T. Sempronius crossed from Lilybaeum to the island of Melita, which was held by the Carthaginians. On his arrival Hamilcar, son of Gisgo, commander of the garrison, with a little under two thousand soldiers, and the town on the island were surrendered to him. So Livy, Decade 3, book 1. And we have shown that the name Melite itself is Punic. The Melitans, then, were part of the Barbarians, like the other Punic peoples in Africa, from whom the region itself was at length named Barbaria. These, then, when they saw κρεμάμενον τὸ θηρίον [kremamenon to thērion], the beast hanging, that is, the viper, from the hand of Paul, etc. For θηρίον [thērion] signifies not only a beast in general but also a serpent, or a venomous beast. Thus Sir 12:17 Τίς ἐλεήσει ἐπαοιδὸν ὀφιόδηκτον, καὶ πάντας τοὺς προσάγοντας θηρίοις; [Tis eleēsei epaoidon ophiodēkton, kai pantas tous prosagontas thēriois?] Who will pity a charmer bitten by a serpent, or any of those who approach beasts? supply venomous, that is, vipers or serpents. Dioscorides, book 1, the chapter On the chaste-tree: Τὰ φύλλα ὑποθυμιώμενά τε καὶ ὑποστρωννύμενα θηρία διώκει· [Ta phylla hypothymiōmena te kai hypostrōnnymena thēria diōkei;] which Pliny renders thus in book 24, chapter 9: By fumigation too, or when strewn beneath, they (the leaves) drive away venomous creatures. Hence throughout the books of the physicians θηριόδηγμα [thēriodēgma] and θηριόδηκτος [thēriodēktos] are used of one who has been bitten by a serpent, and θηριακὰ φάρμακα [thēriaka pharmaka] of remedies that help against venomous creatures. Of the same kind is the fact that for Josephus, Antiquities, book 2, chapter 5, Ethiopia is a land θηριοτρόφος [thēriotrophos], because it nourishes many serpents. And in Galen the Marsi are θηριοτρόφοι [thēriotrophoi], because they feed on serpents. And in Dionysius of Halicarnassus the letter Σῖγμα [Sigma] is θηριώδης [thēriōdēs], because it imitates the hissing of serpents. So too the same word חיה is for the Hebrews any wild beast, and for the Arabs a serpent. And among the Chaldeans the words חיוא and חויא differ little: the former means beast in general, the latter serpent. Thus in Luke, then, τὸ θηρίον [to thērion] is a serpent, and indeed a viper; and when the barbarians saw it hanging from the hand of Paul, to which it had fastened itself, they concluded that he was a murderer, that is, guilty either of homicide or of some other grave crime. The species stands for the genus. By the same figure one of the Furies is called Τισιφόνη [Tisiphonē], ἀπὸ τοῦ τίειν τοὺς φόνους [apo tou tiein tous phonous]; for she was believed to be the avenger not of homicide alone but of other crimes too. III, 143 And this was the barbarians' reason for passing so barbarous a judgment on a holy man: they saw him, scarcely escaped from one evil, presently fall into another, as though ἡ Δίκη [hē Dikē] would not allow him to live. Ἡ δίκη [Hē dikē], that is, Justice, a goddess; for so the ancients called her. Hesiod, in the Works, verse 254:


Ἡ δέ τε παρθένος ἐστὶ Δίκη, Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα,
Κυδνή τ᾽, αἰδοίη τε Θεοῖς, οἳ Ὄλυμπον ἔχουσιν,
Καί ῥ᾽ ὁπότ᾽ ἄν τίς μιν βλάπτῃ σκολιῶς ὀνοτάζων,
Αὐτίκα παρ᾽ Διῒ πατρὶ καθεζομένη Κρονίωνι,
Γηρύετ᾽ ἀνθρώπων ἄδικον νόον, etc.

Ἡ δέ τε παρθένος ἐστὶ Δίκη, Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα, Κυδνή τ᾽, αἰδοίη τε Θεοῖς, οἳ Ὄλυμπον ἔχουσιν, Καί ῥ᾽ ὁπότ᾽ ἄν τίς μιν βλάπτῃ σκολιῶς ὀνοτάζων, Αὐτίκα παρ᾽ Διῒ πατρὶ καθεζομένη Κρονίωνι, Γηρύετ᾽ ἀνθρώπων ἄδικον νόον, etc. [Hē de te parthenos esti Dikē, Dios ekgegauia, Kydnē t', aidoiē te Theois, hoi Olympon echousin, Kai r' hopot' an tis min blaptē skoliōs onotazōn, Autika par' Dii patri kathezomenē Kroniōni, Gēryet' anthrōpōn adikon noon]


Virgo autem est Dice, Iove prognata, clara, et veneranda diis, qui coelum tenent. Et, cum quis ipsam laeserit oblique convitiis incessens, statim, patri Iovi Saturnio assidens, narrat hominum iniquam mentem. Orpheus Argonauticῶn versu 349.

But there is a virgin, Dice, born of Jove, renowned and venerable to the gods who hold heaven. And whenever anyone harms her, assailing her with crooked insults, at once, seated beside her father Jove, son of Saturn, she tells of the unjust mind of men. Orpheus, Argonautica, verse 349.


— — — τούτου δ᾽ ἐπιμάρτυροί ἔστον col. 372
Ἰθύντειρα Δίκη, καὶ Ἐριννύες αἰνοδότειραι,

— — — τούτου δ᾽ ἐπιμάρτυροί ἔστον [toutou d' epimartyroi eston] col. 372 Ἰθύντειρα Δίκη, καὶ Ἐριννύες αἰνοδότειραι, [Ithynteira Dikē, kai Erinnyes ainodoteirai,]


Hujus (juramenti) testes sint rectrix Dice, et Furiae ultrices. In Euripidis Medea, Iason Medeae sic imprecatur, postquam communium liberorum caede manus polluit, versu 1389.

Of this (oath) let the witnesses be Dice the directress, and the avenging Furies. In Euripides' Medea, Jason curses Medea thus, after she had defiled her hands with the slaughter of their common children, verse 1389.


Ἀλλ᾽ ὁ Ἐριννὺς ὀλέσειε τέκνων,
Φονία τε Δίκη· — —

Ἀλλ᾽ ὁ Ἐριννὺς ὀλέσειε τέκνων, Φονία τε Δίκη· — — [All' ho Erinnys oleseie teknōn, Phonia te Dikē]


Sed te perdat Erinnys caesorum liberorum, et caedis vindex Dice. Aristoteles, aut quisquis est, in fine libri De mundo, ubi de summo Deo; Τῷ δὲ ἀεὶ ξυνέπεται Δίκη τῶν ἀπολειπομένων τοῦ θείου νόμου τιμωρός· Illum semper sequitur Dice, eorum, qui a divina lege defecerint, vindex futura. In Orphei Hymno in Horas, Dice una est filiarum Θέμιδος καὶ Ζηνὸς ἄνακτος, Themidis et Iovis regis. Graphicam hujus picturam nobis exhibet Chrysippus apud Gellium, libri decimi quarti capite quarto, Παρθένος δὲ εἶναι λέγεται, κατὰ σύμβολον τοῦ ἀδιάφθο-ρος εἶναι, καὶ μηδαμῶς ἐνδιδόναι τοῖς κακούργοις· μηδὲ προσίεσθαι, μήτε τοὺς ἐπιεικεῖς λόγους, μήτε παραίτησιν, καὶ δέησιν, μήτε κολακείαν, μήτε ἄλλο μηδὲν τῶν τοιούτων. ὃς ἀκολούθως καὶ σκυθρωπὴ γράφεται, καὶ συνεστηκὸς ἔχουσα τὸ πρόσωπον, καὶ ἔντονον καὶ δεδορκὸς βλέπουσα, etc. Virgo dicitur, ut significetur esse incorrupta, nec malis ullo modo cedere; non orationem modestam, non deprecationem, aut peditionem, non adulationem, non denique tale quidquam ab iis admittere. Quamobrem merito tristis et corrugata fronte pingitur, et vultu contento et torvo, etc. Apud Plutarchum libro De sera Numinis vindicta, si qui sunt, qui scelerum poenas in hac vita nondum perfecte luerint, III, 144 τούτους Δίκη μετὰ τὴν τελευτὴν ὁ δαίμων παραδίδωσι, hos daemon post mortem Dice tradit gravius puniendos. In Arati Phaenomenis aurea aetate cum hominibus familiariter convixisse legitur: argentea quoque, quamvis rarius: sed aenea, postquam coeperunt boves operarios edere, in coelum secessisse,

But may the Erinys of the slain children destroy you, and Dice, avenger of slaughter. Aristotle, or whoever the author is, at the end of the book On the World, where he speaks of the supreme God: Τῷ δὲ ἀεὶ ξυνέπεται Δίκη τῶν ἀπολειπομένων τοῦ θείου νόμου τιμωρός· [Tō de aei xynepetai Dikē tōn apoleipomenōn tou theiou nomou timōros] Him Dice always follows, to be the avenger of those who have fallen away from the divine law. In the Hymn of Orpheus to the Horae, Dice is one of the daughters Θέμιδος καὶ Ζηνὸς ἄνακτος [Themidos kai Zēnos anaktos], of Themis and of Jove the king. Chrysippus, in Gellius, book 14, chapter 4, presents us with a vivid picture of her: Παρθένος δὲ εἶναι λέγεται, κατὰ σύμβολον τοῦ ἀδιάφθορος εἶναι, καὶ μηδαμῶς ἐνδιδόναι τοῖς κακούργοις· μηδὲ προσίεσθαι, μήτε τοὺς ἐπιεικεῖς λόγους, μήτε παραίτησιν, καὶ δέησιν, μήτε κολακείαν, μήτε ἄλλο μηδὲν τῶν τοιούτων. ὃς ἀκολούθως καὶ σκυθρωπὴ γράφεται, καὶ συνεστηκὸς ἔχουσα τὸ πρόσωπον, καὶ ἔντονον καὶ δεδορκὸς βλέπουσα, [Parthenos de einai legetai, kata symbolon tou adiaphthoros einai, kai mēdamōs endidonai tois kakourgois; mēde prosiesthai, mēte tous epieikeis logous, mēte paraitēsin, kai deēsin, mēte kolakeian, mēte allo mēden tōn toioutōn. hos akolouthōs kai skythrōpē graphetai, kai synestēkos echousa to prosōpon, kai entonon kai dedorkos blepousa] etc. She is called a virgin to signify that she is incorruptible and in no way yields to the wicked; that she admits from them no modest speech, no plea for pardon or petition, no flattery, nor anything at all of that kind. For this reason she is rightly painted as stern and with a frowning brow, with an intent and grim countenance, etc. In Plutarch, in the book On the Delays of Divine Vengeance, if there are any who have not yet fully paid the penalty of their crimes in this life, III, 144 τούτους Δίκη μετὰ τὴν τελευτὴν ὁ δαίμων παραδίδωσι [toutous Dikē meta tēn teleutēn ho daimōn paradidōsi], these the daemon after death hands over to Dice to be punished more severely. In Aratus' Phaenomena we read that in the golden age she lived familiarly with men; in the silver age too, though more rarely; but in the bronze age, after they began to eat the working oxen, she withdrew to heaven,


— — — πρῶτοι δὲ βοῶν ἐπάσαντ᾽ ἀροτήρων,
Καὶ τότε μισήσασα Δίκη κείνων γένος ἀνδρῶν
Ἔπταθ’ ὑπουρανίη. — — — —

— — — πρῶτοι δὲ βοῶν ἐπάσαντ᾽ ἀροτήρων, Καὶ τότε μισήσασα Δίκη κείνων γένος ἀνδρῶν Ἔπταθ’ ὑπουρανίη. — — — — [prōtoi de boōn epasant' arotērōn, Kai tote misēsasa Dikē keinōn genos andrōn Eptath' hypouraniē]


Quo alludens Nazianzenus Carmine tertio,

Alluding to which Nazianzen says in his third Poem,


Παρθενικὴ δ᾽, ἀπὸ σεῖο φυγὰς, πρὸς Χριστὸν ἀνέλθοι,
῞Ως τε Δίκη τοπάροιθε βοὸς κταμένου ἀροτῆρος·

Παρθενικὴ δ᾽, ἀπὸ σεῖο φυγὰς, πρὸς Χριστὸν ἀνέλθοι, ῞Ως τε Δίκη τοπάροιθε βοὸς κταμένου ἀροτῆρος· [Parthenikē d', apo seio phygas, pros Christon anelthoi, Hōs te Dikē toparoithe boos ktamenou arotēros]


Virginitas, a te fugitiva, ad Christum redibit, ut Dice olim bove aratore caeso. Nec mirum, Graecae deae famam ad Melitenses devenisse, quorum plerique Phoenices erant: cum ante, quam Romani Melitam occupassent, inter Graecos et Phoenices hujus insulae imperium ita alternaverit, ut modo hos, modo illos penes fuerit summa rerum, ut alibi probavimus ex idoneis testibus. Hujus igitur deae cultum, a Graecis mutuati, illi tribuunt, quod Paulus, e maris periculo ereptus, in aliud statim incidit, priore non minus grave. In quo judicio id quidem placet, quod scelestos statuunt admissi facinoris poenam haudquaquam effugere. Vere enim Plato libro quinto De Legibus, Τιμωρία δ᾽ ἀδικίας ἀκόλουθος πάσης· Poena omnis injustitiae comes est. Et Horatius libri tertii Oda secunda,

Virginity, fleeing from you, will return to Christ, as Dice once did when the ploughing ox was slain. Nor is it surprising that the fame of a Greek goddess reached the Maltese, most of whom were Phoenicians. For before the Romans occupied Malta, rule over this island alternated between the Greeks and the Phoenicians, so that supreme power lay now with these, now with those, as we have proved elsewhere from reliable witnesses. It is to the worship of this goddess, then, borrowed from the Greeks, that they attribute the fact that Paul, snatched from the peril of the sea, at once fell into another, no less grave than the first. In this judgment one thing at least is pleasing: that they hold that the wicked by no means escape the penalty of the crime they have committed. For Plato says truly in the fifth book of the Laws: Τιμωρία δ᾽ ἀδικίας ἀκόλουθος πάσης· [Timōria d' adikias akolouthos pasēs] Punishment is the companion of all injustice. And Horace, book 3, Ode 2,


Raro antecedentem scelestum
Deseruit pede poena claudo.

Rarely has Punishment, though lame of foot,
abandoned the criminal who goes before her.


Et viperas quoque a Deo in impiorum poenam adhiberi, habetur Eccles. XXXIX, 35. (al. 38.) Θηρίων ὀδόντες, καὶ σκορπίοι, καὶ ἔχεις, καὶ ῥομφαῖα ἐκδικοῦσα εἰς ὄλεθρον ἀσεβεῖς· Ferarum dentes, et scorpii, et viperae, et gladius ulciscens ad internecionem impios. Idem de aspide, Thermuti dicta, persuasum fuit Aegy- ptiis. Aelianus libri decimi capite trigesimo primo, Φείδεσθαι μὲν αὐτὴν τῶν ἀγαθῶν, τοὺς δὲ ἀσεβοῦντας ἀποκτιννῦναι. Bonis quidem parcere, impiis au- tem necem afferre: quod si ita se habeat, inquit auctor, τοῦ παντὸς ἂν ἡ δίκη τι-μήσαιτο τὴν δὲ τὴν ἀσπίδα, universi justitia hanc aspidem honoraverit: id est, Dice dea, quae per hanc in malos animadvertat, ut habetur in sequentibus. Itaque in barbarorum judicio de Paulo aliquid fuit non omnino contemnendum. col. 373 Sed et in eodem constat, illos peccare multipliciter. Primo in eo, quod impiorum poenam non referunt ad verum Deum, sed ad idolum, ab hominibus confictum, quod ab his Δίκη, ab aliis Themis, ab aliis Astraea, aut Erigone, III, 145 ab aliis denique Nemesis appellatur, aut Adrastia. 2. Quod sic agunt, quasi ab impiis in hac vita semper reposcantur poenae, cum in futuram saepe differantur, ubi judiciorum tarditatem Deus gravitate compensat. 3. Quod neminem putant in gravem calamitatem incidere, qui non sit idem graviter reus: cum etiam optimis mala accidant, Iobo puta, et caeco nato, quamvis neque ipse, neque parentes ullius insignis peccati rei fuerint, Ioh. IX, 3. Proinde non est metienda cujusquam virtus, aut perversitas, ex prosperis et adversis rebus. Sed eorum, quae latent, judicium Deo soli permittendum, qui summus est omnium arbiter. 4. In eo quoque peccant, quod praeceps judicium de Paulo ferunt. Neque enim eventum exspectant. Sed eum pronuntiant jam periisse, tanquam de ejus exitio tam certi, quam si jam evenisset. Itaque in praeterito dicunt, Iustitia (vel Dice) non permisit eum vivere: ut qui de Davide dicebant Ps. XLI, 9. Grave aliquod scelus ei adhaeret, et, qui decubuit, non resurget amplius. Tamen e lecto surrexit David, contra quam putaverant. Atque idem hic Paulo accidit. Neque enim periit morsu viperae, quam ex ejus manu barbari videbant dependentem.

That vipers too are employed by God for the punishment of the impious is stated in Eccles. XXXIX, 35. (var. 38.): Θηρίων ὀδόντες, καὶ σκορπίοι, καὶ ἔχεις, καὶ ῥομφαῖα ἐκδικοῦσα εἰς ὄλεθρον ἀσεβεῖς [thēriōn odontes, kai skorpioi, kai echeis, kai rhomphaia ekdikousa eis olethron asebeis]; The teeth of wild beasts, and scorpions, and vipers, and the avenging sword, to the destruction of the impious. The Egyptians were convinced of the same about the asp called Thermuthis. Aelian, book 10, chapter 31: Φείδεσθαι μὲν αὐτὴν τῶν ἀγαθῶν, τοὺς δὲ ἀσεβοῦντας ἀποκτιννῦναι [pheidesthai men autēn tōn agathōn, tous de asebountas apoktinnynai]; that it spares the good, but brings death on the impious: and if this is so, says the author, τοῦ παντὸς ἂν ἡ δίκη τιμήσαιτο τὴν δὲ τὴν ἀσπίδα [tou pantos an hē dikē timēsaito tēn de tēn aspida], the justice of the universe would have honoured this asp: that is, the goddess Dike, who through it punishes the wicked, as is stated in what follows. Thus in the barbarians' judgement about Paul there was something not wholly to be despised. col. 373 But it is also clear that in this same judgement they erred in many ways. First, in that they do not refer the punishment of the impious to the true God, but to an idol invented by men, which is called Δίκη [Dikē] by these, Themis by others, Astraea or Erigone by others, III, 145 and by others finally Nemesis or Adrastia. 2. In that they act as though punishment were always exacted from the impious in this life, whereas it is often deferred to the life to come, where God compensates for the slowness of his judgements by their severity. 3. In that they think no one falls into grave calamity who is not also gravely guilty, whereas evils befall even the best, Job, for instance, and the man born blind, although neither he nor his parents were guilty of any notable sin, John 9:3. Consequently no one's virtue or wickedness is to be measured by prosperity and adversity. Rather, judgement of hidden things must be left to God alone, who is the supreme arbiter of all. 4. They also err in passing a hasty judgement on Paul. For they do not wait for the outcome, but declare that he has already perished, as certain of his death as if it had already happened. Thus they speak in the past tense: Justice (or Dike) has not suffered him to live, like those who said of David, Ps 41:9. Some grave crime clings to him, and he who has lain down will rise no more. Yet David rose from his bed, contrary to what they had supposed. And the same happened here to Paul. For he did not perish from the bite of the viper, which the barbarians saw hanging from his hand.


Quin, bestiam in ignem cum excussisset, nihil mali passus est. Ita impletum est, quod Christus Apostolis promiserat, fore, ut serpentes tollerent, Marc. XVI, 18. Et videtur ille serpens Pauli manui se alligasse, non, ut laederet, sed ut ornaret. Fuit enim apud veteres inter armillarum genera ὄφις ἐπικάρπι-ος, aut περιβραχιόνιος, cujus meminere in Athenaeo Nicostratus, Philostratus Epistola trigesima nona, Hesychius et alii: ut a Nonno Dionysiacῶn libro quinto monile describitur, quod

Indeed, when he had shaken off the beast into the fire, he suffered no harm. Thus was fulfilled what Christ had promised the Apostles, that they would take up serpents, Mark 16:18. And that serpent seems to have fastened itself to Paul's hand not to harm it but to adorn it. For among the ancients there was, among the kinds of bracelets, the ὄφις ἐπικάρπιος [ophis epikarpios] or περιβραχιόνιος [peribrachionios], mentioned by Nicostratus in Athenaeus, by Philostratus, Epistle 39, by Hesychius and others; just as a necklace is described by Nonnus, Dionysiaca book 5, which


Ὡς ὄφις ἦν ἑλικῶδες ἔχων δέμας,

Ὡς ὄφις ἦν ἑλικῶδες ἔχων δέμας, [Hōs ophis ēn helikōdes echōn demas,]


Tanquam serpens erat tortuosum habens corpus. Si Oecumenio credimus, vipera in ignem se sponte projecit, tanquam poenas a se exigens, quod corpus invasisset nihil ad se pertinens: Κατὰ τῆς πυρᾶς ἥλατο, inquit, ὥσπερ δίκας ἑαυτὴν εἰσπραττομένη, ὅτι τῷ μηδαμόθεν προσήκοντι προσέβαλε σώματι. Sed Lucas diserte asserit, Paulum illam excusisse, idque in vicinum ignem, non procul in aërem, ut in Prudentio habetur:

Was like a serpent, having a twisted body. If we believe Oecumenius, the viper threw itself into the fire of its own accord, as if exacting punishment from itself for having attacked a body that in no way belonged to it: Κατὰ τῆς πυρᾶς ἥλατο, he says, ὥσπερ δίκας ἑαυτὴν εἰσπραττομένη, ὅτι τῷ μηδαμόθεν προσήκοντι προσέβαλε σώματι [Kata tēs pyras hēlato … hōsper dikas heautēn eisprattomenē, hoti tō mēdamothen prosēkonti prosebale sōmati]. But Luke expressly states that Paul shook it off, and into the nearby fire, not far off into the air, as we have it in Prudentius:


Excussumque procul decutit aspidem:
Abjectus coluber verberat aëra.

And he shakes off the asp, flung far away: the snake, cast off, beats the air.


Hoc ad veterem serpentem, id est, diabolum, referunt, qui, fideles frustra aggressus, in ignem Gehennae detrusus est. Arator ubi supra,

This they refer to the old serpent, that is, the devil, who, having attacked the faithful in vain, was thrust down into the fire of Gehenna. Arator, in the place cited above:


— — — digito nam bestia pendens Excutitur projecta rogis, bene reddita flammae, III, 146 Quam dedit ipsa prius, quae culpae protulit ignem, Unde Gehenna calet. — — —

— — — for the beast hanging from his finger is shaken off, flung onto the pyre, fitly given back to the flame, III, 146 since it had first given that flame itself, which brought forth the fire of guilt, whence Gehenna burns. — — —


Fuit id Pauli miraculum, barbaris maxime improvisum, qui putaverant, αὐτὸν μέλλειν πίμπρασθαι, ἢ καταπίπτειν ἄφνω νεκρὸν, fore, ut intumesceret, aut concideret statim mortuus. Πίμπρασθαι proprie est ardere et exuri; deinde etiam prae ardore inflari et intumescere. Hesychius, Πιμπρᾷν· ἐμπυρίζειν, φυ-σᾶν, καίειν. Aelianus libri primi capite quinquagesimo septimo, Psyllos ait facile sanare eos, qui a ceraste morsi sunt, modo vocentur, πρὶν ἢ πρηθῆναι τὸ πᾶν σῶμα, id est, priusquam totum corpus intumescat. Nam totum corpus iis, varicum modo, tumere scribit Dioscorides. Etymologus de bupresti, oleris specie, Βούπρηστις δέ, φασι, λέγεται διὰ τὸ τοὺς γευσαμένους αὐτῆς μεγάλως πίμπρασθαι, τουτέστι φυσᾶσθαι· Buprestis dicitur, ut ajunt, quia, qui eam de- gustant, maxime intumescunt, quod Graece est πίμπρασθαι. Et Nicander de bupresti animali Alexipharmacῶn versu 344.

This was Paul's miracle, wholly unforeseen by the barbarians, who had supposed αὐτὸν μέλλειν πίμπρασθαι, ἢ καταπίπτειν ἄφνω νεκρὸν [auton mellein pimprasthai, ē katapiptein aphnō nekron], that he would swell up, or suddenly fall down dead. Πίμπρασθαι [Pimprasthai] properly means to burn and to be burnt up; then also to be puffed up by heat and to swell. Hesychius: Πιμπρᾷν· ἐμπυρίζειν, φυσᾶν, καίειν [Pimpran: empyrizein, physan, kaiein]. Aelian, book 1, chapter 57, says that the Psylli easily heal those bitten by the cerastes, provided they are called πρὶν ἢ πρηθῆναι τὸ πᾶν σῶμα [prin ē prēthēnai to pan sōma], that is, before the whole body swells. For Dioscorides writes that their whole body swells like varicose veins. The Etymologicum, on the buprestis, a kind of herb: Βούπρηστις δέ, φασι, λέγεται διὰ τὸ τοὺς γευσαμένους αὐτῆς μεγάλως πίμπρασθαι, τουτέστι φυσᾶσθαι [Bouprēstis de, phasi, legetai dia to tous geusamenous autēs megalōs pimprasthai, toutesti physasthai]; It is called buprestis, they say, because those who taste it swell up greatly, which in Greek is πίμπρασθαι [pimprasthai]. And Nicander on the buprestis, the animal, Alexipharmaca line 344:


Ἡ καί που δαμάλεις ἐριγάστορας ἄλλο τε μόσχους col. 374
Πίμπραται, — — — — —

Ἡ καί που δαμάλεις ἐριγάστορας ἄλλο τε μόσχους [Hē kai pou damaleis erigastoras allo te moschous] col. 374 Πίμπραται, [Pimpratai,] — — — — —


Quae interdum juvencas, interdum ventriosos vitulos inflat. Et in Theriacis de haemorrhoo versu 306.

Which sometimes swells heifers, sometimes pot-bellied calves. And in the Theriaca on the haemorrhous, line 306:


Τῆς γὰρ ὀδαξομένης τὰ μὲν ἀθροὰ πίμπραται οὖλα,

Τῆς γὰρ ὀδαξομένης τὰ μὲν ἀθροὰ πίμπραται οὖλα, [Tēs gar odaxomenēs ta men athroa pimpratai oula,]


Cum illa mordet, intumescunt totae gingivae, aut etiam ardent. Ita enim Scholia- stes, Πίμπραται· ὑποκαίεται, καὶ πυροῦται. Et paullo post, Πυρακτοῦνται, καὶ ἀναβράζουσι. Neque aliter sumitur in Luciano, cum de dipsade dicit, πίμ-πρασθαι ποιεῖ. Sequitur enim, Καὶ βοῶσιν ὥσπερ οἱ ἐν πυρὶ κείμενοι· Et clamant (qui icti sunt), ut qui in igne jacent. Potest igitur in Luca utroque modo reddi. Proinde Arabum unus hic habet, Exspectabant fore, ut يحترق arderet. Et Castalio, illis futurum exspectantibus, ut arderet. Sed Hierony- mus, Existimabant eum in tumorem convertendum, id est, fore, ut intumesceret. Quod sequuntur Arias et Beza, et multi alii recentiorum. Neque id immerito, cum inter symptomata, quae accidunt ex morsu viperae, hoc sit unum e praecipuis, et maxime conspicuis, quod demorsa pars statim intumescit. Dioscori- des libro sexto, Τοῖς δὲ ὑπὸ ἐχίδνης δηχθεῖσιν οἰδεῖ, καὶ ἐφ᾽ ἱκανὸν τὸ σῶμα ξηραίνεται· Iis, qui a vipera morsi sunt, corpus tumet, et vehementer arescit. Nicander, ubi de morsis a vipera, Theriacῶn versu 240.

When she bites, the whole gums swell, or else burn. For so the Scholiast: Πίμπραται· ὑποκαίεται, καὶ πυροῦται [Pimpratai; hypokaietai, kai pyroutai]. And a little later: Πυρακτοῦνται, καὶ ἀναβράζουσι [Pyraktountai, kai anabrazousi]. Nor is it taken otherwise in Lucian, when he says of the dipsas, πίμπρασθαι ποιεῖ [pimprasthai poiei]. For there follows: Καὶ βοῶσιν ὥσπερ οἱ ἐν πυρὶ κείμενοι [Kai boōsin hōsper hoi en pyri keimenoi]; And they (who have been bitten) cry out like those who lie in fire. In Luke, therefore, it can be rendered either way. Accordingly one of the Arabic versions has here: They expected that he would يحترق [yaḥtariq] burn. And Castalio: as they expected that he would burn. But Jerome: They supposed that he would be turned into a swelling, that is, that he would swell up. Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot] and Beza follow this, and many other more recent writers. And not without reason, since among the symptoms that follow the bite of a viper this is one of the chief and most conspicuous: the bitten part swells at once. Dioscorides, book 6: Τοῖς δὲ ὑπὸ ἐχίδνης δηχθεῖσιν οἰδεῖ, καὶ ἐφ᾽ ἱκανὸν τὸ σῶμα ξηραίνεται [Tois de hypo echidnēs dēchtheisin oidei, kai eph᾽ hikanon to sōma xērainetai]; In those bitten by a viper the body swells and dries up severely. Nicander, where he treats of those bitten by a viper, Theriaca, line 240:


— — — φλύκταιναι ἀραιαὶ, Οἷα πυρικμήτοιο χροὸς, κλαδόωσιν ὕπερθεν· III, 147 tumores noxii, ac si corpus sit igne combustum, superne ebulliunt. Ita etiam Paulus Aegineta, Pustulae in commorsa parte erumpunt, veluti in ambustis. Et Aëtius ex vulnere, a vipera inflicto, enasci scribit tumorem biliosum, fervidum, bullosum, subrubrum, etc. Et Avicenna in capite De morsu viperarum ima pagina 137. ثم يظهر ورم حار احمر ذو بثور كثيرة ونفاطات كحرق النار Tunc apparet tumor calidus, ruber, multis bullis, et pustulis plenus, tanquam ex adustione ignis. Quae quidem conveniunt. Sed iis, quae habentur in fine ejusdem capitis, واكثر ما يهلك يهلك في ثلثة ايام وربما بقي الي السابع Plerique eorum, qui pereunt, tertia die pereunt, et quandoque permanent usque ad septimum, videtur posse opponi, quod putabant Melitenses, fore, ut Paulus, a vipera morsus, caderet illico mortuus, quasi morsum viperae sequeretur mors repentina. Respondeo, apud Aëtium τοὺς ἐχιοδήκτους intra septem horas plerumque mori. Et Plinii libri undecimi capite quinquagesimo tertio Scytharum sagittas, viperina sanie tinctas, mortem illico afferre levi tactu (quamvis in Aristotelis Mirabilibus solum legatur, μιγνύουσι τῷ τῆς ἐχίδνης ἰχῶρι, καὶ οὕτω ποιοῦσι θανάσιμον.), et in Pausaniae Boeoticis narratur a Phoenice quodam, ἄνθρωπον ἀποφεύγοντα ὁρ-μὴν ἔχεως, ἐπί τι ἀναδραμεῖν δένδρον, τὸν δὲ ἔχιν. ὡς ἦλθεν ὕστερος, ἀπο-πνεῦσαι πρὸς τὸ δένδρον τοῦ ἰοῦ, καὶ οὐ ζῆν ἔτι τὸν ἄνθρωπον, Hominem, ut insequentis viperae impetum declinaret, in arborem quandam celeri fuga se recepisse, quo cum paullo post venisset vipera, venenum arbori afflasse, et hominem vivere desiisse. Sic apud Arabes جارية giaria viperae genus est, quae statim occidit. Unde Damir in Proverbiis de vipera, رماه الله بافعي جارية وهي التي يموت لذيعها من ساعته Deus objecit illum viperae giariae, id est, conjecit illum in malum immedicabile: quia, qui ab hac vipera morsus est, moritur ipso momento. Nempe perniciosior est viperae morsus pro loci aut col. 375 alimenti ratione, et si jejuna mordet, et aestivis diebus, et prius provocata. Tum enim, accensa bili, venenum fit multo acrius, Praeterea quaedam corpora, et in ipsis corporibus quaedam partes veneno minus obsistunt. Cum igitur tam multae sint causae, cur aut lentius, aut citius viperae morsu perimant, tempus futurae mortis non potest certo definiri. Sed, quae Paulum invaserat, poterat videri venenum habere praesentissimum, quia e mediis ignibus commotior et concitatior eruperat. Itaque ex illius morsu cum timeretur prompta mors, et barbari diu exspectassent, nec Paulo quidquam incommodi accidisset, μεταβαλλόμενοι ἔλεγον Θεὸν αὐτὸν εἶναι, mutati illum Deum esse dicebant, quem prius homicidam esse statuerant. Nempe III, 148 Rustica progenies nescit habere modum.

— — — φλύκταιναι ἀραιαὶ, Οἷα πυρικμήτοιο χροὸς, κλαδόωσιν ὕπερθεν· [phlyktainai araiai, Hoia pyrikmētoio chroos, kladoōsin hyperthen;] III, 147 harmful swellings boil up on the surface, as if the body had been burnt with fire. So also Paul of Aegina: Pustules break out on the bitten part, as in burns. And Aëtius writes that from a wound inflicted by a viper there arises a bilious, hot, blistered, reddish swelling, etc. And Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)], in the chapter On the bite of vipers, at the foot of p. 137: ثم يظهر ورم حار احمر ذو بثور كثيرة ونفاطات كحرق النار [thumma yaẓhar waram ḥārr aḥmar dhū buthūr kathīra wa-nuffāṭāt ka-ḥarq al-nār] Then there appears a hot, red swelling, full of many blisters and pustules, as from burning by fire. These indeed agree. But against what is found at the end of the same chapter, واكثر ما يهلك يهلك في ثلثة ايام وربما بقي الي السابع [wa-akthar mā yahlik yahlik fī thalātha ayyām wa-rubbamā baqiya ilā al-sābiʿ] Most of those who perish, perish on the third day, and sometimes they survive until the seventh, it seems possible to object that the Maltese thought that Paul, bitten by the viper, would fall down dead on the spot, as though sudden death followed a viper's bite. I reply that according to Aëtius τοὺς ἐχιοδήκτους [tous echiodēktous] mostly die within seven hours. And in Pliny, book 11, chapter 53, the arrows of the Scythians, dipped in viper's gore, bring death at once by a light touch (though in the Mirabilia of Aristotle one reads only μιγνύουσι τῷ τῆς ἐχίδνης ἰχῶρι, καὶ οὕτω ποιοῦσι θανάσιμον [mignyousi tō tēs echidnēs ichōri, kai houtō poiousi thanasimon].). And in Pausanias' Boeotica a certain Phoenician relates ἄνθρωπον ἀποφεύγοντα ὁρμὴν ἔχεως, ἐπί τι ἀναδραμεῖν δένδρον, τὸν δὲ ἔχιν. ὡς ἦλθεν ὕστερος, ἀποπνεῦσαι πρὸς τὸ δένδρον τοῦ ἰοῦ, καὶ οὐ ζῆν ἔτι τὸν ἄνθρωπον [anthrōpon apopheugonta hormēn echeōs, epi ti anadramein dendron, ton de echin. hōs ēlthen hysteros, apopneusai pros to dendron tou iou, kai ou zēn eti ton anthrōpon], that a man, to escape the attack of a viper pursuing him, took refuge in swift flight up a certain tree; when the viper came there a little later, it breathed its poison upon the tree, and the man ceased to live. So among the Arabs جارية [jāriya] giaria is a kind of viper that kills at once. Hence Damir, in the Proverbs on the viper: رماه الله بافعي جارية وهي التي يموت لذيعها من ساعته [ramāhu Allāh bi-afʿā jāriya wa-hiya allatī yamūt ladhīʿuhā min sāʿatihi] God has cast him to a giaria viper, that is, has thrown him into an incurable evil: because whoever is bitten by this viper dies that very moment. For a viper's bite is more deadly according to its place col. 375 or food, and if it bites when hungry, and in summer days, and when it has first been provoked. For then, with its bile inflamed, the poison becomes much sharper. Moreover, some bodies, and some parts within bodies, resist poison less. Since, then, there are so many causes why vipers kill by their bite either more slowly or more quickly, the time of the coming death cannot be fixed with certainty. But the viper that had attacked Paul could seem to have a most potent poison, because it had burst out of the midst of the fire more agitated and roused. So since a speedy death was feared from its bite, and the barbarians had waited a long time, and no harm had come to Paul, μεταβαλλόμενοι ἔλεγον Θεὸν αὐτὸν εἶναι [metaballomenoi elegon Theon auton einai], changing their minds they said he was a god, whom they had previously judged to be a murderer. Indeed, III, 148 The rustic brood knows no measure.


Et

And


Dum stulti vitant vitia, in contraria currunt.

While fools avoid vices, they run into the opposite ones.


Ut homicida non erat Paulus, ita nec Deus, sed fidelissimus Dei servus. Antea in charitatem, nunc in fidem graviter peccant. Nimirum, ut notat Oecumenius, gentiles ita solebant, πάντα ποιοῦντά τι παράδοξον Θεὸν νομίζειν, pro Deo quemlibet habere, qui mirabile aliquid ederet. Ita Lystrenses huic eidem Paulo divinos honores decreverunt, quia claudum sanaverat: sed et eundem iidem paulo post lapidaverunt: Act. XIV, 10. 19.

As Paul was not a murderer, so neither was he a god, but a most faithful servant of God. Before, they sinned gravely against charity; now against faith. For, as Oecumenius notes, the gentiles were accustomed πάντα ποιοῦντά τι παράδοξον Θεὸν νομίζειν [panta poiounta ti paradoxon Theon nomizein], to take for a god anyone who performed something marvellous. Thus the people of Lystra decreed divine honours to this same Paul because he had healed a lame man; but a little later the same people stoned him: Acts 14:10 19.


Multi quaerunt, quorsum Iudaei, aut Pharisaei passim a) vocentur γεννή-ματα ἐχιδνῶν, progenies viperarum. Et ad id alludi plerique putant, quod vipera ex eroso matris utero nasci traditur. Quia Iudaei in Deum et Prophetas, quos patrum loco habere debuerant, ingratos se praestiterunt. Vide praeter eos, qui in Matthaeum et Lucam ex professo scripserunt, Isidorum Pelusiotam Epistola centesima quinta, et Parabolarum Evangelii interpretationes, quae Athanasio tribuuntur, Quaestione vigesima. Mihi non fit verisimile, ad rem fabulosam alludi; neque Deum et Prophetas hac ratione cum viperis conferri. Iis igitur accedo, qui pessimorum parentum pessimos filios hic intelligunt. Nempe κακοῦ κόρακος κακὸν ὠὸν, Mali corvi malum ovum est. Quo respiciens martyr, Stephanus, Iudaeos ita compellat Act. VII, 51. O duri cervice, et incircumcisi corde et auribus, vos semper Spiritui Sancto obsistitis. Quales fuerunt patres vestri, tales et vos estis. Et multo ante David Psalm. LXXVIII, 8. Ne sint ut patres eorum, generatio contumax et rebellis, etc. Nec multum repugnabo, si quis viperarum nomine daemones intelligat, qui cur per serpentes significentur, neminem latet. Daemonis porro filii censentur, quotquot in Deum sunt rebelles. Proinde magum, Elymam, Paulus vocat filium diaboli Act. XIII, 8. Et Christus Iudaeis dicit Ioh. VIII, 44. Vos ex patre, diabolo, estis, et desideria patris vestri vultis facere. Aliud δεινῆς ἐχίδνης θρέμμα in Trachiniis Sophoclis versu 1106. Ibi enim ἐχίδνη non est vipera, sed fabulosa Echidna, ex qua natus Cerberus. De illo enim ibi agitur.

Many ask why the Jews, or the Pharisees, are repeatedly a) called γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν [gennēmata echidnōn], brood of vipers. Most think that this alludes to the tradition that the viper is born by gnawing through its mother's womb, because the Jews showed themselves ungrateful toward God and the Prophets, whom they ought to have regarded as fathers. See, besides those who have written expressly on Matthew and Luke, Isidore of Pelusium, Epistle 105, and the Interpretations of the Parables of the Gospel ascribed to Athanasius, Question 20. To me it does not seem likely that a fabulous matter is alluded to, or that God and the Prophets are in this way compared with vipers. I therefore side with those who understand here the very wicked sons of very wicked parents. That is, κακοῦ κόρακος κακὸν ὠὸν [kakou korakos kakon ōon], A bad crow lays a bad egg. With this in view the martyr Stephen addresses the Jews thus, Acts 7:51. O stiff-necked, and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers were, so are you also. And long before, David, Ps 78:8: That they might not be like their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation, etc. Nor shall I much object if someone understands by the name of vipers the demons; why these are signified by serpents is known to everyone. Moreover, all who rebel against God are reckoned sons of the devil. Accordingly Paul calls the magician Elymas a son of the devil, Acts 13:8. And Christ says to the Jews, John 8:44. You are of your father, the devil, and you want to do the desires of your father. The δεινῆς ἐχίδνης θρέμμα [deinēs echidnēs thremma] in Sophocles' Trachiniae, line 1106, is something else. For there ἐχίδνη [echidnē] is not a viper but the fabulous Echidna, from whom Cerberus was born; for it is he who is spoken of there.


a) Bochart, III, 148 Matth. III, 7. et XII, 34. et XXIII, 33. Luc. III, 7.

a) Bochart, III, 148 Matt 3:7 and XII, 34. and XXIII, 33. Luke 3:7.


Part 2, Book 3, chapter 3: Chephir and sachal are also names of serpents
------------------------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/chephir-sachal.html

III, 149 col. 375 CAP. III.

III, 149 col. 375 Chapter 3.


Probatur, כפיר chephir, et שחל sachal, non solum lconum, ut vulgo, sed et serpentum esse nomina.

It is proved that כפיר chephir and שחל sachal are names not only of lions, as is commonly held, but also of serpents.


Leonis nomen nonnnullis animalibus commune est, a leone diversissimis. Sic col. 376 Diphilus in Athenaeo, Plinius et Aelianus λέοντα θαλάττιον, leonem marinum describunt inter astacorum genera. Lacertae vel stellionis species est ὁ χαμαιλέων, id est, terrestris leo; qui idem Arabice vocatur a) ليث عفرين leo Iphrina, ab Arabiae loco, in quo frequens est. Quale, quod ليث, leo, in Alcamus est ضرب من العناكب, araneae species. Et in serpentum genere cenchris, seu cenchrine (1), a nonnullis vocatur λέων αἴολος, leo varius. Nicander in Theriacis versu 463.

The name of the lion is shared by several animals very different from the lion. Thus col. 376 Diphilus in Athenaeus, Pliny and Aelian describe a λέοντα θαλάττιον [leonta thalattion], a sea lion, among the kinds of lobster. A species of lizard or gecko is ὁ χαμαιλέων [ho chamaileōn], that is, the ground lion; in Arabic the same animal is called a) ليث عفرين [layth ʿifrīn], the lion of Iphrin, from a place in Arabia where it is common. Similar is the fact that ليث [layth], lion, in Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] is ضرب من العناكب [ḍarb min al-ʿanākib], a species of spider. And in the serpent kind the cenchris or cenchrines R1 is called by some λέων αἴολος [leōn aiolos], the variegated lion. Nicander in the Theriaca, line 463:


Δήεις κεγχρίνου δολιχὸν τέρας, ὅν τε λέοντα
Αἴολον αὐδάξαντο, περίστικτον φολίδεσσι·

Δήεις κεγχρίνου δολιχὸν τέρας, ὅν τε λέοντα Αἴολον αὐδάξαντο, περίστικτον φολίδεσσι· [Dēeis kenchrinou dolichon teras, hon te leonta / Aiolon audaxanto, peristikton pholidessi]


Invenies cenchrinis longum monstrum, quem et leonem varium vocarunt, squamis maculosum. Ad quae verba Scholiastes, Ἔστι δὲ οὗτος μακρὸς κατάστικτος, ὃν καὶ λέοντά φησι καλεῖν· ἢ διὰ τὸ πολύστικτον τῶν φολίδων· ἢ διὰ δὲ γενναῖον λέοντα ἐκάλουν αὐτόν· ἤτοι διὰ τὸ ὀρθὴν τὴν οὐρὰν βαστάζοντα διεγείρειν ἑαυ-τὸν εἰς μάχην· ἢ διὰ τὸ δάκνειν, καὶ ῥοφᾷν τὸ αἷμα τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, ἅτινα δὲ καὶ λέων ποιεῖ. In quibus verbis cur dicatur leo vocari διὰ τὸ πολύστικτον τῶν φολίδων, propter squamas maculosas, cum in leone nihil tale est. Sed scripserat Scholiastes, ὃν καὶ λέοντα αἰολόν φησι καλεῖν. Itaque mens ejus haec est, leonem quidem vocari propter generosum animum; aut quia erecta cauda ad pugnam se incitat; aut quia leonum more mordet, et humanum sanguinem exsorbet: varium autem appellari propter maculas, squamis adspersas. Utut sit, hinc patet, Graecos quoque leonum nomen serpentibus adhibuisse: ne cui novum videatur, quod Hebraea leonum nomina כפיר chephir, et שחל sachal, etiam ad serpentes pertinent. Inde est, quod, cum כפיר chephir proprie leunculum sonet, tamen a Senioribus nonnunquam pro dracone sumitur. Sic Iob. IV, 10. Hebraea ושני כפירים נתעו, Et dentes chephirim (seu leunculorum) avulsi sunt, reddunt mira libertate, γαυρίαμα δὲ δρακόντων ἐσβέσθη, draconum autem gloriatio extincta est. Et Iob. XXXVIII, 39. pro Hebraeis וחית כפירים תמלא, An animam leunculorum III, 150 implebis? iidem habent, Ψυχὰς δὲ δρακόντων ἐμπλήσεις; Animas autem draconum an explebis? Nempe כפיר chephir apud Hebraeos non solum le- unculum, sed et dracunculum sonabat (2). Quomodo Arabicum شبل sabl, quod Hebraeo כפיר chephir plane respondet, et pro leunculo fere sumitur. Tamen etiam de catulo draconis usurpari, docent haec Arabici paraphrastis Thren. IV, 3. والتنانين خلعوا ثديهم اشبالهم ارضعوا Et draco- nes mammas eduxerunt, catulos suos lactarunt. Dracones nempe marini, id est, cete, ut Hebraice תנין, et Graece δράκοντες hoc ipso loco.

You will find the long monster of the cenchrines, which they have also called the variegated lion, spotted with scales. On these words the Scholiast says: Ἔστι δὲ οὗτος μακρὸς κατάστικτος, ὃν καὶ λέοντά φησι καλεῖν· ἢ διὰ τὸ πολύστικτον τῶν φολίδων· ἢ διὰ δὲ γενναῖον λέοντα ἐκάλουν αὐτόν· ἤτοι διὰ τὸ ὀρθὴν τὴν οὐρὰν βαστάζοντα διεγείρειν ἑαυτὸν εἰς μάχην· ἢ διὰ τὸ δάκνειν, καὶ ῥοφᾷν τὸ αἷμα τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, ἅτινα δὲ καὶ λέων ποιεῖ [Esti de houtos makros katastiktos, hon kai leonta phēsi kalein; ē dia to polystikton tōn pholidōn; ē dia de gennaion leonta ekaloun auton; ētoi dia to orthēn tēn ouran bastazonta diegeirein heauton eis machēn; ē dia to daknein, kai rhophan to haima tou anthrōpou, hatina de kai leōn poiei]. In these words, why should it be said that it is called lion διὰ τὸ πολύστικτον τῶν φολίδων [dia to polystikton tōn pholidōn], on account of its spotted scales, when there is nothing of the kind in the lion? But the Scholiast had written ὃν καὶ λέοντα αἰολόν φησι καλεῖν [hon kai leonta aiolon phēsi kalein]. His meaning, then, is this: it is called lion because of its noble spirit; or because it rouses itself to fight with its tail erect; or because it bites in the manner of lions and sucks out human blood; but it is called variegated because of the spots sprinkled over its scales. However that may be, it is clear from this that the Greeks too applied the name of lions to serpents, so that no one should find it strange that the Hebrew names of lions, כפיר chephir and שחל sachal, also apply to serpents. Hence, although כפיר chephir properly means young lion, it is nevertheless sometimes taken by the Elders for a dragon. Thus in Iob. IV, 10 they render the Hebrew ושני כפירים נתעו, And the teeth of the chephirim (or young lions) are torn out, with remarkable freedom as γαυρίαμα δὲ δρακόντων ἐσβέσθη [gauriama de drakontōn esbesthē], but the boasting of the dragons is extinguished. And in Job 38:39, for the Hebrew וחית כפירים תמלא, Will you fill the appetite of the young lions? III, 150 they have Ψυχὰς δὲ δρακόντων ἐμπλήσεις; [Psychas de drakontōn emplēseis;] Will you satisfy the appetites of the dragons? Evidently כפיר chephir among the Hebrews meant not only young lion but also young dragon R2. So too the Arabic شبل [shibl] sabl, which corresponds exactly to the Hebrew כפיר chephir, is generally taken for a young lion. Yet that it is also used of the young of a dragon is shown by these words of the Arabic paraphrast on Thren. IV, 3.: والتنانين خلعوا ثديهم اشبالهم ارضعوا [wa-l-tanānīn khalaʿū thudīyahum ashbālahum arḍaʿū] And the dragons drew out their breasts, they suckled their young. Sea dragons, that is, whales, as is the Hebrew תנין and the Greek δράκοντες [drakontes] in this very passage.


Ita vox שחל sachal, cum alibi leonem sonet, tamen Psal. XCI, 13. pro aspi- de, aut alio serpente, sumunt vetustissimi interpretes. Ubi Hebraea verba על שחל ופתן תדרך, Seniores exponunt, Ἐπ᾽ ἀσπίδα καὶ βασιλίσκον ἐπιβήσῃ. Et Vulgatus, Super aspidem et basiliscum ambulabis. Et Hieronymus, Super aspi- col. 377 dem et basiliscum calcabis. Et Apollinaris,

Likewise the word שחל sachal, although elsewhere it means lion, is nevertheless taken by the most ancient translators in Ps 91:13 for the asp or some other serpent. There the Elders render the Hebrew words על שחל ופתן תדרך as Ἐπ᾽ ἀσπίδα καὶ βασιλίσκον ἐπιβήσῃ [Ep᾽ aspida kai basiliskon epibēsē]. And the Vulgate translator: You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk. And Jerome: You shall tread upon the asp col. 377 and the basilisk. And Apollinaris:


Ἀσπίδα θαρσαλέως ἐπιβήσῃ, καὶ βασιλίσκον.

Ἀσπίδα θαρσαλέως ἐπιβήσῃ, καὶ βασιλίσκον. [Aspida tharsaleōs epibēsē, kai basiliskon.]


Et Syrus, ܥܠ ܓܪܣܐ ܘܥܠ ܚܪܡܢܐ ܬܕܘܫ Et Arabs, تطا علي الافعي والحية التنين Et Aethiops, ላዕለ፡ ተኵላ፡ ወከይሲ፡ ትጼዐን፡ Omnes eodem sensu. Neque enim eorum ullus leonem hic intelligit voce שחל, sed serpentis aliquod genus. Quamvis de specie inter illos non conveniat. Nam Arabi שחל est الافعي, vipera, Syro ܓܪܣܐ, amphisbaena, Aethiopi ተኵላ፡ serpentis genus, a lupino ingenio sic appellati. Et toto illo versu על שחל ופתן תדרך תרמס כפיר ותנין, Davidem verisimile est solum egisse de serpentibus, adeoque vocibus כפיר et שחל tam angues intelligi, quam vocibus פתן et תנין; quarum illa aspidem, haec draconem significat. Sic enim omnia melius cohaerebunt; quam si leones cum serpentibus permisceas: ut novi interpretes, qui fere hic habent: Super leonem et basiliscum ambulabis, conculcabis leunculum et dra- conem. In quibus verbis praeter quam ferae junguntur plane diversae naturae, nemo facile dixerit, quid sit ambulare super leonem, aut calcare leunculum. Neque enim quisquam est, qui leonem ambulando calcet, quomodo solemus aspides et anguium reliqua genera (3).

And the Syriac: ܥܠ ܓܪܣܐ ܘܥܠ ܚܪܡܢܐ ܬܕܘܫ [על גרסא ועל חרמנא תדוש]. And the Arabic: تطا علي الافعي والحية التنين [taṭā ʿalī al-afʿī wa-l-ḥayya al-tinnīn]. And the Ethiopic: ላዕለ፡ ተኵላ፡ ወከይሲ፡ ትጼዐን፡ [lāʿəla takʷəlā wakayəsi təṣēʿan] All in the same sense. For none of them understands a lion here by the word שחל, but some kind of serpent, although they do not agree on the species. For to the Arabic translator שחל is الافعي [al-afʿī], the viper; to the Syriac ܓܪܣܐ [גרסא], the amphisbaena; to the Ethiopic ተኵላ፡ [takʷəlā], a kind of serpent so called from its wolf-like nature. And in that whole verse, על שחל ופתן תדרך תרמס כפיר ותנין, it is probable that David dealt only with serpents, and therefore that by the words כפיר and שחל snakes are meant just as much as by the words פתן and תנין, of which the former signifies the asp, the latter the dragon. For thus everything will cohere better than if you mix lions with serpents, as the modern translators do, who here generally have: You shall walk upon the lion and the basilisk, you shall trample the young lion and the dragon. In these words, besides the fact that beasts of entirely different nature are joined together, no one could easily say what it means to walk upon a lion or to tread on a young lion. For there is no one who treads on a lion while walking, as we commonly do on asps and the other kinds of snakes R3.


III, 151 Iam, si quaeras, quod anguis genus significetur nomine שחל sachal, respondebo, ut in leonibus שחל sachal dicitur, qui niger est, ut suo loco b) docuimus, ita etiam nigrum serpentem eadem voce designari. Cujusmodi Nicander in Theriacis multos describit: ut cum scribit de aspide versu 172.

III, 151 Now, if you ask what kind of snake is signified by the name שחל sachal, I will answer: just as among lions the one called שחל sachal is the one that is black, as we showed in its place b), so also a black serpent is designated by the same word. Nicander in the Theriaca describes many of this kind, as when he writes of the asp in verse 172.

Color autem in scabro dorso quandoque melinus occurrit, et varius, quandoque cinereus, saepe etiam fuliginosus, atratus sub gleba Aethiopum, quale lutum plenus Nilus multis ostiis in mare fundit, et in pontum infligit. Et de haemorrhoo versu 288.

The colour on its rough back sometimes appears quince-yellow and mottled, sometimes ash-grey, often also sooty, blackened under the soil of the Ethiopians, like the mud that the Nile, when full, pours into the sea through its many mouths and drives into the deep. And of the haemorrhous in verse 288.

Sometimes it is fiery in colour, sometimes sooty. And of the dipsas in verse 337.

Et tophus scaber, et nigris exesa chelydris Creta. — — — — — III, 152 Aelianus quoque nigras habet aspides et nigros haemorrhoos, Historiae lib. 6. cap. 38. et lib. 15. cap. 13.
