And rough tufa, and chalk eaten out by black chelydri. — — — — — III, 152 Aelian too has black asps and black haemorrhoi, Historia book 6, ch. 38 and book 15, ch. 13. Aëtius describes the ammodytes, marked with black spots; the chelidonian asp, black on the back like swallows and white on the belly; the dipsas with a black tail; and dragons, some black, some red, some ash-grey. Pausanias in the Boeotica says: Ἐν Αἰθιοπίᾳ μέλανας τὰς ἀσπίδας οὐ μεῖον ἢ καὶ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἡ γῆ τρέφει [En Aithiopia melanas tas aspidas ou meion ē kai tous anthrōpous hē gē trephei]; In Ethiopia the earth nourishes black asps no less than black men. In Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] the swallow serpent, that is, the chelidonian asp, col. 378 لونها يشبه لون الخطاف [lawnuhā yushbihu lawn al-khaṭṭāf] is in colour like a swallow, that is, with a black back. And the colour of the basilisk inclines الي سواد وصفرة [ilā sawād wa-ṣufra] to blackness and yellowness. The haemorrhous too and the cerastes (in the barbarous writers aufudius and sabrin) have نقط سود وبيض [nuqaṭ sūd wa-bīḍ] black and white spots sprinkled over their body; and heads and tails sometimes سودا وحمرا وبيضا [sūdan wa-ḥumran wa-bīḍan] black, red and white. On the body of the dipsas, too, there are اثار سود كثيرة [āthār sūd kathīra] very many traces of blackness: ولون موخرها الي الاذناب الي السواد [wa-lawn muʾakhkharihā ilā al-adhnāb ilā al-sawād] and the colour of the hind part towards the tail inclines to blackness. And the same author says of dragons: ولها وجوه صفرا وسودا [wa-lahā wujūh ṣufran wa-sūdan] They have yellow and black faces. Nor do the more recent writers say otherwise. For Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)], an eyewitness (αὐτόπτης [autoptēs]), in the Observations book 1, ch. 31 and book 2, ch. 14, describes the jaculus as sprinkled with black spots like eyes. And Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium] describes the typhlops as dusky over the whole body, or darkly spotted. And Olaus Magnus, in his description of the Northern lands, says that serpents of black colour inhabit partly the waters, partly the land; and that serpents dwelling among rocks are mostly black, which in the vernacular of the people they call Snok. I understand snakes, which are called Snake in English. Rightly, then, does the greatest poet say in book 1 of the Georgics:


Ille malum virus serpentibus addidit atris:

He added baneful poison to black serpents:


id est, quorum multi sunt atri coloris. Tamen serpentum unus est prae caeteris niger, quique ob id ipsum Arabice اسود asuad, id est, niger, vocatur. Alcamus, الاسود الحية العظيمة Alasuad (niger) serpens magnus (4). Quidam سالخ salich addunt ἐπιθετικῶς, quasi exeuntem III, 153 dicas, quod Damir ita explicat: الاسود السالخ نوع من الحيات شديد السواد سمي بذلك لانه يسلخ جلده كل عام Alasuad assalich, serpentis genus nigredinis intensissimae, qui sic vocatur, quia quotannis pellem exuit. Aliud exemplar habet نوع من الافعوان viperae genus. Nigras aspides intelligo, quas sub viperarum genere multi complectuntur Arabes. Eae nimirum aspides nigerrimae sunt, quod praeter Nicandrum docent Pausanias, Aelianus, Aëtius, atque Arabum nonnulli. Quo dato, veteres שחל sachal recte aspidem interpretantur. De nigro serpente multa fabulatur Damir, quae piget hic referre. In his Iesum, Mariae filium, lignatori praedixisse, fore, ut illa ipsa die in summum vitae discrimen incideret: qui, cum lignatum ivisset, et rediisset sub vesperam cum fasce ligni, cumque jussu Christi solvisset, reperit in illo حية سودا, serpentem nigrum. Tum, Iesu rogante, quid fecisset, et illo negante, se quidquam fecisse, nisi quod transeunti mendico sui panis partem dederat, regessit Iesus, بهذا دفع عنك Propterea Deus a te malum avertit. Alii de col. 379 Saleh, propheta, idem narrant, et dicunt, serpentem اسود سالخ asuad salich crassum fuisse مثل الجذع instar trunci palmae.

that is, many of which are black in colour. Yet one serpent is black above the rest, and for that very reason it is called in Arabic اسود [aswad] asuad, that is, black. Alcamus: الاسود الحية العظيمة [al-aswad al-ḥayya al-ʿaẓīma] Alasuad (the black one), a great serpent R4. Some add سالخ [sālikh] salich as an epithet, as if you were to say one coming out III, 153, which Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] explains thus: الاسود السالخ نوع من الحيات شديد السواد سمي بذلك لانه يسلخ جلده كل عام [al-aswad al-sālikh nawʿ min al-ḥayyāt shadīd al-sawād summiya bi-dhālika li-annahu yaslukhu jildahu kull ʿām] Alasuad assalich, a kind of serpent of the most intense blackness, which is so called because it sheds its skin every year. Another copy has نوع من الافعوان [nawʿ min al-afʿuwān] a kind of viper. I understand black asps, which many Arabs include under the kind of vipers. These asps are indeed very black, as besides Nicander is taught by Pausanias, Aelian, Aëtius, and some of the Arabs. Granted this, the ancients rightly interpret שחל sachal as asp. Damir tells many fables about the black serpent, which I am loath to relate here. Among them: that Jesus, son of Mary, foretold to a woodcutter that on that very day he would fall into the gravest danger to his life. When he had gone to cut wood and returned towards evening with a bundle of wood, and at Christ's command had untied it, he found in it حية سودا [ḥayya sūdā] a black serpent. Then, when Jesus asked what he had done, and he denied having done anything except that he had given part of his bread to a passing beggar, Jesus replied: بهذا دفع عنك [bi-hādhā dafaʿa ʿanka] For this reason God has turned evil away from you. Others tell the same of col. 379 Saleh, the prophet, and say that the serpent اسود سالخ [aswad sālikh] asuad salich was as thick مثل الجذع [mithl al-jidhʿ] as the trunk of a palm.

Et quod Nicander, poeta, colubrum miliarem λέοντα αἰόλον vocat, inde ne hoc quidem potest concludi, adhibuisse Graecos leonum nomen serpentibus, multo minus vero, Hebraeos.

R2 Rosenmüller, III, 150 But nothing can be weaker than this opinion of Bochart, since it rests solely on the authority of the Alexandrian translator. And from the fact that the poet Nicander calls the coluber miliaris λέοντα αἰόλον [leonta aiolon], it cannot even be concluded that the Greeks applied the name of lions to serpents, much less the Hebrews.


(3) Rosenmüller, III, 150 Cum vero, ut vidimus, nomen כפיר sine ratione pro serpente sumatur, ac nihil III, 151 nihil significet, praeter leonem, sequitur, posse nec שחל, quod hoc loco τῷ כפיר respondet, ex legibus parallelismi membrorum, alia, quam usitata leonis significatione sumi. Nec me movet, quod vulgari interpretationi Bochartus opponit, eam sensum efficere non satis aptum. Intellige enim leones cubantes, quos nemo impune pede offendat. ut nec serpentes quisquam inultus calcat, et nihil erit incongrui in hac poetae Hebraei imagine.

R3 Rosenmüller, III, 150 But since, as we have seen, the name כפיר is taken for a serpent without reason, and III, 151 means nothing but a lion, it follows that שחל, which in this passage corresponds to כפיר, cannot, by the laws of the parallelism of members, be taken in any other sense than the usual meaning lion. Nor am I moved by Bochart's objection to the common interpretation, that it yields a sense that is not apt enough. For understand lions lying down, which no one strikes with his foot with impunity, just as no one treads on serpents unpunished, and there will be nothing incongruous in this image of the Hebrew poet.

Part 2, Book 3, chapter 4: Achsub is the asp

III, 154 col. 379 CAP. IV.

III, 154 col. 379 Chapter 4.


Probatur, עכשוב achsub esse Aspidem.

It is proved that עכשוב achsub is the asp.


Quaeritur, quid sit עכשוב achsub, in his Psal. CXL, 4. חמת עכשוב תחת שפתימו, Venenum achsub sub labiis eorum. Chaldaeus exponit, אורסא דעכוביתא, venenum araneae, quasi עכשוב κατ᾽ ἀναγραμματισμὸν sit idem, quod עכביש. Arabs سم الافاعي, venenum viperarum. Alii venenum aspidis: quibus assentior potius, quia, praeter Graecos interpretes, et Latinum, et Syrum, et Apollinarem, et Hieronymum, et ex Hebraeis Kimchium, Mardochaeum, et Pomarium, insuper Paulum, Apostolum, suffragatorem habent, qui Psaltis verba sic effert Roman. III, 13. Ἰὸς ἀσπίδων ὑπὸ τὰ χείλη αὐτῶν. Videri possit עכשוב achsub alludere ad vocem עכס eches, quam alii serpentis venenum, alii viperae speciem explicant. Prius his verbis asserit Rabbi Selomo in Esa. III, 16. עכס הוא ארס של נחש, Eches est venenum serpentis. Posterius auctor Mechiltae, ex quo Aquinas, עכס הוא מין אפעה שכשרואה העוף פורח באויר יתחבר אל צלו ואיבריו נושרין וזהו צלמות צל ועמו מות, Eches est viperae species, quae, cum avem volantem videt, consociatur umbrae ejus, et pennae ejus defluunt, et haec est umbra mortis, seu umbra mortifera. Sed uterque fallitur. Nam עכס eches nihil quidquam est, quam Graecum ἔχις, id est, vipera mas. Neque illam vocem Graeci ex Hebraeis, sed Hebraei recentiores ex Graecis mutuati sunt. Itaque nugatur, quisquis עכשוב achsub, vocem vere Hebraeam, conatur ad hanc revocare.

The question is what עכשוב achsub is in these words of Psal. CXL, 4: חמת עכשוב תחת שפתימו, The poison of achsub is under their lips. The Chaldee renders it אורסא דעכוביתא, the poison of the spider, as though עכשוב were, κατ᾽ ἀναγραμματισμὸν [kat᾽ anagrammatismon], the same as עכביש. The Arabic translator has سم الافاعي [samm al-afāʿī], the poison of vipers. Others have the poison of the asp; I rather agree with these, because, besides the Greek translators, the Latin, the Syriac, Apollinaris and Jerome, and among the Hebrews Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], Mardochaeus and Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)], they also have Paul the Apostle on their side, who renders the words of the Psalmist thus in Roman. III, 13.: Ἰὸς ἀσπίδων ὑπὸ τὰ χείλη αὐτῶν [Ios aspidōn hypo ta cheilē autōn]. It might seem that עכשוב achsub alludes to the word עכס eches, which some explain as the poison of a serpent, others as a species of viper. The former is asserted by R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] on Isa 3:16 in these words: עכס הוא ארס של נחש, Eches is the poison of a serpent. The latter by the author of the Mechilta, and from him Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)]: עכס הוא מין אפעה שכשרואה העוף פורח באויר יתחבר אל צלו ואיבריו נושרין וזהו צלמות צל ועמו מות, Eches is a species of viper which, when it sees a bird flying, joins itself to its shadow, and its feathers fall off; and this is the shadow of death, or the deadly shadow. But both are mistaken. For עכס eches is nothing other than the Greek ἔχις [echis], that is, the male viper. Nor did the Greeks borrow that word from the Hebrews, but the later Hebrews from the Greeks. Therefore whoever tries to trace עכשוב achsub, a genuinely Hebrew word, back to it is trifling.


Sed verum ejus etymum mihi videor ex Arabica lingua deprehendere, qua عكس achasa est retorquere, et reflectere rem ad principium suum, sive id fiat recta linea, ut in repercussu solis, qui dicitur انعكاس in Avicenna a), sive per circulos et gyros, ut cum, capite ad caudam obverso, serpens in spiram se colligit. Hinc Alcamus, تعكس في مشيته مشي مشيا الافعي Incessit incessu viperae, id est, in gyrum se convertendo. Forte Hebraeis idem fuit עכש, unde עכשוב, litera Beth in fine adscita. Quomodo ex כרך, ambire, factum כרכוב, ambitus, Exod. XXVII, 5. Et a Chaldaeo תעל, Arabicum ثعلب, vulpes. Et ערבוב, mistio, a Verbo ערב, miscere. Et זרבוב, fusorium, a Verbo זרב, fluere. Et si quae alia sunt hujusmodi. Aspi- col. 380 dis certe naturae plane convenit hoc nomen; cum, Nicandro teste b), soleat κατ᾽ ἐναντίον ἕρπειν, in contrarium serpere, id est, بالعكس c). Ut taceam, quod idem Nicander pugnantem ita describit versu 166.

But I think I detect its true etymology from the Arabic language, in which عكس achasa means to turn back and to bend a thing back to its starting point, whether this happens in a straight line, as in the reflection of the sun, which in Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] is called انعكاس [inʿikās] a), or by circles and coils, as when a serpent, its head turned toward its tail, gathers itself into a coil. Hence Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: تعكس في مشيته مشي مشيا الافعي [taʿakkasa fī mashyatihi mashā mashyan al-afʿā] He walked with the gait of a viper, that is, turning himself in a circle. Perhaps among the Hebrews עכש was the same, whence עכשוב, with the letter Beth added at the end. Just as from כרך, to go around, comes כרכוב, circuit, Exod 27:5. And from the Chaldee תעל the Arabic ثعلب [thaʿlab], fox. And ערבוב, mixture, from the verb ערב, to mix. And זרבוב, a casting-vessel, from the verb זרב, to flow. And any others of this kind. This name certainly fits the nature of the asp col. 380 perfectly, since, as Nicander testifies b), it is wont κατ᾽ ἐναντίον ἕρπειν [kat᾽ enantion herpein], to crawl in the contrary direction, that is, بالعكس [bi-l-ʿaks] c). Not to mention that the same Nicander describes it fighting thus, in line 166:


III, 155 Ὁλκῷ δὲ τροχόωσαν ἅλων᾽ εἰλίξατο γαίῃ. Σμερδαλέον δ᾽ ἀνὰ μέσσα κάρη πεφρικὸς ἀείρει· Describit tereti sinuosa volumina tractu, Horrendumque caput medio sic tollit ab orbe.

III, 155 Ὁλκῷ δὲ τροχόωσαν ἅλων᾽ εἰλίξατο γαίῃ. Σμερδαλέον δ᾽ ἀνὰ μέσσα κάρη πεφρικὸς ἀείρει· [Holkō de trochoōsan halōn᾽ eilixato gaiē. Smerdaleon d᾽ ana messa karē pephrikos aeirei] It traces winding coils with rounded trail, and thus raises its dreadful head from the middle of the circle.


Ita etiam Etymologus, Συστρέψαν ἑαυτὸ πολεμεῖ, καὶ μάχεται· Contorquens se ipsum bellum gerit, et pugnat. Συστρέφειν ἑαυτὸ Arabice est تعكس. Sic Oppiani Cynegeticῶn lib. 3. versu 446. ichneumon aspidem dilacerat

So too the Etymologicum: Συστρέψαν ἑαυτὸ πολεμεῖ, καὶ μάχεται [Systrepsan heauto polemei, kai machetai]; Twisting itself together, it wages war and fights. Συστρέφειν ἑαυτὸ [Systrephein heauto] in Arabic is تعكس [taʿakkasa]. Thus in Oppian's Cynegetica book 3, line 446, the ichneumon tears apart the asp


— — — ἑλισσομένην ἑκάτερθε,

— — — ἑλισσομένην ἑκάτερθε, [helissomenēn hekaterthe]


hinc inde convolutam. Et in Phylarcho, quem citat Aelianus lib. 17. cap. 5. mansuetae aspides τὴν μὲν λοιπὴν σπεῖραν ἐῶσι κατὰ τοῦ δαπέδου, ἀρᾶσαι δὲ τὴν κε-φαλὴν περιλιχμῶνται, reliquam quidem spiram humi relinquunt, capite autem sublato circumlingunt. Idem animal εἰς κύκλους πολλοὺς ἑλισσόμενον καθεύδειν, in plures circulos convolutum dormire, asserit Aristophanis Scholiastes in Vespis. Hi circuli Graece dicuntur Οἶμοι. Hesychius, Οἶμον, οἶμος· ὁδὸς, κύκλος, τρίβος. ὅθεν καὶ τῆς ἀσπίδος κύκλους οἴμους ἐκάλεσαν. Arabice انعكاس recte dixeris. Proinde Hebraeum aspidis nomen עכשוב videtur inde deduci, qua ratione diximus. Neque alia est ratio Graeci nominis. Ἀσπὶς enim tam pro clypeo, quam pro serpente sumitur. Rotundos autem fuisse Graecorum clypeos, vel ex Poeta disce, a quo Polyphemi oculus orbicularis describitur d),

coiled on this side and that. And in Phylarchus, whom Aelian cites in book 17, ch. 5, tame asps τὴν μὲν λοιπὴν σπεῖραν ἐῶσι κατὰ τοῦ δαπέδου, ἀρᾶσαι δὲ τὴν κεφαλὴν περιλιχμῶνται [tēn men loipēn speiran eōsi kata tou dapedou, arasai de tēn kephalēn perilichmōntai], leave the rest of the coil on the ground, but with head raised they lick round about. That the same animal εἰς κύκλους πολλοὺς ἑλισσόμενον καθεύδειν [eis kyklous pollous helissomenon katheudein], sleeps coiled into many circles, is asserted by the Scholiast of Aristophanes on the Wasps. These circles are called Οἶμοι [Oimoi] in Greek. Hesychius: Οἶμον, οἶμος· ὁδὸς, κύκλος, τρίβος. ὅθεν καὶ τῆς ἀσπίδος κύκλους οἴμους ἐκάλεσαν [Oimon, oimos; hodos, kyklos, tribos. hothen kai tēs aspidos kyklous oimous ekalesan]. In Arabic you would rightly say انعكاس [inʿikās]. Accordingly the Hebrew name of the asp, עכשוב, seems to be derived from this, in the way we have said. Nor is the reason for the Greek name different. For Ἀσπὶς [Aspis] is used both for a shield and for a serpent. That the shields of the Greeks were round you may learn even from the Poet, by whom the round eye of Polyphemus is described d):


Argolici clypei aut Phoebeae lampadis instar.

Like an Argive shield or the Phoebean lamp.


Hinc in Homero passim e) ἀσπίδες εὔκυκλοι, et ἀσπίδες ὀμφαλόεσσαι, ubi Scholion, στρογγύλαι, περιφερεῖς. Et Diodoro f), τὸν τῆς ἀσπίδος κύκλον μιμη-σάμενος, clypei circulum imitatus. An clypei nomen ἀσπὶς a serpente sit ductum, ut placet Scholiasti Aristophanis, aut serpentis a clypei forma, quam spiris suis videtur exprimere, ut vult Etymologus, nobis disquirere non libet; quia ad rem nostram non facit *).

Hence in Homer everywhere e) ἀσπίδες εὔκυκλοι [aspides eukykloi] and ἀσπίδες ὀμφαλόεσσαι [aspides omphaloessai], where the Scholion has στρογγύλαι, περιφερεῖς [strongylai, periphereis]. And in Diodorus f), τὸν τῆς ἀσπίδος κύκλον μιμησάμενος [ton tēs aspidos kyklon mimēsamenos], imitating the circle of the shield. Whether the name ἀσπὶς [aspis] for the shield was derived from the serpent, as the Scholiast of Aristophanes holds, or the serpent's name from the shape of the shield, which it seems to reproduce with its coils, as the Etymologicum would have it, we do not care to investigate, since it is not relevant to our subject *).

Arab. عكش, colligere) sub labiis eorum. This conjecture seems to me to be rejected chiefly for this reason: in the first part of the verse there had preceded שננו לשונם כמו נחש, they sharpen their teeth like serpents, so that the parallelism of members requires in the other part of the verse another name of a serpent; and that this is עכשוב itself Bochart, I think, sufficiently shows in this chapter.


Part 2, Book 3, chapter 5: Pethen is the asp
--------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/pethen.html

III, 156 col. 380 CAP. V.

III, 156 col. 380 Chapter 5.


Probatur, פתן pethen esse Aspidem.

It is proved that פתן pethen is the asp.


Aliud est aspidis nomen פתן pethen. Ita enim hanc vocem plerique reddunt. Et veram esse hanc versionem, suadent aliquot loca de veneno פתן pethen *). col. 381 Sic Iob. XX, 14. מרורת פתנים בקרבו. Ubi Seniores, Χολὴ ἀσπίδος ἐν γαστρὶ αὐτοῦ· et Vulgatus, Fel aspidum intrinsecus. Et paullo post versu decimo sexto, ראש פתנים יינק. Ubi Seniores, Θυμὸν δὲ δρακόντων θηλάσειεν. Sed Graeci interpretes alii, Χολὴν ἀσπίδων μυζήσει· et Hieronymus, Caput aspidum suget. Rursus Deut. XXXII, 33. וראש פתנים אכזר, Et venenum pethanim crudele. Pro quo Graece, Καὶ θυμὸς ἀσπίδων ἀνίατος· unde Vulgatus, Et venenum aspidum insanabile. Ac si pro אכזר legerint אין זר, non est curatio. Nam זר est curare vulnus, Esa. I, 6. Et מזור, vulneris curatio, Ier. XXX, 13. Nempe venenum aspidis est omnium acutissimum, et vitalia celerrime penetrat. Aeliani verba sunt lib. 9. cap. 61. Ὀξύτατόν ἐστι τὸ ἐξ αὐτῆς φάρμακον, καὶ διαδραμεῖν ὤκιστον. Unde vulgatum adagium in Apostolio et Erasmo, Δῆγμα ἀσπίδος, Morsus aspidis, pro immedicabili vulnere; quia, qui ab aspide demorsus est, raro sanatur. Quod testatum faciunt scriptores, non contemnendi. Aristoteles lib. 8. Historiae cap. 29. Τὰ δὲ τῶν ὄφεων δήγματα πολὺ διαφέρουσιν. ἥτε γὰρ ἀσπὶς ἐν Λιβύῃ γίνεται, ἐξ οὗ ὄφεως ποιοῦσι τὸ σηπτικόν· καὶ ἄλλως ἀνιάτως. Serpentum morsus multum differunt. Aspis enim in Africa nascitur, III, 157 ex qua faciunt unguentum putrefactivum: et alioqui immedicabiliter, supple mordet. Plinius lib. 8. cap. 23. Colla aspidum intumescere (vulgatum est) nullo ictus remedio, praeterquam si confestim partes contactae amputentur. Aelianus lib. 1. cap. 54. Ἀσπίδος δὲ ἀκούω μόνον δῆγμα ἀνίατον εἶναι, καὶ ἐπικουρίας κρεῖττον· Aspidis solum morsum immedicabilem esse audio, et omni remedio potentiorem. Et lib. 6. cap. 38. Τῶν ὑπ’ ἀσπίδος δηχθέντων οὐ μνημονεύεται οὐδεὶς ἐξάντης γεγο-νέναι τοῦ κακοῦ. Ἔνθεν τοι καὶ τοὺς βασιλεῖς ἀκούω τῶν Αἰγυπτίων ἐπὶ τῶν δια-δημάτων φορεῖν πεποικιλμένας ἀσπίδας, τῆς ἀρχῆς αἰνιττομένους τὸ ἀνίκητον. Eorum, qui ab aspide morsi sunt, nemo a malo (id est, a morte) traditur fuisse immunis. Unde est, quod Aegyptiorum reges in diadematibus pictas aspides ferre audio, ut invictum imperii robur sic significent. Et infra, Οἱ δηχθέντες ὑπ’ ἀσπίδων οὐ περαιτέρω βιοῦσι τετάρτης ὥρας· Qui ab aspidibus morsi sunt, ultra quartam horam non vivunt. Phile cap. 59.

Another name of the asp is פתן pethen. For so most render this word. And that this rendering is correct is suggested by several passages on the poison of the פתן pethen *). col. 381 Thus Job XX, 14. מרורת פתנים בקרבו. Here the Elders have Χολὴ ἀσπίδος ἐν γαστρὶ αὐτοῦ [cholē aspidos en gastri autou], and the Vulgate translator The gall of asps within. And a little later, in verse sixteen, ראש פתנים יינק. Here the Elders have Θυμὸν δὲ δρακόντων θηλάσειεν [thymon de drakontōn thēlaseien]. But other Greek translators have Χολὴν ἀσπίδων μυζήσει [cholēn aspidōn myzēsei], and Jerome He shall suck the head of asps. Again Deut 32:33. וראש פתנים אכזר, And the cruel poison of pethanim. For this the Greek has Καὶ θυμὸς ἀσπίδων ἀνίατος [kai thymos aspidōn aniatos]; whence the Vulgate translator has And the incurable poison of asps. As if for אכזר they had read אין זר, there is no cure. For זר means to treat a wound, Isa 1:6, and מזור the treatment of a wound, Ier. XXX, 13. The asp's poison is, of course, the sharpest of all, and penetrates the vital organs very swiftly. Aelian's words, book 9, ch. 61, are: Ὀξύτατόν ἐστι τὸ ἐξ αὐτῆς φάρμακον, καὶ διαδραμεῖν ὤκιστον [oxytaton esti to ex autēs pharmakon, kai diadramein ōkiston]. Hence the common proverb in Apostolius and Erasmus [=Desiderius Erasmus, Adagia], Δῆγμα ἀσπίδος [dēgma aspidos], The bite of an asp, for an incurable wound; because one who has been bitten by an asp is rarely healed. This is attested by writers not to be despised. Aristotle, book 8 of the History, ch. 29: Τὰ δὲ τῶν ὄφεων δήγματα πολὺ διαφέρουσιν. ἥτε γὰρ ἀσπὶς ἐν Λιβύῃ γίνεται, ἐξ οὗ ὄφεως ποιοῦσι τὸ σηπτικόν· καὶ ἄλλως ἀνιάτως [ta de tōn opheōn dēgmata poly diapherousin. hēte gar aspis en Libyē ginetai, ex hou opheōs poiousi to sēptikon; kai allōs aniatōs]. The bites of serpents differ greatly. For the asp is born in Africa, III, 157 from which they make a putrefying ointment; and besides, incurably—supply it bites. Pliny, book 8, ch. 23: That the necks of asps swell (it is commonly known), and there is no remedy for their stroke, except if the parts touched are immediately amputated. Aelian, book 1, ch. 54: Ἀσπίδος δὲ ἀκούω μόνον δῆγμα ἀνίατον εἶναι, καὶ ἐπικουρίας κρεῖττον [aspidos de akouō monon dēgma aniaton einai, kai epikourias kreitton]; I hear that the bite of the asp alone is incurable and stronger than every remedy. And book 6, ch. 38: Τῶν ὑπ’ ἀσπίδος δηχθέντων οὐ μνημονεύεται οὐδεὶς ἐξάντης γεγονέναι τοῦ κακοῦ. Ἔνθεν τοι καὶ τοὺς βασιλεῖς ἀκούω τῶν Αἰγυπτίων ἐπὶ τῶν διαδημάτων φορεῖν πεποικιλμένας ἀσπίδας, τῆς ἀρχῆς αἰνιττομένους τὸ ἀνίκητον [tōn hyp’ aspidos dēchthentōn ou mnēmoneuetai oudeis exantēs gegonenai tou kakou. enthen toi kai tous basileis akouō tōn Aigyptiōn epi tōn diadēmatōn phorein pepoikilmenas aspidas, tēs archēs ainittomenous to anikēton]. Of those bitten by an asp, none is recorded to have escaped the evil (that is, death). This is why, I hear, the kings of Egypt wear asps depicted on their diadems, to signify thereby the invincible strength of their rule. And further below: Οἱ δηχθέντες ὑπ’ ἀσπίδων οὐ περαιτέρω βιοῦσι τετάρτης ὥρας [hoi dēchthentes hyp’ aspidōn ou peraiterō biousi tetartēs hōras]; Those bitten by asps do not live beyond the fourth hour. Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)], ch. 59:


Τῆς ἀσπίδος τὸ δῆγμα δῆγμ’ ἔστι θανάτου. Μὴ, μὴ, Γαληνὲ, μηδὲ φάρμακον χέῃς. Repente mortem morsus infert aspidis. Ne, ne, Galene, pharmacum ne infuderis.

Τῆς ἀσπίδος τὸ δῆγμα δῆγμ’ ἔστι θανάτου. Μὴ, μὴ, Γαληνὲ, μηδὲ φάρμακον χέῃς. [tēs aspidos to dēgma dēgm’ esti thanatou. mē, mē, Galēne, mēde pharmakon cheēs.] The bite of the asp brings sudden death. Do not, do not, Galen, pour in a drug.


Quem frustra sibi objicit, cum id abunde confirmetur ipsius Galeni suffragio lib. 1. De Theriaca capite 8. ubi de aspidibus haec habet: Πολλάκις ἐθεασάμην ἐγὼ ἐν τῇ μεγάλῃ Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ τὸ τάχος τοῦ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ γιγνομένου θανάτου. ὅταν γάρ τινα, τούτῳ τῷ νόμῳ τῆς κολάσεως κατακριθέντα, φιλανθρώπως καὶ ταχέως ἀποκτεῖναι θέλωσι, προσβάλλοντες αὐτοῦ τοῖς στέρνοις τὸ θηρίον, καὶ ποιήσαντες ὀλίγον περιπατῆσαι, οὕτω ταχέως ἀναιροῦσι τὸν ἄνθρωπον. In magna Alexandriae urbe saepe vidi, quam cito mortem inferant. Quoties enim aliquem, hujus supplicii lege damnatum, humaniter citoque interimere volunt, ad-motam pectori bestiam aliquantulum inambulare jubent, et hominem hac ratione stastim enecant. Proinde aspides calcare maxime periculosum est. Et Psaltes, ut virum bonum etiam inter hostes infensissimos a Deo servari significet, illum aspides et dracones ait impune calcaturum, Psal. XCI, 13. Quale est, quod apud veteres Onirocriticos in Suida,

He addresses Galen in vain, since this is amply confirmed by the testimony of Galen himself, book 1 On Theriac, chapter 8, where he says this of asps: Πολλάκις ἐθεασάμην ἐγὼ ἐν τῇ μεγάλῃ Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ τὸ τάχος τοῦ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ γιγνομένου θανάτου. ὅταν γάρ τινα, τούτῳ τῷ νόμῳ τῆς κολάσεως κατακριθέντα, φιλανθρώπως καὶ ταχέως ἀποκτεῖναι θέλωσι, προσβάλλοντες αὐτοῦ τοῖς στέρνοις τὸ θηρίον, καὶ ποιήσαντες ὀλίγον περιπατῆσαι, οὕτω ταχέως ἀναιροῦσι τὸν ἄνθρωπον [pollakis etheasamēn egō en tē megalē Alexandreia to tachos tou hyp’ autou gignomenou thanatou. hotan gar tina, toutō tō nomō tēs kolaseōs katakrithenta, philanthrōpōs kai tacheōs apokteinai thelōsi, prosballontes autou tois sternois to thērion, kai poiēsantes oligon peripatēsai, houtō tacheōs anairousi ton anthrōpon]. In the great city of Alexandria I often saw how swiftly they bring death. For whenever they wish to kill humanely and quickly someone condemned under the law of this punishment, they put the beast to his breast and make it walk about a little, and in this way they kill the man at once. Therefore treading on asps is extremely dangerous. And the Psalmist, to signify that a good man is preserved by God even among the most bitter enemies, says that he will tread on asps and dragons unharmed, Ps 91:13. Similar is the saying of the ancient interpreters of dreams in the Suda:


Ὄφεις πατεῖν, τὰ κέντρα τῶν ἐχθρῶν λύει· Qui calcat angues, vitat insultum hostium.

Ὄφεις πατεῖν, τὰ κέντρα τῶν ἐχθρῶν λύει· [opheis patein, ta kentra tōn echthrōn lyei] He who treads on snakes escapes the assault of enemies.


Neque ullus est, qui ad aspidis aut basilisci foramen ultro accedat. Aut, si quisquam ita insaniat, is magnum adit vitae discrimen. Hinc, ut doceat Esaias, magnam fore sub Christi regno rerum conversionem, Tum, inquit, ludet infans על חור פתן, super foramen aspidis: et super cavernam basilisci puer, a lacte col. 382 depulsus, manum injiciet, Es. XI, 8. Id est, Gentes cum Iudaeis in unam ecclesiam III, 158 convenient: et tutus patebit accessus ad eos, qui fidelibus olim erant tam terribiles, quam sunt pueris anguium maxime venenati et pestiferi, aspides puta et basilisci. Quamvis etiam ad literam hoc aliquando fuisse impletum, his verbis narret Sulpicius Dialogi primi cap. 5. Panem Abbas per duos pueros miserat, quorum major habebat annos aetatis quindecim, minor duodennis erat. His ergo, inde redeuntibus, aspis mirae magnitudinis fit obviam; cujus occursu nihil perterriti, ubi ante pedes eorum venit, quasi incantata carminibus, coerula colla deposuit. Minor e pueris manu adprehensam, ac pallio involutam, ferre coepit. Deinde monasterium quasi victor ingressus, in occursum fratrum, inspectantibus cunctis, captivam bestiam, resoluto pallio, non sine jactantiae tumore, deposuit. Sed et jam olim in Aegypto mansuetas aspides cum pueris innoxie vixisse, et digitorum crepitu vocatas ex cavernis prorepsisse, narrat Phylarchus in Aeliano lib. 17. cap. 5. Verba sunt, Τοῖς παιδίοις (τὰς ἀσπίδας) συντρεφομένας μηδ-ὲν ἀδικεῖν, καὶ καλουμένας δὲ ἐξέρπειν τῶν φωλῶν, καὶ ἀφικνεῖσθαι· κλῆσις δὲ αὐτῶν ὁ τῶν δακτύλων ἐστὶ κρότος. Idem de Psyllis refert Lucanus lib. 9. versu 909.

Nor is there anyone who would willingly approach the hole of an asp or a basilisk. Or, if anyone were so mad, he would run a great risk to his life. Hence, to teach that there will be a great reversal of things under the kingdom of Christ, Isaiah says: Then the infant shall play על חור פתן, over the hole of the asp, and the child weaned from milk col. 382 shall put his hand on the den of the basilisk, Isa 11:8. That is, the Gentiles will come together with the Jews into one church III, 158, and safe access will lie open to those who were once as terrifying to the faithful as the most venomous and deadly of snakes, namely asps and basilisks, are to children. Yet Sulpicius, in the first Dialogue, ch. 5, relates in these words that this was at some time also fulfilled literally: The abbot had sent bread by two boys, of whom the elder was fifteen years old and the younger twelve. As they were returning from there, an asp of wondrous size met them; they were not at all terrified at its approach, and when it came before their feet, as if charmed by incantations, it laid down its dark-blue neck. The younger of the boys seized it with his hand, wrapped it in his cloak, and began to carry it. Then, entering the monastery like a victor, he went to meet the brothers and, while all looked on, he unfolded his cloak and set down the captive beast, not without a swell of boasting. But Phylarchus, in Aelian, book 17, ch. 5, also relates that long ago in Egypt tame asps lived harmlessly with children, and when called by a snapping of the fingers crept out of their holes. His words are: Τοῖς παιδίοις (τὰς ἀσπίδας) συντρεφομένας μηδὲν ἀδικεῖν, καὶ καλουμένας δὲ ἐξέρπειν τῶν φωλῶν, καὶ ἀφικνεῖσθαι· κλῆσις δὲ αὐτῶν ὁ τῶν δακτύλων ἐστὶ κρότος [Tois paidiois (tas aspidas) syntrephomenas mēden adikein, kai kaloumenas de exerpein tōn phōlōn, kai aphikneisthai; klēsis de autōn ho tōn daktylōn esti krotos]. Lucan, book 9, line 909, reports the same of the Psylli:


— — — — pignora gentis
Psyllus habet, si quis tactos non horruit angues,
Si quis donatis lusit serpentibus infans.

— — — — the Psyllian holds these as pledges of his race: if any infant did not shudder at the snakes he touched, if any infant played with the serpents given to him.


Et Aelianus Historiae lib. 1. cap. 57. eosdem ait legitimos liberos suos in dolium, cerastis plenum, injectos, ex eo agnovisse, quod ad illorum contactum cerastae ἐμαράνθησαν, extabescerent. Quin hodieque in Africa circa Segelmessam montes quindecim esse perhibentur, quorum incolae cum serpentibus familiariter degunt, ita, ut cum iis pueri ludant. Ita narrat Vincentius le Blanc partis 2. cap. 23.

And Aelian, History, book 1, ch. 57, says that the same people recognized their legitimate children by throwing them into a jar full of cerastes, from the fact that at their touch the cerastes ἐμαράνθησαν [emaranthēsan], wasted away. Indeed, even today in Africa, around Segelmessa, there are said to be fifteen mountains whose inhabitants live on familiar terms with serpents, so that children play with them. So relates Vincent le Blanc, part 2, ch. 23.


In Aegyptiis serpentibus aspides esse multo maximas, scriptores docent. Ammianus lib. 22. Serpentes quoque Aegyptus alit innumeras, ultra omnem perniciem saevientes: basiliscos, amphisbaenas, et scytalas, et acontias, et dipsadas, et viperas, aliasque complures: quas omnes magnitudine et decore aspis facile supereminens, nunquam sponte sua fluenta egreditur Nili. Nicander μῆκος longitudinem iis tribuit ὀργυῇ μετρητὸν, orgya (seu ulna) mensurabilem. Quod sequutus Strabo lib. 17. Διττὴ δ᾽ ἔστιν, inquit, ἡ μὲν σπιθαμιαῖα, ἥπερ καὶ ὀξυ-θανατωτέρα· ἥδ’ ἐγγὺς ὀργυιᾶς. Duplex est aspis: una quidem dodrantalis, quae celerius necat; altera vero fere orgyiae. Apud Aelianum libri 16. cap. 39. Aegyptii dicunt ἀσπίδας τετραπήχεις γίνεσθαι πολλάκις, aspides saepe esse quatuor cubitorum. Sed et, eodem teste lib. 6. capite 38. γίνονται καὶ πεντα-πήχεις, sunt etiam cubitorum quinque. Aëtii Tetrab. 4. Serm. 1. cap. 21. tres aspidum censentur species; terrestres, chelidoniae et ptyades: quarum terrestres III, 159 majores sunt, et quandoque usque ad quinque cubitorum longitudinem reperiuntur. Quomodo in Avicenna de aspide sicca dicitur, هي في قدرها ما بين ثلثة اذرع الي خمسة اذرع Est in quantitate sua a tribus ad quinque cubitos. Quam molem serpentes cum attigerunt, incipiunt dici dracones. Hinc Aëtius, in capite De Draconibus; Alii cubitorum quinque sunt, alii decem: sunt et, qui ad triginta cubitos se extendant, et quidam etiam majores narrantur. Et Avicenna, اصغر اصناف الثنانين علي ما ذكره بعضهم خمسة اذرع واما الكبار فتكون col. 383 من ثلثين ذراعا الي ما فوق ذلك Minima draconum species, ut quidam referunt, est quinque cubitorum: maximi vero sunt triginta cubitorum, et supra. Cum igitur crescant aspides usque ad draconum molem, non immerito Hebraeum nomen פתן pethen draconi fuit cum aspide commune. Proinde pro felle פתנים pethanim Syrus habet, ܡܪܪܬܐ ܕܬܢܝܢܐ, et Arabs مرارة التنين, fel draconis: et Graeci θυμὸν δρακόντων. Illi Iob. XX, 14. hi paullo post versu 16. Addo, פתן pethen, et תנין thanin (vulgare draconis nomen) ut fere synonyma poni Psal. XCI, 13. et Deut. XXXII, 33. Quo loco pro Plurali פתנים pethanim, Ionathan habet פיתוניא pithunja, tanquam a Singulari פיתון pithun. Atque huc alludere videtur Graecum PYTHONIS nomen, quo caesum in Parnasso draconem ab Apolline poetae vocant. Draconem tamen non fuisse, sed hominem, scripsit Ephorus, ex quo refert Strabo lib. 9. Apollinem sagittis confecisse χαλεπὸν ἄνδρα, Πύθωνα τοὔνομα, ἐπίκλησιν δὲ Δράκοντα, virum atrocem, Pythonem nomine, Draconem cognomento, postquam scilicet caedibus et latrociniis diu fuisset Parnassiis infestus. Idem pro Pythone Delphynes nominatur a Suida a) post Apollonium b). In his tenebris si quid video, fuit is praedo insignis in Phocide, cujus verum nomen erat Delphynes. Python cognomen inditum a Phoenicibus, in vicina Boeotia tum degentibus, ob tumultus concitatos et latrocinia commissa. Nimirum apud Arabes (quibus Phe est loco Pe, quia litera Pe carent) فتن phathana est concitare tumultus: فتنة phithna, seditio, caedes: فتان phatthan, seditiosus, latro, grassator. Sed idem ex grassatore draco factus est a fabularum architectis; quia Syris ܦܬܢ pethen, vel ܦܝܬܘܢ pithun, draconem significat. Itaque etiam Python dictus est. Ab hoc Pythone Pythii ludi; et Delphorum urbs Πυ-θὼ, vel Πυθών atque ipse Apollo Πύθων vocatus. Macrobius lib. 1. cap. 20. Hoc nomen (Πύθων) ex nece draconis inditum Deo Graeci fabulantur. Itaque III, 160 Actor. XVI, 16. πνεῦμα Πύθωνος est spiritus Apollinis, quo daemone mulier illa ἐγγαστρίμυθος plena esse credebatur. Unde ipsos etiam ventriloquos Εὐρυ-κλέας πάλαι, νυνὶ Πύθωνας appellant, ait Plutarchus in libro De defectu Oraculorum. Eo sensu, pro Pythone, Hebraei פיתום Pithom scribunt, voce leviter deflexa. Atque ariolorum id genus non ex ventre, sed ex axillis, vocem emisisse somniant. Talmudici in Sanhedrin cap. 7. fol. 65. a. בעל אוב זה פיתום המדבר משחיו, Baal Ob idem est, qui Pithom, seu qui loquitur ex axillis suis. Et ibi Glossa, מעלה את המת מן הארץ ומושיב לו בשחיו תחת זרועותיו ומדבר Mortuum ex terra educit, quem sub axillis et brachiis suis constituit, ut loquatur. Proinde Rabbi Selomo in Deut. XVIII, 11. explicans, quid sit שואל אוב, consulens Ob (seu Pythonem), זה מכשפות ששמו פיתום ומדבר משחיו ומעלה את המת בבית השחי שלו, Haec est divinatio, quae vocatur pithom, qua loquitur quis ex axillis, mortuum ad axillarum locum evocans. De hoc ritu, qui plura volet, Maimonidem consulat in tractatu De Idololatria, statim initio cap. 6. Auctor Aruch פיתום Pithom dici vult quasi פי־תהום pi-thehom, os abyssi. Quin פיתום pithom, et Πύθων idem sunt: et utrumque factum ex פתן pethen, col. 384 vel פיתון pethun, ut diximus.

Writers teach that among the Egyptian serpents the asps are by far the largest. Ammianus, book 22: Egypt also nourishes countless serpents, raging beyond all destructiveness: basilisks, amphisbaenas, and scytales, and acontias, and dipsades, and vipers, and many others; all of which the asp easily surpasses in size and beauty, and it never of its own accord leaves the streams of the Nile. Nicander assigns them a μῆκος [mēkos], a length, ὀργυῇ μετρητὸν [orgyē metrēton], measurable by the orgya (or ell). Strabo, following him, says in book 17: Διττὴ δ᾽ ἔστιν, ἡ μὲν σπιθαμιαῖα, ἥπερ καὶ ὀξυθανατωτέρα· ἥδ’ ἐγγὺς ὀργυιᾶς [Dittē d' estin, hē men spithamiaia, hēper kai oxythanatōtera; hēd' engys orgyias]. The asp is of two kinds: one a span long, which kills more quickly; the other nearly an orgyia. In Aelian, book 16, ch. 39, the Egyptians say ἀσπίδας τετραπήχεις γίνεσθαι πολλάκις [aspidas tetrapēcheis ginesthai pollakis], that asps are often four cubits long. And, on the same witness, book 6, chapter 38, γίνονται καὶ πενταπήχεις [ginontai kai pentapēcheis], there are also some of five cubits. In Aëtius, Tetrab. 4, Serm. 1, ch. 21, three species of asps are reckoned: terrestrial, chelidonian and ptyades; of which the terrestrial III, 159 are larger, and are sometimes found up to five cubits in length. Just so Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] says of the dry asp: هي في قدرها ما بين ثلثة اذرع الي خمسة اذرع [hiya fī qadrihā mā bayna thalathat adhruʿ ilā khamsat adhruʿ] In its size it is from three to five cubits. When serpents have reached this bulk, they begin to be called dragons. Hence Aëtius, in the chapter On Dragons: Some are five cubits, others ten; there are also some that extend to thirty cubits, and certain ones are even said to be larger. And Avicenna: اصغر اصناف الثنانين علي ما ذكره بعضهم خمسة اذرع واما الكبار فتكون col. 383 من ثلثين ذراعا الي ما فوق ذلك [aṣghar aṣnāf al-thanānīn ʿalā mā dhakarahu baʿḍuhum khamsat adhruʿ wa-ammā al-kibār fa-takūn min thalāthīn dhirāʿan ilā mā fawqa dhālika] The smallest species of dragons, as some report, is five cubits; but the largest are thirty cubits and more. Since, then, asps grow to the bulk of dragons, it is not without reason that the Hebrew name פתן pethen was common to the dragon and the asp. Accordingly, for the gall of פתנים pethanim the Syriac has ܡܪܪܬܐ ܕܬܢܝܢܐ [מררתא דתנינא], and the Arabic مرارة التنين [marārat al-tinnīn], the gall of the dragon; and the Greeks θυμὸν δρακόντων [thymon drakontōn]. The former at Iob. XX, 14, the latter a little later at verse 16. I add that פתן pethen and תנין thanin (the common name of the dragon) are set as virtual synonyms in Ps 91:13 and Deut 32:33. In the latter passage, for the plural פתנים pethanim, Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] has פיתוניא pithunja, as if from a singular פיתון pithun. And to this the Greek name PYTHON seems to allude, by which the poets call the dragon slain on Parnassus by Apollo. Yet Ephorus wrote that it was not a dragon but a man; from him Strabo, book 9, reports that Apollo killed with arrows χαλεπὸν ἄνδρα, Πύθωνα τοὔνομα, ἐπίκλησιν δὲ Δράκοντα [chalepon andra, Pythōna tounoma, epiklēsin de Drakonta], a savage man, Python by name, Dragon by surname, after he had long harassed the people of Parnassus with murders and robberies. The same figure is named Delphynes instead of Python by Suidas a) following Apollonius b). If I see anything in this darkness, he was a notorious brigand in Phocis, whose real name was Delphynes. The surname Python was given him by the Phoenicians, then living in neighbouring Boeotia, because of the tumults he stirred up and the robberies he committed. For among the Arabs (with whom Phe stands in place of Pe, since they lack the letter Pe) فتن [fatana] phathana is to stir up tumults; فتنة [fitna] phithna, sedition, slaughter; فتان [fattān] phatthan, seditious, a robber, a highwayman. But this highwayman was turned into a dragon by the fabricators of fables, because among the Syrians ܦܬܢ [פתן] pethen, or ܦܝܬܘܢ [פיתון] pithun, signifies a dragon. So he was also called Python. From this Python come the Pythian games; and the city of Delphi was called Πυθὼ [Pythō] or Πυθών [Pythōn], and Apollo himself Πύθων [Pythōn]. Macrobius, book 1, ch. 20: The Greeks tell the fable that this name (Πύθων [Pythōn]) was given to the god from the slaying of the dragon. Thus III, 160 in Actor. XVI, 16. πνεῦμα Πύθωνος [pneuma Pythōnos] is the spirit of Apollo, the demon with which that ἐγγαστρίμυθος [engastrimythos] woman was believed to be filled. Hence ventriloquists themselves were formerly called Εὐρυκλέας [Eurykleas] and are now called Πύθωνας [Pythōnas], says Plutarch in the book On the Failure of Oracles. In this sense, for Python the Hebrews write פיתום Pithom, the word being slightly altered. And they dream that this kind of soothsayer uttered his voice not from the belly but from the armpits. The Talmudists in Sanhedrin, ch. 7, fol. 65a: בעל אוב זה פיתום המדבר משחיו, Baal Ob is the same as Pithom, that is, one who speaks from his armpits. And there the Gloss: מעלה את המת מן הארץ ומושיב לו בשחיו תחת זרועותיו ומדבר He brings up the dead from the earth, and sets him under his armpits and arms, so that he speaks. Accordingly R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] on Deut 18:11, explaining what שואל אוב is, one who consults Ob (or a Python): זה מכשפות ששמו פיתום ומדבר משחיו ומעלה את המת בבית השחי שלו, This is the divination called pithom, by which one speaks from the armpits, calling up the dead to the place of the armpits. Whoever wants more on this rite should consult Maimonides [=Moses Maimonides (Rambam), Mishneh Torah] in the treatise On Idolatry, at the very beginning of ch. 6. The author of the Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome] holds that פיתום Pithom is so called as if פי־תהום pi-thehom, mouth of the abyss. Rather, פיתום pithom and Πύθων [Pythōn] are the same, and both are formed from פתן pethen, col. 384 or פיתון pethun, as we have said.


Obiter nota, ventriloquum, ut Graecis Πύθωνα et Εὐρυκλέα, ita Babyloniis Σακχούραν fuisse dictum. Sic testatur Photius Auctore 94. ex Iamblicho De amoribus Rhodanis et Sinonidis, Καὶ ἐγγαστρίμυθον, ὃν καί φησιν, ὥσπερ Ἕλ-ληνες μὲν Εὐρυκλέα λέγουσι, Βαβυλώνιοι δὲ Σακχούραν ἀποκαλοῦσι· Sacchuras fortasse est Arabum ساحر sachir, vel سحار sacchar, quomodo magum illi vocant. Pro mago ساحر sachir occurrit Actor. VIII, 9. et XIII, 8. et Deut. XVIII, 10. et Plurale سحرة sachara, Act. XIX, 19. Et a Singulari سحار sacchar Plurale سحارون saccharuna Gen. XLI, 8. 24. Et Foemininum سحارة sacchara pro venefica, Exod. XXII, 18. Et سحر sichr pro magia et veneficio, Act. VIII, 9. et Galat. V, 20. in Pentateucho et Novo Testamento Erpenianae editionis. Et Verbum سحر sachara, vel in secunda Conjugatione sacchara, incantare, in Nubiensi Geographo Clim. 1. part. 7. يسحرون الحيوان الضار Incantant noxia animalia. Vel, quod mihi sit verosimilius, sacchuras est זכורו zacchuru, vel zechuru, quomodo a Chaldaeis et Syris ariolum appellari notius est, quam ut probatione egeat. Exempla vide in Chaldaeis et Syris paraphrasibus, Levit. XIX, 31. Deut. XVIII, 11. et 1 Sam. XXVIII, 3. etc. Et in Sanhedrin fol. 65. 2. et 105. 1. et in Vajekra Rabba Sect. 26. etc. Sic ex zacchuru fieret sacchuras, Z et S permutatis, ut in Sagunto pro Ζακύνθῳ (ita enim vocat Stephanus): et in smaragdo pro زمرجد zmargiad.

Note in passing that a ventriloquist, as among the Greeks he was called Πύθων [Pythōn] and Εὐρυκλῆς [Eurykleēs], so among the Babylonians was called Σακχούρας [Sakchouras]. So Photius testifies, Author 94, from Iamblichus, On the Loves of Rhodanes and Sinonis: Καὶ ἐγγαστρίμυθον, ὃν καί φησιν, ὥσπερ Ἕλληνες μὲν Εὐρυκλέα λέγουσι, Βαβυλώνιοι δὲ Σακχούραν ἀποκαλοῦσι· [Kai engastrimython, hon kai phēsin, hōsper Hellēnes men Eurylea legousi, Babylōnioi de Sakchouran apokalousi]. Sacchuras is perhaps the Arabic ساحر [sāḥir] sachir, or سحار [saḥḥār] sacchar, which is what they call a magus. For magus, ساحر [sāḥir] sachir occurs in Actor. VIII, 9. and XIII, 8. and Deut 18:10, and the plural سحرة [saḥara] sachara in Acts 19:19. And from the singular سحار [saḥḥār] sacchar the plural سحارون [saḥḥārūn] saccharuna, Gen 41:8 24. And the feminine سحارة [saḥḥāra] sacchara for venefica [sorceress], Exod 22:18. And سحر [siḥr] sichr for magia [magic] and veneficium [sorcery], Acts 8:9 and Galat. V, 20., in the Pentateuch and New Testament of the Erpenian edition. And the verb سحر [saḥara] sachara, or in the second conjugation sacchara, "to enchant", in the Nubian Geographer, Clim. [=climate (section) of al-Idrīsī's geography, in the Latin Geographia Nubiensis] 1, section 7: يسحرون الحيوان الضار [yasḥarūn al-ḥayawān al-ḍārr] They enchant harmful animals. Or, which seems to me more likely, sacchuras is זכורו zacchuru, or zechuru, as the Chaldeans and Syrians call a soothsayer, which is too well known to need proof. For examples see the Chaldee and Syriac paraphrases, Lev 19:31. Deut 18:11 and 1 Sam 28:3 etc. And in Sanhedrin fol. 65. 2. and 105. 1., and in Vajekra Rabba Sect. 26, etc. Thus from zacchuru would come sacchuras, with Z and S interchanged, as in Saguntum for Ζάκυνθος [Zakynthos] (for so Stephanus calls it), and in smaragdus for زمرجد [zumurjud] zmargiad.


*) Bochart, III, 156 FORSKAL in Descript. Animall. p. 15. mentionem facit serpentis cujusdam, quem Colubrum Baetaen vocat, cujus nomen Arabicum scribit بتن, quod tamen, ad vulgi pronunciatum expressum, male scriptum puto pro فتن, quod ipsum nostrum פתן est. Eum serpentem Forskal his verbis describit: Totus maculatus albo nigroque. Longitudo pedalis; crassities fere bipollicaris. Ovipara. Morsus in instanti necat, corpore vulnerato intumescente. Parum verisimile mihi videtur OEDMANNI sententia (Vermischte Sammlung. Fasc. V. Cap. X. pag. 85.) hunc colubrum non esse diversum a Colubro Lebe tino Linn., qui in insula Cypro frequens est, ubi ἀσπιδος nomen gerit. Longitudinem corporis Forskal (pag. 13.) dicit subcubitalem esse, Hasselquist vero (p. 239.) unius pedis. Uterque tamen consentit in eo, morsum ejus somnum inferre letalem. Vulgus in insula Cypro hunc serpentem surdum existimat, unde et κουφη, surdus, appellatur (vid. POCOCKII Itinerar. T. II. §. 402. et FORSKALII Descript. Animall. p. 14.). Atque cum Ps. LVIII, 5. פתן surda dicatur; MICHAELIS in Supplemm. P. VI. p. 2056. et OEDMANN l. c. p. 84. Hebraeorum פתן eundem serpentem esse putant cum Colubro Lebetino Linn. Sed cum non unum serpentum genus surdum credatur, ut ostendit Bochartus Cap. sequ., et Coluber Lebetinus Cypro tantummodo domestica esse videatur; ego certius puto, colubrum Baetaen Forskalii pro Hebraeorum פתן habere.

*) Bochart, III, 156 Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)], in Descript. Animall. p. 15, mentions a certain serpent which he calls Coluber Baetaen, whose Arabic name he writes بتن [btn]. This, however, rendered according to the popular pronunciation, I think is miswritten for فتن [ftn], which is our very פתן. Forsskål describes this serpent in these words: Spotted all over with white and black. Length a foot; thickness almost two inches. Oviparous. Its bite kills instantly, the wounded body swelling up. The opinion of Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde] (Vermischte Sammlung. fasc. 5, ch. 10, p. 85) seems to me hardly probable, that this snake is not different from the Coluber Lebetinus Linn., which is frequent on the island of Cyprus, where it bears the name ἀσπιδος [aspidos]. Forsskål (p. 13) says the length of its body is under a cubit, Hasselquist [=Fredrik Hasselquist, Iter Palaestinum (1757)] (p. 239) one foot. Both, however, agree that its bite brings on a lethal sleep. The common people on the island of Cyprus consider this serpent deaf, and hence it is also called κουφη [kouphē], deaf (see Pococke, Itinerar. vol. 2, § 402, and Forsskål, Descript. Animall. p. 14). And since in Ps 58:5 the פתן is called deaf, Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer] in Supplemm. vol. 6, p. 2056, and Oedmann loc. cit. p. 84 think that the פתן of the Hebrews is the same serpent as the Coluber Lebetinus Linn. But since more than one kind of serpent is believed to be deaf, as Bochart shows in the following Chapter, and the Coluber Lebetinus seems to be native only to Cyprus, I think it more certain to take Forsskål's Coluber Baetaen for the פתן of the Hebrews.

Part 2, Book 3, chapter 6: The deaf asp and the charming of serpents

https://openseforim.org/bochart/aspis-surda.html

III, 161 col. 384 CAP. VI.

III, 161 col. 384 Chapter VI.


De Aspide surda, quae aurem obturare legitur, ne audiat vocem incantantium, Psal. LVIII, 5. 6.

On the deaf asp, which is said to stop its ear so as not to hear the voice of the charmers, Ps 58:5–6.


Superest, ut de aspidum, adeoque serpentum omnium, incantatione dicamus col. 385 in verba Psaltis πολυθρύλλητα, Psal. LVIII, 5. 6. Venenum est ipsis simile veneno serpentis: sicut aspidis surdae, obturantis aurem suam, ne mussitantium vocem audiat, et divini incantationum periti. In quibus primo quaeritur, quorsum aspis surda dicatur. Respondet Bustamantinus libri tertii De Scripturae animantibus capite undecimo, surdam ideo appellari, quod, ut acutissimi visus, ita sit auditus hebetissimi. Sed consulti naturae plane contra statuunt, aspidem auditu multo plus valere, quam visu. Nicander in Theriacis versu 162.

It remains for us to speak of the charming of asps, and indeed of all serpents, col. 385 on the much-discussed (πολυθρύλλητα [polythryllēta]) words of the Psalmist, Ps 58:5–6. Their poison is like the poison of a serpent: like that of the deaf asp, which stops its ear so as not to hear the voice of the whisperers, and of the diviner skilled in incantations. Here the first question is why the asp is called deaf. Bustamantinus, in book 3, chapter 11 of De Scripturae animantibus, answers that it is called deaf because, as its sight is very sharp, so its hearing is very dull. But those versed in nature hold exactly the opposite: that the asp is much stronger in hearing than in sight. Nicander, in the Theriaca, line 162:


— — — — ὑπναλέοις δὲ
Αἰὲν ἐπιλλίζουσα φαείνεται ἐνδυκὲς ὄσσοις.
Ἀλλ᾽ ὅταν ἢ δοῦπον νέον οὔασιν, ἠέ τιν᾽ αὐδὴν
Ἀθρήσῃ, νωθρὸν μὲν ἀπὸ ῥεθέως βάλεν ὕπνον.

— — — — ὑπναλέοις δὲ Αἰὲν ἐπιλλίζουσα φαείνεται ἐνδυκὲς ὄσσοις. Ἀλλ᾽ ὅταν ἢ δοῦπον νέον οὔασιν, ἠέ τιν᾽ αὐδὴν Ἀθρήσῃ, νωθρὸν μὲν ἀπὸ ῥεθέως βάλεν ὕπνον. [— — — — hypnaleois de / Aien epillizousa phaenetai endykes ossois. / All᾽ hotan ē doupon neon ousin, ēe tin᾽ audēn / Athrēsē, nōthron men apo rhetheōs balen hypnon.]


— — — — somnoque gravatis
Torpida continue nictare videtur ocellis.
Ast ubi vel murmur, facili vel percipit aure
Vocem aliquam, segnes rejicit de corpore somnos.

— — — — sluggish, it seems to blink continually
with eyes weighed down by sleep.
But when with ready ear it catches either a murmur
or some voice, it casts the lazy sleep from its body.


Plinius libri octavi capite vigesimo tertio, Iam primum hebetes oculos huic malo dedit (rerum natura), eosque non in fronte ex adverso cernere, sed in temporibus: itaque excitatur, sed saepius auditu, quam visu. Frustra regerit Bustamantinus, haec de aspide chersaea dici, non de ptya et chelidonia. Nam de toto genere aspidum Nicander et Plinius agunt. Neque vero quisquam alius a ptyis et chelidoniis chersaeas aspides ita distinxit, ut illas visu, has auditu praepollere somniaret. Omnibus enim aspidibus eadem est oculorum hebetudo, et aurium acrimonia. Mercurialis, Omnibus aspidibus haec communia sunt, visus imbecillus, incessus tardus, auditus subtilis (1).

Pliny, book 8, chapter 23: First of all (nature) gave this pest dull eyes, and made them see not forwards from the front but from the temples; and so it is roused more often by hearing than by sight. In vain does Bustamantinus retort that this is said of the land asp, not of the ptyas and the chelidonia. For Nicander and Pliny treat the whole genus of asps. Nor has anyone else distinguished land asps from ptyades and chelidoniae in such a way as to dream that the latter excel in sight and the former in hearing. For all asps have the same dullness of eyes and sharpness of ears. Mercurialis: Common to all asps are these: weak sight, slow gait, keen hearing R1.


III, 162 Itaque alii surdam aspidem dici volunt non natura, sed consilio; quia, ut addit Psaltes, obturat aures, ne vocem incantatoris audiat. Theodoretus, Προσ-φυῶς αὐτὸν ἀσπίδι παρέβαλλεν, οὐ κωφευούσῃ κατὰ φύσιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ βυούσῃ τὰ ὦτα, καὶ τῆς ἐπῳδῆς ἀποθουμένῃ τὴν προσβολήν· Apposite illum aspidi comparavit, non natura surdae, sed aures obstruenti, ut incantationis vim prohibeat. Quomodo etiam Suidas in Κωφῆς. Et Augustinus, „Sicut aspidis sur-„dae] Unde surdae? unde „Et obturantis aures suas?] ideo surdae, quia obturat aures suas. Mediam viam insistit R. Selomo, scribens, aspidem in senectute una aure obsurdescere, alteram opplere pulvere, ne incantatoris vocem audiat, quod merum commentum est. Sed neque id satis certum, quod, ut ex vulgi rumoribus acceptum, referunt Augustinus, Cassiodorus, Beda, Isidorus, alii, aspidem, cum coeperit pati incantatorem, unam aurem ad terram col. 386 applicare, alteram obturare cauda, ne via pateat incantationi.

III, 162 Others therefore hold that the asp is called deaf not by nature but by design, because, as the Psalmist adds, it stops its ears so as not to hear the voice of the charmer. Theodoret: Προσφυῶς αὐτὸν ἀσπίδι παρέβαλλεν, οὐ κωφευούσῃ κατὰ φύσιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ βυούσῃ τὰ ὦτα, καὶ τῆς ἐπῳδῆς ἀποθουμένῃ τὴν προσβολήν [Prosphyōs auton aspidi pareballen, ou kōpheuousē kata physin, alla kai byousē ta ōta, kai tēs epōdēs apothoumenē tēn prosbolēn]; He aptly compared him to an asp, not deaf by nature, but stopping its ears so as to ward off the force of the incantation. So also Suidas under Κωφῆς [Kōphēs]. And Augustine: “Like the deaf asp” Why deaf? Whence “And stopping its ears?” It is deaf because it stops its ears. R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] takes a middle course, writing that the asp in old age grows deaf in one ear and fills the other with dust so as not to hear the charmer's voice, which is a pure fiction. But neither is it certain enough what Augustine, Cassiodorus, Bede, Isidore and others report, as taken from popular rumor: that the asp, when it begins to suffer the charmer, presses one ear to the ground col. 386 and stops the other with its tail, so that no way lies open to the incantation.


Verum, ut tota res clarior fiat, necesse habeo pauca praefari de serpentum incantatione, quos censet Augustinus a) ideo moveri magis hominum carminibus, quam ullum aliud genus animantium, ut hoc esset argumento, primum hominem a diabolo fuisse per serpentem in Paradiso seductum. Itaque integras gentes videas hoc fascini genere infames. In his Marsi et Psylli, quod omnes sciunt. Sed et idem praestare Aegyptios μαγείᾳ τινὶ ἐπιχωρίῳ, magica quadam ratione, illi genti propria, in Aeliano legas Historiae libri sexti capite trigesimo tertio. Et de Melindensibus hoc ipsum tradit Geographus Nubiensis, primi Climatis parte septima, يزعمون انهم يسحرون الحيوان الضار حتي لا يضر الا لمن ارادوا ضره Dicuntur noxia animalia ita incantare, ut nemini noceant, nisi cui ipsi voluerint. Et de Nigritis Cadamustus, Sunt etiam fascinatores, id est, incantatores eximii. Fascinant praesertim serpentes. Et de Peruanis in Orbe Novo Spitillus in Collectaneis: Puer festi tempore coronatus, altera manu telo instructa, altera vipera viva dependente, positam in loco quodam ornatissimo sedem occupat. Unde facile colligitur, daemonis esse artes, cum a vipera non mordeatur. Et de Indis Teixeira li-bri primi Historiae Persicae capite 29. Los vemos comunmente en la India adò suelen los gentiles traher culebras encantadas, algunes muy grandes, y terribles, por las calles, y casas, haziendo las baylar al son de una flauta, y las rebuelven al cuello, y hazen con ellas otros semejantes ademanes, tratando las con las manos sin III, 163 offensa suya. Y aunque algunos los attribuen a no tener dientes, porque dizen se los sacan siendo chiquitas. La experienzia muestra lo contrario, puez siendo algu- nas vezes ensannadas, o no tan ligadas con el encanto como convenia, se ha visto, que hazian grande estrago en los aspectantes. Quae Latine sic sonant: Illud in India saepe vidimus, ubi serpentes incantatos, eosque aliquando valde magnos et terribiles, per vias et domos deducere gentiles solent, quos manibus illaesi tradunt, et ad fistulae sonum saltare jubent, et collum retorquere, atque alios hujusmodi ge- stus agere. Quae ideo fieri quidam dictitant, quia sunt edentuli, et dentes, quos parvos habent, iis facile avelluntur. Sed experientia refelluntur, qui sic sentiunt: cum iidem hi serpentes irritati, nec incantatione ita vincti, quam par erat, non- nunquam visi sunt magnam spectatorum stragem edere (2).

But to make the whole matter clearer, I must say a few things first about the charming of serpents. Augustine a) holds that serpents are moved by the songs of men more than any other kind of animal, so that this would be a proof that the first man was seduced by the devil through the serpent in Paradise. And so you may see whole nations notorious for this kind of enchantment. Among them are the Marsi and the Psylli, as everyone knows. But you may also read in Aelian, History book 6, chapter 33, that the Egyptians do the same μαγείᾳ τινὶ ἐπιχωρίῳ [mageia tini epichōriō], by a certain magical art peculiar to that nation. And the Nubian Geographer, first Clime, part 7, reports this very thing of the people of Melinde: يزعمون انهم يسحرون الحيوان الضار حتي لا يضر الا لمن ارادوا ضره [yazʿumūn annahum yasḥarūn al-ḥayawān al-ḍārr ḥattā lā yaḍurr illā li-man arādū ḍarrahu] They are said to charm noxious animals so that they harm no one except whom they themselves wish. And Cadamosto [=Alvise Cadamosto, Navigazioni (1455-56)] of the Negroes: There are also enchanters, that is, outstanding charmers. They enchant serpents above all. And Spitillus in his Collectanea of the Peruvians in the New World: At festival time a boy, crowned, with a spear in one hand and a live viper hanging from the other, takes a seat placed in a very richly adorned spot. From this it is easily inferred that these are arts of the demon, since he is not bitten by the viper. And Teixeira [=Pedro Teixeira, Relaciones (1610)] of the Indians, History of Persia book 1, chapter 29: Los vemos comunmente en la India adò suelen los gentiles traher culebras encantadas, algunes muy grandes, y terribles, por las calles, y casas, haziendo las baylar al son de una flauta, y las rebuelven al cuello, y hazen con ellas otros semejantes ademanes, tratando las con las manos sin III, 163 offensa suya. Y aunque algunos los attribuen a no tener dientes, porque dizen se los sacan siendo chiquitas. La experienzia muestra lo contrario, puez siendo algunas vezes ensannadas, o no tan ligadas con el encanto como convenia, se ha visto, que hazian grande estrago en los aspectantes. In Latin this runs: We have often seen this in India, where the heathen are accustomed to lead charmed serpents, some of them very large and terrible, through the streets and houses; they handle them unharmed, make them dance to the sound of a pipe, twist them round the neck, and perform other gestures of this kind. Some keep saying this happens because they are toothless, and that their teeth, which are small, are easily pulled out. But those who think so are refuted by experience, since these same serpents, when provoked and not bound by the charm as firmly as they should be, have sometimes been seen to cause great slaughter among the spectators R2.


Neque haec superstitio hodie et heri nata est. Ejus enim vestigia in vetustissimis scriptoribus passim videas. Sic Eurydicem, a serpente ictam, ideo fingitur Orpheus ex inferis revocasse, quia

Nor was this superstition born today or yesterday. You may see traces of it everywhere in the most ancient writers. Thus Orpheus is fabled to have recalled Eurydice, struck by a serpent, from the underworld, because


— — ὑπὸ ὄφεως αὐτὴν τῷ ὄντι δεδηγμένην
Καὶ κυνδυνεύσαν θανεῖν, ταῖς ἐπῳδαῖς, αἷς οἶδε,
Καὶ ἀγχινοίᾳ, μέσῃ τε, καὶ πολυμαθείᾳ
Αὐτὴν ἐζωοποίησεν· — — — —

— — ὑπὸ ὄφεως αὐτὴν τῷ ὄντι δεδηγμένην Καὶ κυνδυνεύσαν θανεῖν, ταῖς ἐπῳδαῖς, αἷς οἶδε, Καὶ ἀγχινοίᾳ, μέσῃ τε, καὶ πολυμαθείᾳ Αὐτὴν ἐζωοποίησεν· — — — — [— — hypo opheōs autēn tō onti dedēgmenēn / Kai kyndyneusan thanein, tais epōdais, hais oide, / Kai anchinoia, mesē te, kai polymatheia / Autēn ezōopoiēsen · — — — —]


Ab angue ipsam re vera morsam, et vita periclitantem, incantationibus, quas no- verat, et solertia, et musa, et multa doctrina ad vitam revocavit. Ita Tzetzes Chiliadis secundae Historia quinquagesima quarta. Neque Orpheum hanc artem III, 164 latuisse, idem probat ex ipsius Orphei verbis in opere De lapidibus (quod tamen opus Timocli Syracusano cum Suida tribuere malim),

She had in truth been bitten by a snake and was in danger of her life; by the incantations he knew, by his skill, his muse and his great learning he restored her to life. So Tzetzes, Chiliad 2, History 54. And the same writer proves that this art was not unknown to Orpheus III, 164 from the words of Orpheus himself in the work On Stones (a work which, however, I would rather ascribe with Suidas to Timocles of Syracuse),


Ῥοῖζόν τε στῆσαι χαμαὶ ἐρχομένοιο δράκοντος,
Εἴσεται, ἠδ' ὄφεων ἰὸν σβέσαι ἑρπυστήρων·

Ῥοῖζόν τε στῆσαι χαμαὶ ἐρχομένοιο δράκοντος, Εἴσεται, ἠδ' ὄφεων ἰὸν σβέσαι ἑρπυστήρων· [Rhoizon te stēsai chamai erchomenoio drakontos, / Eisetai, ēd' opheōn ion sbesai herpystērōn ·]


Stridoremque sistere humi venientis draconis sciet, et serpentum repentium venenum (aut vero jaculum) exstinguere. Haec verba ideo profero libentius, quia ad ea Paulus palam alludit Ephes. VI, 16. Illa porro reperias in proëmio operis Περὶ col. 387 λίθων, sed corrupta. Nam pro ῥοῖζόν τε στῆσαι, metro et sensu repugnante, nostrae editiones habent Ῥοιζῶντες, καὶ, etc. Eodem pertinet, quod Apollonii Argonauticῶn libri quarti versu 147. Medea legitur

He will know how to stop the hissing of the dragon coming along the ground, and to quench the poison (or rather the dart) of creeping serpents. I cite these words the more gladly because Paul plainly alludes to them in Ephes. VI, 16. You will find them, moreover, in the proem of the work Περὶ col. 387 λίθων [Peri lithōn], but corrupted. For instead of ῥοῖζόν τε στῆσαι [rhoizon te stēsai], our editions, against both metre and sense, have Ῥοιζῶντες, καὶ [Rhoizōntes, kai], etc. To the same point belongs what we read of Medea in Apollonius, Argonautica book 4, line 147:


Ἡδείῃ ἐνοπῇ θέλξαι τέρας,

Ἡδείῃ ἐνοπῇ θέλξαι τέρας, [Hēdeiē enopē thelxai teras,]


suavi voce mulsisse monstrum, id est, draconem, velleris aurei custodem. Proinde sequitur non multo post,

that she soothed the monster with sweet voice, that is, the dragon, guardian of the golden fleece. Accordingly there follows not much later,


— — — αὐτὰρ ὅ γ' ἤδη
Οἴμῃ θελγόμενος δολιχὴν ἀναλύετ᾽ ἄκανθαν,

— — — αὐτὰρ ὅ γ' ἤδη Οἴμῃ θελγόμενος δολιχὴν ἀναλύετ᾽ ἄκανθαν, [— — — autar ho g' ēdē / Oimē thelgomenos dolichēn analyet' akanthan,]


Hujus igitur cantu deliniti longa spina resoluta est. At Ovidius idem Iasoni tribuens libro septimo Metamorphoseως,

So, soothed by her song, his long spine was relaxed. But Ovid, ascribing the same thing to Jason in book 7 of the Metamorphoses:


Hunc postquam sparsit Lethaei gramine succi,
Verbaque ter dixit placidos facientia somnos.

After he had sprinkled him with herbs of Lethean juice,
And thrice spoken the words that bring peaceful sleep.


Ad id ipsum magiae genus alludunt haec Platonis libro secundo De Republica, Θρασύμαχος φαίνεται ὑπό σου ὥσπερ ὄφις κηληθῆναι· Thrasymachus videtur a te ut serpens delinitus. Sed disertiora qui volet, in fine Mirabilium, quae Aristoteli tribuuntur [cap. CLXII.], longam historiam legat de serpente, sacro dicto, magae Thessalae carminibus exanimato. Quale est, quod serpentum morsibus Indos ἐπῳδοὺς Alexandri comes, Nearchus, et tibicines Theophrastus mederi tradunt: ille apud Strabonem libro decimo quinto; hic Gellii libri quarti capite decimo tertio. Et quod sub Lagi filio scripsit Antigonus, Psyllos, ab aspidibus ictos, nihil pati, Mirabilium capite decimo nono.

To this very kind of magic Plato alludes in these words in book 2 of the Republic: Θρασύμαχος φαίνεται ὑπό σου ὥσπερ ὄφις κηληθῆναι [Thrasymachos phainetai hypo sou hōsper ophis kēlēthēnai]· Thrasymachus seems to have been charmed by you like a serpent. But whoever wants something more explicit should read, at the end of the Mirabilia attributed to Aristotle [ch. 162], the long story of a serpent called sacred, killed by the spells of a Thessalian witch. Of the same kind is the report that the Indian ἐπῳδοὺς [epōdous], charmers, cure the bites of serpents, as Nearchus, the companion of Alexander, relates, and by flute-players, as Theophrastus relates: the former in Strabo, book 15; the latter in Gellius, book 4, chapter 13. And what Antigonus wrote under the son of Lagus, that the Psylli, when struck by asps, suffer nothing, Mirabilia, chapter 19.


Hujus porro fascini multa genera. Aliis enim serpentes manu et tactu fascinare moris erat. Virgilius libro septimo Aeneidos, versu 754.

Of this enchantment, moreover, there are many kinds. Some were accustomed to enchant serpents by hand and touch. Virgil, Aeneid book 7, line 754:


Spargere qui somnos cantuque manuque solebat.

Who was wont to scatter sleep by song and by hand.


Silius. Italicus libri primi versu 411.

Silius Italicus, book 1, line 411:


Nec non serpentes diro exarmare veneno Doctus Atyr, tactuque graves sopire chelydros. III, 165 Et libri octavi versu 500.

And Atyr, skilled to disarm serpents of their dire poison and by touch to lull the noxious chelydri to sleep. III, 165 And book 8, line 500:

Monstravisse ferunt, tactuque domare venena.
