showed baneful herbs, and tamed poisons by touch.


Symmachus libri septimi Epistola decima nona, Quis Colchus, aut Thessalus, cantu, aut manu has offensiones levasset? Alii orbem describebant, et medicamina adhibebant. Ita Thessalam mulierem in urbe Teno narrat Aristoteles, aut quisquis Mirabilia scripsit, ut sacrum serpentem exanimaret, κύκλον γράψα-σαν, καὶ τὰ φάρμακα θεῖσαν, εἰσβῆναι εἰς τὸν κύκλον αὐτὴν καὶ τὸν υἱὸν, cum circulum descripsisset, et pharmaca in eo posuisset, in illum circulum cum filio esse ingressam. Et in Luciani Philopseude Chaldaeus, ut serpentes evocaret, in agrum mane veniens, sacra septem nomina ex vetusto libro legit, θείῳ καὶ δαδὶ καταγνίσας τὸν τόπον, περιελθὼν εἰς τρὶς, sulphure ac face lustrato loco in orbem ter obambulans. Rursus alium fascini ritum his verbis describit Seneca in Medea Actu quarto,

Symmachus, book 7, letter 19: What Colchian or Thessalian would have relieved these injuries by song or by hand? Others drew a circle and applied drugs. Thus Aristotle, or whoever wrote the Mirabilia, relates that a Thessalian woman in the city of Tenos, in order to kill the sacred serpent, κύκλον γράψασαν, καὶ τὰ φάρμακα θεῖσαν, εἰσβῆναι εἰς τὸν κύκλον αὐτὴν καὶ τὸν υἱὸν [kyklon grapsasan, kai ta pharmaka theisan, eisbēnai eis ton kyklon autēn kai ton huion], having drawn a circle and placed drugs in it, entered that circle with her son. And in Lucian's Philopseudes the Chaldaean, to call forth serpents, came into the field in the morning and read seven sacred names from an old book, θείῳ καὶ δαδὶ καταγνίσας τὸν τόπον, περιελθὼν εἰς τρὶς [theiō kai dadi katagnisas ton topon, perielthōn eis tris], having purified the place with sulphur and a torch, walking round it three times. Again, Seneca describes another rite of enchantment in these words in the Medea, Act 4:


Et triste laeva complicans sacrum manu,
Pestes vocat, quascunque ferventis creat
Arena Libyae. — — —

And folding the grim rite with her left hand,
she summons the plagues, whatever the sand
of burning Libya breeds. — — —


Laminae, etiam lapides, ligna, figurae Talismanicae, quas vocant, in eum usum adhibitae. Arnobius libro secundo, Adversus ictus noxios, et venenatos colubrarum morsus, remedia saepe conquirimus, et protegimus nos laminis, Marsis et Psyllis vendentibus. (Alii, dubito, an melius, Protegimus nos labiis, Marsis, Psyllisve dentibus). Et Nubiensis Geographus (Climatis primi parte tertia) circa Nigritarum urbem Cucu ligeum quoddam nasci fabulatur, quod عود الحية lignum serpentis ideo vocant, quia اذا وضع علي حجر الحية خرجت اليه مسرعة cum latibulo serpentis apponitur, statim ad illud egreditur serpens. Imo, si credimus, quisquis hoc lignum manu tenet, ياخذ من الحيات ما شا بيده من غير ان يدركه col. 388 شي من الجزع ويجد في نفسه قوة عند اخذها serpentes, quotquot voluerit, ita manu capiet, ut interim nullo timore percellatur, quin in iis captandis quandam in se sentiet fortitudinem. Alii tamen aliter referunt: nempe, si quis hoc lignum manu teneat, aut collo appendat, لم تقربه حية البتة serpentem ad eum nullo modo accedere. Idem de Emesa, urbe, haec habet Climatis tertii parte quinta, وهي مطلسمة لا يدخلها حية ولا عقرب ومتي ادخلت علي الباب المدينة هلكت علي الحال Illa sic talismanizata est) id est, III, 166 οὕτω τετελειωμένη, talibus τελέσμασι, seu talismanis instructa), ut nulli eam serpentes aut scorpiones ingrediantur, quin, si ad portam civitatis inferantur, sta- tim exspirent. Addit, in quadam testudine lapidem esse infixum, in quo scorpii figura est incisa, cujus tactu sanatur is, quem scorpio pupugit, aut momordit. Qua fide apud Plinium libri vigesimi octavi capite tertio, Attalus affirmat, scorpione viso, si quis dicat DUO, cohiberi, nec vibrare ictus. Et Alcamus, اوس os, vel اوسه osoh, esse كلمة تقال للحية فتنخضع vocem, quae cum serpenti dicitur, is se demittit. An quia serpentis sibilum videtur imitari? Sic enim in libro Mirabilium Thessala, maga, ut sacrum serpentem in suum circulum evocet, dicitur μιμεῖσθαι τὴν φωνὴν τοῦ θηρίου, bestiae vocem imitari. Quod Arabice uno verbo صدا dicitur. Nempe صدا est, serpen- tem incantando illius sibilum imitari, quomodo Echo nostram vocem imitatur. Nam صدي Nomen est echo, ex quo Nomine fit Verbum صدا.

Metal plates, also stones, pieces of wood, and so-called talismanic figures were employed for this use. Arnobius, book 2: Against harmful strokes and the poisonous bites of snakes we often seek remedies, and we protect ourselves with plates sold by the Marsi and Psylli. (Others read, I doubt whether better, We protect ourselves with the lips, with the teeth of the Marsi or Psylli.) And the Nubian Geographer (Clime 1, part 3) tells the fable that near the Nigritian city of Cucu there grows a certain wood which they therefore call عود الحية [ʿūd al-ḥayya] serpent's wood, because اذا وضع علي حجر الحية خرجت اليه مسرعة [idhā wuḍiʿa ʿalā juḥr al-ḥayya kharajat ilayhi musriʿa] when it is placed at a serpent's lair, the serpent immediately comes out to it. Indeed, if we believe it, whoever holds this wood in his hand ياخذ من الحيات ما شا بيده من غير ان يدركه col. 388 شي من الجزع ويجد في نفسه قوة عند اخذها [yākhudh min al-ḥayyāt mā shā bi-yadihi min ghayr an yudrikahu shay min al-jazaʿ wa-yajid fī nafsihi quwwa ʿinda akhdhihā] will take as many serpents as he wishes in his hand, in such a way that meanwhile he is struck by no fear; rather, in catching them he will feel a certain strength within himself. Others, however, report it differently: namely, that if anyone holds this wood in his hand or hangs it from his neck, لم تقربه حية البتة [lam taqrabhu ḥayya al-batta] no serpent at all approaches him. The same author has this about the city of Emesa, Clime 3, part 5: وهي مطلسمة لا يدخلها حية ولا عقرب ومتي ادخلت علي الباب المدينة هلكت علي الحال [wa-hiya muṭalsama lā yadkhuluhā ḥayya wa-lā ʿaqrab wa-matā udkhilat ʿalā al-bāb al-madīna halakat ʿalā al-ḥāl] It is so talismanized) that is, III, 166 οὕτω τετελειωμένη [houtō teteleiōmenē], furnished with such τελέσμασι [telesmasi], or talismans), that no serpents or scorpions enter it; rather, if they are brought to the gate of the city, they immediately expire. He adds that in a certain vault a stone is set in which the figure of a scorpion is carved, by touching which a person whom a scorpion has stung or bitten is healed. With the same credibility, in Pliny, book 28, chapter 3, Attalus affirms that if anyone on seeing a scorpion says TWO, it is checked and does not dart its stroke. And Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] says that اوس [aws] os, or اوسه [awsah] osoh, is كلمة تقال للحية فتنخضع [kalima tuqāl li-l-ḥayya fa-tankhaḍiʿ] a word which, when said to a serpent, makes it lower itself. Is it because it seems to imitate the hissing of a serpent? For thus in the book of Mirabilia the Thessalian witch, in order to call the sacred serpent into her circle, is said μιμεῖσθαι τὴν φωνὴν τοῦ θηρίου [mimeisthai tēn phōnēn tou thēriou], to imitate the voice of the beast. This is expressed in Arabic by one word, صدا [ṣadā]. Namely, صدا [ṣadā] means to imitate a serpent's hissing in charming it, as Echo imitates our voice. For صدي [ṣadā] is the noun for echo, from which noun the verb صدا [ṣadā] is formed.


Sed hujus fascini praecipua vis esse creditur in cantibus et carminibus, quae Hebraei לחשים, id est, susurros, aut mussitationes vocant; quia magi cantus suos solent inter labia demurmurare (3). De his agit Psaltes hoc loco, cum surdam aspidem dicit obturare aurem suam, ne audiat vocem מלחשים, mussitantium, seu incantatorum. Cantu nempe magico credebantur serpentes, 1. Primo e cavernis elici atque evocari. Sic Plinius libri octavi capite decimo sexto eos ex- trahi cantu, dicit, cogique in poenam. Et Aelianus de Aegyptiis, libri sexti capite trigesimo tertio, Τῶν φωλεῶν τοὺς ὄφεις, ἐπαοιδαῖς τισι καταγοητεύσαν-τες, εἶτα μέντοι προσάγουσι ῥᾶστα· Serpentes, carminibus quibusdam primum incantatos, e latibulis postmodum facillime extrahunt. Et Seneca in Medea,

But the chief power of this fascination is believed to lie in chants and songs, which the Hebrews call לחשים, that is, whisperings or mutterings, because magicians are accustomed to murmur their chants between their lips R3. The Psalmist treats of these in this place, when he says that the deaf asp stops its ear so as not to hear the voice of מלחשים, the mutterers, or charmers. For by magic chant serpents were believed, 1. first, to be drawn out and called forth from their holes. Thus Pliny, book 8, chapter 16, says that they are drawn out by chant and compelled to punishment. And Aelian, on the Egyptians, book 6, chapter 33: Τῶν φωλεῶν τοὺς ὄφεις, ἐπαοιδαῖς τισι καταγοητεύσαντες, εἶτα μέντοι προσάγουσι ῥᾶστα [Tōn phōleōn tous opheis, epaoidais tisi katagoēteusantes, eita mentoi prosagousi rhasta]; Serpents, first charmed with certain songs, they afterwards draw out of their lurking places very easily. And Seneca in the Medea:


— — tracta magicis cantibus
Squamea latebris turba desertis adest.

— — drawn by magic chants
the scaly throng is present, its lairs deserted.


Ut in Luciani Philopseude ad Chaldaeum magum ἧκον, ὥσπερ ἑλκόμενοι πρὸς τὴν ἐπῳδὴν, ὄφεις πολλοὶ, καὶ ἀσπίδες, καὶ ἔχιδναι, καὶ κεράσαι, καὶ ἀκον-τίαι, Venerunt, tanquam incantatione tracti, multi serpentes, aspides nimirum, et viperae, et cerastae, et jaculi. Lampridius in Heliogabalo. Serpentes per Marsicae gentis sacerdotes collegisse fertur. Hieronymus in Psal. LVII. Ille ho- mo, qui incantat, Marsus dicitur, et trahit eos de tenebris ad lumen. Augustinus III, 167 libri undecimi De Genesi ad literam capite vigesimo octavo, Putantur audire et intelligere serpentes verba Marsorum, ut, eis incantantibus, prosiliant plerumque de latebris. Et libri Quaestionum 65. Quaest. 44. Ut de antris ad verba Marsorum exeant, permittente Deo, coguntur a diabolo. Et in De Haeresibus capite decimo septimo, ubi de Ophitis; Habent etiam verum colubrum, quem nutriunt et venerantur. Qui et, incantante sacerdote, egreditur de spelunca, et col. 389 ascendit super altare innixum speluncae. Cadamustus de nepote principis Budomel, Navigationum capite vigesimo octavo; Designato in terra circulo, fascinatione serpentes eo concedere compellit. Scaliger in libros anim. libro primo capite vigesimo octavo sectione 123. Nos aliquando vidimus cantationibus e cavernis exciri serpentes. Eodem facere multi credunt, quod magum Hebraei חובר chober, quasi consociatorem, appellant; quia evocata animalia in unum consociat et congregat. Sic Deut. XVIII, 11, חובר חבר, juxta Selomonem est, שמצרף נחשים או עקרבים או שאר חיות למקום אחד, qui consociat serpentes, aut scorpiones, aut reliqua animalia in locum unum. Quae ex his Ionathanis sumpta sunt in paraphrasi, ומחברין ואסרין חיוין ועקרבין וכל מיני רחשין, Qui consociant et li-gant (magicis scilicet verbis) serpentes, et scorpiones, et omnes reptilium species. Cui paraphrasi Hierosolymitana non est absimilis. Neque videtur alia mens fuisse Psaltis, cum in hoc ipso loco dicit, Non audit vocem incantatorum, neque חובר חוברים מחכם, (ad verbum) periti consociatoris consociationum, id est, ejus, qui callet artem serpentes ad se evocandi, ut in unum congregentur. Proinde Chaldaeus hic reddit, דלא מקבל לקל מלי חרשיא אסורי נחשין, Quae (aspis) non audit vocem et verba magorum, qui ligant serpentes (4).

As in Lucian's Philopseudes, to the Chaldaean magician ἧκον, ὥσπερ ἑλκόμενοι πρὸς τὴν ἐπῳδὴν, ὄφεις πολλοὶ, καὶ ἀσπίδες, καὶ ἔχιδναι, καὶ κεράσαι, καὶ ἀκοντίαι [hēkon, hōsper helkomenoi pros tēn epōdēn, opheis polloi, kai aspides, kai echidnai, kai kerasai, kai akontiai], there came, as if drawn by the incantation, many serpents, namely asps, and vipers, and cerastae, and javelin-snakes. Lampridius in the Heliogabalus: He is said to have gathered serpents by means of priests of the Marsian people. Jerome on Psal. LVII.: That man who charms is called a Marsus, and he draws them from darkness to the light. Augustine III, 167, book 11 On Genesis according to the Letter, chapter 28: Serpents are thought to hear and understand the words of the Marsi, so that, when these charm them, they very often spring out of their lurking places. And in the book of 65 Questions, Question 44: That they come out of their caves at the words of the Marsi they are compelled by the devil, God permitting. And in On Heresies, chapter 17, on the Ophites: They also have a real snake, which they feed and venerate. And, when the priest charms, it comes out of the cave and col. 389 climbs up on the altar set against the cave. Cadamosto, on the nephew of the prince Budomel, Navigations, chapter 28: Having drawn a circle on the ground, by fascination he compels the serpents to come into it. Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)] on the books on animals, book 1, chapter 28, section 123: We have sometimes seen serpents roused from their holes by chants. Many believe it points the same way that the Hebrews call a magician חובר chober, as it were an associator, because he associates and gathers together into one the animals he has called forth. Thus at Deut 18:11, חובר חבר, according to Solomon [Rashi], is שמצרף נחשים או עקרבים או שאר חיות למקום אחד, one who associates serpents, or scorpions, or other animals into one place. This is taken from Jonathan's [=Targum Jonathan] paraphrase: ומחברין ואסרין חיוין ועקרבין וכל מיני רחשין, who associate and bind (namely by magic words) serpents, and scorpions, and all kinds of reptiles. The Jerusalem paraphrase is not unlike it. Nor does the Psalmist seem to have had another meaning when he says in this very place, It does not hear the voice of the charmers, nor חובר חוברים מחכם, (word for word) of the skilled associator of associations, that is, of him who knows the art of calling serpents to himself so that they gather into one. Accordingly the Chaldee renders here דלא מקבל לקל מלי חרשיא אסורי נחשין, Which (the asp) does not hear the voice and words of the magicians who bind serpents R4.

Plutarchus in Catone, de Psyllis; Τὰ θηρία κατεπάδοντες ἀμβλύνουσι, καὶ κηλοῦσι· Serpentes cantu obstupefaciunt et demulcent. Philostratus in Apollonio, libri tertii capite secundo: Scripta incantatoria verba draconibus dicuntur somnum inducere: Graece, ὕπνον ἐγγοητεύσαντες τοῖς γράμμασιν. Plutarch in the Cato, on the Psylli: Τὰ θηρία κατεπάδοντες ἀμβλύνουσι, καὶ κηλοῦσι· [Ta thēria katepadontes amblynousi, kai kēlousi] By song they stupefy and soothe the serpents. Philostratus in the Apollonius, book 3, chapter 2: Written incantatory words are said to induce sleep in dragons: in Greek, ὕπνον ἐγγοητεύσαντες τοῖς γράμμασιν [hypnon engoēteusantes tois grammasin]. So Theodoret, on Psalm 57, says that the asp stops its ear while the magician sings, ὥστε μὴ θέλγεσθαι ταῖς ἐπῳδαῖς [hōste mē thelgesthai tais epōdais], so that it may not be soothed by the incantations. And on the same passage Hilary: Nor does he here mention the chants of the Marsi, or the lulled hissing of vipers. Cadamosto, in the place cited above: He went and restrained the serpents with a spell, and returning at once he addressed his guest thus: The serpents had besieged the house to lay it waste, had I not met so great an evil with an incantation, which we use rather frequently.


Cantu insuper crediti serpentes ab omni veneno expurgari, ut ne morsu noceant. Ita Isidorus Originum libri noni capite secundo, Marsos scribit illae- col. 390 sos esse carminum maleficiis. Quo pertinent haec Alcimi libro secundo De peccato originali,

Moreover, serpents were believed to be purged of all poison by song, so that they do no harm by their bite. Thus Isidore, Etymologies book 9, chapter 2, writes that the Marsi are unharmed by the evil effects of charms. col. 390 To this belong these lines of Alcimus, book 2, On Original Sin:


Concutit interius secreti carminis arma, etc. Mox impune manu coluber tractatur inermi: Et morsus tantum, non virus, in angue timetur.

Within he wields the weapons of a secret charm, etc. Soon the snake is handled with impunity by an unarmed hand: And in the snake only the bite, not the poison, is feared.


Et Maimonidis, De Idololatria capitis undecimi sectione decima; הן אומרים שח׳ אומר כך וכך על הנחש או על העקרב אינו מזיק, Si magus, ut ajunt, hoc vel illud serpenti aut scorpioni dixerit, is non nocebit amplius. Quin, apud Delrium libri secundi Disquisitionum magicarum Quaestione decima tertia, asserit Petrus Chieza, vere ne an secus, lectoris esto judicium, omnes Andinorum montium vastos serpentes omnem ferociam vimque noxiam posuisse, vetulae cujusdam carminibus olim exarmatos: ita, ut nunc etiam aspectu tantum terreant, caetera sint innoxii.

And Maimonides [=Moses Maimonides (Rambam), Mishneh Torah], On Idolatry, chapter 11, section 10: הן אומרים שח׳ אומר כך וכך על הנחש או על העקרב אינו מזיק, If a magician, as they say, has said this or that to a serpent or a scorpion, it will do no further harm. Indeed, in Delrio, book 2 of the Disquisitiones magicae, Question 13, Pedro Cieza asserts (whether truly or otherwise, let the reader judge) that all the huge serpents of the Andes mountains have laid aside all their ferocity and harmful power, having once been disarmed by the charms of a certain old woman: so that even now they terrify only by their appearance, and are otherwise harmless.


Putatur quoque virtus carminis eos sanare, quos morsu laesit, aut tactu serpens. Quo nomine apud Strabonem Indos commendat Nearchus. Cum enim in India serpentes et reptilia quaevis magno numero scateant, et locorum incolis sint multis modis molesta: ibi refert ἐπῳδοὺς περιφοιτᾷν πεπιστευμένους ἰᾶ-σθαι, καὶ εἶναι σχεδόν τι ταύτην μόνην ἰατρικὴν, circumvagari incantatores, qui III, 170 mederi putantur, et hanc fere solam esse medicinam. Sic de Umbrone Poeta libro septimo,

The power of a charm is also thought to heal those whom a serpent has injured by its bite or touch. On this account Nearchus, in Strabo, commends the Indians. For since in India serpents and reptiles of every kind swarm in great numbers and trouble the inhabitants in many ways, he reports that there ἐπῳδοὺς περιφοιτᾷν πεπιστευμένους ἰᾶσθαι, καὶ εἶναι σχεδόν τι ταύτην μόνην ἰατρικὴν [epōdous periphoitan pepisteumenous iasthai, kai einai schedon ti tautēn monēn iatrikēn], charmers wander about who III, 170 are believed to heal, and that this is almost the only medicine. So of Umbro, in the Poet, book 7:


— — — et morsus arte levabat.

— — — and by his art he relieved bites.


Et Lucanus libri noni versu 933.

And Lucan, book 9, line 933:


— — pestis nigris inserta medullis
Excantata perit. — — —

— — the plague implanted in the black marrow
perishes, charmed away. — — —


Hoc praecipuum, quod angues, Mago cantante, rumpi dicuntur, et crepare medii. Lucilius,

The chief point is this: snakes, when the magician sings, are said to burst and to split in the middle. Lucilius:


— — — Marsu', coluber
Distendit cantu, venas cum extenderit omnes.

— — — the Marsian bursts the snake
with song, when he has stretched out all its veins.


Virgilius Ecloga octava,

Virgil, Eclogue 8:


Frigidus in pratis cantando rumpitur anguis.

The cold snake in the meadows is burst by chanting.


Ovidius libri septimi Metamorphoseωs Fabula secunda sub persona Medeae,

Ovid, Metamorphoses book 7, Fable 2, in the person of Medea:

I burst the jaws of vipers with words and charm.

By a charm snakes burst asunder, their jaws torn apart.


Et De Medicamine faciei,

And On Cosmetics for the Face:

Nor let snakes be split in the middle by Marsian chants.

Caputque Marsa dissilire naenia.

Lucan, book 6, line 488:


— — — gelidos his explicat orbes,
Inque pruinoso coluber distenditur arvo,
Viperei coëunt, abrupto corpore, nodi.

and is stretched out on the frosty field;
the viper's knots join again, its body broken.


Nemesianus, Ecloga quarta, de Mycale venefica;

Nemesianus, Eclogue 4, of the sorceress Mycale:


Cantavit quod Luna timet, quo rumpitur anguis.

She has chanted what the Moon fears, by which the snake is burst.


Et Philosophus ubi supra, Ὡς δὲ προσῆλθεν ὁ ὄφις εἰς τὸν κύκλον, λύσιν εὐθὺς γενέσθαι αὐτου. Quamprimum serpens in circulum est ingressus, eum (ajunt) statim fuisse solutum, id est, solutis compagibus extinctum.

And the Philosopher, in the place cited above: Ὡς δὲ προσῆλθεν ὁ ὄφις εἰς τὸν κύκλον, λύσιν εὐθὺς γενέσθαι αὐτου [Hōs de prosēlthen ho ophis eis ton kyklon, lysin euthys genesthai autou]. As soon as the serpent entered the circle, it (they say) was at once dissolved, that is, killed, its joints loosened.


Interim quosdam esse serpentes, qui incantari non possint, vel ex Scriptura videtur posse elici. Nam Ierem. VIII, 17. minatur Deus, se in Israelitas immissurum III, 171 נחשים צפעונים אשר אין להם לחש, serpentes regulos, contra quos nulla sit incantatio. Complutenses, οἷς οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκσπᾶσαι, a quibus non licet se avellere: sed alii melius, οἷς οὐκ ἔστιν ἐπάσαι, quos incantare non licet. Et Ec- cles. X, 11. Solomon בעל לשון, obtrectatorem nihilo meliorem (id est, tam perniciosum) esse dicit, quam אם נשך הנחש בלא לחש, si mordeat serpens sine incantatione, id est, non incantatus, vel qui incantari non potest. Et in loco Psaltis, in quo versamur, aspis surda dicitur aurem suam obturare, ne incanta- toris vocem audiat. Nempe duobus modis incantationi serpens putatur obluctari, aut cum recanit, aut cum obsurdescit ad cantum. Recanere ἀντᾴδειν, vel recantare si mavis, est contrario sibilo incantationem repellere et retorquere. Plinius libri vigesimi octavi cap. secundo, Non pauci etiam (credunt) serpentes ipsas recane- col. 391 re, (ita cum Turnebo b)) lego, et hunc unum esse illis intellectum. Aristoteles de saga Thessala, Εἶτα μιμεῖσθαι τὴν φωνὴν τοῦ θηρίου· τὸ δὲ ἀντᾴδειν, καὶ προσι-έναι· Deinde imitari (coepit saga) vocem serpentis: serpens vero recanere et acce- dere. Serpens, in quem irrita est incantatio, quia cantui sic occinit, صل sil dicitur Arabice, ut اصم asammo, id est, surdus, qui cantu non afficitur. Proprie صل sil est serpens tinnulus, vel stridulus, id est, qui, stridore quodam edito, mago occentat et obsibilat. At phrasi, tam Hebraeis et Arabibus familiari, quam Graecis et Romanis ignota, ad cantum obsurdescere, vel, quod idem est, aurem obturare dicitur serpens, cum cantu nihilo magis afficitur, quam si vel surdus esset, vel auribus obtusis. Ita accepit Kimchius in loco Psalmi, ubi de aspide dicit, זה הנחש הקשה לא יועיל בו לחש כאילו הוא חרש וכאילו יאטם אזנו שלו ישמע מה שלוחשים לו, Durus est ille serpens, in quem non magis proficit incantatio, quam si vel surdus esset, vel obduraret aurem, ne audiret car- mina, quibus illum incantant. Eadem phrasi, qui erga pauperes durus est, et immisericors, aurem obdurare dicitur a clamore pauperis, Prov. XXI, 13. Et vir pius aurem obturat, ne audiat caedes, Es. XXXIII, 15. id est, a cruentis et sanguinariis consiliis tam alienus est, neque ad ea magis attendit, cum ab impiis proponuntur, quam si aures haberet obturatas. Sic, cum de Aenea dicitur libro quarto Aeneidos,

Meanwhile, that there are some serpents which cannot be charmed seems deducible even from Scripture. For in Jer 8:17. God threatens that he will send among the Israelites III, 171 נחשים צפעונים אשר אין להם לחש, serpents, reguli, against which there is no charm. The Complutensian edition has οἷς οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκσπᾶσαι [hois ouk estin ekspasai], from which one cannot tear oneself away; but others better, οἷς οὐκ ἔστιν ἐπάσαι [hois ouk estin epasai], which one cannot charm. And in Eccl 10:11 Solomon says that a בעל לשון, a slanderer, is no better (that is, just as pernicious) than אם נשך הנחש בלא לחש, if a serpent bites without charm, that is, uncharmed, or one that cannot be charmed. And in the passage of the Psalmist with which we are concerned, the deaf asp is said to stop its ear, so as not to hear the voice of the charmer. Indeed, a serpent is thought to resist a charm in two ways: either when it sings back, or when it grows deaf to the song. Recanere [to sing back], ἀντᾴδειν [antadein], or recantare if you prefer, is to repel and turn back the charm by a contrary hissing. Pliny, book 28, ch. 2: Not a few (believe) that the serpents themselves sing back, col. 391 (so I read with Turnebus b)), and that this is the only understanding they have. Aristotle, of the Thessalian witch: Εἶτα μιμεῖσθαι τὴν φωνὴν τοῦ θηρίου· τὸ δὲ ἀντᾴδειν, καὶ προσιέναι· [Eita mimeisthai tēn phōnēn tou thēriou; to de antadein, kai prosienai;] Then (the witch began) to imitate the voice of the serpent; but the serpent sang back and approached. A serpent against which the charm is ineffective, because it sings against the song in this way, is called صل [ṣil] sil in Arabic, as one that is not affected by the song is called اصم [aṣamm] asammo, that is, deaf. Properly صل [ṣil] sil is a ringing or shrill serpent, that is, one which, uttering a certain shrill sound, sings and hisses against the magician. But by a phrase as familiar to the Hebrews and Arabs as it is unknown to the Greeks and Romans, a serpent is said to grow deaf to the song, or, what is the same, to stop its ear, when it is no more affected by the song than if it were deaf or had its ears stopped. So Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] took it in the passage of the Psalm, where he says of the asp: זה הנחש הקשה לא יועיל בו לחש כאילו הוא חרש וכאילו יאטם אזנו שלו ישמע מה שלוחשים לו, That serpent is hard, against which a charm avails no more than if it were deaf, or hardened its ear, so as not to hear the songs with which they charm it. By the same phrase, one who is hard and merciless toward the poor is said to harden his ear to the cry of the poor, Prov 21:13. And the pious man stops his ear, lest he hear of bloodshed, Isa 33:15, that is, he is so averse to cruel and bloodthirsty counsels, and attends to them no more when they are proposed by the wicked, than if he had his ears stopped. So also when it is said of Aeneas in book 4 of the Aeneid,


— — — sed nullis ille movetur
Fletibus, aut voces ullas tractabilis audit.
Fata obstant, placidasque viri Deus obstruit aures.

— — — but he is moved by no weeping, nor does he listen yielding to any words. The Fates stand in the way, and a god blocks the man's gentle ears.


Id est, ad Didus et Annae preces tam inflexum reddidit, ac si obstruxisset aures. Aspis pari ratione tum ad cantum surda est, et aurem obturat, cum in eam cantus tam parum valet, quam si esset plane surda, atque aures obturasset. Antecedens III, 172 pro consequente. Neque aliter ab Avicenna sumi puto, cum repetit toties, hunc vel illum serpentem esse e genere surdorum, ut pluribus infra docetur.

That is, he made him as unbending to the prayers of Dido and Anna as if he had blocked his ears. In like manner the asp is deaf to the song and stops its ear when the song has as little power over it as if it were entirely deaf and had stopped its ears. The antecedent stands for the consequent. III, 172 Nor, I think, is it taken otherwise by Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] when he so often repeats that this or that serpent is of the kind of the deaf, as is shown more fully below.


Porro, sive recanat serpens, aut ad cantum obsurdescat, non eluctari solum, sed et mago creditur creare periculum. Sic apud Aristotelem, cum Thessalae veneficae sacer serpens occentaret, parum abfuit, quin in soporem lethiferum illa dilaberetur. Atque, ut testatur Alcimus ubi supra,

Furthermore, whether the serpent sings back or grows deaf to the song, it is believed not only to escape, but also to create danger for the magician. So in Aristotle, when the sacred serpent sang against the Thessalian sorceress, she very nearly sank into a deadly sleep. And, as Alcimus testifies in the place cited above,


Interdum perit incantans, si callida surdus
Adjuratoris contempsit murmura serpens.

Sometimes the charmer perishes, if the deaf serpent has scorned the cunning murmurs of the adjurer.


Sive tota vis incantationis, justo Dei judicio, cedat in perniciem auctoris; sive serpens incantatori lethale vulnus inferat. Quo pertinet celebre exemplum c) Salzburgensis illius magi, qui, cum omnes ad unum milliare serpentes in quandam foveam cogere niteretur, tandem ab ingenti uno et annoso, in eum insiliente, necatus fuit. Itaque magos etiam morderi a serpentibus Sirachides his verbis docet Ecclesiastici capitis duodecimi versu decimo tertio, Τίς ἐλεήσει ἐπα-οιδὸν ὀφιόδηκτον, καὶ πάντας τοὺς προσάγοντας θηρίοις; Quis miserebitur incantatoris, a serpente demorsi, aut ullius eorum, qui accedunt ad venenatas bestias? Ibi enim θηρία non feras quasvis, sed venenatas significare, jam ante d) probavimus.

Either the whole force of the charm, by the just judgment of God, turns to the destruction of its author, or the serpent inflicts a lethal wound on the charmer. To this belongs the celebrated example c) of that magician of Salzburg who, when he was striving to drive all the serpents within one mile into a certain pit, was at last killed by a single huge and aged one that leapt upon him. Accordingly the Son of Sirach teaches that magicians too are bitten by serpents, in these words of Ecclesiasticus, chapter 12, verse 13: Τίς ἐλεήσει ἐπαοιδὸν ὀφιόδηκτον, καὶ πάντας τοὺς προσάγοντας θηρίοις; [Tis eleēsei epaoidon ophiodēkton, kai pantas tous prosagontas thēriois?] Who will pity a charmer bitten by a serpent, or any of those who go near venomous beasts? For there θηρία [thēria] signifies not any wild beasts whatever, but venomous ones, as we have already proved earlier d).


Qui porro serpentes recanant, vel ad cantum obsurdescant, vel quorum serpentum virus quovis fascino credatur esse potentius, Graecorum nullus explicat. Nisi quod Aelianus libri primi capite quinquagesimo quarto hoc aspidi videtur tanquam proprium assignare, quod in illius morsum neque medicamina, neque incantationes quidquam prosunt: Καὶ ἔχεως, inquit, δῆγμα, καὶ ὄφεως, ἀλλ᾽ οὖν, φασὶν, ἀντιπάλων μὴ διαμαρτάνειν φαρμάκων. Καὶ τὰ μὲν αὐτῶν ἀκούω πόματα εἶναι, τὰ δὲ χρίσματα· καὶ ἐπῳδαὶ δὲ ἐπραΰναν τινῶν ἐγχει-σθέντα ἰόν. Ἀσπίδος δὲ ἀκούω μόνον δῆγμα ἀνίατον εἶναι, καὶ ἐπικουρίας κρεῖττον. Viperae quidem et aliorum serpentium morsus ajunt non carere re- col. 392 mediis, quae malo opponantur. Quorum alia propinari, alia inungi audio: in nonnullis etiam incantationes impactum venenum mitigaverunt. Sed solius aspidis morsum insanabilem esse accepi, et omni auxilio superiorem. At rem, a Graecis intactam, accurate et dilucide exponit Avicenna post Arabes philosophos in capite De speciebus Serpentum, quod sic incipit e): ان العلما بامر الحيات وطبايعها قسموها ثلثة اقسام شديدة الحدة III, 173 لا تمهل من الحال الي فوق ثلث ساعات ولا علاج للسوعها وهي الصم والاصلال ولا ينفع فيها الا قطع العضو في الحال او الكي البالع النافذ بالنار فانه يحرق السم ويضيق المجاري Philosophi in libris de serpentibus, et natura eorum, trifariam illos dividunt. In prima specie veneni vis tam intensa est, ut mors a tempore morsus non differatur ultra tres horas, ne- que ulla sit curatio. Sunt enim e genere surdorum et stridulorum (id est, ut docuimus, eorum, qui vel ad cantum videntur obsurdescere, quia illo non magis afficiuntur, quam si surdi essent, vel etiam τῷ ἐπαοιδῷ ἀντᾴδουσι, incantatori recanunt, ita, ut in illos incantatio sit irrita). Itaque nihil prodest praeter mem- bri amputationem in eodem momento, vel combustionem ad intima penetrantem; quia venenum exurit, et constringit meatus. Addit, ad hanc speciem pertinere الملكة, regulum, qui solo visu et auditu interficit: et الخطاف aspidem chelidoniam: et الاسفيس اليابسة, aspidem siccam, seu χερ-σαίαν· quarum haec ante tres horas, illa ante duas necat: et البزاقة, aspi- dem ptyadem, a qua morsus interit قبل ان توجع, priusquam doleat, id est, sine dolore moritur; Latinus interpres absurde, antequam redeat; quia legit ترجع pro توجع. Quale est, quod paullo post idem interpres in hoc eodem censu ponit surdos arcuatos, qui multiplicantur in terris Aegypti. Surdos arcuatos, id est, الصم المقوسة. Quomodo legisse videtur nullo sensu, pro الصم المقعصة, qui sunt serpentes surdi, cito mortem infe- rentes. Cujusmodi sunt praeter regulum et aspidem, المقرنة, cerastes, et اوبريس, hydrus, et كرسودروس, chersydrus, quos omnes surdis accenset Avicenna in sequentibus. Sic in capite de Basilisco, هو الاول من الصم Is est primus surdorum. Et capite, De aspide Chelidonia, وهي من الصم Etiam haec est ex surdis. Et infra, وعلاجها علاج الصم Et curatio ejus est curatio surdorum. Quod ipsum habet in Aspide chersaea. Et in Ptyade, علاجها من جنس علاج الصم Curatur eo modo, quo surdi. Et capite De Ceraste, هي جنس من الصم Est e genere surdo- col. 393 rum. Et De Hydro, seu Chersydro, هي اصغر من الاصله صما Est dryino minor, surdus. Ut jam nemini sit obscurum, surdos ab Arabibus dici serpentes omnes, quos credunt ab incantatione esse immunes. Hinc Alca- mus diserte, الاصم من الحية لا يقبل الرقي Surdus de serpente is III, 174 est, qui incantationem non admittit. Tales porro ab iis habentur ii omnes, quorum virus in supremo gradu intensum est, reguli puta, aspidis, cerastae, hydri, chersydri. Cui doctrinae consonare videbitur, quod aspidem regius Psaltes; et regulum, seu basiliscum, Ieremias in illo genere ponunt. Quasi certis experimentis constet, aut serpentum id genus incantationem magos nequaquam aggredi; aut, si aggrediantur, illis adeo non succedere, ut saepe etiam cedat in perniciem auctorum.

Which serpents, moreover, sing back, or grow deaf at the chant, or whose poison is believed to be stronger than any spell, none of the Greeks explains. Except that Aelian, book 1, chapter 54, seems to assign this to the asp as its peculiar property, that against its bite neither medicines nor incantations are of any avail: Καὶ ἔχεως, he says, δῆγμα, καὶ ὄφεως, ἀλλ᾽ οὖν, φασὶν, ἀντιπάλων μὴ διαμαρτάνειν φαρμάκων. Καὶ τὰ μὲν αὐτῶν ἀκούω πόματα εἶναι, τὰ δὲ χρίσματα· καὶ ἐπῳδαὶ δὲ ἐπραΰναν τινῶν ἐγχεισθέντα ἰόν. Ἀσπίδος δὲ ἀκούω μόνον δῆγμα ἀνίατον εἶναι, καὶ ἐπικουρίας κρεῖττον. [Kai echeōs … dēgma, kai opheōs, all' oun, phasin, antipalōn mē diamartanein pharmakōn. Kai ta men autōn akouō pomata einai, ta de chrismata; kai epōdai de epraynan tinōn encheisthenta ion. Aspidos de akouō monon dēgma aniaton einai, kai epikourias kreitton.] The bites of the viper and of other serpents, they say, are not without remedies to be set against the evil. col. 392 Of these I hear that some are given to drink, others are rubbed on; in some cases even incantations have mitigated the injected poison. But I have learned that the bite of the asp alone is incurable and beyond all help. But the matter, left untouched by the Greeks, is set out accurately and clearly by Avicenna, following the Arab philosophers, in the chapter On the species of serpents, which begins thus e): ان العلما بامر الحيات وطبايعها قسموها ثلثة اقسام شديدة الحدة [inna al-ʿulamā bi-amr al-ḥayyāt wa-ṭabāyiʿihā qassamūhā thalathat aqsām shadīdat al-ḥidda] III, 173 لا تمهل من الحال الي فوق ثلث ساعات ولا علاج للسوعها وهي الصم والاصلال ولا ينفع فيها الا قطع العضو في الحال او الكي البالع النافذ بالنار فانه يحرق السم ويضيق المجاري [lā tumhil min al-ḥāl ilī fawq thalath sāʿāt wa-lā ʿilāj li-lusūʿihā wa-hiya al-ṣumm wa-al-aṣlāl wa-lā yanfaʿ fīhā illā qaṭʿ al-ʿuḍw fī al-ḥāl aw al-kayy al-bāliʿ al-nāfidh bi-al-nār fa-innahu yaḥriq al-samm wa-yuḍayyiq al-majārī] The philosophers, in their books on serpents and their nature, divide them into three kinds. In the first species the force of the poison is so intense that death is not delayed beyond three hours from the time of the bite, nor is there any cure. For they are of the class of the deaf and the hissing (that is, as we have shown, of those which either seem to grow deaf at the chant, because they are no more affected by it than if they were deaf, or even τῷ ἐπαοιδῷ ἀντᾴδουσι [tō epaoidō antadousi], sing back to the charmer, so that the charm is ineffective against them). Therefore nothing helps except amputation of the limb at the same moment, or a burning that penetrates to the inmost parts; because it burns out the poison and constricts the passages. He adds that to this species belong الملكة [al-malika], the regulus, which kills by sight and hearing alone; and الخطاف [al-khaṭṭāf], the chelidonian asp; and الاسفيس اليابسة [al-asfīs al-yābisa], the dry asp, or χερσαίαν [chersaian]; of which the latter kills within three hours, the former within two; and البزاقة [al-bazzāqa], the ptyas asp, from which the bitten man perishes قبل ان توجع [qabl an tūjiʿ], before he feels pain, that is, he dies without pain; the Latin translator absurdly has before it returns, because he read ترجع [tarjiʿ] for توجع [tūjiʿ]. Of the same sort is that a little later the same translator places in this same class arched deaf ones, which multiply in the lands of Egypt. Arched deaf ones, that is, الصم المقوسة [al-ṣumm al-muqawwasa]. So he seems to have read, without any sense, instead of الصم المقعصة [al-ṣumm al-muqʿiṣa], which are deaf serpents that bring death swiftly. Of this kind, besides the regulus and the asp, are المقرنة [al-muqarrana], the cerastes, and اوبريس [ūbrīs], the hydrus, and كرسودروس [kursūdrūs], the chersydrus, all of which Avicenna counts among the deaf in what follows. Thus in the chapter On the basilisk: هو الاول من الصم [huwa al-awwal min al-ṣumm] It is the first of the deaf. And in the chapter On the chelidonian asp: وهي من الصم [wa-hiya min al-ṣumm] This too is of the deaf. And below: وعلاجها علاج الصم [wa-ʿilājuhā ʿilāj al-ṣumm] And its cure is the cure of the deaf. He says the same of the chersaean asp. And of the ptyas: علاجها من جنس علاج الصم [ʿilājuhā min jins ʿilāj al-ṣumm] It is cured in the same way as the deaf. And in the chapter On the cerastes: هي جنس من الصم [hiya jins min al-ṣumm] It is of the class of the col. 393 deaf. And On the hydrus, or chersydrus: هي اصغر من الاصله صما [hiya aṣghar min al-aṣla ṣamman] It is smaller than the dryinus, deaf. So that it is now obscure to no one that the Arabs call deaf all serpents which they believe to be immune to incantation. Hence Alcamus says expressly: الاصم من الحية لا يقبل الرقي [al-aṣamm min al-ḥayya lā yaqbal al-ruqī] A deaf serpent is one III, 174 which does not admit incantation. Such, moreover, they hold to be all those whose poison is intense in the highest degree, namely the regulus, asp, cerastes, hydrus, chersydrus. With this doctrine it will seem to agree that the royal Psalmist places the asp, and Jeremiah the regulus or basilisk, in that class. As if it were established by sure experience either that magicians never attempt to charm that kind of serpent, or, if they attempt it, that they succeed so little that it often even turns to the ruin of those who try.


At his duo possunt objici: primo, nullam apparere causam, cur in aspides, hydros, regulos et cerastas magi non idem possint, quod in reliquos serpentes. Quidni enim regulus, aut aspis, potentia daemonis tam facile evocetur, aut obtorpescat, aut dissiliat, aut veneno exarmetur, quam quivis alius serpens? Et magis hic haerere calculum quis crediderit, cum majora in aliis artis suae specimina videantur edere? Praeterea hos quoque serpentes incantationi esse obnoxios, multi scribunt. In Philopseude Luciani a mago evocantur ἀσπίδες, καὶ ἔχιδναι, καὶ κεράσαι, καὶ ἀκοντίαι, aspides, et viperae, et cerastae, et jaculi. Virgilius Umbronem dicit cantuque manuque sparsisse somnos

But two objections can be raised against this. First, no reason appears why magicians should not be able to do against asps, hydri, reguli and cerastae the same as against the other serpents. For why should a regulus or an asp not be called out by the power of a demon, or grow numb, or burst asunder, or be disarmed of its poison, as easily as any other serpent? And who would believe that their reckoning sticks here, when they seem to give greater proofs of their art in other things? Further, many write that these serpents too are subject to charming. In Lucian's Philopseudes a magician calls out ἀσπίδες, καὶ ἔχιδναι, καὶ κεράσαι, καὶ ἀκοντίαι [aspides, kai echidnai, kai kerasai, kai akontiai], asps, and vipers, and cerastae, and darting snakes. And of the Marmaridae, or Psylli, book 3:

Est scilicet cerastis πρὸς τοὺς καλουμένους Ψύλλους ἔνσπονδα, οἵ περ οὔτε αὐτοὶ δα-κόντων ἐπαΐουσι τῶν δηγμάτων, καὶ τοῖς τῷ τοιούτῳ κακῷ περιπεσόντας ἰῶνται ῥᾷστα, foedus cum iis, qui Psylli vocantur, qui nec ipsi mordentium sentiunt morsus, et eos, qui in id malum incidunt, facile sanant. Ita Aelianus Historiae lib. 1. cap. 57. Neque aliter affectae aspides erga eosdem Psyllos. Antigonus Mirabilium cap. 19. Ὑπὸ τῶν ἀσπίδων οὗτοι μὲν (Ψύλλοι) οὐδὲν πάσχουσι τυπτόμε-νοι· τῶν δὲ λοιπῶν οὐκ ἔστιν, ὅστις διαφεύγει δηχθείς· Psylli, ab aspidibus icti, nihil patiuntur incommodi, cum aliorum nullus, ab iis morsus, mortem effugiat. Varro apud Priscianum, Admota aspis, cum pupugerit, si non occidat, sciat ex Psyllorum stirpe esse. Cinna apud Gellium lib. 9. cap. 12.

The cerastae, namely, have πρὸς τοὺς καλουμένους Ψύλλους ἔνσπονδα, οἵ περ οὔτε αὐτοὶ δακόντων ἐπαΐουσι τῶν δηγμάτων, καὶ τοῖς τῷ τοιούτῳ κακῷ περιπεσόντας ἰῶνται ῥᾷστα [pros tous kaloumenous Psyllous ensponda, hoi per oute autoi dakontōn epaiousi tōn dēgmatōn, kai tois tō toioutō kakō peripesontas iōntai rhaista], a treaty with those who are called Psylli, who neither feel the bites of those that bite them, and easily heal those who fall into that evil. So Aelian, History book 1, ch. 57. Nor are the asps otherwise disposed towards the same Psylli. Antigonus, Mirabilia ch. 19: Ὑπὸ τῶν ἀσπίδων οὗτοι μὲν (Ψύλλοι) οὐδὲν πάσχουσι τυπτόμενοι· τῶν δὲ λοιπῶν οὐκ ἔστιν, ὅστις διαφεύγει δηχθείς [Hypo tōn aspidōn houtoi men (Psylloi) ouden paschousi typtomenoi; tōn de loipōn ouk estin, hostis diapheugei dēchtheis]; the Psylli, when struck by asps, suffer no harm, whereas none of the others, when bitten by them, escapes death. Varro in Priscian: If an asp, when brought near, has stung him and does not kill him, let him know that he is of the stock of the Psylli. Cinna in Gellius, book 9, ch. 12:


Somniculosum ut Poenus aspidem Psyllus.

As the Punic Psyllus the drowsy asp.

And Silius:

Et Plutarchus, Αὐτά τε τὰ θηρία κατεπάδοντες ἀμβλύνουσι, καὶ κηλοῦσιν· Ipsosque adeo serpentes incantationibus stupefaciunt et demulcent. Et Hesychius, Ψυλλικὸς γόης, ὁ τῶν Ψύλλων, οἱ δὲ Ψύλλοι ἔθνος Λιβύης· Psyllicus magus, id est, ex Psyllis, quae gens est Libyae. Sulpicius denique, qui totam Aegyptum peragraverat, ubi sunt aspides magna copia, eas credidit posse incantari: alioqui non dixisset, quod jam f) ex illo citavimus, Aspis mirae magnitudinis, etc. quasi incantata carminibus, coerula colla deposuit.

And Plutarch: Αὐτά τε τὰ θηρία κατεπάδοντες ἀμβλύνουσι, καὶ κηλοῦσιν [Auta te ta thēria katepadontes amblynousi, kai kēlousin]; and the serpents themselves they stupefy and soothe with incantations. And Hesychius: Ψυλλικὸς γόης, ὁ τῶν Ψύλλων, οἱ δὲ Ψύλλοι ἔθνος Λιβύης [Psyllikos goēs, ho tōn Psyllōn, hoi de Psylloi ethnos Libyēs]; a Psyllic magician, that is, one of the Psylli, which is a people of Libya. Finally Sulpicius, who had travelled through all Egypt, where asps are in great abundance, believed they could be charmed; otherwise he would not have said what we have already f) quoted from him: An asp of wondrous size, etc. as if charmed by spells, laid down its blue neck.


Iam, ut duae objectiones allatae diluantur, ad priorem respondemus, A col. 394 diabolo hydrum, et aspidem, et cerastem, et basiliscum, tum facile posse compesci, quam quemvis alium serpentem, si modo permittat Deus: sed Deum nolle, ut diabolo omnia in mundo liceant. Utut enim superbe jactet impurus ille spiritus g) omnia sibi fuisse tradita: tamen illi Deus id ipsum, quod mari, dixit h), Huc usque venies, nec procedes ulterius. Unde est, quod in Aegypto magi, qui sanguinem, et serpentes, et ranas in specie produxerant, cum ad pediculos ventum est i), haerent, Deo non permittente, ut praestigiis suis Pharaoni pergerent illudere. Et in Evangelio k) daemones, nonnisi cum Christi venia, Gergesenorum porcos invadunt. Ad posteriorem respondemus, frustra objici Luciani Philopseudem, cum ex ipso titulo mentiri se profiteatur. Frustra etiam Marsos et Psyllos, de quibus quae produntur, si vera sint, naturae potius tribui debent, quam vi magicae. In qua sententia video fuisse plerosque veterum. Plinius de Psyllis lib. 7. cap. 2. Horum corpori ingenitum fuit virus exitiale serpentibus, ut cujus odore sopirent eas. Et paullo post, Simile et in Italia Marsorum gente durat, quos a Circes filio ortos ferunt, et ideo inesse iis vim naturalem eam. Et Solinus, Gentem Marsorum serpentibus illaesam esse, nihil mirum. A Circae filio hi genus ducunt: et de avita potentia deberi sibi sciunt servitium venenorum: ideo venena contemnunt. Et alibi, Supra Garamantes Psylli fuerunt, contra noxium virus muniti incredibili corporis firmitate. Soli morsibus anguium non interibant, et, quamvis lethali dente appetiti, incorrupta durabant sanitate. Ita Strabo lib. 17. Τοὺς Ψύλλους τοὺς πρὸς τῇ Κυρηναίᾳ φυσικήν τινα ἀντιπάθειαν ἔχειν πρὸς τὰ ἑρπετά· Psyllos, qui in Cyrene sunt, naturalem vim quandam habere contra serpentes. Et de iisdem Lucanus libri 9. versu 894.

Now, to refute the two objections brought: to the first we answer that the hydrus, the asp, the cerastes and the basilisk col. 394 can be restrained by the devil as easily as any other serpent, provided God permits it; but that God does not will that everything in the world be allowed to the devil. For however proudly that impure spirit boasts g) that all things have been delivered to him, yet God has said to him the very thing he said to the sea h): Thus far shalt thou come, and no further. Hence it is that in Egypt the magicians, who had produced blood, serpents and frogs in appearance, are stuck when it came to the lice i), since God did not permit them to go on mocking Pharaoh with their illusions. And in the Gospel k) the demons enter the swine of the Gergesenes only with Christ's leave. To the second we answer that Lucian's Philopseudes is objected in vain, since by its very title it professes to lie. In vain also the Marsi and Psylli: what is reported of them, if true, ought to be attributed to nature rather than to magical power. I see that most of the ancients held this view. Pliny of the Psylli, book 7, ch. 2: In their body there was an innate poison deadly to serpents, so that by its smell they put them to sleep. And a little after: A similar thing persists in Italy in the people of the Marsi, whom they say are descended from a son of Circe, and that for this reason this natural power is in them. And Solinus: That the people of the Marsi is unharmed by serpents is no wonder. They derive their descent from a son of Circe, and know that from their ancestral power the service of poisons is owed to them; therefore they despise poisons. And elsewhere: Beyond the Garamantes were the Psylli, fortified against noxious poison by an incredible firmness of body. They alone did not perish from the bites of snakes, and, though attacked by a lethal tooth, remained in unimpaired health. So Strabo, book 17: Τοὺς Ψύλλους τοὺς πρὸς τῇ Κυρηναίᾳ φυσικήν τινα ἀντιπάθειαν ἔχειν πρὸς τὰ ἑρπετά [Tous Psyllous tous pros tē Kyrēnaia physikēn tina antipatheian echein pros ta herpeta]; that the Psylli who are in Cyrene have a certain natural power against serpents. And of the same Lucan, book 9, verse 894.


III, 176 Ipse cruor tutus, nullumque admittere virus
Vel cantu cessante potest, natura locorum
Iussit, ut immunes misti serpentibus essent.
Profuit in mediis sedem posuisse venenis.
Pax illis cum morte data est. Fiducia tanta est
Sanguinis. In terram parvus cum decidit infans,
Ne qua sit externae Veneris mistura timentes,
Lethifica dubios explorant aspide partus.

III, 176 Their very blood is safe, and can admit no poison
even when the chant has ceased; the nature of the place
has ordained that they be immune, though mingled with serpents.
It has profited them to have set their dwelling amid poisons.
Peace has been granted them with death. So great is their trust
in their blood: when a little infant has dropped to the ground,
fearing lest there be some admixture of foreign Venus, they test the doubtful offspring with the deadly asp.


Circa Hellesponti Parium eadem vis insita fuit Ophiogenis, de quibus, post Cratetem Pergamenum, Varro, Strabo, Plinius, Priscianus, etc. Quid, quod Celsus lib. 5. cap. 27. Psyllis nihil quidquam tribuit supra vulgus hominum, praeter audaciam, usu ipso confirmatam? Ac si idem iis acciderit, quod Mithridati, de quo Poeta:

Around Parium on the Hellespont the same power was inborn in the Ophiogenes, of whom, after Crates of Pergamum, Varro, Strabo, Pliny, Priscian, etc. have written. What of the fact that Celsus, book 5, ch. 27, attributes nothing whatever to the Psylli beyond the common run of men, except boldness, confirmed by practice itself? As if the same had happened to them as to Mithridates, of whom the Poet says:


Effecit poto Mithridates saepe veneno,
Toxica ne possent saeva nocere sibi.

By often drinking poison Mithridates brought it about
that cruel venoms could not harm him.


Praeterea, quamvis Arabes serpentum alios posse incantari scripserint, alios ab incantatione esse prorsus immunes, quos surdos vocant, Davidis tamen, Solomonis et Ieremiae loca eo referre necesse non est. Neque enim Sancti Prophetae serpentes uspiam ita distinguunt. Sed ex illorum verbis hoc solum elicias, saepe magos id frustra conari, sive aspides, sive regulos, sive aliud quodvis serpentis genus cantu suo delinire et demulcere conentur. Itaque, ut his Scripturae locis sua constet veritas, non opus est sibi fingere, quasdam esse serpentum species, in quas magorum carmina nihil possint. Quippe in eadem serpentis specie potest diversus esse successus, prout varie Deus diabolo habenas aut adducit, aut remittit. Nec daemon paredrus, a quo pendet incantationis tota vis, ad magi nutum semper se accommodat. Unde est, quod illius conatus non semper voto respondet.

Moreover, although the Arabs have written that some serpents can be charmed, while others, which they call deaf, are wholly immune to incantation, it is nevertheless not necessary to refer the passages of David, Solomon and Jeremiah to this. For the holy Prophets nowhere distinguish serpents in this way. From their words you may gather only this: that magicians often attempt it in vain, whether they try to soothe and calm with their chant asps, or reguli, or any other kind of serpent. Therefore, for these passages of Scripture to hold true, there is no need to imagine that there are certain species of serpents against which the magicians' spells have no power. For in the same species of serpent the outcome can differ, according as God variously draws in or slackens the reins on the devil. Nor does the familiar demon, on whom the whole power of the incantation depends, always accommodate himself to the magician's nod. Hence it is that the magician's attempt does not always answer to his wish.

R4 Rosenmüller, III, 167 But that this interpretation of the verb חבר is hardly probable, since neither the word itself nor the passages of the Old Testament in which it occurs bid us think of a gathering of serpents and similar creatures, is rightly observed by DAV. MILL in his Dissertation on the חרטמים and other Magi of the Orientals (the eighth of his dissertations published together, Utrecht 1724), §9, p. 130. Mill himself, however, thinks that the magi were called חברים, binders, from חבר, he bound, because they were accustomed not only to join to themselves, to summon and bring whatever they wished, but also to constrain effectively and to bind; and so they were believed able to take away the power of harming and to bring things to obedience. He tried to prove this view at length in §§10-14, but in such a way that he uses only examples drawn from Greek and Roman antiquity, and adduces none from which it would appear that this belief in the power and efficacy of the magic art also prevailed among the ancient Hebrews. I therefore agree with CHRIST. BENED. Michaelis in his Philologemata Medica §10, p. 13, who compares the Hebrew חבר with the Arabic خَبَرَ [khabara], he knew, so that חובר properly means knowing, and then magus, charmer, just as the Chaldee מְחַבַּר and the Syriac ܝܕܘܥܐ [ידועא] signify a charmer. For among the Orientals, words carrying the notion of being wise and knowing have passed also to charmers, sorcerers and magi, because these are thought to know more than others. Thus from חָכַם, he was wise, III, 168 he was wise, in Exod 7:11 החכמים, the wise men, are joined with המכשפים, the sorcerers, and החרטמים, the Egyptian magi; and in the very passage this chapter examines, Ps 58:6, one is called חובר חברים, charming (i.e. practising, employing) charms, and מחכם, trained in wisdom, namely in the magic arts. So the Arabic طَبّ [ṭabba] means both he excelled in knowledge and he used fascination and sorcery; and عَرّاف [ʿarrāf] means soothsayer, from the root عَرَفَ [ʿarafa], he knew. But among the Latins too the saga [wise woman, witch] was named from sagire, i.e. from knowing keenly, as CICERO expressly says, On Divination book 1, ch. 31: “Sagire is to perceive keenly; hence SAGAE for old women, because they want to know many things.” Likewise we Germans call a saga eine weise Frau, from weise, wise.

Part 2, Book 3, chapter 7: Tseboa is the serpent called hyaena
------------------------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/tseboa-serpens.html

III, 177 CAP. VII. col. 395

III, 177 Chapter VII. col. 395


Probatur, צבוע tseboa esse Serpentem varium, quem Hyaenam vocarunt Graeci et Aegyptii.

It is proved that צבוע tseboa is a spotted serpent, which the Greeks and the Egyptians called hyaena.


Vallem Seboim, de qua mentio 1 Sam. XIII, 18., nomen habere vult Iunius ab urbe Benjamitica SEBOIM, Nehem. XI, 34. Sed, cum illa vallis Hebraice dicatur גי הצבעים, cum Articulo praefixo voci Seboim, constat, ibi Seboim nomen esse Appellativum. Proinde Hebraei omnes, R. Selomo, Kimchius, et Esaias in Notis in hunc locum, R. Mardochaeus in Concordantiis, Baal Aruch, Pomarius, et Aquinas in Lexicis suis voce SEBOIM serpentis genus intelligunt. Et praeiverat Ionathan in Chaldaea paraphrasi, ubi, pro valle Seboim, reperias חילת אפעיא, vallem viperarum (sic enim illi accipiunt). Quale est, quod in tractatu Talmudico Bava Kama cap. 1. fol. 16. a. אמר רב יוסף צבוע הוא אפה Dixit Rabbi Ioseph, TSEBOA est vipera. Ibi enim אפה idem est, quod אפעה, elisa Gutturali, ut observatum a Kimchio. Nolim tamen intelligi viperam, proprie dictam, sed maculosi serpentis genus: cujusmodi in Arabum scriptis non pauci describuntur. Sic in Avicenna Tom. 2. pag. 139. الحية الرقشا ذات الالوان المتخلفة Serpens raksa, qui variorum est colorum. In Damire, الارقم الحية التي فيها بياض وسواد كانه رقم اي نقش Arkamo, serpens, albo et nigro distinctus, tanquam Phrygium opus, seu interpunctum. In Giauhari, الحريش نوع من الحيات ارقط Alharis, varii serpentis species. Denique in Alcamus, السف الارقم من الحيات والتي تطير Assuph (vel assiph) serpens varius, et qui volat. Est et in hoc censu Graecorum cenchris, seu cenchrites, Arabice جاورسية giavversia, de quo Nicander Theriacῶn versu 463.

The valley of Seboim, mentioned in 1 Sam 13:18, Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] would have take its name from the Benjamite city SEBOIM, Neh 11:34. But since that valley is called in Hebrew גי הצבעים, with the article prefixed to the word Seboim, it is clear that Seboim is there a common noun. Accordingly all the Hebrews, R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)], Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], and Esaias in their Notes on this passage, R. Mardochaeus in his Concordances, and Baal Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome] [=Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome, the ʿArukh], Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)] and Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)] in their Lexicons, understand by the word SEBOIM a kind of serpent. And Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] had led the way in the Chaldee paraphrase, where in place of the valley of Seboim you find חילת אפעיא, the valley of vipers (for so they take it). Similar is the passage in the Talmudic tractate Bava Kama, ch. 1, fol. 16a: אמר רב יוסף צבוע הוא אפה, Rabbi Joseph said: TSEBOA is a viper. For there אפה is the same as אפעה, with the guttural elided, as Kimchi observed. Yet I would not have it understood as a viper in the proper sense, but as a kind of spotted serpent, of which not a few are described in the writings of the Arabs. Thus in Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)], vol. 2, p. 139: الحية الرقشا ذات الالوان المتخلفة [al-ḥayya al-raqshā dhāt al-alwān al-mutakhallifa], the serpent raksa, which is of varied colours. In Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: الارقم الحية التي فيها بياض وسواد كانه رقم اي نقش [al-arqam al-ḥayya allatī fīhā bayāḍ wa-sawād ka-annahu raqm ay naqsh], Arkamo, a serpent marked with white and black, like Phrygian work, or embroidery. In Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ]: الحريش نوع من الحيات ارقط [al-ḥarīsh nawʿ min al-ḥayyāt arqaṭ], Alharis, a species of spotted serpent. Finally in the Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: السف الارقم من الحيات والتي تطير [al-saff al-arqam min al-ḥayyāt wa-allatī taṭīr], Assuph (or assiph), a spotted serpent, and one that flies. In this class too is the cenchris or cenchrites of the Greeks, in Arabic جاورسية [jāwarsiyya] giavversia, of which Nicander, Theriaca, line 463:


Δήεις κεγχρίνου δολιχὸν τέρας, ὅν τε λέοντα
Αἴολον αὐδάξαντο, περίστικτον φολίδεσσι.

Δήεις κεγχρίνου δολιχὸν τέρας, ὅν τε λέοντα Αἴολον αὐδάξαντο, περίστικτον φολίδεσσι. [Dēeis kenchrinou dolichon teras, hon te leonta Aiolon audaxanto, peristikton pholidessi.]


Reperies (in Lemno, Samothracia, etc.) cenchritem, monstrum oblongum, quem leonem varium appellant, squamis distinctum. Et Lucanus lib. 9. versu 716.

You will find (in Lemnos, Samothrace, etc.) the cenchrites, a long monster, which they call the spotted lion, marked with scales. And Lucan, book 9, line 716:


Pluribus ille notis variatam tingitur alvum,
Quam parvis tinctus maculis Thebanus ophites. col. 396

His belly is dyed, varied with more marks than the Theban ophites is tinged with small spots. col. 396


Hujusmodi serpentem voce צבוע tseboa, significari, suadet primo, quod צבוע tseboa proprie tinctum, aut pictum sonat. Secundo, quod illum Hebraei varium esse asserunt. Kimchius enim in Notis sic nominari docet; לפי שעשוי בגוונים ובמיני הצבוענים, quia coloribus et picturis distinctus est. Et Pomarius, מין III, 178 נחשים ונקראו כן על השתנות הצבעונים, Species serpentum, qui sic vocantur propter colorum varietatem. Et multo ante Beresith Rabba, הצבוע הזה מטפה של לובן הוא ויש לו שס״ה מיני צבועים כמנין ימות השנה של חמה, Serpens, nomine tseboa, ex albi seminis guttula constat. Et tamen colores habet trecentos sexaginta quinque: quot nimirum sunt solaris anni dies. Ex qua insigni hyperbole hoc saltem elicimus, serpentes varios significari voce TSEBOIM. De eodem Baal Aruch in voce ברדלס bardales, ברדלס זו אפא וז׳ שנים הראשונים שהוא זכר נקרא צבוע וכשמתהפך לנקבה נקראת נפרזא ורעה היא יותר מן הזכר Bardales est vipera, quae primis septem annis, dum est mas, appellatur tseboa. Sed, cum mutatur in foeminam, vocatur niphreza, et est mare multo pejor. Bar- dales et niphreza deflexa videntur ex πάρδαλις et νέβρισσα. Huic serpenti utrumque nomen ab Hellenistis inditum propter varios colores. Variam enim esse πάρδαλιν, nemo nescit. Ita etiam νεβρὶς, id est, hinnuli pellis, aut cer- vi. Proinde cervi passim a poetis στικτοὶ vocantur, et κατάστικτοι, id est, varii et maculis distincti. Sic, in Electra Sophoclis, Agamemnon in Dianae luco interfecisse legitur στικτὸν κεράστην ἔλαφον, varium, cornutum cervum. Et cervorum genus describit Oppianus libro 2. Cynegeticῶν,

That a serpent of this kind is meant by the word צבוע tseboa is suggested, first, by the fact that צבוע tseboa properly means dyed or painted. Second, by the fact that the Hebrews assert that it is spotted. For Kimchi teaches in his Notes that it is so named לפי שעשוי בגוונים ובמיני הצבוענים, because it is marked with colours and patterns. And Pomarius: מין III, 178 נחשים ונקראו כן על השתנות הצבעונים, a species of serpents, which are so called on account of the variety of their colours. And much earlier Bereshith Rabba: הצבוע הזה מטפה של לובן הוא ויש לו שס״ה מיני צבועים כמנין ימות השנה של חמה, The serpent called tseboa comes from a little drop of white seed. And yet it has three hundred and sixty-five colours: as many, namely, as there are days in the solar year. From this remarkable hyperbole we at least gather that spotted serpents are meant by the word TSEBOIM. Of the same Baal Aruch, under the word ברדלס bardales: ברדלס זו אפא וז׳ שנים הראשונים שהוא זכר נקרא צבוע וכשמתהפך לנקבה נקראת נפרזא ורעה היא יותר מן הזכר, Bardales is a viper which for the first seven years, while it is male, is called tseboa. But when it changes into a female it is called niphreza, and is much worse than the male. Bardales and niphreza seem to be derived from πάρδαλις [pardalis] and νέβρισσα [nebrissa]. Both names were given to this serpent by the Hellenists on account of its varied colours. For no one is unaware that the πάρδαλιν [pardalin] is spotted. So too the νεβρὶς [nebris], that is, the skin of a fawn or of a deer. Accordingly deer are everywhere called by the poets στικτοὶ [stiktoi] and κατάστικτοι [katastiktoi], that is, spotted and marked with spots. Thus in the Electra of Sophocles we read that Agamemnon killed in the grove of Diana στικτὸν κεράστην ἔλαφον [stikton kerastēn elaphon], a spotted, horned deer. And Oppian describes a kind of deer in book 2 of the Cynegetica:


Στικτὸν, ἀρίζηλον, ποταμηπόρον, ὑψικάρηνον,

Στικτὸν, ἀρίζηλον, ποταμηπόρον, ὑψικάρηνον, [Stikton, arizēlon, potamēporon, hypsikarēnon,]


Varium, eximium, flumini-gradum, capite arduum. Et, apud Nonnum Dio- nysiacῶn lib. 4. Actaeone in cervum mutato, canes ejus

Spotted, conspicuous, river-crossing, high-headed. And in Nonnus, Dionysiaca, book 4, when Actaeon has been changed into a deer, his dogs


Στικτὸν ἐθοινήσαντο νόθον δέμας ἄφρονι λύσσῃ,

Στικτὸν ἐθοινήσαντο νόθον δέμας ἄφρονι λύσσῃ, [Stikton ethoinēsanto nothon demas aphroni lyssē,]


Varium adulterinum corpus insana rabie devorabant. Unde Pollux, Ἔστι δὲ τοῖς ἐλάφοις τὸ χρῶμα ἐπίξανθον, κατάστικτον λευκοῖς γράμμασι· πλείω δὲ αἱ θήλειαι τὰ στίγματα ἔχουσι, καὶ μάλιστα τῶν ἐλάφων οἱ νεβροί. Cervorum color subflavus est, albis lineis distinctus; foeminae vero plures habent maculas, et hinnuli inprimis. Itaque a vocibus νέβρος et νεβρὶς serpens tseboa propter maculas primo νέβρισσα (ut Hispaniae quoddam oppidum): deinde, corrupta voce, נפרזא nephriza, vel (ut hodie efferunt) nephreza est appellatus. Atque eodem recidunt tria haec ejusdem serpentis nomina צבוע tseboa, ברדלס bardales, seu πάρδαλις· et נפרזא nephriza, seu νέβρισσα. Illis enim omnibus hoc commune est, quod maculosum serpentem sonant. Sed nomini צבוע tseboa aliquid est peculiare, quod jam notandum. Proprie צבוע tseboa Hebraeis est hyaena, etiam ipsa a maculis ita dicta. Hyaenae enim

“They devoured the spotted, counterfeit body with insane frenzy.” Hence Pollux: Ἔστι δὲ τοῖς ἐλάφοις τὸ χρῶμα ἐπίξανθον, κατάστικτον λευκοῖς γράμμασι· πλείω δὲ αἱ θήλειαι τὰ στίγματα ἔχουσι, καὶ μάλιστα τῶν ἐλάφων οἱ νεβροί. [Esti de tois elaphois to chrōma epixanthon, katastikton leukois grammasi; pleiō de hai thēleiai ta stigmata echousi, kai malista tōn elaphōn hoi nebroi.] “The colour of deer is yellowish, marked with white lines; the females have more spots, and the fawns above all.” Thus from the words νέβρος [nebros] and νεβρὶς [nebris] the serpent tseboa, because of its spots, was first called νέβρισσα [nebrissa] (like a certain town of Spain); then, the word being corrupted, נפרזא nephriza, or (as they pronounce it today) nephreza. And so these three names of the same serpent come to the same thing: צבוע tseboa; ברדלס bardales, or πάρδαλις [pardalis]; and נפרזא nephriza, or νέβρισσα [nebrissa]. For all of them have this in common, that they mean “spotted serpent.” But the name צבוע tseboa has something peculiar to it, which must now be noted. Properly, צבוע tseboa among the Hebrews is the hyaena, itself also so called from its spots. For the hyaena’s


— — — ἔῤῥαπται δέμας αἰνὸν
Κυανέαις ἑκάτερθεν ἐπίτριμα ταινίαισιν·

— — — ἔῤῥαπται δέμας αἰνὸν Κυανέαις ἑκάτερθεν ἐπίτριμα ταινίαισιν· [errhaptai demas ainon / Kyaneais hekaterthen epitrima tainiaisin]


— — — cutis horrida corpore toto Coeruleis dense conspergitur undique vittis. III, 179 Ita Oppianus lib. 3. Cynegeticῶn versu 274. Qui proinde στικτὰς, varias paullo infra nominat. Atque, ut tseboa serpens sexum alternare creditur, ita etiam tseboa quadrupes, id est, hyaena. Quod cum multis probaverim in capite De hyaena a), hic sufficiet ejusdem Oppiani verba proferre,

— — — “grim hide over the whole body is thickly sprinkled on every side with dark-blue stripes.” III, 179 So Oppian, Cynegetica book 3, line 274. Accordingly, a little further on, he calls them στικτὰς [stiktas], spotted. And just as the serpent tseboa is believed to alternate its sex, so too is the quadruped tseboa, that is, the hyaena. Since I have proved this with many arguments in the chapter On the hyaena a), it will suffice here to cite the words of the same Oppian:


Θαῦμα δὲ καὶ τὸ δ᾽ ἄκουσα περὶ στικτῆσιν ὑαίνης,
Ἄρσενα καὶ θήλειαν ἀμείβεσθαι λυκάβαντι·

Θαῦμα δὲ καὶ τὸ δ᾽ ἄκουσα περὶ στικτῆσιν ὑαίνης, Ἄρσενα καὶ θήλειαν ἀμείβεσθαι λυκάβαντι· [Thauma de kai to d’ akousa peri stiktēsin hyainēs, / Arsena kai thēleian ameibesthai lykabanti]


Miraculum etiam hoc audivi de pictis hyaenis, marem et foeminam alternare quotannis. Merito igitur tseboa, id est, hyaena, vocatur serpens, qui utrumque hoc cum hyaena commune habet, pellem variam et sexus alternationem, ab col. 397 Hebraeis supra observatam. Et iisdem de causis hic idem serpens Graecis et Aegyptiis hyaena dictus. Gesnerus de quadrupedibus in Hyaena pag. 556. Aelianus et Orus in Hieroglyphicis hyaenam, non quadrupedem, sed serpentem, per vices marem et foeminam esse prodiderunt. Nempe in Aeliano legerat, Historiae lib. 1. cap. 25. Τὴν ὕαιναν ὄφιν τῆτες μὲν ἄῤῥενα εἰ θεάσαιο, τὴν αὐτὴν ἐς νέω-τα ὄψει θῆλυν δέ· Hyaenam serpentem hoc anno, si marem videris, illam ipsam anno altero foeminam videbis. Et in Horo Hieroglyphicῶn libri 2. cap. 65. Ὕαι-ναν ὄφιν ζωγραφοῦσιν· αὕτη γὰρ ὅτε μὲν ἄῤῥην γίνεται, ὅτε δὲ θήλεια· Hyaenam serpentem pingunt (ut hominem parum constantem designent): haec enim modo mas est, modo foemina. Ita habebant libri, quos Gesnerus consulerat. At in nostris editionibus vox ὄφιν utroque loco desideratur; quia illam editores tanquam superfluam induxerunt. Quod malo exemplo videtur et praeter rationem esse factum: cum, praeter Graecos et Aegyptios, Hebraei quoque צבעים tseboim, id est hyaenas, inter serpentes censeant, et illis eandem tribuant sexuum vicissitudinem. In Horo igitur et Aeliano vox ὄφις, delata perperam, est omnino restituenda: et Hebraeorum Lexicis addenda vox צבוע tseboa, quae et hyaenam quadrupedem, et hyaenam serpentem sonat. Quamvis pro fabuloso habeam, quod Hebraei, Graeci et Aegyptii vel hanc, vel illam sexum per vices mutare scribunt *).

“This marvel too I have heard about the spotted hyaenas: that male and female alternate every year.” Rightly, then, the serpent is called tseboa, that is, hyaena, since it has both these things in common with the hyaena: a spotted skin and the alternation of sex, observed above by the col. 397 Hebrews. And for the same reasons this same serpent was called hyaena by the Greeks and the Egyptians. Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium], on quadrupeds, under Hyaena, p. 556: “Aelian and Horus in the Hieroglyphics have reported that the hyaena, not the quadruped but the serpent, is by turns male and female.” He had evidently read in Aelian, Historia book 1, ch. 25: Τὴν ὕαιναν ὄφιν τῆτες μὲν ἄῤῥενα εἰ θεάσαιο, τὴν αὐτὴν ἐς νέωτα ὄψει θῆλυν δέ· [Tēn hyainan ophin tētes men arrhena ei theasaio, tēn autēn es neōta opsei thēlyn de] “If this year you see the hyaena serpent as a male, next year you will see the very same one as a female.” And in Horus, Hieroglyphica book 2, ch. 65: Ὕαιναν ὄφιν ζωγραφοῦσιν· αὕτη γὰρ ὅτε μὲν ἄῤῥην γίνεται, ὅτε δὲ θήλεια· [Hyainan ophin zōgraphousin; hautē gar hote men arrhēn ginetai, hote de thēleia] “They paint a hyaena serpent (to signify an inconstant man): for it is now male, now female.” So read the books that Gesner had consulted. But in our editions the word ὄφιν [ophin] is missing in both places, because the editors struck it out as superfluous. This seems to have been done on a bad precedent and without reason, since, besides the Greeks and Egyptians, the Hebrews too reckon צבעים tseboim, that is, hyaenas, among serpents, and ascribe to them the same alternation of sexes. In Horus and Aelian, therefore, the word ὄφις [ophis], wrongly deleted, must certainly be restored; and to the Hebrew Lexicons must be added the word צבוע tseboa, which means both the quadruped hyaena and the serpent hyaena. For my part, though, I regard as fable what the Hebrews, Greeks and Egyptians write, that either the one or the other changes its sex by turns *).


a) Bochart, III, 179 Part. I. lib. III. cap. XI. pag. 832.

a) Bochart, III, 179 Part 1, book 3, ch. 11, p. 832.


*) Bochart, III, 179 Sed non praetermittere debuit Bochartus, quae GESNERUS de Hyaena serpente in libro De Serpentibus p. 59. dicit. Is enim, postquam illam de sexus mutatione fabulam ex Aeliano et Oro retulisset, addit: Sed plures hoc de hyaena quadrupede scribunt. Et sane incertum est, num tale quoddam sit serpentis genus, nec etiam verisimile, talem sexus mutationem in eo deprehendi posse. Omnino vero satis mirari non possum, Bochartum futilibus Rabbinorum commentis tantum tribuere, ut sola horum auctoritate vocem צבוע etiam ut serpentis nomen in Lexica immigrare jubeat.

*) Bochart, III, 179 But Bochart ought not to have passed over what Gesner says about the hyaena serpent in his book On Serpents, p. 59. For after relating that fable about the change of sex from Aelian and Horus, he adds: But more authors write this of the four-footed hyaena. And it is indeed uncertain whether there is any such kind of serpent, nor is it even likely that such a change of sex could be detected in it. Indeed, I cannot wonder enough that Bochart attributes so much to the futile inventions of the Rabbis that, on their authority alone, he bids the word צבוע enter the lexicons also as the name of a serpent.


Part 2, Book 3, chapter 8: Tsimmaon is not the dipsas but a thirsty place
------------------------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/tsimmaon.html

III, 180 col. 397 CAP. VIII.

III, 180 col. 397 Chapter 8.


Probatur, צמאון tsimmaon non esse Dipsadem, ut quidam post Hicronymum reddunt, sed siticulosum locum, Deut. VIII, 15.

It is proved that צמאון tsimmaon is not the dipsas, as some render it following Jerome, but a thirsty place, Deut 8:15.


Dipsas est viperae similis, sed minor, vix dodrantalis, albo corpore, cauda gracili, et duabus lineis insigni, quam incedendo sursum attollit, ut observant Arabes. Omnes in Africa describunt. Sed et in Arabia nonnulli. Aelianus Historiae lib. 6. cap. 51. Γίνονται δὲ ἄρα ἐν Λιβύῃ τε καὶ Ἀραβίᾳ μᾶλλον. Ita etiam Suidas. Et in Aegypti desertis Gregorius Nazianzenus Iambico 22.

The dipsas is similar to the viper, but smaller, scarcely a span long, with a white body and a slender tail marked with two lines, which it raises upward as it moves, as the Arabs observe. All writers describe it in Africa. But some also place it in Arabia: Aelian, History book 6, ch. 51: Γίνονται δὲ ἄρα ἐν Λιβύῃ τε καὶ Ἀραβίᾳ μᾶλλον [Ginontai de ara en Libyē te kai Arabia mallon]. So also Suidas. And Gregory of Nazianzus, Iambic 22, places it in the deserts of Egypt:


Διψὰς τὶς ἐστι τῶν ἐχιδναίων γενῶν,
Τούτων, ὅσ᾽ ἡ ἔρημος Αἰγύπτου φέρει·

Διψὰς τὶς ἐστι τῶν ἐχιδναίων γενῶν, Τούτων, ὅσ᾽ ἡ ἔρημος Αἰγύπτου φέρει· [Dipsas tis esti tōn echidnaiōn genōn, Toutōn, hos' hē erēmos Aigyptou pherei]


Dipsas quaedam est viperini generis serpens, ex iis, quos fert Aegypti desertum. Alii etiam in Syria. Avicenna Tom. 2. pag. 139. وقال قوم ان اكثر ما تكون هذه في بلاد لوبية والشام Nonnulli dicunt, eam ut plurimum esse in Africae et Syriae regionibus. Apud Aelianum nonnulli pre- col. 398 sterem vocant, causonem alii, et melanurum, et ammebaten, et centriden. Sed vulgare nomen est διψὰς, ab inexplebili siti, quam morsu suo excitat. Isidorus reddit situlam. Et Avicenna, per periphrasim, الحية المعطشة serpentem, sitim excitantem; quasi desit proprium nomen: quod mirum, cum dicatur esse in Arabia frequens, et in vicinis locis, ut in Aegypto et Syria. De hoc serpente plura qui volet, praeter Nicandrum et medicos, Aelianum legat, ubi supra, et Lucianum libro De dipsadibus, et Lucanum libri 9. versu 738. et Nazianzenum in loco, quem citavimus, et Epiphanium in Marcosiis, et Isidorum, qui post Solinum eum in genere aspidum perperam censet, cum ad viperam maxime accedat.

The dipsas is a serpent of the viper kind, one of those which the desert of Egypt produces. Others also place it in Syria. Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)], vol. 2, p. 139: وقال قوم ان اكثر ما تكون هذه في بلاد لوبية والشام [wa-qāla qawm anna akthar mā takūn hādhihi fī bilād Lūbiya wa-l-Shām] Some say that it is found mostly in the regions of Africa and Syria. In Aelian, some call it prester, col. 398 others causon, and melanurus, and ammobates, and centris. But the common name is διψὰς [dipsas], from the insatiable thirst which its bite produces. Isidore renders it situla. And Avicenna uses a periphrasis, الحية المعطشة [al-ḥayya al-muʿṭisha], the serpent that causes thirst, as though it lacked a proper name. This is surprising, since it is said to be common in Arabia and in neighbouring places such as Egypt and Syria. Whoever wants more on this serpent should read, besides Nicander and the physicians, Aelian in the place cited above, Lucian in the book On the Dipsads, Lucan book 9, line 738, Nazianzen in the passage we have quoted, Epiphanius on the Marcosians, and Isidore, who, following Solinus, wrongly counts it among the asps, although it comes closest to the viper.


Legitur etiam in Hieronymi versione Deut. VIII, 15. Et ductor tuus fuit in solitudine magna atque terribili, in qua erat serpens, flatu adurens, et scorpio, ac dipsas. Sed Hebraea voce צמאון tsimmaon, quae ibi dipsas redditur, aliud significari, nempe sitim, siccitatem, siticulosum locum, multa sunt, quae non suadent modo, sed et persuadent. Primo perpetuus vocis usus in ea notione, quam diximus. Sic Psalm. CVII, 33. Posuit flumina in desertum, et aquarum scatebras לצמאון, in siticulosum locum. Graeci, εἰς δίψαν· Vulgatus et Hieronymus, in sitim: Chaldaeus, היך צחותא, sicut siccitatem: Syrus, ܠܨܗܝܐ III, 181 in siccitatem: Arabs, عطش, sitim: Aethiops, ምጽማእ: locum sitis. Rursus Esa. XXXV, 7. Et erit locus aridus in stagnum, וצמאון, et locus siticulosus in fontes aquarum. Hieronymus, et sitiens. Nec alii multo aliter. Graeci, τὴν διψῶσαν γῆν. Arabs, الارض العطشانة, terram siticulosam. Chaldaeus, בית צחונא. Syrus, ܒܝܬ ܨܗܘܢܐ, locum siticulosum. Sed et in ipso loco, in quo versamur, idem intelligunt omnes omnino interpretes, praeter solum Hieronymum. Neque enim eorum ullus est, qui dipsadem hic intelligat, aut aliud serpentis genus. Et falsum est, quod multi scribunt, Hieronymum hic sequi Graecos, in quibus pro צמאון non legitur διψὰς, ut volunt, sed δίψα, sitis: ut in Samaritano ࠑࠌࠀࠅࠍ et in utroque Arabe edito عطش, quae itidem sitim sonant: at in MSS. مفازة, et in utroque Chaldaeo בית צחונא, et in Syro, ܒܝܬ ܨܗܘܢܐ, locus siticulosus. Praeterea post צמאון Moses addit ἐπεξηγητικῶς, אשר אין מים, id est, locus siticulosus, in quo non sunt aquae. Itaque צמאון, ipso Mose interprete, non est dipsas, sed locus, in quo non sunt aquae, quod idem est cum loco siticuloso. Res clarior erit ex totius periodi lectione, quae sic ha-bet: Qui deduxit te in solitudine vasta et terribili, in qua prester et scorpio; וצמאון, et loco siticuloso, in quo non sunt aquae. Sic incidendam esse periodum, monet punctum Zakeph-Katon super vocem עקרב, scorpio. Sed Hieronymus illam incidit post vocem וצמאון, quam reddidit ac dipsas. Et sequentia אשר אין מים exponit, ac nullae omnino aquae, vocula ac de suo addita, ne referrentur ad proximum antecedens, quia nullus fuisset sensus horum verborum, Dipsas, in qua non sunt aquae. Denique, si צמאון esset dipsas, in harum vocum ordine נחש שרף ועקרב וצמאון posset id desiderari, quod scorpio inseritur inter duas serpentum species.

It is also found in Jerome's version of Deut 8:15: "And he was your guide in the great and terrible wilderness, in which there was the serpent burning with its breath, and the scorpion, and the dipsas." But that the Hebrew word צמאון tsimmaon, rendered there dipsas, means something else, namely thirst, dryness, a thirsty place, there are many arguments that do not merely suggest but convince. First, the constant use of the word in the sense we have stated. Thus Ps 107:33: "He turned rivers into a desert, and springs of water לצמאון, into a thirsty place." The Greeks: εἰς δίψαν [eis dipsan]; the Vulgate translator and Jerome: into thirst; the Chaldee: היך צחותא, like dryness; the Syriac: ܠܨܗܝܐ [לצהיא] III, 181 into dryness; the Arabic: عطش [ʿaṭash], thirst; the Ethiopic: ምጽማእ [məṣəmāʾ], a place of thirst. Again Isa 35:7: "And the parched place shall become a pool, וצמאון, and the thirsty place springs of water." Jerome: and the thirsty [ground]. Nor do the others render it much differently. The Greeks: τὴν διψῶσαν γῆν [tēn dipsōsan gēn]. The Arabic: الارض العطشانة [al-arḍ al-ʿaṭshāna], the thirsty land. The Chaldee: בית צחונא. The Syriac: ܒܝܬ ܨܗܘܢܐ [בית צהונא], a thirsty place. Moreover, in the very passage we are dealing with, absolutely all the translators understand the same thing, except Jerome alone. For none of them takes it here as the dipsas or any other kind of serpent. And what many write is false, that Jerome here follows the Greeks; for in them צמאון is not rendered διψὰς [dipsas], as these writers claim, but δίψα [dipsa], thirst; as in the Samaritan ࠑࠌࠀࠅࠍ [צמאון] and in both printed Arabic versions عطش [ʿaṭash], which likewise mean thirst; but in the MSS. مفازة [mafāza], and in both Chaldee versions בית צחונא, and in the Syriac ܒܝܬ ܨܗܘܢܐ [בית צהונא], a thirsty place. Furthermore, after צמאון Moses adds by way of explanation [ἐπεξηγητικῶς, epexēgētikōs] אשר אין מים, that is, a thirsty place, in which there are no waters. So צמאון, with Moses himself as interpreter, is not the dipsas but a place in which there are no waters, which is the same as a thirsty place. The matter will be clearer from reading the whole period, which runs thus: "Who led you through the vast and terrible wilderness, in which were the prester and the scorpion; וצמאון, and through a thirsty place, in which there are no waters." That the period is to be divided thus is indicated by the accent Zakeph-Katon over the word עקרב, scorpion. But Jerome divides it after the word וצמאון, which he rendered and the dipsas. And he renders the following words אשר אין מים as and no waters at all, adding the little word and on his own, so that they would not be referred to the immediately preceding word; for these words would have made no sense: The dipsas, in which there are no waters. Finally, if צמאון were the dipsas, in the order of these words נחש שרף ועקרב וצמאון one might find fault with the fact that the scorpion is inserted between two species of serpents.
