Part 2, Book 3, chapter 11: Kippoz is the acontias, the darting serpent
------------------------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/kippoz.html

III, 194 CAP. XI. col. 408

III, 194 Chapter 11. col. 408


Probatur, voce קפוז kippoz, Es. XXXIV, 15. neque Hericium, ut veteribus, neque avis speciem significari, ut recentioribus visum: sed serpentem Acontiam, sive Iaculum.

It is proved that the word קפוז kippoz, Isa 34:15, signifies neither the hedgehog, as the ancients thought, nor a kind of bird, as the moderns thought, but the serpent acontias, or iaculus.


Bostram et Idumaeam ferro et igne ita vastandam interminatur Esaias capite trigesimo quarto, ut, omnibus incolis vel pulsis, vel extinctis, feris tantum et solivagis animalibus sit deinceps habitabilis. In his nominatur קפוז kippoz, de quo sic agit divinus Vates versu decimo quinto, Ibi nidificabit kippoz, et liberabitur, et rumpet, et congregabit in umbra sua. Sic Hebraea sonant ad verbum. Sed, verbis תמלט, et בקעה, et דגרה, ex generali significatione translatis ad specialem, recentiores Hebraei hunc versum recte reddunt: Ibi nidificabit kippoz, et pariet, et excludet, et fovebit in umbra sua. Nempe מלט malat in genere est liberare, vel liberari; hic parere, ut Es. LXVI, 7. המליטה זכר, ubi nostra versio ad verbum, Elle a est è deliuree d' un masle, phrasi tam Hebraica, quam Gallica. Idem verbum ملط malata etiam Arabes de partu usurpant, sed de eo proprie, qui abortivus et intempestivus est. Assyria Venus, quam praesedisse partui, atque eandem fuisse cum Lucina et Ilithya, multis contendit Seldenus in libello De Diis Syris, ab hoc Verbo videtur nomen habuisse Μυλίττας, ut col. 409 est in Herodoto; vel Μυλήτας et Μιλίτης, ut est in Hesychio; potius quam a Verbo ילד, generare, prout conjicit Scaliger: cum ut verbi sonus, ita etiam significatio congruat magis. Lucina enim in partu juvat, non in generatione. Etiam בקע in genere est findere, vel rumpere, hic ovi ruptione parvulos excludere: ut Esa. LIX, 5. Ova basilisci בקעו, ruperunt, id est, excluserunt. Sic Latine dicitur pullus ex ovo erumpere. Denique דגר apud Chaldaeos, a quibus desumtum est hoc Verbum, in genere est congregare, hic congregare sub se ova vel pullos, ut calore materno foveantur. Non aliter sumitur Ier. XVII, 11. ubi Propheta dicit, קרא דגר ולא ילד, Rusticula congregat (id est, fovet) quae non peperit. Nec a Chaldaeo interprete, cum Hebraeum תחמם, calefaciet, de struthionis ovis, reddit תדגר, congregabit, id est, fovebit, Iob. XXXIX, 14. (al. 17.). Insuper in haec verba, בקעה ודגרה, excludet et fovebit, notandum, conjunctionem et idem esse quod cum, vel postquam: ac si Propheta scripsisset, Excludet ova, postquam ea foverit. Sic Exod. XIV, 21. Redegit mare in siccum, et divisae sunt aquae: id est, postquam divisae sunt aquae. Et Esa. LXIV, 5. Iratus es, et peccavimus: id est, cum peccavimus, vel quia peccavimus. Ita Kimchius. III, 195 Sed haec nemini non sunt obvia: quid sit קפוז kippoz, non item; Cum alibi nullum occurrat animal hujus nominis, nec in Scriptura, nec in Talmude, nec in Syrorum aut Chaldaeorum libris. Dicam tamen de ea voce quid senserint cum veteres, tum recentiores interpretes. Graeci, Chaldaeus, Syrus, Arabs, Vulgatus, Hieronymus, Pomarius, Schindlerus reddunt hericium, ac si קפוז kippoz sit idem, quod קפוד kippod, paullo ante versu 11. Ita suadente scilicet soni vicinitate, et literarum Z et D facili permutatione. Kimchius item, et Selomo, et Mardochaeus, et Aquinas, et Hebraei fere quotquot sunt, kippod et kippoz pro eodem habent. Sed kippod, adeoque et kippoz, alius testudinem exponit, alius noctuam, alius in genere avem solitariam. Solus Aben Ezra, quod sciam, kippod et kippoz diversas aves esse vult, sed quales, non explicat. Sed et eorum interpretum, qui nostro aevo in novis versionibus elucubrandis utilem operam navarunt, non parva hic est dissensio. Santes exponit hericium, Castalio bubonem, Iunius merulam, Deodatius il gufo, id est, scopem; Angli the great Owe, id est, magnam ululam; Galli, post Mercerum, le martinet, id est, cypselum; Arias ipsam vocem Hebraeam in Latinum textum inserit, ingenue professus, eam a se non intelligi.

In chapter 34 Isaiah threatens that Bozrah and Idumaea are to be laid waste by sword and fire, so that, all the inhabitants being either driven out or destroyed, it will thereafter be habitable only for wild and solitary animals. Among these is named קפוז kippoz, of which the divine Prophet speaks thus in verse 15: There shall kippoz nest, and shall be delivered, and shall break, and shall gather in its shadow. So the Hebrew runs word for word. But, taking the verbs תמלט, בקעה and דגרה from their general meaning to a special one, the more recent Hebrews rightly render this verse: There shall kippoz nest, and lay, and hatch, and brood in its shadow. For מלט malat in general is to deliver or to be delivered; here it is to bring forth, as in Es. LXVI, 7, המליטה זכר, where our version has, word for word, Elle a est è deliuree d' un masle, a phrase as much Hebrew as French. The Arabs also use the same verb ملط [malaṭa] malata of birth, but properly of one that is abortive and untimely. The Assyrian Venus, who, as Selden argues at length in his little book De Diis Syris, presided over childbirth and was the same as Lucina and Ilithyia, seems to have taken from this verb the name Μυλίττας [Mylittas], as it is in Herodotus, col. 409 or Μυλήτας [Mylētas] and Μιλίτης [Militēs], as it is in Hesychius, rather than from the verb ילד, to beget, as Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)] conjectures; for the meaning, like the sound of the word, agrees better. Lucina, after all, helps in childbirth, not in begetting. Likewise בקע in general is to split or to break; here it is to hatch the young by breaking the egg, as in Isa 59:5: The eggs of the basilisk בקעו, they broke, that is, they hatched. So in Latin a chick is said to break out of the egg. Finally, דגר among the Chaldeans, from whom this verb was taken, is in general to gather; here it is to gather eggs or chicks under oneself, so that they may be kept warm by the mother's heat. It is taken no otherwise in Ier. XVII, 11, where the Prophet says קרא דגר ולא ילד, The partridge gathers (that is, broods) what it did not lay. Nor otherwise by the Chaldee translator, when he renders the Hebrew תחמם, she will warm, said of the ostrich's eggs, by תדגר, she will gather, that is, she will brood, Job 39:14 (var. 17). Moreover, on the words בקעה ודגרה, will hatch and brood, it should be noted that the conjunction and means the same as when or after, as if the Prophet had written, She will hatch the eggs after she has brooded them. So in Exod 14:21: He made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided, that is, after the waters were divided. And in Isa 64:5: You were angry, and we sinned, that is, when we sinned, or because we sinned. So Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim]. III, 195 But these things are obvious to everyone; what קפוז kippoz is, is not, since no animal of this name occurs anywhere else, neither in Scripture, nor in the Talmud, nor in the books of the Syrians or Chaldeans. I shall, however, state what both the ancient and the more recent interpreters thought of this word. The Greeks, the Chaldee, the Syriac, the Arabic, the Vulgate translator, Jerome, Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)] and Schindler render it hedgehog, as if קפוז kippoz were the same as קפוד kippod a little before, in verse 11; persuaded, of course, by the closeness of sound and the easy interchange of the letters Z and D. Kimchi likewise, and Solomon, and Mordecai, and Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)], and nearly all the Hebrews there are, take kippod and kippoz for the same thing. But kippod, and therefore also kippoz, one explains as the tortoise, another as the little owl, another in general as a solitary bird. Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] alone, as far as I know, holds that kippod and kippoz are different birds, but of what kind he does not explain. And among those interpreters who in our own age have done useful work in producing new versions there is no small disagreement here. Santes explains it as hedgehog, Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)] as eagle-owl, Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] as blackbird, Diodati as il gufo, that is, scops owl; the English as the great Owe, that is, the great owl; the French, following Mercerus [=Jean Mercier (d. 1570), commentaries on Job and Proverbs], as le martinet, that is, the swift; Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot] inserts the Hebrew word itself into the Latin text, candidly confessing that he does not understand it.


Nunc, ut modeste aperiam, sed libere, quid in singulis desiderem: Primo hoc haberi velim pro certo, קפוד kippod et קפוז kippoz, utut sono similia sint, tamen esse nomina diversorum animalium. 1. Quia in eadem serie contextus ab Esaia proponuntur ut diversa. Eam, inquit, possidebunt pelecanus et KIPPOD. Et, paucis interjectis, Ibi nidificabit KIPPOZ. Quae inanis est repetitio, si kippod et kippoz idem essent (1). 2. Hoc potissimum, quod, cum קפוד kippod hericium esse, suo loco a) probaverim, id est, animal quadrupes viviparum: contra describitur קפוז kippoz ut animal oviparum (2): Ibi nidificabit kippoz, et pariet, et excludet (ova scilicet), postquam (illa) foverit in umbra sua. Quid expressius? Itaque Santes et Schindlerus in Lexicis suis, voce בקע, plane videntur ignorasse, quod animal sit hericius: alioqui nunquam dicturi, quod faciunt in hujus loci expositione, nidificare hericium, et rumpere ova, et, iis ruptis, pullos suos excludere. III, 196 Secundo, quidquid sit קפוז kippoz, cum a saltu nomen habeat, neque te- studo est, neque cypselus avis. Neutri enim convenit saltus. Non testudini, quae ne graditur quidem aliter, quam reptitando. Sed neque avi cypselo, quam alii apodem vocant, quia pedum usu caret, et incessus fere est expers. Plinius col. 410 lib. 10. cap. 39. Plurimum volant, quae apodes; quia carent usu pedum: ab aliis cypseli appellantur hirundinum specie. Item, His quies, nisi in nido, nulla. Aut pendent, aut jacent. Eadem etiam alii scribunt. Praeterea, cum cypselus marina sit avis, aut riparia, quorsum nidificare dicatur in Idumaeae aridis locis? Frustra Mercerus urget, cypseli vocem ab Hebraea קפוז kippoz non abludere. Neque enim id tanti est, cum caeterae notae desint. Ut taceam, ab Hebraea lingua male repeti vocem, quae palam est Graecae originis. Cypseli enim dicuntur ἀπὸ τῶν κυψελίδων, ab alveolis, quos e luto sibi construunt. Philoso- phus Historiae libri 9. cap. 30. Οἱ δὲ ἄποδες, οὓς καλοῦσί τινες κυψέλους, νεοτ-τεύουσιν ἐν κυψελίσιν ἐν πυλοῦ πεπλασμένας μακραῖς. Sic, apud Herodotum in Terpsichore, Eëtionis filio Cypseli nomen inditur, ἀπὸ τῆς κυψέλης, in qua latens ex periculo mortis evaserat.

Now, to state modestly but freely what I find lacking in each: first, I would have this held as certain, that קפוד kippod and קפוז kippoz, however similar in sound, are nevertheless names of different animals. 1. Because in the same sequence of the text they are presented by Isaiah as different. The pelican, he says, and the KIPPOD shall possess it. And, a few words later, There shall the KIPPOZ make its nest. This is an empty repetition if kippod and kippoz were the same R1. 2. Above all this: whereas I have proved in its place a) that קפוד kippod is the hedgehog, that is, a viviparous quadruped, קפוז kippoz, on the contrary, is described as an oviparous animal R2: There shall the kippoz make its nest, and lay, and hatch (the eggs, that is), after it has (them) warmed in its shadow. What could be more explicit? Thus Santes and Schindlerus in their Lexicons, under the word בקע, seem plainly not to have known what kind of animal the hedgehog is; otherwise they would never have said, as they do in expounding this passage, that the hedgehog builds a nest, and breaks its eggs, and, when they are broken, hatches its young. III, 196 Secondly, whatever קפוז kippoz may be, since it takes its name from leaping, it is neither the tortoise nor the bird cypselus. For leaping suits neither. Not the tortoise, which does not even walk except by crawling. Nor the bird cypselus, which others call apus, because it lacks the use of its feet and is almost incapable of walking. Pliny col. 410 book 10, ch. 39: Those called apodes fly most of all, because they lack the use of their feet; by others they are called cypseli, of the swallow kind. Also: They have no rest except in the nest. They either hang or lie. Others too write the same. Moreover, since the cypselus is a sea bird, or a bird of the riverbanks, why should it be said to nest in the dry places of Idumaea? Mercerus urges in vain that the word cypselus is not far from the Hebrew קפוז kippoz. For that counts for little when the other marks are lacking. Not to mention that a word plainly of Greek origin is wrongly derived from the Hebrew language. For cypseli are so called ἀπὸ τῶν κυψελίδων [apo tōn kypselidōn], from the little cells which they build for themselves out of mud. The Philosopher, History, book 9, ch. 30: Οἱ δὲ ἄποδες, οὓς καλοῦσί τινες κυψέλους, νεοττεύουσιν ἐν κυψελίσιν ἐν πυλοῦ πεπλασμένας μακραῖς [Hoi de apodes, hous kalousi tines kypselous, neotteuousin en kypselisin en pylou peplasmenas makrais]. So in Herodotus, in Terpsichore, the son of Eëtion is given the name Cypselus, ἀπὸ τῆς κυψέλης [apo tēs kypselēs], in which he had lain hidden and escaped the danger of death.


Tertia interpretatio, quae קפוז kippoz merulam exponit, plus habet verisimilitudinis. 1. Merula enim Graece est κόσσυφος, quod ex Hebraeo, kipphoz, ut efferebant veteres, factum videri queat per literarum metathesim. 2. Et cum solitariis animalibus videtur posse censeri, cum merulam dici velint Varro b), Festus c), Isidorus d), eo quod mera, (id est, sola), volitet. 3. Eadem avis קפוז kippoz recte dicatur a saltu, cum subsultet potius, quam ambulet. Plinius lib. 10. cap. 38. Avium ambulant aliquae, ut cornices; saliunt aliquae, ut passe- res, merulae. Has rationes habuit Iunius, cur kippoz merulam redderet. Sed vir doctissimus non cogitavit, Prophetam ibi agere de φιλερήμοις animalibus, quorum inhabitatione cultus antea locus vastus atque horridus fiat. In quo numero merulam esse, nemo dixerit, quae avis est innoxia, habitu corporis decens, voce suavi, sapore grato, fimo ad laetificandos agros utilissimo, quamque adeo in Ornithotrophiis cum lusciniis vult ali Varro lib. 3. De Re Rustica cap. 5. Merulam quidem dici volunt, quia fere vagatur sola, nec nisi propter sobolem cum avibus sui generis solet inire societatem. Sed hanc originationem, cum aliis Varronis deridet Quinctilianus lib. 1. cap. 5. Cui, inquit, non post Varronem sit venia? qui agrum, quod in eo agatur aliquid; et graculos, quia gregatim volent, dictos; Ciceroni persuadere voluit (ad eum enim scribit): cum alterum ex Graeco sit manifestum dici, alterum ex vocibus avium. Sed hoc tanti III, 197 fuit vertere, ut merula, quia sola volat, quasi mera volans nominaretur. Et merulam quidem dici, quasi merivolam, merum commentum: merula tamen pro mera, id est, sola, dici potuit diminutiva voce. Verum, undecunque nomen traxerit, eam in habitatis locis degere, nemo est, qui nesciat, atque unam merulae speciem plerumque ἐπὶ τῶν κεράμων, super tectorum tegulas versari, ut observat Philosophus Historiae libri noni capite decimo nono. Unde est, quod huc nonnulli referunt illud Psaltis, Fui sicut passer solitarius super tectum.

The third interpretation, which explains קפוז kippoz as the blackbird, has more probability. 1. For blackbird in Greek is κόσσυφος [kossyphos], which could seem to have been formed from the Hebrew kipphoz, as the ancients pronounced it, by a metathesis of letters. 2. And it seems it can be reckoned among the solitary animals, since Varro b), Festus c) and Isidore d) would have merula [blackbird] so called because it flies mera (that is, alone). 3. The same bird could rightly be called קפוז kippoz from leaping, since it hops rather than walks. Pliny book 10, ch. 38: Some birds walk, like crows; some hop, like sparrows and blackbirds. These were Junius's reasons for rendering kippoz as blackbird. But that most learned man did not consider that the Prophet is there dealing with φιλερήμοις [philerēmois] animals, desert-loving ones, by whose habitation a place formerly cultivated becomes waste and dreadful. No one would say the blackbird is of that number: it is a harmless bird, comely in form, sweet of voice, pleasant in taste, its dung most useful for enriching fields, so much so that Varro book 3, On Agriculture, ch. 5, wants it kept in aviaries together with nightingales. They do indeed say it is called merula because it usually wanders alone and does not usually associate with birds of its own kind except for the sake of its brood. But this derivation, along with others of Varro's, is ridiculed by Quintilian book 1, ch. 5: Who, he says, would not be pardoned after Varro? who wanted to persuade Cicero (for he writes to him) that ager [field] was so called because something agitur [is done] in it, and graculi [jackdaws] because they fly gregatim [in flocks]; although it is manifest that the one comes from the Greek, the other from the cries of the birds. But it was worth so much to him to make the turn, that merula, because it flies alone, was named as if mera volans [flying alone] III, 197. And indeed that merula is said as if merivola is pure invention; yet merula could have been said for mera, that is, alone, as a diminutive. But wherever it got its name, there is no one who does not know that it lives in inhabited places, and that one species of blackbird mostly frequents ἐπὶ τῶν κεράμων [epi tōn keramōn], upon the tiles of roofs, as the Philosopher observes in History, book 9, chapter 19. Hence some refer here that saying of the Psalmist: I was like a solitary sparrow upon the roof.


Hoc vitavit incommodum Deodatius ὁ μακαρίτης, qui קפוז kippoz, Italice gufo, id est, scopem, interpretatur; avem non modo solitariam, et φιλέρη-μον, sed et nocturnam, et deformem, et ominosam, vocisque absurdae et absonae (3). Homeri vetus Scholiastes, Σκῶπες· ὄρνεα νυκτίνομα, κακόνομα, κακόφωνα, οἱονεὶ σκαιόπές τινες. 2. Accedit, quod merito קפוז kippoz, id est, saltatricula, nominari posse videtur avis, quae saltatione tam delectatur, ut, aucupe saltante, capi legatur ἀντορχουμένη, id est, ex adverso saltitans. Quocirca scopem Athenaeus e) iis accenset animalibus, quae saltantem intuentia νευ-ροσπαστεῖται, id est, moventur ad instar sigillariorum νευροσπαστῶν (Gallice des marionettes) et ut — nervis alienis mobile lignum. Unde σκὼψ f) appellatur saltationis quoddam genus, varietate motuum et gesticulationum insignis. Et σκώ-πτειν proprie est, scopis instar, imitatione ridicula aliquid effingere. 3. Quid, col. 411 quod pro scope veteres fere copem g) scribebant, sine Sigma praefixo. In his Epicharmus, Speusippus, Metrodorus et Alexander Myndius, qui Homerum etiam et Aristotelem asserit κῶπες scripsisse, non σκῶπες. Quod ideo observamus, quia κῶψ magis accedit ad Hebraeum קפוז kippoz. Et vox Italica gufo videtur ex utroque posse deduci: cum gli cufi, vel gufi, sint veterum copes, vel scopes. Phavorinus, καὶ δοκοῦσι σκῶπες εἶναι, οὓς κούφους ἢ γούφους οἱ Ῥωμαῖοί φασι. Idem est in Eustathio, nisi quod, pro κούφους ἢ γούφους, nostra exemplaria perperam habent κουκούβας. Videt cordatus lector, ultimam hanc interpretationem maxime esse probabilem. Neque aliud eos voluisse puto, qui bubonem, aut magnam ululam, eandem vocem reddiderunt. Tamen hoc certum est, scopem III, 198 non potuisse dici קפוז kippoz, eo quod sit ὀρχηστικὴ, et ab aucupe saltante capiatur ἀντορχουμένη. Neque enim Hebraeum קפז est ὀρχεῖσθαι, sed ἅλλε-σθαι. Proprium vocis usum didicimus ex Arabibus, qui tria verba prope synonyma زج zaggia, طفر taphara (Chaldaice טפז tephaz) et قفز kaphaza (Chaldaice קפז kephaz) ita promiscue usurpant, ut زج zaggia plerumque significet prosilire in plano, طفر taphara, e sublimi loco in inferiorem desilire, قفز kaphaza, sursum exsilire ex inferiore loco. Hinc in Avicennae capite h) De speciebus exercitii, القفز Alcaphzo fit الي شي ليتعلق به ad rem aliquam, ut ab ea quis suspendatur. Et in Sacris paraphrasibus قفز kaphaza occurrit passim pro verbis Hebraeis דלג, et זנק, et נתר, quibus ἅλ-μα, et πήδημα, non ὄρχησιν, significari, notum est. Ergo קפוז kippoz, ut res nomini respondeat, oportet esse animal ἁλτικὸν, non ὀρχηστικὸν (Gallice propre a sauter, non a dancer). Quae duo quam differant, nemo non videt. Neque id omissum a Scaligero, qui, Aristotelis locum explicans, quo capite le-gitur otus ἀντορχούμενος Historiae lib. 8. cap. 12. Ἀντορχούμενος, inquit, vicissim gesticulans. Ὄρχησις aliud est quam ἅλμα.

This difficulty was avoided by the late Diodati (ὁ μακαρίτης [ho makaritēs]), who renders קפוז kippoz in Italian as gufo, that is, scops [scops-owl]: a bird not only solitary and φιλέρημον [philerēmon], but also nocturnal, ugly and ill-omened, with a harsh and discordant voice R3. The old Scholiast of Homer: Σκῶπες· ὄρνεα νυκτίνομα, κακόνομα, κακόφωνα, οἱονεὶ σκαιόπές τινες [Skōpes· ornea nyktinoma, kakonoma, kakophōna, hoionei skaiopes tines]. 2. Add that the name קפוז kippoz, that is, little leaper, seems fitly applicable to a bird that so delights in dancing that, when the fowler dances, it is reported to be caught ἀντορχουμένη [antorchoumenē], that is, dancing in return opposite him. Accordingly Athenaeus e) counts the scops among the animals which, watching a dancer, νευροσπαστεῖται [neurospasteitai], that is, are moved like puppets νευροσπαστῶν [neurospastōn] (in French des marionettes), and like — a piece of wood moved by another's strings. Hence σκὼψ [skōps] f) is the name of a kind of dance, notable for its variety of movements and gestures. And σκώπτειν [skōptein] properly means to mimic something with ridiculous imitation, like the scops-owls. 3. Moreover, col. 411 for scops the ancients mostly wrote cops g), without the prefixed Sigma. Among them are Epicharmus, Speusippus, Metrodorus and Alexander of Myndus, who asserts that Homer and Aristotle too wrote κῶπες [kōpes], not σκῶπες [skōpes]. We note this because κῶψ [kōps] comes closer to the Hebrew קפוז kippoz. And the Italian word gufo seems derivable from either, since gli cufi, or gufi, are the copes or scopes of the ancients. Phavorinus: καὶ δοκοῦσι σκῶπες εἶναι, οὓς κούφους ἢ γούφους οἱ Ῥωμαῖοί φασι [kai dokousi skōpes einai, hous kouphous ē gouphous hoi Rhōmaioi phasi]. The same is in Eustathius, except that, instead of κούφους ἢ γούφους [kouphous ē gouphous], our copies wrongly read κουκούβας [koukoubas]. The judicious reader sees that this last interpretation is by far the most probable. Nor, I think, did those mean anything else who rendered the same word eagle-owl, or great owl. Yet this is certain: the scops III, 198 could not have been called קפוז kippoz because it is ὀρχηστικὴ [orchēstikē] and is caught ἀντορχουμένη [antorchoumenē] by a dancing fowler. For the Hebrew קפז is not ὀρχεῖσθαι [orcheisthai], but ἅλλεσθαι [hallesthai]. We have learned the proper use of the word from the Arabs, who use three nearly synonymous verbs, زج [zj] zaggia, طفر [ṭafara] taphara (in Chaldee טפז tephaz) and قفز [qafaza] kaphaza (in Chaldee קפז kephaz), so interchangeably that زج [zj] zaggia mostly means to leap forward on level ground, طفر [ṭafara] taphara to leap down from a high place to a lower one, قفز [qafaza] kaphaza to leap upward from a lower place. Hence in Avicenna's [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] chapter h) On the kinds of exercise, القفز [al-qafz] Alcaphzo is done الي شي ليتعلق به [ilā shayʾ li-yataʿallaqa bihi] toward some object, so that one may hang from it. And in the sacred paraphrases قفز [qafaza] kaphaza occurs everywhere for the Hebrew verbs דלג, זנק and נתר, which are known to signify ἅλμα [halma] and πήδημα [pēdēma], not ὄρχησιν [orchēsin]. Therefore קפוז kippoz, if the thing is to answer to the name, must be an animal ἁλτικὸν [haltikon], not ὀρχηστικὸν [orchēstikon] (in French propre a sauter, non a dancer). How much these two differ, everyone sees. Nor was this overlooked by Scaliger, who, explaining the passage of Aristotle where the otus is said to be ἀντορχούμενος [antorchoumenos], History book 8, ch. 12, says: Ἀντορχούμενος [Antorchoumenos], gesticulating in return. Ὄρχησις [Orchēsis] is something other than ἅλμα [halma].


Itaque tam in avium, quam in quadrupedum genere קפוז kippoz, frustra quaesitus hactenus, docti judicent, annon potius pertineat ad serpentes, ex quorum numero est acontias, sive jaculus, ita dictus διὰ τὸ ὁρμᾶν ὥσπερ τὰ ἀκόν-τια, quia jaculorum instar impetu fertur. Ita Nicandri Scholiastes. Nec multo aliter Aelianus lib. 6. cap. 18. Ἤδη δὲ καὶ ἀκοντίων δίκην ἑαυτόν τις μεθίησι, καὶ ἐπιφέρεται. καὶ τὸ ὄνομα ἐξ οὗ δρᾷ ἔχει· κέκληται γὰρ Ἀκοντίας. Est et serpens quidam, qui in modum jaculi semet ipsum emittit (Apostolius i) legit μεθί-στησι transfert) et irruit: et ex eo, quod facit, nomen habet; vocatur enim Iaculus. Itaque fere omnes illi ἅλμα tribuunt, et προσπήδησιν. Agatharchides cap. 50. de hoc serpentum genere, Τὴν πληγὴν δὲ δίδωσι παλλόμενον εἰς ὕψος· Plaga infert vibratum in altum. Quod potest ferri. Tamen ἁλλόμενον constanter scribunt posteriores. Artemidorus apud Strabonem libro 16. Ὄφεις δὲ σπι-θαμιαῖοι, φοινικοὶ τὴν χρόαν, προσαλλόμενοι, etc. Serpentes sunt trium palmorum, coloris punicei, assilientes, etc. Diodorus lib. 3. pag. 126. Δάκνουσι δὲ προσπηδῶντες, καὶ ἁλλόμενοι πρὸς ὕψος· Mordent prosilientes, et in altum saltantes. Aelianus Historiae libri 8. cap. 13. Ἔστι ἁλτικὸν θηρίον, καὶ διαπηδῆσαι καὶ εἴκοσιν εἰ δέοι, πήχεις οἷόν τε· Est serpens saltu valens, quodque viginti cubitorum spatium, si sit opus, transilire queat. Galenus cap. 8. Ad Pisonem, Ὁ III, 199 δὲ ἀκοντίας, ἐκτείνας ἑαυτὸν πάνυ, καὶ ὥς πέρ τι ἀκόντιον ἐφαλλόμενος τοῖς col. 412 σώμασιν· Iaculus se ipsum multum extendens, et in jaculi modum in corpora insiliens. Isidorus Originum lib. 12. cap. 4. Exsiliunt in arbores, et dum aliquod animal obvium fuerit, jactant se super illud. Et Avicenna k) Tom. 2. pag. 139. ربما كمنت علي الاشجار راصدة وترمي بانفسها علي من يمر بها وتثب منزجة اليه Quandoque super arbores in insidiis latet; et, si quis prope illas transeat, se jaculatur, et desiliens in eum irruit. Unde est, quod acontias Arabice vocatur ab Avicenna قفازة kipphaza, et طفارة tipphara; quasi assultricem dixeris, et desultricem. Nam قفازة kipphaza proprie dicitur, cum sursum nititur; puta ex solo in arbores: et طفارة tipphara, cum e sublimi desilit; puta ex arboribus in viatores. Prius nomen omnino factum ad instar Hebraei קפוז kippoz, vel kipphoz, ut veteres legisse et extulisse certum est. Eaedem utrobique literae Radicales, et eadem pene nominis forma, quantum ferre potuit, linguarum diversitas. Tantum in Arabico قفازة kipphaza addita est Foeminina terminatio, quam in nomine קפוז kippoz desiderari docent Foeminini generis quatuor verba, huic adjuncta. Quamvis ideo diversa sit terminatio, quia Hebraeum serpentis nomen נחש Masculinum est, et Arabicum حية Foemininum (4).

Therefore, since קפוז kippoz has hitherto been sought in vain both among the birds and among the quadrupeds, let the learned judge whether it does not rather belong to the serpents, among which is the acontias or iaculus, so called διὰ τὸ ὁρμᾶν ὥσπερ τὰ ἀκόντια [dia to horman hōsper ta akontia], because it rushes forward like javelins. So the Scholiast on Nicander. Not very differently Aelian, book 6, ch. 18: Ἤδη δὲ καὶ ἀκοντίων δίκην ἑαυτόν τις μεθίησι, καὶ ἐπιφέρεται. καὶ τὸ ὄνομα ἐξ οὗ δρᾷ ἔχει· κέκληται γὰρ Ἀκοντίας [Ēdē de kai akontiōn dikēn heauton tis methiēsi, kai epipheretai. kai to onoma ex hou dra echei; keklētai gar Akontias]. There is also a certain serpent which launches itself like a javelin (Apostolius i) reads μεθίστησι [methistēsi], transfers) and rushes upon its prey; and it has its name from what it does, for it is called Iaculus. Accordingly almost all ascribe to it ἅλμα [halma] and προσπήδησιν [prospēdēsin]. Agatharchides, ch. 50, on this kind of serpent: Τὴν πληγὴν δὲ δίδωσι παλλόμενον εἰς ὕψος [Tēn plēgēn de didōsi pallomenon eis hypsos]; It strikes its blow when hurled aloft. This can be accepted. Yet later writers consistently write ἁλλόμενον [hallomenon]. Artemidorus in Strabo, book 16: Ὄφεις δὲ σπιθαμιαῖοι, φοινικοὶ τὴν χρόαν, προσαλλόμενοι [Opheis de spithamiaioi, phoinikoi tēn chroan, prosallomenoi], etc. There are serpents three palms long, of a scarlet colour, leaping at one, etc. Diodorus, book 3, p. 126: Δάκνουσι δὲ προσπηδῶντες, καὶ ἁλλόμενοι πρὸς ὕψος [Daknousi de prospēdōntes, kai hallomenoi pros hypsos]; They bite, springing forward and leaping aloft. Aelian, History, book 8, ch. 13: Ἔστι ἁλτικὸν θηρίον, καὶ διαπηδῆσαι καὶ εἴκοσιν εἰ δέοι, πήχεις οἷόν τε [Esti haltikon thērion, kai diapēdēsai kai eikosin ei deoi, pēcheis hoion te]; It is a serpent strong at leaping, and able, if need be, to leap across a distance of twenty cubits. Galen, ch. 8 of To Piso: Ὁ III, 199 δὲ ἀκοντίας, ἐκτείνας ἑαυτὸν πάνυ, καὶ ὥς πέρ τι ἀκόντιον ἐφαλλόμενος τοῖς col. 412 σώμασιν [Ho de akontias, ekteinas heauton pany, kai hōs per ti akontion ephallomenos tois sōmasin]; The iaculus, stretching itself out greatly and leaping upon bodies like a javelin. Isidore, Etymologies, book 12, ch. 4: They leap up into trees, and when some animal comes their way, they throw themselves upon it. And Avicenna k), vol. 2, p. 139: ربما كمنت علي الاشجار راصدة وترمي بانفسها علي من يمر بها وتثب منزجة اليه [rubbamā kamanat ʿalī al-ashjār rāṣidatan wa-tarmī bi-anfusihā ʿalī man yamurru bihā wa-tathibu manzajatan ilayhi] Sometimes it lies in ambush up in trees; and if anyone passes near them, it hurls itself and, leaping down, rushes upon him. Hence it is that the acontias is called in Arabic by Avicenna قفازة [qaffāza] kipphaza and طفارة [ṭaffāra] tipphara, as if you were to say the one that leaps at and the one that leaps down. For قفازة [qaffāza] kipphaza is properly said when it strives upward, say from the ground into trees; and طفارة [ṭaffāra] tipphara when it leaps down from on high, say from the trees onto travellers. The former name is formed entirely after the pattern of the Hebrew קפוז kippoz, or kipphoz, as it is certain the ancients read and pronounced it. The radical letters are the same in both, and the form of the noun nearly the same, so far as the difference of the languages allowed. Only in the Arabic قفازة [qaffāza] kipphaza a feminine ending has been added, which is lacking in the noun קפוז kippoz, as the four feminine verbs joined to it show. The ending differs, however, because the Hebrew word for serpent, נחש, is masculine, and the Arabic حية [ḥayya] feminine R4.


Haec de verbo: rem quod attinet, inter Africae pestes nulla est hoc serpente deterior. Aëtius ubi supra cap. 27. Ab hujus morsu sequuntur omnia, quae de vipera dicta sunt, atque etiam graviora. Avicenna, Accidit ex morsu ejus dolor vehemens, et ulcus calidum toto corpore, atque ex eo mors. Et morsum ejus ἀνίατον vel ἀνήκεστον, id est, insanabilem esse, scribunt Agatharchides, Diodorus et Strabo. Proinde in Agatharchide hoc serpentis genus dicitur esse ἰωδέστα-τον πάντων, omnium venenosissimum. Is enim videtur ita scripsisse, non ἰδιώτα-τον, ut habent nostrae editiones. Neque vitabile est hoc telum, cum ex insidiis erumpat tanto impetu, ut praevertat omnem fugam. Missili volare tormento, III, 200 dicit Plinius: et Solinus, ex arboribus vi maxima turbinatum, penetrare animal, quodcunque obvium fortuna fecerit. Et Aelianus, Ἁλλόμενον δὲ παραχρῆμα ἐνέ-φυ, Insiliens statim adhaeret, nempe iis, quae saltu appetit. Tam praeceps rapiditas a Lucano sic describitur lib. 9. versu 822.

So much for the word. As for the thing: among the plagues of Africa none is worse than this serpent. Aëtius, in the place cited above, ch. 27: From its bite follow all the things said of the viper, and even worse ones. Avicenna: From its bite there arise violent pain and a hot ulcer over the whole body, and from it death. And Agatharchides, Diodorus and Strabo write that its bite is ἀνίατον [aniaton] or ἀνήκεστον [anēkeston], that is, incurable. Accordingly in Agatharchides this kind of serpent is said to be ἰωδέστατον πάντων [iōdestaton pantōn], the most poisonous of all. For he seems to have written thus, not ἰδιώτατον [idiōtaton], as our editions have it. Nor can this missile be avoided, since it bursts from ambush with such force that it outstrips all flight. It flies as if from a missile-engine, III, 200 says Pliny; and Solinus says that, whirled from the trees with the greatest force, it pierces whatever animal fortune has put in its way. And Aelian: Ἁλλόμενον δὲ παραχρῆμα ἐνέφυ [Hallomenon de parachrēma enephy], Leaping, it clings at once, namely to whatever it attacks with its leap. Such headlong speed is described thus by Lucan, book 9, line 822.


Ecce! procul saevus sterilis se robore trunci
Torsit et immisit (jaculum vocat Africa) serpens,
Perque caput Pauli transactaque tempora fugit.
Nil ibi virus agit, rapuit cum vulnere fatum:
Deprensum est, quae funda rotat, quam lenta volarent,
Quam segnis Scythicae strideret arundinis aër.

Behold! far off, from the wood of a barren trunk, a savage serpent (Africa calls it the iaculus) twisted and hurled itself, and passed through the head and pierced temples of Paulus. No poison does its work there; death seized him with the wound. Then it was found how slowly the stones that the sling whirls fly, how sluggishly the air hisses with the Scythian arrow.


Sunt, qui hunc serpentem levi saltu defungi colligunt, nec attolli supra hominis ilia, ex his Strabonis in Latina versione; Serpentes etiam, spithamam longos, colore puniceo, usque ad ilia assilientes, quorum morsus incurabilis est: sed fallit eos prava versio, eaque nata ex prava Graeci textus interpunctione, qui sic legitur: Ὄφεις δὲ σπιθαμιαῖοι, φοινικοὶ τὴν χρόαν, προσαλλόμενοι καὶ μέχρι λα-γόνος, τὸ δῆγμα ἔχοντες ἀνήκεστον· cum sit legendum προβαλλόμενοι, καὶ μέ-χρι λαγόνος τὸ δῆγμα, etc. Neque enim sensus est, eos salire usque ad ilia; sed vulnera, quae assultu suo infligunt, toto corpore usque ad ilia esse insanabilia, cum alioqui sanari possint, nempe si sint infra ilia, puta in cruribus, aut femoribus. Haec enim ex Artemidoro sumpsit Strabo, et Artemidorus ex Agatharchide, cujus verba sunt: Δῆγμα δὲ ἀνίατον, ἂν τὸν λαγόνος ἀνώτερον αἱ-μάξῃ· Morsus est insanabilis, cum supra ilia sauciat. Itaque jaculus, de quo Lucanus, non solum ad ilia saltu se extulit, sed col. 413

There are some who infer that this serpent manages only a slight leap and does not rise above a man's flanks, from these words of Strabo in the Latin version: "Serpents also, a span long, of a purple colour, leaping up as far as the flanks, whose bite is incurable". But they are misled by a faulty version, and this arose from a faulty punctuation of the Greek text, which reads thus: Ὄφεις δὲ σπιθαμιαῖοι, φοινικοὶ τὴν χρόαν, προσαλλόμενοι καὶ μέχρι λαγόνος, τὸ δῆγμα ἔχοντες ἀνήκεστον· [Opheis de spithamiaioi, phoinikoi tēn chroan, prosallomenoi kai mechri lagonos, to dēgma echontes anēkeston]. It should be read προβαλλόμενοι, καὶ μέχρι λαγόνος τὸ δῆγμα [proballomenoi, kai mechri lagonos to dēgma], etc. For the sense is not that they leap as far as the flanks, but that the wounds they inflict by their spring are incurable over the whole body as far as the flanks, whereas otherwise they can be healed, namely if they are below the flanks, say on the shins or thighs. For Strabo took this from Artemidorus, and Artemidorus from Agatharchides, whose words are: Δῆγμα δὲ ἀνίατον, ἂν τὸν λαγόνος ἀνώτερον αἱμάξῃ· [Dēgma de aniaton, an ton lagonos anōteron haimaxē]; "The bite is incurable when it wounds above the flanks." Thus the iaculus of which Lucan speaks not only raised itself by its leap to the flanks, but col. 413


Perque caput Pauli, transactaque tempora fugit.

"Through the head of Paulus, and through the pierced temples, it flew."


Et in Isidoro jaculi exsiliunt in arbores: et in Aeliano transiliunt καὶ εἴκοσιν, εἰ δέοι, πήχεις, etiam viginti cubitos, si sit opus; cui saltus longitudini necesse est, ut altitudo sit proportione par. Ex his intelligit lector, vasta omnino et inculta oportere esse loca, quae tali peste foecunda sunt. Atque hoc est, quod vult Esaias, cum acontiam in Idumaea scribit non modo diversaturum, sed pariturum etiam, et exclusurum ova, quibus incubuerit. Si quis Libyci serpentis genus Iudaeis neget aut Idumaeis fuisse notum, audiat haec Marcellini libro 22. Serpentes quoque Aegyptus alit innumeras, ultra omnem perniciem saevientes, basiliscos, et amphisbaenas, et scytalas, et acontias. Alii Arabiae adscribunt. Lucanus libri 6. versu 677.

And in Isidore the iaculi "leap up into trees"; and in Aelian they leap across καὶ εἴκοσιν, εἰ δέοι, πήχεις [kai eikosin, ei deoi, pēcheis], "even twenty cubits, if need be"; and for such a length of leap the height must be proportionately equal. From this the reader understands that the places which abound in such a pest must be utterly vast and desolate. And this is what Isaiah means when he writes that the acontias will not only lodge in Idumaea, but will also give birth there and hatch the eggs on which it has brooded. If anyone denies that this kind of Libyan serpent was known to the Jews or the Idumaeans, let him hear these words of Marcellinus in book 22: "Egypt also nourishes innumerable serpents, raging beyond all destruction: basilisks, and amphisbaenas, and scytalae, and acontiae." Others assign them to Arabia. Lucan, book 6, line 677:


Non Arabum volucer serpens: — —

"Not the winged serpent of the Arabs": — —


id est, jaculus. Idem enim lib. 9. versu 720.

that is, the iaculus. For the same poet says in book 9, line 720:


III, 201 Et natrix violator aquae, jaculique volucres.

III, 201 "And the natrix, violator of water, and the winged iaculi."


Ut de Agatharchide, Diodoro et Strabone taceam, qui in Sabaeis describunt, ad quos Iudaei navigare coeperant jam inde a Solomonis aevo.

To say nothing of Agatharchides, Diodorus and Strabo, who describe them among the Sabaeans, to whom the Jews had begun to sail already from the age of Solomon.


Sed, ut res clarior fiat, juvat Esaiae singula verba perpendere. Ibi] inquit, in Idumaea, Arabiae parte, Aegypto contigua, in qua serpentes acontias describit Ammianus. Nidulabitur Kippoz] id est, jaculus, seu acontias, ut Hebraice קפוז kippoz, sic Arabice قفازة kipphaza dictus a saltu. Nidulari, fateor, maxime proprium esse avium, quod mihi olim objecit vir doctissimus: sed et nidus καταχρηστικῶς aliis animantibus tribuitur. 1. Homini puta, ut Eccles. XXXVI, 28. Τίς γὰρ πιστεύσει, etc. ἀνθρώπῳ μὴ ἔχοντι νοσσιὰν, καὶ κατα-λύοντι οὗ ἐὰν ὀψίσῃ· Quis credet homini, qui non habet nidum, et divertitur ubicunque advesperascit? Hinc Iob. XXIX, 18. In nido meo moriar. Num. XXIV, 21. de Kinaeo, In rupe posuisti nidum tuum. Ierem. XLIX, 16. et Abd. 11. de Idumaeo, Quamvis exaltares ut aquila nidum tuum. Hab. II, 9. Vae inhianti lutro malo pro domo sua, ut ponat in excelso nidum suum! 2. Leoni in Graeca versione Nahum II, 12. Ἔπλησε θήρας νοσσιὰν αὐτοῦ, Praeda implevit nidum suum. Hebr. חריו, foramina sua. Alcamus, العرزال عريسة الاسد وما يجمعه في ماوا هلاشباله مما يمهده كالعش Alirzal, antrum leonis, et quod in lustro suo colligit catulis suis, ut tanquam nidum substernat. 3. Sui. Columella lib. 8. cap. 9. In cubili suum quisque matrem nidus exspectat, id est, porcelli, in hara jacentes, tanquam in nido. 4. Hystrici. Callimachus Hymno in Dianam,

But to make the matter clearer, it is worth weighing Isaiah's words one by one. There], he says, that is, in Idumaea, a part of Arabia adjoining Egypt, in which Ammianus describes acontias serpents. The kippoz shall nest], that is, the iaculus or acontias, called from its leap קפוז kippoz in Hebrew, as in Arabic قفازة [qaffāza] kipphaza. I admit that to nest is most properly said of birds, as a very learned man once objected to me; but nest is also applied καταχρηστικῶς [katachrēstikōs] to other animals. 1. To man, for instance, as in Sir 36:28 Τίς γὰρ πιστεύσει, etc. ἀνθρώπῳ μὴ ἔχοντι νοσσιὰν, καὶ καταλύοντι οὗ ἐὰν ὀψίσῃ· [Tis gar pisteusei, etc. anthrōpō mē echonti nossian, kai katalyonti hou ean opsisē]; "Who will trust a man who has no nest, and lodges wherever evening overtakes him?" Hence Job 29:18 "I shall die in my nest." Num 24:21 of the Kenite: "You have set your nest in the rock." Jer 49:16 and Abd. 11. of the Idumaean: "Though you should set your nest as high as the eagle." Hab 2:9 "Woe to him who gapes after evil gain for his house, that he may set his nest on high!" 2. To the lion, in the Greek version of Nahum II, 12. Ἔπλησε θήρας νοσσιὰν αὐτοῦ [Eplēse thēras nossian autou], "He filled his nest with prey." Hebr. חריו, "his holes." Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: العرزال عريسة الاسد وما يجمعه في ماوا هلاشباله مما يمهده كالعش [al-ʿirzāl ʿarīsat al-asad wa-mā yajmaʿuhu fī māwā hlʾshbālh mimmā yumahhiduhu ka-l-ʿushsh] Alirzal, "the lion's den, and what he gathers in his lair for his cubs, to spread beneath them as a nest." 3. To the pig. Columella, book 8, ch. 9: "In its own sty each litter waits for its mother" (nidus), that is, the piglets lying in the pen as in a nest. 4. To the porcupine. Callimachus, in the Hymn to Artemis:


Καὶ κοίτην ἐλάφοιο, καὶ ὕστρικος ἔνθα καλιαὶ,

Καὶ κοίτην ἐλάφοιο, καὶ ὕστρικος ἔνθα καλιαὶ, [Kai koitēn elaphoio, kai hystrikos entha kaliai,]


Et cubile cervi, et hystricis ubi nidi. 5. Hericio. Esa. XIII, 22. Καὶ νοσσοποιή-σουσιν ἐχῖνοι ἐν τοῖς οἴκοις αὐτῶν· Et nidificabunt hericii in domibus eorum. Isacius ad Lycophronem versu 1093. Hericius, cum praecognoscat, qui venti spirare debeant, ἀποφράττει τὸ πρὸς τὸν μέλλοντα πνεῖν μέρος τῆς καλιᾶς αὐτοῦ, ὑπανοίγει δὲ τὸ ἕτερον, nidi partem obturat, oppositam ei vento, qui spiraturus est, et alteram aperit. 6. Phycidi pisci, de qua Plin. lib. 9. cap. 26. Eadem piscium sola nidificat ex alga, atque in nido parit. Et Ovidius in Halieutico,

"And the lair of the stag, and where the nests of the porcupine are." 5. To the hedgehog. Isa 13:22 Καὶ νοσσοποιήσουσιν ἐχῖνοι ἐν τοῖς οἴκοις αὐτῶν· [Kai nossopoiēsousin echinoi en tois oikois autōn]; "And hedgehogs shall make nests in their houses." Isaac [Tzetzes] on Lycophron, line 1093: "The hedgehog, since it knows in advance which winds are going to blow," ἀποφράττει τὸ πρὸς τὸν μέλλοντα πνεῖν μέρος τῆς καλιᾶς αὐτοῦ, ὑπανοίγει δὲ τὸ ἕτερον [apophrattei to pros ton mellonta pnein meros tēs kalias autou, hypanoigei de to heteron], "blocks the part of its nest facing the wind that is about to blow, and opens the other." 6. To the fish phycis, of which Pliny, book 9, ch. 26: "It alone among fishes makes a nest of seaweed, and gives birth in the nest." And Ovid in the Halieutica:


Atque avium dulces nidos imitata sub undis.

"And imitating beneath the waves the sweet nests of birds."


7. Crocodilo. Solinus, Metatur locum nido naturali providentia. 8. Vermibus. Sic Plinius lib. 11. cap. 28. dicit, in fimo nidulari vermiculos. 9. Culici, muscae, api, vespae, crabroni. Lucianus in Muscae encomio, Νεοττίαν δὲ, ἢ καλιὰν, col. 414 III, 202 οὐκ ἐνὶ τόπῳ κατεστήσατο· Nidum autem, aut nidulum, non uno in loco constituit. Et in Icaromenippo, Ἅπαντα διαγινώσκεις τὰ ἐπὶ γῆς· τοὺς ἀνθρώ-πους, τὰ θηρία, μικροῦ δεῖν, τὰς τῶν ἐμπίδων νεοττίας· Omnia, quae in terra sunt, dignoscis; homines, feras, et, pene dixerim, culicum nidos. Iosephus de Samsone libri 5. Antiquitatum cap. 10. Ἐπιτυγχάνει σμήνει μελισ-σῶν, ἐν τῷ στήθει τοῦ λέοντος ἐκείνου νενοσσευκότων· Incidit in apum examen, quae in leonis illius pectore nidificaverant. Chaldaea paraphrasis Iudic. XIV, 8. והא קנא דדבריתא בפגרא דאריא, Et ecce nidum apum in cadavere leonis! Et Arabica, واذا في صدر الاسد نحل قد عششت هناك وقد سال العسل من عش النحل Et ecce in pectore leonis apes, quae nidificaverant illic, et mel effluebat ex apum nido. Ut 1 Sam. XIV, 26. Mel decurrebat من عش النحل ex apum nido. Et Chaldaea rursus versu sequente, Extendit caput baculi, quem in manu ha-bebat, et intinxit illud בקינא דדובשא, in nido mellis. Virgilius lib. 4. Georgicorum, de apibus:

7. To the crocodile. Solinus: By natural providence it marks out a place for its nest. 8. To worms. Thus Pliny, book 11, ch. 28, says that little worms nest in dung. 9. To the gnat, the fly, the bee, the wasp and the hornet. Lucian in the Praise of the Fly: Νεοττίαν δὲ, ἢ καλιὰν, col. 414 III, 202 οὐκ ἐνὶ τόπῳ κατεστήσατο [Neottian de, ē kalian, ouk eni topō katestēsato]; But it has not set up its nest, or little nest, in a single place. And in the Icaromenippus: Ἅπαντα διαγινώσκεις τὰ ἐπὶ γῆς· τοὺς ἀνθρώπους, τὰ θηρία, μικροῦ δεῖν, τὰς τῶν ἐμπίδων νεοττίας [Hapanta diaginōskeis ta epi gēs; tous anthrōpous, ta thēria, mikrou dein, tas tōn empidōn neottias]; You discern all things that are on earth: men, beasts and, I might almost say, the nests of gnats. Josephus on Samson, Antiquities, book 5, ch. 10: Ἐπιτυγχάνει σμήνει μελισσῶν, ἐν τῷ στήθει τοῦ λέοντος ἐκείνου νενοσσευκότων [Epitynchanei smēnei melissōn, en tō stēthei tou leontos ekeinou nenosseukotōn]; He came upon a swarm of bees which had nested in the breast of that lion. The Chaldee paraphrase of Iudic. XIV, 8: והא קנא דדבריתא בפגרא דאריא, And behold, a nest of bees in the carcass of the lion! And the Arabic: واذا في صدر الاسد نحل قد عششت هناك وقد سال العسل من عش النحل [wa-idhā fī ṣadr al-asad naḥl qad ʿashshashat hunāka wa-qad sāla al-ʿasal min ʿushsh al-naḥl] And behold, in the breast of the lion bees which had nested there, and honey was flowing from the bees' nest. So too 1 Sam 14:26. The honey was flowing down من عش النحل [min ʿushsh al-naḥl] from the bees' nest. And the Chaldee again in the following verse: He stretched out the end of the staff that he had in his hand and dipped it בקינא דדובשא, in the nest of honey. Virgil, Georgics book 4, on bees:


Progeniem nidosque fovent. — —

They cherish their offspring and their nests. — —


Plinius lib. 11. cap. 21. Vespae in sublime e luto nidos faciunt, et in iis ceras: crabrones in cavernis ac sub terra. Et rursus, Vespae, quae ichneumones vocantur, unum genus ex araneis perimunt, phalangium appellatum, et in nidos suos ferunt. Item, de crabronibus; Nidos vere faciunt fere quadrifores, in quibus opifices generentur. Iis educatis, alios deinde nidos majores fingunt, in quibus matres futuras producant. Et cap. 22. de bombycibus; Nidos luto fingunt salis specie, applicatos lapidi tanta duritia, ut spiculis perforari vix possint. Epiphanius Haeresi 44. de vespae genere, quam ζώπυρον vocant: Ἐπὰν δέ τις διερχόμενος τὸν αὐτοῦ φωλεὸν, ἢ καλιὰν, καθέλοι· Si quis viator latebram illius nidumque diruat. Ζώπυρον est Chaldaice זיבורא zibbora, et Arabum زنبور zanbur, de qua Damir, يتخذ عشه تحت الارض Nidum sub terra sibi sumit. 10. Formicis. Sic in tractatu Talmudico Nedarim legas קיני דשומשמני, nidos formicarum. Et in Horo lib. 2. cap. 60. Τιθεμένων (νυκτερίδος) τῶν πτερῶν εἰς τὴν νεοσσίαν τῶν μυρμήκων, οὐ προσέρχεται αὐτῶν τις· Vespertilionis pennis ad formicarum nidos admotis, nulla illarum egreditur. Et Apulejus lib. 8. Cujus in ipso carioso stipite inhabitantium formicarum nidificia burriebant (al. bulliebant). 11. Muribus, et aliis animalculis. Minutius Felix, Mures, etc. nisi abigatis, in ipso Dei vestri ore nidificant. Et Arnobius lib. 6. Non videtis sub istis simulacrorum causis (al. cavis) stelliones, sorices, mures, blattasque lucifugas nidamenta III, 203 ponere, atque habitare. 12. Locustis. Unde est, quod, cum David se excussum fuisse queritur ut locustam Psalm. CIX, 23. Kimchius et Aben Ezra observant, agi de locusta, שאין לו קן, quae non habet nidum. Et Damir, postquam locustam parturientem cauda sua petras durissimas diverberare dixit, donec in rimam pateant, atque ova sua in ea rima ponere, addit, فيكون له كالافحوص ويكون حاضنا لها ومربيا Et (haec rima) pro nido illis est, in quo foetum foveant, atque educent. 13. Serpentibus denique certum est nidos non raro tribui. Cic. lib. 2. de Divin. Ut in cunis fuerit anguis, non tam est mirum, in Selonio praesertim (qui est campus agri Lanuvini), ubi apud focum angues nidulari solent. Perperam legunt nundinari. Epiphanius in Physiologo cap. 16. Ὅταν ἐπὶ col. 415 τὴν πηγὴν τὸ ὕδωρ πιεῖν ἔλθῃ ὁ ὄφις, οὐ φέρει τὸν ἰὸν, ἀλλά γε ἀφεὶς αὐτὸν ἐν τῇ νεοττίᾳ, οὕτω καθαρὸς πορεύεται· Cum serpens ad fontem venit, ut bibat, virus non defert, sed, illo in nido dimisso, ita purus accedit. In nido, id est, ἐν τῷ φωλεῷ, in lustro, ut idem habet in Ophitarum Haeresi cap. 8. R. Selomo, explicans, quid sit foramen aspidis Esa. XI, 8. ait, esse foramen terrae, שהנחש מקנן בתוכו, in cujus medio nidificat serpens. Et Arabs interpres ibidem pro foramine aspidis habet عش الافاعي, nidum viperarum.

Pliny, book 11, ch. 21: Wasps make their nests of mud up on high, and their wax in them; hornets in caves and underground. And again: The wasps that are called ichneumons kill one kind of spider, called the phalangium, and carry it into their nests. Likewise, on hornets: In spring they make nests, generally with four doors, in which the workers are bred. When these have been reared, they then build other, larger nests, in which they bring forth the future mothers. And ch. 22, on silkworms: They form nests of mud in the shape of salt, fixed to a stone, of such hardness that they can hardly be pierced with spear-points. Epiphanius, Heresy 44, on the kind of wasp they call ζώπυρον [zōpyron]: Ἐπὰν δέ τις διερχόμενος τὸν αὐτοῦ φωλεὸν, ἢ καλιὰν, καθέλοι [Epan de tis dierchomenos ton autou phōleon, ē kalian, katheloi]; If a traveller destroys its lair and nest. The ζώπυρον [zōpyron] is in Chaldee זיבורא zibbora, and the Arabs' زنبور [zunbūr] zanbur, of which Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] says: يتخذ عشه تحت الارض [yattakhidhu ʿushshahu taḥta al-arḍ] It takes its nest for itself under the earth. 10. To ants. Thus in the Talmudic tractate Nedarim you read קיני דשומשמני, nests of ants. And in Horus, book 2, ch. 60: Τιθεμένων (νυκτερίδος) τῶν πτερῶν εἰς τὴν νεοσσίαν τῶν μυρμήκων, οὐ προσέρχεται αὐτῶν τις [Tithemenōn (nykteridos) tōn pterōn eis tēn neossian tōn myrmēkōn, ou proserchetai autōn tis]; When a bat's wings are placed at the nests of ants, not one of them comes out. And Apuleius, book 8: In whose very rotten trunk the nests of the ants dwelling there were swarming (var. bubbling). 11. To mice and other small animals. Minucius Felix: Mice, etc., unless you drive them away, nest in the very mouth of your god. And Arnobius, book 6: Do you not see that under the bases (var. hollows) of these images geckos, shrews, mice and light-shunning cockroaches make their nests III, 203 and dwell? 12. To locusts. Hence, when David complains that he has been shaken off like a locust, Ps 109:23, Kimchi and Aben Ezra observe that it refers to a locust שאין לו קן, which has no nest. And Damir, after saying that the locust, when about to bring forth, beats the hardest rocks with its tail until they open in a crack, and lays its eggs in that crack, adds: فيكون له كالافحوص ويكون حاضنا لها ومربيا [fa-yakūnu lahu ka-l-ufḥūṣ wa-yakūnu ḥāḍinan lahā wa-murabbiyan] And (this crack) serves them as a nest, in which they cherish and rear their young. 13. Finally, it is certain that nests are not seldom attributed to serpents. Cic., On Divination, book 2: That there was a snake in the cradle is not so wonderful, especially in Solonium (which is a plain in the territory of Lanuvium), where snakes are wont to nest by the hearth. Some wrongly read nundinari [to hold market]. Epiphanius in the Physiologus, ch. 16: Ὅταν ἐπὶ col. 415 τὴν πηγὴν τὸ ὕδωρ πιεῖν ἔλθῃ ὁ ὄφις, οὐ φέρει τὸν ἰὸν, ἀλλά γε ἀφεὶς αὐτὸν ἐν τῇ νεοττίᾳ, οὕτω καθαρὸς πορεύεται [Hotan epi tēn pēgēn to hydōr piein elthē ho ophis, ou pherei ton ion, alla ge apheis auton en tē neottia, houtō katharos poreuetai]; When the serpent comes to the spring to drink, it does not carry its poison with it, but, having left it in its nest, approaches thus pure. In its nest, that is, ἐν τῷ φωλεῷ [en tō phōleō], in its lair, as the same author has it in the Heresy of the Ophites, ch. 8. R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)], explaining what the hole of the asp is in Isa 11:8, says that it is a hole in the earth שהנחש מקנן בתוכו, in the midst of which the serpent nests. And the Arabic translator in the same place has for hole of the asp عش الافاعي [ʿushsh al-afāʿī], the nest of vipers.


Iam in Esaia quae sequuntur, Ibi nidulabitur acontias, et pariet, et ova excludet, quae foverit umbra sua, ipsissima verba sunt, quae in hoc argumento naturae consulti usurpant. Philosophus de serpentibus, Historiae lib. 5. in fine; Ὠοτοκοῦσιν ἔξω· ὅταν δὲ τέκῃ, εἰς τὴν γὴν ἐπωάζει. ἐκλέπε-ται δὲ καὶ ταῦτα τῷ ὑστέρῳ ἔτει. Ova foris edunt: quae cum pepererunt, in terra fovent. Ea autem excluduntur anno sequente. Unde Plinius libri 10. cap. 62. Ova pariunt serpentes, etc. Et contexta in terra incubant, et foetum sequente excludunt anno. Et Celsus lib. 5. cap. 27. Perniciosissimi sunt (serpentes), cum incubant. Ergo in Esaia מלט, est ὠοτοκεῖν, ova parere: דגר, ἐπωάζειν, fovere, incubare: בקע, ἐκλέπειν, excludere. Atque ipsemet Esaias alibi eodem Verbo ovorum basilisci exclusionem exprimit, ut supra l) notavimus.

Now what follows in Isaiah, There shall the acontias nest, and lay, and hatch out the eggs, which it has kept warm in its shadow, are the very words which the naturalists use on this subject. The Philosopher, on serpents, History book 5, at the end: Ὠοτοκοῦσιν ἔξω· ὅταν δὲ τέκῃ, εἰς τὴν γὴν ἐπωάζει. ἐκλέπεται δὲ καὶ ταῦτα τῷ ὑστέρῳ ἔτει [Ōotokousin exō; hotan de tekē, eis tēn gēn epōazei. eklepetai de kai tauta tō hysterō etei]. They lay their eggs outside; when they have laid them, they keep them warm in the ground. And these are hatched in the following year. Hence Pliny, book 10, ch. 62: Serpents lay eggs, etc. And they incubate them woven together in the ground, and hatch the young in the following year. And Celsus, book 5, ch. 27: They (serpents) are most deadly when they are incubating. Therefore in Isaiah מלט is ὠοτοκεῖν [ōotokein], to lay eggs; דגר is ἐπωάζειν [epōazein], to keep warm, to incubate; בקע is ἐκλέπειν [eklepein], to hatch out. And Isaiah himself elsewhere expresses with the same verb the hatching of the eggs of the basilisk, as we noted above l).


Etiam Verbum דגר, congregare proprie, vel ova congregata et connexa vovere, etsi tribuatur avibus, tamen in serpentem maxime quadrat, cujus ova non modo sunt simul collecta, sed et mutuo nexu cohaerent monilis III, 204 instar. Aristoteles ubi supra, Τὰ δ' ὠὰ ἀλλήλοις συνεχῆ ἐστιν, ὥσπερ αἱ τῶν γυναικῶν ὑποδερίδες· Ova sunt sibi mutuo connexa ut mulierum monilia, id est, ut margaritae in monilibus. Damir etiam, postquam serpentis ova descripsit longa, coloris fusci, viridis, nigri, albi, varii, punctis quibusdam distincti, lucidi, cum tantae varietatis causa non appareat satis, atque egit etiam de sanie intus latente, وهو في جوفها منضد طولا علي خط واحد Per ventrem, inquit, in longitudinem super lineam unam connexa sunt. Et Scaliger, Ea ova vidimus nos agglutinata inter se, globulorum modo, quibus preces numerant mulieres. Sunt, qui Hebraice id dici putant שלל של ביצים, sed proprie שלל של ביצים est, ovorum in gallinae ventre conglobatio, cum ad maturitatem vergunt. Ut אשכול של ביצים botrus ovorum, dicuntur ova minora, ex semine primum conglobata. Vide Talmudicos in tractatu Betsa fol. 7. a.

Also the verb דגר, properly to gather together, or to keep warm eggs gathered and joined together, although it is applied to birds, nevertheless fits a serpent best of all, whose eggs are not only collected together but also cling to one another by a mutual bond, like a necklace. III, 204 Aristotle, in the place cited above: Τὰ δ' ὠὰ ἀλλήλοις συνεχῆ ἐστιν, ὥσπερ αἱ τῶν γυναικῶν ὑποδερίδες [Ta d' ōa allēlois synechē estin, hōsper hai tōn gynaikōn hypoderides]; The eggs are joined to one another like women's necklaces, that is, like the pearls in necklaces. Damir too, after describing the eggs of the serpent as long, of a dusky, green, black, white or variegated colour, marked with certain spots, shining (though the cause of such great variety is not sufficiently apparent), and after treating also of the fluid hidden inside, says: وهو في جوفها منضد طولا علي خط واحد [wa-huwa fī jawfihā munaḍḍad ṭūlan ʿalī khaṭṭ wāḥid] Through the belly they are joined lengthwise along a single line. And Scaliger: We have seen these eggs glued to one another, in the manner of the little beads with which women count their prayers. There are some who think that this is called in Hebrew שלל של ביצים, but properly שלל של ביצים is the clustering of the eggs in the hen's belly, when they are approaching maturity. Just as the smaller eggs, first clustered together from the seed, are called אשכול של ביצים, a cluster of eggs. See the Talmudists in the tractate Betsa, fol. 7a.


Neque id omittendum, quod acontiam ova בצלה, umbra sua fovere dicit Propheta, dicturus potius sub alis, aut sub pennis, aut sub alarum umbra, si de ave res esset. Forte etiam his ipsis verbis insinuat divinus vates, hoc serpentis genus de suis ovis magis esse sollicitum. Amphisbaena saltem, quam Avicenna jaculi speciem esse suspicatur, legitur apud Albertum serpens esse vigil, et sollicitus de suis ovis valde, cum ea incubat (5).

Nor should it be passed over that the Prophet says the acontias keeps its eggs warm בצלה, in its shadow, whereas he would rather have said under its wings, or under its feathers, or under the shadow of its wings, if the subject were a bird. Perhaps also by these very words the divine seer hints that this kind of serpent is especially solicitous for its eggs. At least the amphisbaena, which Avicenna suspects is a species of iaculus, is described in Albertus as a serpent that is watchful, and very solicitous for its eggs when it incubates them R5.
