III, 222 col. 428 CAP. XIV.

III, 222 col. 428 Chapter 14.


De Draconibus.

On Dragons.


Hebraice תנין thannin duo significat, nempe draconem et cetum; ac si cetus sit draco marinus. Quin aliquando תנין sumitur pro serpente quovis, plane ut נחש. Ut cum virga Mosis mutari legitur לתנין in thannin, Exod. VII, 9. id est, לנחש, in serpentem, ut explicat ipse Moses Exod. IV, 3. et VII, 15. Ita Nasrius, scriptor Arabs in Oxoniensi bibliotheca, cum refert in Ὀνειροκριτικοῖς (lib. 3. sect. 21. cap. 30.) de muliere quadam, quae somniavit se peperisse الحية, col. 429 serpentem, et peperit magnum et celebrem oratorem: quia تنين thannin est bilinguis. Patet, eum تنين thannin, et حية, id est, serpentem, pro eodem usurpasse. Tamen non solum Hebraeis, Syris, sed et Arabibus, proprie תנין thannin est draco. Atque, ut alia taceam, patet id ex paraphrastis, qui pro dracone תנין constanter habent in libro Revelationum Iohannis. Hinc تنين thannin in Alcamus definitur, حية عظيمة, magnus serpens (1). Et III, 223 apud Arabes التنين, draco vel est السماوي, coelestis, vel الارضي, terrestris, vel البحري, marinus. Et coelestis, inquiunt, qui Persice هستبر obscurior quaedam albedo est, quae sex occupat signa, et cum Planetis locum mutat. Draco marinus, Graece δράκων θαλάσσιος, (Gallice vive) est araneus Plinii, de quo Avicenna lib. 2. et 4. Canonis. Terrestrem idem describit his fere verbis lib. 4. Fen. 6. tractatu 3. cap. 53. Minimus in specie draconum, ut quidam referunt, est quinque cubitorum; maximus, triginta et supra. Oculi magni: in mandibula inferiore quid eminens instar barbae. Dentes plurimi. Ajunt reperiri multos in Nubia et India, sed Indos esse majores. Ionici in Asia quatuor cubitos non excedunt. Indis, praeterquam quod maximi sunt, et de caetero qua specie diximus, facies sunt flavae et nigrae, ora amplissima, supercilia oculos obtegentia, colla squamis obsita. In unaquaque maxilla tres dentes (id est, dentium ordines).

In Hebrew תנין thannin means two things, namely dragon and sea monster, as if the sea monster were a sea dragon. Indeed תנין is sometimes taken for any serpent whatever, just like נחש. So when the rod of Moses is said to be changed לתנין, into a thannin, Exod 7:9, that is, לנחש, into a serpent, as Moses himself explains, Exod 4:3 and VII, 15. Thus Nasrius, an Arab writer in the Oxford library, when in his Ὀνειροκριτικοῖς [Oneirokritikois] (book 3, sect. 21, ch. 30) he tells of a certain woman who dreamed that she had given birth to الحية [al-ḥayya], col. 429 a serpent, and she gave birth to a great and celebrated orator: because the تنين [tinnīn] thannin is double-tongued. It is plain that he used تنين [tinnīn] thannin and حية [ḥayya], that is, serpent, for the same thing. Yet not only for the Hebrews and Syrians but also for the Arabs, תנין thannin is properly a dragon. And, to say nothing of other evidence, this is plain from the paraphrasts, who consistently have תנין for dragon in the book of the Revelation of John. Hence تنين [tinnīn] thannin is defined in the Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] as حية عظيمة [ḥayya ʿaẓīma], a great serpent R1. And III, 223 among the Arabs التنين [al-tinnīn], the dragon, is either السماوي [al-samāwī], celestial, or الارضي [al-arḍī], terrestrial, or البحري [al-baḥrī], marine. The celestial one, they say, which in Persian is هستبر [hstbr], is a certain fainter whiteness which occupies six signs and changes place with the planets. The sea dragon, in Greek δράκων θαλάσσιος [drakōn thalassios] (in French vive), is the araneus of Pliny, on which see Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)], books 2 and 4 of the Canon. The terrestrial one the same author describes in roughly these words, book 4, Fen 6, treatise 3, ch. 53: The smallest in the species of dragons, as some report, is five cubits; the largest, thirty and more. The eyes are large; on the lower jaw there is a projection like a beard. The teeth are very many. They say that many are found in Nubia and India, but that the Indian ones are larger. The Ionian ones in Asia do not exceed four cubits. The Indian ones, besides being the largest and otherwise of the form we have described, have yellow and black faces, very wide mouths, brows covering the eyes, necks covered with scales. In each jaw there are three teeth (that is, rows of teeth).


III, 224 Unum in eo genere nos vidimus, qui densos habebat pilos ab utraque parte colli.

III, 224 We ourselves saw one of this kind which had thick hair on both sides of the neck.


Libet hic obiter explicare barbara draconum nomina, quae citantur ex sequentibus, quae ubique sunt corruptissima, sed in Latina versione longe magis, quam in fonte, id est, in textu Arabico. Primo se offert Albedisimon Persin. Ita Latini interpretes. Sed textus Arabicus habet اغاذنيمون والسير agadanimon et alsir, vel assir, qui ab Avicenna censentur in genere draconum. Fallor, aut prius nomen factum ex Graeco ἀγαθοδαίμων, quod draconis fuit cognomen. Philo Bybliensis apud Eusebium De praeparatione Evangelii lib. 1. cap. 7. postquam Phoenices et Aegyptios, auctore Taauto, docuit, draconum et serpentum naturae divini aliquid tribuisse: Φοίνικες δὲ, inquit, αὐτὸ (τὸ ζῶον) ἀγαθὸν δαίμονα καλοῦσιν· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ Αἰγύπτιοι Κνὴφ ἐπονομάζουσι· Hoc autem animal Phoenices agathodaemonem appellant, et Aegyptii similiter Kneph vocant. Lampridius de Heliogabalo, Aegyptios dracunculos Romae habuit, quos illi agathodaemonas vocant. Servius in haec Poetae de vipera,

It is worth explaining here in passing the barbarous names of dragons cited in what follows, which are everywhere very corrupt, but far more so in the Latin version than in the source, that is, in the Arabic text. First comes Albedisimon Persin. So the Latin translators. But the Arabic text has اغاذنيمون والسير [aghādhnīmūn wa-al-sīr] agadanimon and alsir, or assir, which Avicenna counts among the kinds of dragons. Unless I am mistaken, the first name is made from the Greek ἀγαθοδαίμων [agathodaimōn], which was a by-name of the dragon. Philo of Byblos in Eusebius, On the Preparation for the Gospel, book 1, ch. 7, after showing that the Phoenicians and Egyptians, on the authority of Taautus, attributed something divine to the nature of dragons and serpents, says: Φοίνικες δὲ αὐτὸ (τὸ ζῶον) ἀγαθὸν δαίμονα καλοῦσιν· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ Αἰγύπτιοι Κνὴφ ἐπονομάζουσι· [Phoinikes de auto (to zōon) agathon daimona kalousin; homoiōs de kai Aigyptioi Knēph eponomazousi;] This animal the Phoenicians call agathodaemon, and the Egyptians likewise call it Kneph. Lampridius on Heliogabalus: he had Egyptian little dragons at Rome, which they call agathodaemons. Servius on these words of the Poet about the viper,


— — — coelumque exterrita fugit,

— — — and terrified it shuns the sky,


lib. 3. Georgicorum: id est, tectis gaudet, ut sunt ἀγαθοὶ δαίμονες, quos latine Genios vocant. Quo Lucanus alludens de draconibus dixit lib. 9.

Georgics book 3: that is, it delights in houses, as do the ἀγαθοὶ δαίμονες [agathoi daimones], whom in Latin they call Genii. Alluding to this, Lucan said of dragons, book 9:


Vos quoque, qui cunctis innoxia numina terris.

You too, harmless deities to all lands.


Et Sir, et Isidori Sirena, (imo Siren) Sirenae, inquit, sunt in Arabia serpentes cum alis. Et Eucherius, Sirenae in Esaia daemones, aut dracones magni, cristati pariter et volantes. Et multo ante Hieronymus in Esa. XIII, 22. Sirenae autem תנין vocantur; quas nos aut daemones, aut monstra quaedam, vel certe dracones magnos interpretati sumus, qui cristati sunt, et volantes. Melius Sirenes dixissent, quas poetae multo aliter describunt. Sed Patribus Siren est draconis species; col. 430 quia in Graeca versione aliquoties occurrit pro תנין: ut Iob. XXX, 29. Esa. XXXIV, 13. et XLIII, 20. Inde igitur factum Arabicum سير sir pro dracone.

And there are the Sir and Isidore's Sirena (or rather Siren): Sirens, he says, are winged serpents in Arabia. And Eucherius: Sirens in Isaiah are demons, or great dragons, crested and also flying. And much earlier Jerome on Esa. XIII, 22.: But the Sirens are called תנין; these we have rendered either demons, or certain monsters, or at any rate great dragons, which are crested and flying. They would better have said Sirenes, whom the poets describe very differently. But for the Fathers the Siren is a species of dragon, col. 430 because in the Greek version it occurs several times for תנין: as in Iob. XXX, 29. Esa. XXXIV, 13. and XLIII, 20. From this, then, the Arabic سير [sīr] sir for dragon was formed.


Sequitur caput De morsu draconis marini, ubi araneum non intelligit, sed scorpionem marinum Aetii, ut conferenti patebit.

There follows the chapter On the bite of the sea dragon, where he means not the araneus but the sea scorpion of Aetius, as will be plain to anyone who compares them.


Excipit caput, cui Latine titulus est De haren carmen, sed Arabice في حيوانان بحريان De serpentibus marinis. Et intelliguntur σμύραινα, muraenae, quas idem vocat سوريا. Sed Latinus interpres hic habet semurion, et doctorem esse putat sic appellatum, cum sit σμύραινα piscis. Me vere conjectasse, planum erit Aëtium cum Avicenna conferentibus. Ibi enim ipsissima Aëtii verba de muraena pisce describit Avicenna.

There follows a chapter whose title in Latin is De haren carmen, but in Arabic في حيوانان بحريان [fī ḥayawānān baḥriyyān], On sea serpents. And what is meant is σμύραινα [smyraina], muraenae [morays], which the same author calls سوريا [sūriyā]. But the Latin translator here has semurion, and thinks that a doctor was so named, although σμύραινα [smyraina] is a fish. That my conjecture is correct will be plain to those who compare Aëtius with Avicenna. For there Avicenna reproduces the very words of Aëtius about the moray fish.


III, 225 Sequenti capite titulus est De Alhatraf et Hauden, quae rursus esse volunt inter genera draconum. Sed in Arabe est طروغورون truguron, pro quo طروغون τρύγων, id est, pastinaca marina, de qua agi, apparet ex ejusdem Aëtii collatione cum Avicenna. Haec in Phil-Arabum gratiam. Iam e diverticulo in viam.

III, 225 The title of the following chapter is De Alhatraf et Hauden, which again they hold to be among the kinds of dragons. But in the Arabic there is طروغورون [ṭrūghūrūn] truguron, for which read طروغون [ṭrūghūn], τρύγων [trygōn], that is, the sea stingray; that this is the subject is apparent from a comparison of the same Aëtius with Avicenna. So much for the benefit of the lovers of Arabic. Now from the digression back to the road.


Dracones a serpentibus mole praesertim differunt. Proinde draconem in Alcamus definiri diximus حية عظيمة, magnum serpentem. Et notum est Graecorum adagium, Ὄφις, εἰ μὴ φάγῃ ὄφιν, δράκων οὐ γενήσεται· Serpens, nisi serpentem comederit, draco non fiet. Nec immerito Augustinus in Psalm. CXLVIII. Magna quaedam sunt animantia dracones: majora non sunt super terram. Sed nemo facile dixerit, quousque crescant, cum hic veteres multa fabulentur, neque major sit uspiam mentiendi licentia, quod gradatim jam ostendemus. Plinius lib. 8. cap. 13. ex Iuba refert, apud Asachaeos Aethiopes cristatos generari dracones vicenum cubitorum. Aëtius et Avicenna a quinto cubito scribunt usque ad tricesimum augeri. Quod et aliunde confirmatur. Nam apud Aelianum Historiae lib. 2. capite 21. dracones in Phrygia crescunt ad decem orgyias; quarum singulas tricubitales esse, docent Hesychius et Eustathius. Et Pausanias in Corinthiacis, τοὺς ὄφεις τοὺς Μεγαλαύνας, serpentes Megalaunas circa Epidaurum supra triginta cubitorum magnitudinem excrescere tradit; quales in India, et in Africa feruntur progenerari. Sic Philostratus lib. 3. cap. 2. ubi de draconum speciebus in India; Οἱ μὲν δὴ ἕλειοι νωθροί τέ εἰσι, καὶ τρια-κοντάπηχυ μῆκος ἔχουσι· Palustres quidem tardi sunt, et triginta cubitos longi. Quae eadem mensura fuit draconis Aegyptii, qui vivus Alexandriam ad Ptolemaeum Philadelphum adductus est. Fallitur enim Tzetzes, qui illum facit τριακον-ταπεντάπηχυν, triginta quinque cubitorum, Chiliadis 3. Historia 113. cum is, quem sequitur, Diodorus lib. 3. hunc nonnisi τριάκοντα πηχῶν, triginta cubitorum fuisse disertis verbis asserat. Qualem unum se vidisse, testatur his verbis Agatharchides lib. 5. cap. 41. Τῶν μέν τοι ὑπὸ τὴν ἡμετέραν ὄψιν πεπτωκότων ὁ μέγιστος, πέφηνε πηχῶν τριάκοντα· Maximus illorum, qui in nostros obtutus incidit, videbatur cubitorum esse triginta. Et apud Strabonem libro decimo sexto, δρακόντων εἴρηκε μεγέθη τριάκοντα πηχῶν ὁ Ἀρτεμίδωρος, ἐλέφαντας καὶ ταύρους χειρουμένων, dracones triginta cubitorum describit Artemidorus, qui tauris et elephantis sunt superiores. Per me igitur licet, ut pro vero id habeatur, quod testantur tam multi veterum, dracones mole sui corporis triginta cubito- col. 431 rum, aut, quod idem est, quadraginta quinque pedum mensuram adimplere. Sed eorum, quae sequentur, pleraque fidem superant. In Periplo rubri maris apud Aelianum lib. 17. cap. 1. Alexander se vidisse refert serpentes quadraginta cubitorum longitudinis, ad quam latitudo et crassitudo proportione respondebat. III, 226 Philostorgius lib. 3. cap. 11. in Oriente et Meridie dracones memorat, πά-χος μὲν δοκῶν οὐκ ἐλάττους, τὸ δὲ μῆκος εἰς δέκα πέντε παρατεινόμενον ὀργυί-ας, crassitudine tignis non minores, longitudine vero ad quindecim orgyias (id est, cubitos XLV.) extensa, quorum pelles, Romam allatas, ipse viderit. Augustum narrat Suetonius cap. 43. anguem quinquaginta cubitorum pro comitio publicasse. Et sub eodem meminit Dio lib. 50. Τοῦ δικεφάλου δράκοντος τοῦ ἐν τῇ Τυρσηνίδι φανέντος, καὶ ἐς πέντε καὶ ὀγδοήκοντα πόδας ἐξικνουμένου, πολλά τε κακώ-σαντος, εἶτα κεραυνωθέντος, bicipitis draconis, in Hetruria visi, longi pedes octoginta quinque, qui, cum multa devastasset, fulmine percussus est. Tale est, quod Strabonis lib. 16. in Coele-Syriae campo, Macra, narrat Posidonius τὸν δρά-κοντα πεπτωκότα ὁραθῆναι νεκρὸν, μῆκος σχεδόν τι καὶ πλεθριαῖον, πάχος δ᾽, ὥς θ᾽ ἱππέας ἑκατέρωθεν παραστάντας ἀλλήλους μὴ καθορᾷν, χάσμα δὲ ὥς τ᾽ ἔφιππον δέξασθαι, τῆς δὲ φολίδος λεπίδα ἑκάστην ὑπεραίρουσαν θυρεοῦ, visum fuisse draconem mortuum plethri (seu centum pedum) longitudine, et tanta crassitudine, ut equites, utrinque assistentes, se non viderint invicem: et oris hiatu tanto, ut hominem, equo insidentem, reciperet, qui denique exuvii squamas singulas habuerit scuto majores. Iam quid notius dracone centum viginti pedum, quem non procul ab Utica ad Bagradam flumen stabulantem reperisse fertur Regulus. Qui, cum telis et jaculis a toto exercitu frustra impeteretur, tandem ballistis tormentisque, ut oppidum aliquod, est expugnatus. Et pellis maxillaeque usque ad bellum Numantinum Romae in templo duravere. Haec testantur multi scriptores. Sed videndi inprimis Tubero apud Gellium lib. 6. cap. 3. Livius apud Valerium lib. 1. in fine, Plinius lib. 8. cap. 14. et Orosius libri 4. cap. 8. Quid, quod molem tam portentosam non exaequare modo, sed et superare leguntur Aethiopici atque Indici dracones. Aethiopicis enim triginta orgyiarum, id est, cubitorum nonaginta, seu pedum CXXXV. longitudinem tribuit Aelianus Hist. lib. 2. cap. 21. (2). Et in eadem fuere, qui dracones centum cubitorum, id est, centum quinquaginta pedum, longos se vidisse palam assererent: sed illorum fidem esse suspectam, his verbis testatur Diodorus lib. 3. Serpentum multa genera, et magnitudine incredibilia, videri ajunt, qui prope desertam et feris frequentem (Aethiopiae) regionem incolunt. Ἑκατὸν γὰρ πηχῶν τὸ μῆκος ἑωρακέναι τινὲς ἀποφαινόμενοι, δικαίως ἂν οὐχ᾽ ὑφ᾽ ἡμῶν μόνον, ἀλ-λὰ καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων ψευδολογεῖν ὑπολεφθείησαν, centum enim cubitorum longos videri quidam pronunciantes, jure merito non nobis solum, sed et aliis omnibus mendacii suspecti sunt. Indicos quod attinet, unum memorat Aelianus, III, 227 lib. 15. cap. 21. longum cubitos septuaginta, seu pedes centum et quinque, oculis ad instar clypei Macedonici, ab Indis in antro quodam summa religione cultum, quique solo flatu et sibilo totum Alexandri exercitum terruerit ac turbaverit. Sed, quasi hoc parum esset, apud eundem lib. 16. cap. 39. refert Onesicritus, Aposisarem Indum duos nutrivisse dracones, quorum minor fuerit cubitorum octoginta, id est, pedum centum et viginti; major cubitorum centum et quadraginta, id est, pedum ducentorum et decem, quos videre Alexander maxime appetiverit. Quod ipsum in Tzetze legas Chiliadis tertiae Historia 113. Sed Strabo, qui, pro Aposisare, Biasarum vel Abiosarum scribit, hujus commenti fidem ita elevat. Ἐν τοῖς ὄρεσιν ἡ τοῦ Βιασάρου (MSS. Ἀβιοσάρου) χώρα, παρ᾽ ᾧ δύο δράκοντας ἀπήγγελον οἱ παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ πρέσβεις τρέφεσθαι, col. 432 τὸν μὲν ὀγδοήκοντα πηχῶν, τὸν δὲ τετταράκοντα πρὸς τοῖς ἑκατὸν, ὡς εἴρη-κεν Ὀνησίκριτος, ὃν ἐκ Ἀλεξάνδρου μᾶλλον ἢ τῶν παραδόξων Ἀλεξάνδρου ἀρ-χικυβερνήτην προσείποι τις ἄν· In montibus est Biasari (vel Abiosari) regio, apud quem legati, ab eo missi, duos nutriri dracones nuntiaverunt; quorum alter octoginta, alter centum et quadraginta fuerit cubitorum, auctore Onesicrito: quem non tam Alexandri navis, quam incredibilium gubernatorem merito quis appellaverit. Nondum tamen hic mendaciorum finis. Levicula enim haec videri possunt, prae eo, quod Abiosaro rex vicinus, Taxiles, Alexandro ostendisse traditur draconem quinque plethrorum, id est, quingentorum pedum. Ita habet Maximus Tyrius Serm. 38. Ἔδειξε καὶ ζῶον ὑπερφυὲς, Διονύσου ἄγαλμα, ᾧ Ἰνδοὶ ἔθυον, δράκων ἦν μῆκος πεντάπλεθρον, Ostendit immensum quoddam animal, Bacchi simulacrum, cui Indi sacrificabant, draconem scilicet quinque plethrorum longitudinis. Interim Graeci Arabibus sunt longe modestiores, quorum unus apud Damirem asserit, se vidisse تنينا طوله نحو فرسخين ولونه مثل لون النمر مفلسا مثل فلوس السمك بجناحين عظيمين علي هية جناح السمك وراسها كراس الانسان لكنها كالتل العظيم draconem longum fere duabus parasangis (id est, passuum octo millibus) coloris pardi, piscis squamis squamatum, pinnis quoque magnis instructum, quomodo pisces, et humanum caput habentem ad instar excelsi collis.

Dragons differ from serpents chiefly in bulk. Accordingly, as we said, the dragon is defined in Alcamus as حية عظيمة [ḥayya ʿaẓīma], a great serpent. And well known is the proverb of the Greeks, Ὄφις, εἰ μὴ φάγῃ ὄφιν, δράκων οὐ γενήσεται [Ophis, ei mē phagē ophin, drakōn ou genēsetai]· A serpent, unless it has eaten a serpent, will not become a dragon. Nor without reason does Augustine say on Psalm. CXLVIII.: Dragons are certain great animals; there are none greater upon the earth. But no one could easily say how large they grow, since here the ancients tell many fables, and nowhere is there greater licence for lying, as we shall now show step by step. Pliny, book 8, ch. 13, reports from Juba that among the Asachaean Ethiopians crested dragons of twenty cubits are bred. Aëtius and Avicenna write that they grow from five cubits up to thirty. This is confirmed from elsewhere too. For in Aelian, History book 2, chapter 21, dragons in Phrygia grow to ten orgyiae; and that each of these is three cubits, Hesychius and Eustathius teach. And Pausanias in the Corinthiaca relates that τοὺς ὄφεις τοὺς Μεγαλαύνας [tous opheis tous Megalaunas], the Megalaunian serpents around Epidaurus grow beyond a size of thirty cubits; such as are said to be bred in India and in Africa. So Philostratus, book 3, ch. 2, where he treats of the species of dragons in India: Οἱ μὲν δὴ ἕλειοι νωθροί τέ εἰσι, καὶ τριακοντάπηχυ μῆκος ἔχουσι [Hoi men dē heleioi nōthroi te eisi, kai triakontapēchy mēkos echousi]· The marsh ones are sluggish, and thirty cubits long. The same was the measure of the Egyptian dragon that was brought alive to Alexandria to Ptolemy Philadelphus. For Tzetzes is mistaken, who makes it τριακονταπεντάπηχυν [triakontapentapēchyn], of thirty-five cubits, Chiliad 3, History 113, since the author he follows, Diodorus, book 3, asserts in express words that it was only τριάκοντα πηχῶν [triakonta pēchōn], of thirty cubits. That he saw one such, Agatharchides, book 5, ch. 41, testifies in these words: Τῶν μέν τοι ὑπὸ τὴν ἡμετέραν ὄψιν πεπτωκότων ὁ μέγιστος, πέφηνε πηχῶν τριάκοντα [Tōn men toi hypo tēn hēmeteran opsin peptōkotōn ho megistos, pephēne pēchōn triakonta]· The largest of those that came under our eyes appeared to be thirty cubits. And in Strabo, book 16: δρακόντων εἴρηκε μεγέθη τριάκοντα πηχῶν ὁ Ἀρτεμίδωρος, ἐλέφαντας καὶ ταύρους χειρουμένων [drakontōn eirēke megethē triakonta pēchōn ho Artemidōros, elephantas kai taurous cheiroumenōn], Artemidorus describes dragons of thirty cubits, which overpower bulls and elephants. I am willing, therefore, that what so many of the ancients attest be held true: that dragons in the bulk of their body reach a measure of thirty cubits col. 431 or, what is the same, forty-five feet. But most of what follows surpasses belief. In the Periplus of the Red Sea, in Aelian, book 17, ch. 1, Alexander reports that he saw serpents forty cubits in length, to which their breadth and thickness corresponded in proportion. III, 226 Philostorgius, book 3, ch. 11, mentions dragons in the East and the South, πάχος μὲν δοκῶν οὐκ ἐλάττους, τὸ δὲ μῆκος εἰς δέκα πέντε παρατεινόμενον ὀργυίας [pachos men dokōn ouk elattous, to de mēkos eis deka pente parateinomenon orgyias], not smaller than beams in thickness, and extending in length to fifteen orgyiae (that is, 45 cubits), whose skins, brought to Rome, he himself saw. Suetonius, ch. 43, relates that Augustus exhibited a snake of fifty cubits before the comitium. And under the same emperor Dio, book 50, mentions Τοῦ δικεφάλου δράκοντος τοῦ ἐν τῇ Τυρσηνίδι φανέντος, καὶ ἐς πέντε καὶ ὀγδοήκοντα πόδας ἐξικνουμένου, πολλά τε κακώσαντος, εἶτα κεραυνωθέντος [Tou dikephalou drakontos tou en tē Tyrsēnidi phanentos, kai es pente kai ogdoēkonta podas exikneoumenou, polla te kakōsantos, eita keraunōthentos], a two-headed dragon seen in Etruria, eighty-five feet long, which, after it had laid waste much, was struck by lightning. Of the same kind is what Posidonius in Strabo, book 16, relates of the plain of Coele-Syria, Macra: τὸν δράκοντα πεπτωκότα ὁραθῆναι νεκρὸν, μῆκος σχεδόν τι καὶ πλεθριαῖον, πάχος δ᾽, ὥς θ᾽ ἱππέας ἑκατέρωθεν παραστάντας ἀλλήλους μὴ καθορᾷν, χάσμα δὲ ὥς τ᾽ ἔφιππον δέξασθαι, τῆς δὲ φολίδος λεπίδα ἑκάστην ὑπεραίρουσαν θυρεοῦ [ton drakonta peptōkota horathēnai nekron, mēkos schedon ti kai plethriaion, pachos d᾽, hōs th᾽ hippeas hekaterōthen parastantas allēlous mē kathoran, chasma de hōs t᾽ ephippon dexasthai, tēs de pholidos lepida hekastēn hyperairousan thyreou], that a dead dragon was seen, a plethrum (or a hundred feet) in length, and of such thickness that horsemen standing on either side could not see one another; and with a gaping mouth so wide that it could take in a man sitting on a horse; and finally, each scale of whose skin was larger than a shield. Now what is better known than the dragon of one hundred and twenty feet which Regulus is said to have found lurking by the river Bagradas, not far from Utica? When it was attacked in vain with missiles and javelins by the whole army, it was at last overcome with ballistae and siege engines, like some town. And its skin and jaws lasted in a temple at Rome until the Numantine war. Many writers attest this. But see especially Tubero in Gellius, book 6, ch. 3, Livy in Valerius, book 1, at the end, Pliny, book 8, ch. 14, and Orosius, book 4, ch. 8. What of the fact that Ethiopian and Indian dragons are read not only to equal so portentous a bulk but even to surpass it? For to the Ethiopian ones Aelian, Hist. book 2, ch. 21, R2, assigns a length of thirty orgyiae, that is, ninety cubits, or 135 feet. And in the same country there were those who openly asserted that they had seen dragons a hundred cubits long, that is, a hundred and fifty feet; but that their credit is suspect, Diodorus, book 3, testifies in these words: Those who inhabit the region (of Ethiopia) near the desert and full of wild beasts say that many kinds of serpents, incredible in size, are seen. Ἑκατὸν γὰρ πηχῶν τὸ μῆκος ἑωρακέναι τινὲς ἀποφαινόμενοι, δικαίως ἂν οὐχ᾽ ὑφ᾽ ἡμῶν μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων ψευδολογεῖν ὑπολεφθείησαν [Hekaton gar pēchōn to mēkos heōrakenai tines apophainomenoi, dikaiōs an ouch᾽ hyph᾽ hēmōn monon, alla kai hypo tōn allōn hapantōn pseudologein hypolephtheiēsan], for some, declaring that they have seen them a hundred cubits long, are justly suspected of lying, not only by us but by all others too. As for the Indian ones, Aelian, III, 227 book 15, ch. 21, mentions one seventy cubits long, or a hundred and five feet, with eyes like a Macedonian shield, worshipped by the Indians with the greatest reverence in a certain cave, which by its breath and hissing alone terrified and threw into confusion the whole army of Alexander. But, as if this were too little, in the same author, book 16, ch. 39, Onesicritus relates that Aposisares the Indian kept two dragons, of which the smaller was eighty cubits, that is, a hundred and twenty feet, the larger a hundred and forty cubits, that is, two hundred and ten feet, which Alexander greatly desired to see. The same you may read in Tzetzes, Chiliad 3, History 113. But Strabo, who writes Biasarus or Abiosarus instead of Aposisares, thus undermines the credit of this fiction: Ἐν τοῖς ὄρεσιν ἡ τοῦ Βιασάρου (MSS. Ἀβιοσάρου) χώρα, παρ᾽ ᾧ δύο δράκοντας ἀπήγγελον οἱ παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ πρέσβεις τρέφεσθαι, col. 432 τὸν μὲν ὀγδοήκοντα πηχῶν, τὸν δὲ τετταράκοντα πρὸς τοῖς ἑκατὸν, ὡς εἴρηκεν Ὀνησίκριτος, ὃν ἐκ Ἀλεξάνδρου μᾶλλον ἢ τῶν παραδόξων Ἀλεξάνδρου ἀρχικυβερνήτην προσείποι τις ἄν [En tois oresin hē tou Biasarou (MSS. Abiosarou) chōra, par᾽ hō dyo drakontas apēngelon hoi par᾽ autou presbeis trephesthai, ton men ogdoēkonta pēchōn, ton de tettarakonta pros tois hekaton, hōs eirēken Onēsikritos, hon ek Alexandrou mallon ē tōn paradoxōn Alexandrou archikybernētēn prosei pois an]· In the mountains is the country of Biasarus (or Abiosarus), with whom, as the envoys sent by him reported, two dragons were kept, one of eighty, the other of a hundred and forty cubits, on the authority of Onesicritus, whom one might justly call the chief pilot not so much of Alexander's ship as of incredible tales. Yet this is not yet the end of the lies. For these may seem trifles compared with the report that Taxiles, a king neighbouring Abiosarus, showed Alexander a dragon of five plethra, that is, five hundred feet. So Maximus of Tyre, Oration 38: Ἔδειξε καὶ ζῶον ὑπερφυὲς, Διονύσου ἄγαλμα, ᾧ Ἰνδοὶ ἔθυον, δράκων ἦν μῆκος πεντάπλεθρον [Edeixe kai zōon hyperphyes, Dionysou agalma, hō Indoi ethyon, drakōn ēn mēkos pentaplethron], He showed a certain immense animal, an image of Bacchus, to which the Indians sacrificed, namely a dragon five plethra in length. Meanwhile the Greeks are far more modest than the Arabs, one of whom, in Damiri, asserts that he saw تنينا طوله نحو فرسخين ولونه مثل لون النمر مفلسا مثل فلوس السمك بجناحين عظيمين علي هية جناح السمك وراسها كراس الانسان لكنها كالتل العظيم [tinnīnan ṭūluhu naḥwa farsakhayn wa-lawnuhu mithl lawn al-namir mufallasan mithl fulūs al-samak bi-janāḥayn ʿaẓīmayn ʿalī hya janāḥ al-samak wa-rāsuhā ka-rās al-insān lākinnahā kal-tall al-ʿaẓīm] a dragon nearly two parasangs long (that is, eight thousand paces), of the colour of a leopard, scaled with the scales of a fish, furnished also with great fins, like fishes, and having a human head the size of a lofty hill.


De forma quoque draconum valde ambigitur. His enim pedes, cristas et alas multi tribuunt. Et de pedibus quidem ita Paulus Iovius lib. 18. Asserunt Georgiani regni incolae, in his vallibus dracones esse alatos, qui anserinis pedibus gradatim humi serpant. Et Scaliger apud Gesnerum, Genera omnia draconum pedes habent. Et rursus, Draconibus crura esse, notum est. Cristatos quoque apud Plinium describit Iuba. Et Ovidius lib. 4. Metamorphoseωs Fabula 15.

There is also much doubt about the form of dragons. For many attribute feet, crests and wings to them. About feet, Paulus Iovius says in book 18: The inhabitants of the Georgian kingdom assert that in these valleys there are winged dragons which creep step by step along the ground on goose-like feet. And Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)] in Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium]: All kinds of dragons have feet. And again: That dragons have legs is well known. In Pliny, Juba also describes crested ones. And Ovid, Metamorphoses book 4, Fable 15:


III, 228 Lubrica permulcent cristati colla draconis.

III, 228 They stroke the slippery neck of the crested dragon.


Et lib. 7. de dracone, velleris aurei custode.

And in book 7, of the dragon that guarded the golden fleece:


Qui crista linguisque tribus praesignis. — —

Conspicuous for its crest and three tongues. — —


Et Philostratus lib. 3. cap. 2. Τὸν ἐν τῷ τῆς Νεμέας ἄλσει (δράκοντα) φασὶ καὶ λοφιὰν ἔχειν. Ὅπερ οὐκ ἂν περὶ τοὺς ἑλείους εὕροιμεν· Draconem in Nemeae luco cristatum esse, dicunt, quod nos in palustribus non invenimus. Et de montanis draconibus idem, Τούτοις καὶ λοφιὰ φύεται· νέοις μὲν ὑπανίσχουσα τὸ μέτριον, τελειουμένοις δὲ συναυξανομένη τε, καὶ συνανιοῦσα εἰς πολύ. His etiam crista nascitur; juvenibus quidem mediocriter erecta, sed aetate provectis grandior et valde remissa. Et infra, Ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν λόφων, πυρσῶν ὄντων, πῦρ αὐ-τοῖς ἄττει λαμπάδος πλέον· Ex cristis autem, quae rubrae sunt, ignis plus quam ex face scintillat. Et Aelianus lib. 11. cap. 26. Ὁ μὲν δράκων ὁ ἄῤῥην τὸν λόφον (ἔχει) καὶ τὴν ὑπήνην δασεῖαν· Draco mas cristam habet et barbam densam. Et Hieronymus in Es. XIII. תנין dracones magnos interpretati sumus, qui cristati sunt, et volantes. Et Isidorus lib. 12. Originum cap. 4. Est autem (draco) cristatus ore parvo, etc. Volucres denique esse dracones, plerique putant. Lucanus lib. 9. versu 732.

And Philostratus, book 3, ch. 2: Τὸν ἐν τῷ τῆς Νεμέας ἄλσει (δράκοντα) φασὶ καὶ λοφιὰν ἔχειν. Ὅπερ οὐκ ἂν περὶ τοὺς ἑλείους εὕροιμεν· [Ton en tō tēs Nemeas alsei (drakonta) phasi kai lophian echein. Hoper ouk an peri tous heleious heuroimen] They say that the dragon in the grove of Nemea is crested, which we do not find in the marsh dragons. And the same of the mountain dragons: Τούτοις καὶ λοφιὰ φύεται· νέοις μὲν ὑπανίσχουσα τὸ μέτριον, τελειουμένοις δὲ συναυξανομένη τε, καὶ συνανιοῦσα εἰς πολύ. [Toutois kai lophia phyetai; neois men hypanischousa to metrion, teleioumenois de synauxanomenē te, kai synaniousa eis poly.] These too grow a crest; in the young it is moderately raised, but in those advanced in age it is larger and much relaxed. And below: Ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν λόφων, πυρσῶν ὄντων, πῦρ αὐτοῖς ἄττει λαμπάδος πλέον· [Apo de tōn lophōn, pyrsōn ontōn, pyr autois attei lampados pleon] And from their crests, which are red, fire sparkles more than from a torch. And Aelian, book 11, ch. 26: Ὁ μὲν δράκων ὁ ἄῤῥην τὸν λόφον (ἔχει) καὶ τὴν ὑπήνην δασεῖαν· [Ho men drakōn ho arrhēn ton lophon (echei) kai tēn hypēnēn daseian] The male dragon has a crest and a thick beard. And Jerome on Es. XIII.: תנין we have rendered as great dragons, which are crested and flying. And Isidore, Etymologies book 12, ch. 4: And (the dragon) is crested, with a small mouth, etc. Finally, most people think dragons are winged. Lucan, book 9, line 732:


— — — ducitis altum
Aëra cum pennis. — —

— — — you draw the high air with your wings. — —


Hieronymus jam modo, Cristati sunt et volantes. Augustinus libri tertii De Ge- col. 433 nesi ad literam capite nono: Dracones autem, etc. in aërem sustolli perhibentur. Et in Psalmum CXLVIII. De speluncis procedunt, feruntur in aëra. Iovius ubi supra, Asserunt Georgiani regni incolae, his in vallibus dracones gigni alatos. Scaliger quoque, Quaedam genera draconum alas habent. Cui sententiae id favere videri possit, quod Apoc. XII, 7. draco mysticus in coelo, id est, in summo aëre, cum Michaele pugnat, tanquam alis eo subvectus.

Jerome, just cited: They are crested and flying. Augustine, On Genesis Literally, book 3, chapter 9: Dragons, however, etc. are said to be lifted up into the air. col. 433 And on Psalm CXLVIII: They come forth from caves and are borne into the air. Iovius, as above: The inhabitants of the Georgian kingdom assert that winged dragons are born in these valleys. Scaliger too: Some kinds of dragons have wings. This opinion might seem to be supported by the fact that in Apoc. XII, 7 the mystical dragon fights with Michael in heaven, that is, in the highest air, as though carried up there by wings.


Tamen in hac draconum descriptione non puto quidquam esse veri. Nam, ut a pedibus ordiamur, veterum scriptorum nullus est, qui draconi pedes tribuat. Et Augustinus in loco, quem nuper citavimus, eum esse ἄποδα, diserte docet. Dracones, ait, sine pedibus et in speluncis requiescere, et in aërem sustolli perhibentur. Neque gradi, sed serpere dicuntur in his Lucani,

Yet I do not think there is any truth in this description of dragons. For, to begin with the feet, there is no ancient writer who attributes feet to the dragon. And Augustine, in the passage we just cited, expressly teaches that it is ἄπους [apous, footless]. Dragons, he says, without feet, are said both to rest in caves and to be lifted up into the air. Nor are they said to walk, but to creep, in these lines of Lucan:


Vos quoque, qui, cunctis innoxia numina terris,
Serpitis aurato nitidi fulgore dracones.

You too, dragons, divinities harmless to all lands, who creep along shining with golden gleam.


Nempe draco est serpentis genus, quem in ventrem serpere jussit Deus Gen. III, 14. Iam de cristis ita Plinius libri undecimi capite trigesimo septimo, Draconum III, 229 cristas qui viderit, non reperitur. Et libri octavi capite decimo tertio, Id modo mirum, unde cristatos dracones Iuba crediderit. Alis denique, iisque cartilagineis tam vastam molem attolli, nemo facile in animum sibi induxerit. Maxime, cum nihil tale philosophi tradant, nec fideles historici. Nam, quod ajunt, Strabonis libro decimo sexto Indicis ac Libycis draconibus alas tribui, habetur quidem in Xylandri versione, at in Graeco textu longe aliud est. Neque iis πτερὰ alae, sed πόα ἐπιφυκέναι λέγεται, herba innasci dicitur. Quod ex Iphicrate videtur sumptum, qui ejusdem Strabonis libro decimo septimo in occidua Aethiopia δράκοντας λέγει μεγάλους, ὥστε καὶ πόαν ἐπιφυκέναι, dracones describit tam vastos, ut iis herba innascatur. Nec a mystico dracone ad naturalem valet argumentatio. Quamvis ille ipse draco mysticus alas habere nusquam legatur. Quin ἄπτερον esse, colligas ex eo, quod mulierem illam, quae aquilinis alis avolat, non insequitur: sed, quod unum potest, aquarum vim in eam evomit, Apoc. XII, 14. 15. Ut in aquilae cum dracone pugna apud Nicandrum in Theriacis, cum aquila volatu ex periculo se eripit,

For the dragon is a kind of serpent, which God commanded to creep upon its belly, Gen 3:14. Now about the crests, Pliny, book 11, chapter 37: No one is found who has seen III, 229 the crests of dragons. And book 8, chapter 13: This alone is strange: whence Juba came to believe in crested dragons. Finally, no one will easily persuade himself that so vast a mass is raised aloft by wings, and cartilaginous ones at that. Especially since neither the philosophers nor trustworthy historians report anything of the kind. For as to what they say, that in book 16 of Strabo wings are attributed to Indian and Libyan dragons, that is indeed found in Xylander's version, but in the Greek text it is something quite different. It is said not that πτερὰ [ptera], wings, but that πόα ἐπιφυκέναι [poa epiphykenai], grass grows upon them. This seems taken from Iphicrates, who, in book 17 of the same Strabo, speaks of δράκοντας μεγάλους, ὥστε καὶ πόαν ἐπιφυκέναι [drakontas megalous, hōste kai poan epiphykenai] in western Ethiopia, describing dragons so vast that grass grows on them. Nor is an argument from the mystical dragon to the natural one valid. And in fact that mystical dragon itself is nowhere read to have wings. Indeed, you may infer that it is ἄπτερος [apteros, wingless] from the fact that it does not pursue the woman who flies away on eagle's wings, but, doing the one thing it can, spews a flood of water after her, Rev 12:14–15. So too in the fight of the eagle with the dragon in Nicander's Theriaca, when the eagle escapes the danger by flight,


— — ἱπτάμενον δὲ πέριξ ἀτέλεστα διώκει
Σπειρηθεὶς, καὶ λοξὸν ὑποδρὰξ ὄμμασι λεύσσων,

— — ἱπτάμενον δὲ πέριξ ἀτέλεστα διώκει Σπειρηθεὶς, καὶ λοξὸν ὑποδρὰξ ὄμμασι λεύσσων, [— — hiptamenon de perix atelesta diōkei Speirētheis, kai loxon hypodrax ommasi leussōn,]


Volantem circumcirca frustra insequitur (draco) in spiras convolutus, obliquis et torvis oculis illam intuens. Elatam enim in sublime non potest attingere.

it (the dragon) pursues it in vain as it flies round about, coiled in spirals, glaring at it with sidelong and grim eyes. For it cannot reach the eagle once it has risen on high.


Itaque nullus video, unde apud vulgus invaluerit haec opinio, dracones esse alatos, nisi ad mythologos et poetas eam referamus, quibus, cum pictoribus,

Therefore I do not see where this popular opinion that dragons are winged came from, unless we trace it to the mythographers and poets, who, together with painters,


Quidlibet audendi semper fuit aequa potestas.

have always had an equal licence to dare anything.

Driving the chariot through the air, he lashed the spotted backs of the ear-bearing dragons. So Nonnus, book 13 of the Dionysiaca. Sed draconum nomine naves significari, docent illi ipsi veteres: ut in Eusebii Chronico celeberrimus scriptor Philochorus, cum, sub Eleusinis rege Celeo, Tri- ptolemum tradit μακρῷ πλοίῳ προβαλόντα ταῖς πόλεσι τὸν σῖτον διαδοῦναι· ὑπονοεῖσθαι δὲ πτερωτὸν ὄφιν εἶναι τὴν ναῦν, ἔχειν δέ τι καὶ τοῦ σχήματος, longa navi delatum urbibus frumentum distribuisse; et per alatum serpentem navem significari, cum figura sit aliqua ex parte similis. Adde, si lubet, Draconis nomine potuisse insigniri navem, quae pro insigni draconem habuit: ut, apud Plutarchum libro De virtutibus mulierum, pirata, Chimarrus, a Bellerophonte occisus, ἔπλει πλοίῳ λέοντα μὲν ἔχοντι πρώραθεν ἐπίσημον, ἐκ δὲ πρύμνης δρά-κοντα, vehebatur navi, quae in prora leonem, et in puppe draconem habuit pro insigni. Et, apud Euripidem in Iphigenia in Aulide, Boeoticis navibus pro signo fuit Cadmus

But that ships are signified by the name of dragons is taught by those very ancients: as in Eusebius' Chronicle the most celebrated writer Philochorus, when he reports that under Celeus, king of Eleusis, Triptolemus μακρῷ πλοίῳ προβαλόντα ταῖς πόλεσι τὸν σῖτον διαδοῦναι· ὑπονοεῖσθαι δὲ πτερωτὸν ὄφιν εἶναι τὴν ναῦν, ἔχειν δέ τι καὶ τοῦ σχήματος [makrō ploiō probalonta tais polesi ton siton diadounai; hyponoeisthai de pterōton ophin einai tēn naun, echein de ti kai tou schēmatos], having been carried in a long ship, distributed grain to the cities; and that the ship is signified by the winged serpent, since its shape is in some respect similar. Add, if you like, that a ship could be marked with the name Dragon which had a dragon as its ensign: as in Plutarch, in the book On the Virtues of Women, the pirate Chimarrus, slain by Bellerophon, ἔπλει πλοίῳ λέοντα μὲν ἔχοντι πρώραθεν ἐπίσημον, ἐκ δὲ πρύμνης δράκοντα [eplei ploiō leonta men echonti prōrathen episēmon, ek de prymnēs drakonta], sailed in a ship that had a lion on the prow and a dragon on the stern as its ensign. And in Euripides, Iphigenia in Aulis, the Boeotian ships had as their sign Cadmus


Χρύσεον δράκοντ᾽ ἔχων
Ἀμφὶ ναῶν κόρυμβα·

Χρύσεον δράκοντ᾽ ἔχων Ἀμφὶ ναῶν κόρυμβα· [Chryseon drakont᾽ echōn Amphi naōn korymba;]


aureum draconem habens in navium rostris. Eodem pertinet, quod in Fabulis, col. 435 qui draconibus vehuntur, non nisi e maritimis, nec nisi ad maritima loca proficiscuntur. Sic Ceres, Proserpinam quaerens, cum totam Siciliam absque draconibus peragrasset, etiam insulae littora tandem adiit:

holding a golden dragon on the beaks of the ships. To the same point belongs the fact that in the Fables col. 435 those who are borne by dragons set out only from coastal places and only to coastal places. Thus Ceres, seeking Proserpina, after she had travelled over all Sicily without dragons, at last came also to the shores of the island:


Quo simulac venit, fraenatos curribus angues Iunxit, et aequoreas sicca pererrat aquas. III, 232 Ita Ovidius libro quarto Fastorum. Et Circe ex Colchide draconum curru vehitur in Italiae promontorium Circeium: Medea, liberis caesis, Corintho Athenas: Triptolemus Athenis Patras, Achaïae maritimam urbem, ubi Eumeli filius, An-theas, exemplo Triptolemi, dracones jungere ausus, de curru excussus periit, id est, naufragium fecit, cum navigandi imperitus mare attentasset. Historia habetur in Pausaniae Achaicis. Sed frustra disputamus, cum Coroebi, aut Margitae (id est, fatuorum,) sit, credere, Τριπτόλεμον ἐλάσαι διὰ τοῦ ἀέρος ἐπὶ δρακόντων ὑποπτέρων, Triptolemum alatis draconibus per aërem vectum fuisse: ut in Philopseude vere asserit Lucianus, haec poetarum commenta ridens. Qua mente etiam Augustinus, aut quisquis libri auctor est, Soliloquiorum libri secundi capite decimo quinto: Non enim, cum dicitur junctis alitibus anguibus Medeam volasse, ulla ex parte res ista verum imitatur: quippe quae nulla sit, nec imitari aliquid possit ea res, quae omnino non sit. Alae tamen draconibus non aliunde natae sunt, quam ex hujusmodi commentis.

As soon as she arrived there, she yoked bridled snakes to her chariot, and roams dry over the waters of the sea. III, 232 So Ovid in book 4 of the Fasti. And Circe is carried from Colchis in a chariot of dragons to the promontory Circeium in Italy; Medea, after slaying her children, from Corinth to Athens; Triptolemus from Athens to Patrae, a coastal city of Achaea, where the son of Eumelus, Antheas, who dared to yoke dragons after the example of Triptolemus, was thrown from the chariot and perished; that is, he suffered shipwreck, having attempted the sea without skill in navigation. The story is found in the Achaica of Pausanias. But we argue in vain, since it is the part of a Coroebus or a Margites (that is, of fools) to believe Τριπτόλεμον ἐλάσαι διὰ τοῦ ἀέρος ἐπὶ δρακόντων ὑποπτέρων [Triptolemon elasai dia tou aeros epi drakontōn hypopterōn], that Triptolemus was carried through the air by winged dragons, as Lucian rightly asserts in the Philopseudes, mocking these fictions of the poets. In the same spirit Augustine, or whoever is the author of the book, in the Soliloquies, book 2, chapter 15: For when it is said that Medea flew with winged snakes yoked together, that thing in no respect imitates the truth; for it is nothing, and a thing that does not exist at all cannot imitate anything. Yet wings grew on dragons from no other source than fictions of this kind.


Sed aliae notae non desunt, quibus a vulgo serpentum dracones dignoscantur. In his prima sit vasta moles, in draconibus tam frequens, quam in reliquis serpentibus rara et insolita. Secunda, sub mento barba et palearia. Nicander,

But other marks are not lacking by which dragons are distinguished from the common run of serpents. Among these let the first be vast bulk, as frequent in dragons as it is rare and unusual in other serpents. The second, a beard and dewlaps under the chin. Nicander,


— — — νέρθε δὲ πώγων
Ἔπλεθ' ὑπ' ἀνθερεῶνα χολοίβαφος,

— — — νέρθε δὲ πώγων Ἔπλεθ' ὑπ' ἀνθερεῶνα χολοίβαφος, [— — — nerthe de pōgōn Epleth' hyp' anthereōna choloibaphos,]


Infra autem sub mento flava est barba. Aelianus libri undecimi capite vigesimo sexto, Ἔχει γοῦν ὁ μὲν δράκων ὁ ἄῤῥην τὸν λόφον, καὶ τὴν ὑπήνην δασεῖαν· Cristam quidem habet draco mas, et barbam hirsutam. Avicenna, وتحت الفك الاسفل نتو كالذقن Et sub inferiore maxilla eminentiam (habent) tanquam barbam. Philostratus non omnibus barbam tribuit, sed draconum certo generi: Οἵδε δὴ πυρσῖται, inquit, καὶ περιόνωτοι γίνονται, οὗτοι καὶ γενει-άσκουσι· Qui colorem igneum et dorsum serratum habent, iis etiam barba adnascitur. Tertia, dentium ordo triplex: siquidem vere Nicander,

But below, under the chin, is a yellow beard. Aelian, book 11, chapter 26: Ἔχει γοῦν ὁ μὲν δράκων ὁ ἄῤῥην τὸν λόφον, καὶ τὴν ὑπήνην δασεῖαν· [Echei goun ho men drakōn ho arrhēn ton lophon, kai tēn hypēnēn daseian;] The male dragon indeed has a crest and a shaggy beard. Avicenna: وتحت الفك الاسفل نتو كالذقن [wa-taḥt al-fakk al-asfal nutūʾ ka-l-dhaqan] And under the lower jaw (they have) a protuberance like a beard. Philostratus does not attribute a beard to all, but to a certain kind of dragons: Οἵδε δὴ πυρσῖται, he says, καὶ περιόνωτοι γίνονται, οὗτοι καὶ γενειάσκουσι· [Hoide dē pyrsitai … kai perionōtoi ginontai, houtoi kai geneiaskousi;] Those that have a fiery colour and a serrated back also grow a beard. The third, a triple row of teeth, if indeed Nicander is right,


— — — ἐν δὲ γενείῳ
Τρίστιχοι ἑκάτερθε περιστιχόωσιν ὀδόντες,

— — — ἐν δὲ γενείῳ Τρίστιχοι ἑκάτερθε περιστιχόωσιν ὀδόντες, [— — — en de geneiō Tristichoi hekaterthe peristichoōsin odontes,]


In maxilla autem tres dentium ordines utrimque digesti sunt. Avicenna solum ha-bet, وفي كل لحي ثلثة انياب Et in unaquaque maxilla tres sunt dentes. Sed puto, aliquid esse omissum, puta vocem صفوف aut سطور, id est, ordines. Quarta nota sit color, qui quidem est varius. Observat enim Aëtius, alios esse nigros, alios rufos, alios cinerei coloris. Et, juxta Avicennam, III, 233 لها وجوه صفر وسود Facies ipsis sunt flavae et nigrae. Et multo ante Nicander,

And in the jaw three rows of teeth are ranged on either side. Avicenna has only وفي كل لحي ثلثة انياب [wa-fī kull laḥy thalātha anyāb] And in each jaw there are three teeth. But I think something has been omitted, namely the word صفوف [ṣufūf] or سطور [suṭūr], that is, rows. Let the fourth mark be colour, which is indeed varied. For Aëtius observes that some are black, some red, some ash-coloured. And, according to Avicenna, III, 233 لها وجوه صفر وسود [lahā wujūh ṣufr wa-sūd] Their faces are yellow and black. And long before, Nicander,


Φράζεο καὶ χλοάοντα δαεὶς κύανόν τε δράκοντα,

Φράζεο καὶ χλοάοντα δαεὶς κύανόν τε δράκοντα, [Phrazeo kai chloaonta daeis kyanon te drakonta,]


Etiam peritus describe flavum, et nigrum draconem. Tamen fulvi, aut flavi, aut aurei, aut rufi coloris, quod fere idem est, plerumque describuntur. Lucanus,

Being skilled, describe also the yellow and the black dragon. Yet they are mostly described as tawny, or yellow, or golden, or red in colour, which is nearly the same thing. Lucan,


Serpitis aurato nitidi fulgore dracones.

You dragons, gleaming with golden brightness, crawl.


Pausanias in Corinthiacis, Δράκοντες δὲ οἱ λοιποὶ, καὶ ἕτερον γένος, ἐς τὸ ξαν-θότερον ῥέποντες χρόας, ἱεροὶ μὲν τοῦ Ἀσκληπιοῦ νομίζονται· Caeteri quoque col. 436 dracones, sed (inprimis) aliud genus, in fulvum colorem vergens, Aesculapio sacri habentur. Et Philostratus ubi supra, postquam πυρσίτας (id est, ignei coloris) dracones serrato dorso et barbatos esse dixit, addit: καὶ τὸν αὐχένα ὑψοῦ αἴρουσι, καὶ τὴν φολίδα στίλβουσι δίκην ἀργύρου, et cervicem altius attollunt, et eorum squamae instar argenti fulgent: ut hos in draconibus doceat maxime eminere. Ut non frustra scripserit Poeta summus Iliad. β΄. versu 308.

Pausanias in the Corinthiaca: Δράκοντες δὲ οἱ λοιποὶ, καὶ ἕτερον γένος, ἐς τὸ ξανθότερον ῥέποντες χρόας, ἱεροὶ μὲν τοῦ Ἀσκληπιοῦ νομίζονται· [Drakontes de hoi loipoi, kai heteron genos, es to xanthoteron rhepontes chroas, hieroi men tou Asklēpiou nomizontai;] The other col. 436 dragons also, but (especially) another kind, inclining to a tawny colour, are held sacred to Aesculapius. And Philostratus, in the place cited above, after saying that πυρσίτας [pyrsitas] (that is, fire-coloured) dragons have a serrated back and are bearded, adds: καὶ τὸν αὐχένα ὑψοῦ αἴρουσι, καὶ τὴν φολίδα στίλβουσι δίκην ἀργύρου [kai ton auchena hypsou airousi, kai tēn pholida stilbousi dikēn argyrou], and they raise the neck higher, and their scales shine like silver: so that he teaches that these stand out most among dragons. Thus the supreme Poet did not write in vain, Iliad 2, line 308:


Ἔνθ᾽ ἐφάνη μέγα σῆμα, δράκων ἐπὶ νῶτα δαφοινός·

Ἔνθ᾽ ἐφάνη μέγα σῆμα, δράκων ἐπὶ νῶτα δαφοινός· [Enth' ephanē mega sēma, drakōn epi nōta daphoinos;]


Ibi apparuit magnum signum, draco dorso rubens (aut rufus). Nec multo aliter divinus scriptor Apoc. XII, 1. 3. Signum magnum apparuit in coelo, etc. Et ecce draco magnus rufus! Quamvis aliud significetur: diabolus nempe, qui sanguineus est, et homicida ab initio, Ioh. VIII, 44. et bile succensus, et ardens, quia tempus ipsi breve, Apoc. XII, 12. Quo respiciens Syrus interpres reddit, ܬܢܝܢܐ ܕܢܘܪܐ, draconem ignitum. Et Arabs, تنين بلون النار draconem coloris ignei. Qui Philostrato πυρσίτης, et Iohanni πυῤῥὸς, id est, πυρόεις τὴν χροιάν.

There appeared a great sign, a dragon red on the back (or ruddy). Not much differently the divine writer, Rev 12:1 3. A great sign appeared in heaven, etc. And behold a great red dragon! Although something else is signified: namely the devil, who is bloodthirsty and a murderer from the beginning, John 8:44, and inflamed with wrath, and burning, because his time is short, Rev 12:12. With this in view the Syriac translator renders ܬܢܝܢܐ ܕܢܘܪܐ [תנינא דנורא], a fiery dragon. And the Arabic: تنين بلون النار [tinnīn bi-lawn al-nār] a dragon of fiery colour. Which is in Philostratus πυρσίτης [pyrsitēs], and in John πυῤῥὸς [pyrrhos], that is, πυρόεις τὴν χροιάν [pyroeis tēn chroian].


Rictum draconis alii parvum, alii magnum describunt. In priore sententia Solinus fuit, qui draconibus ora dicit esse parva, et ad morsus non dehiscentia. Adeo, ut verbere potius, quam rictu noceant. Quod sequutus Isidorus, est, inquit, ore parvo, et arctis fistulis, per quas trahit spiritum, et linguam exerit. Vim autem non in dentibus, sed in cauda habet, et verbere potius, quam rictu nocet. Sed Aëtius contra, Maxime hiante sunt oris rictu. Et Avicenna, qui viderat, لها افواه شديدة السعة Illis ora sunt valde ampla. Quod idem Posidonium sensisse patet, cum draconi πλεθριαίῳ in Macra Coele-Syriae tribuit χάσμα ὥστ᾽ ἔφιππον δέξασθαι, talem hiatum oris, ut cum equo sessorem admiserit. Et Megasthenem, cum scripsit, in India serpentes (id est, dracones) in tantam magnitudinem adolescere, ut solidos hauriant cervos, taurosque; auctore III, 234 Plinio libri octavi capite decimo quarto. His cum Ieremia magis convenit, apud quem ecclesia non diceret a), Nebucadnetsar me deglutivit ut draco, si draco animal esset tam parvi hiatus et innoxii.

Some describe the gape of the dragon as small, others as large. Solinus was of the former opinion: he says that dragons have small mouths, which do not open wide to bite, so that they do harm by a blow rather than by their gape. Isidore follows him: It has, he says, a small mouth and narrow pipes, through which it draws breath and puts out its tongue. Its strength, however, lies not in its teeth but in its tail, and it does harm by a blow rather than by its gape. But Aëtius says the contrary: They have a very wide gape of the mouth. And Avicenna, who had seen them: لها افواه شديدة السعة [lahā afwāh shadīdat al-saʿa] They have very wide mouths. That Posidonius held the same is clear, since to a dragon of a plethron's length [πλεθριαίῳ (plethriaiō)] in the Macra of Coele-Syria he attributes χάσμα ὥστ᾽ ἔφιππον δέξασθαι [chasma hōst' ephippon dexasthai], such a gape of the mouth that it could have taken in a rider together with his horse. So too Megasthenes, when he wrote that in India serpents (that is, dragons) grow to such a size that they swallow stags and bulls whole, on the authority of Pliny, book 8, chapter 14. III, 234 Jeremiah agrees better with these, in whom the church would not say a), Nebuchadnezzar has swallowed me up like a dragon, if the dragon were an animal of so small and harmless a gape.


Idem Propheta recte omnino cum draconibus confert onagros, qui, inopia pabuli fatiscentes,

The same prophet quite rightly compares with dragons the wild asses, which, exhausted for want of pasture,


— — — — coelum
Suspiciunt patulis captantes naribus auras.

— — — — look up
to the sky, catching the breezes with open nostrils.


Onagri (inquit capitis decimi quarti versu sexto) stantes in clivis attrahunt ventum ut dracones. Quamvis dracones non solum ventos, sed et aves supervolantes aspiratione sua legantur ad se attrahere. Mela libri primi capite decimo nono, Circa (Rhyndacum) angues nascuntur immanes, neque ob magnitudinem modo, sed ob id etiam mirabiles, quod ubi in alveum ejus aestus solemque fugerunt, emergunt atque hiant, supervolantesque aves, quamvis alte et perniciter ferantur, absorbent. Plinius id ipsum scribit libri octavi capite decimo quarto, tanquam ex Metrodoro. Et Aelianus libri secundi capite vigesimo primo, Δράκοντες περὶ τῷ ποταμῷ τῷ καλουμένῳ Ῥυνδάκῳ, τὸ μέν τι τῆς σπείρας ἀπήρεισαν εἰς τὴν γῆν, τὸ δὲ λοιπὸν σῶμα ἀναστήσαντες πᾶν, ἀτρέμα, καὶ ἡσυχῆ τὴν φά-ρυγγα ἀνατείναντες, καὶ μέν τοι καὶ τὸ στόμα ἀνοίξαντες, εἶτα τὰ πτηνὰ ἕλ-κουσι, οἱονεὶ ἴϋγγι, τῷ ἄσθματι. τὰ δὲ εἰς ἐκείνων εἰσπίπτει γαστέρας, ὑπὸ τῆς περὶ αὐτῶν εἰσπνοῆς συρόμενα αὐτοῖς πτεροῖς. Circa fluvium (Ponti), Rhyndacum nomine, dracones, parte voluminis terrae innixi, reliquo corpore erecto, collo tacite et quiete extenso, et ore hiante, aves aspiratione sua, tanquam amatoria illecebra, ad se attrahunt. Illae autem in eorum ventrem decidunt, ipsis suis alis draconum spiritu ductae. Phile capite quinquagesimo nono de draconibus id col. 437 ipsum tradit,

The wild asses (he says in chapter 14, verse 6) standing on the slopes draw in the wind like dragons. Yet we read that dragons draw to themselves by their breath not only the winds but also the birds flying over them. Mela, book 1, chapter 19: Around (the Rhyndacus) huge snakes are born, remarkable not only for their size but also because, when they have fled into its bed from the heat and the sun, they emerge and gape, and swallow the birds flying over them, however high and swiftly they are borne. Pliny writes the very same thing in book 8, chapter 14, as if from Metrodorus. And Aelian, book 2, chapter 21: Δράκοντες περὶ τῷ ποταμῷ τῷ καλουμένῳ Ῥυνδάκῳ, τὸ μέν τι τῆς σπείρας ἀπήρεισαν εἰς τὴν γῆν, τὸ δὲ λοιπὸν σῶμα ἀναστήσαντες πᾶν, ἀτρέμα, καὶ ἡσυχῆ τὴν φάρυγγα ἀνατείναντες, καὶ μέν τοι καὶ τὸ στόμα ἀνοίξαντες, εἶτα τὰ πτηνὰ ἕλκουσι, οἱονεὶ ἴϋγγι, τῷ ἄσθματι. τὰ δὲ εἰς ἐκείνων εἰσπίπτει γαστέρας, ὑπὸ τῆς περὶ αὐτῶν εἰσπνοῆς συρόμενα αὐτοῖς πτεροῖς. [Drakontes peri tō potamō tō kaloumenō Rhyndakō, to men ti tēs speiras apēreisan eis tēn gēn, to de loipon sōma anastēsantes pan, atrema, kai hēsychē tēn pharynga anateinantes, kai men toi kai to stoma anoixantes, eita ta ptēna helkousi, hoionei iyngi, tō asthmati. ta de eis ekeinōn eispiptei gasteras, hypo tēs peri autōn eispnoēs syromena autois pterois.] Around the river (of Pontus) named Rhyndacus, dragons, resting part of their coil on the ground, with the rest of the body raised, the neck stretched out silently and quietly, and the mouth gaping, draw the birds to themselves by their breath, as if by a love charm. And the birds fall into their belly, drawn wings and all by the dragons' breath. Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)], chapter 59, on dragons, col. 437 reports the very same:


Δράκοντες Αἰθιόπων δέ τ᾽, εἰ θηρᾷν δεοῖ,
Χαίνοντες ἀσθμαίνουσιν εἰς τὸν ἀέρα,
Καὶ τῶν πετεινῶν τὰς κρεμαστὰς ἀγέλας,
Ἴϋγξι θερμῆς εἰσπνοῆς καλουμένας,
Καὶ σπωμένας ἄνωθεν εἰς γῆν ἀθρόας
Ἐκ τῶν γνάθων ἕλκουσιν εἰς τὴν γαστέρα.

Δράκοντες Αἰθιόπων δέ τ᾽, εἰ θηρᾷν δεοῖ, Χαίνοντες ἀσθμαίνουσιν εἰς τὸν ἀέρα, Καὶ τῶν πετεινῶν τὰς κρεμαστὰς ἀγέλας, Ἴϋγξι θερμῆς εἰσπνοῆς καλουμένας, Καὶ σπωμένας ἄνωθεν εἰς γῆν ἀθρόας Ἐκ τῶν γνάθων ἕλκουσιν εἰς τὴν γαστέρα. [Drakontes Aithiopōn de t', ei thēran deoi, / Chainontes asthmainousin eis ton aera, / Kai tōn peteinōn tas kremastas agelas, / Iynxi thermēs eispnoēs kaloumenas, / Kai spōmenas anōthen eis gēn athroas / Ek tōn gnathōn helkousin eis tēn gastera.]


Aethiopici dracones, si aucupio egent, hiantes in aerem anhelant, et avium suspensos greges, calidae aspirationis illecebra demulctas, et ex alto ad terram frequentes attractas, ex maxillis in ventrem trahunt. Quo Tertullianus alludens III, 235 De corona militis capite decimo, Draco etiam terrenus, inquit, de longinquo non minus spiritu absorbet alites. Ubi absurde Pamelius draconis nomine basiliscum intelligit.

The Ethiopian dragons, when they need to hunt birds, gape and breathe out into the air; and the flocks of birds hovering aloft, beguiled by the charm of their warm breath and drawn down in numbers from on high to the earth, they draw from their jaws into their belly. Alluding to this, Tertullian, III, 235 De corona militis, chapter 10, says: Even the earthly dragon absorbs birds from afar no less by its breath. Where Pamelius absurdly understands the basilisk by the name of dragon.


Hebraeorum antiquissimi, qui dracones, ut diximus, erectos, et diductis faucibus hiantes, sursum aspirare observarunt, id ita sunt interpretati, ac si, ore in coelum obverso, per suspiria et gemitus, ad Deum de sorte sua conquererentur; quodque omnibus odiosi, desertisque ac feralibus addicti locis, longam quidem, sed miseram, vitam aegre traherent. Ac proinde Iob dracones cum struthionibus jungens capitis trigesimi versibus vigesimo octavo et vigesimo nono, Surgens, inquit, in congregatione clamavi. Frater fui draconum, et socius struthionum. Micheas itidem capitis primi versu octavo, Super hoc plangam, et ululabo, etc. Faciam planctum velut dracones, et luctum sicut struthiones. Fortasse etiam horrendos draconum sibilos respiciunt, quibus deserta personant. Aelianus libri decimi quinti capite vigesimo primo, de dracone quodam in India; Συριγμὸν μὲν οὖν ἀφῆκε μέγιστον, καὶ φύσημα, ὥστε ἐκπλῆξαι πάντας, καὶ ἐκ-ταράξαι· Maximum igitur sibilum et flatum emisit, ita, ut omnes terruerit et conturbaverit (in Alexandri copiis). Et libri decimi sexti capite trigesimo nono idem in Chio alterum memorat δράκοντα μεγέθει μέγιστον, οὗπερ οὖν καὶ τὸν συ-ριγμὸν ἐπιπεφρίκασιν οἱ τὴν Χίον κατοικοῦντες, draconem immensae magnitudinis, cujusque adeo sibilum exhorruerint omnes Chii incolae. Praeterea, ut struthiones a clamore dicuntur בנות יענה, ita draconum nomen תנים thannim alludit ad תנות thannoth, quod θρηνεῖν, plangere explicant vetustissimi interpretes Iudic. XI, 40.

The most ancient of the Hebrews, who observed that dragons, as we have said, rear up and, gaping with wide-open jaws, breathe upwards, interpreted this as if, with mouth turned toward heaven, they were complaining to God about their lot with sighs and groans, and because, hateful to all and consigned to desert and deathly places, they dragged out with difficulty a life that was long indeed, but wretched. And accordingly Job, joining dragons with ostriches in chapter 30, verses 28 and 29, says: Rising up in the assembly I cried out. I was a brother of dragons, and a companion of ostriches. Micah likewise, chapter 1, verse 8: For this I will lament and howl, etc. I will make a lamentation like the dragons, and mourning like the ostriches. Perhaps they also have in view the dreadful hissings of dragons, with which the deserts resound. Aelian, book 15, chapter 21, on a certain dragon in India: Συριγμὸν μὲν οὖν ἀφῆκε μέγιστον, καὶ φύσημα, ὥστε ἐκπλῆξαι πάντας, καὶ ἐκταράξαι [Syrigmon men oun aphēke megiston, kai physēma, hōste ekplēxai pantas, kai ektaraxai]; It therefore emitted a very great hiss and blast, so that it terrified and confounded everyone (in Alexander's forces). And in book 16, chapter 39, the same author records another in Chios, δράκοντα μεγέθει μέγιστον, οὗπερ οὖν καὶ τὸν συριγμὸν ἐπιπεφρίκασιν οἱ τὴν Χίον κατοικοῦντες [drakonta megethei megiston, houper oun kai ton syrigmon epipephrikasin hoi tēn Chion katoikountes], a dragon of immense size, whose hiss all the inhabitants of Chios dreaded. Moreover, just as ostriches are called בנות יענה from their crying, so the name of dragons, תנים thannim, alludes to תנות thannoth, which the most ancient interpreters explain as θρηνεῖν [thrēnein], to lament, Judg 11:40.


Venenum habere draconem, multi negant. Plinius libri vigesimi noni capite quarto, Draco non habet venena. Aëtius, Animal hoc venenum non jacit. Isidorus, Innoxius est a venenis. Proinde a dracone morsis parum dolere scribit Nicander. Verba sunt:

Many deny that the dragon has poison. Pliny, book 29, chapter 4: The dragon has no poisons. Aëtius: This animal does not cast poison. Isidore: It is harmless as regards poisons. Accordingly Nicander writes that those bitten by a dragon feel little pain. His words are:


— — — — οὐ μὲν ὅ γ᾽ αὐτῶς
Ἐγχρίμψας ἤλγυνε, καὶ ἢν ἔκπαγλα χαλεφθῇ.
Βληχρὸν γὰρ μυὸς οἷα νυχηβόρου ἐν χροῒ νύγμα
Εἴδεται, αἱμαχθέντος ὑπὸ κραντῆρος ἀραιοῦ.

— — — — οὐ μὲν ὅ γ᾽ αὐτῶς Ἐγχρίμψας ἤλγυνε, καὶ ἢν ἔκπαγλα χαλεφθῇ. Βληχρὸν γὰρ μυὸς οἷα νυχηβόρου ἐν χροῒ νύγμα Εἴδεται, αἱμαχθέντος ὑπὸ κραντῆρος ἀραιοῦ. [ou men ho g᾽ autōs Enchrimpsas ēlgyne, kai ēn ekpagla chalephthē. Blēchron gar myos hoia nychēborou en chroi nygma Eidetai, haimachthentos hypo krantēros araiou.]


Non is aeque (ac alii serpentes) pungens dolorem excitat, etiamsi graviter laedat. Nam a debili dente cruentato levis in cute punctio apparet, tanquam a mure, qui noctu vorat (alii μυχηβόρου, qui in penu vorat. Tamen in Cantico Moses, Deut. XXXII, 33. Venenum draconum, vinum eorum. Et Sap. XVI, 10. Τοὺς δὲ υἱούς σου οὐδὲ ἰοβόλων δρακόντων ἐνίκησαν ὀδόντες· Filios autem tuos nec venenatorum draconum vicerunt dentes. Sed, ne dicam, Hebraeum תנין posse pro III, 236 quovis serpente sumi, etiamsi draconem intelligas, facile erit haec conciliare. Nam Graeciae dracones, de quibus Nicander et alii, veneno carere, verum est: nisi quod noxias herbas, data opera, leguntur edere, ut suo morsu plus periculi creent. Homerus Iliad. χ´.

It does not (like other serpents) cause equal pain when it strikes, even if it wounds severely. For from the weak, bloodied tooth a slight puncture appears on the skin, as from a mouse that devours by night (others read μυχηβόρου [mychēborou], that devours in the larder). Yet in his Song Moses says, Deut 32:33: The poison of dragons is their wine. And Wis 16:10 Τοὺς δὲ υἱούς σου οὐδὲ ἰοβόλων δρακόντων ἐνίκησαν ὀδόντες [Tous de huious sou oude iobolōn drakontōn enikēsan odontes]; But your sons not even the teeth of poisonous dragons overcame. But, not to mention that the Hebrew תנין can be taken for III, 236 any serpent, even if you understand it as dragon, it will be easy to reconcile these. For it is true that the dragons of Greece, of which Nicander and others speak, lack poison; except that they are read to eat noxious herbs on purpose, so as to make their bite more dangerous. Homer, Iliad χ´ [chi]:


Ὡς δὲ δράκων ἐπὶ χειῇ ὀρέστερος ἄνδρα μένῃσι
Βεβρωκὼς κακὰ φάρμακα· — —

Ὡς δὲ δράκων ἐπὶ χειῇ ὀρέστερος ἄνδρα μένῃσι Βεβρωκὼς κακὰ φάρμακα· — — [Hōs de drakōn epi cheiē oresteros andra menēsi Bebrōkōs kaka pharmaka]


Ut in lustro draco montanus exspectat pastus malas herbas. Et Aelianus libri sexti Historiae capite quarto, Μέλλοντες δὲ τινα ἐλλοχᾷν, ἢ ἄνθρωπον, ἢ θῆρα, τὰς θανατηφόρους ῥίζας ἐσθίουσι· Cum homini aut ferae cuipiam moliuntur insidias, mortiferas radices edunt. Apud Eustathium alii dicunt, ὅτι δράκων, ἐσθί- col. 438 ων μύρμηκας, καὶ κανθαρίδας, ἰοῦ πληροῦται, καὶ εἰς λύσσαν ἄγεται, draconem, formicas et cantharidas comedentem, veneno impleri, et in rabiem agi. Alii item intelligunt πόαν τινὰ χολῆς γεννητικὴν, ἣν ἐσθίων ὄφις εἰς χολὴν ἐρεθίζε-ται, herbam, quae bilem generat, qua cum vescitur, bilis ejus irritatur. Sed in Africa et Arabia hac arte nihil est opus, cum venenum habeat lethiferum. Quod his verbis a Lucano est observatum,

As in its lair a mountain dragon, having fed on evil herbs, awaits a man. And Aelian, History book 6, chapter 4: Μέλλοντες δὲ τινα ἐλλοχᾷν, ἢ ἄνθρωπον, ἢ θῆρα, τὰς θανατηφόρους ῥίζας ἐσθίουσι [Mellontes de tina ellochan, ē anthrōpon, ē thēra, tas thanatēphorous rhizas esthiousi]; When they plot an ambush against a man or some wild beast, they eat deadly roots. In Eustathius others say ὅτι δράκων, ἐσθίων col. 438 μύρμηκας, καὶ κανθαρίδας, ἰοῦ πληροῦται, καὶ εἰς λύσσαν ἄγεται [hoti drakōn, esthiōn myrmēkas, kai kantharidas, iou plēroutai, kai eis lyssan agetai], that the dragon, eating ants and cantharides, is filled with poison and driven to madness. Others likewise understand πόαν τινὰ χολῆς γεννητικὴν, ἣν ἐσθίων ὄφις εἰς χολὴν ἐρεθίζεται [poan tina cholēs gennētikēn, hēn esthiōn ophis eis cholēn erethizetai], a herb that generates bile, on eating which its bile is stirred up. But in Africa and Arabia there is no need of this device, since there it has a lethal poison. This was observed by Lucan in these words:


Vos quoque, qui, cunctis innoxia numina terris,
Serpitis aurato nitidi fulgore dracones,
Pestiferos ardens facit Africa. — —

You too, dragons, who glide gleaming with golden splendour, harmless divinities in all lands, burning Africa makes pestilent. — —


Proinde Heliodorus, de sagittariis agens ex Aethiopiae regione cinnamomifera; Οἱ δὲ μικροῖς μὲν τοῖς βέλεσιν, ἰῷ δὲ δρακόντων πεφραγμένοις ἐιστοξεύοντες, ὀξύν τινα καὶ ἀπότομον θάνατον ἐπέφερον· Illi autem parvas quidem sagittas, sed veneno draconum infectas, conjicientes, citam et accrbam mortem inferebant. Et Prudentius Hamartigeniae versu 481.

Accordingly Heliodorus, treating of archers from the cinnamon-bearing region of Ethiopia: Οἱ δὲ μικροῖς μὲν τοῖς βέλεσιν, ἰῷ δὲ δρακόντων πεφραγμένοις ἐιστοξεύοντες, ὀξύν τινα καὶ ἀπότομον θάνατον ἐπέφερον [Hoi de mikrois men tois belesin, iō de drakontōn pephragmenois eistoxeuontes, oxyn tina kai apotomon thanaton epepheron]; But they, shooting arrows that were small indeed, but tainted with the poison of dragons, inflicted a swift and bitter death. And Prudentius, Hamartigenia, verse 481:


Ecce! Iebusiacae fervent ad praelia turmae:
Aurea tela quibus, de sanguine tincta draconis,
Mortifero splendore micant. — — —

Behold! The Jebusite squadrons burn for battle: their golden darts, dipped in the blood of the dragon, flash with a deadly gleam. — — —


Et Apollinaris Psalmo septuagesimo tertio,

And Apollinaris, Psalm 73:


Ὤλεσας ἰοβόλων κεφαλὰς ῥοθίοισι δρακόντων,

Ὤλεσας ἰοβόλων κεφαλὰς ῥοθίοισι δρακόντων, [Ōlesas iobolōn kephalas rhothioisi drakontōn,]


In fluctibus draconum venenum ejulantium capita perdidisti. Et Psalmo nonagesimo,

In the waves you destroyed the heads of the dragons that spew poison. And Psalm 90:


Ἰοβόλον δὲ δράκοντα ποσὶν καὶ θῆρα πατήσεις,

Ἰοβόλον δὲ δράκοντα ποσὶν καὶ θῆρα πατήσεις, [Iobolon de drakonta posin kai thēra patēseis,]


Venenatum draconem et leonem pedibus conculcabis. Et Leo Africanus libro nono, III, 237 Atlantici dracones sunt virulenti admodum: et, si casu quenquam vel contingant, vel mordeant, carnem emolliunt et debilitant. Sed et in Africa, et Numidia serpentes quivis pestilentius habent venenum, quam in terrarum aliis. Unde Horatius libri tertii Oda decima,

You shall trample the poisonous dragon and the lion under your feet. And Leo Africanus, book 9: III, 237 The dragons of Atlas are extremely poisonous: and if by chance they either touch or bite anyone, they soften and weaken the flesh. Indeed in Africa and Numidia all serpents have a more deadly poison than in other lands. Hence Horace, book 3, Ode 10,


Nec mauris animum mitior anguibus.

Nor gentler in spirit than Moorish snakes.


Et libro secundo Satyrarum in fine,

And at the end of book 2 of the Satires,


— — — — velut illis
Canidia afflasset, pejor serpentibus Afris.

— — — — as if Canidia had breathed on them, worse than African serpents.


Nemo est, qui serpentes nesciat vini esse avidissimos. Id enim docet Philosophus Historiae libri octavi capite quarto, Οἱ δὲ ὄφεις καὶ πρὸς τὸν οἶνόν εἰσιν ἀκρα-τοὺς. Διὸ θηρεύουσί τινες καὶ τοὺς ἔχεις εἰς ὀστράκια, διὰ τὸ τιθέναι οἶνον εἰς τὰς αἱμασίας· λαμβάνονται γὰρ μεθύοντες. Serpentes vini avidi sunt. Proinde viperas aliqui, vino in testis ad sepes disposito, venantur: ebriae enim capiuntur. Et Plinius libri decimi capite septuagesimo secundo, Serpentes, cum occasio est, vinum praecipue appetunt. Sed, vini potu, serpentum et draconum venenum acrius et intensius fieri, non aliunde didici, quam ex Chaldaeo Ionathane, qui, pro Mosis verbis, Venenum draconum est venenum eorum, Deut. XXXII, 33. sic habet in Paraphrasi, הי כמרירתהון דתניניא כי הנך הוון מן חמרהון בגין כן יהי מריר כס דלוות דישתון ביום פורענותהון, Ecce! ut est fel draconum, cum sunt a vino suo (id est, postquam vinum biberunt) ita erit fel calicis, e quo bibent in die ultionis eorum.

Everyone knows that serpents are extremely fond of wine. For the Philosopher teaches this in History, book 8, chapter 4: Οἱ δὲ ὄφεις καὶ πρὸς τὸν οἶνόν εἰσιν ἀκρατοὺς. Διὸ θηρεύουσί τινες καὶ τοὺς ἔχεις εἰς ὀστράκια, διὰ τὸ τιθέναι οἶνον εἰς τὰς αἱμασίας· λαμβάνονται γὰρ μεθύοντες. [Hoi de opheis kai pros ton oinon eisin akratous. Dio thēreuousi tines kai tous echeis eis ostrakia, dia to tithenai oinon eis tas haimasias; lambanontai gar methyontes.] Serpents are greedy for wine. Accordingly some hunt vipers by setting out wine in earthenware vessels by the hedges: for they are caught drunk. And Pliny, book 10, chapter 72: Serpents, when there is opportunity, especially crave wine. But that by drinking wine the poison of serpents and dragons becomes sharper and stronger I have learned from no other source than the Chaldee Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan], who, for the words of Moses, The poison of dragons is their poison, Deut 32:33, has this in his Paraphrase: הי כמרירתהון דתניניא כי הנך הוון מן חמרהון בגין כן יהי מריר כס דלוות דישתון ביום פורענותהון, Behold! as is the gall of dragons when they are from their wine (that is, after they have drunk wine), so shall be the gall of the cup from which they shall drink on the day of their punishment.


Draco sectatur solitudines, τὴν ἐρημίαν πρὸ τῶν ἀστικῶν διατριβῶν, inquit Aelianus libri sexti capite sexagesimo tertio. Acute igitur Plutarchus libro De defectu oraculorum negat verum esse, quod ajunt, Delphos olim fuisse desertas, quia draco ibi degebat. Cum contra ibi draco degeret, quia locus erat desertus. Ἡ γὰρ ἐρημία τὸ θηρίον ἐπηγάγετο, μᾶλλον ἢ τὸ θηρίον ἐποίησε τὴν ἐρημίαν. Ideo Prophetae toties b) urbes populosissimas praedicunt fore draconum domicilia, aut habitandas a draconibus. Quibus verbis extremam illis desolationem minitantur. Aquila igitur non male Ps. XLIV, 20. Contrivisti nos ἐν τόπῳ ἀοι-κήτῳ, in loco inhabitabili, pro eo, quod est Hebraice, in loco draconum. Sed, utut dracones saepe degant in siticulosis locis, tamen, ubi liberum est, in irriguis vallibus sedes figunt multo libentius. Itaque etiam de veris draconibus suo col. 439 III, 238 modo verum est, quod de mysticis draconibus, id est, gentibus, a veri Dei cognitione remotis, sed suo tempore vocandis, prophetavit Esaias c), fore, ut dracones glorificent Deum, cum posuerit in deserto aquas, et flumina in solitudine. Et Nehem. II, 13. fons draconis prope Ierusalem dici videtur a dracone, ibi stabulari solito, dum urbs erat desolata. Sic Pausanias in Boeoticis fontem describit prope amnem Ismenium, cui draco custos a Marte scilicet fuerit appositus. Et Philostratus libri tertii capite secundo Homerum observat draconem in Aulide statuisse circa fontem περὶ κρήνην. Hoc longe verisimilius, quam, quod conjicit Villalpandus, fonticulum hunc magnos illos pisces aluisse, qui Hebraice dicuntur תנים. Sed et id videtur coactum, quod asserit vir doctus, fontem Siloë vocari a lento et serpente fluxu, de quo Es. VIII, 6. Graeci reddunt πηγὴν τῶν συκῶν, fontem ficuum; quia, pro תנים, legerunt תאנים. Syrus autem ܥܝܢܐ ܕܬܠܠܐ fontem collium, quasi תלים legerit.

The dragon seeks out solitary places, τὴν ἐρημίαν πρὸ τῶν ἀστικῶν διατριβῶν [tēn erēmian pro tōn astikōn diatribōn], says Aelian, book 6, chapter 63. Plutarch therefore acutely denies, in his book On the Obsolescence of Oracles, that what they say is true, that Delphi was once deserted because a dragon lived there; rather, the dragon lived there because the place was deserted. Ἡ γὰρ ἐρημία τὸ θηρίον ἐπηγάγετο, μᾶλλον ἢ τὸ θηρίον ἐποίησε τὴν ἐρημίαν. [Hē gar erēmia to thērion epēgageto, mallon ē to thērion epoiēse tēn erēmian.] This is why the Prophets so often b) foretell that the most populous cities will become the dwellings of dragons, or will be inhabited by dragons. By these words they threaten them with utter desolation. So Aquila rendered not badly at Ps. XLIV, 20: You have crushed us ἐν τόπῳ ἀοικήτῳ [en topō aoikētō], in an uninhabitable place, for what is in Hebrew in the place of dragons. But although dragons often live in thirsty places, yet, where they are free to choose, they settle much more gladly in well-watered valleys. Thus also of real dragons, in its own col. 439 III, 238 way, what Isaiah c) prophesied of mystical dragons, that is, of the nations far from the knowledge of the true God but to be called in due time, is true: that the dragons will glorify God, when he has put waters in the desert and rivers in the wilderness. And in Neh 2:13 the dragon's spring near Jerusalem seems to be named from a dragon that used to lurk there while the city lay desolate. So Pausanias in his Boeotica describes a spring near the river Ismenus, over which a dragon was set as guardian, by Mars, of course. And Philostratus, book 3, chapter 2, observes that Homer placed the dragon at Aulis by a spring, περὶ κρήνην [peri krēnēn]. This is far more probable than what Villalpandus conjectures, that this little spring nourished those large fish which in Hebrew are called תנים. But it also seems forced, what a learned man asserts, that the spring of Siloam is named from its slow and creeping flow, of which Isa 8:6. The Greeks render πηγὴν τῶν συκῶν [pēgēn tōn sykōn], the spring of the figs, because for תנים they read תאנים. The Syriac, however, has ܥܝܢܐ ܕܬܠܠܐ [עינא דתללא], the spring of the hills, as if it had read תלים.


Apocal. XII, 9. diabolus vocatur magnus draco, et serpens antiquus, quae fere eodem recidunt. Serpentes enim fama est longo decursu annorum tandem fieri dracones. Praeterea draco non appellatur quivis daemon, sed qui seduxit Evam. Eum porro daemonum principem esse, plerique volunt, et draconis nomine significari, illum inter daemones tam eminere, quam in vulgo serpentum magnus draco. Proinde hunc ipsum daemonem draconem vocat etiam Philo Iudaeus d), qui ante Iohannem scripserat. Ταῦτα δὲ, inquit, οὕτω μὲν λεγόμενα φάσμασιν ἔοικε, καὶ τέρασι, δράκων ἀνθρώπου προϊέμενος φωνὴν, καὶ ἐνσοφι-στεύων ἀκακωτάτοις ἤθεσι, καὶ πιθανότησιν εὐπαραγώγοις γυναῖκα ἀπατῶν· Haec, quae referuntur, spectris et portentis propiora videri queant, draco huma- col. 440 na verba emittens, et argutiis innocentissimos mores corrumpens, et persuasionibus, quibus facile imponatur, mulierem decipiens. Sed et eundem Hebraei הנחש הקדמוני, serpentem antiquum vocant. Quod pridem observarunt Drusius in hunc locum, et in Genesim Paulus Fagius. Neque obscura est ratio nominis. Primo enim serpentis figura seduxit Evam. Secundo, Satan occulto, et ex insidiis, nos aggreditur, et

In Apocal. XII, 9. the devil is called the great dragon and the ancient serpent, which come to almost the same thing. For it is reported that serpents, over a long course of years, at length become dragons. Moreover, not just any demon is called dragon, but the one who seduced Eve. Most hold, further, that he is the prince of demons, and that the name dragon signifies that he is as eminent among the demons as a great dragon is among the common run of serpents. Accordingly Philo Judaeus d), who wrote before John, also calls this very demon a dragon. Ταῦτα δὲ, he says, οὕτω μὲν λεγόμενα φάσμασιν ἔοικε, καὶ τέρασι, δράκων ἀνθρώπου προϊέμενος φωνὴν, καὶ ἐνσοφιστεύων ἀκακωτάτοις ἤθεσι, καὶ πιθανότησιν εὐπαραγώγοις γυναῖκα ἀπατῶν· [Tauta de ... houtō men legomena phasmasin eoike, kai terasi, drakōn anthrōpou proiemenos phōnēn, kai ensophisteuōn akakōtatois ēthesi, kai pithanotēsin euparagōgois gynaika apatōn;] These things, as they are related, might seem closer to apparitions and portents: a dragon uttering human col. 440 words, and corrupting the most innocent character with subtleties, and deceiving the woman with persuasions by which she is easily imposed upon. The Hebrews too call him הנחש הקדמוני, the ancient serpent. This was observed long ago by Drusius on this passage, and by Paulus Fagius on Genesis. Nor is the reason for the name obscure. First, he seduced Eve in the form of a serpent. Second, Satan attacks us secretly and from ambush, and


— — — latet anguis in herba.

— — — a snake lurks in the grass.


Tertio, ut astutus est serpens Gen. III, 1. ita diabolus longe callidissimus. Hinc Evam seduxisse legitur, ἐν τῇ πανουργίᾳ αὐτοῦ, 2 Cor. XI, 3. Quarto, ut serpentis venenum per totum corpus: ita daemonis virus per totam animam effunditur. Denique serpente homini nihil est odiosius, quodque fugiamus magis.

Third, as the serpent is crafty, Gen 3:1, so the devil is by far the most cunning. Hence he is said to have seduced Eve ἐν τῇ πανουργίᾳ αὐτοῦ [en tē panourgia autou], 2 Cor 11:3. Fourth, as the poison of the serpent is spread through the whole body, so the poison of the demon is spread through the whole soul. Finally, nothing is more hateful to man than the serpent, nothing that we flee more.


III, 239 Unde Theophrastus in Characteribus de cavillatione, Τὰ δὴ τῶν ἠθῶν μὴ ἁπλᾶ, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπίβουλα, φυλάττεσθαι μᾶλλον δεῖ, ἢ τοὺς ἔχεις· Mores, qui non sunt simplices, sed insidiosi, fugiendi plus, quam viperae. Et apud Theocritum Praxinoë, ut sternaces equos doceat se maxime horrere;

III, 239 Hence Theophrastus in the Characters, on cavilling: Τὰ δὴ τῶν ἠθῶν μὴ ἁπλᾶ, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπίβουλα, φυλάττεσθαι μᾶλλον δεῖ, ἢ τοὺς ἔχεις [Ta dē tōn ēthōn mē hapla, all᾽ epiboula, phylattesthai mallon dei, ē tous echeis]; Characters that are not simple but treacherous must be shunned more than vipers. And in Theocritus, Praxinoë, to show that she dreads above all horses that throw their riders, says:


Ἵππον, καὶ τὸν ψυχρὸν ὄφιν, τὰ μάλιστα δεδοίκω·

Ἵππον, καὶ τὸν ψυχρὸν ὄφιν, τὰ μάλιστα δεδοίκω· [Hippon, kai ton psychron ophin, ta malista dedoikō;]


Equum et frigidum anguem maxime timeo. Et in Mercatore Plautus,

A horse and the cold snake I fear most. And Plautus in the Mercator:


Nempe ruri est uxor tua, quam dudum dixeras
Te odisse aeque atque angues. — —

Your wife, of course, is in the country, whom a while ago you said you hated as much as snakes. — —


Ut Horatius libro primo Epistolarum,

As Horace in the first book of the Epistles:


— — cane pejus et angue
Vitabit. — — —

— — he will shun it worse than a dog and a snake. — — —


Ita inter genus daemonum atque hominum grave odium intercedit, de quo Gen. III, 15. Sed hoc solum obiter attingimus, quia sunt alterius loci.

So between the race of demons and that of men there is a bitter hatred, of which Gen 3:15 speaks. But we touch on this only in passing, since these matters belong to another place.


III, 240 LIBRI TERTII APPENDIX.

III, 240 APPENDIX TO THE THIRD BOOK.


De Serpentibus in genere.

On Serpents in General.


[Ne quidquam in nostra Bochartiani operis editione desideretur, quod aliqua ratione utile et fructuosum esse possit, visum est, huic libro mantissae loco subjicere, quae Bochartus P. I. L. I. Cap. IV. de serpentibus in genere disputavit, cum his multa insint, quae in reliquo opere non recurrant, digna tamen, quae ab interprete V. T. inprimis Cap. III. Genes. non negligantur.]

[So that nothing that could be in any way useful and profitable should be missing from our edition of Bochart's work, it seemed good to append to this book, by way of a supplement, what Bochart discussed in vol. I, book I, Chapter IV on serpents in general, since it contains much that does not recur in the rest of the work, yet deserves not to be neglected by the interpreter of the O. T., especially of Chapter III of Genesis.]
