Serpens est ζῶον ἑρπετὸν, ἔναιμον, φολιδωτὸν, animal reptile, sanguine praeditum, cortice tectum. Hujus propria pars גחון gachon, Gen. III, 14. id est, venter oblongus, in quem serpit. Philosophus a), Τὴν δὲ κοιλίαν ὁ ὄφις ἔχει, οἷον ἔντερον εὐρυχωρέστερον. Sunt, qui serpentem in creatione quadrupedem fuisse putant, aut saltem, draconum instar, bipedem, et pertinere ad poenam, quod hodie serpit in ventrem. At mihi non fit verisimile, propter peccatum hominis Deum in natura serpentis quidquam mutasse. Tantum, quod erat naturae, cessit in poenam, ut in homine nuditas, et in muliere partus. Neque vero id satis certum, draconem ullum esse bipedem, aut, quod ait Plinius b), visos esse serpentes pedibus anserinis. Augustinus lib. 3. De Gen. ad lit. diserte asserit, dracones esse sine pedibus. Et Philosophus, in libro De incessu animalium, multis probat, neque duos, neque quatuor pedes posse serpenti sufficere propter enormem corporis longitudinem, neque posse plures haberi, quia τῶν ἐναίμων μηδὲν οἷον τ᾽ εἶναι πλείοσι σημείοις κινεῖσθαι, ἢ τέτταρσιν. Unde necessariam esse concludit in serpente τὴν ἀποδίαν.

The serpent is ζῶον ἑρπετὸν, ἔναιμον, φολιδωτὸν [zōon herpeton, enaimon, pholidōton], a creeping animal, endowed with blood, covered with scales. Its proper part is the גחון gachon, Gen. III, 14., that is, the elongated belly on which it creeps. The Philosopher a): Τὴν δὲ κοιλίαν ὁ ὄφις ἔχει, οἷον ἔντερον εὐρυχωρέστερον [Tēn de koilian ho ophis echei, hoion enteron eurychōresteron]. There are those who think that the serpent at its creation was four-footed, or at least two-footed like dragons, and that its now creeping on its belly belongs to the punishment. But it does not seem likely to me that God changed anything in the nature of the serpent on account of man's sin. Only what belonged to its nature was turned into a punishment, as nakedness in man and childbirth in woman. Nor indeed is it sufficiently certain that any dragon is two-footed, or, as Pliny says b), that serpents have been seen with goose's feet. Augustine, book 3 De Gen. ad lit., expressly asserts that dragons are without feet. And the Philosopher, in the book On the Progression of Animals, proves at length that neither two nor four feet could suffice a serpent because of the enormous length of its body, and that it could not have more, because τῶν ἐναίμων μηδὲν οἷον τ᾽ εἶναι πλείοσι σημείοις κινεῖσθαι, ἢ τέτταρσιν [tōn enaimōn mēden hoion t᾽ einai pleiosi sēmeiois kineisthai, ē tettarsin]. Hence he concludes that τὴν ἀποδίαν [tēn apodian] is necessary in the serpent.


In maledictione serpentis merito dictum de semine mulieris, Illud conteret tibi caput, Gen. III, 15. quia caput est in serpente longe potissima pars, qua il-laesa raro succumbit. Isidorus Orig. lib. 12. cap. 4. Dicit autem Plinius, si credetur, quod serpentis caput, etiamsi cum duobus evaserit digitis, nihilominus vivit. Aeliano teste scilicet c), τὴν καρδίαν κεκλήρωται ἐπὶ τῇ φάρυγγι, cor in III, 241 gutture fortitus est, in vicinia capitis, cum in caeteris animalibus medium pectus occupet. Unde est, quod Epaminondas, ut Thebanos recta in Lacedaemoniorum agmen impelleret, d) Μέγιστον ἔχιν συλλαβὼν ἔδειξεν αὐτοῖς, καὶ πάν-των ἐναντίον τὴν κεφαλὴν τοῦ θηρίου συντρίψας, Ὁρᾶτε, ἔφη, ὅτι τὸ λοιπὸν σῶμα ἄχρηστον, τῆς κεφαλῆς οἰχομένης. οὕτω δὴ ἢν τὰς τῶν πολεμίων κεφα-λὰς, τὸ Λακωνικὸν τοῦτο συντρίψωμεν, τὸ λοιπὸν σῶμα τῶν συμμάχων ἄχρη-στον. Maximum serpentem arreptum ostendit ipsis, et ejus capite attrito in conspectu omnium, Videtis, inquit, capite adempto, reliquum corpus esse inutile. Ita, si hostium capita, nempe Laconicum hoc contriverimus, reliquum corpus sociorum nullius erit usus. Quapropter serpens in pugna fere in eo totus est, ut caput periculo eximat, Epiphanius in Physiologo cap. 15. Ὅλον τὸ σῶμα παραδίδωσι, τὴν κεφαλὴν μόνην φυλάσσει. Et in Ophitas, Haeresi 37. Ἐν τῷ διώκεσθαι, γινώσκων ὅτι ἐν τῇ κεφαλῇ αὐτοῦ ἡ πᾶσα ζωὴ αὐτοῦ τυγχάνει, ὅλον τὸ σῶμα ἐνειλήσας ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ κρύπτει μὲν τὸ κρανίον ἑαυτοῦ, παραδίδωσι δὲ τὸ ἄλλο σῶμα· Ab aliquo appetitus, cum in capite vitam omnem suam residere sentiat, toto in caput complicato corpore, cranium quidem suum occultat, tradit autem reliquum corpus. Chrysostomus in Psal. CXIV. Ὁ ὄφις τὸ λοιπὸν σῶμα προΐεται, ὥστε τὴν κεφαλὴν διασῶσαι. Serpens reliquum corpus exponit, ut caput conservet. Caesarius, Dialogo 4. Quaest. 192. Ὁ γὰρ ὄφις ὑπὸ βροτοῦ δυ-νάμει καταλεφθεὶς, ὅλον μὲν τῷ παίοντι τὸ σῶμα περοΐεται, τὴν δὲ κεφαλὴν ἄτρωτον φρουρεῖν μηχανᾶται. Serpens enim, ab homine vi correptus, totum quidem corpus percutienti objicit, caput autem illaesum servare conatur. Isidorus Pelusiota, lib. 1. Epist. 126. Ὅσαις γὰρ ἂν περιστάσεσι καὶ πληγαῖς ὁ ὄφις συνέ-χηται, τὴν ἑαυτοῦ φυλάττει κεφαλὴν ἀβλαβῆ· Quibuscunque enim casibus et plagis serpens prematur, caput suum servat illaesum. Et Isidorus alius, nempe Hispalensis, Orig. lib. 12. cap. 4. Totum corpus objicit pro capite ferientibus. Tzetzes Chil. 9. cap. 263.

In the curse of the serpent it is rightly said of the seed of the woman, It shall bruise your head, Gen 3:15, because in the serpent the head is by far the most important part, and while it is unharmed the serpent rarely succumbs. Isidore, Orig. book 12, ch. 4: Pliny says, if it is to be believed, that the head of a serpent, even if it has escaped with only two fingers' length of body, nevertheless lives. For, as Aelian testifies c), τὴν καρδίαν κεκλήρωται ἐπὶ τῇ φάρυγγι [tēn kardian keklērōtai epi tē pharyngi], it has its heart allotted in III, 241 the throat, near the head, whereas in other animals the heart occupies the middle of the chest. Hence it is that Epaminondas, in order to drive the Thebans straight against the line of the Lacedaemonians, d) Μέγιστον ἔχιν συλλαβὼν ἔδειξεν αὐτοῖς, καὶ πάντων ἐναντίον τὴν κεφαλὴν τοῦ θηρίου συντρίψας, Ὁρᾶτε, ἔφη, ὅτι τὸ λοιπὸν σῶμα ἄχρηστον, τῆς κεφαλῆς οἰχομένης. οὕτω δὴ ἢν τὰς τῶν πολεμίων κεφαλὰς, τὸ Λακωνικὸν τοῦτο συντρίψωμεν, τὸ λοιπὸν σῶμα τῶν συμμάχων ἄχρηστον. [Megiston echin syllabōn edeixen autois, kai pantōn enantion tēn kephalēn tou thēriou syntripsas, Horate, ephē, hoti to loipon sōma achrēston, tēs kephalēs oichomenēs. houtō dē ēn tas tōn polemiōn kephalas, to Lakōnikon touto syntripsōmen, to loipon sōma tōn symmachōn achrēston.] seized a very large serpent and showed it to them, and having crushed its head in the sight of all, said: You see that, once the head is taken away, the rest of the body is useless. So, if we crush the heads of the enemy, namely this Laconian one, the rest of the body of the allies will be of no use. For this reason the serpent in a fight is almost wholly intent on keeping its head out of danger. Epiphanius in the Physiologus, ch. 15: Ὅλον τὸ σῶμα παραδίδωσι, τὴν κεφαλὴν μόνην φυλάσσει [Holon to sōma paradidōsi, tēn kephalēn monēn phylassei]. And against the Ophites, Heresy 37: Ἐν τῷ διώκεσθαι, γινώσκων ὅτι ἐν τῇ κεφαλῇ αὐτοῦ ἡ πᾶσα ζωὴ αὐτοῦ τυγχάνει, ὅλον τὸ σῶμα ἐνειλήσας ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ κρύπτει μὲν τὸ κρανίον ἑαυτοῦ, παραδίδωσι δὲ τὸ ἄλλο σῶμα· [En tō diōkesthai, ginōskōn hoti en tē kephalē autou hē pasa zōē autou tynchanei, holon to sōma eneilēsas epi tēn kephalēn autou kryptei men to kranion heautou, paradidōsi de to allo sōma] When attacked by someone, since it perceives that its whole life resides in its head, it coils its whole body around its head and hides its skull, but gives up the rest of its body. Chrysostom on Psal. CXIV.: Ὁ ὄφις τὸ λοιπὸν σῶμα προΐεται, ὥστε τὴν κεφαλὴν διασῶσαι [Ho ophis to loipon sōma proietai, hōste tēn kephalēn diasōsai]. The serpent exposes the rest of its body in order to preserve its head. Caesarius, Dialogue 4, Question 192: Ὁ γὰρ ὄφις ὑπὸ βροτοῦ δυνάμει καταλεφθεὶς, ὅλον μὲν τῷ παίοντι τὸ σῶμα περοΐεται, τὴν δὲ κεφαλὴν ἄτρωτον φρουρεῖν μηχανᾶται [Ho gar ophis hypo brotou dynamei katalephtheis, holon men tō paionti to sōma peroietai, tēn de kephalēn atrōton phrourein mēchanatai]. For the serpent, when seized by force by a man, offers its whole body to the one striking it, but tries to keep its head unharmed. Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, Epist. 126: Ὅσαις γὰρ ἂν περιστάσεσι καὶ πληγαῖς ὁ ὄφις συνέχηται, τὴν ἑαυτοῦ φυλάττει κεφαλὴν ἀβλαβῆ· [Hosais gar an peristasesi kai plēgais ho ophis synechētai, tēn heautou phylattei kephalēn ablabē] For whatever mishaps and blows the serpent is beset by, it keeps its head unharmed. And the other Isidore, namely of Seville, Orig. book 12, ch. 4: It offers its whole body in place of its head to those striking it. Tzetzes, Chil. 9, ch. 263:


τυπτόμενος εἰς φόνον,
Παντοιοτρόπως τὴν κεφαλὴν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ συγκρύπτει.

τυπτόμενος εἰς φόνον, Παντοιοτρόπως τὴν κεφαλὴν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ συγκρύπτει. [typtomenos eis phonon, Pantoiotropōs tēn kephalēn tēn heautou synkryptei.]


An huc pertinet, quod scribit Sirachides e), Οὐκ ἔστι κεφαλὴ ὑπὲρ κεφαλὴν ὄφεως· Non est caput supra caput serpentis? Non puto, quia sic sensus esset subobscurus. Haud dubie igitur auctor libri Hebraice scripserat לא ראש על ראש הנחש, quod vertendum, Non est venenum supra venenum serpentis. Nempe ראש tam venenum significat, quam caput. Sic Deut. XXXII, 33. Vinum eorum, ראש פתנים, venenum aspidum. Toto coelo aberraret, qui redderet caput aspidum. III, 242 Venenum illud partim in felle est, Iob. XX, 14. Fel aspidum in interiori ejus. Plinius lib. 11. cap. 37. Ne quis miretur, fel venenum esse serpentium. Et lib. 29. cap. 6. Non aliud hoc esse, quam fel serpentium, et inde venis sub spina ad eos pervenire, diligentissimi auctores scribunt. Partim etiam in dentibus, Eccles. XXXIX, 35. et in vesicula quadam sub lingua; ideo Iob. XX, 16. Occidet eum lingua viperae.

Does what the Son of Sirach writes e) belong here: Οὐκ ἔστι κεφαλὴ ὑπὲρ κεφαλὴν ὄφεως [Ouk esti kephalē hyper kephalēn opheōs]; There is no head above the head of a serpent? I do not think so, because then the sense would be rather obscure. Without doubt, therefore, the author of the book had written in Hebrew לא ראש על ראש הנחש, which should be translated, There is no poison above the poison of the serpent. For ראש means poison as well as head. Thus Deut 32:33. Their wine, ראש פתנים, the poison of asps. Whoever rendered it the head of asps would be utterly wide of the mark. III, 242 That poison is partly in the gall, Job 20:14. The gall of asps within him. Pliny, book 11, ch. 37: Let no one be surprised that the gall is the poison of serpents. And book 29, ch. 6: The most careful authors write that this is nothing other than the gall of serpents, and that it reaches them from there through the veins under the spine. Partly also in the teeth, Sir 39:35, and in a certain small bladder under the tongue; therefore Job 20:16. The tongue of the viper shall slay him.


Linguae extrema, λεπτὰ ὥσπερ τρίχες f), capillamenti tenuitate. Quo David respiciens, Psal. CXL, 3. Acuerunt, inquit, linguas suas, sicut serpentes. Plautus bilingues non semel vocat. Ita in Persa, Tanquam proserpens be-stia, est bilinguis et scelestus. Et in Asinaria Libanius Philenium ad osculum ita invitat, Fac proserpentem bestiam, duplicem ut habeam linguam. Nempe, si Salmasio credimus, serpentes tam tremulo motu linguam crispant, ut non una, sed gemina videatur esse. Quomodo sarissam duplicare dicebantur, qui vibrabant eam et crispabant, quasi duplicem quatiendo facerent. Unde Hesychius, Πτύσσει· κραδαίνει, τὰ δόρατα διπλοῖ, id est, vibrat hastas et duplicat. Et in Apuleii Apologia Laelius ἴϋγγας vocat inlices bicodulas, quod caudae assidua vibratione quadamtenus duplicem eam faciunt, et sic duas videntur caudas ha-bere. A quo caudae motu Iynx σεισοπυγὶς, et motacilla dicta. In qua ipsa sententia fuisse nonnullos veterum, docent haec Isidori de serpente, Orig. lib. 12. cap. 4. Nullum animal tanta celeritate linguam movet, adeo, ut triplicem linguam habere videatur, cum una sit. Sed haec, utut speciosa, tamen haudquaquam vera sunt. Neque enim propter celerem linguae vibrationem bilinguis a Plauto dicitur serpens, sed quia eam habet bisulcam; ut ipse in Poenulo testatur, Bisulci lingua, quasi proserpens bestia. Proinde Philosophus asserit, ubi supra, δι-κρόαν αὐτῶν εἶναι τὴν γλῶτταν ἄκραν, summam eorum linguam esse bifidam. Unde Arabes in Damire, capite الحية, seu De serpente, لسانها مشقوق ولذلك يظن بعض الناس ان لها لسانين Lingua ejus divisa est, propterea nonnulli putant, eum habere duas linguas. Et in capite الضب, seu De crocodilo terrestri, ولما سال الامام ابو حنيفة عن ذكر الضب فقال انه كلسان الحية اصل واحد له فرعان Et postquam inquisivisset sacerdos Abuchanipha de virga crocodili terrestris, dixit, eam esse ut linguam serpentis, quae radicem unam habet, sed bifida est. Alii trisulcam esse asserunt. Ita Plinius g), Lingua tenuissima serpentibus, et trisulca est. Quod poetae fere sequuntur. Virgilius, Georg. lib. 3. et Aen. lib. 2.

The tips of the tongue are λεπτὰ ὥσπερ τρίχες [lepta hōsper triches] f), as thin as hairs. With an eye to this David says, Ps 140:3. They have sharpened their tongues like serpents. Plautus more than once calls them bilingues [two-tongued]. Thus in the Persa: Like a creeping beast, he is two-tongued and wicked. And in the Asinaria Libanus invites Philenium to a kiss thus: Be a creeping beast, so that I may have a double tongue. That is, if we believe Salmasius [=Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), Plinianae exercitationes], serpents flicker their tongue with so tremulous a motion that it seems not single but double. In the same way those who brandished and shook a sarissa were said sarissam duplicare [to double the sarissa], as though by shaking it they made it double. Hence Hesychius: Πτύσσει· κραδαίνει, τὰ δόρατα διπλοῖ [Ptyssei; kradainei, ta dorata diploi], that is, he brandishes the spears and doubles them. And in the Apology of Apuleius, Laelius calls ἴϋγγας [iyngas] inlices bicodulas [two-tailed lures], because by the constant vibration of the tail they make it in some measure double, and so seem to have two tails. From this motion of the tail the Iynx is called σεισοπυγὶς [seisopygis], and motacilla [wagtail]. That some of the ancients held this very opinion is shown by these words of Isidore on the serpent, Orig. book 12, ch. 4: No animal moves its tongue with such speed, so much so that it seems to have a triple tongue, though it has only one. But these things, however plausible, are by no means true. For the serpent is not called bilinguis by Plautus because of the swift vibration of its tongue, but because it has a forked one, as he himself testifies in the Poenulus: With forked tongue, like a creeping beast. Accordingly the Philosopher asserts, in the place cited above, δικρόαν αὐτῶν εἶναι τὴν γλῶτταν ἄκραν [dikroan autōn einai tēn glōttan akran], that the tip of their tongue is cleft. Hence the Arabs in Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], in the chapter الحية [al-ḥayya], or On the serpent: لسانها مشقوق ولذلك يظن بعض الناس ان لها لسانين [lisānuhā mashqūq wa-li-dhālika yaẓunnu baʿḍ al-nās anna lahā lisānayn] Its tongue is divided; for this reason some think it has two tongues. And in the chapter الضب [al-ḍabb], or On the land crocodile: ولما سال الامام ابو حنيفة عن ذكر الضب فقال انه كلسان الحية اصل واحد له فرعان [wa-lammā saʾala al-imām Abū Ḥanīfa ʿan dhakar al-ḍabb fa-qāla innahu ka-lisān al-ḥayya aṣl wāḥid lahu farʿān] And when the priest Abuchanipha had inquired about the penis of the land crocodile, he said that it is like the tongue of the serpent, which has one root but is forked. Others assert that it is three-forked. Thus Pliny g): The tongue of serpents is very thin, and three-forked. The poets generally follow this. Virgil, Georg. book 3 and Aen. book 2:


III, 243 Arduus ad Solem, et linguis micat ore trisulcis.

III, 243 Towering toward the Sun, it flickers in its mouth with three-forked tongues.


Ovidius de dracone, a Cadmo caeso, Metam. lib. 3.

Ovid, on the dragon slain by Cadmus, Metam. book 3:


— — — corpus tumet omne veneno,
Tresque micant linguae.

— — — its whole body swells with poison,
and three tongues flicker.


Et de dracone, in Colchis, velleris aurei custode, Metam. lib. 7.

And on the dragon in Colchis, guardian of the golden fleece, Metam. book 7:


Qui crista, linguisque tribus praesignis.

Who, conspicuous for his crest and his three tongues.


Seneca in Medea, versu 686.

Seneca in the Medea, line 686:


Hic sera serpens corpus immensum trahit,
Trifidamque linguam exertat.

Here the savage serpent drags its immense body,
and thrusts out its three-cleft tongue.


Silius lib. 6. versu 222.

Silius book 6, line 222:


— — — trifido vibrata per auras
Lingua micat motu, atque assultans aethera lambit.

— — — the tongue, brandished through the air with three-cleft motion,
flickers, and leaping up licks the sky.


Et versu 264.

And line 264:


— — jamjamque extrema trisulca
Lambebat lingua fessi certamine terga
Quadrupedis.

— — and now, now with the tip of its three-forked
tongue it was licking the back of the steed
wearied by the struggle.


Statius de Pythone, lib. 1. Thebaidis versu 565.

Statius on the Python, book 1 of the Thebaid, line 565:


— — Castaliis dum fontibus ore trisulco
Fusus hiat.

— — while, stretched out, it gapes with three-forked mouth
at the Castalian springs.


Et de serpente, a quo caesus est Archemorus, lib. 5. vers. 580.

And on the serpent by which Archemorus was slain, book 5, line 580:


— volat hasta tremens, et hiantia monstri
Ora subit, linguaeque secat fera vincla trisulcae.

— the spear flies quivering, and enters the gaping
jaws of the monster, and cuts the fierce bonds of the three-forked tongue.


An eo referendum, quod maledico, qui linguam in quoscunque exerit, et vibrat more serpentis, lingua triplex tribuitur in Chaldaea paraphrasi, Iob. XXXVI, 33. Ps. CI, 5. et CXL, 12. Eccles. X, 11. etc.? Omnino ita videtur: Neque aliter interpretor haec Sirachidis XXVIII, 15. Γλῶσσα τρίτη πολλοὺς ἐσάλευσεν, et vers. 17. Γλῶσσα τρίτη γυναῖκας ἀνδρείας ἐξέβαλε. Alii aliter explicant, ut infra observabimus.

Should we refer to this the fact that the slanderer, who thrusts out his tongue against anyone and flickers it in the manner of a serpent, is assigned a triple tongue in the Chaldee paraphrase, Iob. XXXVI, 33. Ps 101:5 and CXL, 12. Eccl 10:11 etc.? It certainly seems so. Nor do I interpret otherwise these words of Sir 28:15 Γλῶσσα τρίτη πολλοὺς ἐσάλευσεν [Glōssa tritē pollous esaleusen], and verse 17, Γλῶσσα τρίτη γυναῖκας ἀνδρείας ἐξέβαλε [Glōssa tritē gynaikas andreias exebale]. Others explain them differently, as we shall observe below.


Sed hanc interpretationem valde confirmant verba Psaltis, quibus cum lingua serpentis maledici lingua confertur.

But this interpretation is strongly confirmed by the words of the Psalmist, in which the slanderer's tongue is compared with the tongue of a serpent.


Addo, ex Arabum fide, rem a Romanis et Graecis scriptoribus praetermissam, serpentes alios non modo acutam, sed et aculeatam habere linguam, aut III, 244 vero rostrum et nasum; alios, scorpionum instar, etiam cauda ferire; alios gemino aculeo ex utraque parte pungere. Alcamus, النكّاز حية لا ينكز الا بانفه ليس له فم لا يعرف ذنبه من راسه لدقته من اخبث الحيات Nicchaz, serpens, qui nonnisi naso pungit, ac si ore careat, cujus caput ita tenue est, ut a cauda non secernatur. Deterrimum est serpentis genus. Nempe نكز nahaza de serpente, est naso, vel rostro pungere. Ibidem, ذو الطرفين من الحيات لها ابرتان احدهما في انفها والاخري في ذنبها Dultaraphina, serpentis genus gemino aculeo, quorum unus in naso, alter in cauda est. Unde est, quod serpentis punctionem a morsu ita distinguit Solomon, Prov. XXIII, 32. Velut serpens mordebis, et ut basiliscus יפרש punget. Ita in Iucatana, Novae Hispaniae contermina, serpens ex eo, Polpoch dictus, quod sibilus ejus videatur hunc fere sonum referre, scribitur et ore mordere, et caudae aculeo pungere h)). Et in Australi America, apud Chiribichenses, Petrus Martyr i)) aspidum meminit, quae scorpionum instar cauda feriunt.

I add, on the authority of the Arabs, a fact passed over by the Roman and Greek writers: that some serpents have a tongue that is not only sharp but armed with a sting, or else III, 244 a sting in the snout and nose; that others, like scorpions, also strike with the tail; and that others prick with a double sting, one at each end. Alcamus: النكّاز حية لا ينكز الا بانفه ليس له فم لا يعرف ذنبه من راسه لدقته من اخبث الحيات [al-nakkāz ḥayya lā yankuzu illā bi-anfihi laysa lahu fam lā yuʿrafu dhanabuhu min raʾsihi li-diqqatihi min akhbath al-ḥayyāt] Nicchaz, a serpent that pricks only with its nose, as if it had no mouth, whose head is so slender that it cannot be distinguished from its tail. It is the worst kind of serpent. For نكز [nakaza] nahaza, said of a serpent, means to prick with the nose or with the snout. In the same place: ذو الطرفين من الحيات لها ابرتان احدهما في انفها والاخري في ذنبها [dhū al-ṭarafayn min al-ḥayyāt lahā ibratān iḥdāhumā fī anfihā wa-al-ukhrā fī dhanabihā] Dultaraphina, a kind of serpent with a double sting, one of which is in the nose, the other in the tail. Hence Solomon distinguishes the prick of a serpent from its bite, Prov 23:32: You will bite like a serpent, and like a basilisk יפרש you will prick. So in Yucatán, bordering on New Spain, a serpent called Polpoch, because its hiss seems to give roughly this sound, is written both to bite with its mouth and to prick with a sting in its tail h)). And in South America, among the Chiribichenses, Peter Martyr i)) mentions asps that strike with the tail like scorpions.


Sibilus serpentum terribilis, Sap. XVII, 9. exilis tamen, ut observatur a Philosopho k)? Quocirca Ieremias, cap. 46. versu 22. de Aegypto disserens, a Chaldaeis opprimenda, Vox illius, inquit, quasi serpentis ibit; quia, servitute pressa, vix audebit hiscere et mussitare. Tale illud, Esa. XXIX, 4. Humiliaberis, de terra loqueris, et e pulvere humile erit eloquium tuum. At Ieremiae locum ita reddit Syrus interpres, ܩܠܗ ܕܚܝܠܐ ܐܝܟ ܚܘܝܐ ܕܪܚܫ Vox exercitus erit ut serpentis reptitantis. Et Chaldaeus, קל כחוש זיניהון כחון זחלין, Fragor collisionis armorum eorum erit ut serpentium repentium. Ac si fragorem armorum in Chaldaeorum copiis conferat cum strepitu, quem inter rependum edunt quorundam serpentum cortices, cerastae puta, vel haemorrhoi, de quo Nicander in Theriacis,

The hiss of serpents is terrible, Wis 17:9 yet thin, as the Philosopher observes k)? Therefore Jeremiah, ch. 46, verse 22, speaking of Egypt, which was to be crushed by the Chaldeans, says: Her voice shall go like a serpent's; because, weighed down by servitude, she will scarcely dare to open her mouth and mutter. Like this is Isa 29:4. You shall be brought low, you shall speak from the ground, and your speech shall be low out of the dust. But the Syriac translator renders the passage of Jeremiah thus: ܩܠܗ ܕܚܝܠܐ ܐܝܟ ܚܘܝܐ ܕܪܚܫ [קלה דחילא איך חויא דרחש] The voice of the army shall be like that of a creeping serpent. And the Chaldee: קל כחוש זיניהון כחון זחלין, The crash of the clashing of their arms shall be like that of creeping serpents. As if he compared the crash of arms in the forces of the Chaldeans with the rustling that the skins of certain serpents make as they creep, for instance the cerastes or the haemorrhous, of which Nicander says in the Theriaca,


— — — φολίσιν δὲ, καὶ οἴμῳ Παῦρον ὑποψοφέων καλάμης χύσιν οἷα διέρπει· — — — dum serpit debile murmur Squamarum attritu, calcatae ut arundinis, edit.

— — — φολίσιν δὲ, καὶ οἴμῳ Παῦρον ὑποψοφέων καλάμης χύσιν οἷα διέρπει· [pholisin de, kai oimō Pauron hypopsopheōn kalamēs chysin hoia dierpei] — — — as it creeps it gives a faint murmur from the rubbing of its scales, like trodden reeds.


Et Aelianus, De animalibus lib. 15. cap. 13. Ἕρπει δὲ ἥσυχος ἐπιθλίβων τὰς τῆς νηδύος φολίδας, λοξὸν δὲ οἶμον πρόεισιν· ἠρέμα γοῦν ὑπηχεῖ. Lente serpit III, 245 ventris squamas premens, tortuosa autem via progreditur, et leniter substrepit. Et de ceraste Aetius l), In serpendo sonum, sibilo similem, edit. Avicenna m) etiam plane ut Nicander, ceraste et haemorrhoo reptantibus, sonum edi scribit parvi stridoris, ut قصبا الغاب خشخشة, fragoris arundinum. Iam Rabbinorum audi nugas. Eliezer in Capitulis, et R. Selomo in Ieremiam, eum agere putant de antiquo illo serpente, qui, cum in peccati poenam pedibus truncaretur, tam horrendum exclamaverit, ut ab uno orbis extremo ad alterum auditus fuerit. Sic Ionathan, Exod. VII, 9. ait, omnes terrae fines clamorem serpentis audivisse, cum nudatus est a fundatione mundi.

And Aelian, On Animals book 15, ch. 13: Ἕρπει δὲ ἥσυχος ἐπιθλίβων τὰς τῆς νηδύος φολίδας, λοξὸν δὲ οἶμον πρόεισιν· ἠρέμα γοῦν ὑπηχεῖ. [Herpei de hēsychos epithlibōn tas tēs nēdyos pholidas, loxon de oimon proeisin; ērema goun hypēchei.] It creeps slowly III, 245 pressing the scales of its belly, and advances by a winding path, and makes a gentle rustling. And of the cerastes Aetius l): In creeping it makes a sound like a hiss. Avicenna m) too, just like Nicander, writes that when the cerastes and the haemorrhous creep, a sound of slight rustling is made, like قصبا الغاب خشخشة [qaṣabā al-ghāb khashkhasha], the crackling of reeds. Now hear the trifles of the Rabbis. Eliezer in the Chapters, and R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] on Jeremiah, think he is speaking of that ancient serpent which, when it was deprived of its feet as punishment for sin, cried out so horribly that it was heard from one end of the world to the other. So Jonathan, Exod 7:9 says that all the ends of the earth heard the cry of the serpent when it was stripped, from the foundation of the world.


Serpentes aut in aquis degunt, Amos IX, 3. aut in aridis locis, Deut. VIII, 15. puta, in petris, Prov. XXX, 19. in sepibus, Eccles. X, 8. in terrae latibulis, Es. XI, 8. Quae tria uno versu complectitur Nicander, de cervis agens, qui, ut serpentem pervestigent,

Serpents live either in waters, Amos 9:3 or in dry places, Deut 8:15 for instance on rocks, Prov 30:19 in hedges, Eccl 10:8 in holes in the ground, Isa 11:8 Nicander embraces these three in one verse, speaking of deer which, to track down a serpent,


Τρόχμαλα θ᾽ αἱμασίας τε καὶ εἰλύους ἐρέουσι, Saxa petunt, sepesque, cavernarumque latebras.

Τρόχμαλα θ᾽ αἱμασίας τε καὶ εἰλύους ἐρέουσι, [Trochmala th᾽ haimasias te kai eilyous ereousi] Seek out rocks, and hedges, and the hiding places of caves.


Serpentes censentur in παμφάγοις· nam et carnem edunt, et herbam, et sunt λιχνότατοι τῶν ζώων n), cupediae dediti prae caeteris animantibus. Itaque serpenti pulvis assignatur in cibum, Gen. III, 14. Esa. LXV, 25. et Mich. VII, 17. non quod vescatur solo pulvere, sed quia, cum humi repat, non potest, quin pulverem in os cum aliis cibis simul ingerat. Ita David in luctu queritur, se comedisse cinerem sicut panem, Ps. CII, 10. quia, pronus in cinere jacens, pane, in terram projecto, vescebatur. Talmudici tamen in tractatu De Sabbatho; טועמין את הארץ כחויא, Terram comedebant ut serpens. Et Nicander, de chersydro o), cum exsiccata prorsus illum defecit aqua, νέμεται διψήρεας ὄγμους, aridos sulcos depascitur. Et Phile cap. 59. de serpente quodam Indiae, qui videtur esse sepis species,

Serpents are reckoned among the παμφάγοις [pamphagois]; for they eat both flesh and herbs, and are λιχνότατοι τῶν ζώων [lichnotatoi tōn zōōn] n), more given to dainties than other animals. So dust is assigned to the serpent as food, Gen 3:14. Isa 65:25 and Mic 7:17 not because it feeds on dust alone, but because, crawling on the ground, it cannot help taking dust into its mouth together with other food. Thus David in mourning complains that he has eaten ashes like bread, Ps 102:10 because, lying prostrate in ashes, he ate bread thrown on the ground. The Talmudists, however, in the tractate On the Sabbath: טועמין את הארץ כחויא, They ate earth like a serpent. And Nicander, of the chersydrus o), when the water has dried up completely and failed it, νέμεται διψήρεας ὄγμους [nemetai dipsēreas ogmous], feeds on the dry furrows. And Philes, ch. 59, of a certain serpent of India, which seems to be a species of seps,


Νωδὸς γάρ ἐστι, καὶ ψιλὸν χοῦν ἐσθίει. Soloque vivit pulvere, estque edentulus.

Νωδὸς γάρ ἐστι, καὶ ψιλὸν χοῦν ἐσθίει. [Nōdos gar esti, kai psilon choun esthiei.] It lives on dust alone, and is toothless.


Sed et eodem cibo vesci alia putantur animalia. In his lumbrici et vermes. Plautus in Casina, Act. I.

But other animals too are thought to feed on the same food. Among them are earthworms and worms. Plautus in the Casina, Act 1.


Post autem nisi ruri eruum tu comederis, Aut, quasi lumbricus, terram. III, 246 Et الحباحب cicindela, de qua Algiahid, غذاوها التراب لم تشبع منه قط خوق ان يغني تراب الارض فتهلك جوعا Alimentum ejus est pulvis, quo nunquam saturatur, ideo solum, quia timet, ne deficiat terrae pulvis, atque ita fame pereat. Quomodo in avibus aquaticis مالك الحزين malich alhazin, aliis البلشون balscun, id est, ardea, quam aqua parcius uti, adeoque a potu tamdiu abstinere scribunt Arabes, ut prae siti moriatur, ne aqua deficiat, si biberet paullo largius. Quod symbolum est avari divitis, qui inopiae metu suum defraudat genium. Dicuntur et scorpiones terram habere pro cibo. Bardisanes in Eusebio, De Praepar. lib. 6. Σκόρπιος γῆν ἐσθίει. Plinius lib. 10. cap. 72. Scorpiones terra vivunt. Et talpa in Porta coeli, fol. 22. c. ומן היסוד העפרי יתהוה באשות הנקרא טלפא אשר מזונה העפר, Et ex elemento terrae facta est talpa, cujus alimentum est pulvis. Ut de eadem Vincentius p), In terra habitat, vermium esca vivit, in fame quoque terram comedit. Quin et aves terra vescentes se vidisse ait q) Cardanus. Sed dubitat, utrum id factum sit fame adigente, an ut aliquid eruerent, vel salsedine, vel alio nomine suae naturae conveniens. Sic, auctore Philosopho r), Τοὺς λύ-κους φασὶν, ὅταν πεινῶσιν, ἐσθίειν τινὰ γῆν. Lupi esurientes dicuntur quoddam terrae genus edere. Et apud Pisidam in Hexaëmero,

But afterwards, unless you eat vetch in the country, or earth, like an earthworm. III, 246 And الحباحب [al-ḥabāḥib], the glow-worm, of which Algiahid says: غذاوها التراب لم تشبع منه قط خوق ان يغني تراب الارض فتهلك جوعا [ghidhāwuhā al-turāb lam tashbaʿ minhu qaṭṭ khawq an yughnī turāb al-arḍ fa-tahlik jūʿan] "Its food is dust, with which it is never sated, only because it fears that the dust of the earth may run out and it may thus perish of hunger." So among the water birds the مالك الحزين [mālik al-ḥazīn] malich alhazin, called by others البلشون [al-balshūn] balscun, that is, the ardea [heron], which the Arabs write uses water so sparingly, and abstains from drinking so long, that it dies of thirst, lest the water run out if it drank a little more freely. This is a symbol of the avaricious rich man who, for fear of want, cheats his own appetite. Scorpions too are said to take earth as food. Bardesanes in Eusebius, De Praepar. book 6: Σκόρπιος γῆν ἐσθίει [Skorpios gēn esthiei]. Pliny, book 10, ch. 72: "Scorpions live on earth." And the mole, in the Porta coeli, fol. 22. ch.: ומן היסוד העפרי יתהוה באשות הנקרא טלפא אשר מזונה העפר, "And from the element of earth the mole was made, whose food is dust." As Vincent p) says of the same animal: "It lives in the earth, it lives on worms as food, and in hunger it also eats earth." Indeed Cardano q) says he has seen birds feeding on earth. But he doubts whether this happened under the compulsion of hunger, or so that they might extract something suited to their nature, whether saltiness or something else. Thus, according to the Philosopher r), Τοὺς λύκους φασὶν, ὅταν πεινῶσιν, ἐσθίειν τινὰ γῆν [Tous lykous phasin, hotan peinōsin, esthiein tina gēn]. "Wolves, when hungry, are said to eat a certain kind of earth." And in Pisides, in the Hexaëmeron:


Λύκοι δὲ τὴν γῆν, οἱ λαγοὶ δὲ κανθάρους. Lupique terram, et cantharos lepores edunt:

Λύκοι δὲ τὴν γῆν, οἱ λαγοὶ δὲ κανθάρους. [Lykoi de tēn gēn, hoi lagoi de kantharous.] "And wolves eat earth, and hares beetles":


sed in morbis duntaxat pro medicina. At elephantos Vincentius s) mori tradit, si terram comederint, nonnullos tamen huic cibo ita assuefieri, ut illius consuetudo sit pro altera natura.

but only in sickness, as medicine. But Vincent s) reports that elephants die if they eat earth, yet that some become so accustomed to this food that the habit of it is to them a second nature.


Serpentes ὠοτοκεῖν, ova foris edere, et εἰς τὴν γῆν ἐπωάζειν, in terra fovere, quae anno sequente excludantur, scribunt Aristoteles t) et Plinius u). Ita etiam Esaias XXXIV, 15. Ibi nidificabit קפוז, acontias, et pariet, et excludet ova, quae fovebit sub umbra sua: et LIX, 5. Ova basilisci excluserunt.

Aristotle t) and Pliny u) write that serpents are ὠοτοκεῖν [ōotokein], lay eggs outside the body, and εἰς τὴν γῆν ἐπωάζειν [eis tēn gēn epōazein], incubate them in the earth, and that these hatch in the following year. So also Esaias XXXIV, 15: "There the קפוז, the acontias, shall make its nest, and lay, and hatch eggs, which it will brood under its shadow": and LIX, 5: "They have hatched the eggs of the basilisk."


Genes. III, 1. serpens legitur fuisse ערום supra omnem terrae bestiam. ערום alii recte πανοῦργον, callidum, vafrum, astutum, versutum, versipellem, soli LXX. φρόνιμον, prudentem interpretantur. Quibus tamen haudquaquam velim hoc nomine dicam scribi, cum etiam alibi ערום prudentem sonet, ut passim in Proverbiis x). Et videatur ipse Christus hanc interpretationem confirmare, III, 247 cum cohortatur discipulos, ut sint prudentes tanquam serpentes, Matth. X, 16. eodem verbo, ni fallor, usus, quo Moses. Quamvis ad alteram alludant haec Apostoli 2 Cor. XI, 3. Ὁ ὄφις Εὔαν ἐξεπάτησεν ἐν τῇ πανουργίᾳ αὐτοῦ, Serpens Evam seduxit calliditate sua. Brutis animantibus quo sensu tribuatur vel πανουρ-γία, vel φρόνησις, alibi dicam. Hic solum observabo, perperam hanc phrasin ex Theophrasto confirmari, cujus librum citat Laërtius y) Περὶ τῶν ζώων, ὅσα λέγεται φρονεῖν. Ibi enim pro φρονεῖν legendum esse φθονεῖν, ex Photio scimus, qui hujus libri compendium nobis exhibet Auctore 178.

In Genes. III, 1, the serpent is read to have been ערום above every beast of the earth. Others rightly render ערום as πανοῦργον [panourgon], cunning, crafty, astute, wily, shifty; the LXX alone render it φρόνιμον [phronimon], prudent. Yet I would by no means wish to bring a charge against them on this account, since elsewhere too ערום means prudent, as frequently in Proverbs x). And Christ himself seems to confirm this interpretation, III, 247 when he exhorts the disciples to be prudent as serpents, Matt 10:16, using, if I am not mistaken, the same word as Moses. Although these words of the Apostle, 2 Cor 11:3, allude to the other meaning: Ὁ ὄφις Εὔαν ἐξεπάτησεν ἐν τῇ πανουργίᾳ αὐτοῦ [Ho ophis Euan exepatēsen en tē panourgia autou], "The serpent beguiled Eve by his cunning." In what sense either πανουργία [panourgia] or φρόνησις [phronēsis] is attributed to brute animals I shall say elsewhere. Here I shall only observe that this phrase is wrongly confirmed from Theophrastus, whose book Περὶ τῶν ζώων, ὅσα λέγεται φρονεῖν [Peri tōn zōōn, hosa legetai phronein] is cited by Laertius y). For there φθονεῖν [phthonein] must be read instead of φρονεῖν [phronein], as we know from Photius, who gives us a summary of this book in Author 178.


Ad serpentis calliditatem refero, quod in via stans cerastes, vel ammodytes, et in iis, quibus concolor est arenis latens, ungulas equi mordet, Genes. XLIX, 17. et calcaneo hominis insidiatur, Gen. III, 15. et solis exertis corniculis, quae frumenti granis similia sunt, aviculas, quasi ad escam advolantes, intercipit. Item quod, auctore Luciano z), ad struthionum ova, quae Garamantes maxime expetunt, dipsades sunt in insidiis, accedentes demorsurae. Proinde serpentes Philosophus tradit a) esse μάλιστα ἐπιβούλους, maxime insidiosos. Et apud Aesopum cancer, societate cum serpente inita, eum adhortabatur μετα-βαλέσθαι τῆς πανουργίας, ut mutaret calliditatem suam: ὁ δὲ οὐδοτιοῦν ἑαυτὸν παρεῖχε πειθόμενον, ille autem minime se praebebat obsequentem.

To the cunning of the serpent I refer the fact that the cerastes, or ammodytes, standing in the way and hiding in the sands, whose colour it shares, bites the hoofs of the horse, Genes. XLIX, 17., and lies in wait for the heel of man, Gen 3:15, and, putting out only its little horns, which resemble grains of corn, catches small birds flying up as if to food. Likewise the fact that, according to Lucian z), dipsades lie in ambush by the ostrich eggs, which the Garamantes greatly covet, ready to bite those who approach. Accordingly the Philosopher a) reports that serpents are μάλιστα ἐπιβούλους [malista epiboulous], most treacherous. And in Aesop the crab, having made a partnership with the serpent, urged it μεταβαλέσθαι τῆς πανουργίας [metabalesthai tēs panourgias], to change its cunning: ὁ δὲ οὐδοτιοῦν ἑαυτὸν παρεῖχε πειθόμενον [ho de oudotioun heauton pareiche peithomenon], but it showed itself not at all compliant.


Prudentiae serpentis quatuor argumenta profert Epiphanii Physiologus. Primum, quod, cum senium praesensit, quaerit petram, et ῥαγαδαστεύει, προκύψας δὲ διὰ τῆς ὀπῆς ὠθεῖται περάσαι, καὶ ἐκβάλλει τὸ γῆρας, in rimam se insinuat, pronusque per foramen transire nititur, et senectutem exuit. Atque id uno ore omnes asserunt. Secundum, quod, cum ab homine vestito fugiat, cum eundem nudum videt, καταθαῤῥεῖ αὐτοῦ, illum aggreditur confidenter. Atque hoc quoque videri possit rationi consonum: tamen contrarium alii diserte docent. Eustathius in Hexaëmero, Ἐὰν δὲ γυμνὸν θεάσηται ἄνθρωπον οὐ πρόσ-εισιν· εἰ δὲ ἐνδεδυμένον, ἐφάλλεται· Hominem nudum si aspexerit, non adit; sed, si vestitum viderit, aggreditur. Hieronymus, vel quisquis auctor est Epistolae ad Praesidium sub Hieronymi nomine; Coluber nudum hominem timet, vestitum prosequitur. Isidorus lib. 12. cap. 4. Fertur autem, quod serpens hominem nudum non sit ausus attingere. Damir, ومن عجيب امره انها تهرب من الرجل العريان E mirabilibus naturae ejus est, quod fugit ab homine nudo. Et id se non raro expertum scribit Olaus. Favorabile, inquit, verbum Isidorus de natura serpentum profert, quod hominem nudum et dormientem III, 248 nunquam laedant: idque mihi, in pueritia et adolescentia, serpentibus sine laesione saepissime congredienti, contigit. Tertium serpentis prudentiae argumentum idem profert, quod ab homine appetitus solum caput servat illaesum, et reliquum corpus objicit. De quo cum jam plura dixerim, hoc solum addam ex Caesario, Dial. 4. Quaest. 190. Κατευναζόμενος δὲ, καὶ καθεύδων (ὁ ὄφις) τρο-χίζων ἑαυτὸν, μέσην ὅλου τοῦ σώματος κεφαλὴν ἀσφαλίζεται, οἱονεὶ τειχίῳ τῷ ἐφεπομένῳ ὁλκῷ περιοχυρῶν αὐτήν· Cum quieti se tradit ut dormiat serpens, sese contorquens, medium intra totum corpus caput communit, consequente tractu, ut muro, illud circumvallans. Quartum, quod, cum ad fontem venit, ut bibat, οὐ φέρει τὸν ἰὸν, ἀλλά γε ἀφεὶς αὐτὸν ἐν τῇ νεοττίᾳ, οὕτω καθαρὸς πορεύεται, virus non defert, sed illud in nido dimittens, ita purus accedit. Quod Haer. 37. idem ita edisserit: Οὐ συμπαραλαμβάνει τὸν ἰὸν μεθ᾽ ἑαυτοῦ, ἀλλὰ ἐν τῷ φω-λεῷ καταλιμπάνει, καὶ οὕτως ἐλθὼν λαμβάνει τὸ πόμα τῶν ὑδάτων· Virus non effert secum, sed in latibulo relinquit, et sic accedens aquarum potum sumit. Et Eustathius in Hexaëmero, Ὅταν δὲ διψήσῃ τὸν ἰὸν πρότερον ἀποτίθεται, καὶ οὕτως ἐκπίνει τὸ ὕδωρ ἐκ τῆς πηγῆς· Cum sitit, virus ante deponit, atque ita aquam ex fonte bibit: nempe ne eum venenum, aqua concretum, occidat, ut addit auctor Epistolae ad Praesidium. Non absimile est, quod multi scribunt, viperam, cum muraena coituram, virus suum prius evomere, tanquam αἰδουμένην τὸν γάμον, nuptias reveritam, ut ait Basilius Hom. 7. in Hexaëm. Sed ut fabulosum id rejicit Andreas b) in libro Περὶ τῶν ψευδῶς πεπιστευμένων. Quamvis, praeter Basilium c) et Ambrosium, auctores habeat Nicandrum d), Aelianum e), Oppianum f), Licinium Macrum g), Achillem Tatium h), Philen in Iambis i), et Isidorum k), aliosque non parvo numero.

The Physiologus of Epiphanius offers four proofs of the serpent's prudence. First, when it senses old age coming on, it seeks a rock and ῥαγαδαστεύει [ragadasteuei], προκύψας δὲ διὰ τῆς ὀπῆς ὠθεῖται περάσαι, καὶ ἐκβάλλει τὸ γῆρας [prokypsas de dia tēs opēs ōtheitai perasai, kai ekballei to gēras], it slips into a crevice, and, bending forward, strives to pass through the hole, and puts off its old age. And this all assert with one voice. Second, although it flees from a clothed man, when it sees the same man naked, καταθαῤῥεῖ αὐτοῦ [katatharrei autou], it attacks him confidently. This too might seem consistent with reason; yet others expressly teach the opposite. Eustathius in the Hexaemeron: Ἐὰν δὲ γυμνὸν θεάσηται ἄνθρωπον οὐ πρόσεισιν· εἰ δὲ ἐνδεδυμένον, ἐφάλλεται [Ean de gymnon theasētai anthrōpon ou proseisin; ei de endedymenon, ephalletai]; If it has seen a naked man, it does not approach; but if it has seen a clothed one, it attacks. Jerome, or whoever is the author of the Letter to Praesidius under Jerome's name: The snake fears a naked man, and pursues a clothed one. Isidore, book 12, ch. 4: It is said, moreover, that the serpent does not dare to touch a naked man. Damir: ومن عجيب امره انها تهرب من الرجل العريان [wa-min ʿajīb amrihi annahā tahrub min al-rajul al-ʿuryān] Among the marvels of its nature is that it flees from a naked man. And Olaus writes that he has experienced this not rarely. Isidore, he says, offers a favourable word about the nature of serpents, that they never harm a naked and sleeping man III, 248: and this happened to me in boyhood and youth, when I very often encountered serpents without harm. The same author offers a third proof of the serpent's prudence: that when attacked by a man it keeps only its head unharmed and exposes the rest of its body. Since I have already said much about this, I shall add only this from Caesarius, Dial. 4, Quaest. 190: Κατευναζόμενος δὲ, καὶ καθεύδων (ὁ ὄφις) τροχίζων ἑαυτὸν, μέσην ὅλου τοῦ σώματος κεφαλὴν ἀσφαλίζεται, οἱονεὶ τειχίῳ τῷ ἐφεπομένῳ ὁλκῷ περιοχυρῶν αὐτήν [Kateunazomenos de, kai katheudōn (ho ophis) trochizōn heauton, mesēn holou tou sōmatos kephalēn asphalizetai, hoionei teichiō tō epheponemō holkō periochyrōn autēn]; When the serpent gives itself to rest in order to sleep, coiling itself up, it secures its head in the middle of its whole body, encircling it with the following length of its body as with a wall. Fourth, when it comes to a spring to drink, οὐ φέρει τὸν ἰὸν, ἀλλά γε ἀφεὶς αὐτὸν ἐν τῇ νεοττίᾳ, οὕτω καθαρὸς πορεύεται [ou pherei ton ion, alla ge apheis auton en tē neottia, houtō katharos poreuetai], it does not carry its poison along, but leaving it in its nest, it approaches thus pure. The same author sets this out as follows in Haer. 37: Οὐ συμπαραλαμβάνει τὸν ἰὸν μεθ᾽ ἑαυτοῦ, ἀλλὰ ἐν τῷ φωλεῷ καταλιμπάνει, καὶ οὕτως ἐλθὼν λαμβάνει τὸ πόμα τῶν ὑδάτων [Ou symparalambanei ton ion meth' heautou, alla en tō phōleō katalimpanei, kai houtōs elthōn lambanei to poma tōn hydatōn]; It does not bring its poison out with it, but leaves it in its lair, and approaching thus takes its drink of the waters. And Eustathius in the Hexaemeron: Ὅταν δὲ διψήσῃ τὸν ἰὸν πρότερον ἀποτίθεται, καὶ οὕτως ἐκπίνει τὸ ὕδωρ ἐκ τῆς πηγῆς [Hotan de dipsēsē ton ion proteron apotithetai, kai houtōs ekpinei to hydōr ek tēs pēgēs]; When it is thirsty, it first lays down its poison, and so drinks water from the spring: namely, lest the poison, congealed by the water, should kill it, as the author of the Letter to Praesidius adds. Not unlike this is what many write, that the viper, when about to mate with the moray, first vomits out its poison, as if αἰδουμένην τὸν γάμον [aidoumenēn ton gamon], revering the marriage, as Basil says, Hom. 7 on the Hexaem. But Andreas b) rejects this as fabulous in his book Περὶ τῶν ψευδῶς πεπιστευμένων [Peri tōn pseudōs pepisteumenōn]. Although, besides Basil c) and Ambrose, it has as authorities Nicander d), Aelian e), Oppian f), Licinius Macer g), Achilles Tatius h), Philes in the Iambics i), and Isidore k), and others in no small number.


His ex Plinio addi queat, serpentem, hyberna latebra visu obscurato, oculos marathro inungere ac refovere. Si vero squamae obtorpuerunt, spinis juniperi scabere, et draconem vernam nauseam lactucae succo restinguere. Quae naturali solertia fieri verisimilius, quam qui quadam θεηλάτῳ, prout Arabes sibi fingunt. In his الزمخشري Azzammachsari, scriptor, prae caeteris fabulosus, cujus verba sunt: حكي ان الافعي اذا اتت عليها الف سنة عميت وقد الهمها الله ان تمسح عينيها بورق الرازيانج الرطب فير اليها بصرها وربما كان III, 249 في برية بينها وبين الريف مسيرة ثلثة ايام فتطوي تلك المسافة علي طولها وعلي عماها حتي تهاجم في بعض البساتين علي شجر الرازيانج لاتحظيه فتحك به عينها فترجع باصرة باذن الله تعالي Vipe- ram ajunt, cum vixit mille annis, excaecari, et inspirare illi Deum, ut ungat oculos suos recentis foeniculi folio, et recuperare visum. Quin nonnunquam est in deserto; et inter eam et locum cultum trium dierum iter intercedit. Quod spatium, quantum quantum est, illa emetitur, donec in aliquem hortum ingressa in foeniculi plantam incidat, a qua haudquaquam aberrat, et ea confricat oculos, et cum bono Deo redit illi visus. Non dissimilem fabulam narrat Abugiani Thaugidaeus الشمسية, id est, Solarem dici serpentis genus, qui, cum oculi debilitari incipiunt, septem diebus continuis eos per horae spatium ad solem obvertit, at-que ea ratione visum illius acui et intendi.

To these may be added from Pliny that the serpent, when its sight has been dimmed in its winter hiding place, anoints and refreshes its eyes with fennel; and if its scales have grown stiff, it scrapes itself on the thorns of the juniper; and that the dragon relieves its spring nausea with the juice of lettuce. It is more probable that these things happen by natural skill than by some θεηλάτῳ [theēlatō] impulse, as the Arabs imagine. Among them is الزمخشري [al-Zamakhsharī] Azzammachsari, a writer fabulous above others, whose words are: حكي ان الافعي اذا اتت عليها الف سنة عميت وقد الهمها الله ان تمسح عينيها بورق الرازيانج الرطب فير اليها بصرها وربما كان III, 249 في برية بينها وبين الريف مسيرة ثلثة ايام فتطوي تلك المسافة علي طولها وعلي عماها حتي تهاجم في بعض البساتين علي شجر الرازيانج لاتحظيه فتحك به عينها فترجع باصرة باذن الله تعالي [ḥukiya anna al-afʿā idhā atat ʿalayhā alf sana ʿamiyat wa-qad alhamahā Allāh an tamsaḥ ʿaynayhā bi-waraq al-rāziyānaj al-raṭb fa-yr ilayhā baṣaruhā wa-rubbamā kāna fī barriyya baynahā wa-bayna al-rīf masīrat thalathat ayyām fa-taṭwī tilka al-masāfa ʿalā ṭūlihā wa-ʿalā ʿamāhā ḥattā tuhājim fī baʿḍ al-basātīn ʿalā shajar al-rāziyānaj lā tukhṭīhi fa-taḥukk bihi ʿaynahā fa-tarjiʿ bāṣira bi-idhn Allāh taʿālā] They say that the viper, when it has lived a thousand years, is blinded, and that God inspires it to anoint its eyes with a leaf of fresh fennel, and it recovers its sight. Indeed sometimes it is in the desert, and between it and cultivated land there lies a journey of three days. This distance, however great it is, it traverses, until, having entered some garden, it comes upon a fennel plant, from which it by no means strays, and it rubs its eyes on it, and with God's favour its sight returns to it. Abugiani Thaugidaeus tells a not dissimilar fable: that a kind of serpent is called الشمسية [al-shamsiyya], that is, the Solar, which, when its eyes begin to weaken, turns them toward the sun for the space of an hour on seven successive days, and that by this means its sight is sharpened and strengthened.


Etiam huc referunt, quod aspidem dicit Psaltes aures obturare ad cantum, Psal. LVIII, 7. Quasi mira quadam sagacitate, cum primum aspis audit incantatorem, aurium unam terrae applicet, alteram cauda obturet, ne incantationi via pateat. Sed suo loco Arabes nos docebunt, haec multo aliter accipi.

They also refer to this the Psalmist's statement that the asp stops its ears against the chant, Ps 58:7: as though, with a kind of wonderful sagacity, as soon as the asp hears the charmer, it presses one ear to the ground and stops the other with its tail, so that no way lies open to the incantation. But in their place the Arabs will teach us that these words are to be understood quite otherwise.


Consalus Pontius de Leon in Notis ad Epiphanii Physiologum serpentis solertiam sitam esse vult in agilitate corporis, quam in dracone potissimum commendat antiquissimus ille Taautus, cum apud Eusebium lib. 1. Praeparat. draconem tradit esse πνευματικώτατον τὸ ζῶον πάντων τῶν ἑρπετῶν καὶ πυρῶδες. παρ᾽ ᾧ καὶ τάχος ἀνυπέρβλητον διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος παρίστησι, χωρὶς ποδῶν τε, καὶ χειρῶν, ἢ ἄλλου τινὸς τῶν ἔξωθεν, ἐξ ὧν τὰ λοιπὰ ζῶα τὰς κινήσεις ποιεῖται, καὶ ποικίλων σχημάτων τύπους ἀποτελεῖ, καὶ κατὰ τὴν πορείαν ἑλικοειδεῖς ἔχει τὰς ὁρμὰς, ἐφ᾽ ὃ βούλεται τάχος· Omnium reptilium maxime spiritualis, et igneae naturae, unde est, quod per solos spiritus eximiam celerita- tem consequitur, absque manuum, aut pedum, aut exterioris ullius organi adju- mento, per quae reliqua moventur animalia; et in varias figuras se conformat, adeoque inter gradiendum flexuoso fertur impetu quamlibet citissime. A qua sententia parum recedit Laurentius Ramirez Pentecontarchi sui capite primo, ubi serpentem contendit non alia de causa dici φρόνιμον, Gen. III. et Matth. X. quam quia nullum est animal, quod se insinuet magis. Unde ortum vult habere, quod angues in Mercurii caduceo impliciti finguntur, quia summi oratoris, qualis credebatur Mercurius, munus vel praecipuum est insinuatio. Addit, Evam lusitare solitam cum serpente, eoque sinus ornare, et collum, ac brachia: ideoque monilia hodieque fieri ad serpentum similitudinem, quae Graeci III, 250 ὄφεις appellant. Quod, praeter Nicostratum et Athenaeum, testatur etiam Clemens lib. 2. Paedagogi. Sed hae illius conjecturae longius petitae sunt, quam ut me in assensum trahant. Maxime cum ערמה aut φρόνησιν, vel pro corporis agilitate, vel pro insinuatione sumi nusquam legerim: et, ut demus, alibi sic usurpari, tamen in Christi verbis, Este φρόνιμοι, prudentes sicut serpentes, et simplices sicut columbae, ratio oppositionis docet, vocem φρόνιμοι intelligendam esse, ut sonat. Neque enim corporis agilitas, aut insinuatio, sed prudentia simplicitati opponitur. Unde Martialis lib. 10. Epigr. 47.

Consalus Pontius de Leon, in his Notes on the Physiologus of Epiphanius, holds that the serpent's shrewdness consists in the agility of its body. This is what that most ancient Taautus especially praises in the dragon, when, in Eusebius, book 1 of the Praeparatio, he relates that the dragon is πνευματικώτατον τὸ ζῶον πάντων τῶν ἑρπετῶν καὶ πυρῶδες. παρ᾽ ᾧ καὶ τάχος ἀνυπέρβλητον διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος παρίστησι, χωρὶς ποδῶν τε, καὶ χειρῶν, ἢ ἄλλου τινὸς τῶν ἔξωθεν, ἐξ ὧν τὰ λοιπὰ ζῶα τὰς κινήσεις ποιεῖται, καὶ ποικίλων σχημάτων τύπους ἀποτελεῖ, καὶ κατὰ τὴν πορείαν ἑλικοειδεῖς ἔχει τὰς ὁρμὰς, ἐφ᾽ ὃ βούλεται τάχος [pneumatikōtaton to zōon pantōn tōn herpetōn kai pyrōdes. par᾽ hō kai tachos anyperblēton dia tou pneumatos paristēsi, chōris podōn te, kai cheirōn, ē allou tinos tōn exōthen, ex hōn ta loipa zōa tas kinēseis poieitai, kai poikilōn schēmatōn typous apotelei, kai kata tēn poreian helikoeideis echei tas hormas, eph᾽ ho bouletai tachos]: of all reptiles the most spiritual and of a fiery nature; hence it attains extraordinary speed by its breath alone, without the aid of hands or feet or any external organ by which the other animals move; and it shapes itself into various figures, and so, as it goes, it is carried with a winding impetus as swiftly as it pleases. Not far from this opinion is Laurentius Ramirez, in the first chapter of his Pentecontarchus, where he contends that the serpent is called φρόνιμον [phronimon], Gen. III. and Matth. X., for no other reason than that no animal insinuates itself more. From this, he holds, arose the fact that snakes are represented entwined on the caduceus of Mercury, because insinuation is the chief, or nearly the chief, task of the supreme orator, such as Mercury was believed to be. He adds that Eve used to play with the serpent and adorn her bosom, neck and arms with it; and that for this reason necklaces are made even today in the likeness of serpents, which the Greeks III, 250 call ὄφεις [opheis]. This, besides Nicostratus and Athenaeus, Clement also attests in book 2 of the Paedagogus. But these conjectures of his are too far-fetched to draw me into assent. Especially since I have nowhere read ערמה or φρόνησιν [phronēsin] taken either for agility of body or for insinuation; and, granting that they are so used elsewhere, yet in Christ's words, Be φρόνιμοι [phronimoi], prudent as serpents, and simple as doves, the logic of the antithesis shows that the word φρόνιμοι [phronimoi] must be understood as it sounds. For it is not agility of body or insinuation, but prudence, that is opposed to simplicity. Hence Martial, book 10, Epigr. 47:


— — Prudens simplicitas, pares amici.

— — Prudent simplicity, friends who are equals.


Et Paulus Rom. XVI, 9. Volo vos sapientes, id est, prudentes, esse in bono, et simplices in malo. Itaque serpens vere ערום, id est, φρόνιμος, prudens, vel πανοῦργος, callidus est, quantum in brutum cadere possunt calliditas, aut prudentia.

And Paul, Rom 16:9: I would have you wise, that is, prudent, in what is good, and simple in what is evil. Therefore the serpent is truly ערום, that is, φρόνιμος [phronimos], prudent, or πανοῦργος [panourgos], cunning, so far as cunning or prudence can belong to a brute.


Quod ipsum in causa fuit, cur hoc organo diabolus uteretur ad seducendum hominem. Quasi fuerit vero similius, a tam vafro animali tam vafra consilia proficisci, ne fraudem suboleret Eva. Id vero cum Satanae successisset ex voto, Deus non illi solum, sed et serpenti maledixit, tanquam instrumento seductionis. Ita judex falsarium una cum calamo damnat, et sicarium cum suo telo. Et si quis cum jumento rem habuerit, divina lex jumentum etiam morte mulctari jubet, Lev. XX, 15. Et bovem cornupetam Deus una cum domino occidi voluit, si quem feriisset per domini negligentiam, Exod. XXI, 28. 29.

This very thing was the reason why the devil used this instrument to seduce man: as though it were more plausible that such crafty counsels should proceed from so crafty an animal, so that Eve might not scent the fraud. But when this had succeeded for Satan as he wished, God cursed not him alone but also the serpent, as the instrument of the seduction. So a judge condemns the forger together with his pen, and the assassin with his weapon. And if anyone has lain with a beast, the divine law orders the beast also to be punished with death, Lev 20:15. And God willed a goring ox to be killed together with its owner if it had struck someone through the owner's negligence, Exod 21:28–29.


In parte maledictionis est mutuum inter serpentem et hominem odium. Ponam inimicitias inter te et mulierem, Gen. III, 15. Cujus odii ratione scribebat Hyperides 1) in Oratione contra Demadem, τοὺς ὄφεις μισητοὺς εἶναι πάντας, odio dignos esse serpentes omnes; et Theocritus, Idyll. 15.

Part of the curse is the mutual hatred between the serpent and man: I will put enmity between you and the woman, Gen 3:15. On account of this hatred Hyperides 1) wrote in his Oration against Demades, τοὺς ὄφεις μισητοὺς εἶναι πάντας [tous opheis misētous einai pantas], that all serpents are worthy of hatred; and Theocritus, Idyll 15:


Ἐκ παιδὸς τὸν ψυχρὸν ὄφιν τὰ μάλιστα δέδοικα, A teneris fuit horrori mihi frigidus anguis.

Ἐκ παιδὸς τὸν ψυχρὸν ὄφιν τὰ μάλιστα δέδοικα [Ek paidos ton psychron ophin ta malista dedoika], From childhood the cold snake has been my horror.


Plautus etiam in Mercatore, Act. 4. Nempe ruri est uxor tua, quam dudum dixeras te odisse aeque atque angues. Hinc Artemidorus, Onirocrit. lib. 2. Ὄφις ἔχθραν ἐπάγει· ὅπως δ᾽ ἂν διαθῇ τινα, οὕτως καὶ ὁ ἐχθρὸς τὸν ἰδόντα διαθή-σει. Serpens, in somnis visus, inimicitias conciliat: quomodocunque igitur aliquem (in somnis) divexaverit, eodem modo, quisquis viderit, ab hoste investabitur.

Plautus too, in the Mercator, Act 4: Your wife, of course, is in the country, whom you said a while ago you hated as much as snakes. Hence Artemidorus, Onirocritica book 2: Ὄφις ἔχθραν ἐπάγει· ὅπως δ᾽ ἂν διαθῇ τινα, οὕτως καὶ ὁ ἐχθρὸς τὸν ἰδόντα διαθήσει [Ophis echthran epagei; hopōs d᾽ an diathē tina, houtōs kai ho echthros ton idonta diathēsei]. A serpent, seen in dreams, brings about enmities: in whatever way, then, it has harassed someone (in dreams), in the same way whoever has seen it will be assailed by an enemy.

R1 Rosenmüller, III, 222 SCHNURRER, in his Dissertat. in Esaj. XXVII. (in his collected Dissertations, p. 323 ff.), following ED. POCOCK in his Comment. ad Mic 1:8, holds that two names must be distinguished, similar indeed, but nonetheless truly different. The one is תן, the jackal, or wild dog [which among the Hebrews is called by other names, אי and שועל; see above vol. 1, book 3, Chapter 12, 13]; it does not occur in the singular in the surviving Hebrew literature, and has a plural of several forms, תנים, תנין and תנות. The other is תנין, for which in Ezekiel תנים occurs twice, perhaps only through the carelessness of copyists; its plural is תנינים, and it means dragon and things similar to it. This is confirmed not only by the authority and agreement of the Arabic dialect, in which تِنّينٌ [tinnīn] is dragon, great serpent, while تِينان [tīnān] is wolf, which is closely related to that wild dog, but also by R. Tanchum, a Jew of Jerusalem and a most excellent commentator, who in his Arabic commentary, a copy of which exists in the Bodleian Library at Oxford, in several places (on Mic 1:8. Jer 9:10. Lam 4:3. Mal 1:3) denies that the meaning dragon can apply, and teaches that the animal called ابن اوي [ibn awī], ibn awi, or ابن واوي [ibn wāwī], ibn wawi, is to be understood. To this is added the authority of the Syriac translator of the Old Testament, who uses now a word agreeing with the Hebrew, ܬܢܝܢܐ [תנינא], now another name, ܝܪܘܪܐ [ירורא], meaning wild dog or jackal. Nor does the Syriac translator use these words indiscriminately and at random, but in such a way that he is readily seen to have kept a fixed and consistent rule. For he employs the word ܝܪܘܪܐ [ירורא] wherever the Hebrew text has the plural תנים, or תנין, or תנות, with the single exception of Ps 44:20. Conversely, whenever תנין occurs in the singular (to which the form תנים, used twice by Ezekiel, XXIX, 3. and XXXII, 3., also belongs), or its plural, III, 223 תנינים, the Syriac too uses the name that corresponds exactly to it, ܬܢܝܢܐ [תנינא]. The Chaldee version agrees with the Syriac in this way: where the latter uses the word ܝܪܘܪܐ [ירורא], the former puts ירורא, which was indeed usually taken in the sense of dragon, but plainly arose from the confusion of the similar letters ד and ר, and so is to be restored to ירודא and taken in the same sense which, as POCOCK attests, the Syriac writers themselves give to the word ܝܪܘܪܐ [ירורא], namely jackal. [But what if the confusion of the letters ? and ; occurred in the Syriac version, so that, on the evidence of the Chaldee version, which consistently has ירודא, ܝܪܘܕܐ [ירודא] should be restored for ܝܪܘܪܐ [ירורא]?] CHR. LI, 9.), its bellowing (Mic 1:8). Moreover, that in Lam 4:3 the תנין are said to give the breast to their young, and that in Jer 14:6. Ps 74:13 their heads are described as standing above the waters to catch the air, suits the hippopotamus best. Although this view has something to commend it at first sight, it is entirely without the support of the other dialects cognate with Hebrew and of the agreement of the ancient translators. To me, from the primary meaning of the verb تنّ [tanna], which the Arab lexicographers, as ALB. SCHULTENS reports in his Comment. ad Iob. XL, 20, p. 1170, explain by the synonym قصع [qaṣaʿa], that is, to swallow, to swallow down, with jaws wide open, تنين [tinnīn] and תנין seem to embrace any terrible beasts of immense size, aquatic as well as terrestrial (a meaning most fitting in Isa 34:13. Jer 9:10), yet so that it is sometimes also used of certain particular huge and harmful beasts, such as serpents, Exod 7:9 compared with IV, 3. VII, 15., the crocodile, Ps 74:1314. Esaj. XXVII, 1., in which places תנין and לויתן are used interchangeably, and sea monsters, Genes. I, 21. Ps 104:26. CXLVIII, 7.

Part 2, Book 4, chapter 1: The names and kinds of the locusts
------------------------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/locustae-nomina.html

III, 251 col. 441 CAP. I.

III, 251 col. 441 Chapter I.


Locustarum nomina et species.

The names and kinds of locusts.


Vt Hebraeorum terra locustis, ita lingua locustarum nominibus est maxime foecunda. Nam, ut Talmudica taceam, quae magno numero occurrunt, in solis Prophetarum scriptis doctores decem numerant. Ea sunt 1. ארבה arbe. 2. גוב gob, vel גובי gobai. 3. גזם gazam. 4. חגב chagab. 5. חנמל chanamal. 6. חסיל chasil. 7. חרגל chargal. 8. ילק jelek. 9. סלעם solam. 10. צלצל col. 442 tselatsal. Quarum vocum origines, cum pleraeque parum notae sint, hic obiter explicare operae pretium esse duximus: quia res latet in verbis, et ex nominibus multa eruuntur, quae ad horum animalium naturam pertinent.

As the land of the Hebrews is most fertile in locusts, so is their language in names for locusts. For, to say nothing of the Talmudic ones, which occur in great number, in the writings of the Prophets alone the doctors count ten. They are: 1. ארבה arbe. 2. גוב gob, or גובי gobai. 3. גזם gazam. 4. חגב chagab. 5. חנמל chanamal. 6. חסיל chasil. 7. חרגל chargal. 8. ילק jelek. 9. סלעם solam. 10. צלצל col. 442 tselatsal. Since the origins of these words are for the most part little known, we have thought it worthwhile to explain them here in passing: for the thing lies hidden in the words, and much that pertains to the nature of these animals is drawn out of their names.


I. Primum ארבה arbe, Aben Ezra in Leviticum recte deducit מלשון רבוי, ex significatione multitudinis. Nam רבה raba multum esse, vel multiplicari significat. Unde ארבה arbe, praefixo Aleph, ut passim. Nec obscurum, cur a copia locustae nomen traxerint, cum nullum animal sit foecundius. Hinc de Ma- col. 443 dianitis Iud. VI, 5. Et veniebant ut locustae, ipsi, et cameli eorum innumeri. Et Iudic. VII, 12. Diffusi erant in ea convalle, tanquam locustae multitudine. Et Psal. CV, 34. Et venit locusta et bruchus; cujus non erat numerus. Et Ierem. XLVI, 23. de sylvae arboribus, Quia plures sunt locustis, neque illis est numerus. Et LI, 14. Nisi te impleam hominibus, quasi bruchis. Et Ioel. I, 6. de locustis, Iudaeam devastaturis, Gens ascendit contra terram tuam valida et innumerabilis. Et Nahum III, 15. Esto tam copiosa quam bruchus, tam copiosa quam locusta. Et III, 252 Iudith. II, 11. Conveniebant ad eos ut locustae, et ut arena terrae: innumerabiles enim erant prae multitudine. Et de locustis Aegypti Exod. X, 5. Operient super- ficiem terrae, ita, ut non possit quisquam videre terram. Hinc Hieronymus in Ioelem, Quid locustis innumerabilius? Et vulgare Arabum proverbium, مال كالدبا Opes (vel pecudes) ut locustae, id est, valde copiosae. Sed haec nemini non nota sunt (1).

I. The first, ארבה arbe, Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] on Leviticus rightly derives מלשון רבוי, from the meaning of multitude. For רבה raba means to be much or to be multiplied. Hence ארבה arbe, with Aleph prefixed, as often. Nor is it obscure why locusts took their name from abundance, since no animal is more prolific. Hence of the Midianites col. 443 Iud. VI, 5: And they came like locusts, they and their camels without number. And Judg 7:12: They were spread out in that valley like locusts in multitude. And Ps 105:34: And the locust came, and the bruchus, of which there was no number. And Jer 46:23, of the trees of the forest: Because they are more than locusts, and there is no number of them. And LI, 14: Surely I will fill you with men, as with bruchi. And Joel 1:6, of the locusts that were to lay waste Judaea: A nation is come up against your land, strong and without number. And Nahum III, 15: Be as numerous as the bruchus, as numerous as the locust. And III, 252 Jdt 2:11: They gathered to them like locusts, and like the sand of the earth: for they were innumerable for multitude. And of the locusts of Egypt, Exod 10:5: They shall cover the face of the earth, so that no one can see the earth. Hence Jerome on Joel: What is more innumerable than locusts? And the common proverb of the Arabs, مال كالدبا [māl ka-l-dabā] Wealth (or cattle) like locusts, that is, very abundant. But these things are known to everyone R1.


II. At locusta cur Hebraice dicitur גוב gob, vel גובי gobai, Amos VII, 1. et Nahum III, 17. et Arabice جاب gab, vel جابي gabi, adhuc nescirem; nisi me docuissent Arabes, apud quos جبا gaba Verbum e terra emergere significat, quod locustarum proprium. Aristoteles lib. 5. Historiae capite 28. Ὅταν τέκωσιν (αἱ ἀκρίδες) ἐνταῦθα γίνονται σκώληκες ὠοειδεῖς, οἳ περιλαμβάνονται III, 253 ὑπό τινος γῆς λεπτῆς, ὥσπερ ὑφ᾽ ὑμένος· ἐν ταύτῃ δὲ ἐκπέτονται. Cum locustae pepererunt, ibi fiunt vermes ovorum specie, qui terra quadam praetenui, tanquam membranula, ambiuntur, unde evolant. Gaza, Qua dissecta, emergunt locustae, ac evolant. Plinius lib. II. cap. 29. Hae pariunt in terram demisso spinae caule ova condensa autumni tempore. Ea durant hyeme sub terra: subsequente autem exitu veris, emittunt parvas, etc. Eodem refero, quod ab Aethiopibus et Troglodytis locustae vocantur አንበጣ፡ anbat. Nempe Arabice نبط nabata est scaturire, atque e terra emanare ac emergere. Quod quidem fontium proprium, sed et ad alia transfertur καταχρηστικῶς (2).

II. But why the locust is called in Hebrew גוב gob, or גובי gobai, Amos 7:1 and Nahum III, 17., and in Arabic جاب [jāb] gab, or جابي [jābī] gabi, I would still not know, had not the Arabs taught me, among whom the verb جبا [jabā] gaba means to emerge from the earth, which is characteristic of locusts. Aristotle, History book 5, chapter 28: Ὅταν τέκωσιν (αἱ ἀκρίδες) ἐνταῦθα γίνονται σκώληκες ὠοειδεῖς, οἳ περιλαμβάνονται [Hotan tekōsin (hai akrides) entautha ginontai skōlēkes ōoeideis, hoi perilambanontai] III, 253 ὑπό τινος γῆς λεπτῆς, ὥσπερ ὑφ᾽ ὑμένος· ἐν ταύτῃ δὲ ἐκπέτονται [hypo tinos gēs leptēs, hōsper hyph᾽ hymenos; en tautē de ekpetontai]. When the locusts have laid, there arise there egg-shaped grubs, which are enclosed by a very thin earth, as by a little membrane, from which they fly out. Gaza: When this is split open, the locusts emerge and fly out. Pliny, book 11, ch. 29: These lay their eggs, packed close, in the ground in autumn, letting down the stalk of their spine. They last through the winter under the ground; and at the following end of spring they send forth small ones, etc. To the same I refer the fact that by the Ethiopians and Troglodytes locusts are called አንበጣ፡ [ʾanəbaṭā] anbat. For in Arabic نبط [nabaṭa] nabata is to gush forth, and to issue and emerge from the earth. This indeed is proper to springs, but it is also transferred to other things καταχρηστικῶς [katachrēstikōs] R2.


III. Tertium locustae nomen גזם gazam, Ioel I, 4. et II, 25. et Amos IV, 9. Hebraei deducunt a גוז guz, vel גזז gazaz, quod tondere est et abscindere. Et Finale Mem Servile esse volunt; quamvis simile Nomen nullum proferant. Quippe חנם, gratis, ריקם, frustra, דומם, quiete, יומם, interdiu, אמנם, vere, quae hic citant, non sunt Nomina, sed Adverbia. Itaque vera Radix est Verbum גזם gazam, quod Talmudici in abscindendi et amputandi notione quandoque usurpant: ut in Avoda Zara fol. 50. b. אין מגזמין וסכין שמן בגזום, Non amputant ramos arborum, sed oleum ungunt in locum amputationis. Sic Arabice in Alcamus, جَزَمَ النحل, Putavit palmam. Aethiopice etiam occurrit pro ἐκκόπτειν Matth. III, 10. et VII, 19. Luc. III, 9. et XIII, 7. 9. In quibus locis aeque agitur de arborum amputatione. Inde igitur locustae dictae; quia praeacutis dentibus non solum gramen, et segetes, atque arborum folia, sed et cortices, ipsosque arborum teneriores ramusculos ita erodunt, ac si amputarent. Plinius ubi supra; Multa contactu adurentes: omnia vero morsu erodentes, et fores quoque tectorum. Hieronymus in Ioelem cap. 1. Iudaei putant, in diebus Ioel tam innumerabilem locustarum super Iudaeam venisse multitudinem, ut cuncta complerent, et non dicam fruges, sed ne vinearum quidem, et arborum cortices ramosque dimitterent. Sed et Amos IV, 9. Hortos vestros, et vineas vestras, et ficeta vestra, et oliveta vestra יאכל הגזם, comedet Gazam (seu locusta). Proin- col. 444 de Pisidas locustarum agminibus tribuit μυριόστομον ξίφος, ensem decies mille acierum. Haec ex Hebraeorum mente, qui summo consensu statuunt, גזם gazam esse locustae speciem: Chaldaeum scilicet sequuti, cui gazam est זחלא, locusta repens, III, 254 seu ἄπτερος, ut infra docebimus. Syrus quoque reddit ܡܫܘܛܐ eodem sensu. Inversum enim est ܡܫܘܛܐ ex Chaldaeo שמוטא. Et שמוטא censetur inter locustae species, ut Hebraeum חסיל, pro quo habetur in Ionathane 1 Reg. VIII, 37. et Ioel. I, 4. (3). Sed Graecis et Hieronymo גזם gazam est κάμπη, eruca. Quam versionem etsi multis asserere conetur Fullerus in Miscel- laneis lib. 5. cap. 20. mihi tamen haud quaquam persuadet: cum, quia Hebraei, Chaldaei et Syri aliter sentiunt; tum, quia Nomen גזם gazam, a ramorum ampu- tatione factum, videtur erucae minus convenire, quam locustae, cujus fortior est morsus. Exurit enim potius, quam amputat erucae morsus. Columella,

III. The third name of the locust, גזם gazam, Joel 1:4 and II, 25. and Amos 4:9, the Hebrews derive from גוז guz or גזז gazaz, which means to shear and to cut off. And they hold that the final Mem is servile, although they produce no similar noun. For חנם, gratis [freely], ריקם, frustra [in vain], דומם, quiete [quietly], יומם, interdiu [by day], אמנם, vere [truly], which they cite here, are not nouns but adverbs. Therefore the true root is the verb גזם gazam, which the Talmudists sometimes use in the sense of cutting off and pruning: as in Avoda Zara fol. 50b, אין מגזמין וסכין שמן בגזום, They do not prune the branches of trees, but they smear oil on the place of the pruning. So in Arabic, in Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī], جَزَمَ النحل [jazama al-nakhl], He pruned the palm. In Ethiopic too it occurs for ἐκκόπτειν [ekkoptein], Matt 3:10 and VII, 19. Luke 3:9 and XIII, 7. 9. In these places too the subject is the cutting down of trees. From this, then, locusts were named, because with their very sharp teeth they gnaw not only grass, crops and the leaves of trees, but also the bark and the more tender twigs of the trees themselves, as if they were cutting them off. Pliny, in the place cited above: Scorching many things by their touch, but gnawing everything with their bite, even the doors of houses. Jerome on Joel ch. 1: The Jews think that in the days of Joel so innumerable a multitude of locusts came upon Judaea that they filled everything, and left, I will not say the crops, but not even the bark and branches of the vines and trees. And also Amos 4:9: Your gardens, and your vineyards, and your fig groves, and your olive groves יאכל הגזם, the Gazam (or locust) shall eat. Accordingly col. 444 Pisides attributes to the swarms of locusts a μυριόστομον ξίφος [myriostomon xiphos], a sword of ten thousand edges. So much according to the mind of the Hebrews, who with the greatest agreement hold that גזם gazam is a species of locust: following, of course, the Chaldee, for whom gazam is זחלא, the creeping locust, III, 254 or ἄπτερος [apteros], as we shall show below. The Syriac also renders it ܡܫܘܛܐ [משוטא] in the same sense. For ܡܫܘܛܐ [משוטא] is the Chaldee שמוטא inverted. And שמוטא is counted among the species of locust, as is the Hebrew חסיל, for which it stands in Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] on 1 Reg. VIII, 37. and Joel 1:4 R3. But for the Greeks and Jerome גזם gazam is κάμπη [kampē], caterpillar. Although Fuller [=Nicholas Fuller, Miscellanea theologica / sacra (1612–22)] in his Miscellanea, book 5, ch. 20, tries to defend this version with many arguments, he by no means persuades me: both because the Hebrews, Chaldeans and Syrians think otherwise, and because the name גזם gazam, formed from the pruning of branches, seems to suit the caterpillar less than the locust, whose bite is stronger. For the bite of the caterpillar scorches rather than cuts off. Columella:


— — — serpitque eruca per hortos,
Quos super ingrediens exurit semina morsu.

— — — and the caterpillar creeps through the gardens,
And, advancing over them, scorches the seedlings with its bite.


Itaque, ut ab erodendo ERUCA, sic ab urendo URUCA etiam appellatur. Glos- sae veteres Latino-Graecae, a Stephano editae, pag. 347. Uruca, κάμπη. Et Graeco-Latina pag. 501. Κάμπη λαχάνου, Eruca, uruca. Et pag. 516. Λα-χάνων κάμπη, urica. Quae tria loca cum se mutuo confirment, horum unus non debuit Fullero esse suspectus (4).

Therefore, just as it is called ERUCA from gnawing [erodere], so it is also called URUCA from burning [urere]. The old Latin-Greek Glosses edited by Stephanus, p. 347: Uruca, κάμπη [kampē]. And the Greek-Latin ones, p. 501: Κάμπη λαχάνου [Kampē lachanou], Eruca, uruca. And p. 516: Λαχάνων κάμπη [Lachanōn kampē], urica. Since these three places confirm one another, none of them ought to have been suspect to Fuller R4.


IV. Quartum locustae nomen חגב chagab notum esse asserit Aben Ezra in Leviticum מלשון ישמעאל, ex lingua Ismaelis, id est, Arabica: quod falsissimum. Quamvis enim apud Arabes quamplurima sint locustarum nomina, tamen huic simile nullum occurrit. Interim origo vocis potest esse Arabica. Nam III, 255 Arabicum Verbum حجب chagaba velare significat. Sic Avicenna capite De anatomia oculi, tunicam ἀραχνοειδῆν ideo subtilem esse docet, quia, si densa esset, يحجب الضو عن الجليدية lumen velaret ab hu- more glaciali, seu crystallino, id est, lumen ab eo arceret, tanquam oppanso velo. Unde حجاب chigab est velum Matth. XXVII, 51. et Hebr. VI, 19. et حاجب chagib, id est, janitor, Gen. XLIII, 16. 19. editionis Parisiensis; quia januam claudens ei quasi velum obtendit. Locustas igitur indidem חגבים cha- gabim, dictas fuisse putaverim; quia, cum turmatim volant, solis lumini velum videntur obtendere, ut infra docebimus in Ioel. II, 20. (5).

IV. Aben Ezra on Leviticus asserts that the fourth name of the locust, חגב chagab, is known מלשון ישמעאל, from the language of Ishmael, that is, Arabic: which is utterly false. For although among the Arabs there are very many names for locusts, none similar to this one occurs. Yet the origin of the word may be Arabic. For III, 255 the Arabic verb حجب [ḥajaba] chagaba means to veil. Thus Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)], in the chapter On the anatomy of the eye, teaches that the ἀραχνοειδῆν [arachnoeidēn] tunic is thin for this reason, that if it were dense, يحجب الضو عن الجليدية [yaḥjub al-ḍaw ʿan al-jalīdiyya] it would veil the light from the glacial humour, or crystalline, that is, it would keep the light from it as if by a veil spread before it. Hence حجاب [ḥijāb] chigab is the veil, Matt 27:51 and Heb 6:19, and حاجب [ḥājib] chagib, that is, doorkeeper, Gen 43:16 19. in the Paris edition; because in closing the door he as it were draws a veil over it. I would therefore think that locusts were called חגבים chagabim from the same source, because when they fly in swarms they seem to draw a veil over the light of the sun, as we shall show below on Joel 2:20 R5.


V. Quintum חנמל chanamal, Psal. LXXVIII, 47. pro locusta sumitur a R. Selomone et R. Chasane, quem citat Aben Ezra. Sed alii melius chanamal statuunt aliquid esse grandini analogum. Ut de more sint ἀντίστροφα duo ejusdem versus hemistichia, quae sic habent, Et occidit בברד, in grandine vites eorum, et sycomoros eorum בחנמל, in Chanamal. Ita Hebraea ad verbum. Itaque Aben Ezra lapides grandinis hic intelligit. Sed Saadias et Kimchius, id, quod Arabes vocant יאלצקיע, id est, pruinam (6). Recte omnino. Ita enim Graeci veteres, Καὶ τὰς συκαμίνους αὐτῶν ἐν τῇ πάχνῃ. Unde Vulgatus, Et moros eorum in pruina. Et Arabicum Psalterium vetus apud me manuscriptum وتوثهم بالصقيع. Et Aethiopicum, ወበለሶሞን፡ በአስሐትያ፡ omnes eodem sensu. Praeterea in Midras חנמל chanamal per metathesin dici asseritur pro נחמל nachamal; quia נח ומל nach vemal, quiescit et incidit. Quorum utrumque pruinae valde convenit. Hinc Theophrastus lib. 5. De causis cap. 19. nivem cum pruina conferens, Ἡ μὲν οὐκ ἐπιμένει, inquit, ἀλλ᾽ ἀποτήκεται ἀπὸ τῶν col. 445 κλημάτων, καὶ τῶν βλαστῶν· ἡ δὲ πάχνη (ἐπιμένουσα, id enim supplendum, ut oppositio constet) ταῦτ᾽ ἀποκαίει, illa quidem non diu manet, sed a palmiti- bus et germinibus liquescens delabitur: at pruina (diu manens) haec exurit. Et infra, Τμητικοτέρα δοκεῖ ἡ πάχνη τῆς χίονος εἶναι, Vim incidendi pruina quam III, 256 nix majorem habere videtur. Plinius quoque pruinam satis persidere scribit, id est, diu insidere. Verba sunt libri 17. cap. 24. Pruina perniciosior natura est, quoniam lapsa persidet. Pruinam igitur potius quam locustam voce חנמל significari, vero valde consentaneum est. Aliud ἐρυσίβη, rubigo. Tamen in Graeco Scholiaste in Psalmos ἐρυσίβη ἐςὶ κατὰ τὸν Ἡρωδιανὸν τὸ ἐπικάθιζον τοῖς καρ-ποῖς παχνῶδες, καὶ διαφθεῖρον αὐτοὺς, rubigo est juxta Herodianum pruinosum id, quod fructibus insidens eos corrumpit (7).

V. The fifth, חנמל chanamal, Ps 78:47, is taken for the locust by R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] and R. Chasan, whom Aben Ezra cites. But others more rightly hold that chanamal is something analogous to hail, so that, as usual, the two hemistichs of the same verse correspond (ἀντίστροφα [antistropha]). They read: And he destroyed בברד, with hail their vines, and their sycomores בחנמל, with Chanamal. So the Hebrew word for word. Accordingly Aben Ezra understands hailstones here. But Saadias and Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] understand what the Arabs call יאלצקיע, that is, hoarfrost R6. Quite rightly. For so the ancient Greeks: Καὶ τὰς συκαμίνους αὐτῶν ἐν τῇ πάχνῃ [Kai tas sykaminous autōn en tē pachnē]. Hence the Vulgate translator: And their mulberry trees with hoarfrost. And the old Arabic Psalter in manuscript in my possession: وتوثهم بالصقيع [wa-tūthahum bi-l-ṣaqīʿ]. And the Ethiopic: ወበለሶሞን፡ በአስሐትያ፡ [wabalasomon baʾasəḥatəyā]; all in the same sense. Moreover, in the Midrash it is asserted that חנמל chanamal is said by metathesis for נחמל nachamal, because נח ומל nach vemal, it rests and cuts. Both of these suit hoarfrost very well. Hence Theophrastus, book 5, De causis, ch. 19, comparing snow with hoarfrost, says: Ἡ μὲν οὐκ ἐπιμένει, ἀλλ᾽ ἀποτήκεται ἀπὸ τῶν col. 445 κλημάτων, καὶ τῶν βλαστῶν· ἡ δὲ πάχνη [Hē men ouk epimenei, all᾽ apotēketai apo tōn klēmatōn, kai tōn blastōn; hē de pachnē] (ἐπιμένουσα [epimenousa], for this must be supplied for the opposition to hold) ταῦτ᾽ ἀποκαίει [taut᾽ apokaiei], the former does not stay long, but melts and slips off the shoots and buds; but hoarfrost (staying long) burns them. And below: Τμητικοτέρα δοκεῖ ἡ πάχνη τῆς χίονος εἶναι [Tmētikotera dokei hē pachnē tēs chionos einai], Hoarfrost seems to have a greater power III, 256 of cutting than snow. Pliny too writes that hoarfrost persidere [settles in], that is, stays settled long. The words are in book 17, ch. 24: Hoarfrost is more destructive by nature, because once fallen it stays settled. It is therefore very consistent with the truth that the word חנמל signifies hoarfrost rather than the locust. Ἐρυσίβη [erysibē], blight, is something else. Yet in the Greek Scholiast on the Psalms: ἐρυσίβη ἐςὶ κατὰ τὸν Ἡρωδιανὸν τὸ ἐπικάθιζον τοῖς καρποῖς παχνῶδες, καὶ διαφθεῖρον αὐτοὺς [erysibē esti kata ton Hērōdianon to epikathizon tois karpois pachnōdes, kai diaphtheiron autous], blight, according to Herodian, is that frost-like thing which settles on the fruits and spoils them R7.
