Part 2, Book 4, chapter 3: The locusts of Egypt
-----------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/locustae-aegyptiae.html

III, 282 col. 460 CAP. III.

III, 282 col. 460 Chapter III.


De Locustis Aegyptiis, Exod. X, 4.

On the Egyptian Locusts, Exod 10:4.


In Prophetarum scriptis tres de locustis occurrunt vel historiae, vel prophetiae, prae caeteris insignes, ac proinde hic explicandae. Prima est de Aegyptiis locustis, id est, in Aegyptum a Deo immissis, post septem plagas atrocissimas, quibus frangi non potuerat Pharaonis contumacia [Exod. X, 4. seqq.]. In qua col. 461 historia, ut intelligantur, quae habentur de locustis, haec tria sunt observanda. 1. In genere, quantam locustae perniciem creent herbis, segetibus, arboribus, atque omni terrae proventui. 2. Quid in his locustis fuerit peculiare. 3. Quomodo in Aegyptum adductae fuerint, et ex Aegypto abductae. Et de primo frustra ageremus, si locustae nobis tam notae essent, quam Arabibus et Africanis, qui experiuntur indies, quam grave sit hoc malum. Cum jam paratis messibus, aut pratis, et pascuis, aut hortis, et pomariis incumbunt locustarum mille myriades, quae, totius anni laborem paucis horis absumentes, miseris incolis famem indicunt. Quam voracitatem et ingluviem Arabes exprimunt verbis احتنك ingurgitare (a حنك id est, faucibus, deducta voce) نعص vel لعص, vorare (Lam et Nun permutatis); دبش, decorticare (quod tamen de terra et agris, non de arboribus accipiunt, quasi fruges et herbae, quas absumunt locustae, sint terrae cortex); بشر, corii instar radere, et laevigare: جرد, deglabrare et depilare: unde et ipsi locustae nomen جراد. Nimirum haec animalcula, quidquid in agris viret, ingurgitant, vorant, excorticant, radunt, deglabrant. Neque solo morsu nocent, sed et contactu adurunt. Quin لعابهم سم ناقع للنبات والشجر لا يقع علي شي منه الا اهلكه saliva earum virus est, herbis et arboribus tam noxium, ut, in quodcunque incidat, id deperdat; ut in Damire legere est. Quae tamen levia videri queant, cum saepe multo plus damni mortuae quam vivae inferant, tetro et viroso odore aërem inficientes, unde gravissima sequitur lues, adeoque plures hominum myriades tali peste paucis diebus abripiuntur, quam diuturnis bellis; ut dicetur suo loco. Unde idem Damir, ليس في الحيوان اكثر افسان Nullum est animal perniciosius. Et Mahumetes, ut ajunt, الله خلق الف امة منها ستماية في البحر واربعماية في البر وان اول هلاك هذه الامم الجراد واذا اهلك الجراد تتابع هلاك الامم كنظم السلك Mille animalium species creavit III, 283 Deus, sexcentas in mari, et quadringentas in terra. Sed horum prima pestis est locusta, qua destruente sequitur reliquorum exitium, ut monile consertum: id est, ut baccae, in monili consertae, se mutuo subsequuntur (1).

In the writings of the Prophets there occur three histories or prophecies about locusts that are remarkable above the rest, and which must therefore be explained here. The first concerns the Egyptian locusts, that is, those sent by God into Egypt after the seven most dreadful plagues, by which the obstinacy of Pharaoh could not be broken [Exod 10:4 ff.]. In this col. 461 history, in order to understand what is said about the locusts, these three things must be observed. 1. In general, how great a destruction locusts cause to herbs, crops, trees and every produce of the earth. 2. What was peculiar in these locusts. 3. How they were brought into Egypt and carried away out of Egypt. On the first point we would labour in vain if locusts were as well known to us as to the Arabs and Africans, who learn daily how grievous this evil is. When the harvests are already ripe, or upon meadows and pastures, or upon gardens and orchards, a thousand myriads of locusts descend, which, consuming the labour of a whole year in a few hours, impose famine upon the wretched inhabitants. This voracity and gluttony the Arabs express by the words احتنك [iḥtanaka] to gulp down (a word derived from حنك [ḥanak], that is, the jaws); نعص [naʿaṣa] or لعص [laʿaṣa], to devour (Lam and Nun being interchanged); دبش [dabasha], to strip the bark (which, however, they take of the earth and the fields, not of trees, as if the crops and herbs that the locusts consume were the bark of the earth); بشر [bashara], to scrape like a hide, and to make smooth: جرد [jarada], to make bare and to strip of hair: whence also the very name of the locust, جراد [jarād]. Indeed these little creatures gulp down, devour, strip, scrape and make bare whatever is green in the fields. Nor do they harm by their bite alone; they also scorch by their touch. Moreover لعابهم سم ناقع للنبات والشجر لا يقع علي شي منه الا اهلكه [luʿābuhum samm nāqiʿ li-l-nabāt wa-l-shajar lā yaqaʿu ʿalā shayʾ minhu illā ahlakahu] their saliva is a poison so harmful to herbs and trees that whatever it falls upon, it destroys; as one may read in Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]. Yet these things may seem slight, since they often inflict much more damage dead than alive, infecting the air with a foul and poisonous stench, from which a most severe pestilence follows, so that more myriads of men are carried off by such a plague in a few days than by long wars; as will be said in its place. Hence the same Damir says: ليس في الحيوان اكثر افسان [laysa fī al-ḥayawān akthar afsān] There is no animal more destructive. And Muhammad, as they say: الله خلق الف امة منها ستماية في البحر واربعماية في البر وان اول هلاك هذه الامم الجراد واذا اهلك الجراد تتابع هلاك الامم كنظم السلك [Allāh khalaqa alf umma minhā sittumiʾa fī al-baḥr wa-arbaʿumiʾa fī al-barr wa-inna awwal halāk hādhihi al-umam al-jarād wa-idhā halaka al-jarād tatābaʿa halāk al-umam ka-naẓm al-silk] God created a thousand species of animals, III, 283 six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land. But the first plague of these is the locust; when it destroys, the ruin of the rest follows, like a strung necklace: that is, as the beads strung on a necklace follow one another R1.


III, 284 Sed in Aegyptiis locustis aliquid fuit solito gravius. Cum enim in Aegypto pestis nulla sit frequentior, tamen Moses diserte dicit a), his locustis neque pares unquam fuisse, neque in posterum futuras; sive fuerint mole majores; ut locustae illae Indicae, quas Plinius scribit lib. 9. cap. 3. quaterna cubita implere, et lib. 10. cap. 29. ternum pedum longitudinis esse, cruribus et feminibus serrarum usum praebentes, cum inaruerint: sive, quod credo potius, numero superaverint quidquam unquam fuit uspiam locustarum in uno loco, et magis noxiae fuerint. Quod suadent Prophetae verba, has terrae superficiem ita cooperuisse, col. 462 ut non potuerit quisquam videre terram; adeoque resedisse in universa Aegypti terra, cum in hunc vel illum agrum involare soleant, aliis praeteritis; et absumpsisse omnem herbam, et omnem fructum arborum, et quidquid residuum fecerat, quae praecesserat grando.

III, 284 But in the Egyptian locusts there was something more grievous than usual. For although no plague is more frequent in Egypt, Moses nevertheless says expressly a) that there had never been locusts like these, nor would there be in the future; whether because they were larger in bulk, like those Indian locusts which Pliny writes, book 9, ch. 3, fill four cubits, and book 10, ch. 29, are three feet in length, their legs and thighs serving as saws when they have dried out; or, as I rather believe, because they surpassed in number whatever swarm of locusts had ever been anywhere in one place, and were more harmful. This is suggested by the words of the Prophet: that they so covered the surface of the earth col. 462 that no one could see the ground; and that they settled over the whole land of Egypt, whereas locusts usually fly into this or that field, passing over others; and that they consumed every herb, and all the fruit of the trees, and whatever the hail that had gone before had left.


Ad quae verba si roges, Quod fuerit hoc residuum, cum grando percussisse legatur, quidquid erat in agris in tota terra Aegypti, et omnem herbam laesisse, et omnem arborem confregisse, Exod. IX, 25.? Respondeo, 1. Triticum et zeam a grandine non fuisse laesa. Ita enim habet sacer textus versib. 31. et 32. Linum autem et hordeum laesum fuit; quia hordeo erat calamus, et lino culmus. Triti- cum vero et zea laesa non fuerunt, eo quod erant serotina. Nempe triticum in il-lis locis hordeo serius provenit. Unde Clemens Alexandrinus lib. 6. Stromatum, III, 285 Προπετεστέρα εἰς ὥραν θέρους τοῦ πυροῦ, μᾶλλον ἡ κριθή· Hordeum est tritico citius tempore aestatis. Et Plinius lib. 18. cap. 17. In Aegypto hordeum sexto a satu mense, frumenta septimo metuntur: id est, uno mense serius (2). Hinc, cum hordeo collata אפילות, id est, serotina, vocantur. Non, quod sub terra plane laterent, ut ex Kimchio reddunt Iunius et Tremellius; pridem enim se exeruerant: sed quod, adhuc tenera, lenta flexilique sua mollitie ingruentes grandinis ictus evitarent et subterfugerent; ut a Fullero recte observatur Miscellaneorum lib. 3. cap. 11. Porro ut triticum et zeam, sic herbas quasdam, et gramina, nonnullarum quoque arborum ramos et fructus, grandinis impetum evasisse, vero consentaneum est. Itaque non citra hyperbolen grando laesisse legitur omnem herbam atque omnem arborem. Quod sequens exceptio aperte docet. Vel omnes herbas atque arbores ita laesisse dicenda est, ut non prorsus corruperit.

If at these words you ask what this remainder was, since we read that the hail struck whatever was in the fields in all the land of Egypt, and damaged every herb, and broke every tree, Exod 9:25? I answer: 1. The wheat and the spelt were not damaged by the hail. For so the sacred text has it in verses 31 and 32: But the flax and the barley were damaged, because the barley had its stalk, and the flax its stem. But the wheat and the spelt were not damaged, because they were late. For in those places wheat comes up later than barley. Hence Clement of Alexandria, book 6 of the Stromata, III, 285 Προπετεστέρα εἰς ὥραν θέρους τοῦ πυροῦ, μᾶλλον ἡ κριθή [propetestera eis hōran therous tou pyrou, mallon hē krithē]: Barley comes sooner than wheat in the summer season. And Pliny, book 18, ch. 17: In Egypt barley is reaped in the sixth month from sowing, wheat in the seventh: that is, one month later R2. Hence, compared with barley, they are called אפילות, that is, late. Not because they were still entirely hidden under the earth, as Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] and Tremellius [=Immanuel Tremellius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] render it following Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim]; for they had long since come up. Rather, being still tender, by their pliant and flexible softness they avoided and escaped the blows of the falling hail, as is rightly observed by Fuller [=Nicholas Fuller, Miscellanea theologica / sacra (1612–22)], Miscellanea book 3, ch. 11. Further, it is likely that, like the wheat and the spelt, certain herbs and grasses, and also the branches and fruits of some trees, escaped the force of the hail. Thus it is not without hyperbole that the hail is said to have damaged every herb and every tree. The exception that follows plainly shows this. Or it must be said that it damaged all herbs and trees in such a way that it did not destroy them entirely.


Plerique, ut hunc nodum solvant, sibi fingunt multos menses, aut annum etiam intercessisse inter plagam grandinis et plagam locustarum: atque interea temporis crevisse nova gramina, novas segetes, novos arborum fructus, in eorum locum, quos grando perdiderat. Quae videntur frustra dici, cum Moses diserte scribat, locustas absumpsisse, quidquid grando reliquum fecerat, Exod. X, 5. 12. 15. Nec dici possit grando id reliquum fecisse, quod nondum erat, aut super terram nondum exstabat. Praeterea ab eo tempore, quo in Aegypto coepit Moses patrare miracula, usque ad ejusdem obitum, fluxerunt anni praecise quadraginta. Agebat enim annum octogesimum, cum convenit Pharaonem, Exod. VII, 7. Et anno aetatis centesimo vigesimo mortuus est in ora terrae Chanaan, quam viderat a monte Nebo, Deut. XXXIV, 1. 5. Per hos porro quadraginta annos dicuntur Israelitae per desertum iter fecisse Ios. V, 6. Quod stare non posset, si Moses annum integrum in Aegypto trivisset in miraculis patrandis. Nam annus ille demendus esset ex annis quadraginta morae Israelitarum in deserto. Falsum est igitur, quod hi supponunt, inter Mosis miracula multum spatium intercessisse. Neque id satis convenit cum Dei bonitate, ut, populo suo jam ad incitas redacto, tam lente subvenisset, et tot moris interpositis. Sed et justitia ejus requirebat, ut in tam gravem Pharaonis σκληροκαρδίαν continuis plagis animadverteret, nec ullo ei dato respirandi spatio. Proinde iis accedimus, qui decem plagas, Aegyptiis inflictas, intra breve tempus contrahunt, puta menstruum, aut circiter.

Most, in order to untie this knot, imagine that many months, or even a year, passed between the plague of hail and the plague of locusts, and that in the meantime new grass, new crops and new fruits of the trees grew in place of those that the hail had destroyed. This seems to be said in vain, since Moses writes expressly that the locusts consumed whatever the hail had left remaining, Exod 10:5 12. 15. Nor could the hail be said to have left remaining what did not yet exist, or did not yet stand above the ground. Moreover, from the time when Moses began to perform miracles in Egypt until his death, exactly forty years passed. For he was in his eightieth year when he met Pharaoh, Exod 7:7. And in the hundred and twentieth year of his age he died on the border of the land of Canaan, which he had seen from Mount Nebo, Deut 34:1 5. Through these forty years, further, the Israelites are said to have journeyed through the desert, Josh 5:6. This could not stand if Moses had spent a whole year in Egypt performing miracles. For that year would have to be subtracted from the forty years of the Israelites' stay in the desert. It is therefore false, as these suppose, that a long interval passed between the miracles of Moses. Nor does it accord well with the goodness of God that, when his people had already been reduced to extremity, he should have come to their aid so slowly and with so many delays. And his justice too required that he punish so grave a σκληροκαρδίαν [sklērokardian] of Pharaoh with continuous plagues, granting him no breathing space. We therefore side with those who compress the ten plagues inflicted on the Egyptians into a short time, say a month or thereabouts.


III, 286 Quod prope omiseram, non solum agros, sed et Aegyptiorum domos implebant hae locustae, Exod. X, 6. (3). Neque tantum terrae frugibus arborum, sed et hominibus putantur fuisse noxiae: atque eo haec pertinere de ecclesiae hostibus; Sap. XVI, 9. Οὓς μὲν γὰρ ἀκρίδων καὶ μυιῶν ἀπέκτεινε δήγματα, καὶ οὐχ εὑρέθη ἴαμα τῇ ψυχῇ αὐτῶν, ὅτι ἄξιοι ἦσαν ὑπὸ τοιούτων κολασθῆναι. Quos quidem locustarum et muscarum morsus occiderunt, neque inventum est reme- col. 463 dium animae (id est, vitae) ipsorum, quia digni erant, qui ab hujusmodi rebus punirentur. Sed libri auctor niti videtur verbis, quibus Pharao liberari petiit ab hac plaga, Exod. X, 17. Rogate Dominum Deum vestrum, ut auferat a me mortem istam. Unde tamen haudquaquam sequitur, has locustas hominibus mortem inflixisse. Mors enim etiam agrorum est, et herbarum, atque arborum. Sic Aegyptii dicunt Gen. XLVII, 19. Cur moreremur coram te, tam nos, quam terra nostra. Et de arbore Iobus XIV, 8. Si senuerit in terra radix ejus, et in pulvere mortuus fuerit truncus ejus. Et David Psal. LXXVIII, 47. Occidit grandine vites eorum. Et Paulus 1 Cor. XV, 36. Quod tu seminas, non vivificatur, nisi prius moriatur. De qua locutione plura habentur statim initio hujus operis (4). Praeterea locustae homines et bruta occidunt, saltem ex consequenti, III, 287 quod ajunt; quia consumptis illis, quae fuissent vitae subsidio, sic ad mortem eos adigunt (5). Utroque igitur respectu Pharao potuit rogare, ut Deus auferret mortem istam, id est, mortiferas istas locustas.

III, 286 A point I had nearly omitted: these locusts filled not only the fields but also the houses of the Egyptians, Exod 10:6 R3. And they are thought to have been harmful not only to the fruits of the earth and of the trees, but also to men; and to this, it is thought, refers what is said of the enemies of the church, Wis 16:9 Οὓς μὲν γὰρ ἀκρίδων καὶ μυιῶν ἀπέκτεινε δήγματα, καὶ οὐχ εὑρέθη ἴαμα τῇ ψυχῇ αὐτῶν, ὅτι ἄξιοι ἦσαν ὑπὸ τοιούτων κολασθῆναι [Hous men gar akridōn kai myiōn apekteine dēgmata, kai ouch heurethē iama tē psychē autōn, hoti axioi ēsan hypo toioutōn kolasthēnai]. For the bites of locusts and flies killed them, and no remedy was found for their soul col. 463 (that is, their life), because they deserved to be punished by such things. But the author of the book seems to rely on the words with which Pharaoh asked to be freed from this plague, Exod 10:17. Entreat the Lord your God, that he take away from me this death. Yet from this it by no means follows that these locusts inflicted death on men. For there is also a death of fields, of herbs and of trees. So the Egyptians say, Gen 47:19. Why should we die before you, both we and our land? And of a tree, Job XIV, 8. If its root grow old in the earth, and its stock die in the dust. And David, Ps 78:47: He killed their vines with hail. And Paul, 1 Cor 15:36: What you sow is not quickened unless it first dies. On this expression more is said at the very beginning of this work R4. Moreover, locusts kill men and beasts at least by consequence, III, 287 as they say, since by consuming what would have served to sustain life they thus drive them to death R5. In either respect, therefore, Pharaoh could ask that God take away this death, that is, these deadly locusts.


De caetero, ut vento קדים Kadim, id est, Orientali, in Aegyptum illatae fuerant hae locustae: ita vento ים, maris, , id est, Occidentali, abductae sunt, et in mare rubrum projectae. Locustas enim vento vehi, tralatitium est. Plinius ubi supra, Est et alius earum obitus. Gregatim sublatae vento in maria, aut stagna, decidunt. Hieronymus in Ioelem cap. 2. Etiam nostris temporibus vidimus agmina locustarum terram texisse Iudaeam: quae postea misericordia Domini, etc. vento surgente, in mare primum et novissimum praecipitatae sunt. Orosius lib. 4. cap. 11. de locustis Africanis, Repentino arreptae vento, atque in globos coactae, portataeque diu per aërem, Africano pelago immersae sunt (6). Ventus autem קדים Kadim, qui locustas in Aegyptum advexit, quamvis proprie Orientalem sonet, tamen etiam pro Australi sumitur, ut probavimus b) in capite De miraculo Coturnicum. Itaque Graeci interpretes Νότον et Λίβα reddunt, id est, Notum, et Africum, et καύσωνα, ventum urentem. Neque fortasse erit extra rem ita hic interpretari: cum ventus Orientalis nonnisi ex Arabia locustas potuerit in Aegyptum advehere: sed Australis ex Aethiopia, quae hac peste multo est foecundior. Proinde الحبشان alhabsan, locustae genus, nomen habet III, 288 ab Abasenis, seu Abyssinis, in quorum solo nascitur. Et in Aethiopia nonnullae gentes ex solis locustis vixerunt, quas copia vix credenda eo advehebant venti, partim occidentales, partim meridionales. Idque circa vernum aequinoctium, quo ipso anni tempore in Aegytum adductae sunt. Agatharchides ubi de Acridophagis, Ὑπὸ δὲ τὴν ἐαρινὴν ἰσημερίαν, ὅτε Λίβες παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς καὶ Ζέφυροι πνέουσι παμμεγέθεις, ἀκρίδων πλῆθος ἀμύθητον ἐκ τῆς ἀνιστορήτου μετὰ τῶν ἀνέμων παραγίνεται χώρας. Et Diodorus lib. 3. Κατὰ γὰρ τὴν ἐαρινὴν ὥραν παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς Ζέφυροι καὶ Λίβες παμμεγέθεις ἐκρίπτουσιν ἐκ τῆς ἐρήμου πλῆθος ἀκρίδων ἀμύθητον. Et Strabo lib. 16. Ζῶσι δ᾽ ἀπὸ ἀκρίδων, ἃς οἱ ἐαρινοὶ Λί-βες, καὶ Ζέφυροι, πνέοντες μεγάλοι, συνελαύνουσιν εἰς τοὺς τόπους τούτους. Proinde hi ipsi venti locustas ex iisdem locis videntur in Aegyptum attulisse, id est, ex Aethiopia (7). Nam, quod eas plerique volunt a Deo fuisse creatas, mihi vix persuaserint; quia Scriptura nihil tale refert, sed a vento fuisse advectas, qui tota die flaverit, et tota nocte. Nec miracula confingenda sunt absque necessitate. Qualis hic nulla apparet, cum in Aethiopia prope Aegyptum plures locustae procreentur, quam in ulla parte terrarum. Miraculum igitur non fuit in eo, quod produxit Deus, sed in eo, quod adduxit nutu suo tam prodigiosam locustarum multitudinem. Et quod idem, qui adduxerat, ad Mosis, servi sui, col. 464 orationem statim abduxit, alio vento excitato, occidentali scilicet, quem Hebraei vocant רוח ים , ventum maris; quia mare habent ad occasum. Et, illo vento magna vi flante, in mare rubrum projectae sunt locustae omnes, ne una quidem relicta in cunctis Aegypti finibus. Cum enim ad Orientem Aegypti sit mare rubrum, has occidentali vento eo propelli oportuit.

Moreover, just as these locusts had been brought into Egypt by the קדים Kadim wind, that is, the east wind, so they were carried away by the ים wind, the wind of the sea, that is, the west wind, and cast into the Red Sea. For that locusts are carried by the wind is commonplace. Pliny, in the place cited above: "There is also another way in which they perish. Lifted up in swarms by the wind, they fall into seas or pools." Jerome on Joel ch. 2: "In our own times too we have seen swarms of locusts cover the land of Judaea: which afterwards, by the mercy of the Lord, etc., when a wind arose, were hurled into the first and the last sea." Orosius, book 4, ch. 11, on the African locusts: "Seized by a sudden wind, and driven together into masses, and carried for a long time through the air, they were plunged into the African sea" R6. But the קדים Kadim wind, which brought the locusts into Egypt, although properly it means the east wind, is nevertheless also taken for the south wind, as we proved b) in the chapter On the Miracle of the Quails. Thus the Greek translators render it Νότον [Noton] and Λίβα [Liba], that is, Notus and Africus, and καύσωνα [kausōna], the burning wind. And perhaps it will not be beside the point to interpret it so here: since the east wind could have brought locusts into Egypt only from Arabia, but the south wind from Ethiopia, which is far more fertile in this pest. Accordingly الحبشان [al-ḥbshān] alhabsan, a kind of locust, takes its name III, 288 from the Abaseni, or Abyssinians, in whose soil it is born. And in Ethiopia some peoples lived on locusts alone, which the winds, partly westerly, partly southerly, carried there in an almost incredible abundance. And this around the spring equinox, the very time of year at which they were brought into Egypt. Agatharchides, where he speaks of the Acridophagi: Ὑπὸ δὲ τὴν ἐαρινὴν ἰσημερίαν, ὅτε Λίβες παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς καὶ Ζέφυροι πνέουσι παμμεγέθεις, ἀκρίδων πλῆθος ἀμύθητον ἐκ τῆς ἀνιστορήτου μετὰ τῶν ἀνέμων παραγίνεται χώρας [Hypo de tēn earinēn isēmerian, hote Libes par᾽ autois kai Zephyroi pneousi pammegetheis, akridōn plēthos amythēton ek tēs anistorētou meta tōn anemōn paraginetai chōras]. And Diodorus, book 3: Κατὰ γὰρ τὴν ἐαρινὴν ὥραν παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς Ζέφυροι καὶ Λίβες παμμεγέθεις ἐκρίπτουσιν ἐκ τῆς ἐρήμου πλῆθος ἀκρίδων ἀμύθητον [Kata gar tēn earinēn hōran par᾽ autois Zephyroi kai Libes pammegetheis ekriptousin ek tēs erēmou plēthos akridōn amythēton]. And Strabo, book 16: Ζῶσι δ᾽ ἀπὸ ἀκρίδων, ἃς οἱ ἐαρινοὶ Λίβες, καὶ Ζέφυροι, πνέοντες μεγάλοι, συνελαύνουσιν εἰς τοὺς τόπους τούτους [Zōsi d᾽ apo akridōn, has hoi earinoi Libes, kai Zephyroi, pneontes megaloi, synelaunousin eis tous topous toutous]. Accordingly these same winds seem to have brought the locusts into Egypt from the same places, that is, from Ethiopia R7. For as to the view of most, that they were created by God, they will hardly persuade me of it; because Scripture relates nothing of the kind, but says that they were brought by a wind which blew all day and all night. Nor are miracles to be invented without necessity. None such appears here, since more locusts are produced in Ethiopia, near Egypt, than in any part of the world. The miracle, therefore, lay not in God's producing so prodigious a multitude of locusts, but in his bringing it at his nod. And in that the same God who had brought them, at the prayer of Moses, his servant, col. 464 immediately took them away, raising another wind, namely the west wind, which the Hebrews call רוח ים, the wind of the sea, because they have the sea to the west. And as that wind blew with great force, all the locusts were cast into the Red Sea, not even one being left in all the borders of Egypt. For since the Red Sea lies to the east of Egypt, they had to be driven there by a west wind.

R1 Rosenmüller, III, 283 How much damage swarms of locusts inflict on the regions of Syria and Egypt will be better understood from what the writers both of histories and of travels report to us. GREGORIUS BARHEBRAEUS, also called ABULPHARAGIUS, in his Chronicle, written in Syriac, copied by Bruns from a Bodleian manuscript and edited by Kirsch, p. 134: ܒܫܢܬ ܐܨܗ ܕܝ̈ܘܢܝܐ ܐܬܐ ܩܡܨܐ ܦܪܚܐ ܘܚܒܠ ܙܪ̈ܥܐ ܘܐܪܡܝ ܙܪܥܐ ܘܢܦܩ [בשנת אצה דיוניא אתא קמצא פרחא וחבל זרעא וארמי זרעא ונפק]. ܘܡܣܒܟ ܗܘܐ ܘܣܠܩ ܒܫܘܪ̈ܐ ܘܐܣ̈ܐ [ומסבך הוא וסלק בשורא ואסא]. ܘܥܐܠ ܡܢ ܟܘ̈ܐ ܘܬܪ̈ܥܐ ܠܒ̈ܬܐ [ועאל מן כוא ותרעא לבתא]. ܘܐܬܡܠܝܘ ܡܢܗ ܐܦ ܓܪ̈ܒܐ ܕܡ̈ܝܐ ܘܬܫܘܝ̈ܬܐ ܘܦܬܘܪ̈ܐ ܘܠܓ̈ܐ [ואתמליו מנה אף גרבא דמיא ותשויתא ופתורא ולגא]. ܘܟܕ ܡܢ ܦܢܝܬ ܬܝܡܢܐ ܥܐܠ ܗܘܐ ܠܒܝܬܐ ܡܢ ܓܒܐ ܓܪܒܝܝܐ ܢܦܩ ܗܘܐ [וכד מן פנית תימנא עאל הוא לביתא מן גבא גרבייא נפק הוא]. ܘܐܟܠ ܥܡ ܥܣܒܐ ܘܐܝܠ̈ܢܐ [ואכל עם עסבא ואילנא]. ܐܦ ܡܐ̈ܢܐ ܕܥܡܪܐ ܘܢܚ̈ܬܐ ܕܒ̈ܢܝܢܫܐ [אף מאנא דעמרא ונחתא דבנינשא]. ܘܟܕ ܓܡܪ ܠܟܠܗ ܦܢܝܬܐ ܕܐܘܪܗܝ ܘܣܪܘܓ ܥܒܪ ܠܡܥܪܒܐ [וכד גמר לכלה פניתא דאורהי וסרוג עבר למערבא]. In the year of the Greeks 1095 (which was 784 after Christ) flying locusts burst in, spoiled the crops and laid eggs; and those hatched from them, after they had grown wings, climbed the walls and partitions, and entered the houses through the windows and doors [cf. Exod 10:6. ומלאו בתיך ובתי כל עבדיך ובתי כל מצרים, They shall fill (the locusts) your houses, and those of your courtiers and of your subjects]. The water jars, the floors, the tables and the dishes were filled with them. After they had entered the houses from the southern side, they went out on the northern side, having consumed the plants, the trees, even the woollen garments and the clothing of men. When the whole region of Edessa and Sarug had been laid waste, they passed on towards the west. And the continuator of Barhebraeus, in dem Neuen Repertorio für bibl. und morgenl. Literat. edited by Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)], vol. 1, p. 67 f. [the Syriac, 10 lines, not transcribed here]: In the year 1774 (1463 after Christ) many locusts came from the east, and wingless ones at that [so, it seems, the words ܘܕܒܒܐ ܐܝܬܝܗܘܢ ܗܘܐ [ודבבא איתיהון הוא] should be rendered, which Bruns translated: and flies burst in. But ܕܒܒܐ [דבבא] here undoubtedly agrees in meaning with the Arabic دُبَّاءٌ [dubbāʾ], a locust not yet winged]. They came as far as Egypt, ate the crops, vineyards, fruits, trees, even the grass, and left nothing green on the face of the earth. The vineyards, fruits and trees failed, gnawed bare and devoured by the locusts. LEO AFRICANUS in the Descript. Africae III, 284 book 2, ch. 11, p. 77, Zurich edition 1559: When I was staying among them (the people of Tagtessa), a great multitude of locusts had invaded that region; I would dare to affirm that they had grown so large that they far exceeded the ears of grain, which had then reached ripeness, so that the very surface of the ground was completely covered with locusts. [Cf. Exod 10:15. ויכס את עין כל הארץ ותחשך הארץ They covered the whole surface of the earth and darkened it.] And this was in the year 919, which was 1510 of Christ. The same Leo, book 9, ch. 61, p. 512: In Africa locusts are generally seen in such numbers that in flight they cover the rays of the sun like a cloud. They eat the very trees together with their leaves and fruit. When about to depart they leave eggs, from which others spring up (although these do not fly), and wherever they are met with they eat everything down to the bark of the trees, and leave behind a great dearth of grain, especially in Mauritania. LE BRUN, Voyages au Levant p. 252, mentions a swarm of locusts that had consumed everything green within the space of two hours, and the places in Cyprus through which these insects had passed were as though laid waste by fire. Russell [=Alexander Russell, The Natural History of Aleppo (1756)] relates the same in the Natural History of Aleppo p. 62 (Of the noxious kind may well be reckoned the locust, which sometimes arrive in such incredible multitudes, that it would appear fabulous to relate, destroying the whole of the verdure where-ever they pass). Whoever wants more should consult OEDMANN in den Vermischten Sammlungen, fasc. 2, ch. 6, p. 95 ff., and our Scholia on Exod. X, 14. p. 450 ff., second edition.

Non quod ex Hebraeorum sententia vita sit animalis propria, ut docti putant. Plantis enim inesse vitam, agnoscunt Aben Esra et Ramban in primum caput Geneseos. Atque id ex Scriptura clarum, cum pollicetur homines victuros ut frumentum, Os. XIV, 7. Quo allusum ab Apostolo 1 Cor. XV, 36. Proinde occidi dicuntur arbores et emori, id est, vita privari. Sic Ps. Eodem faciunt haec Iobi de arbore cap. 14. vers. 8. Si senuerit in terra radix ejus, et in pulvere mortuus fuerit truncus ejus. Et Aegyptiorum ad Iosephum quiritatio, Genes. XLVII, 19. Quocirca plantam vivere, etiam apud Hebraeos in confesso est. Sed quia solum animal sentit, appetit et movetur, interdum illi vita tribuitur, tanquam propria, ut quae multis gradibus supra plantae vitam assurgat. “

R4 Rosenmüller, III, 286 Vol. I, book 1, Chapter 1, p. 1. I shall add the words that bear on this: "Just as an animal is called ζῶον [zōon] in Greek, so in Hebrew it is called חיה by reason of life. Not that in the view of the Hebrews life is proper to the animal, as the learned think. For Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] and Ramban, on the first chapter of Genesis, acknowledge that there is life in plants. And this is clear from Scripture, when it promises that men shall live like grain, Hos 14:7. To which the Apostle alludes, 1 Cor 15:36. Accordingly trees are said to be killed and to die, that is, to be deprived of life. Thus Ps 78:47: He killed their vines with hail. On these words Kimchi says: גם יתכן בצומח מיתה אחר אשר בו נפש הצומחת, Death also befits a plant, since there is a vegetative soul in it. Hence Horace, book 1, Epist. 12: But whether you slaughter fish, or leek and onion. And Seneca, Epist. 58: For it is held that crops and shrubs have a soul: and so we say that they both live and die. To the same point are these words of Job about a tree, ch. 14, v. 8: Though its root grow old in the earth, and its stock die in the dust. And the outcry of the Egyptians to Joseph, Genes. XLVII, 19: Why should we die before you, both we and our land? For the land is said to die when it lies uncultivated and desolate, since it lives in some way in its produce. Hence Martial, book 13, Epigr. 12: — — lest the suburban field should die. And Statius, book 5 of the Thebaid, on the serpent by which Archemorus was killed: — the grass, struck by its hot breath, falls where it bore its jaws; the field dies at its hissing. Therefore that the plant lives is admitted among the Hebrews too. But because the animal alone feels, desires and moves, life is sometimes attributed to it as its own, since it rises many degrees above the life of the plant."

Part 2, Book 4, chapter 4: The locusts of Joel, chapter 1
---------------------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/locustae-ioel1.html

III, 289 col. 464 CAP. IV.

III, 289 col. 464 Chapter IV.


De Locustis quid habeat Ioel capite primo.

What Joel says about locusts in his first chapter.


Hactenus de locustis Aegyptiis, quibus similes Israelitis propheta Ioel gravissimis verbis interminatus, tandem desinit in verba pacis, et Dei nomine iis multa bona promittit. Nostrum igitur est, e Ioele edecumare, et pro viribus interpretari, quaecunque de locustis habet, prout occurrent, et servato Prophetae ordine. Qui, ut attentionem captet, statim ab initio nova et inaudita se dicturum profitetur cap. I, 2. Audite, inquit, hoc senes, et auribus percipite, omnes incolae terrae: An fuerit istud in diebus vestris, et in diebus patrum vestrorum? Primo senes compellat, qui aetatis beneficio plura viderant atque audiverant. Ut Moses Deut. XXXII, 7. Interroga senes, ut tibi dicant. Et Iob. XXXII, 7. Dies loquentur, et numerus annorum docebit scientiam. Propheta igitur significat, locustas, de quibus statim dicturus est, eam cladem intulisse, qualis nulla memoratur ab omni aevo illata. In Iudaea scilicet. Eo enim haec pertinent, Audite hoc, senes; et auribus percipite, omnes incolae terrae, supple col. 465 Iudaicae, de qua hic res est. Sic, cum de Aegyptiis legitur Exod. X, 14. An-tea non fuerant locustae, istis pares, neque postea futurae sunt: haec ad Aegyptum sunt restringenda. Alioqui cum Ioele pugnaret Moses, aut cum Mose Ioel. Caetera enim, quae Hebraei afferunt, sunt minus ad rem, ut infra docebimus.

So far concerning the Egyptian locusts. With locusts like these the prophet Joel threatened the Israelites in the gravest terms, but at last he ends in words of peace and in God's name promises them many good things. It is therefore our task to pick out from Joel whatever he says about locusts and to interpret it as best we can, as each passage occurs and keeping to the Prophet's order. To capture attention, he declares at the very outset that he is about to say things new and unheard of, ch. I, 2: Hear this, he says, you old men, and give ear, all you inhabitants of the land: Has this happened in your days, or in the days of your fathers? First he addresses the old men, who by the benefit of age had seen and heard more. So Moses, Deut 32:7: Ask the old men, and they will tell you. And Job XXXII, 7: Days will speak, and the multitude of years will teach wisdom. The Prophet therefore signifies that the locusts of which he is about to speak wrought such destruction as none recorded in any age. In Judaea, that is. For this is the point of Hear this, you old men; and give ear, all you inhabitants of the land: supply col. 465 of Judaea, which is the subject here. Likewise, when we read of the Egyptians in Exod. X, 14, Before them there were no such locusts as these, nor shall there be after them, this must be restricted to Egypt. Otherwise Moses would conflict with Joel, or Joel with Moses. For the other explanations which the Hebrews offer are less to the point, as we shall show below.


Versu tertio, Haec filiis vestris narrate, et filii vestri filiis suis, et filii ipsorum aetati alteri] Quod Poetae verbis dixeris,

In the third verse, Tell this to your children, and your children to their children, and their children to another generation] Which you might express in the words of the Poet:


Et nati natorum, et qui nascentur ab illis.

And the children's children, and those who shall be born of them.


Neque enim insignia Dei facta sunt oblivione sepelienda, sed eorum memoria ad posteros sedulo propaganda atque in posterum conservanda. Ut vel beneficiis acceptis grati simus, et pleni fiducia, vel poenis illatis trepidi et cauti magis. Hinc David Psal. LXXVIII, 3. etc. Quae audivimus, ac novimus, et patres nostri narraverunt nobis, non celabimus filios eorum, generationem alteram, ut narrent Domini laudes, et virtutem, et mirabilia, quae fecit, etc. Et mandavit patribus nostris, ut filiis suis nota facerent, ut sciat altera generatio, filii qui nascentur, surgentesque enarrent filiis suis. Et ponant in Deo spem suam, neque obliviscantur operum Dei, etc. Vide et Deut. IV, 9. et VI, 6. 20. Ios. IV, 6. etc.

For God's remarkable deeds must not be buried in oblivion; their memory must be diligently passed on to posterity and preserved for the future. Thus we may either be grateful and full of confidence for benefits received, or more fearful and cautious because of punishments inflicted. Hence David, Ps 78:3 etc.: What we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us, we will not hide from their children, another generation, so that they may tell the praises of the Lord, and his might, and the wonders that he has done, etc. And he commanded our fathers to make them known to their children, so that another generation might know, the children yet to be born, and that they might arise and tell them to their children. And that they might set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, etc. See also Deut 4:9 and VI, 6. 20. Josh 4:6 etc.


Versu quarto, Residuum gazam comedit arbe, et residuum arbe comedit jelek, et residuum jelek comedit chasil.] Hae sunt locustarum quatuor species, ut III, 290 jam ante a) monuimus, quas Hebraeis nominibus hic appellamus, quia Latina non suppetunt. Sic infra capitis secundi versu vigesimo quinto, Et reddam vobis annos, quos comederit ARBE, IELEK, CHASIL et GAZAM. Ubi gazam, quae prima fuerat, postrema nominatur. Quod observandum in Hebraeos, qui has quatuor locustarum species quatuor annis continuis, gazam nempe primo anno, arbe secundo, jelek tertio, chasil denique quarto, Iudaeam devastasse putant. Quod mihi sit parum verisimile; quia, si locusta, gazam dicta, in Iudaeam primo anno fuisset immissa, non poneretur ultimo loco Ioel II, 25. Et in his plagis enumerandis Propheta eundem utrobique servasset ordinem. Praeterea, si singulae species singulis annis assignatae fuissent, non diceretur arbe comedisse residuum gazam, et jelek residuum arbe, et chasil residuum jelek: neque enim hujus anni proventus sunt praecedentis reliquiae, nec quae futuro provenient in hujus anni reliquiis haberi possunt. Itaque, sive annotina fuerit haec locustarum plaga, aut, quod ex Ioel II, 25. videtur recte concludi, in plures annos propagata: non tamen singulas locustarum species singulis annis assignandas, sed omnes eodem anno in Iudaeam puto ingruisse. Ita, ut, uno agmine ex agro aliquo discedente, alterum succederet, praecedentis reliquias, si quae essent, depasturum ac consumpturum: Idque repetitum toties, quoties fuit necesse, ut nihil omnino, quo vel homines, vel bestiae vescerentur, in agro superesset. Nihilo magis probo, quod volunt, Iudaicam hanc plagam ab Aegyptia in eo differre, quod Aegypto unum locustae genus (ארבה arbe nimirum), at Iudaeae quatuor illae species incubuerint. Quamvis enim arbe sumatur εἰδικῶς pro certa locustae specie, cum reliquis opponitur, ut in Ioele et Levit. XI, 21. plerumque tamen γενικῶς usurpatur pro toto genere locustarum. Quomodo sumsit Moses, ubi egit de τῷ arbe, in Aegyptios immisso. Ita, ut etiam ילק jelek, et חסיל chasil, atque aliae locustarum species includerentur. Proinde David de Aegyptiis Psal. LXXVIII, 46. Dedit τῷ chasil proventum eorum, et laborem eorum τῷ arbe. Et Psal. CV, 34. Dixit, et venit arbe et jelek sine numero. Itaque non solus arbe, sed et chasil et jelek in illos a Deo immissi sunt. Merito igitur apud Pisidam Deus in Aegyptios instruit παγγενῆ τὴν ἀκρίδα, locustam omnigenam. Quatuor in Ioele locustarum species, gazam, arbe, jelek et chasil, col. 466 quomodo Chaldaei, Syri atque Arabes efferant, hic dicere nihil attinet. In Graeca et Vulgata hae sunt, ἡ κάμπη, ἡ ἀκρὶς, ὁ βροῦχος, ἡ ἐρυσίβη, eruca, locusta, bruchus, rubigo. Quarum prima et ultima ad locustarum genus non pertinent. Nam ἡ ἐρυσίβη, rubigo, ne animal quidem est, sed morbus segetum. Itaque huic versioni haud quaquam stamus. Nobis enim id persuasissimum III, 291 est, Hebraicis quatuor vocibus quatuor locustarum species significari. Quod uno ore hic asserunt Hebraei omnes: quamvis illae species, quomodo inter se differant, definire non possint.

In the fourth verse, What the gazam left, the arbe has eaten, and what the arbe left, the jelek has eaten, and what the jelek left, the chasil has eaten.] These are four species of locusts, as III, 290 we noted earlier a), which we call here by their Hebrew names because Latin ones are not available. So too below, in chapter 2, verse 25: And I will restore to you the years which the ARBE, IELEK, CHASIL and GAZAM have eaten. There gazam, which had been first, is named last. This should be noted against the Hebrews, who think that these four species of locusts laid waste Judaea in four successive years: the gazam in the first year, the arbe in the second, the jelek in the third, and finally the chasil in the fourth. To me this seems hardly probable. For if the locust called gazam had been sent into Judaea in the first year, it would not be placed last in Joel 2:25. And in enumerating these plagues the Prophet would have kept the same order in both places. Moreover, if each species had been assigned to a single year, it would not be said that the arbe ate what the gazam left, and the jelek what the arbe left, and the chasil what the jelek left. For this year's produce is not the remainder of the previous year's, nor can what will grow in the coming year be counted among this year's remains. Therefore, whether this plague of locusts lasted one year or, as seems rightly concluded from Joel 2:25, extended over several years, I think that the individual species of locusts are not to be assigned to individual years, but that all of them fell upon Judaea in the same year. Thus, as one swarm left a field, another followed, to graze off and consume the remains of the preceding one, if any were left; and this was repeated as often as necessary, until nothing at all remained in the field on which either men or beasts could feed. Nor do I any more approve of their claim that this Judaean plague differed from the Egyptian in that a single kind of locust (namely ארבה arbe) fell upon Egypt, but those four species upon Judaea. For although arbe is taken εἰδικῶς [eidikōs] for a particular species of locust when it is set against the others, as in Joel and Lev 11:21, yet it is mostly used γενικῶς [genikōs] for the whole genus of locusts. So Moses took it when he dealt with the arbe sent upon the Egyptians, so that ילק jelek and חסיל chasil and other species of locusts were also included. Accordingly David says of the Egyptians, Ps 78:46: He gave their produce to the chasil, and their labour to the arbe. And Ps 105:34: He spoke, and the arbe came, and the jelek without number. Thus not the arbe alone, but also the chasil and the jelek were sent by God against them. Rightly, then, in Pisides God arrays against the Egyptians παγγενῆ τὴν ἀκρίδα [pangenē tēn akrida], the locust of every kind. How the Chaldeans, Syrians and Arabs render the four species of locusts in Joel, gazam, arbe, jelek and chasil, col. 466 is of no concern here. In the Greek and the Vulgate they are ἡ κάμπη [hē kampē], ἡ ἀκρὶς [hē akris], ὁ βροῦχος [ho brouchos], ἡ ἐρυσίβη [hē erysibē]: eruca [caterpillar], locusta [locust], bruchus [bruchus], rubigo [blight]. Of these the first and the last do not belong to the genus of locusts. For ἡ ἐρυσίβη [hē erysibē], rubigo [blight], is not even an animal, but a disease of crops. We therefore by no means stand by this version. For we are fully persuaded III, 291 that the four Hebrew words signify four species of locusts. This all the Hebrews assert here with one voice, although they cannot define how those species differ from one another.


Sed hae voces quidquid sonent, gravis agitatur quaestio, nempe, an, quae de locustis hic dicuntur, ad literam sint explicanda. Mysteria enim hic multi quaerunt, quasi non verae locustae intelligantur, sed Iudaeorum hostes. Inter utramque sententiam ita fluctuare videtur Hieronymus, ut ad ultimam magis propendeat. Primo enim haec refert ad quatuor imperia, quae singula successive in Iudaeos insurrexerunt. Erucam, inquit, quae Hebraice גזם gazam, Graece dicitur κάμπη, Hebraei Assyrios interpretantur, Babylonios atque Chaldaeos; qui, de uno orbis climate procedentes, tam decem tribuum, quam duarum, hoc est, Israelitici populi, cuncta vastarunt. Locustam autem Medos interpretantur, et Persas; qui, subverso imperio Chaldaeorum, Iudaeos habuere captivos. Bruchum Macedonas, et omnes Alexandri successores, maximeque regem Antiochum, cognomento Epiphanem, qui instar bruchi sedit in Iudaea, et omnes priorum regum reliquias devoravit. Rubiginem referunt ad imperium Romanum; qui, quarti et ultimi, in tantum oppressere Iudaeos, ut de suis finibus eos pellerent. Haec ille, tanquam ex mente Hebraeorum, qui tamen, ipso fatente, agnoscunt, etiam ad literam contigisse, quae de locustis hic habentur. Iudaei, inquit, putant, in diebus Ioel tam innumerabilem locustarum super Iudaeam venisse multitudinem, ut cuncta complerent; et non dicam fruges, sed ne vinearum quidem et arborum cortices ramosque dimitterent. Sed hanc Iudaeorum sententiam ita refellit in sequentibus, Hoc utrum factum, necne sit, liquido affirmare non possumus. Neque enim Regum et Paralipomenων narrat historia. Quod utique si fuisset, nunquam Scriptura tacuisset. Tantum dicimus, quod sub metaphora locustarum hostium describatur adventus. Deinde, quasi inter utramque sententiam ambiguus; Ni fallor, inquit, videor mihi in hoc Propheta aliquid reperisse. Narratur impietas hostium sub figura locustarum. Et rursus sic de ipsis locustis dicitur, quasi hostibus comparentur: ut, cum locustas legeris, hostes cogites; cum hostes cogitaveris, redeas ad locustas. Videtur Hieronymo Cyrillus assentiri, qui per has quatuor pestes, Salmanassarem, Nabuchodonozorum, An-tiochum et Romanos intelligit. In eodem tamen haec legas; Ἀληθὲς μὲν οὖν τὸ χρῆμα, κἂν εἰ ἐπὶ ἀκρίδος τυχὸν νοοῖτο, βρούχου τε, καὶ κάμπης· Verum quidem hoc est, etiamsi de locusta, bruchoque, et eruca accipiatur. Theodoretus, postquam nonnullos tropice haec interpretari scripsit de quatuor Assyriae regibus, Theglaphalasare, Salmanassare, Sennacheribo et Nabuchodonozoro! Ἐγὼ δὲ, ait, ἀληθῆ μὲν ἡγοῦμαι καὶ ταῦτα· ὑπολαμβάνω δὲ καὶ τὰ κατὰ τὸ ῥη-τὸν νοούμενα τῷ ὄντι γεγενῆσθαι· Ego vero, inquit, vera quidem haec esse censeo; III, 292 sed et quae ad literam intelliguntur, re vera contigisse arbitror. Chaldaeus literalem sensum plerumque amplectitur. Nonnunquam tamen in mysticum delabitur: ut Ioel. II, 25. ubi pro quatuor locustarum speciebus, arbe, jelek, chasil et gazam, habet עממיא ולשניא ושלטוניא ומלכותא פרענות, populos, et linguas, et imperia, et regna vindictae; id est, quibus Deus usus est ad rebellium in populo suo ultionem. Ex Hebraeis commentatoribus Iarchius, Kimchius et Aben Ezra literae mordicus haerent. At his posterior Abarbenel, Hierony- col. 467 mum sequutus, hunc Prophetam venisse asserit, להתנבאות על ממשלת ארבע המלכיות בבל ופרס ויון ורומי, ut prophetaret de dominatione quatuor imperiorum, Babylonici scilicet, et Persici, et Graeci, et Romani. Et a literali sensu usque adeo alienus est, ut, de iis agens, qui ad locustas haec referunt, in ipsa praefatione exclamet, חלילה לי מלהאמין בזה, Absit a me, ut hoc credam: quasi id esset valde absurdum. Sed, cum nihil objiciat, quod non sit futilissimum, non dubito, quin a Propheta verae locustae intelligantur, quae paullo post prophetiam ejus Iudaeam devastaverint. Neque enim hostes infensi solent cum locustis conferri, nisi ratione numeri: ut cum de Madianitis et Amalekitis dicitur Iud. VI, 5. Venerunt quasi locustae multitudine. Et Iud. VII, 12. Diffusi erant in ea valle tanquam locustae multitudine. Et Iudith. II, 2. de copiis Assyriorum; Et multi miscelli, ut locustae, ad eos conveniebant. Et de Trojanis et Aethiopibus, quos Memnon adduxerat, Q. Smyrnaeus libri secundi versu 195.

But whatever these words may mean, a serious question is raised, namely, whether what is said here about locusts is to be explained literally. For many look for mysteries here, as though not real locusts were meant but the enemies of the Jews. Jerome seems to waver between the two opinions in such a way that he leans more towards the latter. For first he refers these things to the four empires which one after another rose up against the Jews. "The caterpillar," he says, "which in Hebrew is called גזם gazam, in Greek κάμπη [kampē], the Hebrews interpret as the Assyrians, the Babylonians and Chaldeans; who, coming from one region of the world, laid waste everything of the ten tribes as well as of the two, that is, of the Israelite people. The locust they interpret as the Medes and Persians; who, after overthrowing the empire of the Chaldeans, held the Jews captive. The bruchus as the Macedonians and all the successors of Alexander, and above all King Antiochus, surnamed Epiphanes, who settled in Judaea like a bruchus and devoured all the remains left by the earlier kings. The blight they refer to the Roman empire; who, fourth and last, so oppressed the Jews as to drive them from their own territory." So he writes, as if from the mind of the Hebrews, who nevertheless, by his own admission, acknowledge that what is said here about locusts also happened literally. "The Jews," he says, "think that in the days of Joel so countless a multitude of locusts came upon Judaea that they filled everything; and left, I will not say the crops, but not even the bark and branches of the vines and trees." But he refutes this opinion of the Jews in what follows: "Whether this happened or not, we cannot clearly affirm. For the history of the Kings and Chronicles does not narrate it. And if it had happened, Scripture would certainly never have kept silent. We say only that under the metaphor of locusts the coming of enemies is described." Then, as if undecided between the two opinions: "If I am not mistaken," he says, "I seem to have found something in this Prophet. The impiety of the enemies is narrated under the figure of locusts. And again, the locusts themselves are spoken of as if they were compared to enemies: so that when you read of locusts you think of enemies; when you have thought of enemies, you return to the locusts." Cyril seems to agree with Jerome, understanding by these four plagues Shalmaneser, Nebuchadnezzar, Antiochus and the Romans. Yet in the same author you may read this: Ἀληθὲς μὲν οὖν τὸ χρῆμα, κἂν εἰ ἐπὶ ἀκρίδος τυχὸν νοοῖτο, βρούχου τε, καὶ κάμπης· [Alēthes men oun to chrēma, kan ei epi akridos tychon nooito, brouchou te, kai kampēs] "This is indeed true, even if it be taken of the locust, the bruchus and the caterpillar." Theodoret, after writing that some interpret these things figuratively of four kings of Assyria, Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, Sennacherib and Nebuchadnezzar, says: Ἐγὼ δὲ ἀληθῆ μὲν ἡγοῦμαι καὶ ταῦτα· ὑπολαμβάνω δὲ καὶ τὰ κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν νοούμενα τῷ ὄντι γεγενῆσθαι· [Egō de alēthē men hēgoumai kai tauta; hypolambanō de kai ta kata to rhēton nooumena tō onti gegenēsthai] "I indeed consider these things true; III, 292 but I also think that what is understood literally really happened." The Chaldee mostly embraces the literal sense. Sometimes, however, he slips into the mystical: as in Joel 2:25, where for the four kinds of locusts, arbe, jelek, chasil and gazam, he has עממיא ולשניא ושלטוניא ומלכותא פרענות, "peoples, and tongues, and dominions, and kingdoms of vengeance"; that is, those whom God used to take vengeance on the rebels among his people. Of the Hebrew commentators, Jarchi [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac), called Jarchi by the Christian Hebraists], Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] and Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] cling tenaciously to the letter. But Abarbanel [=Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), commentary on the Bible], later than these, following Jerome, col. 467 asserts that this Prophet came להתנבאות על ממשלת ארבע המלכיות בבל ופרס ויון ורומי, "to prophesy concerning the dominion of the four empires, namely the Babylonian, and the Persian, and the Greek, and the Roman." And he is so averse to the literal sense that, dealing with those who refer these things to locusts, he exclaims in the very preface: חלילה לי מלהאמין בזה, "Far be it from me to believe this", as though it were utterly absurd. But since he objects nothing that is not most futile, I do not doubt that real locusts are meant by the Prophet, which laid waste Judaea shortly after his prophecy. For hostile enemies are not usually compared with locusts except in respect of number: as when it is said of the Midianites and Amalekites, Iud. VI, 5., "They came like locusts in multitude." And Iud. VII, 12., "They were spread out in that valley like locusts in multitude." And Jdt 2:2, of the forces of the Assyrians: "And many of mixed stock, like locusts, gathered to them." And of the Trojans and the Ethiopians whom Memnon had brought, Quintus Smyrnaeus, book 2, line 195.


— — — — τοί δ' ἐκέχυντο
Ἀκρίσι καρποβόροις ἐναλίγκιοι, αἵ τε φέρονται
Ὡς νέφος, ἢ πολὺς ὄμβρος ὑπὲρ χθονὸς εὐρυπέδοιο,
Ἄπλητοι, μερόπεσσιν ἀεικέα λοιμὸν ἄγουσαι·

— — — — τοί δ' ἐκέχυντο Ἀκρίσι καρποβόροις ἐναλίγκιοι, αἵ τε φέρονται Ὡς νέφος, ἢ πολὺς ὄμβρος ὑπὲρ χθονὸς εὐρυπέδοιο, Ἄπλητοι, μερόπεσσιν ἀεικέα λοιμὸν ἄγουσαι· [— — — — toi d' ekechynto Akrisi karpoborois enalinkioi, hai te pherontai Hōs nephos, ē polys ombros hyper chthonos eurypedoio, Aplētoi, meropessin aeikea loimon agousai]


Ipsi autem effundebant se, locustis frugivoris pares, quae feruntur ut nubes, aut immodicus imber super latam terram, innumerae, tetram hominibus famem allaturae. Alioqui enim, cum homines locustis comparantur, id ad contemptum pertinet, et πρὸς τὸν ἐξουθενισμόν. Quale illud de Israelitis, cum Anakaeis gigantibus collatis, Num. XIII, 34. Quibus comparati ut locustae videbamur. Et de hominibus prae Deo Es. XL, 22. Qui sedet super gyrum terrae, et incolae ejus sunt quasi locustae. Nec dissimile illud Luciani in Hermotimo, Οἷον μύρμηκας ἀπὸ τοῦ ὕψους ἐπισκοποῦντάς τινας τοὺς ἄλλους, Alios homines tanquam formicas e sublimi contemplantes. Itaque magna imperia cum his animalculis nusquam conferri videas: sed cum leonibus, pardis et ursis, ut Danielis capite septimo. Sed, ut res sit manifestior, jam sequentia dispiciamus.

But they poured themselves forth, like crop-devouring locusts, which are borne along like a cloud, or a heavy rain over the broad earth, countless, bringing a dreadful famine upon men. For otherwise, when men are compared to locusts, this serves to express contempt, and πρὸς τὸν ἐξουθενισμόν [pros ton exouthenismon]. Such is the statement about the Israelites when compared with the Anakim giants, Num 13:34. Compared with them we seemed like locusts. And about men in comparison with God, Isa 40:22. He who sits upon the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like locusts. Not unlike this is Lucian's phrase in the Hermotimus, Οἷον μύρμηκας ἀπὸ τοῦ ὕψους ἐπισκοποῦντάς τινας τοὺς ἄλλους [Hoion myrmēkas apo tou hypsous episkopountas tinas tous allous], Looking down from on high upon other men as if upon ants. Thus you will nowhere see great empires compared with these little animals, but rather with lions, leopards and bears, as in the seventh chapter of Daniel. But to make the matter clearer, let us now examine what follows.

Dentes ejus ut dentes leonis, et molares ut leaenae.] Ad quae Abarbanel, לא אמר הנביא זה באמת על הארבה כי איך יקראהו גוי וקהל גוים, Propheta certe id non dixit de locustis: eas enim quomodo gentem vocaret, et congregationem gentium? At Propheta habuit, quem sequeretur, regum sapientissimum, cujus verba sunt Prov. XXX, 25. 26. הנמלים עם לא עז, Formicae, populus invalidus. Et, שפנים עם לא עצום, Choerogrylli, populus non fortis. Ridiculum enim est, quod ibi habet ex Midras, etiam eo loco Solomonem per quatuor animalcula quatuor imperia significasse. Fateor quidem, gentis nomen de homine proprie usurpari, nec transferri ad bestias, nisi per metaphoram. Sed ea metaphora nihil quidquam est usitatius. Hinc poetarum antiquissimus, idemque optimus, dixit Iliad. β´. versu 87.

In verse 6, For a nation has come up against my land, strong and without number. Its teeth are like the teeth of a lion, and its molars like those of a lioness.] On which Abarbanel says, לא אמר הנביא זה באמת על הארבה כי איך יקראהו גוי וקהל גוים, The Prophet certainly did not say this of the locusts: for how could he call them a nation, and an assembly of nations? But the Prophet had someone to follow, the wisest of kings, whose words are Prov 30:25–26. הנמלים עם לא עז, The ants, a people not strong. And, שפנים עם לא עצום, The choerogrylli, a people not mighty. For what he cites there from the Midrash is ridiculous, namely that in that passage too Solomon signified four empires by the four little animals. I admit, indeed, that the word nation is properly used of man, and is not transferred to beasts except by metaphor. But nothing is more common than that metaphor. Hence the most ancient of poets, and also the best, said in Iliad β´, verse 87,

And again,


Ut bina regum facies, ita corpora gentis.

As the kings have two aspects, so do the bodies of the nation [gentis].


Et libro primo Aeneidos,

And in book 1 of the Aeneid,


— — cum gentis adultos
Educunt foetus.

— — when they lead forth the full-grown young of the nation [gentis].


Quod loquendi genus, ne quis poetis proprium esse putet, etiam in Columella occurrit libri decimi capite tertio, Gens universa totius alvei consumitur. Et capite nono, Intestino bello totae (apum) gentes consumuntur. Et capite decimo de rege apum, cui detractae sunt alae, Ne ditionis quidem populo suae permittit longius evagari. Et capite decimo tertio, Duo populi conjungi debent. Et de fucis capite decimo quinto, Nec ad occidionem gens interimenda est. Quale est, quod Aelianus libri sexti Historiae capite decimo nono, τὸ τεττίγων φῦλον, cicadarum nationem dixit. Ita enim scripserat, non φῶλον, vocem nihili, quam III, 295 habent nostrae editiones. Sed et Arabice أمة umma, gentem, de quovis animali dici, notant Arabum Lexicographi, Giauhari et Alcamus. Ut in celebri Pseudo-prophetae dicto de animalibus, quod supra b) citavimus; خلق الله الف امة منها ستماية في البحر واربعماية في البر وان اول هلاك هذه الامم الجراد Mille animalium gentes (ita ad verbum habetur) creavit Deus, sexcentas in mari, et in terra quadringentas. Et prima harum gentium pestis est locusta. Quidni igitur locustas Ioel hic appellaverit גוי, gentem, et עם, populum, capitis secundi versu secundo.

Lest anyone think this manner of speaking peculiar to the poets, it also occurs in Columella, book 10, chapter 3: The whole nation of an entire hive is consumed. And in chapter 9: Whole nations (of bees) are consumed by civil war. And in chapter 10, of the king of the bees whose wings have been removed: He does not even allow the people of his own dominion to roam farther. And in chapter 13: Two peoples must be joined. And of the drones, in chapter 15: Nor is the nation to be destroyed to the point of extermination. Similar is what Aelian, book 6 of the History, chapter 19, called τὸ τεττίγων φῦλον [to tettigōn phylon], the nation of cicadas. For so he had written, not φῶλον [phōlon], a meaningless word, which III, 295 our editions have. Moreover, the Arabic lexicographers Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ] and Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] note that in Arabic too أمة [umma] umma, nation, is said of any animal. So in the celebrated saying of the pseudo-prophet about the animals, which we cited above b): خلق الله الف امة منها ستماية في البحر واربعماية في البر وان اول هلاك هذه الامم الجراد [khalaqa Allāh alf umma minhā sittumiʾa fī al-baḥr wa-arbaʿumiʾa fī al-barr wa-inna awwal halāk hādhihi al-umam al-jarād] God created a thousand nations of animals (so it reads word for word), six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land. And the first plague of these nations is the locust. Why then should Joel not have called the locusts here גוי, a nation, and עם, a people, in chapter 2, verse 2?


Iisdem leonum dentes et molares assignantur: ut Apoc. IX, 8. Ὀδόντες αὐτῶν ὡς λεόντων ἦσαν, Dentes eorum ut leonum erant, id est, duri, validi, acuti. Proinde Plinius de locustis, Omnia morsu erodentes, et fores quoque tectorum. Quae vis est stupenda prorsus in tam vili animalculo. Ut non immerito Hieronymus ad haec verba exclamet: Quid locustis fortius, quibus humana industria resistere non potest? Et Cyrillus, Ἄμαχον τὸ χρῆμά ἐστι, καὶ ἀκατα- col. 469 γώνιστος κομιδῆ τῶν τοιούτων ἡ ἔφοδος, ἱκανή τε ἄρδην ἀπολέσαι τὰ ἐν ἀγροῖς. Res est insuperabilis: et prorsus inexpugnabilis est earum impressio, et ad perdendas ruris opes plane sufficit. Quod ab illis demorsum est, Arabes تاشر vocant, id est, denticulatum in serrae modum. Nam اشر est serra secare (1).

To them are assigned the teeth and molars of lions, as in Rev 9:8 Ὀδόντες αὐτῶν ὡς λεόντων ἦσαν [Odontes autōn hōs leontōn ēsan], Their teeth were as those of lions, that is, hard, strong, sharp. Accordingly Pliny says of locusts: Gnawing everything with their bite, even the doors of houses. This strength is truly astonishing in so paltry a little creature. So not without reason does Jerome exclaim at these words: What is stronger than locusts, which human industry cannot resist? And Cyril: Ἄμαχον τὸ χρῆμά ἐστι, καὶ ἀκαταγώνιστος κομιδῆ τῶν τοιούτων ἡ ἔφοδος, ἱκανή τε ἄρδην ἀπολέσαι τὰ ἐν ἀγροῖς. [Amachon to chrēma esti, kai akatagōnistos komidē tōn toioutōn hē ephodos, hikanē te ardēn apolesai ta en agrois.] col. 469 The thing is invincible; their onset is utterly irresistible and fully capable of destroying the wealth of the countryside. What they have bitten off the Arabs call تاشر [tāshur], that is, toothed like a saw. For اشر [ashara] means to cut with a saw R1.


Versu septimo, Posuit vitem meam in desolationem, et ficum meam in confractionem. Penitus nudavit eam et abjecit: albuerunt rami ejus.] Vitem, ait, et ficum; quia bruchi et locustae utrique infesti sunt. Proinde, ut a vitibus bruchi arceantur, hoc praescribit Didymus libro decimo Geoponicῶn, Περὶ τὸ στέ-λεχος τῆς ἀμπέλου παρὰ τὴν ῥίζαν, τρεῖς κόκκους σινήπεως χῶσον· φυτευόμε-να γὰρ ταῦτα τῇ ὀσμῇ τὸν βροῦχον ἀναιρεῖ. Circa vitis truncum ad radicem tria sinapi grana defode: illa enim consita bruchum odore suo perimunt. Et de ficubus Plinius libri decimi septimi capite vigesimo quinto: In Boeotia derosae a locustis ficus iterum germinavere. Quae sumta sunt ex his Theophrasti libri secundi Historiae capite quarto, Ἐν δὲ τῇ Βοιωτίᾳ καταβρωθέντων τῶν ἔργων ὑπὸ τῶν ἀττελέβων πάλιν ἀνεβλάστησε. Itaque pro τῶν ἔργων legendum τῶν ἐρίνων. Nempe ἔρινα sunt ficus sylvestres, vel ficus quaevis immaturae; ut III, 296 in Alexi apud Athenaeum. Hebraeum לקצפה reddo in confractionem, cum Graecis, qui hic habent εἰς κλασμὸν, aut συγκλασμόν (2). Quae vocis, alioqui inusitatae, versio confirmatur ex Arabismo. Arabice enim قصف est frangere, et القصيف est fractus arboris ramus. Ita Giauhari et Ibno-maruph. Quod maxime ad rem facit. Modo ad summos arborum ramos referatur, quos locustae depascuntur. Itaque a nonnullis dici putantur ἀκρίδες, παρὰ τὸ ἄκρας τῶν ἀσταχύων καὶ τῶν φυτῶν νέμεσθαι. Hieronymo קצפה est decorticatio. Is proinde hic habet, Ficum meam decorticavit. Et arbores a locustis decorticari non semel scribit. Ut in Oseae caput decimum tertium, Locusta noxia est in tantum, ut arbores quoque et vineas decorticet. Et in Ioelem: Iudaei putant, in diebus Ioel tam innumerabilem locustarum venisse multitudinem, ut ne vinearum quidem et arborum cortices ramosque dimitterent. Et infra, Locustae in tantum cuncta populantur, ut derodant arborum cortices. Chaldaeus, qui vocem קצפה reddidit multo aliter, tamen arbores a locustis decorticari, conclusit ex sequentibus de ficu, חשף חשפה, nudando nudavit eam; quae sic interpretatur, מקלף קלף, decorticando decorticavit. Sed, ut nudari dicatur arbor, corticem adimi necesse non est. Sufficit enim, ut folia, et fructus, vel flores auferantur. Unde Poeta vetus, in Descriptione quatuor anni tempestatum,

Verse 7: He has laid my vine waste, and my fig tree broken. He has stripped it bare and cast it away; its branches are made white.] He says vine and fig tree, because bruchi and locusts are harmful to both. Accordingly, to keep bruchi away from vines, Didymus prescribes this in book 10 of the Geoponica: Περὶ τὸ στέλεχος τῆς ἀμπέλου παρὰ τὴν ῥίζαν, τρεῖς κόκκους σινήπεως χῶσον· φυτευόμενα γὰρ ταῦτα τῇ ὀσμῇ τὸν βροῦχον ἀναιρεῖ. [Peri to stelechos tēs ampelou para tēn rhizan, treis kokkous sinēpeōs chōson; phyteuomena gar tauta tē osmē ton brouchon anairei.] Bury three grains of mustard around the trunk of the vine at the root: for when planted they kill the bruchus by their smell. And of fig trees Pliny, book 17, chapter 25: In Boeotia fig trees gnawed by locusts sprouted again. This is taken from these words of Theophrastus, book 2 of the History, chapter 4: Ἐν δὲ τῇ Βοιωτίᾳ καταβρωθέντων τῶν ἔργων ὑπὸ τῶν ἀττελέβων πάλιν ἀνεβλάστησε. [En de tē Boiōtia katabrōthentōn tōn ergōn hypo tōn attelebōn palin aneblastēse.] Therefore instead of τῶν ἔργων [tōn ergōn] one should read τῶν ἐρίνων [tōn erinōn]. For ἔρινα [erina] are wild figs, or any unripe figs, as III, 296 in Alexis in Athenaeus. I render the Hebrew לקצפה into breaking, with the Greeks, who here have εἰς κλασμὸν [eis klasmon] or συγκλασμόν [synklasmon] R2. This rendering of a word otherwise unusual is confirmed from Arabic usage. For in Arabic قصف [qaṣafa] means to break, and القصيف [al-qaṣīf] is a broken branch of a tree. So Giauhari and Ibno-maruph. This is very much to the point, provided it is referred to the topmost branches of trees, on which locusts feed. Hence some think they are called ἀκρίδες [akrides], παρὰ τὸ ἄκρας τῶν ἀσταχύων καὶ τῶν φυτῶν νέμεσθαι [para to akras tōn astachyōn kai tōn phytōn nemesthai]. For Jerome קצפה is decortication. Accordingly he has here, He has stripped the bark from my fig tree. And more than once he writes that trees are stripped of bark by locusts. So on Hosea chapter 13: The locust is so harmful that it strips the bark even from trees and vines. And on Joel: the Jews think that in the days of Joel so innumerable a multitude of locusts came that they did not spare even the bark and branches of the vines and trees. And below: Locusts lay everything waste to such a degree that they gnaw away the bark of trees. The Chaldee, who rendered the word קצפה quite differently, nevertheless concluded that trees are stripped of bark by locusts from what follows about the fig tree, חשף חשפה, stripping he has stripped it, which he interprets thus: מקלף קלף, barking he has barked it. But for a tree to be said to be stripped, it is not necessary that its bark be removed. It suffices that the leaves and fruit, or flowers, be taken away. Hence the old Poet in the Description of the Four Seasons of the Year:


Fronde nemus denudat hyems, amnesque rigescunt.

Winter strips the grove of its leaves, and the rivers grow stiff.


Id Graece dixeris ψιλοῦν. Theophrastus libri quarti Historiae Plantarum capite decimo sexto, Ἐν Μιλήτῳ δὲ τὰς ἐλαίας, ὅταν ὦσι περὶ τὸ ἀνθεῖν, κάμπαι κατεσθίουσιν; αἱ μὲν τὰ φύλλα, αἱ δὲ τὰ ἄνθη ἕτεραι τῷ γένει· καὶ ψιλοῦσι τὰ δένδρα. Mileti oleas, cum florent, erucae erodunt, aliae frondem, aliae, genere diversae, florem, atque arbores ita denudant. At in Ioele sequitur, fici ramos exalbescere: quod non videbitur aliter posse fieri, quam si cortex detrahatur, ut detegatur alburnum, quomodo factum a Iacobo, Gen. XXX, 37. Respondeo, ipsum arboris corticem, cum putrescit, exalbescere. Hinc Theophrastus libri quinti De causis capite duodecimo, Διὰ τὴν ἀτροφίαν ἐκλευκαίνεται καὶ ἀπόλ-λυται τὰ δένδρα· Alimenti defectu arbores exalbescunt et pereunt. Arbores autem locustarum contactu perire et exarescere, dicetur infra. Utut sit, ex Abyssinorum historiis constat, locustas non solum corticem, sed et fruticum exscindere truncos, cum ad alius pabuli inopiam deventum est (3). Ita asserit Scaliger in Cardanum Exercitatione centesima nonagesima secunda.

In Greek you would call this ψιλοῦν [psiloun]. Theophrastus, Historia Plantarum, book 4, chapter 16: Ἐν Μιλήτῳ δὲ τὰς ἐλαίας, ὅταν ὦσι περὶ τὸ ἀνθεῖν, κάμπαι κατεσθίουσιν; αἱ μὲν τὰ φύλλα, αἱ δὲ τὰ ἄνθη ἕτεραι τῷ γένει· καὶ ψιλοῦσι τὰ δένδρα [En Milētō de tas elaias, hotan ōsi peri to anthein, kampai katesthiousin; hai men ta phylla, hai de ta anthē heterai tō genei; kai psilousi ta dendra]. At Miletus caterpillars gnaw the olives when they are in flower, some the leaves, others, of a different kind, the flower, and so they strip the trees bare. But in Joel it follows that the branches of the fig tree turn white. It will seem that this cannot happen unless the bark is stripped off so that the sapwood is exposed, as was done by Jacob, Gen. XXX, 37. I reply that the bark of a tree itself turns white when it rots. Hence Theophrastus, De causis, book 5, chapter 12: Διὰ τὴν ἀτροφίαν ἐκλευκαίνεται καὶ ἀπόλλυται τὰ δένδρα [Dia tēn atrophian ekleukainetai kai apollytai ta dendra]; For lack of nourishment trees turn white and perish. That trees perish and wither at the touch of locusts will be shown below. However that may be, it is established from the histories of the Abyssinians that locusts cut off not only the bark but even the stems of shrubs, when they are reduced to a lack of other fodder R3. So Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)] asserts in the 192nd Exercitatio against Cardano.


III, 297 Versu nono, Excisum est fertum et libamen e domo Domini, lugent sacer- col. 470 dotes, ministri Domini.] Ut versu decimo tertio, Venite, et pernoctate in saccis; quoniam prohibitum est e domo Dei vestri fertum et libamen. Ex utroque hoc loco colligit Abarbanel, templum a Babyloniis fuisse tum excisum: cum sequatur contrarium, nempe templum extitisse. Neque enim exscindi et prohiberi potest sacrificium ex domo, quae non amplius exstat.

III, 297 Verse 9: The meal offering and the drink offering are cut off from the house of the Lord; the priests, the ministers of the Lord, mourn. col. 470] As in verse 13: Come, and spend the night in sackcloth; for the meal offering and the drink offering are withheld from the house of your God. From both these passages Abarbanel infers that the temple had then been destroyed by the Babylonians; whereas the contrary follows, namely that the temple was standing. For a sacrifice cannot be cut off or withheld from a house that no longer exists.


Versu decimo, Vastatus est ager, luget terra; quoniam vastatum est triti- cum, erubuit mustum, languit oleum.] Unde primitiae et decimae Domino offerebantur, Num. XVIII, 12. Deut. XIV, 23. et XVIII, 3. 4. Sed et ex iisdem fiebant ferta et libamina. Itaque cum haec tria deessent, non erat, unde fierent solitae oblationes. Lugere terra dicitur, ut apud Hebraeos quaecunque vastata et desolata sunt, et in deterius mutata. Ut Es. XXIV, 7. Luget mustum, vitis languet. Thren. II, 8. Fecit, ut lugerent antemurale et murus: pariter elangue- runt. Eodem tropo oleum languere et mustum erubescere dicuntur (quomodo vitis versu duodecimo) tanquam pudore affecta, quod hominum exspectationi respondere non possint. Sic Es. XXXIII, 9. Luxit, languit terra, erubuit Li-banus. Lugenti terrae opponuntur frugum pabulique laetus ager in Sallustii libro secundo Historiarum, et laetae segetes apud Poetam. Unde et fimus, quo stercorantur agri, vulgo laetamen vocari, scribit Servius, quod Italis est letame.

Verse 10: The field is laid waste, the land mourns; for the grain is laid waste, the new wine has blushed, the oil languishes.] From these the firstfruits and tithes were offered to the Lord, Num. XVIII, 12. Deut. XIV, 23. and XVIII, 3. 4. And from the same the meal offerings and drink offerings were made. So when these three were lacking, there was nothing from which the customary oblations could be made. The land is said to mourn, as among the Hebrews is said of whatever has been laid waste and made desolate and changed for the worse. So Es. XXIV, 7: The new wine mourns, the vine languishes. Lam 2:8: He made the rampart and the wall mourn; they languished together. By the same figure the oil is said to languish and the new wine to blush (as the vine in verse 12), as though affected with shame because they cannot meet the expectation of men. Thus Es. XXXIII, 9: The land mourned and languished, Lebanon blushed. To the mourning land is opposed a field glad with crops and fodder in Sallust, Histories, book 2, and glad crops in the Poet. Hence too the dung with which fields are manured is commonly called laetamen, as Servius writes, which in Italian is letame.


Versu undecimo, Erubescite, agricolae; ejulate vinitores, propter triticum et hordeum: quia periit messis agri. 12. Vitis erubuit, etc.] Ordo esset, „Eru-„bescite, agricolae, propter triticum et hordeum; quia periit messis agri. Ejulate, vinitores, quia vitis erubuit.“ Sed haec transponuntur per figuram, qualis χιασμός. Tale illud de ecclesia Cant. I, 4. (al. 5.) Nigra sum, sed formo- sa: ut tentoria Kedar, et aulaea Solomonis. Id est, „Extrinsecus, et hominum III, 298 „judicio, nigra sum, ut cilicina Kedarenorum tentoria: sed formosa intrinsecus, „et coram Deo, ut magnifica Solomonis aulaea.“ Itaque par μετάθεσις.

Verse 11: Be ashamed, O farmers; wail, O vinedressers, for the wheat and the barley; because the harvest of the field has perished. 12. The vine has blushed, etc.] The order would be: "Be ashamed, O farmers, for the wheat and the barley, because the harvest of the field has perished. Wail, O vinedressers, because the vine has blushed." But these are transposed by a figure such as the χιασμός [chiasmos]. Such is that said of the church, Cant. I, 4. (var. 5.): I am black, but comely, as the tents of Kedar, and the curtains of Solomon. That is, "Outwardly, and in the III, 298 judgement of men, I am black, like the haircloth tents of the Kedarenes; but comely inwardly, and before God, like the magnificent curtains of Solomon." So there is a like μετάθεσις [metathesis].


Versu duodecimo, Erubuit vitis, et ficus languet. Malus punica etiam, palma, et malus, omnes agri arbores exaruerunt, quia periit gaudium a filiis hominum. Quo scilicet in messe et vindemia afficiuntur, et cum colliguntur arborum fructus. Unde Es. IX, 3. Laetati sunt coram te ea laetitia, quae in messe est. Et Psal. IV, 8. Majorem animo meo laetitiam indidisti, quam tempore, quo frumentum et mustum illis abunde provenerunt. In his cum planum sit, agi de damno, terrae frugibus ac arborum fructibus a locustis illato, tamen reperit Abarbanel, quod objiceret. Nempe, si res sit de locustis, frustra dici, vitem, et ficum, et omnes agri arbores exaruisse: cum fructus quidem locustae absumant, sed ipsas arbores haud quaquam laedant. Unde hanc pestem patet illi fuisse minus notam. Locustam enim Plinius scribit multa contactu adurere. Et Pisidas in Opificio mundi,

Verse 12: The vine has blushed, and the fig tree languishes. The pomegranate too, the palm, and the apple tree, all the trees of the field have withered, because joy has perished from the sons of men. That is, the joy they feel at harvest and vintage, and when the fruits of the trees are gathered. Hence Isa 9:3: They have rejoiced before you with the joy that is at harvest. And Ps 4:8: You have put greater gladness in my heart than at the time when their grain and new wine abounded. Although it is plain that these verses concern the damage inflicted by locusts on the crops of the land and the fruits of the trees, Abarbanel nevertheless found something to object. Namely, that if the matter concerned locusts, it would be pointless to say that the vine, the fig tree and all the trees of the field had withered, since locusts consume the fruit but do not harm the trees themselves in the least. From this it is clear that this plague was little known to him. For Pliny writes that the locust scorches many things by its touch. And Pisides in the Creation of the World:


Τήκει τὰ δένδρα, καὶ μαραίνει τὴν πόαν,

Τήκει τὰ δένδρα, καὶ μαραίνει τὴν πόαν, [Tēkei ta dendra, kai marainei tēn poan,]


Arbores tabefacit, et herbam marcidam reddit, Et Damir, لعابه سم ناقع النبات والشجر لا يقع علي شي منه الا اهلكه Saliva ejus plantis et arboribus venenum est praesentissimum: ita, ut, in quamcunque incidat, eam perdat. Quod idem post Valeriolam his verbis tradit Muffetus: Nec solum morsu segetibus, pascuis, pratis, hortis, pomariisque nocent: sed stercore item nigro, viridi, mordace, gravi, biliosaque inprimis atque acri saliva, quam multam ex ore inter rodendum fundunt.

It makes trees waste away and renders the grass withered. And Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: لعابه سم ناقع النبات والشجر لا يقع علي شي منه الا اهلكه [luʿābuhu samm nāqiʿ al-nabāt wa-l-shajar lā yaqaʿu ʿalā shayʾ minhu illā ahlakahu], Its saliva is a most potent poison to plants and trees, so that whatever it falls upon, it destroys. Muffet, following Valeriola, reports the same thing in these words: They harm crops, pastures, meadows, gardens and orchards not only by their bite, but also by their dung, which is black, green, biting and heavy, and above all by their bilious and acrid saliva, which they pour from their mouths in quantity while gnawing.


Versu decimo quinto, Heu diem illum! quia propinquus est dies Domini, et ut vastitas ab omnipotente veniet. Dies Domini, quo nempe sedebit tanquam col. 471 judex, ut in Iudaeos animadvertat, locustarum agmine in eos immisso. Diem enim pro judicio hic sumi, docti recte observant. Ut 1 Cor. IV, 3. Mihi parum est judicari ab humana die, id est, humano judicio. Quomodo loqui Cilices, unde Paulus oriúndus, scribit Hieronymus ad Algasiam Quaestione decima. Quod illos a vicinis Syris crediderim esse mutuatos. Ut vastitas ab omnipotente] Hebraice כשד משדי, eleganti paronomasia. Ac si quis Graece dixerit, ὡς ἀπώ-λειαν ἀπ᾽ Ἀπόλλωνος· aut ὡς δήωσιν ἐκ Δηοῦς. Tamen Dei nomen שדי saddai vastatorem non sonat, sed παντοκράτορα, omnipotentem, ut Arabice شد sadda est roborare.

In verse fifteen: Alas for that day! for the day of the Lord is near, and it shall come as devastation from the Almighty. The day of the Lord, that is, the day on which he will sit as col. 471 judge to punish the Jews by sending the swarm of locusts against them. For learned men rightly observe that day is taken here for judgment. So in 1 Cor 4:3. With me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of man's day, that is, by human judgment. Jerome writes to Algasia, in Question 10, that this was how the Cilicians spoke, from whom Paul came. I would believe that they borrowed it from their neighbours the Syrians. As devastation from the Almighty] In Hebrew כשד משדי, an elegant paronomasia, as if someone were to say in Greek ὡς ἀπώλειαν ἀπ᾽ Ἀπόλλωνος [hōs apōleian ap᾽ Apollōnos], or ὡς δήωσιν ἐκ Δηοῦς [hōs dēōsin ek Dēous]. Yet the divine name שדי saddai does not mean devastator, but παντοκράτορα [pantokratora], almighty, just as in Arabic شد [shadda] sadda means to strengthen.


Versu decimo sexto, Nonne coram oculis nostris cibus succisus est, e domo Dei nostri gaudium et exultatio?] Unde rursus apparet, agi de templo adhuc stante, III, 299 non a Chaldaeis subverso, ut placet Abarbaneli. Gaudium autem intelligitur, quo illi afficiuntur, qui sacrificiis et primitiis, in Dei templo oblatis, hilares vescebantur, Lege ita jubente Deut. XII, 6. 7. Eo adducetis holocausta vestra, et sacrificia vestra, decimasque vestras, et oblationes manus vestrae, etc. Ut ibi comedentes coram Domino vestro laetemini, vos, et familiae vestrae, etc. Et Deut. XVI, 10. 11. Celebrabis festum septem septimanarum Domino Deo tuo voluntaria oblatione, etc. Et laetaberis coram Domino Deo tuo. Et 1 Paralip. XIX, 21. 22.
