Roasting the thighs, they feasted, delighting in a splendid banquet. But this joy ceases when offerings are lacking. And they were lacking, because the locusts had left nothing untouched.


Versu decimo septimo, Putruerunt grana sub glebis suis, desolatae sunt cellae, destructa sunt horrea; quia exaruit frumentum.] In hujus versus primo commate, עבשו פרדות תחת מגרפותיהם, e quatuor verbis tria sunt, quae nusquam alibi reperiuntur. Proinde hic haerent interpretes, neque dissensus major uspiam. Graeci enim reddunt, Ἐσκίρτησαν δαμάλεις ἐπὶ ταῖς φάτναις, Subsultaverunt juvencae in praesepibus suis (4). Et Hieronymus, Computruerunt jumenta III, 300 in stercore suo. Et Chaldaeus, אתמסיו גרבי חמר תחות מגופתהון, Effluxerunt dolia vini sub operculis suis (5). Et Syrus rursus aliter (6). Nos cum Hebraeis, Computruerunt grana sub glebis suis. Nempe עבשׁו idem, quod עפשׁו, Beth et Pe permutatis, quae literae sunt homogeneae et facile permutabiles. Porro Talmudicis עפשׁ est putrescere. Recte igitur Hieronymus, computruerunt. Et פרדות grana vere exponi suadet, quod Syris ܦܪܕܬܐ est granum. Hinc in Syra paraphrasi Matth. XIII, 31. ܦܪܕܬܐ ܕܚܪܕܠܐ est granum sinapi. Ioh. XII, 24. ܦܪܕܬܐ ܕܚܛܬܐ, granum frumenti. 1 Corinth. XV, 37. ܦܪܕܬܐ ܕܚܛܬܐ ܘܕܣܥܪܐ, grana tritici et hordei (7). Denique מגרפות esse glebas, III, 301 suadet similitudo vocum גרף (unde מגרפות) et רגב: quarum haec in Iobo bis occurrit pro gleba. Et vero glebae dici videntur מגרפות, a Verbo גרף, quod, de torrente usurpatum, avehere significat. Sic Iud. V, 21. Torrens Kison גרפם avexit eos. Et Arabice in Alcamus, جرفته السيل, illum avexit torrens. سيل جراف Torrens omnia avehens. جرف terrae gleba, quam torrens avehit. Itaque מגרפות sunt proprie רגבי נחל, glebae torrentis, quomodo vocantur Iob. XXI, 33. deinde etiam glebae quaevis (8). Grana porro (seu semina) III, 302 solent sub glebis suis (id est, in terram jacta) putrescere, cum nimii sunt col. 472 imbres. Proinde Plinius, libri decimi capite vigesimo quarto, sationem locis humihumidis III, 303 vult celerius fieri, ne semen imbre putrescat. Et Kimchius in hunc Ioelis locum, יתעפשו גרגרי הזרע מפני הגשמים, Putrescunt grana seminis propter pluvias (9). Et Iunius, Mucida facta sunt sata ex nimiis imbribus, semen corrumpentibus. Quo eodem sensu Cl. Deodatius, Accenni che le semente sarebbero guaste da soverchie piogge (10). Sed haec non cohaerent cum sequentibus, quibus describitur summa siccitas. Eo enim haec pertinent versu decimo nono, Ignis consumsit pascua deserti, et flamma adussit omnes arbores agri. Et versu vigesimo, Etiam agri bestiae ad te clamant, propterea quod exaruerunt alvei aquae et pascua deserti absumpsit ignis. Ignis, et flamma, id est, immodicus aestus. Ut Psal. LXXXII, 13. (al. LXXXIII, 15.) Ut ignis comburit sylvam, et flamma montes incendit. Hinc loca, solis ardore retorrida, חררים, vocantur Ierem. XVII, 6. id est, ardentia, vel adusta. Satorum igitur putredo, de qua Ioel, non venit ex pluviis, sed ex summa siccitate. Qua, si proprie loqui velimus, semina non tam putrescere, quam vanescere dicuntur. Plinius ubi supra: Sationem locis humidis celerius fieri ratio est, ne semen imbre putrescat: siccis serius, ut pluviae sequantur, ne, diu jacens, atque non concipiens, vanescat. Quale est, quod capite praecedenti dixit, ventos noxios exinanire grana. Sed, sive imbre grana putrescant, aut siccitate vanescant, Hebraeum עבש, vel עבש, potuit utrumque complecti (11). Ut in Hesiodi Clypeo cadaverum ossa III, 304 Σειρίου ἀζαλέοιο κελαινῇ πύθεται αἴῃ,

In verse 17, The seeds have rotted under their clods, the storehouses are desolate, the granaries are destroyed, because the grain has withered.] In the first clause of this verse, עבשו פרדות תחת מגרפותיהם, three of the four words are found nowhere else. Hence the interpreters are at a loss here, and nowhere is there greater disagreement. For the Greeks render it Ἐσκίρτησαν δαμάλεις ἐπὶ ταῖς φάτναις [Eskirtēsan damaleis epi tais phatnais], The heifers have leapt at their mangers R4. And Jerome: The beasts have rotted III, 300 in their dung. And the Chaldee: אתמסיו גרבי חמר תחות מגופתהון, The jars of wine have run out under their lids R5. And the Syriac again differently R6. We, with the Hebrews: The seeds have rotted under their clods. That is, עבשׁו is the same as עפשׁו, with Beth and Pe interchanged, letters which are homogeneous and easily interchangeable. Further, in the Talmudists עפשׁ means to rot. So Jerome rightly has computruerunt [have rotted]. And that פרדות is truly to be explained as seeds is suggested by the fact that in Syriac ܦܪܕܬܐ [פרדתא] is a seed. Hence in the Syriac version, Matth. XIII, 31, ܦܪܕܬܐ ܕܚܪܕܠܐ [פרדתא דחרדלא] is a grain of mustard seed; John 12:24, ܦܪܕܬܐ ܕܚܛܬܐ [פרדתא דחטתא], a grain of wheat; 1 Corinth. XV, 37, ܦܪܕܬܐ ܕܚܛܬܐ ܘܕܣܥܪܐ [פרדתא דחטתא ודסערא], grains of wheat and of barley R7. Finally, that מגרפות are clods III, 301 is suggested by the similarity of the words גרף (whence מגרפות) and רגב, the latter of which occurs twice in Job for clod. And indeed clods seem to be called מגרפות from the verb גרף, which, used of a torrent, means to carry away. Thus Iud. V, 21: the torrent Kishon גרפם, swept them away. And in Arabic, in Alcamus: جرفته السيل [jarafathu al-sayl], the torrent swept him away; سيل جراف [sayl jurāf], a torrent sweeping everything away; جرف [jurf], a clod of earth which a torrent carries away. Thus מגרפות are properly רגבי נחל, clods of the torrent, as they are called in Job 21:33, and then also clods of any kind R8. Further, grains (or seeds) III, 302 usually rot under their clods (that is, when cast into the ground) when the col. 472 rains are excessive. Hence Pliny, book 10, chapter 24, wants sowing in humid places III, 303 to be done earlier, lest the seed rot from the rain. And Kimchi on this passage of Joel: יתעפשו גרגרי הזרע מפני הגשמים, The grains of seed rot because of the rains R9. And Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible]: The sown crops have become mouldy from excessive rains, which spoil the seed. In the same sense the distinguished Diodati: Accenni che le semente sarebbero guaste da soverchie piogge R10. But this does not agree with what follows, where extreme drought is described. For this is what verse 19 refers to: Fire has consumed the pastures of the wilderness, and flame has scorched all the trees of the field. And verse 20: Even the beasts of the field cry to you, because the channels of water have dried up and fire has consumed the pastures of the wilderness. Fire and flame, that is, excessive heat. As in Ps 82:13 (var. LXXXIII, 15.): As fire burns the forest, and flame sets the mountains ablaze. Hence places parched by the heat of the sun are called חררים in Jer 17:6, that is, burning or scorched. So the rotting of the sown crops of which Joel speaks comes not from rains but from extreme drought. By this, if we wish to speak properly, seeds are said not so much to rot as to come to nothing. Pliny, in the place cited above: The reason for sowing earlier in humid places is lest the seed rot from the rain; in dry places later, so that rains may follow, lest, lying long and not germinating, it come to nothing. Such is what he said in the preceding chapter, that harmful winds empty the grains. But whether the grains rot from rain or come to nothing from drought, the Hebrew עבש, or עבש, could cover both R11. As in Hesiod's Shield the bones of corpses III, 304 Σειρίου ἀζαλέοιο κελαινῇ πύθεται αἴῃ [Seiriou azaleoio kelainē pythetai aiē],


Sub arido Syrio in nigra putrescunt terra. Quasi etiam siccitas sit causa putredinis. Atque illa ipsa siccitas, cujus Propheta meminit, causa fuit, cur locustae uberius provenirent. De iis enim ita Plinius libri undecimi capite vigesimo octavo, Vernis aquis intereunt ova, sicco vere major proventus. Et de attelabis Philosophus libri quinti Historiae capite vigesimo nono, Φθείρεται δὲ αὐτῶν τὰ ὠὰ ὑπὸ τῶν μετοπωρινῶν ὑδάτων, ὅταν πολλὰ γένηται. ἂν δὲ αὐχμὸς συμ-βῇ, τότε γίνονται μᾶλλον ἀττέλαβοι πολλοὶ, διὰ τὸ αὐτὰ μὴ φθείρεσθαι ὁμοίως. Eorum ova corrumpuntur autumnalibus aquis, si multae sint. At sicco autumno largior est attelaborum proventus, quia tum similis non est illorum corruptio. Hinc Tertullianus De Anima capite trigesimo secundo, Siccitatibus gaudent locustae, papiliunculi, chamaeleontes (12). Itaque, ut locustarum ova destruantur, ex Valeriola et Peucero docet Muffetus, in eorum loca primo vere derivare torrentes, qui totam terrae superficiem, aut maximam ejus partem, abunde humectent. Haec ad primum caput Ioelis; jam ad secundum.

Under parching Sirius they rot in the black earth. As though drought too were a cause of rotting. And that very drought which the Prophet mentions was the reason why the locusts came forth more abundantly. For of them Pliny says thus in book 11, chapter 28: The eggs perish from spring rains; in a dry spring the yield is greater. And of the attelabi the Philosopher, book 5 of the History, chapter 29: Φθείρεται δὲ αὐτῶν τὰ ὠὰ ὑπὸ τῶν μετοπωρινῶν ὑδάτων, ὅταν πολλὰ γένηται. ἂν δὲ αὐχμὸς συμβῇ, τότε γίνονται μᾶλλον ἀττέλαβοι πολλοὶ, διὰ τὸ αὐτὰ μὴ φθείρεσθαι ὁμοίως. [Phtheiretai de autōn ta ōa hypo tōn metopōrinōn hydatōn, hotan polla genētai. an de auchmos symbē, tote ginontai mallon attelaboi polloi, dia to auta mē phtheiresthai homoiōs.] Their eggs are destroyed by autumn rains, if these are heavy. But in a dry autumn the yield of attelabi is larger, because then they are not destroyed in the same way. Hence Tertullian, On the Soul, chapter 32: Locusts, little butterflies and chameleons rejoice in droughts R12. Therefore, so that the eggs of locusts may be destroyed, Moffett, following Valleriola and Peucer, teaches that at the beginning of spring torrents should be diverted into the places where they lie, so as to soak the whole surface of the ground, or the greater part of it, abundantly. So much for the first chapter of Joel; now to the second.

(4) Rosenmüller, III, 299 Quod ἐσκίρτησαν verterunt, rationem existimo non fuisse hanc, quod pro עבשו legerint בעטו, ut conjecit CAPPEL-LUS Crit. S. T. II. pag. 631. edit. Vogel-Scharfenberg., in qua conjectura sequacem habet I. D. MICHAELEM in Supplemm. P. VI. p. 1825., aut פשו, obesi facti stulte egerunt, ut voluit I. FR. FISCHER in Proluss. de Verss. Graecc. Librr. V. T. pag. 13., aut פשו, saliunt, quod verisimile visum Scharfenbergio ad Cappelli l. c.; verum quod Hebraeum עבש ludendi significatione sumserint, quae inest Arabico عبث, quae ED. POCOCKII est sententia in Commentar. pag. 84. vers. lat., aut quod עבש cum أفز, assilire, comparaverint, quae minus probabilis est BOYSENII opinio, in libro, vernacula lingua scripto, cui index est: Beyträge zu einem richtigen System der Hebräischen Philologie, T. I. p. 342. Pro פרדות Alexandrinum et Syrum interpretem פרות in suis codicibus legisse, Mercerus, Cappellus, Fischerus, Michaelis, alii, colligunt ex eo, quod ille δαμάλεις, hic ܥܓ̈ܠܐ, vitulos posuit. Quibus et Vulgatum Latinum accensent, qui vertit, jumenta, quamvis quibusdam videatur iisdem consonantibus legisse vocem, at non iisdem vocalibus: ac si numerum pluralem formasset a פרדה, quod genus foemininum est nominis פרד, mulus; uno bestiarum genere expresso, quo ceterae similis naturae comprehenduntur bestiae vel catuli in genere. Denique loco ejus, quod nos hodie legimus, מגרפתיהם, interpretem Graecum III, 300 Alexandrinum in suo codice invenisse הרפתיהם, Fischerus concludit ex eo, quod is ἐπὶ ταῖς φάτναις αὐτῶν vertit; רפתים autem alio quoque loco (Habac. III, 17.) iisdem interpretibus dicuntur φάτναι. MER-CERUS tamen in Commentario ad hunc locum, tam hanc Graecorum versionem, ἐπὶ ταῖς φάτναις αὐτῶν, ad praesepia, sive in stabulis, ipsorum, quam Vulgatam latinam, in stercore suo, putat quam maxime niti derivatione vocis a radice גרף, quatenus denotat avertere, quia stercus avertitur sub pecudibus, vel ex eorum stabulis.

R4 Rosenmüller, III, 299 That they rendered ἐσκίρτησαν [eskirtēsan], I think the reason was not that they read בעטו for עבשו, as Cappellus conjectured, Crit. S. vol. II, p. 631, Vogel-Scharfenberg edition (a conjecture in which he has a follower in I. D. Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], Supplemm. vol. VI, p. 1825); nor פשו, having grown fat they behaved foolishly, as I. Fr. Fischer would have it in Proluss. de Verss. Graecc. Librr. V. T. p. 13; nor פשו, they leap, which seemed probable to Scharfenberg on Cappellus, loc. cit.; but rather that they took the Hebrew עבש in the sense of playing, which belongs to the Arabic عبث [ʿabath], which is the view of Ed. Pococke in his Commentary p. 84, Latin trans.; or that they compared עבש with أفز [afaza], to leap up, which is the less probable opinion of Boysen, in a book written in the vernacular entitled Beyträge zu einem richtigen System der Hebräischen Philologie, vol. I, p. 342. That the Alexandrian and the Syriac translators read פרות in their manuscripts instead of פרדות, Mercerus [=Jean Mercier (d. 1570), commentaries on Job and Proverbs], Cappellus, Fischer, Michaelis and others infer from the fact that the former put δαμάλεις [damaleis], the latter ܥܓ̈ܠܐ [עגלא], calves. To these they also add the Latin Vulgate, which renders jumenta [beasts of burden], although to some it seems to have read the word with the same consonants but not the same vowels: as if it had formed a plural from פרדה, the feminine of the noun פרד, mule; one kind of beast being named, under which the other beasts of similar nature, or young animals in general, are included. Finally, Fischer concludes that instead of what we read today, מגרפתיהם, the Greek Alexandrian translator III, 300 found in his manuscript הרפתיהם, from the fact that he rendered ἐπὶ ταῖς φάτναις αὐτῶν [epi tais phatnais autōn]; and רפתים is in another passage too (Hab 3:17) called φάτναι [phatnai] by the same translators. Mercerus, however, in his commentary on this passage, thinks that both this Greek rendering, ἐπὶ ταῖς φάτναις αὐτῶν [epi tais phatnais autōn], at their mangers or in their stalls, and the Latin Vulgate, in stercore suo [in their dung], rest above all on deriving the word from the root גרף, in so far as it denotes to sweep away, because dung is swept away from under the cattle, or out of their stalls.


(5) Rosenmüller, III, 300 Rectius Chaldaica haec in Bibliis Polyglottis latine ita redduntur: computruerunt dolia vini sub operculis suis. Quae interpretatio firmatur auctoritate Abu Walidi, doctissimi Hebraeorum Grammatici, ab Ed. Pocockio, ut saepe, ita et hic laudati (pag. 80.), qui Chaldaei interpretis verba ita explicat: خبجت دنان الخمر وعفنت من طول مكثها فارغة dolia vinaria foetent, vel rancida et mucida redduntur, quod tamdiu vacua maneant. Patet, Chaldaeum interpretem verbum עבש mucescendi, putrescendi significatione sumsisse. quae inest Chaldaico, sono cognato, עפש. Verba autem Hebraea cetera, quae non satis intellexisse videtur, libera paraphrasi reddidit.

R5 Rosenmüller, III, 300 These Chaldee words are more correctly rendered in Latin in the Polyglot Bibles thus: the wine-jars have rotted under their lids. This interpretation is confirmed by the authority of Abu Walid, the most learned grammarian of the Hebrews, cited by Ed. Pococke here as often (p. 80), who explains the words of the Chaldee translator thus: خبجت دنان الخمر وعفنت من طول مكثها فارغة [khabijat dinān al-khamr wa-ʿafinat min ṭūl makthihā fārigha] the wine-jars stink, or become rancid and musty, because they remain empty so long. It is clear that the Chaldee translator took the verb עבש in the sense of growing musty, rotting, which belongs to the Chaldee עפש, cognate in sound. The other Hebrew words, however, which he seems not to have understood well enough, he rendered by a free paraphrase.

R6 Rosenmüller, III, 300 ܥܒܫ ܥܓܠܬܐ ܥܠ ܐܘܪܝܘܬܗܝܢ [עבש עגלתא על אוריותהין], words which the Latin translator in the Polyglots renders thus: the heifers remained unfed at their mangers. But Ed. Pococke, p. 80. 82, notes that the verb ܥܒܫ [עבש] is more correctly rendered they are parched or scorched, so that the more usual meaning of the Syriac ܥܒܫ [עבש] is retained, and that the Syriac translator expressed the notion of being dry, which belongs to the Arabic عبس [ʿabasa], agreeing in spelling and sound with the Hebrew עבש. Cf. our note 11 below. That parched or dried-up heifers are heifers wasted by hunger scarcely needs pointing out.


(7) Rosenmüller, III, 300 Vocis פרודות notionem nemo exposuit melius, atque simul varias ejus interpretationes diligentius expendit Eduardo Pocockio in Commentario, quem, quia neglectum fere hodie video, atque in paucorum manibus versatum, immerito tamen, quum refertus sit solida atque exquisita eruditione, apponam ex eo, quae maxime ad rem faciunt. „A radice פרד, quae Hebraeis, Chaldaeis et Arabibus significat separare, vel separatum esse, possunt deduci nomina, quae denotant quid singulare et separatum ab aliis, ut frumenti granula et semen, quod seminatur ac terrae mandatur. Atque eo sensu et hic accipi posse nomen hebraicum, absurdum non est, III, 301 quamvis formae admodum peculiaris sit, cum nominis substantivi loco in SS. literis nullibi usurpetur, nec ulla ejus occurrat occasio, sicut Syriaci ܦܪܕܐ, quod in N. T. versione occurrit ea significatione grani, vel sati, et in plurali granorum, vel satorum; unde apparet, haud sine praegnanti ratione sic esse redditam, et a quibusdam Iudaeorum explanatam גרגרי החטה והשערה, grana tritici et hordei, vel גרגרי הזרע, grana seminis, quae seminantur, separantur et dissipantur per solum; vel ut Abu Walid Arabice الحبوب المبذورات للزراعة grana disjecta seminando, et R. Tanchum, الحبوب المعدودة للزراعة لانها تغرق في الارض grana praeparata ad seminandum, ita dicta, quia sparguntur per solum. Manuscripti Arabici auctor [intelligit versionem V. T. arabicam, quam possedit et saepe laudat, quamque a R. Saadia Haggaon concinnatam putat in Praefat. p. 16.] eandem ei tribuit denotationem, atque ab eadem radice deducit reddendo المتفردات (quod ad literam sonat separatum), ubi peculiari nota exponit, se intelligere קמח אלבדאר אלדי הו קמח מפרד לם פיה זואן, semen tritici, quod est triticum separatum, cui non immixtum est lolium, לאן כאן דאב אלנאס יבדדו אלגל מן אלקמח, quia mos hominibus est, seminare praecipuum (vel exquisitum) tritici. Ita quidem et Abarbinel accipit, sed etiam significationis adducit causam, scilicet, non quod alterum ab altero sit separatum et distinctum, vel a lolio seiunctum, sed quod separatum sit (vel subductum) ab oculis hominum atque occultum in latebris soli semen. Atque sic omnibus his convenit in eadem significatione eademque nominis radice, utut in derivationis ratione nonnihil vacillent.“ Haec Pocockius.

R7 Rosenmüller, III, 300 No one has explained the meaning of the word פרודות better, and at the same time weighed its various interpretations more carefully, than Edward Pococke in his Commentary. Since I see that it is almost neglected today and in the hands of few, though undeservedly, for it is full of solid and exquisite learning, I shall add from it what is most to the point. "From the root פרד, which among the Hebrews, Chaldeans and Arabs means to separate or to be separated, nouns can be derived that denote something single and separated from others, such as grains of corn and the seed that is sown and committed to the earth. And it is not absurd that the Hebrew noun can be taken in this sense here too, III, 301 although its form is quite peculiar, since it is nowhere used in Holy Scripture as a substantive, nor does any other occurrence of it appear, as with the Syriac ܦܪܕܐ [פרדא], which occurs in the version of the N. T. in the sense of grain or seed sown, and in the plural grains or seeds sown. Hence it appears that it was not without weighty reason rendered thus, and explained by some of the Jews as גרגרי החטה והשערה, grains of wheat and barley, or גרגרי הזרע, grains of seed, which are sown, separated and scattered over the ground; or, as Abu Walid puts it in Arabic, الحبوب المبذورات للزراعة [al-ḥubūb al-mabdhūrāt li-l-zirāʿa], grains scattered in sowing; and R. Tanchum, الحبوب المعدودة للزراعة لانها تغرق في الارض [al-ḥubūb al-maʿdūda li-l-zirāʿa li-annahā tughraq fī al-arḍ], grains prepared for sowing, so called because they are scattered over the ground. The author of the Arabic manuscript [he means the Arabic version of the O. T., which he possessed and often cites, and which he thinks was composed by R. Saadia Haggaon, in the Preface, p. 16] assigns it the same meaning and derives it from the same root, rendering it المتفردات [al-mutafarridāt] (which literally means separated), where in a special note he explains that he understands קמח אלבדאר אלדי הו קמח מפרד לם פיה זואן, seed wheat, which is separated wheat, with which no darnel is mixed, לאן כאן דאב אלנאס יבדדו אלגל מן אלקמח, because it is the custom of men to sow the choicest (or most select) of the wheat. Abarbinel too takes it so, but he also adduces the reason for the meaning, namely, not that one grain is separated and distinct from another, or set apart from darnel, but that the seed is separated (or withdrawn) from the eyes of men and hidden in the recesses of the soil. And thus all these agree in the same meaning and the same root of the noun, however much they waver somewhat in the explanation of the derivation." So Pococke.


(8) Rosenmüller, III, 301 Abu Walid, inquit POCOCK p. 84. 85., quem eorum, quos habemus, Grammaticos inter Iudaeos, censemus antiquissimum, habet خطوطها, sulci illorum, quibus intelligit الخطوط التي يخطها الزارع بالسكة بعد البذر quos agricola dentali suo ducit, postquam frumentum satum est, qui sunt, addit, sicuti خدوش في الارض scalpturae in fundo. Et in eandem sententiam alio loco (in Rad. פרד) rursus ait, sic nominari تشبيها بالخدوش propter similitudinem scalpturarum sive vulnerum, quae fiunt in cute alicujus unguibus, quae sunt fracturae cutis. Eadem voce tantum non utitur R. Tanchum, adeo, ut et illi תחת מגרפותיהם sit תחת חרושהא sub scalpturis illorum, III, 302 illorum, i. e. تحت الخطوط التي يحفرها الحراث التي كانها كسور في الارض sulcis (lineis) quos aratrum fodit, qui sunt tanquam lirae in terra, quomodo et alias (Psal. LXV, 10.) eadem fere ratione vocantur גדודים, incisiones (nostr. sulci), a גדד, incidere. Huic significationi fulcrum quaerunt ex voce אגרוף, quae reperitur Exod. XXI, 18., et nostratibus, aliisque tum Iudaeis, tum Christianis, redditur pugnus, sed illis (Abu Wa-lid in Rad. גרף) شادخ كاسر aliquid quod vulnerat, vel facit incisuram, كل يجرح او يشدخ به. Interim apparet, his lineis vel scalpturis (ut eas vocant) non intelligendos sulcos excavatos et apertos, sed terra obtectos, qui aratro, vel occa ducuntur per eam, quippe vox תחת, sub, ei adjuncta, hoc necessario requirit; atque ideo Aben Esra exponit eam per העפר, pulverem, vel terram, et Kimchi per חתיכות העפר, fragmenta, vel particulas pulveris; hinc nostrates reddunt glebas, cum recentioribus interpretibus plerisque. Quod quidam confirmare conantur ex lingua Arabica, qua جُرْفٌ significare perhibetur glebam terrae, quam aqua convolvit, vel secum abducit, ita, ut pro quavis gleba possit usurpari. A radice hujus vocis hebraica גרף et Arabica أجرف, quae significat et convolvere, et abducere, vel dispergere, non incommode forsitan posset deduci nomen, quod denotet terram fractam, superfusam, convolutam, vel projectam super frumentum aratro vel occa glebae denotatione confirmata a الجرفة, significante frustum panis fracti, atque ita forsan quaedam fragmenta, vel frusta fracta alius rei, sicut glebae terrae. Restat interpretationis vocis alia ratio, cujus meminit auctor Ms. Arabici (etsi ipsa hebraica voce exprimat مجارفهم), nimirum انادر, quae designat vel granaria, vel acervos frumenti in granariis, التي منها يجرف القمح ويودا الي الصحرا a quibus triticum (vel semen) remotum est (vel aversum, vel ablatum) et delatum in campum, ut terrae demandaretur, ita, ut eandem notionem habeat haec radix, quam praecedens, nimirum demendi vel auferendi. Hac ratione etiam accepisse nonnullos, refert Grotius, qui habent acervos, ac si semina vel grana fuissent corrupta at-que ad seminandum inidonea reddita jam in acervis, quo congesta erant. “ — Cum Arabicum مِجْرَفَةٌ ligo sit, vel tale instrumentum, fimo ejiciendo vel pulveri extergendo aptum; eadem significatione etiam Hebraicum מגרפה sumendum censet MICHAELIS in Supplemm. ad Lexx. P. II. pag. 361. verbaque nostra vertit: grana minuuntur sub paleis. Qui sensus, jam per se jejunus, etiam ideo non potest admitti, quod עבש contrahendi, sive minuendi notione sumit, quam in nulla dialecto cognata habet. Sed multo magis improbanda est ECKERMANNI interpretatio, comma hoc vertentis: seposita (a פרד separare) evanuerunt palearum ergo (תחת, caussa, ergo, ut Ierem. V, 19.), i. e. propterea, quod de eo, quod in horreis sepositum fuerat, continuo paleis absumebatur.

R8 Rosenmüller, III, 301 "Abu Walid," says Pococke, pp. 84–85, "whom we judge the most ancient of the grammarians among the Jews that we possess, has خطوطها [khuṭūṭuhā], their furrows, by which he understands الخطوط التي يخطها الزارع بالسكة بعد البذر [al-khuṭūṭ allatī yakhuṭṭuhā al-zāriʿ bi-l-sikka baʿda al-badhr], those which the farmer draws with his ploughshare after the grain has been sown, which are, he adds, like خدوش في الارض [khudūsh fī al-arḍ], scratches in the ground. And to the same effect he says again in another place (under the root פרד) that they are so named تشبيها بالخدوش [tashbīhan bi-l-khudūsh], on account of their likeness to scratches or wounds made in someone's skin by the nails, which are breaks in the skin. R. Tanchum uses almost the same word, so that for him too תחת מגרפותיהם is תחת חרושהא, under their scratchings, III, 302 i.e. تحت الخطوط التي يحفرها الحراث التي كانها كسور في الارض [taḥta al-khuṭūṭ allatī yaḥfiruhā al-ḥarrāth allatī kaʾannahā kusūr fī al-arḍ], the furrows (lines) which the plough digs, which are like ridges in the earth; just as elsewhere (Ps 65:10) they are called, on almost the same principle, גדודים, incisions (our furrows), from גדד, to cut. For this meaning they seek support from the word אגרוף, which occurs in Exod 21:18, and which our people and others, both Jews and Christians, render fist, but which for them (Abu Walid under the root גרף) is شادخ كاسر [shādikh kāsir], something that wounds or makes an incision, كل يجرح او يشدخ به [kull yajraḥ aw yashdakh bihi]. Meanwhile it is evident that by these lines or scratchings (as they call them) we are to understand not hollowed and open furrows but ones covered with earth, drawn through it by the plough or harrow, since the word joined to it, תחת, under, necessarily requires this. Accordingly Aben Esra explains it by העפר, dust or earth, and Kimchi by חתיכות העפר, fragments or particles of dust; hence our people, with most of the more recent interpreters, render it clods. Some try to confirm this from the Arabic language, in which جُرْفٌ [jurf] is said to signify a clod of earth which water rolls along or carries off with it, so that it could be used for any clod. From the root of this word, Hebrew גרף and Arabic أجرف [ajrafa], which means both to roll together and to carry off or scatter, a noun could perhaps not unsuitably be derived denoting earth broken, poured over, rolled together, or thrown upon the grain by plough or harrow; the sense 'clod' being confirmed by الجرفة [al-jurfa], meaning a piece of broken bread, and so perhaps certain fragments or broken pieces of some other thing, such as clods of earth. There remains another explanation of the word, mentioned by the author of an Arabic manuscript (although he expresses it by the Hebrew word itself, مجارفهم [majārifuhum]), namely انادر [anādir], which designates either granaries or heaps of grain in granaries, التي منها يجرف القمح ويودا الي الصحرا [allatī minhā yujraf al-qamḥ wa-yūdā ilā al-ṣaḥrā], from which the wheat (or seed) is removed (or turned away, or taken away) and carried into the field to be committed to the earth, so that this root has the same notion as the preceding, namely of taking away or removing. Grotius reports that some have taken it in this way, rendering heaps, as if the seeds or grains had been spoiled and made unfit for sowing already in the heaps into which they had been gathered." — Since Arabic مِجْرَفَةٌ [mijrafa] is a mattock, or an implement of that kind, suited for throwing out dung or sweeping away dust, Michaelis in Supplemm. ad Lexx. vol. II, p. 361, holds that Hebrew מגרפה too should be taken in the same sense, and renders our words: the grains diminish under the chaff. This sense, already meagre in itself, cannot be admitted also because he takes עבש in the sense of contracting or diminishing, which it has in no cognate dialect. But much more to be rejected is the interpretation of Eckermann, who renders this clause: the things set aside (from פרד, to separate) vanished on account of the chaff (תחת, because of, on account of, as in Jer 5:19), i.e. because what had been set aside in the barns was continually consumed together with the chaff.

(10) Rosenmüller, III, 303 Sed non secus egisse Bochartum cum Deodatio, quam cum Kimchio, idem ille asserit Pocockius, l. c. „Verum equidem est, inquit, verba ejus citata extare in editione Genevensi in quaternis 1607., scilicet grana esse corrupta da soverchie piogge, per nimiam pluviam, sed inveniuntur in posteriori editione (Genev. 1641. in forma maxima), verba, quae omnino contrarium indicant, videlicet non potuisse progerminare per lestreme ioccita, propter summam siccitatem, ac si ambiguus haereret cum aliis, num haec vel illa illata sit noxa vel pluviarum frequentia, vel raritate nimia, vel, ut placet quibusdam, utramque conjungere, post diuturnos imbres, saevientem siccitatem, seu aestum solis. R10 Rosenmüller, III, 303 But that Bochart dealt no differently with Diodati than with Kimchi is asserted by the same Pococke, loc. cit.: "It is true," he says, "that the words of his that are cited are found in the Geneva quarto edition of 1607, namely that the grains were spoiled da soverchie piogge, by excessive rain; but in the later edition (Geneva 1641, in largest format) words are found which indicate exactly the opposite, namely that they could not sprout per lestreme ioccita, because of extreme drought, as if he remained in doubt with others whether this damage or that was brought on either by the frequency of rains or by their excessive scarcity, or, as some prefer, by joining both, after long-lasting rains, a raging drought, or the heat of the sun. But Kimchi, as has been said, does not attribute it to an abundance of rain, but to a lack or want of rain."


(11) Rosenmüller, III, 303 „Verum antiquus ille Grammaticus, Abu Walid (in verbis עבש et פרד) conatur significationem verbi עבש eruere comparando eam cum voce Arabica عبس, quatenus idem significat, quam يبس, exarescere, quod optime huic loco arbitratur convenire, eo, quod damnum, hic descriptum, magis videatur illatum siccitate, quam humiditate, ut verba עבשו פרודות III, 304 nihil aliud velint, quam אלתשניע ואלהעטים לאמר אלקחט אלדי נאלהם התי יבשת אלחבוב תחת אלארץ אד לא ינזל עליהא מטר פלם תנבת, exaggerare turpitudinem et magnitudinem famis, quae illos obruebat, ita, ut grana sub terra arefierent, quia pluvia non cadebat super ea, atque ita non poterant protuberare. R. R11 Rosenmüller, III, 303 "But that ancient grammarian Abu Walid (under the words עבש and פרד) tries to draw out the meaning of the verb עבש by comparing it with the Arabic word عبس [ʿbs], inasmuch as it means the same as يبس [yabisa], to dry up, which he judges to fit this passage best, because the damage described here seems to have been caused by drought rather than by moisture, so that the words עבשו פרודות III, 304 mean nothing other than אלתשניע ואלהעטים לאמר אלקחט אלדי נאלהם התי יבשת אלחבוב תחת אלארץ אד לא ינזל עליהא מטר פלם תנבת, to heighten the horror and the magnitude of the famine that overwhelmed them, so that the grains dried up under the earth, because rain did not fall on them, and so they could not come up.
