Vide Ioelem capitis primi versibus 18. 19. 20. At Amosi capite quarto Deus pluviam alibi dimittit, alibi non dimittit: et, parte una compluta, altera exarescit. Ibidem solus gazam, in Ioele praeter gazam tres aliae locustarum spe- col. 484 cies Iudaeam depopulantur, nec solum arborum proventum absumunt, ut in Amoso, sed et ipsas arbores corrumpunt ac tabefaciunt, Ioel. I, 12. Et populi, quibus Amos ἀμεταμέλειαν objicit, in Ioele ad Deum convertuntur, jejunioque et precibus ejus misericordiam implorant. Rursus Amosi capite septimo locustas non format Deus, nisi post foenisecia, cum foenum cordum jam succrevisset. Itaque, jam peracta messe, solis herbis sunt noxiae. At in Ioele vastatur frumentum et hordeum, et perit messis agri. Amos denique, solus pro Israele intercedens, malum ingruens statim avertit. Sed in Ioele sacerdotes, et e populo senes, juvenes, ipsi pueri, adhuc ab ubere pendentes, in domum Dei clangore tubae convocantur, ut communibus suffragiis Deum exorent. Neque is facile flectitur, sed postquam continuasset hoc malum in plures annos. Parum igitur verisimile est, Amosum ut completa illa ipsa narrare, quae praedixerat Ioel, cum in tam multis diffideant.

See Joel, chapter 1, verses 18. 19. 20. But in chapter 4 of Amos God sends rain in one place and not in another, and while one part is rained upon, the other withers. There the gazam alone appears; in Joel, besides the gazam, three other kinds of locusts lay waste Judaea col. 484, and they not only consume the produce of the trees, as in Amos, but also damage and wither the trees themselves, Joel 1:12. And the peoples whom Amos reproaches for impenitence turn to God in Joel, and implore his mercy with fasting and prayers. Again, in chapter 7 of Amos God does not form the locusts until after the mowings, when the aftermath hay had already grown up. So, the harvest being already completed, they harm only the grass. But in Joel the wheat and barley are laid waste, and the harvest of the field perishes. Finally Amos, interceding alone for Israel, at once averts the approaching evil. But in Joel the priests, and from among the people the old men, the young men, even the children still hanging at the breast, are summoned to the house of God by the blast of the trumpet, to entreat God with common supplications. Nor is he easily moved, but only after this evil had continued for several years. It is therefore hardly probable that Amos narrates as fulfilled the very things that Joel had foretold, since they disagree in so many points.


Sed et Amos duas clades refert, suo tempore per locustam illatas: unam capite quarto, quae praecessit messem, et cum siccitate, uredine et rubigine conjuncta fuit. Nempe in siccitate locustas uberius provenire, jam b) docuimus. Et easdem in Aegyptum impellit ventus קדים kadim, Exod. X, 13. A quo ipso vento שדפון, uredo, et ירקון, rubigo. Unde est, quod utrumque malum ἀνεμοφθορία graece dicitur. Et in Graeca paraphrasi modo pro ירקון occurrit; ut Agg. II, 18. modo etiam pro שדפון, ut Deut. XXVIII, 22. et 2 Par. VI, 28. Quod sequuntur Aquila, Symmachus et Theodotion in eo ipso loco, in quo versamur, id est, Amos IV, 8. ubi seniores ἐν πυρώσει. Et Gen. XLI, 6. 27. spicae שדופות קדים, id est, uredine percussae a vento kadim, in Graeca editione uno verbo vocantur ἀνεμόφθοροι, Ab eodem igitur vento kadim, a quo siccitas, uredo, et rubigo, locustae quoque, in Iudaeam adductae, hortos et vineas, id est, hortorum et vinearum proventum, ficusque et oleas consumpserunt, id est, omnes fructus arborum. Nam praecipuae nominantur, et hortorum nomine reliquae continentur. Hic enim horti sunt paradisi, ut Syrus interpres recte reddidit: id est, agri consepti, atque omnis generis plantis diligenter III, 322 consiti. Hic porro cum neque pascuis, neque segetibus infestus fuerit gazam, sed solos arborum fructus legatur consumpsisse, huic locustae speciei potuit id esse proprium, ut non aliunde vesceretur, quam ex arborum proventu. Atque ipsum nomen id suadet. Nam, ut suo loco notatum, apud Talmudicos, Arabes et Aethiopes Verbum גזם est abscindere et amputare, non quidvis, sed ramos arborum.

But Amos also reports two disasters brought on by the locust in his time. The first is in chapter four; it preceded the harvest and was joined with drought, mildew and blight. That locusts come forth more abundantly in drought we have already b) shown. And the wind קדים kadim drives them into Egypt, Exod 10:13. From this same wind come שדפון, uredo [mildew], and ירקון, rubigo [blight]. Hence both evils are called ἀνεμοφθορία [anemophthoria] in Greek. In the Greek paraphrase this word occurs sometimes for ירקון, as in Agg. II, 18., and sometimes also for שדפון, as in Deut 28:22 and 2 Chr 6:28 Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion follow this in the very passage we are dealing with, that is, Amos 4:8, where the Elders have ἐν πυρώσει [en pyrōsei]. And in Gen 41:6 27. the ears שדופות קדים, that is, struck with mildew by the wind kadim, are called in the Greek edition by a single word, ἀνεμόφθοροι [anemophthoroi]. By the same wind kadim, then, from which come drought, mildew and blight, the locusts too were brought into Judaea and consumed the gardens and vineyards, that is, the produce of the gardens and vineyards, and the figs and olives, that is, all the fruits of the trees. For the chief ones are named, and the rest are included under the name of gardens. Here gardens are paradises, as the Syriac translator rightly rendered it: that is, enclosed fields carefully III, 322 planted with plants of every kind. Further, since the gazam here harmed neither pastures nor crops, but is said to have consumed only the fruits of the trees, it may have been peculiar to this species of locust that it fed on nothing other than the produce of trees. And the name itself suggests this. For, as noted in its place, among the Talmudists, Arabs and Ethiopians the verb גזם means to cut off and to lop, not just anything, but the branches of trees.


Haec de prima locustarum in Iudaeam irruptione Amos IV, 9. Quae cum Israelitas ad poenitentiam non provocasset, Hortos vestros, etc. comedit גזם gazam (inquit Dominus) neque tamen ad me conversi estis: alias locustas immisit Deus, de quibus ita Propheta capitis septimi versu primo, Sic ostendit mihi Dominus. Et, ecce! formabat locustas, cum surcrevisset foenum cordum: et foenum erat post regis foenisecia. Foenum cordum, Hebraeis לקש, solet in Italia autumno provenire. Columella de agnis libri octavi capite tertio, Aluntur commodissime autumnali foeno, quod cordum vocatur. Quo ipso anni tempore locustas parere, nos docent Aristoteles et Plinius. Ille Historiae libri quinti capite vigesimo octavo, Τίκτουσι δὲ λήγοντος τοῦ θέρους, Pariunt aestatis exitu (non veris, ut habet Gaza). Hic libri undecimi capite vigesimo nono, Hae pariunt, etc. autumni tempore. Et naturalis quidem est ille partus, ut reliquorum animalium. Quod ibidem Philosophus multis verbis docet, quorum summa est, foeminas parituras in terram defigere τὸν πρὸς τῇ κέρκῳ αὐλὸν, cauliculum, quod in cauda habent, et circa finem aestatis universas eodem loco foetus deponere, ut quasi favus videantur. Nec summae telluri committi, sed rimis et fissuris, quibus terra dehiscit. Ubi cum tota hyeme latuerunt, ineunte aestate inde emer- col. 485 gunt nigri vermes ovorum specie, rupta quadam terra tenui, qua tanquam membranula ambiuntur. Ex quibus Plinius haec solum, Hae pariunt in terram, demisso spinae caule, ova condensa autumni tempore. Ea durant hyeme sub terra: subsequenti autem exitu veris emittunt parvas, nigrantes, et sine cruribus et pennis. Et paullo post, alios sequutus; Alii duplicem earum foetum geminumque exitum tradunt. Vergiliarum exortu parere: deinde ad Canis ortum obire, et alias renasci. Quidam Arcturi occasu renasci. Nempe, prout varia sunt climata, locustis quoque varium est nascendi tempus et denascendi. De eodem hoc argumento multa legas apud Arabes. Damir, وهو اذا اراد ان يبيض التمس لبيضه المواضع الصلدة والصخور الصلبة التي لا تعمل فيها المعاول فيضربها بذنبه فتفرج له ثم يلقي بيضه في ذلك الصدع فيكون له الافحوص ويكون حاضنا لها ومربيا Cum paritura est locusta, ovis suis loca salebrosa eligit, et petras durissimas, quas non attigerit ferrum, easque III, 323 cauda diverberat, donec in rimam pateant. Tum vero in illa rima ovificat: eaque illi pro nido est, in quo foetus suos foveat atque educet. Sed aliter Alkazui- nius, وانا رعت ايام الربيع طلبت ارض طيبة التربة رخوة ونزلت هناك وحفرت باذنابها حفرا وباضت فيها كل واحد ماية بيضة وطارت Cum verno tempore pascuntur, terram agri foecundi et mollis quaerunt, in quam descendant: et cau- dis fossas fodiunt, in quibus cum singulae ova centum ediderunt, inde avolant. Ad quem ovorum numerum proxime accedit Ibno Omar, cum inter Mahumetis manus locustas decidisse fabulatur, in quarum alis scriptum fuerit, نحن جند الله الاكبر لنا تسعة وتسعون بيضة ولو تمت لنا الماية لاكلنا الدنيا بما فيها Sumus exercitus Dei magni. Nobis sunt ova nonaginta novem: et, si centuria perficere- tur, totum mundum absumeremus, et in illo quidquid est. Sequitur in Alkazui- nio, ثم اذا اتي ايام الربيع واعتدل الزمان شققت البيض المدفون فظهرت مثل الدبيب الصغار علي وجه الارض فاكلت زرعها حتي قويت ثم نهضت الي بيض اخر وباضت كما فعلت في العام الاول Dein- col. 486 de verno tempore, cum temperatius est anni tempus, sepultum illud ovum finditur: et ex eo emergit parvi reptilis genus super faciem terrae, quod comedit ejus semina: donec aetate robustius ad aliam ovificationem pergat, atque ovificet, ut anno prae- cedente factum fuerat. In Alcamus سرا sara, et قصم kasam, et مكن machin est locustae ovum: مزكوت mazcuth est locusta gravida: متح ma- thaha, vel متخ mathacha, سخت sachatha, زر zarra, et قلز kallaza totidem verba sunt, quae de locusta usurpantur, cum غرزت ذنبها في الارض لتبيض caudam suam terrae infigit, ut ovificet. Ipsa dicitur صفرا saphra cum ova posuit, quia tum flava est. Foetus ipse, nuper editus, دبا da- ba, et دبر dabar, et قمص kamas. Ex his cum satis constet, locustas a Natura formari, tamen locustarum formationem Propheta Deo tribuit. For- mabat, inquit, locustas, cum primum ascenderet foenum cordum. Et quidem usus verbo יצר, quod adhibet Moses, ubi agitur de formatione hominis et reliquorum animalium, in historia creationis Gen. II, 7. 8. 19. Non quasi Deus locustas de novo creaverit, post primam illam rerum omnium productionem; aut, ut locustis peculiare aliquid tribuat cum Mahumetanorum Theologastris, qui Deum locustas finxisse fabulantur من الطين التي فضلت من III, 324 خلق ادم عليه السلام de (meliore illo) luto, quod superfuit ex creatione Adami, cui sit pax: sed locustarum formatio Deo tribuitur, cum praeter solitum foecundae sunt, atque in immensum multiplicantur. Quia id non accidit absque speciali Dei providentia, qui his utitur in poenam peccatorum. Itaque minarum divinae Legis haec una est Deut. XXVIII, 38. Semen multum in agrum conjicies, et parum colliges; quia absumet illud locusta. Et versu quadragesimo secundo, Omnes arbores tuas, et fructus terrae tuae (tanquam) haereditario jure obtinebit locusta. Proinde sic loquitur Deus 2 Paral. VII, 13. Si praecepero locustae, ut terram absumat. Quale est, quod de Aegyptiis legitur Psal. LXXVIII, 46. Proventum eorum brucho dedit (Deus) et laborem eorum locustae. Et Psal. CV, 34. Dixit (Deus), et venit locusta, et bruchus sine numero. Hinc locustas non solum Hebraei, sed et Arabes appellant Dei exercitum, ut supra c) observatum est in Ioel II, 25. Et Propheta suo cum Abdalla sedente, locustam fingunt in eorum mensam cecidisse cum hac inscriptione in tergo et alis, انا الله لا اله الا انا رب الجراد وزارقها ان شيت بعثتها رزقا القوم وان شيت بعثتها بلا علي القوم Ego sum Deus, neque ullus est praeter me, locustarum dominum, qui eas alo, et, cum libet, immitto, ut sint esca populis: sed et, cum libet, immitto, ut iisdem plaga sint. Unde poeta anonymus de locustis,

So much for the first irruption of the locusts into Judaea, Amos 4:9. When this had not moved the Israelites to repentance (The gazam גזם ate your gardens, etc., says the Lord, yet you have not returned to me), God sent other locusts, of which the Prophet speaks thus in chapter 7, verse 1: Thus the Lord showed me. And behold! he was forming locusts when the second-crop hay had sprung up; and the hay was after the king's mowings. Second-crop hay, in Hebrew לקש, usually comes up in Italy in autumn. Columella, on lambs, book 8, chapter 3: They are most conveniently fed on autumn hay, which is called cordum. Aristotle and Pliny teach us that locusts lay their eggs at that very season of the year. The former, History book 5, chapter 28: Τίκτουσι δὲ λήγοντος τοῦ θέρους [Tiktousi de lēgontos tou therous], They lay at the end of summer (not of spring, as Gaza has it). The latter, book 11, chapter 29: These lay, etc., in the autumn season. And that birth is indeed natural, like that of the other animals. The Philosopher teaches this at length in the same place; the sum of it is that the females about to lay fix in the ground τὸν πρὸς τῇ κέρκῳ αὐλὸν [ton pros tē kerkō aulon], the little stalk which they have at the tail, and that towards the end of summer they all deposit their young in the same place, so that they look like a honeycomb. Nor are these committed to the surface of the earth, but to the cracks and fissures with which the ground gapes. When they have lain hidden there all winter, at the beginning of summer they emerge col. 485 as black worms in the form of eggs, after a thin layer of earth, by which they are enclosed as by a little membrane, has burst. Of this Pliny has only the following: These lay in the ground, letting down the stalk of their spine, eggs packed together in the autumn season. These last through the winter under the ground; and at the end of the following spring they release small, blackish young without legs and wings. And a little later, following others: Others report a double brood and a twofold emergence: that they lay at the rising of the Pleiades, then die at the rising of the Dog Star, and others are born again. Some say they are born again at the setting of Arcturus. That is, as climates vary, so too the time of birth and of death varies for locusts. On this same subject you may read much among the Arabs. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: وهو اذا اراد ان يبيض التمس لبيضه المواضع الصلدة والصخور الصلبة التي لا تعمل فيها المعاول فيضربها بذنبه فتفرج له ثم يلقي بيضه في ذلك الصدع فيكون له الافحوص ويكون حاضنا لها ومربيا [wa-huwa idhā arāda an yabīḍa iltamasa li-bayḍihi al-mawāḍiʿ al-ṣalda wa-al-ṣukhūr al-ṣulba allatī lā taʿmalu fīhā al-maʿāwil fa-yaḍribuhā bi-dhanabihi fa-tanfariju lahu thumma yulqī bayḍahu fī dhālika al-ṣadʿ fa-yakūnu lahu al-ufḥūṣ wa-yakūnu ḥāḍinan lahā wa-murabbiyan] When the locust is about to lay, it chooses rough places for its eggs, and very hard rocks which iron has not touched, and III, 323 beats them with its tail until they open into a crack. Then it lays its eggs in that crack, and this serves it as a nest in which it warms and rears its young. But Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt] has it otherwise: وانا رعت ايام الربيع طلبت ارض طيبة التربة رخوة ونزلت هناك وحفرت باذنابها حفرا وباضت فيها كل واحد ماية بيضة وطارت [wa-anā raʿat ayyām al-rabīʿ ṭalabat arḍ ṭayyibat al-turba rikhwa wa-nazalat hunāka wa-ḥafarat bi-adhnābihā ḥufaran wa-bāḍat fīhā kull wāḥid māyat bayḍa wa-ṭārat] When they graze in springtime, they seek the ground of fertile and soft land, into which they descend; and with their tails they dig pits, in which, when each has laid a hundred eggs, they fly away from there. Close to this number of eggs comes Ibno Omar, when he tells the tale that locusts fell into the hands of Muhammad, on whose wings was written: نحن جند الله الاكبر لنا تسعة وتسعون بيضة ولو تمت لنا الماية لاكلنا الدنيا بما فيها [naḥnu jund Allāh al-akbar lanā tisʿa wa-tisʿūn bayḍa wa-law tammat lanā al-māya la-akalnā al-dunyā bi-mā fīhā] We are the army of the great God. We have ninety-nine eggs; and if the hundred were completed, we would consume the whole world and whatever is in it. There follows in Alkazuinius: ثم اذا اتي ايام الربيع واعتدل الزمان شققت البيض المدفون فظهرت مثل الدبيب الصغار علي وجه الارض فاكلت زرعها حتي قويت ثم نهضت الي بيض اخر وباضت كما فعلت في العام الاول [thumma idhā atā ayyām al-rabīʿ wa-iʿtadala al-zamān shuqqiqat al-bayḍ al-madfūn fa-ẓaharat mithl al-dabīb al-ṣighār ʿalā wajh al-arḍ fa-akalat zarʿahā ḥattā qawiyat thumma nahaḍat ilā bayḍ ākhar wa-bāḍat kamā faʿalat fī al-ʿām al-awwal] Then col. 486 in springtime, when the season is milder, that buried egg splits, and from it there emerges a kind of small creeping thing on the face of the earth, which eats its crops, until, grown stronger with age, it proceeds to another laying and lays eggs, as had been done the preceding year. In the Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī], سرا [srā] sara, and قصم [qṣm] kasam, and مكن [mkn] machin is the egg of the locust; مزكوت [mzkwt] mazcuth is a pregnant locust; متح [mtḥ] mathaha, or متخ [mtkh] mathacha, سخت [skht] sachatha, زر [zr] zarra, and قلز [qlz] kallaza are so many words used of the locust when غرزت ذنبها في الارض لتبيض [gharazat dhanabahā fī al-arḍ li-tabīḍa] it fixes its tail in the ground in order to lay eggs. The locust itself is called صفرا [ṣafrā] saphra when it has laid its eggs, because it is then yellow. The young itself, newly hatched, is دبا [dabā] daba, and دبر [dbr] dabar, and قمص [qmṣ] kamas. Although it is sufficiently clear from this that locusts are formed by Nature, the Prophet nevertheless attributes the formation of the locusts to God. He was forming, he says, locusts, when the second-crop hay first came up. And he uses the verb יצר, which Moses employs where the formation of man and of the other animals is treated in the creation account, Gen 2:7–8. 19. Not as if God had created locusts anew after that first production of all things; nor to attribute something peculiar to locusts, as do the petty theologians of the Muslims, who tell the tale that God fashioned locusts من الطين التي فضلت من III, 324 خلق ادم عليه السلام [min al-ṭīn allatī faḍalat min khalq Ādam ʿalayhi al-salām] from the (better) clay which was left over from the creation of Adam, on whom be peace. Rather, the formation of locusts is attributed to God when they are fertile beyond the usual and multiply immeasurably. For this does not happen without the special providence of God, who uses them as a punishment for sins. Thus this is one of the threats of the divine Law, Deut 28:38. You shall cast much seed into the field, and gather little; for the locust shall consume it. And in verse 42: All your trees and the fruits of your land the locust shall possess (as it were) by right of inheritance. Accordingly God speaks thus in 2 Chr 7:13. If I command the locust to consume the land. Such is what we read of the Egyptians in Ps 78:46. He (God) gave their produce to the bruchus, and their labour to the locust. And Ps 105:34 He (God) spoke, and the locust came, and the bruchus without number. Hence not only the Hebrews but also the Arabs call locusts the army of God, as was observed above c) on Joel 2:25. And they tell the tale that, as their Prophet sat with Abdalla, a locust fell onto their table with this inscription on its back and wings: انا الله لا اله الا انا رب الجراد وزارقها ان شيت بعثتها رزقا القوم وان شيت بعثتها بلا علي القوم [anā Allāh lā ilāha illā anā rabb al-jarād wa-zāriquhā in shiʾtu baʿathtuhā rizqan al-qawm wa-in shiʾtu baʿathtuhā balāʾ ʿalā al-qawm] I am God, and there is none besides me, the lord of the locusts, who feed them and, when I please, send them forth to be food for peoples; but also, when I please, send them forth to be a plague upon them. Hence an anonymous poet on locusts:


فسبحان من يهلك القوي الاكول بالصعيف الماكول

فسبحان من يهلك القوي الاكول بالصعيف الماكول [fa-subḥāna man yuhliku al-qawī al-akūl bi-al-ṣaʿīf al-makūl]


Laus illi sit, qui perdit robustum cibum (id est, segetes, unde panis) per infirmum col. 487 comedonem (id est, per locustam). Neque aliud sibi volunt haec Plinii, Deorum irae pestis ea intelligitur. Et vota, et sacrificia, etiam ab ethnicis, diis suis oblata, ad hoc malum avertendum. Sic Casii, montis, incolas, cum fruges eorum locustae vastabant, Seleucidum avium adventum a Iove precibus impetrasse, a quibus absumerentur, testatur Plinius libri decimi capite vigesimo septimo. Quod idem ab Apolline in Sarpedonio templo petiisse Ciliciae Seleucienses, legas apud Zosimum libro primo. Et Athenis Apollo Parnopius dictus est a locustis pulsis, ut habetur in Pausaniae Atticis: quomodo in Oëta Hercules Cornopion, auctore Strabone libro decimo tertio.

Praise be to Him who destroys the strong food (that is, the crops, from which bread comes) through the weak col. 487 eater (that is, through the locust). Nor do these words of Pliny mean anything else: this plague is understood to be a sign of the wrath of the gods. And vows and sacrifices were offered, even by the pagans, to their gods to avert this evil. Thus Pliny, book 10, chapter 27, testifies that the inhabitants of Mount Casius, when locusts were laying waste their crops, obtained from Jupiter by their prayers the arrival of the Seleucid birds, by which the locusts were consumed. That the people of Seleucia in Cilicia sought the same from Apollo in the Sarpedonian temple, you may read in Zosimus, book 1. And at Athens Apollo was called Parnopius from the locusts he drove away, as is found in Pausanias' Attica; just as on Oeta Hercules was called Cornopion, on the authority of Strabo, book 13.


Notanda haec in Arnobium, qui hujusmodi animalcula negavit esse Dei opus, et professus est se nescire, a quo condita fuerint. Non, inquit, si negemus, III, 325 muscas, scarabaeos, et cimices, nitedulas, curculiones, et tineas, omnipoten- tis esse opus regis, sequaciter postulandum a nobis est, ut, quis ea fecerit institue- ritque, dicamus. Possimus enim nulla cum reprehensione nescire, quis et illis ori- ginem dederit, et obtinere non esse a Deo superiore prolata tam supervacua, tam vana, tam ad nullas pertinentia rationes. Haec ille libro secundo ex Marcioni- tarum lacunis hausta, qui apud Tertullianum adversus Marcionem libro primo ita loquuntur: Sufficit unicum hoc opus Deo nostro, quod hominem liberavit sum- ma et praecipua bonitate sua, et omnibus locustis anteponenda: id est, omnium locustarum creationi, quam Deo affingitis. Hinc Hieronymus in Prooemio in Epistolam ad Philemonem, Quod si non putant eorum esse parva, quorum et ma- gna sunt; alterum mihi conditorem, juxta Valentinum, Marcionem et Apellem, formicae, vermium, culicum, locustarum: alterum coeli, terrae, maris et angelo- rum debent introducere.

These points should be noted against Arnobius, who denied that such little creatures are the work of God and professed that he did not know by whom they had been made. If we deny, he says, that III, 325 flies, beetles and bugs, dormice, weevils and moths are the work of the almighty King, it does not follow that we must be required to say who made and formed them. For we may without any reproach not know who gave them their origin, and yet maintain that things so superfluous, so empty, so unrelated to any purpose were not brought forth by the supreme God. This he wrote in book 2, drawn from the puddles of the Marcionites, who in Tertullian, Against Marcion, book 1, speak thus: This one work suffices for our God, that he has freed man by his supreme and pre-eminent goodness, which is to be preferred to all the locusts: that is, to the creation of all the locusts, which you ascribe to God. Hence Jerome, in the Prologue to the Epistle to Philemon: But if they do not think that the small things belong to him to whom the great things also belong, then, following Valentinus, Marcion and Apelles, they must introduce one creator of the ant, the worms, the gnats and the locusts, and another of heaven, earth, the sea and the angels.


In Propheta sequitur, Cum autem absolvissent comedere herbam terrae, dixi, Domine Deus, condona, obsecro, etc.] Agitur de locustis, quae, post messem creatae, solis herbis vescebantur. Tum enim deerant segetes. Nec volatu poterant in arbores se attollere, cum alas nondum haberent, nec nisi humi reptitarent. Hujusmodi locustas bruchos a multis appellari, observavimus d), atque ex illis primo attelabos fieri, et postmodum locustas proprie dictas. Priusquam igitur hi bruchi, in majus aucti, plura damna inferrent, pro populo intercedit Propheta, et precibus suis obtinet, ut amoveatur haec pestis.

In the Prophet there follows: And when they had finished eating the grass of the land, I said, O Lord God, forgive, I beseech you, etc.] The subject is locusts which, produced after the harvest, fed on grass alone; for at that time the crops were gone. Nor could they raise themselves into the trees by flight, since they did not yet have wings and only crept on the ground. We have observed d) that locusts of this kind are called bruchi by many, and that from them first attelabi come into being, and afterwards locusts properly so called. Therefore, before these bruchi, grown larger, could inflict more damage, the Prophet intercedes for the people and by his prayers obtains the removal of this plague.

Part 2, Book 4, chapter 7: John the Baptist's locusts
-----------------------------------------------------
https://openseforim.org/bochart/locustae-ioannis.html

III, 326 CAP. VII.

III, 326 CHAPTER 7.


Iohannem, Baptistam, veras locustas habuisse pro cibo.

That John the Baptist had real locusts for food.


Locustis patuit hactenus vix ullum esse animal humano generi perniciosius. col. 488 Tamen his quoque suus usus est, quem alii multis explicant. Nobis docere sufficiet, locustas non paucis gentibus in cibum cessisse jam olim, et cedere hodieque, in verba de Iohanne, baptista, πολυθρύλλητα Matth. III, 4. Ἡ δὲ τρο-φὴ αὐτοῦ ἦν ἀκρίδες, καὶ μέλι ἄγριον. Et Marc. I, 6. Ἐσθίων ἀκρίδας, καὶ μέλι ἄγριον. Quae verba cum clare et aperte doceant, locustas et mel sylvestre pro cibo illi fuisse: tamen, quasi non sit ferendum, ut vir sanctus locustis vitam sustinuisse credatur, veterum et recentiorum multi in omnes formas se transformarunt, ut haec alio detorquerent. Agmen ducunt Ebionaei, in quorum Evangelio haec de Iohanne legebantur. Τὸ βρῶμα αὐτοῦ μέλι ἄγριον, οὗ ἡ γεῦ-σις ἦν τοῦ Μάννα, ὡς ἐγκρὶς ἐν ἐλαίῳ· Cibus ejus erat mel sylvestre, sapore Mannae, tanquam lagani in oleo fricti. Ad quem locum Epiphanius illos asserit hoc sibi proposuisse, ut veritatis sermonem in mendacium mutarent, et ἀντὶ ἀκρίδων ποιήσωσιν ἐγκρίδας ἐν μέλιτι, ex locustis facerent lagana in melle fricta. Occasione haec confingendi ex eo sumta, quod ἀκρίδες et ἐγκρίδες sunt voces simillimae. Atque in Evangelio junguntur ἀκρίδες καὶ μέλι, ita de Manna dicitur Exod. XVI, 31. Ejus autem sapor erat ὡς ἐγκρὶς ἐν μέλιτι, ut lagani in melle (sive cum melle,) fricti. Quomodo si sapuerint Iohannis in deserto cibi, non magnum id fuerit austerae vitae argumentum. Alii aliter sentiunt, nempe ἀκρίδες hoc loco esse ἀκρόδρυα, vel τῶν φυτῶν ἀκρέμονας, arborum et herbarum extremitates, quibus Iohannes in illo deserto vixerit. Ita Isidorus Pelusiota libri primi Epistola quinta vult, ut monachus, a Iohanne edoctus, contentus sit ἀκρέμοσι βοτανῶν καὶ φυλλῶν πρὸς ὀλίγην τροφήν, herbarum et foliorum extremis ad tenue alimentum. Et Epistola centesima trigesima secunda ita mordicus haeret huic interpretationi, ut iis, qui ἀκρίδων nomine locustas intelligunt, his verbis dicam scribat: Αἱ ἀκρίδες, αἷς Ἰωάννης ἐτρέφετο, οὐ ζῶά εἰσιν, ὥς τινες οἴονται ἀμαθῶς, κανθάροις ἀπεοικότα· μὴ γένοιτο. ἀλλ᾽ ἀκρέμονες βοτα-νῶν, ἢ φυτῶν. Illae acrides, quibus Iohannes vescebatur, non sunt animalia, scarabaeis similia, ut quidam imperite existimant; absit: sed herbarum aut arborum extrema. Ita etiam Paulinus in carmine de Iohanne, baptista,

It has been shown so far that there is scarcely any animal more destructive to the human race than locusts. col. 488 Yet these too have their use, which others explain at length. It will be enough for us to show that locusts served as food for not a few peoples long ago, and still serve so today, with regard to the much-discussed (πολυθρύλλητα [polythryllēta]) words about John the Baptist in Matth. III, 4: Ἡ δὲ τροφὴ αὐτοῦ ἦν ἀκρίδες, καὶ μέλι ἄγριον [Hē de trophē autou ēn akrides, kai meli agrion]. And Mark 1:6: Ἐσθίων ἀκρίδας, καὶ μέλι ἄγριον [Esthiōn akridas, kai meli agrion]. Although these words teach clearly and openly that locusts and wild honey were his food, nevertheless, as though it were intolerable to believe that the holy man sustained his life on locusts, many ancients and moderns have twisted themselves into every shape in order to bend these words to another sense. The Ebionites lead the column; in their Gospel the following was read about John: Τὸ βρῶμα αὐτοῦ μέλι ἄγριον, οὗ ἡ γεῦσις ἦν τοῦ Μάννα, ὡς ἐγκρὶς ἐν ἐλαίῳ [To brōma autou meli agrion, hou hē geusis ēn tou Manna, hōs enkris en elaiō]· His food was wild honey, with the taste of Manna, like a cake fried in oil. On this passage Epiphanius asserts that they set themselves this aim, to change the word of truth into a lie, and ἀντὶ ἀκρίδων ποιήσωσιν ἐγκρίδας ἐν μέλιτι [anti akridōn poiēsōsin enkridas en meliti], to make out of locusts cakes fried in honey. The occasion for this fabrication was taken from the fact that ἀκρίδες [akrides] and ἐγκρίδες [enkrides] are very similar words. And just as in the Gospel ἀκρίδες καὶ μέλι [akrides kai meli] are joined, so it is said of the Manna in Exod 16:31: And its taste was ὡς ἐγκρὶς ἐν μέλιτι [hōs enkris en meliti], like a cake fried in honey (or with honey). If John's food in the desert had tasted like that, it would not have been much proof of an austere life. Others think otherwise, namely that ἀκρίδες [akrides] in this passage are ἀκρόδρυα [akrodrya], or τῶν φυτῶν ἀκρέμονας [tōn phytōn akremonas], the tips of trees and plants, on which John lived in that desert. Thus Isidore of Pelusium, in the fifth Letter of book 1, wants the monk, taught by John, to be content with ἀκρέμοσι βοτανῶν καὶ φυλλῶν πρὸς ὀλίγην τροφήν [akremosi botanōn kai phyllōn pros oligēn trophēn], the tips of plants and leaves for slender nourishment. And in Letter 132 he clings so tenaciously to this interpretation that he brings a charge against those who understand locusts by the name ἀκρίδες [akrides], in these words: Αἱ ἀκρίδες, αἷς Ἰωάννης ἐτρέφετο, οὐ ζῶά εἰσιν, ὥς τινες οἴονται ἀμαθῶς, κανθάροις ἀπεοικότα· μὴ γένοιτο. ἀλλ᾽ ἀκρέμονες βοτανῶν, ἢ φυτῶν [Hai akrides, hais Iōannēs etrepheto, ou zōa eisin, hōs tines oiontai amathōs, kantharois apeoikota; mē genoito. all᾽ akremones botanōn, ē phytōn]. Those acrides on which John fed are not animals resembling beetles, as some ignorantly suppose; far from it: but the tips of plants or trees. So also Paulinus, in his poem on John the Baptist:


Praebebant victum facilem sylvestria mella,
Pomaque, et incultis enatae cautibus herbae.

Wild honey furnished easy sustenance, and fruits, and herbs sprung from untilled rocks.


Et Pantaleon, diaconus, in Sermone De luminibus sanctis, Ὁ τοῖς τῶν μελισσῶν κατὰ τὴν ἔρημον πόνοις, καὶ τοῖς τῶν βοτανῶν συντρεφόμενος ἐκ βρέφους ἀκρίσμασι· III, 327 Qui apum in deserto laboribus, et herbarum extremis ab infantia nutritus est. Et Theophylactus, Τινὲς δὲ (λέγουσι) τὰ ἀκρόδρυα, ἤτοι ὀπώρας ἀγρίας (εἶναι τὰς ἀκρίδας·) Acridas quidam dicunt esse extrema arborum, aut poma sylvestria. Et Euthymius, Locustas vero quidam herbarum esse virgulta dixerunt. Et Nicephorus Callistus libri primi Historiae capite decimo quarto, Ibi teneriori- bus arborum summitatibus, ἄκροις δρυῶν, pro cibo utebatur. Et superiore saeculo Cajetanus, Suspicor, aequivocum esse nomen ad animalia illa, locustas, et ra- dices, vel summitates teneras virgultorum, seu ramusculorum, seu aliquid hujus- modi, quo crudo vescimur. Quo torrente abreptus Baronius ad annum 31. Quid, inquit, de his sentiendum sit, definiendum nobis non est, sed totum relinquimus lectoris arbitrio. Nam constat, Graecam dictionem ἀκρίδας, et locustam, insecti col. 489 genus, infirmas habens alas ad volandum, et summitates arborum significare. Imo constat, ἀκρίδας et ἀκρόδρυα multum differre, nec a scriptoribus vere Graecis usquam confundi haec duo vocabula. Quod tamen illi veterum, qui a locustarum esu abhorrebant, eo fecere libentius, quod ἀκρόδρυα sciebant nonnullis pro cibo fuisse. Sic, in Paedagogo Clementis lib. 2. cap. 1. Matthaeus, apostolus, σπερμάτων, καὶ ἀκροδρύων, καὶ λαχάνων, ἄνευ κρέων, μετελάμ-βανεν, seminibus, et arborum summitatibus, et oleribus sine carnibus vescebatur. Sed ibidem Iohannes eo ipso a Matthaeo distinguitur, quod ὑπερτείνας τὴν ἐγκράτειαν, ἀκρίδας, καὶ μέλι ἤσθιεν ἄγριον, continentiam ulterius promovens, locustas et mel agreste comedebat. Ut illi aliud fuisse scias ἀκρίδας, aliud ἀκρό-δρυα. Sic Epiphanii aevo nonnulli in jejuniis suis usque adeo rigidi erant, ut etiam abstinerent ἀκροδρύων, καὶ ἑψημάτων, ab arborum summitatibus, et ole- rum jusculis: quasi hoc nimium fuisset. Haec ille in Expositione fidei, cap. 23. Tertia sententia eorum est, quibus αἱ ἀκρίδες sunt herbae genus. Euthymius, Locustas vero quidam herbarum esse virgulta dixerunt: quidam autem herbam, di- ctam locustam. Theophylactus, Τινὲς λέγουσι βοτάνας εἶναι τὰς ἀκρίδας, ἃς καὶ μέλαγρα καλοῦσι· Acridas quidam herbas esse dicunt, quas etiam melagra vocant. Ut alludatur ad μέλι ἄγριον. Itaque, ex hac sententia, idem erunt mel et locustae; herbae scilicet genus, aliunde prorsus ignotae, quae tamen Io- hanni pro cibo sola suffecit. Nihil absurdius fingi potuit. Tamen etiam haec sententia suos habuit sectatores: in his Surianum, monachum, a quo Iacobus de Vitriaco cap. 53. Historiae Hierosolymitanae se didicisse profitetur, ἀκρίδας Io- hannis non fuisse locustas, sed herbam quandam, monachis in Syria apponi solitam. Fortasse etiam Dionysium Carthusianum, qui nonnullos per locustas intelligere scribit herbas deserti, cum non videatur probabile, quod Iohannes, qui nec pane vescebatur, carnes animalium, aut aliquid coctum, comederit. Et Hermo- laus in Dioscoridem Corollario 256. eam herbam ait intelligi, quae Arabice dicitur رجل الجراد pes locustae; id est, blitum, ut quidam volunt; aut, ut III, 328 alii, rapunculum. Quarta sit sententia, quae Iohannis ἀκρίδας aviculas esse vult. Christianus Druthmarus, qui in Matthaeum scripsit nono post Christum saeculo, De locustis audivi quendam dicere, quod istae locustae aviculae fuerunt parvae cum rubeis tibiis. Quod ferendum esset, si solum volucres dixisset. Nam e locustis volucribus nonnullae sunt rubris pedibus. Sed cum aviculam dixerit rubris pedibus, quid aliud intelligamus, quam Graecorum ἐρυθρόποδα? Fringillae speciem esse volunt. Druthmarum certe patet veram avem intellexisse, cum hujus sententiae auctorem ita refellit; Quare laudaretur (Iohannes) de abstinentiae rigore, si volatilia ederet, quae desideraverunt Iudaei? Quinta, locustas esse pisces marinos, quos Iohannes ex Iordane habuerit, ut refert idem Druthmarus: quod est perridiculum. Neque enim in fluviis, sed in ipso mari has locustas reperire est. Ut taceam, locustas marinas a Graecis non dici ἀκρίδας, sed καράβους. Denique cum locustae marinae in deliciis habeantur, hic quoque merito objicit Druthmarus, non esse, cur Iohannes ab abstinentia laudetur, si marinas delicias ederit. Quae eadem in illos objici queant, qui ἀκρίδας in κα-ρίδας, id est, squillas, mutant; quibus in toto cancrorum genere nihil est praestantius. Huic sententiae, quae sexta est, septimam addo viri maximi et piissimi, qui conjicit, Evangelistas hic scripsisse ἀχράδες, id est, pira sylvestria, et exigua mutatione hoc nomen deflexum esse in ἀκρίδες (1).

And Pantaleon the deacon, in his sermon On the Holy Lights: Ὁ τοῖς τῶν μελισσῶν κατὰ τὴν ἔρημον πόνοις, καὶ τοῖς τῶν βοτανῶν συντρεφόμενος ἐκ βρέφους ἀκρίσμασι· [Ho tois tōn melissōn kata tēn erēmon ponois, kai tois tōn botanōn syntrephomenos ek brephous akrismasi] III, 327 He who from infancy was nourished on the labours of the bees in the desert and on the tips of herbs. And Theophylact: Τινὲς δὲ (λέγουσι) τὰ ἀκρόδρυα, ἤτοι ὀπώρας ἀγρίας (εἶναι τὰς ἀκρίδας·) [Tines de (legousi) ta akrodrya, ētoi opōras agrias (einai tas akridas)] Some say that the acridas are the tips of trees, or wild fruits. And Euthymius: But some have said that the locusts were shoots of herbs. And Nicephorus Callistus, History book 1, chapter 14: There he used for food the tenderer tops of trees, ἄκροις δρυῶν [akrois dryōn]. And in the last century Cajetan: I suspect that the name is equivocal, applying both to those animals, locusts, and to roots, or the tender tops of shrubs or twigs, or something of this kind that we eat raw. Swept away by this torrent, Baronius, under the year 31, says: What we should think of these things is not for us to decide; we leave the whole matter to the reader's judgement. For it is agreed that the Greek word ἀκρίδας [akridas] signifies both the locust, a kind of insect col. 489 having weak wings for flying, and the tops of trees. On the contrary, it is agreed that ἀκρίδας [akridas] and ἀκρόδρυα [akrodrya] differ greatly, and that these two words are nowhere confused by truly Greek writers. Yet those of the ancients who shrank from eating locusts did this all the more readily because they knew that ἀκρόδρυα [akrodrya] had served some people as food. Thus in the Paedagogus of Clement, book 2, ch. 1, the apostle Matthew σπερμάτων, καὶ ἀκροδρύων, καὶ λαχάνων, ἄνευ κρέων, μετελάμβανεν [spermatōn, kai akrodryōn, kai lachanōn, aneu kreōn, metelambanen], ate seeds, and tops of trees, and vegetables, without meat. But in the same place John is distinguished from Matthew precisely by the fact that ὑπερτείνας τὴν ἐγκράτειαν, ἀκρίδας, καὶ μέλι ἤσθιεν ἄγριον [hyperteinas tēn enkrateian, akridas, kai meli ēsthien agrion], carrying abstinence further, he ate locusts and wild honey. So you may know that for him ἀκρίδας [akridas] were one thing and ἀκρόδρυα [akrodrya] another. Thus in the age of Epiphanius some were so rigid in their fasts that they abstained even from ἀκροδρύων, καὶ ἑψημάτων [akrodryōn, kai hepsēmatōn], from the tops of trees and from vegetable broths, as though this were too much. So he says in the Exposition of the Faith, ch. 23. The third opinion is that of those for whom αἱ ἀκρίδες [hai akrides] are a kind of herb. Euthymius: But some have said that the locusts were shoots of herbs, and others a herb called locust. Theophylact: Τινὲς λέγουσι βοτάνας εἶναι τὰς ἀκρίδας, ἃς καὶ μέλαγρα καλοῦσι· [Tines legousi botanas einai tas akridas, has kai melagra kalousi] Some say that the acridas are herbs, which they also call melagra, as an allusion to μέλι ἄγριον [meli agrion]. So, on this opinion, the honey and the locusts will be the same thing: namely a kind of herb otherwise entirely unknown, which nevertheless alone sufficed John for food. Nothing more absurd could be imagined. Yet even this opinion had its followers, among them Surianus, a monk, from whom Jacques de Vitry, ch. 53 of the History of Jerusalem, professes to have learned that the ἀκρίδας [akridas] of John were not locusts but a certain herb that used to be served to monks in Syria. Perhaps also Dionysius the Carthusian, who writes that some understand by locusts herbs of the desert, since it does not seem probable that John, who did not even eat bread, ate the flesh of animals or anything cooked. And Hermolaus, on Dioscorides, Corollary 256, says that the herb meant is the one called in Arabic رجل الجراد [rijl al-jarād] locust's foot; that is, blitum [blite], as some hold, or, as III, 328 others, rapunculum [rampion]. Let the fourth opinion be the one that holds the ἀκρίδας [akridas] of John to be little birds. Christian Druthmar, who wrote on Matthew in the ninth century after Christ: About the locusts I have heard someone say that these locusts were small birds with red legs. This would be tolerable if he had said only winged creatures, for among flying locusts some have red feet. But since he said a little bird with red feet, what else are we to understand than the ἐρυθρόποδα [erythropoda] of the Greeks? They take it to be a species of finch. That Druthmar understood a real bird is certainly clear, since he refutes the author of this opinion thus: Why would (John) be praised for the rigour of his abstinence, if he ate the flying creatures that the Jews longed for? The fifth: that the locusts were sea fish, which John obtained from the Jordan, as the same Druthmar reports, which is quite ridiculous. For these locusts are found not in rivers but in the sea itself. Not to mention that sea locusts [lobsters] are called by the Greeks not ἀκρίδας [akridas] but καράβους [karabous]. Finally, since sea locusts are counted a delicacy, here too Druthmar rightly objects that there would be no reason to praise John for abstinence if he ate marine delicacies. The same objection can be raised against those who change ἀκρίδας [akridas] into καρίδας [karidas], that is, squillas [shrimps], than which nothing in the whole crab family is more excellent. To this opinion, which is the sixth, I add a seventh, that of a very great and most pious man, who conjectures that the Evangelists here wrote ἀχράδες [achrades], that is, wild pears, and that by a slight change this word was turned into ἀκρίδες [akrides] R1.


Sed nihil opus est quidquam mutare, cum in receptam lectionem conspirent libri omnes; neque illa quidquam habeat, quo lector eruditus merito pos- col. 490 sit offendi. Certum enim est, locustarum esum in iis, quae vel ad ortum, vel ad austrum sunt, regionibus fuisse receptissimum. Quae Hieronymi verba sunt in Iovinianum lib. 2. cap. 6. Orientales et Libyae populos, quia per desertum et eremi vastitatem locustarum nubes reperiuntur, locustis vesci moris est. Sic, ab Alexandri aevo, inter Aethiopum populos Graecia descripsit Acridophagos, a locustarum esu sic dictos. De his Agatharchides lib. 5. cap. 27. Ὑπὸ δὲ τὴν ἐαρι-τὴν ἰσημερίαν, ὅτε Λίβυες (lege Λίβες) παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς καὶ Ζέφυροι πνέουσι, παμ-μεγεθῶν ἀκρίδων πλῆθος ἀμύθητον ἐκ τῆς ἀνιςορήτου μετὰ τῶν ἀνέμων παρα-γίνεται χώρας. τῇ μὲν δυνάμει τῆς πλήσεως τῶν ὀρνίθων μικρὸν παραλλάττον, III, 329 μακρὸν δὲ τῷ σώματι. ἀπὸ τούτου δὲ τοῦ ζώου τρέφονται πάντα τὸν χρόνον, ἄλλως τε τούτοις καὶ τεταριχευμένοις χρώμενοι. Sub vernum aequinoctium, cum apud eos spirant Africi et Favonii, inenarrabile locustarum praegrandium agmen ex ignotis terris una cum ventis advolat, quae vi quidem volatus parum ab avibus, sed corpore plurimum differt. Hoc autem animalculo quovis tempore vescuntur, sive cum sale, aut aliter condito. Ita etiam Diodorus lib. 3. editionis Steph. pag. 113. Ἐκ τούτου δαψιλεῖς τροφὰς ἔχου-σιν ἅπαντα τὸν βίον: Ex eo uberem victum habent per omnem vitam. Et Artemidorus apud Strabonem lib. 16. Ζῶσι δ' ἀπὸ ἀκρίδων, ἃς οἱ ἐαρινοὶ Λίβες καὶ Ζέφυροι, πνέοντες μεγάλοι, συνελαύνουσιν εἰς τοὺς τόπους τούτους· Locustis vivunt, quas verni, Africi et Favonii, vehementius flantes, in ea loca impellunt. Et Solinus, Confines Mauritaniae certo tempore locustas terrestres legunt, duratasque salsugine in praesidium vitae solas habent. Et Plinius libri 6. cap. 30. Pars quaedam Aethiopum locustis tantum vivit, fumo et sale duratis in annua alimenta. Et lib. 11. cap. 29. Parthis et hae in cibo gratae. Et de Nasamonibus Eustathius in Dionysium, Ἐσθίουσι δὲ ἀττελάβους πρὸς ἥλιον ξηράναντες· εἶδος δὲ ἀκρίδος ὁ ἀττέλαβος· Attelabos, locustae speciem, ad solem exsiccatos, comedunt. Et Dioscorides, ubi de asiraco, locustae specie; Χρῶνται δ' αὐτῇ κατακόρως οἱ κατὰ Λέπτιν Λίβυες· Ea utuntur in cibo usque ad satietatem Libes, qui ad Leptim incolunt. Porphyrius quoque lib. 1. De abstinentia a carne scribit, exercitui, in Libya inedia laboranti, locustarum nubes se obtulisse.

But there is no need to change anything, since all the books agree on the received reading, and it contains nothing at which a learned reader could rightly col. 490 take offence. For it is certain that the eating of locusts was very widely accepted in the regions that lie either to the east or to the south. These are Jerome's words in Against Jovinian book 2, ch. 6: Among the peoples of the East and of Libya, because clouds of locusts are found throughout the desert and the vastness of the wilderness, it is the custom to feed on locusts. Thus, from the age of Alexander, Greece described among the peoples of Ethiopia the Acridophagi, so called from eating locusts. On these Agatharchides, book 5, ch. 27: Ὑπὸ δὲ τὴν ἐαριτὴν ἰσημερίαν, ὅτε Λίβυες (lege Λίβες) παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς καὶ Ζέφυροι πνέουσι, παμμεγεθῶν ἀκρίδων πλῆθος ἀμύθητον ἐκ τῆς ἀνιςορήτου μετὰ τῶν ἀνέμων παραγίνεται χώρας. τῇ μὲν δυνάμει τῆς πλήσεως τῶν ὀρνίθων μικρὸν παραλλάττον, III, 329 μακρὸν δὲ τῷ σώματι. ἀπὸ τούτου δὲ τοῦ ζώου τρέφονται πάντα τὸν χρόνον, ἄλλως τε τούτοις καὶ τεταριχευμένοις χρώμενοι. [Hypo de tēn earitēn isēmerian, hote Libyes (lege Libes) par᾽ autois kai Zephyroi pneousi, pammegethōn akridōn plēthos amythēton ek tēs anistorētou meta tōn anemōn paraginetai chōras. tē men dynamei tēs plēseōs tōn ornithōn mikron parallatton, makron de tō sōmati. apo toutou de tou zōou trephontai panta ton chronon, allōs te toutois kai tetaricheumenois chrōmenoi.] Around the spring equinox, when the south-west winds and west winds blow among them, an indescribable swarm of very large locusts flies in together with the winds from unknown lands; in the force of their flight they differ little from birds, but in body very greatly. On this little creature they feed at every season, either salted or otherwise preserved. So also Diodorus, book 3 of Stephanus's edition, p. 113: Ἐκ τούτου δαψιλεῖς τροφὰς ἔχουσιν ἅπαντα τὸν βίον [Ek toutou dapsileis trophas echousin hapanta ton bion]: From it they have abundant sustenance throughout their whole life. And Artemidorus in Strabo, book 16: Ζῶσι δ' ἀπὸ ἀκρίδων, ἃς οἱ ἐαρινοὶ Λίβες καὶ Ζέφυροι, πνέοντες μεγάλοι, συνελαύνουσιν εἰς τοὺς τόπους τούτους· [Zōsi d' apo akridōn, has hoi earinoi Libes kai Zephyroi, pneontes megaloi, synelaunousin eis tous topous toutous] They live on locusts, which the spring south-west winds and west winds, blowing strongly, drive into those places. And Solinus: The neighbours of Mauretania at a certain season gather land locusts and, having hardened them in brine, keep them as their only means of subsistence. And Pliny, book 6, ch. 30: A certain part of the Ethiopians lives on locusts alone, hardened with smoke and salt as their yearly food. And book 11, ch. 29: among the Parthians these too are welcome as food. And on the Nasamones, Eustathius on Dionysius: Ἐσθίουσι δὲ ἀττελάβους πρὸς ἥλιον ξηράναντες· εἶδος δὲ ἀκρίδος ὁ ἀττέλαβος· [Esthiousi de attelabous pros hēlion xēranantes; eidos de akridos ho attelabos] They eat attelabi, a species of locust, dried in the sun. And Dioscorides, where he treats of the asiracus, a species of locust: Χρῶνται δ' αὐτῇ κατακόρως οἱ κατὰ Λέπτιν Λίβυες· [Chrōntai d' autē katakorōs hoi kata Leptin Libyes] The Libyans who live near Leptis use it as food to the point of satiety. Porphyry also, in book 1 of On Abstinence from Meat, writes that clouds of locusts presented themselves to an army suffering from hunger in Libya.


Quid, quod in ipsa Graecia idem cibus fuit in usu; quod probare est obvium? In Aristophanis Acharnensibus, Actus quarti Scena prima, Boeotius rusticus inter venales cibos, quos fert Athenas in forum, aliquid habere se dicit

What of the fact that in Greece itself the same food was in use, which is easy to prove? In Aristophanes' Acharnians, Act 4, Scene 1, a Boeotian peasant, among the foods for sale that he brings to the market at Athens, says that he has something


Τῶν ὀρταλίχων, ἢ τῶν τετραπτερυλλίδων,

Τῶν ὀρταλίχων, ἢ τῶν τετραπτερυλλίδων, [Tōn ortalichōn, ē tōn tetrapterullidōn,]


gallinarum, aut locustarum, quas τετραπτερυλλίδας vocari observavimus a) a quatuor alis, quibus instructi sunt. Et Scena 7.

of hens, or of locusts, which, as we have observed a), are called τετραπτερυλλίδας [tetrapterullidas] from the four wings with which they are furnished. And Scene 7:


Δ. Βούλει περιδόσθαι κἀπιτρέψαι Λαμάχῳ,
Πότερον ἀκρίδες ἥδιόν ἐστιν, ἢ κίχλαι;
Λ. Οἴμ' ὡς ὑβρίζεις. Δ. Τὰς ἀκρίδας κρίνει πολύ.

Δ. Βούλει περιδόσθαι κἀπιτρέψαι Λαμάχῳ, Πότερον ἀκρίδες ἥδιόν ἐστιν, ἢ κίχλαι; Λ. Οἴμ' ὡς ὑβρίζεις. Δ. Τὰς ἀκρίδας κρίνει πολύ. [D. Boulei peridosthai kapitrepsai Lamachō, Poteron akrides hēdion estin, ē kichlai? L. Oim' hōs hybrizeis. D. Tas akridas krinei poly.]


D. Vis pacisci et Lamacho permittere, (ut dicat) utrum plus sapiant locustae, aut turdi? L. Hei mihi! quam tu injurius es. D. Locustas praefert. Et III, 330 ibi Scholiastes. Διασύρει τὸν Λάμαχον, ὡς ἀκρίδας ἐσθίοντα, ἢ ὅτι πρό-τερον εὐτελεῖ ἐχρῆτο τῇ διαίτῃ· Lamachum insectatur, tanquam locustis vescentem, aut quia antea vili cibo usus fuerat. Plutarchus in Convivio tyrannum, qui mancipiis mavult praeesse, quam viris, colono similem esse dicit, qui vellet ἀκρίδας, καὶ ὀρνίθας, ἀντὶ πυρῶν, καὶ κριθῶν συγκομίζειν, locustas et aves, pro frumento et hordeo (edendas) colligere. Apud Theophylactum in Epistolis rusticus quidam, laute se exceptum fuisse jactitans, Ἰσχά-δες, inquit, ἦν μοι, καὶ ἀκρίδες, τὰ ὄψα· ὁ δὲ θεσπέσιος οὑτοσὶ νεανίας τῶν ἰσχάδων τὰ πλεῖστα ἐκβέβρωκε καὶ τὰς ἀκρίδας, οὐκ οἶδ᾽ ὅπως, ἐξερ-ροφήσει. Habebam, inquit, caricas et locustas, pro obsonio; divinus autem ille juvenis plerasque caricas voravit: locustas etiam, nescio quomodo, absorbuit. col. 491 Sic animalcula, locustis simillima, cicadas scilicet et cercopas, quae sunt cicadae minores, esitasse veteres, et quidem ad provocandam orexin, testatur Athenaeus lib. 4. Verba sunt, Ἤσθιον δὲ καὶ τέττιγας, καὶ κέρκωπας, ἀναστομώσεως χάριν. Ibidem Anaxandridas, in apparatu nuptiarum Iphicratis, cum Cotyis, Thraciae regis, filiam in uxorem duceret, τέττιγας ὀπτοὺς, cicadas coctas, inter caetera recenset. Et ex Aristophanis Anagyro haec citantur, Πρὸς Θεῶν ἐρᾷς τέττιγα φαγεῖν, καὶ κερκώπην θηρευσαμένη καλάμῳ λεπτῷ. Per Deos cicada et cercope libenter vesceris, quas tenui calamo venaris. Et lib. 9. Aristophanes in Horis Athenas laudat, quod etiam hyeme ibi vendat institor κίκλας, ἀπίους, σχαδόνας, ἐλάας, πύον, χόρια, χε-λιδόνα, τέττιγας, turdos, pira, favos, oleas, colostrum, choria (id est, edulia ex lacte et melle) hirundines, cicadas. Ut lib. 2. Alexis anum introducit, cui pro consueto cibo sunt, ut ipsa ait, κύαμος, θέρμος, λάχανον, γογγυ-λὶς, ὦχρος, λάθυρος, φηγὸς, βόλβος, τέττιξ, faba, lupinum, olus, rapa, ervilium, cicercula, oesculi glans, bulbus, cicada. Quin Philosophus lib. 5. Historiae cap. 30. et post eum Plinius lib. 11. cap. 26. docent, quo potissimum tempore maxime sapiant. Et hic gentes ad Orientem iis vesci testatur, in quibus Parthi, licet opibus abundantibus. Unde est, quod Aelianus Historiae lib. 10. cap. 6. graviter indignatur in sui saeculi homines, quorum alii Musis sacrum animal, cicadas, in lineam digestas, ad coenam vendunt, alii iis emptis avide vescuntur.

D. Do you want to make a wager and leave it to Lamachus (to say) which taste better, locusts or thrushes? L. Alas! how unjust you are. D. He prefers the locusts. And III, 330 there the Scholiast says: Διασύρει τὸν Λάμαχον, ὡς ἀκρίδας ἐσθίοντα, ἢ ὅτι πρότερον εὐτελεῖ ἐχρῆτο τῇ διαίτῃ [Diasyrei ton Lamachon, hōs akridas esthionta, ē hoti proteron euteleī echrēto tē diaitē]; he mocks Lamachus as one who feeds on locusts, or because he had formerly used cheap food. Plutarch, in the Banquet, says that a tyrant who would rather rule over slaves than over men is like a farmer who would want ἀκρίδας, καὶ ὀρνίθας, ἀντὶ πυρῶν, καὶ κριθῶν συγκομίζειν [akridas, kai ornithas, anti pyrōn, kai krithōn synkomizein], to gather locusts and birds instead of wheat and barley (to eat). In Theophylact's Letters a certain rustic, boasting that he had been lavishly entertained, says: Ἰσχάδες, ἦν μοι, καὶ ἀκρίδες, τὰ ὄψα· ὁ δὲ θεσπέσιος οὑτοσὶ νεανίας τῶν ἰσχάδων τὰ πλεῖστα ἐκβέβρωκε καὶ τὰς ἀκρίδας, οὐκ οἶδ᾽ ὅπως, ἐξερροφήσει [Ischades, ēn moi, kai akrides, ta opsa; ho de thespesios houtosi neanias tōn ischadōn ta pleista ekbebrōke kai tas akridas, ouk oid᾽ hopōs, exerrophēsei]. I had, he says, dried figs and locusts as a relish; but that divine young man devoured most of the figs, and the locusts too, I know not how, he gulped down. col. 491 So too Athenaeus, book 4, testifies that the ancients used to eat little creatures very like locusts, namely cicadas and cercopes, which are smaller cicadas, and indeed to whet the appetite. His words are: Ἤσθιον δὲ καὶ τέττιγας, καὶ κέρκωπας, ἀναστομώσεως χάριν [Ēsthion de kai tettigas, kai kerkōpas, anastomōseōs charin]. In the same place Anaxandrides, describing the preparations for the wedding of Iphicrates, when he took to wife the daughter of Cotys, king of Thrace, lists among other things τέττιγας ὀπτοὺς [tettigas optous], cooked cicadas. And from the Anagyrus of Aristophanes this is quoted: Πρὸς Θεῶν ἐρᾷς τέττιγα φαγεῖν, καὶ κερκώπην θηρευσαμένη καλάμῳ λεπτῷ [Pros Theōn eras tettiga phagein, kai kerkōpēn thēreusamenē kalamō leptō]. By the gods, you gladly eat the cicada and the cercope, which you hunt with a thin reed. And in book 9, Aristophanes in the Horae praises Athens because even in winter the huckster sells there κίκλας, ἀπίους, σχαδόνας, ἐλάας, πύον, χόρια, χελιδόνα, τέττιγας [kiklas, apious, schadonas, elaas, pyon, choria, chelidona, tettigas], thrushes, pears, honeycombs, olives, beestings, choria (that is, dishes made of milk and honey), swallows, cicadas. Likewise in book 2 Alexis brings on an old woman whose usual food, as she herself says, is κύαμος, θέρμος, λάχανον, γογγυλὶς, ὦχρος, λάθυρος, φηγὸς, βόλβος, τέττιξ [kyamos, thermos, lachanon, gongylis, ōchros, lathyros, phēgos, bolbos, tettix], the bean, the lupine, greens, the turnip, the bitter vetch, the chickling, the acorn of the oak, the bulb, the cicada. Indeed the Philosopher, History book 5, ch. 30, and after him Pliny, book 11, ch. 26, teach at what season above all they taste best. And Pliny testifies that peoples in the East eat them, among them the Parthians, although abounding in wealth. Hence Aelian, History book 10, ch. 6, is greatly indignant at the men of his age, some of whom sell the cicadas, an animal sacred to the Muses, strung in a row, for dinner, while others buy them and eat them greedily.


Sed, quod rei caput est, etiam inter Iudaeos edulis fuit locusta. Testatur id Mosaica lex Levit. XI, 21. 22. ubi in esum conceduntur quatuor locustarum species, arbe, solam, chargol et chagab. Et Talmudici doctores, qui tractatus Cholin cap. 3. fol. 65. et 66. multis disputant, quibus notis dignoscantur mundae locustae ab immundis, id est, quas licet edere, ab iis, quarum esus Lege prohibetur. Proinde ad Exod. X, 19. ubi ventus, a Deo immissus, III, 331 abripuisse, et in mare rubrum conjecisse legitur, quidquid in Aegy- pto locustarum erat, ita, ut ne una quidem remanserit in omnibus Aegy- ptiorum finibus. Ionathan in paraphrasi id excipit, מה דמלחין במנייא לצרוך מיכלהון, quod in vasis suis sale condierant in cibi usum (2).

But, and this is the heart of the matter, the locust was edible among the Jews too. This is attested by the Mosaic law, Lev 11:21–22., where four species of locust are permitted for eating: arbe, solam, chargol and chagab. So too the Talmudic doctors, who in the tractate Cholin, ch. 3, fol. 65 and 66, argue at length about the marks by which clean locusts are distinguished from unclean, that is, those which may be eaten from those whose eating is forbidden by the Law. Accordingly, at Exod 10:19, where we read that a wind sent by God III, 331 carried off whatever locusts were in Egypt and cast them into the Red Sea, so that not even one remained in all the borders of the Egyptians, Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] in his paraphrase makes an exception: מה דמלחין במנייא לצרוך מיכלהון, what they had preserved with salt in their vessels for use as food R2.


Arabes quoque idem docent. Damir in capite De locustis, titulo الحكم sive De usu, اجمع المسلمون علي اباحة اكل الجراد Musulmanni in id consentiunt, locustarum esum esse licitum. Freti nimirum Abdallae auctoritate, cujus verba sunt, غزونا مع رسول الله صلي الله عليه وسلم سبع غزوات ناكل الجراد فيها Bellicas expeditiones septem suscepimus cum Dei propheta, cui Deus sit propitius, locustarum carnem comedentes. Hinc est, quod Deum illas immittere dictitant, modo ut sint رزقا القوم esca populis, modo ut sint بلا علي القوم plaga in populos. Exemplo sint pauca haec, petita ex Alcamus, الصراح طاير كالجندب يوكل Sorrach, volucre animalculum bruchi instar, quod comeditur. جرد شري جلده عن اكله Giarida, pustulae effloruerunt in carne ejus propter illius esum; id est, propter esum locustae, de qua antea. جرد شكا بطنه من col. 492 اكله Giurida, propter ejusdem esum venter doluit. المرتجل من يقع برجل من جراد فيشتوي منها Almurtegilo, qui, in locustae pedes incidens, eos assat. الحنتف الجراد المنتف المنقي للطبخ Alchantapho, locusta, quae, ut coquatur, depilata, et mundata est, الوهيسة ان يطبخ الجراد وتجفف ويدق ويخلط بدسم Alvvahisatho, cum coquitur locusta, et arefacta con- tunditur, et cum adipe miscetur: nimirum ut sit pro cibo. His adde recentiorum testimonia. Ut Nicolai Clenardi in Epistolis, Plaustra, plena locustis, advehunt Fessam; nam hos hostes vulgo hic comedunt. Et Leonis Africani III, 332 lib. 9. Arabiae desertum et Libyae populi earum adventum pro felici habent omine: nam vel elixas, vel ad solem exsiccatas in farina tundunt, atque com- edunt. Et Hermolai Barbari Corollario in Dioscoridem CCLVI. Hodie quo- que locustas comedunt Aegyptii (3).

The Arabs teach the same. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], in the chapter On locusts, under the heading الحكم [al-ḥukm], that is, On use: اجمع المسلمون علي اباحة اكل الجراد [ajmaʿa al-muslimūn ʿalā ibāḥat akl al-jarād], "The Muslims agree that the eating of locusts is lawful." They rely, of course, on the authority of Abdalla, whose words are: غزونا مع رسول الله صلي الله عليه وسلم سبع غزوات ناكل الجراد فيها [ghazawnā maʿa rasūl Allāh ṣallā Allāh ʿalayhi wa-sallam sabʿ ghazawāt naʾkul al-jarād fīhā], "We undertook seven military expeditions with the prophet of God, on whom God be gracious, eating the flesh of locusts." Hence they keep saying that God sends them, sometimes to be رزقا القوم [rizqan li-l-qawm] food for the peoples, sometimes to be بلا علي القوم [balāʾ ʿalā al-qawm] a plague upon the peoples. Let these few examples, taken from Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī], suffice: الصراح طاير كالجندب يوكل [al-ṣurāḥ ṭāʾir ka-l-jundub yuʾkal], Sorrach, a small winged animal like the bruchus, which is eaten. جرد شري جلده عن اكله [jurida shariya jilduhu ʿan aklihi], Giarida, pustules broke out on his flesh because of eating it; that is, because of eating the locust mentioned before. جرد شكا بطنه من col. 492 اكله [jurida shakā baṭnuhu min aklihi], Giurida, his belly ached from eating the same. المرتجل من يقع برجل من جراد فيشتوي منها [al-murtajil man yaqaʿ bi-rijl min jarād fa-yashtawī minhā], Almurtegilo, one who, coming upon a swarm of locusts, roasts them. الحنتف الجراد المنتف المنقي للطبخ [al-ḥantaf al-jarād al-muntaf al-munaqqā li-l-ṭabkh], Alchantapho, a locust that has been plucked and cleaned for cooking; الوهيسة ان يطبخ الجراد وتجفف ويدق ويخلط بدسم [al-wahīsa an yuṭbakh al-jarād wa-tujaffaf wa-yudaqq wa-yukhlaṭ bi-dasam], Alvvahisatho, when a locust is cooked, and after drying is pounded and mixed with fat: that is, to serve as food. Add to these the testimonies of more recent writers. Thus Nicolaus Clenardus in his Letters: "They bring wagons full of locusts into Fez; for here people commonly eat these enemies." And Leo Africanus III, 332 book 9: "The desert of Arabia and the peoples of Libya regard their arrival as a happy omen: for they pound them into meal, either boiled or dried in the sun, and eat them." And Hermolaus Barbarus, Corollary 256 on Dioscorides: "Today too the Egyptians eat locusts" R3.


Sed et idem in Iudaea fieri, multi scribunt. Sic Beda, De locis san- ctis cap. 14. a sancto episcopo, Archulpho, qui ad ea loca peregrinatus erat, se accepisse tradit, notissimas esse locustas in Palaestina, quae corpusculis in modum digiti manus exiguis et brevibus, in herbis facile captae, coctaeque oleo pauperem victum parent. Et Euthymius in Matthaeum, Dicunt usque ad hodiernum diem in illis partibus, plerosque illud (insecti genus) edere fu- mo siccatum: habere autem gravem odorem, malumque gustum. Iacobus quoque de Vitriaco, Ptolemaidis episcopus, ubi supra b) testatur, locustas in Iu- daea et recentes edi solitas, et servatas.

But many write that the same is done in Judaea as well. Thus Bede, On the Holy Places ch. 14, reports that he learned from a holy bishop, Arculf, who had made a pilgrimage to those places, that "in Palestine there are very well-known locusts, which, with little bodies slight and short like a finger of the hand, are easily caught in the grass and, cooked in oil, provide a poor man's fare." And Euthymius on Matthew: "They say that to this very day in those parts many eat it (that kind of insect) dried in smoke, but that it has a strong smell and a bad taste." Jacques de Vitry too, bishop of Ptolemais, in the place cited above b), testifies that in Judaea locusts were customarily eaten both fresh and preserved.


Summa eorum, quae diximus, haec est, praeter Acridophagos, omnibus notos, Nasamones etiam, et Leptitanos, et Parthos, et Graecos, et He- braeos locustas olim pro cibo habuisse. Quomodo Arabes quoque, et Nu- midas, et Mauritanos, et novos Palaestinae incolas jam inde a multis saeculis. Itaque, quod locustas edebat Iohannes, novum non fuit, nec inauditum: sed hoc in illo fuit singulare, quod in deserto solum locustis et agresti melle vescebatur, iisque forte oblatis, nec aliunde comparatis; ut virum illum Iudaei scirent extraordinarium habere munus, atque ad ejus conciones essent attentiores. Causa igitur non fuit, cur Isidorus Pelusiota eos accusaret III, 333 imperitiae, qui locustas hic intelligunt. In quo numero multi fuerunt illo longe celebriores: ut Theophilus Antiochenus, Origenes, Hilarius et Chrysostomus in Matthaeum; Ambrosius in Lucam, Clemens Alexandrinus lib. 2. Paedagogi, Hieronymus lib. 2. in Iovinianum, et Epistola 23. ad Marcellam, Augustinus lib. 10. Confessionum cap. 31. Scriptores denique quotquot sunt Isidoro vetustiores, praeter unicum Paulinum in sacro poemate de Iohanne, baptista, cui facile sit alios Poetas opponere, nobiscum sentientes. Ita enim de eodem Iuvencus lib. 1. Historiae Evangelicae,

The sum of what we have said is this: besides the Acridophagi, known to all, the Nasamones too, and the people of Leptis, and the Parthians, and the Greeks, and the Hebrews once had locusts for food; as have the Arabs also, and the Numidians, and the Mauretanians, and the new inhabitants of Palestine, now for many centuries. Therefore that John ate locusts was nothing new or unheard of. What was singular in him was that in the desert he fed only on locusts and wild honey, and these perhaps as they chanced to come his way, not procured from elsewhere; so that the Jews might know that this man had an extraordinary office, and might be more attentive to his preaching. There was no reason, then, for Isidore of Pelusium to accuse of III, 333 ignorance those who understand locusts here. Among their number were many far more celebrated than he: such as Theophilus of Antioch, Origen, Hilary and Chrysostom on Matthew; Ambrose on Luke; Clement of Alexandria, book 2 of the Paedagogus; Jerome, book 2 Against Jovinian and Letter 23 to Marcella; Augustine, book 10 of the Confessions, ch. 31. In short, all the writers older than Isidore, except only Paulinus in his sacred poem on John the Baptist; and against him it would be easy to set other Poets who agree with us. For thus Juvencus writes of him in book 1 of the Gospel History:


Arvis qui solitus ruralibus esse locustas.

He who was wont [to eat] locusts in the country fields.


Et Prudentius, Cathemerinωn Hymno 7.

And Prudentius, Cathemerinon, Hymn 7:


Parvum locustis et favorum agrestium
Liquore pastum corpori suetus dare.

Accustomed to give his body a meagre fare
of locusts and the liquid of wild honeycombs.


Et Amoenus in Enchiridio,

And Amoenus in the Enchiridion:


Perfundit fluvio pastus Baptista locustis.

The Baptist, fed on locusts, bathes [them] in the river.


Et Paulus Diaconus in Hymno De Nativitate sancti Iohannis, baptistae,

And Paul the Deacon in the Hymn On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist:


Praebuit hirtum tegimen camelus, col. 493
Artubus sacris strophium bidentes,
Cui latex haustum, sociata pastum
Mella locustis.

The camel provided a shaggy covering, col. 493 sheep a girdle for his sacred limbs;
for him water was drink, and food
was honey joined with locusts.

He was moved chiefly by this reason: that the tree is common in the desert in which John is said to have lived, and which today is called the desert of St John. To state this opinion will be the same as to refute it, for no argument can prove that ἀκρίδας [akridas] and κεράτια [keratia] mean the same thing.
