III, 341 col. 496 CAP. IX.

III, 341 col. 496 Chapter IX.


De Musca.

On the Fly.


Vel in ipsa Scriptura, vel in vetustis Scripturae versionibus, septem leguntur muscarum species. I. Musca, proprie dicta, Hebraice זבוב zebub, Graece μυῖα, Eccles. X, 1. Muscae mortuae faciunt, ut foetorem eructet unguentum pigmentarii. Esa. VII, 18. Sibilabit Dominus ad muscam, quae est in extremo fluminum Aegypti. II. Apis, Hebraeis דברה debora; Graecis μέλιττα, Deut. I, 44. Persequuti sunt vos, ut faciunt apes. Iud. XIV, 8. Et, ecce! examen apum in corpore leonis. Psalm. CXVIII, 12. Circumdederunt me ut apes. Esa. VII, 18. Sibilabit Dominus ad muscam, etc. et ad apem, quae est in terra Assyriae. III. Vespa, vel crabro, Hebraeis צרעה tsira: Graecis σφὴξ, vel σφηκία, ut habent Graeci interpretes Exod. XXIII, 28. Mittam crabronem ante te, qui expellet Hevaeum, etc. Deut. VII, 20. Etiam crabronem immittet Dominus Deus tuus in eos. Ios. XXIV, 12. Misi ante vos crabronem, qui expulit eos a facie vestra. IV. Οἶστρος, oestrum, seu asilus: ad cujus nomen alludentes Graeci dicunt Ezech. II, 6. Διότι παροιστρήσουσιν, Quia, ut oestro perciti, insanient, et Os. IV, 16. Ὡς δάμαλις παροιστρῶσα παρεῖστρησεν Ἰσραήλ· Ut juvenca, oestro percussa, insanivit Israel. V. Κυνόμυια, seu canina musca, in Graeca versione saepe nominatur. Sic Exod. VIII, 21. Ἰδοὺ, ἐγὼ ἐξαποστέλλω ἐπὶ σὲ κυνόμυιαν. Et passim reliquo capite. Et Psal. LXXVII, 45. Ἐξαπέ- col. 497 στειλεν εἰς αὐτοὺς κυνόμυιαν. Et Psal. CIV, 31. Εἶπε, καὶ ἦλθε κυνόμυια. Sed Hieronymus in fine Epistolae ad Suniam et Fretellam, legi vult κοινόμυιαν. Pro quo Aquila παμμυῖαν habet, quia Hebraeum ערב arob a mixtura putatur sumptum. Itaque sunt etiam in Hebraeis, qui sic interpretantur. Sed de his infra suo loco. VI. Ad muscarum species potest referri κώνωψ, culex, de quo Matth. XXIII, 24. Οἱ διυλίζοντες τὸν κώνωπα, τὴν δὲ κάμηλον καταπίνοντες, Excolantes culicem, camelum autem deglutientes. VII. Ut et σκνίπες (vel, ut alii legunt, σκνίφες) Exod. VIII, 16. Ἔσονται σκνίπες ἔν τε τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, καὶ ἐν τοῖς τετράποσι καὶ ἐν πάσῃ γῇ Αἰγύπτου. Et Psal. CIV, 31. Καὶ σκνίπες ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ὁρίοις αὐτῶν. Vulgatus quoque interpres et Hieronymus, sciniphes. Sed Hebraeum כנים Iosephus et Hebraei recentiores pediculos verius reddunt. Iam dicemus de musca, proprie sic vocata.

Either in Scripture itself or in the ancient versions of Scripture, seven kinds of fly are found. I. The fly properly so called, in Hebrew זבוב zebub, in Greek μυῖα [myia], Eccl 10:1: Dead flies make the perfumer's ointment give off a stench. Isa 7:18: The Lord will hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt. II. The bee, in Hebrew דברה debora, in Greek μέλιττα [melitta], Deut 1:44: They chased you, as bees do. Iud. XIV, 8: And behold, a swarm of bees in the body of the lion. Ps 118:12: They surrounded me like bees. Isa 7:18: The Lord will hiss for the fly, etc. and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria. III. The wasp or hornet, in Hebrew צרעה tsira, in Greek σφὴξ [sphēx] or σφηκία [sphēkia], as the Greek translators have it, Exod 23:28: I will send the hornet before you, which will drive out the Hivite, etc. Deut 7:20: Moreover the Lord your God will send the hornet among them. Josh 24:12: I sent the hornet before you, which drove them out from before you. IV. Οἶστρος [oistros], the oestrum or asilus [gadfly]. Alluding to its name, the Greeks say at Ezek 2:6 Διότι παροιστρήσουσιν [Dioti paroistrēsousin], For, as if stung by the gadfly, they will rage, and at Hos 4:16 Ὡς δάμαλις παροιστρῶσα παρεῖστρησεν Ἰσραήλ [Hōs damalis paroistrōsa pareistrēsen Israēl]: Like a heifer struck by the gadfly, Israel has raged. V. The κυνόμυια [kynomyia], or dog-fly, is often named in the Greek version. Thus Exod 8:21 Ἰδοὺ, ἐγὼ ἐξαποστέλλω ἐπὶ σὲ κυνόμυιαν [Idou, egō exapostellō epi se kynomyian], and throughout the rest of the chapter; and Ps 77:45 Ἐξαπέ- col. 497 στειλεν εἰς αὐτοὺς κυνόμυιαν [Exapesteilen eis autous kynomyian]; and Ps 104:31 Εἶπε, καὶ ἦλθε κυνόμυια [Eipe, kai ēlthe kynomyia]. But Jerome, at the end of his Letter to Sunnia and Fretela, wants κοινόμυιαν [koinomyian] to be read. For this Aquila has παμμυῖαν [pammyian], because the Hebrew ערב arob is thought to be taken from mixture. Accordingly there are also some among the Hebrews who interpret it so. But of these below, in their proper place. VI. To the kinds of fly may be referred κώνωψ [kōnōps], the gnat, of which Matt 23:24 Οἱ διυλίζοντες τὸν κώνωπα, τὴν δὲ κάμηλον καταπίνοντες [Hoi diylizontes ton kōnōpa, tēn de kamēlon katapinontes], Straining out the gnat, but swallowing the camel. VII. As also σκνίπες [sknipes] (or, as others read, σκνίφες [skniphes]), Exod 8:16 Ἔσονται σκνίπες ἔν τε τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, καὶ ἐν τοῖς τετράποσι καὶ ἐν πάσῃ γῇ Αἰγύπτου [Esontai sknipes en te tois anthrōpois, kai en tois tetraposi kai en pasē gē Aigyptou]. And Ps 104:31 Καὶ σκνίπες ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ὁρίοις αὐτῶν [Kai sknipes en pasi tois horiois autōn]. The Vulgate translator too and Jerome have sciniphes. But Josephus and the more recent Hebrews more correctly render the Hebrew כנים as lice. Now we shall speak of the fly properly so called.


Musca, ut Hebraice זבוב zebub, sic Chaldaice דבובא debuba; Syriace ܕܒܒܐ debaba; et Arabice ذباب dsebab, dicitur levi mutatione. Nominis originem, Hebraeis et Syris ignotam, aperiunt Arabes, apud quos ذب dsabba, incertis sedibus divagari, nec in uno loco consistere significat. Quod muscae III, 342 convenire, nemo est, qui nesciat. Hinc Lucianus in Muscae encomio, Νεοττιὰν δὲ, ἢ καλίαν, οὐχ᾽ ἑνὶ τόπῳ κατεστήσατο, ἀλλὰ πλάνητα τὴν πτῆσιν κατὰ τοὺς Σκύθας ἐπανῃρημένη, ὅπου ἂν τύχῃ ὑπὸ τῆς νυκτὸς καταληφθεῖσα, ἐκεῖ καὶ ἑστίαν καὶ εὐνὴν ποιεῖται· Nidum autem, aut nidulum, non uno in loco constituit, sed, Scytharum in morem, vago volatu sublata, ubicunque a nocte fuerit deprehensa, ibi domum et cubile facit. Eodem pertinet, quod, qui maxime vagus est et inconstans, Arabico proverbio dicitur esse اطيَش من ذباب Musca in- constantior (1).

The fly, as in Hebrew זבוב zebub, so in Chaldee is called דבובא debuba, in Syriac ܕܒܒܐ [דבבא] debaba, and in Arabic ذباب [dhubāb] dsebab, with slight change. The origin of the name, unknown to the Hebrews and Syrians, is disclosed by the Arabs, among whom ذب [dhabba] dsabba means to wander about with no fixed abode and not to stay in one place. That this suits the fly, there is no one who does not know. III, 342 Hence Lucian in the Encomium of the Fly: Νεοττιὰν δὲ, ἢ καλίαν, οὐχ᾽ ἑνὶ τόπῳ κατεστήσατο, ἀλλὰ πλάνητα τὴν πτῆσιν κατὰ τοὺς Σκύθας ἐπανῃρημένη, ὅπου ἂν τύχῃ ὑπὸ τῆς νυκτὸς καταληφθεῖσα, ἐκεῖ καὶ ἑστίαν καὶ εὐνὴν ποιεῖται [Neottian de, ē kalian, ouch' heni topō katestēsato, alla planēta tēn ptēsin kata tous Skythas epanērēmenē, hopou an tychē hypo tēs nyktos katalēphtheisa, ekei kai hestian kai eunēn poieitai]: She does not establish a nest or a little nest in one place, but, borne up in wandering flight after the manner of the Scythians, wherever she happens to be overtaken by night, there she makes her home and her bed. To the same point belongs the fact that one who is extremely fickle and inconstant is said in an Arabic proverb to be اطيَش من ذباب [aṭyash min dhubāb], more inconstant than a fly R1.


III, 343 Muscarum esum concedunt nonnulli Arabum; quia saepe ex rebus concessis generantur: puta ex faba, quam corruptam ajunt Arabes in muscas ita mutari, ut nihil supersit praeter corticem. Sed Hebraei muscas vetabant, freti lege, quae habetur Deut. XIV, 19. Omne reptile volucre immundum est: non comedetur. Quam Ionathan sic παραφράζει· וכל דיבבי וזיבורי וזיזי דטלופחי ופולי דפרשי מן אוכלא ופרחין הי כעופא מסאבין אינון לכון לא יתאכלון, omnes muscae, et vespae (seu apes) et vermes lentium et fabarum, qui, a cibo separati, avis instar evolant, vobis erunt immundi, non comedentur. Idem concludunt ex his Levit. XI, 20. Omne reptile, volucre, et quadrupes, abominatio erit vobis. Ubi Ionathan, וכל ריחשא דעופא דמהלך על ארבע זני דיבבי וזני אורעי וזני זובורי שיקצא הוא לכון ברם דיבשא דזיבורי יתאכל, Et omne reptile, volucre quadrupes, species muscarum, et species crabronum, et species apum, abominatio erunt vobis: tamen mel apum comedetur. Et ibidem R. Selomo, הם הדקים הנמוכים הרחושים על הארץ כגון זבובין וצרעין ויתושין וחגבין, Haec minuta sunt animalcula, quae super terram repunt, ut muscae, et crabrones, et vespae, et locustae. Si muscas, crabrones, vespas et apes objeceris in censu reptilium quadrupedum ab Hebraeis perperam poni, cum muscarum genus non sit τετρά-πους, sed ἑξάπους· duos pedes anteriores respondebo non haberi pro pedibus; quia manuum vicem potius gerunt. Neque enim iis incedunt, quomodo quatuor reliquis, sed oculos, pulvere obsitos, abstergunt, cibos sumunt, et, quidquid tollendum est, evehunt. Lucianus de musca, Ἑξάπους δὲ οὖσα, τοῖς μὲν τέσσαρσι βαδίζει μόνοις· τοῖς δὲ προσθίοις δυσὶ, καὶ ὅσα χερσὶ χρῆται. Ἴδοις ἂν οὖν αὐτὴν ἐπὶ τεττάρων βεβηκυῖαν, ἔχουσάν τι ἐν ταῖν χεροῖν μετέωρον ἐδώ-διμον ἀνθρωπίνως πάνυ, καὶ καθ' ἡμᾶς. Cum sit sexipes, quatuor tantum pe- col. 498 dibus incedit; aliisque duobus anterioribus utitur tanquam manibus: ipsam igitur pedibus quatuor gradientem videas, et edule aliquid manibus in sublime tollentem, humano prorsus nostroque more. Sed et Philosophus libri quarti De partibus capite sexto, Τοὺς δὲ πόδας τοὺς προσθίους μείζους ἔνια τούτων ἔχει, ὅπως διὰ τὸ σκληρόφθαλμα εἶναι, ἐπειδὴ οὐκ ἀκριβῶς τὴν ὄψιν ἔχει, τὰ προσπίπτοντα τοῖς προσθίον ἀποκαθαίρωσι σκέλεσιν· ὅπερ καὶ φαίνονται ποιοῦσαι αἵ τε μυῖαι, καὶ τὰ μελιττώδη τῶν ζώων· ἀεὶ γὰρ χαρακίζουσι τοῖς προσθίοις σκέλεσι. Pedes priores nonnulla (animalia) longiores habent, ut, quoniam propter oculorum duritiem non exquisite cernunt, prioribus illis pedibus id abstergant, quod in III, 344 oculos incidit. Quod et muscas facere videas, et mellifica quaecunque sunt animalcula. Semper enim prioribus pedibus (tanquam palis) quidvis in sublime tollunt. Ita reddendum. Nam χαρακίζειν hic est μετεωρίζειν, ut est in Hesychio; non vallare et protegere, ut voluit Gaza. Plinius libri undecimi capite quadragesimo octavo, Insectorum pedes primi longiores, duros habentibus oculos, ut subinde pedibus eos tergeant, ceu notamus in muscis. Damir, والذباب ليس له اجفان لصغر احداقه ومن شان الاجفان ان تصقل مراة الحدقه من الغبار فجعل الله له يدين يصقل بها مراة احداقه فلهذا تري الذباب ابدا يمسح بيديه عينيه Muscae non habent palpebras propter pupillae parvitatem: sed, cum palpebrarum proprium sit, ut a speculo pupillae pulverem abstergant, Deus illis dedit manus, quibus id praestent. Illas igitur subinde videas oculos his manibus detergentes.

III, 343 Some of the Arabs permit the eating of flies, because they are often generated from permitted things: for instance from the bean, which the Arabs say, when corrupted, is so changed into flies that nothing remains but the husk. But the Hebrews forbade flies, relying on the law found in Deut 14:19. Every creeping thing that flies is unclean: it shall not be eaten. Which Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] paraphrases [paraphrazei] thus: וכל דיבבי וזיבורי וזיזי דטלופחי ופולי דפרשי מן אוכלא ופרחין הי כעופא מסאבין אינון לכון לא יתאכלון, all flies, and wasps (or bees) and the worms of lentils and beans which, separated from the food, fly out like a bird, shall be unclean to you; they shall not be eaten. They conclude the same from these words, Lev 11:20. Every creeping thing that flies and goes on four feet shall be an abomination to you. Where Jonathan has: וכל ריחשא דעופא דמהלך על ארבע זני דיבבי וזני אורעי וזני זובורי שיקצא הוא לכון ברם דיבשא דזיבורי יתאכל, And every creeping thing that flies, four-footed, the species of flies, and the species of hornets, and the species of bees, shall be an abomination to you: yet the honey of bees shall be eaten. And in the same place R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)]: הם הדקים הנמוכים הרחושים על הארץ כגון זבובין וצרעין ויתושין וחגבין, These are the minute little animals which creep upon the earth, such as flies, and hornets, and wasps, and locusts. If you object that flies, hornets, wasps and bees are wrongly placed by the Hebrews in the class of four-footed creeping things, since the fly kind is not τετράπους [tetrapous] but ἑξάπους [hexapous], I shall reply that the two front feet are not counted as feet, because they rather serve as hands. For they do not walk on them as on the other four; rather with them they wipe their eyes when covered with dust, take their food, and carry off whatever has to be lifted. Lucian on the fly: Ἑξάπους δὲ οὖσα, τοῖς μὲν τέσσαρσι βαδίζει μόνοις· τοῖς δὲ προσθίοις δυσὶ, καὶ ὅσα χερσὶ χρῆται. Ἴδοις ἂν οὖν αὐτὴν ἐπὶ τεττάρων βεβηκυῖαν, ἔχουσάν τι ἐν ταῖν χεροῖν μετέωρον ἐδώδιμον ἀνθρωπίνως πάνυ, καὶ καθ' ἡμᾶς [Hexapous de ousa, tois men tessarsi badizei monois; tois de prosthiois dysi, kai hosa chersi chrētai. Idois an oun autēn epi tettarōn bebēkuian, echousan ti en tain cheroin meteōron edōdimon anthrōpinōs pany, kai kath' hēmas]. Though it is six-footed, it walks on four feet only, and uses the other two in front as hands: so you may see it stepping on four feet and lifting up something edible in its hands, col. 498 entirely in human fashion, as we do. And the Philosopher too, book 4 On the Parts, chapter 6: Τοὺς δὲ πόδας τοὺς προσθίους μείζους ἔνια τούτων ἔχει, ὅπως διὰ τὸ σκληρόφθαλμα εἶναι, ἐπειδὴ οὐκ ἀκριβῶς τὴν ὄψιν ἔχει, τὰ προσπίπτοντα τοῖς προσθίον ἀποκαθαίρωσι σκέλεσιν· ὅπερ καὶ φαίνονται ποιοῦσαι αἵ τε μυῖαι, καὶ τὰ μελιττώδη τῶν ζώων· ἀεὶ γὰρ χαρακίζουσι τοῖς προσθίοις σκέλεσι [Tous de podas tous prosthious meizous enia toutōn echei, hopōs dia to sklērophthalma einai, epeidē ouk akribōs tēn opsin echei, ta prospiptonta tois prosthion apokathairōsi skelesin; hoper kai phainontai poiousai hai te myiai, kai ta melittōdē tōn zōōn; aei gar charakizousi tois prosthiois skelesi]. Some (animals) have longer front feet so that, since because of the hardness of their eyes they do not see precisely, they may wipe off with those front feet whatever III, 344 falls into their eyes. This you may see flies doing too, and all the honey-making little animals. For they always lift up (as on stakes) anything with their front feet. So it should be rendered. For χαρακίζειν [charakizein] here is μετεωρίζειν [meteōrizein], as it is in Hesychius; not vallare [to fence with stakes] and protegere [to protect], as Gaza would have it. Pliny, book 11, chapter 48: In insects that have hard eyes the front feet are longer, so that they may wipe them with their feet from time to time, as we observe in flies. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: والذباب ليس له اجفان لصغر احداقه ومن شان الاجفان ان تصقل مراة الحدقه من الغبار فجعل الله له يدين يصقل بها مراة احداقه فلهذا تري الذباب ابدا يمسح بيديه عينيه [wa-l-dhubāb laysa lahu ajfān li-ṣighar aḥdāqihi wa-min shaʾn al-ajfān an taṣqul mirāt al-ḥadaqa min al-ghubār fa-jaʿala Allāh lahu yadayn yaṣqul bihā mirāt aḥdāqihi fa-li-hādhā tarī al-dhubāb abadan yamsaḥ bi-yadayhi ʿaynayhi] Flies have no eyelids because of the smallness of the pupil; but since it is the property of eyelids to wipe dust from the mirror of the pupil, God gave them hands with which to do this. So you may see them constantly wiping their eyes with these hands.


Nec sine causa, reptilium, atque in his muscarum, esus Iudaeis prohibitus est: cum musca sit foedum ac foetidum animal, quodque ex immunditia nascitur, atque in immundis libenter haeret. Et, sive ad hominum mensas, aut ad Deorum aras accedat, dapes impudenter diripit, contactuque omnia foedat. Quid, quod pusilla bestia, ad myropolium volans, et in narthecio casu mortua, unguentum, in eo reconditum, totum inficit? Unde illud Solomonis Eccles. X, 1. Muscarum mortuarum una facit, ut foetorem eructet unguentum pigmentarii. Sic parum stultitiae foetere facit hominem, sapientia et gloria eximium. Quomodo dicit Paulus, parum fermenti totam massam corrumpere, 1 Cor. V, 6. Nam multo facilius corrumpitur, quod bonum est, quam emendatur, quod malum. Proinde notat Aggaeus capitis secundi versu duodecimo, et decimo tertio, rei secrae contactu rem immundam non consecrari; sed, contra, sacram pollui contactu rei immundae (2).

Nor was it without reason that the eating of creeping things, and among them of flies, was forbidden to the Jews: for the fly is a foul and stinking animal, born from uncleanness and gladly clinging to unclean things. And whether it comes to the tables of men or to the altars of the gods, it shamelessly plunders the feast and defiles everything by its touch. What of the fact that the tiny beast, flying into a perfumer's shop and dying by chance in an ointment box, taints all the ointment stored in it? Hence that saying of Solomon, Eccl 10:1: One of the dead flies makes the ointment of the perfumer send forth a stench. So a little folly makes a man eminent in wisdom and honour stink. Just as Paul says that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump, 1 Cor 5:6. For what is good is corrupted much more easily than what is bad is amended. Accordingly Haggai, chapter 2, verses 12 and 13, notes that an unclean thing is not consecrated by the touch of a holy thing; but, on the contrary, a holy thing is polluted by the touch of an unclean thing R2.


III, 345 Quaeritur, cur cum muscis conferantur Aegyptii in his Es. VII, 18. Sibilabit Dominus ad muscam, quae est in extremo fluminum Aegypti: et varii varia afferunt. Hieronymus, Muscas autem Aegyptios vocat propter sordes idololatriae et imbellem populum. Basilius respici putat τὸ εὐτελὲς τῶν ἀντικειμένων III, 346 δυνάμεων· μυῖα γάρ ἐστι ζῶον ἀπὸ κόπρου τὴν γένεσιν ἔχον, ὀχληρὸν τοῖς ἀν-θρώποις γένος, καὶ μυσαρὸν ὂν, καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ὀχληρὰ, καὶ ὁ θάνατος βδελυ-κτὸς, vilitatem copiarum, quae Israelitis oppositae sunt: musca enim ex stercore generatur, et genus est hominibus infestum, et abominandum, cujus vita molesta est, et mors execrabilis. At Cyrillus Aegyptios muscis comparari asserit διά τοι τὸ πλῆθος, καὶ τὸ μὴ λίαν εὔηχες τῆς φωνῆς, propter multitudinem et sermonem absonum atque inconditum. Quasi non tam sit sermo; quam muscarum susurrus. Videtur simplicissimum, ut ad multitudinem id referamus cum Chal- col. 499 daeo interprete, cujus paraphrasis sic habet: יכלי יי לעם קטרי משרית גבריא דסגיאין כרבביא וייתינון מארעא דמצרים, Clamabit Dominus ad populum ligationum exercitus virorum fortium (id est, in quo copiae virorum fortium simul junctae et conjuratae), qui multae sunt ut muscae, et adducet eos de terra Aegypti. Sed et R. Selomo hic intelligit חילות רבות כזבובים, exercitus, muscarum instar, numerosus. Et Abarbanel, המשיל אותם בזבוב לקלות מרוצתם ולרוב האספם, Confert eos cum muscis propter levitatem cursus eorum, et propter multitudinem congregationis eorum. Quorum prius ex Kimchio: posterius est ex Chaldaeo et Solomone; quod praeferendum puto, quia Aegyptus olim supra fidem fuit populosa. Ad Dianae festum Bubastim convenisse hominum septingenta millia: et urbium in Aegypto viginti millia sub Amasi culta fuisse, narrat Herodotus libri secundi capite sexagesimo, et centesimo septuagesimo septimo. In Ptolemaei Philadelphi regno, cujus maxima pars Aegyptus fuit, recenset Theocritus Idyllio decimo septimo oppidorum plus triginta tria millia. Recte igitur Aegyptii cum muscis conferuntur, quorum immensa est multitudo. Unde Plautus in Truculento, Actus primi Scena prima,

III, 345 It is asked why the Egyptians are compared with flies in these words of Isa 7:18. The Lord shall hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt; and various writers offer various answers. Jerome: But he calls the Egyptians flies because of the filth of idolatry and because they are an unwarlike people. Basil thinks the reference is to τὸ εὐτελὲς τῶν ἀντικειμένων [to euteles tōn antikeimenōn] III, 346 δυνάμεων· μυῖα γάρ ἐστι ζῶον ἀπὸ κόπρου τὴν γένεσιν ἔχον, ὀχληρὸν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις γένος, καὶ μυσαρὸν ὂν, καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ὀχληρὰ, καὶ ὁ θάνατος βδελυκτὸς [dynameōn; myia gar esti zōon apo koprou tēn genesin echon, ochlēron tois anthrōpois genos, kai mysaron on, kai hē zōē ochlēra, kai ho thanatos bdelyktos], the worthlessness of the forces that are opposed to the Israelites: for the fly is generated from dung, and is a kind hostile and abominable to men, whose life is troublesome and whose death is loathsome. But Cyril asserts that the Egyptians are compared with flies διά τοι τὸ πλῆθος, καὶ τὸ μὴ λίαν εὔηχες τῆς φωνῆς [dia toi to plēthos, kai to mē lian euēches tēs phōnēs], because of their multitude and their discordant and uncouth speech, as though it were not so much speech as the buzzing of flies. The simplest course seems to be to refer it to multitude, with the Chaldee col. 499 translator, whose paraphrase runs thus: יכלי יי לעם קטרי משרית גבריא דסגיאין כרבביא וייתינון מארעא דמצרים, The Lord shall call to the people of the bands of the army of mighty men (that is, in which forces of mighty men are joined together and sworn in league), who are many as flies, and he shall bring them from the land of Egypt. R. Selomo too understands here חילות רבות כזבובים, an army numerous like flies. And Abarbanel [=Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), commentary on the Bible]: המשיל אותם בזבוב לקלות מרוצתם ולרוב האספם, He compares them with flies because of the swiftness of their course and because of the multitude of their gathering. The former of these comes from Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], the latter from the Chaldee and Solomon; I think the latter is to be preferred, because Egypt was once populous beyond belief. Herodotus, book 2, chapters 60 and 177, relates that seven hundred thousand people assembled at Bubastis for the festival of Diana, and that twenty thousand cities in Egypt were inhabited under Amasis. In the kingdom of Ptolemy Philadelphus, of which Egypt was the greatest part, Theocritus, Idyll 17, counts more than thirty-three thousand towns. Rightly, then, are the Egyptians, whose multitude is immense, compared with flies. Hence Plautus in the Truculentus, Act 1, Scene 1:


Nam nunc leonum, et scortorum plus est fere,
Quam olim muscarum est, cum caletur maxime.

For now there are almost more pimps and harlots than there once were flies, when it is hottest.


Et Homerus, Iliad β'. versu 469. Graecorum copias in prato Scamandrio magno numero constitisse ait,

And Homer, Iliad 2, line 469, says that the forces of the Greeks stood in great numbers in the Scamandrian meadow,


Ἠΰτε μυιάων ἁδινάων ἔθνεα πολλὰ, Ut confertarum muscarum gentes plurimas.

Ἠΰτε μυιάων ἁδινάων ἔθνεα πολλὰ [Ēute myiaōn hadinaōn ethnea polla], Like the very many tribes of thronging flies.


A musca nomen habet Beel-zebub, Deus Accaronitarum, 2 Reg. I, 2. LXX. explicant μυῖαν Θεὸν Ἀκκαρὼν, muscam, Deum Accaronis. Quod sequuntur multi veterum. Ita Iosephus libri noni capite primo, Ochoziam misisse narrat πρὸς τὸν Ἀκκάρων Θεὸν μυῖαν, τοῦτο γὰρ ἦν ὄνομα τῷ θεῷ, ad Accaronis Deum, muscam, id enim erat nominis Deo. Et apud Suidam, voce Ἠλίας, scriptor vetus de eodem Ochozia; Ἐχρήσατο μυίᾳ τῶν ἐν Ἀκκάρων εἰδώλῳ, Musca usus est, Accaronitarum idolo. Quo alludens Nazianzenus Oratione quarta, III, 347 Οὐδὲ ζητήσουσι μυῖαν Θεὸν Ἀκκαρὼν, ἢ εἴ τι ταύτης ἐστὶ γελοιότερον. Neque quaerent amplius muscam, Deum Accaronis, aut si quod aliud numen est illo majus ridiculum. Nempe Graeci Patres hunc Deum putant sub muscae imagine fuisse cultum. Theodoretus in hunc locum, Τί μυσαρώτερον μυίας; ἀλλ᾽ ὅμως τὴν εἰκόνα ταύτης Θεὸν ἀνηγόρευσαν. Musca quid est odiosius? Tamen ejus imaginem Deum esse pronuntiaverunt. Et paullo post, Ἣν ζῶσαν ταῖς ῥιπίσιν ἐλαύ-νουσι, ταύτης τὸν τύπον Θεὸν προσηγόρευσαν· Quam vivam muscariis abigunt, ejus figuram Deum appellaverunt. Quos sequutus Philastrius in Catalogo Haereticorum, qui ante Christum vixerunt, Muscaccaronitas censet, qui, inquit, muscam colunt in civitate Accaron. Sed et Procopius eidem Deo, muscae, tribuit imaginem. Dubitat tamen, an fuerit daemonis nomen, aut vetulae, in divos relatae. Quod commentum refellit Hebraeum nomen בעל־זבוב , Beel-zebub, ex masculinis vocibus conflatum. Malo igitur Latinos sequi, quibus Beel-zebub non est Nominativo casu Deus musca, sed Genitivo Deus, vel Dominus muscae. Augustinus in Iohannem Tractatu primo, BEEL-ZEBUB interpretatum dicitur princeps muscarum. Hieronymus in Ecclesiasten capite decimo, Ab his muscis etiam princeps appellatus est daemoniorum BEEL-ZEBUB, qui interpretatur aut idolum muscarum, aut vir muscarum, aut habens muscas. Et in Matthaeum capite decimo, Beel-zebub idolum est Accaron, quod vocatur in Regum volumine idolum muscae. Liber nominum in Iohanne, BEEL-ZEBUB habens muscas, aut vir muscarum. Isidorus Originum libri octavi capite undecimo, BEEL-ZEBUB, col. 500 idolum fuit Accaron, quod interpretatur vir muscarum. Malim deus, aut dominus, aut princeps muscarum, ut in Augustino habetur. Nam בעל Baal, cum idoli nomen est, virum non sonat, sed deum, aut dominum. Neque ratio nominis est obscura, cum etiam Graeci deum habuerint Μυιώδην, vel Μυίαγρον, vel Ἀπόμυιον, sive is Iupiter, aut Hercules, aut alius aliquis Deus fuerit, a muscis abigendis sic appellatus (3). In quam rem diserta sunt loca veterum. Plinius III, 348 libri decimi capite vigesimo octavo, Elei Myiagron deum (invocant), muscarum multitudine pestilentiam adferente (4); quae protinus intereunt, qua litatum est illi die. Alii, quam litatum est illi deo. Et libri vigesimi noni capite sexto, Nullum animal (musca) minus docile existimatur, minorisve intellectus: eo mirabilius est, Olympio sacro certamine, nubes earum, immolato tauro deo, quem Myiodem vocant, extra territorium id abire. Pausanias in Arcadicis, ubi de nundinis Alipherarum; Ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ πανηγύρει Μυιάγρῳ προθύουσιν, ἐπευ-χόμενοί τε κατὰ τῶν ἱερείων τῷ ἥρωϊ, καὶ ἐπικαλούμενοι τὸν Μυίαγρον. Καὶ σφισι ταῦτα δράσασιν, οὐδὲν ἔτι ἀνιαρόν εἰσιν αἱ μυῖαι. In illis nundinis uni ante omnes Myiagro rem divinam faciunt, heroëmque super hostiis precati, et Myiagri nomine implorato, postquam haec praestiterunt, muscae illis non sunt amplius molestae. Et in Eliacis prioribus, Φασὶ δὲ Ἡρακλεῖ τῷ Ἀλκμήνης, θύ-οντι ἐν Ὀλυμπίᾳ, δι᾽ ὄχλου μάλιστα γενέσθαι τὰς μυίας. ἐξευρόντα οὖν αὐτὸν, ἢ καὶ ὑπ᾽ ἄλλου διδαχθέντα, Ἀπομυίῳ θῦσαι Διῒ, καὶ οὕτως ἀποτραπῆναι τὰς μυίας περὰν τοῦ Ἀλφειοῦ· Λέγονται δὲ κατὰ ταῦτα καὶ Ἠλεῖοι θύειν τῷ Ἀπομυίῳ Διῒ ἐξελαύνοντι τῆς Ἠλείας Ὀλυμπίας τὰς μυίας· Ajunt etiam, Herculi, Alcmenes filio, cum Olympiae sacrificaret, maximam muscas exhibuisse molestiam. Eum itaque vel proprio inventu, vel monitu alieno, sacra fecisse Iovi Apomyio (quasi dicat muscarum abactori) atque ita muscas trans Alpheum fuisse profligatas. Ac proinde dicuntur Elei Apomyio Iovi sacra facere, qui ex Olympia Elidis muscas abigat (5). De quo eodem ritu multa Aelianus Historiae III, 349 libri quinti capite decimo septimo, et libri undecimi capite octavo. Et Antipha- nes Comicus apud Athenaeum libri primi capite quinto. Clemens etiam in Pro- treptico, Ἀπομυίῳ Διῒ θύουσιν Ἠλεῖοι, Ῥωμαῖοι δὲ Ἀπομυίῳ Ἡρακλεῖ. Et Solinus capite primo, ubi de sacello Herculis Romae in Boario foro; Divinitus illo neque canibus, neque muscis, ingressus est. Etenim, cum viscerationem sacri- colis daret, Myiagrum deum dicitur imprecatus. Quod idem ex parte refert Plinius libri decimi capite vigesimo nono, Romae in aedem Herculis in foro Boario, nec muscae, nec canes intrant. Ut in Papho περὶ τὰ θυρώματα τὰ τῆς Ἀφροδίτης, circa fores Veneris (nisi sit legendum περὶ τὰ θυσιάσματα, circa sacrificia Veneris) musca nulla est. Ita ex Androne memorat Apollonius Mirabi- lium Historia octava. Et in Leucade e fano Apollinis Actii muscae discedunt, bovis sanguine saturatae, ut habetur in Aeliano libri undecimi Historiae capite octavo. Nec in monte Cretae, Carina, IXM. passuum ambitu muscae reperiuntur, si Plinio credimus libri vigesimi primi capite decimo quarto. Sed et in templo Dei Hierosolymis tale aliquod miraculum obtigisse, Iudaei referunt in Pirke Aboth capitis quinti sectione quinta. Verba sunt, לא נראה זבוב בבית המטבחים, Musca nulla visa est in domo mactationum. Quae si vera sunt, diabolus, ut solet, fuerit hac in parte Dei simia. Atque ut Apollo Athenis PARNO-PIUS, et Hercules in Oëta monte CORNOPION appellatus est propter pulsas locustas: et ab Erythraeis Ἰποκτόνος propter ἶπες interemptos, seu vermiculos, a quibus vites infestantur. Ita quisquis Deus muscos abigere creditur, ut Graece μυίαγρος, μυιώδης, et ἀπόμυιος· sic Hebraice BEEL-ZEBUB dictus fuerit, id col. 501 est, muscarum dominus. Qualem se prodidisse creditus est, eas a sacris suis amovendo, atque abigendo. Itaque hoc idoli illius verum nomen fuisse reor. Nec viro magno (6) assentior, qui putat, a cultoribus suis בעל זבחים Beel-zebachim, id est, Deum sacrificiorum, appellatum, quod per contemptum in בעלזבוב Beel-zebub, id est, muscae dominum, Israelitae detorserint. Nam, ut taceam, zebub et zebachim voces esse tam dissimiles, ut inter illas vix videatur quaesita fuisse allusio; nec vero esse consentaneum, ut ab oblatis victimis deus ullus nomen traxerit, cum omnibus id fuerit commune, ut victimarum oblatione colerentur: certum est, Ochoziam serio egisse, cum dixit, Ite, et consulite Beelzebub, deum Accaron, an ex hoc morbo convaliturus sim. Neque enim eum deum ludos habuerit Ochozias, quem in morbo jubebat de salute sua consuli. Itaque nomen Beel-zebub tam apud Philistaeos, quam apud Israelitas in usu III, 350 fuisse reor (7). Sed cum in Evangelio legatur Beel-zebul, cum L in fine, ac si dicatur a voce זבל zebel, quae stercus sonat, posteriores Iudaeos putaverim interpointerpolasse III, 351 nomen, ut inter stercoreos deos Beel-zebub sic rejicerent (8). Quamvis nihil sit necesse, cum in linguis illis B finale quandoque mutetur in L. Ita sinus Arabici ostium vulgo Babelmandel dicitur pro Arabico باب المندب Bab-elmandab. Et nablium, Hispanis rabel, Arabibus est رباب rebab. Pari ratione Beel-zebul dici potuit pro Beel-zebub.

From the fly Beel-zebub, the god of the Ekronites, takes his name, 2 Reg. I, 2. The LXX render μυῖαν Θεὸν Ἀκκαρὼν [myian Theon Akkarōn], the fly, the god of Ekron. Many of the ancients follow this. Thus Josephus, book 9, chapter 1, relates that Ahaziah sent πρὸς τὸν Ἀκκάρων Θεὸν μυῖαν, τοῦτο γὰρ ἦν ὄνομα τῷ θεῷ [pros ton Akkarōn Theon myian, touto gar ēn onoma tō theō], to the god of Ekron, the fly, for that was the name of the god. And in Suidas, under the word Ἠλίας [Ēlias], an ancient writer says of the same Ahaziah: Ἐχρήσατο μυίᾳ τῶν ἐν Ἀκκάρων εἰδώλῳ [Echrēsato myia tōn en Akkarōn eidōlō], He consulted the fly, the idol of the Ekronites. Alluding to this, Nazianzen in his fourth Oration says: III, 347 Οὐδὲ ζητήσουσι μυῖαν Θεὸν Ἀκκαρὼν, ἢ εἴ τι ταύτης ἐστὶ γελοιότερον [Oude zētēsousi myian Theon Akkarōn, ē ei ti tautēs esti geloioteron]. Nor will they any longer seek the fly, the god of Ekron, or any other deity more ridiculous than that. The Greek Fathers, that is, think that this god was worshipped under the image of a fly. Theodoret on this passage: Τί μυσαρώτερον μυίας; ἀλλ᾽ ὅμως τὴν εἰκόνα ταύτης Θεὸν ἀνηγόρευσαν [Ti mysarōteron myias? all᾽ homōs tēn eikona tautēs Theon anēgoreusan]. What is more loathsome than a fly? Yet they declared its image to be a god. And a little later: Ἣν ζῶσαν ταῖς ῥιπίσιν ἐλαύνουσι, ταύτης τὸν τύπον Θεὸν προσηγόρευσαν [Hēn zōsan tais rhipisin elaunousi, tautēs ton typon Theon prosēgoreusan]· The creature which, when alive, they drive away with fly-whisks, its figure they called a god. Following them, Philastrius, in his Catalogue of the heretics who lived before Christ, lists the Muscaccaronites, who, he says, worship a fly in the city of Ekron. Procopius too ascribes to this same god the image of a fly. Yet he doubts whether it was the name of a demon, or of an old woman raised to the gods. This fancy is refuted by the Hebrew name בעל־זבוב, Beel-zebub, which is compounded of masculine words. I prefer therefore to follow the Latins, for whom Beel-zebub is not, in the nominative, the god fly, but, with a genitive, the god or lord of the fly. Augustine, Tractate 1 on John: BEEL-ZEBUB is said to be interpreted prince of flies. Jerome on Ecclesiastes, chapter 10: From these flies the prince of demons is also called BEEL-ZEBUB, which is interpreted either idol of flies, or man of flies, or having flies. And on Matthew, chapter 10: Beel-zebub is the idol of Ekron, which in the book of Kings is called the idol of the fly. The Book of Names, on John: BEEL-ZEBUB, having flies, or man of flies. Isidore, Origins, book 8, chapter 11: BEEL-ZEBUB col. 500 was the idol of Ekron, which is interpreted man of flies. I would rather say god, or lord, or prince of flies, as in Augustine. For בעל Baal, when it is the name of an idol, does not mean man, but god or lord. Nor is the reason for the name obscure, since the Greeks too had a god Μυιώδης [Myiōdēs], or Μυίαγρος [Myiagros], or Ἀπόμυιος [Apomyios], whether he was Jupiter, or Hercules, or some other god, so called from driving away flies R3. On this matter the passages of the ancients are explicit. Pliny III, 348, book 10, chapter 28: The Eleans (invoke) the god Myiagrus when a multitude of flies brings pestilence R4; and they die at once, on the day on which a sacrifice has been offered to him. Others read: once a sacrifice has been offered to that god. And book 29, chapter 6: No animal (the fly) is thought less teachable or of less understanding; all the more wonderful is it that at the sacred Olympic games, when a bull has been sacrificed to the god whom they call Myiodes, clouds of them depart out of that territory. Pausanias in the Arcadica, on the festival of the Aliphereans: Ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ πανηγύρει Μυιάγρῳ προθύουσιν, ἐπευχόμενοί τε κατὰ τῶν ἱερείων τῷ ἥρωϊ, καὶ ἐπικαλούμενοι τὸν Μυίαγρον. Καὶ σφισι ταῦτα δράσασιν, οὐδὲν ἔτι ἀνιαρόν εἰσιν αἱ μυῖαι [En tautē tē panēgyrei Myiagrō prothyousin, epeuchomenoi te kata tōn hiereiōn tō hērōi, kai epikaloumenoi ton Myiagron. Kai sphisi tauta drasasin, ouden eti aniaron eisin hai myiai]. At that festival they first of all offer sacrifice to Myiagrus; and when they have prayed to the hero over the victims and invoked the name of Myiagrus, after doing this the flies no longer trouble them. And in the first book of the Eliaca: Φασὶ δὲ Ἡρακλεῖ τῷ Ἀλκμήνης, θύοντι ἐν Ὀλυμπίᾳ, δι᾽ ὄχλου μάλιστα γενέσθαι τὰς μυίας. ἐξευρόντα οὖν αὐτὸν, ἢ καὶ ὑπ᾽ ἄλλου διδαχθέντα, Ἀπομυίῳ θῦσαι Διῒ, καὶ οὕτως ἀποτραπῆναι τὰς μυίας περὰν τοῦ Ἀλφειοῦ· Λέγονται δὲ κατὰ ταῦτα καὶ Ἠλεῖοι θύειν τῷ Ἀπομυίῳ Διῒ ἐξελαύνοντι τῆς Ἠλείας Ὀλυμπίας τὰς μυίας [Phasi de Hēraklei tō Alkmēnēs, thyonti en Olympia, di᾽ ochlou malista genesthai tas myias. exeuronta oun auton, ē kai hyp᾽ allou didachthenta, Apomyiō thysai Dii, kai houtōs apotrapēnai tas myias peran tou Alpheiou; Legontai de kata tauta kai Ēleioi thyein tō Apomyiō Dii exelaunonti tēs Ēleias Olympias tas myias]· They also say that when Hercules, son of Alcmene, was sacrificing at Olympia, the flies caused him very great trouble. So, either by his own discovery or on another's advice, he sacrificed to Jupiter Apomyius (as if to say the driver-away of flies), and thus the flies were routed across the Alpheus. And accordingly the Eleans are said to sacrifice to Jupiter Apomyius, who drives the flies away from Olympia in Elis R5. Of this same rite Aelian says much in the History III, 349, book 5, chapter 17, and book 11, chapter 8. So does Antiphanes the comic poet in Athenaeus, book 1, chapter 5. Clement too in the Protrepticus: Ἀπομυίῳ Διῒ θύουσιν Ἠλεῖοι, Ῥωμαῖοι δὲ Ἀπομυίῳ Ἡρακλεῖ [Apomyiō Dii thyousin Ēleioi, Rhōmaioi de Apomyiō Hēraklei]. And Solinus, chapter 1, on the shrine of Hercules at Rome in the Forum Boarium: By divine power it is entered neither by dogs nor by flies. For when he was giving a distribution of sacrificial meat to the worshippers, he is said to have invoked the god Myiagrus. Pliny reports the same in part, book 10, chapter 29: At Rome neither flies nor dogs enter the temple of Hercules in the Forum Boarium. So too at Paphos, περὶ τὰ θυρώματα τὰ τῆς Ἀφροδίτης [peri ta thyrōmata ta tēs Aphroditēs], around the doors of Venus (unless we should read περὶ τὰ θυσιάσματα [peri ta thysiasmata], around the sacrifices of Venus), there is no fly. So Apollonius records from Andron in the History of Marvels, 8. And at Leucas the flies, sated with ox blood, depart from the shrine of Apollo Actius, as is found in Aelian, History, book 11, chapter 8. Nor are flies found on the mountain of Crete, Carina, nine miles in circuit, if we believe Pliny, book 21, chapter 14. And the Jews report that some such miracle also occurred in the temple of God at Jerusalem, in Pirke Aboth, chapter 5, section 5. The words are לא נראה זבוב בבית המטבחים, No fly was seen in the house of slaughtering. If this is true, the devil, as usual, will have been God's ape in this respect. And just as Apollo at Athens was called PARNOPIUS, and Hercules on Mount Oeta CORNOPION, because of locusts driven away; and by the Erythraeans Ἰποκτόνος [Ipoktonos], because of the ἶπες [ipes] he killed, that is, the small worms by which vines are infested: so whatever god was believed to drive away flies, as in Greek μυίαγρος [myiagros], μυιώδης [myiōdēs] and ἀπόμυιος [apomyios], will in Hebrew have been called BEEL-ZEBUB, that col. 501 is, lord of flies. Such he was believed to have shown himself, by removing and driving them away from his sacrifices. I therefore think this was the true name of that idol. Nor do I agree with a great man R6, who thinks that he was called by his worshippers בעל זבחים Beel-zebachim, that is, god of sacrifices, which the Israelites in contempt twisted into בעלזבוב Beel-zebub, that is, lord of the fly. For, to say nothing of the fact that zebub and zebachim are words so unlike that a play on them seems hardly to have been sought; nor that it is likely that any god took his name from the victims offered, since it was common to all to be worshipped by the offering of victims: it is certain that Ahaziah was in earnest when he said, Go, and inquire of Beel-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I shall recover from this sickness. For Ahaziah will not have mocked the god whom, in his sickness, he ordered to be consulted about his recovery. I therefore think the name Beel-zebub was in use among the Philistines as much as among the Israelites III, 350 R7. But since in the Gospel we read Beel-zebul, with L at the end, as if derived from the word זבל zebel, which means dung, I should think the later Jews altered III, 351 the name, so as to relegate Beel-zebub in this way among the dung gods R8. Yet this is not necessary, since in those languages a final B is sometimes changed into L. Thus the mouth of the Arabian gulf is commonly called Babelmandel for the Arabic باب المندب [Bāb al-Mandab] Bab-elmandab. And the nablium, in Spanish rabel, is in Arabic رباب [rabāb] rebab. In the same way Beel-zebul could be said for Beel-zebub.


Difficilior est quaestio, cur Matth. XII, 24. et Luc. XI, 15. Pharisaei sive Beel-zebub, sive Beel-zebul, daemonum principem esse voluerint, qui Hebraeorum aliis אשמודי, Asmodaeus. Neque habeo, quod respondeam, nisi quod Philistaeorum urbs, Accaron, etiam scribitur Acharon ab Hieronymo, et aliis: quo cum Acheron proxime alludat, potuit ab ignaris deus-Acharon cum III, 352 Acherontis deo, id est, cum Plutone, confundi, quem praefecit inferis gentilium theologia. Notum enim est, Hebraeos posteriores non pauca suae linguae vocabula e Graeca deduxisse. Quale est, quod τὰ Ἱεροσόλυμα Iosephus ita dici vult propter τὸ ἱερὸν, id est, templum, ibi conditum. Et torrentem Iabok is ipse Iobacchum vocat: tanquam ab Iobaccho, deo, appellatum. Idem iis fuit animus, qui, pro torrentibus Kedron et Kison, χει-μάῤῥους τῶν κέδρων, et τῶν κισσῶν, primi dixerunt, ac si a cedris et picis sic vocarentur. Et Scitta, urbs, Scythopolis dicta est, tanquam a Scythis. Et AR Moabitarum, Ἀρεόπολις, quasi Martis urbs. Et nomen Taphnes mutatum in Daphnes, ut vocari crederetur παρὰ τῶν ἐκεῖ πολλῶν φυομένων δαφνῶν, a multa lauru ibi consita. Denique pari de causa ex Philistaeis facti Ἀλλόφυλοι, ex Pibeseth Βούβαστος, ex Gibliis Byblii, ex Horaeis Heroum urbs, ex Iabneel Ἰάμνια, quasi hoc nomen habuerit, ὅτι Ἰάμνους ἐκά-λουν τοὺς καθύγρους, καὶ τεθηλότας τόπους, quia locos humidos et virentes ἰάμνους vocabant. Ita Stephanus. Et Ptolemais, pro עכו Accho, Ἄκη dicta est, tanquam ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀκεῖν, quia ibi sanatus Hercules.

A more difficult question is why, in Matth. XII, 24. and Luc. XI, 15., the Pharisees held that Beel-zebub, or Beel-zebul, was the prince of demons, whom other Hebrews call אשמודי, Asmodaeus. I have no answer to give, except that the Philistine city Accaron [Ekron] is also written Acharon by Jerome and others. Since this closely echoes Acheron, the god of Acharon could have been confused by the ignorant with the god of III, 352 Acheron, that is, with Pluto, whom the theology of the gentiles set over the underworld. For it is well known that the later Hebrews derived not a few words of their own language from the Greek. An example is that Josephus holds that τὰ Ἱεροσόλυμα [ta Hierosolyma] is so called because of τὸ ἱερὸν [to hieron], that is, the temple built there. And the same author calls the torrent Iabok Iobacchus, as though it were named after the god Iobacchus. The same was the intention of those who first said, for the torrents Kedron and Kison, χειμάῤῥους τῶν κέδρων [cheimarrhous tōn kedrōn] and τῶν κισσῶν [tōn kissōn], as if they were so called from cedars and pitch-pines. And the city Scitta was called Scythopolis, as though from the Scythians. And AR of the Moabites became Ἀρεόπολις [Areopolis], as if the city of Mars. And the name Taphnes was changed into Daphnes, so that it might be believed to be called παρὰ τῶν ἐκεῖ πολλῶν φυομένων δαφνῶν [para tōn ekei pollōn phyomenōn daphnōn], from the many laurels planted there. Finally, for the same reason, from the Philistines were made Ἀλλόφυλοι [Allophyloi], from Pibeseth Βούβαστος [Boubastos], from the Giblites the Byblians, from the Horites the City of Heroes, from Iabneel Ἰάμνια [Iamnia], as if it had this name ὅτι Ἰάμνους ἐκάλουν τοὺς καθύγρους, καὶ τεθηλότας τόπους [hoti Iamnous ekaloun tous kathygrous, kai tethēlotas topous], because they called moist and verdant places ἰάμνους [iamnous]. So Stephanus. And Ptolemais, for עכו Accho, was called Ἄκη [Akē], as though from τοῦ ἀκεῖν [tou akein], because Hercules was healed there.

III, 343 Quod argumentum quam sit incertum, quisque intelliget ipse. R1 Rosenmüller, III, 342 Yet since the species of flies and gnats are innumerable, it is not clear which in particular ذباب [dhubāb], זבוב designates. Perhaps it is a general name, comprehending all those insects which the Latins include under the name of muscae [flies] and culices [gnats]: for example, the gnat of Egypt, with white joints, the size of the common gnat, of a dusky grey colour; the fly of the Buphthalmum, common in Egypt, smaller in size than the common bee, with four wings, short, club-shaped antennae stretched forward and bearing a bristle on the back, an oblong, convex, shining, dark green thorax, and six legs on the thorax. These two insects were carefully described by Hasselquist [=Fredrik Hasselquist, Iter Palaestinum (1757)], in his Travels p. 470. 471. German trans. Further, the troublesome gnat of Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)] (in Descript. Animall. p. 85), in size and appearance like the common piping gnat, hairy over the whole body and the legs, with bristle-like antennae and dusky wings, which is found in immense numbers at Rosetta, Cairo and Alexandria, is a nuisance to sleepers at night, and can scarcely be kept off except by a well-closed curtain. Finally, the black fly also seems to belong here, with bristle-like antennae and a thorax with yellow spots, which Forsskål briefly lists among the insects of Arabia observed by him, p. 24. Eugène Roger, in his Description of Palestine, written in French (La Terre Sainte, Paris, 1664, 4to), p. 84, mentions small black flies called Bargaches (the sound of the word is to be rendered with French pronunciation, for it is the Arabic بَرْغَشْ [barghash], the same as بَعُوضْ [baʿūḍ], gnat, or a certain species of gnats, in Golius [=Jacobus Golius, Lexicon Arabico-Latinum (1653)] p. 259), whose swarms, borne in like dense clouds, attacked the camp of the Arabs with such violence that men and animals were almost deprived of the ability to breathe. And Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde], in the Vermischte Sammlungen, fasc. 4, ch. 9, p. 81 ff., thought it credible that the same species of flies is denoted by the Hebrew זבוב, chiefly on account of the passage Isa 7:18, where the incredible multitude of Egyptians who would invade the territory of Israel is set forth under the image of flies called זבוב. But in fasc. 6, ch. 9, p. 79, he himself changed his opinion, understanding it of that species of gadfly or oestrus which Bruce [=James Bruce, Travels to discover the source of the Nile (1790)], who often saw it in Ethiopia, described at length in his Travels vol. 5, p. 190 ff. of Volkmann's German trans., where you will also find a picture of this insect, plate 39. The Ethiopians call it Tsaltsalia. This species of oestrus was unknown to Linnaeus. But Gmelin [=J. F. Gmelin, 13th edition of Linnaeus, Systema naturae (1788–93)], in the Notes on Bruce's Travels edited by Hassencamp, p. 31, thinks it should be designated by the name oestrus fusco-pilosus, alis immaculatis. Compare, however, what Blumenbach remarked on Bruce's description of this insect, vol. 5, p. 291 f. German trans. Oedmann, however, considers that oestrus to be the זבוב of the Hebrews, moved by no other reason than that he thinks it more suitable to the passage Esaiah VII, 14 than that black fly which Roger described loc. cit. III, 343 How uncertain this argument is, everyone will see for himself. With the same right, and perhaps greater, he could have referred here some species of the flies which we mentioned above from Hasselquist and Forsskål. It will be safest to regard זבוב, like the Arabic ذباب [dhubāb] and the Syriac ܕܒܒܐ [דבבא]?, as a general name for various species of flies and gnats.


(2) Rosenmüller, III, 344 Mirus tamen interpretum dissensus est in his verbis explicandis. Ut a veteribus initium faciamus, Alexandrini hunc versum ita vertunt: Μυιαι θανατουσαι σαπρι-ουσι σκευασιαν ἐλαιου ἡδύσματος· τίμιον ὀλίγον σοφιας ὑπὲρ δόξαν ἀφροσυνης μεγαλην. Omittunt Hebraeum יביע, quod non intellexisse videntur, ut nec totius similitudinis sensum sunt assequuti. Attamen eos sequitur Vulgatus, qui reddit: Muscae morientes perdunt suavitatem unguenti: pretiosior est sapientia et gloria, parva et ad tempus stultitia: atque inter recentiores ZIRKEL, qui prius commatis membrum (זבובי-רקח) ad caput praecedens referendum existimat, ut verba יקר — מעט novam sententiam formarent, eum sensum exhibentem, quem Alexandrini exprimunt: parum sapientiae pretiosius est stultitiae gloria: quem tamen sensum non nisi mutato textu masorethico III, 345 elicere potuit: vocabulum scilicet מעט ante מחכמה ponit, praeeuntibus Alexandrinis, qui ὀλίγον σοφίας habent, atque hoc מעט מחכמה, ab ipso formatum, ad verbum vertendum censet: ὀλίγον ἀπὸ σο-φίας, quod sensu idem esse pronuntiat, at-que ὀλίγον σοφίας. Quod interpretationis artificium vix alii probetur. Ad caput praecedens priorem commatis particulam refert etiam I. E. CHR. SCHMIDT, sed alterum membrum, יקר מחכמה מכבוד סכלות מעט, ita vertit: praestantior sapientia atque honore est stultitia et inopia (Besser, als Weisheit und Ansehn, ist — Thorheit und Dürftigkeit), cujus παραδόξου sensum esse dicit hunc: praestare, egenum esse, et pro stulto haberi, quam sapientiae speciem prae se ferre, ut admiratio hominibus moveatur. Cui interpretationi praecipue obstat, quod מעט nusquam egestatis notione occurrit. In alia omnia abit DOEDER-LEIN, qui in Scholiis in Libros poeticos V. T. ad h. l., insolita sane, ut ipse inquit, et audaci interpretatione, locum nostrum ita vertit: Lethales exsiccat fluxus, qui fontes aperit olei unguentarii: respondere sibi putat voces יבאיש et יביע per modum antitheti; יביע dici de aqua erumpente e fontibus, ut Prov. XV, 2. 28., באש autem significatione convenire cum יבש, arere, in quarta conjugatione arefacere; זבובים esse fluxus, a זוב fluere, et זבובי מות fluxus lethales, vulnera et ulcera, ut כלי מות arma mortifera, עץ מות lignum lethiferum; his esse oppositum שמן רוקח oleum unguentarii, salubre et recreans: hinc sensum effici hunc: quemadmodum fluxus lethiferos, haemorragias et similia, exsiccat, qui oleum unguentarium, cujus magna vis laudatur in vulneribus, effundit; ita vir sapiens, qui verbis mollibus utitur, multas noxas mitigat et tollit. Verba vero ultima vertit: decus per sapientiam praestat honore, qui stultitia, vel minima, acquiritur. Vides, et in hac interpretatione vocibus novas et insolitas notiones adfingi, atque omnino totam orationis seriem mirum in modum contorqueri. Quare simplicissimum erit, verba nostra ea ratione interpretari, qua supra Bochartus; sive Syrum, veterum interpretum doctissimum, sequi, qui versum primum ita vertit: ܐܝܟ ܕܒ̈ܒܐ ܕܡܝܬܝܢ ܡܣܪܚܝܢ ܠܡܐܢܐ ܕܡܫܚܐ ܒܣܝܡܐ. ܝܩܝܪܐ ܗܝ ܡܢ ܚܟܡܬܐ ܘܡܢ ܣܘܓܐܐ ܕܬܫܒܘܚܬܐ ܣܟܠܘܬܐ ܩܠܝܠܐ Sicut muscae mortuae foetidum reddunt vas unguenti suavis, praeponderat sapientiae et gloriae multae modica stultitia. Omisit tamen verbum יביע. Sed nulla difficultas erit, si utrumque יבאיש יביע ita conjungas, ut alterum, יביע, adverbialiter vertas, foetere facit eructanter, sive indesinenter, i. e. facit, ut foetor, instar aquae scaturientis, ebulliat, sive eructet: de quo Hebraismo videndus est GLASSIUS in Philol. S. pag. 272. ed. Dath. Similiter A. SCHULTENSIUS in Commentar. ad Prov. XIII, 5. pag. 122. verba nostra vertit: Musca mortua effervescere facit cum foetore, ebullire balsamum seplasiarii. Sub זבובי מות tamen ego intellexerim muscas mortiferas, sive noxias, sicut כלי מות, Ps. VII, 14. sunt arma lethifera.

R2 Rosenmüller, III, 344 There is, however, a remarkable disagreement among interpreters in explaining these words. To begin with the ancients, the Alexandrians render this verse as follows: Μυιαι θανατουσαι σαπριουσι σκευασιαν ἐλαιου ἡδύσματος· τίμιον ὀλίγον σοφιας ὑπὲρ δόξαν ἀφροσυνης μεγαλην [Myiai thanatousai sapriousi skeuasian elaiou hēdysmatos; timion oligon sophias hyper doxan aphrosynēs megalēn]. They omit the Hebrew יביע, which they seem not to have understood, just as they did not grasp the sense of the whole simile. Yet the Vulgate translator follows them, rendering: "Dying flies spoil the sweetness of the ointment: wisdom and glory are more precious than a little and short-lived folly". Among the more recent interpreters ZIRKEL follows them too. He thinks that the first member of the verse (זבובי-רקח) should be referred to the preceding chapter, so that the words יקר — מעט form a new sentence, yielding the sense the Alexandrians express: a little wisdom is more precious than the glory of folly. Yet he could draw out this sense only by altering the Masoretic text III, 345: he places the word מעט before מחכמה, following the Alexandrians, who have ὀλίγον σοφίας [oligon sophias], and holds that this מעט מחכמה, which he himself formed, should be rendered word for word ὀλίγον ἀπὸ σοφίας [oligon apo sophias], which he declares to be the same in sense as ὀλίγον σοφίας [oligon sophias]. This interpretive device is hardly likely to win anyone else's approval. I. E. CHR. SCHMIDT also refers the first part of the verse to the preceding chapter, but renders the other member, יקר מחכמה מכבוד סכלות מעט, thus: more excellent than wisdom and honour is folly and poverty (Besser, als Weisheit und Ansehn, ist — Thorheit und Dürftigkeit). He says the sense of this paradox [παραδόξου (paradoxou)] is that it is better to be needy and to be thought a fool than to put on a show of wisdom in order to excite people's admiration. The chief objection to this interpretation is that מעט nowhere occurs with the meaning poverty. DOEDERLEIN departs from all of these. In his Scholia in Libros poeticos V. T. on this passage, with an interpretation that is certainly unusual and, as he himself says, bold, he renders our passage: He dries up deadly fluxes who opens springs of the perfumer's oil. He thinks the words יבאיש and יביע correspond to each other by way of antithesis: יביע is said of water bursting forth from springs, as in Prov 15:2 28., while באש agrees in meaning with יבש, to be dry, in the fourth conjugation to make dry; זבובים are fluxes, from זוב to flow, and זבובי מות are deadly fluxes, wounds and ulcers, as כלי מות are deadly weapons and עץ מות a death-bringing tree. Opposed to these is שמן רוקח, the perfumer's oil, wholesome and refreshing. Hence the sense results: as he who pours out the perfumer's oil, whose great power in wounds is praised, dries up deadly fluxes, haemorrhages and the like, so a wise man who uses gentle words soothes and removes many harms. The last words he renders: glory through wisdom surpasses honour acquired by folly, even the least. You see that in this interpretation too new and unusual meanings are attached to the words, and the whole course of the discourse is altogether twisted in an extraordinary way. It will therefore be simplest to interpret our words in the way Bochart did above, or to follow the Syriac translator, the most learned of the ancient interpreters, who renders the first verse thus: ܐܝܟ ܕܒ̈ܒܐ ܕܡܝܬܝܢ ܡܣܪܚܝܢ ܠܡܐܢܐ ܕܡܫܚܐ ܒܣܝܡܐ [איך דבבא דמיתין מסרחין למאנא דמשחא בסימא]. ܝܩܝܪܐ ܗܝ ܡܢ ܚܟܡܬܐ ܘܡܢ ܣܘܓܐܐ ܕܬܫܒܘܚܬܐ ܣܟܠܘܬܐ ܩܠܝܠܐ [יקירא הי מן חכמתא ומן סוגאא דתשבוחתא סכלותא קלילא] As dead flies make a vessel of sweet ointment stink, a little folly outweighs wisdom and much glory. He did, however, omit the verb יביע. But there will be no difficulty if you join the two, יבאיש יביע, so as to render the second, יביע, adverbially: makes it stink, belching forth, or ceaselessly, i.e. makes the stench bubble up or belch forth like gushing water. On this Hebraism see GLASSIUS, Philol. S. p. 272, ed. Dath. Similarly A. Schultens [=Albert Schultens, Liber Jobi (1737)], in Commentar. ad Prov. [=Albert Schultens, Commentarius in Proverbia Salomonis (1748)] XIII, 5. p. 122, renders our words: A dead fly makes the perfumer's balsam ferment with a stench and bubble up. By זבובי מות, however, I would understand deadly flies, or harmful ones, just as כלי מות, Ps 7:14 are deadly weapons.

The beasts left in the field are consumed by the flies, and only the bones are left. The Jesuits saw this; they were at first amazed III, 348 when the Ethiopians bade them flee, adding that the flies were coming; yet they fled, and afterwards recognized from the bones of the animals what a plague they had escaped. I would not vouch for all of this, for it may have been exaggerated; but that Ludolf related it I know on sure testimony, that of my father, who spent some months as a guest at the house and table of Job Ludolf.“ Thus Michaelis [=J. Namque et morientium muscarum multitudo foetore inficere aëra potest; et cibos obsidentes atque inquinantes, febrium putridarum fieri at-que dysenteriarum caussa possunt. R4 Rosenmüller, III, 348 „How the flies brought pestilence, although Pliny does not record it, is nevertheless easy to conjecture. For the multitude of dying flies can infect the air with stench; and by settling on food and fouling it they can become the cause of putrid fevers and dysenteries. Thus DIO CASSIUS, book 68, §. 31 (p. 1145 of Reimarus's edition), reports that Trajan was forced to raise the siege of the city of the Agareni because dense swarms of flies settled on the food and filled everything with nausea. He is silent, indeed, about diseases arising from this; but the mere nuisance of flies would hardly, it seems, make a man like Trajan raise a siege and abandon an expedition. Dio's words are these: καὶ ὁπότε ἂν δειπνοιεν, μυιαι τοις βρωμασι καὶ τοις ποιμασι προσιζάνουσαι, δυσχερειας ἅπαντα ἐνεπίμπλων [kai hopote an deipnoien, myiai tois brōmasi kai tois poimasi prosizanousai, dyschereias hapanta enepimplōn].“ Thus Michaelis in the passage cited, note 17; he, moreover, takes the Myiagros worshipped as a god not for an idol but for a bird that feeds on flies, since it is mentioned among other birds held to be gods because they give help against plagues.

Is Phoenicum בעל זבוב eundem esse putat cum Graecorum Plutone, hac maxime ratione motus, quod Matth. XII, 24. et Luc. XI, 15. Βεελζεβουλ sive Βεελζεβουβ vocatur ἀρχων δαιμονιων, daemonum princeps, talem autem fuisse Plutonem, quippe qui a Porphyrio apud EUSEBIUM in Praeparat. Evangel. L. IV. Cap. XXIII. ἀρχων δαιμονων appelletur, a CLEMENTE ALEXANDRINO in Protrept. ad Gentes pag. 31. μεγαλοδαιμων, atque a Graecis Romanisque poetis βασιλευς ἐνερων, rex inferorum. Deinde Beelzebubo, utpote daemonum principi, tribui in evangeliis ingentem in daemones potestatem; eandem vero potestatem adscribi a gentilibus Plutoni, daemonum praefecto. Et quemadmodum Plutoni, tanquam mortis domino, sub cujus imperio essent Parcae, quarum arbitrio vitae mortalium tempus permissum, commendare solerent salutem suam et victimas vovere solerent; ita Achasum 2 Reg. I, 2. Beelzebubum de valetudine et vita sciscitatum misisse. Denique convenire etiam nominis Hebraei sive Phoenicii, בעל זבוב significationem: זבוב enim, quod proprie insecta quaecunque noxia denotet, apud scriptores Talmudicos saepe usurpari pro daemonibus, veluti in מדרש ילקוט שמעני, Midrasch Ialkut Simeoni Part. II. fol. 14. col. 1. et part. III. fol. 111. col. 3. זבובין esse malos daemones, hinc בעל זבוב in Evangeliis recte explicari ἀρχων δαιμονιων. Sed tota haec Millii sententia III, 351 entia magis ingeniosa atque artificiosa videtur, quam vera. — NOLDIO in Annotatt. et Vindicc. ad Concordantt. Particularr. not. 636. p. 802. ed. Tymp. Βεελζε-βουβ in N. T. non est idem, quod בעל זבוב, Accaronitarum Deus, verum Syriacum ܒܥܠܕܒܒܐ ܒܥܠ ܕܒܒܐ, hostis, inimicus, seu διαβολος, Σατανᾶς, quae sententia et placuit STORRIO, qui in Dissertat. de sensu historico p. 38. Iesum a Iudaeis eo nomine appellatum censet, quod hostem religionis patriae eum putarent, coll. Ioh. VII, 12. 47. VIII, 48. IX, 28. Cui sententiae praecipue obstat, quod lectio genuina in N. T. non est Βεελζεβουβ, ut Vulgata, ab Hieronymo mutata, cum Syro vetere habet, verum Βεελζεβουλ, quae lectio est constans omnium, qui hucusque consulti sunt, codicum graecorum, expressa quoque a patribus Graecis, e. g. Theophylacto et versionibus, antiquis latinis ante Hieronymum, Saxonica, Gothica, Coptica, Syriaca recentiore, Russica, atque utraque Arabica, in Polyglottis, et ab Erpenio edita.

R7 Rosenmüller, III, 350 The same view was also favoured by Vossius, book 2, de Idololatria, ch. 4, and by Grotius on Matt 10:25; against them, however, several objections were raised by Selden, de Diis Syris, Syntagma 2, ch. 6, by Clericus in his Commentar. ad 2 Reg. I, 2., and by Jurieu in his Histor. Dogmatum et Cultuum vol. 4, tract. 4, ch. 3, p. 628 ff. — Drusius, in Matth. XII, 24., thinks that בעל זבוב, the god of flies, was so called from a resemblance he bore to a fly: For among the ancients, he adds, it was the custom to carve the statues of the gods in a form that represented a man in the body, but some animal in the head and face, say a bird, or a lion, or a fly; or conversely, it had a human face and represented some animal in the rest of the body; and he confirms this by the testimony of Porphyry from the book περι των ἐμψυχων ἀποχης [peri tōn empsychōn apochēs]. But this rests on mere conjecture, and a very uncertain one. — Simonis, in his Onomasticon Vet. Testam. p. 46, interprets זבוב as wandering, i.e. a crowd of men wandering hither and thither (compare Arabic ذبّ [dhabba], he wandered about without fixed abode), so that בעל זבוב would be the lord of wandering, i.e. the god of the Philistines as exiles, since they named almost all their things from exile and wandering, such as גרר, פלשת, אשדוד, עקרון etc. Nor is this interpretation of the word בעל זבוב wholly displeasing to J. D. Michaelis in the Supplemm. ad Lexx. [=J. D. Michaelis, Supplementa ad lexica Hebraica] Hebrr. vol. 1, p. 203, yet in such a way that he thinks בעל זבוב was a surname of Hercules, a deity of the Phoenicians, the same as Horace's wandering Hercules, because he had travelled through the whole world. — Joh. Alberti, in his Glossae N. T. p. 30, holds that בעל זבוב denotes καταπινοντα μυιας [katapinonta myias], swallowing flies, and that זבוב and בעל, which the Alexandrians rendered καταπινειν [katapinein] at Iesaj. XVI, 8., stands by metathesis of letters for בלע, he swallowed. Jac. Basnage, in his Antiqq. Iudaicc. vol. 1, believed that the God of hosts and of arms is designated by this name, because the Phoenicians could easily have turned the Hebrew צבאת into זבוב. — A new view was proposed by D. Mill in the dissertation de Beelzebub et Miphlezet, which is the sixth of his Dissertationes selectae, Utrecht 1724. He thinks the Phoenician בעל זבוב is the same as the Pluto of the Greeks, moved chiefly by this reason: that at Matt 12:24 and Luke 11:15 Βεελζεβουλ [Beelzeboul] or Βεελζεβουβ [Beelzeboub] is called ἀρχων δαιμονιων [archōn daimoniōn], prince of demons, and that such was Pluto, since he is called ἀρχων δαιμονων [archōn daimonōn] by Porphyry in Eusebius, Praeparat. Evangel. book 4, ch. 23, μεγαλοδαιμων [megalodaimōn] by Clement of Alexandria in the Protrept. ad Gentes p. 31, and βασιλευς ἐνερων [basileus enerōn], king of the underworld, by the Greek and Roman poets. Next, that to Beelzebub, as prince of demons, an immense power over demons is ascribed in the Gospels, and the same power is ascribed by the gentiles to Pluto, the ruler of demons. And just as people were wont to commend their welfare to Pluto, as lord of death, under whose rule were the Parcae, to whose decision the span of mortals' life was entrusted, and to vow victims to him, so Ahaziah, 2 Reg. I, 2., sent to inquire of Beelzebub about his health and life. Finally, that the meaning of the Hebrew or Phoenician name בעל זבוב also fits: for זבוב, which properly denotes any harmful insects, is often used by the Talmudic writers for demons; for instance in מדרש ילקוט שמעני, Midrasch Ialkut Simeoni section 2, fol. 14, col. 1, and section 3, fol. 111, col. 3, זבובין are evil demons; hence בעל זבוב is rightly explained in the Gospels as ἀρχων δαιμονιων [archōn daimoniōn]. But this whole view of Mill III, 351 seems more ingenious and contrived than true. — For Noldius, in the Notes and Vindicc. ad Concordantt. Particularr. note 636, p. 802, Tympe's edition, Βεελζεβουβ [Beelzeboub] in the N. T. is not the same as בעל זבוב, the god of the Ekronites, but the Syriac ܒܥܠܕܒܒܐ ܒܥܠ ܕܒܒܐ [בעלדבבא בעל דבבא], adversary, enemy, or διαβολος [diabolos], Σατανᾶς [Satanas]; this view also pleased Storr, who in his Dissertat. de sensu historico p. 38 holds that Jesus was called by this name by the Jews because they considered him an enemy of the ancestral religion, compare John 7:12 47. VIII, 48. IX, 28. The chief obstacle to this view is that the genuine reading in the N. T. is not Βεελζεβουβ [Beelzeboub], as the Vulgate, altered by Jerome, has together with the Old Syriac, but Βεελζεβουλ [Beelzeboul]; this reading is constant in all the Greek codices consulted so far, and is also rendered by the Greek fathers, e.g. Theophylact, and by the versions: the Old Latin before Jerome, the Saxon, Gothic, Coptic, the later Syriac, the Russian, and both Arabic ones, that in the Polyglots and that edited by Erpenius.


(8) Rosenmüller, III, 351 Apud Iudaeos seriores pro religione fere habitum fuisse, idolis atque idolorum cultui indere nomina probrosa, inter quae commune fuerit זבול, stercus, ex scriptoribus Talmudicis probavit LIGHTFOOT in Horis Hebraicis ad Matth. XII, 25. Sed MICHAELIS in Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. P. I. pag. 205. et in Notis ad version. vernacul. Matth. X, 25. Βεελζεβουλ, quod in N. T. legitur, diversum plane censet a בעל זבוב, deo Accaronitarum, neque ex eo formatum, sed explicandum ex astrologia iudiciaria. „Haec“, inquit, „coelum in XII domos dividit, cuique domui unum ex planetis praeficiens, qui dominus domus vocabulo illius artis vocatur. זבול est habitatio, maxime autem siderum, proprie ergo בעל זבול planeta, dominus domus coelestis, ut, Venus domus virginis: hi autem planetae, cum ab ethnicis, astrologiam intime cum cultu vanorum numinum conjungentibus, dii, a Iudaeis dii gentium mali daemones haberentur, quid magis in promptu, quam principem daemonum, forte non unum omnium, sed tamen primarium alicujus ordinis, et reliquis praevalentem, dominum domus coelestis vocare? Iam et egregie lucebunt verba Christi, habebuntque aliquid allusionis et acuminis, εἰ τον οἰκοδεσπότην (רב הבית, vel, ut est in evangelio Hebraico, בעל הבית) Βεελζε-βουλ (בעל זבול) ἐκάλεσαν.“ Quae sententia nec mihi displiceret, modo Michaelis exemplis probasset, usurpari vocem זבול in astrologia ea significatione, quam ipse ei tribuit.

R8 Rosenmüller, III, 351 That among the later Jews it was held almost a matter of religion to give idols and idol worship opprobrious names, among which זבול, dung, was a common one, Lightfoot has proved from the Talmudic writers in his Horae Hebraicae on Matth. XII, 25. But Michaelis, in the Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. vol. I, p. 205, and in the Notes on the vernacular version of Matth. X, 25, holds that Βεελζεβουλ [Beelzeboul], which is read in the N. T., is altogether different from בעל זבוב, the god of the Ekronites, and not formed from it, but is to be explained from judicial astrology. "This," he says, "divides the heavens into 12 houses, setting one of the planets over each house, which in the terminology of that art is called the lord of the house. זבול is a dwelling, but above all a dwelling of the stars; properly, then, בעל זבול is a planet, the lord of a heavenly house, as Venus is of the house of Virgo. And since these planets were held to be gods by the heathen, who closely joined astrology with the worship of vain deities, and since the Jews held the gods of the nations to be evil demons, what was more natural than to call the prince of the demons (perhaps not the one prince of all, but yet the chief of some order, and more powerful than the rest) the lord of the heavenly house? Now the words of Christ will also become wonderfully clear, and will have a certain allusion and point: εἰ τον οἰκοδεσπότην [ei ton oikodespotēn] (רב הבית, or, as it is in the Hebrew gospel, בעל הבית) Βεελζεβουλ [Beelzeboul] (בעל זבול) ἐκάλεσαν [ekalesan]." This opinion would not displease me either, provided Michaelis had proved by examples that the word זבול is used in astrology in the sense that he himself assigns to it.


Part 2, Book 4, chapter 10: The bees: the name, and the lion's carcass

III, 352 CAP. X. col. 502

III, 352 Chapter X. col. 502


Apum nomen et origo. Quomodo repertae legantur in Leonis cadavere. Easdem audire, aeris tinnitu terreri, fumo pelli, et fortitudine esse insignes in varia Scripturae loca.

The name and origin of bees. How they are read to have been found in the lion's carcass. That they hear, are frightened by the ringing of brass, are driven out by smoke, and are remarkable for their bravery, on various passages of Scripture.


Hebraeum דבר non solum loqui significat, sed et ordinare, regere, ducere, deducere, ex Chaldaeorum usu. Exempla vide 1 Sam. VIII, 21. Psal. XLVII, 4. et XVIII, 48. Inde apis Hebraice דברה debora; Chaldaice דברא dabbara, dicitur a mirabili ductu et ordine: ut Arabice دبر dabron est examen apum (1). Politicum enim est hoc animalculum, reges habens, et populos, et III, 353 urbes, et praetoria. De quibus e Graecis potissimum consulendi, Aristoteles, Aelianus, et scriptores Geoponicῶν; ut, e Romanis, Varro, Virgilius, Colu- mella, Plinius; et ex Arabibus, Damir et Alkazuinius: quorum scrinia in argumento tam trito compilare, mihi non vacat.

The Hebrew דבר means not only to speak but also to order, to rule, to lead, to lead down, following the usage of the Chaldeans. For examples see 1 Sam 8:21. Ps 47:4 and XVIII, 48. Hence the bee is called in Hebrew דברה debora, in Chaldee דברא dabbara, from its wonderful guidance and order; just as in Arabic دبر [dbr] dabron is a swarm of bees R1. For this little creature is a political one, having kings, peoples, III, 353 cities and palaces. On these, among the Greeks, the chief authorities to consult are Aristotle, Aelian and the writers of the Geoponica; among the Romans, Varro, Virgil, Columella, Pliny; and among the Arabs, Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] and Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt]. I have no leisure to plunder their book-chests on so well-worn a subject.


Apes non solum ex apibus, sed et ex bove progenerari, constans fama est apud scriptores. Antigonus Mirabilium Historia vigesima tertia, Ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ τὸν βοῦν ἐὰν κατορύξῃς ἐν τόποις τισὶν, ὥστε αὐτὰ τὰ κέρατα τῆς γῆς ὑπερέ-χειν, εἶθ᾽ ὕστερον ἀποπρίσῃς, λέγουσιν μελίττας ἐκπέτεσθαι· σαπέντα γὰρ αὐτὸν εἰς τοῦτο διαλύεσθαι τὸ ζῶον. In nonnullis Aegypti locis si bovem ita de- foderis, ut cornua supra terram extent, quae deinde serra amputes, ajunt apes evolare: eum enim putrefactum in hoc animal mutari. Varro itidem de bove, Rusticorum libri secundi capite quinto, Scio, ex hoc putrefacto nasci dulcissimas col. 503 apes, mellis matres: a quo eas Graeci βουγόνας appellant. Et libri tertii capite decimo sexto, Apes nascuntur partim ex apibus, partim ex bubulo corpore putre- facto. Columella libri primi capite quarto, Progenerari apes posse juvenco per- empto, Democritus et Mago, nec minus Virgilius prodiderunt. Mago quidem ventribus etiam bubulis idem fieri affirmat. Philo Περὶ θυόντων, Μέλιττα ζῶόν ἐστιν οὐ καθαρὸν, ἐκ σήψεως καὶ φθορᾶς νεκρῶν, ὡς ὁ λόγος, βοῶν γεννώμενον· Apis impurum est animal, quodque ex mortuorum boum putredine et corruptione nasci ajunt. Plinius libri undecimi capite vigesimo, Sunt, qui apes in totum amissas reparari (putent), ventribus bubulis recentibus, cum fimo obrutis. Plut- archus in extremo Cleomene, Μελίττας μὲν βόες, σφῆκας δὲ ἵπποι κατασα-πέντες ἐξανθοῦσι· Apes quidem boves, vespas autem equi putrefacti emittunt. Aelianus in fine libri secundi, Ἀποθανὼν δὲ βοῦς γενναῖόν τι χρῆμα, καὶ ἀξιέ-παινον· μέλιτται γοῦν ἐκ τῶν ἐκείνου λειψάνων ἐκφύονται. Bos etiam mortuus res eximia est, et magni facienda; cum ex ejus reliquiis enascantur apes. Gale- nus libri, An animal sit, quod in utero continetur, capite quinto, Οὐ δὲ γὰρ ὅπως ἐν φυτοῖς σκώληκες γίνονται, ἢ ἀφ᾽ ἵππων καὶ βοῶν οἱ σφῆκες, καὶ μέ-λιτται, ῥᾴδιον ἡμῖν λέγειν· Neque enim vobis facile dictu est, quo pacto vermes in plantis gignantur, aut ex equis bobusque vespae et apes. Origenes contra Celsum III, 354 libro quarto, Cum non miremur, etiam nunc ex homine mortuo serpentem fieri, e dorsi medulla, ut quidem ajunt; et ex bove apem, ex equo vespam, ex asino scarabaeum. Servius in librum quartum Georgicorum, Apum sunt multa genera. Proprie ta- men vocantur apes de bobus, fuci de equis, crabrones de mulis, vespae de asinis. Et qua ratione id fiat, narrat pluribus Florentinus libro decimo quinto Geoponi- cῶn, capite [2] Περὶ μελισσῶν, καὶ πῶς ἂν ἐκ βοὸς γένηται ὃ καλεῖται βου-γόνη, De apibus, et quomodo ex bove fiat, quod vocatur BUGONE. Concinunt multi poetae, ut e Graecis in Antigono Philetas; is nempe, quem testatur Sui- das Ptolemaei secundi fuisse praeceptorem, et Elegias atque Epigrammata scripsisse.

That bees are generated not only from bees but also from an ox is a constant report among writers. Antigonus, Account of Marvels 23: Ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ τὸν βοῦν ἐὰν κατορύξῃς ἐν τόποις τισὶν, ὥστε αὐτὰ τὰ κέρατα τῆς γῆς ὑπερέχειν, εἶθ᾽ ὕστερον ἀποπρίσῃς, λέγουσιν μελίττας ἐκπέτεσθαι· σαπέντα γὰρ αὐτὸν εἰς τοῦτο διαλύεσθαι τὸ ζῶον [En Aigyptō ton boun ean katoryxēs en topois tisin, hōste auta ta kerata tēs gēs hyperechein, eith᾽ hysteron apopris ēs, legousin melittas ekpetesthai; sapenta gar auton eis touto dialyesthai to zōon]. In some places of Egypt, if you bury an ox so that the horns stand above the ground, and then saw them off, they say that bees fly out; for it, when putrefied, is changed into this animal. Varro likewise on the ox, On Agriculture book 2, chapter 5: I know that from it, when putrefied, are born the sweetest col. 503 bees, the mothers of honey; from which the Greeks call them βουγόνας [bougonas]. And book 3, chapter 16: Bees are born partly from bees, partly from the putrefied body of an ox. Columella, book 1, chapter 4: That bees can be generated from a slain bullock, Democritus and Mago, and no less Virgil, have reported. Mago indeed affirms that the same happens also from the bellies of oxen. Philo, On Those Who Sacrifice: Μέλιττα ζῶόν ἐστιν οὐ καθαρὸν, ἐκ σήψεως καὶ φθορᾶς νεκρῶν, ὡς ὁ λόγος, βοῶν γεννώμενον [Melitta zōon estin ou katharon, ek sēpseōs kai phthoras nekrōn, hōs ho logos, boōn gennōmenon]; The bee is an impure animal, which they say is born from the putrefaction and corruption of dead oxen. Pliny, book 11, chapter 20: There are some who (think) that bees wholly lost are restored by fresh ox bellies covered with dung. Plutarch at the end of the Cleomenes: Μελίττας μὲν βόες, σφῆκας δὲ ἵπποι κατασαπέντες ἐξανθοῦσι [Melittas men boes, sphēkas de hippoi katasapentes exanthousi]; Putrefied oxen put forth bees, and horses wasps. Aelian at the end of book 2: Ἀποθανὼν δὲ βοῦς γενναῖόν τι χρῆμα, καὶ ἀξιέπαινον· μέλιτται γοῦν ἐκ τῶν ἐκείνου λειψάνων ἐκφύονται [Apothanōn de bous gennaion ti chrēma, kai axiepainon; melittai goun ek tōn ekeinou leipsanōn ekphyontai]. Even a dead ox is an excellent thing and to be highly valued, since bees spring from its remains. Galen, in the book Whether What Is Contained in the Womb Is an Animal, chapter 5: Οὐ δὲ γὰρ ὅπως ἐν φυτοῖς σκώληκες γίνονται, ἢ ἀφ᾽ ἵππων καὶ βοῶν οἱ σφῆκες, καὶ μέλιτται, ῥᾴδιον ἡμῖν λέγειν [Ou de gar hopōs en phytois skōlēkes ginontai, ē aph᾽ hippōn kai boōn hoi sphēkes, kai melittai, rhadion hēmin legein]; For neither is it easy for you to say how worms are generated in plants, or wasps and bees from horses and oxen. Origen, Against Celsus III, 354 book 4: Since we do not marvel that even now a serpent comes from a dead man, from the marrow of the spine, as they say; and a bee from an ox, a wasp from a horse, a beetle from an ass. Servius on book 4 of the Georgics: There are many kinds of bees. Properly, however, those from oxen are called bees, from horses drones, from mules hornets, from asses wasps. And in what way this happens is related at length by Florentinus in book 15 of the Geoponica, chapter [2], Περὶ μελισσῶν, καὶ πῶς ἂν ἐκ βοὸς γένηται ὃ καλεῖται βουγόνη [Peri melissōn, kai pōs an ek boos genētai ho kaleitai bougonē], On bees, and how what is called BUGONE comes from an ox. Many poets agree, as among the Greeks Philetas in Antigonus: the one, namely, whom Suidas attests was the tutor of Ptolemy II and wrote Elegies and Epigrams.


Βουγενέας φάμενος προσεβήσαο μακρὰ μελίσσας, Taurigenas haec fatus apes longinquus adisti.

Ἵππων μὲν σφῆκες γενεαὶ, μόσχων δὲ μέλισσαι· Vespae ab equis, sed apes taurorum ab origine natae.

Whom Nicander imitates thus in the Theriaca, line 741.

Discerpti enim a lupis equi vespas, et tauri apes, corporibus corruptis, pro- generarunt. (Ubi obiter nota, σκῆνος, tabernaculum pro corpore sumi, ut a Paulo 2 Cor. V, 1. 4.). Et Ovidius libro decimo quinto Metamorphoseωs,
