III, 365 col. 510 CAP. XI.

III, 365 col. 510 Chapter XI.


Loca quaedam de Apum mellificio, quae tanquam ex Scriptura proferunt Graeci Patres.

Some passages on the honey-making of bees which the Greek Fathers cite as if from Scripture.


Apes commendat inprimis mellis conficiendi artificium, de quo in Hebraeorum col. 511 sacro textu hoc solum reperias Iud. XIV, 8. Et, ecce examen apum in corpore leonis, et mel! Examen apum, et mel: id est, examen apum mellificarum, aut mel conficientium, per figuram ἓν διὰ δυοῖν. Sed Graeci Patres e penu suo tres alios textus proferunt. Primus est Psalmi CXVII, (Hebraeis CXVIII,) 12. Ἐκύκλωσάν με, ὡσεὶ μέλισσαι κηρίον· Circumdederunt me, sicut apes favum. Ita ex Graeca versione citant Augustinus, Hieronymus, Theodoretus. Neque aliud habent nostrae editiones. Aethiops quoque idem sequitur. Et Arabs, quem habeo manuscriptum, احتاطوا بي مثل النحل بالشهد Circumdederunt me, ut apes favum. Sed pro الشهد, id est, favo, editi habent الشمع ceram. Quasi Arabes κηρὸν Graece legerint, non κηρίον. At in Hebraeo solum legitur, סבוני כדבורים, Circumdederunt me, ut apes. Et illud κηρίον videtur perperam additum. Agit enim David de hostibus suis: nec eos confert cum apibus, quae favum circumstant, cum in eo nihil sit hostile, sed cum apibus, quae hominem aut brutum agminatim circumdant, ut infestis aculeis pungant. Quomodo apud Statium Thebaidos lib. 10.

Bees are commended above all for their skill in making honey. On this, in the sacred text of the Hebrews, col. 511 you will find only Iud. XIV, 8: And behold, a swarm of bees in the body of the lion, and honey! A swarm of bees, and honey: that is, a swarm of honey-making bees, or of bees producing honey, by the figure ἓν διὰ δυοῖν [hen dia dyoin]. But the Greek Fathers bring out three other texts from their own store. The first is Psalmi CXVII, (Hebraeis CXVIII,) 12: Ἐκύκλωσάν με, ὡσεὶ μέλισσαι κηρίον· [Ekyklōsan me, hōsei melissai kērion] They surrounded me, as bees a honeycomb. So Augustine, Jerome and Theodoret cite it from the Greek version. Nor do our editions have anything else. The Ethiopic also follows the same. And the Arabic, which I have in manuscript, reads احتاطوا بي مثل النحل بالشهد [iḥtāṭū bī mithl al-naḥl bi-l-shahd] They surrounded me, as bees a honeycomb. But for الشهد [al-shahd], that is, honeycomb, the printed editions have الشمع [al-shamʿ] wax, as if the Arabs had read κηρὸν [kēron] in the Greek, not κηρίον [kērion]. In the Hebrew, however, one reads only סבוני כדבורים, They surrounded me, like bees. And that κηρίον [kērion] seems to have been wrongly added. For David is speaking of his enemies; and he does not compare them with bees that surround a honeycomb, since there is nothing hostile in that, but with bees that surround a man or a beast in a body, to sting with hostile stings. So in Statius, Thebaid book 10:


Sic, ubi pumiceo pastor rapturus ab antro
Armatas exegit apes, fremit aspera nubes,
Inque vicem sese stridore hortantur, et omnes
Hostis in ora volant. — — —

So, when a shepherd, about to plunder them, has driven the armed bees from their pumice cave, the fierce cloud roars, and they urge one another on with buzzing, and all fly into the face of the foe. — — —


Sed de his supra jam actum.

But these matters have already been dealt with above.


III, 366 Secundus textus est Prov. VI, 8. ubi post locum de formica πολυθρύλλη-τον, Vade ad formicam, o piger, etc. Graeca editio sic habet: Ἢ πορεύθητι πρὸς τὴν μέλισσαν, καὶ μάθε, ὡς ἐργάτις ἐστι, τήν τε ἐργασίαν ὡς σεμνὴν ποιεῖται· ἧς τοὺς πόνους βασιλεῖς καὶ ἰδιῶται πρὸς ὑγίειαν προσφέρονται. πο-θεινὴ δέ ἐστι πᾶσι, καὶ ἐπίδοξος· καίπερ οὖσα τῇ ῥώμῃ ἀσθενὴς, τὴν σοφίαν τιμήσασα προήχθη. Quae in versione sua Castalio sic expressit, Aut apem adi, et disce, quam operosa sit, quamque augustum opus exerceat: cujus laboribus et reges, et privati vescuntur salubriter. Eaque omnibus est amabilis et illustris: et, quamvis viribus infirma sit, tamen sapientiae studio promovit. Arabica quoque versio, او انهب الي النحلة واعرف انها مثل الفاعل هي تعمل صناعتها طرفة عجيبة * واتعابها تحمل الي الملوك * والعامة يستعملوها لحفظ الصحة * وهي عند جميع الناس ماثورة مشرفة * مع ضعيفة في قوتها قدمت لانها اكرمت بالحكمة وفضلت * Aut vade ad apem, et scito, eam, velut operarium, opus suum fabricare arte mirabili. Et labores ejus deferuntur ad reges. Et vulgus iis utitur ad tuendam sanitatem. Estque apud omnes homines excellens et nobilis. Etiamsi debilis sit viribus, tamen antecellit; quia commendatur sapien- col. 512 tia, et praestans est. Eundem locum citant multi veteres: ut Clemens Alexandrinus lib. 1. Stromatων; Origenes in Numeros Homilia 27. et in Esaiam Homilia 2. Basilius in Hexaëmeron Homilia 8. Ambrosius in Hexaëmeron lib. 5. cap. 21. Hieronymus in Ezechielem cap. 3. Theodoretus De Providentia Oratione 5. An-tiochus, Abbas Sabae, Homilia 36. Iohannes Damascenus lib. 2. Parall. cap. 89. Tamen, ut vere observat Hieronymus ubi supra, hoc Hebraea non habent exemplaria. Itaque nec in Chaldaea, nec in Syra, nec in Vulgata versione ullum est hujus loci vestigium. Et saepe mirari subiit, unde id sumpserint Graeci interpretes, ut et quaedam alia, quae variis locis passim inserunt. Neque enim credibile est, illos de suo haec fuisse addituros, nisi in quibusdam Hebraeorum exemplaribus jam inserta reperissent.

III, 366 The second text is Prov. VI, 8, where, after the much-celebrated (πολυθρύλλητον [polythryllēton]) passage on the ant, Go to the ant, O sluggard, etc., the Greek edition reads: Ἢ πορεύθητι πρὸς τὴν μέλισσαν, καὶ μάθε, ὡς ἐργάτις ἐστι, τήν τε ἐργασίαν ὡς σεμνὴν ποιεῖται· ἧς τοὺς πόνους βασιλεῖς καὶ ἰδιῶται πρὸς ὑγίειαν προσφέρονται. ποθεινὴ δέ ἐστι πᾶσι, καὶ ἐπίδοξος· καίπερ οὖσα τῇ ῥώμῃ ἀσθενὴς, τὴν σοφίαν τιμήσασα προήχθη. [Ē poreuthēti pros tēn melissan, kai mathe, hōs ergatis esti, tēn te ergasian hōs semnēn poieitai; hēs tous ponous basileis kai idiōtai pros hygieian prospherontai. potheinē de esti pasi, kai epidoxos; kaiper ousa tē rhōmē asthenēs, tēn sophian timēsasa proēchthē.] Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)] rendered this in his version as follows: Or go to the bee, and learn how industrious she is, and how majestic a work she carries on: by whose labours both kings and private persons are wholesomely fed. And she is beloved and renowned among all; and, although weak in strength, she has nevertheless advanced by her zeal for wisdom. The Arabic version also: او انهب الي النحلة واعرف انها مثل الفاعل هي تعمل صناعتها طرفة عجيبة * واتعابها تحمل الي الملوك * والعامة يستعملوها لحفظ الصحة * وهي عند جميع الناس ماثورة مشرفة * مع ضعيفة في قوتها قدمت لانها اكرمت بالحكمة وفضلت * [aw inhab ilá al-naḥla wa-iʿrif annahā mithl al-fāʿil hiya taʿmal ṣināʿatahā ṭurfa ʿajība * wa-atʿābuhā tuḥmal ilá al-mulūk * wa-al-ʿāmma yastaʿmilūhā li-ḥifẓ al-ṣiḥḥa * wa-hiya ʿinda jamīʿ al-nās maʾthūra musharrafa * maʿa ḍaʿīfa fī quwwatihā qaddamat li-annahā ukrimat bi-l-ḥikma wa-fuḍḍilat *] Or go to the bee, and know that, like a workman, she fashions her work with wonderful art. And her labours are carried to kings, and the common people use them to preserve health. And she is excellent and noble among all men. Although she is weak in strength, she nevertheless excels, because she is commended for wisdom, col. 512 and is outstanding. Many ancient writers cite the same passage: thus Clement of Alexandria, book 1 of the Stromata; Origen on Numbers, Homily 27, and on Isaiah, Homily 2; Basil on the Hexaemeron, Homily 8; Ambrose on the Hexaemeron, book 5, ch. 21; Jerome on Ezekiel, ch. 3; Theodoret, On Providence, Oration 5; Antiochus, Abbot of Saba, Homily 36; John of Damascus, book 2 of the Parallels, ch. 89. Yet, as Jerome rightly observes in the place cited, the Hebrew copies do not have this. Accordingly there is no trace of this passage in the Chaldee, the Syriac or the Vulgate version. And I have often wondered where the Greek translators took it from, as also certain other things which they insert here and there in various places. For it is not credible that they would have added these things of their own accord, unless they had found them already inserted in some copies of the Hebrews.


Utut sit, in hoc de ape loco quaedam notanda. Primo: apem cum formica jungi, ut passim apud scriptores. Sic Philosophus Historiae lib. 1. cap. 1. postquam apem et formicam politica et gregalia dixit esse animalia, addit: τὸ τῶν μελιττῶν γένος εἶναι ὑφ᾽ ἡγεμόνα· μύρμηκες δὲ, καὶ μυρία ἄλλα ἄναρχα, apum genus esse sub duce, formicas autem et infinita alia sine duce. Et lib. 9. cap. 38. Τῶν δ᾽ ἐντόμων ζώων ἐργατικώτατα σχεδόν ἐστι, καὶ πρός τ᾽ ἄλλα συγκρίνεσθαι πάντα, τότε τῶν μυρμήκων γένος, καὶ τὸ τῶν μελιττῶν· Insectorum III, 367 animalium sunt laboriosissima, et reliquis omnibus praeferenda, formicarum et apum genera. Cicero Academicarum Quaestionum lib. 4. Cujus quidem (Dei) vos majestatem deducitis usque ad apum formicarumque perfectionem. Plutarchus in libro, An seni gerenda sit respublica, Τὸ κοινωνικὸν, καὶ πολιτικὸν, ὃ καὶ μύρμηξιν ἄχρι τέλους παραμένει καὶ μελίτταις· Vita communis et politica, in qua ad finem usque permanent tam formicae, quam apes. Aelianus Historiae lib. 5. cap. 49. Μέλιτται, μύρμηκές τε, καὶ ἐκείνοις, ἐκφορᾶς νεκρῶν μέλειν ἡ σοφωτάτη φύσις ἔδωκεν· Apibus et formicis id sapientissima natura tribuit, ut mortuos suos efferrent. Phocylides, aut quisquis est, postquam formicam pluribus descripsit, de ape addit continuo post,

However that may be, certain points should be noted in this passage about the bee. First: the bee is joined with the ant, as is common among writers. Thus the Philosopher, History book 1, ch. 1, after saying that the bee and the ant are political and gregarious animals, adds: τὸ τῶν μελιττῶν γένος εἶναι ὑφ᾽ ἡγεμόνα· μύρμηκες δὲ, καὶ μυρία ἄλλα ἄναρχα [to tōn melittōn genos einai hyph᾽ hēgemona; myrmēkes de, kai myria alla anarcha], the race of bees is under a leader, but ants and countless others are without a leader. And book 9, ch. 38: Τῶν δ᾽ ἐντόμων ζώων ἐργατικώτατα σχεδόν ἐστι, καὶ πρός τ᾽ ἄλλα συγκρίνεσθαι πάντα, τότε τῶν μυρμήκων γένος, καὶ τὸ τῶν μελιττῶν [Tōn d᾽ entomōn zōōn ergatikōtata schedon esti, kai pros t᾽ alla synkrinesthai panta, tote tōn myrmēkōn genos, kai to tōn melittōn]: Of insect III, 367 animals the most industrious, and to be preferred to all the rest, are the races of ants and of bees. Cicero, Academic Questions book 4: Whose (God's) majesty you bring down even to the perfection of bees and ants. Plutarch, in the book Whether an Old Man Should Engage in Public Affairs: Τὸ κοινωνικὸν, καὶ πολιτικὸν, ὃ καὶ μύρμηξιν ἄχρι τέλους παραμένει καὶ μελίτταις [To koinōnikon, kai politikon, ho kai myrmēxin achri telous paramenei kai melittais]: The communal and political life, in which both ants and bees remain to the very end. Aelian, History book 5, ch. 49: Μέλιτται, μύρμηκές τε, καὶ ἐκείνοις, ἐκφορᾶς νεκρῶν μέλειν ἡ σοφωτάτη φύσις ἔδωκεν [Melittai, myrmēkes te, kai ekeinois, ekphoras nekrōn melein hē sophōtatē physis edōken]: To bees and ants most wise nature has granted that they carry out their dead. Phocylides, or whoever he is, after describing the ant at some length, immediately adds about the bee:


Κάμνει δ' ἠερόφοιτος ἀριστοπόνος τε μέλισσα,

Κάμνει δ' ἠερόφοιτος ἀριστοπόνος τε μέλισσα, [Kamnei d' ēerophoitos aristoponos te melissa,]


Operatur quoque aëria laboriosa apis. Celsus apud Origenem hominem stulte asserit a brutis ideo non differre, quia civitates condidit, et civili administratione utitur, καὶ γὰρ μύρμηκες, καὶ αἱ μέλισσαι, formicae enim et apes idem praestant. Sed eum accurate refellit Origenes lib. 4. Tertullianus lib. 1. contra Marcionem cap. 14. Imitare, si potes, apis aedificia, formicae stabula, etc. Pontanus lib. 1. De stellis,

The airy, industrious bee also labors. Celsus, in Origen, foolishly asserts that man does not differ from the brutes on the ground that he has founded cities and uses civil government, καὶ γὰρ μύρμηκες, καὶ αἱ μέλισσαι [kai gar myrmēkes, kai hai melissai], for ants and bees do the same. But Origen refutes him thoroughly in book 4. Tertullian, book 1 Against Marcion, ch. 14: Imitate, if you can, the buildings of the bee, the stables of the ant, etc. Pontanus, book 1 On the Stars:


Sola hyemi metuens latebroso pumice condit
Triticeos populata hominum formica labores.
Idem amor atque apibus eadem experientia parcis.

Alone, fearing winter, the ant stores in hollow pumice
the wheaten labors it has plundered from men.
The same love and the same skill belong to the thrifty bees.


Scaliger in carmine, cui titulus Avara militia;

Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)], in the poem entitled Avaricious Warfare:


Formica, et apis, utraque deponit in annum.
Hanc sedulitas, hanc studium facit virilem.
Huic alveus, illi satis est cavum pusillum.

The ant and the bee both lay up for the year.
Diligence makes the one, zeal the other, manly.
For this a hive, for that a tiny hollow is enough.


Et in titulo, Labor pater fruitionis,

And in the one entitled Labor, the Father of Enjoyment:


Formica et apis nos operariae docebunt
Pro parte laborare, dein frui labore.

The ant and the bee, workers, will teach us
to labor for our share, then to enjoy our labor.


2. Neque id praeter Scripturae morem est, quod ex brutis petuntur exempla vitae: ut ex formica in eodem versu; ex bove et asino, Esa. I, 3. ex turture, grue, et hirundine, Ierem. VIII, 7. ex serpentibus et columbis, Matth. X, 16. Deo ad classem inferiorem, nempe ad brutorum scholam, sic eos ablegante, qui in sua schola nihil profecerunt. 3. Hoc quoque tralatitium est, quod apis hominibus imitanda proponitur. Seneca Epistola 84. Apes, ut ajunt, debemus imitari, quae vagantur, et flores, ad mel faciendum idoneos, carpunt, deinde, quid- col. 513 quid attulere, disponunt, ac per favos digerunt, etc. Lucretius libro tertio, III, 368 Floriferis ut apes in saltibus omnia libant, Omnia nos itidem depascimur aurea dicta,

2. Nor is it contrary to the custom of Scripture that examples for life are sought from brute animals: as from the ant in the same verse; from the ox and the ass, Isa 1:3; from the turtledove, crane and swallow, Ierem. VIII, 7.; from serpents and doves, Matth. X, 16. In this way God sends down to a lower class, namely to the school of the brutes, those who have made no progress in his own school. 3. This too is commonplace, that the bee is set before men for imitation. Seneca, Epistle 84: We ought, as they say, to imitate the bees, which wander about and pluck the flowers suitable for making honey, then arrange whatever col. 513 they have brought and distribute it through the honeycombs, etc. Lucretius, book 3: III, 368 As bees in flowery glades sip at everything, so we likewise feed upon all your golden words,


Horatius libri quarti Oda secunda,

Horace, book 4, Ode 2:


— — — ego apis Matinae
More modoque
Grata carpentis thyma per laborem
Plurimum, circa nemus uvidique
Tiburis ripas operosa parvus
Carmina fingo.

— — — I, after the manner and
fashion of the Matine bee,
that gathers the pleasing thyme with much
labor, around the grove and the banks of moist Tibur, small as I am, fashion
laborious songs.


Plura hujusmodi ex Platone, Plutarcho, Luciano, et aliis nemini non sunt obvia. Neque aliud volunt, qui mulierem frugi ex ape natam esse fingunt, ut apud Stobaeum capite septuagesimo primo Simonides,

More of this kind from Plato, Plutarch, Lucian and others are familiar to everyone. Nor do those who imagine that a thrifty woman was born from a bee mean anything else, as Simonides in Stobaeus, chapter 71:


Τὴν δ᾽ ἐκ μελίσσης, τήν τις εὐτυχεῖ λαβών·
Κείνῃ γὰρ οἴῃ μῶμος οὐ προσιζάνει·
Θάλλει δ᾽ ὑπ᾽ αὐτῆς κἀπαέξεται βίος.

Τὴν δ᾽ ἐκ μελίσσης, τήν τις εὐτυχεῖ λαβών· [Tēn d᾽ ek melissēs, tēn tis eutychei labōn;] Κείνῃ γὰρ οἴῃ μῶμος οὐ προσιζάνει· [Keinē gar oiē mōmos ou prosizanei;] Θάλλει δ᾽ ὑπ᾽ αὐτῆς κἀπαέξεται βίος. [Thallei d᾽ hyp᾽ autēs kapaexetai bios.]


Natam ex ape qui duxerit, felix est: in hac enim sola culpa non residet; floretque, et ab ea augetur res familiaris. Et Phocylides,

He who has married one born from the bee is fortunate: for in her alone no fault resides; and the household flourishes and is increased by her. And Phocylides:


— — — ἡ δὲ μελίσσης
Οἰκονόμος τ᾽ ἀγαθὴ, καὶ ἐπίσταται ἐργάζεσθαι,

— — — ἡ δὲ μελίσσης [hē de melissēs] Οἰκονόμος τ᾽ ἀγαθὴ, καὶ ἐπίσταται ἐργάζεσθαι, [Oikonomos t᾽ agathē, kai epistatai ergazesthai,]


Quae autem ex ape nata est, rem oeconomicam probe callet, et novit operari. Hinc in Oeconomico Xenophontis capite decimo tertio, ἡ τῶν μελισσῶν ἡγε-μῶν, dux apum, confertur pluribus cum matre familias. Itaque etiam illustres mulieres apis nomine appellari non dedignatae sunt: ut apud Hebraeos DEBORA duplex; una, Rebeccae nutrix, Gen. XXXV, 8. et altera, prophetissa, quae judicavit Israelem, Iudicum IV, 4. Et apud Graecos Iovis nutrix, ME-LISSA, nympha; et MELISSA, Epidamni filia, de qua Stephanus in Δυῤῥά-χιον· et MELISSA, Periandri uxor, regis Corinthiorum: et MELISSA recentior, cujus Epistolam edidit Aldus in volumine Graecarum Epistolarum. 4. Est etiam id receptum, ut apis dicatur ἐργάτις, opifex, vel operaria. Aristoteles Historiae libri noni capite quadragesimo, Εἰσὶ δ᾽ αἱ μικραὶ ἐργά-τιδες μᾶλλον τῶν μεγάλων. Quibus similia haec Varronis libri tertii Rusticorum capite decimo sexto, Sylvestres minores sunt magnitudine, et pilosae, sed opifices magis. Et quod Anthologiae libri primi capite sexagesimo apes in Antiphilo vocantur

But she who is born of the bee is well versed in household management and knows how to work. Hence in Xenophon's Oeconomicus, chapter 13, ἡ τῶν μελισσῶν ἡγεμῶν [hē tōn melissōn hēgemōn], the leader of the bees, is compared at length with the mother of a household. Accordingly, even illustrious women did not disdain to be called by the name of bee: as among the Hebrews there are two named DEBORA: one, the nurse of Rebecca, Gen. XXXV, 8, and the other, the prophetess who judged Israel, Iudicum IV, 4. And among the Greeks there is MELISSA, the nymph who nursed Jupiter; and MELISSA, daughter of Epidamnus, of whom Stephanus speaks under Δυῤῥάχιον [Dyrrhachion]; and MELISSA, wife of Periander, king of the Corinthians; and a later MELISSA, whose Letter Aldus published in the volume of Greek Letters. 4. It is also an accepted usage that the bee is called ἐργάτις [ergatis], craftswoman or worker. Aristotle, History, book 9, chapter 40: Εἰσὶ δ᾽ αἱ μικραὶ ἐργάτιδες μᾶλλον τῶν μεγάλων [Eisi d' hai mikrai ergatides mallon tōn megalōn]. Similar to this is Varro, Rustica, book 3, chapter 16: The wild ones are smaller in size, and hairy, but better workers. And in Anthologia, book 1, chapter 60, bees are called in Antiphilus


Αἰθερίου πτηναὶ νέκταρος ἐργάτιδες, Aetherii volucres nectaris artifices. III, 369 Ut de Luciano taceam, qui in Halcyone apem appellat μέλιτος ἐργάτιν, quomodo etiam Pisidas τὴν σοφὴν τὴν ἐργάτιν. 5. Sed nemo alius, quod quidem sciam, harum ἐργασίαν σεμνὴν vocavit. Quod Ambrosius reddit operationem venerabilem, Hieronymus opus castum, Castalio augustum opus, Godefridus Tilmannus, opus munditiae et honestatis plenum. Malim opus pretiosum, aut mirabile; quia magis ad rem est: et σεμνὸν, vel σεπτὸν, sic sumi, docent lexicographi veteres. Hesychius, Σεμνή· (lege Σεμνὰ) τίμια, σώ-φρων. Idem, Σεπτά· θαυμαστά. Quod sequutus Arabs hic habet, apem fabricare opus suum عجيبة طرفة, arte mirabili. (Male editum طرقة). Quid si σμήνων legas pro σεμνὴν, hoc modo, τήν τε ἐργασίαν σμήνων ὡς ποιεῖται, et quomodo faciat opus alvearium, id est, mirabile illud opus, quod fit in alvearibus? Quod ingens naturae arcanum est, neque dum satis perspectum. Philosophus ubi supra, Ὅταν δὲ εἰς σμῆνος ἀφίκωνται ἀπο-σείονται, καὶ ἀκολουθοῦσιν ἑκάστῃ τρεῖς, ἢ τέτταρες. τὸ δὲ λαμβανόμενον οὐ ῥᾴδιόν ἐστιν ἰδεῖν, οὐδὲ τὴν ἐργασίαν, ὅν τινα τρόπον ποιοῦνται, οὐκ ὦπται· Cum autem in alveare (a florilegio) redeunt, se excutiunt, et unamquamque apem tres aut quatuor sequuntur. Sed quid accipiant, videre facile non est. Neque dum observatum est, quomodo opus suum faciant. Scitu dignum, mo- col. 514 do verum, quod de illo referunt Alkazuinius et Damir, وقد صنع ارسطاطاليس لها بيتا من زجاج لينظر الي كيفية ما تصنع فابت ان تعمل حتي لطخته من باطن الزجاج بالطين Fecit illis Aristoteles alveare vitreum, ut introspiceret, qua ratione ad opus se accingerent. Sed abnuerunt quidquam operari, donec interiora vitri luto oblevisset. 6. Sequitur in sacro textu, Ἧς τοὺς πόνους βασιλεῖς καὶ ἰδιῶται πρὸς ὑγίειαν προσφέρονται· Cujus labores reges et privati ad sanitatem adhibent. Apis labores, id est, mel: ut in Hesiodi versu de fucis notissimo Operum versu 303.

Αἰθερίου πτηναὶ νέκταρος ἐργάτιδες [Aitheriou ptēnai nektaros ergatides], winged craftswomen of heavenly nectar. III, 369 Not to mention Lucian, who in the Halcyon calls the bee μέλιτος ἐργάτιν [melitos ergatin], as also Pisides calls her τὴν σοφὴν τὴν ἐργάτιν [tēn sophēn tēn ergatin]. 5. But no one else, so far as I know, has called their ἐργασίαν σεμνὴν [ergasian semnēn]. Ambrose renders this venerable operation, Jerome chaste work, Castalio august work, Godefridus Tilmannus work full of cleanliness and honesty. I would prefer precious work or wonderful work, because it fits the matter better; and the old lexicographers teach that σεμνὸν [semnon] or σεπτὸν [septon] is taken in this sense. Hesychius: Σεμνή· (read Σεμνὰ) τίμια, σώφρων [Semnē (Semna): timia, sōphrōn]. The same: Σεπτά· θαυμαστά [Septa: thaumasta]. Following this, the Arabic version here has that the bee makes her work عجيبة طرفة [ʿajība ṭurfa], with wonderful art. (Wrongly printed طرقة [ṭrqa].) What if one were to read σμήνων [smēnōn] for σεμνὴν [semnēn], thus: τήν τε ἐργασίαν σμήνων ὡς ποιεῖται [tēn te ergasian smēnōn hōs poieitai], and how she does the work of the hives, that is, that wonderful work which is done in hives? This is a great secret of nature, and not yet sufficiently understood. The Philosopher, in the place cited above: Ὅταν δὲ εἰς σμῆνος ἀφίκωνται ἀποσείονται, καὶ ἀκολουθοῦσιν ἑκάστῃ τρεῖς, ἢ τέτταρες. τὸ δὲ λαμβανόμενον οὐ ῥᾴδιόν ἐστιν ἰδεῖν, οὐδὲ τὴν ἐργασίαν, ὅν τινα τρόπον ποιοῦνται, οὐκ ὦπται· [Hotan de eis smēnos aphikōntai aposeiontai, kai akolouthousin hekastē treis, ē tettares. to de lambanomenon ou rhadion estin idein, oude tēn ergasian, hon tina tropon poiountai, ouk ōptai] When they return to the hive (from gathering flowers), they shake themselves off, and each bee is followed by three or four. But what they receive is not easy to see. Nor has it yet been observed how they do their work. Worth knowing, if only it is true, is what Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt] and Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] report about this, col. 514 وقد صنع ارسطاطاليس لها بيتا من زجاج لينظر الي كيفية ما تصنع فابت ان تعمل حتي لطخته من باطن الزجاج بالطين [wa-qad ṣanaʿa Arisṭāṭālīs lahā baytan min zujāj li-yanẓura ilā kayfiyyat mā taṣnaʿ fa-abat an taʿmal ḥattā laṭṭakhathu min bāṭin al-zujāj bi-l-ṭīn] Aristotle made them a glass hive, in order to look in and see how they set about their work. But they refused to do any work until they had smeared the inside of the glass with mud. 6. There follows in the sacred text: Ἧς τοὺς πόνους βασιλεῖς καὶ ἰδιῶται πρὸς ὑγίειαν προσφέρονται· [Hēs tous ponous basileis kai idiōtai pros hygieian prospherontai] whose labours kings and private persons use for health. The labours of the bee, that is, honey: as in Hesiod's well-known line on drones, Works, line 303.


Οἵ τε μελισσάων κάματον τρύχουσιν ἀεργοὶ,

Οἵ τε μελισσάων κάματον τρύχουσιν ἀεργοὶ, [Hoi te melissaōn kamaton trychousin aergoi]


Quique apum laborem absumunt otiosi. Et apud Euripidem, Iphigenia in Tauris, censetur in inferiis

And who, idle, consume the labour of the bees. And in Euripides, Iphigenia in Tauris, there is reckoned among the funeral offerings


— — — — ξουθᾶν πόνημα μελισσᾶν,

— — — — ξουθᾶν πόνημα μελισσᾶν, [xouthan ponēma melissan]


flavarum apum labor. Hinc adagium de juvene, qui in re pervulgata explicanda tempus inutiliter terit; Σύγγνωθι τῷ μειρακίῳ τὸ μέλι πόνον με-λίττης κηρύττοντι, Ignosce juveni, qui mel apis laborem esse praedicat. De quo Tzetzes Chiliadis octavae Historia ducentesima octava, III, 370 Τοῦτο τὸ σχῆμα γίνωσκε τυγχάνειν εἰρωνείας. Καὶ τίς γὰρ, ὃς ἠγνόηκε πόνον μελίσσης μέλι;

the labour of the tawny bees. Hence the proverb about a young man who wastes time uselessly explaining something commonly known: Σύγγνωθι τῷ μειρακίῳ τὸ μέλι πόνον μελίττης κηρύττοντι [Syngnōthi tō meirakiō to meli ponon melittēs kēryttonti], Forgive the young man who proclaims that honey is the labour of the bee. On this, Tzetzes, Chiliad 8, History 208: III, 370 Τοῦτο τὸ σχῆμα γίνωσκε τυγχάνειν εἰρωνείας. Καὶ τίς γὰρ, ὃς ἠγνόηκε πόνον μελίσσης μέλι; [Touto to schēma ginōske tynchanein eirōneias. Kai tis gar, hos ēgnoēke ponon melissēs meli?]


Hanc figuram scito esse ironiae. Quis enim est, qui nesciat, laborem apis esse mel? Porro mel πρὸς ὑγίειαν, ad sanitatem adhiberi, vere dicitur. Ita enim statuunt veteres. Hippocrates capite quinquagesimo De Affectionibus, Μέλι, ξὺν ἑτέροις ἐσθιόμενον, καὶ τρέφει, καὶ εὔχροιαν παρέχει· Mel, cum aliis comestum, et nutrit, et bonum colorem exhibet. Et capite quinquagesimo quarto, Οἶνος καὶ μέλι κάλλιστα κέκριται ἐν ἀνθρώποισι, ἢν πρὸς φύσιν καὶ ὑγιαίνουσι, καὶ ἀσθενέουσι, σὺν καιρῷ, καὶ μετριότητι, προσφέρονται· Vinum et mel optima judicata sunt in hominibus, si juxta naturam et sanis, et debilibus, cum temporis opportunitate ac mediocritate, exhibeantur. Diophanes libro decimo quinto, in Geoponicis, Οὐ μόνον ἡδὺ τοῖς χρωμένοις, ἀλλὰ καὶ μακροβίους ποιεῖ· οἱ οὖν γήρᾳ μέλιτι μετὰ ἄρτου μόνου τρεφόμενοι, ἐπὶ πλεῖστον βιοῦσι· καὶ τὰς αἰσθήσεις δὲ διαφυλάττει πάσας ἐῤῥωμένας. Mel utentibus non solum suave est, sed et eos longaevos facit. Qui igitur in senectute melle cum solo pane vescuntur, diu vivunt; et sensus vegetos facit ille cibus: Proinde Λύκος πολυχρονίους φησὶν εἶναι τοὺς Κυρνίους, διὰ τὸ μέλιτι ἀεὶ χρῆσθαι, longaevos esse Corsos, tradit Lycus, quia melle semper utuntur. Ita Athenaeus libri secundi capite septimo. Et ibidem, Τῶν Πυθαγο-ρικῶν τροφὴ ἄρτος μετὰ μέλιτος, ὥς φησι Ἀριστόξενος, τοὺς προσφερομένους αὐτὰ ἀεὶ ἐπ᾽ ἀρίστῳ λέγων ἀνόσως διατελεῖν. Pythagoricorum nutrimentum panem cum melle fuisse, scribit Aristoxenus, addens, sine morbo vivere, qui ea ad prandium semper adhibent. Quod videntur ex praeceptore suo, Pythagora, didicisse, de quo Eustathius in Iliad λ᾽. Ὡς δὲ καὶ τρόφιμον τὸ μέλι Πυθαγορᾶς μαρτυρεῖ, ὃς, εὐτελέστατα διαβιοὺς, πολλάκις μέλιτι μόνῳ ἠρ-κεῖτο. Mel etiam posse alere, testatur Pythagoras, qui, frugaliter admodum vivens, plerumque solo melle contentus erat. Eodem facit vetus de Glauco proverbium, Γλαῦκος πινὼν μέλι ἀνέστη· Glaucus, poto melle, revixit: id est, si Paroemiastae mentem capio, e gravi morbo convaluit. Et quod Democritum scribit Athenaeus, cum de eo jam esset conclamatum, διαζῆσαι ἡμέ-ρας ἱκανὰς, τῇ ἀπὸ τοῦ μέλιτος ἀναφορᾷ μόνῃ τρεφόμενον, in dies aliquot vitam prorogasse, solo mellis odore nutritum. Nempe, ut ibidem sequitur, mellis usu maxime delectabatur. Itaque Πρὸς τὸν πυθόμενον, Πῶς ἂν ὑγιῶς τις διάγοι; ἔφη, Εἰ τὰ μὲν ἐντὸς μέλιτι βρέχοι, τὰ δὲ ἐκτὸς ἐλαίῳ· col. 515 percontanti, qua ratione vitam quis sanus degeret? respondit: si corporis interiora melle rigarentur, exteriora oleo. Nec multo aliter Diophanes, Δημό-κριτος δὲ, ἐρωτηθεὶς, Πῶς ἂν ἄνοσοι καὶ μακραίωνες γίγνοιντο οἱ ἄνθρω-ποι; εἶπεν, Εἰ τὰ μὲν ἔξωθεν ἐλαίῳ τοῦ σώματος, τὰ δὲ ἔνδοθεν μέλιτι III, 371 χρήσαιντο. Pro quo malim χρίσαιντο. Indidem petitum Pollionis apophthegma, de quo Plinius libri vigesimi secundi capite vigesimo quarto, Multi senectam longam mulsi tantum nutritu toleravere, neque alio ullo cibo, celebri Pollionis Romuli exemplo. Centesimum annum excedentem eum Divus Augustus hospes interrogavit, quanam ratione maxime vigorem illum animi corporisque custodisset? At ille respondit: intus mulso, foris oleo. Mulso, id est, τῷ οἰνομέλιτι. Patet igitur, mel poni merito inter regum et magnatum dapes. Quod facile sit probare exemplis, ex Scriptura petitis. Sic enim ad Iosephum, Aegypti pro-regem, pro eximio munere mel mittitur, Gen. XLIII, 11. et regi Davidi, cum esset in oppido Mahanajim, mel obtulerunt vicini nobiles, 2 Sam. XVII, 29. Solomon quoque ita loquitur Cant. V, 1. Comedi favos cum melle meo. Ut Ionathanem taceam, regis filium, cujus oculi et vires mellis esu refectae sunt, 1 Sam. XIV, 27. Quibus si profana jungimus, Iliad. λ΄. versu 630. Hecamedem reperiemus Nestori et Patroclo in convivio μέλι χλωρὸν, mel flavum, aut mel recens apposuisse. Et Odyss. υ΄. versu 69. Venerem Pandari filias nutrivisse τυρῷ, καὶ μέλιτι γλυκερῷ, caseo et dulci melle. Sic Suetonius de Nerone capite vigesimo septimo, Indicebat et familiaribus coenas, quarum uni mellita quadragies sestertium constiterunt: id est, centena aureorum millia, ex Budaei supputatione. Sed vocem mellita, quam habent vulgares editiones, mutavit doctissimus Casaubonus in mitellita, quia sic legunt codices vetustissimi. Interim mitellita quid sint, ingenue fatetur se ignorare. Hodie, post saccharum inventum, multum de mellis pretio decessisse, nemo mirabitur. 7. Additur, apem esse apud omnes ποθεινὴν καὶ ἐπίδοξον, amabilem et claram. Mel enim ubique nascitur, ut notat Plinius libri vigesimi secundi capite vigesimo tertio, et ubique est in pretio, ab ultima Scythia usque ad Afros et Aethiopes. Augustinus, aut quisquis est, Sermone decimo quinto Ad fratres in eremo, scribit, Philosophum, Aristodemum, annis multis insudasse in natura apis investiganda. Sed pro Aristodemo Aristomachum libens scripserim, de quo Plinius libri undecimi capite nono, Ne quis miretur amore earum (apum) captos Aristomachum Solensem duodesexaginta annis nihil aliud egisse: Philiscum vero Thasium, in desertis apes colentem, Agrium cognominatum. 8. Conclusio denique haec est: Quamvis (apis) sit infirma viribus, τὴν σοφίαν τιμήσασα προήχθη, quia sapientiam coluit (id est, sapientiae studio) provecta est. Nempe, ut serpenti prudentia, sic api sapientiae studium tribuitur καταχρηστικῶς, quae naturae instinctu id facit, quae si facerent homines, sapientum catalogo merito inscriberentur. Qua καταχρήσει sapientem esse apem, non pauci scribunt. Ita Lucianus in Halcyone apem appellat σοφὴν θείου μέλιτος ἐργάτιν, sapientem divini mellis opificem. Et Plutarchus Περὶ φιλοστοργίας, Τὴν μέλιτταν ἡμεῖς σοφὴν καλοῦμεν, καὶ νομίζομεν, ξανθὸν μέλι μηδομένην· Apem nos sapientem III, 372 vocamus et censemus, quia mel flavum operatur. Phile capite vigesimo septimo de ape,

Know that this figure is irony. For who is there who does not know that the labour of the bee is honey? Further, it is truly said that honey is used πρὸς ὑγίειαν [pros hygieian], for health. For so the ancients hold. Hippocrates, chapter 50 of On Affections: Μέλι, ξὺν ἑτέροις ἐσθιόμενον, καὶ τρέφει, καὶ εὔχροιαν παρέχει [Meli, xyn heterois esthiomenon, kai trephei, kai euchroian parechei]; Honey, eaten with other things, both nourishes and gives a good colour. And in chapter 54: Οἶνος καὶ μέλι κάλλιστα κέκριται ἐν ἀνθρώποισι, ἢν πρὸς φύσιν καὶ ὑγιαίνουσι, καὶ ἀσθενέουσι, σὺν καιρῷ, καὶ μετριότητι, προσφέρονται [Oinos kai meli kallista kekritai en anthrōpoisi, ēn pros physin kai hygiainousi, kai astheneousi, syn kairō, kai metriotēti, prospherontai]; Wine and honey have been judged best for human beings, if they are given in accordance with nature to both the healthy and the weak, at the right time and in moderation. Diophanes, book 15 of the Geoponica: Οὐ μόνον ἡδὺ τοῖς χρωμένοις, ἀλλὰ καὶ μακροβίους ποιεῖ· οἱ οὖν γήρᾳ μέλιτι μετὰ ἄρτου μόνου τρεφόμενοι, ἐπὶ πλεῖστον βιοῦσι· καὶ τὰς αἰσθήσεις δὲ διαφυλάττει πάσας ἐῤῥωμένας [Ou monon hēdy tois chrōmenois, alla kai makrobious poiei; hoi oun gēra meliti meta artou monou trephomenoi, epi pleiston biousi; kai tas aisthēseis de diaphylattei pasas errōmenas]. Honey is not only pleasant to those who use it, but also makes them long-lived. So those who in old age eat honey with bread alone live a long time; and that food keeps the senses vigorous. Accordingly, Λύκος πολυχρονίους φησὶν εἶναι τοὺς Κυρνίους, διὰ τὸ μέλιτι ἀεὶ χρῆσθαι [Lykos polychronious phēsin einai tous Kyrnious, dia to meliti aei chrēsthai]: Lycus reports that the Corsicans are long-lived, because they always use honey. So Athenaeus, book 2, chapter 7. And in the same place: Τῶν Πυθαγορικῶν τροφὴ ἄρτος μετὰ μέλιτος, ὥς φησι Ἀριστόξενος, τοὺς προσφερομένους αὐτὰ ἀεὶ ἐπ᾽ ἀρίστῳ λέγων ἀνόσως διατελεῖν [Tōn Pythagorikōn trophē artos meta melitos, hōs phēsi Aristoxenos, tous prospheromenous auta aei ep' aristō legōn anosōs diatelein]. Aristoxenus writes that the food of the Pythagoreans was bread with honey, adding that those who always take these at their midday meal live free of disease. They seem to have learned this from their teacher, Pythagoras, of whom Eustathius on Iliad λ᾽ [l']: Ὡς δὲ καὶ τρόφιμον τὸ μέλι Πυθαγορᾶς μαρτυρεῖ, ὃς, εὐτελέστατα διαβιοὺς, πολλάκις μέλιτι μόνῳ ἠρκεῖτο [Hōs de kai trophimon to meli Pythagoras martyrei, hos, eutelestata diabious, pollakis meliti monō ērkeito]. Pythagoras also testifies that honey can nourish; living very frugally, he was mostly content with honey alone. To the same effect is the old proverb about Glaucus, Γλαῦκος πινὼν μέλι ἀνέστη [Glaukos pinōn meli anestē]: Glaucus, having drunk honey, came back to life; that is, if I grasp the meaning of the Paroemiographer, he recovered from a grave illness. And Athenaeus writes of Democritus that, when he had already been given up for dead, διαζῆσαι ἡμέρας ἱκανὰς, τῇ ἀπὸ τοῦ μέλιτος ἀναφορᾷ μόνῃ τρεφόμενον [diazēsai hēmeras hikanas, tē apo tou melitos anaphora monē trephomenon], he prolonged his life for some days, nourished only by the smell of honey. For, as follows in the same place, he took the greatest delight in the use of honey. So Πρὸς τὸν πυθόμενον, Πῶς ἂν ὑγιῶς τις διάγοι; ἔφη, Εἰ τὰ μὲν ἐντὸς μέλιτι βρέχοι, τὰ δὲ ἐκτὸς ἐλαίῳ [Pros ton pythomenon, Pōs an hygiōs tis diagoi? ephē, Ei ta men entos meliti brechoi, ta de ektos elaiō]; col. 515 to one who asked how a person might live his life in health, he replied: if the inner parts of the body were moistened with honey, the outer with oil. Not much differently Diophanes: Δημόκριτος δὲ, ἐρωτηθεὶς, Πῶς ἂν ἄνοσοι καὶ μακραίωνες γίγνοιντο οἱ ἄνθρωποι; εἶπεν, Εἰ τὰ μὲν ἔξωθεν ἐλαίῳ τοῦ σώματος, τὰ δὲ ἔνδοθεν μέλιτι [Dēmokritos de, erōtētheis, Pōs an anosoi kai makraiōnes gignointo hoi anthrōpoi? eipen, Ei ta men exōthen elaiō tou sōmatos, ta de endothen meliti] III, 371 χρήσαιντο [chrēsainto]. For this I would prefer χρίσαιντο [chrisainto]. From the same source is drawn the saying of Pollio, of which Pliny, book 22, chapter 24: Many have sustained a long old age on the nourishment of mead alone, with no other food at all, as in the famous example of Pollio Romulus. When he was past his hundredth year, the Divine Augustus, his guest, asked him by what means above all he had preserved that vigour of mind and body. And he replied: within by mead, without by oil. Mulsum [mead], that is, τῷ οἰνομέλιτι [tō oinomeliti]. It is clear, then, that honey is rightly placed among the dishes of kings and great men. This is easily proved by examples taken from Scripture. Thus honey is sent as a choice gift to Joseph, viceroy of Egypt, Gen 43:11 and to King David, when he was in the town of Mahanaim, neighbouring nobles offered honey, 2 Sam 17:29 Solomon too speaks thus, Song 5:1. I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey. Not to mention Jonathan, the king's son, whose eyes and strength were restored by eating honey, 1 Sam 14:27. If we add profane sources to these, in Iliad λ΄ [l'], line 630, we shall find that Hecamede set before Nestor and Patroclus at a banquet μέλι χλωρὸν [meli chlōron], yellow honey, or fresh honey. And in Odyssey υ΄ [y'], line 69, that Venus nourished the daughters of Pandarus τυρῷ, καὶ μέλιτι γλυκερῷ [tyrō, kai meliti glykerō], with cheese and sweet honey. So Suetonius on Nero, chapter 27: He also imposed dinners on his friends, of which one cost four million sesterces for the honeyed dishes; that is, one hundred thousand gold pieces, by Budé's reckoning. But the word mellita [honeyed dishes], which the common editions have, the most learned Casaubon changed into mitellita, because the oldest manuscripts read so. Yet he candidly admits that he does not know what mitellita are. Today, since the invention of sugar, no one will be surprised that honey has lost much of its value. 7. It is added that the bee is ποθεινὴν καὶ ἐπίδοξον [potheinēn kai epidoxon], beloved and renowned, among all. For honey is produced everywhere, as Pliny notes, book 22, chapter 23, and it is valued everywhere, from farthest Scythia to the Africans and Ethiopians. Augustine, or whoever the author is, in Sermon 15 To the Brothers in the Desert, writes that the philosopher Aristodemus toiled for many years in investigating the nature of the bee. But for Aristodemus I would gladly write Aristomachus, of whom Pliny, book 11, chapter 9: Let no one wonder that men have been captivated by love of them (the bees), that Aristomachus of Soli did nothing else for fifty-eight years, while Philiscus of Thasos, who kept bees in the wilderness, was surnamed Agrius [the Wild]. 8. Finally, the conclusion is this: Although (the bee) is weak in strength, τὴν σοφίαν τιμήσασα προήχθη [tēn sophian timēsasa proēchthē], because she honoured wisdom (that is, through the pursuit of wisdom) she has been advanced. That is, as prudence is ascribed to the serpent, so the pursuit of wisdom is ascribed to the bee καταχρηστικῶς [katachrēstikōs], since she does by natural instinct what, if human beings did it, would rightly enrol them in the catalogue of the wise. By this καταχρήσει [katachrēsei] not a few write that the bee is wise. Thus Lucian in the Halcyon calls the bee σοφὴν θείου μέλιτος ἐργάτιν [sophēn theiou melitos ergatin], the wise maker of divine honey. And Plutarch, Περὶ φιλοστοργίας [Peri philostorgias]: Τὴν μέλιτταν ἡμεῖς σοφὴν καλοῦμεν, καὶ νομίζομεν, ξανθὸν μέλι μηδομένην [Tēn melittan hēmeis sophēn kaloumen, kai nomizomen, xanthon meli mēdomenēn]; We call and consider the bee wise III, 372 because she produces yellow honey. Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)], chapter 27, on the bee,


Ἡ σύντονος δ᾽ οὖν, καὶ σοφὴ, καὶ τεχνικὴ,

Ἡ σύντονος δ᾽ οὖν, καὶ σοφὴ, καὶ τεχνικὴ, [Hē syntonos d' oun, kai sophē, kai technikē,]


Illa igitur vehemens, et sapiens, et artifex. Et capite vigesimo octavo,

She, then, energetic, and wise, and skilled in craft. And in chapter 28,


Καὶ ζῇ μὲν ἁγνὸν ἡ σοφὴ σχεδὸν βίον,

Καὶ ζῇ μὲν ἁγνὸν ἡ σοφὴ σχεδὸν βίον, [Kai zē men hagnon hē sophē schedon bion,]


Et sapiens puram vitam solet vivere. Pisidas De mundi opificio versu 137.

And the wise one is wont to live a pure life. Pisides, De mundi opificio, verse 137:


Τίς τὴν μέλιτταν τὴν σοφὴν τὴν ἐργάτιν col. 516
Γεωμετρεῖν ἔπεισε, καὶ τριωρόφους
Οἴκους ἐγείρειν ἑξαγώνων κτισμάτων;

Τίς τὴν μέλιτταν τὴν σοφὴν τὴν ἐργάτιν col. 516 Γεωμετρεῖν ἔπεισε, καὶ τριωρόφους Οἴκους ἐγείρειν ἑξαγώνων κτισμάτων; [Tis tēn melittan tēn sophēn tēn ergatin geōmetrein epeise, kai triōrophous oikous egeirein hexagōnōn ktismatōn?]


Quis apem sapientem opificem geometriam exercere induxit, et trium contignationum domos excitare hexagono aedificio? Et infra,

Who induced the wise, craftsmanlike bee to practise geometry, and to raise houses of three storeys in hexagonal construction? And further on,


Μή που σε κέντρον τῆς σοφῆς διδασκάλου
Πλήξῃ μελίττης, καὶ μαθεῖν ἀναγκάσῃ·

Μή που σε κέντρον τῆς σοφῆς διδασκάλου Πλήξῃ μελίττης, καὶ μαθεῖν ἀναγκάσῃ· [Mē pou se kentron tēs sophēs didaskalou plēxē melittēs, kai mathein anankasē;]


Ne sapientis magistrae apis aculeus te percutiat et discere cogat. Didymus libro decimo quinto Geoponicῶn, Ἡ μέλιττα πάντων τῶν λοιπῶν ζώων ἐστὶ σοφωτά-τη, καὶ εὐμηχανωτάτη, καὶ σύνεγγυς ἀνθρώπῳ κατὰ τὸ συνετόν: Apis est omnium animalium sapientissima, et artificiosissima, et ad hominis solertiam maxime accedens. Poeta denique, poetico more rem in majus efferens, voluit apes partem habere divinae mentis. Verba sunt,

Lest the sting of the bee, that wise teacher, strike you and compel you to learn. Didymus, in book 15 of the Geoponica: Ἡ μέλιττα πάντων τῶν λοιπῶν ζώων ἐστὶ σοφωτάτη, καὶ εὐμηχανωτάτη, καὶ σύνεγγυς ἀνθρώπῳ κατὰ τὸ συνετόν [Hē melitta pantōn tōn loipōn zōōn esti sophōtatē, kai eumēchanōtatē, kai synengys anthrōpō kata to syneton]: The bee is the wisest and most ingenious of all animals, and comes closest to the shrewdness of man. Finally the Poet, magnifying the matter in poetic fashion, held that bees have a share of the divine mind. His words are:


His quidam signis atque haec exempla sequuti
Esse apibus partem divinae mentis, et haustus
Aethereos dixere. — — — —

Following these signs and these examples, some have said that bees have a share of the divine mind and draughts of the ether. — — — —


Tertius de apum mellificio locus ex eo libro sumtus est, qui neque Hebraice exstat, neque ab Hebraeis pro canonico agnoscitur. Sed verba Graeca sic habent Ecclesiastici XI, 3. Μικρὰ ἐν πετεινοῖς μέλισσα, καὶ ἀρχὴ γλυκασμά-των ὁ καρπὸς αὐτῆς· Parva in volucribus est apis, et principium dulcedinum est fructus ejus. Parva in volucribus; id est, una e minimis, non absolute minima volucrium, ut hic habet Drusius. Nam ape minores sunt musca et culex. Sic Beth-lehem parva fuit in millibus Iuda, non tamen minima omnium, Matth. II, 6. Principium dulcedinum: id est, summe dulcis, primas tenet inter dulcia. Ut Amos VI, 6. ראשית שמנים, principio unguentorum ungunt se, id est, unguento primario. Nempe inter dulcia primas tenet apis fructus, qui est mel. Unde Hebraeum proverbium, Dulce ut mel, de quo infra. Iungendus est hic de ape versus cum proxime praecedente, Μὴ αἰνέσῃς ἄνδρα ἐν κάλλει αὐτοῦ, καὶ μὴ βδελύξῃ ἄνθρωπον ἐν ὁράσει αὐτοῦ. Non laudaveris virum ob pulchritudinem III, 373 ejus, neque hominem dedignare propter speciem ejus. Quibus verbis non significat, homini a forma nihil accedere commendationis; nam

The third passage on the honey-making of bees is taken from a book which neither survives in Hebrew nor is acknowledged as canonical by the Hebrews. The Greek words of Ecclesiasticus XI, 3. run thus: Μικρὰ ἐν πετεινοῖς μέλισσα, καὶ ἀρχὴ γλυκασμάτων ὁ καρπὸς αὐτῆς· [Mikra en peteinois melissa, kai archē glykasmatōn ho karpos autēs;] The bee is small among flying creatures, and her fruit is the beginning of sweet things. Small among flying creatures: that is, one of the smallest, not absolutely the smallest of flying creatures, as Drusius has it here. For the fly and the gnat are smaller than the bee. Thus Bethlehem was small among the thousands of Judah, yet not the least of all, Matt 2:6 The beginning of sweet things: that is, supremely sweet, holding first place among sweet things. As in Amos 6:6. ראשית שמנים, they anoint themselves with the beginning of ointments, that is, with the chief ointment. For the fruit of the bee, which is honey, holds first place among sweet things. Hence the Hebrew proverb, Sweet as honey, of which below. This verse about the bee must be joined with the one immediately preceding: Μὴ αἰνέσῃς ἄνδρα ἐν κάλλει αὐτοῦ, καὶ μὴ βδελύξῃ ἄνθρωπον ἐν ὁράσει αὐτοῦ [Mē ainesēs andra en kallei autou, kai mē bdelyxē anthrōpon en horasei autou]. Do not praise a man for his beauty III, 373, nor disdain a man because of his appearance. By these words he does not mean that a man gains no recommendation from his looks; for


Gratior est pulchro veniens e corpore virtus:

Virtue is more pleasing when it comes from a handsome body:


Solum igitur vult, viri laudem in eo potissimum non esse sitam, quod forma sit eximius; cum vera laus non tam in corporis, quam in animi bonis consistat. Proinde neque quisquam propter externam speciem spernendus est. Puta, si sit deformior, aut statura brevior. Saepe enim

He means only that a man's praise does not chiefly lie in his being outstanding in form, since true praise consists not so much in goods of the body as in goods of the mind. Accordingly, no one is to be despised for his outward appearance, say, if he is rather ugly or short of stature. For often


Major in exiguo regnavit corpore virtus.

Greater virtue has reigned in a slight body.


Quod probatur apis exemplo, quae, quamlibet parva, tamen producit fructum insignis dulcedinis. Cum haec auctoris sit vera mens, tamen Epiphanium, in Physiologo capite vigesimo primo, eundem locum multo aliter intellexisse, probant illius verba, A sapiente dicitur, parva in volucribus est apis; et principium dulcedinum fructus illius. Sic etiam Dei opera sunt ἀνεξιχνίαστα ἐν ἀνθρώποις, καὶ θαυμαστὰ ἐν ὑψηλοῖς, καὶ γλυκύτερα ὑπὲρ μέλι, inscrutabilia in hominibus, et mirabilia in excelsis, et melle dulciora. Quae ex parte petita sunt ex ejusdem Sirachidis versu quinto, Ὅτι θαυμαστὰ τὰ ἔργα Κυρίου, καὶ κρυπτὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ ἐν ἀνθρώποις· quasi quintus ille versus cum tertio cohaereret, qui est de ape: cum cohaereat cum quarto proxime praecedenti, quo homini dixerat, non esse gloriandum, nec esse, cur se efferat, cum ab aliis honoratur. Nam Deus, cujus opera (id est, judicia,) mira sunt et inscrutabilia, potest superbos uno momento de statu suo dejicere, et in ruinam impellere: ut Nabuchodonozori obtigit, Dan. IV, 31. et Herodi, Act. XII, 23. Quem verum esse loci sensum, confirmant sequentia versu sexto et septimo de tyrannis, solo afflictis, et potenti-bus, ignominia affectis, et illustribus, traditis in manus aliorum.

This is proved by the example of the bee, which, however small, yet produces a fruit of remarkable sweetness. Although this is the true meaning of the author, nevertheless Epiphanius, in the Physiologus, chapter 21, understood the same passage quite differently, as his words show: It is said by the wise man: the bee is small among flying creatures, and her fruit is the beginning of sweet things. So too the works of God are ἀνεξιχνίαστα ἐν ἀνθρώποις, καὶ θαυμαστὰ ἐν ὑψηλοῖς, καὶ γλυκύτερα ὑπὲρ μέλι [anexichniasta en anthrōpois, kai thaumasta en hypsēlois, kai glykytera hyper meli], inscrutable among men, and wonderful in the heights, and sweeter than honey. This is partly drawn from verse 5 of the same Sirach: Ὅτι θαυμαστὰ τὰ ἔργα Κυρίου, καὶ κρυπτὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ ἐν ἀνθρώποις· [Hoti thaumasta ta erga Kyriou, kai krypta ta erga autou en anthrōpois;] as if that fifth verse were connected with the third, which is about the bee. But it is connected with the fourth, immediately preceding, in which he had told man not to boast, and that there is no reason for him to exalt himself when he is honoured by others. For God, whose works (that is, judgements) are wonderful and inscrutable, can in a single moment cast the proud down from their station and drive them to ruin, as befell Nebuchadnezzar, Dan 4:31 and Herod, Acts 12:23. That this is the true sense of the passage is confirmed by what follows in verses 6 and 7 about tyrants brought down to the ground, the mighty covered with disgrace, and the illustrious delivered into the hands of others.


Part 2, Book 4, chapter 12: Honey and wax

III, 374 CAP. XII. col. 517

III, 374 Chapter 12. col. 517


De melle et cera.

On honey and wax.


Sequitur, ut de melle dicamus, de quo Scriptura passim. Mel Hebraice voca- col. 518 tur דבש debas, aequivoco nomine, quo appellantur etiam dactyli. Kimchius in Lexico, ונקראו התמרים דבש, Etiam dactylos DEBAS (id est, mel) vocarunt. Quomodo sumi volunt R. Selomo et idem Kimchius 2 Paral. XXXI, 6. ubi Israelitae leguntur obtulisse primitias frumenti, musti et olei, ודבש, et debas, id est, inquiunt, dactylorum. Addit Kimchius, veteres ita sumere Deut. VIII, 8. in quo loco promittit Deus, se eum introducturum in terram זית שמן ודבש, oleae oliferae et debas. Huc facit, quod in Alcamus دبوس dubous sunt خلاص تمر يلقي في مسلاء السمن فيذوب فيه dactyli selectiores, qui in butyrum liquefactum conjiciuntur, ut in eo colliquescant. Et دبس dibs, vel dibis, غسل التمر وغسل النخل mel dactyli et mel palmae, id est, dactyli, vel palmae succus. Qui jure merito cum melle habet commune nomen, cum sit vicini saporis. Iosephus libri quinti De bello Iudaico capite tertio, ubi de valle Ierichuntina: Pulcherrimos paradisos ac densissimos educat, palmarumque irriguarum multa genera, tam sapore, quam nominibus varia. Τούτων οἱ πιότεροι πατούμενοι, καὶ μέλι δαψιλὲς ἀνίασιν, οὐ πολλῷ τοῦ λοιποῦ χεῖρον· Harum pinguissimae calcatae plurimum mellis emittunt, non multo deterius alio melle. Et Iosephus alius, propior quidem tempore, sed loco remotior, Indus nimirum Navigatione capite 138. Mense Augusto Indi palmam putant. Et quoniam tunc arbores potissimum luxuriant, gemunt incisae, lacrymasque instar sauciatae vitis emittunt. Has vasis excipiunt tribus solum diebus ab arbore sauciata, etc. Qui vero saccharum efficere voluerit, is aquam hujusmodi sumat emanantem intra triduum, et ahenis impositam tantisper coquat, donec vix tertia pars supersit. Tunc sic decocta mel efficitur suavissimum. Patet igitur, cur ab Hebraeis inditum fuerit mellis nomen vel dactylorum, vel palmae succo (1). Quin R. Selomo in Levit. II, 11. id extendit multo latius, quasi דבש debas significet כל מתיקת פרי, omnem dulcedinem fructus (2). Utut sit, hic agimus de melle proprie dicto.

Next we must speak of honey, which Scripture mentions in many places. In Hebrew honey is col. 518 called דבש debas, an ambiguous name, by which dates are also designated. Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] in his Lexicon: ונקראו התמרים דבש, They also called dates DEBAS (that is, honey). R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] and the same Kimchi wish it to be taken in this way in 2 Chr 31:6, where the Israelites are said to have offered the first fruits of grain, of must and of oil, ודבש, and of debas, that is, they say, of dates. Kimchi adds that the ancients took it thus in Deut 8:8, in which passage God promises that He will bring him into a land זית שמן ודבש, of oil-bearing olives and of debas. To this point belongs the fact that in Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] دبوس [dabūs] dubous are خلاص تمر يلقي في مسلاء السمن فيذوب فيه [khalāṣ tamr yulqā fī maslāʾ al-samn fa-yadhūbu fīhi] choicer dates, which are thrown into melted butter, so as to dissolve in it. And دبس [dibs] dibs, or dibis, is غسل التمر وغسل النخل [ghasl al-tamr wa-ghasl al-nakhl] the honey of the date and the honey of the palm, that is, the juice of the date or of the palm. It rightly shares its name with honey, since its taste is similar. Josephus, The Jewish War, book 5, chapter 3, speaking of the valley of Jericho: It produces most beautiful and very dense gardens, and many kinds of irrigated palms, varying both in taste and in names. Τούτων οἱ πιότεροι πατούμενοι, καὶ μέλι δαψιλὲς ἀνίασιν, οὐ πολλῷ τοῦ λοιποῦ χεῖρον· [Toutōn hoi pioteroi patoumenoi, kai meli dapsiles aniasin, ou pollō tou loipou cheiron] The richest of these, when trodden, give out a great deal of honey, not much inferior to other honey. And another Josephus, closer in time indeed but more remote in place, namely the Indian, in his Voyage, chapter 138: In the month of August the Indians prune the palm. And since the trees are then at their most luxuriant, when cut they groan, and emit tears like a wounded vine. These they catch in vessels for only three days after the tree has been wounded, etc. But whoever wishes to make sugar, let him take water of this kind flowing out within three days, and put it in copper pots and boil it, until scarcely a third part remains. Then, thus boiled down, it becomes a most sweet honey. It is therefore clear why the Hebrews gave the name of honey either to dates or to the juice of the palm R1. Indeed R. Selomo on Lev 2:11 extends it much more widely, as though דבש debas meant כל מתיקת פרי, all sweetness of fruit R2. However that may be, here we are dealing with honey properly so called.


III, 375 Hujus duo sunt genera: domesticum unum, ex apibus, quae domi aluntur; et alterum sylvestre, quali legitur Iohannes in deserto vixisse, Matth. III, 4. Cibus ejus erant locustae et mel sylvestre. Et Marc. I, 6. Comedens locustas et mel sylvestre. Cum ibi μέλι ἄγριον, mel sylvestre diserte scribant Evangelistae duo, mirum, quosdam esse, qui μελαγρίαν intelligant herbae genus, si credimus, in deserto crescentis. Suidas, Μελαγρία· εἶδος βο-τάνης φυομένης ἐν ἐρήμῳ. Alii τὰ μέλαγρα scribunt, quasi herba sit hujus nominis, quam aliter ἀκρίδας vocent. Theophylactus, Τινὲς λέγουσι βοτάνας εἶναι τὰς ἀκρίδας, ἃς καὶ μέλαγρα καλοῦσι· Acridas quidam herbas esse ajunt, quas etiam melagra vocant. Quae utut concederemus, tamen extra rem essent. Neque enim legitur Ioannes comedisse μελαγρίαν, aut μέλαγρα, sed μέλι ἄγριον. Nihilo magis placet, quod afferunt Beda in libro De locis sanctis, et Thomas in Matthaeum ex Arnulpho, vel Archulpho, in deserto Iohannis arbores fuisse latis et rotundis foliis, lactei coloris, et mellei saporis, quae, natura fragi- col. 519 lia, manibus confricentur atque edantur, et hoc dici mel sylvestre. Nec Christiano Druthmaro assentior, cui mel sylvestre hoc loco est illud ipsum Manna, quo filii Israel pasti sunt per quadraginta annos. Mannae quidem sapor fuit כצפיחת בדבש, ut sapor lagani melliti, Exod. XVI, 31. Ac proinde a nonnullis Manna vocatur δροσόμελι ac ἀερόμελι (3). Tamen aliud Manna, aliud sylvestre III, 376 mel. Nec scripturae vocibus novae notiones sunt affingendae, cum receptae quadrare possunt. Hic igitur nihil quidquam intelligo, quam locustas et mel sylvestre. Et locustas jam probavimus a) in illis locis esse frequentes, adeoque in cibis receptas. Idem de sylvestri melle vel ex ipsa Scriptura probare est obvium. Notum est illud Solomonis Prov. XXV, 16. Mel reperisti? comede, quantum satis est. Et haud dubie pertinet ad sylvestre mel, quod in agris passim reperiebatur. Ita cum in agro Samson in leonem incidisset, eumque dilacerasset, III, 377 anno sequente mel reperit, quod in ejus cadavere apes elaboraverant, Iud. XIV, 8. Quale est, quod legitur 1 Sam. XIV, 25. 26. Populus venit in sylvam, in qua erat mel על פני השדה, in agri superficie. Et in eam sylvam populus ingressus est, et ecce הלך דבש, fluxum mellis. Id nempe fuit sylvestre mel, quod apes vel in nudo solo, vel in cavis arborum, vel in fissuris rupium confecerant. Qualis rupes Hebraice vocatur צור דבש, rupes mellis, Ps. LXXXI, 17. Et mel inde manans דבש מסלע, mel e petra, Deut. XXXII, 13. Sic a voce יער jaar, quae sylvam sonat, (ut jar Punice lignum apud Augustinum in Psalmum XXIII.), יער jaar, vel יערה jaara, est favus proprie in sylva repertus. Ut 1 Sam. XIV, 27. Extendit Ionathan summitatem virgae, quam habebat in manu, et immersit eam ביערת הדבש, in favum mellis. Et Cant. V, 1. Comedi יערי, favum meum cum melle meo (4). Neque est, quod quis hoc credat Iudaeae fuisse peculiare, quod ibi passim apes in agris aut sylvis mellificabant. Nam idem de Scythia et Moscovia, ex idoneis scriptoribus jam b) didicimus. Et Maldonatus in Matthaeum refert, se pauperes homines in Boetica vidisse, qui mel ex sylvis colligerent, eoque vendendo quaestum factitarent. Itaque apum, III, 378 quae vel in cavis arborum, vel in arundinetis, aut in antris nidificant, poetae passim meminere. Hesiodus Theogoniae versu 230.

III, 375 Of this there are two kinds: one domestic, from bees that are kept at home; the other wild, such as John is said to have lived on in the desert, Matt 3:4. His food was locusts and wild honey. And Mark 1:6. Eating locusts and wild honey. Since the two Evangelists expressly write μέλι ἄγριον [meli agrion], wild honey, it is surprising that there are some who understand μελαγρίαν [melagrian] as a kind of plant which, if we believe them, grows in the desert. Suidas: Μελαγρία· εἶδος βοτάνης φυομένης ἐν ἐρήμῳ [Melagria; eidos botanēs phyomenēs en erēmō]. Others write τὰ μέλαγρα [ta melagra], as though there were a plant of this name, which they otherwise call ἀκρίδας [akridas]. Theophylact: Τινὲς λέγουσι βοτάνας εἶναι τὰς ἀκρίδας, ἃς καὶ μέλαγρα καλοῦσι [Tines legousi botanas einai tas akridas, has kai melagra kalousi]; Some say that the acrides are plants, which they also call melagra. Even if we granted this, it would still be beside the point. For we do not read that John ate μελαγρίαν [melagrian] or μέλαγρα [melagra], but μέλι ἄγριον [meli agrion]. No more acceptable is what Bede in his book De locis sanctis, and Thomas on Matthew, report from Arnulphus or Archulphus: that in the desert of John there were trees with broad, round leaves, of milky colour and honeyed taste, which, being naturally brittle, are rubbed in the hands and eaten, and that this is called wild honey. col. 519 Nor do I agree with Christianus Druthmarus, for whom the wild honey in this passage is that very Manna on which the children of Israel were fed for forty years. The taste of Manna was indeed כצפיחת בדבש, like the taste of a honeyed wafer, Exod 16:31. And accordingly Manna is called by some δροσόμελι [drosomeli] and ἀερόμελι [aeromeli] R3. Yet Manna is one thing, wild III, 376 honey another. Nor should new meanings be foisted onto the words of Scripture when the received ones can fit. Here, therefore, I understand nothing other than locusts and wild honey. And we have already shown a) that locusts are frequent in those regions and therefore were accepted as food. The same about wild honey is easy to prove from Scripture itself. Well known is the saying of Solomon, Prov 25:16: Have you found honey? Eat as much as is sufficient. And this doubtless refers to wild honey, which was found here and there in the fields. Thus when Samson had come upon a lion in the field and torn it apart, III, 377 in the following year he found honey which bees had produced in its carcass, Iud. XIV, 8. Of the same kind is what we read in 1 Sam. XIV, 25. 26: The people came into the forest, in which there was honey על פני השדה, on the surface of the field. And the people entered that forest, and behold הלך דבש, a flow of honey. This, namely, was wild honey, which bees had made either on the bare ground, or in hollow trees, or in clefts of rocks. Such a rock is called in Hebrew צור דבש, rock of honey, Ps 81:17. And the honey flowing from it is דבש מסלע, honey from the rock, Deut 32:13. So from the word יער jaar, which means forest (as jar in Punic means wood according to Augustine on Psalm 23), יער jaar, or יערה jaara, is a honeycomb, properly one found in the forest. As in 1 Sam. XIV, 27: Jonathan stretched out the tip of the rod that he had in his hand, and dipped it ביערת הדבש, in the honeycomb. And Cant. V, 1: I have eaten יערי, my honeycomb with my honey R4. Nor is there reason for anyone to believe that it was peculiar to Judaea that bees made honey here and there in fields or forests. For we have already learned b) the same of Scythia and Muscovy from reliable writers. And Maldonatus on Matthew reports that he saw poor men in Baetica who gathered honey from the forests and made their living by selling it. Accordingly the poets frequently mention bees III, 378 that nest in hollow trees, in reed-beds, or in caves. Hesiod, Theogony, line 230:


— — — οὔρεσι δὲ δρῦς
Ἄκρη μέν τε φέρει βαλάνους, μέσση δὲ μελίσσας,

— — — οὔρεσι δὲ δρῦς Ἄκρη μέν τε φέρει βαλάνους, μέσση δὲ μελίσσας, [ouresi de drys / akrē men te pherei balanous, messē de melissas,]


In montibus autem summa quidem quercus fert glandes, media autem apes. Nempe ἐν τοῖς κοιλώμασι τῶν στελέχων, in truncorum cavis; ut ibi Scholiastes. Phocylides, aut quisquis est, in Νουθετικῷ versu 160.

On the mountains the oak bears acorns at its top, and bees in its middle. That is, ἐν τοῖς κοιλώμασι τῶν στελέχων [en tois koilōmasi tōn stelechōn], in the hollows of the trunks, as the Scholiast there explains. Phocylides, or whoever he is, in the Νουθετικῷ [Nouthetikō], line 160:


Κάμνει δ' ἠερόφοιτος, ἀριστοπόνος τε μέλισσα,
Ἠὲ πέτρης κοίλης κατὰ χηραμὸν, ἢ δονάκεσσιν,
Ἢ δρυὸς ὠγυγίης κατὰ κοιλάδος·

Κάμνει δ' ἠερόφοιτος, ἀριστοπόνος τε μέλισσα, Ἠὲ πέτρης κοίλης κατὰ χηραμὸν, ἢ δονάκεσσιν, Ἢ δρυὸς ὠγυγίης κατὰ κοιλάδος· [Kamnei d' ēerophoitos, aristoponos te melissa, / Ēe petrēs koilēs kata chēramon, ē donakessin, / Ē dryos ōgygiēs kata koilados;]


Operatur quoque aëria et laboriosa apis, aut in antro cavae petrae, aut in arundinibus, aut in antiquae quercus cavitate. Virgilius libro quarto Georgicorum [vs. 43. seqq.].

The air-roaming and hard-working bee also labours, either in the cave of a hollow rock, or among reeds, or in the hollow of an ancient oak. Virgil, Georgics, book 4 [vv. 43 ff.]:


Saepe etiam effossis (si vera est fama) latebris
Sub terra fodere larem, penitusque repertae,
Pumicibusque cavis, exesaeque arboris antro.

Often too (if the report is true) they have made their home in hollows dug beneath the earth, and have been found deep within porous rocks and in the cavity of a hollowed tree.

Quale est, quod Iob. XX, 17. memorantur נחלי דבש וחמאה, torrentes mellis et butyri. Quae locutio sic est hyperbolica, ut melli ex parte conveniat; quia e favo mel defluit, cum copiosum est. Mellis ille fluxus apud Hebraeos et Sy- ros varie signficatur. Primo voce הלך halach, quae proprie est ire, vel ince- dere. Sed 1 Sam. XIV, 26. הלך דבש est fluxus mellis. Ita in Ovidio supra,

Such is the mention in Iob. XX, 17 of נחלי דבש וחמאה, torrents of honey and butter. This expression is hyperbolic in such a way that it partly suits honey, because honey flows down from the comb when it is abundant. This flowing of honey is expressed in various ways among the Hebrews and Syrians. First by the word הלך halach, which properly means to go or to walk. But in 1 Sam 14:26, הלך דבש is a flow of honey. So in Ovid above:


— — jam flumina nectaris ibant,

— — now rivers of nectar went [flowed],


id est, fluebant. Secundo, nomine נופת nopheth, quod distillationem sonat, ut נוף nuph, Verbum stillare, vel aspergere. Sic Psal. XIX, 11. נופת צופים est distillatio favorum. Et Cant. IV, 11. נופת תטפנה, Distillationem stillant labia tua. Et Prov. V, 3. Distillationem stillant labia meretricis. Ut Prov. XXIV, 13. ונופת, Et distillatio dulcis est palato tuo. Et Prov. XXVII, 7. Anima satu- rata calcat נופת, stillationem, supple mellis, aut favorum. Id enim ubique supplendum. Tertio, a Verbo צוף, id est, fluere, צוף tsuph nomen est favus proprie fluens. Sic Prov. XVI, 24. צוף דבש, mellis favus (fluens sunt) sermones amoeni. Et Psal. XIX, 11. Iudicia Domini melle dulciora sunt, ונופת צופים, et distillatione favorum (fluentium). Quarto, Verbum רדה rada, quod Hebraei accipere reddunt, Syri Iud. XIV, 9. ex suae linguae idiotismo referunt ad mellis fluxum, quia illis ܢܕܼ fluere est. Itaque haec verba de melle, a Samsone reperto, וירדהו אל כפיו, Et accepit illud in manus suas, a Syro interprete sic exponuntur: ܘܢܕܼ ܗܘܐ ܕܒܫܐ ܥܠ ܐܝܕܘܗܝ ܘܡܗܠܟ Et defluebat mel super manus ejus, et ibat. Et rursus in eodem versu, Non significavit ipsis, quod e corpore leonis רדה הדבש, sumpserat mel. Ita Hebraei; sed Syri ܢܕܼ ܕܒܫܐ, fluxerat mel: ut 1 Sam. XIV, 25. (vel 26.) ܘܢܕܼ ܗܘܐ ܕܒܫܐ Et fluebat illud mel. Quinto, ibidem Chaldaeo fluxus mellis est בריז דובשא. Nempe برز baraza Arabice est egredi. Inde בריז brez, vel briz Chaldaice est fluxus mellis, ex favo egredientis. Quo fortasse pertinet, quod mellis inventor, Bacchus, Brisaeus dicebatur, aut Bressaeus. Thus in Ps 19:11. נופת צופים is the distillation of honeycombs. And in Song 4:11. נופת תטפנה, Your lips drip distillation. And in Prov 5:3. The lips of a harlot drip distillation.
