Then to you, Alecto, and to you, never joyful Megaera, the chosen bodies of woolly two-year-old sheep fall down;
they pour honey over them, and the tribute of Bacchus and of milk.


Sed ut doceamus simul et semel, nullum fuisse deorum, qui melle gaudere non crederetur, legendus est Pausanias in Eliacis prioribus, ubi, postquam aras minimum quinquaginta recensuit, in Iovis Olympii templo variis numinibus erectas, et quasdam in illo censu omnibus diis sacras; Ἑκάστου δὲ ἅπαξ τοῦ μηνὸς (inquit) θύουσιν ἐπὶ πάντων Ἠλεῖοι τῶν κατειλεγμένων βωμῶν, θύουσι δὲ ἀρ- col. 530 χαῖόν τινα τρόπον· λιβανωτὸν γὰρ ὁμοῦ πυροῖς μεμιγμένοις μέλιτι θυμιῶσιν ἐπὶ τὸν βωμόν. Semel quolibet mense ad omnes, quas recensuimus, aras Elëi sacra faciunt, vetusto quodam ritu, thura et melle subactum triticum adolentes. Persas etiam describit Strabo libro decimo quinto in omnibus sacrificiis ἀποσπέν-δοντας ἔλαιον, ὁμοῦ γάλακτι καὶ μέλιτι κεκραμένον, oleum, cum lacte et melle mixtum, libantes. Proinde Homerus, vel quisquis est, Hymno in Mercurium, mel vocat

But to show once and for all that there was no god who was not believed to delight in honey, one should read Pausanias in the First Book of Elis. There, after listing at least fifty altars erected to various deities in the temple of Olympian Zeus, some of them in that list sacred to all the gods, he says: Ἑκάστου δὲ ἅπαξ τοῦ μηνὸς θύουσιν ἐπὶ πάντων Ἠλεῖοι τῶν κατειλεγμένων βωμῶν, θύουσι δὲ ἀρ- col. 530 χαῖόν τινα τρόπον· λιβανωτὸν γὰρ ὁμοῦ πυροῖς μεμιγμένοις μέλιτι θυμιῶσιν ἐπὶ τὸν βωμόν [Hekastou de hapax tou mēnos thyousin epi pantōn Ēleioi tōn kateilegmenōn bōmōn, thyousi de archaion tina tropon; libanōton gar homou pyrois memigmenois meliti thymiōsin epi ton bōmon]. Once every month the Eleans sacrifice at all the altars we have listed, by a certain ancient rite, burning frankincense together with wheat kneaded with honey. Strabo, book 15, also describes the Persians in all their sacrifices as ἀποσπένδοντας ἔλαιον, ὁμοῦ γάλακτι καὶ μέλιτι κεκραμένον [apospendontas elaion, homou galakti kai meliti kekramenon], pouring libations of oil mixed with milk and honey. Accordingly Homer, or whoever it is, in the Hymn to Hermes, calls honey


— — — Θεῶν ἡδεῖαν ἐδωδὴν,

— — — Θεῶν ἡδεῖαν ἐδωδὴν, [Theōn hēdeian edōdēn]


Deorum suavem cibum. Et mus, in Batrachomyomachia ranae suas delicias cum jactantia enumerans; Non me fugit, inquit, panis ter pistus non placenta sesamo condita, non pernae frusta, non jecora, non caseus,

the sweet food of the gods. And the mouse in the Batrachomyomachia, boastfully listing his delicacies to the frog, says: I do not lack thrice-kneaded bread, nor cake seasoned with sesame, nor slices of ham, nor livers, nor cheese,


Οὐ χρηστὸν μελίτωμα, τὸ καὶ μάκαρες ποθέουσιν,

Οὐ χρηστὸν μελίτωμα, τὸ καὶ μάκαρες ποθέουσιν, [Ou chrēston melitōma, to kai makares potheousin]


Non optimum ex melle dulciarium, quod etiam dii desiderant. Cujusmodi sacrificia νηφάλια, καὶ μελίσπονδα, vocat Plutarchus in libro De ira cohibenda, et Symposiacῶn libri quarti quaestione quinta. Taceo frequentem mellis usum inter inferias et libationes pro mortuis. Sic in Patrocli funere Achilles Iliad. ψ′.

nor the excellent honey sweetmeat which even the gods desire. Sacrifices of this kind Plutarch calls νηφάλια, καὶ μελίσπονδα [nēphalia, kai melisponda] in the book On Restraining Anger, and in the Symposiaca, book 4, question 5. I pass over the frequent use of honey among funeral offerings and libations for the dead. Thus Achilles at the funeral of Patroclus, Iliad ψ′ [psi]:


Ἐν δὲ τίθει μέλιτος καὶ ἀλείφατος ἀμφιφορῆας,

Ἐν δὲ τίθει μέλιτος καὶ ἀλείφατος ἀμφιφορῆας, [En de tithei melitos kai aleiphatos amphiphorēas]


Imposuit (feretro) mellis et olei amphoras. Et Odyss. ώ. crematur Achillis cadaver, III, 396 — — ἐντ᾽ ἐσθῆτι θεῶν, καὶ ἀλείφατι πολλῷ, Καὶ μέλιτι γλυκερῷ, — — —

He placed (on the bier) jars of honey and oil. And in Odyssey ώ [ō] the body of Achilles is burned, III, 396 — — ἐντ᾽ ἐσθῆτι θεῶν, καὶ ἀλείφατι πολλῷ, Καὶ μέλιτι γλυκερῷ, — — — [ent' esthēti theōn, kai aleiphati pollō, Kai meliti glykerō]


in veste deorum, et cum oleo multo et melle dulci. Et apud Euripidem Iphigenia in Tauris inferias Oresti, fratri, parat

in the garment of the gods, and with much oil and sweet honey. And in Euripides, Iphigenia in Tauris prepares funeral offerings for her brother Orestes:


Πηγὰς τ᾽ οὐρείων ἐκ μόσχων
Βάκχου τ᾽ οἰνηρὰς λοιβὰς,
Ξουθᾶν τε πόνημα μελισσᾶν,

Πηγὰς τ᾽ οὐρείων ἐκ μόσχων Βάκχου τ᾽ οἰνηρὰς λοιβὰς, Ξουθᾶν τε πόνημα μελισσᾶν, [Pēgas t' oureiōn ek moschōn Bakchou t' oinēras loibas, Xouthan te ponēma melissan]


Fontes sanguinis ex montanis vitulis, et Bacchi vinosam libationem, et flavarum laborem apum. Ita habetur versu 163. Et rursus eundem tanquam moriturum alloquens versu 632,

Streams of blood from mountain calves, and the winy libation of Bacchus, and the labour of the tawny bees. So it reads at line 163. And again, addressing him as one about to die, at line 632:


Πολύν τε γάρ σοι κόσμον ἐνθήσω τάφῳ,
Καὶ τῆς ὀρείας ἀνθεμόῤῥυτον γάνος
Ξουθῆς μελίσσης εἰς πῦρ ἐμβαλῶ σέθεν,

Πολύν τε γάρ σοι κόσμον ἐνθήσω τάφῳ, Καὶ τῆς ὀρείας ἀνθεμόῤῥυτον γάνος Ξουθῆς μελίσσης εἰς πῦρ ἐμβαλῶ σέθεν, [Polyn te gar soi kosmon enthēsō taphō, Kai tēs oreias anthemorrhyton ganos Xouthēs melissēs eis pyr embalō sethen]


Multum enim ornatum tibi in sepulchro ponam, et montanae flavae apis delicias, ex floribus manantes, in rogum tuum injiciam. Taceo item

For I will place much adornment for you in the tomb, and I will cast onto your pyre the delights of the tawny mountain bee, flowing from the flowers. I likewise pass over


Melle soporatam et medicatis frugibus offam,

the cake drugged with honey and medicated grain,


Cerbero ab Aenea objectam. Ubi non probo, quod vir, sui aevi facile doctissimus, y) legendum esse saporatam, tanto molimine contendit. Quamvis enim saporatum pro condito dixerint Tertullianus, Arnobius, Marcellinus, atque alii posterioris aevi scriptores, tamen Augusti aevo vox fuit ignota prorsus, neque a quoquam usurpata. Et, quamvis ullam esse in melle soporandi vim perneget vir eximius, tamen aliter sensisse veteres, Coelius Rhodiginus z) ex Orpheo probat, qui Saturnum a Iove mellis appetitum insidiis, et consopitum fuisse narrat. Quibus addo haec Iamblichi apud Photium auctore 94. Οἱ δὲ τῷ μέλιτι καρω-θέντες μόλις ἀνίστανται. Illi autem, melle soporati, vix expergiscuntur. Sed haec de melle plus satis. Tantum addo, Deum, ob id ipsum, quod in daemonum sacris mellis usus pene perpetuus fuerit, pro impuro illud habuisse, et in suis sacrificiis offerri noluisse (11).

thrown to Cerberus by Aeneas. Here I do not approve of the reading saporatam [flavoured], for which a man easily the most learned of his age y) contends with so much effort. For although Tertullian, Arnobius, Marcellinus and other writers of a later age said saporatum for conditum [seasoned], yet in the age of Augustus the word was entirely unknown and used by no one. And although that excellent man flatly denies that honey has any power to induce sleep, Coelius Rhodiginus z) proves from Orpheus that the ancients thought otherwise: Orpheus relates that Saturn was ensnared by Jupiter through his craving for honey and lulled to sleep. To this I add these words of Iamblichus in Photius, author 94: Οἱ δὲ τῷ μέλιτι καρωθέντες μόλις ἀνίστανται [Hoi de tō meliti karōthentes molis anistantai]. But those stupefied by honey scarcely wake up. But this is more than enough about honey. I add only that God, for the very reason that honey was used almost constantly in the rites of demons, regarded it as impure and did not want it offered in his own sacrifices R11.


III, 397 Alius apis labor est cera, melle non minus utilis. Ex cera enim cerei fiunt, quibus tenebrae fugantur. Martialis,

III, 397 Another product of the bee is wax, no less useful than honey. For from wax are made tapers, by which darkness is put to flight. Martial:


Hic tibi nocturnos praestabit cereus ignes.

This taper will furnish you with fires by night.


Eadem praestat usum glutinis. Virgilius,

It also serves as glue. Virgil:


Pan primus calamos cera conjungere plures
Instituit. — — — — —

Pan first taught to join several reeds with wax. — — — — —


Nec minus cera, quam melle condiebantur cadavera. Sic Herodotus libro quarto Scythas refert regis mortui corpus κατακεκηρωμένον per totam Scythiam circumtulisse, antequam terra conderent. Et libro primo idem de Persis, κατα-κηρώσαντες τὸν νεκρὸν γῇ κρύπτουσι. Unde Cicero libro primo Tusculanarum, Persae jam cera circumlitos condiunt, ut quam maxime permaneant corpora. Et col. 531 Strabo libro decimo quinto, Θάπτουσι δὲ κηρῷ περιπλάσσοντες τὰ σώματα. Itaque موميا mumiae vox notissima, deduci videtur ex موم mum. Persae ceram, et Arabes προπόλιν sic appellant. Et Esaiae verba capitis sexagesimi quarti versu secundo, כקדוח אש המסים מים, Seniores sic reddunt, Ὡς κηρὸς ἀπὸ προσώπου πυρὸς τήκεται. Quia pro מים, id est, aquis, מום, id est, ceram, legerunt. Et כקדם אש, ut coram igne, pro כקדוח אש, ut conflagrat ignis. Itaque jam tum pro cera erat in usu vox מום mum, unde mumia. Cerae etiam multus fuit usus in scriptura, et pugillaribus, et in pictura, et in fuco, et in sigillis, qui hodieque durat. Sed haec sunt alterius loci.

Corpses were embalmed with wax no less than with honey. Thus Herodotus in book 4 reports that the Scythians carried the body of a dead king, κατακεκηρωμένον [katakekērōmenon], throughout all Scythia before burying it. And in book 1 the same author says of the Persians: κατακηρώσαντες τὸν νεκρὸν γῇ κρύπτουσι [katakērōsantes ton nekron gē kryptousi]. Hence Cicero, Tusculan Disputations book 1: the Persians embalm them after coating them with wax, so that the bodies may last as long as possible. And col. 531 Strabo, book 15: Θάπτουσι δὲ κηρῷ περιπλάσσοντες τὰ σώματα [Thaptousi de kērō periplassontes ta sōmata]. So the well-known word موميا [mūmiyā] mumia seems to be derived from موم [mūm] mum. So the Persians call wax, and the Arabs call προπόλιν [propolin]. And the words of Isaiah, chapter 64, verse 2, כקדוח אש המסים מים, the Elders [=the translators of the Septuagint] render thus: Ὡς κηρὸς ἀπὸ προσώπου πυρὸς τήκεται [Hōs kēros apo prosōpou pyros tēketai]. For in place of מים, that is, waters, they read מום, that is, wax; and כקדם אש, as before fire, in place of כקדוח אש, as fire burns. So already at that time the word מום mum was in use for wax, whence mumia. Wax was also much used in writing, in writing tablets, in painting, in cosmetics, and in seals, a use that lasts to this day. But these matters belong elsewhere.


Cum cera, ad ignem liquescente, multa conferunt sacri scriptores. Sic David Psalm. XXII, 15. Cor meum simile cerae est, liquescit, in visceribus meis. Et Psal. LXVIII, 3. Ut coram igne cera liquescit, ita coram Deo improbi pereunt. Et Psal. XCVII, 5. Montes ut cera liquefiunt coram Domino. Et Mich. I, 4. Liquefient montes sub eo, et valles diffindentur, ut cera coram igne. Unde scriptor libri Iudith, quisquis est, capitis decimi sexti versu decimo octavo, Petrae III, 398 a conspectu tuo ut cera liquescent. Ita etiam profani passim. Theocritus in Pharmaceutria,

The sacred writers often compare things with wax melting before fire. Thus David, Ps 22:15: My heart is like wax, it melts within me. And Ps 68:3: As wax melts before fire, so the wicked perish before God. And Ps 97:5: The mountains melt like wax before the Lord. And Mic 1:4: The mountains shall melt under him, and the valleys shall be cleft, like wax before the fire. Hence the writer of the book of Judith, whoever he is, chapter 16, verse 18: The rocks III, 398 shall melt like wax at your presence. So too the profane authors everywhere. Theocritus in the Pharmaceutria:


Ὡς τοῦτον τὸν καρὸν ἐγὼ, σὺν δαίμονι, τάκω,
Ὡς τάκοιθ᾽ ὑπ᾽ ἔρωτος ὁ Μύνδιος αὐτίκα Δέλφις.

Ὡς τοῦτον τὸν καρὸν ἐγὼ, σὺν δαίμονι, τάκω, [Hōs touton ton karon egō, syn daimoni, takō,] Ὡς τάκοιθ᾽ ὑπ᾽ ἔρωτος ὁ Μύνδιος αὐτίκα Δέλφις. [Hōs takoith᾽ hyp᾽ erōtos ho Myndios autika Delphis.]


Ut hanc ceram ego, Deo juvante, liquefacio, ita statim liquescat prae amore Myndius Delphis. Unde Virgilius,

As I, with the god's help, melt this wax, so may Delphis of Myndus at once melt with love. Hence Virgil:


Limus ut hic durescit, et haec ut cera liquescit
Uno eodemque igni, sic nostro Daphnis amore.

As this clay hardens, and as this wax melts in one and the same fire, so may Daphnis with love of me.


Lucretius de nubibus libri sexti versu 512.

Lucretius on clouds, book 6, verse 512:


Praeterea cum rarescunt quoque nubila ventis,
Aut dissolvuntur solis super icta calore,
Mittunt humorem pluvium stillantia, quasi igni
Cera super calido tabescens multa liquescat.

Moreover, when the clouds too are thinned by the winds, or are dissolved when struck from above by the heat of the sun, they let fall rainy moisture, dripping, as when wax wasting over a hot fire melts abundantly.


Ovidius de Narcisso libro tertio Metamorphoseως,

Ovid on Narcissus, book 3 of the Metamorphoses:


Non tulit alterius, sed ut tabescere flavae
Igne levi cerae, matutinaeque pruinae
Sole repente solent: sic attenuatus amore
Liquitur, et tecto paullatim carpitur igni.

He could bear it no longer, but as yellow wax wastes in a gentle fire, and morning frost in the sun, so, worn away by love, he melts and is slowly consumed by a hidden fire.


Et libro decimo de statua Pygmalionis,

And in book 10, on the statue of Pygmalion:

Cera remollescit. — — — —

It yielded under his fingers and gave way, as Hymettian wax softens in the sun. — — — —


Lucanus de Sabello, quem seps serpens momorderat, libri noni versu 783.

Lucan on Sabellus, who had been bitten by the seps serpent, book 9, verse 783:


— — manant humeri, fortesque lacerti,

Nix resoluta cadit, nec solem cera sequetur.

— — his shoulders melt, and his strong arms; his neck and head flow away; not faster does snow dissolve and fall before the warm South Wind, nor will wax yield to the sun.


Asclepiades Anthologiae libri septimi Epigrammate vigesimo sexto,

Asclepiades, Anthology book 7, Epigram 26:


Τήκομαι ὡς κηρὸς παρ᾽ πυρὶ, κάλλος ὁρῶν·

Τήκομαι ὡς κηρὸς παρ᾽ πυρὶ, κάλλος ὁρῶν· [Tēkomai hōs kēros par᾽ pyri, kallos horōn;]


Liquefio ut cera ad ignem, pulchritudinem videns.

I melt like wax at the fire, beholding beauty.


Cera Hebraice dicitur דונג, sed Chaldaice שעוה, unde Hebraeum Verbum השתעה, est cerae instar mollescere, si magistris credimus, qui haec Es. XLI, 10. אל תשתע כי אני אלהיך, in hunc sensum fere reddunt, Ne (ut cera) mollescas, quia ego sum Deus tuus. Ita R. Selomo. Et observat Kimchius, sic interpretari majores suos, nempe in Berescith Rabba sectione 65. his verbis, כיון שאמר III, 399 יצחק ליעקוב גשה נא ואמשוכך בני נשפכו מים על שוקיו והיה לבו רפה כשעוה וזמן לו הקדוש ברוך הוא שני מלאכים אחד בימינו ואחד בשמאלו והיו אוחזין אותו במרפקו כדי שלא יפול הדא הוא דכתיב אל תשתע כי אני אלהיך, Cum Iacobo (sub Esavi veste latenti, ut benedictionem consequeretur) dixit Isaac Genes. XXVII, 21. „Accede, quaeso, fili mi, et tangam te:“ sudore diffluxerunt col. 532 crura ipsius, et cor cerae instar emollitum est. Sed Deus sanctus et benedictus illi praeparavit duos angelos, unum a dextris, alterum a sinistris, qui eum sub axilla tenerent, ne caderet. Unde est, quod dicitur Es. XLI, 10. „Ne (ut cera) mollescas, quia ego sum Deus tuus.“

Wax is called in Hebrew דונג, but in Chaldee שעוה; hence the Hebrew verb השתעה means to soften like wax, if we believe the masters, who render these words of Isa 41:10, אל תשתע כי אני אלהיך, roughly in this sense: Do not soften (like wax), for I am your God. So R. Selomo. And Kimchi observes that his forebears interpreted it thus, namely in Bereshit Rabba, section 65, in these words: כיון שאמר III, 399 יצחק ליעקוב גשה נא ואמשוכך בני נשפכו מים על שוקיו והיה לבו רפה כשעוה וזמן לו הקדוש ברוך הוא שני מלאכים אחד בימינו ואחד בשמאלו והיו אוחזין אותו במרפקו כדי שלא יפול הדא הוא דכתיב אל תשתע כי אני אלהיך, When Isaac said to Jacob (who was hiding under Esau's garment to obtain the blessing), Genes. XXVII, 21. „Come near, I pray, my son, that I may touch you“: his legs ran with sweat, col. 532 and his heart softened like wax. But God, holy and blessed, prepared for him two angels, one on his right, the other on his left, to hold him under the arm so that he would not fall. Hence what is said in Isa 41:10 „Do not soften (like wax), for I am your God.“


Vocem נכאת necoth, perincertae significationis Genes. XXXVII, 25. et XLIII, 11. Ionathan שעוא, et Arabs Erpenianus شمعا, id est, ceram, exponunt, ut et auctor Beresith Rabba sectione 91. prope in fine. Et in Onkelo putant שעך id ipsum esse, quia accedit ad שעוא. Utut sit, alii interpretes multo aliter explicant. LXX θυμίαμα, vel θυμιάματα· Aquila, στύρακα· Hiero- nymus in priore loco aromata, in posteriore storacem, ut Aquila; Syrus ܪ̈ܗܛܢܐ resinam; Samaritanus ࠒࠈࠐ balsamum; Arabs Parisiis editus, خرنوبا, ut apud Kimchium nonnulli חרוב siliquam; Arabes duo manu-scripti in Suecia صمغا gummi; Rabbi Moses Sacerdos, et Kimchius, דבר נחמד, rem desidera- bilem; Rabbi Selomo, כנוסי בשמים הרבה, collectiones plurium aromatum. Posteriores in re dubia e vetustioribus hunc, vel illum sequuntur, prout visum est. Solus Iunius, privatam insistens viam, myxaria reddidit, quae Arabice, inquit, dicuntur NUKETA, teste Aegineta, Aëtio, Psello et Actuario, voce pro- xime ad Hebraicum NEKOTH accedente. Sed virum, alioqui pium et doctum, fugit ratio. Nam Arabicum myxariorum nomen مخيط mucchait, prout Arabes constanter scribunt, ne unam quidem literulam communem habet cum Hebraeo נכאת nechoth, quod statim agnoscet, quisquis in his linguis non est prorsus ἀναλφάβητος. Neque Arabici nominis ii meminere, quos ille citat, sed Graecorum unus Charito, quod quidem sciam, qui scribit μουχαῖτας, ut officinae mukeitas et mokaitas. Recentiorum plerique alii נכאת necoth, θυμιά-ματα, aromata exponunt, cum Graecis, et Hieronymo, et Hebraeorum nonnullis. Quod vix stare posse patebit legenti duo Scripturae loca, in quibus occurrit haec vox. Prior enim sic habet Gen. XXXVII, 25. Sublatis oculis aspe- xerunt; et ecce turmam viatorum Ismaelitarum, ex Galaade venientium, quorum cameli ferebant נכאת nechoth, et resinam, et stacten: et ibant, ut ea in Aegyptum deportarent. Et posterior Gen. XLIII, 11. Sumite de laudatissimis hujus terrae fructibus in vasis vestris, ut ad virum illum munus feratis, parum resinae, נכאת nechoth, et stacten, et pistacia, et amygdala. Ex quorum lectione attento lectori constabit, נכאת non esse θυμιάματα, vel aromata, vel rem desiderabilem III, 400 in genere, sed peculiare aliquid, ut mel, resinam, stacten, etc. quorum ibidem fit mentio. Et cur Aquila maxime placeat, qui storacem reddidit, plures habeo rationes. Quarum prima haec esto, quod in Syria storax abunde provenit. Plinius libri duodecimi capite vigesimo quinto, Proxima Iudaeae Syria supra Phoenicem styracem gignit circa Gabala et Marathunta, et Casium Seleuciae montem. Dioscorides libro secundo postquam stryacis praestantissimi notas attulit, Τοιοῦτος δέ ἐστιν ὁ Καταβαλίτης, καὶ Πισσιδιακὸς, καὶ Κιλίκιος, ubi pro ὁ Καταβαλίτης, legendum, ὁ Γαβαλίτης, id est, ex Syriae urbe notissima, Gabalis, de qua Plinius. Alii Phoeniciae adscribunt, ut Artemidorus apud Stephanum in Κάρνη. Et Iosephus Galilaeae, libri decimi quinti Antiquitatum capite vigesimo tertio. Secundo, merito censetur storax inter laudatissimos terrae fructus, cum ejus usum medici inter aromata maxime commendent. Tertio, ut hic Ismaelitae, sic, apud Plinium libri duodecimi capite 17. Arabes ex Syria revehunt styracem. Quarto, a Mose non frustra jungitur styrax cum resi- col. 533 na, melle et myrrhae stacte, cum ad illorum naturam accedat. Proinde a Dio- scoride storax optimus ῥητινώδης, resinosus describitur, καὶ ἐν τῷ μαλάσσεσθαι ἀνεὶς ὑγρασίαν τινὰ μελιτώδη, et cum subigitur emittens melleum quendam li- quorem. Eidemque tribuitur δάκρυον κόμμι ἐοικὸς, διαυγὲς, σμηρνίζον, lacry- ma gummi similis, translucida, qualis myrrha. Ita etiam Isidorus libri decimi septimi capite octavo, Storax calamites, pinguis, resinosa, odoris jucundi, hu- mecta, et veluti mellosum liquorem emittens. Hinc apud Plinium styrax adultera- tur cedri resina, vel gummi, alias melle. Quinto, Hebraei nominis originem, ignotam hactenus, videor mihi deprehendere. Arabicum verbum نكت nachatha est 1. hasta terram ita verberare, ut nota impressa maneat: 2. hasta confossum aliquem in caput dejicere: et النكت talis confossio: et النكات qui sic confodit. Quidni huc alludat Hebraeum styracis nomen נכאת nechoth, cum ex stryace arbore fiant τὰ στυράκινα ἀκοντίσματα ἐοικότα τοῖς κρανεΐ-νοις, styracina hastilia iis, quae ex corno fiunt, similia? Ita habetur in Strabo- ne libro duodecimo. Ac proinde apud Hesychium Graecum σύραξ non solum styracem, arborem, aut aroma, sed et lanceam significat, et hastae partem, sive infimam, sive supremam. Neque enim convenit satis inter veteres. Polluci libri primi capite decimo, Τὸ μὲν τέλος τοῦ δόρατος σαυρωτὴρ, τὸ δὲ προῦχον αἰχμὴ, καὶ ἐπιδορατὶς, καὶ στύραξ, ima pars hastae est sauroter, et summa cu- spis, et styrax. Tamen eidem libri decimi capite trigesimo primo σαυρωτὴρ et στύραξ idem sunt. Ita etiam Hesychio, Suidae et Etymologo. Et apud Athe- naeum libro duodecimo ab Heraclide Cumano describuntur Persarum μηλοφόροι, melophori, ἐπὶ τῶν συράκων μῆλα χρυσᾶ ἔχοντες, habentes in styracibus (id est, summis hastilibus) aurea mala. Atque id ipsum est στυράκιον libro secundo Thucydidis, ubi legitur Plataeensis quidam urbis clausisse portas στυρακίῳ ἀντὶ III, 401 βαλάνου χρησάμενος ἐς τὸν μοχλὸν, cuspide hastilis pro vecte in serram trajecto. Et verbum συρακίζειν Hesychio est κεντρίζειν, pungere, tanquam hasta vel hastae cuspide. Sexto, si auctoritate certamus, Aquilam, cui נכאת nechoth est σύραξ, sequitur Hieronymus Gen. XLIII, 11. ubi storacem reddit. Et in libro Nominum legas, NECHOTA, styracem, vel aromata. Quod ipsum sensisse suspicor Syros, qui resinam, et Arabes, qui gummi explicarunt, nomine generico abusos, quia speciale illos latebat. Cum נכאת nechoth, aromate Hebraei perperam confundunt נכותה necotha, quod plane aliud est Es. XXXIX, 2. et 2 Reg. XX, 13. ut alibi dicetur (12).

The word נכאת necoth, of very uncertain meaning, in Genes. XXXVII, 25. and XLIII, 11., is explained by Jonathan as שעוא and by Erpenianus [=the Arabic version edited by Thomas Erpenius (Pentateuch 1622; New Testament 1616)] as شمعا [shamʿan], that is, wax, as also by the author of Beresith Rabba, section 91, near the end. And in Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] they think that שעך is the very same thing, because it comes close to שעוא. However that may be, other interpreters explain it very differently. The LXX have θυμίαμα [thymiama] or θυμιάματα [thymiamata]; Aquila, στύρακα [styraka]; Jerome in the first passage aromata [spices], in the second storacem [storax], like Aquila; the Syriac ܪ̈ܗܛܢܐ [רהטנא], resin; the Samaritan ࠒࠈࠐ [קטף], balsam; the Arabic version published at Paris, خرنوبا [kharnūban], just as some in Kimchi have חרוב, carob; two Arabic manuscripts in Sweden صمغا [ṣamghan], gum; Rabbi Moses the Priest and Kimchi, דבר נחמד, a desirable thing; R. Selomo, כנוסי בשמים הרבה, collections of many spices. In this doubtful matter the later writers follow one or another of the older ones, as seemed good to them. Junius alone, taking a path of his own, rendered it myxaria [sebesten plums], which, he says, are called in Arabic NUKETA, according to Aegineta, Aëtius, Psellus and Actuarius, a word very close to the Hebrew NEKOTH. But this man, otherwise pious and learned, has missed the point. For the Arabic name of the sebesten, مخيط [mukhayṭ] mucchait, as the Arabs consistently write it, has not a single letter in common with the Hebrew נכאת nechoth, as anyone who is not entirely ἀναλφάβητος [analphabētos] in these languages will at once recognize. Nor do the authors he cites mention the Arabic name; among the Greeks only Charito, as far as I know, does so, writing μουχαῖτας [mouchaitas], as the apothecaries write mukeitas and mokaitas. Most of the other more recent writers explain נכאת necoth as θυμιάματα [thymiamata], spices, with the Greeks, Jerome and some of the Hebrews. That this can hardly stand will be evident to anyone who reads the two passages of Scripture in which this word occurs. The first reads thus, Gen 37:25. Lifting up their eyes they saw; and behold, a company of Ishmaelite travellers coming from Gilead, whose camels were carrying נכאת nechoth, and resin, and stacte; and they were going to carry them down into Egypt. And the second, Gen 43:11. Take of the most praised fruits of this land in your vessels, to carry a gift to that man, a little resin, נכאת nechoth, and stacte, and pistachios, and almonds. From reading these the attentive reader will see that נכאת is not θυμιάματα [thymiamata], or spices, or a desirable thing III, 400 in general, but something particular, like honey, resin, stacte, etc., which are mentioned in the same place. And I have several reasons why Aquila, who rendered it storax, pleases me most. Let the first be this: that storax grows abundantly in Syria. Pliny, book 12, chapter 25: Syria, next to Judaea, above Phoenicia, produces storax around Gabala and Marathus, and Casius, the mountain of Seleucia. Dioscorides, book 2, after giving the marks of the best storax, says Τοιοῦτος δέ ἐστιν ὁ Καταβαλίτης, καὶ Πισσιδιακὸς, καὶ Κιλίκιος [Toioutos de estin ho Katabalitēs, kai Pissidiakos, kai Kilikios], where for ὁ Καταβαλίτης [ho Katabalitēs] one should read ὁ Γαβαλίτης [ho Gabalitēs], that is, from the very well-known city of Syria, Gabala, which Pliny mentions. Others assign it to Phoenicia, like Artemidorus in Stephanus under Κάρνη [Karnē]. And Josephus to Galilee, Antiquities book 15, chapter 23. Second, storax is rightly counted among the most praised fruits of the land, since physicians particularly commend its use among the spices. Third, as here the Ishmaelites, so in Pliny, book 12, chapter 17, the Arabs bring back storax from Syria. Fourth, it is not without reason that Moses joins storax with resin, col. 533 honey and stacte of myrrh, since it approaches their nature. Accordingly Dioscorides describes the best storax as ῥητινώδης [rhētinōdēs], resinous, καὶ ἐν τῷ μαλάσσεσθαι ἀνεὶς ὑγρασίαν τινὰ μελιτώδη [kai en tō malassesthai aneis hygrasian tina melitōdē], and when kneaded giving off a honey-like liquid. And to it is attributed δάκρυον κόμμι ἐοικὸς, διαυγὲς, σμηρνίζον [dakryon kommi eoikos, diauges, smērnizon], a tear like gum, translucent, like myrrh. So also Isidore, book 17, chapter 8: Storax calamites, fat, resinous, of a pleasant smell, moist, and as it were giving off a honeyed liquid. Hence in Pliny storax is adulterated with cedar resin, or gum, at other times with honey. Fifth, I think I can detect the origin of the Hebrew name, hitherto unknown. The Arabic verb نكت [nakata] nachatha means 1. to strike the ground with a spear so that a mark remains impressed; 2. to throw someone pierced by a spear on his head; and النكت [al-nakt] is such a piercing, and النكات [al-nakkāt] one who pierces thus. Why should the Hebrew name of storax, נכאת nechoth, not allude to this, since from the storax tree are made τὰ στυράκινα ἀκοντίσματα ἐοικότα τοῖς κρανεΐνοις [ta styrakina akontismata eoikota tois kraneinois], storax javelins similar to those made of cornel? So it is in Strabo, book 12. And accordingly in the Greek Hesychius σύραξ [syrax] means not only storax, the tree or the spice, but also a lance, and a part of the spear, either the lowest or the highest. For the ancients do not agree well on this. In Pollux, book 1, chapter 10: Τὸ μὲν τέλος τοῦ δόρατος σαυρωτὴρ, τὸ δὲ προῦχον αἰχμὴ, καὶ ἐπιδορατὶς, καὶ στύραξ [To men telos tou doratos saurōtēr, to de prouchon aichmē, kai epidoratis, kai styrax], the lowest part of the spear is the sauroter, and the top the point, and the styrax. Yet in the same author, book 10, chapter 31, σαυρωτὴρ [saurōtēr] and στύραξ [styrax] are the same. So also in Hesychius, Suidas and the Etymologicum. And in Athenaeus, book 12, Heraclides of Cyme describes the μηλοφόροι [mēlophoroi] of the Persians, the melophori, ἐπὶ τῶν συράκων μῆλα χρυσᾶ ἔχοντες [epi tōn syrakōn mēla chrysa echontes], having golden apples on their styraces (that is, on the tops of their spear-shafts). And this is precisely the στυράκιον [styrakion] in book 2 of Thucydides, where we read that a certain Plataean shut the gates of the city στυρακίῳ ἀντὶ [styrakiō anti] III, 401 βαλάνου χρησάμενος ἐς τὸν μοχλὸν [balanou chrēsamenos es ton mochlon], driving the butt of a spear-shaft into the bar instead of a bolt-pin. And the verb συρακίζειν [syrakizein] in Hesychius is κεντρίζειν [kentrizein], to prick, as with a spear or the point of a spear. Sixth, if we contend by authority, Aquila, for whom נכאת nechoth is σύραξ [syrax], is followed by Jerome at Gen 43:11, where he renders storax. And in the Book of Names you may read NECHOTA, storax, or spices. I suspect that the Syrians, who explained it as resin, and the Arabs, who explained it as gum, held the same view, but misused a generic name because the specific one was unknown to them. With נכאת nechoth, the spice, the Hebrews wrongly confuse נכותה necotha, which is plainly something else, Isa 39:2 and 2 Reg. XX, 13., as will be said elsewhere R12.

R4 Rosenmüller, III, 377 But J. D. Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], in Supplemm. ad Lexx. [=J. D. He adds that in v. 27 Jonathan is said to have dipped his staff ביערת הדבש, and that it is not credible that someone who had disturbed with a staff the honey stores of bees placed on the ground would have gone unpunished. Into this honey lying on the ground Jonathan could dip his staff with impunity. — Much less acceptable is the opinion of Rabbi Nathan the Ishmaelite, who interprets יערת דבש as forest of honey, understanding by that name a thicket of sugar canes; this opinion was followed by R. Solomon Jarchi [=Rashi (R. Further, and this alone is enough, who, travelling through sugar canes, could dip a staff into them and bring honey extracted from them to his mouth?" — Let the meaning honeycomb stand, then, which the passage Song 5:1 virtually demands: I have eaten יַעְרִי עִם דִּבְשִׁי, my honeycomb with my honey, as the Vulgate translator has it. R9 Rosenmüller, III, 386 But PETR. ADRIAN. VAN KOOTEN, in Observatt. ad nonnulla Canticor. loca (under the presidency of SEBALDUS RAVIUS, Utrecht, 1774), p. 16 ff., refers that comparison used by the Hebrew poet not to pleasant speech but to the saliva of the beloved, which the later Oriental poets are accustomed to compare with honey. Thus NUWEIRI (in REISKE on Tarafa, last page), listing the flowers of the Arab poets which they use in praising their beloveds, mentions this one among others: شبهوا اللما بالخمر والريق بالشهد [shabbahū al-lamā bi-l-khamr wa-l-rīq bi-l-shahd] they compare the gum to wine, the saliva to honey. And MUTANABBI (in the Excerpts published by Reiske, p. 43, verse 7), describing his beloved, says: مظلومة القد في تشبيهه غصنا [maẓlūmat al-qadd fī tashbīhihi ghuṣnan] مظلومة الريق في تشبيهه ضربا [maẓlūmat al-rīq fī tashbīhihi ḍaraban] Her stature is wronged if it is compared to a branch; her saliva is wronged if it is compared to honey. So too IMRU' AL-QAIS, in the Poem adorned with the prize, edited by Lette, verse 15, addresses his beloved thus: فقلت لها سيري وارخي زمامه [fa-qultu lahā sīrī wa-arkhī zimāmahu] ولا تبعدني من جناك المعسل [wa-lā tubʿidīnī min janāki al-muʿassal] I said to her: let him (the camel) go with slackened rein, and do not keep me from your most honeyed fruit. By the most honeyed fruit he means her saliva, or kisses that equal honey in sweetness. TOGHRAI uses the same figure where, imagining himself pierced and nearly slain by the spears, that is, the eyes, of his beloved, he says (verse 25): يشفي لديغ العولي في بيوتهم [yashfī ladīgh al-ʿawlī fī buyūtihim] بنهلة من غدير الخمر والعسل [bi-nahlatin min ghadīr al-khamr wa-l-ʿasal] He who is wounded by spears will be healed in their tents by even a single draught from a pool of wine and honey. These passages moved Michaelis, in the Biblioth. Orient et Exeget. vol. 7, p. 169 ff., to think that in that passage of the Song lascivious kisses are meant, such as the Florentine kiss (a kiss given with the tongue inserted into the other's mouth and licking the tongue). But Velthusen, in his commentary on the passage, p. 364, contends that the common interpretation, which understands that passage of pleasant and sweet speech, is to be retained, chiefly because of the parallel passages IV, 3. V, 16. II, 3. Prov 5:3.

(10) Rosenmüller, III, 391 Magis tamen mihi placet I. D MI-CHAELIS conjectura, in Supplemm. ad Lexx. P. II. p. 393. conferentis Arabicum دَبْشٌ, decorticatio, ut ab attritu atque exulceratione gibbus cameli דבשת dictus sit.

R10 Rosenmüller, III, 391 I prefer, however, the conjecture of I. D. Michaelis in the Supplemm. ad Lexx. vol. 2, p. 393, who compares the Arabic دَبْشٌ [dabshun], stripping off of the skin, so that the camel's hump would have been called דבשת from its chafing and ulceration.

(11) Rosenmüller, III, 396 „Sed si Deus ideo solummodo sibi melle fieri sacrificia prohibuisset, quod in gentium ceremoniis locum invenisset; pari ratione et thus, et sal, et oleum, inter vetita posuisset, quae ab ultima cultus ethnici memorra, in gentilium sacris usurpata reperiamus“. Haec recte, meo judicio, in Bocharti sententiam, quae et Maimonidis est (in More Nebochim, P. III. C 46.), monet SPENCERUS de Legibus Hebraeorum Ritualibus, lib. II Cap. IX. Sect. I. pag. 280. seq. edit. Hagae Comit. 1686. 4. Sed multo minus placent, quas ipse adfert rationes vetiti mellis, quarum gravissima videtur III, 397 esse haec, quam et lib. III. Dissert. II Cap. II. Sect. II pag. 140. commendat, „mel et fermentum ab altari suo rejecisse Deum, eodem temporis articulo, quo salem adhiberi jussit, ut tacite significaret, salem purioris antiquitatis usu cohonestatum, mel autem et fermentum (inter alia multa) nuper excogitata fuisse, et, ob rationem aliquam e theologiae profanae mysteriis arcessitam, sacrificiis addita. Cum enim Deus legem traderet, id egisse videtur, ut cultum publicum a ritibus novis et superstitionem olentibus liberaret, eumque ad simplicitatem, patrum aevo receptam, reduceret.“ Eadem tamen fere est sententia SYKESII, Angli, in libro, quem inscripsit: an Essay on the nature, design and origin of Sacrifices, Lond. 1746. pag. 117. seqq. vers. germ. (quae prodiit Halae 1778. cum notis et praefatione I. S. Semleri).

R11 Rosenmüller, III, 396 "But if God had forbidden sacrifices to be made to him with honey only because it had found a place in the ceremonies of the gentiles, by the same reasoning he would also have placed among the forbidden things frankincense, salt and oil, which we find used in the rites of the gentiles from the earliest memory of pagan worship." This, in my judgement, is rightly urged against Bochart's opinion, which is also that of Maimonides [=Moses Maimonides (Rambam), Mishneh Torah] (in the More Nebochim, vol. III, ch. 46), by SPENCER, de Legibus Hebraeorum Ritualibus, book 2, ch. 9, sect. 1, p. 280 f., ed. The Hague 1686, 4to. But much less satisfactory are the reasons he himself adduces for the prohibition of honey, the weightiest of which seems III, 397 to be this one, which he also recommends in book 3, Dissert. 2, ch. 2, sect. 2, p. 140: "that God rejected honey and leaven from his altar at the same moment at which he ordered salt to be used, in order to signify tacitly that salt had been honoured by the usage of a purer antiquity, whereas honey and leaven (among many other things) had been devised recently and added to sacrifices for some reason drawn from the mysteries of profane theology. For when God gave the law, he seems to have aimed at freeing public worship from new rites that smacked of superstition, and at bringing it back to the simplicity received in the age of the patriarchs." Yet nearly the same is the opinion of SYKES, an Englishman, in the book he entitled an Essay on the nature, design and origin of Sacrifices, London 1746, p. 117 ff. of the German trans. (which appeared at Halle in 1778 with notes and a preface by J. S. Semler).


(12) Rosenmüller, III, 401 Illam tamen vocis נכאת derivationem, quam Bochartus dedit, nimis longe esse petitam, ideoque parum verisimilem, quisque sentiet ipse. Neque magis placet sententia LUDOVICI DE DIEU, in Animadversionibus ad Genes. XXXVII, 25. conferentis Arabum نكيث, quod, docente Firuzabadio, est ex numero τῶν سواك, quo nomine omnia dentifricia designantur, quae in quotidiano usu sunt apud Arabes, inter quae maxime aestimantur aromata quaedam, quibus non tantum dentes mundantur, sed praecipue fragrantia halitui oris conciliatur. Verum نكيث an recte comparetur cum Hebraeo נכאת, ego dubito. Multo minus autem videtur probanda esse interpretatio HILLERI, qui in Hierophyt. P.I. p. 212. נכאת tusa, contusa vertit, a כתת, tudit, ut נכאת scriptum sit pro נכתות, posita א pro ת repetenda, quemadmodum ימאס, liquefiet, dictum sit pro ימסס Iob. VII, 5.; שגיאה, error, pro שגיגה, Ps. XIX, 13.; רבאות pro רבובות, myriades, Esr. II, 69., more Syrorum, qui pro רגג dicunt ראג, concupiscens, Gal. V, 17., pro רותת, Thau in Aleph mutato, ܪܬܝܬ, tremens, Act. XVI, 29. Nomine vero tusorum h. l. intelligenda censet olea tusa, cum et Exod. XXVII, 20. XXIX, 4. Levit. XIV, 2. mentio injiceretur שמן זית כתית, olei olivae tusi, lucernis in templo et oblationibus sacris impensi. Sed in Institt. Linguae Sanctae p. 409. sub tusis aromata contrita, pulveres aromatarios intelligit. Verum, ut taceam, exempla, quae Hillerus adfert, positae א pro ת repetenda, valde incerta esse, cum voces illae ad diversas potius radices sint referendae (veluti ימאס ad מאס, שגיאה ad שגא etc.), dubito etiam, נכאת, si vere tusa significet, absolute positum pro oleis, sive aromatibus tusis usurpatum fuisse. Aliorum multo minus probabiles conjecturas qui scire cupit, evolvat CLODII Lexic. Hebr. Select. pag. 339. Mihi maxime placet ea interpretatio, quam PAULUS attulit in Clavi in Iesaiam, Cap. XXXIX, 2. p. 275. (quamquam quod ibi occurrit, נכתה, recte a nostro נכאת diversum putat). Is Hebraeum נכאת comparat cum Arabum نَكَأَةٌ, quod in GO-LIO idem esse dicitur, quod نُكَعَةٌ, summitas τοῦ طُرْثُوث, rubicundo cortice conspicua, florem referens amaranthi, seu flos ejus rubicundus, quo tingi solet. It. Gummi tragacanthi: quae posterior significatio locis Genes. XXXVII, 25. XLIII, 11. apprime apta fuerit.

R12 Rosenmüller, III, 401 Yet everyone will himself feel that the derivation of the word נכאת which Bochart gave is too far-fetched and therefore hardly probable. Nor is the opinion of LOUIS DE DIEU more satisfactory, who in his Animadversiones on Genes. XXXVII, 25. compares the Arabic نكيث [nakīth], which, as Firuzabadi teaches, is one of the سواك [siwāk], the name by which are designated all the dentifrices in daily use among the Arabs, among which certain aromatics are most esteemed, by which not only are the teeth cleaned but above all a fragrance is imparted to the breath of the mouth. But whether نكيث [nakīth] is rightly compared with the Hebrew נכאת, I doubt. Much less, however, does the interpretation of HILLER seem acceptable, who in the Hierophyt. vol. I, p. 212, renders נכאת as things pounded, crushed, from כתת, he pounded, so that נכאת would be written for נכתות, with א put in place of a repeated ת, just as ימאס, it will melt, is said for ימסס Job 7:5; שגיאה, error, for שגיגה, Ps 19:13; רבאות for רבובות, myriads, Esr. II, 69., after the manner of the Syrians, who for רגג say ראג, desiring, Gal. V, 17., and for רותת, with Thau changed into Aleph, ܪܬܝܬ [רתית], trembling, Acts 16:29. By the name of pounded things here he thinks pounded oils are to be understood, since in Exod 27:20. XXIX, 4. Lev 14:2 mention is made of שמן זית כתית, pounded olive oil, used for the lamps in the temple and for the sacred offerings. But in the Institt. Linguae Sanctae, p. 409, he understands by pounded things crushed aromatics, aromatic powders. However, not to mention that the examples Hiller adduces of א put in place of a repeated ת are very uncertain, since those words should rather be referred to different roots (for instance ימאס to מאס, שגיאה to שגא etc.), I also doubt that נכאת, if it truly means pounded things, was used absolutely for oils or pounded aromatics. Whoever wishes to know the much less probable conjectures of others may consult CLODIUS, Lexic. Hebr. Select. p. 339. To me the most satisfactory interpretation is the one Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)] offered in the Clavis in Iesaiam, Chapter XXXIX, 2, p. 275 (although he rightly considers the נכתה occurring there to be different from our נכאת). He compares the Hebrew נכאת with the Arabic نَكَأَةٌ [nakaʾatun], which in GOLIUS is said to be the same as نُكَعَةٌ [nukaʿatun], the top of the طُرْثُوث [ṭurthūth], conspicuous for its reddish bark, resembling the flower of the amaranth, or its reddish flower, with which one is wont to dye. Also gum tragacanth: the latter meaning would fit the passages Genes. XXXVII, 25. XLIII, 11. exceedingly well.
